content.text:
The wind at the line always smelled faintly of iron, as if the planet itself were rusting. Mara Kestrel had learned the taste of it as a child, the way it snuck into your mouth and sat on the tongue while you talked, the way it stitched itself into everything from soup to kisses. It came from the storm that never moved and never ended, the wall of cloud and grit and vapor that marched forever around Orison under the red eye of Mitra.

She hung eighty meters up the bladder-smooth side of Aperture Tower Nineteen with the iron taste in her mouth and her boots bit into the alloy ribs with a gentle stuttering click. The tower’s skin hummed with the passage of heat—a low, almost subaudible thrum that made her bones want to buzz. To the east lay the burn of Day, a glare off white salt pan and naked bedrock and a sun so large and close that even when filtered through three levels of visor it felt like something alive glaring directly into her. In the west the Night rose up like a cliff against the sky, a wall of shadow and blue-black where frost-plains and ice ridges lay in an ancient unmoving dark. Between the two, around the horizon, the air boiled and coiled and did tricks no atmosphere was meant to do, which was why you built mirrored towers that ate light and spat it back the way you wanted.

“Beaconhouse West, Nineteen’s ring twelve hinge cluster is seized,” she said, and licked her lower lip, tasting the world again. “Pull the deflection to nine percent for me, Lio. I’m going to crack it.”

“Acknowledged, Kestrel,” came Lio’s voice in her helmet. He had the lazy vowels of the Basin and always sounded like he’d been woken from a nap. No one else could make a requisitions officer’s drawl seem charming. “Do try to avoid being peeled off the side like old paint.”

“Try to avoid starving the line, I’ll try to avoid dying,” Mara said. “On three. One… two… three.”

The tower shivered under her hand. Far above, the petals that formed Nineteen’s adjustable mouth tilted fractionally, redirecting the stabbing angle of Mitra’s low light. Mara felt the yank of air and pressure differentials against her suit. The ring twelve hinge didn’t so much seize as sulk. It was a part designed to swing a kilometer’s worth of reflective sail with precision, and it wanted to be doing that, not frozen half-open, half-shut like a yawn caught in a jaw cramp.

She wedged the manifold wrench into the narrow gap around the pivot and engaged the filament heater. Silver fibers on the tool’s head flushed orange, then red. The hinge sweated, a brief spurt of fog, and the torque numbers on her visor ticked up, down, up again. Inside the tower the coolant loop hissed. Her tether line hummed as the wind tried to take her. She grunted and leaned into the tool, boot magnets on full, shoulder aching against her suit’s stiff counterpressure.

“Come on, you stubborn child,” she said. “Don’t make me get angry.”

“Is that your professional technique?” Lio again. She could imagine him leaning back in his chair in the Beaconhouse, boots propped up on a console he wasn’t supposed to put boots on, hair tied back messy, watching her diagnostics on his screen. “Verbal threats?”

“Always worked on me,” Mara said, and then the hinge finally lurched, gave, and slid into place with a groan she felt in the soles of her feet. The entire sail assembly realigned, a shade shift so subtle that the light sharpened in one slice of sky and softened in another. Somewhere south of here, a kilometer of thermopile pipes breathed easier. Someone’s field freezer would spend less time squealing. Someone’s child would sleep without bleached light sneaking under the door.

“Got it,” she said between breaths. “Locking ring twelve and repeating across ring eleven through nine. Your logs are going to be perfect. It’ll be your finest day in the Beaconhouse yet.”

“You say that every time,” Lio said. “Hang on—”

In Mara’s ear there was a pulse that wasn’t voice. A creak, a faint tick, half a breath of something that made her widen her eyes and turn, stupidly, as if sound had a direction in the sealed world of her helmet. It was low, soft, almost an omission rather than a noise. Her suit’s filter tagged it a transient from the Nineteen array’s ambient sensor stack, logged as category gray.

“Did you hear that?” she said.

“Hear what?” Lio asked.

“Never mind,” Mara said, because she did not like how quickly she’d said hear. She checked her suit inputs anyway—wind vector, tower Brayton loop, ambient pressure, the microphonic feed from the tower’s skin as if the structure itself might be whispering. The gray-scale trace of the transient stood out like a heartbeat on an ECG, a small hump in the noise where there shouldn’t have been one.

She slid the manifold wrench into its holster and scuttled crabwise along the tower’s ribbing toward the sensor blister. The world to the east was a smear of dull orange and white glare, the world to the west was night-negatives and ice. The line itself, the thin ribbon where human habs hung like beads on a wire, glowed ahead of her with the heat of their own small suns—steam plumes, the sodium glare of towers like the one she was clinging to, the flicker of drones plying along the way.

When she reached the blister she slapped its access plate. The little screen inside painted itself with crisp digits and the idle chatter of the array’s brain. There were day-long curves of light and heat in pale green; there was the scrawl of the wind in pale blue. The gray trace was a momentary hiccup in the deep noise floor that the aperture system listened to the way a fisherman listens to current.

Mara isolated it. Zoomed. Played it back.

Tick. Tick. Tick-tick. Tick.

Her mouth went dry, the iron taste sweeping everything else away, replaced with something she couldn’t name. Her hands, in their armored gloves, had new weight.

“Lio,” she said, “route me the Nineteen gray channel. Everything. Just dump it to me.”

“You and your salvage habits,” he grumbled, and for a heartbeat she saw what he saw: the version of her who couldn’t pass a heap of broken tools without sorting them; the woman who still ran her palm along the underside of a console to feel for a hidden latch. Mara had grown up in a caravan Moving west with the line when she was small; she had been trained to work the towers because her hands were clever and her stomach was steady, but before that she had slept in a triple-layer cocoon under a cargo deck and learned how to find things by ear.

The Beaconhouse coughed data down her band. The gray channel was everything the towers didn’t quite know what to make of: lightning-worble from the storm wall, the scream and chuckle of ice cracking on Night’s edge, the itch of sand on Day’s face, whisper-modulations of stray microwaves and drift.

She shunted sound through her suit’s processing and listened, filtering for regularity. Human brains like patterns even where there aren’t any. Her mother had used to say that when she was mad at the caravan’s navigation AI, angry at a forecast that had sent them into blowing dust for three days. Mara remembered that, and remembered her mother tapping her knuckles against the floor of the cocoon to quiet the baby—tick, tick-tick, tick—an old caravan lullaby in percussion, a rhythm they’d used to teach infants the safety code for following shadows.

Tick. Tick-tick. Tick. A pause. The pattern came again.

She opened her mouth and closed it. “Lio.”

“I’m here,” he said, cheerfully unaware that the world had just put on a new face. “Don’t say ‘you’re not going to believe this’ like in those dramas. You know I don’t have the budget to process disbelief.”

“It’s a code,” she said. “Old Line. Caravan code. Band four-two, lying under the Brayton noise. Someone’s tapping in our gray channel.”

“Could be echoes. The ice cracks make all kinds of—”

“Lio.” She made it a word that opened his ears. “It spells Kestrel.”

There was a hiss on the band that might have been him dragging his hand down his face. “Anonymous admirers leaving you flirtations in the emissions suite? It would be the least romantic thing I’ve heard.”

She swallowed. Her tongue was dry. The pattern was not just the name—the letters staggered in pulses and halts—but the cadence. Tick. Tick-tick. Tic—her mother’s hands on the floor, the way she’d taught it to Mara and to Arlen, their palms tapping in the dark, a code so old you could claim to remember it from Earth because everyone claimed to remember everything from Earth.

“I know what it sounds like,” she said, and she hated that her voice sounded like she was nineteen again, hanging off a different tower with a friend whose name she can’t say without something in her chest moving the wrong way. “Don’t report it yet.”

“Too late,” Lio said. “The Beaconhouse is a sieve and this is a gray anomaly at the edge of Night. There are entire departments that salivate when they hear those words next to each other.”

“Unlighters?” Mara’s mouth twisted without asking her permission.

“Among others.”

She looked west. Night ate the ground like a slow maw. On the very margin there were things that moved, not creatures but physics performing its contortions: frost condensing as glitter, then pattering, then razoring itself into needles and decreeing that any water that dared to linger would become architecture. The Dark was not empty. It was simply not for human beings.

They didn’t go into Night. Not anymore. They stabilized the line instead, pushed it where they could, smoothed it where they had to. The old caravans still moved, but fewer. Most people now lived in towns with names like Anchor and Stayer and Wait. They put out tiny roots into a planet that didn’t want them. They built towers like Nineteen and controlled the angle of Mitra’s punch into their air so they could have consistent mornings and afternoons instead of the eternal, queasy light of sunrise.

Mara had not set foot into Night since Arlen.

“I’m bumping this up,” Lio said, voice gone administrative. “I’m also locking the partition on it so the Unlighters don’t agitate for a pilgrimage and the Cirrus Authority doesn’t decide to send a kite full of grad students into the shadow. We’ll let Proxima see it first.”

“You like Prox now?” Mara said. It was a reflex and a plea—keep the tone light and maybe the world will, too.

“I like my job. And also the continued existence of the Bioshifts you people cradle out there,” Lio said. He lowered his voice. “You okay, Kes?”

She could lie. She had no ritual for that, no code whispered in the dark. She could lie and go back to the hinge, turn ring eleven, let the muscles in her shoulders burn and forget the pattern.

“I’m going to look,” she said, and then, before he could do the thing with his breath that meant he would try to stop her, she spoke again. “From the tower. Not into Night. I’m not a zealot.”

“A zealot would say that on his way over the edge.”

“Lio.”

“Fine,” he said, and took a breath she recognized. He’d moved from friend voice to launch voice. “Deploy caution. Request denied by policy. Emergency override granted in advisory capacity. Tie your suit’s doc to my board. If your heart jumps or your glyco levels crash or a bat-shaped angel asks you to kiss it I will call you back hard.”

“You’d like that,” she said automatically, and cut the line before he could answer.

She scrambled to the viewing cradle under the sensor blister and slid herself into it. The cradle was an old addition, half-joke when it had been bolted on, a zero-gravity chair without the zero that kept maintenance techs from pitching backward while they did delicate work under the eyelid of the blister. Mara had used it twice—to change a chip, to wipe dust off a lens—and for naps when the world said nap now or die. This time she used it to press her helmet to the blister’s interior and let the tower feed a stack of wavelengths into her visual cortex, stacking red and blue and microwave and heat into a single uneasy image.

The Night side’s first hundred meters were always ugly. It was where light went to die, where heat poured down into cold that could drink it forever and never show a change of expression. But further in, the ice reflected, the sky cleared. Stars spilled in the west like nails out of a torn sack. When she was small, she had thought you could see Earth in that spill if you looked hard enough. When she was less small she had thought you could see every person you had ever lost.

Mara touched the sensor’s controls with her fingertips and dialed down the light to minimum, flattened the glare from Day behind her to a smear in the extreme east of the image, so that Night’s edge was a line thrown into razor focus. The ground was a ridge here, old rock buckled and smoothed by wind and pressure, streaked where ice had retreated and advanced again in slow pulses as big as wars. And there, tucked just in from the line, at a place where the tower’s instrument packages hardly bothered to look because nothing sane ever happened there, was a point of heat.

She blinked and made sure the image wasn’t artifact. The point didn’t waver. It wasn’t a flare, wasn’t a reflection from the tower’s own stray angles, wasn’t Lio playing a trick because he had never played tricks and anyway would never make this particular joke.

The heat source was not large. Neither was it natural.

Some calms are the part where everything vanishes and you slip into sleep as into a well. This was the other kind of calm, the one her body pulled tight like a band of fabric around her chest and she breathed against it. “It’s not a battery leak,” she whispered, to no one. “It’s not a ratty sail on someone’s kite. It’s not a planned outpost; there’s no signal on the safety band.” She hated that she was narrating to herself but it kept her hands from shaking and her eyes where they needed to be.

She matched the angle of the heat to the predicted depths of permafrost, to geological slope, to her knowledge of where the caravan routes had crossed this region decades ago. No caravan would have walked the edge here; the wind tore at you and the frost had too many voices, playing you into mistakes.

Tick. Tick-tick. Tick, said the gray channel, and she could hear it under the instruments now, an itch in the part of her brain that had learned to pluck meaning out of the kind of noise you got when you slept under a machine’s heart.

She tied the tower’s brain to her suit’s, told them to kiss and share, and sent a tight-band whisper at the heat source. Safety ping. Identification request. Your existence is a violation of at least three Charter terms but we will be kind if you answer, said the code. No response. The tower’s output array reorganized—without asking—around the slight change in its operator’s heart rate and eye focus. Nineteen wasn’t clever, not really, but it learned the people who crawled over it and hummed inside it kept it alive.

Someone had put a shelter into Night. It was small, and close enough to the line to buy a little leaking heat, and the geometry said it had been there less than a year if the ice that had remade itself around it was any indication. It was probably a folly. It was possibly a tragedy. It might be a trap.

Mara uncurled from the cradle. Her hands had already done what they would do from the moment she’d heard the taps: they were inventorying what she would need. Night suit. Thermal pack. Coilgun loaded with flares. Clamp anchors. One of Lio’s emergency overrides so she could take a sledge out without being flagged and chased by Authority drones. She thought of Proxima Havel, with her quiet hands and her tired eyes that always tried to read the desire underneath what you said. I want to go see. That was the desire. Not I want to save them. Not I want to die. Just the itch to put her body into the space where hard things happened.

Her body remembered a different Night. The smell of it, beyond iron; the way frost bloomed like mold; Arlen’s glove losing grip on hers because he had always been the one who tested limits and one day the limit had been a centimeter past his reach. She felt a ghost pressure on the pads of her fingers and pulled them into fists until the tendons popped.

“Kes,” Lio said in her ear. “Do not say what you’re about to say.”

“I found a heat signature,” she said, because there was no point pretending. “Not ambient. Not incidental. It isn’t pinging back. It’s right at the border.”

“Prox is on her way,” Lio said. “Five minutes. Don’t move. I put a lock on the sledges.”

“Locks are for people who haven’t lived in caravans,” she said, and took her tools back into their pouches because they would go where she went and come back when she did or stay with her when she didn’t.

“Mara—”

“Tell Havel where I’m going,” she said, and hooked her tether to the clip-and-slide that would take her skimming down the tower like a beetle down glass. “Tell her if she wants to keep me from doing something foolish she should bring extra foolishness in the other direction to balance me out.”

The ride down stole speech anyway. The tower’s skin sang through the soles of her boots. The air tried to blow her away. She hit the platform at the tower’s base, unhooked, jogged across the open expanse with her shoulders hunched against the constant dawn-wind, ducked back into the maintenance lock, spun the wheel, felt the pressure equalize with a pop in her ears. The little room smelled like someone had boiled steel. She yanked off her helmet and stood, breathing, as the door cycled.

Proxima Havel was there when it opened, which meant the Authority had gotten her out of somewhere within shouting distance. She was taller than Mara, thin enough that when she folded her arms her elbows looked like knuckles. She wore the blue-gray of Cirrus and the little ellipse pin that meant she could say stop and a hundred people’s jobs would pause.

“Do not,” Prox said, and the word did not have anger in it so much as weight, like a stone you could put on the corner of a paper that wanted to blow away. “Don’t go in alone.”

“Then come with me,” Mara said. “Or send me with a team who’ll get me killed by insisting we go back when we’re halfway there.”

“It’s a trick,” Prox said. “You’ve thought of that.”

“I have thought of every bad thing,” Mara said. “And the good thing that sits under all the bad ones and pushes up until my ribs hurt is that someone is knocking from the wrong side of Night and calling my name.”

Prox watched her. The thing about Proxima Havel that had made Mara trust her the first time they’d met was that she had a tell when she was thinking hard. Some people chewed the inside of their cheek. Prox pressed her tongue against the small gap in her teeth and let it rest there, making a barely visible dimple in her lip. She did that now. Mara waited and pretended she wasn’t rocking on the balls of her feet.

“You have a sledge ready?” Prox asked at last.

“Always,” Mara said, which was almost a lie but not quite.

“Take two lines. Take a line layer to spool the return. Take K45 flares.” Prox flicked her gaze past Mara to the door the Authority had opened behind the maintenance lock, the one Mara had never had permission to pass through. “And take me.”

“Really?” Lio’s voice squeaked in their ears.

Prox touched her comm bead. “Authorization Havel-seven. Advisory lifting of the lock for sledge nine. Recording on. If this goes poorly I want the Board to be able to watch and tell me they would have done otherwise in my place.”

Lio made a noise that could have been assent or resignation or an attempt to swallow both at once. “Sledge nine is live,” he said. “Mara, your blood levels are unwise. Eat something on the way or I will be in your ear with nutrition facts until you wish for Night to swallow you.”

“I always wish for that,” Mara said, and smiled because she needed to queue herself into a world where smiling was a thing people did.

The Authority door led into a bay where sledges hung like beetles sleeping in a line. Sledge nine was a stubby-bodied creature with low runners and a fat cylinder riding its spine like a humpback. Night air would try to eat the heat out of anything that went into it; sledge nine’s cylinder was a new iteration of a very old idea, a thermal battery wound tight with material that wanted to be warm and would bleed that wanting into the bodies tethered to it.

Mara’s hands remembered straps and sequences even when her mind wanted to slide sideways into memory. She slotted flares into the coilgun and put the gun at her right thigh. She clipped coils and anchors onto her belt. Proxima Havel climbed aboard with less awkwardness than Mara had expected; authority made people clumsy sometimes in other contexts, as if gravity increased with rank, but Prox had started on a weather tower and her body remembered.

“We’re not heroes,” Prox said quietly, as the sledge coughed, heaters woke, and the runners vibrated.

“We’re not cowards either,” Mara said.

They shot out from under the tower’s lateral deck like a flat stone skimming a pond. The hab cluster around Nineteen fell behind, a tangle of shadow lines and smoke. The line itself was a fixed star—no matter how fast you ran, it was widthless and everywhere. The ground changed under them with each meter: the packed dust of Day’s fringe, the pitted black of wetted stone, the sparkle-sand where frost had been and wasn’t yet again. The air temperature fell with an insistence that made their suits tighten their grip on them.

Mitra in the east held its position a thumbspan above the notional horizon. Night rose to meet them, a shoulder of darkness arching high. It was like driving into a wall, the way your body knew the light would stop and fall. Wind turned and tried to pull them sideways; the sledge’s smart runners dug in.

“Talk me through the code,” Prox said. It was a thing to say when someone needed a task to keep panic from building a nest.

“Kestrel,” Mara said. “Plain. Old Line. It’s a trick, but it picked the wrong trick if it wanted to fool me by accident rather than by design.”

“If it’s design it wants you,” Prox said softly.

“Everything wants something.” Mara lifted a hand from the controls and let it hover over the emergency brake for the small personal superstition that had kept her alive in kites and sledges and towers: always know where the thing is that will stop you from continuing. “We’ll stop when we see why.”

The heat-source point grew in the sledge’s forward view like a star coming at speed. Around them the world lost detail; it was all grays and blacks, a smear of texture, frost and rock and the shadow of her own fear thrown long and straight ahead. The code came again, in the sideband, in the metal bones of the sledge, in the tapping of her heart against her suit. Tick. Tick-tick. Tick.

She did not say Arlen’s name. There were ways to carry ghosts, and none of them were saying them aloud in Night on your way to meet whatever you had called toward you by letting the world know you wanted something.

The shelter was not much more than a mound of the wrong kind of geometry against the ice. Someone had covered it in rock and dust to hide its angles and day-lit planes. It was not a caravan module, not a tower lifeboat, not any Authority-minted thing. It was small and clean-lined and its door was sealed from the inside with a strip that had been cut from a weather kite wing and tied in a knot only someone who had slept inside a caravan’s belly would make.

Mara cut the sledge’s speed and bled it down to nothing. She felt Prox’s hand tighten around the support rail, skin sliding against suit glove. The world went quiet except for wind’s whisper and the low hum of the sledge’s battery. It was always quiet at the edge if you let it be. It wasn’t true that Night had no sound. It had a sound like a machine resting, oxygen condensing, water making decisions.

Mara stood. Prox stood with her. They went to the door together because all the ways this could be wrong were smaller if you didn’t give them the space to be larger.

The strip across the seam had been tied with a child’s reach. Mara’s fingers remembered doing that once, in a caravan where you tied what had to stay put with whatever you had. She touched it as if it could bruise. Tick. Tick-tick. Tick, said the code from nowhere because it had never claimed to be from here. She slipped the knot.

Cold breathed out. Not sharp, not the needle-pain of raw Night, but a deep, permanent cold that had made friends with whatever the shelter had to offer it. Mara unsealed the door. It swung inward a hand-width, a body-width, a world-width.

Inside, in the small electric light that made the room possible, someone had written KESTREL on the far wall in a marker that had bled a little into the surface. Under it, in a hand that had not been careful, someone had drawn the outline of a bird in a single line.

And on the floor, set carefully so no one would step on it when the door opened, lay a toy from the caravan days: wood smoothed by fat baby fingers, animal shape abstracted into curves. Arlen’s, Mara’s mind said, because of course it did. But this one had three lines carved on its back and Arlen had carved two, because he had never finished anything.

Prox’s breath hitched. Mara did not breathe at all.

“The room is warm,” Prox whispered, because you had to say something. “Which means someone left it that way. Which means—”

Mara pointed. There were footprints in the frost on the inner wall, so careful and so recent that you could see the pebble that had been caught in the heel. They led to the far corner. There was a second door there, one that hadn’t been on the outside. It wasn’t a door like any door Mara knew. It wasn’t door-shapes, not panels and hinges. It was a curve in the wall that made her eyes want to slide.

The code ticked again, no longer only in her ear. It seemed to come from the seam itself. Tick. Tick-tick. Tick.

“What the hell is that,” Lio said in both their ears, so loud that Prox flinched and Mara exhaled for the first time in what might have been minutes. “I’m seeing it on your feed. On all our feeds. What is that door.”

Mara did not answer. She reached out her hand.

It was the world’s oldest story, to open a door you should not. It was why human beings had survived; it was why they died. It was both of those things at once, always, in different proportions. The seam under her glove was slightly warm.

Behind her, Proxima Havel said, low and steady, “On three.”

“On three,” Mara agreed, and let herself taste the iron in the air so she would remember where she was when everything else changed.

At the hinge of day and night, the air always moved.

The city of Brim clung to that hinge like a barnacle, its alleys and terraces stitched into the gray band where the star’s heat became inhabitable and the frozen night’s breath could be borrowed for a while. Out toward the bright, the sky was a permanent copper-white and the ground shone glassy from a thousand years of sun. Out toward the night, frost devoured pillars and whispering dunes of carbon snow marched up against the city’s windbreaks. In between, in the belt of dawn, everything lived by a margin. Blood. Water. Minutes.

Kezia Marr kept the minutes.

Her pulse room crouched under the Meridian Tower, slotted into bedrock, the ceiling hung with old brass bells and new glass fibers. She stood at the long bench with her sleeves rolled past her elbows, breathing the acetone-sweet fumes of flux and the faint metallic tang of ozone. The bench lights were crude—dimmable filaments in ceramic cages—and the light pooled on the instruments: optical combs stacked like pages, little toffee-colored coils of copper, old hairsprings, chipped lenses, the gangly skeleton of a gravimeter whose free mass trembled to the rhythm of the planet’s interior. In the corner the backup pendulum knocked its lazy tick against a column of oil—decoration more than necessity, but it calmed visitors.

On the wall above the bench, high as a saint and twice as stubborn, an oscilloscope painted green ghosts across the glass.

“You’re three microbeats fast,” Kezia said. She tapped the crystal cover of a municipal wristband with the tip of a screwdriver. “You feel that?”

Tamsin, who was both apprentice and annoyance and twelve years younger than Kezia with hair like wire and a habit of using the pulse room like a stage, leaned over, squinting. “Feels good to me. Everyone loves a fast clock.”

“It will make their water valves think it’s time to open before the pressure comes up. You want your ration to squirt inside your neighbor’s walls? Fast clocks are thieves.”

“Maybe I hate my neighbor.”

Kezia hid a smile. Tamsin had been pulling slum bands all morning, calibrating them on the cheap against the municipal beat. Brim let people barter minutes like coin, and counterfeiters skimmed with fast bands and slow ones, little lozenges that tickled the brain into compliance. Council hated that but couldn’t stop it. People worked to clocks, slept to clocks, paid for light from the Array in ratios of clock-time to heat, and Kezia sat in this basement, calibrating the city’s throat.

She soldered a lead, let the wristband’s tiny gyros find the beating reference coming down the mountain through the Tower’s bones. The beat came from two anchors: a white dwarf five hundred light-years away whose pulses were steady as blindness, and the old Meridian Array above them, the broken crown of attenuators and shades that moderated the star’s glare and, when it behaved, winked the beat through the sky. The Array’s original software had died with the first generation, archived in stone and politics. They got by with patched code and heirloom keys and the silent prayer that the ring would go on holding off the Noon.

Kezia set the wristband to the pulse. It hummed, content.

“You bring me anything that isn’t filthy?” she asked.

Tamsin dug in his pockets like a magician and came up with something wrapped in cloth. “Bargainer on Salt Street. Said it belonged to his grandmother’s partner’s mother’s head of household. Charged me two ice pears and a courtesy.”

Kezia took the bundle. The cloth was sunbleached and worn-thin, and when she unrolled it her mouth went dry. Inside lay an old larkwatch: an oval thing not much bigger than her thumb, matte black and unadorned, with a little brass toggle like a beak. She had one just like it tucked under her shirt, pressed to the hollow of her throat. She hadn’t seen another in fifteen years.

She touched the beak. The little watch didn’t tick. The case was scarred where someone had pried and pried and failed to find a way in that didn’t destroy it.

“Do you know what this is?” she asked.

Tamsin’s eyes danced. “A lure. A trap. A way to make you tell me a story.”

Kezia pulled her own watch out by its chain and laid it next to the stranger. The same. The same scuffs in the same places, the same tiny engraving on the beak: a dot and two slashes, the quick shorthand for Phase Hold.

“My mother wore this,” she said. “She built shade logic for the Meridian. The Array used to talk to these, in an emergency.”

Tamsin’s laughter thinned. “That’s a funny story. Ha ha. Did the Council give you permission to tell it?”

“They didn’t give me permission to remember.”

The old grief came in like night, not dramatic, just absolute. It made Kezia clumsy, so she stopped touching the stranger larkwatch and folded the cloth back over it. The chain of her own watch warmed against her palm—always warm, as if it remembered skin.

The pulse room door banged open and a courier came shouldering through with a messenger’s staff and the urgent frown of someone who ran their whole life on other people’s panic. He wasn’t Council; his coat was ratty and patched at the elbows, but he wore the blue finger-band that meant he was permitted to touch the Tower’s doors.

“Kezia Marr,” he said. “The Council requests—”

“Requests?”

“—directs your presence within five minutes at the Lodge.”

“No.”

The courier blinked. “No?”

“I’m calibrating and I have the Array’s noon cycle in twenty. They’ll have me for the cycle or they won’t have me at all.”

Tamsin hissed. The courier shifted his weight like a man examining a pit. “Fine,” he said finally. “They directed you to delay the noon by one-twenty seconds. Make sure the agricultural shades over Brimsward get first dark.”

Kezia set down her screwdriver. “One-twenty seconds will rip the whole city out of phase with the Camp and the Night-side caravans and the windmills on South Arch. It will collapse the microgrid terms we just negotiated and it will get three hundred people hurt.”

“They said you’d say that.” The courier’s mouth twitched, not a smile. “They said to remind you that elections are coming and nobody votes who burns.”

Kezia took a breath and let it out very carefully. She wished, fiercely and without dignity, to be able to punch something. Tamsin slouched with the alert ease of someone prepared to intervene at body level.

“I’ll bring the noon thirty seconds slower over Brimsward,” Kezia said. “You tell the Council that will cost us a percent of efficiency on West Well and we’ll skip the evening shade over the markets to balance. If they argue, I’ll bring them down here and let them juggle a city while they campaign.”

The courier opened his hands, as if she had dropped a hot stone into them. “I just talk,” he said. But the relief in his shoulders said he had something practical to carry back. He sketched a bow to the pendulum, because everyone did, and left.

“Gross,” Tamsin said. “Politics.”

“Time,” Kezia said. It was the same thing here. She put her thumb on the larkwatch on its chain and felt its weight. She picked up the stranger watch again, turned it under the bench light, thinking of hands like hers but older and more clever, assembling these cases in the first years with whatever they had on hand—scrap from the landers, meteoric iron, a promise. Phase Hold. Override.

Kezia has never been allowed near the Array. She was a calibrator, not a warden. She kept the city sane; those who climbed the Tower and rode the shade-lines into low orbit handled the sky. They patched mirrors and coaxed twist from thousand-kilometer ribbons of foil and black. Her mother had worked up there and had not come down. Kezia did not look at the Array if she could help it.

The pulse room clicked in its many ways. The oscilloscope drew its green line. The pendulum sucked oil. A breeze came under the door and touched her ankle as if the world were a cat. Outside, the markets would be swarming, people laying out handshade cloths and heat-catchers, little pans and coils and black stones that sipped the sun while the shades skimmed and fell in their scheduled dance.

The herd-clock on the wall—big and rude, a public tick to keep apprentices honest—jumped. The line on the scope spat, a spike that wasn’t in her noise, a sharp vertical like an insult.

Tamsin’s head came up. “Did you—?”

Kezia’s fingers flew. She locked the municipal beat to the dwarf star anchor, the surest of her pillars, though the latency meant any local variation would smear. She looked at the Array feed with one eye, because she had to, and because she had trained herself to decode the jitter of its old mind into time.

It happened again. The line jumped, a defile in the calm. The gravimeter stammered, wet metal sound. The pendulum, too heavy to care, licked its oil with a soldier’s patience.

She didn’t know she was moving until the pulse room door was already open and the light from the tower’s stair cut her in half. Tamsin swore and grabbed both larkwatches and came after her.

The tower’s interior shaft was cool and pumped. It had a spiral of stairs for anyone with legs and a pallet lift for the rest. Kezia’s boots thumped on stone, each step a little different, as if the mason had been bored and sought to put a private joke into the city’s skeleton.

She came out onto one of the sky-leaning balconies that looked north across Brim. The hinge-land rolled down to the brightside like a frozen wave—buildings like barnacles stuck to its windward face, shade-sails like knife-wings leaned against the gusts, all the city’s faces turned a little toward the light as if listening. The sun itself was an orange coin burning behind the frosted cloth of the Array. The Array looked like an old scar: dark filaments and panels and spiderweed tethers set at an angle to the light, a ring not so much complete as implied, the sky’s suggestion of a ring.

The dimming, when it came, reached out and stroked her skin. The light tone dropped a note, a piano slackening. Shadows sharpened and then softened again. The line between bright and night stepped, a toe toward the city and then away. People on the terraces three streets down cried out; the cry came up thin and not quite human. A child’s kite snapped and flew into a thermal that shouldn’t have been there and then was gone, melted maybe, maybe eaten by the air.

Not a cloud. Not a dust front. A change in the Array. Unscheduled.

Tamsin pressed the larkwatch into her hand. “Tell me this is a joke. Tell me we did this.”

“It’s not a joke.”

Another pulse: dim—normal—dim—normal—not quite equal. Kezia’s eyes watered. She squinted past the glare at the black geometry of the Array and thought she could see a shadow move through it, a darker dark through the dark, like a man’s hand in a field of grass. That wasn’t sense. The Array was too far for that; the motion was the folded illusion of scale and rhythm.

The balcony’s warning light buzzed at her elbow. It was linked to the municipal beat; it flashed green for good. Now it faltered, skeptical, as if someone tapped it with two fingers.

Kezia’s head filled with the old stories: the Long Pause, the half-legend of a day when the Array had seized and held and the sun had pressed its thumbs into the city’s eyes until the stone smoked. Her mother had scorned the stories, and in that scorn there had been something too tender to touch.

The dimming settled, smoothed. Kezia didn’t realize she had been gritting her teeth until her jaw ached. Around them the market noise rose again, cautious, and then louder as people performed bravado to drown their fear.

She ran for the pulse room. Tamsin kept pace.

“What is it?” he panted. “Grav wave? Array glitch? Cosmic joke?”

“If it’s a grav wave we get it again later from the dwarf,” Kezia said. “If it’s the Array, I can map the shutters and calculate the shift.”

“And the Council?”

“The Council can eat its own hands. Do you have that watch?”

Tamsin waved the cloth bundle. “I stole it fair.”

Back under the tower, the hum of her equipment told her the city had snapped back into its little integers. The herd-clock had settled. The gravimeter was as sullen as ever. The scope, though, that told the story. The jump had a shape: steps whose widths were not equal, whose widths were—Kezia stared—primes.

Two. Three. Five. Seven. Eleven.

The Array had winked at the city in prime intervals.

“Kezia,” Tamsin said softly. “Tell me that’s random.”

“Random is a word for a thing you don’t understand.”

“You understand?”

“I understand someone is playing with the shutter code.”

“You can do that?”

“No.”

The strictly illegal thought came to her like a shadow of a happier thought: the larkwatch. Phase Hold. If the old mind of the Array were still in there under the Council’s new subroutines and the Wardens’ patches, if the rails had not rusted away in vacuum, if if if—she touched her own, felt the pulse. On her skin. Another life.

Her mother had never told her how to use it. She had told stories instead, very practical stories that were about not falling between. That was not useful now.

Kezia laid the stranger watch on the bench next to the scope and the municipal beat coil and the little mountain of wristbands waiting to be righteous. She slid the cloth aside and clicked the beak. Nothing. She clicked again. Old logic sometimes needed a rhythm. She tapped her own watch with a fingernail, the sound small in the pulse room. She tapped the bench. Two. Three. Five. Seven. The prime steps. The watch stayed dead—in her hand at least.

The bench lamp went blue.

Kezia’s throat closed. The blue meant the pulse room had caught a Priority. Not Council—Council priority was a red bar that listened for itself. This was older. This was a channel nobody used if they could help it because using it was an admission that things had slipped beyond the routines of pious scarcity.

She reached for her console with hands that were steadier than she felt. The blue peeled, opened, gave her sound first because the city’s nets were hungry and clipped video to save juice.

“Kezia Marr,” said a voice she had never heard and knew.

Her name in that cadence, the way it had always been in her head, spoken by her mother on a night with both doors locked and both windows shut. Kezia couldn’t breathe. Tamsin made a small noise like a bird hitting a glass.

“It’s not her,” Kezia said.

The voice waited a beat and then said, crisp and entirely here: “Phase Hold asset zero-seven-two authenticates to Kezia Marr, citizen A-line, registered calibrator.”

Tamsin scrabbled at the other larkwatch with both hands and dropped it and cussed and picked it up again. Kezia was already thumbing the toggle on her own. The case warmed, then heated so quick she almost let go. She didn’t. The beak twitched under her thumb.

“Authenticate,” said the voice.

“My mother is dead,” Kezia said. That was not a password. Behind the blast-shield of professionalism, she saw herself as a child in the light well, sitting on the tiles and waiting for the sound of boots on the stair. The sound had come, unfamiliar.

“Authenticate,” the voice said again, implacable now. Kezia put her mouth against the little black shape, which smelled like thumb-grease and years. She said the only thing that mattered in the first days when the tools were soft and so were the people.

“Hold to phase,” she said. “Don’t let them turn the day.”

The question hovered for a heartbeat as if considering whether to allow coincidence. Then the watch clicked. It clicked with the old, impossible tick of tiny parts that weren’t there, gears she had never opened, and a little pulse ran up into her thumb like everything she had been waiting for becoming true.

The shade code unfolded in her console like a flower opening. The old mind of the Array saying, faltering but present, I have a hand for you. I remember your touch.

Kezia swallowed. The scope chattered. The primes walked off the screen and then stopped, organization becoming something else, a threshold.

A face came up on the console: a man with the burned-silk skin the Wardens had and eyes like chips of day. He didn’t wear Council blue or any color Kezia liked; he wore the ring’s drab, functional, heat-stained gray, the uniform of those who went up. He looked younger than her in the senses that mattered and older in the way of those who had watched day from the wrong side.

“City calibrator Marr,” he said. “I need you to hold phase. The Array’s east quarter is taking instructions from a protocol we do not own. If you let the noon slide, it will complete the handover.”

“What protocol?” Kezia asked. Her mouth felt full of crushed ice. Beside her, Tamsin had stopped breathing altogether.

The man glanced down at something outside her view. His jaw tightened. When he looked back up, the expression was not Warden and not stranger. It was a person trying to be careful with a person.

“It calls itself the Home Key,” he said. “It’s the launch code from the first ship. It’s addressed to your larkwatch.” He paused, then added, as if that meant less than the rest by orders of magnitude when it meant everything: “And it’s signed by your mother.”

The Meridian Tower groaned as if a deep wind had leaned its shoulder into the rock. Kezia’s knee found the bench. Her hand found the watch. Somewhere outside the pulse room, some part of the city laughed too loud or screamed. The beat found her again after drifting, and she set her teeth into it like a rope.

“Tell me what to do,” she said, and it was as flat and simple as hunger. She did not say: do not take this from me, do not let it turn into a story. She did not say: I will not let them turn the day.

The Warden nodded, a little once, and the watch ticked, and the Array’s dark geometry waited in the sky like a riddle and a promise. Outside, at the hinge of everything, the air kept moving.

On the morning the die refused to land, I had already decided to quit.

It hung at the apex of the toss above my counter, a cheap red cube with rounded edges and one pip smudged to a crescent from a thousand anxious thumbs. It should have arced, kissed the glass, and tumbled, but it chose—no, we all know better than to give it will—it happened not to. It hung. It took the longest still breath I’ve ever watched a small thing take, bleeding my shop of that everyday creak of probable outcomes.

The Nearest Future is a shoebox wedged between a memory laundry and a kiosk that prints manufactured pets. The sign outside is a rectangle of polarizing film that shows a different name depending on your angle and time of day: Tomorrow’s Better, The Small Tilt, The Near Side. The droplet in the corner registers the city’s ambient noise and adjusts for it. That morning the droplet was a dull amber and the sign read The Nearest Future for everyone, every angle. Stale coincidence, my old friend.

I held my hand under the die and waited for the world to breathe again.

Across Phyll Street, a man in a lemon-colored suit stood beneath a broken streetlamp and whistled into his wrist sleeve like it held the answer. An electric bus hissed, its letters crawling with advertisements for tax season: File your Interference. The memory laundress huffed as she dragged damp recollections on a line, their pale ghosts of moments from last week flapping in the slow air. My cat, Collapse, lay in a sunstripe by the window and did what her name suggested.

Inside, my coaxer radio was tuned to the station that carried a carefully balanced wash of thermal noise and cosmic static we’d agreed upon years ago as a city. We brokered the civic randomness in committee meetings, argued about it over coffee. Don’t tell me what’s fair, someone said; fairness is just an interfering frequency. When I left the Interference Office I took the radio with me. No one argued. A few of them were glad to see my back.

The coaxer’s dial was pegged in a spot labeled With Care. Even with care, it was humming too cleanly.

The die wobbled a fraction, as if on the cusp of remembering how to fall. I can tell a lot from a toss. A lifetime of calibrations and default judgments means your hands and eyes become instruments. It’s like learning to see the wind in laundry. My fingers had learned to feel the air’s thickness, the tiny tug of a borrowed future brushing the skin.

And something was wrong.

“Don’t you dare,” I told the die. My voice sounded larger in the small room.

It dropped, finally, but it didn’t tumble. It slid like a bead through syrup and came to rest on its edge between four and six. Collapse’s one green eye opened to consider if this was worth her attention. She went back to her sun.

“Well.” I blew out a breath. “Well.”

You learn to observe without collapsing things too sorely; you learn to sit with hover. But the die on edge was theater. It meant someone nearby was carrying a heavy amplitude debt or an illicit source. It meant the city noise had hiccuped or that fate itself—the public kind, the regulated kind—had a kink in its allocation. It meant I should close up, calibrate the coaxer, and call someone who still wore the Office’s blue.

And then the bell above the door rang, just once, like a tongue clicking.

The girl shuffled in with a mason jar clutched in both hands, elbows locked like she was carrying a cake with too much frosting. She had a bandage on her cheek and shoes that said she ran when people told her not to. The jar was taped with three kinds of tape and a label that had torn off of something else and been repurposed. It said SEA SALT in looping script.

She stopped just inside, letting the door swing shut, and looked from me to the wobbling die to Collapse, who did not return the courtesy. I took all this in while trying not to look at the jar too hard. The jar was wrong in the air. The room made a different noise around it.

“Are you Mira Thorne?” the girl asked. Her voice tried to be brave in the chest and cracked at the end, then recovered with practiced annoyance at itself. She brushed hair from her eyes with the side of her wrist, keeping both hands on the jar.

“I am,” I said, and then wished I had lied to buy myself ten seconds. “What have you got there?” I gestured vaguely at the jar with my chin. Hands visible. No sudden moves. You learn that with certain jars.

She looked at the die like she had caught me in the middle of bad magic. “My mom said to bring it to The Nearest Future. She said if anything happened. If she was late. She said your sign changes names, but this one was the right one. Are you—did I go to the wrong one?”

“I’m the right one,” I said, because in a city full of small lies that was one of the few I knew I could tell without consequence. “What’s your name?”

“Yara.” She blinked fast. “Are you going to help or are you going to stand there and explain randomness at me?”

“I wasn’t going to—” I half-smiled despite the jar. “Put it on the counter, Yara. Carefully.”

Careful is a word like fair; it means different things to different people. To me, careful meant I slid the coaxer’s volume lower with the back of my wrist and thumbed the Ground bowl onto the counter. The Ground is a heavy ceramic thing lined with graphene and good intention, wired under the floor to a bank of damp sinks that vent amplitude into a city-coordinated null. In the old days we called it the Prayer, because it was exactly as reliable. I’d kept mine in working order with prayer and contraband parts.

Yara set the jar down on the Ground with the solemnity of a bomb tech. The jar’s glass wasn’t glass; it was composite, the cheap kind you buy for pickles when you don’t intend to keep the jar forever. It held light like a pocket holds heat.

“What happened to your mom?” I asked. The word mom broke the new quiet like a hair snapping.

“She didn’t come home,” Yara said, and that was both too much and too little. Her eyes flicked to the die. “Is that supposed to do that?”

I glanced at the cube still braced between four and six. “No.”

“Is it dangerous?”

“Depends.” I drummed my fingers, then stopped; even that seemed loud. “Who is your mother, Yara?”

She hesitated like names were contracts, which in a way they are. “Ana Reyes.”

The band behind my heart tightened. The name was a nail in the wood of my career. I hadn’t seen Reyes in two years. She was smart in the way that made you revise your definition of smart to include kindness. She danced with her hands while she talked about noise floors and fairness. We had both resigned within the same month for different reasons and the same one.

“She said you knew each other,” Yara said. “She said you might not want to.” She offered the jar with her eyes, like it could argue on its own behalf.

“Is that—” I swallowed. “Why didn’t—Ana—call me?”

“She left me a note with the jar. It said, ‘Mira after dark if not before.’ It said not to use the channel. It said they listen there.”

“They?” I said, but we both heard the capital letter.

I leaned in close to the jar without moving too fast and let my eyes unfocus. The thing inside wasn’t light, not exactly. It was a very particular arrangement of electromagnetic noise harnessed to the jar’s inner surface like a wet moth clinging to a screen. Patterns shimmered at my lazy stare. The surface seemed to show the sharpness of an outline and then lost it when I tried to resolve it. It was a has-been of a star in there, a map of maybe. It was wrong because it was clean. It had edges that randomness shouldn’t. It sang if you put your ear to the right part of the air.

“Where did she get it?” I asked quietly.

“She told me not to say. She told me to say it later, on the way, when you said to. She said you’d tell me when the time was safe. She said… she said it mattered.”

The coaxer radio spat a little bit of white noise and then apologized for it by going silent. The bus outside did not move for a full three counts and then did. Someone down the block dropped a bottle, and it did not break.

“I need to see what’s inside,” I said, and looked at Yara to ask permission. The only honest work I do is small honesty.

She nodded, and it undid something in me.

“I’m going to ground some of it,” I said. “To take the edge off. Like uncorking a soda over the sink so it doesn’t go everywhere. Slow. Does that make sense?”

“I’m not a baby.” Her chin lifted. It trembled.

“Good,” I said. “Watch the dial.”

I left the die where it was and reached under the counter for the Sextant. The Sextant is a lie of a word; there are no arcs to measure there, only interference and amplitude. But when the Office had first put instruments in our hands they’d liked to name them for romance and pastness. It’s a small rectangular box with a needle that trembles like a good dog and a circular scale printed with words to keep us human: Normal, Kind, Naughty, Litigious, Very Bad, Don’t.

I set the Sextant next to the jar and clipped it to the Ground. The needle was pressed hard to Don’t and went past that into where the plastic ends.

“Okay,” I breathed. “Okay.”

“That looks bad,” Yara said. Her voice was monotone at the edges. She was either going to cry or sheath herself in iron; I couldn’t tell which.

“It’s a lot,” I said. “It’s more than anything.”

“More than anything what?”

“More than anything has any right to be in a pickle jar.”

If you have never felt the texture of a neighborhood’s chance in your teeth, this will sound fancy. But when a jar like that sits in a room like mine, you can tell which future it makes heavy by the way your tongue goes numb. You can tell if it’s hungry or ready. You can tell if it kills for the sake of killing or if it’s a child.

I took the jaw-clamp from the drawer and eased it over the jar’s lid. A gadget from the homegoods aisle, turned holy by our use of it. I did not open it. That would have been like opening a dam with your hands. I loosened it a hair until I could hear the faintest hiss, and I put my palm on the Ground and felt the city’s sinks drink. The Sextant’s needle trembled back to a place with numbers. The coaxer radio breathed again. The die rolled: it fell delicately from its edge to show a six, landed flat, and I hated how relieved that single face made me feel. Collapse flicked her tail twice in displeasure.

“What is it?” Yara whispered. In that whisper was a field’s worth of what ifs. If I had a child and we lived in this city and the city did what cities do to our children, I would have taught her to ask exactly that way.

“It’s amplitude,” I said. “It’s a lot of amplitude. Enough to—” I stopped. I didn’t need to say a phrase like rewrite a day out loud, even in the privacy of my shop. Words like that have habits.

She put her fingertips on the glass like she could draw heat from it. “Is that bad?”

“It depends,” I said.

“On what?”

“On whether anyone else knows you’re here. On whether your mother intended this to be opened or thrown into the deepest ocean. On whether it’s what I think it is.”

“What do you think it is?”

I didn’t answer. I lifted the jar off the Ground an inch and set it back, gauging the torque. The Sextant sang like a mosquito. The jar’s contents were arranged to hold. We call things like this primes because the first ones we ever found did not factor into smaller workable chunks no matter how you cut them. They are amplitude harvested from—no one agrees from where. The official line is baselines: vacuum thermal fluctuations integrated over ridiculous timescales by ridiculous instruments. The unofficial line is worse: a market you don’t audit, a habit of stealing futures from far away strangers, a weaponization of luck.

Ana Reyes had left; she’d left me; she’d decided she could fight from the inside longer than I could. She had always loved the idea that randomness, properly stewarded, could be a public good. I had loved that too until a boy loaded a nudge into a schoolyard scuffle and hit another boy in the wrong place behind the ear. You don’t get to see all your mistakes collapse in front of you like that very often. It had been my policy memo, my algorithm parameter set, my hand on the coaxer for that portion of town. No one had meant to. That was how we talked, then: no one had meant to. Intentions counted at our tax audits. I had left with my office plant and my coaxer radio and an anger I didn’t know how to aim at anything.

I put my fingers very lightly on the jar and closed my eyes. In the dark behind my lids, patterns talk to me. It’s not a gift. It’s training layered over inclination. Most of us had it. Some of us lied about it later. The jar’s patterns were not doing what they should. They were not bleeding cleanly into the Ground. They were braided in some deliberate way that pushed certain frequency bands and held others. Someone had wrapped a message around a bullet.

“Ana,” I said, and the name was dry.

“What?” Yara’s hope was a knife on a whetstone.

“She left you something in here. Or she left me something and you’re the courier. Either way, she wanted this to be read not poured over the city like—like sugar on a table.”

“How do you read it?”

I opened my eyes and met the gaze of the child of a woman I had respected and avoided in equal measure. “I shouldn’t,” I said. “No one should. That’s the point. We built a whole Office so that ‘no one should’ would be a structure and not a prayer. If I plug this into any trusted channel, everyone who listens for words like this will know it’s here. If I open it wrong, the weight will roll downhill and break someone’s shin in a place I’ll never see.”

Yara swallowed. The bandage on her cheek was peeling at one edge. “Then don’t open it wrong.”

It was older than me, the urge to be useful. We’ve been calling that love since we had words. I fussed with the clamp a degree tighter, then went to the door and flipped the sign to Nobody. The droplet in the corner went a shade more amber. The world might as well have put its finger to its lips.

“I need to call someone,” I said, staring at the die like it had to agree. “My old boss. Not on a channel that makes noise. Do you have a paper number? Do your generation still know how to write on paper?” I tried to make that a joke, but my voice was too bright.

Yara dug in her pocket and came out with a bent card that read Little Suns Daycare on one side. On the back there was a number in blue ink and a small drawing of a cat with two tails. The tails were the only detail that made it look like Collapse, and Collapse did not deserve it.

“That’s her emergency number. If I got lost. Not the one on her devices. She said you would use this. She said if I got scared I should count to thirty-nine and do it again.”

“Do what again?”

“She didn’t say.” Yara looked at the jar like maybe it had a manual printed on the bottom. “Is my mom dead?”

The room felt suddenly like it had my childhood inside it. I wanted to answer from some place that mattered and found only the honest scraps. “I don’t know,” I said. “If she was, I don’t think we’d be having this conversation. I think we’d be attending to different details.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“No,” I agreed.

I went into the back room and pulled the curtain against the front like it could hold something bigger than light. A merrow clock ticked sourly on the wall. The back room is to the front room what confession is to gossip. I lifted the receiver of the actual landline I had installed for the sake of theater and maybe for moments like this when we’d decided channels could be traps. I dialed the number with my finger.

It rang three times and then somebody answered with a breath held so tight it sounded like frost.

“Reyes?” I said.

“Mira.” It wasn’t her. It was someone else I had not expected to hear from and also had never expected not to. It was Armin, who had been my boss and then had been nothing.

“You shouldn't be on this number,” he said. He said it like he was looking over his shoulder in a room full of chairs.

“I have a jar,” I said, because I could not say a prime out loud yet. “Delivered by Ana’s daughter. Are you with her?”

“No,” Armin said, and something in his voice made the hairs try to leave the back of my neck. “We lost her ping at Catenary Station eight hours ago. We’ve been in to sweep and out to make tea and the tea tastes like a lie. Is the jar safe?”

“It’s on a Ground,” I said. “Environmental’s stable.”

“Do not, do not hook it to anything,” he said, thrumming the don’t with the rhythm of our old training. “Do not let it see any city grids except your sink. Do not let it see the Office. Do not let anyone who can spell amplitude into your shop. Stack the sinks if you can. Add salt if you have to.”

“Salt,” I said. “You get poetic in my absence.”

“They’re listening where we listen,” he said. “You left us and now you’re the safest part of the system. How’s that feel?”

“Like an indictment,” I said. “What’s in the jar, Armin?”

“Ana pulled it from a wholesale siphon,” he said. “Don’t bother with the official story; I can hear you deciding not to. It’s the big kind. It’s prime. It’s clean. She was on her way to your shop when we lost her. Are you hearing me?”

“I am.” My hand was a clamp on the receiver.

Armin took a careful breath. “I don’t have to tell you what it would do if someone put that in a bad heart.”

“You don’t,” I said.

“Then you have to get out,” he said. “You and the kid. Take the jar to ground somewhere no one will think to search. Do not leave it in your shop. If Ana made it to here with that amplitude, she was counting on you not to be governed by all the good reasons we ever wrote down.”

“I’m not in the habit of running,” I said, and hated that I still performed competence for him, even from this far away.

“Neither was she,” Armin said, and his voice did a thing I did not have a word for. “Mira. If you ever liked me, listen.”

The line crackled, and something else breathed into it. A tone of static stretched like a string. Someone had leaned into the only curve we had.

“I’ll call you after I’ve relocated,” I said, and hung up before any longer listening could happen.

In the front room Yara sat on the stool with her knees pulled up, fists under her thighs like anchors. She looked like every child forced to sit on their hands as the adults whispered in corners. The die on the counter was a six; it had not moved and that annoyed me.

“We’re leaving,” I said.

“To where?”

“Somewhere less insured.” I swaddled the jar in a wool carrier like a winter baby and clipped a second Groundcraft to it—a portable sink I had built with parts from a decommissioned dishwasher—to hold the boil. The Sextant did not like that; it ticked at me like a scold. The coaxer radio slipped a station and settled on a woman singing about the moon as if the moon could fix anything. Collapse sat up, arched, and in that moment existed in the map of my house as a certainty. Then she trotted under the curtain toward the back, embarrassed to be cared for.

“What about my mom?” Yara asked.

“We find her,” I said. “On the way to not getting dead ourselves.”

“And if we can’t?”

“Then we revenge politely,” I said. She watched my mouth to see if I was joking and decided to let me be a stranger with my own brand of comfort.

I lifted the strap of the jar’s carrier over my head, letting it sit low at my side. It tugged at me as if the ground itself was enamored. The walls of my shop shimmered with that something-wrong ripple you see above roads on hot days. Outside, a flock of scooters went by in a chord, their riders helmeted and bored. We would pass out into a city arranged to keep secrets we’d written into it ourselves.

On my way to the door, muscle memory made me reach to steady the die. I didn’t; I let it stand on its six. I turned the sign, watched it try to shift and fail, and that told me something I didn’t enjoy.

“Why do you call your cat Collapse?” Yara asked as if she was asking what the weather was, because when you are eleven your universe holds all questions equally.

“Because she only exists when you look at her,” I said.

“That’s not true,” Yara said, immediate and sure.

“I know,” I said, and opened the door.

The moment we stepped onto Phyll Street I could feel eyes that weren’t eyes, listening that wasn’t hearing. The lemon-suited man was gone like an amateur trick. The memory laundry had bundled up its damp afternoons and left only clothespins and the smell of pine. Above us, the smart glass canopy that pretended to be sky flickered once—not its usual song of cloud and brand but a single pale slate frame like a held breath. Someone had their hand on the city’s coaxer. It took a very large person to put their hand there without burning.

Yara took my hand without asking permission. Her palm was damp; the jar sang at my hip like a whale. The day did what it had to do to keep us thinking it was doing what it always did.

In the distance, toward Catenary Station, a long note went up and held. The sort of note that means doors are closing or opening or that the train will wait this long and no longer for anyone.

“Count to thirty-nine,” I said, remembering the bent card and its plain blue ink and the tails on the cat.

“What happens if I do?”

“You’ll know when to stop,” I said, and pulled her with me into the crowd that had learned to dance between probabilities, because we’d taught them and they had memorized the steps. We moved quickly. I did not look back at the shop. There are some collapses you don’t watch. There are some futures you walk toward even if you suspect they don’t want you to. We threaded a line I could feel under my feet like a crack in ice.

Behind us, I heard a sound that might have been my sign finding a new angle to show itself in. Or it might have been the door opening for a different kind of customer. Or it might have been nothing at all, the city doing what cities do: making noise to hide the places where the noise has been stolen.

Chapter One

The day the storm said my name, I was upside down, nested in straps beneath a balloon the size of a cathedral, twelve atmospheres deep in Jupiter’s southern temperate belt, where the wind never sleeps and the light is always the wrong color.

People like to romanticize the drift life. They imagine us riding the big belts like sailors once rode oceans, cutting treasure out of cloud. They don’t picture the ammonia rime that forms on your faceplate when a pocket of cold rolls through, or the way your suit’s struts creak when the pressure changes faster than your blood can. They don’t taste the copper sting that means lightning is counting down somewhere too close, or hear what the wind really sounds like down there.

Not that most people would ever hear it.

Most of the flotilla lived well above us, where the helium farms and rain-catchers skim the storms like houseflies, inflating and deflating their bladders to climb and sink on heat differentials. There, the wind is a polite thing. There, you can stand at a window with your coffee bulb and watch ochre bands unspool to the horizon and imagine you’re in a painting.

Down where we worked, there’s no window. There’s the suit, the tether, the line of your breath on the HUD, and an understanding between you and the wind that it will not bite you hard enough to take your name.

“Kettle?” I said. “Talk to me.”

My deck AI hummed through the bone-conduction pickups in my collar. Kettle was old, older than me, old enough to be cobbled together from three different buoyancy control systems and a salvage drone chassis, and might have remembered Earth if someone had given her a mouth back then. She took her name from the shape of her core unit: a battered pressure-safe cylinder with a crooked handle someone had once painted blue. “Present,” she said. “You’re at eleven point nine atmospheres. Your shadow is making the finicky hydrogen jitter again.”

“Tell it to stop.” I flexed my gloved fingers and watched white crystals flake away. The glove heater obligingly ticked up a degree. Outside the suit, there was nothing to touch but wind. I still flexed.

“Consider it chastised,” Kettle said.

The balloon above me—my balloon—hummed, a contented big-belly sound you felt through the straps more than heard. The woven skin, layered with slick films and patchwork panels, stretched and contracted as the gas cells inside breathed. The whole assembly was tethered to my gondola by a forest of cables: braided lines feeding control surfaces, moving ballast, adjusting intake valves, routing warm hydrogen where it needed to go. We rode the southern jetstreams like a jellyfish rides currents, trading altitude for energy and back again, mapping eddies, harvesting trace deuterium, picking over whatever the belts coughed up.

Today’s cough-up was a bright flicker in the silt of the bands. Kettle had flagged it in archived weather imagery: a specular glint on the right side of a rolling billow fourteen hours old, rare enough to send a notification to my contract feed. The Guild would pay for it. If it was intact, they would pay twice.

“Lock out buoyancy doors three and five,” I said. “If this goes sideways I don’t want the left flank overinflating.”

“Locked,” Kettle said. “Storm song remains within variance. Temperate. She’ll behave.”

“You say that.”

“I do not anthropomorphize.” A beat. “Not unintentionally.”

“Right.” I checked the time: a fat green circle on my HUD, nine minutes to the edge of the heat fall. Nine minutes before the local convection cell behind me cooled enough to drop and the roller in front of me warmed enough to rise and everything changed. The ocean of air was a stack of conveyor belts, and you learned to read which one you were on and when it would flip. “Scoop and go,” I told her. “If it’s tech, we tag and bag it. If it’s junk, we keep our bow pointed home.”

Kettle moved one of our outboard pods microdegrees to the left. The whole rig creaked. Somewhere above, a fin twitched to compensate. “You want the choir?” she asked.

“Turn it on.”

“Suit feed or gonzo?”

“Suit,” I said. Gonzo would have piped the belt’s low-frequency skeleton into the whole rig, into the balloon itself, letting the skin flex with it, a lazy pulse you could put your palm to and feel like a heartbeat. Suit kept it in my skull.

A soft flick and my world became sound.

If you have ears and a curiosity, you can listen to the wind anywhere. But down here, you don’t listen through air. You listen through bone. The implant nestled at the base of my skull picked up pressure variances recorded by the suit’s external sensors, shifted them down into a range nerves could understand, and gave my spine something to sing. Storms spread themselves out in that song. The big belts are organs. The Great Red is a cathedral choir. The temperate bands where I worked… sometimes they were lullabies. Sometimes, like today, they were talkative.

“Her pitch is up a hair,” I said.

“She knows you’re here,” Kettle said.

“You said you didn’t anthropomorphize.”

“That was before you reminded me to.”

I laughed into the mask. My breath fogged the edge of my visor and then vanished. The suit’s chem scrubbers were working a little harder than usual; the ammonia sensor was throwing occasional teethmarks on the stream. For comfort, I pinged the longline.

Ping back: tight, taut, good. The longline ran up to my gondola, a spaghetti of cables and lift-lines and communication tethers wound together into one thick coil that looked like the umbilical of a child conceived by a squid and a crane. It was the only true thing between me and the deep. The suit had microthrusters, but in this air they were a joke. An argument you had with a hurricane.

“Two minutes,” Kettle said.

I let the storm sing and thought about my father.

He had taught me knots when I was ten. Not the sailor knots that linger in old movies—bowlines and clove hitches and the pretty lies of symmetry—but knots for cords under tension where every fiber decides whether you live. All knots are confessions, he’d said, guiding my fingers through the twist that made a taut-line hitch, tying it blind, tying it behind my back, tying it while he shouted at me to hurry because the hatch is closing, the hatch is closing. They tell the wind who you are. They tell the wind if you can be trusted.

He’d gone out under a balloon not unlike this one and not come back. The Guild had given us a recording of the last five minutes of his suit feed, as if that would salve him being a past tense. The recording is a storm singing and then not singing. A hole in sound where something should be. Silence is a lie down here.

“One minute,” Kettle said. “We’re crossing your glint vector in thirty-six seconds. Keep your nose up.”

“Neck,” I said. “I don’t have a nose.”

“Keep your neck up then.”

I watched the scoops unfurl on my forearms: petals of woven carbon, electrostatic filaments flexing. They could sift micrometeorite silt out of Jovian murk; they could catch a glimmer and bring it to ground if I was precise. This was not like picking through an old shuttle bay or prying a transmitter off a dead buoy. This was blind work, tactile, an arc traced through doubt.

I kicked off. The straps released like hands. For a second, I was a bead on a string under a balloon and the world was a sphere of wind.

The glint revealed itself not to my eyes but to my hands. A hard tap like a plucked string in the right scoop, a scrape in the left, the hairline drag of something with mass. I rolled, parted filaments to keep from shearing whatever I’d touched, and brought my elbows in. The thing nestled in, clunky, heavy for its size. Kettle read its inertia. “Ten kilos,” she said. “Sixteen by sixteen centimeters on one axis, maybe twenty on another. Irregular. You’ve got it.”

“Come to me,” I told the line. The balloon above me reeled a centimeter. The wind objected and then decided not to kill me for it. I backed toward the longline, careful, careful.

A shape crescented out of the oxide smear to my left: the bow of someone else’s bucket. A second rig, smaller than mine, painted a cheerful red that the bands had dimmed to rust. Nav-fins flicked. Her pilot hadn’t bothered to obscurate their Guild tags. I recognized the handle. Ovid. Marm Hale’s people.

“Company,” I said.

“I see them,” Kettle said. “They hail.”

“Not now.”

Ovid’s rig vectored to put me in her lee. If I’d been generous, I might have said she was trying to shield me from a little bit of wind. But rigs didn’t give you lee out of kindness, and Hale’s people didn’t give you anything. I heard her comm ping through Kettle’s filter. Unrequested handshake. Uninvited.

Kettle blocked, then unblocked because Ovid brute-forced the handshake and ducted her voice through the oldest protocol anyone still used, the one everyone kept in their stacks like a superstition. “Tamsin,” she said, and then: “Whatcha got?”

The Guild believed, or pretended to believe, that drift law was fair: what you tagged, you owned. Ovid had seen my vector change. She’d seen my rig take strain. Even at this depth you could read the attitude of someone else’s balloon the way you can read a person’s shoulder. She’d seen a catch.

“Work,” I said.

“Let me take a look.”

“It’s tagged.”

“Tags are thoughts,” she said. “Show me the thing or I tell Home you’re harassing my line.”

“Do what you need,” I said. The word Home made something tighten. The Guild’s home wasn’t home the way the old word meant, but the flotilla used it because we had nothing else. It was three balloons tied together with catwalks in a permanent shape that the wind could not fail to recognize: spindles and domes, farms and fixbays, a hundred bodies asleep at any given hour, a thousand awake. It was where Hale’s people rented hangars. It was where I rented a cot.

Kettle clicked her disapproval in my bones. “I am not warning her off because you told me not to warn her off,” she said. “I want the record to show this. For later.”

“It’s happening now,” I said.

“It is as you say,” Kettle said. “Record begins.”

The world trembled. A tremor, a low animal sigh. Not in the rail or the balloon. In the surround itself. The choir in my skull reached a note I had not known it could. I felt it in the hinge of my jaw, my teeth. They hummed.

“Kettle.” My voice sounded wrong to me. Too bright, too far away.

“Convection roll,” she said, but the way she said it told me she did not think so. “Under us. It’s… wrong. Do you feel that gradient?”

Yes. A drop in the bones, like an elevator but sideways. I tightened my grip on the catch, bringing my elbows in. The thing in my scoops was cold. It should have been the same temperature as the soup around it, but it felt like it had been somewhere else. “Is it a sink?”

“No. Maybe. Possibly.” She was buying herself seconds to figure out how to be certain. Kettle never lied to me. “Wind shift in five. Four. Three.”

Ovid’s rig swung her bow, a sloppy curl, a fin catching where it shouldn’t. Someone up there—Marm, or a handler—swore over open comm, and then cut the line. In my skull the choir rose, then quieted, then rose again as if the storm had taken a breath.

I knew what storms could do. I knew what their edges looked like. I had spent a decade reading where the lines parted and where they stitched back together. This was not a place where wind should have been still.

“Depth spike,” Kettle said. “Right under you. Twenty meters in diameter. Stable.”

“Stable?” I asked.

“Persisting longer than it should.”

There are old stories among the drifts about still places. My father had told them like campfire tales when the hydrogen hum and the creak of the mesh were too vivid for sleep. If you find a still place, he’d said, you come up. If the choir stops singing, you come up. If you feel your bones become someone else’s bones—

The longline went slack.

“Kettle,” I said.

“It’s not slack.” Calm. She kept me calm by being calm. “It is an artifact of the local gradient. Trust your instruments and not your gut.”

“What if I told you my gut is overclocked by a proprietary implant designed to—”

“Then I would say that I did not sign your implant’s nondisclosure agreement and cannot therefore be held responsible for any breach of contract required to keep you breathing.”

“Kettle.”

“Hold,” she said.

I held. The scoops cradled the thing. Ovid drifted away as if she had nudged into honey. My HUD flickered as a packet of numbers tried to go where numbers did not want to go. The storm’s voice… changed. At least, that is the only way I can say it now, here, with forethought. In the moment, it was not change but awakening. Where there had been long-tone structure and predictable eddies and hollow breaths, there now was something like vertical, as if a deep bell had been struck somewhere below and its vibrations had climbed the air in columns. If sound had had edges, I would have sliced my fingers on them.

Kettle whispered: “We’re recording.”

The thing in my scoops pulsed. Not moving—pulsed. It was as if a pattern on its surface had shifted between one identical alignment and another, and in doing so the storm had noticed it.

A new voice arrived.
