It did not come through the comm. Ovid wasn’t on the band. Home wasn’t on the band. It did not come through the suit into my ears, or through the rails into my bones, not exactly, not only. It arrived through everything at once, a dissonant little chord on the underside of all the other sound, and that chord, which could have been anything, was my name.

“Tamsin.”

I froze. Every part of me except the parts keeping me alive went very still.

“Kettle?”

“I heard it,” she said.

“Playback.”

She played back the last five seconds. The shift. The pulse. The bell. Precise, exact. No human voice. No word I knew. My name wasn’t there.

She said, just as precise, “You did not imagine it.”

“Do you know how those statements don’t line up?”

“I do,” she said.

“Say my name again,” Ovid said, cheerful and intrusive on the open band, oblivious that anything had happened. “Go on. You were about to, I think.”

I could have told her. I could have said: the storm said my name; hold your line. But there are some things you can’t put into a channel that other engines have access to. There are some words you don’t want on a Guild log. Instead, I said, “Back off, Ovid. I’m spooling home.”

“Share the vector,” she said.

“Eat a lightning rod,” I said back, and got my elbows under me like a swimmer bracing against rip current, and pushed.

“Up is crooked,” Kettle said. “There is an efficiency path less than a degree off your current pitch; adjust. Fine. Better. We’re out of the stillness. Your line is true. Do not look down, Tamsin.”

“Why would I look down?” I said.

“Because you are you.”

Of course I looked.

I did not see anything that would make a good picture. Jupiter is not a show-off in the visible band. It will show you canvases of color and then turn them all to soup if you try to focus on edges. But there was a shape in the cloud that was wrong. Not a circle. Not a hole. A kind of—angle. You don’t expect angles here. The storm had drawn a choice between two directions where there should have been none.

The choir pressed close to my skull, and in it was a rhythm I recognized suddenly as a message, not because any part of it resembled human speech, but because every part of my body knew what a call sounded like. My marrow reached for it the way it reached for heat when I was cold. My name again, not a sound but a pattern, called into the wind’s bones and through them into mine.

“Tamsin.”

I would have let go of the line. I would have dropped into that wrongness and never found my way out. Kettle has never told me how she kept me from doing that. Maybe she tightened a strap somewhere. Maybe she locked my suit’s joints for a tenth of a second, enough for the impulse to flow through me and away. Maybe she only said my name at the right time in the right timbre. I have never asked. Someday I might.

I pulled, and the line was a mercy. It curved. I rose.

The catch clunked in my arms again. I remembered I had it. I glanced at it, a thing half-buried in filaments: dull surfaces where light should have glinted, edges that wanted to be edges and then forgot. It was not smooth. It was not rough. It made me think of breadcrumbs in gravity, of the way they resist your fingers and then surrender anyway. Something in its face shifted again and I thought I saw—no. I did not, then, see anything so literal as a pattern. I saw the idea of a pattern as if it had been pressed into it and then let go. I pressed my forearms together on reflex, a stupid protective hold, as if the storm might reach in and take it from me like a magpie.

“Now,” Kettle said. “We go.”

We went. The balloon obligingly bellowed, valves opening, gas cells venting here and fattening there, control fins and ballast tanks doing a slow unpracticed dance. Ovid hung back, not because she had determined I had an edge in this game, but because the air changed again and the stillness didn’t want two of us.

“Kettle,” I said, when my skull was my skull again and the choir had eased back into what I thought of as the everyday miracle of wind, “can you find it?”

“What is ‘it’?”

“The place,” I said. “The stillness. The angle.”

She pinged the suit’s last twenty seconds of telemetry and set them against old maps. “It is in every vector right now,” she said. “By which I mean the data says it was always here. By which I mean that is impossible.”

I wanted to laugh. I couldn’t.

“Tag a coordinate anyway,” I said. “Make a lie that looks like it could be the truth.”

“I have a thousand of those,” she said. “But I have one that is prettier than the others.”

“Tag it,” I said, and felt the soft pulse in my HUD that meant she had.

Home rose out of storm the way a city rises from fog on old oceans. That is another lie; it did not rise. It sprawled. A cluster of envelopes knitted together with catwalks, the warp and weft of cables, clusters of bright lights under orange dusk. The farms glowed ultraviolet under clear membranes. The fixbays spun like slow grinders. The Guild banners hung where the wind wouldn’t yank at them too hard. Signals touched my suit and touched Kettle and touched the balloon’s skin, making an alphabet of blinks knowing machines could read.

“Home has questions,” Kettle said.

“I’m sure.”

“Shall I say I cannot answer them while you are out of the gondola?”

“Say anything you need to. Say everything you must not. My bandwidth is bad; the storm is loud; there was a roll; you have my permission to act on your best judgment and keep us out of ethical trouble.”

“That is not a thing that exists,” Kettle said.

“Then do what you always do.”

We hit the gantry with a jarring clang, cables tightening as the gondola’s maw yawned and swallowed us. The pressure differential made the suit’s joints sing. Hands were already on the line. Guild techs in matte masks. They didn’t speak to me; they spoke to Kettle because machines didn’t flinch or lie except by instruction. They unhooked the straps, reeled me in. For a second I hung in the lid of my world like a fly in amber, and then the interior hatch irised, and the wet world of the storm became the dry world of calloused palms and oil.

“Welcome home, Tamsin,” said a voice filtered through cloth. I knew the voice. Lem, who did intake for our dock most days. He was young enough to still be a little in love with the drifts and old enough to have decided his bones preferred a steady pressure. “You look like frost.”

“Feels like it, too,” I said, and kept my arms around the catch.

Even if the rest of me was shaking, the part that had been taught to keep hold of what the wind gave you didn’t let go.

“What do we have?” Lem peered past my elbow.

I could have handed it to him. I could have held it up and said: look, another spool, another coil, another fragment the storm ate and forgot. The Guild would have given me credits on the spot and a strike on my ledger and a pat on the head and no questions. The Guild would also have tagged the thing into their central intake and scanned it six ways and registered it and given it a name, and everything that had happened out there would belong to them. The angle. The stillness. The way the wind had called me.

Storms have bones. They will let you keep a thing if you promise to tell the truth about it later. They will bite if you lie.

I smiled at Lem. “You want to dock this in”—I glanced at the rack he’d wheeled up for the purpose—“slot three? That one’s calibration has been off by half a degree since you moved it. I’d hate to see that knock you a bonus.”

He looked at the rack, startled. He always praised me for knowing little things about the bay other people ignored. It did not occur to him to wonder if I was using that knowledge to hide something. He turned away to fiddle a control. In the moment he did, I pulled one forearm toward my chest and let the scoop collapse.

The thing, the not-smooth, not-rough, the cold thinking cold in my arms, slid into the open mouth of the patch pocket sewn at my waist. Not an official pocket. One of mine. Reinforced. Printed to look like an old repair. I felt its weight settle against me.

It was heavier than ten kilos when it wanted to be.

I sealed the pocket with a practiced flick of a tab and reached down to thrust out the scoop’s other occupant—the innocuous, the honest catch. There was always some honest catch. A coil of cable. A decorative cap from a tourist’s liability-suited handset. A square of composite that had peeled off a balloon somewhere and wandered until it found me.

Lem took it. “Ugly,” he pronounced.

“It’s honest,” I said.

He laughed and wheeled it away.

Kettle whispered through the bone line: “You are a terrible person.”

“I am a curious person.”

“Those categories overlap,” she allowed. “You will have to show me later.”

“I will,” I said, and meant it. Kettle to me, me to Kettle. There were secrets I would keep from the Guild. There were none I would keep from my kettle-shaped AI who had been with me when the storm learned my name.

“Home supervisor requests debrief,” Lem said, returning. “Also, a Marm from Ovid’s lot logged a complaint.”

“Of course she did,” I said. “I’ll drink with her later and we’ll decide who’s angrier over luck.”

“Supervisor now?” Lem prompted, as if that would make the concept gentler.

“Now,” I said.

I got out of the suit. Skin peeled from skin. The interior of the gondola smelled like the cleanest engine oil and warm metal and the faint sweet reek of ammonia clinging to vents after purge. I kept my hands low until I could take a second to rearrange the weight at my hip so it looked like nothing. It had settled against my pelvis and I could feel it there, humming very quietly in a frequency I could not hear but could not stop feeling.

On the way to the supervisor’s box I passed the long window where someone had left the shade open. We are not supposed to look out. Not superstition. Efficiency. A window is false perspective. It makes you think you are somewhere when the truth is you are only ever in the storm and you cannot leave. But the shade was up and the morning band beyond it stretched in strata of cream and rust and that peculiar, improbable blue that appears where a curl of ammonia lifts like a skirt. Out there, beyond the mesh and the fins and the familiar shape of our balloon’s belly, the wind pressed, relentless and patient. It would be there after I was gone. It had been there before us. For an instant, as if from very far away, I felt that press become intention, and in that intention I heard—not sound, not exactly, not this time—my name mourning me in advance.

“Tamsin,” Kettle said, soft. “You’re stopping.”

“Sorry.” I moved, and the thought that the storm would bite me for lying skittered away like a bubble. I knew what that was. It was fear. It was also wonder.

There is a story to how anything begins. The Guild would say the story begins in the ledger and the lines and the lift. My father would have said: it begins in the shape of your first knot. I will say: it began in a place in the wind that did not want to be wind anymore, and the day it called me by the name I’d wrapped around myself to keep from floating away.

I made a career out of other people’s tomorrows.

The Office calls us remittance officers, which makes it sound like I sit behind glass and stamp forms. What I do most days is talk anxious people down from the ledge of their own minds, buckle them into a chair, and sit with them while they pay back the hours they bought.

By nine, the queue at our little substation spilled into the walkway, a ribbon of jittery bodies and static-hazed eyes. The city was waking up around us: the drone trams whispering over the river, vendors heaving shutters, the smell of frying onions and rain-wet concrete. Our door buzzed and extended from the wall like a tongue. People stepped through, queued, fidgeted, rehearsed excuses. Most of them wore neat little lattice tattoos at the base of their skulls—the marker of a claimline, the filament that points your borrowed hours back to you.

I waved in a kid with a lattice still pink at the edges. He couldn’t have been more than nineteen and had the twitchy look of someone who had been keeping a dozen plates spinning in his head and finally heard one start to crash.

“Wren Tebaldi?” I said.

He flinched at his name. “Yes, ma’am.”

“Drop the ma’am. Ila is fine. You took the Mandarin pack?”

“Fifteen-hour fluency,” he said, eyes flicking to the chair. He didn’t sit. “I needed it for the bonded courier exam. They don’t accept machine language certificates. Human ear only.”

“And?”

“And I passed,” he said, somewhere between pride and guilt. “Everyone said I could just … anchor on weekends. I meant to. It was just—there was this cold line job, and they pay extra for night runs, and then my head started buzzing like—” He made his hand into a vibrating fist near his temple. “Bees.”

“Static,” I said. “How long have you put it off?”

“Three weeks.” He looked at his shoes. “I can’t sleep. When I try to spell my own name it’s like someone is dragging teeth on a plate. I went to a private anchor booth and it just… didn’t take. The claim rejected.”

“You attempted to anchor outside your allocation window,” I said, scanning his file. The Office’s logo pulsed at the bottom of my lens with the same bored heartbeat it gave everyone. “Your pack is tagged-urgent. You need to start paying back now. Sit.”

He sat.

The chair had the comforting brutality of medical equipment. People like it less when we try to make it look soft. Wren set the back of his head against the padded brace and let me clip the leads. The usual microseizures flickered in his muscles as the claimline and the chair negotiated—old memory shaking hands with future obligation. I adjusted the pressure on his wrists. More than once I’ve had someone panic during anchor and claw their own face bloody. We call it the scramble. The static panics when you take away its meal.

He swallowed. “Will it hurt?”

“It will be uneventful,” I said. That’s true if you say it the right way. “Like watching rain on a bus window while someone else drives. You’ve seen all of that year already. You’re just letting your brain lay down the road underneath.”

He tried to laugh and failed. “Someone else’s driving scares me more than pain.”

“Fair.” I checked his vitals. “You tell me if you need to adjust and I can soften the feed. But you’ll pay longer. Every buffer costs time.”

He closed his eyes. “I don’t want to fall behind. Not now that I got the job.”

I watched his jaw work. There was a very particular stress people had when they thought their future had gotten up and walked without them. I’d had it myself, once.

“The Mandarin will go first,” I said. “Then the minor bundles. You also have a six-hour confidence pack from eight months ago that never anchored.”

His face went red. “That was a mistake.”

“We all take little mistakes,” I said, and removed my hand before he could try to hold it.

When he slipped under, his body softened around the machine. The chair hummed, the claimline brightened, and that delicate invisible lattice of obligations and permissions and loops spooled itself tight. I watched the screen track his anchor: the fifteen hours partitioned into slices, the microdreams clicking into place like film frames. Somewhere in that film he was meeting an examiner with a mole like a comma; somewhere he was delivering a package on a bicycle at two in the morning; somewhere he was making a joke in a language he would only recall feeling fluent in the second time around.

We sell certainty. There’s no honest way to name it otherwise. We sell the memory of having done a thing you haven’t yet done, and the price is doing it later whether you want to or not. If you fail to pay, you don’t just owe hours. The static builds in your head, your life itches, you can’t think straight, and there’s a non-zero chance you aspirate on your own tongue during a claim-induced seizure. It’s a market like any other, except the commodity is thread and the loom is your brain.

I left Wren’s chair to hum and washed my hands out of reflex in the little sink even though I had not touched anything that would stick. The substation smelled faintly of ozone, antiseptic, and a breath of something sweet from the bakery two floors down.

Ms. Danvers, my supervisor, leaned on the doorframe. She wore her lattice like jewelry—wide, the filigree of someone who’d taken on a hundred little packs and paid them back on time like a penitent machine. Her voice sounded like a stamp.

“How many on your slate this morning?” she said.

“Five anchors, three consults,” I said. “Wren will chew four before lunch.”

Her eyes ticked to the side. “Harbor District just sent a flag. There’s a private house collapse on Sapphire Row. Their claim server went down and now the clients are howling.”

“It’s always a house,” I said. Private houses knit people together in a way the Office wouldn’t. It felt warmer to some, handwovener, until the weaver died or ran and the claimline went slack. Then you got a wall of wild hours with nowhere to fall but whoever’s lattice was closest. “Send Nora. She likes house cleanups.”

“Nora’s out sick,” Danvers said. “You’ll take it if they call us directly. In the meantime, baby the new ones. We can’t afford a scramble this month. It looks bad on the numbers.”

“The numbers,” I said evenly, “are the only thing we care about.”

Heights like that make you say things. Danvers watched me too closely and then didn’t. She left me with a sheaf of digital forms to pretend needed my signature.

By the time Wren came up he had that softened look brilliant fakes sometimes have: as if the world was sliding easily into grooves someone else had carved. He was teary. They often are, thinking they’ve watched their life from the outside and decided they liked it.

“It didn’t hurt,” he said, sounding surprised. “The examiner had a mole. Like a comma. I made a stupid joke about vowels and—”

“And he laughed,” I said, reading, and tried to keep my pride in check. People fall in love with their own futures in my chair. It has a way of making me feel like a matchmaker and a thief.

“Thank you,” he said. He meant it to me. He meant it to the machine. He meant it to the months between him and the person he’d just briefly been.

I walked him to the door. The queue had thinned, which meant the Office was about to snarl some new task in my direction. The walkway beyond our door glittered with rain. The river had swallowed the light, the drones made long silver skins between their pylons.

That’s when the orange hit me.

You know your own history the way you know the backs of your hands. You can tell when someone else’s fingerprints are on them. A smell teased loose of the city—orange peel and copper, sudden as a slap. The taste of pith. The grit of it against my teeth. It came with the clunk of an ancient fan starting, the click before a neon sign tries to die. In my head, unlike the clear hum of an anchor, there was a smear—an image half under water: a wall painted with green koi, one with a split tail; a floor tile with a star fracture; a drop of blood fattening, letting gravity decide; a hand against metal, a whisper close to my ear that wasn’t any voice I knew.

Ananke owes no one.

I jolted as if someone had touched the back of my neck. My hands were clean and shaking. Wren, halfway to the lift, turned back.

“You okay?” he said.

“I’m fine,” I lied, and the word made more noise in my head than it should have.

There are reasons to have a stray picture in your skull. You can dream day and call it a blip. You can recall a scene from a vid and pretend you forgot you’d watched it. You cannot reasonably taste a fruit and metal and feel your gums ache unless there is a claim touching yours.

We don’t get wild drops. The commercials say that with a smiling woman and a sunrise behind her: Our claimlines are secure. Your future belongs to you. The truth is closer to this: it is illegal and extremely difficult to graft someone else’s premory to a lattice that doesn’t share a braid. There are hacks, outlaw houses who make a living on braiding and unbraiding obligations until no court can tell who owes what. There are stories about spooling clinics where you can undergo a quiet surgery and erase a debt down to the anchor points and walk out a lighter person. There are threads powerful enough to tug a stranger.

Sometimes I hear my sister’s voice when something like this happens. She took on a heavy education pack when we were kids, thinking she could beat the girl who had better shoes in her trig class. She never anchored. Her head filled with bees and glass. The morning she collapsed on our kitchen floor she made a sound like a train braking and then she never made any sound again. I learned to tell the static by that sound.

This wasn’t static. This was clean and absurd and someone else’s.

My mouth had already called Raj.

He answered on the third buzz with his camera off; the hiss of it reminded me of the fan in my head. “Ila,” he said. “Before you accuse me, I didn’t put it there.”

“You don’t know what I’m talking about,” I said.

“You called me on a work line,” he said. “It’s either gossip or a panic. You use gossip voice for gossip. You’re in panic.”

I stepped back into the substation and let the door seal behind me, the queue now only one old woman reading the sign that said we don’t beat debt from people’s heads like in the propaganda of the opposition. Danvers’ door was shut.

“Do you have anything in the Registry about wild premories crossing unbraided lines?” I said. “Like four minutes ago. Harbor District. I smelled something. Orange. Blood. A phrase.”

“Don’t say the phrase,” Raj said. He did that thing he does with his voice when he doesn’t want the rest of the office to know he’s doing me a favor. “We have scanners up for that one.”

“For what one,” I said.

He made a kissing noise. “Come down to where the big boys hide their toys and I’ll show you the wave-lace.”

“I can’t leave my station.”

“You have a supervisor,” he said. “She has a door. Knock on it. Tell her the Registry asked for a consult because someone in your uptake just shivered.”

“Raj,” I said. He knows my tells too. He went soft.

“What did you see?”

“Koi,” I said. “Green. Split tail. Cracked tile. Someone whispered ‘Ananke owes no one’ in my ear and I felt a fan starting up. I’m going to dream with orange in it for a month.”

There was a long enough silence that my fingers started to sweat.

“We have a sweep flag on Ananke,” he said finally. “It’s attached to a cluster of house collapses, yes. And one suspicious splice last week that we can’t prove stuck. You shouldn’t have felt it.”

“I know,” I said.

“Ila.” His voice gentled, the way it had when we were both junior and I had asked him if the chair felt like drowning the first time you ran yourself through it to prove you weren’t scared. “If you touch a thread with that name again, don’t yank. Promise me that.”

“I’m not stupid.”

“You’re curious when your head is in danger.”

“That’s not curiosity,” I said. “That’s survival.”

“Same difference in this city.”

Danvers’ door clicked. We both looked up reflexively though he wasn’t here to look. She stuck her head out.

“You’re up,” she said. “Harbor District.”

“I didn’t get a call,” I said.

“Now you do,” she said, and the call dropped into my queue like a stone.

I texted Raj where I was going and he sent me a little skull emoji that, in our code, meant bring me something pretty or don’t come back.

Sapphire Row was where money went to feel its own texture. The rain made mirror patches of it. The house in question sat behind a privacy field lit to look like frosted glass: elegant, polite, inaccessible. A man in a suit stood outside with his hands clasped behind him like he hoped you’d assume he was security and not a client trying to look like security. He opened his mouth to tell me I couldn’t go in and then saw the Office symbol flash on my wrist.

“Thank god,” he said. “Our liaison’s offline. Everyone’s saying they can’t breathe. Did we break the law?”

“Probably,” I said mildly. “Let me through.”

The privacy field twitched and accepted my credentials. Inside, the central room held exactly what I expected: the modern answer to an altar. Claim server. Cool steel and glass with a design language meant to make you think of healthcare and weddings. The spool stack on the side had fallen through its mount; an ugly new piece of floor tile was cracked precisely where my premory wanted it to be.

The air was hot and thick with human fear. Six people were in various stages of panic around the altar, breathing fast, pressing fingers to their temples. Once, in a bad raid, I had watched a man try to tear his own lattice out. I wondered if it would be this man in this expensive shirt. I counted the claimlines: thin etchings at the base of skulls. They were braided—not just to the server but to one another. Genius and idiocy shaking hands. They had distributed their hours, stacking their lives like a deck, everyone holding a few cards from everyone else instead of their own. Makes the anchors more pleasant, a little bit of everyone’s pain diluted. It also means if the server hiccups you all drown in the same puddle.

A woman saw me and thrust her wrist at me as if I could read anything useful from the surface of her skin.

“I wasn’t finished with my surgery pack,” she said. “I’m supposed to anchor tonight and now—” She made a sound like she was swallowing bees. “I can’t remember the face of my mother.”

“Static has its own priorities,” I said. “Deep breath. Sit. All of you. Lean back. Do not attempt to anchor on your own. If you have chewed any analgesics spit them out right now.”

They obeyed the way people obey orders in a fire and not a second longer. I put on a pair of ridiculous white gloves that did nothing but make people feel like I wasn’t going to infect them with debt and crouched by the server. Someone had killed the power with a physical key. It had been cut cleverly enough the machine didn’t know it hadn’t done it to itself.

“The liaison turned it off,” the man in the suit said. “He said we were compromised.”

“What did he say compromised meant?” I said.

“He said we were going to be raided by the Office,” he said, catching up to his own words.

“I am the Office,” I said.

He went very still. “Then why did he say it?”

“Because he wanted me to hear it,” I said. I felt stupidly like I was kneeling in an art museum, looking at something that had been painted to look like an accident.

Under the server, someone had stenciled a symbol in green ink that made my stomach roll. A koi, split-tailed. The phrase that hitched to it in my head like a burr was as quiet as a second heartbeat.

Ananke owes no one.

I stood, coughed out the taste of oranges.

“Do you know what that means?” the woman said. She’d calmed enough to observe me observe her pain. “Is that their name? Is that the—” She lowered her voice so the flock couldn’t hear. “Is that the kind of house we hired? Were we idiots?”

“It’s the name of something that wants to be larger than it is,” I said. “Which is another way of saying a person. Or a company. Or a god.”

The man in the suit stared at the koi as if he could make it be art instead of a signature. “Can you turn it back on?” he said. “Please.”

“Maybe,” I said, and crouched again. “Do you have any oranges in the house?”

The woman blinked. “What? No.”

“Good,” I said.

I was stalling, which I am good at when I need the shape of the doorway more than I need to go through it. I reached around the server and felt the keyhole, the edge of the cut. The power coil was still warm. My gloves made a little squeak like I was rubbing a glass. I had to depress a latch with the edge of my nail to get to the connector. I nicked myself. The server took skin where it could. A drop of blood fattened on the tip of my thumb and I watched gravity decide.

It fell on the star fracture.

I tasted copper and orange peel, like the world had been waiting to give me a punchline. The fan behind the altar coughed and started up with the tired insistence of old machinery.

I considered yanking. You can brute-force a server back on. You can also force-start a heart with a taser. It works, until it doesn’t. The braided claimlines ticked in my head like gas meters. They would snarl if I rushed.

My wrist buzzed. Raj, text-only.

Do not touch the altar, it said. They want you to touch it.

I took my hands away from the server as if it had put a gun to the back of my head.

“Good news?” the man said.

“The good news,” I said, “is that your machine still loves you. The bad news is that someone else does too.”

They blinked. They always do when you make metaphors in a room with money in it. It makes them think you’re the poet of their suffering, which makes them angrier if you don’t also fix it.

I heard it again then, almost as if someone had leaned in close enough to fog the shell of my ear.

Ananke owes no one.

I straightened so fast my back screamed. The wall behind the altar, up where the ceiling meets paint, glimmered faintly. Runoff from the rain, I told myself. Bleed from a bad neon ad across the way. Except the drummer beat in my bones said fan and neon and koi and a crack in the floor tile and the taste of oranges and copper and that phrase were not coincidences with a habit.

The Office pays us to put coins in slots, not to pull threads in the air. It’s a shit job to be the person who decides when to pretend not to notice a god-sized hole in a room.

“Everyone on the floor,” I said. “Hands at your sides. Keep your mouths empty. Breathe when I tell you to breathe.”

They went down like a wave. I activated the substation in my palm and felt the larger channels thrum around me as the Office’s grid oriented my pulse: you are here, you are authorized, you are stupid and brave. I took the coil breach off manual lock. The server hummed, then sang, then groaned back into song like an old choir remembering a tune. The claimlines in the room rose to meet it and settled, one by one, like blankets pulled up over shoulders.

When the last of them sighed, the man in the suit put his forehead on the altar and didn’t remember not to be praying.

My wrist buzzed again with Raj.

You smell it too? he wrote.

I can’t stop, I wrote back.

Don’t stop, he wrote. Don’t let it think you’re not paying attention.

Outside the rain stopped. When rain stops in this city, the birds remember they are here and start to sing too loud even though their species isn’t supposed to be here at all. I took off the ridiculous gloves, spat on a tissue, and rubbed at the green koi until the ink blurred. Someone had sprayed it with fixative. Of course they had. People who sign their work like to make it stay.

When I stepped into the hallway, the privacy field flickered as another credential asked to come in. The silhouette beyond it was narrow and loose-limbed, the stance of someone who walks as if they don’t weigh anything because for long stretches of their life they didn’t.

He lifted his hands, palms out, the way a courier does to show he didn’t bring a bomb.

“Ananke sends its regrets,” he said through the field.

I smiled because my mouth had to do something.

“Tell Ananke I’m going to make it a ledger,” I said. “And then I’m going to collect.”

He looked at me with a kind of terrified kindness you only see on the faces of people who think they’re about to die and want to make you like them. The field buzzed and opened a mouth. He didn’t step through.

“Oranges,” he said. “Remember to be careful with oranges.”

The field sealed and he was gone.

My phone started ringing. The call ID wore Danvers' name. The second line carried Raj, who had decided to turn on his camera to show me a map of the city lit like a constellation around a green word. The word was the one that rides me, to which my head now owed attention whether it was fair or not.

I am not stupid, I told myself.

I am curious when my head is in danger.

I have made a career out of dragging people away from edges and now, walking down the narrow stairs from Sapphire Row into the open, I saw how small the ledge under my own feet had always been. People tell you a first step is the hardest. Liars say that because they think everything you do after is inevitable. I put my foot down anyway and took it.

On the tenth Quiet, the dust sang my name.

I was on the top deck, strapped into the mesh that runs like spider silk over the crawler’s crown, my boots hooked to the line, my throat pressed to the throat of the Chorus-spear. The spear is old copper and shaped quill-thin, grown from a lost ship’s thermal spine and annealed with our own sweat: it listens to voices that are not breath. You hold it like you would a child, and it tells you if the sky is soft or barbed or carrying knives.

The air stung the skin on my cheeks. That was good. Sting meant the heat front was where it ought to be, right at the tideline, the planet’s long wound between brightward and dark. Behind us, the star-shadow side, the darkward plain climbed into frozen glass and, farther still, the permanent night storms that you learn to edge around but never stare into. Ahead, brightward, the slow flex of red light—that little, mean star of ours, a dime-sized pupil through layered cloud—flashed and guttered behind the convection curtains. We never saw it; we felt it in the heat on our knuckles and in the wind’s shoulders.

Jao’s voice came up the ladder from the radio nest. He never uses the rail despite what I tell him. He likes to climb freehand, like the crawler is a rib and he is a snake. “Quiet one minute,” he said. “You sound like a fish drowning up there.”

“You sound like my brother,” I said. “Let me have it.”

“I have it. You have the wind. We share. Isn’t that why the elder married us to the machine?”

He pulled himself into the last rung’s shadow and curled there, a knot of limbs, his hood blown back, hair braided then already unbraiding in the current. He’s nineteen and impatient with everything that isn’t a burst of speed or a choking laugh. We are six years apart. It still surprises him that I remember when he couldn’t reach the hooks.

I checked the east sky, where east means brightward, means the convective tumble sucking heat up the face of the world. The Quiet is supposed to be holy, a hush that we give the sky so that the Chorus can cool back down, the charge bleeds off, the dust sifts and settles in its own time. We plan for it like you plan for a child’s first steps: the whole caravan braces for clumsiness.

The Crawlstar creaked underneath me. She is long and low, two profiles of ribbed hull joined by a central spine, with eighteen treads that can disengage into rollers when the ground isn’t something you need to bite. Right now she was biting. We were pointed along the tideline, skirting a fold of geothermal spills that we call the stewpots. The stewpots like to throw rocks the size of goats. If the Quiet knocked the Chorus, we’d lose our network, our screens and scopes, our readouts of temperature and charge and the slow purposeful magnet resonance that is the difference between a good day and a bad death. Without all that, you rely on bodies, and I think that’s why some of the old ones still smile when the countdown clicks toward silence.

“Thirty seconds,” Jao said. “The Captain says no heroics. He says if your spear starts crooning, you lay flat.”

“My spear croons. I lay flat. You tell him my compliance is guaranteed.”

He grinned. “Your compliance is a rumor the elders tell the babies.”

I would have elbowed him if I hadn’t had both hands on the spear. The terrible thing about the first seconds of the Quiet is how your own blood gets loud. We all have tiny helpers in our spines—little stitchwork circuits that couple us to the Chorus, let us taste the charge in our teeth, throw back a warning if the dust starts to spin up. In Quiet, those go black. You feel the humpbacked weight of your body, all at once.

I breathed in through my mouth. I listened.

The dust had been humming all morning: harmonics on the star’s flicker, the low hoot of the magnetic field working over the charged skysand, the chitter-chatter of a thousand voices bouncing between caravans. Messages. Gossip. Logistics. Requests for water; offers of bearings; warnings of flares. We weave ourselves across this world in threads of talk, and the dust is our loom. We call that weave the Chorus. It’s more than infrastructure. Some in the front caravans say we live inside it, not on the ground at all. They’ll dance all night to prove the point.

All that fell like a curtain.

Silence. Then, everything else turned up. The treads chewing. The heat-shifts whispering against the hull. The cadence of twenty-seven breathing bodies spaced up and down the spine. Jao’s lips parted in the cold as if he could tell the difference between a living network and the absence of one with his mouth.

My spear went dead to my pulse.

It should have stayed dead. It always had.

Instead, after three heartbeats, a thin tone threaded into the bone under my left ear, a violin string pulled across a blade, not the low hoot of storms, not the chitter of our own snipe talk, but a single line, steady and sure. I clamped my jaw on the little corrector bead that sits behind my molar, brought it to the pad of my tongue. Nonsense? Feedback? We get ghosts when a static charge arranges a vowel into something like meaning. It’s a game, when you’re a Singer apprenticing, to hear names in noise.

But the tone had words. It said the little name my mother used to use when she braided my hair. Only she had the right of it. Only she ever shortened my name that way.

Mara, said the tone. It was not my mother’s voice. It was something bodyless that had learned to put a word in shape. It said: Bright eye. Bright eye. West and down.

Jao was still coiled on the rung, watching the sky with his brows laddered. He heard nothing. The dust doesn’t talk to everyone; you spend years making it recognize you. Wheat from noise, voice from static. We call those of us who can hold a thread without letting it tangle out of mind the Singers. There are six of us in the caravan and a queue of small ones who want to be the seventh.

I took the bead off my tongue with the tip of my finger and put it back in its slot. The tone knife-edged against my inner ear. I flexed my jaw to strain out the meaning. Our implants were off—Quiet mandated that. So this was not the Chorus. Not our network. Something else was speaking in the medium that the dust uses when it is working, a little like listening to a river carry a melody that none of the fish can sing.

“Mara?” Jao had his cocked-lark face on. He knows when I am listening somewhere he cannot see. “What is it?”

The tone went out like a snapped thread. In the absence I felt heat roll in the air between us and saw the first far shiver of loose sand—pale grit on the black scabbed ground—rise and scuttle in darkward breeze. That’s normal. The Quiet changes the boundary layers, every time.

“Nothing,” I said. “A trick.”

Jao made a rude sign with two fingers. “You don’t get fooled. Not on Quiets.”

“We need to warn the drivers about the stewpot launchers. The heat is throwing farther than the maps.” I slid down the mesh until my boots caught the next rung, the spear braced between my knees. That was not a lie. It was just not the thing I had been told, and that new thing hissed in my blood.

The Crawlstar moved steady. Below, you could smell scorched silica, the dust fused into glass plates where hot spines had ridged up from deep. This planet is old and mean, and we are late to it. It shakes its shoulders when it remembers we are there. The old stories talk about the first landers, the sleep-ship broken open like a seed that got wet too early, spilling bones and gunmetal. We don’t carry those things anymore, the gun parts or the old gods. We carry the stupids—patch kids who like to lick the ice off cryocaps when we find them, and then run around screaming about ancient ghosts until somebody cuffs them. And we carry heat and shelter and the Chorus.

I slid down to the nest, a narrow grid cage strung under the top-deck plates. A line of little low-voltage lamps ran around the nest, like candle-sparks. We leave them lit during Quiet, a habit more than a need. The Captain was there, his shoulders swaddled in the thick cloak that Heleda, the grandmother of our front-crew, had woven for him out of twinned cables. The cloak sheds heat when heat needs shedding and hoards it when you must hoard. He wore it like it was his last piece of home.

“Report,” he said.

“Heat front is throwing two kilometers long. Closer to four in some downdrafts.”

“How long?”

He was thirty-five but had carry-lines in his face like someone older, skin drawn tight along high bones, eyes that never learned soft. He had been born on the same crawler he now commanded. This world, one of the older caravans liked to say, makes us into knives and then asks us what we meant to cut.

“Two hours, maybe less. The stewpot on our right is coughing like a smoker. We’ll be peppered.”

“Gear our flanks,” he said to Jao. “Drop the mudskirts. I want the treads dredging low.”

Jao slid down like a bead on a string, throat alight. He likes orders when he gets to fulfill them with his hands. Heleda’s laugh rolled up from the long line where the engine crew lives like a bell dragged along rough stone. She and her three grandsons called themselves the Firelegs—they tended the crawler’s heat exchangers, the heart of our body, the boots she walks on. She has one eye milk-white from a fall; the other shines.

“You want the skirts?” she hollered up. “You should ask their mother.”

“The skirts,” the Captain said. He does not do hollers. He throws the same words in a tight line and expects physics to carry them. “Now.”

Heleda’s one good eye twinkled. She loves him like a son and likes to make him fret like one. “Now, now,” she said, to mock the double, then clacked her tongue at her grandchildren. In a minute the crawler shuddered as panels on both sides shook free of their nested housings and fell into place, stiff rubberized canvas rimmed with the flexible bones of old printer frames.

The sheep—our two rag lines of sand-chewers, all horns and patience—were hitched behind the last wheel teams. They don’t mind heat much. They knit the silicon beneath our feet into something they can use. They breathe oxygen from rocks and shit glass. Their coats grow like splinters. They are ugly and perfect, and Jao loves them. He’d wrap himself in the harm itchy blankets we spin from their coats and refuse to admit that the itch was why the younger Singers would always pick my bunk over his when they wanted a story.

“Have you got a bead on the Quiet?” the Captain asked me softly when the bustle actually started moving around us. He always gives me the quiet question when his hands want something to squeeze.

“It’s right,” I said. “The first breath tells you. The heavy pull.”

“And the dust?”

“Still.” I wanted to be sure. I pressed the spear to the ridge of my collarbone, where the deep nerves branch. It made my tongue prickle. “Still.”

He looked past me toward brightward, eyes narrowed. There’s a new scar along his left forearm. A ribbon of bubbled skin. He took it two weeks ago when we misjudged an edge flare from the star and a coronal belch kissed the runsweeps. He put himself between heat and child because that’s what he believes captains are for.

“It will be over fast,” he said. “Quiets come and go. People like to make them drama.”

“People like to tell a story,” I said. “Stories go down easier than what you give them.”

That got me the corner of his mouth bent up, a private thing. He used to bring me fruit when we were children and steal my beads. We are still children by the measure of the elders. When the elders die, a new measure must be made, and I am not sure we will be equal to it. He drew his cloak closer and glanced at Hani, the second singer, where she knelt by the lower hatch with her own spear braced between her boots. Hani is older and mostly good at chewing younger mouths into behaving.

I opened my own mouth to say his name. Say, There is a voice in the dust.

A cheer rose up from the midline. It came from a group of tinny voices that had not learned Quiets are an edger’s game. Not the elders. Not even the adults. A cluster of children had ducked the rule of their guardians and pressed their faces to the clear plates of the belly viewports. Each of those plates is a dark circle set into the spine; they let you see the ground like small moons. Any shock will crack them. In Quiet, you should be lying still enough to be mistaken for equipment. I started to say their names to shame them down.

Then I saw what they were seeing.

Darkward, where the world is black velvet stitched with cold stars, the edge storms had jerked into a motion we never see. It started like an opening of a fist: the black wall—its color from ground-dust thrown so high it erases the sky’s red—puckered and then ringed itself around a new darkness, like a throat swallowing. Nothing like that is supposed to happen. It’s a child’s drawing to call a storm an animal, but when it turned its eye toward us, in one twist of the roiling, we all had animal words in our heads. The old ones sometimes talk about the oceans they lost when they left their first home. I thought of a wave cresting.

“Hold,” the Captain whispered, and the word ran down the spine, spine into bones, bones into treads.

The dust did not move. It sang my name again. It did it like it was testing its own tongue.

Bright eye, it said. West and down.

West is the wrong word on a world like ours. We make directions out of things we have lost. West and down are where the stewpot fields are not. West and down are where the heat fell heavier last season and made a run of slick air that the moth-sails from Caravans Two and Four rode like calm water.

West and down is brightward.

Down is into the stew.

“What?” Jao breathed. His hand was on my arm and a little too tight for talk.

“Nothing.” If you say a quiet thing aloud, it stops being what it is. Also, I did not want twenty-seven heads turning toward me all at once.

There was something else in the tone, under my name and the phrase it had chosen, something like the scrape of stone against stone. A sequence. A pattern. Numbers lulled into a chant. I gritted my teeth. The pitch shifted with each syllable, and I saw the world behind my eyes as a grid laid over what the spear could feel: the long injuries of the convection lane ahead, the safer canyon the Captain had chosen to snake into—see? I can lay lines of caution with the rest of them—and the little cluster of stewpots to our right: not little. A field. A rib of the world where heat broke from below, punched into air, and didn’t care if bodies were in its way.

West and down. That tone held direction in the way a willow holds rain: quietly and without showing the strain.

The Quiet ended with a click. Everyone who has heard it knows it is not anything as simple as a click. This was my grandmother’s joke, telling me as a child that the end of Quiet is like somebody clipping a thread between your fingers. The truth is you feel a rush. Your spine hands itself back to you. The dust floods into the narrow corridors of charge that we use for talk; the beads in our mouths chime. The first thing always is a hiss of overlap as every other caravan that was holding its breath speaks at once.

“Mara,” said Hani, our second, down the clean new sword of a channel. “You have overwatch. Go.” She had seen the children. She had seen, maybe, the way my shoulders knotted. Hani sees too much, even when the sky is loud.

“Check,” I said, and the bead clicked in my teeth with the assent code. I switched my spear back to the Chorus fork and let the old comfort roll in: the choir of us and ours, the long exhale as if the world had been standing on a cliff and now had decided not to jump.

It was in the middle of that relief that the sky spoke again, not through our channels but around them, a plumbline dropped through the noise. It said: This is Earth. It said a number. It said: Hello, Mariam.

No one calls me that. People pretend that’s my name on birth papers because Elder Sarai liked the way it sounded when she called me out of a sleeping stack for petty tasks. My mother would laugh at that and tilt my head into her hip, fingers in my hair, and say the short form only she could use. The voice in the dust had not heard those fights. The voice had correct bookkeeping and the gravity of a city I’ve never seen.

Earth is a word with religious weight. I felt the Captain’s attention like somebody had folded a hand around the back of my neck and squeezed.

“Say that again,” he said, in my ear and in the bead, quiet as an apology.

I did not have to. The dust had the drama we denied it. It began to whistle in the Chorus frequencies we keep free for emergency. Hani hissed in a breath; she had caught it too. So had three other Singers, all brightward caravans, none darkward. That was not right. The Chorus is local to the dust above you. If the dust is speaking across four caravans, it is using something we don’t know. It is running a note through a throat it should not have.

“This is Earth,” it said again, and then: “Mariam Qadri. With coordinates. Repeat. Brightward rim, lahar field, vent cluster forty-seven. West-by-down.”

Behind me, Heleda’s grandsons muttered a prayer, the one meant to keep machines honest. The Captain swore once, simply and tidy, as if he were cutting a rope.

Our map-bone is a long screen that folds like a fan from a slot along the nest’s left wall. I breathed on it and it woke, its black surface blooming with color in the exact shape of the ground our treads had bitten in the last hour. I spread two fingers; it widened. Hani’s coordinate marker pulsed bright where our white line slalomed between stewpot fields. I pulled west and down in the map’s language, thumbed a vector. It burned hotter red over a cluster of vents that none of our last-rotation charts had flagged as active. We don’t go there because heat there is extravagant and the ground shelves into old melted channels. You get a sink there and the Crawlstar will wear it to her grave.

“It’s a trap,” Hani said, on open line. “Tell it your mother’s name. See if it can guess.”

The dust chose not to answer her. It is wise that way, sometimes. Or deaf. The children had stopped pressing their faces to the viewports. Heleda herded them back, just with that voice of hers, that says: If you do not come, the ground will open and eat you, and I will not pull you back out. She has pulled back too many not to be believed.

The Captain raised his eyes to mine. “Do you know this voice?”

“I know the word it uses for me.”

“Mariam,” he said. He almost never does that. He is one of those who thinks names are as sacred as clean water. He uses the ones I’ve given, the ones I’ve refused.

My tongue stuck to the roof of my mouth. I slid the bead sideways and bit down hard enough to get copper. “I don’t know any voice from Earth,” I said, slower than my heart. “I don’t know Earth like a place. I know it like a story.”

“We’re not going to vent cluster forty-seven,” Heleda said, as if that was the stupidest debate to be had. “We’ll burn the skirts off the Crawlstar and I’ll have to knit her new ones from my own hair.”

Jao, who worships heat, had the look he gets when a cliff says jump and the wind says maybe it will carry you if you lean just so.

Hani said: “I’ll stake my beads that brightward caravans Four and Five are thinking about it.”

As if she had called them up by name, their signals popped into our near channels like excited birds. Four’s pilot graced us with a stream of talk that could have meant Are you hearing this? or I am already rolling or the names of his last three lovers, the way he goes. Five’s Captain, who is an aged woman of zero humor, said: Singer Hani. Confirm. Coordinates. We heard Earth. We heard a code.

That was the stone-on-stone I had guessed at in the tone: a code built of pulses, periods, phases. The shape of old Earth talk, the one they say their stations used when they threw voices through vacuum to listen for echoes. We don’t use it much. Our dust doesn’t like it; it prefers hooks and loops, harmonics and patience.

“It’s wrong,” said Heleda. “Do not thumb your nose at a wrong that comes from the sky. It has teeth you do not see.”

I should have agreed. That is one of the rules to get as old as Heleda: when the old warn, listen. But the dust was still humming that place-name in my head, and under the dread something else had started to pump into my veins, not courage, not even curiosity that is a cousin to courage, but something more petty, more young: the fierce itch of a mystery putting its hand on your neck. I am not the last of anything or the first of anything, I told myself the way I have since I started to follow wind by feel and not by meter. I can lay my ear down and hear trains a kilometer away. I can tell you the weight of rain by the way my knee hurts in the hour before. I can sense the start of a dust shear just by the mood of the sheep. But this—this is something that knows my name from a place I’ve only had as rumor.

“Captain,” I said.

He looked at me. He did not say my name this time. He waited.

“I can go,” I said. “Not the Crawlstar. A light rig. One coil to brightward, down the shelf, to the rim. Two hours out. Two back. I can take Jao.”

“No,” Heleda and Hani said in the same instant. Jao said, “Yes,” because he has never said no to anything that looks like a bad idea he can hold in both hands and grin over.

“Absolutely not,” Heleda said again, in case anyone had missed her meaning. “You are not taking my wheel team.”

“She is not your wheel team,” Jao said. “She is my sister.”

“That is worse,” Heleda said. “Blood makes you stupid twice.”

Four had stopped wisecracks. Five sent a private whisper to me: If this is Earth, Singer, and if they have a thing that can speak in Quiet, then we must touch it or we have to admit we live in a ghost’s stomach. If it is not Earth, if it is our own dust learning a new trick, we must still touch it. Or we will be ashamed that we flinched.

I do not love Five’s Captain. She called me green for a full year because I told her a crosswind was going to be mild and it was not, and we broke a bird-sail, and she used one of her own as a patch, and it stank. But she is right more often than she is unkind.

“We can’t go as a full,” the Captain said. “We won’t tank heat on a hunch.”

“It’s not a hunch,” I said, and hated the waver in my voice. “It spoke my full. My mother’s name for me. It was never in any registry.”

“Child,” Heleda said, and the single word had salt in it. “You think the Chorus does not know your nicknames? You think every elder who had a flirtation did not shout them into the dust to see who would echo them back?”

“It is possible to set a voice at a distance,” Hani said, thoughtful now instead of sharp. “But in Quiet? It is not just wrong, elder. It is new.”

“It could be trap by the dark caravans,” someone in the midline muttered. “Make us roll to bright, burn us. Then they take our sheep.”

“Darkward has its own hazards,” the Captain said. He didn’t even turn his head to answer the mutterer. “We trade with them when the lanes allow.”

“Because we have to,” the mutterer said, too soft for the Captain to scold.

The dust did not wait for our consensus. It spoke again, and this time it did not use my name first. It used a construction that no one in our caravans has used for as long as I’ve been old enough to listen. It said: For verification, prove identity with family phrase.

There was a pause that held in it the past and the future and a fist around a throat. I had not told anyone the phrase. It is what my mother said into my ear when the world was too bright and my body too loud and I could not stand the way dust feels like a living thing on skin, the way it swarms, the way it takes sound into itself and returns it thinner. It is a nonsense phrase. It is the point at which you cannot argue with yourself that everything is normal anymore.

“Mara,” Hani whispered, soft and new-mother gentle. “What did your mother say? You can lie to the dust and to us and to yourself, and you can tell it a different phrase, if you like, and then you can go down to your sleeping stack, and you can pretend that the world did not just speak to you in a way we do not have words for.”

I did not want to. That was the smallest true thing I have ever known.

I swallowed. The copper taste was gone, and in its place the taste of the earth of a place I have never seen rolled up in my mouth, a taste like a city, like rebar under concrete, like sweet fruit burst in fingers. I said: “Hands to the ear. Heart to the sand. Little coil, little star.”

I have never said it aloud in full voice since the day she died.

The dust sang back to me the thing my own mother used to sing when I could not sleep. It got it right. It said: Confirmed.

Then it put a new thread into the Chorus, and this time even the elders who pretend their bones antedate all of our devices heard it and stiffened. It sent an image through the skim: a map that no one had drawn for a generation, with names that have become sacred in their absence, points marked that corresponded to places we circle in our maps with red lines and don’t cross. It showed a doorway where the vent cluster is, west and down, in the mouth of heat. It showed—if the pixels can be believed—the white bone of a structure buried under glass that our instruments have always told us is just stone.

On my tongue the bead chimed three times for urgent and three more for nonsense, and then it shut itself down in the old behavior our beads have when they are told something that is bigger than their makers thought they would ever have to hold.

“Captain,” Five said, not to him, not to me, but to the space in which we both existed. “We will go.”

“Two is going,” said Four.

Heleda swore in her mother’s language and spat over the rail, a waste of water she would beat any child for.

The Captain’s hand found the rail by my head. Not rough. Not kind. Simple. Which is what he is. He did not look at me, and somehow that made the choice harder, not easier.

“Fine,” he said. “We’re not losing this. Not to Four. Not to Five.” He has pride for our line that he thinks is invisible. It is not. “We go. Not as full. A coil, yes. Your coil, Mara. Take Jao. Take Hani. Take the second runner. Name me a path that does not eat us.”

My mouth opened. Closed. The dust whispered nothing new and everything changed. Hani glanced at me and then at Jao, and her mouth did that tiny tight purse it does when she plans to allow somebody a thing she will hold over them later. Heleda threw up her hands to make a shape between us that was supposed to be a ward and looked like surrender.

I raised the spear to my shoulder and laid my forehead to its shaft. The ground ahead was worse than any map. The stew pots will throw. The vent field will spit. The heat will break over us and maybe break us.

West and down, said the dust, with what felt almost like patience. Bright eye.

“Path,” I said, and the bead said: Ready, in its small blind way.

I mapped it and then I gave it a name that I have never given a path before, a ridiculous, childish piece of blasphemy that made Jao snort a laugh even as his hands twitched for the grips: I called it Earth.

Chapter One

The ring sings when it wants blood. You learn to hear it: a dry grain-whisper along the hull, rising from dust hiss into a low glass edge, like a finger pressed too hard to a wineglass rim. The pitch tells you what to tighten, what to throttle back, whether your luck will hold.

I listened without meaning to, one hand on the magline, boots braced in the cradle of my skiff’s forward pylons while the quick little thrusters ticked and whispered. The gas giant took up half the sky, its banded belly smeared with thunder. We were all tethered to it, in one way or another. There was an aurora spilling down its night limb, a curtain of teal and fierce white.

“Wind’s five minutes out.” Hollow’s voice was small and soft in my ear, synthetic but with the burr I’d tuned into it over years. It was in my suit and in the skiff’s cabin and in the bead of transparent plastic lodged under my skin: my only constant crew. “Eastward radial. Gusting. We should anchor.”

“We are anchored,” I said. I glanced at the magline, that steel-blue cable the width of my wrist that tethered the Needle to the ring’s slow river. It was hooked to a dock’s dead-beat anchor spire on a scrap island of ice, and tension made it sing. The salvage code said it wasn’t an anchor until your hull had taken one full spin of the ring while attached. I’d never met a code that had saved a life. Threads saved lives. Tethers. Predictions. Listening.

“Then we should reel in,” Hollow said, slightly peeved. It did that to keep me company.

“I see our ghost,” I told it. “Two degrees starboard. Twenty meters deeper.”

Hollow angled the LIDAR sensors and the skiff’s cockpit HUD sketched a scattering of dots in pale green across my vision. The ring itself was a tireless river of ice cobbles and dust and old machinery: shattered survey satellites, fragments of long-ago ore tasters, wave-shredded construction struts from the days when humans first banded the planet because they thought it would be a miracle and not a job. Now there were millions of us, living on the habitats that tumbled in that glare and made a ragged crown around the world, eating the harvested water, breathing air pulled from steam, trading the same old stories on a thousand different frequencies.

“Ghost has strange edges,” Hollow said. “Spectral returns are too neat. Hull? Or…mimic? No, not with that albedo.”

I rolled my shoulders against the suit’s weight and clicked a drone into life. It wriggled loose from the skiff’s belly and unfolded into four little limbs and a coil of sensor like a whisker. It had a name too, painted in chips on its flank: Whisker, because some days my imagination ran dry before breakfast. It scuttled into the ring like a crab slipping from a net, delicate thrusters fluttering.

“Keep it tight,” I said. “No tangles.”

“I keep reminding you, that’s what I’m for,” Hollow said. “Three minutes on the wind.”

I lazily started reeled us in anyway, not because Hollow was right (Hollow is never right; that’s our game) but because a line full of snapping harmonics is no way to die.

“Is this one of those days where you’ve decided you are tired of this and would prefer to arrive home in multiple pieces?” Hollow asked.

“Don’t jinx.” My ribs were sore from yesterday’s haul, when I’d dragged a half-disintegrated solar kite out of a pinch zone and it had kicked like an enormous fish as I tried to net it. I still had the bite of the harness printed into my skin, a faint wash of bruise at my collarbone.

The ghost was there, in the scatter, a geometry that was too regular to be ice, too quiet to be a streaming latch. It slid bright as a fish and then dimmer, as if something were flexing light around it.

“Angle nine degrees, notch the thrusters,” I said.

Hollow did it, finetuning on my breath and on the little muscle twitches the bead under my skin could read. Whisker drifted closer, its camera pivoting. The ghost grew in greyscale on the HUD and in the next breath it stepped out of things, not scattering light but full-throated with it.

It was a skiff. It was a skiff I knew.

I didn’t think that, not at first. Recognition is slower than you expect. It comes in flavors: the shape-of-it, the weight-of-it, the snapshot-of-a-knot-in-a-strap that your hands know better than your head does. She emerged from the ring as if tipped up on a platter, a dark little crescent of engine and cockpit nested to twin booms, thruster bells scabbed with pale carbon frost. One pylon was damaged—no, not damaged; patched, with a square of violet composite that I had cut myself from the guts of a wrecked hauler because it had been the only thing that would fit onto the Needle when she mangled her footing thrashing in a jet stream two months ago. The violet square had a crack that I did not remember. On her nose was a smear of hand oil exactly where my glove had always left it, a darker sheen on the grey. Her nameplate had been half-pried free once, when someone tried to rob me and only managed to shuck off the letters Nee. I still write NEE in grease pencil over it so I don’t have to listen to all the jokes.

Whisker’s camera drifted along the hull and fixed like a fly on the portside pylon. There, under the seam, was a scrape as thin as a hair. I’d only put that there last week.

“Hollow,” I said. I sounded very far away, even to myself. “Read the transponder.”

I could feel Hollow reaching out, like a shiver down my arm.

“Silent,” it said. For once there was nothing frivolous in its voice. “No broadcast. Passive only. Shielded. Mara… That’s your signature block.”

“It can’t be,” I said, which was a stupid thing to say because there it was.

We drifted like swimmers. The magline hummed under my palms and the taste of metal rose in my mouth. The ring sang a thinner note, then steadied. The wind that Hollow had predicted began to build, not air-wind but the coupling of magnet and dust, the little electrostatic tides that could shove a skiff sideways if you didn’t watch them.

“You said there were imprints in the ring,” Hollow said, because if it couldn’t think of a joke it could at least think of an argument. “Old trajectories, folded places where the field lines do strange things. I have told you for five years to treat such stories as stories.”

“And yet here we are,” I said. “Whisker?”

Whisker latched, magnet toes finding edges to cling to. It crawled along the hull with embarrassing familiarity. It found the belly hatch and blinked its beacon once.

“Pressure reads a whisper,” Hollow reported. “Eight kPa. There’s frost along the joints.”

“That’s practically homey,” I said.

I reeled us in the last of the way and bumped the Needle’s nose into the twin pylon cradle of her sister so gently I didn’t sound the hull alarms. The skiffs were a matched pair for a breath. It felt like looking at two stills from a film, one a fraction of a second after the other.

I fitted the umbilical cuffs, watched the seals set, and then crawled hand-over-hand along my own hull until I was sitting with my boots on my own ghost’s flank. The ring slid in a cold spangle under me. The gas giant’s aurora cracked.

“Do you want to call Control?” Hollow asked me abruptly. There were always a dozen voices you could pick out of a background else-chatter: Control at Ringdock Cline, the salvage net, the moorings’ friendly channel. Kade would be on duty today. Kade would pick up the call with a laugh you could pour like tea.

“No,” I said. “Not yet.”

“You could assign salvage rights,” Hollow pressed, with a theatrical lawyer’s pucker. “Say the words that would make this ours. Of all the foolish things.”

“Of all the foolish things,” I said, and opened the hatch.

I was breathing too fast. When you’re in a suit you can hear your blood in your teeth. There was a little exhale as the pressure equalized across the seal. The interior light was out, but in the faint magnet glow and the starlit wash the cockpit was a familiar skeleton. The pilot’s cradle. The scarf that I had stitched with red thread across the headrest to make it mine. The little rack of yellow tags that held the spare filters. A smear of grease on the third switch from the left.

Something else too, something that did not belong: a small red case, buckled to the deck by a harness line, right in the footwell where no sane person would tether a thing. I bumped against it with my boot. It thunked, solid. The buckles were new. The case was the kind you use for doors you never want to hack—with wafer chips embedded and a ceramic core that could survive a fire.

“Mara,” Hollow said. “Do you see—”

“I see it,” I said. I reached for the filters and found exactly three, one with the corner bent like a dog’s ear. I touched the scarf. I touched the scar on the cradle where I had once dropped a wrench and chipped the composite.

There was a little crackle in my ear. Not our channel. Not Control, not the net. Not anything I could name. Just a warm cough of static and then a voice, my voice, so close to my own I thought I had spoken without knowing. It said:

“If you’re hearing this, it means the shear came early.”

I froze. The ring went on singing. Hollow said nothing at all.

“You won’t want to sit down,” my voice said. “Do it anyway. And keep your suit on. I tried this without gear the first time and regretted it.”

I folded into the pilot’s cradle because the speech had the same cadence, the little dry lilt, the thing that is only yours. I strapped one strap across my shoulder because my muscle memory did it for me. I put my boot against the red case because I wanted to, to prove that it was there.

“I know you have questions,” my voice said. “There isn’t time. You have less of it than I did, if the way the currents have been behaving is any indication. Listen to me. Things you know: don’t call Control. Don’t tell Kade. Don’t blurt this on the net. Someone is listening who has no business doing so and you don’t know them yet. Hello, Sable. Try not to smile.”

My breath stopped in my throat. That name had no place here. Sable was a contact from a year in my life I never told the ring. Sable was a shadow, a rumor passed down the moorings at the spines of my childhood: a fixer with an old pilot’s collar, cigarette out-the-side-of-her-mouth, eyes like augers. She bought futures with chips no one else knew about. I had met Sable exactly once and then made lifelong habits out of not thinking about it.

“You’ve already noticed what you’re sitting in,” my voice said in my ear. “Yes. It’s the Needle. It is also not. Everyone’s going to have an opinion about that later. For now: there’s a cascade coming. The magnetopause will flare and throw the ring into a shade-state that even the old timers won’t recognize. The salvage code will die for a week. People will float who have never floated. And there is something in that flare that isn’t just field. It’s seeded. They have been seeding it in the outer line with the drive dirigibles. Don’t look for their brand. You won’t find a logo. Look for the parts that are too uniform. Find Naris on Spindle Nine and say salt-flowers. He’ll tell you who bought his silence.”

The channel hissed. The voice in my ear was breathing. I was breathing. Hollow had not said my name again, because it had learned when not to.

“I only figured out one thing,” my voice said, smaller now. “You’ll get your wave before mine. That’s why you have a chance to move where I didn’t. I’m going to leave you something—don’t open it here. Don’t open it until you’re on the far side of the skin and the wind is quiet. It screws with the lines. I know you will touch it anyway. I did. You’ll tell yourself you’re different from me. You’re not. I’m so sorry.”

I looked down. The red case pressed against my boot as if it might bruise me. There was a marker scrawl across the buckles. It said in my handwriting: IF FOUND: ASSUME THIS IS A WEAPON.

I laughed, a high sharp thing, because a weapon was the last thing I ever brought into the ring. Task hooks, cutting saw, a spool of silk line, a lunch that was two-thirds sugar, sure. A weapon was for a different kind of life.

“I have to go,” my voice said. “They’re knocking.”

The channel cut. It didn’t fade. It was midsentence and then it was gone.

“Mara,” Hollow said then, as if we had both been underwater. “That is your voice.”

“It’s a fake,” I said. I needed it to be, tilt it like that toward a safe angle.

Hollow ignored me for once. “I am reading motion. I am reading magnet churn beyond the long horizon above your head. Small, in the hundred-meter scale. Bigger things too. The wind is early.”

My tongue tasted like coin metal again. The ring’s hum shifted. The magline’s harmonics went from a bright C to a flatter note that I did not have a name for.

“Whisker,” I said. The drone clung like a burr to the exterior. The little light on its back blinked once: cheerful, oblivious, the way I had programmed it, because sometimes you choose what loves you back.

In the pocket beyond the cockpit, the storage where I kept the spare heat blankets and the bag of microwave noodles I had not eaten in two years because I thought I might want them someday, a small light flickered. It found my eyes like a tap on the wrist.

The small light was the internal transponder—my transponder—waking like a firefly because my suit had passed nearby with a signature it knew. It showed three dots: me, the hull, and a third tag, almost too faint to read.

For a heartbeat my stomach got up and walked away for a life of its own.

“There’s someone—” Hollow began.

The hatch behind me shuddered.

I know how things sound in vacuum. That knowledge is under my fingernails. You can’t hear a knock unless you are touching what’s being knocked upon. I was. The hatch quivered against my boot. Three deliberate hits, as if someone had found a spot with a palm and tapped.

Nobody knocks on a skiff out here. You ping a suit channel. You flash a light. You keep a distance you can survive.

I put my gloved hand to the hatch. Through the glove through the hatch was a human rhythm. Tap-tap…tap. A pause. Again.

“Don’t move,” Hollow said suddenly.

“Why?”

“There’s an echo in the signal,” it said. “I can’t parse it. But it came with the knock.”

The tap came one more time, steady as a metronome. Then, through the old emergency panel that I had never bothered to remove because it was riveted on the first day and the rivets were cheaper than my patience, a voice bled into the skiff, small and hungry and matching my throat’s cadence so perfectly I wanted to be sick.

“Mara,” it said. “Open. Please.”

I was a child at the moorings again, playing under the spines with the other kids, letting our hands skate along frost cables that could take your fingers off if the field spiked. My mother taught me to tie a line so that it would hold you if you were pulled in two directions by a flood. I had been pulled in two directions since I was old enough to choose what to want.

“Say something,” Hollow said in my ear. It was trying to be calm. It sounded like a kettle simmering.

“What would you like me to say?” I asked. My mouth was dry. “Hello, me. You look terrible. This is awkward.”

The knocking stopped.

The wind came early like my voice had promised, and the ring didn’t so much shudder as ripple, as if something that was not water had become liquid and was pausing to decide what to do with us. The aurora’s line doubled in the sky. The magline sang.

“Brace,” Hollow said. “Please brace. I don’t even have to say it, you’re already braced, I know, but say that you are stupidly for my peace of mind.”

“I’m braced,” I said.

I put my palm flat to the hatch. Cold came through the glove like teeth.

“Who are you?” I asked.

The answer came with the lag of any suit-to-suit patch with no proper handshake: a slow syrupy two seconds that stretched and pulled.

“You,” the voice said. “Now please. You get one chance. You don’t get the better one that I got. You’re not going to like that. Open the hatch, Mara.”

I had spent my life with warnings. You get born into the ring, you learn that warnings are not proverbs; they are instruments. Don't step on the yellow line. Don't dismount while the spindle is moving. Don't glance back at a mooring and imagine it will always be there when you want it. I have dodged warnings like they were bad weather. I have also clung to them like they were rope.

Behind my head the red case bumped against the cradle once, very gently, as if whatever was inside it had turned over in sleep.

“Don’t,” Hollow said, so soft no one who didn’t know Hollow would have heard it as a plea.

The never-lit sunlight came over us like a God we hadn’t hired, and the ring shed a thousand motes of dust into a shimmer that made the skiff’s skin itch under my palms. I could see the habitations across the curve of the ring like beads on a broken string—Spindle Nine a dark spindle, Cline a long spindle with ships lined up like teeth. If I opened the hatch, a dozen new stories would begin and I would be the kind of person they were about. If I didn’t, then I was some other person.

My hand moved without talking to me. I undogged the wheel. The seal hissed like breath drawn for the first time. I cracked the hatch.

Cry air poured in, freezing and thin, scented of metal and that slightly sweet dead scent that even the best scrubbers never take out entirely. Through the little gap I saw a face in the dark, a slick white oval under a patchy helmet, visor spiderwebbed and blind. It tilted and caught a wash of aurora light, blue slid across bone. I saw my own mouth, the notch of scar on the upper lip that I had gotten pulling wire as a child and falling into it face first.

“I came earlier,” said my voice with my mouth, and it was raw, frayed. “I came earlier and it wasn’t enough. For you it might be. There’s a ship on a slow arc into the ring. You’ll want it and you can’t have it. Not without the case. Not without Naris. Not without—”

The wind hit the magline and the skiff shuddered. The hatch slammed into my palm hard enough to spark pain up my forearm. Above us the gas giant rolled its belly and every salvage alarm on the net went off all at once: a bright rising peal, a shiver down the length of the ring like laughter in a dead city.

I had already made my decision in the second before pain, before the alarms, before Hollow could say anything else. I did not even tell myself I had.

I pulled the hatch all the way open. The other me fell forward into my arms like something I had lost at the bottom of the river and only now remembered had been mine.

The babies were on the ceiling when Naima got the call.

She was two blocks away, knee-deep in the Hinge, where gravity went cheap and the city slouched between one paid-for curve and the next. It was a Tuesday, which meant Meridian Systems had de-tuned a few alleys to cover a midweek invoice—you could always tell by the way the pigeons forgot how to land and the tourists from Uptown took spills, clutching coffees as if the cups had stopped believing in bottom. Naima had a coil of carbon filament over one shoulder and a splice kit on her hip, hair braided tight and threaded with copper so her collar could read her pulse. She had leveled three shopfronts that morning and set a 0.97g over a kitchen where old man Simic weighed out spices like tiny moons. The Hinge would keep its feet until Friday.

Her collar buzzed a second channel to the bone. Hospital, her dispatcher's voice said, without hello or apology. Memorial District. NICU. The line for the coordinates lit red, a string of numbers that detailed a place she knew from childhood immunizations and her mother’s gallbladder surgery. Ceiling adhesion in effect. They’ve strapped the incubators. Meridian won’t authorize a hard reboot—there’s a lien on the block.

“I don’t care about the lien,” Naima said, and swung the coil off her shoulder. A kid on a scooter dragged himself along a railing beside her, cheeks pale, feet kicking in the syrup of almost-weightlessness.
