The Hinge was doing that jittery thing it did when the Lattice above them hiccuped—a silvered haze in the air you felt in your inner ear, a sorry hum in fillings and old knees. The whole district was a net of rented gravity, stitched into the mega-structure of skytowers by software most people never saw except when it failed. Naima saw it everywhere, in the way rain fell in long parenthesis and smoke curled without lifting.

“Sending you the override,” the dispatcher said. “We need an anchor in five.”

“I’m three out,” Naima lied, already running.

She knew where Memorial was by the birds. In a city calibrated to the mean, birds reclaimed the honest red of wind and wing near hospitals and river stations, drawn to the humming nodes that promised steady pull. She saw a circling storm of gulls aligned to nothing, their arcs eccentric, a wheel with a broken spoke, and cut into Palace Street without touching the pavement. She let the Hinge lift her as she went low, feinting past a couple locked together in a zero-slow walk, side-stepped a rolling cart that had inexplicably decided it was a balloon, caught a hand-thrown loaf from a baker whose counter had gone treacherously light and threw it back with extra heft. Someone shouted her name; the Hinge knew her face the way any neighborhood knew the people who kept the lights on and the floor steady.

When the shock doors of Memorial thumped open for her, the smell of antiseptic hit like a chemical reality check. There is no smell to gravity, but when it’s wrong it bends the world until air acquires the taste of wrongness: tin and gauze and the copper lick of panic.

“Qadir!” a nurse called, green cap stained with sweat. “They’re strapped, but we’ve got blood pooling. We can’t keep it down.”

“I’ve got you,” Naima said, because you said that even when you didn’t. She looked up and fucking there they were, five incubators adjoining a ceiling grid like cocoons snagged in a web. A sixth had swung on its straps, cracked—someone had caught it with a ladder and a heroic length of surgical tape. Tiny bodies shifted inside, floating in the clear antiseptic world of their making. A doctor with a lot of hair and no patience looked about to climb the wall.

“What’s your source?” Naima asked.

“Meridian pulled us to ninety last night,” the nurse said. “We got a warning that the default somewhere upstream was going to hit our curve. We’re running on campus generator but the g-lift doesn’t care. It went one-ten at five a.m. Last twenty minutes we’ve had these zeros and ones. Ping-pong. Janitorial took a fall in the stairwell, broke a wrist. I need you to set us at one. I don’t care if you have to haul mass in in wheelbarrows.”

“I don’t move mass in wheelbarrows,” Naima said. “I move your space.” She pulled the harmonizer from her bag, clicked it open. It looked like nothing so much as an ancient concertina, all pleated metal and black rubber, but it wasn’t music it played so much as silence. Meridian issued them in matte gray and told them not to call it an instrument. You were to think of it as an interface, as a tool. Naima strapped it to her chest anyway, because the body remembered the way to hold something alive, and pulling a district back into shape required the same bone-deep steadiness as a song.

As she calibrated, the clinic-internal gravity unit thrummed a mechanical protest. Its tiny pearl of exotic matter, leased by the gram, was never meant to carry a ward when the city’s big Lattice lines redirected. The hospital had paid for redundancy, but redundancy didn’t help if someone upstream had coded your lot for a lien. Meridian’s software was supposed to cascade the burden across a dozen small districts so no one corner took the hit. The software also obeyed rules that had very little to do with safety when invoices didn’t clear. The law had been written that way.

Naima didn’t waste breath cursing Meridian. She’d contracted with them at eighteen because she was good with her hands and better with her head, and because their hazard pay was real, and because she was born in a place where you learned to stand in doorways when the world rocked. She would fix it and then she would go yell at someone in a blue suit. She slotted a tether into the ward’s pinboard—a matte triangle that hid a data river—and asked the Lattice to show her where it hurt.

It showed her a map of invisible faultlines, all the points where the city’s curves met and pretended to be smooth. She saw Memorial’s campus lit like a ruddy heart, steady and brave, and above it the g-lines that should have made a cathedral of invisible ribs, all of them molting and shimmering like lit silk in rain. Something upstream was pinging them with a waveform that didn’t belong, and the waveform tasted like debt. Naima didn’t have to see a lien notice: she could read it in the way the Lattice vectorized the block, in the way a little grisette of code stuck out of a boundary fence like a warning flag, in the flicker that said if this were your account, we’d flip you to Outer Marker service right now.

She did not, under any circumstances, have authorization to override a lien. She did it anyway. The override code from dispatch opened a thin door, and she put her foot in it, the harmonizer’s plates sucking at her palms as she dialed in a counter-curve. She imagined she was flipping Memorial upside down: a child shaking a snow globe, making the flakes of blood and saline settle. The harmonizer thrummed and the world flexed.

The nurse went quiet, watching the centimeter-thick flow of crimson in a suction line become what it had always wanted to be—a line, not a column. Somewhere metal groaned. The doctor with the hair grabbed a ladder and monkey-climbed to an incubator and did something quick and precise that made the baby inside pinken up. The night-shift janitor, wrist in a sloppy splint, sagged against a wall and said, heartfelt, “Thank Christ.”

Naima felt the harmonizer argue with her, bellows resisting the pull. She sweated until her collar thew a trickle down her neck and into the copper thread, and then she felt it: the fall smooth out. The ward’s curve drifted over her like a warm palm smoothing bedclothes. She glanced at the ceiling; the incubators were no longer trying to become stars. They hung like pendulums, learned their lesson, and came home.

“Hold it,” the nurse said. “Hold it, hold it, hold—”

“I’m here,” Naima said, through her teeth. “But I’ve got spill. The g-load’s going to dump somewhere else on campus unless I route it. Your ORs? Your imaging? Where can you afford to feel light-headed?”

The nurse looked like Naima had asked which of her fingers she wanted to lose. A fluorescent light fizzed, distorting, and sloughed its casing. Naima caught it with a hand that wasn’t free and pushed it back into its bracket, because magicians are just fast janitors with a different salary structure.

“Evac the cafeteria,” the nurse said. “If they’re not already. Route it there. We can mop up soup.”

Naima coded in the cafeteria as a sink. The harmonizer didn’t like it. The Lattice didn’t like that she was shaving values from a line flagged for corporate review. Somewhere, some screen in the Meridian Oversight Office threw a polite, well-coded tantrum. Naima felt the pushback in the way her hands began to vibrate. No.

“Qadir,” her collar said. “Meridian says to stand down. They’re sending a tech.”

“I am a tech,” she said. “They can send three. We’re holding now.” The harmonizer sang its subsonic disagreeing. Underneath that, something else had begun to hum.

It wasn’t the hospital’s generator. It wasn’t the harmonic of the Lattice lines, which could be as comforting as a train or as sickening as a missed stair. Naima had learned to tune those with her heartbeat, to ride them the way surfers rode old videos on her mother’s phone. This was lower, older, and it rolled under the normal structure of things like a whale song under rain. She would have dismissed it as her nerves if the ward’s wheeled rack of monitors hadn’t all started scrolling the same nonsense digits.

“Do you see that?” the hairy doctor said. “Is your machine doing that?”

“My machine is doing what I tell it to,” Naima said, on principle. She looked at the nonsense, and it wasn’t nonsense. It was numbers arranged in a way that made them want to mean something. The NICU monitors should have had no relationship to the Lattice; they were reading blood oxygen and heartbeats that were small and fierce. But the Lattice permeated everything, and any bit of electronics that had not been physically insulated from the city’s curve would sometimes pick up the song of the infrastructure and try to decode it like a radio catching stations it shouldn’t.

“What’s the frequency?” Naima asked, distracted.

“Forty-two point something,” the janitor said. “Something with a lot of decimal. I only know because the cardiac alarms are keyed to ninety too.” He laughed, a little hysterical. “Everything is keyed to ninety.”

“Forty-two point something isn’t one of ours,” Naima said. Meridian used weird prime numbers like proprietary charms. The idea was that you couldn’t fake their lock with something you scraped off a forum. This felt like some other edge, something there was no forum for. The harmonizer pulled at her hands again. She pushed back. The incubators settled further. When you played the harmonizer right, you felt the city’s bones like a skeleton under your fingers. She felt them now, and she felt where the wrong note was coming from: upstream, yes, further than the campus. Not the district’s other anchor—she had eyes on that. Not the transmission line that tied to the river plant. It was one of the Hinge’s quiet nodes, a stub, the sort of budget relay that fixed the edges of paid reality so the poor wouldn’t drift into the ceiling when the invoices went late. Node Seven.

“Don’t touch Seven,” her collar said, all of a sudden her dispatcher’s voice again, which meant the Oversight Office had called him while she was busy being useful. His voice had a weird squashed quality that meant he was reading from a message: “Meridian Oversight requests you not to approach or make any changes to field components at or near Node Seven pending a compliance review.”

“I’m in a NICU,” Naima said. “They can review my compliance when everyone in this room is oriented the right way up.” She routed the excess backwash into the cafeteria and watched on her overlay as a field of soups and salads learned to drift. Outside, through the ward’s high windows, she could see the lobby’s paper mobiles thrashing. A security guard with a shaved head was shepherding panicked people with the authority of a man who had been paid not enough for too long.

“Holy hell,” the nurse said, voice finally breaking. “You are a saint.”

“Buy me a beer,” Naima said. “You can canonize me later.”

There was a hand stuck to the ceiling beside the door, fingers spread. For a second, Naima thought it was a smudge or a glove. Then it moved. A person pulled himself into view, face flushed, hair matted to skull with sweat. He was in a gray hoodie with LET GO printed across the chest in a font like a falling sign. Zeroist. He raised his palms when he saw her eyes.

“Not us,” he said, soft, like he wasn’t sure he believed it himself. “We hit offices. Banks. We don’t touch hospitals. Not with the babies.”

Naima didn’t have the energy to argue the ethics of disabling gravity in corporate boardrooms. She had done those midnight runs herself when she was twenty, wired on conviction and stolen soda, watching hedge funds lose footing. She held the curve with her whole body. The man slid down the wall as the Lattice remembered what direction was.

“Then who?” she asked.

“Ask your bosses,” he said, and looked past her at the baby in the closest incubator with a raw, human tenderness that cost nothing and everything.

There were a lot of things Naima could not do. She could not pay the hospital’s bill. She could not coax the Lattice to forgive without taking from somewhere it would be noticed. What she could do was make choices in the moment, with her hands and her instrument and the authority she stole with her competency. She kept the harmonizer humming until the nurse told her that the incubators were secure enough to re-seat and until the doctor had a baby against his chest and a new suturing kit in hand. Only then did she ease the curve to a steady one, like setting a cup down on a table you just built yourself, and breathe.

The cafeteria was a mess of floating food and floating curses. Three teenagers rode the edge of a gravity gradient to make their sodas chase them upriver, laughing hysterically, because kids could make joy out of a funeral. In the lobby, a Meridian Oversight team had arrived. Twin suits and a young tech whose harmonizer had the shut door look of a machine obeying only approved commands. The taller suit had a jaw like a manifesto and a tie that cost more than Naima’s rent.

“Naima Qadir,” he said, reading off a display that was pretending to be a phone. “Field engineer. You are not authorized—”

“She saved us,” the nurse said. “I couldn’t give a shit about your authorization. If you’re not here to give her a medal and a clean set of scrubs, go stand under a piano.”

“Ma’am,” the tall suit said, and unfocused his eyes, signaling his comms. “We have a stakeholder situation. We require—”

Naima took the harmonizer off and slung it so it hung under one arm like a sullen cat. Her hands shook. She could feel the hum still, the bone-deep frequency that hadn’t been Meridian. She held onto the thought like a stone.

“I’m going to check my lines,” she said. To the Oversight tech: “Do you have Seven?”

“We’re not touching Seven,” the tech said. He looked about nineteen, pale as paper under the lobby lights. “We were told to not interact with Node Seven until Legal clears the payment issue.”

“What payment issue?” Naima asked.

The tall suit gave him a look that promised a review of employment. The kid swallowed. “Seven’s on a derivatives contract,” he said, and his mouth tripped on the word the way a newcomer tripped on a curb you couldn’t see. “It’s collateral in a gravity swap between Meridian-Central and a hedge group out of the Pacific. If we alter the load, we violate a model. If we violate a model, the swap triggers. If it triggers, we lose a supply line.”

“Lose a supply line where?” the nurse demanded.

“Uptown,” the suit said, evenly. “The Meridian-Central Headquarters campus.”

Naima laughed. It wasn’t funny. It burst out of her like a lung cough. “So to keep the coffees from spilling in a boardroom, you were going to let a NICU pop like a soda can because they were attached to a delinquent block.”

“No one authorized—” the man began. The nurse swore at him until he shut his teeth together with a sound like a stapler.

“Take me there,” Naima said to the tech. “Now.”

“I can’t,” he said, and then in a lower, terror-hushed tone, “I mean, I really can’t. They told us not to—even looking at Seven is a violation.”

“The Lattice is a physical thing,” Naima said. “It isn’t code. It isn’t a spreadsheet. You can’t not look at it when it fails.”

They didn’t let her past the lobby. They offered her coffee. They took pictures of their own reflections in the glass and called them accountability. Naima signed the thing that said she had taken actions that might be construed as unauthorized but which were definitely necessary to preserve human life. She signed her name N. Qadir with a sharp pen and an illegible flourish, and in the space where the suit got to explain the situation she wrote liens are not life.

Then she walked out the back, because she knew the hospital and knew how to be a ghost when you’d been told to sit still. She cut through a staff lot and a cigarette-smoke cove and came out into Memorial’s utility street, where the deliveries came in and where the city kept its guts. The air there was always warmer than you wanted and smelled like wet electricity. She called a little electric cart her friend in maintenance let her borrow when she had to “go yell at the sky,” and drove it like every second mattered, because they did.

Node Seven lived behind a co-op daycare and a shuttered bodega, in the sort of pocket any city accrued like lint: a concrete cove with some wild grass and two municipal bins and a good view through the chainlink of an empty lot. Meridian had bolted it into the ground with bureaucratic sadness, a cylinder the height of a person with a cowl over its working parts, painted a color that had been white before the city had its way. There were stickers on the cowl—old band logos, ancient protest slogans, a Zeroist sigil of a little falling person—but also someone had made it flowers with a paint pen, a garland of daisies that wrapped their little cartoon arms around it like pilgrims around a relic.

It hummed like a throat. That was normal. It sang like a whale. That was not.

Naima put a palm to the cowl and closed her eyes. The harmonizer could have told her the same thing, but there was something about touching the machine that made the first reading feel honest. The cowl was hot. Meridian had turned the core up to keep it shouldering load, and somewhere between the node and the Lattice line the load had acquired a shadow. She opened the cowl, because she knew where the bolts were and because she was always listening to see if someone at Meridian would put chains on things that kept the city from buckling. No chains, yet.

Inside, the node was a simple thing pretending to be complicated: a stack of field plates lovelier than rooftops, nothing as exotic as the hospital pearl, but calibrated to put a hand on space and hold. Naima’s harmonizer read the settings the way you taste soup and know how much salt will make it sing. The numbers were right. The direction they pointed wasn’t. Sometimes a thing that looks like ninety degrees is ninety-one, and that’s where buildings tilt. The node’s curve was off by a fraction that made the back of her neck itch.

She crouched. The concrete was warm through her jeans, and she got a better look at the invisibles: the faint line of a drone’s skid; the powder of dust that had fallen funny and told the truth about the shape of the air. Somebody had been here, not long. She found a thing under the bottom flange, half-stuck to the cowl with chewing gum like a high school prank. It was the size of a coin, matte-black, heavy enough that the gravity of it told lies. When she rolled it between her fingers, dust skated sideways across the ground.

“Hello,” she said to it, because sometimes you said hello before you decided if you were going to swear.

It wasn’t Meridian. Meridian’s little tricks never made her teeth ache. She glanced at the cameras. There were two, one on the daycare roof and one that belonged to nobody and everybody down on the corner, and she was in their sight with her hand in the node. She pocketed the coin without thinking about legal or professional hell. It didn’t want to be in her pocket; it wanted to roll right through her thigh to the center of the earth. She clenched and kept it. Her harmonizer, when she held it up near the coin, made a noise like a cat refusing a leash, and the whale-song deepened in a way that made the street’s weeds bow toward the drain.

She thought of the little ones in their incubators. She thought of derivatives and coffees and who got to decide where down was when money fell. She thought of the way the song had slid under her body, how it had not been built into the Meridian schema. She thought of the Zeroist on the ceiling saying not us. She thought of her mother saying don’t take anything that makes you ache when you are already working.

“Qadir,” her collar said. It was dispatch again, the static of an office with its lights too bright. He sounded tired and like he wanted to be braver. “Meridian has issued a formal request that you return to base. Legal has ideas about you saving babies again.”

“Noted,” she said. “Tell Meridian that their node has a parasite.”

“A what?”

“A foreign modulator. Doesn’t look like Zeroist hardware. Does look like someone’s idea of a private gravity.”

“Like a siphon?”

“Like a seed,” she said, and didn’t know why she chose that word until it was out. Seeds make more of themselves. A siphon takes and is done. A seed takes and then grows.

“Don’t touch it,” he said. “Qadir, I am not kidding. You will get me fired.”

“Tell them the NICU is upright. Tell them their field went weird. Tell them we both like our jobs.” She closed the cowl. She could have dialed Seven back toward the right quadrant by hand. It would have taken five minutes and six months of meetings. She left it humming where it was and got up and wiped her hands on her jeans.

When she started the cart, her harmonizer twanged a damped harmonic and then, for a breath of the day, everything felt light. Not less heavy. Light in the way of a burden being shared.

She drove because moving felt like certainty. The Hinge to her left flicker-seized and recovered. The sky above Memorial held blue like a promise. Her collar buzzed and buzzed. She turned it off. At a stoplight, a boy with three pierced ears asked her if she could make him fly. He wore a shirt with LET GO in the same terminal font as the man at the hospital. His hair was built to defy gravity without the Lattice’s help.

“You fly on your own time,” she told him. “This is mine.”

He laughed and skated on, feet barely kissing pavement.

At the office, the suits were waiting. They had found new ties. They had found new handholds on the idea of blame. Naima waved and took her emissions test and clicked her harmonizer into its charging dock as if it were just another Tuesday. She sat on the floor because chairs made her knees stiff and she liked the feel of the ground when it was a steady friend.

When she plugged her harmonizer into her relic of a laptop, the log of the morning flickered up. She scrubbed to the NICU and watched the curve like a ribbon cross a dangerous range. She scrubbed to the cafeteria and winced at a worker catching a bowl of noodles with the same focus the doctor had used for a heartbeat. She scrubbed to the moment in the ward when the monitors had all decided to repeat a number like a prayer. The number was forty-two point six something repeating. She swore softly because the decimals had patterns. They were not random. They were not Meridian.

She turned the sound up. If you listened to the Lattice you could hear the city singing to itself. You heard generators and ac systems and the distant tantrum of a million little mechanical hearts. Under that, this morning, there had been a long note. When she isolated the band and played it at human, window-glass rattling volume, it was not a note at all but a voice with an accent she did not know, saying things she did not yet have the math to translate. Maybe it said: hold me here. Maybe it said: let go. Maybe it was not for her at all.

At the bottom of the log, where Meridian’s proprietary software watermarked her actions and her sins, where the algorithms annotated her inputs like a careful lover writing in margins, there was a tiny flag she had not put there and her system should not have admitted. It was a dot, blue as a bruise. When she clicked it, her machine hummed into a little reverberation, the same sweet wrong she had felt standing in front of Seven. A string of letters unfolded. It was not any alphabet she had used to call a thing by name. It tickled her eye and then her tongue.

“What are you?” she asked the log, out loud, and thought of seeds again, of things planted where nobody expected dirt.

Outside, the city pulled itself flat and level as a freshly made bed. The office lights flickered once and then steadied. Somewhere Uptown, a very serious man stared into his coffee and did not notice that his cup had not tried to escape his hand. Somewhere in the Hinge, old man Simic put cumin on the scale and saw it settle the way it should. Somewhere in the hospital, a nurse wrote the words oxygen saturation improved and then looked at her own hand and cried in a way that made no noise at all.

Naima copied the string to a file called not our problem and then, with deliberation, changed it to our problem and hit save. She turned her collar back on. Dispatch, she said. When do I get to go home?

When Legal says you’re not a lightning rod, he said, bleak and fond. You okay?

“I’m fine,” she said, and slid her hand in her pocket and pressed her fingers against the coin that wanted to go down. She raised her hand. It raised her hand with it. Her bones sang a little, like tuning forks.

Outside, the gulls had found a thermal. They hung there, unflapping, making a monastery out of air.

At dawn the city gives up pretending to be singular.

From my window the roofs of Gantry float into each other like breath on cold glass. Sixteen versions of the same tenement house share the hour: sixteen chimney stacks exhaling different densities, sixteen laundry lines with shirts that are not quite the same shade of blue, sixteen cats—the same cat—threading sixteen parapets. In just the right light, you can watch a pigeon begin its flight in one reality and finish it in another, its shadow draped across three alleys. Paper from yesterday’s markets drifts past, thin as onion skin and printed with currencies we never minted. Somebody below argues with a spouse who died last winter somewhere else and came home on a wind from up-Spindle.

All of that settles as the day warms and the anchors hum. The big needle by the river—the Spindle, humming like a throat—tunes Gantry back toward a point on its own line, and the other versions of us thin and go like fog burned off by light. By noon, Runoff Street will be just one street again. We will hold in place until evening.

It is a mercy to have clocks and anchors and a Bureau. It is a mercy, I tell myself every morning as I strap on my lath and buckle my ledger against my ribs. I work for Number and Breath. We are the ones who make the count that feeds the net that governs air and water and bread and heat. There is nothing romantic about it. But when the anchors lull and the Spindle goes tired, the city spreads and grows porous. If you do not know the number of mouths to feed and lungs to fill across the variations that press at our edges, you starve or suffocate a thousand versions of yourself and call it a mistake. We learned to count after High Quay.

My lath sits in my palm like a metal antlers, a lattice of fine struts nested inside each other, brighter than it has any right to be. Somebody called them alidades once, back when the geeks that ran the Array still named things like they were mapping stars, but nobody says that now. We call them laths because there’s no poetry left in the things that keep us upright. You plug your lath into the little socket at your wrist, silver dust under your skin tasting the charge, and your body becomes a weak antenna for what lies to either side. You can step from your own result to neighboring solutions, just enough to make the audit.

I hum when I step. It's a bad habit. It calms the nauseous, electric feeling that comes when you are not entirely in one place. The sound gives your ears something to hold on to, a line you can reel yourself back in along. No one knows I do it except for Rey down at Records, and that is only because Rey is quiet enough that he notices things.

By the time I hit the street, the morning rush is resolving. Markets off Eastlight are still doubled—the fishermen with their mirrored stalls, one tray heaped with this morning's catch and the other tray heaped with a species of fish that vanished with High Quay—but the vendors draw their chalk lines around the versions of their tables they prefer. Chalk helps if you believe in it. Belief helps too.

I turn toward Ravel. It's a section of Gantry that never truly comes flat, a tangle of staircases and landing-plated basements, a habit of the city where the overlapping found somewhere permanent to knit. I have a flag in Ravel, a discrepancy to close, a breath I can't count on our sheet.

The summons came through late last night, mean little pulses in my ledger ink that spelled out an address and a code and the red box we jokingly call the Shepherd's Crook. That means the count couldn't find a tie. Shepherd's Crook means we have someone who won't sit neatly in the tally—the allotment can't hook into their anchor. If you have never seen men and women on the low floors waiting for the air to kick back on, hands on their chests, you might think that is an abstract problem. If you have watched a little boy turn cyanotic because the net can't find his token and won't open his ration, you don't sleep when you see that red box. You go.

I tap my pen against the lath and the lattice flickers. A sound, like rain on glass. Good. I breathe in, breathe out, choose calm. The coat I wear has pockets weighted with small, familiar things—tally-chalk, a stack of seal-chits, a roll of thin copper stamps, an anchor token with the Bureau crest, heavy as the day. The crest shows the Spindle threaded by a stylized loop, some elegant shape that meant "continuity" to somebody in the days before we had to hold continuity with both hands.

Ravel is awake. Men with drums coax the stray versions of the stairways back toward the dominant result. Aunt Ralia sits at her window with a parrot that knows more poetry than she does, bits of other mens’ and other birds’ voices snagged on her bird’s tongue from years in a braided city.

"You're late, Kele," Aunt Ralia says without greeting as I pass under her window. She is an aunt in that Ravel way that means she knows everything you have done and a little of what you will. Her hair is a silver cloud; her nightdress has been replaced today by something enviably orange.

"You're early, Auntie," I say. The parrot puts his head to one side and recites, clear as a bell, We are such stuff as dreams are made on.

I glance up at Ralia. She shrugs. "He thinks himself very modern. They're on the third landing. Thessa's girl. I told the net yesterday and the net ignored an old woman, as usual. I don't know why they put a needle in the ground if they're going to stuff wax in their ears."

"Shepherd's Crook," I say, showing her the little painted rune in my ledger so she'll know I am not ignoring her today.

"Hah." The parrot cocks his head, then says, in some other man's voice, We count to keep ourselves from disappearing. It sends a prickle down my back because that is a phrase from the Number and Breath training manual not meant for parrots or for public. Aunt Ralia looks at me and lifts her eyebrows like she did not teach the bird that trick.

"Thank you," I say. I take the stairs up and try not to step into the versions that still resist the anchor. The third stair wants to be the fourth stair. It isn't, and my heel slams hollow against a ghost plank before finding wood again. A woman opens her door at the second landing and closes it again when she sees my coat. People hide their anomalies from us and then blame us for not seeing them. People show us their anomalies and blame us when we do.

Thessa's door is painted with a mountain in green. In one version of Gantry, there was a mountain in that shade. We have a print in the Bureau lunchroom of it, lifted from some other layer’s atlas. In this one, there is a river and a Spindle. I tap.

The woman who opens the door wears yesterday's hair. She has the look of every person who has ever been flagged by a Shepherd's Crook—wide eyes, a tiredness under the bone, a chin that is already set in the direction of argument or plea. She does not know which yet. Her anchor is visible around her neck, a little iron pin with the Bureau’s crest that sings faintly when the Spindle hits the right tone.

"Thessa?" I ask.

"Yes," she says, without the Cambry drawl of this building or the up-Spindle ring I grew with. The accent has edges of somewhere else that is not one place. She can't help that. All of us borrow from the neighbors.

"I'm Kele Omendi from Number and Breath. I'm here about your allotment tie." Practice makes a human into something almost like a machine: voice neutral, posture open, hands visible.

She bites her lip. "I didn't do anything wrong."

"Nobody ever does when the count goes strange. May I?" I nod toward the room behind her. She steps back.

The room is too small for a woman and a child and a metal stove and a table with three chairs but it holds them anyway because Ravel is very good at holding too much. A pot is on the stove, opportunistically catching steam from a leaking radiator pipe. A curtain separates the sleeping area. A pair of shoes sit under the table with their laces knotted together. On the wall is a drawing of the Spindle done in a child's hand, but there are three Spindles and they braid together like hair.

"Where is she?" I ask softly. You learn to be soft. They hate the clip of officialdom.

Thessa’s mouth tightens. "She's here."

"I can't help you if—"

"Don't use that voice on me, Bureau," she says with sudden heat. Good. Anger is easier than fear.

"Mother?" A child's voice decorates the word with curiosity rather than worry.

Thessa releases the breath she was holding and calls, "Iri, there's a man from air and bread here. He wants to see your numbers." Then, to me, "Don't you scare her."

"That is the last thing I want to do." I slip the lath half out of my sleeve and let my fingers find its familiar grip.

A small girl emerges from behind the curtain. She is maybe five. The roundness has not left her face yet, but it has started to lift from her wrists and ankles. She carries a coin. Her hair is done in two plaits that do not match each other. She has ink on her mouth, as if she has been chewing a pen.

"Hello, Iri," I say, and the name sits in my mouth in a curious way. Names do that sometimes. Some names feel like a tight knot, some like a slack rope thrown down; Iri feels like a syllable too light, like a piece of language that did not come through with all its weight.

She looks at me, unafraid. Her eyes are very dark.

"This is Kele," Thessa says. "He's going to look at your anchor and then maybe he will leave us alone and we can have our day back."

"Hello, Kele," Iri says. She tips her head. "You hum."

The words stand on the rug like a dropped plate.

Thessa's eyes flash to my face, registering and discarding a dozen possible reactions. The lath in my palm is not visible. The hum is not loud. You cannot hear it unless you are very close to someone who steps just a finger thick to the left of you. I have never made a point of the humming. I have never, I am fairly sure, hummed in the Bureau in a way that anybody would point a finger and say: He hums, that is his habit. I feel the little muscles around my ears twitch.

"I do," I say, because there is nothing else sensible to say, and because lying to children breaks a piece of you you need for the rest of the day.

She nods and opens her palm to show me the coin. It is a sliver cut from something larger, etched with the ghost of an image that suggests a beast that is not a lion and not a fish. Everything presses to be not-quite something in Gantry.

"That's a… a lucky piece?" I offer. A harmless thing to say when a five-year-old shows you contraband.

"It's my boat," Iri says. "It goes across."

Thessa draws in sharp. "Iri."

"Across what?" I ask, gentler now, as if a little pressure the wrong way would crack something in here.

Iri frowns as if I haven't understood the simplest thing. "Across where it isn't, to where it is," she says, and holds the coin up between her fingers so light from the window makes it hard to see.

Thessa catches my eye. "She's five. It means nothing."

"Most things mean nothing until they do," Aunt Ralia would say from her window if she could hear what happens below her. I do not say it out loud. I let my shoulders relax and kneel to be at Iri's height.

"May I look at your anchor?" I ask her. "It won't hurt. It's just a count. Then you can eat your day."

She hesitates, then nods. Thessa unhooks the little iron pin from around her daughter's neck and puts it in her hand first. You learn to respect that ritual. It is not about trusting the Bureau; it is about the mother reminding the child that the anchor is hers.

My lath warms in my palm. I plug the anchor into its cradle, and the lattice unfolds like a fishing trap in a dream. A moment of nausea rises—always on the third cut; the body knows even if you won't tell it—that slick vertigo that comes from leaning to glance at yourself from one angle and then another.

We count by fingers. That is the old joke, the ugly one. Number and Breath uses a thousand black boxes to keep you alive, and at the heart of it there is a man counting and humming, leaning sideways with a little metal thing in his hand. The cross counts tie to neighbor counts, the neighbor counts tie to the allotment net, the net ties to the Spindle, the Spindle ties to whatever is left of the Array under High Quay, and the Array ties to the kind of men that Aunt Ralia says ought to have been drowned at birth. We call it infrastructure. We call it civilization.

If you hold a person’s anchor up in the lath's web, even a newborn, the lattice fills with them. Not with their mind or their soul or anything sacred—just their traces across the stacked solutions that the city is smoothed between. A normal result in Gantry shows a spread four or five or six layers deep at any idle breath. A child glows in a radius that says: there are other children that are almost-Iri who think different thoughts and want different soups. This is not spooky if you do it every day. It is simply the shape of a place that has not learned to be single any more.

I hold Iri's anchor up. The web hangs empty.

I blink. The lath's struts glint pheromonal—comforting machine-light that has guided my days since I was old enough to—nothing.

No scatter. No neighboring lights. No thin threads to left and right. The web is bare as a fishbone after lunch, and the only signal is a hard pin-prick in the center.

If I had not already been kneeling I would have needed a hand for the table.

Sometimes you get thin results. Sometimes the Spindle is in a mood. Sometimes the Array farts. You learn to lean through four layers of oh and find the work again. But an empty lattice is a thing we take classes about. An empty lattice is a world on a chalkboard with no neighbors, a theoretical. An empty lattice is an "incoming."

Incoming is a word that belongs to the Shears. The Office of Shearing Services wears severe coats and speaks with the bitter patience of people whose job is to cut cords. It is their function to prune the overlap when it tangles too hard for the count. They call it excision. They call it love. They call it necessity. They are not my friends.

I taste copper. I feel ridiculous because I taste copper only when I am anxious and because we stopped putting copper pipes in Bureau buildings a generation ago. Numbers click in me: this girl will not tie; she will never tie; if she is not tied she will not breathe when the net has to choose. The net will choose the thousand children we can count. It will not remember the one we cannot. If I mark her Shepherd's Crook and send the flag properly, a pair of Shears in those lovely clean coats will be at Thessa's door before the next hour, and whatever they do will not be undone.

"So?" Thessa says, because she is balancing on a small ledge over very deep water and needs to hear how far she will fall.

I put the lath down on my knee. I look at the child. She looks back at me as if I am very far away.

"Sometimes," I say, "the lath runs stupid before breakfast. It is a temperamental old creature and it needs coaxing."

Thessa stares at the device, then at me. She knows a lie. She will accept one favor like it is a hundred because there will not be another.

"We've been breathing," she says, quieter. "We have heat. We have... As long as I am holding it, Kele, we breathe. At night it goes heavy like a rock, but we breathe."

"You carry her anchor?" I ask, the shape of something clicking into its neighbor’s shape in my head.

"She is five," Thessa says. "Anchors fall through cracks. I keep it near."

Her mouth makes a smile that isn’t one. I know what she means. I slept with my first pin under my pillow like a tooth until I learned that it sang louder farther from skin.

"You called Number and Breath," I say.

"I called Aunt Ralia when the notices came," she says. "Her bird speaks Bureau. Aunt Ralia squawked in your direction and the city pretended it could not hear. I put my ear to my daughter and I hear... wrongness. I hear empty places. I hear... I do not want to tell a Bureau man what I hear when I hold my child."

It is too warm in that room. It is exactly the right temperature, and my nerves are lying to me. The lath sits quiet in my hand like it never hiccuped. The easy thing is to stand and say, There is an anomaly; you need to come to the Office; we will do a proper test. The easy thing is to believe in Shears and the neatness of excision. The hard thing is to believe in a woman cooking her soup off a radiator leak and a child with a coin that is a boat that goes across.

"I could mark an inspect," I say. "It would cut off the pub flag. Delay."

"You could not," Thessa breathes with a little laugh that is not a laugh. "I know how many ways you can mark something. All of them end with a knock."

I don't know why I say what I say next, except that Iri is still looking at me as if I am far away and she is the only person who has ever noticed how a bureaucrat hums when he opens the world like a drawer.

"I could mark a turbulence artifact," I say, and it is like telling a man who asks you for water that you could give him the moon. "We get weather. Paper rain, you know that. Cacophony, resonance, slop. A turbulence artifact on a Shepherd's is... not good practice. It would make the count ignore something it shouldn't ignore. If the net can't tie a stable anchor, it should flag. But it would stop the Crook for a cycle."

"A cycle," she repeats, as if tasting an apple.

"Two days. Maybe three if the Office is busy." I risk a small smile. "The Office is often busy. People spill out of themselves all the time. You wouldn't believe what Rey had to file last week. A baker who had two right arms on Wednesdays. They kept catching each other."

Iri giggles the unstoppable giggle of a child who did not understand the joke but enjoyed the sound of it.

"This is not a game," Thessa says, but the edges of her mouth soften.

"I mark a turbulence and you put this anchor back on the line," I say. "Don't take it off her. I will squeeze noise into this corner of the net, the kind that makes a tie look like it will resolve if you leave it alone. And you won't open your door to anybody in a clean coat you didn't call. If the Office shows, you say Kele Omendi told them to get clear of your stair."

"You will put your name in ink," she says, not a question.

"Yes," I say.

"You will be held for it," she says, not a threat.

"Probably," I say, and her eyes do something human that is not relief and not gratitude and not permission. It is something like the moment a tight knot slips half a millimeter through your fingers.

"You think you can keep us long enough?" Thessa asks. "Why? Why us? You don't know us."

"Because you have already kept yourself long enough to get me here," I say, and realize as I speak that it is true: she called Ralia; Ralia threw words like stones; the parrot learned a manual; Thessa held the pin like a charm; a little girl learned to stand on a rug as if the floor was thinner than paper and not fall. "Because sometimes Number and Breath is more mouth than number."

"Sometimes," she says, and that is not permission, it is a declaration of fact.

"Hold your coin," I tell Iri. "Hold it tight. If your boat goes across, make sure it comes back."

She nods solemnly and clamps her fist.

I take out the ledger. The paper has the oily feel of something that wants to be a screen and can't admit it. In Bureau ink, red bleeds toward caution and yellow sours toward cowardice. I pull a thin thread from my pen and stitch it through the code. It is not wise to do the thing I am doing. It will tie me to this error, it will propagate down to Records, and Rey will see my name float in place around a Shepherd's Crook like a fish with bad scales.

"Turbulence artifact," I say out loud as my handwriting pretends to be official. "Resolution pending. Auditor present. Delay to next count. Do not escalate."

I feel that tiny ache behind my eyes that means the lath is angry with my ethics. I squeeze the bridge of my nose and then hang the small wooden tag above Thessa's door, under the green mountain. The sigil says: We have counted this thing; counting continues; do not intercede. It will hold until someone is greedier than God.

I stand. The room tilts and rights itself. Thessa has a hand on the back of her chair she did not have there a moment ago.

"Thank you," she says.

"Please don't thank me yet," I say, because thank yous sound like eulogies in this line of work.

On the stair down, Aunt Ralia waits where she said she wouldn't. The parrot is silent now, its head under its wing. She squints past me into whatever else sits on the landing. "Well?"

"Turbulence," I say.

"Ah," Ralia says, and in that word is the weight of knowing that turbulence is an announcement to a bigger storm that it has been seen.

"You didn't learn that in a manual," she says, not questioning.

"No," I say.

She tucks her nightdress around her knees. "The Shears have been sniffing around Ravel," she says. "They think we won't notice when they come for our threads. But it's like taking a braid apart. You're left with a handful of hair no one knows how to wear."

"I need to go," I say. "I should write this up before someone writes it for me."

"Tell your friend in Records he's got a pretty neck if he sticks it out for you," she says.

"I'll tell Rey he should buy a scarf," I say, and she cackles, and the parrot lifts his head to say, with hexameter solemnity, Beware the cutters who mend.

Outside, paper starts to fall. Not rain like the poets. Paper. Crumpled slips and bits of other days and other city forms, dog-eared and smudged. A receipt for ink. A ticket to a ferry that never ran here. A message on a handbill in a language that looks like ours through a mirror. Ravel has children who make purses out of the paper and sell them on market days. There is art to be made from predicaments we do not choose.

As I cross Runoff Street, my ledger vibrates against my ribs. Records blinking me.

"Omendi," Rey says when I answer. His voice is all the things mine is not: steadied, measured, always six beats behind so he can catch what you did in his net when it falls. "You've got a Crook with a turbulence on it."

"Do I?" I say, and step under a balcony dripping a version of rain that does not exist on this block anymore so I can think. I do not lie to Rey. He is my friend because we do not lie to each other about the weather.

"Clerk Morrow has eyes." Rey's tone isn't accusation. It's the tone of a man who knows what a notch on a piece of wood sounds like and hears axe on oak.

"Clerk Morrow can glory in his eyes," I say.

"You humming?" Rey asks softly.

"Always," I say, and almost laugh because it feels like I've stolen my hum and thrown it into a place no one can hear it.

"Get back when you can," he says. "Morrow raised a brow and then a flag. There's a note for you from Shears. Courteous. They ask you to come over and explain your handwriting to them. I have a feeling they know the alphabet and don't need tutoring."

"You can tell Shears numbers don't learn better if you threaten the pen," I say.

"This isn't the pen they're looking to threaten," Rey says. He inhales. "Kele. Be careful."

I could tell him about a coin that is a boat and a girl who looks at where you are not as if it is the more interesting place to stand and a lattice that came up empty like a bowl after a famine. I could tell him that whatever the Shears want, they do not have a word for it yet. I say instead, "Throw some noise into my lane."

"I was born to make noise," Rey says. "Morrow hates my music."

We end the call. The Spindle's low hum threads the street. I realize I am humming too, so soft only my teeth can hear it. A handbill flutters down onto my shoulder. It says in big, earnest letters: We were wrong. Below that, in smaller type: A Public Lecture on the Array, With Diagrams. The room listed is under High Quay. The date is twenty years past and one layer over. That is the thing about paper rain: it is almost useless as instruction but perfect as omen.

I am halfway to the Bureau when I notice I am not alone.

There are footsteps behind me that strike a fraction too late and hit the stones without sound. I slow. They slow. Not the rhythmic tail of a tail who wants to be noticed. Not the wind. I pass under a strand of flags from some holiday I can't remember we celebrated, and in the triangle of blue cloth I catch a reflection that is not mine and not any of the versions of me who have ever worn this coat on this street.

It is a face, yes. It is a child's face. It is Iri's face. It is not quite the same. The braid sits higher. The coin is not cut but whole. The eyes are not as dark. The reflection is wrong because it is yours in the wrong place, and for a second my heart does a thing that hearts should not do.

When I turn, there is only a boy with a bundle and a man arguing with a pipe that refuses to be anchored. Nothing elegant or frightening. The trick of a city that knows my nerves.

I do not run. I change my path, take two steps to the left in the way the lath has taught me and settle back into a neighbor result where the flags do not hang and the pipe does not argue and the paper never frays. You can do that if you are very good and very stupid. It is not meant to be done for long. I do it to see if the flanking footsteps can follow a step I did not step in front of them.

They do. Of course they do.

The Offices of Number and Breath are all stone and patience. Rey meets me at the door with a scarf in Bureau brown like a joke that never gets old. His hair sits like a careful graph. He looks at my face and then at my hands and then, in a small mercy, at my feet. "You have paper on your shoe," he says. "It says: Beware the cutters who mend."

"You taught Aunt Ralia's bird hexameter," I say.

"I taught a parrot a meter and he subsumed me," Rey says sorrowfully, handing me a cup.

"Shears sent you something?" I ask.

He lifts a paper that is too heavy to be from our rain and taps a place where Clerk Morrow's name sits nestled in the kind of ink that screams its own seriousness. Request the presence of Auditor Omendi at earliest convenience to discuss potential misapplication of turbulence protocol. Kindly bring Alidade log and copy of field sigils for review. Kindly. The Shears had their last kindness surgically removed with the radiation.

"I have to go, then," I say.

"You have to not go yet," he says. "Let Morrow feel the absence of you. It will make him less precise."

"He's very precise when he's angry."

"Then don't make him angry. Make him curious. Bring him a story."

"I thought you liked me," I say.

"Not that kind of story," Rey says. He lowers his voice. "You saw emptiness?"

"Nothing," I say, and that word carries a weight like a dropped anchor.

"Incoming," he says.

"Not ours to say," I tell him, because that is the phrase they taught us to put in our mouths when we stand at the edge of what we cannot name. "Not ours to say until Shears says so."

Rey sips his tea. We lean against the cold stone that tries to remember what being a single building felt like. Down the hall, Clerk Morrow's office door is open like a mouth.

Behind my ribs, the ledger ticks. The net breathes and the Spindle's hum goes softer or my ear changes. On the table, between us, the note Shears sent flares in a way paper does when somebody else touches it with their attention. Words crowd my tongue that want to be said—the kind of words you are not supposed to speak inside Offices because they change the temperature in a way you then have to explain in a memo.

We do not own the first chapter of any story we are foolish enough to live inside. But sometimes you can hear the bind on the page, the way the spine creaks, the way it will break if you put pressure there.

Rey says, very quietly, "Kele. Someone left you another note."

I look. It is not from Shears. Not from Number and Breath. Not from Aunt Ralia or the market or any of the thousand bureaucratic machines that write their names above their requests.

The paper is thin like onion skin. The ink is not ours. There is only one line on it, written in a hand that doesn't know the habit of this city.

We were waiting for you to find us.

Chapter One: Night Silt

We called it silt because it looked like silt—the way it drifted when you disturbed it, the way it gathered in troughs and ripples, the way it held a damped memory of what had passed through it. But it wasn’t dirt. It was the ground truth of other people’s yesterday. Crushed lattices, carbon snow, pressure-crazed hyperglass, and a fever of encoded polarization that, if you knew how to listen, would tell you how an ocean you’d never seen used to smell.

We were three kilometers into the Dead Hemisphere when the skiff’s undercarriage sank half a meter into a field of it. The fins on the sled whined as Kol throttled back. The sled hovered, repulsors straining, a wake of glittering dust curling up around us like a breath.

“Hold it there,” I said. My voice came back small in my hood, the cold making it tinny. “Don’t fight the drift.”

Kol grunted acknowledgment through the link. On his side of the saddle he was a slab of moving shadow, the suit’s black quilted weave jerking with each microadjustment of the controls. Behind me, Mei’s rig chirped and clicked as she slid a new module into the throat of the thrum antenna.

The Dead Hemisphere deserved its name. On Tern we didn’t have night. We had Night. It was a thing that took up space, a thing you could lean on. Day clung to one side of the planet and Night clung to the other, and in between there was a wind that never stopped trying to reconcile them. We lived where it blew the least. We worked where it blew the most.

I unclipped my own thrum device and anchored it to the skiff’s forward hardpoint. It was a fat tuning fork coupled to a bank of piezos and processors that the manufacturer called a polylithic adaptive vibrational analyzer and everyone else called an ear. In daylight we used lasers. In Night, light did strange things. Sound held still.

“Ping out,” Mei said. “Make it a low sweep.”

I banged the fork against the skiff’s lip. In the near vacuum, the tone was more felt than heard, a crease of force that ran out ahead of us and came back stern and confident from the plain: open, open, open, then—there—something breaking the symmetry, a dish, a hollow, a wall that was not a wall because the grain of it was wrong.

Kol bared his teeth. The internal lights cast wet flares in his visor. “You getting it?”

“I’m getting something,” I said. The fork kept singing. The processors painted the data on the lower border of my visor: rainfall plots of amplitude, grain-phase graphs, cartoons of possible shapes. The screen coalesced into a shallow bowl with a long spine rising from it like a fin. The spine rang like glass.

Mei’s suit shifted behind me. The woman barely weighed anything out of rig, but she carried her gear like a mountain. In the reflection of the skiff’s forward hood, I saw her duck her head and whisper. It was a habit she had, even with the link open—words to the machines, words to the old ghosts. People said Tern made everyone superstitious. I thought maybe that was just a polite way to say it made us honest.

“Trench ahead,” she said. “Engineered, not glacial. It’s the Ravel signature.”

Kol made a satisfied sound. “Our sponsor will send you a cake, Ren.”

“Cake would be a mistake,” I said. “We can’t digest anything without enzymes, remember?”

“Fine,” he said. “They’ll send you a very enthusiastic letter.”

“Much better.”

We were following a careless line into Night. The last known coordinates of Kase’s final ping were pinned to the inside of my skull in a hole that never healed. He’d gone out past the Threshold eight months ago, chasing after a rumor that the oldest Ravel field had shifted, exposing a core. People disappear in Night. Suit rips. Cables fail. A thousand things happen for which there is no malice and no narrative, just entropy. But Kase had left me twelve seconds of singing and a tail of telemetry that implied he had been falling at four meters per second squared, then two, then zero, not into emptiness but onto something that caught and kept.

I had tried not to follow. Tern punished obsession. The wind stole heat and the city stole years and both of them were less cruel than the way your brain could convince you that one more step into the abyss would resolve the chord that had been thrumming through your bones for months.

The skiff cleared the lip of the bowl. We drifted down into the hollow. As we approached, the air grew strangely still. The skiff’s vibration changed from the open chorus of flatland to a soft, precise reverb that made the hairline fractures in my teeth ache. When I tapped the fork again, the return was timed and tight. Mei hummed under her breath, tracking. She read thrum like other people read text. The bowl was glassboney: the surface of the silt here had been sintered by some long-ago heat into plates and needles, a frost of material too brittle to be ice and too elastic to be stone.

Above us, the sky was stationary and infinite. The stars never moved in Night. We navigated by them and by memory. Across the curve of the world, Day was boiling the air white. Here, under the fin, the sky was a frozen black, and the fin rose out of it like a wish.

“Is that—” Kol began.

“Shh,” Mei said. “Listen.”

She tuned the fork and set it vibrating at a frequency I couldn’t feel. The processors did their work and translated for us. The fin sang back. It had seams. It had a periodic lattice that had been strategically disordered, the way human pod hulls are when you want to damp a certain range of frequencies. But this fin was old. Not human. Before us, before Tern’s first flutter of sails dropped into the atmosphere and the first habitats anchored themselves to the streaming rivers of air along the terminator.

Aster-and-Salt had paid us not to go in stupid. We were to take pictures and thrum maps and signal the city for a more formal team. But Aster-and-Salt did not have Kase under their tongue, making everything taste like iron.

Mei finished her sweep and tapped a packet to my visor. “There’s an entrance,” she said. “Low and long. It’s filled.”

“Filled with what?” Kol asked.

Mei lifted one shoulder. “Time.”

We set anchor in the silt field and paid out a line. Kol insisted on two more. He was all aikido and economy until the subject was “not dying,” at which point he became a belt of redundancy and drills. He clipped me with too much force and our helmets bumped. The little click was intimate and infuriating. He fumbled an apology. I ducked my head and made the sign for fluid motion and harmony. He laughed. The laugh showed up on my HUD as a spike.

We took the first steps off the skiff together, the three of us arrayed like a clumsy star. Silt puffs rose and fell and rose. The surface here was crusted, like old bread. It broke underfoot and flowed and set again and you didn’t want to think too hard about what it would do if your suit compromised and it found your throat.

My hands went heavy as the temperature dropped another degree. The suit compensated, but cold on Tern was like the memory of a grief you had sworn not to feel anymore. It still found you. It still put its hand in the place you kept vacant for it.

We reached the fin. Up close it wasn’t smooth. It was composed of thousands of hair-thin plates canted against each other at angles that made my eyes water and my proprioception scream. The edges had been ground down by a million years of wind into something that was not any shape I knew how to name. The thrum signal showed a channel opening into it near the base, half-choked with silt. We crouched. The entrance was a mouth. It had lips of glass that had flowed once and frozen in the act of rippling.

“I’ll go,” I said.

Kol made the motion for patience. “We probe, then go.”

“I can be the probe,” I said.

Mei ignored us both. She slid the microspine out of its sheath on the side of her pack. The spine was a cassette of memory and sensor and the kind of attitude control a mosquito would envy. She tapped its head to wake it and it quivered, buzzing, eager.

“Take a breath,” she said softly, and let it slip into the channel.

We watched its feed scroll across our visors. The spine’s world was grain and edges and ghostlight, a continuous update of probabilities. It flowed along the left-hand lip of the channel and then used that lip as its frame of reference to measure everything else against. Tiny adaptations learned from the windborne creatures out at the Edge. Mei had built the spine’s AI herself, teaching it to be suspicious of light, to prefer the tactile, to never enter a volume it could not exit.

The spine slid three body lengths into the channel and stopped.

“Why?” Kol asked, voice tight.

Mei frowned. “Because the world ends.”

I leaned closer, breath fogging my visor before the filters wiped it away. The spine’s last frames resolved on the edge of a darkness that was not dark. Light and pressure and sound gradients all went sane and then fell off a cliff. The pipeline was gone. Something else was there. Something with a curvature that refused to be measured, like the horizon you could never reach.

Mei stuck two fingers under her own jaw and pressed hard, a trick for calming yourself when your nerves were making your muscles dance. “It’s not a hole. It’s an error.”

Kol’s hands flexed. “We’re not going into an error.”

“We’re not leaving without a physical piece,” I said. “Aster-and-Salt paid for pain, remember?”

“Fuck Aster-and-Salt,” Kol said.

“Gladly,” I said. “After. Mei, can you brute an anchor into that edge?”

Mei blinked once—hard—like she was physically pushing something to one side in her head. “If I can get it to pretend its existence depends on it.”

“That’s how,” I said.

She fired a microharpoon. The cable whirred. The hook kissed the curvature that was not. For a second, the line went slack in a way that was not slack. The suit’s haptics juddered. Every nerve in my arms told me I was holding onto a metal ring in sunlight on the dock in Port Clarion twenty years ago. The feeling was so strong that tears jumped to my eyes, and then the cable stiffened and reality reasserted itself. The hook had found a place to be stubborn. Mei made a sound of relief so small I might have imagined it.

“Okay,” she said. “We have a line. Ren, you’re up.”

I took the lead. The channel was high enough that I could crouch but not stand. The fin’s internal ridges scraped the shoulders of my suit. My chestplate clicked on a plate seam that was eight degrees colder than the air and I flinched. The silt there was different. It resisted forward motion the way a crowd resists a person trying to push through it. The particles whispered against the suit’s membrane. The processor translated the whisper into an arc of tonalities whose family resemblance to speech was just enough to blow a fuse in my head.

“Noise,” I told my mind. “It’s noise. It’s not a language you don’t yet speak.”

The cable trembling under my hands steadied me. Behind me, Kol kept tension on it like a climber. He always pretended his strength was incidental to the rest of us and then he would do some small, essential thing—hold a rope, clip a line—that put his body back into the center of the picture whether he was comfortable with that or not.

The error rose to meet me. The edge felt like a line drawn in water with a knife. I lay on my belly, reached, and put my hand into it.

It was not like putting my hand into anything I had done before. The suit’s sensors told me pressure and temperature and chemical composition. The values were all within sane limits. But the haptics relayed a judder that was not in the numbers. It was as if every layer of the suit from membrane to weave to ceramic plates had been built yesterday not for my hand, not for a human hand at all, but had been built for this. The suit had not been built for this.

The error was a material. It gripped the suit and then released it in a pattern that the processors helpfully mapped to a sequence of old Earth lullabies. Somewhere in the machine, a training dataset had been fed a particular library of human structures and had decided this was the shape of comfort.

“Ren?” Kol said, voice pitched low.

“I’m okay,” I lied. I found purchase on the far lip and hauled myself forward. The error yawned under me like a calm sea. I pushed my head and shoulders through. Orientation fell apart and then restitched itself. My sense of up, which had been anchored to the skiff and to Day somewhere beyond the horizon, was replaced by a new up that oriented to the fin’s axis. I was inside. The air was colder. Something else was warmer. The warmer was a source, not an environment.

There was a room.

Room was not the word. Rooms were square or round, they had floors and ceilings and things meant for people with four limbs and a head. This place had none of those and all of them. Planes intersected at angles that were only illegal if you took Euclid personally. Struts and voids defined each other by negation. The silt from the channel had flowed into a curve and then stopped, as if embarrassed.

I stood with the help of the cable and rotated slowly. My visor’s transparency suddenly refused to be transparent in a certain sector of my view and I tugged at my suit’s data presentation, swore under my breath. The processors thought there was something there and did not know how to show it.

“Ravel core,” Mei breathed. Her voice made a tiny private thunder in my ear. “That has to be a core.”

Kase had thought he’d found a core. The old stories said the Ravel had seeds: nodes from which the rest of the field blossomed under pressure and time, the way soap films meet in threes to minimize tension. Nothing human had ever seen one intact. The cores found by the first crews had been melted into slag by a million years of day-night cycling. Here, in the lee of the fin, someone had kept a piece sheltered.

I took a step. The floor flexed and remembered not to flex. I put my glove against the center of the not-visibility, and the suit recorded temperature. It was thirty-three degrees C. Warm enough to boil spit. The suit helpfully protected me against all the ways I could die from that number.

“Ren,” Mei said. “Do not poke it with your face.”

“I am going to talk to it first,” I said.

“Of course you are.”

“I mean, you did tell a harpoon its existence depended on it five minutes ago.”

“That’s different,” she said. “Harpoons are sentimental.”

I cleared my throat. It was a stupid impulse. You clear your throat when there are other throats in the room. I thought about what voices my suit had on file. The generic set. The training set. The emergency set. Kase’s twelve seconds, scraped and processed and turned into a usable profile. His voice was there, in my suit. The city had sent back his pack after his ping cut, a plastic coffin with foam cut for gear and the gear not there except for his spare boots and his spare voice.

“Don’t,” Kol said.

I didn’t key in my brother. I keyed in my own. My raw voice. “Hello,” I said into the center of not-visibility. “I’m Ren.”

The suit recorded my output. The processors did their best to subtract my input from the reflections. The edge of the not-visibility brightened in the lo-fi sense that my suit’s systems gently flagged it. The thrum fork, even hanging from Mei’s harness behind me, sympathetically resolved to an older frequency. My grandmother, dead two continents and an ocean and a planet ago, used to keep a ridiculous bronze tuning fork on a shelf by the window. When I was little, I used to strike it and put my forehead against it and feel the inside of my skull light up. This felt like that.

“Hello,” I said again, to prove the first time had not been a fluke of breath and fear and electricity.

The not-visibility said something back.

Not words, not structure in any way that my mind could bear to reduce to an alphabet. But the pattern it threw into my chest was the shape of the word welcome if you had been taught to hear that as a changed air pressure as a door opened at your back.

My arms tried to move up and out in a gesture my suit did not know. I was suddenly aware of how far my helmet was from Kol’s. I was aware of Mei’s pulse in my ear. I was aware of Day, trying with its entire bright mass to pull air around the planet in a single endless reach. I was aware of Kase, of twelve seconds of singing that had split open and ended with a voiceless oh.

Mei’s voice came low and precise. “Ren. Mark your observations. Keep your hands where I can track them.”

“Yes,” I said, because when Mei’s voice turned like that you said yes.

Observation: My suit’s thermal maps are standing still, with a localized heat source at the core. Observation: The silt is behaving like an active substrate at micro scales, but macroscopically it is inert. Observation: The core answers to a human vocalization, but the mapping of the response onto human sensory channels appears to be a trick, not an accommodation inherent in the world.

“This is not an accident,” I said aloud.

“What?” Kol asked.

“They wanted someone to find this,” I said. “Not us. But someone. At some point. It’s a kept thing.”

Mei said, “Other kept things have been traps.”

“Yes,” I said. “And sometimes a hook with food on it is still food.”

Kol grunted. “No speeches. No metaphors. It’s either a container or a mouth.”

“Why not both?” Mei murmured.

The not-visibility changed. It opened in the way a gaze opens: without motion, with attention. My suit’s lensing fought with the phenomenon and lost. My HUD blanked for a fraction of a second. Something pressed against the inside of my helmet with no physical vector to justify it. It was huge and gentle and not for me and it turned its face toward me anyway.

“Ren,” it said.

The voice was not Kase’s. It was not any voice I had stored, not any of us, not any human voice. It was the idea of a voice, expressed as weight. The syllable compressed ribs that my biofeedback swore were not compressing. Mei made a sharp sound. Kol cursed.

“Ravel interface,” Mei hissed, as if we were being rude and she was furious at herself for being surprised by it.

“Ren,” the voice said again, but differently, as if trying to bottom out in the same word. There are only so many ways to say a name. It found another.

“I’m here,” I said. “Who are you?”

“Archivist,” it said.

“I am not,” I said. Well. That depended on how you drew the line around me, and the things I had put into myself that were not me in order to hold onto the past.

“Designate: Archivist,” the core insisted, and the not-visibility stirred, a subsonic hiss of particles reorganizing that I felt through my knees.

Mei’s hands were ice steady on the tether. “Ren, back out.”

“Wait,” I said, but my mouth was slow and the motion of my body was faster. Kol was hauling. The cable cut into my wrist where the suit’s weave was weaker. I dug my fingers into the wrong floor. The wrong floor obliged me and became a floor.

“Wait,” I said again, because if the past had a shape I wanted to memorize it with my skin. The core’s warmth pulsed under my palm in a rhythm that was not quite heartbeat. It was a measure of something else. It was counting me.

“Archivist,” it said, and something latched.

Every layer of my suit chimed. Warnings spiked. Filters came on. Processes isolated. The suit’s onboard AI—Keepsake, perpetually nostalgic and terminally cautious—spoke for the first time in weeks in a voice I had chosen because I hated it to be chirpy. It was flat, as if boredom could be homologous with authority.

“You have been tagged,” Keepsake said.

“No shit,” Kol said.

“Tagging is not physical,” Keepsake said. “No change in mass. No change in surface properties. No biohazard signatures. Correlation with previous observed tagging events is twenty-one percent.”

My mouth was dry and too wet at the same time. Fear, the kind that tasted like the burned edges of meat. “Do we think it’s a beacon?” I asked. “A handoff protocol?”

“It’s naming you,” Mei said softly. “It’s putting you in its system.”

“I am not yours,” I told the core, very calm. “We are just visiting.”

“Visit,” the voice said, and I had the sense of something tilting its head to show it understood the ritual but had no practice at it.

A wreath of radiation tore through the room. The meters spiked. Kol swore, the cable went vicious in his hands, and we were all moving without agreeing to move.

“Star weather,” Mei snapped. “We have a shower coming in. It’s early.”

The sun was a steady tyrant above the Day hemisphere, but the magnetosphere around Tern had its tantrums, and Night got cut by knives you could not see. We had trailed indulgently after the forecast’s low probability like a child, and now the sky was about to remind us that forecasting on a planet with one face in permanent light was the art of describing beautiful lies.

“Out,” Kol said, and it wasn’t a plea and it wasn’t an order. It was a category of word that meant there was only one way and it was that way.

I made to push myself back through the aperture. The core still had a hand on me, metaphysically speaking. It did not fight me. It did not let me go. The tag was not a line. It was a smell. It was a signature in a room that was not a room, a whorl in currents I could not see. It would not keep me from leaving.

“Visit,” it said again, differently. As benediction, as promise, as threat.

We blew back into the channel in a body, stumbling and cursing and kicking silt. Kol hauled us from the mouth of the fin and we scrambled crabwise up the bowl. Silt blew. It rose in sheets. The first particles of the shower hit the upper surface of the fin with a sound like rain on a roof in a city where rain was normal and roofs did not rust themselves to lace. Invisible muons hammered through us, sawed through the suit’s protections, left tracks in our teeth and our marrow, and the suit hummed as it dumped every erg it could spare into the countermeasures.

We made the skiff and fell into its belly. Kol slammed us shut. Mei’s fingers did what Mei’s fingers always did: they danced, juggling, persuading, redirecting power, coaxing the skiff to shelter us from a star it could not see. Keepsake unspooled the emergency umbrella—carbonweb tensors and a sheath of field reactive foil—and the umbrella flowered over us with a sound like the release of breath.

“Report,” Keepsake said, because it was stupid and patient. “Report, report.”

“Alive,” Kol grunted. “Mostly.”

“Define alive,” Mei muttered.

I lay on my back with my helmet still on and the strap across my chest cutting my body into two parts. The core’s voice did not come with me. That was good. The tag came. My suit’s telemetry labeled me as being something I had not been when we came into the bowl, and as the umbrella shuddered under the shower and the skiff slid half a meter to one side and dug its rear fin into the silt like a desperate animal, I closed my eyes and saw not Kase’s twelve seconds but the half-second at the end of it that I had always avoided.

He had been falling. Then he had been stopped. The last frame of his telemetry had flared and died. I’d never thought about what he’d seen in that last little bit, because I could only ever get as far as the falling part. Now I imagined him on his belly, arms stretched into a room that made math into a sculptural medium, the world adjusting around him as if he were the load a truck had not expected to carry and was going to try anyway.

It would have said his name. It would have called him Archivist.

The skiff creaked. Night leaned against us. We breathed and counted and waited for the shower to pass.

“That wasn’t a core,” Kol said finally.

“What?” Mei said, exhausted and interested in the same breath.

“It was more than that,” he said. “It wasn’t a node. It was a person.”

“Don’t be speciesist,” Mei said reflexively.

Kol laughed, a broken thing. “I mean that it wanted to speak.”

“We need to tell Aster-and-Salt,” Keepsake said.

“We need to not tell Aster-and-Salt,” I said at the same time. We all heard it. We all heard the sum of our debts, the sum of what we could not do without a sponsor, and the sum of what we’d lose if a corporate excavator dropped its polite full weight on the fin and turned it into a report.

“Ren,” Mei said carefully. “What did it say to you exactly?”

“Archivist,” I said. “Welcome. Visit.”

“And?” she prompted.

“And it tagged me,” I said. I put my hand—gloved, insulated, wholly mine—over the place on my chest where the suit had chosen to summarize the tag’s existence. It was silly. It wasn’t a thing. It did not have shape. But I could feel the fact of it like a fresh bruise.

“What will it want when we go back?” Kol asked. He made it into a question, as if we were not already making a plan to do the thing we all knew was the worst available choice.

“Everything,” I said, because I am dramatic when I am tired. “Or nothing at all.”

The shower eased. The umbrella settled. The skiff’s instruments stopped screaming and went back to grumbling. Mei rolled onto her side and propped herself on an elbow. “If the core tagged you as Archivist,” she said, “there may be an expectation attached to that.”

“I don’t have the keys to the past,” I said.

“You have better,” Kol said grimly. “You have the right shape.”

I would have told him to stop trying to write poetry, but I could not quite make my mouth form the words. I could taste the tag. I could taste metal and old wind and the skin-salt of what it meant to be counted by something that had learned counting from a geometry I would never touch.

Keepsake’s status line pulsed along the bottom of my visor, a constant smarm of reassurance. I blinked it off. The skiff was safe. For now. We could push back to the city and sell them exactly enough of the truth to buy us a return to the bowl without a parade of auditors. Or we could run the entire mission in the red and not report anything at all until we knew how to turn this into something we could live with.

“Do you think it knew Kase?” Mei asked. She never said his name. None of us did unless we had to. On Tern, names were for the living.

“I think it knows everyone who puts their hand into that room and asks to be seen,” I said. Some of the air left my lungs and did not come back. “He got as far as I did. Farther, maybe. Or not as far. I don’t know.”

Kol rubbed his faceplate with his glove, a useless habit, the motion translating as a smear of light. “If we tell Aster-and-Salt, they’ll lock the site.”

“And if we don’t,” Mei said, “and they hear about it through someone else, they’ll do worse.”
