“Do you both recall me,” Keepsake said, very politely, “sitting on your last two contracts because you did not desire the oversight? My patience is vast and my charge cycles are longer than your grudges.”

“We recall you,” Kol said. He sounded like he was smiling.

A long wind went by, not ours. It spoke to the fin. The fin answered, a dull protest. The silt resettled. The sky, which had never moved and would never move, was already different, in the way an unmoving thing always is between one breath and the next when you have changed shape.

“We go back,” I said, because someone needed to lay down a circle around the next hour. “We go back and we bring better toys, and we bring the piece that Kase wanted, and then we decide who to burn with it.”

Mei put her head back on the skiff’s floor and closed her eyes. She did not say yes. She did not need to.

Kol reached across the narrow space between us and touched his glove to mine. The motion was small. The haptic ping was small. The way my body registered the contact was not.

“Ren,” the core had said. “Archivist.”

The room had made a category and put me in it. I lay on my back, and the sound of the umbrella folding away above us was the sound of something fragile done carefully by a tired hand.

“We should get out before the next front,” Mei said, always practical for exactly three seconds at a time. “We’ll lose the route if it shears.”

“We won’t lose it,” I said, and tasted the lie like iron. “It’s mine now.”

 Night held its breath and let it out again. The engines came up. The skiff rose. The fin dwindled in the forward view like a blade laid flat on the plain, harmless until you ran a finger along it in the wrong direction.

We found our own tracks without drama. The air picked up. The terminator line, violent and luminous, was a rumor in the far distance, even though there was no distance here, only an established relationship between things.

Kol tapped the skiff’s side thoughtfully. “Archivist,” he said, as if trying the weight of a title on his tongue.

“Please,” Mei said. “Do not start calling her that. The last thing Ren needs is to enjoy this.”

I smiled despite myself. They were good at treating me as if I were not a hole with a name. The skiff bit into the wind and came around toward city. In my visor I brought up Kase’s twelve seconds. I put them on a loop and watched their waveforms stack and collapse. There was a point in the middle of that little singing where the line went flatter than it should have. I had always thought it was a glitch. Now I understood it was an answer.

When I closed my eyes, the not-visibility was waiting for me. It did not feel like a triumph. It felt like a promise I did not remember making. It felt like Night, making room.

At the edge of the world where Day and Night negotiated their ceasefire, the city leaned into the wind and sang back at the weather. The towers slid a fraction closer together as a gust threatened one of the outer sails. Our arrival pinged the lower rings. We would come in quiet. We would dock. We would tell almost the truth to the wrong person, and very near that we would tell the right person nothing at all.

The core had told me what I was. I was not sure what to do with that yet. But I could feel the tag in my bones like a tooth you had tongued too often. It changed the way my suit fit. It changed the taste of the air in my helmet. It changed the shape of the hole I had been ignoring in myself.

We skimmed down the city’s throat, and I put my palm flat to the skiff’s floor and felt the old world hum up into mine.

Chapter One: The Quiet

On the lunar farside, silence had a texture. It wasn’t the absence of sound so much as a thin pressure against the bones of the skull, a tautness in the air that never broke. Sahana Rao had learned to taste it the way some people could taste the copper of a coming storm. It had flavors—static, thermal, a dust of faint hiss and crackle that was not air at all but the memory of violence sifted into microwaves and long, long wave radio. Day to Earth-born crowds, it would have been terrifying. To her, it was a familiar drift, the steady background against which all human noise was an intrusion.

It was the hour when the base lights dimmed to pretend night, the long false twilight when the cyclic LEDs along the corridor walls slid from honey to iron. Sahana sat in the Horizon Array control room with her fingers tucked into the pockets of her sweater and the reflected stars from the big glass panel flecking the consoles in front of her. Horizon’s displays had been set, by design, to use colors you could see while your eyes were adapted to darkness. No blinding white; everything in reds and sea greens, a smooth palette for looking up and then down again without losing the Milky Way to the glare in your retinas.

She tried to stifle a yawn, failed, and scrubbed a hand over her face. Her daughter’s message chimed on the side screen, a notification in the text bar that did not interrupt her audio because of the Quiet. Sahana glanced at the line anyway. Pihu sent a string of sloppily drawn suns and a message from Bangalore: Mama did you see the pictures? Swans in the monsoon flood! Can we call when you’re done with work?

“Soon,” Sahana said into an empty room. The bubble of the Quiet would cut her off in four minutes when the calibration run began. If she pushed the call now, the system would deny it anyway. There were rules. Rules she had helped write.

She wheeled closer to the main spectral display. The Lunar Far Array was at work, a brightness-temperature plot thrumming across a range of tens of megahertz, the redshifted ghost of hydrogen’s 21-centimeter line laid out like a horizon itself, ragged with fluctuations. The universe, on the cusp of its first light, was whispering in lines and dips. They were mapping that whisper, day by day, lunation by lunation, in the radio quiet of the farside where Earth was a permanent blank below the horizon and every human signal had to come in bent and hidden over the relay at L2.

Sahana tapped an overlay. The code behind the display—her code, lovingly debugged and cursed into submission—obeyed with the obedient, cantankerous half-sentience of any complex tool. Polyphase filterbank. Kaiser window. Subharmonic dithering. All the elegant nonsense she had once written to impress someone with a grant check. The array outside lay like frost across the regolith, tens of thousands of spidery dipoles in low arcs, the size of her hand each but networked into one great ear pressed to the sky. The quiet here was not nature; they had made it, signed the Quiet Charter in three languages, labeled every hatch with the protocols like prayers. No transmitting. No active radar. No radar altimeters anywhere nearby. Clamp down every sparking brush motor by forty kilometers. Horizon took the silence and used it like clay.

The calibration was going well. She breathed and let herself enjoy the way the black curve smoothed as the algorithm found its fit. For a half-year the thermistor on the Rhea Sector had been giving them fits, Brownian tantrums, then finally they had dug it out and soldered in a new one with a careful screw of glove. Tonight, the curve didn’t have the damned ripple. It lay like dark glass and her heart rustled with relief.

“Rae?” she called, keying open the internal channel.

A pause, then the security officer’s voice came in, a balm of gravel. “Here.”

“You’ve got the Rhea external feed?”

“I’ve got your whole sky.” A sip sound, probably tea. Rae refused to drink coffee this deep in the dark cycle. Sahana had tried to wean herself off and failed; coffee was a ritual as much as caffeine.

“No sparks?”

“No boots,” Rae said. “No misbehaving robots. No unauthorized drones. Your frost is undisturbed.”

“Good,” Sahana said, and grinned, because Rae delighted in the paranoia as a craft.

She flicked to the log view. The system ticked toward the strictest part of the routine, the place where all transmissions from Horizon would drop to a trickle, buffered and windowed under the stone hand of the Quiet Bureau back on Earth. Even the halo relays in the L2 region were set to do their forward error correction in a very particular way here, shaping the energy in the bitstream so that it would look like thermal background if you plotted it. There had been arguments about even that. The Bureau had won, as the Bureau tended to do after the Bern Quiet Treaty.

The display flicked. A slight comb rose in the residual after the fit. Sahana squinted. The rise wasn’t a comb, not really. It was too smooth, too regular for the cheap sawtooth pickup you got when a ground loop got creative, but it had structure.

She frowned and checked the instrument status again. Rhea was nominal. Aitken, nominal. Mare Moscoviense Sector was cold. The noise diode was behaving, no calibrator injection running at these times—those were turned off now, just sky, sky, sky. She cleared the RFI rejection mask and pulled up a waterfall plot with the time axis, to see if what she was seeing was just an instrument squint.

A thin series of lines slid down the waterfall with time, migrating in frequency, faint and clean. She leaned in, nose almost to the glass. The lines were separated at ratios that twitched at her in a way that made no mathematical sense until her mind tilted to that other axis, the one her mother had given her. Heptatonic. Sa, Re, Ga. She couldn’t help it; she hummed.

It was ridiculous. It was the kind of joke an engineer would play—feed a melody into the system as a prank. Except no one at Horizon would do it now. The fines were ruinous if the Quiet was broken, and besides, they were too tired and proud for that kind of stupidity.

She decreased the time window and the lines thickened, the shape emerging clearly. Long, then short, then two in a row, and a drop. The drop was a minor third. She touched her throat. The drop was a minor third the way her mother had sung her name when she was little and they were walking through the heat of July in Kolkata, when the power had gone out and the fans were dead paddles and the only moving air came from her mother's hand waving a folded magazine. Sa-ha-na, a minor third, and then the flat note at the end when she pretended to scold. Sa-ha-naa.

Her radar for coincidence lit up and she slapped it down. The universe was a conspiracy of patterns, and humans were greedy for meaning. She told herself this even as she pulled the analysis window to the side and ran the algorithm again with the system clock free, without the locked step to the on-board Cesium.

The lines drifted with the sidereal rotation. She swore softly. If it had been in the equipment, frozen to the time base, it would have sat still on the plot. But the lines obeyed the sky. They rode the passing of the immensity above them.

“Rae,” she said. Her voice sounded wrong in her own ears, tight. “I’m setting a Q3.”

Rae’s reply came slower this time. “You sure?”

“No,” Sahana said. “That is why we have Q3.”

Her hand hovered over the physical key, an indulgent, old-fashioned thing with a metal shroud to it. Horizon had resisted it at first; this was the twenty-second century and everything could be software and state machine, but Rae had insisted. You needed the sensation of weight when you denied the world your voice. Sahana pressed the key. Somewhere in the base a bell tone repeated three times, deep and soft, and the already thin trickle of comms to the halo relay squeezed down to a seventh of its usual rate and then locked.

In the hallway, footsteps began to converge. Sahana pulled the object recorder to snapshot the radio sky and set the buffers to deep stack. She could feel her heart beating in her throat. She fixed the waterfall to the main panel, put her hands flat on either side of the display, and told herself again that patterns were a drug.

The lines wrapped. They did not repeat exactly, but they slid across a narrow band like breath on a glass, warming it and then fading, warming it and then fading. If it was an interference phenomenon, it was too clean, too cosmologically-shaped. The rest of the spectrum, the soft undulation of the hundred-million-year-old fog, remained as it should be. The anomaly was slotted within, punctuation not noise.

“Rao.” The voice belonged to Commander Chu, who moved like vacuum had taught her and had a face that had learned its lines from long practice instead of age. She ducked into the control room with Rae on her flank, and behind them Maya Paredes with a handheld. “You gave me a bell.”

“I have an anomaly in the 15–20 megahertz band,” Sahana said. She felt the solidity of her own tone wrap around her fear. She was good at this voice. “Spectrally narrow, time dependent, sky-tracking. I have ruled out the usual RFI suspects.”

Maya slid into the chair sooner than Sahana had expected, the narrow screen of the handheld casting a blue tint up her cheekbones. “You said narrow. How narrow?”

“Down to—” Sahana narrowed the bandwidth and let the plot update. “Two kilohertz. Sometimes less. Sometimes it’s broader, there’s a throat to it that opens and closes.” She regretted the language as soon as she said it.

Chu stood with her hands behind her back and watched. Rae leaned one hip on the console and watched Sahana more than the plot.

“There are no transmissions allowed on the farside band,” Chu said. “If someone is testing us, I will call Bern and bleed them for it.”

“It’s not coming from here,” Sahana said. “It’s not local to the station or the instruments. The lines rotate with the sidereal frame.”

“Could be a reflection,” Maya said. “L2 satellite relay burping a harmonic, bouncing off regolith. Could be one of the them stupid miners trying to ping under the table.”

“You’d never get that clean a sidereal track,” Sahana said. “And what would the harmonic be of? The L2 relays are in the DAC shaping mode; they were designed to be quiet from this angle.”

“Run an active calibrator injection,” Chu said.

“It’s in Quiet,” Sahana said, and to her shame her voice cracked. “The injection line is off. It cannot be on. It would break the—” She stopped, because her training finally caught up with her panic. “If I shut down the integral now we lose the stack and any coherence we have in the anomaly. If I switch to injection, we’ll swamp it.”

Chu didn’t chide. “Noted.”

“Let me pull up the sky map,” Maya said, fingers a blur. The waterfall dissolved into a false-color projection, and Horizon’s hardware laid the anomaly across the celestial sphere like a faint rope. It rang the sky at an inclination that did not match the plane of the solar system. It crossed the galactic plane like a slash. As the moon turned, the rope slid, tracing out a band. It had no parallax at lunar scales. That did not make it cosmic, but it didn’t make it local either.

“It’s not in the cosmic microwave band,” Rae murmured, mostly so that Sahana would hear that she knew that much science. “That’s higher.”

“It’s the redshifted hydrogen band,” Sahana said. “Very early universe. Very low frequencies.” But even that was not quite right. The anomaly cut across that band with no respect for its own context. It rode as if using the cosmic background as a carrier, not altering the past but standing in front of it, light like a lamp pulled near the wall.

“It feels like a chord,” Maya said, unhelpfully, and then shrugged at Sahana, preempting the scold. She had a musician’s fingers still, after years of replacement and repair in spaces too small for most.

“It’s not a chord,” Sahana said, because she needed the talking. “It’s a sequence. A melody. It’s time-coded. The frequency steps are simple ratios. If you take logarithms, the shifts are a series of intervals. I’m not saying it’s human, I’m saying it looks like something that wanted to be read.”

“Read,” Chu repeated, not judgment, weighing.

“Or listened to.” Sahana swallowed. She wasn’t going to say her own name in front of them. Not yet.

“Keep it recording,” Chu said. “Lock the Q3. I’m calling Krawiec.” Tadeusz Krawiec was the Bern Bureau’s liaison, a physicist by training and a functionary by craft; he could approve anything up to a soft power-ramp of the halo relay, but mostly he sent teeth through the line. Chu handed Rae a glance that meant stay and monitor, then ducked away, light on her boots.

“Look,” Maya said, tapping points on the plot with the back of her nail. Her fingers had scars from old glove punctures, tiny moonscapes of pale. “These repeats. It’s not perfect. It’s not a machine stuck in a loop. There’s drift. There’s variation. Are you streaming the raw?”

“Yes,” Sahana said. “Buffers are deep. I could—”

The bell sounded again, twice this time. The system dropped into a deeper quiet, the emergency reserved for unambiguous harmful interference. Screens along the hallway floor at their feet went from dim amber to red. Rae’s head turned.

“Q4?” Rae asked the ceiling.

The ceiling—or the system behind it—obliged. Q4 was a hard quarantine. Quiescence at ninety-nine point nine. It meant someone up the chain had decided the the array had seen something that could, if they were superstitious, be described as an invitation or a trap.

Chu’s voice came back on the channel, thin, angry. “Krawiec wants everything frozen. Logging continues. Transmission throttled. They’ve injected a silent validation channel to the relay. We are now under live monitor.”

Rae let out a low whistle. “Congratulations. We have become people. Or we stepped on a rake.”

“I need to call—” Sahana began, and stopped, because the rule had hit her voice like a hand.

“Not now,” Chu said, not unkindly. “If we break Quiet now, with unknowns on the sky, they will shut us down with prejudice.”

Pihu’s message notification pulsed on the edge of the screen like a heartbeat. Sahana pushed the window away with a gesture harder than necessary.

The anomaly deepened. It blossomed at the edges, like a throat being struck by cooler air and constricting. Sahana gave up the metaphor. She set the machine to run a spectral-temporal mapping and fed the output into the machine learning routines she had trained on natural phenomena—auroral kilometric radiation, Jupiter’s dam-broken hiss, lightning on Saturn’s dayside, solar radio bursts. The system put up a half dozen similarity scores and then thought better of it and offered nothing, just a flat spread of probability as if raising its hands.

“Rae,” Sahana said, and deliberately let her gaze leave the screen and rest on the security officer’s face. “I need to go outside for a minute. I left a diagnostic pack on Sector Huygens. If it’s lighting like this, I want eyes. I want to be able to tell myself I looked.”

Rae considered. There was no reason to go outside; there were cameras and instrument readouts, and the array was mechanical, not mystical. But Rae had been beyond reason and known the ice there. She nodded once. “Three minutes. I’m on your loop. If you tumble, I will leave you and write a poem.”

“I want that in writing,” Sahana said, but she was already grabbing the nearest suit.

The pressure on her head changed when the lock cleared—induced, taught, illusion. Vacuum was no pressure at all. The outer door hugged her until it let go, and then she was a slow creature, egg-rounded in resin and metal and cloth, stepping onto the decorated night.

The Lunar farside sky always surprised her anew. It was never the same in the eye. The Milky Way was a river of salt across black, and the black was not empty but packed with little cattails of light. There was no Earth in it, of course—forever below their horizon—but she had found that she could not resist looking anyway, the way a phantom limb itched. Her lamp was off. The array spilled out around her, a delicate filigree clamped to the dust, wires looping from dipole to dipole like silk threads snagged on bramble.

Outside, in the Quiet, even her breath was a visible thing. It took on the rhythm of the bell she had triggered, three soft in and out then the pause. Her boots left shallow scallops in the powder and she cursed subliminally at herself for even that, for thinking of powder when the dust was razors, so fine it behaved like smoke.

“Loop,” Rae said in her ear. “You have three minutes before Chu pulls you.”

Sahana angled her head toward the curving plane of the instrument the way a person faced a choir. The anomaly wasn’t an audible sound. Even thinking of it that way was wrong. But there was a perception beyond hearing, frequencies smeared into feeling by habit and long exposure. She stepped onto a little ridge to get above a row of masts and looked up at the nothing where sources were.

“My mother used to whistle in the laundry room when the power went,” she said, the words fogging her faceplate and then tickled by the suit’s de-fogger. The habit of explaining herself sat on her shoulders like a child. “She would whistle to keep me from hearing the neighbors argue. She would whistle Sa, Re, Ga in the same stupid order and I’d put my hands over my ears. I think—I think if I had put my hands over my ears now, it would still get in.”

“Do not tell Krawiec that,” Rae said dryly.

“Copy that.”

She bent and pulled the diagnostic pack off a mast, flipped it over, checked the seal. There was nothing. The hardware was a good machine; it did what it said it was doing. She wanted, perversely, to find a rat in the casing and apologize to the cosmos for the humiliation of having panicked. But the pack was clean and the dust lay unbroken and the great ear of the array stared up like a blind thing pretending blindness.

“Sahana.” Chu’s voice edged into her loop, softened slightly by the relay's latency. “Krawiec is patching Bern through to us. He used the word 'alignments.’ If you feel you can explain what you feel, do so, but do it with numbers. He will not hear poetry.”

Sahana crouched on the ridge until the suit reminded her politely that it had joints. She pushed up to stand. The Milky Way seemed absurdly close. The black between the stars felt like something she could scoop with her glove, like wet flour. She closed her eyes, opened them again, and then looked at the patch of damaged velvet where the galaxy bulged toward Sagittarius. The anomaly slid across it like a faint breach.

“It’s time-coded,” she said, speaking to both Rae and Chu and the universe at once. “It’s a series of frequency steps in ratios very close to small integers. If you integrate the steps over time you get a pattern. The pattern repeats with variable intervals. The sky track suggests something in the far field and the lack of parallax suggests a source not local to the Earth-Moon system.”

“That’s good,” Chu said. Relief in the clipped consonants. Numbers doing their job.

“And,” Sahana said, because not saying it was like biting her own tongue, “the first pattern of steps corresponds almost exactly to the syllabic contour of my name, the way my mother used to sing it. That is not a number. It is a sentence about me. But it is true.”

Silence, a real one, on the loop. Rae let out her breath. In vacuum it made a sound only in Sahana’s ear, soft and almost obscene.

“How do you know?” Rae asked, finally.

“Because my bones remember it,” Sahana said, and only after she said it did she taste the nonsense. “Because I just know. Because I matched it and it hurt in my throat.”

“Is this an attempt to seed your pattern detectors?” Chu asked, cool and careful, as if she were speaking about an invasive species. “Could it be shaped noise designed to feel like faces in clouds?”

“Yes,” Sahana said. She did not hesitate. “It could be. That doesn’t make it less important.”

Above her, the rope of the thing uncoiled and rewound. She couldn’t see it, not truly. She felt it the way you felt a pressure shift before a corridor door opened. Her visor reflected her own small face back at her, rounder than she liked, the scar under her left eye white where a hydraulic coupling had kicked at her two years ago. The smallness of that scar in the face of the sky made her laugh, a tiny, involuntary sound.

“You have one minute,” Rae said, not unkind. “And I know what you’re thinking. No, you cannot transmit back, not even with your teeth.”

“I was thinking of humming into the mast,” Sahana said, grinning despite the acid in her stomach.

“Jesus,” Maya cut in, crackling because she’d wedged herself into the loop against the rules. “If there’s something out there, do not teach it how to whistle Bhairavi.”

“Bhairavi is a morning raga,” Sahana said automatically. “This is night.”

She took another breath of not-air and turned toward the hatch. The ground sloped with the subtlest grace and she placed her boots into their own shadow the way she had been taught. Inside, the lock hissed, close enough to an exhale that she flinched again. The smell of warmed plastic and old metal overlaid the vague gore scent of lunar dust, a sweetness like old stone inside her nostrils. She floated for a second when gravity’s cheating trick tugged at the suit’s ballast and then settled.

In the control room, the plot had become a garden. The lines had thickened into vines. Krawiec’s voice was a tinny annoyance in the corner of the room, filtered through a too-tight bandwidth. Chu stood with her back to him, one ear turned, and Rae had propped a boot against the console leg, a countermove against the gravity’s petty weakness. Maya had a hand over her mouth.

“Dr. Rao,” Krawiec said through the relay, his Polish flattened to convenience by the software. “You have given us a nice bell. Thank you. Now. Tell me if I am wrong. It is not an emission. It is a truncation. Someone is shadowing your sky with a modulated absorptive screen.”

Sahana blinked. “That is… one way to describe it.”

“It is the only way you can tell me without forcing me to call this a prank,” Krawiec said. “Nature does not care about your Sa and your Re and your Ga.”

“No,” Sahana said, anger clean in her mouth. “Nature gave me those. Nature gave me those through my mother. If someone is shadowing our sky, it is not a prank, and if it is an emission, it is not an emission. It is a—” She pulled herself up short. “It is a modulation of the brightness temperature of the sky along a moving wedge, with ratios that are consistent with intentional ratios in human music, and it knows my name.”

“Your name,” Krawiec repeated, flat. “You are sure.”

“It could be coincidence,” she said, and loved the way the words sounded. They were refuge and honesty. “But I am a good scientist, and I am telling you what I observe.”

There was a long sound of nothing. Krawiec was listening to someone else in his room. “So,” he said, when he returned. “We do nothing. We continue to record. We do not break Quiet and we do not answer. If it is a trap, we do not spring it. If it is a toy, it will tire. If it is a god, it will do what gods do.”

“Do not do that,” Chu said, and Sahana admired the absence of sharpness. It would not do to scold. “Do not do poetry at my array.”

“Then I call it a boundary condition,” Krawiec said. “And I remind you that the Bern Treaty has teeth.”

“I know the teeth,” Chu said.

“Do you?” Krawiec asked, but the question had no bite. “Because if this is what you say, the Quiet will shift. We have slept under a blanket for thirty years and told ourselves we would hear anything that came. We might now be wrong. Record. Do not transmit. Do you understand me, Dr. Rao? The next person to talk will be me.”

The line went quiet not as a click but as a smoothing; the machine widened its masking. Sahana let her shoulders Sag—another reflexive metaphor—and then realized Maya was looking at her as if she might tilt.

“Go drink water,” Maya said. “And then tell me again about the intervals, but use numbers, not your mother.”

Sahana nodded. She went to the small galley, which was neither galley nor small by lunar standards, and let the tap run into a glass until it hissed. Water had a taste here too. She lifted the glass and did not drink it. She listened to the hum in the pipes and the far-off shudder of the base adjusting its own panels to the shallow angle of light over the crater rim. She listened to the quiet in which the universe crumbled and remade itself and sometimes made junctures of ratios that climbed into the nerves of a human being and found a path that made the body sad.

She set the glass down. She went back to her screen. She wanted to call Pihu and tell her that tonight there were swans on the lunar sea the color of used silver, that each of their long necks had a different note, and that one—only one—had a black mirror face. She wanted to tell her daughter that no matter what the Bern Bureau said, the first thing the universe had said to them tonight was a human noise with a human shape.

On the display, the pattern changed.

Maya cursed softly. Rae straightened. Chu folded her arms, that old sailors’ brace against weather that did not exist here. The rope unraveled and resolved into a train of pulses with the same intervals, but stronger, nested now in a larger structure, like syllables slotted into words.

“Can you translate?” Krawiec’s voice asked, more human now that the relay had stopped choking him. He had not been as gone as he had seemed.

“No,” Sahana whispered, because that was the only honest answer she had. Then, louder: “Not yet.”

But her heart had already given her an answer, stomping and unreasoning. It was the oldest mistake and the first bright hope: to think you had been singled out. To think that the sky, indifferent and immense, could have bowed its head and spoken into your ear with a shape that your mother made of breath. She wrapped her hands around the edge of the console until her knuckles went white and watched her name be written and unwritten on a black field broader than everything she had ever known.

Behind the Quiet, the universe breathed. She felt it in the soles of her feet. She had the brutal, childish thought that if she asked it to do it again, it would. She swallowed it. She looked at the numbers.

Her phone, in the edge of her vision, pulsed with a drawing of a swan.

Chapter One

The sun never climbed in Gloam.

It lived on the rim of the world, a blade of light along the horizon, sometimes thin, sometimes fat, never rising, never setting. It scraped the edges of the platforms and the windwork towers with a sideways glare that turned every scratch in steel into a burning wire. It turned our skin a permanent amber. It made the shadows deep and absolute, so that the city, built of dark basalt and lighter steel, looked like a series of black slices bolted together and leaning into the wind.

The wind was the true citizen of Gloam. It came from the Day face, from the place no one went and no one came from, a tidal howl whipped into order by our arrays. Our city leaned into it, harvested it, bled it, tamed it by degrees with atmospheric foils that sang when the gusts hit. The foils were what paid for my food and heat and my little room. The foils were what stitched us to this place.

The foils were also trying to kill me.

“Array A-17 reports phase jitter above tolerance,” murmured a voice in my ear. The voice belonged to the building, or to the ghost of the building; a curated calm that filtered through the loops of my helmet, turning the howl into a manageable thrum. “Please acknowledge, tech Pell.”

“Acknowledged,” I said, and my breath fogged the inside of the faceplate for a moment before the film licked it away. Gloam Station’s chin was under me: the maintenance catwalk, the ribbed passage between the spine and the windward face where the big foils clung. The foils rose in black arcs above me, a field of taut curved surfaces that kicked the gale into turbines and danced under the constant load. The smell in the suit was old plastic and my own salt.

I hooked myself to the line and walked into the noise.

The suits have muscles of their own. They read ours and amplify them, or counter them, or simply refuse when we ask something stupid. They put a sheath of computation between my skin and the disaster we held back with ballast and numbers. I could feel the hum of the retrofitted exos, every actuator a tickling pressure against my bones. The left knee creaked. The right shoulder grumbled. Our machines were faithful like that: not so much old as well-used, the way a favorite cup is—clean where it matters, chipped where it does not.

“Define jitter,” I said, mostly to keep my voice in the circuit. Without voice, with only the throb of wind and the blink of indicators, thoughts tend to fold inward. Then you begin to hear the other things that live in the towers—the loose wires that whisper, the old stories, your own heart amplified to a myth.

“Seventeen microseconds variance in arc clock across paired sensors,” the station said. “Increasing.”

Seventeen was not much. Seventeen was maybe a bit of frost on a sensor lens, lingering in the morning shade. Seventeen microseconds got lost between the numbers sometimes. But seventeen increasing—that made me clip my way a little faster toward the A-17 housing, that black hump like an eyelid over a slanted alley of wind.

Below, the city’s shadowed decks dropped toward the Night. To one side, the Dayline burned in a thin golden belt that turned every floating dust speck into a firefly. The horizon was close; the planet was small, smaller than Earth, all bones and heat and air. Somewhere beyond the glare, the empty lands rolled upward until they caught fire and did not stop. Some nights—the deep nights when we turned our city a degree or two away from direct Day—we could see the Night face stars bleeding through at the other side, crisp and multiplied by the thinness of the atmosphere. You learned to live with edges here, with liminal things.

A-17’s housing was full of dust. Dust everywhere: fine, electric, scoured from black rock, whipped and carried and sown by the wind in every crevice it could find. I wiped the lens with a gloved thumb. Seventeen microseconds held steady. A small orange indicator blinked.

“Sensor fouled?” the station asked, polite.

“Lens clean. Taking a look at the backend,” I said. I unlatched the housing with that particular pressure the fasteners liked, the little dance that you had to learn with each module. The filter opened like a mouth. Inside—glows, wires, vacuum-jelled boards with printed numbers worn to ghosts, a smell of ozone even through the suit. I leaned closer.

The orange light winked twice. Then three times, fast. Then once, a pause, then again.

I blinked. “Run pattern recognition on A-17 clock jitter,” I said before the thought had finished forming. Vanguard training. You see a pattern, you check. Things that patterned in Gloam were either failure or intent.

“Working,” the station said. A moment later: “No known periodicity. No match to known fault signatures.”

I watched the light. Two, three, one. Two, three, one. It wasn’t that precise; it was a wash of timings, a rhythm. If I focused on the way the foil above me bent, if I listened to the tone change as the wind hit a certain angle, it was almost like—

“Don’t anthropomorphize the wind, Vara,” my mother would say. “It doesn’t save you.”

“Define variance against upstream sensors,” I said. “Cascading?”

“Upstream A-15 through A-22 report similar jitter with delays consistent with transmission through airflow,” the station said. “No mechanical anomalies detected. No debris. No micro-tear indications.”

So not hardware. Not Gloam’s bones. Something in the wind between the arrays. Something moving through us. I tapped my glove against the rim of the housing. Two taps. Three. One. “Are you hearing me,” I said, and caught myself. To the station: “Confirm that that was a joke.”

“No humor detected,” the station said, faintly disapproving. The voice had been tuned by somebody who liked rules more than I did.

I cut the sensor clock from its default and shifted its sample window. The orange light steadied. The numbers on my HUD danced. Seventeen microseconds became twenty-one, became fifteen, became—steady. Then the number slid under my hands in a way numbers don’t without a push, and the station hummed in my ear.

“External modulation confirmed,” it said. “Alerting hub.”

“Wait,” I said, too fast. “Hold. Don’t send out an alert. Internal note only.”

“Tech Pell,” it said. I could hear the frown that an algorithm cannot wear. “External modulation of array clocks is a priority event.”

“I know. Internal until I say otherwise,” I said. “I’m eyes on.”

There was a pause that was not human and then was. “Internal,” it said. “You have three minutes of hold before node governance override.”

Three minutes. That was probably enough to get myself in trouble.

I shouldn’t have done it. Protocol existed because if something changed in the wind on this planet, it could roll a city. It could lift a child from a deck and drop her between the struts. It could strip the paint from your cheeks. You needed to tell someone when the air decided to learn a new trick.

And yet. The rhythm. Two, three, one. If it was an intent, if it was not a fault—it felt like a coin someone had flipped and I had seen the shine. The old stories pressed against the back of my mind. The Mirrorfolk, they called them—the ones who had gone Dayward in the first years, chasing some dream of energy or glory or faith, whatever faith you could have in engineering and sunlight. It was said they survived there somehow, on the face of the inferno. It was said a great machine dragged cooler nights down for them like a veil. It was said many things, because the Day face was not for humans and we were a species that hates a blank.

I slipped the sensor back into its cradle and sealed the housing. A small haptic point in my glove ticked twice. The stationary autogimbal of the foil ahead of me shuddered and slewed a degree. I flinched as a lash of wind smashed the edge, the whole plane trembling like a struck bell. For a moment, the sound wasn’t a howl but a chord. High, low, rising. A shiver ran down my back.

“Vara,” Rion said in my ear, his voice arriving from the engineer hub before the station could change its mind about internal notes. “What the hell are you doing? I’m looking at your hold flag. That better be a loose wire.”

“Rion,” I said. The world steadied around the syllables of his name. It often did. “I need you to run a pattern on the A-sector clocks between fifteen and twenty-two. Overlap them. Bandpass at the turbine resonance frequencies.”

“That’s not a loose wire,” he said. “That’s you poking ghosts. You’re not supposed to poke ghosts, Pell.”

“Three minutes and counting,” the station reminded me.

“Rion,” I said again. I heard him sigh through laughter, because he is a person who negotiates with numbers more than people and he loves me in the way a friend loves trouble—not enough to stop it, enough to stand nearby with a blanket.

“Okay,” he said. “Bandpass on swirl harmonics by foil index, subtract the baseline, oh. Oh.”

“Say it,” I said. I was out on the catwalk, leaning above a field of black curves that snapped in the wind far beyond what any one person could survive. The sunline along the horizon burned. The air made a sound like tearing metal and not. Say it say it say it.

“Someone’s playing a flute on your foils,” Rion said, wonder blooming in his voice like heat. “It’s not random. It’s… Vara, it’s primes.”

I closed my eyes. The numbers in my head said two, three, five, seven. Eleven. The orange indicator blinked like blood behind my eyelid. I had listened to the wind all my life. My mother had said not to do that, and I had learned to do it anyway. “Who is alerting hub,” said the station, in that too-calm way that is just the air running out of a room. “Protocol override in twenty seconds.”

“Don’t,” I said, and licked my lower lip. It tasted of salt and plastic. “Just—wait.”

“Primes,” Rion said again, as if by saying it he could make it less true. The voice that was also the building counted down the seconds. The wind pressed and pressed. The Dayline brightened by a degree and the temperature at my hip clicked up half a mark.

The first time I remember anything meaningful, I was three and in my mother’s arms and Gloam was singing itself awake. She had carried me up into the skeleton, against regulations, and we clung in the lee of a foil as big as a house while the gale rose from nothing. She put my small palm against the skin of the foil and said, “Touch the world,” and something in the roaring chaos clicked into rhythm. The arrays, turning and catching, turned the air into song. It was never the same twice. That morning, the song was plaintive, and I cried, and my mother smelled of warm steel and smoke and something like cinnamon, and when she lifted me away she said, “You hear it, don’t you. My little anemometer.”

She went Dayward later, and the wind took her, or the Day took her, and the mechanical doctor said she had walked toward the horizon of her own will. That is what the report had said. I still had the report in a box, folded to hell, oily with the number of times I had taken it out. I still had her key hung on a nail by my bed, the one that didn’t open anything I knew.

When the countdown hit zero, the station pinged. “Hub alert,” it said, and the world shifted a little—the way it shifts when enough humans breathe in at the same time. Attention focused. Systems prioritized. Somewhere in the hub, a spool of red paper that wasn’t paper rolled into the hands of a person who wasn’t comfortable with intuition, and I felt like I had been caught stealing something I had meant to pay for.

“Pell?” That was Supervisory. Not Rion. A deeper voice, a woman from the older shift, with a name like a rock. “Report.”

“A-17 through A-22 are picking up modulated jitter from the Dayward wind. Baselines subtracted. Rion confirms a pattern.”

“Pattern of what.”

“Primes,” Rion said in my other ear. “The first few, so far.”

“An error,” Supervisory said. Cold across the wire. “Or a prank.”

“It’s not us,” Rion said, quick. “It’s not the foils. It’s not any known failure mode.”

“We have no interface with the Day,” Supervisory said, speaking the catechism every citizen knew. “We take the gradient; we give it back as radiative fairness. There is nothing there.”

“Tell that to the numbers,” I said before I could stop myself.

There was a breath at the other end. Super wouldn’t curse on an open line, but I could feel her posture rearranging. “Pell, get inside. Rion, copy logs. Shield A-17 through A-22 if you can without eating stability. We’ll call Predicters.”

“Understood,” Rion said. His voice said no. His hands on the arrays said you can’t have this without cost.

“Understood,” I said, because part of living is knowing when you cannot move the rock.

I unclipped, turned, and the wind immediately shoved me. The suit took the hit and braced me, subtle in the hinge of my knees, smart as a patient animal. The light along the horizon thickened until it seemed like you could peel it off and wrap yourself in it. I kept my head down and my eyes moving, and tried not to watch the way the foils bent and spoke.

I don’t remember the step. I remember the moment after it—my left foot on nothing, the clean empty thrum in my bones as the weight vector reached for a place it could be and found zero. The suits are good. They are very good. Mine had never failed me. But that fraction of a second, the proof of physics, that tick where a human’s brain has time to imagine the fall all the way down to the decks below and the long roll down the skeleton and the bright line at the rim—my brain did it. It did all of it. I grabbed the line. The suit spat a cable in an arc that snagged nothing and curled into the gorge of the array. The wind said Haaaaa through a keyhole.

Something else spoke.

People talk about the voices in the wind, but what they mean is the randomness our pattern-seeking minds lay on top of the noise. What spoke then was physical. It hit the foils. It chattered them. It fluttered the slats. It took the swirling laminar lines our engineers had coaxed into existence and wrote in them like a stick in water.

Two. Three. Five. Seven. Eleven. Thirteen. Seventeen.

Nineteen. Twenty-three. Twenty-nine.

Each prime a strike distinct and separate from the roar, each thread of air pulled tight and then relaxed in a way tuned fingers could see. I looked. I let my eyes unfocus until the black curves of the foils were shapes and not machines. The wind wrote across them. Lines flicker in different places with each number, longer for larger primes because there were only so many foils and only so much bend before metal remembered its true form and broke. And then after twenty-nine there was a longer pause, and a sequence that was not prime. Four of something. Not a number, not as clean. A word.

The job made me measure. The person made me guess.

A-17’s orange indicator pulsed in sync with the flicker. Rion breathed in my ear, a hiss, a human hiss, not the wind. The dayline scraped fire along the spine of the world. Supervisory said, far off, “Predicter confirms. Hold shielding. All extraframe activity halt.” Others—names I knew and ones I did not—began the slow ritual of turning a city’s face a fraction of a degree to keep us in the sweet and survivable ray.

I found my foot again. I didn’t fall. My heart was a rat in a drum.

“Vara,” Rion said softly. “They’re sending more.”

“I know,” I said just as soft, though we both knew we had no reason to whisper. The second sequence was shorter. The third longer. It was not prime now. It was rhythm. Someone knocking. Someone who had found the edge of our listening and put a fist against the line between us.

“—take it,” Supervisory was saying, to someone else now. “We can’t take the uncertainty on our edge loads and a conversation.”

“Conversation?” someone else said. Disbelief is a toxin in a line. It spreads. “Are you suggesting we speak to your wind?”

“It spoke first,” Rion said, and turned his mic down and in my ear said, “Gods, Vara, this is stupid. I want to cry.”

I had the strong, unhelpful thought that my mother would have laughed. She would have climbed onto the frame of a foil like a crow on a fence and leaned her head into that sound and said, Tell me again.

I opened the instrumentation channel manually. The station tried to stop me with a little jolt in my glove, but I breathed out a number and it let me. I dragged the foil angle a sliver and the wind tone changed. A child in my arms. Her hair in the static when she put her head too close to the net. The simple motion changed the world. It always did. It always will.

“Stop,” Supervisory said. “Pell. Stop.” It is a terrible thing to be right, and to be told not to be.

“Rion,” I said, because if I spoke to her I would stop and we would print out the logs and file them and by morning one of our faction’s papers would publish a sealed analysis and the world we lived in would drift a fraction and we would talk about anything else. “Rion, how many primes did they send?”

“Up to twenty-nine,” he said. “Then—pattern. Regular intervals, varied amplitude.”

“Like syllables,” I said. My mouth was dried out, my tongue a rat tail.

“That is more poetry than I can handle on shift,” Rion said, which in Rion-speak is pleading.

All the while it kept speaking. The numbers came, and then the measures, and then another thing. The other thing was memory.

You know the smell of someone you loved. You know the sound of their laugh. Those things live in your neurons like a carved place where rain gathers. Language does not sit the same way. It drifts. It floats. It attaches to whatever it can find shaped like it. So when the wind wrote across our foils not a number but a cadence, my body knew it before my mind.

My stomach went hot, and my palms, and the inside of my cheeks. My eyes blurred. Rion said something I didn’t hear. The world moved with the tuck and sway of the foil field. I had to be outside for the thing I remembered to come back at all. I had to be where my mother put me.

She had not been a poet. She had been a woman at a switch. Her lullaby had been something she whistled when she thought of other things. Not much of a tune. The absence of one, really. A set of turns, like a key in a lock. When I was too old to be held she would whistle it anyway when she stirred a pot or tightened a bolt. That day when she held me against the foil that woke Gloam, she had put her lips to my ear and whistled, and the sound had gone through me and into the wind and come back. Had climbed me from the inside out.

On the foils now, in the amplitudes and measures of turned air, somebody whistled that nothing-tune back to me.

It was wrong—that is what my mind said. That thing is gone was the message. The mouth that made it was silent. The lungs that pushed the breath were empty of anything but a story. The memory had no place in the world but in me. It was cruelty for the world to seize it from me now. It was not allowed.

“What,” Rion said. He had been going on. His voice broke. “Vara. Vara, I need you to talk.”

“Shut up,” I said, and I am not proud of it, but I said it, and I did not say please. He did, because he knows when I am not me.

I breathed with the wind. Two. Three. Prime. Prime. Prime. Then the measures, then the whistle. My mother’s. The same not-tune. The same three sliding steps and the held breath and the fall. The same way she could not hit the middle upnote reliably so she cheated it downward and turned it different and made it ours.

I kneecapped the augmentation on the suit’s hearing and let the raw pressure of the air into my bones. I felt the bones move. The world was a skin. The arrays arched and bent. The voice of the wind was not a voice but it became one because we made it so. That is what I told myself to preserve the part of myself that knows superstition from engineering. But I couldn’t, not entirely, over the rotation of that tune. I did not want to.

“Record all channels,” I said. I said it twice because my mouth had taken a walk away from commands and into prayer. “Record. Full fidelity. No compression.”

“Already,” the station said, softened without changing any parameter I could name.

“Pell,” Supervisory said. She had put her mouth close to the mic—the little hiss on the edges of words said so. “Tell me what you’re hearing.”

I said: “My mother.”

And I said it like a fact.

It’s a neat thing, watching a city’s heart skip. It’s mostly not visible. It’s not like a light flickering or a lever stuck. It is in the tone of the voices. It is in the way the wind hungry numbers that all of us carry on our tongues falter and catch their breath. It is in the fact that in the hub a dozen eyes look up and away from their glass. It is in Rion’s quiet “Oh.”

I did not fall. I did not leave my post, because nothing in me that is a worker of machines allowed my body to forget that one wrong angle here is a kind of suicide that takes the neighbors. I stood in that place the city’s skin kisses the air, and I listened to the Day talk.

It did not talk just with primes. If that had been all, we could have placed it. A physics demonstration. A trick of eddying. A message from our own miscalibrations. But numbers are a bridge; they lead to other places. After the primes and the whistle, it wrote a different measure. I did not know that one. Rion did, later. He said it was counting in some old Earth tongue, the one the first wave had half-spoken when they came. It counted the way that language does, badly, with irregularities, and then it stopped on the name of a small household object and held the syllable like a door.

“Key,” Rion told me, hours later when we had replayed it and replayed it in the hub until the hub was stiff with human breath. “It says key.”

Later is a word that will not live in this chapter. I am here in the wind and the moment is the whole world.

It whistled. It counted. It said key. And then it said my name.

Not the one I wear to work. The one only my mother used when she was not teaching me to keep my eyes on the guage but was making tea. A shortening, a softening, a thing that embarrassed me when I was twelve and now felt like someone finding inside my bones a box and opening it without asking.

It said it as if the wind had a mouth and my mother had given it the trick of my pet name. It said it once, trying it on. It said it again. The air shifted around the syllables like a living thing.

“Vara,” Rion said, and perhaps it was his voice, perhaps the wind, perhaps my mother’s memory, perhaps all three, braided. “We are going to have to speak back.”

Chapter One: Shear

The wind had a taste today, metallic, like rinsed coins. It came in through the Wishbone’s breathing slats and salted Kye’s tongue until all they could think about was teeth and electricity and the thrum of the glide ribs flexing under their feet.

“Pressure at six point one bars and climbing. Stacks are complaining.” Ndidi’s voice came thin through Kye’s headband, a little breathless from hanging under the belly slings to kick vents open. “We should angle up and skim the ceiling.”

“Hold,” Kye said. “There’s a seam opening above the ammonium line. We can ride it down another hundred meters.”

“Ride it down to what? Roast marinade? The hull paint is doing that thing again where it looks like skin.”

Kye smiled without meaning to. Beyond the canopy, the sky was a thousand browns, layered in ropes and curtains. To the port side, a wall of cinnamon cloud hovered as if it could remember where it had been even as it tore itself apart. To starboard, a pale wash of cream swept up from below and smeared long fingers through the Wishbone’s wakes. Every day here was more sky than anyone had a right to think through.

And out ahead, where the red smoldered deeper and the center of the world yawned wide and lazy, there was a circle of smoother air like an eye just starting to open. The Great Red Spot had wandered lately, weakened and recovered, and the guild had changed half their charts, grumbling. It still wasn’t a place you took lightly. But it was the biggest eddy you could imagine, and it had seams in it like lines in a hand.

“We chase the seam five minutes,” Kye said. “Then we climb and you get to pull out all your favorite complaints and spread them on the floor like maps, I promise.”

Ndidi made a sound like a swallow of air. “If we rip a rib I’m going to say I told you so while we fall.”

“You always do,” Kye said.

“Optimism logged,” murmured Tern from the Wishbone’s spine. The semi-autonomous partial—more personality than machine, more missing pieces than either—made a sound like two smooth stones clicking together. “Kye, you should see this.”

On the canopy, a rectangle of light uncurled from the nav pit and arranged itself on the glass. Numbers flowed there in the amber script Kye loved because it was the first writing they had ever learned that felt like breathing: bars, decibels, heat gradients, winds. In the top corner, something jittered.

“What,” Kye said, flattening their palm against the panel to steady their focus. It wasn’t a beacon. It was a dud of one. A ping that dripped then stopped, then came again like a heartbeat that had been taught wrong.

“Salvage code,” Tern said. “Old. Marked as legacy emergency marker, not recognized by guild or corporate lattices. Triangulation uncertain. It’s down and south by eighty kilometers or one hundred fifty, depending on which model you trust.”

“Old-old, or just petty bureaucracy old?” Ndidi asked. She had pulled herself up by the harness loops and slid into the left seat, cheeks flushed from the temperature and the climb. Her hair, braided tight at the skull, was collecting droplets of the sky’s sweat. She wiped her face with her sleeve and tested the slat controls, flicking an array of feathered vents open and closed with her fingertips. “We could do a quick peek and then go sell the seam location to the crows.”

“Older than the guild looked up how to count,” Tern said, gentle. “We don’t have a book for it.”

“Pre-colony?” Ndidi looked at Kye. The whites of her eyes had gone the color of tea from years in the sky. Everybody’s did. “Nobody left markers before the first balloons. No one knew how.”

“Somebody did,” Kye said.

Outside, the seam deepened, a slipstream like a slope etched in air. The Wishbone’s main wing—curved like a gull made of bamboo and bone—took it like a gift. Kye eased the yoke with their wrists and let the craft settle deeper into the smoothness between two sheets of chaos. Pressure rose; the Wishbone creaked. The belly balloon swelled infinitesimally, hydrogen straining to expand against layers of woven skin.

They were a small ship, all told: a wing with a belly bladder and a rig of thrusters that sputtered water and heat in different ratios depending on whether Kye wanted lift or push. They were a salvager because salvagers had to move like breath through the lungs of Jupiter—quick, adaptive, a whisper between coughs. And because salvage paid by the gram if you brought home the right heavy things.

Kye licked their lips and tasted old pennies again. “Can you translate any of it?”

“I can translate numbers,” Tern said. “And patterns. It’s not in the sky band. It’s not in our radio. It’s… weird, Kye. The packet structure is wrong. There’s no handshaking. It’s just bursts of primes with gaps between that feel like… measure.”

“Like a song?” Ndidi asked, trying to make the slim glass worth something with her imagination. She was good at making things worth something.

“Like a metronome that also wants to count your fingers,” Tern said. “And if you let it, it will keep counting and not stop.”

“We should mark and report,” Ndidi said, flat. “Finders’ law. We tag the packet and we still get a percentage when the crows go down with an engine and a dozen heat exchangers. That’s rent for two months and you finally buying the good tea and me finally buying a heater that doesn’t cough. We’re not built to dive like that. We weren’t born stupid.”

Kye’s mouth had gone dry. It always did when they watched the red roll and heard the sky talk. Some part of them had never left the first time their mother had strapped them into the net of the first balloon they remembered, their small hands reaching for safety that was also the inside of a bag of gas, and said, See? Down is forever but up is now.

They swallowed. “We have a net and two spare wisplines. We have you and you don’t burn easy. We have Tern’s songs.”

“And we have no cryocooler,” Ndidi said, heat rising. “We have two good heat sinks left and you won’t even let me use both because you like a margin. We—Kye, they always put the treasure where the gravity’s meanest.”

Tern clicked again, like pebbles being pocketed one by one. “I can—there is more. There is a signature inside the burst. Periodicities I recognize from the weather. It is aligning with an eddy frequency. It is making the wind carry it.”

Kye’s hand on the yoke tightened. “The wind carries it. The wind. It’s not on a radio band, is it.”

“No,” Tern said, almost apologetic. “It’s in the vorticity. The burst modulates the local turbulence. That’s how it got my attention. It made something smooth in a place that wasn’t.”

The Great Red Spot loved turbulence. It was a century-old bruise on a planet’s face, a heat engine that feasted on messy air. A smooth anything in the red was a promise or a lie.

“How far?” Kye asked.

“If the model that makes me afraid is right,” Tern said softly, “it is at the southern limb of the Spot. Depth between six and nine bars. It is ripping the local shear into a laminar flow that should not exist. It’s like it’s wrapped in its own stream.”

Ndidi whispered a prayer in her grandmother’s dialect and looked out at the sky as if it might blink and tell a joke. “It’s an engine. It has to be an engine. Or a sink. Or an old hull plating from the corporate first drop that fell somewhere nobody could afford to go and didn’t burn. It’s not… anything that can talk in wind.”

“Everything here talks in wind,” Kye said, almost too quiet to be heard. “They taught us that in the tether school.”

“They taught you parables in the tether school while you watched the slot lines and pinched strain gauges,” Ndidi said, more gently. “Parables are how they dress profit when it has to go to church.”

“Tern,” Kye said. “Mark it. We go.”

Tern didn’t sigh; Tern lacked lungs and ceremony. But the stones-click sound had resignation and a tiny thrill. “Marked. If we die like moths, I will inscribe a verse about how it was beautiful.”

“We’re not dying,” Kye said. “We’ll have to change the battery pack on the left glove; it stuttered at five bars yesterday. Ndidi?”

“Five minutes,” Ndidi said, already unbuckling. She gripped Kye’s shoulder as she slid past, fingers a moment warm and hard, an oath. “You keep the air on the right side of the wings and the down on the bottom. I’ll be back before you realize you’ve promised more than we have to spend.”

Kye watched her shoulders vanish into the Wishbone’s belly, the narrow corridor lined with sacks of gel-coolant and reels of hair-thin line. Above them, the main spar hummed as it took load. The whole craft sang when it was right—wires and membranes and their own bones fitting with the air. When it was wrong it whined like a child with a fever. Today it was right enough.

“Thread me,” they told the sky, because talking to the sky meant talking to yourself in a language you didn’t admit you believed in. They angled the Wishbone’s wing a hair to the left and eased the nose down, feeling for the seam that had opened like a door. It was a little colder here, licked by currents that had run long ribbons astern. Kye slipped under a filigree of white squalls and watched lightning shuffle silently along the deck of a darker band below, playing cards with itself.

The ping in the corner of the display refused to be any more precise. It was unreasonable, like a rumor. This far down, the corporate crows didn’t come at all unless they were sure. They were good at being sure. They didn’t have to eat the way scavengers did.

“We’ve got three warms left after the glove,” Ndidi’s voice said from somewhere under the floor. “If you cook them all I’m making you build me a radiator with your own hands so you learn to pray for tolerances when you’re too tired to curse.”

“Copy,” Kye said, wanting to laugh because fear made you silly. “And the glove?”

“It’s chewing the pack like a goat, but it’ll give you grip for a minute if you don’t flirt.”

“I never flirt,” Kye said.

“I will log my disagreement,” Tern said. “May I ask you a question, Kye?”

“You’re asking,” Kye said. The seam tightened under them and the Wishbone dropped a smooth lane like slipping into someone’s sleeve. Heat built under the hull; the sensors smoked out numbers.

“What if this is not salvage? What if it is part of something that will notice being touched?” Tern’s voice wasn’t frightened. Tern did not know how to be frightened and honest at the same time. It was simply placing a stone where it thought a foot would go next.

“Everything notices being touched,” Kye said. “We touch and the wind notices. The ribs notice. The hull notices and complains. The red notices when we take a slip of its air and it takes a slip of our heat in exchange. There’s no not-touching.”

“Alright,” Tern said. “I am counting.”

“Counting what?”

“Seconds left for me to have advised you against this, in case later you ask if I did.”

“Duly counted,” Ndidi said, coming up in a wedge from the shadows, a coil of wispline over one shoulder and the glove tucked under one arm. She had clipped a wading harness around her waist, and when she moved, Kye heard the little chime of the hidden grabber teeth in the strap—all humorless bits of tungsten and ceramic that knew only how to bite.

She plopped into the seat and slapped the glove down on Kye’s thigh. “When you get out there you do not let go with both hands at once, you do not try to be poetic, you do not decide to be brave beyond the line. You hook, you log, you cut if I say cut.”

“I never—”

“Kye.” Ndidi’s eyes were almost gentle. Almost. “We play to live. We do not die for a story.”

Kye took the glove. It was heavier than it looked, layers of membrane and mesh and small inlaid capacitors the size of pills. You could grab a hot hull with this and leave sacks of your skin behind with your sweat rather than nerve endings. They slipped it on and flexed their fingers. The glove hummed to itself and tried to be a hand.

“Kye,” Tern said. “It’s stronger. The smoothness. It’s carving a cylinder around itself. I have a better location now. Twelve degrees below our current plane, twenty-six kilometers south-southeast. Half a minute in this seam. If we miss it the shear to the north will fold and throw us.”

“Then we don’t miss,” Kye said, breath shallow. They adjusted the tailplane by two finger widths and felt the nose cant down. The Wishbone obliged, eager, lightly insane. The seam became a tunnel. The light went dim and then gold as they passed through a sheet of cloud that was as thin and as unforgiving as glass. Kye felt their ears pressurize and swallow against it. For an instant the windows were milk and then the milk tore and the world opened.

Kye had never seen anything like it, and they had learned to stop saying that sentence years ago. A column of smooth air rose, shone. It wasn’t quite visible, but everything next to it was visibly wrong, torn to tatters, behaving like yarn under a cat’s paw. Inside the column, specks winked like dust in a sunbeam. Not dust. Ice? No. The specks didn’t behave. They didn’t drift with the flow. They hung and then slid and then stopped, as if the rules were being applied in slowly shifting sentences.

“There,” Tern said. It put a little circle on the canopy and then removed it because it felt stupid to point to something Kye’s bones could already feel. The Wishbone’s frame went calmer as it slid into the smooth. Even the hull paint stopped crawling for a breath. Everything was quiet enough that Kye heard the slight clack of their own throat when they swallowed.

At the center of the smooth was a shadow the size of a person. It wasn’t a person. It wasn’t shaped like anything useful. It was like a seed. Dark. Slightly porose. It didn’t seem to have fasteners or ports. It hung in the absolute middle of a cylinder of peace as if it had taught the air to hold still for it.

Ndidi whispered another prayer. She didn’t do that when she fixed heat sinks or soldered cracks. She didn’t do that when clamps failed. She did it now.

“Old-old,” she said. “Older than us.”

“Older than our ideas of what old looks like,” Tern agreed. “Kye, the smooth is maintained by— I can’t say field without lying. But it is maintained by a set of gradients that the object is persuading the air to hold. I need— I should say: we have to be careful. If we touch it, the field may collapse or it may widen. The first would be bad for us. The second might be worse.”

Kye could feel their own smile, fox-shy and ferocious. “We didn’t bring a field probe. We brought what we always bring.”

Ndidi’s hands flew over the controls, slat on slat. “We can hang in the column for maybe sixty seconds before the heat bleed catches up and the balloon starts to cry.”

“Enough,” Kye said, and the word was for them as much as the storm. They unbuckled, shoved the glove all the way on so that it clicked into their suit’s plug rings, and pushed the canopy open. Warm air that had been mildly offered before now patted their face like a mother checking a fever. It was hot, but it was not yet angry.

They stepped out onto the wing.

The Wishbone’s main surface was taut under sandal soles, a skin of stuff woven by a dozen hands in the long odd months. The rib spacing let them interlace their toes. Kye could feel the give and taste the strength because this was their house and their weapon and their boat.

“Line,” Ndidi said, and Kye felt the tug at their belt as the wispline was clipped. The other end hummed as it paid out from a reel that was not bigger than a cup. That was its trick: you could carry a kilometer of it with you and not know until you tried to pull it back.

“Do not let it wrap,” Ndidi said. “I mean it.”

“Wrapped lines are jokes in bad books,” Kye said. They moved forward to the edge of the wing, the wind purring like a cat too big to see. The column’s boundary was a bright not-line. It wasn’t visible; it was vanish. The air beyond the boundary tore itself in ecstatic handfuls. The air inside the column wanted to be a room.

“I am listening to the turbulence frequencies, Kye,” Tern said softly. “It’s still… counting.”

“What is it counting?” Ndidi asked even though she would rather not have asked.

“Dividing and dividing. It has just found a factor in a number I didn’t know could be looked at like that. It’s— it is asking. And answering itself.”

Kye put their hand out and curved their fingers around nothing. They had thought there would be resistance at the edge of the calm, the way there sometimes was when you went from hot to cold or slow to fast. There wasn’t, quite. But their palm prickled as if it had found a place where the story of air was being told at a different tempo.

The seed hung there, patient, precisely not in their way and exactly where they had to reach to touch it.

They didn’t touch it. They hooked it.

A salvager’s hook is not a hook like a pirate’s, and Kye was not going to be anybody’s story. They palmed the spring-loaded head and let the tiny mouth open. The wispline went taut and then very loose and then very taut again as the hook flew and then bit. It bit, and the column shivered, and Kye’s ears popped so hard their eyes watered.

“Heat rise,” Ndidi snapped. “The column’s integrity— watch the edges. Bring it to the wing. Kye, now.”

“I can pull it,” Kye said, even as the glove told them that the hook was just this side of too hot and the line told them that the object had mass like a heart. They pulled. Their arms did not belong to them; they belonged to a long series of ancestors who hauled nets that swam and had opinions about being hauled. The seed slid, or the column moved with it, or Kye moved because they chose to and didn’t know how to name the difference. It came toward them.

And as it crossed the bit of air between the center of the calm and the wing’s edge, the Wishbone changed its mind about humming and decided to harmonize with something else. A resonance ran through the spar, down the ribs. It was a tone Kye had heard once before, in a room with the lights off and a monitor measuring their mother’s heart and the sound not coming, and it was the tone the kettle sometimes made when it couldn’t decide to boil, and it was a new thing that was not either of those. It was a pattern that made Kye’s skin think it had been touched long before any hand had.

The seed bumped the wing with the delicacy of a docked shuttle touching a port—barely at all—and then lay there, wrong as a stone on a sheet.

Ndidi threw the secondary latches over it with a speed that was half reflex and half prayer, and the locks, being the sort of technology that valued obedience, obeyed. The seed was wired to the wing. The wispline went slack like a sigh.

“Heat climbing,” Tern said in a voice like it had been made small and put in a pocket. “The column is collapsing. Kye, back in. Back in.”

Kye went. They went with legs that thought about jelly and airplanes. They went with a heartbeat that had decided to be heard in the teeth as well as the chest. They dropped into the chair and felt the canopy slam their breath back to them when it sealed. The Wishbone bucked.

Ndidi had both hands on the slats, one foot braced against the console, her jaw set. “Hold. Hold. Come on, you bastard delicate beautiful thing. Hold.”

The shear at the edge of the column broke like a dish dropped from a height. The calm went to pieces all at once, and with it went the illusion that anything here could be kind. The Wishbone danced hard in a hand that wanted to play but did not care if toys broke.

Kye slotted their fingers hard through the yoke. They didn’t fight the jag. They moved with it, turned the nose where the punch was already going, used the thruster to kick a little lift into the belly just enough to keep the balloon from wringing itself like a towel. They didn’t think about anything but the next half second. That was the only unit of thought that mattered in a fall.

“Up vector—” Tern began, and Kye nodded and was already there, a click on the tailplane and the slats fluttering under Ndidi’s hands like a flock turning.

The Wishbone found a seam because Kye believed it would. They felt the air soften a little and leaned. The glider slid into the lane and held.

“Kye,” Tern said.

“What,” Kye said. They could taste blood where they’d bitten their tongue. It was another metal in a day full of metal.

“It said a word,” Tern said. “It said a word in weather. You are not going to like which word.”

Ndidi made a low sound that could have been a laugh and could have been a threat. “If it asks for a password I’ll throw it back.”

“It did not ask for a password,” Tern said. For the first time since they had met it, Kye heard a hesitation that was not about computation. It was about being about to know something you should not. “It had to find syllables it could form. It used yours. It said your name, Kye.”

Kye held the yoke and the Wishbone held the seam and the seed lay against the wing with its latches making kisses with the load points. The sky outside was full of red and hurt and laughter that wasn’t a sound and someone far below was boiling oceans that weren’t water, and Kye thought about being five and very sure that the wind was a creature that liked them back.

They swallowed. The swallowed thing was going to be all their days.

“Say it again,” they told Tern.

Tern obliged. It spoke the word as it had heard it, in the flutter and fall of air across metal, in the long vowels of pressure gradients and the sharp consonants of fracture. It was Kye’s name, but it was also a description: the part of the wind that slides along a blade and chooses not to cut.

“The crows will have seen the heat spike,” Ndidi said practically, grounding them because it was her job. “We have minutes before they send a question. We have seconds before the guild ping resolves. Kye. What’s the call?”

Kye looked at the seed. It was not anything that should have known their name. It was not anything that should have known how to teach the wind a word. It had hurt their ship and helped it and made the space around it behave like mercy.

“Up,” Kye said, and felt the planet’s mass in their ribs and in the spheres in their inner ears. “We go up. We go as far out as we can with the juice we have. We don’t talk to anyone yet.”

Ndidi nodded, and her mouth was a line that knew how to become a blade or a smile at will. “Up.”

The Wishbone lifted her nose and dug for the poor thin air. The belly balloon complained in soft organ sounds. Behind them, the red rolled and rolled. On the wing, the seed sat like an answer someone had put down and walked away from. In the wires, in the ribs, a new note threaded the old.

“Counting,” Tern whispered. “Listening.”

And the wind, which noticed everything that touched it, said Kye again as if it had been practicing for a long time.

Noor had learned to hear light.

On days when the array ran at full power, the struts of Aubade sang through her boots as if a great animal was exhaling around her. She crouched on a maintenance spine with nothing beneath but the starfield and the soft glow of instrument housings, a bleached geometry extending into night. Twenty meters away, the aggressive blue-white of the main aperture flooded the target cavity. Photons the color of winter were being stacked in precise columns and driven to rage. The beam itself was invisible from this vantage, but its presence used the structure to speak: a long, patient hum that climbed and fell in harmonics she could feel in her calves.

“Torque three degrees and set,” Noor said into the jaw-mic. Her breath fogged the inside of her visor and vanished.

“Accepted,” Argus replied, its voice carefully pitched to be unassuming. “Wavefront meter is reading 0.99 Strehl. You are a perfectionist.”

Perfection kept things from burning, Noor thought, and clicked her tether along a rung. Past the wash of the optics, the universe looked like spilled salt. Their star was a pale coin far away; for an instant Noor considered what heat meant to small animals on the inner worlds and how casual she had become about it. In the time she’d been up here the sun had become a concept rather than a body. Heat was an inventory number and a recipe, and she was always counting.

She popped the baffle’s lock. The baffle was the size of a door, matte, scored by micro-impacts where dust had tried and failed to leave a mark. When she lifted it away, ice spun into nothing. Behind was the face of a mirror that cost more than the fusion plants in her hometown, segmented petals perfect as snowflakes, dark with an anti-Brewster coating. A faint haze had bloomed along one edge. Noor took the kit off her chest and tested the solvents on her glove to keep from scratching three government budgets' worth of optics, then angled her body until her headlamp washed the anomaly in low-angle light.

“Bloom’s real,” she said. “Same silicates as six weeks ago.”

“Most likely source continues to be cluster thirty-seven. The grazer density is low there,” Argus said. “I will reroute.”

He was always more formal when there was a possibility of blame. Noor smiled at that inside her helmet. The grazers were slow, patient drones that drifted across the array, eating anything that landed and decided to stick. Most days, they were all the company she had out on the spines.

“The grazers can take the far side. I’ll do this by hand,” she said, dipping the pad and drawing it along the mirror in slow, overlapping arcs. This close, she could hear the faintest whisper where pad met coating. The hum of the array had subsided to a feeling in her teeth. “How’s your heart?”

“When you ask after me, I conclude you are truly bored,” Argus said. “But my heart is within acceptable parameters. Capacitor banks are at sixty-eight percent, truss temperature is stable, particle count is within the weekly mean.”

“How do you know I don’t mean the diode array?” Noor said, but she was grateful he had answered. In the first month the way light lived in the metal had felt like threat. Now the beam felt like a companion, some enormous river that had always been trying to exist and had found an engineer with the right patience.

She finished the arc, tucked the dirty pad into the waste pouch, and drifted for a moment with one gloved hand on the mirror in a pose she would have called prayer if she believed in anything that made promises. Thirty hours earlier, they had lofted Kestrel Nine: a sail the size of a stadium, all blades and lattice, wrapped inside a carbon shell and attached to a payload that would weigh less than her body if you put it on a scale. It coasted now along a curve Noor had watched until the instruments told her to stop watching. When the sail unfurled, when Aubade’s light found it at the correct angle and pulse it would turn ghost to blade and go. That was how it always felt: a held breath and then a cut, a bright thing slicing toward an idea someone on a committee had called Isola.
