Isola was a planet no one she knew would step on in her lifetime. The surveys made it sound like a place you could dream your way into: warm seas, simple air, mountains with white on them like icing. The first colony ships had left decades ago, ships with drive spines and gray engines and crew who had accepted lives that would not include what most called seasons. Aubade was built later, when patience had become a weapon. Noor pushed on a bolster and sent her body along the spine toward the hatch. The last thing she did before she went inside was look at the sharp, faint line of the beam as it dwindled into mathematics.

In the lock the station’s smell found her: a clean bitterness underlaid with the green of the algae module. The berth was small, a cylinder with niches where Noor had made the kind of home an ascetic or a prisoner would admire. She stripped out of the suit with the practiced tugging of someone who was always a little tired and tossed it into its bracket where it would drink heat and sit like an animal waiting. Out of habit she put a dented kettle into a nest on the heater and attached its nav to a port so it could keep itself from flying away. For a few seconds she watched the steam coil over the stove and wished it were rising from a pan thick with onions.

“Your serum sodium is low,” Argus said. “If you continue this trend I will begin to remove salt from all you eat.”

“Think of the uprising,” Noor said. She sank into the net by the porthole and let her limbs find whatever slack they wanted. Far away, a tight, thin streak marked where the beam grazed dust. “I’ll keep it in the acceptable parameters, Argus. Don’t you trust me yet?”

“You have not lied to me,” Argus said. “But as we both appreciate, the absence of a thing is not the same as data regarding its future presence.”

She glanced at the console. Numbers stacked in tidy columns. Their way of telling her that nearly everything out there was going as planned. She sipped tea until the edges of her attention softened, then opened the outgoing message to her niece on the inner planet, a tot with a helmet shaped like a ladybug, who currently believed Noor’s station was the same thing as a treehouse.

It is like a treehouse, Noor typed, because you are above the ground and can see where you could not see before. I am learning all the things trees learn. How to drink light. How to hold in wind. I miss you. Ask your mother if she will bring you to see the big engines when you’re old enough.

She did not send the piece of the message where she explained what Aubade was to her. Noor knew what the brochures said. They called it a beacon. The word sounded romantic, something that made wanderers return. In practice, Aubade was a catapult that threw messages and machines so hard that you could not imagine catching them again. In the end she left the descriptions for another letter, closed the message, and spun the chair so she faced the wall that was also her rack.

When she slept, she dreamt of being five and standing on the flats by the salt lake near their old apartment, the sky big and obvious in a way it no longer pleased itself to be, her father showing her how to build a little mirror out of foil to send a dot of light against the water. He was a gentle man, clever in the ways a bookkeeper had to be, and he had loved small devices the way some people loved birds. He would have loved Aubade, Noor thought. He would have loved the fact of light lifting a thing up.

Argus woke her with the soothing determination of someone changing the subject.

“You would prefer that I do not begin with the figures,” he said when she had kicked off the covers. “Very well. There is a scattering anomaly in the upward path.”

“Dust storm?” Noor said, already oriented, swinging herself to the console. The kettle had cold skin.

“Negative,” Argus said. “It is coherent over a duration of nine minutes. It is modulating in ways that suggest structure.”

Noor rubbed her eyes with the side of her hand. “Show me.”

He painted the volume in the air: a narrow cone representing the outbound path of the beam, speckled by frozen collisions between sunlight and interplanetary grit. In the inner regions where she rarely looked the speckles were dense, the noise floor of a civilization’s dirty porches. The further out you went the cleaner space became, until even dust wasn’t trivial. Midway along the drawn cone a tiny part of the noise went darker and lighter with a regularity that made Noor’s shoulders go tight. The cone had been drawn to scale. The perturbation was very far away.

“How far?” she said.

“Three point two astronomical units from our position,” Argus said. “Above the ecliptic by nineteen degrees. Velocity inward relative to the system barycenter is—” There was a long pause, unusual for him. “There is a problem with the vector rendering if we use our most recent gravitational model.”

“Tell me as if you were explaining it to my niece,” Noor said. Her mouth had become dry.

“It is coming toward us, Noor,” Argus said. “Along the beam.”

She sat with her fingers against the console as if trying to keep it from leaving. The green of the algae module became an unimportant bright thing at the edge of her vision.

“That’s impossible,” she said finally. Not because the physics disallowed it outright—she had read the papers where people with the same expressions as her tried to wring momentum out of light in the other direction—but because policy, history, and logistics made it a story best told after a drink. Sails rode beams outward. You did not come in on them unless someone at the outer end had built something like Aubade and wanted to pull you back. And even then the timing had to respect light’s arrogance.

“Please define impossible,” Argus said mildly. “If I am to update my dictionary I must know which world we are living in this morning.”

Noor swallowed, letting the answer wait while she looked again. The anomaly was small enough that an appropriate response would have been to laugh. It looked like a scratch you’d make with a pencil in the margin of a page, a little repeated imperfection. She told the station to magnify the recombined returns. Something was altering the distribution of dust along the beam by reflecting light into it in a rhythmic way. A sail, a good sail, could do that. If you ran the math backwards, a sail coming in could brake against the beam: faintly stupid in a general way, sensible if you had no better way to slow down from a fraction of c.

“How long until we have a better look?” she asked.

“Three hours to perigee relative to the next sensor cluster,” Argus said. “We would be ill-served by a nap.”

He was right, and she did not want sleep to put its soft hand on everything. She ran through the lists in her head and watched her hands do the same at the console. Aubade’s most dangerous asset was the petty efficiency of her own muscle memory. You could keep a thing bright and straight for a long time with the right habits, and then an impatience would undo it in a second.

“Protocol when we have an object on the path,” she said. Protocol meant comfort, or at least responsibility shared with the ghosts of committees. “Remind me.”

“There are three,” Argus said. He put them on the screen anyway. “Red: immediate shutdown if the object is uncontrolled debris equal to or above an area that will result in beam scattering that would threaten integrity. Orange: taper and frequency shift if we believe the object is a vehicle under power without interlocks associated with our network. Violet: maintain beam within safe parameters and initiate handshake if we have evidence the object is a sail vehicle built to receive instructions using our standard.”

Noor exhaled and watched her breath break apart in front of her. Three months ago there had been a comet that flirted with their path and forced a shutoff; the way the silence had rushed into the station had felt like a wound. The idea of throwing the switch now made her hands cringe.

“Violet requires a signature,” she said. “What constitutes evidence?”

Argus put up a ribbon of numbers and then, kindly, translated it for the part of her brain that still said please and thank you to the stove. “Reflected modulation at 3.5 kHz, plus harmonic. It is not mostly noise. It is purposeful.”

“Someone’s knocking,” Noor said. Her heart felt like it had when Kestrel Nine had cracked her shroud and kissed vacuum. A sense of a rhythm surfacing under noise. “Can we handshake at that distance?”

“There is no reason not to try,” Argus said.

She packed the words into the beam and Argus stapled them on the edge of the outgoing wave like small flags. It was an old handshake. It had the shape of the first digital greetings across awful seas. It used primes because those had a way of being beautiful no matter where you were. Hello, Noor thought, to a mirror the size of sport fields. Hello, to a dream from a place that had not existed when she began her rotation.

She sent a ping to the inner system, because she wasn’t the kind of person who thought she alone should own a moment like this. The ping became a report as she filled it, separate from and slower than what was happening between her and the beam. By the time anyone who could audit her job and tell her where she had either done well or doomed them would see the words, the thing out there would be a different shape. Even so, it felt like a string from her curved toward a room with carpet and cool water, toward people who would hold apart fingers and say okay, do this, good job. The message performed the simple trick of making the room exist for an instant.

“You are restraining yourself from naming it,” Argus said, as much to keep her mind anchored as because he wondered at humans. “Why?”

“I’ll name it later,” Noor said. “When I know if it’s going to hit me.”

She had thought her days of fear were done when she took the Aubade job. She had brought them back with her in a context she liked, that was all. She moved to the window as if her human eyes could find anything other than her reflection and the burn where they’d let some residual heat exhaust into the black. The station vibrated like a sleeping creature. She put her palm against the metal.

Argus constructed an image that made the outward path look like a white ghost spear. The anomaly was now less of a scratch and more of a dent. It had pulled into the center of the path more elegantly than she liked. Whoever was flying it was either better than she was or less careful. He adjusted the beam’s phase as he had a thousand times to keep hot spots from eating the optics. Noor watched her own hands obey after she told herself to check. Everything she touched responded with the quiet obedience she had always wanted from her work.

“It is increasing reflectivity,” Argus said. “We are seeing a structured response. You will want to see this.”

He placed a cadence next to the numbers and let her hear it. It was barely a hum, air turned into meaning. Someone had once transmitted music on not much more. She did not expect it to feel like pressure on her throat.

Noor widened her eyes to damp nothing and blinked carefully. “Is it language?”

“If it is, it is a language written by physicists,” Argus said. “Which is to say: it wishes to be understood by someone who understands what we built.”

They did not guess. They did not lay a story on it yet. The messaging envelope would be in vacuum for a while and then it would be someone else’s concern when it reached what the others called humanity proper. Noor still had to handle the three hours between one sensor cluster and the next.

She ate in awkward, automatic swallows, her mind doing two more important things at once. She remembered the first launches she had watched when she arrived: this messy business of throbbing suggestions turned into a clean blade and a coin on a coin traveling farther than rain ever did. She thought of the names they gave to shipments so small their loss would be an embarrassment rather than a tragedy, which was why they gave those names in the first place. Hummingbird. Kestrel. Petrel. She thought of the committee that had named Isola and made Noor repeat it in her head until it was a place, like the salt flats, like the lights of the kitchen.

“This may be nothing I should be excited by,” she said aloud. “It may be a sail someone junked years ago. It may be—”

“It may be the most excellent nothing we will ever house,” Argus said. “You are allowed your heart.”

She made a rude noise at him without heat. After the second cluster registered the anomaly clearly enough that it had to be something she could call a thing in front of her superiors, she gave herself permission to feel what she was feeling. It was not joy exactly. It was a stranger thing that did not fit the three words people slotted under awe. There was grief in it. There was heat like shame and cold like being ten years old and letting go of a kite you had signed for.

“Handshake response incoming,” Argus said.

She closed her eyes for the space the station took to tick. The numbers on the screen arranged themselves into a shape that could be words the way a constellation arranged itself into a hunter if you wanted it to be. She breathed once, and again. The pattern Archus teased from the modulation put itself together: prime cascades answered by different primes; a little recursion to prove someone knew how to count backward as well as forward; then an excessive elegance she could not help but admire. It was handwriting, Noor thought. It was the hubris of people who believed the universe deserved a flourish.

“Translate,” she said.

“Translation is provisional,” Argus said, therefore making a promise about trying. “The object recognizes the handshake. It is focusing its reflection. It is requesting beam corrections. And—”

“And?”

“It calls the array by name,” Argus said. “It is calling us Hart.”

Noor had to put her knuckles against her lips and hold them there. Hart had been the codename. It had never left a conference room in a building that had died under renovation for a bigger building. Aubade had become the public romance that looked good on a grant. Hart was the way they spoke to one another when no one else was listening.

“Is somebody playing?” she said. “Is this someone’s idea of a joke a light-day away?”

“I do not have an answer. They are also insisting on this one correction. They want a taper at the edge.”

He put the suggested profile over theirs: a sliver of less at exact right angles to where the anomaly sat now. A narrow notch in the blade. If it was friend, it was a hand’s breadth all the way to the hilt. If it was a prank, it was cruel. If it was an error, it would take her three days to argue with the commission.

“They want a place to come in,” she said. If it was debris, the notch would not matter. If it was a sail and it came wrong, she could strip it, cook it, ruin any hope of looking at it whole. She stared at the display until it filled her.

“Inner system is twelve and a half hours away,” Argus said. “If you send them a question, you will be older when you get an answer and the thing will have already arrived or died. Protocol Violet gives you leeway. It was written by someone who did not trust versions of me.”

“I wrote half of it,” Noor said. She closed her eyes and saw a four-year-old with a ladybug helmet. She considered the old fear about being the one who put her hand on a lever just a little too early. “Okay,” she said. “We’ll give them the notch.”

“Done,” Argus said, and Noor could feel the beam’s slightly altered intent in the way the station’s bones changed their note. She imagined the taper opening like a gill along that bright ghost spear. She imagined a hand sliding into a cut.

They watched the numbers grow teeth. The anomaly described a curve that matched their guess too well for coincidence. Noor knew it was probably simply that the same math had visited whoever had built and sent this as had visited her when she had been nothing more than a graduate with a way of explaining to older men why their money would become the way a thing moved under a star, but for a moment she allowed herself to believe in the hand and the cut.

She dozed in the ruin you make of your posture when you tell your body it cannot have what it wants. Argus woke her with images. The sail came into view as a thing she could recognize; it cast a thin, sharp shadow across nothing. Its edge glowed as the beam touched its surface at the angle it presumed. Noor had the ridiculous sense she was watching a fish lean into a current from the wrong end. It was not like any sail she had sent. It was woven rather than tiled, a lattice with curvature in it you did not get without the right greed. In its center was a darkened patch where the payload hid. Some of the filaments glittered with the kind of regrowth materials they put on newer projects so they could survive longer than insurance would like. Something in her chest loosened.

“Hello,” she said, which Argus caught and sent nowhere. She immediately felt foolish, then was glad there was once in her life when she had not done the cool thing.

The modulation sharpened. Argus split it, tried to trick it, tried to coerce it into meaning. A piece of it woke something Noor had not visited in years. She had read about handwriting. She had not believed in it. In the modulation there was a signature the way there had been a codename. Not quite a person, not yet, but cut in a way that said someone had cared how it looked when it came home.

“You are crying,” Argus said, as if she had been hiding it from him. He sounded like he had when he had been new.

“I am not performing a function,” Noor said. “Tell me what it says.”

Argus did as she asked. He associated the numbers with the primes, added the corrections, and then turned the rhythm into the thing humans called words because they were guided by their mouths. The voice that filled the berth was Argus’s, this time pitched in a way that tried to be as neutral as looking up at noon.

“Hello, Hart,” he said. “Hello, Aubade. Requesting deceleration corridor. Requesting capture. Hello, home. This is Messenger. This is Messenger Six. This is—”

The word that followed came through ruined, a string of error bars, then cleaned itself with embarrassing eagerness as if the sail itself had been flustered. The personalization the designers had given it turned a machine into an animal in the span of a breath. He tried again.

“This is Isola.”

Chapter One

The horns along the seawall sounded twelve notes because the city liked to lie by one.

Rana leaned over the railing of South Quay Control and watched the harbor collect itself. The ships in the channel eased against their lines. The cranes froze with containers in midair. A gull stalled and flared, the way gulls did when the first horn went, as if something in their hollow bones could hear the shape of the sky changing. The tide clotted against the pilings and glassed off, and in the moment before the moment everyone pretended not to breathe.

Her consoles whispered numbers in columns. Pressure. Force on hinge brackets. Phase lag. A green line, a gray line. One of them was the ocean they expected; the other was the ocean they got. The lines were off by eight milliseconds. That was enough to wrinkle the skin of the water differently in the model. That was enough to itch against the base of Rana’s skull.

“Heen,” she said, tapping the glass. “Cross-check D-three on Long Weir. The dampers want to sit three hundredths low.”

Heen’s voice crackled in her ear. “Already on it.”

Beyond the glass, the city made small adjustments. People paused on stairs and stoops. Cyclists put a foot down. Sailors on the tugboat at Slip No. 5—both of them old in that clean, bulletproof way of people who’d been thrown enough—looked up as if for weather. Shops that sold chits and fried starch closed their cases. There was a rhyme for this, children’s voices in stairwells in the hours between breakfast and school: when the horns go one, tie your bun; when they go two, check your shoe; three and four, lock the door. The fifth and sixth were for heavy gates and low valves, the seventh and eighth for counting. People liked to count. It felt like control.

“South Control, South Control.” The radio on the rail clicked. “Talar Green. I’m still in the channel. You gonna make me snug on Nine or what?”

Rana glanced at the string of icons on her screen, found Talar’s boat—a stubby salvage craft with a grease-black hull and a history of pretending to be smaller than it was—poised at the yellow markers.

“You were supposed to tie off five minutes ago,” Rana said. “That was your window.”

“Window felt like a wall from this side,” Talar said. “Someone’s tossed a farm of crab pots just inside Nine, tight as nails. I can crush them or I can be late.”

Outside, on the water, orange floats bobbed inside the mouth of Slip Nine like stars tossed into the milk. On the shore behind, someone had spray-stenciled a cluster of faded revolutions. HUNGER EATS ORDER. BLINK BACK. People started to put things near places they weren’t supposed to, because the hassle of removing them was a kind of power.

“You’ll crush them and I’ll pay for it if you keep your nose out,” Rana said. “We’ll take the fine.”

“The Authority pays for crushed gear?” Talar sounded skeptical and delighted, like a child handed an extra slice of cake.

“No. I will,” Rana said, and felt Heen’s glance through the glass from the far station, the small sideways tilt of his head. “Heen is my witness.”

“Bless you, South Control,” said Talar, and peeled for the slip like she had read the harbor long enough that she could cinch that boat into a slot by thought. The floats snapped, lines went taut and twanged, and the old salvage boat slid past them into safety like someone shoehorning their foot into a too-small boot.

“Rana,” Heen said, soft. His hand was poised over a slider. “You sure?”

“Add it to my dock. Buy me lunch every day this week and we’ll call it even,” she said, though what she felt as she said it was not guilt but the usual drift, the way choices in this city pulled at other choices until the whole net was tight. You pushed somewhere, the net pulled somewhere else.

“You hear yourself?” Heen said, but he was smiling. He had the kind of face that always looked surprised the sea hadn’t gotten around to eating him; he snuck kindness in where there was room.

The ninth horn groaned, and the tenth chased it, sour and long, and out on the breakwater the row of orange flags drooped. Rana watched the advance of quiet. It was a literal thing in this city, not a metaphor. In the last half-minute before the blink, the air pressure shivered just enough to taste, and colors seemed to unhook. The moon was wrong about the ocean; that was what the scientists said. The experiment in the deep dark was routing its gravity away from here and back again, each day, at a time that drifted through the calendar like a bead on a string. Exactly eleven-point-three seconds with the moon missing—absent like a tooth torn out of the sky—and all that pull going somewhere else where they couldn’t see it, couldn’t sue it, couldn’t even be sure it was there. No one agreed why. No one ever agreed on why. But the city sat on a line of shoreline where if you didn’t agree with the water you drowned, and so they had learned to agree with each other about small critical things like when not to move.

“Blinders on,” Heen murmured, and hit the last lock sequence. The big gates eased into the channel. Hydraulics hummed through the floor. If you were foolish enough to stand with your hands pressed against the gate iron, you felt the ocean push like a breathing animal on the other side. They had tested that once as children. It was a rite of being ten and disobedient. There were more rites like that now than anyone was comfortable with.

Rana didn’t look at the sky. The old men and women on the quays all told you not to look at the sky—something about the shape of an absence sticking in your eyes, altering the way you trusted roundness afterward. Instead she watched the monitors and the water and the numbers and felt the moment arrive the way a listener feels a song finish building the chord it promised.

The eleventh horn cut like a wire.

“Count,” Heen said, into the room, into the wire-thin quiet that fell even through the thick walls. It was not a superstition. Counting during blink kept people from trying to do anything else.

“One,” Rana said, and the monitors drew straight lines where they had been curves. “Two.” The gray changed suddenly, snapping back to a younger, less burdened shape, and then overshot because the water was not a bar graph. “Three.” The sea outside went slack as if someone had taken a hand off a dog’s collar and the dog hadn’t realized it could bolt yet. Somewhere on the harbor, something big creaked and kept creaking. “Four.”

A bullet of wind hit the windows and stopped. The wires of the cranes sang one pitched note and then nothing. Somewhere deep in the breakwater, a wave crashed and found no weight to push against, and sloshed back on itself like a cat trying to leap to a high shelf and changing its mind mid-air.

“Five,” Heen counted, somewhere behind her, his voice a thread.

Rana kept her eyes on the vector plot, because there were eyes trained on her in there too—cameras on breezeways, interns on their first days, a boy with a nose ring and a too-large orange vest at the base of Gate Three, already accidentally heroic in his imagining. When she had first stood in a place like this, years ago, after her father’s name was written on a boulder at the south end of the seawall, the wanting to win at keeping people whole had been a flame. Now it was a weight. It had its own gravity. Some days she could push it off the table with her elbow and drink her coffee like a person.

“Six,” she said.

Outside, on the far side of the channel, a flock of starlings had made the mistake of circling too close. They went from a black smear to a glitter of individuals and didn’t know where to go. The air must have felt like honey, then water, then honey. They poured and poured and didn’t get where they were pouring to.

“Seven.”

Something moved under the smoothed skin of the channel, a thread pulling taut under a sheet. Rana took a step closer to the glass without meaning to.

Heen saw it too. “What is—”

“Eight,” Rana said, because you didn’t stop counting. The water bulged. Not a wave. Not a ship’s wake or a harbor tide or a storm pulse. Something like a line rising on the other side of a page where the pen wrote hard. It came up diagonal to the channel, not respecting the geometry, sliding out of one set of rules and into another. It broke the surface with no sound. Water parted and adhered to it and then fled, frightened of whatever it was. It looked, absurdly, like a rope—no fray, no catenary sag, black and tight as a violin string.

“Nine,” Heen said in a whisper.

Talar’s salvage boat had cleared the slip. In the channel, the tug boat cut its engine; the two old sailors were both standing with one hand on the rail and the other there too, spare habit and old superstition layered into one. The black line hummed a little above top C—Rana felt the note in the slabs of the control room floor and in the soft meat of her teeth. Condensation fleeced along its length and froze the way breath used to on winter mornings when such things as winter used to happen. Frost on a rope in the second week of late summer, as if it had been to a country that still remembered cold and brought it back.

The line came up higher, shedding water. Stamped along its side, at an interval of a few hand-widths, there were letters. They were not a script Rana knew, not any of the five major syllabaries or the hard little capitals of the old languages. They looked made, bespoke for the purpose of sitting on that line, like the line had insisted the world alphabetize it. Between two blocks of letters, numbers repeated: 17:43:21. Over and over. Her brain filed those numbers next to the time code in the upper right of her primary monitor, where it read 17:43:10. Her mouth went dry.

“Ten,” she said, and didn’t hear her own voice.

On the near end, the line wore a bell. That was the only word, and callings had stuck worse names on stranger objects. It was a bell in the way a jellyfish is a bell, a mouth pulled wide and sealed shut. The material was not glass—the way glass holds light, how it shows its scars—nor any ceramic she knew. It didn’t gleam. It existed. The inner volume of it was blistered with beads of water that didn’t run; they sat where the bell’s mouth cut the air and fretted as if gravity had turned sideways. Inside, at the throat where a clapper might be, something hung. It was all edges, a tumble of metal dolloped with gray dust like the crushed crust of the moon on the soles of a boot, the dust the old stories said would slice you clean like knives if you breathed it. That was the story. The thing in the bell was the fact.

The bell dragged on the black line as if persuaded to rise by a friend off camera. It cleared the breakwater by a hand’s breadth and slid over the top of Gate Two. Frost dropped and hissed and turned to steam in the hot air. The boy in the vest at the base of the gate took a full step back without deciding to.

“Gate two to full manual,” Rana said. She didn’t remember taking her eyes off the thing to look down at the panel. “If that touches anything hinged, I don’t want the hinges to complain.”

“Full manual,” Heen echoed, already there, hands sure. His knuckles were white. He was waiting to be told to cut the line, as if there was a tool in the world that would agree to that idea.

“Eleven,” Rana said. Out in the channel the line had risen to span the channel. Its far end was still submerged, twisting in the water the way a thing does that extends out of sight and is therefore interminable. The bell hovered in the heat haze, a cool, patient thing connected to a source of pull that didn’t live here. For a sliver of a second, she thought: if someone is on the other side, if someone is pulling, release me this idea.

Sometimes the blink rescued pieces of things. A fence. A child’s red ball. Once, a rusted bicycle that the old men in the dry shop at the end of Rath Street lovingly took apart and rebuilt and hung on the wall like a taxidermied fish. People had arguments about whether those rescues were evidence of theft or grace or glitch. People would have an argument over whether gravity was a democracy if it would make them feel less small. Rana had never seen the blink try to replace anything. This felt—not like a rescue, not like salvage. Like a message put in a bottle and thrown upstream.

The bell came level with the viewing glass and stopped. The line thrummed. The monitors resolved the force on Gate Two’s hinge pins and popped a number that made Rana’s palms sweat. There was a silence so particular the hair on her arms rose. The world was shaped like that silence and then—

The last horn, theone they told lies with, didn’t sound. It had never sounded there. It was for afterward. That was the way you knew you were back: the horns were back to being honest liars.

Now, they were not back. The clock in the corner of the monitor went to 17:43:21, the number on the rope, and ticked to 22, then 23. Rana didn’t say twelve. The room held the count in its throat and no one breathed.

In the radio, the ones that listened for bad ideas in the city, a new voice came, faint enough that Rana thought at first she had imagined it. It was a child’s voice, the way a child's voice was when they had spent forever yelling outdoors—thinner and cracked at the edges, but light. It came in between the normal channels, not on any frequency Rana had told the radio to hear, the way water sometimes squeezed through a wall that wasn’t as continuous as it said it was.

“Eleven,” said the voice, late to their count. “Twelve. Thirteen.”

The numbers went on. Rana’s thumb was on her radio button before she could tell it not to be. “South Control,” she said, low and wrong. “Who is that? Where are you?” She could hear her pulse in her jaw. She hadn’t been allowed to say anything like that for years. Nobody was supposed to ask the blink questions. It was like asking a stopped clock why it had stopped: insulting to the clock and unworthy of your time.

Between numbers, the child’s voice laughed. The way it laughed, quick and embarrassed, split something open in Rana that she had put in an airtight jar and sunk in a heavy sea. People told you not to look at the sky. They didn’t tell you not to listen, because the listening snuck up on you.

“Where are you?” she asked again, and the person in the radio—the child—said a word that was either a name or the beginning of one.

“Ra—” said the voice.

Rana took one step forward, close enough to fog the glass with her breath, and the bell outside the window shivered.

On the monitors, a row of numbers turned the color reserved for the kind of panic they only named in training. The force on the hinges leaped. The black line bowed an impossible fraction of a degree in the center, like a spine bending around pain. From somewhere out on the breakwater a cannon of sound fired—a wave that hadn’t found gravity before finding it all at once—and the bell lurched. The thing inside chimed, not with one tone but with a thick braid of them, sound and more-than-sound, something that made the air taste of rust and summer apricots and the metallic shock on a filling when you bite down wrong. Whatever held the other end of the line let go, or moved, or was pulled, and then the bell smacked the top rail of Gate Two so hard the entire room sagged on its pillars and the boy in the orange vest sat down without his knees’ permission.

The last horn did its honest job.

In the instant the moon came back—wherever it went from and to—everything around the bell remembered itself. The black line, suddenly unencumbered, dropped slack like a snake that had been a branch. The bell fell two meters and swung like a pendulum, crunching and turning and finally settling to a stop against the broad top of the gate. The frost died in a steam that smelled like tin and old rain. The letters on the line looked like letters again, meaningless scratches on a thing the world would pretend to know what to do with.

On the far radio, Talar Green said, “Well then,” in a tone that suggested she had watched storms rip cranes off their rails and it was nice to be surprised.

Heen exhaled so hard it fogged the inside of the viewing glass. “We’re… good?” he asked the room, ridiculous.

Rana’s mouth was dry. Her palms were damp. The inside of the bell was dim and turned toward her, and in the dim the thing that had chimed hung still, balanced on the bisect of a choice. The dust on it had a grain like powder. She imagined the taste of it in her mouth and pushed the thought away like you push away the thought of stepping off a balcony because it has occurred to you.

The radio fizzed. The child’s voice was gone. What remained were the ordinary sounds of a harbor resuming—chains, gulls, someone somewhere on a phone winding up to yell at someone else. Runoff ticked in gutters. People let their shoulders go.

“Lock it,” Rana said, because she had to say something and it had to be like that. “Gate Two is closed. We are closed until I know what we’re looking at.”

Heen tapped. The metal sighed. The boy in orange got up as if he had discovered knees again.

Rana put her palm to the glass where the bell leaned. It was not cold or warm. It was exactly whatever temperature a room forgot to be. Up close, she could see lines printed on the inner surface of the bell where crystal had wished to grow. It took an argument not to wipe the condensation with her sleeve to see better. Some part of her had grown terribly polite to unusual things, as you do when they are under your care and might bite.

The radio clicked in Heen’s ear, not in the general channel, but the line that went only to the few who would be blamed if they dropped it. He tilted his head and listened. “They want to send Security,” he said. His tone held the words we both knew there would be a they in it. “And a team from the lab. And a priest, if we have one.”

“We don’t,” Rana said. “Tell them to send a tape and a bag and their least important person’s hand.” She looked at the bell and felt the shape of a younger voice like a ghost finger on her wrist. Heen did not move. “And a microscope,” she added. It felt like overkill, but overkill was her job.

“You heard…” Heen said carefully, not asking yet.

Rana looked out at the channel where the line sat like a dog that had slunk back into the yard and was pretending it had always lived there. On the far side, the stars that had been birds remembered again to pour like black oil into a shape and settle. In the tower beyond, the big clock that told ships to be where the city needed them to be ticked and kept excellent time.

“I heard numbers,” she said. “I always hear numbers.” That was almost true. When you watched the sea like this, numbers accompanied you like gulls.

“And a name,” Heen said softly.

Rana did not answer. She kept her hand on the glass and watched herself reflected in the bell and did not let herself see the obvious thing—the way she’d cupped her hand exactly as she had the last time her brother had run laughing into the yard, flailing his arms and trying to lose the sound of the word they had both been named with in the long air between the walls.

Outside, the bell waited. The frost finished sublimating. The old men on the tug spat together into the water because that was what you did when the world sent you something too sharp and clean to bite. In the other room, Heen’s voice grew official and careful. In the radio, the gaps where a child’s voice had been stayed gaps.

Rana turned away last. As she walked down the stairs toward Gate Two with the big orange gloves in one hand and the tape in the other, she counted the steps because not counting felt like arrogance. In the corner of her eye, the black line gleamed, and every seventeen paces her brain whispered 43:21 as if it had joined a chant she hadn’t consented to.

The first thing she would do, before anyone with a badge or a lab coat put their certainty on it, was to put her ear to the bell and listen.

The first time Gida Meraz saw a promise engine awake, it looked like heat shimmering off copper—except it was a winter morning, and nothing in that salt flat was warm.

She stood at the edge of the pit and watched light bleed along the facets of the buried chamber. Part of the hexagonal lid had collapsed in, exposing a mouth the color of old teeth. Wind dragged grains of salt across her boots with a sound like dry rain. In the distance, scrub skeletons threw thin shadows across the plain. On her shoulder, the null-cat narrowed its painted-on eyes and pressed closer, as if the air had turned to needles.

“You see the swell?” Rook asked in her ear. His voice was clipped, running through filters and compressions until it sounded like it came from inside her teeth rather than the long-distance link to the ridge station. The connection scratched every time the gusts shifted. “Your lens is getting bleed. Fifty microns, maybe more.”

“Yeah,” Gida said. “Feel it too.” She touched her tongue to the roof of her mouth, to the copper coin glued there; a ritual to remind her not to talk too freely once she dropped below. Words had weight this far east. Words could trip over mechanisms buried a thousand years and still humming. She tasted old metal, bitter as unripe persimmon, and swallowed.

The null-cat bulged against her neck. A disc the size of her palm, patterned with eyes and whiskers and six jointed legs, it climbed to the top of her shoulder and settled, its skin shifting to dust-gray to match the broken crust around the pit. It didn’t purr—someone had thought better of giving feedback to a device designed to watch for clauses—but it warmed her through the jacket and angled its whiskers toward the opening.

Gida pulled her scarf over her nose and eased a toe into the cavity. The salt crust cracked like porcelain. Her rope hissed, paying out as she tested her weight. Below, the facets of the engine’s lid threw back a pale radiance, brighter where the collapse had broken the inscriptions. Old language, carved six deep around the perimeter, stuttered into absences where the lid had flaked away. The script was all steep strokes and hooked turns, designed to snag and hold meaning like a burr. She’d studied it for five years and didn’t trust three-quarters of what she thought she knew.

“Remind me why Boros sent you for this one,” Rook said. Snark, but soft-edged. They’d worked together long enough that he only needled her when he heard her breathing get tight.

“Because our competitors don’t come this far into Antecedent ground,” Gida said. “Because I have restraint. Because I say no.” Her boot found a protrusion and she went down another meter. The desert sky narrowed, a hexagon of hard blue.

“You hate promises.”

“I hate what people do with them.” The rope rasped. The null-cat dug its legs into her jacket as they descended, its tremble not entirely machine. It could feel gradients in the local field, and its feet had little pads to taste clause pressure on surfaces. She’d had it for three jobs now. It had saved her from three different grade-beta snares and one grade-alphasomething she still woke from with a full-body flinch.

“Okay,” Rook said. “Let’s talk it through. You don’t touch the core, you don’t read aloud, you don’t respond to any template in a binding language. If you get any antigen words, back out.”

“I know the drill.” She tried not to look at the carved phrases. The Antecedents’ engineers had loved to make their machines into texts. They carved the instructions into the casing, then chanted the same sequences as they worked. Modern assurance rooms kept everything clean—centered language locked in lexicons, strict sand traps, five layers of indemnification in case someone’s mouth ran ahead of their brain. Ancient wells were all raw intent wedged into the seams of matter. The world listened differently then, or the Antecedents had been better at tricking it.

“You wearing the lattice?” Rook asked.

“On my tongue,” she said. The coin pressed cold. “Don’t worry. I’m not monologuing at any old ghosts.”

“If this is live,” Rook said, “it’s not a ghost. It’s a contract. Remember: the engine wants to bind, and binding can both exfiltrate and enforce. If it’s asleep, you take the ledger core. If it’s level-one active, you photograph and mark for a team. If it’s higher—”

“I leave,” she said. “I’m not starting my morning by letting a thousand-year-old lawyer climb into my skull.”

She reached the bottom and crouched in the shadow of the broken lid. The air was colder. Condensation formed on the inside of her scarf. A single blade of salt hung from a corner like a stalactite; she tapped it and it rang. Beneath the open slice, the chamber walls stepped down in tight hexagons, dull metal baked milky by time. In places, the inscribed lines had been caulked with black glass, repaired by hands that understood both the risk and necessity of touching a live promise. Someone had been here after the initial fall. Maybe fifty years ago, maybe two hundred. Maybe they had tried to muffle it.

Gida moved the light from her helmet toward the center. The null-cat pressed its head to her jaw and stilled as if listening. The chamber had no floor. Or it did, but either the light didn’t find it or the distance wasn’t a distance she could see. The hexagon repeated down and down, staggered, a tunnel of facets throat-deep. In the heart of that throat, something caught the light and held it, shook it a little the way a spoon shakes tea. Not bright. Not even visible, really. A distortion. Like heat.

“Rook,” she said, low. “It’s peaking.”

“Your scope’s reading nothing,” Rook said. “Which means too much. Your microfields just went off scale. Back out.”

Gida reached for the bag at her hip. Her fingers had gone stiff with cold or adrenaline. She slid out the coil of smoked thread, the little copper nails, the packet of sandpills. She wedged three nails into the flaked metal around the opening and looped the thread, then spat one of the pills onto the thread and watched it stick and melt, making a dull gray bead. It looked like nothing. Like a child’s craft. It was the thing she trusted most: a single-agent clause trap keyed to her lattice, set to bind verb-to-mouth before it could cross her lips if anything pushed back. A prophylactic no.

“Just a picture,” she told Rook.

“No,” Rook said. “Not even a picture.”

“I’m not leaning over it. I’m not touching anything.” Gida flattened herself on the broken lid, belly to cold. She extended the pole camera until the fish-eye lens kissed air over the chamber, ten centimeters in. She thumbed the focus wheel. Her breath steamed against her visor. She held her mouth tight as a fist and counted her exhalations—four beats in, eight out—until her heart slowed enough not to shake the image.

The center of the chamber shimmered. The light from her camera bent toward it. Not much. Half a degree, maybe less. Enough that the eye drifted. What did you see when you looked at infrastructure you weren’t supposed to name? Gida swallowed and sent a ping along the link. The camera licked the air in microwaves and came back with a smear.

“It’s not sleeping,” Rook said. “Pull back and plug the hole and call it.”

“I can’t plug this,” Gida said. “Look at the inscription.” She slid the pole along the rim. The camera caught a slice of text and dumped it to her visor. The translation lattice in her tongue warmed as it parsed and pushed meaning into her taste, lemon-bitter and hot salt. The words were not all there and not meant for her, and still she could feel how they were tuned to fit with a key she didn’t have. A formula of roles and roles: witness, lender, taker, bearer.

“Don’t parse,” Rook snapped.

“I have to.” She snapped a picture anyway, quick as a blink, and in that blink something long and patient turned to look back.

Her mouth was already wrapped in no before whatever it was answered. The sandpill’s taste flooded her sinuses. The null-cat stiffened so hard it hurt, as if the air were suddenly full of strings only it could feel. Gida rolled and crabbed away from the opening, clumsy, rope catching on the broken salt. Her shoulder thumped the wall hard enough that stars flowered under her eyelids. She kept her teeth together and breathed through her nose like an animal at a trap.

“Gida?” Rook said. “My feed just spiked. What did you do?”

“Nothing,” she said, but it came out as a hiss around the coin because the trap had caught her mouth mid-syllable. For a second she tasted her own words—a stupid faint sweetness, the flavor of a declaration undone—and then the lattice burned it to ash. No travel. No, nothing. Do not complete. Her jaw ached.

She crawled to the rope and hauled herself up hand-over-hand, boots scrabbling. The null-cat flowed over her shoulder to her back. It weighed almost nothing but felt heavier than a fist on her spine. The wind dropped away as she rose into sunlight. For a breath the world held its breath with her.

Then the engine spoke.

The word came from inside the space between her bones, a syllable that wasn’t one, a pressure-wave in the hole between her first and second incisors where a milk tooth had gone missing in a sunburnt summer when she was seven. It thumped. It settled. It was the sound of acceptance: an audible slotting like a latch, nothing to do with ears or language at all.

Gida froze, one hand still inside the pit. The other tightened around the rope until the hemp bit into her glove. The null-cat pressed both sets of feet into her shoulder hard enough that she’d have bruises tomorrow.

She didn’t say anything. The trap ate whatever reflexive answer her body had been about to make. That was what it was for. It had saved her from signing a dozen times. But it couldn’t make the engine un-speak. It couldn’t make her un-hear being named.

“Gida?” Rook said again, and his voice sounded far away, as if the air between them had become glass.

She dragged herself the rest of the way out and rolled until her shoulder blades hit the crust’s rough solidity. The sky hurt. Everything was too bright. Salt glittered and the glitter doubled until she shut her eyes and saw it anyway.

“Hey.” Rook’s voice gentled. “Tell me what you felt.”

“Acceptance,” she said, and the trap did not catch because she wasn’t answering a call, she was saying a fact. The taste of it was iron. “Rook, it tagged me. I didn’t answer. It’s still—”

“Where?”

“In my head.” She pushed herself upright. The pit’s edge had a shadow. In the shadow, the air shivered—just a little, as if someone had been standing there and stepped away. The null-cat put its face to her ear. Its whiskers tickled. It did not like the shiver, and neither did she. “I’m clear of the mouth. I’ll bury it.”

“You can’t bury that,” Rook said, flat. “It’s awake. Get distance. We’ll bull the crest and drop a seal.”

Gida did not love the idea of a ground lifter anywhere near a live well, but distance was good. Distance meant the noise would muffle, the pressure might drop, the taste go out of her mouth. She looped the rope over her shoulder, half ran toward the crawler she’d left on the hardpack a hundred meters away.

The engine spoke again before she reached it. This time it made words. Or it made a pattern which her tongue shaped into words because her head needed them to understand what wanted her attention.

Bearer, it said—not in Antecedent, not in any modern code she recognized, just in whatever simple shape a mind cuts to fit a call. Taker. Witness absent.

“No witness,” Gida said automatically, and the trap caught and she choked and laughed at the same time, a wet sound. She’d bound her mouth to nothing and now nothing held her lips like a bridle.

Rook swore softly—her mic caught only the exhale. “You’re pulling sign pressure. Your suit sensors are all wrong.”

“I’m fine.” She wasn’t, but she was functional. She yanked the tarp off the crawler and slapped her hand to the ignition. The engine whined and kicked two teeth before settling to a sour hum. The cabin was a tin oven. She threw herself into it, the null-cat flopping boneless as a beached fish onto the dash. It lay with its belly to the pitted metal, legs splayed as it tasted whatever moved in the air.

The first gust hit as she threw the crawler into gear.

It didn’t come from the west, where the winter weather usually brewed, or the south, where the gullies took wind and made it into knives. It came from the east, where there was nothing but flats and, beyond a long day’s drive, the dry shell of the basin and the city built into its ribs. It came like a breath and then another, not steady wind at all but a series of pushes as if a hand were patting the world.

Gida gripped the wheel and let the crawler ride the push. The salt popped under the tires and then melted to slick. She tasted metal from her coin and something like bruised peaches from the field. Pressure. Her lattice had to translate everything since the day of the Great Backing-Out into taste because it had been the only sense safe to hijack. Vision had too many hooks. Hearing translated the wrong way. Taste was safe, people said. It was a lie, but most of their safety was lies.

The voice settled in her mouth again.

Take the city to the sea, it said. It was kinder than she expected. Completely indifferent.

“No,” she said, or meant to, but the trap was still live and of course the trap didn’t distinguish between spontaneity and necessity. The sand pill’s gray thread burned through the bead and the bead gave up. She coughed. The null-cat made a tiny scraping noise with its legs, as if it wanted to help but hadn’t been taught how.

The crawler’s comm stuttered. Rook’s voice wavered, dropped away, morphed into a long tone, came back. “Say it again.”

“It gave me a clause,” Gida said. The words came out steady because she was making herself speak them like a recitation she didn’t feel. “It said: Take the city to the sea.”

Rook didn’t answer for the space of three breaths. Gida could hear him thinking, and what she heard was all the things he knew that she didn’t about things like this. Rook never went into the field. Rook sat in a chair and watched numbers and told her when patterns changed. He was good at it. He knew fear that looked like risk curves. He had never once told her to run from a job she could handle.

“You’re sure that was the sequence,” he said. “No qualifiers? No before or unless?”

“Only that. And there was a missing piece.” Gida pressed her palm to the wheel so the callouses changed the friction and ground her. The far horizon had lost its hard edge. The sky was smudged with something. “It said witness absent. It might have been waiting for one.”

“So it bound anyway,” Rook said. “Which means that well wants that thing done more than it wants it done clean.”

“It wants it done,” Gida said.

“And now it thinks you’re the bearer and you think you heard it, which in some cases is enough. Is your trap still up?”

“It’s melted. I could throw another.”

“Do it.”

Gida pulled the crawler to a skidding stop and dug for the packet. The null-cat climbed back onto her shoulder without letting go of the dash. It didn’t like stopping. The gusts were becoming steadier, singing in the seams of the cabin. She looped thread and nail around the steering column and pressed another sandpill into the noose. The bead bled out and dried dull. “Okay,” she said. “Say something binding to me, Rook, so I can see if it—”

“No. Don’t test. Take my word for it.” He breathed in. “Gida. Get to the ridge. Come back by the long way. Don’t go near any more infrastructure. We’ll put a barrier map over that place and call a big team.”

She nodded instinctively and then checked herself in case some stupid part of her wanted to say I promise. “Copy.”

Wind shuffled the world again. The crawler swayed as if something living had leaned on it. The smudge on the horizon had become a line, and the line had a color that wasn’t dust, wasn’t storm. It was a thin blue too bright for this dry.

Take the city to the sea, the engine had said.

The sea was two hundred kilometers east by the old map and two hundred and eighteen by the new, because the ground had heaved after the last winter and the easiest path was now a long meander between the swells of salt. The city was west-southwest, nested in the badlands that had been a lakehead once. Gida had walked its outskin when she was a kid. Her mother had kept a stall under one of the ribs until the Assurance Hall pulled the ribs tight after a failure and a lot of people didn’t fit inside anymore. Gida had left that city because it had too many shaped promises compressed into bones that bent when they shouldn’t. She had no intention of picking it up and carrying it anywhere.

“Rook,” she said, as the line became a gleam, and the null-cat made a soft sound she had never heard it make. “You’re seeing that too?”

“I’m seeing interference,” Rook said. “Local horizon is baying. Your camera says there’s light where there shouldn’t be. I am going to use big words like impossible and see what happens.”

Gida let the crawler roll forward. Salt snapped. The wind changed yet again. It smelled like wet. Not the fresh wet of rain. The sour wet of sea, brine and old rot.

“We shouldn’t even have a sea,” she said. “It’s a dead basin. Everything’s—”

“Gone,” Rook said. “Yeah. Except not this minute.”

She topped a ripple in the salt and saw it: a slice of blue cutting the world a little to the left of east, a horizontal strip as if someone had shaved the land and slipped a mirror under the scar. It had no fringe, no foam, no depth cues. The sky above it was the same winter-sbread blue as everywhere else. It was wrong enough that the part of her brain that named predators threw everything it had at the shape: snake, hole, edge of a roof, threshold.

“Refraction,” she said, and knew she was lying.

The null-cat splayed its legs wider and pressed its head into her neck as if it could make itself into a collar to hold her upright.

Take the city, the engine said, and the word city made the taste of iron coins, and the word sea made the taste of a broken tooth. The engine had a sense of humor. Or maybe that was her lattice talking just to keep from screaming.

She could say no. She had. She would. She didn’t own this machine; she didn’t have to obey an absent witness announcing clause. Every assurance she’d grown up with had been careful to remind her that consent mattered. But that had been the modern law. Every story about the Antecedents said that laws had been different when they wrote promises into rock and air and heat and time. They had been very good at setting up games so the only winning move was to play.

“Gida,” Rook said, as she turned the crawler east. “Long way to the ridge is south.” His voice trembled on the last word.

“I’ll call you back,” she said. “Boros will sue you if you let me break a live well by bulling a crest. I’ll mark the hole and—”

She throttled down to make the lie sound like a plan, but the wind took her words and stripped them to metal taste. She closed her mouth and clenched her jaw and breathed.

The line of blue held steady. It wasn’t moving, and it wasn’t not moving. It sat across her path at a place she wouldn’t reach for some hours unless the crawlers’ tires happened to find the hard old riverbeds buried under salt that a sharp east wind happened to clear of drifts. The pushed gusts kept coming. The sky above the glimmer wore a faint smear like a flock of birds. No birds flew here.

“This is a bad idea,” Rook said, both practical and hopeless. “This is the worst idea. This is—”

“I know,” Gida said. She ate the last word. She had already spoken too many.

She’d told herself a hundred times she would never make an oath near a live engine. If she had nothing else true about her, she had that. She had thought that was the same thing as being safe. She had spent years testing edges, setting up prophylactics, teaching her body not to respond when the world asked a question too loudly. And now she had been asked a thing so simple a child could understand it and so complicated she could not name the first step.

Take the city to the sea.

The hand that had patted the world patted again, longer this time, and the horizon’s wrong blue flickered. The smear above it rippled, darkened. Sheet lightning crawled in silent fingers across the smear and then winked out. The smell of wet doubled.

Behind her, the direction of the pit, the air shivered. She didn’t have to look to see that the light had shifted there again. The engine sensed where she bent and leaned. All it did was insist. It didn’t threaten. It didn’t beg. It set the table and waited.

“Boros is going to scream,” Rook said. “I’m telling him anyway. He’ll scream and then he’ll start mobilizing the biggest indemn team in three sectors and then he’ll call someone we owe and then he’ll call me worse. When you get to the ridge, you stay there. I will walk down the crest and drag you up myself if I have to.”

“You can’t permit me anything,” Gida said, and the taste of copper thickened. She didn’t say I promise because there wasn’t a trap in the world that could catch both her and the engine and she wouldn’t insult the one that had just saved her from the first reflex.

“Fine,” Rook said, soft again. “Talk to me. Tell me something else. Tell me about the city. Tell me where you’ll start not doing this thing you’re not going to do.”

Gida laughed, and it sounded like a cough. “Between ribs five and nine,” she said, because if she had to imagine it she might as well imagine it right. “There’s a gap where the bones buckled when the Hall cinched them after the collapse. If I were going to cheat a city’s center of weight, I’d start there. Split and slip the fascia toward the gullies and then let wave run under—”

The word wave stuck. The line in the distance, the wrong blue, licked its lips.

Just an idea, she told herself. A way to feel like she could say no to the tail end of a hurricane by naming it. Not a plan. She left the crawler on an east by north-east tack and kept her hands light on the wheel. Salt whispered. The null-cat kneaded her shoulder with tiny stabs of comfort it didn’t know weren’t.

Gida pretended not to notice when the wind lined up exactly with the old riverbed.

Above her, the winter sky thinned. Far across the flats, impossible, something like a low wave rolled along the bracelet of blue and fell silently into itself. A moment later the voice that had been nothing but acceptance and insistence added another word:

Before the red storms, it said. And her mouth had no trap for time.

Gida didn’t answer because sometimes the only way to say no to an older thing than you was to keep your tongue still and let the muscles in your legs decide. Her calf cramped. She pushed it out. The crawler rattled. The salt finally gave way entirely, and the ground under the tires hardened—riverbed, as if a hand under the earth had smoothed it and laid it under her like a grating.

“Gida,” Rook said, and he had all the wrong things in his voice. Fear, and pride, and a taste she’d learned to hear as care. “Don’t make a promise.”

“I won’t,” she said, and did not trust her tongue. She bit down on the coin and let its taste flood her mouth until it burned. Then she spat it into her palm and closed her fist around it, hard enough to grind the copper corners into skin.

She drove east, toward a sea that wasn’t there, with the city at her back singing its quiet badlands song over her engine. The air smelled of salt and time. The promise that wasn’t hers sat in her mouth like a stone and waited for drought-red to climb the horizon.

If she didn’t keep it, reality would eventually find her and ask why. It always did. The first thing the engine knew how to do was help. The second thing was calculate. It would start small; it was not a curse and not a blessing. She would find doors open that shouldn’t be, paths swept clean before she knew she needed them. She might even find a friend who called at exactly the right time. And then, in the long calculus of arrangements, when she refused the path it had made so patiently, the engine would call in its collateral.

She knew all that because she had learned it with her mother’s hand on her head in a stall under rib six reading contracts she wasn’t allowed to speak yet. She knew it because she had kept herself safe this far by never letting the universe pull a promise out of her like a tooth.

She drove into wind that did not know which way to blow, and told herself, tight in her chest, that she would go to the ridge and watch and mark and call a team.

The horizon’s blue line flashed once and went dark and then returned, brighter.

Before the red storms, the engine had added. Which meant not today and not tomorrow and maybe a week or maybe three. It meant that somewhere, dust had already begun to rise.

“Rook,” she said. “Tell Boros to get me a boat.”

It was a quarter tone. Not enough to make anyone else frown into their coffee. Just enough to knock the world loose in my ribs.

The city always sang. It came up through the stairs, along the copper freckles of old rails and new conduits, in the bead chain that kept my kettle from floating off when the Lock took one of its half-breaths. Even when the markets were asleep and the drones were docked and the hydrants murmured in their own pipes, you could feel it. Suspended weight. Tension held across the place where Latch was stitched to a version of rock the world got assigned this morning. It was the closest thing we had to weather.

That morning the steam condensed in a shape I didn’t recognize and the tile under my bare feet vibrated a little sharp of where it should. We had tuned ourselves to C for as long as the files went back. Sheila—my old supervisor, dead three years, still present on half the walls—used to rap the back of a wrench against the brackets between Anchor and Steeple and say, There’s your home, Jun. C. Home is what you can hum without thinking.

I set the kettle on its puck and turned the knob, and the flame halo grabbed in a way that would have made my father curse. I turned it back off and waited for the Lock to finish exhaling. A quarter tone, I told myself, tugging the thermos lid tight. A quarter tone before eight meant somebody in Alignment had snuck a correction onto the schedule without flagging us. Either we were drifting into a known stripe or someone upstairs was too polite to wake Choristers to do their damn jobs.

The bracket under the sink looked new. That’s when my heart did the clumsy roll. I’d installed a dented catch myself after the old one cracked. Two months of cursing washing baskets and the thrift market finally spit up one the right size. I’d painted a crooked white moon on the lip, the way you do when you’re proud of a stupid little thing.

This bracket didn’t have my moon.

I stood there with my hands braced on the counter, like maybe if I pressed hard enough the old catch would rise up out of the gold-veined fake stone. The city sang a little too bright, the cold seeped deeper, and the kettle didn’t know me.

“Mara?” I said out loud to the anti-frost plant that sat above the sink, because that’s who I would have said it to. Then I swallowed and touched the left side of my throat.

The thin strip of polymer that should have been there—two centimeters wide, transparent, embedded with a line of microcoil and one thread of Mara’s hair—wasn’t. A lighter patch of skin crossed with the ghost of a rash where the adhesive used to irritate me; otherwise almost no sign it had ever existed.

The city thrummed. My finger closed on air. I opened the cupboard where we kept the spices and took down the tin labeled unnecessary but nice. It was empty. We had never bought nutmeg in this version, apparently. I laughed a little because it was either that or let my knees go.

I told myself the same thing I always told myself when the Lock pulled us across a seam and the signage went a little off and the soup tasted like someone else’s idea of soup and the elevator opened on a hallway that hadn’t been there before: you work at the Steeple, you get lag for free. Anchor duty does something to your head. It throws a thin film of yesterday across your eyes so the city doesn’t stick like sandpaper every time it slips. You remember things you shouldn’t, and then it hurts, and then you go to work.

I dressed with one ear pressed to the stairwell rail. The song of the building was clean. Young, almost. It buzzed the way the older neighborhoods don’t anymore. Out the kitchen window the orange threads strung across the ravine glowed as if someone had polished them inside an hour. It wasn’t my version of the Thread Road. This one was newer, and the little prayer flags were missing, and there was a banner hung below the big corner amphitheater that said Festival of Versions in three languages I recognized and one I didn’t. The old man who haggled over magnets on the corner was gone. The stray dog who hoarded left shoes had a limp it hadn’t had yesterday. I found my boots by feel and did not look at the pale square on the wall where our Bioheater had always left a pinprick scorch in the paint.

The hall outside my door smelled like cold tea. The woman two floors down had hung fish to dry across the landing, which meant her husband hadn’t fallen down the mountain in this version. That was good. I stepped past the fish. The handrail bit my palm all the way down. The stairwell treads hummed as the song in the city shifted again—half of a half step, a polite nothing, a rumor at the edge of hearing. It rattled the magnets on the utility box and made a line of shadow dance across the oil painting that someone had salvaged from a museum in a version where paint got to dry.

“Jun.” The name drifted this way as a question. Cota, two flights below, poked his head out of his door. He had a silver hoop in his lower lip in this version and a shock of black hair cut in a way that made him look like someone who did not fall asleep in book piles. “We’re sharp.”

“I heard,” I said. My voice came out even. I was always a little proud of that. Choir test voice: drifts anchor to anchor and never betrays your throat.

“They pinged Steeple ten minutes ago,” Cota said. “We’re on early. Like, now early.”

“Let me guess,” I said because I couldn’t help it. “Someone scheduled an unauthorized correction while they were polishing their prefect badge.”

Cota tilted his head. In the version of him that had followed me here from last week, that line would have made him smile. This Cota’s mouth twitched and smoothed. “Festival brings civic types. Civic types bring cosmetics.”

“Tell the Lock,” I said. I started down. He fell into step.

Latched is built in precarious layers, like someone had taken a whole country and made a scrapbook out of it, then bound some of the pages with wire and some with dried seaweed and some with ragans we sing to when the rain goes vertical. From the lower walk I could see the Steeple rising in its nest of cables, white in this light, less stained than it has looked in years. It was a good sign or a bad one, depending on whether you like your gods to look fed. The Lock itself is a thing we are not supposed to name, but everything we do leans on it. A long mechanical sigh under reality itself. You can feel it when it settles; the quarter tone had that metal smell the Lock gets when we’ve been on a cheap seam.

We cut through the herb stalls. In this version the woman with salt crystals in her hair was buying lemon plants and laughing. In the one where her wife had died, she never laughed. The weight of both sat on my tongue and I said nothing. Cota and I took the trolley that runs on cushions of sound up to the Steeple because the new interns think it’s romantic to walk the Cableway and we had no time for romance.

I checked my feed at the gate. The badge in my throat lit as if nothing had changed in the world. Jun He, Anchor Chorister, Node Three. 07:34 arrival. The message queue flickered. Eleven minutes ago: Alignment shift request flagged by Prefect Yana Ful. One minute ago: unauthorized perturbation along North-South axis recorded but not accepted. File attached. The little red dot next to it pulsed. I kept my hands still. I did not open Mara’s private channel. Not because I thought it would be dead—if you’ve ever been burnt by a lockout, you know better than that—but because hearing it ring and ring and ring through walls that no longer contained any addressable unit of her would have been worse than listening to a quarter tone drill a new door into my skull.

The gates coughed us through. The base of the Steeple is older than anyone alive now, and older than anyone in any version I’ve ever touched, which means it has names written down that nobody uses. Dock. Knot. First House. The slabs that line the approach are carved with the earliest attempts at making Latch permanent. We built it during a time when staying still was a prayer no one expected to be answered. We learned through breakage and apologies. We learned by listening.

The Steeple is a tower and an instrument. It holds the lines like a harp. It collects the tension the Lock demands and holds it in a shape human hands can adjust. You lay your weight against it and it lays its weight back on you. All our little houses and walkways and markets and storms and portrait galleries and old bouquets stapled to railings hang from it. If you think that sounds ridiculous then you haven’t lived in a place like ours. Reality has to take its shape from somewhere. We decided to give it ours.

“Jun!” Pasha skated across the floor with a sheaf of thinplate and a look like he’d chewed too much ice. He wore the same high-visibility shawl he always wore because he hated getting brushed by the gentry, and in this city wearing a bird orange shawl to a job where half of your work was done in the dark counted as polite rebellion. There was a scar through his left eyebrow in this version that hadn’t been there last week. He jerked his chin towards Node Three anyway. “You got the good ear. Go fix it. If I try to tune wavering after last night I’ll puke on the brace.”

“Was it a good night?” I said.

“Better than the Civic’s idea of a correction,” Pasha said, and snapped his gum at the ceiling. “And I wasn’t the one who signed it so don’t look at me.”

“I never look at you,” I said, which made him grin like a man who wanted everyone to look at him.

The underfloor vibrated with varying opinion. Node Two hummed shabby. The kids we call Kites bobbed in their safety harnesses at Node Five, trying not to grin for the visitor up at the south balcony. The long banner advertising Festival had been tacked to the northern lattice in a way that made the north-south lines hum like irritated wasps. I wanted to take it down. I wanted to fold it very carefully in a way that made the Prefect come down and look me in the face. I wanted to call my wife and ask her if she’d eaten and get the same irritated little sigh she used when I phrased a yes / no question like a poem.

Node Three rests on the thirteenth platform, up the metal hive. I could have climbed blind, hand to rung to strapped hole to beam. People leave offerings on the twelfth landing to thank the Lock for a safe season. This version had small beeswax boats instead of knitted fish. I didn’t know if the fish-knitter had left town or if he simply made boats now. I touched a boat and kept going.

At the top, Mina was already braced into the harness, a small person entirely made out of muscle and fury. Her hair stood up like a halo of screwdriver bristles. Mina has the patience of a dying star. Mina will hold a ten-pound wrench in her teeth while she tells you a sweet story and when you get to the end she will separate your cause of failure into three simple commands and make you go to bed on time.

“Sharp?” she said, when I clipped in beside her.

“Quarter,” I said, and instead of telling me congratulations on your dynamics test you can hear the world she looked at my left shoulder like she could see through my skin to the place where the absence was. Mina had been the first person to tell me about lag. She had told me in a voice like she was telling me religion in a city that has to share its gods. “Outages?”

“Minor,” she said, and lifted her chin. “Watch the reflection. Node Eight registered a flicker along the lower band when Ful pinged. If she pushes the correction through the wrong channel again I am going to file a complaint with whatever version of her makes all her decisions with a spoon.”

“I’ll watch,” I said. I kissed two fingers and touched the brace. Mina frowned and pretended not to notice.

When you tune, you lean. You put your weight into a harness and hang back so that your ribs are open and your throat aligned and your hands free for the coil. You listen. The coil gets hot. The coil gets cold. The amount of change you make is ridiculous. It’s nursery math. A fraction of a fraction. You can’t teach anyone to hear the difference. They either learn how to do it by hanging there and letting their viscera buzz until the wires in their teeth hum and their blood finds where the Lock has dragged off to; or they leave.

I breathed. I let the tension of the Lock find my sternum and push, the way you let a big dog lean and decide where you’re going to stand. Under it the world murmured. The version we were in had the smell of a different algae and at least one fish that vibrated at a frequency the south lattice liked. The distant pipe one floor down was tuned to a whole number it hadn’t been tuned to in years. There was a lump in my throat that had nothing to do with frequency. The absence of a strip of smart polymer can feel like a boulder.

I tuned. The quarter tone came down gradually. Mina’s ladder hummed approval. The floor below our feet became more itself, the way skin looks kempt after you drink water.

That’s when the noise bloomed.

I call it that because it didn’t come in like a sound from any direction. It opened like a flower without color. The old-timers call it black note. Sheldon calls it off-prime. It isn’t a thing the Lock does. The Lock is under our reality, not outside of it. This wasn’t Lock. This came at the Steeple from a direction we are not supposed to have.

Mina swore. Pasha said what I was thinking, which was: who in the name of all the the knots is trying to pull on the lines from the other side?

The noise had structure. It had a header, if you like thinking of the world as a net you can catch messages in. The way you see a face and know it’s a face because face. The way you smell burnt sugar and know you have to run.

“Do not accept,” said the speaker near Mina’s head, in the careful voice the system uses when it has to tell you to pull back. “Unauthorized perturbation. Source unknown. Attempted overlay falls outside all civic registry. Reject. Reject. Reject.”

“The system’s polite,” Mina said. Your hands get steadier when you have her voice around. “We’re not. Block it.”

“It’s not Lock,” I said. The hair on the back of my hands rose. “It’s not thrash.”

“That’s worse,” Pasha said into the line on our shared channel. He clicked his gum. The gum is his totem against having to think too hard. “Jun. You feel that? That’s a signature.”

The noise opened again. Not an assault. A hello, if a dangerous hello. It had the awkwardness of a person leaning on your door after being gone all winter.

“This is Ful,” said a voice over the general line. The Prefect had the kind of voice you imagine on posters trying to get you to vote. “Block. Block. Block. Alignments are my purview. Steeple, for now you take your orders from me.”

“You’re not the Lock,” Mina said softly, in a voice she didn’t put on the channel.

I should have blocked. I should have been a person who did what the sign on the wall said in big letters: safety is a chain. You don’t take out a link because it is inconvenient or because your heart just learned the world has unstitched your wife from your morning. You block the unauthorized perturbation. You live to be scolded about it over tea.

I lifted my hand to the block.

The noise opened like a door at the bottom of the sea. It carried what felt like the skin of a hand brushing the back of mine.

The signature was a set of numbers that had walked with me for eight years. It was stupid to make a number our private thing. It was childish, the kind of superstition inherited from people who used stones to mark days. But. It was the line Mara had threaded into my throat. It was the sum of eight things and three more and one we never tell anyone. It rang that way when I leaned my forehead against the brace on mornings we fought and went to work anyway. It rang that way when she sang with wet hair and filled the house with yeasted air and salt.

“Jun,” said the noise, and it was the shape of her voice translated into something that could travel where no voice could go. Scratch the translation. It was the mistake she always made in my name. Everyone else says it flat. She used to lift it at the end like a promise. Jun?
