I have never seen Mina’s jaw drop. In some version of the city, that moment was the first.

“Do not lock,” the voice said. “Follow the chalk.”

It cut.

Pasha cursed, which sounds like a child being thrown into very cold water. The line hissed. Mina swore in a language I didn’t know. The Prefect’s voice came back saying block block block and my hands hovered, useless.

“Follow the chalk?” Pasha said. “What chalk?”

Mina’s eyes cut to mine. “We block,” she said. You don’t ask a question like a question when the line is open and the Prefect is listening. The Lock hummed under our feet like someone holding their breath to count.

“I—” I said.

The corner of Mina’s mouth moved. It could have been a tic. It could have been permission, if I was the sort of person to see permission in the twitch of a woman whose job is to hold ladders. “We block,” she repeated softly, for the record.

I flipped the block. The system made the tired grateful noise it does when you do what the sign says. The black note went away like stepping out of wind.

We counted to twenty out loud for the civics and the gods. We updated the log. Knit three; purl one. We tuned with the quarter tone until it was gone. The banner on the north lattice slept without anger. Mina’s knuckles went white and then red. The kids at Node Five bragged about how they would have handled it if it had been theirs. The Prefect preened in our ear about swift response and civic trust. I kept my hands moving so that they would not shake.

On the way down the first stair my boot scuffed white.

At first I thought someone had chalked something as part of Festival. Children draw ladders that lead to the Lock, strings that tie the Steeple to a big cartoon hook in the sky, the way they teach you to when you’re small and want to say thank you to the thing that hasn’t dropped you yet. Tired Choristers chalk notes to themselves when their hands are too numb and they don’t trust the line. Mina chalks a three-prong fork in a place that machinery should not be because she distrusts every map.

But this chalk wasn’t on a sensible surface. It rode the dark mouth of a maintenance shaft on the thirteenth platform that had been welded shut in my city five years ago. The weld was gone. The hatch was old. The chalk had been laid with two strong fingers, thick as a toddler’s wrist. The line was an arrow, down. The arrow had a tiny curved tail.

No one in the Steeple draws their arrows with tails.

I stood very still so that the Lock could decide if gravity was going to be kindergarten easy or shipboard mean. Under my palm the railing felt less cold than it had thirty seconds ago. The song in the struts shifted by a not-large measure. In my collarbone, a place sang that had never belonged to me.

“Jun?” Mina said. The question lift. Had I taught her that? Or had she learned it from a version of me who had not learned it from Mara yet?

“I’ll be back,” I said. I heard my own voice from far away and hated it, and I loved it for being calm.

The prefect was still talking. The Kites were still preening. Pasha’s gum clicked like a metronome to a dance I have never known how to do. I knelt, put my hand to the chalk, and came away with white dust on my skin that smelled like what dust always smells like, in every version: rocks, boring, faithful.

Follow the chalk, the impossible voice had said. If this was a test devised by civics to see if we’d dethrone faith with curiosity and let the city split along seams it wasn’t ready to travel, I was going to fail it. The maintenance shaft mouth breathed cold air on my face.

I flicked my wrist and cut my private channel alive. Protocol says you do not open private channels during unauthorized events. Protocol also says you do not draw chalk on maintenance hatches. The channel hummed.

“Mara,” I said, and swallowed. “If you’ve made me follow someone else’s children’s art into a shaft we sealed because a man got lost in it and came back wrong, you owe me so many nutmeg tarts you will carry the smell in your hair for a month.”

The shaft breathed deeper. The chalk tail pointed down.

I slid in.

At 09:17, the Winnower breathed wrong, and the city answered.

If you’ve lived under the shadow of the towers as long as I have, you know the way the city hums on a good day. Traffic curls through the grid like blood in capillaries. Drones knit invisible threads. Crowds move with the indifferent grace of fluids. Noise has a texture, warm and even. Chance itself feels tame, like a dog that knows its boundaries.

At 09:17, all that stopped. There was a shiver under my feet that had nothing to do with earthquakes, a cough from the depth of the building that wasn’t mechanical and wasn’t quite human. Every system hiccuped, just once. On my left, a maintenance drone sneezed bolts across the floor—tiny silver pings that should have skittered into the gutter and disappeared. Instead, each bolt described a neat curve and screwed itself into a waiting hole on the underside of a rack that had been missing three fasteners for months. On my right, Jae’s paper cup slipped from his hand, rotated in midair, and landed upright on its ring stain with the coffee still inside.

He blinked at it, then at me. “Did you—?”

“No,” I said, though a part of me wanted to claim it just to try on the power. The screen above my head filled with ash-tinted noise, the way old televisions used to when we still had antennas and weather. A coil of conduit on the far wall, loose since before my apprenticeship, swung with sudden purpose and settled into its clamps as if repenting.

And as if someone had pulled a drawstring under the sky, the noise of the city drew tight. The distant cadence of pneumatics and wind turbines sharpened. A motorcycle whose muffler had been hanging on by hope and rust fell off, clanged on the street, and then bracketed itself back into place. My comm buzzed so hard against my collarbone that I smacked it without thinking. The time stamped in my vision went from 09:17:03 to 09:17:03 and stuck.

“Okay,” Jae said carefully. “The Winnower is not supposed to do that.”

No, it wasn’t. The Winnower—the Confluence Control Core, if you wanted the official name—was the densest stack of probability management ever built. It was three hundred meters of gyred metal and latticed crystal and humming algorithms folded into a vertical labyrinth, sunk into the bedrock beneath Tower Two. Every light pulse in it went through at least nine redundant pathways. Its sole job was to nudge our world away from the knife-edge of its unlikelier disasters.

Nudge was the word they drilled into us. We were not gods. We did not cheat. We tuned the city’s calcium-rich mess so that the skull didn’t crack so often. We shaved tails off distributions—just a little—and redistributed the saved luck where the budget allowed. We were gardeners of randomness. If it coughed, it was not a metaphor. It meant there was dust in the air of our vault where no dust had any business being.

I had already sprung the latch on the access panel. The face-plate swung out on its oiled hinges. Behind it lay the bowels—spiral waveguides like veins in slate, rooms of vacuum thick as silence, incantations coded in languages we didn’t speak anymore, only maintained. I ducked my head and the scent hit me: cool metal, ozone, the faint sweetness of old capacitors. Beneath that, something else, like the smell of the wall behind an old painting when you take it down and there’s a square of a different time.

“See if it’s localized,” I said. Jae’s fingers were already flying over his console. Cher was in the air above us, her avatar’s face projected in semitransparent blue from the ceiling. She was the building’s system voice when we drilled, which is to say she had once been a person, and now she was permissions and reminders and the click of doors. We didn’t ask what she had been before. You learn not to.

“There are reports,” Cher said. “Citywide anomalies. Probationary calibrator Omondi, proceed with caution.”

I crawled into the service crawlway on my belly and elbowed forward. My torch cast a thin oval. The cable harness looked like a waterfall frozen in black, flowing down to the heart. I ran my hand along it like a ritual, the way I had when I was thirteen and a tour guide had snuck us into the lowest public deck and told us to listen with our bones. We had crowded against the glass and listened for the heartbeat of the city. I heard it now, the old thrum, and something behind it like breath caught in a throat.

Everyone in the towers has their superstitions. I was raised on the lower terraces, where when you spill salt you throw the grains backwards over your shoulder and make a face. When the Winnower coughs, I touch the crown of my head with three fingertips and think of my mother’s voice.

Nothing is coming for you, she would say. It is just the weather of numbers. Be clever. Be kind.

I reached the first junction and toggled my pad to manual. The map lit in lines of light, my volumetric HUD overlaying the last inspection with the reality. Everything was where it should be. That was the problem. There were no popped seals, no heat blooms or sagging lines. My pad pinged again. The building had found me with its eye.

“Thread 7H’s variance thresholds have been applied retroactively to distribution cluster Cranial Nine,” Cher said. “Please assess for damage.”

My throat went dry. “Retroactively?”

“Affirmative.”

“Nonsense.” Jae’s voice carried down the crawlway. “Cher, nothing is applied retroactively. That’s the point. The point is the forward constraint.”

“Affirmative. Retroactive application is not permitted. It has occurred.”

I pulled myself around a right angle and into a box room the size of my body. Here in the dark was Sibyl, the so-called oracle. It was half irony and half marketing, because it wasn’t prophetic at all—it was a set of monitoring lattices that speckled the city and gave us early warnings of the highest-probability avalanches. She looked like a bundle of seaweed and stained glass, an old algorithm recarved every time a new failure mode had tried to kill us in the last fifty years.

Sibyl had lit up with thousands of dots. They weren’t the cold green we used for potential. They were orange, which we used for anomalies only when we were very sure the anomaly was not going to be fatal. If Sibyl had gone red I would not have been able to hear her, because I would have been hearing the city screaming. Orange dotted the map like a rash.

“Patch me to street-leads,” I said. “I need a sample.”

Jae grunted. “You’re patched. Hold.”

He didn’t need to say hold. I was, against my will, listening to the city’s layer of voices. It took a second to pick them out from the hum. Trade channel: “My knives curved into the board instead of out, slice clean, ten in a row, what the hell.” Health channel: “Patient on floor thirteen inhaled a bee took breath, bee came out again alive, no swelling. Ah—no, never mind, swelling now.” Logistics: “Two pallets self-centered with no operator input, they shouldn’t have done that, they could have cut someone’s fingers off, thanks, they didn’t.” Lounge channel: “The lemon slice went back in my glass without getting it wet. You know? Like it missed? Like the drink had a perimeter?”

And from the lower terraces where the tower’s shadow falls longest: “The bullets hit the stop signs instead of the kids,” someone said, voice breaking. “Tell the Winnower I saw it.”

The bridge of my nose stung and that wasn’t dust. I put my head against the cool metal and breathed.

“Small sample,” Jae warned. “I’m filtering them. There’s noise. People are making things up because people do that when they’re afraid.”

“I know,” I said. “Sibyl doesn’t.”

She spared me a flicker; I read it as embarrassment because that was easier than thinking of a system of stones that way.

“You’re on Cranial Nine,” Cher reminded us. “Please assess. Thread 7H appears unstable.”

Thread 7H fed the old quarter along the river where the markets never closed. It was where my mother sold spoons for two decades. I crawled another meter and flipped open its panel.

Inside were spin cans small enough to cup in one hand. You wouldn’t know that things so little could tug on the world until you held one. The Tulane pattern—my pattern—shone on their edges like a ring of writing: the physics and ethics our city had inherited from engineers who had mortgaged their neural architectures for its first draft. Each can sat in a saddle of ceramic foam. The fourth can on the left was loose. Its clamp had not come undone. It had not cracked. It had gone wrong in the way things do when your intuition tells you a story that math makes contradictory: it was both deeply in and slightly out, one line of text misaligned, so all the force of the page landed in the margin instead.

I touched it. It clicked into place like a tooth aligning in a bite. Down in my inner ear, where the Winnower keeps its whisper, the home frequency settled.

“Found it,” I said. “7H had an oscillation in—no, that’s not right. It—what did you do?”

“I didn’t do anything,” Jae said, which was true. Jae did nothing. Jae had always done nothing and would retire on the reputation of having done the minimum with elegance. He had a slow smile and a mole under his eye and a habit of using humor as a safety valve. He had also pulled me out from under a collapsing scaffolding when I was fourteen and working a day job, so I liked him even when I would have liked to throw a spin can at his head.

The can was warm. As my fingertips warmed with it, my hand shook. That embarrassed me. Calibrators are taught to keep their autonomic nervous systems under the same kind of gentle constraint as the city. The body is a probability distribution; the mind is a filter. Breathe. Hold. Release.

“What does retroactive application mean?” I asked. “We cannot have retroactively reassigned anything. That’s not how time works.”

“Well,” Jae said, and I could hear the shape of his shrug, “it’s how ledgers work.”

I shut my eyes. The phrase variance debt ticked past my mind like a long advertisement on a bus. We were not supposed to imagine it as a ledger. The training left welts when we did. But it was. You can shave luck but you have to pay it back. Not to the same people—never to the same people, the algorithm avoided a return to the mean that tidy. It paid it back to the city, to opportunity and heartbreak in aggregate. Every time we avoided a pileup on the bridge by switching traffic across four lanes, someone else’s bread fell butter-side down. Everyone learned to live with it, because torn bread heals and bodies sometimes do not.

“Cher,” I said, “how far back?”

A pause. Cher did not pause to think. She paused when she had a human fact to deliver. “Seven years, three months, twelve days, eight hours, twenty-one minutes.”

I swore and rested my forehead against the frame again. Seven years was farther back than anyone liked. That was before I took my first oath. That was before I had the right to touch the cans with my bare hands. Something in this thread had been saving luck and not paying it out, scraping pennies into a jar and not putting them back into circulation, and now the jar had broken. The city was being paid back at once. There would be more oranges. There would be some reds. Causal chains we had nudged a hair were going to snap back with the energy of spring steel.

“Why didn’t we see it?” Jae whispered. He never whispered. “Why didn’t Sibyl see it? She’s not supposed to miss seven years of an out-of-band oscillation.”

Sibyl made a noise like a cat coughing up a hairball, which was Cher’s way of reminding me that the building was never exactly literal. “Sibyl is not prepared to model retroactivity. Please refrain from anthropomorphizing your tools.”

“Please refrain from acting like you aren’t one,” I said, and then, because I couldn’t help it, I laughed. The kind of laugh you have when you don’t believe and you believe too much. It echoed in the room and died.

When I crawled out from the panel, Jae was sitting cross-legged in the corridor amid a halo of bolts the drone had sneezed and then replaced. He had his hands in his hair and that ugly mole under his eye seemed closer to his eye because his face had gone tight. He looked up at me.

“I have a street cam rolling highlights,” he said, and jerked his chin at the far wall. I turned. The feed came in with an oblique tremble, the edge of a building like a knife above, the street below a shallow bowl.

A child sprinted along the edge of a fountain. She was airborne for a second, her foot aimed at slick tile. Someone gasped off-camera. She would fall and break a wrist, I thought, and the thought ribboned through me—familiar, because if you grew up where I did, you learned to pre-mourn. Then an advertisement banner that had been drooping for months lifted itself in a breeze I couldn’t see, snapped taut, and caught her by the hip as gently as a strong hand. She laughed and swung and didn’t even know. A man at a food cart slid a knife along the trick of his fingers and the knife went where he wanted without drawing blood, and behind him a stovepipe tilted and then corrected, a shimmer of heat like a prayer. Two policemen startled as their partner’s gun slid out of his holster and thumped gently on the pavement by his shoe. He picked it up as if it were an apple and put it back in with his palm over the mouth, cheeks red.

The reel spun. That was the city taking its due the wrong way around. It was wrong, and it was also for once in my life distributed upward. I felt the tick in my bones that I’d felt when I was seven and stepped into the ring of the Winnower tour and looked down on its first deck, and the guide had said, You are part of this now whether you like it or not.

“Fix it,” I said, and it wasn’t to Jae, and it wasn’t to Cher.

“We can’t fix it globally,” Cher said calmly. “We can stabilize, but the debt will pay. It is a matter of where and how fast, not if.”

I pressed my palms together. There were tricks to this. We could widen the aperture in neighborhoods that could take the hit. We could slow the payback so that it didn’t produce spikes. We could tell the city our moral priorities so that the ledger balanced more kindly. That was what the job was when you stripped away the myth and the math. It was telling the machine what we value. It sounds clean until it’s your mother on the other side.

“Pull 7H from the ring,” I said. “We’ll tie a bypass to 7I and thicken the dampers. We’ll take a hit on the river markets, but the schools—”

“You can’t,” Jae said hoarsely.

“What?”

“You can’t pull 7H. It’s bound.”

Bound wasn’t a word we used outside of training. Bound was for rare, rare times when the algorithm adapted itself to contingencies we had not foreseen. It was for events that spooked Sibyl, when the city itself had decided to lean hard on some brittle corner and we had nodded and let it because the catastrophe tree’s branches had been heavy with fruit. When a thread bound, we were not supposed to cut it, because cutting meant a return to the raw distribution of wild space. We liked wild space as a concept. We liked it on t-shirts and murals. We did not like it actually.

“Bound to what?” I asked, though my mouth had gone dry again.

Cher did not answer in words. The wall lit up with a schematic, a thread-map, a cluster of nodes tied in loops I did not recognize. It was beautiful, the way deep things are beautiful when you don’t yet know that they have teeth. It spiraled inward, showing nested neighborhoods, reference systems, and then it hit its center. The tether point flashed.

Subject: OM-134210-LE: Omondi, Laleh Amund.

I misread it the first time. I saw my mother, and then I saw my name. It is always uncanny to see your full name in a font you did not choose. Even on government forms it makes your skin think of eyes.

“Cher,” Jae said flatly. “That’s not funny.”

“I would never attempt humor,” Cher said.

My name sat there like a blood spatter. The thread lines rose and fell around it, weighting, balancing, singing. I reached out and my fingers touched light.

“It’s a bug,” I said. “It’s a mislabel.”

“What are the odds,” Jae said softly, “that a mislabel has your name on it?”

I winced. That was not how odds worked. But in this building, in this job, in this year, a joking calculation like that landed heavy.

A noise came through the feed from the river quarter. Pop. Pop. Pop. Firecrackers, I thought, the way you think “It’s just thunder” when the sky is where it should be and the thing that tears through it isn’t. The cam turned. Three boys crouched under the shadow of the stairwell. They had something cupped in their hands that threw sparks. One looked up and mouthed a word, and the cam did me the mercy of not letting me read it. The sparkler flared and then went out. It should have blown—those boys were not carrying registry and the powder was cut with nonsense and the fuse was greedy. The boy’s friends gaped and then laughed, and the boy looked briefly like a saint in a stained glass window with the fire halo around his fingers. I realized my nails were digging crescents into my palm.

The Winnower owed this city a string of unlikelihoods, and it was paying them through me.

That was not quite right. It was bound to me by some old decision, and whether the binding had happened seven years ago at some threshold I didn’t register, or last week when I signed a form, or this morning when I detoured to bring a child a sweet bun because she had told me she had never had one, did not matter. The threads had tangled. My balance had tipped.

“There will be an audit,” Cher said. One could always rely on her for the dullest part of an emergency.

“Yes,” Jae said. “There will be a bonfire with words in it.”

He stood up and put a hand on my shoulder. The underfloor heat had warmed the paint on his palm, so his hand left a ghost on my shirt when he took it away. We have no gods in our tower except the ones we manufacture, so we sometimes improvise absolutions. He didn’t say anything else. I was grateful.

“What do I do?” I asked the room, which was stupid, because the room was just metal and calculation.

“You stabilize 7H,” Cher said. “You widen buffers in adjacent threads. You prioritize schools and hospitals, restrict the river quarter for the next ninety minutes, and you answer when the Oversight calls and you say, yes, sir, yes, ma’am, we have identified a binding, we don’t yet know why, yes, we’re handling it. You do not pull the thread. You do not run.”

I was not going to run. I had spent my life inching my way deeper into the guts of this place. Running would mean peeling myself back out of the machinery one piece at a time, and I did not think it would let me. But I wanted, suddenly and ferociously, to be back on the lower terraces with my mother, whose hands were spoon-shaped by spoons, making soup that took a whole day, the kind that tastes like the slow work of survival.

My comm ticked. The ID tag pulsed. Oversight. I breathed and opened the line.

“Omondi,” said a voice that belonged to a person whose shoes made no noise in a carpeted hallway. “Explain.”

So I did. I did it clean, with no metaphor and no plea. I spoke as the person I was when I had shaved my hair and stood in a room full of light and said I would nudge and not push, I would care and not own. I said retroactive. I said Sibyl. I said bound. I said my name. On the other end, there was the kind of silence that meant someone was painting their face on with an iron.

“And you’re sure you can’t pull,” Oversight said.

“I can’t without popping constraints we don’t have a map for,” I said. “If I pull without a map, I make wild space.”

“We like wild space on t-shirts,” Oversight said dryly.

“We like it less when it eats our children,” I said, and then bit my tongue. There was another silence. I would pay for that later or I wouldn’t. That is, I realized, also how odds work.

“Stabilize,” Oversight said. “Audit incoming. Do not leave your post.”

“Where would I go?” I asked, and it slipped out warmer than I intended. Oversight didn’t dignify it with a reply.

The line went dead. Jae was watching me with those eyes that always seemed to be laughing and were not now.

“You good?” he asked.

“No,” I said. Whether I liked this job or not, whether it liked me back, I was about to have to learn more about it than I had wanted to know. That’s another superstition we keep in the tower: the machine has layers. The first layer is what you learn on tours. The second is what you learn when you apprentice. The third is what you learn when the building breathes wrong and says your name.

“Laleh,” Jae said, and that was a thing too—he rarely called me by my name. “We’ll fix it.”

We, not you. He stood in a room that smelled like old dust behind a painting and he said we. I nodded. I opened my palm. The crescents my nails had made were white. I pushed my fingers into the foam under the spin cans. I clicked another into place. The city hummed. The ledger spun.

On the feed, the child on the fountain balanced on one foot and then stepped down. On the corner, a bus driver whose brake line had been one shift from snapping took a breath and checked his gauges, and for once the gauge told him the truth before it failed. A woman in a green coat dropped her keys and they bounced and landed in her hand. Somewhere else, something bad that had been meant to happen did not. Somewhere, something that had been meant to go right cracked on a tile floor.

I have never loved the Winnower for its power. I have loved it for its honesty. It cannot stop the wind. It can only tell you how to plant your trees.

“Cher,” I said, “show me everything bound to OM-134210-LE.”

She hesitated, and in that microsecond of hesitation I understood there was a fourth layer to the machine after all.

“There are things,” Cher said very softly, “that I am not permitted to show you.”

“You will,” Jae said, in his slow, pleasant, devastating way. “And you will tell us who told you not to.”

“I will show you what I can,” Cher said, “and I was told by the people who wrote the first draft of your ethics that you do not pull 7H.”

“Then we won’t,” I said. I was lying and we both knew it. I would pull it when I had a map and a way. I would pull it if I found that the binding had been no accident.

The lights flickered. The hum steadied. The scent in the air changed from ozone to clean metal.

And the city, outside, breathed in.

Chapter One

By the time the dry lightning crawled back into the clouds, the tower was warm enough to burn her palms through the gloves. Sena paused three rungs from the top to watch the desert give itself back its heat: the pale perspex of the water farms sweating, the ragged quilts of salt flat reappearing from the night’s chalk. The city’s bones—two hundred Loom pylons—stood in perfect hexes across the plain, each with their blinking sentry lights in slow-phase sync, the pulse that kept people sane. Maybe not kept. Anchored.

“Your biometrics just spiked,” Eyo said in her ear. The line was clear this morning; the storm had scoured the sky clean of dust. “You are not supposed to enjoy this.”

“I’m not enjoying it,” Sena said, and climbed the last three rungs. “I’m trying not to think.”

“You could just… not think without hovering over a two-hundred-meter fall.”

“This is lower than the west spires,” she said. “And I promised I’d stay on leash.”

The leash tugged at her belt when she shifted her weight. It was a narrow braided band of clocksilk, a whisper-light substance that was only heavy to the hand if it needed to catch you. It was new issue. Her old gear had been retired with the incident report.

Sena set her bag against the warm radio deck and crouched. She could see the market streets to the east where the caravans would begin unrolling their awnings to pretend the day’s sun wouldn’t hurt them. The tower’s grattach had a film of night still on it—dew that shouldn’t exist here, forming purely because the Loom had allowed enough slack for humidity to gather in a line of pearl along the galvanic seams.

She touched the dew with a fingertip. It didn’t quite feel like water. It felt like something thinking about water.

“This is a good place,” she said, more to herself than to Eyo.

“I had a bed in mind,” Eyo said. “A possible second good place. We are not so creative.”

“Tell the seed to go live in five.” Sena took the cicada out of the bag and thumbed it on. A soft buzz filled the air around her faceplate and then her chest and then the tower itself, like finding the frequency of the day.

“In five,” Eyo said. A pause. “Are you sure, Sen?”

The cicada sang to boundaries. It was an old machine in a new shell, a thing their teachers had taught them to treat like a pet and a god. It found leeways when the bigger rigs ignored them—those small drafts in causality that smelled like ozone and onionskin, that made matches burn backwards and stories stutter at the critical line. The Loom was supposed to keep such pockets brief and harmless, like eddies behind stones in a river. The city paid people like her to map them and bind them and make sure nobody with a stupid idea and a borrowed sledgehammer decided to widen one for a miracle.

Sena set the cicada on the deck grating. It vibrated, legs clinging to the metal, and sang a little louder.

“Your five is up,” Eyo said. The smile in their voice went away. “We are live. Skin cameras are posting.”

Sena let her faceplate darken against the rising sun and slid her hand along the grating until her fingers found the hairline seam she’d felt in the night’s cold. There. A temperature mismatch. She unfurled a ribbon of thread from her bag and laid it across the seam. A unit of dust from her fingernail drifted up instead of down, watched it hesitate, then go with up as if it had considered arguments and changed its mind.

“Okay,” she said, low. The word became breath on her faceplate. “Okay.”

She breathed with the cicada. The tower vibrated with it. Somewhere below, on the plaza floor, a hawker would be clapping synthetics together and calling for early buyers; further out a Loom tech would be checking a gate phase and whistling the Hush song without knowing it. Sena felt the city the way she had been taught to feel it: not as a place, not as structures and people and the daily economy of salt and sun, but as patterns. This was the frame of her work and the part she loved. She ran her palm above the seam again and felt the place where friction slid sideways.

“Hello, beautiful,” she said, and the cicada trilled, flaring up to a harmonic that made the world blur and snap.

The dew under her fingers unformed, beads abandoning spheres to become pearled neutron storms of idea, and then in the span of a breath they were either gone or doing something backwards. Sena drew her hand back fast. Brush a leeway wrong and you might leave fingerprints on a future you weren’t supposed to touch.

“I have it,” she said. “Eyo, do you see it?”

She heard Eyo’s exhale. “We have you,” they said. “The seam is clean. Six meter arc. It’s very pretty. Like cut glass.”

“Start logging resonance.” Sena slid the tether seed out of the bag. It looked unimpressive for what it did: a matte disk, a coil of clocksilk, a tiny flag antennal as if the machine had a sense of humor. “I’m going to drop the seed.”

“Sen—”

“I know.” She set the seed at the end of the ribbon. “I am alive, and I am careful.”

“You can be one without the other,” Eyo said.

“Not my experience,” she said, and nudged the seed.

It rolled into the seam like a coin finding a slot and then went quiet in the way only very active things could go quiet. The flat light of early day trembled. Sena held her breath out of habit. The cicada’s trill stepped into a deeper register, the kind that made this job feel like prayer, and her skin broke in little gooseflesh knots along her forearms.

Then something on the seed’s little flag lit and blinked, a pattern outside of the patterns she knew. She frowned at it and then glanced at the readings on her sleeve. Numbers were behaving in a smug way. She set two fingers on the grating to check for what the numbers refused to admit. The warm of the metal was wrong. Heat pulled toward the seam instead of away, as if the leeway had hunger.

“Sena?” Eyo again, voice gone thin. “Your complaint dice are starting to throw.”

She liked that the lab had been forced to adopt the slang. “Ah? Show me.”

The screen on her forearm overflowed with small gray squares, each one a tiny simulation of what would happen if she did X instead of Y. Sensors had a sense of humor too. The dice were skewing. A thing not supposed to be possible under the Loom’s maintenance. It wasn’t dramatic. It was a half percent shift in a probability distribution that had done nothing interesting for eight years and seven months.

“Hold the logs right there,” she said, even though she knew Eyo was recording. “Don’t bump this one. I want to see where it stabilizes.”

“Sena,” Eyo said, and the second time they said her name differently, like they were trying to remind her what it was. “The Hush is in… twenty-one minutes. If this is a sympathetic drift—”

“I know,” she said. The seed flickered again. She reached out and touched the little flag. A hiss in the radio made her flinch.

The voice came in sideways, as if it had to paw its way through the metal of the tower to reach her ear. It wasn’t the durable, clean tone of network speech through the Loom’s channels. It was like hearing someone through the kitchen wall during a storm.

“Sena Kade,” the voice said, and she stopped breathing on an old reflex, the one that made her heart hop. She had never told the equipment her name. It did not need it.

Eyo’s breath, a curse, then: “That’s not me.”

“I am at Tower Forty-Three,” the voice said. It had a grain in it that didn’t belong to anyone she knew. Not Eyo, not Tal, not any of her team. It did not belong to the city, older than anyone alive there was old. “Do not bind this seam. Do not call it. We need this leeway.”

Instinct made her peel back, as if the seam itself had thrown the words. She grabbed the ridge of the grating and anchored.

“Identify,” she said. Professional. The training voice. “Speak your name. Speak your sequence. Where are you anchored? What Loom channel are you using?”

The cicada whined, offended or hysterical. The seed’s little light flickered. Somewhere far below a dog barked twice and then couldn’t figure out how not to bark a third time, so barked twice again.

“The channel is not yours,” the voice said. “The channel is after. We are… do you say it this way? We are a later iteration. We have a hold on this seam and we cannot afford to have you bind it now.”

“Sena,” Eyo said, and they weren’t pretending to be calm anymore. “It is a girl with my aunt’s voice when she is ill. It is giving me a headache.”

“Say your sequence,” Sena repeated. Her mouth was dry. Her own voice seemed flimsy enough that if she touched it, it would crumple. “Say your anchor.”

“Sena Kade,” the voice said. “Anchor sequence: Bolus-94, Frequency gate: Stalwart. Your anchor is registered as—”

“Stop,” Sena said.

The silence when the voice obeyed was worse. Heat crawled down the tower skin. The cicada’s song jumped again, lost a half tone, found it again.

“I have you simple,” the voice said, smaller. “I know it is not proper. We are not permitted. I am permitted less than others, because I am kin to you in a way that lingers. It would be good to hear you laugh. We have so many recordings. Your voice always makes the old ones—”

“Stop,” she said again, and some weight fell into the word that even she had not expected. “Do not—”

“Do not bind,” the voice said, fast, eager as a dog offered a job. “We will pay. What do you ask. We can trade—”

Eyo made a startled sound. “Sena,” they said. “Do you see this? The Loom logs are not updating. I am watching the Hush timer and it is choking. There is a hitch, like what you get in a spool that was not wound clean. This is not us. This is not this tower. I am pinging the district station and they are playing dumb.”

Sena wiped her faceplate with the back of her wrist out of a habit from when her breath used to fog glass. No fog now. The desert took. It took and left scratches.

The Hush was the noon alignment. The Loom took a deep breath and all the little machines that kept the world from grinding its teeth went quiet at once. Some people prayed when it happened. Some people coughed. Nobody liked to be doing anything complicated during the Hush if they could help it, because sometimes you lost the thread in what you were doing, the precise step, and then had to wait for sense to return like someone stepping back into a room.

If the Hush had a hitch—

“Let me hear you say my name again,” she said, to the seam. It was petty, but she wanted what she wanted.

“Sena Kade,” the voice said, and this time she heard the way the vowels were sickle-sharp, the way someone would say them who had learned to make hard words around tighter lungs. “I am sorry. You must think of us as grief. We are not supposed to talk to you.”

“Then do not,” Eyo muttered. “Do not talk to us.”

But the voice spoke on, as if apology itself had momentum that carried it over common sense. “We do not get to ask for mercies like this,” it said. “Do not bind the leeway. We use it to feed the far things, to pull them along. Ropes. We are roping something that will keep the children alive in a place that does not want their lungs. If you bind it now the slack is lost to us. It is not your fault. It is the order in the Loom. But the orders are wrong.”

Sena looked down at the coil of clocksilk by her knee. A minute ago it had been a coil. Now it was laid nearly straight, as if someone had been unwrapping it in slow forgetting. She caught it and it tightened as if embarrassed to be caught doing something without permission.

“Don’t bind it,” Eyo said, very quietly. “We cannot do a thing like this without telling. There is so much need for telling. But for the moment— Sen, if the Hush is hitching and you have an unknown actor running that close to one of our spires, we do not bind it from one tower with one set of gloves. We tell, and we get eyes, and we get a coverage rig, and we name it something that will look harmless in the paperwork—”

“What would you name it?” Sena said, absurdly, because naming things was a comfort. “Tell me a harmless-Supply name, Eyo.”

“A petty seam,” they said. “Pseudorandom drift. Children playing at the fence. A phrase that makes the managers feel like they could step on it by accident and not feel bad.”

The cicada had begun to hum in irregular pulses. Sena could tell Eyo was hearing the same pattern because they both, without remarking it, began to breathe in that rhythm, as if it made the waiting easier.

“Do you think a petty seam learned to talk?” Sena said. “Do you think it knows my name on an appetite?”

Eyo didn’t answer. Far below the market had found its stride; she could see the flash of solar cloth stiffening into tent shapes. A child ran with a string of cooling disks in a chain behind them like a tail. This was supposed to be an easy morning. This was supposed to be a check, a seed, a bind, a report, a drink on the way home because the air had been cleaned out by last night’s lightning. She had promised to be dull. Eyo had said yes, and Tal had said nothing which was worse, and she had to come back the following week with everything still true.

She looked again at the seed. It looked like a toy somebody had left on the roof of the world.

“How do you think it knows my name,” she said, to Eyo, and not to the voice.

“Because you are on every list,” Eyo said, gently, as one whispers that a bruise is almost gone but not yet. “Because you do this with your sleeves rolled up where everyone can see. Because when you fell you had your mic open and the whole district heard you sing. Because they made you an example, Sena. Stop pretending you are not lit.”

Right. The fall. The suspension. The loss that belonged to a better chapter, but she carried it with her like a spare battery. Tal had not forgiven her. She had tolerated the way the Loom had, too. Not justice. Not exactly.

“I am sorry we made you an example,” the voice said, startling her into remembering it had not gone away, it was a presence, it was listening. “I am sorry we will do it again in some axes. I am sorry you are going to—”

Sena touched her faceplate with the heel of her hand, hard, as if it might shake the voice out. “What is your name,” she said, very calm. “You know mine, and I cannot abide that between us.”

The pause this time had weight. She could imagine a person on the other side, somewhere unkind, somewhere with a bitter sun. Imagine a hand over a microphone, a look to the side, a shake of someone’s head. A fight. The kind that happens between the line of one breath and the next when choices are too heavy to carry. It helped to picture it as human. It made saying the next thing about a person and not a seam.

“I am Ariyeh,” the voice said, quick as if it would cost less if it came out fast. “I am Ariyeh Kade.”

Her stomach dropped. She tasted something tinny. The skyline bent for half a heartbeat and then straightened.

There were a number of ways to share a name. None of them were accident. It felt like being handed a photograph and a knife and told to choose one.

“We are our grandmother’s failure,” Ariyeh said, and there was that knife, as if Sena had not already found it. “We do not like the Loom. The Loom does not like us. We need ropes. Do not cut this one.”

No one had called her grandmother. Not Tal, who would say your mother’s mother or say the name or say nothing. No one could be that to her who had walked out. It was possible this was a cruelty made to order. It was also possible it was simply the shape of later, and she had to put her hands somewhere in that shape and not let them shake so bad she lost something.

“Eyo,” she said, and her voice sounded normal. “Logging?”

“Logging,” they said. “I have four redundant recordings and two analogs and a piece of paper I am burning under my own desk. The Hush timer has a wobble I have not seen in a decade. District is answering with old words. I think they have their own wobble. Sen, I think this is what Tal calls a bad day.”

“I will not bind it,” Sena said to Eyo. To a person she could hug later. To the work she could answer to. “Not yet. I will set flags and we will call it petty. We will call it… leak with a boundary. Leak with a personality. Something to make them bored. And we will come back with a crew that knows how to be alive all day.”

Eyo blew out air. “Good. Good. Make it dull. Make me a cup of something that makes my bones stay inside.”

Sena reached for the seed, fingers careful, and posed the call to retrieve. The little flag on the seed flicked as if a fish under it had decided it was very tired of being a fish. The cicada dropped to a whisper. In the market a bell rang the Hush pre-note: three descending tones, like the city practicing forgiveness.

“Sena,” the voice said, Ariyeh, and it felt so much like an intimacy it made her want to take off her gloves and press one hand flat against the tower skin. “I love you. Not in a way you can use. But there it is, spent. Please. Please.”

She snapped the seed’s tether and let it spin back into her glove. The seam held a hollow in the air where the seed had been, the way a bed had a body shape even hours after someone stood. Then the air forgot itself and filled in.

“Do not call me grandmother,” she said, not to Ariyeh in particular, but to the tower and the sky and the idea that the world could stick that name on her without her permission. She tucked the seed into its case. “We will be back. Try not to leave.”

The Hush struck. It was as if the city had been wound tight on a spindle and someone took the spindle out. The pulse from the Loom pylons rolled across the plain and people who had forgotten the sensation of silence remembered it and winced. Sena felt the hitch in it, small and wrong, like a skip on a record that has always played smooth, and something in her chest answered in sympathetic skip.

Below her, in the market, a row of red peppers that had been hung in the shade shivered and lifted themselves an inch and then decided to be peppers again and went limp. A dog barked twice and then considered a third time and found it had run out of time to bark for the moment. Eyo said nothing; she could hear them listening.

The hitch passed. The city coughed the way it always did when breath returned. The bell rang a reassurance. The Loom lights resumed their slow pulse as if they had never thought to stop. The seam under her hand—which she had promised not to touch with skin, but promises were flexible sometimes when you were mourning a thing that wasn’t yours yet—stayed cool for the span of ten heartbeats and then warmed, as if her attention had been a blanket.

“Sena,” Eyo said, and their voice had gotten its shape back. “You came home, yes? Do not get ideas about sleeping on the tower.”

“I’m coming down,” she said. She clipped her bag closed and slung it over her shoulder. She looked once more at the line of the desert, the good clean cut of it. Lightning still held itself like a ledger in the clouds, a faint geometry that hadn’t quite faded.

“Ariyeh,” she said into the seam, and hated herself a little for how it felt to say the name. “There will be a call. A formal call. Do not talk to anyone who sounds like me.”

A static that might have been a laugh. “We are not that lucky,” the voice said. “We talk to so many of us. None of them are you. None of them say my name like that.”

Sena carefully silenced the cicada. The tower’s song became just a tower’s creak, metal cooling and complaining. The clocksilk leash tugged when she stepped down, a polite warning, and then settled.

Half a dozen rungs down she stopped because something soft touched the back of her hand. She looked up, expecting an insect. The sky had gone very clear, very bright. A flake floated in the air. It landed on her glove and bit through the material like a slow thought. She shook it off and it cut a neat arc through the sunlight as it fell, etching light into a line. A second flake landed, and she hissed. The air smelled like cold iron and rain that did not belong here.

“Eyo,” she said. “Are you getting—”

“Snow,” Eyo said. “But it cuts. I have a boy on the station roof bleeding from his fingers trying to catch it. I am putting the words together for a petition. I am going to write so many petitions forming a stack that the wind will steal them.”

The flake melted. The biting stopped. A third flake drifted down and then decided, midair, to be just light and was gone.

“Petty seam,” Eyo said. “We are very petty this morning.”

“Very petty,” Sena said, and began to climb in earnest. The tower felt different under her hands, a little more like a thing that could have a mood, a little less like a fact. She could see Tal, later, at the long table, all the maps spread, all their bright, brittle talk, and she could feel the shape of the argument they would have like a bruise coming. She would say Ariyeh’s name and it would be a fight or a silence or another shape she could not name yet.

The city below kept pretending to be ordinary for the sake of people whose hands were full. The Loom lights blinked in their arrangement, dutiful and blind. Sena dropped the last rungs and felt the tower give her to gravity, a gentle handoff, as if the world could be careful with her just this once. She landed on the tile and thought of rope. Of leeways as ropes thrown backwards.

When she turned it felt like the seam at the edge of her vision flicked like a fish in a very still pond. She did not look away from where she was going.

She had a voice in her ear. She had a story that didn’t fit in any report. She had a new word stuck in her mouth like a seed.

On the walk back to the stairwell she gave that word the smallest part of her attention so it would not demand more. She rolled it on her tongue the way a child would taste a fruit they had not yet learned to like.

Ariyeh.

Chapter One: The Knife’s Edge

When Tamsin was a child, the rails sang her to sleep.

The sound came whenever the city shifted its weight, a deep thrumming that rose like a whale breaking under black water, shivered through apartment beams and thin ceramic walls, and finally settled into a hum like a heartbeat. Her father would set a cup on the windowsill and the surface would tremble, making the light from the sunline break into a thousand long, bright slivers across the floor. He would say, There’s comfort in machinery, Tama. Warmth needs a carrier. Sound needs a medium. Love needs a vessel.

At the time she believed him. She could not imagine the rails failing. She could not imagine a day when the song vanished, when the city might outpace its own careful calculations and skate too far toward the day or the night and be lost in torment or freeze.

Now, at twenty-seven, standing on the underside of Heliotrope’s forward gantry, watching the anemometers twitch and tremble and smell the metal heating under her boots, she knows how foolish that belief was. Everything fails, given time. Even sound. Even love. But still the rails sing, and she listens as if there will be a question contained somewhere in the vibration that she will be required to answer.

The sun is a permanent blade on the horizon, a knife’s edge of white fire that the city keeps always at the same insulting angle. The air tastes of copper today and grit. There is a shallow fog lying low over the frostline behind them, that border where day-thaw becomes night-bite, where the street radiators exhale and the ground exhales and the breath comes back as glitter. To their left, toward the day, the heat-louvres are angled to bite off the worst of the flux. To their right, the night expands forever, a black plain with slow rivers of glass and old dunes that crack like cast iron.

“Don’t think I don’t see you worrying,” Jun says, squatting beside her to clip his tether into the gantry’s spine. He gives the line a perfunctory tug. The wind pulls his words sideways, so she turns her head so he can shout them into her short-cut hair instead of open air. “You look like my father in tax season.”

“We have a rail anomaly and a very expensive, very reluctant city,” Tamsin says. She checks her own tether. Her little heat ledger, clipped to her chest, blinks an admonition: conserve. Pre-allocations for this trip were generous—Frontline Maintenance always gets enough for the suit pumps and the glove heaters—but she grew up counting calories in square centimeters of radiator fin and will never be able to stop. “I have a right to worry.”

Jun grins behind his clear visor. He has drawn a little smiley face in grease pencil just above his left eyebrow. It looks defiant, or possibly drunk. “What do you think it is? One of the old refugium boxes breaking through? A dune collapse?”

“We don’t evolve new dunes on top of rails, Jun.” She glances through the gantry lattice at the dark shape that lies ahead, straddling the track, just close enough to be utterly their problem. It is not a dune. It is not any kind of rock she has ever seen on the Knife. It’s glossy under the low light like something oiled. It eats the light. “And the anchor drones came back with low–no return. You see that, right? They pinged that thing and got…nothing. I don’t like nothing.”

Mira climbs out of the belly of the forward sled, swearing eloquently and in at least three languages. She’s the only person Tamsin knows who can make swears sound like poetry. She swings her legs over the side, the suit joints hissing delicate steam for a moment, so quickly the droplets freeze at the ligament edges and it looks like she has lace at her knees. “We burned a drone,” Mira says. “How often does that happen? Why do I let you people talk me into waking up early for this?”

“Because you like to flirt with my discomfort,” Jun says, and Mira kicks him gently in the shin. The three of them have been partnered for two years. They know each other’s tells. They know when to give space and when to offer banter like a handhold. Out here, balance is everything.

There is a crackle over the open channel. Riko’s voice, the shift marshal. When Tamsin first met Riko, she thought the woman had sunlight in her bones. Now she knows better; Riko has tungsten. “Maintenance, talk to me. We’re five degrees shy of threshold on forward slip. I want that obstruction cleared before I have to crank the city’s shoulders.”

“We see it,” Tamsin says. She gives her card number; she listens to the fractional weight of responsibility beep into her ledger: this amount of heat is yours to spend. “We’re going to approach on foot. Sled’s going to be more problem than help at that angle.”

“Got it. And Tamsin?”

“Yes.”

“Be careful.” The channel clicks off.

Tamsin checks her gloves: the filaments are warm and humming. She feels the heat pumps in her boots trying to push back against the cold that leaks up through steel, through composite, through nothingness. Her breath fogs her visor for an instant, clears. All these little proofs of life. She clicks the sled’s little beacon into standby. It blinks an indignant blue at her that says, Why bring me if you won’t use me? Husky things, machines. Full of opinion.

“First round is on you,” Jun says, “if this turns out to be a maintenance prank and we walk all the way out there to find someone’s sculpture.”

“If it’s a prank,” Mira replies, beginning to move along the gantry in the slow, careful footwork of a dancer on ice, “I will personally wire whoever did it directly into the dayface and leave their boots on the frostline for dogs to collect.”

“There are no dogs anymore,” Jun says.

“Then I will start a program to breed cold-hardy dogs,” Mira says, “so that I can leave their boots to them.”

Tamsin smiles because she is supposed to, because this is their ritual and ritual is ballast. She keeps her eyes on the object. If it were a stone, it would be dull; if metal, there would be some structure. It looks like a burn without a fire. The rails around it gleam—naked, exposed. Once these rails were covered, armored against drift. That was when the city was new and the ledger was fat. The louvres were shiny then. The student towers along the sunline still wore their first paint. The water towers sang at night. They sang.

Pacing forward along the gantry takes longer than she wants. The wind pushes at her shoulder, sends sound past her ear like whispers. Between the slow-sky day and the slow-sky night lie all the little eddies of weather, geography’s grudges and favors. They move through a pocket that tastes like lime. They move through a pocket that tastes like dust.

By the time they reach a point where a sensor ping should have returned enough to draw a map of the obstruction, they still have almost nothing. The HUD ghost in Tamsin’s visor shows a silhouette, more absence than presence, a shadow chewed into data. The thing sits atop the east rail and bleeds across the gap to smear onto the west. There is a hummock beneath it where the ballast has heaved up in little frozen bubbles.

“Old gods,” Jun says, not meaning it, because the saints were all burned for heat long before any of them were born. He reaches out a gloved hand toward the object and then stops because he has been trained since childhood to not touch strange things.

“Mira,” Tamsin says, “you have the fancy sampler today?”

Mira flicks the catch on the tube at her hip. The sampler’s mouth opens like a flower. “I can take a shaving,” she says. “If it lets me.”

“Careful,” Jun says softly, and for once he doesn’t sound like he’s mocking anyone.

“On it,” Mira says. She leans forward carefully, making sure her tether isn’t going to swing and thump the obstruction—if it is a sensor, if it is a bomb, if it is a God, nothing could be more disrespectful than a thump. The sampler scrapes very lightly across the surface. There is a sound—not a song, but a single syllable that Tamsin hears in her teeth rather than her ears. It is not in any human language. It is not in any language at all, except that it means stop.

Mira yanks the sampler back like the object bit her. The flower mouth is rimed with a frost that wasn’t there before. “It took heat,” Mira says. She sounds a little breathless. “It took heat out of the sampler.”

“Conserve,” the little ledger on Tamsin’s chest says, cheerful and idiotic.

“Pull back,” Tamsin says. Her mouth is dry. “We need to see whether it reacts to proximity. Step back slowly.” They step back slowly. The object does nothing. The rail humbles quietly underneath it, as if embarrassed to have company. The glow from the sunknife catches the edges of the obstruction where it is not absolute; Tamsin sees a slight corrugation, like growth rings, like something that has layered itself over time.

“Is this a human device?” Jun asks. “Tell me someone put this here.”

Tamsin shakes her head. She points at the tiny drift trails all leading inward. “Exogenous,” she says. “Came in from outside the rails. Look at the way the ballast—” She stops. The ballast stones nearest the object are microfractured and frosted, as if they have been subjected to a very fast, very cold shock. The effect diminishes with distance. It is not a method she recognizes. Not any tool they have. There is a little field of tiny glittering bits just beyond the reach of their boots.

When Tamsin was fourteen, she skipped classes and went out with a boy named Saro to the frostline beyond the northern pumps where the city stutters as it tilts its shoulder to slide around a granite extrusion. Saro put his hand under her parka and said things that would sound good later, because he was beautiful as a knife and terrible for heat budgets. They lay side by side with their backs against the cooling tower, its fins angled like a book open in supplication, and watched the sky. The night side was clear and so full of stars she thought she could fall into them. Saro said, Do you ever wonder what it’s like in the night? Really in the night, not this soft stuff. He meant the antumbra. He meant the far-dark. He meant a little death like an experiment. And she felt something in her wake that choice. Like a lurch in the rails.

Now, with cold flowers blooming instantly on the sampler and a new sound in her teeth, she feels something again. It is not curiosity, not exactly. It is a vector, a pull.

She calls Riko. “We have an external object bonded to both rails approximately three meters by half. No good return. It appears to be leaching heat from anything that contacts it. It’s not responding to proximity at this distance. Orders?”

There is a tiny pause, the sort that tells Tamsin that Riko is not alone and not speaking only for herself. The city is run by consensus, by the ledger and by those who argue best; it is also run by those who can spend and those who can deny. “We need to keep moving,” Riko says after the kind of pause she allocates to prayer. “Is there a way to drop it?”

Mira, distracted, says, “We can cut it,” at the same time Jun says, “We can haul it.”

“Neither,” Tamsin says. “We don’t know what cutting does, and hauling means putting it on the sled, and I’m not going to put an unknown leech on my sled. I need a micro” —she swallows, hating herself even as she says it— “detonation.”

There are three men in the city who call themselves decommissioners, and all three used to be preachers before they traded words for blast ratios. To most, the word detonation is obscene when you are speaking of rails. The rails are older than any of their grandparents. They are the inherited spine. Humans built them in the first dawn of the city, when ships still came sometimes through the day to spit colonists blinking and sweating into the Knife, and those early engineers used their wealth to lay steel like promises. It is very bad luck to threaten that.

But Tamsin thinks of the way the sampler’s heat ran raining into nothingness. She thinks: whatever this is, if it wakes when the whole city rolls over it, it will drink like a god. It could leach the forward locomotors dry in a minute. It could freeze the couplings. It could stop them. And if the city stops in the Knife…

“Something gentle,” Tamsin says, because even her voice alone near the rails feels like an affront. She knows every hairpin and bolt and shim in this stretch; she has replaced them with her own gloved hands. “Half a spoon of old metal in a dissolving capsule. We slide it under at angle and take out the bond on the east side away from the rail head. We don’t touch the rail itself. We don’t even cough on it. Then we pull it into the shadow and let it think about its life choices.”

Silence. Sometimes Tamsin wonders if that is how it feels to be a saint, hearing the city in your head, waiting for judgment. Then Riko says, “Approved. Be quick. We’re at four degrees.”

Jun takes the tiny capsule from his kit. It is a thing of beauty, so small, so contained. Mira hovers, ready to grab Jun by the back if he does something un-Juned for once. Tamsin drops to her knees on the gantry, feels the cold try to drink her through the composite. She slides her gloved hand under the edge of the obstruction. It resists her, not with weight but with a kind of sticky reluctance, as if it has very strong feelings about that particular patch of world. She coaxes. She is, in her most effective moments, a liar. She whispers to the thing without words: we are not your enemy. We are your ghosts.

Jun lays the capsule on her glove. It smokes at once. She snaps her wrist, gets it under the overhang, against the ballast, the angle she wanted. She pulls her hand out so gently it feels reverent. They are held by a mutual breath that fogs and clears, fogs and clears. The little capsule dissolves. The bit of metal within falls, strikes, flashes.

The sound this time is not in her teeth. It is in her eyes. There is a thing that happens when hard light meets harder cold; it shears in a way that the world can’t catch. For an instant, she sees the inside of the object.

It is not empty.

There are layers. The corrugation is not surface detail but structure: like the growth rings she thought of before, but not wood. Not stone. A stack of planes—ten, twenty, fifty—each fractionally offset from the one below, so that what should be a flat face is actually a staircase. The steps are molecules thick. Between each step lies a gas or a gel or something her suit can’t count. It is colder than she knows how to say. It is arranged.

Her mouth is open; she hears herself make a small noise, like someone has poured a cold drink down her spine and she’s trying not to flinch. Jun is saying, “I think it cracked, I think it cracked,” and Mira is saying, “Pull,” and there is a lurch as the bond lets go, and they do, they pull.

The object slides over the rail like a thought sliding out of speech. It has weight; it is more honest than it looks. They get it onto the gantry shadow. Tamsin’s gloves spike heat to keep her fingers from the sweet hard pain of cold damage. The sampler at Mira’s hip hisses gently where she has pressed its hot mouth to her thigh in a thoughtless human attempt to comfort. Jun laughs, the sound high and odd, so it might be fear. Tamsin can feel a little field of wrongness around the object, like the way the air feels near a floodlight, except inverted.

“Cover it,” she says. “Blanket.”

Jun shakes out the multilayer. It is a thing made to keep the city’s secrets in and the night’s teeth out. He throws it over the object and the wrongness diminishes as if someone has drawn a curtain across a scene too bright. Tamsin likes that metaphor. Curtains can be pulled back later.

“Give me two more minutes,” she tells the air, and hears Riko’s exhale that could be laughter. She kneels again, very close now. Under the blanket, the object hums like a held note in a throat. She has never wanted to touch something more and touch something less.

She says, “For the record, I think this thing is alive.”

“You can’t…” Jun begins, and then says, “You can’t just call that. You don’t know.”

“I know the way it is.” She wants to say: I have cold in my teeth that was not there before. I have a syllable that has lodged under my tongue. It has steps inside it as if it was built to slow something down, like it is a staircase in a place where time falls.

“What do you want to do?” Mira asks. Her voice is flat, neutral, a blade made ready to be law enforcement or emergency therapy or riot music. Anything. She is always asking Tamsin what to do. It is the gift and the burden of it, to be the one who decides.

Tamsin sits back on her heels. The ledger on her chest is blinking a polite counter. The city hums. The rails’ song ticks upward in little uncertain halftones; the locomotors are losing patience; the day’s schedule yawns wider with every minute. The object whispers in her mouth the word that means stop in a tongue only teeth understand.

“Bring it,” she says.

Mira says, “Bring it where.”

“To the cold lab,” Tamsin says. “Into a thermal box. Under quarantine. We keep it away from the main loops.” She can feel Riko bristling across the channel even before the marshal speaks. “We can’t destroy it without knowing what it is. We can’t push it off and leave it to sit where it will, because what if it is a lure. What if there are more, and this is the polite one.”

Riko’s voice has tungsten in it when it comes. “We are not a research outpost, Tamsin. We are a city, with children and stewpots that need to come to boil. We run on ledgers, not curiosity.”

Tamsin says, very deliberately, knowing she is writing debt she does not know how to pay, “I will cover the heat cost for the box, out of my ledger. I will cover the heat loss for the sled. The lab has backfeed from the medical wing; we can share budget with them. If the council needs someone to swear their skin on it, I swear.”

Jun makes a whistling noise. Mira does not move. Riko is quiet long enough that Tamsin’s heart tries to declare independence.

“Fine,” Riko says at last, three degrees colder than fine meaning. “You take it. If it breathes weird on you, you take it to the dumps and I never hear about it again. You have sixteen hours to make your case that this is not a new way to die. Move.”

Tamsin wants to say thank you, but the ledger on her chest is blinking now not admonition but promise. A new number has appeared, in red, a debt forecast with her name on it. The kind of number that means her apartment goes cold for a month. The kind of number that will mean thin soup and a new appreciation for blankets.

“Jun,” she says quietly. “The sled.”

He moves like a conjurer. They angle the sled like a cradle. They lift the blanket-wrapped thing like a baby pulled from a river. It is not heavy, but it resists being moved again—not with friction, with intention. They coax. They lie. Their suits hiss. Their breath condenses. The wind chuckles and then gusts mean. On the horizon the knife of the sun has a halo today, particles shy around it; it looks like a saint’s idea of God. Tamsin refuses to be superstitious and stops herself from touching the rail for luck as they slide the object home into the sled’s body.

“Let’s go,” she says. “Slow. Easy. No bumps.”

The sled’s little motor whirs. Its treads bite like the teeth of a patient animal. The city’s shadow grows as they approach. Tamsin can see the sunline’s fabric shining with the sweat of a thousand breathers, the luck-lanterns that some fools still hang, the banners advertising conservation programs and knitting circles and workshops on ferments that don’t spoil hot. A child leans out from a balcony big as a bread slice and waves, seeing nothing but the three bright suits and the glitter of the sled. Tamsin waves back, a reflex.

There is a sound. Not the rails. Not wind. It is a sort of thrum at the edge of hearing. Tamsin turns her head. The blanket over the object has tightened slightly, as if a muscle listened to it and flexed.

“Do you feel that?” Jun says.

Tamsin arranges her face into a shape like calm. “It’s nothing,” she says, and then catches herself too late. She does not lie to them, not if she can help it. “I feel it,” she amends, and because confession without comfort is cruelty, she adds, “It’s probably just a resonance. The city’s flux makes pockets. Everyone gets spooked at the same edge sometimes.”

Not true, whispers the syllable in her teeth. Not true, human. Her mouth floods with that metallic taste again, and for an instant she thinks she can make out a second syllable, a neighbor to stop. The shape of it is like a hand raised palm-out. She swallows and the syllable goes to lie down in her bones.

They leave the gantry and step into the city proper. The change is immediate and every time it surprises her. Out there, under the white line of the sun and the black fan of the night, everything is a sharp edge. In here, the edges soften. The alleys hold heat like gossip. The smell of stew and chemical yeast and harsh tea lives in the markets like a kind of congregation. Even the soft scratch of the knitting circles’ needles is a kind of rain.

People on the forks make way for the sled. They are not fools. Rumors travel faster than weather. There will be whispered against walls before they are three blocks deep: Frontline brought something in. Frontline paid with their skin. Frontline brought the night to bed. Tamsin lifts her chin and does not meet anyone’s eyes.

They deliver the sled through the cold lab’s airlocks. The lab is a luxury the city still permits itself, because sometimes the Knife throws them gifts—ice from a comet; spores from the high day; a pig that wandered too far from a festival and lost its ears and gained wisdom. Inside, the cold is cultivated. It is clean. The countertops gleam and the thermoclines are posted on the wall in bright letters like traffic laws.

Doctor Keshe lets them in because she is curious first and always. She has the lines at the corners of her mouth of a person who tasted something good once and never found it again. “Whatever you have,” she says, “it had better be prettier than the last thing. That last thing looked like a lung set on joyless fire.”

“It’s alive,” Tamsin says before she can stop herself.

Keshe looks at her like she’s said she believes in saints. Then she looks at the blanket and the little twitches it is making and says, very softly, “Oh.”

They settle it onto the table that keeps itself as close to the night as possible without offending anyone. Keshe flicks the blanket back like a magician unveiling, and the object—under the careful light of the lab—looks less like an absence and more like an answer to a question Tamsin has had all her life and never articulated. It hums, a little. It has steps inside it like someone built a labyrinth for heat.

Keshe glances at Tamsin’s chest, sees the debt rendering there, and says, “You’re an idiot.”

Tamsin says, “I know.”

Keshe grins. “All the right people are. Who else would take the Knife and make a city.”

They set the monitors. They draw a boundary in chalk on the floor—Tamsin knows it’s nonsense and also that some nonsense is necessary. Whenever the object shivers, the chalk’s dust rises in a tiny motes and hangs, and then in slow motion it falls all at once as if the air within the lines pauses and then remembers itself. Keshe murmurs equations like a lover’s pet names. Jun draws another smiley face on his [visor], on the other side this time. Mira leans in the doorway to play obstruction for the curious.

Riko comes in only long enough to look. She puts her hand briefly on Tamsin’s shoulder, a human heat that the ledger cannot calculate, and then leaves to go be tungsten.

Around midwatch, when the lab has settled into a rhythm of readings and caution, Tamsin makes the mistake of touching her lips with the back of her glove. The glove is cold; her lips taste metal; the syllable that means stop rushes back to the front of her mouth—and this time it is joined by a second that really is a word: don’t.

It does not come in a voice. It does not come in any language. It is an arrangement of heat that her tongue reads. It is a shape she knows because she has held hot spoons and kissed cold skin under a cooling tower and learned the Knife by kissing the rails of it with her work. It is as real as hunger. It is an instruction, or a plea, or an aesthetic. Don’t, it says, not stern but horrified. Don’t don’t don’t.

She leans over the object. Her breath makes a little fog that drops and shatters on the steps. She whispers without heat: Don’t what? And feels very foolish.

The syllable blooms. It tastes like salt. It lands in her bones like a coin thrown into a well. It says: don’t bring the sun.

She closes her eyes over reflexive tears that have nothing to do with heat budget. She sees the city with its louvres angled like eyelids. She sees the rails humming with their weight. She sees the horizon, blade-bright. She sees the long-ago dream of people like her father, who believed machines could be a vessel for love. And she sees far beyond the frostline into the antumbra, into the night that is not none but full of its own slow music.

“Keshe,” she says, and her voice is flat, not neutral, only flat because if it is anything else then she will have to declare herself a priest and stand in the market and proclaim. “I think there is something living in the night.”

Keshe glances up from the monitors. Her face is bright and intent. “We’ve always known there are things that can live with less heat than we can imagine.”

Tamsin shakes her head. She is not good with words when she is full of them. “Not bacteria. Not… not simple. Something that sends. Something that wants. It told me—”

Keshe’s eyes sharpen, and Tamsin knows she has just said something expensive. “It told you?”

“I don’t know what to call it.” She swallows, tastes the metal. The syllable sits there like an unspent coin. “It told me not to bring the sun.”

Keshe is quiet long enough that Tamsin hears the rails sing again, a little irritated now, a tone that means the locomotors are being throttled to buy them time. Then Keshe says, “We always thought the day was the danger. We always thought light would save us.”

Tamsin thinks of Saro in the frostline. She thinks of the first ship’s promise. She thinks of the way the object has steps like it is built to trap heat like flies. She thinks of the ledger blinking red over her heart. She thinks of the city and the knife and the song. She thinks of love and its vessels.

“What if,” she says, “we aren’t the only ones with a ledger.”

The syllable shifts under her tongue. She feels something like laughter, except it tastes forlorn. Don’t bring the sun, it says again, and then, in the space where heat could be, it makes a shape like a map. Not with lines. With a cooling pattern. A road in negative. A path through absence. It lays itself along her palate like frost.

Mira leans her head in. “We’ve got council,” she says. “Riko wants you. Bring your religion or don’t.”

Tamsin looks at the object. It is very patient. It is very old or very new; she cannot tell. It asks a question of her that is not one she has heard before. When she was a child, the rails sang her to sleep. When she was a child, she thought that meant there would always be a song. Now she knows different.

She sets a hand on the lab table very gently, to steady herself, to borrow heat and give it, both at once. “Coming,” she tells Mira, and then, to the thing on the table, in the language that is no language, the only one they share, she puts a little warmth in her words and says: wait.

It hums a note that tastes like patience and like the moment before a coin flips and lands heads or tails and either way changes everything. And then the rails sing again, louder, impatient, like a throat cleared before a pronouncement, and Heliotrope strains at its leash toward the blade of an indifferent star.

The Sun had never looked like mercy until they put gauze over it.

Lin hung from a seam line along the underside of the Parasol and watched the giant disc blur behind the lattice. It made her visor’s filters strobe amber and then settle to a pale lemon as the mesh breathed in thermal stress. The sound came through her suit in bone, not air: a continuous, almost musical tension as millions of square kilometers of film and filigree flexed against heat and gravity and wind that wasn’t wind. She had learned to tell moods from that hum. Today the Cloth was fretful.

She planted her boot spikes against a rib and let her body drift while the spool on her back extruded a ribbon of refractive film. The ribbon fluttered as if eager for a home. When she touched it to the edge of a tear, the film drank it up, the micro-hooks in its belly aligning to the rip’s ragged polymer and knitting themselves molecule by molecule. She nudged with her left glove to straighten the seam, nudged again, and held her breath as she touched the arc-lighter to cure. The heat felt far away, as if she were cooking a meal in someone else’s kitchen.

A cloud of stitcher moths gathered in the corner of her vision. They were no larger than thumbnails, flat and translucent and slightly opalescent, each with a sliver of sail that allowed them to skate momentum out of photons. Technically not moths at all but 3D-printed thrips with logic limited to ten simple behaviors. They were attracted to blueness: the corrected scatter from a damaged patch, the scattering of her visor, the deliberately blue lure diodes set into her wrists. They smelled hunger here. They trailed her like confetti and then swarmed the edges when she moved away, fastening themselves to brighten or dim the local reflectivity until a sensor looked and told them to stop. When she was a child she had chased dragonflies over brackish water. It was the same chase impulse, turned inside out. Now things chased the brokenness she made whole.

She brought the arc-lighter up and kissed the seam closed. The hum of the Cloth shifted, the tension redistributed, the line of the tear becoming just another score in the giant instrument.

“Lin, how’s my seamstress?” Osei’s voice came into her head with its usual dry breakfast warmth. Somewhere behind him Lin could hear the faint clatter of utensils. Ground control was unromantic that way.

“Fifteen patches down for the hour,” she said. “And some of these patterns are weird.”

“Weird how? Weird like meteor cascade weird or weird like you’re about to tell me you found God spelled out in pinholes weird?”

The corner of her mouth twitched. She tilted her helmet slowly and let the visor take in the field. Wearing the suit made the world a theater; your eyes took in too much and your brain learned to prioritize.

Over the last fifty meters, the tear sites marched in a formation that was on the wrong side of random. Not a simple straight line, not a simple log spiral. Their spacing widened and narrowed in a way that sent a pinprick of recognition through her. It made her think of old bamboo blinds back home, of woven mat mistakes that repeated with a stubborn rhythm because that’s where the weaver’s hand hesitated, that’s where the thread had a knot.
