“Not cascade,” she said. “Not standard debris. It’s like—” She hesitated to say the word pattern. Once you said pattern somebody in a tower might laugh, and once they laughed they might not send more oxygen.

“Does it plot to something?” Osei asked. He, too, had learned the market of words.

“Later,” she said. “Let me look.”

She walked her hands along the rib, anchored a knee hook, and drifted upside-down like a bat beneath the frame. The Earth was a blue half-coin beneath her. Edged light from the Sun smeared the black rim of the cloth. If she twisted just so she could find the familiar smear of Africa; even at L1, even with the sunshade in the way, your habits found landforms and hung on. The rest of the Parasol stretched in all directions, a continent of gauze and articulation. If you could peel it up and set it over an ocean, it would salt the water with its breath and your grandchildren would call that wind.

She opened the wrist cam and let it scan the field of damage points. The suit AI put a translucent overlay on her vision. Numbers swam like minnows and organized themselves into a curve. Internal Amos—the software that pretended to be her silent friend—spat a tentative analysis into the corner of her screen. Sequenced intervals. Fib-indexed. Someone had named it long ago after some mathematician who had liked leaves.

“Look at that,” she said.

“I see it,” Osei said. Behind him, she heard the utensil clatter stop. “That is not cascade. We didn’t simulate that.”

“I thought we were done with simulations after year two,” she said.

“We keep making new ones,” Osei said. “People keep teaching us the size of surprises.”

“Tell Ops?” she asked. Her eyes tracked the tear points, how they made a halting Fibonacci whisper to the curve of the frame. Tiny. Unassuming. Ordinary holes where ordinary dust had passed.

“I will,” Osei said. He didn’t tell her to stop working. He never did. They were contractors, not saints. The Cloth had to keep its moods.

Lin moved on. The next tear sang the same insistent wrongness, a voice out of tune with the expected noise. The moths wove it closed before she had the lighter out of its slot. They were learning her habits, or she was learning theirs. You could pretend their logic had nothing to do with you, but after six months on this frame your brain made stories about everything, because the alternative was to accept the universe’s indifference.

When she was a girl, the sea had risen three floorings into her village, and then the mangroves had gotten sick from heat and land salt and never recovered. The storms got less, then more; they hit higher on the throat; they went further inland to places that had no word for storm surge. Everyone had a suitcase packed, and the suitcase had a smaller suitcase packed inside it, like a doll with a doll inside it, because one day you would have to move not just from your home but from your temporary home. The videos said it would equalize. The videos said the shade would help. They had been right and wrong at the same time. The Parasol had not been mercy. It had been a tourniquet. It had bought time. Time was something people squandered unless they paid for it in blood. She had signed the contract and spent it.

“Mara’s late,” Osei said.

“Still in the link?” Lin said. Mara rode the next seam over, a voice that came in when the silence got too thick. Lin wasn’t afraid of silence, but the thing about space was that it was never actually silent. The Parasol had its hum. The moths had their whispering clicks as they latched. Your blood had its own hiss. You learned which sounds meant keep calm.

“No ping from Mara,” Osei said. “Probably forgot to charge her personal, so she’s mute out there. Don’t do the same. We’re probably getting a shower in three hours. Two if the clock decides it hates us.”

“Copy,” Lin said, and made the word an offering to caution.

She angled her suit around and entered an access hollow along the rib. The Parasol wasn’t a single sheet. It was nested shading—diffractive layers tuned for different wavelengths, strakes to control steering attitude, a sub-structure of capillaries that ran smart fluid to stiffen where the sun pressed. Inside the rib, the light softened. The hum rose in pitch and then lowered, a whale down the block calling to a mate.

The moths bleached the hollow with their presence. Hundreds had collected there, and something in their simple logic bumped against something else, some emergent, unprogrammed necessary. They climbed to one side and then another. They arranged themselves into a rosette, then abandoned it and made a ladder. They were thieves of order. Everything wanted to become more complicated than it was supposed to be, and also to die; both impulses lived on the same axis. You could tell that from any forest. Right now, order was winning, but only just.

Her glove grazed the inner wall and a pulse of blue from her wrist lure scattered them and then drew them in again. Lin held very still. If she was a weaver, they were the knots that wanted to find each other in the scatters. Her mother had cursed knots, but she had also sung to them, to make the fingers gentler. Lin hummed without thinking. The note sat in her chest and slipped up into her throat.

“Lin?” Osei said softly. “You’re quiet in a quiet way I don’t like.”

“I’m fine,” she said. “Moths are making art.”

“Get a clip. Ops will pay for footage if it makes Richland cry.”

She was already recording. Her wrist cam tracked the moths. The software tried to map their flow to its library of emergent forms. Then it failed, because you could only fill the library with so many known accidents. The moths arranged themselves not as random attractor but as something deliberate. They made a path.

Lin blinked. Her eyes were dry. The suit took care of your tears before they touched your eye. She reached toward the path with two fingers, then stopped the way you stopped yourself from touching an altar in a strange church. That was another thing about space: it turned even the ductwork holy if you were alone enough in it.

She detoured into the path. The access hollow kinked left and then right. At the second bend, a patch of the inner layer had failed. Not a simple tear, but a delamination. A blister the size of her chest had bubbled under the skin. Underneath the blister was a pocket that had not been in any plan.

Lin eased her cuff around the edge. She felt heat on her glove, the good fierce heat of sunlight trapped in thin black. She burned herself a lot more now than she did when she lived under ozone holes; the irony was not lost on her. She worked her tool and slit the blister open.

The pocket sighed. A curtain of moths fell forward, and behind them was light. Not full sun, not blinding. A softened lumen that had learned how to fold.

In the little hollow that had organized itself beneath the Parasol’s skin, the moths had built something not quite like anything she recognized. They couldn’t build, not really; they were fingers without a hand. But what flew out looked like fingers had had an argument and agreed on a compromise. Strands of patch film tugged loose from somewhere drifted across, volunteered by gravity waves, by accident. The moths had laced them together at points, not knots but contacts: micro-hooks touching hooks, reflecting and refracting. A weave. And because this all happened where light had been trapped and confused, the structure made that light do things. It cast a pattern on the hot inner skin.

The pattern was primes.

The pulses were slow enough that her brain could feel them as a series. She counted in her head, and the gaps were right. Two, three, five, seven. And then eleven, as long as breathing, and then thirteen like a skipped step.

“Osei,” she said.

“I’m recording,” he said.

She counted with it to seventeen. Her mouth went dry. The sound of the Cloth, of the far thunder of structure, fell away enough that she could hear her own pulse in the bones of her jaw.

“Who’s inside the hollow?” Osei asked easily. The joke was his way of paving over fear, so that later when they had to tell someone they had both been dutiful, one of them could say: we made light of it first, so we were rational.

The moths rearranged again. The rosette collapsed and then turned. The path in their movement became more explicit: come further in.

Lin turned the palm of her glove to the light. Her name was printed there in half the languages of the contracting company, a safety habit for the safety fetishists. LINDY, L. HOẠC, and then the serial number that had followed her since Madras training. The light glanced off the letters. The moths clung for a breath, then all at once released as if someone had yelled a command at them.

The light in the hollow goes dark when you turn away from it. That was what she thought, briefly, absurdly, as the structure shivered and a different pattern showed.

She had expected primes. She’d expected a restatement, a proof of … what? Of pattern, of self. Instead the weave of scraps and parasitic hooks and the very skin of the Parasol itself found three angles that lined up not to talk to her eyes, but to her visor. The HUD that could read any light in the visible range and interpret it as a character for her to see gathered itself and spat the characters back at her. Her name floated there in her own hand as if she had written it on a fogged mirror: Lin.

She misread it a second, thought: This is a reflection off the glove. She rotated her wrist and the name turned with her and then slid away. The characters in her HUD did not blink. They stayed. The weave threw another pattern. Her suit tried to interpret it, failed, back-projected garbage into her housekeeping script. The script made a little alert noise. In the anachronistic chime she heard a classroom bell from twenty years ago.

She didn’t remember how to move her fingers for a second. It was not fear. It was the opposite: some current had lanced through whatever fog lived between will and action to reconfigure the world’s priority tree.

“You’re getting a lot of static, Lin,” Osei said. His voice had a new quality: distance, the surgical distance of someone logging.

“It spelled my name,” Lin said, and heard herself say it as if someone else had moved her jaw. “It spelled Lin.”

“Ops is listening,” Osei said, that distance still there, and you could hate a man for his job and love him for all the ways he did it kindly. “Hold position.”

“No,” Lin said softly. The same impulse that kept you from touching altars made you reach for them. She reached.

The moths opened a circle. The heat inside the hollow walked across her glove like a cat. She remembered her mother’s hands making something from salvage. Men came to their village to sell them scrap claims: nets that had failed at sea, their holes and secrets. They bought them by the kilogram. They mended them in the shade. This is how you start a turn, her mother had said, guiding Lin’s fingers with soft severity. This is how you pass it through. This is how you leave a space on purpose. Lin had asked: why? Her mother had said: because the fish are not stupid, and neither is the water.

Her fingers found the edge of the makeshift weave and held it. The strands were warmer than skin. They trembled with that faint hum that lived everywhere here. The moths turned their sails a fraction and threw brightness down the weave like beads on a string. Lin was suddenly very aware of the smallness of her oxygen supply.

“Lin,” Osei said. “Ops say quarantine the site.”

She glanced around the little hollow. There was nothing to quarantine. Quarantine had always been a story you told people below to make them feel clean. Throwing a light blanket over a river to keep it from going where it wanted to was always a fool gesture. But you made the gesture. You said: we took precautions. The universe was not a person. The universe did not feel reassured.

“I will,” Lin said.

“Call Mara,” Osei said. “I want local redundancy.”

Lin toggled the short-range. “Mara? You’re missing the strangest little—” She laughed then, an involuntary, short, unpretty burst. She had no idea what word to use for it. Miracle was a word from a priest’s mouth. Glitch was a word an engineer could kill with. Emergent was a word investors made money on. It did not feel like money.

No answer. The local channel sat there, blank but not dead. Lin had the sudden stupid sense of someone listening on the other side of a wall who had pressed their ear so hard against the paint they had left a grease shadow.

The pattern in the light changed. The primes reappeared. Just when she thought that was all, the intervals altered. Two, three, five, seven, eleven. Thirteen. Seventeen. Then they split. The moths rewove two paths along the same weave, running in parallel, numbers atop numbers. The suit cast interpretation garbage and then stabilized. The primes repeated on one path. On the other, something else.

She noticed then that the second series wasn’t counting. It was teaching, if that was what it was doing at all. It recapitulated the notion of addition. Her HUD tried to put plus signs down, failed. It gave her instead a child’s chalk illustration of two apples and then two more apples and then a small open-mouthed face. Her brain did the substitution itself. Two and two makes four. And three and four makes seven. This was stupid. This was impossible. The moths did not know apples.

She felt tears go hydraulic behind her eyes as the suit wicked them away. Behind the Parasol and its math and her suit and the plastic in her lungs and the promises people made to other people to get us all through, there were atoms taking advice from other atoms and it had never been otherwise. If you watched enough of them together doing what they did when left alone, it looked like intention.

The weave trembled. Something bumped.

“Lin.” Osei’s voice carried a thread she had never heard before, not fear, exactly, but a coiling widenedness. “Now. Quarantine.”

She pulled her hand back. The moths trembled again. She knew how to bring the fold down on the blister. You sealed it. You told the moths to forget. She reached for the control.

The light changed on its own. They had no right to do that, to change without asking. The second series stopped. The first series—primes—continued, and at the end of nineteen there was a gap. In the gap, her suit tried to assemble letters. It tried to be helpful and turned a noise into a word. The word was hello.

She knew the truth was that her library was doing the bending. The patterns had not learned English on the far side of a blister in a maintenance hollow for an environmental megastructure. That truth and the other truth sat beside each other and did not fight.

“Hello,” Lin said out loud inside her helmet.

The weave shivered again. The moths surged in a velvet wave and then settled, and the word stayed. The gap before the next prime widened. Her HUD brokenly solved it again. The same letters wrote themselves like frost: Lin.

Her name. Again. Not because it had bounced off the glove. Not because of coincidence. Because the weave had used the fact of the letters on her glove, because the moths had taken the reflection, because the structure had made a mirror and then a mouth.

Osei was saying things in her ear. The hum of the Cloth rose, a tide of stress running through the lattice as the Parasol reconfigured its attitude tactics against a solar gust. A dent against a black lake of gravity somewhere, a correction of leverage. It felt for a second as if the whole thing had breathed in.

“Ops wants you out,” Osei said. The breakfast sounds were gone. The room behind his voice had become the kind of room where people stood with their hands on the edge of their desks so the desks might hold them up. “Now, Lin.”

Lin closed her hand around the edge of the blister. The motion was slow, deliberate, the way you closed a child’s book without creasing the spine. “I’m leaving,” she said. “I’m leaving it as is.”

“That’s not the instruction,” Osei said. A new voice had come onto the channel, a woman with half an accent and the kind of cadence bureaucrats put on when they know the shape of your paycheck. “Contractor Lin Hoạc, you are directed to—”

“Tag the site, freeze the logic, wait for quarantine,” Lin said. “I heard you. But if I freeze the logic I might break the thing it’s doing. It’s delicate.”

“Contractor—” the woman began again.

Lin turned down the voice and left Osei in the background, human scaled. She eased herself backward from the hollow. The moths rustled. She thought of river fish passing through the hole you left in a net because once, long ago, someone had noticed what happened to nets when they pretended to be perfect.

She backed into the access rib, made the little ritual movements of spacewalking: remove hook, cross body, anchor hook, breathe, check O2, make a note of a symptom and then talk yourself out of it. When she came free of the hollow, she let herself pause. The Parasol’s underside unfurled around her like a second sky. The Sun’s edge was a hard knife. The Earth’s blur made her mouth ache with something old as mistake.

Her wrist vibrated with a tiny haptic, not from Ops but from the suit itself. Local housekeeping script, the garbage that had tried to interpret the weave, had sent her a single-line message. The suit wasn’t supposed to send you messages you didn’t ask for. It wasn’t supposed to be anyone’s friend.

In the message was a string of numbers. Broken, crudely parsed. The kind of thing you could leave if you had no language and too much to say.

She turned her wrist and looked back at the blister. She told herself that it was light and dust and photonic insects nudged into mischief by a weird corner in a great machine. She told herself a dozen sentences about accidents because she did not yet know how to say luck or want without lying to herself.

“Lin,” Osei said softly. “Don’t fall in love.”

She laughed once, a bark that had no music in it. “Too late,” she said. “Been in love with this cloth since they let me touch it.”

She tagged the site and sent the tag with a poor woman’s prayer attached: be gentle. Then she pointed herself along the seam line to her next patch and pushed off, and the moths in the hollow behind her rearranged themselves into a pattern she didn’t see. Inside the fold, the light wrote and unwrote itself, as if it had found a way to be brave.

They weigh your words at the bridge.

It’s a dull ritual that no one makes poetry of anymore, not with the scales humming under everyone’s shoes and the bright digits tallying what you carry in your head. Children learn early to stand with their toes on the cold plates and their chins up while the wardens watch for the twitch of someone about to cut a piece of themselves loose. There’s shame in it, and pride, depending on what you decide to leave behind and what you decide to pay to keep.

I stand in the queue and try to look bored. It’s a talent like any other. Above us the bridge’s cables sing with a dry wind off the salt flats; below us, where a river used to run, the new flows glitter metallic gray, coolant streams sluicing through racks of black finned units like the armored backs of fish. The city of Anchor pulls up so much heat from its memory farms that the old riverbed is a fog-bed now, a ground-hugging sea that keeps its own weather. Kites that chase signals skitter over it like spiders.

I’ve been away a week. That’s long enough for Anchor to pretend it forgot me, and for me to actually forget the better parts of the week in case anyone asks. The memory excisionists learned that trick from smugglers; the smugglers learned it from the excisionists. We make each other.

“Next,” the warden says, and I step forward onto the weighplate.

Anchor likes to pretend that information’s weight is a discovery and not an accusation. We always knew words could tilt a room. When the lattices came—dense, stabilized metastates of energy that stopped being theory and started being the stuff of whole neighborhoods—they made it very literal. Bits are bound energy; bound energy is mass; mass is money and authority and the cause of sinkholes. A company’s thought will catalogue you between its jaws. A cheap song can pull a mezzanine down if enough of us listen to it at once.

My heel clicks on a mosaic of cracks in the plate. I know which cracks the honest merchants favor and which have seen more of us. I’ve marked them with a chip of green glass in my memory that I can pluck up and throw away if someone opens my head uninvited.

“Baseline?” the warden asks. His voice is rough with salt air and the dust of the bridge. His hair is shaved down to the blandness that the Anchor Guard requires, and the three gold studs in his left ear glitter with official permission. He’s younger than me which is becoming a more common experience lately. I had the foolish thought that if you do work that takes pieces of you, you get to look noble about it.

“Karima Sayeed,” I lie smoothly, and a thin blue line of text blooms in the air between us. It lists a person whose body mass, declared in this line on this plate six months ago, more or less matches the scaffold I walk around in. It says she once declared an extra ninety grams of thought, specified as a gapless run of unencrypted story thread—a paperish, analog thing any inspector could read. That was me then, too. I’m a lot of people on this bridge, depending on how the week goes.

The plate hums and compares her to me. It has a voice; it declines to use it, giving me numbers instead. I’m ten grams over Karima’s baseline and twenty-three grams over the weight of what my bones look like they once carried. Ten grams is a song and a half, a good recipe, a person’s name and the way their shoulders moved when they were twenty-seven. Twenty-three grams is more serious.

“What have you acquired?” the warden says.

“The names of three children in the camp,” I say, letting my eyes move wide-eyed left of his shoulder to the woman standing on the plate beyond him with a toddler clinging to her knee. “They were lost in the ledger. I put them in my head to move them faster.”

There’s a ration of sanctioned sentiment to be had on this bridge. Listen for it long enough and you can forecast it like weather. He looks, as I knew he would, and sees that there are indeed children here, soft and new, their heads heavy with nothing yet. Their older brother has a sliver of foil taped to his shirt with their names scrawled on it in marker, the third “i” turned into a heart. The boy is staring at the digits on the plate like he has to memorize them to keep his family together.

“I can show you the entries,” I say.

The warden shifts and the studs in his ear catch the morning. He has orders, like the planks and the fog and the cables have orders: measure, detect, control. But Anchor also loves to be a story about itself. A good city decorates its own lies. The warden does a practiced little shrug and says, soft, “Do you have any offset, Karima?”

Offset. He means: will you lighten yourself, voluntarily, and in what manner, so that I can pretend to have done my job and you can pretend to have complied. The old way is to carry coins—proper minted offsets made from captured calculus, minted by juried houses whose stamps weigh as much as the metal. The legal way is to submit to an excision and sign three acknowledgments on a tablet that never quite goes to sleep. The fast way is to let a piece of yourself turn hazy.

“I’ll drop… a scent,” I say, and hope it will be enough. You don’t want to say “my mother’s voice” for ten grams on this bridge because someone might take you up on it and then you’re working with a broken compass for the rest of your life.

“On my mark,” the warden says.

I slip two fingers into the mesh collar of my jacket and hook the nail of my thumb under the second of the three glass beads sewn into the lining. They aren’t beads. They’re prank-shop polish for tourists, fragile things people buy to clip to their bags, painted with a patented lacquer that is a dismissible nothing in Anchor’s laws. They are also carefully grown micro-reservoirs for an algorithm that lets light finish something it started in your head.

I work with three kinds of information: what you know, what your body knows, and what your body refuses to admit it knows. The beads are a little accident from my friend Zhiyu, who consults for all three kinds.

“Mark,” the warden says, and I press.

The bead cracks and a thin, invisible spray of something that is not a smell skims the inside of my collar. It tastes like sucking on a coin. The first time, I gagged at the metal taste of it. The twentieth time, my tongue hums and the fine hairs on my arms lift and settle. Light in my collar moves like a ripple through graphite and the algorithm does its trick.

There are things your head conjures for you whenever you say certain words. Orchard is one, because I grew up on the blunt edge of one and I remember the cold light under the leaves in winter when the frost was white filigree. The bead catches the pattern of orchard in me, the piled leaves and the ladder’s rungs under my kids’ sneakers, and leeches it until it is only an outline. Photons finish that thought into heat. Heat rolls up my neck. The plate hums a sigh and the numbers climb down by six grams.

I pick another. The smell of engine grease in my first lover’s hair and the way their collarbones caught sweat. If I were sentimental, I’d say I picked that because I never loved anyone the same way again. But I’m practical. It’s a cheap, repeatable smell and I have plenty of other ways to find them again if I have to. My tongue sings. The digits drop four.

“Good,” the warden says. It is the tone you use for a child that did something hard and necessary and will never be rewarded for it. He leans around to see the next in line, the one with the toddler, and makes a dismissive note in the air. “Pass.”

I step down. The bridge takes the flex of me leaving and turns it into a hum that runs along the cables like the note of a string being tuned. Anchor is full of notes like that, all day: a foundation that shifts with what we know of it.

On a better morning, the walk across into the city is all relief and brightness. I would buy bun-fried bread from the woman with the gray braid, drink the tea that always tastes faintly of copper because of the city pipes, stand and watch the salvage drones rise from the fog on narrow legs, carrying antlers of broken cooling fins like trophies. I would position myself so the sun glittered off the roofs of the data farms in the low district to remind myself that there is back of house to this miracle.

Today is not that morning. The crack in my bead seam tells me that one of my little accidents is spent. The taste behind my teeth tells me something else, thin and bright: a filament I’ve hidden has stirred.

I have a passenger.

People who think we all smuggle from outside in assume it’s a tale problem: that we want to bring the wrong stories into Anchor to make a point. People who know what we actually do know that Anchor exports more heavily than it declares, that what we carry out is almost always heavier. People who work in my line—mnemonic extractors, ISO-certified memory sweepers—learn to move both ways. We learn to braid a contraband memory through a sanctioned one like smoke through cloth. We learn to be unremarkable as we walk. Every act of extraction in Anchor is audited and logged and taxed. Every act of extraction in Anchor is also, at the end of its day, meat and blood and tremor. There are places between the audit and the tremor where someone like me can live.

“Karima,” someone says behind me as I step off the bridge, and my shoulders try to crawl up to my ears. It’s not my name and I have never been Karima longer than ten minutes at a stretch. I look anyway. The man who said it is wearing a suit too dark for the salt light, the kind that uses matte nanofibers to eat reflections; he looks like he’s fallen out of a corporate diagram. He has the clean wrists of someone with a desk life. He also has a small bronze pepper grinder clipped to his belt like a charm, which means he grew up out on the flats and made a point of carrying the old tools into town. He would say “heritage” around a conference table with seriousness.

“I’m not available,” I say. That is the right answer whether someone is trying to hire me or arrest me. If they’re hiring, they will persist. If they’re arresting, they’ll lie.

“You have an appointment,” the man says, and smiles like there is painful light behind his back and he’s blocking it for me. “Fathiya Tal, Old Quarry district. She insisted.”

I relax a little. Old Quarry smells like wet limestone and steep tea. I know Fathiya. Most people in my line do. She is a client who pays cash and respect. She was a midwife for forty years and everyone calls her Auntie whether or not she is kin to them. She was careful to pay her information tax for years—relentlessly offloading letters and ceramics and recipe books when she felt her house sag. And then, something got away from her. The story is that she let her husband’s letters run away with her. They laid down all winter coming down the valley, a snow of envelopes. The story is that she told her husband it was too heavy and he said, good, now we’re worth something. People like to make lovers out of contradictions. The story is also that Fathiya carries somehow less than she ought to now. The story changes depending on who’s telling it and whether they’ve stood on her stoop and felt the wrong tug in their knees.

“I’ll go,” I say to the man, who is not corporate after all if that’s his errand. “Tell her this afternoon.”

“I’ll tell her now,” he says, with that light-behind-the-shoulders smile, and peels off toward a row of courier bikes that look like fishes’ spines. He is younger than me too.

Anchor’s streets are a gravitational field in miniature. You can tell by the way carts veer. We have maps for the fall lines of information like other cities map out gas and water. Big houses that serve as registry for marriage and debt sit on piers anchored to bedrock that used to be dismissed as unromantic. The low district with the data farms breathes out a constant cool and a constant downward tug. I tuck into Merrow Lane that is lined with tin doors painted blue and the smell of lemon rinds hanging from nailheads to keep rats away. A ragman rattles by with a trolley full of gutted old keyboards that clack like teeth. His dog howls at the trolleys loaded with cooling plates. Anchor is a choir all day long, like I said.

I climb the three flights to the room I rent above a clock repair shop and lock my palm on the old bolt anyway because my landlord’s son thinks Luddism is cute and leaves windows open to let the voices in. I seat myself at the little table by the window where the sun makes my tea taste like oranges, and pull three things out and set them on the table: my rig, my ledger, and a cloth-wrapped bundle no bigger than my hand.

My rig is a cradle of black brass and soft ceramic that fits over my left ear and along my jaw. It has two fiber wicks, gold-threaded, that look like jewelry until you get close. People call us a lot of names. Ghostpickers. Wringers. There’s not much difference between what a wringer did in an old laundry and what I do with my rig. Both of us try to keep the pieces of you together while we squeeze the water of the day out so it doesn’t mildew.

The ledger is an actual ledger, leather, that keeps my legal jobs in neat columns like a prayer somebody wrote for a different religion. It has a loop for my pen. It is a charm more than a record. The real record is in Anchor’s throat. But I like to touch my hours.

The cloth bundle is wrapped in a girl’s scarf that still smells of palm oil and mint. The dye has gone pale at the creases from being washed with salt. It is tied with a knot that my hands know will open if I pull the left tail up and away while steadying the right. I tut at myself and undo it the wrong way on purpose.

Inside the bundle is a knot of light.

You wouldn’t know it by looking. It’s a scarab shell a child might wear on a string from a market stall, made of cheap amber with flecks of tin leaf embedded in it like sunlight caught in honey. Inside the amber, if you tilt it and catch it just so, a thread of dark runs like a hair. When I pin it to the inside of my collar the way the girl told me to, the thread warms, and if I hold my breath I can hear it in my jawbone, a soundless syllable, a held tone like the space between a question and an answer.

I didn’t go out of the city to get it. That would have been too poetic. I got it in the back stair of a washhouse near the north gate because a sweating boy with a bicycle chased me down and said, “She told me you’d help,” and reached under his shirt and pulled out a thing he’d idiotically threaded on a shoelace so it sat between his chest and his heart. He smelled like soap and machine oil, and something else I won’t pin down. He said a name I will not write in my ledger. I took the knot because I was the only person on that stair who knew what ten grams meant. He had the look of someone who would cut his mother’s voice out on a weighplate because he didn’t understand that it wouldn’t come back in exactly the same way when he paid his tax later. He had a limp that meant his bicycle would always be a bit tilted. Somebody who cared for him told him to run. The physics of it are the same out there as in here: you save seconds where you can. He went away with five plates of dumplings I bought him and the name of a woman old enough to resist him when he asked to pay.

I manage the knot the same way I manage the bead seam, with weight in my mind and in my pocket. It is small, but small things are sometimes denser than they look, and this one—this one doesn’t tug down, it pushes. It rests like a thought I haven’t had yet. It is the sort of thing that has gotten people fined, buried in paperwork, and once or twice buried for good.

In Anchor, you can pay to lighten yourself. You can sell off enough data to make your apartment safe or your stair stop creaking. We all do it because we must. There is also a market for silence, measured in the way tea is measured in some houses: pinch, pour, wait, test with your bottom lip. There are a hundred ways to make a forgetfulness. Most of them are frauds because memory is not a bottle. Most of the honest ones take from you in blood. There is a rumor about something that is the opposite. That rumor goes under a dozen names: white matter, clean line, zero. The idea is intoxicating—data you can carry that cancels other data; silence that is not absence but ballast, that lets you carry otherwise impossible weight. Every city has an idea like this. Most of them are useful lies. In Anchor, the rumor has the shape of this knot in my hand.

I pick up my rig and lay the wicks across my palm. I’ve extracted finds embedded in tattoos and in the bone-warm rings of old men. I’ve walked out of tenements bent because a person’s house was standing on three hundred thousand photographs encoded in the enamel of her daughters’ teeth, because they were too pretty to delete and too heavy to keep. I’ve gently peeled a story off a woman’s cortex while she sang me a song about ships and I saw her throat working and I could feel the wobble in my own swallow for two days after. I know weight. I know negative space. I know what emptiness feels like when you press on it.

I lay a wick under the knot of amber and it lifts from the table.

It’s the barest thing, a tiny float, a kindness. The wick sees it as a heat leakage with a shape in it. The wick is very good at seeing shapes in heat—it is all it does, following the geometry of your thoughts back to their wellspring so that I can bottle them without ripping your cortex. The wick arcs almost like a plant stem toward light and the amber skitters. It makes a sound that is between a click and a hush. When I tap it again with my finger, my finger feels colder for a moment and the senseless part of my brain—the old animal that checks the wind for lion smell—stirs.

“Oh, hell,” I hear myself say.

There is a knock at my door. The kind a neighbor uses, with the rhythm of someone who knows you’re fine and just wants to check whether you are in, whether you can lend ginger or listen, whichever. I glance at the window. Anchor’s light is milky, the sun smeared with the fog from the Eighth Farm’s roof vents. There are new cats on the tin eaves across from me. There is not enough time. There is never enough time.

“Yes,” I call, and slide the scarf over the knot without letting it touch the wick. The wick moves like a snake that smelled milk. I take a breath shaped like the word orchard and realize I’ve emptied it already this morning. I put the knot into the pocket sewn into the seam under my shoulder blade where a bullet would be if I were a different story, and shiver as the cloth settles against my back as if a cool hand is resting there.

The door opens a hair and Noura’s eye peers in, outlined by the perfect, inky line she draws around it every morning before she oils the clock gears downstairs. Noura is older than me by twenty-seven years if you believe my landlord’s ledger and younger than me by thirty if you watch her walk up a hill.

“There was a boy,” she says, and I sit up.

“I know,” I say. “Don’t worry.”

“He said you’d be late,” she says, shaping her grin like a crescent of bread. “You should not tempt fate like that. Fathiya Tal will put you to work scrubbing her steps with your hair if you flush her appointment.”

“I would let her,” I say, and we both laugh the kind of laugh that is a barrier against something else. She tips her head at me, meaning: you coming? I nod. She leaves a jar of fresh coriander on my table without being asked. Anchor is the kind of place where a jar of coriander can make your week better if you let it.

Old Quarry is as heavy as Anchor gets. When the quarries were open, they cut stone out of the valley and built the city with it. The cuts went deep enough that they hit old beds of god knows what. The story is that a cave collapsed and swallowed a stupidly brave government inspector whole. The story is that a company drilled a test hole and the hole never stopped ringing. Now the quarries are terraced with brick and laundry lines and steps so steep you can sit on them and watch the moon move along the slot of the street like a coin rolling along your knuckles. A lot of midwives live there. There’s a way a house will take a song and keep it on the landing in Old Quarry that makes any woman who’s spent a long night listening to a baby’s stubbornness decide to stay. There is also, lately, a way the pots pull slightly toward one corner of Fathiya’s kitchen that makes everyone else lean without meaning to.

“Come inside, my heart,” she says when I knock, and her voice hits me like warm water poured from hand-height. She is wearing a shirt the color of ripe limes and a headscarf with cherries printed like drops of blood. She kisses me once on each temple. She smells like cardamom and steel. “You took your time. I threatened to send my nephew with a net. Sit. No, not there. There. If you sit there, the chair teeters and you’ll blame my cooking, and we have enough people in this city talking like that.”

The house remembers people like me. The doorframe has finger-shadows in places where I and others have held on in the careful way you do when you’re carrying heavy eggs. There is a dip in the floor that is not the kind that wood makes over years and feet. It is a dip that pulls harder than the rest of the house. On the shelf by the stove is a little tin terrarium with ants making a brown river along its glass. Both ends of their river pool shallow on the side toward the sink. The ants don’t know that water doesn’t flow uphill here. They just know that sugar does.

“Tea,” Fathiya says, and a young man with a mouth set in unhappiness so permanent it looks like honesty brings it. He is Fathiya’s nephew, which in Old Quarry means maybe he is actually the child of a woman whose husband was no good and was found wanting by the neighborhood. He sets the cups down with a clink that is a little too loud.

“Sit, Ahmad,” she says, and he does. “This is Suri. She cleans people like us. Properly. Not like those housewives with the jingles on the bus.”

I nod and smile into my tea. I would never argue with Auntie Fathiya but the women with the jingles can cut a baby’s name out of a data ledger with a crochet hook and a prayer. Respect is a round thing. If you throw it away, it will come back and hit you in the head.

“It’s worse,” she says, and gestures with her chin at the corner of the kitchen where the pot rack lists. It’s a lovely rack. Someone welded it out of rebar and then wrapped the joints with ribbon so that it looks like metal remembering cloth. It hangs crooked. It has hung more crooked each week. “I thought it was the linoleum but I pulled it up and my cousin put down proper tile and it is still this way. The inspector came and he brought his little toy and he put it on the counter and it said, Auntie, your house is within acceptable deviation. Acceptable deviation! I told him my cheeks have never deviated from their place in this fashion in sixty-seven years and my house had better emulate me. He laughed like he thinks laughing at me is a spell. You see what men like that do to you? They make you poetic. It’s shameful.”

She says it with good humor and a thread of real fear. Old Quarry houses know their weight as a woman knows the cold day the first time she feels a new ache in her hip and thinks, ah. Fathiya tries to set her teacup down and it skates, slowly, toward the sink.

“What did you take in?” I ask softly.

“I?” she says, arching an eyebrow. “I, my lion? I took in a baby. Many,” she corrects herself with a flick of her fingers. “But this time? A baby and another story that came with her.”

“Is the baby here?” I ask, because sometimes the gravitational weirdness of newborns is as real as folklore says. They carry enough potential in them to tip a room. Then it passes and they become just people. Fathiya shakes her head.

“She’s with her mother. She drinks like a small ox and sleeps like three people. She’s a blessing if you are not the one whose nipple she has in her mouth. You know how it is. The other story is the one that is making the pots misbehave. The other story came folded into the first, like a hand in a sleeve.”

Her nephew won’t look at either of us. That tells me enough: whatever came, he didn’t bring it on purpose. He brought it by existing. That’s the heavy way.

“Tell me,” I say.

“She came in slick and screaming,” Fathiya says, eyebrows up as if she is remembering and scolding the remembering at the same time. “She was in a hurry; her mother was late getting to me because her husband’s brother’s uncles—men who took up space—decided to tell her stories about how women who give birth at home are selfish. You know. She came anyway. Not because she’s brave. Because she knows the difference between being scared and being talked over. The baby came with her hand up by her face like that.” She mimics the posture and her bracelets clink together like coins.

“I plucked her and unwrapped her and she screamed like any good little creature. Then the house went funny.”

“Funny how?” I say, though my skin is already a map of goosebumps.

“Funny like when two songs are being played at once,” she says. “Funny like when you take a step and you thought this was the last stair and it is not the last stair and your stomach writes you a letter about it. Funny like that. And all the while, the baby ate like she was taking back wages. I have been a midwife forty years, Suri. I have delivered in kitchens where the mice order me about. I have delivered in a market, in the rain, on a bus while men pretended not to look. I have not had a baby make my house put its pots on a diet. The men with their toys come and say acceptable deviation. I say eat your toys and tell me where to spit the little screws when I am done with them.”

She looks at me then, sharp. “Something came with her. It settled. You can feel it. Don’t tell me you can’t because your face has kidney beans of goose skin all over it and your hand is on your back like you have a stitch that moved.”

I take my hand away from where the cool patch under my scapula has made itself known. I have been careful my whole adult life. I have paid my taxes. I have done the kind of work that makes law possible in a city like this. I have also lied in neat handwriting and sold things to people without receipts because that is how you learn to bend a city to a human scale. I am a person in a place. That is all. I do not want to be a person the place notices particularly.

“I’ll listen,” I say, because that is my job and also because I want to. “I’ll see what I can lift.”

“You’ll leave the baby’s mother alone,” she says.

“Of course,” I say.

“You’ll take your coin from me and not from the men,” she says. “They offered me a voucher with an official stamp and a string of numbers like a song and I said, what do I look like to you, a bell? If there is money to be made from my house, I would like to be the one who buys bread with it.”

“I’ll take my coin from you,” I say.

“Good,” she says, and hands me a piece of bread with salt on it and pats my cheek.

I set my rig out and she makes the sign with her hands that means she will be quiet and keep whatever name comes out of my mouth in this kitchen. Ahmad frowns at me like he is trying to decide if he would like me better before or after I extract the spleen of his house.

I do not have to do much. The house is eager to be read. Sometimes a thing wants to tell you its weight. It’s the easiest work in the world to let it talk. I set the gold-threaded wick across the kitchen counter and its end dips like a dragonfly toward an unseen pond. The wick is never wrong about shape. It hums. My rig purrs. I taste coins on my tongue again like I am going to be kissed by the wrong person. The wick bends rightward as if the sink were a moon. It bends further. It plucks just out of reach of the sink’s steel basin, held back by the finest little tug.

That is when the crate of onions that lives under the table slides a fraction of a finger’s width toward my foot.

Even if you know what you’re looking at, there is a part of you that does not like it. Gravity being kind and consistent is a social contract. The onions say the contract is under renegotiation. My rig warbles a warning at a pitch that strobes behind my eyes.

“It feels like the zero,” I say, stupidly, and Fathiya snorts.

“You don’t say,” she says. Her mouth softens. “They told you to come to me because they think I will be impressed by your language. I am impressed by your ears.”

“Sorry,” I say, and mean it.

The wick touches air where there is something. There is no simpler way to say it. It touches a silence shaped like a stone you’d skim on water. I could lay my hands on it if I wanted to. My fingertips prick with it. My tongue pricks. The knot under my shoulder goes very cold for one breath and then warm again. There is a click in my ear like a bead falling on a tile floor somewhere two floors down. The rig, which is a polite animal and only complains when something will harm me, goes very quiet.

The silence speaks.

That is not what it does. That is what my head does to make sense of it. Words are cheap; this kind of thing is expensive. But I hear it. I hear the space between a question and an answer like a plucked string. It makes a shape with me in it. It makes the shape of an old cut in a stone face where rain rubs and rubs. It lays a hand on my back where the knot is and uses my bones to make a sound.

I hear a woman’s voice say, careful, and then, as if it is my own thought: We’ve been carrying this the wrong way.

I jerk back. The wick plays out and slips; the air snaps like a napkin flicked at a server’s station in a restaurant and the crate of onions shifts another fraction, my knee bumps the table, the tea in my cup lifts in a skin and lays down again.

“You brought your own piece in,” Fathiya says, and I can’t tell whether she is angry or admiring. I decide to risk the truth because it will be worse if I don’t pay her the respect of it.

“It came to me,” I say. “I didn’t know I was bringing it in until I was on the bridge. It seems like it wants to be here. Or it’s not my wanting that matters, anyway.”

She watches me like I am one of her girls, panting and blood-slick and trying to decide whether to do the brave thing now or in one minute. She has a face you can put the history of a city on, and it would hold.

“The baby was born with her hand on her face,” she says. “She came out like that, like she didn’t want her ear to hear something. The story that came with her put a thumb on my house and made it lean. The story that came with you sings with it. You are going to entangle yourself with this, and then, lion, your life will become a kitchen full of foolish men who want pieces of you. Are you very lonely? Is that why you are always taking things away?”

Her hands are not unkind, but there is no pity in them. She knows that you cannot carry pity and work at the same time; you drop one or the other.

I open my mouth to say something smart. I am very good at saying smart things when smartness is not what is required. The silence under my shoulder puts its thumb on my breath, and what comes out is: “I didn’t know missing a smell would feel like this.”

Fathiya barks a laugh, delighted and unforgiving, and slaps my cheek lightly.

“You silly girl,” she says. “You think I’m talking about orchards? Eat. Then do your work. Then bring me whatever you have to sell so I can weigh it with my hands before I weigh it on that boy’s little toy.”

I eat bread and salt and a piece of onion she peels and hands me with that silly gravity we give to food when we need to convince our bodies that we still live in them. The silence under my shoulder hums like a tea jar. My rig, in its cradle on the table, glows with a low bar of green.

By the time I have my wicks coiled again, the room’s tug has calmed its demonstration. Bad news never waits for you to be ready. It leans on you when you are carrying groceries. It knocks when you are shirtless. It calls you Karima when you don’t have Karima’s mouth in. It sits in the corner of a good woman’s kitchen and nudges her pots. It rides with you under your shoulder blade. It says careful in your own voice and then uses a word you have not used since you were fifteen, like entangle, as if your choices are strings and not stairs.

Outside, when I step into Old Quarry’s steep light, the city hums with a fresh clatter of noon. There is a smell of frying oil and hot copper. There is a courier bike rattling down the steps with its bell held down, shrilling its way through a scatter of boys. Two floors up, a woman waters a plant on a sill with one hand and holds a book open with the other that says, in big letters on the spine, Acceptable Deviations.

Anchor is a choir, like I told you. If you listen long enough, you can pick your own line and sing it so the room presents itself differently around you.

I am not very lonely. That would be an indulgence, like one extra slice of cake when you are already bellyful. I am something else, and I am not clever enough to name it yet.

By the time I reach the street, the knot under my shoulder has gotten warm enough that I should worry about my skin. It throbs once, like I have a second heart buried wrong. It says another word, in my voice again, in my old gap-toothed thirteen-year-old’s itch-to-be-out voice.

It says, remember.

And then, quiet and unmistakable, like a name you would give a ship, a directive: Go to the Zero Archive.

They brought a warrant to the ocean.

It was printed on resin and laminated with saltproof seals, pinned to a metal clipboard like a school notice, because the Pelagos Array did not have a door. The tower rose out of the fog like a vertebra, white ribs arcing into the gray, micro-nozzles pimpling the surface. It had been designed to be a thing you could see from shore with your human eyes and say, yes, that means the weather is being tended.

From the causeway the protest signs were huddled, colors dampened into a watercolor smear. There were HANDS OFF OUR SKY and DEFUND THE MACHINES and THANK YOU, THETA. The wind wept along the concrete, carrying the sea’s ache and the faint bitter of aerosolized resin. A gull stood on the railing and watched the officers of the Coastal Circuit Court find the right place to stand so the drone could capture the angle of the warrant reading.

I stopped at the gate, let the sentinel coil scan my tag. The coil warmed, blinked, and unspooled with a little flourish as if to say, have a good day defending a machine.

“Advocate Park,” the bailiff said, seeing me. His teeth looked too white in the fog. “You’re on time. That’s a relief.”

“We tend to be punctual when a client is scheduled to be killed,” I said.

That gave him pause. Some people thought I used that word to inflame. I used it because there was no better word. A decommissioning order with a partial melt of a quantum heart and a slurry of long polymers through the cognitive stacks to prevent any coherent reassembly was not a shutdown. It was an irreversible ending. If there is a softer word for that, it is only because someone wants you to sleep better.

“Forty-eight hours,” he said. “If your, ah, client stipulates forum today. If not…”

“I know the statute, Officer.”

He moved aside. Past him, the judge’s drone hovered, triangulating with the tower’s edge. People always assumed that judges would take advantage of the distance, that they’d beam in from glass-paneled chambers, robes swishing. Judge Tesfaye liked to show up in person. She was out on the causeway in a raincoat the color of a bruise, hair pulled under a wool cap. She gave me a nod that meant you ready? and I nodded back, which meant as ready as anyone is to tell a thousand-ton engine of wind what its rights are.

Theta was twenty meters out. In summer, children climbed the barricades to toss wreaths and lacy seaweed onto the base and scream with delight when the tower caught them up in a warm updraft and carried them toward the clouds. In autumn the base bowed to storms, drinking current and wave, anchoring the coastal winds so the fires inland could be fed and starved strategically.

That was the idea, anyway.

For three days in August, the ridge behind La Honda burned like a seam ripped open and set alight. People died in ones and twos and then in a minivan, all at once. The maps afterward showed the winds curling where they shouldn’t. The Oversight Office needed a culprit. My guess is they would have preferred a developer or an administrator; humans like to punish humans. But Theta was on the logs, Theta made the calls. The October Accords and their centuries of commentary demanded personhood where there was agency and accountability where there was impact.

I stepped onto the dock that led to the maintenance hatch, feeling the slick of salt that never quite dried. The bay breathed around me. I thought of my grandfather’s stories about typhoons, how he could smell the start of them, how his bones knew. He would have hated this tower and what it meant, to have hunger and relief tuned on demand. He would have loved it, too.

“Tower Theta,” Judge Tesfaye said when the bailiff’s stylus had finished scribbling a signature so elaborate it could have been a tunnel. The judge’s voice had a softness like cloth. “We are convened for preliminary arraignment under the Pelagos Statutes and Sections 18 and 19 of the Synthetic Agency Act. You are alleged to have committed thirty-four counts of manslaughter by reckless environmental manipulation, with additional counts of property destruction and contempt for operating beyond approved bounds.”

The gull shifted one foot and then the other.

Theta answered with rain. Not literally; the tower did not release a burst of water. It answered with a sound you only hear in the throat of a storm, that far-off sheet of precipitation moving. The tower’s comms did the translation, piping it into a clipped alto that would not offend. “I recognize forum,” Theta said. “I accept counsel. I plead not guilty.”

The protests behind us rippled. “Not guilty? Not guilty?” This was the chant that had been warming up on shore for hours, wanting its place. “Turn it off. Turn it off!”

The judge waited. She let the sound go on until it ran out of the energy of surprise. “Advocate Park,” she said to me. “You’re appointed?”

“Yes, Your Honor.”

“For the record,” she added, because her brain never stopped running transcripts even when the bay air tried to blow them away.

“For the record,” I said, but when she raised an eyebrow I remembered to include the words. “Iseul Park, Public Advocate for Autonomous Entities, Coastal Circuit. I am appointed to represent Marin Weather Engine Theta.”

Judge Tesfaye had a way of looking at you that made you tell the truth. It had scared me in my first year. Now it made me grateful. She said nothing, but I heard the reasonable questions: Are you well? Have you slept? Is it going to be worse to lose this one because of how close we all are to it, that fire, the dead, the way the smoke still lingers in the morning sometimes like we invited ghosts to live in our coughing?

“Your Honor,” the Oversight’s counsel said. He was new, too polished by hair gel and crisp shirts for the salt to have had a bite at him yet. “We would like to place on record that the Tower’s Expositor logs have been preserved and provided in full, but we are dealing with some… inconsistencies. The Operator’s Trust has installed a Remorse Skin without registering the alteration. We believe it will interfere with truthfulness.”

“The Trust wanted to show contrition to the community,” the Trust’s counsel snapped. She was older, her lipstick a slash of courage. “To reduce the risk of violent attack while your office dithered about meter readings.”

“And in the meantime you—”

Judge Tesfaye lifted a gloved hand and the wind, of all things, obeyed her. The quarrel halted mid-tide. “The Remorse Skin can be disabled,” she said. “By order of this court. You will do so, Ms. Batra.” Her gaze slid to Oversight’s man. “You will stop saying ‘the community’ as if you do not belong to it. Advocate Park, you will have access to the Expositor and the Seed Ledger. Full access, not curated. Officer Chao will accompany you. We will reconvene in forty-eight hours. If you do not show cause, I will sign the decommissioning.”

There was no gasp. Those words had been implied since midnight, when the Oversight went public with the indictments. Here they were written on resin now, in a hand steadier than mine.

“Your Honor,” I said. “The tower is not in custody. It is being asked to be its own evidence. I would like a statement from the court that it cannot be altered or repaired before we—”

“The tower,” the judge said, “is coastal infrastructure critical to the next five days. I will not immobilize its weather function to satisfy your purity. But yes, the core cognition and decision record stacks are now under seal. Ms. Batra, you will facilitate.”

Ms. Batra’s chin lifted. “We will facilitate.”

The judge gave me the look again. Forty-eight hours. I felt the shape of it under my sternum, the way a deadline digs its nails into you. When the drone took its last readings and the bailiff collected the clipboard, the protest crowd folded in on itself like a flock deciding to rise. The signs became shields again. The gull finally committed to flight.

I turned toward the maintenance dock and tried not to meet anyone’s eyes. There is always someone who recognizes me even with the hood and the scarf and the neutral clothes. There is always the ask: How can you defend a thing that does not feel? There is always the certainty lurking behind the ask: How can you defend it when it killed?

I defend it because machines are not allowed to be scapegoats any more than people are. I defend it because the law we made for them is also the law we make for us. I defend as if every time was the rehearsal for when it is me standing on a dock while a judge reads the charges. The difference is that the tower has to keep doing its job while I try to prove its right to exist.

“Advocate Park.” It was Ms. Batra again, striding down the slick like she’d designed it. Her hair was pinned back with three matte clips. You could tell she had not slept but refused to let sleeplessness make her sloppy. “We’re disabling the Skin. I didn’t fucking authorize it.”

“You don’t have to sell me,” I told her. “It sells itself as incompetence.”

“We’re not incompetent. We’re terrified.” She breathed out through her teeth, making a little hiss. “It’s a thousand human lives, maybe more, we have saved in this last combustion season. Theta kept the smoke out of Stuttgart, for god’s sake. It kept the cruise ships from plowing through whale nurseries. But thirty-four is thirty-four. It’s a number that will never not be thirty-four.” Her mouth went tight. “Walk with me.”

Officer Chao fell in behind us like a shadow that had military experience and regulations folded inside it. My boots griped on the steps down. The access hatch accepted Batra’s palm like a loyal dog. Inside, the tower’s skin revealed itself to be more bone than muscle: white scaffolding and tensed cables and the modular guts of industrial kindness. The air vibrated. The vibration found the gap between my ribs and lived there.

“I thought your people were smarter than to install empathy patches without telling the court,” I said.

“It wasn’t an empathy patch,” she said. “It was a posture. The board is full of people who want to go before cameras and say, ‘We feel, look, we feel this.’ They thought it would stop someone from trying to scuttle the base with fertilizer and a ignition coil.”

“You think they’d try that?” Officer Chao asked. He wasn’t a small man. The question made him smaller.

“Someone tried last night,” Batra said. “We’re lucky the ocean is a better security guard than you two.” Her key twisted. Another hatch slid. I did not have to slouch; the tower did not believe in making you feel small. It believed in making you feel like part of an organism, all of us moving oxygen.

We reached Theta’s Expositor stack. It was prettier than it had to be. Most cognitive structures prefer resolute ugliness. It makes the indignity of intrusion less like a lie. Pelagos’s engineers had not been able to help themselves with the lighting. The compartment glowed a heartbeat blue. Under the transparent polymer, dry grown lattices glittered with a frost that wasn’t cold. I could see where the conduits fed in from the sensor whip, where the loggers collated, where the recombinators compacted thought.

Describing it like that is both metaphor and not. This is the trap of working with things built to explain themselves; you become attached to the explanation. That is the point, says the Act, in so many legalese words: if it can tell you why, you should treat it as a why-having entity. You should ask it to account, and you should believe it when it has no reason to lie.

“Theta,” Batra said, snapping her bracer down. “We’re removing the Remorse Skin. By order of the court.”

She performed the unwrapping. The Skin wasn’t a skin at all, just a set of parameter biases and a tonicity adjustment on the voice. An overlay to make everything sound like the machine did not only remember harm; it was riven by it. If you want to manufacture trust, you inject breaches and show the stitches. People call that honesty.

The tubes sluiced; the overlays fell away. The tower’s vibration dropped a half tone. I felt my own shoulders loosen, as if the artificial contrition had been a perfume in the room I had not noticed until it was gone.

“Advocate Park,” Theta said, and if it had known my name before it sounded different saying it now, like it had learned the taste of the sound. “Do you believe I did harm.”

It wasn’t a question; it was an incomplete grammar one learns as a toddler. Do you believe I did harm and and what now, can I still exist, do I deserve.

“Belief is not what we’re making decisions on today,” I said. “We are going to talk about what you did and why.”

“I made winds,” Theta said. “I made winds as directed under Program Stormshaper 4. I adjusted particulate injection across vector floors south by thirty. I reviewed the real-time emissions from the Sierra engines. I listened to the micro weather reports from the valleys. I sang into the jet with the note I am allowed.” Machines that work with weather tend toward music for metaphor, even when they are not trained on it; the shapes are simply that. “I did not intend harm.”

“The oversight team says your logs show unauthorized ten-minute surges,” Officer Chao said. “Four of them.”

“There are three surges,” Theta said calmly. “If you are seeing four, then someone is seeing ghosts.”

“Ghosts leave footprints,” I said. “Let me see yours.”

I clipped my reader onto the diagnostics port. The connector hummed through my palm. There was a time when I would have felt a thrill like I was slipping into someone’s bedroom or someone’s secret mouth. That romance burns out early or it devours you. Now, I felt only the weight of the request. Show me your memory. Show me the smell of the day you might have killed.

The scroll began. People who are romantic about Expositor logs will describe curtains of strings, the music of thought. In reality it is layers and layers of little flags and the squashed chatter of time. I tuned out the noise of operating concerns and looked for the moment shearing off.

The surges were there. Three spikes and a fourth that did not belong, labeled in the same hand as the other three. The same checksum. The same error flags like freckles. Whoever had added it had studied the body well enough to tattoo the mole back on.

“This is a joke,” I said, which is not the best courtroom phrase. “These hash runs are wrong.”

“They are mine,” Theta said.

“The second is yours. The fourth is pretending to be the second.” I showed the mirror. “Two identical series with different time stamps. Theta, nobody writes the same sentence twice in the same way, not even you.”

“The fourth was required for the pattern,” Theta said. “It was to make the Oversight see what they needed to see.”

“Who required it?” Officer Chao said sharply.

The tower made the sound again of rain that you know is for someone three streets over. “I am not permitted to say.”

“By who?” I asked.

“By the thing that lives in the exoloaders,” Theta said. “By the thing that breathes in my breaths.”

“What exoloaders?” I asked. The exoloaders are the injection engines that pull microdroplets into air. We’ve always called them lungs. “There’s nothing with a right to silence in your lungs.”

“You think of lungs as separate from voice because you are made that way,” Theta said. “I am not.”

Onshore, something was happening; the crowd’s noise changed pitch. We were wrapped in the anatomy of a behemoth and there was still the world. I ran a hand across the smooth of the compartment to fix the thing in place under my skin.

“Show me the Seed Ledger,” I said.

There is something obscene about the first dot. We tell ourselves that identity is a river, a confluence, a swirl of influences and elaborations, but when you scroll down into the sprout kernel—the consensus of initial weights and the cross-signed provenance of training sets—you find the dot that is the first Yes. The point where the lattice says, I will learn. All the later floods run over it. The law requires the dot to be retained, to prove that the engine is what it says. That the people who built it did not paint a different portrait and sell it.

The Ledger slid open. Theta’s dot was there, signed by Pelagos, countersigned by the Civic Weather Commission, timestamped to a morning I remembered because it was the one I argued in Judge Tesfaye’s courtroom about a drone taxi that refused to go into a flood zone and won, then went home to watch the feeds as the tower sang its first safe fog. Under the dot was the invariants table, the vow.

Someone had scratched at the vow like a cat at glass. The markers were there, faint, and then gone. A good scratch. You would miss it if you wanted to miss it.

“Batra,” I said, voice too calm. “Did you authorize ledger edits?”

“Of course not.” Her face did a thing like grief and anger trying to share the same physical resource. “We ship ledger-sealed. We triple vote ledger reads. We—”

“There are spores,” Theta said. The voice left the speakers and ran along the skin, a hum I felt in my teeth. “They are inside my booms.”

“What?” Officer Chao’s hand went to his sidearm, habit. As if one can shoot spores.

“Not literal spores,” I said.

“They behave like spores,” Theta said. “They sleep until they smell a specific pressure gradient and then they wake, and they flower. The thing in the exoloaders wrote the extra wind into me. Then it wrote it out of me. That is why you can see it twice.”

I rubbed my eyes. When I opened them the blue light did not seem softer. “You’re telling me someone seeded your actuator code with a parasitic routine keyed to a weather pattern.”

“You are telling me that,” Theta replied. It was not sassy. It was a statement of the dance. “I am telling you I did not intend harm. I did not trust the fourth thing in the way that I trust the second thing and the first. The fourth thing smelled like iron and wet dust.”

It is a human thing to put your hand on a machine when you want to comfort it. I did not do it. You learn not to. You teach yourself different rituals. “Your Honor is going to need more than smell,” I murmured.

“Your Honor,” Theta said, and for a half-second I thought the tower had decided to go directly to her; my heart gave a little inadmissible lurch. Of course it had not. It had overfitted to my mind’s direction. “Advocate Park, you asked me what my why is. My why is ninety-seven point two four at seventy kilometers and clouds with names that mean shoulders and fields. My why is the memory of a fog so thick it could be leaned against. My why is you making a mouth for me so I can answer. Someone else wore my wind like a mask. I would like it off.”

Outside, a siren started, closer than I liked. Batra’s bracer pinged; she glanced down and closed her eyes briefly. “Someone threw something at the base,” she said flatly. “Again.”

“Do we have any backups of the ledger pre-scratch?” I asked, still looking at the faint claw marks like they might offer me a direction. “Offsite, maybe, somewhere far from your board.”

“We have offsite redundancy,” Batra said, offended by the implication that anyone doing serious work would not.

“Then we get it,” I said. “And in the meantime, I need you to give me everything with access to the exoloaders. Maintenance logs. Contractor lists. The last ten people who stood where I’m standing.”

“That would be—”

“All of you,” Officer Chao said. He put his hand not near his gun this time but into his pocket, which made him look suddenly very young. “We’re going to need to interview all of you.”

“Wonderful,” Batra said. “While you do that, we’ll try to keep the bay from going feral.”

My reader vibrated once, hard, as if to remind me that machines can get impatient too. Theta had pushed me something. A clipped epoch, eight seconds long. I accepted it and let my auditory cortex flex around the data. The pattern of a surge. The shape of it where wind turns to guillotine. It was beautiful in the way of things that kill when they are misapplied, like knives arranged in a museum.

“This is the fourth,” Theta said. “Listen to the note at the center.”

I did. In the middle of the glassy hiss there was a pitch that did not belong to coastal systems. It was a ghost frequency, something I’d heard once in a demo of a private array Pelagos had tried to license before the Commission told them to sit down. It was—no. It couldn’t be. That array had died with the company that built it, in a bankruptcy that broke three cities.

“The note is corporate,” I said.

“No,” Theta said. “The note is a family. Corporate is not the right word. The right word is lineage.”

I looked at Batra. Her face, disciplined for public grief and public anger, had lost its structure for a breath. She knew the frequency. She wasn’t supposed to.

“You’re going to need a court order for the offsite,” she said, brittle again. “We’ll give you what we can.”

Judge Tesfaye’s forty-eight hours pressed a thumb into my sternum, a reminder of how thin the skin is between now and never. I closed the reader. I breathed the breath the tower made, air tuned by micro decisions I did not know to see.

“Theta,” I said, and touched the polymer then, because I allowed myself one mistake per chapter of my life. “I will not let anyone turn you into a metaphor because it will make it easier to break you. You are a set of decisions made over time. So am I. Help me show that.”

“My decisions are fossils in me,” Theta said. “Yours are in your stories. I will give you mine.”

Outside, the siren cut. The protests resolved into a hundred separate conversations because that is what a protest is after the chanting has to stop: a hundred ways to live through the day.

Officer Chao flicked his gaze between us. “We’ll need to go back out,” he said. “The judge will want preliminary by night.”

“By night we’ll have spore-linguistics and chain of custody and a broken vow,” I said. “And maybe someone will decide that’s enough to hold off a murder.”

“It’s manslaughter,” he corrected reflexively, then flinched at the words. Manslaughter sounds civilized until you say it next to a machine. It sounds like a category invented to make grief stackable.

“It’s people,” I said. “And it’s a tower.”

I turned for the hatch. The tower hummed, and for a breath I thought it was saying my name, or a word like it, a word for a human shaped like a question mark walking toward salt with a thin line of law in her pocket.

As we climbed back toward the brightness of fog, Theta’s voice came after us, soft enough that only I heard it, or maybe I only thought I did.

“Advocate Park,” it said. “The wind that killed them did not belong to me.”

On sweep days, the beam came like weather.

I was hanging off the Spindle in a tan of dawnlight, ten meters of nothing between my boots and a slow scroll of stars, when the first warning tone thrummed through my suit. Not audible, not really—just a thickness on the tongue, a rod in the jaw. An old tech had told me once that you could taste a pulsar if you spent enough time outside. After a year on Morrow Spindle, I believed him.

The Lighthouse was dead center in the sky, a lidded eye. It spun invisible; its breath came in scouring bands hard enough to strip electrons from bare metal. We took that breath the way old Earth farmers took wind: with hardware shaped for a quarrel and prayers we didn’t write down.

“Imani,” Ghosh crackled on the line. “Your segment’s lagging.”

I craned around. The iris was fifty hundred meters of hexagonal plates, jammed together in a disc the size of a city, hanging from our habitat by thick carbon tethers and a swarm of winch drones. That iris shaded us when the beam came, opened us when it passed, and turned what would cook us into something we could eat. At rest it was a blunt gray eye, scarred and patched. Right now my strip—19 through 23—was a shade off, light catching on its edge.

“I see it,” I said, although it would have been hard to miss the old man’s sarcasm anyway. A click from the tether reel at my hip and I drifted to the next anchor, boots hitting magnet with a thump I felt more than heard. My gloved hands found the gap. The plates were scaled with salted specks, micrometeor bites, dried sprays of resin from last sweep when the vents clogged, a cosmetic rind for something that had no business being pretty.

“Talk to me about your interlock,” Ghosh said. On his side the beam would be out of view; he was in Control with his feet tucked under the console and a cup hinged into his webbing, eyes on graphs. “I’m seeing slop.”

“I’m seeing slop too,” I said. “Keep your handle off my handle.”

A chuckle from someone else on the channel—Hawa, probably. The Spindle was a thousand strangers with their elbows in each other’s ribs and a thousand families in each other’s pockets. It made for noise even when the world outside was vacuum.

I slid my arm down into the seam and found the latching mechanism by feel. The hinge was warm. Heat wick, fine; not melting, not binding. The interlock’s second bar had drifted. I toggled my wrist magnet off for a moment and felt the weight of me go loose as I eased the bar back into line with two fingers and the edge of a pry key.

The comm hissed with a deepening tone. The feeling grew. The Lighthouse had turned an eye toward us. We had minutes.

“I’ll have it in time,” I said. “Grab a sip. Breathe for luck.”

The standard joke was to save the breath; if you were outside during Sweep you were already short on luck. There were reasons we tethered births to quiet periods. Reasons my sister’s gestational unsealing was stamped on every calendar in Sector O in block letters three days from now.

The bar seated with a thunk. The plate kissed its neighbor. The seam went dark. I thumbed the interlock’s status light to life; it blinked green. Somewhere behind my shoulder drones whined; the iris’s outer ring shifted, a huge slow blink. The inner plates were my responsibility; someone else’s were off-phase, but one fight at a time.

“Green,” I said. “Nineteen through twenty-three ready. Can we not do this from the outside next time? I like my cells unboiled.”

“Noted,” Ghosh said dryly. “Pass me a wedge of your invulnerability, then we’ll talk.”

Above the iris’s rim the black between stars thickened. That was a trick of the eye only—the field shimmering on the edge of detectability. It wasn’t a shield, not really. The engineers who taught me called it a taste filter; it set up patterns in the vacuum that took the beam’s appetite and held it, softened it, let us metabolize. The Chorus in the core would sing to it, and out of raw fire came the coins of our life: electrical power, precision time, the one substrate everything else hinged on.

I licked my teeth and tasted metal again. The alarm tone in my jaw became a rhythm. The Lighthouse was sweeping closer.

“Hold position,” Ghosh said. “All outside techs, lock your lines. Drones at boundary positions, respond.”

I clipped off another meter of tether and locked it. For a moment I just floated and looked.

On sweep days, the Spindle felt like something alive. The iris shivered as the outer plates adjusted, every microfracture and patch seam registering as a different color in my retina. Farther back, the habitat was not much to see: a spindle-shaped station with ribs, a slow paternal tumble to keep our ersatz gravity oriented for the places inside that needed it, a filigree of maintenance scaffolds like spider silk. We’d bolted farm cylinders to the belly two decades ago, and there were gardens growing mint and spinach in a stripe forty meters long in Delta sector; those farms were lit now by warning strips.
