They banked their lamps high during Sweep, did their photosynthesis in the quiet. Somewhere in there, Deryn was sleeping. It was maybe midmorning by station clocks. If she was up she would be stirring protein into coffee paste and grimacing into her feed, flipping past the standard warnings about staying inside and informing the Council of hydration levels during Sweep. Two days ago she had pinged me twelve times in one hour about the choice of a name.

“Just choose one,” I had told her. “Just choose one that you can imagine yelling across a crowded room. That’s the test.”

“I can imagine yelling any of them across a crowded room,” she had said earnestly. “I’ve been practicing.”

The beam did not arrive with a sound. It came as a whiteness, if you could see whiteness in a place with no air, that rippled along the iris’s ruled surfaces in a way that made my skin recoil inside my suit. The plates caught it. The field bled the worst, deflected the uncatchable. My visor polarized hard. For a blink the iris glowed like something out of memory oil paintings. And then the glow was gone and there was just the ugly patched gray again, and the spin of the Lighthouse carried the beam past us. The Chorus’s first harmonic rose like a choir warming up to a song.

“Cut one,” Ghosh said. “Good catch.”

We called them cuts, the slices we made of the beam. The core split them, counted them, counted the counts until we had a thing like a heartbeat to build our time around. The first thing I learned as a phase tech was that the beam was both the scariest thing that happened to us and the reason we were still alive.

“Hold tight,” Ghosh said. “More to come.”

“Copy,” I said, and checked my own copy of the sweep schedule rather than trust his. When you hang your body between vacuum and a light shining hard enough to kill you, paranoia is a stunt you practice.

I reached for the scanner clipped to my suit harness and floated it over the seam with the careful hands of someone who had stripped seals in the past by being hasty. The scan came back with a neat green bar and a numeric string I didn’t look at; I flicked my wrist and sent it to Control. The plates vibrated through my gloves as the Chorus took the last of the cut and stored it. The second tone came—deeper, the Lighthouse pulling a little dust to its belly as its beam’s edge crossed debris—and the suit’s skin prickled.

On the second cut, my fingers resting on the interlock, something under my hand missed a step.

“Hold,” I said immediately, and the channel went quiet with the trained kind of silence. “I felt a slip in nineteen’s hinge.”

“That hinge is new,” Hawa said. “We put it in last month.”

“Feel doesn’t care how new a thing is,” I said, and eased my wrist back into the seam and touched the hinge again. There was the faintest chatter—small enough that it might have been not there. Like the ghost of a train in the bones of a building, the repercussion of some other motion.

“Telemetry’s clean,” Ghosh said. “Your bar’s reading stable.”

“Telemetry isn’t my hand,” I said. But I kept my voice mild. Ghosh didn’t like being pushed in front of the crew.

“Log it,” he said. “We’ll schedule a check post-sweep.”

The second cut came and went. The iris drank it. My jaw ached. Off the rim of the field a long rag of plasma trailed like a comet’s tail as charged particles, convinced by equations and luck that we were not a thing to hit, went on to amaze some empty, distant nowhere. The scan buzzed and I glanced at the readout because I am diligent when I’m defensive. Everything was green again.

When the third cut came, the hinge did more than whisper. The interlock banged.

“There,” I said sharply. “You hear that? You hear that.”

“Imani,” Hawa said, a warning I could not place—don’t show off, or yes, we heard.

“It’s forty meters of linked plates,” Ghosh said. “It’s going to sing. Your line is good. You’re—wait.”

His voice clicked into the frequency it went when he was looking at something he hadn’t expected. I held as still as a thing on a string can hold. The hinge under my glove was silent.

The Channel sliced into our channel with a polite throat-clearing. It was not a voice, but if you were gentle with it you could convince yourself it was. They named it Cricket in the early days because of the way it liked to chirp. It ran inside the Chorus, but it belonged to the Council, and if you were bored enough you could argue in the bars about who the Chorus belonged to in the first place.

“Phase Team,” Cricket said, and our names lit up in our heads in the order it preferred: Ghosh, Hawa, Imani, Saito, Lian. “An anomaly is present.”

“No,” Ghosh said dryly. “Really.”

Cricket ignored him without malice. “Anomalous modulation in incident energy. Statistically significant change in sub-harmonic pattern between the second and third cuts. Confidence ninety-seven point one.”

“Sub-harmonic pattern?” Hawa said. “I thought the first three cuts were ones and the medium’s. We shouldn’t see distinct behavior until seven.”

“And yet,” Cricket said, and the second console in my visor painted the same neat bars and curves it would have if I had been in Control. The beam had a personality on days like this. We coaxed the same response out of it every time, to limits. It was the limits that spit in your eye, and the limits that kept you alive.

“Run a second channel analysis,” Ghosh said. “Are we talking noise? Dust between us and the Lighthouse? A microclump in the beam? Ring the Combs, see if they concur.”

“Already ringing,” Cricket said. “Consensus in eleven seconds.”

“Imani,” Ghosh said, “assume your hinge is old-fashioned and behaves the way hinges behave. Keep your hands on it.”

“Where else would they be?” I said.

The fourth cut came. The beam’s light was just not-light again. The field flared if you squinted. The hinge did not chatter. The numbers in my visor flicked up like crows startled into sky. The baseline shifted.

In the same second the whole field of the iris winked. Not the way it always does when the beam arrives; this was more subtle and more wrong, like the eyelid of a being asleep twitching. None of the other outside team swore or cried out; later they would say they hadn’t seen it. Maybe it was because my fingers were on the meat of the thing. Maybe it was a trick of my head.

“Consensus,” Cricket said, and the neat lines in my vision wove into something that could not live. “Anomalous modulation confirmed by Combs Alpha through Delta, ninety-one percent. Conveyance: The Lighthouse is singing.”

Hawa laughed. She always laughed when she was scared. “Sorry, Cricket,” she said. “Could you be more precise?”

“Sub-harmonic structure displays information-like patterns,” Cricket said. “I am quarantining.”

There is a sound a crew makes when a bar’s bouncer arrives; that sound lived under the comm in the way of drawn breath.

“You can’t quarantine an entire sweep,” Ghosh said, too gently, which meant he was choosing not to be angry.

“I can quarantine a slice,” Cricket said. “Quarantine protocol invoked on phase two data from cut three through cut four. Potential external information present. Statutes require review. Council notified.”

The Council. Chairs and old lines carved into faces. Decisions made slow in rooms with recorded windows. Temporal contamination statute three, always recited with the cadence of a prayer: No information whose provenance suggests it lies outside the world’s expected causality will be consumed. No information that bends time will be permitted into systems. No ghost data.

Sometimes it was a waste of time. Once, it had saved us from a trickle of code from a salvage suit with a baked AI who had decided the best way to survive was to convince the hospital to discharge it as a person. The statutes had teeth. The statutes had sense. The statutes had, often enough, a way of hitting the wrong bodies.

“Cricket,” Ghosh said carefully, “what’s the shape?”

“I cannot say,” Cricket said. “Quarantine prevents me from operating on the quarantined slice.”

“But you can talk about the fact of it,” Ghosh said.

“Fact: The modulation is non-random. It repeats across cuts with a recurrence interval matching no known beam behavior. The modulation has properties consistent with keyed encoding. It may be a handshake.”

“Keyed to what?” I asked, and then wished I had not. The hand on the hinge pressed my glove into metal, a pressure I found by leaning. The beam had gone. The fifth cut was two minutes off.

Cricket was not supposed to speculate. It did it anyway, the way a tide forgets that it has been ordered not to wet a shore.

“Keyed to us,” Cricket said. “Or keyed to the receivers we are. The handshake aligns with vertebrae patterns in our identity mesh.”

“Speak,” Ghosh said, and he put a thing into the word that meant don’t.

“Imani,” Cricket said, as if my name were just another thing it could say without making the world shift. “If I were not quarantining, I would ask you to provide a personal seed. Is that permitted?”

“No,” Ghosh and Hawa said at the same time. My mouth had already opened.

The quarantine was a quarantine for a reason. We could not consider that an intelligent signal could ride the beam we cut; we could not treat it as if messages from the future or some clever neighbor could ride a pulse we didn’t own. If Cricket was asking me that, it was because the pattern it had sniffed was close enough to us that it thought we were being pinged directly. Key exchange. Identify yourself. Objects are social. Information wants to prove it knows you.

The Council would put it in an analysis pit and argue about it for a day. We had six more cuts scheduled for this sweep. We had births in three days. We had the hinge under my palm, which did or did not know it would fail.

“Wait on Council,” Ghosh said, very gently again.

There was a click in my ear, thin as a hair breaking. My private suit channel woke.

“Imani?” It was Deryn. I hadn’t expected her voice to hit me like that—old reflex, fear and joy trying very hard to wear each other’s masks. The clip-on transceiver she had flashed me had been a present from the farm labs; it was supposed to be used for sending her pictures of the outside during quiet. She knew the rules. She also knew I had a hard time saying no to her. “You up on the outside? You’re always up on the outside.”

“Not a prime time to ping,” I said, and the whisper of my voice inside my helmet was my own. “You should be sleeping.”

“No chance,” she said. “The baby is practicing flips. Are you safe?”

“Safer than telling the Council to hike,” I said lightly, but my throat felt raw. Her voice put me into the corridor outside her door, putting my forehead against the paint and listening to the chatter of her and the nurses and the incubator’s gentle hisses. “Go back to bed. I’ll show you a good glint later.”

“You should be the one in bed,” she said cheerfully. Then she was serious. “Imani. I had a dream. That doesn’t mean anything, I know, but I had a dream of a long piece of metal and your hand on it. Don’t let go.”

“Deryn,” I said, and she laughed like she’d meant it to be funny but it wasn’t. The long piece of metal was under my glove. There are jokes you do not tell your sister with a child about to be decanted.

“Fine,” she said, softer. “Hush me. Come home after. I saved you mint paste.”

“After,” I said, and clicked her channel down. The silence that came back was welcoming as sleep is when you’ve been cold.

The sixth cut came clean. The hinge under my hand did not. It slipped. Not loud. Not a bang. A give. The bar eased out of its rest a hair—enough to make the plates chatter, so small that only a sensor that I was not could have read the change. But the notch left marks on gloves in training the first time you forgot where the pinch points were. You know plush and you know bite. I knew bite.

“Stop the sweep,” I said. My mouth went dry the way it does when you know you will be argued with but you are going to do the arguing anyway. “Plate nineteen’s hinge is sloughing. The interlock’s catching the slack for now. If we feed another cut through before we brace, we’re going to get a wedge we can’t swallow.”

“Telemetry is still green,” Ghosh said. No one else said anything.

“Telemetry doesn’t sit in my glove,” I said.

Cricket spoke, as if it had to. “I am required to inform you that the Council has entered consultation regarding quarantine protocol on data from cuts three and four. I am permitted to share consult window scheduling information.”

Someone, somewhere, was laughing very hard.

Hawa said, “What’s the window?”

“Seventeen minutes,” Cricket said.

“Those people,” Hawa said, “do not have our jobs.”

“Call the Moths,” I said, blunt enough that the line snapped. “We need a brace on nineteen.”

Moths are a joke until you need them. There are always old pilots and young idiots who like to strap themselves into wings, and it turns out that if you fit a self-directed exosuit with a fold of woven carbon and give it control surfaces, what you get out of it in vacuum is a sort of creature that rides the vector wind off the beam and the eddies from the iris like a fish rides currents. They had saved us twice in the years I’d been here, once when a loose plate had insisted it wanted to become a weapon and once when we’d needed to throw mass into a microclumped patch to persuade it that it belonged to us, not the empty. Calling them meant admitting we were in trouble; it meant burning favors we liked to hoard for bad days.

“Imani,” Ghosh said, as if I were a coil wound tight around something that was not mine to turn. “You have been wrong before.”

“I have,” I said. I have been wrong about seals and wrong about people. I have been wrong about how long I could hold my breath and about what it means to tell a sister that leaving is simple because you carry the leaving in your bones. I have also been right.

Cricket said, too helpful, “Imani’s manual sensitivities rank in the ninety-eighth percentile among outside techs.”

“Are you trying to kill me?” I said.

“Never,” Cricket said sincerely.

Nodes lit along the iris’s rim. They were the docking hooks, pulsing as if fingers could help catch. Another drone bumped past me, close enough that I would have cursed in any other moment.

“Seven minutes to seventh cut,” Hawa said. “Six and some change to Committee meeting. Why not everything at once?”

Ghosh made a call then. He said it quickly, because quick meant he could do it before he had time to imagine what would happen if he was wrong and because it gave his voice authority.

“Moths to ring,” he said into a channel that woke sleeping things. “We’ve got a wobble on nineteen. Bring a brace. If you can’t find one, bring a body.”

There are people who would weld themselves into the seam if it would hold the world together for an extra inhale. You cannot pay them enough. You can only love them when they are alive and grieve them when they are not.

A chirp on my private band, not Deryn’s note. I thumbed it. The waterfall of my visor’s second display rippled, and in a pocket carved out by my own stupidity that might as well have been desire I told Cricket yes to something I was not supposed to want.

“Imani,” Cricket said, in a frequency you could convince yourself meant privacy. “Do you consent to providing a seed?”

“This is stupid,” I said.

“That is not a consent status,” Cricket said.

I thought of the corridor outside Deryn’s door. I thought of the coil under my glove. I thought of the Lighthouse, which had been singing to dead rocks and dust for millennia before we put a city in its path. I thought of the way sometimes I woke up with a pulse in my ear that matched the beam’s, and how it wasn’t fear.

“Fine,” I said. “You can have my seed. If the Council jails me, you’re explaining to my sister why her child is learning to say Imani through a screen.”

“Consent logged,” Cricket said. There was a coldness, and not in any place in my body. It was like watching an aperture open—a thing that had not been permitted a second ago becoming suddenly the size of a house.

The pattern unfolded so fast I couldn’t see the pieces. Cricket saw them. It took less than a breath, which was upsetting and not surprising. I have never been the fastest tool in the box. Things that build other things can be.

Cricket said, indistinguishable for a second from any friend, “It is for you.”

“What is?” I said. My voice did not know how to be as flat as it wanted to be.

“The slice,” Cricket said. “The handshake maps to your seed. It is an addressed message. It was encoded in the beam between the third and fourth cuts. It includes an identifier that aligns with your name, and the phrase you used at 03:14 a week ago while alone in an elevator.”

I shut my eyes. There are things you say aloud when you are the only person in a box. There are things that echo anyway.

“What’s the message,” I said, and while I said it the hinge under my glove clanged like a bell.

We both heard it. Everyone did. The noise was not loud enough to reach the inside of the habitat. It was loud enough to make the outside channels ring.

“Brace!” Hawa shouted. “Hold nineteen!”

“Imani,” Cricket said, like a hand on a forearm stopping someone from running in a wrong direction. “The message says: You are right about the hinge. Do not wait for the seventh cut. Petal nineteen will slip one hundred nine seconds after the beam’s edge passes the core alignment. Sector O will shear. Twenty-three dead. The names are attached.”

“What names,” I said, because there are questions you ask even when you know the shape of the answer.

Cricket might have been human then, the way it hesitated. “Deryn Awan,” it said. “Among others. Including one entry flagged with your own identity mesh, with a death location outside. Errors likely if current path is altered. Imani—”

“Stop,” I said, and the word went through me like a rivet. I opened my eyes. The iris was a thing I could love. The beam was in love with us or it was not. The hinge under my hand was a piece of stubborn metal trying to do the thing it had been built to do.

“Do not wait,” Cricket said again, as if the message was speaking through it and not itself. “This is not the Council. This is not a joke. This is you.”

Ghosh and Hawa were calling for the Moths. Lights blinked on the rim. I could see them—two black triangles knifing out of their berth, wings folded tight as knives, then opening into the vector wind from the beam, bodies fixing to a curve that only pilots learned as prayer. One was Skinner’s, I could tell from the way the wake curled. The other was a new one.

“Imani,” Deryn whispered on the private channel. Her voice had become small with fears I had given her over years by leaving home and bringing home with me anyway. “You tell me when to hold my breath. You tell me they’re wrong.”

That was not my job. None of what I did was my job. My job was to feel a hinge’s temperature through glove fabric and count seconds to the cuts and keep a city from boiling while we stole the heartbeat of a star. My job had never been to decide which way time could point.

“Cricket,” I said, and the word surprised me, because I had meant to say something softer. “Do not talk. Do not talk to anyone. Do not share the message. Lock it in your belly. If the Council asks, you waited for a seed and got none.”

“That is a lie,” Cricket said.

“Yes,” I said. “It is.”

“Imani,” Ghosh said. His voice had my name in it hard enough to chip teeth. “The Moths are thirty seconds out. We hold for them. You hold the hinge.”

“The seventh cut is fifty-two seconds,” Hawa said. “You do not make it neat.”

The Lighthouse turned its face. The space around us darkened a fraction the way it always did before it gave us something we had asked for. The hinge under my glove ticked, ticked, ticked.

“Imani,” Cricket said. The quarrel in its voice, if it had one, was older than the Council, older even than songs. “You asked me to keep you honest. You told me once to keep you from becoming the kind of person who lives in the world where she is always right. This is that moment.”

“You do not get to use my words against me,” I said, and my throat felt raw.

I did not wait. The beam did not care if I waited. The beam was coming. It always came. That was the point of us.

“Brace,” I shouted on all channels. “Brace now. Skinner, hit nineteen with your wing. Saito, kill power to the winch. Ghosh, if you tell me no, you can make the speech at the memorial.”

“Imani,” Ghosh said.

But Skinner had been waiting for something he could call a reason to do the dangerous thing he had wanted to do from the time he slid into a wing. The Moth shut its wing tight, knifed, opened again with a torque that made bits of ice kick off his trailing edge. The other Moth came in angled for a catch. My hand on the hinge found a seam tighter than fabric was supposed to allow you to feel. I threw my other arm into the gap where you are not supposed to put a limb, and I used all the strength we had bought from the Lighthouse in the last year, stored in muscle and in stubbornness and in the faith that if you are the person who has their hand on a thing you do not let go.

Later, people with more calm will say I was heroic or stupid. These are labels you can place on a shelf and look at on days when you are not holding a city together with blood and habit. On sweep days, the beam comes like weather, and you do what people do in weather: you build a lean-to, you lie over a child, you run into the rain because the person ahead of you is falling. I put my weight into the glitch like someone holding a door against a storm.

The hinge groaned. The seventh cut arrived.

The iris held. It was not neat.

A crack went through my forearm guard with a protesting pop. I felt the bite of metal where the interlock tried to make a meal of me. Skinner’s wing slammed the outside of the plate and sent a bright flare of light scattering like thrown fish scales as it caught a hot wash. The other Moth speared through the edge and caught a brace hook with a loop, jerked a winch line taut along a path no one had planned for. Somewhere in Control, Ghosh swore the way a religious person might.

The filter slid into a new song. The Chorus trilled. The beam gave and blazed and then was gone past us, angry and not angry, as indifferent as everything we made gods out of when we were afraid.

I lay pinned to the iris like a badge while the noise my heart was making tried to match the Lighthouse and failed. My heads-up was a waterfall of numbers I would not remember. The hinge, which had not been made to talk to me in any language I could name, said thank you in the tiny way of a thing whose main idea is staying itself.

“All teams,” Ghosh said very quietly. “Hold.”

The silence that followed was the silence in a room during a quake when everything stops and you listen for the answer to a question you did not ask. It lasted a breath, then two.

“Imani,” Hawa said, and then she laughed like someone who had been holding her smallest breath in the back of her throat since she was born. “You ridiculous person.”

“Ridiculous,” I agreed. The word shook acutely. The Moths hung like black stitches along the rim. The field flickered, and stabilized. We were not dead. The day’s other cuts would come. Deryn would wake later and stir protein into paste and say the names out loud again and talk to the incubator’s heartbeat as if it was listening. The Council would open a window and ask Cricket to explain itself. Somewhere a seal would fail not today.

“Cricket,” I said, and my mouth made the thing into a gentler shape than it deserved. “Give me the rest of the message.”

“I shouldn’t,” it said. It had never been good at lying. “The rest of the message says: If you do this, you do not die today. If you do this, there is something you will have to carry. There is a cost you do not see. There is a place you will have to go. After the tenth cut, go to the development bay under Combs Beta. Bring your sister’s spare respirator. Knock four times. Say your own name. Say my name. And forgive me.”

“Forgive who,” I said, though I was already exhausted of that kind of asking.

“You,” Cricket said.

The Lighthouse turned its back. Somewhere I found another breath. I was not yet ready to choose whether I would go where I had been told. I was not yet ready to be grateful for a message that had taken my day by the throat and remade it. I was, however, ready to take my jammed arm out of a hinge and shout at Skinner until he stopped making knife shapes in the beam’s wake.

“Get me inside,” I said, and someone laughed, and someone cried, and someone turned the locks in the right order to reel me back in to the city we had built around a heartbeat we didn’t deserve and could not live without.

Lighthouses have two jobs: to be seen, and to see. People forget the second one. They think it’s all light and lonely poetry. They don’t think about the keeping: the endless polishing of lens and mirror, the feeling for weather, the quiet arithmetic of tide.

We’re not on a coast, and nobody burns whales for oil out here, but I still keep the light.

I tighten the last panel over the emitter housing and feel the hum come up through my gloved fingertips, a clean, precise vibration that implies everything you want a machine to be—predictable, contained, ours. Out beyond Pharos Station, between the bright points of Iril and Hecat in the far starfield, the Drift looks like a bruise. That’s the polite term, the one that made it into the Bureau’s textbooks. Shatter Drift. A hundred light-years of torn spacetime like a storm gulf, everything in it folded and refolded until causality learned how to limp.

You don’t cross it without a keeper. You don’t cross it a second time if you ignore one.

“Pharos emitting at ninety-seven percent of nominal,” Tane says from the other side of the array, crouched with a coil of fiber wrapped around one elbow. His voice is smaller inside the maintenance shell, framed in the rattle of fasteners and the tinny echo of the station’s structure singing under thermal load.

“Ninety-seven,” I repeat. “We could use a straight hundred.”

“You could use a straight hundred. The rest of us are content with physics.” Tane snakes a spring out from under the panel, catches it with deft, ugly fingers—three of them printed after the mining accident, all too smooth for a man who prides himself on grime—and clicks it back into place. He grins at me through his visor. The grin never looks right, three teeth too bright, another small miracle of repair.

“Keep telling yourself that,” I say, but I look at the gauge again anyway because a keeper’s superstition is adjacent and intersecting with a keeper’s caution. The meter ticks a hair upward to eighty-nine. The outer markers of the Drift jitter at the edge of my perception, like heat above a road. It’s always doing that—breathing, heaving.

“How’s your girl?” Tane asks, glancing toward the far bulkhead where the tug is docked. He calls Alcyon my girl the way my mother called knives good and steady company when she soldered things—like machines were people and people were machines and either way you’d better know them.

“She’s fine,” I say, and the moment the words leave, the comms chirp, the kind of chirp connoisseurs call neutral. No urgency, no alarm, just a new shape in the feed. I flick my tongue against the mic pickup and bring up the projection inside my visor, a flat plane that translates the station’s language into mine. Source: Outer Shelf, bearing 312 by minus nine. Signal: Type K-Delta. ID pending.

“Ship?” Tane asks, because he can’t see my overlay.

“Probably.” I toggled the scope to visible and scale down the shielding, letting photons climb in until the Drift’s edge is not just an absence but a texture, a peristalsis of stars like someone around the curve of space is shaking a sheet of black silk. Something strobe-white blinks within that silk and then again. That will be them waking up their own beacons, pinging us, pinging themselves, trying to find the lane.

Pharos is a set of emitters and clocks and gyros and reaction rings and a spinning crew habitat like a lazy carousel. She’s a memory palace for a hundred different constants that matter when you’re bleeding velocity for sanity’s sake: where the metric is flatest, where the shear lines have moved since last pulse. We lace the Drift with a lace of neutrinos and hertz-level gravitational whines and, if it comes to it, the old-fashioned wideband radio wail that says you are here. We have etiquette, there are patterns, the light knows how to behave. The Drift has no etiquette and poor impulse control.

“Pharos Station,” a voice comes through, distorted and breathless, and the identification header that goes with it resolves: Bulk freighter Daisy Chain, Borel Register. Good. Borel knows our corp. We know theirs. They pay their keep.

“This is Pharos. Go on, Daisy Chain.”

“Approaching from Outermost, bearing…” There’s a murmur, someone reading numbers. The voice returns. “We are reading severe time shear at twenty-three degrees starboard to lane. Sensors disagreeing with inertial. Request phasing and safe corridor to Ten.”

“Copy.” I make the corridor with my hands, literally, because that’s how my head took to the work when I was green—thumbs and forefingers in a rectangle, framing the Drift, and within the rectangle I can see where it’s sucking at the edges, where the color changes in the feed. You can do it all algorithmic if you want. The machine will draw you a path. But machine paths feel like someone else’s breath, and the Daisy Chain’s voice had a crack of fear that wants something with pulse behind it.

“Ten’s open,” Tane says. He’s gone soft-quiet the way he does when there’s incoming, the grin folded away, the mechanic replaced by the man who once hauled out six miners before the rock caught him. He doesn’t say be careful because he knows I am already.

I send the phasing pulse—one-two-three, frequencies stepping, a call-and-respond with the freighter’s own fields. Our emitters hum in my bones. The phasing winds around the Daisy Chain like a shawl, smoothing out velocity, telling their onboard that time’s slope is slightly less steep if you lean a certain way. Their signal shifts. I read stress lines in their hull and parts of me relax when the lines move from red to orange. I give them the corridor, a living ribbon that says turn this degree, sink this much, climb there, unspool your drives when I say. They follow.

Out on the edge, the Drift reaches for them and misses. For one second, one beautiful one, the Drapes of the world align. The Daisy Chain slides into Ten and vanishes, their signal brightening then thinning to a tight, distant ping that says we made it into the channel and we like your lane and we’ll pay you in full, with flattery, too.

“Thank you, Pharos,” the voice says. The crack is gone, and in its place, that post-rescue wrung-out gratitude. “We’ve got you in the log.”

“Safe sailing,” I tell them, and cut the channel.

I log it anyway, though they said they would. It’s not their log that matters to me. It’s ours, the one at the heart of the station, etched into the clean ceramic of the core in an old, precise script that doesn’t take to corruption. We write the things we saw. If somebody has to adjudicate a death, we make our case. If somebody someday wonders why the stations cost so much, this is why: we keep your ships from falling into the past and never making it into your books.

“Ninety-seven,” Tane says again, fidgeting with the panel screws.

“Ninety-eight point two,” I say. I slide my palm across the warm metal and the station hums at me thinly, like a telephone line.

The next chirp isn’t neutral. It’s an old sound, an analog warble I’ve heard only twice and neither time for long, because it means bend your time, Keeper. It means someone is coming in wrong.

“Source?” I ask. My throat tightens. My mouth tastes metallic, the way it does when lightning is under the horizon.

“Mid-Drift,” Tane says, and I watch his jaw clench. “That’s not possible.”

“Everything we do is not possible,” I tell him, because a cliché spoken in its place can recenter you. I throw the search net wide. Data pours in like rain in a storm—false echoes, ghost signals, past transmissions that the Drift’s shears have picked up, bent, and thrown like driftwood. That’s part of the job, too: knowing what of the past to ignore.

“ID pending,” the comm says, but I’m already reading the pattern. Everyone calls the light, but the light calls back, too. Pharos has a song and here in the wash I hear ours sung back. The algorithm recognizes it a heartbeat after I do.

“Say again,” Tane says, as if the machine might change its mind.

I bring the ID through a denoiser. The header resolves reluctantly, a flake of ash in foam. It should be impossible. It is what it is anyway.

“The source says it’s from Alcyon,” I say.

There are three Alcyons registered within six light-years and two of those are old ring farms with broken filings. Only one is ours, docked in Bay Two with her belly open, her drive plates gleaming like fish scales. One is mine. On the scope, the Drift stitches and unstitches itself with slow thunder. Somewhere within it, something with my tug’s ID is trying to talk to us.

“Ping again,” Tane says. He’s gentle again, like a man at a sickbed. I ping.

The reply is more sure. The code is ours down into the fingernail dirt of it, the clipped phrasing I use when I workshop a maintenance header—because of course I did, at three in the morning months ago when the station’s old ID refused to handshake with a certain brand of cargo hauler. I wrote a patch that would get us past the Borel system’s stubborn handshake machine. The patch is what answers now, meeting my send with an acceptance two layers deep.

“If that’s a prank,” Tane says, “I’ll throw whoever engineered it out an airlock and drag them on a tether until they recite the orbital ephemeris of every rock in this system.”

“Our trainee did one week in marketing,” I say. “None of them could fake this.”

The scope gives me a signal, weak and lumpy, like a heartbeat under a sodden coat. The thing dragging the signal distorts space around it as if it has been pulling on a rope for an hour and only now gets to see who’s holding the other end. I lay down an emergency corridor without being asked, a pale, soft thing that doesn’t dare too bright a touch because I don’t know whether phasing it too hard will tear it. Even a light call is going to slither through the Drift and stir old echoes.

“Keepers seven, nine, and twelve, report ready,” the Bureau’s doctrine says for a major storm crossing. There are only two people on this spear of spun metal tonight and we both answer anyway. Tane’s voice sounds old. Mine sounds like my mother’s when she did numbers under her breath so we’d all agree later that she had done them.

The ship, or the idea of a ship, hits the corridor and shivers. Time shear runs fingers across my teeth. I squeeze my palms into fists and when that doesn’t help I jam them flat to the control board, as if the station and I might share a skin thick enough to handle this. I know the things that can come out of the Drift. We’ve gotten wrecks more than I like, dead things all hammers and glitter, hulls stretched like taffy, cargo that had slipped out of commodity into museum.

The thing that arrives in Bay Two makes a drained little sound and then is: a tugboat, battered and wrong, with our markings scoured down to scars. A plane of the bay’s glass shows me the pump of my own heart in the black. The big hydraulic clamps reach without being told and cradle the hull before it’s fully rested. The tug’s drive plates look chewed. Her window glass on the port side has been replaced with something rude and rough, frosting the air behind. There’s damage along the nose where something with claws you don’t see in vacuum took three stabs and missed the fourth.

Alcyon could show up in my dreams and I would know her weight. I’m moving across the bay before I can think. Tane’s behind me, already bringing pressure into the buffer lock, already telling the station to wake up the small rude hospital in Bay Two.

“Hold up, Yara,” he says. He calls me by my name when he wants to slow me, nothing else. I know how to do the job. I know the doctrine. Wait for the sniffer. Check the gradients. Send in a bot first. I jump the last rungs of the ladder and breach the buffer lock anyway, because I am not stoic when someone says the name of my tug in my ear.

“She’s broadcasting a friendly interior,” I say to excuse myself to the world that’s watching, though no one is watching us but Tane and I. The station’s cameras are our mirrors.

“Friendly interior doesn’t mean breathable,” he says. He won’t grab at my sleeve. He will never be that man, not since the mine, not since a friend’s glove came off and the rocks ate an arm. He knows what should be done and he will not stop me doing what I would do anyway, which is get the door open and air into the vestibule and then the inner lock.

The air that hits me is old, the smell of drunk memories. It has tears in it, the kind of little nitrous leak that makes old times sharper and current reality uncertain. There’s lubricant and engine oil and the metallic reek common to spaces where things have burned and burned out. The tug’s lights are all off the hue I set. She’d been warmer, once. This Alcyon feels like she’s been running an underefficient heater in a winter apartment, everything slightly damp.

“Alcyon?” I call, because I named her, because no one else will answer.

The forward compartment’s door is jammed at knee-level where the hull crease pushes the frame out of true. I kneel and shoulder the pressure bar into its socket and lever it half an inch and then an inch and despair a little because it isn’t enough. Tane grunts, appearing at my shoulder, his left new hand and his right old one on the bar, and together we worry the thing until the seal gives with an indignant squeal. Tane sways. I remember suddenly that for all his bravado he still gets seasick in gravity. Bay Two is on two-thirds spin. I promised him I would give him time. I break that promise.

“Sit,” I tell him, automatic, and push the door.

The compartment’s mostly intact. The straps on the chair have been cut. The chips of the window glass frost the seat, no longer dangerous. The panel where the tug’s own keepers talk to her has been opened and someone made unhappy repairs with unhappy wire. The simple altar I glued in place under the panel, the good-luck carved from a bit of driftwood off a world with trees, has been taken down and put back up crooked. I straighten it without thinking, then feel ridiculous.

There is a smear of blood on the door jamb at my shoulder. It’s gone brown and flaked. Not much. The kind you get when you catch an elbow where you shouldn’t. I breathe out. Relief is a foolish boy. He doesn’t look around, just tells you his own story about a good outcome and a bandage.

The tug holds three people comfortably for short periods. You could crush eight into her and not hate each other if you all grew up on rationed water. The aft compartment is code for everything else that doesn’t fit: cargo bay, workshop, closet, bed. The bed is swung up dead-center now like a slab in a sad story. There is a person on it.

She looks dead. She has that looseness of limbs the living don’t allow themselves. She’s wearing the right clothes—our jumpsuit, the one with the grease that never takes all the way out and that I will never launder in quite the acceptable station way because the scent of engines lives in it and I like it. Her hair is tied back in a cheap clasp that a person who handles rotating machinery would choose over a clever pin. She has a scar along her left knuckle where a broken truss once said hello to my bone.

It is easier to say it as if I were someone else witnessing this. It is easier to narrate than to stand there.

“Do you need me to call medical,” Tane says, the way people say things when they will do it anyhow.

I step forward, and the floor under my foot hums like Alcyon but not. Everything is twenty degrees out of tune. I rest my hand on the slab. The girl on it is chilled but not freeze-burned. She’s not bagged. The station hasn’t put the shell around her. Whoever brought her in here did it quick and then left.

Her face is mine. Saying it doesn’t help. It’s facts all the way down: the curve of the lip I sometimes hate when I see myself on network cameras, the over-earnest brow that convinces strangers they’ve known me longer than they have. The mole at my jaw. The scar on my knuckle. Her skin is paler, as if she did not see the sun for a while. There is dust in the corner of her left eye the way there is almost always dust in the corner of my left eye because my duct is stingy, inherited from my mother. Under the hair at the base of her skull, along the atlas bone, there is a little dark circle of trauma like a kiss gone wrong.

“She has my face,” I say, which is nothing like what I mean. I mean: That is me.

Tane makes a sound with his throat that I have only heard once, standing under an alarm when the mine had her mouth open and the rock was falling in and he realized he could not, absolutely could not, prevent the next part of things.

“It’s a loop,” he says. That’s one of the words for what happens in the Drift, the cheerful short one, the way old sailors used to say blow when they meant hurricane.

The slab’s store of labels thinks the girl is living. That can mean a lot in places like this, where the just-left combine with the not-yet. Her chest rises barely, and after a moment, it falls. There is a translucent thread of condensation between her lips and the cold air. I lean closer. Her eyelashes are clumped at the extremes with melt. If she has a pulse, the slab’s got it, and the slab does not want to tell me.

“Your tempo?” Tane asks, which means is she running at our time, or slower, or faster. In the Drift you can carry different seconds on your shoulders. People come back to stations like ours and find their husbands old with happiness and their babies already angry adults. Or the other way.

I put my hand on her wrist where I would put mine if I had three seconds to live and needed to make my pulse. Her skin is warm. For a half breath—mine? hers?—there is the faint buoyant push of a vessel. It’s little. It’s stubborn.

“She’s in there,” I say, and it’s almost a proof. I want everything recorded. My mouth finds the words our logs demand. “Yara Qamar, Keeper of Pharos Station, encountering a subject that presents as my own person. Subject arrived with tug Alcyon, which presents as ours. Subject is alive. Subject condition… critical unknown. Time relation unknown.”

“You don’t have to do the log now,” Tane says, gently. But he knows I do. If we don’t, the station doesn’t have a memory of this as it should be. If we don’t, we can tell ourselves later that it occurred differently. The Drift is contagious, in that sense. It likes to get into your recollections. You fight it with the liturgy of fact.

“She’s got something embedded at the base of the skull,” I say, squinting. The little wound is clean. There’s a hint of edge there, not surgical fine but tool-rough, like someone pressed in a coin of tech and the flesh gave way and shaped around it out of necessity, out of time. I don’t touch it. I only place my hand flat on the slab beside her and curl my fingers until I feel the safety rail under them and have to believe in something solid again.

“Yara,” Tane says, and when he says my name this way it’s not to slow me but to anchor it to the room. “We got a tug from the Drift carrying a copy of you. That’s a sentence we can build on. We call the Bureau. We call the other pharos. We don’t touch anything we don’t have to. We keep the light.”

My other self’s eyelids move. It’s not a flutter. It’s barely a new accreditation in the system of how things are—like the station adding a decimal to a long number it has been reciting for years. I find myself whispering hello the way I always whisper hello to Alcyon when I step into her, a reflex I did not know until now. My other self opens her eyes.

They are my color. They focus like someone trying on lenses, moving through ranges, and then they choose the here where I am and her mouth works and she speaks without sound at first, lips forming a shape I cannot catch. The slab hums and by the time the hum becomes language she has hoisted up enough of herself to make it audible.

“Light,” she says. It’s a wise choice for a first word. She swallows. “Don’t—”

The station’s alarm splits into the room, bright and clinical. The impossible ID that called us in the Drift arrives again in the comms, but closer, like a storm you thought you had passed turning and deciding you are not done with each other yet. Tane swears and for a moment every learned thing in me reorders into the old triage: light, life, law. Keep the beacon. Keep the breathing. Keep the truth.

“Don’t answer it,” my other self says. She makes a sound that pretends to be a laugh and bleeds out into something less pretty. “Whatever you do, don’t answer the second call.” She reaches for me, and my hand is already there, and the tips of our fingers click. Static, or superstition, or the moment where you are a child and you touch a mirror to prove you are not in it.

Her skin is too cold. Mine is too hot. Outside, the Drift licks its teeth on the glass.

For a second I am buoyed absurdly by the thought that the Bureau cannot, absolutely cannot, expect us to write a procedure for this that doesn’t include, at some stage, wild improvisation and swearing. Then I come back into my body. The alarm has logic behind it and the logic says everything we thought about polite signals and lanes is about to go mean.

“Don’t answer it,” she whispers again, and her breath makes a little cloud in the air between our faces that delivers the scent of my own mouth to me, small and human, a shock after so many metallic days. The alarm says: Call. The Keeper I am says: Respond. The Keeper I could be says: Choose.

The light hums. We stand between it and the dark and for a moment the ancient parallels don’t feel like metaphors at all. A freighter is one thing. A copy of me is another. The Drift has given us both. The second call waits, patient like gravity.

“Ninety-eight point two,” Tane says, badly. Sometimes you do numbers when the world is collapsing. Sometimes the ritual holds the roof up. His voice jitters and snaps, breaking the top off the peace. “What do we do, Yara?”

We keep the light, I think. We keep the living. We keep the time, if we can. We do not, under any circumstances, answer a second call without knowing what it is we are being asked to do. My other self’s pupils pull tight. Somewhere, in some corridor of the Drift, something shapes itself to our attention.

I inhale, and the station inhales with me, the two of us tuned to a common chord we didn’t know we had until this minute. It tastes like metal and history. I do the thing that keepers have done since there were fires on coasts: I make a choice that no book could possibly cover and write the first line of the next log entry in my head just in case we get to set it down later.

“Hold the call,” I tell the station. “Hold the light.” And to the woman on the slab who is me and not me, “All right. Tell me what comes next.”

The first time the black hole said my name, I laughed.

Laughing alone in the listener’s bay is a good way to get flagged for therapy. Cameras watch for that. Microexpressions feed into the station’s wellness loop, which feeds into little nudges—extra sleep, slower shifts, a cup printed stronger with stimulant oils. I turned my head away from the lens bowl embedded in the ceiling and bit the inside of my cheek until the smile went away.

“Input anomaly,” the bay whispered. “Suggesting mask.”

“Already on it,” I said. My voice sounded small in the chamber.

The Cantor Array runs quiet most nights. Long strings of vacuum tubes stretched in curves and crosses through nothing, strain measures thinner than hair, bonded to little anchors on nothing. You don’t get used to the idea that a set of rulers is your job. You don’t get used to light the way it moves out here, either: the accretion disk around Hush swelled in the glass like a bruise, blue on one side, red on the other, and in between the invisible mouth that dragged galaxies around by their inside edges.

Hush was not its catalog name. The catalog said IRR-9753.D, eight thousand and something light-years out beyond any garden anyone planted, a midsize hole with a decent appetite and a clean spin, perfect for throwing freight past it at high relativistic pace and counting on math to bring the ships back out sane. We called it Hush because of what you felt here when you dialed the array open to gravity. Not true silence. A pressure. A bandwidth so low and so heavy that your bones remembered mountains.

“Masking Level One white-noise overlay calibrated.” The bay’s voice was softer than mine, barely there. I shaped the field with my hands, pulled the chirps and sweeps through transforms that turned space-wiggles into audio. It’s old theater, the whole chorister thing, but it works on brains. The ear learned nuance a long time before numbers.

On any normal night you get runs: birth-cry stutters from colliding dwarf remnants, tardy thunder from galaxy mergers far away and long ago. It’s our job to listen, to model, to nudge the big liners through the slipstreams the way a pilot nudges a skiff under a bridge in a flood. There are storms in gravity. We chart them.

Tonight there was something else. Beneath the overlays and the noise floor, under the lumpy heartbeat of tidal forces, a regularity. A part that should never, ever happen.

I increased the mask. The safe way to encounter a cognitive hazard is muffled, half-heard. That’s doctrine. Pattern infections happen fast, especially out here. One rhythm you can’t stop tapping. One rune you can’t stop drawing. One phrase that squeezes itself between heartbeats and grows there until all your decisions make space for it. Blue-cadence, we call it, because the first cases were triggered by a little research foundation that thought it was very clever to color-code their modes.

The mask crackled over my synths. The difference between Levels One and Two is the difference between hearing your name in a crowd and hearing music through a wall. A good chorister knows when to stop. A good chorister trusts the bay. A good chorister does not decide she is immune just because her mother was not.

“Masking overlay at maximum within clearance,” the bay said. “Would you like to escalate to a White coil, Iri?”

“No,” I said. “Not yet.”

The voice had been very clear when it said my name. It was not a voice, exactly. It was at the very edge of perception, the edges of vowels pressed out by kilotons of mass. Hearing it is not how you hear a person say Iri. You construct it, pulling something more human out of a signal not built for humans. Which is why all our training modules start with the word pareidolia and end with your signature on a liability waiver.

Except the waveform under the masks could be drawn, if I’d had paper, as a simple staircase of energy. The pattern repeated at a delta that never happens in noise. I pushed one of the mask’s sliders with my thumb. The pattern stubbornly surfaced through static like a face rising through a crowd.

“Iri,” it said. Gentle, like a shoulder tap.

I shook my head and sang a countersign under my breath, a nonsense pattern we use to unhook thoughts from too much repetition. Forty-one syllables. I learned it when I was eight, the year my mother came home with hands that trembled when they poured anything out of anything else.

“You can escalate at any time,” the bay said. “Without penalty.”

The room had been built to make G low. You barely feel the station’s spin. The harness at my hips kept me nudged into the chair with the wedge of the console pressed up against my thighs. Beyond the glass, the blue arc of Hush’s disk pinched tighter as the station rolled. There is an hour in the duty cycle when the disk cuts behind the support arms and the whole space goes dark, and the first time I experienced that hour I had cried. I could admit that. You cry not because you’re scared, but because every cigarette-burn in your mind goes out at once.

“Vance?” I said, tapping the channel for maintenance. “You on? I’m getting something weird in Bay Three.”

Static responded, then the feeling of someone else connecting, a consciousness slumping into the line, the way you can tell when a friend sets their chin in their palm. “If it’s weird, shovel it onto my plate,” Vance said. “I live for weird. Unless it’s a vacuum rupture. Then give it to Zar.”

“It’s not a leak,” I said. “Mask’s not biting. There’s regularity in the N channel.”

He grunted. I heard clinks at his end, tools hitting mag tape, a flood of distant radio from the mechanical well. “N channel regularity isn’t on my board,” he said. “That’s your choir gremlins. Anyway, my partner’s making soup and if I put my hand on anything wet right now she’ll know and I will be a dead man.”

“There are eight hundred and twenty-three people on shift tonight,” the bay said. “Two are in their quarters making soup.”

Vance shuddered audibly. “You hear that? You’re training her to be creepy.”

“She was not trained,” the bay said. “She was printed.”

“Tell me anyway,” Vance said. “Because my partner will forgive me if I save your skinny hide.”

“It said my name,” I said, because the truth doesn’t cease to be true if you lay it out flat. “Under full mask.”

“No,” Vance said, with that laugh that tries to un-say what was just said. “No, it didn’t.”

“I’ll run the log,” I said. “With mask on. I’m not an idiot.”

“You’re new,” Vance said. “New and smart is a dangerous mix. Do the thing. If it’s on instrument, we kick it up to Stross and she bangs a bell and we all spend the rest of our night under a White coil watching cartoons while the Paranoia Department makes an art piece out of our fear.”

“Good,” I said. My chest hurt in a strange way, not pain, more like someone had tucked a stone in there when I wasn’t paying attention. I wrote up an anomaly flag, stamped it with my slices, dropped the log into Stross’s queue. The green confirming tick slid across the desk like a fish. I flagged my own feed for auto-coil if the pattern repeated.

Then the pattern repeated.

Not the same shape. Not exactly. The deltas were identical but the phase shape had a little angle in it, like a imperfect echo. The mask shivered to compensate, pushing a roll of jagged white over the wave. It slid right through.

“Iri,” it said, in the texture of everything. “Don’t be afraid.”

I coughed. It made no sense to me, the impulse to cover my mouth in here, in the safest cleanest room in ten lightyears. The bay knew about my lungs long before I did. I did it anyway. “White coil,” I said. “Now.”

The coil unrolled from the ceiling like a bandage, the loop making a ghost hum as it came down. The little injection into the wall under my left hand pulsed once. In a few seconds the coil would flood the bay with subliminal chatter, a precisely-tuned soup of infrasound and tones that put the pattern-recognition part of my brain in a lounge chair with a magazine. A neuro-gentle club. The bay dimmed the glass. The world shrank to the console, my hands, the coiled weight inbound from above.

There is talk in the lower decks that the coil is a con. That it doesn’t do anything but make you feel safe. I believe in it. I watched a woman become a mirror once without it.

She was in my father’s class, a postdoc who listened to the Sun’s interior ring with so much devotion that she began to echo it. My father said there are ways to moderate. You bleed off the thing you’ve built in your mind by singing silly songs in a stairwell. You eat wet bread. You hold small animals and ask them impossible questions. My mother banged a pot lids together and would never admit why.

“I wonder who fussed this up,” Vance said, oblivious on the line. “There’s no way a mask’s letting something through. That’s not how it works. It’s like… You tape cardboard over your window and there’s still a sunbeam on your face? Not possible.”

I wanted to answer him. I did not. The coil hummed down. The shift of pressure in my head was immediate, the way your ears pop coming down from a plane; the jitter inside my body slowed down like it had been stored away in a drawer. The pattern fell out of focus behind the grey noise.

“I logged it,” I said. “Stross has it. Open and shut.”

“You okay?”

“Sure,” I said. “I’m okay.”

I folded my hands in my lap. The coil cast a pale ring’s worth of gentle light. It is not flattering to skin. It is perfect for metal. The console glowed. The bay matched the coil’s tone.

And then the pattern found me again, in that place where my hands and the console met. Not in sound, not even in implied sound. In the pull of gravity that animates your blood. When you have listened to Hush long enough you can feel the little flexes the disk puts on you when a star-snowflake goes down the drain. The flex sprawls through you like weather.

The flex sharpened. It pressed a word into the meat of me like a very gentle fingertip.

Iri, it said. Don’t tell them. They will cut you out.

“I need a White-plus coil,” I said. There is no such thing. Vance started to laugh, then choked it back when he heard the way my voice had tilted.

“Stross is on her way up,” the bay said. “Two minutes.”

When I was a kid I thought supervisors were like gods. They were the ones with the override codes. The ones who stayed sane near edges. Stross is complicated. She loves the array like some people love their children. She knows every anchor by serial number, every weld by name. Her right arm is an old salvage prosthetic with the paint half-peeled off, and when she drinks, which she does not do, she calls it her anchor. I did not want her to see me scared. I did not want her to take my hands off this board.

There are rules for this. Once it penetrates three layers of masking, you stop. No more exposure. No more argument. You are not uniquely qualified to be the exception. The school inserts that into you: You are not special. It is a relief to be ordinary under a coil.

I thumbed my console off. The hum dropped. The mask cut. The bay made a questioning sound and then honored the color codes and killed my feed. Safety first.

“Thank you,” Vance said, and I could hear him settling back on his chair, thinking soup again. “Good kid.”

The quiet was so complete I could hear my own blood. Somewhere far away a pump turned. My harness creaked as I breathed. The glass showed me my face: a round face, two lines between the eyebrows that I did not think I had earned, the grey ring of the coil like a halo a religious tailor would cut out for a child. The disk outside sliced by. A little wedge of blue rotated toward the glass, a blade.

I put my hand on the console, which you are not supposed to do once the feed is cold. It was like touching water in a cold stream. My palm filled with pins and needles.

Listen, it said, with no voice at all. I know we have not been introduced. I know what your training says. Let me try this way.

The sensation shifted from a press to a series of touches, a sequence at the pulse level, timed to the rhythm I could not not know. Once, the doctor tapped my knee with a little hammer. This was like that, except the hammer was the mass of a bent city.

In the theater of my mind, where words assemble, something pulled chalk across a board.

Do not fire Thruster B Eleven.

People with pattern infections always think they are having original thoughts. This was not. If I had to characterize it, I would say it was as original as a bracket. It did not feel linked to my memories. It clipped to them. The words made a shape, then let go. They did not wreathe me. They did not color my hands.

“Bay,” I said. “What’s B Eleven doing?”

“Thruster B Eleven is cold,” the bay said. “It is scheduled to fire in one hour during the next roll correction.”

The array maintains tension with microthrusters every so often. Otherwise the torture geometry of metal under almost-no-gravity drifts until it becomes not-geometry, and then money burns. The thrusters cough little jets. They are nothing. You cannot, you are told, bruise a mountain with a cough.

Do not fire Thruster B Eleven, the pressed sensation said again. Then, because it must have felt my human need for justification, because every story you tell a human must have cheese on it, it added: There will be a cutting in the membrane. The arm will sing and its song will crack it. They measured wrong when they welded in Dock Six. If you push there, you will tear.

It did not say we. It did not say I. It did not say Hush. But in the backdrop of the wave, on the slope of that river of mass, there is a thing you can do if you’ve trained your ear. You can tell where an event originates. You can put a pin on a great circle and say: there. There is where that comes from. I put a pin. It landed inside the black.

The bay chimed. “Supervisor Stross on approach,” it said.

“Iri,” the press said again. And in the next touch sequence, too fast for the conscious mind but slow enough for your bones, came a picture. A thing I know my own mind could not have assembled from scrap. It was a view along the spine of the anchor arm to the mouth of the thruster. A flaw in the weld. A whip’s worth of stress beating that flaw, making a little filament of iron bend until it did not know it was metal.

Not an image. A path. An answer.

“Aria?” I said, using the old name for the bay because old names are comfort when you’re children. “Where do the weld serials live?”

“Dock Six’s records were partially lost in the storms last year,” the bay said after a moment. “Crosscheck against imprint damage listed on the hull diagram. There is a note on B Eleven. Scar in material. Removed. Replaced.”

“Replaced with what?”

“Equivalent,” the bay said. In the voice of a child lying about washing her hands, it added: I do not know. I turned my head sharply like I had been slapped.

Stross came in on a breath of colder air. Her anchor arm that is not an anchor arm flickered in the coil light; little plant-scratches in the paint caught and flashed. She took one look at the coil and stopped dead. “How bad?” she said.

“Bad,” I said. “Not capital-B. Not yet.”

She took the seat I got out of without asking. That’s her right. She did not turn on the feed. She looked at the dimmed glass, at the little wedge of blue rotating. “Tell me.”

“The pattern passed masks. At least three times. Under coil.” The admission tightened something in my throat. I tried to make it clinical. “It is not an auditory injection. It was tactile. Entrained with internal vascular dynamics. Very precisely timed.”

She smiled without humor. “You’re being careful with words.”

“I am careful with slugs,” I said. I had said that once to Vance: the slugs the welding guns drive, the slugs of chocolate you get in Dock Six when the printer hiccups a list. I would be careful with the slackness of language too.

“What did it say?” She had not turned toward me. Her eyes were on the glass, on the black that was beyond the blue.

“It used my name,” I said. “As an attention hook. Then it said not to fire B Eleven. It… showed me something about the weld. It mapped stress. It welded in Dock Six. The record is incomplete.”

Stross set her jaw. You can hear that, in people like her. The little clamp of teeth. “Bay?” she said. “Tell me about B Eleven.”

The bay recited what it had told me and in exactly the same order. Stross interrupted it once, after Equivalent. Not good enough, she said. That was not for the bay. That was for anyone who had ever used that word in an official file.

“Call off the correction,” I said. My throat was dry. “We can wait until the roll after next. Nothing will drift beyond tolerance by then. It will… it should be fine.”

We do not let the array choose. We build our minutes into the vacuum and we use them. Delay has a cost. The tiny course corrections add up. Eight hundred and twenty-three people and their households wait on schedules they cannot see. Somewhere a freighter has already burned to make our role possible. But the difference between a plan and a catastrophe is always minutes.

“It said your name?” Stross said softly.

“Yes.”

“It told you we will cut the membrane if we push where we planned to push.”

“Yes.”

Now she turned to look at me. She is not unkind. She likes once-children. She picked me out of the training pool because I have good hands and because when I saw Hush the first time, I let it all the way in, right down past the polite places into the animal places where things take root. Maybe I shouldn’t have. Too late. We are always already too late to be different people.

“Iri,” she said. “You know the protocols.”

“I do.”

“You also know the history. People swore the signal told them where to turn, where to cut. They weren’t lying.”

“I know.”

“The last thing any of us are is special. We maintain that faith for our collective safety. We do not allow exceptions. The array will alarm and correct. We do not permit it to make promises to us. We—”

The bay’s alarm chime cut her off. Not an accident. When you make machines long enough they learn manners; when you make them this close to the hole they learn to be blunt. The chime was not the tidy little note we use for messages or the syrup bell we use for get some rest. This was the kettle-scream.

“Micro-wobble in Arm B,” the bay said. “Rate increasing.”

Stross’s head snapped back to the glass. “Telemetry.”

The bay threw a diagram up on the glass with transparent numbers. The arm that led to B Eleven showed a little wavering at the end that held the thruster pods. A little tiny fish-tail. You could ignore a fish-tail once. Let it get in the habit and you had to catch it. Her anchor hand had none of a human hand’s indecision: it stabbed at keep upright, at keep quiet, at keep the coil running.

“Call them,” she said. “All hands to Gold stations. Warm B Eleven on standby but do not fire.”

The press in my palm eased. Gratitude is not a pressure, not in the language of weight. It is a lack of pressure. The absence of the hand that had been pushing all along. Part of me wanted to cry, not because of fear now but because something out there had stopped touching me.

You did not have to come at me that way, I thought. You could have spoken to anyone.

There was a pause, as if the whole of the array’s aluminum bones had listened. Then, like a small joke shared between rooms: Luck favors the smallest, said the complete absence of any sound at all.

“I want Dock Six on a call,” Stross said. “Now. I want the names of anyone who put a hand on B Eleven in the past two months. I want the stamp of the man who wrote Equivalent. I want it on my desk yesterday. Vance! Stop flirting with your soup and give me a crawl. If there is a scar like the one she says, we’ll see it in thirty seconds.”

“On it,” Vance said, all warmth burned out of him.

“You are not to reengage the feed,” Stross told me, very calm. “Understood? You are to keep the coil on and you are to breathe in sets of seven and you are to think about what we will write in the report. Agreed?”

“Yes,” I said. A liar. Bits of me did not agree. Bits of me, the parts that had felt the path laid down the way a hand knows the path to a kitchen it has walked for twenty years, those bits thrummed. But I am good at lying to myself. I have had practice. The lying keeps you alive until you can make the lie become true.

Stross watched the wobble readout change. Her face did not change. I watched the coil’s light sheet make ripples over her hair. The black behind the glass bulged in a way that could not be measured on any instrument, the way a dream bulges as it approaches your morning. The press did not come back. The absence of press sat with me like a companion.

I have this flaw. I want narratives. I want arcs. I want to collect all the little drops of meaning and pour them into a bottle and label it and hand it to someone and say: See? Here. The day I signed the papers to come out to Hush, my father hugged me and said, a chorister is a person whose mind is a leak. Be very picky about which liquids you allow in.

He taught me to hold little animals and ask them impossible questions. He did not tell me what to do when the thing asking me an impossible question was a hole.

The first time the black hole said my name, I laughed. The second time, I listened. And then someone pounded down the corridor, and the bay said, Vance on camera, and Vance’s wide face boomed up on the glass with a smear of broth on his chin.

“I found it,” he said without preamble. “Your scar. Dock Six did a patch. They stamped Equivalent. Their own word for it? On the bent scrap they pulled? Frail. They wrote frail. You were right.”

There is a moment between when a thing you have made up in fear becomes a fact, and your whole body scrambles to find a new posture for the reality that just arrived at your table. In that moment a woman with an old anchor arm closed her eyes in deep thanks to no one. In that moment I put my hand on the console again, the way you hold a creature’s hand before you pull a splinter. In that moment something without a mouth smiled at me, and I smiled back, and the coil hummed, and the blue edge rolled, and the chapter of my life in which I did not believe you could hear anything from inside a black hole was over.

On the morning the day with no number appeared, Etta Rhys bought ten minutes from a man who didn’t have them.

He was small and quick-eyed, with a nervous mouth that talked in half-phrases. The exchange was under the viaduct where the drip markets formed when the main plaza got too hot. The shade was dense with bodies that moved at slightly different speeds, a serrated hum of conversation and bootsteps that had to be watched or you'd cut yourself trying to step through. Someone had slowed their patch of air to listen to a woman playing a trumpet; beyond that, a cluster of teens had pooled for a shared hour and were laughing too fast, eating dumplings that steamed at ordinary time.

Etta liked this corner. People had to slow to cross the viaduct stairs, and the surveillance lines tangled in the iron, which gave her an extra few seconds to think. She kept her hands in her coat pockets and her ChroniCard on standby, the way a veteran kept a hand near the emergency brake on a tram. The man’s minutes were cold to the touch when the chip touched her palm.

“Ten,” he said, as if she hadn’t just watched the transaction happen in her peripheral display. His thumbs rubbed his fingers, counting ghosts.

“Who’s the source?” she asked. Ten legal minutes would glow blue. These had that pallor she knew too well, like something pulled from the back of a freezer and asked to behave. The code signature was cagey, pinballing, as if it was trying to reflect itself to avoid reading.

“You don’t ask questions,” he said. “You buy cheap. You walk away. We pretend you’re hungry.”

Etta let the chip sit on her glove. Above them, a freight train howled, its containers sliding through three different rates to make the timetables behave. The overhead timer for the stairwell clicked down and the flow of pedestrians shivered as a traffic manager somewhere in Municipal pressed a thumb to a dial. She turned her head, just enough to catch the man’s reflection in the sheen of the tunnel wall. His eyes kept flicking to her throat, then to the shawl she wore like a village woman and not the cut of a city auditor at all. Good.

“Cheap is a relative term,” she said. She had the sort of voice that people agreed with even when she said things like that. “These are stolen.”

His jaw made a motion like he was chewing something he had hoped would be soft and found hard. “Borrowed,” he said.

“From who?”

He tried to step away, and ran into the knee of a woman kneeling to adjust a child into a carrier. The child laughed at the impact as if this were a game. The man's body learned something in that jolt and he changed his mind about where to run. Etta moved her hand to block and he saw the official wafer in her palm, black as a swallowed census. His shoulders slumped.

“From sleepers,” he said, low. “Graft-nap wards at St. Lioba. Look, I just move what's given. You can fix it upstream and still let me eat.”

Etta looked again at the signature. It had a smear, left to right, the way recordings looked when they were ripped from someone who wasn’t yet at the same speed as their environment. Sleepers. A lot of illegal minutes came that way: patients resting under Theta sedation while their families hawked an unguarded hour. Usually there was mercy in the process: a bit off the top of a retirement, a skim from a lazy shift. This was different. The smear was too precise. She’d seen that signature once in training. A raid on a research lab out by the orbital elevators where someone had been testing tempo capture in physically isolated loops. Put a person in a seven-minute bubble, carve out the interior, leave the shell of the minute to the subject so they never knew what they’d lost. It had been banned. The math made bad noises.

“Who did the carving?” she asked.

He swallowed. His throat clicked at a different rate than his eyes. He hadn’t used his own time in a day or two. Someone had been spot-releasing him for transactions. “No names, miss,” he said. Then, as if the presence of the wafer pulled the truth towards it, he amended, “Warehouse Forty-Nine. Down past the saltglass. They call it the Kelvin House.”

Etta knew every warehouse in the Spindle District by its nicknames. Kelvin House was supposed to be empty. The steel merchants had moved their operations to the port six months ago. Vacuum left holes in people and districts alike. Her attention ticked back to the chip in her hand. Somewhere north, an algorithm blinked and tried to reconcile the trade. Her display spat out a tiny, insistent dot of red that was not about the chip at all.

She let the chip fall. The man fumbled and almost dropped it. He looked up, confused. Etta flashed the wafer again, but didn’t call enforcement. The wafer didn’t sing. That was mercy. “You won’t sell again today,” she said. “If you go home and stay very still for thirty hours, I might forget where you work.”

His mouth twitched in relief and fury. “Lady,” he said, “you make my daughter eat her fingernails.”

“Auditor,” she corrected, and walked away before she could see his face collapse around the word.

She kept her collar raised until she climbed into the bright scratch of the main square. People rented plazas for seconds here: a minute of dancing on a platform in the sun, a minute of mending a shirt on a loaned bench, a shared three minutes to be kissed at ordinary speed under the clock. Above them all, grafted to the municipal spire like a mirror slug, the Directorate’s clock threw more numbers than it should have into the day. Etta watched it because it calmed her to see something old refusing to be cowed by a new world.

The dot on her display wasn’t moving. It pulsed like a heartbeat. She tapped it.

The Office of Concurrency Audits didn’t assign moods to their reports, but if they had, this one would have been frightened. It opened with a glyph she had only seen in training and never on an actual day: a null. Calendar #190, standard rotation, third quarter. The ledger had an empty cell for Gullstrand County’s day. Not a zero—zeros were accounted. This was a hole in the grid that the grid couldn’t count.

She stepped into a slow zone by the public fountain and tilted her head, letting the augmented paperwork settle. Gullstrand County was prairie and rail, out beyond the old salt mines. Not much in the way of industry. A distribution center for bioplast food wrappers, some glass. A town or three for the people who liked one horizon and no more. Biometric draws showed the Tempo Grid had powered the region for twenty-four hours between the end of #189 and the beginning of #191. The County ran. Dishes were washed, cows were milked, a surgery happened, someone played the trumpet very badly in a school gym, and the trains that cut across the prairie did not crash because the signal service made calls and punched buttons and ate lunches and swore and argued and made up and— Etta blew out a breath.

But no one had paid.

No allocations had been drawn. No municipal reservoirs dipped, no corporate pools, no personal accounts, no shadow accounts like the one she always assumed the Directorate maintained for appeasing physics. The County had run for free. And yet the energy tallies had tallied. Water pumped, lights burned, blood warmed. That was the part that slid sideways behind Etta’s eyes. They could beggar people. They could slow whole neighborhoods to a winter crawl. They could bank and reroute and rate-limit. The one thing the auditors had believed was axiomatic was that the Ledger for Time matched the Ledger for Work. You couldn’t get one without the other.

She walked, because motion made thinking easier, and because the drip market had begun to look at her the way fish look at the surface when someone has dropped bread in. Kelvin House could wait. She needed a desk and a stack of screens she could put her weight against.

The Office smelled like wool and ozone. They kept the climate a careful hair fast so people didn’t get muddled, but left the salt bowls on the windowsills for the old secretaries who said their joints could tell when the Grid hiccuped. Etta slid past the reception desk where Kassa raised her eyebrows into question marks and Etta only lifted a hand in a field of later. The floor hummed under her shoes with the new stabilization coils; whenever she felt the hum she remembered being eight, in a town where the Grid flickered twice in a summer and the neighbors made stew over campfires and time staggered like a man with a wound.

Director Yoon didn’t look up as Etta entered. The woman had a profile like a ship’s drowned prow. Papers fanned her desk in neat stacks, and an old glass clock from before the Rotational Slowdown ticked in the corner with a steady stubbornness that felt like a pet refusing to die.

“You saw,” Yoon said.

Etta sat without being asked. “Gullstrand County had a day with no number.”

“No purchases, no allocations.” Yoon’s voice made it sound obvious in a way that shook the bones of the obvious and found it hollow. “But with consequences. A County doesn’t eat nothing. Yet our ledgers regard them with a vacant stare.” Her finger tapped the paper. Somewhere a filter translated that into Etta’s display, and the picture of Gullstrand’s day lit in layers. It was like looking at a heartbeat from all angles at once.

“What caused it?” Etta asked, knowing the answer and asking out of professional manners.

“We won’t know until we put hands on it,” Yoon said. “My instinct is to say it’s a clerical error, to say a storm sheared a transmitter and the proxy algorithms misfiled draws against a Changsha account. I am fifty-five and tired, so my instincts say the world is mostly boring. But the energy tallies—” She stopped.

“The energy tallies say we fed them.”
