“Everyone else will say we have a theft on our hands, on our throats. My colleagues at the Directorate view time as coins in a jar. Someone might reach in and take. But you know where I came up. On the ships.” She waved a hand at some non-existent porthole. “Nothing goes anywhere by itself. If a day ran, a day came from somewhere. The question we must answer before anyone else asks is where from.”

Etta rubbed her forefinger and thumb together, an old habit, a way to find where the edges were. “You want me to go.”

“I want you to go and do what auditors do best,” Yoon said. “Ask questions that make good people hate you. And another thing.” She hesitated. Etta had not seen that in Yoon before. “The preliminary psychological sweeps returned something I do not like.”

Etta had to smile. “You like very little about psychological sweeps.”

Yoon grimaced back. “True. But this I like less. We sampled seventy residents on public nets. Twenty-two report that they remember a day that no one else does. They are annoyed in the usual ways about the usury of the Directorate, but they are not surprised in the way we would expect if the Grid had brought them back from a stall. Eleven report a specific intrusion.”

“A burglary?” Etta asked, thinking of Kelvin House, thinking it would be neat if the world put its mysteries in one box at a time.

“A woman came to their house,” Yoon said softly. “Each describes her differently, but the through-line is a woman in her thirties, wearing a gray shawl like a village woman, hair half pinned, and her left shoe squeaks.”

Etta looked at her own shoes. They were good ones, with the City’s badge stitched in the insole. She had a shawl; she wore it when she went to the drip markets. She lifted her left foot, and pressed. The shoe squeaked. The tiny sound hung between them, absurd as a gull in an office.

“And?” she asked, keeping her voice level.

“And two of the respondents used your name,” Yoon said. “Etta. And one wrote a note during the day that we cannot find in our day. The note remained. It has your signature. Very neat. I had my analysts swear they did not falsify to curry favor. They swore a lot.”

The room’s hum seemed suddenly too close to Etta’s nerves. She had the sensation she sometimes had in old houses when she had to mount a staircase that sagged in the middle and promised to drop away. “That’s not possible,” she said. It sounded inadequate.

“No,” Yoon said. “It isn’t. Go put your hand through it and tell me what it is. Take field status. Leave your chip; take a recorder. Use the old tricks. If you see a Kelvin House on your way, do not be lured. This may be unrelated, or related only in the nest of things that is the City.”

Etta could not decide whether she was relieved or annoyed that Kelvin House had become a footnote. “Who else knows?”

“Three in this office. One at the Directorate. I told him it was a clerical error and did not let him finish saying the word conspiracy. He is allergic to complexity and listens to himself when he sneezes.” Yoon’s mouth tightened. “You leave in an hour.”

Etta stood. There were three routes to Gullstrand; all required patience with trains. Once, when she was younger and brave in a way that made her bones cold to recollect, she had hired a spinner-driver out of the Slough and held on to the frame while the road rippled like a rumor beneath them. She would take the train now. She didn’t need to get there fast so much as arrive threaded to the grid.

On the way out, Kassa reached for her sleeve. “They’re saying ghouls out there,” Kassa murmured, always happiest when a situation admitted a ghost story. Her hair was a watercolor of red that day. “People who slip through and take your hours while you sleep. I told them we use machines for that now.”

“What would a ghoul do with hours?” Etta asked.

Kassa leaned on her elbows. “Garden,” she said. Then sobered. “Be gentle. The last time someone did an audit of a prairie county, three families applied to sell all their hours to the State and leave. The forms are in triplicate and depressing.”

“I’m always gentle,” Etta said.

“You have elbows like a logic problem.”

Etta smiled despite the sick knot in her stomach. “I’ll try not to bruise anyone with them.”

The train out of the city ran along the old river and then across it, a silver insect that forgot to fear water. The car was half full, people with the look of time in their pockets or the hunger to be near those who did. A woman in a quilted coat dozed with her hands in fingerless gloves wrapped around a basket of jars that flashed with something slow inside. Two children played a game with cards that changed suits depending on how fast you flicked them. Etta sat facing backwards, the way she always preferred, so that the present poured towards her and the past retreated, orderly.

She let the city spool itself away. The oversized clocks shrank. The neighborhoods turned into boxes with small stories inside. She could map them the way an avid reader maps a beloved series. There was the block where the butcher sped his window to keep the sausages from attracting flies. There the corner where the old woman who ran a pawn stall kept time on low to punish browsers who treated her like a museum. And the gates, where time thickened for a minute to preempt arguments. She watched until the buildings surrendered to winter-brown fields and the pitches of the train’s stabilizers became the default. Behind her, a man argued softly into his cuff with someone who did not plan. The conductor moved up the aisle, cheeks pink, rubber soles squeaking. Etta flinched at the sound.

It should not be possible for a day to tuck itself, unbought, into the precise and petty machine of their world. During the Stall, when the world had learned that the sun could stretch an afternoon to an ache if you asked it with massive, careful machines, the old astronomers had pleaded to be left alone. Time had been a thing they measured. City men and women came with graphs and sweet words and reorganized everything. The Grid hummed, and it made life better at first. Firefighters could burn a building out of its own fire while the rest of the block watched, slow. Surgeons could extend seven minutes into a half hour without asking any god to turn the earth back. But it had created debts. Debts had invented the Directorate. And people like Etta had acquired jobs that put them in rooms with tired women and glass clocks and told them to weigh the unweighable.

She thought of Yoon’s face when she’d said Etta’s name in the mouths of strangers. There was a part of her that wanted to laugh it off. Small towns were full of women with gray shawls. The grid played tricks on shoes. And yet. There was the wafer in Etta’s coat pocket, the one with the city seal that could quiet a crowd like cold rain. It stung her side the way guilt stings. She pressed her palm to it until it warmed.

The land flattened. The horizon grew unashamed. Here and there, in low hollows, the saltglass lay like ponds. In summer the kids came from the cities with hammers and carved sculptures that flowed slowly all winter. The saltglass was what the first grid techs had blown when they flooded the fields with uncalibrated time. It hung in the soil’s memory like a bad habit. Etta had been fifteen the first time she saw one. She’d thought they were frozen lakes. Then she’d seen a dragonfly beating against its own moment at the center, and she had backed away quickly, like from a sleeping dog.

The Gullstrand station stood alone, a barn-shaped building with old painted advertisements on one side for the sort of nostalgic product no longer made. A girl with hair the color of dried wheat sold coffee pour-over style that tasted of tin and patience. Etta shouldered her bag and stepped down onto the platform, which hummed the same way as the city's floors. It sounded wrong under this much sky.

He was waiting for her. He had a sheriff's badge turned into a paperweight and a smile that said he had been told city auditors were vipers, and that he would hold still and let it bite because that meant it had seen him, and a man liked to be seen. He held out his hand.

“Arlo Makepeace,” he said. “Gullstrand Public Safety. We don’t usually rate visits.”

Etta took the hand. It was big, warm, human. “Etta Rhys. Office of Concurrency Audits. You rated a day.”

He lifted his shoulders in a motion that was not a shrug so much as an adjustment of weight. “We did. Or didn’t, depending on who I’m listening to. You want a ride?”

“I want to see the edge,” she said. “Where your day begins.”

He didn’t pretend not to know what she meant. He gestured to a battered truck whose interior smelled like hay and engine and something sweet like apples. The dash held three photographs of a child growing, and a sprig of dried prairie grass hung from the rearview mirror like a bit of folk magic. He drove without music. People here were used to hearing the day.

“You’ll get your Bureau story,” he said finally, as the truck rolled toward the low spine of the town. “We had two dawns. My mother always told me not to look a thing like that in the eye. The first was usual. The second was pale, like paper.”

“Two dawns,” Etta said, binding her voice to the cadence of his so he’d keep talking.

“A handful of people slept right through,” he said. “A handful woke up hungry like you wouldn’t believe. Everyone else remembered it in that way that makes you doubt your teeth. Folks noticed the clocks of course. The school got a call from a Directorate subroutine that told them to hold morning classes, and Ms. Carver wrote it down and then the paper it was on burned lemon-right at the edges and went away and she told us and we made her tea and said it was the wind. You know.” He smiled, then let it go.

“What about the edges,” Etta asked again, softer.

He took a right, and then a left, and the town thinned to pasture. The sky sat heavy and patient. Ahead, a fence cut the flat in a line that rippled in places as if heat were playing tricks. Arlo stopped the truck fifty meters from the fence. He swallowed.

“There,” he said. “We put up a fence because Chief Caro said people were going to start cutting pieces to bring home. It’s wrong to bring home pieces of something you don’t understand, I told her.” He flexed his hands on the steering wheel. “She said people do that all the time.”

Etta got out. The fence was chain-link, with ribbons tied in one place as if someone had held a festival here. Beyond it, nothing had changed, and everything had. The grass was a little greener, but it was the wrong green: too literal, like paint in a child’s box. The clouds had the slow rolls of summer cumulus even though it was late autumn. And at knee height, an invisible line lay in the air where the light bent, so soft that if you looked at it direct you would miss it. If she turned her head and watched with the meat of her eyes instead of the lenses, she could see a series of tiny flickers, like heat bugs in a field at dusk, but colder, less convinced.

She turned on her recorder. It whispered awake. The sound of the prairie didn’t change.

She took a step toward the line and Arlo made a noise and then swallowed it because men here swallowed things like that. She looked back. “I won’t break it,” she said.

“You don’t know that,” he said, reasonable. A gust of wind moved his hair. He was not a man who would speed up his backyard for anything. That made him admirable or doomed.

“I don’t know anything,” she said, more honest than she meant. She stepped.

The world did not lurch. There was no friendly cinema trick of frames jittering and then re-aligning. Her body did one brief complicated adjustment that made her think, for no reason and for a second only, of falling out of a tree as a child and finding midair.

Her ChroniCard buzzed her wrist. A line of text appeared that made the skin of her arms go to sand: Account credited +1d.

She stared. The card had never given before.

The air smelled different. The almanac smell of prairie was the same, but there was a sweetness under it—old paper, or apples left too long in sun. The sky had the same patient hills of cloud. But the low hum she had learned to associate with a city floor was missing; she realized she had been hearing it in the soil since stepping off the train. Here there was only the hum of living things and the very faint whisper of the recorder.

Something clicked.

She turned her head. Thirteen cows chewed and looked at her with the sort of calm that either meant idiots or saints. A girl with a dog watched from a hundred yards away. The dog’s ears saw her before the rest of him did; he dropped and crawled, tail flicking. The girl steadied him with a hand like a punctuation mark. And there, at the base of the fence where others had tied ribbons, someone had tucked a little thing of glass into the wire. It was the size of a plum, clear as clean ice. Inside, something was caught like a fly in amber. Not a fly. Etta leaned closer. The shape was roughly insect, but with too many angles. It pulled at her like the curiosity of a cut.

Arlo exhaled a swear under his breath. “They keep leaving those,” he said. “We tried to collect them. They crack if you carry them outside the line. My grandmother used to say there were birds that lived in winter all year. I thought she was being poetic. Now I think maybe she was an auditor for a day and didn’t know the word for it.”

Etta didn’t answer. The thing in the glass seemed to move, but only if she wasn't looking. Its wings had veining that was familiar and not. If a carpenter bee tried to imitate a paperclip and then grew confused somewhere in the middle. The glass was warm. When she put her palm near it, her ChroniCard pulsed again like a finger tapping a table.

“You see it?” Arlo asked, voice a little hoarse.

“I see it,” Etta said. She thought of Yoon’s note. A woman with a shawl and a squeak. Someone had been here. The note. She straightened and scanned the fence posts. On one, under a ribbon of blue, a scrap of paper had been glued with sugar-water and patience and an impulse that said, this will matter. The writing was neat. The letters had the schoolmaster’s corrections still in their bones. Her handwriting.

Do not stand here long, it said. If you stand long, you will remember standing. Once is enough.

Her mouth went dry. She could feel her tongue make room for words and then refuse to issue them.

“Miss Rhys?” Arlo asked. “You’re white as cheap bread.”

Etta folded the paper. It resisted, as if the air wanted to keep it flat. She put it in the hidden pocket sewn inside her coat and felt wrong, like a thief. “We’re going to need to talk to your Ms. Carver,” she said. “And anyone who saw a woman with an unfortunate squeak.”

“I can take you to the school,” Arlo said. “After you tell me what it is.”

Etta looked at the line where the light bent. She thought of the signature on the stolen minutes in the drip market, the smear of a person half-present while someone else dipped a ladle. She thought of the feeling she’d had stepping over. She thought of an old story about a river you could only cross once, and all the men who argued with the story because they wanted to be the one who proved it wrong. She thought of the card in her wrist suddenly fat with a day she had not earned.

“I think,” she said, choosing the bald line that auditors were taught to use when they should lie but the truth was tidier, “that your County borrowed a day from a place that did not know it could lend.”

“From where?” Arlo asked.

Etta opened her mouth and all the possible answers crowded it: from us, from a future, from a past, from the debt we pretend is a river and not a lake. The recorder in her pocket whispered, a faint feedback, and in that whisper, for the length of a breath and no longer, she heard her own voice, a little older and flatter, and saying her own name.

“From me,” she said. Then shook her head. “From somewhere I am going to have to stand in the wrong place to see. Let’s go to the school.”

The garden was supposed to die a little each day; that was the only way to keep it alive.

Isola Venn knelt among the glasswork branches and watched a leaf make up its mind. It looked like frost, like the delicate fern of ice that would climb a window back when windows were still things that opened to weather, but this was no winter’s flourish. The leaf had a long petiole of spun diamond lattice and a blade as thin as a thought, and the pattern it wove as it formed was the sum of a trillion collisions she would never see. It hesitated at a fork—one branching would give rise to a spiral that trapped a gram of low-temperature motion in its lanes; the other would shunt a whisper of order out of the pond and back up the conduit to the black wires and the reservoir beyond. Isola touched it with a filamented glove and the leaf's veins brightened, taking the path her fingers argued for.

“No greed today,” she told the tree. The voice in her helmet fed the words back to her forehead with a tiny latency that was half of the distance to the reservoir and back. “You hoard and you shatter. Breathe.”

The tree, of course, did not hear her. The tree was a scaffold for gradients and nothing else. The hearing was for her.

She sat back on her heels and scanned the bed. Frond, bud, vein, knot—so many points of decision and she was only one pair of hands. Her console wove the flow mapping in pale light between the branches, running predictive heat-death on a billion outcomes, but the console’s utility was always after the fact. Algorithms could catch catastrophe and explain it, but they were never any good at asking for beauty.

Above her, the sky was the color of old slate, uniform, eternal, and unbroken by stars. The garden’s bubble held a faint haze where the manufactured gradient pulled at the outer dark, a bruised ring that shivered when a conduit carried too much load. She could taste the strain in the air when she pulled her helmet open, a metallic bitterness that caught on the back of her tongue. Somewhere under her boots, a pump older than any of her parts drew from the last well in this quadrant of thin existence—a black hole in a cage, a whisper of a downflow from a cosmic string, the physics manuals called it several names—and from that well the garden drank.

She moved on, looping the coil of her tuning comb over her shoulder, passing the pond where the time-lilies were sleeping under the dark glass. They flowered once every four days, white cups that unfurled their matte petals and caught a thickness of motion in them that one could scoop with careful hands and carry to someone with money and an appetite. People sent orders in from centuries away, slow packets on cold ships: I will pay eleven hours out of my future if you will ship me back eight that smell like rain. I will give a year if I can hold a day that hurts less. Their letters came to her encrypted and weightless; when the ships made the long arc back, thick with time wrapped in thin metal, she was always somewhere else. The trade was handled by the Registrar in the vault stations. She was the world-end gardener; she was a licensed thief of forgetfulness. The money funded her pumps and the occasional visit from a human voice.

“Flux,” said the console at her waist, making it a word instead of a graph. “Seven milli-Kelvins above plan in Sector C3.”

She paused mid-step. “Conduit?”

“Within operating margins.”

“Edge?”

“Stable.”

“Leak?”

“No leak.”

She frowned and reached out with her comb, touching the air and listening. The comb was a harp of microwires and microgravimetric sensors. In the hands of the archivist who had trained her, it had been something like a musical instrument; in hers it was more a stethoscope. The pitch of the space between the trees was a shade brighter near the pond, a note fattier and warmer. She thought of belly heat, of ovens. Her stomach twitched.

She ghosted the pond’s rim and saw at once that it was not the lilies and not the pond. It was the soil, if one could call that latticework substrate soil at the end of time. A small rise had swelled up near the third anchor stone, ribs of condensed probability, a knot of interference lines tightened upon itself like thread. At its center, something lay suspended, a blur in the air like a heat ripple. The ripple was small, not much larger than both of her fists, and it was wrong.

Things did not condense here. The gradient did not thicken into... objects. Not on its own. That was how you got runaway crystals, devouring heat, collapsing your bubble into a brittle sculpture that would look very beautiful for the ten seconds of cold it would be allowed before it shattered beyond measure. That was how you lost your license and your pumps and your life in one drift of glitter.

“C3 variance,” the console said, more softly this time.

“I see it,” Isola murmured. She laid the comb down on the anchor stone and took out the flux knife. It was not a knife; it had no edge. It was a teardrop of magnetotactic material keyed to the pulse of the garden, and if you moved it swiftly through a flow, it made seams. She’d cut seeding crystals with it before. She’d shaved runaway beads from the underside of the lily disks, had cut her own hair with it for lack of a better tool. She did not remember a time when she had owned more than seven objects that were hers alone.

The ripple pulsed. She swore and flipped the knife to its obverse. She could starve it. The purse-string filaments tense in her glove bit her fingers in acknowledgment.

She closed her helmet. “Registrar, this is Isola Venn at Palinode, Orchard 3b. I have a spontaneous aggregation in—” She checked the garden grid. “—Sector C3 near the lilies. Unscheduled, unseeded. I’m stabilizing and request a protocol check.”

Static. Then the whisper-click of the link settling into a higher-power channel. Then, “Palinode registered. Registrar listening. Aggregation? Send imagery.”

They did not greet each other. They had never met, whoever sat in the vault station, and in their displacement of time it was entirely possible that the registrar she knew in her ear had died a thousand years ago and the voice was a simulation with good taste. She shaped the comb’s image capture and sent what it saw.

A pause. “I have a funhouse,” said the Registrar dryly. “Send spectrum.”

Isola flicked the comb through the ripple and tuned her filters. The taste in her mouth grew stronger. The comb’s lines went from pale, to bright, to saturated, until the little blur at the center stopped being a blur and became a thing with a boundary. It was smooth-surfaced and seed-shaped, not entirely symmetric, ridged like a fingerprint. Its outer layers were cooled to the pond’s standard measure, but something inside it was giving off noise. Not heat, exactly—noise. Something that did not belong.

“Protocol nine,” said the Registrar. The voice had acquired a layer of interest. “Whatever it is, it’s an object. That’s a breach nucleus. You need to quench.”

“You want me to freeze it or starve it out?”

“Either. Both. We will likely lose lily yield for two cycles. Which is better than losing the garden.”

Isola’s hands did not move. Good practice was to obey the voice that paid for the pumps, the fuel, the maintenance bots and the food-things that came in a pack smelling of nothing. Good practice was to cut, to starve, to burn. She had given the lilies entire nights of thickened motion and the lilies had given her eight rich hours in a jar that smelled like chalk dust and sunburnt wood; she had sent those hours to someone whose child had lost a practice device in an accident. She had cut her palm with the flux knife and bled red as the old myths said and the pump had pulled her blood into the garden and the garden, obligate thief, had enlisted it into a pathway of repair. It was easier, in general, to let the instructions do your ethics.

She moved the knife.

The ripple pulsed again. She went to stare into it with her helmet a hand’s breadth away. The seed-shape hung in air. Within, in the noise, a pattern stuttered and settled, stuttered and settled, looking for a rhythm like a thing that has become aware of its own edges. Isola felt the edge of a memory join that noise. It was unrequested and unwelcome and so clean it was painful: a field where grass was not engineered, not laid in arrays, but grew long by accident; a smell of green; a sequence of the sky with clouds in it. A shadow passed over her face in the memory and the memory had a heartbeat.

She jerked backward so fast she cracked her helmet on the anchor stone. The yard-long living crease in the anchor stone’s matrix tightened and closed the crack before it finished opening. She found herself breathing hard into a stale tank.

“Palinode?” the Registrar asked after a slice of time it took to cross two voids and back. “Report.”

“It—” Isola looked down at the seed. “Echo. I touched it and it threw me a childhood that I did not have.”

“Describe.”

“Grass, smell, clouds.”

“Not physical description,” the voice said, as patient as a book. “Spectrum.”

Isola steadied herself and pushed the comb back in. The thing’s noise was not thermal and not purely entropic either. It had a signature that the comb translated as a slow whine, like the sound old cables made in wind. The pattern in the noise that she had thought was heartbeat was in fact periodic, roughly at one-sixty to one-ninety per minute, but variable in a way that biological things were variable. The seed had a pulse.

“Registrar,” she said slowly, “I am going to put hands on it.”

Silence.

“Palinode,” the Registrar said, very carefully. “Why?”

“I think I know what it is.”

“Say it.”

“A pocket,” Isola said, and her mouth went dry in her helmet. “A pocket from before. Not from a vault, not a crystal. Not cut. A true one. Somebody wrapped a thing that was alive in a knot and threw it forward. They threw it to a gradient. They threw it to a gardener, of all people. They threw it to me.”

The voice did not answer. She imagined someone in a well-lit room, hand over the mic, mouths moving out of sound.

“How likely is that,” said the Registrar eventually, and did not make it a question.

“Not,” Isola said, and that was true. “Not at all.”

“Quench. We will dispatch an inspector. Do not breach the nucleus. Do not touch—”

Isola closed the channel. It would reopen on priority, and there would be penalty shunts on her allotment for doing it, but there were worse fines to pay than credits. Her fingers had learned to move while the voice spoke. They had rarely betrayed her as thoroughly as they did then.

She put her palm on the seed.

The pain was not heat-pain. It was an alignment and a misalignment all at once, like setting a miscounted bone. The seed adjusted itself around the shape of her lifeline. She felt her pulse go into it and the thing’s pulse come back. Her glove sequenced its own protective layers, trying to float her skin free of contact; the seed ignored the glove’s protests the way roots ignore stone.

The first memory was the grass and the sky again, all angles, all brightness. The second was a hand on her hand, smaller than here, warmth with a particular weight. The third was a taste of salt in wind. The fourth was a shape unrelated to any sense—an orientation in a manifold Isola did not know how to hold in her head, as if someone had rotated the world and she had seen briefly that it had pivots in directions she never had words for. That sight was terrifying, and afterward everything looked thin.

“Stop that,” she whispered to herself, to the seed. “Stop.” To stop was to live, sometimes. Her teacher had told her that once, kneeling in another orchard in another bubble, drawing a curve of frost away from one of the Archivates’ crystal spines. “We do not re-enact. We do not make. We hold.”

She took her hand away and sat with her elbows on her knees and her gloves pressed against the visor of her helmet. Right outside the shield, a bubble of impossible warmth beat like a heart. Her console waited for her to ask it for a number. She did not.

It occurred to her that the thing inside the seed might be a lie. She had caught lures before. The universe at the end had predators too, if one was inclined to call them that: accumulations that were hungry for gradient, that had learned to mimic the shapes that stabilized them. The archivists’ manual had sketches of their trickery, had admonished them to call things what they were. But the manual had never told her what to say about the smell of green.

She stood and keyed her comb to cut. The comb sang a culling note up the spectrum. She set the flux knife to starve, to pinch the outflow from the reservoir until the garden would struggle, until the lilies would die for a cycle, until the tree leaves would choose the branch that returned the order to the world. She raised the knife, as heavy as the fate of this tiny place could make a tool out of a toy, and brought it down in a line a hand’s breadth from the seed. The air shrieked. Flows rarified. The seed did not dim.

Instead it did a small thing. It rolled. It tipped itself, like a bird’s egg struck by breath, and came to rest against the side of the anchor stone. It left a damp little circle of reality in the air where it had been. She did not know if it had used her gradient to move or if it had taken pity on her indecision.

“Do not,” she said to it, and felt foolish.

Something moved in the distance. She looked up. Past the tree’s fingers and the pond’s black skin, at the far edge of the bubble, the ring-light thinned and tore. She had starved the edge with her rashness, had pulled too much to the center in too little time, and the edge was going to come in, and any little thing without purchase would be scraped. The bubble would not collapse, but it would contract. The lilies would be safe under the pond; the trees had roots in good anchors; she had built the anchors into the stone with an obsessive’s care. The thing with no place in any design would be cast out into the old dark and make a very brief brightness there and then be nothing, and she would have to tell the Registrar that she had thought it was a child and then had killed it like a weed.

She put down the knife and ran.

It was a graceless run. Her boots had traction only where anchors were pegged, for the substrate’s surface was a mercy to nothing that put weight on it. She slid twice and pulled her knee on the spar of a root. There was no useful friction in the world anymore; everything was too close to too smooth. The bubble’s edge came in like a sigh, the bruise darkening and swelling. The pressure change nipped her ears through her seals. Her breath sounded like an animal she could not place.

She reached the seed and scooped. It was too hot for her gloves to want it, but she took it anyway. It lay in her palms and settled into the cup she made like it had done that a thousand times. She loped toward the one place in all the garden where a thing could hide from contraction.

The lily pond was a disk of vitrified substrate, its lip painstakingly burned by a person who, for a week and three days early in her tenure, had forgotten to sleep and had cut by hand because cutting by code felt too neat to be true. The pond’s skin looked black because it was deeper than it had any right to be. It kept that depth by exchanging a steady breath with the reservoir; it was a door, a little one. She skidded on the lip, found her balance by putting a hand, palm-down and bare, onto the hot glass—she would regret that later—and tucked the seed under her arm. With the other hand she reached into the pond up to her elbow and felt the thick motion in it muscle her bones. The seed jammed hard into her ribs, then into the sticky material of her suit as it seized. For a moment she was a hinge. Then she shoved, and the pond took.

The seed slid out of her grip and into the dark. The pond’s surface trembled and smoothed. The bubble’s edge rebounded. The trees whispered. She stood motionless with her arm in the pond until its ache told her where her skin ended and the world began again.

She reeled back and sat at the pond’s edge. Her gloves steamed. The place where she had laid her palm on the pond to steady herself had bubbled. In a few hours it would heal as if nothing had happened at all.

The channel opened by itself with a throatless little click.

“Palinode,” said the Registrar. “You dropped your link with a breach alert on metrics. A contraction shows on our mirror. Your edge is intact. You will report in detail.”

Isola considered lying. She considered a grand defense of intuition. She considered the screaming that would happen and the fines she would pay and the fact that there were no fines in this world that would matter more than the pump. She considered the smell of green.

“I stabilized a nucleus with a temporary submersion,” she said, choosing words the way she picked leaves to fall. “It was an aggregation that evidences interior patterning. I did not quench it. I am holding it in Medication One.”

“Medication One is for thermal noise.”

“And yet,” Isola said quietly.

“It will crack your gradient. The intrusion will hazard your yield and possibly the archive.” The voice was close to what in any other time would be anger. “This is not a home for your whims.”

“It was not a whim.”

“Names,” said the Registrar, because if every conversation came back to the human, sometimes the only way to keep them from drowning in their feelings was to give them forms.

“Palinode, Orchard 3b, Sector C3, lily pond, Medication One,” Isola said, half to the voice and half to the garden, to enter the act into the fabric that kept it alive. “Incident at—” She glanced at her grid. “—local tick 9:10:37. Intervention recorded.”

There was a long pause. When the Registrar spoke, the voice had changed. “An inspector is en route,” they said. “Estimated arrival in two weeks at your rate. We will keep a pull on you. Do you hear me? Do not feed it. Do not talk to it. Do not give it names. Do you hear me?”

“I hear you,” said Isola.

“Do not think you are the first to hope,” said the voice, almost tender now.

The channel cut. The gradient settled into a new slow rhythm, as if the garden were sleeping a little lighter. Isola took off her helmet. The air bit her eyes. The pond stared up at her with its blank face as the lilies stirred and resettled under their covers.

She could go and sit under the glass tree and take out the reed flute she had made with the flux knife and push air through it until the comb’s sensors mistook the vibrations for a collapse and scolded her. She could drink a powder that would call itself tea and taste like time left too long on the coil. She could be obedient the way her hands had not been and go around the bubble and check the anchors and sing to the leaves because it made no difference and it made all the difference. She could do the work, which would mean that she would be still.

Instead she lay on her stomach and slid her arm into the pond again, deeper this time, to the wrist, to the elbow, to the upper arm, until her cheeks puddled on the lip and the skin of her chest squealed against the glass where it had bubbled. She reached through the thickness as if through honey and there, under her hand, found the seed.

It did not move. It had let itself be taken into the pond the way a tired creature lets itself be carried. Around it the water that was not water moved in patterns its sensors would have translated into any number of comforting lies about flows and quench and return. It had no obvious seam. It nested like an orphaned thought. She curled her fingers, not closing on it, simply letting. The pod pulsed.

A sound came, very faint through the pond and her bones. It was not a melody. It was not language. It was the simplest of sounds, the oldest, the first thing the world had taught her when she was nothing but noise: a heartbeat, irregular and precious as sin, twice then pause, then twice again, looking for someone to learn it.

She drew back, hands numb, and lay with her cheek on the hot lip of the pond, the smell of cooked glove in her nose. The garden ticked around her, a place for endings, a place that remembered on purpose. In the dark beneath the lilies, something that did not belong to endings refused an instruction.

“Very well,” Isola Venn said to the pond and the seed and the ridge-backed outer dark beyond the garden’s curve. “Then we’ll need to make you a name.” She closed her eyes. The sound in the depth kept time with the little muscular engine in her chest. Outside, the old universe burned through another fraction of whatever it had left. Inside, under her hand, someone had been thrown forward like a prayer.

She had two weeks, a garden made of patience, and all the disobedience she had never permitted herself.

The birds hung like commas in the slowed air.

They were starlings mostly, flashes of graphite and oil over the municipal lawn, their wings beating two, three times a minute instead of ten in the subsidized afternoon. People paid good money for hours like this. Grass grew audible. Shadows took their time crossing faces. The fountain at the plaza’s center didn’t so much spray as sculpt, glass ropes suspending beads in a helix.

I checked my ledger as I stepped over the little lip of rate at the park’s gate. The readout ghosted above my wrist: Bureau Float 3.4 days, Personal 12.0 days, Scheduled Harvest zero. No red. The cuff whirred under my sleeve as it negotiated my entrance, slender algorithms smoothing my stride to match the bubble’s ten-percent rate—just enough velveteen drag to feel like stepping into warm water.

Sareet Alar sat on a slatted bench facing the fountain, cardigan knotted at the elbows. She had the intense concentration of someone trying to memorize the way sunlight lands. Beside her, a paper bag rested on a cane. Real paper—she’d split her time for this, I thought. Inside the bag, three apricots lapped by still air.

She recognized me before my image stopped wavering into her. Clients always did. I had a Bureau face whether I wanted it or not—the way we held ourselves inside rate gradients, the way we didn’t fidget because we knew exactly what a fidget cost.

“You’re early,” she said. Her voice lilted a fraction lower, the slow air pulling vowels like taffy.

“We send the warning a quarter hour before clawback,” I said. “I give you ten. The reclaimer arrives in twelve.”

Sareet’s mouth twisted. “And you’ll go back to your office and drink a coffee at a hundred-and-five and never think of me again.”

“I don’t drink coffee,” I said. It was reflexive and petty. She smiled despite herself, then the smile hardened.

“I’m not running,” she said, and reached into the bag. Her fingers closed on an apricot. She lifted it with the care of someone lifting a child’s hand. It took her a long time to bring it to her mouth because the bubble insisted on dragging every muscle fiber back into the indulgence she’d purchased. When she bit, the flesh gave like a small sun. The smell was thick and immediate: sugar, pitch, the salty ghost of stones.

“You have to know,” she said, not looking at me, “that I would not take what I could not afford if this was only for me. I am not that sort of thief.”

“You’re eighty-one,” I said. “We flagged you last month. You signed the plan.”

“I signed the plan because my granddaughter is twelve and cannot stand still,” she said. “She thinks the world is a story you skip through. I wanted her to learn the way afternoons used to feel. To sit with me while water had texture. She can almost do long division in this air because her thoughts have room to stack without toppling.”

“You can’t stack them if the reclaimer takes the whole shelf,” I said. “Your account is overdrawn. The Bureau won’t just reclaim the hours you stole, they’ll schedule compression to recoup the penalty.”

Sareet stared at the fountain. A child inside the bubble had walked out onto the wide stone rim. His mother, frozen in the faster street beyond the park, had turned to watch through the gate, reduced to a tableau by the mismatched rates. The starlings made another of their heartbeat pulses; for a moment they looked like an idea, then they were birds again.

“You could authorize a de-accel patch,” she said, a little too casually. “You people carry a few spare minutes down your cuffs. Everyone says so. Give me ten seconds of Bureau grace and I’ll find a way to make it right.”

“I don’t have that authority,” I said. “And grace is an accounting fiction, not a thing that grows on trees.”

She turned. Her eyes were very clear. “Then why is your cuff humming?”

I lifted my sleeve and glared at it. The band made a small apologetic chime. You learned how to be unreadable doing this job, but the cuff pulsing meant I’d been thinking about my own float, about the round, cold weight tucked against the inside of my boot—an old habit from when I was new and too poor to forgive other people’s thinking. One unmarked day of pure, unallocated rate: a coin the Bureau insisted didn’t exist. I’d found it in a raid on a backroom time-lender two years ago, rolling under a freezer. It had taken me six minutes to decide not to log it. Weeks to decide not to spend it.

“I’m sorry,” I said, because there were only two honest moods in a park like this: apology and greed. “If you walk with me out of the bubble now, I can put you on an installment that doesn’t crush you.”

“And leave this,” she said, and gestured at the birds as if they were the point. “Leave this—knowing I had it, and I gave it up? What would I do with the rest of my days? Little fast dry days like burnt bread?”

The reclaimer pinged me. Twelve minutes outside was one hundred twenty inside the bubble. The programmed compressor would glide down the street, invisible until it touched the boundary, then bulge the park air like a thumb pushing through plastic. I could stand in its mouth and argue, and none of it would matter.

“We don’t have a lot of time,” I said, and then laughed at my own choice of words. No one ever thought it was funny but us. Sareet rolled the stone of the apricot in her palm. The starlings pulsed again.

“Show me,” she said. “Show me the thing you have that you’re not supposed to have. Then I’ll walk out of here on my own legs.”

“I can’t do that,” I said, too quickly. Her gaze sharpened. She had been reading people since before my mother could tie her shoes. She heard the button you never press when you want a machine to behave.

“This used to be a city,” she said softly. “Before we let the owners of it ration the way sunlight lands. If you have anything left that is not theirs, use it on me.”

It was a neat little knife of a sentence. It slid right under the armor I’d welded together at twenty-two. The Bureau had words for what she was trying—coercion by moral premise; unauthorized leverage via guilt—but the Bureau also had coffee brewed at 105% and the way my cuff had hummed when she asked me for grace.

And I had done this before. Not often. Only when the number shaped itself into a face. Only when the ledger felt wrong the way a note felt wrong in a song.

“You’ll walk,” I said. “You’ll walk with me the second the compressor bites the fence.”

She watched my hands. There were three starlings to one second if you watched them right here. I curled my fingers around the coin in my boot and tried not to notice the way my pulse climbed to meet it. It was smooth and cool, denser than it should have been—time in a blister, minted illegally by some genius with a gravity well in a warehouse, the kind of thing that can buy an afternoon or a prison sentence.

The reclaimer arrived. You could feel it even if you couldn’t see it: the pressure front of rate differentials resolving, the air tautening inexplicably. Outside the park, people blurred a little as the city’s underlying metronome shifted to accommodate the park’s violation. The gate’s guard-strip flickered red.

“Now,” I said.

The compressor pressed its mouth to the fence. The air inside the park indented. The fountain’s ropes of water bowed. The starlings lost their neat punctuation and scattered toward the deeper slow.

And then I cracked the coin.

It was not dramatic. There was no flash. I didn’t shine. Nothing perked or curdled. I pressed the little blister against the back of my cuff. The cuff made a queer little swallow-noise, a hungry infant at a breast. A chilled river ran under my skin. For a heartbeat the world jumped to a tempo I had never stood inside. Then my ledger ticked.

Bureau Float 3.4 days, Personal 13.0 days.

I didn’t look up. I didn’t want to see the way the park also tilted, the failure of accounting to stay inside its borders. I palmed the coin—emptier now, light now, gone now—and pushed a smear of myself into the compressor’s plan. It met the fence. It tasted what it would compress. It recalculated. The bubbling pressure went butter-soft. Instead of collapsing the park into a half-time jitter, reclaiming everything like a misprinted page, it shaved a little. Five minutes off a five-hour indulgence.

The starlings made their last pulse and flew.

Sareet had her apricot. She held it like a sacrament. She stood up without any theatrical slowness and picked up her cane.

“You shouldn’t do that,” she said conversationally, moving toward the gate. “I know you already know. I used to tell my kids not to walk in traffic. It didn’t stop their legs from being fifteen.”

“I’ll file your plan,” I said. “It’s not going to be easy.”

“Nothing easy is worth a prayer,” she said, and tucked the stone into the paper bag as if it might sprout something in the right earth. People in the fast street glanced at us with the usual sideways interest as we crossed out: their eyes sliding over the sheen of the bubble on our skin, the gate’s scanners shuddering a polite little wave at my Bureau credentials. The periphery of the park quivered as the compressor took its bite: a shimmer that wobbled a man’s hair as he passed, an annoyance at the corner of your eye. Then the rate inside went from velvet to cloth. The birds became birds again. The fountain remembered it was plumbing.

“Tell Álina,” Sareet said, her mouth close to my ear. “She listens to you. Tell her you spent something on me and I did not squander it.” She made the little blessing people in District Three still made with their index finger, a dot on the air as if punctuating her own life, and folded into the Monday crowd.

I stood at the gate until the red guard-strip cooled back to white. Then I walked into a day that belonged to someone else.

The Bureau office on Bray Avenue was three stories of glass the color of old seawater and two stories of servers that breathed like cattle belowground. During our seven-day shift it ran at a comfortable rate of one-oh-five to keep our casework flowing ahead of the city, which is to say we always had the taste in our mouths of an hour we had just outrun. My badge asked the door to open. The air tasted of citrus and the buzz of a thousand tiny clocks.

“Metronome,” said Maddy from her desk, which was one of six along the south wall. She was chewing on a pen cap and flicking through depositions. “Someone sent you a plant. For your windowsill. Have you enemies?”

“It’s a succulent,” I said. It was also a rate-hungry thing a quarter of our clients used to get rid of their overages—a biological metronome with the Bureau’s seal in its pores. “Put it near the reheater and it’ll flower.”

“You hear that, Theo?” said Maddy. “We can have flowers if we cook them.”

“Theo went to Systemic,” said Álina from the doorway of the glass-walled conference suite. Her hair did that thing it did when she’d been in the server room: coiling tighter from the static, shaping itself to her skull as if it liked order. “He stole a chair. He said if he brought it back they’d let him sit at meetings he’s not invited to.”

“We had a reclaimer on Ten-West,” I said. “Any blowback?”

“Only the usual,” said Álina, and tilted her head at me the way she tilted at data—like the second angle might help everything line up. “Walk with me?”

I followed her past the Devotions wall—that ugly mural somebody thought would make us feel better about our job, all clocks and grain and the phrase Time is a Favor not a Fact—and into the conference suite. She closed the door and the room slid half a rate quieter, a courtesy that made me always feel like my bones were being unknotted by small hands.

“You look like someone who found a baby on a subway,” she said. “Happy, guilty, and attached.”

“You’re mixing me up with the me who likes trains,” I said. “What’s Systemic want?”

“Not Systemic,” she said. Her mouth made a shape that meant either laughter or fear. “The Auditor.”

Nobody used “the” deliberately in the office unless there were capital letters in it. The Auditor existed the way mountains exist—visible from a distance, unwise to pretend you could simply walk over them. They came when someone had siphoned too much or too cleverly. They came when a district’s float started humming discord under its cover.

“Already?” I said. I had not yet opened the file to write up my day. I hadn’t even set the dead coin under the edge of my mat to remind myself I had done a risky thing and had better be very careful about doing it again.

“Your casework has a pattern,” said Álina, and then raised a hand in a warding gesture. “Don’t. They’re not going to say it like that. They’re going to say there’s a discrepancy in our float, and would we please account for the missing quarter-day between block 3d and 3g. But you know it’s you they mean. And also—”

She reached into the inside pocket of her jacket and pulled out a strip of translucent film. It looked like trash: glove-skin from a surgery. She stuck it to the glass of the conference door and a list swam up, letters forming as if ink were learning to be words. My name bloomed there. Under it, my ledger. The readout refreshed, second by second.

Personal 12.0 days.

“What,” I said. Then: “What?”

“You’re missing,” said Álina quietly. “It’s not the Bureau’s float. It’s you. You’re down. One day vanished from your personal ledger without a counterparty, without a timestamp. You didn’t file a transfer. There’s no drawdown or grant. The system says your tomorrow doesn’t belong to you.”

“That’s not a thing,” I said. My mouth felt numb, the way the air had felt when I cracked the coin. “We can’t—my personal ledger is closed except for my salary and my own contracts. You can’t negative a day without someone taking it.”

“Unless,” said Álina, “you gave it away.”

“I didn’t,” I said. And then I thought about the cold slick rush, the drumbeat thump of the reclaimer, the way an illegal unit had fit into my cuff so neatly it seemed as if the cuff had been waiting for it. “That was a Bureau day. It was Bureau grace.”

“You and I both know that’s a catechism against thieving,” said Álina. “The float hummed. It hummed for two minutes. Some of it evaporated and became someone else’s weather. The cheap way to clean that ledger is to put it on someone who volunteers.”

“I didn’t volunteer,” I said. It came out as a hiss. “What do I do?”

“You meet the Auditor,” she said. “You wear the suit you never wear. You let me sit right behind your left shoulder and pretend I did not come out of the same house you did, with the same hunger and the same bad instincts. And Mara—”

She reached into her jacket again and this time pulled out a little folded page, the kind of silly physical note only old people used. She smoothed it on the table. It was torn from the corner of a newspaper. The ink had bled in a way that said it had been in someone’s pocket, forgotten for an hour.

“For you,” she said. “It was on your chair when we came in this morning. Theo thought it was porn. He was disappointed.”

I unfolded the note. The letters were neat and square but shaky—someone minding their hands. There were six words.

I owe you a day. Run.

It was signed the way I sign when my cuff is dead and my patience is, too—a stylized M like a heart broken in the right place.

There are secrets that taste like pennies. There are secrets that taste like summer. This one tasted like the future curling in on itself, hot metal, apricot stone. I turned the paper over. There was a trace of citrus on it from the office air, and another smell underneath that lifted a memory I had not taken out of its box: the way my mother’s kitchen smelled at dawn the day she left for the fast ward, sharp, green, the last time the world felt like one pace for the two of us.

“What does it mean?” said Álina.

“I thought you told me,” I said. My voice was steady. I was glad of that. I am very good at being steady in rooms built to fold people in half for whatever the Bureau calls mercy. “It means I’m down a day.”

“It means,” she said, and she was looking at me like I was a pattern she’d traced but couldn’t get to line up with the other placemats, “there is a timetable for you that doesn’t belong to me.”

“Is that envy?” I said.

“It’s logistics,” she said sharply, and then, softening: “Mara, listen to me. Don’t run. That’s what they want, if it is what it says. They want you to do something they can call a breach.”

“I have never run,” I said. “I walk at the pace of other people’s misfortune.”

She made the face she made when she knew I was pulling out a mask she did not like. “Please. Don’t do the thing where you turn into a proverb and call it a plan.”

The lights over our heads ticked and breathed. I could taste the office’s pace settling around us, a pulse that insisted we were on the right side of order. When I looked at the note again the M that was not-not mine looked like a hole I could put a finger into and touch what lay behind my life.

I folded the scrap of newspaper carefully, as if it might break, as if it might be old. I slipped it into the inside pocket of my jacket. The edge of it scratched my sternum.

“When do we meet the Auditor?” I said.

“Eleven,” she said. “In the glass room everyone pretends not to fear.”

“Then we have time,” I said, and watched her flinch minutely at the word we both had used until it lost meaning.

“What will you do?”

“Finish my paperwork,” I said. “Tell Theo to return his chair. And send a message to District Ten-West.”

“To say what?”

“To tell a girl named Álina that an old woman asked me to tell her I spent something of mine on hers, and that she did not squander it.”

“You’re sentimental,” said Álina, but her eyes were the eyes of the kid who held my hand on the day we stood at the gate of the hospital ward where an entire floor ran at 150% and asked to see our mother, and the nurse shook her head because we did not have the right contract.

“I’m practical,” I said, and the way my cuff hummed when I lied told me nothing but the truth.

Chapter One

The sky above Noor wasn’t sky at all, just a black ocean studded with broken reflections. Dead things drifted there: antennae folded like praying hands, mottled tanks with regulators teethed off, foil that had peeled and rewrapped itself like the skin of an onion. Below, the Earth was a blue bruise under her boots, soft-looking and far too big to hold.

“Two o’clock, seventy meters, old bus, likely Soviet,” Lio said in her ear. His voice came tinnier through the cheap ENV link they used on suit-to-suit. The expensive one built into the hull of the Hama was reserved for when they were both safely docked and could argue about money without trying to catch their breath.

Noor thumbed her thrusters and drifted. The Hama hung a hundred meters behind them, a fat cylinder with a spine of net launchers and roll-up tanks and a paint job the sun had scoffed off years ago. Their tether lines curled back into her chest winch like translucent snakes. She hated looking at the winch. When it stopped moving, that meant something had gone wrong and she was about to become a new piece of sky junk.

“I’m not seeing a bus,” Noor said. Her visor populated itself with green text. She didn’t love augments, but she loved that feeling of being able to pull field from the vacuum with her eyes. The catalog scrolled like a prayer flag: KOSMOS-18XX series, GLONASS stage 2, NOAA, SHIYAN. No bus.

“I’ve got the glide,” Lio said. “See the hard-edge glint? That’s a bus. They all look like that.”

Noor saw what he saw when she dialed down all the overlays and let sunlight do the finding. A hard line cutting the black, edges precise where so many things were whittled into curves by heat and drag. It tumbled once every twenty-three seconds. Every time it flashed, the inside of Noor’s chest tightened; a bright white memory of a road and a headlight.

“Got it,” she said, and toggled her suit to “stupid,” the mode in which the dampers let her make the micro-stupid errors that made human salvagers worth more than magnets and remote nets. You got taught to feel wrong moves in this mode. Your body got scolded until it learned. She fired her ankle jets, moved too much, corrected. Her tether went taut and sang.

“Slow down,” Lio said. “We need it whole. For the bounties you need the bus intact, panels attached.”

“You’re frightened of me,” Noor said.

“I’m frightened of losing my lease,” Lio said. “And you. In that order.”

The bus rolled toward her as she spread her net. It was a gray coffin with the paint blanched, no numbers, no flag. It was the size of her body and older than her father. It had given someone weather or surveillance or television. Now it gave Noor rent.

She thought she was going to catch it clean. The net pillow blossomed and swallowed the bus, jets firing little puffs to curb its spin, and Noor made the mistake the stupid mode wanted her to feel—the instinct to yank. The tether spanked her shoulder. The bus was heavier than the sim let her believe; inertia could lie still and then suddenly throw a punch.

The bus urged itself out of the first net like a seal sliding out of a careless fisherman’s snare. Noor fired the second, smaller and stickier, and this time she let it tug her, let it keep its angular momentum while her body found a way to lean in to vacuum. They spun together, a slow dance with no friction to tattle on missteps.

“Beautiful,” Lio said, and she could hear his grin because he didn’t say it about people often.

Noor burped thrusters to bring them both down the line toward the Hama. The old bus came like a stubborn child. Earth turned beneath them, and she saw a smear of ocher she knew was the Sahara. Once, when she was a kid and they were still living quadmate in Cairo, she could climb to the roof in the morning and pretend she could see every desert at once. Her grandmother had laughed at that, with cigarette smoke curling out of her nose like the steam from a kettle.

Her grandmother would have loved the Hama. The old woman loved anything that had been sued and re-sued and still worked.

The bus bumped against the Hama’s spine, magnets thunking. Lio was already there, boot soles stuck, gloved hands guiding it into an open belly like a midwife. The net released with a shiver; the contract would auto-fill most of the key fields if the Hama’s hull could sniff a serial number in the bus’s guts. They got paid for kilograms, for intact solar, for gold solder and rare dopants. They got paid more if the registry recognized a name.

“Whoever made it did not want to be identified,” Lio said. He scrubbed at a panel where often, even after decades, a manufacturer’s mark would cling inside, protected from the LE radiation. There was nothing. Noor filed the feeling away. She trusted feelings. They had saved her from a very nice boy who would have definitely learned to day-drink at her expense.

They bolted the bus in place. The Earth swung, the stars held still. Noor’s augments flickered, and for a moment the text streamed nonsense. This happened sometimes when the Hama’s dampers shivered under a little debris stream: the electros went brittle and screamed. But it cleared too fast for debris.

She pinged the net. A slowness moved through the overlay, the way thick syrup moves when you tip a plate. A gap. A something that wasn’t nothing. The catalog tried to smear a label across it and then gave up. The something drifted beyond the Hama, maybe a kilometer away. No number, no orbit file. No station would admit to it.

“You seeing this?” Noor said.

Lio had the bus half-open. “Seeing what?”

“A hole,” she said, and she heard how that sounded and winced. “An object without a registry.”

“Plenty of those,” Lio said. “We call them rocks.”

“Rocks have mass,” Noor said. “My LIDAR kissed it and got kissed right back. It’s… not.”

Her grandmother would have laughed again. The old woman had died under a ceiling fan that squealed, and Noor had inherited an ashtray that still smelled like her hair oil and a phrase: who told you the world goes in the direction you point?

“Go take a look,” Lio said, but he didn’t look up; a place in the bus had his attention now. He had that squinty way when he smelled a metal everyone else missed. “I need a minute. Might be niobium wiring. Please be niobium wiring.”

“Please be a new job,” Noor said, and she unspooled the work line off her hip, careful. The nothing-thing drifted in a slow slide that defied her sense of where orbital families kept their lanes. It sat just out beyond their shadow line, and when she tipped her visor on manual light it didn’t light up until she turned her lamp away. Noor sucked on her mouthpiece without meaning to. The astringent bite flagged high CO2. She forced her breath long and thin again.

All her data wanted to smear. A trick of the angle, of glare. She tried to love the world as if it wasn’t trying to deceive her, but space wasn’t the right place to practice faith.

She nudged forward. The Hama became a darker limb she could swing back to. The black beyond had depth; there were currents in it if you lived here long enough to see them. Hammers of pebbles sometimes, like being inside someone else’s hailstorm. Or a fog of paint dust that turned sunlight into a loose, cold milk. She had learned those early. The thing she chased rode on a flat calm bubble. Her suit whispered numbers she ignored.

It was small. Space had lied to her and made it big. When she got close enough, the augment stopped flickering and drew that thin green wire around it as if embarrassed to have lost track. A cube, maybe eight centimeters on a side. Not a material she knew at a look, its surface not reflective, not matte. If she had to say what it looked like she would have said deep water a second after you turn the light off: a color you still somehow see. It tucked itself and didn’t tumble and didn’t drift when she faced it; it faced back.

The suit light washed over it. The cube didn’t gather the beam, but it didn’t cast shadow either. Her mouth went dry. Somewhere in the back of her head, someone else’s voice said, Act normal.

“Looks like a little battery brick,” Noor said, trying to sound bored so Lio wouldn’t come. He was good; he would take things out of her hands without meaning to. It was easy to forget the things that felt like yours weren’t. Company policy enforced it. Orbit enforced it harder.

“Battery brick my ass,” Lio said. “Wrap it. Fast.”

She tied a loop in her net with fingers that stopped obeying her when she thought too much about them. The cube waited. When she got close enough to feel the suit hairs on her forearms lift where the electrostatic went weird, something brushed inside her ear. Static first, then a thin tone like a telephone left inside a glass. Her gut clawed. She came all the way here because she knew there was a thing, and the thing was rewarding her for knowing.

“Noor,” the Hama said in Lio’s voice, very quietly. “Noor, you hearing that?”

She swallowed relief. “What? The tone?”

“No.” He sounded far. “The lullaby. The one with the spoons.”

Her skin pebbled with sweat; the suit had to chase it away for her. Her grandmother had tapped spoons on the house pipes when she sang, when the power went out, when the neighborhood kids had to go up to the roof to feel air. Noor hadn’t told Lio that story.

“I don’t hear any lullaby,” she lied. The cube didn’t pulse or open or show seams. It simply became heavier under her glove. She had that bone ache you get a second before a thunderstorm. She swung the net around it, and when the mesh brushed the cube, the mesh hiccuped, as if for a fraction of a second its wires decided they were something else.

“Back now,” Lio said. He was done pretending he wasn’t worried.

“On my way,” Noor said, and she locked the cube inside a pouch at her hip, the kind she used for loose screws and sometimes her father’s old brass worry coin. The pouch felt heavier; the coin felt jealous.

The tug back to the Hama was there if she wanted to lean into it. She did. The suit gulped, took a breath for her. Her visor smeared the world once more—Noor’s eyes refused to believe the cube was behind her—but then the Hama rose like a horizon, and beyond it, the shimmer of a debris swell.

“Shit,” she said, but she was quiet and calm about it. The swell looked like nothing if you didn’t live here. If you did, and if you remembered the last time a swarm had come through and turned a Bollywood satellite into shrapnel, you felt the hairs inside your nose raise. This one was a glint-mist. Paint, screws, and a wing of polyimide film that had been a sunshade once and was now a kite for hitting people who weren’t looking.

“Get inside—get inside,” Lio said, words gritted. He toad-slinked down the Hama’s spine, boots thunking metal. The Hama had no real inside. It had a pressure drum you could climb into and sit in while you waited for a lawyer to respond. Otherwise, you glued yourself to the hull and made yourself small. You angled yourself to present the smallest cross-section to the spray and hoped nothing thick came at you going fast.

Noor keyed the winch to take her in. It whirred. It also made a noise that was not whirr. Her heart tried to jump out her throat.

“Tether’s snagged,” she said. Calm. Saying out loud that a thing is true can make it bearable. “I’ll manual.”

She pinwheeled around her line and reeled herself, hand over hand. The swell came in like a translucent hose. In another life, she’d had a stack of summer afternoons on the Qasr El Nil bridge where she watched boys with scabbed knees throw themselves into the Nile rips. They’d grin while the current took them. They’d stay underwater just long enough to make girls scream. She had loved and hated them with equal force.

“There’s a panel coming,” Lio said, too loud. “Eight o’clock. Duck.”

She tucked and felt it flow over her like a sharp blanket. Her suit’s shell chittered. A ping like a pebble off a bicycle rim. Another. Her visor chimed; a crack spidered and stopped, stopped. The cube in her pouch warmed against her thigh and then went cold. Noor hissed without meaning to.

Lio was a few meters away now, one boot glued to the Hama, body bent into a question mark trying to be small. Paint dust turned the sun into a halo around his head. A screw chimed off his skull. He said a word Noor had only heard old priests use before barbering: a kind of oath that sounded like grandfather iron.

“Hold,” Noor said, because there was nothing else to say. The swell came and went. It didn’t last long. That was the thing about orbits: everything wanted to be on its own line. Chaos in space rated a low on the scale. Chaos elsewhere was greedy.

It passed. Movement at last had texture again. Noor licked her lips. The suit complained about dryness she hadn’t noticed.

“Alive?” she said.

“Yes,” Lio said, with feeling. He tilted his head, trying to see her without moving too much. “You good?”

“Peachy.”

“What the hell was that? New wake?”

She kept her eyes on her hands and not on the pouch. “We’re on a pancake lane. Some idiot probably popped a tank at the wrong speed.”

“Some idiot,” Lio said, not meaning Noor. “We’ll get a hailstorm penalty on the bus intake. Look.” He pointed with his chin. The old bus had taken three new dents, shallow but visible. The contract would swallow them and spit out a smaller number.

Noor wanted to tell him that the bus wasn’t interesting anymore; that this morning she had been a certain kind of person and now she wasn’t. That was a thing you didn’t say to your partner when the company cut your share each time your heartbeat climbed above a threshold during a job. She stuck to her line and reeled in.

Inside the Hama’s drum they took their helmets off, very slowly, hair stuck to foreheads. The drum smelled like stale tea and singed dust. Somebody had taped a photograph to the bulkhead, a teacher making a face while throwing confetti over a classroom of kids. Noor had brought that from Cairo. She didn’t know the teacher. She had liked the confetti because it was the opposite of orbit: chaos that stayed in a room because gravity said so.

Lio kicked his boots free of their clamps and floated along the longitudinal, toes curling like a dancer’s. His hair, left long in the back because he thought retro made him interesting, fanned out, and a paint flake got caught in it and spun there. He didn’t notice.

“You’re bleeding,” Noor said, and flicked the flake out. It left a weal of red on his scalp about the size of a pistachio.

“I like it,” he said. He liked any wound he could show somebody at the bar who’d never been up. He peeled his glove down and fingered the seam on the bus. “No registry, no ID, but there’s a cavity here. Haven’t seen this layout.”

“Means nothing good,” Noor said. The pouch at her hip tugged at her like a child again. She put her hand there and felt the shape through the fabric and made herself take it away.

His brow creased. He reached for a tool he called the auntie: a thin, patient scraper you slid under things that didn’t want to be slid under. He worked at the seam while Noor unhooked herself. She kept her body between him and the pouch. There was no reason to. He wasn’t watching her. She did it anyway.

Her father would have said, this is how people go crook: side-step by side-step, each one small and easy. Her father also would have said, don’t bring home anything that eats.

The personal line pinged in her visor. No audio, just a soft pulse like a finger tapping. Her augments couldn’t block it. The Hama’s system logged it as a ghost. Somebody out there had flagged their container with a ping. Lio didn’t get it or pretended not to.

“Hama, this is Tower,” came the hull’s tight-beam speaker, the expensive channel. The voice was a woman with accents Noor couldn’t place, the kind who had been trained to sound like gravity. “Traffic density alert in your sector. Recommend you clear to eight twenty-kilometers and hold.”

“We’re not taking advice today,” Lio said mildly. He never refused anything directly. He pushed away from the bus and drifted to the mic to toggle reply. His mouth had gone hard. “Copy, Tower. Holding six eighty.”

“Negative,” gravity-voice said. “We have superusers requesting your vector cleared.”

“Superusers can—” Lio started, injectively jovial, and Noor gave him the face that meant, stop being the child they think you are. He swallowed his grin. “We don’t have the prop to stair-step at your leisure, Tower.”

A pause. Noor used it to slide the pouch free. She shouldn’t. She did. She hid it under the bench with the tape and the spare seals and the ancient sandwich bag she and Lio kept full of metal washers because they acted like freedom if you let them float.

The voice came back. “Apologies, Hama. I have an override. Clear the sector now. Vector follows.”

“Who is pushing you?” Lio said, softly now.

“Tell me who told you to tell me to go,” he meant, but out loud he said the thing that makes you a person, not a device.

Another pause, longer. Noor scratched at the sweat drying in her hairline and thought of her grandmother’s thumb working a cigarette lighter wheel with a knowing that seemed older than lighters. She could tell when the woman in the tower was going to say the words.

“Military,” the Tower said. “Unspecified. I don’t recommend antagonizing. Transmitting vector now. Four minutes to compliance.”

“This is our lane,” Lio said, but he didn’t hit the mic. He looked at Noor, and the look said, did you bring home something that eats?

She considered not saying anything. She considered showing him the cube and letting them both feel the way the air folded around it. The absence of air. Company policy was clear: unregistered, unknown finds went to quarantine. Quarantine meant ten different lawyers from eight flags, meant hands that were not hers, meant a find would vanish, and somewhere down the line a patent would appear with a name on it that sounded like a brand and not like a person.

“Yes,” she said, because she liked Lio alive. “Under my bench.”

He bent, found the pouch, unzipped. The thing inside didn’t light or hum or deploy needles. It lay like a subdued animal. Lio stared at it, and then he did something she liked him very much for: he closed the pouch, fastened it, and then he put it back under the bench and he put his foot back over it.

“Okay,” he said. “We will comply.”

“Think they saw us pick it?” Noor said.

“No,” Lio said, and his mouth couldn’t decide if it was smiling. “They knew it existed before we did.”

The Hama’s maneuver jets were small and foul-smelling and efficient. They pushed the cylinder into a new orbit like a hand nudging a bead along a wire. Lio strapped in grudgingly. Noor didn’t bother with the harness; she knew the Hama like a body. She braced her boots and shoulder and became part of the bulkhead.

The vector displayed on her visor. It was a little prayer string leading them out and up and then up again, clearing a volume that no one had ever cleared for them before. Hull creaks announced temperature differentials. The bus wept a flake of white.

The personal line pinged again. This time it resolved into a voice that had almost no qualities; it was like the voice that reads when you make your phone read but the machine is old and the app is free. It said: “Noor.”

Her tooth roots hummed.

She didn’t answer. Answering was half a contract.

Lio was either ignoring it or not hearing it. “We log the push,” he said. “We call Avinash. We get credit for the detour and the hazard. We are going to be so annoying that next time the first thing they clear out of a lane is us.”

“Okay,” Noor said. She put her hand down on the bench and felt the pouch through the metal the way you sometimes feel thunder through a floor before you hear it. The voice in her ear said her name again. Her grandmother’s kind of voice would have laughed and lit another cigarette.

“You shouldn’t have found me,” the voice said. “No—that is a lie. You have to find me at least six times, and this was one of them.”

Noor closed her eyes. She should tell Lio. The taste in her mouth said: don’t. The shape in the pouch said: don’t. The way the tower’s voice had flattened when it said military said: don’t. Every authority in her life had taught her to keep her interesting secrets for when the day gets thin.

“What are you?” she whispered. Long practice made that kind of whisper not carry to the room mike.

“Out of range,” the voice said. “Inside range. Do you remember the river with the green road across it? I liked that. You cried there.”

Noor tried to stand up and couldn’t because her stomach had opened. When she was small, she had stood on the Qasr El Nil and watched the green laser in the shape of a road shoot across the river on festival nights. She had not told Lio that story either.

“Who are you,” she said, teeth against tongue.

The voice inhaled in the faintest, mangled electronic way. “You made me. Not yet. Don’t give me to them.”

“Too late,” Lio said, to someone else. He tapped the console. “We’re giving everybody everything today.”

The Hama rotated. The Earth beneath them swelled. Noor looked down without meaning to. She could see, burnt into her, streets and their empty little rivers, a child’s toy city draped in exhaust and sun.

If she pretended very hard, she could believe gravity would stay if she asked it nicely. If she pretended very hard, she could be the kind of person who followed the rules around interesting things.

“Okay,” she said to the voice, very quietly. “Okay.”

“Okay what?” Lio said, not looking, his fingers on the vector controls as if he could do better than the cheap autopilot could.

“Okay I’m not going to throw up,” Noor said. “Scalp wounds make me queasy.”

He laughed, and it broke some of the spell in the room.

Outside, lanes cleared like curtains being pulled, and three things that were not in Noor’s catalog slid through where they had been. Smooth, no protrusions, colors that her eyes didn’t decide on. They moved without pushing anything, without carrying their own wake. They moved like math. Lio stiffened. Their cheap ENV link, that stateful little radio which had carried arguments about rent and long compliments for broken machinery, suddenly and peacefully died.

“Compliance acknowledged,” said the tower, to the wrong people. “We never spoke.”

Noor rubbed her thumb along the place in her palm where her grandmother’s lighter had worn a scar once. The cube warmed under the bench. The ship hummed like a throat making up a lie.

She had the sense, seldom so precise, that a trajectory had been altered not by a burn but by a choice. People in orbit liked to pretend they couldn’t choose much. Choices were expensive. She wished the sensation felt less like relief.

“Let’s go home,” Lio said. He meant, let’s send messages and start fights and sleep. He meant, let’s not die today.

“Sure,” Noor said. “Home.”

Her grandmother would have tapped a spoon against a pipe and sung the first low note of a lullaby and said: home is wherever you keep the thing that changes everything about you. The Hama rolled. The Earth was a big patient thing that didn’t look up. The three unlisted strangers didn’t look at them as they passed, but Noor felt seen. The word for that was older than any registry. She put her hand over the bench, over the little pouch, as if she could keep something quiet by making it warmer, as if she was a sky and not a person.

Chapter One: Collections

Our city sells hours.

Water is rationed, energy is metered, air is filtered. Those are utilities. Hours are different. They sit beneath everything, you don’t see them until you do, and then you can’t stop. People buy them by the slice: a luminous minute for a proposal, seventy-four thick seconds to watch a meteor shower, a rich afternoon to hold your mother’s hand through snow we will never have again. We call it Resolution. We sell clarity. We sell time you will keep.

I take it back when you can’t pay.

They teach you how to smile at the Academy. Make your eyes soft. Speak with the weight of someone who has been forgiven and now forgives; don’t apologize for policy; never leave them their anger. Be a person they can accept losing to.

I carry the Meter under my jawbone where it taps against my pulse. It catalogues and invoices and, when I need it to, it lowers the lens.

Today I step off the eastbound tram into a fog that has swallowed the salt towers. The street lamps float like ghosts and the sea is a nothing behind the concrete wall, only a taste, only the ghost of cold. Across the slick road, a child presses his hand to the aquarium glass and the fish press back. His mother checks her day-feed.
