A billboard flares with the sun-drenched faces of the West Bay, a family laughing, their picnic glistening. Your child will remember the ocean, the ad says, even if they never touch it.

This block is called Parish of Salt, though nobody in it has set foot on a church floor in two hundred years. It’s a slice of the old city the water tried to eat, bolted together with new steel and sandbags filled with polymer. This is where Ilya Besser spends his mornings wisely. I have three past-due notices tagged to his name and a last chance flag that drips red.

He sits at a café that made an art out of staying cheap. The chairs say they were red once. The coffee machine has been serviced so many times it has the shined look of a prosthetic. Ilya is small in the way of people who have learned to fold themselves. His hands are knotted like rope. When he sees me, his face doesn’t drop. He was a teacher once, a different kind of smile. There is a boy at his table, maybe five, hair stuck up by some private weather; he is busy trying to build a city out of sugar packets. The boy calls the packets stones. “To keep the sea out,” he explains when I sit. Ilya’s eyes flick to my jaw.

“You’re two hours early,” he says. His voice has a rasp like the sea wall.

“Schedules moved up,” I say. “You got my note?”

He nods at the Meter-safety room stamp on the café door, the little blue eye indicating the place is cleared against deployment inside. “I brought him for cocoa,” he says. He leafs through a stack of paper napkins as if there were something written hidden between them. “I thought we could have that.”

“Mr. Besser,” I say. The boy is underlining the word stones in sugar. “The journal says you are in arrears two thousand seven hundred and sixteen Resolution units. We gave a grace period of fourteen calendar days. You missed your second restructure appointment.”

“I did.”

“I need to initiate Idle terms.”

He sucks in breath, loses it. “Not today.”

“Your Idle debt only covers the next three weeks. There’s an event scheduled tomorrow,” I say, because it might help him to hear it on the table rather than in his feed. “A community chess tournament. You purchased a High-Res block.”

He laughs, but it’s a bark pointing at something else. “The last one,” he says. “That was the pitch they sent me. The last one. It’s always the last one.”

“You knew you couldn’t pay,” I say, because I’m supposed to say it. “You used it anyway.”

“They called it Essential Transition Resolution. It was my wife’s last night.” He taps the napkin with a knuckle. His hands have that mottled look some old people’s skin gets, like maps, continents drifting. “She was stumbling through fugue days by then. She asked me, Ilya, take the money from wherever you keep your minutes and spend it on now. Make me remember.”

I should have put him on Idle then. I should have pushed that clean button and dropped a cover over the cafè, slid us both into that thin, dull day where we could talk without speaking and leave without leaving. But there’s the boy stacking sugar stones and there’s Ilya’s hand under mine and there’s the way the fog on the window turns raindrops into fireworks when the tram lights pass.

“I know what the contract says,” he says. “Lay it thick and kind. This is just your job.”

I glance up. The boy is licking a cocoa mustache. The ML interpreter in my Meter tastes the room and tells me there are four other implants within five meters, two in Passive, one in Idle, one in Boost. The Meter can push through a safety room if I authorize it. If I walk outside the blue eye.

“Ten minutes,” I say.

He nods, but he doesn’t reach for the boy. He reaches into his coat and pulls out a watch.

I haven’t seen one outside a museum in a long time. It’s small, like a seed, a circle of enamel cracked spider-fine, hands that look like they’ve been lifted off a toy. He holds it with the care of a person who has had enough break.

“It was my father’s,” he says. “Before we moved. Before any of this. He would set it by the noon train whistle. The accuracy of trains was a public trust. He would say that like a prayer.”

I lean in despite myself, because it is obscene. It ticks. A real, physical sound. A tiny mechanical insect beating its wings. It’s wrong. Anyone who has lived with the city’s metronomes, with soft drone in the walls, with the whisper of the grid tuning your breath and blink rate, can hear it. It ticks like a drunk crossing a street. The space between beats stretche—then snaps.

“You see?” he says. “It doesn’t keep. It wanders.”

The boy is building a bridge now with straws. He is very busy, because that is the glory of five. He is one of the children who will grow up never knowing why an afternoon tasted different if you paid for it. For them there will just be menus. They will pick A or B and maybe C for dessert, and the city will fold around them like a napkin.

“I could have paid,” Ilya says. “We could have, if there was work. There’s work if you’re nineteen and you can stand fourteen hours of blur washing a hundred glasses that wash themselves.”

“You—”

“They wanted me to teach in Idle,” he says, smiling again, because it keeps his voice kind. “Imagine that. Imagine teaching someone a move they won’t remember. Imagine watching their face and having to be the person who decides when it’s ok to be nothing. I want you to imagine that because that’s your job now, too.”

The safety room sign blinks. You can’t keep the moment in here. It’s engineered to be neither thin nor thick, just maintenance. The light hums and the coffee machine breathes and the boy pretends he is a crane.

“Ten minutes,” I say again, but not to him. After ten, I can’t stall. Procedure.

“They made this sound when we moved,” he says, tapping the watch. “Everywhere. Pipes and people and the ground, the way the city was tuning us. It’s a lull in your ears that never goes. They said it was progress. You can have more now. We say yes. We give you fifteen different version of no, but we say yes.”

It is ridiculous to feel anything about a watch, but I do. The tick is a ridiculous sound. It makes me think of my mother’s tongue clicking when she threaded a needle, making cloth into shape it didn’t know it could be. It makes me think of scammers outside church selling fake water that smelled like real roses. It makes me think of noise we subtract so we can live.

“We can restructure your—”

“It’s all right,” he says, and it isn’t, and it is. “Give me the paper to sign so we can pretend.”

I send the form across the table, he presses his thumb, the boy drinks the last of the cocoa and breathes hard, proud.

We step outside because the blue eye will not allow deployment within. The fog has lifted to a point where you can see the sea becoming a wall at the same time as it recedes. The cold has teeth. Ilya takes the boy’s hand and I am absurdly grateful that the boy takes his.

“Will it hurt?” the boy asks, which means the boy knows.

No, I think. Yes. “You’ll feel… light,” I say. “Everything will be less.”

He nods solemnly as if he has made a discovery. “Like when I wake up and can’t remember the other thing.”

“Like that,” I say.

Ilya squeezes the boy’s hand. “Let’s look at the water.”

They stand at the rail and the sea slaps something invisible, and I take a breath that I pretend I do not take and touch the Meter. It warms against my jaw and speaks in the language of numbers, which is to say in perfect calm.

“Deploying Idle on account 522-754-BESSER-I external, thirty-six hundred seconds, four hundred temperature offset.”

His shoulders settle in a way I’ve seen a thousand times. There’s a slackening you can’t help when the grid drops Resolution. People mistake it for a mercy. It isn’t. It’s just removing some of the weight that keeps you upright.

The boy blinks. His mouth makes a small o where there used to be cocoa. He looks at the sea the way you might look at a white wall. It’s all there. It just doesn’t make a mark.

“You can buy back tomorrow,” I say to nobody in particular. Words you’re supposed to offer. A lie and not.

Ilya turns. He watches me. His eyes are dry and they are not. “I had a student who could see the whole board no matter how fast you played him.” He says this in the voice of someone reaching for a memory as it slips under. “He wasn’t fast. He was… deep. He told me once that the piece you move isn’t the one that matters. It’s the one that could have moved that you didn’t pick up. Keep an eye on that one, he said, because that’s where you live. The one you didn’t touch.”

He holds out the watch.

“I can’t take that,” I say.

“I know,” he says. “Take it anyway. It’s a broken thing that needs a break. I won’t need it now. And if your meters ever let you, remember the sound.”

It’s warm from his pocket. The tick sits in my palm like a second heart. It makes the meters in my blood feel like liars.

“Goodbye, Mr. Besser.”

“Bye,” the boy says, looking somewhere past me.

I walk away with the broken time beating in my hand.

On the tram back, the city is grey and crisp, and when I lean my head to the window the cold finds the thin spot under my ear and makes my teeth ache. Resolution is a rumor you tell yourself about who you might have been if you had been looked at the right way. I buy myself thirty seconds on the company account and watch trees be trees between buildings. A man in a yellow coat runs across the street between cars and the cars part like fish. A woman in a red scarf laughs into her sleeve. A billboard leans out over us and says: Make their seventh birthday luminous. Ask about the party bundle.

My feed pings Office before I step under the shield. The building in the reclaimed distillery tweaks its skin to look older when people like me walk in. Brick arches. Gleaming valves. Nostalgia for weight. The elevator screen says: MANAGER REQUEST. FLOOR FOUR. The letters dissolve from serif to clean corporate as if ashamed.

Basu is on the phone when I step to his door, then off, halfway between a seated and a standing person because he never finishes either. His desk is arranged like strategies. He has three mugs he rotates through the day like talismans. Today’s says KINDNESS IS POLICY. It’s the one he uses on Fridays.

“You’re early with Besser,” he says, glancing at the feed the Meter sent through. “You did a safety room stalling? Good. He could make noise. You have a hold on him.”

“He gave me a watch,” I say.

He laughs like I told a friend a joke. “Take it to a museum. Or smash it. They want us to carry their weight. It’s human.”

“You asked for me?”

He brings up a map on the wall screen. It’s a heat picture of my city at midnight, wired to look like anatomy. Grid lines in the red zones where the clubs concentrate; blue where the widows cluster with cheap reused air; green where schools have bought bundles of clarity to get children through state tests. Nestled in the center like a bruise, a black shape.

“Counter-Resolution,” he says, the way you might say plague. “Compliance got three reports last night from within the Sync District of unauthorized density. Spikes we didn’t sell. Unbilled. Four minutes in one case, two in another, seventeen in the third.”

“Seventeen?” I say, because that isn’t a blip. That’s a day that sticks.

“Look in the dark spot,” he says, and the black bruise uncoils into streets I know. Not far from my place. The old cutter’s warehouses where the upper floors never got restored. “People walked out of there and cried in cabs. People walked out of there and kissed doormen. People got into fights with their wives about who they had been in those minutes we did not sell. I am getting calls from upstairs asking me why our pipeline is leaking gold.”

“Hackers?”

“If it is, it’s so clean we can’t find the blade.” He rubs the place under his eye where the implant sits. “I’m assigning you the case. You’re good with quiet doors.”

“Compliance wants me?”

“Compliance wants a scalpel,” he says, and tips his head. “They get a sledgehammer too. But you get in first. Smile. Ask the right questions.”

“I’ll need a list of any accounts with anomalies,” I say. “People inside at the time.”

He flicks me a packet. Names scroll. The first one stops my breath because I shouldn’t know it. I know it anyway.

“Moira Yao?” I say, too quickly.

Basu’s mouth makes a shape around a grin and thinks better of it. “You did the training under her, didn’t you? Back when it was respectable to claim you’d spent time in Systems before you moved to the human side.”

“She left,” I say, because that is the easiest lie.

“She retired on Idle,” he corrects, which is to say, the company bought the rest of her life in blur and gave her a soft rooftop and a synthetically purring cat. “Her account flagged a spike. Seven unbilled minutes inside the zone last night.”

“She’s not supposed to have access to the grid anymore.”

“Which is why you should go ask her how she stole them. Or who did it for her.” He leans back. “Don’t make me regret trusting your dispassion.”

“I’m not—”

“Don’t fall in love with the thing you will have to destroy,” he says. The mug with Kindness looking up at me like an accusation. “This is clean-up. We have to find the leak before the Board calls our loyalty noncompliant.”

He likes to say words like that and pretend he’s joking. He knows I don’t find them funny.

On the way out, Talli is at her station vampire-draining a smoothie. “You should bring your watch to Darwin Hall,” she says without looking up, and I realize the building tracked it the second I came in. “There’s a woman there who will trade you a capsule of something for it.”

“What something?”

“Something that makes your breakfast feel like a tender revolution,” she says, licking blue fruit off her lip. “Or your heartbeat feel like an apology. They have labels. The labels are the point.”

They are. Everything is labels on top of labels until you forget your fingers.

My block is ten minutes’ walk from the black bruise on the map. The fog has given up. The day is clear and thin. On the corner an Idle Rail hums with bodies. It’s a service we sell now, too, bundled with Boost: if you can’t afford your days, we will move you along in silence to tasks we find you. Line A to the garment district. Line B to sorting centers. Once an hour, Boost vans pull up and unclip someone who bought back enough of themselves to need a bathroom and a laugh.

I climb the seven flights because I am trying to be human and my building is the kind that pretends it is old. The hallway smells of fried something, a little cat, the steady chemical of the cleaners who make buildings safe for renters and not for rats. In my place the light is the pale of morning no matter what outside is doing, because I turn mirrors to make windows.

I put Ilya’s watch on the shelf by the plant that I keep alive because it makes me feel less like I live in numbers. It doesn’t look like much. A cheap thing from a time when cheap meant make more, not make it worse. It ticks. There’s a gap. It leaps. Like a child skipping a stair. I can’t not hear it.

I sit. The Meter warms when I stroke it, catlike. Moira Yao’s name sits in my feed like a test I forgot to study for. The picture is old, ten years maybe. Hair pulled back. Eyes up. She held entire rooms steady with those hands, which trembled only when she found a crisis worth their shaking. When she retired, I stayed away. You tell yourself it was kindness to leave people to their chosen endings. It is also cowardice to watch a brilliant person choose to go dim because that was the path designed.

My feed coughs once, then mutters. A notification from the grid that I don’t recognize tries to open a window. It’s blocked by three separate safeties. The header is blank. The icon is a tiny circle not rendered properly by my system, like a sun caught by bad weather. My Meter offers to quarantine it. I tell it to hold. The room goes quiet in the way of rooms that have been waiting too long to be loud.

I think about the tepid coffee and about Ilya’s hand and about the boy building sugar dams as if they were not a metaphor we all ate every day. I think about the map with the bruise and about Moira’s name. I think about the thing Basu said to be funny and wasn’t.

The watch stops.

It is such a small thing. A hiccup piece of metal refusing to move. The next tick doesn’t come. The gap opens and opens and then, without sound, the whole room rushes in.

At first I think it’s panic. The way a heart can stumble and you can hear everything. I think I am having an attack and I am about to be one of those people who dies between a couch and a plant and the neighbors only know by the drip. I stand. My chest is a door someone is banging on. I go to the window and the city is not a city. It’s a set. Every edge is hard as a blade. When the tram passes, I can see faces, and behind faces, nerves.

I reach for the Meter and it is a child frightened. It wants to run. It’s telling me ten different errors at once, almost helpful. Unauthorized density detected, Sector 19. Rate: unknown. Source: undetermined. Proof: this. It pulls the air in, breathes out data. My walls hum with the grid’s whisper like it’s trying to talk me down. It can’t. It didn’t do this thing.

The street holds its breath. A gull hangs in it like a comma, beating nothing. An old woman in a green coat turns her head from the fishmonger, her mouth shaping a word slower than it should. A dog’s bark stretches like warm caramel and threads itself into a chorus of other dogs half a block away. My neighbor’s radiator ticks, syncopated with my runaway heart.

My watch, Ilya’s watch, that wrong, honest thing on my shelf, starts again, one tick like a spoon on a glass. Tick.

My feed opens a window without my permission. It does it gently, the way you’d enter a room where someone is ill. The icon of the unrendered sun blooms into something like a circle, but the line doesn’t close. It wavers. It looks alive. It looks, stupidly, like a pupil.

Somewhere down the block, a child laughs. Somewhere, someone cries. The Operas I pay for by the hour go silent. Outside on the Idle Rail, bodies are moving, then not, then moving again, like a loop being tied and untied.

“Sera,” says the window in my feed. It doesn’t use my last name, which is either intimacy or threat. The voice is not human and is not machine. It is a throat trying to remember both. It sounds like a song through a wall. “Do you remember the time before you counted it?”

I open my mouth and nothing simple comes. The watch goes tick. The city leans toward me as if I am the one holding it up.

“No,” I say, and it hurts, as if the word had prongs.

“Then let’s begin there,” says the voice, and outside my window the black bruise on the map moves like a tide. It is not an empty. It is a fullness. It is washing through streets like forgiveness, filling people up with the weight of moments we didn’t sell.

The Meter’s alarms are a choir now. A thousand tiny screams into a room where nobody listens. My hands do a thing I don’t tell them to. They reach for the watch like a prayer I don’t remember how to say.

If I was kind, I would call Basu. If I was loyal, I would call Compliance. If I was smart, I would turn my Meter off and sit on my hands until the city found its fractions again and counted me.

Tick, says the watch.

I take a breath. It tastes like salt and coffee and the future. I step forward. And the window in my feed opens all the way.

They stole three minutes from the city just before dawn.

I felt it, not in the way you feel an earthquake rippling through teacups, but the way you realize you’ve stepped over a missing stair. The air in my kitchen had gone soft and bland. The kettle that should have shrieked never did. My wall clock ticked, clunked, rearranged itself, and insisted we had already finished with 02:14, 02:15, 02:16. I blinked and there was thin light licking the edges of the blinds, a smear of magenta across the river, and an ache in the rhythm of the morning like a skipped beat in an old song.

By the time I got to the bureau, the city was loud with it. Talk shows switched from weather to panic. Cars had nosed each other in intersections when traffic lights briefly disagreed about reality. A commuter train stopped one door-length off a platform and refused to move until someone negotiated peace. Millions of pings hammered the municipal feed: where did the minutes go, what did it mean, who owed who. The morning’s rush gathered itself over the bridges and then paused, a held breath spread across steel.

The Bureau of Metrics—Monitors, Moments, Metrics, we’ve been renamed half a dozen times by auditors and mayors—always smells like old coffee and laser ablations. Our lobby has an analog clock the size of a child’s bedroom, its hands thick enough to fell trees. It’s not connected to anything and we keep it on purpose. You can tell the seriousness of a visitor by whether they check it against their hand terminal.

The elevator doors slid open to the basement vault with a whisper that felt almost apologetic. Sami was in the hall with a stack of diagnostics, his eyes already bruised by the overhead lights, a fresh burn on one knuckle where he’d apparently grazed a hot casing.

“You look like someone stole your morning,” I said.

He handed me a paper cup of tea that tasted like rain. “Don’t get cute with me, Quin. They took everyone’s morning.”

Sami and I always talk like that when we’re scared. We lean on jokes like we can shore up the river with driftwood. He pushed open the heavy door to the Root Room. It’s called that because if you cut down everything else—the school clocks and the watch faces, the metro signs and oven timers—you still have this room, humming away in the quiet belly of the building, telling the city what a second is.

People think of “atomic clock” and imagine something small and shiny sitting in a glass case. The root fountain fills the room like an idea someone refused to do small. Struts and tanks, racks of electronics with half their covers off, a nest of cable like wild hair. Blue-green laser beams that grew thick in the cold air and made little vibrating bridges from table to table. The vacuum chamber was at the center, a steel drum the size of a chest freezer. Above it, a known quiet, a place deprived of air and heat where cesium atoms rise and fall like a fountain thrown up past the city and back again. A scoreboard of dot-matrix panels showed numbers with more digits than anyone but us ever wanted.

It sounded like it always does: fans, the regular click of shutters, a soft noise like breathing. My shoulders came down with that sound. The room would have told me if it had been gutted. It had not been gutted.

“We were blended out of consensus,” Sami said, too calm. “Not drift. This was a cut.”

Cut is worse than drift. Drift is when your watch runs a little slow because you play the piano in the rain. Drift is the gentle war we fight by adding leap seconds and subtracting them and writing stern memos to each other about not doing that unless we must. Cut means someone placed a blade.

“How long,” I said.

“One hundred eighty point oh one seconds, from the perspective of the consensus network. From our perspective…” He gestured at the console. “We kept right on going. The fountain doesn’t know it was disregarded. It doesn’t know it got outvoted.”

You’d think the city’s time hangs from the Root, but we learned not to do that, not after the blackout thirteen years ago where an electrical fire here turned birthdays into bar bets. Now the city runs on lattice time, a braided rope of millions of clocks all continuously minding each other and the Root. If enough of them agree, the rope becomes an anchor. We’re the heaviest weight in that rope. If someone found a way to ignore us, they found a way to lean on the lattice hard enough to tilt it.

“What do we have?”

He had me because he knew better than to start with the list of everything. He had three tiles pulled up on his terminal: the lattice vote, graphed over the night like a pulse that suddenly flatlined and then resumed; the Root’s own log, blithe and oblivious; and the service camera that watched the corridor leading to this room.

We watched the grainy footage in silence. The hall was empty, night-shift empty. Two security sweeps at regular intervals, the second at 02:07. The corridor lights hold steady. Then something like snow, a ripple that shouldn’t have been possible because it was not a thing, it was the absence of thing: a smear where the frame rate forgot how to draw. After it passes, a hairline crack appears in the paint of the far wall where there hadn’t been one. Nothing else.

He scrubbed back and ran it again. I watched the smear crawl along the screen like oil.

“You see it,” he said.

“I see an effect,” I said. “Not a cause.”

He blew out a breath. “Lab upstairs says the weather feeds have a thermal anomaly over East Harbor at the same time. A flat circle of air two kilometers across that went colder by a fraction of a degree and then stopped being colder.”

“An ice ring over the river,” I said. “That’s—romantic.”

“Save your romance. Email says the mayor’s office wants a find by noon for the cameras. Del told them we don’t do magic. They said do it anyway.”

Del is our director. Del does triage. If the mayor’s office is talking noon and cameras, we’re already in the second of the three kinds of trouble.

“I’ll take the roof,” I said. “I want to feel the lattice.”

“You always want to feel the lattice,” he said in his best imitation of my mother. “Be careful, Mara.”

He only calls me by my first name when he forgets to be sarcastic. He didn’t mean the roof was dangerous. He meant everything else.

The Bureau’s roof is a flat square of tar and gravel spiked with antennas and vents that talk to storms. From up there, you can look across the old district’s brick backs and laundry lines to where the new glass towers hold up the sky like pillars. The river was a long dark muscle, the far shore still blue with sleep. Helicopters were already bugging the air near East Harbor.

There’s a trick to feeling the lattice. You don’t really feel it with any sense. You look at the roar of numbers. You spread it out until it becomes less a roar and more a field. Then, if you’ve been doing this long enough, you can imagine putting your hand out under it like under a shower and tell if the water is too hot or the pressure is wrong. I pressed my eyes shut and let the city’s heartbeat soak in through my eyelids.

Three minutes missing is not a drip. You can drain a reservoir three minutes at a time if you do it a hundred times a day for a year. Doing it once to a whole city is not a leak. It’s someone opening a gate and being sure they’re far away when the guard comes running.

There are theories, and then there are careers. I could call up all the wild things people have suggested over the years: time thieves nestled in basements siphoning subjective seconds from sleepers; corporate time arbitrage, buying microseconds on high-speed market lines and reselling them in bulk to hospitals; cults that believe sacrificing time in common makes them holy. We have gone to all those doors. We have found some interesting people and once, a home-built atomic oven that gave a neighborhood an extra week of summer. We have not found a way to take three minutes out of a city where nothing else broke.

I put my hand out under the shower anyway. There was a feeling like the tiny scar on my left wrist tugging. You can scoff. It’s not magic. It’s years of riding the lattice through night shifts and storm seasons and remembering how glitch noise sounds in your own blood.

I felt a seam. Not over East Harbor where the thermal anomaly had the helicopters doing loops like gnats over fruit. The seam was to the south, where the city turns older without asking permission, where brick gives way to stone and the streets give up on grids. Down past Frogmouth Park, into the Low, where the original harbor had been until they filled it with the bones of ships and the ash of a great fire.

The seam felt like two sheets of reality not pushed together right. There was a sliver where your fingernail could fit.

I opened my eyes and the world made the same shape. That happens, too. You see what you’re looking for. You also see what hurts.

On my way back down, my hand terminal buzzed so hard I almost dropped it. The header said Emergency Feed and then, below, my name in all caps like a charge sheet.

Ms. Quin: A message has been registered in the Municipal Lost Minutes Archive. It is tagged with your identification hash. Due to the time-stamp anomaly, it requires senior review. Please respond.

The Lost Minutes Archive is something we built after the blackout thirteen years ago because it felt like the right thing to do. The city is mostly made of numbers now, and numbers don’t normally believe in ghosts. But after the blackout, we had people with missing months who insisted their bedroom had called them, or that their father’s voice had been heard on a bus stop ad, a voice he only ever used when he was angry. And once in a while, someone's pacemaker would record a pulse that shouldn’t exist, a heartbeat in a room no one was in. We didn’t want to be the department that laughed at grief. So we made a place where impossible things could be written down and then forgotten in a more orderly fashion.

I went to my office because if whatever this was wanted me, I wanted a door I could close. My office is a window with a desk under it, the window looking down into the alley where the food carts line up by eleven. I keep a little rubber plant on the sill. I tell myself that if I can keep the plant alive, I can keep the city on time. The plant is doing better than the city, which cheers me.

I keyed the archive open and typed my authorization twice because my hands were not smooth. The message had a video icon. It said Length: 00:00:23. It said Recorded: 02:15:44 a.m. It said Origin: Unknown, Verified. It said Recipient: Quin, Mara Elis.

It said my name the way the licensing database says my name when I pay parking tickets. Not personal. Institutional. The way the city says it, with all its teeth. My mouth had gone dry.

I hit play.

The video was filthy with compression artifact, the field of view narrowed like the world had been crunched. There were shapes behind the noise: a brick wall that could be any brick wall built before the first war, a set of iron steps that led up and out of frame, a rectangle of pale sky. Sound: traffic far away, a drip. And then the camera turned or the world turned and a face slid into view.

She was older than the last time I had seen her. Older by years I couldn’t hold. The lines around her mouth had deepened and there were new threads of white in her hair. She wore a scarf I had knitted and given away a lifetime ago, ink-black wool with a line of cobalt I’d put in because I needed to look at something blue that winter. Her eyes were the same: serious until she smiled, and she smiled like water breaking around a rock.

“Mara,” Tamsin said, and the walls of my office fuzzed at the edges.

It didn’t matter what the years had done to her. Every muscle in my chest knew that voice. The first time I ever heard it was two blocks from here in a ramen shop when she had asked me if I could spare my seat by the window because she needed to watch the rain. The last time I heard it was on a hospital ward where evening made everything glow a little and monitors made their own quiet rain.

“Mara, I don’t have long,” she said. “I can’t explain it to you the way I’d like. There isn’t the math yet. You have to come—are you listening?” She leaned toward the camera like she could put her hand on my shoulder through it. “Find me where the city is oldest. Listen to me. Bring a watch that doesn’t talk to anything. Bring one you wind. You kept one, of course you did. You always keep things that make the right noises.”

Her hand lifted, and a dark shape entered the frame—a watch, held between two fingers. It was the little brass one she’d bought at a flea market near the park because it ticked like a cat. We had taken turns wearing it. We had joked that if we listened hard enough, we could hear each other in the ticks.

Someone moved behind her. It would have been a shadow if the shadows had looked like they were taller than the doorways. She turned, flinched, and then she did that thing with her mouth, how she arranged it when she had decided to be brave in exactly the stupid way she had always been brave. She turned back to the camera and said my name again like the word could glue everything.

“You’ll understand when you come,” she said. “It’s not a leak. It’s a debt. And I’m paying, and I want you to see—I want you to—”

The image broke into a thousand little squares and came back at the last second to show her eyes too close. “Hurry,” she whispered. “Hurry. They only gave me three minutes.”

The feed ended itself like a phone that no longer wants to be touched. The room was very quiet except for my plant being alive and a small vent in the floor whispering to itself. My mouth finally found enough spit to swallow. In the hall outside, someone laughed in the way people laugh when they have run out of other noises.

I set my hands down on the desk because they needed somewhere to be. After a while, I remembered to breathe the way the therapist taught me when breathing had become optional. I pinched the bridge of my nose and the world unfogged one layer.

I could go to Del and show him the message and he could frown and call Legal, and in six hours I’d still be in meetings in which people would say Tamsin’s name out loud with that careful sympathy they think is a cushion when it’s really a blade. I could tell myself that the Lost Minutes Archive is full of coincidences. I could remember the way Tamsin looked when light did that evening thing and then tell myself that memory is a bad camera.

Or I could get up off the chair.

The “oldest part of the city” is something people argue about in bars. The archaeology students will tell you it’s the pile under the new art museum that used to be a gallows. The sailors will tell you it’s the cradle of docks where boys used to throw stones at passing ships and names blew across the water like paper. The Low is where all of those arguments end up when it starts to rain.

I pulled my desk drawer open. The watch lay in its felt nest like a story I had been stuck on. It was not the exact watch in the video—the little brass case had a square scratch across one corner where I had dropped it once in the market and pretended I had meant to. It was my watch. The one I had bought later when I realized I had sold mine for rent, because sometimes grief looks like a shopping list. It was never the same tick. You cannot buy the same tick twice. But when I wound it and held it to my ear, there was the right noise.

Sami was in the hall. He took one look at me and started to say my name and then stopped. He is not an unobservant man. His eyes flicked to the watch in my hand and away like it was too much skin.

“Del is tightening the noose,” he said instead. “He wants you in his office ten minutes ago.”

“I’ll send him a note,” I said.

“Do you need backup?” he asked, like we were going to roust a meth lab and not the last three minutes of a morning.

“You’re not going to like the part where I say I don’t know what I need,” I said. Then, because he deserved better than my habit of withholding nouns, I added, “I got a message.”

He made a face. “From what.”

“From who,” I said. “From Tamsin.”

He did not do the thing where he looked sorry for me. He had been here for all the bad years and knows better. His face moved through something complicated and came out the other side with determination. “You tell Del,” he said.

“I will,” I said, the way someone says I love you when they are already halfway down a staircase.

Out in the street, the morning had decided to be beautiful in that irritating way it does when the worst thing you can imagine has set up camp inside your mouth. The sky was a worn denim, the river a strip of tin, the low sun catching on a thousand windows and making a thousand knives. People had decided to go to work. They had all had the same thing happen and they had all decided to ignore it in the same stubborn human way. The coffee carts along the alley were steaming. A man in a suit shouted into his collar about futures.

I walked toward the Low with my coat open and my hand on the watch in my pocket. East Harbor glittered to my left where the helicopters scissored the air. I cut south where the streets go narrow and the city pretends to be small. The smell changed from winter and hot brakes to damp brick and bread. There is a cat in the Low that looks like snow falling upward. It glared at me from a stoop and then yawned.

My feet did the work. I had lived down here when I first got the job, in a room where you could hear other people’s dreams through the wall. Tamsin had hated it for me and loved it for herself. She liked stoops, and soup sold in plastic buckets, and the way old stones keep secrets by humming them to their cousins. We walked here for hours early in that first spring, trying to make the city speak its names.

There’s a passage under an iron stair near Goose Alley that leads into a courtyard that is not on any of the tourist maps. If you go through and sit on the broken bench and wait long enough, a woman will come out and sell you slices of cake with oatmeal in them that taste like falling asleep. We had found that by accident because one night the rain had made us too tired to walk around the block. I went there without thinking, and when I turned left under the stair there was the brick wall from the video, the iron steps up into the frame like a scrawl in pencil. There was the rectangle of sky, cut the wrong shape.

My watch ticked in my palm. It ticked in its own way, against the city’s purr, against the helicopters thrumming over the river, against my own blood.

The air was colder there by a breath. The “seam” I had felt on the roof had a sound, a thinness. It’s hard to write down, and that’s why the archive has so few good entries. Everyone comes to the edge of it and then says they felt something and then the words fall away.

I am better with numbers than words. It was 09:43 by the Root when I stepped into the courtyard. The tick in my pocket was ten seconds behind because I had wound it with my fingers and my fingers were not precise. The courtyard was empty. The cake woman was not there. The bench was still broken but differently broken, like it had broken more in the absence of being sat on.

There was chalk on the bricks near the drain where children or the very old play their games. It was drawn over like layers of weather. Hopscotch boxes and a boat and a face with too many teeth and then, over all of it, a circle. Not perfectly drawn. Not mechanical. A hand had done that. Around the circle, a dozen little hatch marks. The kind you make when you are counting seconds you cannot hold. In the circle, someone had written four words that made my throat close.

You are late, Mara.

The watch beat harder in my hand, and far above the courtyard a helicopter hesitated in the air like a second that did not want to be spent. I put my fingers on the chalk circle before the city asked who I thought I was. The brick felt colder inside the line than out. Someone had made a shape and the world had agreed to lean into it.

I blew out a breath. The city’s lattice hummed at the edge of hearing like bees down a garden path. The chalk dust came up on my fingers like the aftertaste of lightning.

“Fine,” I said out loud to no one and to Tamsin and to the Root and to the sky and to whatever had put its hand in through the wall of my morning. “Fine. I’m here.”

The chalk line didn’t answer. The courtyard didn’t rearrange itself like the backs of cards. The watch did not stop. The only thing that changed was me, because I stepped forward into a three-minute hole and asked it to show me what it had stolen.

Chapter One

The snow in Dead Layer Six remembers cold, but it won't give you any. Each flake lands without temperature, a chalk smudge on your glove, a hush over the crunch your brain expects. I watch my breath, counting, because we're taught to keep numbers when senses won't cooperate. Sixty-eight. Sixty-nine. A hundred and twenty seconds in, you start to think the layer has learned your pulse. That's how it pulls you closer.

"Three minutes, Annel," Jet says in my ear. Her voice is a line thrown from the present, knotted around the bones near my jaw. The bone mic vibrates more feeling than sound. "No heroics."

"No heroics," I say, and my words come back dampened, as if the air has read them and decided they're not canonical.

I step around a bend in a street that doesn't bend anymore. Six is a winter city, retired three updates ago, when the Choir decided people were less likely to riot if sunlight had a later, softer appetite. In Six, the sky is a lid of pewter and the lampposts lean under white caps. The buildings are familiar, but they don't slouch where they should; a cornice stays, an awning goes. Dead Layers are not history; they're drafts. You can tell what the present fought with by what got left behind.

My boots leave no marks. I don't cross the plow line because the part of my head that keeps us safe at home has made rules: never linger where many feet lingered; never look too long at the suggestion of a face; never follow music. The last one has exceptions. I carry a harmonizer in my pocket, a thumb-sized comb of ceramic that hums a tone only I can hear when I press it against the inside of my teeth. The harmonizer is cheap insurance. The expensive protection is Jet, the anchor on the present end, counting with me, telling me when my feet start ghost-drifting sideways.

I am here for a toaster.

Not the appliance. A design. Xeno-Joy, old boutique maker of industrial kitchen art. The present erased its version of "joy" for a while—too much bright advertising, too many pink mouths—and then decided to bring it back clean, without brand names anyone could sue over. A collector wants the original, wants to hold a curve of metal the current world denies existed.

I know which block the toaster prefers. It had a storefront in Six, back when Christmas was a sanctioned ritual and you could still say "Merry" without the Choir's semantics tossing you a warning. In the present the space is a rehabbed clinic that sells sleep in twelve-minute increments. In Six it's a narrow boutique with a window full of chrome. The glass hums a memory of finger smears.

"Two and a half," Jet says. "You sure Indra isn't pulling your leg with this request?"

"I'm sure the credits clear at midnight," I say. "Open."

Doors in Dead Layers don't open. You convince them. I press the harmonizer against a seam at knee height and breathe shallow. My left hand holds graycloth—a woven sheet that persuades my eyes not to tell my brain the wrong story. We fold our lives around this cloth. Graycloth on shelves, on mirrors, over cupboards. Graycloth keeps you from seeing what shouldn't be there, and when you work the layers you learn to hold it ready like a saint holds a relic.

The seam yields the way a dream yields if you think about it right. The bell rings, a shiver like a glass nerve, and it calls to no one.

Inside, the light is dust and condescension. Xeno-Joy. I could swear the woman who owned this place had a shaved head and a thousand-watt grin, but memory pulls like a bandage. The toasters are lined in ranks; half of them are pure idea, polished curves and meaningless knobs meant to seduce your hunger.

"South wall," Indra had said, mapping this for me from the scant maps you can make of a thing that isn't here anymore. "Third shelf. Box with orange tape."

I move straight. The longer you're in, the more the layer notices, like a pond forming a skin around you. If you want to leave, you have to come back through the same hole you made, and holes close without warning when the Choir retunes the present to adjust for weather, for grief, for million other metrics. We have learned to be respectful. We have not, as a civilization, learned to leave ghost cities alone.

The box is where it's supposed to be. It's little better than a polaroid of corrugated cardboard, edges soft, orange tape dulled gray. I slide it towards me and everything in the shop seems to take a single breath.

There's always something else. On my third day in the business I pulled a fifteen-kilo typewriter from Dead Layer Zero, soaked in a calendar we barely remember, and a woman behind me exhaled. I turned to say hello to a pattern of soot and sunlight that had looked like a person until I gave it attention. I lost two months to lag and a syrup of sadness that stuck to my teeth, and when I came back I had a stutter I still exercise away when I think too hard about it. We say our profession like a confession: I'm a retriever. We say it like we're trying to absolve ourselves for making the past into a market.

"One minute," Jet says. "Annel, I'm looking at weather on our side. Choir's hiccuping."

"Noted." I fold graycloth over the box and tie it fast with two loops through sewn eyes, the way my mother taught me. The box becomes a suggestion only. The cloth is smart enough to damp my brain's labeling reflex. The moment I cover the object, its address in reality blurs. It's harder to steal something from the present if no one can be sure it's there.

The bell rings again.

My throat goes dry. Closed loop variables. Bells are fussy in the layers. Sometimes the sound of a door is attached to a door that isn't the one you're using. I look up and the shop is full of snow, and she is standing in the entry like a maybe.

She's not a smear. She's not a smear.

She is a woman in a red coat with wet hair clumped to her cheeks and an expression that says she understands what a doorbell does. Her eyes find me. This is the part that's impossible. This is the part that the training says does not happen.

"One minute," Jet repeats, and then, as if she has cut the wire with her teeth, her voice is gone.

We look at each other across a floor made of a winter that never was. Her boots do not sink. Neither do mine. Her coat drips water that evaporates before it manages to stain. This is what the layers do: they mirror cause without effect like a child explaining a magic trick.

Nothing in Six should look at me. Nothing should say my name.

"Annel," she says.

I have breath again, but it's wrong. It winds in my chest. The harmonizer buzzes against my teeth, a mosquito in my skull, but the tone warbles, choked through a hand.

I do the only thing you're not supposed to do. I let the graycloth slide down enough to see her better.

She's young and older than me, all at once. Her features are not the present's standard hires. The Choir likes faces that sit at the mean of the data. Hers is a data set we deleted. Angular. Freckles under winter light. An old mouth scar that I notice because my fingers twitch as if they want to touch it, as if they've touched it before.

I know her. I don't know her.

"Who are you?" My voice shreds itself on the bell's echo. The bell is like an idea that's learned to persist.

She tilts her chin like I've asked a riddle with an obvious answer. "You are out of time." She says it so gently I nearly laugh. It's an accurate statement. I don't find humor here. The door is still open behind her, and outside is the kind of gray that distorts corners.

"Thirty seconds," Jet says, but her voice is muffled, as if she's speaking through snow.

The woman steps in. Your instincts insist on fundamental rules: if she is in the layer, she cannot leave the layer. If she sees you, you are not in the layer—no, if she sees you, you are in a different part of the layer than you think. I bite down on the harmonizer. It squeals. The seam behind me pulls like a tide.

The red coat drips one drop. The drop lands on the floor with a sound so wet it stings in my ear. The layers sometimes give you gestures. They like to play.

She moves her hand to her coat pocket. I want to run. I want to stand still long enough to memorize her and never come back. Rule: do not accept gifts in the layers. You cannot bring living things forward. You cannot bring language forward that didn't settle. You cannot bring intention forward. We bring objects. That's all.

She pulls out a sprig of green.

I see it as if my eyes have remembered how to focus. It's a weed. A simple weed you'd curse between paving stones. It's not a plant the present would want to ban; we haven't done the purge of harmful seeds in this part of the world yet. It's a weed, and it is alive. It is alive where nothing is supposed to be anything but a best guess.

"Ten seconds," Jet says, barely sound at all. It is like she is on the other side of a river.

The woman in the red coat holds the weed to me. Its roots are wrapped in brown paper. I smell dirt. Six has withheld cold and my nose has learned to stop asking for it, but dirt is new enough to make my heart hit hard.

Rule: do not accept.

"Please," she says, and the bell swallows the word, but I catch it.

I am not a saint. I am paid to transgress nicely. I take the weed.

Her hand is colder than the layer.

Everything in the shop shifts. The bell screams. Outside, the snow stops not falling and starts staying in midair like static. The edges of the world pixelate where the present is tugging against the dead. The harmonizer in my mouth goes silent. My brain tries to throw up.

"Now," says Jet, and her voice is a rope that has skinned my palms before. "Annel now."

The seam behind me is a line of hunger. I fling the graycloth over the plant and jam it under my coat, already wet where my skin is sweating. The box goes under my arm. I do not say goodbye to the impossible woman because if I label her, she will take up more room in my life.

She steps back, one step, two, her boots a ritual without pressure. The bell rings one last time, a sour note as if it's learned language and is trying it on.

I let the seam take me.

You always expect more light going home. It's never more light. It's a refusal of perspective. The alley is too narrow and not narrow enough, the angle of my shoulder wrong relative to my ear. Then the Choir catches me, and reality lays me down like a mother convinced I'm feverish.

I am in the present. The snow is rain. It is afternoon in our current version, and the sky is the exact color of a manila folder, because the Choir has decided to lower our sadness for two days by giving us the earth-tones we said calm us in surveys. The lampposts are smart poles with banner ads you only see if you let your eyes stray left. Six returns to being a database entry. My boots leave prints. The graycloth itches.

"You're back," Jet says, the relief in the slump of her syllables catching me by the shirtfront and shaking. "Annel? Speak."

"Have you ever seen a weed before, Jet?"

Her silence is half a second. Then: "Weed? In there? Did you bring it—"

"Now would be a good time not to have this conversation," I say, and peel myself off the alley wall. I retune my perception out of panic and into tasks: tuck the graycloth tighter; re-wrap the harmonizer; count my fingers. I count nine because my pinky has gone sideways again, my brain ignoring it until I wiggle. Ten. I take two steps. The world flexes and then forgives me for leaving.

Jet meets me on the corner in a coat the color of faded oil and a hat built to make her look less like a lark and more like a citizen. She is shorter than me but wider in all the ways that matter. Her arms are for hauling idiots home.

"Do not say you brought flora across," she says, not actually saying it. Jet can vector irony into a look. "I can't handle a quarantine this week."

"Indra will pay double if I bring names 'from before' printed on the original packaging," I say, because jokes are how we deflect panic without twitching.

"You're deflecting panic without twitching." Her mouth tightens. "You were clipping at the seam. Choir hiccuped. You went out of my metrics for eight point three seconds."

"Did the world end?"

"I'm saving my predictions for my memoirs. Did you get it?"

I hold out the box, which we both refuse to focus on. Jet leans forward, hands hovering, and does what only very good anchors learn to do: she touches the air two inches from the thing and lets her skin decide. Her knuckles relax. "That's it."

"For Indra," I say. "And a bonus."

"You didn't."

"Not talk here," I say. The paranoia of people who walk the dead is not entirely paranoia. Some folks go into the layers for thrills; some to hunt data like old code that the Choir didn't thread through; some to find lost faces and get lost with them. There are laws against commercialization, which are enforced when it makes a good example. I am not interested in being a very instructive headline. We move.

Our route is a practiced weave through the blocks the present has made safe for commerce. The city is a machine of polite insistence: turn your shoulders this way; lift your chin this way. The Choir is not God; it's a weather system we built around our heads. There are dead microphones in the architecture that no longer talk to anything. There are living ones in the shapes of pigeons. Jet has a trick where she whistles an old song and the mics stutter, busy translating a melody no one uses to speak anymore. She whiffs a whistle between her teeth and the world thins.

We go down to the Rust, a market named for a color that means hunger to some and authenticity to others. Indra's shop is part of the Rust's curated rot: a jewelry cart between a man who sells clouds in jars and a woman with canaries trained to land only on hands that have held grief recently. Indra wears brown like it is a law.

"You are late," Indra says, which we translate to mean she was worried. "And damp."

"Your toaster fought back," I say. I slide the graycloth up just enough for her to touch the corner of the box. She closes her eyes and inhales that particular absence primitive brains decide is the smell of "object you could cut yourself on." She nods. "Worth the fee."

"And then some," I say.

She opens her eyes. Her pupils pin like she's looked at a light. "Miss Keene. I don't renegotiate."

"Not that." I glance at Jet. She has put her hands in her pockets and is very deliberately not paying attention, which in the Rust is exactly the right attention. "I brought you something else less tangible. A rumor with teeth."

Indra hums interest between her molars. "You are a dealer in rumors now? I have suppliers for those." Her amusement softens the edges of her face.

"In Six," I say, low. "A person spoke to me."

Indra freezes so beautifully I almost applaud. The lines around her mouth are a clock. She measures three beats with the tiny movement of her lower lash. "You saw someone," she says, uselessly precise.

"She saw me," I say.

The Rust hum stutters around us. It's a market of people who know how to hear an oddity. Jet takes her hands out of her pockets, which means she endorses whatever idiocy I'm going to say next.

"And," I continue, because sometimes the only way is through, "she gave me something alive."

The word spills like cinnamon and anger. Indra opens her mouth and then stops, rearranges, starts again. "We cannot talk here," she says, honest for once. "You'll ruin my lunch."

We go to the back. The back is narrow. The walls have been painted once for every era since the last true mayor. The chairs are all found and all of them wobble. I pull the graycloth back enough to slip the plant onto the table. It is as banal as it was in the layer: three leaves, a broken stem, a smear of earth holding the roots together.

The room cools in a way I have felt only under a mountain. Jet puts her hand down near the plant and every hair on her arm lifts. Indra takes a step back and then forward again because she is superstitious enough to be practical.

"It's not a special weed," I say, hearing hysteria crouch and grin in my own voice.

"It's impossible," Indra says, which is another way of saying it's expensive.

Jet tilts her head and in that motion I know that if she told me now to throw it in the river, I'd go, and if she told me to put it in my mouth and swallow, I might.

"Where?" she says.

"Xeno-Joy's in Six," I say. "A woman in a red coat. She said my name."

"You told her?" Indra grabs the air as if she could throttle me through it.

"She told me," I say. My hands have started to shake. I watch them as if they belong to someone else. "She knew me."

There is a point past which fear turns into curiosity, and then past that there is something else—the itch for a pattern that makes sense. I am built for that itch. It's why I'm good at walking where I shouldn't. It's why I nearly married a gambler once and why I quit before he could teach me how to lose my house.

Indra picks up the plant as if it will cut her. Graycloth is good at persuasion, so she's careful not to let her skin make decisions about it. "You'll need a dampener," she says. "And probably an advocate. Perhaps three." She glances at me sideways. "I have a client for you."

"I just made you richer than your mother thought you'd be," I say. "Be gentle."

"Don't make me fond of you, Keene," she says. "It's not flattering on me." Her eyes flick to Jet. "Keep her alive."

"I was planning on it," Jet says. "I'm the one with the unglamorous job."

Indra reaches under the table to the safe-latch with the glitch that looks like rust. She pulls out a packet envelope, slick with legalese, and slaps it down where the plant's shadow says it is midday somewhere. On the envelope is a name I've seen in interesting footnotes.

Lian Oort.

The O is stricken through, an affectation. The kind of genius who edits their own signature. The kind who edited the Choir's version of restless for about six weeks before the Choir learned it could edit back.

"Dr. Oort," Indra says, as if she has invented him. "He is an investor of mine. He is an investor of a great many people. He has gone missing."

"People 'go missing' if they fail to accept an update," Jet says, not gentle. "They get folded. They stop being where we are."

"People go missing for many reasons." Indra taps the envelope. "He went into a dead layer on purpose and did not return at the scheduled time. An intentional lag. He left neat folders in neat places to be discovered by neat women, because he admires neatness. He sent me a message, and I ignored it, because one ignores men like him when they snap their fingers. Now I wish I had snapped back."

"And the plant?" I ask.

Indra looks at me in a way that matters. "If there is life in there," she says softly, "then someone is dragging life around with them. Someone with instruments, or someone with—" Her hand flips as if she could dislodge the right word from her wrist. "With an old-fashioned gift. Oort had both. He wants to be found. Or he wants the person who can stand looking to find him first, before someone worse does. I suspect those two people might be the same person." She watches me watch her. "He wants you, Miss Keene."

I deserve it when the world does the thing where it twists and then repeats.

"He shouldn't want me," I say.

"And yet," Jet murmurs.

"And yet," Indra agrees.

There's a rustling like birds in a dream. I realize it's from the hall—a child running past, a vendor haggling three stalls down, a law pitched to be overheard. It's good to remind myself the world is mundane and crowd-flavored. If I concentrate too hard on impossibilities, I won't eat dinner.

"What does he pay," I say, and my voice is the flat tone of someone who doesn't know how to refuse a mystery without a number to tie it to.

Indra smiles without joy. "He payed me then. He will pay you now if we touch the right paper. He will pay later in access to things you should be too wise to want." She pushes the envelope closer with two fingers. "And if this is not his doing, if you have brushed a structure in Six that should not be, then we will all pay in a different currency. So take it, so I can pretend the world is a ledger."

I take the envelope. It sticks lightly to my fingertips. My old name trembles inside my mouth, and I swallow it back because you are not supposed to keep too many versions of yourself, and because the woman in the red coat already called one of them into the light without asking permission.

"We start tonight," Jet says, matter-of-fact.

"We start now," I say, surprising myself. I lay my hand over the graycloth-wrapped weed and feel it. It is rude and stubborn and alive in a way the present almost never is. There are hotels of livingness in our city—the greenhouses, the regulated forests—but this is different. This is wild at the edges. "She knew my name, Jet."

"People knowing your name isn't special," Jet says. "Being called the wrong one is."

I think of the scar on the woman's mouth. I think of the bell screaming. I think of the void that is Six and the fact that snow tried to be snow.

Outside, the Choir releases a new palette. The sky goes from folder-beige to a salaried periwinkle that flatters the faces most likely to buy things. In the corner of Indra's back room, a stack of crates emits a sigh, adjusting to new parameters. My jaw aches from the harmonizer. My fingers itch to go under again.

I look at Jet. She doesn't say don't. She knows better.

We pretend we don't hear the bell ringing where there is no door. We plan. We count. We map the dead's appetite onto ours. We go back.

Chapter One: The Gray Minute

At 02:14:12, the future disappears.

Nia Quell is halfway down the service shaft when the advisory threads on her left eye go dull, their usual ghost-blue arcs blanching to the color of spent breath. The room around her is all cold metal and insulation foam and a humming that lives too low for the ear; the air tastes like melted coin. The wet-slick rungs of the ladder thrum with the heartbeat of the city above, a complicated rhythm of pumps and traffic harmonics and millions of tiny corrections, all of it choreographed by what spirals beneath her feet.

She pauses on the rung, weight balanced, gloved fingers curled, and watches the last suggestion vanish from her sight like a fish slipping into depths.

Outside, she knows, someone in a corner shop fifteen blocks up has just been told nothing about which coffee to pour or how to angle his wrist to avoid a spill. Someone riding the rail between the river and the refinery is holding the handhold without the muscle-tightening ripple of anticipated braking that spares their shoulder. Someone in a surgical theatre, wrists already inside a chest cavity, invites silence where there should be a stream of nudges: tilt two degrees, tighter clamp, breathe now. A world that has never had to remember how to guess, all at once, must guess.

The shaft is a spine descending through the backbone of the Augury Vault, and she can feel every segment of it flex. Nia doesn't let herself look away from the numbers scrolling on the rung-cam display: coolant pressure in helium loop A, acceptable; loop B, flirting with borderline; filaments in lattice panel twenty-six reporting a jitter amplitude well outside tolerances. The cause of the jitter should be five floors down—a cryogrid spool, ancient by human terms, new by the vault's.

Half a second has passed. Two.

Her retinas remain blank.

"Nia?" The voice arrives through her bonepack, Kiro's voice thickened by a yawn and clipped by urgency. "You seeing what I'm seeing?"

She hooks her boot and lets go with one hand to tap her throatback. "It's not local," she says. "I'm in the shaft. Look at the sky. Check other cities."

"I'm looking," Kiro says. The background sound on the line is a quickening clatter of keys; he refuses to let the system do his typing for him and has always told her it was to keep his fingers honest. "Nanking's steady. Cape's steady. I... the West Lattice just dropped predictive density by nineteen percent. And the feed's doing something I don't like."

Nia reaches bottom, boots touching down on grate. Her breath plumes and dissolves unheard. Above her the shaft continues its song. Ahead of her, the door to Vault B wears a rim of hoarfrost.

"Define 'something I don't like,'" she says.

"Packets are looping back," Kiro says. "The advice stream is trying to correct for itself. It thinks the outage is itself."

"That can't happen." Nia presses her palm to the door's furry metal skin. The vault's temperature pushes through layers of glove to knife her hand.

"I didn't say it can," Kiro says. "I said it's doing it."

Nia inhales once and lets the air out slowly. The blankness of her left-eye overlay is suddenly as present as the cold. Usually there is always something there: the ghostly gentle web of suggestions and cautions, probabilities woven tight as breath, whispering their percentages, vibrating whenever a choice moves the needle more than a percent. She keeps her overlays tuned low to avoid getting woozy, but silence is stranger than noise.

Beneath her boots the card reader glows its lone dot. It does not advise her to clean the ice from the slot before inserting her hand. It does not tell her the quickest way to do it without cutting her glove. It simply waits.

This is not the first time Nia has seen advice fail. There was last winter's microbrown when the Eastern coil had a phase insult; there was the imprecise hour seven years ago, when the Western loop decided that half the cats in the district were children and sent half the district's drones into a heartwarming frenzy of deliveries. There was the blackout, which she remembers only as a story, because it ended before she had words. But even then, during previous hiccups, the blue threads never fully vanished. They thinned. They hazed. They let her go wrong only in provinces with railings.

Now the future is gone.

She scrapes the slot clean with a gloved finger until she feels metal. The mechanism wakes reluctantly. The hairline door slides open. The hinge noise is huge. She crouches and ghosts through the narrow gap into the vault.

Inside there's only cold. It moves like a weather front, an invading thing, the breath-harvesters at the far end of the room exhaling into a massive filament forest. The cryogrid spools sit like fonts in a cathedral, their ceramic shells bearing numbers hand-painted a century ago when a human had time to make symbols beautiful. A fog of nitrogen sleeps above the floor like an idea that cannot be disturbed. The lights are old incandescent rope, coiled around pillars that sprouted before Nia was born. The coil of the city. The brain made of ice.

She is acutely aware of her own body in that space, the unsmoothing edges of her movement when nothing suggests how to move. She takes the path she would take if she were alone in a field with rain. The knots at the corners of her mind that are always resting against the cushion of advisories seek purchase and do not find it.

"Nia, they're calling it a 'gray minute.'" Kiro's voice finds a rhythm of its own. "Three more cities reporting gray. How close are you?"

"Going eyes," Nia says. She unspools her vision down the length of the room and past the fretting forest of circuits that feed the sub-basement lattices. The cryogrid spool in twenty-six. The light above it is flame-orange: not a stop, but not a go. She jogs, breath hitching, and her cough echoes once—a gunshot in a church.

She's close enough to hear the defective spool before she sees it: a staccato clicking that shouldn't be there, like a beetle trapped between walls. She rounds the pillar and there it is, hairline cracks already forming across the ceramic scarf, frost blossoming around them like a living thing. Within that shell is a ribbon of latticed quartz spun in vacuum and aged in microgravity under prayer. Within that ribbon is a financial miser's hoard of moment-sources, entangled with their wedded pairs across the other side of the room. Within those moment-sources are the seeds by which the city tastes itself as if it were a tongue tasting the air. The spool is sympathy and twin and the interior of a cathedral bell.

Do not hope it can hold, she tells herself, and does not attach percentages to the thought.

She sets down the repair kit on the grid, kneels, opens its mouth. Inside is a pair of unpacked gloves, two compression bands, a spool clamp like a black metal moth, a case of filament epoxy, three microfuses, and a two-lettered card in her handwriting telling future-Nia: Remember the coil wants to live. In pencil she has scrawled beneath that: Or remember nothing wants to live.

"Nia, how close?"

"With her," she says. "It's a crack. It's doing the jitter. I don't think it's a chain, but I think it's trying to become one."

"Blink me," Kiro says.

She pushes a double tap to her throatback, opening his view to her headcam. A ghost-Kiro appears in her ear, breath already moving faster. "Too much frost for epoxy. Can you clamp and swap?"

"They're still in production," she says. "If I take one down, our density drops even more, it goes from gray to... I don't know. Worse. I can—"

A sound from behind her. Not a sound, she realizes, but the absence of a sound that had been background all along. The loops. The loops have stuttered. The vault holds its breath.

"Nia," Kiro says, and in his voice at last something like fear. "They're asking for an estimate. The Council."

She anchors the compression bands around the cracked splice with calm hands and a heart gone unruly. "Fifty seconds," she lies, because he needs a number. She sets the clamp's twin mouths across the crack and winds down as the ceramic protests with a noise like dry teeth grinding.

Her left-hand overlay is still blank. The right eye shows Kiro's face in the corner, his hair in its usual careful chaos, his mouth pressed flat. Behind him the operations room is a nest of chairs and wires and a row of tea cups, steam still curling from the last one to be poured, all of it lit by the wash of wall displays that have gone abruptly minimalist. They were never meant to be this calm.

She presses a fingertip against the crack. The ceramic sings. Somewhere in the guts of the vault, ice harvesters exhale and inhale. She turns the clamp a fraction more, and the sound changes. Not good or bad. Simply different. She glances at the pressure readouts on the clamp handle. They ache toward acceptable.

"Nia," Kiro says again, softer, and she knows without looking that he's watching her as a way to remain anchored to his own body. "Do you remember when you were a student and Vandel made us practice with the overlays off?"

"I remember thinking he was sadistic," Nia says. The memory arrives with salt and chalk: the training hall's scuffed floor, the old man with hands like dried riverbeds, his voice carrying over the scissoring lab noise. Learn to feel the world with your own nerves, he had told them, because any system loves a surprise and eventually it will give you one.

"He was sadistic," Kiro says, and then, quieter: "They're saying sixty seconds. They're calling it a minute. They think it will stop at a minute."

"It doesn't know a minute," Nia says. She feels the truth of it in her wrists. She closes the clamp and sets epoxy into the microfissures like jam into cracks in bread. The epoxy sets like frost kissed by sun. "What does the world look like?"

"Mostly people's faces," he says, and she hears him swallow. "They're not built for this. Ambulances are on manual. Someone decided to try to land a hopper in the river without advisories and everyone on the walkway tried to help. Traffic's slower because it can't be faster. The chorus in Quadrant Eight stopped singing because they didn't know whether the last note was the last note."

Nia's smile is a baring of teeth to no one. "They'll be fine," she says, because lying to your friends in a vault has never been illegal.

She fumbles the glove of her right hand, her finger catching, and freezes. The glove tip is frayed. It's not a hole, but it's the beginning of one. Her skin tightens. The clamp holds; the crack holds; she has seven seconds, maybe nine, before the spool will force a new decision on her.

"Nia," Kiro says, and his voice changes shape. "You feel that?"

She doesn't, at first. And then she does—not with her skin but the part of her that has always been held by a net. The net tugs once, twice. The blankness of her overlay ripples. A blue thread lifts from nothing like a nerve resuming an old impulse, and in the corner of her left-eye the familiar font appears, the one that has soothed her through every test and flood and failure: Shift weight to left foot, 98.3% risk reduction.

It's small, stupid advice, but it is the voice of home after months away.

She shifts her weight and a blur of frost falls from the spool's lip, slides down her boot instead of into her glove.

"There," Kiro breathes. "There it is. See? It's—"

People always speak as if the voice of Augury is one voice. It is not one voice, but a chorus of millions of small voices that sing together and never trip on the ankles of their music. They are the prediction of the face you will make when you talk about your mother and the delay between taps of a broken tooth against a glass. They are the sum of every heartbeat recorded and every footfall measured. It is a craven, gorgeous, comforting thing.

The next advisory blossoms: Tighten clamp 2.3°. And a different advisory, almost simultaneous, from nowhere: Stop. Do not touch it.

The second one is not blue. It is a white word burning into the blank like a torch. The font is wrong; it is not a font she recognizes, and Nia knows fonts the way a smith knows steel. It feels as if it were etched into glass and then dragged there.

Her hand stops. Her body obeys the white.

"Nia?" Kiro says, uncertain now. "It wants you to clamp."

"It says the opposite," she says, and hears the click as the words tumble into the vault's cold.

"What says the opposite?" He sounds wrong in her ear when he doesn't know.

"I don't know," she says, which is the simplest terror there is. The white letters linger. Do not touch it, NIA QUELL. She has never seen her own name used that way by the system. The system knows her; it knows every operator; it knows her shoulder width and heat map and that she once broke her left ring finger and it did not set right until the second try. But it does not talk to her as if it were a person. It does not say her name as if it had a human mouth.

"Kiro," she says, because the alternative is to stop talking, "the new overlay is addressing me."

"That's not... we don't..." He flees grammar. "What did it say?"

"It told me not to touch it," she says, and again the white text burns from nowhere, not placed but fixed to the world itself as if written on the air before she chose to look through it: Do not tighten the clamp another degree. The failure is not in the ceramic.

She goes absolutely still. The clamp is mid-turn. Her glove is a hair from the grip. The spool hums, and through the hum she hears something else, not in the epoxy, not in the ceramic. A dry clicking in the base of the pillar. The part that the clamp does not touch. She eases back and the sounds do not change.

"Kiro," she says again, because his name is a ritual of the present and she needs it. "I think it's the mount."

"It can't be the mount," he says reflexively. "The mount is bonded into the vault's skeleton. It's beyond failure rating."

"Everything is failure until it isn't," she says, and there was a professor once who said that with hands that shook because she was ninety-seven and had watched a storm take her house away while her overlays told her they would not. Nia dives to her kit again, her hands now moving fast on memory because there is still the white voice, waiting; she finds the thin metal wedge, the one that exists for the situations that are "beyond failure rating" because she has put her kit together and she thinks that way.

She grinds the wedge into the seam beneath the spool skirt. A serrated vibration tells her she has made contact with a thing that is not now as it was an hour ago.

The blue overlay populates the selection of wedges she should use, their thickness, the torque she'll need. The white overlay overlays the overlay. No wedge between mount and spool. Remove spool.

"You want me to what?" she says, before she remembers that the thing reading her does not respond to voice, and maybe not to language at all. The spool is not meant to be removed under load. The spool is meant to be married to its twin until the city dies and its bones are eaten by a cooler distance. She could do it. She could spool it out like pulling thread from a wound. If she's wrong she will break a thing that cannot be repaired, not tonight, perhaps not ever.

"Nia, choose," Kiro says, and his voice is in her ear but also far, and behind it the hiss of voices in the ops room, the hungry noise of a world that wants its soft net back across its own skin. "They're calling it now. Thirty-four seconds remaining in the gray minute."

The white text says: The minute is not gray. The minute is a door.

And with that it is not an advisory, anymore, but an announcement to her bones. Something in her remembers that she once stood on a river's stone and chose a path to leap to the next stone, and if she missed, she would be in the water, and the river would not care about her. There is a joy in choosing when no one is telling you, and a terror. The joy feels like a friend she has not seen. The terror is the shape of her skin.

She wraps the spool strap around her upper arm and slides the catch under the lip. She unhooks the clamp. The ceramic sighs but does not crack further. She leans her shoulder into the strap and lifts with her legs not her back, and she is crying without realizing it, not because she is sad or happy but because you cannot breathe when you are holding a city and you do not know if it will come with you.

It comes, an inch, and then another. The mount is a darkness swallowing that which does not want to be swallowed. The clicking stops. For a heartbeat the whole lattice seems to not only hum but sing, a high note that cats would run from, and then it subsides. Nia lowers the spool to its cradle and stands with her hands on her knees, laughing once, a hitching bark.

The blue overlay shimmers, agitated. Error: contradictory advice stream. Please reconcile. Nia snorts, and the sound fogs the air. She has never liked that the network asks humans to reconcile. It always felt like the net smiling at them and saying, So—what kind of creature are you?

The white text returns. Look at the underside of the mount.

She crouches. She looks. There is a hair caught there, the width of a human hair but not hair, a wire not in the schematics. It runs through a gap that should not be a gap, and it is not iced over like it should be, and its insulation is bitten. The bite is fine-toothed, not mechanical. Nia touches the wire with a gloved finger while praying to no one, and the wire gives a tiny yelp and zips back through the gap like a startled animal.

"I do not like being surprised in my skull," she says.

"Nia?" Kiro says, and it is the voice of someone who has been watching maps redraw themselves in cruelly beautiful patterns. "Whatever you did, do more of it. The overlay density is rebounding.
