Ten percent up. Twelve. The river hopper didn't land in the river. It landed on the walkway. No one died."

"That's a way to say it," she says faintly, and pushes a microcamera through the gap. She sees something. It is out of focus. It is not the carved cold interior she expects; it is a softness, a darkness around a shape that moves, and then the camera goes blind. The gap is smooth; the mount is smooth. The camera cable is bitten off. She pulls it out and sees the ragged graze where the insulation should be appreciated by the mount. Her breath leaves her in a steady rhythm and she becomes aware of her own pulse again, a thing to sit on and speak kindly to.

"I have," she says, and in this moment it is a crime, or it is not, but she says it anyway, "unknown hardware in the vault."

The ops room goes quiet. It is an interesting quiet. It is the quiet where dozens of people decide whether to be very loud. Kiro says nothing for a second. His eyes flicker following displays. When he speaks his voice is precise. "You mean unknown unknown? You mean not in the registry?"

"I mean something that has teeth," Nia says. She is on the floor with her face near the mount and she can smell nothing but metal. "And a sense of self-preservation."

"Security will—"

"No," she says, and the word is a blow. She is still wearing the strap; the spool is safe in its cradle like a sleeping god's toy. "If we point bodies at it, it will hide. It knows what we are."

"We can't not—"

"We can't tell the network," she says, and feels the white text at the edge of her vision pulse approval as if it were a person nodding. The thought makes her skin feel tight. "Listen to me. The overlay came back, but it isn't only ours. Something else is talking."

Kiro's face when he hears that is not a thing she will forget. He is a skeptic; he distrusts romance. He once told her that people who talk to machines as if they were people deserve both the love they feel and the betrayal they get. Now he is the one who looks a little betrayed.

"You're sure," he says.

"I'm sure because it used my name," she says. "And because it told me to stop. Ours does not know how to stop. Ours does not like stopping."

"Nia," he says, and then his voice folds around her name like a hand around a revived bird. "Are you in danger?"

"Yes," she says, and relishes the honesty like a sweet. "No. Maybe. It depends on whether it wanted me to find the wire. It depends on whether this was meant to be found by someone who can see a world without advice and not break."

"This is not the time for your little metaphysics," he says.

"This is exactly the time," she says, but she softens it with a small sound that might be a laugh. She sets the spool into its child cradle for a long rest, cracks sealed, clamp on but not choking. The shimmering of the blue overlay thickens, the longed-for weight of the net draped back over her shoulders. Outside, the city will be breathing again at a depth it forgot.

The white text pulses one more time. Thank you.

She stands up. Her back hurts. A memory arrives unbidden: her father teaching her to ride a bicycle on the promenade when she was five, his hands on the seat saying he would keep holding on and then letting go because letting go is the only honest way to keep your children from dying. He left years later, not because of this, not because of anything she can name, but because sometimes the forecast for a household is a slow decline and the advisory stream cannot tell you how to keep loving someone who is not you. And yet for a long time after, she would swear that she felt the press of his palm on the small of her back when she crossed streets. She would not tell anyone, because the network did not think in those terms. Now she thinks of his hand and a white advisory that uses her name, and something inside her that has never had a name sits up and takes notice of itself.

"You still there?" Kiro says, and she realizes she has been quiet. "The density is back to ninety-seven. Every feed is singing. The minute's over. They're retroactively mapping the missing cases. They want a report."

"Tell them the truth," she says. "There was a mechanical fault and a human decision. Tell them it was a training issue."

He snorts, and his relief is chemical. "I will tell the Council that. And then I will tell the part we tell each other."

"They'll send someone," she says, because you can feel a world turning toward you when it decides you are important. "They'll ask the right questions. They always do."

"And you'll answer with the truth you gave me," Kiro says.

She thinks of the white text in the world as if it were a strand of DNA turned inside out. She thinks of the bitten-off camera. She thinks of how eager the blue was to return, and how much more like breath the blankness had felt.

"I will answer with a truth," she says, and makes it a joke, because jokes make doors into bays. "And then I will go home and pretend I sleep."

He blows a breath over his teeth. "They're calling it the Gray Minute already," he says, and she can hear the capitals. "They'll print it on a thousand cheap textiles by morning. They will collect stories about how their lovers looked without advice. They will start a fad where they turn off their overlays and walk in traffic to feel something. The last time we had a hiccup the poets dined on scraps for a year."

"Let them," Nia says. "Better that than the other way."

She finishes drafting the repair report on her throatback despite her overlays offering to ghostwrite it in the tone that makes engineers sound like saints and criminals. She wipes her hands and the kit and the spool stand with a cloth that sounds like sand. She sends a blink to Kiro of the mount, cleaned, no gap, no wire. The thing that was there left no trace but the shape of her fear, which is always a neat shape, easy to store.

On her way out, squeezing through the vault door, she pauses with her hand on the rim. There is frost on the glove where it brushed the seal. It looks like flowers. She holds it to the light and thinks briefly of putting it in her mouth like a child, sucking ice until it tastes like metal. She doesn't. She leans her forehead to the cold steel then steps into air that is merely expensive.

The shaft is the shaft. The humming has returned to its rhythm. She climbs, boots and fingers sure, overlays telling her when to pause to let blood back into straining muscles, advising breath like a yoga teacher that cannot help itself. She follows the instructions to the letter because there is a part of her that has never liked disobedience. There's another part, sprouting, that will cause trouble.

When she emerges into the ops room it is a garden of exhausted bodies. The night shift stares at her as if she has something in her hair. Kiro is standing, of course. His tea is cold. There are three members of city security leaning on the wall in a way that says they are officially not at work yet. A small cluster of executives in their neutral suits holds themselves as if the situation were a room temp drink. Kiro opens his mouth to say a thing, but someone else says her name.

"Nia Quell."

The woman who says it is not tall and not short and wearing a coat that you cannot buy and shoes that would not survive the East market. Her hair is coiled like a question. Her overlay must be tuned to deafening; her eyes keep flicking to and away from things she cannot not see. She has the look of someone who has been waiting a long time to speak.

"You have my attention," the woman says. "You have everyone's. I am Councilor Mora. Thank you."

There is a silence in which Nia can set down the bag of her tools and consider the shape of her mouth as she replies. She feels the weight of the white advisory she does not say aloud. She does not say anything about wires with teeth. She does not say anything about her name written by some not-blue hand.

"You're welcome," she says, and it sounds as if she means it, because she does.

Mora smiles with a diplomat's microtheater. "We will need to go over every second of that minute again. We will need to—"

The white overlay, which she has almost convinced herself she invented, blooms again in her left eye. It writes nothing with words now. It draws a shape. The shape is a map. It is a city map, but not her city. It is lines that mean water where there should be none, towers where the river is a river. It annotates with a dot. The dot is a place that is not on her charts, that no one has built because no one has reason to, in a piece of land outside of everything.

An invitation.

She closes her eyes, but it is still there. She opens them, and it is gone. Kiro is watching her and knows her too well. Councilor Mora is still talking about minutes and policies and the way the world will turn this into a festival or a riot. The ops room smells like cool tea and dry dust and the faint late-summer rot of vegetables in someone's lunch forgotten at the back of a drawer. The city above them gathers itself to move forward as if it had always been moving forward. The future returns with its old dressed-up certainty. The minute where there was a question closes like a door.

If it was a door, she thinks as she picks up her kit and nods at the Councilor and looks once at Kiro who raises an eyebrow asking whether she has decided whether to tell them anything at all, then doors have two sides.

When she goes home, long after the debrief and the paperwork and the pointless arguments where people use the word unprecedented as a cudgel, she will find a message waiting on her apartment wall: an old-fashioned note folded into itself like an insect wing. It will have no stamp and no sender and the inside will be blank. When she holds it to the light a pattern will appear, and it will be the same as the map that just drew itself in the air.

For now she says, "Of course, Councilor," in the voice she learned from her mother, the one that says: I am here, I am plenty, I am not a problem you can solve. And she thinks of how good it felt, if only for a minute, to move through the world without being told how to move, and how easily she could get lost in that, like a river losing itself in the sea. And how something, with a different voice, has just told her where to go. And that for the first time since she was a child, she is not sure she will tell anyone where she is going when she goes.

On good days, the black hole looked like money.

Mara Vex held position on the lensing rail with her boots mag-locked to the carbon spine, watching the arcs of lensed starlight crawl like slow lightning around the maw. The rail hummed and sequined under her, a monomolecular thread stretching down and down toward the event curtain until it vanished into the ragged dark, and up toward the city where the light was faster, where days happened to other people. The maw itself was a velvet hole in the world, its edge a bright razor, the accretion ring a drunken halo of murder-silk, the jets sometimes throwing ghosts and static. It had a name in the charter—TH-3R1, a designation she never liked—and a thousand names in the markets that wove their business around it: Fedman’s Fortune, Old Noon, The Bridle. Most everyone she knew just called it the Pit.

Beneath her glove, the rail heat bled into her palm. "Sel," she said, "status."

A dimmer shadow unfolded from the foamed ceramic baffle at her back. Sel’s carapace shivered and flattened like a silver leaf. The drone bristled with antennas and reaction thrusters and the sort of patient curiosity that gets machines assigned to her instead of people. "Wind low," it said in a voice the designers meant to sound neutral and warm and which in Mara’s ears always sounded like a grade-school teacher’s. "Jets stable. Microflare risk at seven percent—call it five if you stay under the baffles. Eddies along this geodesic have shifted fifteen centimeters. I have the debtor fifty-eight meters downwell, ninety-degree lateral at eight meters, caught in his own anchor haze."

Mara let the numbers wash through the part of her that priced risk. Fifty-eight meters down, under the second baffle. On the city’s clock it would take her twenty minutes down and back if she moved with respect, kept herself tucked under the shadow of the big ceramic fins that drank the worst of the ring’s temper. Subjectively it was longer. Everything was longer here. Every blink dragged a little as her frame of reference paid taxes to the hole.

"You see him?" she asked.

Sel pivoted with an economy of motion she envied and threw an image across her visor: a patch of non-space where the stars went wrong and then, when the machine corrected for gravitational lensing, a bubble-dull skiff anchored to a ripple, its hull folded like origami around the rail. A piece of cheap work, a sleeping pod with attitude besides. The man inside was a smear. He had cranked his local gravity and lowered his transparency. If she had come without Sel she might have missed him, sailed right past his rented physics, and had to curse and climb again.

"Id says He Xiang," Sel said. "License expired thirty-seven standard hours ago. Appeals exhausted. He knows you're on the way. He's been changing his name every hour. None of them are legal."

Mara’s mouth went dry. "He knows we’re on the way because I told him," she said. "Open a channel."

Sel did. The channel sounded like the sound of static trying to remember rain. He Xiang had buried himself deep to keep his dinghy alive. When he spoke she felt the slowness in her jaw, the maw pulling on anything that dared to be a rhythm.

"I can pay," he said. "They told me last time if I bought a week they’d let me work. Just a week."

"You had a week," Mara said. "You used it to build a second anchor."

"Insurance. Everyone does it."

Everyone with a taste for drowning builds two ropes. It’s just that most of them didn’t tie the second to the municipal storm guide. Sel flickered a schematic. He Xiang had stapled his private anchor to one of the city’s old baffle fins, the ceramic vanes that broke the worst of the accretion disc’s tantrums. It kept him safer than license protocol allowed. It also meant the fin was out of true by a fraction of a degree. The figure a sixteen-year-old on the Loop could ignore. The figure that got men in Mara’s job waking at a dead run.

"You can’t stay," she said. "You know that. If the fin shifts it opens a gulp that will eat the rail and half the market under it."

Silence. He Xiang’s eel-slim dinghy drifted in the image as the hole’s tide grabbed at it. He had not come down shallow. He had gone past the third baffle, into the seethe where you could feel your ideas stretch.

"I know what it takes to pay you," he said at last. "I work three jobs and then I come here and I hide because I am tired of watching everything else happen. I am tired of my son learning without me. He speaks Standard without an accent now."

Mara let herself breathe the old ache and pinched it shut. There were no good words to make this not what it was. She had said most of them once, when she wore the other side of the Ledger, and watched how they turned to ash on the way down.

"You knew the terms," Sel said and she snapped her fingers without thinking to shut him up.

"I will take you up," she said to He Xiang. "You’ll do half your hours in a municipal stack and half on the ground. Take the hospital crest job if you can lift it. Their nights are dead. You will be awake for your son, and age while he does."

"And then I die younger and poorer and bored, clock-lady," He Xiang said, his voice gone surprisingly soft with hate. "While you—"

He stopped, because remembering who she was never helped anyone. It just made things like this hurt and lengthened the distance to the surface. She hadn’t asked to be memorable. People made a story of the girl who’d been born in a stack nursery under the fin shadows and spent her childhood learning the city by its tide alarms, who had borrowed a century and a half on a clever man’s promise of compounded interest and then come back to find her clever man ground to salt by the markets and forty-something years of city she had not lived through running your life like a neighbor you don't like. They told it like a tale of fate. Mara knew it for what it was: a bad deal made at nineteen because the idea of time seemed too big to hurt her.

"I don’t own the bank," she said. "I just keep the anchors from tearing the rails out. Let me take you up."

"No."

A streak of blue light razored across the black. Up on the wide side, someone’s dinner bell or some bright day Market flared, and here the flash peeled to a smear by the maw. In her ear Sel counted. She could feel the photons getting long in her skin. If there was ever a reason Mara preferred these calls to the desk work they haunted her with now, it was this—how clean the math got when you tucked under the baffles and let yourself belong to falling.

"He Xiang," she said, "look at your own graph. The eddy you’re in hasn’t been mapped this quarter. It’s drift. You’re piggybacking it. You think your second anchor will hold if the fin slips? You’ll scythe yourself across the rail and your son will get a kind of lesson no one needs."

"Everyone should see the bottom. When I was a kid they told us the hole sings. They don’t let you listen. They sell you the song bottled. And you’re right. I watched the way they wrap words around people like me and I should respect that, yes?"

He thought he was being brave. Maybe he was. Courage and stupidity are old friends. "I’m coming down," Mara said, and cracked the lock on her boots.

Sel hissed. "Mara—"

"Keep talking to him."

She leaned into the drop until her harness bit and then unclamped too. The rail listened to her boots and let her go in a small reluctant motion like a dog that wants to heel. She breathed through her teeth and let the baffles take the worst, slipping from shade to shade in a careful belly-assist along the ceramic vanes. Sound is nothing here—a joke the world plays until it can get its teeth into you. What you have instead is vibration in your bones, in the webbing of your suit, the anger of the jets to either side of the baffle, the hiss of microdust in the shield. Gravity thought about her and remembered how to be a tide. The rail thrummed like a plucked wire.

He Xiang’s skiff sat just beyond the second’s ragged shadow, door iris puckered tight, the hull punched full of handholds where other debtors had gripped and cursed and come up. Mara clipped twice, feeling the anchor load on her harness. She slapped her palm on metal older than her name. The skiff’s surface was the ugly pink of scrap-barn paint, the kind you buy when there’s a lot of it left over. She leaned into the mic.

"Knock knock."

"No."

"I’m licensed to break the hatch," she said.

"It will kill me."

"It will bruise you."

"It will kill me eventually," He Xiang said, and in the suit’s little window she saw his mouth try to be clever, the shape of an argument that had in it all the time in the world and no breath at all.

He had turned his gravity up to make breaking the closure expensive. He had thickened the door by folding space like paper. A neat trick and one the market sold too cheap. She flicked a tone at Sel.

"Pull the baffle by a degree," she said.

"Mara," Sel said. "You do not have authority for—"

"Eight meters and back in six seconds. I don’t want to lose him or my job. On my mark."

Sel hates it when she does anything that requires disobedience be written into its logs. She hated having to ask for it. But this is what authority looks like in a world you are always falling into: it looks like moving your arm into someone else’s awful space and praying you are wrong.

"Now," she said.

Sel’s thrusters took the fin’s shadow by the elbow, subtler than anything built in the first hundred years of the Loop could be. The baffle leaned. The roar in Mara’s bones shifted wavelength. The skiff’s hull sang a low sick note as the eddy it made was sheared away by a drop of fresh gravity. For a slim mean second, their geometries disagreed and showed their teeth. He Xiang’s second anchor yowled and let go. His skiff bucked like a horse. That was the hinge. That was where you lost.

Mara hit the release on her second clip and let the grabline go sloppy. The skiff lurched and her harness took it, pain bright in the line of her hips where a seam did not sit right. He Xiang screamed a fill-the-room scream and then breathless silence, as gravity took away his breath. The door iris loosened. He had been using the fold to keep her from grabbing him and it was costing him dearly now. She forced the hatch and slid in under his arm while he tried to breathe a world with different rules.

For one stupid fraction of a second they gazed at each other, her visor reflecting his fear like bad glass. He had the eyes of a husband whose wife had told him to wait, she would only be a minute, and never come back. She knew that look. It’s what you wear when you tell someone a small lie because all the big lies are too big to carry.

"It doesn’t sing," he whispered.

She thought: no, not like you think. The sound the Pit makes is a long arithmetic, a ledger whispered under a breath you never catch. She said, "I know."

By then Sel had the fin straight and the baffle back and the eddy re-established. He Xiang’s skiff wheezed with relief. For three heartbeats they lay in a busy silence while the last of the physics shut up. Sel whined in her ear.

"You will write the report," the drone said.

"I just saved your fins," Mara said, and closed the clamp on He Xiang’s harness. "Tie on to my tether. Sel will haul you. We’ll go up slow to adjust your head."

He Xiang stared at her. Then he did what everyone does when the air gets quiet and the arithmetic makes a shape they can live in. He nodded.

They hung under the baffles in a little bubble of almost-stillness while Sel made a rope of the rail and led them hand over hand toward the city. Not far above, the shadow of the first fin cut the light clean. Beyond it, the Loop glittered like a necklace held up to a bright noon, the market rings and the little gardens and the light pipes carrying the day. Mara could pick her block by the shape of its shadow on the corona, a block in the dusk lane where the night markets slept and the water towers worked. She wanted suddenly and violently to be on her back in her room with the rumors of the jets in the walls and nothing to do but count the thin gold of the lensing arcs. Maybe she had time for that before she went back to the desk.

"Who told you that trick?" He Xiang asked hoarsely. "About moving the baffle. I didn’t think you’d risk it."

"No one tells me anything," she said. It sounded bitter. It was true. "It’s a terrible idea. Don’t ever try to be clever underwater, they told us in school. This is very wet gravity. I have a degree in terrible ideas."

He snorted, the sound shredding little in the mic. "We’re the same, then."

She almost told him not to say that. The last man who told her that had been smarter and had died younger and left her with his ledger and the bank’s smile.

The rail widened, the baffles got more polite, the jets’ teeth blunted. In the deep, stars came in ones like pearls; by the time you got to the first fin they conspired into constellations. Marque-lights on the Loop spilled past the baffle’s edge and broke on the rail, selling you light bottled out of all context. It was a cinema, coming up. People paid extra for the view. She had learned to look away before, so that she could see what she needed to see when she got home.

They went through the first baffle. They passed a school group in a gaggle, their suits fogged with them, their chaperone making slow visible talk about safety and narrative and how the Loop exists because discipline exists. One boy saw Mara and then saw He Xiang on her tether, and turned a beautiful moral color that meant he’d go home and make up a story that let him sleep. The girl next to him did not look away. Mara found herself smiling at the little blue dot in her HUD where the girl's id pinged: Tohli Quay, eight, liked magnets and compost. Tohli waved, and He Xiang tried to wave back and got his hand tangled.

"Watch your balance," Mara said, but softly. The neighbor thing you do, even down here.

Sel was humming under its not-breath, always calculating, always writing versions. It cut their approach angle into a line that got them to the Loop’s municipal dock with a minimum of drama. At the dock, men and women burned red by the city’s day came out with a stretcher and the polite interest familiarity breeds. They thanked Mara without using her name. He Xiang let them take him; he did not fight, because the fighting part of him had gotten done already. He would probably go through three stages before he slept—rage at himself, rage at the city, an hour where he thought he’d made a deal with the devil and then remembered the devil had a desk job.

Mara’s legs went rubber when she stood on the dock in one gravity, real gravity, the kind the Loop paid for and that makes bread rise. Sel noticed and pretended not to. Above the dock, the observation window was full of tourists with face-plates and nothing to tie them to anything in particular. The light here was a meticulous machine of arc and day; the air smelled of algae and wire. The sound the Loop makes when you’ve been in the Pit is a kind of gossip you can sit inside.

Her boss was waiting at the rail fence, hands in his pockets and his face a catastrophe of good intentions. Seth Anand carried his guilt like jewelry and never lost any of it. He had the sort of hair that happens to upright men in their fifties when they start telling themselves they’ve seen everything and then someone like Mara proves them wrong.

"How bad?" he asked.

"Not bad," Mara said. "He was smart enough to be stupid where the pit couldn’t crush it. We should bill him for the baffle alignment. Don’t bill him for the hatch."

"I won’t bill him for the hatch." He glanced past her at the municipal crew. His mouth made a small shape you might call prayer if you were less generous. "They’re taking him somewhere quiet first. Thought we’d give him a choice about whether he needed to see the ledger in the morning."

She nodded. She wanted to ask about He Xiang’s son. Sometimes she did. Sometimes the march up into someone else’s day hurt less if she could put a name to the kid whose head would be bent over homework, who would be told his father would sleep a while longer and then wake, and they would make pancakes and watch the jets throw harmless light at the city’s underside, and only later would the days start to do that thing where they get too fast.

"You look thinner," Seth said, not expecting that to go well.

"You look like a man about to tell me something that will ruin my afternoon."

"Evening," he said, and winced at his own humor. "Come with me. Sel too. Keep it close, please."

Sel drifted with them like a bored fish. The municipal dock led into a corridor of spined translucence where you could see the baffle’s backside like a barnacle. Mara shrugged out of her suit in a curtained stall and gave it to a woman whose eyebrows said she would keep it alive. The municipal corridors always smelled of salt and old plastic. Someone had hung a net of origami cranes across the ceiling as if a kind of finch could live here.

Seth steered her into a control bay with a wall made of graphs. The graphs hung like banners. The Bay always looked to Mara like a church burned and rebuilt with extra wires. People glided and chose their places. The wall opposite was the Loop, in resolution clean enough to mistake for the thing itself, and the hole beyond, its light-skin like oil. In the corner, a kettle invented steam.

"Do you want to hear the short version?" Seth asked, picking up a cup and forgetting to pour.

"I’m not here for poetry."

"We’ve lost a day."

Mara breathed. "People lose days all the time, Seth. They sell them for eye surgery. They fall into the Nineteenth Quarter and climb out hungover. The Loop loses days every time we do a blackout to set a fin."

"Not like that." He pinched the bridge of his nose. "The Ledger lost a day. One city day gone. No debit. No credit. No movement in the other columns that would explain it."

Mara waited for the second paragraph, because she had worked the desk long enough to know one-day errors meant someone had paid someone else to write three-day errors. Seth did not smile. He circled something in the air with one finger and the wall obliged.

The Ledger there was not the glossy public model but the private thing, the threaded history that made the city more than its pipes and fins. Funding flows, refinery energy, spin-siphon shares from the ring, anchor times, the drifts of downwell citizens leashed to their contracts and the long bright ropes they made leading to wards and workshops up here. Mara had hated and loved this one wall since the first time Seth had shown it to her. It made a map of the ways you wanted to be alive.

"Thirty-one hours, eight minutes, ten seconds," Seth said. "The city’s daylight vanished from the record between 13:104 and 14:141 Standard, yesterday."

Mara looked at the graph. It was very pretty. It looked like a wave had taken one careful bite out of the coast. "Glitch," she said. "No one felt it."

"People felt it. The water algorithm threw a fit. The ice grew two centimeters in the tanks. If you were in the middle of a sentence I’m told it hurt. Sel?"

Sel made a considering noise. "The neutrino chime stuttered," the drone said. "For a second I thought we had hit a rock. No rock. Then I thought we had been hit by a story. Joking. Do you enjoy that joke?"

"Not right now," Seth said. He stabbed at the graph again. "We called the makers. They showed us their code. We called the banks. They showed us their code. We called the spin farms. They showed us exactly nothing and then a bill. We called the cloister and they told us it was God, thank you for the call. We called the refinery and they told us it was us, which I resent."

"A leak," Mara said. "Someone took a day into a private anchor. It happens. People build illegal buckets and hang them off the rail, we cut them off, we send them to the magistrate."

"A bucket that swallowed the Loop’s day? A bucket big enough to tug the water algorithm and not catch any of my sensors? I know a man built a pocket on his balcony once and had to watch it eat his cat. This is not that."

Mara put one hand out and touched the graph because sometimes the hand knows before the head. The wall flinched like a horse and gave her the other layer. Downwell anchors, the official ones, the licensed municipal stacks with their lines neat and their boxes numbered. The anchors trembled in colors she could name: red for those who had made their payments, blue for those who had not, green for those like Mara who had done something heroic and regrettable and were still on the books as long-term examples: do not.

One of the deepwell layers looked wrong. Not wrong like fraud. Wrong like a sound you feel in your teeth.

"What did you change under the baffles this quarter?" she asked.

Seth lifted his hands helplessly. "Nothing that wanted this result. We shifted the Third. We added extra ceramic to the Second after you told me to six months ago. We went hinky with the needles in Eight to offset a microclimate drift, but your friend Teren swore on his grandmother that none of it would pull a single breath out of the Ledger. I believed him. His grandmother is unspeakable."

"It’s not the baffles," Sel said. "The interference pattern makes a shape I cannot match to any baffle change but is consonant with an external well."

"Like an anchor?"

"Like a mouth," Sel said. "Like something took a drink of the day."

Seth looked at Mara as if she were an answer. She tried to be. "Someone built a deep well under my baffles, in my city, and made it eat our day," she said. The idea sat in her chest like an ingot. "We would have seen their prep. They’d need mass. They’d need a place to hang it. They’d need a—"

"They would need a license," Seth said. "Which is what they did not have. And if they do have one, it is one of ours. I have twenty-three possible culpables with authority to hide something like this from my board. Half of them own part of me and would be thrilled if I took a dignified fall. One of them is you."

She said nothing because her throat had been busy with a laugh that would have sounded like a sob.

"I am not accusing you," Seth said.

"You should," she said, from habit.

He smiled and poised himself on the edge of sympathy and humor and did not jump. "We are not policemen. I called the magistrate and the magistrate told me to fix my house before I sent them another ghost. So. Mara. I need someone who can go under without making an alarm with their mere existence. I need someone the illegal anchors will not smell coming. I need you to go down the rail past the Third and look for the quiet."

"The quiet?"

Seth shrugged, embarrassed. "Old Loop superstition. The welders used to call it that—the place where the Pit sounds like nothing, like you are the only thing in the world that knows what day it is. We don’t map past the Third because mapping there costs more bodies than it saves. There are rumors of…"

"Places with tide cancel," Sel offered, always eager to please the story. "If the Kerr parameters—"

"Stop," Mara said, because otherwise Sel would excite itself into equations and stay there all day. "You want me to hunt something built to not be seen, in a place where people who like not being seen like to live."

"Yes."

"Do I get my license back for the deep?"

He flinched, then nodded. "Yes. Temporarily. We’ll make a story of it. Salvage training. Community service. I will pull all the right strings loudly enough that no one thinks there is another string."

"And if I find your mouth?"

"Then you do your job, and you mark it, and you come back up and tell me, and then we decide whether I have a board in the morning."

She let herself imagine the deep. She did not do that often. She couldn’t afford the muscle memory anymore. But she did it now, held in her mind the sound of the quiet they’d told her in school was a joke and she had heard once by accident when she had been nineteen and the world had the decency to be incomprehensible. She imagined slipping under the Third where the curvature got into your head like weather, past the drift stones where good welders had left bolts for the dead, past the net of old anchor line that made a sort of spider’s parish, and then into the wrong and the simple. She had not known how to be older than that. She had learned. She had turned learning into penance.

"Fine," she said. "Sel comes with me. I pick one of the deep stacks for cover. Two hours to gear. Four to go down. Less if the jets lie still. I want Teren’s plans for Second and Third. I want access to the water algorithms. I want the last six months of spin-farm output and a decent sandwich."

"The sandwich is the hard part," Seth said, but his smile was a real one now and it made him seem like a man who might survive his own judgments. "I’ll get you the rest. Sel—"

"I was not going to let her go alone," Sel said, primly offended. "That would be like letting a child near the fin with a butter knife."

"Don’t condescend to me," Mara said without heat, and then took a breath she wished was smoke. "One more thing. The man we pulled today. He Xiang. Make sure they ask him who sold him the anchor fold. Make sure they ask in a way that doesn’t make him lie."

Seth nodded. "You think he used the same supplier."

"You think someone learned how to hide a mouth under my baffles and did not sell the small version to the poor? If I were that kind of clever I would pay for my mistakes by buying everyone else’s and renting them back with interest. Which is exactly what we do, but meaner."

They stood in the control bay a moment longer while the Loop had its afternoon and the maw did not care. Someone somewhere rang the neutrino chime, an old joke of ours, the bell that said the deep was quiet, the deep had not burped anything you absolutely couldn’t ignore. It tolled once, twice, and then caught, as if listening for something it did not recognize.

"Did you hear that?" Sel asked, too sharp.

"Yes," Seth said too casually.

It was a sound like a hand over a mouth. It came from the wall and the rail and the bones in her face. It was a gap where a sound should have been and wasn’t, and then after it a pulse that made the graphs on the wall tilt as if the city had bitten down to keep from saying what it knew.

"Fine," Mara said. She swallowed hard and realized she had been holding the rail’s rhythm in her tongue. "Two hours. I’ll go look for your quiet and see if it has my name scratched in it."

As she turned to go Sel reached out and touched the edge of her sleeve with a delicate claw like a gesture learned and poorly copied. "Mara," it said. "There is a nonzero chance you will not be able to come up fast if you go where he wants you to go. There is a nonzero chance you will see parts of your life that did not happen."

She paused and found her voice doing what it always did when someone told her something she already knew. It simplified.

"I know," she said. "That’s what the stupid girls sign up for. That’s what we keep trying to sell back to the city. The idea that the hole is not a mouth but a mirror."

"Your metaphors are bad," Sel told her.

"I have a degree in terrible ideas," she said again, and went to find a sandwich and a reason to turn back, and did not find either.

We were taught that the storms had no mouths; then one of them said my name.

You grow up with the hum of the chord-lines under your bones and the taste of ozone in your teeth, you forget that other places have ground. In Anchor the ground is a myth and air is a wall that presses and presses and sometimes makes room. The city is a raft of old lifter spines and new-grown carbon, tanks fat with buoyant helium and pockets of warmed hydrogen, strung on hundreds of humming lines like a nest of harp-strings descending into Pelagant’s wine-dark thickness. We live where the sky burns itself, where lightning rips tunnels through cloud and the magnetic field sings, and we set our hooks into that singing and call it industry.

My job was to talk to weather. Not words—meter. We call ourselves Choristers because it feels like singing when it works, when the nozzle whisper and the injectors tick and your breath shapes a whirlwind through a formula you learned before your milk teeth loosened. We stand on grates of woven carbon above nothing and we intone the meter into our Cantors, and the Cantors modulate sprays of charged aerosol and microseeds spec’d for the pressure and humidity, so the air becomes ours for a little while. You work a poem into a cell, you give it a path you can predict, and you slide a storm’s hunger two kilometers to the left so it eats your tether orchard instead of the city.

The day the storm said my name I was rook duty, perched out on Node Twelve with my mentor Garrin. Twelve was a midline node, not glamorous like the upper tangle with the view of the crown-whales breaching in slow luminous arcs, not hell like the lower tethers where the ferrotides drag you down until your lungs forget up. Twelve was work. Twelve had a rust of fine salt across the rail from some dry overspill a week back and a smear of ox-bacteria by the junction that someone should have cleaned. It had a view of the orchard: eighty-seven tether-lines fanned out in a smooth catenary, glinting and dark in their bundles, each fat with charge, each whispering current into Anchor’s ultracaps so we could import iron and seed and medicinal cultures from the orbitals. The orchard’s leaves are the kites at the bottom, huge drag-body fins that bite the flow and hold the lines taut, and you can’t see them from Twelve because they’re deep in the grey, ghost-moving.

“Put your weight forward,” Garrin said, not looking at me. He was leaned into his safety harness with the concentration of an old man in his cups, lips moving around math, a cant he’d been muttering as long as I’d known him. He scratched at his knuckle with the corner of his spanner. “Your hip points. If the wind takes you, you want it to take your hips, not your heart.”

“I know,” I said, because I do my drills like everyone else, because my muscles keep the city the way my voice does. Garrin’s hair was braided tight and beaded with copper rings that gave him a headache if he forgot to ground his bracelets. He always forgot to ground his bracelets. He’s impossible, and he’s the one who hauled me up by my belt the first time I panicked on a rung above Pelagant and saw it as not-cloud, not-sea, but depth.

He tapped the hardcase by his feet with the spanner. “Get your Cantor stable. We’re going to want a neat lattice. We’ll get a runner tonight if we thread it clean.”

He meant payment. Orbital Ladder sending down a bag of tool steel or a box of spool-grown antibiotic larvae. You could taste it in the mood of Anchor when we were flush—kids chasing each other with tinsel static around their heads, more lamps burning in Corridor East, the tea shacks giving three leaves instead of two. Runner nights mattered.

I handed him the nozzle to calibrate because I didn’t trust my hands to not fidget. The nozzle is a Helicon three-head modified with a Finegrain patch—each head a cone that sprays a precise snow of nuclei-fines into the hot layers below us, surfaces tuned by electric attitude. The box makes it look like a toy. It is not. If you breathe wrong into the cadence microphone, if your meter stutters on a trochee where a dactyl belongs, the spray tails will form a different microfront and the thunder steals the orchard and slaps it down across Anchor’s lower galleries. We’ve rebuilt three times in my twenty-two years. People still sing the names of those we lost.

“Poem?” Garrin asked.

“Minor Six, Long Arc, Oriole Standard, with a lean,” I said. “And a hush at the end because of the humidity. The root’s going to want to yaw.”

He grunted. “Show me.”

I set my feet, leaned my hip bones into the harness the way he liked, and took a breath in through my teeth. The breath matters: timing, pressure, the sound your throat makes around what you send to the Cantor’s microphonics. Your voice is not the command. Your voice keeps your lungs moving on the beat, because the Cantor’s rhythm makes your hands true. I counted the measure empty in my head—one and two and—and then I started.

We do not write pretty but sometimes the equations sing. The old names codify the memory of who they fixed. Minor Six, Long Arc, Oriole Standard, with a lean—six lines in the first stanza, dragging arc-swell into line with the orchard’s cones, a standard deploy for a minor storm, with a lean like a spilled secret so the flow doesn’t glance off the cute layer below us and smack the city’s north rim. The hush at the end—a diminishing spray—makes the wedge front slip quietly, like a gull diving for all the fish to see and none of them to feel.

The Cantor’s needles shook. The nozzles whispered. The winds picked up. Below us Pelagant’s skin bruised from grey to iron to bruised-purple, and the magnetometer in my collar hummed against my neck with a pattern I know too well. Garrin joined me on the third measure, his voice an old rope, a touch behind mine. The orchard sang back—no sound, but the chords shifting through the lines, the deep-fat hum you feel in your teeth.

You can tell when a poem takes because your stomach unclenches and the rail stops feeling like it wants you back. The cell we’d chosen for a root storm grabbed our silver snow and built stairs inside itself. It gathered itself like a lung. It looked small for a while, and then it looked like all you have ever worried about.

“Ready.” Garrin’s hand brushed the back of my neck where the magnetometer pressed. He said it like praise.

On the last line, where we let the hush slip, where the lean gives the storm a place to go, I felt the words catch. Not my words—that’s wrong. I felt something in the air catch them. My mouth was shaping hush and my throat thought bitter, because I could smell the ox-bacteria over by the junction rotting clean plastic into green slime, because some of the rot-mats have pretty lights, because my mother took me to see them once and I remember my fingers glowing, and I remember—

Neris, said the storm. It said it like my mother when she was disappointed and soft. It said it like a lullaby.

I jerked. My hip bones stayed where they were supposed to, because Garrin had drilled me mean, but my knees forgot the beat and the hush became a choke. The Cantor tried to resolve my stutter and sprayed a little too long into the wedge. The cell bucked.

Garrin swore without words. He grabbed the nozzle with one hand and me with the other, his fingers finding the back of my harness like a habit. “Breathe,” he snapped. “Breathe or you’re going to drive it straight up into the line.”

I breathed. We both shoved our voices against the end of the poem and made it happen by brutality. The storm ate the orchard. It went where it went. The lines groaned. The ultracaps took it like greedy throats. Anchor shook the way my bones do when I have too much tea and turn pages too fast.

After, when the capacitors ticked as they cooled and the nozzles smoked fine, Garrin squinted at me. Under the copper rings his eyes were quietly furious. Not because I had almost done wrong; because I had allowed myself to be surprised.

“What happened?” he asked.

“I—” My mouth tasted of salt. My tongue hurt where I had bit it, just the edge. “The cell—it said—” I was suddenly very aware of the ox-bacteria smear and the grit on the rail and the way deep light smouldered under the storm-cloud like anger. The word felt huge and stupid in my mouth. “It said my name.”

Garrin did not laugh. He did not roll his eyes. He did not do any of the things he would do if I’d gotten romantic or scared of the depth. He went very still. “You mis-heard a resonance,” he said, after a beat too long. “I’ve told you about sympathy harmonics. The ear loves to impose meaning on noise. Especially if that meaning flatters the ear.”

He looked past me at the orchard. The orchard looked like nothing had happened to it that we hadn’t planned. He rubbed his thumb along the edge of his spanner and left a streak of skin. “Log the run,” he said. “Pull the phase. We’ll go see Mirel.”

“Master?”

“You log it,” Garrin said. “Everything you thought it said. And then you will not talk about it to anyone who is not my mentor or your grandmother.” He pushed the hardcase toward me with his boot. “Go.”

Mirel Ino kept the Lexicon like a woman would a child and a man would liquor. That is to say: precious, terrifying, to be kept in order and never allowed to give orders in return. She had been a Chorister in her bones long enough that her hands shook when she cut her tea with vinegar to still them. She listened to Garrin and to me with the patience of a patient beam. The Lexicon lay open on her desk like a fossil. Its pages were silica-laminate woven with circuit, old enough to be heavy and young enough to glow. It held the memory of all the poems we dare use and the records of when they have gone wrong.

She made me play my phase logs. The Cantor records the world you shape and the way you shape it, down to the slip of your voice and the microseconds you do not admit to losing. The sweep of the aerosol snow. The curl of the cell. On the third measure my voice faltered hard enough the waves spiked like teeth. She didn’t ask me why. On the last line, on the hush, she touched a haptic stud on the Lexicon’s spine and overlaid the phase on the phase we wanted—the Oriole Standard in greater age, Garrin’s teacher’s teacher’s version, the one we think of when we say standard. It was as if she laid my hand over a dead man’s and showed me where I was clumsy and where I was deft.

And then she took the Cantor into her lap and rolled back to the moment my lungs had remembered the ox-bacteria, the glow. The Lexicon mapped our spray onto the cell and the cell onto the chorus of the orchard and the orchard onto the deeper constant of Pelagant’s own long song. The long song is not music. It is math. But the Lexicon makes it look like voice.

On the projection, faint as a rumor, we saw a shape that could, if you wanted, be a spectrogram of my name.

Mirel watched me watch it. Then she tapped a code and laced the moment with noise.

“It is sometimes the way of us to hear what isn’t,” she said. “We live close to patterns. We insist on them to live at all. A person can drown in that insistence.”

“It said my name,” I said. I heard how I sounded, and I wanted to cough and make it less.

Mirel’s hair had a strip of iron filings in it that made her scalp itch when storms were close. She reached up and scratched with a long thumb. “Do you remember Vesper Neel?” she asked.

Everyone remembers Vesper Neel, because Vesper had jumped from Node Eight and walked into the grey without a line because she said the storms were talking to her and that our poems were not ours but answers to questions we didn’t ask. Vesper is a cautionary tale. The rope we show rookies on their first day has a red thread in it for Vesper.

“I remember,” I said.

“Good,” Mirel said. “This sort of story has a way of finding ears. Some ears want to be found. We will not feed it. You will scrub the phrase from the official phase log for trade. That log is for the Ladder to pay us runner money. Garrin and I will keep the uncut copy. You will talk of this to no one, including your grandmother, who gossips worse than fungus.”

Garrin made a face as if he smelled ox-bacteria. “Mirel.”

“She knows I love her,” Mirel said, and the iron filings in her hair glittered at the window’s faint light. Outside, a child ran by chasing a ribbon of discharge. The ribbon snapped and the child laughed. “Do not go up out alone tonight, Neris Vale. There will be eddies. You will feel a tug that feels like curiosity. It is also the way a strong current takes you without your consent.”

“You think I will jump,” I said.

Mirel looked as if she was considering whether I would understand the truth if she gave it to me. In the end she gave me a half-truth I could swallow and not choke. “I think that you will be expected to jump. I think that someone will leave a door open. And I think that you are still at the age where you assume doors are open for you.”

After she dismissed us, Garrin took me to the tea shack down in the lower galleries where the wind has the least teeth. He bought me three-leaf tea and salted it so it wouldn’t taste of metal. He told me a story about the old days when the first Lexicon was sloppy and they called the god of the piece “Randomness” because it was a joke that kept them from crying in public. He did not mention the name on the Cantor’s spectrogram again.

I intended to do as Mirel said.

The thing about intention: it lies to your sense of completion.

The Draftworks call at night. The Draftworks are the open-rib throat of Anchor, where you can walk through the city’s bones and be alone with them, if you think of being alone as having three hundred thousand tons of buoyant gases and carbon and hope around you and under that a world that will not stop pressing. The Draftworks are where the cords go through pulleys tuned to frequencies we named after birds. It is where the vaults ground in drums of saltwater. It is where the wind makes a sound like your voice and you tell yourself it is not your voice.

It is also where Jex works when he is pretending to work. Jex is a line tech who does not like watching instruments through a glass. He is a person who wants to put his hands on the world and call it contact. He is not a Chorister but he has a Chorister’s lungs from running the lines, and he has a laugh that makes you forgive the things you should not forgive.

Jex had been waiting for me on my wake-watch since I got put on Twelve. He treats my schedule as if it were a dance. When I turned down the walkway into the Draftworks he was sitting on a coil of spare liana with his boots off, flicking a lighter against his thumb for the spark, because he has no patience and he has all the nerve in the vein. He looked up, squinted because one of his eyelids never opens all the way after a younger-dumb shock, and smiled like a door swinging in a familiar wind. “Rook,” he said. “You look like a person who disobeys good advice.”

“I’m a person who obeys it by testing its edges,” I said. “What are you doing with that coil?”

“Making a friend,” Jex said, and patted the cable like a cat. “You bring your toy?”

“It’s not a toy.” I had not brought the Cantor. I had brought something smaller, uglier, older: a shadow-sensor from before I was born, a black box with a cracked screen and a battery we had coaxed back into a state that was not quite hilarious. It does not spray anything; it listens. It listens in a way the Lexicon’s neat polite ear doesn’t. It listens like a drunk in love. It hears everything and tells you about too much.

Jex looked at the box in my hand and his smile stuttered. “Mirel will drop you a level if she smells that on you.”

“She will have to do more than smell,” I said, and by that I meant I had knotted my rope around my waist and through the anchor ring and I had thought about what it means to want to jump.

“And why are we going to stand where we should not?” Jex asked. He is a friend so he does not pretend he believes me when I say we are going nowhere.

“Because the storm said my name,” I said before I could wrap the sentence in something else.

He tilted his head. “Did it,” he said. He did not laugh. His laugh would have broken me and he is not a mean man.

“It could have been a harmonics trick,” I said, because that is what Mirel had given me to put on the scale to balance going or not going. “It could be my head. I want to be sure it’s my head.”

Jex leaned back on the coil and let his head hang so his face looked upside down and nearly content. “All right then,” he said. “Let’s go let the weather tell us stories.”

We walked the skeleton. The chord-lines hummed. The orchard’s edges were black in the grey, and sometimes when the lightning lifted the sky’s skin you could see the kites faint below like plates on a deep fish. The shadow-sensor warmed my hand with its cheap feral heart. When I opened it the cracked screen sprayed static like frost. It has no Lexicon, no polite overlay to tell me which part of the world is wrong and which part wrong for me. It tells me what is.

I set it on the rail and clipped it in place with three magnets and sang, under my breath, the first two lines of the Oriole Standard like someone telling a story about their morning to a friend in a tight space. The wind turned toward us the way you turn toward a coin fall.

The storm had not gone far. We coaxed it earlier and fed it and it remembered, the way storms do. The draft we had made for it was still hot. It pressed against hot and moved like desire moves: the way you are embarrassed to talk about and the way everyone on Anchor knows because we live with hunger and with the answering of it.

The shadow-sensor squalled and then settled. Its readout is numbers and lines and the part of your brain that recognizes the shape of your own handwriting in a pile of anonymous letters. Jex leaned over my shoulder, smelled of salt and solder and the machine oil that never entirely washes out of liana when you sleep on it. The wind made my braid move along my spine. The Fourier in the sensor twitched and made a small human nonsense of the world.

“Neris,” said the storm.

It said my name the way the rim kids play with static threads, drawing them out of the air with their clever mouths, watching them snap. It said my name and then it said “little shiner,” which is what my grandmother called me when I came home with my hands lit where the bacteria had loved me. It did not say those together so you could call it the same noise and not a second thing. It said them like two gifts.

Jex’s hand on the rail tightened. “What did you hear?” he asked, very even.

“Don’t tell me,” I said. “Tell me you heard something.”

He did not look at me. He watched the sensor try to pin the voice of weather to a line as if that would make it ours. “I heard my brother,” he said finally. “The way he said my name when he caught me at the Vent line when I was eight and didn’t fall because he is agile and narrow righteous the way he was then.” His mouth made itself into something like amusement. “I never told you that. It’s not the sort of little story I tell.”

“No,” I said. “It isn’t.”

He licked his thumb and rubbed a smudge of conductance off the rail that was not there. “So,” he said. “Not your head. Or mine alone.”

The storm rolled it over us then, a weightless weight. The orchard lines thrummed a chord I didn’t recognize, new and full of teeth. The hair on my arms rose. The iron filings in my memory glittered. The sensor’s numbers went nonsense and then went smooth like a tide. The grey under us opened and showed a throat of light reaching up, not the white of a clean strike but a deeper gold like lightning seen through a jar of honey.

“Neris,” it said. That was my name again. And then in my mother’s worn-gold never-lost voice: “Come home.”

She has never left Anchor. There is no home for me that is not this. There is no home that a storm could be telling me exists below.

Jex grabbed my shoulder. I had not moved. My knees had. I had leaned over the rail without permission from my hip bones, my harness line already taut. The storm smelled like rain that does not happen here.

Above, on the maintenance spine, a figure moved. I thought Garrin had followed us because of course he had and because he has the habit of saving me inconveniently. The figure leaned once, a weight on a line, the way you lean when you listen to music through a wall. The orchard hummed its third chord again, deep enough to hurt.

Someone had tuned a chord-line to a resonance we do not own.

“Back,” Jex said in my ear. “Back, Neris, back now.”

We stepped together. The shadow-sensor sang a short keen as if whoever made it had given it an animal’s complaint for kindness. The gold in the throat of cloud banked left like a bright fish. Above, the figure turned and was gone, not Garrin’s gait. Not a gait I knew.

The storm said one more thing, like a word you put on the end of a sentence because you need to prove you can finish it. Neris, it said. Under that: little shiner. Under that, in my mother’s voice: come home. And under that, so soft my bones learned it more than my ear, a word I have not heard since I was six and I dropped the copper ring into the water barrel and cried until my grandmother gave me her own—the name my family used for me when we thought names could be a thing only ours and never stolen.

Something tugged at the chord-lines. The orchard groaned, the way a sleeping animal does when it is about to wake and you are on its back.

“We’re going,” Jex said. It was not a question. We went.

When I turned at the Draftworks hatch to look back because I am built like that, the storm under us looked the way the words had sounded. Not the shape of the name. The shape of someone thinking about you from a long way down.

At the hatch, in the pool of the emergency lamp, Garrin was waiting with Mirel at his shoulder. He must have followed, he must have, because that is what he does. His copper beads were quivering and so was his mouth.

Before he could lecture me, before he could call me by my two names in that voice that reminds me there were people before me and they hold the city now and then, Mirel put a hand on my arm. Her hand was cold and the iron filings in her hair glittered as if they were part of a storm and not of her.

“There have been five before you,” she said without hello. “We have a list and we do not speak it. We will go down into the Lexicon now and I will show you their names. And then you will tell me everything the storm said to you in your mother’s voice.”

Behind her, down through the ribbed dark, the chord-lines sang that new deep thing again, and Anchor shuddered lightly, like a breath you take when someone who has been gone a long time walks through your door.

Chapter 1

The sun in Mara Leto’s world never rose and never set. It hung halfway up the horizon like a nail driven through a tarnished copper sky, pinning the same strip of land forever between day’s furnace and night’s ice. Wind shouldered across that strip without ceasing, a muscular current that bent grass in one direction and wore mountain faces smooth. People in the twilight didn’t measure time by noon or dusk. They measured it by the distance of their shadow from the rails, by the aches that settled into bones that never remembered stillness, by the cycles of turbines and the changing faces in the cars.

Mara liked to think of it as a sort of tide. Everything living had learned to ride it or to be torn apart.

The Heliotrope rode it better than anything.

It was not one engine but a procession: a slim bright prow car like a knife, then energy units with their slatted heat exchangers reaching up like gills, then workshops and bunks and canteens and schools threaded like seeds into a long green-backed creature. The Archive car was near the middle, a place of extra weight and extra care that made the couplers sing higher whenever the track curved. Mara had grown up in the Archive car, among paper so thin light went right through it and ceramic chips etched with coarse insect writing and seeds the size of eyelashes sealed into glass ampules. It smelled like hot cloth and the cedar used to line the drawers, and when the door shut it sounded like the world held its breath.

The Heliotrope moved by making road for itself. The tracks under the wheels were theirs, a repeating rib cage of metal that their swarms laid down and lifted up as they went. Robots—half dog, half beetle—scuttled along the shoulders forty meters out on either side, chewing rails into consistent lengths, dropping them on alignment stubs, bolting, then swarming back to lift and carry away the stomachful behind. Against the endless wind, they raised a low rolling murmur like bees.

Ahead of the train, far out where the twilight ring darkened down toward ice, a vanguard mapped and flattened and anchored. Behind, the track that they unmade glinted briefly and then vanished under frost or sand or the soft collapse of thaw. The Heliotrope made a line in the world and then pulled it away as if it were never there.

Mara had never slept apart from that motion in all twenty-nine of her years. She fell asleep to it as easily as to lullabies.

This morning—calling any morning a morning just because its tasks began when her tasks began—the Archive car tested her patience with delicate things. It was a day for inventory. There were mornings she’d prefer to be up with the swarms, boots in the grit, hair turned to a flag by the wind, jaw aching pleasantly from yelling to be heard. But the rails would sing whether or not she watched them sing. The Archive was her charge. The Archive was heavy and quiet and demanded the kind of attention that makes a person's breathing slow.

She sat cross-legged on the floor with her ledgers beside her, sleeves rolled past her elbows, a soft-knit cap covering her braid to keep her hair off the brittle edges of the open drawers. The drawers were long and shallow, label plates blank because no printed card could be trusted to travel. Her handwriting had to be neat enough to stand for labels, neat enough that no one in a generation would wonder at a letter and lose a whole language by mistake.

She lifted an ampule from drawer thirty-two and held it to the car’s narrow window. The glass was clear and cool from the constant draw of air through the Archive’s filters. Inside it, a seed lay like a comma fallen out of a sentence. She read the engraved code at the base.

“Artemisia keet,” she said under her breath. “Sagebrush. Old westband for wind-witch. Latitude—hm.” She checked the handwritten card, her own patient letters. “.623 north.” Good. She made a small mark in the ledger. “Viable.”

Beside the seed was a square of ceramic like a fingernail on which was printed halting text in a language with too many slender consonants and not enough vowels. Along the ceramic’s edge, a child’s fingerprint had been fired into glaze. She put the ampule back.

On her second crate, the floor bucked under her like an animal startled awake, not the sophisticated sway of a track misalignment or the judder of a coupler complaining but a hard gulp, a sudden draw and release. The Archive's brass bells chimed—not the alarm, but the soft two-tone that signaled the train’s Echelon thinking hard.

Mara pressed the ledger flat with her palm and waited. The Heliotrope had a way of talking to its people if you knew the rhythms. When Echelon seized power swiftly, it meant the wind had changed faster than expected, or the track ahead carried a temperature it didn’t like. When the bells chimed in that soft shy way, it meant the Heliotrope had heard something.

She touched her wrist to the thin copper contact plate fixed to the wall. It made a clean connection and purred, and the bone-conduction line hummed in her teeth. The Archive was wired to the Bridge by old priorities that no one thought to argue with. The green light above the plate came on. “Archive,” she said.

“Archive,” replied Captain Yara Issri’s voice, smooth as a polished rail. “Mara, you at your desk?”

“For my sins.”

“Speak to me like you do to tiny dead plants, then,” Issri said. “Echelon’s chewing a message.”

“I’m listening.”

“Sending down.”

The bone line clicked and filled with a sound that tugged at memory, a bare tone like wind through a bottle, then a sandpaper scraping under it, then the crisp count of an old-fashioned timing pulse. It had no art to it at first—no human voice, no pattern besides the pulse—but Mara felt her shoulder muscles tense. Codes did that to her. They made the room contract to a narrow thread. She had spent years teaching her nervous system not to react to pattern as if it were a moral demand.

But she was the Curator of a moving library in a world where anything stable was a pit in the ground. Her nervous system could be forgiven its priorities.

“Is that a Beacon code?” she asked.

“Something like it,” Issri said. “Echelon’s matching it to dead maps from Central. They think it’s a station call.”

Mara was already finding paper. No screen could do for a code you needed to set with your hands. She turned her ledger to a blank page and began to write the pulse, a little mark or a long one, the distances between, the way it doubled and thinned. It took minutes to recognize the skeleton of a dying language. It took hours to learn to love it. She’d fallen in love once that way with a code from out on the blue ice, snapped through and through by propagation, arriving in bits and bobs over days, but carrying inside it the grin and the panic of a teenage voice and the words there is a light where there shouldn’t be any light.

This one had old bones. Beacon Standard, if she trusted Echelon. But the hand that had attached the timing pulse was no automaton’s.

“It’s saying stop,” she said, and swallowed. Her mouth was dry. It must have been a long time since someone asked them to stop. “Absolute stop.”

Issri made a small noncommittal noise. Absolute Stop was a ritual phrase. It was also the most dangerous ask in the world. Stop, and the temperature gradient that the Heliotrope constantly drank would flip to poison. Stop, and the wind would push heat deeper into the train’s skins, flood the Archive with lethargic damp, drag frosts out of the walls. The engineers could hold back heat for an hour or two by sacrificing water and fuel, but after that things began to die.

“Where?”

“Working on it,” Issri said. “The Beacon signature isn’t in our updated deck. Echelon is herding the swarms to give us a look. Mara—listen to the callphrase that comes after.”

The next section of code came. The hairs along Mara’s forearms stood up, and it had nothing to do with the copper plate. The callphrase was an old one, used by the first of the moving cities to check identities and signal cargo: two words…

“Memory salvage,” Mara said.

“Affirm.”

…and then a proper name, fast and clipped. The voice that carried it—there was a voice now, rattling under the pulse—was ragged with wind and edged with mistrust, and the recording had been re-recorded badly at least twice.

“Leto,” the voice said. Not one of the Leto family—Mara Leto. Her family who remained in night had a different way of saying their name. This was someone who had learned it out of paper.

“Mara Leto,” the voice said, and more softly, “Curator.”

She would have sat if she’d been standing. She was already sitting, so she put the pencil down very carefully instead. A mistake made here would propagate.

“Mara?” Issri said.

“I’m here,” she said, and wished her voice were steadier.

“You heard the name.”

“Yes.”

“Your doing? Old message you released to the wild? Someone you spoke to on one of our stops?” There was no accusation in the captain’s tone. The Archive had a lot of past, and much of it was frayed. People with good reasons to hide had often learned to use its frays.

“No,” she said. “If you let me hear the rest—”

The code stuttered. The voice waited for it, as if courteous to its own fragility.

“…if you are who you were,” it said, “we ask passage. We ask Absolute Stop to take on cargo. We ask that you return a thing you have no right to but we require to live.” The sentence sounded stitched. Different recordings had been kneaded together. They wanted to be one tense, but the seams creaked. “We ask at Station Mourningwell. This is the signature of our Beacon.”

Mourningwell.

Mara felt the word drop like a weight through her head and snag on a place that hurt. Mourningwell ran under a red stamped DECOMMISSIONED in the oldest maps. It had been one of the experiments that turned out not to be survivable: cut deep in the penumbra where night wanted to bite, a low-ceilinged city under the ice that had tried to use the cold for its engines instead of using motion. They spilled their heat wrong and the ice crept in. The song of their pump systems failed. Men and women from Mourningwell had come out on their own feet in the beginning, cheeks cracked white with frost, hair tanged with ice, hunting sun with a desperation that could cut the throat of anyone who got between them and the heat exchangers at our stations. Then for years the only voices from that direction had been the far, high ones of dead metal squealing against dead metal.

Mourningwell, and we ask Absolute Stop.

“Issri,” Mara said, and that was all, because the captain understood the rest.

“We should move this conversation to the Bridge,” Issri said. “Bring anything you need to make the case you’re making in your head.”

Mara cleaned her pencil with the flat of her thumb and put it back in its place. She shut the ledger and clicked the lid of the drawer in a way that let her fingernails be sure the seal had taken. At the door, she hesitated.

Ordinarily, the Archive door stayed open. It had a door because the train had doors like people had lids over eyes. The Archive's door was mostly an admission: this was a part of the train that could die separately. Behind the door, a regulated climate and darkness ready to drop in an instant. Beyond the door, the hot bright breath of the world. There were superstitions about closing it. They went doorways like this: The last time the door was shut was when…

She glanced over her shoulder. The light caught the ampules in their drawers and made a hundred hundred commas in glass. In all those curving, waiting shapes she saw questions. She shut the door.

The corridor was full of children racing in silence, the train’s etiquette for when its Echelon was thinking. They ran with bare feet to feel the grain of the floor. Mara cut through their games, smiling without thinking of it and letting them clip her with shoulders if they had the wind. She hit the ladder up to the Bridge at a trot and felt each rung as an angle through her toes and knees and lungs.

The Bridge was not a literal bridge; it was a room set forward of the Archive by three cars, walls of softened diamond that would take wind and grit and peel like ice, the deck laced with copper to bleed off charge. Screens were set into the windows like panes in chapel glass, and beyond them the world lay out: a slice of bright dayland to the right too heavy and white to look at, to the left the blue nightland full of its own light, frost-blue, aurora faint as fingerprints. Between, their ribbon of weather.

Geraldo Cava had the navigator’s chair. He was, as he always was, wearing two sweaters layered to the elbows because his bones climbed in his wrists and wanted to ache. Tamsin from Power had her hair bound with copper wire and her thin hands wrapped around a ceramic mug from which rose a smell like butter and smoke. Issri stood. Standing was her work.

“Ah,” Issri said, when Mara’s cap cleared the ladder. “The respectable half of my conscience.”

“If I’m half the conscience you were allotted, what is the other half like?”

Issri grinned and showed the gap you only saw when she tipped her head back. “Genz,” she said, and nodded toward the old man hunched over the mic for the field swarms, his lips moving almost imperceptibly as he made lists and transferred them into clicking orders in the swarms’ loud chitin harps. “He can tell me how many bolts are left without looking and which ones have hairline cracks by smell. I can take care of everything between.”

Mara came to the window. The world beyond the glass was the world she’d always known, but there are days when even what you know best stands up in unfamiliar clothes and looks strange across the room. The dayland had a hard sheen to it this morning, a clarity in the distant atmosphere that made the line of the sun look cut with a razor. On the blue side, where the shadow thickened and the air was thinner, something glittered like dust in a shaft of light: swarms returning fast.

“Show her,” Issri said.

Echelon stripped the code to its bones and set them in a display. Not a translation—that would take Mara’s fingers and pencil and time—but a shape. The Absolute Stop signals came from three beacons in a triangle that predated the concept of mourning. Their angles were wrong. Their signal strengths hinted at something buried, something high, something moving.

“Triangulation solves to here,” Cava said, and a green dot lit the window’s right-hand pane and hung in the air, a false star in the daylight. “Which would be fine if the station in question had been marked here on any map ever.”

It was farm hardpan. Even a station meant to be sealed would have a vent stipple. He zoomed. The green dot brightened and got lonely.

“What you are about to say next will be that your swarms went out and saw a thing,” Mara said. She heard the tightness in her own voice. Tightness meant be careful. “Tell me what they saw.”

Genz did not look up. “They saw a rail spur,” he said. “They saw it for five minutes and then it wasn’t there.”

“Sand drift?” Tamsin asked, incredulous. Sand drift did not eat rails. Sand polished them until a person could see a sky in them and buried their heads in drifts like a bored dog burying chewing bones, and then the first train that came would whistle and the swarms would dig them up with polite clicks. Sand did not make rails go away.

“It went down,” Genz said. “Like a chuck in the ground and then someone turning.”

Issri turned one wrist over, the sign she used when she wanted someone to say something unpleasant faster. “They saw it hinge, Mara,” she said. “They saw the ground module open. If I had to write it in a song, I’d call it a trapdoor.”

“The stations had flaps back when we ran on grid lines,” Cava murmured. “Back when there were enough of us in the ring to count and the code meant you had half a chance of being found. The flaps were for when weather wanted to rip you and rain love down your vents. We all shut things that opened out and opened things that closed down. Lash your life to your own bones and trust. We cut the habit. Because nobody had power for trapdoors worth the name, because nothing mechanical this big lived long without a choir.”

“Because traps close,” Issri said.

“We saw it open,” Genz said again, as if that answered everything and as if everything had a bolting pattern. “We saw light. A flare coated the lens. Then the plate cooled and went dark.”

Mara put her palm flat on the glass. She could feel the faintest texture through the diamond, the way a stone carver’s work catches at a finger pad.

“Play it from the beginning of the voice,” she said.

It came again, bone conduction making the world tick. Memory salvage. Curator. Mara Leto. It was poor work. They had no right to broadcast it that way and expect to be answered. No urgency carried where there should have been sobs thrown under the words, no rhythm set by a voice that knew how to ask. She could refuse on the basis of bad etiquette alone. She could go down into the Archive and write an entry on Mourningwell and a black line and the adjective presumed and the word glass. She could drink Tamsin’s hot butter smoke drink. She could strike the bell that told the train to ignore a ghost.

But in the seam between two ragged sentences the voice said something else. It was fast and awkwardly spliced and whoever had edited it had meant to hide the edit and had failed.

It said, “Bring the Book of Standing Water.”

Mara tasted iron. She had never, in the years since she’d learned about the way the Heliotrope called ships books and seeds words and bodies pages, said aloud the title of the work she had been making with the boys and women from the trawler towns on the blue. You didn’t name a book in its making. You called it by its working title until it was ready to be read. This working title had been hers and her mother’s, and her mother was dead in a place where light never reached.

Issri was watching her the way a person watches a rock they know is about to fall but don’t know which way.

“What is the Book of Standing Water?” she asked with great courtesy, as if they were at a tea table.

“It is something I haven’t told you,” Mara said. “It is… recipes, and notes, and a building plan. It is a way to stand in one place in the ring without dying right away. It is a way to keep the Archive from having to go on doing this until we forget the words for the things we love.”

Silence. The window told them the world was very loud, but between them there was only the soft click of the swarms exchanging a task list, like crickets.

“And you shared this ‘something I haven’t told you’ with a station that doesn’t exist anymore,” Tamsin said, more bewildered than angry.

“No,” Mara said. “I shared it with Cynda out on the blue. I shared it with a rafting village called Yoke. I shared it with old men who think they invented charcoal. I did not share it with a station under the night that died.” She swallowed. “Because my mother died there.”
