The Bridge shifted around that sentence as if the car had hit a wave. Issri was too good at her work to let the movement show in her face, but the danger came up into the room’s corners like weather.

“Say we answer,” Cava said very softly. “Say we try. Let us lay the thirty kilometers of spare track we keep in our belly out in a U to curl us toward the Beacon. We burn water. We trade two days’ reserve for heat to keep babies’ fingers pink and the copper manageable. We will be thirty-two hours slow to Long Ditch. We will have to write apologies to the laundress there and to the midwife who planned to lay her daughter’s bones to rest in the rail trench when we passed. The wind will not change just because we want it to. And if Mourningwell is a trap, it will be a good one.”

“If it is not a trap,” Tamsin said, “it is a miracle.”

“If it is even a station and not a tongue on the end of a thing that wants to taste us,” Genz said. Practical, always. “We have had wolves that learned to cry help. We have had men that cut their beards to look like women. We have had codes copied by birds that spend a whole day shouting a stranger’s name because a worm fell when it heard that name, once, and a mouth never forgets.”

Mara closed her eyes and in her head set the words of the voice in lines so thin the ink split. Mourningwell. Absolute Stop. Bring the Book of Standing Water. She could almost feel where the words had been lifted like slices of meat and laid elsewhere. Behind them a hand she did not know reached—a hand that had touched paper. The grief in her chest and the anger in her throat tuned themselves slowly into a third thing, no easier to carry but cleaner to look at.

“It may be a trick,” she said. “If it is a trick and we move toward it, we die. If it is not a trick and we do not answer, we betray something that is the whole point of us.”

Issri breathed out through her teeth, very quietly.

“I could take a scout car,” Mara said. “I could take two and a half kilometers of track and the beetles and four of the rail dogs.”

Issri shook her head even though it was a suggestion in her favor. “If it is a trap that has teeth for a train, it has teeth for a car. No. We go or we don’t. We do not break apart to be bitten separately.”

“Captain,” Cava said, “your conscience has split in two. Which half are you going to listen to today?”

Issri looked, this once, not at the window but at the floor. The deck under her boots was a brass plate engraved with the names of people who had died to keep the train from stopping before they intended. Two of the names were people who had died in order to stop the train when it had to stop. One of the names was a child whose body had been found on the coupler with both hands out like a bird.

“Echelon,” she said, and the lights above the windows warmed. “Calculate a turn in toward the Beacon to bring us within visual of this hinge without braking more than ten percent. Genz, begin a lay of a spur off our own head to give us a handhold we can throw away. Tamsin, write me a budget of water and weep about it very loudly. Cava, write me a prayer. Curator Leto—”

Mara had not expected the Captain to decide so quickly. She’d asked and people died for asking and there was no time for the careful grief she owed them.

“Yes,” Mara said.

“You will bring up whatever it is by that lovely name. You will bring me its recipes and its notes and its plans. If we must stop, we will stop with better art than anyone has ever managed before. If we must bleed out water, we will bleed it into vessels that mean we can pick it up again.”

“I should go down and tell the laundress,” Tamsin said into her cup. “Before the apology you had me practice two months ago becomes a lie.”

Cava’s eyes were on the window. “I have written your prayer. It goes like this: Please let the teeth be a door.”

The Heliotrope leaned. It leaned slightly, almost nothing. The rails under it sang a little higher. The children in the car below Mara’s shifted their fleet game and their bare feet drummed a new pattern, a storm on a roof. Out on the horizon a line of dust rose where the rail dogs found purchase and a vanguard became a wedge.

Mara left the Bridge last. The moment she set foot on the ladder she could taste metal and water like tears at the backs of her molars, the way she did when the Echelon forced a sharp draw on the heat gradient. In the corridor she passed the laundress, who had a basket piled with threadbare green towels and a baby asleep facedown belly-first on top of them, and she felt sudden, stupid love as sharp as hunger.

In the Archive she opened the door and the breath the world had been holding let go. She found the notebook that was full of systems that were not just recipes and not quite machines. The cover was old leather with her mother’s name on the inside, in pencil so faint you had to know it was there to see it. She had written in it with three pencils from three different stations and a charcoal stub and a polisher’s stone. The book smelled of the Heliotrope in rain and of her mother’s hair when her mother had been a hand-width shorter than a town wall.

Mara threaded the thin copper strap back over her head and down to the plate and tuned her breath to the humming metal. She said, “Echelon, play the message again.”

It came. When the voice said her name it sounded as if whoever spoke had thought saying her name would win them something. As if they remembered her before she had become who she had become. She drew a copy of the hinge system onto paper as if making the drawing could bring it into being closer to her and less capable of harm.

When the Archive bells chimed the second time that day, low and round like big slow hearts, the movement had begun. The Heliotrope leaned more. In an hour the rails would split away not behind them but before the prow. Out on the hardpan at the edge of night, a trapdoor blinked its eye and waited.

Mara shut the Book of Standing Water and clipped it under her arm. The sun never moved, but they would.

The ring is not silent.

They teach you that on your first hour in a suit, when the trainers still look like saints and your hands still shake without gravity to tell them where down is. The whisper of micro-impacts taps at your boots. The baritone groan of a kilometer slab rolling in slow frustration leaks through spines and helmets and into teeth. Static from charged dust nests in your hair. It is not silence that presses in on you out there; it is everything speaking in a language most of us forgot how to hear when we moved into walls.

So when the ring began to sing my name, I almost missed it under the expected noise.

My pack perched in the shadow of a pitted ice fin—a cliff face of dirty frost that rose and curved like a slice of frozen surf. Beyond it, Uranus took up a third of my view, washed pale in sunlight that had traveled nine hours to get bored and old and still make us squint. The planet’s bands were subtle, the color like bruised milk, not like the textbook images that burn with false blues. The rings themselves were nearly invisible unless you caught the angle right; then the dust lit in a smear, and the big ones, the ones we had fattened and fused over lifetimes, threw a knife-edge of darkness over the planet like scratches on glass.

My pack was five drones, each the size of a child’s bag, studded with thrusters and sensors, glossy dark to shed ice and static. In my ear, in that bare slice of sound the ring did not own, they purred and wheezed and murmured their little diagnostics like old cats. I named them years ago in a moment of superstition and humor and then never changed the names: Kettle, Pan, Jar, Spoon, and Tongs. When the husher tradition says you should name the things that listen with you, what else do you call them but the tools that hum and clang and live in heat?

“Pack,” I said, tapping my jaw to switch through their feeds, “we’re on a five. Wake all channels. Tongs, you go first. Pick up my hand?”

My gloves were thick. The nodes in my fingers sent a gentle shock into Tongs’ hull when I touched it. It pushed away from the fin and drifted in the thin snow that always fell in the ring: dust and shatters and breath.

“Picking up,” Tongs agreed in its soft procedural tone, which was just a software engineer’s idea of a personality, someone back in Hab Three who wanted hushers to feel less alone. “Victor India Bravo Gibberish… sorry. Debris field interfering. Calibrating.”

“Don’t apologize,” I told it, and angled my helmet HUD to open the model of the section ahead.

The section was called Azure’s Chord. Someone with poetry in their lungs named it long before my rotation. None of the ice here was blue. The ice, when it was pure, was white; when it was worked, it was grey; when it was old, it was black. Azure was probably for the planet, an old story about colored light under certain angles. The Chord was for the way this ring arc caught shepherd resonance and snapped like a string when the moons lined right.

Shepherd moons had been domesticated as much as anything giant and indifferent could be domesticated. We built baffles on them, turned their slight gravity sharper with towers and mass lines. We tugged at their paths the way you might lead an ox with a rope through its nose and a prayer it wouldn’t gore you. Even so, every so often their dance with the rings got mean. Waves marched. A boulder tumbled. A wave met a wave and made a wall. And eighty thousand people living in a city built into a ring of ice wanted the walls to behave.

We hushers made the walls behave.

I flicked my teeth against the implant switch, and the world went from image to sound. It was a bad habit. We had displays and models and predictive overlays for a reason. But if I didn’t take a taste of the raw, early in the job, I felt—wordless and superstitious—blind.

A tremor shrugged my bones, too slow to be heard as anything but a thought, and then it came up through the boots, a rolling thunder too low to be sound in air, too high to be tectonic in instinct. It was almost the note of a whale, if the whale were the size of a nation and made of frozen time.

“Feel that?” I asked the pack, knowing they didn’t.

“Azure’s Chord is at 0.31 increase on predicted amplitude,” said Kettle. “External knocks detected. Twelve incoming dust trails from the outer edge. One magnetized speck of unknown composition. Please advise.”

“Keep your voice down,” I told Kettle, because she always sounded like she was shouting secrets across a cafeteria. “You’ll wake the ice.”

“Ice is not sleeping,” Pan, who was dry and literal, informed me.

The husher channel chimed. Ziya’s voice threaded in, a little breathless with hurry or laughter—you could never tell with Ziya—carrying the spin of the habitat behind her, the squeak of a chair catching a boot heel, the far tinny chorus of a market arguing about mushrooms and heat. We hung humble on our little part of the ring, but we complicated it with living.

“Mara,” she said, cheerful. “You still out there pretending you can hold back Newton with five soup bowls and a prayer?”

“Six,” I said. “Don’t disrespect Jar.”

“Jar is sulking,” Jar reported.

“And pretends to be modest to get what it wants,” Ziya said. “Listen, can you—

A tone cut her off. It wasn’t the usual intercom reminder. It was the triple chirp we never ignored—a system alert from Chief Lark himself.

“Team Three,” said Lark. He didn’t like callsigns. He liked you reminded that you were a team and he had three of them. “Line twelve on Azure’s Chord is picking up a potential cascade along a two-kilometer face. Influence from Miranda’s wobble. We’re seeing a probable impact cluster in five. It’s dark stuff. It’s coming in hot.”

“Dark stuff?” Ziya said at once. “As in—what kind of dark?”

“As in the visual sensors can’t see it and the magnetometers don’t like it,” Lark said. “As in don’t lick it when it goes by, okalo?”

Ziya laughed. I didn’t. “I’m on the chord,” I said. “I can pre-hush the face.”

“Hush it,” Lark said. “Hard. This is going to be a walk on the ridge. I want no sound in my house tonight worse than the sound of my own snoring.”

The channel clicked off.

“Jar,” I said. “You’re forgiven. Take the left shoulder. Spoon, right. Kettle, middle sweet spot. Pan, go high and look humble. Tongs, you’re with me and you keep your sass to a minimum.”

“My sass is factory standard,” Tongs said.

The pack moved. Their thrusters whispered, spitting faint needles of compressed air to get purchase on nothing. They anchored themselves into predrilled sockets on the face of the fin and burrowed their clamps into the ice. I watched the ring’s model show a thin ripple moving toward us like a pale blush along a cheek, and I watched the predictions stack up, little hazard cones blossoming and fading as the algorithms argued about the future. I let the implants push the deep notes into bones, let me feel where the ring was a choir that would balance my drones and where it was a stubborn drunk who would pick a fight.

“Starting hush?” Ziya asked.

“In five,” I said.

“We pulled a scan on the magnetized object,” Ziya said. “It’s weird.”

“Everything’s weird at this distance,” I said.

“No, this is weird. It’s not on any composition tree I’ve got. It’s recording, too, like a little black box that forgot it’s dead.”

“That’s not what black boxes do,” Pan said, patient and sure.

“Humans named a fox a box when they were panicking,” Ziya said. “And Mara Qis, don’t you dare hush without me listening. I want to bite the raw first.”

“You’re not in a suit,” I protested.

“I have simbones,” she said, as if that were an answer. “Let me in.”

I flicked the share. There was a second’s lag while the software turned the ring into a sound you could pump through headphones instead of marrow and tooth. Then Ziya exhaled as the big note rolled up under us and through her.

“Oh,” she said softly. “Gods.”

“Language,” Pan said, because that is what Pan said in the absence of gods.

“Miranda’s wobble,” Ziya murmured. “She’s jealous.”

I watched the far edge of the fin. Dust like snow. Ice like cliffs. The place where habitat lights probed out into the ring, little lances of yellow in all that black.

“Kettle,” I said, and sent the hush pattern.

Kettle hummed. They all did, in their way. They pressed into the ice and vibrated at frequencies you could almost mistake for headache. The hush worked like a singer who knew exactly where to pitch her voice to make a glass not shatter. The pack listened at a dozen depths and sent back the note the ring didn’t want to hear, filling it with the right wrong sound so that the cascade would pick another path, fold softer, burn itself out in harmless waves and grumbles.

Azure’s Chord obliged. The first ripples came, and we canceled them, and the ice held as if I had put a flat palm on a stray dog’s ribs and told it to stay. The cascade rolled past us, frantic and beautiful, and did not find a home. On the HUD, danger cones winked and gave up. On the other channels, other hushers called, cussed, laughed, sang.

I was about to let myself smile, to say something bright to Ziya, when Kettle made a sound she had never made.

It was not language. It was a hiccup dropped into a drum. It made my list of instincts unroll like a paper fan. Somewhere behind me, where no air carried sound, my heart kicked out a new rhythm.

“Kettle?” I asked.

“Interference,” Kettle said. She did not apologize. Kettle never apologized. It had been a joke. I swallowed.

“What kind?”

“Unidentified. External. Resonant.”

“I’m not hearing it,” Ziya said.

“Because it’s in my bones,” I whispered, before I could stop myself.

“You’re doing the implant again,” Ziya said. “You’ll fry your jaw.”

“Shut up,” I said without heat, because the word had no edge when you said it to the person who had salt on your towels and burned taste still hanging in your tiny kitchen from the night before.

“Jar?” I said. “Pan? Tongs? Anyone else picking up an unpredicted input?”

“Nothing,” Pan said.

“I am blind and honorable,” Jar said, insulted at the implication.

“Tongs?” I asked.

Tongs hesitated.

“Repeat,” I said softly. “Tongs, repeat.”

The drone whispered, and in the whisper was a tremor I had never heard in my pack. They were not built to fear. They were built to be sure.

“Mara,” Tongs said. “I believe the ring is asking for you.”

Ziya swore. I would have too if all the breath I had were not busy falling out of me.

“What do you mean?” I asked. The question was so absurd that even saying it out loud felt like folktale.

“There is a modulation,” Tongs said, reverting to sterile terms as if they would keep us safe. “Superimposed on the low-frequency ripple from the cascade. It is not any natural interference pattern I know. It repeats. It appears shaped by intentional variation in amplitude over time, not by phase. The pattern matches your name.”

“Mara,” said Ziya disbelieving, incredulous, already hungry. “Mara, are you hearing it?”

“I don’t hear my own name,” I said, because I wasn’t a child anymore, because I didn’t want to be the story about the husher who stared into the snow and saw her dead mother waving. “I hear an unnatural modulation.”

“It’s your name,” Tongs insisted.

“Tongs,” I said, patient to mask the small knives that had unsheathed along my spine, “what does my name sound like?”

“It sounds like your name,” Tongs said, and I made a mental note to strangle the next engineer who thought they could save on compute by making the drones overconfident instead of right.

“Send me the raw,” Ziya said on the shared channel. “No smoothing. No filters. Don’t chisel it into something you think a human will understand. Give me the bones.”

I shared. The wave rolled through us again. The hush caught it and broke it like an oar through water. Underneath the big sound, something faint and frankly ridiculous was rattling at the edges.

Ziya breathed in. I held still. The planet hung and listened with us because the planet could not do anything else.

“Mara,” Ziya said slowly. “My cool and competent love, someone is knocking in the snow.”

I wanted to laugh. I wanted to turn off my teeth. I wanted to tell Lark we had a pretty story to tell the babies back this shift, and then I wanted to dig with my hands until my nails bled and see if there was a heart under all that hard.

“Kettle,” I said, keeping my voice level, “model the interference impact if we do not correct for it in the hush.”

“Local amplitude will increase by 0.41 within one hundred seconds,” she said. “Load exceeds safe thresholds for socket #12 and #32. Probability of a slab snap rises to nine percent.”

“Which is more than anyone at Hab Three will enjoy hearing,” Ziya said.

“This is not a when-your-lover-says-something-mean-and-you-pretend-you-didn’t-hear situation,” Pan said. Pan had learned sarcasm, but like a child who had just been handed a knife.

“I can do two things at once,” I said, though I wasn’t sure if I could. “I can hush the cascade. And I can leave a little room for the… knock.”

“This is a rationalization,” Pan said.

“You are a pot that never built anything,” I said.

“Mara Qis,” Lark said, cutting into our headspace nicely, as if he had been waiting to be the voice in the story that comes in exactly at the worst second. “Status.”

“We judged no cascade,” I said, mechanical. “We’re catching the wave. There is an anomalous input. We are assessing a possible correlation with the magnetized object.”

“A real answer,” Lark said.

“There’s a voice in my ice,” I said, before I could stop myself; and then, because I heard the words leave my mouth and become idiocy because nothing I could do would call them back, I added, “and this is where you say, yes, I need you to hush the voice too.”

Lark was silent, which was not usual; he was not a man who left space around words because space made echoes he did not trust.

“You’re not the only one hearing it,” he said at last, and the hairs on my arms that hadn’t gone back down lifted again. “Three arcs down, Team One just sent me a markup of a modulation on their face. It reads like code. Not our code. Then their feed cut.”

My tongue went dry. “Cut how?”

“Like a hand across a mouth,” Lark said. “Don’t be poetic, Mara. Do the job. You hush the cascade. The magnets can send a trawler for the object. Hushing is what keeps the air in our pipes.”

“Yes,” I said, because he was right. Because if the ice wall snapped under us, it wouldn’t be romantic at all. It would be metal creaking around your thighs and a ten-second blizzard and the subsequent long, quiet after.

He cut the feed. Ziya’s breath filled the space he left.

“Pan,” I said. “Spoon. Kettle. Give me a mirror hush. Tongs, you ghost it.”

“Ghost?” Tongs asked, eager.

“You’re going to echo the interference faintly at a second harmonic on the opposite phase,” I said. “You’re going to pretend to be stupid and sloppy. You’re going to make it look like a natural error. You’re going to see if the interference follows you like an idiot or keeps to the main wave like a plan.”

“That’s unkind to idiots,” Ziya said, but her voice had the edge it got when she was listening hard. “Do you think it’s riding the cascade? That someone is… surfing into us?”

“I think this is how my grandmother would have talked to the next farm down the snow if all the long lines were cut,” I said.

“Your grandmother did not have a ring,” Pan said.

“She had fields,” I said.

We played our little dangerous game. The hush went on in earnest, catching, crushing, whispering the big wave into behavior. Tongs pushed a little tremble into the face, a mirror of the interference but wrong in a way that an amateur would be wrong, that an accident would be wrong.

The interference did not follow Tongs.

“It’s not chatting with you,” Ziya said softly. “It’s talking to the ring.”

“Or through it,” I said.

Kettle chimed again. “Magnetized object will cross our visual in twenty seconds.”

“Can you tag it?” I asked.

“With what?” Kettle asked.

“What the hell would you tag it with,” Ziya said, amused and terrified. “Paint?”

Tongs could spit magnetic dust. We used it to draw interior maps of broken hollows sometimes. It was a child’s trick and a good one.

“Dust,” I said.

“No dust,” Lark said, back in our ears like he’d never left. “The magnets, uppercase M, want to catch this thing clean.”

“Tell the magnets to catch my sweat,” Ziya said. “We’re out here with spatulas.”

We missed the dust window. The object tumbled into view like a stain. If a shadow could be thrown onto nothing, it would look like that: a shape not there until it was, a darkness darker than the dark behind it, a thumbprint smudged over stars. It passed the edge of the fin a meter from Tongs, slow as a prayer and fast as a bullet.

Something in my teeth sang.

“Tongs,” I said sharply. “You don’t follow that.”

“Understood,” Tongs said, sounding like a child with her hands twisted into her skirt to keep from reaching.

“What is it,” Ziya whispered, as if quiet could make it less.

“Nothing I know,” I said, because there was no proof to argue with the old forms. “A rock that forgot light, maybe.”

“You do not forget light,” Pan said.

“When I fell asleep with a flashlight under the covers, I forgot light all the time,” Ziya said. “My mother slapped the sheet and burned me with brightness. Tongs, don’t you go. Mara, you’re shaking.”

She was right. My fingers trembled on the clamps. I wanted to grip the ice with my bare hands and make sure it was as dumb and familiar as it had always been.

“It spoke your name,” Tongs said again, stubborn.

“What if it’s not a voice,” Ziya said. “What if it’s a pattern we read because we are apes and want to make faces out of leaves?”

“Then it’s a good face,” I said. “Then it’s better than listening for hours and hearing only the itch in your own hair.”

“Mara,” Ziya said. “Look.”

She pinged me a grid. Clean, simple. Old. It was a picture of a hash pattern we teach apprentices to look for as a joke and a history lesson. Eight in, eight out, lines and dots. One of the first encodings we used to send messages in the very early days of the rings, when half of our equipment was salvaged and the other half was invented drunk. You flash it in magnet, in light, in pressure. You can drive it with whatever you can push.

It was in the ring. It was in the interference. It was faint and broken and wrong—but wrong in the way the hand of an old friend is wrong when it shakes in cold.

“What does it say?” I asked, voice thick.

Ziya swallowed. Those faint raw sounds carried in. Once, in a setting with walls, I heard a person press their forehead to a door and talk to the wood. It sounded like this did.

“Hold,” she said. “Wait. No. That’s not a letter. That’s a calling sign.”

“Don’t dramatize,” Pan said, but even Pan’s voice had a little lift in it now, as if a kettle had started singing in a cold kitchen.

“It’s a calling sign,” Ziya said, sure now, excited, careful. “It’s mangled, Mara, but it’s there. Eur— no. That’s not a Greek letter, that’s just my brain wanting to make it one. Eury— wait.”

My tongue knew the name before she said it. We had chased it as a game, as a campfire story, as an if. We’d drunk and told one another how we’d have followed its wake. We’d sniggered at the people who named their kids after lost ships.

“Eurydice,” Ziya said softly. “Mara, it’s calling the Eurydice.”

“Don’t be a poet,” Lark said at once, reflexive, frightened.

He stayed in anyway. We all did.

The Eurydice had gone out to the halo many years before I was born. A sailship towed by a captive magnetic filament. Thirty crew, one to be married when she came home, one who wrote poems about fields. She’d broken tether, the story went. She’d drifted. She’d fallen in. She’d gone to the cold. We told the story to remind ourselves to always check our clips.

“Nobody calls the dead,” Lark said. “Nobody calls what they cannot get to with a hand and a wrench. We do not have boats for the halo. We have soup bowls on strings.”

“What if the dead calls us?” Ziya asked, and I loved her then in a way that had nothing to do with wanting and everything to do with the dangerous hope in her ridiculous question.

“Pan,” I said. “Normalize for wave interference and spit the pattern back. Low. Gentle. One of the old codes. Say hello like you would to a dog you eventually want to put a leash on.”

“I do not greet dogs I want to leash,” Pan said, offended.

“Pan,” I said.

Pan graphed. Pan sent. The hushers hummed. The cascade fitted itself around us and went off elsewhere to be drama in someone else’s pockets. The magnetized object rolled away and took its shadow with it, like a hole in the world closing.

A second stretched. Then another. The only sound was the deep slow singing and the contradictory zero of space around it.

And then it came back.

It was not my name. It was a simple note, sharp and desperate and trembling, heat in the cold. It came braided with the ring’s mass and with the dust. It came up through my boots and bit my bones.

I knew it like I knew the shape of my own hand. It was the first line of a school algorithm, repeated, repeated, as if the rememberer were not sure if we had left and wanted to keep us at the door.

Hello, it said in a language old enough to be new. Hello. Hello. Hello.

Everyone spoke at once. The channel filled with unhelpful noises, joy and terror and the crackle of appetites and old aches. Lark made a sound I had never heard out of him, not a word, something like a folder closing on fingers.

“Mara,” he said. “Do not be foolish.”

“I’ve never been anything else,” I said, and because the hush held and the face did not crack and the pack did not fail and the planet did not fall, I sent hello back again.

The line we built our lives on — if you push, it pushes back — turned and faced me. I had my hand on the ribs of something that was not sleeping. I had always told apprentices that the ring is not silent and now I had a chance to show them what else it was not.

Ziya laughed, a bright thing in the dark. Behind her, the market shouted about mushrooms. Behind me, the ring rolled on.

“Tell me a thing I can fix, Mara,” Lark said, which is what he said when the world made the wrong kind of music.

“We can fix this when we see it,” I said. “We can see it when it tells us where it is. It will tell us where it is when it thinks we are listening.”

“You are not hearing your name,” Tongs insisted, one last time, stubborn and clear, and if a machine could offer benediction, that was what it sounded like.

I put my glove over the clamp and felt the tiny sting of frost through the insulation, a reminder and a promise. My mouth was dry. My implants were hot. Often the ring spoke and I was the only one listening; often I spoke and the ring did not reply. Now the universe had done us a vulgar courtesy and said hello first.

“Hold the hush steady,” I said. “Let the song in the edges get louder if it wants. We are not going to break the face. We’re going to meet our neighbors.”

On the far side of the fin, something knocked. It was not in air. It was in structure, which is to say it was in everything that held us up.

The object’s shadow had drifted already, on a curve I could predict and then not, because something in me did not want to predict it anymore.

The first chapter is the part of the story where the ocean leans in and shows you a hand. There is a math to it and there is a superstition too. You look up and see the planet like a lamp behind old paper and you put your mouth to the ice and you say hello until you are sure you are heard.

Hello, I sent. My pack hummed. The ring took it in and tossed it like a fisherman throwing back a silver fish that will not feed his children now but may grow.

Hello, came the answer, like a whisper dropped into a drum. And then, before I could tell Ziya not to cry because the valves didn’t like salt, came the next line, clipped, broken, foolish, hopeful between the storm and the hush:

Mara.

The city makes a sound when the tide turns. It’s not what you’d expect—no romantic whistles through broken towers or mournful whale-song of steel. It’s teeth on glass. All that submerged facade and fractured window-frame flexing a little as pressure equalizes, a soft clatter like wind chimes in a house no one lives in anymore. I taste it through the regulator, something metallic and bitter that always conjures someone’s kitchen. My mother’s, sometimes. If I let it.

I don’t let it today.

“Three minutes to slack,” Miro says over the suit’s bone-mic. Above us, on the skiff, he’s a warm hum more than a voice. I imagine him hunched over the feed, chewing algae gum and squinting at currents like they were bookkeeping. He calls everyone cousin, as if that throws a blanket over the fact that none of us are really watching out for each other out here. “Nai, you’re leading. Don’t fall in love with the pretty lights.”

I give him a little click, an acknowledgment without words. I can’t roll my eyes with a visor on, but I do anyway. The pretty lights are the reason I’m down here at all.

The mantaray drones slide past me, silver ovals against the bruise-blue. Their bellies are yellow with hazard paint and they blink their green ‘I’m thinking’ LEDs as if I’m stupid enough to trust them. They send out a ping that ripples down the street and comes back fractured—this block used to be Dorn Avenue, if I believe the rusted street sign speared by a sea urchin the size of a tire. On both sides the old office towers rise forty floors into the dark, floors that no longer hold anyone’s breath or paperwork. The coral does, though. It blooms on the edges, all scalloped ridges and bone-white shelves, glimmering faintly with engineered algae feeding on the city’s old heat.

Ahead, in the place where Dorn met Eddystone, the shape is unmistakable even in ruin. A triangular bite of steel and glass, slumped sideways and pinned on its neighbor like a collapsed dancer. The signage has rotted down to a single letter—A, enormous and arrogant, half-obscured by barnacles. Administrative Archive, probably. One of a hundred. Good enough.

“Lock your tether,” Miro says. “I want you to tie off on any structural that isn’t trying to make art.” His laugh is sandpaper. “Hey, Sela? Laish? We’re not robbing the roof. We’re pulling the reef.”

“Copy,” Sela says. Her voice always sounds like someone else is speaking through her. “Cameras are rolling. Nai, your feed is clean.”

“It’s only clean because I scrub it,” I mutter, but I flick the wrist to send my visuals up anyway. The HUD is a skeleton of lines over a slow ballet of silt and light: manta #2 on my left flank, a school of translucent fish making a silk scarf of themselves, the Archive’s main entrance yawning ahead like a throat. The door has been smashed by currents, replaced by the round mouth of a coral fan that has chosen to grow where the welcome mat used to be.

“Ready,” I say. I adjust my ballast; the suit compensates, humming through my ribs. The tether unspools from the drum at my waist with a neat little purr. Above, clouds move. We’re down long enough that I’ve learned to feel the shifting brightness as a shadow on my skin.

I love it, even when I pretend I don’t. The city drowned before I was born, and like everyone my age I belong equally to salt and rust. The surface is where the quotas get shouted and the markets hustle; down here is where stories fossilize.

“Remember,” Miro says, the humor gone from his voice, “no unauthorized pockets. SA’s crawling. They’re hungry for a score.”

“Copy,” I say, which means I heard him, which is the minimum requirement. The Surface Authority would take a finger for an unlogged find if they were in a good mood. A hand for a bad one. I keep my hands; I keep my fingers.

The coral fan at the archive’s mouth is a living thing too beautiful to be true, petals aligned into a spiral that would make a mathematician weep into their swill. As my glove brushes a ridge, tiny polyps pull in with synchronous shyness. A tremor shivers through it, and it’s not just water. It’s signal.

“There,” Sela breathes in my ear. “You see that overlay?”

It’s faint, a haze stitched into my feed by the analysis program, but it’s there: a dull gold scatter that resolves into a lattice if you squint. We call it memory glitter, because we are too irreverent to name things properly. The reef has grown over an old datacenter. Sometimes the algae and the coral take on the algorithmic rhythms of what they’re devouring, like shells absorbing a song. We strip it, we coax it, we render it into fragments of the world that was. Weddings, shipping schedules, scavenged novels, tax records. Everyone always wants lost images of love and catastrophe; what pays our rent are the spreadsheets.

The drone slides up to the coral and kisses it with a micro-vibration. “Waking him gently,” Sela murmurs. “Be nice.”

“Be quick,” Miro says. “You’ve got—two. Tide’s turning faster.”

I slide in through the fan and into the lobby. The floor is a raft of silt resting on the bones of security bars. The coral here is thicker, more elaborate and more aggressive—boulder corals and brain corals muscling over each other, a slow motion gang war that carved space into narrow aisles. The lights on my shoulders paint everything false; in the periphery, creatures flicker. An eel in an elevator. A cloud of jellies floating past what was once a reception desk. The weight of water and time is a cathedral.

Voices are dangerous down here—you hear things—but I have to try. “Sela, I’ve got eight meters to the left-hand server farm. Manta #3 is flagging increased signal density.”

“Confirm,” Sela says. “It’s thick like winter soup. Give me a slab if you can.”

I squeeze into an aisle so narrow my left tank whispers against a rib of coral. Someone once said this must be what it’s like to move through a sleeping animal’s throat. I think of it every time, and every time I curse them on their grave.

“There’s a rumor,” Laish says in a stage whisper. He’s up on the skiff with Miro, his feet hung over the side, probably dreaming of the god’s share of our take. “Tide traders say SA found a pocket yesterday full of clean prints. Old code. Think they’ll auction it dry to the patent mills.”

“Shut it,” Sela and Miro say at the same time.

I stop moving. Not because of Laish’s rumor, though it lands in me like a low ache. Because there is a second signal.

It slides under the drone’s steady rhythm like a bass note, so low it might be a pressure artifact or my own heart. I close my eyes, the childish gesture of someone trying to listen with her skin, and it swells, not louder but closer. It feels personal.

“Nai?” Sela says, alert. “Your vitals spiked.”

“Just tight space,” I lie. “Hold my hand, why don’t you.”

The hum shapes itself. You hear a lot of voices down here if you want to. Grief makes tape loops; hope does too. But this isn’t one of the archive-echoes you can dismiss as your brain trying to make words out of noise. This is syllables hiding in the wave. This is breath on my neck in a room where no one has breathed in twenty years.

“Nai,” the signal says. My name. No one calls me that except people who knew me when my legs were shorter and my curiosity had fewer scars.

I freeze hard enough that my knee locks in place and the joint tells me about it. Silt showers up around me like a curtain. I have to force myself to reduce the panic cascade to manageable parts. I count the seconds. I breathe. I let the mantas push their green LEDs close until they seem like beetle eyes.

“Nai,” the voice says again, and it is close to my ear without any of the artifacts of comms, none of the dryness of radio. It is a woman’s voice, low, a little hoarse. It is my voice, older.

I have never believed in miracles. I believe in angles and leverage. I also believe, reluctantly, in patterns you can’t immediately explain.

“Say that again,” I whisper. “Say it again so I can pretend you’re real.”

Miro is all sharp consonants now. “Nai, report.”

“There’s a bleed,” I say. “Electrical. Don’t panic.”

“Who’s panicking?” Laish says, already panicking.

I inch forward. The aisle doglegs to the right and dumps me into a chamber, some offshoot of the main server room. The racks here have collapsed, their aluminum bones splayed like broken umbrellas, and the coral has made a low, dense canopy over them. The memory glitter is everywhere. It’s in my teeth. The mantas hesitate, confused by the density. My suit’s receiver yanks at the hum like a kid pulling at his mother’s sleeve.

I reach out and lay my palm on one of the smooth coral domes.

Heat pours into me. Not literal, not enough to cook anything, just a wash like when you step past a bakery vent into winter air. Then the voice—not just syllables now, but cadence and rhythm like walking into a room and knowing your own footstep is already there waiting.

“Nai,” it says. “If you’re hearing this, it worked.”

A ridiculous laugh tries to get out of my chest. I stop it by biting the inside of my mouth. “What is this?” I ask no one, then realize my bone-mic is probably catching it. “It’s—Sela, I’m getting a cross-modulation. It’s like the reef retained a training set.”

“Run a check,” Sela says, polite-homicide cool. She does not ask me what it is doing to my heart rate. “If it’s echoing, we can map it.”

“It’s not an echo,” I start, then stop, because what would I call it? The voice goes on, ignorant of me.

“I’m you,” it says, and I feel myself recoil against the suit and the suit respond with its little haptic that says calm down. “Don’t do the thing where you refuse to entertain the impossible because it played a trick on you once. Breathe. You will want to be clever. Please don’t be. We don’t have time.”

I taste salt that has nothing to do with the Pacific. It is something childish and angry and frightened in my mouth. I am about to be angry for a very long time if this is some elaborate SA trap, or a story someone embedded to make a diver lose her edge.

“Tell me something only I know,” I say under my breath. I realize as I say it that there are versions of me who would rather not know it, who have wrapped certain memories in newspaper and stuck them in the freezer to deaden their smell. But that has always been the deal with salvage—you go down for something you might not want to bring home.

“When you were eight,” the voice says, “you stole strawberries off the hydroponics at the school and hid under the expansion joints on the roof. You let them warm in the tar, then you ate them slow. You licked your fingers so long the guard thought you were crying. You told your brother that you had been fasting, so you were holy. He laughed and said you smelled like something holy had died in your mouth.”

The mantas blink. My body is a city whose power grid just surged and then settled. Miro, Sela, Laish are saying things, I am sure of it, but they are in another layer of water, far above.

I move both hands to the coral. “How.”

“I don’t know,” the voice says. “I don’t know the map. I know it can imprint voices in the lattice. Someone taught the coral to learn, and then the coral learned to keep. Then someone taught me how to write into what the coral keeps, and that someone’s bones are good calcium now.”

A bubble of air escapes my regulator and rushes up, and I watch it like a spell. On the skiff, Miro is swearing in three languages at once.

“You have to get the seed out,” the voice says. “It’s small. It looks like a pillar coral’s bud but it resonates. Don’t give it to Miro. Don’t give it to Sela. They’re not bad; they’re just alive. Give it to Aris, second shift, the noodle stand under the brown tarp, the one that does too much ginger. He’ll take it to the right place. And don’t—do not—go to the Spindle on Day 220. Wait until 236. The ladder will have settled by then, and Jit won’t be working the pulley. I know you like Jit. Don’t. Trust. Jit.”

I find myself laughing. I can’t stop it. I sound, in my own ears, crazy. I will blame nitrogen if anyone hears me. The Spindle is the half-collapsed vertical market that rides the tide levels in Exe Sector; everyone goes to the Spindle because everyone has to.

“You’re not me,” I say, not to the voice and not to anyone else, but to the version of myself that is already starting to be careful in the wrong ways.

“On Day 228,” the voice says, patient in a way I have never been, “the SA will sweep Miro’s skiff. Laish will jump and break his left wrist on the rail. Sela will smile and say it’s a lucky day for the lottery, isn’t it, and they will take her in for an hour and then let her go because that is what she is. They won’t find what you hide if you put it where—”

“Stop,” I say, and then, more usefully: “Where is the seed.”

I can hear Sela hissing my name in my ear now, not unlike an eel. “Nai. Send us a shot. What are you doing, Nai.”

“Working,” I say, and pivot my camera so that she sees what I want her to see and not what I don’t.

“The bud under your left palm,” the voice continues, the warmth of it filtering through the bone of the coral into my glove. “Twist it like a jar. If it stings, let it. You have fifteen seconds before the reef wakes its defense.”

“Defense?” Laish says, because of course that word penetrates. “No one told me the rocks bite.”

“Only if you make them,” I say. “Keep your toes in.”

I wrap my fingers around the almond-shaped nub. It is slicker than I expect, and when I turn it, there is a little give. The reef shivers. Something in my forearm stings like static, a little thousand-needle fizz that travels up toward my elbow and stops. The bud loosens and comes free with a pop you can’t hear, and instantly the entire chamber seems to flick. The mantas retreat half a meter. My own blood, for an irrational instant, insists that there is a sharp fin slicing past my thigh.

I cradle the bud in my palm. It is a thing that might be a seed or a pearl or a worthless bit of calcium. It hums in that same not-sound that rides my bones.

“Good girl,” the voice says, and the warmth there is so close to my mother’s that for a heartbeat I am inside an evening that will never happen again. I can smell the algae stew. I can see the cheap bowl with its crack down one side. I can feel my brother’s shoulder pressed to mine, both of us pretending we are not afraid of becoming other people’s problems. I hate the warmth even as I lean into it.

The reef wakes. I feel it like a slow muscle flex, a tightening under the mantle. The polyps on the dome unfurl, and they are not teeth, not exactly, but I do not want them to brush bare skin. A current draws past my ear, not water, something else, a momentum in the posture of the colony that says: not yet a bite, but ready.

“Time,” Miro says, this time just a professional countdown. “Nai, we are done. Tide’s shifting hard. Out in sixty.”

“Copy,” I say, so gently I hope he thinks it means something. I open my hand, press the bud against the little hinge in my suit’s wrist that I should not have, that no diver should have because the SA will take your hand for it. The hinge opens like an eyelid. The bud disappears into the suit, into the space between my skin and the world. It is a violation, what I do next. I am good at violations because I know how to be small when necessary.

The reef’s shiver becomes a quiver. A thin thread of mucus lashes at the spot where my glove had been. The mantas back up a little farther and turn red to show their disapproval.

“Out,” Sela says, not unkindly. “Don’t be greedy.”

“I’m never greedy,” I say, and snake back through the dogleg, through the aisle, through the temporary cathedral. The coral fan at the entrance is less shy now. It brushes my helmet with a touch like inadvertent intimacy. Above, the light has shifted—there’s a sheen like oil on the world. My tether tugs because the ocean wants a little piece of me and my suit says, no, this one is mine.

We breach and the day’s sound comes crashing back in. The skiff’s deck is a hot slap after the cool. My helmet yanks off with a wet willingness, air hits my face like an insult, and Miro’s smile is a knife with teeth.

“You look like someone told you you could retire,” he says. He helps me unbuckle because if there’s one true thing about Miro, it’s that he needs the river to keep being the river and his divers to keep breathing. “Did you get me something sweet?”

“We’re rich forever,” I say. I never learned how to be cautious at the right time. “Sela, feed?”

Sela has a visor on, her eyes two moonless insides. She nods, distracted, already dancing with the data. “We got a good slab. Clean overlays. If the mills don’t mind off-white, we’ll get enough for fresh fruit and the right kind of soap. Laish, stop trying to see through my head.”

Laish has wrapped his left wrist in elastic. He always wraps something in elastic. It makes him feel attended to. He leans toward me like a plant finding water. “Did you hear it?” he asks, his fear already ticklish with hunger. “I heard it. Sela, tell her I heard it.”

“No one heard anything,” Miro says. “No one hears voices in the sewer. We listen to data. We don’t speak to ghosts because there are no ghosts; there are only back pay and tariffs. The SA is cold. I can feel them scenting.” He points with his chin. In the middle distance, a black hull sits low, arrogant. No flag, because they don’t need one. “Laish, hide all the bottles that don’t have a tax stamp. Sela, button our faces on. Nai…”

His gaze does a thing it doesn’t do often. It meets mine. He is the kind of man who only looks directly at you when there is nothing you can do to his advantage. Today, for a moment, he looks because he is worried. It makes him human and I hate it.

“Nai,” he says, and his hand hovers over my arm like he might touch me, and doesn’t. “You went quiet down there.”

“Had to squeeze through a narrow place,” I say. “I had to think thin.”

“Keep thinking thin,” he says, and claps my shoulder so hard my clavicle complains. “SA’s going to do a polite little sniff. Give them your teeth and save your tongue.”

He turns away and begins to be himself again, loud and necessary, waving his cheap cigarette in the humidity like a scepter. Sela nudges my hip with hers as she passes, barely moving her mouth. “You good?”

“I’m funny,” I say. “Ask me to tell you a joke.”

She bumps me again, humorless. “Be careful.”

The SA men arrive like they always do: too clean for this water, too certain of their own teeth. They will talk, and we will pretend to listen, and some water will change pockets. The sun glares at the optics in their helmets and turns them into blank syllables.

I stand at the rail while Miro does his rituals. The city’s teeth-on-glass song is gone now; the tide snaps in another direction. The skiff rocks and someone swears because someone always does. The seed warms under my skin where I hid it, a little fever. I put my palm there and try not to think of infection.

“Aris,” I say under my breath, because saying names sometimes makes plans more real. The noodle stall under the brown tarp in the Exe, too much ginger. I haven’t been there in months because of how the owner smiled like he knew exactly what kind of trouble I would bring him one day.

“Nai,” a SA helm says above me. The voice is filtered into neutral. The man inside is younger than me by a slice. “Any unreported acquisitions?”

“Just my charm,” I say, and the helm’s head does an irritated tilt that gives me joy out of proportion to its size.

That night, the storm that was a line at noon becomes a field. The skiff creaks against its moorings in a chorus, and the market—the part of it that doesn’t float away—is a lantern festival made anxious. I leave after doing exactly enough to keep Miro from sending someone after me. I wedge myself into the stream of bodies moving toward the Exe Sector, where the Spindle hunched over its own wreckage like a tarantula and the noodle stands do their best to perfume the compactor-sweet air into something like appetite.

Aris’s stand is where I remember, shamefully unchanged except for the new crack in the tarp and the addition of a little chalk drawing of a fish with teeth. He sees me and rolls his eyes so hard they would be a liability on a ladder.

“I told the ginger about you,” he says, before I can speak. “It was insulted.”

“I’ve upgraded my tongue,” I say. “It can take more abuse.”

He flips noodles with a movement that is very close to affection. Aris has the hands of someone who knows how to lift a person by their elbows without making them feel like cargo. He slides a bowl toward me. “Payment?”

I could pretend. I could carry on a small play in which I am a good girl telling lies. But something about the voice has burned that part of me down to the tin. I tilt my wrist so he can see the small square of my skin that is slightly warmer than the rest, the place where the suit’s hinge sits like a second mouth.

Aris does not start. He sighs like a mechanic presented with a familiar error message. He keeps flipping noodles. “Of course,” he says. “Of course today.”

“Do you want to see it before you say no?” I ask. My own voice sounds too bright. I am not a canary, I tell myself. I am a gill.

He turns his face toward me, really looks. His eyes are old. The rest of him is not. “You think I’m going to say no?”

“I think you should,” I say. I slide onto the low stool and let the steam make my eyes water. “But the person who told me to come to you sounded like someone who knows my poor habits.”

He touches my wrist, two fingers, light. The hinge opens at the heat of his skin like a secret doing a tired trick. I press my palm flat on the counter between us. It’s not the bud anymore. The bud is gone. In its place is a line of chalk-bright white etched at the edge of my hand like a tidemark.

Aris whistles once, under his breath. It is an exhale with a purpose. He reaches for the noodle ladle as if his muscles think he must keep doing the thing he always does, but he doesn’t pick it up. He stares, then he closes his hand around my fingers and lifts my palm to his ear. He listens to my skin.

“What did you do,” he says, like an old priest asking a girl where she left her shoes on the morning she was supposed to go up the mountain.

“I stole something,” I say, because that is the answer I have always liked best. “From the past. Or from somewhere that thinks it is. It told me not to go to the Spindle on Day 220. It told me to find you. Please be the Aris under the brown tarp who does too much ginger.”

He laughs once, too loud, and then he stops. He turns away and pretends to fix a burner. “You will need a poor cup and a good cup,” he says. “We’ll drink from the poor one. We’ll leave the good one full so the ghost doesn’t think we’re greedy.”

“I don’t believe in ghosts,” I say. It is a lie only in the way a bandage is a lie: it conceals, it hopes.

“Of course you do,” he says. “You just call them something else.”

Behind us the market throws its voice in a hundred directions, and the sea lifts its head and considers. The seed hums in my hand. The marks on my skin begin to glow, faintly, as if someone is drawing a map in the milk under my palm, a map that doesn’t match any coastline I have ever seen, a map of lights where lights do not yet exist.

The road stopped the way a torn seam stops, threads springing loose into white.

Sori took her foot off the accelerator but did not brake. The chassis hummed under her, tires singing on cracked asphalt. The windshield ahead showed nothing but a wall of blankness where the highway used to be, a flat, pale pressure that made the shapes of the world around it sharper. On either side, the scrubland, the leaning billboards for old brands and new, the ribcage of a wind farm—they all seemed suddenly staged, hung props on the last few meters of a stage.

Her spooler drone lifted from the passenger seat like a gull taking a thermal. It hovered to the right, its three counter-rotors almost silent. A thin ribbon of data-light unspooled from its belly, flickering as the drone sniffed the edge, sampling the seam.

“Edge Sweep seventy-seven beeline,” Sori said, not to the drone but to her log. Her in-eye confirmed: Arclight Continuance—Sori An—Auditor grade—Field radius: five hundred meters—Attention stream quality: marginal: ninety-two minutes since last paid break. Please consider opening an entertainment loop to maintain baseline.

She ignored that. The drone chirped, and the ribbon snapped taut.

Sori rolled forward until the nose of the rover almost kissed the white. A dull chill leaked off it, the way the back of a refrigerator leaks into a kitchen. No sound from beyond, no air movement. The end of the world smelled faintly of disinfectant and of static, as if rain had never learned what to do there.

She killed the engine. In the quiet, the white hummed in a frequency that wasn't quite sound. A tiny shiver went through her, the way the first cold of a fever gets into your bones.

“Show me the weave,” she said.

The spooler pulsed a cone of invisible pressure at the seam. Gridlines ghosted into being on Sori's in-eye overlay—continuity crosshatching like the warp and weft of a fabric, thinning out where it met the white. Scrolling diagnostics followed: Edge delamination—two hundred and thirteen centimeters deep at center line—fray trending—local residents reported stalling. No anchors in place within the last forty-eight hours. Her appointment was hours late. The call had gone out at dawn. They always went out at dawn. People fought harder in the mornings.

She got out and stood barefoot on the warm blacktop. Her boots thunked as she set them on the hood. The habit was old, from before Arclight issued the self-sterilizing soles. She liked the ripple of heat through skin. She liked the feel of a road that had led somewhere once.

Beyond, a stranded billboard advertised Continuance Assurance, smiling families climbing a ladder of light. The bottom half of the ladder had been eaten by white, and the father's forearm ended in a clean, impossible line.

Sori unrolled a soft case and took out a disc the size of her palm, heavy for its smallness, matte black. An anchor. She hummed without meaning to, a few bars of an old song her mother had taught her when she was small, something about counting, about keeping steps. Maybe that was why she’d started this work. Maybe she just liked the ritual of it: eye, hand, throw, catch.

She balanced the disc on her fingers. The white resisted her gaze. It gave back nothing to look at, and that nothing took effort. Her attention slid on it like a skater on glare ice. She turned the disc, felt the raised ridges of its ridgeline code, felt the notch at the one o'clock position that would let her index finger drop at the moment of release.

The spooler pinged. “Please commence anchor test,” it said in its bright, sexless voice. It had named itself Salt. They all did that now, some quirk in the factory net. Salt had papered her in-eye with tiny reminders and cheery animations since Uttara: winning streaks, above-average performance, curated playlists to keep her attention weighted, cutesy seam-cat cartoons. Sori tapped the corner of one window and it shrank like a scolded animal.

She breathed out and threw.

The disc cut the hot air, sundial shadow spinning across the pavement. It struck the white and vanished without sound. For a heartbeat there was only the humming dullness. Then a circle opened where the disc had gone, a shallow bowl pressing itself into the blank, like a thumb pushing into wet paper. Color bled from the world into the circle. Sori tasted copper. The hair on her arms prickled. The bowl deepened. White receded away from the anchor, and reality made a place around it for a few meters as if coaxed, as if reminded of what it had agreed to be.

Road. Cracked. A pale weed pushing up where a seam had lifted. The faint vibration of bugs that live under guard rails. A slant of shadow.

“Anchor integrity at thirty-two percent,” Salt reported. “Attention density marginal. Consider opening an entertainment—”

“Later,” Sori said.

She walked closer. The bowl lip shimmered, and the smell the white had carried was replaced by hot asphalt and sage. Her in-eye showed the circle as a fragile thing of numbers and thin wires. Her body told her its own truth. The edge of the bowl pushed like a muscle resisting.

Somewhere behind her, there were footsteps, light, hesitant. Sori didn't turn. If she scared them, they would run.

“I’m not armed,” she said. “Just here to stitch.”

The footsteps stopped. She heard someone breathing. Finally, a voice: a girl, nine, maybe ten, the age of articulations and hard opinions.

“You're the one in the car,” the girl said. “With the wing that buzzes.”

“It’s called a spooler,” Sori said. “He gets offended if you don’t call him by his name.”

Salt chirped obligingly. Sori glanced back. The child was thin under a shirt two sizes too big, its graphic bleached into abstraction. Her bare legs were scratched from thorns. She stood with her weight on one foot, ready to run. Her hair was cut blunt, as if someone had done it with a kitchen knife. In the child's eyes, the white had mirrored itself: a flatness that had learned not to expect return.

“You’re not supposed to be here,” Sori said gently. “Who are you with?”

The girl pushed her chin out. Bravado in the face of the big fact that had eaten the road. “We live,” she said. “Over that way. It comes closer sometimes, and the goats get dumb.”

Sori placed her palm flat against the lip of the anchored circle and the world pressed back, cool as the inside of a wrist. “You called it in? The seam?”

The girl nodded without taking her eyes from the anchor's bowl. “The road was shorter. Yesterday it wasn’t so much. Mama said to call if it took the sign. It took the sign.”

“Where is your mama now?”

The girl blinked, and for a moment Sori saw a flicker under the child's face, a ripple of something that wasn't bravado, wasn't even fear—more like indignation that the rules you had been taught could betray you. “She went to see.”

Sori did not look at the white now. She kept her gaze on the child, on the shade of the girl's collarbone. “She went in?” Sori asked. “Into the blank?”

“She said it was quieter in there,” the girl said. “Quieter than here. She said she would just look. She told me to wait on the warm, where the bees fly. I waited.”

“How long?”

“I don't know. Two songs and a cow truck.”

The featureless hum of the white crowded the edges of Sori's hearing. If the girl had stood alone with that pressure, with the blank pressing its forehead against this small road, for the time it takes two old songs to play on a scavenged radio and one cattle hauler to grind by on a length of road that should not exist—that was a kind of heroism Sori recognized. It had nothing to do with Arclight and everything to do with being poor.

She reached into her kit. Anchors could make a circle, a gate, a cul-de-sac. They could not keep open what the world did not pay for. Arclight bought and sold Continuance by neighborhood, by city. Metrics were tightened when a district went delinquent; streets vanished from maps; morning fogs came and did not lift. The white—not really white, not really anything—waited under everything like blank paper under paint.

She had been told in training that the white was neutral. Not malice, not hunger. The white was a useful concept by which to understand the absence of the streaming computations that bound objects, forces, and the consensus of cause and effect. The white was unrendered.

Her mother had laughed and said, in the old apartment, in the old city that had later been eaten from the edges inward: unrendered, that’s a fancy way to say it’s where they don't pay to remember you.

Sori grabbed a second anchor disc. The budget on her in-eye ticked down: two left in her kit until the month cycled, unless she called in a request and a spooler from a better-fed district came to relieve her. She had been a good auditor lately. She had pleas in reserve. But there were rules. The rules said: no deeper than one circle without team support. The rules said: objects lost into white must be written off unless anchored within six minutes of loss. The rules said: persons lost—she did not think about that line.

“If you go in,” the girl said, and swallowed. “If you go in and see her, tell her I waited.”

“I’ll tell her,” Sori said. “What's your name?”

The girl dug her toes into the road. “Una,” she said, quickly, daring Sori to make fun of it. “It means one.”

It meant hunger, in Sori's first language. It meant kindled. It meant a thread between two things.

“Sori,” she said. “Stay back from the lip. Salt? Mark our entry.”

“Logging,” Salt said. “Anchors spooled for two minutes at current attention. Strongly suggest opening an entertainment—”

“I said later,” Sori said.

In her peripheral feed, Arclight pushed a cartoon: cats mending a sock. The cats played banjos and sang about how everyone had to do their part, and how attention was the coin of love. Sori blinked it away. She would pay for this on her ledger; the anchors drew from a pool that drew from beholden eyes, and hers were sullen this morning. But the rules, the rules.

She threw the second anchor. The circle deepened, doubled into a lens. The white hissed like sugar poured on a hot plate and retreated an optimistic five meters. The anchor-lens quivered, held, then settled, as if someone had breathed out. Inside, the road continued in a thin slice and then fell away. Beyond, something moved. Sori leaned toward the lip and the hair at her jaw lifted in a wind she couldn't feel.

It wasn't wind. It was presence.

Sori stepped into the circle.

The blank pressed around her like a sheet being tucked into a bed. The world behind her was a thin, shaking coin. Taste of iron. Sharp scent, unnameable. The hum became a texture under her teeth. She placed her boot soles on the road and took three steps forward.

Everything that wasn’t the coin of reality tried to deny the existence of her hands. She saw the lines of her fingers only because she wanted to, because she kept seeing them. The anchors held a memory of road and sky. She carried a pocket-sized version of both.

And yet: to her left, shadow. Not the absence-of-light shadow of white-on-white, but a thing cast. A shape that interrupted. Something tall, twigged. It was as if a palimpsest under the white whispered something else, an older writing. She took another step. The lens strained.

It was green.

It was green in a way the parks in the city never were, not even the rich neighborhoods whose Continuance budgets could afford seasons and a drift of leaves in November. Those leaves had always been too symmetrical, their veins too regular, their scatter algorithm taught. This was not that. The thing growing just beyond the reach of the anchor's memory was a living insistence. Leaves hung in a ragged plume. Their edges were chewed. Their surfaces reflected light in a way that confused old machine-learning models, light caught and hoarded in cells that had never seen an in-eye. Sori smelled it and the breath punched out of her. She had no word for it at first. It came to her the way a child's name does when you wake in the dark and your heart is running: this is called sap.

She reached out. The anchor's circle tightened in response, trying to keep her within itself. Sori held her breath and leaned toward the green, toward a world that had been discontinued. A single leaf trembled, and for a moment—the smallest fraction of the smallest time—a drop of something cold touched her wrist. It was as undeniable as glass breaking. It rolled. It left a thread of wetness that made a clean line on her skin as if a new thought had been written there.

The hum under her teeth shifted. Somewhere far away and very close, as close as her bone marrow, something spoke.

It did not speak in words. It spoke like an old radio tuned at night, voices braided under static. It smelled like the chalk of her first school classroom. It felt like the weight when her mother had fallen asleep with Sori's head on her thigh. It touched her with the certainty of someone calling you from another room and you knowing who it is without being told.

Sori pulled back. The world-shape of the circle yawned. The green shivered as if in a wind. The voice came with the next breath, and this time it had a shape that language could use.

Sori? the blank said.

She could have sworn it was her mother’s voice.

She stumbled backward without grace, bumping the heel of her boot against the lip of the circle. Salt's rotors flared as it tried to compensate for a change in pressure. The drone bobbed like a buoy.

She fell out of the circle into air that smelled like heat and summer trucks. Her balance fell back into her, heavy, grateful. Una was on her feet now, not brave—MP shoulders, ready to run. Sori put one hand out, palm open, to show she held nothing dangerous or magical. Her hand was trembling. A dark line of wet ran from her wrist to the heel of her palm. She wiped it off on her pants and it left a darker streak.

“What did you see?” Una demanded.

Sori would have answered with one of the soothing scripts Arclight had hired poets to write: stitching the sky costs more when the wind is bad; this is a natural shedding; your love will not be wasted even if our anchors cannot retrieve a body. She had recited those to men and women and once to a pack of teenagers who had saved up their attention for months to hold their basketball court on weekends. The scripts worked often enough to keep Arclight's numbers to a tolerable burn.

She could not say any of them now. The word she wanted to say felt like a crime.

“Green,” she said softly. “I saw a tree.”

Una looked past Sori as if she could force her own vision there by will. Her eyes were trained on the anchors, on the circle that hummed and shook. “Is Mama there?”

Sori opened her mouth. Closed it. A bee wandered a lazy pattern over a crushed flower by the road and then launched itself up in a line. Sori took a breath and made a decision that her supervisor would call misconduct and her mother would call intention.

“We have one minute left on the anchor,” she said. “And I broke a rule by going in. I can't go deeper without a team.”

“Rules aren't for when someone you love is in,” Una said with child's certainty.

“They are,” Sori said, and watched the child's mouth harden. “But not all the rules are good.”

Her in-eye chimed. Someone had noticed her attention stream's quality dropping and sent a polite escalation. A name flashed with the push: Javek, her supervisor, old field agent turned desk. You know the frays out there go feral when the budget expires, he wrote, and then a second message, softer: Don't get yourself lost.

“Can you pull your attention in?” Sori asked Una. “Look at the anchors. Just look. Hold them.”

“What is attention,” Una said, sullen, as if the word tasted like grown-ups.

“It’s what they buy,” Sori said. “But yours isn't on anyone’s meter. Do you see? You can look and it won’t cost anyone anything but me.”

Una did not nod. But she shifted her weight, and she focused the way a child focuses when watching a magician and trying to understand the trick. Sori felt something tighten in the world, some little pulling-together. The anchor's numbers steadied, three percent, four. Salt made a surprised sound that wasn't in its programming.

Una's gaze made a tiny hollow in the white, as if whoever had built things had not understood to make a place for an uncounted child's seeing.

Sori reached back into the bowl. The green was farther now. The white had filled in where it could. The trace of water had dried on her palm. But the voice—her mother? A trick? A cruelty spun out of a statistic about her lost-stamped relative?—it fluttered on her periphery as you might feel someone step into a room you can't afford to heat.

She let go of the green. Not because she wanted to. Because if she reached again, she would fall.

She closed the anchor. The circle tightened like a mouth and swallowed itself. The hum changed key and dropped away, leaving a tinny silence. The road ended again, against a wall of white.

Una stared at it the way a kid stares at a dog that has bitten them twice and is wagging its tail. “Did you tell her?” she said. “If you saw my mama. Did you tell her?”

“I didn’t see her,” Sori said. She felt everything in herself stiffen around the lie. She had seen a tremor in the green, a shadow of a figure that might have been a woman, might have been an old piece of fence, might have been the gesture the blank itself made when asked to imitate a human. She had heard a voice that was her mother and not. None of that would help this child. None of that would stitch a road.

“But you heard—” Una began.

Sori crouched, the heat of the road bleeding into the bones of her boots. They were the nice ones, the self-cleaning, Continuance-branded, the ones that bought you a little polite respect in stores when you flashed them under a clerk's gaze. They had not made her fit any better in the parts of the world where she had learned her first curses. She balanced her forearms on her knees and looked up at Una so the girl could decide whether to slap her or cry. “We’re going to put three small anchors on the lip,” she said, choosing a plausible compromise. “They won’t hold it back all day, but they will slow it until my team gets here. I’ll call in a bigger budget, I promise.”

“You promise promises are expensive,” Una said with raw literalness.

“They are. But sometimes you can steal a little. I know how.”

Una didn't smile. She didn't believe in smiles that didn't feed goats. But she nodded. Maybe it was the only tool the child had to bargain with adults.

They set the anchors together. Sori showed Una where to place her hands, how to square her shoulders behind a throw. The discs struck and sank. Three small bowl-shapes pressed into the white. The world sighed.

Salt circled, its belly-light stitching invisible netting between the anchors. In her in-eye, Sori opened an entertainment loop for the first time that day and let ads edge her vision. She gave the world thirty-two seconds of a man telling her how his face had improved since he bought a different razor, a woman whose yard had become perfect when she rented a weather plan, a little animated seam-cat juggling balls of light. Attention was the coin. She paid in a small way to save a larger debt.

Her ledger ticked down. Javek pinged her again. You always liked the edges, he wrote. Come home when the team gets there. Don't put yourself between the bill and the god.

She closed the loop. The anchors held steady, made a squeak-sound in the overlay like a chair pushed back from a table. Una sat on her heels, face as intent as a monk's.

“When will they come?” Una asked.

“When the numbers say it's worth it,” Sori said, and then, because it was cruel to make this child into a metric: “Soon. I'll make it soon. If anyone comes out of the white, don't step after them. Not even for love.”

“My mama wouldn't call me and then step back,” Una said.

Sori thought of the voice. It had not called her by the name Sori An. It had called her Sosori, the name her mother used to use when she was clipped and irritated and affectionate and the rent was due and the light was not paid.

She stood. She pressed her palm against the girl’s hair; she did not know when she had last touched a child's head. The bones under skin were small and indignant. “Stay where the bees fly,” Sori said. “I’ll be watching. Salt will come if the anchors sag. He worries when he isn’t useful.”

“I don't like him,” Una said, the honesty of the feral and the just. “He sounds like the radios that lie.”

“That's fair.”

Sori returned to the rover. The cabin was an oven. Her seatbelt buckle burned her palm. She stared through the windshield until her eyes watered and the white blurred.

The first chapter of a life had opened at a seam twenty minutes back. She could not name what kind of book it was. She knew only that in the place where the world had ended, something in her had opened a door, and she had heard a familiar voice from a room no longer under rent.

When she put the rover in gear, Salt bobbed once at the window and then zipped to a hover above the anchors. “Local cache uploaded,” it said. “Javek is calling. Ignore?”

“Not yet,” Sori said. “Let him hear me breathe.”

She drove back down the highway that wasn't quite there and watched in her rearview as the anchors glowed, small coins of resistance in the white. The land to either side was ordinary, generous with heat and stubborn things low to the ground. Far beyond, the city rose on its own budget. The towers shimmered in the noon. It always looked like a mirage until you were inside it and paying with your eyes for the privilege of doors that opened.

Her in-eye buzzed. Javek's voice came gray and textured, like the inside of a grandfather clock. “Report,” he said, language wrapped in fatigue. “An. I see you burned anchors.”

“Edge delamination two meters at center,” Sori said. “Una and her mother live within the effect radius. Mother went in before I arrived.”

“Did you go in?”

“Yes,” Sori said, because lying to Javek was like lying to a piece of road. You could call it something else, and it would still carry your weight until it broke.

“Don't do that,” he said, sighing it like a prayer. “We are not paid for that bravery anymore. What did you see?”

Sori stared at her own knuckles on the wheel. A drop of something she'd carried out from the white had dried to an almost invisible salt track there. She rubbed it away with her thumbnail and it flaked. “Nothing,” she said. “Just white.”

When she hung up, she swallowed once and tasted sap.

She drove until the heat flickered invisible over the blacktop like water. She drove until the city got bigger instead of smaller. Behind her, at the seam, a child sat and watched three little circles of resistance hum. The bees flew without regard to anchors. The goats hammered their hard foreheads into fence posts. And inside the white, whether malice or mercy or just some stranger kindness, a voice that sounded like Sori's mother spoke her private name again and waited, patient as a tree.

Chapter One: The Salt Archive

The library had forgotten it was a library and learned to be a reef.

Where shelves had stood there were now curtains of brown kelp, frilled and patient, combing the current for sifted sunlight. Coral licked at marble steps and climbed the columns in slow, bruised pastel. A lionfish, all grand finery and poisonous thought, nested in a ventilator shaft and watched the intruder’s ghost-light drift over the titles—Linnaeus, Woolf, an atlas of the polar regions from when the poles had been clean and cold and unremarkable. Each spine was so furred with sponge that Ari could read nothing with her eyes. She read with her hands.

Her suit’s gloves were thin at the fingers: soft pads of graphene rubber that transmitted texture and pressure back to the nerve. She swept the pads along the rows and waited for the haptic chatter of something denser than bone. The coral hummed with shrimp clicks and algae-creak. The library murmured. The suit translated some of the murmur into simple icons along her wrist: salinity climbing, pressure stable, battery at 62 percent. The rest was noise the body understood without translation. Ari’s shoulder ached where the exosleeve had rubbed against an old scar. Her tongue could taste the copper tang of an algae bloom through the rebreather, even though no water had touched her mouth in years.

Near her left, a shelf broke free from whatever had grown it in place and sighed into silt. A galaxy of motes spiraled, caught in the beam from her helmet. She had to tilt her head, sorry without words. There was no saving paper here. The stacks had been drenched and dried and drenched again as the city’s pumps stuttered over the years; salt had made lace of the pages. The legal fiction of salvage rights held that what you could retrieve and catalogue, you could keep or sell. The physical truth of it was that culture had become a cartilage, a thing that had bones but no flesh. You couldn’t sell a poem you couldn’t read. The only things a diver could barter were the media that kept their guts intact: drives, crystal, metals that did not flake to white ash when the water kissed them.

She found one, under a spill of waterlogged pulp that might once have been an art history. Her fingers hesitated, then closed; the glove filled with the clean, smooth geometry of a data rod. Not the cheap ones with a telltale seam like a healed wound, but a pre-Compaction rod, glassy and perfect. Pre-Compaction meant two things at auction: redundant metadata and guilt.

“Kafo,” she murmured out of habit, and her helmet caught the syllables and leaked them back into the water as a vibration. The Atlantic did not care. The suit’s assistant did. It peeled the name’s waveform apart somewhere in Ari’s earpiece, matched it, and sent back the old greeting in her grandmother’s language with perfect tone, like a relative she didn’t have.

Kafo. Patience.

Ari slotted the rod into the vacuum sleeve along her thigh. She took a slow breath, counted six, let it out. In the end, she was grateful for the silt. It kept the frenzy at bay. If you came to a place like this and looked for everything at once you could drown without a drop of water in the lungs. You had to look for the gleam and file it in your head without exultation.
