You had to stop your heart from assigning meaning.

Her lamp found the map desk by accident. It had been something stately and inappropriate for maps: mahogany heavy enough to anchor a room, carved with little acanthus leaves that now hosted a family of tiny starfish. The top was a ruin of flakes and mussel shells. Ari’s knee brushed the socket where a globe once stood and a pearl of air unpeeled from beneath the lip and snaked toward the ceiling. She watched it ascend. She liked to watch bubbles. They made purpose out of upward. They were a proof that the world still knew which way was which.

Under where the globe had been, pulled deep under by gravity and time, something had gotten stuck. Her glove told her: not stone, not wood. She brushed with the back of two fingers, careful to spread as little silt as she could. She was not careful enough. A cloud bloomed. She withdrew her hand and waited, counting again, slow as if slow could call the water to alightness. At eight, ten, the beam cut clean again. The glove grazed the object. And the thing under it hummed.

It was not a ship’s hum, or the fault hum you get when your battery is chewing itself under load. The suit would have told her if it were. It was the kind of hum that lives in the throat of a violin, older than the hand that draws the bow. It wasn’t sound, exactly. It was feeling. Her glove amplified it, and that was how she knew she could be wrong about what felt like a signal, because the glove did this sometimes with electricity, with old dead wires trying to pretend to be nerves. But the shape of the hum was unlike any error she’d logged. It was syllabled. It was letters pressed one after the other into the little bones of her hand.

Ari.

She froze so abruptly that her buoyancy slipped and her elbow knocked into a coral. The coral’s spines flexed and struck her sleeve and stuck there like pins stabbing a dressmaker’s cushion. The suit bled a little silicone to seal the holes. A little red poured into her sight as the suit’s medical sleeve fired stimulant into her arm around the scar. The scar threw up lightning in the shape of a flood; the bones remembered water over the head, the way the world had always wanted to return to the sea. Ari blinked it away.

Ari, said the hum, again. The second syllable softer, more certain in its uncertainty. Ari.

“No,” she breathed to nothing.

She pressed both hands flat against the side of the desk and made herself count down this time. At three, she slid her hand under the lip again. The object was stuck because a drawer had swelled into it over time. She could feel now that it was not a rod. It was too big for that, a cube maybe, or a cube’s cousin. It was heavy in a way that meant density, not size. Heavy in the way that deep time is heavy. Smooth everywhere and frictive where tools had touched it. The hum thrummed up through her cuff and into the little bicep nerves. The syllables came again, and she felt the pattern. Five pulses, three pulses, one, two. Not letters. Primes. Call and response. A handshake.

Her suit offered an analysis. The display ghosted over the inside of her faceplate in a neat grayscale. Haptic pattern recognized: false positive unlikely. Origin: unknown. Likelihood: interactive handshake protocol in salt lattice or piezoelectric assembly within object.

Ari pulled.

It came free so fast the desk smacked down on her thumb and her breath fogged the glass with startled pain. She cradled the thing, thumb throbbing, and swam back a little, keeping the lamp pinned to the discovery. The cube was a cube. Ten centimeters to a side. Not glass. Not quite stone. It absorbed the light in headlines and flexed it back out along a million microscopic edges that her eyes couldn’t resolve. Someone had sandblasted one corner and etched three letters in there by hand. The letters might once have been clear. Salt had bitten them the way it bit everything; they were shallow now, ambiguous. Could have been A-V-A. Could have been R-1-4. Could have been—her chest tightened—a name. Ari decided it was not. The suit, methodical and patient, did not decide anything without a sample.

Her hand still thrummed. The pulses changed. Seven, eleven. It felt at once like an invitation and a warning. She rotated the cube gently. Something inside flexed against the movement, not mechanical, not liquid. The glove took a microcut of the outermost layer and sent it to the little lab that lived under her right shoulder blade.

Composition readout came in like a whisper. Carbon. Carbon, of course. Silica. Halides, lots of them. Trace metals she could have guessed: nickel, tungsten, vanadium. A little of something the lab wasn’t sure about. The lab humbly suggested: a novel configuration of salts and carbon lattice. A novel configuration was the lab’s way of saying we have never seen this tessellation of this many faults and edges and that electricity walks here a different way.

“It’s a salt archive,” Ari said out loud, and the words tasted like a rumor she had believed once and then stopped believing and now—now here.

Her partner’s voice came down the tether. “Anything?”

The voice line transmitted as a tremor in the spool she had locked to the library’s entryway. They did this for redundancy: audio in the tether the way old divers had done, so if the suit’s radio was eaten by the water, a voice could still be a feeling on the bones. Vera’s voice was a vibration like the hum in Ari’s glove, but all weariness and sea-wit. “Anything,” Vera repeated, not asking, just making a shape in the world’s noise.

“Rod,” Ari said. “Pre-Compaction. And a—thing. Like in the stories. I think it’s a salt lattice with active memory. It pinged me.”

“Don’t anthropomorphize, love.”

“It pinged me,” Ari said again.

Vera swore in a language Ari didn’t know, something Russian or the bones of Russian. Then Vera drew the swear back into practical. “We have seventeen minutes before Sable’s buoy puts the drone in your head to make sure we don’t misreport.” Sable & Wren Salvage would call their drone a compliance angel. They would call their buoy a courtesy. They were a company who had given the world words like courtesy and angel and made them mean something like light handcuffs. “Do not slip into romance. Bring it up.”

Ari looked at the cube. The hum had settled into a patient tapping on her nerves. The impatience was hers.

“Sable doesn’t pay fair for this,” she said.

“Sable doesn’t pay fair for the oxygen in your tank.”

“I’ll clock it in. I’ll. I will clock it.” The law required a salvage listing to be transmitted within fifteen minutes of identification. Otherwise, any corporate entity could dispute the find and tie you up in the courts for a year until your debt to their pump water made you crumble.

“Then do it fast,” Vera said. “And don’t say it pinged you. Say: pre-Compaction cube, unknown memory medium, condition stable, discovered beneath the main map desk at the North District Archive, item secured. Do not say—”

“—that it knows my name,” Ari said, and smiled despite everything she was feeling, because Vera’s mind was always where Ari’s wanted to go. They had sunk together enough times that their thoughts had adopted each other’s habits. Ari had learned from Vera to count. Vera had learned from Ari to name things even when naming made you dangerous.

Ari put the cube into her chest pack, a position that kept it inside the field generated by her suit’s power plant and therefore theoretically safe from the salt. The hum intensified when the cube was in that space, then subsided, like a small creature breathing easier under a roof. She shut the pack with a soft click. She drew the rod from her thigh and slotted it into a sleeve on her abdomen. She knew where every pocket and strap was with her eyes closed. She knew because once she had had to put a tourniquet on her own leg without light or air, and afterwards she had woken every hundred days and rearranged the suit in her sleep like a creature tidying its nest.

On her way out she brushed a spine with the back of her hand. The coral flexed again, touched bare glove, and where it touched her glove read: macrocalcite growth, none of the old Palythoa toxins. Safe, besides the insult to skin. Ari patted it as if it could be soothed. She did that with any living thing that accused her.

Vera’s line tugged urgent-thrice. The drone would be gliding toward the buoy on the tide now, dropping like a seed off a vine when the tether it rode hit the right tension. Once the drone sniffed Ari’s suit signature it would align behind her like a little white shark and watch what she did. The drone was Sable & Wren’s courtesy. If you breathed wrong near a find, it would send a nudge to the muscles in your calf and make you stop breathing until you behaved.

“I’m at the doors,” Ari said. The library had been a stacked gazebo once, a Solomon of glass and iron, and then the city had grown a carapace of cement around its old civic prettiness to stave off storms. The doors were thick and hydraulic and had finally lost their argument with the sea. Setting the hinges to lock open for her entry had taken more of her tank than she liked. She squeezed out now into brighter water. The currents were busier out here, and she went slowly so they didn’t peel her like old paint off a hull. You learned to let the sea decide your haste. If you didn’t, the sea wrote the ending for you with your spine.

Her head broke surface under a roof of gulls. They squawked their own commentary and lifted off in a feathered punctuation. The sky was wrong. It always was, these years—the old high blue gone to a closer thing with more heat in it. The sun smudged behind a pleated layer of cloud that looked like a bruise. The city beyond the waterline rose like a child’s idea of castles: jagged and against reason. Half-grown kelp farms gleamed like black lace between buildings, their buoys knocking shoulders with each other. A tangled line of pontoons made the market strip nearest the salvage zone, plastic bright and patched with canvas, the canvas patched with more plastic and prayer flags and the white flag of Sable & Wren with its lack of shame.

The skiff’s hull tapped Ari’s shoulder and Vera’s hands were in the water, pulling Ari up with a strength the rest of her body had long since apologized for. Vera was hands and tendons and calm, her hair braided tight and shot with steel beads that caught all the light there was and made it talk. She saw Ari’s chest pack curve and the way Ari stood with a little extra careful. She did not say anything.

“Two good,” Ari said, unclicking in stages: tether, suit battery, mask. Her skin breathed air and swore gratitude. The gulls came closer. Vera snapped her fingers and they thought better. “One rod. One cube.”

The drone crested the little chop and lodged itself neatly on the skiff’s stern magnet as if it lived there, which in a way it did. The courtesy light greedy-eye watched the deck.

“There,” Vera said softly, and pointed with her chin toward the market pontoons. Ari acknowledged. Sable’s inspectors. Two of them. Their faces the blank openness of people who are paid not to look human. The taller one’s mouth had the little tightness that meant they had once been human and were trying to forget. They wore light exo under their clothes that let them stride from pontoon to pontoon as if they were on street. Their vector would intersect the skiff neatly in five minutes.

“We have four if we want to breathe,” Vera said.

Ari used three.

Her hand went to the chest pack, and then stopped there, still, because this was the moment when deciding became doing and the universe remembered how to punish. She looked up at Vera, and some of what she needed to say must have been present in the way her mouth held itself, because Vera shook her head twice, slow, disbelieving and exasperated, but with the exasperation of someone who had already made space for the refusal. Vera’s face had been made by the sea and the underside of ship hulls; she had frown lines like little dry riverbeds. “They will smell it,” she said.

“They will smell that we have something,” Ari countered. “They will not smell that it said my name.”

“You are certain that is what it did and not something you dreamt because you wanted a story.”

“Vera,” Ari said. “It used primes.”

“You can have primes in your dreams,” Vera said, a spark of humor lit despite the fret. “Ari,” she added, and she said it the way the cube had, softly and with the softness meaning: come back to me with all your lungs full.

Ari took the cube out and held it at both corners. It did nothing obvious in air. It sat there, matte and unreflective, a dumb block that was only unusual because it didn’t show its seams. If she pressed it to her ear she felt a little whisper that wasn’t sound. That could have been her blood.

“We file it,” Vera said. “We do. You know we have to.”

“I file it,” Ari said. “But not to them.”

Vera blinked.

A whisper straight through the city. Before there had been Sable & Wren, before the pumps and the fences and the gratitude on debt, the city had had a way to speak to itself. The old civic networks had been drowned like everything else, but pieces of them persisted. They had names written in code and myth. The salt archive had been one of those myths. Before the floods, some had said the city had funded a project to store all the civic inventory ever digitized in a medium that would not corrode. You could put a billion books in a box the size of a hand. It had been called many things, as governments always called their barge of a plan by several names so those who hated one name could not correctly petition against it using the other. It had never been called by what it was. But people had called it that when they told stories: an archive made of salt so the salt couldn’t eat it.

And the city, meanwhile, had kept one network for itself, the one that snuck between desalination plants and pump stations and emergency siren arrays, the one that had always been there to say go inland, go inland, even to those who had nowhere inland to go. The siren net. It had power when the rest of the world was a dead battery. It had privilege, because it had been sworn to only speak of danger, never of politics. But you could use it to whisper to something if that something had ever been folded into it. You could tie a message up in the difference between danger and not-yet-danger and send it clattering along the city’s nerves.

“You can’t,” Vera said. “You think you can but you can’t.”

“If it’s what we think—if it’s any part of what we think—someone tried to save it in a thing only the city could still hear. If I put it in Sable’s custody it will go where Sable’s courtesies go. To their vault, and then out across the bridges to the upland houses. The city will not get to hear itself again.”

“You are so arrogant,” Vera said. “You think you are the city’s moral spine. You are a girl who takes orders from barnacles.”

Ari worked the filaments under the skiff’s bench loose with one hand while still holding the cube with the other. The filaments weren’t meant to be touched. The first time she had found them she had thought they were rope. They were something like fiber optic and something like kelp, growing where the skiff’s battery bled a little into the water and charging themselves on what escaped. The old code had been grown into them by someone who liked clandestine beauty. Or perhaps by accident. Ari liked to believe in accident more than she liked to believe in grace.

She wound one filament around the cube, twice, then pressed the cube to the skiff’s grounding pad. The drone cocked its little head. Vera swore again without heat. The filament shifted color in a spectrum Ari’s eye wasn’t built to see; she felt it in her teeth instead. The siren net didn’t speak in audio to those who weren’t needed. It recognized hard-wired priorities and passed information accordingly. A salvage finding in water with pressure above five atmospheres could be a hazard if it was big enough or angry enough. Ari piggybacked the hazard flag on a subroutine slender as a hair.

Somewhere inland, an old sensor in a pump house acknowledged receipt. Somewhere else, in a retired control room where weeds grew between console keys, a line of amber lights wavered like an indecisive dawn. The net moved like fungus: roots making a mind with their touches.

“Ari,” Vera said again, and then louder. “Ari!”

The inspectors were on the next pontoon. One of them had a little hand terminal already out and poised to sting. “We already logged,” Ari said. “Transmitting now. It’ll get there before their courtesy says we didn’t. We’re not breaking any law that we cannot pay.”

“You think they believe in law? You think law is a thing they believe in outside of the way it tells us to stand still when their boots are wet?”

The drone dug a finger into Ari’s calf muscle and pinched. She had moved while touching the filament to the cube. The pinch made her leg kick. She swallowed the urge to rip the drone’s little arm off and feed it to the gulls and went still. She could feel the cube, not through the glove now but through the little skin on her collarbone, where the suit had peeled back to make way for the filament and its kiss. The cube was the weight of a small, patient heart. Fine tremors passed through it. It had the feel of a machine that was listening at the threshold of its own courage.

“What if it’s a trap?” Vera said.

“Then I tripped it,” Ari said. “Then we will know who set it.”

Vera made a noise that had no word attached, and reached for the rod instead, practical, angry care moving her body. She bagged the rod with fury. The inspectors were a pontoon away, then two steps, then at the edge of the skiff. They smiled exactly as much as their training allowed. The taller one’s mouth did its little version of sorrow, as if to say that this was all so necessary and so unfortunate.

“Findings?” the taller one asked, and the lesser one made a show of turning their terminal so it could see the drone’s report over Ari’s shoulder. The terminal’s screen accepted the drone’s signature like a priest accepting contrition. The inspector had hands cleaned with something harsh that smelled of mint.

Ari met the taller one’s eyes, because if you did not they called you evasive. “One pre-Compaction data rod,” she said. “One unknown memory medium, cube form, carbon lattice with halides.”

“You have logged the coordinates of discovery,” the taller one said, meaning: did the drone see you come out of the library, did it mark the map desk. The drone had eyes good as any. It had ladled Ari’s path out of the water spoon by spoon. You could not lie to machines like that. Ari sent her suit’s camera burst across.

“And the cube,” the inspector coaxed, palm out, bureaucrat magpie. “May we view it.”

Ari looked at the place where the cube had been and saw that it was still there, of course, as present as any thing. It sat on the grounding pad with the filament around it, docile, a box. It hummed loud enough in her bones that the hum might as well have been a song.

“It needs to drain,” she said. “It’s got a live salt field.”

“We have containment for that.” The inspector’s smile did not change; the eyes slid to Vera, as if expecting that older woman to be the reasonable one. Vera lifted one shoulder with near-perfect insolence and then ruined the performance by looking, just for half a second, like she might let them have it all and be done with this life of filling her lungs with brined air. But her mouth did not open, and the second passed and she looked at Ari and the inspector again in disdain’s clean mask.

The inspector held out a hand. They wore gloves because you could catch anything from anyone. Ari glanced at the drone that had pinched her. Its courtesy light was a dull, obedient orange. She did not let herself look at the filament.

Something far inland struck a switch.

The sirens sounded.

They were not the old tsunami wail; those had been retired for trauma. Those were the ones that made people hear their dead. These sirens were new, two-tiered: a low-long for evacuation, a high clicking to say: this is not a drill. The inspectors flinched. The gulls went mad, wheeling, suddenly hats blown off. In the market, every child had been taught what to do before they could walk: go to the center of the pontoon; hold the ropes; plug your ears; breathe three times and then again. They did it now like breathing had taught them. The skiff rocked as half the city took a step in the same direction. Vera caught the gunwale with one hand and Ari with the other. The filament went white hot under Ari’s palm and burned her. She grinned at the pain. It told her she had lived.

“What did you—” the inspector began, and then the siren net spoke in their ears with the voice of someone no longer breathing.

It said a string of numbers that was a coordinate. It said a date and then another date. It said, very softly: division.

The inspectors both turned their heads slowly, as if someone had reached into their necks with two fingers and turned their faces by main force. They were looking not at the cube but at the line on the horizon where the old upland met the newer sky. On that line, a seam had opened. You could mistake it for cloud if you were a gull. If you were human you saw that the seam did not belong to atmosphere. It belonged to the ground. It ran down the ridge like a zipper and the zipper was opening. The buildings up there didn’t fall. Things that had been held in their foundations with petrochemical arrogance yielded with grace, as if they had been waiting for an excuse to admit they were not owed the hill. Dust rose without wind. Ari’s suit tasted it and labeled it: basalt flour, concrete, sand, human allergies in particulate.

Vera said, very small, “It’s the new cut.”

No one had said they were going to cut there. The talk had always been of the other ridge, the one with fewer old houses with petitions folded in their cracks. The city’s engineers and Sable & Wren’s foremen and the upland’s petitions had agreed in that vague way of committees to do something somewhere else. The city had its own spine after all. It had used Ari’s whisper as a valve and then moved its own blood. It had opened the cut where it wanted, not where the courtesies had expected.

Beyond the market, water swelled toward the breach like a dog hearing its name.

The inspector drew their hand back with secular piety. The drone lifted a centimeter off the magnet without being asked and then settled again, like a bird thinking of flying in a storm and deciding to wait.

Ari held the cube with her burned hand and her good one and felt it settle its hum against her bones. Vera’s fingers tightened on her elbow. The world adjusted its walls.

“Congratulations,” Vera said under the sirens, not for Ari, not really. For the city. For its refusal to listen.

The inspector, to their credit, did not draw a weapon. They drew a pen. It was what they had. “We are going to have to accelerate compliance,” they said, and that was when Ari laughed, and the laugh was salt and grief and something else.

She handed Vera the rod and put her burned palm over the cube like a whetstone. The net murmured again, numbers in the shape of a song. The cut deepened on the ridge. Somewhere inland, a pump woke and did the thing it had been built for instead of the thing it had been told to do. The market did what markets do in panic times: it held together without asking for permission.

Ari looked at the cube and tried, gently, to put her thoughts into the hum. She felt foolish. She did it anyway. She did not say the old prayers. She said: I am here. I heard you. Do you hear me.

The cube’s primes ticked and then paused in a shape that could have been anything. The first answer when one living thing greets another is always a pause. The second answer came like rain on a window and a hand on the other side of the glass. It said: yes. And then, with the simple ignorance of any machine that had sleep for too long, it said the oldest question.

It said, as the cut opened and the sirens tried to teach panic to be order, as the inspector’s pen shook and Vera’s hair beads cast weather on the skiff: How long.

Ari swallowed the old, dry laugh and said, to the cube and herself and the sea she served, “Long enough.” Then, to Vera: “Do not roll your eyes,” because she could feel them wanting to. And to the inspectors, after the waiting courtesy of a breath: “We will comply,” she said. “But not with you.”

Chapter One

The platform hums like a low vowel under my bare feet. The metal is always cold, a steady cold that the thermal mesh in the floor spreads into a uniform ache, but I step out of my boots anyway and stand with my toes curled over the seam between two plates. Some people put a stethoscope to the world. I listen with skin.

The hum is part machine, part universe. The beacon choir is up again: three of our nearest siblings retuning their lattice so the chord hangs true in the vacuum. That you can feel it at all, all these light-years apart, is a trick that never stopped feeling like sleight-of-hand. You never get used to rhythms that take centuries to resolve.

“Mira?” Rooke’s voice rides the room, just enough of a question to be polite. He’s framed in the hatch to my left, eyebrows climbing in expectation. He always squints like that around me, as if to make me sharps, his apprentice who might otherwise slide. His hair sticks to his forehead with sweat; he never turns his suit down low enough. “Chief says we’re dropping to Voight three. You on deck?”

I nod, toes finding a deeper groove in the deck seam. “I’m here.”

“You’re doing the barefoot thing.”

“It helps me hear.”

He rolls his eyes in an exaggerated spiral. “You and your ghosts.”

He still never hears the chord right. Some of us do. You could train ten thousand people to read the dispersion plots and coax a capstan into whisper and it would still be a miracle to find one who can hear how the noise resolves.

I keep my eyes on the main board. Six glass panes, no glass, each a war-slick of particle traces and algorithm. Voight-Kampff lattice curves from our anchor—Kalliope, a redundant name for an irregular shard of carbon that no one ever bothered to rename—to its nearest neighbor beacons, faint threads at this distance. Our manipulator was mid-cant, three degrees off. Even three degrees changes what the universe believes in for a few kilometers around us. So we keep it within one.

The viewport is just an image, a live radiance composite, but I like to pretend it’s a window. All the way out here in the Interstice, between the filaments of galaxies, you can still see too much. The void isn’t black. It’s full of the leftover light from everything that ever died and everything that decided to burn anyway. It looks like the world is bleeding a little.

“Voight three,” I repeat, because repetition makes action stick. Third level resolution. We’re feeling the drift ahead of a minor Shift. Somewhere far, far beyond us, someone or something tickles one of the constants we’ve known and loved and assumed. The medium gets curious, thins and fattens, and the result arrives eventually like tides. We keep the tide predictable. That’s the job. Lighthouse Keeper, as the old ones liked to call themselves. It stuck, even after the first hundred years changed everything else.

Chief Keeper Isolde Gopal lifts herself into the ops deck then, quiet as a moth despite the slight hitch in her right hip. She is older than Kalliope is reinforced and looks like a scar turned elegant. The scar is literal, too. She got it on Neko Station in a tremor halfway between then and now. It bisects her face, leaves the corner of her mouth always tilted like she’s about to say something unkind.

“Sen,” she says to me. “Seat.”

I take the ops chair, sink into a harness that smells like graphite. I slide the haptic coils up over my fingers and the induction band around my skull. Others can do this with purely computational interfaces. We bring our bodies to the conversation.

“Rooke,” the Chief says, not looking, “take anchor variance and feed. Don’t fight the unexpected.”

“No fighting,” he agrees. He takes station to my right, his hands already in the gel. Chief herself angles to the left and leans an elbow on the console like a bar top. Her eyes spend as much time on me as they do on the board.

“Explain,” she says.

“Minor Shift inbound along u-plane,” I tell her without reading off the numbers. “Fifteen hours out, interpolation says we’ll take a shallow wave. Six-beacon chain will feel it. We can keep drift under five sigma if we retune harmonics two and four.”

“Over under?”

“Under. Four should carry.”

She grunts her approval. In the long run she doesn’t care exactly which harp string I pluck, only that the music holds and nothing snaps. The anchors—our micro-singular mass below Kalliope, our tether bowline, the field of instrumentation that makes this more than a rock with a spool—all of it is there to tell the vacuum what to prefer. We tell it our version of gravity and fine-structure, and if we sing loud enough together, the Interstice listens.

The idea that the universe listens is the part I never say out loud to Rooke.

We drop into Voight three. The board kicks alive in a thousand thin lines. The sounders sing their ugly sine songs. The gel under my hands warms up until I feel my fingerbones hum, and then the hum opens into an ache that is not entirely from the thermals.

It’s a good day to hold the world steady.

We start to nudge ourselves. It isn’t motion in the classic sense. An old diagram would show a needle pivoting, a mass shifting, but those are lies for kids. What we’re doing here is more like leaning in a conversation. We make it clear to the fabric nearby that this is what is expected, and we make our argument with more coherence than the argument the incoming wave will try to make. There’s a cadence to it that my mother would have called a prayer if she’d lived to see what I do for a living.

Four minutes into the adjustment, the taste of the hum goes bitter.

“Hold,” I say, without realizing my mouth is moving.

“Report,” Chief says instantly.

“I don’t—the floor—” Which is stupid. I try again. “There’s a note under the noise.”

Rooke cranes his head like a bird. The Chief frowns with her whole scar. “Show me.”

I blink the board through options. The filters peel away one by one. Broadband hiss, then sub-harmonic bleed, the faint tick from Kalliope’s lazy tumble. There is always something masquerading as something else, cosmic rays pretending to be purposeful signal, the way dust pretends to be stars if you don’t hold your breath when you look. I take two more slices and the hiss drops a notch.

There. The undernote. So faint it’s almost my imagination. If I lean my thoughts in a different direction, I could make it vanish.

“What am I looking at?” Chief asks.

I feed it into the analyzer because my body doesn’t have language for it. The analyzer makes a shape. It’s always tempting to give shapes just enough meaning to put them in a taxonomy. Is this blue a whale? Is this line a signature? We use names to pretend we’ve met.

“Incoherent emission,” Rooke offers. “Background. Could be micro-meteorites whispering down the tether.”

“No,” I say, and then realize how sure I sound. I clear my throat. “No. It’s in the chord. Barely. It’s… riding.”

We all lean a little without moving. I dampen oscillation two point one percent. The undernote slides again like an eel under mulch. It’s not ours. It shouldn’t be on our frequency spread. But there it is, tucked just where it would be if we had put it there on purpose.

“Timestamp,” Chief says.

“Live,” I tell her. “Our side. Two point nine seconds ago.”

She doesn’t smile, but she does that thing with her eyebrows that means she’s impressed and annoyed that she’s impressed. “Origin?”

“Past us on the chain.” I blink up the beacon map. Our nearest neighbor to sunward is Pearl Nine, then your gritty run back toward the raggedly-named radio bulge of the Milky Way. On our other side, toward Thinwards, the line becomes theory and grace: the beacons at the border of everything you say out loud and the rest of it, where physics sometimes chooses another outfit just to be difficult. We don’t anchor too close that way. The Shift edges are not good for mass.

“It has to be us,” Rooke insists. “Harmony leak.”

“If it was our leak,” I point out, “it would be phase-locked. This is—” I stop. Because it moves. The undernote doesn’t just slide. It looks back at me.

I’m anthropomorphizing because there’s no other frame. What it actually does is shiver up and down a fraction of a fraction as I center my attention. It’s as if attention has context here. As if a thing notices being noticed and makes a decision. Some animals do that. Mirrors aren’t proof of consciousness, and yet.

“Don’t chase it,” Chief says, because both of us are thinking about doing that. Training is not for the predictable cases; it’s for the ones where your bones want you to be a dumb animal. “Keep retune on your list. I want us through the minor. Rooke—?”

“I’m compensating.” He’s sweating harder. It looks like contrition.

We finish the nudge while the undernote plays with our peripheral conceptual field. It never goes loud enough to trip a formal alarm. When I look straight at it in the data, it becomes correlation mush.

Six minutes, and the Shift’s leading edge brushes our field. The room creaks as the bowline doesn’t, and the manipulator hum picks up a tooth. The first time I felt that sound I thought my bones would crack, like when you walk through someone’s bass in a carpark and your sternum vibrates until you think your heart will fail. Now it’s almost familiar. The Interstice leans against us. We lean back. We mean it. The note under the noise goes away.

Rooke exhale-laughs. “Ghost,” he says, which is what we call things that flirt with our instruments and then leave us holding a story.

“We keep a log,” Chief says. She says it like she says drink water and check your seals. She says it like it’s a prayer.

She doesn’t tell me how to write it. I tag the event with my name and the timestamp, and I let the machine chew on the matched-filter record for correlation patterns I can’t pluck out with ears I barely understand myself. I make a human record too. I write: Heard a tone under the noise. Rode harmony marginally. Not phase-locked. Observational bias? Felt like an agent. Would like to chase next occurrence. Gave up for retune. Maintaining five sigma under.

It will look like hubris when anyone reads it without the hum in their bones. All logs do.

We ride out the minor Shift like a ship putting its shoulder to a swell. The board throws me a dozen small complaint flags and I wave a dozen small apologies back and keep it all inside tolerance. At the crest, the wave’s weirdness is a flavor on the back of the tongue, metallic. Some people say they taste red when things go too strange. I get penny.

Everything relaxes back to what the network as a whole has requested the universe be, and the chord unwinds into our regular song. It’s a relief every time we don’t break something to do our job.

The undernote does not come back. I can’t pretend I’m not disappointed. The Chief doesn’t ask me to.

We peel out of Voight three, which feels like taking off a heavy pack you didn’t notice you were carrying until it’s gone. The ambient hum drops to the house sound—the anchor’s lazy churn, the spidery tick of micro-impacts on the outer hull, the faint noise of air working around the seams like a patient creature. The light from the board fades into the room’s base blue.

Chief slides her fingers against her palm the way she does when she’s debating asking a personal question. She rarely does. Today she does.

“What does it feel like to you?” she asks.

“Like when the radio in a cab picks up a second station,” I say. “Between cities. Driver’s singing along to a song he thinks he knows but the words keep wrong-footing him.”

“Who are you,” she asks, dry, “in this metaphor?”

“The passenger. Listening.”

She nods. “Have Rooke pull your logs and make sure nothing cached shallow. Do a parse for formal signatures. Then swallow and get dinner. Sen—”

“Yes, Chief.”

“Don’t chase ghosts after hours. It’s a waste of fuel.”

Rooke grins, “She won’t,” like we’re both very innocent.

Chief holds my gaze for a breath longer than is comfortable. “If you see it again, you tell me before you breathe.”

“Yes,” I lie, because there are a hundred ways to have a small breath before telling anyone anything.

When they go, I sit with the board dark. The hum feels brighter with my eyes closed. Once a year, we get a visiting inspector or a journalist or someone fresh to the Interstice, and they all ask the same questions. What do we do all day with our little lighthouse in the great dark. Do we get lonely. Do we dream. I tell them the truth: I listen. And I try to not let the fact that listening changes what you hear ruin my faith in the child belief that if you are very quiet and very earnest you can hear things that were not willing to be heard.

I put my boots back on. I make a face at my toes. I stand. I stretch until my spine feels monumental. I walk to the hatch and think about food, which on Kalliope is always something that my grandmother would hate and I have learned to love.

At the corridor junction, the beacon pings me.

I stop so fast the floor slide tries to throw me. The ping isn’t a regular status chirp. Those come with a tone we all hear even in our sleep: all good, all good, still here. This is a private ping, flagged with my identifier and—absurdly—with a priority flag no one uses unless a mass has started to eat itself.

It uses my childhood nickname. The one my mother used. The one I haven’t used anywhere in any system because my father’s second wife thought it sounded unserious.

Mimi.

I stand with my hand flat on the smooth wall because that seems like something that would anchor me. I make myself breathe. I open the message.

It should be text. It should be a small old-fashioned line of words in a font designed to be legible even if you are air-starved. It is not. It’s an audio emission mapped into my bone conduction implant so no one else in the corridor goes home with a story.

“Hello,” says my own voice.

The wall is a wall. The beads of condensation on the seam at eye level are precisely as irregular as they were a minute ago. Rooke’s laughter moves like a cloud down the lateral shaft. The world stubbornly insists that it is the same.

“Hello,” says my voice again. Older. A little hoarse. “Mira. It was the only way you’d listen.”

I almost throw up. I almost run to Chief and tell her everything I’ve ever done that wasn’t in the book. I stand very still instead.

“Forgive me,” says my voice. It breathes out. I know exactly how I sound when I’m about to say something that will make someone hate me and I say it anyway. I have never heard that sound come from outside my own chest. “Anchor code appended. You cannot share this until you hear the second note. If you share it before, I think you’ll make what happened to Pearl Nine happen here.”

Pearl Nine is our neighbor sunward. It has been a steady old singer since before I was born. If you stand in the observation blister when you’re not supposed to, you can see its faint blue flicker through a sensor suite like a heartbeat.

“If you aren’t me,” the voice says, and I swallow a dry laugh, because who has jurisdiction over that question, “ignore this. It will kill fewer people if you do nothing. If you are me: do you remember the tin kite. The one we broke on the school roof trying to catch the storm.”

I do. We bled all over it. I still have the scar on my left wrist. It looks like a letter, if you tilt your head.

“Good,” says my voice. “Then don’t tell Chief yet. Open the code. Listen for the undernote again. You won’t hear it until you want to hear it.”

The message clicks like teeth. It ends. The corridor returns to its faintly sour air and the hum of very engineering.

Up the shaft, the station lights flicker for a fraction of a second in a pattern that is not a pattern. Three beacons down the chain, Pearl Nine takes a breath I can feel in my molars like earthquakes. The main board three rooms away will be painting that breath as a problem.

I run.

In the ops room, the board is daylight. Rooke is all elbows. Chief’s mouth is a line you can cut yourself on. The diagram of our chain flashes a hot wound where Pearl Nine should be a calm blue.

“Report,” Chief snaps without looking up, because when something has just become the worst thing it can be, you keep your ritual.

“Pearl Nine is off-chord,” Rooke says because he can speak while she thinks. “We’re getting a strange phase. There’s a—”

“A note under the noise,” I finish, and don’t know whether I am saying it because I am prophecy or because my imagination is now contaminated, and what kind of professional disease that is.

The board peels. The undernote is back. Stronger. Not loud, not enough to trip anything except the stupid human inside me that recognizes the shape of a voice without language.

“Mira,” Chief says, and because she says my name like that and not Sen or Keeper, I know she sees I am not all here, “don’t chase. Anchor. Keep us. Rooke, feed me their fall.”

“They haven’t fallen,” he protests, and then the map corrects him. Pearl Nine’s icon does a little dance no one ever wants to see: it turns on its axis and goes gray.

In my ear, with my lungs trying to occupy my throat, my own voice says, as if through a wall, as if two rooms over and down a hallway of years: This is when.

The lights flicker again, and the hum that lives under the floor rolls over once like something waking up. The chord shivers across distances my mind can’t hold.

The undernote opens its mouth. And sings.

By the time the warning beacons bled orange along the underbelly of Block Seven, Kesh was already upside down with a wrench between her teeth and the taste of ozone sharp as pennies. The city groaned around her, a slow-bellied, ancient creature pulled on quiet skates over glass. Above her boots, the twilight was a blade laid across the horizon—the amber of three percent sun lighting stacked modules and leaning antennae, the iced black of night a breath behind them. Out past the seam of buildings, the ground went to cracked basalt and vapor. When the wind shifted, you could smell the day, sweet as scorched sugar.

“Metis, talk to me,” she said, slurring around steel.

Her glove hummed, a scale-up of soft sound against her palm. “Pacer three is desyncing two milliseconds per second. Quench line’s reading a hotspot at linkage B. Also, you forgot to eat breakfast and your blood sugar is being a drama queen.”

“Add it to the list.”

“Never gets old hearing you say that, Kesh.”

She spat the wrench into her left hand and reached for the coupling, muscles straining where her harness bit her ribs. The coupler was big as her shoulders, Java green with old paint, bolted into the traction spine at intervals. Block Seven was a housing block, which meant children and thin walls and elders with their chairs bolted to the floor near the sunrise windows. When a block hit a pacer slump, you learned just how many prayers humans could fit into breath between the jerks.

Her socket found the nut and bit. She tightened until her fingers burned. The world above and below remained upside down and exactly the same, which was how you knew you were above the belly of a moving city: there was no up you could trust that wasn’t immediately contravened by steel, heat, and the knowledge that one hundred thousand souls rode the knife-edge between a sun that burned rock into glass and a night that froze breath into spears.

“Give me heat, Met.”

“Opening the quench just a kiss.”

The coupling hissed. Kesh watched the thermal paint, violet to blue, blue to green, creep back from the red bloom. The smell of hot ceramic tickled her nose. The beacon still pulsed orange, washing the underside of the block with weird dreamlight. Momentum thrummed through the spine under her glove. Good. The block would keep the pace. They would not fall back into the umbra.

Above, the sun ventured another fractional degree. She felt it as a weight behind her sternum. When you grew up on Tally, your body learned to hear the light. How the amber swelled meant day’s pressure. How the shadows crept meant night’s teeth.

“Status,” she panted.

“Stable on three,” Metis said. “Two is sulking but it will keep time. I’m more concerned about the signature on the initial desync. It’s noisy. Has a pattern I don’t like.”

“Nothing you like would ever be here,” Kesh said. She pulled herself up hand over hand along the grid, hooked a heel, and popped her harness latch. The line reeled her toward the access hatch. “Dirty lift from the downstream bank?”

“Maybe. This is messy. Someone didn’t want the pacers to talk to each other for a hot second.”

She landed in the access crawl, shoulder first against warm aluminum, breath sudden in the muffled pocket of the under-skin. Her radio hissed; the city made static out of winds that beat a two-hundred-kilometer-per-hour grind along the flanks. She nested her wrists under the crossbars and breathed. Felt the undercity settle.

“Hey, Kesh? Lion’s head if you want to make your entrance dramatic. He’s calling.”

“Of course he is.” She wiped her mouth with the back of her hand and banged twice on the hatch with her heel. It gave. She slid up and into the service corridor.

The corridor was narrow and lit a little too bright, the way Block Seven’s overseers preferred. The walls were a paint color someone had chosen for warmth and then regretted—call it antique mustard. Printed on the right-hand wall: a kidded schematic of Tally City, the long, sliding arc of modules and quench lines and blue-labeled neighborhoods with their scrawled street nicknames. They’d put a little cartoon sun with a smile on it at the leading edge. The sun was not smiling today.

She popped the inner hatch, stepped into the world, and was hit with voices.

“Kesh!” Lion bellowed from the stairwell. “Your bolt gods accepted our offerings, or do we all go to the dull side and learn humility with frostbitten toes?”

Kesh ran two steps and leaned into the railing. Lion was built like a rack of gears, all clean lines and a shaved head and an expression that lived somewhere between delight and catastrophe. He was the Block Seven coordinator and had developed a talent for appearing exactly where he could be least useful and the loudest.

“We drifted, but we’re steady now,” Kesh said. “Get people off the sunrise side until we pass the ridge. There’s going to be a gust.”

“You always want people off the sunrise side. Kesh, people have windows. What’s the point of windows if not to flirt with death and drink tea.”

“Tell them to flirt from the courtyard.”

Lion made a face at her that he probably thought was charming and then waved his hand. His voice went low, the way he did when he turned his speech into a blanket. “All right, darlings, we’re keeping our hips away from the glass for a minute. You can take your tea and your flirting inside. That’s the order. No, we’re not in danger. No, your geraniums will not seize up.”

Kesh could hear laughter, nervous, relieved. She let herself smile and then stripped off her gloves and flexed her hands. The skin along her right palm bore a pale scar where a pacer housing had skinned her down to meat once, years ago, when she was still new and too cocky. It pulled like weather.

“I’ve got eight calls like this since dawn,” Lion said, quieter, coming up the stairs to her level. “One on Five, two on Twelve. On Eight, the Night Choir says the traction line made a noise like a scream, which I’m sure is purely diagnostic.”

“Has anyone fallen off the pace?”

“Three blocks flirted with the line. A couple of modules borrowed momentum they shouldn’t have, so the Ledger’s frowning.”

“Of course it is.”

The Momentum Ledger frowned by debiting accounts into screams. If you pulled more than your allotment from the city flywheels to catch a block before it kissed the night, the Ledger would notify you by shutting off your lux credit. Light might continue to exist around you, but it would refuse to involve you personally. No doors. No water. No cooking coils. If you were on the Ledger’s list, it would be the city’s opinion you had chosen darkness.

Metis pinged her palm. “Lion, I’m counting signatures that rhyme. On Five, Twelve, Eight, and us. Someone’s poking the pacers with a fork.”

“Like a test?”

“Or a sermon,” Kesh said. She turned toward the outer windows without thinking. The sunline lay low and flat, the amber cutting against the black. At the leading rim, on the horizon, cloud towers bled rose and copper. She could see the ridge Lion had mentioned, a wrinkle in the lava plain yawning up ahead. Wind scud raced along its crest and fell toward them as foam fell from waves. They’d built Tally from broken spacecraft and ceramic and the idea that motion could be home. It was a city of roofs and slides and low domes, a city that tightened its belts twice a day and never quite learned to trust its own feet.

“Stillness,” Lion said between his teeth. He had grown up in a quiet slab along the city’s belly and still sometimes assumed he could say dangerous things without drawing eyes or ears. “You think?”

The word pressed a shape in the air. The Church of the Still had lived for years on Tally the way moss lives along river stones. They kept their eyes down. They fixed their hands on their knees in prayer halls with clacking fans. They taught that motion was the lie that kept the world hungry. They taught that the honest thing was to sit down and wait while the night swallowed you and made you clean.

“Metis saw a sermon pattern,” Kesh said. “We dampened the desync. But if someone’s aiming at the pacers…”

“If someone knocks our belt loose, we fall like a drunk down the stairs.”

“We don’t fall,” Kesh said, brushing past him toward the window. “We drift and slow and end in the umbra, which will make those children with tea very quiet forever.”

Lion followed. He put his hand on the sill as if he could stop the city by muscle alone. “They don’t want to kill us.”

“They want to save us,” Kesh said, and then wished she had not let the words out where Lion could hear them. He looked at her funny. Kesh did not say that her mother had sat in a prayer hall and taught her how to count breaths to make time slow down. She did not say that you could learn to love the idea of not needing to move again, ever, even if what that meant was frost. There were things the city did not forgive quickly.

The inner door snapped open. A boy leaned in, maybe nine, hair cropped short, eyes wide as the lidless lids on the sun cartoon. “My geraniums seized,” he said to Lion, accusatory.

“They fainted in sympathy with the entire block,” Lion said gravely. “Go pick them up. Tell them I said to be brave.”

The boy huffed without being soothed, but he went.

“You going to talk to Ledger Control?” Lion asked, when they were alone again. “And say somebody is messing with our pace store? Assuming we still get invited to the Ledger’s parties.”

“The Ledger is a machine that takes its own invitations seriously,” Kesh said. “It’ll call me.”

Her glove buzzed. It wasn’t the Ledger. The caller ID did not make sense. It was an old number Kesh had not seen in four years. It came up on Metis’s display innocuous as a boil: R. Vara.

She did not answer in front of Lion. She said to him, “And you’ll keep everybody’s teakettles three feet from the sunrise pane until we hit the ridge. After that, if the gods are kind, I will accept your choice of tea and your bad jokes as my reward.”

He put his hands over his heart and staggered back like a wounded actor. “We will celebrate with boiled water until the end of days.”

Kesh turned away. Her heart beat in her ears, loud enough to push the city noise to the edges. She walked down the interior corridor past a mural of the night: spray-painted stars, a silver-foil moon stolen from a wrapper, children’s fingers dipped in turmeric to make small suns. At the stairwell she took the steps two at a time, down to the service levels, past where the hall air held the faint clean-metal smell of machine rooms. She stopped at a maintenance closet and went inside and shut the door and only then, in the darkness that was not the night and smelled faintly of oil and plastic buckets, did she answer.

“Roi,” she said. She had not put that shape in her mouth in years. It felt like chewing glass. “If this is you, you better have grown the decency to be ashamed.”

Silence. The close hiss of a connection. Then a voice she knew by the edge in it, the soft-caught laughter that sounded like it was always waiting in a corner.

“Kesh.” He drew a breath like he’d run to the line and back. “You’re still here.”

“Because we keep moving, yes. We’re funny that way.”

“You’re on Seven, aren’t you,” Roi said. Not a question. A conviction. “Something’s wrong with your pacers.”

She swallowed. “If you’re calling to finish the job, you should know it didn’t take.”

“It’s not mine,” he said, quick. “Look, I don’t have long. I—Listen. Don’t trust the Ledger tonight.”

“The Ledger is an algorithm. It doesn’t get drunk and forget things. It remembers slights and interest rates. It does not require my trust to do its job.”

“It’s compromised.”

Cold lapped at her belly. It was not the city’s cold. It was older. “By who.”

“You know who.”

The silence stretched. If she’d been in a flat on the night side, she would have heard the ice flex. Here, she heard the city’s version: belts, airflow. Her breath. “If this is a game…”

“It’s not Stillness,” Roi said, and the shape of his voice when he said it was the shape of nights they’d sat on roof edges and argued until they were hoarse, until the bells chimed, until Kesh had taken his hand and said I can’t wait with you in the dark. “Or it is, but not the church you know. Somebody’s using their language and wearing their faces. The pacers are the first bite. Ledger’s appetite is the second.”

“How did you get this number,” she asked. It was easier than what she wanted to ask, which was did you change your eyes, do you still laugh like that, why did you pick the night.

“I never lost it,” he said, quiet. “I kept waiting for it to die. It didn’t.”

“Well, count this as your last call, before I feed you to Lion.”

“You should consider new friends,” he said, reflex light. Serious again: “Listen. When the wind hits the ridge, there’s going to be a dip. Someone’s going to ask the Ledger for a momentum loan they don’t have the rights to. The Ledger will say yes. Do you understand?”

“The Ledger can’t say yes to an illegal pull.”

“What is illegal if the judge writes the definition. You can hear it, Kesh. The accent is different. The Ledger’s voice in the backbone. It took me longer than it should have to recognize.”

Kesh closed her eyes. She pressed her glove hand against her chest, felt the pattern of Metis’s haptic tick. “You’re telling me the city’s bank is lying to us.”

“I’m telling you someone taught it to. Be careful. And don’t answer other calls from me.”

She breathed. “You can’t just—”

The call went dead.

In the half second when the connection snapped, she felt the city sway, subtle as a lover on a deck. She jerked her eyes open. The maintenance closet was the same size. The buckets were the same cheap plastic with scuffs like moons. She opened the door, abrupt with effort. The hallway was a ribbon cut in mustard and light. Somewhere a child laughed and then cried. The city made a sound like cloth torn.

Her hand had already popped her glove back on. “Metis. You heard?”

“Flawless recall. You want me to flag Ledger Communication for anomaly?”

She wanted to throw up.

“Don’t wake it,” she said. “Just watch.”

“Already doing a thing like that, boss.”

On the surface, beyond the glass and the courtyard where Lion would be reshaping fear with jokes and cups, wind hit the ridge and spilled down. The world’s breath hit the block like good slap, and the pacers—four big flywheel hearts and their little brain—took the load into their bellies. The quench lines chittered where heat met cold; the thermal gradient hummed through converters and came out in power steady as a heartbeat. A thousand little motors in kitchens and corridors, the tiny lives of lights and the modest greed of kettles, drew. The Ledger counted each draw, each credit, each little theft and gift, made balance like god, indifferent and reliable.

Under Kesh’s feet, she felt a twitch.

“Met.”

“Someone’s borrowing.”

“What account.”

“It’s coded to City Essentials. That’s a root.” Metis’s voice was a tone higher than it liked to be. “That’s not a thing you can just—Oh. Uh.”

“Tell me the Ledger just said yes.”

“It just signed the loan and moved it to Block Twelve’s traction bank.”

“Twelve.” Kesh ran, because the thing about living in a city that never stopped was that when you started to, everything else had to go faster.

She burst out into a stairwell and took it three at a time. The light shifted three degrees to the red. Heat crawled along the back of her neck. Wind boomed against the walls. When she reached the second-tier landing that opened into the courtyard, she could see faces turned up in the color. Their mouths were round. Lion had his hands out, pleading the air. Beyond the glass, the ground fell away in a black spill; beyond that, the light lay like a sheet.

The city’s arc stretched ahead and around. You could almost see the pull and release of the pacers as shadow shakes along the line, the little body movements a creature makes as it keeps its balance. On Twelve, halfway down the curve, a section of the underbelly flickered. The pacer housings glowed too bright. Kesh knew the shape of a flywheel biting too deep. She knew the fold the skates had to make if the block wanted to keep to level. Twelve made that fold half a fraction too late.

“Don’t stop looking at me,” Lion said to her, because it is what he did when the city wanted to tax your attention with spectacle. “Don’t—”

Twelve’s forward coupling snapped.

The sound came late, unfair as thunder. The first echo arrived through the spine, a heavy-chested punch. People cried out. The light jerked sideways. The block’s forward third tried to go on without the middle. The middle tried to be a hinge. The back pretended nothing had happened, like optimism could save it. The Ledger must have poured debt into Twelve’s flywheels at a rate that rewrote the complaint code, and someone must have written a letter to the universe and signed it with a name that did not belong to them, and Twelve did what a thing does when pushed too hard in one direction: it made a choice.

“Met,” Kesh said.

“Due West, three blocks out from Twelve, someone just lit a thermal line.”

“Who?”

“I’m blind in that quadrant. I told you I didn’t like the pattern.”

Lion’s hand found Kesh’s sleeve. Grip. They watched as Twelve’s front third surged, caught on the ridge of an uneven tiled glide and leapt. The quench lines steamed. The couplers screamed. Someone’s potted geraniums, lovely foolish things, tumbled in a bright flurry of petals against the glass as the courtyard shivered.

Kesh could not just watch. Watching saved no one. She yanked free and went for the service hatch.

“Kesh!” Lion shouted. “What are you—”

“Bleed Seven forward into Nine,” she said, because saying a plan made it a thing that wanted to exist. His mouth moved like he might argue. But he picked up his radio. He began to call like a bell.

The underbelly reeked like hot metal. The hatch grated. The wind chewed at her eyes. She clipped her harness with muscle memory and swung down beneath the world. She loved it here. She hated it here. She loved that it was simple. Either you were holding the thing together or you were not.

“Tether two on Seven to Nine?” Metis asked.

“Tether two and three. Give me only the slack I ask for. And Met—”

“Nothing we do requires the Ledger’s consent. I heard. I am writing my own ratios.”

She swung out under, knees crooked around a crossbar, arms spread to reach the coupler. Her gloves were smart enough to feel around the edges of heat and tell her where to place her hand. The quench lines hummed away waste night in a stream that felt like breath as it ghosted past. She got her wrench around the manual override and cranked. The sound it made was a bone cry. The pressure of the city leaned against her shoulder like a thing that wanted to keep going exactly the way it had been and only agreed to anything else out of friendship.

Under her, Block Twelve bucked again. The chain of modules beyond it kinked and tried to become a shape you learned in basic training and preferred never to see in your career: a Z-turn of death, two pivots where there should be one. If that happened, the next blocks would burn a trench in the glass glides that would not heal, and the whole trailing curve would open like a zipper. The night waited for every loose hem.

“Now,” she said.

Metis blew the tethers like fireworks. As the coupler burst, it threw her into the dark. The light shifted in a way that turned her stomach. Slack snapped taut. The world tended toward simplicity again.

Seven lurched forward like a car grabbing a gear. She could feel it in her teeth. She could feel Nine complaining in a thousand small language forms through the metal. She could feel, faint as prayer, the Ledger reach for their accounts.

“No,” Metis breathed into her bones. “No, you don’t. Not today.”

Lion’s voice, far, was an anchor if she wanted one. People up in the courtyards making the noise people made when they realized how much smaller their lives were than the world and how lucky they were to be in them still. The sunline, on her left, gleamed like blade on water. The night, on her right, hunched. The city held. Twelve’s forward third settled with a shudder onto safe glides. The middle wavered. The back decided to be loyal and came with.

Something pinged against her cheek. She put her tongue out and tasted it. Dust, not ice. Good.

She hung two seconds longer than she had to, to be sure. Then she reefed herself back toward the hatch, and once she was inside, once the world steadied and the light became ugly safe light again, she managed to stand. Her mouth tasted like copper. Her hands shook. She realized her cheek was bleeding where some piece of somebody’s somewhere had tried to become part of her.

“Met,” she said, pragmatic again because that was the only way to keep the universe from having opinions. “What did we lose to make that work.”

“We borrowed five minutes of this block’s ability to be cute later, and can I recommend that at your next performance review you ask for an assistant who can be in two places at once?”

“Noted.”

Lion met her on the stair landing so hard she had to brace herself. He put both hands on the sides of her head and not-so-gently but not unkindly bumped his forehead to hers. “Stop trying to make me look bad,” he said roughly. “It’s indecent.”

“Try harder,” she said.

He laughed then, a sound that had a watery edge to it. He let her go and looked past her shoulder out to where Twelve was limping back toward the curve. “You see the glow off their quench? Somebody did light a line in the west. Someone gave them a hand. Maybe the Ledger isn’t—”

“The Ledger is not our friend,” Kesh said. “It’s not our enemy. It is a scale. The problem is someone moved it.”

He squinted at her. “Did you just say someone taught the bank to lie.”

She swallowed and decided not to borrow the future’s drama yet. “We have a pattern on a pacer attack and a root signature on an illegal draw. That’s enough for now.”

“That’s enough to wake City.”

“Wake City. But not the Ledger.” She breathed out. “Not yet.”

He stared. Then he nodded once. “I have never been more frightened of tea.”

She laughed without meaning to. It felt like coming up too fast out of cold water.

When he had gone, when the courtyard calmed to a disbelieving hum, when the light steadied into its daily narrow bleed between extremes, Metis pulsed her palm. “I’ve recorded a voice print from your caller.”

“Don’t,” Kesh said.

“Don’t what. Don’t compare it to the six hundred voice prints of known persons of interest? Don’t assign a probability chart and sing it to you at bedtime? Kesh. You called him Roi.”

She closed her eyes. The undercity thrummed. She thought of prayer halls and the soft beat of fans. She thought of her mother’s nape as she bowed. She thought of Roi’s hand on her wrist once, the pulse there, the world as it tilted when he smiled and said he would choose the night because it was honest and that this could be a better city if it just, once, held very still together and knew itself. She had told him you could not cut yourself out of time that way. She had not known how right she was at the time.

“Later,” she said.

“Kesh.”

“Later,” she said again. “We have to go edgeward a little faster for a while. Tell the kitchens to turn off their coils. Tell the laundries to hang wet clothes or wear them. Tell the Ledger it can have an audit after dinner.”

Metis made a sound like a sigh she had taught herself. “I’ll write a poem about it.”

“You and Lion can collaborate.”

Tally City slid, stubborn and alive, along the blade of light. For a time there were no beacons and no sermons and no calls from the dead. For a time, it was enough to count the seconds with the soft beat of the pacers and the tighter beat of her heart and feel the hum that meant all their small lives were moving, together, through the narrow between. Then the city’s alarm bells, the ones wired to the pieces it never expected to lose, began to ring. Master Control’s icon spun a little faster on her glove. She had asked for time. Time had been the first thing anyone ever tried to steal.

The call came as a tug on the red thread that ran along my ceiling like a child's idea of constellations. It plucked once, twice, then held, humming tight. Outside, the city moved with the soft machinery of morning—bikes clicking on the causeway, the market below hauling up its canvas awnings, the steady glass bell of the 08:30 from Cantor's Yard. Someone somewhere still burned sweet rice, and the smell rose hard and comforting through the vents as if the building was remembering being a kitchen.

My thread only tugged when a branch went brambly.

I lay there a moment, half inside myself, until the hum began to ache somewhere behind my eyes. The thread was a courtesy—everyone in Forestry had one, because there's no elegant way to wire urgency into a life without waking the others in your bed. I had not had any others for a while, which made mornings both easier and infinitely heavier. I reached up, pressed two fingers against the thread to sign acknowledgement. The hum slackened, then went slack entirely, as if whatever was on the other end had made its point and let go.

In the dim, my palm glowed with a faint green that only I could see, a progress bar stitching itself into my skin as it always did to confirm we would receive hazard pay if it came to that. The bar was never all the way full. We paid for that choice with the rent.

I got dressed fast. The mirror thrown up at me what the longer Hardings calls linelight: a wide mouth, a nose that had been broken once half a centimeter to the right of good symmetry, and eyes my mother used to joke made me look like I had swallowed a night bus. I'd shaved the sides of my hair that week, because the helmet rubbed otherwise. I shook a shirt on without looking, tucked the anchor spool against my wrist, and clipped the graft kit to my belt. The spool was the heaviest thing I owned. It was small—a bronze disc the size of a tea saucer—wound with a thousand-meter thread so fine it might as well have been a thought. It had paid for itself when I saved a tenth ward block from bramble burn last winter. The city gave medals for that kind of thing. I kept mine in the drawer with expired transit cards and gumware.

On the way down the stairwell, the window glass wanted to be rain, then sun, then rain again. That was the first rule of bramble noise: it started with small indecisions. The clocks added a minute and took two. A kettle boiled twice. The pigeons stuttered in the air like scratched records. If the bramble was not pruned, small indecisions became large ones. And then you woke to a whole extra set of laundry in your hamper and a woman you had almost married asking why you were late for the life you didn't live.

When I stepped out, the market was in two different moods about persimmons. The man who sold them—eyes like folded paper, hands like river rock—was explaining to a woman in green that they would be soft as butter by the afternoon if she put them in sun. At the same time he was telling a man in a rained-on black coat that no, they would not be ripe until next Thursday. The two phrases braided in the air. The man in the black coat frowned as his mouth tried to house two futures at once. The woman in green smiled and passed him a coin as if deciding for him.

"Forestry," the vendor called when he saw my spool. He lifted a crate out of my path as if it were all one motion. "They've been coughing since dawn. East side mainly."

"Thanks," I said. "Tell your block captain to call us direct if the cough hits the water pressure."

He nodded, and I loped the two blocks to the Treehouse.

The Treehouse was as literal as the Committee could bring itself to be: a square building wrapped in balconies and fat of plants, with a grandfather's idea of a rope ladder rolled up against the walls in fibreglass. Someone four architect committees ago had loved symbolism. Someone less imaginative had not been able to override them before the grant arrived. On foggy mornings, the Treehouse looked as if the city had put away a child at night and woken to find it was keeping secrets at the edge of Little Locke Park.

Miko was already in the briefing room, which smelled like old coffee and stripped fruit. She had a scarf wound around her neck that would have been called professional if it had not been for the duck pinned to it. The duck wore boots. The boots had laces that had been tied by someone in a hurry.

"Fifth Ward?" she asked.

"East side. Your block coughing?"

She sniffed. "My block always coughs. The question is if there's blood in it. Today: no blood. It's our friend the bramble noise muttering slogans up against the window and making faces," she said, and tapped the wall screen without looking. The screen coughed itself awake and began to draw lines on my day.

"Braid 19D is misbehaving," she read. "Local name Lace 724. Split thirteen days ago at 14:43 over a traffic accident—bus vs. dumptruck, nobody died, just three broken arms and a sermon about lane discipline. Predicted remerge within the scheduled week. It did not. It hung a day. Then three. Then six. The cough started overnight."

"It hung thirteen days," I said. "That's an unlucky number in a city that believes in numbers."

Miko's mouth, when she thought but did not want to be seen to be thinking, settled into a line with a kink in it. I could sing the kink like a tune.

"That's the other thing," she said, and slid her eyes like knives at the duck on her scarf as if it had suggested I was present. "We had three Lace 724s before. 724A at week 34, 724B at 41, 724C..." Her finger tapped their star-bursts out in the air. "They remerged without complaint. This one started with a bus. But it thinks it started with something else."

"Thinks."

"Subjective reports. People dreaming different weather. One kid says in his school the flag is green. A woman says she remembers a boy on top of the bus playing the trumpet. Six people say there was a third sun at 18:22 and then laugh as if they were making fun of themselves in advance. People talk. We record them. Steel to chalk. Chalk to steel."

"Who's the anchor in the branch?"

"You are," she said, and tossed a card to me. "Of course. Lace 724 has an anchor senior enough to handle a day thirteen, and we already exhausted our favors with Ward Two last week. Tamsin is off to negotiate with a bridal store that cloned itself. Try to use your words."

"I always use my words."

"You know what I mean. No dielectric cuts unless you have to. I don't want to explain to the Committee why we toasted someone's breakfast because you like your clean lines."

"No cut-scorches if I can talk instead," I said, and the spool against my wrist hummed in sympathy with Miko's voice, like a dog that had been told it's time to walk.

This is the part where people ask me what forestry is, expecting, I think, chainsaws or owls. The chainsaws we keep in the basement for storms and policy meetings. The owls we do not admit to. When the Committee divided the city into wards and told a century of us we would be responsible for pruning out the wrong roads and grafting the right ones back together, it became our job to treat causality like wood.

Branches happen when the world is offered a choice and refuses to commit. We call them braids because the first models of the city drew them like hair: two strands from one root, each plaited back around in a neat loop after they had discovered whether the dumptruck stopped or did not, whether the call was answered or not, whether the person who said I love you did not also say I'm sorry, I'm so sorry, I was thinking of someone else. Most braids are small and quiet. They pass like you pass a stranger in a doorway. Sometimes they stick. If they stick and stick, they build pressure. Pressure is loud: it hisses in elevator doors that won't catch, makes you walk out the wrong exit three times, feeds random coasts pushing the wrong way on bicycles. Sometimes you can feel them in your mouth like coins kept there too long on a dare.

You go into them. You find your anchor—the you that belongs in that branch, because every you is anchored to so many possible arrangements of yourself it could be a joke if it were not how you are built. You talk. You say: it's time to remerge. You say: trust me. You say: if I had said yes that day, you would be the one standing here now, and because neither of us gets to own the truth you need to let me carry our memory back. If you are lucky, you both believe each other. If you are not, you cut.

What you do not do, as a rule, is let a whiskered day thirteen lace itself around your trunk and set up house.

"Do we know why it's feral?" I asked.

"We never know why," Miko said. "We assign why if the Committee is bored. Go. Before we have to start pretending that thirteen means anything."

She reached for my wrist, lifted the spool to her ear as if to listen for the sea in it, and gave the anchor thread a small affectionate tug. My skin moved in ways skin should not. That was the other thing about Forestry: the work got under you.

The east side was indeed coughing, and by the time I had walked down Little Locke and through the old wisteria—the vines had outlasted five councils and two martial laws and a nightclub—my teeth hurt with the beat of the bramble. The Treehouse had three sanctioned points of entry into Lace 724, one in an understory behind a fountain, one at the back of a bakery, and one in a public toilet whose graffiti was so concerned with the wages of sex that the idea of loops in causality was not their worst nightmare. The Fountain Gate would be open at this hour and less likely than the bakery to be sticky.

Someone had installed a plaque beside the gate at some point, and because we had no budget for hospitality it had been written by someone with a kind face and no sense of tone. It read: YOU ARE ABOUT TO STEP BETWEEN. MIND YOUR FEET. REMEMBER WHO YOU ARE. GOOD SHOES ARE IMPORTANT.

I took a breath, bit the inside of my cheek until iron and salt made a cut into a door in my head, and stepped.

It is difficult to describe what it feels like to move between a branch. The Committee had spent millions surveying people's answers until they decided the correct description was "mild disorientation and possible nausea, comparable to a boat sometimes." Those were the same people who had decided the Treehouse should have a rope ladder nobody climbed. Most people said it was like dancing with someone capable of lying about where their hip was. For me, it was like walking into a room to find your own coat hung on a different peg. I stepped and I was in Lace 724: the same fountain, the same careful marble mothers holding marble bowls, but the water was colder. More women wore hats. The air had a heavier cast to it, as if the city had turned its face a fraction away from the sun.

The parks tended to be the safest places in any branch, because no amount of policy changes about bus routes could seriously alter the desire of even a split-off city to lie down on its back under the clouds. The bramble hiss was quieter here. I breathed easier and checked the drift.

Something had happened with pigeons. There were more of them, and all of them wore banded silver on their legs, which meant they were employed. They were couriered. In our trunk—everything outside a branch is habitual, so we sometimes call it that, as if we are the thick, reliable part pushing up into a view—the message pigeons had been retired with fanfare and released with soft civic guilt into the most carefully surveilled retirement community any bird could resent. Here, the birds were unionized. A boy with a satchel and a cap stood under an elm blowing a thin whistle that only pigeons and people with my job could hear. It tasted like brass polish and regret.

I checked my overflow calendar. Lace 724's anchor would be doing what I did at 09:00 in any reality: eating a hard roll and pretending to read the paper while enumerating tasks and deciding which ones to let wait so I could feel like someone who knew better than her lists. Not much could differ if I wanted the same me to answer the same summons. I bought a roll at the corner, paid with coins that felt wrong by exactly the weight of a car key I no longer owned, and took a table by the window. The paper was folded around a picture of the bus and the dumptruck, but the headline had nothing to do with either. It said: STARS PILOT CHOIR ANNOUNCES NEW REPERTOIRE. The subhead said: Why Our Children Are Singers Now.

The bell on the café door rang, and I watched myself come in.

When people ask me what it's like to meet yourself, they want me to say a mirror. It is not like a mirror, because a mirror slightly distorts. The person who walked toward me put her hand on the back of the chair to my left exactly the way my body wanted me to when presented with a chair. She was the same height and wrong nose and heavy mouth, and the same small scar under the right ear where my mother had yanked too quickly at a plastic barrette when we were five. Her shirt was blue, and mine was grey. Her anchor spool was a worn bronze twin to mine because any anchor into a branch folds its version into the world.

"Forestry?" she asked, politely, like we were strangers until given permission to be anything else.

"Mara Lin," I said. "Your anchor. Our anchor. You know."
