She smiled then, and the skin around her eyes did the thing my father called crinkle and my last girlfriend had called the trap. It made people who did not love me think they might. I watched it and wanted to swat at my own face. It is exhausting to know your lies that well.

"Mara Lin," she repeated. "We do know. I'm glad you came. I—" She stopped. Her hand tightened on the chair until I could see the tendon pop against the skin. "We're less formal about it here," she said, lightly, but the light was a bird thrown against a window.

"Less formal." I kept my voice quiet. No one else in the café turned. In most branches, there is an agreement we don't sign and must pretend not to have with the versions of us that are attached to the same knots: we do not break each other in public.

She sat. The waiter put a hard roll in front of her that looked like a fist. She broke it apart as if doing the work would feel like doing the work would help. Little steam rose from the loaf, and it was comforting in ways that had nothing to do with bread. We are a species that learns to associate heat with benediction.

"We should remerge," I said.

"Yes," she said, without flinch. "My block is coughing."

"It will get worse."

"This is the part where you tell me it always gets worse in prolonged lays." She smiled at me in that way I used on people who argued about the necessary. "I do this work too."

"Branches don't usually know that," I said. The thread at my wrist chimed once; Miko checking in.

"Don't they? What do they do, out there?" She flicked the corner of her roll toward my step, meaning the trunk. "Here, they open with the line about chickens."

"The line about chickens is good."

"It is a very good line. The city paid a poet. We liked it. But we knew we liked it because we'd been told we would. That's not me being clever. That's me saying you can feel it when you are being written."

"You're being written by physics and the economic self-interest of a thousand municipal contracts."

"Sweetheart." She swallowed and pinned me with my own eyes. "Don't talk to me about the economic self-interest of a thousand municipal contracts. Your scarf left the job because the Committee told her the numbers were God. She cried for a week quietly in the staff toilet and then came back smelling like cedar and said she was all right. And you said nothing because she was not yours to save and you were not hers to keep. Don't tell me we don't feel money in our bones. You asked me what it's like here? It's like being told you're a poem written by a procurement algorithm. It is funny until you realize you're not the one who gets to keep the rights."

"You said we were less formal," I said. "Which means you're going to refuse me."

"Don't perform being surprised," she said, gently enough to make me hate us both. "It isn't charming."

We sat. The waiter brought coffee. The sugar bowl had been replenished recently, and the sugar was in conical lumps like small pale roofs. I put one in my coffee and watched it dissolve. I was stalling. The spool against my wrist was warm like a cat who had decided on your good books in a sunbeam.

"What's the hold?" I asked finally. There is always a hold. It is never the hold it says on the complaint forms.

She put her hands around her cup. The anchor thread on her wrist was the same old bronze as mine but banded with something else, a matte grey like a storm that wanted to be loved. I did not like that. We do not wear our threads. We wear what we are given when we are nailed to ourselves.

"You said this branch started with the bus," she said.

"It did."

"It didn't," she said.

"Okay," I said slowly. "Tell me what it started with. And please don't say trumpets on a bus."

"There was a man," she said, and looked out the window at the fountain's marble mothers as if they required help. "He wore a hat with a red feather. He was too old to wear it that way and know anyone would believe him, which is how you know when the world is wrong: it asks you to believe that kind of thing. He came into my office three days before the bus and asked to leave a message for the person who would come to remerge with me."

"You laughed him out," I said.

"I did not laugh. I told him he was in the wrong office. Then I told him to sit and wrote what he wanted. He said the name of the woman who made my first anchor spool."

"There was only one woman who made our spool," I said, and the room tilted sidewise under me for a second. "She's dead."

"Is she dead in your place?" My anchor nodded at my wrist with her chin. "In ours she lives two more weeks. She dies with her hands inside one of us like she is fixing a throat. The Committee calls it an accident. We learn new words for accident. We say it quietly as if the wrong gods will hear. The man with the red feather told me to tell you he couldn't find a counterpart who would know his name, so he would do this the old way. He said: They'll call it Lace 724 even though it isn't a lace at all. He said: don't let them cut. He said: sing if you have to, even if you are someone who thinks you don't believe in choirs."

"You wrote it down."

The coffee had a sweetness in it that was not sugar. The bramble hiss was quieter than outside, as if the café were isolated like a sensible ship. I watched the light on the table pretend to be afternoon and then drag itself back into morning in a way a person who didn't know where to look would mistake for a cloud. "No one knows that name. We burned the files after she died."

"We always burn the files we are told to burn." She smiled without malice. "In some worlds, that's the right choice."

"Sing if I have to?"

"Our Stars Pilot Choir changed repertoire," she said, nodding at the own copy of the paper. "You saw. The Bends are deeper in this year. They need the kids to hold a different kind of tone."

"We don't talk about the Choir on duty," I said. "Miko says it gives the interns ideas about cosmic glory and a sick taste for collapse."

"I'm not giving you cosmic anything," she said. "I'm saying: do not cut. Not yet. I will remerge with you. But not today. Give me—" She looked down and counted in the fine lines at the base of her thumb. "Give me one more day."

"No," I said, and it was like shutting a door on the hand of my own child. "We cannot leave a day thirteen. It will skip on the groove and make lines through the trunk."

"I know," she said. "We will make lines through the trunk anyway."

Outside, a man on a bicycle put his foot down and then put the same foot down again and then frowned at his foot like it had betrayed him. A woman crossing with a baby strapped to her chest counted her steps and then counted them again and the baby's eyes were like dark hidden rooms in a house I would never own.

"You're asking me to trust your feelings about a man with a feather," I said.

"I am." She reached into her bag and took out a small metal thing—a rectangle of matte grey like the band on her spool—and slid it across the table. It did not reflect right. It sucked at reflection like a mouth and made the inside of my eyes itch. "He left this. He said if I showed it to you, you would know it isn't ours. He said it would itch you like a word you misheard that wasn't, in fact, never said."

I did not touch the rectangle. The last time I had laid my hand on a sympathy device brought to me by a version of myself who spoke lightly, I had lost three hours and gained a flowering scar on the root of my spine that my new lover had liked to kiss. I did not have the lover anymore. I still had the scar.

"Where did he say he came from?" I asked.

"He said he fell. He said he was a courier from above. He said the Choir was late and we were going to sing the wrong thing. He said—" She swallowed hard, and when she put her hand to her throat it trembled like a string on a badly tuned instrument. "He said this branch was not an accident. He said it was being grown."

The air in the café tasted like old coins and wet copper, the taste of the inside of a bitten lip and the thin metal smell before a lightning strike. My spool sang one clear note and then went dead-still under my skin as if what it wanted to do was decide that it belonged to someone else.

"You cannot keep this branch," I said. "If you keep it, you will eat us. The bramble is already on the east side."

"You're not listening to me." She reached across, grasped my wrist. Her hand was my hand. It was different like wind the day before a storm. "He said if we cut we sever the seed. He says if we sever the seed, it will look for us elsewhere and graft itself into a place that cannot bear it. He said if we hold, if we anchor, we can pull the seed through with us and put it into quarantine. He said to give you a word."

I closed my eyes. I could feel the city outside, grinding like teeth.

"Say the word," I said.

"Anchorline," she said, and the café rippled sideways.

Someone somewhere cut. In the trunk. In a council I would run to later with my voice cracking. The fountain mothers froze in the act of pouring. The bicycles out on the street elongated and snapped back like rubber being pulled and released, and the pigeons lifted in shuddering squares as if someone had thrown a net at them and then thought better of it. My spool went hot and then green then white.

"Don't cut!" my not-self shouted, standing so fast her chair bit the tile and fell backward. "Don't—"

And then the world did the thing I had trained my body never to let it do: it doubled.

For a moment, there were two coffees in front of me and both of them were mine. One had sugar in it. One didn’t. My right hand had a ring on the ring finger that was not there. It was heavy. It was a narrow band of black carbon with a ridge where two pieces had been fused together after being broken. It was warm like a person. It was the weight of a life.

I looked down, and there were two coffee cups, and in the reflection of one of them the woman I had almost married looked back at me and said, with unbearable patience, you're late.

And then the cups laid into each other and there was only one and it was mine and it was cold.

The café was very quiet. The man on the bicycle was crying silently because his foot could not decide if it had ever touched the ground. The bramble hiss was a scream held between two teeth. Miko's voice slashed into the world through the thread on my wrist, flat and terrified, the only way she ever spoke when she let me know she loved me.

"Do not," she said, "cut. Do not, do not, do not—"

"I didn't," I said, though no one had asked me. My anchor self was looking at me with a pity I had reserved for the very few people I thought I had forgiven. The rectangle on the table hummed like a refrigerator in a house that wasn't connected to electricity but refused to admit it.

"I gave you the word," she said. "Pull when I tell you. Hold until then."

"How long?" I asked, through a mouth that had learned to love a life it could not remember and could not bear the thought of losing.

She took a breath, looked at the ceiling like it kept time, and said, "Until you hear the choir."

"Which one?"

"The one that makes your teeth hurt."

I left my coffee on the table. The ring was still on my finger when I stepped back through the gate. The fountain mothers in our trunk were still. The pigeons were squares of grey in the air, waiting for a signal that wasn't coming. The breath of the city came in short shallow draws. The red thread at my wrist was a shout.

Miko met me at the Treehouse door with her duck kicked crooked. There was blood on her scarf. The blood was mine in a branch where I had cut my finger open on a sympathy device and laughed until I cried because it felt current hard enough to be a body. She grabbed my wayward hand and put her palm over the ring.

"Where did you get this," she said hoarsely. "Do not tell me."

"Do not cut," I said. "Hold."

"We are already holding," she said, the words thick like she had bit them raw. "It is cutting itself against us. The trunk is—"

"I know," I said. The rectangle had burned its line into the wood of the café table in Lace 724. I could feel it. A small grey thing like a word misheard that wasn't. "He said the seed is being grown. He said if we cut, it will go somewhere worse."

"We don't have any worse," Miko said. "We have the city. That's all. I don't have anywhere to put worse."

"You have your toilet," I said, because sometimes you use your words to hold anything like laughter that wants to go black.

She closed her eyes. When she opened them, she looked past me at the park, at the gate beyond, and at the shape of a dozen mornings stacked on top of each other and trying to go through the same door. The duck flailed a bit against her throat like it was trying to fly. She reached up and unpinned it and put it in her pocket.

"Okay," she said. "We don't cut. For one day. We sing. Get me the Choir."

"You get the Choir. I keep my anchor."

"Which is you," she said.

"Which is me," I said.

"And if your anchor walks away?" Miko asked, low, because she had been there the day mine did. "If the one you are standing on refuses to be stood? If Lace 724 turns and puts teeth in you?"

I looked down at the ring. It was warm and it was a weight, the way anything you call home is heavy enough to tug your neck when you leave. In some possible world I could feel like a poem written by procurement. I had decided to be the kind that stayed in the mouth.

"If it bites," I said, "then I bite back. But not with a cut. Not today."

"How then?"

I thought of the boy with the cap and the whistle that only pigeons and people like me could hear. I thought of the rectangular sympathy device on a café table in a world that had been told it was an accident. I thought of a woman who died with her hands inside a spool like she was fixing a throat and of a man with a feather who had said choir like a prayer he didn't want to cheapen.

"With a song," I said. "With whatever is left after you stop believing in cutting."

We stood there, two women with old bronze at their wrists, and the world in our city changed shifts. Somewhere very far above us, beyond the rooftop gardens and the last municipal budget and the soft light polluted clouds, something vast cleared its throat. The bramble hiss ran up my spine like a wire and settled in my teeth until it hurt.

Miko grinned, fierce and scared and beautiful the way anyone is when they jump knowing how hard the ground is.

"That's our queue," she said. "I hate them when they're on time."

"Me too," I said, and the ring on my finger pulsed once in the rhythm of a song I hadn't learned yet that was nevertheless mine. "Me too."

People in the high towns count birthdays like hail. Down in the basins, they count lines in the rock. My ledger is worse than both. I count crossings.

First time I clipped into the Ladder and leaned my weight into a fall of years, I puked copper and saw my own hands trail a fraction behind my wrists. The world stretched, then rolled back like nothing had happened. My mentor laughed until her visor fogged. “That’s the ratewind smelling you,” she said. “You’ll get used to it.”

I never did, not really. It still tastes like rain after striking iron, like mint spooned out of a well.

This morning the tastes are sharp. The sky over the Escarpment is a pale bruise, sun low and glare-crazed on the glass of the pylons. I stand on the grating, a thousand meters of air under my boots, and my harness hums against the bones of my hips. The Ladder climbs and twists along the cliff face in a grid of bridges and tethers and tensile rings anchored into stone older than the concept of a calendar. The drop beside me is not just distance; it is a fall through rate. The higher you climb from the basin, the faster time runs. Up among the high towns, children outgrow their boots in half of a basin year. Down in the low, a bruise can last a decade. In the middle—my place—everything mixes, frays and knits in a way that makes mistakes expensive.

“Adi, you still there?” Bel’s voice crackles in my ear, familiar as my own footsteps. The signal comes with a tiny, fussy delay; she’s perched a terrace above, where the rate difference makes words a little thinner.

“I’m here,” I say. “Just enjoying the view.”

“You always say that when you’re doing something ill-advised.” I can hear her chewing. Bel chews when she worries. “You get the new beatwatch calibrated? They bumped the standard.”

“I have it,” I say, and tap the round coin of the watch on my wrist. It ticks in a rhythm that has nothing to do with heartbeats and everything to do with how many seconds per second my body is experiencing. The Wardens of Rates send down new definitions every season in a rustle of law—the Second Standard, the Crossfall Rules, safety marks painted at precise terraces so we don’t accidentally add or shave too many days off our lives.

“They’re calling for an inspection at Halvor Gate,” Bel says. “You should see the notice.”

Halvor Gate is the high town where my sister lives and where I sleep in a room that never seems to know what year it is—it’s the sun that tells you, not the calendar. Halvor is fast enough to make people born there grow a little wiry with the pace of it. Miri took to that pace. I took to the fall.

“I’ll be back before midday,” I say. “I have an early run to Lent.”

There’s a little hiss that is not a word. Bel has opinions about Lent—the little market town that hangs on a crumpled terrace halfway down the Ladder, where the rate is just slow enough to keep fruit sweet for longer and wages honest for less time.

“You picking up for the Wardens?” she asks.

“Private,” I say. “But legal. Mostly.” I can almost feel her frown over the link. “Tell me the drift numbers anyway.”

She sighs at me. “Don’t make me your planner when you break the Crossfall.”

“I don’t plan to break anything,” I say, and step off the decking.

The kite catches me. It’s a harness, yes, but there are also foils that you flick out with your knees and a spooling drum of anchor line at your hip, and a fan of thin, intelligent fabric that feels the insertion of your weight into the ratewind and knows exactly how to ride that invisible slope. The fall isn’t a waterfall you can see. It’s more like a hum in the light, a tension in the air. The pylons that run the length of the Escarpment gleam with it, constantly measuring, constantly whispering to each other about it; they manage tiny fields and counterfields so we don’t get torn into years and seconds all at once. People like me trust them, or at least pretend to.

I lean, the foil catches, and the world tips. The high-town noise drops away—the clatter of carts, the bark of a dog that will get old this afternoon—and the sound that replaces it is the wheeze of my own breath in my helmet and the soft hiss-snap of the line paying out. My metron, clipped at my shoulder, shows a ribbon of light sliding along a bar. That’s my rate relative to Crossfall Standard. I’m dropping into slow. It feels, paradoxically, like moving into syrup—everything is plush and sweet and my thoughts have edges. If I don’t run my checklist, I forget steps.

Anchor check. Foil check. Beatwatch pulsing, green. If you don’t keep the routine in your head out here, the fall eats it the way riverwater eats stones.

Lent is a skein of platforms strung out over a bulge of sediment, awnings knotted in bright colors so that from a distance it looks like someone spilled paint down the cliff and forgot to scrub. Children doze on the parapets with strings of drying fish, their cheeks round, and the elderly have fewer wrinkles than their years because their years go sly in this rate. The market smells like spilled oil and yeast and old rope. A woman taps an iron nail against the pylon near her stall, listening to the ricochet hum. Some people claim they can hear the difference between a day of fast and a day of slow in that hum. I can’t. I feel it in my gums.

“Adi,” Old Ilar says when he sees me. He sells clocksalt and sugary figs and advice. He was gray thirty years ago, back when I was a mid-rate brat with no harness. He is gray now, but the gray is not the same. It’s strange to know that and not be able to say how. “You running for me today?”

“I’m running for Coldhouse,” I say.

Ilar’s eyebrows go up. “The Wardens could use a courier with sense. That’s news. Cleaning their heads out down there?”

“Private,” I repeat. He snorts.

Coldhouse is what the locals call the municipal store in Lent where anything that will keep better in slow gets tucked away—library paper, seeds, microbes like sleeping cities, legal attestations. Some of Halvor’s archives live down here in Coldhouse capsules, because Halvor’s days are too fast to keep a paper page from going yellow between morning and night. The door is metal, the inside air wrung dry as old bones.

The clerk is a girl with hair braided in a pattern I don’t recognize. She could be fifteen or fifty. That’s the game along the Ladder.

“You Kole?” she asks. Her voice is flat, not unfriendly.

“Ariadne Kole,” I say. She checks my beatwatch, the stamp on my harness. The Wardens insist on stamps for anyone who takes passage across more than one fall a week. I have six stamped into my shoulder strap, each with an embossed date that means different things at different terraces. Half of my life is metal.

She slides a crate onto the counter. It is about the size of a cat sleeping under a blanket. It hums faintly. I press my hand to the lid and feel heat and the whirr of a controlled pump.

“What’s in it?” I ask.

“Woodsleep bees,” she says. “You know the Larchfields up at Halvor had a blight—sugar crystals in the comb, bad queen lines. The Coders up there want fresh stock, and they want it without losing two seasons to rate drift. You’re their answer.”

Woodsleep bees. They breed them down here because their eggs go pliant with slow time, take longer to harden, so the queen lines can be shipped without losing half the brood to the pace up-top. I’ve ferried bees before, felt the faint fuzz of their lives through the box. If you listen long enough, you hear them dream. Not really, of course, but it feels like it.

There is a name scratched into the side of the crate. It is my name.

ARIADNE KOLE — in block letters, the kind a kid uses when practicing authority.

I look at the clerk, who doesn’t look at me. “Funny,” I say.

“Wasn’t me,” she says, and pushes the box toward me with her fingers careful as a surgeon’s. “Message inside, too. Coders’ seal. Hurry’s better than caution.”

We both pretend the bees don’t care about that distinction.

I clip the crate to the chest plate of my harness. The weight settles against me, not heavy but significant. I taste iron again. Outside, the market breathes around me. I stop just beyond the door to test my own superstition: I take a pinch of Ilar’s clocksalt and touch my tongue to it. It’s sweet as a high town noon. That tells me almost nothing except that Ilar’s salt is good. But rituals matter in the fall.

“Bel,” I murmur. “I’m turning. Rate differential?”

Her answer walks toward me through the delay, clumsy in the syrup of Lent. “You sure about that run? Wardens are sniffing. Something about a Gold Cross breach up near the Gate.”

Gold Cross is what we call the safe apex of the Ladder—a rate steep enough that a crossing will age your teeth a little if you do it wrong, but not lethal. Anything above Gold is High Red, and if you hit that without training, you don’t recognize your own reflection when you crawl home.

“What kind of breach?” I say.

“Rumor is an inversion,” Bel says. “Wardens say it’s fine. I say rumor has teeth.”

Inversions are not something we joke about. The pylons hum to keep the gradient smooth; if they hiccup, whole strata will swap their rates like dance partners. In a soft inversion, you just get headaches and a sudden desire to sleep. In a hard inversion, carts roll into terraces and never exactly hit them. A hard inversion can make you a painting on the inside of your bones.

“I’ll be quick,” I tell Bel. “Put coffee on. Miri home?”

“Stayed late. She’ll be under a mountain of blueprints at the office.” There is a pause. “Be careful.”

I step off Lent’s decking into the fall and let the kite take me. The bees vibrate against my chest. The foil snaps in a gust I feel only as pressure in my sinuses. A long time ago—before Hephaestus seeded the pylons with their invisible teeth, before the Wardens had their laws—people tried to walk this cliff. They left scuffs where their boots bit rock and bones where the falls bit back. It is easier now. It is not easy.

Halfway between Lent and the next resting ring up, the hum changes.

It’s not the hum in the pylon—which is steady, a bass note in the flesh. It’s something else, a mismatch so small it could be imagined. My metron ribbon doesn’t move. The beatwatch ticks the same. The hairs on my arms rise anyway.

The kite hiccups. My line spools too fast, then drags. For a fragment of a second, the sky goes the color of blade metal after you pull it out of the fire: that oil-slick sheen that thieves call mercy.

The beatwatch flashes yellow and then green again. My stomach climbs into my throat, then goes home.

It could be nothing. The Ladder is a machine, and machines twitch.

“Bel,” I say. “You see that?”

There is a delay long enough that I measure it in the number of times the bees thrum. “See what?”

“Small inversion. Burp. Between Lent and Terrace Nine.”

“Wardens didn’t flag anything,” she says, but the annoyance is gone from her voice. “You want me to get you a lock at the Nest? You can wait it if you—”

“I have a living crate,” I say, and I am so angry at how my voice shakes that I could burn my tongue to smooth it. I could turn. I could go back to Lent and sit in the Coldhouse’s dry air with my hands around my harness line and wait for some Warden in a clean coat to tell me when it is safe to do my job. But the bees will stale. The Larchfields will go one more season with bad queen lines. Halvor eats seasons like candy. They don’t have many they can spare.

“Call the Nest anyway,” I say, because I’m not stupid. “Tell them I’m riding.”

By the time I reach Terrace Nine, the fall feels normal again, which is worse. The Nest is a Warden facility that looks like a hedgehog: spines and antennas and tiny offices poking outward. The Wardens built one every three terraces the year I turned twelve and then forgot to paint them. The metal is the color of dust. A woman in a black regulation harness with luminous chevrons clipped along her shoulders waits for me on a gantry. Her hair is shaved close. Her belt is starched. Everything about her says new.

“You Kole?” she asks. She doesn’t offer me a hand. The big Wardens don’t. They like their distance.

“Ariadne,” I say. “You called the Nest?”

“We heard your blip,” the Warden says. “Warden Lam. STE-S1 Lam if you have to tangle with forms later. I saw your stamp. Six runs this quarter across Gold. You know the rules.”

“I’m paid to know them,” I say. In the Cage behind her, technicians with poor eyesight on purpose—that’s what I always think when I see Wardens, people with sharp shapes and approximations of faces—stare at screens where my trajectory is a cartoon. “You going to tell me not to move?”

“Are you going to tell me you won’t?” Lam regards the crate on my chest. “Living?”

“Woodsleep bees.”

Her mouth goes sideways. “Convenient. This is why the private licenses are a mistake. Market makes people brave. Market makes people dead.”

“Wardens make people dead too,” I say, and I should bite my tongue, but something about the way the hum changed has stripped off my careful. “When the pylons hiccup.”

The technicians go very still. Lam doesn’t move, but in a different way. “The pylons did not hiccup. There was a minor rate surge. It is within tolerance. The Nest can issue you a lock to hold you here while we—”

“I can’t hold,” I say. “I have to ride.” I think of Miri’s lips pursed over a pencil, of the way she speaks to the high-town stones as if they are animals she could coax. I think of the Larchfields—the fields that look like green lace slapped onto granite, the way their berries smell when you are tired. I think of the name scratched into my crate.

Lam’s eyes tick. “You know the law. We can chain your gear if you—”

“You could,” I say, and we both look at the staircase etched into the cliff face beyond the Nest. Sometimes the Wardens do chain couriers to the metal teeth of the Ladder until the Crossfall is smooth. You stand there and taste metal until the hum goes honest again. I have done it twice. I still wake with my teeth buzzing some nights.

Lam looks at my watch, at my stamps. “You’ve got sense,” she says grudgingly. “Ride. Strap your line through the Guide Two channel. If you feel a change, you hard-anchor and keep your head down. We’ve got a crew sniffing the pylons near the Gate. If there is an inversion, it will be higher than you.”

“What’s at the Gate?” I ask.

She shakes her head. “You know what’s at the Gate.” Money and law and the point where high-town speed goes into a sheen like electricity. “Keep it honest, Kole.”

There’s something in Lam’s eyes when she says my name. Something that makes my shoulders prickle. I don’t know her. She knows me. I file that away next to the taste of steel.

The climb from Nine up to Halvor Gate is a gauntlet of familiar. There are rust streaks in the rock that line up with the way I carry my weight. There is a wind that hits you leftward on the third span and rightward on the sixth. There is a place where the Ladder kinks around an outcrop and you can see, if you look, the long fall all the way down to the basins, where the rate is so slow that you could watch a shadow cross a field for three days and call it altarpiece.

There is a harness curled around a pylon post at Guide Three, melted to the metal.

It’s an old burn, by the look of it. The fabric is glassed, fused. Only the buckle survived, warped into an oval. Someone cleaned the worst of it. Someone then tied a strip of blue rag around the post. That’s what we do for our dead. I don’t know why I didn’t see it yesterday.

I reach to touch the rag and stop my hand just short. It is superstition to touch a blue rag without asking, and the dead are bad with permissions.

A boy sits on the parapet nearby with his legs dangling over nothing. He has a knife in his hand that he is not using to cut anything. He looks at me with eyes that are river-dark. “You Kole,” he says.

“Ariadne,” I say again. He waits. “Yes.”

He flips the knife, catches it by the blade. “She said you’d stop. She said you’d look.”

“Who?” My voice is rope. He flicks his chin at the rag. The bees hum between my ribs. The metal tastes like blood.

“Lady with the scar,” he says. “Left ear. She said tell you that if you see the rag, you should go to the Ladderside Chapel and put a coin in for her, because she forgot money and doesn’t want to be seen staying long. She said you would know which coin.”

It makes no sense, which is how I know it’s for me.

“Okay,” I say, because what else is there. “What’s her name?”

He grins and there is a chip out of his front tooth. “She didn’t say. She never does.”

I peel a small metal circle from the inside of my harness strap. Bel idiot-scrawled on it with a stylus a long time ago: FOR WHEN YOU RUN OUT OF GOD. I keep it there because it feels like luck, not because I think it buys anything. I flip it to the boy. “Buy yourself a fig,” I say.

He regards the coin as if it might change his life and then tucks it behind his ear. “You smell like bees,” he says.

“I’ve been told worse,” I say, and step back into the hum.

The Ladderside Chapel is a cave with a roof someone sweated seven thousand stars into. It’s for the ones who live in the in-between, not high-town gods or basin saints. There’s a dish the size of a soup bowl where people drop coins. The coins are dented and warm. Above the dish, someone carved the words WE STAND IN THE MIDDLE. Someone else scratched YOU ARE MISSING THE POINT.

I fish the “when you run out of god” coin back out of my harness. I don’t know what I am doing until I am doing it. I let it fall.

It rings. In the very tiny space after it rings and before I step back, the sound hangs. It ripples in the air in a way that makes my teeth feel like they are going to crack. The chapel dampens the Ladder’s hum, but this sound cuts through the dampening like light through salt water. For a second the stars in the roof look like they are falling.

Then the sound is gone. A woman coughs behind me, and the rope over the entrance sways. I realize I’ve put my hand over the crate as if to shield the bees from a god’s attention.

When I make it out into open air again, the beatwatch shows green. The metron light is a steady line. The sky is perfect blue. People above me are moving slightly too quick in that way that makes intuitive sense only if you grew up watching your father go down to the basins to haul up apples and come back with them wrinkled and his hair longer by an explanation he cannot offer.

I climb.

Lam is wrong. The inversion is not higher than me. The inversion is a door in the air, and someone opens it when I am exactly between spans, exactly where there is no easy anchor, exactly where I am most afraid of the feeling of not touching anything.

There’s no scream of metal. There is no siren. There is only the sense of a wall where there used to be a corridor. I lean into the kite—and it doesn’t catch the way it should, because I am not moving through a slope anymore. I am moving through a different slope at a different angle, and the sheet of intelligent fabric at my back doesn’t know what to be intelligent about.

The crate bucks against my chest. My harness strap cuts into my collarbone. My line pays out in a gush and then seizes. If it seizes too hard, it will tear out the bolts in my hip plate, and then I will be two things falling at once: a person and a very astonished pile of bees.

“Anchor,” I say, but that is not a word that is useful without a thing to bite into. My hand scrabbles at my belt anyway. The anchor is a fired rope with a smart knot that can find any hole in stone and make it into a fist. There is no stone here. There is only air and the belly-laugh of the Ladder’s hum gone inside out.

I do the stupid thing. I throw the anchor anyway.

It bites. It bites something that is not a hole in stone. It bites a line, one of the Guide’s braided spines, and the knot locks as if it were designed to. The harness whips me sideways, the kite fabric capsizes, and for a second I see the whole Ladder tilt like a drawing someone has just flipped. The pylons blaze. I swear I see them talking to each other—not in words, but in the way black water talks to a dock post when the wind goes wrong.

My back hits iron. The breath is burned out of me, then drags back in with the grit of an unlit match. I taste mint. I taste metal. I taste something like old paper.

The inversion relaxes. I feel it let go the way a hand lets go a sleeve. My beatwatch slaps back into green. The metron ribbon remembers what a straight line is.

I am alive. The bees are alive. The line sings with the kind of tension that means if I move wrong, I’ll go again.

Bel’s voice is a stitch in my head. “Adi? Adi. Say something.”

I don’t say the thing I want to say. I say, “I’m fine. There was a hard-snap at... between Ten and Eleven. It felt like a... like a backwater. Like the field knotted.”

“That’s not possible,” Bel says. I can hear the Nest’s comms in the background of her voice. “Wardens say the Gate is stable.”

“I don’t care what the Wardens say,” I say, and I realize I am laughing. I don’t know if it's because I am so scared, or because I am so happy to be able to be scared. “I just rode the knot.”

“You’re an idiot,” Bel says, and her voice is wet. “You’re a heroic idiot.”

The laughter dies. It dies because I look down at my chest and see, pressed against the bees’ crate, a strip of paper jammed into the edge where the lid meets the box. I didn’t see it before. It wasn’t there when I left the Coldhouse, because I would have felt it. I pull it free with fingers that feel like other people’s. It is a cheap note, a bit of thin, crisp wood-pulp that hasn’t had the benefit of slow. The letters go wobbly when the sweat from my gloves spreads.

Ariadne, it says. Do not take this up.

Nobody signs it. There is a brown smear where a thumb pulled bluntly away from ink, a smudged half moon.

I look at the bees. I look at the sky. I look back down into the place where the fall just knotted.

“Bel,” I say. “I have a problem.”

“You think?” she says, and there is a thump like someone’s headset hitting a table, and then a new voice slides across the link, slick as oil.

“Kole. Warden Lam. You hold?” She doesn’t wait for my yes. “Gate’s flagging. We have interference. Keep your head where it is. There’s an event at Halvor. Evacuation orders. You know anyone at the Coders’ Hall?”

“My sister works four doors down,” I say. It takes everything in me not to swing the line and make for the Gate like a shot arrow.

“Then you listen to me,” Lam says. “There is no time for heroics. The pylons are singing a song I don't like. Stay pinned until we—”

The link snaps. Not a tidy click. Not the hiss of a normal cut. It is a sound like cloth tearing from throat to belly.

Silence steps into my ear.

The hum is loud as a storm. The bees are a tiny, private thunder against my sternum. In the distance, toward the Gate, a glitter of scaffolds and sky-bridges that is my birthright flexes once, as if someone took a breath wrong.

I put my hand on the crate like the pressure of my palm could do anything in a world where years blow past like dandelion seeds.

In the first season of my life, my mother taught me to count the rungs on the Ladder between our house and the market so I wouldn’t get lost in days. I counted so well that when she died between one crossing and the next, I counted on anyway. The numbers lined up. The stone didn’t move beneath my feet. What changed were the sentences people used to talk about her. Past tense smuggled itself in with milk and bread.

Do not take this up, the note says.

My fingers make a fist around a paper that was not there before, ink that smells like the inside of a chapel.

“Bel,” I say to the silence. “Miri.”

I pull the anchor tight like it is a prayer. I look up at the Gate and down at the knot. If I go up, I climb into fast time and maybe into a falling city. If I go down, I carry the bees into the place where someone put a message for me that shouldn’t have been put.

The fall breathes on my teeth. The Ladder hums its two notes. The pylons are lit like wet bones with ghosts inside.

I choose, and the choice is a kind of gravity all its own.

The universe had a heartbeat if you knew how to listen.

Mira Sen leaned back in her chair and let it thrum through her bones. On the wall, the array’s output drifted in sheets of pale blue, long-breathed troughs sweeping under bright pinpricks where distant black holes had waltzed jaw to jaw, somewhere that wasn’t here and some time that wasn’t now. The data was text and numbers and vector fields if you wanted it to be, but the good listeners always ran a translator in their skulls and turned it into sound. Her implants rendered spacetime strain as a soft garden of tones, the bass of the cosmic background like the breath of a sleeping animal and the treble prickles of micrometeoroids flashing across the lattice like insects in summer.

The room smelled faintly of metal and citrus cleanser. A strip of condensation beaded along the inside of the viewport in a straight, dutiful line. Beyond, the dark was comfortingly black. The Far Array was a thin spray of infrastructure looped through the outer system like a cobweb, its nodes anchored to nothing but mathematics and tensile faith.

It was third shift, which meant the station was quiet enough that the hum of the coolant pumps felt conversational. The other tech on the floor, Kaito, had fallen asleep with his face pressed into a nest of printed schematics. His breath fogged the mat in a slow metronome. He kept promising to print less; every week the promised less became a different heap.

Mira pulled a blanket over his shoulders and slid his stylus out from under his cheek. His implant murmured a question into her inner ear—soft chime, a purple note—then went back to streaming the universe’s heartbeat.

The Authority liked to call them analysts. The crew called themselves tidelisters. Between stars there are tides, the slow flexing and sighing as mass moves through the fabric. You learned to read them. You learned to tell the difference between a whale song and a bootprint. Somewhere in the middle of the last century—Mira had been an infant—the Continuity Authority had declared ungated folding a Class-One offense. The war that followed had a dozen names, most of them poetic and useless. People who hadn’t been there liked to argue labels. People who had didn’t speak much about it at all.

After the Great Severance—she hated that one in particular—they built arrays like this and hung them in the dark, and people like Mira learned to listen for the things you weren’t supposed to do to space.

She sipped cold coffee. It tasted like a penny. She tapped a heel against the underside of her console to stay awake. Across the room, the status boards kept a faint green insistence, thousands of lines full of okay. Somewhere two decks down, a maintenance drone ticked. A dehumidifier sighed. The universe went on humming.

Out in the black, a small object passed through one of their interferometer arms at too high a relative velocity, and the hardware bickered for a fraction of a second. Mira whispered to the console and smoothed it out. She liked this, the feeling of extraneous panic settling back into a steady beat under her hand. The array was big and temperamental and as alive as anything designed by people, and it liked to be petted.

Kaito snuffled, turned his face the other way on his papers, and muttered something about nautiloids. Mira smiled. The implant was filling her with a library of noise. A pair of neutron stars had collided thirty million years ago and their ghost was still chasing itself past the edges of her awareness; closer to home, a mining rig on a misaligned trajectory somewhere in the belt was making the interference pattern thrum weirdly every twelve seconds. She filed a mark with Traffic to tell them. The message went out along a beam and would reach them in nine minutes.

For a little while there was nothing unusual at all, and she let the world go fuzzy around her and thought about the taste of oranges.

Oranges, because sometimes the noise would pull up a memory with no mercy. She had been nine and sticky with juice and there had been a song. No, not a song. Humming. A pattern carried in breath and vibration. She had been under a lift cradle with her hands full of screws she wasn’t supposed to have, and above her someone had been coaxing mathematics into place, and the hiss of the anti-laser and the whine of the coil had woven into it and made a fabric she could still feel in her teeth.

It was a stupid thing to remember. Or not stupid, just irrelevant to a life that mostly consisted of telling the difference between whale songs and bootprints. She pushed her thumb against the inside of her right wrist, a habit she had when the old memory currents ran too hard. The skin there was smooth and a little paler than the rest; the Authority didn’t let you keep jewelry at your console station, but you could keep the ghosts of habits that used to involve rings.

The implant pinged again, purple edging toward indigo. Mira sat up.

“Not now,” she told the universe, softly, which never helped but always made her feel better.

A bootprint, if it was from a fold without a regulator, had a contour all its own. It was not the smooth, auditable rising of amplitude you saw when something passed through one of the Authority’s sanctioned gates. It was an ugly thing, a jagged tug on the interference fringes, like a hand grabbing a tablecloth. It often came with incorrect symmetry, tremors where the algorithm failed to match its own output. The Authority taught you the obvious signatures first—spikes, dephasing—and then the subtle ones. She had learned the subtle most quickly. Her supervisor had said, a little unkindly because he had not slept much, that there were two kinds of listeners: those who chased big fish and those who liked the minnows. She had replied that a minnow was still an organism.

She pulled the anomaly into her personal channel and let it expand, an eddy that had been a rumor on the baseline resolving into itself. The pattern didn’t trip the board’s automatic alarms; it was too small, too polite. But it was there.

“Kaito,” she said softly. “Hey. Kai.”

He snored in direct defiance.

Mira leaned over him and poked the tiny muscle at the base of his skull just hard enough to wake him without making him jerk. Kaito flailed anyway, flung up a hand, blinked. “What?”

“Listen.”

He groaned, pulled the blanket over his mouth, and groaned again. He put two fingers to his temple and synced to her feed. His eyes unfocused. “Huh,” he said. “You got a freighter doing something illegal?”

Mira shook her head. The pattern was too clean and too personal. It had that patience she associated with craftspeople. An ungated fold had to destroy its own mistakes quickly or else the local metric twisted and started to chew on itself. Sloppy work left scars. This was…gentle.

“Artifact,” she said, almost hoping it was. “Interference from the mining rig? Did Traffic ping you back?”

“Not yet,” Kaito said. He pushed himself into a sitting position with the same lack of grace he’d used to fall asleep. He was younger than her by seven years and his beard was always either too short or too long. He blinked, squinted, and then had the nerve to sigh contentedly. “The background is particularly lovely tonight.”

“Headline,” Mira said. “Please.”

“Right.” He scratched his cheek thoughtfully. “It’s very low amplitude.” He dragged the wave into three dimensions on his own screen and stacked it against qualifiers one, two, three. “No spectral spikes like you’d expect for a brute force. No sloppy tears. It’s…weird. Like someone’s taking a partial derivative with their fingers.”

“Don’t say that,” Mira said. “Our components are superstitious.”

He grinned. “We’re lucky. They like you.”

“Don’t invoke luck either.”

She sank back into the sound. The wave had a total duration of 0.31 seconds. It teased the array rather than pulling on it. It had lobes where it shouldn’t. It had a tiny asymmetry that made her tongue itch.

She isolated the asymmetry. Then she did the thing she did when the data felt like it had a soul: she hummed to it.

“Are you singing?” Kaito asked.

“Syncopation test,” she said.

“You’re singing.”

She was. Her voice was very quiet. The array’s translation, the little flicker of the anomaly, and the hum of the machines under the floor braided together and made a line. She cleared her throat and took the line apart and put it back together. She inverted it. She smoothed and stepped the lobe. She took out the background and the rig’s twelve-second mischief. She watched the anomaly increase relative amplitude by a fraction; that made no sense. It should not respond. She told herself she’d misinterpreted the way the visualization shifted scale.

She hummed the old pattern without meaning to, the one that had sat under an engine cradle and smelled like oranges and oil.

Kaito looked up at the ceiling as if he might see the physics up there. “Are we getting echo?”

Mira wasn’t listening to him. Her skin had gone cold.

“Give me the Authority’s gate catalog,” she said. “All of them.”

“It’s right there,” Kaito said, and highlighted it on her screen. He looked at her. “Hey. You’re pale.”

She took all the registered gate signatures; she subtracted them. She took their schedule; she subtracted it. She took the fifteen most recent illegal fold attempts on record, all of them broken and half-crushed and light-years away; she subtracted them. The anomaly remained. It did not care what she asked it to be.

She took a breath and pushed every piece of music she’d ever known into the back of her throat. She hummed anyway, because she couldn’t not, because there are behaviors that climb out of you without asking.

The pattern on the screen reached up and drew a line through her hum.

No, not possible. She adjusted for lag. Light took time. Space had an opinion about how quickly information could move. What she was hearing had happened hours ago, properly speaking. It did not matter. It was happening to her now.

On the floor, Kaito’s foot bounced. “Is it…is it a handshake?”

“No one handshakes a listening array,” she said. “We’re not supposed to have hands.”

He spread his arms. “Tell that to whoever just shook you.”

Her implants blazed white. Not alarm. Recognition. The Authority, to keep its machines and its humans in polite conversation with one another, allowed a tiny set of personal libraries to be loaded into station systems. Mira’s library was small and she’d embarrassed herself when she’d asked for it; the intake psytech had raised a brow and told her that was a peculiar request. It was a recording of a woman’s humming, low and careful, unadorned by words.

Her mother’s hum had a stumble in it three notes in, a tiny catch where she’d broken a tooth and never had it replaced, not out of poverty but out of superstition. That catch cut the third tone by an irrational fraction and made a little lean-to where there shouldn’t have been one, and the little lean-to was the place nine-year-old Mira had died under that engine cradle because she’d fallen in love with it and then everything else had been downhill.

“Mira?” Kaito said, more softly. “Hey. Hey.”

She would not cry at her console. That was a rule. She had not written it down. You only needed to write down rules when you didn’t keep them. “Run a private match,” she said, and pushed the hum file into the anomaly with the same careful motions she would use to coax a shy animal out from under a bench. The console blinked once. The match percentage floated up like a bruise.

Ninety-three point four.

Kaito’s eyebrows jumped. “Huh,” he said, because he was tactful. “Do you…want me to wake Voss?”

“In a second,” she said.

There were a dozen ways to fake a match. People did it all the time; the Authority’s threat models were full of eerie mimicries designed to set off exactly this kind of psychological trap. She’d been lectured, at length, about what would happen if someone tried to use her to get a better reaction time out of a listening station. The Authority had invested heavily in algorithms that could tell whether your hands had started shaking and adjust the threshold of when something counted as an emergency accordingly. The algorithms were sometimes wrong. So were people. Together they hoped to make a reasonable compromise of being less wrong.

She adjusted for those known traps. The percentage sharpened, dropped, rose. Ninety-one point nine. Ninety-four point two. Ninety-three point four again, as if being precise didn’t interest it overly much.

Her mother had died on a tarmac a long time ago. The Authority had said so. The Authority had given her the hum and called it evidence and therapy both. They’d used simple words for a messy thing. They’d said a crash. They’d said a protest the morning after. Mira had not gone. She’d been nine. The smell of oranges and oil had been replaced with the antiseptic of the Authority’s offices and the smell of sleep-deprived official sympathy.

Mira pinched the bridge of her nose until her head hurt.

Kaito’s voice came from a long way off. “I’m going to wake Voss.”

“Wait,” she said sharply enough that he flinched. She took a breath. “Not yet. Let me—if it’s a fake I can catch it.”

He hesitated. The station’s ethics required that if one operator’s judgment was impaired the other one take the chair. He knew that. She knew that he knew. The decision sat between them with its legs dangling.

“You have thirty seconds,” he said eventually, and leaned back to pretend he had stepped away without moving.

That was generous and also the maximum anyone could give without lying. Thirty seconds, then, to decide whether to call the Authority and let the anomaly go into the long, grinding machinery of other people’s decisions. Thirty seconds to listen to the way the wave turned on itself.

She told the station to cease routine data sharing for ten seconds for maintenance. It obeyed. The world on the board turned a shade less green. Somewhere, a process spawned a note that would go into a log and be read by a tired minor official in fifty minutes. She took the anomaly apart and found what she’d felt coming. It wasn’t a fold event by itself. It was at an angle to one.

Her mother hadn’t been an engineer of gates. She’d been a maker of little things. She’d crafted partials. The Authority called them catalysts, little packets of instruction that might help a fold happen properly—more smoothly, with less damage to the metric. They were not supposed to be used without the Authority’s stamp. The problem with making little things is that you can sneak them into big systems.

The anomaly contained a catalyst. It was a strange, tiny, folded shape of noise designed to unfold exactly one way when it met the tug of a particular larger event. It wasn’t the event itself. It was what you sent ahead to tell the event how to be gentle.

The catalyst was keyed. The key was a pattern. The pattern was a hum.

It had her name in it, too.

Not spoken. Not written. Not in any strict human way. It surfaced like a fish flashing its belly white for a fraction. She recognized it where it lived in mathematics: the old game she used to play with vectors, the silly one with vocabulary they never used in the ear, where you could fold letters out of phase. An M, made of a slope and a return. An I with its dot dragged an unacceptable distance to the left. An R, refusing to be symmetrical. An A, refusing to be an A at all. Childish. Too much ambition in the constraint. Her mother had been unable to keep art out of math and math out of music. Mira had been unable to keep any of it out of anything else since.

Her thirty seconds were up. Kaito stuck his hands in the pockets of his cardigan like it might anchor him. “Mira.”

“It’s not an event,” she said, and heard her own voice like it belonged to someone else. “It’s a seed.”

“A what?”

“A seeding packet,” she said. “From—someone with access to…look.” She pulled the shape into transparency and rotated it so he could see the ghost of the larger thing it wanted to attach to. The predicted seeds of stress lined up like teeth. “It’s not going to rip. If it completes, it’ll do it clean. If it completes.”

Kaito was pale, too. “Which means somebody is about to do something they are not permitted to do.”

“Yes,” she said. “Or already did. Four hours ago.”

He drew a breath through his teeth. “We have to wake Voss.”

“We will,” she said. “I just. The thing’s addressed to me.”

He stared at her. Then he looked at the screen. Then he said something under his breath in a language she didn’t know, very softly, without any heat. He tapped the comm on his wrist. “Supervisor Voss to Array floor. Priority Amber.”

She heard more than saw Voss’s response: a murmur of gruff, a scraping of chair. He would arrive in eighty seconds, give or take. She had eighty seconds to decide whether to do something very stupid or something boring and correct.

Her hand trembled, a little. She clenched it and hated that Kaito might see, and then hated herself for caring about his seeing more than the thing that had made her hand tremble to begin with.

She opened the catalyst fully.

It unrolled like a paper purse.

The Authority did not like you to open things addressed to you if those things came wrapped in the fabric of spacetime, for what might be an intuitive set of reasons. Every nerve in her body agreed. Something about it felt like stepping into a room she had already spent a life in and finding all the furniture moved by a fraction of an inch.

A voice spilled out, at least that was the simplest way to think of it, riding on the same hum that had wrapped around nine-year-old Mira’s bones while hardware sang above her. No words. She thought there should have been, briefly fell in love with the idea that there might be, but no. A sequence of notes, a measurable array of strains, mapped to a coordinate set and a time and a direction and a set of conditions. The conditions were the worst part. They were there like a dare.

She read what wasn’t meant for anyone else. She read the place. She saw the time: nineteen hours from now. She saw the gate it wanted to cowl itself under, dead and shuttered since before she’d been tall enough to change a light bulb. She saw the parenthesis in the conditions: only if you come.

As if a fold would care about her presence. As if the metric would know that a medium-sized woman with scars on her right hand had decided or not decided. It was nonsense. You could make seeds robust against error or fragile and easily quenched. This was something in between, not error correction but intention. It called to a person who might be present at a certain place and time and gave up a certain behavior—constrained itself as a courtesy—if that person was not there.

Nineteen hours. There were protocols for what to do with announcements like that. The Authority would send a team to the old gate, they’d pack it with quenching mass, they’d wait with all the grim competence the Authority had always had, and if anyone tried to thread there they’d find themselves pushing through salted air.

If the person who had built the seed had wanted a clean fold, she had given the Authority all the time it needed to make sure there wasn’t one.

It didn’t fit. It didn’t fit and that was what made it hers.

Her mother, the Authority had told her, had been a skilled engineer with a quaint set of ideas about decentralization and public goods and the ethics of how big you were allowed to make your tools. She had died for the quarrel between people who wanted big tools and people who wanted small ones. That had been a long time ago.

“Mira,” Kaito said, very carefully. “What are you seeing?”

“A location,” she said. “The old Sable Gate.”

Four decks down, Voss’s boots hit the ladder too fast and rang. “Are you joking?” Kaito said.

“It’s there,” she said.

“The Sable is dead,” he said. “It’s ash.”

“It’s ash if you believe Authority press releases,” she said, and then “I’m sorry,” because it wasn’t fair to say it like that to him, because it made her sound like a person who put herself on one side of a line and him on the other, which were just cartoons people used so they didn’t have to stare at the way things really shook.

Voss arrived with his collar half-buttoned and his hair making subtle comments about the last time he had found a mirror. He looked at them both and then at the screens. His jaw tightened. “What did you hold,” he asked without saying good morning, which was fair, because good mornings were lies in their place and time.

Mira stood. “Sir, I—”

He took their feed without asking. He didn’t have to. He had been a listener when Mira’s mother was still alive. There were scars on his hands you could only get from soldering in gloves you couldn’t afford to break. He listened for five heartbeats and then said, quietly, “Who?”

“I don’t know,” she said, which was true and not.

He closed his eyes, lifted one hand, and then dropped it. He looked older every time she saw him. He was not yet fifty. He had the eyes of a tired grandfather. “You pulled data sharing.”

“Ten seconds,” she said. “We’re resynchronized. I added a note to maintenance so we don’t look like we’re hiding. It was within discretionary threshold—”

“I’m not here to count ticks,” he said, not unkindly. His gaze moved to Kaito for a fraction. Kaito put his palms up. “I told her to wake you,” he said.

Voss scruffed his hair, stared at the Sable coordinates, and swore in a language Mira did know because he had taught her the words himself. “We call it,” he said. “That’s the law. We call it and they decide. I can lose a stripe for waiting. I can sleep at night for waiting. I’ve lost sleep enough other ways.”

He was right. That was the problem with him.

“Sir,” Mira said, and stopped. The station’s lights made a moody pale oblong on the floor. She put her foot in it. She took it out again. “Sir. It’s addressed to me. It—”

“To you?” His voice cracked on the last word and got vicious with restraint. “Good. Then you get a broom and you sweep your name off it because the last thing any of us are is special.”

Her mouth tasted like copper. She nodded.

Voss turned to the comm and spoke the protocol words that woke up the Authority sleepers and made them walk to their ancient switches. Amber to Red. Red to Black. The message sent itself as if it had been waiting all along. Far away, the Continuity Authority rolled over and opened one eye.

Mira stood still enough to feel the vibration of her heart against the bones of her wrists. Kaito whispered, “You did the right—” and then didn’t finish it because he had been taught not to lie where it mattered.

The reply came faster than it should have. Not seconds—nothing human could travel that way—but faster than bureaucracy ordinarily allowed. The Authority had already been awake. The Authority had been listening, too. Of course they had.

Proceed to Sable Gate, said the message, auxiliary embers to follow. Do not engage beyond observation. Do not allow local interference. Report all anomalies. She saw Voss count heads and resources and decide whether he had to pretend to be surprised for their sake. What he settled on was grim amusement, which is a cousin to despair. “They’ll send the quench,” he said. “We can beat them there in thirteen hours if I take the express.”

“She wants me there,” Mira said before she could stop herself.

He looked at her like a man trying to decide between believing in the shape of his hands and believing in ghosts. “She?” he repeated, very softly.

Mira swallowed. Her voice went away and refused to return. She lifted one shoulder. She could feel the line under the floor where the old cable trunk ran, the tiny crow-hops of power crossing connectors. She could feel the thread she wasn’t supposed to touch.

Voss shut his eyes. When he opened them they were made of the same metal as the rest of him. “You’re not family to me,” he said. “You’re a station operator. You keep that in your mouth if you can. If you can’t, you call me and I’ll put it there for you.”

“I hear you,” she said.

“And if whoever wrote that seed thinks she can pull my people into her story because she wrote a clever hum,” he said, almost gently, “then she’s not as smart as she thinks and nothing we do here makes any difference.”

Kaito, reckless in the way of people who do equations for people who are bleeding and think the arithmetic matters more at the moment than the blood, said, “What if it does?”

Voss stared at him; then he pinched the bridge of his nose in eerie mimicry of Mira and said, “Pack a bag,” with the resignation of a man who already knew he was going to put too much on too few bones because the better men had died thirty years ago and still expected him to get up on time. “Sen, you’re with me. We’re going to go look at a dead thing.”

Mira nodded and tried not to let the relief show too nakedly. The feeling was not honorable. People who made good rules did not let their hearts leap at the chance to break them in a neat way.

They had thirteen hours on the express and then nineteen hours and then the end of a line. Maybe the Authority would pack the Sable with salt before anyone could try anything. Maybe this was a trap so petty it would only burn three of them and a few kilograms of equipment and nothing else.

She shut down her console. She left a note in the maintenance log that would read as her trying to be good. She took the blanket off Kaito’s shoulders and folded it into a square she hoped looked like care rather than farewell. She thought about oranges again. She wished she hadn’t.

As she followed Voss out, her implant flared one last color, a soft gold she had never seen it use. The anomaly had tired itself out; its ghost made a shape on the baseline like a sleep-warmed pillow. The last fold of the seed unrolled at a lazy angle and showed her something she hadn’t expected: a second coordinate set, a second time, a cheat tucked under the obvious candy. It was smaller. It was not for machines.

It was a place you could walk if you went to the old Sable observation deck and took the stairs you were not supposed to take and opened a door that a certain maintenance code held closed. It was a niche. It was the space under a lift cradle of a particular vintage that had been bolted into the observation deck for tourists back when the Authority had allowed tourists to see what they did to the world. It was, in plain insult, the only place the old smell might still be.

She wasn’t special. She was a vector. The difference mattered and didn’t.

“Nineteen hours,” Voss said, as the lift took them away from their quiet hums. “Hope you like getting dressed in a hurry.”

She smiled a little because you always told a story about yourself as you fell. You could make yourself look like a reasonable person and maybe, if you practiced it enough, you would be. “I brought a toothbrush,” she said.

He snorted. Kaito made a face. The elevator hurtled.

The array kept listening. The universe never stopped. Under the floor, under the skin, there was a hum almost too soft to feel: a person’s voice, the ghost of it, the way mathematics remembers the shape of the hands that made it, the angle of the head as she had leaned down and breathed and coaxed and said without words that the trajectory of a life was a thing you could tilt if you were careful and a little unreasonable.

Mira did not know whether she would be careful. She was certain of the other part. She thought that should count for something. Outside the viewport the dark had one bright pinprick. It had always had that pinprick. It would keep it when she was gone.

It was a good trick, being small and not stopping. It was the only trick anyone had ever had.

Chapter One: The Street That Thinned

The street thinned at 09:13, not with fog, but with the subtraction of one of its angles. At least, that’s how Mara’s brain described the first ripple—a subtle, heart-sick feeling that the geometry of the day had buckled. She was two blocks away when the alert chimed, en route with a lukewarm breakfast bun clenched between her teeth and her anchor pack already digging a familiar groove into her shoulder.

“Class C crossfade, Sable District tram stop at Fawn and River,” Kestrel said in her ear. The dispatcher's voice always sounded like it came from a room where things were stacked neatly. “Confirmed reports of partial overlays and at least one body interphase. All units respond.”

“Unit Beta-Four responding,” Mara said, swallowing the bun and tossing the wrapper into a bin that decided, fleetingly, to be a piece of twisted bronze before it remembered being plastic. She jogged into a lope, boot soles slapping wet pavement. It had rained before dawn, and puddles showed two kinds of sky—one gray, one a fractured hummingbird blue that didn’t belong to the weather there.

Everyone thought crossfades looked spectacular on the feeds—pearlescent veils, strange architectures breathing through your own—but what you noticed when you worked them wasn’t beauty. It was the smell. It smelled like a power station nested inside old books and rain-rotted wood, an ozone tang undercut with the sweet rot of dislocated time. It smelled wrong, like a hospital corridor in a cathedral.

By the time she turned onto Fawn, the shimmer was visible. Air knit with a filmy density that ate detail. You could stare through it and feel your eyes give up, your brain too sensible to commit to any one version of a corner, a roofline, a tram that had never run on this track. People were slowed at the perimeter, a knot of onlookers, some cautious, some idiots already reaching with their phones to film their own deaths.

“Ishaan?” she said as she wove through them. “You on my six?”

“Three minutes out,” came Ishaan's voice, breathless. He always sounded like laughter was something he was saving for later. “Got hung up by a delivery bot deciding to be a pond. Don’t start without me.”

She would start without him. Class Cs were the worst kind—long enough to do damage, not long enough for the edges to settle. Mara muscle-memory scanned her kit in her mind: tethers and sinks, a skein spool with four hundred meters of threadable constant, pulse beacons, a handful of splints, two injector pens, foldable goggles. She didn’t believe in personal lucky charms, not since she’d watched a man’s silver stag pin become a spring-loaded nightmare and take off half his ear, but she kept her anchor coin in the small front pocket anyway. Thin, palm-sized, etched with tidal lines. She had won it by passing the municipal interference exam on her first try, a record for Sable District. It wasn’t luck, she told herself. It was weight. Every tool needed a counterweight.

“Beta-Four on site,” she told Kestrel, stepping into the pale veil.

The world changed temperature. It was like walking through a draft from a cavern; heat stripped from her skin and left every hair on her arms prickled. Old training slid into place. She saw the tram stop canopy stutter between its actual canopy and something like an iron gazebo with filigreed vines. She saw flagstones inlaid where concrete ought to be. She saw five people who were not from this city at all. They were dripping, dressed in long coats that seemed made of braids, faces turned toward her with that same dazed startlement she recognized from her own side—the beached fish look of a brain tugged into a place it had no map for.

“Hey!" she barked to the perimeter. The old part of her that had been a teenage lifeguard woke up and took control of her throat. “Back. Everyone back. You, the scarf, drop the drink. If it crossfonts you, it’s going to fuse to your hand. You’ll never get the smell off.”

The woman with the scarf laughed a shaky laugh and obeyed. The cup was full of something that reflected three different colors in bands. It wasn’t the coffee she’d bought.

Mara squinted past the veil. The overlays had done something to the tram’s power rail—she saw spitting lights trying to be different voltages at once. A child cried. The sound came skittering across like a marble. She followed it with her body, not her eyes, trusting where the hairs on her arms pulled.

There. To the right of the bench where old Mr. Lant re-read the same paperback every morning. There was a corridor, a hallway that was not hallway-shaped in their world, and in it, a child with a mop of hair and a red jacket screaming quietly. Some people knew how to scream loud. Some made sounds very deliberately, as if they were counting each one.

“Hey, little comet,” she said, kneeling to bring her face down close to the level where the overlay turned to a watery misalignment. Her voice sounded like it had been recorded a second ago and played back. “You want to come with me?”

The child’s eyes were the wrong gray. They looked like polished fish stones. He stared behind her, through her, at the place where her back was in an alternate, not at her actual face at all. Across the threshold, the air had the quality of a lens dipped into sugar syrup.

“Don’t cross without anchor,” Kestrel snapped into her ear. “Read me, Beta-Four?”

“Reading you,” she said, even while her left hand was already on her anchor coin. The coin was cool and pleasant, perfectly boring. She slid it from the pocket, into her palm, and pressed two sink nails between her fingers in the other hand. Sinks were ugly—stubby rods that smelled faintly of vinegar, heavy with dense mass and equations locked in by an engineer she’d never meet.

She set one sink nail into the tram platform, felt it bite. For a second, it didn’t want to be there. It wanted to be an idea of a nail, a variable. Then it clicked into a more satisfying version, hard reality pinning down like a thumb on a jumping line.

“Thread out,” she said. The skein spool hummed against her thigh. She thumbed it, and an almost invisible strand uncoiled, glistening like breath in winter. The thread carried a calibrated constant—something that said here is here—and in training they taught you not to think about the way “constant” was a word that sounded arrogant. You fed it into the air and hoped the world agreed.

She bounced the thread off the sink, wove it between her fingers, threw a loop into the veil, and felt the tug when the other side took it. That was the weirdest part, always: that you could feel when a place accepted your idea of it. It was a tug not just on the thread but in the back of her molars, a small ache as if she had bitten down on hard candy.

“Listen,” she said to the child. “I’m going to throw you a line. When it lands in your hand, close your fingers and do not let go. Can you do that?”

The child blinked. “Are you supposed to be blue?” he asked, perfectly polite.

Mara didn’t look at her own hands. “Sure,” she said. She looped the thread gently through the veil, used the coin to weight the throw. The coin vanished differently than other things when it crossed. It slipped with a tiny sigh, like a parent sinking into a chair.

The child caught the loop badly, on his wrist. Mara wrapped the line back around, made another loop, all while the veil flickered and the filigreed gazebo tried to become real. The thread thrummed once, hard. Someone on the other side, a woman with coffee-colored skin and braids coiled into a crown, reached to steady the child, then looked up at Mara. Her mouth shaped a word: not help but here.

Don’t engage, they taught. Cross-residents weren’t your responsibility. They weren’t your liability insurance. They weren’t survivors you could tally in your report. The city had decided not to count them, because counting a thing meant admitting it mattered.

Mara tugged. The boy stumbled forward, then sideways, and then through. It was like watching birth. He popped into their air and sucked it like a fish does, desperate and angry. The thread went slack. The anchor coin slapped the top of the tram bench and spun to a stop with a chime that sounded like a dropped spoon. For a second, the coin’s etching was not her coin’s etching—the tidal lines were deeper, and there was a scratch across the face that she didn’t recognize.

“Nice catch,” Ishaan said, sliding into position beside her. He dropped his backpack like it had insulted him and took a knee, eyes already tracking the saturation. He reached to steady the boy, and the boy flinched away, then flinched toward him as the veil breathed.

“Watch the rail,” Mara said. Sparks were throwing interesting shadows. And there, to the left, the worst thing—someone had turned into the wrong material. A man, fused at the hip to one of the iron filigree struts. His pants were doing their best to be both denim and some kind of harness. He wasn’t bleeding because whatever he was bleeding into wasn’t a place where blood had the right rules.

“Sir,” Mara said softly, finding his eyes. “Sir, my name is Mara, I’m with Interphase Response, we’re going to get you loose.”

His mouth chattered. She couldn’t tell if he was cold or if his jaw was trying to be two positions at the same time. She wanted to put her hand on his cheek, to ground him like you ground a skittery horse, but her hand might be not-hand by the time it reached his face.

“I’m okay,” he whispered, and then louder, as if louder would make it true, “I’m okay.”

“We need a cut,” Ishaan said, eyeing the joint where iron and denim and personhood met. He pulled the micro-saw from his pack, thumbed it on. It sang a disagreeable song. “If I take it at ten degrees—”

“Don’t. The angle wants to be twenty-three right now.” She felt the angle the way she felt weather, pressure in her sinuses. She shifted, got her shoulder under his, and Isaac—no, not Isaac, she didn’t know his name yet; he was always Isaac in her head until she learned his real name—put his weight onto her without meaning to, so light, so grateful.

“Two minutes left on saturation,” Kestrel said. “Beta-Four, do you have bodies? I have reports from perimeter of—”

“We’ve got one extracted minor, one partial interphase, three cross-residents present. Ishaan is cutting.”

“Copy. Keep the beam tight.” Kestrel didn’t say don’t get attached. She didn’t need to.

Mara took a breath, smelled the other place again. It wasn’t just ozone and paper. It was something like spices burning, like orange peel and cloves and resin. Not this neighborhood’s smell. In the overlay, the tram was something else—a rain shelter for a market maybe. She heard, weirdly, the sound of metal bells. She let the thread in her left hand anchor her to her own place, fed a second strand out with her right, stitching reality with little, smug movements.

The man fused to the strut gagged. The gag sounded too loud and then snapped to be too quiet. His eyes rolled and for a second, they looked like her father’s.

That was when she saw her mother.

It was not her mother. It was a woman who had her mother’s height and the exact same way of holding her jaw when she was watching a pot boil and pretending not to be impatient. She stood on the other side of the veil under the iron gazebo, wearing a coat made of the braided fabric and a scarf the color of copper pennies. She held a paper bag in both hands. She saw Mara and something like recognition flared across her face—surprise that someone had not died after all.

Mara’s hands didn’t move. If she moved, she would throw everything off. She simply let herself have a heartbeat that hurt so much it had to be funny later. The copper-scarfed woman took a step forward, as though to give Mara the bag.

“Don’t,” Mara said aloud, to the air, to herself. Her mother had died in an entirely boring way when Mara was nineteen, failing organ by organ over seventeen months, and those months had been long enough to teach everything there was to learn about carrying on. Crossfades did not get to rewrite those lessons.

Ishaan’s saw bit through the wrong iron. It whined. The man cried out, and the sound helped Mara. She focused on the part where pain meant the body was feeling one version of itself. She swung the thread high, looped it and anchored it again. The tug in her molars went sugary and then clean.

“Saturation down,” Kestrel said. “We’re at fifteen percent, holding at nine and sliding.”

The veil thinned. It sucked back the way frost retreats in a sunny patch, reluctantly. The tram stop remembered its canopy. The filigree iron sighed out. The bells stopped. The copper-scarfed woman—who was not her mother—blinked out mid-breath. The child at Mara’s side lost interest in everything and began to cry in relief and the devastation of anticlimax, which sounded exactly the same.
