The coin lay on the bench where it had spun. Mara leashed it with two fingers as if it might run, then pressed it to her palm. Warm. It shouldn’t have been. Everyone’s breath in cold air, yes. But warm meant it had been somewhere that believed in heat differently.

Ishaan finished his cut. The man stumbled, freed. His pants were half melted into the memory of a harness that would have bruised him in strips. He hugged Mara like he knew her. She hugged him back and handed him to someone with a blanket and a job in the next part of the day.

“Nice work, Beta-Four,” Kestrel said. “Hold for debrief and live account for the feed. Public Affairs is begging me with their eyes.”

“Tell Public Affairs to eat my anchor,” Ishaan muttered, too low for the mic. He grinned at Mara, then let his face sober. “You okay?”

She nodded. It was honest. “You?”

“I am in love with that saw. I want to write poetry to it and send it small gifts it will not appreciate.”

The child was wiping tears off his face with the heel of his hand. He was so serious about it. “Your coat is not blue,” he told Mara solemnly. “It is green but wrong.”

“Mine too,” she said. “You need a better coat? We’ve got blankets. And a warm drink that wants to be hot chocolate if you tell it nicely.” Public Affairs always had little foil packets of feelings.

He sniffed in the general direction of the idea of hot chocolate and then nodded once, so decisive it broke her heart.

They made statements. They let themselves be filmed because the city liked to see itself being brave, liked to see people who had faced the weirdness and come back jokes intact. Mara had a good face for the camera. She looked like someone you would want to hold a ladder for you; she didn’t look like someone who would bring you bad news. She said the phrases Kestrel liked: “working together,” “stability,” “no reason to panic.” She did not say, I saw my mother. She did not say, my coin came back warm.

Only when the perimeter had dissolved into morning again and the tram hissed in for its 09:40 as if it hadn't been a gazebo seconds ago did she let herself sit on the bench and press the anchor coin against the inside of her wrist.

On one side, the coin still said what it had always said—Interphase Response, municipal seal, and a tiny motto in Latin chosen by some bored city council in a different decade. On the other side, where the etched tidal lines nested, there was a scratch that hadn’t been there before. It ran a shallow diagonal across the rings. It looked like the kind of mark you got from dropping a coin onto stone.

She rubbed at it with her thumb. The warmth wasn’t normal warmth; it felt like wine does two minutes after you’ve swallowed it and your chest thinks about glowing. She put the coin down on the bench and pulled one of her sink nails from the pouch. She laid the coin on top of the nail.

Metal likes metal. Her father had said that, once, about razors. He had been half right and half poetic.

The coin stuck. It wasn't magnetism; it was a kind of consent. The edges of the coin lined themselves up with the nail’s short axis with a tiny twist, like a dog nesting into a bed. For a second, the etching on the coin seemed to ripple. She had the unsettling impression of looking down at a very shallow, very fast river.

“Beta-Four,” Kestrel said in her ear, voice lower now the feed was off. “I’m sending you a private brief. We got a forecast update from Central. The incidence curve is…a little bucky. Nothing to sell soap with yet.”

"Bucky how?" Ishaan asked, hearing the same channel. He was leaning back against the tram map, eyes slitted against the light. He’d tucked a packet of Public Affairs hot chocolate into his vest like a medal.

“Spiky,” Kestrel said. “Unknown driver. A cluster of micro-events calculated for Sable, Piedmont, River’s Mouth. Times are…well, if I say volatile I sound like Public Affairs. Let’s say ‘not nailed down.’ Chief wants field eyes. You two see anything at site that would suggest a local attractor?”

Mara’s thumb paused on the coin. She could say: a scratch. She could say: a face. She could say: a warmth in my hand where there shouldn’t be. All of those things sounded like feelings and feelings didn’t go into the kind of report engineers trusted.

“We had more cross-residents visible than expected for a C,” she said. “Counted five at one point. None persisted past saturation drop. Rail picked up a weird hum but so did my fillings.”

“I only have three fillings,” Ishaan said. “So there were thirty percent fewer hums.”

“Not helpful, Ishaan,” Kestrel said, humor a layer beneath her words. “Okay. Keep me posted if you see anything that wants to be a lever. Chief is going to pretend to nap and then read every syllable of my reports with a magnifying glass.”

“Understood,” Mara said.

They packed up. You always packed the skein back carefully. You always counted your sinks and told yourself you always got the same number back that you had taken out, because admitting you misplaced mass on a Tuesday would make you weird. People drifted back into their day, grateful to have something to complain about. Trams were always late; trams always smelled like east wind; trams always carried other people with their wet umbrellas and their music turned up too loud. Nobody wanted to talk about the gazebo.

Mara walked, coin in her pocket again, down Fawn toward the river. After a crossfade she liked to take a long route to the station, to put the world through her body step by step. She loved this part of the city in an unbalanced way. The buildings didn’t know yet whether they were destined to be expensive or bare. The river was close enough to hear even when you couldn’t see it, ferry horns scolding the air. Someone had scrawled a new bit of graffiti on the retaining wall overnight, a stylized cat with a halo. It was persistent; it seemed unwilling to crossfade into anything else. She liked that about it.

A man in a suit stopped her. “Weren’t you just—” he started, breathless and embarrassed both. “At the tram. I saw you. Are we okay? Are these…getting worse? My little boy…”

Her instinct was to say what Kestrel would prefer. “We’re okay,” she said. “We’re trained. The systems are good. The city is learning how to be itself again.” She hated that last phrase, because it sounded like the end of a poem, but it also felt true the way the right angle had felt true under her hand.

“Right,” he said, visibly soothed by sentences that had verbs in the right places. “Right. Thank you. For the boy—the other boy. For the…for doing that.”

She nodded and moved on. She had said the line wrong. She had said, the city is learning, as if cities did the learning, not the people in them. As if people didn’t do all the work of every metaphor.

At the station, Ishaan peeled off toward the locker room for whatever ritual he used to shuck off a job. He hummed under his breath. He only hummed when he was thinking hard. He would call her later with a joke and maybe with a math problem, because his brain found math comforting the way other people found baths.

Mara went into the equipment bay. She logged her skein out, signed two forms that still used paper because someone had decided paper was immune to crossfades on account of yearning. She cleaned her hands twice and then a third time, because some of Sable District’s water had been other water sometimes, and her hands remembered they might not like that. Then she sat on the edge of the folding chair by her locker and took the coin out again.

Up close, the scratch looked older than this morning. It had the softened edges of something that had been worried at by pockets and worry itself. When she tilted the coin, the scratch caught the light and for a breath she felt she could see depth under it, as if the etching had stopped being surface and started being topography. She looked away and the impression went with her gaze. She looked back and it was just a scratch.

“Don’t be superstitious,” she told herself gently. That tone belonged to someone else. She had learned it from the nurse in her mother’s ward who had brought her extra pudding and lectures in equal measure. “But do pay attention.”

Her locker door had three magnets on it. One held a note from Ishaan picturing a stick figure with hair like Mara’s beating a west wind with a rolled-up map; one held a picture of her father from a summer before the hospital, laughing and tanned and looking like a version of the future that hadn’t fitted; one held the municipal emergency contact list printed on paper in case all the digital systems decided to be birds. She slipped the coin under the emergency list magnet. It clanked lightly. It stuck in a way that was not magnetism at all. Her tongue told her the room had a new taste.

“Beta-Four,” Kestrel said, closer now, at the door. Mara jumped and then hated that she jumped. Kestrel was a small woman who dressed like thunderheads—blue, gray, occasionally white, rumpled by hands that knew other things to do. She had a pen behind each ear and a third in her hair for luck she would never admit to. “Good work. Except the part where you did not wait for your partner.”

Ishaan materialized behind her like a more cheerful shadow. “Hey now,” he said. “I was only thirty-eight seconds shy of being present for the hero’s first act.”

Kestrel ignored him. She leaned her shoulder against the locker frame, eyes scanning the bay. Her presence changed the room’s air pressure. “We had another small one up the hill while you were coming in,” she said. “No injuries. Mrs. Delrine’s shed decided to be a conservatory and then a cave. She wants to know if the city will pay for new hyacinths.”

“The city will pay for different hyacinths,” Ishaan said, deadpan, and Kestrel snorted in spite of herself.

“There’s a meeting at twelve with Central,” Kestrel said. “They used the phrase emergent behavior. If you are lucky, they will use it on each other to feel clever and not require us to take notes. If you are unlucky, they will ask you questions.”

“Always unlucky,” Ishaan said, but his eyes slid to Mara. He saw everything about her that changed, not just the obvious stuff.

“Go eat something,” Kestrel said. “The city has more mornings.”

When Kestrel had gone, Mara reached up, tugged the coin back into her hand. It came reluctantly. The scratch caught a different light this time—window light, dirty with exhaust and river brightness. Something pricked at her palm, a small static shock. She sucked in a breath and tasted—ridiculous, impossible—orange and clove.

“Did you just get shocked by your membership in our noble municipal service?” Ishaan asked, watching.

“It wanted to be somewhere else,” she said. She turned the coin again. The etching seemed a little deeper, but that could be light, could be wanting it to be. “We had more cross-residents. And my mother was there.”

His face changed in increments. He leaned his hip against the locker and made the jokes vacate his mouth. “Do you want me to say she wasn’t your mother? Or do you want me to say that every face we know must be somewhere under some other sky, living an absolutely average morning?”

“I don’t want you to say anything,” she said. “I want you to stand there for thirty seconds so I can look at you and decide you are true.”

He stood. He had always been good at that.

In the twelve o’clock meeting, the Chief said emergent behavior six times. Central’s liaison, a man with expensive fingernails, said the word volatility until it lost all useful meaning and became a trick of the tongue. They rolled graphs onto the wall like tides. Nobody mentioned feelings. They talked about anchors, about constant propagation, about the failure modes of the skein. They did not talk about the way sometimes, now, dogs woke and barked just before a veil slid in, or about how the city’s crows had started to fly differently—low, strung out, like beads on a wire.

By the time Mara stepped back into the afternoon, the sky had decided to be one uniform thing again. Her body was tired the way a runner’s is—deep, fatigued joy in muscles that had been used for the right thing. She would go home, she decided, and nap, then go to the grocer who liked to argue about figs. She would not do the thing where she looked up variations of her mother’s birthday on the municipal incident log. She would not write down the scratch on the coin in her notebook and then pretend she didn’t keep a notebook.

Halfway down the station steps, her coin thrummed in her pocket. Not a ring—a hum. It moved up her bones. It was as if someone plucked a string that ran from her hip to her heart and then out to something at the far end of the river.

She stopped. Ishaan, behind her, bumped her shoulder. “What?”

“The coin,” she said. “Do you feel—”

He shook his head. His face did a precise impression of someone who was trying to feel something that wasn’t there. “No. Is it doing your palm static again? That happened to my cousin when she was pregnant. She said money shocked her right up until the kid was born.”

“It’s not that,” she said. The hum built. It was steady, not urgent yet, a standing wave inside her that wanted to align with a different wave out there. She turned, slowly. When she faced the river, it quieted. When she looked away, it strengthened.

“Do you have anywhere you need to be?” she asked Ishaan.

He brightened. “Nowhere as interesting as wherever you’re about to decide we’re going.”

They crossed to the river. Traffic studded the bridge. Ferries cut wakes like stitch marks. People were their noisy, normal selves. The coin kept humming. Mara took it out and held it on her open palm. It was warm again. The scratch shone. If she had been someone else, she might have named the feeling destiny; she’d always hated the romance of that. It didn’t feel like destiny. It felt like a certain kind of rightness you get when you align two pieces of wood and their grains nest into each other.

“There,” she said, without meaning to. There mattered. It was a warehouse on the far bank with windows like blank eyes. It had a big painted name that had been sanded off by time and paint and time again, leaving only the palimpsest of letters that might have spelled GEORGE, or might have spelled NOTHING. It was unimportant in every way except that her coin wanted it.

“Are we allowed to follow our equipment on mysterious errands?” Ishaan asked amiably.

She smiled, feeling the kick of too much coffee and too little sleep, and the hard bright of a day you don’t tell anyone about because you want to keep one thing secret. “We are if we don’t tell Kestrel until after,” she said.

He considered this. “I cannot be fired if we don’t talk about it. That is science.”

They went. The city obligingly gave them crosswalks, and once, the cooperative red of a traffic light that held a line of cars with surprising politeness. The coin hummed less now that they were closer, as if the noise of desire quieted when it was almost sure of being met.

The warehouse yard was fenced but unlocked because everyone believed the chain would convince itself to be useful. A cat slipped under the gate and didn’t sparkle, which Mara took as a good sign. They stepped over a coil of rope that wanted to simultaneously remember being a snake and an electrical cable; they ducked beneath a pipe that seemed honestly resigned to being a pipe. The door was not locked. It opened with a push like a held breath let go.

Inside it smelled like rope, oil, rain that had dried in past seasons, and something else—the now-familiar bite of crossfade air diluted down to a hint. The space was big enough to swing a boat in. The windows let a gray river light slant across the floor in hard bars. The dust was wrist deep on the unused table in the center.

On the table sat a thing that twinned her coin.

It was not a coin. It was a disc, palm-wide, with etched lines not of tide but of some other calculus, neat and self-satisfied. It sat exactly where a person’s hand would put it if they had been interrupted in the middle of doing something precise. It was the size of the warmth in her palm. It hummed, and her coin answered. The two notes met and made a third—the kind of thing you hear sometimes when you lean your forehead against someone you like and the day goes quiet around the edges.

“Do not touch it,” Ishaan said reflexively. He said it the way you say don’t jump at the cliff edge when you are joking, but also when you are not.

Mara laughed once, softly, and set her coin down beside it. The two discs spun lightly, aligning their scratches and etches into a single line that resolved like a picture snapping into focus. Lines ran from coin to disc to the edges of the table, out like the spokes of a small, strange wheel.

“What is it?” Ishaan whispered.

Mara did not know. The city did not have a form for she found something that wanted me back. There was a new tremor in the air, very slight. Her molars ached, the way they did when a thread took. The wrong sky blue flickered at the edges of the windows like a joke they weren’t meant to hear.

She had been about to tell Kestrel where they were. She had been about to put sensible words together, to make her voice sound like paperwork. Instead she reached out, and her finger touched the edge of the disc.

It wasn’t heat. It wasn’t shock. It was the sensation of a staircase exactly where you expected one being half a step lower. It was the feeling of her mother’s breath on her forehead when she was ten, and the memory had gone brittle with repetition in the way memories do when you’re careful with them. It was the sense of something clicking into the notch it had been carved for.

Outside, a ferry horn called, ordinary, low. Somewhere upriver, someone dropped a crate and swore. In the corner of the warehouse, a small skittering thing with too many legs that had lived there long enough to belong paused in its important business and decided not to cross this floor at this moment.

On the table, the lines brightened. The air smoothed. The world felt it, or her body tricked her into believing it did. The discs made a sound like the sustain pedal, like a piano when the player lifts their foot and lets the notes mingle.

“I think,” Mara said, and her voice was steady, “that we just found a lever.”

Chapter One

They say time is a tide. In Peregrine’s shadow, it feels like a rip current.

From the maintenance arm that held me over the Relay’s throat, the black hole was not a hole. It was a lens, a bruise in the starfield, pulling a ring of sickle-bright light from the background and bending it around nothing. The light shivered in the vibrations of my suit. It was closer than sense said it should be, farther than fear allowed. The tether at my hip went taut and sang along my spine, and I pulled myself hand over hand a meter closer to the grim black center.

The Relay itself was an elegance of old engineering: a platform of Rorschach silhouettes—clocks, coils, radiation shrouds—circled along the perigee track around Peregrine, dipping toward the blackness to skim the edge of its time well and slingshot back out. There were two rings of devices, counter-rotating to cancel torques, linked by struts that flexed like the ribs of a whale. The perigee track was a compromise between physics and nerve. Any closer and we’d flirt with Roche rending. Any farther, and the tide wouldn’t take.

The first time I came out here, fresh from an orbital lab and full of textbook boldness, I laughed in my helmet and spun myself to look at the Station, at the tiny cluster of modules drinking light from Peregrine’s faint halo, and I shouted at the live mic until Sumi on the line told me, laughing, to rein it in before I spooked the prayer group listening from Jupiter. The image of my breath misting my visor against that impossible curve still lived in my chest. It never stopped being wrong and beautiful.

Today there was no prayer group. Today, the listening lists were empty. We were between scheduled drops. There would be a lull—no one orbiting the black well to lay a message into the future, no packet climbing time’s slow incline to reach us millennia in a moment. Which made it the best time to fix things before the next song swelled.

I reached the joint at Strut 22A and let the suit’s magnets bite the thermimmune plating. The plating thrummed faintly with heat that didn’t come from the sun. Peregrine hummed in every atom, a song below hearing. The coupling here had begun to worry itself loose, a creep measured in atoms over years. Most of our work was measured like that. The big disasters happened quickly, but the things that made them possible took quiet patience to grow teeth.

I wedged the wrench into the slot and gritted while I put torque on the thing.

“Status?” Orin’s voice came through the suit.

“Out,” I said. “At twenty-two A. Gravity nominal, thermal within parameters, I’ve got torque on the coupling. Who invented torque ratings? I have bones.”

“Bones were your idea,” Orin said. “You’re welcome for your bones.”

He wasn’t watching me, not directly. He was two hundred meters away in the Operations module, inside a bubble lit with soft blue-tinted glass, surrounded by circles of nested chronometers and their whispers. You could work line by line in Ops, half-hypnotized by the Reflexion Clocks and their precise quarrels with each other over what to call a second. People liked to take their coffee in there and dare the oscillations to find a rhythm in their heads. Orin had been on the Relay longer than anyone alive and wore time’s quarrels like a coat. His hair had long since gone colorless, and his face had reorganized itself around the eyes.

The coupling settled with a lurch that ran up my arm and rattled my teeth. I swore and then laughed through it. In that sound, I caught old Sumi’s voice again and the snort she’d make when her instruments were being finicky. It was almost enough to be a ritual, the things you say while you put your hands on the bones of a machine. We who worked at Peregrine had a lot of rituals. People thought we were priests of a sort, or witches. All we did was set clocks and keep the tracks true. The rest is gravity.

“Twenty-two A is home,” I said. “Moving to twenty-three B. Put the kettle on.”

“The kettle’s a myth,” Orin said. “We drink our coffee cold and bitter like time.”

“Put the kettle on,” I said. “I want to smell water.”

The station’s kettle had a rusted hinge and a patched whistle and lived on a shelf near the Reactor door in defiance of all safety signs. It was one of my favorite things here: a relic of Earth that came in on a supply shuttle before I was born. I wasn’t born on Earth. I’ve never been on a planet. When I want to think about gravity in a social way, I imagine a kettle on a stove, its lid rattling and its steam worrying at the room.

Twenty-three B was worse. The thermistors were singing high, the plating here rippled like skin over muscle, and the field monitors spat numbers Orin wouldn’t like.

I put a hand on the strut and felt, through glove and plating, a tremble like a heartbeat that was not mine.

“You seeing this?” I asked.

Orin’s pause seemed to have shape. “Numbers are stubborn today,” he said. “Peregrine’s sneezy.”

“We can’t afford a cold,” I said. “It thinks it’s spring.”

“Finish the strut,” he said. “Then get inside. We’ve got an external sync to run before the next pass.”

I was finishing the strut when the beacon pinged a register tone that made the inside of my skull feel cold. It was not the tone we expected. It was not any tone I knew.

“Orin?” I said, already knowing he was hearing it too.

“A ghost note,” he said softly. His voice lost and regained itself between syllables. “Suit, confirm. Suit, record. Iri, finish quickly.”

The tone came again, and despite the suit’s baffles my hindbrain thought of animal calls in forests I’ve never stood in. Something somewhere cleared a throat.

The Relay works like this: you have a message you want to survive the kinds of storm that erase everything else. You pack it onto a device built to keep time better than anything we know how to build, you put it on the perigee track, and you throw it around Peregrine. The device dives in toward the event horizon and, for you watching from outside, its time slows. Hours for the device become years outside, then decades, then centuries if you keep your nerve and your equations true. We call it a drop, because the thread you hold on to is a drop shot into a well, and you wait for the ripples to come back. You can’t talk to the past. But you can whisper forward, and time’s tide will carry the words.

The tone we heard meant something was about to claw its way up.

I made myself breathe slow and steady while I checked my work. A strut out of true during a drop could translate into mass lost at perigee, and mass lost at perigee meant direction lost and then you were writing letters to a ghost on the inside of a throat that only swallowed. The toolbench magnetized itself to my thigh with a comfortingly solid clonk. The suit’s thrusters nudged me along the strut to the next handhold.

“I want you in Ops,” Orin said. “Now.”

“Suits don’t move faster when you shout,” I said, but he was right. I kicked off gently, hugged my tether, and let the Station pull me home. Peregrine’s swirl widened behind me. Space that had been quiet bled photons across my periphery as my angle to the lensed background stars shifted. By the time I reached the airlock and slapped my palm to the reader, the tone had resolved into a pattern.

The lock cycled, the interior door opened with its accustomed stutter, and Station air met my tongue with the taste of metal and yeast and coffee long boiled and recirculated. Someone had, against my orders and their better sense, heated water.

“Iri,” Orin said. “Ops. Now.”

I went.

Operations was a circle of circles. The Reflexion Clocks hung in nested rings around our console like cages for invisible birds. Each clock did math differently, and none could agree on the exact tempo of the universe, but if you listened long enough you could hear the shape of truth in their arguments. On the central panel, Peregrine’s perigee track traced a perfect oval, white for our ring and red for the counter-rotating, with little patient diamonds moving along like fisherman’s floats in a breathing sea. The bottom of the oval flickered as the perigee nodes hit their deepest dive.

Orin stood with his knuckles on the console, squinting as if that would change the numbers. He looked up when I came in. His eyes were bright.

“What are we looking at?” I asked.

“An echo,” he said. “Or a prank from the early Commonwealth codes. A salvage out of L-archive that someone flushed and forgot. Or a ghost out of the event horizon sent to tell us how clever we aren’t. Pick your poison. It’s not on the books.”

“Drop?” I asked. “You said—”

“Four minutes out,” he said. “Unscheduled. Untagged.”

“You’re kidding me.” I didn’t bother to take off my helmet. I set it on the stool and leaned toward the console like the device could be soothed by my curiosity. The Reflexion Clocks whispered. The note rose again, like a coin rolling on a table as it nears rest.

“Who sent it?” I asked.

“We don’t know.” He pointed. “It’s using Commonwealth Format Nine stripped of the registry layer. That’s…not done anymore. Not since the Tulliver collapse. There’s no header for a sender, no baton. Just payload and parity. Someone wanted their words tight.”

“Someone old,” I said, and didn’t mean to sound the way I did.

When I was nine, which was a lifetime ago and not so long, I took a class field trip to a museum in Venus orbit while my mother refueled a tug. The museum had a wall of letters from the first decades of the Relay, when everyone with a ledger and a grandparent wanted their thoughts to outlast the end of anything. The letters were rude and tender and full of recipes. None of those senders thought they were writing to me. The Relay collected their words and put them on a shelf where you needed a room full of temporal versions of the same clock to reach. When we learned to make better clocks and to pack more bits into the spin of a particle, we learned to be less human. Format Nine was one of our awkward adolescent attempts at forever. Old.

“I want to see the outside,” I said.

Orin nodded, and I touched the control to throw the camera feeds onto the wall. The wall was a cheap thrill made for patrons and recruits. It wrapped us and made the Station a transparent bubble over the black, and the perigee track a ring of pale sequins that a clawed hand without a body held over a drain. If I thought about it too long, my knees vibrated. I didn’t close my eyes. You don’t look away from something that is about to speak to you.

I found the diamond that had begun to blink three perigees ago and traced it with a fingertip thought, unconsciously, the way I used to trace the lines of my palm when the ship my mother worked pushed into a burn. The blinking diamond was old, so old that the invisible numbers next to it were full of canned jokes from engineers who had been dead longer than I had been alive.

“Three minutes,” Orin said.

“The Regulation Sequencer’s awake?” I asked, because the question was required in the script we all carried.

“It’s awake and wearing its Sunday clothes,” he said. He forced his voice into its old banter. It was like watching someone recall the map of a city after an earthquake. “We’ll follow the book.”

The book said this: Unscheduled drops do not get to talk to us without going through three layers of quarantine. First, a physical ring of checks that verified the payload hadn’t picked up any rogue physics at perigee that would make our devices sing themselves apart. Second, a math ring that looked for malicious content, self-targeting loops, and the kinds of message that made people’s minds go back and back on themselves. Third, a human ring—us. The book had more pages about the human ring than the others, because we were the ones who broke when something had to.

“Orin,” I said. “Who else is on?”

“Just Binta in Life Support. She’s chopping fungi. Everyone else is asleep or hanging out in G-lab trying to coax the microstacks to behave like nodes and not teenagers. I didn’t call anyone.”

I looked at him then. At the little tells. At the way his knuckles had gone white and stayed. “Because?”

“Because if this is Century One trash,” he said, “I don’t want a livestream of me sighing. And if it’s not trash, you are the person I want in the room when we decide whether to open it.”

“I’m younger than your boots,” I said, but it was a protest without teeth. He carried loves and frustrations and calculations I would never know. But he had started saying my name like a place to tie a tether.

“Two minutes,” he said. “What do you hear?”

“The clocks are fighting on the half-second,” I said. “There’s drift we didn’t account for. Something’s overfeeding the coils at twenty-three B. That’s what I felt. If we don’t fix it before the next set of scheduleds, we’re throwing error into the stack.”

“You felt that outside?”

“It’s in the plating.” I rubbed my thumb against my glove as if I could still feel the ripple. “It’s not big.”

“Everything’s big here,” Orin said. “Even the smalls are big. One minute.”

The tone made a clean interval of itself and became a carrier. The feed told a quiet lie by smoothing the reality of the radiation into an elegant gradient. In truth, particles sang knives out there. In truth, we were listening at the edge of a hurricane. I let my breath find a rhythm that fit with the carrier and did not think in words for a few breaths. Then the packet hit the first ring, and our board lit with green and kept lighting.

“Clean on physics,” Orin said. His voice was ragged. He had sweated in the time between one second and the next. “It’s clean. That’s absurd. Who builds something a million years ago that walks physics this tight across this many perigees? Who stays lucky that long?”

I wanted to answer with a history lesson, to say words about the Deep Makers and the people who left notes under rocks for children they’d never meet. I kept my mouth closed. The second ring opened like a flower in sped-up footage. It read and read and folded and read and did not find an obvious throat full of teeth.

“Do we…” Orin said.

The human ring was us. We did what a committee in a much safer room had once decided was a good idea. We looked at each other and decided which way to turn a key. The key was metaphorical and literal. It lived under a cracked cover checked by three independent hardware locks and a string of curses in Old Belt Cantonese. Orin flipped the first two. I flipped the third. The panel accepted that we were, in fact, at least as foolish as it was.

“Display,” Orin said in a voice that was not like any I’d heard him use. It was softer, somehow, as if he didn’t want to startle a bird.

The wall sputtered. Letters were old-fashioned. People in the first hundred years loved letters because they wanted things to look like they were supposed to, because it made them feel that they weren’t inventing a religion. Words in standard were still the easiest thing to pass through fourteen kinds of censorship. The text bloomed across the wraparound display in gray chalk lines as if someone stood in air with a piece of chalk and wrote in front of us.

Hello, it said. If you are reading this, it worked.

Dates and credentials scrolled under that in the tiny mathematical filigree that proved the structure of the message. I didn’t look at them. I was looking at the line below.

Iri, it said. Are you awake?

My name in my mother’s voice. Not the syllables of it. The cadence. There are jokes about how you can hear your mother say your full name across vacuum—how she can get a message past baffles you thought were built for cosmic rays. I hadn’t heard my mother say my name in six months, not since her tug had gone behind a planet that was mostly bureaucracy and lost itself in paperwork and taxes and then in an explosion no one would own. I had her voice in postcards and old message fragments. I had it in my mouth sometimes, when I was tired enough to talk to myself and too proud to call it that. Now it was in front of me, the shape of what she used to do when she wanted me to say I was listening.

I forgot how to swallow and then did it twice.

Orin half-turned his head. “Iri,” he said. He was warning and comfort both.

I had to reach forward to make my fingers behave. The interface offered me a polite little sidebar, as if we were doing research in a pleasant library: Would you like to resume? Would you like to save? Would you like to forward to your stream?

I hit resume.

Good. If you are awake, then the cold is doing you good and you don’t need me to tell you to put on socks. This is going to be messy. You have to forgive me the mess. There was no other way to get it to you. You shouldn’t open this with everyone looking over your shoulder. Orin, if you’re there, hello, I’m sorry, you know I am, and there’s a line for you at the end if the buffer holds.

“I don’t—” Orin began, and then stopped. His face had gone as blank as the inside of a helmet.

You are going to get three more unscheduled drops in the next six days. Only the first one is clean. Do not open the second. Let the third pass through and don’t let your hand shake even a little when you do the thing with the switch.

A fragment of an old lesson came and went: we teach the kids not to give orders across time because it makes them think about causality like an arrow you can aim. We teach the kids to say please and thank you to ghosts because politeness does not collapse anything you don’t want collapsed. There was no please here. I would have known my mother by the way she used imperatives even if I had been someone else reading this for the first time.

The second drop will say my name. It will tell you something you’ve wanted to hear since you were nine and some teacher told you the Relay was a benign lie. It will say: the math is wrong. It will offer you proof. It will be lying.

“It’s a joke,” I heard myself say, without meaning to. “It’s a sick—”

“It’s too clean to be a joke,” Orin said. He had found the cushion for his voice again, the one that went under and around me when I was pulling a bolt that wouldn’t line up with the hole. “Let it talk.”

I’m sorry, my mother’s voice wrote in gray chalk on the wall of the universe. I am sorry to both of you. Orin, the bearing at twenty-three B has drifted a half-micron in the wrong breath at the wrong time and the coil wants to bite. You felt it outside, Iri. I know you did. You have to let it bite. Do not trim. If you trim, you won’t like what happens three days from now when the third drop wants to breathe. Trust me. I know you don’t like that. Trust me. If you can’t trust me, trust the person who sent this before I did. Her note will reach you two minutes after this one ends. She is dear to me. You’ll like her. But do this first. Let the coil bite and cache the pain.

I had my hand out without meaning to, fingers splayed on the console glass. The Reflexion Clocks murmured like the inside of my skull when I haven’t slept. Muscle memory told me where the trim control lived. Everything in me that had ever been a technician flexed itself to fix the tiny drift she mentioned. The fix was a simple gutting line with a wrench. You could call it a tweak and be forgiven.

“If we don’t trim,” I said, and the sentence broke its own spine against my teeth. “If we don’t, we’re going to feed error into the pass.”

“We will,” Orin said quietly.

“And that error will—”

“Make the scheduled drops get weird.” He had his eyes on the perigee track. “It will upset people who cared enough to pay for their words to travel time. It may drop a bit or two in the wrong direction. It may turn recipes into metaphors and prayers into jokes.” He looked at me. “It may keep us from having to decide something worse in three days.”

My mother’s voice went on, and I was glad it could not see my face. There are moments when I am certain faces should be private. If you let the coil bite now, the third drop will be at a phase we can catch without looking like thieves. If you don’t, things line up too well and everything gets simple in the way knives are simple.

She had written this long before my mother had a tug, long before I had a body. She had written this so precisely that it reached into a day when I was standing beside Orin with sweat cooling on my neck and told me to do the opposite of everything I had been trained for. It was like being told to stop your own heart for a moment and trust that you are your own life support.

“Who sent it?” I asked, not meaning my mother and meaning it anyway.

No sender, no baton, no gift registry. Only the payload and parity. The math underneath the letters sang a structure that had been taught to students when reactors used water and stars were a metaphor instead of a place.

“Orin,” I said. “If the coil bites, Ops gets dirty. We’ll have to pretend we didn’t notice to pass the second ring on the scheduled drops. We—”

“We will lie to a machine about a machine,” he said. “We’ll sleep later.”

The wall text stopped long enough for my heart to climb up my throat and decide it was time to stop pretending to be attached to anything. Then there was the barest breath of scrolling.

Iri, when you were nine, we had to sell the old scope and you didn’t talk to me for six days. You put the scope in a bag like a pet and took it with you everywhere for a month. When you finally said my name again, you said it as if you had decided to forgive me in installments but you had to be hard to make it count. You’re still like that. I’m asking you to do the thing you don’t do: bend without giving. Let the coil bite. Do not cut its teeth off it or it will bite somewhere we can’t afford to bleed. There’s tea in the kettle. Drink it before it’s bitter. Orin, again: sorry. I wouldn’t do this to you if there were a better way.

The text blinked, and then, almost as an afterthought, a string of numbers spilled across the bottom like the tail of a comet. It was a coordinate in a space I knew the feel of like the back of my hand, and a time window that put a little red slash through my afternoon three days from now.

Then another bracket unfurled, and a signoff came as if my mother were stepping out of the room and leaving a hand on the doorframe.

I love you. Do not tell anyone about the second drop. Let it howl past you. Tell them it was dirty and smelled wrong. You can say it like that and it won’t be lying. You’re good at that. My hands are out of time. I’ll be late. Be late with me. M.

The message ended. The Reflexion Clocks did not. Peregrine did not. The Station breathed the way machines breathe: a beat of fans, a click in the wall, the sigh of circulating air that tricked the part of my brain that had been shaped by people who were shaped by sky into thinking of leaves.

Another tone announced another packet brushing the first ring.

“That would be the next note she promised,” Orin said hoarsely. He didn’t look up from the console. He didn’t look at me. “Do you want to call the others?”

I thought of Binta with a knife full of fungi, of the G-lab kids arguing about their rebellious microstacks, of the prayer group we didn’t have and the donors with their recipes and regrets. I thought of the Regulation Sequencer and its honest unblinking face. I thought of my own hand reaching for the trim control and how badly I wanted to make a number be the number it was supposed to be.

“I want to drink tea,” I said. “I want to hold the kettle and feel heat on my hands and believe that there are rooms where you can pick something up and put it down and nothing is ruined.”

“You want me to—”

“I don’t want to open that second ring,” I said. “I want you to stand there with your hand over the key and let our shoulders touch while you don’t turn it, and we will write in the log that a cat walked across the board and the Sequencer had a bad minute and that will be the truth we tell.”

The packet whispered against the physics ring and slid past like a swimmer diving. The machine prepared to stand in judgment, polite and unafraid.

Orin breathed once. Twice. He took his hand off the key.

“Binta is going to be cross,” he said. “She’s been waiting for a drop with a poem in it for three months.”

“Binta can have the third,” I said, and it wasn’t bravery, but it sounded like it in the mouth. I put my hand flat on the console. “Let the coil bite.”

I did not move toward the trim. The number that said twenty-three B’s drift jittered like the eye of an animal that did not know if it was being hunted yet. Somewhere, a bearing made a sound that only the clocks could have heard if they had had ears.

“Tea?” Orin asked gently.

“Tea,” I said.

We left the room with the wrapped wall still showing the black throat and the tiny diamonds blinking their way around it. The second packet knocked on the second ring, and the Regulation Sequencer was, for the first time in its honest life, ignored by two human creatures with bones they had insisted on and voices they couldn’t put away, walking toward a kettle that might whistle if it was treated with the right kind of love.

The kettle’s hinge stuck as always. I set it on the heating ring and waited while water thought about boiling. Orin leaned against the wall and closed his eyes. When the kettle finally found its voice and announced itself, I felt an absurd urge to cry. I poured the water and watched it turn dark and then darker.

On the wall in Ops, unnoticed by us, a third tone began the shape of its approach.

Chapter One

The first lesson they teach you at the Bureau is that cause and effect are not married, only engaged. The second is to never be the one who suggests postponing the wedding.

Ada Nadir stood in the chalky dawn at the edge of a stream of red tape and listened to the city misremember itself. The tape didn’t flap in the wind; it pulsed, little light-beads along its length winking in a pattern her eye had learned to read: a steady-lagging oscillation, about three seconds of misalignment. Something had wrinkled the past here and the present was trying to pull it flat again.

“Your anchor’s stable,” Gerrit said into her ear. He always sounded like he was speaking through a coat. “Coherence index point-nine-three. Don’t let it drop.”

“Wouldn’t dream of it,” she muttered. The anchor’s weight sat against her collarbones like a reassuring hand. In the early years they wore them as belt packs; now they were a loop of braided fiber and tuned ferrites, warm from her skin, humming when the city did.

They’d called her at four, the Bureau’s red glyph crawling up her wall. By four-thirty she was sliding into boots and telling herself she remembered coffee. By five she was stepping off the tram into the Old Dock district, where apartment towers leaned in shoulder to shoulder like tired men, and overhead the spindown turbines pinwheeled the dawn into a haze. Across the street she could see the river, strapped into its canal, pretending to be tame. She could also, if she didn’t look directly at it, see the river as it had been yesterday at noon, sun-shot and noisy with pleasure boats. That was one of the tells—in a healthy block you couldn’t catch other days out of the corner of your eye.

The convenience store had two names at once: CAMDEN FOOD & FUEL in flaking red even though no one had bought petrol here in ten years, and NEW YEAR MARKET in spray paint on a piece of plywood nailed across the window. It had also, if you understood the way the soot clung to the threshold and the way the glass granules on the sidewalk reflected light as if it were coming from somewhere else, both burned down and not burned down. The front door hung politely open at a ninety-degree angle. Her watch told her 05:12. The CCTV rig above the door told her 05:12, too—on the wrong day. Tomorrow.

Ada pulled the hood of her jacket up to keep the ash out of her hair and stepped under the tape. Her drone, Tessel, followed, its glossy black body sliding along at shoulder height. Tessel had the ungenerous shape of a housefly scaled up and peeled down to essentials: wings too narrow to be useful, eyes like shallow bowls. It also had good manners. It held steady, humming, while she took a shallow breath and let her anchor hum back.

Inside, the store smelled like rain on bricks and ozone, like someone had microwaved static. Rows of metal shelves sat politely, their mouths full of bread and brand-name sugar—bright as new money, which told her this was the not-burned version asserting itself. Behind them, the wall was a mural of smoke, all the metal spines of the shelves bent in one direction. She raised the cone—a delicate wand, like a caliper without jaws—and let it integrate light against its own memory of light. The cone didn’t care what the shelves looked like. It could see the entire event as a ripple. She watched the little graph in her goggles build and dip, a diamond turned on its side. Something had propagated through here faster than the neighbors’ ability to absorb it. The Bureau called events like that kinks for the way they tightened everything around them. The press called them afterbefores. Ada called them trouble.

“Talk to me,” Gerrit said. “What’s your feel?”

“Knotting at the threshold. Two separate peaks of energy deposition, one thermal, one—” She frowned. “One is clean. Not heat. Coherent.”

“Laser?”

“Not with this signature. And get this: the camera thinks this is tomorrow. And it believes it.”

Gerrit made a sound like something soft tearing. “Tomorrow bleed. L3 rating if the footprint extends beyond the building. They cut budget and then blame time for not standing up. You alone?”

Tessel clicked, meaning yes and no at once. Bureau regs wanted two Inspectors per callout, but Old Dock was thin on staff and Ada had a good anchor. She could hold a block steady by glare alone, Gerrit liked to say. She didn’t laugh when he did anymore.

There were burn marks, yes, looking like tide patterns in black wax. But there were also other marks—a gentle deformation in the linoleum where something heavy had rested that had not, in any version, been part of the store. Ada crouched and pressed two fingers to the dent. The dent was cool. “We’ve got foreign mass signature,” she said softly.

“Planted?” Gerrit’s voice lighter. Planted meant a prank, a suit in a lab testing a new toy, some grad student trying to goose a metric. Planted meant the Bureau could throw a permit number at the Mayor’s Office and be done by lunch.

Ada glanced down the aisle. A jar on the shelf announced Acacia Honey in a script your grandmother would have called trustworthy. It had two prices at once. The higher one was handwritten, and the ink changed color as she watched. She looked away. When she looked back the handwriting was a different hand.

“They don’t make pranks with coherent peaks,” she said. “They make them loud.”

“How’d you like backup?”

“I’d like causality to sit down and use its indoor voice. But yes. Send me Vey.”

“I can send you Vey in fifteen.”

“I’ll take Vey in ten.” She flicked the cone on the edge of her goggles. Tessel drifted higher, mapping the thermal residues. “And tell Dispatch to rotate the blue-light units off Stephen Street. Their sirens are kicking the coherence down another point.”

“Copy,” Gerrit said. “I’ll bring you coffee when I come. Keep your head, Nadir. No heroics.”

Ada smiled without showing teeth. Heroics were what happened when you confused your own story with the city’s. She had made that mistake once and her sister didn’t speak to her any longer.

Something stuttered in the back room. A sound, or the absence of one, like the pause when a thunderstorm is deciding if it wants to be a disaster. Ada moved toward it. Through the beads of plastic curtain, the little office went blurry and then snapped into iron clarity. She had to squeeze sideways between a toppled filing cabinet and a steel desk that had been bored through by something not the size of any bullet she knew. The edges of the hole were glassy, as if a much slower drill had melted its way and then changed its mind. On the far wall a calendar from a neighborhood pizza place hung wrong. The little box for next Friday was circled twice and in pencil the word PARTY had been written and then erased hard enough to tear the paper.

Ada said her own name at a normal volume, just to hear something she recognized. Tessel whined in sympathy. There was a thing on the floor under the desk, not a piece of store, not a piece of office.

It was a sphere the size of an orange. Not quite a sphere—if you looked hard lines formed themselves across its surface and then slid away again. She’d seen something like it once in footage from a lab at the University of Axioms. They’d called it a seed. A seed is the most ordinary word for the most dangerous thing: a small, contained discrepancy in the way time handles itself. In the lab they’d anchored theirs to a bank of massively boring machinery that was supposed to keep it from falling like a ball in the slope of its own desire. The lab had burned down three weeks later. The Bureau had said faulty wiring and signed her pay slip and told the press kinks were rare and manageable.

This seed lay in dust and burnt receipt paper like it had always been there. It made the air above it vibrate a little, like heat does in the distance on a road. When it throbbed Ada felt it in the capillaries beneath her eyes.

“Gerrit,” she said. “I have an OP node. Passive. No obvious anchor. Handbuilt, I’d say.” Origin parity reversal was the polite way to name a piece of the future that insisted on being born yesterday.

Silence on the line. Then, careful: “How big?”

“Hold a breath. Hold it too long.”

“Don’t touch.”

“What do I pay you for?” Ada shifted, getting the desk between herself and—what? The door, where something could enter. The ceiling, where time sometimes fell. She talked to fill the space. “I’m going to field-anchor it. Vey gets here, we cage it and call Central.”

“If you field-anchor and it parasitizes your loop we’ll be digging you out of antinewton sludge.”

Ada snorted. “Don’t be lyrical.” She reached under her jacket, unhooked the secondary from the anchor at her neck. It was a little loop of itself, light as thread, and if you didn’t know better you’d have thought it was pretty. In her goggles it haloed her hand, her fingers silhouette against a nothing bright as cold water. She flicked the little switch on the clasp. A number wrote itself in the corner of her vision. She had always been good at that moment, at lining herself up against whatever the city was trying to do and refusing. It was the warmest form of stubbornness she knew.

She lowered the ring. The seed didn’t move. The ring touched. There was a noise like a child half-sobbing. Ada’s eyes watered. The number in her goggles slid and steadied.

“Tessel,” she said. “Be kind.”

Tessel dipped and laid a grid of light like lace across the scene. The seed’s signature wrote itself in the pattern. Ada felt, not saw, the moment when her anchor’s math lapped around it like a hand around a throat. The seed quieted. Instead of beating it hummed very softly in ragged time with her pulse.

“Got you,” she said, and then swore, because in the cut of the quiet something else was trying to be a world. Not a thunderstorm this time. A voice, made of signal noise.

“Nadir,” the voice said.

Gerrit was still in her ear, breathing deliberately. Tessel’s motors sang the key of C. Neither of them said her name like that, with the stress on the wrong syllable, with exact intimacy fallible as handwriting.

“Nadir,” it said again. “You will hear me. Do not fix this.”

Ada lifted the ring away. You didn’t leave yourself attached to a thing that said your name like you owed it something.

“Nadir, please. The seed will climb your loop if you cage it. If you cage it it will ride you home. If it rides you home it will see your wall and laugh. Don’t. Leave it.”

She sat on the edge of the metal desk and said, because there were rules even for this, “Identify your origin.”

The voice was quiet for a half second in a way that meant it was searching for language on a path between two not-agreed-upon now. “I come from today,” it said. “I come from the other today. The one that wasn’t supposed to hold. You tell me that phrase. Later. You tell me to save you the trouble of inventing it. So here. I am doing that.”

“You’re adorable,” Ada whispered. She had steadied hundreds of people who were certain they remembered tomorrow. Forty percent of them were traumatic stress. Thirty percent were opportunists. Twenty were honest anomalies that could be combed and folded and filed. Ten percent were stories that made her teeth hurt and her boss drink in his office with the lights off. Nobody meant them harm. Not in a personal way. Nobody until the Axioms lab.

“Tessel?” she said.

Tessel’s light-grid flexed, made of algorithm and what could only be called mood. It chimed, then gave her a tiny arrow, pointing, not at the seed, but toward the front of the store.

Something was happening out there. Something that had learned to walk in the wrong direction down the curve of the street.

“Later,” the voice said, urgent, almost musical now. “I wanted to tell you in a room that wasn’t on fire. I wanted to tell you with coffee. You don’t—” It broke if you could call it that, into sound that wasn’t language but all the stress of language. It found itself again. “Do not fix this the way you do.”

Gerrit said, “Nadir, pee-bees out front.”

“Passengers?” Ada stood, very slowly, because her anchor didn’t like abrupt shifts.

“Parametric bleed. Traffic van just arrived twice. Operator thinks he’s late for last Thursday. Sends out a signal like a lighthouse for idiots.”

As if summoned by Gerrit’s lack of humor, a shadow rolled across the tiled floor. It did the wrong thing in light: it moved across darkness and became brighter. Ada stepped back, away from the door, as a van—the sort that had once hauled soft drink deliveries, now repurposed to ferry boxes of gray plastic—ghosted into the aisle. It wasn’t actually in the aisle. The van was outside on the street. But what it did to light and time made it look like it was shouldering past boxes of cereal.

The engine coughed. The whole world coughed with it. The anchor at Ada’s neck kicked against her bones. Tessel’s hull bloomed with warning flower petals of orange and blue. Ada kept her hand on the seed, not touching it, but letting it know she was there, as if it could be soothed like a dangerous dog.

The van’s door opened under no one’s hand. A man hopped down from a place that was not the height of the sidewalk. He wore a jacket too crisp for this neighborhood with a little sigil on the breast Ada didn’t know. Maybe she did and would, later. His hair was the color of plastic that had sat in the sun too long. He didn’t look at her. He looked at the back room as if it were a lighthouse and he’d been wrecked all night.

“Ada?” he said, as if he hadn’t thought about how his voice would sound saying it.

She did not say yes.

He reached into the van and pulled out a hard case with Bureau gray and Bureau catches and Bureau drawl. Bureau. Except the gray was a shade the procurement catalog had stopped ordering two years ago. The catches had a slightly mismatched sheen. He put the case on the floor, and the case decided what was the floor and what wasn’t.

“Director,” he said, not to her but past her, to a version of her that maybe had a different coat. “You told me to bring it. If you say you didn’t I don’t care.”

Ada glanced at Tessel. Tessel had flattened itself against the ceiling in a posture of synthetic terror. Its little camera mouth was open in a line. Its light grid now spelled the Bureau’s emergency glyph, not helpful.

“Leave,” she said. “Now.”

The man seemed to think about the word as if he’d never encountered it. “You said you wouldn’t yet,” he said, and smiled in a way that wished it were charming. “I always like you before you become yourself. No offense.”

“None taken,” she said. “Go anyway.”

He touched his ear like he was checking for a comm. Blood smeared his fingers. Not his. The wrong color. He lifted his hand and looked at it and said, “Oh,” which was how some people say the Great Ship is sinking, or I am about to tell the truth.

Outside, another van drew up, and then the same van left, both sounds inserting themselves under her skin. Two uniforms stepped out, not Bureau but city cops in their crisp silent boots. They wore their anchors like medals, and they were too tight in the shoulders. One of them raised a gun.

Ada’s brain did the thing it did when the world wanted to argue. It put a sheen of calm over everything, like someone had polished her from the inside. “Nobody fire,” she said, and realized by the way the sentence sounded like she was speaking through water that one of them had already. Several times. She could see the holes. The bullets had not been here yet. They left a smell like cheap fireworks. The holes crawled forward along the drywall in a tidy line, moved by a hand that would not lift a finger for another half second.

She stepped left. The air where she had been shredded in a neat school of punctures. Shards of calendar fluttered down in shapes like punctuation. Under her palm the seed hummed like a guilty heart.

“Nadir,” Gerrit said into her head, and this time she heard him not as a voice but as pressure against her anchor. “Backup in two.”

“Kick the sirens off Stephen Street,” she said, and then ducked as one of the cops moved to the wrong place too quickly. Their partner reached out, grabbed their anchor strap, yanked them back like a child at a river’s edge. Ada made a note to get that partner a drink. She did not know either of their names yet. She might or might not ever learn them. The Bureau had a mural in the lobby for names it did not learn fast enough.

The man with the case had put it on the desk next to her without her permission. It gaped a few millimeters and inside cables and foam made promises about containment and safety statistics. The screen on the lid lit with a line of text: Hi, Ada. We’re late.

“You brought me a portable cage,” she said, not a question. Her voice sounded like someone else’s patience.

“You told me to.” He spread his hands. He was about her height, with a different sort of anchor around his throat, something hammered-looking wrapped in tape. “We can save us a week if we stop the seed here. You were on about budgets. You’re very persuasive when you think you’re doing the right thing.”

“I’m always persuasive,” she said, and found in herself a bitter little fissure that wanted to laugh.

“Yeah,” he said. “It’s why I loved you.”

The seed made a sound like a bell in a glass of water.

Tessel dropped out of the air like something had cut its string and then caught itself—its motors shook as if protesting a bad dream. In her goggles the number that was her coherence drifted and then returned so sharply that the moment had edges.

The case’s screen put up its hand in a polite little animation. Unlock Me, it said.

“How?” she asked, before she could stop herself.

“By being yourself,” the man said, and then flinched as if someone had tugged a fishhook in the tender part of his ear. His face went slack for a fraction. “Shit,” he said. “It’s going to pull me.”

“If you know that, you know how to—” Ada began, and then stopped, because she had watched enough people be taken back by the more stubborn part of time to recognize the way his skin became the wrong kind of pallor, like someone had overexposed him a little. His hand on the case slipped and left fog.

“Find the spindle,” he said with an intensity that made room for itself in her memory. “You won’t understand for three days. Don’t use the cage.”

“Whose spindle?” she demanded, and threw her weight against the part of the world that made him less solid. “Where?”

“You told me not to tell you,” he shouted, which would have been funny if he hadn’t looked like it hurt. “Please. I’m not supposed to be here. I kill a thousand head of cattle if I stand another minute. Don’t fix it your way. For once—”

There was always a moment when the choice looked like an accident and then another when it didn’t. Ada stepped back from him, because she could not anchor him without tying him to herself, and she did not like the odds that he would make sensible choices on her behalf. He wavered and went sideways, not left or right but another axis entirely, the one that led you through the same door two days in a row and into different houses. He was there, not there, there. He left air chewed up like the wake of a boat.

“Spindle,” she said again, as if the word itself could hold him. He shook his head, and went. He left the wrong amount of shadow where he had been. The case stayed. The van made the opposite of an engine sound and rewound itself around the corner. The store inhaled.

On the street the cops breathed. Ada heard someone cry and go quiet. Footsteps rearranged themselves. A girl somewhere in a third-floor window asked her mother if it was already tomorrow, and the mother said, very carefully, no, not yet. Somewhere a siren turned itself off and lay down. The number in Ada’s goggles ticked back toward one.

The seed, quiet as a hand on a fevered forehead, did not hum for a count of two, and Ada experienced something like silence, the absence of strain. Then it resumed, this time nestling just under the same beat as her pulse.

“Nadir,” Gerrit said.

“I have a case I didn’t bring,” she said.

“Don’t open it.”

“I’d already—” She stopped, and let herself be honest in the small ways. “I wasn’t going to.”

“You say that and I think you mean the opposite on principle.”

“Don’t valorize my flaws. How far out?”

“Vey’s in the alley,” Gerrit said, and then without his humor: “Are you all right?”

Ada looked at the desk, where the seed did its best impression of a paperweight from the future. She looked at the case, which had very politely turned its screen dark. The calendar on the wall had become last month. NONETHELESS WE PERSIST had been written across a day in a hand she almost recognized. The wrong bullet holes in the drywall did not unspool, exactly. They compromised. The tidy line broke.

“I feel like I’ve been given advice by a version of me less annoying than usual,” she said. “It’s a novel sensation.”

“You’re shaking,” Gerrit said, and she realized she was. The anchor vibrated friendly and fierce as a cat.

Tessel drifted to her shoulder and put its hull against her cheek like affection. She scratched its beaten-up casing and felt it hum under her nails.

“What’s your call?” Gerrit asked. It was not a casual question. It was the kind of leash bosses gave you when they wanted to see if you’d hang yourself.

She looked again at the case. It was designed to be the answer. She could lock the seed into a mat of carbon memory and borrowed inertia and ride the whole thing back to the Bureau’s beige vault with its chemical floral smell and its safe labels. She could do the thing she had been trained to do for six years and loved most days: she could make a problem into a waveform on a set of graphs and then a paper and then a line in a report that made a politician open their mouth and say, in tender confusion, “We’re doing fine. The Bureau has it. We’ve got it.”

The voice in the seed had been wrong about a dozen things—the swoop of her name, and the particularity of telling her she loved budgets—but she could not shake the way it had said please as if it had learned the word at cost. She could not shake the way the man had said spindle. She had touched, once, a broken toy at a fair that had an axis with no friction point, and you could spin the hemisphere forever. It had delighted her and then frightened her for reasons her mother told her later were philosophical and would pass. Not all of them had.

“Vey,” she said into her microphone. “I’m in the back room. Bring two cages. Leave the doors open. We’ll ghost it.”

“Copy,” Vey said. She and Vey had been trainees together. Vey had a laugh like she’d been told a joyless city didn’t need.

Gerrit exhaled the kind of breath managers practiced. “We’re not taking it home.”

“We are not,” Ada said. “We are going to do a thing they didn’t invent yet. We’re going to build a shadow of a cage around it and leave the cage empty. And then we’ll see who knocks.”

She slipped the secondary loop back onto its clip, feeling the way the anchor’s hum changed when it wasn’t doing double duty. The seed made another little sound, almost like it was disappointed in her. Or relieved. She couldn’t tell. That was the third lesson at the Bureau. The world does not speak your language. You can teach it a few words. It will never apologize.

Ada stood, smoothed her jacket, and picked up the case anyway. It was heavier than it looked. It fit her hand. It was keyed to a person she was not yet, and that fact put a thin line of discomfort down her spine she decided to sit with instead of solve.

She walked out into the store. Bread was bread again, cheap and wrapped in paper damp with morning. The burned part looked less insistent. Outside, for a moment, the river was only water.

On the sidewalk a boy stood behind the red tape. He was serious the way boys get when their friends are watching and their fear is an unmanly animal. He had a gap where a tooth would be. He said, “Did my dad die already or not yet?”

Ada’s anchor did not help with that kind of question. She went down on one knee to put her eyes level with his. She said, “We’re going to make it so things only happen once. Then we’ll know.”

He nodded solemnly, as if she had given him a hot stone to hold. “Okay,” he said. “I remember you.”

“Do you,” she said lightly, and felt something in her step sideways.

Vey rounded the corner at the sprint Vey always used when the city needed to be outrun and grinned when she saw Ada. “You look like you’ve already done something an ethics board would ask you about.”

“Premature,” Ada said. “We have time.”

“Ha,” Vey said, and slid under the tape with the grace of a seal.

Somewhere, some version of Ada was calling a press conference and choosing a tie. Somewhere, some version of Ada had opened the case. This Ada walked back into the store that had both burned and not burned and told her hands not to shake and her mind not to make sense prematurely.

“Director,” the case had said, falsely. “Hi, Ada. We’re late,” it had written, truthfully.

She’d made late decisions before. Sometimes they were the only kind anyone could afford.

Behind her the boy’s mother called his name and he answered like he had always lived here, and would, and perhaps had, and that this morning would be a story he told and some parts of it would be wrong and some would be right and he wouldn’t know which and it would not matter much unless the Bureau did its job.

She touched the seed briefly with her knuckle, casual as you would the head of a cat you were pretending not to love, and then let go.

“Let’s make a shadow,” she told Vey and Tessel and the room. “Let’s see who thinks it’s real.”

On calm days the Bloom pretends to be water.

From the pier above it, glassed over with the first shy light, you might think you could skip a stone and hear it tick across the surface. Children in Port Grey used to try, back before the Guild strung up the netting and the warning bells. They'd lean over the railing, mouths open, as if they might catch sweet air, and they'd come up dizzy with strangers' laughter clinging to the back of their throats.

I learned early not to open my mouth.

The morning I found the thread that shouldn't have been there, I checked the wind—southerly, cool—and spat over the side to see how fast the tide was moving. It took a long time to carry that drop of spit away. The Bloom had gathered thick in the bay overnight, miles of it, a fine opalescent scum just under the skin. It swelled as I watched, a breath you could almost see. Far across the water the breakwater and the fishwright's arches were slumped silhouettes, and beyond that, the three rusted stacks of the old thermal plant pointed at the sky like knuckles.

"Grey day, Greywater," Jun called. He was sitting on the winch housing with his feet on the rail, black curls askew under his cap. Jun always called me Greywater, because Port Grey still clung to people like a wet coat and because my name never fit right in his mouth. "You ready to be choir?"

"You want to clip me in or you want to watch me fall?" I asked.

"Both has appeal."

He grinned and made a little trumpet flourish. The harness rasped as he hauled it out. I wriggled into the straps, the canvas cold against my shirt. Tamsin came up from the cabin as Jun checked the buckles. Tamsin moved like an old crane on greased wheels; she had never lost a diver and it was the only thing she had ever boasted about.

"North net's snagged," she said. "Harbor says a fouled personal drift—some idiot with a hobby mask last night. If the alarms go you're back up. No heroics, Mara. We got four pulls to fill for Finn's."

"Finn's always wants a mouthful of first kisses and not enough funerals," Jun said. He offered me the mouthpiece like a cigarette. "Go on. Be their little saint of secondhand joy."

The mouthpiece smelled like rubber and mint. I fit it between my teeth and felt my tongue itch against it. "If the bells go off," I said around it, "you pull me up even if I beg."

"Especially if you beg," Jun said.

Tamsin placed her hand for a moment on my shoulder, the way she always did. Anchor touch. There was a time when a diver would let their mother do it, and the human brain doesn't forget things like that easily. A pressure. A weight. A steady thing to lean against when the Bloom got loud.

I swung over the rail and stepped into the net cradle. The Bloom lapped against it, leaving iridescence on the ropes like snail tracks. Under the surface its nacreous mass trembled, a million million mouths tasting the air. A gull hung on the wind and cried something that wasn't words but could be, if you listened too hard.

"On your timing," Tamsin said. The winch motor throbbed. The cradle creaked. The world tilted cool and white.

They train you to keep your tongue hard against your teeth until the filters kick. They train you to listen to your heart and count if you need to. They train you, above all, to remember who you are.

Tell yourself your name: Mara Iri Kaminski. Tell yourself where you were born and when: Shed-town, on the freshwater canal, March 18. Tell yourself something ridiculous: You once bit a prefect in year six and it tasted like chalk. Fill the front of your head with declared things, and the back would behave.

The water gave way to Bloom. It's always a strange moment. Liquid has weight, it has the decency to press evenly, to remind you in every thin finger of current that physics is still in charge. The Bloom slides around you like a caul. The suit's gland vents activated and pumped out nutmeg and bitter green to dull the receptors in my sinuses and tongue, a blanding fog to keep the synesthetic edges from flaying me open.

It didn't matter. The first thread brushed my left shoulder and I was five years old and scratching mosquito bites behind my knees with sandy fingers and someone's mother was calling, baked wind and peeled paint and the aching good hurt of running, and then it slid, sweetness dissolving into heat and stubble against my jaw and the taste of someone else's mouth and the thought there's always a window, always, if you keep looking—

I blew out air hard through my nose and squeezed my eyes against the lights that weren't there. I wrapped the catch line twice around my wrist. The Bloom caressed my faceplate with oily whorls. Sound shivered faintly through the suit: the city's low breath, the cluck of a lone boat hull, the far-off thump of the thermal plant waking up a turbine.

Salt. Tin. Cardamom, tanged with dread.

"You're below," Jun said in my ear. Tamsin somewhere behind him, a silence pressed into a human shape. "Lucky. Sine's boat just got sniffed by the Bureau. Two riders."

"Stay off the comms beyond status," Tamsin said. "No talk about names."

"I'm down," I said. My voice sounded low and fuzzy. "Bloom's thick. Pulling west quadrant first. Keep me four meters from the net."

Jun muttered agreement. The cradle rope hissed as they let me drift.

There's an art to harvesting. You can't snatch. You can't ignore. The waiting and the going are the same motion. The Guild teaching songs call it listening, but it's not sound. The threads of memory in the Bloom aren't neat foreign bodies you pluck like pearls. They're polymer sacks full of a thousand quickly written letters jostling to be read. They bump and tumble and give off their flavors, and if you push your face against the glass they will push back and try to get in.

We are porous. That is the terrible beauty of us.

I opened my hands and let the suit's tiny strobes emit a pulse train, a tiny shimmering lure. Mnemosytes are simple, hungry things. They flocked to the glitter and warmth. They liked sugar. They liked saline. They liked drama.

The first strong thread came right, a bright slick rope of it like a jellyfish axle, and I hooked a loop without touching it, letting the harness spool it into a capture bladder at my hip. The bladder hummed, nanofilters nibbling away until what lay in its solution was only a clean copy of the train the Guild used, a sequence of chemical doorways we could open back at the shop and let a citizen of Port Grey step through and be ten years and twenty-eight centiliters in love for a few minutes for twenty credits.

First pulls are always lovers and the first taste of mango. People shed their happiness without trying. It drifts to the top like foam. I got three in a row, then an old dog dying in a lattice of afternoon light, then a crash—metal screams and the hollow in a chest where something used to beat. The flavor of the crash was sour and left my lip numb through the mouthpiece. The dog made me think of mine, a long-dead thing with wet eyes named Slug, and I swore at the Bloom inside my helmet for its kindness. It did not care.

I collected a birthday where everyone was late; I collected a stage fright so sharp I had to flex my fingers like they weren't mine. I bagged them neat and labeled them in my head and let the suit's paddle jets push me along the line Tamsin had set in my route map.

And then I felt it. No, that's wrong. Feeling is like a fresh cut, hot and close. This was the sense of a room two doors over catching fire. The cold change of air before a storm blooms in the bones.

The Bloom around me slid. If you had asked me later to find the word for it, I would have said it leaned.

What tastes like blue and tin at the same time? The breath before lightning. The memory hitting my shoulder didn't so much touch me as mean to. It pressed not into the suit but through it, a closeness like the inside of my own mouth. The suit vented more blanders. The syrinx in my mouth pushed an extra spray. It sliced through like perfume through fog.

Don't open your mouth. Don't swallow.

I was walking down a staircase. It was lightless and narrow and it had a dampness to it that told me it was close to the sea, even if you didn't see the green on the bricks. I could smell iron. My hand was on the rail, and it was thick and worn in the places where rings had rubbed it for a hundred years. Someone had left a shopping bag on the landing two steps down, white plastic that caught at my calf.

The weight of what was waiting below me was wrong and right, like the heaviness of a storm overhead when you know you forgot to bring the laundry in. There was grit under my shoe.

And I knew this staircase.

Every diver has anchor places. The Dockside Steps were one of mine. Every schoolchild in Port Grey had fallen on them at least twice. I could hear the city through them: the slap of water on stone, the shift of gulls. I could hear someone breathing below. No—someone not wanting to breathe. Someone shaping silence with their whole body.

My hand slid on the rail. I was careful. I counted: nine to the first landing, twelve to the second, nine again. I could feel the place where the brick was chipped on the seventh, where someone—me?—had done it with the heel of a boot last summer when Jun was making me laugh so hard I couldn't see.

I stopped on the ninth step.

You stop there because that's where the view shifts; the wall on your right ends and you get a slice of the lower landing and the warped painting someone had stapled to the corkboard. You stop there because if you go any further the person below you will know you're coming.

On the ninth step I knew three things at once.

I knew that the smell of iron wasn't from the rail. It was thicker, sweet. It was blood.

I knew the person below and the shape of their shoulder and the way their hair lay against their neck where it always escaped the clip, and that knowing opened a hole in me like a hatch ripping off the side of a plane.

I knew it was my hand on the rail. My hand with the small white scar down one knuckle from the time I had slid on the concrete outside Finn's and counterweighted myself on a trash bin to keep from falling on a basket of egg tarts.

I knew it was me.
