The Bloom shook me like a dog, three points of impact from three different directions. Something scraped along my back. My mouth was open. I was saying words that I had not yet said.

"Find me on the ninth step, and don't bring the Bureau."

There isn't much you can do inside a dive suit when your body decides it's somewhere else. The technicians would tell you the more accurate term is entrainment: your own little knots of microcircuitry begin to vibrate at the frequencies they've evolved to mimic, and because of the way our brains love a pattern, your big circuits try to make sense and snap to. The blanders smother, the strobes confuse, your training tells you to breathe and check your heart rate, recite your anchors and kick for the surface if you have to.

I didn't kick.

A diver who believes more than she should is a hazard to herself and to others. I wasn't believing anything. I was making lists in my head very quickly and dropping each item into a bucket labeled maybe so that I could throw the whole bucket into Tamsin's face and then run.

On the ninth step. Do not bring the Bureau.

There are people in Port Grey who would call it a Drift, capital D. Drifts are illegal. It's not what drones on the morning shows say they are, it's not a dirty little sex-high you get to excuse your weak morals. It's a harm. It's a wrong. It's when the Bloom sets up housekeeping in the corners of your mind and begins to misfile everything. You leave the stove on and you are happy about it. You don't recognize your wife's laugh and it tastes like soap. You forget the shape of the letter b. Drift too far and you wake up and the person in your head with your name is someone you don't like.

What I had was not a Drift. What I had was a thread in my capture bladder that didn't have a license signature, didn't have a remnant of someone's breath patterns, didn't have the aftertaste of a stranger. It tasted like my own mouth.

I moved very carefully. My knees were shaking. My heart was either too fast or too slow. I did two pulls in quick succession and labeled them in a way that didn't hang in front of my face, and then I palmed the bladder with the staircase memory and slid it under the right strut of the cradle where the suit camera would register it as a stray.

"Status, Mara," Tamsin said. Her voice sounded like a rope across a stone.

I forced breath past the thing that had caught, counted four, counted four again. "Third strap full. Moving toward west catch for Finn's. Bloom is high tin. Blander efficiency down to seventy. I'm fine."

"You got tin?" Jun said, sharply. "You taste any cardamom? You need me to bump you?"

Don't bump me. If he pulled me up fast with that in my bladder and the Bureau riders decided to be thorough, if they came aboard and did what they are so fond of doing and took my breath into their little pops and ran it over their little boards, they would find everything I had been within the last fifteen minutes and they would fine us out of our next three months of permits and take away Tamsin's pride in one sideways look.

"I got it," I said. "I can sit with the tin."

"Hum a scale for me," Tamsin said.

"E flat," I said.

"Don't be cute."

"E, F sharp, A, B," I sang, very quietly. The notes were steady. The inside of my mouth was a citrus wedge and the outside of my face was a calm sea.

They let me finish the pull. I packed bladders and labeled them, cheap in my head, fixable if the Bureau demanded to see the logs. I did not touch the rail of the cradle with my left hand because it felt like if I did I would fall straight into myself and would keep falling. At one point a gull landed on my helmet and let its claws scratch down. The Bloom laughed in my ears like cousins around a table after a funeral. I sang scales until Tamsin told me to stop threatening her sense of music and to get my ass out of the water.

Jun hauled me in hand over hand like we were in some fairy tale and I was an eel. My knees went soft and he caught me with a hand under my harness and I slid into the grate with an undignified grunt. Tamsin reached down and clicked me out of the mouthpiece and lifted it away. The morning air hit me like a slap. Everything stank of fuel and salt and yeast from Finn's dough shop and a faint perfume that might have been my own fear.

"Well?" Jun said. "Are you choir or are you tornado?"

"Slim pickings as always," I said. I peeled off the gloves and flexed my hands. The left shook. I tucked it under the right and pretended it was cold. "Got you some first kisses. A right good wedding in too much sunlight. A broken collarbone. You don't get enough broken collarbones in your repertoire. Builds character."

Tamsin crouched and peered at my mask, held it up to the light and made approving mouth noises. Her big hands gentled over the catches and bottles at my belt, did the count without letting me see her count. She didn't comment on the missing one. She knew how many I had supposed to come up with. She knew my tells.

"We'll take them to Finn's before noon," she said. "You go home, take a shower, drink something that isn't made in a vat, and don't suck on a cinnamon stick like you're clever. If you sneeze blue, you call me."

"Who sneezes blue?" Jun said. He leaned over to retie the coil. "If she sneezes blue, I get half her take."

"If she sneezes blue, you get me to the hospital and you tell them she didn't go past the line," Tamsin said. Her face had gone flat. "And you keep your mouth shut about riders."

Jun shut his mouth. His eyes flicked over my shoulder and I didn't turn to look.

"Two on the water," he said after a moment.

The Bureau riders were never subtle, and they never needed to be. They like to make you look at them. The boat that pulled up alongside was clipped, metal sorted by someone with an anxious hand. Two riders in sea-leather, Tyrian jackets over it like they were bored of their own sin. Wet hair combed back. Tag pistols where you could see. The man in front had a freckled face and perfect teeth. The woman behind him was blank as a chalkboard.

"Guild operators," the freckled one said. "Routine survey. Any unlicensed drift or personal harvest this morning? Any large-scale Bloom disturbance?"

"No and no and no," Tamsin said, all bland. "You want to step aboard and inspect? We are always happy to assist the Bureau in safeguarding the minds of the people of Port Grey."

They did step aboard. They always do. The freckled one took my belt in his hands with a movement that was almost intimate and sniffed at the bladders like he had a dog in his head that would tell him if I was lying. He made a note on his slate that hummed when his fingernail touched it. His partner moved around with a sensor that was mostly theater. She held it near my face for a long breath too long.

"You been under long, diver?" she asked. Her voice didn't fit her mouth. She'd been raised inland.

"An hour and thirteen," I said.

"Any singing?"

"I'm as tone-deaf as my crew will complain about all day," I said.

She didn't smile. She clicked her sensor off. Freckles flipped through our work tickets and made a show of frowning at taxes and then passed them back without saying the word fine, because they didn't want to write anything down for a morning this small. It was enough to be seen.

"Keep your lines," he said, which was Bureau for be good. "There's talk of a heavy east current. The plant's spinning up. You know what that does."

We knew. When the thermal plant draws big, the Bloom shivers and thins and can tear in great flower-petal rips across the bay. It moves strange. It can spit up deep things. It can tuck secrets into corners you thought clean.

"We'll mind," Tamsin said.

They went away, and Jun exhaled in a way that made him seem younger by a year. Tamsin thumped the deck, once. She didn't look at me.

"What did you put under the cradle?" she asked.

"Tin," I said.

"Tin," she repeated.

"Someone's iron. Old steps," I said, evasive as smoke. "I'll come back for it."

"No," she said. "You'll tell me what you put under the cradle. And then you'll come back for it and do what you're supposed to do with it."

I crouched and reached under, fingers finding the warm plastic of the stray bag by feel. The little fish-hook things we use to keep them from drifting had snagged it door-tight. I pulled it free and cradled it like a bird. When I held it the hair on my arms rose.

"It's a Dockside Steps," I said.

"Those steps have fifty threads a week," Jun said. "Every fool's been kissed and kicked on those steps since the city started falling in love with itself."

"It's mine," I said.

Jun made a soft, rude sound in his mouth with his tongue on his teeth, something he did when he suspected me of lying in a way that was going to cost him something.

"You've never been that arrogant," he said. "Not out loud."

"It's about me," I amended. "It belongs to me. And it hasn't happened yet."

The silence after that wasn't the kind that falls. It was the kind that arrives on purpose and sits down and waits for you to explain yourself.

"Drift," Jun said, not like an accusation, but like a diagnosis.

"No," I said.

Tamsin took the bag from me without hurry and held it up the way she had held my mask. She didn't unscrew the top. She didn't have to. She tilted it back and forth and watched the golden smear inside reorient itself with the gravity of the boat. She was a woman who could tell a wind direction from the color of a shirt hung in a window two streets away; she could tell a mood from a posture at thirty yards. She watched the smear like it was telling her a story in a language she only half-remembers.

"You going to tell me why you didn't toss this the instant you knew it had your taste?" she said.

"I wanted to know," I said, and that wasn't the whole of it. The whole of it had a shape like a person standing at the bottom of a set of steps with their back turned to me and the simple dull knowledge that if I didn't go there now, some door would close that wouldn't open cleanly again.

"You know what happens when the Bureau decides a diver's picking personal?" she said.

"I didn't pick it," I said. "It picked me."

"Oh, is that so?"

"It's on the ninth step," I said. "There's blood."

Jun made the soft sound again. "Whose?"

"I don't know," I said, and that was the truth, but in the place in my chest where I keep things I won't say I did know whose hair that was escaping its clip, I did know the step where my heel would catch because I'd been cocky once when I was drunk. The Bloom didn't make such small things. I did.

"There's a rule," Tamsin said finally. "Always has been. You don't steal. You don't swallow. You don't talk about seeing around corners, because no one's going to believe you if they don't want to and the ones who do will bite you and put you in a jar. You want to keep working? You want to keep your lungs? Then we play it square. Obey the rule."

"Yes," I said. "After."

"After what?"

"After noon," I said. "After Finn's. After you collect the vouchers. After I go to the Dockside Steps and see whether anyone left a bag on the landing."

"No," Tamsin said.

"Yes," I said.

Jun looked between us like a crow looking for the shiniest trouble.

"You'll bring her," Tamsin said to him. "You'll bring her back by the ear if you have to."

"You just told me not to bring the Bureau," I said.

"I didn't," she said. "Whatever voice in your head did can go to hell. I am not the Bureau. I am your boss. I will stand on the landing and knit and watch you have your little private drama, and if a man in a jacket the color of grapes shows up I will hit him where it hurts and you will run."

A slow heat flowered under my ribs. The shape of the world steadied the way it does when someone older than you consents to your sin.

"Okay," I said. "Noon, then."

"No," Tamsin said again, softer. "Now."

"You just said—"

"I said we'd deliver to Finn's before noon," she said, "and we will. You'll be up and down those steps quick as the gods used to be. We'll do it before the plant yanks the Bloom into wrack and someone else sees what you saw and decides it belongs to them."

Jun grinned without humor. "You picked a good morning to flirt with fate, Greywater," he said. "I can hear it whispering."

There are cities where fate has better things to do. In Port Grey it watches the tide in and out with patience it learned from the sea.

We wrapped the bladders and stowed the bulk into the lockbox welded to the deck and drew the canvas and threw the chain. Jun took the tiller in hand like he loved it and coaxed the old boat away from the pier, and the Bloom eddied around our hull like breath made visible.

The Dockside Steps were cut into the seawall between the Deux-Ports statue and the place where the Wharf Rats liked to believe no one would notice their trading. There were three sets. If you were from the south side you had loyalties, you argued about which set was true, you got shoved into the one you hated and you fell on your tailbone into a fish scale mosaic. The one I knew like my own teeth was the middle. Someone had painted a warning on the wall there once: Do Not Feed the Bloom. Rain had run it into a watercolor of grief.

I went first. Tamsin had a coil of rope around her shoulder as if this were a rescue and not a decision she had allowed. Jun wore his cap pulled down and hid a wooden spoon in his sleeve, for luck or for a joke.

The city at mid-morning was itself: a market of fish and paper, a shout, a clank, a smell of oil and salt and cheap sugar. A girl with kohl around her eyes and a swoop to her walk leaned against the statue base and pretended not to see us. She saw everything. Everyone did. The riders' boat idled in the middle distance, stupid as a thumb.

I counted in my head. Anchor. Name. Year. The small white scar on my knuckle. There were nine steps to the first landing. There had always been nine.

When I put my foot on the first one a film of something slick took my weight and held it differently, as if the stair had been waiting all morning for the foot that made it true.

"Nine," I said.

"Don't be poetic," Jun muttered behind me.

"I don't know how," I said, and put my foot on the second, and then the third. A gull cried the same not-words, and the light at the bottom was a round coin of green and the air smelled of iron and the wind pushed in coming from the south.

The plastic bag was there on the landing.

It was white, with red letters bleeding from a bakery on Thirteenth, and it was tipped so that it caught someone on the calf if they weren't looking and the ridges of the steps fit into its creases like fingers closing.

Tamsin made a sound. It wasn't surprise. It was the sound she makes when she sees a man about to walk under a falling thing and she can't get to him but she can get to his answer.

I didn't wait. I stepped down one more step and looked. There was a person on the lower landing, their back to me, their shoulders hunched and the line of their spine like the stroke of a pen writing no. Their hair had come out of its clip in a little handful at the nape.

She turned. The blood on her hands was so bright it was like a painting of blood.

"Mara," she said, and it was my name like a bell.

I don't remember moving. I was on the ninth step and then I was on the seventh without having put my foot down and then I was kneeling on the landing where the damp gets into your clothes and stays, and the person I'd known would be there was there, a friend I loved and had been avoiding, and on the stones beside her a body lay on its side with the face turned away and the blood making a halo like iron in water, and the city above us went on selling fish and sugar and pretending the sea was only water.

In the hush between pulses, Arin could hear the ship think. The thought was not a sound, not in the way voices or alarms were sounds; it was the memory of a vibration, the ghost pressure of a drumbeat that had just stopped. Under the insulation and polymer and water of the deep bay, the Transit Grace hummed in a tone too low for bone but perfect for blood. Arin had learned to know what the hull meant when it carried that tone.

Now it meant a question.

He drifted on his back in the observation well, palms tucked to his ribs, the suit’s webbing tight across his shoulders. The water around him was so clear it didn’t exist until he moved, until his knee brushed through and sent long threads of air spiraling like loose silk. Beside him and above him and below—orientation had lost the right to own those words—twelve thousand cubic meters of ocean cupped itself inside the starship like a held breath. Arin had grown up in lakes, freshwater green and silt-tasting. This was not like that. Salt lifted him higher; his tongue clicked with brine; everything was lighter than he remembered the world being.

“Ease,” he said, and the binaural mics stitched his voice into a line and dropped it into the bay. The water carried it slow, the way a word travels across a long room. “Darya, ease.”

The oldest singer in the pod hung a few meters beyond his toes. She could have fit three of him in her throat. Her skin was a galaxy of scars: pale slashes from long-ago ice, puckered circles from implant ports grown over and sealed smooth. When she opened her mouth, her baleen was a dark fence of hair; when she closed it, her eye blinked once, then again, independently, the way she always did when she was thinking hard.

She was thinking hard now. They all were. The whales were quiet, which was not their nature. They would be more honest for it later.

Another tremor came through the hull—there and gone, under the range of the ship’s official senses, but not beyond the membrane. Arin felt it in his ribs, not as a sound but as the absence of one. Something had rung the Grace, and somewhere beyond the etching in the light-years that their flight would carve, the ring had hit a boundary and reflected.

He flicked two fingers and drew the hud into his visor. The scatterplots leapt into existence, bundles of pale-blue lines like hair caught on a comb. The ship’s gravitational lidar—nonsense, an engineer would have called it that. The naming mattered, to Arin, to the singers. We name that which saves us. Call it what it is. They called the instruments Lensors and they called the redshifted hum the Choir. Maps of the Choir draped across space, revealing not the stars themselves but the persistent curves of their ability to bend what passed by.

The curves before him were wrong.

“Grace,” he said. “Say that again.”

The ship obliged. Its voice was patient and human-warm and almost gendered, and it would have sounded tender even if it had been fed through the hull and out of range. It obeyed the pronunciation preferences he had coded into it and lengthened its vowel just enough. “Arin? We registered an event in the segment ahead. A transitory curvature. Duration six microseconds, amplitude at sensor deck two. Would you like to view in projected? Warning that the mapping error is above hundred percent. Arin, we are yet within the safe interval to correct course.”

He turned the projection around with his hand. The safe corridor—threading between nodes of mass like a needle whose eye flexed in and out—looked fine. It was fine. They had been living with fine for days. The Transit Grace was on a course cut by the last ship to make it through the Sagittarian Sheaf intact. That one had dropped comms for thirty hours, then emerged with half its mirrors cracked clean through and a wake like a bell’s aftersound. The pilot on that run had logged nothing but the word noise eight hundred times in a row, as if the repetition could capture it.

After that, the Fund had insisted on singers. Quiet never stays quiet when money is frightened. The whales had been pressed back into service.

Arin shifted in the harness until his stomach touched the bay’s central column. He folded his arms across it and let the column’s slight warmth seep into his skin. It was an old habit. He had done the same when he was twelve, pressed against a weir strut as Darya passed him and the water lifted him in her slipstream.

“Darya,” he said, softer now. “What do you hear?”

The whale turned her head and showed him her pale underside. Her left pectoral fin—longer than his old apartment—flexed in place, the internal musculature rolling like dunes. The photic implants along its trailing edge pinged a code, low and lazy: Remember when you asked if the rain could be taught to fall.

They always answered in jokes. It was their way of having two conversations at once.

Arin blinked back his reply on the same channel: The rain only thinks it chooses. We put our buckets where we know it will pass.

A younger singer, Quince, skated past Darya and rocked on his side. His paint blazes—thin lines of pigment sealed under skin—rose and fell with his breath. The pattern marked him as of Caribbean stock, though everyone in the pod carried fragments from three oceans like ancestry braided into their bodies. Quince’s reply was a fast flicker: I did not ask about rain. I asked what it is that bangs walls without hands.

“That’s fair,” Arin said. “You always were impatient.”

Outside the bay, the ship’s upper decks hummed with their own impatience. He could picture it: Mx. Sun-Ya, their administrative lead, threading her fingers together and taking them apart again as the nav staff recited numbers at her. Khouri at Flight, his hair in rough ropes, shrugging as if that could draw tension off his chest. They would be waiting for him to say yes, they should burn a little, slide a little, choose a lane that did not pass so near to whatever was making the Grace ring.

He was supposed to say yes. The Fund’s recommended protocols were very clear. If your whales grew quiet, you listened to your whales but you also moved.

“Crew to Bay One,” the ship said. “Arin. Mx. Sun-Ya requests you at the aft projectors.”

“I’m in the water,” he answered.

There was the barest hint of disapproval in the ship’s pause. It didn’t come from the AI. It came from the syndicate that owned and maintained this particular stack of algorithms. In their opinion, caretakers did not swim during instrument check. In their opinion, the animals did not need to see our eyes when we asked them to work.

Darya closed the space between them and slipped beneath him. Being near her made him younger. She had never tried to drown him, not even when he was small and she was angry and the line had been shoved through her and cinched to a bar, when they had been doing it all wrong. She had let him put his hand on her eye and feel the muscles there click and twitch against his palm. Once, twenty years later, in a storm on an open sea he had thought was their last, she had done the same.

“I will come up,” he told the ship. “Give me sixty seconds.”

He dipped his face beneath the surface and opened his eyes. The world sharpened, as he had known it would, and a hundred lines of light leapt across the whales’ skins as the implant nets talked and laughed. Something had shifted in the pod's posture. They were not just quiet. They were waiting.

For what, he didn’t know. But he could guess. They belonged to a world of gradient and persistence, of long swells, of notes thick enough to push whole bodies. The electric laughter around their fins was theirs but not primary. When something spoke that did not belong to that first world, they felt it like a wrong pressure against their tongues.

The event that had made the ship think was shaped like song.

He popped up, wiped his face with his forearm, and swam for the ladder. When he turned, Darya had followed him to the edge of the well; her rostrum was there, like a cliff’s face rising out of a night sea. He caught the rail and held himself up in the water and put his hand against her lip ridge. She nearly smiled. That particular quirk was her favorite thing she had learned that belonged to humans and not whales.

“Sing it to me,” he said.

She did not sing in the voice that would rattle the marrow out of him. The bay was not where they practiced that voice. She used her projectors instead—a row of precision plates along her spine that could vibrate with micrometer calibration, throwing energy into the water at frequencies the hydrophones could catch and reshape. He felt the first line in his face, not his ears; the pattern slid right under his skin and made a place there like it had been waiting since he was born.

Something else waited with it. A signature. No. A fingerprint.

“It’s not from us,” Quince flashed. Darya’s big left fin flicked assent.

The map in Arin’s visor tracked the song. The song was not notes. It was a carved framework of time. It said: here and here are holes in the slope; you may put your keel here. It said: the cliff seems sheer but there is a shelf. It said: you may cross a river if you learn it. The shelf was not supposed to exist. No chart put it there. No mathematics of the region permitted anything stable that close to the primary well.

“Grace?” he said. “Overlay that with the last-known traversal of the Aster Demeter.”

The translucent line of the older ship appeared, ghosting through their corridor and then arcing away. It didn't intersect what Darya was singing. It nearly did. There was a gap there, a thin wedge, a thing like any sailor would look at and see and decide: not this time.

He flipped up the visor. “Darya, where did you hear that?”

She blinked, once and then again. Her implants flittered: Do not turn away yet.

“It’s returning?” The sudden dryness in his mouth surprised him. “You think it’s an echo.”

The word was imprecise. They all were. Their physics teams taught accuracy and scarcity. The whales had other uses. Their best translations of the word Arin needed were a kind of negation: you threw something out into a canyon. It did not come back like itself. It came back wearing a story. That story was imposed by the canyon. It carried news of the canyon’s shape.

“Arin.” The ship slid back in, softer than before. “Khouri would like—”

“Tell Khouri to wait.”

He pulled himself up the last rungs, stepped onto the platform, and let the drainage fans strip the water from his skin in a white roar. A strip of cloth with the pod’s symbol lay on the handrail. He wrapped it around his wrist because he always did. The doors opened for him with an almost audible relief at the human in the corridor again.

He moved odd in the gravity—the small constant fraction the Grace kept to protect her spin and her fragile parts. The wolf-cat gait of space workers had never suited him. He liked having legs. He preferred the way the bay let his body be a long and flowing thing.

Khouri stood in the projector room with his mouth set to polite. He was a big man who had run out of space to carry his strength and started laying it across his grin. He had stopped grinning some months ago. This mission would pay him enough to happy himself for a while, provided he lost nothing crucial between here and the other side.

“We can push fifteen meters up,” he said as soon as Arin stepped in. “Aim us off the line. We can buy ourselves breathing room. We can buy you time for your…for the singers.”

“They need more than fifteen meters.”

“They can have hundreds when we are not about to get hammered by something I cannot name.”

“It’s a song,” Arin said.

Khouri blinked and then did not roll his eyes and still managed to project the sense of having done so. “And your whales know it.”

“My whales are hearing it.”

“Captain.” Mx. Sun-Ya had a talent for making a man with bars behave like a boy in a school. She wore her silver hair in a coil that might have been steel cable. The left side of her jaw shone faintly with an overlay implant—communication, control, a hundred microtools the Fund had bought her after the second time she kept a ship and its cargo alive by doing math no human should have to do. Of the three people in the room, she had survived the most to arrive at the privilege of impatience.

She gave Arin a look he knew too well. It measured him and decided how much of him she could afford to cut away. “The whales are trembling,” she said.

“Yes.”

“They are braver than I am. Khouri, fifteen meters won’t do it. If we’re going to move, we move.”

“We stay,” Arin said. “At least as long as it takes me to—” His hand wanted to drift to his wrist, to the strip of cloth, and he folded his arms to keep from fidgeting. “We’ve been following a corridor that was cut by a ship half-blind. It wasn’t hearing this. Something’s there. We wanted a better map. We kill our one chance to have it if we break now.”

“If we die,” Khouri said very gently, “the map is worse.”

Sun-Ya turned her face slightly to the glass. Through it, the bay shimmered, a bowl of black with stars pricked in it where sensors looked back at sensors. The whales moved like planets. The lights under their skin glowed, brief as caught breath, communicating to one another and to the ship, knitting a world Arin had learned to read as if it were script.

“Show me,” she said.

He pulled up the recording and laid it into the projector. Shy as it was, no human ear would have caught it—the pattern lay at the edge where the Grace’s senses, hard and stubborn as they were, could just barely lay hands on it. The projector broadened it, bent time, shaped the long line into something it could show on a human scale.

It sounded lonely. Arin had the unscientific sense that if he spoke back to it, it would lean.

Khouri rubbed his face. “It’s not geological,” he said, and then laughed and shook his head at himself. “What does geological even mean here.”

“Something is giving the bay a series of shapes,” Sun-Ya said. “What are we hearing the first of? Seven? Ten?”

Arin found himself whispering. “It’s singing.”

“Not the whales.”

“No.”

“And the signature on it?” Sun-Ya’s eyes turned to him. She was a woman who never asked a question without already knowing the answer. It was her way of shepherding you toward your own.

He could have lied. Pretended it was new. He didn’t know why it mattered that he did not.

“The timing increments,” he said. “The ratio between the long pulses and the short—if you plot it against the conversions we use when we teach the pod their interlocks, the way we keep them on axis.” He gestured, impatient with the need to put math in his mouth. “The phrase is mine.”

Something close to curiosity softened Sun-Ya’s expression. “What phrase.”

“It’s a piece I use when they’re tired. It means: Wait. Rest your throat against the warm wood. I’ll fill your cups. I used to hum it to Darya when we were hauling her along piers that were too small. It isn’t one of the Fund’s patterns. It’s ours.”

Khouri let out a breath that might have been a laugh if he had remembered how. “Of course it is.”

“It doesn’t mean someone’s out there who knows you’re here,” Sun-Ya said, not unkindly. “It means something used the shape of something you made because your whales were near and that was the easiest way to get a message across. It means your whales have been teaching the void songs, Arin. It means the void sings back with your vowels.”

“Of course it does,” he said. His hands had a life of their own and wanted badly to be in water again. He took a step toward the glass instead. Darya had not left the edge of the well. She was waiting for him to come back and say what he would do.

The deck trembled. It was not a shiver. It was a slow-centering weight, the way a body sets itself before lifting something it knows is heavy. Every projection on the wall tremored, then steadied into lines that were cleaner than they had been; the error bars contracted as the ship’s model found something to fasten on.

The signature returned.

It came not at their instruments’ edge but right into their hands. It was louder. It had chosen them or had been amplified by the canyon of space in a way that made choosing irrelevant. Arin did not trust himself to speak for a moment. If it was his, it could not be anything good. Good things did not know how to wrap their mouths around your name.

“Grace,” Sun-Ya said, very calm. “Where is it.”

The ship was no longer patient. It had the sound of a woman holding two doors open with both hands and wanting badly to know which one would be slammed first. “A vector from starboard aft. Negative three degrees. Danger potential unresolved. Mx. Sun-Ya. The carve indicated is—there is no carve. Arin, there is no carve. The space is not there. The track is not there. The map says no.”

“Maps can be wrong,” Arin whispered.

“Gravity,” Khouri said under his breath, like a prayer or a curse. “The worst of teachers.”

“Darya,” Sun-Ya said, and her voice softened not because she knew how to talk to whales but because she had watched men and women and animals die as responses to tone as much as to action. “Precious. Do not answer.”

Darya’s fin-lights pulsed once, polite acknowledgment. Quince’s followed, impatient as ever. Another, older calf—Sera—flashed a chaotic bristle Arin interpreted as I want to. They would hold, for a breath. They would not hold for long. They were made to sing back. All animals are, and some men, and some machines.

Arin had thought he would have more time before this choice fell into his hands. He had believed he would go a dozen voyages with whales and learn to be good at it and come away with money and a limp and the immense relief of having chosen nothing beyond yes and no, forward and back.

A voice spoke in the projector room that was not the ship’s, and not the whales’, and not a handsome sequence of numbers strung like beads around a curve. It came in the same precise register that the hydrophones had learned to favor, because it helps to tune a signal to the shape of the ear that will receive it. It said three words in a tone that was very like his mother’s when she put a hand on his hair as if she would calm him by writing something at the base of his skull.

Hold vector, child.

All the air in the room became salt; Arin tasted it and almost choked. It could have been anyone. It was the oldest of phrases. It was the kind of thing engineers taught ships to say when men couldn’t hear them and needed to pretend tenderness was a tool. It could have been a ham-fisted piece of art drawn by the void to keep them here until some tidal effect crushed them flat.

Then the voice did the thing that unstitched him, that gave his shaking mind the shape of an answer whether or not any answer existed. There is a way to speak to whales that is not theirs and not ours. It is a small push on a joint you will only find if your hand has rested there a thousand hours. The voice made that push. The bay’s water trembled along the exact curve of the hymn he had taught Darya when she could not stop hurting after the metal bit had torn her jaw. She had carried it for years without singing it to any other human.

“Khouri,” Sun-Ya said. “Lock.”

He did. Arin heard the stutter of clamps and felt the fine shift as the Grace tucked her metaphorical knees into her chest, making herself small and careful.

“We do not have time to calculate,” Sun-Ya said. Her hands were open, empty. “We will not be idiots. We will not chase phantoms into walls. But we will not throw away a shelf handed to us by something that knows how to speak our names. If this is a trap, it has earned our attention. Arin. Give me a way to keep them alive.”

He was already moving. The commemorative cloth on his wrist clung wet and stubborn. He wanted to rip it off and throw it into the bay the way he had when he was seventeen and ready to hate every person in a white coat who told him to be careful with something he loved. He did not. He drank a breath and dropped into the ladder and let himself fall back toward the water that knew what to make of his weight.

The whales had taken the shape of the circle they made when they wanted to decide something. Darya at one side, Quince opposite, Sera hovering between, the smaller ones arranging themselves like notes hung across a staff. Their lights showed the words they did not yet put into water. They needed permission the way only creatures who had once been denied it need it.

“Listen to me,” Arin said, loud enough that the hydrophones would not have to guess. “We are going to hear and not answer. Tie your tongues to your teeth. Touch the bottom of your mouths with your minds and say stay. Do not throw yourself against an opening the way you did when we were young and silly and thought we could make storm-windows hold the sea back. Darya. I am going to speak into you and show you the line I think there is.”

He had no right to do this. He was a translator, not a pilot. But all the old names frayed in the spaces between stars.

He pressed his palm to Darya’s implant port and felt the comfort of a thing you had built that had not broken. He sent the phrase. It was simple and ugly and functional—too many corners, not enough the long, loving curve whales preferred. She took it anyway, softened it, wrapped it in a fabric of air and mineral and distributed weight that remade it into something that could move a ship and not tear it apart.

The hull hummed again. This time the tone had an answer, not just a question.

Sun-Ya’s voice pinged the bay. “Khouri. On his mark. Grace, confine failsafes to parameters beta one through three. I will take your hands if you try to stop me.”

“Affirm,” the ship said, and if there was an echo of affection in its tone, Arin did not imagine it. He had taught her the place in the joint, too.

The voice returned. It did not say anything simple. It delivered a sequence of closures and releases in a cadence that made his chest ache. It showed him a very small way through something very large. He thought of walking down the spine of a rotted log and putting his feet only where the moss was just visibly thicker. He thought of his father kneeling in a boat with his hand under the keel, feeling for hidden rocks. He thought of Darya once in a long-ago river, laughing so hard under a bridge that she had tipped him off and let him stay under, nose pressed to skin, trusting him to know the difference between danger and joy.

“Mark,” he said.

Darya’s song went from thoughtful to teeth. The pod’s body became a chorus. The Transit Grace leaned into the shelf that did not exist. The hull made a sound like a whale’s back when it broke a wave. On the other side of the glass, stars bent around them like reeds around a barrel. The projector room lights went out for an instant and came back blue. Khouri did not swear; he made a noise like he had once learned the taste of fear and found it tolerable in small doses.

The bay’s pressure changed. The pod did not complain. When they had been at this long enough, the whales had taught Arin a difference he had not known how not to know. Some pressures are sudden and singular and almost clean, like getting bitten. Some are long and changing and involve your whole skin. They were in the second kind. He could see in the way Darya’s eye kept moving that she was counting.

The voice came one more time, soft and tender and thin as wire. It fell into his ear with the weight of grief he had been waiting for since it said child.

Hold vector. When you come out, do not look behind you.

Everything in him wanted to ask why. Darya’s fin touched the water near his head, a momentary cool shadow. The contact was accident and intention in equal measure. It broke the little rant his brain had been spinning and let him think.

He breathed. He fixed his hands on the ladder because it gave the animal parts of him something to hold. He waited for the part of the mind that thought in desiccated, nice words like vector to be useful.

He did not look behind him.

The Transit Grace slid into a space the map refused to show. The bay moaned once, a long note that Arin knew a human ear would never have considered music. He held the rung. The water pressed at his shoulders. He counted with Darya. Somewhere in an unkind piece of geography a long time from now, something terrible would break or had broken and they would hear it later. For now, they were inside the canyon. The canyon taught them its shape.

When it let them out, Arin would discover whether the way back was gone forever and if the map needed to know that. He suspected it did. He would discover whether the voice that had come out of the Choir belonged to a trick of the void, to someone’s remnant, or to himself. He would later remember that he had already known at the moment it spoke—because it had found the joint of Darya’s jaw and set a finger there gently—and that knowing would haunt him for longer than it should have.

Now he was content to count and not look behind him and sing a quiet line in his head to keep the whales from getting tired, a line he had taught them when they were silly and was teaching them again now that they were very, very wise.

Rain fell upward on Tiamene, rising in thin, silver needles from the mirror-lake to the sky. Keziah Renn stood at the edge of a pier that wasn’t a pier but the fused spines of an extinct leviathan, the bones polished smooth by centuries of wind. The rain traced her reflection in the water in reverse, her face smudged into a ghost by the shimmer of the pier’s field.

“It’s not weather,” the client said, or the translator said for the client, its voice settling on a human alto for reasons of its own. The client was a torus of translucent tissue and chitin that undulated in the air, three meters from the water and three meters from Keziah, because it had requested symmetrical distances to everything live when it first established the meeting space. Veins pulsed faintly through its skin, carrying pale honey light. A hound-shaped drone lay down at Keziah’s boots with a soft clank and began to recharge off the pier’s hardlight rails, its ears occasionally flicking at the upward rain.

“What is it,” Keziah said, “if not weather?”

“Song,” the client replied. Its ring narrowed and widened, a gesture that the translator claimed was akin to disdain. “This lake sings itself back into the sky. It is a generational song, colonizer. Your underwriters cannot repo a song.”

Keziah smiled despite herself. The hound drone exhaled a small, static-laced sigh. Her ship orbiting above the cloudline sent a ripple of acknowledgement through her jawbone implant, a reminder of the time window. It was early morning by local reckoning and her second case of the day; there were two more sunsets before the enforcement drone cluster deorbited to install the pumps and spindles they’d ordered for this repossession.

“Not repo,” Keziah said. “Salvage. Different regulations. You signed—well, your ancestral cluster signed—a collateral agreement when you took out the ocean-quieting loan.”

The torus rippled. It emitted a hum that the translator ignored, which meant it was untranslatable or offensive, or both. “The storm maps we were given were lies.”

“That’s a claim,” Keziah said. “You can file it. The Cooperative will adjudicate. I’d even advise that you file it. But on the matters of collateral, I have to enforce. This is banal, but banality keeps us all breathing.”

The client was silent long enough that the translator filled the air with a faint pink noise, polite filler. Keziah watched the lake. The upward rain was more rapid at the lake’s center; the effect created an illusion of a silver tree growing out of the water and atomizing at the crown. A flock of flesh-kites wheeled above it, each kite trailing a ribbon of muscle and light that read the humidity and wrote equations in air as performance art. Keziah had enough time to admire the way the kites’ shadows wrote the same equations inverted on the bones of the pier and to decide she would buy a noodle cone from the vendor at the shore on her way back to the shuttle.

“My clutch will be destroyed,” the torus said finally. It dimmed, which the translator whispered meant seriousness. “Our unborn depend on this cycle.”

“Then help me classify,” Keziah said. “Is your lake's song natural? Indigenous to the lake before your engineering? If so, your contract classifies it as domestic-kinectic, and domestic kinetic features are protected. Or was it induced by the underlake vibratory towers you installed after you took the loan? If so, the song is an artificial byproduct of the installation, and it’s excluded.”

“The towers are old,” the client said, and dimmed further, then flared. “They were old when we took them. They were like bones, like this pier. We turned them on. We do not understand them.”

Keziah held up her hand, which told the drone dog to stop broadcasting local thermal maps and told her ship to overlay files. A skein of text ghosted in her left eye, thick with references in three languages and four numerologies. Tiamene’s public admixture registry suggested the underlake towers had been there long before the torus’ people farmed these shores, long before anyone she could trace. Someone had nipped into the towers’ code around the time of the ocean-quieting agreement and inserted a throttle.

“Run me the initial claim,” Keziah said to the air. “Name-stack and wet signatures.”

The hound drone, which the ship routinely used like a portable terminal for meetings where showing a visible console looked unfriendly, lifted its head and projected a neat column of glyphs onto the air above the pier. The underlake towers were indeed listed as heritage infrastructure, recognized under half a dozen interstellar archaeological compacts. The throttle insertion was brash, spackled in a style popular with human civil-military contractors a century ago.

“Not your work,” Keziah told the torus. “Not your ancestors’ work.”

“Not weather,” the torus insisted stubbornly.

“Song then,” Keziah conceded. She pulled a key from the column of glyphs, let it sink through the air toward her open palm, and watched it dissolve into threads that slithered up her sleeve and into her implant. “Song classified as domestic kinetic soundscape under Heritage, with local continuity predating loan agreement. Which makes it protected, and I can’t touch that part of it if it endangers your clutch.”

The torus brightened in a way the translator could not resist labeling relief.

“But,” Keziah said. The torus dimmed again. “The loan you defaulted on wasn’t to harm your lake. The ocean-quieting was justified because the rogue cyclogenesis was killing your littorals. We can still salvage your default. The enforcement cluster wanted to install three pump arrays and a set of suctions that would cut through your lake’s resonance. That won’t do. But I can propose a swap: they tune their pumps to the humpback currents in the north, where your song doesn’t reach, and I take your default out in brine harvest rights from the kelp farms.”

“You want salt,” the translator breathed, and for the first time Keziah thought maybe it was watching her, siding with her, anthropomorphizing her warmth.

“I want to get the Cooperative off your lake,” Keziah said. “You can’t pay them back in songs. But salt’s salt.”

The torus rotated slowly, its veins glowing in an intricate pattern, then failed to finish whatever gesture it had begun. “Salt reduces,” it said. “Salt is sacred. But it is yours to ask.”

“It is yours to agree,” Keziah said.

“Give us three days,” the torus said, most of its volume turning opaque in emphasis. “We will have the salt ready. No pumps in our song.”

“Two days,” Keziah said. “The enforcement cluster is eager and stupid. I can keep them hung on formalities, but only so long.” She smiled again, and this time it was practiced. “You have my wet to hold them off.”

The torus pulsed acceptance. It extruded a thin golden thread and touched it gently to the hound drone’s snout. The drone’s eye-slit blinked a soft blue as the thread vanished and the drone’s main drive accepted the handshake. Contract resonance. Local gods appeased. Underwriters assuaged.

“Pleasure doing business,” Keziah said. The hound rose and shook itself, sending droplets of upward rain skittering sideways against the pier’s field. Keziah turned toward the shore, toward the noodle vendor and the shuttle that would take her up through the singing rain to the ship that was her home when she wasn’t pretending any place could be.

The message arrived halfway back across the bones, and it arrived in the old way, a hard-angled ache that started in her left molar and sank into her jaw, not the soft suggestions the ship preferred for the purpose of her sleep hygiene. It bypassed the niceties because it had an older priority, the sort of thing buried in protocols written when the first relay between Sol and the stars had lit up a boy’s face on a Cape Coast beach.

She stopped. The rain hissed around her. The hound froze, its paw half-lifted. She let the ache bloom and opened the message.

Notice of Default, it said. The font was plain, the legalese short. Because that was all you needed when you were calling every bondholder to attention at once.

Asset: Stellar Body 1 of its system
Common Name: Sol
Local Alias: the Sun
City: N/A
Coordinates: RA 18:36:56, Dec +38:47:01 (transformations provided)
Lienholder: Interstellar Indemnity and Retrieval Cooperative, collated
Debtor: Solar Assembly of Terra and Sibling Bodies [dissolved], per Assignment B twelve-zero-kappa
Trigger: Silence. Two centuries. No remission.
Proceed with Repossession Plan Theta.

Her first thought was that the coordinates were wrong. Her second was that of course they weren’t; she hadn’t looked up Sol’s corrected coordinates since she was seventeen, when she’d left with everyone else whose family could convert everything they owned into cred and passage. Sol walked the galaxy with the rest of it, and there was more sky now where it had been then.

The third thought was banal but like she had told the torus on the pier, banality keeps you breathing: the way the notice named the debtor. Solar Assembly of Terra and Sibling Bodies. Not Earth Government. Not United Nations. Not any of the flags she had seen and later watched burn, at least on screens. The Assembly. A creature older than any of those, designed by lawyers to outlast ideologues, writing itself into the future in thick, careful lines. The Assembly had used the stars for collateral when the stars had been too far away for almost anyone to reach. And then it had fallen silent.

“Docet,” Keziah said, tugging the noodle vendor’s debt marker free of her bay account without thinking, dropping the heavy paper cone into the hound’s waiting maw. The hound automatically inverted its mouth to keep the noodles safe from upward rain as it trotted behind her. “Tell me it's a bad joke.”

On the other end of the uplink, in orbit, her ship considered how to speak to her now that the ache had subsided and the message had slotted itself into her work queue as if it were any other case. The ship called itself Docet because she had given it that name when she was young and hopeful about being taught. It had a full legal name longer than gardens.

“Not a joke,” Docet said. If it could have sounded gentle, it would have. It tried anyway. “The notice is real. The broadcast channels are burning with it. Ten thousand threads on the co-op board in the time it took you to walk fifty meters. Subtitle fights in five different dialects. Somebody has already minted a memorial coin. Somebody is selling commemorative starshades.”

“Shut up,” Keziah said, and stepped off the last spine and onto the shore.

The noodle seller offered her a paper umbrella. Keziah took it, because the umbrella was printed with tiny dancing fish who appeared to be trying to swim down the umbrella and up the rain, and she was not yet ready to yell where anyone could hear.

“Proceed with Theta,” Docet went on. “Not Beta Eight with all the disclaimers, not Staggered Discretionary. Theta means shades. theta-one means we put the collectors in and you get frost in the tropics by the first winter.”

The noodles in the hound’s mouth steamed gently. Keziah took the cone back and fed the hound a single dumpling. It accepted delicately and licked her knuckles, the motion stuttering slightly as it compensated for the field and the rain. The upward-falling needles of water ticked faintly on her cheeks.

“I can't take it,” she said. “Conflict. History. You know that.” She started walking toward the shuttle. It hunkered on the beach like a beetle, sand and rain sliding off its hull. She wanted it to open and she wanted it to be closed forever.

“The notice was sent to your queue specifically,” Docet said. “I can prove trace. You are primary on the Assembly series. You filed the last sign-of-life two hundred and five years ago.”

She stopped again. A new ache started under her sternum. She didn’t have a word for it.

“That was a child's formality,” she said. “I sent them a packet of signatures from a schoolhouse.”

“And they sent you a mug,” Docet said softly. “Ceramic from a kiln in Lagos. It’s in the galley. It’s chipped.”

Keziah had not been on Earth when they sent that mug. She had been on a ship like a long-boned sea creature, except in the dark instead of an atmosphere, and gravity stuttered when you tipped your head too fast and everyone got nosebleeds and learned to lick them up and laugh. There had been teachers and they had liked what she liked, which was the way systems connected if you could hold them in your head long enough. There had been a girl who sat with her during latencies and taught her to play Spindle while pretending it was a love letter. There had been a photograph she had taped above her bunk, a photograph of a sea she had never seen, a horizon she could not claim.

“It’s not like we can repossess a sun,” she said, and felt the foolishness of the sentence as she said it.

“We cannot move it,” Docet agreed. “But we can cover it. We can extract. We can starve everything that breathes under it. We can leave it a black coin in the sky on a world that will call us demon in a thousand thousand dialects.”

“You sound like you have an opinion,” Keziah said.

“I have many,” Docet said. “I am not expected to share them unless asked. But I know you are going to ask.”

“Not yet,” she said, and then she whispered, “all right. Tell me the escape hatches.”

We tell ourselves there is always an escape hatch. Part of it is faith and part of it is training, and the part that’s training is solid enough to stand on. Docet had a deep cold memory full of documents that had been amended and amended again, accreted around a central fear: that one day the things we mortgaged to build bridges between stars would come due and the bridges would lead home.

“There are time windows we can wedge,” Docet said. “The default was set by silence and dissolution. Silence is hard to speak to; it is what it is. Dissolution can be argued. If the Assembly is not dissolved in a particular legal sense, Theta might be paused. If there exists a surviving sub-entity recognized under prior compacts, we can file remission. We can argue that the collateral was pledged under constraints that no longer apply to the present circumstances of the species; there is precedent for a stay under hardship. Hardship is broad.”

Keziah laughed once. It had no humor in it and it tasted like the metal of the pier had tasted as a child, when she had licked a handrail because it looked like sugar. “Humanity as hardship. Good luck with that.”

“I said precedent,” Docet said. “Not victory. The shades, once deployed, take months to seat. They are cheap to launch and expensive to calibrate because the companies that build them are paid to make mistakes. Our underwriters will not wait for a miracle, but they will be forced to listen to it if there is something to hear.” The ship paused, and when it spoke again it was careful. “You could also take the case to arbitration.”

“No,” Keziah said, too quickly. “No Councils.”

“The Councils will come whether you like them,” Docet said. “There is too much collateral at stake, too many other liens anchored to Sol’s outgoing. It is not just your people who will suffer if Theta proceeds. There are thousands of smaller economies riding the beams.”

“I know,” Keziah said. Her hand had clenched so hard around the umbrella’s stick that a seam had opened along the paper and a line of upward rain had found its way through, needling her palm. The hound rubbed against her shin, trusting that whatever she smelled like now was not fear but the iron-distilled scent of decisions.

They reached the shuttle. Its carapace unfolded like an insect opening its back, a ribbon of humming light leading up into a white interior. The view beyond the threshold was the same view she always had when she climbed in: the slope of the couch that would cradle her, the constellation of status lights that would mirror her heartbeat and lie to her if she begged them to.

She turned back to the lake. The upward rain had thickened; the silver tree now looked like an attempt to reach a god and yank them down by the ankle. The torus client hung a measured distance from the surface, its veins playing a slow, soft song. In the distance, someone had unfurled a sail, and the sail was catching the rain that fell upward, and the boat attached to the sail was doing something like moving.

“You said the Assembly dissolved,” Keziah said, as if Docet had not told her and she had discovered it herself at the bottom of a well where no one could climb to pull her out. “What about—what about the municipal superset? The parliaments? The diaspora? The—”

“Names,” Docet said. “Severed names. Pieces that fit under different umbrellas. The lien sits with the Assembly. It was careful. It was greedy. It did not permit anyone to take its debt without taking its teeth.”

“Comms?” Keziah said.

“Yours are better than most,” Docet said. “If there is a voice left on the home side of the old stargates that can answer a formal call, you can be the one to hear it.”

There are days when you are a vector for someone else's debt and days when your own debt arrives in a neat envelope with your name written in a handwriting you recognize from the inside of your childhood shoe. Keziah stepped into the shuttle, and the shuttle understood that her weight had changed and the day had changed around it. The hound hopped up after her and found its niche, processing the noodles with the content twitch of something that believed in immediate satisfactions. The umbrella folded itself and sucked its paper back into its spine and presented the biodegradable core to a bin labeled with an arrow that probably pointed at a recycling reservoir but could as easily have pointed at a polite hole in the wall.

“Take me up,” Keziah said. “Show me the board. Put in a hold with the Tiamene enforcement cluster. Two days.”

“Done,” Docet said. There was nowhere for the ship to nod in recognition, but it found a sound that meant the same thing, a quiet frictionless click.

As the shuttle rose, the upward rain turned to sideways mist and then to a fine dusting of shining particles that clung to the shuttle’s field in a yearning that made her teeth ache again. The bone pier slipped away like any beautiful lie, the lake spread out like any truth you thought you could hold. The noodle seller waved in a way that suggested he waved like this at anyone who bought noodles from him, but she let herself pretend he waved to her in particular.

In orbit, Docet was already awake in the way that ships were always awake, a readiness that had nothing to do with sleep and everything to do with the number of lives they would hold if something moved wrong. It brought up the board: names and times and debt ladders and a new, bright, terrible line at the top that said SOL in a font more severe than any music. It brought up a satellite photograph of her old sea in case she wanted to look at it. She didn’t.

“Who else is headed there?” she asked.

“Everybody,” Docet said. “The insurers. The harvesters. The scavengers. The altruists. The nostalgics. A dozen universities with grant money like guilt. A warlord from Interstice who has no reason to go but the need to say she was there. And us.”

“Us,” Keziah repeated, and let the shape of the word remind her of the girl who had taught her to play Spindle. The girl had been named Alix or Alya or something that felt like a kiss. She had died at thirty-two on a world with a sky like a bruise, her last message a photograph of a table laden with fruit she had never tasted. Keziah did not save the message. She saved the table.

“Do you want to notify anyone?” Docet said. “Friends, colleagues, exes you use to measure the distance between yourself and the person you could have been?”

“You learned a lot from a mug,” Keziah said.

“I learned a lot from you,” Docet replied, and if she had not been strapped into the couch she would have seated herself more deeply in it anyway, the way you do when someone tells you they know you and you realize you would like, once in your life, to be known in that direction rather than the one you provide for them.

“Send the notice to Jiro,” she said. Jiro would grumble about the jurisdictional mess and then get excited about the clause that would save them all if they argued it right. He would send her a sketch of a lizard he had seen that morning on the walkway to his office, and the lizard would have speech bubbles where it extolled the virtues of subparagraph thirteen. “And to Dai. And to Kamericana. And to anyone who owes me favors who still thinks I am worth paying back.”

Docet pulsed the messages. Traffic thundered around them, literal and otherwise. She could feel it through the couch, a hum that had been absent from her bones for centuries and now suddenly returned, like the feeling when you visit your childhood street and nothing is as you remember and everything is exactly as you feared.

“We will have to arrive inside the shades’ approach,” Docet said. “If we come in late, all we will be able to do is watch.”

Keziah closed her eyes. She opened them because the dark behind them was worse. The ship put Sol on the screen and there it was from an old array’s distant glance: a yellow star a little meaner than she’d told herself it would be, light reflecting off the dust of a great many tragedies. It was small and ordinary and the center of everything that had ever taught her what a center could be. Her hands were steady on the console. Her body was a trustworthy thing for once.

“Plot it,” she said. “Burn for home.”

“Are you sure?” Docet asked, because it loved her enough or had been trained to mimic love enough to give her the chance to take the words back into her mouth and chew them until they were unrecognizable.

“No,” she said. “But I am standing on a very old contract.”

Docet laid in the course. The drive whispered. On Tiamene, the upward rain sang and fell. The lake gathered itself and rose. Somewhere, a torus that had nearly lost its clutch spun slow and bright and told its people that the stranger with debts had left them their song. Somewhere else, the first of a million starshade units shivered loose from its cradle and began to unfurl like a flower that had learned to take.

Keziah watched Sol and did not speak the names she had for it. They would have to be different, now. They would have to be new. She had three days, four burns, and every escape hatch she could wedge open before somebody tried to turn her sun into currency.

“Docet,” she said softly. “When we get there, you remind me of the clause that let a small fishing platform on Salanka refuse a multinational mining concern.”

“That clause was never supposed to apply to this kind of case,” Docet said, amused and appalled in the way you are when a child flicks a dragonfly from a spider’s web. “We will make it apply.”

“Good,” she said. “And remind me to take the mug down from the galley and throw it away.”

“Will do,” Docet said.

“And then,” Keziah said, and it took her a moment to find the angle for the words, so that they would sit in the right place around the ache, “we will go home.”

Chapter One

The bell in Truss always rang twice—once for the living and once for the daylights.

The first ring rolled across the city as the sun climbed over the glass flats, a bronze sound that shook droplets from the elevated gardens and sent delivery drones skimming along their routes. It woke citizens in the ridge towers, told teachers to unlatch their doors, reminded vendors to ice their vats and trellis their trays. For us, it meant the racks would hum to life. It meant bodies.

I came down at Dock Three, where the racks stacked like scaffolding against the ocean-bleached concrete. The attendant kiosk blinked my kernel on its screen: a pulse of green, a line of license text, the name my register gave me—Anah–277–daylight. The kiosk was always polite. It asked if today I preferred a standard build, if I had any allergies to the new polymer batches, if I consented to municipal recording. It spelled consent in full and on a clear backdrop, and I ticked yes to everything. Saying no closed routes. Saying no meant someone somewhere would add a yellow line next to your number, and when the bell rang at dusk your body would give back to the city and you wouldn’t spool tomorrow.

The racks sighed. The foam-lattice unrolled like bread dough rising, soft and blushed, a thousand thousand wet cells knitting into a shape I had preregistered: five-seven, light, a scar on the left shoulder from an old mold line that never quite smoothed out. The first breath always tasted like acetate and rain. I flexed fingers, counted the micropricks as nervous threads found edges, blinked as the retinal grid warmed.

The kiosk greeted me with a chirp. “Good morning, Anah,” it said. “Today’s jobs have been optimized for weather and skillset. Next-of-kind payout will be debited upon close of day.”

“Good morning,” I said. My voice felt like a borrowed instrument, clean and a little stiff. My tongue registered the crack of salt in the air. Truss did that—lay salt on everything so you couldn’t forget who owned you. The ocean had receded a half-century back, the maps said; it had taken walls and highways, and in their place the city had climbed on stilts and trusses and taut cables. The old shore was a skeletal thing we all moved through, glass flats laid over the silt. The water was distance and hunger and a certain kind of freedom, if you were built for it.

Tulla was beside me, spooling into a narrow build with long hands she liked for threading filament through the uprisers. She reached over to flick the edge of my ear. “You got the shoulder again,” she said. “Why don’t you file a request? If they reprint the mold, we all benefit.”

“Because the scar feels like me,” I said, and realized I meant it. A tiny prickle ran up my spine; it was too early for philosophy. Tulla snorted, and we snagged our mesh aprons, our job slates, the little pouches of seed nan lab stamped with the city’s crest that we would use to coax algae off the intake screens and into buckets.

The work wanted us. It always did. You can tell yourself you’re a person distinct from the tasks you do, but when a thing knows the shape of you the way a tool knows the hand, it’s easy to forget.

We took the canal run first. The intakes throbbed, slowly, like sleeping hearts. Yesterday’s bloom had been heavy, a pink slick the consistency of broth poured over the glass. We scattered the seed nan along the edges, watched it form a fizzing lace that the algae loved and climbed, then dragged the whole sheet free with hooked poles. The slurry sloshed thick into our buckets, neon under the slate water. Our job slates chimed approvals as we reached the metrics, a cascade of small good sounds. The mesh aprons clung to our thighs. Tulla hummed under her breath, a song I didn’t know but felt like afternoon: a sound that leaned toward heat, where the flats out on the old freeway would shimmer and you could hear kids on the ropeways above throwing out their laughter like nets.

People moved over us, less than they used to. Citizen traffic had been light the last few seasons. Those who could afford slow lived high, their societies built on months and years; those who moved through days lived down with us. There were citi-bots in their company livery rolling across walkways, sweeping dust, checking for micro-cracks in the supports with clever light. Sometimes citizens would come down. They watched us like we were a street performance: the way our hands moved in synchronized rhythm, the way the algae peeled. None of them said the word daylight to our faces.

The second job was sweets—a cardboard tub of preserved fig syrup to be carried to the Ridge Market, a child’s treat her aunt had purchased across the nets. “Courier,” the kiosk had said. Couriers only went to those parts of the city with laws asking for bodies to bring some things by hand, a ritual—so someone would make eye contact, share a sentence, an exchange of oxygen and information. “I like that,” Tulla said, kicking at the trolley with her toe. “Being the kind that carries.”

“It’s heavier than I thought,” I said. We lifted it between us anyway.

At the market, an aunt with an elbow crutch and her hair braided with red wire met us at a shade stall. “You’re quick,” she said to me. Tulla’s job slate chimed pivot and sent her toward the upriser yards, so she raised a hand without looking back and slid into the crowd.

“She’s quick,” I said. “I’m just—”

“You’re you,” the aunt said, and grinned like she had told you a secret she wasn’t sure you’d like. She pressed coin credit into my slate, more than the municipal rate, and said, “When I was a kid, the bell was a different tone. All things change and change and change.”

“I wouldn’t know,” I said, careful in the way you are careful when you feel a shape in the conversation you can’t see. It was true. I didn’t know the bell from any other time than my own.

“You working late, Anah?” she asked. She had read my tag when we walked up; everyone could, if they didn’t mind feeling a little rude.

“Till the bell,” I said.

She reached out, slow enough that I could move away if I wanted to, and touched that scar at my shoulder. Her fingers were warm. “Find someone to eat with before,” she said. “Bad for a body to go out alone. You come by, and I’ll fry you something after the heat falls. No charge.”

“I don’t—” I began, because it seemed important to tell the truth: that nothing I ate would follow me; that the coins went into the fund for my origin, not my tongue.

She waved me off. “I know what you are,” she said. Her voice was soft. “I also know what I am. All of us live on borrowed mornings. Don’t make me say the poetry of it. You and your friend come by.”

I promised. People liked promises. They made the minutes sound less empty, less like a room you were meant to hurry through.

The heat fell like a sheet around the time we finished the uprisers. The ropeways were full of kids again, and the ribs of Truss hummed, a low throbbing that came on when the solar banks bled their power over into the night grid to prevent the slamming of demand at nine. That meant the second bell was coming. My job slate chimed the ceremonial list: return aprons, return slates, return anything you borrowed or were. Municipal courtesy.

Tulla rejoined me at Dock Three, hair stuck to her forehead, eyes bright. “You get asked to eat?” she asked without preface.

“Yes,” I said, surprised.

“Everyone’s soft today,” she said. “It’s because the long tide is due this week. Makes people generous.” Her voice softened. “My first day and my second day I got asked and I didn’t go both times. My origin ate alone those nights, and I don’t know why, but I felt it. Or I tell myself I felt it. Either way, I go now.”

We handed our aprons to the rack, walked the long way around the Dock to bleed off adrenaline. Daylight bodies weren’t supposed to get wound, not in a way that carried trouble. But something about the crush of the return always did it—the knowledge of the hour. There were three hundred of us in the Dock’s return hall, a space that had once been a swimming pool and now was a kit of drains and catchment basins, the giant fans overhead spinning slowly to keep the air sweet. We lay down on mats we’d used a dozen times before, or picked up new ones if we were new enough for everything to still be new. There were songs sometimes, murmured like prayers. Today it was just the hum of the fans, the little rattle of someone’s foot.

“One more,” Tulla said, turning her head to look at me. Her eyes were dark as the canal.

“One more,” I said.

The bell rang. The first tone was for the citizens and citi-bots and the scaffolds of the city, something that made the hair along my arms lift, an agreement between the stakes in the ground and the wires in the walls. Then the second began—a frequency you knew even if you were barely printed, a tone engineered to coax the field that held your mind to decouple. The bell built slowly. Your body warmed, the foam-lattice in your bones loosened, your sense of yourself pulled toward a shared slow gravity. “See you in the morning,” Tulla said, and her voice already had that doubled sound to it, like a voice heard through water.

“See—” I began, and the room went soft at the edges.

It went soft. It did not go away.

The second tone thickened until it was almost taste. My fingers tingled. Across the pool, I watched a dozen bodies sigh and spill, the lattice of them relaxing, a kind of melting that wasn’t grotesque because there was no pain in it. Daylight minds, released, tagged, routed, compressed back into their city-kept kernels, into the cold servers in a blockhouse by the uplink station. The mats were designed to wick; the drains took what was left. You didn’t think about the reuse. You didn’t think about your bones tomorrow being made from someone’s work today; you didn’t think, because there was no tomorrow, not until you dropped and woke again.

I lay and stared and did not spill.

A fan ticked. It was a small sound, easy to ignore if everything else was as it should be. It wasn’t. I turned my head and the room tilted in a way that had nothing to do with heat or exhaustion. A dozen mouths had fallen open in slack surprise before they fell apart; a dozen chests shuddered on their last held breath. Tulla’s hand lay palm-down on the mat, and I reached for it because I had planned to do that as soon as my fear let me, as soon as we both slumped. My hand touched hers. It was already not a hand. It was a map of it, the foam-lattice expressing its memory in slow collapse.

I sat up.

No one sits up when the bell is still ringing. The tone flattened, lengthened, loosened, finally quieted. The silence that followed felt like an uninvited guest.

“Anah,” said the Dock attendant speaker. It was the same voice as the kiosk’s, but without the polite smile coded into it. The microphone picked up the little crackle of dust in its grill. “You appear to be noncompliant. Please remain on your mat. Sweepers will assist.”

I was a minute past propriety. That is all it takes to become something the city has to correct.

I stood. My legs felt odd, waking to a weight they hadn’t expected to carry. The pool room was a geography of slack forms, most already draining, some not. A few daylights sometimes didn’t go right away—coherence takes time to unravel in the odd build or the odd body—but always within ninety seconds. Ninety came and went. I counted because I had been taught to count many things, because the city loved numbers that proved it was thinking.

“Please remain on your mat,” the speaker said again. There was a tiny change in the tone the way there is when a human takes a breath before they raise their voice. “Anah–two-seven-seven, you are in violation.”

“What happens if I don’t?” I asked, and heard the thin thread of my voice pulled tight by something I could not name. The sound bounced off tile, hit no ears that would give me answer.

A shape moved at the far end of the pool room: a gray sweeper drone unspooling from its charging column, its arms folded like a praying mantis’s, its tanks brassy and full. You could see your reflection in its side panels. I saw myself: a standard build, summer brown, eyes too wide. I saw behind me the slow collapse of those who had been mine, who had been me. The sweeper’s arms tasted the air, feeling for charge, for particulate, for coherence. It moved like a thought about purpose.

I had the stupid instinct to hide under a mat. I had a dozen other instincts layered under that: to run for the door; to lie down again and pretend; to call out to the attendant that I was sorry, I should, I would, I was just scared. The mat would not save me. The door would be locked. The attendant had already flagged me.

I ran anyway. The body the city had printed for day-work turned out to know stairs better than I did. My feet found the metal grate, my hand found the rail. The sweeper spun quickly, quicker than the last time I had seen one move like that; it skated on its little air-casters and was suddenly a long thin thing behind me. I threw myself up the second flight and into the supply corridor—and collided with a woman.

She didn’t fall. She didn’t even sway. She grabbed my shoulders as if I weighed less than the trolley had and threw me against the wall hard enough that the world flashed. Then she put a finger to her mouth.

She was old, or had chosen a face that read old—they weren’t the same. The hair along her jaw was white; her face had a map of lines that had nothing to do with cutting or coding. She wore a workman’s vest with a municipal patch half pulled loose, the threads fraying. She smelled like iron and night air and something sweet I couldn’t place. She tilted her head toward the stairs. The sweeper hummed in, arms out.

“Noncompliant daylight detected,” the sweeper said politely, in the same vote of the city I had lived my minutes by. “Assistance required.”

“Hi, lovely,” the woman said to the machine, softer than I would have believed possible. She put her palm against its brass side panel, over the mark where my face had just been. Her thumb pressed down and began to make circles, slow, affectionate. The sweeper’s arms dipped, a fraction, like a dog leaning instinctively into a hand. She leaned closer, said a word that wasn’t English into the little seam above its intake valve, and the hum staggered. I felt it in my knees. The sweeper paused, then folded its arms back to its body and drifted, calm and blank, to dock itself again, like a brilliant idea that had chosen to make itself a later problem.

I thought very hard about breathing and did not. When I realized I had forgotten how, the woman squeezed my shoulder until my chest twinged, and my lungs did what they knew. Oxygen slid into me; the world steadied.

“You shouldn’t be here,” the woman said. Her voice had the drawl of the lower city and the tribe of the old salt fences; it was not a municipal voice. It was not anything the city had chosen. She took her hand off my shoulder and peered at my arm as if reading a sign. “Anah–two-seven-seven. Somebody’s little bright. Look at you standing up when you should be a puddle.”

“I didn’t,” I said, and had to stop. The word didn’t wasn’t a sentence. It was a doorway with nothing behind it. “I didn’t go.”

“No,” she said. “You didn’t.”

“What do I do,” I asked, hearing the drop in my voice when the word I hit my throat and fell through, “now?”
