She tilted her head as if listening to water under floorboards. “You don’t go home,” she said. “You don’t go to anyone whose name is attached to yours. You drop your slate right here.” She held out her hand. I gave it to her because when someone handles a sweeper that way and knows your name and speaks like she built the bell in her kitchen, you do what she says. She slipped the slate down the front of the vest and it disappeared as if there had been a pocket there since the vest was woven. “And you keep your feet under you.”

“My origin,” I said. The word was a stagger. It felt like swallowing a pin. “Rian. They—”

“You’re not for them now,” the woman said, not cruelly. “And they are not for you. That’s a tangle for a morning when you have a different sort of time.” She glanced at the stairs and the door beyond, where the Dock’s return hall hissed and drained. “You got any food in you?”

“No,” I said.

She nodded like that confirmed a suspicion. “Then it’s my lucky day, because I like to fry late. Come on.”

“Why are you helping me,” I said, too quick, stumbling after her as she slid down the corridor with the fluid fast pace of someone who had a map in her bones.

“Because you asked it,” she said, and for a second her mouth smiled without it touching her eyes. “Because I am old enough to remember when the bell was a different tone, and I like to put a thumb on what tries to sound the same and change it a little. Because you’ve got that look. Because I owe someone a favor and the city owes me fifty. Pick one you like. It’ll make the story better later.”

We cut across a maintenance yard littered with coils of cable and stacks of glass sheets, through a door that said PRIVATE and another that said DO NOT ENTER WITHOUT CITY PERMISSION, up a steep stair that smelled like old oil and sea. The city vibrated under my feet. The low throbbing in the truss bones shifted, like a big thing had turned over in its sleep.

“What’s your name,” I asked between one breath and the next, finding that I wanted the anchor of syllables.

“Sael,” she said. “Sael if you like me, Sal if you think I’ll throw you to the sweepers, Sala if you are trying to be respectful. The city called me Worker Nine at a time in my life when it mattered and Catastrophe One when I argued. You can call me old, if you have to call me any damn thing.” She held the door for me into a room with low ceilings, pale walls, a line of shelves where a dozen small potted vines climbed cleverly shaped pieces of copper. It was a kitchen, the kind built into service corridors for municipal staff: a two-burner, a chipped sink, a kettle with a cork handle.

She turned on the burner. The electric click caught, blue flame under black pan. She cracked eggs into the pan with one hand and shook a salt packet like rain. I stood by the door as if expecting it to do tricks. Through the glass of the far window, I could see the lights of the ridge towers winking awake, the ropeways pulsing with their little glow, the long plate of the east flats slick with night.

“I don’t have any days,” I said, because if there was a moment to say a true thing, it was when someone had just saved you and put a pan on a flame. If there was a moment to say a small thing, to see how it sounded in someone else’s air, it was now.

Sael nodded without looking up. “None of us do,” she said. “That’s the trick the bell plays. But you’ve got an hour, right now. Some hours are better than days.” She folded the eggs like letters and slid them onto a cracked plate. She handed it to me with a plastic fork, the kind with a tine already bent. I put the fork in my mouth and tasted something warm that hurt me with how good it was. I made a sound that probably embarrassed me and didn’t care.

“Eat,” Sael said. “And listen. I know a thing or two. This wasn’t you alone.”

“What do you mean,” I asked, but the words were thick, full of egg.

Sael picked up a copper pot with a dent in its side, held it up to the light, turned it like you would a baby to see if it was all there. “I mean what I said. The bell slips. It always has a margin, like machines do. Once in a generation, twice, ten times in a bad year, somebody stands up when they shouldn’t. Sometimes they sit back down when someone looks hard at them. Sometimes they run out and tangle themselves in trouble that wasn’t meant for them.” She set the pot down quietly. “And sometimes, once in a long while, the slip isn’t a slip for just one person.” She looked at me then. The copper vines on the shelf rustled as if a draft had threaded through the room. “Did you hear anything?” she asked. “When you lay down.”

“The bell,” I said. “Everyone hears the bell.”

“Anything else.”

I hesitated. Memory is slippery in the edges, and daylights teach themselves not to hold too hard. But there had been a shape in the noise, a flicker in the long tone, a little catch the way a voice catches when it doesn’t want to say a word. I had thought it was my fear. I had thought it was my ribs learning the measure of my breath. I hadn’t thought it was someone else.

“Something like a—” I said, and struggled. “A knock.”

Sael nodded as if this pleased her and frightened her all at once. “All right,” she said. “All right. Don’t go quiet now. You’ve got an hour. Maybe two, if the city’s slow. So we’ll spend it. We’ll spend it well.” She poured water into the kettle and set it to boil, then looked back at me. “Eat,” she said. “I’ll tell you about the folks who don’t spill when they should. I’ll tell you about the long tide. I’ll tell you a story, Anah, and you tell me if any of it sounds like yours.”

Outside, the city breathed out. In the Dock, the drains gurgled and carried away what was left of my day. The bell in Truss had finished its work; it would not ring again until morning. It was quiet enough that I could hear my own heart not understanding the shape of this hour. The window glass trembled lightly in its frame. The evening lay down like a map.

I ate. Sael began, and her first sentence was an old shape bent in a new way.

“Once,” she said, “we used a bell to call boats home. Once we rang it to tell people where the high water was. The bell the city built is a different instrument, loud and clever, tuned to the math of how your mind sits in your bones. But it’s still a bell. And bells carry. Sometimes they carry farther than the hands that made them intended.”

She pointed her finger toward the east, beyond the flats, past the old freeway, toward the thin dark line of the horizon where the sea lay like a coin. “Sometimes,” she said, “they carry under water.”

Chapter One

On Titan, silence had weight.

Safiya El-Hashim could feel it through the hull, a pressure that wasn’t pressure, a hum of absence pressing against the skimmer’s aluminum ribs. Ordinarily there would be sound even in this world’s hush—the slow burp of the methane sea slapping at her pontoons, the rustle of thick air across her rotors, the tidy metronome of the navigation beacons belting their identifiers through the soup of orange haze.

Bead Nine was supposed to ping at forty hertz, a slow, old-fashioned heart. Nine was supposed to say: I am here, and I am bright, and the lanes are clear.

She heard nothing.

“Finch,” Safiya said, never quite certain whether the drone preferred being addressed by name. Its frame was folded on the bulkhead like a black iron praying mantis. “We’re still outside of Nine’s last broadcast radius?”

Finch flicked awake. The cockpit filled with a faint electronic trilling, Finch’s idea of clearing its throat. “We are inside the thirty-kilometer ring,” it said, voice clipped, the cadence still more groundschool than lived experience. “Beacon Nine’s last scheduled transmission was seventy-four minutes ago. I detect no signal on standard bands.”

Safiya adjusted a dial with one knuckle, eyes on the sickly glow beyond the windscreen. The sea was a matte slab, darker than the sky—a blacker black beneath the orange. The air wasn’t clear enough to see the far curve of the world; there was only the immediate, the near, the slow fireworks of ice crystals glittering at the limit of the skimmer’s lamps.

“You think god took Nine, Finch?” she said. The joke was old, but Titan made you reuse your words the way you reused water. It taught you thrift.

Finch rotated one multifaceted sensor in a gesture that carried, somehow, the suggestion of a shrug. “Operative ‘god’ is not indexed. I suspect human failure. Or weather. Or both.”

“Always with the optimism.” Safiya pushed the throttle and felt the skimmer’s twin impellers bite into air as thick and useful as syrup. The vessel lifted slightly onto its foils and began to kiss the methane just under the surface rather than plow through it. At Titan gravities you didn’t need much to lift a person and a machine. You didn’t need much to fly, and yet you were never far from falling.

The sea here was Kraken Mare, greatest of the hydrocarbon seas. Lanes crisscrossed it in precise loops, schema imposed on a world that had its own slow ideas. Bead Nine sat—should have sat—at one of those intersections, a stainless steel heart designed to endure a century. Each Bead listened to the others and stitched together a net of reliable position in a place where you could lose yourself by turning twice in the fog.

Nine had been her friend for three months. She timed her patrols by Nine’s slow pulse, the way she timed sleep by the distant thunder of the Orbital Authority’s blares, timed boredom by the count of minutes it took the central heater to kick again, the trickle of condensation down the steel. That was the thing about Titan that she grew to respect, even to love: it was a place made of systems, human ones and alien ones, and to survive here you learned to hum with both.

She had chosen this life. People always assumed otherwise. That she was in exile, that the Titan rangers were a league of quiet criminals. There was no reason they couldn’t be right, Safiya thought; it just so happened she had signed her contract with clear eyes and a better option in the other hand. The better option had been people, meetings in bright domes, appointments in greater gravity. Her nephew’s school on Earth would have been there—the one her sister wanted help with now—and in the background, always, the weight of other people’s schedules pressing her into their shape.

Here, schedules pressed too. They just smelled of solvent and cold metal, and they lived in machines with her.

Finch extended its arm toward the windshield, indicating the ghost of a ghost of a light in the haze. “Contact ahead,” it said.

Safiya squinted. The light was the color of old coins, then in the next second it wasn’t there, then it was closer, brightening in pulses that felt irregular only because of the way the air turned and smeared the world. As they approached, the pulse resolved into a steady blink. She wanted to read it—she wanted desperately to read “Nine” in that blink, to find the pattern her brain had already decided she should find. But the cadence was wrong.

“That’s a buoy,” she said. “Not Nine.”

“It reads as emergency,” Finch said. “The buoy’s code indicates a severed tether in the lane. Proceed with caution.”

She throttled down and the skimmer settled from flight to float, pontoons biting into the sea. Methane slapped metal with a sound like hollow palms clapping. The buoy was a simple thing, a metal drum with a strobing LED and a set of low-grade chirpers set to scream in any direction someone might be listening. Its top was slick with a skim of frost, and a rime of pale chemicals clung to its shadow side where the light never quite reached.

Safiya reached out with the boat hook and drew the buoy close. It greeted her hand with a pulse so eager it was almost hungry. “Easy,” she murmured, as if it feared being scolded for what had happened. She popped the maintenance hatch with her wrist wrench and watched the diagnostics scroll across her visor in a green that felt warmer than Titan’s blue cold.

“Severed at fifty meters,” she read. “Tension spike recorded four minutes before failure. Tension spike magnitude: Off-scale.” She whistled, and the thin noise of it sounded almost obscene in Finch’s microphones. “Off-scale. That’s not weather.”

“Could be mass,” Finch said. “A ship hit the mooring, overloaded the line, and fled without saying?”

“There are three ships on Kraken today,” Safiya said. “Arctic Prism at the southern run, Hye-sun Twelve holding at Raspel, and Sigrún out by the islands. Nine’s in our lane and our lane is empty. And any captain dumb enough to hit a mooring in this visibility would be dumb enough to call crying about it before his insurers could choke him.”

She did not say: before Orbital audited his license and repossessed his ship. On Titan, licenses were life support in more than the metaphorical way.

She toggled the skimmer’s underbelly sonar and sent a low-frequency moan into the sea. The return rolled back seconds later: a bunk mass of cold indifference—flat seafloor, the mild irregularity of the weighted Bead base—except the Bead base wasn’t where it should be. The plot showed a pit where the base had been, its edges fuzzy, and a long smearing trail moving away like something had dragged weight across a snowfield.

She toggled the winch and fed out the eel.

The eel was a flexible camera and sensor package made of sapphire-sheathed fiber and an idiot brain at the end that loved nothing more than wiggling along a surface and showing you what it found. Safiya watched the thin line unspool into Titan’s sea, watched the numbers on her visor: 5 meters, 10, 20, 30. The eel hadn’t seen daylight in weeks. It made an eager little chirp when it hit fluid and then went quiet as its mics filled with cold.

At forty-nine meters the line went slack in a way Safiya recognized—the eel had hit bottom. She zipped the feed into three windows: sonar on the left, the eel’s optical in the center, chem-sense on the right.

Unless a miracle of tectonics had happened in the last hour, Titan’s seabed was what it had always been: regolith of complex organics—tholin dust that had sifted down for a billion years—over a crust of water ice firm as granite. It wasn’t sand like home: particles could behave like fluids in chemical cold, a thing that made motion weird, inevitable, uncanny.

The eel’s camera cut through the gloom with a beam whose brightness the world did not deserve. The beam found opaline dust motes lazily suspended. It found the pit. Even before she brought the skimmer around to hang directly above the thing, she could tell this was no simple collapse. The pit’s edges were crisp and defined, not the scallop curves of a natural slump. They were scallops, yes—regular scallops, like tooth marks on a soft apple. She recorded a quick scroll of footage, and her breath was loud in her own head.

The Bead base had been set into the ice. Someone, or something, had torn it free from its anchor points with enough force to shear the fixtures. The fixtures were meant to outlast storms, collision, neglect. They had gone all at once. Off-scale.

“Finch,” Safiya said. “Give me thermal.”

“Safi,” said the drone, and she allowed herself the mild warmth of hearing her name softened. Finch had learned to do that on its own, without any fiddling from human hands. A strange thing. “It is minus one hundred and seventy-eight on the surface and colder beneath. There is no thermal to give.”

“Humor me,” Safiya said. On Titan, you learned to ask for the things that could not be.

Finch overlaid a false-color map on her visor anyway, inventing a way to visualize a landscape that wanted no cameras. The eel’s chem-sense tickled green as it nosed along the trail leading away from the pit.

The trail was complicated, and at first Safiya almost fooled herself into thinking it was the random chatter of kerogens clumping under a slow slope, the way tholins would sometimes skitter like ball bearings under gravity so light a child could push her way into the air with one hand. But the trail had pattern. It had bilateral symmetry.

The eel’s light caught the imprint the way moonrise catches cat tracks in a dusting of snow. A pad shape, then another, offset. Pad, pad. As big as her gloved hand. Spaced evenly. And deep. Three-fingered. Once the eel saw one, it found hundreds, arranged in the somber purposefulness of something that knew how to walk.

Walk.

Humans had made Titan walk in many ways. Machines trundled across its plains. Submarines had crawled along its seabed on triangular treads. People, once, in the early days, had bounded about in exosuits like astronauts on a playground for adults. She had seen the old vids: men laughing, their voices crackling through speakers as they kicked up fans of pale grains. It had not been this.

She traced the line of the trail with the eel. It went away from the Bead base for just under forty meters, then it ended abruptly in a burr of disordered sediment. The eel coughed to itself, then refused to go further. She coaxed it. The eel insisted that its chemistry sensors were angry.

“What are you smelling?” she murmured. “What did you taste?”

Finch bent and watched the reels of data, head cocked. “Spike in nitriles,” it said after a moment. “Ordinary enough. Slight rise in acetylene. Trace hydrogen cyanide, also ordinary enough. But there is also—” It paused, a human affectation it had acquired in the long winter. “A polymer I do not have in my tables.”

Safiya raised the eel, inch by inch, and watched glitter shake off the fiber line like dandruff. It looked like snow, if snow could fall upward from a sea. She reached and caught some on the back of her glove and watched it frost there, a delicate skin of something that had once been fluid, or wanted to be.

“Cement,” she said, not because she believed it but because she couldn’t not say it.

Finch made a daytime noise, a little negative hum. “Unindexed polymer could be contamination from the Bead’s casing. From the anchor. From the buoy’s paint. Or from our own hull.”

“Yeah,” she said. “Or from that, too.” She watched the trail dissolve into disorder on the screen, then flipped the overlay off. The world returned to orange and grey and black.

The radio in her right ear clicked. Orbital Authority dispatch, the voice of water and air and jobs. The voice was scrubbed of accent, steady and unobtrusive. “Ranger El-Hashim,” it said. “Routine check. Please confirm status of Bead Nine. We read a service anomaly.”

Safiya stared at the lightless gap where Nine’s pulse had been. She saw it, in that moment, as something other than a machine: one of the beads on her string, one of the points that made her horizon. She did not want to tell anyone what she had seen. She did not want to tell anyone ever. She wanted to keep this trail and its terrible regularity to herself like an indecent secret.

“Bead Nine is offline due to weather,” she said. “I am performing diagnostics. Will advise in thirty.” She felt her mouth shape the lie and then it wasn’t a lie; it was policy, like all the best lies. You didn’t cry wolf on Titan. You did not call the Authority with “something in the sea” unless you wanted orbital to drop a bundle of measures so heavy they would leave dents in the world. Titan had seen its share of panics. People had filmed myths here already, and there was nothing Orbital hated more than uncontrolled stories.

“Copy,” said the voice. “Recommend deploying a replacement transmitter if possible. We have Sigrún turning inbound on a tight schedule.”

“Understood,” she said. She cut the channel before the voice had time to say anything human.

Finch’s sensors tracked her face. It was a polite invasion. “You said weather,” Finch said.

“There is weather,” she said, and gestured at the world. “There is always weather.”

Weather was a wall of aerosolized hydrocarbons rolling in from the eastern plains, a storm of sand finer than flour. Weather was the slight buck and yaw of the skimmer as a swell passed under like an indifferent animal. Weather was the way frost scribed calligraphy across the inside of her windshield if she let her heater drop a degree.

She told herself, for the discipline of it, that the trail might be all of those things and none of the other. She reeled the eel back in, wiping frost with practiced motions, and locked it back into its recess. She secured the buoy with a new link—a quick job with a lazy outcome, something Finch would be able to watch and judge. Then she went to the storage rack and shouldered the replacement Bead kit.

Titan was unfeeling; you had to be unfeeling right back. You saw a hole in your net, you rewove the net.

She set the replacement cylinder gently on the deck and opened its case. Inside was a tight bundle of radio, batteries, and a clever little brain. Not as clever as Finch’s, and not required to be. It would hum, and it would listen, and if it failed, it would shout until someone like her came. You couldn’t ask a machine for more than that. You shouldn’t ask a person.

“Finch,” she said. “May I request a thing you will not approve?”

The drone’s head tilted. It wanted, Safiya suspected sometimes, to be more than it was. That was a dangerous want in a place that rewarded those who stayed within the boxes people had built for them. “You may request,” Finch said, cautious. It was better than most people.

“Open your free channel,” she said. “Record. Encrypt. Hide in the noise.”

Finch’s motors hummed in minor chords. “Are we making a story?” it said. “Are we not supposed to make stories?”

She looked past it at the window, at her own reflection—brown face, tucked hair, things to keep skin from cracking under the heater’s breath—and at the sea beyond. The sea did not look back. The sea had never promised to look at all.

“Not a story,” she said. “A note. For me. For later.” She did not add that if the worst thing—if the best thing—were true, then later would be a thin light in a far place, and her future self might be grateful to the past that had left her bread crumbs.

Finch, who had learned to pause, paused again. “Recording,” it said.

Safiya told herself the thing she needed to hear in her own voice: There were prints. They were real, inasmuch as the eel had seen them, which was as real a seeing as any other in this place. The prints were made by an entity with bilateral symmetry and regular stride length. The entity had pulled Bead Nine from its mooring with a force beyond expectation and had left behind polymer traces unknown to Finch’s tables. She, Safiya, had made a choice to lie because she wanted more information before the Authority applied the hammer it applied to all nails: more hardware, more rules.

She stopped. She listened to the shape her breath made in her sinuses. “Button that,” she said. Finch clicked and tucked the packet away inside the randomness of sideline communications, where it would be a twist of phase a casual reader would not even see.

“Thank you,” Finch said, and she laughed, because it had been the thank-you of a friend who had accepted a burden with grace.

Installing the replacement Bead was muscle memory. She slung the toolkit over her shoulder, boots clanking on the deck, and eased herself out onto the catwalk. The cold ate at her joints even through the suit’s heaters, a gnawing creep that told her the environmental variables she carried with her would always be insufficient. The orange light seeped through the haze, made beautiful everything it touched and lied about all distances.

She worked quickly and well. She braced her legs apart because Titan always tried to teach you to float, and sometimes you didn’t want to. She fed the new Bead’s base with stiff hands, guided the cable toward the spot her sonar told her was flat enough to accept a friend. The line sang as it unspooled—this was imagination, she knew; lines did not sing here, not with nitrogen that thick—but her brain supplied the note anyway, because she was a human animal and her ears longed for some sign there were other animals nearby.

She had almost finished when the skimmer’s cheap, rear-facing camera saw movement and screamed, a calorie of panic in her ear.

“Finch?” she said, brow creasing under her helmet.

“Relative bearing sixty-one,” the drone said. It had stopped observing politeness. “Depth five meters. Object unknown. That is—”

The thing surfaced five meters off the starboard pontoon. It was not dramatic. This was not a story about waves. It came up like a piece of wet furniture rising from a flooded basement, a blunt rectangle impelled by some internal buoyancy, the liquid sliding off its skin in sheets. Safiya’s first thought was that it was a crate. A crate from some outdated shipping process, a box with the corners knocked clean by sea time.

Then the rectangle turned, and the angle of its surface caught the skimmer’s light, and she saw that it was not a simple box but the jointed segment of something larger. It was built—or had built itself—of cells like ice honeycomb, each cell full of something darker than the world. It had a skin like resin. It looked like a rib. It looked like a toy. It looked like the idea of a tool.

Safiya didn’t reach for the boat hook. She didn’t move at all.

The segment floated for the length of three of her heartbeats—long, extravagant heartbeats drawn out by the heater’s efforts—and then it tilted, exhaled a cloud of bubbles that weren’t bubbles, and sank. As it went down, it brushed against the buoy she had reattached. The buoy bobbed like a bobbing thing, offended and helpless. The segment sank with the deliberateness of a thing not quite sure whether down was the direction it wanted to go.

It disappeared. The world returned to orange.

Safiya stood as still as hardware. On her visor, the backend camera for the eel had begun to show excited lines; Finch had thrown up industrial labels like confetti and then realized labels were not the right tools for now and swept them away.

“That,” Finch said, and stopped. Safiya knew then that it had used up its quota of newness for one day.

She took a breath. She took another. She said, to the air, to the sea, to the thing that had touched her buoy, “Hello?” The word fogged her visor. She wiped it. The heater breathed harder. She wanted to laugh.

The radio in her ear clicked again. Orbital, not the speech-scrubbed channel but the one where they sometimes let themselves be themselves. “Safi,” said a woman whose name was Abioye. The vowels were long and soft; the consonants landed like parachutes. “Do we have Nine? Sigrún wants to leave by dusk.”

Safiya swallowed. She looked down into the black. The black looked back, or didn’t. Who could say? “Working,” she said, and then, because she had said too many lies in a row without anchoring one in fact, “Replacing now. Give me fifteen.”

“We’ll give you ten,” Abioye said, and cut the line without rancor. On Titan, you did not squander a ranger’s attention on conversation. You would never get it back.

She finished the job. She watched the replacement Bead spin up, watched it test its own pulse and approve it, and when the pulse went out and returned rich with echoes of the other Beads, when Nine’s gap knitted closed into a familiar net, she allowed herself to breathe in a way that felt reckless.

She wrote the new Bead’s registration code into her report. She omitted the segment that had surfaced. She omitted the trail. She omitted the taste of unfamiliar polymer and the way the buoy had bobbed like a kicked ball.

Back on the bench, she slotted the mule battery into the skimmer’s secondary port and let the heater have a drink. Outside, the sea looked as if it had always been that way. Inside, the air smelled like dust that had once wanted to be stone.

Finch eased its frame down beside her and angled its face toward hers. “Are we going to tell them?”

“Tell who?”

“Any them,” Finch said. “The Authority. The captains. The biologists. The ones who will be very excited or very frightened.”

Safiya leaned her head back against the cold bulkhead. Out beyond the haze, there was a city on stilts like a room full of furniture, there were domes with gardens printed under the plastic like green messages, there were people who woke at arranged hours and ate arranged meals and kept arranged thoughts in arranged heads. She liked many of those people very much. She did not want them to have this yet. She did not want the hammer.

“Not yet,” she said. “We tell me. We tell Finch.” She touched the drone’s arm and felt it flex infinitesimally, as if startled. “Tomorrow, we tell the person we both decide deserves it.”

The drone’s low motors made a sound like agreement. Or like a room settling. Or like nothing. Sometimes she pretended she could tell.

She throttled up. The skimmer lifted. She aimed its nose at the next Bead on in her patrol because that was what a ranger did, and because the shape of the job held her like a hand.

As she left Bead Nine behind, she looked once over her shoulder. The buoy bobbed. The sea smoothed. The haze swallowed everything.

On Titan, nothing walked. It shouldn’t.

But something had.

Chapter One: Anchorbeat

From the hullglass walkway, the hole looks like a bruise in the sky. Not black. Not empty. A bent place, the color of swallowed light, a ring of stars smeared and doubled around it like fingerprints on a mirror.

We keep the ring alive by listening to that bruise.

I’m two hours into a sweep on the underside of Spindle Six when the Anchor begins to sing out of tune. It’s a thin thing at first, a fractional warble in the ping that we take for granted, like your own heartbeat miscounting one beat. Tavi’s voice crackles in my teeth as the audio bone goes active.

“Hear that?” he says. “Anchor’s drunk.”

“Hold,” I answer, more to the instruments than to him. I steady my glove on the net strut and feel the tension come back against my palm. The light net is a thousand filaments of dust, glass, and memory, stretched out to catch photons that have been bent around the hole twice before they get here. Our grandmothers would’ve called it a harp. If the harp could measure time by the way the strings keep trying to slip out of tune.

The Anchor ping hits again. Even through layers of insulation and vibration dampers, I feel the pulse. Thin. Then fat. Then thin. Dilation is supposed to happen out there, where Kera drags it, where we sell it by the barrel. Not in the Anchor.

“Seul.” Tavi’s singing voice goes flat. He only uses my real name when he’s afraid.

“I hear it,” I say. Above me, the spindle extends into the ergosphere where space itself is co-opted and spun. It hums like a long, sympathetic bone inside the ring, chewing on frame-drag to pull a trickle of energy from the hole. We’re careful with our grazing. The early stations burned themselves by trying to get greedy, by sawing too close to the throat. The bruised sky swallowed them without leaving a scream.

I count three warbles, thirty-nine heartbeats apart, which makes no sense. Anchor’s a fixed light, out in the far blue normal time, deliberately placed beyond any well. She’s there so our ledgers don’t lie; she’s there so clients know our numbers are honest. She’s there so the kids’ lullabies have the same rhythm in every creche.

“Bringing net nineteen into high,” I tell Tavi, and thumb the release. The net lifts in slow breath, the curving threads catching star and lens, and the feed pumps a thousand points of light into my glove and up my arm.

I learned to read light nets when I was six. Dad’s hands were big enough to cup my whole head, and he used those hands to move mine along the filaments, naming each gap and node. This is your lucky seam, sweetheart. This bright where the Crab doubles itself? That’s your Anchor. When you’re scared you can find it blind and you can find your way home.

Since he left, I’ve kept nets tuned like prayers.

“You think someone’s sitting on Anchor?” Tavi asks.

“Who?”

“Pick a megacorp. Pick a state with a grudge. Pick a pirate with an overclocked death wish.”

“And what? They tug Anchor’s beam through a well to make us look bad?”

“War by audit. I’ve seen stupider.”

“Shut up with stupid. I need quiet.”

He shuts up. I squeeze my eyes against the sting of the chill and the tiny, heroic ache that the vacuum always leaves in my teeth. I should’ve brought a fresh respirator pack. The one I have tastes like old iodine and lemon rinds. It fogs the back of my mouth with metallic cold.

We’re not supposed to be afraid of Anchor. Anchor is the one piece you don’t question. Every other clock lies. Every other measure we have is smeared by gravity and speed. Anchor has been watching us since before we built the first net from unpacking struts and the cable of my grandmother’s hair. We struck a light out there and agreed to blink on it together. It is not supposed to sing wrong.

The net hum surges and steadies. I feel the pull even out of the suit’s muscle film, a kindness that keeps me from coming apart when I lean too close to the thick of it. The lens blur shifts and I see the smear of Anchor’s light as a thickened smear. A pulse too long. A pulse too short. If I keep breathing like we’re in magnetic calm, I can pretend the timing drift is within corrections.

The silly, safe part of my brain imagines Anchor asleep at her console, drooling into the blink switch. I picture some technician in blue-shift, yawning, tapping the time, grinning when she realizes the whole ring is taking its breath from her. The part of my brain that got me hired out of the creche knows better.

Tavi breathes like a metronome on the line. He used to sing me rhymes in freefall when we were nine and sent out to scrape ice off the Hush—quiet ducts that keep the ring cool enough to not cook us in our own recycled air. He always wanted to pilot Clockbirds, the maintenance drones that skate the in-between near the spindles. He ended up with accounts, the Ledger life, moving lags like coins, hunting discrepancies like smugglers. We all end up doing some mix of what we love and what keeps the ring buying limes.

“What do you see?” he asks now.

“Anchor’s ping smeared by 0.17 pulses on the long side. 0.19 short,” I say. “If it’s us, the whole ring’s bowing. If it’s them, someone’s tugging their beam.”

“Net the ring,” he says, breath quick with the idea. “We can see if a bend is local.”

“That would be a Charter-floor call,” I say.

“You’re Charter,” he says. “Your mother kept Spindle Six from chewing itself in half the year I was born. They owe you the keys to the mess hall, let alone a net pull.”

“And yet my access doesn’t open the vault for soup. Hold your horses.”

“You have no horses.”

“That’s because you ate them.” I lift my hand from the net and brush a thumb across the patch sewn into the glove: a little stitched tide mark with two black stitches below it. Dad sewed it there when I turned twelve. It’s the mark of the old House of Tides, back when we still pretended the ring had Houses and not committees. The patch is frayed to threads. I keep meaning to sew it down. I keep finding other, less vulnerable things to mend.

The Anchor ping pops again. And again. The fifth drift is bigger than the fourth by an unlovely margin. Not a natural smear. A hand shoving on the beam.

“Tavi,” I say. “Call it.”

He inhales. “To who? We ring the Charter and they’ll ask if our nets need a wash.”

“Ring them anyway. Tell them I want—”

The line goes cold.

For a second I think he’s hung up. Then every sound in my suit goes thin at once: coolant flow, oxygen hiss, the friendly rumble of Spindle Six. I am suddenly very aware of my own blood in my ears.

Anchor is silent.

You know something is wrong, truly wrong, when the thing that has been background since birth empties itself. Silence falls on us like a dropped bell. The suit begins to count down emergencies in the tone of a patient, distracted teacher.

“Loss of Anchor. Loss of Anchor. Loss of—”

“Shut up,” I tell the suit. It flips to a red blink in my mask and goes mercifully dumb. I press both hands into the net until I feel the sting of thin threads notch into my palms—fake pain through glove sensors designed to convince you that this is real and you should care. The nets don't catch anything heavy. A sparrow would rip them. A shrug of careless body would tear them. They’re for catching a different kind of thing.

For a few heartbeats, there is nothing but the bruised light of the hole and the white weight of the starfields we have stretched into arcs around it. And then my own voice says my name in my ear.

“Seul,” I say in a whisper four hours old. “If you can hear me, step away from the spindle.”

I do not move.

An echo of my breath. The soft, exhausted little laugh I make when I have been awake too long. I listen to myself as if I were a stranger under the bed.

“Please,” past-me says. “The spindle’s going to cough. It will look like a flare in the nearest nets and you will think you can ride it. Do not. I’m telling you because I didn’t and it hurt.”

The com logs aren’t supposed to be polyphased without a Charter key. If old-me is whispering to new-me without a ticket, something has gone very wrong between then and now.

“I love your stubbornness, but not like this,” my voice says, and I can hear Tavi behind me in the recording, the way his laughter sits on the bones of his throat. He sounds tired. He sounds like something is behind him in the room, a dark standing up.

The net pops its gentle warning in my glove. I am too close to a rising tide line.

I undo my hands and swan backward in the slow, sultry gravity we keep for safety. The ring pretends to be gentle with us, until it decides not to. I push off the net and catch the rung on the frame, letting my body swing back toward the walkway. As if on cue, the spindle coughs.

It is not a flare the way we see flares from the suns we set to seed the dark. It is a curl of space, light bending itself into a knot that doesn’t unravel. The net flashes a color I do not have a name for, a color like the feeling of your tongue going to sleep, a color like losing and finding in the same breath. The curl collapses into simple light again. The spindle moans.

I taste metal so hard my jaw locks.

The hole is quieter than I have ever known it. No hum, no background thrumming. We live by the song, and it’s gone.

“Seul, if you do step away you will have a minute and a half. Use it to run the nadir sweep. There will be a signature down there. You’ll only get it once before the Charter closes the ports. Please hear me. Run the sweep.” My own voice breaks. I hate how well I can hear my own fear. “When you get to the end of the minute you will think I am lying. I am not. Take the sweep and then call Amanu.”

“Amanu?” I whisper to the suit. It obligingly throws up the contact. Amanu Iro. What a name to have in a ghost call. The last time I saw Amanu, she was wearing a jumpsuit stained with coffee and reactor varnish, and swearing she would never set foot out on the underside of the ring again. She lives in the Deep Charter now, where old women with eyes like razor blades sort out whose grief gets paid for.

My father’s name is below Amanu’s. He has been out beyond Anchor for fifteen years. He sometimes sends me recipes, like a man who forgot how to write “I miss you.” I stare at the two names like they are the keys to a door, then I look down.

The nadir sweep is not in my checklist for the day. The nadir is the bottom, which is a silly idea on a ring that has no up or down. But we have our ways of talking. The nadir sweep is the one you run when you don’t believe what you think is true. You run it because sometimes the ring lies to you to keep you from seeing the thing that is going to kill you.

“Tavi,” I say into the dead line, forgetting for a handful of breaths that the line is dead. “Start the sweep. I need you to—”

The suit gives me a double tone. Local circuit only, like a cup-and-string between two kids peeking around doorframes. Tavi’s breath fills my helmet; the ring’s echo of him has a hollowness to it.

“I lost the Charter,” he says. No greeting. No pretense. “We lost—it dumped me out of ledger and I’ve never been dumped out before. I think I watched a million hours vanish. I think I—Seul, I need to not be in charge. What do you see?”

“A bandage on a bruise,” I tell him. The thing I always say when I’m too afraid to say what I see. He makes a sound like he believes me and like he doesn’t.

“If we talk like civilians will you run me a sweep like a goddess?” he asks, begging in humor. “Quick. Please.”

“You sound small,” I tell him.

“I am,” he says. “And I’m too old to say my prayers to holes. I need numbers.”

“Run my hand,” I say, and let him take the net feed. He jacks the thread into the ledger algorithm and the ring does its sweet, precise dance. The net makes it a song again: ping ping ping, silence where Anchor should be, a harmonic that slides sideways like a fish.

It is not nothing. If the hole sat in a perfect, empty night, we would die of boredom and vacuum. But everything around here moves. Space is full. The far dust of the galaxy carries records if you have the patience to read them: old starlight, spilt heat, the breath of living worlds, and whatever this is. Something brushes the ring’s skirt and we hear it in the net as a whisper of motion.

“Sorry if I sounded like a futurist there,” I say, the way people apologize when they are about to give you bad news.

“You’re perfect,” Tavi lies. “What do we have?”

“A signature, near-nadir,” I tell him. My own voice in the future told me true. It is like the cold satisfaction of stepping barefoot onto the stair that you knew would be there. “Something… there. Blue on the long. A smear we don’t own. It looks negative.”

“Negative?”

“You’ve never seen it. I’ve seen it once. In a textbook about things you are not allowed to try unless you’d like the ring to pinch shut like a mouth.”

“Stop teasing me. Tell me.”

“Penrose,” I say, and it is like spitting. “Someone is doing a deep-drag on the far side. They pulled a sliver of negative energy out of the spin.”

“That’s illegal in every language,” Tavi says, reverent and horrified. “You can’t do that within a parsec of a habitat. That’s—”

“That’s how you steal from a hole,” I say. “That’s how you commit suicide in public.”

“Who?”

“You tell me.” My suit tells me I have been out on the spine for forty-one minutes past the safe window. It does not tell me anything about the safe window that exists now. The window we used to have, the window before Anchor shut her eye. I have to invent safety from the shape of my breath. “What’s in the ledger?”

He is quiet, and that quiet is worse than the Anchor’s. “A lot moved in the last six hours,” he says at last. “We were blissed with new time. Poured in from accounts I didn't recognize, then vouchered and laundered through old names. It looked clean by the time it hit stores. I thought we’d sold a beautiful slow to someone important.”

“Maybe we did,” I say. My glove vibrates again, gently, like a hand on a wrist. The nadir signature deepens. We are looking at someone’s hook sliding into our fish’s cheek.

From the far side of the ring, in the line reserved for emergency talk you aren’t supposed to even know exists, a voice older than the station says, “This is Amanu Iro. I need a sweep of the nadir for the last eighteen minutes.”

“Done,” Tavi says before I can take a breath. “Ma’am. We’re seeing Penrose bleed.”

For a moment there is noise like paper being turned in an empty hall. Then Amanu says, conversational as a woman asking for more tea, “We are blind. Kera is humming us into the floor. Who is on Six?”

“Seul Hye,” I tell her. “Crewborn. House of Tides.”

“You’re not House anything,” she says automatically, and it cuts me good. “I need another sweep in five. I want you ready to move when I give it.”

“Move what?” I ask.

She doesn’t say “us.” That would be honest beyond her habit. She says, “Assets,” like a prayer.

That is when the first flock of Clockbirds goes dark.

The Clockbirds are little and white, and when you are on the inside of the ring you can see them skating along the spindles like bored minnows. They keep us clean, they keep us mended, they keep their own counsel. They love the song of the spindles—the way swarmbots love a hum, the way people love a heartbeat. They fail safe. That’s their point. When one fails, the others tug it back like a spider saving the fly for later, and the faulty one goes to hospital for a friendly scrub.

On my visor, six of them wisp out of existence like someone took a pencil to them.

“Seul,” Tavi says. “I’m going to throw up.”

“Please don’t. The suit hates it.”

“We’re being robbed,” he says. “It feels so polite. I hate it.”

I picture someone on the far side of the ring, a stranger with a tug like God’s hand, reaching into the ergosphere with a mechanic’s charm and a gambler’s nerve. I picture a skiff with a name painted over twice, ridden quiet by a man or a woman who learned the math from a feed we stamped with a polite NO. I picture how it will go when the spool we’ve kept turning since before I was born snags on the thief’s hook and tears.

“You have sixty seconds,” my older voice tells me, the one from the future. “You will want to run. Don’t. You can’t outrun this. Your body will think it can do more than it can. Use your hands. Use your eyes. Get me the curl.”

I do not remember saying these things. I believe the woman who said them because she sounds like me when I am lying to someone I love, and because she keeps saying please to herself like a promise.

“Spit me the numbers,” Amanu says, impatient, alive with the kind of fear that can move a city. “I need the curl. Give me the curl.”

“Yes, Charter,” I say, and I feel the old, ridiculous gratitude that someone older than me knows what to do. I take the net in both hands. I move it like Dad taught me. I watch the bruise not as a hole but as a map.

“Seul,” Tavi says, his humor back, thin as a ribbon. “If we live, I am going to make you late for every party you ever want to attend.”

“If we live,” I say, “I’m going to let you.”

He laughs like a man who knows where the laughter stops. “All these years selling time and I didn’t think about what it would sound like when someone stole it.”

“They’re not stealing time,” I say, because he needs a better lie. “They’re stealing spin. We live on time. We’ll make more. We always do.”

The net catches. Light sings, if light can sing. The curl sheared loose from the spindle is right there in my glove, imprinted in the flight of photons like a fingerprint left on water.

“There,” I say. “There.”

I transmit. Amanu swears softly in a language I don’t speak anymore. The suit ticks down eight seconds to something it cannot explain. The holes under my feet are empty as eyes.

“Seul,” Amanu says, with a warmth that is not mercy but necessity, “you are now a vector on my map. Congratulations. Keep your head down. Do not, under any circumstances, cut the net without telling me first.”

“I’m not an apprentice,” I say, reflex sharp as a burr.

“Good,” she says. “Then you know what happens the first time someone thinks they’re the exception.”

She cuts the line. Anchor stays silent. The hole hums in a note lower than my blood.

In my ear, I hear my own voice one last time. “We didn’t die here,” I say, and I can tell I am smiling, and I can tell I am lying. “Not yet.”

I look up at Kera, at the bandage on the bruise, at the smears of stars drawn out and multiplied by the curve. The ring carries weight like a word in your mouth you haven’t spoken yet. Somewhere not so far away, someone is playing thief with the slow, patient thing we have built. They have the math and the will. They have a hook in our jaw.

“Okay,” I say to the suit, to the net, to the hole. To Tavi, who opens and closes his mouth like a fish and laughs like a man about to jump into cold water. “Okay.”

I do not know if my father is sleeping in a common bunk on a ship beyond Anchor, or if he has his hands on a similar net and is feeling the drift begin. I do not know if Amanu will be able to push a committee into a shape quick enough to save us. I do not know if the thief will take their sliver and leave or bring the whole ring along behind like a ribbon tied to a fleeing child’s hand.

I do know where my hands belong when the music changes.

We have traded in patience for as long as I have been able to hold a wrench. We have calibrated tenderness and greed. We have used math to hold off the worst of what the universe wants to do to us. A part of me has always been ready for the day someone more patient than we are comes to take what we think we own.

“Seul,” Tavi says for the last time before the Charter takes his line. “If we drown, let’s drown together.”

“We do nothing halfway,” I tell him, and drop with the net toward the nadir, to listen to the way the hole sleeps.

By the time you smell burnt sugar, it’s already moving.

They tell you the scent comes from the coolant cycling too fast, from all the heat your body makes when someone starts pulling years out of it. I learned a different truth early: your sense of smell holds to the oldest part of you. When you stand in the room and the air tilts sweet, it’s the mammal inside, the one before language and bank contracts, recognizing the sudden bright fact that life is being translated into something else.

Haven 12 is a concrete rib cage on the leeward side of the river. The elevators are broken, and on the way up I pass a girl with a chipped violin case and a bald man carrying a column of green bottles he sells as home-brewed chromatography kits, because somebody always thinks they can cheat the sensors by fixing their own. On the tenth landing someone has painted over the CCTV eye with a thumbprint of soot. It looks like a star seen through tears.

My collar buzzes. “Ari?” Shirin’s voice, precise, grainy with a compression algorithm I built three years ago and won’t ever get a bonus for. “You’re five minutes past window. Compliance is pinging.”

“Stairs,” I say. My shirt sticks to my back where the strap of the case cuts. “I’m almost there.”

“Asset is high-risk. Flagged for relocation.” She pauses, then adds, “Please be efficient.”

Shirin rarely puts please in front of anything. I know what that means. The asset has a name and that name has a cousin in our building or a sponsor in a block where we pretend to wear our green jackets with the logo because people there throw things.

Len Mills opens the door before I can knock. He must have been watching the hallway through the tiny gap between the jamb and the wall. He looks like every accountant I’ve ever met: square, neat, the genderless tidy that comes from living with a heap of rules. He shouldn’t be a high risk. His hair is the kind that had a plan and then a plan to replace the plan when the first one wore thin. He reminds me of my father.

He glances at my jacket, at the italic letters of Aevum that arc from my ribs to my shoulder, at the case. He doesn’t widen the gap in the door to let me in.

“I have thirty days,” he says.

“You had thirty days,” I say. “Mr. Mills, we talked. You acknowledged service. You missed the grace extension. The lien attached when the sun set on Friday. It’s Sunday.”

He doesn’t move. My collar hums once, with the soft urgency of a vibrating moth.

“We can do it in increments,” I add. “We don’t have to collect all at once.”

That’s the script the PR team wrote for us, and it fits like something bought in the wrong season: plausible but never comfortable. Aevum likes the words incremental, compassionate, structured. Aevum likes us to use them.

He lets me in. The room is efficient to a fault: a couch that folds, a table that is a screen and a desk and a warming plate for a kettle. Two plants sit under a lamp that makes light like the memory of noon. On the far wall, a series of shelves and in them, rows of glass vials, each with a little paper label, each filled with something that catches and holds the light.

“Herbs?” I ask, despite myself. You learn to ask unimportant questions so people have something else to look at besides your case.

“Cuttings,” he says. “From wild types. Before they were patented. I work in seed acquisition. Worked. I’m between contracts.”

He says that with the careful mouth you get because you’ve practiced in front of a mirror for the call from your mother, the one where you said you’re still fine.

I set the case on the table, snap the latches. The metronome purrs under my fingers as if it’s a small carnivore pleased to see me. It’s called a CQ-9 in the system but everyone in the field calls them metronomes because when you place it on the table it ticks to the beat of a human resting pulse until it doesn’t. It’s small and matte and harmless-looking, the way a pocket stone is harmless-looking right until you throw it and it breaks a window. Inside are two coil heads, a film of adhesion, a delicate spool of silver that unravels into a thread so thin it is mostly a boundary condition.

He watches me lay it all out. He doesn’t ask me how much this will hurt because he knows the answer. It depends. He doesn’t ask me how long it will take. That depends too, on resistance and the labyrinth between intention and flesh and the proprietary quantization metrics the legal team says are trade secrets and the research team says are almost right if you squint.

“You told me you wouldn’t—” His voice is steady but quiet. He clears his throat. “You said you’d come after the holiday.”

“I said if you showed proof of income before the end of last week, we could defer.”

He sets his hands on the back of a chair like he needs an anchor. When people are about to lose time, they always reach for furniture or door frames. The body is smarter than the mind. It knows the house will be the same in an hour and time will not, and it wants to be tied to something.

“How much,” he says.

I tap the screen. His ledger blooms: sixty-nine minutes of house arrears from the last year compounded to months with penalty fees, an advance on a niece’s education that he co-signed for, a half-year for a surgery that kept his sister walking after a scaffold collapsed.

“A total of three point seven years,” I say. “We can take it as four monthly segments. It costs more overall that way.”

He looks past me, and his eyes snatch to a movement in the doorway to the little bedroom. A girl stands there. Nine, maybe ten. Her hair is the brown of dried river weed and she’s wearing a shirt that says SOLVE in faded letters and something else under it in a language people were still arguing about when I was in school. She has the look kids get when they’re pretending to be older to make fear behave.

“Nina,” he says. “Back to your—”

“No,” she says.

She doesn’t say it to him. She says it to me.

“That’s not your decision,” I say as gently as I can.

She steps forward until she’s in the edge of the light and I can see she has the kind of rigid dignity that gets you hurt. “He already paid for us,” she says. “He already gave them what they asked. It isn’t fair.”

I have a list of phrases for this. None of them work, and none of them are for her to hear.

“Grandfather,” she says, and the word catches like a held breath, and even though I really don’t want to I think of my sister, who refuses to speak to me, and I think of her daughter, who knows not to call me anything at all because we made that bargain.

“Nina.” Mills puts a hand out but stops himself before touching her. “Go in, please.”

She goes, like it costs her a piece of bone to do it, and the room feels emptier and bigger after she’s gone, the way a mouth is when you lose a tooth.

“We can pause between segments,” I say because I’m supposed to offer the pause. “You can eat. You can sleep.”

“I don’t want to be asleep in pieces,” he says. “If we’re doing this, do it.”

He sits. He rolls up his sleeve.

The coil heads go to the carotids because that’s where the line is easy. The adhesion film warms under my palm as it bonds. The silver thread hums a little against my finger like a tuning fork when a piano hits middle C.

“You’re not the first to collect from me,” he says. “Two years ago. For her. I thought, if I give them enough of mine, they’ll never take hers.” He smiles then. It’s a very small smile that he puts down carefully between us like a knife. “I was wrong.”

I don’t tell him about the clause that ties guarantees across three degrees of kin. He knows that. He signed it. Everybody signs it now, because everybody wants a little longer, wants to have a baby or save a house or fix a spine. And yes, they tell themselves: I’ll pay it back when the promotion comes, when the next contract is renewed, when my side project sells. Yes, they tell themselves: we’ll pay it together. Yes: we are not the kind of people who end up like this.

The metronome’s indicator changes from open to listening. The room loses a little depth. People think time is a line but it’s more like a fabric with a particular weave and the metronome’s job is to hook that thread in you and pull without tearing.

“You’ve done this a lot,” Mills says.

“Yes,” I say.

“How do you do it? How do you go home after?”

I almost say practice. I almost say a different name than mine. But I say, “I take the train. I put my jacket in a bag. I watch a show with other people’s faces in it. I take a long shower. The steam helps.” I’m not sure if any of that is true anymore. “You signed.”

“I signed,” he says. “She wanted to study ecologies. They told us it was a good investment. They had charts. The first man to sell his years for wine was named Esau. Part of my job used to be reports like that. Stories that hold a mouth open long enough to pour the numbers in.”

He’s trying to talk me into kindness. He’s also trying to see me. It’s not unkind, but it is dangerous.

I tap the accept.

There’s always a beat between agreeing and loss. Your body considers whether this is a good idea; the part of you that knows stone and fire and wolves turns toward the door. Then the metronome ticks once, twice, and the air goes sweet and thin and a sound rises out of the marrow of things. It’s a sound you almost can’t hear until you’ve heard it too many times. It’s the sound of something unfastening from a place no hand has ever touched.

Mills closes his eyes. He breathes. The interface on the table fills with pale color like dawn behind a shade. Somewhere inside the metronome, a wheel I have never seen turns very slowly.

I watch the numbers. They change, not like digits flicking over in a meter, but like a tide going out, the surface lowering so gradually that if you stare you convince yourself you’re imagining it. It used to take seventy-two hours to reclaim a month if the donor held still and slept twice. That was before the CQ-9s. That was when if a man moved his hand you could lose a week to noise and quantization error. We have gotten better at getting what we want.

At point eight six, the interface hiccups. Not a big stutter. A skip, like a heartbeat that trips when you see someone you forgot you loved.

The metronome’s screen shows me a message in system font two sizes smaller than legible. It’s like a secret whispered through a door.

Secondary correlation detected.

“Hold,” I say. The metronome doesn’t know the word hold but my hand knows what to do. I ease pressure on the coil, tilt the spindle a degree. The screen brightens like a cat being scratched behind the ear.

“Is there a problem?” Mills says.

“No,” I lie.

Secondary correlation means another line, near the one I’ve thrown, vibrating. It means something else is moving when I pull this. It means a family guarantee usually. It means a spouse somewhere is giving up a bit of hair to the drain at the same time. But the error detail opens, a spasm of data that tastes like salt in the back of my throat, and I see the stringified ID tag.

ARI NEVALIS 27-13-9072.

I feel it as a skip in myself. The room tilts, the ceiling slides an inch. For a moment it’s like I’m watching my hands on a screen through old plastic.

“Ari?” Shirin’s voice, dry, thin, almost transparent with urgency. “Are you at target? Compliance is blind on your feed. Reconnect.”

“I have a—” I swallow. “We’ve got bleed.”

“Seal and continue,” she says immediately. The words click out of her mouth like pieces of a lock falling into place. “Legal will sort. Reconnect your feed now.”

The girl is in the doorway again. She shouldn’t be—kids can move like insects, finding the gaps in everything. She looks from the machine to her grandfather’s face to mine. When her eyes touch mine I have a moment of disorientation, like stepping down expecting another stair and finding floor. It’s a stupid metaphor, cheap, but that’s how it is, the empty drop that isn’t dangerous but shocks you enough to shame.

“Grandfather,” she says.

“It’s okay,” he says, and looks at me, and in that look is all his long decisions, the nights he woke and counted things he could sell, the afternoons he tells himself he still has time.

The thing about a secondary correlation is you can’t explain it to a client without also explaining how a metronome spins threads between kin through the thinnest possible place and uses the way humans hold each other to make a cleaner cut. If you told that truth, you would make the whole city stand up and scream. So there are a lot of PowerPoints that say network optimization and proprietary dynamic cluster assignment. And there are lawsuits in other districts about whether family is something that happens to blood or something corporations can measure.

The bleed shows my name like someone whispered it into a glass and then pressed that glass to my ear across a very great distance. I don’t have a contract in default. I don’t have liens. I have a mortgage with rates that would make my grandmother kick the wall of her grave if she were ashes in ground instead of ash in a paper box under my sister’s kitchen sink. I have nothing they can take that I have not already labeled as theirs.

“Shirin,” I say, still looking at the neat numbers. “I think we have an orphan segment.”

Silence. Then, too bright, too careful, “What?”

“On the correlation. It’s tagged to me.”

“That’s impossible,” she says. “You’re not on—”

“Do you smell that?” says Nina. She takes a step forward. “I smell… it smells like—”

“Sugar,” Mills says, and he shuts his eyes, and his hand moves as if he is reaching for a rail on a ship.

People always say sugar because it’s nice to think of sugar. To me it’s caramel on the edge of burning, black wrap around a stick, a certain winter when my mother spent a week making candy she couldn’t afford not to sell and burned the pan twice.

“Ari, collect,” Shirin says. “Do not stop. If there’s an orphan we’ll run analytics. There’s a new package on your collar. You shouldn’t be seeing that tag.”

“I am,” I say. “What is it?”

A pause, and I know she’s glancing to the left at her second screen where the conversation that has my job in it just erupted. I can imagine Compliance—three letters, petty gods—trying to make sense of this and doing it without me.

“Someone is playing with us,” she says finally. “You’re clean. Collect and get out. There’s a mobile unit inbound if you aren’t done in four minutes.”

Corporate enforcement. We don’t call them that. We call them mobile optimizers when we feel like living in a word made of gauze.

“Who else has been here?” I ask.

Mills opens his eyes. He considers the ceiling like a man decides whether to lie to his priest.

“Yesterday,” he says, and leaves it there.

“What did they say?”

The room sluggishly refocuses. The numbers on the screen tick like a heart that runs too fast and then stumbles. He runs his tongue over his lower lip. It’s pink, almost obscenely alive.

“She said,” he says. “She asked me to hold as much as I could for another day. She told me it would matter. She left me a jar. She said if I couldn’t hold it, to give that to whoever came to take it. She called it a seed.”

“She?” I say.

He looks at Nina very quickly and back at me. “She knew you. She knew your name.” He smiles that small knife smile again. “She said to tell you kite string."

I have not heard those two words spoken in that order since I was fifteen and a boy I loved stood on the floodwall with me and asked, bold and stupid, if I was going to jump. The same year, my mother said kite string, and tied the pantry door shut with it so I couldn’t steal sugar to make candy like the women at the market did, and then at the market a woman sold me two minutes of her life for a bag of crushed pomegranate seeds.

“Kite string,” I repeat, and the room remembers being a street and the table remembers being old wood and the metronome ticks twice and waits.

“What jar?” I say through my teeth.

He nods toward the shelf. I step around the coil and the thread and the breath and the sweet ache in my throat and pick up a glass vial. It has one of his paper labels: S24-RED. Inside is a red grain the size of a dry pea, more matte than a thing like that has any right to be. My fingers feel it as heat through the glass. When I turn it, it doesn’t roll quite right, as if the inside of the jar is not the same kind of space as the room.

“It’s not for you,” he says. “She said to give it to you if I couldn’t hold them back. And you are here, so I couldn’t.”

Shirin is an insect in my ear. “Ari, you will finish this collection now. You will not accept unregistered objects from a defaulted client. Do you hear me? That order is explicit.”

For a second, I am fifteen again, and my mother’s hand is on my wrist and people are shouting and a man is holding a bag of salt out of reach of a skinny dog. Then I am me, standing in a man’s neat apartment with a machine that burns sugar and a glass vial in my palm that feels like a small sun.

“Mr. Mills,” I say, “who was she?”

He shakes his head. “She had a coat that looked like it belonged to someone with better shoes.”

Outside, something purrs in a way that is too smooth to be a cat, too round to be a drone. The mobile unit is here early or the neighbors’ building is doing an arrest or the city just moved its breath to make space for something.

“Ari,” Shirin says.

Three point seven years is a lot. It is enough to turn a hairline crack in a life into a fracture. It is also exactly what we are meant to take because a contract is a contract and if we don’t claw it out of this man someone else’s mother will die years early because a hospital budget will wobble.

I have done this job long enough to know that none of that is true and all of it is. I have done this job long enough to learn that decisions don’t happen in your head but in the tendons of your fingers.

I pick up the metronome with my left hand and with my right I slip the little jar into my jacket pocket because if I don’t, someone will. The device in my hand hums and my collar stings me like a bee and the mobile unit outside equivocates between leaving and coming up the stairs.

“I will take the first segment,” I say. “We will reassess.”

“That will incur additional—” Shirin starts.

“I know,” I say. “Put it on my compliance score.”

“Excuse me,” she says, cold as space, and the communication drops.

I bring the wheel a fraction back to take pressure off the thread. The room sighs. The sweet smell lingers but clears. Mills opens his eyes and looks ten days older and exactly who he was. The numbers freeze in their march, pause on a cliff’s edge I can’t name.

The girl steps forward once, then stops herself. She is learning too many kinds of control in one morning.

“You shouldn’t do that,” Mills says to me. “They won’t like it.”

“They don’t like a lot of what I do,” I say.

There’s another sound then. A deep note, not machine, not entirely. A hum like air made from glass. It comes from outside, from the sky. I look out of habit.

Above the river, too high to be a drone and too low to be a weather satellite, the Halo glows. It’s pale in daylight, almost polite, not something you notice until you do and then you can’t look away. The Halo is a chain of vessels linked like pearls around our planet, not quite touching, a necklace we bought by the second to keep our atmosphere clean and the storms gentle. We pay for it with years, of course. We are told that’s cheaper than all our throats.

On mornings when I ride the train, the Halo looks like a god seen through fog, something you would have sworn was a lie if you hadn’t read the contract. Today it has a dark seam running along it like a wound closing in reverse.

“Do you see that?” I ask.

Mills does not look. He is looking at the metronome and the thin silver thread and the way my hand shakes. He reaches, slowly, very slowly, and puts his fingers on the edge of the table.

“Kite string,” he says again, softly, as if the words are not a code but a prayer with a chord in it.

There is a knock on the door, precise and administrative, like someone practicing what politeness sounds like. Nina goes rigid and is small again, a child again, all the dignity gone like a coat taken off and folded.

“Aevum Recovery,” a voice says through the crack. The politeness is almost human. “Open, please. We’re here to assist with your optimization event.”

I should finish this. I should set my hand and take what we came for and leave before the mobile unit takes me with their carbon calm. I should not think about boys on floodwalls or my mother’s pantry or a jar that feels like a star in my pocket.

“You need to go,” Mills says.

“I think they want me to stay,” I say.

The door knocks again, more insistently, and then the precise sound of a corporate key in a communal lock. The lock was made to open to that kind of key. Of course it was.

“Do you know what’s in it?” I ask, my hand on my pocket where the red seed sits like a blood cell that learned a secret.

He shrugs, a careful slope of the shoulders. “No. But it felt like… something that calls back.”

“Calls what?” I say.

He looks at me, really looks, and for the first time all morning I feel seen in a way that isn’t my job, isn’t the jacket I wear or the case I carry. “Time,” he says. “Or you.”

The door opens a fraction and a person shaped like a person in a uniform we all have seen on screens puts a hand through. The Halo’s pale seam tightens in the strip of August sky. The metronome ticks. The air tastes sweet and dangerous. I will tell myself later that I did not decide. The decision rose through me like a buoy moves through water, because the hand is in the room and the sky has a seam and someone told my name to a glass to carry across the city and a man who looks like my father once did is watching me hold his years like a handful of coins.

I pull the thread free with a motion so slight it could have been an accident. The metronome hums down to its resting note. The numbers stabilize. Three point oh nine remaining.

“Hi,” I say to the person in the doorway, and I smile like a streetlight going red. “We’re between segments. The client needs to eat.”

“Policy restricts—” the person starts.

“Policy,” I say, “can find me on the train.”

I put the metronome back in the case. I snap the latches. I touch the pocket where the jar sits, warm as luck.

Outside, the Halo tightens. Somewhere under all the noise, the words kite string hum like a connection you can’t see and a path you haven’t taken yet and a debt you didn’t know you owed.

“Run,” says a voice that is not in the room.

For a moment, I think I have imagined it. For a moment, I am sure it is my own scared animal brain trying to name the right way out. Then the jar in my pocket warms to pain and the voice says again, distinctly, like someone speaking in the next room with the door almost shut:

Run. They can see you.

Chapter One: The Weather Writes Back

On the morning the weather learned to write, Sori Anene was balanced on a maintenance rung with the Atlantic thrumming beneath her boots.

The array spread below her like a spiderweb flung across the continental shelf. Thousands of hexagonal floats railed the swells, each anchored down into the cold with braided cable, each topped with soft-shouldered towers and mirrored wings. Wave-eaters along the skeleton gulped energy and shoved it into the grid. Sky keels unfurled and furled to push air into the paths they needed. Sori had grown up inland, the brown harmattan dust in her hair, but it was the taste of salt and ozone she’d come to call home. The array sang when she walked it—tiny shifts in tension, the human weight it had not been designed for and yet had learned to accept.

“Anene,” Jae’s voice said in her earpiece, thick with stale coffee. “Kelvin gating is five by nine. Your little tantrum upgraded out of wavelets.”

“They always do,” Sori said. She hooked her knee against the rung and leaned out over Slipway Seven, the vertical drop where they launched the skates. A crew of five in orange soft-armor was prepping a cluster of sonic emitters—black globes the size of watermelon, enmeshed in smart-mesh like strange fruit. A skate drone skimmed the troughs, its white body sleek and mottled with dried salt, the underside pitted where it had butted a coral tower earlier in the week. Its flippers were carbon sails; when it skimmed, it moved like something alive.

“Say that louder,” Jae groaned. “Management loves it when you anthropomorphize the atmosphere.”

“They are alive,” Sori said. On her wrist, the fields came through her haptic band as textures: the low burr of shelving inversion, the melody of shear at three altitudes. The cutter currents from the Azores. The warm tongue leaking west from the Gulf of Guinea like a sigh.

Weather had been Sori’s first language, even before she knew how to name it. Back when she was small and Kenshin Road had not yet rearranged itself into endless stacked housing, she and Tunu would stand on the roof and watch the bruise-code of storms unfurl from the sea blade. Tunu would make up songs out of thunder. Shhhhh, she’d say. Listen. It’s talking.

The event that had made Sori into a Cloud Shepherd was not cinematic. It was slow. It was days of rain too warm to be kind, then inland rivers climbing out of their beds and walking through houses. It was Tunu’s door swelling in its frame. It was an ambulance that could not clear the overpass because the bridge had settled into its new posture and nobody had yet updated the weight limits. It was Sori carrying a suitcase of damp paper family and looking up and thinking: we let it get this way.

“My god, you’re already listening, aren’t you?” Jae said softly. “You have that voice.”

“My voice is the same,” Sori said. She slid down the rung into the launch well. The air was cool and sharp this early. The day would grow into a glare, but now the light was grey and interested. By midday the tropical depression straddling the Precover would either lay down and die or gather itself. It had that look Sori did not trust. If it found the right energy, it could push itself south, roll under the belly of the array into Zones Six and Seven where the non-intervention treaty prevented them from laying a finger on it, and then slip into Angolan waters fat and smug. Stormlaw had complicated everything. Storms had always been political; Sori just hated that now she had to say it out loud.

“The new ensemble’s up,” Jae said. “NeuroBayes wants us to do a crisp cap injection at ninety-one kilometers.”

“NeuroBayes can want a lot,” Sori said. She signaled the launch crew. A technician gave her a silent two-finger salute and nudged the skate onto the tongue of water slicking the rails. The drone slid forward with the grace of a stingray and dropped. Sori’s band filled with a new texture and she closed her eyes and let it in. The drone’s cameras were good, but this was better: the claws of arpeggio where cell convection tugged the surface, the whispered hiss in the transition layer like a finger over glass.

She tapped the band, shiftily, pulling back one layer of abstraction until the raw numbers scrolled by. They had names for the patterns they learned to love or fear: onion ring echo, seahorse tail, dry slot, sting jet. This wasn’t any of them. The pattern lived somewhere between scale and scale, not fully statistical, not really human-readable. She dropped her hand and watched the horizon where the cloud wove its own horizon in pure white.

“Say it for me,” Jae prompted, a ritual of theirs. “Describe it so I can pretend I’m out there instead of in here watching dashboards turn green.”

“Think of a musician warming up,” Sori said. “Not a song. Not yet. Little broken scales. Someone teaching themselves to press their mouth a different way.”

“Christ,” Jae said, and then, because he knew when to stop poking, he went quiet.

Sori signaled for the emitters to start their test. The black globes unshuttered and dipped into the sea, hummed in perfectly ordinary ways. They were not magic. They were instruments. They pushed small sonic pulses into the boundary layer where sea became air. They could not stop a storm—you learned to stop thinking in absolutes if you worked here—but they could encourage cells to peel off, disrupt rotational couplings, feed the right fish while starving the wrong whale. It was work of millimeters and seconds, and it mattered.

Above Sori, two gulls passed like gossip. The air smelled of machine oil and salt.

Her earpiece clicked. “Atlantic Pivot Station, this is Nairobi Flight Seven requesting corridor. We have a research hawk requesting a high-altitude pass over your Zone Five. We need a clean sky by thirteen hundred.”

Sori glanced up. The local airspace manager was two bays down with a harmonizer looped around her neck, braiding drone flight requests into the rest of the morning’s noise. “You hear that?” Sori said. “They want a corridor through the field in five.”

“The hawk can thread a needle,” Jae said. “Just give them a line.”

“Tell them to stay above nineteen thousand if they can,” she said. “We’re going to kick the messy stuff up there soon.”

“Yes, ma’am, we will certainly relay your request to the birds,” Jae said drily. He was a good manager in here because he had not forgotten how anything outside looked.

“Don’t call me ma’am,” she said, and then the glove bit into her palm in a way that was not pain but was not not pain.

The band translated suddenness as a sharpness, a new edge under the old song. The depression’s envelope thickened, then thinned, then this: a braid snapping and rebraiding itself, the fast-hand of an expert knotter.

Sori swore. “Slipping south faster than projected,” she said. “It found a path. Halson—”

“I’m here,” said Halson, a calm alto from the treaty desk. Halson’s job was a perfect marriage of law and ruin. “Where are we with the line?”

“The line is a joke,” Sori said, then regretted it. Halson didn’t write the treaties; Halson cleaned the blood off old ones and made new ones look presentable. “It’s going for the white.”

On everyone’s prints, a translucent strip of ocean hung like a bandage just below Zone Six. White Zone. That was the good, neutral word. The long name was the Biomass Sanctuary Corridor, a ribbon of water where everything living had been so thoroughly gouged and hacked and starved that the global commons had finally barricaded it off. No industrial fishing. No wave capture. No aerosol injection. No sonic disruptions. Some of the plankton species rebounding there were the sort that made old whales remember something. A few biogenic cloud seeds had been cataloged that did not behave like any of the modeled ones; some of them interfered with electrics in messy ways. The treaty logic was iron.
