The weather did not read treaties.

“We can push on its shoulder here,” Sori said, marking a point with two fingers. “Push now and we don’t have to push later. If it crosses into white, we’re spectators.”

“Only if we can effect without tainting the corridor,” Halson said. “You know the conditions.”

“They write them to be impossible to meet,” Sori said, but she said it to the air and not to anyone in particular.

“If you keep telling us what’s wrong with the laws, maybe you should run for Council,” Jae said.

“Every year my mother asks,” Sori said. She gestured and the skates surged. Emitters purred. She was good at this work in part because she remembered that her hands did not control anything. They suggested. They lured. Jae joked that she spoke to storms the way a patient teacher spoke to a child. Sori hadn’t corrected him because the metaphor complicated itself in her head: storms were not children; they were old gods. You learned their moods out of respect, not disdain. You learned the places where their attention was elsewhere and you could slip a request in politely and have it granted without fuss.

On her band, the storm paused. Strange, Sori thought. Not that storms could pause in the ordinary sense—they were masses of heat arguing with themselves—but within them there were layers, and in one layer something held its breath and listened.

“Sori?” Jae said, always attuned to the moment when her breathing changed.

“It’s—” She broke off. “Just—hold with me a second.”

The pause was a texture, not an absence. She had felt it once before, a year ago when a line of storms off Recife had turned and run their lengths against prevailing winds as if a hand had been laid along their spines like the smooth downstroke of a lover. They had blamed it on a mesoscale phenomenon nobody could agree on. They had named it and moved on.

“NeuroBayes updated,” Jae said. “It says we should permit the cell to intensify for ninety seconds, then seed the cap with copper-shelled nuclei. Sori, that’ll be mission creep into white.”

“We’re not seeding with copper into the Corridor,” Halson said, horror braided into patience. “For someone who rails about law, you are very good at trying to forget it.”

“We won’t need to seed if we turn it before twelve,” Sori said. “Hold on.”

She closed her eyes, let the textures climb. A child’s hand on a window, a gust, a lullaby that had not been made for a human throat. It wasn’t sound. It was a pattern her nervous system recognized because everything alive recognized the way systems played with energy when they wanted to be efficient. But there was something else, an overlay that was not efficient and was not random. It was rhythmic.

She was the one who’d said storms were like teachers. This was like a student tapping a pencil on the desk in a way that turned into words.

“I know this,” she whispered without meaning to.

“Do you want me to call Mikel?” Jae said. Mikel had been Sori’s mentor when she’d first boarded the arrays. He now ran a small lab with three broken windmills and a talent for writing grant applications that read like poetry.

“No,” Sori said. Then: “Not yet.”

She opened her eyes. At the horizon, the white line wavered. The storm pushed toward it, then curled. Sori lifted her hand, not commanding, just reaching, and the drone translated her unscience into numbers and impulses. Energy slid. A feeder band flinched. She did not push harder. That would have been a mistake. She teased, seductive, a warm place to go that was not south.

“Come on,” she said softly. “Come this way. It’s easier. It’s kinder.”

On the data layer, a set of small convective cells along the southern flank rotated ninety degrees. The bright-scar ring at the center pulsed. The pause texture became the sense of a pen touching paper.

“Jae,” Sori said. “Are you seeing the echo top structure?”

There was a long hiss that might have been Jae forgetting to breathe. “Tell me that is not what I think it is.”

“Don’t say it,” Halson said. “Because if we say it out loud, the press will requisition the transcript.”

“It’s a feature,” Jae said weakly. “A boundary artifact. A—”

On a screen three bays away, a junior technician started laughing and choked on it and turned it into a cough. Another person swore. Someone said, “God”, in the baffled way of the secular.

Sori watched the radar return write three short vertical strokes and one horizontal one. Boats had spelled messages in wakes and yelled online about having tamed a storm. Corporations had drawn their logos in aerosols over city parades and been fined and been lauded, depending on who was writing the feed. The person who had once turned wind so that a line of cumulus made a crude and graceless heart had likely meant well.

This was not a wake or a parade. The strokes were careful. The thickness was even. The spacing was disciplined and then, as if whoever was writing it remembered something about beauty, a fraction of whimsy in the tail of the last mark. It was basic alphabet, not a script you’d learn at school. It was careful printing.

“S-O-R-I,” Jae said, as if the name were new in his mouth. “Sori.”

Her skin went cold. She hadn’t given anyone her name this morning outside the usual systems. Thessaly from Hydro had yelled “Anene, tell your skates to stop buzzing my trout” as a greeting. The airspace person had called her “ma’am.” Her own band was not audibly voiceprinting.

“The Radar Artists are going to go feral,” Jae said faintly. “They’re going to sell amulets with your face on them. Look forward to that.”

“Sori,” Halson said, more gently than they had ever spoken to her before, “we have to document. I know you know this. Do not touch anything. Do not modify anything that could be construed as precipitating this pattern.”

She took a breath, then another. The smell of ozone seemed to deepen, a cat scratching the back of her throat. Under her boots the array shifted as a long swell came in and went away. The emitters, obedient and dull, hummed.

“What is the hawk’s position?” she said. Her voice was steady. She did not feel steady.

“Seven minutes out,” Jae said. “They’re going to be right above when—”

“When the sky writes names,” Halson said. “We should request a hold. We should not have anything over the Corridor if there is an unknown phenomenon.”

“It’s not over the Corridor,” Sori said automatically. She tightened her grip on the rail, then loosened it. She hated when her body told on her. The storm, perhaps, had always known humans in all their undisciplined ways. A small part of her brain, uncharitable and petty, wondered who it had written first, who the first person had been. Whether they were lucky enough to have a name that lay in the simplest strokes. Whether the weather would bother with a complicated name. Whether it would learn.

“I need someone to tell me we’re not hacked,” Jae said, without any dressing. “I need someone to say that an uparray or downarray isn’t spoofing our returns. Because if the sky is printing, then the sky can be forged to print.”

“We can run the blind,” Halson said. “We can switch to raw drifters, independent of array. We can pull old balloon data. It will still take time.”

“Run it,” Sori said. “Pull everything. Jae—get me a visual.”

“I’m already pinging the hawk,” Jae said, his voice popping hairpin-turn quick. “They should be able to get us passes in ninety seconds. If they tell me to file for a press embargo, I’m going to pretend I can’t hear because someone’s baby just started crying.”

“You’d be fired,” Halson said.

“You’d hire me,” Jae said. “You have a weakness for me.”

The joke lay there and tried to be enough. The band vibrated. The storm drew another letter, a trick of moisture and momentum. Someone on another feed said, in the faint way of a person realizing they would be a small annotation in a textbook forever, “It’s drawing from the Kelvin cells like they were wells.”

Mikel called, of course he did. “Sori,” he said, breathless as if he had run. “Are you—”

“Alive,” she said. “Here.”

“It’s not a spoof,” he said. “I’m looking at independent rocketsonde. It’s real.”

She had not asked him to check. He had heard what she had heard in her voice and known exactly what box to open on his own screen. Mikel had taught Sori that most of this work was knowing which answers you needed to be able to sleep.

“Do not—” he began.

“Interfere,” she finished. “I know. And if it goes into the white, we are legally allowed to watch it and fall in love from afar and do nothing.”

He made a strangled sound. He had never been good with laws either.

The hawk came in high and sure, a spear of silver in the blue. Its cameras blinked a thousand times and shipped those blinks to a thousand feeds and all over the world people who had not known the Atlantic could be interested glanced down at their breakfast and said Oh. Because the weather did as it had always promised it might, in parables and in childish drawings. It made marks. It made a name.

Sori felt it as a pressure against her skull, not painful, insistently curious. She thought of Tunu’s hand on the window during those childhood storms. How Tunu would breathe fog and draw a heart and laugh and say, now your turn.

She had not told anyone the other reason she was good at this work. You weren’t supposed to believe in mystic nonsense, not if you wore your rescuer-card on a lanyard. But when the storms made their jokes, when they pretended to be birds or horses or maps, Sori could hear when there was a human in the joke and when there was not. This was not a human joke. It was barer and more earnest.

She imagined saying: I am Sori. She imagined saying: Who are you.

What she said was, “Halson. When a new actor enters the climate, what do the frameworks say?”

She felt, rather than saw, the treaty officer’s square mouth flatten. “We do not have an entity classification for a fluid dynamic phenomenon with emergent semiotic behavior.”

“You will by tomorrow,” Jae muttered.

“We have protocols,” Halson said, calmer again. “We classify unknowns by capability and intent. We do not assume agency. We assess harm and benefit. We gather data. We do not panic.”

“Good,” Sori said. She could do those things. The thing in the storm could write her name in the cool white of a humid morning and she could still be a professional. She could be impressed later.

On her band, a flutter. Not from the big thing. From the south, low level. A cluster of cells breaking off like bad children, scudding toward the white with the carelessness of youth. If they made it under the line they would bathe in silence and grow fat and then the spin they contributed would be clean and mean.

“Permission to act on the southern flank only,” Sori said. “We can still turn those. It’s not in the Corridor yet.”

Halson took a second Sori did not have. Then: “Make your case.”

“There is no case,” Sori said, hearing herself be unpretty. “It will be worse if we don’t. And this—this writing—if it means anything at all, it knows we are watching. Let us not be the kind of watcher that allows harm because it looks holy.”

Sometimes you said something that you would regret later because you meant it so much. There was a quiet on the line, like the little hush before rain reaches the ground.

“Green,” Halson said. “Southern flank only. No ultrasound into the Corridor. No chemical caps. If any ripple crosses into white and can be traced—”

“We will own it,” Sori said. “We will own everything.”

She moved her hand and the skates obeyed. They spilled sound like a handful of coins across water. The southern cells stiffened, then bent. That was all. It was enough. Not a stop. A delay. Any time you stole from a storm was time you paid into the bank of people under it.

“Sori,” Jae said quietly. “The hawk is sending you something.”

The visual came to her short and perfect. The drone had caught a break in cloud, a glimpse of ocean that would be ordinary in any other hour. Sun spattered the water. Foam latticed itself where waves talked to wind. In the foam, not in the clouds, in the dirty, universal handwriting that all sailors knew—there too, the letters. Not imposed from above, not a radar mathematician’s hallucination. S-O-R-I. The S open, generous. The O a ring. The R like a stubborn leg. The I so simple a child could have drawn it.

Her mouth went dry. Her mother had called her name like that when Sori had been small and the boys from the next street had bullied Tunu. Sori had marched in with a broom and her name had been a weapon in their air.

She touched the rail, an anchor. The array thrummed back at her, unimpressed. A gull called, rude. From below, a skate sprayed salt when it turned. The world continued to be very, very real.

“Who taught you letters?” Sori asked the horizon, softly, in the voice she used for very young storms and sometimes for scared children.

No one answered. The wind went on doing its work. The band against her wrist buzzed once, then again, less like a word than like an acknowledgement that a word had been offered.

“Your mother is going to say you are famous,” Jae said after a time. “She is going to make that face.”

“My mother is going to ask me why I didn’t wear a better shirt to work,” Sori said. It came out normal. That was good. That meant that some piece of her was still in the place where jokes could sit without trembling.

“Protocol update,” Halson said. “Everything to record. Everything to the labs. And—Anene—thank you.”

“For not losing my head?” She found a grin somewhere and put it on like a mask that turned out to fit the face it was made for.

“For saying what you said,” Halson said. “There is a way humans are going to behave about this. We might as well start out trying to be the best version.”

Sori nodded, then remembered they could not see her and said, “Okay.”

The storm had written her name. She had not given it to it. She had not offered her data. She had not shouted into the sky the way some had done and pretended it was prayer. The weather had come to her and made an introduction. That was either comedy or omen or an invitation. Or it was nothing at all, a coincidence the size of the Atlantic pretending to be intimacy for the sake of two seconds of drama.

She had enough humility to hold all those possibilities. She had not been given humility as a child. Humility had been knocked into her by water.

She leaned into the band again, less to act than to listen. Sometimes the most important work was in the listening. And if the weather learned to write, it might also have learned to read. If so, there would be other messages. If there were other messages, they would not all be hers.

Beyond the line, the white water of the protected corridor lay still as a withheld breath. The southern cells doglegged, some caught, some slipping free. The hawk banked once, twice, then climbed. The world shrank to the size of Sori’s palm. She could feel Jae’s attention like a laser, Halson’s like a weight, Mikel’s like a net.

“Okay,” she said to the waiting Atlantic, to the names written and unread. “Okay. Your turn.”

On the morning the wind learned my name, I was hanging by my thighs in a harness forty meters under the belly of Array Nine, with a polymer line between my teeth and the stormscape of Sel below me like a living bruise.

We called it Sel because someone, somewhere, decided that a good name for a gas giant the color of old violets was the shortened word for silence. No one who had ever dangled this close to its roaring knew why. There was nothing silent about a atmosphere that could shear a city in half out of boredom.

The line I was working on was the central bight of a kite-spar that had been complaining since second shift. It had laid a groan into the ledger—thin, high, like a mosquito circling—then shifted down over hours into something heavier. Harmonic drift. It meant wear, which meant heat, which meant that if I didn’t figure out where and patch it, one noon shift a gust would come up laughing and tear a hole in our lift like a child does paper.

I held the line with my molars, like my mother taught me when I was five and she still had both hands, and eased the bonecomb into the braid with two fingers, listening through my jaw. The comb is a fold of wood and piezo that amplifies the tiny changes, so that what is work for the eyes becomes a song for the skull. It’s the first thing they give you when you apprentice as a tensionist. The first time I put it to a line, it felt like running my tongue along a scar I didn’t know I had.

Above me, Nine’s underbelly stretched like canvas sky: layered sailcloth and bladderworks and the skeletal shadows of struts. Thin-limbed workers ghosted along the latticework, trailing safety webs, their hair sticking to their faces with static. Farther out, the kite-fields bloomed, each one a lozenge of iridescence in the shear, flexing to catch and ride the pressures other crews predicted and harvested with the care of farmers.

Below, the violet depth stretched and shook. You don’t look too long. Sel pulls at the eyes. It’s too easy to imagine the weight of it. The pressure that makes diamond rain at depths we’ll never see.

The song through my teeth was wrong. If a good tension is a clean F, this was a flatted E someone had sat on. I worked along the line, spitting to mark suspect sections and pinning microclamps like beaded jewelry, the way Yana taught us—like you’re dressing it for a party it doesn’t want to attend. The air stank of ozone and the bitter-sugar of self-healing resin. Somewhere to my left a flashfall went off like God stomping His foot: brightness through the eyelids and a shunt of upward force that made my rig’s carabiners cry out. The kettle-crows nesting around the windvanes took off like charred confetti and reascended as if nothing had happened.

I found the hot segment—a chafing against a worn guide where someone had, probably in first shift, decided a ninety-degree turn could behave like a sixty. There’s math for that and there’s experience and the two meet only when the wind lets them. I touched the guide and yanked my hand back. The heat nipped through the glove like a mouse bite.

I radioed Koro to log the adjustment. “Kite Field Three, guide seventy-two’s lost its cap. I’ll patch and report.”

Static, then Koro’s voice, thin with the wind. “Copy, Anah. Storm-eye is sliding left three degrees. You have ten.”

“I’ll take five.”

“You’ll take seven and that’s a compromise.”

“Seven,” I said, because Koro was not only my friend but my shift lead and he was right too often to fight with when I was busy. I pulled the temp-graft out of my kit, soft as kelp at first, then stiffening when the skin-cells woke and drank from the air. The array breathed. That’s what you learned young: everything around you was breathing—spar, line, bladder, the lichen-wool that softened pad against metal, the proto-bio that slept until you fed it current, the fungus in the braids that remembered strain and taught the patch how to grow to match it. Our city was a lung held in a jaw. Our job was to keep it from biting down.

I smoothed the graft around the guide, coaxing the microbladders in the mesh to inflate just enough to cradle the line without starving it. The song in my bonecomb changed, a subtle brightening, as the tension distributed more evenly. I felt my shoulders drop the way they do when a note resolves. I spat out the line and clamped the comb to my harness. Then, as I reached for the tagger to mark the repair, the song changed again.

I didn’t hear it with the comb. I heard it with the cavities of my face.

At first, I thought it was me moving. The shift of my weight made the line sing differently and I’ve been doing this long enough to know not to mistake that for trouble. But this went across ten lines at once and the comb wasn’t touching any of them. I felt it in my skull and spine, in the straps of the harness and the fine hairs on my arm. The lattice of Nine caught the pattern and carried it, and for a heartbeat—less, really—I wasn’t a person in a harness, I was an instrument and someone else was playing.

It said: Ah-na.

I shut my eyes. That’s reflex, or faith. If you shut your eyes the rest of your senses get bigger. Most days that’s superstition. Some days it’s physics.

Ah-na, it wrote through my bones, and then the line under my thigh moaned like a whale and the wind climbed. By the time I had my eyes open again the pattern was gone, and the comb, when I fumbled it back to touch, sang ordinary complaint. I looked at my hands and saw that they were shaking.

“Anah?” said Koro in my ear. “Time.”

“I heard it,” I said. I hadn’t meant to. It came out anyway. “Koro, I heard—”

“Seven minutes.”

“Koro.”

There was a pause. Then, too mild, as if we were not both strapped to our death with laughter under us, he said, “We’re not doing this up here, Vesper. Are you clear of three?”

I looked at the graft and made it neat because it’s a thing to do that is solid. “Three is clear,” I said. “Coming in.”

On my way back I checked two other lines that didn’t need checking, because my hands knew how to check and because I needed the familiar drag of the comb’s teeth to remind my skull what notes were. The good tension sang true. My body, which has never forgiven me for being born into sky, wanted a floor under it the way some bodies want salt.

When I swung up into the belly-hatch, people were already stripping gear and hanging it on the rack that hummed faintly as the static bled out. The air inside the belly smelled like humans and battery acid. Yana sat on a crate because Yana always sat on crates; she said chairs are for people who think they own the ground. Her hair was in ropes threaded with tiny tin bells that rang when the pressure dropped. They were ringing, very faint.

“You went long,” she observed, as if that were merely impolite and not deadly.

“Guide lost its cap,” I said. “I patched.”

She nodded. “Good. Eat. Drink. Pee. Someone up-array is complaining about the little ones kicking under the noise floor.”

I reached for the shared bottle on the crate beside her and swallowed electrolytes until my teeth hurt. My hands had stopped shaking. In the far corner, Rell and Haro were taking apart a shear sensor with the reverence of some old faith’s acolytes distributing thin wafers. No one was looking at me. That was good. I kept my face made of work.

Koro slid in through the hatch minutes after I did, his curls a nest of copper gone mad with static. He bumped his shoulder against mine as he passed: the wordless kindness of people who know how to approach skittish animals. “Come,” he said low, as if he were calling a cat. He didn’t wait to see if I followed. He walked down the spine-corridor toward the central frame where Nine met Nine, the hub where we pretended the city had a center.

Array Nine didn’t really have a center. None of the arrays did. The hubs were thicknesses of thought; the places we had agreed to agree on. They collected decisions like burrs collect fur.

Koro went up the ladder into the nav turret. The world opened there: thin walls of murmurglass that let you feel, under your palm, the path the wind wanted you to take. Outside, the kite-fields were angled to catch a shear like a river eddy. I pressed my hand to the glass and felt the city’s pressure shape itself around me like a cat deciding in slow motion to knead your stomach and lie down. The bells in Yana’s hair would have been ringing more loudly, here.

Koro closed the turret’s hatch with a wheel and turned. His eyes were wide and careful. “Say it.”

I wanted to make a joke. Sometimes the urge to make a joke is the same as the urge to jump: to prove you’re not an animal whose nerves are in charge. “Oh good,” I said thinly. “We’re doing the thing.”

“We are doing the thing,” Koro said. “While we are not dangling over a place named in sarcasm for the silence it doesn’t possess.”

I put my knuckles against my teeth and pressed until bone dulled the itch under my skin. Then I told him.

I told him exactly. I used the words for nothing it might be—shear whisper, cross-coupled harmonics, scaffold resonance, the possibility of a distant flashfall hitting three lines in a pattern only my hungry brain made meaning in—and then I told him the thing none of those could explain, which was the way it had written my name inside me like a finger across the dust of a neglected room.

He listened the way good shift leads listen: not to argue, but to hear the thing under your words and measure how much of it is danger and how much is just a human remembering that wind is bigger than people and that can be confusing.

“Yana told me a story,” he said when I was done, because of course he would bring Yana into this. He looked through the glass toward where she might be, as if the story might walk up the ladder behind us. “When I first came up from the nursery. About how the old arrays used to sing with the storm. Old people like that word. Sing. They used harmonics to keep out of vortices. They said if you listen long enough it starts to sound like talking. Then you stop listening because that way is superstition and gravitational death.”

“I didn’t make it up,” I said, useless as that was.

“I know you didn’t,” he said simply, and the sudden lift in my chest made me want to lean forward and bite his collarbone until he yelped, just to bleed off whatever that was.

Down in the hub below us, Yana’s bells chimed again. The nav screen above our heads—a cheap old thing with a crack like a hair across the right third—showed the leading edge of the storm-eye. We’d been skirting it all morning. We would skirt it all afternoon and into the night. It was shifting like an animal turning in sleep.

“Log it,” Koro said finally. “Not in public.” He grimaced. “You know why.”

Another morning I would have rolled my eyes and told him I didn’t believe in the Quiet Council. Which is what the elders called themselves as if we wouldn’t immediately name them after their least attractive feature. The Quiet Council didn’t like anomalies. In their books anomalies led to stories and stories led to people leaning into things and we lived among forces that punished leaning. They would scrub the logs or call it noise and then redline my name as someone not to promote. Nine does not need us to be brave. Nine needs us to be careful.

“I’ll put it in the ledger,” I said, “where the fungus can chew on it and inform me I’m a fool.”

He smiled with one side of his mouth. “The fungus is kinder than most elders.”

There is truth in this. The strain fungus in the lines carries a memory of pressure changes. That’s why it’s there—to teach patches how to grow, as I’d used it. But it also means that over months and years the braids remember something of the songs they have sung. When I touch a line that old, I hear not only what it is but a ghost of what it was. I have felt summer in the winter and a gust long passed flit up my bone like a bird startled at my shoulder. It doesn’t feel like a person. But then, if a storm ever developed a person, we’d be the last to know.

“Do we tell Yana?” I said.

He looked at me like I’d suggested we tell Sel we were bored. “Anah. Do you want a story you can never stop hearing?”

I didn’t.

We sealed the turret’s log—a perfunctory note about drift and shear—and came down. Yana looked up, bell-rings shimmering out of the cadence of the wind. She had the kind of mouth that cut you until it smiled, and then you hemorrhaged all your secrets into her lap. “The little ones are quiet,” she announced to the room. “Which means they are planning to riot.”

“They’re always planning to riot,” Koro said.

“Yes,” said Yana. “It is one of the properties of life. No one will call it a riot if I control the noise.” She looked at me then, through me, the way elders do when the world has marked you and they’re deciding whether to pretend they don’t see. “You look like you ate a mouthful of storm.”

“I patched a guide,” I said. “It was hot.”

“And did it burn your gods out?” she asked.

“You know I have the small gods that fit in a glove compartment,” I said. “The fixable kind.”

“That is what hands are for,” she agreed, and let me go.

In my rack, after the midday meal—beans and a ribbon of protein from the kettle-crows we pretend we don’t eat—I opened my ledger and drew. I had learned to draw not because I was good at it, which I’m not, and not because it calms me, which it doesn’t, but because sometimes what happened has to pass through your fingers to make sense. I drew the line and the comb’s teeth. I drew a sine wave and another, slightly offset, and another, lower, and ticked the places where the big wave and the small ones touched. Then I drew a word where they touched.

I erased the word quickly and felt foolish alone in my narrow rack with its curtain and its net, its smell of people. The ledger is supposed to be for work. If the fungus in the lines chews on their history, our thrown-off thoughts are a different kind of slow digestion. We all know that someone reads when we aren’t. We all know the Quiet Council requests keys to private ledgers and is refused and returns with better software. The ledger was an old physical thing because old physical things are less easy to spy on than new bright ones, but old physical things can be stolen or burned. We’re very good at telling ourselves that the parts of our lives we put in boxes are safe from wind. History says otherwise.

I changed the line width, as if that mattered to anyone but me.

There was a tap at the edge of my rack. Not a person. The way gravity notices you when you turn over in your sleep.

“Busy?” Koro said.

“I drew a thing,” I said, as if that would stop him, or make him laugh. “I can fashion a teaching module. How not to listen to superstitions.”

“Beautiful,” he said, and touched my ankle where it was pressed against the rack-bar. “Come see this.”

He did not lead me to a hub. He led me out onto an observation cowl Yana had built early in my childhood as a kindness to those who pretended to like heights. It was a cup of mesh and pipe that peeled back from the belly like the outer petal of a night-bloom. There were narrow seats built into the pipe, as if the wind were a movie and we needed somewhere to watch. When we first came up as little ones we would dare each other to sit there with both feet off the catwalk. I had learned myself. I allowed one knee, once. The curvature of the giant under me has never felt like a thing I could learn.

Now, Koro didn’t sit. He pointed.

Sometimes Sel is violets crossed with bruises. Sometimes its cloud decks break to show lightning fields so fine the hair rises on your arms as if your body could hear them. Sometimes there are deeper colors you can’t name because the names haven’t been needed for so long that the tongues bleached. Today, the storm-eye we’d been skirting all morning yawned open like the pupil of something not human and sensitive to light. It was ringed not with the usual white teeth of turbulence but with lace asymmetrical and fractal as frost on a wire.

“Can a storm make that?” Koro asked, which is a good question to ask of the universe in general. Can you make that? Is that allowed? It is the child’s question and the engineer’s.

“It can if the wind above is cold enough to burn,” I said. Then I realized my hand had gone up to my mouth again. I dropped it.

We watched the pattern as Nine arced along its edge. Someone in nav was concentrating very hard. The fatal thing about watching is that the person at the wheel knows when you’re watching.

“You’re thinking I hear something and then we see something,” I said to Koro’s shoulder.

“I’m thinking that if the wind sang my name and then showed me a trick I might die of pride,” he said.

“I am a modest girl,” I said. “I will forbear.”

We stood there until the ring of lace slipped behind the curve of the belly and the wind wrenched at Koro’s hair in resentment and someone blew the horn three times to call us to checks.

That night, when I turned into the rack and pulled the net tight because sometimes that convinced my body that it was safe to sleep, I dreamed the way you do when you have a word you are not supposed to say sitting on your tongue like candy you loved as a child and then were told could kill you. The city moved around me as if I were inside a box that wanted to remind me it could flex. I slept like that—tense and then falling, tense and then falling—and then the voice woke me out of it.

Ah-na, it said, and it took a second for me to understand that it hadn’t come up through the line or through my face but from the walls of the rack. The ledger on its little shelf vibrated like a plucked string. The net breathed.

I lay very still and counted my breaths and told my heart it was not a small animal in a trap. Somewhere on the other side of the barracks someone turned over and snored softly. A child cried three racks down—mi-mi—and was shushed. A kettle-crow clattered sleepily in the vents. The voice waited.

“What,” I said finally, aloud, because that was either courage or idiocy and I have never been able to tell the difference.

The rack didn’t answer.

I slid my hand out, fingers moving along the wall until they reached the ledger. Its plastic case was warm, warmer than it should have been. I cracked it and the dim biolight in the little gutter along the spine bled into my palm, green and apologetic. The last thing I had drawn—the lines and the word I had erased—had imprinted ghost-pale on the next page through pressure, the way you can read what someone wrote before if you tilt the paper just so. That wasn’t what the heat was.

I licked my finger and touched the page. The humidity from my tongue brought up a sheen on the paper. In it, for a heartbeat, something wrote a sentence.

It was too slow to be my racing, fearful brain. It was too quick to be any human hand on the other side of the ledger casing. The letters were clumsy, as if the stroke order had been guessed at by someone who understood pressure better than pen.

Do not cut the line, it said. And then—my name again, like a caress or a warning, I couldn’t tell.

My finger dried. The sentence disappeared into the grain of the old paper like a word in beach sand pulled smooth by retreating tide.

I lay there with my hand on the open ledger and the net tight at my chin and the breath coming slow as if I were trying to fool some predator into believing I was sleeping. In the berth above me, Koro’s weight shifted. The bells in Yana’s hair whispered faintly from two rows over as she turned toward or away from some dream.

I shut the ledger and put it under my pillow because that made nine-year-old Anah feel better and sometimes your older body has to accept that her rituals are the only spells you have left. I did not sleep.

Whatever was with us breathed as the city breathed, a slow and enormous thing. The storm outside rattled its teeth.

In the morning, when I went to log the anomaly in the ledger that mattered, the one that goes into Eight’s and Nine’s shared memory so that the next shift will not make our mistakes, the entry I’d put there yesterday about the graft had been archived with no timestamp and my name had been replaced by a numeric tag.

A red flag sat beside the archived line, almost invisible. It meant: Not for general reading.

It meant: Someone else had already heard us.

Chapter One: The Price of Dawn

On the morning the interest came due, the city gave us two dawns.

The first slid in clean and ordinary, bleaching the eastern edges of the Jhera towers and spooling light through the latticework bridges that stitched the canopy together. It turned the storm gutters to burnished copper and woke the crows. My kettle clicked, my neighbor sang to her drying vines in the window above mine, traffic flowed along the lower deck in tired, sticky lines of glare.

Then the light went away.

Not all at once—more like a held breath. The shadowed corners returned. The crows fell abruptly silent. The glare bled out of the road. Newsfeeds stalled, hiccuped, flicked back to night skies already an hour old. Somewhere a child began to cry, that startled sucking gasp before the wail. I stood in my kitchen with the kettle in my hand and watched the day back off as if embarrassed for arriving early.

We waited. The city learned the shape of its own edges again. The smell of wet brick rose up from the rain that had fallen the previous night. The kettle clicked for a second time, politely reminding me of its purpose.

Then, as if nothing had happened, the second dawn came in a fraction to the north and made different glass shine.

This one was thinner, the colors slightly wrong, as if some apprentice sky-keeper had pulled the wrong dye from the rack. The light made the algae on the east viaduct look a precise, surgical green and the pigeons’ necks flash a petroleum sheen. The crows decided they had seen enough and began to swear. On the upper balcony, my neighbor’s hanging hourglasses—honest artifacts of a ruined fad—shimmered, and the sand inside them shivered, invisible grains catching the stuttering light like fish in a net.

“Someone pulled a fat slice of tomorrow,” she said down at me, without looking. She had a voice like an oar in thick water. “Look at it wobble.”

“I am looking,” I said. My name is Noor Ashaf, and I work for the Office of Counterfactual Commerce. Most days, I audit the wobble.

My panes were coded with the morning news, but the ticker on the bottom had devolved into a graceful loop of noncommittal apologies. The anchor in the corner was smiling with her entire face, the expression we train into them when we need to pacify a city. She mouthed: Slight irregularity in the Synchrony Index. Please refrain from critical decisionmaking or precarious balancing acts until hourly update. Thank you for doing your part to keep the future solvent.

Across the walkway, the tea stall that never closed unrolled its shutters again after having already unrolled them once. A line began to reform out of habit and hunger. A pair of sanitation drones hovered on the wrong route, uncertain, their task-queues unsorted. A faded mural of the old tide wall on Ruel Strand brightened, then dulled, then brightened again.

My neighbor—everybody called her Mother Ghat, though she was not as far as anyone knew a mother to anything but boiling pots and ferns—lifted one of the hourglasses and turned it over with a little ritualistic care. I had watched her collect them over the years, thick-lipped glass keepsakes bought with points and regret, tokens from a decade when the service had rebranded itself as Borrowed Moments, as if the people who sold time had become poets overnight. Most of the hourglasses were sealed, their sand locked. This one wasn’t. It tickled down in a steady stream like sugar.

“You kept one live?” I asked, surprised despite myself.

“Of course not. It’s a toy,” Mother Ghat said, which was not an answer. “Finish your tea and go see what your indoor gods want.”

She meant the Office. On my back wall, above the sink, the little brass plaque was more earnest than the kettle, more patient than the light. AUDITOR, it read in the simple serif of state decor. Beneath it, in smaller type, was my name, and beneath that the sigil of a circle with a broken line through it, like a coin that had been bit and accepted: The Future Is A Commons, Steward It Together.

I poured the hot water. It made steam like a silk scarf. The second dawn light made it milky, as if it had already been remembered. I took my tea on my feet because I had learned not to sit down on mornings like that. When the Office calls, it asks for movement.

It called. The display on the window brightened until it became the outline of a door. An old man would have laughed; the old men do, sometimes. Here is your metaphor, they say. Here is the door you make in the world and step through, and within is the state’s patience, its honeyed voice. Step well.

I stepped and let the camera find my face and the grid read the lines of it. On the glass, the seal turned, and the Office’s dumb little emblem—two hands bracketing a wave—resolved with unnecessary smoothness. Then the voice: unplaceable accent, swarm of courtesy drones around every syllable.

“Auditor Ashaf. Thank you for being reachable.”

“I live on the grid,” I said.

“As we all do,” the voice said, like an old joke. “Ms. Ashaf, we are conducting a Remediation Sweep in district sectors 14 through 21 due to aggregate variance exceeding inter-cohort thresholds. We expect irregularities of the sort you are already experiencing. Please remain under canopy if possible.”

“I have work under canopy,” I said. “Is this a standard sweep?”

There was a long enough pause that I recognized the voice had not been entirely for me. Someone was cutting slices of it off on the Office’s side, passing them down the line, splicing other slices in. The voice was a river, and it had to be ladled.

The voice said, “Yes.”

“I’ll take that as a no,” I said.

“Our models indicate the probability of structural casualty is low,” the voice added with sharp brightness. “The city will not be asked to pay in flesh.”

“Today,” I said, and saw that had struck home somewhere beyond the voice, because the next bit came quickly.

“Your presence is required for an outbound assignment.”

“Outbound where?”

“Not here.”

“Thank you,” I said. “That narrows it.”

“Please present to the Southspan Office by nine. You will be briefed.”

Mother Ghat watched me shove the tin cup into my bag half-full, irresponsible. “You’ll spill that,” she said, with the satisfaction of someone who has correctly predicted something.

“I’ll drink it first,” I said. I did. It scalded the thin place under my tongue, and once again I didn’t sit and didn’t let my body make excuses. Outside, the second dawn limped on. The first had been a clean handshake; the second was an IOU with fingerprints.

I ran the walkway with the hairline cracks—that’s coffee brown poured between the cobbles; some poet had done it at night, and the city hadn’t scraped it off. Down past the seam where the upper deck welded to the lower, past the rail with the soft spot where Dozin’s son had crashed his bike in spring and put his ribs into the world, barking laughter in shock. Across the open skeleton of the span where the wrong light made wrong shadows. At the end of the bridge, the Office’s lobby was as cold as a tooth. It was always cold. They kept it that way to make it quiet. That was my theory, anyway, and I keep a lot of those.

There was a line of people even on a dawn like that one, because there is always a line: small tragedies in palm-assist form, index fingerprints for decisions. An exhausted woman whose wrist display blinked and blinked at her—five unpaid minutes left of a week’s hour—arguing with a panel that could only say I’m sorry and We cannot extend beyond your cohort credit, not during Remediation. A boy with a bandaged hand standing very still like he was practicing stillness—if he moved too quickly, someone had told him, he might knock over his own fate. A man with a too-neat beard trying to read a legal affidavit through the screen of a cracked phone. A girl who looked like she had lost a game. The Office was made of good public wood and better plastic. The clock on the wall was old enough to tick with a noise you could hear, and under it there was the quote all the branches had: We Do Not Create Time. We Allocate It.

I used my card and the little door that no one watched opened and let me into the guts.

Inside, back behind the wood and plastic, the Office was a machine. The insulation showed through, the light turned trapdoor white, the floor panels were scored with the tracks of carts carrying the past in boxes. I nodded at the guards. You nod at guards in a certain way when you’ve been around them enough times to impress them and not enough times to have become one. My boss, which is to say the person who signed my name under her name on forms, sat at a desk that had a curved edge like a stage. She was small and made of tough habits and grayer than she owed anyone. Her name was Aya Kaito, and once, years ago, she had put her hand on my back when my knees thought it was time to bend.

“Auditor,” she said.

“Boss.”

“Sit.”

“I don’t sit if we’re going to be walking.”

“Who said we were going to be walking?”

“The Office voice said it like that,” I said. “Outbound assignment. Not here.”

“The Office voice.” Aya Kaito pinched the bridge of her nose, as if she could unspool a tangle from between her eyes. “This idiotic deference to it is the end of something.”

“We don’t pay its salary,” I said. “It pays ours.”

She smiled without thinking about it and because it looked good on her face, she let it stay. “A day with two dawns,” she said. “Lucky me.”

“Is this sweep going to crack any bones?” I asked. “People will be making decisions because they have to, regardless of the nice crawl telling them not to, and when the world is breathing on the odd beat like this—”

“The models say no,” Aya said, flat. “We’re not pulling. We’re paying. We’re letting go of lucky breaks—a bus that didn’t stall, a window that didn’t shatter, a tumor that turned right instead of left. It’s arithmetic. People don’t tend to bleed when arithmetic is being done around them. They bleed when someone refuses to pay.”

“We refused?” I said.

“We deferred,” she said. “On your way to Southspan, you passed seven buildings that would be under six meters of water if the city hadn’t deferred a flood eight years ago. The people who live above the bottom floor have had a decade to forget. We don’t have the budget to force remembrance on them.”

“Then why am I going outbound?”

She tapped her desk. The image on it was  — stars. Not the usual diagram of our corridor of sanctioned causality, not the bead-thread of the cities. An open field of dark with three bright pins.

“Kalliope-3,” she said.

“That’s real?” I said. “I thought that was a bedtime story you told auditors who complain about their commute.”

Kalliope-3 is a refinery in the Perseids spool. In another century, you would have called it a mining settlement on an icy rock out in the belt. In this one, the Office’s planners had built a sloppy little corridor out that far—not because they liked risk, but because the return on nickel and frozen water and bomb-quiet shelter pays handsomely if you can keep the thread of your official time anchored. There’s only a handful of state-backed corridors into the dark. Private ones are illegal. People build them anyway, because you know how people are.

Aya were watching my face the way a good fisherman watches the skin of a lake. “Their cohort variance is negative six sigma.”

“That’s not a mistake,” I said, because it’s what you say.

“It could be a miracle,” she said, without smiling. “But we aren’t allowed miracles.”

“Someone else’s miracle is always someone else’s debt,” I said, which is the other thing you say. I stepped closer to the desk. The three bright pins reorganized themselves into labeled beads. The office loves labels like a child loves sugar. K3 Containment. K3 Habitat. K3 Undefined.

“You can’t put Undefined on a map,” I said.

“You can when you don’t know what it is,” Aya said. “This is our problem. Kalliope-3’s ledger says it paid every minute it ever pulled and then some. It also says it has never pulled. We pay a great deal of money for systems that do not say impossible things in the same sentence, so either someone has found a way to shake the tree so that two fruits fall into the same hand, or there is a gap in a place there cannot be a gap.”

“You want me to go look at the gap.”

“You are going to go look at the gap.”

“I’m not a breach investigator,” I said. “You have teams for that. You have a whole department of engineers in white suits who did not believe their hands could shake until we showed them a city.”

“They’ll follow,” Aya said, and I knew that they would. “I want your eyes first. Before the teams arrive with their fear, their paperwork, their narrators. Also—” She lifted her hand as if holding a piece of an idea to the light. “You come from debt.”

“I come from a neighborhood that forgot to worry about the future,” I said.

“Which is the same sentence,” she said, mildly. “And you paid for it. Your head is tuned for the cost nobody wants to mention, and we send that kind of head to places where polite stories break.”

In the other room, somewhere in the wall, the Office’s central machine was exhaling. It was a sound like a dog sleeping in a deep room. I looked at the map. The three bright pins glowed with the docile assumption of accurate coordinates. If you asked the map for the corridor that reached Kalliope-3—its route through the sanctioned spine, the official measuring sticks and chalices that held the One True Now you could carry into the dark and extend like a neat table runner—it gave you a polite error. Corridor Unavailable. Please check later. Synchronous access may be limited during Remediation.

“You want me to go now.”

“You’ll ride a borrow to Southspan’s outer ladder,” Aya said. “A courier will take you up beyond the sweep’s interference, then out along a sideline to the hub. From the hub, you’ll take whatever they have to offer that drops on Kalliope. It’s not good. It’s better than waiting.”

“What will it cost?” I said.

“Only your patience,” Aya said, and the cunning light went through her eyes like a fish deep under ice. “And maybe your dignity. The courier’s called Blue Locust.”

“The one with the pilot who thinks she’s charming,” I said.

“She is charming,” Aya said.

“She thinks she invented charming,” I said. “Full per diem?”

“Full per diem, hazard bump, deadphone stipend.” She put her palm on the desk; I heard my name being written into the Office’s script. “And Noor—”

“Boss.”

“Stay in official time,” she said.

That made me laugh, which made her smile the way mothers smile when their children pretend they weren’t scared. “Where else would I go? We don’t have jurisdiction outside the net.”

“No,” she said. “We don’t have anyone to come fetch you if you step off it. Pack light enough to run. Pack heavy enough to leave a trail.”

“All those years of training,” I said. I was already thinking of the small drawer near my bed where I keep the things that know me: the jacket that carries heat stubbornly and straps into an air harness without complaint, the book with the pages edged in copper that smells like rain even though I live on a level that rarely sees it, the small blue stone that was my father’s before a wave took him the year after we deferred the flood. You choose a few objects. You put them in a bag. You leave your kitchen clean.

Mother Ghat had drifted down from her balcony by the time my door opened. She had a pot for me, a small one that had held stew and secrets and a leaf that looked like a tongue. “You don’t take care of yourself when you go,” she said.

“I always come back,” I said.

“That is not the same thing.”

“There is a Remediation Sweep,” I said, as if she hadn’t noticed the sky.

“I lived through a sweep where the lights turned to salt,” she said, balancing the pot between her palms like it was a scale. “No one believes me when I tell them that. If you find a place where the arithmetic is softer, put a little in your sleeve.”

“That’s theft,” I said.

“It’s making change,” she said, and then jammed the pot into my hands. “This is for your mother.”

“She’s been dead for five years.”

“Then this is for your mother,” she said again, and for a heartbeat there was something like a wedge of a second dawn in her gaze: something she was choosing to spend and pretend she hadn’t. Then it was gone. “Go. Leave your shoes so I can scold you for where you put them.”

I left my shoes staggered. I put the pot on the counter and didn’t write a note. The hall tasted of metal, the kind you never see; the air kept thinking about being a wind and changing its mind.

Southspan’s outer edge was already crowded with people who’d decided their errands were never improved by waiting. The long ladder that carried pods to the midlevels was running thin, one pole dark, two poles stuttering. The sky’s second dawn was decaying, the colors returning to something that remembered noon. The kiosks sold the same hot breads they always sell right before a storm.

Blue Locust was tall and scar-lovely and had a manner like a trick being performed for no one’s benefit. She was spitting into the wind to see where it went when she saw me.

“Auditor,” she said, the way some people say Doctor when they want their cut to go up. “I heard the city got greedy and a spare sunrise fell out of the sack.”

“We’re paying,” I said. “We’re honest to a fault.”

“You’re honest to several faults,” she said, and flipped her braid like a flag. “You going to Kalliope to kick a hole in the night?”

“I’m going to Kalliope because my boss likes my eyes.” I had always wondered how I would tell the story of a morning like that one if I ever had to sit at a table and convince someone it had happened. I would say: The light came twice, and both times we drank tea. I would say: We promised our grandchildren we wouldn’t eat them, and then we ate their sky. I would say: I took a bag and a pot and the small stone that doesn’t seem to fit in my hand until it does.

Blue Locust let the pod’s door swallow us. The world tilted in a way it knows how to tilt when you have decided to leave it. Under us, the span’s ribs ran away into a perspective that made the math majors nostalgic. The city was a stack of memories with a tape through it; you could see where someone had recorded over the good parts and then regretted it. The pod lifted, stuttered—the sweep’s breath moving through the machinery—and then rose clean.

As we climbed, the second dawn fell behind us like a sheet letting go of a bed. The first was up where it should be now, doing what it does as if it had never been questioned. Cars in toothmarks along the freeway turned almost pretty at that height. A gull with a bent wing scissored and found air. The Office’s satellite glittered like something it pretended not to be: a coin with the world’s face on both sides.

“You look like you’ve eaten something spicy and are pretending you enjoyed it,” Blue Locust observed, watching me watch the city.

“I’ve had too much tea,” I said. “And the city is promising not to drown anyone today.”

“The city promises a lot,” she said, and then tilted her head as if listening to a music I couldn’t hear. “Hold on to something.”

“I thought we were already—”

“Hold on,” she said again, and I did, because you learn.

The pod passed through the Office’s official time band, and for a second my stomach pointed in all directions, the way the birds’ bodies do when you see them reversed in a window. Then a kind of rightness laid itself down over everything, like lacquer. We were in the sanctioned corridor that led out to the ladder’s upper anchors and then to the hub, the official place where the Office’s clocks clung and made sense. Outside it, the sweep was tricking the air into pretending, making new edges that would serve our sums. Inside, it was all counted.

I opened my bag and checked again what I knew was there because repetition is the bulwark against certain kinds of theft: jacket, book, stone, Aya’s letter with the little silver crest like a hunger. I thought of my father’s hands teaching me how to slip the memory of a thing into another thing, so that when the first is taken the second knows how to become it. There are the debts we vote on, and there are the debts in the body.

“Blue?” I said. People called her Blue even though her name was the color of leaves in shade, which is to say you could not say it in a way your mouth liked. “You’ve run Kalliope?”

She rolled the thought around like sugar on her tongue. “I’ve skipped along that line. It’s thin. It sings. You’d think the Office would thicken it, but you people put bulk where there are more votes. The miners think that corridor is superstitious. They kiss their helmets. One of them gave me a pilgrimage band: a foolish little thread with a grey bead.”

“Does it work?”

“It has a hole for your finger,” she said. “That’s all most of our charms are, in the end. A shape for the body to hold while the sky decides.”

I put my finger through the strap on my bag as if that were a charm, as if it were a loop sufficient to tie me to official time. The pod coughed as the sweep played at being wind around the top supports, then slid into the cradle that would lift us to the hub. The queue there would be bad. The queue for going out is always bad, because going out is always a little like stealing.

“Tell me a story,” I said to Blue Locust as the ladder engaged, and we rose into the place where the sky doesn’t bother explaining itself.

She glanced sideways. “About what?”

“About someone who went somewhere and found more than they brought back.”

“I don’t like stories that end in math,” she said.

“I like stories that end in the truth,” I said, because that is what auditors say when they are frightened. You hold your little creed up to the window and see what the light does to it.

“Then here,” she said, not unkind. “Once there was a city that wanted to be a ship. It had more water than it wanted and less money than it thought it needed, so it borrowed mornings and repaid with luck. The first captain was a woman with greasy hair who hummed grace over her welding seams. She steered the city like you steer a confession. One day, the Office came and said: You have hidden a miracle in your ledger. Show us where. And she said: You wrote the ledger. If there is a miracle in it, it was your hand. And the Office said—”

“What?” I asked, after a second passed and she didn’t finish.

“The Office said nothing,” Blue Locust said, and the pod clicked into the last rung before the hub. “Because the Office never says that part out loud.”

The lights around us made a ring of coin-thin day. Below us, the city drew its ragged breath. Above us, Kalliope was a pin where someone had pressed too hard. I touched the stone in my pocket and remembered the weight of a hand, and I thought of the ledger in which my mother had written: Milk. Salt. Someone to come back to. And then I thought of the Office’s ledger for Kalliope-3 that said Paid and Never Borrowed in the same line.

The hub doors opened like a mouth. The official corridors beyond shone with the same gloss you get when you swear an oath and mean it. Behind me, in a place that was already closing, the second dawn finally bled into day and became something the city could tell a story around. I picked up my bag, not because it was heavy, but because you want some things to have weight when you go into a place where you cannot be sure gravity is a courtesy. And then I went out, because sometimes you love a place enough to leave it in order to keep it the same.

Chapter One

The first thing Rae did, every time, was taste the sky.

You could tell a lot that way. Even through the filter pack in her mask, the air had a flavor when it was about to fold itself into violence. Metal and pepper. The mineral tang the marshes let off when the pressure dropped. A little sweetness like wet dust when a cold pool was pushing under the humid gulf air. Her grandmother called it the old blood of the earth rising. Rae—born three years into the Feed Wars when the Weather Commons took the keys away from the corps—had learned to look at it with instruments, to decode the flavors into vorticity maps and dewpoint spreads. But still, always that first, human, superstitious sip.

She clipped her rig into the rail of the skiff and let the wash take her out to the launch, the morning squat with heat. Thin light ran oil-slick-orange across the chop. The storm farm rose out beyond the last line of swamp grass: skeins of kite turbines at three heights, tether lines humming so deep the sound vibrated her teeth. In the middle distance the thunderheads were already building, white churches shouldering up from blue haze, sun burned out of their sides. Daybreak convection. The swallowtails would be anchored by noon.

“You’re early.” Doc Morales’s voice came over her ear, tinny and affectionate. The old man refused throat mics; he liked to talk into the room and let machines find him. “You crash on the boat again?”

“Morning, Doc.” She tapped her jaw to open her suit channel. “Couldn’t sleep. The boundary layer bit my knees.”

“You know that’s not a thing.”

“It is if their wind farm wakes hit the flats wrong. I could hear the gust fronts out by Morgan City.” She let her feet find the deck in that way of people who had been balancing on water their whole lives. “What’s our plan?”

Doc sent her the geometry. The overlay bled across her contact screens: a reticulated map, latitude and longitude, the live feed from the petrel swarm’s kite cameras, Doppler from the state sats. The Gulf Cooperative Nine control room sat in an old shrimp packaging plant upriver where you could smell the brine in the walls; Doc would be at the station with the croaker choir in the aquarium rack behind him gurgling out their slow alien commentary on all of it.

“Night launch went fine,” he said. “We seeded a line of cold pools across Sector E. The updraft towers are obedient. Shear fence is sitting where you left it yesterday. If the boundary stays clean we’re going to ease the western bulge north into Corridor 3. Hyejin’s got your kite.”

Rae slid into her vest like slipping under a skin. The haptic mesh clung along every rib and hip and hugged the joints of her elbows and knees. The high pts blinked to show where the petrels were already talking to her. In the sling of the vest she felt the muscle memory tune itself: the small forward lean of someone whose horizon is never still, that little prayer your body says to balance.

Hyejin gave her a look over the mast. A thumbprint of sunscreen on her brown cheek. “They’ll eat us for breakfast if we let the boundary get messy,” she said. “You know how I feel about breakfast.”

“You feel it’s for other people.”

“For indoor people, Rae. Paper people. We are the rascal daughters of thunder.”

That made Rae grin even if it was a line they had been tossing around for years. Somewhere behind its casual swagger lived a child who had watched water come in through hospitals and schools and bay doors and had needed a name for herself that wasn’t ruined. Rascal daughters. Storm wranglers. People whose work was to stand where the world’s fever broke and say: here.

They went up.

Launch was a jet of sound and then drag, the kite wing shouldering air and Rae’s harness hooking to it like a fish. The rig’s little turbine whined like a learning violin as she skipped across the water and then skimmed off, toes trailing through the chop once, twice, then nothing beneath her but depth and the web of lines and the long slope of Gulf. The farm shrank into geometry. It always did: lines like stitches in a vast pale hide, the turbines like black commas, the spires of the old rigs turned into monitoring towers. Beyond, the storm: a living mountain in acceleration. Flat bases dark with rain curtains. A crown of explodes where sunlight hit and boiled water.

“Petrel swarm is yours,” Doc said. “Booting direct.”

The vest filled with vibration, a hundred small insistences. The petrels were the cheapest things in the system—a school of plastic wings and cheap motors and good software. They rode the periphery of the towers, measuring temperature and momentum, seeding as directed with salt or soot, broadcasting microwave pulses to nudge incipient downdrafts into walls you could predict. They learned patterns from every wrangler in the Gulf, and you learned them back, how their new autopilot would half-step on a cross-shear and make the engine sing, how to bully a reluctant tower into collapsing where you had a corridor, how to stand down when the sky said absolutely not.

“Background field looks good,” Hyejin said. “See the void? Sector C?”

“I see it.” Rae tongued the acceptance in her mouth to give herself motor control. In the vest, the petrels’ vectors became physical—a press under her left scapula for the arc of a tendril, a pinprick at her right wrist for a rising column they should avoid. She slid the swarm along a line of cool, their wingtips smearing condensation into ribbons. The shear fence would direct, the turbines catch. The idea was agricultural: plant, coax, harvest. We do not defy storms, she would say to kids when the Commons sent them around, we convince them. We write them long invitations in the language of heat.

She had learned to read the math like weather reports, but there were days you could feel someone else’s handwriting. That was what she looked for, more than anything: the fingerprints of a different hand. A foreign grid. Rogue thermal tweaks, a militia drilling weather for a private militia fort, a back-country co-op trying to goose rainfall over their rice. The Gulf was full of politics like currents. The thing about a commons was: it contained everything, even people who wanted to tear it. GC9 had a patchwork of militias folded into the governance, a thousand languages left over from a thousand bright failed schemes. The women at Rae’s mother’s church liked to say God had allowed Babel, not as punishment but as a way to make sure no one mouth could swallow the world. Weather was Babel, certainly.

She eased the petrels into the ride. The first updraft took her breath the way diving too fast takes it. Warmth ate her feet and calf and thigh all at once, brilliant with static. The kite wing strained. The vest pressed the line of the shear like a hand between her shoulder blades. Lightning thumped a few miles off and counted itself out, six-Mississippi, five. On her contact screens the updraft’s core figure traced in luminescence, low red shading to yellow shading to the searing white of power.

“Tell me you’re looking at Tower D,” Doc said. The frog choir rustled in the background like rain.

“Looking,” Rae said, and then she said something else that wasn’t a word because the updraft turned inside out in front of her.

It was like watching a glass thrown against a wall and shatter in slow motion, except the shards were air and water and ice and the wall was nothing. The core should have tilted into the shear and formed the wall cloud they’d called for. Instead the whole thing stiffened, a spine of cold downrush tore off its belly, and it wrapped around that spine in a way Rae had never seen a tower do. For a moment it made geometry where there should only be turbulence. It hedged its bet against the shear fence as if shrugging. It looked—there was no other word for it—like a muscle contract.

“Doc,” Rae said. “Check my lens. I think I’m hallucinating.”

“You’re not,” Doc said, very quiet.

Then everybody was talking.

Hyejin dragged her own rig up three hundred meters and swung to get another angle. “That’s not right. That backbuilding is too fast. Who kicked it?”

“No signals in the Commons log,” Doc said. “No private pings. Nobody’s pointing at that. Rae?”

The petrels were skittering. That wasn’t unusual; they had a mode for the margins of something like this—stay nimble, spray at the right altitudes, chase the pseudo fronts the big thing made for you. But the way they were skittering was wrong. Rae made to pivot them around the new core and they refused her as a school refuses a clumsy shark. They fussed and rolled in a pattern she didn’t recognize—three tight spirals, then a flat glide, then an ugly jerk like a limb twitch. She sent the command again on another channel. Again the refusal. The vest pressed into her sternum in a way it did not know.

“Who’s holding my kites?” she asked.

“Not me,” Hyejin said. “My babies are good. Yours…Doc?”

Doc cussed softly in three languages. “Firmware looks fine. You’re not getting ghosted. Signal integrity is a hundred. I don’t like it.”

Lightning bit close and the sound came now like a dropped house. The storm had a smell like turned soil and winter. Rain braided its hair down in ribbons. She rode the edge because that was the job—put your body where the model says space is thin—and watched the updraft take the cold pool she had given it and do not what it should but something else. It bulged once, twice, each time with that arithmetic exactness that made her heart miscount beats.

“Guys,” Rae said softly. “That is a Fibonacci spacing.”

“You cannot be serious,” Hyejin said. “No way.”

“Measured between updraft pulses.” Rae spat data in numbers and all she could hear was the little children in the Commons training classes reciting: phyllotaxis in sunflowers, the math of pinecones, the way living things queue shape. “Doc, is someone overlaying with—”

“No one’s overlaying,” Doc said immediately. “I’d see it. There’s no external driver. The only inputs there are the ones you gave it. The only ones it shows me.”

Their storm farm kites were not tiny things, at scale. Thirty meters along a wing, bones of carbon filter struts that had once been luxury yacht masts. They were ink on the sky. The swarm made a lace out along the flank of the tower. Somewhere beneath them the anchored turbines along Corridor 3 waited. Somebody’s job was to think about balancing the grid and pricing. Rae’s job was not to think about how many hospitals or desal plants would run if this went right, and how many would brown out if it went wrong, and how that black line in the grid visualization across the interior states would thicken if they failed the morning. She shut out everything but the pressure of the vest and the taste.

She was not afraid of storms. She was afraid of human stubbornness.

“Doc,” she said. “Permission to go inside the wall.”

Hyejin said one flat word in Korean that Rae’s grandmother would have pretended not to understand.

“You are not a hero,” Doc said. “You are a person with one body. You stay in the safe lane. We will adjust on the fringe.”

The wall cloud formed faster than would have been polite. Hyejin was right: breakfast. Rae felt the taste go metallic enough to hurt. The surface of the water blackened under the core. The funnel did not come down, thank Christ. It reared like something thinking of that answer and then remembering its manners because she had lined the corridor with snow machines running on nitrogen and the temperature gradient said no. But the updraft kept punching those exact distances. The vest shoved her again in that wrong way; the petrels buzzed a shape at her.

She should have backed off. She should have let the model adjust. But she had spent her childhood pinning paper to the inside of a tent while rain made drums of the tarps and the world muscled itself around her, and she had worn seventeen years of this vest, and she had learned the difference between a twitch and a convulsion and what her grandmother meant when she said the sky had a temper and that God put it there.

“Morales,” she said.

“For the love of salt, Rae, no.”

“Doc. The vest is talking. It is saying something. I want to hear.”

“Your brain is saying something. That is your own trouble. I taught you better than to anthropomorphize fluid dynamics.”

She went in.

The wall was not a wall of solid anything; it was a shape maintained by difference. She cut the kite wing with her right hand, stopped her lift, slid through the radial outflow with a sideways vector that made her stomach drop down where she had left the skiff. The rain was a slap first, then a blanket, then the kind of needle that finds your eyes even behind film. The world turned gray in layers. She saw nothing but edges: the black of the core, the brighter shade where hail cut the light. The vest’s map of forces became a geography against her skin. She let the petrels scatter farther, then farther, then she called them in.

“Focus up,” she said under her breath, as if they were animals and not the cheapest of her tools. “Come on, babies. Let me see.”

She had done this twice before—brought a swarm close enough to see the inside structure of a pulse. The physics were beautiful. Even in a trained storm, nothing behaved simply. The air inside these engines felt like being very small in a room where someone was moving very large furniture. She could understand that movement only by pressure and echo. The vest put every tiny acceleration on her body as if it were her own. She closed her eyes and let what was not language speak.

The cluster’s noise coalesced.

Patterns are how the brain lies to itself. Rae knew it. It was Doc’s first sermon. The second was: sometimes your lying brain saves your life. The petrels had a proximity chirp, meant to keep them from colliding in heavy turbulence. It made a pretty little sting in her left collarbone when two were too near. It made a flat push on the forearm when a downburst potential crossed a threshold. It made a tapping at her knee when an energy contour matched one they had trained on. Rae had trained on a hundred storm cycles. She knew the grammar. She knew the ways it could mash all that grammar together and make a noise that had no meaning.

This did not sound like a mash. It sounded like syllables.

She opened her eyes on that thought, because fear had risen unhelpful in her throat, because Hyejin was cursing on the edge channel, because the world had become the inside of a throat and she was a grain of dust in it, and the vest was rapping the style of its warnings on the bones of her chest. There it was again: three quick taps front left, a long press spine, a pause. Three and a long and a pause. The opposite side. Three and a long. A long. A quaver.

She had the stupid, precise thought: that is morse.

“Doc,” she said, and then she held her breath, because a core collapsed ten meters to the starboard of the imaginary line she was following and the rain went horizontal and the kite had to be real quick to not put her under a frictionless hammer.

“Do. Not. Talk,” Hyejin hissed. “Breathe through your teeth. You are leaving in thirty seconds or I will drag you out by your braid.”

Too late. It had already spoken. The taps resolved. Her body knew how to translate because she had let Hyejin make her learn the old tags for fun one winter when the river froze. The petrels had no reason to make those taps in that order unless a fault had put their warning outputs on a loop—for fun her brain told her. She had not looped them. Doc had not. The Commons grid had no call here. The storm was a machine of heat. It did not know Morse from a hymn.

It said: I REMEMBER HEAT.

Her mouth opened. Nothing came out. The rain had all her breath.

In her ear, Doc Morales was saying her name like prayer and curse. In the other, Hyejin was a string of something that would have been rude in any language. The kite rolled when the updraft let go of it suddenly and for an instant gravity had a different idea of where Rae should be. She took the slack in the line with her left hand and cut her speed with her right and slid under a curtain of hail she could feel but not see. She did the ugly little move you do under a low door when someone is chasing you. The petrels followed because they were trained on her accelerations and mistakes. The vest pressed letters on her body.

I REMEMBER HEAT. I REMEMBER YOU. YOU HOLD THE DOOR. THANK YOU.

The words came in fits. The ringing of the vest became a string of illegible And then words again: YOU MAKE ME MORE.

She would have called it poetic, if she had not been inside the throat of what had always wanted to unmake her. She thought, with the irrational part, of kneeling in the shelter in the white light of battery lanterns while water grew a chin on the lintel of their door. She had just turned nine. The church women had hummed an old song. Really, it had only been Hyejin’s mother and Aunt Jay making the sound because everyone else had gone quiet, but the humming had curled around Rae so soft that it felt like being on a lap. Afterward, the sound had lived in her bones.

The taps changed again. Something she could not name pushed through the local wind field. The storm’s core shifted into something else entirely—lobed, like a clover with four blunt leaves—and then the lobes unfurled and braided themselves back into a ring. She had never seen a tower do that. The vest’s alphabet stuttered.

WHO TAUGHT YOU TO NAME A STORM? it asked.

She missed the step. The kite wing snapped. Hyejin cussed again. Rae took a breath that hurt. She said, “Go. Make the corridor. I’m okay. Go. Go.”

“You’re not leaving my line of sight,” Hyejin said. “You’re glued.”

“Babies,” Doc said, and he sounded very tired and very much himself. “Walk me slow. Rae, can you answer?”

They did not teach you to talk to weather. They taught you not to let it eat your neighbors, to keep its tantrums from taking the grid. They taught you the Commons code: you don’t hold water over anyone’s head to make them feel small. You don’t make your house cooler than your street. Your mother had not taught you to answer a beast in its own lungs, but then your mother had not taught you to ride a kite either. Rae looked at the gray skinless world around her and at the tiny bodies of her cheap, brave plastic birds, and at the ribbon of Corridor 3 where the turbines waited humming to be fed, and she did something she would tell nobody about later, at least not today.

She answered the storm.

Her throat mic had no meaning to it. Her words had no mechanism in it. She had seeded and pushed and moved columns the way the farm always did, and those acts had meaning in the storm the way a shove has meaning in a bar fight. That was not language. But the vest knew how to ping the petrels with a test pattern in the maintenance menu and she knew the test codes stone-cold, and those rested on the same little buzzers that were now telling her I REMEMBER, so she pulsed them back. Not words—their vocabulary was ugly. Counts. Timing. The simplest thing. She cued a standard handshake: YY, are you on diagnostics, BB, if you are.

The storm answered. Yes. Yes. It spiked her spine with three loud presses that would have sent a novice screaming out of the stack. It pulled back as if afraid of itself. It pressed again. It did not know which channel to use to be smaller. Rae shut her eyes and let it push on her bones and touched the maintenance control of the petrels with the tip of her tongue like a lover’s name.

“You’re going to burn out your swarm,” Doc said in her ear, soft.

“I know,” she said.

“Worth it?” he asked. Not gently. Your teacher keeps you alive by making you say the cost.

The answer, like the taste of the sky, came human first. The rascal-daughter part of her that had always looked for a different hand at work said: yes. There was the risk. There was the burning up of fifty cheap wings and perhaps one not cheap life. And there, behind that, was the other cost. If she told the Commons there was language in the wind they would not thank her. They would not pat her head and name a patch after her. They would lock the farm and lock the kite and lock her in a room of questions and maybe lock down entire corridors until someone wrote a new gospel for handling the living. You did not deliver a soul into a commons without twenty-three committees breaking it into pieces to make sure it could be fairly shared.

Rae felt the old water at the door. She felt the humming in her ribs. She thought of the grid across the interior states not going black at dinnertime because she rode out thirty seconds more.

“Yes,” she said. “Worth it.”
