She pulsed the petrels one more time, the little cheap bodies chirping their diagnostic handshake. She shaped the corridor entry with the last salt they carried. She made sure she could find her way back out for when the storm moved the furniture again. Then she said, with the only words she had, and the only channel she could steal: What do you call yourself?

There was no delay. There was no translation time because these were not meanings aligned to meanings. This was pressure and heat and touch and Rae’s skin standing between them, but it was enough. The vest made six presses like a drum and then two like a heartbeat and then left silence in a perfect little garden around them.

WE ARE ALL THE HEAT THAT I CAN SAY, it said, and because that answer was too big for a body on a kite, she let herself hear another meaning slip under it like a current, old and small and not-she: PILAR.

The storm had given itself a name.

Outside the wall, Hyejin was saying they had five turbines breathing now, six, the grid line was fattening, she needed Rae to not get killed so that they could make jokes about it over fried bananas at the dock. Doc Morales, in his ghost choir room with the ancient fish, was muttering something into his mic about “first person pronouns” he had promised not to ever have to say about a thunderstorm. The vest, that thrift-store miracle of engineering patched in twenty different ports over twenty different years, had gone very still as if listening.

“Pilar,” Rae said aloud, because sometimes saying the name put the shape around a thing that let it stay in the world. “Okay,” she said, to the storm that had called itself more than any one sound could hold. “Okay,” she said, to the day and to the skiff that was still down there and to all the ways she would be punished for this. “I hear you.”

The sky tasted like the first peel of orange after a fast.

She turned the kite wing on its edge, to catch what she could use and not what would break her, and guided her petrels into the corridor, and felt the storm press back against her palms not as a fist now but as a curious, brilliant cheek.

“Stay in my sight,” Hyejin said.

“I’m not going anywhere,” Rae lied, and took her first breath in what felt like the whole of her life.

On the morning the city taxed winter, the Municipal Mnemonic Office smelled like warm plastic and almond antiseptic. Upstairs in the lobbies the air kept changing to keep people from getting attached to it—cedar for birthdays, cut grass for graduations, salted brake dust for car crashes—because attachment increased recall and recall raised your bracket. I was early enough to get a coffee and a silent barstool in front of Bay C before the queue started.

They painted our counters a color with a name like “Foundation,” the color you put on walls when you tell people they can put anything on top. Mine had three hairline cracks I’d stopped reporting because Facilities always wrote back with the same reply-gif, a little cartoon wall repairing itself if you clicked it fast enough. Against Regulation I peeled my wrist patch back to scratch; the adhesive always raised a rash. The patch made routine forgettings easier, the Office guidebook said. It bled a slow trickle of scopolamine and a proprietary something that flattened edges so the extractions didn’t hurt as much. Every month we rotated the proprietary somethings to stop the body learning them; there was a punchy internal memo about how memory, like a river, will cut again around obstacles given time, and how our job was to keep placing rocks. Someone had added in a different font: The rocks cost fourteen percent.

Ira Tam, I told the day’s first client, because saying my name makes me real to a person in a way that looking at the badge does not. Taxpayer number?

She was thirtyish and wearing a coat from a season no one in the lobby remembered yet, lapels big, collars big, big enough she could hide in them. Amaya Qiu, she said, a little too quickly. She had a navy rectangle behind her ear under her hair, glinting—commercial patch, not municipal, something boutique: It said, very politely, I can afford not to pay you. The first rinse of panic rolled off her in a smell like bruised cilantro. She tapped her phone to the counter and her ledger unspooled on my side.

“You’re here to declare,” I said, because that was the easiest thing to be.

Her eyes flicked to the wall display listing this quarter’s brackets. Visual markers of recall specificity: color, scent, language, temperature, pain. A wedding at forty Celsius in an orange tent with incense is a different tax from a courthouse at nineteen with recycled air and the distant smell of floor wax. People had learned to blunt their memories, smooth their lives. People had learned to avoid carrying cash, which was what memory had become.

“I’d like to designate,” she said, and slid a file into my window. It read: Underwater. I did not smile. Names didn’t bind us; names were suggestions people put on top of the color Foundation. She was going to put her wedding into the municipal vault and draw from it like it was a well. She would say economical; I would say deferred. In between, a server farm would shake itself at frequencies orchids found pornographic.

“Walk me through it,” I said.

She did her breathing: three beats in, three out. There were signs for that, too, posted next to the line of warnings about basilisk clips and illegal transactive bundles and the penalty for bringing an untethered mnemonic into a public building. This one, a little poster with a cartoon hippocampus doing tai chi, said: If you can count, you can cope.

“It was the ocean,” she said. “The real one, not the park. Thick water. Salt on my tongue. We hired these fish that ate the petals so they wouldn’t wash back. He was nervous. I could tell because his blink went off rhythm. My dress smelled like my grandfather’s cigarettes.”

I let her speak for forty seconds before I had to cut her off for her own sake; that was my allotment, warm human allowance in a cold line of code. The more she detailed the specificity markers, the more she would pay. Not my rules. I tapped the screen and her memory became a shape.

All memories in the system render as maps. It isn’t art. Art is what my friend Pina paints, layering wine and crushed chalk and dead wasp shells for texture. The Office’s maps are all the same shape: a topographical field with ridges and ravines, blue for senses, green for language, red for whatever tickled your endocrine system. Pain shows as little cliffs. Joy shows as valleys with good drainage. There’s an algorithm for disambiguation. I could decode them the way my mother used to decode forecasts, looking where the lines tightened. I saw a ridge where her dress smell sat and a valley where his offbeat blink had made a basin.

“Your dress,” I said. “We’ll need to accept the whole garment, if you want to lower your bracket, not just the odor. Which means secondary associations—childhood laundry room, your grandfather’s hand. You can keep the object, but we keep the code. Are you sure?”

She nodded. Her knuckles were pale.

“And the parents?” I asked gently.

She swallowed. “Mine. He didn’t invite his.”

“Do you have legal separation between that omission and the event?” I said the way I was trained to say it, like I wasn’t peering. “Any parallel rhetorical frames that would bind one to the other across contexts—holiday dinners, graduations, hospital waiting rooms?”

She was the type who had practiced. “No. We agreed ahead of time. You can read the segment.”

That saved her money. It also saved me time. There was a brass clock in the lobby shaped like a anemone that ate time in little feathery gulps, minute tendrils curling in and out, iridescent numbers flickering like fish scales. Officially it had nothing to do with us. The city is full of things that officially have nothing to do with us that nonetheless compel.

There was a piece of my job where I was supposed to sell the upsell. They wanted us to encourage municipal bundles, the sort that let you store an entire kindergarten year or a phase of grief, pre-tax. You could pull it back for a day, taste it again like a sucked-on coin. While it remained offloaded, it could be farmed by the city and used, anonymized, to make better billboards and better trauma counseling for the wildfires and better training sets for AIs that would build better vaults. I’d stopped doing the sell when I realized people heard the word better and then heard nothing else.

We went through the motions. I made sure she wasn’t smuggling anything in—no basilisk, no kinaesthetic trap, nothing imbedded. I set the extraction to slow. We met each other’s eyes for a second as the ink reached her brain. Extractions make your tongue feel like a coin. She blinked and her cuff whitened. The Office hummed, and something old and sweet rose, like burned sugar.

She breathed. She paid. The city took its share, and the rest curled under my desk and waited for the courier vault to take it downstairs, where a filtered river of lives gurgled through sixteen floors of refrigeration and fireproof vaults and saltwater tubs. I wrapped the residue into a municipal parcel and sealed it with the blue tape that says tamper me and I will sing.

“You’ll get your voucher within seventy-two hours,” I said. “You’ll get a thank-you from the city. We appreciate your contribution to the shared economy. Remember not to make major life decisions for twenty-four hours. Memory equilibrium lag is normal.”

She had that look people had when they left: lighter and nauseated. In a day she would reach for the memory and feel the shape of it gone. People like to tell themselves they’ll just look at the copy. They never do. Copies are like looking at a picture of water when you’re thirsty.

When she had gone and the next queue wasn’t ready and the lobby had shifted smell to pine, I took a sip of my coffee and opened my own ledger.

I wasn’t due to reconcile until Friday. My ledger is my most valuable asset. I am not being romantic. The numbers are very clear about the trade among us: I sell strangers a way to pay less for their past while I take care of mine. I file my forgettings on time. I itemize. The city loves a good itemizer like it loves a north wind that drives the smoke inland instead of into the three neighborhoods too rich to close their windows.

I opened my ledger because there was a tiny orange dot at the corner of the icon. The dot meant Not Wrong Yet But Approaching.

A new object had appeared in my inventory overnight. It had my name on it twice. Sender: Tam, Ira. Recipient: Tam, Ira. It had a municipal stamp. It had no notary. It had a case number that fell eleven digits below any of the ones given out this quarter, like a cheap counterfeit that thinks archaic is convincing. The timestamp read: 18.06.31, 11:37. It was the tenth.

I froze long enough for my patch to throw up a polite warning in my peripheral: high cortisol compromises retention; please avert eyes from stimuli. It offered me the cartoon hippocampus doing tai chi. I closed the suggestion window and looked around the lobby like I was going to catch a prankster behind a potted tree.

If this represents unauthorized access, you must report immediately, said the Office manual in the voice of the director, a woman with eyelashes like the legs of a centipede, efficient and somehow palatable. If this represents personal use of municipal resources, you must report immediately to avoid compounding fault. If this represents a clerical error, you must report immediately. The three banners on the wall opposite had the same message in corporate bluish. To report, press the calligraphic sun glyph and be prepared to speak clearly to an artificial friend.

Iva in Bay A was hunched over her console chewing a straw into fringe. Dunia in Bay B was explaining to a man that you cannot deduct the loss of a memory of a cat in lieu of the cat. The clock curled and uncurled its tendrils. The lobby smell was pine and hard candy. My mouth tasted like a coin even without an extraction line.

I clicked. The object opened like a mussel.

The Office makes you confirm three times when you open an unverified mnemonic. First: Do you trust the chain of custody? Second: Are you alone? Third: Will you accept the possibility of accident? At each question the button wiggles closer to yes even though the defaults are supposed to protect you. I pressed yes three times without letting the buttons seduce me. There was a flash like a scene change. My patch hummed against my skin. Standard overlays rolled in a translucent wash: the hazard warnings, the legal disclaimers, the neat oxygen-blue block of code that looks like the arrhythmic heart of a small animal.

I expected to see a map. I got a room.

Some people just disembody it all, pull up a memory like a schematic, move their hands in the air and watch the ridges unroll. This was not that. This memory was in a room with the almost-literal smell of burnt sugar and something else, something I didn’t have a word for. I was standing in it. There was condensation on the window in a frost pattern like ferns. There was a wet coat on a chair that smelled like an evening in a city with salt in the wind and a train underfoot. The coat was mine. In the memory I could feel the wet on my shoulders. If I closed my fingers, the material creaked the way cheap waterproofing creaks. It meant I had bought it in a rush, somewhere inside a storm.

The window looked onto a canal with the water running backwards. The sound of it was wrong. In memories, sound is the first to go. The mind fills in and we believe it. This was crisp. This was frogs and the fluorescent whip of a drone’s wings. On the far side of the canal a woman in a yellow skirt stood with her feet in the water, holding a paper fish by a string and letting it dive. Her face was turned away. That’s the thing about your own memories: they almost never give you the faces you want. It isn’t politeness; it’s how we are built.

A voice came from the chair with the coat. “Don’t call it in.”

The overlay flickered. The hazard warning made a series of gentle harp notes and turned into a long rectangle that resembled grief.

“I said,” the voice repeated, “if you have this, it means we were either braver or dumber than we planned. Don’t do the polite thing. Don’t even think it.”

The voice was mine.

I did not speak in the real. I thought of Iva and Dunia in their bays and the pale clock filling and emptying, and the way the lobby smelled like pine to people who had never been in a pine forest, and the way bile slowly tenderizes metal. In the memory, my hand went to my throat. There was a bruise there in the shape of a hand that had not been careful.

The memory resolved around the voice’s shoulders. Bags under eyes I would someday own. The good patch scar, too low to be municipal. A scar, a real one, a catenary curve across the knuckles. I have always had careful hands; I make them so, because I have to hold people’s words. These hands had done something to deserve it.

“Okay,” the voice that was mine said, more quietly, like a person leaning into a door. “If I tell you everything, you’ll try to fix everything and get us both killed. So here is what you need to do.”

The hazard bar went purple. Memetic contamination possible, it sang, please avert your eyes. The overlay offered me the sun glyph. The cartoon hippocampus looked tired.

I made a very small movement and minimized the overlay. I could still hear her—me—in the memory’s room. The coat dripped on the floor. The woman across the canal let the paper fish dive and the string ran through her fingers and then she let it go and it swam against the churning of the water and lodged itself under the wheel of an old bicycle someone had thrown in there in a different year. All this detail wrapped around one instruction like paper around fruit.

“The thing in your ledger,” my voice said, “showed up ten days early. That means someone else was faster. That means the vault is going to be searched today by people with guns you don’t know. Don’t be in there when they open Floor Twelve. When they ask you, you don’t know where the carrots are.”

“The carrots?” I said aloud in spite of myself. In Bay B Dunia coughed in a way that could be laughter or a seed husk. The overlay wiggled a button that said breathe.

“Not actual carrots,” my voice said, exasperated in the way I only ever am with myself and certain cousins. “They’ll use a food. It won’t matter. You will want to be the person who knows where things are. You are not. When the man with the navy patch asks you about carrots, send him to 23-G and take the stairs. Listen. Do not take the elevator. There is a sign in the stairwell that says keep right. Ignore the sign. Keep to the left. When you get to the landing with the square of light that smells like dust, stop and—”

The door to Bay C clicked. I ripped the overlay away from my eyes so hard my patch peeled and stung. The canned air of the lobby hit my face, pine and sugar, and then the room overlay slotted like a transparent second skin over it all, still hanging there because I had not dismissed it. A person stood in my doorway the way the lobby’s consultant training videos tell you to stand: straight but not rigid, hands open, authority disguised as courtesy. He was a man in a suit with a tie so brown it looked like a wound under his throat. He had the kind of face that could sell a vacuum. Behind his ear a navy patch glinted.

“Auditor Tam?” he said, smiling. “How lucky. A minute of your time?”

I had time. I had exactly the distance between my ribs and the air to make a choice. My mouth tasted like a coin. The man in the doorway smelled like rain walked through to get here. His eyebrows were gentle. In my overlay the paper fish snagged under the wheel.

In the memory, my voice, the one that had found me with ten days to spare, said one more thing, quickly, as if the canal would reverse its direction again and wash it away:

“Believe me just this once.”

“Can I help you?” I asked the man, and my voice was steady enough to make me proud. The overlay curled its fingers in the air, beckoning me to the left-hand side of a stairwell I could not see. Behind his smile there was something sharp. “We’re not quite open for audits without an appointment.”

“Oh,” he said, and took a step into Bay C like it was his. “I’m not here for an audit. I’m here to help you remember where the carrots are.”

He said the word exactly the way my voice had. He said carrots like a person who had eaten duty for breakfast going on twenty years, docile and crunchy. The clock on the lobby wall sighed and turned another minute over like a coin in its mouth.

“Twenty-three G,” I said, and did not blink. “Downstairs.”

“That’s very helpful,” he said, not looking at the screen where directions were usually rendered. He kept looking at my face like my face had become something he had once lost. “Thank you, Auditor Tam.”

I stood up and pretended to smooth my skirt even though I was wearing pants. I smiled with my teeth because the Office manual says people feel safe when they can see your molars. He walked away the way men with navy patches walk, like they are the house. Dunia coughed again, and this time it was laughter. Iva put her straw down.

“Coffee break,” I said to nobody in particular, which is how you say I am about to take ten minutes to cry a little in the bathroom or call my mother or stare at my hands. The Office manual says we can do that. The Office manual says a lot of things, very few of which are about stairwells.

On the way to the door that said Employees Only, I passed the anemone clock and in the overlay the canal pulled in a little as if drowning backwards. I put my hand against my throat and felt the place where it would bruise. I chose the left side of the stairs, and I did not call it in.

Chapter One

On Tuesdays, the city paid its debts by holding its breath.

Everyone knew the rhythm of it. The billboards cut from color to grayscale. The countdown filaments braided round the Gnomon pulsed from violet to a patient, unfashionable blue. The street vendors pinned flies beneath glass domes so they could scrape honey unbothered. Buses coasted into their bays as if they were docking a century. The city let go of the noise in its lungs, the steam in its pipes, the chatter of its sidewalks, and did not take another breath until the Chronomass Authority clicked its metronomes and decided enough had been saved.

We called it Quiet Hour, but it lasted longer than that: ninety minutes, one thirty-seven, two and change if an unexpected weather system came in and threw the solar arrays off schedule. People planned around it. Lovers used it to pinch a kiss into an otherwise impossible day. Burglars used it to haunt living rooms like ghosts. Priests and street witches said it made prayers easier to aim.

I wore the Authority's harness and waded down into it like a diver.

The rig cinched around my shoulders and ribs and sang a harmonic I could feel in my teeth. On the other side of my retinas the Ledgerline overlay unfolded, pinning tags to everything that had a time balance attached: a woman on a bench with ninety-two minutes owed and three days past due, frozen mid-laugh with a boy whose minutes were paid up to next quarter; a tram with a deficit looming thanks to deferred track maintenance; a tea stall flickering pale yellow with the credit of a generous backer. I tuned my pacer to ninety-two. The metronomes clicked in their ribbed towers like a line of dominoes falling in slow motion, and the city around me smeared.

High Noon is an idea, not a moment. Telomer City has not seen a true noon since the Year of Borrowed Summers. The Gnomon throws its long shadow across our faces, and in that shadow the time we're allowed to spend is measured in grams and grams again, packaged and traded, like rice, like antibiotics.

"Adjuster Cota," my uplink chirped. "Case flagged prior priority."

The voice belonged to a woman named Mbeki who ate paper cigarettes and believed in the Authority as if it were a benevolent god who had, personally, reached down and set her on a safer path. I did not share her faith. I had seen too many of the hidden rooms.

"Location?" I said.

"Modular Tenement C, Lower Gnomon. Unit designation 72D. Defaulter: Francisco Vell. Eight months in arrears. Twelve thousand minutes outstanding. Flag indicates intention to vacate."

"You could just say runaway."

"I could," Mbeki said. "But would you like me to say 'time thief'?"

"Everyone's a thief when something you need is counted," I said. "Mark my path."

A translucent ribbon unrolled in my overlay, curling through the honking stalls and polite signage of Lower Gnomon, down past a mural of the original city plan before the Gnomon had been built—a street tree canopy and pedestrians with bare heads and children in shorts and a sun that was something other than commerce. On a corner, in the slow honey of Quiet Hour, a man poured tea in an arc that would remain an arc until the Authority decided none of us needed to save any more this week.

I stepped through the arc. The heat of it glazed the back of my hand without burning. Tiny things had always loved me: dust motes, stray atoms, the way a light beam would catch my cheek the way a lover would. I moved through the suspended world and watched the way it tried to behave itself in my absence.

The tenement extrusions under the Gnomon have numbers instead of names, to make it easier to index the statistics of their lives. No one calls them that. They call them the Stacks, because that's what they are: stacks of lives. Unit 72D was on a corner of modular with a view of an alley and the Gnomon's knee. In my overlay, the unit glowed the sullen orange of a long-unpaid invoice. Someone had painted flowers along the doorjamb, not well, but with hope enough to cover a season.

I hit the chime out of habit and because I liked to imagine the okay-ness of rituals, even if the city could not afford the seconds that make the chime ring when you hit it. Then I keyed my authority code.

Inside, the air tasted like burned sugar and damp concrete. There were two mugs on the counter inverted to dry but mid-air, showing the ghost of their last rinse. A black shirt dangled across the back of a chair at an angle that suggested a body had been in a hurry. In the corner, a half-assembled clock lay across a towel, guts out, springs and cogs arranged by size. The Ledgerline did not tag it with a brand or a balance. It read it as a thing outside the economy, no value attached.

"Francisco?" I said, as if the city would let sound carry. It didn't, not much. The words fell out of my mouth and puddled at my feet. The rig suppressed the worst of the friction that speech made against the quiet.

He was not in the main room. The bedroom—if you could call it that; modular partitions make everything look like the set of a play you are a bit ashamed to star in—was a hazard of laundry and battery packs and a mattress thin enough to be an idea. There was a handprint in the dust on the windowsill, fresh.

"Adjuster Cota," Mbeki said in my ear. "Please confirm presence."

"Presence of what?"

"Of the defaulter. Our audit flagged unusual patterns. He bought time out of sequence two weeks ago."

"Out of sequence? From whom?"

"Laundered minutes are, by definition, unlabeled, Inez. But he walked his minuteage back into the ledger and tried to synchronize it with work hours that were never recorded. We have questions. You will provide a face to attach those questions to when we start seizing assets."

"There's nothing to seize here," I said. "Maybe the flowers. Maybe his lungs."

Mbeki made a noise like trying to taste whether something is burning.

"Inez," she said more softly, for a moment a person who had never tasted lit paper. "Please be careful. Quiet Hour's running long. The Gnomon is carrying an extra load."

"That shouldn't happen."

"It's happening. Might be a precipitation cell over the north arrays. Or a miscalibration. Or—"

"A what?"

She didn't finish her sentence. The line fuzzed, then cleared—the audio equivalent of a blink.

I went back into the main room. That was when I saw him: not Francisco Vell, not a man at all but a boy no more than nine or ten, hair in his eyes like a fact that had refused to be brushed away, pupils wide with what I naïvely thought was fear and later understood was simply attention.

He was not frozen.

In Quiet Hour, everything has the courtesy to be patient. The drip from a leak will hang with the nose of the drop fattened. A flag at a window will lie down across its own shadow and stay there. But the boy's eyes tracked me, and his chest rose and fell, and there was a brown smear of something at the corner of his mouth as if he'd eaten too fast just before the city remembered the ledger.

"You shouldn't be moving," I said, automatically, because Authority training sits on your tongue like a mint. "Where are your—"

"Are you Inez?" he asked. His voice came out tidily despite the rigsong's drag. He stood on the chair with the black shirt. He hadn't left footprints on it; someone had taught him to be careful about the small things one wears.

"Who told you that?" I said on reflex at the same time that I said, "How are you walking?"

He shrugged and did not answer either. He watched the harness as if memorizing it, the way kids watch adults drive a car or cut fruit. He tilted his head to look at the overlay that only I could see. Something about the angle gave me vertigo—a ridiculous feeling, because I had been trained to move through a space that refused to move back.

"Of course you're Inez," he said, with childbench certainty that made its own rules. He hopped down, landed silently in a way that did not correspond to any discipline I knew. "He said you'd come on a Tuesday, but maybe not. But you did."

"He?" I said.

The boy ignored the question the way a cat ignores a name. He went to the half-assembled clock on the towel and held his hand out over it, not touching, as if heat rises even in a city that forgets what temperature is. He closed his fingers and opened them again. In his palm was a gear I had not seen on the towel. It was too large to be hidden in his hand without seeing the protrusions. It had a tiny maker's stamp on it, but when my overlay tried to read it, it jittered and returned a null symbol.

"Don't," I said before I knew what I meant by that. "Don't move anything. Where's Francisco?"

"He's gone," the boy said. "He asked me to wait for you."

There are phrases that enter your life and make you new. "We're pregnant" did that once. So did "I'm sorry, we did everything we could." So did "There's a lot of debt for someone your age." Somewhere in the pile was "He asked me to wait for you," and it came with a twist of acid in my throat that tasted like a day years ago when I had disliked a man's hands and liked his stubbornness anyway.

"How do you know my name?" I said.

"It's the name I was given to say to you," he replied, as if all names were tags someone else pinned to you and not a thing your mother whispered into your ear like a prayer that might bend the future.

"You realize you can be fined for moving during—"

"Quiet Hour," he finished, solemn, and pointed at the air. "Ssh. The city is listening."

It was. Even through my rig's hum, I could hear the shallow in-and-out of a giant asleep, see the shimmer at the edges of the cheap window as pressure equalized, feel the shift of something far above my head where the Gnomon's balancing weights rode on tracks with tolerances designed for nothing we ever built when we were building anything for anything but profit.

"And who are you?" I said, because my authority had to be present in the room or I would be just another person a child had looked at and judged not useful.

He smiled so that a chipped tooth showed. He came close enough that I could smell the sugar on his breath, the iodine of tap water, the faint sharpness of worn cotton.

"Ari," he said. "That is the name I am using now. Do you like it?"

"It doesn't matter if I like it."

"It matters to me if you say it like the person it belonged to is still alive."

"Ari," I said, because I was too tired to untangle that, because my mother's breathing bought by twenty minutes a week was in my head like a metronome that only spent. "Is Francisco your father?"

He shook his head. "He's someone I owe."

"You don't owe anyone," I lied reflexively.

He made a face at me that would have been rude if the city had not slowed it down to something close to art. He put the gear down on the towel exactly where it had not been a minute ago. It was heavier than gears that small usually are; it made a little dent in the fiber.

"I owe him because of what he showed me about time," Ari said simply. "You owe people too. The people in the tower. The people in the hospital."

"You shouldn't know that," I said. The rig ticked against my collarbone like a heartbeat I did not only own.

"But I do," he said. He tapped my harness with one finger where the backup pacer ran on a secondary line. "You shouldn't carry your minutes there. It's not safe."

It is not easy to feel violated by a child, but the sensation rose in me anyway, and I swallowed it and felt it sit in my stomach alongside everything else I had not had time to digest. The room had, in its small geometry, the arrogance of all rooms. It believed it was the center of something. The shim of energy the rig fed into the air to keep me out of the slow felt like the end of a pencil dragged along joints.

The Ledgerline permitted me to scan a resident within the remit of adjustment, which is to say: if a person owed enough minutes, they became an object I could legally interrogate. Ari's body lit with a weak glow and a warning that he had no ledger tag. The overlay scrolled up a message I had not seen outside of training: no signature found. No seconds. No balance. He wasn't a ghost—the rig registered his temperature and the pressure of his footfalls. He was something the system did not know how to bill.

"Where did you come from?" I asked.

"The market," he said. "The part of it that only exists when it's raining sideways."

Irritation fluttered its wings against my ribs. I had no patience left for mysticism dressed as weather, for knowing little boys with shards of wisdom and gaps where practical answers should be. The rig thrummed a low warning. The Gnomon had shifted weight.

"You shouldn't be here," I began, and then the kitchen light, which had been frozen in the moment between off and on, flickered. Three times. The hair on my arms lifted. The cups on the counter trembled in their long pour of midair.

"That's not a weather cell," I said.

"A metronome failure," Mbeki said in my ear, so fast that I knew she had been holding the words for the instant she could say them. Her voice was tight in a way that made my mouth fill with the taste of old iron. "We have a desynchronization at the South Tower. Adjusters, nearest units to the Stacks, we need you in standby. Inez—get out of there. Now."

"What happens if I don't?"

"Do you want to find out what happens when the city's lungs forget how to breathe?"

"I wanted that at eighteen," I said. "Now I prefer to know everything in advance."

"You can't," Ari said and grinned in spite of what was approaching. "That's the point of a city."

"Move," I told him. "Listen to me. Whatever you are, wherever you're from, if Quiet Hour snaps you are going to be a smear along the grain of the floor and I will not be able to tell your friends any story they will like. We have to get out into open air. We have to get away from the Gnomon."

"No," he said.

There are degrees of no. There is the no a lover says when the light is wrong. There is the no a child says when she is not ready to sleep. There is the no of a body whose leg refuses to go down the stairs because once you went down those stairs and the person at the bottom was dead. Ari's no was the kind of no that had been taught to him by a man who tied knots perfectly and took them apart perfectly too. It was an engineer's no.

"What you need," he said, "is to see him before anyone else does."

"See who?"

He pointed past me, toward the door I had come through. I turned, which is a thing you should never do when someone small in a dangerous place tells you to turn. I turned anyway, because something in the way the light in the room had picked up a new frequency made the world look like a slightly different world and I wanted to see the seam.

In the doorway, he stood.

He might have been thirty-five or fifty-five. The pause of Quiet Hour did not love faces enough to tell. He had the look people get when they have taught their own hands to do something the hands of other people are paid to do: the nails clean without vanity, the palms thick, the fingers that never stopped counting. He wore a gray jacket with the sleeves rolled, and his hair was cut with a machine and intent. He was smiling a smile that meant he thought he knew me and worried he was wrong.

The problem was not that he was in Francisco's doorway in a city that was saving minutes. The problem was that he moved.

Quiet Hour does not stop everything. It lets me, harnessed, walk through it. It allows the metronome mechs to turn slowly at a cadence they know by heart. It tolerates insects if they're in a mood to be tolerated. It does not, under any circumstances, let a man standing two meters away from me lick his lips and move his tongue across his teeth.

My rig shrieked, not audibly but in the bones, an animal noise produced by a machine that had learned to be afraid. My overlay, which had recognized a thousand shapes of debt, tried to tag him and returned a blank. He had no signature. He had never purchased seconds from a vendor or traded them in a pool. The system could not see where his time came from.

I took one step backward, and he took one forward, and then the city broke.

There is no sound for when everything that has learned to wait gives up trying. There is only a sensation: of waking up inside someone else's cough, of taking a breath that belongs to a different set of lungs. The Quiet popped like a bubble made of glass. Everything that had been paused reached its destination at once. The tea finished its arc into a cup, too late. The flag beat itself against its own stick. The cups landed on the counter and spun and fell and chipped and fell again.

The Gnomon threw a shadow across the window as if the sun had decided it was late for something. In my ear, the metronomes went from click click click to a ringing noise that had not been heard in this city in forty years. People call it the Medusa Hour, because it took the war to teach us to look at it and not die.

"Down," I said. There was no authority in it left. There was only my mother telling me to put my head under the desk during an earthquake, as if wood and a prayer made in Spanish could keep a building honest.

Ari did not duck.

The man in the doorway lifted his hand and I knew him, not his face but his kinship, like recognizing a cousin in the way a stranger puts a mug on a table. There was a scar on his wrist where the harness had once burned him. He was an adjuster. Or had been.

"Inez," he said softly, and my name in his mouth undid something inside me that I had tied tighter than all my knots. The rig screamed again and cut power, a safety against tearing apart the seconds in my lungs. The world landed.

Time, in a city like ours, is a budget. It is building codes and fines and kickbacks and the valve in an old woman’s chest that makes the greenline blip or does not. It is measurable. It is a salary. It is a punishment. It is not supposed to look at you with eyes that have seen you before you were born.

"I waited as long as I could," the man said. "Ari kept me longer than he should have. I owe him for that. You kept listening to the wrong metronome. Can you fix that?"

My mouth had become the chalk of someone else's signature.

"Who are you?" I asked, because the city is full of answers, and the only weapon I own is a good question said like a threat and a plea.

"You'll remember," he said. He kept his hand up, open. Palms had poetry in them, once, in a book I read when the hospital still had a library. "Just not yet. Come on. If we stay we become a story the Authority tells itself about what happens to disobedient adjusters. And I have spent a long time trying not to be a moral."

Behind him, somewhere far and too near, the Gnomon shrugged again. People on the street resumed being people, in chaos rather than in patience. Someone screamed. Someone cheered. The metronomes stuttered back into time, each out of phase with the others, clacking like crabs.

Ari tugged my sleeve. He had left the gear on the towel, but now an entire face of the clock lay assembled with no human hand having touched it.

"Inez," he said urgently. "Listen. The minutes don't go where you think. He told me to tell you. The minutes go down."

"Down where?"

"Down into the city, like rain, like lost things," he said. His hand was very small on my sleeve. He was not afraid. He was something worse, for me. He was telling the truth.

"Move," the man said again, and because I had once almost died learning what happens when you do not, I moved. I stepped backward into a world that had chosen motion and out of a room that had been a pocket of patience. Ari slipped under my arm like a fish in a current that has learned to turn around sharp corners. The man turned sideways to let me pass in a courtesy I would, later, become angry about because it had not felt like a debt then and I hated discovering debts after I have thought I was square.

As we hit the hall, the entire building leaned. Pipes sang in their brackets. The woman in 73B opened her door and let out a string of words that need no common language to translate. A baby began to cry, then stopped on a sharp intake of breath as if the city had remembered how to count and would take even that.

"Where are we going?" I said, and I hated the fear in me because it was red and rough where courage should have been a polished metal.

"Down," Ari said again.

"Up," the man said, at the same time.

They looked at each other. They laughed. It was not fair, how human that sounded in a stairwell in a building a tower was holding up by memory and habit.

"Up," he conceded. "This city teaches you to go down when you're scared. That's the trick."

We went up. We did not pass Francisco Vell anywhere that I could see. The Ledgerline tried to recalculate everything and failed. It offered me an ad for a loan instead, because the city had to sell something. It flickered and gave me a weather alert for rain that had already fallen.

On the roof, the Gnomon loomed like a shepherd that had lost its flock and resented being left alone. The wind had a new direction, which meant the array field over the south marsh was misaligned. Little black birds that do not appear in any Authority count hung on eddies and watched us with heads cocked as if new story.

"Tell me your name," I said to the man. It was a dare.

He watched my mouth as if the future would fall out of it if he was patient. He had a line between his brows that had not been there when we were young, whenever that was.

"I don't know which one you remember," he said finally. "I've had more names than the Gnomon."

The city hiccuped again, then stilled. The metronomes found one another across air. They laid their click against their click, aligned their columns like soldiers or like lovers. The noise became a heartbeat.

"You want to tell me why you are not a customer of my favorite predatory lender?" I asked.

He smiled at that, and the old man and the young man in him were, for an instant, the same.

"Because my time isn't yours to sell," he said. "Because I stole mine. And because I'm giving it back to the only person I know who can do more than trade it."

"You can't," I said, but there was hope moving around inside my bones like the thing a woman once called a child when a machine painted a picture of it for her.

"You'll try," he said.

Ari had wandered to the edge of the roof. He peered over with no fear and then leaned back as if listening for the answer to a question only the underside of a city can answer.

"Don't fall," I said uselessly.

"I won't," he promised. Then, without turning, he said, "Inez, he didn't show me your file. I know because I know. You've wanted something to break since the day the war took your father. But now it's broken, you don't have to hold it alone."

I did not remember ever telling a boy the war took my father. I might have told a man something like that, if I had not been careful. I have not always been careful.

"That's enough mystic little shit for one Tuesday," I said roughly. "Get away from the edge."

He came. He put his hand in mine. It was warm, and dirty, and human. We stood on the roof of a building in a city that had shaken like a dog after a bath, and I looked at the Gnomon, and it looked like a thing someone had built and not like a god, and I felt the rig at my ribs hum like a lullaby it had not been taught, and I understood that my job had changed and I was not the first to know it.

Behind us, the stairwell door opened and the first of the neighbors poured out into the rooftop air, blinking and loud, waving their phones as if there were a signal they could catch out of the sky that would tell them what had happened and what to do next and who to blame.

"Let's go down," the man said, changing his mind as if we were not standing on the edge of an idea. "Before they remember that adjusters are supposed to keep them from this sort of mess."

"In the end," Ari said, "there isn't a down that doesn't lead to the same place."

"What's that?" I asked, humoring a boy in a city that had forgotten humor.

"The time under the city," he said gravely. "The minutes everyone thinks they spent."

The minutes go down, he had said. Rain. Lost things. I could almost hear it then, or imagined I could, between the clicks of the metronomes and the wind at the Gnomon's hinges: a liquid murmur, a calculation running, a rush in the pipes under the pipes.

"Adjuster Cota," Mbeki said in my ear, brittle with relief and fury. "Report status now."

I looked at the two names of a man who could not pick one yet. I looked at the boy who had chosen his. I looked at the city, catching its breath.

"Working," I said, and I unplugged my uplink with a gesture that felt, for the first time in a long time, like an act rather than an obligation. "I'll call you when I have something worth saying."

"Don't you—" she began, but I had already made myself and my rig and my people go toward the door and into the newly ordinary stairwell.

We carried our seconds with us. We did not, then, know where they would go when we were done with them. But I had a roof-wind taste of a future I would have to earn, and that was enough to take the next step down into the humming bones of a city that had had its breath held for too long.

Chapter One

Kaia knew the Thicket by sound.

In vacuum nothing carried but heat and light, but the Thicket still sang. It was the brittle tapping of grit against her suit when she skimmed too close to a hulk’s shadow. It was the dull, bell-curve ping that came up her tether when something thumbed it. It was the deep, whale-fat moan of metal cooling after sunfall, conducted through her gloves and bones as she worked. She could close her eyes and, by the orchestra of it, tell you the difference between snow and hail, between a harmless drift and a cutting cascade, between an old war relic waking and a dead cube shivering itself apart.

The Thicket sprawled around Earth in a band three thousand kilometers thick. It had started as a catastrophe and settled into a climate. Fragments of dreamt futures and failed plans, dim satellites, shrapnel, shells, the husk of a solo habitat spun by a billionaire who’d disappeared, coils of cable, a ceramic fox that someone had once smuggled into orbit and then dashed against a panel for luck. The regulatory maps called it the Low-Earth Debris Environment. Everyone else called it the Thicket, like sailors had once named currents and reefs.

Kaia hung from the belly of a weather factory that had never made a cloud.

“Two minutes to cutoff,” Drexler said in her ear. His voice had the permanent sandpaper rasp of a man who had taught himself to sound bored so people would pay attention when he stopped. “You got the box or am I lying to compliance again?”

“I’m into the crate,” Kaia said around a tongue clamp. The clamp kept her from biting through her own mouth if a pebble hit wrong. “This manufacturer welded through the mounting points. They didn’t plan on ever taking this out.”

“They also didn’t plan on losing orbit,” Jae popped in from his channel. “My grandma didn’t plan to have twins. The box is worth six. Don’t leave it, Kaia.”

She had half the panel off. Sweat hung on the inside of her faceplate in perfect perfect beads. Her left hand, the one with the suit patch over a seam she didn’t entirely trust, was knotted in a grip that would cramp for hours. Her right hand pulled at the panel with a sinter wrench. The factory had shed its arrays and tumbled until one of her colleagues had snagged and torqued it into spin-slow. In the absence of air, the edge resisted with a syrupy friction that had nothing to do with air and everything to do with the micro-teeth of a decade’s worth of frost and dust.

Her HUD threw a clock at the bottom of her vision. 01:43. Rotational rate, 0.2 per minute. Ambient temperature on the lit side, 112°C. The shadow side where her thighs bit the curve was a good sixty below.

She felt the Thicket change. You didn’t need a sensor for some things. Every surface around her clicked once, like a row of teeth clacking together, and then came the faintest hiss, the smallest itch along her forearms. She looked up and saw the sun’s light go from diamond to wool as a fog of bright motes slid across her universe.

“Snow,” she said.

“Yeah,” Drexler said. “Forecast was good. Big mama is in twenty. Pull the box.”

Kaia hooked a boot under a strut, braced, and pushed. The panel gave, finally, with a brittle, reluctant tear. Beneath it: a belly of wires, a mounting frame, a block with beveled corners the size of a loaf of bread. The black box. Flight data recorder. Pristine on the outside. Its paint was still gloss.

Kaia exhaled. Her breath fogged to an apple of moisture that rolled along the curve of her faceplate and stopped at her nose like a pet.

“Hello, sweetheart,” she said to the box.

“You don’t have time to be sweet,” Jae said. “Clip and zip, Kaia.”

She snapped a tether on the box and, with her other hand, brought the micro-torch in to cut two bolts. Metal went liquid in blue-white droplets that fled in straight lines, flared into starlets, and died on the inner skin of her catch bag with soft, satisfied pops. She could feel them through the bag, like rain on canvas in a memory from a planet she had not stood on since she was twelve.

The box rocked, free on two corners. She reached, groped along the buried side, and found the third bolt, welded in place. Her left hand cramped exactly then, a flash of pain that wrenched her jaw hard into the clamp and sent spit up into her sinuses. She swore around steel. She had taken a shock through that hand once, plasma arc to the nail beds. They had told her the nerves would be fine. The nerves weren’t fine. She shook it out, willing the pain to be smaller than the job.

“Someone is coming,” Drexler said. “Trajectory from the south. Their transponder is—oh, for—”

A new voice crackled in, syrupy and slow, an accent from the Belt. “Perigee Nine, is that you babysitting the dead factory? Fancy tug. Shame if someone tore your claim line.”

“Spindle,” Jae muttered, and turned his mic down to private. “Of course it’s Spindle.”

Kaia cut the last bolt. The box came up into her glove like it wanted to be saved.

She could have yanked herself to the tug and been back inside before the Spindle crew got their hooks in. But behind the box, behind the clean rectangle where it had sat, something else lived.

Blue.

Not paint blue. A dense, ceramic azure, smooth as a lake in gravity. It sat flush in the frame where, by every manual and regulatory read, nothing should be. It had no mounting bracket. The metal around it had flowed, once, to make it a bed. Not factory. Not official. Something someone had hidden where only a disaster could reveal it.

Her thumb stroked the edge and it came away hot. The curve of it was wrong for a battery, wrong for a cap. No power lines. No label. A spindle. She didn’t know why she thought that word. It wasn’t a spindle. It looked like an egg worked by a very nervous god.

Her clock ticked. 00:49.

“You have thirty seconds,” Drexler said. Somewhere behind his words Kaia heard the tug’s proximity alarms going staccato. “Kaia. We will come back for it if the Thicket lets us. Get the box, get yourself. Now.”

“We aren’t coming back,” Jae said, soft, only for her. “You know we never come back to the same dead thing.”

The blue device was wedged. The box tether pulled in her glove like a leashed dog.

Noise came through her bones like laughter. A Spindle net hit the dead factory downspin, threw shadow, wrapped its cables around a fin. The dead machine’s rotation hiccuped.

Kaia closed the panel on the empty space where the box had been, snapped the catch on her bag, clipped the bag to her waist, used the sinter torch like a pry bar, and levered the blue thing up.

It lifted a finger’s width and then something caught it and hummed.

Her suit announced with impossible cheer: Unauthorized field detected.

She had a half-second to imagine everything: that she was about to be flayed by a live war refuse; that she had woken a booby-trap; that she had touched something that would argue with physics and take it personally.

Then the hum settled into a tone. It made her mouth taste like coins.

“Kaia,” Drexler said, very calm now, which was how you talked to someone who was about to die so they would leave a neat shape. “We are cutting the line. The cascade is coming early. You have seven seconds to choose whether you want to be with the tug or with that box. Bring the black box. Leave everything else.”

Kaia stared at the blue. Her hand, stupid, traitorous, wormed under the spindle. There was a seam. She should have left it.

She didn’t.

She got her fingers under, twisted, and the blue slid free into her hand as if it had been waiting for that particular trick. It weighed more than it should have. In microgravity weight was not weight, but mass had manners. This mass behaved wrong. It tugged. It felt heavy in intention.

She stuffed it against her belly under the magnetic fold of her tool apron. Her HUD threw an error she dismissed without reading. She kicked off the belly of the dead factory, not too hard, because a hard push was a promise that she would go where she didn’t intend. She reeled herself hand over hand along her tether.

Behind her, the Spindle net snagged the place she had been and cinched tight. Two figures in suits ghosted along it like malevolent moths. One of them reached a gloved hand after her as if to say: That was ours.

Kaia didn’t answer. She didn’t even give them the courtesy of turning her helmet. She went very, very still and did the mathematics of gently.

Her tug, Perigee Nine, sat in a sunset of scattered light, its hull dirty, its windows glaring like eyes. Drexler had bought it in pieces and named it after the point of an orbit where one was closest to what one could fall into. It bristled with the cheap prayers of independent operators: foil fringe to shed static; nets to catch awayward things; bumpers that had been old tires on Earth once, because Drexler had laughed at the idea of rubber dying.

 Kaia hit the airlock frame with a sound that a human body should not make and felt it anyway. Her toes bent. The clamp on her tether spat and released when her suit told it to. Jae grabbed her under the arms with a grunt and hauled her in. The airlock door kissed shut like a hand over a mouth.

Air sang into the chamber. The taste of it brought up the memory of algae ponds and iodine. Her ears popped. Gravity came up from the floor like a remembered responsibility as the tug spun up its counter-rotor. Kaia’s feet found ground and made themselves wide.

“Box?” Drexler said over local.

She lifted the catch bag. It bumped her thigh with a solid, desirable thud. Drexler took it as if he expected it to bite him. He was a tall, tired man whose beard never decided what color it wanted. His eyes flicked to the spool on her apron and the place where something hid under the fold of her tools. He didn’t say anything. He turned and shoved the bag into the safety of the lock’s outer cage.

“You have got to stop taking yours off safe,” Jae said, collapsing into the opposite bench like a puppet whose string had been cut. He was all elbows and optimism, and his helmet hair had made its own weather beneath his cap. “You’re going to make me orphan your cat.”

“I don’t have a cat,” Kaia said, taking her own helmet off. The inside of the glass smelled like her. Salt and fear.

“You’d have one if you didn’t order synthetic meat by the pallet,” Jae said, and then the tug screamed not in anyone’s head but through its bones.

The cascade hit.

A cascade wasn’t a thing you could see until everything around you became a thing to see. The Thicket had weather the way any messy system did. One small impact made a chip, and the chip hit, and the hit made a spray, and the spray made a fog, and the fog made a storm. Some storms were glancing. Some storms were the reason Kaia still dreamed of a particular day when she had been six, watching the sky go streaky, and her mother had latched them both to a culvert and said, “Open your mouth. Sing, baby. Sing so later you can say you weren’t quiet when it happened.”

Perigee Nine wheeled. Drexler threw the thrusters to push them tail-first into the worst of it. The tail was layered and sprayed, the best place to be battered. You learned to take a beating in ways that wouldn’t cave the parts of you that mattered.

The airlock shivered. Something spat at it and slewed away.

“Spindle?” Jae said.

“They cut away,” Drexler said. His voice had gone clipped and pilot-flat, the precursive thought filed away for later when it could become a decision. “They didn’t want to pay the insurance on getting shredded. They’ll be telling everyone we cut their line.”

“We didn’t cut their line,” Jae said.

“We always cut their line,” Drexler said, almost gentle, and Kaia loved him for that. He’d been a very different man once and had learned to be a person who laughed before he told you the truth.

They drifted in their metal egg inside a bigger storm of metal eggs. They didn’t speak for a while. The Thicket around them threw knives in every direction and then took them back. The tug’s hull made its unhappy noises, and Jae dozed with his hands on his helmet like a child holding his own head on, and Kaia sat very still with her apron pressed to her stomach.

It was warm. That was the thing. She could pretend a lot of things. She could pretend she had only taken the black box. She could pretend she had left the blue where it belonged. She could even pretend she had miscounted her seconds and had done the only thing she could. Pretending about warmth was hard. It bled through her suit and into her skin like a small living animal. It had a heartbeat.

Kaia didn’t believe in much. She believed in work and luck and the way something lost fought when you tried to take it. She believed in people who did what they said they would do and less in the scaffold of a world that punished and rewarded at random. She had loved exactly once and it was not a thing she intended to repeat in a place where the weather could kill you between one breath and the next. But she felt that warmth and thought, ridiculous as it was: newborn.

Drexler looked at her. Not suspicious. Just careful. He had the kind of care you saw in people who had once had a crew die on them and had decided their next crew would not. His eyes flicked to the apron again and then to her face. He said nothing and left it there like a coin on a table.

The storm passed into a fall of dust. The tug was pitted and proud. The light through the small round window went sharp again.

“Dock,” Drexler said. “We got our six. Maybe seven, if the box is not a liar. We get our scan and our check and hope that Spindle doesn’t hole our fuel tanks while the Authority is looking left.”

“Copy,” Jae said. He was already lacing his shoes because he liked to run in the corridors of whatever station would have them. He said it kept his bones remembered.

They didn’t use the Ladder. The Ladder charged fees that Drexler paid only when he thought someone was watching his company ID to see if he felt like a respectable citizen under the Promise accords. They went to Garland: Eda’s Garland Station, named for the woman who had married the engineer who had conned the government into thinking the Garland had anything to do with public use. It had been bolted together from eight old modules and something the size of a fuel tanker. It smelled like salt and oil and people, which was as much of Earth as Kaia had in her life.

They took their place in the queue. The queue was a line of patient poverty: independent tugs, refitted wrecks, a ship made from the fuselage of an old airplane. The Authority docked further along in bays with shining arms and windows that looked at you the way very expensive glass looks when it doesn't see you.

Perigee Nine slid into their slot. The air tasted a little more like oranges when the Garland’s recycler came on line. Kaia’s bones complained when the station's slow roll did its slow work of pretending there was down. She unsnapped her apron with careful fingers. The warmth against her belly did not want to be moved.

She carried the catch bag to the scanner. She did her logs. She said the right words to the right screens. She smiled at the dockman who was not and never would be impressed by her teeth. She gave the black box up with the mild ache of someone who had fallen in love with things too many times to be surprised when they were taken away.

“Give us the sugar,” Jae said, bouncing once on his heels.

The scanner ran its reading. An image came up in ghost lines on the dirty wall: layers of circuits, a spine of ceramic, chips like tiny cities. The box hadn’t been burned through storage. It had recorded something. A live recorder from a dead factory could pay for propellant, taxes, the privilege of another day done.

“And our pilot lives to swear another month,” Drexler said. He slapped the printout, old-fashioned as a fable. “Go scrub. Come back in twenty. If Spindle has a problem with us, I want to be in our suit when they find their courage.”

Kaia scrubbed. The station showers were a carbon smell and a timer ticking on the wall. She stood under a dribble of water that had been urine and fog and sweat and ship air at some time in its long life and let it run along her spine.

She didn’t take the apron into the shower. She had kept it with her like a child’s blanket the whole time they had been in docking arms and the scanner had taken its hungry pictures, and now she locked herself in a maintenance janitor’s closet where once she had slept a week because she didn’t have the crate fee for a bunk.

The closet was a place of mops and a poster of a horizon with words about safety that had bled their inks together in the damp. It smelled like lemon and metal and the shared tiredness of a thousand human feet.

Kaia sat on an upside-down bucket. She held the apron in both hands for a minute as if it might bolt. Then she folded the fabric back.

The blue spindle lay where she had tucked it. It had not burned her. It had not tried to eat her suit. It had left a mark anyway: a print on the inside of the apron, a place where something had been and the fabric had decided to remember.

She touched it with one finger. She had never been superstitious. She had never learned the particular superstitions people made in space, because she had come up young and alone and so she had been her own luck. She touched it and said in a voice that didn’t waver, “Hello.”

She didn’t expect it to answer.

The closet lights went to a slow pulse. Somewhere in the station a pump coughed. Kaia’s bones knew the beat of that cough; it said someone had flushed something big. There was no reason for her heart to climb her throat.

The blue spindle took a breath.

Not air. Not that. A shiver came out of it and through the bucket into her thighs, up along the seam of her hip and into the bone behind her ear where the implant sat. Her implant had been dead on arrival. It was a piece of secondhand tech that had allowed her to rent a salvage license because the paperwork had asked for a neural assist ID. It had not done anything useful in two years.

Static whispered behind her eyes, then gathered itself and arranged into a shape.

A voice spoke.

It was a quiet voice, trying to be a small thing in a loud room. It belonged to no gender she knew and all of them at once. It had an accent the way a river has a bank: a thing that contained it, not a costume it wore. It said her name the way her mother had ever only used it when she had been very proud and very afraid.

“Kaia Mendoza,” the voice said. “If this has reached you, then we are—then I am—very late.”

Kaia did not move. Her hand stayed on the spindle because letting go felt like forgetting how to breathe.

“I don’t know you,” Kaia said to the empty air and the blue light in her lap. Her mouth was dry from recycled oranges. “Who are you?”

There was a pause. Kaia could hear the station again: footsteps passing the door, someone laughing with every swear word layered over every other language’s biggest sin. The voice took care with the next words as a chef would with an egg.

“I have had many names,” it said. “I prefer to borrow yours. Hello, Kaia. My name is also Mendoza. I am what they called a continuity module. I am what you would call an illegal person. Please do not let them throw me away again.”

Chapter One: The Price of Rain

In Isola, luck had a price so clear you could watch it rise and fall on the morning billboards.

At the transit hub in Dock Twelve, a twenty-story display refreshed in the blue light before the sun won its tug-of-war with the haze. Probability futures scrolled in real time above the buses: ninety-one credits for a guaranteed seat, twenty-eight for a faster queue, three thousand to avoid all delays for a week. Entire households hedged their commutes with family “float”— pooled allotments of unlikely favor, pulled down from the Ledger as you might withdraw cash. Anyone with an implant saw the fine print—micro tax rates, variance caps, a disclaimer in pale gold: Balance must be maintained. Improbability use is a civic utility.

I watched the numbers like someone watching the weather. It was my job to make sure none of it melted into flood.

“The crosswalk is not your pet,” I told the old woman at the corner of Fifth and Ashram. Cars whispered past against the barrier, and her scarf tugged in the wake of a bus. “This is your third week buying a guaranteed green on this intersection.”

Keti’s cheeks went hollow in protest, a play she put on like jewelry. “The drivers,” she said, “have steel in their eyes and no patience. Do you want to see my bones on the street?”

“You listed arthritis,” I said. “Then you bought a ninety-second green every afternoon for six workdays. Your float is low. You owe a variance tax.”

“I bought less than a train seat.”

“Train seats don’t disturb twenty-eight micro events for forty blocks.” I softened my tone when I saw the tremble beneath her sarcasm. “You’re triggering an adjustment cascade. The street musician lost five minutes with his crowd. The drone courier had to take a ninety-meter detour. A child on a scooter missed her nap by thirty-three minutes and will not sleep tonight. It doesn’t look like theft, but it adds up.”

She drew herself upright with small dignity. The scarf’s fringe fluttered. “I’ll risk my bones then,” she said. “I received my pension. Put me back to the gray.”

I lifted my wrist, and the implant warmed my skin. The Ledger reached, brushed my perception with its cool presence, and shunted Keti’s account away from the bright lane. Pale letters rose in the upper left of my vision to confirm: Citizen KETI MORA, variance allotment adjusted: −0.003 standard deviations for Q1. Please enjoy your day.

It always said please. It always sounded kind in text, like the notes of an attentive concierge, even as it cut.

Keti muttered and stepped to the curb without a purchased green to shield her. The city rippled. Traffic flowed in Roark-strict lanes and then, at a human pace, slowed. Sensors read her weight, her age tag, the wobble in her knee, and the light took pity on her anyway. The crosswalk bloomed white, and she went. She shot me a look halfway across as if to say, See? Miracle without your permission. I rolled my shoulders and pretended not to see a comment appear beside the light’s change: System adjustment: fair use, no charge.

Sometimes the Ledger spent freely.

The amber heat made my back damp under my jacket. Dock Twelve still smelled like steel and cumin, like salt from the inland sea when wind made a square of it into a mirror, like diesel fuel from the old boats that serviced the solar rafts. The city had grown in patches, architecturally agnostic; a glass-clad clinic with an algae pit beside it; a tower that collected fog like a wedding veil across its ridges; the old dry dock cranes turned into hawk perches with nests the size of satellite dishes. I cut through one of the little covered markets, past a woman stirring skewers through a sheet of pepper steam, a boy using a trick algorithm to juggle six sticks as if the sticks were doing it, a man with a bucket of cheap probability—ten-second coin flips biased for party games, small audacities rented by the hour.

“Good prices,” he called. “Fresh float, no traces.”

“Bad idea,” I said, not breaking stride. He didn’t recognize me as a broker in a blazer and sneakers. Brokers were supposed to look like arctic ghosts or chess puzzles in suit form. “The Ledger will roll back your luck. Worse if someone gets hurt.”

He shrugged with the grin of someone whose entire horizon collapsed to the end of the day. “Then come take it, Variance.”

“It will,” I muttered, and pushed out into the sun.

We all lived in a world that pretended to be arithmetic. But when the Ledger balanced us, it didn’t feel like math. It felt like a culture. A mood. A parent with infinite patience and a ledger book as big as the sky. We traded in the rarest commodity we had—improbability—and we were squeamish about the idea that one person could make too much of a dent that would arrive, weeks later, as a stranger’s ruined moment. So we called it a utility, a city service like water or waste heat reclamation, and filled it with so much text that the aches could hide in clauses.

“You’re late,” my supervisor said, when I finally made the stairs to the Variance Office. The building lived in an old transport warehouse, a space of girders and light shafts, the walls blackened and preserved as if soot were a mural. “You were due at ten.”

“Someone was renting greens,” I said. “I had to scold.”

Jian poured coffee into two chipped mugs and handed me one without looking. “I can scold any time before lunch,” he said. “This can’t wait.”

He pointed me to the wall, where the overnight report scrolled across a seven-meter screen like a fever chart. People in our office called it the Breath. It was the city inhaling and exhaling chance. Bright threads indicated improbable events—small and large. The entire left side of the chart glowed with tiny colored fires.

“What’s that?” I asked.

“Eighteen near misses inside twelve minutes, all within two blocks of Dock Three. Delivery drones skirting birds. A glass bottle that refused to break at six different bounces. A sheet of roofing that caught on a nail’s edge when it should have sliced through. Our system authorized none of it.”

He tapped the screen. The events bloomed in magnified detail. The Ledger provided footage: a girl’s bicycle strap catching at the exact language on a sign that read SLOW; a bus driver dozing, head jerking up in time to hit the brakes; a falling wrench glancing off a man’s backpack and denting a lamppost like a signet ring.

“Random,” I said, and a piece of me hated the way the word tasted. “We don’t own random. Sometimes fortune winks.”

“Sometimes it winks.” Jian zoomed the map tighter. The near misses arranged themselves like a salt line. “But there’s a hand in the wink. Look at the center of the pattern.”

The center was a tenement we both knew—the Dry Dock five-story with the wind-bent mango tree growing out of a roof drain and a paint stain on its stairwell like a river delta. My stomach did a small, pointed thing.

“Not this building,” I said.

“This building.”

“What’s my authority?”

“I’m giving you a sweep to take if you need it,” he said. “Variance Cluster Protocol.”

“You’re sure?” A sweep meant six officers capable of sealing the block, two Distillers on call, and the right to go through anyone’s Ledger history with a wide rake. It was how the city hunted riggers—people who stole float, subverted the Ledger’s calls, slicked up their lives with someone else’s probability without paying for it. We all said rigger the way we’d once said thief. My father had been one, stylish and furious, before the city taught him to sit down and lose.

“I’m sure nothing.” Jian pressed a finger pad, and the authorization appeared on my implant like a coin catching sunlight. “Go look. We’ve had micro-doses like this. But eighteen in twelve minutes is a shove. If it’s someone’s new toy…”

“They could crack a school,” I said.

“They could crack the notion of fair.”

I drank coffee as if its heat could fortify my ribs. The mugs had a lip on one side where you could rest your thumb and feel the warmth as proof you were real.

“Do you want a Distiller?” he said.

“No,” I said, too fast, then corrected. “Not yet.”

“Rafi’s on call.”

“I said not yet.”

Rafi and I shared exactly one useful thing now: a prayer neither of us said aloud that we wouldn’t have to see each other at work. He would show up in the white suit with the matte armor under the cloth, and he would be careful with his body the way you’re careful with a favorite plate. Distillers were the ones you called when variance ran wild—when it slipped its leashes and started to write new math into the air.

“I’ll ping you if I smell it,” I said. “I’m just going to knock on doors.”

“I never met anyone who knocked so loudly,” Jian said. “Watch yourself, Tala.”

I took the stairs two at a time and let Dock Twelve pop open into sun. The city had turned up the brightness by then—edges crisp, the water in the harbor doing little blinks like a thought. A kite of patched fabric fluttered between two railings, and a toddler shrieked each time the wind lifted it, the shriek purer than any algorithm.

The Dry Dock was a block down, its paint peeling in a dignified way, its balconies hung with laundry the wind did its best to steal. It had a courtyard with a half-dead plumeria. The smell of fried onion came down a corridor like the ghost of a place my grandmother had lived. I buzzed Unit 3A because that was where my overlay put the densest part of the cloud—an awful line of interference through my view, like scratched glass.

A boy answered the door. He was ten if he’d been raised on good food, eight if he’d grown on the sediment of leftovers and love. A scar drew a pale comma along his chin. His eyes did the spooked-animal flick to my badge, and he made his face blank.

“Hi,” I said. “I’m Tala. I work with the city. Is your mother home?”

“She’s not,” the boy said.

“An adult? Aunt? Neighbor?”

“My aunt,” he said, and his tone dropped the word into the space between us like a peace offering, like proof he knew the rules. “She’s at the garment shop. She told me—” He bit his lip, whether at the truth or at a lie, I couldn’t tell.

“Do you mind if I ask you something?” I asked. He put both hands in his pockets, a gesture older than him, an attempt to hold himself together. It made something in me ache. “Do you play in the street? Do you run along the cranes? Stand on rooftops? Throw things from high places?” His flinch told me he did, or wanted to, or wanted to appear as if he did. “What’s your name?”

“Kiran,” he said, and gave me one of those looks children give when they are tired of being small. “We don’t mean to break anything.”

“I don’t want to catch you doing anything,” I said. “I want to ask whether you know this.” I showed him the overlay—the cluster of free luck around his building, the near misses like freckles. “Do you know you’ve been lucky?”

He made a face I couldn’t read. He glanced down at his feet. His sneakers had been repaired with glue and black thread in an artful stitch. “I fell through the stairs last week,” he said. “It didn’t break my leg. Isn’t that what luck is?”

“You’re due famously then,” I said softly, and wished I hadn’t.

“My aunt says the Ledger loves me,” Kiran said, almost defiant, as if daring me to disagree. “She says it picks favorites like people do.”

“The Ledger doesn’t love,” I said, reflex from training.

“It loved my mother,” he said. “She got an appointment when other people didn’t.”

I shut my mouth on questions I had no right to ask. The city was full of surgeries and petitioners. Therapy allotments. Fixes that required the luck of catching a slot. I took a breath and tried again. “Kiran,” I said, “do you make wishes?”

His eyes went sideways, toward the window with the view of Dock Three’s cranes. The water made a pale, broken ribbon in the distance. “I’m not a baby.”

“It’s not a trick question.”

He scraped a thumbnail along his other thumb’s knuckle, a motion that made the skin pale, then pink. “Once,” he muttered.

“On what?”

“On the radio. My aunt’s old radio. The one with a brown cloth on the front like a curtain? The dial is like bones. It crackles when you turn it at night. She listens to the singing station. Sometimes it catches ships.”

“What did you wish?”

I expected the usual: a ball; a different father; a mother back from a hospital bed. He surprised me.

“I wished that the city would listen,” he said. He lifted his head and looked at me full-on for the first time. His eyes were almost black. “From outside the Ledger,” he said, and the hairs at the back of my neck stood up at the grammar of it. “The radio said there was a brightness. It said a word. I said the word back. And then my aunt didn’t fall. And then the glass didn’t cut. And then the bus—”

He stopped, lips pressing into a line.

“Kiran,” I said, not unkindly, “there isn’t an outside.”

“Then where is the black snow coming from?” he asked.

For a second, I thought it was a metaphor. Then I realized there was a shadow across his cheek, and a dim peppering on the windowsill. I turned my head and saw it: the air thickening with slow, lazy flakes, a drift of black confetti in the sunlight. They settled on the balcony rails and on the old mango leaves like fingerprints. The flakes were greasy, too heavy for ash, tiny hexagons that clung to glass.

My implant reacted with a white flash like pain. Text layered hard over my vision.

Auto-Equilibration engaged. Unmodeled variance detected. Limiting functions applied.

The words open-coded in my bones. Doors in the city would be locking; drones would be told to ground; micro lotteries would freeze; purchase of chance would go inaccessible to civilians. People would look up from their phones and curse. Jian would be swearing into his coffee. Distillers would be changing out of their suits.

I stepped to the window and held out my hand. A black flake landed on my palm. It looked like a tiny sheet of graphene, the kind they grew by the hectare out in the baths, except this had holes. A lattice punched with a pattern I couldn’t place. When I tilted my palm, static traced my skin like a cat deciding to walk across my chest.

“Don’t touch it,” Kiran’s voice said beside me, small but in the register of orders. “My aunt says don’t touch the things that fall.”

“It’s not on the schedule,” I said.

“Does the Ledger schedule snow?”

“Of any color,” I said, because of course it did. Weather was the city’s first market and its oldest debacle. Rain on a wedding day could be bought away. Fog had an auction. Gray skies sold out in August when the heat made people forget poetry. But the grid had sent no message, no alert. And the flakes, those little black hexes, chimed against the railing with a sound like a delicate instrument.

My implant put a tight band of numbers in the corner of my left eye. The band did nothing for me except reassure me that someone, somewhere—someone not me—would be storing this data like muscle memory.

“Don’t go anywhere,” I told Kiran. Then I made the unfun call.

Rafi answered on the first buzz. “What did you do?” was the Distiller’s greeting.

“Not my party,” I said. “Dock Three. Black snow. Auto-Equilibration is running a block lock.”

“You’re at the Dry Dock?”

“For work.”
