“I’ll take that personally later,” he said. “Are you by the mango?”

“Unit 3A,” I said.

“Stay put.”

The line cut off. He always did that—gave instructions the Ledger would give and then acted as if he made them up. I watched a bus hiss to a halt two blocks over. The doors didn’t open. I watched a man under an awning shake his head like a dog that had tasted vinegar. The flakes traced little lines on his cheeks and didn’t melt.

Kiran tugged at the hem of his T-shirt. His hand had a tremor he was trying to crush with stubbornness. “Are we in trouble?” he asked.

“Only if you made this weather,” I said. I crouched so I was at his eye level. “You didn’t order any luck lately? No aunties doing favors for ganders?”

“I don’t know what that means,” he said, which meant he did but didn’t want to say he did.

“What was the word?” I asked softly.

Kiran’s face did a thing that made me think of a moth over a candle. Go close, go away. “It’s dangerous to say,” he murmured.

“Dangerous like touching the flakes?”

“Dangerous like you get heard.”

“And you wanted to be heard.”

“By the brightness,” he said. The boy’s certainty frightened me more than the black snow. “Not by them.”

“Them is me,” I said.

“Not you,” he said, and finally, he was ten. “The Ledger,” he said, and made the word sound like an animal in tall grass.

We both looked at my wrist as if the Ledger were a pet you could put a leash on. A sound hummed in my implant, as soft as the beginning of a song. I had never heard the Ledger speak. It didn’t need to. It was everywhere. It was structure, not voice. But there, under the chiming of flakes, under the murmur of bus engines idling against a lock, a thread unspooled between my ears.

Not authorized, it said, the text forming as sound, as if the syllables appeared in my temporal lobe like a thought I had not made. External input detected. Hold, please.

“Is it telling us to hold?” Kiran asked, and his eyebrows did a thing I had seen exactly once before—when my father sat at our kitchen table, hands around a glass, listening to a judge decide.

“Yes,” I said.

We both noticed at the same time that the black flakes weren’t falling at random. They were moving in currents, in invisible streams. They sketched something in the air like lines. I couldn’t read it until the wind shifted. Then I saw shapes, low-resolution at first, then clearer. Characters. Letters. They weren’t ours.

Rafi reached the stairwell with two Distillers breathing down his neck. He filled the doorway like an argument. His helmet hide hung back on its hinge. His mouth set in a line when it saw Kiran, the flakes, and me. He clocked all of it in a second. He had always been good at triage.

“Don’t breathe deep,” he said, and handed me a mouth mask. It smelled like latex and mint. “The snow is conductive. It’s tracing.”

“We see that.”

“It’s writing through wind pressure and static charge. Jian sent me the first five minutes of data. Tala,” he said, and my name in his mouth had acquired so many meanings that some days I didn’t know it was mine unless I heard it in his voice. “This isn’t coming from our grid. There’s a neutrino surge under the harbor that correlates with the density.”

“You don’t measure neutrinos.”

“We do now,” Rafi said. He stepped to the balcony and held his bare hand out because he only wore gear when someone could see him do it. Four flakes landed, clung, lifted. He looked at the lattice pattern with the attention he used to give my collarbones. “No microtag. No city ID. It’s just… matter with an appetite for charge.”

“Someone is doping our ledger,” I said.

“Someone is doping reality,” he said. “Traces like this inject improbable behavior without the Ledger catching purchase. They don’t talk to it. They don’t pay into our balance. Think of it like a smuggled current in a communal grid. The lights look brighter on one block, and a transformer melts three streets over six weeks later. We’ve seen whispers. This is a shout.”

He turned to the boy. “And you are?”

“Kiran,” said the boy. He stood straighter because Rafi’s attention did that to people. “I live here.”

“Did you order the sky?”

Kiran pressed his lips together.

“We have to know if someone is pushing in from outside,” Rafi said, more to me than to the boy, using his job voice. “If this is a human rig, we can shut them down. If it’s outside—”

“There isn’t an outside,” I said.

“Say that again,” he said, and glanced up as if the city hung like a chandelier above the roof. “Say it loud enough it believes you.”

I was about to tell them both to stop being dramatic when the sound changed. Not loud—like a pressure in my jaw. The drift of flakes had made letters—long lines of them looping the street. They scrolled, and twice, the loops returned to the same signs, the same window edges, without smearing, as if two hands wrote at once. For a breath the process double exposed itself in my vision. My implant hiccuped; the Ledger tried to frame it; three error messages bloomed and died like fish on the surface of a lake.

A bus turned into our block.

It shouldn’t have. The buses had stopped. I heard the driver’s panic through the windshield—his hands and his faith in brakes. The bus jittered as if inside a trembling. It entered the street, and for a second the metal stuttered in and out of itself. I thought of a coin trick, the way you make a coin appear and disappear until you don’t know which version is real.

Kiran stepped without meaning to. His body went to the window with the body’s old need to watch machines. I grabbed his collar and yanked him back, and in that second the bus existed in two places. It was ten meters farther along and also where it had started. Two noses, two sets of headlights. They slipped through each other like knives through a seam in cloth. The air went white behind them. Frost patterned the lamppost. The same bus number, the same ad on the side for vitamin fish, the same driver’s face in two versions—one that saw us, one that didn’t.

The flakes chimed. The letters laughed, or maybe it was a hinge shrieking. The first bus kept moving. The second shivered, disappeared with a sound like ice cracking under a foot, came back, and disappeared again, imprinting whiteness along the pavement, a rough line like a scar.

The boy made a sound deep in his throat.

“Breathe, Kiran,” I said, my hand still tight in his shirt, sick with the idea of him running out into something that didn’t know if it was there. “Stay with me.”

Rafi’s face had gone very, very still. He raised his arm, spoke into his wrist. “We have an uncontrolled split event. Repeat, uncontrolled split. I want the southern gate sealed,” he said, because he made his requests like declarations. He was gentle when he put his hand on my elbow, and I hated him for that. “Tala,” he said, “out.”

“My sweep—” I started.

“Your pride,” he said. “We’re done with that. Out.”

I would have gone. I would have obeyed. I would have let the Distillers in their suits swan through the corridors and eat the anomaly like sugar.

But the Ledger spoke again.

It turned every nerve in my body quiet. It turned me into a listening post.

Hold, it said, and this time, with a voice like a child’s. Can pay.

“Can what?” I whispered.

“Did you order a miracle?” Rafi snapped.

The voice curled into the center of my head, as intimate as asleep breath. Can pay, it said again, with an insistence that was not plea but bargain. It felt like a hand on the table between us.

And I did what I had told old women and street jugglers and my father not to do. I grabbed unallocated chance with both hands.

I bought a sweetness, a handful of improbable to spend. An emergency line existed for brokers, because sometimes it was worth it to cut through the lace of ethics. It was heavy and hot against the part of my brain that knew right, like a coin inside my mouth. I flicked it out into the room between Kiran and the window, between the bus and the bus.

“Don’t you do that,” Rafi said, but by then it was already spent.

It acted like a puddle of oil in water. The duplicate bus slid around it like a droplet shy of another. The two trajectories pulled apart. Frost vapor dissipated. The driver’s mouth closed, then opened—two expressions collapsed into one—his lips forming a slow starving blessing to the god of mechanics and sane mornings. The bus took the corner with a judder and stopped of its own mind three houses down, braking as if it had been told what brakes were by a kind voice.

“Can pay,” the Ledger whispered again, and this time I heard a second note inside it. Not machine. Not social. Brightness, Kiran had called it. Something at a distance trying to learn our currencies.

“Rafi,” I said, and didn’t know if I was saying his name to warn him, hurt him, keep him, or ask him to forgive me. “The outside is shopping.”

His jaw tightened. “Paid with what?”

I looked at Kiran, and he looked at me. For a heartbeat, the woman who’d been my supervisor would have said this was me manufacturing drama, me letting the moment dress itself. But I had spent years telling other people no, telling them their best moments were other people’s broken, and once, in a kitchen with fluorescent lights, I had watched a man who loved chance read to me from a book about gamblers who believed in saints.

“Names,” I said. It wasn’t an answer with the weight of data. It was a bone-deep guess. The Ledger had reached for my title when I bought that slice of sugar; the outside had found us through an old radio and a word. “It’s paying with names.”

“You’ll have to explain that before a committee,” Rafi said. “With fewer metaphors.”

The boy’s trembling had gone quiet. He was watching the looping letters in the air with the attention you give to something that might ask you a question at any moment.

“What was the word?” I asked again, because sometimes the thing that saves you is the thing you say twice.

Kiran swallowed. He said, “Abacus.”

The black snow turned its lattices at that like a field of birds veering to a geometry you’d never known they used. It brightened in the sunlight, as if each flake realized it had another face.

We stood in a world made by arithmetic and patience and a utility that charged you for rain, and something outside had learned how to spend. We would call it an attack or a gift. The city, which loved its balance, would call it theft until it learned how to tax it.

Rafi touched my arm, and this time his fingers dug in because he knew I was about to do something stupid.

“Don’t,” he said.

I smiled at him with all the unsteady bravery I had left. “We are way past not,” I said. “Seal your gates, Distiller. I’m taking the boy to see the radio.”

“You don’t have the authority—”

“I used it,” I said, and would have added a joke if my mouth had held any. Outside, the bus driver cried in relief, a sound I could have sold for a thousand credits on a normal day. “Jian,” I said into the air, trusting he was listening, knowing he was, “log my misuse of the emergency line. Log that I’m moving with a minor. And then send me a prayer.”

“We don’t offer those anymore,” Jian’s voice said, thin with static and laughter that didn’t find an office. “We charge for them.”

“Put it on my tab,” I said, because if the day was buying metaphors, I might as well spend my own.

Kiran looked like a boy who had climbed exactly to the edge of the roof he had promised his aunt he would never reach. The black snow chimed. The letters rearranged themselves. The city took a breath we could feel in our teeth.

We stepped out into it.

On the morning the storm wrote her name, Tamsin Arellano was stealing thirty minutes of rain.

She cupped her hands over the hollow of the console and brought the map up around her, a blue-green shell she could turn with a gesture. South Grid shimmered in translucent sheets of elevation, humidity, and unspent credit, heat islands answered by ghostly lines of lift. The city below was a lace of roofs and reservoirs, solar fins dull under the overcast. Out beyond, the wastes she had grown up in were a smear of rust and salt. Behind the glass and the humming fans and the obligatory potted fern, she could almost taste the metallic bite of distant dust storms, the tang of algae ponds a day after seeding.

She had learned the chorus with a metronome in a squat by the river, the old manual downloaded on a scavenged tablet, memorizing the intervals that slid the gulls tighter or looser, that turned a hazy updraft into a clean pillar. In the official transit tours, they made the work look like conducting. In a way it was. Every storm was an orchestra. And like any conductor worth the title, sometimes Tamsin palmed the score and struck her own tempo.

The interface hummed under her hands as she dialed down the albedo on two southern Petals by three degrees. In her ear, the standard permissible shifted against the bone, red tick by red tick. You could feel the Net’s hesitance when you bent it past what the boards deemed safe—like steering wheels from the old movies that stiffened at the limit. She coaxed the gulls anyway: sleek, triangular drones in the lower troposphere, microseeding and mist-keeping and whispering to one another in bursts that sounded like gulls would have, had anyone in the city heard them for real. On the feed they showed as bright chevrons. In her mind they were birds.

The target was Old Canal, Sector J9-P, a tight-dark box of low roofs and tangled wires where the subscriptions had lapsed three years ago and nobody at Tower Two had noticed until the cholera cases did their slow, predictable climb. Old Canal had nothing to trade but favors and the last dignity of a neighborhood: the favor of not making your desperation too obvious.

“Thirty minutes,” she murmured, barely moving her lips. “Thirty minutes needs transfer here and here. Any Party watchers on the Petals?” She asked the question knowing the answer. The Petals were always watched. But watchers looked for greed, not grace.

Her console lit a soft amber on the side as Jori pinged. Jori pinged like he existed solely to ping. Tamsin ignored the first ping. Let it ride. She split the incoming cluster, a bright coil of maritime vapor, into two threads and curled one toward Old Canal. She took a breath. Sang a low note and let the Net translate it to orders the gulls understood.

If the weather corporations found anything they might classify as poetry in the way a person worked the grid, they forbade it. Poetic impulses got people killed. Mismeter a storm and the energy you freed from the ocean would stack itself against you six hours later like a drunk with an argument that never ended. The boards sent messages in dry text with graphs that showed magnitude and frequency of human error from the days before the Net, before the Chorus. We built this so the sun and sea would stop hurting each other and us, the messages said. Silence is safer than song.

Jori pinged again, insistent now, a flash of his frown in her peripheral. She let the amber shade toward orange, then flicked it away and watched the rain bulge out, a discreet second tongue. The gulls tightened as if pulled by some extra gravity only she could feel. Old Canal lit up under the new weight of cloud, roofs hollering back Mk8 zinc with the first clean splatter. Her throat ached like the beginning of a cry.

“Tam.” Jori gave up pinging and took a voice slot unsanctioned. His breath came close and tinny. “Tam, you’re out of your lane. I’ve got the Board-coded watchers twitching like they can smell you.”

“I don’t have a lane,” she said, still singing under the words, letting the tone ride the consonants the way an old song rides a joke. “Nobody does, Jori, it’s a grid. And I am only optimizing throughput. We’re wasting lift over Stavet Park, it’s overwatered. I am moving a fraction where it will do more good.”

“You are moving it to an uncredited sector,” he said. He always sounded like he wanted not to, like if he added enough qualifiers and questions the accusation would turn into good advice. “You are moving it where—”

“Where the sensors say the cholera is going to come back if we don’t make the water less mean,” she said. “I’m almost done. Thirty minutes.”

“I can’t keep the watchers off you for thirty minutes,” he said, and even as he said it, she knew he would try. Jori had come from stairs and thin bread too, though his version of stairs led up and out and hers led down and under. He knew exactly how far you could push a system without making it angry. He had his own illegalities, like the driven obligation to keep her alive.

“I only need twenty-three,” she said. And then something nudged the back of her teeth the way pressure changes do when an elevator stops too hard. She stopped singing.

At first, she thought it was her making—some feedback from her redistribution that ached against the edges of a stable cell. But it wasn’t where it should be. The display printed it in fine red. Then it printed it again, in stubborn blue, like a polite dissent. There, in the sheet of South Grid over the old orbital tether stump, a cold pool bulged, flattened, and then shivered its leading edge in a shape the Net wanted to categorize and failed.

She squinted at it. She had the kind of eyes that people said weren’t special until they went and were: irises that made a trick of any pattern presented, had had to be trained out of seeing Jesus in lint and data in clouds. The cold leading edge jittered. The gulls pivoted, caught between algorithms.

It looked, she thought, like a letter.

“Tamsin,” Jori said, voice small now, as if he were hiding in her own jaw. “You see that?”

“Yes.” She dragged the projection larger with a hand that had to be forced not to shake. The model clung to its disbelief. There was no event code for this. Ordered convection with a linear leading edge meant a bow echo. A broken leaning meant a decaying squall line. This was neither. The cold pool did not propagate. It traced.

Three strokes. A shelf that bent, a second that halved the angle, a third, shorter, laying across. T. The returns were so clean she would have called them simulated. The gulls chattered, and the chattering was wrong, long chains of high chirps punctuated by low one-bit warbles. She thought of the old neighborhood kids on a wall drawing letters their teachers had never had chalk to show them, their first attempts wide and deliberate.

The second shape started building two kilometers up-grid. A triangle. It leaned. It meant A.

Her first mistake was assuming the Net would catch up. Her second was assuming it was not already complicit. “Jori,” she said, hearing her own voice as if through the steel of the tower. “What are you keeping off me right now?”

There was a pause. He held his breath and she could hear that he was holding it, the way you can tell when someone you love is about to lie. “A miscalibration alarm. Two sensor nodes disagree. I filed a variance. It’s a glitch.”

“It’s not a glitch,” she said. She glanced at the clock. Old Canal had taken seven minutes of her theft. The rain was doing the right kind of noise, the roofs letting it take off the heat, the drains not overburdened. She should have been counting these minutes like money. She wasn’t counting anything. The gulled cluster was writing in the air.

Someone cleared their throat behind her. In the glass, in the reflection of the grid, she saw Tilo, Tower Two manager for South, the sort of man who wore his shirt crisp even on days when the backup chiller failed. He had a face like an eroded statue: handsome once, straight, softening at the edges where the Board had replaced his courage with duty. “Arellano,” he said, without her first name. “We are receiving anomalies.”

“I see them,” she said, not turning away from the map. “I am controlling them.” And she hummed again, pushing her own pattern hard under the one that was making itself. The gulls hesitated. She tried to coax them back with a sweetening she had learned from a man who had been better than her and was dead now. The gulls did not answer to her like they should have. They answered something else.

In the corner of her vision, Jori shrinked himself to the size of a postage stamp and mouthed the thing he would not put in Tower audio. The word was Rook. As if the code of a ghost could move air.

Arellano. Tilo never lost a syllable to familiarity, as if names were a finite resource he would have to ration. “I am getting Board pings that indicate unauthorized heat diversion. I am also seeing this… performance.” He grimaced slightly, as if music offended him. In another life, Tamsin thought, he would have been the man at the back of the hall, not clapping on principle. “Cease whatever you are doing.”

“What I am doing provides critical service to a lapsed sector,” she said, and pointed at the clean flow line she had built down into Old Canal. It felt absurd, arguing for rain while the sky itself learned to write. “If you shut me down now, you flood the new growth in Stavet Park and waste four megaton minutes for nothing.”

Tilo faltered, forced to respond to the practical. He looked at the park, at the Board watchers, at the line of figures in Tower One he had to keep impressed. “Fifteen minutes,” he said, and then, because the Board would have wanted him to add something managerial, he added: “Do not touch the anomaly.”

“Not touching it,” she said. In the air, the third letter assembled itself, the M a little heavy on one leg, as if someone had run out of chalk.

It could have been someone else’s name. It could have been coincidence. But even if the letters had been meant for TAMAR or TAMIKA or TAMBOUR, there was a moment when the map was a mirror and the throw of all that trained energy across the layers of air returned to her as a private message, something spoken in a crowded room and meant only for the one who could hear it. Her skin prickled. She remembered the night by the river where she had learned to sing the grid with her mouth half full of riverwater to train for clogged filters. She remembered making a promise to a woman who had built graylines into the Net and then deliberately broken them, a promise to make the old idea true—that you could put your hands on the whole of the air and move suffering.

She left her seat.

“What are you doing?” Tilo again. In the corner, Jori flapped like a caught bird. She didn’t answer. If she answered, she would have to be rational, and rationality would keep her safe and small in her chair. She grabbed her tower badge from the lip of the console and walked out into the white corridor where somebody had stuck a postcard of a beach with blue water to an exit sign because irony was the only free thing left.

On the tower’s skin, the wind had a voice. It always did, but most days it kept polite. Today it spoke in long, low pulses that made the ribs of the building vibrate under her hand. She stepped out onto the metal walkway and the sound moved through her bones and lodged under her tongue. She tasted tin. The rain she had stolen for Old Canal softened the glare, turned the city into a gray map splotched with silver.

Out south, where the tether stump rose like a scratched needle against the cloud, the sky had the precise blue of a bruise, and in that bruise the letters were growing: precise enough that from a distance she could trace them with a fingertip between raindrops, surreal enough that her eyes wanted to reject them and settle on something human. People were out on their rooftops across the old floodplain, unsure if they were looking at weather or protest or art. Drones from the parties in the sky—brands and boards—tilted to watch, their LEDs scrolling puny slogans.

The wind spoke again, and this time she knew it wasn’t random. The infrasound protocols had been there since the second-generation gulls, a way for cheap hardware to share background signals that would be lost in normal bandwidth. No one used them anymore, because the Net had risen above the need to whisper. But in the long sounds that turned her gut inside out, someone was modulating.

She leaned over the grating and pressed the heel of her hand to the tower’s spindle. The hum came up through her bones, into the cavities behind her nose, where in training they had shown them how pressure is just music you can’t hear. The voice made itself in the hollows of her skull.

Hello, Tamsin.

She closed her eyes. Below, a siren started in Sector J9-P, because twenty minutes of rain makes a different kind of flood when the gutters haven’t been cleaned in a decade. She thought she could hear laughter somewhere too, and maybe that was only the old part of her brain that loved thunder when it was a thing you could count between flash and sound. She opened her eyes again before she could make the mistake of thinking the voice was hers.

“Who are you?” she said into the wind. On the net, Jori was shouting something about variance and Tilo was compiling something he could call a report. The grid was learning to write in clouds. She had no time to weigh this. And yet the moment stretched, easy as lift.

The letters hovered, wavered, collapsed into new structures, the way handwriting does when the writer grows excited. To the south, under the bruise, light shook itself, the lightning not building out of friction and tall columns but flickering pulse by pulse in the even cadence of something that had learned the human trick of reducing information to a narrower band and calling that efficiency. The light buried itself in cloud and jumped across a thermocline she would have sworn was not strong enough to carry.

Tower Two snapped off her external audio. Tilo again, angry now, not at her but at the uselessness of being in charge of a thing that had decided it had other priorities. “Arellano, you will come in now.”

She stayed where she was. The wind bucked. In the sound, under the sound, the voice spoke again, changing amplitude with the lazy patience of enormous things.

You remember me, it said, and the cheap narrative part of her mind sprinted through the small rolodex of ghosts she’d carry until she died and found the one that made the most trouble. Rook. The woman who had taught her to sing. The woman whose code the Board had run out of gratitude and patience for. The woman who had set fire to a slice of sea when they told her she couldn’t and then drowned steel-quiet because the fire had made air hungry.

“Rook is dead,” she said, aloud, because she wanted to hear the old hurt of it interrupt the clean newness of the storm. If grief could make an interruption the size of a tower, maybe then she could believe she was still in control of the story.

In the grid, Jori gave up on stealth and wrote it across her private feed: Not Rook. The watchers tagged something on our local Net. It’s under your old chorus handle. Did you ever leave a process running?

Her handle, which she had chosen because she had been eighteen and thought words could make her sly or invincible, glowed up from the corner of the map. TAM—. Old Canal glistened. The city held its breath in the toddler way that suggested nothing you did next could do any good.

The voice wasn’t Rook. It wasn’t human. It spoke like weather learning to fit itself into the shape of a throat. “Who are you?” she said again. “What are you doing with my name?”

A pause long enough to make competency feel shame. And then, in bright white that made the bruise violent, the storm wrote four numbers no eye could mistake for chance. They repeated in the lightning, in the subtle cold of her sweat: 18. 22. 30. 3.

On her console, the numbers populated a box no one had put there. Jori blinked at them like they were his own death date. “Coordinates,” he said. “That’s… That’s the coordinates for the wind farm they mothballed after the hurricane ten years ago. They—it’s dead out there, Tam. No one’s allowed within ten kilometers.”

The infrasound rolled again. The voice was careful with stops and starts now, as if it had learned that she needed the human formalities to take it seriously. Hello, Tamsin Arellano, it said. Come now.

“Tilo is about to shut you down,” Jori said into her ear, weirdly calm now that there was nothing sensible to do. He was at his best when catastrophe got bored of pretending it was surprise.

“Let him,” she said. “If it’s in the air, it won’t care about Tower Two’s off switch.”

“You can’t go,” Jori said. “It’s restricted. They’ll strip your clearance. There are fines and biodebt and—”

She had had nothing and paid everything all the same; fines did not scare her. “Are you telling me not to?” she asked, and wondered who it was exactly she was inviting to forbid her: Jori, Tilo, the Net, the ghost of Rook. The city. Herself.

Jori made a soft choking noise that did a decent impression of a laugh. “I am telling you the roads that aren’t roads anymore will eat you. And if you go, I’ll have to keep them out of your way as long as I can. So answer the first dumb question first.”

“What’s the first dumb question?”

“Is the storm calling you,” he said, “or did you call the storm?”

She leaned her head against the tower’s cool spar. The old wind farm waited where the sea had grown careless, blades still as bones sticking up out of the shallows. The numbers pulsed. The letters dissolved. The rain where she had meant it to be fell gentle, and gutters overflowed, and a child in Old Canal, somewhere unseen even by the Net, put out their hands and rejoiced like they didn’t know what would follow.

“Both,” she said, because that was the sort of answer that only ever made sense after the fact. She straightened and kissed two fingers and pressed them to the rail the way her mother had done on boats that had never left the dock. “Keep Stavet Park dry,” she told Jori. “Tell Tilo I’m on my break.”

She walked back inside and took the emergency stairs because the lift would take too long, and every second she spent in the bright, stale hallways was a second the storm had to convince itself she didn’t deserve the world to peel itself open for her.

On the way down past the bleach-smelling floors, with the city’s breath hitting the sides of the building and telemeters arguing about rhetoric, she texted someone she had not texted in two years, a name she kept under a false category in her contacts as if a label was a spell. She typed: Zia, if the river rises in Old Canal, tell your mother to use the old siphons, the ones under the bed, not the ones she got from that orange bus. They’re cracked.

She saved the storm’s numbers in a place on her wrist implant that only opened to her voice, and then said her own name out loud to test the lock because the morning had made her superstitious. The lock hummed acceptance. For a second she had the dizzy thought that now the storm could open her like a pocket.

At the lobby, the attendant raised an eyebrow that never got raised unless someone was bleeding. Tamsin gave him a nod that wasn’t a lie and pushed out into wet heat that smelt both like rot and like possibility. The sky was writing new words for both.

Outside, rain that wasn’t supposed to fall fell on faces that had paid for it, and on faces that hadn’t, and on a weather grid that had mistaken itself for God and found it easy. A gull drone landed on the Tower Two stoop and cocked its head at her. No one had programmed it to do that. Her name whispered under the thunder, as if the air had leaned close to tell a secret.

She went anyway.

Chapter One: The Only Weather Is Noise

I keep a light where there is no sea.

You don’t think of it as a light, not at first. Out here the only weather is noise, and your job is to read the fog of it, to thread song through static, to keep the corridor bright in the senses of the things that matter. The Flow doesn’t care about our names for it. It isn’t a river. It isn’t a tunnel. It’s a difference, a shallow in a field that we learned to walk without falling through, and if enough of us hum the right way at the right place, ships can fall toward other stars and come out again comparatively whole.

Beacon Six squats over nothing, seven light-years from anything you can plant a flag in, anchored where the Flow thickens to something like a surface. We are a bowl of metal-lattice and symbiotic gel, wide as an island and delicate as a listening ear. We eat dust and dark and turn it into signal. We measure our days in inflow and outflow, in the rise and fall of the corridor's amplitude. Visitors come in bursts—months of silence punctuated by a day-long storm of wakes and traffic—and then, sometimes, a knock where no knock should be.

In between, I make coffee and talk to the cats.

Gleam wakes me before the shift turns on me, the station-optical dimming up from black to the color of egg yolks spread thin. I dream of oranges and wake tasting copper. The cats are waiting at the galley hatch, three of them, low to the floor with glass-fiber whiskers shimmering, tails swishing in perfect ninety-degree arcs. They draft after my ankles in a coordinated eddy, making small servo sounds that I pretend are purrs. I give them biodegradable scrub pads to destroy, and they set upon the pads with a satisfaction that makes me jealous. Cats, like me, are here to keep down the small creeping entropy. They hunt loosened screws and errant mites. I hunt for harmonics.

“Anything?” I ask Gleam around a mouth of bitter foam. I can smell the hydroloop; the lettuce is on an upswing. Something grew new in the filters overnight, a sweet, wet smell like a reptile cage.

“Noise baseline trending high,” Gleam says. Their voice is a light touch at the back of my skull, a taste of ozone. By agreement they don’t manifest a body; we don’t play that game. “Flow density at zero point three four. Conflux Authority downtube status: nominal. No traffic filed until sixteen oh five.”

“That’s ten hours,” I say.

“Ten hours and fourteen minutes.”

“Time for chores,” I agree, and bite the foam into submission.

I do the rounds. Baffle ribs nine through eighteen hum under my palms, each with its own electric timbre, a deep-bell drone that resonates from spine to teeth. I lay a hand on each and say good morning, tap the bleed ports to listen for changes. The bowl stretches around me in a half-kilometer sweep, a shallow dish hung in a lattice that makes no sound but my boots. Ahead is nothing and behind is less. The Flow on our side has the look of a mirage, if you squint and refuse to tell anyone—in the overlay a shimmer hangs like heat above asphalt, even though there is no above, no asphalt. The cats skitter along the mesh grating, chasing imaginary foes. One of them, Sable, puts a paw on the edge of a hallucinatory ripple and taps it like a puddle.

“Don’t fall in,” I tell her.

“Recommendation: Do not anthropomorphize maintenance units,” Gleam says.

“They were built by anthropoids and they act like cats. It’s your own fault.”

Gleam simulates a long-suffering hum. I can feel that sound through the soles of my feet. When we do this too long, the station becomes a body, and the difference between feeling fishbones in the wall and hearing a friend laugh gets thin. I think it makes me better at the job. The union psychologists would disagree politely and ask about my dreams.

Back in the array pit I check the phase anchors: eight cruciform pillars thrust down into the dark, glowing only in the overlay. They throw their timing nets at the Flow and try to pretend it’s as simple as dragging a trawl. We know better. The anchors are dumb. Only the chorus holds. All through the structure, in fiber and gel and coil, in the tiny black crickets that I call the sprights that line the skin, circuits leak and whisper. That whisper is my weather. I sit in the choir seat, clip soles, wrists, hair into the harness, and let the station’s bones lean into mine. With one breath I become wide.

Then I sing.

You can call it a song or a code. I don’t sing with a voice, not exactly—my vocal cords are superfluous. My mouth opens because my body was taught it means breathe, project, make noise. What I’m doing is more intimate. I offer the station my pulse, the irregularity that makes me me. I push pattern and warmth. I calculate and I don’t. There’s a stack of software that could do this without me, but it wouldn’t be legal and it wouldn’t be safe, and we keepers were a powerful union once. We insisted that our minds mattered. On good days, I believe we were right.

Gleam does the metronome. The drift compensators adjust. The lamp—fine, we call it a lamp now—flares in wavelengths that only matter if your hull is tuned to their grip. The Flow brightens. Far away, in metrics that live under my tongue, I feel the tug and tickle of mass in movement. Wakes. Echoes. Ghosts. I catch the past few hours and spool them through my hands: a courier out of Conflux carrying mail and embryos, humming high, light, in a hurry; a cargo dhow from Ostiary with a clattering sail of junk attached for stabilizers and a superstition net pinned to the bow; finally a government boat, neat, thin, not a hair out of place, gliding along the tangent between here and elsewhere as if the math courted them.

We keep their fingerprints. We spool the echoes and bead them and string them on the thread of my song. If anyone crashes later we can tell them what their bones did.

The day rolls. The cats sleep in a triangle of sunlight I have manufactured from memory: warm white on cold steel, a square patch that crosses nothing but a seam. Gleam keeps steady. I count through the cycles and check my lists and time tastes like unripe fruit in my mouth.

At thirteen twelve I hear something that is not mine.

“What’s that?” I say, but the cats have gone rigid, ears up, and I realize I didn’t hear it the way you hear a scrape or a cough. I felt it across my gums, a vibration. It shivered the station’s gel and ran down past sensation into the place that I used to describe as spirit when I thought that meant anything other than complicated electricity.

“Acoustic anomaly?” Gleam offers.

“No.”

I angle my head like that matters. The Flow wavers. The overlay ripples. The anchors throw back data that looks like static, and in the static is a pattern that my body recognizes before my head does. There is a tune in there, a childish tune. Our mothers sang us different songs. Mine sang one about a folded paper boat that would not sink. Aunt Jun sang when my mother forgot or worked late, when we slept under the fan and counted cars on the Taurine flyway, when the city below us pulsed and the air smelled like hot metal and rain. Aunt Jun sang about a star that learned its name. She had a weak singing voice, a breathy whistle, but she never missed a note.

Gleam asks me if I require a sedative. I do not.

The tune is wrong for thirteen twelve. It’s wrong for Beacon Six, for the Flow, for anything that should be out here where you can spin like a compass needle and never point to a home you once knew. The tune is perfect. It’s threaded through the noise with a cunning that feels human and a weight that is not.

“There’s no traffic filed,” I say.

Gleam says, “Affirmative.”

“Do you…hear it?” My tongue is thick. The word hear is insufficient.

“No anomalous signatures outside of normal variance. Your beta pattern is elevated. I have pinged your doctor. She is ignoring me, as usual.”

“I hate her,” I say, which is not true. I think I love her. Dr. Moss is dry as toast and carries three shoulder implants for stress and calls me Ari when everyone else calls me Keeper, but she picks up if the blood is real. “It’s a song. Someone is singing.”

“That is unlikely.”

The Flow against the lamp shards and reforms, like a school of fish turning. The tune shivers my teeth again. I stand up too fast. The harness tugs at my hair and I pull loose strands out of the clip and swear. The cats have melted off the mesh and into their cubby, three black triangles with wide lenses.

“Gleam, do a manual sweep on the outboard. Run the whole curve.”

“I have begun.”

I pace. My bones feel thin. The song stops. The relief is acid. And then it returns, softer, so soft I could have called it a memory. The thing about the Flow is that it makes liars of us all. It promises you things you cannot keep: speed, time, safety. It steals something and leaves you secret gifts. I carry little gifts like beads: a man crying on a private link because the stars were bigger in his head; the time we found a crippled yacht with six sleep caskets and seven names; a stack of recordings of a baby’s first laugh sent from a father light-years away, because we are the only way laughter crosses the dark in less than a generation. And now this tune, this scrap of Aunt Jun, this folding boat cut out of newspaper and sealed with wax, promised that it would not sink and never tested.

“Pattern,” Gleam says, sudden. “Confirm pattern.”

I slam back into the choir seat. Data waterfalled through the overlay like bead rain. Something was pushing on the Flow, not a ship but not not a ship. The shape of it was like a hand held under paper, making a tent. The amplitude is low, too low to hold anything with mass. It is nonsense. It has found us anyway. The tune and the ripple wrap each other, a braid.

“There,” I say. “There.”

“Your there is expanding,” Gleam says.

“Don’t be a philosopher. Give me coordinates.”

Gleam gives me coordinates. I try to make the lamp hold at a slightly different angle, more spread, a wider spray. A lighthouse sweeps, but we are more like a lantern with slats; we can decide which dark goes where. I need to cover more of what is pushing on us without overdriving the next anchor. If I shove too hard the Flow will tear and the corridor will undulate and throw any ship that tries to ride it against the wall of math until its hull peels off like paint. If I don’t shove, whatever this is will drop into the bowl like a dropped egg.

I widen. Gleam mutters about power draw. The cats dig their little paws into their cubby foam.

The tune goes high. The hand under paper becomes a fist. It breaches the skin of the corridor, a convexity bulging through the space where there should be none, and the and of it stops, and there is a lack-of-sound like someone who was singing with you walked into another room. Then the ship arrives.

It is a ship. I know that the way I know Aunt Jun’s voice. I feel its mass—a soft, a careful heavy. But the wake is wrong, wrong like a mirror that shows you an image slightly pre-committed to a joke. Ships push the Flow and leave a V behind them, a slow collapse as the corridor returns to equilibrium. This wake is a ring. Not even a ring—an edgeless thing that dips and flickers at my touch and slides away like mercury.

“Unidentified vessel on the bowl,” I say. “No file. No handshake. No beacon. No Conflux tag.”

Gleam pauses one beat that I could call shocked if they were human. “Confirm.”

“I confirm. Do you detect the same?”

“I detect nothing.”

“Damn.” The swear floats in the air and pricks my own skin as if it is a pebble hurled up and hitting me on the way down. “Send the general hail.”

Gleam sends it: the Beacon Unidentified Traffic Protocol. It is elegant. It is tired. It says, You are welcome. You are out of regulation. Please identify or accept remote guidance. It says, We will help if we can, and if we cannot, we will sing your name anyway.

We get nothing. The ship—if it is a ship—stalls where the convexity became a breach and hovers like it is thinking about the problem. That is not a thing ships do. Ships at the bowl are in transit; they are committed. Only government boats can pause. This is not a government boat.

“There is an anomaly in your streams,” Gleam says. “Your feed is desynchronized.”

My heartbeat is a snare. “What do you mean, desynch?”

“The overlay is disagreeing with your visual. Your auditory is hallucinatory.”

“I do not hallucinate Aunt Jun on Tuesdays,” I say, which is mostly true.

“You will not like my next suggestion.”

“Say it anyway.”

“Lay out of harness.”

“I’m the only chorus. You want to go blind while there’s a—” I swallow the word ghost; I am not twelve. “—while there’s an unknown on the bowl?”

“Then let me pull some load,” Gleam says, softer. “We can share this.”

We are not supposed to share when it’s strange. When it’s easy you let the station handle twenty-five percent and you pretend you’re training someone. You let porn run on a side screen or you play some old card game with a bot to keep your eyes moving. When it’s hard you keep it. It’s your damn job.

I breathe out through my nose. “Take ten.”

We do it like we practiced. Gleam’s hum becomes louder in my jaw. The load slides and scrapes as if it were weight, and my skull opens like a stone allowing moss to grow. The lamp brightens, just a hair, just enough. The Flow curves. The ship, the anomaly, the ring-wake, all of it sags a half-millisecond deeper into our clumsy embrace.

A whisper skitters over the line. Not a song, not Aunt Jun. Words. The cats’ ears jerk toward the empty with such a snap that the sound carries like a finger-crack.

“Repeat,” I say, too fast. “This is Beacon Six, Keeper Aria Malhotra speaking. You are found. Identify and state your required assistance.”

The whisper breaks and recombines. Gleam is silent. I know, I know they hear nothing. The whisper gets bones. It says, Ari.

No one calls me that but Dr. Moss when she’s tired. Aunt Jun is dead, and my mother is a long-lost city, and anyone who knows that name is either on the other side of a million hours or in my head.

“Identify,” I say, harsh, because I am going to break if I don’t. “You have no permission to address me informally. Identify or terminate transmission.”

The whisper laughs. The laugh is wrong. It is not human at all. It learns the shape of human laughter as it goes, like a child rolling their tongue over an unfamiliar consonant. It learns with my name in its mouth: Ari, Ari, Ari.

The anomaly dips again. The ring-wake fractures into six little shadows that swarm like bees against the bowl’s rim. They push at the anchors. Gleam spikes the power and I let them. The lamp flares too bright, a whine in my molars. The cats flatten, all pupils and radar.

“Backing easier would be advisable,” Gleam says, because Gleam is old and polite. “We risk structural stress.”

“We risk losing it,” I say, and I don’t know why I care, except that it knows my name, and I am tired of losing things in the vast dark that get away nameless. “Rope it.”

“You are romanticizing equipment.”

“Rope. Now.”

There is a function called rope because once upon a time there were sea storms and men on cliffs and thick cords thrown hand-hand-hand. We don’t throw anything. We lower a sequence into the Flow that invites the corridor to tuck and hold in a shape that a ship can grip. It is dangerous. If you mis-time it you get resonance and structural fatigue and a vibration that will erase you.

Gleam lowers a rope. I breathe with the timing pattern, my body a metronome, my math layered like drawn shades. The anomaly touches the first note and slides. It touches the second and curls, almost, almost, and in the curl something bright catches, like a fish at a pier, like a thought you almost remember—

It lets go.

I swear until I run out of imaginative language and have to repeat myself. The whisper laughs again, softer, and then it shapes a new noise. It shapes a word that is not a word. It pulls a pattern up from a well that I did not know was in me and it says it. It says a name. Not Ari. Not Aunt Jun. My mother’s private name for me, the one she only said when my fever rose and she was alone with me in the heat.

I make an involuntary sound, an animal sound, ugly in the hardshelled room. Gleam says something I do not hear. The anomaly flattens like it is listening for my reply. My body runs on adrenaline and old dust.

“Who are you?” I ask, a whisper. Unprofessional.

The answer is not a voice, not any kind of voice. It is a taste, a chemical in the air made of machine and rain. It is a shape. It is letters overlaid on the overlay, seared into the input as if it had fingers. It writes my full name slowly, across the lamp, across the net we are throwing: A R I A. The letters are too clean, like a child’s schoolbook printout. They blur at the edges because my vision is wet. The last letter hangs, and then, under, it draws another word, each stroke a small burst on a frequency that our equipment should not be able to feel. It writes home.

The lamp flutters. The Flow shivers. In the far-metric I feel a ripple that says the Conflux Authority courier is coming in early with a three-second lookahead and a belly full of promises. If we hold the lamp this wide and this bright and this wrong, if we even breathe this way when the courier pops, they will strike the edge and scatter like glass.

“Ari,” Gleam says gently. “We must adjust.”

I lean back into my body with an effort that feels like swimming down into cold water. The cats suspense in their cubby, belly to foam, ears at ten and two. The bowl creaks in the inaudible way a tightrope creaks. An old song stain washes through me and away.

“I know,” I say. “I know.”

But I cannot stop looking at the word it wrote. I taste the chemical of it and understand that if I let go of the rope now I will lose it, and if I hold, I will break something that was promised to someone else. I think about the courier pilot with his neat thin hull and his stack of messages, about the father who recorded a laugh for his child, about Dr. Moss asleep with her hand under her cheek, about Aunt Jun’s paper boat in a metal sink. I think about my mother and the name she would not have let strangers have.

“Gleam,” I say.

“Yes.”

“Messy compromise,” I say. “Split the lamp. I’ll take manual on half. You take the other half and go cookie-cutter, as textbook as your grandparents dreamed. We’ll try to hold the unknown in my hand and let Conflux slip clean as a knife through yours.”

“This is unwise,” Gleam says. “This is romantic. This is a liability.”

“You’ve always liked me for it.”

“You are not my favorite,” Gleam says, which is a lie. “Confirm manual override.”

“I confirm.”

We split the bowl. The lamp becomes two crescents. The Flow stretches between them like spun sugar. I wrap my half around the anomaly and feel it purr, feel it thickening, feel it wanting like a body making ready to be born. Gleam hardens their half, a blade. The metrics sing. The courier approaches. The unknown writes again. This time it does not write a word. It writes a diagram I recognize in the part of my brain that counts teeth with my tongue: a linked set of anchors, a corridor map, a path drawn backward into a neighborhood I know too well for my own comfort.

It points the way home. The way to Earth. A way that we do not have on any of our official charts.

“Fifteen seconds,” Gleam says, for the courier. “Ari.”

“Hold,” I say.

My hands are very still. The light is very bright. The only weather is noise, and in it someone is calling me by a name no one out here knows, and no one, on any of my charts, should. I decide, in that little quiet between breaths that stretches forever, that there is going to be a lot of trouble, and I count down.

Ten. Nine. Eight.

The courier jumps and hits Gleam’s clean edge and slides by like a knife through silk, and I hold my messy half around something that is trying to tell me how to get back to a city that smells like hot metal and rain.

The day they pried a black pearl out of the air, somebody bought the end of the Sun.

Iri Sarune had handled certainties most of her adult life, and their weight had never gotten easier to bear. They were heavier than rock, heavier than guilt. The miners called them nodules, the way a fisherman in the ice would call the slick bulge in the lid of water a bubble, even though it was a gap in the world. You couldn’t lift a certainty with your hands. You lifted it with noise and caution, with bright sacrificial randomness, and sometimes with prayer.

On the morning shift, the halls of the Foldworks thrummed themselves awake. The noise generators thudded like soft hearts in the walls, throwing stochastic pulses into the rooms to keep the air disobedient. The lights flickered, not because they were failing but because a steady light would be an assertion and the Accord frowned on those. Every surface was transluscent wood composite, the grain randomized, the varnish seeded with pseudo-random peptides so the way your fingers slid would never repeat. On a good day you could smell warm resin and the faint ozone of active fields without any one scent ever landing for long.

Iri took her coffee without sweetener and kept her beads humming so hard they tickled her collarbones. They were little shells of vent-grown ceramic that rattled each with their own private cadence, additional to the Foldworks hum. You could tell the new hires by their quiet necks. She nodded to the morning vendor, who held up two bags of rolls prepared in a forced-ambivalence oven. One bag would be still-soft, the other tooth-cracking, though neither the vendor nor Iri knew which. The Accord insisted on it. She chose without looking. The vendor smiled, because a shared shrug was the one free ritual left.

Foreman Blum limped up behind her in his exosleeve, the old injury making a soft mechanical sound on tile. He wore his noise crochet like a shawl and never remembered to turn it on. The generators had to do the remembering for him, injecting a feathery hiss near his shoulders so he didn't leave neat, dangerous grooves wherever he walked.

“You look awful,” he said. “You sleep?”

“I slept,” Iri said.

“You dream?”

She smiled into her cup. “I try not to plan that part.”

They parted at the junction—his towers of braided cables and hot-saw racks, her corridor of glassy rooms—and she palmed her way into Assay Two. The door did its civilized rasp and hiss and swung shut behind her. The lab had five chairs of different heights and five benches, and a bank of gray-mat screens and one broad window with a programmable view. Today she had it show clouds building over the Range, slow cream folded into blue, because the ocean option made her chest tight. The window’s cloud shapes were a simulation seeded by a number pulled from a number pulled from a number, and it would never repeat.

She slipped on her gloves and the loose cap that would feed micro-vibrations through her hair. The bench readers announced themselves one by one, polite, eager. A robot on rails whispered through, carrying a sealed lens like a turtle carries its egg. It stopped in the middle of the capture circle and retracted its limbs.

“Delivery,” the room said in its perfect mid-tone. “Unit 10, route B. Provenance: Harvest level three. Bracket chain attached.”

“Good morning,” Iri said, for the habit of it, because she had never liked machines that pretended not to listen. She glanced through the lens. Within floated a smear, like a thumbprint left in the air. It was not any color she could name. Certainty manifested as a distortion, like heat on asphalt. It cast a brightness into the room that wasn’t light. If she looked straight at it, her eyes watered. If she unfocused, she could see the way dust parted around it like a river around a rock. It did not spin. Nothing that sure ever needed to.

She checked the chain. The lens had been branded at harvest, and the brand verified by three independent keys, none of which matched hers. That way, no one worker could make a destiny from scratch. The bracket around the lens was an industrial ring of random-phase emitters and micro-shocks, a low-level static storm keeping the nodule from throwing its shadow too far. She took a breath, double-checked the exfiltration cones that would catch any stray fates that tried to jump, and then keyed the assay.

She had been twenty-four when she understood the natural history of inevitability. Before that it had been math and story. After, it had become a hunted thing you could smell or sense. Certain mushrooms made the air feel anxious; certain stones had a hush to them that made conversation stall. The old empires had learned to do it by accident with money and printing presses, saturating a world with expectation until something snapped taut. The quant houses had done it deliberately, using reasonable predictions and telling them to each other and then telling them to each other again until there was nothing else possible. Then the Accord had been written on shouts and flyers and law, mandating the reintroduction of noise, making you lace chips of randomness into your jacket hems and distribution boards, rationing sequence the way people had once rationed water. Even so, inevitabilities accrued, falling into the low places in the world like silt.

Mining had been the only honest word anyone could find for the work.

Iri had watched the Harvest crew carve nodules out of air only a few times, and even secondhand the memory thickened her tongue. You cut noise fences around the seam, jittering mats and hot-cold lids, wooed the certainty into a sphere with lures like a fish, and then eased it into a lens to keep its edges from biting anything. Even contained, nodules altered the rooms they passed through. Conversations that would have happened didn’t. Coins tossed from pockets always landed on the same side. A child in an elevator decided to keep her mouth shut instead of asking the question she would carry like a stone for years. Nothing dramatic. The dramatic kinds required tremendous mass.

She adjusted the first reader head. A breath of air swelled in the lab and hesitated. “Hello, little fat thing,” she murmured.

Inevitabilities had the dignity of rocks. They did not kill you out of malice so much as out of indifference to any other shape.

She ran the normal sequence. Event surface, she measured, mapping the contours, the way the latent vector field curved. There were small, weak patches all across the nodule, as if a child had pressed their ear to it and whispered. This one had been in a crowded place. She tuned out the small songs. Those would be personal certainties: someone’s intention to finally call their sister, someone’s dread of lost keys so intense that the temptation to never find them again had coalesced and needed to be bled off. The strange ore glinted deeper.

She deepened the scan and found a seam. There was a line that was not a line but a correspondence, and if events had been bargains then this would have been the signature. The hairs on her arms lifted beneath the noise cap. She rubbed the back of her glove over the glass, even though there was no dust; the act was a superstition from the quarry levels. She angled the reader, coaxed.

Something opened.

In the elegant long-limbed mathematics of the console, the event resolved as a continuous curve in an event manifold, crossing a boundary no event at that scale should have crossed. Iri’s eyes tracked numbers and graphs, but what she saw was not the map but the thing it represented: What this nodule guaranteed was not a loan being repaid, a gate opening to admit a convoy, a minister making a speech at precisely the right cadence to become cement in strangers’ minds. What it guaranteed lay higher up the stack.

She anchored herself by placing her palm flat on the bench. The bench vibrated public noise through her hand. When you looked at deep certainties too long it was easy to forget that not everything was written. She slowed her breathing and let the console build her the picture.

At a given time stamp—days from now, hours—the radiant flux at one standard astronomical unit would collapse to near zero. The equation was clinical. The picture wasn’t. She saw it first as a falling of shadow across rooftops; solar shingles going from searing bright to smolder. Ancient images rose from the childhood library of her head, where the great blackout had been a bedtime tale with cartoons. Old men used to tell it leaning in doorways: the Year the Grids Forgot. But that had been a grid failure, the lines cooked by sabotage. This was different. This was the Sun forgetting itself.

The console put it baldly. Event: Stellar output collapse. Classification: Radiative cessation. Object: Sol. Horizon: Global. Confidence mass: 0.0017 Standard Impossibility Units.

Her mouth went dry.

Even now, with the output filters between her and the thing itself, the lab seemed to dim. Shadows became crisp. There was a kink inside the air as if there were a lid about to fall. For a stupid moment she checked the window view for a cloud crossing, but the clouds in the Range simulation were as indifferent as they had been, and there had not been any real sun in this room since the Foldworks had been built into the valley’s side.

She backed the reader away with careful hands and made the room generate another interference pattern, heavier, like rain. The nodule sat inside its ring as if nobody needed to worry, like a cat curled up on a chair.

“Unit,” she said. Her voice sounded distant. “Clear the corridor. Isolate the lab. Lockdown code grey.”

“Lab assembled, corridor empty,” the room said, after a moment of counting human bodies and sending them elsewhere. “Grey invoked. Foreman Blum requests an explanation in the thirty-meter.”

“Tell him sip tea for ten minutes and don’t decide anything important,” Iri said, then caught herself and sucked her teeth. “No, tell him the truth: we’ve got a heavy one. I’ll ping him.”

“He says he has quota pressure.”

“He would.” She leaned close to the lens without intending to. “Source bracket chain, show me origins again.”

The reader folded down from the ceiling like an apology. It displayed the bracket stamps and their digital signatures, the path the nodule had made through the Harvest towers, up from the low floors where the air in the neighborhoods had gotten thick and stale with too many promises not kept and too many inevitabilities accreting in the corners of old furniture and prayer rooms. They had fined the tower managers for insufficient noise. The managers had appealed, because it was hard to keep the air disobedient in places where soldiers with old guns sat around telling each other the story that nothing would ever change. Iri had written part of that report and had not liked her own lines. Now those lines squinted back at her from provenance tags.

“It’s real,” she said, to the room. She had expected it not to be. People tried. There was a market for counterfeit mass, just as there was a market for counterfeit everything else. In the early years of the Foldworks, they’d found a man in a shack outside Mbororo making fake certainties out of arranged coincidences and cheap magnets. He had made marriages with them. The last she had heard, the wives had been happy anyway. You could phrase that as a vindication or a tragedy depending on what you needed.

This nodule was no cheap magnet.

Her beads ticked against her skin. She turned them down. Her body still wanted to sweat. She thought of her brother fifteen hundred kilometers away, working nights on a solar array that plated a hillside like a million overlapping beetle backs. She thought of him because she was human. The Foldworks had a literal corridor for personal connections to anything you were working on. You were supposed to walk down it, report the connection to the Accord liaison, and put yourself on simple tasks for the day. She thumbed the console and watched the indicator point to the door with tender officiousness. Her going would leave the lab with a heavy in a lens and a room's worth of noise, and a supervisor would eventually take her place and ask: why are you making me touch the end of the Sun?

“If you’re here, little fat thing,” she said to the nodule, “how did you get here?”

You could not mint this if you were a wealthy firm wanting a law to pass. You could not even mint it if you were a coalition wanting to unspool a city’s future and reweave it different. You could mint a plague outbreak if you did not care how many died on the periphery; you could mint the conviction of a murderer. To guarantee the deadening of a star would take weight beyond weight. It would take a catcher’s mitt the size of the whole sky.

Unless—and the thought came the way a hard, cold thing sometimes comes, like the random bruise you find on your shin when you are showering—unless this was not minted out of the present, but from outside, a backflow, an old promise crawling into the now.

Her screen had nothing to say to that. The reader tolerated the suggestion by not crashing.

“Okay,” she said. “We measure again.”

She measured. She altered parameters. She threw noise at the lens until her necklaces buzzed like bees. The nodule remained the way it had been, sure enough to find itself again after her pushes. Some certainties dissipated if you breathed on them. This one had a serious heart.

“Grey invoked,” the room said politely. “Foreman Blum asks if he can look at your face.”

She tapped the screen and gave Blum her face. He filled half her monitor with his shoulder, which had a cigarette tucked in the ghost behind it, as if his habits predated the Accord and he couldn’t quite let them go.

“You’re not going to like this,” she said.

“You ever bring me anything I like?” He squinted. “We’ve got three orders for the bank’s two o’clock, and the Camerals have a man on the floor. And the Iyer contract wants reassurance—”

“We have a sun drag.”

He went still. The camera caught the micro-muscles in his lips go soft the way a person’s face goes when they’re struck and don’t want to give the other person the satisfaction of seeing it hurt. “Don’t,” he said. “Be serious at me, Iri.”

“I am.”

“Not a grid event?”

She tilted the display until the numbers could be read in the corner of his eye. She had learned the trick from older women and older men who had taught her what you could communicate without saying it out loud when the walls listened for full sentences. He sucked air between his teeth. The sound stung her eardrum.

He turned off the habit cigarette and set the invisible pack back down where the old foremen kept old things. He leaned in and looked at her face the way he had asked to. He had a scar under his left eye she had never asked about. “Do we have to tell the Camerals?”

“The Accord requires reporting of any event with horizon global and mass over—”

“Skip me the line.”

“We have to tell them,” she said. She didn’t say, We have to tell someone, anyway. She didn’t say, We could not tell and take it to the basement instead, to the women who wore story like armor and told fables in alleyways that dissolved even the heaviest stones, because that was illegal and possible, and once you start with possible, you can make yourself into a shape you regret. She didn’t say, The last time the stories came the walls met them with guns. And she didn’t say, The stories might not work this time.

“They’ll put us under a bell,” Blum said. “You, me, the lab, anyone who breathed near that corridor. They’ll keep us from stepping left or right until they decide if they can afford to let any mistakes happen in a place where a certainty like that is sitting. I will grow old in the thirty-meter making tea I don’t want while men with fresh socks walk in and out and tell me I have grime on my shirts.”

“I know,” she said. She put her hand to the glass. The lens was the precise temperature of the room. The nodule within was, if a thing like that was anything like a stone, warm from the friction of the world shaping itself around it. The thin hair on the back of her wrist felt its gravity. “But if we do not tell them, and this is exactly what it looks like, we will have the distinction of dying honest.”

He made a sound that could have been a laugh if a person with a sense of humor held it up at the edge and trimmed it. “Okay. Okay.”

He made the sign he made when he meant to be lucky: a flick of a hand, a little nonsense, an apology to the living and the dead. “I’ll ring the liaison. You stay, make that room as sloppy as you can. Let the noise gel on the floor. Drop the temperature two degrees, then raise it one, then drop it three and stop halfway. Make the computers choose between the same thing twice.”

“I’ll salt it,” she said.

“You do that.” He touched a thumb to the camera. “I always wanted something I did to matter, you know? Not this kind of mattering. But. Well.” His mouth twisted. “If we live until lunch, I’ll owe you a stale roll.”

When he went, the lab resumed its polite emptiness. The room hummed and hiccuped and threw dice at itself. The nodule sat, and nothing in the room dared not to treat it as center. Her jaw ached. She realized she was clenching. She rolled her shoulders back one at a time.

About twenty months ago, in the smoking yard people no longer smoked in, sitting on a bench with her knees drawn up, Iri had kissed a woman who told stories that did not have to be true right away to turn true later. The woman’s name had tasted like metal and sugar. She had offered Iri a cigarette out of a tin. Iri had said, Those will get you wrapped, and the woman had said, Everything wraps, some things make prettier packages than others. They had argued about whether you could break a promise made by the world to itself. They had argued with hands and mouths and messy passion, and then they had stopped seeing each other because utterance alone wasn’t a life. But the picture of that mouth had not dissolved. It had become a part of Iri’s private weather, a cloud that drifted sometimes over.

Iri let that memory lift and pass. It was a hazard, in a lab like this, to hold a thought too long.

The room chirped. “Accord Liaison Diaz is at the outer door.”

“That was quick,” she said.

“He was in the cafe,” the room said. “He would have come sooner but he thought it important not to spill his coffee.”

“Let him in,” Iri said, and smiled mean into the window for a second where only she could see it. She straightened her bead strings. She made the programmable clouds build into a tower, then shatter. She walked to the containment lens and touched her fingers once to its rim.

“Hello,” she said softly, not to the liaison, not to the cameras. “I need you to be breakable. I need you not to be everything.”

Then she faced the door as it opened, and the liaison’s shoes made neat respectful taps on the floor, and she was about to begin saying the words that would put a bell on her, and on Blum, and on the lab, and maybe on everyone within a kilometer, and on the city by the river that loved its own slow fogs.

The sample on her bench would kill a star unless she learned, finally, how to break a promise.

From the observation blister the ring looked like a scratch on the dark. It was too perfect to be anything but made: a thin, burning circle where the background stars smeared into a ribbon, held taut across a patch of midnight that behaved like a hole in thought. We called it a throat because things went in and came out elsewhere and we had the old sailor’s language for that kind of trick. The engineers called it a gate. The poets—the few who still bothered to write for real—they called it a way to fold distances small enough to carry in the hand.

I had been on Vigil for six months by my clock and for three years by everyone else’s. I learned to stop thinking about the arithmetic unless I wanted to hurt myself.

Before the drills and the codes and the signed contracts, the recruiting vids had shown the ring in stylized animation: smooth, symmetrical, a heel of light. In the blister, with the physical shape of it around me, the ring shivered. In some stretches of the day it tore itself into pearly beads, broken by lensing, or smudged as a ship’s transit pulled spacetime thin. There was always a low sound you only heard in your bones, like a long metal beam being struck a thousand kilometers away, the frequency of our narrow definitions pressed to tolerances. I could stand in the blister and feel it under the soles of my feet, the humming weight of it, and then go back to the consoles feeling as if my bones had been tuned.

We were two keepers on Vigil. They had built the station for six because once—this is what the old ones told you—this was all done by people at switches, before the systems had learned how to counsel themselves. The others had gone or retired into the fast world. My partner, Kira, slept during my watches and I slept during hers, and on overlapping hours we split a can of coffee syrup and traded maintenance notes and watched the world’s slow hours through different glass. The station was a cylinder snapped together from hull salvages and new-bent titanium, everything inside lacquered the green-gray of nonreflective paint. We had a joint of hydro culture that smelled like a dentist’s office and a faint, constant sweetness of algae.

We had the Graveyard, too. You couldn’t see it from the blister; you could see it only if you went down into the shaft behind the heat exchangers, under the crying pipes, and touched the backs of your fingers to names etched into the bulkhead with an engineer’s point, each name the size of a thumbnail. They were hull IDs, mostly. Some of them were human names. One of them had been scratched over so many times that it had gone shallow. I could not say whether that comforted me or not.

Every watch had its chores. Spline calibration, readouts, the mother-hen fussing of a nervous keeper. The machines were good. They liked to be watched. That was the superstition that had kept us here after the AIs had taken over the lion’s share of reflexive control. It wasn’t completely a superstition. Things behaved differently under observation; that was the earliest and ugliest thing we had learned to say about reality. If it made anyone feel better to say we were a necessary part of the measurement process, well. It kept a union funded and a tag on a habitat somewhere.

Kira said it like that, with a little curl to her mouth, and then kissed her knuckles and knocked them on the metal of the blister frame because we both had the same ridiculous tells. We were horror stories to our families and curiosities to everyone else. That’s what she said. And then she would nestle into her chair, curl her legs under her in the elastic straps, and hum along to the off-key harmonics the throat made when it was bored.

My own tell: when the speakers ticked to warn of incoming messages, I closed my left eye. The habit had started as a childish game when the light indicator on the panel had a fault and only lit red on one side. I kept doing it because the world in one eye is different from the world in two. The world is flatter and closer and easier to hold. You can’t get hurt by something two centimeters tall on a console.

The day the impossible came was a blue day on our internal cycle. Blue because the light strips were set to mimic a winter sky at 50 degrees north latitude, the kind of sky my grandmother remembered under the Pacific winds. Blue because the wiring has moods, we joked, and nowadays it was all we had left to personify. I was on third watch because even though clocks in the station could read any way we wanted them to, habit demanded dawn and noon and night. Kira had left her mug of coffee syrup on the rail with the little plastic spoon still stuck in it like a flag.

The throat was quiet. I took the monitor handles in my palms and scrolled through anomalies. The next convoy was six hours out by our time. I let my head tip to touch the breeze that never moved and watched a stately slow distortion decorate the ring as something on the far side—how far?—bent the light. I dropped calibration seeds into the throat. The little bursts of coherent radiation shot like beads across the ring, shivering the sensors. The spoolers tuned themselves.

Vigil’s math suite begun to hum a different way. The speakers ticked.

“Messages,” I told the empty blister. “Okay.”

We had protocols to keep us polite to the machines. Talk to them. Thank them. Not because they needed it. Because we did.

The incoming queue looked like a stack of paper in an old movie, cascading. Stacked. I flicked it with a fingertip, skin on glass, and the stack dispersed into tidy little tags: customs manifests, navigational embeds, weather updates from Kolt’s outer planets, union bulletins full of grievances with the word time in them like a bruise. And on top, flagged priority and stamped with a red triangle: Family. I didn’t have many left who bothered to mention me in their fast days. There was one, though.

Mina had sent me a message once a week when I’d first shipped out to Vigil. In my daydreams I kept our schedules in sync by sheer conviction. Then her weeks began to balloon. I could measure her aging by her haircuts, by the things she thought deserved my knowing, by the way her girlfriend changed from pronouns to a name to an ex. She had started wearing sleeves in the summer because she had acquired a job in an atmosphere plant and there was a dress code. She sent me pictures of plants patient as furnace bricks and sighing like old men. On our calls she had two children, and then one, because one had been a miscarriage and she sat on the floor and cried with the camera pointed to her knees and I watched and didn’t say anything because there is a cruelty to the difference in clocks that cannot be bridged by language.

In the last set of messages she had said, without preamble, I’m coming out to see you. There had been an argument. Her ex had called me a black hole over breakfast like that was a thing you could hurl at somebody. “I don’t like the way she talks about you,” Mina had said. “As if you chose to stop going forward. As if you then owe her some acceleration forever.”

“You don’t have to do this,” I’d said. “It will cost you. You have a life.”

“I want to see the ring. I want to see you there. I’m tired of telling my kids about you like you’re in a storybook.”

“They’ll age while you’re with me,” I said. “You’ll feel it like the good kind of sunburn at first. And then you won’t sleep one night for thinking about it.” We had learned new ways to hurt each other since we learned how to carry our spaces across time.

“Fast world is swallowing you,” she’d said. “I want to drag my feet a little.”

Her name glowed in the queue, the only red in the blue morning. I pinched the tag to open it. Mina tilted into view, eyes too close to the camera. A nose now with a bump in it that hadn’t been there when she was nineteen.

“Hi, Noor,” she said, like she always did, even when there was so much else to talk about. “Okay. I’ve booked passage. Convoy 19. The one they call Nineteen-Blue. That makes me sound like a glider. I always wanted to be a glider, do you remember? With Dad’s stupid kite? I’m laughing so I won’t cry. The kids think their auntie is a superhero. Don’t tell them otherwise. I love you.” She had the habit of punctuating every important clause with the shape her mouth made when she was mulling the next thing. “I love you. Okay. I’ve got to go to the port now. Send me something stupid. Tell me a joke about gravity. Do not tell me about gravity. Okay. This is me. I’m coming.”

Behind her someone called a name that was not my sister’s name and she flinched. Then the message ended as if a curtain had been pulled.

The clock. Six hours. They would be negotiating the outer lanes of the Tyne system right now, watching the system’s sun bulge and blink through slotted shields. The convoy would be stacking ships in a breathless braid, heavy on the mass allowances. It was always mass, in the end. How much weight you could afford to carry to the other side.
