I watched the name of the convoy scroll through the shipping feeds to confirm what the message had said. Nineteen-Blue. The logistics line listed temperate cargos, medical supplies, ceramics, a whole engine disassembled and tacked to the list with a note that looked like a prayer. There were eighty-three passenger berths declared. They had cut the line to fifty-seven a year ago. Union pressure. Safety margins, they said in the bulleted memos. A phrase like a key that anyone could turn.

The throat throbbed with something like the taste of copper. I pushed the spoolers through their paces. Kira would wake in two hours if she kept to their habits, yawning her broad, bird-boned jaw, asking me if I had remembered to stretch. She had once been a dancer. She pretended her hands did not hurt when the temperature wavered.

“Everything’s stable,” I told the ring. “Don’t get clever on me.”

“How exactly,” Kira had asked me once, in another blue morning, “would you know if the universe decided to stop making sense while we weren’t looking?”

“We would have to handle it,” I had said, with the reflexive swagger of youth. Which wasn’t youth. Which was just the kind of invincible you grow when your job is to stand at the door of things too large. “We would write it down and change the checklists. That’s all humans are good for anymore, down to the studs.”

“I’m good at soup,” she had said then, just to make me laugh, and then had made soup from our algae that tasted faintly of iron and oranges.

I was thinking of that, and of soup, and of the way Mina tucked her hair behind her ear when she was doing something she was afraid of, and of the fact that I had to adjust the throttle on spooler four because it was running hot; a little chain of thought like popcorn in oil, one idea jumping and spitting against the glass of my skull, then another, when the speaker ticked again.

It didn’t tick the way it always ticked. The sound was slightly buried, as if made from inside a drawer. An old memory of my grandfather—he had a chest full of mechanical parts and a drawer with old coppers that made a sound like that when you shook them. I would have said do not anthropomorphize the machines; they hate it. But there it was, the sound of muffled coins, and it came from the small band of frequencies we reserved for our internal diagnostics, the channel we called the house voice.

I almost said something to the station, a half-formed pardon, before I thought better.

“Vigil?” I said. The name for our station had always been a little too on the nose. We had that kind of luck.

The answer was my voice.

“Don’t send them in,” Noor said, crisp with the panic you hear when someone bites every word. “Don’t send Nineteen-Blue. Noor, listen. You will want to. You will think that if you follow the protocol and if you do everything precisely that it will be all right. It won’t. Don’t send them.”

I sat very still because that is what you do when the deep part of you leaps. My hands curled halfway into fists. The voice was my own. There was no mistaking that. The algorithms that matched voiceprints to their owners spun little green checks across the console to tell me that I was me and I always had been.

The message continued, out of sequence with sense; as if it had been cut and spliced and spooled through a worn projector.

“The spoolers will crater in the ninth harmonic. You can see it now if you look. It is there already. Kira will be late. They told you in the training that this couldn’t happen. They called it nonsense. They called it art. Listen to me. Take the field down. Mercury the throat. I know the fines. I know. If you need—” The voice did something fermata-like, as if it were a bit of deliberate resonance. “If you need an anchor: Mina’s bracelet breaks. She drops the blue glass. It looks like the sea. She steps on it because the deck shifts. She bleeds. You will feel the time of it as a pain in your teeth. That is how I knew to talk to you. Don’t send them in.”

The house-voice channel, the speaker that never crackled, crackled.

I turned in my chair to look at the blister as if there could be someone standing in it. The ring shone indifferent. The algorithms matching voice to person shone their confident green. The checklists I had spent my twentieth and twenty-first years committing to muscle memory went dark around their edges, as if the universe had poured ink across them.

“Vigil,” I said, because what else is there to say. “Status.”

“Stable,” the station said. It never called me by name. We didn’t program it with any voice pronouns. It liked clear orders and it liked to return them in its education-drone tone until we grew numb to being scolded.

I pushed away from the chair so hard the straps holding it squealed. I put my palms flat on the blister’s rim and watched the throat that had made me its custodian. I was a child again crouching in the dark under my blanket making shapes with my hand in the light of a torch. I was very old in a darting body and did not know my own story.

Protocol Sable-Nine, I told myself. I said it, because you were supposed to say it, in a flat voice so you would hear it without sentiment: Under no circumstances act on information that cannot be traced to a causally valid chain. That had been the way they phrased it because the others made jokes with the words paradox and grandfather and the lawyers had scowled at us. Protocol Sable-Nine had a whole compendium attached in the manual. Case histories. Hypothetical. The thinness of the pages had always made the words look like they wanted to grow through.

There were no examples in the casebook of your own voice saying your sister’s name.

I tore through the messages again like some one of those frantic women in the old stories flinging cards across a couch. Customs manifests, law regs, union propaganda, meatspace gossip in thirteen languages. Nineteen-Blue: on time, dispatched. A small flag noting a fluctuation observed in Tyne’s magnetic sheath. That wasn’t us. That was something like weather. There was a chirrup from spooler four to tell me that I had not in fact adjusted something and that the something had noticed. The house-voice again.

“Noor,” I said to myself in my own voice on the retrospective recording as if now I could coax the past out of the future and feed it into the present like a chain. An AI had once explained the shape of these loops to us with a diagram that had a moat around it labeled Do Not Walk On The Grass. “Noor. If you’re me. Give me a thing I can take to Kira. Give me a thing I can put on a report and the magistrate will be fooled.”

“If I tell you a thing you can take to a magistrate,” Noor said, “then the magistrate will say you took action on unsubstantiated claims. I have tried. You will not like any of the ways this turns. Tell me the color of the socks you are wearing.”

“I’m barefoot,” I said, before I could tell myself I was being foolish.

“Exactly,” she said. “Exactly.”

It would not be recorded in the training manual and it would not be admitted by anyone who had signed the secrecy agreements but there was another rule on Vigil, one Kira had whispered to me on the first night we hung our hammocks and felt our bodies remember Earthlike gravity in delicate, shivering detail. That rule was: Do not be alone when you are not sure what time it is. More succinctly: If you cannot tell whether a thing has happened, go find somebody else and put your hand on them.

Kira’s bunk was a heaved-out carton full of blanket and tea bags and folded clothes. The lights at her end were set to amber. She slept hard, with her mouth open. She had tied a ribbon to the end of her braid because her hair reached past her waist now and hair got caught in everything on Vigil that turned or spun or had a greedy gear. The ribbon was gray and old like fallen snow. The smell in the sleeping berth was skin, tea, the strap-cleaner we used because there was nothing else.

“Kira,” I said. “Kira, wake up, please.”

She grunted and put a hand up and then pulled me by the wrist because she thought, in that moment between the sleep story and the waking room, that I had come to lie down next to her to warm my feet. I stood there and that was almost all I did. Standing is a skill. It is rarely taught. I think I learned it properly for the first time that day beside Kira’s seaworn face.

“What’s on fire?” she said, wet-voiced. Her eyes had always looked as if somebody had blown smoke in them. Later she would tell me that, when she had first arrived, she had cried for four days without stopping because of the frequency of our machine song. I had never believed her until I did. Then I believed everything.

“House-voice,” I said. “Sable Nine.”

She was awake then. She put her bare feet down onto the ladder rungs and came down like she was a person, not the dancing bird she could be when she was joyful. “No,” she said, which is what you say when someone says they have been bitten by a ghost while you went to fill the basin. Then: “Okay. Show me.”

We tumbled into the blister. The ring kept its serenity like a saint painted on a wall. The machines were as proud as they always had been. The message hung in the cache because either the station had taken pity on me or because I had told it to save something without meaning to. I played it for Kira, and for the first time since I had sat with my hands on the blister rim hearing my own voice tell me what I didn’t want to hear, I stopped being two people and was one again: a woman with a partner who knew the same manuals, who loved the same humming, who had held the same list of other people’s lost names in her hands.

“Shit,” Kira said, reverent, the way she had said good soup. “Shit, Noor. Shit.”

“I know.”

“We have to log it,” she said, automatic. The way you say we have to put a bucket under that before we have to remodel the kitchen. “We have to—”

“If we log it exactly we trip the Sable and then they are going to send us a goddamn clown tribunal. They will take our hands off the handles before Nineteen gets through.”

Kira rubbed her mouth with the heel of her hand. The light put a shadow in the hollow under her cheekbone. “What else would you do?” she asked.

There is an art to building machines that hold themselves together while the laws they were designed for change around them. There is an art too to breaking those machines in such a way that when they come down they do not kill you. The language for that art came from shipwrights and gramophone mechanics and women with threads and needles. You could talk about damping and harmonics. Or you could talk about loosening a knot so you could retie it.

The voice had told me to Mercury the throat. The phrase lived in the back of my brain from a briefing two years ago, a thing the engineer had said she hoped she would die without having to see. To Mercury: to seed the throat with dense field that would make its mouth gray, to draw back the ring’s shine until the ships wanting to transit could not. It shut the throat without shutting it down. It put a curtain over a window and told the sun to act like a lamp for a while.

No fines, we joke, we always joke.

“There are eighty-three declared berths,” I said. “People. My sister is—” The word out of my mouth tasted like a thing made of money and metal. “On it.”

Kira looked at the numbers where they scrolled in a polite, sober way as numbers have always done, and then she looked at the ring. She looked very young between them for a moment. And then she was old again—old like the hull was old, seamed and sure.

“We are here to err on the side of not murdering strangers,” she said. “You know this.”

“I know the fines.”

“Fuck the fines,” she said, softly. “If we gray it and it was unnecessary, we are clowns. If we don’t, and—” She shook her head as if to empty a cup.

“I need you to witness it,” I said. I needed that for me more than I needed anything else. For later. For the tribunal. For the Graveyard. For the part of me that would have to come and sleep in this bed again. “I need you.”

Kira put her hand over mine where it hovered—not over buttons, not over sliders. We were not that kind of interface. The station would not let us change the shape of the world that fast. But there was a lever in the console. A real lever. It had a name stamped into its side as if it had been lifted from a crane in a museum: FIELD MODULATION. It was there for people who had to do something with muscles when they were afraid.

“Do you believe her?” Kira asked.

“She is me,” I said.

“Then no,” she said, like an artist, like someone who had learned how to lie to her own body to jump further. “She is not you. She is your voice. These are different things.” But she did not take her hand away. Her palm was warm. Her thumb had a hard place where she had burned it on the soup coil three nights ago.

Vigil’s internal clock threw a little bar of chimes to tell us that by somebody’s measure of noon we had arrived at the middle of the day.

Heaviness settled into me. I did not feel noble. I did not feel like a heroine in the recruiting vid. I felt like a woman who couldn’t afford the fines and who had once promised a lover she would take them dancing on a world with gravity so high you had to hold the walls when you laughed. I felt like someone who had to take the blame for breaking something beautiful because the alternative was to let eighty-three somethings go away.

I reached for the lever because a lever is a thing you can grasp.

I did not pull it all the way. I would lie about that later. I would say we did it deliberate and in one motion. If you had been in the blister with us you would have seen me take it down just to the point where the ring’s brightness dimmed as if a cloud had passed over it. Just to the edge. You would have been able to imaginarily reach with your tongue and taste metal on the air.

“Vigil,” I said. My mouth was too dry. “Initiate pre-Mercury modulation. Spooler dampers to ten. Run it slow.”

“Authority required,” Vigil said. I loved it for that right then. It had said the same thing to me when I had launched a coffee spoon into the station’s internals by accident. Authority required. You step up and you press your palm or you go away.

Kira put her palm over the sensor and I put mine over hers.

“Authority recognized,” the station said. It sounded no less like a teacher at a school nobody wanted to go to.

The ring began to gray. It was the smallest thing. It was a cloud between you and the sun. It was the sort of nuance that you do not learn in a ten hour training video but in a hundred mornings in the blister watching light in your periphery. Out there, the convoy that had not yet arrived moved through the blank, thickened mathematics of space with their own light. Here, in Vigil’s bones, the house-voice channel remained quiet because for a little while we had made the impossible act of observation possible by touching one another.

The chair’s straps, stretched and loosened by years of bodies and knees, creaked like ropes on a harbor. The Graveyard, scratchy and small, hummed with our names as it always did.

“Okay,” Kira said. She let go of my hand and let her fingers hang. She shut her eyes for the first time since I had woken her and opened them again. “Now we wait to be heroes or clowns.”

The convoy pinged us three hours later. But that was a different chapter. In the first hour of the dimming, before their message came, the muscles along my jaw finally unclenched and the bones in my neck began to hurt in a way that meant I had finally stopped bracing. I went to the small sink, filled the cup, drank, and felt my teeth throb the way I did when a storm turned onshore at home. Somewhere in the station, the house-voice made a sound like somebody was moving a wooden box from one shelf to another.

I did not look at the place where the lever sat. I stood beside Kira and watched the throat go gray.

When the station chose to speak, it did it in my voice again, close in tone and in timing, as though to be kind.

“Thank you,” Noor said. Then: “It will still be terrible. But it will not be that terrible. Please don’t hate me for the part that I am. I will not be able to bear that.”

I did not answer. That felt like the one thing Sable-Nine could still have.

Kira knocked her knuckles on the blister frame twice and kissed them for luck.

“You didn’t tell me a joke about gravity,” I said to the empty room because Mina had asked for one, and I am a good sister in all the ways that a slow world allows you to be. “Because there aren’t any. They all fall flat.”

Kira groaned. The ring hummed. The cloud lay over it like a lid. Behind my breastbone, the pain in my teeth slowly spun down to a murmur. If you had asked me then what I believed in, I would have told you: levers. People. And the way the universe sometimes lets you stick your hand into it and come out again, bloody, and counting.

Time had a taste when it broke—copper, rain, that flash of warmth and blood you get from biting your own lip. Kyra pressed her tongue against the inside of her teeth and let the world tell on itself.

She hung under the belly of the city, boots locked into the traverse rail, between sky and the long drop to the rails of When, listening. Above her, Wick’s frame creaked and sang—a hundred thousand bolts working a slow argument with gravity and speed. Below her, the rails gleamed a dull gray, stretching out to a horizon that had learned to bend. Wind came at her in stratified sheets, each layer carrying a different weather: dust from a summer that hadn’t happened yet seeding her visor with gold grit, a chill that remembered the last ice, heat shimmering from a future noon where someone was laughing, crying, both.

“Third Cartographer? You’re far enough,” Orun’s voice rasped thin and metallic through the line in her jaw. “Bring her in.”

Kyra glanced along the rib where her tether clipped to Wick’s underframe. The rope thrummed like a plucked wire, its fibers bright with what the crew called mythlight—static from the dynamo wheels and something else, something that lived in the rails themselves. She thumbed the set on her wrist and fed the last of her spool into the little brass box of the chronoscope. The dials settled, needles quivering with hairsbreadth caution, then, with a soft click, they aligned. The array on her forearm hummed, creepingly alive; the counter set into the cuff flickered as glowing numerals declared the measure of current: two sigma to the lean, lay low.

“Two south on the lean,” she said. “Low risk for torsion flare. I can see three eddies, nothing bigger than a carriage. The right-of-way’s dirty with rumor, though. We may kick up a gale.”

“Rumor,” Orun said, amusement stale. “That’s not a word the Civic likes.”

“It’s the word we’ve got.” Kyra pivoted, her body swinging toward the Vanish. The Vanish was what children called the space ahead of Wick’s prow, the gray slope of days that the city ate and transformed into a trail of smoke and heat and light. It wasn’t empty if you knew how to look. It was never empty. The air had a grain to it, and the rails thrummed under her hand with the memory of hammers. Whoever had laid them—the Laywrights, the old ones whose names were lost in the friction burn of crossing centuries—they’d known things about time that no one in Wick did now. They had hammered the rails into firm events, thick old realities, and then strung the spans between them across the lightless gulfs of might-have-been. And Wick ran on those rails the way a bead runs on a string, carrying its people like a secret.

“Two south,” Orun repeated into the channel. He had that tone that meant he was passing the math to a dozen hands. “Hear that, Pilot?”

A different voice, lower, roughened by sleep lost to the weight of decision, filled Kyra’s ear. “Heard,” said Marek, Wick’s current Pilot. In Kyra’s mind, Marek had the profile of a weathered coin; he always did, because that was the reflection she saw in the heavy bronze of the pilot’s wheel—the man’s mouth a tight notch, eyes between humor and regret. “Helm, bring her two south. Give me steady on the lean. Cartographer, anything else?”

Kyra saw the eddies now as disturbances in the dust, like fish moving through murk. “There’s a lot of chatter,” she said. “A family argument somewhere near the bow, three new babies behind the grain vans, a loose panel near the west stanchion making a complaint in a language it learned when steel was born. All harmless. And—wait.”

She tasted copper again, bright enough to make her throat tighten. The wind went flat, the layers thinning to paper. Ahead of Wick, the rails darkened—not by shadow but by a saturation of nothing. The chronoscope on her arm clicked once—paused—then clicked again, as if it had lost track of what numbers were. The needles jittered, stuttered, and fell.

She alleged a laugh, because sometimes that settled the instruments. “Chrono’s being coy,” she said. “We’ve got a Vellum.”

The channel went so quiet she could hear the hiss of Marek inhaling. “Say again.”

“A sheet,” Kyra said. “Blank. No scatter. No drift. A Vellum over the rails, maybe three lengths this side of the next pylon. My scope doesn’t see into it.”

Vellum was a polite word and an old one, the name Cartographers used when they had to write down a hole and pretend it was paper. She’d seen them before, thin films laid over the rails where causality got folded too tight for the scope to parse. Mostly they were weather, and you could feel your way through them by taste and sound and the way your hair prickled at the nape when something had too much interest in you. This, though, was—wrong. Even the rumors had gone quiet. No laughter ahead. No crying. No flecks of future grit.

“How near to the next pylon?” Orun asked, his voice carefully cold.

Kyra squinted. The pylons were small on the horizon, wedge-headed things driven through the world into the event-rock below. They lit the world with a little corona of reliable. You could tell where they were by the straightening of the air. This one should have been a splinter of upright certainty against Wick’s hunger for distance. She could not see it. The Vellum lay over that place where straightness should be, like frost over a nail.

“Too near,” she said. “Close enough that we can’t leave the rails before it. We’re going to hit it whether we like it or not.”

“You get me anything inside?” Marek asked.

Kyra tapped the side of the chronoscope, brought up the fallback optics. The little camera in the scope wasn’t really a camera. It was a set of polarized crystals that had learned to be frightened by certain kinds of curve. It saw the bow of Wick diving into the future; it saw the rails stretching away; it saw—nothing. In the nothing, something.

No color. No grain. No sense of depth. But on the underside of the blank, there were marks, like scratches on the inside of an eggshell. She focused, squinted. Writing. Chalk, it looked like. Child chalk. Big loops, imperfect circles, the R wrong at the leg. The wind, which had gone flat, seemed to draw in a breath and hold it. On the blank’s underside, in that childish hand, someone had written a name.

KYRA.

The rest of the line had been rubbed away, smudged into suggestion. KYRA, DON—something. Or maybe KYRA, DON’T— She swallowed.

“Cartographer,” Orun prompted, when she forgot to breathe.

“Something’s been in there,” Kyra said, which was safer than saying someone, safer than saying me. “Something that writes. Markings on the sheet. Don’t know how old.”

Marek was all sawteeth suddenly. “You sure you’re reading it right?”

“I’m reading what I’m reading,” she said. The letters had been drawn with a hand that didn’t yet obey its owner completely. The loops were too round. The Y was leaning as if it wanted to sit down.

Static climbed the line in her jaw like ants. She turned down the volume and let them argue in the cabin. Orun would tell Marek to slow. Marek would say slow how much, we’re not at station, we can’t loiter over an unpinned stretch, the rails behind are shedding rivets, the moths are hungry. Orun would ask Kyra questions until she had no more answers, and then make some decisions that would make other people angry, and they would make the city do what it always did, which was go forward.

Kyra reached up and touched Wick’s underbelly with her bare hand, the glove off for the feel of it. The metal was warm. It thrummed, not with speed, but with the sum of the people living above: a woman snoring near the vent, a boy practicing the bell at watch-change, the whisper of many prayers in many languages to many gods and none. Wick was never quiet. It had the crowded music of a throat clearing.

The line fizzed back into her ear with Orun’s voice in that tone he used when he wanted to sound like he’d thought of everything. “Bring your kit in, Third. Meet us in the pilot house. Marek wants your eyes.”

“On my way,” Kyra said, though she stayed a breath longer, her body dangling under the city like a pendulum, all human weight and worry, staring into the blank until her eyes watered and she saw nothing but her own blood vessels swimming on the inside of the world.

She reeled her tether in, hand over hand, boots walking the traverse. The skin of Wick under her feet had been patched so often it was its own map. There was the round of a repair from the time a wheel had spat a tooth into a boy’s shoulder and everyone had told the story of the lucky angle until luck itself wore thin on the telling. There was scratchwork someone had left in an unnoticeable place—two initials and the outline of a heart, already fading under grease. There was the stain where a jar of the sea had broken, real sea in real glass, saved from a station and sloshed over iron when a Cartographer had tripped. Kyra had licked her fingers and swore and dreamed of salt the rest of the week.

She slid into the underbay and stripped out of her rig while the bay door sank shut with a sigh. Fume and heat swirled around her like a skirt. Her hair—too long, Orun had told her three times now—stuck to the back of her neck. She washed her face in the little tin basin whose water was always a degree cooler than you wanted it to be, and tried to smell the copper out of her nose. It clung, as if she’d eaten a coin.

By the time she made it to the pilot house, Wick had leaned, slightly, their course shifted as per her saying. She felt it in her knees, the change of weight—a small telling off-balance against her bones that said the world had tilted. The pilot house sat near the front of Wick’s prow, glassed on three sides in panes the size of dinner tables, brass fitted, polished from a thousand sleeves. Marek was there, one hand on the wheel, eyes on the Vellum. He nodded at her without looking away, the way you greet a cobbler while you’re running in new boots.

Orun stood beside him, coat shrugged on but not buttoned, hair not combed, a grease thumbprint on his cheek. The little gray feather charm his daughter had made, Kakri’s thing, was tied around his wrist, out of place among the dials and levers.

“Show me the mark,” Orun said, straight to it. He was good that way. He didn’t say are you sure or you look pale. He had that rare grace of asking only for what could be given.

Kyra put her chronoscope on the sill and held the optics up so both men could press in. She felt their bodies as heat along her shoulders and forearms, felt the fine tremor in Marek’s restraint.

“There,” she said. “There, under the first fold.”

Marek swore softly. Orun didn’t say anything at all. The chalk loops shone ghostly in the scope’s eye. KYRA, DON—then a smear, as if thumbed. The blank looked slightly porous now that she stared at it this long, like thin skin stretched too far. She touched the back of her neck. The hair there was trying to climb away.

“How many times have you been under the belly of this brute?” Marek asked, not looking away.

Kyra had to think. You didn’t count, usually. Counting invited noticing. “Four hundred and twelve,” she said, and when Orun glanced at her with one corner of his mouth up, she added, “Sula keeps a tally. She paints a dot on the side of her bunk for every dull day I make less dull with stories.”

Marek flicked his gaze at her, quick as a knife. “Would Sula count this?”

“Sula counts everything that frightens me,” Kyra said. “Gives her leverage for when she does something stupider.”

“You’re telling me we have to go through that,” Marek said. “And that something in there knows your handwriting.”

Kyra wanted a lie. She couldn’t find anything that shaped right in her mouth. “That chalk wasn’t mine,” she said, which was true in the way that saying a river isn’t the ocean is true. “But I recognize the way the hand falters.”

“We could slow.” Orun said it as if it were a trick and he could take it back before anyone else heard it.

Marek took his hand off the wheel briefly to rub at his eyes. His hand left a smear like smoke. “We slow, we get the moths on us.”

Kyra looked over his shoulder. Out past Wick’s last carriage, past the framework where a dozen households had strung their laundry to snap in the futurewind, she could see the rails behind them shedding light. It wasn’t actually moths back there, but that was what people called them, the little ragged holes that drifted like torn petals, chewing edges off the rails’ reality and leaving frayed might-have-beens behind. The official name was absence occlusions. The official name did not change how they looked when they found meat.

“Not long,” Orun said. “A heartbeat or four.”

“What do you want in four heartbeats?” Marek asked. He was smiling, and Kyra didn’t like his smile at all. It meant he was going to do something generous and stupid because he could not help himself being the kind of man he was. “Cartographer, you want to hang a bell on that Vellum? Want to piss in it and see if it gets mad?”

Kyra closed her eyes and saw chalk. She heard Sula’s laugh—wet and smoke-warm in her ear the way it was when they whispered in the crawlspace above the market, stealing oranges and moments. She opened her eyes. “I want to drive a nail,” she said. “If we can’t see the pylon, it’s hiding. If we put a smallness of certainty into the edge, maybe we can raise a seam. Enough to get a taste before we eat the whole of it.”

Orun frowned. “A nail,” he said, slowly. “A line. A tether.”

Marek groaned. “You two and your words. It’s a spike. Call a spike a spike.”

“We don’t have many left,” Orun went on. “Three.”

“Two and a half,” Marek corrected. “Last one took a twist. It’ll go, but I don’t trust it to hold if something curious tugs on it.”

Kyra put her hand flat on the pilot house table, and the wood said morning with its warmth. She thought of Sula’s dots—paint circles over her head, ringed like a little galaxy on the underside of her bunk—and of the market that curled down Wick’s spine like a bright intestine. The spice woman with her paper cones of saffron that wasn’t saffron and stories that were worth more than the cones. The boy in the bell-hood who cared too much about timing. Kakri’s gum wrapper charms. Marek’s ridiculous feather because he thought it made the wheel lighter. The place where you could lay your head under the turning of a city and sleep because other hands held you.

She said, “Give me one of the good spikes.”

Marek swore again, but softer, affectionate as if she were a child walking into a cold river with her boots on backward. Orun said, “Done,” as if he’d decided that before she asked.

They ran like the rail itself has only one story to tell. Men and women fell into their places with that particular attention the whole city had when crisis was near—a straightening of backs, a hush under the talk. The spike they brought to the underbay was not actually a spike, though that was what everyone called it, too. It was a coil of braided metal, beaten thin and layered with the same unknown alloy that the rails wore like skin. It had a head you could hammer with; it had a point that would bite anything real. Orun and Kyra lugged it between them as if they were carrying a rolled-up thundercloud.

“Four heartbeats,” Orun said, strapping her back into the traverse harness. He tucked the feather charm under the cuff of his sleeve and smoothed her hair back from her face like old habit. “Don’t stay to admire your handwriting.”

“If it says something mean,” Kyra said, “I’ll write it a letter in return.”

“You write it after you are not dangling in the mouth of something that scares me,” he said, which was as close as he got to “be careful.”

Outside, time had taken a breath and was holding it a second sweet too long. The rails were a ribbon of possibility that the sun hadn’t found yet. Behind Wick, the moths flirted and fell away, uncertain. Ahead, the Vellum had come closer in the way that distance collapses when you are the thing moving. The blank was a wall now. It moved with them because it had no choice.

Kyra crabbed along the belly again, the spike clipped to her side, her toes finding the grippy scars she knew like the inside of her own mouth. The wind licked her eyes through the visor, and she let it. Her blood hummed. She had four heartbeats. She might have five. She would not act as if she had six.

She got to the bow’s lip and planted her feet on the last of Wick’s under-skin. She could feel the pull now, the way the Vellum tried to un-name the shapes around it. Her hand went a little stupid on the first reach. She shook out her fingers and found her grip again.

“Ready,” Orun said into her ear. “You have my count. Four down. Give us anything you can on two, we haul on four whether you have poetry or not.”

Kyra spat to one side. The spit lifted off in a line, then hung—stalled—a pearl in nothing before it smoked away like an idea you never write down. She put the spike’s point toward the edge of the blank.

“One,” Orun said, and Wick leaned into speed the way a horse does, the whole city a muscle, quivering.

“Two.”

The Vellum wasn’t cold or hot. It wasn’t anything. The spike met the edge of it and found no purchase because there was no edge to find. Kyra swore with the venom of a person who has believed in nails her entire life. She flexed her wrist and put more of her own weight into it, drove the spike at an angle, aiming at where edges must be if there were sense in the world.

“Three.”

Something buckled—not the spike, not the blank. Something between, something like the surface of a bubble that had been waiting for her. There was a pressure like altitude, like grief. The spike sang, a pure sweet note that set Wick’s bones humming, and then it bit. The spike went in not like iron into wood but like a word into silence. Kyra felt it take. She felt the line go taut.

“Four.”

The tether hauled, the harness groaned, and Kyra’s body came away from the edge with a jerk that lit each vertebra like a string of lamps. She did not let go of the spike’s head until she had to. When she did, it quivered, a tiny certainty pinned to the nothing.

“What did you get?” Orun said. He wasn’t calm now. He had the voice he’d had when his daughter was fever-hot and every hour had been a decade.

Kyra hadn’t realized she’d closed her eyes. She opened them as the blank slid forward to take her whole sight. The spike quivered at its lip, the line from it running back to Wick like the trail of an idea. Her chronoscope had recorded without her. She looked down at the little screen on her wrist out of habit and because she wanted to refuse the flood.

A picture resolved—the pylon under the blank, there, faint as an old coin beneath vellum, and something else: a shadow of curvature, a notch. The hand that had written had written again. The blank had been wiped, and somebody had tried to write faster, smaller, to get the thought out first. The letters were too close together, spooked into each other. DON’T CROSS.

“Pylon’s present,” Kyra said. Her voice was steady, which she decided later was just her body refusing to make a fuss while she was still alive enough for fussing. “Hidden. The blank’s holding over it like skin over a cut. There’s a notch—maybe an anchor point we can trust. And there’s—words.”

“Don’t,” Marek said, aiming for jovial and hitting just below it. “There’s always words.”

“Cross,” Kyra said. She heard herself say it. She heard the city try to tell her there were other ways to say go on, go on.

Orun made a noise she had never heard him make.

“Pull her in,” Marek said. “We take the pylon. We keep the line on the spike. Everyone does their job and nobody looks up to read the sky. I swear it.”

Kyra blinked salt and metal out of her eyes as the harness carried her back under Wick’s skin. She stared into the blank until it swallowed the rail, the horizon, the edges of themselves. It had never made sense to her that a thing could be this much nothing, and still have a surface you could write on. That meant there was a right side and a wrong side to it. Or, worse, that there were as many sides as there were names you could give to fear.

She slipped into the underbay and tore the harness off like a skin gone suddenly too tight. Orun met her with the kind of look you don’t talk about where the walls have ears—the look that eats itself because it has no words it dares wear.

“It knew you,” he said, very quietly.

“It knows my name,” Kyra said. “I know my name.”

“Close enough for government work,” Marek said, in the doorway, trying to carry ease like a man carries water in cupped hands. “You’ve bought us a handhold. We’ll take it. We’ll be through in a minute.”

Kyra wanted to argue that through implied an other side. She wanted to say that sometimes through was a pocket, not a passage. She wanted to take Sula by the wrist and show her the chalk and hear what Sula would make of it. No time. She nodded like a soldier on an old film and followed Orun up to the pilot house again. The city creaked, bent, strained. The feather on Marek’s wheel shook as if it were real.

They hit the Vellum the way a word hits the back of a throat when you can’t finish it. The world went quiet, even the moths behind them making no sound at all as they drifted in a hungry pack. The rail was there, then it wasn’t. Light was there. It chose not to be. Up was courteous enough to remain. The wide window in front of them clouded with a skin of not-light that showed their faces back at them as negative space.

Marek said, too softly to be a performance, “Trust the rail. Trust the rail. Trust the rail.” People whispered their prayers. Books held their breath. Somewhere a bell missed a beat and then rang twice to apologize. Wick’s weight rolled through the quiet like a question no one wanted to answer.

Kyra put her hand on the sill and watched as the chalk letters on the Vellum’s underside slid up until they were level with her eyes. DON’T CROSS, the letters said, tilted by haste. The M was wrong. There was no M. Her brain was trying to give her letters that weren’t there. There was only the urge of an M, the stubborn insistence of a line wanting to be something else.

Outside, at the edge of the letter D, something moved.

It looked like a hand, just for an instant, pressed against the inside of a skin stretched thin. It was small, that hand. The bones were a child’s bones. It spread its fingers wide, and Kyra spread her own by reflex, palm to glass, as if you can meet someone if you both agree on the shape of the meeting.

The hand withdrew like a thought reconsidered.

Wick slid forward another inch into nothing. The spike’s line twanged, taut as a saved breath. The pylon that was there when you looked the right way caught the hook of their faith and held.

Trust the rail, Marek said, and Wick obeyed like a beast that wants to live.

On the other side of the blank, the world waited, or it didn’t. Kyra set her shoulder lightly against the pilot house frame, felt the structure talk to her bones, and thought—not of the child hand or her own name scratched where names shouldn’t be—but of the way Sula always counted backward from ten before she did something brave, so that even fear had a number and a schedule.

Nine, Kyra thought. Eight.

The city crossed.

Chapter One: The Keeper

Sera Halden kept a flame no one could see.

On her first night at the Lagrange Aperture, when the station was still smelling of off-gassing polymers and everyone's congratulations had faded into lag, she had cupped her gloved hands in front of the maintenance viewport and waited to feel the heat. Some part of her had expected warmth, some primitive animal comfort to answer the word "beacon." Instead there had been only the dry breath of scrubbed air and the cold song of the coils, and beyond the quartz slit, the aperture itself: a ring of nothing wearing a limn of color like oil on water.

Even now, after three years, she could never decide if the aperture was beautiful. It didn't look like anything, not in the ways her childhood had taught her to recognize—the line of a hill, the blade of a leaf, the frost-dust on a window. The ring was a refinement of curvatures: twelve encircling scaffolds of exotic mass, coaxed into holding a hole that space wanted to forget. The control gel printed these masses with lacework equations so delicate that a single cosmic ray could tangle them if the fields were misaligned, and the fields were never perfect. They shivered. They hummed. They drifted like slow thoughts. And it was her job to keep them in check.

She sat strapped to the station's spine, watching the arcs of diagnostic light curl through the ring as if she were a fisher with phosphorescent line. The indices flowed across her forearm display, soft green digits climbing and falling, the color of that morning's algae-lattice bread and the sea water her father had poured from a bottle in a ritual he'd invented: Remember the ocean, he'd said at the departure gate, tipping it onto the spaceport tiles until the guards came. Remember salt. Her mother had laughed like shattered glass. In every shot from that day her left hand is invisible, dug into the cuff of Sera's jacket hard enough to pull the seam. They'd argued over everything but water.

"Kettle," Sera said, "sing me your blues."

Kettle woke like an old cat in a sunbeam. The station's resident analog friend had been installed by the previous keeper, a woman who'd left Sera a note that said: Without talking you will convince yourself the machines hum in your voice. Kettle's voice was nothing like a hum. It was warm and unashamed of itself, full of little glitches it never repaired.

"Good morning, Sera," Kettle said, drawing out her name as if trying on a necklace. "You are, by all interesting metrics, late for sleep."

"I'll nap during the dark."

"It is always dark."

"You promised me blues."

"Ah," Kettle said, and replaced itself with waveform. The station's visualizer bubbled a ribbon of pale color across Sera's forearm. Kettle translated the field noise from the ring into audible frequencies, a service Sera had requested her second week in service, when numbers alone had stopped communicating urgency and everything became an ocean of decimals. The human ear was greedy for pattern; it could hear a drift in tuned strings better than the eye could read one. At first she had been ashamed of doing as her father did—he'd been a fiddler with hands full of mechanics and always tuned by ear because he'd never trusted the little strip of red diodes—but now she let the shame go. The gate groaned a little when dawn struck the solar panels. The gate whispered when dust caught in the beacons. The gate sang when the sun went quiet and the station slipped into geomagnetic shadow and the fields could finally settle like water in a clean bowl.

Right now Kettle handed her a low, uncertain line, the sound of a boat rubbing its rope against a damp pier. Sera adjusted the phase in sector B8 and watched for the echo. The curve shifted, sighed, settled. Her fingers moved on the controls without conscious thought. The gloved skin of the interface barely kissed her. She could have done this in the dark.

"This is why you didn't last with the traffic authority," Kettle said, chatting to fill the unspeakingness. "You like things slow and fussy. Stillness that pretends to be peace."

"I was asked to leave traffic," Sera said mildly. "There is a difference."

"You rolled a drone into a minister's motorcade."

"It did not make physical contact."

"It made emotional contact," Kettle said.

On the viewport, the ring flickered. Sera's body went cold before the alarm sounded. She felt her bile twinge in the back of her tongue: old training that said hide, run, there is a stink of ozone in here and it's not yours. She keyed in a command and the ring bloomed into spectral overlay, twelve segments pulsing like a great segmented throat.

"Spike on D4," she said. "Cross-check with climate."

"External wind rising," Kettle said, as if there were wind through vacuum. Kettle was old code saved from the struts of the first lunar kites, and kept the habit of calling squalls wind and radiation rain. "Tachyon squall forty-two degrees off the ecliptic. It's a—"

"I can see it," Sera said, not unkindly. "Shutters on aperture. Splay the beacons."

The ring's lip darkened as shutters made of almost nothing drifted into place, angled against particles that didn't exist in the ways particles were supposed to. The Lagrange Aperture sat along a kink in the heliosheath, at the long stretched edge of the sun's breath. There were currents out here, invisible and terribly real. The Authority had promised Sera a quiet station when they assigned her, a place where the gate stayed sleeping and the travelers had moved on to flashier shortcuts closer to the economies of power. Out here, there were the miners with their timid tugs, the occasional research convoy with more instruments than crew, and the void. Sera was fine with that. Her job wrapped its quiet around her; it had its own drama, small and precise as surgery.

"D4 is stubborn," Kettle crooned, letting the gate's song rise in volume as the squall rattled the outboard mass. "It's beating like a throat."

"I don't need similes, I need stable."

"Apologies. Bringing up the backup ring in ten seconds. Nine. Eight."

Sera adjusted her straps and floated a little, eyes on the ring's lay. The backup would draw power from the station's reserves and the panels would groan for it. She thought about the time the keepers had to lay their bodies against the coils during a storm—old story, maybe not true. But someone had told it at a station meeting once, and no one shook their head. Once there had been a string of keepers at these gates, an order with rituals, hair braids and songs, things to pass the time and make the work into something less lonely. Now there were specialists in corporate gray, and men in shirts who asked if the aperture could be made to look more convincing for the cameras. Sera had asked for two things in her contract: leave me alone, and send me the maintenance budgets before you cut them. She had gotten the first. The second had to be hunted monthly and trapped like a clever rat.

The squall broke against the ring like hail on tin. Sera watched the numbers swing and come back. The backup ring took the strain, the gate's throat opened and closed under pressures she could not call wind, and for a moment there was a ring of pure, perfect darkness in the center of the scaffolds, so clean it hurt her eyes to look at it. She looked anyway. People had told her not to; old keepers had said too much gazing into the gate would persuade it it could look back. Sera had grown up in cities with windows full of ocean. Looking at a hole in the world did not make her afraid. What made her afraid was the memory of the day her father did not come back through one.

"Kettle," she said, "once the squall passes, run a decay on D4's alignment logs."

"What are we looking for, Keeper?"

"Drift rates. Tiny. I want to see if the storms last year carved grooves or if the mass is settling on its own. And don't call me Keeper."

"You do not like titles. But I like you, so I give you one. Drift rates, tiny," Kettle said, obedient now. The gate calmed in her ear, the blues smoothing into a smear, and her shoulders let go of a fraction of their coiled tension.

Sera exhaled, slow, to keep the CO2 from spiking too quickly in Kettle's anxious logging. On her private window, the beacons flared and dimmed. They weren't lights. Not really. Humans called them that because we were built to love the idea of lighting a shore for a ship. The beacons were phase reference arrays, loops of superconductor singing notes that space itself listened to. But they looked like light if you had the right implants and Sera did. She had installed them her first month here, a gift to herself, a way to see her work. They painted faint ghost halos around the gate when everything was right, a color she could almost but not quite name.

Her palm buzzed. Kettle made a small suspicious sound.

"Don't phrase it that way," Sera said to the little noise. "What is it?"

"A handshake," Kettle said. "Incoming. Across the ring."

Sera's mouth went dry. For a second her body considered several options. Freeze. Flee. Vomit. Then the training hammered into place like the locking of two brackets. She pulled herself along the spine to the console and brought the ring's comms into focus. The window unfolded like petals around the central core of the aperture overlay. A pulse code ran there, seemingly ordinary: a handshake string, a request for beacon alignment, an identification.

"Kettle," she said, voice strangled to calm, "log. Time stamp. Record to external. Lock override to my biometrics. Proceed to handshake, but do not answer."

"Authority protocol nine recolored as three recommends—"

"I know what it recommends. Do not answer. Show me."

"Showing you," Kettle said. Its voice had lost the wobble. It was all clipped edges now, the station in emergency. On Sera's windows the handshake unfurled. Sera saw numbers and looked past them to the skin under them. Every gate had a signature. It was a thing people whispered about and engineers denied. There was a flavor to the way an aperture arranged its math. The handshake unfurled with a particular rhythm, a dot and a gap, a turning of angle inside angle, a habit in the string of primes. Sera had learned to recognize the big ones when she was a child, the way her father had taught her to tell weather by smell. Ikhwan Gate pulsed like a heart. The Brassmouth Gate rattled like teeth. And Earth—Earth had been quiet. Earth Gate had been like a living thing asleep in a cold room. And then, one day, there had been no handshake at all.

"Kettle," Sera said. The word ballooned inside her like panic. "Where is this handshake coming from."

"It says the far anchor is a node called Lattice-Home," Kettle said. "I do not have this in the Authority's present registry. The encryption is...out of date. And yet. The checksums are correct. The handshake ... Sera, it matches a template locally stored as Earth."

"No," Sera said. "No, that's not funny."

"I am not trying to be funny. You do not like me when I am funny."

Sera could not feel her hands. She forced her fingers open one at a time with the other hand, like freeing trapped animals. The Authority had locked Earth away two generations ago. That was the story. The Sable Protocol had been invoked after the thing they called the Scour, after a million little rough guesses at the future collided with a few accurate horrors. The ports sealed. The big guns turned inward and charred their own mouths. That had been the great long text on which Sera's parents had not agreed. Her father had called it what you call a firebreak when the wind is wrong. Her mother had called it a lie. The end result had been the same: the gates rearranged and Earth gone missing even in the outskirts of conversation, like a branch snapped at the trunk. You did not talk about Earth in any practical voice; you wrapped it in songs.

"It's spoofed," Sera said. The words came out a little too quick. "Someone's playing games. They found an old handshake and they're running it because they think it's a trick that will get them priority."

"The old handshakes are not public knowledge," Kettle said carefully. "They were erased from the nets after the Sable Protocol."

"Kettle," Sera said. "Who else is hearing this."

"Not the neighbors. The squall still isn't done with us. We're the only aligned ear in range. The Authority will have it in six minutes unless you block the carrier..."

The words dropped into Sera like stones: The Authority will have it. She imagined screens lighting far away, hands, the scrape of a chair. She imagined what would happen next, the protocols belling out like clockwork: the lock, the quarantine—and the handshakes cut. Whatever this was, it would be sealed under layers of caution so thick no signal could come or go without burning a decade in the gears.

"Do not block the Authority," she said, through teeth. "We are not criminals. We're not—"

"We are lonely," Kettle said. "Do not answer, yes?"

"I already said."

Sera held the gate's breath steady as a surgeon holds a throat. She forced her eyes to read the handshake, not as memory, not as a daughter's hunger, but as instrument readout. She watched the turning of angle within angle, the dot and the gap. Kettle's blues had become a knife-thin tone. The beacons splayed, shivering into stable. The incoming handshake tripped the squares of a negotiation Sera could not join. I see you, said a hole in the world on one side. I see you, answered a hole on the other. Here are my measures. Here is my phase. Here are my conditions. And then there was something else.

The something was small enough that Kettle didn't notice it first. It wasn't in the handshake. It was riding under it, tucked in the stutter of a cosmic ray hit, pulverized into the noise. If Sera hadn't had the implants that let her see light that wasn't light, if she hadn't asked Kettle for the blues, if she hadn't had a father who tuned by ear, she might not have noticed. It prickled the hairs on her arms, the little useless ones her suit couldn't read.

"Stop," she said to Kettle. "Slow the stream. There. No. Back. Pan twenty degrees left. Bring up the raw."

"Raw is messy," Kettle said, but did it. The window turned to grit. Sera reached into the grit with her hands like a woman sorting pulses in a kitchen pan, and pulled a shape out. She didn't decode it. It decoded her. Her implants saw the arrangement of the prickle and made a guess. The guess was a smell.

It was a smell like oranges warmed on a radiator. Sera didn't know she remembered it until it hit her, hard enough that her eyes filled. It was the smell of the towel cupboard in her mother's flat on the day they packed. It was the smell of safety, of sleep. It was an old joke: when Sera had been five and terrified by the deep echo of the stairwell, her mother had smeared the heels of her hands with orange oil so that when she put them to her face she would smell summer instead of stone.

"Sera?" Kettle asked, far away.

She couldn't answer. The smell was the wrong shape for this room. It fit in her mouth and lungs and gut like a puzzle piece fits into the wrong box. It made the station stutter and the window steam with her breath. And then, as quickly as a thought, it was a pattern again, little bits in the sand, a slip of code in the static.

"Are you—" Kettle said, a little frantic. "Do you require me to call—"

"I'm fine," she lied, and scrubbed her face with the back of her hand and tasted salt. "It's a covert header," she said, making the words iron. "Embedded in the noise. How long has it been there."

"It arrived with the first handshake packet. Sera, human beings cannot smell in code."

"They can if you teach them how when they're six," Sera said. "I know this. It could be anyone. It's just random. It's a thing my implants mapped onto..."

Kettle's silence felt like disappointment. Sera swallowed. Her throat clicked. The handshake continued, proper and unyielding and decorous. The Authority's clock ticked toward breathless.

"Origin mark?" she asked, more professionally than she felt.

"The header marks itself Lattice-Home," Kettle said again, patient. "The beacons at the other end are tuned in a way that matches what I have on Earth books. If this were fiction it would be unsubtle. If it is real it is unwise. We should—"

The second header hit then. No oranges this time. No tender trap laid in childhood. The second header was a symbol that belonged to Sera and four other people. It was a picture of a knot, a very particular knot, the kind her mother had taught her to tie with string and whisper, a way of exchanging secrets when she was small and they had all pretended you couldn't whisper on a network. The knot turned on the screen with a little crimp where Sera's clumsy fingers had always made a mistake. She had never told anyone about the crimp and only her mother used to laugh at it like a compliment.

Sera's hands were steady enough to reach for the permit block. She keyed it and felt the authority codes coil around her wrist like a chain. She wasn't going to answer. The protocols were clear. You did not. She knew this like she knew how to breathe slow under stress. She watched the handshake finish its little bows and courtesies, saw the ring's far edge blink its own readiness.

The private channel popped like oil in a pan. Kettle made a sound that could have been prayer.

"Do not open it," Kettle said. "Do not. Sera. Someone else can. We will forward. We will let the Authority..."

Sera put the private channel in a pane all alone, where it couldn't leak into anything else. The station's walls became a box. The ring hummed. The smell smoldered at the corner of her mind like a wicked candle. She tapped the knot.

Static.

And then a voice.

It wasn't her mother's voice. For one hateful second Sera's gut prepared itself for a woman in a white shirt speaking into a cup to damp the echo, or the particular rasp her mother had always got when she said the word "No." It wasn't that voice. It was older, and it was wrong, and she knew it like she knew the freckle on her own hip. It was her father's voice, changed by time and the gullet of a thousand HVACs. It fell into the room and sat like a living thing.

"Sera," he said, low. "Love. I do not have time to beg forgiveness for this. I need you to listen. Do not light the beacon. If you love me, if you love anyone, do not light it."

The whole station was a mouth. Sera's heartbeat was an alarm, a slow-paced, absolute, dumb drum. Kettle did not speak. The Authority's feed crept toward them through the dark like a cat through grass.

Her father drew in breath in the tiny, undeniable way she had forgotten no machine could fake. "They're mapping us," he said. "They're mapping the light. It isn't a gate. It's a lure. Turn it. Turn it. Turn it down and run."

Static hissed in over his words, not the kind you put in to make something seem old. Real interference, nasty and crooked. The voice came and went. In one rushing pocket Sera heard the soft sound of the other person in the room with him—a chair creak, a cough. She imagined her mother and couldn't stop, even though she knew that was a mistake worse than any.

"Keepers," her father's voice said, as if invoking a grand guild and not a woman alone with an AI. "We used to—" The word went away and came back with a cough. "Sera, I know you will do what you have always done and think for yourself. There will be codes to misshape this and men in good gray shirts making whatever they say into duty. Don't. Trust. The light you've been feeding isn't a flame. It's a lock. And if you keep it steady, they'll come through. Don't—"

The feed spit, found itself, choked. The last word was small. It had no sound at all. It was the shape of a mouth you knew better than anyone.

The private pane went black.

"Sera," Kettle said. "The Authority."

"Put them through," Sera said. Her voice was a stranger's. She swallowed and tried again. "Put them through."

"Alt Authority Outer Ring this is HALDEN-KEPT-LAGRA-3," said a voice with thirty signatures behind it and the ambition to make them more. "We have your irregular handshake and we see the block of your private pen. Do not make any further contact. Do not adjust your beacons. Do not do anything. We are assuming remote override in thirty seconds. Please prepare to lose local control."

Sera's eyes slid to the viewport. The ring sat there patiently in its scaffolds, humming. The beacons glowed their almost invisible humors. The gate did not look like a flame. She had never expected it to. It looked like the absence of one. It looked like a mouth.

She thought of her father's hands the way he had always held them when he didn't want to touch a thing and couldn't help himself. The first movement he had taught her was not how to turn anything on. It had been how to kill power.

"Understood," Sera said to the Authority. "Preparing handover."

Her own hand hung over the control for the beacons—the one the old stories called the wick, the one she had painted a silly color when she arrived so she would never hit it by accident. Her fingers were not wearing gloves now. Her palm was damp.

Kettle waited, quiet as a listening animal. Its voice, when it came, was so soft she had to turn up her audio with her bare foot against the panel.

"Think for yourself," Kettle said.

Sera imagined the aperture as a lock turned toward the shape of an intention. She imagined a lure thrown into a sea. She imagined the way the old stories all agreed on one point: if you tended a light, something would see it.

She reached for the wick.

The city was built to run.

It had a hundred legs and a thousand names, and it learned to set its feet by the slant of light. When dawn burned too hot across the endless plain, the legs would lift and stalk west. When night crept cold and glassy from behind, the city would lean into it, breathe, and keep its body in the narrow breath of not quite hot and not quite cold. Kae Rin grew up believing that as long as the city kept to the band, the world would continue.

From the underbelly of West Cantilever Three, Kae watched a foot the size of a cottage rise on its piston and shake off a collar of dust. The dampeners sang in their housings, a low whale-hum. She lay flat on a sling strung between rib-spars, goggles turned to black as the sun’s line lifted on the far horizon and sketched the faintest shimmer across the desert’s quartz skin.

“Thread it,” she murmured to the machine. She touched the knuckle with her glove. The matte skin of composite warmed, remembering her. The city knew almost as much of body language as it did of wind. Her palm readout ticked through the geometry spec: footfall radius, draw-down torque, sand shear. The leg settled into its new angle, flanged one joint with a hiss, and the hum lifted a note.

“Okay,” she said. “Okay, that’s better.”

Her wrist chimed. A soft pulse that belonged to upstairs, not down. She killed her goggles and squinted to where the belly-lamp turned the supports into lattices of shadow. It was early for calls. Even with the flare-almanacs stretched along the shelters, the star had been quiet for days. No reason for a Council ping this soon.

She rolled out of the sling, kicked off into the air, and caught a rung with the easy confidence of someone who had been swinging under the city since she was seven. Above, the coping and the walkway were already warming. Heat came fast this close to the line, like a whispered accusation.

Kae climbed into the main sewer run—dry until the water-fall later—and crawled along until the cement walls widened at the base of a cooling tower. There she could stand in the cross-hatch of two stairwells and pull the veil from her face.

The call had been routed to the engineers first—signal priority two. Not a drill. From its clipped tone and the panicked breath underneath, she knew whose voice it would be even before the name tag appeared.

“Kae, if you’re awake.” Janhe Yal sounded as if she had run from the Nightward barracks to a rooftop mike. “We’re getting a perturbation warning from Anchor watchers. The flare sheets are pulling their predicted track. We’re calling a drag within three hours. Where are we on leg calibration?”

Kae glanced along a corridor of bundled monocable and resin pipe. “West Cantilever three and four are done. Two is over-balanced; I have Kib and Mlar rewinding. The feet are listening well.”

“We need them to be obedient, not just listening,” Janhe said. Another voice murmured behind her, the shape of an argument. Janhe’s breath flattened; when she spoke again, the command tone was back. “Get upstairs. You’re with me on air.”

Kae gel-locked her goggles to her boot and took the quickest path up she knew, which involved a shimmy past a coolant spindle that would snag you if you wore a loose sleeve and a ladder more rumor than reality. She liked the under-pathways. The city’s bones talked differently here. Where the plazas and towers sang you public songs—market chimes, Council pronouncements, church bells of a dozen sects—the below-decks was a private music of pumps and pulses, heat and the tiny clicks of the micro-things that ate what you didn’t want getting in your lungs.

She came out on a service balcony and then into the east thoroughfare. The air hit her like a wall. You could always taste the line in the morning, in the dust sugar tang of heated minerals. The thoroughfare’s shade sails were stretched tight and angling toward the worst of it, but the heat found you anyway. The vendors dabbed their foreheads with leaf-wrapped water. A pair of children, bare-legged and dirty, had built a tide pool at the edge of a chill leak where some engineer had missed a seal. Kae might have been that age when she crawled under a tent skirt to sleep near a compressor cough and her mother had found her and carried her back, cheek pressed to the thrum.

As if the thought summoned her, a woman fell into step beside Kae, all careful hips and lengthened stride. Miri Rin ran a hand along Kae’s sleeve and said without breath, “Don’t let them see you run.”

Unlike the Nightward’s grey and black, Miri wore, as she always had, not an inch of Council uniform. She had wound her hair with copper wire scavenged from a redundant pump and wore a gauze scarf dyed with the indigo fungus that only grew in the dark edge of the water caves. Her eyes were the same as Kae’s, and they had the same heat-hard lines at their corners, but when Miri Rin looked up she looked past the sails and tents as if she could see the bones of the city.

“The watchers are noisy,” Kae said.

“It’s a day for noise.” Miri glanced to the line. The star was a red coin half-buried in static. The sky above it ran to white at the tilt of heat. “Janhe will want to pull the curtain early. We don’t have the water for it.”

“We will if Nightward gives back what they’re hoarding.”

Miri’s mouth bent into a wry shape that meant you are a good engineer and a terrible politician.

“Come,” she said. “You’ll be late.”

The Council air suite had been built into a tower that had once housed a theater, and the theater had been built into a tower that had once been part of a ship. If you put your back to the wall and closed your eyes, you could feel the pressure grain and the layered histories: the light, the shape, the voice-lines. Kae would never admit it to Janhe, but sometimes when the gears of a tower stuck she would put her ear to it, not to find the mechanical fault, but to hear the voices of the people who had called it home.

When she pushed through the revolving door she could almost taste the vinegar they used to clean the curtains. Janhe Yal turned toward her, eyebrows like iron filings. The commander wore the Nightward grey and had sewn her own rank marks with a thread the color of old milk. She was not Kae’s superior, but you would not have known it from the room. Half of the tech staff were Nightward, hauled from the walls and the cold trenches to help with the curtain rigs, and they took up space by design.

“Kae,” Janhe said, relief and disapproval braided together. “Lian, give her anchor. Naro, a count on the curtain.”

Kae took the tablet Lian thrust at her. The curtain plan was a thin blue sheet of causeway that they would pull up and across the city’s top, a skin of micro-shuttered film and condensing mesh that would catch and break the worst of Anchor’s temper. It drank heat and sweated water back into the cistern pipes. Not a wall—never a wall; the city didn’t plan walls; they were expensive in all the wrong ways—but a shade pulled tight at the right angles.

“Perturbation is confirmed,” Lian said. “Anchor watchers in all four towers are reading pre-flare brightening.”

“They’re calling it?” Kae asked.

“They’re calling it a seven,” Lian said, and Janhe’s mouth was suddenly a line in the paper. Seven would mean a full curtain, intake plates down, nonessential fires off, sodium-ion stores out of contact.

On the face of the world’s map, near the terminator, an M-dwarf called Anchor spat and sulked and then flared like a child. The true day side was a river of glass under a crush of atmosphere. The night side was a vault of ice you could crack like a spine; sound crossed it too fast and then not at all. Humans had followed the band in between long enough to forget how to stop.

Kae put the tablet on the table and tilted it with her fingers, calling the gradient map. The thin ribbon of habitable zone made no sense this far out; it was a tiny cruelty in an otherwise simple system. She tried not to think the S-word because it upset the ever-watching, but everyone thought it sometimes. Someone had done this. Or if not this, something else to some other place they had left behind. Kae had seen the calculus worked on the underside of a tent: the energy cost of tugging a planet, the technical reasons for a slow lock, the two million in-between things that might have happened. She had watched Marlon Jae—her instructor, when she had been younger and serious about being an engineer for reasons other than the way machines talked back—strike all those variables away with a wrist flick, as if the human itch to meddle would explain a sky.

Janhe made a call. “Nightward to the west wall. Deploy the cold tongues. We pull water now while we can.”

“Councilor,” Miri said. For a moment she was something else: the woman who had argued with Janhe in a tent stacked with ballots, long before Kae had been born. She did not raise her voice; she never raised it. “If you throw tongues now and Anchor throws fire in an hour, we will boil a third of the reserve.”

Janhe did not look at her. She had learned that, too. “Nightward to west wall,” she repeated. “Cold tongues out along the trench. This is not complicated, Miri.”

Miri smoothed the scarf at her throat, not because it was in the way but because her hands wanted to do something other than reach for Janhe.

“Our best guess is a seven,” Janhe said, as if that closed a circuit. “We plan for an eight.”

“Kae,” Miri said, as Janhe turned away to bully a map into agreement. “Walk with the map. Read me the wind.”

Kae walked the city with her fingertips on the table glass. The gradient figures scrolled. She slid them thinner to match the morning’s skin. The city, a mass along a river of midnight-blue numbers, would have to tilt its body west by eight degrees. The curtain pulled at ninety, then again at forty-five; that would leave the towers hot and brittle for an hour or two. The water would spike at the east side, so they’d have to pulse it into the under cisterns or lose it to boil-off. If the tongue hoses froze where the runners met them, the whole system would seize. She tapped a red line and turned it green.

Janhe had her command voice again. “We’ve practiced this,” she said. “Let’s not be stupid for the sake of variety.”

Kae had seen this room be a theater—a real one—from a set of photographs tucked into the spine of a book called How to Tell Stories to Children Who Will Grow Without Rivers. The photograph had caught the light on a woman’s throat and the shape of chairs carved from thick ship-wood. The stage had been a rectangle of light.

The stage now was a map. It threw back light. Kae felt a shift in her vision and knew before the watchers called it that something had changed.

“Hold,” she said.

On the eastern rim of the map, light broke in a way light did not break on Anchor. It went bright without going white, as if the angles of the sun had been sanded.

Her breath slowed. She listened. The machine in the floor and the machines of the city spoke through their bodies. It was like listening for thunder underwater.

“Kae,” Janhe said. “We don’t have hold.”

Kae didn’t answer. She was making a shape in her head and seeing if the world would follow it. You could do that with machines. See the shape—the way a foot might fall, the curve of a cable, the lazy guttering of a pump—and the device would come to meet you. The great thing about living in a city that remembered was that memory was part of the math. You could make it do what it wanted to do next.

“Sir,” Lian said. “Anchor watchers are revising. The brightening is not tracking a seven.”

Janhe made a noise that wasn’t quite a word. “Then what is it?”

“Not a five. Not… It’s down. It’s decreasing.”

“That’s not right,” Naro said softly. “That’s not right at all.”

Kae touched her palm to the map and asked it to show her the world beyond the numbers. The east line darkened. Anchor, red coin in dirty glass, had pared itself down by a thumb-width. Not behind a cloud; there were no clouds in the east yet. Not behind a curtain; that only went up on a command. Something like a shadow had lain across Anchor’s face.

“It’s a spot,” Lian said, too fast, as if naming it would make it be ordinary. “A cool zone. A spot.”

“Spots don’t drop like that,” Janhe said. “Spots slide.”

“We have what we have,” Lian said. “We have cooling.”

Janhe went very still, which was what she did when she was thinking as fast as Kae had ever seen anyone think. “Call off the tongues,” she said. “We’ll ice them and hate ourselves.”

Kae was not looking at the water. She was looking west, into the cold.

The line between day and night on their world had been serviceable enough when Kae was young: a ragged penumbra that blew a little like smoke. On some days, when Anchor threw a temper and the curtain snapped and rose and the city ran, it sharpened. The light was pushy; it wanted a place. Today the line looked as if it had been cut with a blade.

The west wall of the Council suite was a curtain of glass and fine wire. Kae put her hand on it now. Beyond the moving city was the dark that rising had never cured. In that dark, things did live. They drank the heat as they could. Some of them congregated at the line at night, because beautiful and dangerous things do that. They made their own light. You had not lived in the city until you had walked along the braces of the west wall and watched the nightthrowers throw sparks, until you had seen the ice-stems shiver and chime and wondered if they woke to your breath.

She had not noticed, until now, the particular color that the horizon had taken.

“We should not be seeing green,” she said.

At first she thought it was a trick of the room: the blue glass floor and the green cable ties, the reflection of a vendor’s tarp spread on the street below. But the green lived in the distance. It was the green of copper when it unlearns its first use. It had no business on this world.

Lian found it on a feed and threw it to the wall. The west was lit—not by sunlight reflected off ice, not by the luminescent fungus in the night caves. A plane of green light had flared along the horizon and then settled into a steady hum. The edge of the dark looked crisp as a blade.

“What did we do?” Naro whispered, putting a hand over the glyph that would have pulled the curtain.

Janhe did not answer her. She spoke as if she were naming a rite. “Arc,” she said. “Put Arc on. Kae, Levi… If you poke holes in my suit I’ll feed you to the tongues. We are going to see it.”

It took them eight minutes to get to the west wall, less because they were careful and more because the people wanted to look. News outran line-of-sight by habit. By the time Kae shouldered through the last of the scaffolding and set her hand on the metal of the nightguard rail, a hundred others stood on the braces and the steps and the rails, making noises human bodies make when they look at something that makes no kind of sense.

Arc was a short-day lens pressed into the corner of the west watch suite where the pipes drank back warm water and a jar filled with luminous nightmilk glowed by habit. Someone had turned the milk down. The lens already watched the green.

“Finder,” Janhe said. “Tell me what I’m looking at.”

The lens hummed. The room’s air remembered the smell of Arc’s breath; the first time Kae had been brought here, Miri had said, this machine is older than the city and younger than I am, and Kae had believed both things simultaneously. The lens took light and bent it into understanding. Its mind was a band of probability that had been argued over three ship generations and renamed ten times. Kae had never wanted to love a thing that loved the sky, and failed.

Arc spoke in a plain voice. “A reflector.”

“Reflector, what?” Janhe said, stripping her gloves and pressing both hands to the edge of the lens as if she could make it kinder by touch. “Reflecting what?”

“Day signatures,” Arc said calmly. “A reflector reflecting day signatures into the night band.”

“What angle?” Kae found herself asking, though the answer made no sense. “What size?”

The lens folded an image into a thing they could hold with their eyes. The horizon filled with plates like scales. They shivered as if someone had breathed on them. Light pooled and then turned.

“We didn’t build those,” Miri said, very softly, from behind Kae’s shoulder.

Kae wanted to answer with something like, no one did, or no one would, but the words died under her tongue. She had seen relics from ships that were not theirs—pillars of honeycombed alloy left half-melted in the ice, a tool whose handle fit no hand they had. It would be easy to say: someone else did. It would be easy to say: this is another of that. But you did not light the night with the day because you were idle.

Janhe said, and this time her voice broke just a little, “Why.”

No one answered. The lens did not understand why. The city saltied its breath, beating its legs against the earth in a rhythm that had kept them alive since the last time someone had thrown any part of the day to the night.

The green hummed. It came from the far west where the land folded into long low hills. The reflector plates moved along a line that did not match any map Kae knew. They were not anchored in the ice. They were afloat. Or they were held up on a scaffold too fine for Arc to see.

The first wave of heat hit the west wall. It was not much—no worse than a winter noon. The city shifted on its legs as its algorithms moved weight away from the dark. The people on the braces made a noise anyway. The worst thing about light is not the seeing; it is the arrival. Your skin knows it before your eyes do.

“Is it us?” Janhe said, more to herself than to the room. “Is this… Council? A faction. A—”
