“Then it is the best-kept secret since the city learned to say its own name," Miri said dryly. She stood with her hands folded and her scarf undone, indigo stripes grown dark. “No one moves plates like that quietly. No one pulls a scaffold into the night without a thousand runners knowing.”

Kae had half a thought and then it was a whole thought and then it had teeth. “We shouldn’t be seeing the plates,” she said. “The angle’s wrong. If they’re reflecting, and we’re seeing the green, we should be seeing glare. Not the structure. Those plates shouldn’t be visible at this angle.”

Janhe’s eyes flicked to her. “So?”

“So they’re not plates. Or they’re plates folded with—" She reached for a word that did not exist thirty years ago and existed now because someone had given her a way to get invaded by it. “—with skin.”

The lens’s image sharpened and then blurred. Arc was trying to decide whether it was allowed to believe Kae. Sometimes that made Kae want to shake it by the throat. She had once, privately, asked it a question that was only half about mechanics and half about why her mother never stood in a doorway like other people did, and Arc had said, the answer is not mine to give, and Kae had wanted to cry and laugh and put her ear to the machine to listen for the world’s apology. You wanted to forgive your machines when they were honest about their limits.

The green stepped up a note. Heat touched Kae’s cheeks—strange, from the west—and the city made a collective sound that wasn’t quite fright. The legs adjusted again, shifting west but not fast, and not as if they wanted to run.

Janhe looked like she wanted to put her face into wind and scream, which was not her way. “Do we have a voice?” she said suddenly. “Is anyone talking to us?”

The west watch had always been mostly eyes, not ears, but it had a scattering of mics pointed toward the cold. Naro tuned them, the way you might tune a guitar. It filled the room with the small breaths of ice and the larger breath of the city in the distance, a low throb.

Then, through that, something else.

A signal long and plain and patient. It could have been a foghorn if the night had been water.

Miri straightened. “Play it.”

Naro played the sound twice, three times. The room, which had been full of murmurs, quieted. It was rude to speak when someone else was translating.

Arc said, “Sentence markers. Old keys. The fourth and second of your—” It stopped for a fraction of a second, terrible for a machine that did not stutter. “The fourth and second. A word once used in ships like your mothers.”

“What word,” Janhe said, very softly.

“Arrival,” Arc said.

Kae’s body did something she could not name. Her hands went cold and her mouth filled with the taste of the coolant they’d used that morning on Cantilever Two. She knew that word, and not only because she had read it in books and heard it at funerals and uttered it at festivals. She knew it because when she had been ten, her mother had put her palm to a piece of city metal and said, do you feel that. Do you feel how it moves. Do you feel how it remembers.

Behind the tabletop calm of the lens and the mapping and the water plan, the city had other voices, and those voices had always counted themselves as a we. The first time Kae had tried to think of the city as a single body, she had choked on the laughter of it. That’s the kind of thing a person does when she wants a god who will listen and finds one who hums.

On her wrist, where she had set her own filters too low for ordinary noise to get through, the old band vibrated with a signal so old no one used it for anything but materials inventory. It said, very quietly, the way a person speaks to the back of a sleeping animal’s neck: Kae Rin, arrange your ears. It said: We have arrived.

Her mother’s hand found her elbow. Miri did not squeeze. She did not have to. “Don’t jump,” she said, and Kae realized, with a distantly terrified part of her brain, that she could feel the city’s legs wanting to.

“What does it mean,” Janhe said. “Arc. Answer me.”

Arc did not answer. It did that thing where it turned its head toward a place outside the room, even though it did not have a head. Kae had never liked that. It made her feel as if some part of their house had decided that the walls were not as trusted as it had once thought. Then Arc inclined itself toward Kae like a person, which it never did, because it never had cause to address a mechanic who was not an operator.

“Kae Rin,” Arc said. “There is a protocol keyed to your family name. There is a door in the west wall. Please open it.”

Kae’s heart kicked. She knew, of course she knew, that a family could set a private protocol into a machine and that the machine would remember it after the family had gone. There were songs for that. They sang them at child namings. They sang them when someone died.

But her mother had never been that sort of woman. Miri did not like doors that belonged to one person instead of a we. She did not like the kind of inheritance that could get your neck broken and your house burned. She had once turned down a Council seat because she hated the taste of power and that kind sucked it like sugar.

Kae did not look at her mother. She looked at Janhe Yal, who looked back at her with a face made blank by will.

“Open the door,” Janhe said.

And that was how, on a day when the star pretended to be less hot and the night learned to glow with a color that had never belonged to it, Kae put her hand to a piece of night-cold metal in the west wall that she had never seen before, and felt it open along a line that fit her palm.

Behind it, darkness waited. Not the cold dark of ice and breath stopped with fear. Not the theater-dark of curtains and hush. This was the kind of dark where you could walk, and the sort where you could talk to something older than your city and know it would talk back.

“Don’t go in,” Miri said, her voice very careful. “Not alone.”

Kae stepped forward, and something on the horizon—a line of emerald, bending; a wall of light with skin—shivered in answer. The city lifted its legs. The world held its breath. A voice, not quite the machine’s and not wholly human, said from inside the dark:

Say my name, Kae Rin. Then step where the city has been saving a place for you.

She had not thought until that moment that a place might be saving her. She had thought, like most who were born to machines, that she was the one who did the saving.

Behind her, someone began to pray. In front of her, the dark tasted like old ship air. She opened her mouth.

And somewhere outside, in the green-lit night, something else answered.

On some mornings the tide dragged in the future still dripping with other weather and left it in smeared pools among the rocks below Pier Seven. It had the smell of hot dust and snow, of scorched books and cut apples, of the inside of a watch left too long on a radiator. The air above the Port of Glass made Kade’s teeth sing, and the hair along their arms stood up in a faint, ridiculous salute to the distant thunder that was not thunder at all.

Kade had grown up to that hum. They could sleep with it—lean into it like a body against a railing—as easy as other people slept to the sigh of actual sea. It was a comfort until it wasn’t. The day the Strand took Lio, the hum had become a scream, and afterward Kade learned to hear a jaggedness under the regular throb, a tooth chipped in some enormous cog beyond the sky, catching and letting go.

They told themselves this morning was not jagged. The burn of cold on their face was fine, the layers of their slicker worked, and the rope around their waist had a new splice that lay like silk. The wind was obstinate, but the thin rain it flung had only one edge. Below, the Strand showed its slow belly. Banks of pearled foam leaned toward the canted pilings. Between them, the surface looked like a tilted sheet of lead; under that sheet, slow gears turned and turned.

Kade stood on the plank at the end of Pier Seven and slung out their line. The line was twice-woven: hemp core, copper sheath. The copper was for luck. It glittered dull grey this morning; good. Anything too bright meant charge in the air would ride it straight back into your hands, and then the Chronology Office would have to scrape your fingerprints off the hammers again. Mama Sant would say they had better things to do.

“Kade!” Noll’s voice, gruff as a cleat. He was halfway down the ladder of Pier Six, his cap jammed low.

“I’m on Seven,” Kade called back without turning. “Your eyes still work? You can see there’s six meters between seven and six.”

“You never learned to count. You know I’m telling you to meet me at Five. Color’s wrong on your side.”

Kade squinted against the rain. He was right. The gray of the water near Pier Five was the softer of the two, and in the softer gray you could wade to your knees and have only your boots knocked sideways. On Seven, the gray shattered as if it had just remembered an insult. Kade’s weight shifted to the balls of their feet. The line went taut and sang.

“I’ve already got something,” they said, because stubbornness had carried them this far in life and would probably carry them to the end. “You want it or should I—”

“Hold it. We’ll haul at Five.” Noll’s steady steps on wood. The way he moved was a map Kade could read blindfolded: the set of his shoulders, the pause at each bolt where the pier’s repaired section began. Eleven years a partner and he still moved like he expected the deck to sink.

Kade paid out rope hand over hand and fixed the copper-sheathed length into the clips that lined the pier’s edge. The clips were anchored into bedrock with time-hardened spikes and sainted according to some dock superstition older than this town. Kade believed in the spikes. They pretended with their whole mouth that they didn’t believe in the saints.

The rope tugged. There was weight on it like a thing alive, jerking twice and then lying.

“Easy,” Noll said close behind. He was big and damp and smelled like clove oil. “Feel that?”

“I feel it wanting to go where it goes.”

“Like you,” he said, but his hands wrapped around the rope just above Kade’s, thumbs against the copper, taking some of the drag. He had an ugly scar across the back of his right hand from a day he hadn’t been quick enough. Kade pretended not to watch that hand.

“Anchor,” Kade said. Noll nodded. He drove the first of the anti-echo stakes in with two fast blows of the fall hammer. The hammer was weary wood, its metal head welded up from three older heads; it sucked the ring out of its own strikes. After the second blow, the rope settled. Whatever it held, it was not going back to wherever the tide had been. At least not today.

“You picked Seven because you like a fight,” Noll said conversationally. “Or because you think you can keep me from seeing what you’ve netted by making me work for it.”

“Don’t be stupid,” Kade said, and both of them pretended it was a joke.

The tide flexed, and along Pier Nine the yellow horn lit. It didn’t sound—sound would spook the Strand into one of its moods—but the light was warning enough. A skimmer boat darted out from the Chronology Office’s dock, bright crimson in the gray. Two Office Wardens in long oilskins swayed aboard, their pale faces looking already scoured of curiosity. Mama Sant would be in there too, somewhere, keeping her hands out of her pockets so no one could say anything about bribes sticking to them.

“We should hurry,” Kade said.

“As if I ever do anything else with you,” Noll said, and tore the last knot through his brass ring. “On three. One—”

They hauled. They had hauled anchors heavy as cars, had hauled crates full of tools that had not been invented yet, had hauled rope twisted into shapes Kade did not have the math to name. This weight was like something full of water but also full of light: sloshing and resisting, sticky on the skin of the world.

Kade leaned back, boots braced, rope biting across their palms through the gloves. The rain thickened. The copper in the rope warmed, then cooled. Kade felt the exact moment when the thing on the other end found the lip of the shelf below the pier and scraped against it, and the sting of that friction sang along their bones.

“Careful,” Noll hissed. “No sudden—”

“I know.” Kade eased to one side, letting the rope play around the second stake so it made a neat angle, a neat little law describing the world. The weight shifted and slid, and then the surface between the turn in the rope and the pier went barn-flat again.

“Back it up,” Noll said, because the Strand loves sudden lurches and will take anything it can get. They both took a step back, then another, so that they came up next to the block and tackle mounted on Pier Seven’s last pile. They pulled the line through the tackle’s hungry throat and Noll snapped shut the catch. The catch’s little inscription—NEITHER HERE NOR THERE—was almost completely worn away by years of palm oil and salt.

The rope creaked. The stakes shuddered. The thing under the water rose like a whale that had been pretending to be a shipwreck.

It broke the skin of the Strand with a tidy, triumphant slap. Water sheeting off it lagged behind by a heartbeat, as if the body of the tide had to decide to let go. It was a chest. Not large—maybe the size of a traveling trunk—brass-bound in the old fashion, with a rounded lid and the green stains of copper rot seeping down the sides. It wore a fur of barnacles that were not barnacles, made of brittle glass, and the locking plate was a new design Kade had never seen before and had been trying not to tell themselves they had already seen in dreams.

“Don’t,” Noll said softly.

“What?” Kade’s mouth was dry. Their palms were slick inside their gloves. That was fine. Hearts should beat. Bodies should leak.

“You’ve got a look on your face,” Noll said. “The same look you had when you started carrying your lock picks in your boot.”

“I never—”

“You’re wearing that boot,” he said. “I know it. I’m telling you not to take anything off without me.”

Kade tried to swallow. The Strand splashed the pier with water not water, and their teeth clicked against one another twice.

Around them, the port woke. People had been waiting at the rails, half-hoping, half-praying the Strand would bring their lost things back. A woman with a scarf over her head made the sign against reflection—two fingers drawn across mouth and forehead. A boy with slate eyes, ferrying a basket of eel chips, stopped dead. The skimmer from the Office cut a tidy wake, that crimson splitting gray. The horns at Pier Two lighted as well; the Strand was surging in some new way to the south. Today was going to be a difficult day.

Kade and Noll got the chest up and over the lip of the pier. It thunked solidly and lay there like it had every right to, like they were the ones who should explain themselves.

“Get rid of those.” Noll nodded toward the glass barnacles. Kade took the scraper from their belt and worked them loose. They cracked like sugar, and under them the wood of the chest was burnished dark.

As soon as Kade cleared the lock plate, their breath stopped.

It was stamped with a maker’s mark in the brass, worked into the metal with a neat little punch: three nested circles, offset so they suggested a spiral, and a notch taken at the lower left like a bite out of a coin. Not just any maker’s mark. The one Kade had drawn a thousand times in the back of a throwaway notebook and on napkins and once on the underside of Noll’s hat brim: the mark they had settled on for their shop if they ever got out from under debt in this port and took their hammers inland, the mark they had not yet used, because to use it you had to pay the registry fee and you had to be brave, and Kade, for all their foolishness, had not been that.

It wasn’t exactly the same. The notch was a hair higher. The inner circle was turned a fraction. Tiny things, only a hand would know them. Only Kade’s hand.

Noll saw the way Kade had gone very still. He leaned in, squinting. “Well,” he said. It was not disgust or amusement. It was the word he used when something impossible and important had just set its plates down in the middle of his day.

Kade’s mouth found words. “It doesn’t mean anything.”

“No,” he said gently. “It doesn’t mean anything.”

The sound of the Office skimmer grew louder. Kade heard the little slap of waves against its hull and the ridged hum of its motors. Mama Sant would step on and off its deck without looking like she was stepping, and her eyes would skid over a dozen little deceptions and snag on the one that mattered.

“We register it,” Noll said. “We do it right. If it belongs to you, it will still belong to you in an hour.”

“Does ‘belong’ even mean anything here?” Kade said. The Strand had a sense of humor about property. They thought of the debt ledger kept in the back room of Sunside Tavern. They thought of their grand plan scratched out in tiny precise letters on a paper they kept folded and folded in the inner pocket of their jacket: a drawing of a sign, a list of costs, a plan for a wall. The three circles. The notch.

Noll’s jaw moved, twice. “Don’t be a fool.”

“I’d have to be one to be here at all,” Kade said, and the words came out with a brightness that made Noll’s eyes narrow. They put the scraper away. They rested their palm on the chest’s dark lid. The wood was warm, and in that warmth there were pulses, faint and regular as breath. For an instant, Kade had the sick, exhilarating sense that the chest was already opening, that the future had little hinges that clicked as gently as a mouth.

They took their hand away. They wiped it on their slicker. The sound of the skimmer swelled.

“Fine,” Kade said. “We register it.” They bent and slid their pry iron under the lock plate and used their body weight to lever the chest up and into the glass net they kept bundled under the cleat. “And we don’t tell anyone anything we don’t have to. Not yet.” That was the compromise Noll would take. It meant they had thirty breaths and a lie before the Office put their stamp on the day.

Together they heaved. The net slipped around the chest and the weights clicked into place. Noll ran the tag through the clip, stamped it with the day and the pier number. He was meticulous about tags. Mama Sant said that’s why he’d lived this long.

They got the chest onto the dolly, lashed it. The dolly’s wheels squeaked and then fell into silence—it was as if they had remembered who they were and what they were doing. Kade and Noll pushed, their boots squeaking on the wood, and Kade kept theirs on the left wheel to brake if the Strand drafted a spiteful wind up through the slip and tried to yank the whole thing into the drink.

A Warden stepped onto the head of Pier Seven. He had the gray cap they all wore pulled low and the little blue triangle pin Mama Sant had pushed through legislation last year pinned to his collar. The pin was supposed to mean they had remembered that the Strand took Lio, that you did not waste people by making them argue while the world shifted underfoot.

“Morning,” he said, pleasantly enough.

“Is it?” Noll said, and because they were old acquaintances, the Warden laughed.

“Wind wants to teach us something. That it has hands too, I think.” He glanced at the chest like it was a person he did not want to meet eyes with. “Chronology Office will have a look.”

“It will,” Noll said. He did not say anything else. The Warden blinked, perhaps a hair thrown: Noll normally had a comment, a small weather report or a joke. Then he didn’t push. Another thing to love about the Office in this port: you could lean on the rules, but if you leaned too hard, the rules leaned back.

“Pier Two’s gone yellow,” the Warden said. “You’ll want to pull off.”

“We’re pulling,” Kade said, because if they didn’t say something they were going to say the wrong thing. “We’ll stop at Five for the muck scrape.”

The Warden nodded. “Mama’s on Four,” he said, and Kade’s stomach dropped with the little click of incoming. It was always better to meet Mama Sant when you had three hours of paperwork in a buffer between you and whatever it was she wanted you for.

They trundled. Kade kept their mouth shut, which took work. The Strand flung a handful of steel-smelling spray and the dolly skated an inch. Kade corrected. The rain slicked their knuckles when they adjusted the lashings on the net.

Noll said, so low that Kade felt the words in the bones of their wrist where their hand touched the dolly: “Keep your face straight.”

“What face?”

“The one that thinks all plans are knives.”

“I don’t—”

“You do. I like you. I have to say it out loud more than once: I like you. Keep your face. And keep your mouth, Kade.”

They hit the plank that connected Seven to Six and the dolly bumped. The chest inside the net bumped in sympathy. A sound came from it then, the most ordinary thing in the world: a thump and then a sliding knock as if books shifted against one another in a satchel. Kade held their breath.

On Pier Five, the muck scrape had already made a business of itself. Two teens in oilskins were up to their calves in Strand scum, pushing it with squeegees toward the catch grates that fed into the back-room filters they cleaned for half a cup of soup and a story. Mama Sant said if you could make money and keep the Strand off your pilings at the same time, you did it. Anything else was more romantic than she had time for.

“Kade,” the shorter of the teens said. “You got something fat today.” Her grin was all needle teeth. Kade liked her because she asked the right questions and also because she asked very few.

“Ask your mother for a higher grade,” Kade said, and the girl laughed.

They pulled the dolly to the scrape station. The station was a joke, really: a name given to a hose and a rack and the right to use a broom on things that had never technically touched the ground. Noll hosed the chest; the Strand water that ran off it smoked faintly where it touched the pier’s old wood then blew cool. He scrubbed with a stiff brush. He carved off the last of the glass that didn’t want to be glass anymore.

“Tag on this is fine,” a voice said, and Kade’s heart did a neat trick where it trotted into the next second and looked back. Mama Sant stepped onto Pier Five with the little gliding gait, like her soles did not quite touch the wood because she was ninety percent knee and elbow, all focus. She had a thin scar on her lip that moved when she smiled, cutting the smile in half.

“Morning,” she said to both of them, but her eyes stayed on Kade. “How’s your sister?”

Kade felt the bite of the name in their chest and wondered, not for the first time, if Mama Sant did it on purpose to see if their face would crack and the light inside their head leak out.

“She’s dead,” Kade said.

“Right,” Mama Sant said. “Some mornings you forget what carried you to work.”

“Some mornings,” Noll said, and his voice made the words soft. Mama’s eyes flicked to him and then away.

She touched the chest with two fingers like she was checking a pie for heat. “You get this out of a soft patch or a hard one?”

“Hard,” Kade said. There was no harm in that. Everyone on the pier could see the way their shoulders carried the morning.

“I like a hard patch,” Mama Sant said. “It makes the paperwork easier when I can write ‘risk was assumed.’” She bent and studied the face of the lock. Kade held very still. For a second Mama’s gaze snagged on the maker’s mark—but she had a hundred of those in her head, a thousand—and then slid off. Kade felt sick with the relief of not being known.

“You try it yet?” Mama said.

“We don’t try,” Noll said.

“The day you don’t try is the day you can’t use your hands anymore,” Mama Sant said, as if she were tired of this particular lie of his and didn’t have time to play. “Bring it in. You get a receipt. You get a cut when it learns how to belong to somebody again. And I get a chance to take noisy things out of it before they fall into someone’s living room at midnight and scare their children.”

“Seems reasonable,” Noll said.

“It’s reasonable the way gravity is reasonable,” Mama said. “Even God had to deal with gravity.” She tapped the lid again with her knuckles. “If this is food or medicine or a bomb, the day is different. If it is letters, I will make you wish my parents had never met because I like to watch people cry on my floor.”

Kade couldn’t help it. “What if it’s just a box?”

“Then I will send you back to the Strand to find me a better story,” Mama Sant said. It was a joke. Some part of Kade, the part that had watched Lio’s hair go like a ribbon in a machine and then not be, did not think the word “just” belonged to anything on this pier.

They pushed. Mama Sant walked beside them like someone taking the last flanking place in a parade. All the while Kade’s palm itched where it had rested on the chest, as if the wood had left a shadow under their skin, a warm oval that did not know yet whether it was a brand or a benediction.

The Chronology Office in the Port of Glass was a long low building with a back full of machines, most of which were less impressive than they sounded. Kade had seen them up close: flux sinks the size of bathtubs, timekeeping pendulums thick as Noll’s waist, arrays of little vibrating forks that sang a note you couldn’t hear unless you put your teeth right against the panel. The front of the Office was for people. It had a queue and a counter and a hunk of glass mounted on the wall behind the counter that everybody loved to stare at. The hunk of glass was a slice of something they called collapse froth—a sound made into matter. If you looked long enough you could see a letter trapped in it, a letter you had written once, or would write. It was a trick of the eyes. Kade had never looked long.

They wheeled the chest to Station Three, because Station One had a couple from the caravan arguing about whether a net full of tin cans was theirs by virtue of the net or the river, and Station Two had a fisherman Kade knew getting into a pleasant lying contest with a Warden about the age of a boot he had found. Mama Sant took Station Three’s notebook from under the string that held it to the counter and wrote in her neat, exasperated script. She flipped to a new page and wrote Kade’s name and Noll’s, and the number of the pier, and the time, and a description: chest, wood, brass. She left out the mark. Kade watched the way her hand paused over that detail, then decided to make a note to herself in her head rather than on paper.

“Here then,” Mama said. She made a little circle with her finger in the air above the lock. Noll rolled his shoulders; Kade felt the little ripple that went through the room when the three Wardens in it realized they were going to see it opened. There was not much to watch in an Office day that felt like both a miracle and a form. You took what drama you could get.

The lock was nothing Kade knew. They knew locks the way some people knew cards. They could glance and tell you the lineage: this one’s father was a marrow-bone latch from a monastery, this one’s mother was a car trunk, this one learned to lie from a violin case. This lock looked like a mouth that had been taught to lie and then taught to be ashamed of it.

They could have picked it. It would have taken three hours and a tool the size of a cigarette. Kade thought of the tool immediately: the texture of its knurling, the way it would sit in the first three fingers of their right hand and torque just so. They saw themselves making it tonight, with Noll snoring and the Strand breathing and everything in their life briefly manageable because it had turned into work.

Mama Sant took out a key. It was ugly brass, looked like a church key that had been stepped on. She put it in the lock, breathed once to smooth the world, and turned it. The lock unscrewed itself with a short violent sigh like an apology. There was a smell like cloves and hot paper. The lid lifted a finger-width on its own and then stopped.

“Ready?” Mama said, though she was already lifting.

Inside, there were letters.

They were stacked in a bundle tied with twine, thick envelopes of cream paper with their corners softened by having sat against one another for a long time. They wore stamps from a post office that did not exist—small thin rectangles imprinted with a sun that was not ours, more triangular than round. The twine had been sealed with wax. The seal was the three circles, the notch.

On top of the stack, loose as a leaf dropped on a step, lay a single envelope, addressed in a hand Kade had taught themselves, years ago, by practicing their signature over and over on any blank they could find, until they could do it with their eyes closed, so that if anyone ever asked them who they were, if anyone ever said, Show me, they could show it neat and necessary.

Kade Nazari, it said.

It did not look like a threat. It looked like duty catching up. Kade did not move. They heard Noll’s breath go out and knew it was in time with their own.

Mama Sant did not reach for the letter. If anyone in the room had reached for it, the Strand would have reached through the ceiling and broken their hand. Maybe. Either that, or Mama Sant would have broken it for them.

“There are rules,” she said softly. “We don’t read things that aren’t ours.”

“It’s mine,” Kade said. Their voice came from the back of their throat, scraped with rust. They had not planned the words. They weren’t certain if they believed them or not. It didn’t matter. The room had already decided. Even the collapse froth on the wall seemed to twist a little and lean.

Mama Sant nodded once. “There are still rules,” she said. She handed Kade a pair of gloves thinner than their own, the kind with silver filaments in the tips. “Sit,” she said, as if Kade had been standing rude in an old woman’s kitchen. Noll angled the dolly so the chest’s lid propped against the counter and Kade could see into it without having to hunch. The light in Station Three fell narrow and clean across the paper in the chest. It was a pretty light, the kind you gave to a painting or a knife.

Kade put the gloves on. The letter was cool under their fingers. The ink on the front had not bled into the paper in the places Kade always made it bleed. The tail of the z in Nazari had a flick they had not used yet but had thought about using. They slid a finger under the flap and lifted. The wax gave with a little click.

Inside, there was a single sheet of the same heavy paper. It was folded in three. It had the smell of metal burned so clean you could see your face in it. Kade unfolded the paper, one crease at a time.

The handwriting was theirs.

It was not only like theirs. It was theirs written after a cold day, after a bad hour, hands clean and steady from work, heart of a shape Kade did not know yet how to make in their chest. There were words. Kade did not see the words at first. Their eyes ran forward and backward along the letters like a dog getting a scent, and the imperfections were little taps under their skin: the way the cross of a t went a fraction long, the way they crowded a line when they were afraid of running out of space. They had taught themselves those imperfections. The first thing Kade had ever made out of nothing was the way they wrote their name.

Then the words stood up and Kade read them.

Kade,

Do not let me in.

If they make you, if you cannot keep this from the door, do not let me over the threshold. You will want to. You will think it is your duty, or a kindness, or a test you have to pass to be the version of yourself you think I am. It isn’t.

I know this won’t be enough. It wasn’t enough for me. There will be more letters. There is a lock I know how to make and I know you don’t yet. There will be a map and there will be a day when you will think about walking out of town. You will think you can walk around the edge of the tide and outsmart it because you were born here and you think that means something to a machine this large. You can’t.

I’m not writing this because I think you will listen. I think you will open the door.

When you do, tie your left boot twice. Take Noll’s spare key even though he will say he needs it. Wear the copper in your left pocket, not your right. It matters.

If you can avoid opening it, burn this letter and tell Noll you are going to buy oranges and then go home and sleep with your head under the pillow. Do not come out.

There is a person with my face who is coming to the port to ask you for your help. Your instincts will be right and wrong in equal measure. You will think the only way to keep everyone safe is to do the most painful thing first.

Do not let me in.

—K

The paper made a tiny, disloyal sound when Kade’s glove tightened around it. On the counter, the hunk of collapse froth split a long bubble along its length and then sealed it again as though it had decided there was nothing to see here after all.

Noll’s fingers at Kade’s elbow, light and deliberate. “You tell me what it says,” he said softly, the little rattle in his voice when he tried to make a humor of things edged out with something like fear.

Kade moved their mouth. Nothing came. They looked up because that was what you did when you were drowning and you wanted to pretend you were just dealing with rain.

Through the Office’s front window they could see Pier Four and then the smear of the Strand beyond it, bruised and luminous. People were moving along the piers in the way they did when something had happened and they were trying to look like they weren’t running. Kade saw a girl with needle teeth leap from one plank to another and felt pride rise stupid and raw in their chest like a sob. The wind came up again and pushed against the glass with both palms, as if to say, Knock, knock.

Mama Sant said, not unkindly, “If you bring that to me, Kade, I will burn it in front of you. If you keep it, you will wish I had. Either way, it will make the same shape in the air.”

Kade swallowed. The letter was real in their hand. Their breath fogged the air in front of their face and then went away again.

“When?” they said.

“When what?” Mama Sant said.

“When do I not let me in?”

No one in the room laughed.

Noll’s grip tightened. “It says?”

Kade did not look at Noll. They kept their eyes on the pier beyond the glass, that browning edge of the world where the unbelievable came ashore every morning and asked to be believed. Their own letters on the page winked like a bad light.

“Soon,” Kade said.

As though he had been waiting for his cue, someone banged on the Office’s door. Not the tentative double-touch of a person who didn’t want to buy trouble. Not the authoritative knock of a Warden with the breath of law on his neck. A knock like an answer.

Mama Sant’s mouth did its little half-cut smile. She did not turn. “Don’t,” she said to Kade, and then she said, “Lalla, mind the door.”

The clerk in blue behind the counter went and opened it. The wind came in with the sort of politeness that is always followed by destruction. Along with it, a shape.

Kade knew it before they knew it. That was how this port worked. The Strand did not deliver strangers without practicing their faces on you first.

She stood in the doorway and she was younger than Kade by two years and she had their mouth and their the wrongness of their left eyebrow and their sister’s old coat. The coat had the patch Kade had sewn on with cheap thread the week before Lio died; Kade had unpicked that patch the night after and put it under their pillow like an apology. It wasn’t there, now, because it was here.

“Kade,” she said, breathless and angry and grateful and all the things Kade had found out you could braid a name into if you did it right when you said it.

Noll’s fingers moved against Kade’s sleeve, spelled out in the old dock alphabet: okay?

Kade’s left boot laces were tied only once. The copper they kept in their pocket sat against the wrong thigh.

Do not let me in, the letter said.

Everything in Kade was already moving toward the door. They were a person who hauled on the pier that morning. They were a person who believed things about thresholds. They were a person whose first instinct was a knife, yes, but a knife can cut bread as well as ropes.

They said, their voice their own and not their own, “Hi,” and Mama Sant made a sound like a matched set of coins hitting the bottom of two cups, and the Strand outside shifted its weight and waited.

There is a crisp sound when the world agrees with you. Not a sound you hear—no bell or chime—but a click in the gut and a very small deposit of credit into your ledger that somehow tastes like mint for the span of a breath. If you do it right, if you do it well, your days are a string of those mint clicks, little confirmations that you have correctly divined the next thin sliver of the future.

My kettle does not boil unless enough of us have agreed that it will. That is an exaggeration, technically, though there is a thin corridor of truth hiding in it. We are raised to see prediction the way old ocean people saw the tide: always coming, always going, and intimately ours. Every door hinge in Atrium District knows when it will squeal. Every bus knows who will miss it. We know the odds not because the city loves us, but because we feed it numbers until it is full, and in return it lets us drink. It is a civic exchange, the same way clean water used to be.

It is 06:58 and the kettle at the end of my counter is a stained thing with a blistered enamel belly. My room is four paces by seven, a slice of the tower with a window that faces east toward the old estuary. Down there, beyond the grey grid of roofs and the soft neon hives of the farmers’ stalls, a raft of foam laps at the shore where the tide fences keep the salt out. Above, the civic lattice drapes data into the air in a wash of transparent translucents, a second sky of numbers beyond the window’s treated glass. Radials of probability simmer in my field of view. The boil vector for the kettle hovers at 0.78 with a gentle upward slope. It will click off at 07:03:21 local time.

I put in my claim anyway. 07:03:20. One second tighter than the market consensus. Ninety-three microcredits on the line. The feed pulls in my kitchen humidity, the room temperature, the kettle’s previous boil history, my building’s hard water content, and the fact that last week I splurged on gum for the first time and therefore might be rebalancing my spoiling tendencies. It weighs a thousand such stupid facts and returns a tiny Yes, all right, maybe, if you breathe like you did yesterday.

The kettle clicks over at 07:03:20.12 and the ledger down my wrist vibrates against my skin. I breathe mint. The city and I have agreed.

I make tea the way my grandmother in Abbasine taught me, terming the steeps out with an app for time because bubbles and leaves are not my native language. My grandmother never registered as a forecaster. She claimed she could smell weather with her jaw. She would leave peeled pages of old books under the bed to collect dreams. She is dead and I can’t ask her, but sometimes I fancy those books were some primitive ledger too, a secret way of telling the future by the way paper wrinkles in thick air.

The wall by my sink displays contracts as I drink. There are the big civic ones—Bus 4 departure timing on the Junction to Circle run; Ferry C spillover from Midshore; the lecture hall fill rate for the equity school two blocks away—and there are the thousands of little ones like my kettle, offered by citizen-emitters for the price of shaving a sliver off their own entropy. It is a thing the Bureau used to teach us in primary: nothing stops anyone from having their own guesses in their own heads, of course, but the city runs on shared guesswork. We emit, we stake, we settle. If you are consistently right, you become important in the same way a bridge is important. People walk over you. Cargo is routed your way. The city changes its shape a little to favor your correctness.

It has been three years since I left the rookie floor at Forecast Standards and started living on my own emissions. I am not a bridge. I am a woman with neat nails and tidy scores and a knack for seeing what buses will do. My full name is Roya Anwar. There is a heavy glass ring around the edge of the city called the belt-road that everyone simply says Belt, like they mean the thing around your waist. Belt has ten bus lines that feed and feed from it, and I can tell you when those buses will sneeze or hiccup or surge. My apartment is small because buses do not pay as well as weather, and weather is owned by a god of men with wet labs under their houses who do not share.

I put on my shoes. The screen on my wrist blinks a new frame over my veins, and the bus claims, like tiny birds, hop from my wall onto my arm like feeders.

Don’t anthropomorphize the numbers, Roya. That was something Kord used to say when we both wore the navy jackets of the Bureau and the small enamel crows on our collars—the crows meant you were authorized to normalize. Kord’s jacket hangs behind my door on a nail, the crow glinting with cheap enamel, weightless and ugly. After three months in Standards I learned to pick out the weight of the city’s gaze even from inside that bravado. You cannot normalize people for long without feeling like you have been sandpapered into somebody else’s idea of smooth.

The belt-road outside is a glazed ribbon. At this hour it looks like it had been polished by the shoes of a million ghosts. The first of the buses whistle along their magnetics, fat trolleys with soft noses. People stand in the spill of the morning and stare at their overlays and taste whatever they taste when city and self agree.

Bus 4, Junction to Circle. The contract sits behind my eyes, waiting. So do the little feeder contracts: will there be a delay at Tsai Intersection due to the scaffolding on the mural; will the platform at Bluerift oversell by more than nine percent; will the boy in the heavy coat try to skip the fare again? There are microcredits to be had in these virulent moments, if you know how to look.

I like the boy. He knows he cannot skip. He is bone tall and brown, with a face like a knife from one side and like a bowl from the other, and the bus cameras have long decided he is a nuisance. But he does it anyway because something in him prefers being told no to not being seen at all. This is also a kind of contract. I stake it: he will try.

When Bus 4’s nose drifts past, the crowd tilts. A woman with a floral headscarf flicks an eye at my elbow and reads my emission displays. That is allowed. Forecasts are social goods. You’re allowed to take but not to copy wholesale. The bus’s door breathes and people become a flow solved by an algorithm seventy years old and updated every morning with the miles of the day. It all works until, once a week or so, a scooter decides to love a bus, and then we have to be humans again with voices and fingers and the soft weak parts behind the eyes. The cameras catch the boy’s foot hitching past the gate. He looks at me as if he knows I have staked him, which of course he cannot. The bus says no. The bus is very polite. The boy shrugs. The mint on my tongue is small and sharp.

We used to say in the Bureau that the world is not a function of our belief, which is true, and also a thing we repeated because we didn’t want to start thinking that it could be.

Bluerift Station is full. It shouldn’t be. Then again, most days the shouldn'ts come in pairs. People mask immediacies. The mural on the scaffolding at Tsai is turning out to be some saints pulled from oil and data. The scaffolders idle like ants clinging to a slice of sugar. The bus lifts its front to the magnet, kisses the rail. I can feel the weight of seven hundred thousand microforecasts pressing into this block of the morning. Bus drivers used to be people with hats who squinted at the weather. Now the algorithm has fat cheeks, and we call it Aurora like it is a niece we don’t want to disappoint.

Aurora purrs. The gridded overlay of the civic lattice hangs over Bluerift like a bowl with a map drawn on the inside. When we were younger and Kord and I were chewing tough bureau rations, he would say that the lattice looks the way the sky must look to god. I told him if there was a god he would be fired for redundancy.

I step off at Circle because there is coffee there and a long bench that is always slightly warmer than it should be because of the engineering of its guts, and because I like the way the building to the east throws a low, soft shade in the morning. The bench has its own little contract market for whether it will have room when I arrive. I have a thirty-eight percent superstition that my body heat nudges the forecast by one tenth in my favor.

The world goes wrong three minutes later in the time it takes to finish half my coffee.

It is not a noise not-heard thing like the mint click when you get it right. It is a full-body drop in a lift that forgets to stop making you weightless. My overlays go white, which is not a color the lattice uses lightly. White means undefined. White was something we practiced for at Standards with our bright screens and our fake emergencies. White was a theoretical banner hung in emergencies that some of us laughed off and some of us had nightmares about. White means your numbers do not apply. White means your mind—the part of you that clicks mint—has nothing to bite.

When white happens, proper citizens do nothing. That is what we were taught. You freeze so that your energy doesn’t push a wrong that topples into a worse wrong because some turbulence in the lattice has already taken up all the room for chaos. You breathe like your grandmother taught you or like a screen tells you. You do not try to be clever.

Someone on the bench stands so hard their knees hit the underside with a hollow whang. A girl’s paper cup tilts and a fan of brown arcs toward the ground, the simulation of a head-on with gravity. The arc hangs, wrong; for a heartbeat my eyes refuse to write a smooth path through it. The coffee slaps the ground six inches wider than my brain thinks it should. That is the kind of wrong we get: petty, intimate. The bus in the Circle glides and then shivers, the magnet hum backing off then reasserting itself in a sick cat purr. People are not screaming because white does not scream. White is blank. White is a low breath throughout the district and the feeling of every overlay shuddering and then ceasing to be useful.

I set my coffee down. I feel the part of me that would click mint lean forward and then sit back because there is nowhere to lean. The circle moves in this strange gelatinous way. For the first time since I left Standards I realize that the person who taught me to freeze—Kord with his stick elbows and his crow badge shining like a cheap star—was probably mostly making that up. There is no freeze when you are a body in air and other bodies are in air too.

Behind the bus, a child trips. She does not fall like any of us have practiced falling. There is a physics you get used to in a city like mine; the way it fails to hurt you too badly when you tumble because a net knows when you will slip and deploys under your future. The white is a famine. There are no nets in a famine.

It isn’t heroism. It is impulse. The child is exactly one stride away from the bus’s slow-firing nose gear and exactly one half-second into a fall that is not going to end in a normal place. My body inhabits the space where my mind is supposed to be. My hand catches the back of a lumpy sweater. We pivot. The bus slides. The child’s breath hits my face in a hot, fat sob that breaks like a wave on all that white. The bus hums past the place where a head wasn’t a moment ago and then stops four centimeters later than it was modeled to.

What I do is lift. It is any morning. It is the kind of thing you do without thinking while thinking about thinking. The worst thing about white is that there is a little taste of metal in your mouth, and you know what that taste means: time without a net.

Then the lattice snaps back. Not gracefully. There is no mint when a white ends. There is something like stale bread, as if your success had sat too long and now you have to eat anyway. The overlay slouches into place with a muttered apology: mostly in the right place, a little frayed. Aurora, as always, has a very smooth voice when she is bleeding. Civilians blink and read. People make sounds that aren’t quite human. The contract market for the bench is a mess; no one will ever untangle it right. The weather line does not move for two heartbeats and then accelerates like a mother in a bad dream running toward a door.

The child’s mother is there suddenly with her hands like claws and her voice like milk going bad and her eyes swelling with thanks and terror. I hand over her child and feel the shock in the little body, a high-pitched whine without sound that the overlay politely distills into a suggestion to stay still for six minutes and to accept a voucher for an apology drink. We accept apologies in the city like communion.

The boy with the knife-bowl face is here too, looking at me with enormous, solemn eyes. He says, in a tone of awe he probably learned on television, “You moved before you knew.”

I have a whole thought I do not say to that. I think: We always do.

Two things happen in the next minute. The first is that two Bureau jackets appear, their crows winking in the white’s afterglow. They step into my field with the too-still calves of people trained to be the same height wherever they are. They do not look at me but their internal overlays have me highlighted because I can feel my shoulders itch the way you itch when a mosquito circles.

The second thing happens between blinks. I see him. Or her. Or them. For the rest of my life my mind will put male clothes on this shape because it simplifies me to do so, and the shape resists being pinned as if it were a helium balloon trying very gently not to be held. They are one person in a crowd of hundreds who are all trying to rejoin the lattice with their eyes and lips. They are unremarkable except that, as they move, the overlays on my retina forget they are there. The white recedes from the whole Circle like a tide, but this little body carries its own absence with it, a not-color like oil on newspaper. People step around this person without ever fully locating the reason why.

A zero, says a thin voice in my head I do not like. The Bureau term is aharmonic, which is a better lie because it sounds like a choice about music and not like a hole in a wall where a person should be. When we were rookies we would whisper the other word: a null. A break in the sum. A person who throws off prediction the way rain throws off light.

That is fairy talk, Kord used to tell me. But he whispered it too.

By the time I stand, the aharmonic body has already found the stairs out of the Circle and slipped into them with three other human shapes that rearrange themselves unconsciously to make room for the one who shakes the numbers. The Bureau jackets have drifted toward an old woman whose cane left a black streak on the ground that no overlay is clearing. They look young under the hats they no longer wear. We used to carry hats for the color. Hats make your silhouette easy to find. The Bureau stopped wearing them the year a riot used them as flags.

I am no longer with the Bureau. I am a woman who guesses bus hiccups. This is what I tell myself while my spine lifts its head like a turtle from a shell it doesn’t love.

I do not follow the aharmonic down the stairs. You get to draw a line across yourself and say Here, here, this is where my life ends and the life of those who sign things for me begins. I draw it. Then I redraw it because that is also a prediction. I drink the rest of my coffee which has cooled past its correct taste and into a sort of muddy resignation.

When I get home there is a message, which is a kind of old-fashioned word we keep to make ourselves feel like communication is a letter between people and not a pulse that pages you like a sudden fever. It waits on my wall where I keep my worse secrets. It has no sender. That is, it has an address, but the address is one of those Bureau legal numbers that looks like a god did it by accident while doing something else. I do not answer those quickly.

The message has no text. It has a motion graphic of a crow looking at its own reflection in a puddle.

I used to like those. When I was a first-year my crow pin felt like the smallest and smartest bird and I liked the way it made me a person in a city of systems. I press my thumb to the air and the message opens. It is not the Bureau. The Bureau does not animate. This is someone with a sense for staging.

Ms. Anwar, the voice says. It is a field voice. You get them when you have enough money to pay a throat to borrow at leisure. Neither male nor female, not too deep, the nice clean vowels of someone who grew up far from the river and who learned to speak in rooms where echo is considered vulgar.

We would like to arrange a meeting. The word we is not the Bureau we. It is the we of the parts of the city that never make their own forecasts, only purchase yours.

You pulled a child from the white. That is admirable but not the reason we are interested. We are interested because you saw something that our instruments recorded but our people did not admit to seeing.

Like water with heat under it, something in me collects bubbles that are not yet visible. I watch my own face in the reflection of the window. It has the dark, hard look of my mother’s in photographs. There is a nick in my left eyebrow, visible only when I am tired, which is always.

The voice carries on, gentle. There are persons, rare, whom the lattice fails to allocate. If you prefer a Bureau term, you may say aharmonic. If you prefer a true one, we will call them zeros. The voice waits on the word like it wants me to kick it. My stomach does something small and unpleasant and hungry.

We would like you to meet one, not in white, not in a crowd whose attention is burning holes in the floor. We would like to hear your readings while you do. We would like to pay you. A pause, because these are people who respect the rhythm of consumption. We assume you would like to be paid.

On my wall the list of my bus contracts rustles like a dry tongue. I can see where the white has already cost me. You cannot be paid when numbers have been subtracted and then redrawn around their absence. People are forgiving. The lattice forgives less. You took its hand and it dropped you and now it will ask you to prove you know its steps again.

There is a picture now, as if the voice knows that numbers are not enough for us primitive animals. It is a picture of a glasshouse on a roof I know but have never stepped on—an old greenhouse with ribs like a whale’s, full of dark plants drinking from misters and the blur of faces like fish behind the ribs. The text that swims under it is a time I could find in the lattice and a ladder I could climb and a request to bring nothing with a lens except the ones in my head.

If this were the Bureau, there would be paperwork first. Even ignoring that I am not Bureau anymore, I could send this to Kord, who is, and watch him sharpen his teeth on it until his jaw clicks. I look at the crow staring at itself in a puddle and try to decide if the crow looks surprised. It does not. Crows never do. They know the shape of their own minds and theirs are not nice shapes.

I write, with my finger in the air because sometimes it feels good to be manual: Why me?

The answer comes with a speed that tells me it was waiting in exactly this shape.

Because you believe in the lattice, Ms. Anwar. But you do not like being held by it.

This is false. This is also not untrue.

I put my kettle on. I watch the boil vector gather like a skirt. I do not stake this one. I make tea badly on purpose and let it steep too long and decide I will go.

This is a bad decision.

You can always tell because the mint doesn’t come. You can tell because nobody else had the chance to say yes. You can tell because the city does not lean with you, or because it leans too much like a friend too eager to pull you into trouble.

When I sleep that night a riot of numbers flows through my jaw and my grandmother’s paper pages wrinkle under my cheek and somewhere a child breathes out long and slow because she did not die. When I wake I am wearing the navy jacket from the nail behind my door and I do not remember putting it on. It is too small and too heavy and the enamel crow scratches my collarbone when I lift my hair to tie it.

The glasshouse is three stops from my building if you go the long way and five if you are careful not to pass over too many stray contracts that will pull at your pockets. I try to choose the long way and the careful way at once, a thing I have done all my life and which never ends well for anyone. On the belt-road, a bus pulls in and sighs contentedly because the morning has decided to be excellent about buses now, to make up for earlier. My overlays float along like docile jellyfish: status unremarkable, expected flows steady, civic appetite good. Somewhere above, the weather gods have put a lid on rain. You can hear the lid when the wind catches the edges of the skyscrapers and the air gives up on being cold.

I go up a ladder wet with last week’s fog. I think of the type of person who can call themselves we and send crows and ask me to climb. My hands come away clean. Halfway up, a middle-aged man with hair like a shorebird leans out of a neighboring window and says, breathing like a fish does when you take it out of its own prediction ocean: They got you too?

It could be a joke. I grin the grin of people who are not certain how many versions of themselves might exist at once if we took scissors to everything. They got me, I say, and keep climbing.

There is a door at the top of the ladder. It opens on pressure before I can lift a knuckle. It smells like wet leaves. The air in the glasshouse is the kind you can eat. Everything is damp. Plants bulge in all the wrong ways because a climate this controlled has to make up for something. The path is gravel to erase footfall. If I were the Bureau I would think about cameras and heat maps. If I were the person in the crowd with the oil-slick around them, I would think about the places I could stand without being seen by the seeing.

There are three people inside. Only one is wearing a face I can read easily. Their jaws do not move in the way rich people’s jaws do when they try to pretend they are made of fruit and bread like the rest of us. There is no low table with things on sticks that would make it easier to bite down a shaky throat. The one with the readable face holds up a hand.

Ms. Anwar. Thank you for coming.

He has the same field voice as the message. Either he is the throat it borrowed or he borrowed himself. He would like to be twenty-five and is instead forty-five and not mad about it. I do not look past his shoulder yet, because I am an idiot and because I understand a little theater. I can feel the aharmonic the way you can feel a low-frequency speaker without hearing it: a thudding you locate in bone. The overlay on my retina does not go white. It is not cruel. It slides to a dark grey like a morning that will not decide to be day.

The readable man gestures like a polite conductor and the orchestra hushes. You saw a turbulence today, he says. What we call a white. He does not say what he calls the person behind him.

I breathe. I lie without effort because this is a skill that served me and hurt me equally when I wore a crow on my collar. I say: I saw a child fall. I saw my hand reach to catch them.

His mouth tips as if I have quoted a favorite passage. And then you saw an absence. It is a statement and a question and the thing in the grey behind him shifts its weight and the world has to decide whether to allow that shift to count. The lattice blinks, very, very slowly, and then rerenders reality around that small motion like a film crew adjusting for a lighting change they are not allowed to admit happened.

The zero in the glasshouse looks up and gives me a look I have been avoiding all morning by focusing on the wrong things.

It is not a look that says Please help me. It is not a look that says I am dangerous. It is a look a mirror would give you if it could choose what to reflect.

They smile without neon. The overlays roll and die and roll and try again, as if unpredictability were a wind I could lean into and be held.

On the first day of the new fiscal year, I took the childhood of a stranger.

Outside, a weather system the color of old nickels crawled inland off the bay, making the city’s skin itch. The fog horns from the lower wharves had the slow patience of animals. Up here on the thirtieth floor, the air smelled like disinfectant and boiled coffee. I set the eidetap on the table and waited for Mr. Vale to stop shaking.

“Hold still and we’ll be done in fifteen minutes,” I said.

He was a spool of wire coiled inside of a man. His left eye watered; his right eye was an old aftermarket—one of the post-Ceramic models with a viewfinder iris that clicked faintly as it focused on the eidetap. He had taken off his cap when I came in. The cap sat on the radiator and steamed.

“You make it sound like a haircut,” he said.

It was. It wasn’t. The device sat in the middle of the table in its cradle, a shallow chrome bowl nested in a carbon frame like a half shell. Blue indicator lights freckled the rim. To the right, a glass vial marked with a pale yellow stripe waited to be filled. My gloves creaked when I tested the dampers.

“It’s a tap. You set it to fifty milliliters of glucose draw, pair it to the hippocampal lattice, and it siphons out what you sign for. Painless. Localized. A prick.” I smiled. It didn’t reach any of the places that mattered. “You’ll be a little soft on names for a day or two. They come back.”

“They don’t come back,” he said, and braced his hand on the chipped tabletop. “Not the good things.”

The ledger had his file open. KAI, VALE; MARCUS; citizen grade bronze. Forty-nine years old. Three infractions: late tithe, possession of uncertified memory patches, striking an auditor. The last was five years back, and the note on the infraction from the field office read: auditor refused to press charges. Grief event: wife, pneumonia, thirteen months ago. Net balance due: eight hundred thirteen credits or one hundred thirty minutes at current valuation.

He had eighty-six credits in his account.

“We can negotiate content,” I said. “You choose what. The law protects milestones, primary anchors, and trauma sequences. People protect those, anyway. You know this,” I added, softer. “You’ve paid before.”

He nodded. He had. Most people did. The Memory Tithe had been on the books since before I was born, an ugly compromise left over from the years when the state had run out of cash but discovered there was something better to extract: us. Our attention, our tasting of the world, our associative maps—the raw feed of human experience the models needed to learn what we were and were not. It was all captured, aggregated, anonymized, and warehoused in soundproof cold.

That was the story we were told, anyway.

The truth veered hard depending on whether you wore a suit to work or cleaned blood out of elevators for a living. If you believed the Agency’s campaign materials, your twice-yearly contribution went toward better traffic systems, better triage, better ration distribution. If you believed the collection of fretted conspiracists on the third level of the east market, your contribution went toward an enormous simulation that had already replaced most of reality, which was why nobody noticed the sea moved differently now and why half the birds had learned to sing the tone used to reset public kiosks.

Me? I believed in the way people looked down at the table when you gave them the options, in the way their right hands found their left wrists.

“Names come back,” I said again, and slid the bowl toward him.

He reached for the harness, then stopped. “When my wife… They asked me to pick a slice, after. To cover the hospital. I couldn’t sell her laugh, I couldn’t. So I gave them the day we moved into the old apartment on Harbor. Papers and cardboard and the elevator breaking between floors. The hallway smelled like fish skin and lemon cleaner. We were happy.” He made a small sound in his throat. “They took how the floorboards sounded. I step into that building now and it’s like walking into a photograph. No sound. Flat.”

“We don’t take all of anything,” I said. “Just a thin. You’ll remember. Just with less weight.”

He stared at the device as if it might open into a mouth.

People always asked if it hurt. The answer was no. The device interfaced with the hippocampal lattice through the glove and the harness, an old trick half pulled from surgery and half from advertising. The sedation gel made everything lullaby-soft. It was the after that hurt—when your tongue tripped over a name and the hole it left in your day became a pattern.

I rubbed the dampers between my fingers to warm them. “Do you want to select your own slice?”

He swallowed, nodded. “My first trip to the stadium,” he said. “My father and me. There was a player who used to—”

“If it touches an anchor, the system will reject it,” I said, and tried not to picture a small boy’s hand in a larger one. He scowled at me, then closed his eyes.

“Fine,” he said, and after a moment, “I’ll give you the sound of rain on the old tar roof of my school. Primary school. The way it was when I was seven, eight. We had buckets. We put them out to catch it. They told us not to touch, it was dirty.” He opened his eyes to look at me. “You said you wanted something that wouldn’t bruise me.”

I nodded. “That will do.”

“Will the Agency get the rain like I knew it?”

“It gets what you sign for.”

He made a face, lifted the harness, and fitted the carbon rings behind his ear and along the hinge of his jaw. The harness looked delicate in his hands. It never did, in mine.

While he adjusted, I tapped the vial icon on my slate. The outtake would be recorded to an Agency capsule for transfer to the city reservoir—a data warehouse branded with sunrise-blue vinyl banners and armed guards who looked like librarians in flak vests. The reservoir smelled like a winter garden and fire suppression foam and was the quietest place I had ever been.

The eidetap chimed when he tightened the chin strap. I adjusted the skin sensors at his temples. I told him to breathe the way the training suggested—long, deep waves in the belly—and I thumbed the dampers to five. His fingertips, which had been twitching on the table, sighed open.

The device’s halo lit to an ice-blue, then a ghostly green. My slate bloomed with the mesh of his activity. The AI in the tap recognized the pattern his mind took when it followed rain and went looking for more of that shape in the tangle of his history. A hundred responses thrummed, then narrowed to a thread. Consent, the display prompted.

“Marcus Vale, do you consent to the capture of the following experience?” I asked, looking at his face.

He nodded. “Take it before I think of my father.”

I let out the breath I’d been holding, and touched the prompt.

Sometimes, even though the auditors are taught not to look at the stream, not to lean close to the eaves of somebody else’s life, you hear things. Our devices flatten, anonymize, filter. They turn a concert into an equalizer, pixels into maps. But memory isn’t a video file. It’s a muscle, a smell, the sudden weight of a shirt on your shoulders. And when the device bites that muscle, you feel it clamp your teeth around something more than a number.

Rain, then. The machine hummed, the vial misted, and I caught—only a sliver, because I didn’t mean to—the smell of chalk and wet wool, the flash of a child’s arm scrawling a number on a page, the tectonic rightness of being told what to do. I felt, absurdly, buckets. The hollow glug-glug-glug of water hitting water. When his father’s voice tried to wander in from the hallway, the tap redirected it away, found the roof, the drip, the ache of something you cannot fix but learn to live alongside.

The vial filled to its line with something that wasn’t liquid at all. The device called it a condensate because the Agency preferred its metaphors tidy. People called it a tear. The condensate glowed faintly blue as data spun into it, as if a ghost had caught itself in that strange glass. It pulsed when his pulse did. I watched the vial to keep from watching him.

When the line went opaque, the device chirped. Marcus Vale let out a shaky sound and swiped his mouth. The eidetap’s halo dimmed to a soft green. I capped the vial with a noise like clicking a pen and slid it into the padded slot beside the slate.

He took off the harness as if it had insulted him. He rubbed the red circles the pads had left at his temples. His hands were steady now.

“Done,” I said. In my ear, the Agency’s back-end ticked off the balance and updated his ledger. His account now read: four hundred eighty-seven credits due by the second quarter or at the next tithe. His jaw tightened as the numbers updated, as if the debt itself had applied pressure to his tendon and he’d caught it before it spread.

“You didn’t even count to fifteen,” he said.

“It took twelve,” I said. “You’re efficient.”

He snorted. “I’ve been doing this since I was eighteen,” he said. “You learn which parts of your life are expensive.”

He walked me to the door because he was the kind of man who would. The hall outside his apartment was a long, low slope that led to the stairwell and a patchy view of the bay. The door opposite his was open, spilling the smell of fish and frying oil into the hall and revealing a narrow kitchen crowded with a family in mismatched pajamas and a boy with an at-home tutor raising its hands for attention.

We both winced at the same time. Different reasons.

“Next time,” he said, “I’ll just pay in blood. Blood grows back.”

“Only if you’re young,” I said, because people liked to be argued with when they’d chosen to be generous. It made generosity feel like defiance. “And blood costs more by the gram.”

He watched me for a moment as if trying to decide whether I was giving him something with that, then gave up and nodded at the little case. “Take care of that.”

“I always do,” I said.

What I didn’t say: take care of what’s left.

I walked the stairwell instead of waiting for the elevator, because I preferred the feeling of earning my descent to being plummeted in a box of moving parts I hadn’t inspected. The fog had thickened to the texture of raw wool, and by the time I made it to street level, the city wore a slip of wet like sleep. All down the block, neon signs notched the day with their angling, patient light—pharmacies, pawn brokers, stamp offices, a stall that offered to fix the cracked glass on your slate with a laser and a prayer.

The Agency had its field office four blocks over beneath an obsolete viaduct. It occupied a trimmed, repurposed firehouse with a flag out front and a pair of benches on which people rarely sat unless they wanted to be seen waiting for forgiveness.

The clerk at the front desk buzzed me in with her chin. Her hair was the color of cinnamon sticks, shaved close on the sides. She wore the Agency grey with the faint smugness of people who believe uniforms make them safe.

“You’re late,” she said, because this was the way we were with each other.

“Fog,” I said. “Worth at least seven minutes.” I slid the case along the counter. “Vale, Marcus. Rain on tar roof.”

She typed, took the case, slid me a receipt with the small flourish of a magician producing a coin.

“Quell wants to see you,” she said.

The back office smelled like lemon and printed paper. Quell’s economics certification hung in its frame above his desk with a tiny crack in the glass at the lower left corner, as if someone had been tempted once and played at punching it before remembering their pension. He wore the clean, colorless suit of someone who had never had to step onto a wet stoop and ask a father to pick between birthdays.

“Sera,” he said, as if my name were a data point. “Sit.”

I sat. The chair was not designed with bodies in mind. The way the back cut into my shoulder blades made my left arm go a little numb. Quell was a thin man, the kind of thin that tells you hunger once sat at his table until he learned to heel it.

He glanced at his slate, then at me. “You pulled a flagged file this morning.”

I frowned. “From Vale? There was nothing—”

“Not from him,” he said, and flicked the file into the space between us. It hung there in the cheap slow holo like a moth pinned to a dull sky. The file number was long and teethy. The tags along its edge shifted like a school of fish when I focused on them: reserve, restricted, pre-ledger.

An ice smell slid under my tongue.

“Where,” I said very slowly, “did that come from?”

“Someone routed it to your personal digest. It credited to your ID at 08:09. It tried to bypass Oblivion entirely.” He leaned back. His chair didn’t squeak. “We’re fairly sure you didn’t ask for it, because you haven’t asked for anything since they make auditors sign the ethics pledge on language you can read. Which makes me want to ask who sent it to you. Or who wants us to think they sent it to you.”

“I didn’t ask,” I said, and watched the tags again. I knew most of the categories the Agency used. The ones I didn’t know made me itch. “What’s in it?”

“We didn’t open it,” Quell said. “It’s flagged Oblivion. It is very literally my job not to know what’s inside. You’ll escort it down to the basement and give it to Grey Linen. They will put it wherever they put those things.” He paused. “Do not look.”

“They routed it to my digest,” I said. “Am I permitted to know who in God’s steady mouth would do that?”

“You are permitted to take it downstairs,” he said, and slid me the transfer capsule. It was white and bland and looked like a vitamin. The file wobbled over his desk. “What you’re not permitted to do is stick your tongue out and balance fate on it.”

“I hate your metaphors,” I said.

“I know,” he said, and was suddenly, briefly human. “This kind of thing is a bruise. If you press it, it will only spread. Carry it, Sera.”

I took the capsule between two fingers like plucking a bee out of air.

In the old days—if there were old days that were ever exactly anywhere—we called it the Forgetting Division. Now it was Oblivion. The name implied softness, a mercy. It was a division for the removal of what could ruin the ledger if it made it into the reservoir. They invested a lot in making sure they got the words right. No one felt less erased because the door was labeled with a scented noun. No one came up from that basement and said anything useful.

“Downstairs,” Quell said again, and returned to his ledger.

I stepped into the corridor with the white cylinder in my hand and felt the buttoned-down wind of the building as if it had a mood. I leaned against the wall outside his office and let it thud gently, once, twice, against the back of my head. It didn’t help.

Curiosity is a prickle. Ignore it long enough and it becomes a rash. Scratch it and it bleeds. I held the capsule up to the fluorescents and watched the milk interior hold the light. The file orbited my slate when I pulled it up again like a small pale moon.

You are not special, Sera, I told myself. You are a conduit. You are grey thread. You hold one end and you hand the other end to a person wearing a different shade of the same shirt. If the Agency wanted you to know, they’d have sent you the training with the pictures.

I put my thumb against the capsule’s seam.

Downstairs was two levels down past the cashier’s cage and the legal office with its dusty plants. The sign for Oblivion had indeed been written in the kind of font they reserved for household goods and rescue shelters. The door was closed. This floor was cooler than the rest, and the air had the metallic taste of machines left always-on.

I could have pushed through. I could have set the capsule on the desk of the man in the grey linen suit who would look at my hair and check my slate and say thank you, auditor, and slide the white cylinder into a slot. The day could have continued in the pattern it had yesterday, and the day before that, and the day before that.

Instead, with my shoulder leaned against the cool wall, I tapped the file with my nail. It wobbled. I pulled it open enough to look through the crack.

The rule was not to look. The rule was, if you looked, look at the edges. Nobody ever kept the rules exactly the way the memos meant them.

The file opened with a sound like air leaving a room you had just discovered you loved. My slate stuttered, then stabilized to a cold grey. The tags attempted to rearrange themselves and failed. A field bloomed, not a video but a space. My fingers tightened involuntarily around the capsule.

It was a corridor, long and far too bright. The kind of institutional light that makes bones feel porous. The walls were a pale green I had never seen used outside of hospitals and courtrooms in old films. The floor was polished, and along the far wall, a run of windows that should have shown light showed instead a long blank like old paper.

My own breath made the little microphone in the slate pick up static. Someone else was breathing in the file.

“Stay still,” a voice said. Female. Not old, not young. The accent made my neck itch in a way I couldn’t explain. “Don’t turn your head. They’ve tightened the bands. If you turn too much you’ll feel it.”

I didn’t turn. The memory did. It moved as if the person inside it had learned to move carefully, with the management of someone who had been given speed once and had it taken away. The corridor widened. A door opened. A smell reached me so complex and sudden that my eyes closed, because it wasn’t a smell my life had handy: hot metal, bleach, something like crushed greenery, and underneath it the electric buzz of lit air.

A room, then. Large and full of machines. Not machines in the way the Agency used the word. These had roundness and a tightness of purpose, a way of looking as if they were always already mid-task. A half ring of mirrored panels hung like a crown that had just been lifted off a head. On the far end of the room, a woman stood with her hands in her pockets like it was summer.

She turned.

It’s a myth that when you see your younger self, you faint. I didn’t faint. I did stop breathing for a heartbeat and a half. Inside the memory, the person whose eyes I was using did not even flinch. The woman in the room wore her hair in a blunt, heavy cut I knew I had worn the year I was nineteen. The scar along her jaw was the scar I got at twenty-one when the protest on Char Street turned inside on itself. She was a quarter inch shorter than me, and the left eyebrow had that way of asking too many questions. I knew how that woman’s shoulders ached in rain.

“Don’t tithe this,” she said, and in the way light sometimes chooses to move differently, she looked up at the ceiling where there was no camera and at the exact place where I was not and could not be, and she said my name.

“Sera.”
