The memory stuttered. The room jumped softly like a deck on bad water. The capsule in my hand clicked. The file tried to route a copy to Oblivion by itself like a startled animal finding a hole and forgetting how to be caught.

I almost choked on the shape my mouth made when it tried to call a name I didn’t remember knowing how to say anymore.

“Stay with me,” said the woman who wore my history like a well-loved coat. “If you forget this we don’t get to win again.”

“She’s in the corridor,” someone else said, and the memory swung. I saw, for a fraction of a second, the threshold behind the woman with my scar. The numbers stenciled on the wall were wrong. The font wasn’t any Agency font. The numbers themselves did not belong to our systems. The world had a brand it had been forced to wear and this room had not accepted it.

I snapped the file closed.

I stood very still in the hallway outside Oblivion and counted the beats it took my heart to remember how to come down. My thumb throbbed where it had pressed into the seam of the capsule. Upstairs, a phone rang. Somewhere a door shut with a bureaucratic little sigh. The cooling system in the floor at my back exhaled.

The trick with fear is positioning. You put it to the side so that it can walk with you without bumping your hip. If you put it in front of you, it becomes a wall. If you put it behind you, it becomes a hand at your spine.

I put the capsule in my pocket, and I walked into Oblivion.

Grey Linen sat behind his desk and did not look up right away. His suit was the color of the cheap static that haunts bad lines. His face had the calm of a no waiting room and a long, practiced absence where curiosity should have gone. He held his hand out without looking and I placed the capsule in it. He put it into a grey drawer. He closed the drawer. He pressed a button I could not see. He lifted his eyes to mine.

“You didn’t look,” he said, with the kind of voice that knows where lies breed.

“I didn’t look,” I said.

He smiled with his mouth and not at all with his eyes. “It’s good that you didn’t,” he said gently. “It’s good that you can’t.”

I smiled in the way auditors do when we lie on paper for other people for a living. I left the basement with my hands in my pockets like it was summer and went upstairs and did three more tithes in a row on the list Quell had pushed to my slate. I did not think about the woman who stood in a room the Agency did not own. I did not think about the way my name had sounded when spoken by my mouth.

At five, I went home. The fog had lifted and the city had its edges back. My building smelled like curry and cat litter and the kind of flowers that smell better after they’re cut. My door recognized my palm. My apartment was the size of the kind of small sailboat that tips easily when a passenger stands up too fast.

I had three messages. My mother, asking whether I was coming on Sunday for soup. Quell, asking whether I could go to North Hill in the morning because someone had failed to put their tithe on their calendar. And one with no caller ID, no return route, no mark at all but a single word in the subject line: Remember.

I stood in the kitchen with the cool edge of the counter under my hands and watched the light do that late-day trick where it makes everything repainted with luck.

There is a thing you learn, doing what I do. The state may own what I have paid. They may move my bucket into their garden to water what they like. But there are corners even they can’t find. There are cupboards inside the self where we put who we are when we have to go to the door and pretend.

I went to the cupboard. I pulled out a memory I had never tithed, the one I didn’t ever take out because once you take it out you risk dropping it. I held it and let it open, and it was me at six under a table while rain found all the nails in the roof. It was my mother’s voice telling me that nothing real is ever lost, Sera, it just changes its name.

The message pinged again.

Remember.

I made the kind of choice that rearranges your life so gently you’ll tell yourself for months afterward that it was inevitable, that you had been walking that way the entire time. I opened the message.

The face that appeared in the air over my slate wouldn’t have been allowed on an Agency billboard if they still let the Agency put faces on things. She had the wrong kind of certainty about her around the eyes. There was a smear of oil along her cheekbone, as if she had fixed something on her way to telling me this.

“Sera Kade,” she said, and that my mother’s surname was in that mouth broke something and made something else. “If you are receiving this, then you looked even though you shouldn’t have and you gave our present away even though you couldn’t help it. They have your forgetting. We need your memory.”

She leaned close, too close, and the file grain blurred. “Don’t tithe this,” she said again, in case the gods of small repetitions were listening. “Find the place with no birds. Come before they ask you to go.”

The message ended. The light in the apartment made the small mirror on my wall look like another door.

Outside, the bay did what it had always done: took the city and returned it, took the city and returned it. The night shift’s horns began to blow.

I put my head on my arms on the cool kitchen counter. I listened to my heart decide. I listened to my lived life argue with the life in the message. Somewhere downstairs, Mrs. Lithgow’s cat knocked over a plant. Earth spilled across the hallway. Someone cursed, and then laughed very softly, as if remembering something.

The first chapter of a life ends the way a tide does. You think it’s gone until you look down and see your feet are in the water. I took my slate off the counter. I called my mother and told her I loved her and would come Sunday and bring bread. I wrote Quell that North Hill was fine. I put my gloves into my bag. I checked the location of a place I didn’t remember ever hearing of and saw, with a little shiver, that the city still called it by a name that was more like a pause than a word.

Then I turned off the lights. I went downstairs. I took the night train east. I pressed my palm against the glass and watched the city drain. I did not look back because I knew the looking would be the kind of tithe nothing could repay.

Chapter One

The night the city splits into ten thousand not-quite mornings, I’m the one with my hand on the chorus key.

There are protocols. There are safeguards. There are twelve separate glass-covered switches that don’t look like switches at all, because someone decided people obey better when their world looks like it has outgrown levers. There are the soft, sad hums of helium in the Josephson forests, blue-white frost across the superconducting trunks like winter trapped in cages. There is the anchor, a buckydiamond sphere the size of a melon suspended in a spider-lattice at the center of the room. We call it the keelstone. Everyone else calls it the thing that lets their mornings be better.

Outside, Heliotrope is sleeping. The library above my head is quiet. Even the motion-activated stacks are dark. It’s one of the reasons the Department kept the Loom under a public place: as if it were a small crime. Put it somewhere with old stone arches and a reading room that smells like dust and sun and you can pretend the secret you’re keeping isn’t a secret at all.

“Rae.” Mendel’s voice pops in my implant, stripped of its tobacco rasp by the way the chorus engine carries sound. He’s in Bay Two, calibrating qubit gardens we won’t touch for another month. “Still with me?”

“Still in love with your trees,” I say, and pull my fingers away from the keelstone’s security field as if I’ve been caught in the sugar jar. The field hums on my skin for a second, the ghost of a bee.

“Creep,” he says cheerfully. “You’re on schedule?”

The schedule is burnt into the top left of my vision: a ladder of luminous dots, the color shifting as the minutes slide past. At 04:17, the city’s sleepers twitch. At 07:00, the maintenance crews at the ferry terminal will roll out their soaps and hoses for a day that may or may not include a procession of schoolchildren and a paper dragon. At 09:17, the Loom will close its hands on a single thread, and the song the city sings for the next twenty-three hours will become the only song it could have sung.

We do not admit this in public. We talk about predictive architecture, about guidance. It matters how you talk about what you force people to live in.

“I’m on schedule,” I say, even though the top right corner of my vision has been pulsing red since I came down the stair and keyed open the first of the false bookcases. It’s a subtle pulse, if you don’t know how to see it. If you had the implant and it came baked in, if you grew up with the Loom like I did, you learn to ignore certain pulses.

You also learn not to ignore others.

I stand on the gantry over the core. The room is lightless except for the faint blue from the Josephson trunks and the pale moon-glow from the keelstone. The web around it makes my eyes cross if I look too long. It’s the lattice of invariants: the things so basic the threads can’t change them without snapping off into futures the engine can’t support. The keelstone. The interface seals. The anchor fields. Me, some days, because the maintenance team is integrated into the engine’s stability model and we try very hard not to get ourselves dead.

“We could just not,” says the part of my brain that belongs to the past forty years of philosophers. The part that lives on posters kids in the University quarter keep slapping up over transit maps: DON’T TAKE MY TOMORROWS. SAY NO TO THE LOOM.

“We could,” I say aloud, because Mendel knows when I’m arguing with people who aren’t there. “But then a bad morning kills a thousand people at the tram hub, and everyone wants to know why we let it happen.”

“You’re rehearsing,” he says. “You and Oona still fighting?”

“We don’t fight,” I say, because it isn’t exactly untrue. “We disagree with emotional intensity.”

“It’s love,” Mendel says, and cuts the link before I can tell him to save the Hallmark for someone who didn’t spend their childhood tracing the math behind impossible streets.

I should do the pre-run.

Every night, the Loom generates the chorus, the interleaving set of what-could-bes dense enough that we can taste the harmonics of them in the present. The engine calls it the spectral. We call it the place where our ghosts come from, the hollows that lean over our shoulders and make us reach for keys that aren’t there. People swear more since the Loom’s activation. They have more to swear about.

The pre-run is a ripple. It wakes the city up without touching it. It’s the difference between humming and singing. I slip into the seat in the glass cube, watch my reflection settle into the black, my face a pale slice against the blue. I look tired. Overnight rotations do that, and the argument with Oona that wasn’t a fight. She had reached for a coffee cup that both existed and didn’t. It was a new one from the ceramics stall off Podward Street, the one with little gold cracks painted in. She put her hand on air, and it was what pushed her over the edge.

“I don’t want this,” she said, flatly. “This aftertaste. This sense like I’m always behaving wrong in my own house.”

“You get used to it,” I said, and had regretted it immediately.

I put my palm on the pre-run pad.

The chorus unfolds.

It’s always different when you’re feeding it. Later the engine will stack the threads into their spectral matrix, and the docents will do their analogies for the Council, and the Council will lean back in their chairs pretending they know what’s being said. Later the city will taste like copper and cold blueberries and the hum in your bones when the elevator gets to your floor. But right now, for me, it’s a bloom.

My implants are old enough that I still hear it as a chord.

Morning in Heliotrope: ten thousand suns rising tinted by ten thousand different conditions. My implant shivers hot and throws tiles into the edge of my vision, just the way I like it—a tessellation of possible days. Joggers on the promenade. A woman’s scream that becomes laughter by the third repetition because in that thread the kite doesn’t break free. A delivery drone passing low enough in one world to take the brim off a hat. A small dog that slips its leash and runs slantwise through six mornings in a row before its owner remembers a better grip on a seventh.

The Loom does not give us different cities. It gives us the same one, with different luck.

I let the pre-run wind itself to the point where the spectral harmonics stabilize, where the engine’s predictive nets’ error bars go slim. Then I tap the anchor fields up by a notch, and—

“Rae,” Mendel says. “Heads up. Something weird in the Bay One temp.”

“Define weird.” I wince as the pre-run tosses a stutter across my vision. Someone’s put their fingers into the piano.

“Eight hundredths of a degree in the interface. And you didn’t do that. Right?”

If it were a whole degree, alarms would be screaming. Eight hundredths is enough to raise the hair at the back of my neck. Nothing in Bay One should change without me changing it.

“On my way,” I say, and lock the pre-run with my elbow before my own body and the Loom can disagree about where I am and what I am doing.

Bay One is down a flight of narrow steel steps, up a short ladder where the paint is very new because I fell two weeks ago and bled on it, and then through a pressure door set with a fat old-fashioned wheel that makes me feel like I’m on a submarine. Mendel likes the wheel. “If we’re going to run the city from a machine under a library,” he said the day we installed it, “we might as well own the aesthetic.”

The door opens on the carbon-quiet of cryogenics. I taste cold. Before the Loom I would have said that was poetic. Now I know fear has a very specific flavor: chlorine and cream.

The temp readouts are a neat line of green. Bay One’s Josephson trunks click softly in their cold. The interface field hums with that ghost-bee again as I cross to it.

And I see the mark.

It stops me. Not the door. Not the wheel. Not Mendel, who has followed me down the ladder and is rattling a sensor wand behind me like a maraca. The mark has no right to be here.

It’s a smear the size of a child’s hand at the exact dead center of the interface ring where the field lines cross. Black and gritty, like charcoal dragged across glass. No one has been in Bay One since I signed the seal at midnight. No one could have, without leaving a record in the access logs the way a leaf leaves a record in a puddle.

To the left of the smear, scratched into the stainless steel of the guard plate with something sharp enough to bite, are four letters and an arrow pointing down.

RAE ↓.

“Did you do graffiti on my machine?” Mendel says, coming up behind me.

“I didn’t,” I say evenly. “Don’t be ridiculous.”

“You’re the only one who would write your name.”

“It wasn’t me.”

“You’re sure.”

I am very sure, because my handwriting is better, and I was inside a dream with Oona at midnight, asking her what color we should paint the bedroom. Pale green, she said, as if that would solve the hollows. Pale green.

“Someone is making a joke,” Mendel says, but his tone has moved from cheerful to thin.

“No one knows Bay access codes but six people,” I say. “And two of them are us.”

He leans into the beam of the wand, squinting. “The smear’s in the interface field.”

“I know.” I can feel it. There’s a slightly flat note where the hum should be sweet. I put one hand out and then think better of it. I do not touch invariants with my skin unless I have a good reason to be burned.

“Wipe it,” Mendel says.

“No.” My mouth makes a shape like Oona’s when she’s refusing the coffee I keep offering. “We document.”

We document, because the Loom’s legal gills flare if we do not. I snap flat panoramas of the ring, the smear, the scratch that says my name. I sign a time lock with my breath, because some marketing consultant decided blow-in logins would make people smile a decade ago. I run a particulate sample, and the little hungry sucker makes a wet mouth on the steel and vomits data into my implant: 63.5 percent carbon, 21 percent something that pings as binder, traces of lithium and iron and—paint.

“It’s just soot,” I say.

“Why would there be soot in my interface ring?” Mendel says, in the tone he uses when someone from Council makes a joke with math in it that doesn’t add up. “Also the scratch. Rae. This is not—”

His wand goes pev, that tight sound halfway between a beep and a snapped violin string. He and I look up the way people do on trains when something happens to change the background. Our implants overlay the same thread of the spectral.

In nine thousand six hundred and eighty-seven possible mornings, the mark is there.

I see it in parallel: the morning where rain has driven a thin line between the houses on Barge Street; the morning where a delivery drone arrives at the library early and the courier notices my coffee and reports me to Security for consumption of liquids near delicate stuff; the morning where Oona texts me a photograph of a pale green paint swatch and adds a heart.

In each of those mornings, someone has smeared charcoal across the interface ring and scratched my name into the guard plate. In the handful of threads where it is not there, Bay One is empty.

No trace I know of gets written into the spectral unless it has been recorded in the physical within our set of invariants. The engine is very firm about the rules.

“You saw that,” I say.

“I saw that,” Mendel says. “Don’t like that.”

My heart manages the neat trick of rising into my throat while dropping into my feet. It is a sensation you only get with a Loom implant, and even after a decade it makes me want to sit down and throw up.

“Calibrate,” I say. “We check the anchors. We check the logs. We don’t assume anything.”

By which I mean: We do not assume someone or something has done something that must be impossible: introduced a cross-thread artifact into an invariant. We do not assume someone is sending me a message from a morning that the city will never live. We do not assume we have been touched by a hand coming the other way through the glass.

The anchor logs are clean. The access seal shows my code, Mendel’s code, the locked service code. The housekeeping bot did its rounds, turned in a report so polite I want to adopt it. Security’s little green dot hovers above the library like a side-eye.

“Maybe,” Mendel says, “it’s a garnish. On the dish. Some little extra. Council has a new visualization idea.”

“I will personally garnish the Council,” I say, and hear my own voice shake.

He looks at me. We have been together in this cave for seven years, which is time enough to know where each other’s bones sit.

He says, gently: “Call Oona. Say you’ll be late. We’ll be boring for a few hours.”

I nod, but I do not call Oona. It is 04:39. Oona will be sleeping, crooked on her side because of the crick in her back she blames on the Loom, as if the engine reached up through the mattress and pinched her nerves. I have never seen the city drop a hand into a body like that. The hollows are psychological. They are breaks in habits. I did not say any of that last night because Oona is right about everything that matters until she is wrong, and I love her enough to distrust my own desire for order.

We go back to the core. The smear sits there. My name on the steel shines dull and honest in the light from the trees. The pre-run is locked and waiting for me to bless the city with better luck.

“Do you want to stop?” Mendel says.

I could. We could. The Council would wake up angry and there would be a hearing. The day would be admitted as unaided and the city would be told to wear helmets and keep their knives away from their fingers. That’s what people do when they think the world will fall on them without the net.

I say, “No,” and lean into the glass seat.

We balance the spectral, because that’s what we do. You think not because you think of yourself as thoughtful, but because thought is the only way to keep your hands clean.

At 07:00, the morning audience begins. The Loom is not a secret to the city. It is a secret to the rest of the world, which pretends not to know and sends us students and carefully framed news crews. Heliotrope sips its coffee extra slowly on days when I am on rotation. The docents open the line. Two Councilors log in, one with a tie so red my implants throw a warning for over-saturation.

“Good morning,” I say into the mic. “We’re live.”

“Spare us the poetry,” the tie says. It is Councilor Agati, who is allergic to lighting and wears a hat in rooms no one else would call bright. “Are we on track?”

We are always on track, until suddenly we are not, and then someone writes a smear across places where smears cannot go.

“We are,” I say. “Initial runs show seventeen problematic threads in the 09:00 to 10:00 hour, all avoidable. There’s a weather variance across the peninsula that—”

“Standard,” Agati says. “The algorithm knows what to do.”

The algorithm knows what to do. The docents frown at him through their glass like fish.

“Anything else,” says the other Councilor, a woman from Ward Five whose name I always forget and who always remembers mine.

I could tell them about the smear. The protocol is not clear. You don’t write protocols for this kind of thing; it frightens the people who fund you. I could tell them my name is scratched into invariants like a prayer.

“No,” I say. “We’re humming.”

We hum. The holography in the viewing room above the stacks runs the prettiest visualization because the docents asked it to. Out in the city, Oona turns over in bed and gropes for a coffee cup that is and isn’t there. A child on Barge Street loses her kite in three threads and tugs her mother’s hand harder in the fourth. The joggers reconsider their route in that way that says they are listening to a voice they will not name.

At 09:13, the spectral narrows. The job is less art than editing, at this point. The engine feeds me its recommendation. The math hangs in the air. You think you understand it because it is translucent.

Nine thousand six hundred and ninety-two threads whisper not this one, not that one. The thicker strands accumulate around a day where the ferry has a minor delay and the school tour arrives late and avoids the man who would have spilled coffee here if his cup were not empty, and a meaningless fight becomes only a sentence said and then apologized for. Little things. We sell it in little things. We do not talk about the nights we tune the algorithm harder to avoid the storms.

At 09:16, Mendel leans into my shoulder. His breath smells like peppermint and worry.

“Look,” he says.

The smear has darkened, as if the soot took a breath.

It can’t. The interface field is constant. If I made a movie of Bay One, it would be the same frame over and over again until someone came in and touched something. The guard plate’s scratch looks deeper. The arrow is more aggressive, somehow, like handwriting has inflection.

At 09:16:30, my implant pings. It is not a sound I have heard before. It is like the taste of metal.

The text is bare, bold, floating in the middle of my spectral. It overrides the UI in a way I would have sworn was impossible without a ceremonial tour of passwords and vows. It is not a system message. It is not from Council, or from Mendel, or from the docents. The engine gives it no origin. I know spam when I see it. This isn’t that.

Rae, do not collapse at 09:17.

My mouth goes dry. The spectral warbles. I hear the city singing itself into focus and I could stop it by not breathing, but that is not how breath works, or songs.

Agati is in my ear, and the metaphor of it makes me hate him more than usual. “Engineer Halden,” he says, using my last name like a knife. “We’re ready.”

“Rae,” Mendel says, low. “We could.”

Someone thinks they are me. Someone is me. The arrow on the guard plate points at the smear, which points at the keelstone, which points at nothing, because the keelstone points at everything. You can hide anything in a chorus, if you do it gently enough. Lingering charcoal across the invariants. A name carved into steel. A message that has no source.

We do not have time for this.

I could stall. I could announce a microdelay. I could cough, and the docents would smile at the audience and talk about how the Loom requires us to be careful because care is love. I could listen.

“Rae,” says the message, as if it had eyes.

There are reasons to gather your courage and do what other people tell you not to. There are reasons to be sure. All my training is those reasons quartz-etched into bone.

“Collapse,” Agati says. “Now.”

I touch the key.

The city inhales. The spectral lifts, then falls, like a flock of birds turning. Something in me tries to turn with them and is pinned by the glass, by the field, by the weight of ten thousand days flattening to one. My implant runs the correlations. The algorithms smile. The docents begin their applause. Heliotrope tumbles into a day where the ferry is late and no one’s coffee spills in the library and the paper dragon gets caught on a traffic light and it is funny and not dangerous.

The engine relaxes around the choice like water around a stone. It is always a relief. It is always like this, and the way we say it aloud to ourselves is: success.

In Bay One, the smear remains.

“See?” Mendel starts to say.

Before he can finish, the alarm that is not an alarm goes off. It is in my head and under my tongue, fizzing. I am rarely surprised by my own body in the Loom. The implant has a generous sense of what will upset me.

We do not have alarms for this because we do not have this. The keelstone’s field becomes a tone so low I can feel my fillings answer. The Josephson forest goes still.

In the spectral that no longer exists, I see an arrow pointed down, a handprint in soot. In the only day there is, the scratch on the guard plate is deeper still. The letters are not just my name. Someone has added more.

Under RAE ↓, there are six new words, etched clean in the exact center of the metal, as if something sharp and deliberate has written them there in the one second between yes and yes.

You didn’t listen. Now look outside.

“Rae.” Mendel’s voice is the handheld from when he first took me up on the ferry roof and told me not to be afraid of wind. “Don’t. Don’t.”

I don’t.

It does not matter. The Loom is in me and I am in the Loom and the city is the song that we just chose and I hear it change.

Outside, Heliotrope always has birds. We cultivated them, because there is something about a city that is kinder when it remembers to feed its sky.

The glass in the core gives me a sliver of the reading room up above, the way it always does, a postcard of the world reflected down a shaft. It is enough. Oona would call it the sedimentary of my life, layer upon layer of places I look because my work has taught my eyes to make doors out of windows and windows out of doors.

In that sliver, the birds stop.

Not all at once. That would be too easy, too neat. It is more like a disease, crossing from beak to feather to wingtip, a slow glitch in the morning air. The first one I see is a gull, frozen three inches above the rail, the tilt of its head at an angle that my stomach recognizes as wrong. In the next breath, the others hang, too, suspended in perches that do not hold them. A pigeon with one foot tucked up becomes an ornament. A swallow tears itself mid-arc into a dot.

It takes my brain thirty seconds to name what I am seeing and then to reject the name and then to fight for it again. I taste metal as if I have bitten the city.

Time is not a thing you should be able to smudge.

“What did you do,” Agati says, though he says it like, What have you done to me.

I put my hand out to the glass. My palm meets my face in reflection. I see the hollows queue up like men with suits in the Council chamber, waiting to be acknowledged. I see hands that are and aren’t mine smear soot on steel. I see Oona standing at our sink, one hand on the faucet that streams water and another hand held under a faucet that pours nothing at all.

“We collapsed a good day,” I say, knowing that is not what he asked.

“Correction,” says the message that has no origin, mild as if we were having coffee. It is not in my implant. It is not in the speakers. It is somewhere else. “You collapsed a possible day that had a hole in it. The hole is now the city you live in. Rae. Listen.”

Then every bird in Heliotrope, all the sleepers and all the hunters, all the small brown city wrens and all the cormorants on the ferry pilings and all the pigeons that wait for news on the library rail, begin to fall at once. The drops are not dramatic. They are not cinematic. They are just a series of lines breaking, one after the other, like someone has snipped the wires of a mobile. The bodies do not accelerate properly. Some of them do not move at all, hanging in the seams between beats.

The docents upstairs start to scream. Agati says something I would not repeat to another human being if he paid me. Mendel’s hand finds my wrist, hot and hard.

“Rae,” he says, and I have never heard my name sound like a door slamming.

I am looking at the place the birds were. I am listening to the voice that told me not to do the only thing I am good at. I am tasting the tang of a hundred forever-mornings I will not live.

And because the machine under the library sings whether I do or not, because the city does not know how to stop, the engine begins to run the next second, and the next, and the next.

I swallow blood I do not remember biting into my tongue. I say, stupidly and beautifully, to the air and the Council and the docents and the birds and the message and to Mendel, “We need to reverse.”

“You can’t reverse a collapse,” says Agati, blank with terror.

The voice in the nowhere laughs, not unkindly. “You can’t, Rae. But you can learn how not to do this again.”

“I did this,” I say.

“No,” the voice says, and this time it sounds like someone I have known my whole life, but older. More tired. “We did. The difference now is that this time, you get to see it.”

Chapter One

Tamsin Pell hung two hundred meters above the deathline, and the sail sang in her bones.

They called it a sail because someone, long ago, needed a name that didn’t make you think of the fact that if the rigging snapped, if a seam unzipped under the pressure differential, the entire field would whip itself into the bright and carry you with it like a seed on a hot wind. Sail sounded gentler than metamaterial array. It sounded like a choice, like something you took into weather and coaxed into the right shape, instead of something you clamped between towers and begged not to tear.

The sail above her–below her–was a taut gray plane, bounds glittering where the tension cables joined to carbon pylons and the pylons rooted into Vesper’s outer rim. Its woven surface was a trick, a dance of light absorption and reflection tuned to keep the city alive. On the side turned toward the incandescent day, the membrane flickered low albedo, collecting heat into the superfluid veins and rerouting it into the subterranean mass. On the side turned toward the cold, it shone high-albedo and sent precious sunlight shivering along its length like a rumor. The membrane did not mind the heat. It did not mind the cold. It pulsed and laughed at the wind.

It was finally laughing again.

“Don’t smile,” Quill said in her ear. “I know when you smile. It means you’re about to do something stupid.”

He was on the next line over, ten meters to her left, a dark shape in a dark harness, boots hooked into the sail’s mesh by metal-claw stirrups. Like her, he hung face-down, the world a curve beneath him. Above them, an abyss of black-and-carmine sky. Below them, the line of land that kept everyone sane: the dark of the night side at their backs, the torturing bright of the day side ahead. The terminator carved the world into halves and they worked in the knife edge.

“I’m not smiling,” Tams said.

“You are. I can hear your teeth catching air.”

Tams rolled one shoulder against the harness so the sail hummed into a slightly different register. She wore it the way she wore her balance, low and private. Other people needed instruments to listen to the membrane; they clamped their sensors and analyzed the data and went home convinced. Tams learned listening out here, with carbon-fiber pressing into her sternum and the wind pushing steady at her neck.

The sail had been out of tune for days. There’d been an under-scratch like nervous fingers on a table. They had checked the anchor tension, swapped the bad vanes, cooled the chiral switchboards. The scratch remained and with it a measured two-point decline in power capture. It was small enough that Supervisor Rodrik wanted to schedule the main inspection for next week and try to ride the cycle out. “There’s a flare due anyway,” he’d said. “No point crawling under if the star’s about to kick you off.”

Tams had argued. She’d argued without numbers, which was not the way to win. She had argued by leaning into the railing at Central Dock 6 and telling him how the sail sounded.

“Like a throat,” she’d said. “Dry. Like it wants water.”

There wasn’t water anywhere near the bright. She knew how that sounded. She had known she lost the moment the words left her mouth. But Rodrik had watched her for a moment from under the bristle of his forehead and said, “Half an hour. Take Quill. If the flare sirens start while you’re out, you recall on the beat. No improvisation.”

Out here, improvisation was a survival skill and a death wish. They all did it. They all promised not to.

“Thirty,” said Quill now. “Twenty-three left. Give the thing a scratch and let’s go home.”

Tams swallowed. Her mouth was dry behind the rebreather. Air tasted of metal and sunlight, though the sunlight itself never touched her skin. The membrane sloughed it off, kept it in its clever veins. She slapped a sensor ladder onto the nearest seam, let the haptics trickle into her harness, and filtered out the city noise in her head.

The fabric vibrated in layers, a dozen conversations stacked and shimmering. Some of them were constant: the wind combing the ribs, the thrum of the anchor pylons thrice out past her, the distant, steady chug of Vesper’s mass pumps as they drank heat and sent it under. That was the undertone that never changed, the heartbeat (the word was wrong, but people used it anyway). Then there were the transient harmonics: gusts, birds–the thin, errant seabirds who followed the city for heat–Quill shifting his weight, a side guy line stretching microscopically against its lubricants.

Under all of it, the scratch.

She closed her eyes against the vertigo and touched her left gloved hand to the membrane, fingertips speechless. The glove’s tactile amplifiers rendered the vibrations into a shape in her palm. The scratch wasn’t random. It was high-frequency, then dropping, then high again. It had a period that roamed in a circlet around her.

“How wide?” she asked.

Quill said, “Too wide. It’s in segment D through G at least. Those panels flex wrong and it drags the rest like a tug.”

“No puncture,” Tams said. “No fiber fatigue. No grit.” She would have smelled grit. Grit was the desert’s voice when it whispered up to you and promised to flay you clean. Grit stuck in the crevices of the metamembrane and made it creak.

“You’re going to propose it’s a feeling,” Quill said, resigned.

“It’s a waveform,” Tams said. “It’s being impressed on the sail, not generated by it.”

Quill went quiet a long second. The wind sang. Out ahead, the red little star that owned them rose fat over the bright, and Tams felt the flares waiting in it the way a cat might feel rain: a smell, a stance of humid heat. The star was calm, though. The star was an old coin in her palm.

“You’re saying it’s the pylon,” Quill said. “Anchor B. We checked the B sensors twice. A third time with the good scope.”

“No,” Tams said. “Not from the bright.” She shifted again and the scratch laxed in her palm, shifted its phase and slid in slow motion across the width of her hand, like a breeze turning. She had the stupid thought of someone’s fingers, drumming on the far end of something too tight to see. “It’s transverse.”

“Come again?”

“Sideways,” she said. “Across. Not along the bright/dark axis. Across our line. It goes toward night.”

Quill actually laughed. “Nothing comes from the night.”

The night side was an ocean of black. The only lights in it were the beacon masts–you could count them if you knew where to look, a necklace of old expedition challenges receding into frozen dune and cliff. The permanent shadows smelled like iron and airless glass. The city’s old men told stories about walkers who had drifted that way, convinced by some inner voice or chemistry that they would be safe. They weren’t. In the dark, you made your heat and the dark ate it. In the bright, the heat made you and the bright ate it. In the middle, the terminator, people made contraptions like sails to delay being eaten. That was the story, elegant and pitiless.

Tams lipped the rebreather aside just long enough to spit at the thought. The spittle dried on the membrane before she could see it. Vesper’s Outer Nine were full of people who said what Quill had said without even the laugh: Nothing comes from the night.

Her mother, who still left candles burning on their shelf to the memory of the long-run, said otherwise. Her mother’s stories had too many names and dates and not enough endings. Her father’s name sat in the middle of them like a weight.

Tams leaned forward until the harness took her sternum and the sail hummed into her breastbone. “Hold me,” she said.

“I got you,” Quill said.

She unhooked one boot and slid it forward, slowly. The membrane thrummed. Her left hand splayed for balance. Her right hand dragged the sensor ladder along. They didn’t question why she was moving toward the night side because neither of them needed to say it; the scratch drifted that way and her body aligned with sound before thought caught up.

The city’s rim fell away behind her. Off the corner of her eye she saw Vesper’s towers like spoked bone, white and delicate and braced against a constant dark wind. She counted their number to keep her nerves from burning up: One for the first generation who’d built the keel-rigs, two for the next who had welded their homes under a sky like crushed wine, three for her grandparents who had set down in a city that was already something like permanent. Counting made movements small and precise. She moved the way she played the broken cello her father had given her when she was twelve: with intent tied to listening.

The scratch braided itself into something not like speech but not unlike language. It had repetends. It had gaps. It had a rhythm that made her tongue want to tap against the back of her teeth. She could see it in her head the way people who did numbers saw spirals when they read primes.

“Tams,” Quill said, slow. He sounded like a man watching someone step backward toward a cliff. “That’s not vibration from the pylon. That’s cable talk.”

“It’s too slow for cable talk,” Tams said, hating how breathless she sounded. “Our side lines are tuned stiffer.”

“Not our side lines,” Quill said. “Think bigger.”

She froze. The wind slid past her hood with a silk scratch. On the horizon, the bright turned white, a place no human could stare and keep their sight. The night behind her turned blacker, which was not possible. Her hearing expanded until she felt she could hear Vesper’s boilers individually burping in their undercity cavities.

The sail fields arced along the terminator for many kilometers, a necklace of segments selves with their own pylons and cables and switchboards, all laced to each other by long, long spanners meant to equalize tension in storms. Those spanners were not supposed to talk; they were supposed to be dumb. They wasted nothing on live sensors, on active modulation. Yet she knew a thing from when she had trained under Kafo O, who said things you weren’t supposed to say and showed you the parts you weren’t meant to see. He had knocked on a crossbeam at Dock 3 and said, “Do you feel that? That comes when wind jumps segments. That’s the line telling you about it.”

“Junction spanner,” she said now, almost not aloud. “Someone is touching a junction spanner and we’re hearing the talk.”

Quill swore softly. “From the night side.”

“It’s not from the bright.”

The scratch paused. It came again, a triangular series, like a child in a stairwell stamping every third step. On, off, off, on, off, off. Her hand tingled where the glove transmitted it. She felt stupid tears press behind her eyes, not for sentiment, not even for fear, but because she knew it. She had known it once and hit the same pattern back with the heel of her palm against the Frame 12 ladder in her family’s loft while her father laughed and said, “You’re hearing the chord but what it means is that you know what a chord is, not that the chord says your name, Tam.”

Her father had gone into the dark two years after that. He had not come back. She had received no chords since.

“Tams,” Quill said again. He used her name like a hand on the back of her neck. “You have twenty minutes. Record and go.”

“I’m recording,” she said.

She had been, as soon as she had slapped the sensor on. She let the idiot tear trickle sideways into her hair under the cap. She breathed slow.

The sail hummed and offered more. The triangular pattern resolved into a chain, into a longer phrase. There was a pause, exactly like the one the city took before the first bells of shift-change. Then the pattern came back, the same, an assertion more than a question.

“Tams.”

“I know,” she said. She could feel Quill watching her spine.

In her heads-up, the flare siren indicator sat pale and low. The star held its breath. They could finish this. She could finish this, then go back to the dock and sit through Rodrik’s annoyance and wash grit out of her hair and listen to the recording until dawnlights. She wanted then, suddenly, something irrational and enormous: to take her father’s broken cello from its rack and fit new strings and tune it to the sail and let the entire city hear how the night talked through wire.

It was midday by the city clocks. The bright burned. The night took heat and frowned in its sleep.

“Three more minutes,” she said. “Then we go.”

The membrane rippled as if someone had kicked the pylon. She felt the kick in her teeth and ribs. Quill swore again, louder. He was not a man who used up words like that. “Jump,” he said. “That’s not wind. Someone’s hauling on lacing.”

The flare sirens pulsed on her HUD. Tams’s entire throat went dry. Not a flare yet; a warning. The star had hiccuped. The sensors tuned to jets of plasma that could peel a city like fruit had sniffed something and thought it might get worse. “Twelve minutes,” Quill said. “Eleven, if Rodrik’s feeling like your father today.”

She didn’t correct the grammar of that. She swallowed again.

On, off, off. On, off, off.

You know what a chord is.

She knew what a chord is. Her glove hand shook. She stilled it. She set her thumb against the seam and tapped in response. With the membrane’s vastness, with the number of ways vibrations could run and vanish and scatter, she had no right to assume any response would go back along the same route. But the junction spanners took equalization pulses from anywhere and translated them into tension across the network, and if this was that, if this was a touch on wire instead of a voice on air —

On, off. She tapped. On. She paused. Off, off. On.

Quill’s intake of breath hissed across the channel like a strike. “No, Tams. No, no.”

The scratch fell into a hole. She felt it vanish, as if a door had closed five rooms down in an old house. Her chest folded over an emptiness.

“She’s off,” she said, her voice smaller than she meant it to be. “It’s gone.”

“I swear to you if we die because you wanted to flirt with a frozen wire–”

“Shut,” Tams said, automatic.

The sirens on her HUD stayed amber. She counted ten counts. She counted another ten. She had heard enough of the phrasing to set a model to work in the background out of habit. She had a name‑tag for it already, a ghost’s foolish hope, and she wasn’t proud of herself for the quickness with which she had typed it. She locked the file. She did not let it go to general.

“Pack your ladder,” Quill said. “We’re on return.”

She pulled the sensor back, rolled it into its cylinder, clipped it. The membrane ceased its translation and went back to general polyphonic hum. Tams fixed her boot-straps and glanced back at the city as she swung the harness around and, neatly, lightly, rode the line down one meter to test the anchor. The line softened and caught. Quill made the same motion, one over for redundancy.

Below and behind them, Vesper rose out of the terminator in tiers, its white and blue shells canted inward like a bowl, its streets braided with wind organs that converted sound into stored power and power into cooled air and cooled air into breathing. On a clear day, the organs sang a chord you could hear from the sail. Today they muttered, wait and see, wait and see. Tams watched the sunlight scrape along the edge of a tower and thought with an unreasonable suddenness of the loft shelf where the cello leaned, its neck worn by her father’s left hand.

“Quill,” she said.

“What.”

“What if it isn’t from the far spanner? What if it’s the near one. The Winter Span.”

Quill took a second to process. “That doesn’t go into the dark. That’s internal to Dock 9. We use it when we need to drop the fields to let the cold front through.”

“It’s frozen then,” Tams said. “That’s why it sounds like this. It’s stiff.”

“Nothing’s moving on the Winter. No one’s stupid enough to–”

Another kick. She almost bit her tongue. Quill swore a third time, used her name like a curse. “Okay,” he said. “Enough. Back.”

They went. Crossing outward was easier than returning because you listened different. Tams moved hand-over-hand along the line, boots skimming the membrane with care. You never stepped too hard. You never dug in. The city glided into a rising angle. Her wrists ached from small movements. Her neck had a hot ache from resisting the pull of the harness; if you let it take you, it punished you later. Her bones knew the routine. Her mind hummed on something else.

On, off, off.

It had been a chord too simple to be math anonymous. It was a name insofar as a dog’s name is a precise thing: a sound that got someone’s attention. The file in her HUD ticked translator cycles and spat out nothing helpful. She would go to her mother’s loft and sit with the cello and pluck the peg and the line of it would be wrong and her mother would say why are your hands shaking and she would tell a lie, a half-good one, about the flare.

The amber siren went red.

The sudden button of it in her eye made her flinch. The membrane translated the tension in her boots into a long rippling tone, and Quill hissed, “Do not you make noise. Do not make the sail sing when the star’s about to–”

“It’s fine,” she said. The word was a charm. It worked sometimes. The red blinked and steadied. The star’s calm coin face shivered.

They were close. On her left, the anchor tower rose into the membrane with an angle that never stopped making her body shrink from it. It was a structure designed to let wind pass through and it looked like a thing designed to cut wind into pieces.

There was a percussion beneath her bones. Not the scratch. Not wind. She felt it as a code before she recognized it as a physical thing: the flares, when they came, did not arrive as light alone. They came with particles that found the long cables and could not decide whether to flow or freeze. The protean shrug of it traveled along the metal-headed rope into her harness and into her bones and into the ghost of the cello, maybe. She tasted copper.

“Now,” Quill said. “Now, now. We clip to the tower, we ride her in.”

They did. The tower’s climbing rail accepted her carabiner with a happy click that felt vulgarly intimate. The tower’s hum was an order. Come inside. Stop playing at edges.

Tams turned her head once more, not because she expected to see anything, but because you always looked, a superstition from crews older than hers. The bright was indecent. The dark was a mouth. The sail was a taut breath between.

There was a smear at the very far horizon, something like a line of aurora, by which she had learned in school to mean charged particles darting along field lines. But there were no field lines there. There was no atmosphere that kept aurora in one place. The smear moved like a ribbon pulled taut.

“Tams,” Quill said.

“I see it,” she said.

“Don’t see it. Move.”

They moved. The tower embraced them, a cage shutting around their harnesses. A door swung in. The interior had a smell like cold coins and grease, like old sweat and something else: a scent she did not have a word for that meant safety to people with different bone maps than hers. It made her teeth ache. She wanted, as always, to put her forehead against the pylon’s skin and apologize for something. They had done this to the planet. They had made it sing. And made it sing wrong.

She popped her boots free, unclipped the line from her hip. Quill undid his straps with neat motions, his long fingers quick in gloves. He looked at her once, eyes travelling like a tally. “You’re coming in, right? You’re not going to decide you want to go to Dock 9 to look at the Winter.”

“I’m coming in,” she said.

She meant it. The flare sirens howled then, not in her eyepiece but through air, a long rising call that went through tower metal and through skin and through habit. It made people below them stop what they were doing and fold work up under benches. It made shutters slide. It made children widen their eyes and tuck under tables and recite the difference between light and charged wind and thermal load. It made mothers put their hands on shelves where old cellos leaned and whisper a name and bite the inside of their cheeks hard so they would not say anything else aloud.

The membrane flexed. The tower shuddered. The threshold between dark and bright thickened in a way you could not photograph, only feel. It was like the entire city took a breath in and waited to see if it would get to let it out.

They rode the elevator down. It was articulated to keep movement minimal. The tower’s spine did not like to be asked to think during flares.

“File?” Quill said to her without looking.

“Logged,” Tams lied.

He snorted. “I’m not your supervisor. I don’t care. I want us both to know where to look later, when we’re bored. Rodrik will sleep two hours, easy, if it hits us wrong.”

He did care. He did not care in the way that meant rules broke. He cared like a man who could not unlearn his own curiosity and had learned to tuck it under jokes. It was the better way, probably. Tams envied it. She had only wanting too big and bones a city had tuned for the wrong music.

They came out at Dock 6. The dock was a cavern with windows that looked toward the city’s heart and shutters that could be slammed if the bright decided to kick. Men and women and the others in neutral uniforms moved with practiced briskness toward down-valves, toward panel arrays that would let them absorb as much as they could without burning out the undercity. The dock’s wind organs had already shut. Their mouths gleamed like turned brass.

Rodrik had his hands on his hips and his mouth pursed, and Tams knew before he opened it that he would say, “I said half.”

“Half,” Quill lied easily.

Rodrik’s face did something like a twitch that was the sum of thirty years on this edge. He reached toward a panel and then toward Tams, the gesture incomplete. He changed his mind. “In,” he said. “No heroics.”

“We’re in,” Quill said.

Tams wanted to say a stupid thing then, wanted to say: I heard a chord. She shut up. She unbuckled, she stowed, she ran the check sequence on her harness with the automatic movements of a body that had been trained into salvation. She looked at the dock window when she should not have and saw the smear again, the auroral thing along the far junction line, a color she could not name. She felt the membranes sing a note low enough to knead her liver.

“Pell,” Rodrik said from behind her. “When we ride this one out, go to Central. Someone left a message for you.” He said it like he was passing her a wrench.

Her skin went cold and then hot. “What kind of message.”

“Old format,” he said. “Not on net. Paper. On the glass of the counter like a time capsule. Asks for you by name.” He squinted, then, as the flare’s first edge struck their field and the dock vibrated. “We’re going to have to jump the B-laterals,” he said. “If we don’t want to sweat in our beds tonight.”

“On it,” Quill said.

“Go,” Rodrik ordered, and they went.

The flare came down like a visit from a god who had gotten bored of other people and remembered there was, after all, this small city clinging to a strip of planet near a red star’s heavy eye. It came as light and wind that wasn’t wind, as fingers in antennae, as an ache in her dental work. Tams leaned into her panel and worked her hands the way she had learned, the way her weight learned to trust lines. It was not music. It was its cousin, the cranky one who made dinner and kept you alive.

When the worst of it passed, there was sweat on her collar and her braid had stuck to the back of her neck and her fingers hurt. Quill had a flush across his cheekbones that made him look young enough to be dangerous. Rodrik leaned against the counter with his hand over his mouth like a man who had just had a thought he would not share. The dock gates, visible through the glass, had taken on a reflective sheen that meant heat, that meant working out of debt. The sound downstairs, at the level of the organs and the pipes and the engines they fed, shifted into the hopeful. That was a bad move. Hope made people sloppy. Rodrik began shouting orders again to fix it.

Tams wiped her palm on her trouser and said as calmly as her mouth would allow, “Central.”

Rodrik waved a hand without looking, then noticed and saw her. He held her for a second in a gaze that hurt worse than the flare’s sting. It said what it always said: you are too much like him. It said something else too: we need your hands, and I do not want to know what your wanting will do.

“Go,” he said.

She went.

The hall from Dock 6 to Central curved inward and down. Portraits of past supervisors drifted across the left wall, etched onto thin transparent film that had bubbled at the edges and made everyone look slightly melted. Tams passed them with her chin up. Her heart had the jump in it that meant big trouble or big love. The city smelled like hot bread and ozone. Everyone moved with that sped-up quiet that followed flares, the sense of having. If you breathed, you had been spared.

Central had glass counters and brass railings to make you feel like your requests were old-fashioned and serious. Tams had always resented it. You could not make brass out of this world unless you hauled it a long way. They had hauled it to make weighty railings and to let secrets sit on a counter with all the sanctity of an old method. She felt herself smile with her teeth, finally.

The clerk behind the counter looked up with eyes that had not seen a flare yet. He pointed to a fold of pale paper under the glass, held down by a pen.

“For you,” he said.

The paper was a torn page from an old ledger. The writing on it was black and thin, made by a nib with patience. The script was not Vesper’s hand. The letters had a slant like distant rain.

Tams felt her hands go cold around the edges. She did not read it at once. She looked through the glass at her own warped reflection and at the people moving and at the door, as if someone would come through it and she would know to run or to go still. She put her finger on the corner of the paper.

It said, Tamsin Pell, by name. It said, Don’t report the pattern you recorded. It said, Come to Dock 9 after shift. It said, Bring your listening. It did not sign a name. It drew three short lines. On, off, off.

Behind her in the city, somewhere far across the ring, a wind organ misfired and put the chord into air. People looked up. The sound ran along the ribs of buildings. It fuzzed hair. It made someone bump into someone else and say, excuse me, sorry, I thought you were—

Tams folded the paper once and put it in her inner pocket and let her breath out very slowly. There were rational options. None of them would let her sleep. The voice in her that was unhelpful, that was brave when it should be disinterested, dropped a coin in the slot and made a choice.

She was not her father. She told herself that as if telling her bones would change their mind.

“Dock 9,” she said to no one, and when she turned to go, the city’s lights adjusted to flare-light and her shadow went long along the floor like it had been waiting to remember a shape it had mostly forgotten.

On quiet days, the halls of the Archive forgot there was anything left to collect. Light threaded the air in patient strands, humming with the soft, fractional tonality of the station’s heartbeat. The long curve of the Gallery of Ends ran ahead, every seventh step lifting to remind you the whole thing orbited something else—magnetically anchored to the throat of a captured black dwarf, swinging a slow circle through a region of space so tidy with emptiness that the nearest honest star was a long whetstone away.

Mara Sen walked the gallery before her docent shift and counted her breaths between the doors. Habit. Calibration. She’d learned it from an older curator who could hear the subtle drift in the gravity tide and tell when a micrometeor had smiled across the shield nets. Most people heard nothing. Most people who came here had never trained their ear to the place. They were tourists, mourners, petitioners, the curious intimately or distantly afraid. They had questions. They wanted stories. They wanted mercy.

Door Fifty-One breathed as she passed, just enough to stir the hair along her forearm. The room behind it was sealed for now, but she knew what waited: a lautering ocean made of salt and silica and organ keys, music that ate its singers as they made it. The Orloi Choir. She had fallen asleep to their end three nights in a row after they came in, confirming the metadata and placing the context loops, and she had dreamed of water cracking like hot glass. If she closed her eyes she could still feel their collected mind locking itself into a chord so precise it made heat, see a horizon of throat-bright spires, and the way the light jerked when the sky turned to steam.

She put her palm to the seal and the door hummed its agreement. Not today. Her shift schedule pulled her toward a group of twelve: a school from the Okeanos orbitals, mostly tall and half-grown, one of their teachers bristling at the jaw with the texture of a nanocaster stencil. The schedule overlay ticked in her peripheral:

0900: Survey: Dialogues with Nemesia Planum. 0945: The Farseeder Dust. 1015: The Ji-Arc Blossom Collapse. 1040: Questions.

She might have time to work through the backlog of visitor emails after that, three of them urgent. A woman asking if the Archive had an end for a particular fragment of human culture and whether she could view it privately—No, unless the Requesting Collective consented. A poet offering to sell them a complete suite of mortal shanties allegedly sung by people on the last generation ship to abandon Mars—No, the Archive did not acquire private funerary media without a public matching grant. A ship asking to be recognized as extinct.

At 0858 the Diamonds corridor wavered with the sound of teenagers suppressing the urge to run. Their teacher pulsed a greeting to the wall; the wall considered it and opened. Mara straightened as they filed through, practiced her smile in the reflection of Door Forty-Nine. She almost had it when a shadow pushed off the far threshold and came toward her with the long-limbed swim of the station-born.

“Curator Sen?” he asked, halfway through a bow and looking unsure if anyone bowed here.

“Mara,” she said. “Welcome. Is this your first time?”

“Mine, yes. Their second. The school rotates. I’m not a teacher, exactly. I’m a parent.” He looked as if that word meant more than it used to. His eyes scanned the doors with hunger and something like anger wrapped inside it. It wasn’t an uncommon mix. He was from the Okeanos support belt—Tethys in his accent, the g drift pulling his shoulders a little forward. He’d be thinking about water and what killed water.

“Then you know the protocols,” she said gently. “This is not a reliquary. This is not POV or immersive reconstruction. No one here is living or trapped. You can’t change anything you see. Your presence is a matter of respect, not rescue.”

He nodded, jaw working. “I want my child to—” He paused, searching. “To understand there is an end. That it is a thing with weight. You carry it better if you see how others did.”

Mara had learned not to answer that directly. See how others did was one of the Archive’s phrases, and it was both simple and untrue. They didn’t have the ends of everything. They had what they had, and it was always exactly enough to be unbearable.

She got them arranged in two curved rows and guided them to the thin blue line on the floor that marked the best angle for Door Seventy-Nine. The kids were trying not to lean on the rail, trying not to ask too fast. Their teacher made the formal request, and the door thought about it and slid.

The Gallery of Ends wasn’t made of rooms. That was a metaphor the Archive let people use because it made living nervous systems calmer. The truth of Door Seventy-Nine was an aperture opened into a boundary that was not a boundary at all, a sheet cut through spacetime like glass, cunningly wound in on itself and anchored to this place, a field that made a pocket where photons could build a continuous story. The Archive did not simulate. They did not render. They caught the last opaque wavefronts of a habitable surface, the last bundle of signals measurable as a world held itself together, and they made those photons wait in a way that light was not meant to wait, until someone asked to see them.

The door let the last moments of Nemesia Planum breathe, and the temperature dropped two degrees. The kids flinched. The teacher did not.

The planum was a valley of basalt carved into lace by wind, five hundred million years of sculpting, something like Earth in its memory of water and nothing like Earth in its air, ethane and a hundred sweet poisons. The inhabitants were shovel-headed walkers who wore the light in patterns on their skin, making mathematics in color, talking in angle and occlusion. You could watch them thinking if you knew how to read their albedo. They did not have language. They had geometry. They arranged themselves in circles and made their decisions by rotational symmetry. When the flare hit—not a small one, nothing their cliffs and caves could swallow—the shadows that had been the base of their logic baked themselves flat, and in that one last minute the walkers arranged themselves in a new pattern that was not rotational and not a circle.

“Can you pause it?” one of the kids asked, voice high, gloved fingers white-knuckled on the rail.

“You can slow, and you can stop at the end,” Mara said. “Pausing is a kind of selecting, and we don’t select.”

The teacher touched the rail. “They knew,” he said.

“They did,” Mara said. She knew the translation overlay would be doing its gentle work in the personal devices, letting each watcher understand what mattered in their own language. It would not tell them how Nemesia Planum felt. No one but Nemesia Planum knew that.

When the light winked and the door returned to its rest, half the kids were crying or trying not to. The Okeanos parent had tears hanging in the corners of his eyes and was rubbing at his wrist to keep from wiping them. It was going fine. Mara had been doing this ten years and she could tell when a group made the turn from morbid to reverent.

She took them through the Dust of the Farseeders, a drifting lantern of cleared room, a thousand microtubes suspended, each holding a thread of collected culture the size of a hair. The kids asked how a plague of confused neutrinos could make instruments confess. She said if she tried to answer, they would not hear the rest of the tour. She showed them the Ji-Arc Blossom, a city grown like brain coral on the underside of a red slush moon, unfurling and then taking itself apart when its core found a prime it could not factor. The kids laughed once, weakly, when the teacher made a joke about never learning their multiplication tables.

Mara had just shepherded a boy whose small, hard hand had found her sleeve—what did it feel like? he’d whispered; like being watched by the sky—when her skin lit a polite cold across her sternum. The alert touched the implant along her rib cage and wrote a word across her inner eye in silver.

AMBER.

Her breath caught. She kept her face. The station’s heartbeat did not change. The kids asked and she answered. The alert wrote more, patient because it had to be. She finished the Blossom Collapse and stood the group in the bending hall between doors with its dots of star-graph annotating a thousand missing things. The winch in her chest tugged her toward the Receiving Halo.

“I have to hand you to my colleague,” she said, and the teacher’s eyes tracked her gaze for a second then away, because everyone polite learned not to look directly at an AMBER when a curator had one unless you shared that privilege. The Okeanos parent bowed to her, then bowed to Door Forty-Seven for reasons Mara didn’t think he understood. She didn’t correct him. Someone would.

She walked fast and did not run.

AMBER was not loud by design. The Archive did not ring bells and fling doors to the walls. An arrival was not a show. The silent similes she used when she gave school presentations—an orrery in reverse, a net cast into deep water catching not fish but parts of a sea—did not prepare you for the actual Halo when it woke. No words did. The Halo was a torus wrapped around the station’s belly, a patient coil of exotic matter and anything the donors would call magic if they’d had a word for it, which they certainly did by now. In it, space had been taught a new trick: it could be knotted and unknotted, its gradient made to incline in ways it would rather not, such that the last broadcast, the last emissions, the last light of a thing that died very far away and very long ago could be deflected until it ran down this slope and into this waiting pocket.

There were nine curators on the station. There should always be nine. At this hour, two were on the far side guiding a council of diplomats through the Rooms of Wars We Killed Ourselves With. One was sleeping in the dark tank. Two were at comms. That left her, Director Qel, and a woman from the Weather Conservatory whose job title she never remembered because it changed with the faction in charge of Weather any given week.

Qel was already in the apron when Mara slipped into the control sling. Qel was a slender coil of old scars, half her hair replaced by a cap of implants that ran their cycle like a field of winter wheat in a wind. She turned to look at Mara and Mara saw the way her first mentor had seen, the subtle drift in the gravity of a room.

“You were on the floor?” Qel asked. Her voice was smoke and sugar as always. Some people thought it was a trick voice, engineered to sound like comfort. Mara knew it came from the half of Qel’s lung that was someone else’s.

“I gave them Nemesia and the Blossom,” Mara said. “Farseeder Dust if they come back. Sir, why amber?”

She knew why amber. She knew, by the way the Halo’s edge had brightened a fractional degree, by the way her implant’s feed kept repeating provenance data without committing to a record: Somewhere in the deep, the net had twitched. Something big.

Qel showed her the metadata. They watched it crawl at the speed of bureaucracy over a source that had no patience.

Handshakes: Verified Ladder. Origin: Sol. Epoch: T+8 days. Classification: Terminal Event (Level—)

The classification stuttered, as if the system had chewed a piece of it and broken a tooth. Someone at Comms made a thin sound and swallowed it. The Weather woman sat in a hook against the wall and braided her fingers together.

“Eight days,” Mara said, careful. “Plus or…?”

“Plus,” Qel said. She reached without looking and caught Mara by the wrist, pressed her finger into the gap between two wrist bones, the comfort trick they taught first year to handle human panic. “Possibility. Note the readout. Note the Ladder signature.”

“Orphaned by timeline,” Mara read. “Cross-check—” She swallowed. She, too, had learned to not look directly at the word AMBER on the inner eye. It was a superstition and everyone had it. “We’re sure it’s not a spoof. Or…an artifact of the Receiver.”

“The Receiver doesn’t do art,” Qel said. Not unkind. Just tired.

AMBER meant unscheduled. It meant the Ladder—itself a thing made of many people across many times, a treaty as much as a device—had not sent a formal notice, had not rung the Archive’s bell one standard year in advance to allow for clearance, translation, ethics sign-offs. It meant something was coming like a falling weight, and they would have to catch it before it broke the floor.

“We can deny intake,” the Weather woman said through her laced fingers, looking not at them but at the brightening halo. “We can refuse to anchor. The Charter says—”

“The Charter says we can deny intake if the packet poses risk to the Receiver’s integrity or to the Archive's context integrity,” Qel said. “And that in an AMBER we must weigh the scarcity of the data against the hazard of—”

She stopped. She didn’t like saying data in this context. None of them did. It made the ends feel like things you counted instead of things you held.

“Mara,” she said. “You’ve done eight Anchors.”

“Twelve,” Mara said before she could stop herself, and Qel’s mouth made a tiny shape that some people would call a smile. “I can assist.”

“You’ll lead. Directors should not personally take AMBERs if there is another qualified lead on station,” Qel said. “Else we teach the kids bad habits.”

She pulled the feed down into the shared space. A map of the Halo appeared, a topology of knotted potential colored like a sunrise. There it was: the bright bead of whatever was falling, far out, shivering along decelerated geodesics. The Ladder’s signature unrolled around it like a ribbon, cut off at one end, trailing threads. Orphaned by timeline. The Ladder was a contract made in time. If time misbehaved, the contract couldn’t watch it, and that had reputational consequences.

“This will be delicate,” Qel said softly. “No one say the species yet. No one say the species if you think you know the species. Wait until the pocket is coherent.”

The Weather woman hit the wall with the back of her head and closed her eyes. “You think they can contain themselves?” she asked. “Mara’s a human. Do you think she can contain herself?”

“Do you know how many humans are on the station right now?” Qel asked. “One. The other one caught a shuttle out yesterday to see their grandson grow gills. Guess which one remains.”

Mara put her hands into the gloves. Their interior surfaces tickled her skin in familiar exaggerated friendliness, telling the nerves in her palm all the little lies engineering liked to tell biological tissue to make it accept force feedback. The Halo’s edge softened. The first photons skated the catchment field, trying at once to speed and unable, like a dream when you run and the floor doesn’t agree.

“How do you want to file this?” one of the Comms officers whispered. They didn’t whisper because they had to. The Halo could hear nothing. They whispered because you did, in the presence of an end.

“As a test,” Qel said. “We test the anchor. We test the context. We can declare it art once we’ve held it long enough to call it what it is without becoming a liar.”

Mara breathed once, twice. The gloves passed the motion to the Halo, bleeding the knot into a shape with a mouth. The falling weight found the mouth. It did exactly what all good photons do, which is go wherever the geometry tells them to go.

“Stop watching your hands and watch your end,” Qel said in her left ear, and Mara did that, because she trusted this woman with a thing that had no good name.

It came like a wave meeting a harbor. It came like weather. It spilled itself with reluctant elegance into the pocket, and the pocket stretched to accept it, and then it was there, cupped and cradled, waiting for someone to say yes.

The station dimmed. That was not drama. That was simply what happened when a structure built to be polite to darkness asked for more.

“Context integrity?” Qel asked.

“Seventy-nine percent,” Comms said. “The Ladder meta is torn. We can see two consent tracks and one contested. The contested track is Operating Collective, but the stamp is…old. The standard says we can proceed under dual consent if the third is impossible to notify due to temporal factors.”

“Temporal factors,” the Weather woman said, eyes still closed. “I hate a euphemism that polite.”

“Proceed,” Qel said. She dipped her head to Mara. “Are you ready?”

“No,” Mara said, because the ritual mattered, and because it was truth. “Proceeding anyway.”

The mouth of the aperture took on the shimmer of heat seen from a road. Heat in vacuum was always a strange thing, but then so were a lot of things that were true. The feed told Mara the context had stabilized enough that what they would see would not move. That this would be a real piece of whatever it had been, not a smear of misinterpreted photons. There was a moment when filing kept being filing until it touched you, and then it became a prayer.

The door in front of her was not a door. It was the thinnest part of a thick place. She pulled and the thick place thinned more. It made a sound inside her teeth.

Light.

A horizon curved. Not a planet—you have to know this kind of curve to recognize it—but a blue world seen from above. White wraps of cloud. A brown crescent of land, almost too familiar to be real until familiarity tipped into recognition like a hand finding the bruise it didn’t know it had.

Her stomach dropped to the floor at her feet. Someone behind her breathed her name and made it a question.

The Metadata overlay lied, briefly, by saying nothing. Then it behaved again.

ORIGIN: SOL-III. LOCAL DESIGNATION: EARTH. SUBJECT: HOMO SAPIENS SAPIENS. EVENT CLASS: TERMINAL. WINDOW: T+8 DAYS.

Mara’s hands forgot their training. Her fingers jumped in the gloves, and the gloves told the Halo nothing about that, because the Halo did not care about mammals and their fear.

“Wait,” Qel said softly, and though the word was barely breath, everyone heard it. “No one look without a second. No one decide what this is without at least three counts of we do not know.”

Mara counted. She didn’t think the number would fit in her mouth. She did it anyway, because Qel had taught her, because the Archive demanded it. One: the white at the edge of the world was thicker than she had last seen it in person, years ago, before she had gotten off that well-counted ball. Two: the brown music of the continents had not moved far. Three: the overlay insisted the window was eight days forward and yet did not violate itself with the contradiction of light delay, which meant nothing except that the Ladder had taken steps she did not understand and did not have to.

The image sharpened. Clouds parted as if making a space for them. For her, whispered the part of her that would, no matter how she trained it, always believe in intention.

She could see the limb of the planet, the gradient that had made her child body stretch her hand to cover the sun on watching days. The atmosphere had a bruised look around the edges. That might be the processing. That might be the thing itself.

“Do we ping?” said Comms. “Do we ask the Ladder to confirm? Do we—”

“No,” Qel said. “We don’t send anything anywhere from this room unless we agree on the words. We are not the Authority. We babysit the end of things so people can learn. There are people who will want to fight about this and we will not give them blood to wet the floor.”

“I am a person,” the Weather woman said, standing finally and coming forward, eyes narrowed. “And I want to fight about this without blood. I want to know if the thing we are about to watch is a failure of stewardship, or murder, or an act of God, or if we invented a new category and forgot to name it.”

Mara found her balance. The gloves gripped, the field listened. She could taste copper under her tongue. Home cohered in the aperture, a thing at once completely itself and completely what the Archive taught everything to be: small enough to hold, suddenly larger than she could carry.

“Do we notify?” Comms asked, not asking about the Ladder now.

Qel looked at her. “Mara. You are the lead and the only human. You say the word. We will follow your ethics.”

She could feel the Okeanos parent somewhere on the other side of the station, maybe standing with his child before Door Forty-Seven, possibly feeling the same slow wind of the station’s heart that she felt. She thought of the letters in her queue. She thought of the broken treatises of other worlds and the patience of a place built to say this happened in ways that no one could argue.

“We notify,” Mara said. “We lock the room. We call the Local Assembly of Sol Treaty, the Ladder, the Archive Board, and the public watchers. We do nothing alone.”

She had never been less alone.

The door shivered. The light knotted into clarity. A piece of Earth lay before them, blue and white and brown and green. The overlay slid a subtitle into the air, a courtesy, unnecessary, obscene, perfect.

Last light begins.

The world was wet and wrong in the way of a seam in season. The rain hung a fraction of a second too long in the air, draped in beads that should have fallen but refused, humming with the invisible tension that meant this moment, in some adjacent life, had decided to hesitate. The streetlights were halos. The crosswalk signal kept almost turning red and thinking better of it. A dog on a stoop barked and held its mouth open, bark frozen in a glossy arc.

Mara Qin touched two fingers to the gauge at her jaw, felt the rig’s pulse through her glove. The numbers jittered like nervous fish. She drew a breath that tasted of wet neon and that cold metal tang that clung to the interiors of seams, like you were standing on the inside of a bell that had just rung. In her earpiece, Whistle cleared its artificial throat and started narrating because Whistle could not help narrating.

“Harbor seam, minor, half-life eighteen seconds. Fattened by repetitive weather patterns. Congestion index at three, this is healthy. Anchors holding. Please do not lick anything.”

“I wasn’t going to lick anything,” Mara said.

“You have, in fact, licked things.”

“How would you know that?”
