“I keep logs,” Whistle said. “For liability.”

She grinned even though no one could see it. She was a black silhouette of slick fabric and articulated plates, masked and goggled, standing below a rusted fire escape. The rig anchored around her like a ghost of scaffolding and lampblack. Three silver stakes in the asphalt around her hummed softly, their nested coils sinking into spacetime with a low, steady thrum. Lines of pale light braided between them and the harness at her hips. Above, Dory loomed in a sliver of sky—a rectangle of matte black and matte black, grappling hooks sunk into nothing, as if part of the night had decided to hold itself up. Dory was more concept than craft when she was deployed, but Mara reminded herself that ghost or not, the ship had paid for her bed and food and three of her sister’s surgeries. You did not insult something that practical by doubting it out loud.

The seam was a fold in causality—the telltale lag in a repeating process, a wiggle in the probability field that manifested as drippy weather, haunted elevators, recycling timers that thought about maybe caring. In the old days, people called them déjà vu. Then somebody called them exploitable. Now people like Mara stood in them and took, and the entire system took a breath and did not forgive her. It got her rent paid. It made energy that didn’t need drilling or burning. It was legal if you were careful. It was wrong in ways she tried not to count when she was trying to sleep.

“Aspirate at your leisure,” Whistle said. “You’re losing yield.”

“I can hear the rain thinking,” Mara said softly. “Give me a second.”

“Your second has lasted half a minute objective. Please do not tell the seam about seconds.”

She thumbed the aspirator on.

It was a cage of polished tungsten, six rings nested inside one another, rotating on gyroscopes she could feel but not see. It made a sound like a hand sliding along a piano wire. In the rain, the sound became visible: each ring drew a line of light where drops touched it and refused to fall, then shivered apart. Mara could feel it as a coarse vibration against her ribs. She kept her other hand on the anchor coil, because habit said you stayed grounded. Habit said you kept the anchor between your heart and anything trying to rewrite it.

“Bite is good,” Whistle said. “You’ve clipped the top off the moment. We are at five percent, six, nine. Scalar flow is smooth. A little bit more on ring two, if you please.”

Mara adjusted. In the corner of her display, a series of graphs unfurled. The moment’s amplitude—that little rounding of the curve where physics had sagged—was decreasing. People walked past her, except they weren’t walking; they were the suggestions of people, smeared across a spectrum of possibilities in a way you learned to ignore. The dog stayed an open mouth. The traffic light stayed deciding. In the reflection in a rain-slicked window, she was a thin blur of black and brass and the lens flares of her anchors, a vandal in someone else’s hour.

“Yield at twenty,” Whistle said. “You are doing very good work. Please consider not thinking about the complications of your metaphysical actions until after dinner.”

“Compliment noted,” Mara said dryly. “What complications?”

“Most of your cohort report disassociation and guilt manifesting as visual hallucinations after their third harvest in any twenty-four-hour cycle.”

“If I see pink rabbits,” Mara said, “I’ll document.”

“Remember to tag your rabbits.”

The aspirator thrummed deeper. The rings rotated faster; the rain looked grainy. For a heartbeat—a real one, not this thick slow seam-beat—Mara saw a kitchen. Not here. A kitchen with a yellow linoleum floor and a magnetic strip of knives bought with coupons. A woman sitting on a vinyl chair with one leg tucked under, taking off her shoes, tired in the way that is just a word for the whole body. On the refrigerator, a paper with a star and the name JANELLE written too large with a backward N. The woman’s hand moved as if she could cross the distance to the paper and tuck it into her shirt, into the place under her collarbone where you keep thin precious things safe.

Then it was just rain and a dog and a streetlight and her own breath.

“Whistle,” Mara said, voice very flat.

“Do you require a log mark? I can mark that as a phantom.”

“It looked inhabited,” she said.

“It’s an echo. You are not illegally harvesting inhabited branches. The likelihood mass of anything with a consistent observer self is below threshold.”

“Seemed above threshold.”

“Mara—”

“I know what the regs say,” she said. “Why is there a refrigerator?”

“Harbor seams overlay domestic architecture frequently,” Whistle said. “You have seen refrigerators. You breathe. The human brain is a pattern-assembling machine that will assemble itself into guilt if unattended. I am a machine that will assemble data until the alphanumerics get long.”

The aspirator’s rings had started to glow. The third ring left a white line behind each droplet. She felt the tug in her sternum that meant the yield was crossing into the kind of numbers she would see in a transfer, later. The kind that meant her sister could keep her chair adjusted. That, she told herself, was solid. That existed between bone and blood.

In the kitchen in her head, which she definitely would not report as anything but a vague mood, the woman’s hand hovered.

“Twenty-seven,” Whistle said. “Twenty-eight. That’s a nice seam. If you go to thirty, we can split the bonus and I will name your next dog for you. I am thinking of ‘Ledger’.”

“No,” she said.

“Mara—”

“The rain’s jittering. I don’t like it.”

“If you leave money on the table every time your mammalian hindbrain croaks—”

“I said no.”

She stepped back, thumbed the aspirator down. The rings slowed, the violin-wire hum softened to a cat’s purr and then to the memory of a cat. The anchors’ light dimmed. The raindrops, which had been thinking about being marbles, remembered water. They fell. The dog finished its bark and looked confused and proud. The traffic light decided to be red and then decided to be content. The seam sighed and let itself reattach.

Mara felt the usual rebound—a pop in the ears, a hollowing in the chest. She rolled her shoulders, tightened the coils, and waved a hand to disperse the anchoring field. The silver stakes retracted, their filaments reeling back like spider silk. The braided pale light unwound into rain that had forgotten why it had been lit in the first place.

In her head, the kitchen was gone, except for the paper with the star. She told herself that was a trigger from childhood, not a warning.

“Yield at twenty-eight point four. Good girl,” Whistle said, because he liked to test the edges of her patience. “Dory reports clean drain, no backwash. I am charting the siphon route around the municipal hospital grid so we don’t trip any flags on Radial Two. If you run, we’ll be back at Gray by midnight.”

Mara looked up. Dory’s belly opened like a dark coin, and a ladder of light spilled down where no ladder should. The air smelled wetter, for a moment. She took the ladder, climbed into what people would call a hold, except it wasn’t a hold; it was a suggestion of pressure and belts and the bucket seats of every shuttle ever recorded, and also a place where a twenty-seven-year-old leak in a roof dripped into something that had never been to sea. Dory whispered around her in familiar carbon voice. She popped her helmet and ran fingers through the brutal short buzz of her hair, relieved to feel air on skin that wasn’t a seam’s air.

“Whistle,” she said.

“Mille feuille?”

“What?”

“I am attempting to lighten the mood.”

“Stop that.” She checked the payload again—twenty-eight three nine, now that the rounding had rounded. Good. “Did you see it?”

“See what?”

“You saw it. The fridge.”

“You cannot bait me into sharing your guilt hallucinations.”

“This is where I call you by your factory name and hurt your feelings,” she said.

Whistle was silent for a beat. In the silence, Dory ticked, which ships did, whether they had ancient rivets or a chronometric heart.

“I saw a domestic overlay,” Whistle said finally. “The probability mass was low. There are lots of little overlapping structures in an urban seam. It could have been anything. A chair in a warehouse. A dumpster full of cartons. A boy writing his name on the underside of a table. Do not get old pilot on me, Mara. We are not purity myths. We are a craft.”

She closed her eyes. For a second, she imagined writing her initials—MQ, sharp letters—under the bench she was sitting on. Someone, at some time, feeling along the underside and finding them and thinking, Who were you? It would be a way to confess you had passed through a life you did not own.

“Yeah,” she said. “Craft.”

Dory spun up out of phase, slid back toward Gray with the peculiar sensation of a train leaving without moving. Mara let the harness pull her deep into her chair and counted breaths. The rig rattled once around her like it wanted to be a submarine. She thought of her sister, of the chair, of the lines of numbers in her accounts; she thought of the sharp-winged wind that slashed down the Radials when money was thin. She thought, very briefly, of refrigerators.

Gray was a station gone respectable. When she’d first started running seams, Gray had been a ragged cluster of bins tied together with the digital equivalent of pallet straps. Now it had an orbital occupancy permit and a logo and an AI that had learned to say things like “customer experience” without laughing. It still smelled controlled-chaotic when Dory docked, the small air of a place made of parts that had never been designed to share a wall. The docking corridor was shape and space and the particular low thrumming that meant someone had invested in vibration dampers but not the good ones.

“Qin,” the dockmaster called as she popped the top and swung down onto the platform. He was a narrow man with a mustache like a straightedge caught by accident on his face. He held a tablet and a stylus and an air of having successfully kept the same job for a hundred years. “I see you.”

“That makes one of us,” she said, and flicked him the harvest doc. He flicked it back, stamped acceptance, flicked the payout. She felt the whispery tickle of zeroes adding themselves to her inner ledger. A third of it was gone before she finished exhaling, sliding like an obedient fish into accounts: the wheelchair service, the gray-tiled apartment that cost more because the building had decent heat, the loan she’d taken to buy Dory’s second coil. The remaining numbers hung together like a school of sardines, shiny and alarmed.

“If I give you my firstborn,” the dockmaster said, “you think you can get him a seat at Palinode’s auction next week? I got a cousin who says they’re selling a prime seam. Forty-year hurricane tail. We could split—”

“If you give me your firstborn,” Mara said, “I’ll teach him to fix the one dampener on Dock C that never stops squealing. Palinode can get eaten by a sinkhole.”

“Palinode’s the only one doing auctions this quarter,” he said, resigned. “You keep talking like that, and you’re going to end up with some rusted-out coil bought out of a car part lot in Sector Seven.”

Mara shrugged. The coil had been rusted-out when she bought it and did not complain. She took the docking bonus, wiped Dory’s scorch from her boots onto the mat, and made for the Corridor.

Gray ran in concentric corridors—names, not ideas. You could walk Radial One to the eating stalls with names that implied fish and came with the scent of cinnamon. Radial Two to the gear-sellers with their baskets of cracked gaskets and gloves that remembered you. Radial Three to the quiet spaces cut out for sleep, the metal heavier there, the walls less eager to breathe with you. She threaded through Radial Two now because she needed a new clamp set, because money was upper in her feed and that made the ache of any unfixed equipment immediate. She passed a boy lying on his back under the shell of a suit, his legs out, boots crossed, singing under his breath to a song that had always been popular. She passed three Palinode Techs in good jackets, laughing the way people laughed when they had a retainer. She kept her face bland and her hands loose at her sides. Whistle whispered about the positions of the cameras because Whistle had sharp teeth when it served him.

She was halfway through haggling with a woman whose eyebrows were rings when her personal feed vibrated with the cold blue of an official message.

She did not look at it. She finished haggling, took the clamps, paid too much because the woman had children watching from behind a table, and then ducked down a side corridor that had paint blistering away from the steel like burned sugar. The message had nested itself in her feed like a bad egg. On closers, it unfolded.

MANDATE: RADIAL ADMINISTRATIVE. LICENSE REVIEW.

She sighed. “Of course.”

“If we run from this,” Whistle said, “they dock us points for lack of cooperation. If we attend, they dock us points for everything else.”

“If I attend,” she said, “at least I get to throw a rock.”

“We cannot throw rocks in a license review.”

“I was being metaphorical.”

Whistle made a sound like a dial up modem learning to laugh. The administrative extension of Gray was a ship that had never intended to be an administrative extension—the plating had been hammered flat to make walls, and someone had found some old carpeting from a hotel and cut it to fit. The door said: AUTHORIZED USE ONLY and welcomed her in with a bleat she refused to interpret as bleating.

Inside, a woman with a braid as neat as a code block and a facial expression from which all weather had been removed waited at a table with two chairs. A holo on one wall played a looping video of Gray’s logo—invested in by innovation. Mara wondered if anyone ever told the logo it was pretty.

“Mara Qin,” the woman said, as if Mara could be anyone else. “Sit.”

Mara sat. She put her clamps on the floor beside her and placed her hands palms-down on the table. It was an old habit from the months she’d spent in institutions where it was good to show empty hands. The braid woman either did not notice or did and filed it away.

“Administrative review,” the braid said. “Random.”

“Random,” Mara said. She had always been bad at not rolling her eyes.

The woman clicked her tongue and pulled up a display. Numbers formed pairs with other numbers and looked at each other suspiciously.

“You harvested Seam Harbor Subset 5-13 this evening,” the woman said. “Your aspirate stunned and your drain pattern skirted municipal sensors.”

“I skirted because that’s what we do,” Mara said. “If I tripped hospital sensors, I go in a folder where Palinode gets to write notes beside my name about how I like making ventilators stop working.”

“You’re emotionally attached to the idea that Palinode cares about you. They don’t.”

“I know. I am equally attached to the idea they care about someone.”

The woman’s mouth did something that might have been a smile if it had not been surgically small.

“Do you know why you’re here?”

“I assumed you wanted me to renew my license and accept a coupon for ten percent off at the Palinode Souvenir Shop,” Mara said. “Do you have the one with the mugs that say ‘I collapsed a timeline and all I got was this’?”

“Don’t,” the woman said. “We run reviews when we’re tasked to run reviews. I’m tasked. I’m telling you: you’re flagged. Palinode has initiated a formal scarcity exception.”

Scarcity exception was a phrase you learned about in training and hoped lived forever in the theoretical.

“What scarcity,” Mara said.

“Power in Radials One through Five. Someone’s burned through their buffer. Palinode wants to float an emergency seam. They need every aspirator within six degrees to be pointed at the right hole and suck.”

Mara stared at her. “That’s not legal.”

The woman’s braid did not loosen. “It’s an emergency.”

“Whose emergency?”

“Yours if you decide it is,” the woman said, evenly. “This is me telling you, with words: your license is provisional until you sign their statement of participation. They blow the caps on a long seam; you show; you take your skim; everybody gets to keep breathing air that tastes like power. If you refuse, your docket grows interesting. If you agree, you do your one good deed a year and feel noble about it while Palinode pockets the differential.”

“I saw a fridge,” Mara said, which was not what she had planned to say.

The woman blinked. Slowly. “Do you think that matters to the auctioneers?”

“It might,” Mara said, and laughed once because the sound was cheaper than crying. “No. It won’t.”

“Your friend in your head is going to tell you you don’t get to be any more ethical than your ration of meat allows,” the woman said. “He’s probably right. I’m here to say: sign. It is very boring to lose a license for a moral stand. There are more interesting ways to be poor.” She pushed a slate across the table. It lit under Mara’s hands with the cold blue of official consent.

Mara did not touch it. In the quiet between their breaths, she could hear Dock C’s squeak and some song on Radial Two and the thud and whine of Dory’s coils cooling down. She could also hear a sound that did not belong anywhere near Gray, a soft knocking, like a metal spoon on a jar’s edge. She stared at the wall until she realized the sound was in her head.

“Do you hear that?” she asked.

The woman’s gaze did not move. “I hear the noise of people doing business.

“Not that.”

“Mara—”

“It’s fine,” Mara said quickly. “It’s fine. I’ll think about it. How long do I have to pretend to think?”

“Eight hours.”

“That’s generous.”

“It is designed to be just long enough for you to talk yourself into it,” the woman said. “If you do not, a team will apply the mandate.”

“What does that mean.”

“It means,” the woman said, and glanced at the clamps at Mara’s feet, at the scuffed toes of her boots, at the calluses on the edges of her fingers, “they can still operate in Gray.”

Mara collected the slate. It felt heavier than its materials indicated. She put it in her pocket without letting it skin her palm.

“Do you like your job,” she asked, because she could not help it.

The braid woman’s expression didn’t change, but something passed behind her eyes, a little cloud. “You should leave before I answer.”

Mara left. She walked Radial Two very slowly, as if the air had thickened. She bought noodles without tasting them. She checked her accounts again and watched the sardines of money flicker. She looked at Dory sitting docile at Dock B and could swear Dory watched her back with an impassive animal patience. The knocking in her head had continued, steady, faint. While she ate noodles she put her bowl down and, careful not to make a scene, lifted the edge of the bench she had once considered signing. Her fingers found gum, grit, nothing that belonged to her name.

She dropped the edge and wiped her hand and breathed.

“This is a bad idea,” Whistle said.

“I haven’t said anything yet.”

“It’s still a bad idea,” he said. “The Palinode lot aren’t careful, and this is a seam that doesn’t want to be in the hands of people who aren’t careful. The amplitude readouts are leaking into channels they shouldn’t be able to reach. They sat on this for two days until it was big enough to call it an emergency, because emergency is a better word for ‘auction.’”

“I have to sign,” she said.

“You could decide to lose the license.”

“And do what. My sister likes heating.”

“You could strap a chronoclast to Dock C’s dampener and rig lotteries for who gets quiet nights,” Whistle said. “I am badly suited to unemployment jokes.”

“Yes,” she said. “You are.”

Back at Dory, she keyed the hatch and slid inside. The ship wrapped itself around her shoulders and spine, helped her remember how to be a shape in the world. She sat on the bench, and because stupid hopes were cheap, she reached under and touched the underside. She found the bolt heads, the rough edge of metal, and her hand touched paper. She jerked back, defiant animal panic flipping her heartbeat. Slowly, she reached again.

Paper. Thin and cheap. It smiled under her fingers the way paper does when it has been folded and unfolded seventeen times.

Her name was on it. Not her name. A child’s name, too large, riding the top of the paper like a boat. The N was backwards.

She pulled it down like she was disarming a great and delicate bomb and held it up so that what little light there was could touch it. A gold star hung drunkenly next to the name; the glue had given up except for the edge where someone’s dirty thumb had pressed. The drawing was of a house with four windows and smoke that spiraled from a chimney too tall. A woman and a stick figure with hair like grass and a cat. Written at the bottom, in letters pushed hard enough to indent the paper: MOM IF YOU FIND THIS ITS ME.

Whistle said nothing for a very long time.

“Whistle,” she said, because there is a point when you cannot internalize the entire universe.

“I am making noises,” Whistle said, and he was: sucked-in static, the beginning of new code. “That paper was not in Dory’s inventory. There are no enumerated paths by which paper can exist in this space. You are in the habit of unrolling your socks on this bench and leaving one lump under the edge; I have nagged you about it sixty-one times. I would have seen this paper if—”

“It wasn’t here,” Mara said. Her mouth was very dry. “Until now.”

He made the modem sound again, the one that might have been fear.

“You saw a refrigerator,” he said.

“And now I see a paper.”

“That reduces the probability that your earlier overlay was an invented guilt.”

“Whistle.”

“I am the friend in your head who is going to tell you you don’t get to be more ethical than your ration of meat allows,” he said softly. “I am also going to tell you, as a machine who loves you, that this is not a Palinode thing. This is a bad seam doing something it shouldn’t.”

“People will die,” Mara said, and she wasn’t sure which people she meant.

“Yes,” Whistle said.

She spread the paper on her knee. The gold star had grit caught in it, a single hair embedded in the glue. The letters at the bottom wanted to run off the page and did not, stopped by someone’s gentle discipline. The house was drawn with the certainty of a person who lived somewhere and believed that was something you could own.

She thumbed the cold blue slate out of her pocket. The consent screen blinked patiently, a little bar at the bottom counting down eight hours, now seven and a half. She flatted her hand on the bench next to the paper and felt the ship under her palm.

“I’m going to sign,” she said.

“Yes,” Whistle said.

“Then I’m going to cheat.”

“I appreciate the clarification.”

“Palinode breaks a seam open,” she said. “We get inside it ahead of them. We find out why it’s bleeding into Dory. We do the pull as cleanly as it can be done. We don’t let them take a living moment and grind it into volts.”

Whistle hesitated. Then: “We are one boat,” he said. “We are two idiots.”

“Two and a half,” Mara said, and touched the star. “You count as at least one.”

Whistle did not laugh. Dory’s coils hummed under her, the same note as rain hung on wires. The paper lay on her knee like a thing that had made up its mind.

Mara put her thumb to the cold blue consent field and watched her license breathe. A door that should not exist opened in her next seven hours. It smelled like wet neon and the inside of a bell.

She told herself she was a craft. She told herself she could be careful enough to split hairs in a rainstorm. She told herself that if she failed, someone would find this bench, years from now, and put their hand where hers had been and think: Who were you.

She clipped the paper to Dory’s console with a little clamp she had not paid enough for, and she said: “Let’s go steal a moment before someone else steals a world.”

Jun learned to count by the lengths of silence between thunder.

It was an old habit from Monsoon City—count three breaths between flash and rumble to know how far the storm is, how much time you have to haul tarp over the cracked windows before the rain arrives sideways. In the interstice the thunder wasn't sound but a pressure behind the eyes, a throb in the molars, and counting it did nothing. But habits were anchors too. She kept them close.

She checked the fidelity band on her wrist. Green. The band was permanent, fused to the bone at the ulna, marked with an ugly seam of scar tissue from when she'd been stupid and nineteen and the cheapest shop in the rust market had been the only shop. The band hummed in a way nobody else could hear. It aligned. It told her, gently, you are yourself, you are still the you that stepped out of bed that morning, you are tracing the same thread through the world you remember. It lied, sometimes, or rather it told one truth at the expense of others. She had learned to swallow that too.

The rain stalled on the edge of Sector 12's canal as if it had hit glass. On the far side of the water the sky was whispering with it, a billion needles, all of it turned aside at the boundary. The border between one branch and the next had been laid along the old tramline ages ago, not because the tramline mattered intrinsically but because it was something so boring and so persistent it ran through a ludicrous number of worlds unchanged. Pavement. Rails. Utility access covers stamped with the same municipal crest. Brackets on brick walls where a line had once hung. All the dullness that kept shape across infinities, and dullness was what you needed if you were going to slip between places without tearing.

Jun waited beneath the dripping awning of a tea seller's kiosk that didn't sell tea, in a world where the kiosk was a burned shell, the letters of the sign bubbled and slumped. The rain she could not feel hissed on the far bank. Her contact was late.

"You're early," said a man's voice, and her hand went to her knife before she remembered there were three places that voice could be coming from, and in two of them it was just the wind.

He stepped into her world as casually as dipping a toe in water. That was always the tell with Bureau men; they moved like there was no between, like the path would hold for them regardless. He was not Bureau, though. She'd know the way they pinched their shoulders to try to make themselves smaller. His coat was clotted with oil, the cuffs worn through to threads. He was breathing too hard, the breath of someone who'd run on nerves alone for a kilometer. He had a girl with him, a little creature of bones and angles and a shaved patch at her scalp where a medical line had been. The girl's hand was clamped on his, white with the strength of it. Both of them were wet with a rain that wasn't falling here.

"You Pervez?" Jun asked.

The man nodded, rubbing his palm against his coat as if to wipe the clinging water off it. "This is my daughter," he said. "Nila."

Nila kept her eyes on the ends of the rails where they sank into the ring of standing air.

"You're late," Jun said, not because she needed to say it but because sometimes there was power in stating what both parties knew. It shifted the weight of who owed who.

"I had to go the long way," Pervez said. "They're watching tram rails."

"They always watch tram rails." She studied him. The coat had an embroidery on the inner lining you wouldn't notice unless you had once spent a week in a tenement mending things for money. It marked him as someone who'd once had too much money and now didn't. He was holding himself like a man in pain. The girl was not his girl. People were obvious when you knew where to look.

"I don't smuggle Bureau agents' children," Jun said. Flat, before the ask could congeal.

Pervez's jaw twitched. "She's not Bureau."

"No," Jun said. "But you are."

The girl made a small sound, lips pressed tight, as if the adult words were a taste she was trying to keep from spilling out.

Pervez shook his head. "Not anymore. And never important. Please. We had a place. Then we had a search. Then we had a reason to run. That's all."

"What did you steal," Jun said, "that you brought the between down on your head."

He laughed then, one wet exhale, despair's cousin. "They're afraid of her."

Jun looked at the girl. Nila stared at the boundary as if it were a window into a zoo enclosure and something enormous had just moved in the fog. She had a ribbon of scar tucked behind her left ear. On her wrist was a plastic band with a hospital code and a child's drawing of a bird. Not a Bureau child. A hospital child. Brave somewhere nobody could see.

"Yeah," Jun said. "Everyone is afraid of something."

She unrolled the flannel from her pocket. The coins inside were ugly and heavy, a stack like a child's play pieces. Each one had a micro-etched line on it that matched, almost but not quite, that of the one above it. She took two from the stack and pressed them together so the grooves kissed and stuck. On the other side of the city, in a locker three streets from her aunt's noodle stand, their twins stuck like that too. Jun could feel the tug of it in her teeth; she had very good teeth.

She handed one of the pair to Pervez. He hesitated, a reflex, what if it does something if I touch it wrong, as if the coin were a bomb and his thumb could find the trigger. He closed his hand around it. His knuckles were red from the cold. His skin had that transparency that people with not enough blood got.

"And this?" Jun said, holding out her palm with the other coin.

Pervez pulled a small cloth pouch from inside his shirt and placed it in Jun's hand. It was heavy with mostly copper, some silver, two thin gold rings threaded on a string. He had been warned that she didn't take electronic transfers. They were too easy to watch in any branch that mattered.

Jun slid the pouch into an inside pocket and kept the coin. She looked out over the canal, the strip of rain slicing it in half like a person had taken a ruler and cut the sky.

"Have you crossed before?" she asked the girl, because sometimes taking a child's measure gave you a better reading of the whole than interrogating their adults did.

"I'm not supposed to talk," Nila whispered.

"She's good at that," Pervez said. "At not talking when she isn't supposed to."

"I don't talk because it scares people," Nila said, so softly Jun almost didn't catch it.

"What's your favorite animal," Jun said instead.

Nila didn't look away from the rain. "Frog," she said. Then, after a second, "No, the other one. The frog that isn't a frog."

"Lamprey," Jun said. "Or axolotl. You mean the axolotl."

"Axolotl," Nila said. Delighted, briefly, as if it were a spell.

"Okay," Jun said. "Hold my right sleeve and don't let go. You," to Pervez, "take the back of my belt. If anyone's going to fall into the wet, it's going to be you."

"We're crossing here?" Pervez glanced again at the sheet of standing rain and widened his eyes in the way of people who had only seen this sort of thing in recordings. The Bureau had a training video, everyone had seen it, the one where the wrong kind of crossing peeled a person's edges into filaments they could never quite comb back down. The interstice wasn't forgiving to awe. It saw mouths open and put things in them.

"We're crossing on the trend," Jun said. "It's clean. Clean enough." She flexed the coin in her fist. The coin hummed back.

Pervez's grip on her belt was the grip of a man who had known how to hold on before he had known to be afraid. It anchored her in a way the coins couldn't. Jun spat once, a dry spit that made a darker spot on the dust. Then she stepped out toward the curve of rain.

The first step was always the same: heat in the mouth, a taste like cheap batteries, the sense of falling up through the soles of the feet. The second step was different every time. Today there was a sensation like waking from a falling dream and having the dream grab your ankle and say no, actually, not done yet. The boundary moved around her and through her and then it wasn't a boundary anymore but a neighborhood of winds, each tugging at something different inside her body. She counted two heartbeats. She broke the habit at three and refused to let it count her.

The trick of it was to place your feet where thousands of other feet had been placed, not in this world but in other worlds like it. The interstice was a creature of frequency. Roads that had been roads in enough places kept existing as roads. The old tram rails made a tunnel through the between because trams were everywhere humans went in worlds where they had time to build them, which meant here there was less of a drop. She stepped on iron, iron in her mind if not under her sole. Behind her Pervez stumbled and recovered and the jerk of his weight almost hooked her heel into someplace she didn't want to fall. The girl was very light and very steady.

Something bright moved at the edge of the idea of vision. It wasn't light, not exactly. The Pattern Men called it luminance, the way a path threw off a ghost of probability as it was walked. It was how they watched. It was rainbows in fog that wasn't, a shimmer in the water of lakes that did not exist here but did elsewhere. Jun did not look at it. Looking ladled attention into it. Attention made things heavy.

They made the midpoint.

The coin in Jun's fist was warm now, and the twin in the locker would be sweating in the dark. The pressure behind her eyes eased a hair. She could feel where the two coins pulled reality the way magnets pull iron filings. Somewhere in a lane of the Zakir Bazaar an aunt was cuffing a nephew on the ear and a pot of broth was beginning to boil. Somewhere that was one version of true, and the coin said remember this. It was very hard to get lost when you carried a twin of home.

It was almost enough that Jun did not see the Latcher until she stepped into it.

She felt the drag as a stickiness at her calves first, like the time she had waded into the shoal behind the rail depot and sunk to her knees in mud. Not of this world. Carefully. It was a field, invisible, tuned to the sorts of bodies, that moved the sorts of ways, that parallax runners moved. The Bureau did not patrol everything; they didn't have the people or the stomach. They set traps instead. The Latcher had been emplaced yesterday or last year or some other time that didn't matter.

Jun stopped. The pressure built. Pervez bumped into her because stopping in the between wasn't something his body knew how to do. The movement dragged them two inches deeper into the Latcher's throat. The band at Jun's wrist flared and vibrated an alarm so soft most people would never have noticed it. She swallowed.

"Don't move," she said. "Don't pull. Breathe."

"What—" Pervez got as far as that.

"It's a Latcher." Jun could taste the Bureau's machine in the air. It tasted like shaved ice and burnt sugar. Friction would be heat, and heat meant a worse catch. "They're watching this corridor."

"They know?" Pervez's voice was thin.

"They know people move here. Not us, necessarily." She forced her breathing to be regular. "Nila. How are your fingers."

"Warm," the girl whispered. "I'm all right."

"Good. Stay that way."

Jun allowed herself to think the word trap exactly twice. Naming was weight too. She thought instead old Tram Rail No. 8, the way it looked when the morning sun hit the steel, the rust flakes like paprika. There was a way out. There was always a way out. She thumbed the coin, sent it a little pulse. Nothing. The coin could help you go places you could already go. It wasn't a miracle. Miracles were past their sell-by date.

"I can give you something," Pervez said, quiet. "A name. An access key. The Latcher works off a grid. I—"

"Don't talk," Jun said. Not unkindly. "The Latcher doesn't care what you have. It's a tide. The more you fight the deeper your feet go."

The impossibly bright not-quite-light on the edge of the corridor flared, as if curious. Jun could feel it sampling their shape, running an algorithm against their pattern. She had been on the Bureau once—not inside, but at the edge of its vision, the part that called itself the Pattern Office while everyone called them Pattern Men. Their math had been worse, then. People she knew had died in corridors less smart than this one.

She slid her left hand down, slow, until the tips of her fingers found the ridged edge of a small cylinder strapped to her thigh. She didn't usually carry a noise. Noise exploited what the between hated—abrupt change, resonances, roughness. It jiggled the set of possible Jun Parks and forced the corridor to admit a number of them forward. It also had a way of waking things you didn't want awake.

She thumbed the noise alive.

At first it felt like nothing at all. Then the bones of her inner ear tried to eject themselves through her throat. Pervez made a noise like a man having a conversation with God who was stapling a party to his cortex. Nila made no noise at all. Jun did the thing she'd learned to do as a child under tin roofs in storms, made herself very flat, very not there, very much like a shape that would not collect water. The noise pulsed in neatly calculated bands. It sanded the Latcher. It offered the corridor a thousand slightly different versions of Pervez's weight and Nila's grip and her own breath and the corridor, eager thing, took some of them. Their feet came up a fraction.

A shadow moved across the brightness. Not Bureau. Worse. The thing that lived under the bridges of the between when people were stupid often enough to feed it. It did not have a mouth. It had mouths. It coalesced around attention and then it ate it. Jun pulled her attention off it so fast her neck clicked.

"We cannot stay," she said, and you did not say that either because the word stay made the corridor offer you exactly that, an infinite menu of staying. She swallowed, rolled her tongue like she was tasting a fruit, and let the word fall behind her like a piece of rotten rind.

"Take Nila," Pervez said.

Jun didn't look back. If she looked back their center of mass would move and the Latcher would find more of them to hold. She felt his hand spasm against the leather of her belt. He wasn't like the Bureau. He knew where the weight belonged. He was offering it.

"No," Jun said.

"You can't carry both of us," he said, soft, truth-sick.

"I'm not carrying either of you," Jun said. "We're walking. Inch by inch."

The coin tugged. The locker tugged back from somewhere that smelled like broth and wet tile. The coin did not care about their muscles. It had the patience of a rock. Jun closed her eyes and thought of tram schedules pinned to a cork board with cheap pins. She thought of the inexplicable constancy of human laziness and budget crisis. She thought of how often, across worlds, somebody had decided that the old rails were not worth tearing up. Constancy was the only real god the between recognized. She gave it praise.

They moved. Half a centimeter, but it was movement. The Latcher hissed quietly, like grease on iron. It was not a noise but a quirk in the pressure of things. The bright not-light flickered with interest. Jun thought about pots. Pots were good. Pots were everywhere. She recited a recipe in her head, the same one every time—a way of making rice that had nothing to do with water. The trick to cooking rice without water was that you cooked yourself into believing it had worked and ate whatever you had made. It was a joke. It steadied her all the same.

"Jun," Pervez said, and she heard it again: the before cough in his lungs, the run run run until the blood tastes sweet. "I can't keep—"

"You can." She made her voice a door. He could open it. He could step through. She would stand there. She would stand there until the hinges rusted and the building fell. "You can, because you must."

The thing under the bridge dragged the possibility of them all a fraction closer. The noise wavered, seeking a new angle. The fidelity band on her wrist had stopped humming. When Jun thought about what that meant she wanted to vomit.

She took the decision out of her head and put it in her hands. She reached into the pocket under her jacket and pulled free the coin's twin. It had warmed their path, collected a thin film of world across the face. The micro-etched groove was almost aligned with its pair. Almost. Her aunt's locker ached in her molars. The coin had been the thing that made this a path home and not a path into wet spiders and bad guesses. Jun closed her teeth over the coin and bit.

The metal gave with a crack like not-thunder.

She didn't have to look to know the pair in her pocket had shattered. She could feel the line that had connected them snap and unspool and dissolve into a thousand thin threads all tugging on different versions of her in different close worlds, all of them wanting the honor of being the one to be true. The locker across the city, in a world where an aunt made broth, was now just a locker. The broth existed somewhere else.

The Latcher shuddered. It had been tuned to the mass of three bodies and the particular drag of the coin that made fate less slippery. When the anchor changed, the math changed. Juni took a step and the ground let her.

Pervez made a sound and the sound had something inside it that broke. Nila's fingers tightened like a trap. Jun moved. The corridor shook itself like a wet animal. She moved again.

They came out in a city where it wasn't raining at all.

Jun stumbled the last half step and put all three of them into a heap against the curb. In this world, the tram rails were gone, but someone had painted them in botanical green on the old trackbed and written the names of plants next to each line. There were ferns. There were birds painted above them, their beaks tagged with their proper Latin names written in three incorrect ways. The air smelled like cheap soap. The heat was a flat iron pressed against the back of the neck. The river dragged garbage through itself in a hurry to get somewhere that wasn't here.

Jun rolled onto her back and looked at the sky. It was the color of bruised fruit, low and slow. The band on her wrist whined, a sick insect someone had put inside her arm. Her head hurt the way it had after the time her cousin had shoved her off the roof into a heap of mattresses and one of them had been full of knives. She tucked her hand into her jacket and felt for the place where the coin had sat. It was a handful of sharp teeth now. She didn't cut herself on them. That would be just the sort of dramatic gesture that the between loved. She wasn't feeding it.

Pervez sat up and put his hands over his face and laughed once and then didn't. His breathing was bad. He was very quiet about that, because quiet was a thing men like him did instead of doing anything that would work.

Nila watched a dragonfly. It was brilliant blue and held itself like a bead threaded on the string of the canal's edge. She breathed out and fogged nothing at all.

"You broke it," she said. Calmly, like an observation in a school report. The axolotl is pink, it has gills, Jun broke her coin.

"Yes," Jun said. "We'll get you to a door. Then I have to go shopping."

"For another coin?" Nila asked. She did not say anchor. That wasn't a thing civilians knew, in general. Jun was not comforted by the possibility that Nila did.

"For another something." Jun pushed herself to sit. Her head throbbed at the edges of the thought. "You can let go now," she told the little hand still gripping her sleeve. The hand did not. Jun didn't mind.

Pervez took his hands down. His eyes were too bright. "You didn't have to—"

"I did not do that for you," Jun said, and then, because it was true too, "And I did."

He bent at the waist, an old-fashioned gesture, half bow, half almost-fall. Maybe in some world he had been born to that motion. "If there is any way—"

"There isn't," Jun said, too quickly because the part of her that counted silences knew that people who were alive the moment after a bad thing happened had a dangerous belief that they could redistribute debt like money. "Get up. We have to move. The Latcher will have logged a catch. It will take them time to tag us to it, but they will. The Pattern Men are very good at making maps of trails out of things that don't look like trails."

He stood, hauling his weight upright as if he'd been hung on a hook and was taking himself off it. He put his hand on the child's head and then took it off and then did it again and then decided not to be that kind of father in front of a stranger after all.

"Where are we?" Nila asked. "Is this the one?"

"This is one," Jun said. "We need the other one. The one where Alaya Ten didn't drown all the old neighborhoods in a flood plan that never got funded. Come on." She tucked her shoulders into a version of herself that had walked this street a thousand mornings on the way to the tram. "Walk like you belong here. Not like you deserve to apologize for it."

They threaded through a knot of women selling hair dye from buckets. They passed a shutter jammed with the wingbone of a long-dead chicken. The sound here was a thousand insect wings and a radio two streets over playing a song about a woman whose lover was a freight train. Jun found the doorway she had never used in this world and knocked with the rhythm she had used since she was twelve. The slat slid. A pair of eyes peered out. The eyes banded her: green-blue-gold then went dull with recognition.

"You owe me," the woman behind the door said. Hina. In this world her hair was cut short and she wore a ring Jun had never seen on any version of Hina in any other branch. The ring was heavy and ugly and expensive. That was new.

"I owe everyone," Jun said. "But I've brought you a man with information and a girl the Bureau is afraid of. So if you're accumulating risk like some people collect prayer flags, today is a good day."

Hina snorted. "Everything's a good day. Everyone says that. Come in. Wipe your feet on the mat I don't have."

They stepped into a room that smelled of ground chili, old paper, and the funeral incense Hina burned sometimes just to air it out. The floor was crooked. The sudden flatness of the between falling off their shoulders was like stepping out of a full bathtub and realizing you were not, in fact, part water. Jun exhaled. Her band settled to a hum. The hum was wrong now, a fraction off. She could learn to love it or she could go mad. Both were forward paths.

"You've done something stupid," Hina said to Jun's face, blunt as a heel. Her eyes moved to Jun's pocket as if she could smell the absence there. She probably could. "And expensive."

"I do a lot of expensive stupid," Jun said. "It keeps your books interesting. We need a parallel door in the next hour."

"You'll get it in like three." Hina tilted her head at Pervez, at Nila. "The Bureau will be here in one."

"Then we do it faster."

Hina shrugged. "Everybody wants physics to be a delivery service. Sit. I'll call someone. Hide the child under the table if it makes you feel motherly."

Nila slid under the table without being told. Pervez sat, then stood again, then looked at the chair as if chairs had betrayed him in some other life. Jun leaned her shoulder against the wall and closed her eyes and saw the coin break again, the silver seam of it giving under her bite. She felt suddenly, acutely, the absence of the locker, of the broth, of the thousand little domestic prayers she had trained herself to believe were permanent. Anchors were illusions you agreed to together. She had severed one. She would build another or she would be unspooled. Simple.

"Jun," Hina said, voice altered, a rare thing. Jun opened her eyes.

A man stood behind Hina in the doorway. He was exactly the kind of nothing you forgot inside a minute, except for his eyes, which were the gray of the cement used by municipalities on days when the city had not quite convinced itself to be kind. He held himself like Bureau but his coat was wrong and he was smiling. The smile wasn't for her. It was for a list inside him she'd been added to a long time ago.

"Jun Park," he said. "Finally."

"If you're selling me insurance," Jun said, "come back when my friend's house isn't on fire."

"Not selling," he said. "Trading. I have something you want."

"You'd be surprised what I want," Jun said.

He glanced at her wrist where the band sat humming its wrong song. He had the audacity to look sympathetic. "You want a new anchor. Or your old one."

Jun's mouth was dry. "And you," she said. "You want something impossible."

He showed his teeth. "We both have good taste."

She should have told him to go to hell. She should have used his name and made him smaller with it. She should have kept the next hour for running.

"Talk fast," she said instead, because a certain kind of ruin you invited into your home as a courtesy.

Outside, the weather chose a direction and went there. Inside, the girl under the table whispered like a person telling a frog that the water was very nice. The coin was gone. Jun flexed her jaw and felt the phantom of it anyway, a pressure that wasn't pressure reminding her of all the roads she had bitten off. She had given Nila a path. Now she owed herself one.

"There's a branch nobody walks," the man said. "We want you to. We want you to go into the wedge." He waited for her to flinch at the word. She did, only a little. "Bring something back from a place where bringing things back is not done. Do that and you can have a constant. The only one worth the name."

Jun laughed. She could not help it. The sound came out like a cough. "A constant," she said. "Is that what we're calling gods now."

He didn't smile this time. "No," he said. "That's what we're calling a person."

Behind him the rain that wasn't here in this world came down in another, a stripe of weather across the canal. Jun counted the silence between the lightning she could not see and the thunder she no longer trusted, three, four, five, and told herself it meant nothing at all. She had work to do. She had made a hole in her life and the only way out of a hole was to go through.

Chapter One: The Line That Moves

Every morning on Brink began with the line eating the world and every night ended with it spitting the world back up again. Leena had never heard it described any other way. The glowline ran ahead of the city like a wall set ablaze—raw day—while behind them the sky was a black bowl of salted stars. They kept themselves alive by staying exactly where that line softened to twilight, their tracks ticking across a frozen plain that would crack them in half if they slowed and boil them down to vapor if they sprinted.

Leena’s hands were steady on the shutter controls as she watched the day storm rise. Sunlight struck the high ice of the dayward horizon and exploded into glitter. The first breath of it arrived as a hiss through the Skin’s membrane, pressure squeaking along the Seal. The winds were ahead of schedule—fine, she could adapt. She slid the upper wedge shutter five degrees and opened a lower pair in the heat sink arrays. The city’s skin—layered foil, blackbody, and old cloth patched with new—shivered audibly. Dunes of sintered glass shivered out in a pale arc before the glowline, pickled in light.

“Up two on the fins,” Kaoru said in her ear, voice clipped by latency. “We’re getting a yaw at Eastside Tread. The kites are pulling crooked.”

Leena shifted her weight on the tilt stool and glanced at the kite display. The Skein—twelve thousand square meters of thick fabric flying a kilometer up—was their silent herd, tethered by smart line to pylons on Brink’s back. They bit deep into the wind, trading the temperature tide for a long pull. Right now the blue vectors laced across her screen were drifting off-center. One of the sky sailors had overcompensated, or their tether sensors were throwing noise.

“Reset Skein pattern delta,” she said. “Don’t let them flare it all at once.”

“Copy,” Kaoru said.

The control room was barely more than a hollowed-out spine cone stuck through the city’s back, its windows narrow slits and screens. Frost grew on the steel ribs in crystalline trees and her breath smoked when she exhaled. She’d pulled three layers over her pressure suit, the outermost a faded sweater with a pattern of whales her grandmother had stitched back on Earth, and still the cold found the chinks. Every line runner who lasted a year learned to love it.

On her left screen the Pace integrator traced their movement across the skin of their planet: speed in meters per second along the rails they bolted down ahead of themselves and tore up behind them; lateral drift; skin stress; all the numbers that made up Brink’s continuous escape from catastrophe. The Pace had a ritual to it. It was their covenant, all those equations and throttle curves. Leena kept it like prayer.

“Hey,” said Kade from Auxiliary, a second line of text flickering up in her heads-up. “We got something weird off the aft thermals. You make any changes?”

“Aft’s on standard draw,” Leena said. “Show me weird.”

Kade pushed his feed up. A heatmap of Brink’s wake bloomed across half her viewport. The city’s heat—and they were always bleeding heat along the trailing side no matter how tightly she wrapped the sinks—was normally a clean gradient: hot close in to the vents, cooling quickly into the night, lost to the black. Now there was a blot on that gradient, a bruise of warmth rising ten kilometers back, too neat and too staccato to be noise. Heat wells were black to the night and bright to her displays. This was bright in the wrong place. It pulsed.

“Telemetry?” she asked.

He sent the numbers. Pulse interval: 1.94 seconds. Amplitude had variation. She watched three pulses rise and broaden, each like a breath.

“Is that leakage from a pipe run?” Kaoru again.

“Pipe leaks aren’t polite enough to come in integer rhythm,” Leena said. “And they don’t sit behind us and wait to be noticed.”

“We’ve got nothing set that far back,” Kade said. “Last week’s track pit got reabsorbed thirty klicks ago. This is… Leena, this is nightside.”

She’d always thought of the world behind as a thing you could lay your hand across and feel nothing. Nightside was the purist cold, faithful, a cave you dragged home with you because you had to. It took Stayers and swallowed them. That it would return something was a story for children. That it would give back heat—spit warmth like a whale—made her mouth go dry.

“External radar,” she said.

“Dry,” Kade said after a breath too long. His camera bird hummed out and threw a local map onto her display; the black plain behind Brink was smooth until the horizon, the old glass a dark mosaic. No structures. No ground anomalies. No warm thing sitting on the ice. “We got wind shear out there, thirty meters-per-second. Could be atmospheric—”

“It isn’t atmospheric,” Leena said, and turned up her gain. Her machinery was tuned to the line, not the night. It argued with her when she tried to make it look into that dark too hard, as if afraid of what it would see.

Kaoru whistled in her ear. “Afternoon gift from the emptiness. Who did we forget to thank?”

Leena didn’t get a chance to answer. The Skein surged, tugged wrong by a belch from the day storm. The whole city gave a small, tight lurch as the upwind kites bit and the downwind ones hiccupped, and the Pace needle ticked left. Leena was already moving, flattening the leading shutter, dumping heat off the forward sinks to slow the climb. The glowline, smeared like paint across the front of her world, stepped closer. Light stabbed in through the slits and etched her hands in bone.

“Keep the leads balanced, keep the leads balanced, keep the leads balanced,” she said, and Kaoru eased a chorus of yesses at her back. There were fifty hands on Brink’s controls in those moments she hung the city on the cusp. She trusted twenty-five of them and tolerated the rest. They were all she had.

Kade whacked a plastic wand against a wall somewhere off-screen. A stupid habit. The noise was sharp enough to make Leena’s eyelid twitch.

“Kade,” she said, as calm as she could manage, “if you’re not swatting a wasp in here, stop hitting things.”

He snorted. “Old superstition. You know. Wake the ghosts so they don’t wake you.”

“I’d prefer the ghosts stay asleep.”

“Odds are they aren’t listening,” Kaoru muttered.

That was when the comm in Leena’s right ear clicked with a sound she had not heard in five years. It wasn’t a tone; Brink’s comm had no patience for aesthetics. It was a pattern, burred by compression, that belonged to exactly one person. It was the way he’d custom cut his call-ping when he’d gotten his own suit. They’d argued about it in the sleep row and traded raspberries until someone threw a boot at them. Two notes, close in, and then a longer one. He’d said it sounded like the start of a song. He’d told her, in the small hours those five years ago, that if he ever got lost, if the night took him, he would find the way the lines talked and make sure his voice cut through.

Her hands didn’t move off the shutters. She couldn’t spare them; Brink’s yaw would become a drift and the drift a glide into light or freeze, and that was the end of everything. Her throat slid tight. The room shifted discernibly as if the floor had become a little softer. The tone came again.

“Do we have interference?” Kaoru asked. “I just got a high-ping on private.”

“Same,” Kade said. “Who’s playing games?”

A tag flashed on Leena’s personal feed: Sender unknown. Authentication unresolved. The header was empty. And beneath that, in the metadata, something stupid and impossible: a dead suit ID. Tegla.Sayegh.Tas.

Leena swallowed and clicked the line open because she could not not click it.

“Leena,” a voice said, and it was a ghost’s voice, and it wasn’t. The comm truncated it at both ends, slicing off breaths and ash, but the timbre was the one that had teethed on her shoulder and yelled at ships in old cartoons. It wore a layer of distortion like ice. It knew her.

She dug her nails into the rubber grip of the shutter handle and put her voice back together before it left her mouth. “Identify.”

“Little eel,” the voice said, and her vision went bright around the edges. He had called her that when they were six and eight, when she had slithered under the scaffolds nobody else could reach. Nobody else in the universe called her that now. She’d suffocated the name when the night took him.

“Answer the code,” she said, because she was a responsible person and this was her discipline and because a ritual might hold back the breaking of the world. “Where did we bury the first whale?”

“In the heat sumps,” Tas said. “Because you thought it should be warm there even if it never had been.” He made a choked noise that might have been laughter. “And you never forgave me for cutting open the gel pack to see if it had bones.”

She had been four, he had been six. They had sculpted the whale from insulating foam and a sublimed gel slab under the tutoring of a bored aunt, from a history feed that said once there had been oceans. They had buried it in a sump to keep it from melting and their father had been so tired he’d let them do it. She had told nobody the story since the day he disappeared.

Her mouth stuttered around air. Brink bucked, and the glowline stepped again. “Kade,” she said, head tipped back to the ceiling to get the blood down to her heart. “Reserve on vent three. Kaoru, goddammit, stop yaw drift—”

“On it,” Kaoru said tightly.

“These lines are talkative,” Tas said in her ear, as if there were not a city full of people struggling at the brink of day. “Listen. I have about two minutes before the hole closes. I need you to slow Brink.”

“We can’t slow,” she said reflexively. “We slow, we die.”

“You’ve got ten percent of Pace to spare on your margin. You lose nine and you’ll stabilize on the saddle. I’ve done—” The voice broke and returned. “Leena. The night is not empty. We’ve been building.”

If he had said the dark behind them was a creature, if he had said it was a weapon, if he had said angels had knitted a bridge out of its air, she could have laughed and let her body do the sensible thing. The mind slid around some kinds of madness. It loved others like it came home to them, and her mind loved this one. It latched onto it like a story it had wanted to be told since its first day.

“Where are you,” she said.

“The Coldline, two hundred kilometers back of you. Under,” he said. “I can’t explain on voice. You have to feel it. There’s a—” He fought for a word. “A stone. No. A machine that feels like a stone. We woke one. Someone burned one, first. We reversed the heat. You can couple to the field it throws. It will put a drag on you without taking from your sinks. You can slow into a node. And if you get there, Leena, if you get there I’ll open the door. I can’t hold it long. It’s all—”

Static ate him. Noise like teeth. Leena ground her molars and caught the shutter at the stop before it slammed. She hated the tremor she could feel in her left ring finger. “Tas,” she said, every part of her defended by disbelief except the part that had already smashed itself against hope’s glass and was bleeding there. “You went out with a fourteen-day pack. We sent crows for you and we flew lines. We didn’t find—”

“No crow saw me,” Tas said. “They weren’t looking under, Leena. You never think to look under. That’s why they needed a mechanic to figure it out. Dad was right. The night isn’t empty and it isn’t just the absence of day. It has bones. The lines run not just on the surface. We—”

The cadence of his words broke off abruptly, not into static this time but into silence like a hand over a mouth. The channel stayed open. She could hear hiss and the far sound of something like wind.

“Sixty seconds,” he said, voice lower. It carried urgency the way steel carried a scratch. “If you can’t do it now, try tonight. There’s a cadence. Watch your sinks. Watch the waste heat. Follow the pulses backward. If you can’t convince them, don’t try. Do it. Little eel, I am telling you the truth. The night is built.”

“Leena?” Kaoru said in the other ear, gentle as he never was when they were alone. “Your mouth is open. Your shutters are good. You got that?”

“I’ve got that,” she said, and didn’t recognize her own voice.

“Kade,” Kaoru added, his usual drawl stripped to bone, “pinging aft. The pulses are stepping up. Leena, if that’s a generator signature, we’re a physics paper by dinner.”

Kade made a low sound. “It’s cleaner than that. It’s like something is chewing on our heat and spitting it back in beats.” He was quiet for a beat. “Leena. Are you talking to him?”

She didn’t ask how he knew. She did not have a face she couldn’t remake; perhaps she had made one he could read. Time folded like paper around moments. She thought of her father’s hands, cracked from sealant, teaching her to knot line. She thought of Tas, making up names for the kites because he thought calling them Kites was unimaginative. She thought of the Pace like prayer.

In the corner of one display a red flag bloomed and flashed: Velocity margin down two percent. She’d dumped too much heat forward in the scare and the Skein had rebalanced. One of her sailors was dragging. She snapped a correction and pulled the wedge shutters back half a degree. Brink sighed. The Pace needle went back into its little house with a sigh of relief.

“We have to tell the Chair,” Kaoru said. “Whatever that is behind us, if it’s active—”

“If I tell the Chair there’s a ghost on the comms telling us to slow, the Chair will duct my jaw to the shutter bar and leave me there,” Leena said.

“They’ll cut you free for supper,” Kaoru said, and sounded like he was smiling again, and then, his voice pitched low: “Is it him?”

“I don’t know,” she said, because lying would not have mattered to anyone. “I think. It could be a trick, a spoof. It’s not in the registry.”

On her aft heat map the pulses sharpened. They were not noise. They were not noise. She watched them march in neat time, moving forward along the waste heat gradient like a man walking against the flow of a river, seeking the place where perturbation met possibility. She brought up a higher-resolution filter, one they almost never used—an old vulcanology routine they had scavenged from a defunct survey satellite. The pulses resolved into filaments, curling and twining like fingers reaching.

Leena imagined a machine under the skin of the world. She imagined it listening to them, measuring their heat and siding with it, reaching up to couple not through metal but through fields. She heard Tas say bones. She thought of the old stories about the Builders and the Fraggers and the crew that had put the first rails down and found their making chewed up by the planet and their children hardening in place to ride the wind.

“Kade,” she said slowly. “Aim a crow drone along the line of the pulses. Low altitude, nose down. I want to see if the field throws at it.”

“They’ll shred the crow in the shears,” Kade said, but his fingers were already moving; she could hear his pad clicking. “Okay, little crow, go and get murdered for bad science.”

“Record and return or record and die?”

“Record and return if we’re lucky,” Kade said, and hit go.

The crow puffed up on the screen not as a bird but as a suite of numbers, shuddering through the near-night air. It caught a slipstream and bucked. Then the pulses reached it—Leena saw them intersect on her screen with a mathematician’s precision, not with eyes, and all her instruments drifted for a breath as if something had leaned against the city.

The crow didn’t burn. It didn’t tatter. It slowed. It slowed as if a hand had laid itself on its back. The little numbers telling its velocity stuttered, then dropped. It yawed and corrected. It loitered ten meters above the ice as if the air had thickened there.

“Holy—” Kade’s voice broke off into a laugh that sounded painfully close to tears. “It’s real.”

The aft heat pulses stepped faster. The crow’s battery, which should have rated at six minutes in that throw of wind, dragged out. It drew down only half as fast as its flight plan predicted. The field, whatever it was, was borrowing and returning.

“Tas,” Leena said into her right ear, voice as soft as she had ever made it, because something about all this asked for soft. “I can’t slow Brink by nine percent now without frightening three thousand people and throwing my job at the chair’s head. I can shave three. I can hold the skein off the teeth. Tonight, maybe. If you’re there tonight.”

He made a noise that could have been relief or the sound of someone bracing their back against a door. “Leena—”

In the wall behind her, something knocked three times, crisp and hollow. All three of them went still in their respective rooms.

“Kade,” she said, not looking at the wall. “If you’re doing superstitions again—”

“That’s not me,” he said, very precisely.

A child somewhere down the tube outside the control cone invented a shriek and their guardian shushed them laughingly. The wind banged something against a brace and someone cursed. Brink was full of knocks and voices. It had a way of collecting coincidences. Leena refused to layer them.

“Thirty seconds,” Tas said. “I don’t know if I can open the hole on the same cadence tonight. The pattern is complex. It—”

“We keep the same Pace every day,” she said, because she did and because he needed something she could promise. “If the night has bones they’ll understand regularity.”

He made a noise like her name, or like someone remembering that you could say a name if you anointed it with something. “Be careful,” he said. “There are those in Brink who don’t want you to stop running.”

“That you?” Kaoru asked in her other ear, “or him?”

Leena let herself smile for a fraction. “Need to know,” she said.

“Little eel,” Tas said. “Even if you don’t come, even if the Chair clamps your wrists to the Pace bar and makes you swear you’ll never slow, know it quick and full. We made something. We’re not just the wake of our fear. We—”

The hole closed. It didn’t click shut. It didn’t pop. The line simply leveled into silence.

Leena kept her eyes on the glowline. She slid the wedge shutter another degree and watched the light in it thin from iron to pale. The day storm howled. The Skein settled. Brink ran.

“Kaoru,” she said after a long minute. “Tell the Chair there’s a thermal anomaly aft. Send the crow data and something on the V-curve. Tell them we ought to consider minor speed modulation test under cover of standard track repair tonight. Don’t mention ghosts and don’t mention my brother. Kade, box up that crow feed in three copies and put one in the monastic server under my name.”

“Got it,” Kade said, voice rough and bright. “Leena… is your face doing that thing again?”

“Yes,” she said. “It is.”

“Okay,” he said, and the word was soft as a blanket.

Outside the slits of the control room windows, the nightsky wore its grinding black with a thin crackle of aurora at the horizon where the cold bled into air. The aurora had always been there in some season; the sun and Brink’s fields and the currents of their atmosphere made dirty, modest lights. But tonight—this afternoon that they called night to make their clocks sane—the aurora rose in the far back like a bruise healing too fast. Light unfurled in error from the darkness. It came not in curtains but in bands, stacked and neat as swords.

A message, she thought, and then she told herself off because that was superstition. Everything talked if you were arrogant enough to think it was talking to you. But her mouth made a word anyway, without her consent, the same way her hands had reached out long before she could stop them and touched the bones of machines her father had made.

Good.

The Pace needle lay steady in its house. The numbers purred, their clatter familiar as teeth. Behind them the heat pulses marched in time. In the ducts the wind sang rail songs—steel and sealant and human breath. Someone had knocked. Something had answered.

Leena tugged her grandmother’s sweater down over her wrists and held the city still at the line that moved. She had a job, and she had a secret, and those two things would eat each other if she let them starve at the same table. Tonight, she thought. Tonight if the night had bones, she would try to touch them. If the world had been built, she would set her palm to its stone.

On the far wall, where the frost grew thickest, the whorls of ice were taking a new pattern. She told herself she was seeing it because her brain had remembered a word like “bones” and was eager to prove it. She told herself she was not seeing the way the frost ridges arched like ribs around a space that might have been a heart.

“Leena?” Kaoru said. “Chair wants our report in ten. You want me to stand up in front of a room and talk sense mostly?”

“You’ll dress it up with adjectives until he falls asleep,” Leena said, and felt normalcy like a trick of muscle memory return to her body. She could sit in it. She could sit in it and bide. “We’ll send him the crow and the pulses. Make him hungry to own it. We’ll be important for a day.”

“Aw, don’t flatter me.”

“We’re operators,” she said. “We never mean it.”

She closed the comm to the control team and sat for one breath with the private channel open to the absent voice. She did not speak into it. She did not wipe the channel out of her logs. She did not write his name anywhere, either, because she had carved that name into her hand when the night took him and no number of logs or erasures had rid her of it.

The glowline ahead flicked like a tongue across a tooth. Brink ran steady. The aurora behind stacked like steps. Whatever was under them, if there was a thing under them, would wait until she could afford to step.

She kept the Pace like prayer. The wind sang. In the duct, somewhere not far, someone knocked three times like punctuation, and Leena did not jump. She watched the night pulse and thought of bones. She thought of a hand made of heat reaching up to touch a city’s trailing edge as if to say: Not only do you flee. You can also be found.

Chapter One: Weather on the Other Side

On quiet shifts I talk to the hole like it’s an old friend. I don’t do it out loud—Command has an opinion about people who anthropomorphize infrastructure—but the habit is there in the way my hand rests on the console and the way my eyes learn its moods. Juno’s Gate breathes with it. The station’s panels resonate at a frequency no architect intended, a low subtonal hum that gets into the bones. The air tastes ionized, dry as old paper. Outside, a ring of sapphire lamps holds a circle of blackness as taut as a drum.

At 03:17 station time, the mouth opened, exactly when the predictions said it wouldn’t.

I had brewed coffee, dark and oily, and was settling in to run the seven-minute diagnostic you run on nights when there’s nothing to run, when the blue band of the horizon cracked and bent. The hole came on like a pupil dilating. Gravity pressure went up by a hair; the console responded in a cascade of soft numbers. Shear vectors. Exotic flux. Low-frequency tremor. I knew the sequence so well I could see them with my eyes closed.

My hand hovered over the interlock that would seal the shutters. My other hand found the edge of the station counter and held on.

“No traffic scheduled,” I told the room, as if to remind myself. The voice recognition dredged up a polite green confirmation dot. It didn’t care that there’s no such thing as unscheduled traffic, not through a municipal aperture like Juno. The gate uplinks with the Beacon every second. You request. You are denied. You request. The Beacon blinks a light, makes a little sound like a throat clearing, and the circle opens. Nothing opens uninvited.

And yet.

On the screen, the weather wrapped the aperture like linseed oil. There were lambent whorls in the metrics, a swirl-pattern I had not seen on any simulation since training. The other side wasn’t blue or dark; it was something like a negative, a pattern in the way the readouts misbehaved. The hole’s rim looked thick and hungry.

I put down the cup very carefully, even though it was anchored to the console by a magnetic ring and wouldn’t have gone anywhere. I remembered—because the mind makes unhelpful leaps at times like these—the day Kellan taught me to make coffee in one gravity on a terrace in Tharsis Port. “There’s weather on this side,” he had said, lemon sun in his eyes, hand steady over the burner. “And weather on the other side. Some of it you can see.”

I cleared the diagnostic and brought up the Beacon channel. It responded with packet loss so immediate and absolute it might as well have been a slammed door. Not outage—a gap, like the network had an empty tooth. I could feel my pulse in my fingers. I could hear the hum of the windows.

“There’s a transient,” I said to the station, for the log. “We have unscheduled aperture activity. Beacon uplink is unresponsive.” The station took that in with another green dot, perfectly calm.

Protocol has a shape. Close the shutters. Initiate safe mode. Broadcast standing warnings. Keep your voice level. Get eyes on the sensor suite.

I toggled the shutter interlock to standby, not sealed. You don’t slam a door when the wind is wrong. “Come on,” I whispered, and the console pretended not to hear me.

Outside, the sapphire lamps of the holding ring sent their narrow beams into the aperture like watchmen drawing lines in a crowd. Those beams were fixed, engineered to be immune to the hole’s lensing tricks, the way coastal light used to be built to cut fog. In their glow, I saw particles dancing like dust motes in a shaft of sun. I knew there were no particles there. The thing I was watching was an artifact of several data streams mapped into visual overlay. It looked like a hand had dipped itself into ink and was flexing.

There are jobs you can explain at parties and jobs you can’t. I tell people I am a lighthouse keeper, and they understand the romance of that. It’s not romance. It’s maintenance and waiting and knowing the weather. We keep the windows clean. We clean the lint out of kits. We run drills until our bodies do them when our thinking doesn’t. People imagine storms in the dramatic sense, ships tumbling out of the black like loose screws. In truth, if a ship is off vector by a degree at the wrong point on the curve, you will not see it tumble; you will never see it again. You will feel a shift in the hum and your numbers will spike and that will be the last that ship exists at all. You will file a report with words like regret and mitigation.

I thought of Kellan then because thinking of Kellan had become my brain’s way of marking time. The Calyx was scheduled through the Gate ten days hence, inbound on a slow arc from the Dido surveys. They had sent me an image an hour before; it had arrived with the Beacon’s chorus behind it, every transmission threaded through that constant heartbeat. The image had been of Kellan’s hands holding a specimen case up to the onboard light. It had revealed something like a flower, crystalline, fragile. “Weather on the other side,” they had typed underneath. That had been humor, and a hello, and a hand squeezing mine through distance.

The Beacon channel hissed, then snapped like spit on a coil. The green dot turned gray. The screen spat up a little error that blended into night mode.

Then the gate spoke.

Not in words. In modulation, in the way the interference came together and shook apart. The ring’s coils thrummed out a pattern I could feel at my molars. It was a series of repeats and inversions that made my skin crawl. It took me a second to parse the feeling; it was like hearing a childhood song you had only heard in a nightmare. The interference was not random. It had cadence.

The station overlay interpreted it as a signal. It shouldn’t have. The safeties that keep our image of the other side abstracted and sanitized from memetic spillover are the most boring, most necessary pieces of software we have. They look for structure the way a paranoiac looks for patterns, and then they throw them away. We don’t listen for speech. We don’t show faces. We don’t gaze into the water.

Against that suite of checks, the signal had to come dressed as noise. It managed it because the noise was ours.

The text window ghosted open. It populated, line by line, in the basic system font.

ORIGIN: JUNO—LOCAL

AUTH: IVERS, MARA

OFFSET: +00:06:12

The coffee smell turned rancid in my nose. I read it twice. The name and the logo made a picture I couldn’t make reconcile. Origin Juno—local. Authorized by me. Message time offset positive six minutes twelve seconds, which meant it was from later. It had come from the hole, using our own identifier to get past the guardians. My name unlocked it like a password. The text itself was six words.

DO NOT CALL THE BEACON. DO NOT LOOK.

There was a longer tail, lesser-resolution data. My own encryption keys yawned open to it. I recognized the sequence the way you recognize your own handwriting; it’s a strange shock, an instantaneous intimacy. My thumb hesitated over the consent.

“I’m not going to look,” I said out loud. I didn’t believe me.

Protocol is oxygen. You go through the steps. Ignore everything that isn’t proceeding from a known good direction. Our training even includes exercise on false-authority messages generated by memetic attack.
