Whoever wrote the line about not looking had used my authority to get straight to the part of my brain that remembers warm hands. And the Beacon—there are only two things big enough to pull the shutters with me with the hole open, and one of them is the Beacon. It was offline; if I called it and it surged back up, the Gate would do what it was told. That was the point of centralization. It kept disasters from becoming competing disasters. It kept twenty different Juno stations from making twenty different choices during a storm.

But I had never seen a Beacon outage. I had never seen a signal from the future. There are words those two sentences should not share. I put my hands flat on the console and pressed down because I had the sensation of floating upward out of my body, and I needed something to push against.

The door from the maintenance wing hissed open. The temperature in the room rose half a degree. No, I thought, and yes, because my body had already noticed it—the shift in air pressure, the change in the timbre of the hum. How quickly you grow to know your house.

A human figure stood in the doorway. They were wearing station pajamas and the basic orange in-suit socks. Their hair was flat on one side and they blinked like someone waking into a dream. It took them a moment to remember their body enough to turn their head.

“You’re not supposed to be up here,” I said helplessly, as if enforcing station regulations could prevent phenomena.

They were me.

The mirror quality hit sideways. It wasn’t only face and height and the little asymmetry in the left eye; it was the stance, the way the hand touched the doorframe. The small white scar on the right eyebrow from the time I misjudged a ladder. It was enough to be nauseating and the mind hates nausea. It tries to make it into something else. For a weird instant I thought: a practical joke, a very expensive prank my colleagues had conspired to pull on me. Then she—my later self—smiled the little apology smile I have perfected for strangers on trains. It is an expression that has never belonged to anyone else.

She had a gray undertone to her skin, like someone who has been too long in vacuum lines. Her eyes were bright. She came in without waiting to be invited. She did not look directly at the aperture. She moved with the careful muscle sequencing of someone on a tremor edge.

“Don’t look,” she said. Her voice had a huskiness I know happens at three in the morning after too much coffee. She stopped close enough for me to see the fine cracking on her lips. I took an involuntary step back.

“Okay,” I said, because that was the thing in front of me. The station clock spoke into the room with a polite chime, marking 03:18. The hole grew slightly darker. The ring carriers answered with microadjustments, all that music around the ear.

“Beacon is out,” I—she—said. “It’s not really out. It’s in the wrong place.”

“That doesn’t make sense.”

“It will.” She—the later me—put her hands on the console as if to brace it between us. Her left hand’s little finger had a nick of callus on the outside edge. She had always hated that; she picked at it with her thumb. She did it now.

“What does the other side look like?” she asked, and I saw her perfect not-looking: the eyes skimming the ring, the screen, the floor, never the black in the center. Don’t look. It sounded in my head like don’t stare at a sun.

“I haven’t looked,” I said. It was true in the sense that our instrumentation throws a filter between us and the hole. It was not true in the sense that I had already looked a thousand times. The aperture is beautiful. It is a mathematical concept that somebody let escape into the world and the world is still pretending to be okay with it. You can look at a shadow of it and think maybe you’re safe.

“Good,” she said. There was relief in it, and sorrow. “You can—” She swallowed and used the back of her hand to wipe her mouth. “You know the emergency shutter?”

“Yes.” My hand went to the lever by instinct. The lever is old-fashioned by design, with a steel ring and a satisfying click. It makes you feel like you are doing something weighty with your hand. The truth is, all you do with the lever is authorize the software that authorizes the hardware to begin. It’s a ritual to make action feel real.

“You’re going to want to close it,” she said. “Don’t. If you close it, they’ll die.”

“You’ve got to give me more than that.” My voice ripped open on the last word. My heart was pounding and my mouth had gone metallic, and some remote part of my brain noticed these facts to file them away. I needed specifics so my mind had something to sit on.

“Okay,” she said. She took in a breath and let it out as if this, too, were something she had been rehearsing to get right. “They is us and not us. They is anyone trying to come through that feels their way by the Beacon, and right now the Beacon is in two places. I don’t know how to say that better. It stutters. It belongs to the hole and the hole belongs to it. The pattern they make has a music. That music is going to tell incoming ships that the aperture is healthy and open and shaped like home. It is not. If we pull the shutter, the feedback will resolve the wrong way and the hole will close on them like a mouth. If we don’t pull, and we don’t call, it will shake itself into a choice. There’s a chance it will choose us.”

The room breathed with the station’s lungs. The hair on my arms prickled. I wanted to ask dozens of questions. The only words that came were: “Where is Kellan?”

She flinched like I’d slapped her. I saw the little timing misstep. Yes, I thought, so this is how the world can still hurt you in a place where you’ve become a message. There was sweat at her hairline. It made a darker comma.

“Not here,” she said. “Not yet. If you do as I say, you might see them. If you don’t—” She shook her head. “You won’t see anyone. Close the shutter and you’re alone forever.”

I had disliked many versions of myself over the years. I had disliked the self who took the Juno posting because it was easy to understand and hard to explain. I had disliked the self who stayed with Kellan after the first time they broke my heart. I had disliked the self who bought a cheap ceramic mug with a planet printed on it and has never broken it for fear of the omen. Looking at that face now, I disliked me intensely. I hated the trick of it, the way she put her weight on the words in places I recognize. She was right that I would understand that alone isn’t a normal person’s fear for me; there are people who like an empty house. It is my terrible secret, much more than my fascination with a hole in space.

“I keep thinking of the quarries,” she said, a non sequitur so wrong it ricocheted off the walls. The station once was a rock quarry in L4, back when ore still came up from Earth’s old wounds. I had read the files. “How they cut faces into the stone and then the stone decides that face is the shape it wants to be, forever. The aperture is deciding its own face, and the Beacon is showing it a picture that is also a picture of something else. We don’t call. We don’t touch. We don’t give it another face to want.”

“You’re giving me metaphors.”

“I’m giving you the only language that holds where I can still stand up.” Her smile was raw. “And a list,” she added. “Humans like lists. Don’t call the Beacon. Don’t look. Don’t close. Do you still run the blue plate on the uplink?”

The blue plate is a manual switch you can throw to route all your outgoing traffic into a narrow, archaic band that is intentionally noisy in the right ways. It was designed for something no one does now: sending status through radiation storms in the early days of Gate experiments. We keep it because we keep things that worked, even if we never need them again. “Yes,” I said automatically. I had polished its handle last week. I like to make the metal shine.

“Use it to send a wide broadcast on the local net,” she said. “You’ll crash half the refrigerator eggs between here and Ariel, but anyone heading for Juno will get the pain in their teeth and they might drink water, pause, wonder if they should reconsider. It buys us time. It buys us not-action. I know we aren’t good at not-action.”

She was right and she was wrong. At school they called us watchers and then we became maintenance and the romance sanded off. They told us stories of heroes who shut windows and saved a convoy of ships. The stories were true. Buried under the stories was the number of times someone held their hand very still and made nothing happen, and that was the actual job.

“And afterward?” I asked. The word rose and fell like a gull. I hadn’t let myself say after. It was dangerous. It made two assumptions: that there would be an afterward, and that I would not be the one bleeding into it in some metaphoric or literal way.

“After,” she said, and in her face I read a complicated thing. In any other situation I would have asked what that face meant in detail; in any other situation I would have been the person who cared enough to learn that language. Now I only saw time. “After, we see if you have a pencil and some paper you like and something you want to write. After, maybe you call Kellan. After, you stop working double shifts to avoid going to the greenhouse. After, you stop judging and start building. After, you find out what I saw when I looked.”

“I thought you said I shouldn’t look.”

Her mouth twitched. “I said you shouldn’t look yet.”

The hole shuddered. I felt it in the soles of my feet through the station’s frame. A series of bright pins pricked my scalp. The ring’s lights flicked; the power stayed. The station clock ticked into 03:19 with a sound like a finger tapped on glass.

“Tell me how we got the message through,” I said, because some part of my brain even now wanted to know where the seams were. “If the Beacon is wrong. If the memetic checks—”

“You taught me a trick once,” she said. “About how to get past a dog who won’t let go of a sock. That if you hold very still, the dog will tug so hard it will unbalance itself. It is very tired on the other side. It is holding so many socks.”

We stood there with the humming and the ring and the blue light and the dark mouth that wanted to be a face. Her hand lay on the console next to my own hand like we were schoolchildren taking attendance. If she was six minutes older than me, some part of the world had lengthened and curled the line.

“Blue plate,” she said again. “Please. And put the shutters on soft hold in case of—” She hesitated, searching for a term that did not exist. “In case of wanting to jump.”

My fingers found the blue plate’s handle. It was cool and slightly greasy from the oil I used to make it shine. I flipped it down. The station let out a sound like a relieved aunt. The uplink indicator went from clean green to dirty gray-blue. Somewhere inside a refrigerator on a rock farm, an egg future rancid.

The console asked me twice if I really wanted to send a wideband pulse that violated at least five historical guidelines. I said yes and key-coded and depressed and swore. Then I broadcast a general hazard message to a deaf and indifferent belt. “Juno Gate experiences anomalous conditions. Avoid vectoring within thirty thousand kilometers. Do not follow Beacon tracking at standard gain. Repeat.” On the third repeat my voice went soft, then I read it without any expression at all.

The other me nodded, once, as if an important piece in a puzzle had snapped. She stepped back toward the door, keeping her face turned to the wall so the aperture stayed in her peripheral ignorance. “I have to go,” she said. The words wavered.

“Go where?” It came out too sharp. I didn’t mean to beg. The begging was in there.

“If I stay, I’ll—”

She stopped. Her eyes flicked, a reflex, toward the hole. She caught herself. She smiled at me again and it was a different smile, one I’d worn with my mouth pressed into a line. “I did good,” she said, and then covered on the grammar. “We. We did good.”

The door hissed. The air pressure shifted back down as if the room took a breath under water. She was gone.

I was alone with the ring of lamps and the circle and the fact of the coffee going cold in a magnet. I watched the numbers run for a heartbeat, two, ten. The aperture hesitated. The music of the Beacon—no, the music that sounded like the Beacon—shifted a half-tone. The gates that had once been all in phase have learned since to sing chords. This was a chord I did not recognize. It was beautiful and wrong.

I thought about not looking. I also thought about the strange mean streak running through my curiosity, the one that has cost me and made the world possible. There are people who can keep their hand on a lever for hours. There are people who can leave a letter unopened. I am not those people. I think hard before I do the thing I want. Then I do it.

The Watch manual says that the difference between discipline and denial is timing. Wait now, it says, and you can look later. Look now, and you might not get a later.

I held the lever in my left hand because I knew I might throw it if I didn’t occupy myself. I folded my right hand around the edge of the console. I counted breathing. I counted to sixty. When I got to fifty-eight, the ring shook. When I got to sixty, I let go of the lever and turned my eyes three degrees toward the black.

I did not look at the center. I looked just past it, where the blue lamps met the rim. The human eye cheats. The human brain betrays itself. Where the blue met the black, there was a line of light thinner than hair. It reminded me of the edges of soap bubbles in the sun. It reminded me of a cut healed over with glass.

Behind that line, something moved. It moved wrong at first, moving into the curve instead of out. Then it moved into us.

There is a way that ships appear when they transit. You teach yourself not to expect noise. You teach yourself to receive a shape, the edge of a hull, the signature blink of a beacon. This was none of that. It was a fold, a pleat unfolding, a dress tugged from a drawer. The aperture gathered itself and exhaled and let into the blue an object that did not have a standard ascribed to it by any of my software. The ring sang, the coils lit. I smelled ozone and a memory of coriander.

The object came through like a seed pod. It spun, slowed, flexed. It had fins like a fish and then no fins at all. It threw off a wash of particles that, if you believe the filters, were nothing.

My hand went to the general hail without getting permission from my brain. “Unidentified,” I said, voice going high and polite. “You are through Juno municipal. Identify yourselves. State your—”

On the screen another window opened, this one with the stick-figure icon that means human occupant. It had a latency of half a second. The handshake protocol introduced itself like neighbors at a fence.

The other side spoke with Kellan’s voice.

“Hello?” they said, unsteady. Then: “Mara? Is that you?” Their laugh came in, half-choke half-relief. “You won’t believe the weather.”

I did what I always do in a crisis; I did the first thing and then the next thing. The hole continued to be a mouth finding its face. The station hummed, a patient animal. Somewhere in my head, a version of me sat on a bench in a quarry and looked at a stone face in a wall and tried to make it smile.

Chapter One: The Weight of Salt

We crossed the dark on what we'd lost.

It wasn't poetry. It was the calibration readout on the Lament engine that ran the Borrowed Light: loss measured in lumens of coherence, in micrograms of salt extracted from skin and synapse, in a set of numbers that told us whether we would fold the distance without shredding ourselves to quiet.

On the boards the variables had austere names—Cohesion Factor, Sorrow Gain, Negative Gradient Efficiency—but we called them what they felt like. Weight. Depth. Salt.

I stood in the Cathedral ring with my hand on the harmonizer, listening to the chorus breathing on the other side of the glass, and told myself I had enough.

"Forty ampullae at nominal," Tsai reported over the intercom from the engine alcove. Their voice carried the thrum of the drive's containment, that soft bone-deep vibration you only felt inside ships that ran on grief. "We need forty-four to hit the threshold the captain wants."

"Sori knows it's a sprint, not a burn," I said. The harmonizer sighed and gave me a tiny ladder of tones. I dragged my thumb across them and the resonance in the Cathedral shifted. The ampullae—tear-bottles in antique glass, my mind insisted, though they were stacks of sensors and field coils and brine—glistened in their cradles.

"Mara," Tsai said, "she can hear you."

She always could. Sori Malik's voice cut in from the bridge a second later, warm and dry as desert wind. "We can do the argument after, Keener. Confidentiality claims in twelve minutes and a Bureau boat behind our tail. I want forty-four."

"Forty-two will get us to Hecate's reef," I said. "Forty-four will crack donors."

"They signed," Sori said, and there it was: that unlovely edge we all carried. Legal, therefore moral, therefore fine. "And they're sedated."

"They're not wood," I said. "They're not fuel. Do you want a weeper, or do you want wreckage?"

Silence, but I knew she was still there, eyes on my telemetry, fingers on her cup. The captain didn't drink when we ran; she held the cup like a talisman. Ceramic from home: a battered curve with a kiln flaw like a tear frozen in clay.

Tsai cleared their throat. "Keener, we don't have fourteen minutes for this. Tell me what I can do."

"Seal the side channels," I said. "I want all auxiliaries routed through the main coil. No leakage. Marauder's gain only."

"That's going to throw the harmonics."

"I'll catch them."

The Cathedral listened to me. The Cathedral always listened. The ring's walls were rippled brushed steel shot through with slivers of carbon. Behind them lay the donors: twenty-four in the first passage, twenty-four in the second, each strapped into a cradle of mesh and fluid and electrode, each breathing our air, each dreaming what I whispered for them to dream.

I looked up at their faces. We didn't put windows on those doors anymore. Not after the press exposés and the riots. But the engineers had left ports for maintenance, thumb-sized circles of transparent ceramic that caught reflections like pearls. If I stood at the right angle, I could see eyes through some of them. I didn't look often. This time I did.

The donor in 1-A had her hair shaved and her lashes gone from derm treatment. She could have been any age, twenty to seventy, grief made her skin the same. On the slate at her side it said Loraine, and below it, in my own hand, a note: son, river. She had told me, awake and trembling, about a boy with a sunburned nose and a rusted lure that had snagged and pulled him out where the current had her name. My job wasn't to pry; my job was to tune. But sometimes they wanted to tell and I didn't stop them.

"Okay," I breathed. The intercom would carry the sound if I let it. I did. "Okay, Loraine. We're going to light the ring. We're going to remember we know how to be heavy."

I touched the harmonizer again and the tones deepened, low vowels, cello strings sighing. The ampullae before me shivered. They weren't glass. They were modules of solution and suspended synthetic neurites, seeded with nanomemories of sorrow, anchored with traces of dried skin and hair, because bodies made fields messy and sorrow wanted anchors. The donations—this was the part the Bureau never managed to make unpretty—were not just contracts. They were swansdown pillows and old shirts, baby teeth and lockets and cracked bowls. A thousand personal relics told us where to pour our gravity.

I brought the loop down. The ring woke. The negative gradient curled under us like a tide and the ship breathed with it, the hull shedding a rising whine. On my boards the Cohesion Factor began its crawl upward.

Tsai's breath quickened in my ear. They hated this part. "Forty-one ampullae engaged," they said. "Forty-two at half. Cadence is off."

"I have it," I lied. My fingers had gone cold, and a streak of sweat ran down between my shoulder blades. Beyond the Cathedral, the Borrowed Light unfurled her antennae like a spider in a forest, beautiful and hungry.

I do this, I told myself. I make sorrow into music. I make loss a road.

We had a word for people like me. Keeners. It had been a joke when the first Lament engine prototypes asked for coherent emotional inputs and someone in the lab said, so what, you want a funeral? But we made the joke into architecture. You can't brute-force a warp bubble. We learned that the hard way, blowing holes in vacuum, killing pristine things you can't see. You needed a map that wasn't about coordinates; you needed one about stories. Grief was a map. It aligned a thousand soft brains into a pattern that tugged at the fabric the right way, curled it, nudged it. It made a dish to pour negative energy into. It made a cup.

And not all grief was equal. That's what we didn't say out loud. Clean sorrow, crisp and singular, slid the field like oiled rope. Guilt snarled. Bitter loss melted at the edges and slopped out. Rage sharpened the gradient too fast and you'd get a spallation event. Muddled regret was good for small turns. Deep love turned inside out was the good stuff, the rare, the expensive, the dear.

Loraine gave me clean, cold sorrow. I could feel it like a river mouth biting my calves. I let it in and I sang to it—seventeen beats to a measure, syncopated, the old call-and-response they taught us in the training rooms under Port Livia when the first legal Laments went live. They called it the Noise Floor Prayer. It wasn't a prayer. My voice wouldn't carry past the glass, but the harmonizer fed it back to the donors in a completely different spectrum, a sound that felt like what I'd said.

"Forty-two at nominal," Tsai said. "Forty-three at sixty percent. Mara, the Bureau boat is closing. They've got nets up."

Nets. My mouth filled with copper. The Bureau's confinement nets didn't hurt. They made a ship behave, that was all. They wrapped you in stitched vacuum and told you to be a good light and shine where they could see you. The last time a Lament ship had let itself be netted, they hauled the captain out and put her on a dais while a panel of ethicists explained why they'd rather have people crossing at eighty years between stars on ice than at eight days on tears.

That captain had put on her best uniform and smiled with every tooth she had and said, "Then you walk," and the room had gone loud with singing and shouting and after that no Bureau boat had tried it again. But here we were, out beyond Hecate, with a boat behind us flying Bureau colors and nets stowed and a list of my crew's names in their buffer, and Sori asking me for forty-four.

"Forty-three," Tsai said, breath catching, "at nominal. The harmonic is stable, Keener. It's clean."

"Don't say that," I whispered. It's bad luck to call a clean burn before you've got your depth, like telling a mother it's an easy birth when the baby's only crowned.

"We need one more," Sori said.

"I can go with us," I said.

Silence again. Tsai made a sound and swallowed it. "No," Sori said, and that was true too. You didn't pour the keener into the field unless you were the kind of desperate you didn't wake from. The keener is the tuning fork. You crack her, you can run her like a bell once, maybe, and then you have powder.

"We've got four minutes," Tsai said. "Mara, the harmonic, hold it—"

"It won't hold. You know it won't." I looked up at the donors again. Somebody's eyelashes fluttered. Somebody's foot twitched in its mesh. They weren't asleep. They were in the place I took them, where their bodies went soft around the feeling and let us carry them. "Give me any two ampullae. Any two with reserves."

Tsai's hands clacked over their keys. "We've got reserves in—this is a joke, right?—B-9 and H-3. Someone loaded B-9 with a redundancy pack under a false flag."

"God bless their ambiguity," Sori murmured.

"I don't like it," Tsai said. Which meant they liked it, but they were a good engineer.

"Take B-9," I said. "Leave H-3. H-3's got—" I consulted my notes. I'd written it in the margin of a manifest on a night I'd been half-asleep and half angry. "—H-3's got bitterness. Someone lied in that one."

"And B-9?"

"B-9's got something that wanted to be a song," I said, and heard the stupidity of it, and said it anyway. "It's not ours," I said. "But it'll vibe. It should."

Sori sighed long and thin. "Do it."

Tsai flipped the route and B-9 lit on my board in a green that was almost black. The harmonics shifted. The ring shuddered like a harp hit by a fist. All at once I could feel the center of the pattern as a cold in my teeth. That was good and bad. Good, because definition. Bad, because my jaw ached.

"Forty-four," Tsai whispered. "We have forty-four."

I leaned into the melody we were making. This was the part I always hated and loved, the part right before the pour, where my voice was a blade and every line I laid down mattered and there were a hundred hands on the other side of the glass trusting me to make the weight into something beautiful. I thought of my brother on the jetty, a thought I always reached for and avoided as late as I could. Finn, not quite fifteen, hair bleached white by a summer we weren't supposed to have, his brown shoulders sharp and his smile lopsided. He'd dropped the pocketknife I saved for him into the crevasse between the rocks and gone after it, and he'd never come back up. I'd avoided that thought for eight years. Every burn I didn't look, because if I looked I'd break, and my job was to bend.

This time I let him go. It was a small letting, a glance. It was enough. The line settled. The numbers went sweet.

"Seal the lid," Sori said. No one uses the old words in a crisis unless they're trying to make you laugh. I smiled and laid the last tone down like a prayer.

Tsai's hands and mine and the breath of forty-eight donors did what physics demanded. The Lament engine surged. The negative energy gradient held. The bubble formed and then rippled, not a circle, not a sphere, but a complicated fold with edges that felt like skin. Space went thin around us in the good way. I felt the long fall and shiver as we slid.

It was beautiful every time. There was no way to explain it to someone who had never had their bones remember the sea that wasn't water. It wasn't speed. It wasn't movement. It was weight becoming direction. We took what hurt and pressed it into the vacuum like a thumb into ball clay and the universe softened for us, just so much, just enough.

On the board the Bureau boat flickered, nets unfurled, and then they were behind the jar of our bubble, swearing.

"That's my crew," Sori said under her breath, and in her voice I heard the old Livia docks, the laughter under the cranes. "That is how we do it."

I closed my eyes and sang the hold lines that would keep the borrow neat. Borrowed Light, I thought, as if she had ears. We called her that because everything in her came from someone else's story. We owned nothing but contracts, a hull, a few cups, our names.

"Keener," Tsai said, and there was something like fear in their voice that didn't belong to physics. "Keener, what the hell is this?"

I opened my eyes. The board for B-9, the ampulla we'd pulled under a false flag, was bright enough to make my retinas fizz. The harmonic it was pushing into the ring wasn't the one I had set. It wasn't out of tune. It was a different song under mine, threading it, tugging at it, pulling a thread loose and weaving it back in a direction I hadn't marked.

"Isolate it," I said. "Isolate and damp."

"I can't. It—" Tsai's voice broke. "It's reading into your channel. It's reading your—"

"My what," I said. My throat felt raw. I cut my pitch and the donors breathed back, hands in their meshes slackening, and still the harmonics were moving.

Your bones, I thought. Your bones, your voice. It's reading your voice.

The tone under the tone made the room go long and pale. My heart thudded. The overhead lights condensed into stars, which was impossible; that was a sensor loop the hull made when we ran at high gain, not something you saw in the Cathedral. And then the glass to the donors clouded and cleared and the condensation on it spelled words, which was madness; condensation doesn't shape. Except it did, and it spelled my name.

MARA, it said. A drop ran down the A like a comet tail.

I am not a person who startles easily. You can't be, if your job is to lean. But that made my fingers numb.

"Tsai," I said. "Do you see —"

"I see changing field geometry. I see your board doing a pretty trick with water. Are you having a neurological event?"

"It's writing my name," I said. "It's writing my name."

Sori's voice came in very soft. "On what?"

"The glass," I said. "The condensation."

"Condensation isn't real," Tsai said automatically. "In a sealed—"

"I can see it."

"Okay," Sori said. "Okay. Now I'm going to ask you if you took anything that would make you—"

"No," I said. "I took nothing." My mouth wanted to ask for a cigarette, which was a sign I was either eight years ago in a low bar in Livia or imagining it, and I had quit eight years ago while wearing a shirt of my brother's I couldn't bear to wash. And then the condensation shaped again. Not letters. A drawing. A quick line, a circle, a sharper curve, the long looping of an orbit. It looked like a small child's picture of a planet and a string and a boat.

I'd drawn that as a child on the underside of our kitchen table, in pencil, where my mother couldn't see. I'd use my thumbnail to scratch the graphite shine off the wood and make it look like the jetty, and the boat, and the moon, and the way the tide tugged the rope. I hadn't told anyone. There was no one to tell. My mother didn't look under tables; she washed above. Finn had left before he could see it. The house burned in the Livia riots and took the table with it, my careless planets charred. No one on this ship could possibly know that curve.

"I want to know where that ampulla came from," Sori said. Now there was no dry in her voice. It was all salt and granite.

Tsai's fingers quivered on the keys. "B-9 was a shipload salvage from a cold storage clinic in the San Benito cluster. Label says redundancy pack, donor IDs sealed per contract. Offloaded by a broker with a Permit. We pinged the index, we got a legal go."

"Which broker?" I asked. My voice sounded normal. That made me angrier.

"There's a hash," Tsai said. "We can query after Burn. Keener—"

The condensation wrote again. I didn't tell them what it wrote. I couldn't. It wrote the name my mother used for me when she was laughing and wanted me to stop doing something foolish and I pretended not to stop. It wrote it with a flourish on the last letter, because I'd made that flourish with a knife I shouldn't have had, on the underside of a dead kitchen table.

And then it wrote a set of numbers.

I didn't think right away of coordinates. They didn't look like that. They were ratios and fractions and exponents and values that tickled the part of my mind that woke up in the night and saw a pattern and couldn't go back to sleep. Then Tsai inhaled fast and said, "That's a radial vector on a spun torus. That's a—"

"A gate," Sori said, very quiet.

"No," Tsai said. "Those numbers don't go anywhere we own. They go somewhere—"

"A gate," Sori said again. "Please tell me I'm wrong."

But I was looking at the numbers and what they did to the field and I wasn't thinking gate. The Lament didn't do gates. Gates took whole cities to sing. We made our own bubble skipping and we went where we had depth for. No one took us directly to where we weren't anchored, because that was how you made ghosts.

"Who is this," I asked, and didn't know who I was asking. My voice felt funny in my mouth. "What do you want me to do."

The condensation paused as if considering. The tone under the tone turned tender. I didn't have a category for that. It was the feeling my mother had when she tied my braid too tight and then redid it gentle because I'd flinched.

Bring me home, it wrote.

"Home where," I whispered. "Home is—"

The numbers brightened on the board. You can't see numbers brighten. They are digits on a screen. But the readout flared and the field with it, and Tsai yelled, "The bubble is pivoting. It's pivoting on an axis—"

"Hold it," Sori snapped. "Keener, can you hold it?"

"Maybe," I said. I was already sliding my hands up the harmonizer, trying to drag the pattern back under my fingers. But the pattern was dancing with me and not wanting to be led. I could choke it. I could shatter B-9. I could do what I had to do to keep my crew within the dotted lines and the good graces of a physics that didn't forgive pride. I had trained for that. The body knows how to break a tune into safety if you teach it enough. That's what the port doctors say when they sign off on your Keener license. Your body knows how to be good.

I looked at the condensation on the glass. It had started to drip for real now. That meant it was neither a glitch nor a hallucination. My eyes burned. I didn't cry when we ran. That was a rule too. Tears are data and you don't put your dirty thumb into the mix.

Bring me home, the glass wrote again. It didn't write please. That was my mother's manner too. She assumed we would.

"Where home," I asked again. "You have to tell me where."

The numbers spun a little like joy. I had once tuned a man whose grief was a set of instructions his wife had left him before she died, written in a comb-binding so old the plastic cracked, and he had said There, you see, she told me where the good knives would be when the remotes broke. The numbers felt like that. They drew an arc in the concept space the ring made and highlighted a fold the Federation's maps did not show.

"Mara," Tsai said, and their voice was full of panic now. "That arc goes into a red zone. Do not—"

"Keener," Sori said, her voice suddenly intimate. "If you do this, if you bend for this, we are out there where no one will see if we die. If you don't, you can choke it and we'll eat Bureau fines and go hungry for six months but we'll eat. You have twenty seconds. I am not going to tell you you are allowed to go with us, because the last time I let you go with us I vomited for a day and you slept for three. But I am going to tell you, because I promised you when we took you out of Livia and glued you back together, that I will go where you go."

That's something good captains say, and it isn't always true. With Sori it was true.

My brother was on the jetty in my head, ten years old, and the knife was cheap and I had saved for it, and he said I can't believe your luck and I said it's not luck, I stole it, and my mother shouted from the kitchen and the stink of fish was everywhere, all the time, forever. The part of me that had learned to make sorrow into neat shapes breathed out and looked at my crew in my mind and measured the angle of where the field asked to tilt. The condensation wrote one more thing.

Hurry.

I stopped holding the fight. I let the field turn.

The ring in the Cathedral made a sound like air going out of a lung. The donors made a soft sound all together that you wouldn't pick up if you didn't stand where I did, a little animal mew, and then they quieted. The ampullae sang. The numbers on B-9 wrote themselves like rain on glass and changed not at all. The Borrowed Light rolled under a sky of nothing, and then there was a stutter in the noise the universe made. We slid through.

Starfields do not differ much to the eye. You have to learn the shapes. But you can feel when the weave changes. The inside of my mouth tasted like something I didn't have a word for. There was a metallic in it, not copper, not blood, something else I had never eaten. I put my tongue to my teeth and tasted old salt. It wasn't mine.

"Where did we go," Sori said. It wasn't a demand. It was a child's question about a road.

Tsai's breath came in small huffs. "I don't know," they said. "I don't know where we are. The map doesn't— That arc is not on any—"

The intercom went dead. The ship hummed louder. It always did, in the moment between folds, when vacuum laid its finger down and took its gift. The lights went dim and came back, as if someone had blinked.

On the glass the condensation smeared, the letters running into one another, and for an instant long enough to be keen I saw, just past the donors, the shape of someone sitting in my mother’s kitchen, legs tucked under her on the chair, hands around a problematic cup. She looked up with my eyes. She was older than me and younger. She smiled helpless and made the little half shrug my brother used when he was about to dare me into something.

Then she was gone, and the Cathedral was ordinary again, and the donors slept, and the ring chimed the end of a turn, and the Borrowed Light settled into a place that smelled like rain.

"Engines stable," Tsai said, faint and incredulous. "Bubble intact. I don't know where we are, but we are somewhere and we are not dead."

Sori laughed, a sound like a match struck in a dark room. "I will take not dead. Keener?"

"I'm here," I said. My throat hurt. "I'm here."

"What did you do," Sori said, but she didn't ask like a judge. She asked like my mother would have, with the line of her mouth half stern and half proud and all fear.

"I listened," I said. "And then I didn't hold."

"Good," Sori said. "You do that well. All stations, report. Tsai, find me something to call this place so I can curse it and sell it later."

"Understood."

"And Mara," she said, plain, as if we were sitting at the same rough table. "Whatever that was, don't talk about it where the ship can listen. Come up when you can walk. I have a cup and ten minutes before I have to tell a dozen people we're on a road laid by a ghost. If this ghost is a bill collector or a saint, I want to know before I pay."

The intercom clicked. The Cathedral hummed. The condensation dried and left no trace but cold on my skin. I leaned my forehead against the glass and let myself have one briny sob, not for Finn or for whatever we had just done, but for the ridiculous way the universe had of using children’s drawings as maps. Then I wiped my face with my sleeve and set my voice in serviceable order and went to tell my captain that home, for something, had not been a place but a promise, and that we had chosen to keep it.

Chapter One

They say the planet makes a sound you can only hear when you fall alone.

Tarna had heard it once when she was thirteen, half a breath past a mistake. Back then she'd been a gangly apprentice with too-big gloves and a kite that pulled like a stubborn animal. The mooring winch had shrieked, the line had snapped, and she’d dropped into the bruised gold of the lower air, spinning and spinning. Somewhere in the spin, when the city and its towers had become a small, faraway geometry above her and the storm trumpets a sweeping floor below, she heard it: a low, continuous hum that wasn’t wind and wasn’t thunder. She’d felt it through her ribs and gums more than heard it. It was like the planet clearing its throat.

It returned to her sometimes, in dreams or in the bone-deep quiet at the end of a dive.

Now, nine years and a hundred dives later, the hum found her again as she let herself slip below the rim-layer. Her kite—a triangular wing of silksteel veined with heating filaments—tilted and cut. The vanes along its leading edge retracted with a whisper, the whole thing changing from a big, forgiving surface to something like a seablade, built to slice instead of float. The air down here was a dense syrup, warm and metallic. Light fell from above in columns, broken by the city’s rigs and the clouds, so that the world was banded: a white layer, a copper layer, a black-green layer.

Her buoyancy corset creaked as the bladder trimmed to keep her neutral. The harness bit her shoulders, doing its dull ache where the straps crossed the old, familiar scar on her back. Tarna adjusted the angle of the wing with a touch of her thumb to the haptic pips along the grip, and the kite obeyed. Its tether—her tether—ran up and up, a curve vanishing into the bright, toward the crawler that would pay out the line as she sank and reel her in when she asked.

She checked, again, the dial on her forearm. The dial was nothing more than a ring of beads under the skin: each bead a sensor’s output, each color a kind of fear. Most glowed a comfortable green. Blue pulsed at the rim: the cold-edge from a transient she worked to avoid. Red would mean shear danger—metal-down-canyon wind that could cut her in half.

“Sinkrider,” came the voice of the crawler pilot, tiny in her ear. “I’ve got you at nine hundred. Smooth descent. Your garden is at one-one-two-zero. You’ve got notches of turbulence below. Watch for teeth.”

Teeth was guild slang for shear pockets.

“Copy, Harp Two,” Tarna said. “I see your trim. Keep it on me.”

“I always do,” Harp Two said with dry affection. The pilot’s real name was Alya, but on the line everyone called each other by their rig’s codename. Tarna was glad to have Alya today. She flew the line like it was a wormsheath buried in her own nerves.

Tarna’s job was simple to describe and complicated to survive. She hunted gardens. “Garden” was what they called the clusters of things that weren’t storm and weren’t living weather. Things that sat against the wind like the planet had grown them and yet were not of the planet at all. The oldest divers swore some were older than the cities themselves, older than the mooring towers and the heat pipes and the big smoothing fans that kept the city in one piece.

Garden meant hazard. Garden meant pay.

Her garden today flitted in the gust pattern like a mirage. The big storms carved lanes through the atmosphere, and those lanes had edges, and like snow blown into drifts, debris would collect along those edges. Only this wasn’t debris. Alya had mapped something in the edges. Tarna had seen the spectrographs: a shimmer of refractive indices where nothing should be.

Eleven hundred came and went. The hum pressed against her teeth.

She left the colonized light of the city and entered the steep gradient that the sinkriders called the throttle. The throttle was where the air went from a polite squeeze to a body in a vice; where every motion took muscle because air was no longer air but an invisible ocean of mass. She added heater juice to the trailing edge filaments; the kite complained and tightened and then bit, and she carved a shallow curve around a feathered cloud. The cloud stretched itself like sugar, strands ghosting behind it in the slow-writhing currents.

“Still seeing you,” Alya said in her ear. “Your wet is climbing. You get another minute before I remind you to breathe.”

“I am breathing,” Tarna said, and drew in a practiced, measured breath through the mask. The gas mix tasted of pepper and cold. She imagined it was all anything had ever tasted like down here: a heat without fire, a wet without water.

There. The first sign of her quarry.

It looked like a sleepwalker at the edge of a cliff: a figure implied by absence. The air around it was too smooth. Sound thinned there. The tiny loose crystals that always pirouetted in layers—ammonium something, tang of cleaning solvent, glitter to the eye—fell away from a shape. Tarna had seen gardens shaped like ropes, like stag antlers, like plankton blooms. This one was a sphere, perfectly resolved against the chaos of the planet, and it was in the process of making itself larger.

“Are you seeing this?” Tarna whispered.

The line popped as Alya chuckled. “Oh, I am. That’s a living pocket if I ever saw one. God’s teeth, Tarna, do not touch it without sniffing it.”

She didn’t need the reminder. She cut her descent and let the kite take up the stress. The sphere had a skin: not a membrane but a velvet border of colder, slower air. She stopped at a distance the guild taught, an arm and a half’s reach plus one panic flinch. She extended the nose of her sampler wand through the border.

The wand hissed softly as it took in the air, ran light through it, sniffed it with a dozen microchemical tongues. Tarna watched the beads on her forearm change color as the counts came in. Her skin prickled along the tattoo that had been her graduation gift: five points for the five simple things that killed divers fastest.

“Okay,” she said, slow. “No caustics. Not radiating. Oxygen fraction is nil. Water none. Temperature’s cooler than ambient, by three. Density lower. It has a stable shell but it is not a life pocket.”

“Not life,” Alya acknowledged. “Which does not mean not dangerous.”

“Also not pressure firings. No microexplosions. Wait—wait—”

The sampler wand chirped. Light along the wand’s shaft drifted in circles. Tarna peeered, breath forgotten. The circles were not random. They curved back on themselves, nested, scaled in perfect ratios. She knew that language. All divers did. The circuits of vault locks, the patterns of message balls, the spool-dance of the old archive cores… they loved their numbers like they loved their bronzes.

“It’s a seedclock,” she said softly, throat tight. “A real one.”

“Could be a fake,” Alya said reflexively. Then, after a beat: “No. You wouldn’t get that clean of a ratio in local flow if it were a snag of drift. Shit. You lucky, ugly bastard.”

Alyas’s voice had gone wary. A seedclock meant the planet was about to tease them with the future. Or the past. No one knew where they came from. They tended to appear in the wakes of the biggest storms, as if the storms coughed them up the way the sea coughed driftwood and dead squid. They were bubbles of air with internal minds. If you cracked them correctly, they released a pattern—sometimes sound, sometimes a geometric thought that you had to hold in your head until it melted into comprehension. The first seedclocks had told the engineers where to anchor the cities. Another had taught the chemists what to feed the heat pipes to keep them clean. A dozen had told jokes in languages no one had heard in a thousand years.

Their guild called them seedclocks because, if you were patient, and if you watered them with attention—if you let them tick through a series of environment conditions—they sprouted. They showed you something. Sometimes the something was a trap. Sometimes the something was a box and the box held a machine and the machine asked to be wound.

The right to collect them belonged, by contract and tradition, to the City-of-Harp as a whole. To take one without registering it, without the guild’s eyes on it, was to go beyond reprimand, beyond cutting your percentage. It was to step into the realm of fines and exile.

Tarna looked at the sphere, at the velvet border of slow air like fur. She looked up into the bright where the line went, toward the towers and Alya and the rigs and her bed and the hab rows and the little market where Ket sold hollowbean stew. She looked down. The dark didn't look back.

“Tag and call it?” Alya asked, careful, keeping her voice on the thin edge between command and suggestion.

Tarna did not answer. Ket would be happy tonight if she called it; they would eat long noodles and sweet pepper leaf and Alya would come down off the rigs and tell stories and the seedclock would go to the Harp’s keepers. And in a week the keepers would call a press and the City-of-Harp would add a line to its knowledge. Tarna would see her name in the ledger: Tarna, finder.

In a month, perhaps, she would get a bonus big enough to shave a glancing blow off Mom’s debts.

Mom, who had fallen into the planet and never come back.

“Tag and call it,” Alya said again.

Tarna touched the seedclock’s border with the wand.

“Alya,” she said, “my sampling is clean. I’m going to get a lens on it. That’s all.”

“Fine. Lens it. Do not do anything else.”

A lens was a legal thing. The guild let divers carry one because the guild liked to see quick-and-dirty data before they lowered their cradle and their Keepers’ cage. Tarna unclipped the lens from her belt. It looked like a ring in her hand, a beveled slice of polished crystal ringed by very clever nothing. The nothing was sharper than a knife and as delicate as snow and if it touched you, you bled. She slid the ring into the velvet edge with shaking fingers, let it seat, and twisted a quarter-turn. The seedclock’s border accepted the ring the way a soap bubble accepted a wet loop to become a soap film. The ring gave her a window.

“Tarna?” Alya said, and there were other voices now in the line noise, feeding off Alya’s channel. Supervisors. A Keeper-aide. Tarna ignored them.

The film bloomed.

She squinted and then cursed, soft and fervent. The seedclock’s interior was not empty. It was not the usual collection of schooling motes, their drift pattern encoded with a message. Instead a skein of something like rain hung within the bubble, lines of bright that seemed to fall and yet did not, because there was no gravity here, only the illusion of falling. The lines knit themselves and unknit themselves with the craft of a dozen Sassil mathematicians, except the Sassil were rock-folk who hated the sky and would rather die than move to a place like Harp.

“What do you see?” Alya demanded.

It looked like a model, Tarna thought. That was the best word. People made models of the city to teach schoolchildren how to not die on stairs. People made models of the mooring towers to teach apprentices where not to put their fingers. This was something like that. A model of the planet, not in shape but in mood. Layers, all gradients and flows, each layer a different kind of air. At the center of it all, where no diver had ever gone, where no mooring line could reach because past a certain depth you could pull on the line forever and the line would, in the end, simply thin and break into heat and nothing, there was… a dark.

Not dark like lack-of-light. This was structured absence. An object the way a promise was an object.

“Tarna?” Alya’s voice was too loud.

“In the center,” Tarna said, unable to tear her gaze away. “There’s a… hole. It’s a hole. A hollow that isn’t supposed to be.”

The line went silent except for crackle for two long breaths.

“Record,” Alya said. “Record now.”

Tarna pinned the seedclock’s edges with small adhesive flags that sang their position in the radio band and pressed the lens to her forehead, warmed it with a breath, spoke the guild words. The ring buzzed like a sleeping cat, numbers crawled along her cheekbones, and she felt the slight heat draw of it taking in extraordinary amounts of detail.

While it ate, the falling lines of light inside the bubble re-knitted into a shape Tarna’s mind had to lean into to hold. She felt the tremor of understanding and held her breath to cradle it.

The hole wasn’t just a hole. It was a machine built in a negative. It was a machine that used absence the way a pump used vacuum. You didn’t build something like that out of metal. You built it out of relationship. From the outside, there would be no seam. From the inside—

The inside wasn’t for her.

There was a noise like a distant voice behind a wall. Tarna flinched and the shape went hazy. Her breath fogged the view. The ring tightened on her skin, anxious in its ring-way. The noise came again: not through her ear, not through the line. It was a pressure on her molars, a ripple in the hum.

“Tarn?” Alya said, all the humor fled from the nickname. “I’m seeing movement in your layer. You need to finish and back out. We’ll get the cage down and—”

“Shh,” Tarna said without thinking. The noise resolved into a word, a half-syllable she had not heard in years.

“Nei,” said the voice. Her mother’s name for her. Not Tarna. Nei-nei, from when she was small, from when words had to be softened because she was afraid of hard ones.

Her mouth filled with cold.

“Nei,” said the voice again, making the old syllable as if from the other side of three walls they had never built. “Listen. Listen to me. Do not call the Keepers. Not yet.”

“I didn’t—” Tarna said, then realized she had, in fact, called, by tagging and recording, and that now there were at least three Keepers gliding toward the rig with knives of law in their hands.

“Tarna,” Alya said. Not Tarn or Tarny or any of the worker-names, but Tarna, the name you used when you wanted someone to know they were being asked to be responsible. “Your window just went from nothing to full-spectrum interference. I don’t like this. Back out.”

“Can you hear that?” Tarna asked, and then realized that of course Alya could not. If the voice didn’t come through the line, the only place it could come from was inside the vector of the lens. And even there it wasn’t sound. It was more like a shape that Brush—no, not Brush; that was a story from a time before Tarna—like a brush passing above a paper and the paper wrinkling in answer.

Her mother was dead. Tarna had watched her mother fall. Everyone had watched; it had been the way of it. The city had loaded the grid, the static had popped, someone on the mooring had made a mistake, and the line had jerked and her mother had gone tilted wrong and the gust had taken her. There had been no hum, not for her mother, because there had been no time. There had been only the touch-sound of the guild’s iron bars as strangers held Tarna still, and the smell of heated ammonia, and the moment just after when everything in the world had gone too sharp to look at and then the world had clouded and never quite cleared again.

She put her hand around the ring like a fist around a throat. “Say it again,” she said. If it was a test, she would fail richly.

“Nei,” came the thought-pressure, in her mother’s voice except the voice had been cleaned, tuned by the filter of a machine far cleverer than any Tarna had ever held. “Do not give me up sweet to the Keepers. The cage will unmake me. I have done this before. They will not let me do it again.”

“What are you?” Tarna whispered.

“Tarn?” Alya said. “What’s happening?”

“I have to take it,” Tarna said.

“Don’t you fucking dare,” someone else hissed through the line—Keeper?—and then Alya was saying Tarna’s name again and again and the numbers on her cheekbone were red and the ring vibrated with a warning tone that meant the lens was exceeding its safe energy draw.

“I’m going to throw you a free,” Alya said quickly, the tone she used with ship-pets when they were snagged in fans. “Just drift for a second. Let the line go slack. I need you clear for a cage. If you stay where you are there’s going to be layer mixing and you’re going to have a bad time.”

“I hear you,” Tarna said, and flicked a thumb to cut the kite’s servo again. She brought the wand up, pulled the ring out of the film with a sucking feel like pulling her hand from gel, and the seedclock wobbled like a thought interrupted. The velvet edge shivered. The falling lines inside braided tighter in alarm.

“Nei,” said the voice. “Nei, please.”

If she was wrong, the guild would break her. She would hang for a week in the market square while all the children stared, while the city’s hydra-fans turned and turned. She would pay the rest of Mom’s debt with the rest of her life. If she was right—

She knew a man, Ket’s cousin once removed, who had gone from sleeping in a heat pipe to living in one of the North Wing gloss rooms because he had found a seedclock and waited a day to call the Keepers and so the thing had had time to show him how to fix the most trivial thing on earth in a way no one had thought of and he had simply kept the knowledge long enough to patent it in his own name. The Keepers had sulked and the law had snarled, but his name had gone down in the ledger and that was that. Lightning had struck once in his life. He had managed to hold a bottle for it to fill.

This felt like that, but bigger. And it used her mother’s voice.

“Do not tell anyone,” the voice said in the small space between heartbeats. “Take me out. Go to the Harp’s southmost pillar, lowest room. Find the very old man with the burned hand. He is the only Keeper who may see me. Do you understand? It is not a trick. It is an eddy. If you let the cage touch me, the strand untwists too soon and nothing that must happen will happen.”

Two places in Tarna’s mind stepped backward. The first was panic, a reflex honed by nearly dying a few times too often to be romantic. The second was a quiet that could fit in the palm of her hand. Somewhere in the quiet she imagined Alya’s face up on the rig, scalplight catching her hair, mouth pressed thin. Somewhere under the panic she felt for the hum.

She cut her tether.

The noise that made up in the rig channel was remarkable. People were capable of a lot with just breath and vowels.

Tarna had practiced the cut in the dark, at night, with a dummy tether, just to know. The guild had a rule about never cutting, but it also had a rule about knowing your own tools. The cutter was a flat, dumb piece of folded fiber stuck to the back of her wrist, a little blade you could fish, press, and pull when your hands were too cold to manage smart things. It worked without a word. It bit the line the way the line bit air. It held the taste of salt because she had licked it before she’d shoved it into its pocket on her sleeve that morning, because an old habit from an old story had stuck with her.

Her hand did the job before the part of her brain that obeyed rules could get in the way. The line went from tight as a promise to nothing at all. The kite bucked. The seedclock jumped against her ring.

“Tarna!” Alya screamed. The channel filled with orders. Tarna felt the sudden irrational love that a falling person feels for all the others not falling with them.

Then she fell. The hum swelled up to meet her like an old song.

She gathered the seedclock in her arms like a child and whispered through her teeth, because names mattered and maybe this thing needed to know her: “I’m Nei to you. We’re going home.”

Her kite tried to tilt; she let it. The air below the rim-layer was never still. The planet was a giant drum and the storms were hands. The hands were beating, and beating, and beating. She found a lean in the beat, turned the wing to it.

If the planet was kind and Alya braver than law, the rig would drag the broken end of her tether with the aerial. They’d spool it like a fisherman line, and they’d dive the cage anyway and they would find her ring song and they would find her, and if she timed her fall carefully and played the kite like it was a kite and not a wing, if she threaded seams and rode the smooth and tacked to avoid the teeth, if she kept the seedclock tucked in her belly where her heat and breathing would give it the variability it needed to stay knit, she might hit the lower upwelling on the edge of the southeast anticyclone. It would spit her back up toward the city’s southmost pillar with enough force to bruise her spleen and maybe, maybe, get her through a door.

Her mother had taught her to ride the upwellings. The day after the funeral, Tarna had skipped her work detail, stolen a kite, and climbed a heat-pipe ladder to the east face. She had flown until she could not see the griefless faces and the city would not let her be a person. The upwelling had found her then too and kissed her hard and thrown her up so fast she missed the ladder and hit the tower like a bug hitting glass and slid down laughing, laughing, because sometimes you had to laugh to remind your chest that you were not going to drown on dry air.

“Nei,” said the seedclock, breathing with her. “Quickly. I am not all in one. Parts of me are in the wind.”

Tarna touched the ring to the seedclock again, let it rest skin to skin. “Come then,” she said, her voice high to keep it from breaking.

Above her, far above, a cage swung into blue. In a room threaded with copper pipes and vibrating like a plucked string, a man with a burned hand put his tools down without knowing why.

The planet hummed. Tarna leaned and the wind caught her and the city of Harp, hung on its pillars like a harp in a giant room, slid on the horizon, steady and waiting and very far away. The first hard tooth of shear snapped at the kite. Tarna smiled feral in her mask and bared her teeth. She bent the wing’s edge, cut, and went on falling.

The wind sang at the edge of the world. It was a long, torn note, rising from the hot glare at the horizon and slipping past the ice-shadow behind, tasting of metal and ash and the breath of a star. Mara Tel stood on the forward gantry of Gnomon and felt it through her boots and bones, a vibration threaded through the steel under her, a hummingbird tremor in the rails that the city rode.

Gnomon never stopped. That was the first law, recited to children at their naming and carved into the faces of the heat engines that churned at the front of the train-city. Don’t stop. Not for hail, not for politics, not for ghosts. If you stopped, even for an hour, the balance of the world would remember you. The front edge—where the red dwarf sun hung forever at a low angle, a double fist of glare—would creep up and cook you, inch by merciless inch. The back edge—blackness scarfed in ice crystals, the night wall—would catch you and squeeze you solid. You lived at the knife line, where the sky was always copper and wine-dark and the clouds above were pulled into a flat river. Don’t stop.

Mara blew into her glove, then checked the seal again by habit. The tendon actuators purred and tightened around her palm. Out ahead, the forward observation drone—Ahead-Eye Three—was a darting smear at low altitude, skating the gradient winds, its belly cameras scanning the track. A thread of its feed rode in the corner of Mara’s goggles; for a run-whispered second it showed a fine, pale lattice where smooth gray rail ought to be, then static.

“Lost Eye Three again,” Nazim grunted.

He loomed at her shoulder even in Gnomon’s stormshields, a thick warm presence with frost on his beard and a coil of cable over one arm. He’d been Track a long time, had the flattened thumb and the hesitant smile to show for it, and a tattoo of the original Founder’s glyph under his ear that he made like to forget. Mara trusted his weight, as she trusted the weight of the forward heat engines and the way the concrete heat sink blocks flexed and groaned under load.

“It always loses there.” She tried to keep the irritation from her voice. Static wasn’t new; there were places on Spindle where the rails themselves threw noise, places where the old world hummed too loud for their toys to peer. “But this time it pinged something new.”

He snorted, and the frost on his mustache puffed. “New isn’t an adjective that likes us.”

“Quaint,” she said, and leaned forward over the gantry rail to look at the track itself. Spindle flew past under Gnomon’s wide belly, broad and clean and dull, the Makers’ metal laid in a nearly perfect circle around the world. It was never rusty, never quite cracked, though over generations it had scabbed and mended and puckered where human maintenance met whatever had been here first. In the immediate foreground, the rails had a slight sheen of frost, and the dust devils danced along the ballast like transparent cats.

“Track speed steady,” her earpiece sang in Dispatch’s pleasant neutral. “Wind shear within tolerances. Forward engines nominal. Net heat gain fifteen percent. Track, you are go for forward deployment.”

“Copy.” Mara thumbed her clip-line carabiner and felt the tug as Nazim did the same. “We’re going down.”

Nazim spat for luck, a dry token into the wind. “Don’t stop,” he said, automatic and under his breath.

The forward gantry opened like a mouth. The air that came over Gnomon’s prow was always warmer than the air that rose from the back, because they made it so: ten thousand bodies and boilers and chemical factories throwing the night’s cold away ahead into the day’s heat in exchange for power. The gantry’s shield bit the wind into manageable bites; still, when Mara edged out onto the ladder and down to the outer walkway, her eyes watered.

Under her, the city’s spine: the forward trucks, the broad steel rollers that gripped Spindle by magnet and weight and heat and took Gnomon along. The smell of hot lubricant and ceramic brake soot cut through the star-salt tang. The rails blurred. The world on either side was color-blocked by physics: to her right the bright shelf of scorched earth, flat and yellow-white with a thousand heat-shattered stones; to her left the thin blue of nitrogen haze over frost-lichen and the white glitter of ice.

Ahead, the flagged anomaly segment was just visible, a subtle warp in the otherwise mindlessly straight line of Spindle, as if a hand had pressed and left a print in wet clay and it had hardened that way. In her ear: Ahead-Eye chirped then died again, its last streaming frames staining her goggles with the image of the fine pale lattice.

They had time. A minute and some. No one liked minutes in Track; minutes were where your hat blew away and your rope went slack and then taut, where your weight fell into the wrong kind of silence. Mara had rationed her minutes since childhood. She checked her tools out of habit: monomolecular wire saw coiled like string, the patch foam canisters along her harness, the thermite beads. “Oh, I hate foam day,” she said.

Nazim laughed. “You love foam day. It went in your yearbook. What I hate is the way foam smells like old mustard.”

“What I hate…” She flicked her wrist and the wire saw clip clicked into place on her glove ring, then to the other glove. “Is not knowing why squish has replaced our metal.”

“Squish,” Nazim repeated, skeptical, and then they were level with the anomaly and there was no more time for types of hate.

Up close, the rails were wrong and wrong again. Spindle’s metal was smooth as bone in a museum, utterly uniform even where generations of welds intersected and disagreed. The anomaly was not smooth. It was a lacework, a bristling coral of thin struts and hollows, tubes growing from tubes, no two quite the same, a frozen foam. It was not white, but an off-not-color that the eye interpreted as something paler than steel, like light under ice. The fast-running dust devils could not cross it; they tripped and blew apart at the lacy edges. Where the city’s forward trucks began to pass over it, they did not bounce. They bit. It was the sound of a mouth finding a rind.

Mara put her gloved hand to one of the foamed struts, intentionally gentle, and felt the hum of the wind move through it. Beneath that, lower, a thrumming, regular and familiar: the beat of Spindle’s blood, the rolling of the city’s mass. Lower still, something she could not cannot name, an almost-sound like two notes just sharp from each other.

“We’ve got thirty and then the whole front half will be riding this stuff,” Nazim said, grim. He had already kicked free the quick-snap cartridge of diagnostic nodes from his belt; the little round things rag-dolled in the wind and magnetized themselves along the edge of the anomaly. “Foam cut, sling patch, and maybe we don’t lose ceramic teeth.”

“Copy.” Even as the word came, Mara’s brain offered her a folded paper memory: a story from her mother, told under a greenhouse tarp when the rain-harvesters hammered on it, about how the rails had never been metal to begin with, but a kind of bone the world had grown like antlers after the first ships came. She had asked if bones grew in circles and her mother had said, do not ask questions of things you will never meet. Mara had decided then that she hated not-knowing. Here it was again, in her hands.

She dropped the wire saw’s loop over one of the larger culms and pulled it tight. The wire cut anything they could not burn or wept to glue. It should have slid through this like a thought. It met it with tooth. She felt the wire sing, a high glassy sound, and shivered in spite of her heated suit. “Feels like heavy honey,” she said.

But the wire did cut. The culm spar felt elastic at first, then snapped with a crunch like ice underfoot. The broken cross-section showed tiny hollow circles within circles, wetly glistening with something that dewed and evaporated and left behind a salt sheen.

Nazim caught the piece on the end of his glove. “Don’t lick it,” he said.

“Wasn’t planning to.”

He was already affixing the foam nozzle. “On three.”

“Wait.”

Her hesitation wasn’t professional. It reached back behind the part of her brain that knew weights and tolerances and the smell of overheated ceramic. It was the same part that had once, years ago, made her stop with a hand on a hatch and listen to the way the wind changed pitch as someone behind it took a breath. It was the part that hated not-knowing. “Give me a second.”

“Mara—”

She put her hand flat to the lattice again, where her cut had left a raw mouth of hollows, and closed her eyes. The lower thrumming teased the bones of her ear. She had the ridiculous thought that the world was trying to tell her a joke in a language she didn’t know, starting over again each time she failed to laugh at the right moment. She tightened the muscles inside her ear, a childhood trick to make the Gnomon’s wind roar into a pseudo-quiet, to hear people through the curtains.

The almost-sound came up, like a phrase, like a…not a word. A pattern of long and short that had tickled her once before.

Her earpiece crackled. Dispatch again. “Track, be advised, we have anomalous thermals on the forward arrays and I would like to keep our wheels.” The neutral was gone; there was an edge.

“Just about to fix your wheels,” Nazim said, not keying his mic. “Mara—”

“Foam,” she said. “Foam and then I want Three back up. I want another look.”

They foamed. The patch resin came out of the nozzle like an obedient river and expanded on breathing, a pale gray balloon that settled and stiffened and then set, building itself molecule by molecule around the broken place. It turned lead-hard when you breathed on it and you could weld it or you could burn it back into its bottles. It did not like to stick to Spindle metal and it did not like to stick to snow. It stuck to the anomaly with a hungry greed that made Mara’s neck prickle.

The front trucks hit the new patch and rumbled, but the rumble was the right kind, a complaint and not a scream. Nazim whooped once. “Go you gummy bastard.”

“Good work, Track,” Dispatch said, seconds later, like a prayer and a reprimand. “Forward speed steady.”

“Is this in the runbook yet?” Mara asked.

“I’ll write you a page,” Dispatch said dryly, which meant no.

Mara wasn’t convinced. There were rules for the places where Spindle changed. The city had fought the first growths along the rails with furious human tools and then learned where to compromise, where to cap and where to wrap and where to back off. Every generation, Track thought it had found the vocabulary of the old stuff and every generation a new tense showed up. Today it was lattice foam that ate resin like caramel. Tomorrow it could be vines or teeth.

“Do you ever think,” Nazim said, “that if we could wake The Makers, they’d laugh at our glue?”

“Let them come glue it themselves,” Mara said. There was too much of her mother in it. The old man heard it and smiled with one half of his mouth.

“We should drop a Mend,” he said.

“Not on this.” Her throat had gone tight. “A G Mend would slag it and run down into the ballast and set us a nice glass laser under our feet.”

“You are conservative today.” He mugged exaggerated surprise and she resisted the urge to shove him into the windshield so the wind could sand his eyebrows off.

“We’re riding on it now. And if you haven’t noticed, it’s chewing into our ceramic teeth. It’s not just a pretty reef.”

They should have retreat. That was the sensible thing. Track never did something sensible until someone else made it inevitable. Mara keyed the Ahead-Eye release and felt the drone drop from the rail cradle and whip away like a dragonfly. Its feed took one heartbeat to stabilize, then it was sending her back a crisp, low-angle view of the anomaly and a good thirty meters ahead of it. More foam. More lattice, wider. In the middle distance the lacework spilled aside like sea foam down the ballast embankments and held itself together. But then, beyond that, the rails resumed their proper dull uniformity. Whatever had happened had a boundary.

Except: though she scanned and scanned, she could not find the seam. The place where smooth metal became growth became smooth again happened not across a joint but as if someone had pulled a sleeve over Spindle and then peeled it back. It left no scar she could see. It left a taste in her mouth like old batteries.

“Why there?” she said.

Nazim had his goggles down now, peering with the kind of intent you sometimes saw in surgeons and gamblers. “Hate you sometimes,” he said. “Because it means we can’t just assume hit from above. That’s not meteor pock.”

“Maybe somewhere the Makers were bored,” she said, staring at the too-smooth resumption. “They started a thing and got called to lunch.”

“You tell Dispatch that. I’ll go warm coffee.”

She pinged their coordinate to the Markers. The transparent little rods would leap off the appropriate chute and bite and blink and the next Track team would see their memory when it reached them. Track’s words were mostly pictures and expletives and knots in rope.

The city rolled forward. The first hundred meters past a bad patch were always the longest of the day. Gnomon flowed, engines hissing, the forward trucks biting and spinning and biting again. They hit a little smear of foam mis-sprayed by Nazim and he swore into his sleeve as the truck’s ceramic shoes squealed. Then the sound passed away and it was rails, steady and simple. Spindle drank the weight of the city and sang it back.

“Track,” Dispatch said, more careful now. “Engineering will be out with you. Schedules are pushing. We’d like a sense of scope.”

“Scope?” Nazim made it sound like a swear. “Scope is a twelve-meter section where someone replaced our rails with sponge. That’s scope.”

Mara tuned them both out. She still had her palm pressed to the edge of the foam patch, to feel how it set. The lower thrumming was clearer now, not drowned in the airy roar of the wind. She found herself tapping with her thumb, an involuntary beat. Long-long-short-long. She stopped, startled. That was the pattern.

The skeleton in her mind stirred, a memory unscrolling. She’d been nine. Her mother had been on night shift in Greenhouse Four, and Mara had snuck to the Track museum, to the section of Spindle they’d amputated and set up under glass, gray and smooth and humming like a big cat. There had been an old Track recording playing on loop, something about resonance and stress profiles, and over it an audio of a weather band. In that band had been a pause and then a sequence of long and short static bursts. She’d hummed it for a week. Her teacher had told her to stop. “You’ll get it stuck,” the woman had said. “That was the old world, sweetheart.”

Long-long-short-long. She tapped the foam. The pattern came back in the rail. Not an echo—never an echo that fast. A reply.

Her mouth went dry. She looked sharply at Nazim, but he was on his own mic with Engineering, drawing imaginary diagrams in the air that meant the difference between cussing and money.

She tapped again, this time with the knuckle of her ring finger. Long-long-short-long, short-short-long.

Silence. The wind pawed the gantry. Something in the rail, deep or shy or both, grew very quiet, as if it had turned to listen. Mara felt suddenly ridiculous. She was talking to a bridge. She flexed her hand and the foam crisped under her glove. If Dispatch saw the minute count they would not thank her for playing games with her old childhood melodies.

She was halfway turned to go when the tiniest haptic in her palm—a tick, a lift of not-quite-weight—made the hair along her wrists stand up under the seal of her suit. The rail pulsed. The lattice beyond the foam, the stuff that had grown like coral and snapped like ice, shivered. The pulse repeated, not quite the rhythm she had tapped but related to it the way a whispered answer is related to a challenge.

Long. Short. Short-long.

Mara forgot to breathe. It was silly, it was dangerous, it was outside the runbook. It was also the most beautiful thing she’d felt since she learned how to gauge a storm by the taste in her mouth. She put her palm down flat again. Long-long-short-long. Short-short-long.

The reply came faster this time, and if she’d had her eyes closed she would have missed it. The lattice’s fine culms, those tiny arteries and capillaries, were not all dead. In the hollows, a fluid she could not see moved. The pale stuff stained slightly darker for a heartbeat then returned to its useless white. She should have been cold through with fear. Instead she laughed. Nazim turned.

“What?”

“Nothing,” she said. The word was high, a bubble. “Stupid. Old song in my head. Engineering wants us for a survey?”

He squinted at her. “You’ve gone weird.”

“Not today,” she said, which was a lie.

Behind them, over the wind and the engine hiss, came another sound. It rose from the city and the track and the air, not mechanical. People, a lot of them, all making the same small noise at once. Not fear yet. Surprise. Mara felt the thin bones in her wrist buzz where they touched the rail. She felt her name in the buzz and shook it off like a fly.

Dispatch’s voice went sideways. “Track—”

Then every light in her goggles scribed a message at once: All-hands. All-hands. All-hands. The display smeared, recalibrated, and there was Premiere Eyo’s face under a hood, eyes narrow against a wind she’d never been near. “We have a run out of East Khepri Sector,” the Premiere said without preamble. “We are getting a wideband from Sky Kites and K-pattern from beneath the rails. Do not cut anything you have not cut before. Mark all anomalies. Reroute public traffic from forward viewing platforms. Greenhouses secure. This is not a drill.”

Nazim whistled through his teeth.

“What’s the K-pattern?” Mara asked. She knew. Everyone knew. They used it on the old parade days when Gnomon crossed the quarter. She wanted to hear a liar.

“Founder code,” Nazim said, voice flat. “The one they carved on their coffins.”

Her mother’s story unrolled like a map and put itself over the world. Bones grew in circles. Don’t ask questions of things you’ll never meet. She put her palm to the rail again in a gesture she could pretend was balance and felt the answering tick. Not long-short now. Not the K-pattern either. It did not matter. It was still a call.

She found herself thinking, absurd and sharp and as natural as hunger: At least it wants to talk before it eats us.

“Track,” Dispatch’s voice snapped back in her ear. “Bridge segment AA-12 going soft one kilometer ahead. Visual confirms foam like yours. You’re our only team forward. Set markers. We’re going to need you fast.”

“Copy,” Mara said. Her voice had all its pieces. She flicked the wire saw closed and back into its tidy coil. She could feel the taste of the old battery in her mouth, metallic and dry.

“Nazim?” she asked.

He’s was watching her too closely. “Don’t stop,” he said.

“Don’t stop,” she echoed, and they moved, rope to rope, clip to clip, along the skin of the city that would not allow itself to pause.
