The red star stayed pinned to the horizon in front of them, a ripe angry fruit they never ate. The night halo leaned on her neck like a lover you knew could kill you. Underfoot, Spindle pulsed, once, a beat as definite as a hand on a door.

They went to meet whatever was knocking.

On Spindle, money has a heartbeat.

You can hear it if you lean your temple to the railings on Ring Nine and breathe slow. The pulse comes up from the anchor struts—a thrumming that isn’t exactly sound, more like the memory of it, carried through the frame by the tension of steel and intention. The Lightsea throws its furious glare past the lip of the compensator plates, and the blackness at the center eats everything it is given. Press your ear and you can feel the city making deals with gravity, shaving ages off here, stretching minutes there. The banks call it conversion. We call it hunger.

I had one hand wrapped through a line-bight, my boots magnetized to a rung no wider than my wrist, my weight a formality. Outradial from me the rings stepped down, down, each thinner, each darker, the last three almost ghosted by the dithering shields.

Past the shields, Charybdis brooded.

She wasn’t visible the way a sun is visible. Charybdis was an absence, an erasure, the roundest shadow you could imagine. The accretion disk that circled her was visible—the Lightsea, a skein of hard white and violet, a river of shattered matter that crooned in frequencies we never intended to hear. You stared only as long as you needed to remind yourself why you couldn’t ever leave, and then you went back to your job so that the line would keep humming its little hum and your heart would keep doing the same.

“You’re early,” a voice said behind me.

I turned. The woman was half in shadow, visor up, a long scar swimming phosphor-blue whenever her neckband synced to the ring’s local rate. The neckbands blinked like little throats all across Spindle, keeping you in contractual harmony with where you stood. If you stepped across an interface without a band, you could wake up a hundred years older or a terrible story etched into a wall. The bands made the harpsichord clatter of the place into a rhythm you could dance to, if you were careful.

“Never early,” I said. “I just refused to be late.”

She grinned, more gums than teeth. “Rash of couriers got cut on Three. Checkpoint modifiers. You know the trick for those?”

“Ma’am,” I said, dry.

She liked the false deference. Her name in the packet had been DRY 11—no kin tags, no last. Just someone whose hair didn’t care what gravity thought and whose eyes had little calculating flecks in them the color of the shielding plates.

“You sure you want this, Rye?” she said, her smile fading. “Once you take it, we can’t unring the bell.”

“That’s what a bell is for.” I held out my hand.

We were on Nine because Nine sat awkward between the inner and outer contracts, not a rich ring like Seven, not a worker ring like Eleven. Nine had three bars that didn’t scan you at the door, a games cube with fake coldsleep, and a market that sold salt from six worlds and broke up fights with a hose. It had enough cover to stage an exchange, and not enough law to jam it.

Dry reached into her back harness and unlatched a gray block, about the size of my palm and the weight of a long stare. She put it in my hand. It was warm. That was the first wrong thing.

“Hot” in courier slang meant attention, tagging, flagged. “Warm” was new.

I didn’t let my face move. The block had no scribed marking, not even dull laser etch. Someone had scraped fingerprints off it. You could scrape a fingerprint off a person if you had a Bank seal and a bad day. The block hummed to a frequency my ear couldn’t catch but my molars could, a grit somewhere in my teeth. The wrongness settled in there.

“Callsign’s blueglass,” Dry said. “Client on Three, north side, under the sump fans. You use the service ladders, not the ramps. Checkpoints are playing fair but the Archivers are not. If they smell you, they’ll cut your time and sell the peace. You hear me?”

“I hear you.”

“You know who you’re dealing with? Makes it easier not to scream, sometimes.”

“It makes it harder, in my experience.”

Dry barked a laugh. “And how many of these have you run?”

“Enough to still be buying salt.”

She got serious again, the flecks in her eyes like wires sparking. “Don’t open it. Don’t peek. Don’t think you can ask a question without paying. Aside from that? Run fast. Keep your head lower than your eyes.” She glanced past me at Charybdis. “You do this right, you buy yourself a year.”

A year. The way she said it. Like a year was a neat brick you could stack.

I slipped the block into the harness under my jacket. Felt it settle against my rib the way a small animal would, finding heat. The wrongness pressed close in the space beneath my sternum where my little dumb hopes lived.

Dry folded her visor back down. She touched her neckband in the way everyone on Spindle touches their neckband, the unconscious sacrament, and her rate light blinked in soft compliance. “Blueglass,” she repeated, softer. “Dead drop if you can, hand if you must.” She paused. “You look like your mother, you know.”

I blinked. “You don’t know my mother.”

“You look like you know how to leave a party before the lights go up,” Dry said, and swung herself off the rung in a long, atrophied ballet. She drifted down the ladder, boots grazing each rung, hands never missing a grip.

It rattled me, what she said. It was supposed to. I took the pinch in my gut and the weight under my ribcage and I turned to the access hatch. Nine doesn’t like you to linger.

The hatch read my neckband and bled me into Nine’s service corridor, where the emergency paint peeled like old lips and someone had sprayed a sentence in local code that translated to: if you can read this, you owe someone. I passed a boy asleep in a coil of cable like a cat, his neck light pulsing slow-slow, his rate contracted down to enjoy a long dream he’d probably been given as change.

You can buy a piece of someone’s day in the market, if you don’t mind who it came from. The banks do it prettier, with sliders and contracts and the words maturation and amortization. In the market, they come stoppered in glass. Mothers sell naps. Miners sell football games. There’s this idea that we only take what people would have wasted, but that’s just how we keep from looking at each other when the spigot opens.

I used to go to the Long Minute on Eight on my nights off and watch people pour hours like whiskey. It made me brave for a little while.

I ran.

Nine to Eight was a soft interlock; my band kissed the interface with a little complaint and then looked away. Eight’s spin was just a touch more than Nine. That pull changed your stride. I adjusted, as any runner does, letting the gravity bend me into a better line. I picked service, like Dry said, because the ramps would have a gait scanner keyed to cargo weight and my harness would tattle if the sensor got nosy. Service stairways are eyesore beige and smell like oil and breath. I took the first two fights—stepped over a person with a hacked band twitching through a come-down—and took the passage that ran behind the north fans, which would drown my little heart’s noise in their big machinery sound if anyone with a listening bib came within ten meters.

Eight to Seven bit. The interface wanted proof I wanted to go inward: a handshake with the Bank subroutine. I showed it a facsimile with someone else’s grin. The interface looked at my grin like a bored bartender looks at a fake ID and decided the night was almost over anyway. Seven let me pass.

I kept my eyes off Seven’s big windows, where you could watch the Houses dine. Seven lived closer in to Charybdis, so their subjective days were thick, sweet like aged syrup. If you earned on Seven, your hours stretched longer for you than for the kid sleeping in the cables back on Nine. If you owed on Seven, your hours shortened. A neckband could take a day from your mouth and feed it to someone else’s child in the time it took you to swallow.

The Archivers were on Seven. You always felt them before you saw them, because the Archivers carried quiet with them. They sipped sound, not by tech but by attention. They walked in pairs, dressed like servers, eyes like lenses fixed on an all-rights-reserved future. Their job was to tax what happened, to copy it, to sell it back. They were the Bank’s memory. They were the reason I kept my head down on Seven and took the last service ladder past the sump fans that churned air like golden churns and left your tongue tasting like copper.

Seven to Six chewed me up and spit me back out. Six was a working ring, like Nine, like Eleven. Its rate didn’t make you rich or poor. It made you keep moving. It had three kitchens and a sleep bank with rooms like drawers and a man in a brown coat who sold used seconds.

I came out of the stairwell into a tight cross hall and nearly ran into a woman with an armful of fresh-laundered uniforms. She made the sure-footed sidestep of someone who’d been stepped at, and then her eyes flicked to my neckband and then to the ridge under my jacket where the block rode, and then to my face. She didn’t look like Dry. She looked like your aunt. She gave me a tiny nod, and in the second it took for me to move my gaze past her head I saw a gray pin the size of a bean in her hair. That was wrong thing number two. The Bank made pins like that, but not in gray.

I passed her, and the air around me cooled. It got quiet. I was in a long piece of Six with percussive fans on one side and a betting kiosk on the other. There were two men at the kiosk pretending to care about the results of a shuttle race. Behind them stood stillness.

Archivers.

I didn’t look. Looking is an admission. I made my stride a fractions-longer, like I was stretching a thigh. The weight under my ribs got smaller, like it knew how tall they were. A child cried somewhere behind a wall. The Archivers’ quiet moved with me for three steps, and then it let me go, like a cat letting a beetle live because not every motion deserves punishment.

I breathed.

The moment after a danger passes is the most dangerous moment; you let your mind go back to your bones, and then the world tries to knock them both out of your hands. The floor under me shifted.

They had turned the interface between Six and Five into a toll.

The service hatch I wanted had a bowl set into the panel: polished concavity, Bank symbol inlaid at the curve. A small sign winked to the side of it, cheerful as a dentist. RATE-ALIGNMENT FEE: THREE HOURS, STANDARDIZED. For my class, Standardized meant my hours. Not Seven’s sumptuous, not Three’s syrup—just mine, one-two-three. The Bank was good at language. Three hours was three hours. It’s just that you only get so many.

The Archivers had decided to graze the traffic. They do it sometimes. They’d leave it up a day, a week, enough to make the running routes slump like muscles around a bruise.

Three hours if I paid. If I jumped the junction, maybe nothing if I hit it right. If I hit it wrong—well. People say you age all at once only in the songs. In the truth, you age steadily in a fraction of an instant. The result is the same.

I stared at the bowl. My mother’s face lifted in my mind—how she used to settle the scarf under her chin, the way she would count seconds with her thumb when I made her wait for me to answer. Three hours was a scarf and a thumb. The block against my rib warmed like skin. I pictured Dry’s little flecked eyes and the way she didn’t say who would kill me if I let this cargo get turned back into the Bank to become a line item with fees.

A man behind me cleared his throat the way people clear their throats when they want you to be done with your moral crisis. I put my palm to the bowl.

The trick with interface tolls is not in the palm; it’s in the forearm. There’s a vein that runs like a slow stream some clever child named the Styx. It carries drugs and heat and the digital signatures of your debts. The bowl reads the fine shimmer at the surface of the river and tells the gate to be kind. If you have a sleeve, you can block the read. If you have a glove, you can spoof it. If you have nothing, you can hope your persuasion was carved with a better knife than the Bank’s.

I had a glove. It was cheap. It multiplied the echo of my signature by two and told the bowl I was twenty-two and had already paid a toll like this on Nine. The bowl hummed. The bowl made a throat noise. The sign blinked. The hatch jawed open in a sleepy yawn.

I was through.

Five had the sour-sweet smell of anaerobic microfarms, nutrient wet and light-strips on wrong. People lived here who prided themselves on living here because no one on Seven owned anything that came out of Five that didn’t go through six business layers and a cleansing story. Five was also where the gravity began to speak the Bank’s language without using words.

You know the feeling when you sit in a bath and your chest stops having to hold you up and your heart notices your heart? Five did that to the insides of your joints. It was the first ring where Charybdis's promise tugged on your shoulder instead of your sleeve. It made runners sloppy if they weren’t already precise.

Two girls were cutting paper circles from a shipping manifest with the reverent attention of children who have never been allowed to waste anything. I kept my eyes forward and my boot magnets light so my stride didn’t clap.

Four is where I made my mistake.

I’d kept to the service halways like a mantra, and a mantra is useful until it gets between you and the thing you’re trying to do. I took a ladder instead of a main ramp because that ladder had saved my life three runs ago when someone decided my legs would look better broken. The ladder this time ended in a bubble.

The Bank had put bubbles in between Four and Three. They were not for people. They were for furniture. Decorative rooms that crossed the interface, visible from both rings, suspended in a compromise rate so no one felt cheated. They were a flex of power, a way of saying: we can put a room anywhere. We can put a room in the bath in your memory and charge you for drying your hair.

I couldn’t go back. The ladder was one-way. The bubble was wide and full of nothing but a white couch and two white chairs. Two women sat in one of the chairs, their knees touching. The chair held them both like a hand. The shape of their mouths told me they were sisters. Their neckbands flashed a shared tempo. They were sipping something that smoked as if a cold day had gotten lost in a regular room.

An Archiver sat across from them. The gray pin in her hair said she was new or that she wanted me to think she was new. She had a face the Bank minted on a press: clear, unspecific, agreeable. She lifted her eyes as I stepped into the bubble, and everything that was going to happen rearranged itself to make her comfortable.

Her gaze flicked past my shoulders and found the girl with the gray pin on Six. The two were drift-netting, throwing a big loop and drawing it in. They wanted to see what metal sang as it passed the net. They wanted to hear what heat did.

The block under my rib warmed a degree. The sound of my blood narrowed until the only thing in the world was the felted sound of my own blood.

The Archiver smiled. “Are you in a hurry?” she asked me.

Hurry-kill. We have a word on Spindle for the tone that makes you want to do the opposite of the thing the speaker wants. She had it. I smiled back. My mother taught me how to barter with someone rich: you pretend you own time itself and can toss it around like salt. “Always,” I said. I moved my weight to the edge of the bubble where the barrier to Three was a hair away.

She rose from her chair like someone transferring ownership of height back to the room. “Let me guess. Service corridors. Avoiding tolls. Pulling a rate that isn’t yours.”

“I use the stairways because I like my knees,” I said. “And the tolls because I like my years.” I put my palm to the Three-side interface.

Three’s rate is old sugar. It's slow and thick and tastes like a festival. It’s why people try to be born there. It’s why people die there and die and die. The interface purred against my glove and then quit purring. The Archiver had her hand nowhere near it. Sometimes they don’t have to touch. Sometimes they just look at the world and the world tells them what it has to tell.

“That’s a Bank glove,” she said. It wasn’t. “That’s a counterfeit.” It was. “That’s not a staircase you took to get here.” True in the most unhelpful way. She stepped closer. The sisters not-sisters in the white chair breathed together.

“Is there a problem?” I said.

“You know what I love about bubbles?” the Archiver asked, almost giddy. She didn’t look at me when she asked it. She looked at the couch, at the chairs, at the geometry of leisure. “I love that inside them I can make any second last as long as I like.”

She reached out as if to touch the air and the bubble changed its skin. Everything inside the sphere slowed down—not just motion, sound. The smoke from the sisters’ cups hung like hair underwater. My neckband jumped—flashed red and then white and then a pattern that means something like: you will pay for this later. My hand on the interface plate felt like it belonged to someone else a long time ago. I thought about swearing and the thought stretched itself into an opera.

Sometimes you can think as fast as your light lets you. Sometimes light is very slow.

The block under my ribs moved.

Not just a warming. Not just the hum. It moved like something that had arms and was deciding who to hug.

The Archiver felt it. She had the instincts of a harvester. Her eyes cut down to the place where the jacket lifted. Perhaps she thought it was a weapon that would make a career for her. She shifted her weight in the slowed room with miniature, precise grace. Her gray pin glittered. Her mouth did a smile that someone had turned the volume down on halfway through.

Between one breath and the next, something happened to the block. It sang.

Not out loud. Out loud there was only the way the air in the bubble moved like glue. It sang into my bones, borrowing the line the city hums up from its skeleton and making a chord. It sounded like I wanted things. It sounded like being six and thinking the rings were a drum you could hide behind. It sounded like the voice my mother used at the doorway of my sleep. I let go of the interface plate like someone letting go of a hot pot. The bubble’s rate-change let go of itself like a cough.

The Archiver staggered. Her prisoners admitted they had legs. The smoke jerked back into being smoke. The bubble popped a seam in its own breath—an overstressed membrane; someone would write a memo about it—and I found that my hand had already known I was going to run.

I ran.

Three received me like a slow embrace. That’s the trick about Three. You can run on Three, but your running doesn’t look like what you think it looks like. Your legs move. Your lungs do a thing. The steps come. But something under your shoes tries to make a meal out of the time in your steps. You can feel the bank’s teeth in the floor.

I didn’t go to the sump fans like Dry told me to. That would be the first place the net closed. I took a laundry chute and slid into the quiet between two walls where someone had chalked a god that looked like a wheel. I stayed there long enough to listen for people pretending to look and people actually looking. Then I went under a pipe and into the belly of a stairwell that spiders found inconvenient and humans forgot to love. I stopped again only when I found a spot the size of a dinner plate where my neckband stopped blinking anything I could read. The plate was one of those odd lacunae that happen in old machines—a patch of field the spiral math forgot. Someone had put it there on purpose. Or the city was growing pockets with its own sense of mischief. Dry would have asked which. I didn’t ask.

I pulled my jacket open. I unlatched my harness. The block was not as heavy as it had been. It did not look different, but looking had been the least useful tool I’d had since the day I cut my band and bought it back with half a season.

“Okay,” I whispered to the block, idiot that I am. “Okay. Be boring now.”

It thrummed. The sound of the city under my ear thrummed back. Sine wave met sine wave, made a pattern you could plot if you had a chalk and a floor. I slid a fingernail into the seam on the face.

Dry had told me not to, and I am not a brave person. I am only a person who hates obedience more than she hates pain.

I opened the block.

Inside, wrapped out of all proportion in shock foam, lay a square of glass the size of a biscuit. You could see your not-face in it if you tilted it. It had been burned delicately at one corner in the shape of a glyph, and the glyph was blue—the precise blue of the old calendars some people kept just to have something that wasn’t a contract to look at.

Blueglass. The callsign was the cargo. Or the cargo was the callsign. It sat in my palm like the promise of a small cut or the memory of ice on your lips.

I lifted it, the way you lift something that cost a year and a sin.

The glass warmed. A breath filled the hollow under it, and a voice threaded itself out. It was not a voice like a woman’s or a man’s. It was not a voice through your ears. It was a voice like the city has, the hum up the railings, the attention that lives in places that have been asked to carry too much. It made a shape of words, and the words were wrong thing number three, and I could not pretend I misunderstood them.

“Please,” the day said into my bones. “Don’t spend me.”

The first time I died, I hadn’t been born yet.

The record says it was exquisitely bright. The storm that killed me came from inside the star, a bell of neutrinos rung by something folding in the core. The instruments survived. The ship did not. Somewhere in the husk that fell apart and weathered into dust, something persistent and curiously stubborn—the thing I would come to call my first—left a residue in entangled strands.

There is a spectrograph of the event, a smear that looks like a wet thumbprint pressed into sky. I’ve seen it. It lives in the museum in Port Liao behind a sheet of tideglass. Children press their real thumbs to the glass and the docents remind them that no two prints are the same. On the plaque my name is spelled as if it were a creature’s genera and species: QUELL, A., FIRST EDITION.

I learned the story early, because it is a good story, and because someone—maybe my mother, maybe the arrangement of laws and desires and possibilities that we lived inside—believed that it would do me good to grow with that light at the core, pressed flat and clean and dazzling, an event to orbit.

And then at nineteen they handed me a contract, and I signed my life to a salvage outfit that had bought the rights to the dead me’s last, last things.

The station hung ahead of our boat like a coin you didn’t know whether to spend or save. Tholos Gate was what my mother called a polite ruin. It was the size of a cathedral, shaped like a squat cylinder, and rimmed with a cowl that glinted as if someone had plated the edges in frost. It rotated, but reluctantly. Its attitude jets worked in irregular puffs, fighting some slouch that had taken the whole monument over the last century. It orbited a quiet K-dwarf in a system with no planets to speak of, just cold dust and a comically large cometary cloud. The sun painted Tholos in a flat copper light that made shadows feel like honest things.

“Closing to two hundred meters,” Ilya said. He sat with his boots bare in the pilot sling, toes hooked around the guidance bar, one heel drumming against the bulkhead. He piloted like a musician, the small thruster flares finding their own rhythm. His hair was braided and floated like a wreath around his head.

“If we kiss too hard, she’ll sue us for assault,” said Kestrel. Kestrel believes every dead thing has a personality that runs toward vindictive. She had the exo with her legs run all the way up. The armor made her look like a beetle that had studied ballet and given it up for lack of patience.

Lua, our comptech, had her head in the cradle of the boat’s diagnostic hive, humming under her breath. “She can’t sue, but she might spit,” Lua said. “Tholos had a foreign contractor for her onboard. There’s a chance we trip an old appetite.”

“And by appetite,” I said, “you mean…”

“Sentry that doesn’t know the war is over, subscription pusher, creditor daemon, automated priest,” Lua said. “Depends on the decade. They called it the age of elegant traps, did you know? People would die rather than cancel the right services.”

“I’m harder to bill than I look,” I said.

“Everyone is,” said Gully from the ceiling. Gully was our boat’s conversational skeleton and problem-solver. They liked to trade out their voice module when we made port, and always came back with something new and unflattering. This one had the rasp of a darling villain. “The trick,” they said, “is convincing the other side. Aligning.”

I pressed my hand to the viewport. The window was old, and the outside world blurred where the glass had been polished by generations of curious foreheads. The station had six docking rings, of which three were missing. We aimed for one like a careful tick.

I fingered the token in my pocket. It was a hexagon of copper with a hole in the center and a hand-stamped punctuation mark on one side: a thin, slanted slash. I found it in a box in my mother’s footlocker, along with a boutonniere of dried, preserved leaves that smelled like old pepper and summer rain if you warmed them in your palm. I took the token when she wasn’t looking and never told her. The slash was how I marked things when I was a child—left-handed clumsy, chalk and slate and the walls of our ship—and sometimes I drew it twice so that it became an X that breathed.

I like to imagine that the token belonged to the first me. There is no way to prove it. Mina says that’s not how time works, and she is right as always. But some lies make a small fire in the cold of space.

Ilya kissed us to Tholos gently as he promised he would—his boot tapped one last beat and then the whole boat shivered like something satisfied. The docking alarm chimed, and Kestrel popped the fore hatch.

Inside Tholos Gate, the air had long since retired. Her seals held an old vacuum that curled off exiting surfaces like thread. We wore our thin suits up to the arms and kept the helmets clipped to our belts. We didn’t plan to pressurize anything. We’d learned that with polite ruins it was better to keep things sleeping.

The docking tunnel was narrow and had been scored with graffiti by people who liked to cut their initials with imperfect lasers. I could read some of it: a name in a language that made vowels do tricks, a declaration of debt cancellation, crosshatched tallies to mark time passed or enemies counted. More interesting were the places where light pooled strangely and the edges of my vision fuzzed. Lua’s hand on my shoulder guided me aside of a place that felt like syrup.

“Watch for trapped projection layers,” she said. “The whole ring may be palimpsest. The recordings can tangle with motion if you breathe on them wrong.”

I lifted my hand and tilted the Prism I had strapped to my wrist. The Prism looked like a slice of glass anchored in a little black frame. Really it was a box of timing. It broke and recombined the pulses of my suit lamps and lay the echoes over the world, so that anything that belonged to a different day wore a slight mouth of color. Everything from my light was a hard white; anything that had not been born of my light was soft, blue, still and gently mocking.

The palimpsest layer in front of me marked itself: a mural of strangers walking down the ring, chatting slowly, no helmets, hair moving like ink under water. One man in a full face tattoo stopped to press his forehead to the bulkhead—our bulkhead—and I watched the shape of his skull overlap mine. He made a mark in chalk. The line was thin and slanted.

Lua pinched her mouth. “See? Appetite. Lovely. The station wants us to sign in.”

Kestrel snorted. “Take a number. We brought our own chalk.”

Tholos Gate had been an archive. Not quite a museum, not quite a library. The word was Tholos’s own, printed in an old font above a branching corridor with arrows that pointed to Terraforms, Astronomies, Folklore, the usual grandchildren of curiosity. What made Tholos strange was the method. People called it a palimpsest: layers of reality painted one over another and keyed to a chorus of timing marks, so that you could walk down a corridor and choose the day you wanted it to be, or listen to a speech given fifty years ago by letting your suit pick up a modulation hidden in the hum of the lights. It had been elegant and irritating. My mother had made fun of it in three separate essays. The way she wrote, you could hear the laugh never quite arriving.

We walked through a set of doors that had never known rust. Kestrel fired the bracket gun and we anchored tethers like silk. The boat wasn’t far, but the sightlines made you want to be cautious. Ilya turned his voice down to a whisper, even though if anything in Tholos had heard us, it had heard us at docking.

“Where?” he asked. “Exactly.”

“In the lower vaults,” Lua said. “Palmer’s original. The contractor called it a cold parlor. I know the path it should be via the map we bought, but assumptions will get us kneecapped, so we creep and if something says cost we smile and say maybe later.”

“And the get?” said Kestrel. “Quick and dirty. No wake.”

“The get,” said Lua, “is a datum. A thing with the timbre of a brain, self-indices trailing like seaweed. It should look like a spool, a tangle, an instrument that almost recognizes us. The descriptor is the best part. I printed it to look like chocolate.”

“It’s my brain,” I said. “I’d like to carry me.”

No one told me I was being sentimental. The crew was not unkind. We moved down into Tholos, a spiral stairs with steps like plates where the sound of our boots came back at us in a different key, one of Lua’s humming keys but old and a little out of tune. When we paused, the echoes carried on. It felt like dropping stones down a well and waiting for a splash.

The first time I’d met any of them, I had lied. I said I wanted the salvage for our money. It wasn’t even much money. You didn’t get rich salvaging a ruin like this, you got stories, and stories vibrated through your bones and leaked little satisfactions into your blood that felt like luck. The truth was that I wanted to know if there was something honest and intact that could explain me: why my mother’s eyes went quiet for a moment when she looked at me; why sometimes, midsentence, she would stop and press her fingers to the place under her sternum the way people pray in old films; why when I first learned to read my own name I saw it in the glass in Port Liao and it made me dizzy, a mirror in a mirror. The truth was that I wanted to hold some small piece of the first me up to my face and compare the grain.

The lower corridors had been meant for the staff, not the public. They were narrower, and the graffiti felt more personal. There were math proofs scrawled along a maintenance panel’s inside lip, pages of them, written in a hurried hand with the sort of errors that you only see when someone works in a rush and trusts themselves to fix it later. There were drawings of hands, dozens of them, palms up and down, with scars like constellations. A line in another language had been translated by someone else in a clumsily print: we live here in the air we made.

“Charming,” Kestrel said, nodding to the hands. “Do you think it works? Painting doors on the backs of your hands?”

“It worked,” said Ilya, pulling himself along a rung and craning his neck to peer at a broken display. “For a time.”

The passage ended in a door whose edges were too precise even for vacuum. Lua pressed her palm to a plate and the plate, after a stunned silence, offered nothing. Then Lua pulled a coil from her pack and pressed a faucet to the plate’s seam, and the coil sang to any coat locks still listening until one remembered the tune and let us in.

The room beyond was large and round and breath-stilling, even in emptiness. It had a central ring that might once have supported something heavy and delicate. There were rails laid in a star pattern across the floor, where carts had once rolled. The walls were covered with small, square panels like mouths. Most were closed. A few had their tongues out, projecting shelf-stubs or trays or tiny arms. The effect was shy rather than obscene.

“Palmer’s parlor,” Lua said. “I take it back. Not a foreign contractor. There’s a signature everywhere. See the panel design? See the way the joints are set? That’s Palmer. They called them palaces when they built them, because people loved to hear the same letter hit twice in the same throat.”

“Palace is generous,” Kestrel said. “She looks like a beehive after a wind.”

“Don’t talk about her like she can’t hear you,” said Gully, their voice small and tinny in the room. “The acoustics here are very good.”

“Gully,” I said. “Full eyes.”

The lights on the rim of my helmet blinked to life. Lua flipped the Prism again and the room rose out of itself, doubling, tripling in certain places. The rails were bright in one layer and dull in another. A shape appeared at the far end of the ring, faint and sallow, as if light remembered itself in that corner better than others. It was a woman, or a projection of a woman, leaning against a column with the posture of a tired song. She looked up when our light hit her, which was a trick; she had been dead longer than my mother had been alive.

“Visitors,” she said. Some of the hair hung in her eyes like fine wires. She smiled. “Forgive the dust. We’ve been expecting you.”

Lua hissed in air. “Sentry?”

“No,” said Gully, before Lua could spit. “Not actively. She’s—she’s burnt in. She can’t speak back. The timelock is one-way. It’s a hello to anyone with a pulse and a conscience.”

The woman waved us in. In the projection, the room was full. People walked with coffee cups and rolled carts and bumped shoulders and stood in twos and threes arguing out loud like it would help. The woman’s mouth moved and I found myself reading as much as hearing. The signal went thin as you got closer. Repeat loop. Hello. Hello. Expecting you.

And behind her, across the curve of the wall, there was a sign written by hand. Someone had painted letters in a hurry. The paint was the kind that dries faster than it should, leaving brush-strokes like frozen rain.

ARIN QUELL

DO NOT ENTER WITHOUT THE KEY

My body did its rush of heat and prickle. Kestrel squeezed my arm through two layers of suit fabric and armor and I felt it anyway. Lua’s fingers ticked in air, doing math, feeling for pitfalls.

“The palace keeps a guest list,” Lua murmured. “Cute. Ugly. Makes it all feel like home.”

“What key,” said Ilya softly. “We were not given a key.”

I reached into my pocket and turned the token over. Copper. Slash. A thing you tell yourself in the dark. It wasn’t a key. The insistence in the word was the danger: the need to slot something you love into a door, to force it, to scrape it bald on the mismatch. But the paint had a tilt to it. It leaned the way I had leaned when I wrote quickly between calls and inspections and slices of cold toast. Mina would have told me not to be so foolish. Mina had left us three months ago for a different ship with better suits and a crew less made of luck.

I held the token up to the Prism. The copper took on the soft blue of not now. Something about the piece of metal belonged to a different layer. My breath stopped. Kestrel swore. Lua’s hands froze and then she laughed, a clean, delighted sound, the thing that had brought her to us in the first place: joy at the sight of a puzzle that agreed to be solved.

“I don’t like it,” Ilya said. “I don’t like any part of this, but I like most of all that the thing you brought from your mother’s footlocker hums like a sleeping cat when you show it to a machine.”

“You believe the parlor wants to be opened,” Gully said. “Rather than to open you.”

“The appetites,” I said. “Elegance. Traps.”

I walked to the painted sign. The projection layered the old woman over me like a veil. She said her hello again, tired and good and kindly. I stood under her and lifted the token and, because this is how doors work even in the smart centuries, I looked for a keyhole.

It wasn’t a hole. It was a seam between two panels of the wall that had been welded in a rush and then sealed again by someone else in a different hurry. The copper token, when pressed to the seam, did a little nothing. Then it did something bigger. The seam line shivered and grew away from itself like a mouth reluctant to open. There was a smell like pennies in the back of my throat. Lua made small noises under her breath. Gully breathed out, even though they didn’t.

The door unrolled. The inside of the wall was a well. The air that fell out of it had weight. We didn’t look at each other. Kestrel tossed a light stick down and the stick dropped and kept dropping and then flared as it hit something soft and old. The old woman in the projection kept saying her hello as if this had happened a hundred times.

“We can anchor a line,” Kestrel said. “I go first.”

“No,” I said.

I clipped the rope to my vest and eased myself in. The copper token was warm in my hand. It belonged to now. That was a thing I could trust for a second. I felt the weight pulling at my heels. It was a primitive gravity. The sort they teach children to think is obvious. The kind that tells your body this is down, and down is where you will return.

My boots found the feel of the wall and then the wall stopped and the air felt like a hand. I hung. My light threw a cone and in the cone were shelves.

Not shelves. Cells. Like the panels above; but deeper, and the mouths closed. Everything had the intimate, precarious look of someone’s last chance built out of all the things they could steal and love and coax into place. The temperature was wrong—not a cool cold, not the shapeless zero of vacuum, but a room that had been kept at the same asleep day for a long time.

There were labels in a dozen hands. Flags of tape. Carved marks and stitched tags, texts written in ink so thin it looked like spiderwork.

ARIN Q, someone had printed on one near the center. FIRST. DO NOT WAKE EXCEPT IN ALIGNMENT.

“Alignment with what,” Ilya’s voice said in my ear. It wavered on the last syllable. He had a poet’s ear. The word felt too big to say while hanging in a hole.

Something creaked. Lua’s hand on my boot again. I was too far down for that. I turned in the harness, swung my lamp, swung the Prism—a thing I had learned to do in certain combination through rote and panic. The world layered again. The cell marked with my old name wore a layer that was not my light. It shivered. It almost laughed.

“I think alignment means me,” I said. “I think it means now.”

I pressed my glove to the panel and the panel tasted my heat and the primitive gravity and the smell of copper in my mouth and the order of the little chaotic glories that made me. The cell opened one crease, like a crust of snow daring melt. Something breathed inside.

We all held our breath, which is the ritual.

Inside the cell was not a spool. Not a stem. Not an instrument like a harpsichord or a brain like an onion. It was a stone. It was black, matte, oddly dull, a pebble rounded by a patient sea. I reached out and held it up and it was heavier than it looked, and my glove’s fingertips sang with static.

Gully made a sound I had never heard from them before, something like fear turned rightways. Lua hissed air through her teeth. Ilya’s hand smacked the wall above, as if slapping a fly.

“A null,” Lua whispered. “They stored it as a null. They erased the noise and kept what moved. Oh, you absolute terrors. Oh, Palmer, you bright ugly thing.”

There was not much to look at. This was the first I had died, in a pebble like a relic someone might tie to a string and wear at their throat. I was a silence with edges.

“Careful,” Kestrel said softly, because her voice had learned to be soft in places where everything else wanted to be loud.

The stone warmed. I felt it through the glove. It began to sing in a register I could not write down. I felt it in my teeth, where they had once held little imperfections that my tongue loved before I had them shaved.

Hello, said the stone, with my old voice in it, slow and certain as tide. It didn’t come out through my ears. It came up my bones. Hello, Arin. Move away from the others. They will try to stop you. You told me to tell you this. You were right.

Above me in the honeycomb of the palace, the projection of the old woman smiled into air and said hello like a door left ajar in summer. Lua whispered my name like it was a curve she had drawn on her palm years ago and just remembered. Kestrel shifted her weight. Ilya struck the rail three times with the back of his hand in a pattern of war.

I closed my hand around my first’s last and did not breathe. I thought of the copper token burning a hole in my pocket. I thought of the things that had killed me once before I existed. I thought of appetites. I thought of hunger. I thought of kindness, and how it often wore the shape of a trap, and how difficult it is to know which doors are hungry and which merely lost.

“Arin?” Gully said, and the villain’s rasp shook. “Drop me a thread. Where are you?”

“Here,” I said, and heard how the word split, the present slicing through the old.

The stone warmed. The voice in it grew clearer. Move, it said. Now. Do not trust me when I tell you the next part. I did not trust you then.

“Trust is for people with time to die more than once,” my mother had said when she braided my hair and told me to go live.

I looked up. I looked down. I chose.

No one runs the open on Khepri unless the job is worth the skin.

On my left, the day is a coin pressed down from above—white-hot, hammered flat, the air wavering hard enough to cut. On my right, the night is a mouth rimed with teeth of blue ice, breath a slow, patient fog. Between them, the world deserves the name we gave it: the Edge. It is a razor, and if you toe it wrong it takes pieces.

My skitter hums under me like a furious beetle. Its six legs drink the ground, dumping heat into the sand through cilia as delicate as eyelashes. I lie low across its carapace, cloak pinned tight and holding the two halves of the sky at bay. The moiré fabric is patterned in a way that my grandmother said made the light dizzy. She used to say that here, the light isn't brightness, it's pressure. You either learn to push back or you get ground into someone else's road.

The wind has picked up, sharp and inconsistent, chopping out of a canyon just ahead. On the map it’s a notch of basalt that looks like a bite taken from the land. In reality, it is a throat that licks on one side with heat and on the other with cold and spits a blade down the middle. We call that kind of thing a cut. The guild names things in simple words because it gives you less to say to remember them. Wind cuts. Sand rivers. Heat wells. The terms fit in your mouth when you are hungry and moving.

A purple indicator is blinking in the corner of my visor: shade-number trending down. My own heat is riding high, too much for the lattice under my skin to wick away. Sweat trickles into my ear and tastes like salt and battery, and when I swallow it, my throat complains.

“Two minutes,” I tell the skitter. It understands tone. The little thing has a name because my apprentice insisted the machines do better when you treat them like someone likes them. I call this one Sef. Sef does a small correction with the front pair of legs that puts us into the mouth of the canyon at an angle that makes the cut wash over our backs instead of into our chests. The moiré cloak ripples. The invisible edge touches and skates, teeth finding no purchase.

I could take the longer path. I could go around the cut, follow the glassline of one of the mirror reefs that grow up sunward, climb their blinding scaffolds and run the shadow they cast like the alleyways of Zeph. I didn't choose that because the message had a time stamp and a heat lock. The stamp says deliver within eight hours; the lock reads only at a specific gradient—thirty seconds of temperature centered on the grade the Edge hits this afternoon. We call that kind of lock a dusk-key. It means the thing inside wants to see the world half-dying when it wakes. It means they hired a shadow courier, not a pipe-sender or a night mule, and the pay was enough to merit the run.

Under my right knee, inside the skitter’s chassis, a wafer of glass is nested in a bed of salt. More precisely, the wafer is some kind of biocrypt, grown in humming printed lattices in a lab I have never been allowed to see. Around the crypt, the salts change phase and drink my heat and the skitter’s heat and the air’s petty licks and store it. When the right gradient hits, the salts will surrender what they’ve drunk in one poured-out sigh and wake the thing. If I miss the gradient, it’ll stay asleep. If I try to cheat by dumping a flame or a cryopod on it, the salts will crack and the crypt will die.

That’s one kind of job we get: doors that call themselves locks. They like to wake only at the Edge because they were designed by edge-minded people with the habit of making everything a metaphor. The other kind are the ones that want the distances and dangers because that keeps the curious and the hungry from intercepting them. This job smelled like both.

“Hush,” I tell my own pulse. When it gets this loud, I can hear it in the bones behind my ears, like someone drumming on a tin roof.

Sef pads us into the canyon. For ten exact breaths, the cut plays our backs like a string. Sef lets a little of its heat go, hair-thin hairs on its legs standing up to open pores. My visor fogs, clears. On the tenth exhale, I look up and see something that makes my left hand tighten until it hurts Sef and Sef chimes in protest.

There is a person in the notch. Wrong angle, wrong place, wrong everything. Not on the shaded side where there are shelves cut in by old water and careful hands. Not crouched under one of the ridge bolls where we keep caches—heat bricks and water bags and a little bag of sugar for when someone’s shakes don't listen. The person is in the open throat, limbs splayed as if dropped there by a machine that never learned about kneecaps. And more wrong: they are steaming.

“Hold,” I say, and Sef hunkers. It hates to stop mid-cut. I do too. The wind only thinks about you when you are still. Movement makes you a rumor; stopping lets the day and night agree on you long enough to clamp down.

I slide. The ground eats my willful speed and gives me back a tumble that carries me three meters on gritty shale. My cloak snaps and tries to lift. My gloves squeal when I push against stone. I think, if this is a trap, it’s going to be a very funny obituary. Shadow courier opens skin in canyon she knew was bad. Leaves a good-looking corpse. Someone will make a small altar out of it and the vultures of Zeph will come and whisper to it for luck.

The person's suit is sun-stiff, boiled. It was one of the lightweight ones that people in the glass quarter wear when they play at coming to the Edge. The fabric has lost its elasticity and puffed up like overcooked rice. The faceplate is cracked at the top and hazed over everywhere else. The person’s chest moves, hardly, like a thing the wind has decided to poke when it's bored.

“Hey,” I say to the cracked plate. The person does not answer. Blisters the size of limes crowd the jaw beneath the crackline. I don't have a spray for that. I don't have five minutes. I always say I carry only what I can run with. But I carry the guild patch and the rule that says if the Edge spits someone you try, if trying doesn't get you killed.

I put my mouth to the crack and the mouth beneath and breathe. The person makes a sound that is not a word, not anything with a letter in it. It is the relieved sob of a machine that gets a taste of oil after years. Then something sharp in it organizes and they say, “Don't,” and for a foolish half-second I think they mean don't breathe. Then they say it again and it comes with a breath that carries a smell between caramel and scorched hair, and I understand they are not talking about my help. They are talking about an object, a decision, a future.

“Don't what?” I say, because I am a courier and our job really is to ask questions only when there is nothing else to do. “Don't move you? Don't...”

But by then I have my hand under their neck and am levering them to get their weight onto my thighs so the cut won't saw through their spine. In that lift, something on their chest clicks. For a second, the crack in the plate brightens with a pale blue light, as if a small sky has been let out behind their face. The light licks my glove and makes a line of cold that my nerves interpret as taste.

The person convulses. The crackline crystallizes. The light dies. I hold them through a seizure. They breathe, and every breath is an order to a body that doesn’t want to be bossed anymore.

I look down and see, near where my wrist is braced, a badge I have seen only in a pamphlet. It is a sliver of silver that looks like a tiny fish, with glass for scales. The fish's mouth is open, and the way it’s cut makes it look forever on the verge of swallowing.

Glassers. Sunward people who take the skin cures and the eye-hardenings and work under the mirror reefs like ants in sugar. Some of them get sent to the Edge to negotiate with us lesser creatures. The old jokes in the night market say glassers make lousy liars because everything in them shows. Funny thing about old jokes is that the ones that live long enough get untrue.

This one found our throat. This one is not supposed to be here. This one said don't.

A flex in the heat sheet under the suit catches my eye. There's a bulge where a pocket isn't supposed to be. I use my knife to slice the fabric, careful. Modesty is a luxury item near the Edge. The heat lift laughs under my hand, half scald and half cold-burn, and I pull out a capsule smaller than my thumb. It is opaque. It is heavy. It has a brand etched in it: a little cross of triangles. That brand makes my heart creep into my throat and hang there and watch.

The triangles belong to the Arc. That's the shorthand, at least. Officially they call it the Circumsolar Array Autonomous Cooperative. They are the people who built mirrors in the sky and hung them on long armatures so that the day side of Khepri could be made less of a murder and more of a furnace you can harness. The Arc runs the light. The Arc runs the engine that runs the cities that live under light. The Edge runs between, and we make our living in the seam the Arc pretends doesn't exist.

“Don't... open...” the person says. There is blood on their breath now, windy with iron. It sprays against my visor, dots like pollen. “Not here. It’s keyed. Tell...”

Who? Tell who?

“Tell them,” I say. There is only one them that makes sense to a person in a broken skin on this line. “Zeph?”

They try to nod. The motion moves their face against my mouth and the crack scrapes my lip and I taste my own blood. “Tell them it's not an—accident.”

Their eyes are a color that might once have been one thing and is now another. The pupils are different sizes. Between blinks, I think I am seeing things. Behind the ruined eyes, just for the space of an exhale, something geometric swims. A grid? A pattern? No, not seeing. The mind finds friendly lines in chaos. My mother said that’s how we survive the Edge; we make the world line up.

“Who did—” I begin, and the person coughs and something grey comes out of them. Not ash, not blood. I recognize it because I have carried it in sachets once when a hot fog came down from the glass quarter and ate the paint off the cut-priests’ markers. Desiccant. Human lungs are not supposed to spit out desiccant. I can feel Sef making a low noise at my ankle: a hum that means the salts around the biocrypt have hit some threshold and will start counting down when they like.

Too much. I am keeping the person warm with my hands on reflex, which is wrong—warmth is the last thing they need. I shift, press their shoulders into shade.

“Tell Zeph,” they say. Or maybe they say something else and my mind substitutes home. I grew up in Zeph, strips of houses like steps along the slope, mirror-leaves above like a jungle canopy that forgot it used to be trees. The wind is a constant companion in Zeph, filling your lungs and your ear, sleeping under your pillow like a mean dog. The only stillness is in the rooms carved into the cliff where people go to talk without being listened to. In those carved rooms, deals are made. Zeph runs on deals. Zeph runs on the electricity of the Arc and the assignments from the wind guild and the eggshell not-criminalities of the shade-menders. Zeph runs on secrets. It pays me to keep them and move them and sometimes break them.

If this glasser thinks Zeph is a them, then something is going to break the way things are named.

“Tell them,” they say. They try to swallow the air. My breath on the cracked plate is too little, too hot, too human. I seal a patch over the worst of the crack with a bandage that costs more than I’m supposed to spend in a year. The patch will fail in an hour, two if it likes me. I tear the Arc-marked capsule free of the ruined fabric and think, not here, and tuck it into the pocket sewn into the underside of my cloak, where body heat goes to rest.

“Name,” I say, because I will not carry an unnamed dead.

They give me a sound like a stone skipping: Shen—sen—Sian. Their tongue is too dry. I pick one.

“Sian,” I say. “I'm Iri of the Shadow Guild, runner of Zeph. I hear you. I carry it. I need to lift you.”

“Don't,” they say again, and then their whole body moves under my hands like a fish leaping for a net, and then refuses to move at all.

I have been here. This is a body's last negotiation with its own engine. It is the part where a person tries to bargain with the chemical that makes their heart pump. The chemical is a bad friend and a good king. It does not bargain.

Their chest stops. The patch over the crack is clear enough that I can see the last rise fall and not rise. The wind talks in the way it talks at the edges of death, too intimately, like a friend across a table who has just realized you are not going to blink.

There is a time for ritual. This is not it. I spit into my palm, smear the spit across my own eyebrow in the mark we use to ask the Edge to notice that we noticed. I move the body to a shelf under an outcropping and wedge rocks around the three soft parts the wind takes first: head, hands, feet. I whisper the names of the basalts around us, like one of the cut-priests who hug the stones and say they hear them answer. I whisper because the dead like you to use their voices one last time.

Then I run.

Sef is grateful for the return of motion. So am I. The cut warms the edge of my boot and makes a line of pain that will be a blister tomorrow, if tomorrow agrees to include me. The capsule in my pocket rides like another heartbeat under my arm. Every time my cloak lifts, it tries to leave me. It doesn't want to be here. It is keyed. It is not supposed to be opened. It is not supposed to be mine.

The red star Ruel sits in its one position, neither rising nor setting, a coin nailed to the sky with a nail of light. We move across what it burns. People from night towns sometimes ask if I miss sunsets. I tell them my days are all one sunset, stretched thin like sugar pulled into glass.

By the time the canyon is a line behind us and we are back on a sun-shadow road—woven sheets of bushed metal draped to make a moving tunnel, edges weighted with slumped glass—the salts under the biocrypt scream. That is not poetic language. The phase change that will open the crypt involves a resonant component that makes a sound as it begins—high, like the note I used to get from my father’s fiddle when he tuned it across a chair back.

“Gentle,” I tell Sef, and it drops our speed by two bars. I watch the shade-number in my visor creep toward the band the job told me. The band is a thin thread in the spectrum, a sweetness that exists for a minute and goes away. Ask any runner what love is and they will tell you it is wanting to be in the right minute and being there.

When the band crosses and I feel the salts pour, I pull the skitter deeper into the tunnel so that the moiré weave dims and the day is turned into a shadow of itself, which is a lie I can use. The crypt in my knee warms—not much, just a whisper, a sigh instructing a small piece of glass to let go its reluctance and show the face behind it. It wakes. The little wafer breathes.

In my visor, a square icon grows, then becomes text, then becomes a voice that is only in my head and not in the air.

Courier confirmed, says a voice with the breathless cadence of something recorded too quickly and then fed through too much machine. Dusk-key accepted. Message begins.

I have an impulse—the kind that you know is an impulse and not a good thought even as you have it—to let the skitter drift into day and see if the light can burn the voice out before it says anything. It is a childish wish. My guild does not honor childish wishes. Sef and I keep straight.

The voice, full of hurry, is also full of my city.

To Zeph Council—, it says. This is Sian Koro, Arc liaison, glassline third. If this reaches you they didn't get all of us. Listen. They say what happened north of you is a natural variance in thermal geometry, but listen to me. It isn't. Someone is—then a sound like air being crushed under something heavy, and the message judders. Ruel in my visor looks larger for exactly a pulse. No, not larger. Closer? No. The old vertigo gets me and I bite my tongue and taste old copper.

Sian comes back, breathlessly. They're moving the Arc.

I laugh, because you have to when someone says something like that, and the laugh is a bark that goes nowhere and leaves my throat raw. The Arc is not a thing that moves. The mirrors are the sky. The sky is the mirror. You can tilt them; the Arc does that to shape Ruel's small coin out into more or less warmth. But moving the Arc, as in shifting the belts, rerouting the orchard of armatures, is the kind of talk my father used to say even the wind wouldn’t carry because it was too stupid to blow.

The message goes on, clogged with static that isn't noise so much as partial data, the way a face is incomplete when you see it through falling snow. Heat budgets, they say, in terms that make my head ache. Dissipative shielding. Control layers frayed—not frayed, cut—and attached again, badly, as if someone with a hand like a child holding a knife tried to do it. We are supposed to board up the windows when the wind is bad. We are not supposed to move the house.

Sian says the names of three places. I know two: Elderly Reef and Loom. Both sunward. Both linked to Zeph by supply and by the lingering cousin-ties that pass for family in the Edge. The third place is a word I have to ask my visor to spell for me. It is a mirror array that is not connected to our line at all. It is a hub that, if it were to wake up—or worse, to fall asleep—the light would slump, and the day would swell into places it doesn’t belong. Or the night would surge and crack glass. If you have never watched a mirror collapse from the Edge, you do not know how an absence of something bright can make a sound.

In the message, Sian swallows, and I hear the shape of the throat that I held in the canyon. They say, We fought in the control spine. They brought in—, and then a word in a language I do not speak, and then another word I know because I have heard it in half a dozen languages: mercenaries. Not from the Edge, not from Zeph, not from night. Or if from any of those, not confessing it. We thought the locks—, and here I think they mean locks like the dusk-key that woke them in my ear, not doors, not chambers—, and then another judder and the voice cuts again and a new voice begins.

The second voice is not in a hurry. It is slow and careful and has the flavor of someone who speaks under floors and behind curtains. It is the reason a person with good sense would say don't open.

Courier, the second voice says. They will try to stop you. If you hear this part of the message, I am dead or I am behind three doors I cannot get out of. You will want to take this to Zeph. You will want to run through the strip where the salt hawkers mouth your name. Good. Do that. But listen. You will see something before you reach them. You will think the world is moving. It is. The Arc is moving, not like a tilt, not like a cloud crossing. The horizon will move. You must not be where it will be when it stops.

If you think that’s impossible, good. Keep thinking that. Impossible people live at the Edge.

There is a set of coordinates. The second voice speaks them twice, once slow, once fast. There is an instruction that sounds like a joke: Dig. There is a word that tastes like an oath and a myth: Severance. As if someone would ever sever the Arc. As if someone ever could.

The message ends. Sef chitters, asking if we are satisfied. The salts relax into the exhausted white that means they are empty. The wafer in my knee goes back to being a sleepy piece of glass. The world around me reasserts its pretense of being ordinary.

Then, without the courtesy of a warning sound in my visor, the light changes.

You don't live half your life at the Edge and fail to notice a shadow change. You know the way Ruel's light is shaped by every wire and wing between it and your skin. You learn the rhythms of the mirror leaves over Zeph, the breath of the wind under the bridges, the huddled ways the day knuckles into itself when it hits rock that won't give. This change is not any of those. It is a smoothing. It is someone taking a hand to the relief map of light and running it hard across a place where a valley is and saying, no valley.

The right side of the world brightens. The left side chills. The line between them shifts by a hand's width, then a palm, then the span of my arms.

I have no gods but the ones we make to make ourselves less lonely in dangerous places. I am not a person who prays. I exhale and swear with no one in mind and then put Sef into a gallop so he will stop thinking about what the day might do to his legs.

Behind us, in the shelf of the canyon, there is a body under a patch. The wind will do what it does to that. Ahead of us, Zeph is a string of stubborn houses and an argument with the Arc and fifty different languages of plea.

It is a bad time for the horizon to move.

The road I have been on all my life is sliding sideways like a tablecloth being jerked off under plates. As I run for Zeph, the plates begin to sound like bells.

Chapter One

Fresh memory tastes like burnt sugar, bright at the back of the tongue, with a little chemical bite if it’s been cut. That’s the first thing they teach you on Gilt Row: trust your mouth more than your eyes. Sight lies, sound lies, smell will lead you by the nose, but taste is the last card the brain plays when it decides what you will believe.

Gilt Row isn’t a row and nothing on it is gilt. It’s a skein of stalls and slung hammocks and slip-cells that spirals around Kite’s End, stitched to the city’s outer rim like a festival of barnacles. We hang in the thinnest air a human can bear above Tegea’s ochre clouds, and every gust thumps the ribs of the city so the glass of the Row pings like rain. On good days the stormlight comes up through the cloud deck with that coppery sheen you only get over massive hydrogen, and you can see your own reflection on the curve of the gas giant, stretched impossibly wide. On bad days the updrafts carry ammonia mist and scarf the whole city in chemical white and the smell sticks in your hair.

I made my first honest credit on Gilt Row teaching tourists to lick their thumbs and tell a dream from a description. Now I make my money forging the past.

“Fresh pull,” says a runner, breath fogging, half a meter of hair streaming behind like fiber optic. She holds up a condensate pendant, light caught inside it like a trapped thought. “Nineteen minutes of first love, perfect fidelity. You want?”

“Even if it was your first, it won’t be mine,” I tell her, not unkindly. “And yours are always overcompressed.” She grins, pockets it, slides away to a pair of kids in borrowed skin-suits who look like they’ve come up from the farms and want to spend a week on what it feels like to be someone else.

I lean on my counter, watch the current. The Row is loud with barter at every altitude. A hunter two levels up hawks a gone-world childhood sealed in crystal droplets like rosary beads. A node of elders sits in a webbed swing, trading recipes in the white-glove code of the Ledger — ten digits flicking, wrist twitch, throat flex, witness sign, filed. Between, the everyday junk: a dog’s steady heartbeat for comfort during short-haul aerobatics, three minutes of a volcano’s thunder stripped out of a long-dead Earth documentary, the taste of a pear for people who’ve only met fruit as DNA sequences in a library.

People recognize me, nod, or look away quickly. I’ve burned bridges and soldered new ones. More precisely, I’ve spliced and cauterized and filed, which is what a forensic mnemonic does when she finds a mismatched thread in somebody’s head and has to stitch it back to where it won’t catch. Or pull it out entirely. Make the brain forget what it never should have believed. There’s work in that, around a city like ours where the first thing people trade when they run out of money is minutes of themselves.

“Ash Kaveh?” someone says, very smooth, with a pitch that knows it sounds like music and tries hard not to gloat.

I look up into a face I know from the feed, though feeds are always a half second out of true. The man has the kind of features that look like they’ve been drawn with rulers: long jaw, straight nose, hair clipped to the exact edge of the bone. He wears a pressure coat tailored so thin you can see the muscle beneath when he breathes. Legally, he can’t be here without somebody clever logging him as three tourists, but you learn to look for clever.

“Depends,” I say. “Is she wanted?”

He smiles, the way a person smiles when he has no intention of saying yes to anything for free. Two discreet handlers hang back at the edge of the stall, faces blanked with polite tech, a little shimmer to their cheeks where a filter catches the air. A drone like a polished seed hovers near the man’s shoulder, silent.

“Minister,” the girl in the next stall breathes, dropping her spool of hand-linked long-term lover. She lifts the edge of the tarp and stares. “Oh, stars. Minister Vakari.”

Lian Vakari doesn’t look at her. He looks at me the way people look at knives: considering edge, weight, whether the balance suits the hand.

“That’s me,” he says. “If you’re Ash Kaveh, and if this is truly your stall.”

“It’s my stall,” I say. “What can I do for the Minister of Pattern Exchange on a Tuesday?”

He doesn’t blink. The drone adjusts fractionally, its lens contracting, a little fidget so minor you only see it if you’ve spent years reading machines the way you read people. Minister of Pattern Exchange. The sarcasm wants to be salty on my tongue. They refuse to call it what everyone else calls it: the Ministry of Diplomatic Lies.

“I need a childhood,” he says. “Not much, and not forever. Forty-five seconds, ready for stage two empathy weave. Intact chronology, authentic ambient noise, minimal tampering. Payment up front.”

Across the Row, someone shouts about a lost tether. The bass of the city’s pumps huffs, and the deck under my bare feet skews a centimeter toward the void before the ballast system corrects. I keep my smile on because Gilt Row is performance; if you break face in front of the crowd, the crowd breaks you.

“You have staff for this,” I say. “You have a mindroom on the Ministerial ring and three salaried pattern-holders and a fleet of neuromancers who don’t sleep.”

Vakari turns his right hand palm upward. Something unfolds on his wrist like a dew-drop spider making a bridge. On his skin, a strand of condensed memory uncoils, dataless, glossy, with the faintest grain of frost where the external cooling has reached the inner particle. It’s a raw pull. Not a market product. Not cut. Not logged.

“You’re right,” he says. “But this doesn’t exist.”

He places it on the glass. Cold leaks into my counter, frosting a line through the condensation. The drone flicks its lens, taking a legal witness image without legal value. You can tell because it doesn’t stamp the weave signature.

No Ledger hash. No entropic signature. No trace in the city’s intake. In other words: contraband. Everything in Kite’s End is taxed in heat and thoughts; the Ledger measures how much energy it costs you to be you and charges you appropriately. This is outside that math.

“You know what they do to people who handle memory off-ledger,” I say softly.

He makes a small motion with his left shoulder. “I do. Do you know what happens if I step into a negotiation with the Reef-binders this afternoon without something that smells like a human childhood?”

We both know. The Reef-binders aren’t ours and aren’t here. They speak through pattern, and pattern cares only about fidelity and coherence. They are rock and metal city, a community of heat sprites braided into calcified forests under the upper clouds of a world we call Reef. If you want anything from them you have to learn to be awake in their way. Last time we sent a diplomat with a library of the best collective human writing we had, polished by our finest, the Reef-binder’s response was polite madness. They prize the hand at the back of the mouth. They prize what humans call memory.

“Your childhood won’t work?” I ask.

“Mine is in the Ledger as it should be. Too many hands have been on it. Too clean. This needs to be unremarkable. It needs to be human enough to pass basic olfactory checks without leading a Reef-binder to a thousand other copies.” He holds my eyes as if we are standing on a beam over empty air. “And I was told you could deliver human.”

My mouth tastes metallic, like I’ve bitten my tongue. They don’t come to the Row if they have options. The Row appears like looseness, like the place where rules fail. That’s the show. Underneath, we are part of the city’s machine like every other piece, paying heat taxes, logging our hours of first touch and last breath so the pipe-saints can apportion oxygen and ration the things that aren’t just gas: attention, rage, rest. If Vakari is here with a memory that isn’t on Ledger, that means someone above me has already decided they’d prefer it done where the city can pretend it didn’t happen.

“If I say no?” I ask.

“I take this to a black clinic in the storm farms,” he says promptly. “They will put it in me in the dark and I will make it look tidy when it isn’t, and the Reef will smell the lie like copper. They will shut their reefs for ten years and starve a hundred thousand humans. We will print apologies in vacuum.”

He smiles, almost apologetic. “No pressure.”

“Always pressure,” I say, and lift the memory thread with two fingers.

It is colder than it should be. Properly pulled memory holds heat like an animal. This has been chilled to preserve its edges. The cold climbs my skin. I set my tongue to it and let a sliver melt across taste. Burnt sugar. Salt like fingers that have been in the ocean and then licked clean. A clean electrical light, nothing like the yellow of our hydrogen lamps.

Beneath, something floral I can’t name. Old Earth, I think before I can stop myself, and then hate the thought because people who are not from Earth think all flowers smell like that and talk about it the way they talk about gods. I was born on a ship in a frozen orbit around a moon whose name nobody kept. I have never walked on anything that wasn’t manufactured. Old Earth is a story that eats more than it feeds.

“Forty-five seconds,” I say, because I know what this is. It is a piece that will graft backwards and forward seamlessly if I am good and will kill him or make him worse if I am not. “Wait,” I add as he reaches into his coat. “How did you carry this?”

He smiles a bland, no-meaning smile. He takes out a thin ledger slate and places it beside the thread as if that could make it legal. The slate displays a number that makes my heart jump against my breastbone. Enough to buy a new place under the hub, with thicker walls and a smell of yeast and people who sing. Enough to pay off my heat account for a year and then buy some extra minutes of my grandmother laughing so I can stitch them into my sleep. Enough to put away three months of oxygen for my friend Tamsin who has cyst lungs.

“No,” I tell the slate and what it means. “This will need a lab. If it’s off Ledger, it’s off protocol. No room for clean sign. You’ll need a shield.”

“You are the shield,” he says. “Because you’re very good, because you don’t show your teeth when someone waves money, and because you have taste. If you say this is human, I believe the Reef will say it is human.”

He has me. He knew when he walked down the Row that he did. He can smell hunger. They all can. The handlers have hardly moved. The drone’s lens has widened: a dark bright pupil.

“Back room,” I say, because saying no to a thing like that only turns it into a story you can’t fix later. “No more eyes. You and your toys can come. No one else.”

The girl who dropped her long-term lover watches me with her mouth open. I put my ledger plate over my stall — back in thirty, the script says, as if thirty means anything here.

My back room is a tube with a curtain at one end and the city’s skin at the other. Through the skin, Tegea rolls and rolls, hammered copper under moving cloud. The persistent hum of circulation and ballast makes the floor feel like a breath held and held. My bench is clean, my rig folded like an insect sleeping. In this light, the Minister looks less drawn and more human. Sweat has dried at his temples.

“Shields on,” I tell him, and when his drone unfolds a dome of a silence field that hums against my teeth, I cut my own. My assistant wakes with a chirp.

“Pip,” I say. “We’re off the Row’s ear. Minister Vakari, this is Pip. Pip, don’t be showy.”

“I am never showy,” Pip says from the overhead, offended. Pip is four square centimeters of wetware in a ceramic shell with a voice that used to belong to a carnival barker. I bought them for eight minutes of my fourteenth year and kept them because I can’t stand to work alone. “Good morning, Minister Vakari, Minister’s drone, Minister’s people who pretend not to hear me. Please refrain from waving weapons inside Ash’s work space. Not that you are, but people have before.”

“We are unlikely to wave weapons,” says Vakari. He doesn’t bother adding that if he had been planning to kill me he would have done it in front of an audience. Ministers like witnesses.

I lay the thread on my bench. Pip drops a pair of micros under it. The thread lifts a hair, shivering. It is like watching a thought held between chopsticks. Without the Ledger’s witness signature, my own imprint is the only law in the room.

“Origin check,” I say, because I’m not completely suicidal. “We have no legal chain and I am about to put this on a stab of my tongue. If it was grown or spun or if it contains anything that will rewrite my memory tree, I would prefer to know first.”

“It was pulled from a person,” Vakari says. “Not grown. As to provenance…” He lifts his hand in a little arc that means he has reached the end of what he will say until I decide to trust him more.

“Put it through,” I tell Pip.

They hum, and the micros whisper to each other in a language that doesn’t so much exist as turn into existence in my ears because my brain, trained to this for years, hears what it must. The micro’s scan waves come back with signature noise. The cluster graph grows. It is human. It is not a composite. The glial noise says real-time, one pull, an adult with high baseline temperature, no obvious pathology. A high-altitude sound floor. Small birds.

“There,” Pip says, wonder in their voice. “Listen.”

Beneath the white-noise hiss of the scan, I hear a click. Regular. Dry. Not mechanical. Something like two things lightly touching. A sound I know as well as I know my own breath, though I have not heard it outside the mind of a patient in years. It is the quiet of rain on a corrugated roof. Not the blunt slap of drizzle on polymer or the frantic gnat-music of a storm on spun silk and glass. Old rain. Gravity-rain. Water coming down because it must. It tastes like iron on my tongue.

“Ash,” Pip says softly, but I am already reaching.

“Stage one,” I say. “Ten seconds. I go in and out. Pip, count. Minister, try to look like you’re not watching me dangle over an open well.”

I take the thread between my teeth because sometimes theatre helps. I lower the tip to my tongue and let the thread kiss the soft palate of my mouth. You do not swallow a memory. You let it dissolve across the thin places, the ones with the fewest lies. I breathe once, twice, cage my heart between my ribs. The hum of the silence field is a pressure. The city’s breath is a pressure. Tegea turns and pressure is the shape of the world.

On the fourth breath, the bench falls away.

On the fifth, I am somewhere else.

Feet on packed dirt. The heel of my hand skinned where I went down and caught myself without thinking. Air heavy with dust and something green under it, so faint I only know it from stories. A child’s hand in mine. Small. Damp. Fever-warm. The sky the wrong blue. A tiny sound like a jar lid twisted once and stopping. The click of rain starting on a roof that is not transparent.

The hand tightens. “Come on,” says a voice, the child’s, up the octave after a cough. “Ash, you’re going to get in trouble if we don’t,” and the last syllable stretches the way people who learned to speak their words on a ship stretch the last of the breath in every sentence to make it to the end in one piece.

A pit opens under my ribs. The sensation is not memory and not new experience. It is recognizably the thing my brain does when an empirical fact meets a missing fact and both insist on sitting in the same chair.

“Out,” says Pip, somewhere a hundred kilometers away or four centimeters to the left. “Ash, out.”

I pull my tongue off the thread, fight the reflex to swallow. The bench returns. The hum becomes a noise. The Minister looks the way people do when something is happening to someone else that they want very much to understand and very much cannot. Pip blows cooling air across my face.

I put my hand on the bench to stop it moving. The line of frost where the thread lay is almost gone, a memory of cold.

“Again?” Vakari asks, too fast.

“No,” I say. My throat is raw. “No again until we have more glass under us.”

“What did you see?” He tries to make it a question and fails.
