“Dirt,” I say, because of all the things I could say — the little hand, the wrong blue, the rain — dirt is the least dangerous. Dirt exists. Dirt doesn’t call names from twenty years ago. Dirt doesn’t make me understand that somewhere, someone who has never met me knows how my name sounds when dragged out in a hurry by a child with ship-breath.

Vakari watches my face as if the answer to other questions will appear there if he is patient. The drone vibrates. Pip says nothing, which is their way of saying everything.

“You’re sure it’s human,” he says, and when I don’t answer, precisely because my mouth cannot form that certitude, he leans in. “The Reef won’t care where the ground came from. They’ll read regret and motion and small fear. They’ll smell the speed of that child pulling you into safer light. That’s the part that matters.”

“It matters to me,” I say, before I can make the sentence a more professional shape.

A pause that is barely more than a breath. “I don’t have anyone else I can ask,” he says, and for one soft second the thing behind the jaw and the coat and the drone shows. It is a man who has to walk so carefully he can’t afford to feel sorry for people, but does.

“Fine,” I tell him, because if I have to be anyone’s knife, I prefer to be one used clean. “There’s damage. There is no witness. You understand. If I take this and lay it on you and it cuts your brain, we will have no priest or paper to say I did it right or wrong.”

“Yes,” he says. “I understand.”

“I’ll need a room.”

He glances around the tube. “This isn’t a room?”

“A lab room,” I say. “With a stretcher balanced like a field gyroscope and a window onto something that isn’t human, very large, to keep you inside yourself when you come back from being five. With a drain in the floor in case you vomit. With a chair I can strap your shoulders to so the empathy doesn’t pick up my hands when I have to go in and around.”

“We have a room like that,” he says. “Of course.” Then, a fraction late: “It’s off-lease.”

“Of course,” I say. “Bring it to my here.”

He blinks. “We can’t move—”

“You brought contraband to a city that is a machine and asked a woman whose business is the machine’s teeth to chew it for you,” I say. “Bring the room or don’t. If you go to the storm farms you’ll get a child’s breath next to your own and you won’t have hands to hold you while you swallow.”

He stares for a long second and then nods like I’m a lever pressed in the right place. He doesn’t look back at his handlers. The drone spins its little field inward. The hum shifts. The air thins and then settles as the silence lifts.

“One hour,” he says. “Be ready.”

He leaves the thread on my bench. He is either very confident or he needs my lab too badly to risk taking it with him. The handlers ghost out through the curtain, each a small change in the room as they go. For a moment it is just me and Pip and the taste of old rain.

“Ash,” Pip says.

“I know.”

“You heard it say your name.”

“Yes.” I put the thread in a bath that looks like water and isn’t. It will hold it at the line between melt and break. I label it in the only way that feels honest. I don’t write Minister. I don’t write Reef. I write Under Roof Rain.

Pip hums to themselves, old carnival music, a roll of brass without brass. “You’re thinking of your mother.”

“I’m thinking of a woman with a name that had four syllables and was too long for ship talk,” I say, before I can lie. “She died in the second heat year. I gave her twelve minutes to the Ledger because I could not bear to choose just one.”

“And you are thinking of a child,” Pip says.

“And I am thinking of a child,” I agree, and don’t say that in the memory the child’s hand felt exactly like mine did when I was little and feverish and the ship’s doctor held my fingers tight to keep me from pulling out the cooling line. I start to take the rig down, then change my mind and set it up twice, once for read only and once for the work I will have to do to keep Ministers from falling apart. The ocean under the city rolls. Out on the Row, someone is singing the long rhyme people use when sharp things change hands. The smell of ammonia and warm plastic and hot copper threads through the curtain.

“You could do nothing,” Pip says, in the voice that is not theirs but I have given them so many borrowed voices they cannot remember which one is their own. “It is always an option.”

“And if I do nothing,” I say, “a hundred thousand people might starve. And the Reef might not speak to us again until I am old and can’t hold a thread without my hands shaking. And also I will not sleep,” I add because that is the part that actually makes decisions for me.

“That too,” Pip says.

The hour is a long time. And not. Tamsin sends a tailwind emoji and a picture of her lunch, which is green for the first time in a week. The pumps cough. The cloud deck darkens and then flashes far below, a sheet of light that runs like fish. Somewhere in the city’s hinge a saint sings a wordless chant that follows the pressure change. The world is too large, and the room is too small, and a child I do not know calls my name from under a roof I have never touched.

When Vakari comes back, he brings the room.

It rolls between the stalls like a casket and opens like a flower. It is everything I asked for. It is clean in the way power is clean, which is to say the dirt has been pushed somewhere you can’t see. We pull it into the tube and it fits because the city is built to be torn and retied. The Reef has sent nothing on our feeds; or if it has, they have not shown us. Vakari removes his coat and the tailored shirt beneath and sits on the edge of the gyroscopic contraption without being told. He is thinner than I thought he would be. His stomach has the hollow of someone who forgets to eat when the work is bad.

I strap his shoulders. He does not flinch. I secure his left hand last. He looks at me beautifully as the straps tighten. “Tell me what you need,” he says.

“Forty-five seconds of under roof rain,” I say, and touch the thread to my tongue to say hello to the story again, and when the first drops begin I hold his hand. He only tightens down once, like a man who knows that if he lets himself take more he will never stop. I have become, in the years of this work, very good at being the thing someone grips.

Before we begin, he says, “If this goes badly—”

“I will tell the Reef a better story,” I reply. “And they will forgive you because they have never had a child, and it makes you brave.” Then I slide the thread into the machine’s mouth, and the city breathes, and somewhere far away in a world that tastes like iron, someone very small says my name, and I try not to answer.

Chapter One

The first thing is the taste: cinnamon gum and iron pennies, and a wet sleeve reverent against my cheek. Somewhere, someone else is sixteen and convinced this kiss will rearrange the geometry of the world. Their teeth knock mine. Heat comes up like a beacon. Streetlight flickers. A dog barks three streets away.

I pull back before it completes. The baffles embedded across my palate hum and swap most of it out for dull, harmless gradients, but the outline still presses me hard behind the eyes. My gloves pop against the crust. Tiny sparks lift from the black glass and waver as if the air is full of insects. Two hours before dawn, the reef is awake.

Rule one: never swallow. Rule two: don’t call it memory, not where anyone with a badge might be listening. It’s spill or bleed, exhaust, ambience — anything but the word that can get you picked up by Hygiene and put on a registry for life.

“Temperature?” Juno asks in my ear, lazy-sleepy because she’s bundled in the truck with the heater on and is only pretending to watch my telemetry.

“Nineteen,” I say. “Surface. Lower layers colder.” The dunes around me are hunched like sleeping animals. My breath moves like smoke toward the highway lights on the horizon. The city throws up a low haze, broken to the south where the old data farms still pulse amber in the frost. I’m in the gully left by what used to be a drainage canal. It holds the richest runs — decades of commuters, their laces whispering, everything accumulating in the low places, accreting with the silica, compacting under its own weight until it goes glassy at the edges.

“Signal saturation is spiky,” Juno says. “You near a blossom?”

“I hear it.” The hummm is sub-audible, a warble in my jawbone more than a sound, as if the reef’s core is speaking but can’t be coaxed into my frequencies. Sometimes blossoms come up when the wind has been right for weeks, when the city has been in a mood, when enough of us have been lonely. They’re where the bleed crystallizes, reorganizing itself around a seeded attractor the way frost makes lacy ferns on a tin roof. Good salvage if you get there first and you don’t let it touch you raw.

I kneel and lay my left hand flat. The glove’s microfilaments palpate the glass. Two fingers pinch a seam and pry; small flakes in green-gray come free with a sound like rice paper peeling. I feed one sliver into the port in my right sleeve and let the baffles map it. The glove chirps and then delivers the impression to my tongue and optic nerve: the taste of mint toothpaste and a flash of a gray tie knotted poorly; fluorescent light; disappointment pooling at the bottom of a metal locker.

Leftovers, a few credits at best, nothing with spine. Tonight isn’t about selling thrillribbons near the university anyway. Tonight is for a debt, and for that I need a kernel: a hard knot, a tight resonance that survived storms and foot traffic and amateur harvesters.

“Ministry drone just pinged north grid,” Juno says, voice sharpening. “It’s branching south, might not be this lot. You have…call it twenty minutes.”

“Plenty.” I move sideways along the gully, mapping the density with my palm. The reef is not uniform, any more than a coral reef is uniform. There are fans where commuters walked in step for years, their metabolisms synced by the city’s rhythms. There are holes where truck tires broke through membrane and scoured out channels. There are colonies driven by tragedy, places where accident after accident in the same paint-slick curve left constellations of shock that can pull you down if you don’t protect yourself.

I have a cheap, old-issue baffling suite — palate, eyelids, cuffs across my forearms and the back of my neck, a matrix under my scalp like a second skeleton. They filter structural motifs, cool hot edges, turn foreign into nonsense before it can teach my neurons to ape someone else’s habits. I maintain them myself because I don’t trust any Guild tech that offers updates like favors.

Tonight, I’m a crack in the surface crust and a ripple under my hand. I inch it wider. The thin glass gives with a breath. Beneath is not sand but a coarse crumble that looks like the dregs of a burnt sugar pan. It smells faintly of ozone and old rain. Good. When bleed goes down a couple seasons and cooks under summer heat, it polymerizes. The good stuff hides there.

My drone is a folded thing like a kite. It sits clipped to the strap of my pack right now, its little camera giving me a high view of the gully on my retina. The highway is a ribbon of amber far away. The truck’s heat signature huddles black-blue, Juno’s head a little red dot as she sits upright suddenly. She swears. “It’s definitely coming. One drone, low. Hygiene. You kicked something?”

“I tasted a high school hallway,” I say. “If that’s now contraband, arrest the whole country.” I wedge my knee into the hole and slide my arm in up to the elbow. The crust edges bite the glove. The crumb is cool. I move my hand slowly, feeling for unnatural density, for the way resonant knots push back at pressure. With the right touch, you can hear it, the way you’d hear a tuned glass vibrate under a wet finger. You can also miss it and end up with a bag of moths, all pretty and worthless and liable to eat you from the inside out if you let them fly.

There. A small, tight thing at the base of my reach, humming just off of an E. I guide the gnarl upward, rolling it against my palm to break the weak bonds around it. Putty gives and then stiffens. When I lift it into the air, it’s a lopsided white lump like an old sea-washed bone. The henning in my jaw climbs. Even before I feed it through the baffles, I know this is worth something.

“Got one,” I say. “Cover me.”

“You know they can hear if we sprint,” Juno says. She starts the truck anyway — a cough that makes cold dust leap. “Hygiene drone is low now. It’ll pretend to be an ambulance until it’s right on you.”

“Come down the farm road and kill your lights at the cattle gate,” I say. “Pick me up at the arroyo; I’ll cut across the old fence line.”

“Mara—”

“I’m not testing it here.” I am. But I’m not testing it here, where the reef can grab me if it wants me. I go to feed a sliver into my sleeve to get an ID — who it came from mostly, a rough date, maybe the predominant sensory modality — and the baffles whine, red-warning glare across my inner vision.

I’ve only seen it do that once before, and the taste it had delivered then had been battery acid and a long fall. I had thrown up and not slept for a day. I pull the sliver back, heart thudding.

“Don’t even,” Juno says, knowing me.

“Just a peek,” I say, knowing me. I shave the lightest dust from the kernel with my thumbnail into the port, enough for impressions but not enough that anything with weight can take hold. The baffles hiss. I press my tongue to the palate disc.

Sun. Heat up from concrete like a second sun. The smell of taxi brakes and orange blossom. My eyes aren’t mine. They are higher than mine by a centimeter and set a little differently, the city sits skewed, unbalanced. A shadow moves over the face of a crowd in the plaza by the Central Archive. All those faces turn up together the way they do when a drone is overhead and you just want to be counted as present, not necessarily good.

Someone is speaking right into me. Right into the inside of me, like they know the address of my first shape and they’re meeting me there. Mara, says the voice. My name in a mouth I’ve never heard, with a cadence I’ve never heard, almost catching on the r like a familiar. Mara Lin. Don’t cut the yellow line. Wait for the third chime.

The sound of metal shearing rides up through bone. The square goes bright. A girl in a green coat breathes out, touched by light from the wrong direction. For an instant I see my own wrist — scar on the inside from a stovetop burn when I was seven — and I am not in the square; I am here in the gully; I am doubled between two thin skins.

I rip my tongue back and the world snaps. I’m on my knees in the gully, knuckles white around the kernel. My palate buzzes so hard my teeth ache. I spit reflexively and bright blood dots the black glass and looks like stars.

“What did you do?” Juno is not pretending now. She is running with the truck, her feet in boots throwing up little puffs on the farm road on my drone’s view. The Hygiene drone is not pretending either — it drops the ambulance shimmer and shows its cross-hatched belly and the little mouth where it keeps its darts.

“I tasted,” I say. I clutch the lump to my chest like it is a baby and a bomb. “It’s hot. Future hot.”

“Mara—”

“It used my name.” The words rip out the back of my throat raw. “It said ‘Mara Lin’ and don’t cut the yellow line and—”

“And you think Hygiene won’t have a lock on an illegal reader in the exact field where something is spiking time index?” Juno says. “Move.”

I move. The gully here is sloped and the crust treacherous. It shivers under my boots like sugar glass. I skirt a soft patch where the ground bows and hums. The kernel buzzes in my hands like it wants back where it was. The old fence runs ahead of me, posts the color of old bone. The arroyo is a dark slash beyond, promising cover and a rattlesnake or three. Above, the drone’s fan noise drops to a purr, the way they do when they’re in watching mode. I slide, catch at a post, and the crust gives entirely. My foot goes through. The reef breathes.

It’s not alive, not the way we learned in school. It’s not neurons firing. It’s patterned residues in a city with too many signals to police and too many bodies to be careful with. It drinks our exhale and our spin and piles it up in drifts. It does not want, except the way crystal wants lattice. But when enough wanting is written in ferromagnetic dust and polysilicate skins, it can feel like a hand reaching for you. Or me. Or anyone carrying a bright knot like bait.

I wrench my leg back with a sound like tearing muscle. It’s my pants, not my calf. Baffles across my thighs blare, soaking up something sharp that might have cut me from thinking in circles all night long. I stumble sideways onto hard ground and run.

Juno is at the gate. The truck noses through, lightless. The Hygiene drone hangs and rotates lazily like a big bug. It’s closer than I want it to be. There is a delay between detection and enforcement like a courtesy; if you give it a show of lawful behavior, it will sometimes give you a pass to keep its metrics clean.

“Don’t look at it,” Juno says, her hands white on the wheel. “Don’t look like anyone who has ever read a manual. Get in.”

I get in. I lean the kernel against my knee and try not to look at it either. It looks like nothing. It looks like something that will ruin us.

“What the hell is ‘don’t cut the yellow line’?” Juno says, driving through a pretense of slowness even while her hands tremble. Her hair is in two stubby braids and her sleeves are pushed up and she has a dot of engine grease on her cheek that I don’t tell her about. She looks like a saint of lost machines.

“Third chime,” I say. “I don’t know. The square. The Archive. It was full daylight.”

“What time index?”

“I didn’t get one.” The baffles were too busy screaming no. “I can pull it clean in the lab.”

“And pay what if they come right now?”

My brain is trying to double again, like a fish trying to throw itself back into water. Daylight in my mouth, the taste of citrus peel and ambulance sirens. I swallow and my stomach tilts and rights itself. Rule one: never swallow. Too late now.

We roll onto the old state road. Dark fields on either side, clumps of brittle chamise making black smudges. The drone follows until the highway, where the real ambulances are, where it can pretend again, and then it thinks better of it and veers away, its belly-lights fading into the haze. Juno lets out a breath that is more like a laugh crying.

“I said twenty minutes,” she scolds, because we are alive enough to trade in relief.

“You know how I get,” I say, because we are alive enough to fight like sisters.

“We have to stop,” she says. “You took a dirty bite. We have to milk you.”

“It’s clean enough,” I lie. Milking is what you do when you have more impression than your baffles can clear — you run a scrubbing loop through your hippocampus and force the foreign patterns to degrade while they’re still plastic. It makes you a little less you for a day. It makes your tongue feel like it does not fit in your mouth. I don’t like it. I also don’t like waking up with a song that isn’t mine and finding out I can’t set a kettle on the stove without crying because someone else’s mother used to hum by a certain sink.

“We’ll stop at Naomi’s,” Juno says, as if my dislike has been cataloged and weighed and set aside. “She owes me for her alternator anyway.”

“Naomi tells everyone everything,” I say. The city is ahead, a smudge and a promise and a list of things that will get you caught.

“You’d rather go home?” Juno says, making home mean our container, our ladder bolted to the side of a warehouse, our two beds offset so we can pretend we are not a single unit drifting. Our plant that is more brown than green. The paper taped over the window when the polar film peeled. Our cheap lock. And the fact that if the kernel is tagged by any of the nets we pass, the lock won’t matter.

“Naomi,” I say.

In Naomi’s yard the skeleton of an old turbine leans against the fence as if it’s thinking about getting back to work. The garage smells like solvent and warm metal. Naomi has her legs out from under a panel truck and a wrench in one hand and a cigarette in the other. She looks at the kernel in my lap and raises an eyebrow so sharp I can feel the cut from here.

“This shop is not licensed for your hobbies,” she says, pushing herself upright and squinting at me through the smoke. She’s in a U.S. Postal Service t-shirt from the year before delivery went all drone, sleeves ripped off. She is strong as a house with a good foundation.

“I won’t plug in,” I say. “We need your chair for a flush. Ten minutes. We can pay.” I look at Juno in the way people do when they are lying about paying.

“Flush is licensed medicine,” Naomi says, which is the exact voice of someone who flushes anybody who asks, for cash and out of loyalty and because she likes sticking it to Hygiene. “And I am so licensed. Wait. Did you bite a hot one, Lin?”

“It said it knows her name,” Juno snaps, making it too real. Naomi’s mouth goes tight.

“Oh, baby,” she says, the tenderness startling. “But who doesn’t know your name? You’re famous. You owe Baek three months and the Guild says you burned their filter and you made that big man cry that one time.”

“Not for this,” I say. My hands will not stop shaking. I could clamp them between my knees but I don’t want to let go of the kernel, as if it could suffer separation anxiety. Also as if I don’t want Naomi to see too much of it. I am greedy like that, and I hate that I am.

Naomi pushes the chair — an old dental seat refitted with a harness and the soft, slow pump of a scrubber — to the middle of the garage. “You know it’ll take whatever you want to keep, too,” she says, almost gentle. “Flushing clears good and bad. You’ll lose something you like. One note of a song. The smell of your first apartment in the November rain.”

I think of my mother’s wrist with the flour on it, and am hit with such vertigo that I have to put my head between my knees. It’s not the flush. It’s the daylight ramming itself up inside my dark morning.

“Wait,” I say. “Two minutes. I need to see it clean.” My lab is a drawer built out of a bread box and lined with foil and filters and a black market reader I bought off a kid in a parking lot. I could set it up in Naomi’s, thrive on borrowed electricity and her generous silence. Or I could feed the kernel whole to Baek and buy a week of grace and never know what it wanted from me. Or I could wait like the voice said — wait for a third chime I can’t hear yet — and pray that if time is folding it is folding politely.

Naomi looks at Juno. Juno looks at me. I am a stupid experiment walking around pretending I am a person.

“A minute,” Juno says finally. “Two. But you sit in the chair while you run it. And Naomi holds the switch.”

Naomi grins. “My favorite job.” She pushes me down, buckles the strap across my chest, pulls the cozy around my head that makes the world a small box. The baffles sigh, grateful to have help coming. My scalp prickles where the scrubbers align with the under-mesh of my filter suite. Juno rolls the bread box closer, unscrews the makeshift lid.

I crack the kernel on the edge of the reader like an egg. The outer chalk flakes. Inside is gelatin clear as candy glass, stretched in fine planes like layers of mica. That’s the structure you want: order like a choir, not chaos like a crowd. I use a ceramic spoon to scoop a shaving into the reader and close it.

The palate hums a friendlier hum as it reads the safe translation, as the baffles negotiate with the raw thing like priests offering a terrified god a bowl of milk. My inner vision fills with a technical grid: provenance unknown, heavy load of olfactory and tactile imprint, a Strand pattern I don’t recognize. Time index: plus twenty-seven hours, six minutes. The program flickers like it doesn’t believe itself. It repeats. Plus twenty-seven hours, six minutes.

In the garage, Naomi’s fridge cranks on and adds its hoarse song. Outside, a dog barks. In my head, the square rises again like a tide. Only this time I have space between me and the water. The milk-baffles do their calm work and the impressions arrive banked instead of crashing.

Central Archive. Now I know it by the way sound behaves in that space, the hard reflections of the old stone. Midday. The drone that throws the first shadow has elegant prop blades, not Hygiene. A ring of students in sweats, each with a red scarf. A pair of municipal workers taking their breaks on the low wall, identical sandwiches in wax paper. A child with a paper crown. The voice again, with its half-catch on the r.

Mara Lin. It knows where I am in the crowd and it climbs to reach me. It is not the memory-maker speaking then, not in the conventional way. This is more like a topography laid out so that it leads to me, so that I cannot help but arrive at it. It is designed. Juno squeezes my wrist where her hand wraps around the chair’s arm, an anchor.

Don’t cut the yellow line, the voice says. Wait for the third chime. Then run south under the arch and do not look back. At the corner, a girl in green will hand you a black case. Do not open it. Do not trade it. Bury it. You won’t want to. Bury it anyway.

Under my tongue the metallic taste rises: not pennies this time, but steel. The scene flexes at the edges, like an image caught through heat waves. A drift of birds lifts. There is a sound I know in my bones — the sound of a heavy thing going light before it falls. Every body in the square pivots instinctively toward the source because that is what bodies do in cities. The third chime, when it comes, is the one the Archive clock makes when noon is already gone, the little after-sound of something older. The light goes white.

“Cut it,” Juno says, but Naomi’s hand is already on the switch, and the world contracts so fast my ears pop. The flush grabs the residual threads and pulls. Relief like water on a burn. I gasp, swallow, choke, cough. Tears jump, uninvited. The garage is a small honest room again.

Two breaths. Three. My heart learns to be a heart.

“You’re a fool,” Naomi says softly, affectionate as you would be to a stray that you cannot quite convince to stop stealing. “What did you stick in?”

“Tomorrow,” I say. “Tomorrow at the Archive.” My mouth is thick, but the words are simple. “Plus twenty-seven hours.”

Juno sinks onto an overturned crate. She looks at the kernel in my lap like it might bare teeth. “You are not going,” she says, and I understand that she believes me enough to be scared, and that makes it more true than any file I could flash in her face.

“I owe Baek,” I say. It is stupid to say that in this moment, but it is the truth that underlies all the other truths. The city counts you the most when you owe. “He will send Perry if he thinks I’ve got something that can cover two months. I can’t bury it without making another debt. If I deliver him nothing in the morning, he knocks our door in by noon.”

“You think this isn’t connected,” Juno says, and at last the name sticks to the shape in my mind. Baek, with his fastidious cuffs and the way he eats grapes one at a time.

“I think it’s all connected,” I say honestly. “But what do you want me to do? I can’t bury a thing I haven’t got, and I can’t choose not to be someone’s address if they already wrote my street.”

“Who sent it?” Naomi asks, pragmatic as ever. “Because somebody did. Kernels don’t coalesce into instruction sets by accident. Somebody recorded it and seeded it and pushed it down the line. They know how the reef blooms. They know how long it takes to harden. They aimed.”

Aimed at me. The thought sits like a coin on my tongue. Don’t cut the yellow line, the voice had said, as if it had watched me in a hundred kitchens making rash cuts to solve small problems. You won’t want to, it had said, and that in particular makes a little itch under my skin that I do not like. Because it is right; I never want to bury anything. I want to keep.

“I’ll go,” I say. The words land in the garage like bones. “I’ll go because the only other thing I have ever done when told not to is not gone, and that has worked out like it has.” Which is to say, badly. “I’ll go with baffles. I’ll go and I’ll leave if my teeth hum. I’ll go and I’ll run south and I won’t cut anything.”

“And in twenty-seven hours,” Juno says, “what do you think ‘don’t look back’ means?”

“That I’ll fail if I do,” I say, which is both the oldest story and brand new.

Naomi lights another cigarette, like one fire is not enough. She waves the smoke away from my face. “Then we put you in a different jacket,” she says, practical as a cup of coffee. “We keep you out of nets on the way. We tuck this bully in your grandmother’s tea tin and hide it under the fake floor where I keep my unlicensed dignity. You stay the hell off the university side of town until then so nobody plucks you for parts. And you don’t tell Baek anything until after you come back.” She says it like a promise to herself. She says it like she has decided this is the story we’re in.

The kernel sits in my lap humming faintly, like something asleep remembering that it will wake. In my mouth, the word Archive tastes like citrus and iron. I touch my tongue to my palate and there is only the slow, comforting thrum of the scrubber, like a hand on the back of my head.

“Rule three,” Juno says, as if making one up will save me. “No new rules at two in the morning.”

“Too late,” Naomi says. “New rules all around. Lin, finish your flush. Tomorrow, we’ll teach you not to look back.” She smiles, baring her teeth, and taps ash into the gullet of a dismantled engine. “And maybe whoever thinks they can aim you will learn something unpleasant about inertia.”

Chapter One

I used to think the star was smooth. From the ground, back when I was small enough to fit beneath my mother’s worktable and swallow my fear of the open air, the light of Crocus seemed like a single roar over the dayfall, an unbroken push that pressed on everything. It made our twilight strip of world bloom and burn and made the night ocean crack and slump and pulled storms like a hand pulling sheets. The teachers made the solar wind into diagrams—arrows and numbers and an overexcited cartoon of a red dwarf with cheeks puffed out, spitting. It looked benign, almost polite.

Out here, clipped to a film of mirror the size of cities, tethered by a waistline lanyard and a spine soaked in glass fear, Crocus’s light is a texture. It rattles. It hums in bones and bearings. It has teeth.

The Fleece gathered it, tamed it, threw it where we told it to go. I leaned my helmet into the reflection and watched my own etched face distort across half a continent. The mirror was only a few molecules thick—a gauze of graphene and doped ice—laid out in a fan of silver that arced south toward the shadow. The bridle-lines trailed off like hairs to their nodes. Beyond, a fraying infinity: the stars burned like pricks through dew. Below, the planet was a black disk bit by a pale ring. The daylight terminator was always a bruise, a perpetual dawn circling like a belt. We lived in that belt. The Fleece fed it.

“Rook,” Sana said in my ear, in my jaw, tapping my molars with her voice through the suit-link. “Stop romancing your reflection. We’ve got a snag.”

“Where?”

“Node three-salvage spool. Listen.”

I took two slow breaths past the copper taste of the scrubbers and tilted my head back, closing my eyes to better catch the net’s song. Sound isn’t supposed to happen in a vacuum. It doesn’t stop people from hearing things. The Fleece had its own language, all tension and strain transmitted through aluminum and bone. It thrummed when the light changed; it clacked at micrometeors; it hissed when the attitude jets coughed somewhere far off, a secret between steel limbs.

Sana was right. There was a hitch in the chord. A stutter. The spool at three-salvage chattered like teeth.

“Crossflow,” I said. “Or a fray.”

“Fray,” Sana said. “Camera shows a glint-flower. Probably a bubble. Your side.”

Always my side when it was something that could cut.

I swung one boot over the lanyard and kicked off. The tension in the line plucked me along like a bead. Out here you learned to trust taut things. Trust that there was a line. I spooled myself hand over hand along the bridle toward the bright error, counting clipped knots, numbering the finger burns I couldn’t get because the gloves took all that sensation away.

The flower appeared as a pale starburst in the near distance, a place where the mirror wrinkled up and tried to throw the light somewhere else. The Fleece couldn’t afford whimsy. One wrinkle could shiver a line of heat down to the planet in the wrong place, scorch a tower, destabilize a winter-sown marsh, cause storms to stand where they shouldn’t. There were plenty of ghosts down there that could point to a fault in our work and say, This was you.

The glint-flower wasn’t pretty up close. It was a boil, a tense swelling capped by a blister of frost. Micrometeors hit the microtexture of the sail all the time. The self-healing membranes filled and smoothed. Most were quiet. This one had trapped a breath of vapor between layers and blown a knob into existence. Over it all, the pressure of Crocus’s wind was running like a river over a rock, singing.

“Manual?” Sana asked. “Do we trust the patch?”

“Manual,” I said, even as the patch kit in my toolbelt tapped my hip like an eager animal.

“You really like your hands,” she said. “You trying to make me feel useless over here?”

“Your jokes make up for it,” I said, unclipping a cutter and a spine needle. I parked my boots wide on the texture tabs and bent, aligning the cutter’s mouth with the boil. The star moved in the curve of my visor. In my ear, the net’s song got louder. I could feel the pull of Crocus’s light on the back of my shoulders like muscle fingers. The planet’s night—our night—crept beyond the mirror’s edge.

I pressed the cutter’s lips into frost. It cracked like a tiny scream. Vapor sighed out into the absence. The boil sagged and salted my gloves with ice-dust. I found the seam and slid the needle in, staple-snapping across the rent to make the layers kiss again, stitching shadow to sheen. The Fleece inhaled. The glint-flower died. The song normalized. We made a thing smooth.

“That was pointlessly heroic,” Sana said. “You could’ve been our martyr. I could’ve told your mother that you died saving a bubble.”

“My mother would ask me if the bubble was union,” I said. “Check three-salvage spool again.”

She hummed for a moment, the habitual low of someone who grew up in a turbine tower, and said, “Stable. It’ll hold unless it snows cobbles on us.”

“Is that forecast?”

“You know the forecast. Crocus does what Crocus wants, we translate.”

A drift of brightness passed over my suit, a pale ghosting that came and went with no source. Reflex tightened my arms. The Fleece felt it too. The chord went faintly up in pitch.

“Sana,” I said.

“Yeah, I saw it. Could be a flare sneeze. Could be glare off a new wing.”

There were eleven wings in the Fleece now, like stylized feathers set around the planet’s shadow. We weren’t supposed to call them wings. The senior engineers insisted on proper terms—sectors, lattices, sails. But from the ground the whole construct looked like a bird trying to carry the dark world into dawn; from here it looked like a halo someone had broken into pieces for shipping. I didn’t know about new wings. No one consulted shearers about additions. We were the ones who climbed barefoot into the fabric of things and made minor wrongs not become major ones.

“All right,” Sana said, brisk again. “I’m going to walk the line and check the other spools. You, uh, you keep communing with your god.”

“I don’t owe Crocus anything.”

“Keep saying that.”

She cut the link and left me with the trough-roar and hum of light. I took the time I allowed myself when the needlework was done to look down. Those of us who worked the Fleece got to see what everyone else pretended not to want: our world from above. The terminator ran in a soft-lit ring around the planet’s equator, a penny line between blinding day and absolute night. Along that ring, human work dotted the bruise. Towers reached up like needles threading into the sky. Behind each tower at this height you could see the long chiffon of convective cloud unspooling into the night. Without the Fleece, that ring would be narrower. Without it, the towers would freeze their own breath into glaciers, and the day would creep in with its ferocious deserts and its spitting storms, and the night would eat heat like a god with a mouth full of teeth.

If you dived your eyes into the dark side, you could find the night ocean: flat, not with calm but with firmness, a plain of nitrogen ice that broke and shifted with the seasons, scored by black fault-lines. There were cities under there. There were speakers set into the slabs, coils threaded through so that we could warm it where we wanted and melt it into harbors where we needed. We’d learned to feed the night. The day didn’t need anyone’s help.

I held onto the line and, because my brain was too much with me, I listened again. Not to Sana’s absence, not to the click of my fans or the small wet sounds of my own body in a machine that pretended it could be a skin, but to the net’s hum. To Crocus.

On some days, when the wind turned particular, when the sunspots flickered just so and the flares reached like plants, you could hear organization in the pressure. The engineers said it was a trick of resonance, interference patterns in the tethers made audible by the geometry of the Fleece. They said that everything that seems like speech in a machine is just your brain shunting anxiety into a familiar shape. They said many things. I had never told them that I could sometimes hum back.

It had started when I was thirteen and I got my first illegal ear-splints. I was hearing too much—the loudness of towers, the data hiss of flood gates in the marsh plains, the constant propaganda the city pumped into air as a comfort blanket for children like me who were a little technically inclined and a lot hooked on horror. You put splints in a child’s ears to dull all that. If the splints happened to be recalibrated and black market and tuned to the old low frequencies the first shearers used before proper link tech, that was my luck.

It wasn’t music, what I heard. It was prime numbers once. It was a simple ratio repeating, echoing up and down the spans, three over five, five over thirteen, until it shaped the barely-there exhalations of gas jets and the creak of frozen members into something you could tap your foot to if you were alone and not proud. It was nonsense too. It was wind. But sometimes it wasn’t.

Today there was a ripple in it—a descending little run of beats like someone walking down a stair. Da-da-da-da-dee. The old humor in our crew said that when you heard stairs in the light, you were about to be promoted to ancestor. I held still, gathering the pattern into memory, trying not to move my jaw and not to look like I was trying. Even up here you could feel watched. The city loved us, it needed us, and it didn’t like the idea of us being alone with the future.

Da-da-da-da-dee. Pause. Da-da-da-da-dee. The intervals between the runs grew precise. I lifted my hand and, because no one could see the inside of my glove, tapped on the palm. The inside skin vibrated. I tapped back the same run, because I am the kind of idiot who hums to wind.

Silence fell. Then: dap. Not the run, just a single knock. And after it a sequence of pauses, long-long-short-long. I felt my mouth go dry despite the wetness forced into it by the suit. The pauses were spacing. Spacing for letters. That childish bit of schoolyard code rose up in me like bile.

“What are you doing?” Sana asked, interrupting herself in my skull from somewhere two spools away. I flinched.

“Nothing,” I said, too quick. “Listening.”

“You hear stairs?”

“Only to the grave.”

“Don’t fall down them,” she said. “Weather says flare chance eighty-three. We might get to watch a pretty fountain.”

“Pretty fountain” meant a day at the lathe for me afterwards making new nodes to replace the ones spalled by charged particles. It meant chewing grit and returning late to my mother’s table with chips in my hair. I made a noise like assent. She went quiet.

The spacing waited. I was sweating now. Sweat ran in lines up from my eyelids toward my scalp because up had ceased to have any meaning except the one defined by my fear. I closed my eyes and counted—one-two-three—how would you program a child to hear this? Then I raised my other hand inside my glove and tapped one measured knock.

If it was random resonance, nothing would happen. If it was one of those stupid psychological tests the city ran to make sure we were pliant, something would happen. If it was something else—

Dap. Dap. Long pause. Dap dap dap.

Three knocks this time. Then stop. Then the descending little run again. And then the pauses clicked into words: long space, short space. The old jokes about the old codes knew what to do. You had to assign something to the spaces. You had to make a guess.

MEET, I thought, which made no sense. Then, stupidly, I let that expectation shape what I felt. That was the danger of making patterns—you could weave whatever blanket you wanted and wrap your terror in it and call it prophecy. I almost laughed at myself. I would have, if the next shape hadn’t come like a slap: the run, the beat, the pause, the hammer of a longer interval, and then the stuttering little triple. It spelled out something no one else could make me believe: my name.

R O O K.

The taps stopped.

“Sana,” I said, and didn’t recognize my voice.

“What?”

“You ever get called by wind?”

“Yeah,” she said. “I get called by you whining for spice buns. What’s wrong?”

“Nothing,” I lied again, because in the culture that built me you didn’t talk about ghosts with your partner when you were both tethered to a thing you couldn’t afford to disrespect. “Spool three is tight. I’m going to sweep the hinge, check for track frosting.”

“I can send Niobe,” Sana said, too quickly. “You need your head in the right place for hinges. I want you to have a head.”

“I have an extra,” I said, which made her snort. My mouth felt cold. I left the bridle and shimmed himself along the hinge-line where, twenty kilometers away, the sail bent into a joint with its neighbor. There the fabric thickened into a subtle seam of braided glint. I liked the hinges. They were where the Fleece admitted it couldn’t be perfect. They were scars that worked.

I thought about the taps. I thought about the way the old teacher in the tower by the marsh had taught us the simplest code, just as a game to keep us from jumping the railings when the winds turned visual and sheets of mist went up like banners: you assign long to dash, short to dot, space to separate, you hear what you want to hear. The city permitted that. The city would even approve if you were building the right kind of sync hallucination. It loved people who found meaning in noise that instructed them to be good citizens. It would like it if I said Crocus told me to reinforce the Fleece. That we were heroes. That we were essential. In the night you could hear the propaganda still, even up here, if you tuned for it.

The hinge was clean. The track glided like a smooth child. Beneath my boots something clicked. The Fleece did that—popped from time to time as sunlight pressure changed, or an old weld let go of its tension and sighed back into true. This click was new: a precise little thing, like a finger on bone. I put my palm on the hinge. The cold bit through glove. I heard the stair-run again, louder now as if it were in the metal. The suit link hummed with it. The taps started, more insistent. Space-space-space, tap tap, space, tap. If you squinted at the old codes—if you dared—you could see a shape for that.

C U T.

“Nope,” I said aloud in reflex, as if answering a stubborn child. My throat was dry. I swallowed processor water that tasted like someone had cried in it. “No. Sana, I’m calling a weather read. I’m seeing weirdness in the hinge. Could be heat differentials.”

“Could be flare halo,” she said. “The forecast just tripped to ninety-two. You need to hustle.”

“On my way,” I said. But I didn’t move. I pressed both hands on the hinge and felt for the taps the way you feel for a pulse. They came again. C U T. Then, spacing rapid like a whisper in a throat: T H E F L E E C E.

My heart kicked. My vision went narrow. The lights in my helmet’s periphery that had been worming along telling me oxygen reserves, CO2 partial, attitude correction, flattened into irrelevance. Cut the Fleece.

The city’s code-of-conduct would have a paragraph for this eventually, for the first shearer who claimed the sunlight told them to sabotage the net. There would be a test. There would be counseling. There would be a careful, pitying meeting with a representative who had never had frost growing on their gloves from the vapor in their breath. They would ask if I felt unsupported. They would ask if my mother drank too much tower-heat. They would tell me that the Fleece was humanity’s greatest work since the chimneys and the night speakers and the first time someone decided that you could make a city out of the kind of air no one should live in. They would look at me with their beloved sorrow and ask me if I wanted to hurt everyone.

I put my forehead against the hinge to cool it.

“Rook,” Sana said, and her voice was different now, edges gone. The co-work rhythm had broken; in its place was our other language, the one we only used in storms or when we called each other from bathrooms. “Talk to me.”

“It said my name,” I said before I could absorb the shame.

“Who did?”

“The net,” I said. “The wind. The—”

“The star,” Sana said, because she had known me since I had climbed the radio tower at seven and slept there because it made me feel tidy inside to be above things. “Okay.”

Her okay was a vast space I could walk around in. It didn’t sound like the city’s okay. She didn’t fill it immediately with an avalanche of kindness. She let me speak.

“It said cut the Fleece,” I said. “It said—”

Something winked in the corner of my eye. Not a flare. Not that fat, showboating growth of brightness from the face of Crocus you could ride by the seat of your suit. This was narrow and precise, a shutter closing and opening in a place where there should not have been shutters. A blade of dark moved across the sun, long and brittle and almost too quick to be noticed, and between my spine and my suit something small went colder than anything we could manufacture on purpose.

“There,” I said, but I didn’t know where “there” meant. How do you point in a sky that is all of everything? The thing had crossed the star in a diagonal like a cut you didn’t know you’d taken until you bled into your glove.

Sana said, “I saw it.”

“What was it?” I asked. It came out like the question of a child who wants her mother to tell her it was a sparrow.

“Something in orbit,” she said. “Between us and Crocus. There’s nothing between us and—unless it’s a wave wing. But it wasn’t shaped like—” She stopped. “Niobe is calling all wings. Stand by.”

The link went bright with channel bloom as our wing’s traffic surged. The supervisors slid in, voices flattened by distance and the particular compression of official channels. They used their crisp names. They said words like possible anomaly and maintain posture and the one I hated the most, while we assess. A trailing hiss came in from a downline wing. Someone had their mic keyed by accident. In the hiss, very faint, the tap-code continued. C U T. C U T.

“Are we seeing flare?” someone asked. “Weather is moving.”

“Hold positions,” the supervisor said. Her voice had that calmness that made sane people docile and me raw. “We need clear spectral data.”

“It crossed the profile,” Niobe said. She was two hundred meters ahead of me, on the other side of the hinge, and you could hear the old trench in her voice from where she had grown up in tunnels under a fish farm. If Niobe sounded unsure, we were not seeing what we thought we were seeing. “Not a wing. Not a wave. It cast.”

They all went quiet. On the ground, a child could have told you why that mattered. Crocus was not big. It was an irritable red dwarf that could throw tantrums, yes, but it didn’t cast much in the way of sharp shadow. Our mirrors caught its photons like a snowfield. The only things that cut it clean were we ourselves and the occasional shard of rock that decided to come home. If you were looking at Crocus and something crossed it and cast, that something had to be large and close and viciously black.

“Sana,” I said, because all the official words were brittle and I needed the one other person who had heard me make a fool of myself.

“Still here,” she said, and then cursed softly in a language her wife spoke when she was sad. “I’m seeing signal on spectrum five. Do you see it? Ground is pinging.”

I tuned my suit to five and the world went amber in my ear, a warm syrup of data that usually meant weather watchers were telling farmers when to pull their nets. Embedded in that syrup was a new tone. Not taps. Not the creak of our work. A bell. A bell struck once, then again, measured and slow, the sound an old city used to make when it wanted everyone to go to the square. Then a voice—not in my skull, not on the link, but in the general broadcast—the kind that made the hairs along my arms think about one day they might be called to be feathers.

“All wings,” it said. No gender. No human throat shapes. It had been made to be comfort. It did not comfort. “Do not adjust. Do not attempt cut. Maintain posture. Observe. Observe.”

Sana said, “That’s ground.”

Niobe said, “No it isn’t.”

I said, because the old code said I had to, “It’s not our ground.”

Something else moved across Crocus. Not a blade. A net, a lace thrown over the face of the star and hauled. Light dropped by a measurable breath. The Fleece tugged against my boots. The hinge sang. My suit chimed shrill with stress. The taps hammered C U T into my hands so hard that I felt it the way you feel someone pounding a door two floors down. The bell of spectrum five was replaced by the bark of a command channel I had no right to hear, ropey and tight with panic: “—repeat, we’re seeing—what is that—telemetry says—”

The official voice came back, trying for calm and missing: “Maintain posture. All wings maintain—”

Sana laughed once, a small animal sound, and said, “Rook.”

“Yes,” I said.

“If you were going to cut,” she said, “you couldn’t cut it all. You could cut a feather. You could feather a wing.”

“I am hearing stupid things,” I said. “I am hearing wind talk. I am hearing spectrum lie.”

“I want you to come back and eat a bun with me tonight,” she said. “I want you to sleep and despise the propaganda tomorrow. I want to watch Niobe beat you at storekeep math. I want the towers to hum in a way that tells me no one did anything heroic and none of us got a statue.”

“The old code says statues are just tall traps,” I said, because I loved her then for making me human and not a piece of wire.

“Let ground call it,” she said. “Let ground be the brave one.”

Something hard struck the Fleece five kilometers off like a thrown coin, a point impact that spread ripples through the silver and made the light do something you wouldn’t know it could do if you had only ever been underneath it—bend and focus and knife. A line of white slid down to the planet and wrote a word we could not read fast across a piece of ocean that should not have steamed. My suit threw warnings at me, and above all the warnings, above Sana and Niobe and the supervisors saying holds and wait and what is that, the old dumb code in the metal rapped three letters in a row so hard it left bruises.

R O O—

I pulled my hands from the hinge as if it had burned me. The tether snugged. The planet swung like a pendulum. Crocus swelled in my visor until it became nothing but a color.

“Rook,” Sana said. “Look. Look up.”

I did. The thing laying itself across Crocus—the lace, the net—resolved as more than the tricks of glare and fear. It was not pretty. It was not human. It was made of parallel lines and angled structures and it had the indecent smoothness of machine skin made for an environment that did not include us. It was so black it hurt. And down from it, along invisible threads, were lines like harpoons sinking into our mirror. The Fleece shivered like a drum. Somewhere far along the wing, a bridle snapped and made a sound through the net that would wake me up for the rest of my life.

“Observe,” said the voice again, that comfort shaped by someone who had never needed it. “Observe. Do not cut.”

My hands were already moving. Not on the hinge. Not in wildness. Into my pack, to the cutters. To the manual latch that separated a feather from its wing if it took a hit we couldn’t cushion. My body wanted to live. The Fleece wanted to live, if by living you mean continuing long enough to matter. The city would say we were vital, but not so vital that I should make better decisions than command.

“Rook,” Sana said again, voice small now with all its parts showing. “If we feather—if we drop—down there—”

“Down there we know how to catch,” I said, because that part was true. The towers had nets. The marsh had floodgates. The night speakers had warmth buried like seeds. We had practiced for parts falling from us.

“The towers—if we take the light wrong—”

“Ground can reshape,” I said. I didn’t know what I was saying. The tap-code hammered nothing helpful. The opposite voice said observe like a prayer. In front of me and every piece of carbon and the air in my suit and the blood in me, something we had never named tried to take hold of the star.

I hooked the cutter’s mouth on the latch and looked down and watched the planet’s bruise shine a little darker, and I thought of my mother at her table under a window that was all safety film and wire. I thought of the way Sana’s wife twitched in her sleep when the tower let go of a sigh and the way Niobe’s hands never stopped moving even when she sat still because she had been a child under a fish farm and had learned to make food out of ghosts. I thought of a boy at seven sleeping in a radio tower because up felt like relief. I counted the beats of my heart, because that was a system I understood.

“On three,” I said. “Sana, you have the other latch.”

“I see your cold bastard logic,” she said. “We will not be thanked for this.”

“Good,” I said, and we counted.

At two, the cutter slid. At three, the latch blew. The feather detached cleanly, obeying design, gracefully, almost primly. The feather drifted. The Fleece roared with light and loss. The thing over Crocus shivered its nets and flexed. The mirror I had just cut from the world turned very slowly under my boots, and the thread of its light, no longer obedient to our parameters, reached down and wrote a simple, terrible line across the night ocean that melted into steam and then was wind.

On the channel, command began to scream. The comforting voice told us to observe a last time and then cut out. Sana breathed in my ear like she had been holding it since the world was new. The taps stopped. For a moment everything, even fear, was very quiet.

“Okay,” Sana whispered. “Okay. We were either brilliant or monstrous.”

“Both,” I said. It came out like a cough.

In the time it took to think that, to be in all my own not-enough at once, I turned my head because I could not bear to look at whatever I had done—at whatever we had invited—and saw the thing over Crocus change its shape.

It was a mouth opening.

That was what my animal saw. I tried to make other geometries make sense of it; failed; came back to the idiot word. A mouth opening. In the direction of our night. And in that movement, in that first leisurely taking of our star, was a lifetime’s worth of chapters crouched and waiting.

Chapter One: The Morning That Wouldn’t Come

The morning was late. Not fashionably—stupefyingly. Dawn hung a street away and refused to cross the river.

Asha had known before she slid out of bed that something was wrong. The city’s hum carried a fractional hitch, like a skipped groove on an old recording. Holo-feeds jittered between frames. Nox drones made loops above the rooftops with a puzzled slowness, blinking as if they’d miscounted their own blinks. Out the window her apartment’s single pane held the skyline like a freckled film still: towers lit in sodium insomnia, the black river smooth as a flex sensor. East should have been softening, but the horizon stayed knife-black, pricked with satellite crawlers that crawled too deliberately.

She put a mug under the kettle anyway, and watched the steam curdle and hang as though it had become reluctant fog. When she touched her thumb-pad to the wall, her apartment’s reference meter flicked from green to amber.

“Dispatch,” she said, voice still sleep-rough.

“Already on it,” said Lale, who had been in Dispatch forever and would be there when time wound down to its last click. “Seven calls from Harbor spine to Eastclad district. Citygrid is reporting light latency anomalies along Vector 0-89 through 0-104. You seeing the same?”

“That’s my horizon,” Asha said. She made the kettle work harder, then gave up and drank plain water. Her own wall meter started to count a thing it usually only numbered once an audit: c-drag, the way the registry measured the world’s old, bright ruler slipping through someone’s fingers. “These aren’t micro-jitters. We’re losing daylight.”

“I’ve escalated to Class Three. Jaro’s already in the van.”

“I’ll meet him on the roof.” She grabbed the harness without thinking about it, little habits her muscles had learned: a quick clip that tethered her to a job that never quite held.

He was on the roof when she pushed through the access door, the fat morning of night sprawling over the river. Jaro looked as if the morning held no surprises. He always did; the man had the lidded eyes and rounded shoulders of someone who had taken on the job of moving the horizon by hand and found it a bit light for his tastes.

“Smell that?” he said.

Asha didn’t answer right away. She didn’t expect smell to carry data, but it did, a stitch of ozone and hot metal, and a faint, spiced sweetness like cardamom bread baking in a neighbor’s oven. Unauthorized geometry always smelled like something left too long in a place it didn’t belong.

“Somebody’s been cooking on our stove,” she said.

Jaro grunted, meaning assent. “Tea?”

“You know there’s no morning yet,” she said, but took the thermos anyway. The tea tasted like a circuit board had been flashed over an herb garden.

Below them the river had fallen strangely silent. Without morning, the ferries were stalled at their pilings, and the early runners in day-glow shoes were stuck at the promenade railing, their breath fog-globs suspended till they remembered how to dissipate. Eastclad’s glasslength towers reflected nothing but themselves. The only bright thing was the Municipal Clock perched on Government House, and even it ticked with a sluggish insistence, as if it had had to lean into each notch of time and push.

Asha flicked open the case that lay at Jaro’s boots. The Constant Registry didn’t fuss with glamor. Their kit was sturdy and old enough that pieces bore previous technicians’ names spelled out in fading paint marker. The Metronome was the centerpiece, a waist-high unit of nested rings and shifting segments, gyros thrumming in their elegant gimbals, a little brass plaque on one arm reading NOETHER LACE CO., YEAR 90. Inside its spinning heart a bluish bead of light beat steadily.

Asha strapped on the harness and clipped into the left arm of the device. Jaro clipped into the right with a grunt and set the Metronome humming. The bead brightened, casting a circle around their feet, a weird little island of clarity on the tar-paper rooftop.

“Vector?” Jaro said.

“Angle ninety-two,” Asha said, watching the bead respond to her words, the way it tugged toward the missing dawn like iron filings drawn under glass. “They’re pulling photons somewhere low. Not the big stuff. Just the easy hoses.”

“Probably municipal side siphon,” Jaro muttered. “Some rich idiot wants a longer night and thought he’d borrow it off the rest of us.”

Asha didn’t answer. There were plenty of rich idiots. There were also plenty of thieves who weren’t idiots at all, people who knew exactly how many minutes of luminosity the city could lose before commuters started getting into accidents, before the ferry captains refused to leave, before birds messed up their circadian rhythms and crapped all over the City Council’s patio, before people noticed in a way they wouldn’t forget. The Constant Registry existed because most people had never been taught that their lives ran on maintained measurements, that someone tended mass and charge and, on bad days, morning.

“Start the sweep,” she said.

Jaro pivoted the Metronome with both hands, and the gyros wound into an octave deeper, a sound that made the hair along Asha’s arms lift. The bluish bead split into three, then five, threads crossing like a cat’s cradle between the rings. They swung the device around until the threads tightened, all pointing toward Eastclad, toward the black notch between two towers that should have been pale glass by now.

The Registry’s van was idling below. They got the Metronome on its casters and grunted it into the elevator—Noether Lace had not designed it for vans, and Jaro swore at every threshold. On the street, people had begun to drift toward the river like it might teach them what was happening. The ferries’ horns let out long nervous calls that rippled against the sluggish air. A man in a bright office shirt demanded, loudly, if someone was going to fix the goddamn sun.

“We’re working on it,” Jaro said, not loudly at all, but the man heard something in his tone and backed off. A child with a prism on a string watched her rainbow stick in the prism’s heart and let out a little shriek of laughter, delighted. Her mother shushed her, eyes on her wrist, her wrist on the clock that wouldn’t quicken.

Jaro took the wheel. Asha stared at the edge of dawn like she could will it to move. The van’s dashboard console had three lights and a physical needle. The Constant Registry was allergic to software not nailed to bedrock. The needle was in the yellow and drifted periodically toward orange, like a nail paring around a magnet, each drift taking longer to recover.

“You ever miss it?” Jaro said.

“What?” Asha asked.

“Living somewhere where none of this matters.” He gestured expansively: the kit, the needle, the people whose faces were slowly wrinkling into fear. “Some rock on the fringe, no Noether lace in the sky, no gauge welders crawling over the weather like ants making a new queen.”

“You think those places are real,” Asha said. “They sound like stories old men tell in bars when they are too tired to be bitter and too bitter to be tired.”

“Stories have to come from somewhere,” Jaro said, turning left on Rivermile and muscling the van between a city bus and a courier swarm. “They don’t come after.”

Asha touched her wrist. The inside of her skin was a lattice of half-forgotten marks. She had grown up in a place that measured differently. Nothing about her bones showed it now. She said, “Let’s find the leak.”

They found it in a place that looked like money had sunk into the earth and hardened. Eastclad’s north corner was a thumb of real estate crowded with the kind of buildings that outsourced their own shadows to save weight: frontages of glass dense with embedded meta-pixels, steps that calculated an ascent for you and offered three. The Metronome’s threads knotted across a narrow alley with crudely charming iron balconies climbing one side. Asha liked that, almost. The knot had caught there like fishing line around a rusted hook.

They parked on a hydrant. Jaro hauled the Metronome around and Asha followed on the harness, feeling the thing’s tug build through her arms and spine. In the alley the air had a static prickle that pulled at her hair.

The door was unmarked. Asha could tell, by the way the street camera folded its gaze away, that it had permission and more than permission; the City’s watchers had been told, specifically, to pretend this part of the wall didn’t exist.

“You going to knock?” Jaro said, almost gently.

“Watch the needle,” Asha said. She pressed her palm against the door.

Sometimes unauthorized geometry wanted to be found. This wasn’t one of those days. The door was smart metal and dumb about wanting to tell secrets. It flowed under her palm without letting her through. She took her hand away and reached into the Metronome’s base for the gauge needle.

The needle looked like a knitting tool made to please a mathematician: a slender shaft with a three-tined fork at one end, a fan of delicate filaments at the other. Where it touched a surface, it made that surface remember what it was shaped to be. It wasn’t a lockpick. Picks forced old arrangements. The needle persuaded a door gently that its correct operation included opening for officers of the Constant Registry.

“Come on,” she said to the door. “We keep the lights on. You owe us.”

Something clicked. The door sighed inward.

The smell caught hard in her throat. Cardamom and circuit boards again, thickened by something like copper coins in her mouth. Light behaved badly inside. It leaned in the corners and refused to fill them; it pooled on the ceiling with a petulance that made the hair on Asha’s neck stay up. The lobby was stripped, furniture indentations in the carpet like fossils of rich people’s sofas. Black rectangles on the walls where things had hung. There were a dozen elevators with their numbers out and a single service stair yawning down.

“Someplace big,” Jaro said softly, like in a church or a museum. He wheeled the Metronome toward the stairs. It wanted down, into the building’s guts.

The first landing had a mural. It must have been commissioned by someone with a taste for the old romantic posters: a woman in blue looking up at a cabled bridge, her hair blown back like a flag. In fine print, small enough that a lawyer must have insisted on it, was a name that made Asha’s stomach turn and then tighten into something sharp: Adler & Co., Gaugebond Services.

Her mouth dried. “Jaro—”

“I know,” he said. “Keep moving.”

They moved. The Metronome pulled them like a dog eager toward a lure. At the bottom of the stairs there was a door where there shouldn’t have been, a door backed by more stairs going down, like the building had found a basement in the bedrock it wanted to hide.

“Registry,” Jaro said, voice pitched even. He had said that word into a hundred rooms like an apology. “If you are down there, and you have papers, now is an excellent time to wave them.”

Silence, then the hiss of the building’s air systems groaning to compensate for something small but significant. Jaro looked at her and raised his eyebrows: on three. They went down.

The hole in the world looked like an art installation someone had been too proud to leave unfinished. An oval, long as a ferry and half as wide, had been cut into the basement floor. The edges weren’t clean; they were stitched, a lace of gleaming calibration filaments anchored to the concrete by little hammered pins. Rings of devices circled the oval, delicate as insects, all blinking in a pattern that made Asha’s stomach try to do arithmetic. And above the hole hung the dawn.

It hovered like a single slow wave caught mid-break. The river beyond it gleamed slick, a ribbon of light trying to unfurl. The sun—no, not the sun, never the sun itself, just the scattering of it off air and particles and the city’s glass, the damp glitter of morning—hung like a print held up to a half-hearted reader. It wasn’t just light. Asha tasted it at the back of her tongue: warmth trying its best to be sweet.

“Class Five,” Jaro said, voice gone flat. It was an old Registry superstition to keep your voice empty when the world was too full. He let go of his end of the Metronome and stepped closer to the filigree of devices around the hole. “They’re running a localized metric bend. Narrow. Efficient. They’ve stacked it against the city’s anisotropy like they know our watch shift.”

“Feeding it into what?” Asha said, throat tight.

“Whatever they like costs the same. Money, time, protected computation, coffee that stays hot for days.” Jaro ran his hand over one of the filaments. It thrummed. “You can siphon light into anything that wants order.” He pointed at a standing cylinder made of triangular panes. Inside it, something darker than shadow spun in a poised slow storm. “That? You could run a walled garden in there the size of a metropolis.”

Asha’s skin prickled. The cylinders, the lace, the stitched edges—none of that hurt like a name in her chest. Adler. The man who had trained her to read the needles. The man who had taught her, kneeling on a rooftop when she was wanted by three different jurisdictions for thefts that sounded like fairy tales, that the world was not a machine that ran on its own. You had to crank it. Wipe the oil. Wind the rests. Whisper to the bearings. For three years he had taught and sworn and told stories about walls that had held lines of force so old the first names for them were myth. Then he had not said goodbye, and he had not left a forwarding number, and he had taken one of the Registry’s hearts with him.

“Check the keystones,” she said, because work was a way not to be in this room with that name writ like a stamp under her ribs.

Jaro nodded and crouched, heavy, his spine like a hinge that needed grease. Keystones were the physical declarations that said this part of the world used these values. You could rub them with your thumb in certain places in the city—the base of a bridge, the handrail of a stair—and feel the assertion there, patient as bedrock: We’ve agreed to mass like this, time like this, light like this, across this much distance, for this much time, by and between these parties. You could break a law and argue your way through court; you broke a keystone and the world itself got offended.

These keystones were wrong. They weren’t declarations. They were citings—a slick legal hack, something that borrowed the authority of a keystone and linked it elsewhere. Jaro traced a fingernail under the carving and cursed.

“Cross-bound. They wrote their authority out to a ghost precinct,” he said. “Classic Adler move. Fuck.”

“I thought he was gone,” Asha said softly.

“Gone and tired aren’t the same thing,” Jaro said. “You know that.”

She did. She had left a city before because its gravity had a particular bitterness at certain hours no one else seemed to notice. Leaving had not undone that bitterness; she carried it with her like sour water in her bones.

A tiny sound shuffled under the machines’ steady hum. Asha straightened. The Metronome’s bead faltered, then brightened. Somewhere plastic crinkled.

“In the file cabinets,” Jaro said. “People always forget the paper.” It was one of his other old lines. He turned, slow, and Asha fanned out with the gauge needle in her palm. Between two cylinders and a rack of silent servers, someone crouched under a desk.

“Registry,” Jaro said again.

“I have a card,” said the person. Her voice was older than her hands, which were young, and shaking. She slid out from under the desk on her hip, one knee snagged on a cable. She wore the pinafore of a lab with no name stitched on its breast. Her hair was buzzed to the scalp and dyed a cheap pink that had washed out to cotton. She carried a wallet in her palm like a talisman. The card was a real physical identity, which already made Asha distrust her. Fake identities avoided paper because paper could forgive a lot and forget very little.

“Sarah Wooten,” Jaro read, squinting. “Consultant.”

“Contract,” Sarah corrected, as if that mattered, then swallowed. “It isn’t wrong,” she said. “It’s not. It’s within allowances. We’re not touching raw; it’s all scatter. It’s harm free.”

“It always is,” Jaro said gently, and Sarah flinched as if he’d struck her.

“We have a keystone,” she added, desperately, and pointed. “Adler—”

“Doctor Adler is retired,” Jaro said, all softness gone. “He is not authorized to set contract keystones under the Registry. You know that. Even if you didn’t, you know this is a Class Five modification on a municipal district without so much as a mention in morning briefs.”

Sarah’s breath went fast. She looked very young then. Asha could taste the cardamom again. Somewhere systems ticked over as night tried to find a way to be morning again and discovered someone had put a fence up. Asha took Sarah’s wrist and turned it to read the imprint under her skin, the little pattern that said which schools had trained her and what she wasn’t allowed to sign. She had the marks of a cheap education and an expensive mentor, a bad combination when you added hunger.

“What are you doing with it?” Asha said, because puzzles were better than punishment.

Sarah swallowed. Her throat worked against Asha’s fingers. “It’s a hedge,” she said, voice going monotone like she wasn’t allowed to say certain words. “We’re building shelter.”

“For whom,” Jaro said flatly.

Sarah glanced reflexively at the dark spinning cylinder. The little air of arrogance she’d been clinging to—that she had a card, that she had language—she puffed it up again, and it failed to cover anything. “For anyone who can afford it,” she said, bitterly. “And for people we owe.”

Asha’s mind snagged. The word rang in it. Owe. Adler had a heavy theology about debt. He had made it sound noble, the binding of yourself to the things you declared true.

“What’s the design?” Asha said. “Let me see it.”

Sarah didn’t move for a moment. Then she let a little laugh out that was more like a choke. She crawled to the nearest console on her knees, because the buzz of the lace made standing a negotiation, and laid her palm on an old reader. A bank of screens lit. The design came up like a flower opening, layers of schematic petals, geometry unfolding into hardware. Asha leaned in.

The world sings it’s laws, Adler had told her once, and some of us can hear harmonies. We can add a counterpoint. The trick is to make it pretty enough that no one notices you, and the world doesn’t notice you either.

She recognized the countersong before she read the math. It was in the tilt of a lattice, the way the lace spidered to hug certain eddies and avoid others, the patience in the anchoring. Adler had used this signature on their first illegal patch, a tiny, harmless thing that had made a courtyard’s worth of wind obey rules old trees remembered and new tenants never knew. They had been very drunk and very proud and very stupid.

“Jaro,” she said softly. “It’s his.”

“I know,” Jaro said. He had moved to the edge of the oval and was watching the glued-up dawn as if it might start talking. “He’s crawling in bedrock on our side of town again.” He rubbed his chin, eyes suddenly winter-cold. “We pull it? We can, you know. We rip up the stitching, call it a loss, and morning comes like nothing happened.”

Asha looked at Sarah. Sarah’s eyes were big and pinned on Asha’s face as if they could fish forgiveness out of it with a glance. She looked at the spinning cylinder and at the console readout that measured capacity in units that had been borrowed from an old religion. Out the rim of the spangled oval, a stray ferry’s horn, very far and very determined, called out for a pilot.

“You made a shelter?” she said again.

“Storms are coming,” Sarah whispered to the floor. “Something is wrong up higher than we get to fix. He said—” She cut herself off, as if a contract had caught her tongue. “He said to prepare an option.”

The Registry had seen the papers, the memos buried in budgets: the little upticks in cosmic rays, the persistent strangeness in the halo those rays cast. Some said the sun was entering a bellicose cycle. Some said the interstellar medium was getting teeth. A few whispered counter–pirate radio that the constants were being arbitraged by entities who had stopped pretending to be divine some centuries back. Asha knew better than to say any of that out loud where keystones could hear.

“Of course storms are coming,” Jaro said, calm. “Storms always come. That’s why we have the house we share.”

Sarah’s gaze darted to the cylinder, then away. “What if the house burns?” she whispered.

Jaro opened his mouth—probably to make a speech Asha had heard him make in three different languages and on one level of atmosphere she hadn’t known a human throat could endure—and Asha put her hand very gently on his bicep.

“Hold,” she said before he could make loyalty taller than people could climb.

Asha turned to the lace, and to the oval that held the shape of a morning, and to the console that sang a familiar harmony. “We’re not tearing this up like we’re gods,” she said. “We’re not gods. We’re gardeners.”

She took up the gauge needle and slipped between two filaments like a needle into skin. The world’s hum grew in her fingers till it sang in her joints. She found an anchoring pin with the cosmological equivalent of gloved hands, and teased it free with a lover’s care. Light shifted. The pasted dawn spilled half an inch farther into the room and caught in the Metronome’s rings like a bird hitting a window.

“Easy,” Jaro warned, as if she were the one who didn’t know the difference between a scar and a bleed. He was very close to her now, his breath a warm human thing in air that had become math.

She pulled another pin. Light flooded another inch. Outside, on the river, a hundred people inhaled their first bright breath of morning. Asha felt it like a tide under her skin.

“We’re going to unbind this slowly,” she said to Sarah without looking up. “We’ll let the city have back what’s hers. And then you are going to take me to Adler.”

Sarah made a sound that might have been Yes and might have been a swallow.

“And if he doesn’t want to be found,” Jaro said softly.

Asha smiled without teeth. The gauge needle nestled into the next pin like it had been made to fit. She had made enough noises like that first man had demanded—like please and sorry and no charge and next time— and she knew when not to make them. “Then he can explain his shelter to the night corps while the Registry adds his name to the litany of debts.”

She pulled the third pin.

Across the river, over the ferries and the quay, morning tried again. This time, it remembered how. The first rays broke over the towers like an apology, and people who had never thought about the price of light made a sound like gratitude.

Behind her, very faint, as if it were a piece of code that had learned how to be coy, the Metronome’s bead flickered, then steadied.

Asha kept working, and the city remembered to breathe. All the while, under the hum of machines and the soft animal sounds Jaro made when he concentrated, she could hear a counterpoint threading the air. It had the patient cadence of a man she had loved for his sentences and hated for his sutures.
