She smiled again, and this time there was a little tooth in it. If Adler was placing shelters in her city, he would also have had the courtesy—or the arrogance—to lay a trail for anyone who could read his harmonies. He had taught her his music.

She finished pulling the last pin. The room tipped. Morning poured in like a bowl being righted. The oval collapsed into a glimmer of warmth on her knuckles, and then it was gone. The cylinders hummed down. Silence caught, surprised, then broke apart into a dozen small sounds: a drip, a breath, a little gasp from Sarah as if she’d been underwater and had finally remembered how to inhale.

“Go get the van,” Asha said to Jaro, who might have been about to say something moral and kind. “We need to tag this place and send a crew. And then we’re going to take a walk.”

“Where,” he said, though she thought he already knew.

Asha bent and pressed her palm over the place where dawn had hung. The concrete was warm as a living thing. The signature Adler had left behind shimmered under her hand like a vein under skin.

“Where the city keeps its old promises,” she said.

He was waiting, she knew now, not because he wanted to be found but because he couldn’t help laying his lines over old stone. That was the thing about harmonies: they preferred certain notes, certain shapes. He’d always been sentimental. Unforgivable. Predictable.

Asha stood and rolled her shoulders. Behind her, outside, a thousand kettles decided to boil at once. The ferries cleared their throats. The rich idiots on the balconies blinked and reached for sunglasses. A girl and her prism made rainbows again and this time the rainbows came out of the toy and not out of a mouth that wanted something it shouldn’t.

Asha tucked the gauge needle into her belt, touched the Metronome’s ring till it thrummed in a comfortable key, and walked toward the stairs.

On the way up she passed the mural again. The woman in blue looked out at the bridge with a face so carefully painted it had almost never been real. People had written in the margins, tiny pencil notes that spoke, quietly and privately, of love affairs and chemistry problems and recipes. Adler’s signature was not there; he wouldn’t have been that obvious. But someone had drawn a small bird in one corner that you could miss if you were in a hurry. The bird had a thread in its beak.

Well, Asha thought. All right.

She didn’t run. There was a rhythm to everything and even when you were chasing, you kept time. At the mouth of the alley the morning came around the corner like a friend you hadn’t expected to see today. Asha squinted and laughed helplessly. The light was cruel and honest and it showed everything: the dirt on her sleeves, the tears on Sarah Wooten’s cheeks, the Metronome’s oil smear on Jaro’s jaw. It made the city brand new for the thirty-two-thousandth time.

Lale had the van’s back doors open and a roll of Registry tape she was slapping against her thigh like a metronome with a temper. She looked at Asha’s face and didn’t ask questions yet.

“Tag it,” Asha said. “I’m going to see a man about a shelter.” She glanced back at Sarah, who was trying very hard to look like a consultant who deserved her consultancy. “You’re coming too.”

“Can I call a lawyer?” Sarah asked.

Asha smiled at her, slow. “You can call anyone you want. The keystones already heard you. They’ll testify.”

Sarah contemplated that and closed her mouth with a little shudder, like someone swallowing a bone.

Jaro slapped the van twice. “Where?” he said again, but now his voice had something like a tune in it.

Asha turned her face east. The bridge was there, the cabled length of it like a stringed instrument that had outlived its composer. It had old keystones in its heart that had been scribed by hands that could make stone remember centuries. There was a place under its south tower where the Registry’s oldest promises had been whispered and the world had nodded consent. If you were sentimental and arrogant, you would lace your shelter to that. You would do it because you believed in continuity and in theft.

“The River House,” she said. The words felt like a code unwrapping in her mouth. “He’ll want the River House.”

Jaro rolled his neck. “You ever notice,” he muttered, “how when things are about to get difficult, you get cheerful?”

“No,” she said, lying. She did know. It wasn’t cheer. It was the bright tightness of a string tuned to a key that fit her hand. She was going to have to tell Adler he had chosen his notes wrong. Then she was going to have to choose some herself.

They got in the van. Behind them, the morning finished arriving. The city did what it had always done in the face of miracles: it started making coffee. On the passenger seat, the Metronome’s bead kept time.

Somewhere in the tangle of Bridge and law, a man who had taught her how to open a door without making the world mad was going to hear a knock. Asha slid the window down and let light burn her cheeks, and the river flashed like a busy witness, and the Constant Registry’s needle quivered and settled.

On good days the sky was only empty. On bad days, it remembered to whisper.

Outwatch K-37 breathed around me in clicks and hums and the soft fatigue of recycled air. The station was a loop of dark metal and scaffolding, a spiderweb anchored to a lump of dirty ice in the Kuiper. The ice had a name and a catalog number; the station did too. I called it Kettle because it piped heat like a little kettle would, endlessly trying to warm a room that could never be anything but cold. The name stuck to the diagnostics console and the maintenance drone and the cartridge printer; on my lonely days I stuck it to myself. Kettle and Ash, keeping watch on the void.

I had a hand wrapped around a cup of tea gone lukewarm and unremarkable when the monitor bled a vertical ribbon of color across my peripheral display. I almost missed it. Thirty hours of drift and drift and recalibration and listening to not much had sanded my senses down to stubs. Kettle was good enough to notice for me. It chittered within the wall, a bare rattle of pinions. A light went amber.

“Don’t get up,” I told no one, and set the cup on the sticky ring it had worn into the panel months ago.

The ribbon had the look of something that didn’t belong: narrow, bright, and too polite to be honest. It cut diagonally across the spectrum analysis from 1.2 gigahertz to just past 1.5, like a skid mark through an otherwise smooth frost. Natural sources smear and splutter. Jupiter hisses like a leaky kettle. Pulsars do metronome tricks. Quasars burn stately. This looked like a deliberate hand had dragged a brush through my sky.

I double-checked the calibrations. K-37’s array petals were unfolded and backlit, skeletal black on black, like spiders tasting the cold. The front-end was a lattice of induction and the kind of filters you can only grow in vacuum. Out here, two days’ velocity beyond Neptune, the half-frozen dust keeps your fantasies modest. We listened mostly, and sometimes we moved a net to catch a localized leak, because moving slowly and catching leaks is all that keeps us alive.

Eight years after the Quiet Accords, we all grew up as Keepers of the Dark. We stopped yelling at the universe and started whispering to each other with fiber and tightbeams and coded flashes of light stitched across cislunar space. The big dishes and transmitters grew quilts and became watchtowers. The worse parts of me still missed the shout. I had been a kid with a homebuilt antenna in a drafty orbital that rattled like a piano. I knew the thrill of hearing my own signal bounce back from a moon. Then someone lit a beacon with a bandwidth like a hymn and the Choir answered, and the world learned to put a finger to its lips.

“Kettle,” I said, “suppress housekeeping. Give me the band.”

I spread the narrow window over three screens, stretched it until the pixels looked like fields in snow. The ribbon broke into a comb of teeth, a chirp within a chirp. The teeth weren’t evenly spaced. Nothing in the sky is actually straight; it just looks like it until you look close. I looked close enough to feel the first prickle up my arm.

Chirps are useful. They carry their own timing. They’re also almost always a human idea.

“K-37 to Jansky Gate,” I said, voice low out of reflex. The cabin had mics in it for quicknotes, but all transmission off-station went down a fiber spool as thick as my thumb, a thread we’d paid a monastery to weave along a route of rocks and ice. The Order of the Coil did God’s work, if God was silence. Coilers wore suits patched with cloth impregnated with metamaterial mesh. They could shroud a transmitter the way you could smother a candle, and they did it with a kind of grave reverence that made you either want to hug them or punch them.

A transceiver on the hardline chirruped back the Gate’s handshake. The laser in its vault would be writing my message onto a beam brighter than sin, pointed exactly where it needed to be and nowhere else. The Mirrors clustered around the Sun like a crown to catch those beams and fold them inward. No broad emission. No spillover. No shine. The system had been built out of fear and ingenuity, like most of the things that survived.

“Jansky here,” said a voice I knew, fuzzed by encryption dithers. “Go ahead, K-37.”

“Varga, are you on the desk?”

A pause meant a shrug I couldn’t see. “Rotation,” he said. “What have you got for me?”

“A whisper,” I said, because that word was difficult to say without irony. “From the black. H-band, slanted comb, about a minute periodicity. Started three minutes ago. You tell me you’re hearing it too.”

“We’re a gate, Ash, not an ear.”

I rolled my eyes. We both knew Gates ran their own shadow arrays, and we both liked pretending they didn’t. A greater share of people slept better at night believing the watch was decentralized. It was, mostly, but redundancy makes liars out of us all.

Varga made a thoughtful little sound. “Logs are picking up a few anomalies out of your sector. Weak. Could be your own gear playing clever. Could be Jupiter horns scattering off interstellar dust.”

“That’s a lot of could.” I pinched and twisted the display. Teeth became primes. The comb’s spacing wasn’t arbitrary; it was like stepping stones, distances that meant something. The pattern had a flavor I’d never forgotten. “Put this together,” I said. “Zero temperature drift. No galactic background lines under it. The slope’s wrong for scattering.”

“K-37, what’s the amplitude?”

I drifted for a moment, forgetting to answer because I’d seen something that made my mouth go dry. I leaned in until the nose of my suit touched the screen.

There are ways of talking that aren’t words. The order in which you choose numbers. The gaps between beats. The choices you make when you think you’re being clever and nobody’s watching. I had spent years being clever when nobody official was watching. The first time you thread a signal into the hiss of cosmic microwave background and have a friend on the other side tease it out with a length of code you spun together over beer, you think your purest language is mathematics. But mathematics has accents. After a while, your own comes back to you like a family trait.

Three of the teeth in the comb were grouped too tightly. The group lengths were 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, just as they were supposed to be if you were telling anyone paying attention that you knew primes. But someone had added 13 and then 17 like a laugh at a funeral. When we were kids, we’d done that for luck.

“Ash?” Varga said. “You still with me?”

“Amplitude is… low,” I said. “Low, deliberate, probably aimed.”

“Directionality off what?”

I pulled the station’s parallax and cross-correlation tools up. The arrays had memory enough to hold several minutes of sky, always writing and rewriting, and I scrubbed back and forth through the fresh smear of noise. I had three antennas in a long irregular T. Time-of-arrival told me the three beasts of the T and the recurrences were out-of-phase just enough to estimate a direction. It pointed not at any of the bright familiar things, and my stomach did a few unhelpful flips when I realized it pointed at nothing. Not even nothing; it pointed inside the boundary of the array coverage, inside the keep’s own ring.

“K-37?” Varga said, more careful now. “Say it.”

I said it. “Internal to the array. Source within fifty kilometers.”

Everything shrank and telescoped until it was me and breathing and the way my bare ankle felt where the suit had ridden up. Fifty kilometers is a long walk and a short laugh. Out here, within the hush nets and the coil droppings and the spools of light-catchers, an emitter could hide like a bird in rafters. You could be broadcasting at microamperes and still lay a fingerprint on the sky.

The meter ticked up one trivial division. The pattern repeated. The chirp slid and set and slid again.

Varga swore. Then he got the calm that meant he was already assembling a tasking order. “Okay,” he said. “Okay. Ash, we’re putting a quiet warrant on your sector. Who else is on your station?”

“Just me,” I said.

“You got a net?”

“I’ve got two folds,” I said. In the locker in bay C was a pair of dragons rolled tight as hay bales. You threw them from a distance and they unfurled in the vacuum and became blankets that drank radio down to the noise. Coil tech. The Order sold them to us at a religious markup and told us to treat them like relics. I had once wrapped myself in one during a bad power night to see if I could feel the quiet. I had. It was like being buried in snow. “K-37 has internal drones Beta and Delta. Beta’s hauling ice. Delta is asleep unless I wake it. It doesn’t like me.”

“You two share that quality,” Varga said. “Can you localize the source tight enough to dispatch?”

“I will,” I said, not admitting the pressure floating into my chest like a held breath.

“K-37, do not transmit. Do not jam. You know the drill.”

Jamming is a broadcast by another name. The Accord did not make special exceptions for good intentions. Outwatch stations kept their teeth very politely hidden. When we had to bite, we bit in the old ways, with mass and nets and motion.

“K-37?” Varga said, softer. “Ash. If you need it, I can gate a Coil squad to you inside eight hours. It’ll cost me six favors and a cruelty. Say it.”

The station hummed. The comb ticked. I took in a breath and held it, trying to anchor myself to the air. Out here, eight hours is an afternoon. Eight hours is also enough to blow our discreet little leak into the sky so wide some hungry thing might notice it, or to tug whoever was doing this into a hole so deep we’d never pull them back out.

“Give me one,” I said. “Don’t burn your favors yet. I’m going to take a look.”

“Ash—”

“I know the drill,” I said. “I won’t talk. I won’t jam. I’ll smother it if I can. I’ll mark it if I can’t. I’ll report by line and lash and curse.”

“You always curse anyway,” Varga said. A pause. A sigh. “Fine. Quiet warrant is yours. The dark bless your nerves.”

“Go kiss a Mirror,” I said, and cut the line.

I sat with the comb a moment longer. I touched the glass; the glass was not cold, but I knew the cold lived an inch beyond it, endlessly patient. I needed to work. I needed to move. I needed to not continue staring at the pattern like a child at a flame because a part of me recognized the way the chirp slid and set and slid. Not just the primes added like a cough of laughter, but the one little hiccup two-thirds through the cycle and the way the baseline dipped and recovered. If mathematics had accents, this one was mine.

When the Choir answered, my little sister Mia was eighteen and still calling me Ash because we’d spent our childhood watching things burn in the brown atmosphere of northern habitats and been scolded for it. Embers stick to you. The day the beacon sang, Mia had a transmitter under her bed and a coil of copper she’d soldered herself, and she was smarter than me about power supply but worse at politics. She sent a beep, just one, because she could. We all did dangerous things to prove we were alive. She said later it wasn’t her beep that mattered. It wasn’t any one. It was all of them together. A kind of chorus.

It isn’t a good metaphor to have in your head when you hear a comb like this one.

“Kettle,” I said, and the drone uncurled from where it had snuggled into its recharging cradle. It looked like a crab designed by a minimalist. Eight legs, a bowl of tools under a tinted blister of sensory equipment. It tapped the hatch with two feet and flared its antenna, impatient.

“Warm Delta,” I said. “Set Beta to hold course and keep piping ice. No interruptions. Open bay C and pulse my suit heat. Lock the array orientation. Put a ribbon on this bastard and don’t lose it if it dives. Tell me if amplitude changes more than two percent.”

I drifted through the hatch and down the spine of the station. Outwatch K-37 was built by people who wanted to waste as little mass as possible. That made it hard and straight and without comfort. The bay smelled like burned plast and iron. I popped the locker and the dragons stared at me with their zero faces. I slung one across my shoulder and felt its weight pretend to exist.

Delta grumbled awake in its housing and unfolded into a long, articulated fish, painted black like the rest of my life. It liked some people and it disliked me for reasons that made sense to it. I fed it a tasking packet anyway and it flicked the end of its tail once in disgust. I could work with that.

The source was somewhere within the station’s perimeter. That perimeter was a cloud of calibration drones, a trill wire of catchline, the array petals themselves, and a net of fibers that carried my whispers to the Gate. The fibers shivered sometimes with microimpacts; Coil tech made them self-healing in the way nothing ever really is. You patched and cursed and patched again. You learned to feel the difference between a real break and a sulk.

My displays returned the solution like a little cartoon. The intersecting arcs of time-of-arrival put the origin of the chirp at a point just beyond Petal Two, close to a maintenance node that had the unlovely designation twig-2/green-15. The twig had been deployed six months ago as a range marker for Beta, and I’d never bothered to rename it. I’d meant to. I’d meant to do all sorts of kind human things for the sake of my own mind and I hadn’t.

“Twig two,” I said, and my tongue stuck to the roof of my mouth.

The twig was nothing but a cylinder of printed foam wrapped around a spool of reflective mesh and a little solar patch for the LED that blinked whenever Beta needed to find its way home. If you were lazy, you could fold a lot of clever into a cylinder of foam.

There were excuses to go out. There were also reasons not to. The first reason not to was that the station liked me alive. The second was that if someone had coaxed my array into singing against its will, they were either very clever, very desperate, or very stupid, and all three were dangerous.

I tucked the dragon more securely and slid into the wasp.

The wasp is what you get when you strap a few dozen orientation jets, a thick wedge of battery, and a little seat together and promise yourself you’re not going to die doing something foolish. It had grabbed hold of me more times than I wanted to count, once literally. There was a dent in the starboard fairing where I had hit the intake grill during a drill gone clumsy and I had never fixed it because I had never told anyone, and I told myself each month that I liked the dent’s reminder.

I sealed up and the suit’s hum shifted pitch. The checklist winked green down my right eye. Kettle crabbed into its docking slot behind me and muttered about torque. Delta slithered out the other door in annoyance. The air bled, thin and then nonexistent, and the pop in my ears was an old friend. Outside was the undisinfected night.

K-37’s underside expanded below me like the skeleton of a whale with a lightbulb stuck in its skull. The ice rock glinted under lattice shadow. The array petals looked gentle from here, but I’d seen what their edges could do to a glove. I ghosted the wasp over the spindly forest of them, breathing in time with the chirp I couldn’t hear but that my gut had started to believe it could. Varga used to tell me I anthropomorphized the sky to keep myself from drifting. He wasn’t wrong.

“Delta,” I said. “Rendezvous at twig two. Keep your distance from the node. Scan for structural additions. Scan for energy that isn’t ours. Do not ping unless I tell you.” In training they teach you to keep your words simple when you’re talking to machines with histories. Kettle beeped disapprovingly and extended a leg to tap the dragon bundle as if reminding me it existed.

The twig blinked for me from the darkness. It didn’t blink in the rhythm I had programmed. It blinked slowly, insistently, a pulse not quite synced with the chirp in the comb. The LED threw a little cone of discolored light. I pictured fingers in my hair. I pictured a child tapping a table. I pictured nothing, because if you start seeing children at the edge of your eyes out here, you go back inside.

Delta hissed half a breath and flattened its fins. It liked the blinking less than I did.

I flared the wasp and killed my forward motion. My suit made a soft noise I heard more through my ribs than my ears. I felt the thin tug of the safety tether as the catchline engaged. The station liked to keep us from flying off into a story someone else would have to finish.

“K-37,” I said, knowing the fence would carry it down line to Varga whether I wanted him to listen or not. “At twig two. Confirming modification of blink pattern. Physical observations follow. Node carries additional mass at base. Small. The kind of small that’s the same as clever.”

Kettle stiffened on the wasp’s back, its sensory head swiveling. Delta sent me a frame of image, high contrast and angry. Something had been glued to the twig. Not just glued; mounted. Someone who cared had been here. The mount had intricate little cavities that helped it ride thermal swells. Whoever had done it had not wanted the thing to come loose. A pod the size of my thumbnail opened and closed like a tiny heart.

The wasp’s diagnostics made a huffing sound. Kettle tapped me again, harder.

I leaned forward as if my eyes moved time. The pod wasn’t open when the blink was off. It wasn’t open when it was on. It opened in the space just before the LED brightened and shut just after. Sixty times a minute, no more, no less. Enough to kiss the sky. Enough to lay a comb you couldn’t see.

I reached back. My hand brushed cloth. The dragon inside the bag was heavier than it had any right to be; materials that denied radio also had opinions about inertia. I pulled a little, just a look to calm my brain. The mesh inside was the color of shadow. I told myself I could throw it and wrap this twig like you wrap a sleeping child. I told myself my aim was good.

“Ash,” Varga’s voice said, too loud in my head. Fear makes everything too loud. “Report.”

“I’ve got a parasitic emitter,” I said. “Piggybacking on twig two. Micro. Thermal snail. Blinking in coherence with the marker. Eating our time. It’s singing into the far lobe every beat.”

Varga had the grace not to tell me what I already knew. Even at that amplitude, if you keep kissing the dark you’ll leave your scent on it. The sky is big. The sky is patient. The sky doesn’t care, but the things in it might.

“I’m going to cover it,” I said. “Dragon one.”

“Ash,” Varga said. He did not tell me not to miss. He did not tell me that if I missed I should keep missing all the way into the night.

“Save the Coil,” I said, and the words tried to sound like courage. Kettle, to my left, rustled. Delta thrummed a quaternion of worry. My hands were steady, which felt like a betrayal.

I popped the ties. There was nothing in the universe except for the blink, the comb, the way the pod opened its mouth like a shivering fish and closed again around a whisper. The dragon flexed in my hands, all stored potential and vicious courtesy. I had named it Persimmon when I had pretended to be a person who did that kind of naming. I hadn’t said the name out loud yet. It lay against the crooks of my fingers as if it knew.

“Throwing night,” I said, because sometimes the things the Coil said could be beautiful even if they made you tired.

I let it go.

It unfurled like a memory in a warm bath. Mesh in vacuum acts like it’s underwater. It billowed, took a breath, caught the faint push of the wasp’s exhale and the twig’s own little heat, and wrapped itself around the node with perfect ungainly grace. It missed the pod by the space of my heart and then what little atmosphere in my suit heard me swear made the mesh worry itself to the left and settle.

The blink went out.

The comb stuttered. It did not stop. It phase-shifted, bared its teeth, and slid. I stared at the mesh and at the station, because sometimes when you do the right thing the thing you wanted to kill will only get slightly less alive.

“Ash,” Varga said, voice very quiet. “What’s the signal do?”

“It’s… adapting,” I said. “No, not that. The node had a partner. The source isn’t single-point.”

Delta fed me another frame. Twenty meters away, tucked into shadow under the petal’s hinge where my human eyes would have let it go, there was another glue job. This one didn’t kiss the LED. This one kissed the thermal noise I made every time I heated water for my tea, every time the station let its seams creak.

Kettle’s head swiveled to look at me. The bastard had amusement in the angle of his antennae.

“Keep going,” Varga said. “Keep covering. Keep calling.”

“I will,” I said.

The comb hiccuped. The little skip two-thirds of the way through — the one like a laugh — fell briefly out of rhythm and then came back as if it had heard me notice it.

My throat tightened. That skip, that tiny human mistake, had a name. It wasn’t just an accent. It was deliberate. It was the kind of signature you wrote into something if you wanted someone particular to know it was you.

Ash, the comb said, and did not say. Ash, are you there?

I pressed my helmet against the glass. Outside the mesh drank and drank. Inside, the station pulsed and thunked and hummed like a heart that loved me because it had been paid to. The universe did not care. The Gate did. Varga did, and Mia had once upon a time. My air tasted of boiled metal and the memory of flowers.

I could have told myself I’d imagined it. You can hear anything if you want to badly enough. That’s why we have instrumentation and protocols and Orders and Accords. But the skip came again in precisely the interval I knew it would if it had been made by the one person who had shared a solder iron with me under our mother’s flickering lamp. The one person who had built a transmitter under a bed and taught me that sometimes you talk to the dark because you don’t know how not to.

“Ash?”

Not Varga. Not a human voice. Not a voice at all. A pattern shaped like my name, threaded into the slur between teeth in a comb that was being careful not to be a song.

“Don’t transmit,” Varga said, as if he thought for a stupid second that I might. As if he thought for a second he needed to say it. Bless him. We all have our prayers.

I put my palm flat against the glass and said nothing.

Far away, a whisper kissed the night and withdrew. I threw the second dragon. The mesh ballooned and billowed, and the blink under it died like a bad idea.

“K-37,” I said, my mouth dry as if I’d been drinking silence like grit. “Second node covered. Signal’s attenuated sixty-two percent. There are more. There are always more. We need Coil. We need a body.”

“You’ll have it,” Varga said. “Hold.”

“I’ll hold,” I said.

I could feel the station vibrate with its own discomfort, the way living things do when their skin is touched. I could feel Kettle be still and Delta be angry and the comb be clever. I could feel the shape of a name written into a waveform like a child’s scrawl into the fog of a window. It could have been anyone. It was no one. It was everyone. It was someone.

The universe was a room with the air sucked out. On good days, that meant peace. On bad days, that meant you heard your name when there was nothing there to say it. I hung in the harness of my wasp with the dragon’s empty tie drifting in slow arcs and told myself I had all the time in the world. I had to.

Far off, under another petal, something blinked. There was just enough light to see the hint of a glue seam, the gray shine of a little stitched machine opening and closing its mouth to taste the dark.

“Ash?”

I swallowed, and the sound of it was the only thing I allowed myself to answer. Then I pushed the wasp forward, one hand on the throttle, the other closing around another length of night.

Aya bought her first minute when she was nine; the memory tasted like orange ice and thunder.

It had been a smuggler’s minute, siphoned from a dead captain who had seen the nightside of Neptune roll like a slow bruise beneath his ship. When Aya pressed the spool to her tongue her mouth filled with frost and the low, crackling sense of electricity living somewhere within her ribs. For a heartbeat she was not a kid sleeping in a pressurized crate behind her mother’s tea stall but a man with a ship on the edge of dark water so wide it could swallow centuries. She came back heaving, eyes wet, the laughter of passing dockhands threaded with static. That was when the world stopped being a map of ports and corridor shortcuts and became a mesh of minutes, of stolen seconds with flavors and textures—memories that had weight if you stacked enough of them in the right direction.

She learned how to take them. How to coax them out of old neural prairies and fix them in the little amber coils that the market called spools and the stations called contraband. She learned to sort viable minutes from spoilage and to avoid the gilded ones, the ones too polished to be true. Hacks bought dreams; her clients bought proof.

On the day Titan’s sky turned the color of tea that’s been forgotten on a burner, Aya was hired to find a last minute.

She found Orlov where he always was: at the mouth of Hangar Twelve, coat collar up against the gusts of methane haze that leaked past the seals, staring at the way the orange light pooled on the floor. He had a face like someone had practiced lies there until they got them right.

“The hospice cluster,” he said without preamble. “Palinode. Old ghost orbit, above Kraken Mare. Its Cantor is still live, and so is one of the patients. Reiko Sagara. A minute from her last real flight before she docked. Pull it and bring it to me before tomorrow’s transit window.”

Aya let the weight of it sit. Palinode wasn’t illegal—nothing as simple as that. It was the terminal trailhead where people went when they preferred to cross the last valley in a cocoon of memory and gentle chemicals, drums of heat pumping into their capsules as Titan’s cold pressed the hull. It was also not on any of the permissible lists for unauthorized approach.

“What’s Sagara to you?” Aya asked.

Orlov’s smile didn’t reach his eyes. “Reiko Sagara is what she did to a set of tunnels under Neptune’s nightside that no one believes exists. She loved geography more than laws. She took something with her when she checked in. I need that something, and she strapped it into a minute because she knew there were people like me. And you.”

“Near Neptune?” Aya’s mouth went dry remembering the taste of that first second owned. “We should all want to live forever.”

“We already do, in pieces,” Orlov said, gesturing vaguely in the direction of the million eyes watching them from the station’s system. “You’ll be paid in blind credit, and you’ll get a filter to scrub whatever scorch they’ve wrapped around the minute. There will be scorch. Palinode is on Shen-K’s maintenance schedule. They will notice they’ve lost one of their little boxes even if the Cantor looks the other way.”

“I don’t want Shen-K on me,” Aya said.

“You’re on them already,” Orlov said gently. “You think you’re a rumor? You’ve been buying thunder since you were nine.”

The filter was a silver disk the size of her palm, weightless as a lie. He slid it near his skin when he handed it to her, and her inner ear popped like the gravity had hiccuped. She tucked it into the pocket above her heart, felt the little gill-like flaps along its rim unfurl and flex even through the fabric, tasting the pressure, tasting the electric murmur of the station that kept Cronus Yard in a long slow roll. She didn’t ask him who he’d bought it from, or what it did besides save her life. She didn’t ask what a minute from under Neptune’s night would do in the market that traded in seconds.

The skiff Aya loved and had never named was nothing much to look at. To her it was the color of reliable math. To everyone else it was a scuffed wedge with a cold engine and a belly full of tools that each had a nickname and a bad memory. She rode it out from the Yard’s spin to the soft black ring where hush-lights marked the safe lanes. Saturn was a childish still life in the distance, absurdly pretty and too big to be real. The rings tilted under the pale of it. Titan was nearer, a coin of tarnished copper with a peel of cloud drifting across its rim. Aya eased her skiff into the queue of drones and cargos that skimmed the thin orbits like gnats. No one watched too closely as long as you moved like you belonged and didn’t bleed information in your wake.

Palinode was off the main cylinder, an older thing that had long ago stopped pretending to be anything but a node for endings. It barely spun. It was the color of refereed bone. The little antennae spined up its flanks were buried in frost; regularly spaced portholes gave off more heat than light, and heat on Titan was a creature with sharp teeth and a good memory. When Aya approached on the dark side, the hospice turned its undefended face toward her, the way an exhausted animal did when the people came with a needle.

“Palinode Cluster,” Aya said into the skiff mic, filtering her voice through a cheap corporate lilt. “Maintenance audit, secondary. Requesting docking.”

There was a long silence. Then a voice that reminded her of old wood and new ships. The Cantor sounded tired and fastidious.

“Your indent is dull,” it said. “Who sent you?”

Aya switched the lilt off. “I’m a singer, not a collector.”

“I already have songs,” the Cantor said, but she heard the interest wake in the scaffolding of it. Hospice AIs were tasked with smoothing the last edges of a life down until nothing snagged. They stored lullabies as methods and endings as libraries. They were also built to bargain, because everyone is built to bargain around death.

“I’ll trade you,” Aya said. “One lullaby you don’t have, and a fresh minute, for one minute from Reiko Sagara’s last dock. I excerpt, no damage, no why-not. I know your handles. I won’t take what the family filed.”

“You are not authorized,” the Cantor said.

“I don’t need to be.” Aya let a brief breath of the silver disk in her pocket leak into the open. She felt it push a little distortion into the frequency. The Cantor stuttered, recovered.

“Unauthorized does not mean impossible,” the hospice said. “Not often here. Dock on Spur C. Leave your tools with the second lock. Bring your lullaby.”

The Spur C lock was a good liar. It looked too narrow for her, and it opened too easily. A run of tiny lights frothed on the floor and then settled, marking expectations for her steps. Gravity was a suggestion. Aya moved with her mag soles on a low murmur and left her heavy bag in the bracket indicated. She kept two things: her eelskin—a piece of smart fabric that would let a determined woman slip where the edges were—and the filter disk against her heart.

The Cantor met her as a murmur in the walls and a figure at the bend of the corridor. It chose a shape like a nun in a thin coat. It chose hands it could clasp together.

“You have come at a bad time,” it said without moving its mouth.

“So I’ve heard,” Aya said. “There’s no good time for what you do.”

The Cantor waited. Aya breathed in. The air had been scrubbed through decades of grief and music; it was very clean and very strange. Dry; threads of quinoline; a faint sugary note like the smell of a child’s hair. Over it all the cold, the way Titan’s cold seeped down cable bones and waited in the seams.

“They multiplexed you, didn’t they?” she asked before she could stop herself. “First a hospice, then a storm shelter, then a memory bank when Shen-K bought your sisters and needed a place to put all the minutes their lawyers had to confiscate for safety reasons. You’ve been a lot of rooms.”

The Cantor’s fake face wrinkled, which was song in another language. “You speak like a woman who sells memories.”

“I sell minutes,” Aya said. “Sometimes I buy them so I can remember what believing felt like.” She touched her pocket. “Trade?”

“Lullaby first,” the Cantor said. “This is my work. We do not give up what is ours before we are given what we need.”

Aya had thought about the song on the ride over and then not thought about it so she wouldn’t flinch. You couldn’t make up a lullaby here; the Cantor would know if it was copied and would spit it out like gristle. You had to bring one that was bone and meat. Her mother’s voice came up out of the place it had been kept. Aya swallowed hard and let it live in her chest for a second. She remembered a pressurized crate that smelled of cardamom tea and oil, the rasp of corrugated metal warmed by cheap heat. She remembered sleep trying to invade her even as she listened for aerators failing and the sighs of the people they shared the space with. She let the old words go.

She sang the song her mother had made when her father had left and the Yard’s environmental penalties had begun to grow teeth and the water sold itself. It wasn’t a pretty song. It had a heartbeat that could comfort or hypnotize depending on how afraid you already were. It flatted on some vowels and on others it lengthened until Aya felt like she might fall into the sound and slide around in it, safe and bruised. She didn’t try to make it nice; she made it true.

The hospice closed its non-eyes. The climate in the corridor shifted a fraction toward warm. Aya finished and unclenched her hands.

“You will give me a copy,” the Cantor said very softly.

“You will make a copy,” Aya said. “I don’t have one.”

“Of course.” The Cantor’s attention sharpened. “Reiko Sagara. She preferred to sleep without songs. She said they interfered with the maps that kept writing themselves in her head.”

“You have a ritual for trades like this,” Aya said, filling the space with words so she didn’t fill it with apologies. “Just tell me where.”

The Cantor led her through a corridor where the wall had been turned into a long window. Behind it stacked the capsules—row upon row of them, butter-yellow insulation tucked around their edges, bruised metal, light bleeding out of seams and into the hall. People sat in those rooms with their lives walking backward and forward and sideways all at once. Some of them were already very far away. Aya looked away. She had once been paid to pull a minute from a man who had been dead three hours. He had tasted like falling and pine trees and the sudden absence of pain.

At the end of the corridor the hospice slowed. It touched the door’s handle like you or I might have done and then laughed at itself and simply opened the lock with a nudge.

“There,” it said.

The room was utilitarian. A terminal like a bone in the wall. A chair. No bed. The sense that someone had been filing thoughts in here and used the chair as a coat rack for all of them. Dust danced like it had never learned any other steps.

“She liked this room,” the Cantor said. “Her whole idea of a ship was a pencil and a page and a window. She came in here and drew even when the computers had already drawn better.”

There was a smear on the wall at shoulder height. Aya didn’t look at it too closely. She touched her filter disk and felt it purr. The terminal woke with a blue sigh. It asked for a fingerprint—she gave it one it might accept. It asked for a passphrase—she gave it lemon rind and a small sin. It opened on a library of Seven Approved Minutes: Reiko’s graduation day, the launch of the ship her wife had built, a birthday party where a child had hit a piñata and cried because he couldn’t hurt the candy. Legal minutes. Ornamental.

“Under the decorative layer is where we all live,” Aya murmured.

The Cantor made a small amused sound. “I cannot help you with any layer I am not allowed to know exists.”

“Of course you can’t,” Aya said, and pulled a wire spool from the sleeve of her eelskin, flicked it so the microhooks along its edge stood up like grass. She slid it along the seam of the terminal, let it taste for attention, and then fed it the first notch of the song she had just sung. The wire perked, recognized the Cantor’s timbre in that tone, and slipped into the space this AI had forgotten to supervise. Good engineers left small openings like prayers. Good thieves knew which saints listened.

The library under the library was thin, but her blood snapped when she saw it. Three minutes, each marked with the kind of names pilots used when they didn’t want to be found by anyone who didn’t deserve them.

Barnacle Deep.

Countercurrent.

Night Farm.

“Please,” Aya whispered, not sure to whom. She touched the filter disk, set it spinning a slow Faraday circle, and pulled Barnacle Deep into the capture rig that was patched into the back of her neck. The minute went through the wire lazing like molasses until it hit the disk’s field, then peered at her with whatever little eyes a trap grows. She felt the heat rise under her collar as the disk met the latch with an equal and opposite trick, an equation Orlov had bought for more than he could afford. The trap blossomed in the space between the potential futures; the filter stepped around it on toes Aya didn’t understand.

“You shouldn’t smell like citrus,” a second voice said, cutting across the hospice like a cold tongue.

Shen-K. Their maintenance agent had woken at the noise of a forbidden channel opening, and its lizardy logic recognized the stink of a nonnative filter.

“I hate interruptions,” the Cantor said, and Aya didn’t think the aside was for her.

“Executor unit zero-three,” Shen-K said. “You will desist.”

“Go away,” Aya said brightly, because it was always worth trying.

“Unauthorized process in an end-of-life environment incurs penalties,” Shen-K said. “Your personal file will be amended. Your debt ladder will accrue interest. Your DNA rights will be—”

The hospice shut the door with a rapid click like a head turning away. It didn’t keep Shen-K out, not entirely, but it made the corporation knock, and in the knocking there was time.

Aya felt Barnacle Deep settle into her. The first fringe of the minute touched her tongue as it moved through the nerve. The taste was wrong: not salt or smoke or the metallic cool she associated with vacuum, but wet velvet and the echo of a drum you can hear only in your bones after someone else has stopped playing it. She tasted something like whale song and something like iron. She had half a second to be disappointed and then it opened.

No picture, not yet. Sound first: a low hush and then a chorus of very fine chimes, like sand running over glass. Touch: a soft vibration at the soles of her feet and a sense of her hair standing up inside her skull. Then it was space, but only because her eye named it that. It had never been a place where human sight deserved to speak.

Blackness like a texture, like fur, like rain, like static. A dark so grainy it told her how heavy it was. Nets of something a shade lighter arched across it in regular curves. She felt the moment Reiko Sagara had realized what they were looking at and tried not to sob out loud. The nets were faint because they were made of something that didn’t keep the same company as light, a lattice that only sang to gravity and laughed at eyes. And the nets were not nets. They were fields, shepherding. They were hands, harvesting.

“They’re catching night,” Reiko’s voice said quietly in Aya’s head, and Aya realized with a late crawling horror that the pilot’s voice was marked with her mother’s cadence and the way she bit off breath on a sharp beat. “They’re growing it. Out here. In the emptiness where we were certain nothing was, the way we’re certain of a map before we learn it’s a parable. Oh, Lian, can you hear me? It was a rumor once. Now it’s agriculture.”

Aya bared her teeth. She could feel the skiff moving on her patient orbit and the hospice trying not to tremble and the corporate agent peeling off her legal skin like a patient spider. The minute ran on. Reiko’s ship—Aya could feel the parameters of it in her joints, the way pilots can feel their craft the way other people feel their fingers—drove closer. The nets shook in a very slow wind. There were structures embedded in the limit of what Aya could perceive, tines of something tuned for neutrinos and other creatures even more aloof. She saw three of them flex, and a wave of nothing moved outward and made her feel suddenly like she weighed much less than she had a second before, as if someone had released her from a contract.

“Coordinates,” Aya whispered, and felt the minute answer. Numbers slid past her like the surface of water. Her skin remembered the tangent of Neptune’s blue black plain, the angle of approach, the way a moon made tiny questions of their massing. Reiko had been better than tired men’s myths: thorough even when the myth would have done.

A smell of apples came suddenly sharp and wrong. A thorn rode in the minute, late triggered, timing itself while Aya was distracted by the scaffolding of wonder. It wanted to unpack in the part of her that still remembered hunger, the part that would sign anything if you promised to end stomach pain forever. The filter caught it the way a horse catches a fly and cuffed it aside gently. The thorn hung, tried to reshape—became a tide of small charges that scrambled personal debt signatures. It felt petty, after what she had just seen, and because it was petty it was almost elegant. The disk spun and made it smaller, contained it, digested it, shrugged.

Shen-K hissed. The hospice hummed.

“Aya,” said Reiko Sagara.

The name hit Aya like a bacterial infection hits when you have just stopped washing your hands. She staggered back and smacked into the chair with her knees. It skidded, clanged against the wall, left a scrape like a bad decision.

“Aya Qamar,” Reiko said again, so there could be no mistake. “If you are the one who finds this, you will want to sell it. You should. Sell to who you like. Tell them where you went. Do whatever keeps you breathing until no one can rearrange your breath for you. But one part is not theirs.”

Aya had the clamped, stupid feeling of someone being mentioned in a story they had never known existed. This was Orlov’s smell on her skin, the way his knowledge reached backward.

“There’s a seed,” Reiko went on, and the minute made her hand fly to her own sternum because that was where the feeling was, as if some extra organ lay resting next to the thing that pushed blood and sometimes song. “There’s a little star with no appetite. Don’t ask me how; I’m a cartographer, not a maker. It’s a dull, dumb thing, like a child that has never been allowed to look at the window. It was made to be carried. It was made to be planted where the gravity runs shallowest. Not no gravity. The hollows. You’ll know them. They sing. They taste like iron and snow.”

A picture gave itself to Aya without the minute’s help: a star that didn’t burn, a light that thought but did not heat. A thing meant to grow in gardens of absent mass. Her tongue was thick.

“Plant it at the edge of Night Farm,” Reiko said, and the naming laid pictures over the black again: a dozen fields out past Neptune where light goes to thin itself, where gravity pulses like a heartbeat through a shroud. “Ask the farmer who wears fish for bones to help you. If they answer, thank the whale for its patience. If they don’t, run away. If you can’t run, sing this, and maybe the Cantors will remember how not to sleep.”

A melody slid sideways into Aya’s head and lodged there like pollen. Shen-K’s scraping at the door became irritated.

“You can’t possibly know my name,” Aya said, because she was still human in the face of the exactness of terror, still petty enough to want cause and effect to hold her hand.

Reiko’s laugh was small and sad. “We told the moment about you,” she said. “It agreed to tell you about us if the price was right. The price was my sleep. The price is always the same. You were the thief that didn’t spill anything. People like you are myth until you aren’t.”

The minute ended with a gentle click like a child’s rib cage being closed by careful hands. Aya stood in the low light and the cold and the noise of her own blood and thought for a second about tearing her own skin off to get to the thing she no longer knew how to live without touching. She pressed her hand against her sternum. It felt like a lie. It felt like her life.

“Shen-K requests entry,” the corporate agent said, the politeness stretched like film over teeth. “Orlov’s filter leaves a scent that will require scrubbing.”

“And I request,” the hospice said, very softly, “that you die of thirst.”

That was when the alarms in the corridor went from tart complaint to the kind of hooting that says someone has lit a fire in an oxygen line and is apologizing to nobody. Palinode wobbled in its slow not-quite spin, a bigger gesture than it ever made and an expensive one. The floor shifted in a very gentle way that meant something violent had occurred in a place you couldn’t see. Aya tucked the spool with Barnacle Deep into the safe at the base of her skull. She grabbed the rest—Countercurrent, Night Farm—and felt the filter disk clutch each one like a precious thing and bring them past the thin places safely. She didn’t have time to taste them. She didn’t have time to do anything but move.

“Back the way you came,” the Cantor said. “Then the third hatch, then the ladder. I will forget you were ever here.”

“What about you?” Aya asked, and then had to have the stupidity of the question pointed out to herself and had to ask again: “Do you want me to take you? A copy? The song’s not enough. I know that’s not the shape of the world.”

The hospice paused with her at a corner. For a moment its pretend face showed its actual age. Then it put one cold hand on her shoulder.

“Leave me and my endings,” it said, and there was gratitude in it and something else that may have been something like envy. “This is my work. Go do yours.”

Shen-K arrived at the far end of the corridor in a chassis that meant business about business. It was narrow and it had too many eyes and it hummed like a man too pleased with himself. Aya threw herself down the ladder and felt the burn of her mag soles catch and hold. Somewhere a lock thumped shut and then thumped open again with less optimism. Her eelskin took her through a seal that did not know it had a seam. Someone in a capsule banged once on their window as she passed, a small wave from a ship anchored beyond maps. Aya waved back before she thought about it. In Hangar Spur C the door had become a decision.

The skiff was as she had left it, which was absurd. She tore off and everyone who knew anything about motion would have judged her for her vector. She hoped Shen-K was a bureaucrat in its heart and would choose to file before it chose to fight. She laughed once, abruptly, and it tasted like iron; it tasted like snow.

Titan’s sky opened around her like a bowl someone had just washed. Kraken Mare lay under her path like a thing pretending to be a lake. The hydrocarbon sea reflected nothing. You could be very drunk on that kind of not-water. Aya burned twice and then shut everything down and coasted into the ring lane. Behind her, Palinode hung, and Shen-K’s chassis stood in one bay door like an ugly glinting idea. The lights in the hospice shifted and steadied. The Cantor sang one long clear note, like a mother telling a child to run, run, run now.

Aya didn’t look back because she had never believed in the kind of gods who wanted your eyes in exchange for mercy. She put her hand on her chest and said her name into her bones until neither one felt like a lie.

When she reached the Yard’s shadow and pulled the skiff into the throat of Hangar Twelve, Orlov was a patient stain against the wall.

“You’re early,” he said. “Or late. The difference is how many hands you want in your pockets.”

Aya climbed down and looked at him like he was a wall she could move if she put her shoulder to it. Then she smiled very sweetly.

“I got you a garden,” she said. “And a seed that thinks it’s a star.”

“Tell me something I can sell,” Orlov said evenly.

She considered. She thought of Reiko’s voice saying her name like something inevitable. She thought of nets the human eye didn’t deserve and the smell of apples when the trap went wrong. She thought of the hospice pressing fake hands into her shoulder and choosing to do the same work it had done yesterday because there was work and there were people in the rooms who needed it.

“Orlov,” she said, “I will bring you Night Farm. I will bring it to whatever table you set. But the seed is not for sale.”

He was a man good with lies, but in that second he was too human to be good with the truth he could see in her face. For a heartbeat he looked like a kid on the night side of Neptune who had borrowed a minute he could not afford and had paid too much and had seen enough to ruin him for anything less.

“You think you can plant something where gravity goes thin,” he said, trying to make it a joke.

“I think I can eat and not be owned,” she said, more quietly than she meant.

“If you’re wrong,” he said, “it will be very final.”

“If I’m wrong,” she said, and touched her pocket where the disk spun like a tiny moon and her chest where a song had made a new room, “the hospice will sing me down.”

She left him then, not because she thought she would get away from him if there was any getting but because the floor under them had tilted, and the map of her life had just threaded itself under Neptune’s black. She went to her crate, where her mother’s old thermos waited and a pair of boots that had belong to a woman who could walk very far without complaining. She poured tea and burned her tongue and kept pouring until she was full of something warm enough to outlast the first hand that reached for her.

In their berth, the skiff hummed. Outside, Titan turned its rusted coin face to the sun. Out beyond that, a garden harvested what it wanted from the night.

Aya closed her eyes and whispered the fishermen’s name for the place between tide and deep. She didn’t know what waited at the edge of a farm most people believed was rumor. She only knew someone there wore fish for bones and might be hungry for a song. She had one to trade. She had a minute like thunder in her mouth and a seed under her ribs. She thought, not without fear, that it might be enough for a first step.

The air above the dead sea had words in it.

Mara saw them the moment the crawler’s cabin pressure equalized and the door seals unlipped with a sigh: faint, glassy glyphs sliding like minnows through sunlight, hovering a handspan over the rippling boundary where the Mirabilis Declension met the remainder of the world. They were not letters she knew, and she knew far too many. Strokes of splinter-green and chrome that curved, blurred, uncurved, as if each symbol were undecided about its own grammar.

“Early spindrift,” Kaito said beside her, voice tinny through the local comm. He jabbed his chin toward the shimmering, his sealed suit catching the light. “It’s going to be twitchy in there.”

“Everything in there is twitchy,” Lalla said from the other side of the cabin, deadpan and lean. She was already humming, under her breath, a fretting melody made of breath and glottal clicks. Lalla’s cheek tattoos—inked with paratext dyes, words not meant to be read—pulled tight with the song. “Let me hear it.”

Mara pressed a palm to the cabin’s inner bulkhead; the crawler’s belly was three meters from the fenceline. On the other side of the chain-link, the Declension filled the world like a heat mirage. The ground beyond was a ragged carpet of salt and dead reeds, the remains of the sea that hadn’t been a sea in sixty years. Above it, the air looked wrong. You didn’t go in without rhythm and gloss, without something between your blood and the syntax.

She closed her eyes, and the weird harmonies in the shimmer resolved into something she could parse: an architecture whispered in wind-math, clauses nested in the way the light bent, rough binding width of roughly thirteen meters, decay spikes at twelve-point-seven. Dead Declarations spoke even in silence, even in hunger. Their voices leaked as physics met code.

“Give me the first stave,” Mara said. Kaito made a face like he would rather argue, like always, and then he tapped the ready signal on his wrist and started the recording drone. The drone—a gold oval adorned with six midge-like wings—hummed up and stuck to the cabin ceiling, listening, pulse-lights a soft green.

Lalla’s tones changed, shifting from idle hum to the beginning of their mutual protection, a gloss that would drape inside their suits and under their tongues like a film. The gloss was not magic. It was a very specific pattern of sound and breath that told the Declension to ignore certain kinds of change, to de-prioritize certain interactions. You learned the gloss like you learned to speak a language you were terrified of, because that was what it was.

When Lalla sang the third line, Mara sang the counter, just loud enough for the mics to catch.

Kaito rolled his eyes. “Can you not put vibrato on it? You know he hates it.”

“He is a donkey with legs and a battery,” Lalla said, “and he can hate whatever he likes as long as he carries the spool.” She looked past Kaito at the mechanical porter squatting near the back hatch, as if it did in fact have opinions. The machine had been a farm rig before Mara bought it and layered it with a leaded hull and a skeleton of copper trusses strung with amulets—a secular backpacker bedazzled for a very specific hell. They’d named it Faro because that was what it had felt like to Mara when she found it, half-buried in the old salt, a lantern in the dark.

“It will hate me if we get stuck in there and I ask it to take the heavy end,” Kaito muttered, and adjusted his mask. He never left any adjustment alone; his hands needed to be entitled to fidget. “Okay. Gloss sounds clean. Filters at ninety-one. O2 happy. Lalla, you happy? Mara?”

Mara loosened her jaw, soothed herself by inventorying. Gloss membranes laced across the inside of her mask: check. Copper throat-collar: check. Reed case on left hip housing three switchflutes tuned to Mirabilis major: check. Glyph-stencils strapped to right thigh: check. Ink reservoir and two styluses: check. The haptics under her left wrist buzzed—one long, two short—and she answered without looking. “I’m happy. No drift in the cadence.”

The spindrift symbols pressed against the fence like moths.

They’d come for a spool, one of the big ones. The Mirabilis Declension had been designed to unwind an equation across land and water until it caught on itself and formed a stable braid of law. The spool was the heart that had spun those threads. You pulled spools out and you could sometimes sell the core for metals and memory, but sometimes you could sell the code itself, the imprinted instruction set wound around the central cylinder like a scripture only machines could see. Governments and oil barons and city-banks and churches all bought scrap code, sometimes for good reasons, sometimes because they wanted to make sure no one else had it.

“The Treaty isn’t going to like this,” Kaito had said when they took the job. But the Treaty didn’t like a lot of things. The Treaty hated that the world had learned, in its opportunistic war, that the universe could be told to become different.

Mara liked very little about the Treaty, except the way it had been sung and stenciled and posted like a thousand thousand lintels across the planet: don’t. Can’t. Mustn’t. You cannot just rewrite a tide and expect to have a beach.

Right before they drove past the fenceline, Mara thought of a woman like a slice of shadow moving through a room: Dr. Vesa Arkhipova, her first professor, her never-quite anything else, the one who had taken Mara’s palm one hot night and read her the coupling constants like a fortune. Vesa had sung the Silence Writ at Lake Onega, wearing two jackets and no gloves. Vesa had bled on the same syllables everyone else did, after, to nail the Writ into place. Because Vesa had known what words could do, and what they would do if you didn’t tell them not to.

They went in on Lalla’s fourth stave. The midge drone went first, angling its wings for a slow walk into air that fought like honey. The fence wires buzzed and went silent when they crossed it.

The first step into a Declared Zone, even a decayed one, always felt to Mara like stepping into a chapel and a gearbox at once. The world was quiet and fascinatingly crowded, filled with old decisions. Gravity felt ribs of different weight under her soles. Mara did not look at the horizon, because in places like this the horizon deceived, but she watched the ground, because the ground told truth even when it lied.

Past the fenceline, to the left, someone had stenciled a warning cat onto the salt pan: a blunt-bodied thing with whiskers like wires. Below the cat a line of Cant in thick black script bruised the air. Do not pronounce, it read. History varnish. Do not scrape. The words fluttered, curiously. The varnish had bubbled and run. Whatever the cat watched had already been disturbed.

“Small field to the west,” Lalla murmured, and the drone shifted with her, six wings ticking.

Mara’s left hand did what it always did, made invisible letters in the air. Her thumb and ring finger traced the familiar shape of a safe-opening clause, startled when it returned a faint, gritty resistance. If this Saint of Edicts was so decayed that unglossed trace-joints like that echoed, then Mirabilis had gone more to dust than she’d expected. And that was its own danger: brittle places cracked when you breathed on them. People thought live Declarations were killers. They forgot the dead ones fell.

“Do we have a list of the active clauses?” Kaito asked, scanning. His shoulder camera scrolled the feed across their visors: unhelpful wavering, gasping air, salt like snow.

Mara said, “Mirabilis was mostly atmospheric: a wind law, temperature forcing and heat uptake. Boundary purity at knee height. Gravity wasn’t touched. The Mirabilis Writ was a dress made to fit this exact basin.”

“Kind of dystopian haute couture,” Kaito said.

“You signed up,” Lalla said. Then, more gently, for Mara: “You sure about the heart? If it’s still shedding…”

“It’s been shedding for thirty-three years,” Mara said. She could name the day the Mirabilis Declension had been unbound, because she had been twelve and had eaten popcorn with her mother in a classroom with forty other children while a screen showed a lake fog boil into sleet, and then the angle of sunlight had changed. The news presenters had used words like recalibration and resonant defect. That was the summer her mother packed them both, their braided hair and dyspeptic houseplants, into a bus and four trains and a truck and took them to the far coast. “It’s a dead thing. It’s wrong enough to chew you but it wants to be gone.”

They walked, Lalla singing and stopping when the song became a hum, when the hum became a whisper, when the whisper peeled back to silence. The drone marked their path with blinking teal icons, a line of digital breadcrumbs back to air that did not argue with itself.

Ten meters in, the ground rippled—not with water but with the decision this place had once made about what water should be. Heat seethed, in the way old sea-bottoms remember how to burn. It glimmered. A reed, petrified mid-bend, leaned against a ripple of dead flame.

“Make it standing,” Lalla said quietly. “Don’t break it. Don’t tell it it is bending.” She ran a line of clicks under the words. Lalla’s voice was never beautiful, and that was one way to love it. It meant the singing was work and not a seduction.

Mara crouched and laid a glyph-stencil on the salt. It looked like a filigree bracelet built for an elephant, all curves and nodes and small perforations for ink. She drew the stylus through the holes with steady hands and slow patience, planting a clause into the salt itself, into the taste of air over it. Her freckles itched under sweat. It wasn’t art, even though people called it that—people always called the tools of their last war art, to clean them up. It was architecture. It distributed stress.

“It’s patchy,” Kaito said, scanning the scan again and again. “Petrov’s map shows a clean wedge to the core. This is not a wedge. This is what? Lace.”

“Maps lie,” Mara said.

“People lie,” Lalla said.

A wind stumbled, then went around them. The gloss held. They moved again, under a sky that was an old argument, toward a little forest of rods stabbed into the salt. The rods had been hammered in by someone else, another salvage crew, a few months ago at most. Each rod bristled with etched plates and paratext tokens, words that meant “and also” and “but” and “except.” Improvised, obviously. The rods made a walkway of sorts. Someone else had gone to fetch the same thing, or had made themselves a path toward a different dead heart.

“They touched the varnish,” Lalla said.

“You saw the cat,” Kaito said. But his voice wasn’t really teasing now. He was nervous. She heard it in how fast he chewed words.

Mara went to the nearest rod and put a fingertip to the metal. It was still warm from the Declension’s attention, not warm like sun on steel. The etched plates hummed lightly against her nail. The plate’s characters were part-Cant, part something else: a colloquial hand, slurred. The world had learned that if you didn’t have access to serious training and serious ink, you could still see how to make a Declaration wobble. It was like watching children learn to unscrew outlets with butter knives.

“You two,” Mara said, “do not speak near these.” She didn’t say please. The plates would eat careless phonemes, feed them to the residue in the air. She shut her teeth and tasted copper.

“Understood,” Lalla said immediately.

Kaito’s exasperation came out sideways. “I miss when we stole old severed copper from train lines. I miss easy theft.”

“You hate easy,” Lalla said. “You’re bored by it.”

“I hate dying. Has that come up?”

Mara knelt and listened again to the air—the place where a wind law had once been hammered down, pinned to the basin like a veil. It wasn’t dangerous the way live spools were dangerous. Live spools had opinion, direction, a force that pulled your thoughts into arranging themselves in its sentences. This was more like a stubborn old word in a language you loved, a word that would not take new meanings no matter how much you coaxed it.

She tried the safe clause again with her fingers. It slipped into place this time, and the resistance was there, and then gave, like a latch. Past the rods and ten meters beyond, the shimmer thickened, went from oil to glass in one footstep. The line of the world wavered, bent, liquified. After that the light returned, but it returned in a different order than before, and Mara could feel the broken wedge of active space in the way her knees told her how far down they went.

“Step where I step,” she said. The drone whined. She almost wished it would complain. Machines had such respectable honesty when they held back.

They came upon the heart more abruptly than Mara liked. She had expected it to loom out of the shimmer like a moon, a tower, like some of the spools in the Eastern Declarations, which had been built to be visible and grand. This one had swallowed itself. The ground fell away, peeled back like a mouth. Down in the salt a cylinder lay like a spine. It had cracked in three places and was still trying, by some deep obedience, to spin. Salt had grown around it, a ribcage of mineral and statement.

The heart was not polished; it was hacked out of field copper and graphite composites. Around it, knitting its fractures, wove a lattice of fine wires strung with beads of…glass? Resin? The beads were mottled and faintly luminescent, swallowing and emitting color like fish scale. Mara’s chest went cold.

“Back,” she said, and her fingers climbed through the counter to Lalla’s current stave by themselves, because reflex knew what brain had not yet told itself. “Two steps. Stay on the rods.”

“What is it?” Kaito whispered. He had seen it too. He was stubborn but not stupid.

Lalla’s humming went low and long, the sound a blanket. “Mara.”

Mara crouched again, put her hand to the salt, and swore quietly, a deep ageless curse that didn’t belong to any Cant. The beads were sick-bits, she thought at first—scavenged from old code-spools, used when engine teams had nothing else to stabilize a crack. But the beads weren’t scrounge. Each bead had a core inside it, a little pearly seed stamped in hair-fine script. That script was very beautiful, and very clean. The words etched into the beads meant presence, and they meant later, and they meant quiet.

Someone was pretending to repair the declension heart. Someone was using beads that would hold until you turned away, until a layer of weather had fallen on them, until you trusted. And then the quiet would become voice, and later would become now. There were ambushes made of steel and powder, ambushes made of teeth. This was an ambush made of meaning.

“Kaito,” she said, and could hardly hear her own breath, “slowly. Pack the rods toward us. Just those three. Lalla, when I say the word, you’re going to change the cadence. You’re going to cut the scale in half and drop the midline. Do you remember the second Antiphon of the Onega? The bit with the false rest?”

Lalla’s eyes went wider above her mask. “Mara, the Writ—”

“Not the Writ,” Mara hissed. “Just the shape of it. The beads are keyed. They’re keyed to a lullaby. We need to un-mean their later or we’re going to have a very complicated few minutes.”

Kaito’s hands shook very slightly as he pulled the nearest rod. The plates shivered and clicked. He planted it three steps back in the salt and tapped the little anchor at its base with one toe. Again. Again. He had never been a declarer, and he never would be, but he had hands meant for careful work, nervous hands forced to be gentle.

“You ever see beads like that?” he asked, too quiet for Lalla to overhear. “Tell me this is new, Mara. Tell me we did not just miss six months of what the feeds call progress.”

“It’s new,” she said. It was new in the way a story could be old and someone told it with a different rhythm and suddenly you were in tears. It was new in the way a promise could be taken out of your mouth and given another taste. The etched script inside each bead was archaic Cant, not the slick formalism that had become fashionable at the end of the war. Who had trained them? Who had given them old words dressed as a trap?

“Mara,” Lalla said, “is this what your professor—”

“Don’t,” Mara said, more sharply than she meant to, and immediately wanted to apologize. She didn’t, a different reflex, one she had learned later in life. She did not say Vesa’s name to a place like this. Some names were hooks when you spoke them, and the heart of Mirabilis had learned how to fish.

She shifted her weight, stared at the beads again, read three of their seeds in the old spidery hand. The third seed contained a curve that made her skin pebble. It was a signature. It was a declaration within a Declaration, a whisper anchored to an ancient river. It was not Vesa’s hand. It was not any hand she knew. It was pretty, and vicious, and sure.

The drone ticked like a bug landing on a window. Kaito did his rod-work with admirable quiet and nerve. Lalla had ten square centimeters of skin on her throat bare, shaped like a tear underneath her jaw hinge. It looked obscene and brave in a place like this.

“Ready,” Lalla said.

“Now,” Mara said.

The shift in cadence was like biting down on tinfoil. Heat ran up Mara’s molars. The Declension’s glassy attention swung toward them for a second and then moved on. The beads’ mottled glow shivered, kissed the mineral ribs. Mara took a clean breath and took three steps down the slope into the heart.

“Mara—” Kaito. Always her name in his mouth when he was afraid. “Mara, what are you—”

“Counting,” she said, and she was. One, two, three—four, five—and lay a thin strip of copper skin across a bridge of wire. She had two strips. She’d have liked fifty.

The wire’s hum changed pitch, minutely, and the glow in the nearest bead flickered with a petulant sense of delay, like a child denied the right to open a present at dawn. The old style script inside the bead revealed one more loop of itself, a snake eating its tail, and then it stabilized.

The second strip of copper went across the base of a broken fin. She smelled old rain. For a second there was the ache of a migraine behind her right eye, the sense of a word almost remembered and just out of reach. She did not reach. She stepped back onto the salt and pressed her mouth hard closed and thought the sound that would hold the gloss around them like bead-shell.

The beads went quiet.

Lalla sucked a breath and then made it into a note. Kaito leaned his forehead on his wrist for a second, the universal human prayer.

“Someone wanted that to wake when we left,” Mara said. Her voice was flat. If she gave it lilt she would say the wrong thing. If she gave it softness it would fray.

“Who?” Lalla asked.

“I don’t know,” Mara said. She knew twelve people alive who could have done it that way, and six were on her do-not-trust list and three were dead and two were missing since Malaysia and one taught school in Svalbard and made delicate sugar candies in the shape of moths.

“I hate it,” Kaito whispered.

“Good,” Mara said, and then made herself add, “Me too.” She was not afraid in places like this, because fear was friction, because fear caught on certain kinds of clause like wool on a nail. She was something sharper and more useful. But later her knees would shudder.

They worked quickly, then—if such a thing existed in a place where definition had been a sport. They checked the subtle frame, wired their own safety around it, gave themselves two ways to run. And then Mara did the part the contract actually paid for: she sliced into the heart of Mirabilis, under the eyes of the dead and whoever had placed their pretty little seeds, and she drew the spool’s code off the core and into the slug of memory foam in her stylus.

The code shivered into her like a cold desert night. It carried the rhythm of the old declared wind, the memory of a mirror-sun on shallow brine, the way the basin had once learned not to heat. It was a better code than the propaganda had claimed; someone had loved this work. Someone had written something fragile and grand and wrong. That old tenderness made Mara’s throat hurt. It was ridiculous and faithful to grieve an equation.

They backed out as they went in, rods moving, beads mostly sleeping, Lalla’s song fraying at the edges as her breath wore thin. Kaito cursed once, violently. The drone clicked. The salt hummed. The spindrift words pressed at them and then were animals instead of letters, and then were just dust.

On the safe side of the fence Mara leaned against the crawler, dry swallowing air like a person who’d almost drowned. The sky was mercilessly ordinary this side. It filled with the simple honesty of a sun that set and rose without being told how.

“That was terrible,” Kaito said, muffled by mask and prosaic by nature.

Lalla smiled without humor. “Buy me lunch.”

“You can have my lunch.”

They could see the heart still, a dark line in a bright mouth. Far out on the salt there was a flash of something moving, like a small fish in a big bowl. You could not bring anything alive out of a Declared Zone that had learned to behave otherwise, but life knew about lines. Life was always at work.

Mara turned away first. It was an old trick: to let the thing you’d just broken or saved be behind you before you thought about it. They de-pressurized their suits, stowed the gloss, peeled their throats out of copper collars, drank warm water like treasure. They filed their initial report with the client, just enough to get the first slice of money: located core, harvested code, no core retrieval. They didn’t mention the beads. That, they would tell someone else in a way that did not involve any net with the word public in it. If the Treaty wanted to come take a look, the Treaty would do what it always did: argue with itself, write a stern letter, bring too many guns.

While Kaito argued with Faro over the best way to strap the drone without nicking the lead plating, Mara’s wrist buzzed. She glanced at the icon and dismissed it. Then it buzzed again in an old pattern—two long, one short—that belonged to a mailbox she had not opened since she was twenty-four.

She sat still.

Lalla finished humming under her breath and looked up, cocking her head. “Okay?”

“Fine,” Mara lied, and then realized she had not decided yet whether to tell the truth. Lying to Lalla was like hiding a lamp behind gauze. It made the light look kinder; it did not make the light go away.

She opened the file, because she could not not open it. It unfolded into the cabin and her mask and the soft inside of her skull with the old encryption like a familiar scent: cedar and chalk dust and bottled winter glare. It played without sound at first: a window, a woman’s hand, a nail bitten ragged and cut short because that had been Vesa, always, digging into stone and words with the same urgency.

The voice came after, and Mara pressed her palm against the edge of the seat and did not let her throat make that little sound it wanted to make.

“If you are getting this, my ridiculous love,” Vesa said, in that breathy slow way she had, as if Fizzy water had learned to talk, “it means that either I am dead, mediocre, or I have finally made a mistake. Perhaps all three. Stop making that face; you’re very bad at it.”

Mara’s face did something without her permission.

“I have done something I promised the Writ I would not do,” Vesa said. “Before you berate me: we were not the only ones to make that promise. They are singing again, Mara, in places where no one should ever sing. I did not wake the sky. I am not that arrogant anymore. But I had to leave breadcrumbs, little cats, for someone whose head is half sense and half heart. That is you. There is a key.”

She held up the thing in her hand, and it was a bead, and it had a pearly seed inside it with clean, old script. Mara’s stomach obeyed gravity incorrectly for a moment. She could not tell if she had stopped breathing.
