“You will hate me for this,” Vesa said gently. “I have taught you well. Hate me later. For now: go to where we took the sugar moths out of a man’s house and left him the rest of his sorrow. The key is in a book, in a chapter with no number. The book will bite you. Don’t let it. And Mara. If you can, if you still can: break my vow.”

The file blinked gray in the way old media does when the last bit has fallen off the edge of the world. The cabin was full of coughs of static that had no home.

Kaito, bless him, pretended not to be listening. Lalla, who could hear a gloss fall two streets away, leaned forward and put her hand on Mara’s forearm just above the copper bracelet.

The sun had the audacity to continue lowering itself toward the salt. The Declension shimmered and pretended not to exist. The beads inside the heart of Mirabilis pretended to be asleep.

Mara let her mouth remember how to laugh, just once, because otherwise she would remember other things. “Lalla,” she said, and her voice was a dull knife but still a useful one, “do you remember the man with the moths in Narimanov?”

“His candies,” Lalla said at once. “You nearly choked. He told you a long story about how his uncle had married a woman who could smell snow.”

“Mhm,” Kaito said, eyes on the donkey’s straps but not looking at them, “and his house smelled like sugar and fear.”

“That house,” Mara said. “There’s a book in there that bites.”

“You think it’s still there?” Kaito asked.

“I think if Vesa put something somewhere, it’s where she put it until the heat death of the universe or until someone with a song she respects asks it to move.” She flexed her fingers, made herself fully present in her body again, counted. “Pack up. We’re going to eat in the truck. And then we’re going to go read.”

“Do you,” Lalla asked slowly, eyes on the fenceline as if someone else might step out of the shimmer, “are you going to tell the Treaty?”

“In my will,” Mara said, and tasted the bitterness under the joke. “No. Not yet. We are going to find what she hid. We are going to decide after we know what the key unlocks. And Kaito—”

He had already started shaking his head.

“—you are going to stop taking side jobs from men named Petrov with bad maps and apocalyptic hobbies,” she finished, because humor could cover a multitude of terror.

Kaito gave up and grinned, brief and cutting. “I always quit the wrong vices.”

“Then quit all of them,” Lalla said. “We will inventory the remainder.”

The drone clicked assent that did not exist. The salt lay bright and unarguable on one side of the fence. On the other side, language curled and uncurled itself in heat.

Inside the Mirabilis Declension, beads with old script warmed themselves like stones on a riverbed. Somewhere very far away, where someone had sung something dangerous about heat, a person who had written those seeds touched their throat with two fingers and smiled.

Mara wiped the wet from under her mask, unhooked the copper from her neck, and climbed into the crawler. The file had been sent a month ago. Vesa was dead. Or mediocre. Or a mistake. Perhaps, as always, Vesa was all three and still a person you could love more than was sensible.

“Okay,” she said. “Let’s go wake a book.”

Chapter One

In the city, time was the last honest currency, and everyone cheated it. You could smell it in the morning rushing off the tiled arcades and nanofabric kiosks—a sharp, metallic prickle like rain that never touched skin, the hum of the Chron mesh counting everything you did and everything you put off. It threaded through your implants and through the pedestrians around you, slid into the speed of their shoes and the cadence of their voice, negotiated their days into denominations small enough to swallow without choking.

I had four hours left until dusk according to the public clocks and three hours and twelve minutes until my accounts ran dry. I could feel the deficit like a hunger deep behind the eyes.

The flea market in Glass Harbor’s Drowned Quarter had been erected on the bones of a drowned railway station. The old tracks ran underfoot like rib bones, slick with algae. Water gurgled in the seams. The arcades gave out onto a channel where gondolas—printed, smart, and ugly—bumped hulls like docile animals. Banners twitched in the slight morning breeze, animated with cheap ads whose AI had been downgraded into good behavior. Somewhere a string quartet performed for pay-by-minute, their movements smooth as thought, their music stretching and contracting with their clients’ pacing.

I was there for a man who sold moments he didn’t own.

“Blanker,” I told myself under my breath, and the tilt of the word in my head hardened my gaze. Not a time-thief—there was no such thing. You couldn’t steal time from the system any more than you could steal oxygen from the sky. But you could cheat, here and there, if you knew what to loosen and had the hands for it. You could strip the tags from moments, scuff their metadata until they slipped out of the ledger. Wild seconds. Untaxed time. The mesh hated it because it was an affront to its story of us.

My badge was warm against my ribs, resting in the left breast pocket of my jacket. Bureau of Hours, Reclamation. It was six months since my last promotion and eleven months since my last complaint. Arlen said I was steady. Arlen also said I had an appetite for lost causes.

The blanker was supposed to call himself Jas, which was either a lie or a joke. He was supposed to favor the west colonnade where the shade was good, selling minutes wrapped in cordovan leather wallets, small as ring boxes. He was supposed to be wearing a hat.

Everyone wore hats in the Drowned Quarter. The Shore Authority didn’t like hair nets near the seafood printers, and the hats gave privacy against stray lenses. The hats looked like mushrooms, like patrol blimps, like outdated espionage fantasies. I bought a porkpie from a girl with skin like ivory and hands that trembled a fraction too fast, tipped it low, and let the Chron mesh tighten the threads behind my ears. The world shifted into audit lines and drifts: the speed signatures of the crowd, the plosive red of a fast lane running like a river along the arcade, green swaths of slow time pocketed around the chessboards and sewing tables and noodle carts.

There. A smudge in the flow, a faint mauve where the mesh’s sampling couldn’t find purchase, like looking at a spider web that refused to glisten. It moved quickly, but not smoothly, catching, stuttering. People in the Quarter learn to live with their counting. When you move on the rations you’re assigned you learn the dance, the public rhythm. The blankers never move right. They keep pacing in their heads.

I cut through a knot of students with face tattoos that rippled when they laughed—bright, fast kids who had all bought the same inspirational lecture because the Bureau subsidized it and would give habit credits for clicking through. Their speech was a little too fast. They had the luxury to burn time on words. The Chron mesh tickled the base of my neck. The mauve signature slid toward the rail tunnel and the smell of fried oil.

“Jas,” I said, projecting, making it conversational. “You’re supposed to enjoy the shade.”

The blanker did not look at me. He had the hat. It was slate gray felt that had seen rain. He had an old coat that hung loose on his bones. He had the pale hands of someone who didn’t work for a living, as the old people used to say, which only meant he did work but not in a way you could hold. He palmed a wallet over to a man with nails painted gold. The wallet looked like every other. It felt like every other. When you opened it, the minutes inside would have that telltale texture, too-smooth, too-quiet. When you wore it for ten seconds, the tenth second would laugh.

“Jas,” I said again.

He moved.

He cut across the west colonnade toward the noodle bar where steam made the air thick and the mesh’s visibility worse. My brain and my implant shivered in synchrony, a thin cold trickle along the spine. I felt the Bureau habit phrases start up in my mouth—Sir, don’t run—and shut them down with a breath. I ran.

The Quarter bucked around me, seconds sluicing like water. A woman stepped into my path at a heartfelt walking pace, advancing on a stall that sold lilies of the valley made from sugar. I hit the fast lane and the world tightened, edges crisping, the flat gray felt of Jas’s hat a flare ahead. He hadn’t paid for any fast. He was unlicensed and slippery.

He ducked around the noodle bar and into the stripped skeleton of the rail tunnel. The rail bed sagged with years of water and disregard. Old bulbs in the ceiling glowed like patience, orange and dim. The mauve signature in my overlay deepened. Jas disappeared into a patch of shadow and his hat became nothing.

“Jas,” I said, taking out my coil.

The coil looked like a ring of dark metal with three pips like seeds sunk in its surface. When I thumbed them it unfolded into a slinky, an elegant cascade of linked loops. I shook it once, and it hummed as the mesh recognized it and surrendered control. It wasn’t a weapon. We weren’t a ministry. We were the namers of losses, which is a clever phrase I stole from someone else. The coil only locked you to the mesh. It only brought you into time, official time, the slow-eating time we all agreed on. People found that crueler than a baton.

“People are eating,” a woman insulted me from the noodle bar. “Take your drama to the fish.”

“Thirty seconds,” I said, and hoped someone believed I was talking to her.

Jas was behind the support pillar, pressed close to the dripping bricks. He had an implant like mine, something that caught signals and chewed them into something he could bear. He had jury-rigged his to spit out little pockets of absence, micro-blackouts. Behind him on the brick a black mold had grown in circular stipples that looked like stars. He was thin and maybe thirty, maybe fifty; you learn not to trust faces when the counting is different for everyone.

“I’m not a thief,” he said, without moving his mouth much, in the way of men who have known too many microphones.

“I didn’t say you were.” I stepped in and threw the coil. It made a quick arc and cinched around his forearm, most of an embrace. The hum deepened. The Chron mesh surged, scentless and invisible, and for a whole second everything in the tunnel, from the droplet about to fall from the iron beam to the noodles curling around a pair of chopsticks on the counter, synchronized.

Jas’s eyes went very wide. He had the look of a man tasting municipal water for the first time. Then his shoulders sagged, and he did the same thing everyone does when that old, agreed-on time comes for them. He dropped his shoulders and begged.

“I have a kid,” he said. “I have two. I’m just trying to put away enough so they don’t have to—”

“—the Bureau doesn’t do sentencing,” I said, automatic. “We do counting.”

“Listen,” he said, and because he heard very well he heard the edge of apology in my automation and pushed. “Listen. It’s not what you think. This isn’t to keep me alive one day more. I’m not hoarding. I’m paying down debt, I swear. I’m not a bad person.”

“Stop talking,” I said, because it gets me in trouble. “You’re wearing a hat in a tunnel. It’s damp.”

He swallowed and laughed once, which pushed a line into his cheek. “You’re funny,” he said. “Is that for you, or for someone you love?”

I did not answer him.

We stood like that under the dim bulbs; my coil hummed, the mesh breathed, the noodle vendor poured broth with practiced slowness, the drip that had been about to fall fell and then was replaced by another. Time had to be rebuilt constantly, like a bridge you were also crossing. I watched the coil’s little indicator mosaic fill, tile by tile. The coil wasn’t just locking him; it was sampling his minutes, tasting everything he’d done on this market day and the seven before and spitting the data in a cloud to the Bureau. It would track the wallets he’d sold to whose palms, map the web. It would tell Arlen whether I had kept my head.

“How much did they promise you?” Jas asked. “To make you count us so hard?”

“They promised me a wage,” I said. “And enough hours to see my mother twice a week while she still knows my face.”

He tipped his head. The coil hum deepened; another tile, another, like little teeth.

“Ah,” he said gently. “Ah. So that’s the salvation, is it. None of this changes anything.”

“Ask theology,” I said. “I’m a bureaucrat.”

He looked at me then like he wanted to trot out something else, something meaningful, and saw that my face had closed, and he looked at the tiles instead. Something in him folded up neatly, like a shirt packed away. When he raised his eyes his mouth was plain.

“You think you’re going to catch the people at the top,” he said, matter-of-fact. “Of all this.” He flicked his pupils skyward to indicate the mesh, the city, the world. “You and your slinky. You think there’s a ledger of ledgers that your coil will look into for you like the district saint. I will tell you something and you can write it down on your Bureau pad in case there’s a bonus for confessions. There’s a place where it doesn’t count. There’s a place where you can walk and all the little teeth stop biting. There’s a place where time is just… what it is.”

“That’s called sleep,” I said, even though a very old memory in my bones flinched. I am not a religious man. I remain sure of very little. But there had been a story my mother told me twice, once when I was eight and once when I was seventeen and angry, about an old gate deep under the city where you could walk without paying. Done right, it was not theft. It was refuge.

Jas shook his head once. He was pale, and his hat made a little brim of shadow along his cheek.

“You won’t see it,” he said. “They don’t let boys like you see it until they have to. But maybe—”

He stopped. The coil chimed, sweet and sterile. In my overlay the mosaic filled, clicked and glowed green. The mesh slotted Jas firmly back into the story of us. The tunnel brightened a fraction and the hum receded into my blood until I almost couldn’t hear it. I took my coil back. He stood there rubbing the ring of skin where it had hugged his forearm like it had been something affectionate. I palmed my badge and the tiny screen on it flashed the ritual—Reclamation Complete, Transfer Engaged—and then was blank. I sent him walking up the tunnel in front of me toward the mouth and the newer air and the Bureau drone that had already angled around the arcades quietly to pick him up and the vendor with his noodles and the string quartet playing to someone else’s pace.

“Do me one favor,” Jas said, still walking. “It doesn’t cost.”

“You are not allowed to ask me for anything,” I said.

“Don’t make your mother spend to talk to you,” he said without turning. “Let her talk slow. If she’s looking at something you loved together, don’t speed her. Let it pass.”

He handed himself to the drone like it was a gentleman with a car door, and the drone wobbled politely and wrapped him in a fog of sleeping scent. The hat stayed on as he slumped and tilted and the drone bore him away. I watched them go because I had to log it. The noodles smelled like the school canteen when I was twelve and the laughter sounded like coins.

The vendors went back to their rhythms. The mauve smear in my overlay had dissolved. I stood in the breathing of the mesh and felt my four hours fray. The Bureau would sell the coil data to prosecution and then to advertisers who would try to sell blank wallets as artistry, and then to someone else who would fillet it down to a pattern of hunger you could paste into any ready mind and call it “an ad for better bread,” and I would get seventy-three minutes for the capture, less the coil maintenance fees and the Stabilization tax and the low-rent Reclaimer penalty because we don’t make good clients.

I walked to the edge of the Quarter and crossed over the water on the bridge with the glass sides. Below, fish threw themselves at floating gardens print-layered with lettuces. The gardens drifted and made little wakes. I would have liked, very much, to walk without counting for a while. I swiped my wrist through the fast lane instead. The mesh delivered me to the Bureau.

The Bureau building had been an insurance building once, and it had the sighing ceilings and the comforting light. We had not been able to afford to tear it down, so we had re-skinned it with moving panels like the underside of a school of fish. The façade told the story of a heartbeat in blunt dots and dashes, and, beneath the dots and dashes, the story of a city’s aggregate day. If the dots slowed, we were in trouble.

I left Jas’s packet on Arlen’s desk. The desk was a slab of old wood with the grain raised where the varnish had been worn down by elbows. Arlen had the kind of jaw that belongs to men in honesty PSAs and the light tan of someone who logged their jogs with their eyes closed. He had a plant on the windowsill that was not dying. He didn’t look up when I came in.

“You were longer than the algorithm predicted,” he said by way of hello. “Did the noodle man talk you to death? He’s been flagged for telling people ghost stories.”

My badge pinged on his reader. “Jas talks fast,” I said.

“They all do,” Arlen said. He tapped his screen. The data glittered up into the office. He didn’t look at me full-on, which meant this would be unfair and he knew it. “You’re on leave from twelve hundred to sixteen hundred.”

“I didn’t request leave,” I said.

“I did for you,” he said. “You’re meaner when you’re poor.”

“I am always poor,” I said, because if I didn’t make a joke I would say something that would catch my throat on the way out. “Do we have a new convert from Compliance who told you I scowled at someone?”

“We have a negative for the Quarter in the neural. It makes Compliance nervous. The last thing this city needs is a rumor that there’s a leak… somewhere.” He looked up then, and his smile was a thin breakwater against annoyance. “You’re my least gullible Reclaimer. I’d rather you weren’t at large when they get poetic.”

“It’s early,” I said. “And my mother…”

He opened a drawer without looking and slid a voucher across the desk. It lay there like a sleeping thing. “Call ahead,” he said. “They like warning.”

I took the voucher. He was still a good supervisor. It is possible to be decent in a job that eats people. He let me leave without telling me the rumor. He knew I would hear it anyway, because it would be shaped like a hope and we always have a nostril for those.

The sanitorium for the old timers was called the Holdfast. It had a proper name and a new logo and a café with chairs that made you feel like a good son while you bought their coffee, but everyone called it the Holdfast because the tanks looked like jars where you would store jam against winter. They were glass and water and gentle light. Inside, people rocked in the slow, and we came to visit them and speed and slow and cry in it.

On the way I made myself walk, no fast lane, no greedy fingers for the mesh. I took a route through the botanical conservatory, and paid twenty-two minutes to see the orchids and fifteen minutes to slow so they would not unfurl like party tricks before me. The conservatory had cool air and a woman with severe blue eyeliner who wrote a name with her finger on the condensation of a greenhouse door and smiled at it like it was a person she loved.

At the Holdfast, the receptionist took my voucher and my eyes and asked me if I was feeling well and if I wanted a water and if I wanted to upgrade my experience today by adding a Memory Technician to accompany me and help me curate my time.

“Do you get commissioned for that question?” I asked.

“Yes,” she said easily. “But it’s also true. It’s also good for you. You look—” She bit back the last bit. Not everyone can be decent in our work.

“Lio Sorrel,” I said. “Room nine. No tech.”

Sometimes my mother was asleep when I arrived and I would count with her, slipping into her pace. Sometimes she was awake and bright and the panel on her tank would show her heart and her brain chatty as sea anemones. On those days she talked about the people who worked in the Holdfast and who was stealing slippers. Today the panel showed her heart neat and strong. The brain looked like a map of a city with good buses. She was awake. She was awake and she saw me when I came in, which hit me in the belly like I’d been punched with a bouquet.

“Lion,” she said. Only she was allowed to call me that. My name is Lio. Close enough. “You look older.”

“You look exactly the same,” I said, and she rolled her eyes as much as the tank would allow.

“That’s because they keep me in jelly,” she said. She lifted her hand and pressed it to the glass. I pressed my palm to where hers was and felt cool and the faint vibration of the mesh working to keep her in pace with me. “This week the boy with the moles has a new girlfriend.”

“That sounds ominous,” I said.

“She’s very nice,” my mother said. “She carries tea with both hands. She looks like a stone at the edge of a river. The heavy kind, the kind no one can push.”

“She’ll be good for him,” I said, and then we were inside all the old games. We talked about the boy with the moles and the lady who stole slippers and whether the orchids at the conservatory looked like moths or like something that lived under your bed and I kept an eye on my hours and whether I was speeding her where I shouldn’t.

We had five minutes left when she asked me about my hands.

“Are you using the coil too much?” she asked. “Your hands look tired. They used to be softer.”

I thought of Jas rubbing his forearm where the coil had kissed it. I thought of the rumor underneath the Quarter like a dry river. I thought of all the moments she’d paid in her life to carry me to places I did not understand yet. I had wanted to ask her about the old story she had told me twice, about the gate. But the panel blinked gently to show the edges of my time with her. The mesh prefers you depart before you beg. The Holdfast liked to taper your minutes at the end so you didn’t yank away hungry. It is so easy to become cruel and call it care. I swallowed and smiled.

“I’ll bring you a plant next time,” I said. “You can yell at me for letting it die.”

She laughed, though we both knew the tanks kept plants alive better than I kept plants alive. She put her palm to the glass again and then moved it down in a sort of wave. “I will like any plant,” she said. “I like the weeds under the steps best. Stay and let me talk slow. Don’t spend.”

I stayed until my voucher nudged me up like a gentle hand under the elbow. The mesh drew the curtain and slowed my senses by degrees until the soft light around her tank thickened into daylight again. I touched the glass. The glass did not answer. A Memory Tech waiting in the hallway thanked me for visiting my mother like it had been a job and not the one good thing in my week.

On the steps outside the Holdfast, the sky was a complicated page. Glass Harbor had been built to show off its weather, and it did, proud of its orchestrations. The Bureau’s alerts crawled along a sliver of my vision telling people in the northern precinct to wear hats and people along the southern coast to watch their step near the sea because the tide had been trained to come in theatrical. I stood under that page and bought a coffee and drank it too fast and gave the dregs to a fern.

My ledger pinged. It pinged in the way everything in the city pings when it has something to sell you that you can’t afford and it wants, very badly, to convince you that you can. I blinked the alert open with irritation that became, as I read, a hollow emptiness in my bones.

Provisional Warrant, said the file. Under the logo: Bureau of Hours, Subsection 4: Internal Compliance. Issued by the system, auto-signed, which meant it had been judged too urgent to wait for a human. It hung in my overlay like a door you didn’t want and someone opened with your keys.

Suspect: Sorrel, Lio, Bureau of Hours (Reclamation). Allegation: Breach of Secured Artifact (HOUR GATE), Unauthorized Access (attempt), Interference with Mesh (unknown vector). Evidence: Pending; Predictive identification (Chron mesh signature: 99.998). Effective: 2:07.

I read it again because the world had gone very quiet and I had to find out whether my head would make sound again. Around me the Holdfast’s café ground ethically sourced beans. The fern sighed. The sky winked a thunderhead without rain and then let it fade for dramatic effect.

“Arlen,” I said softly, as if calling a dog. “Arlen. I didn’t touch your—”

My badge, warm against my chest, trembled. A second file uncurled like a leaflet pushed under a door. It was a still image, a security grab from somewhere camera shy—a gray square, a smear of shadow, a gloved hand, and a face turned toward a lens. My face, mouth set, eyes up, jaw a notch harder than mine was when I was looking at my mother. I knew my own bad news mouth too well.

The timestamp in the corner said the image would be taken in two hours and six minutes. The location tag said Lower North, undercoast, coordinates that my implant refused to show me on a map. The tag that made me coldest said HOUR GATE in the bureaucratic way we use capital letters only to perform skepticism.

On the sidewalk a woman lit a cigarette and groused at the lighter as if it were an ex-husband. She blew smoke rings. They drifted indecisively, uncertain which air to occupy. Two kids chased each other and their times strapped to their wrists blinked encouragement, you can outrun anything if you buy it. The fern had a droplet bowed under a leaf. The droplet fell.

Something bumped my ribs from inside my jacket. For a stupid blind moment I thought it was my heart. Then I reached into my pocket and took out a watch I had never owned. It was old. It was not connected. It had a cracked face and hands that moved. It ticked against my fingertips with an assertion that set my teeth on edge and then soothed me in equal measure. Its weight was honest. On the back, scratched into the scratched metal, was a sentence I had told myself in my head as a joke a hundred times when cases went bad and meters went hungry.

When it stops, run.

Chapter One: The Stutter in the Light

The rails sang when the city ran. The sound came up through the steel belly of Indigo Ladder as a low, unbroken tone that Mira felt in her jawbones and the soles of her feet. When the baton-skids were properly greased and the magnets were balanced and the ice lung was breathing clean, the note was a perfect hollow A, like a bottle blown across the lip. It soothed the crews who worked the underbody walkways. It meant the city was keeping pace with the light.

She was kneeling on the lattice, harnessed twice to redundant rings, with her hand deep in the warm cavity of a skid housing. Shadowflake—fine, porous dust that drank heat—puffed around her wrist like smoke as she tamped it into the reservoir. The shade ink sloshed blue-black in its canister beside her knee. Above and to her left, the canopy sails flexed, a translucent whale-skin stretched between towers, flickering as the orbital shutters feathered sunlight in a cadence you could set your breath to.

“Shade on Twelve looks thirsty,” called Tamsin from the next housing. The woman’s voice was thick with the rebreather and the purr of the rail. “You’re dumping it in there like the Sun owes you money.”

“Sun’s in arrears,” Mira said. Her mouth tasted of copper and salt. “We’re crossing the salt flats. Everything drinks more when it tastes something it lost.”

Her gloved fingers found a scored groove where they shouldn’t have. She stilled, letting the city’s hum tell her the story. Raising heat. Slight drag. The bolts had crept under load, which meant Twelve was biting a millimeter lower than it should.

“Hold,” she said into her cuff. “I’ve got tooth marks.”

“Copy,” came a chorus from a dozen caches and outriders on the underbody—voices remote and compressed. “Holding. Holding.”

The halyards above creaked as the wind pushed at the canopy; the tone of the rails changed a fraction, a quaver that made the hairs along Mira’s forearms try to stand despite the slick of sweat. She slid the skinner into the groove and shaved out the flaked iron. The sunline ahead was a blade, a white ember that cut the horizon in two. Beyond it, day was naked. Behind her, a darkness that would crack steel with cold if the city lagged into it. In between: their moving strip of dusk and gold.

Indigo Ladder had been running since Mira’s great-grandmother was a girl in a cloth canopy strapped to a wagon deck, when the city still stumbled, when they thought the shutters were prayers sent up to tame a red dwarf that wanted them dead. Now it was four linked spines and two million souls, three helix turbines caged in its heart and a hull of plated basalt on its belly. It ran because if they stopped they would freeze or burn. It ran because the terminator was the only place to live.

“Go easy,” Tamsin said, watching her. “We’ve got heat to spare for once.”

“Tell the ice lung that.” Mira jammed the bolt with a wedge of quick-cure and checked the magnet coil for pitting. She spoke the numbers to her cuff and the cuff told the coil, and the coil made a small corrective moan that Mira, after a decade, found comforting. “When we ‘spare’ heat it spends itself where you don’t want it.”

Tamsin grunted, undid her own assembly with a smooth twist, and popped the lid with a hiss. Hot, dry breath washed over them, the outgassing of a desert that had been starved of day for months.

The city’s Cantors began to sing. The low tones came down from the towers through the canopy lattice, voices braided in a pattern of measures and calls: distance to night edge, distance to day, wind-speed and pressure, ice lung tempo, Citizens’ migration rotation in the interior. Mira let the sound slip into her calculation—not because she needed to, not the way the old runners had—but because she missed it when she didn’t. Her mother had been a Cantor for three decades. Mira remembered lying in a hammock as a child and feeling her mother’s voice hum through the strap and into her bones, telling her it would all hold.

“Cantors jumpy for mid-cycle,” Tamsin said. “Hear that skip?”

“I hear it.” Mira braced her boot against the lattice and leaned into the skid housing. “Probably a—”

The light stuttered.

There was no other word for it. The white blade ahead, the holy knife that divided their world, trembled, jagged itself, and then hiccuped backwards a finger-width. The canopy edge threw a ragged fringe of shadow across the underbody. The tone of the rails made a sound like a swallowed shout. The air in Mira’s lungs squeezed. Above, the sails spasmed as the rigging brains fought for purchase. Tower bells rang on their own as the towers flexed. The sunline staggered forward again, two finger-widths this time, and then again, and again, in quickening jumps that didn’t fit any of the shutter cycles they lived by.

Someone up on the belly walkway screamed. Metal screamed. Shadowflake burst from Mira’s reservoir like a bird.

Mira put her forearm hard against the skid and swore, the words muffled by the rebreather. Her body knew without being told that losing contact with the city now would let the only certainty in the world—gravity—throw her under Twelve’s fifteen-tonne kiss. She braced and let the city buck under her and made herself small.

“Locks!” Tamsin snarled in her cuff. “On your locks!”

The rigs locked, the magnets bottomed out, the city swallowed the jerkiness in a rumble that traveled from the front spines to the back. The rail’s song fell off a full tone and then began to climb back, warbling thinly like a violinist with a bleeding finger.

The light steadied. The bells quieted. The canopy found posture.

“Report,” came the Guild’s voice, too calm by half. “Systems. Outriders. Are you stable? We saw a shutter anomaly.”

“Anomaly my foot,” Tamsin snapped. “Magnets lost sync in Six. We’re holding. We’ve got stress cracks on canopies artery two.”

“Shadow reservoirs on Twelve and Fourteen popped,” Mira said. She wiped dust from her visor with the back of her wrist. Her heart was still slamming in the tight cage of her ribs, the afterbeat of surprise. “I’m re-packing. The tone’s wrong. Coil in Twelve’s running at a weird chew.”

The Guild’s tone was controlled, the voice of ten people processed into one. “Copy. The shutters upstream hiccupped. Correction has been issued to the array.”

Mira froze again, but not because anything moved. Hiccupped. They used the same word she had.

“Define ‘upstream,’” Tamsin said, dripping sarcasm like sweet syrup. “Where’s upstream, exactly, oh wise House?”

“Off. We can give orientation if you’d like to jog to the mirror control in your lunch hour,” said a background voice dryly, and was probably elbowed.

Mira tuned them out. She thumbed a link to the kite logs. The kites were a thousand bright disks strung out in skylines around the city, tethered and free, each with a sensor throat that gulped light and air and coded both into numbers. She watched the graph pour itself out on her wrist screen, little bright teeth of data. Pressure drop, pressure jump, radiance, syruped back. The hiccup wasn’t a wind shear. The hiccup was in the light. If it was the shutters, they had stuttered like a cheap fan.

But the cadence—she ran it again, just those heartbeats: a pause, a jump, a pause half that long, a bigger jump. The measure marked itself into her even breaths. She saw numbers. Two, three, five, seven. Little old songs that Cantors used to teach on cold days, the prime counts. It was nonsense to see numbers where there were only off-angle photons. It was nonsense and Mira’s brain did this to her sometimes, saw pattern in the twitch of a gull.

“Mira.” Tamsin’s hand knocked her shoulder. “You still with me?”

“I’m with you.” She stuffed shadowflake back into the open reservoir. Her glove shook and made the black dust look like something alive. “Did you…did the light patter look like—”

“What it looked like was a giant reaching down to smudge our lives,” Tamsin said. “Don’t go making shapes out of it. That way’s for Cantors and gamblers.”

Mira didn’t say: my mother is both. She tightened the housing bolts, wrenched them until her wrist ached. The rail’s song climbed another half-step. The city’s vibrations smoothed, the way a sleeping animal’s breathing deepens after a noise.

Her cuff pulsed. Private line, light-tight. The address lifted in her display made something she’d corked in herself for months come uncorked and ring like a struck glass.

Iseul.

Mira turned away from Tamsin even though Tamsin couldn’t see her. “Private. One minute,” she mouthed. Tamsin rolled her eyes behind her visor and saluted lazily.

She tilted her head to cut the wind noise and opened the line.

Static—and then Iseul’s voice, all hush and grit and pressure, like she was speaking through a closed hand. You always could hear the Dawn in Iseul. Even on nights she slept in Mira’s hammock she still sounded like she was talking across kilometers from the bright edge.

“Mira. Mira. Please tell me you’re on a line that isn’t wrapped in a guildman’s pocket,” Iseul said without preamble.

“I am,” Mira said. Her voice pointedly didn’t shake.

“What you just saw, that was not a shutter glitch.” Iseul never believed in the shutters’ benevolence. She called them bits of broken weather. “You hear me?”

“What is it?” Mira said, trying to keep the hunger out of her words. She used to hate wanting anything Iseul wouldn’t give freely. That hadn’t changed.

“We don’t know enough yet. The Dawn crews are out ahead of the ladder—we’re in glare. Our kites are blind except when the array turns its face. We’ve been doing old tricks with mirror blinks, because the Guild won’t push anything that doesn’t pass through their pretty mouth.” Iseul exhaled, and Mira heard metal flex around the breath. “I’m not supposed to say this. We’ve been told to sit on it and wait while the Houses argue with math, but I can't. Lucky for me I was always bad at rules.”

“That’s a lie,” Mira said out of old habit. “You’re a zealot for rules if you wrote them yourself.”

Iseul laughed, a one-note thing with edges. For a moment the sound made Mira forget that they hadn’t spoken since Iseul took a Dawn contract and left, their last fight like a blown sail that whipped between them until it tore. “Listen. The hiccup’s a signal.”

“I thought that,” Mira blurted, then bit her lip.

Iseul didn’t ask how Mira had thought that. “We counted the pulses over three anomaly windows and there’s a structured interval to them. Prime numbers. It’s not weather. It’s not the old shutter schedules. Somebody is trying to talk to us using ninety percent of the sky.”

“That’s…” Mira started. Religious. Terrifying. Impossible. “Who is ‘somebody’?”

“I can give you speculations and I can give you assets.” Iseul’s voice changed, able now. “Assets say this: whatever is throwing those patterns is not anchored to the array the Houses keep in love with. It’s above. High above. And it has leverage. It can push light back.”

“Push light back,” Mira repeated, because the phrase was so stupid it hurt, like calling a thunderhead a pet. “That’s—”

“—what we saw.” Iseul had always hated metaphors. “I need you to sit your hands on the skids and then lie.”

Mira blinked. “You need me to what?”

“The Houses will stop us. Standard procedure after a wobble like that is to brake the ladder and test every joint. They will slow the city.” Iseul’s voice dropped to a raw line. “If they slow, we die.”

Mira looked up beyond the canopy at the knife of the horizon and then down through the lattice to the rails that were their only bridge between less and worse. “No one slows. We keep momentum.”

“You keep momentum.” Iseul sounded like she was leaning forward against glass. “The Dawn is in glare. We’ve got a five-minute sneak, maybe seven in pockets. We rode under like thieves with our eyes closed to get you this. I’ve got four outriders burned and one lost. I don’t get to tell you we know anything. But the pattern is a hand, and it’s moving the sunline like a pen. If we stop, it crosses us with a line we can’t survive.”

Mira shook her head before remembering Iseul couldn’t see her. “If the Guild says brake, and I say no—”

“It’ll be your ass. I know.” Iseul’s breath roughened. “Lie. Tell them your tone is wrong and your skids are gasping and you need ten minutes to balance because you’re saving this city’s underbody from chewing itself into confetti. Then do what you do. Keep us moving. If they replace your entire section tomorrow for insubordination, then we can be alive to hate me about it.”

There was a quiet in the line then that wasn’t static. It was the sound of two people not saying a thing that both of them could say. The city ran beneath Mira and tried to make a space in her chest for its hum. She thought of her mother in the laminated shade of the Cantors’ gallery, of the woman’s hands, cracked and soft. She thought of the ice lung’s bellows, slow and fat and forgiving if you didn’t ask it for too much at once. She thought of the boy in Tamsin’s dorm who had gone to sleep out of range of the equators’ heaters during a slow brake and woken with his toes blackened like burned fruit.

“Say the word, Mira,” Iseul said. “And then I’m going to switch to a blink we used when we were idiots in love, because if the Guild tries to catch me by my own tail they’ll need today and tomorrow to sew together the arguments.”

“This is so like you,” Mira said, and there was a smile in it and a bruise. She closed her eyes within the closed world of her visor. “Okay. Okay. Say it.”

“Selvedge,” Iseul said, and the word hung there, beautiful and useless until it was not.

Mira opened her eyes. “Selvedge received.”

“Now lie.”

The line clicked dead.

Mira swallowed the taste in her mouth. She turned back into the open, made her face neutral.

“You look like your tongue forgot how it’s supposed to live in there,” Tamsin said. “Guild’s pinging again. Wants status by the breath.”

“Copy,” Mira said, and put all the skill she had into sounding like a person who wasn’t about to do something that would bend a law. She tapped into the open channel. “Guild. Twelve’s coil is chewing. Fourteen’s magnets are yawning out of sync—my readings are outside tolerance and it’s not comfortable for anyone. Give me ten to patch. If we brake hard with this in her belly we’re going to shear pins I don’t have spares for and then we’ll be moving with fewer legs than we brought.”

“Patch within procedure,” the Guild said, with showy patience. “Then signal. Full brake holds in eight minutes unless otherwise countermanded.”

“Understood,” said Mira. She muted the link and watched its little light flash back at her like an eyelid. “Otherwise countermanded,” she muttered. “By whom, exactly?”

“By me,” said Tamsin. Mira glanced at her in surprise. The older woman had her feet braced and her hands on her hips. She looked like something carved off the city’s keel. “You think you’re the only one who doesn’t fancy freezing for the sake of procedure? I saw that light stumble and I saw the way the edge came at us. I’ve spent forty years trying not to make my death an anecdote in a Cantor’s song. Patch fast if it helps you lie better. But we don’t brake, little Mira.”

“I thought you called me ‘little’ to irritate me on purpose,” Mira said, shaken into a laugh, and then wished she hadn’t said it. Her throat felt tight.

“Oh, I do,” Tamsin said fondly. “Mostly. What did I miss?”

“Nothing,” Mira said, and that at least wasn’t a lie.

They went at the housings like sweepers at sprint. Mira flushed Twelve’s lines and bled Fourteen’s magnet until it sang sharp and true. She fed shadowflake into the thirsty cracks and slapped the lids closed with a sound that made her palms sting. The Cantors sang updates down: windspeed up a hair, day-edge angling, pressure stable. The Guild counted them down in the same calm voice they had used to inform the citizens that the pipeline to Tower Three would be delayed for two days because the ice lung needed to eat and sometimes the city’s heart must come first: five minutes to brake, four, three.

Mira could have asked for an override. She could have said the word in three different languages that went through the Guild’s skin and made it attend. Instead she looked up through the netted skin of the city at the white line where day ate night, and she thought about prime numbers written in light across a planet’s face. She thought about a hand on the sun like a piece on a board.

“I’m going to countermand,” she said into the open channel, and she said it politely. “Outrider Twelve reports that braking at tempo one is not advisable. Recommend keeping current speed and reassess in twenty.”

“Denied,” said the Guild, because it had to, because the Guild was a mouth of laws. “All belts, all rails, full brake in two.”

“Negative,” said Tamsin calmly. “Thirteen and Fifteen concur with Twelve. Outriders are binding. You brake us, we splinter.”

“You don’t have—”

“Listen,” said Tamsin, and there was a sound in her voice that made the Guild hesitate. “You’ve got a handful of minutes where you don’t have the right kinds of information, but you do have the right kinds of people. Leave it with us.”

Silence. It lasted one long breath and then another. The city ran. The air smelled of hot iron and salt. Mira could hear her own pulse.

“Proceed,” said the Guild finally. It put clipped edges on the word, like it wanted those edges to be remembered later, when the Council counted. “Outriders are acting in local authority. Continue maintaining speed. Reassess in ten.”

Mira blew out a breath she hadn’t admitted she was holding.

Another hiccup rolled across the sky.

This one was smaller, a nudge rather than a shove. But it had the same voice. Two. Three. Five. Seven. The canopy’s shadow field wavered and steadied, and the rails’ song swelled and then was sweet again.

“Mira,” Tamsin said softly. “You thinking what I’m thinking?”

“That someone is counting out loud?” Mira said. “Yes. And I think they want us to know they are counting.”

They got the city through the ten minutes and then another ten where no one asked them to brake and no one offered faith either. The hiccups came at twenty-minute intervals. The first was primes again. The second, if Mira wasn’t fooling herself, was Fibonacci, one-one-two-three-five, the city’s oldest stair. Tamsin snorted when she said it but didn’t call her a dreamer.

On the third, when the shutters went ragged for a heartbeat that made the white line advance a lick and cut a clean, new burn into the salt pan ahead of them, Mira’s cuff vibrated with a low-frequency pulse. She almost ignored it, head thick with numbers, fingers black with dust. But it was low and ugly and she knew every song the city made.

It was the tone of the ice lung. The lungs operated like animals, like whales: drawing in the cold of the night and letting it unspool into the day. They were old and cantankerous. They didn’t cry wolf.

“Guild,” said the Cantors before the lungs could speak again. The sound of her mother’s voice, clear and firm and no different here than in a kitchen, if they had a kitchen; if they had one still. “Pressure drop at Valve Six on the southern bellows. We are seeing ice fracture. We will require heat to rebind.”

“Negatives upon negatives,” Tamsin groaned. “We’ve been blessed today.”

Mira had the map of the lung in her head, the way some people kept the faces of their lovers. Valve Six wasn’t far. If you barely slowed, if you took the ladder’s under-spine instead of the stairs, you could put your hand on Valve Six in six minutes and touch the threat with your own skin.

“Go,” Tamsin said, reading the thought on her face. “I’ll mind the skids. This is my hinge and always has been.”

“You can’t throw shade that high by yourself.”

“I don’t have to. I just have to be the person who answers when someone looks for one.” Tamsin jerked her chin up the slope of the underbody and at the choking bright beyond. “Go be the person who stops a lung from learning failure.”

Mira ran.

It wasn’t a beautiful run. The city’s belly was a place made to punish running. Ladders with rungs too far apart to keep pace. Nets that moved as if they didn’t like your rhythm. Heat that braided itself in long invisible ropes and hit you when you least expected it. But Mira had grown up in this maze. She knew how to put her hands on the grip tape and swing with the rails’ song, how to duck under low pipes and keep low when the unexpected found the canopy greasy.

She hit the southern bellows on an inhale and the cold slapped the sweat out of her skin. The ice lung ran along the city’s south edge like a sleeping beast, plates moving, bellows flexing. Valve Six was weeping frost from its mouth. A hairline fracture ran from the base of the valve through two plates and into a place she didn’t want to name.

A little boy in a Cantor’s sash stood there with his hands on his thighs, breathing like a fish.

“Where is your mother?” Mira said without taking her eyes from the crack.

“In her place,” the boy said, with violent dignity between breaths. “I was running the stair when the bellows called. I was closest. I came.” His lashes were rimed white.

“You came right,” Mira said, because you said that to children on days like this. “Go on then. Hold this gauge. When I tell you to turn it, you will turn it like the world’s hinge is in it. Not before.”

The boy nodded, solemn as a priest.

Mira set heat tape, quick and careful and mean to the crack. It hissed and smoked. She felt the lung’s breath change, the big animal of it trying to curl around its wound. If they slowed too much the temperature gradients would fall apart like any tuning and the lung would lose its song. She could patch and she could pray and she could count the numbers in the light and none of those would mean the thing that Iseul had asked of her if she didn’t keep the city running.

“Now,” she told the boy, and he turned the gauge, eyes wide. The lung made a terrible sound and then a good one, and then the ice fracture was a seam with a seal in it, and then it was only a story she would tell later with her hands.

She sat down, hard. The rail song sang into her spine. The boy put the gauge down like it contained a sleeping bird.

“I knew you would come,” he said, apparently to the lung. His mouth had the faint bloom of chapped salt.

Mira touched his head with a gloved knuckle and stood up because if she didn’t keep moving she would be crushed by the thought of how many things could break at once and how human all of them were.

As she turned back into the climb her cuff buzzed again. No voice this time. A blink flash in a line they’d used years ago to pretend across a narrow dormitory that language could be a blanket you pulled over two bodies and find warmth in it.

Selvedge. Iseul again. The flash pattern had the order of a secret handshake.

Mira paused on the ladder.

She watched it through once, twice, three times before she let herself admit she knew what it was. It wasn’t primes now and it wasn’t a stair. It was spelled in the cadence of light stutters and their lengths, in a code the two of them had written once for counting steps when they were climbing the tower and didn’t want their legs to know they were tired.

The message said: We are seen.

Mira shut her eyes until the inside of her lids went red.

“Fine,” she said out loud, to no one and to the city and to the thing above the shutters moving the sun around like a coin on a street magician’s knuckle. “Fine. Damn you. Fine. I see you.”

She looked down through the net and saw the rails and the skids and the shadowflake and Tamsin, steady, hands on her hips. She looked up through the canopy and saw the white line of the sun move a hair to the left and then a hair back, a wink.

She moved.

Chapter One

I heard the clock stop before anyone else did. If you live your life by teeth and balance and the click of a pawl against a ratchet, you learn the shape of silence, and you can tell when a silence is wrong.

The Grayhaven clock had been speaking to me all morning. It had said, in shivers up the wood and a tremor in the floor, that the weights were running heavy; that the bearings had been starved a season and then overfed in a hurry; that someone, years before my time, had coaxed a tired machine through winter by jamming any piece of wire to hand into place and calling it a solution. It had said, when I laid my ear against the main plate, that it forgave me for not recognizing it sooner. Machines have long memories.

At noon, the bell had rung late by half a beat and the town pretended not to hear. Grayhaven pretends well—it pretends to be a place of paint and porches and tart apples, a place the river only strolls by, not the place it really is: splinters in the palm, mildew under clapboard, a current that pulls. By two, the peal had found its rhythm again, and the bench of retired men on the south side of the square nodded into their coffee as if fate had been coaxed back into line.

By six, I was halfway up the tower stairs with the pendulum rod on my shoulder when the beat dropped out, just an inch to the left of my heart. The raspy chatter of the escape wheel ceased; the governor upstairs spun down with a reluctant whir; the weight lines went slack, and Grayhaven’s oldest heartbeat missed.

I stopped.

Above me, sixty feet of old fir steps corkscrewed into dim gold. Below me, the square had the layered sounds of a Thursday evening in summer: somebody slamming a screen door, somebody calling a dog, a car idling, the fountain’s constant mutter. Then a ripple—voices tilting higher, not yet panic, not yet.

I set the pendulum rod carefully on the stair and kept climbing.

The tower is older than it looks. Outside, it is a neat column of painted brick grafted to the town hall like an afterthought. Inside, it is a bark-stripped tree, a hollow trunk fitted with planks and iron and mistakes made permanent by the weight of repetition. I have visited towers across oceans and the smell is always the same: oil darkening wood, bat guano in corners, ancient damp in stone, the tang of metal worn smooth by fingers you will never meet.

At the top, the room opened and breathed around me. Late sun came through the four clock faces and turned the dust into a soft weather. Gears taller than me stilled mid-bite; rods froze with their velocities pent-up, like bones mid-swing. Above, the bell hung in the belfry, a black moon. The fly governor that should have been spinning on the strike train had stopped with its vanes canted, bird wings caught in a still frame.

“Easy,” I said, to nothing and everything. “Easy.”

I crossed the flooring to the time train, already looking for the wedge, the loose pin, the foreign thing. A clock like this doesn’t stop because it is tired; it stops because something asks it to.

The escapement sat quiet and perfect. Pallet stones unchipped, pins true, no grit on the teeth. The weight hung unspent. I traced the lines backyard to the barrel—no bind there. For a moment, I thought that maybe it had been a ghost silence after all, one of those trick-silences that come after three days with a stubborn movement, when your ears turn conspiratorial.

Then I saw it. Not the time train. On the strike.

I knelt and put my face level with the fly. Someone had slipped something into the gearing between the second wheel of the strike train and its pinion: a small, oval piece of brass wedged like a child’s myth of sabotage. The teeth had chewed shallow notches into it before they stopped. I eased it out with two fingertips and the whole train shivered as tensions rediscovered themselves, a long chain of almosts. The fly spun once, twice, as if to exhale, and settled.

It was a cufflink.

It had weight to it—the old kind of cufflink that’s meant to anchor a shirt meant for a forearm that makes decisions. The face was a coin of heavy brass, polished and engraved with the town’s crest—the river, the three folded hills, the little sheaf of wheat—and beneath that, in a scroll I’ve always found vaguely embarrassing, the motto: Truth Tends Upward.

In the center was a monogram picked out in cobalt enamel: H.B.

My fingers knew more about it than my mind did at first: the slickness of fresh polish, the warmth of recent wear. Then the association was there, ready, obvious. There are not that many men in Grayhaven with monograms. There is, in fact, one who wears them like armor.

Harold Bexley, three-term mayor. Bexley who speaks in measured, benevolent sentences about charm and heritage and the necessity of change that looks like no change at all. Bexley who called me in New York himself, four months ago, and said without saying, Come home and fix our clock for us.

The shout from below hit the room like a thrown stone. Not a scream—not yet—but high and fast and urgent. It changed the shape of the sounds that followed: the bench legs scraping, the door slamming harder this time, footsteps running, more than one.

I stuck the cufflink in my pocket.

There are moments you tell yourself you are borrowing time, or truth, from the future—that you will give it back when the future can use it better. There are moments when you know you are lying and you do it anyway.

I wound the strike train off a fraction to free its tongue, set the pendulum rod in place, measured the beat against my own breath, and brought the movement back to life. The clock took a moment to remember itself, stuttered, found the center. The tick spread into the wood, down the stairs. The bell did not ring. The strike had been blocking the hammer; someone had intended the silence.

I should have waited. I should have let the evidence sit untouched and waited for someone with a badge to lift it into a bag. Instead, I put my palm flat to the main plate—a habit, a way to tell if heat was building, a way to greet—and listened to the town.

The noise below had clarified into commands and pleas. The siren came late, as it always does, the old volunteer engine’s wail twisting up Main and rebounding off brick. Somebody shouted my name at the bottom of the tower, wafting up thin as smoke.

“Wren!”

I took the stairs down faster than I wanted to. The pendulum’s new heartbeat knocked against the boards as if scolding me for leaving.

The stairwell spit me out into the narrow lobby with the donation box and the case of town ephemera—the faded photograph of a man standing with his feet on the pendulum bob in 1895, the poster for the Trout Festival, the glass jar of brass shavings I tell children is fairy dust. The door to the square stood open. Heat pooled there, sweet with cut grass and spill of ice cream, but under it was something iron, something like rain that isn’t rain.

The square had gathered itself into two rough circles. One was calm and organized, the volunteers in hi-vis vests bending together around the form on the stone in front of the fountain; the other was confetti-shaped, an appetite of faces angling for sightline, and in it a lot of hands lifted identical little rectangles and held them as if that made them part of things.

I recognized the fountain the way you recognize a sheet you’ve bled on—a different version of something you only want to know one way. Father Time leaned on his scythe, frozen beneath algae. The water that usually spilled from the hourglass poured clear and indifferent into the basin. Between the apron of polished stone and the edge of the pool lay Harold Bexley.

I knew him by his silver hair. Even flat against stone, there was a rightness to the way he took space, a habit of being the center of a geometry. His shirt was dark with what it had to be dark with. His hand lay open against the stone as if to catch rain. The left sleeve had collapsed where a cuff should be. His wrist was bare.

The Chief’s voice cut through the whisper. “Make room, please. Make room.” And then: “Wren.”

She was built like a canoe—long, reliable, not easily flipped. Cora Ames had been the town’s police chief for four years and an officer for twenty before that. We had gone to the same high school, fifteen years apart; we had passed each other on a track once when my legs were still good and her hair was still long. She had been the first person other than me to put a hand on the clock when I came back, and she had said, “Good,” in a way that made me feel like I had been given permission to keep breathing.

“Did you do that?” Cora asked, nodding once up at the face where the hands stood, stiffly, at six and twelve.

“I… it stopped. I started the time. The strike’s off,” I said. It felt like telling a stupid story in the middle of a funeral. “Someone jammed it.”

She looked at me the way you look at the sky to see if a downpour has decided. Her eyes glanced to the tower door over my shoulder, then back. “How long?” she asked.

“Less than five minutes.”

Her radio crackled with names and codes that meant that the ambulance was coming even though everyone knew the ambulance would be too late. She stepped aside and lifted the tape as if it were there already. “Come on,” she said. “I don’t want you to get jostled.”

I didn’t want to get jostled either, but I also didn’t want to be closer. Close, things stopped being a scene and became parts: a loose coin, a dark thread clotted at the end, the way blood dries into dirt and ink and then the smell of it when the sun is too warm. I had worked in cadences of quiet and careful and learned that most grief is something you lean against and let pass through you, like a heatwave.

Harold Bexley’s face was not peaceful. There is a peace you see on TV, a tidy gone-ness that is merciful to the viewer. He had not died tidily. His mouth was half-open and his teeth were too white. His eyes were open to the blistered paint of the nave of the summer sky. I looked away and met Elise Bexley’s gaze across the circle.

She stood under the tulip tree in a black dress too formal for Thursday. Elise always looked like she was about to have a photograph taken in black and white and she wanted you to know in thirty years that she had had it together. Her ice hair was pinned up; she held a glass of wine she had brought from somewhere because Elise would always find the glass and the wine. Her lips made a shape that meant she had already decided who she would be with this today.

She saw me see her. Her eyes moved to the tower behind me, then to my empty hands, and something in her went still as a stopped hand.

Behind me someone whispered, loud as a bell: “He jumped.”

“No,” said someone else, certain, “he slipped.”

“Bexley does not slip.”

“Look at his wrist. His watch is gone.”

“He hit the stone—” “—sick, God, that’s sick—” “—call his son—” “—he doesn’t have a—”

Cora put one of her big, competent hands on my shoulder and steered me along the edge of the tape toward the hall. “Inside,” she said. “I need to ask you things before you have them asked of you fourteen times by everyone else.”

“I didn’t—” I began, wanting to tell her I hadn’t moved the body, I hadn’t even touched the rope, I hadn’t—

“We all didn’t,” she said. “Come on.”

The town hall’s foyer felt like a church on a weekday—cool, scraped, the echo wrong. An orange extension cord ran over the runner and up the wall into a hole someone had not bothered to make neat. The bulletin board had the same flyers it had yesterday. The Trout Festival would still be August 17. The PTA was still mad about the new math. On the bottom rung of the coat rack hung a new item: a light summer jacket in navy, a good jacket, the kind that has a pocket that keeps your phone from falling out when you lean over a railing.

Cora flipped open a notebook, clicked her pen, and balanced it on her knuckle the way she does when she doesn’t want to scare you by writing down the first thing you say. “Tell me about the clock,” she said. “Tell me about something jammed.”

“It’s the strike train,” I said. “The part that rings the bell. The time and the strike are separate. You can stop one without stopping the other. Somebody put—something—between the gears. The time train stopped anyway because the fly didn’t run and the tension backed everything up. It’s not common. It’s also not an accident.”

“What was the something?”

I could feel the right pocket of my work jeans like a small, hot planet.

“A piece of brass,” I said. It wasn’t untrue. It wasn’t useful.

“Like a bearing?”

“Like a… like an oval. Like a coin. Polished.” The words were unhelpful and I could see them be unhelpful as they came out of my mouth.

Cora’s eyes sharpened. “Do you have it?”

I wanted to say, I wanted to say, I wanted to say. I heard the siren take in breath and let it out again as the ambulance came around the far corner and the sound reached us half a beat after the sight.

“I took it out,” I said. This time the lie sat squarely. “I left it upstairs. On the bench by the movement. It will be there.”

“Good.” Her pen slid the word down like butter. Her face did not change, which is her gift. “Who else has been up there today?”

“Only me. The custodian let me in at nine and left after I told him to please stop trying to help by spraying everything with WD-40.” I was babbling. “I mean, yesterday Mr. Orr from the Historical Society stuck his head in, because he thinks the pendulum is the community’s pet, but—”

“The door at the bottom?”

“It locks. You need a key.”

She glanced at the key in the lock right now, the one that sat in a little box on the wall by the donation jar between ten and four like quaintness. “Best practices.”

“I asked them for a proper lockout set. I have it on a list.”

Outside, someone started shouting again, chant-like: move back, move back, please. The crowd’s sound rose another notch and you could feel the place where all those eyes turned into one eye. Grayhaven was excellent at turning into one thing.

Cora looked over my shoulder at the square, then back at me. There was a soft click in her gaze, the sound of a mind putting away empathy and taking out procedure. “Wren Calder,” she said in the voice she uses on formality, “where were you between five and six this evening?”

“In the tower,” I said. “Mostly. I went down once to the bathroom at five-twelve. I bought an apple at the farmstand for dinner at five twenty-eight because I forgot to eat. I was back up before five forty. I heard the clock stop at six twelve. I took out the—object—and restarted the time at six thirteen. I came down at six fourteen when people started shouting. I am being too precise to seem casual,” I said, surprising myself. “I write things down.”

“Write them down for me,” she said, and then she smiled because she knows how the muscles of your face can loosen people around you. “And Wren?”

“Yeah?”

“Don’t go back up there until I say,” she said. “I know it will itch. Scratch something else.”

When she went out to be in charge of what came next, I leaned my back against the cool plaster and slid down it until I was sitting on the runner with my knees up like a child. The custodian, Mr. Herrin, peered out from the council chamber door, white-faced and unhelpful. The air smelled like lemon oil and a hint of dust you only notice when it is disturbed. Somewhere upstairs the clock had found its balance and was ticking along as if it had always done.

I put my hand in my pocket and pressed my thumb into the enamel letters until they hurt.

H.B.

When I was ten, my father let me take the enamel dial off the clock we had in the hallway and see the sheet brass beneath, rough and honest, and for the first time I understood that the world mostly hides its workings. I have made a career out of coaxing them into view and making them run in step with their bones. I have told myself that I love clocks because they are what they seem if you look long enough; that their lies are only the simplifications we ask of them, not the malicious inventions we ask of each other.

Someone had jimmied an old mechanism with a symbol of a person and a position and forced a silence at a time when Grayhaven would normally expect a sound. That seemed like language to me. If the clock is a voice, then so is this.

It took a full twelve minutes for the ambulance to leave without a hurry. Twelve minutes is a long time when you are white-knuckling a secret in your pocket. The chairs in the council chamber made their small, habitual noise as the staff inside shifted in the way of people who want to be seen to be ready to do something. The old photograph behind the donation box looked down at me: the one where the man stands on the bob and holds the pendulum rod like a mast and stares into the camera with chin-jutted innocence. He must have trusted the pendulum to hold him up. He must not have wondered if he was meant to fall.

“Miss Calder?” A voice, dry as old paper, from my right. Mr. Orr of the Historical Society had materialized like a regret. He held his hat in both hands, white hair rebellious beneath its absence. “Is it true?”

“Is what true?”

“That the strike stopped right at the—” he waved his hat, groping for the word he wanted that wasn’t the word for a person on the stone “—incident.”

“It is true that the strike stopped,” I said.

“Ah,” he said, pleased to know a thing. “How curious. Why would it? Unless—” He leaned closer and lowered his voice, and I smelled tea. “Unless someone meant it to. To mark something, you know? Or not mark. You know there’s precedent in the literature—”

“Mr. Orr,” I said. “Please.”

He blinked, affronted. “I only meant—”

“Not right now.”

He retreated to a chair and sat, hat held appropriately against grief, and furrowed his brow. Later, he would come to me with clippings and theories. Later, I might even be glad of him. Later was later. Now, I wanted a quiet I could trust.

When Cora returned, she had a young officer with her I recognized as Jordan Mills’s nephew—the kind of pretty boy who will be mean by accident as often as he is kind by accident. She had a paper evidence bag in one hand and her calm in the other. “We’re going up,” she said. “Show me what you saw.”

I stood and they let me go ahead and I put my foot on the first stair. I could feel the stairwell like a throat.

Halfway up, the tower swallowed the square. In the movement room, dust settled as if no rush had passed through. The bit of skin I had left on the edge of a gear the first week I worked the tower itched, a strange, old echo.

The bench was as I had left it. The box of assorted screws that belong to nothing anyone can remember lived under the shelf of cans. The little brass brush I prefer to the nylon one rested against the tin of oil. The rag I had torn from one of my mother’s sheets was folded in a square you could put a ring on as if proposing. There was no cufflink on the bench because there had never been a cufflink on the bench because I had carried it down the stairs in my pocket as if it were something light.

“You said—” Jordan began.

“Yes, I said,” I said.

Cora stood with one hand on the main frame and closed her eyes a moment, not praying, counting. “It doesn’t change that it was there,” she said, eventually. “It only changes what you are.”

“What am I?” I asked, too quickly. My voice came back to me off the faces and I sounded like a stranger who had borrowed my throat.

“Useful,” she said, and smiled in a way that lifted nothing. “And complicated.”

Below us, the clock ticked. It was a sound like small forgiveness, like the town’s one stubborn promise to keep moving forward no matter who said no. I took the cufflink out, finally, and the enamel looked blue as river water in the shivering light.

Truth Tends Upward, the crest said, and I thought, holding a symbol of a man who had died at six twelve on the stone: sometimes truth tends to hide until you bend your ear in the right place. Sometimes it wedges itself into a machine to make one big, undeniable noise.

I put the cufflink into the bag. My thumb, at the last, left a smudge I hope was only oil. Cora reached for it, eyes on my face, and for a second her hand hovered like a second chance.

“You’ll have to give a statement,” she said.

“I will,” I said.

“And Wren?”

“Yes.”

“When you heard it stop,” she said softly, “what did it sound like?”

I looked at the pendulum and the gear and the dust that made its own weather and I thought of silence. “It sounded,” I said, “like someone taking a breath to speak.”

The box wasn’t in the system. That was the first suspicious thing I noticed about it, and in the basement of the Bell Harbor Civic Annex, that made it practically a ghost.

We keep the dead things downstairs: a parade of objects that used to be bound up in people’s lives but now belong to their endings. Phones with shattered faces. Wallets swollen with river. Lighter-fluid cans, bricks of narcotics, kitchen knives that, by their look alone, make you imagine the moment they left a drawer and did what they did. They arrive tethered to numbers and barcodes and sealed-lip bags, every step documented in the chain-of-custody like prayer beads. Untethered, an object is nothing. It is trouble.

The trouble was on a gray metal cart parked crooked by my desk, just past the sign that said PROPERTY MANAGEMENT UNIT – AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. No manifest zip-tied to the handle. No white evidence tape stretching mouth to mouth. A standard banker’s box, the lid slightly askew, a dot of dark soot worked like a thumbprint at one corner.

I stood there with my coffee and let the small, sour thrill of it bloom behind my ribs. I live for the ways the world goes off-kilter. I’m not supposed to live for them, but it’s the kind of gratitude you start practicing if you spend nine hours a day elbow-deep in what's left after everything interesting is over. The fridge hummed to my left, a constant, low F-sharp my hearing aids translated as a velvet ceiling to the room. The light bulbs along the cinderblock wall flickered like worried fish. Upstairs, a court reporter laughed and then swallowed it, like she’d remembered herself.

“Don’t touch that,” Jasper said around the donut he wasn’t supposed to be eating while handling anything. He’d come in on my blind side, a talent that would’ve annoyed me if his cologne didn’t reach me first with that synthetic ocean slap he mistook for clean. He was new enough to still think he could pull casual off.

“I’m not touching it,” I said. I put my coffee down and reached anyway.

Jasper rolled his eyes. “Kline said leave it for Detective Randle. He’s coming down.”

“What’d he say it was?”

“Didn’t. Just said leave it.” Jasper leaned an elbow against the cart, and the box’s lid shifted. We both looked down. He moved his arm very slowly back to his side. “It’s probably a stapler.”

I set my palm on the top and felt the weight of it through the cardboard, something dense in the center pulling all the corners inward. Someone had written, in ballpoint along one edge: BELL HARBOR – WINTER MARKET – 1997.

My mouth went dry. I don’t know why I thought, immediately, of the way snow had squeaked the week the Winter Market burned. I was twelve, my father had left the house in two strides with his turnout gear over his shoulder, and my mother had turned the news up louder than necessary so we could all pretend the noise was company. In the morning, we’d gone down to the lake because that’s where everyone went—Bell Harbor people had this particular sorrow in common, we wanted to see for ourselves—and we’d stared past barricades and a row of bundled firefighters at a row of blackened trusses. Eight vendors had died. The cause, they said, was a tangle of wires behind a spice merchant’s stall. Faulty heaters. January blaming worked that year—a comfort, something to point at that wasn’t a person. The city’s gossip teeth had nothing to chew.

I slid a chair with my foot, both a shield and a stage, and lifted the lid. The room took one small, respectful breath with me.

On top of a bed of brown packing paper sat a ledger. Old-school, long and narrow, bound in cracked tan leather that had sloughed and bubbled with heat, the spine tightened into a grin the fire had forced on it. The edges of the pages had been crisped into delicate, scalloped ash. It was the kind of ledger you see in movies, the kind people used to run their lives through, every name and number neat as a church pew. It belonged in a museum. It belonged, absolutely, to a case file that had been boxed and destroyed twenty years ago when a pipe burst and flooded the south wall a week before I started the job.

“Jasper,” I said, my voice smaller than I intended. “Get Kline.”

“Now?” He leaned in, both at war with his curiosity and his instinct to let anything uncomfortable be someone else’s problem. “What is it?”

“Evidence from Winter Market. Or it wants us to think so.” I snapped on gloves. The latex squeaked. In the corner, the fridge shifted its pitch, a half tone up that my left ear heard and my right ear refused. It does that sometimes—sometimes I do that sometimes—which is why the audiologist gives me pamphlets about neurological fatigue I never read.

“I’ll get Kline,” Jasper said, even quieter, and left.

I pulled the ledger free. It left a brown, prisoner-shaped impression in the paper. The smell that rose was not smoke, not immediately—it was glue, the animal kind, and old dust, and something else I only caught because it was the exact: a thin ribbon of char and pine sap. My father had come home with that smell threaded through his hair. It never leaves the house. I always think of it when I turn on the coffee maker and watch the first black pour.

I set the book on my mat and looked for markings. No barcode. A string of numbers penciled in the top right corner of the flyleaf, faint and precise: 97-2876 WM-L. Our old numbering system. The case number made my throat tighten. The tag stapled to the back page, brittle now, had come along. EVIDENCE – DO NOT BREAK SEAL, from a time before we could afford tamper-evident tape. Someone had scrawled a date: 1/22/97. A name: Lt. Voss.

My father’s name. Not the Fire Department, not the Marshal’s office, not a detective. Just Voss, like the writer knew there was only one. He was.

I didn’t hear Kline come in, either. She is built like a clip: small, sprung tight, meant to hold everything together. “Tell me that’s a copy,” she said.

“It’s not logged.” I angled the book so she could see the penciled numbers. “There’s no manifest. It was on our intake cart.”

Her mouth flattened the way paper does when it’s wet. We have cameras pointed at the door at all times. Kline, who makes lists in her sleep, who can tell you which bin a bag of meth cooked in an RV is in without looking, who wears her hair like a helmet because she’s always braced for an impact, was already imagining the policy notices we’d have to write. The meetings. The detective who would come down and subtract an hour from our lives.

“Randle’s on his way down,” she said. “He was…particular. Don’t open it.”

I had already thumbed the corner of the first page. You do this job long enough, the rules rearrange themselves in your head. At the top is this: Everything exists. The second rule is: Everything should be written down. The third is: If no one wrote it down, the first rule is very important.

“I want to check it against the system.” I turned my monitor toward me like an instinctive lie. “See if—”

“Mara.” Kline exhaled, an entire nap’s worth of sleep leaving her lungs. “You can check the system without letting oxygen into something like that. If Randle wants us to see what’s in it, he’ll—”

The elevator dinged.

Detective Randle always looked like he’d walked to work in the rain and refused to use a towel. He had dark hair that never listened, a stubborn patch of beard on his chin that had the energy of a bruise, and a habit of speaking while he was still finishing his last cigarette even when there was no cigarette. He gestured at the box with a little flourish that said both I’m pretending this is nothing and It’s everything we now have to live with.

“This from the Winter Market?” he asked, and when I didn’t answer, because I was too busy watching the way his eyes skipped right over the case number, he supplied: “That’s the rumor.”

“Where did you get it?” Kline asked.

Randle pointed at the ceiling. “It landed upstairs. Please tell me you didn’t—”

“Open it?” I said, and to demonstrate restraint, I only opened it this much.

I wish I could say the words on the page surprised me because they were scandalous, or because they weren’t there, but they surprised me because they were written in my father’s hand. Large and impatient, pressing through the paper in a second, declarative script. He did this thing where he crossed his sevens, a habit he picked up from an old captain who learned to write on forms that had traveled through more than one language. I know because I used to mimic it, drawing little scars across my own numbers like I was putting starting gates in them.

Mara, the first line said. If you are reading this, I did this wrong.

The ledger trembled under my gloves. It could have been my hands. It could have been the fridge revving into that anxious half-step like a violin warming up onstage.

Kline’s hand landed on my wrist, soft. “What?” she said, but it was an ask for which I needed ten hours and a therapist.
