People also went there when they wanted to be alone and when they wanted to be found. Elsie’s mouth had gone thin, the way it gets when she’s already begun not saying the worst thing aloud.

I grabbed my boots and a headlamp and the battered canvas bag I carried when I climbed into the guts of other people’s clocks. It held oil and brushes and a little brass lantern with a heart stubborn enough to shame a saint. I closed the shop behind me and we stepped into the fog. The street was empty except for a dog that may or may not have existed looking at us from the far corner. Above the salt-cured shingles of the houses, the town hall’s clock tower hunched, a black shape without the ring of light it should have at the four faces. Without the motion of its hands, it looked blind.

“Any power outages?” I asked, stepping around last week’s sand still in a drift at the curb.

“Only righteousness,” Elsie said. “The diner’s bread machine tripped a breaker around ten, less than a square yard of hell in Millie’s kitchen. After that, nothing. Lights stayed. Freezers stayed. Old man Rusk’s ventilator is humming him along fine if you ask his daughter. It seems to be just the things that count time for the satisfaction of doing so.”

“Not just mechanical?” I asked. When you’ve stood over both, you can hear the difference between a spring that’s unwound and a circuit that’s lost its nerve.

Elsie shook her head. “I’ve got three calls on my voicemail about microwaves blinking like they’re trying to learn Morse code. Some kids stopped their phone timers mid-race to see who could hold their breath longest under the pier. Two minutes, seventeen seconds.”

I stopped. “You’re telling me that’s what they had set them to?”

“I’m telling you we’re not going to enjoy whatever explanation paid us a visit tonight.” She squinted up into the fog where the tower should have been more tower-like. “I can do my job without knowing exactly how things tick, Mara. But when they stop ticking, I consult the person in town who speaks their language.”

The person in town who spoke their language had coffee at three in the morning because she had hands that stopped shaking only when they were busy. I would have killed for coffee. Instead I climbed.

The inside of the town hall smelled like furniture polish and mouse. The stairs up into the tower were meaner than my apartment’s, built when men are always young and never fall. The first flight was wood and the second iron and the last a ladder runged into the idea of a wall. There were three platforms, and each had the graffiti promises of teenagers and the molted husks of pigeons like the dried-out versions of their own bad decisions. The trapdoor to the clock room stuck, then gave with a sigh of dust around its edges. I breathed through the cuff of my sweater until the sweetness of old cedar rubbed with brass polish beat back the smell of waste.

When you open a clock, you get its character like a draft. The town hall’s clock had been built by men who believed the town would last longer than they would, from years when the town was full of men like that. The gearing was big and clean, the teeth like the bites of tidy animals. In its best years the clock used to argue with itself and win; in its bad years it would sigh and insist. I loved it even when I hated it. Tonight I hated that it was still.

I set my bag down and switched on the lantern. The light kissed the polished arcs and made shadows of the thin parts. The escapement—where the energy became discrete, the tick-tock, the heartbeat—was poised open like a mouth between pronouncements. The pendulum hung stiff and true as a verdict.

“Tell me something, old man,” I said to it.

There are things you look for first. You check cords and weights, the lines of strain where the tower pulls the wrong way no matter how you argue. You look for coins or pebbles dropped by a bet or a bored child with windows opened onto temptation. You look for nests and webs placed by creatures that have no respect for schedules but a lovely instinct for tension. And then you look for malice.

The malice was subtle. If I hadn’t had the lantern, I wouldn’t have seen it. Between the third wheel and the great ring gear, something was lodged that didn’t belong. It was paper, but it hadn’t wadded in; it had been fed carefully, stage-managed so it would stay exactly where it needed to to catch under the first tooth that wanted to pass. I slid in my little bone spatula because in a menagerie of brass you learn which metals argue with each other and which pass the salt politely.

The paper came free damp with oil. It wasn’t a note from years ago, some list of minutes or repairs. It had been typewritten, uneven and blue-black, the letters a little tired. Someone had cut it and folded it and slid it between the gears with hands that knew exactly where to interrupt the world.

NOT YOURS TO MEND.

“Elsie,” I said.

She pushed up through the trapdoor far enough that her elbows took her weight and her face rode the floorboards like a puppet on the stage. “Tell me you found a piece of baling twine and an apology from the pigeons.”

I held up the paper. She read it upside down and swore. She had always saved her best swears for children running across Water Street without looking; this one was for me.

“Christ’s own courtesy,” she said. “We’ve got a comedian.”

“We’ve got someone with time on their hands,” I said. “And small hands, and the patience to stand here wedging a note into a gear on a Thursday night.”

“It’s Friday,” she said.

I thought of all my clocks downstairs that had missed the handoff. “It will be.”

She pulled herself the rest of the way into the room and stood with her hands in her pockets. She looked at the paper again. “Somebody did this to all the clocks?”

“They wouldn’t have had to. People wind on different days. Some pendulums will pass a piece of grit and some won’t. They’d have to be intimate with a lot of systems and a lot of schedules to make a thing like this happen all at once. If they did it to the tower and the church, it would feel like all at once. The tower’s chime tells people what time it is whether they know it or not. The rest might be coincidence wrapped in drama.”

“You hate coincidence,” Elsie said.

“I’m allergic to it.”

She smiled; it didn’t reach the worry lines. “We’ll secure this, then. I’ll have someone at the door and somebody else watching the rest of the clocks that matter. Can you get it moving again?”

“Once you take the note out of a sore tooth there’s no guarantee the jaw wants to chew for you right away,” I said, to amuse myself. I breathed on my fingers and set the lantern just so and nudged the pendulum. It answered—such a relief, that first defiant tick. The second came. The tower took a breath and remembered how to inhale.

I’ve seen a town draw itself up when it gets its heartbeat back. It’s subtle but it’s there: the way a stoplight’s sequence becomes less arbitrary again, the way a drunk sings with a slightly more determined vibrato on the stoop of a bar. The clock was ticking. We would have to reset it, of course, and convince it we were capable of honesty. For now, tick. For now, tock.

“We need to go to Gull Point,” Elsie said, as if she’d heard what I was listening to and didn’t want to let me wrap it around myself like a scarf.

“Yes,” I said. I wiped my fingers and put the note in a plastic bag I carry for the kind of job where birds make statements. I didn’t like the way the words looked inside it, as if I’d caught a small live thing.

On the way down, I thought of the person feeding the paper into the gear. It takes time to wind a clock, to set a gear just so. It takes nerve to stand in the belly of a town where any door might open onto your back. Someone had come up here tonight and poked the old beast and left me a sentence like a slap on the wrist. Maybe they were here when the clock stopped. Maybe they waited for it, listened for my clocks, too, though that was me assigning them the courtesy of my obsessions.

The fog outside was thicker, the kind that doesn’t stay still; it braided itself around the street lamps, the whole town wearing a scarf it was trying to take off without using its hands. We took Elsie’s cruiser because I had a fatal lack of car and because she preferred her own smell of cinnamon and coffee and detective to anyone else’s. The wipers dragged stripes across the windshield like half-done crosshatching. We drove past Water Street and the dark tangle of the harbor where boats clonked their masts together like bottles under a bar. The lighthouse winked at us between cups of fog, an indifferent eye.

“There’s been a body found,” Elsie said, when we had crossed Harbor Road and were taking the narrow that led out to the Point. She said it the way you say it to a person who has seen bodies before but not tonight. “A fisherman, found him down on the rocks by the old tide pool with the iron rung. Teenagers. They’re still crying. There was nothing to be done by the time they got cell service enough to call.”

“Who?”

“We don’t know yet,” she said, which was true and might also have been kind. “He’s not someone we could pull a name off of with a glance.”

We parked where the gravel turns to rock, and some of the fog unspooled itself enough to let us through. The path down was slick and mean. Knott waited with a flashlight that made everything look more conspiratorial than it already was. He was twenty and earnest and worried he’d never be good at anything besides worrying.

“Chief,” he said, seeing Elsie; and then to me: “Ms. Kearns.”

“Officer,” I said. “You practicing your flashlight voice?”

He almost smiled. His beam found the path’s good parts. We came down over the last of it and there he was, a human shape the sea had been considering and had not quite decided to take.

For a second I saw only the unfairness of gravity and slick rock. Then my eyes adjusted around it and found the particular. He had fallen or been lowered or flung in a way my mind wanted to categorize because that’s what minds do. He lay on his side, one hand curled at his chest. He wore a dark coat that had once been expensive in the way men buy expensive things to carry their most ordinary gestures. His hair had come loose from wherever he had put it. His face–well, the sea had opinions about faces and privacy. He had a watch, though. Most men do, when they set out to be found or not; it’s something to refer to when trying to understand a decision.

The watch was in his curled hand, its chain broken, the case open and its glass cracked in a star. You don’t pick up something from a body unless a police officer has agreed with you that you should. Elsie looked at me and nodded because she had already decided to give me that authority tonight. I eased the watch from his fingers with a gentleness I reserve for primates and machines.

The dial grinned up at me with its coal of a crack and the fine hands pointing as if to lay blame.

“Two seventeen,” I said.

Elsie’s breath went out like a small surrender. “Of course it is.”

“Not just stopped,” I said. “Something forced it. See the dent, here—” I touched the rim where it had struck something hard in such a way the balance would have jumped out of its cup. “Fell from a good height, hit just so. Could stop a watch at that moment whether time wanted to or not.”

Elsie watched my face while I watched the watch. She does this with witnesses and with equipment: she uses other people’s attention as a reflective surface.

“Do you know him, Mara?” she asked.

I wanted very much to say no. The foghorn said something approximating my name. The beam of Knott’s flashlight slid over the rocks and pulled up the memory I didn’t want to put a name to. I knew the coat. There was a tear at the hem I had stitched myself years ago, badly and in the worst possible kind of hurry.

“Yes,” I said. “At least I think I do.”

“Who?” Elsie asked.

I swallowed twice because names, once said, do not want to be put back. “Leonard Croft.”

The name hung there in the wet air. The man who had taught me how to hold my breath over a ticking thing so my own lungs wouldn’t disturb the truth of it. The man who’d sold me The Second Hand for less than a fair price because he’d liked the way I kept my shop windows clean.

Elsie closed her eyes for a heartbeat and opened them on me. “All right,” she said, to the night, to herself, to me. She gestured to Knott, and he radioed words to people who would be asleep for ten seconds longer. She crouched close enough to Leonard’s shoulder that the fog made a halo of her hair. “Mara,” she said, and I heard in it every time I’d gone up the wrong ladder. “You’ll come down in the morning and give a statement.”

“Of course,” I said.

“And after that,” she said, flicking her eyes to the bag with the note in it, then back to me, “you will tell me why someone fed a message to your clock with the patience of a penitent, and what it has to do with the fact that time stopped everywhere in this town so we could be out here together with Leonard Croft.”

I held the watch in both hands because otherwise I would have put them on the rock. The lighthouse blinked in the fog, an indifferent eye, and the clocks, all over Grayhaven, held their collective breath to see by which seconds we would count the night.

Death has a smell, but it isn’t what you think.

People who haven’t spent hours in rooms with the newly dead assume it’s rot, something that claws at the back of the throat and makes you gurgle up your lunch. That smell exists, yes—later, after time and air have had their say—but the first smell, the one that clings to your clothes and follows you home, is quieter. It’s hospital antiseptic muddled with wool, sweat tucked into seams, a hint of soap behind an ear. It’s metal coins, old pennies in a warm palm. Sometimes it is lilies someone thought would help. Often it is the smell of a life that just stopped moving through a body and left everything behind.

On nights like this, winter working its way under the door of the prep room, the smell is also tidewater. The Holloway Funeral Home sits at the edge of Blackwater’s harbor, a shingled house with a slate roof my great-grandfather laid himself, and when the wind is right it sweeps in salt and old rope and the alien sweetness of decaying kelp. The embalming machine hums a steady, machine-heart rhythm, tubes quiver, and in the corner the drain takes what it’s given.

“Is he heavy?” Nate asked when they brought him down from the transport gurney, as if it mattered. He’s young, missing the tip of one ear, steady hands. He calls everyone ma’am and says little prayers under his breath. He still believes he is a visitor in this room.

“Yes,” I said. Conrad Pritchard had been heavy in life, a man who took up space deliberately—sturdy suits, chosen watches, steaks cut with the blade of a knife he’d had sharpened weekly. In death, the heaviness turned to a sort of big-boned stubbornness that made the rolling sheet pull him slow down onto the table.

Sheriff Seth Garner stood in the doorway like he had doubts about this whole enterprise, his hat cradled against his chest. The overhead lights cut shadows into the hollows of his face and threaded gray through his dark hair that hadn’t been there in high school when he could throw a baseball from one end of the football field to the other and make a catcher’s glove pop like a shot.

He cleared his throat. “Mara.”

“Seth,” I said, because we have both agreed never to use our history as punctuation. “You didn’t have to come.”

“I did,” he said. Then, as if that explained anything, “Town’s going to wobble. If they see me bringing him here, it looks like—like normal. The town wants normal.”

He meant it kindly. He always does. That’s our problem. We mistake kindness for safety.

Mayor Conrad Pritchard had died that afternoon in his fishing shed at the end of a rickety little pier he maintained himself as an homage to some ancestor who’d worked sardine boats. A heart attack, someone said, out of breath on the phone to dispatch; then Deputy Nate clarified over the radio, something about him slumped over the workbench with a half-carved piece of cedar in his hand, shavings on his shoes. It was clean, they said. Quiet. He liked to whittle there, to make little birds and give them away at ribbon cuttings.

His widow, Vivienne, had called me herself in the careful, glazed voice of a woman who knows the town will discuss her tone alongside her grief. The Holloway Funeral Home had buried her father and her father’s father; she was a subscriber to legacy. She asked, with exquisite politeness, if we could prepare him quickly. There were council matters. There were optics.

“I don’t have a lot of time,” Seth said, fidgeting in a way that told me he had quite a lot of time and didn’t know what to do with it.

“It’s not a magic trick,” I said.

He flinched, slightly. “Is that what you think I think?”

I adjusted a lamp, light slanting across Conrad’s face. He looked, in repose, like a man about to deliver an unwanted opinion. His white hair had flattened at the back where it had met the bench. He’d been a handsome man in a politician’s way—thin mouth, clear blue eyes—made beautiful in the way old men sometimes are when they’ve shed interest in it. He had a small birthmark high on his right cheek near his ear like a faded fingerprint, something I hadn’t noticed in life. We notice these things in death because the living are always moving and the dead give us stillness to examine.

“Do you need to sign anything?” I asked. I’ve found that when men stand in doorways unsure what they can fix, the offer of paperwork soothes them.

“Already done,” Seth said. “Vivienne signed all that. She declined an autopsy.”

“Of course she did,” I murmured, and he narrowed his eyes.

“Mara,” he said, warning in my name.

“I’m not saying she shouldn’t have,” I said. “He was sixty-two. He had the sort of job that gives you headaches and eats your time. He had lunch at Dory’s four times a week and took his coffee like varnish. Men like that die of hearts.”

“Thank you,” he said.

“But,” I said, soft, and he sighed. “But Vivienne is a woman who cultivates control like orchids and she was quick to decline any questions. And you know I like my answers thorough.”

“You like your people,” he said, not unkindly. “I’ll be upstairs if you need me before I go.”

He left, and the room sighed back into its sounds: hum, shiver, a clock’s distant idiot insistence. Nate busied himself with the stainless-steel counters, laying out things I would ask for before I asked. He’d been with me nine months and had stopped puking at two.

I rolled the mayor’s sleeve—cufflinks shaped like anchors—and examined the veins in the crook of his elbow. There’s a clean choreography to this work, a way you have to prepare yourself to enter another person’s geography. It demands a reverence that is not holy but precise. I had been a perfumer once, before my aunt—June Holloway, queen of teacups, who could look down a nose without appearing superior—left me this house with its stiff curtains and debts. In Paris, they called us noses, and we spent our days figuring out how to memory-trick people with molecules. In Blackwater, where people think of perfume as something teenagers spray on themselves by accident, my sense of smell mainly tells me when Mr. Pearson didn’t really quit smoking even though he told his wife he did.

Still, it lives in me, a set of notes tuned by years around oils and absolutes. I smell cedar where others smell pencil, orange blossom where others smell clean. And on the stainless table that winter night, above the cold weight of Conrad Pritchard, I smelled something that did not belong.

If death has a smell, so does interruption. It threaded itself, a thin silver line, through the expected: disinfectant, latex, sea. Bitter almond, the cliché ran, the thing you were supposed to smell if cyanide had come calling. Except not exactly. People expect a bakery’s marzipan. What I smelled wasn’t sweet. It was a sliver of benzaldehyde, yes, that kernely sharpness, but there was something chemical behind it—strict, medicinal—like a bad imitation of an old-fashioned candy. And it shouldn’t have been there, not under formalin’s must and Conrad’s cologne cut through by time.

I leaned in and breathed carefully through my mouth, then through my nose. It came and went like a word on the tip of your tongue. Nate watched me with the look of a person trying to learn a language by observing someone else’s face.

“Mara?” he asked, and I shook my head.

“Give me the file,” I said. I flipped through it with gloved fingers. Found in his shed at 4:12 p.m. by Councilman Alby Merrick, who’d gone down to ask about the budget line for seawall repair. No signs of struggle. Shallow contusion on left temple where he’d struck the bench edge as he fell, likely postmortem. No prescription bottles on premises other than a bottle of aspirin rattling with two tablets, dust gritty in the bottom, and a box of cedar shavings curling like little tongues in the wastebasket. The shed had smelled of varnish and salt. The file said so because Seth had written it and he notices smells like someone who has lived his whole life fixing outboard motors and thinks the world runs on oil.

“Did you smell anything there?” I asked when he wandered back to ask if I wanted coffee.

“At the shed?” he asked. “Yeah. Gluey wood. The river. His—” He stopped himself before he said body, changed it to “his jacket. Wool. Why?”

“Nothing,” I said, because experience has taught me that telling a sheriff he might have missed what, if I’m right, would become a murder is a poor way to begin a conversation. “Decoction pump,” I told Nate. “Slow. And give me a look at his hands.”

We always start with hands. They tell us nearly everything we want to know about a person’s last several hours. Conrad’s were broad and blunt-fingered, nails groomed to a civilized length, cuticles tidy. There was a crescent of cedar dust under his right index fingernail, but scrubbed into the lines of his left palm, near the base of his thumb, was a faint smear of something blue-green. It looked like oxidized copper but felt like paint. It flaked under my nail and came away gleaming small and stubborn in the light.

“Nate?” I said, and I handed him a small evidence envelope. We are not cops, in case that needs saying. We are morticians in a town that thinks of us as a piece of its furniture, all velvet and hush. But my aunt kept old manila envelopes for this precise purpose, and I have learned which quiet to keep.

Conrad’s lips, recently parted by death, had a fine white line at the corner as if dried saliva had sealed there and then dusted with something. I leaned close. The scent was clearer at his mouth. Bitter almond, slender and strange as a knife. Or I wanted it to be. Memory and desire can trick you. Still, I know what I know, and once you know a smell you can’t unknow it.

“Did he take anything?” I asked, trying to sound like a woman who read a file, not one who was about to break one.

“Like pills?” Seth asked, tossing me a Styrofoam cup he’d retrieved from upstairs with coffee that could have been used to strip paint.

“Like anything,” I said. “Supplements. Homeopathic nonsense. Vivienne is a woman who believes in berry powders.”

“Larkham’s told me he came in last week about his blood pressure.” Larkham is Blackwater’s doctor, as old as the lighthouse and twice as grumpy. “Put him on something. Ate him about salt. He told me about it at the diner. Said the pills made him pee like a racehorse.”

“Could you ask him to send over the list?” I asked. “Of his prescriptions.”

“I already did,” he said. “It’s on its way.”

He hovered. He’s good at that, at hovering dramatically, a man-made ornament in mahogany. I’ve seen women cry into that hovering. It must be nice to embody a place like that.

“You can go,” I said. “I’ll call you if I find anything you’ll wish I hadn’t.”

His mouth tilted, almost a smile, not quite. “Don’t poke the hornets, Mara.”

“I’m not poking anything,” I said. “I’m doing my job.”

He left, finally, and the sound of his boots went up the stairs like punctuation. I turned back to Conrad. I clean because I am polite. I slid the trocar into the right place because I am practiced. And yet the entire time I thought of one afternoon five years ago in a little lab that looked out over the rooftops of Paris, where a journeyman perfumer named Daria slapped my hand away from a beaker.

“No,” she said, in that accent that makes Americans fall in love with things they do not understand. “That is benzaldehyde, it is greedy. It will eat what is next to it and pretend it is sweet. It lies.” She laughed. “Or it is just a molecule and we are people and we give our own sins to oils.”

Later, when Aunt June had begun mixing up sugar with salt and called me in a whisper because there was no one else left to call, I came back to Blackwater and exchanged one set of lies for another. You can make perfume of anything, she used to say. Our job is to make it smell like truth.

My phone buzzed on the counter, lighting up with a text from a number with a Boston area code I didn’t recognize.

Package delivered. Front step.

I frowned. I hadn’t ordered anything. I am an unrepentant list maker; there were no boxes on any of my lists. Outside, it had started to snow, the kind of lazy, indecisive flakes coastal towns get when the air can’t commit. The porch light at the front of the home throws a honeyed circle onto the top step. Sometimes tourists walk past in August and take photos of it, the old wooden sign with its swirled Hs and a painted lily. People like to pretend we are quaint. They do not think about the basement.

“I’ll be back,” I told Nate, who has learned not to be offended when I am abrupt. I pushed through the prep-room door into the hallway, up the narrow passage to the front, where the false parlor sits with its pale sofas, curtains on rings like a prom dress. The house creaked in agreement with the sea as I opened the front door and looked down.

A brown-paper parcel crouched on the step like it was about to run. It was unremarkable except for the fact that someone had tied it with string, actual string, knotted neatly, not taped like a modern person might have. I picked it up. It was heavier than it looked, dense like a dictionary. My name was written on the paper in blue ballpoint in a hand that made its capital Ms like mountains. No return address. The snow took the edges off the sound of the harbor.

“Who’s that?” a voice asked, and I turned to find Mrs. Templeton, who runs a bed-and-breakfast and can see this porch from her bedroom as if it were a stage, looking over from the sidewalk and trying on nonchalance like a shawl.

“Junk,” I said, and smiled like I wasn’t holding a nerve in a box.

“Terrible about the mayor,” she said. “Terrible. Though I suppose he was at that age. Charles went at fifty-seven, and he was a saint.”

“I’m sorry,” I said, because I always am, and shut the door gently on her winter curiosity.

Back in the prep room, I set the parcel on the rolling table I use for makeup and lifted the string with my glove. The knot was one my aunt had taught me because she believed in old ways of doing things, not out of stubbornness but because she thought they kept our hands honest. I undid it and lifted the paper back.

Inside was a book. Red cloth fading toward russet, the title pressed into it in gold once but mostly rubbed away. The cover had a hotelier’s politeness, something that had lived on a shelf behind a desk collecting stories it would never tell. I flipped it open and felt the breath leave me in a long, low sigh that made Nate look up sharply as if I’d injured myself.

“What?” he asked.

“It’s my aunt’s ledger,” I said. I knew the handwriting even before I saw her name inside, black ink on cream, the bend and rush of it like a familiar creek. June Holloway, Registrations, Preparation, Notes. 1978–2018.

“What’s it doing here?” Nate asked, genuinely puzzled because he has only worked in a world where ledgers live in the same cupboards forever. He never saw Aunt June fall asleep with it across her lap in that wingback chair and dream about the living by way of the dead.

“I thought it was lost,” I said. “When we cleared her things.” I had gone room to room after the funeral like a thief in my own house and found nothing but dust and checkbooks, and I had grieved this ledger like a second death. I turned pages. The first half was what you’d expect—dates, names, cause of death written in Dr. Larkham’s miserly hand beside her looping scripts. At the back, her iffy shorthand, which was less a code than an unwillingness to be read by anyone but herself, blossomed. Aunt June wrote like a woman who knew the town too well to trust it. She had little notations beside some names: an X, two dots, a slash that meant nothing yet.

“What’s that?” Nate asked, peering at the page as if proximity would bring comprehension. His breath fogged in the cold air, and I resisted the urge to wipe it away.

“It’s how my aunt kept her suspicions,” I said, before I could help myself. Saying it aloud made something transmit between my own skull and the room, a tiny shiver like static. I don’t know why I told him. Maybe I wanted to say it to someone else so I wasn’t the only person who knew that my aunt—Midwife of the Departed, keeper of casseroles—harbored doubt like an ember and didn’t always blow it out.

“S-suspicions?” he said, stuttering on it as if the word itself were improper in here.

“Of what?” he asked.

“Of stories that didn’t add up,” I said. “Of deaths that felt wrong. Of lives that got ended like a book with pages ripped out.”

He pointed at a mark on a page from 1998, beside a name I recognized because the town still told that story, if sideways. “Stanley Grey?” he said. “Didn’t he drown in the cove?”

“He did,” I said. “After last call at Mulligan’s. After he’d told anyone who would listen that he’d teach a man a lesson.” I could hear my aunt in my head. Some people drown because water wants them. Some because people do. Then I pushed the ledger aside and went back to Conrad because this room doesn’t care for nostalgia. It doesn’t forbid it, but it doesn’t like idleness much.

“Take teeth impressions?” Nate asked, and I nodded. We worked, the sort of work that is patient and medium-blind. I cleaned under Conrad’s nails, and my gloved finger brushed something rough on the pad of his left middle finger. Not a callus; he was a pen-holding man, not a hammer man. A splinter lodged sideways, very fine, with a smear of something dark beneath. I teased it out with tweezers and held it up to the light. Cedar, probably, but stained where it had been wet. It left a small notch in his finger like a healed crescent.

The smell flared again when I turned his head slightly, a little cough of bittered, synthetic almond, and an image came into my mind uninvited: a little blue bottle on a shelf in a shed, tucked behind paint cans, labeled in a hand like mountains. The picture was precise, which meant it might well be wrong. The mind is a carnival. The shed exists; I’ve seen it. The bottle might too. Vivienne could burn me to the ground for opening my mouth on just that.

“Do you want me to call Dr. Larkham?” Nate asked, as if he’d plucked my thought out of the air. He does that sometimes. I chalk it up to wanting.

“Not yet,” I said, which is a way of saying probably. “Give me a sample. Partial, from the jugular. And leave the radial for show.”

“We don’t generally—” He stopped before he told me what we don’t generally do, because I am the we in that sentence. He knelt, steady, and I felt the weight of my choice settle on my shoulders like another layer of wool. We’re not cops, I’d said. We are shepherds at the far end of the field. But my aunt had left me a book that said sometimes you have to circle back.

By the time I had finished, it was well on toward midnight and my bones ached the way they had when I first came back, when I was still translating myself from a life of small glass bottles and summer salons where women asked me to make them smell like secrets. The snow had thickened. Upstairs, the house sounded different at night, less sure of itself, the pipes thudding like old men in a bar.

I found Seth in the front hall, leaning on the banister reading a pamphlet about grief because he is the kind of man who would be embarrassed to be caught staring out a window in a funeral home. He looked up when I came in and took in the ledger under my arm like a quick study.

“Is that—” he began.

“My aunt’s,” I said. “It came in the mail.”

“Tonight?”

I nodded. “You should have someone who sits at a desk find out who sent it. It matters to me.” It was the closest I could come to asking for help without confessing that the note of almond under my tongue made it hard to swallow.

He studied my face. We have had years of practice reading each other, in hallways like this, on bleachers, in borrowed cars. His mother still buys pies from church bake sales because my aunt told her to in 1989. We are, as much as people can be, entangled. It makes us good and terrible at this.

“Is there something I should know?” he asked.

“Do you want me to tell you something I don’t know yet?” I asked, careful, and his jaw tightened. He hates it when I do that. He calls it float talk. He thinks I do it on purpose to make him feel like a man in a boat without a paddle.

“Do you have cause to bring him back into my office?” he asked, and this was his way of giving me the room to say the word that would make everything harder for all of us. Autopsy. He hates them. He hates the way they turn a death into law.

“I have questions,” I said. “And a smell I don’t like.”

“A smell,” he said, almost gentle, and when he isn’t careful his voice slips into protective, as if I am a person to be bracketed and lifted. “You and your damn nose.”

“Yes,” I said. I didn’t smile. “Me and my damn nose. You can ignore me. You probably should. Vivienne will decorate your desk with her newest red handbag if you don’t.”

“I don’t work for Vivienne,” he said, and a pulse ticked at his temple. “I work for this town.”

“That’s what I mean,” I said.

He rubbed at his face, as if to wake it. “I’ll talk to Larkham. Quietly. If you keep this quiet.”

“I live in a house that can hear the harbor breathe,” I said. “I don’t plan on shouting.” I held up the ledger and he took it from me, thumb brushing the edge of the cloth cover in a way that told me he knew books as touch. He opened it, looked at a page, frowned.

“What is this?”

“My aunt’s shorthand. She believed people’s stories could be as suspect as their taxes.”

He looked up. “She was the one who told me when I was a rookie that the worst things in town didn’t happen in alleys. They happened at dinner.”

“She wasn’t wrong,” I said.

He closed the book and handed it back. “I’m going to get home before my mother calls the station and asks if I’ve decided to start sleeping in the embalming room. You’ll call me if—”

“If I smell anything else?” I asked, and despite things we both allowed half a smile.

“Good night, Mara.”

“Good night, Sheriff.”

He left. The house settled, and I stood in the front hall a long time without moving. The ledger was a weight against my hip. The day had been full and terrible in the way of these days, and my body wanted a chair or a bed or a bath. The snow made the world smaller. The harbor dully clinked rigging against mast, bells in mittens.

The phone rang, shrill and sudden in the quiet. It pulled me into Aunt June’s office like a fish tugged through water. I picked it up expectantly, more ready than I had any right to be for Vivienne’s voice with its hoarded grief.

“Hello?” I said.

There was a pause, and then that voice, crisp. “Ms. Holloway. It’s Vivienne Pritchard.”

“Mrs. Pritchard,” I said, and found my hand straightening as if she could see me.

“Thank you for receiving us,” she said, as if she were at my door with a pie and not on the line with a woman who had her husband on a table. “I would like to discuss arrangements. Also, I would like to be perfectly clear on one matter.”

“All right,” I said.

“We will not require an autopsy,” she said, not a question. There was a hardness under it like a bedrock no one had mapped.

“The sheriff said—”

“I have spoken to him,” she said, and there was a sound in the background like ice in a glass. “And to Dr. Larkham. Both have assured me that further insult to my husband’s body is unnecessary.”

“I see,” I said, because I do not argue with a widow on a winter night. It is one of the few rules I keep.

“And one more thing,” she said. “My husband found the world a place of curious shortcuts. He believed that the straightest line between two points was only sometimes a line. I tell you that because I think you should know we took care to make his affairs in order. We do not like surprises, Ms. Holloway. Do you understand?”

I could see her in my mind, immaculate hair, that coat that looks like it costs as much as a used car, the way she holds her body as if she is dancing through a room no one else was invited to. “I do,” I said, and wondered if I did.

She ended the call without goodbye. I stared at the receiver for a second longer than necessary. The house was suddenly too quiet. I flipped open the ledger to the back, the place Aunt June kept her notes that were more feelings than facts, and pressed my finger until the paper dimpled. Someone has rewritten an old rule, I thought, and we forgot to tell the dead.

In the prep room, the mayor lay with his hands neatly folded over the sheet, his face settled into something easier than politics. My aunt used to say that the dead do not ask you for anything. That is part of their charm. But sometimes they leave you an aroma, a smudge of paint, a ledger, a widow with a voice like a blade, and you find yourself nodding to an empty room as if someone has just told you a story that ends with you walking out into the snow.

I turned off the overhead light and the room fell into the sort of glow that makes stainless steel look like water. As I closed the door, I caught it again, faint as a memory you don’t want—bitter almond, ghosting my tongue. I could champion coincidence, call it detergent, call it a trick of nerves. Or I could go back to my aunt’s book and begin reading the marks she’d left, one by pile of dead leaves, one by one, until I understood why, forty years on, she had tied it up with string and sent it to me on the night the town lost its mayor.

Behind the house, a gull cried like a baby in the dark. Upstairs, a pipe clanged. I stood at the bottom of the stairs with the ledger under my arm, and I thought: the straightest line between two points is only sometimes a line.

Then, because I am who I am, I went back down and filled a small glass vial with a shining, thin red crescent and wrote in my careful hand: Pritchard, C. 3/2. And next to it, in pencil, a mark I hadn’t used before, but one I knew from my aunt’s book.

Two dots and a slash.

Chapter One

The night the clock stopped, the harbor forgot how to breathe.

It had been a week of gray-lidded skies and nervous gulls that rode low over Grayhaven, the kind of weather that made even the cannery dogs restless. Boats doubled their lines. Shopkeepers taped Xs across their windows with the resigned ritual of people who had lived through enough late storms to know the difference between rumor and a name. This one had a name—Lisbet—and it was moving up the Atlantic shelf with its shoulders squared.

From my shop on Wharf Street, I could smell the storm before I could hear it: damp copper on the air, a metal-teethed edge that found the gums. I had the window propped and the lamps low so the brass didn’t heat. The carriage clock on the bench was guts-out and sulking when my own sign—Finch Horology & Repair, hand-painted in navy on frosted glass—wavered with a gust. I held my breath, waiting for what I had grown used to without knowing I’d grown used to it—the town clock taking the hour.

Instead I felt the absence. Ten, eleven, twelve—nothing, as if some wide mouth above the square had opened for a note and swallowed silence instead.

I set down my screwdriver and turned the carriage clock’s balance cock between my fingers. Reflexively, my eyes went to the wall. The clocks along it were in their own wonky chorus. A cuckoo that had never been able to keep from getting ahead, seven longcase timepieces with the faces of parade marchers, a banjo clock that had sold a dozen times and come home twice. They fussed and clicked and marked their own versions of passing, but each of them checked itself on the town clock the way we all did. Without the deep bronze of the tower at the top of Main Street, their ticks felt like orphaned metronomes.

If I’d been anyone else, I might have waited. Let the storm crews worry. Let the selectmen send a boy with a ladder. But the tower had been mine for the last year, since I came back from the city and hung my name where my father’s had once been. We’d always had the clock in our pocket, the Finches. When something mechanical lost its nerve, people called us.

The phone on the back wall rang just to make it official. I wiped my hands on a rag and let it ring twice more before I answered, because I am a petty man and because hearing the urgency carries its own weight.

“Finch’s,” I said.

“Eli? Thank God.” It was Nora Bell, whose last name had been a joke for two generations, as her father and her father’s father had been sextons, and Nora herself had grown up with a ring of keys that could arm a small fortress. Now she managed the old stone Congregational that owned the tower’s bones. “It’s gone quiet.”

“I noticed.”

“We’ve got a wedding in the morning.” She said it as if the weather would take it under advisement. “And then the storm. If people don’t hear it, they’ll be down here breaking in windows to ask what time it is.”

“There are other clocks,” I said, because I hadn’t had my evening coffee and because Nora was a person who liked things to be done before you had agreed to do them.

“They want that one,” she said. “You know they do. Please.”

From our side window, I could see the square, the white splash of the church’s front against the bruised sky. The tower rose above it, its four black faces dark and blind as hoods. The idea of it sitting unguided during a storm made the skin at the back of my neck pebble.

“All right,” I said. “I’ll go now.”

“Bless you. I’ll leave the side door open.”

I took my scarf from its hook and a coat that had seen too many winters, found the small canvas roll that held my tools and the tin of clock grease. My father had liked to joke that I slept with a bottle of oil under my pillow. I turned the sign to Closed; the letterforms dampened the light into a soft smudge. When I stepped out, the harbor air hugged me with both arms. The harbor had stopped breathing because everything else had, too, drawing itself up to listen.

Grayhaven after dark is different from Grayhaven at three in the afternoon when the ferry lets out and tourists in lemon-yellow raincoats take pictures of the fishmonger’s chalkboard. The paint peels back then. The porch lights are moth-bitten. The sound the estuary makes when the tide begins to run out is not the same sound as laughter. It’s more like someone trying to remember a song they used to know. I cut across the square, past the bronze soldier with his green shoulders and the bench where the teenagers pretended not to be kissed. My footsteps echoed. The tower door took me like a mouth.

Inside the small vestibule it smelled of old wood and the sort of damp that doesn’t dry. There is dust in every church, the accumulated rubbings of hands and hymns. Another door, and then the stairs that go up and up, narrow, worn stone, no railing. I know those stairs better than I know some people I eat lunch with twice a week. I know which riser will wobble. I know where the drafts come. Halfway up, there’s a slit window that catches ships like pins. I always stop there, as I did now, to see what the harbor is doing, but Lisbet had flattened the horizon and erased the boats into the kind of silhouette painters like and sailors hate.

When you get into the clockroom, you feel it before you see it. A particular chill that lives where metal is made to move. Machines carry sadness the way old houses carry echoes. The gear train—Great Wheel, Second, Third—filled the far wall like a patient animal. I could hear it not ticking. I could hear, in fact, the whisper of its collapse. For the uninitiated, when a tower has struck on the hour for two hundred years, it gets ideas about who it is.

“Hello, old thing,” I said, because I talk to them. My father had done it too. I laid a palm on the crazed paint of the frame.

The mechanism had stopped clean; the pendulum hung mid-swing like a sentence missing its end. That made something in me clench and then unclench. A clean stop means interruption—something has interfered rather than something has broken. It’s easier to fix a fight than it is to fix a fever.

I pulled my lamp closer and looked at the escapement. The anchor sat jaw-open. The pallet stones were intact, the escape wheel teeth neat. No chips. No bite marks. I moved along the gear train with my eyes, the way I had been taught, and then with my fingertips, because sometimes you feel what you can’t see: a misaligned tooth, a burr, a smear of grit. The oil had flung itself a little; there were fine black lines on the brass where dust had married it. Nothing to stop it. I followed the linkage to the strike hammer. Its lifting piece was down, its spring normal, and then—I frowned and leaned in.

There was a threadlike stripe on the lifting lever, right where it brushed the cam. Not a crack. Not wear. Something foreign. I brought the lamp closer and smelled it before I knew what it was. Old pennies and salt. Blood.

It had dried already, a brown whisper in a seam. A droplet had formed at the underside and stopped, surface tension arrested mid-fall. You could have missed it, if you were in a hurry or if you were thinking about storms and weddings and how you’d left the iron on. I don’t miss much with machines.

I touched it. It flaked. I held the flake under my nose and closed my eyes and remembered the way rust smells different from blood by just the slightest sliver of iron, and I felt foolish for making poetry where life is prosaic, and then I lifted my lamp again to trace the line back to its source.

There was fabric caught up in the hinged piece that drives the rack. A snag, a tiny ribbon of blue crushed into the grease, as fine as something a dressmaker would cut and let fall, but slicked and dark now. I worked it free with tweezers, careful not to disturb the geometry. The tower’s strike is a rack system, not a count wheel. That’s neither here nor there for you if you have not spent your life with these things. For me, it means that the bell knows what to do by how many teeth the rack falls. If you wanted to make it lie, you could. You could feed it false teeth in the night and it would swear to them in public.

I rolled the fabric between my fingers. Silk. Not local. Most of Grayhaven buys wool and corduroy and calls it a day. Silk arrives with weddings and tourists and the occasional funeral.

“Whose blood?” I said to the bell-metal blankness. The sound did not carry into the church. Bells are strange that way; they keep secrets until they are told not to.

I tucked the blue slip into the pocket of my coat without thinking. Habit, more than anything. People bring you things to fix—their clocks, their watches, sometimes themselves—and sometimes you collect pieces of them without intending to.

Outside, a gust went shouldering at the tower. The frame creaked. The lamp’s flame drew itself skinny and then recovered. It is never smart to be higher than all your neighbors in a storm. My fingers were already in the grease. I did what I had come to do. There is comfort in procedure. I unlatched the pendulum, checked its bob, checked that there had not been a tiny shift in the leader that would slow everything into a sulk. I wiped the lifting face and the pinions. I took a drop of oil in the place where the lifting lever had been touched because there is very little in the world that oil or kindness cannot make easier.

When I set the pendulum swinging again, the room collected itself. Time, like an old dog, came back to the foot of the bed and settled with a sigh. The governor on the strike train did its quiet nervous dance. I let the clock run against noon. The hour would be wrong, because it had stopped long enough for the town to fall out of step. You can correct a half minute by ear, a minute with a penny on the bob, but when the world is off by more than that you must tell it the truth. I unlocked the setting wheel and brought the minute hand around by the slow, clicking increments that always feel like apostasy.

When you stand in a tower’s clockroom with your hands on a mechanism that outlived your father and will outlive you, you think about scale. A watch in a man’s vest will forgive you anything. A tower will remember.

I set it to eight-fifty-eight by my wrist. A Fourth of July watch my father had given me when I apprenticed in the city, old enough to matter, with a face cracked at the edge from a day that got away from both of us. When the hand kissed twelve, the strike lifted. I stepped back, because no matter how many times you hear it, a bell struck in a room as small as a clockroom is too much. It fills the marrow.

The first tone hit like a shoulder. Low C, our bell, with a mouth big enough to swallow a man. It pulled. Two. Three. Four. The stairs carried the sound down into the hollow church. Five, six.

On the seventh, I realized the governor was running a hair off. It was subtle. The time between the lift and the drop, the breath in the throat. Eight, nine. I put my hand on the regulator out of instinct, though there is nearly nothing you can do mid-strike except watch and say whatever prayers you still know. Ten. Eleven. I counted with it. Twelve.

And then there was that half-breath and another hammerfall.

It struck. Everyone in the square will tell you something different about that moment, because everyone in the square heard it. Children say dragons sang. People who wear ties say it was a rote mechanical error, explainable, boring. Old women say they hadn’t heard thirteen since their grandmothers were girls. I only know what I know. The rack had fallen exactly as I had expected it to. The rack had no more teeth to give. The hammer struck anyway.

The floor under my boots trembled. The lamp’s flame hopped its tin cup. Somewhere below me, the vestibule door banged open—wind or a hand, I couldn’t tell. The thirteenth tone bent just slightly at the end, as if reluctant to own itself.

I stood there with oil on my fingers and my jaw tight and told myself half a dozen sensible things. That a spring had rebounded. That a lost rivet had found itself. That nothing is perfect. None of those sensible things meant what everyone in Grayhaven would think they meant. There’s an old story, and like all old stories it has an old face. When the clock strikes wrong, someone dies. It had a nice meter to it, the kind of superstition that gets told over cod fillets and hung on the back of the mind like a hat. My father got bored of being asked if it was true. He used to say, “Clocks err in all the same petty ways we do. That’s proof against magic.”

All right, I thought. Prove it. I set the gate and checked the rack tail. My hands knew what they were doing again, which was a blessing. When I looked up, the slit window was a single strip of breaking. It took me a second to understand why. The church below me had gone dark.

The storm had taken the power. The square had been lit all evening by a necklace of slightly drowsy street lamps; now they had winked out, one by one, the way people look down when they don’t want to see something. Somewhere out at the harbor, a siren started in a long low hum that barely made it in through the stone. If you are from a place with hurricanes, that sound will make spaces in your heart you will not be able to fill with anything else.

A scream lifted, quick and sharp, from the yard.

The stairs didn’t care that I needed to go down them fast. They went on being narrow and worn because that is what they are, and so I had to go down them the way you go down a throat in the dark, one hand on the damp wall, body sideways. At the slit window, the square flickered; one of the shops had a generator. The light it threw was the wrong color, too warm, too sorry. I reached the vestibule, hit the door with my shoulder because the wind had leaned against it, and the square came to meet me like a story you can’t stop telling even after you know you are wrong.

There were a dozen people out in it—more, as the wind took its own and the first broken leaves of Lisbet began to fall like early confetti. Nora was among them, her ring of keys a clapper at her belt. She had a flashlight, and she had lifted it the way you lift a candle at Christmas services, both reverent and practical. She turned when she heard the door and her face told me enough before her words did.

“Eli,” she said. “Oh, God.”

Between the base of the tower and the bench there is a patch of flagstone they laid in the 1930s when the WPA made sure no American town would forget how to square a shovel. On that stone lay a person. People were already doing the useless things people do when they are startled by grief—saying her name, which no one yet had, pressing at a wrist, pulling their jackets over shoulders. The rain had started, a fine spray that made everything in the world look like it was about to disappear.

I went forward because men like me in towns like this go forward. You learn not to prepare yourself for what you will see. In my work, you get cut by tiny things. It’s never the big pieces of glass. It’s the thin yellow wire that catches the flesh of your index finger and makes you remember for days that you ought to have been gentler. The human body is more fragile and also less dramatic than people think. When I knelt, the stone was cold through my trousers.

The woman’s hair was dark and slick against her cheek. There was a line on her forehead where she must have struck, and a halo of grit. Her coat was red, but a red that in the warm light of the generator looked almost black. Someone had put their hand under her shoulders and forgotten to take it away. I put my fingers where I always do first. The pulse point is a habit I must have learned from every detective novel I pretended not to read. Nothing there. Or my own heartbeat pounding through my thumb.

Nora’s face was very near my own. “She fell,” she said. “Nicky saw—he said she came out of the door. We didn’t know you were up there.”

“I was,” I said. It came out clipped. I had not thought, until that second, about someone else in the tower. “I was up there.”

“She opened the door,” Nicky was saying to no one in particular, to the crowd, to the air. He was seventeen with a face that would have been handsome in five years if he lived that long, his hoodie dark with rain. “She just—she came through, and then wind took her, and then she—”

“It doesn’t matter what you think you saw.” That was Mrs. Greeley, who owns the general store and has never been wrong in her life except when it counted. She had her hand on Nicky’s shoulder and was trying to rub the story off him before it stuck. “It’s wet. She slipped.”

“She’s cold,” someone else said, because they needed to say a fact aloud to keep it from being swallowed.

The woman in red did not have a scarf on. Her throat was bare. That is not a thing you notice right away unless you have just found a ribbon of blue silk in a machine designed to mark out human hours. Then you notice. You notice the way your own coat is a weight over an unfamiliar shape in your pocket. You notice that the generator’s light has made a jewel at her ear. You notice that there is a watch ticking somewhere that you did not wind.

I realized the last as if someone had flicked a knuckle against my sternum. It was not the tower. The tower, even when it speaks, does not tick; it breathes. This was a small sound, precise and self-absorbed, a heartbeat behind the ear. I bent, as if I were going to say something kind to the dead and had already forgotten what it would be, and I listened between the breaths of a dozen anxious people. The tick lived in the pocket of the red coat. I slid my hand in. Not because I am a thief, though the thought occurs to you when your hand is where it ought not to be. Because the sound had made my skin prickle and because the part of my brain that knows times and machines had stepped onto the floor and asked to dance.

It was a watch, a woman’s, old enough to be real rather than clever. Gold on the rim worn thin where flesh had loved it. I lifted it with one hand while the other continued pretending to be the respectful hand of a man who has done this before, who might, if called upon, be able to say a verse. The dial had hairline scratches across the porcelain where a fall had taught it humility. The hands had stopped at 8:59. Locked at the moment the clock above us had refused to speak.

“Do you know her?” Nora whispered, because she had gotten close enough to my ear to know how to ask me something we could safely pretend she hadn’t.

It would have been easy to say no. I could have said no for hours. People who fix clocks are not people who are asked to recognize girls in red coats at the base of a tower. But Grayhaven is small. And a storm had made it smaller. And there are names you put in your mouth against your better judgment and roll there like hard candy.

“Lila Morrell,” I said. The name came with the taste of a tired espresso in the back of my throat and the scratchiness of a booth at Deacon’s Diner where two afternoons ago I had sat with Lila while she told me a story about bells.

“Are you sure?” Nora’s voice, thin.

I looked again, but you do not need to see a whole face for certainty to find you when it wants you. The trouble with memory is that it puts its hands on everyday things. Lila’s hands had had ink stains that resembled small countries. Lila’s laugh had been a penny dropped into a glass jar. Lila had had a blue scarf, the color of the inside of the bay on a good day.

“Her,” I said. “Yes.”

Over our heads, the tower’s bell decided, finally, who it would be for the night. The air had changed as the rain made up its mind. People began to unfold their skepticisms and their plastic tarps. Nora put her keys on the ground in a little hectic pile. Somewhere farther off, a car backfired, and you could feel everyone gather themselves like horses. It is something, at least, to have a task. We could find a blanket. We could call the ambulance that would not be able to cross the causeway now that the tide had started its rush. We could argue, gently, about what we were going to say to people who would ask to be told the story with the most spare adjectives we could afford.

A piece of blue silk in my pocket reminded me that there had been more than wind in the clock. The watch in my hand felt like a clue in a game I had not wanted to play. It was warm, a little, as if it had been sleeping against skin a long time. I looked up at the dark square faces of the tower and thought of my father, who had spent his life with machines and died of a thing no gear could arrest, and I tried to imagine saying to him that I had heard our bell say too much.

“I was up there,” I said again, to no one. It is hard to be believed when you tell a town that its stories are only stories. It is harder to be believed when you tell it that they are also sometimes blue ribbon and blood, mischief and gravity, a watch’s stopped hand and a thirteenth strike that has never belonged to any sensible clock.

Lisbet, out at sea, turned her great head toward us. The generator hummed. Someone began to cry a little. In the half-light, I felt time move a fraction to the left, as if it had been pushed by a shoulder you couldn’t see.

Chapter One

The morning the clock failed, Old Quay sounded like a room holding its breath. The gulls still skated the air in their usual lurching arcs. The harbor cranes still grumbled, the water still lapped and slapped against the quay posts, the buses still sighed as their doors arched open. But the hour did not fall from the tower in its familiar brass-bright peal. Something had been removed from the day, and people did what they always do when something old and constant disappears: they looked up.

Elsie Harrow heard it more than most. Sound had traveled strangely through the high, narrow alleys of the Old Quarter ever since they had narrowed them on purpose centuries ago to thwart winds and invaders. The Harrow & Co. shop faced south, toward the square, and when the tower chimed it sent a faint sympathetic tremor through the glasswork hanging behind her counter, a ripple like a ghost finger along the edges of crystal and polished brass. On that morning, the finger didn’t come.

She stood with a gold pocket watch split open on the bench, its face upturned like a patient mid-surgery. The watch was an old marine chronometer out of a captain’s trunk, heavy as a pebble of time, its balance spring coiled with a stubbornness she both resented and respected. Elsie had been halfway through coaxing its hairspring back to life when the hour failed to arrive. Her own wristwatch, an old self-winder she’d built from a mismatch of parts in her apprenticeship years, ticked sweeter and softer and not in sympathy to anything. She looked up at the glass door, expecting one of the neighborhood men to be standing there already, pointing at the tower as if pointing could reassemble whatever mechanism had come undone.

It took a minute—for word to travel from the square, for the ripple of oddness to accumulate enough weight to push someone toward her door. During that minute, she did nothing. She didn’t go out. She didn’t call anyone. She just listened hard to the absence, to the way it had changed the pitch of everything else. Old Quay without the hour sounded like a song missing its bass.

“Elsie,” said a voice from the doorway, breathless, surprised at itself for having hurried. “You heard?”

She recognized Mr. Poole first by his shoes, polished to a mirror even in rain, and then by his shoulders, which had the permanent set of a man who thought someone was about to give him bad news. He sold umbrellas in the arcade down the lane and also sold information like raindrops when it suited him.

“What time did you think it was?” he asked, smoothing his tie as if making good time of his own.

“I think it’s ten past nine,” Elsie said, and turned the wedge screwdriver once more, gentle, telling the spring what to want. Her voice came out steady, easier than her hands felt. She smelled oil and brass and coffee from the little stove in the back. Something sweet had been baked earlier in the morning by the baker three doors down; a lemon pastry scent hung faint and defiant in the air. “But it isn’t what the city thinks. It’s what the city thinks that matters.”

Mr. Poole came two steps into the shop and looked over her shoulder with a theatrical care for not breathing on the open watch. “The tower stopped,” he said, in the hushed tone of gossiping catastrophe. “Seven past nine I think, my kitchen clock said. Stopped dead. No chime, no tick, like someone strangled it.”

“Don’t say strangled,” Elsie said, without meaning to. She closed the marine chronometer gently and the polished case took her reflection and broke it into curved pieces. Her father’s head would have risen at a word like that. He would have said, nothing is strangled by accident. It would have had weight coming from his mouth, the weight of a man whose life had stopped and started according to other people’s clocks for thirty years, until one day it didn’t anymore.

“Someone should go,” Mr. Poole said, eyes skating again toward the square where people had begun to collect like gulls around a dropped sandwich. “You should go. They’ll need you. It’s that old thing, isn’t it? From the ironworks?”

“It has a name,” Elsie said, out of habit. “Harrow & Finch, turrets double-train with gravity escapement. It was built when things were built.” Her mouth went dry. Finch had been the engineer. Harrow had been her father.

She knew the tower like she knew the bones in her own wrist. Knew the stairs that went tight and tight as a corkscrew up through the square stone shaft. Knew the great gear that looked like a halo when it spun. Knew the sway of the huge pendulum, slow and stern as the nodding of a judge. Knew the smell of old oil that never quite washed out of her hair after a day up there. Knew, too, the trapdoor up into the clock chamber, and the way the draught came through a hairline crack even when the wind outside was still.

“I’m sure the council will call someone,” she said. Hers was the only turret clock business left in Old Quay, but the council had the kind of habits that included chairs and committees. “They’ll tell me to submit a proposal. Then they’ll argue about whether the hour is a public utility.”

“Well, if they do, it’ll be the first time anyone made an argument about the hour,” Mr. Poole said. He smiled, briefly. “I just thought I’d tell you. I thought you’d want to know.”

She did. And she did not. She nodded to him. He drifted away, carried backward by the tide of his curiosity, out into the alley where people were stopping strangers to ask if they had seen the same absence they had seen.

Elsie fixed the spring, reset the balance, closed the little sea in her hand and wrote a neat note to go with it later, telling Captain Rooke that his father’s watch would live another life. It cost her ten minutes. She kept the lights on but put the little hand-painted sign in the door that said Back soon and took her key.

It was only four blocks to the square, but it felt longer, as if the city’s sense of time had lengthened space. Elsie passed the apothecary where Mrs. Sloane was leaning, arms folded, in her doorway like a judge, the needlework shop whose display was a quilt of hours sewn in blues and browns, and the ironmongery whose proprietor had come outside with a handful of padlocks and no plan. Children were gathered like a circus behind a constable at the base of the tower, making comments in the way of children, which is to say candidly.

“Maybe a bird flew in the cogs,” said one.

“Maybe it’s Sunday,” said another, more hopeful than logical.

The tower itself was a square-shouldered thing of sandstone and soot, its four dials looking out in four directions like a creature alert to ambush. The roman numerals were blackened iron. The hands themselves were elongated knives, and at each hour the smallest of them used to take a breath along the long minute between sixty and one, and then leap the smallest distance to kiss the next mark. People were pointing up at the north face, where the minute hand was fixed—there, just after the seven, not quite at the eight, like a man raising a finger to say, wait.

Constable Gowan stood at the base, repeating himself in the long-suffering way of a man who had found the phrase that fit his station and intended to lean on it. “Now then, now then,” he said. “Let the council decide, let the workpeople—excuse me, sir, mind your step—that’s city property.”

Elsie showed him her key without making a production of it. He looked at the name engraved on the brass—Harrow & Finch, but the Finch had been polished by twenty years of thumbs until it looked like a wishbone. “Oh,” he said. Some people heard the name and did a double-take, like they’d just walked past a door with a familiar voice on the other side. Gowan’s face did that now. “Oh. Miss Harrow.”

He’d been a lad when her father was alive. The last time he’d let Elsie into the tower, he had brought up a plate of sugar biscuits from his mother and had left them at the bottom of the stairs with a note: For you and your dad. The handwriting had been thorny, shy. Elsie remembered stupid things. She put the key to the lock.

“I tried it,” Gowan admitted, and looked down at his boots. “Wouldn’t turn for me.”

“It’s stubborn with strangers,” Elsie said. She took a breath and slid the key into the iron lock, the old mechanism whose teeth had known only a few shapes in all its long life, and turned. It gave with a sigh that she felt through her whole arm. She pulled the door open and the tower gave back its own smell: cool stone and iron and a hint of pigeon droppings from where the birds had managed to do what birds always did, which was to infiltrate.

“Wait,” Gowan said, catching her sleeve. “Elsie. Listen, before you—Mr. Anwar’s not answering.”

She felt that like a small lift under her heel, as if she had misjudged a step. “Mr. Anwar?”

“Caretaker,” he said. “Gatekeeper. He—he took over the tower after…the accident.” He did not say the year. He did not have to. Everyone put a hand out to that word. Accident. “He sleeps odd hours. Up and down with it. But they usually see him by now. His bicycle’s there.”

Elsie nodded once and took her sleeve back, and Gowan made a face like he had meant to do it more gently. “I’ll come up,” he said.

“No,” she said, too quickly. She looked at the stairs. If someone had cut great holes in the air and then stacked them in a spiral, you would have something like the tower staircase. “If something’s broken, I’ll see it before you do. And if it’s nothing, there’s no sense in two of us making dust. Wait here. If I call, you come.”

He looked up past her, toward the dark of the interior shaft. He did not like heights. He did not like ladders. But duty is a habit as strong as any other. He nodded. She went in and the tower swallowed her sound.

At the first landing she thought she heard a second set of footfalls and stopped to let the tower settle. Silence moved around her like smoke. She had the sense again of the city holding its breath.

She climbed. All towers smell the same inside. The stones cool even in summer, the faint bite of old rain that had spent decades arriving along hairline cracks, the etching scent of iron where hands have polished a rail over years without intending to. The pigeon smell was there, too, pungent and recalcitrant, and the feather-smell of their nests in high corners no one ever thought to sweep. Elsie’s father had called the pigeons the true citizens. They stayed through war and winter and vacancy, ungoverned.

Halfway up she passed the small room where the tower kept its records haphazardly, in boxes and ledger books and wrinkled maps. Twenty years ago, someone had brought up a desk for Mr. Anwar, though he had never used it for more than piling. A half-empty teacup sat there, faintly tannin-brown around the rim. The tea skin had formed and settled into a slack circle on top, boxing a dried lemon wedge. The chair was pushed back as if someone had risen intemperately, leaving the page open. The ink had sunk and dried, making little furrows where a steel nib had picked up its own path. Elsie could read upside down. The last line in the log read: Quarter past eight. Minute hand catching at tooth 43? Investigate track. Then a blot. Then another word that might have been: humming.

She pocketed the idea of humming and went on. The stairs narrowed and turned her shoulders. She counted steps out of habit, not for luck. The numbers had soothed her once. When a person you love dies in proximity to a place, numbers can serve like a prayer there, a measure you can hold in your mouth to keep from thinking too fast.

At the trapdoor into the clock chamber, she listened again. The tower made its own weather. Somewhere above, a draught whispered under the far clock face. The absence of the pendulum’s beat was a thing she hated in her bones. When the big clock was moving, even if you were not listening for it, you felt the world struck. When it was not, something inside you went out of register.

She pushed up the trapdoor. It complained and then let go. The chamber was full of light that had filtered through a hundred years of city soot and settled into the glass. The four clock faces were great opalescent skins on each wall, and you could see the world as a soft shape through the roman numerals. The mechanism sat like a coronation carriage in the middle of the chamber: iron frame, brass wheels layered like old coins, the escapement assembly at its heart with the graceful gravity arms that dipped and rose, arrested now. A green cloth over the far workbench held tools and pieces of old rope, a leather apron folded square the way Mr. Anwar had done it every evening of his life.

Her hands found the rail around the mechanism and gripped it before her body had told them to. Something was wrong in a way that was too simple to be anything but deliberate. The pendulum, which should have hung in a stern straight line, had come to rest two inches to one side and there was a whisper of silver along the rod like a ring left after a wedding. She leaned in and saw it: a set of shallow grooves on the brass surface where the rod met the crutch—three, slanted, equidistant. Not an accident. Someone who knew where to look had left her a message, or a signature, or a working.

The clock had stopped at nine-oh-seven-and-fourteen seconds, which was where the gear train had refused to yield. The escape wheel held a tooth caught. A tiny shaving of metal bright as a fish scale was caught in the oil at the base, glittering. The oil itself smelled wrong. It had always smelled like almond and iron, like all old oils do, a sweetness that had nothing to do with kitchens. Today the sweetness had a backnote that turned the nose, like an off fruit in a bowl of good ones.

“Mr. Anwar?” she called, for the first time, in a voice that did not carry well through stone. She shifted, and the sound in the chamber changed like a lung. Then—because the city had been holding its breath long enough—something gave that was not mechanical: a soft thud, as if someone had been leaning against a panel for a long time and finally lost their ability to lean.

She went toward it. The panel that led to the narrow walkway behind the north clock face was struck soft, open by an inch where its latch should have held. She pushed it with the back of her hand. It resisted for a second and then allowed her. Cool light lapped at her ankles from the gap below the face where the maintenance gantry crossed. The chalk outlines that Mr. Anwar had always kept very strictly—a line of white marking the safe place to stand, a line marking the unsafe—were scuffed. He had used to scold her for stepping too near the line when she was a girl, his voice finding humor even when it didn't intend to. Don’t make me paint your name down there, Elsie, he would say. She stepped over the chalk because she had to.

He was there by the face, nearly folded into himself, his back to her, as if praying, his hands at odd angles, one glove still on, one glove off. He had been a small man with a big laugh and a spine like a flagpole. Today he was less than both. She didn’t touch him. She leaned and put her ear near his mouth and heard nothing but the draft drawing itself thin between stone and glass.

She looked for reasons. He had loved his tea. He had been older than his bicycle should have allowed. The draft was cold. The tower was high. She told herself a list of things because lists were ladders. He had a grey scarf tucked under his chin, the one with the small hole where Mrs. Anwar had set a needle and then abandoned the mend. There was grit on his shoulder. She reached and pinched a bit between her fingertips without thinking: fine, black, almost silky, not soot. Then she saw the second wrongness: a mark on the inner glass of the north face where someone had pushed a finger against the numerals from inside and drawn an arc. The arc traced between the V and the I. A crescent, perfectly imperfect. She felt suddenly that she was being watched, but it was only the city.

She said his name again. “Mr. Anwar.” The name behaved like a stone you throw into a pond and expect to hear hit water, but it kept falling and falling. She stood up, tasting iron in her mouth and feeling the numbers in her head go strange, like they were sliding away from their pegs.

Behind her, a step on the stairs. Constable Gowan. He drew in a breath, and in the space of that breath the tower rearranged itself around the fact of a body. Later, Gowan would say he’d smelled almonds. He said it now, even: “Almonds,” like he had just been brought a slice of cake he had not ordered. Elsie didn’t answer. She backed out of the narrow walkway and closed the panel with slow care, like one would close an eyelid.

“We should call—” he gestured with the radio clipped to his shoulder, as if the gesture could turn it on. He fumbled and finally found the button. His voice came out flat when he tried to pitch it up and over the tightness in his throat. “Base, Gowan. We have a—” he took a breath he thought she might not see, but she saw it—“we have a situation at the tower. Possible—unresponsive male. Request attendance. And Arkady, you tell them to bring their—tell Doctor Hamish. And a detective.”

His voice said detective as if the word had corners. The radio crackled, a sound that did not belong in a place of gears and ropes, and promised everything would be there in a minute, which in the city’s new grammar might be an hour, or a year.

Elsie, to keep her hands from doing what they wanted to do (and what they wanted to do was to reach and set, to fix, to correct), walked around the mechanism. She observed. She dropped the parentheses in her mind over things she would later have to say out loud. The pendulum crutch was engraved with three small lines, the oil smelled wrong, there was metal in the oil, the escape wheel’s tooth looked not like a tooth that had been ground down by age but like a tooth that had been interrupted mid-bite. There were fingerprints—not obvious, but the absence of dust was its own print—along the railing where no one ever touched. There was a piece of red thread caught on a nail near the access to the east face. She did not know then that she would see red thread twice more before the week was done, and each time it would make the same notch behind her sternum.

“Don’t,” Gowan said suddenly, and she realized her hand had hovered above the pendulum rod like a mother above a feverish child. “Just—please. It's…you know.”

“I know,” she said. She let her hand fall. She moved her eyes instead. The green cloth on the workbench had been folded with care, but its edge was a little crooked, and Mr. Anwar would never have left it so. Beneath it, instead of the neat row of oils he kept in their labeled bottles—winter, light; winter, heavy; summer, light; summer, heavy—one space was empty. A small bottle lay on its side, its label wetted into illegibility. The rag nearest it was clean, which was wrong. Mr. Anwar used clean rags last and dirty ones first, an economy. The clean rag meant someone had wiped something and then placed virtue on top of vice to hide it.

There was a note pinned to the angled edge of the mechanism frame. Not pinned with an old pin, but with something like a tailor’s pin, bright and thin.
