The paper was square, torn from the kind of pad that sits on a desk near a phone. Her name was there in block letters on the outside of the fold: ELSIE. She recognized the printing. Nobody prints like that who doesn’t spend their life around numbers.

She didn’t open it. She looked at Gowan. He was not looking at the note. He was looking at Mr. Anwar, and his face was telling itself a new story in which he had not been able to be at every door when every thing in the city needed him. She reached a hand toward the note and then pulled it back, grief and duty arguing at the cruciform in her chest.

“It might be for you,” she said.

“It might be,” he said, “evidence.”

They were interrupted by another kind of order. Heavy steps on the stairs, voices that moved at a different speed than the city’s. The detective arrived a breath later, a woman Elsie had never seen before in Old Quay: mid-forties, hair that had refused to be made to behave and instead had been shown how to be kept out of her eyes, eyes that did not like being told what they had seen. She introduced herself in a way that did not assume any of them were in need of comfort. “Detective Sergeant Ameena Dacre,” she said, and did not offer a hand until after she had looked and already begun to put the room into her own order. “You are?”

“Elsie Harrow,” Elsie said. She gestured as if that explained the mechanism, the tower, the century. Sometimes it did.

“Harrow,” Dacre repeated like any other person with the city’s memory attached to that syllable. No pity, no extra weight. “And you are the keyholder.”

“I am.”

“Did you touch anything?” Dacre asked, bracing herself for the polite lie everyone always told police.

Elsie looked at the mechanism. The note. The rag. Mr. Anwar. Herself. “I opened the door,” she said. “I climbed the stairs. I looked. I read his log only as much as the last line that was visible. I touched the pendulum rail without thinking. I touched the grit on his shoulder. If you give me a cloth, I can wipe my fingers. The oil smells wrong.”

Dacre’s mouth did not smile but one corner made an adjustment as if to say: we will get along, perhaps. “What do you mean by wrong?”

“Too sweet.” Elsie watched Gowan’s eyes flick towards her. He had said almonds already. “Summer oil can go rancid. This hasn’t gone rancid. It’s…something has been added.”

“Poison,” Gowan said, suddenly sure of something he could say that would make a shape out of the air. He snapped his mouth shut again as if he’d broken something by saying it.

“Anwar has not been declared dead,” Dacre said, reflex like an oath. “And poison is a conclusion, not a smell. You will please leave conclusions to me until we have facts. Ms. Harrow, please step away from the mechanism. Constable, we’ll need the scene preserved, where preserved is still possible.”

They moved. Two more people came up—a doctor with the padded air of a man who was used to pushing through doors marked private, and a scene-of-crime officer with neat hair who produced tape out of a pocket as if magic could also be adhesive.

Dacre took out a small notebook and wrote with a pen that had more weight to it than pens usually have. She glanced at the pin that held the note, at the ridges on the pendulum rod, at the catch tooth. She made a quick drawing of the touchpoints as if she had been taught how to take something apart by drawing it first. “What are those?” she asked, pointing at the three small grooves.

“Reminders,” Elsie said. “Or marks, or instructions. But I don’t know what they instruct, yet.”

“Left by whom?”

“I don’t know yet that, either.”

Dacre nodded. “And that?” She had spotted the red thread.

“I don’t know,” Elsie said, again. It was honest. It made her feel small and sharp and endangered. It also made her feel, absurdly, alive.

The doctor went into the narrow walkway and came back out too quickly, as if the air had bitten him. He had his professional expression on his face: the old school one that invented solemnity as a way to kiss death on the cheek in public. He shook his head once, to Dacre. “He’s gone,” he said softly. “We’ll have to move him before we can say much. But there’s an odor.”

“Almonds,” Gowan said, his voice thin.

“Bitter almonds,” the doctor amended, as if one should apologize to almonds for dragging their good name into this.

“Not everyone can detect that,” the scene officer said, halfway, conversational, halfway defensive of science. “Only thirty percent of the population has the gene.”

“I can smell it,” Elsie said. “But my father always said this oil smelled like marzipan even when nothing had gone wrong with it. It’s going to be easy around here to think of the wrong things because of the right smells.”

“You knew her father,” Dacre said to Gowan, both statement and question.

“Everyone knew Mr. Harrow,” Gowan said. “He made us punctual. He—He died here.” Gowan’s eyes shot to Elsie like he had broken another rule.

“Twenty years ago,” Elsie said, before anyone could decide to speak around her. She met Dacre’s gaze. “He fell, they said. He went through the trapdoor wrong and fell. I was eighteen.” It wasn’t the whole story. The whole story had corners and a drawer with a bottle in it, and a fight about a watch he wouldn’t sell, and a ledger with a page that had been torn out. That was too much for a tower full of people, too much for a first hour. Time cut what it could not contain.

“I’m sorry,” Dacre said, the kind of sorry that can be genuine and also procedural. “If there is any reason that this morning brings you back to something dangerous in your own life, I have to know.”

“The reason is that the city has stopped,” Elsie said, tired suddenly of any place to put her hands. “And I have a key. That’s all.”

Dacre’s pen made another mark, a small one. “We will be asking you to sit down later and tell us everything you can about Mr. Anwar, and about this mechanism, and about the last twenty years of this tower in your opinion. But for now, I can tell you two things and ask you one.” She nodded at the note and let the pause stretch just long enough to mean she understood, too, what it meant to leave a thing unopened. “The two things: Mr. Anwar is dead. This scene is going to be in the news before lunch, and my job is to keep the parts of it that matter from being eaten by it. The question: would you like to be present when I open the note addressed to you?”

Elsie looked at the square of paper. In the face of what can’t be controlled, a human will grasp for the way gravity behaves. A note is a note. You open it and you read it. You have done this a thousand times and the world has only rarely changed because of it. But she had already had a long morning by nine-thirty, and the missing chime had not even yet rippled into the rest of the day.

“Yes,” she said. Her voice had found the steady place. “I would.”

Dacre turned the note over with a gloved hand and slid the pin out. She opened the fold just long enough to read the first line. There was something in it that rearranged her face in the smallest way, a muscle under her eye that twitched and went away again. She held the paper so that Elsie could see, and Gowan, too, because trust is a kind of tool.

In Mr. Anwar’s blocky capital hand it said: IF THIS HAS STOPPED YOU, THEN SOMEONE HAS TAKEN MY SECOND KEY. RETURN WHAT WAS TAKEN, AND TIME WILL MOVE AGAIN.

A second line had been added below that, in a different hand. The letters smaller, neater, a hand that had practiced the way it wanted to be seen. It said: Some things cannot be returned.

Elsie felt the point of the words in her sternum, sharp as the pin had been in the paper. Her finger went to the chain around her neck without thinking, to the weight that hung hidden under her shirt: her father’s old pocket watch, the one that had stopped the week he fell. She hadn’t wound it in twenty years. It had been the one thing she hadn’t tried to fix.

On impulse—not thinking, just pulled—she took the watch out and looked at its face. The crack down the enamel had always been there like a lightning scar. The little hands pointed to nothing that mattered. She pressed the crown because people press crowns when they don’t know what else to press; it clicked without moving.

Gowan saw the watch and flinched like he had seen a ghost. Dacre did not flinch. She looked at the watch as if it were a city map. “What time did it stop?” she asked.

Elsie said it quietly, because you don’t give the night the courtesy of a shout. “Nine-oh-seven,” she said. “And fourteen seconds.”

It was, on the face of it, a coincidence. The city had decided not to hear itself, a man was dead, and the first words left behind were about something taken and something that couldn’t be returned. Outside, in the square, the day tried to be a day. People walked in loops, work had to be done, shoes had to be polished. Inside the tower, the clock stood like a thing humiliated. The great heart of the city had been interrupted mid-beat, and none of them knew how to set it going again.

Dacre slid the note into a plastic sleeve and wrote on the sleeve with her heavy pen, the sort of time you write when you know people will be looking at your numbers later. “Ms. Harrow,” she said without looking up. “You said this mechanism had a name.”

“Harrow & Finch,” Elsie said, and wished instantly she had said it less like a gravestone.

Dacre nodded. “And you are going to tell me later about Finch. About keys. About the way a city decides whether it’s still itself when its hours go missing.”

“I’ll tell you whatever I can,” Elsie said. “But there’s one thing I can tell you now.”

“And that is?”

Elsie looked at the grooves on the pendulum rod. At the red thread. At the unnatural sweet note in the oil. At the man who had scolded her for stepping outside the chalk lines and who lay now beyond any line she could draw. “This wasn’t an accident,” she said. “Someone set this to stop.”

Dacre said nothing. The tower around them, without its beat, felt like a held breath. Somewhere far below, in the square, a child laughed and then was shushed. The city went on even when time didn’t. That was both a comfort and a threat.

“What did Mr. Anwar mean,” Dacre said eventually, the pen waiting like a quiet animal in her hand, “by second key?”

“There were two,” Elsie said. “Always. For the great door. For the smaller one inside, too. You keep only one in your pocket and the other in a place you tell to no one. So that if someone wants to stop the city, they have to convince two people at once.”

Dacre looked at the key Elsie wore on its chain in the old way, under the collarbone next to the watch. “And yours,” she said, “is the first.”

“Yes,” Elsie said. “And the one missing is not this one.”

Dacre nodded. “Then that,” she said as if concluding the first small paragraph of a very long report, “is where we begin.”

The ferry ran with a tired hum, the same note it had sung when I was thirteen and the island still felt like a world. Late afternoon, wind combing the sea into dark ridges; gulls hung like punctuation above the rail. I stood at the bow where the salt could catch in my hair the way my mother used to complain about, a dampish net I brought into the house like any other thing I couldn't leave at the door.

It was cold for September, the kind that looks like steel in the air rather than on it. I watched the water slip away from us, a smudged line we were making again. Maps never show motion. A line is either there or not. When I was a child my mother would draw me our cove from memory, the outcrop like a curled hand, the thin path that wound up to the house. Later, when I learned to draw maps properly, it always bothered me how alive a coast is, how it refuses to stay put long enough to be outlined. The island had been small and then smaller. Half of my life measured in erosion.

"Still staring at the edge, Mara?"

Cal called from the wheelhouse door. Cal, whose real name was Callum something, but Cal was all anybody ever used. He had been my mother's friend and sometimes foe, depending on the day and whether the weather station needed replacing. His beard had gone from salt-and-pepper to just salt, and his cap had faded to ghost.

"I forgot the rest," I said, and he grinned.

"Rest hasn't changed much," he told me. "Which is to say, some of it washed off and the rest grew lichen."

He came to stand near enough that his shoulder almost touched mine, both of us pretending we were here by accident. Behind us somebody's dog yapped at a gull that knew better than to take offense. We didn't mention the envelope in my pocket. We didn't mention the fact that I hadn't been back in fifteen years, not once, not even when there were rumors of a memorial I didn't feel comfortable attending because memorials require bodies and we never found one.

Instead we watched the lighthouse swing.

When I was a girl, the lighthouse on Cairn Hill was a person who never slept. I gave it moods. Sullen when the glass fogged. Jealous of the moon. Now the light had the precise tenor of automation, an eye that swept and swept, indifferent to whether there was anything worth seeing.

"You'll find it all as it was," Cal said, in a tone that allowed for plenty of disagreement. "Except where it isn't."

"I got a letter," I said, and he didn't look at me, which was polite.

"The Trust sent it," he said. "They send letters when they've run out of people to talk to. You know how they get, before winter. Accounts and roofs. Things that must be settled."

"It wasn't from the Trust."

He tilted his head. The gulls turned in place overhead, writing something in a language I couldn't read.

"It was from the Hollow," I said. The hill the house crouched under, the place that made sound on storm nights, that owlish woo that gets into your bones. We had called it the Hollow before we knew that was also the word people used about people.

"Child," he said, and then corrected himself. "Mara." As if child were a curse. "From the Hollow?"

"It was addressed in my mother's hand," I said, and it was absurd that I could say it like that, like an observation and not witchcraft. That beleaguered scrawl, the way she angled her capitals as if they were leaning into the wind. I had unfolded the envelope at my kitchen table in St. John's where I draw coastlines that don't belong to me and I had put my finger on the ink and waited for it to turn to water. It didn't.

"People imitate," he said after a moment. "There's software now that does a person's hand. You can make a dead man write you an apology, is what I read."

"It had her smell," I said, and that shut him up. We both knew what I meant: the particular that belonged to the post office, paper and rain. That and the faint resin of the weather instruments, the old cedar of the barometer that was supposed to be wrong but mostly wasn't.

We passed the black buoy that marks the deep channel. Beyond it, the island gathered itself as if holding its breath. The houses are low-slung, like animals that know better than to stick their heads up when storms move through. The church bell was quiet; it keeps its temper until it needs to be heard. The paint on the fish shed roofs glinted like beetle armor.

"There's Danish money on the wind farm now," Cal said, because he didn't want to talk about ghosts. "Out at the north point. They sent engineers with boots too clean to be trusted. We taught them the names of the rocks so they wouldn't die."

I squinted. Three new white spines along the horizon, all alien and muscular, and in their shadows the old bones of the island seemed even older. The air smelled like dry kelp and diesel.

"How's your father?" I asked, because courtesy is one of the last things to erode.

"Gone to the mainland for a spell," he said. "Says he'll die where the shops are. Says his knees demand good bread."

We laughed and let the laugh hover between us like something we could hold. Then he touched my shoulder, quick as if the ship itself had jarred him into it. "You staying at the house?"

"It's still my address," I said, which was not an answer.

The dock gave itself up to us like an old friend in a bad mood: grudgingly, but with familiarity. There were three cars. There are always three cars, no matter who is there to drive them. A child I didn't know untied the ferry rope with the bored competence of people who grow up with boats. When the gangway dropped, the dog was first off and then the man who goes with the dog, all apologies for his animal's enthusiasm as if anybody here has a right to an unenthusiastic dog.

I stayed on till last because that was our ritual, my mother's and mine, to watch everyone go first. "You should always see who you're traveling with," she used to say. "And who you'll be alone with when they're gone."

They went. Then it was me and my bag and the crunch of my boots on the gangway. Cal said, "I'll be there after supper with a crowbar if you find the hinges swollen. Sometimes the salt swells the wood."

"It always did," I said. He lifted his hand. I lifted mine.

My car started. It smelled faintly of mouse. The upholstery had taken on the pattern of the under-seat springs the way a rubbing takes the pattern of an old coin. Black lichened stone walls marked the lanes, sometimes low, sometimes higher where somebody had decided once to keep sheep and failed. On both sides the grass stooped in the wind as if listening.

The house is a long box of a thing perched under the lee of the Hollow. From the road it's unassuming. From the water it looks like a stern gaze, because you can see the big window that used to be my mother's sorting table and the letterboxes that face the yard. The post office wasn't an addition; it was in the bones. Government built it after the war with a picture in their heads of a working village, stamped it out like a tin toy, supplied it with a window that makes a promise it can't keep. We had the postal window and a door with a bell, and if you wanted stamps you came and touched the polished plank between us and we slid you the world in a red and white book. Behind the postal counter, our kitchen. Behind that, two bedrooms and a narrow staircase that goes up to the room where I used to read by flashlight after curfew, listening to the house talk.

I parked with the nose of the car toward the road. It's a habit of people who grew up here. An easy way to leave.

The front steps had a drift of kelp ragged on the second stair as if the tide had come up to greet us. It hadn't been a storm big enough to throw that high. The door was shut. Not locked. I had the keys, but the keys were a formality. Nobody locked doors here, is what they told tourists, and it was almost true if you didn't count the ways we kept ourselves as private as birds.

Inside smelled like old vocabulary. The dust hadn't decided what to be yet; it hung, considering. The kitchen had the meek, scoured look of a place that is waiting to be used. My mother had been particular about clean. "There's enough chaos outside," she used to say. "We don't need it inside. Inside is the place where we know where we put things." There was one mug upside down on the rack, the blue one with the chip. There was the weather log on its peg beside the door, a hundred columns of dates and pressure and notes about fog in a spiky hand.

And through the hallway, guarded by the sagging map of the island I drew when I was eleven and got wrong where it mattered, the door to the post office proper. It had been nailed, then screwed, then nailed again years ago when they closed the office and folded us into the mainland route. The notice was still taped up, yellow as urine. I could read my mother's apology through the tape. The bell above the door hung cockeyed, still threatening to ring. It hadn't occurred to any of us to take it down. You never know when mourners will need to ring again, I guess.

There was a thin fan of salt under the threshold. I bent and touched it and the grit stuck to my finger and the taste was exactly what you expect. The door hadn't been opened in fifteen years. But the salt was new.

I set my bag on the table and didn't look at the loon clock because my mother hated the idea of something pretending to sound like nature when it was powered by batteries. It had been a gift from the Trust the year they forced everybody to modernize. The Trust loves glossy things that everyone else can see themselves in. If you put a museum in a place where people live, you shouldn't be surprised when everything starts to look like an exhibit.

The envelope was in my coat pocket, bottom corner frayed from my thumb worrying it. I took it out and put it on the counter where everyone always put the mail that needed a second look. It was addressed to me in that slanting way that looks like a lean into the wind. The postmark read: Caitlin's Hollow Post, which is impossible because that is not an issuing authority and hasn't been since I was nineteen. Below that, a date. Today's.

When I called the number on the notice two weeks ago the man at the Trust answered with a sigh. When I told him the stamp and date he told me my phone had a bad connection, and when I told him it did not he put me on hold and then came back and used the soft voice you reserve for the newly bereaved. He said it was probably a prank. He asked whether I'd be coming to empty the house because winter hardens the island in the ways you must plan for.

My thumb had gone over the ink until it polished. Inside the envelope there was a key.

Not a door key. A little thing without teeth, round-headed, the kind of key you use in a child's diary. Its shaft had turned green and then been polished by somebody and then greened again. There was a number on the head. 17.

I didn't know seventeen of what.

I sat down and listened. The house had three known noises. It carried the Hollow's surf in rough weather that'll sag your heart. It ticked when the wind shifted out of the west and slid old salt through the seams. And it creaked when the post bell moved, because the screw was loose on the left. I heard them all in turn and none of them sounded like grief anymore, though they had once. They sounded like the place that made me.

It was a quarter to six. The light outside had taken on that quality of Finnian's brownish paintings where the air is thicker than it should be. I put water on and drank tea because when you come in from the boat you drink tea even if you're a person who has been in apartments long enough to forget tea is anything other than a metaphor.

I took off my coat and then put it on again because the house holds its cold like a grudge.

I walked down the hallway toward the closed door. The nails were in there like stitches, proud heads gleaming. Someone had written Shut on the wood in pencil and then erased it. I could still read the the scrubbed S.

I touched the door and it was cool, which meant nothing. But the bell gave a tiny sigh.

"Mara?" a voice said from the yard, and I jumped in the graceless way of people who are supposed to be comfortable and are not. It was Anna Gear, who used to teach kindergarten and who baked bread like something living. She was small and solid and her hair had turned the color of lightning. Her hands were floury as if she had run over to catch me between rising and the oven.

"You got taller," she said, even though we both knew she was lying. "You carrying more light in your face. You look like Eira."

"Thank you," I said, and we didn't say the rest of my mother’s name. You say a name and it fills the house, sometimes whether you want it to or not.

"You're here then," Anna said for the sake of the obvious. "You're alone then. You're staying then."

"I'm here," I said.

"Cal says you got a letter," she said, because nobody keeps anything to themselves on an island except the important things. "Came from nowhere and meant for you."

"Maybe," I said.

"I brought oat bread," she said, lifting the paper-covered loaf as evidence. "Eat this and you'll stop shaking. We all do when we catch sight of what we left."

"I'm not—"

"You are," she said, and set the loaf on my counter with the same authority she must have used when kids tried to stuff rocks in their mouths. "I'll come by later with jam. Leave the kettle on. The hinges swell in a night like this. Did I see you were headed for the office?"

She looked down the hall and shook her head. "Leave it," she said softly, which is different from don't. "Doors have memory. They forget you, sometimes, if you force yourself on them. Best to knock and wait for the way in."

"I didn't bring a crowbar," I said, because jokes are sometimes a way to give each other a life raft.

"Don't you worry," she said, rolling one wrist. "This island will bring you what you need whether you ask or not."

When she was gone and the oat bread sat like a certainty on the counter, I did what I had promised nobody I would do. The key in the envelope was in my pocket. It had weight. I turned it over in my palm and felt the oil of my hand change it from what it was to what it would be and then back again in the ancient alchemy of handling.

The letter slot was brass. It had dulled. If I were anyone else I would have polished it with lemon and salt and a cloth. Inside, I could see an inch or two of the dark. The slot had a slider my mother used to pull down when she wanted to pretend to go to lunch. I slid it up and the dark behind it felt as if it breathed.

I put my eye there because that is the kind of foolish I am. It was a body's shadow I was looking into, a closed room's night. And then something moved in there—a small shift, a settling—and I found myself speaking like a person who talks to the den where the fox lives.

"Mum?" I said, and it was an absurdity and an act of faith, both.

Something slid forward.

It hit the inside of the brass with a soft metallic sound and then lay there, against the seam.

I stepped back without meaning to. My heart did the performing fish act in my chest, a thud and then a leap and then stillness that is worse than either.

I reached down and my fingers shook in a way that would be funny on any other day. The thing was wrapped in butcher paper greased with age. It had been tied with kitchen string; the knot had tightened and stuck; I worked the knot with my teeth like a child and spit out the taste of old twine.

Inside was something that caught the light and made it a secret. A brass compass, heavy in the hand. The glass was crazed in a web of hair-thin lines as delicate as the inside of an eggshell. When I thumbed the side panel the lid sprang and the needle trembled and pointed in a direction that made the hairs on my neck lift because I'd know that pull anywhere: the Hollow's way, which is a kind of north you don't have to be taught.

On the inside of the lid, scratched in the rough careful hand of someone with a penknife and time, there were numbers.

55°13'04"N 59°27'12"W.

I said them out loud the way you make a wish you aren't sure is safe. My throat caught around the minutes like it had swallowed the string.

They were wrong.

Not wrong as in not real. Wrong as in a place that no longer exists, one of the gnarled corners of the island that the sea lifted like a poor tooth and took. The coordinates marked the edge of Sparrow's Teeth, a row of black points that had snagged boats back when boats were wood and men had to be stubborn to live. It had gone in the winter of the year my mother vanished, when the storm ate half the cliff and took the story with it. You can put your finger on a paper map and say it was here and point to the blankness and not be heard.

The needle trembled and settled and trembled again.

Somebody knocked.

Not at the street door. Not at the kitchen door. At the post office door, the nailed one. Three soft raps, the second a little off, the last the measured hit of someone who knows how wood answers.

My voice didn't come when I asked who.

The bell gave that sigh again. The knock came once more, patient, almost bored, as if this had always been the arrangement: we stand in our rooms and we listen to ghost habits and the answers we believe in come from behind closed doors.

I slipped the little key into my pocket like a charm, because even people who don't think they believe still carry them. I did not go closer. I did not let my palm flatten against the seam. The house has ways of asking this of you, and sometimes you should say no.

Instead, I said my mother's name out loud, and it spidered through the wood and the nails and into the empty room where we used to count stamps. It sounded like a bell in a fog. The island took it. The hollow took it. I stood there and the kettle clicked and the compass pointed at the part of the world that isn't there anymore, and the person on the other side of the door did something that made the old screw mutter.

They slid something else through the slot.

It was an envelope with no stamp. No address. The white of it was too white for anything that had been here long. Across the front, in that leaning hand that leans because if it doesn't it will fall, it said: For when you stop looking for edges.

The bell swung. It did not ring. It held itself, a breath drawn, and then the wind in the Hollow came in low and the house answered it and I put my hand on the letter and felt the future tilt.

Chapter One

They had to lean their weight into the key before the door would remember how to be a door.

Metal ground on metal, a sound like teeth, and then the lock gave with a sigh that seemed to come from the entire facade. The carved limestone above them listed the city’s civic virtues—INDUSTRY, LEARNING, PROVIDENCE—in letters softened by soot and freezing rain and the small indignities of birds. Someone had once gilded the book in LEARNING. The gold leaf was mostly gone now, flaked away so the book was only stone again, a trick of light and good intentions.

“Fifteen years,” Lon Pritchard said, jawing a toothpick from one side of his mouth to the other. He was shaped like the dented thermos he carried, a city employee from boots to breath. The thermos had HARROW WATER carved into it with a pocketknife. “It’s been shut fifteen years. Swear to God I was younger than my collar last time the place was open.”

Mara Kline pressed the side of her face to the seam where door met jamb and listened. You could tell something about a building by what it let slip under its breath—the thrum of an old compressor, a latent hum in the walls, the static presence of its own mass. The library gave her plaster dust and stale wool, damp paper and the faint iron of rust. Nothing mechanical. No life.

Tad Voss, the security contractor, shifted his tool bag and tried to look like he belonged in a city seal. “We doing this or what? I’ve got two more of these stupid mothballs today. Then a bank. Real bank. With money.”

“Patience,” Lon said into his toothpick. “World waited these fifteen years. It can wait the minute it takes Mara to make a face at it.”

Mara stepped back and tucked strands of hair behind her ears. “I don’t make faces.”

“You don’t make them because your face is always making them,” Lon said. “Like your resting face is disappointed in the plumbing.”

She looked up at the columns. The capitals had stylized flames, the lick of carved fire curling around the stone. Once upon a time, the city had believed that when you lit a library you lit everything.

“I did my homework,” she said, unshouldering her leather satchel. “They closed in 2009. Budget. Asbestos. Mold in the lower stacks. They moved the collection to West Fifth. They were supposed to sell this building to a developer with a ridiculous plan for lofts. The deal collapsed. The city keeps it mothballed because demolition would cost thirty percent more than leaving it to rot. We’ve got three buildings like this in Harrow. Today we start figuring out which ones we can keep and which ones we can’t.”

Lon rocked his weight on his heels, looking at the street behind them, where a bus hissed to a stop, took on two gray silhouettes, and exhaled itself away. “That’s why you got the title assess—assesssomething.”

“Preservation and Assessment,” Mara said. She kept her voice even. She had learned, in the years after she left, to braid her breath and tone until they looked like something nobody wanted to pull. “We’re supposed to preserve what can be, assess what can’t. Try to get grants. Make a plan.”

Tad pulled the door. It swung in with a reluctant grace, like a ballroom dancer who had been practicing in the dark and resented callers.

The vestibule tiles were the color of cream and old tobacco, cracked into a settling mosaic. The once-grand clock that had hung above the interior doors had left behind only a pale circle and the anchors where its hands had been bolted through. Someone had taken the hands, as if time were the only thing worth stealing.

It was cooler inside. It smelled exactly the way libraries smell when they have been left alone: like the ghosts of starch and almonds, like brittle glue and the breath of people who were never going to come back for their coat. Sun filtered through clerestory windows high above, the glass rippled, blocks of light laid out on the floor like folded paper.

Lon turned on a flashlight anyway. He swept it across the marble floor, the circulation desk with its date stamps dry as bone, the frieze that ran the perimeter of the room: EX LIBRIS HARROW, the city’s crest garlanded with laurel, a pair of carved owls whose eyes were full of dust.

“Watch for soft spots,” Mara said. “Water damage under the east stair. I saw it in the inspection photos from last year.”

“You saw photos,” Tad said. “That’s like eating a picture of a cake.”

Mara stepped forward. Her boots whispered on the dust. Her heart did a small, unprofessional thing at the sight of the card catalog, still standing in its own overbuilt self-importance, a honeycomb of drawers that had once contained everything you needed to know, if you knew how to read it. She had worked in a library through high school, not this one, but one enough like it, long weeks alphabetizing and typing labels and learning that the order of things was only sometimes what people thought it was.

She realized she was holding her breath and let it out. The air touched the back of her throat like a memory that had waited too long to be told.

“The plan,” Lon said, reading a printed sheet as if it were an insult. “Main floor. Note any major structural. Lower level. Give the mold a stern talking-to. Then upstairs, peek at the balcony. Don’t lean on anything made out of nineteenth-century imagination. We get out in an hour and a half. Lunch at Molly’s. The soup of the day is always soup.”

“Great,” Tad said. He was already moving along the perimeter, rattling a chain on a door marked STAFF ONLY just because it was there. He had the attention span of a jar of marbles.

Mara approached the circulation desk. Behind it were the old stamp pads and a date stamp with the dial frozen on OCT 02 2009, a Friday. She imagined the odd, sudden last day everybody had carried with them since: the patrons who had pressed their lips together and stiffened their shoulders and said thank you anyway; the woman who had ripped up her library card and left it in limp pieces like confetti; the boy who had run his fingers along the spines of a whole shelf as if trying to memorize the vibration.

Lon tapped his thermos against the side of his leg, looking toward the shadowed hallway that led to the children’s room. “We had a story time here where my kid learned all the words to ‘Old MacDonald’ and then proceeded to sing it in the produce aisle at Mariano’s for thirty minutes. That lady with the eyebrows was something.”

“Which lady?” Mara asked.

“The one who was always knitting like she was mad at the yarn. Librarian. Flo. Flora? Eh. She had eyebrows like hawks. Caught me with a candy bar once and asked if I was trying to assassinate the books.”

“She moved to West Fifth,” Mara said. “She retired last year.”

Lon looked at her sharply. She made herself busy with her clipboard, checking boxes she already knew how to check.

Upstairs the mezzanine ran around three sides, its ironwork still elegant in the way things are when they assume their survival. The special collections room, according to the map, would have been behind a pair of oak doors with a frosted pane stenciled SPECIAL MATERIALS. The doors were now boarded over with plywood and caution tape that had leached its yellow away. Someone had added a lock with a hasp like a bracelet on an old wrist.

“We got a call about squatters last winter,” Lon said, reading ahead in his memory. “But security didn’t find anything. Broken window in the basement was fixed.”

“Was that a rumor,” Tad asked, “or one of those true rumors?”

“Shop on Fourth said they saw lights,” Lon said. “But that could be anything from kids with flashlights to a battery dying. Could be a reflection. Could be the past trying to get out of the wallpaper.”

They split the room in a loose V and moved through it like detectives in a movie. Mara took her time. She took photos with her phone and narrated notes into it when her hands were filthy. There were bird droppings in the corners where pigeons had come in before somebody had been thorough enough to screen every opening. There was a soft sinking under the carpet near the east stacks that nearly folded around her foot. There were patterns of spreading, almost elegant black on the far wall that had to be old water. There were footprints in one of the light rectangles, the shallow shape of a human sole laid over the dust that had stratified there since the last cleaning. Mara knelt and touched them. The prints weren’t crisp, but they weren’t from 2009 either. Somebody had walked here long enough after for the dust to lay and then lift.

She followed them, even though the sensible thing was to tell the men and mark it later and remain detached. The prints led down the left-hand aisle of what had been history and travel, past tattered tourist guides to cities that had rearranged themselves twice since the last time they had been mapped, past a row of green cloth bindings whose gold titles were almost too gentle to read: ANOTHER HARROW, OUR HUNDRED YEARS, THE RIVER THROUGH US.

The prints stopped at the end of the aisle, where the stacks met the side wall. That wall was painted a pale gray that had taken on the mottled darker gray of dust through time. There was a hairline crack where the wall met the floor. There was a faint line, waist-high, of slightly darker paint that ran in a rectangle that did not match any furniture in the room.

“Lon,” she called, and heard her voice fishtail under the ceiling.

He came, patient as a snowfall. Tad followed because he did not trust silence.

“What,” Lon said, “am I looking at.”

Mara put her hand on the rectangle. The difference in paint was like a hidden door’s shadow. She rapped her knuckles lightly. The sound came back wrong. Hollow, instead of the solid thrum of lathe and plaster. Somebody had closed something up. Somebody had closed it up with care. The line of nail holes along one edge had been mudded, sanded, painted over with a color several shades off and then dust had done its own blending.

Tad took a step back. “Nope. Nope with a capital rope. That’s a movie wall. That’s where the monster is.”

“It’s what they call a ‘dead space’,” Lon said, but he said it without conviction.

“It’s not original,” Mara said. She crouched and looked along the baseboard. It’s funny how old work looks honest and new work looks guilty. Why are you here, it seems to say. Who told you to stand like that. “Somebody boxed out a section of the wall. It’s not on the original plan. It’s not on the addenda. It’s not on the 2009 survey. It’s newer than that.”

“Squatters?” Lon said. “A hidey hole? Kids?”

“If you were going to hide a bottle of vodka and some cigarettes,” Tad said, “wouldn’t you do it, I don’t know, under a stair? Not in something that took time to finish.”

Mara had the urge to write down that theoretical bottle of vodka and cigarettes, to corral it with a bullet point. She sat on her heels and turned her head, put her ear to the wall, the side that had been closed up. She heard nothing. She heard less than nothing, which is to say, the wall was eating sound. Dead space was right. Maybe storage, back when the library was open. But storage didn’t come to you like this, with the feeling that somebody had drawn a line around a secret and colored it in.

She stood and dusted her hands and looked at Lon. He looked at her the way only people who had known you since before you left town could look: as if your bones had not kept your secrets together half as well as you thought they had.

“You carry a multi-tool,” he said. It wasn’t a question.

She took it from her satchel—the pliers, the knife, the stubby pry that had unsunk more than one paint-sticky sash in neighborhoods the city forgot it owned. Tad said something about liability and Lon rolled his eyes so hard the sound of it would have scratched the floor.

“We’re not demolishing,” Mara said. “We’re looking. We can log this. It’s not like the HPC is going to get mad we looked at a patch of wall that might be hiding a unicorn.”

“Lady, I would absolutely get mad if there is a unicorn,” Tad said. “You think my insurance covers mythical horn trauma.”

Mara slid the pry tool under the edge of the baseboard at the bottom of the rectangle. The baseboard was applied over the newer paint, which made it a later addition. It popped up with an ease that was almost grateful. She eased it off and set it aside. The line of finish nails along the bottom of the panel made a row of tiny smiles. She worked the pry against one and then the next. It wasn’t perfect. It wasn’t museum work. It didn’t need to be. The panel gave, as if it had been waiting for someone to ask.

Underneath the painted gypsum board was a layer of heavy plastic, the kind contractors used to quarantine dust. It had been taped along the edges with care. The tape had long ago lost some of its tack and dust had gathered on its sticky fringe like lint on a sweater. Mara slid the blade of the multi-tool under a corner. She peeled back a hand’s width of plastic and caught a smell like old pennies and eucalyptus.

“Mold?” Lon asked, but he stepped closer.

“Eucalyptus?” Tad said, surprised into it. “Like cough drops?”

Mara slit the plastic enough to get her hand in. Her fingers went from the dry scar of dust to the slick cool of the sealed space and then to something textured like canvas. She felt the bristle of fabric and a hard edge that her brain wanted to lay out and label. Book, the brain said, because it was in a library and everything was a book. But the edge was different, the angle wrong. The hair along her arms rose. She widened the opening and used her phone’s light to see.

The light made a line first, along a canvas-wrapped object leaning upright. Her breath kept trying to leave her and then not bothering. The beam slid over something like a work lamp—an industrial clamp light with a metal shade. It had been wired, once, to something. Beside it a small folding table held a ceramic mug. A mug. It had a chip. It said HARROW PRIDE with a lion doing its best to be friendly. The handle had a crack darkened with use. On the table sat a small glass bottle with a scorched stopper. It was the kind of bottle you might keep essential oil in. Eucalyptus.

The light moved and met skin.

Even after all these years, even after the training and the pictures and the documentaries and the time she had assisted with an intake of a cold case file and its ugly photographs, Mara’s brain took a staggering step and refused. It rearranged what it saw into a doll, a mannequin, anything else. But the hand was a hand, curled with the fingers just loose enough to seem like a gesture. The nails had grown and separated in that peculiar way. The arm had the color of wax left too near a stove. Whoever it had been was now the color and texture of an argument with time.

“Okay,” Tad said, breathing out, flat as a tire. He turned away and then forced himself to turn back. His hand found the wall and opened and closed against it, like he needed to try it for studs.

Lon did not swear. He did not say anything. He took off his cap and held it in front of him like it had been a mistake to wear a hat indoors.

Mara widened the tear in the plastic until she could get both hands in. She lifted it and the air that came out was a breath from a box, sealed and kept, not a tomb, exactly—the space had been climate-controlled by accident and desperation. There were two more canvas-wrapped things leaning behind the body. No, not behind. Framing. The body was seated, propped in a chair like a passenger waiting on platforms she had known, as if someone had meant to talk to her again. A scarf was tied around the lower jaw, an old mortician’s trick to keep the mouth from opening in an expression that would scare living people. Somebody had known that trick. The scarf had once been navy but the dyes had leached; it was now the color of water someone had washed lots of maybe-navy things in. There was a book in the person’s lap. The hands had been arranged on it. The leather cover had a faint pressed-border decoration. The edges of the pages were a thin gray. On the top of the book, under the weight of those hands, sat a brass library date stamp.

No. A calculator. No. It was the old circulation stamp, with the dial for the day and the month. She had worked one of those until the noise it made had followed her home. It lay like a paperweight, the lever snug under fingers that had been fingers.

On the table beside the mug, beside the small bottle, sat a Polaroid photograph, the kind that nineteenth-century ghosts could be caught in if you knew to ask. Someone had set a paperweight atop it to keep it from curling. The paperweight was an encased card with the Harrow Public Library crest.

Mara swallowed. “Don’t touch anything. Don’t breathe more than you have to.” She had to say something normal, something like an instruction, to make the world go back to the right size.

“Call it in,” Lon said, his voice dry, ground down to its essentials.

Tad took a stagger-step sideways, navigating orbits that were suddenly wrong, and fumbled out his phone. He looked at the ceiling, as if reception might be better if you asked politely.

Mara leaned in. She knew she wasn’t supposed to, but there she was, leaning into the thing that had been waiting fifteen years to be discovered. Fifteen or longer. She brought her phone up and gave it the terrible gift of a photograph. The light lit the face and she flinched. You always flinch. The skin had tightened. The eyes had collapsed to a different kind of dark. The hair was pulled back, threaded with gray. There was a stud in one ear, a simple silver ball. There was a dent in the left eyebrow where a scar had cut through a hairline long ago and changed the geography.

“You knew them?” Lon asked. He didn’t say how he knew she knew. He had seen her see. He had known her long enough to recognize the way realization changes the shape of a person’s face from the inside.

Mara thought of a dozen faces she had known in this city. Old faces, younger faces, a face across a reading room saying I’ll be right back, can you watch the desk. She thought of the last time she’d been in a library this quiet, the day she did not say goodbye because she thought she might come back. She thought of the headline back when this building was worth a headline: HEAD LIBRARIAN MISSING. She thought of the postcard she had kept in a box, a photograph of the library steps with somebody’s neat script on the back: For Mara. For when you find your way.

“Edwin Mallory,” she said. The name felt like a coin, smooth and cold. “It’s him.”

She remembered Mallory’s hands, ink-stained in a world where there wasn’t supposed to be ink anymore. He had taught her to reshelve with the care you gave a sleeping child, to read a call number as if it were a short sentence, to know the difference between a book that nobody wanted and a book that people weren’t finding. He had been the kind of librarian who kept a jar of cough drops on his desk and a box of tampons in the top drawer and a stern sign that said PLEASE DO NOT MAKE ME TELL YOU HOW LOUD YOU ARE. He had closed the building on the last day with a face like he was folding a shirt that had been a gift he didn’t think he deserved.

Mara reached, not to touch him, but to touch the book. The leather was stiff. The title was pressed in gold so faint that she had to angle her phone’s light to see it. It was an old ledger—not a published book at all, but an account book. On the flyleaf, in Mallory’s hand, was a single line: For whoever finally does the thing we did not. Beneath it was a call number, neatly lettered: 027.473 MAL.

The date stamp sat against his fingers. The dial read OCT 02 2009.

“Jesus Christ,” Tad said, the words coming out in a different order than how he thought them. “This is going to be on the news.”

There was a sound in the library. Not the sound of the three of them breathing. Not the click of Tad’s phone as he told the dispatcher to send everyone. Not the whine of a distant bus. It was a small, precise sound, from upstairs, near the balustrade on the mezzanine: the soft knock of something very small against iron. A button. A coin. A paperclip. Mara turned her head, drawn to the shadow under the curve of the staircase.

She saw nothing. Or she saw the shape of someone resolving and then unrezzing, the way you sometimes do when you try to make sense of darkness. She told herself it was dust falling in larger pieces from the vibration of their voices, the peel and shiver of the panel coming away. She told herself a lot of things quickly and none of them mattered.

“Stay,” she told Lon and Tad, as if either of them were likely to go bounding up the stairs toward a noise that had the shape of a decision. She stood very still and let her eyes adjust. The carved owls watched her.

The knock came again, a little to the left. Something metallic, touched and let go. Then a tick, once, twice, as if a tiny clock had remembered itself. By the time the police siren bloomed somewhere far away like a white flower and began to come closer, the silence had taken the sound and folded it into its coat.

Lon put his cap back on. He looked at Edwin Mallory the way you look at a person who has finally told you the thing they could not bring themselves to say. He looked at Mara. “You didn’t come back,” he said, and she did not forgive him for knowing.

“I’m here now,” she said, which was both too little and the only thing.

She lifted the Polaroid under the paperweight and looked. It was a picture of the circulation desk as it had been the day before everything stopped. In the foreground, someone had set down a paper cone from the water cooler. In the background, Mallory stood with his hands on his hips, and a younger Mara—absurd, with a haircut that had been fashionable in her head and only in her head—was captured in motion, reaching for a date stamp with a hand that had a tiny ring she had forgotten she had ever worn.

On the bottom border of the photograph, in Mallory’s neat black-ink printing, was a note.

If found: Do not call me. You’ll know why.

She put the photograph back in its place under the weight. She put her hand flat on the painted and dust-soft wall beside the cut rectangle and felt, in the cool of it, the echo of sound coming like something you recognize in a voice on the phone before they say their name.

Outside, the siren came closer. Inside, the library waited, the particular patience of rooms that had been made for people and had been without them too long. The clock the city had stolen the hands from had only the pale ghosts of its numerals and a memory of what regularity feels like.

“Okay,” she said to Lon, mostly to herself. “Okay.”

The last time she had been in a library this quiet, she had been the person who did not come back. She adjusted the strap of her satchel across her shoulder and did not look up at whatever shadow on the mezzanine wanted to be seen. She looked down at the ledger with its call number and at Mallory’s hands and the way he had kept his name in a neat corner of a life. Then she stepped away, the living opening their careful path for the dead.

Chapter One

The city is smallest just before dawn. The river pulls the sky into itself like the hem of a dark skirt, and the warehouses along Dockside throw long, black blades across the cobbles. From the passenger seat of Ray Delgado’s pickup, Greyhaven looks flat enough to roll up and tuck under my arm. That’s how I’ve always thought of it—map-slim, delicate as onion skin, its secrets drawn in India ink. But when Ray kills the engine and the lights go out, the building they’re about to demolish—the old Rookery Cold Storage—looms from the damp like a whale surfacing. You don’t roll something like that up. You put your ear to it and listen.

“You got your helmet?” Ray asks.

“Always.” I tap the hard shell lanterne-glowing on my head. The chin strap is slick with salt.

The foreman’s beard is already wet through, beads of mist clinging to the gray like mercury. He’s been doing this thirty years, he told me last week when we met in his temporary office trailer. “Never found anything more surprising than a wayward possum,” he’d said then. Now his eyes flick to the left, where a knot of six protesters huddles under a drooping banner like a soaked tent. KEEP THE BONES, it says, in strokes so thick the paint might never dry. One of them pounds a drum in a heartbeat rhythm. It’s too early, too cold. Their cheeks are blotched raw.

“We’re not the enemy.” I say it, not because I believe it will change anything, but because it’s what I’m here for. “Two hours to pull any significant fabric and log it. The Witness Tile is our priority.”

“You get your tile,” Ray says, “and by the time the suits roll their lazy asses out of bed, we’ll have the roof off.”

He says it loud enough for the contractor’s field inspector to hear. The inspector, a boneless man in a bright vest, pretends to study a clipboard as if clipboards can absolve you. A van pulls in just then and parks nose-to-nose with Ray’s truck; the door ejects a woman in heels that click wrong against the cobbles. Her coat is fox, or something that wants to be fox. Even in the dull streetlight she gleams.

“Ms. Wilder?” she calls. “You’re the archivist?”

“Etta,” I say, offering a hand. She wraps mine in both of hers as if to warm it. Her skin is cool as the tiles inside Jesus of Good Voyage Basilica—not cold, exactly, but stored.

“Polly Hart, Vale Development.” She beams at Ray too, though he offers only a chin. “We’re all on the same team, yes? I think—”

The drumbeat from the protesters mutates into a chant. “You can’t bury the past! You can’t bury the past!” One of them is a kid with copper hair bleeding out from under a cap, the bills of his nose wide with a particular, fierce grief. It hitches me, inexplicably. I don’t know him.

I shift the strap of my bag higher on my shoulder. The bag is canvas, patched in three places, full of gloves and haze-orange tags and a thin roll of measuring tape. People think archivist and imagine a room full of books like a muffled choir. And yes, there are boxes and acid-free paper and the priest-like quiet of flat files. There are maps for days. But there’s also this: damp mornings in hard hats, chasing rumors of bent staircases and nails hand-cut in a long-gone century. Making lists not just to preserve, but to bear witness.

“Let’s get inside,” Ray says. He glances over his shoulder at the protesters. The redheaded kid meets his eyes, then mine. For a second, I have the sense of a thread going taut between us. It’s gone in the next breath, snapped by a forklift whining. The gate opens, we slip through, and the sound outside dulls.

The Rookery was built in 1918 to hold ice and fish and secrets. It looks like a fortress because in a way it was. You’d think a building that stored cold would feel clean, antiseptic by habit, but the hall that swallows us smells like wet wool. My breath ghosts in front of me. We walk past a series of glazed tile murals, five in all, that run like stations in some industrial liturgy: Net Menders; The Catch; The Buyers; The Scales; and, at the end, Witness.

There’s nothing religious about the tiles except the care that went into them. Terra-cotta glazed white, edged in cobalt; fishmen with knotted hands; women in peaked headscarves carrying baskets of silver bodies that flash and flash. People who lived and breathed and stopped, but still move on these walls. Witness is different from the rest. A boy sits on a pile of crates, his chin in his palm, watching—not the fish, not the adults, not the commerce, but something outside the frame. He’s the only one in the series whose gaze doesn’t resolve.

I pull my gloves on and step up on the low rail. I run my fingers along the grout line, careful not to flake anything away. In the corner, at ankle level, the maker’s mark curls like a snail shell. MARIELA, 1919. She put her name there where it wouldn’t show unless someone knelt. I always do.

“Anything special?” Polly asks. I can feel the impatient pump of her foot through the floorboards.

“Everything,” I say. “These tiles are unique to Greyhaven.” My voice disappears into the high room.

She smiles tightly. “Unique isn’t the same as priceless.”

“It is when a developer wants to pay as little as possible for something that only exists once.”

Ray snorts. The inspector looks up. “Clock’s running, Ms. Wilder.”

“Etta,” I correct him. I turn my measuring tape over in my palm. In the far corner of the room, beyond where Witness ends, a line of bricks makes a kind of punctuation mark. It breaks the pattern twice, three-quarters up the wall. Someone who didn’t spend her life staring would never see it. I angle the light and squint. The mortar in that seam is a shade lighter than the rest. It has dried differently, or perhaps not as long. It is not 1918 mortar. The hair on the back of my neck prickles.

“Ray,” I say.

He’s already looking. “What?”

“Can you get me the length between these pilasters?” I measure from the near one to the far—the corner where brick snuck in under tile. “According to the Sanborn map from 1932, we should have forty-two feet on this interior wall.”

“What do you have?” He produces his own tape like a magician.

I bite off the numbers. “Forty. Exactly.”

Ray whistles. “Two feet is generous in some lines of work.” He puts his weight into the wall with his fist. It thuds. He moves to another spot, higher, lower. When he strikes just above the seam, the sound changes—goes hollow as a drum, fractures a rhythm in my chest.

The inspector ambles nearer, blinking; Polly’s smile needles tighter. “Ray,” she says, warning glittering around his name.

“False wall,” he says, voice flat. “Hazard.” He looks at me. It is not a question. It is a fact that is also a door. “You want to see what’s behind it?”

“Samples first.” My hands are too steady. I cut a sliver of mortar from the seam, slide it into a packet. I take four photographs—glazed tile, seam, my tape set against the measure. This is the part that slows everything down, the part people sigh about. But if the city is a body, this is how we figure out which bone we’ve broken, and how long ago.

“Do it,” the inspector says. And there it is, the permission that will become a report that will become a chain of emails that will become a decision I won’t be invited to, written in words without verbs like ‘regret’ and ‘loss.’

Ray chooses his tools. Not the hydraulic shears, not the jackhammer. A hammer, a wide chisel. The first blows sound like someone hushing too loudly. The seam cracks. Lime dust quickens the smell of salt, and something else—something so dry it is almost sweet. The protesters’ chant seeps through the walls. You can’t bury the past. You can’t bury—

A rectangle of brick gives and slides out, bangs against the tarp we’ve thrown down. Behind it: darkness. Ray steps back, raising his head like a dog scenting. The darkness is not empty. It is air that hasn’t breathed human breath in longer than my mother has been alive. Ray puts the chisel back to work, widening the space until a grown person might squeeze through. He lifts his light, and we all crowd the beam.

At first all I see is the far wall, close and rough; the light dissolves it grain by grain into facets of sand and chipped face. Then a shape resolves in the angle where wall meets floor: a pair of boots, their toes scuffed. There is nothing inside them, no foot, but the leather holds the shape it learned. I see the edge of a tiny shelf, a tin mug burned around the rim, a paper-wrapped packet gone hard at the corners. And then—oh. The light moves, and there is the rest of him, as if the dark has been trying to keep him and has failed.

He’s not seated so much as stored. A man, narrow as if hunger carved him with a small knife. His hair is ink roped into tight waves, his jawline defined by absence. Fabric over bone. His hands are folded awkwardly in his lap—no church; it looks as if he’s just put them down to rest a moment and fallen asleep. The air coming from the cavity has that museum smell I know too well: paper and iron and something like old apples.

Polly’s hand goes to her mouth. The inspector swears softly. Ray, whose hands can strip a roof in an afternoon without nicking a thing we’ve tagged, uses his index finger to cross himself, quick and private.

“Stop work,” he says. “Don’t touch anything else.”

“I’m calling it in,” the inspector says, already backing toward the door, his phone lifting like a periscope above his head.

“Wait.” The word is out before I can pull it back.

It’s a bad word in a room where the shifts of power go to habit. The inspector glares. Polly drops her hand. The protesters outside have fallen silent; whether they’ve felt the change in the air or simply tired of the chant, I can’t tell. Ray doesn’t move his light.

“I’m not going to disturb him,” I say. “It’s just—look.” I tilt my light and aim it to the left, where the man’s bent arm casts a thin shadow over something flat. There’s a box, half-crushed between his hip and the wall. Brass, with a bail handle and a latch shaped like a fish tail. It’s stamped with the City’s seal: a three-masted ship under full sail, a sprig of something in one corner that the original engraver couldn’t decide was laurel or olive.

Polly whispers, “Oh.” The sound is greed, sorrow, and the recognition that none of this is going the way she planned.

Ray holds his flashlight while I ease my gloved hand in. The space is no wider than my shoulders. Dust frost coats the glove with a pale fuzz. The latch on the little box resists, then yields with a tiny sound that is unmistakably a click. Under any other circumstances I would catalog that sound and associate it with three other boxes in three other basements. Under these, it makes my heart hammer twice.

Inside: not money, which is what Polly hoped for, not jewels, which only happen in books, but a ledger. Narrow, leather-bound, the spine eaten away. The top page flakes like pastry where the light hits it. I steady my breath and read aloud the first line I can make out.

“Port Dues, 1918.” The neat hand goes on like a new road. “Paid, cash, five dollars. J. Hart.”

Polly’s head snaps toward me. Hart. The word hangs like a chain. Maybe it is nothing. Maybe it is the city playing one of its small tricks. Her face goes pinched pale, the kind that only shows up in people who are used to being the ones to ask the questions. She remembers herself like a door slamming shut and opens her mouth to say—something.

Sirens sound, distant at first, then a block away, then in the pocket of this room. Someone outside yells. The protest sign tilts in the window like a bird trying to land.

Ray takes his light back and moves to my side, deliberately blocking Polly’s view. “Let’s step out,” he says. His voice has a strange gentleness to it, a note I didn’t know he carried.

I nod, but the light has left a ghost of a circle burned into my vision, and in the center of that circle a face. The man’s features aren’t as intact as my eyes want them to be, but there’s something about the angle of his head that suggests attention. He was listening to something invisible when he was sealed in, and he is still listening.

The first cruiser arrives and noses up onto the curb. The tires squeal in protest. Two officers get out, one young and eager, one older and already taking off his glasses to rub the bridge of his nose. The young one stops when he sees the protesters—there will be a call in his radio feed about how to handle them—but Ray moves fast, intercepts, low-toned and smooth. His wrist flicks toward me and the gap in the wall. The older officer follows me in, slides on latex gloves, sniffs, and grimaces.

“Who are you?” he asks, squinting past me into the dark.

“Municipal archivist.” The words feel both full of permission and empty of it, like a door marked come in please that opens on a closet.

“Name?”

“Etta Wilder.”

He nods once, writes it down on a small pad he keeps in his breast pocket. He does not offer his own, but it’s in the set of his mouth. I’ve read enough reports to know how the tone will fall. By the time he produces the call for the coroner, more cruisers have arrived, and a light bar paints the mural in pulses of blue and red. The boy in Witness stares, unblinking. The kid with the copper hair tries to push through the door, mouth a furious O, but a uniform leans him gently back and says, “Later, kid. Later,” as if later always comes.

Polly is on her phone, voice pitched low. “You don’t understand,” she says to someone who cannot possibly. “It’s the Rookery. It’s all of it. They—no, I am telling you—”

The older officer ducks his head into the cavity as if into a confessional. “Looks like he’s been there a long time,” he says unnecessarily. “You didn’t touch anything?”

“Just the box,” I admit. “It was…” The least bad answer is the most true. “It looked like it was going to fall.”

His eyes flick to the ledger in my hands. For a second, his mask slips and I see the man under the seniority: the one who reads more than he lets on, who knows what a ledger can do. “We’ll take that,” he says, not unkindly.

My palms itch to hold onto it. It occurs to me that of all the things in this room, my fingerprints are the newest. “You’ll let me examine it?” I hear my voice. It is steady. It doesn’t betray what it means to me to ask for a small, precise thing in the middle of all this disorder.

“That’s up to the coroner.” He almost smiles, a smudge in the corner of his mouth. “And the person who’ll be running the investigation.” Which is when he finally gives me his name, like a gift he’ll be taking back. “Detective Rios.”

I nod. I don’t say, nice to meet you. This isn’t, and we both know it.

“What did you mean,” he asks, “when you said ‘the Witness Tile?’”

“The mural,” I say. “This building is one of five in the city that features work by an artist named Mariela.” I could say more—that Mariela came from the Azores with a husband who died here three years later, that the thin line she used around the eyes in this series doesn’t appear in her later work, that she slid her name where only a kneeling person would find it—but that would be pouring water into a sieve. He is asking to locate me on a map. I am here.

“Mariela.” He writes it down. He is a man who catalogs out of habit even when he is not sure he’ll need what he collects. It makes me like him more than I should.

More people crowd the door; a voice radios a call sign I don’t know. The coroner’s techs will arrive in twenty minutes with their slow dignity and their neutral bags. A wall has already gone up between us and the man in the gap, a membrane made of procedure and time.

I start to step back, and my heel catches on something that skitters across the ground. I crouch automatically; my light lands on a thin metal disk no larger than a fifty-cent piece. It is the face of a pocket watch, the glass missing, the hands forever fixed at 3:17. The seconds hand is crooked. Along the rim someone has scratched, with a tool not meant for the job, a series of marks that might be a name or might be nothing at all. The older officer sees it in my light and kneels, pinches it delicately between his fingers.

“You mind?” he says. I shake my head and watch him drop it into an evidence bag.

Somewhere outside, another siren makes a long, defeated sound. The protesters’ drum has gone entirely silent. Polly’s heels click and recede. Ray, who I’d half forgotten was there, scratches his beard and looks at the thin gap where a thin man has waited a long time. “So,” he says, to no one and to the room, to the river, to the empty space already present in walls not yet torn apart, “not a possum.”

I stand in the place where the ledger was; I breathe old air and new. There are buildings you can take in at a glance and buildings that reveal themselves the way a person does, over years. The Rookery has always been of the second kind. I thought I knew it. I am wrong.

On the far wall, the boy in Witness is still watching something outside the frame. Maybe that’s how you knew it then, Mariela—you put a boy who would always look for what was coming.

Later, Detective Rios will hand me his card and I will turn it over in my palm the way I turn a key to make sure it fits. Later, he will ask me for dates, for maps, for anything the city remembers that people do not. Later, Polly Hart will find a way to call her lawyer, and that lawyer will find a way to call the mayor. Later, the kid with the copper hair will show up at my office with a question that is not a question. Later, I will make the mistake of thinking I can stand with my feet on one side of the past and my head on the other and not be pulled in two. But now there is only the flicker of a flashlight across a face that is almost a face. There is only the ledger’s dry pages in my hands, and the word HART like a small, mean bell.

You can’t bury the past, the protesters said, and I believed they were being poetic. But the past, it turns out, is not a thing you bury. It is a wall some unknown mason built one long-ago night with brick and mortar and fear, two feet thick and exactly forty long, a wall that cracked like a knuckle under the right hand at the right time, and opened.

The call woke me from the bottom of a dream in which I was trying to breathe underwater and couldn't decide whether I wanted to. I surfaced to the sound of my phone skating across the nightstand and thrashing itself against the lamp base. In the dark, I could see the display bleach the ceiling with a blue rectangle: Tasha, Ops.

It was 2:17 a.m. No one called me at 2:17 a.m. unless something that breathed was dying.

“Hecate,” Tasha said when I answered. No hello. Her voice was taut with the kind of trying-to-be-calm that frays under the fingers. “Manny says her respiration rate looks weird. He says she’s pale. He says—he doesn’t know how to describe it. I’m sorry. Can you come?”

“I’m coming,” I said. “Tell him not to tap the glass. Tell him dim the white lights, red only. Turn down traffic by her tank. No one else near.”

“Copy,” she said. I could hear keys, the sound of a door shutting on wind. “You want me to call anyone else?”

“No,” I said, already pulling jeans over bare legs, one foot shoved into a shoe while the other hunted blindly. “Just Manny. Keep everyone out of Coldwater.”

My cat lifted his head from the couch and blinked at me, as if considering an objection. “It’s a short one, Chief,” I told him, the lie easy and close to my mouth. His whiskers twitched and he put his head back down with the relief of someone with no tank to worry about.

The night air was the kind that slicked your teeth and smelled like rain three blocks out. Downtown was a string of dark storefronts and sleeping neon. The harbor wind carried kelp and diesel, a deep ocean-throat exhale. There is a hum you learn when you work with water—pumps and chillers and filters and all the machines that keep artificial seas in balance. In the quiet, you can hear it in your bones. Halfway down Bayside, with traffic stalled at a red light meant for daylight, I could already hear it.

The aquarium is a low, stubborn building that crouches down to the bay and pretends, in every way it can, to be rock. In the daytime, the school buses pull up in improbable yellow lines. At night, it is a pause between one tide and the next. My access card stuck on the first swipe; on the second the lock clicked and surrendered blackness kissed with red exit signs.

“Doc?” Manny’s voice came from down the hall like a hand held out. He was a square man in every sense, the guard who had been there longer than anyone except, arguably, the loggerhead turtle that came with the original opening. His radio sat on his shoulder and murmured to itself, a cricket with batteries. He had a white paper cup in one hand and a worry line between his eyebrows that was new.

“What’s she doing?” I asked, walking, my feet finding the path almost without light. The jelly cylinder ghosted to my left—a vertical highway of silent bells turning themselves inside-out. Beyond that, the tropical reef tank spread blue on the floor like spilled light, parrotfish tucked into mucus cocoons against the night.

“Moving fast,” he said. “Like—like she’s looking for something. The color keeps…she goes light, like her suckers—like, you know when she does that salt and pepper thing? It’s like that, then dark. I didn’t tap. I didn’t even look in long. I called Tasha, then I went back to keep people from wandering.”

“Anyone else here?”

“The cleaning guys in the Ocean Theater. They are loud even when you tell them not to be. I told them to take a coffee break. And there’s…well, Jake.”

He said the name like he could have said it sooner and didn’t. We had turned left into the Coldwater wing, where the air changed mood—denser, cooler. The pumps here had deeper voices. The anemone tanks simmered in red light, five thousand little fingers all doing their own small piece of the sea. The sound of water over a cascade. The smell went sharp and metal at the back of my throat and I knew, before my eyes adjusted, that something electrical had been wet recently or something living had bled.

“What about Jake?” I asked, but I was already moving faster. Hecate’s room was past the tide pool touch tank and the hall of temperate fishes that always, no matter the hour, had somebody wide-eyed in front of them. I didn’t need the sign. My hands know doors here the way lungs know air.

“He signed in at midnight,” Manny said. “He didn’t sign out.”

“He told anyone he was diving tonight?” I had my keys in my fist and the key ring clinked against the lock. The steel door stuck a little and then gave, and the humidity rolled over us like an exhale from a giant, sleeping animal.

I hit the panel beside the door and the white fluorescents trimmed themselves down to red. It bent the room into a cave. The tanks along the wall became black syrup. The one in the center was not like a tank at all, but a piece of the Pacific borrowed and gently persuaded to stay. A catwalk ran around the top. The acrylic viewing window, ten feet across, was an idea of ocean, and behind it eight hundred pounds of intelligence and mood hovered like a storm.

“Hecate,” I said, too softly to be heard above the pumps, but still the name left my mouth like a charm.

She hung in the upper third, one great arm draped over a reinforced bar, suckers like milky moons. In red light she was almost black, her papillae studded up in tired mountains. Her mantle pumped faster than I liked, water drawn in through her gills and expelled, the way it always was, but too quick. One of her arms curled into a fist the size of a child’s head and uncurled again, nerves writing something I could not yet read.

There were other shapes in the water. That was the second thing. Stray strands of eelgrass that weren’t hers, a cloudiness where it ought to have been clear. And there was a line taut as a violin string disappearing into the water near the far intake.

“Manny,” I said, and my voice had become someone else’s. “Get on the radio. I want 911. We have a diver in the water, unresponsive until proven otherwise. Animal care incident, Coldwater one.”

He didn’t ask. He moved. His cup hit the floor beside the door and rolled without spilling.

I went up. The catwalk stairs clanged. I kept my body low, because animals read silhouettes faster than anything, and because any prey animal will tell you height is threat. I was talking as I went, low and ridiculous, the way you would talk to a child in a thunderstorm. “Okay, okay, lady, I see you. I know. I know. I’m here.”

Hecate rotated that enormous eye to me and it had the sheen of an old bruise. That arrowhead pupil pinned me, then skated to something behind me, then back. She had a sardine jar she loved, a mason jar that we sometimes baited with crab for enrichment, and in her third arm from the left she held it like a clutch purse. Tension pulled at her skin in little white flecks. Her siphon flared and she flowed herself ten inches sideways, which meant she was not just panicked but calculating.

In the diffuse red, the water was a moving pane of night. I followed the line with my eyes. It rose to the surface near the back of the tank and connected to something just under the water—no, to someone. The bobbing dark belonged to a hood, the sheen of neoprene made slick as the skin of a seal. A regulator mouthpiece protruded like a little black handle. The face behind it looked wrong in the way inanimate faces do, lacking all the minute adjustments that tell the body there is someone home.

I had done drills for this. That did not make my hands any less cold.

“Jake,” I said, because of course it was him, because of course the world would not send me unknowns at two in the morning. “Jake, if you can hear me, squeeze my hand,” which is something they teach you to do even when you know they cannot.

The net gaff hung on hooks along the catwalk—the long aluminum pole with a hoop big enough for thirty pounds of bycatch. I got one down and worked the hoop under the line, under the shoulder. Hecate’s siphon blew water against my forearms with enough force to make me grit my teeth. She slid closer, the jar in her grip now just a toy she would crush if she forgot herself.

“Not yours,” I told her. “Not food.” The old trainer’s litany came out of me without thought, the sounds ridiculous and necessary both. “Crab is food. Fish is food. This is not. This is not.”

I pulled hard. The body tumbled up against the surface. The mask was still on, the strap crooked across the back of his head. The glass was spidered where something had impacted it, hair trapped in the cracks like drift. No bubbles—no merciful sign of ongoing breath. The line that had looked like a lifeline was only a guideline, clipped to the rail. He had not been on surface-supplied air; the tank on his back was his only tank. The submersible pressure gauge, dangling against his hip, told me nothing useful at a glance but left an impression that felt ugly later: the needle hard against the pin.

“EMS on the way,” Manny said from below, his voice laced with radio squawk, his shoes on the metal steps now, too. “They said not to move him if—”
