“I’m moving him,” I said. It is the bargain you strike against every future accusation: You move who you must until there is someone else there to say you should not have. I braced and leaned in and my hands met cold that ate the heat out of them. The mouthpiece was in his teeth. It may as well have been a stick. I thumbed the purge button. A burp of air bubbled out, too small.

“Come on,” I said. The first time I put my fingers under his armpit, something slid against my glove. I had gone into tanks enough to expect silver of herring scales or the slick belch of algae. Instead my thumb came away bright with a little smear that, in this light, had two colors: black and darker. The metallic sting in the air insisted itself.

Hecate’s arm came up strong and curious, suckers trying to taste my wrist. She knew neoprene. She had untied knots under water, unscrewed jars, learned her name and thrown it back at us in her way. She could have taken my wrist and moved me. I put a forearm against her to block, and she took it instead, tasting me, holding to herself the unarguable fact that I was mine. “Not food,” I said again, more for me than her.

We hauled him onto the catwalk like poor fishermen, all weight and awkwardness and knees. The line hooked on the rail and I had to cut it with the knife at my belt. The mask strap lay half a loop over his ear where it had torn, and under my fingers the seam felt wrong. It didn’t have the bunched give of a stretch failure. It felt like the clean edge of a thing that had been born a straight line.

When we rolled him to start compressions, the side of his throat showed through a tear in the wetsuit, mottled dark where suction marks like bruised coins patterned themselves in a rough half-moon. I reached to sweep his mouth, got my fingers past the mouthpiece, found nothing but his tongue and the mortal, ordinary facts of bone. The regulator hose had a kink in it, flattened where it had met metal hard, like an animal that had tried once to pass somewhere too narrow and been refused.

“Manny,” I said, because saying a name can normalize anything, “count.”

We were both breathing loud, the two of us and the pumps and the animal that was the room. Manny’s five–six–seven–eight sounded steady. I leaned on Jake’s sternum until my palms burned, until the bitter little hope that he was going to breathe hit the wall of what was possible and sat down.

I stopped when the room changed—when the door opened and two EMTs made white circles of their eyes in the red light. Their bags came down with the weight of enough. “We’ve got it,” one said, a woman with braid and tattoos that peeked from the sleeves of her raincoat. She met my look, and there was, briefly, in the narrow hall of professionals, no argument about who owed what to whom. I moved back and she moved forward. The bag-valve mask went over the mouth and the elastic strap, and the sound of oxygen pushed into emptiness is sickening and harsh. Manny cleared space like a man who has learned to make himself into a door.

I stood stupid at the edge because there was nowhere else to stand. Hecate had drifted down, disappointed by the lack of jar and the chaos of things that shouted threat in octopus. Her color had darkened near but not to comfort. Below us, far below, her eye watched. Her siphon threw a little pulse at the regulator that had fallen beside the ladder and it spun on the wet metal like a bottle looking for someone to choose.

There are different smells to death. This one had the wet metallic note of a penny sucked as a child, the sharpness of neoprene rubbed raw against aluminum rail, the faint embed of crab from somewhere that was hers alone. When the EMT looked up at me and made the lozenge with her lips that was no but with her face, I felt something small and inevitable as a tide notch into place behind my sternum.

Tasha arrived with her hair not yet believing it was out of bed and her coat unbuttoned, moving too fast in shoes meant for daytime. She pulled up short on the threshold as if something in the air pushed back. “Tell me,” she said to me, because one of the few useful things about having a veterinarian as your head of animal health is that you can ask her that in front of other people and not have to translate. The EMT gave her the words that fit the report, and I gave her my hand on her elbow and the steadiness I have practiced less with people than with panicked things that cannot know why you are cutting them.

“The cameras,” she said to Manny. “Are the cameras up?”

“They blinked off after midnight,” Manny said. “We had that glitch? I put in the ticket. Tech didn’t get here yet.”

It was cold on the catwalk and hot. The pumps continued. The hum was as indifferent as it had been at two seventeen, as it would be at nine-fifteen when the first toddler pressed hands to glass and shrieked at a starfish. I looked at the intake for the octopus tank. There was a rag jammed loosely up under the grate where no rag should ever be, a piece of something blue that would have read as ocean in daylight and read as wrong wherever you put it under this red. Someone, probably Jake, possibly not, had shoved it there to slow the flow, to keep—what? To keep the current from tugging at something. To keep himself from being pulled.

“Did you know he was going to be in the water?” Tasha asked me, baby hairs standing at her forehead, eyes doing triage on three different levels of catastrophe.

“No,” I said. “He didn’t tell animal health.”

“Damn it,” she said, very softly, as if perhaps the octopus would take offense and turn away.

The EMT stopped compressions and looked up with the face nobody wants to practice making. There is a lull after that moment, the kind of vacuum you can feel in your teeth. Manny turned his radio down until it was only a soft bickering in the air. Someone down the hall coughed like a person trying not to cry. Hecate set her jar down with absurd care.

I was very aware of the knife still in my hand.

There is a theory about octopuses that goes around like all theories about animals people love go around—that they are little wet geniuses, that they solve our puzzles and escape our tanks and judge us. Hecate could do tricks. She could also wedge herself into a PVC elbow and refuse to eat if you wore the wrong cologne. What she was not, despite tabloids and terrified school groups and the occasional video of a careless diver, was a murderer.

“Lena,” Tasha said, and her voice had the tone in it that means: I am about to hand you something no one would like to carry. “We’re going to have to—”

“Close the wing,” I said. “We will. I know.”

“And Lena?”

The red light made her look like someone from a painting. “Yeah.”

She dipped her eyes to the torn mask strap that lay like a question on the aluminum, and to the blue rag at the intake that meant something to her because she has been in this building as long as I have. “Do me a favor,” she said. “Look around. Tell me if any of this feels like what it looks like.”

Manny had already fetched a roll of yellow tape from the security closet, the kind that uses exclamation points to make points it should not have to make. He stood there with it like he had found rope at a shipwreck and was willing to be told how to toss it.

I knelt like a supplicant in the red light and looked at the strap again. The edge was clean. When I looked close, I could see the little white cords inside the black that held tension, cut like hair with sharp scissors. I looked past it to the pressure gauge. The needle had not fallen back hard against empty. It had stopped mid-dial, where a flick of a wrist might have stopped a heart. There was a scuff on the rail where the hose had kinked, matte against shine, as if something had been clipped there that did not belong.

Hecate floated now a foot from the glass, her mantle smooth, her chromatophores cooled to a steady mossy dark. She lifted an arm and pressed two suckers against the acrylic, side by side, as if to sign her name. When she let go, neat circles remained, clear as fingerprints.

I told myself not to chase ghosts. People come into water with air tanks and with plans and both fail in stupid, human ways. You can die by inches for no one’s reason but your own bad luck. That was the practical, pragmatic voice of the woman who cleans tools in chlorhexidine and throws away scalpels when they go dull by two slices. It sits close to me like an old dog and believes nothing but what it can measure.

But there was the strap. And the rag. And the cameras that had gotten shy at midnight and stayed that way. There was the fact that Jake did not dive alone without telling any of us in any world where he meant to come up again.

“It doesn’t,” I said to Tasha, to Manny, to the room. “Feel like what it looks like.”

No one said what it looked like, here in a building where we spend all day making the living seem like they are in the wild and all night keeping them from finding the edges of their freedom and chewing through.

The sirens, when they came, slid up the hill and then down it again, bouncing off the water. Someone, maybe Manny, turned the house lights up enough to keep the humans from walking into things. Hecate blinked at me—if you can call it that—and I found my mouth doing something like a smile.

“Go to bed,” I told her, and made the sign with my hands she knew, the one that meant door and dark and leave it. She flowed sideways over the den like a hand pulling a coverlet.

It was not the octopus. I knew that as surely as I knew the pump model by sound or the weight of a herring in my hand. But whatever it was wore water and moved quiet and hated light, and I had the feeling, sudden and useless as a sneeze, that I had invited it in the moment I unlocked the door.

The man who died on Thursday called me on Monday.

He had a patient voice, the kind you hear in waiting rooms and on toll-free lines, and it made my name sound like a polite question when he asked for me.

“Nora Vale, please.”

He shouldn’t have known who handled the paid notices after five, and certainly not my name. My desk phone wasn’t listed anywhere but in a laminated calling sheet thumbtacked above the copier, and even that had the wrong extension from when the Tower Building caught fire last spring and we all moved two floors down.

“This is the Obits desk,” I said, half watching the news editor pace like a metronome along the line of high windows. “I can help you place a notice.”

“Good,” the voice said. “Good, thank you. I’d like you to help me with mine.”

In the newsroom, the sports guys were arguing about whether to call a rainout early. Someone had wedged a pizza box under the leg of the long table to stop it from wobbling. The wire monitor spilled little tragedies and big ones across the screen in loops, and under it I had turned down the sound so far the anchors’ mouths moved like goldfish.

“Your own?” I asked, because sometimes people did that—people with diagnoses and plans to tidy up. A certain kind of person took comfort in laying down the words that would stand in for them in print.

He laughed softly. “Yes.”

“And when did your—when will your death occur?” It felt like the wrong grammar even as I said it.

“Thursday,” he said, as if announcing the date of a luncheon. “Late.”

“Cause of death?” I asked, pen poised. In a paid notice, families could indulge their preferences about that—the euphemisms, the omissions. The paper’s rule was that we didn’t put anything in there that the law might take issue with later, which was an elastic rule in practice and involved my boss’s constant phrase, Let the person say the thing they want to say, Nora, and we will argue about whether it is libel at five fifty-eight on a deadline.

“Fell,” he said.

“Accident?”

“Fell,” he said again. “From the fifth step.”

My pen skidded a long, cursive scratch across the margin. A fifth step isn’t a thing you fall from. A fifth step is not a place you can be specific about unless you and a very small circle of others are in on the joke. And then, after a heartbeat: “Put ‘accident.’ Please.”

I looked past the rows of monitors to the big clock over Metro, the one that always ran slow. It said 4:42. Time in here tricked you; the light was always the same beige, the artificial kind that made your eyes feel grainy by eight p.m. I clicked my pen, a nervous tic that drove the other obit clerk crazy, and I forced myself to keep my voice level.

“Full name as you wish it to appear,” I said.

He gave it to me slowly, appreciating his own syllables. “Hector Finch.”

People say harder names with confidence and apologize over easy ones. Finch didn’t apologize. I wrote it down a little too hard and tore the receipt slip underneath.

“And your age?”

“Sixty.” A pause. “Let’s say sixty-one.”

“Our policy—”

“I turned in April. It’s accurate. You can check.”

“And home address?”

“Just say, ‘of our city.’ I’d prefer to keep my street off the record.”

We don’t keep streets off the record unless it’s a safety thing we know about, but paid notices are the place where preferences become the rules. I wrote, of our city, and heard him breathe once, steady. He had that quality of someone trying to put his voice between two masks. I’ve learned to listen for the pauses. Grief drags the sentences down; it makes people fumble with verbs. The giddy ones—people who are divorcing late in life, people who truly hated the parent whose estate they’re dividing up—talk too fast and chew on their consonants. The guilty breathe like they’ve swallowed a room.

“When will you run it?” he asked.

“Notices planned for Thursday need to be paid and finalized by Wednesday at six.” I let my own words find their prissy, reassuring rhythm. “We’ll need to confirm the death with the funeral home. Do you have someone selected?”

“Yes. Put Ellery & Sons.”

Ellery. The name teased something in the back of my head. There used to be a house with that name in the city, a brick monstrosity the history features editor liked to send freelancers to photograph when she needed a haunted headline. I made a little note (check Ellery & Sons) and bumped the keyboard awake with my hip.

“Services?” I asked. “Memorial, calling hours?”

“No services,” he said. “No reception. If someone wishes to do something, they can make a donation to any public library of their choosing.”

“Okay,” I said. “We can include a charity of choice line. Did you have text prepared?”

“I thought perhaps you could take down what I say.” The voice changed—warmer, a little amused. “You write them, don’t you? The real ones.”

“I’m on paid notices,” I said, because we draw that line even though there isn’t one. “But yes.”

“In that case,” he said, and his breathing had become even again, “start with Hector Finch died on Thursday—no, Thursday, the second of June. He died after a fall. He was sixty-one.”

I fixed the date next to June on the wall calendar with my thumbnail. The square had nothing in it yet; City Council was on Wednesday night; the drunks who slosh out of the ballpark would pour onto the sidewalks Thursday if the rain held off. I held the receiver against my shoulder and typed in the template, catching myself doing exactly what I always told new interns not to do: letting the subject have the lead. In a paid notice, the rule was lay out a life, not the death.

“What would you like to say about your life, Mr. Finch?”

He waited just long enough for me to think he hadn’t heard the question. Then he said, “I taught mathematics for thirty-eight years. I never married. I have a sister, Claire, in Chicago. I tended a garden. I have an allotment on Harbormouth Road; if anyone wants the onions, please take them.”

That was the first thing that made me want to like him. People who think about the onions are the people who leave their winter coats in the closet for someone else to find with the sleeves turned right side out.

“Harbormouth Road,” I repeated, and I wrote it down. I only put a sliver of it in notices, little place names that collect the city to itself: Bixby Park, Gray Street, the Maddox underpass. The names that, when we get a flood, the City Desk calls out like incantations—Do we have eyes on Gray? How bad is the Maddox this time?

He continued, “He loved books. He had the great good fortune to spend his life around them. He will be missed by his grafted rose and his library card.”

“You were a teacher,” I said. “Where?”

“Eads High,” he said. “In the old wing, before they tore it down. Angle your sentences there—no names. Eads will know.”

“Survived by your sister Claire,” I said, typing in the standard survivors line with placeholders for dates and relationships, “any nieces or nephews?”

“No,” he said. “That’s all right.” He added, almost as an afterthought, “I had a friend once. You can put that, if you like. A friend once.”

“I don’t think we can—”

“It’s fine.” He sighed. “Leave it.”

The sound of the newsroom came back to me, like I had been underwater. The pressmen were testing the chutes in the back; the floor thudded twice as a stack dropped square. A courier—one of the freelancers—wove between the desks, brandishing a signed photo of the soccer team, and the photo editor pretended not to care. Lots of us lived inside distractions we didn’t name.

“Anything else?” I asked him.

“Yes. A line from a poem.” He cleared his throat. “Not the line you’d think.”

“I don’t think anything, Mr. Finch.”

“You do,” he said gently. “It’s all right. Put this: ‘The river keeps its burdens if asked kindly.’”

“Who wrote it?”

“E. Carlisle,” he said. “It won’t mean anything to anyone anymore.” A pause. “But it will look nice.”

And then, because this is the line that has become the one I hear sometimes when the newsroom is empty and the night cleaning crew leaves their vacuums in a row like sleeping dogs, he said, “You’ll get me right, Nora?” Not Ms. Vale, not Obits. He said my name, and it fit in his mouth like it had been there awhile.

“Yes,” I said, because we are supposed to say yes to the dead.

He let out a breath that sounded like relief, or maybe resignation. “One last thing. I’d like the first letters of each line to be capitalized. Like in the old days.”

“You mean an acrostic.” I was surprised. Most people don’t know the word.

“Yes.”

“We can’t guarantee layout,” I said automatically. “You pay for inches not lines, and the column width changes depending on ad load. The letters might not align.”

“They will,” he said. “Some things still do.”

He gave me a credit card number in neat, slow pairs. I ran it and it went through, and the receipt machine squealed and produced two curly strips of cheap paper. I read the notice back. He corrected the spelling of Carlisle. He asked me to include his middle initial and then changed his mind. When we were done, he said, “It was nice to talk to you,” the way people say it at the checkout when you ask them if they want their receipt.

“Do we have a contact number in case the funeral home has questions?” I asked.

The silence stretched, thin as a wire. “If you must,” he said. “Write this down.”

He gave me a number with the kind of exchange that still shows up in old phone books, the stubbornness of letters instead of digits. My fingers hesitated over the keys, wanting to make it all numbers, and then I typed it in as he said it: MArket-2304, and the last four in a simple repetition, 2304. The kind of thing you give to a child to remember.

“Thank you, Mr. Finch.”

“You’re very welcome, Ms. Vale.”

When I hung up, my heart was knocking in a place I didn’t know stressed about obituaries. I printed his text. It came across the laser printer like a photograph developing in a tray. I set it in my red folder in the Thursday tab and told myself it was just a pre-need notice, like the dozen we got every month from organized people with file folders labeled Estate.

“Nor?” Les, who had been copyediting municipal fees all afternoon and had ink smudged along his left hand like the side of a charred toast, leaned against the partition. “You have that piece for the mayor’s widow?”

“It’s not a piece,” I said. “It’s a paid notice. It runs on Sunday.”

“Give it a little elbow anyway,” he said. “She’s going to buy a full page and she’ll remember who used her comma before the and.” He glanced at the stack of folders, the fluorescent stickies peeking out like fish fins. “What’s that?” He pulled the top sheet of Finch’s from the corner.

“That’s for Thursday,” I said.

Les skimmed, his eyebrows moving in two different paragraphs. “We don’t do poems in paid notices anymore, do we?”

“We do,” I said. “We do if they pay for two inches.”

He set it down. “You see the City Desk item? Another complaint about Gray Street stairs. Kids throwing bottles. Keep your coat when you leave.”

“Thanks, Dad,” I said, and he snorted and returned to his desk.

It wasn’t until closing that I took Finch’s copy out again and looked at the line breaks the way he had described them. In the software I can do little, quiet violations: a fudge of a kerning here, an unholy bit of manual leading there. You’d be amazed what you can do to make a page behave when your whole job lives inside columns. I bent the poem line so it began on a new line as he wanted, adjusted the “survived by” so the names wouldn’t spill, put Harbormouth on its own.

The first letters of each line, if the column held, would read down as a neat spine: HE, F, HE. I shifted one clause and made it: HEFALLSFIFTH. It wasn’t perfect English. He didn’t need it to be. He wanted a mark he had set himself, private and obvious at the same time, a trick kids used to use when they pulled ancient acrostics out of the backs of the copy Bibles in Eads’s library. He taught there, he had said. It made a certain sad mathematical sense.

On Tuesday I answered questions. The widow of a contractor wanted to say in the first line that he was loved “by most,” and I told her firmly we don’t do that even if he would have liked the joke. A young woman with a tiny, triumphant voice placed a notice for her estranged father and said don’t put survivors, there aren’t any, and then called back an hour later and added herself in. I ate the yogurt I’d been meaning to eat for three days and threw away two apple cores that had gone soft and perfumed my trash can. Mr. Finch did not call back.

Wednesday after lunch a bicycle courier came in with a paper bag stamped with the name of a vegetarian place across from the courthouse. He had the basic messenger uniform: black shorts, calves like wrung rope, a triangle of sunburn where his shirt rode up on his lower back. He looked at my desk like a place where dreams go to be perforated and handed me a sealed envelope with a wax stamp on the back in a deep, pretty green. The seal had a bee on it, its wings caught mid-stutter, old-fashioned enough to make me think of engraved stationery and women who send Christmas letters typed on real ribbon.

“For me?” I asked, and the courier made a noise like everything was for someone and none of it mattered and went away.

Inside the envelope was a receipt for a credit card transaction I had already processed, a second card that had the same name and number as Monday’s and the words KEEP THE OLD FONT written in tidy capital letters across the top of a slip of vellum. I turned it over in my hands. There were people, mostly in Historical, who phoned me about fonts as if I held the keys to the Museum of Baskerville. If he wanted blackletter, he wouldn’t get it. We had a set of house faces that had survived three publishers and the small death of our top-floor terrace garden. But I could give him a little flourish in the drop cap that wouldn’t bother anyone but would scratch whatever itch had made him send a bee.

A green card fell out as I tilted the envelope. It was the size of a calling card and had only a line of text on one side: MIND THE STAIR.

Thursday, it rained hard in the afternoon and turned the gutters into fast brown rivers, the kind that carry off sodas and cigarettes and the little plastic soldiers that kids leave on the storm drains downtown. City Desk called the Department of Public Works a dozen times and got on-hold music and then lies and then a hold that lasted so long someone put a printer on top of the phone and the whole thing started to hum. My folder for the day got thicker and lighter in waves. We ran the car dealer’s gigantic half page. We ran a story about a new heroin spike and a lightly shredded election endorsement. I thought about my mother’s habit of keeping umbrellas in pairs everywhere she sat. I thought about Hector Finch’s onions in their blue bed along Harbormouth Road, soaking.

At 6:15, the phone on the corner of my desk rang with a nervous little trill. We don’t answer after six; we let it go to the good voicemail with the kind recorded voice and the direct line to the funeral home fax. The rings climbed the ladder, and somewhere between one and ten I picked up because everyone else was talking at once and because the sound of it had threaded itself into whatever part of me wanted to keep rules and also break them.

“Obits,” I said, and a woman’s voice said, “Do you know where Gray Street stairs go?”

It wasn’t a question. It was an accusation posed as a question. My mouth had gotten ready for a funeral home’s routine confirmation, to read out the date of birth and the address, to have someone on the other end say, “Yes, yes,” with the weary patience of people who have found a man’s social security card in a drawer he kept taped shut.

“Who is this?” I asked.

“You should come,” she said. “If you’re the one Mr. Finch asked for, you should come. We’ve taped it off but they aren’t here yet.”

“What?” My fingers did a useless dance on the keyboard. “Where are you?”

“The Gray Street steps,” she said, the city in three words. Everybody knows them. They run from Gray down to Bixby through the slash in the hill that the old trolley used to use. They flood. They collect beer bottles. They carry, in chalk, the names of girls boys think they love. They have never been entirely repaired.

“Did someone—” I said, and she said the breathless yes that people reserve for emergencies and pregnancy tests and ice on steep slopes.

“Yes,” she said. “He’s here. He’s fallen. The fifth step, he—we don’t—just come.”

She hung up. I looked down at the Thursday folder with its neat stack of lives and then at the old clock over Metro, which had finally decided to try accuracy for the night and chimed a minute before the digital one ticked.

“I have to go,” I told Les. “Gray Street.”

“You don’t report,” he said reflexively, then took one look at my face and sighed. “Take a police radio. Don’t get yourself on the news.”

It has never been anything glamorous, our building. Even when we were bigger, when people noticed us, everyone’s shoes still squeaked because of the cheap carpet. The lobby smelled like old coffee and unwatered ferns. I used to think of newsrooms as rooms full of people who wanted to run into danger. Our newsroom wanted to run into deadline. But bodies rearrange themselves when something sharp enters the space. People sat up when I swung toward the stairs. The girl from Features who had been painting her nails pulled her little bottle out of the way like the smell might offend the investigation. It is hard, in a life built around the daily repetition of loss, not to recognize a special shape when it presents itself.

The rain had settled into a thin, mean drizzle that fogged my glasses. Gray is three blocks down and two to the right; I know these blocks like I know the bridge of my hand. The cops had gotten two sawhorses out of a trunk and threaded crime scene tape between them and between two trees that have spent every summer of the last decade holding up beer cans and soccer scarves in rotation. The tape made an incongruous cube with sides that breathed. The sirens were off by then. A man in dark clothing stood with his hands in his pockets and didn’t move; if you work long enough around deaths you learn the stance of the police officer assigned to be polite to bystanders. He nodded at me like a neighbor and then didn’t say anything.

Down the stairs, two-thirds of the way to Bixby, there was a cluster of people and steam and umbrellas. A woman in a bright yellow slicker with the city seal on it had a clipboard and that was the worst part, the clipboard. It made the world into a checklist with damp boxes. The stairs were slick with the kind of wet that darkens every surface evenly and makes everything look older.

The fifth step from the top had a dark, ugly newness to it. The angle that means nothing natural did this. The man on the step had fallen backward in a way that looked unpracticed and careful at the same time. If you saw him without context you would have said he was resting; he was too neatly arranged, his coat buttoned, his shoes without mud. The patch of hair at his temple had opened like paper. There was a folded umbrella lying inches from his hand as if he had remembered, in the last moment, not to get the floor wet.

Someone’s dog whined from somewhere behind me. The woman with the clipboard glanced up at me, taking a quick inventory, and found me not useful and looked away.

“Hector Finch?” I asked, to nobody and to all of them.

A paramedic, a kid too young to have given his mother this kind of news before, looked at me like I had read it off some hidden place. “Do you know him?”

“No,” I said. “Not really.”

His ID was open on the patch of cement next to him. The little plastic window had fogged with the rain; I wiped it with my sleeve and saw the name the way I had typed it, first the simple Finch and then the easier letter of his first name. The photograph was the sort taken at drugstores and DMVs, the kind where you can’t help but look like you’re apologizing for something. He had the titsy, rueful smile of a man who has thought carefully about math humor and chosen not to make the joke.

“He called me Monday,” I said to nobody and to all of them.

The woman in the yellow slicker raised her chin. “Are you from Ellery & Sons? We called them. He had a card.”

“I’m from the paper,” I said, and made my voice aim at calm. “From the Obits.”

“Of course you are.” She didn’t smile and I liked her for it. “He fell. Slipped, I guess. Someone said he was walking down talking. To himself.”

A man in a hood stepped back into the wet and lowered his head to light a cigarette even though he wouldn’t be able to taste it in this weather. “He said something about a step,” the man muttered to his lighter. “Like he was counting. One, two, three. The fifth one. Dumb place to trip.”

“Watch your mouth,” the cop with his hands in his pockets said mildly without moving his head.

I looked at the step and it made my stomach do that thing it did in summer when I got dehydrated and stood up too fast. It wasn’t slicker than the step above it or the one below. It had no loose stone, no chunk missing from the lip, no little frog of moss to push a heel out. The only difference was the piece of chalk that someone had used to write the number five in a single digit in the far corner where your eye wouldn’t catch it unless it wanted to. It was the kind of five old teachers draw, top horizontal, stem down, hat perched. Eads High. Old wing. Angle your sentences.

And like a slow penny dropping, after the shock had rubbed round enough to allow the simpler thoughts back in, I remembered the green card that had fallen from the envelope like a trick. It had said MIND THE STAIR. Singular. Not stairs. Not the plural shape everyone in the city understands instinctively. Mind the thing that has been named singular for a reason and then be surprised that it has its own rules.

None of that would go in the paid notice. It never does. We would set it tomorrow, two inches, and it would sit between a car dealer’s special and a plea for help finding someone’s lost dog, a little block of words tidy as a handkerchief. We would clean up his commas. We would check his dates. If I got my wish and the ad load left us alone, the letters of the lines would align the way he wanted them to: an old man’s last harmless puzzle. HE FALLS FIFTH. The kind of thing that makes your mouth form an o without noise.

The paramedic stood, a careful unfolding. “Ma’am, if you’re here professionally, you’ll have to wait until the family is notified,” he said.

“I know,” I said, and I did. I knew this kind of order. It is the whole job, after all.

On my way back to the office, my phone buzzed again. A text this time, from a number that had no name in my contacts, the six digits at the end like the cheap magic trick of repetition: 2304. It said, simply: Thank you. Next line: See the library. And then, because this city loves nothing more than to make the living and the dead complicit in each other’s schedules, the streetlight above the Gray Street sign flickered and went out.

Chapter One

If cloth could talk, it wouldn’t shout. It would whisper in fibers and fray, in puckered seams and scuffed hems. It would tell you who ran and who waited, who kept secrets tucked near the heart. My job was to listen.

I was pinning the hem of a quinceañera dress when Mr. Dahl called. The pink satin pooled across my worktable like a sunset gone too soft; my shop smelled faintly of steam and chalk and the sweet metallic tang of pins between my teeth. It was a little after eight, the street outside my window already emptied of the late summer day—only a nail salon across the way humming under fluorescent light, and a moth shoulder-barging the glass of my door, chasing my lamp’s glow.

“Lena,” Mr. Dahl said without hello. The old man’s voice always made me think of maple syrup left too long on the stove. “You home?”

“In the shop,” I said, mouthful of pins. I spat them into my palm. “What’s wrong?”

“We’ve got one for you. Family wants an early viewing. First thing in the morning.”

I glanced at the clock I still hadn’t hung properly. It leaned against a shelf, eternally ten minutes behind. “Tonight?”

“Tonight,” he said. “Can you come down?”

I looked at the satin puddle on my table, at the careful chalk marks tracing off a future party, a hundred photos, the possibility of a spilled glass and salted eyeliner. I looked at my hands. My mother’s hands, people said. Small and deft, calloused along the side of the middle finger where the needle rested. My mother used to prep the dead for Dahl & Sons. Now I did, when they called, and I paid my rent on time and the town learned that if you wanted your mother’s dress or your grandfather’s uniform to look right for goodbye, you brought it to me.

“I’ll lock up,” I said.

Mr. Dahl breathed out, relief or thanks or both. “It’s that realtor fella,” he added. “Britton. Fell in at Point Wash. Sheriff says it was an accident. Family’s—well, you know how Mrs. Britton is.”

I did. Half the town did. She didn’t just buy things, she bought people’s time. Ten minutes early was her late. A screwdriver set to wrong was your problem.

“I’ll be there in fifteen,” I said.

I turned the shop sign to closed and twisted the deadbolt. As I killed the lights, the moth lost interest and drifted off, a scrap of night torn loose. I walked the two blocks to Dahl & Sons, listening to the town breathe: the squeal of a distant screen door, a voice on a porch, the river talking to its banks in the dark. Winterford had slipped from summer’s gold to that peculiar stale blue that came two weeks before school bells, when people counted how many swims they had left.

My mother used to say Winterford had two clocks: the one in the courthouse and the one in the river. The courthouse clock ticked forward with elections and tax bills and the way people forgot the last scandal when a new one came. The river’s clock ran both ways. It carried things out and brought them back. It kept low things low and raised things up when it felt like it. It remembered.

Dahl & Sons sat on a corner shaded by a maple tree so old the town had chained its trunk when a developer once mentioned parking. The sign was hand-painted and flaked, the S in Sons witty and a little vain. Mr. Dahl had made the letters himself, younger and patient.

The quiet was thicker inside. The air held that careful, disinfected cool, like a hospital that had taken a Sunday. Behind the front parlor, past the photographs of men in black suits shaking hands with mayors long dead, down a hallway the color of the inside of a pearl, the prep room waited. Mr. Dahl met me there, smoothing his tie even though the only eyes around wouldn’t be using them.

“Mrs. Britton insisted he be in the blue suit,” he said as I scrubbed my hands at the sink. My reflection over the tap wobbled in the stainless steel. “Said you tailored it; says you’ll make it right.”

“I hemmed the trousers,” I said. I wiped water off my arms, rolled my sleeves, tied my apron. My dress was black, because it didn’t show stains. “Which makes me complicit if they don’t fit.”

We didn’t say much when we worked together, Mr. Dahl and I. He had already done what he needed to do to make bodies presentable, and he knew where I liked the lights. He knew I kept the analgesic for the sudden ache that came when you looked up and it was someone who once bought you a snow cone at Little League. He knew to leave me alone with the clothes.

Evan Britton lay on the table. Even in death, people carried their expressions. His face didn’t. He was the kind of handsome that made teenagers indifferent and old women generous, expensive teeth, skin that had known good moisturizer, hair with a cowlick he must have fought with product. The river had been kind. It wasn’t always.

His blue suit hung on a rolling rack, the trousers draped carefully, the jacket still lint-free from a closet. Mrs. Britton had sent a shirt, a tie in a demure rust stripe, socks the color of a bruise. She had sent cufflinks with tiny anchors, which made me blink. He wasn’t a boat person. He couldn’t tie a bowline if you drew him a picture. He’d tried to buy the east marsh and was surprised a bird could stop him.

I laid the suit on a clean sheet and ran my fingers over the fabric. Wool blend, quality that wouldn’t bag after a day at the office. I’d let the cuff out back in April after he’d bulked up, a midlife crisis disguised as a trainer named Vince. He’d stood in my shop with his hands on his hips, body sucking and expanding like a fish, while the dog-end of his phone call dictated my Tuesday. He’d been alive then with the bright conviction that money could arrange anything. Now his skin was the color of old first aid and he lay under a sheet and the river outside the prep room murmured the way it always had when my mother worked here, when I sat in the hallway with my knees on the shiny floor, reading.

I checked the jacket. The lining was a pale gray, standard. The inside pocket bulged slightly. The dry cleaner had slipped in a receipt, crisp as an opinion. I put it with the little pile of things that had been in the pockets when the clothes arrived: money clip still hefty, wallet, a house key, the thick glass watch popular with men who wanted a wrist to say something.

The tie had a slight snag, as if it had caught on a rough thumbnail. The collar of the shirt was clean and starched, Mrs. Britton’s housekeeper’s work, a woman with irons for forearms and a fastidious eye. A faint scent hung on the cloth, salt and something bitter: not the river. Pools have a smell of chlorine; the river smells like things becoming other things. This was...different. The kind of saline you buy, not the kind the tide brings.

I buttoned his shirt and slipped his arms into the sleeves. The dead are heavy in their slackness; the way men used to kiss in movies, falling into it, reminded me of this—an absolute surrender. Humility pours out of a body once the muscles are no longer a negotiated contract. I threaded the tie and snugged it at his throat, let my fingers rest for half a second against the pulse that wasn’t.

“Do you want coffee?” Mr. Dahl asked from the doorway.

“I’m fine,” I said. The truth was that my brain was careful, not dull. I make fewer mistakes at night. The town is quieter. Its voice is easier to hear then.

I unzipped a bag at my feet and took out my sewing kit. Mum’s. The leather was worn to a shine where her thumbs had pressed. Scissors nestled beside spools, chalk, thimbles, beeswax. I liked the ritual of it, the small church of straightening what I could. I checked the trousers too, out of habit, even if I’d hemmed them and knew they were true. The stitching at the cuff was mine: small, neat, nearly invisible.

There was grit on the hem.

I rubbed it between finger and thumb. It wasn’t the river’s silt. The river left behind a fine, almost silky mud that dried to a pale stripe. This had a sharper tooth. Sand. Not from our banks. Finer, almost powder, with a smell that brought to mind a new deck being sanded, varnish just opened. And something metallic underneath, a whisper of oil.

Mr. Dahl would have washed him. Anything stuck to Evan now had clung on stubbornly. Some children leave the sandbox with a souvenir in their shoes no matter how their mothers slap the soles against the curb.

I checked his hands as much as for the puzzle as to make the cuff sit right. No defensive cuts; his nails were trimmed and glossy with a buff. Under the crescent of his right ring fingernail, a smear of blue paint. He wasn’t what I’d call a painting kind of man.

I do this too much, I told myself. Decide that details add up to conspiracy when the answer is that people are sloppy and life doesn’t care if you line up your edges. The dead can’t tell me; the living will tell me anything.

I stood back, letting my eyes defocus the way you look at an image hidden in dots, so the overall hung right. Something bothered me. A lot of somethings bothered me, if I let them. There was a rip on the inside seam of his right trouser leg, near the knee. Not from wear. From a caught sharp. I’d stitched that seam six months ago. My work stays. This was fresh. A hook, a nail, a blade. If he fell into the river at Point Wash, there isn’t much to catch you before you hit water. The rocks are smooth as the bald heads of bishops.

I turned to the jacket. The inside lining tugged like skin over a bruise under my hands. On the left, at the edge of the inside pocket, the stitches had been clipped and resewn by someone without patience, longer than mine, rushed. The thread didn’t quite match. When I eased my fingers inside, there wasn’t of course anything as dramatic as a map drawn on paper made from his enemies. There was a tear where a hand had maybe dove for something and missed and got cloth instead.

There was something else.

Down near the hem, where only a tailor or a thief or a frightened person would look, the lining had been opened and closed again with a little ladder of panicked bites; the kind of repair someone does at a kitchen table with a dollar store needle, eyes wet. I took out my scissors. I shouldn’t have. I can say that here. It’s not that there are rules against investigating what the dead wear; it’s simply polite to leave people to their grief and let the police do the nosing. But the police in this town, Sheriff Mason in particular, had already decided something. And my mother’s hands were my hands, and if cloth wants to tell you something and you’ve made a life of listening, silence is the worst rudeness.

I snipped my own stitches. I kept them small. I eased my fingers into the dark between lining and shell, and felt paper.

It was waxed. Old, the kind of waxed paper that came out of the pantry, not office stock. The edges stuck to themselves a little. I heard Mr. Dahl shift his weight, the impatient toe-to-heel roll of a man whose joints announce their moods now. I slid the paper into my apron pocket and smoothed the jacket over it, and my throat went tight, like the tie had slipped onto me too.

“Everything all right?” Mr. Dahl asked.

“Fine,” I said, and my voice sounded light the way glass tinkles when it breaks.

The prep room door swung on its hydraulic whisper and Sheriff Hal Mason put his head in. Hal had grown up two streets over from me; we had eaten the same chalk-dusted carrots in elementary school snack time and danced in the gym to a DJ our mothers called poor at the winter formal. He had been a good catcher and a fair liar and people trusted him because his ears stuck out a little. He had become the kind of man who stands with his hands economically placed on his belt and looks at what’s in front of him hard, as if the world might stop being complicated if you stared a piece of it down.

“Evening,” he said, as if the room didn’t hum with fluorescent. “Lena. Mr. Dahl.”

“Sheriff,” Mr. Dahl said, careful.

“Mrs. Britton sent me to check.” He took a step in. “She wants to be sure we’ve got the navy suit? She said blue, but by blue she meant navy. She didn’t like the other one.”

“This is navy,” I said. It wasn’t, strictly speaking. It was something richer, just this side of cobalt, which made men look younger by pretending at their eyes. It would do. “It’s the one he wore to the school fundraiser.”

Hal’s eyes were light and habitually amused, as if a joke were scratching at the door. Tonight they were flat. He glanced at the table, the tie, me. “Find anything?” he asked, and the roll of those words over his tongue wasn’t casual.

“Like what?” I reached for the anchor cufflinks. My hand didn’t shake. It didn’t.

“Like what people find,” he said. “When they go through pockets. You know.”

“Just receipts,” I said. “A dry cleaning ticket.”

He watched me a second longer. He’d cut his hair too close at the sides. He does that when he’s nervous. “You call me if you run into anything. Need anything.” He looked at Mr. Dahl. “I’ll be by at nine tomorrow morning.”

“We open at eight,” Mr. Dahl said, mild, which in Mr. Dahl meant let go.

Hal’s gaze flicked back to me once more, then away. His footsteps down the hall were neat, as if he laid them gently so the floor could keep the prints unstressed forever.

I finished dressing Evan Britton. I did his hair; it was a petty thing, but I put the cowlick slightly out of place in a way he would never have allowed in a mirror. You have to be careful not to make them unrecognizable to the people who love them, but you also can’t make it look like they’re about to breathe and sit up. There is a middle. I try to find it.

When I stepped out of my apron and hung it on the hook that was my mother’s, the waxed paper in the pocket knocked against my thigh. It made me think of all the times I had carried a note in my pocket as a girl, then forgotten it until laundry, and found ink ghosts and confession stains. Don’t borrow my sweater. You owe me five dollars. I like your brother. Stupid things that felt like entire universes and turned as quickly into lint.

I told Mr. Dahl I’d be back at six. He squeezed my shoulder the way men who were once rough try at tenderness after sixty. Outside, the river had climbed a quarter inch up the granite of the landing. The courthouse clock said ten past nine. The river said nothing.

In my little kitchen above the shop, I clicked on the light and watched a small drab bug scuttle under the toaster. I set the waxed paper on the table like it might jump, and I locked the door out of habit even though Winterford locks more out of ritual than fear. I made tea. You can’t drink tea and open something without feeling as if you’ve been civilized about it. You can’t drink tea and slam a door. I told myself maybe it was a scrap of tissue, a bag for buttons, a grocery list. Sometimes mystery is just mess.

The waxed paper unpeeled with the intimacy of removing a bandage. Dust clung to my fingers where the wax bled. Inside were two pieces: a photograph and a slip of card heavy as a business deal.

The photograph was black-and-white and older than I’d first thought—thirties or forties, men in flat caps and women in coats belted high. They stood in front of the factory that used to be Moccasin Shoe, before it was condos, before Evan tried to turn it into something and got a Building Commission full of skeptical farmers. A rectangle had been slipped along the margin at some time and taped, to frame one face. The tape had left a fat, amberish scab. The face was a man, twenty maybe, hair parted with a knife, eyes low-browed and set wide. He smiled like he had won a fight with someone he liked. He looked like my father.

Not exactly. Not the way a photograph of your father makes your chest do the thing mine does when we pull out albums at Thanksgiving and the room smells like oranges and nutmeg. But enough that my body said yes before my brain did. Enough that the edges of everything came forward and the center went back, and my tea steamed its little ghost into nothing.

My father had gone out on the river when I was seven and come back in pieces of wood and a life insurance check and the hollowed-out look on my mother’s face when anyone asked about the weather. His name was Julian Teller. He’d been small and quick, a man who knew where to step on a boat so it didn’t argue. His boyhood had smelled like cotton waste and oil because he’d swept the floors at Moccasin Shoe. I had the feeling sometimes, lately, the shape like a fish at the edge of your vision, that there were blanks in his story I could not fill with anecdotes about the time he found a raccoon in the attic and named it Frank.

The card was older. Cream paper, deckled edge, printed letters that had soaked a little into the fibers.

In block print, with the stubbornness of someone unused to pens, were six names.

G. Halpern
T. Crowley
J. Teller
A. Palomo
I. Halpern
E.

No last name on that last one, just an initial and a period, as if the person were either fond of drama or had too much to hide. Next to my father’s name someone had drawn a star. The ink had bled there too; it made the star look like an infection.

In pencil, on the back, in a different hand, maybe a woman’s in the way it curved, was written: If you don’t hear by August, wind the clock back.

It was September in two days. No one ever winds the courthouse clock, not anymore. It was connected to a new system, Mr. Leary the electrician said, when he came to fix the way it jumped a minute ahead every Thursday. The river’s clock you wind by going down to the landing and throwing memories in.

I sat there a long time, until the tea lost its heat and skimmed over. A car passed under my window, teenagers laughing too loud. Across the street, the nail salon turned its sign off. The odd bug near my toaster decided my kitchen was a country it could move through freely and popped out to scamper across the counters.

When I finally stood to put the kettle back on, my phone rattled across the old farmhouse table on a call from a number I didn’t know.

It rang once and cut. The screen stayed lit long enough for me to see the area code wasn’t ours and the number was palindromic, the kind a nervous woman might make up to give to a man at a bar so he’ll go away. A second later a text came through.

Don’t cut any more.

I turned, slow, expecting someone to be in my kitchen. The door was locked. The street was empty. The river was outside where it always was. I held my breath. When you’re a child, you blow air into a paper bag so it’ll pop and you smile like you made thunder. Silence can be loud too.

You can’t uncut a stitch. My mother used to say that when she was tired and I tried to pick work back out of the dress we were making, because perfection had a siren call louder than bedtime. It’s untrue if your hands are steady and the fabric is forgiving. The scar faintly shows but the cloth forgives. She’d known that. She’d said it anyway because some things you can’t unlearn, and some things you shouldn’t try.

I folded the photograph and the card back into the wax and set them in the battered biscuit tin that held my needles. I hadn’t put them back into Evan’s jacket. I could say I intended to. I could say I was going to sleep on it, decide in the morning, bring the card to Hal with clean hands. I poured another cup of tea and didn’t drink it, then poured it out and watched the water spiral down the sink like a register of someone else’s debt.

The text lay on my phone like a beetle on its back. I deleted it because I didn’t like seeing that imperative on my screen. The number evaporated with it. I turned the phone face down as if it were a thing that had eyes.

Out on the river, a boat motor coughed to life. The courthouse clock yawned toward ten. I lay down on the couch with my mother’s afghan over my legs and watched the light change on the ceiling from the headlamps of that single car. The slip of card sat in the biscuit tin like a tooth under a child’s pillow, weight disproportionate to its size, and somewhere inside me something I had not noticed in years put its finger under the loop of a knot and tugged.

Chapter One

On the days the city forgets itself, the courthouse smells like wet wool and burnt coffee. The radiators clang to remind the heat they have a job. The windows fog in the corners like lungs pressed against glass. If you sit very still you can hear it: the sound of rooms settling, of papers changing their minds.

I have spent five years catching words the way other people catch trains. My machine sits on its low tripod, keys like a miniature piano that never learned to sing—thick, dumb blocks made elegant only by the hands that know them. When I first started in Department 14, my fingers felt like they belonged to someone else. Now they move without me, muscle memory sprinting ahead while the rest of me watches faces, listens for the thread underneath what people think they are saying.

Voices have textures. Judge Hartman’s has the grain of a baseball bat: sturdy, varnished with age. The Assistant District Attorney’s is green glass: something you could cut yourself on if you’re not careful. The public defender this afternoon—new, hair too neat for this place—speaks like he’s reading his own lines in his head. He says “my client” the way some people say “my dog” when they don’t have one.

“You took the ladder,” Hartman says, peering over his glasses as if the pair he’s wearing is a decoy. “From the hardware store, Mr. Ortiz?”

“I borrowed it,” Ortiz says. He shrugs. The sleeves of his sweatshirt grip his forearms like hands. “I left my ID. I signed the sheet.”

“The sheet says ‘Ori.’ That’s not your name.”

“That’s my name when I don’t want to spell it.”

The ADA does his thing with exhaustion, not moral outrage; it’s past three and he wants this over. I am typing even when I’m laughing in my head. I don’t miss a word, not anymore. You can’t in this room, where everything matters and nothing does and the trick is knowing which is which.

Bailiff Armand leans against the back wall, eyes half closed, like a large dog pretending not to nap. We are regulars at a show the city puts on for itself, day after day, always the same set, always new lines. People forget about us—the ones who brush crumbs from the table after the feast. They forget the court reporter is not a tape recorder, that her hands are human, that she notices the way a defendant’s left foot renders Morse code under the bench.

At four-fifteen, the fluorescent lights hum as if trying to remember a song. Three plea deals and a continuance later, Hartman pushes the day off his shoulders.

“Alright,” he says, gaveling once out of respect for tradition more than necessity. “We’re adjourned. Counsel, keep your calendars open. We’ll reconvene on the Martinez matter tomorrow at nine.”

Tomorrow, it will be domestic violence, a witness who doesn’t want to be one, a scraping of chairs and patience. Today, it is ladders and fatigue and the feeling that my jaw has been clenching for hours. There is a stack of transcripts with little neon flags waiting on my desk like bright whispers. I pack the machine, roll the cover over the keys with a practiced gentleness. People assume court reporters all have perfect posture and buttoned blouses. Mine is a navy knit that pills near the wrists. My hair is pinned up with a pencil traded by a clerk for the last chocolate in my bag.

“Park,” Hartman says as the lawyers file out like a herd trying to look dignified. “You alright on the Nelson transcript?”

“Almost done,” I say. “Just need to fill in some places where everyone decided to talk on top of each other.”

“Gonna start fining them for that,” he grumbles, then softens. “Good work.”

He means it, I think. Some people say “good work” like they’re patting a pony. Hartman says it like he’s defying the part of himself that doesn’t believe in compliments. That part lives in all of us. Mine keeps a tidy house.

The corridors are a maze of beige. The vending machine is a crooked smile. On my way back to the reporter’s room, I pass photographs of men with too-tight ties and dates under their names like expiration stamps. The room itself is a converted closet with three desks and an industrial plant trying very hard not to die. Marcie from Department 9 has a calendar with beaches on it, one for each month, none of them this city.

“Lila,” she says, using my name like a sigh. “Tell me I can go home.”

“You can go home,” I say. “I’ll stay late.”

“You’re an angel. Or a masochist. Text me if the building catches fire.”

“When,” I say.

She laughs, hoists her bag, and is gone. You learn meanings for “goodnight” in this place. Sometimes it means I hope I never see you again. Sometimes it means I’ll always see you again. Right now, it means the elevators are not to be trusted after six.

I like the courthouse at night. It’s emptier and more honest. You can hear the bones of it. The cleaning crew migrates through the floor like a slow tide. Papers stop pretending to be more than they are. Even the vending machine relaxes its jaw.

I sit, plug in the headphones, open the file. Best practice is to transcribe from the stenograph record and the audio backup. The steno catches everything, but the audio catches the way it sounded. There is a difference. You can say “I’m sorry” and mean it, and you can say “I’m sorry” and mean “Watch your step.” The machine renders these the same. The audio does not. Most people don’t hear it. I do. Once upon a time I thought I would conduct orchestras. Then a scaffolding dropped a piano where I was supposed to stand, and I took it as a sign from God or gravity. Now I conduct the city from a chair.

The Nelson transcript is a tangle. The defendant’s mother cried into her scarf. The witnesses stepped on each other like dancers out of time. I fill the gaps, surface for air, take notes about who said “you know” more than anyone else. Around seven, Armand sticks his head in, offers me a peppermint with the gravity of a doctor offering bad news.

“You alone?” he says.

“When am I not.”

“Rooms like company.” He crumples the mint wrapper into something small enough to disappear and leaves it on my desk despite himself. “Lock up when you go.”

I nod. The building creaks. The plant sighs. I finish Nelson, slide it into my outbox with a little ceremony I invented because no one else will give you one. There’s one more on the pile I didn’t expect: an old brown envelope with the official stamp skewed on the flap, the way you stamp things at four-thirty on a Friday. It’s from Records. A note clipped to the front says: Appeal—State v. Fenn, 2003. We only have the tapes.

The note has a smiley face on it. Someone in Records has a sense of humor or a sense of cruelty. Tapes. As in cassettes. As in the last time a cassette was in this room, I still wore my hair to my waist and thought my life would be a different shape.

I peel the envelope open carefully because old paper demands respect. Inside are two smoky black tapes labeled in sharpie, a chain-of-custody log that’s been through a coffee spill, and a sticky note that says: Sorry, Lila. I recognize the handwriting and the small, neat heart in the tail of the y. Jamie in Records. He’s thirty-seven and has been fifty for as long as I’ve known him. He thinks he is flirting with me. Maybe he is. Mostly he is married to his barcodes.

The reporter’s room has an ancient tape deck in a drawer, as if the court system knows it can’t afford to forget anything. I plug it in, turn the knob until the light glows sallow. The machine wheezes like a man with a cold. I feed the tape in, press play. The iron smell of old plastic rises like a ghost.

The sound is grainy, voices far away. The judge in 2003 was Delaney, clipped consonants like a metronome. The defendant, Fenn, has a voice like wet paper. It would fall apart under the right pressure. The lawyers speak in the coded niceties we’re all trained to. There’s a clerk who says “Mmmhmm” under his breath whenever anyone does anything. I lean forward unconsciously, press the headphones too tight against my ears, the way people do when trying to hear a secret.

Fifteen minutes in, there’s a warble on the tape—an artifact, a hiccup of time. That happens on old recordings: the past bumps into itself. I mark the spot, rewind, play it again to see if it’s the tape or my patience. The warble comes again, longer, like something slipping under water.

Then there is a voice.

Not the judge. Not the attorneys. Not Fenn. A low whisper, close to the microphone, intimate as breath.

At first I think it’s bleed-over, the ghost of some other case recorded on the same tape, some clerk in 2003 leaning in to tell Delaney his tie was crooked. Then I hear what it says, and my hands forget the keyboard.

“Fenn didn’t do it,” the voice says. “I did.”

It is so soft I could convince myself I dreamed it if not for the way the waveform jerks on the monitor. The whisper lands between syllables like a stone in a pond, ripples out beneath the regular rhythm of the courtroom. I know what to do in this moment—what I’ve been taught. Note the anomaly. Don’t interpret. Don’t own it.

I pull the headphones off, stare at the tape deck as if it might explain itself. The heater clicks on. Somewhere down the hall a vacuum starts to sing. I press stop. I press rewind. I press play.

“Fenn didn’t do it.” The same voice, the same breath. “I did.”

I have listened to a hundred jailhouse confessions. You learn their timbres—the righteousness, the defiance, the relief. This voice has none of those. It isn’t bragging. It isn’t bequeathing tragedy. It is placing a small, terrible object in my hands and asking me to hold it.

I write the words down without breathing, as if the act might scare them away: Fenn didn't do it. I did.

The rational explanation is that the tape got recorded over, that fifteen years ago someone in a room not unlike this one bumped the record button and didn't notice. But why this tape? Why this spot? And who would lean into the void and confess like telling a stranger in the backseat of a cab that it’s your fault the plants died?

I play it a third time. This time, there are extra words. Or maybe I am ready to hear them.

“I did,” the voice says, and then—so soft it’s in the bones of the sound rather than on its skin—"Lila."

For a second I think I have imagined my own name. That I have conjured it from static like a child conjuring a face from a cloud. My name is not rare, but it isn’t one you hear by accident, either. There’s a world of Lilys and Lilianas between me and the most common I will ever be.

I turn the volume down and then up again as if sincerity lives at a specific decibel. The voice does not grow louder, it grows nearer. “Lila,” it says, like a secret and a dare. “I did.”

My first instinct is not to be scared. That comes later, like pain. My first instinct is professional: it’s a glitch. It’s an overlay. Jamie messed up in Records, or the switch-box patched a call through to somewhere it wasn’t meant to go. This building does that. It loses track of itself.

My second instinct is to tell someone. The oldest lesson: do not be alone with the hole you just fell through.

I take off the headphones and sit very still so the chair won’t squeak. I look at the clock and think about which regulars might still be here. Hartman is gone. The ADA is probably at a bar. The public defender is definitely at a bar. Armand—maybe. Or maybe he’s already in the parking lot giving a lecture to his steering wheel.

I press the intercom button that connects to Records. It blares that hollow courtroom tone before resolving into the world.

“Records.”

“Jamie. It’s Lila.”

“Ominous,” he says. “You never call me unless you want something or to tell me a sad story.”

“I have both.”

“Shoot.”

“I’m listening to a Fenn tape from 2003. There’s an anomaly.”

“Meaning?”

“Meaning a non-case voice in the recording. Like an overlay. A whisper. A… confession.”

There is silence on the line. I picture him. Short-sleeved shirt no matter the weather. A tie someone gave him because they did not want to wear it. The posture of a man who puts things into boxes even in his sleep.

“Could be a bleed,” he says, after a second. “Those old tapes do that sometimes. Layer a bit of some other thing. Old hearings. The security radio. We had one that had soccer on it once. Some kid’s game from who knows where.”

“This one uses my name.”

Another silence, this one with edges.

“Your name?”

“Yeah. It’s not on the case file. You didn’t write it on the envelope as a prank, did you?”

“You think I’m funnier than I am,” he says, but it’s soft, not offended. His voice comes back to itself. “You want me to come up?”

I almost say yes. Then I look at the clock and at the way the plant trembles in the draft and think about Marcie’s advice regarding elevators after six. It occurs to me how little of my life happens with another person in the room, and it embarrasses me in a way that is less shame than the realization of a fact.

“It’s fine,” I say. “I’m probably imagining it. I’m going to log it in the transcript and flag it for the judge.”

“Do that,” he says. “And Lila?”

“Yeah?”

“Don’t stay too late.”

In my experience, the universe does not give warnings. People do. I press stop on the tape. The room collects itself around the absence of sound like water refilling a footprint. I print what I have: the bench conference, the voir dire, the one time a juror admitted to knowing the defendant and Hartman’s face did what only the lucky have seen it do. I put the tape back in its bed. I write a note to myself and to Hartman that there is an anomaly at marker 17:12. I do not write the words “It said my name” because I cannot make my pen do that yet.

The courthouse is colder in the hallways. My breath ghosts. I push through the heavy door to the stairwell because I trust stairs in old buildings more than I will ever trust an elevator. The stairwell has a smell to it—old pennies and concrete. On the landing between four and three, there is a window where you can see a wedge of the city like a pie slice that will never be eaten. The snow from last week still clings to the lip of the fire escape. A man in a hoodie smokes in the courtyard. His smoke does not know it is breaking a rule.

When I open the door into the lobby, it echoes in a way it does not during the day, a phrase repeated back to me out of context. Armand is at the far side, his back to me, signing something for a courier. He looks like a portrait of himself. I raise a hand. He does not see me.

The glass doors have that unintentional mirror that makes you catch yourself at odd angles. Mine is a woman with lines at the mouth that weren’t there two years ago. My mother says they are laugh lines. My mother hasn’t laughed at the same things I have since I was thirteen.

Outside, the last light is the color of printer paper. I pull my coat tight and march in time with my feet because it feels good to have something obey. The courthouse steps are wide enough to make you feel like you should be making a speech. I make it down them without tripping on the fractured tile that eats heels.

I live five blocks away, over a florist that pays its rent late but brings the building pie at Christmas. In spring, when they spray the sidewalk, everything smells like cut stems and green sap. Now it smells like city winter: salt, exhaust, the ghost of summer garbage. My key sticks in the outer door because it is a day that insists on small annoyances being puzzles.

The hallway buzzes. There used to be carpet. Somebody pulled it up one day like a bad bandage and never got around to doing anything else. The flickering light outside 3B has been threatening to die for three months. I made a note to call the landlord about it thirty-two days ago. I find notes in my pockets for weeks, the way people find sand after a beach.

My place is 3A. The front window looks directly at the back of a billboard for an injury attorney, which is a kind of poetry. I kick off my shoes, peel off my coat with the jerk that says it is too cold and I should turn the heat up, and don’t, because money is numbers on a screen and the idea of wasting any of them makes heat feel like a luxury. I balance my laptop on the edge of the counter and watch the kettle as if daring it to contradict Nature. The cabinets make a noise when they close that feels personal.

I tell myself not to think about the tape now. The rule is: leave the building at the building. But the words sift through that filter like flour through a sieve. Fenn didn’t do it. I did. Lila.

If the universe is kind, it offers you something ordinary right when you start to feel unmoored. The kettle boils. The neighbor’s radio plays something with a horn in it. Buses exhale at the stop down the block. A car alarm, distant and uncommitted. I pour water into a mug, watch the tea uncurl like an animal waking up. I feel my shoulders drop. It is possible, I tell myself, that the voice was someone saying some other Lila’s name. It is possible Jamie is right. It is possible someone named their cat Lila and confessed to stealing a dish of tuna.

My phone buzzes. A text from my sister, Hannah: Coming by tomorrow. Don’t pretend to be asleep. I type a thumbs up. She will come by whether I say yes or not. She will bring bagels and opinions you could slice bread with. We are not the kind of sisters who borrow each other’s clothes. We are the kind who will sit on the floor of our mother’s kitchen and eat burnt toast and laugh at the same old story. She does not think mysteries should be solved by people like me. She thinks that is what the police are for. I think the police are for something. I have not decided exactly what.

I take the tea to the window and lean my forehead against the glass. It is an old habit. When I was a kid, I would do this in winter to write names in the fog. Once, it was the name of the boy who sat in front of me in Biology and thought I only paid attention to the frogs. After he moved away, it was the name of a school I couldn’t afford. Then the names got less interesting and more necessary: rent, due. Dad’s appointment, Tuesday. Call the bank. Call him back after you think of what you want to say.

Behind the billboard, the sky bruises then surrenders. I breathe. Somewhere below my left elbow, my building remembers that it is old and clanks to prove it. I am not going to press play. I am going to read a book in which nothing happens and other people’s problems are solved in charming villages by charming people, and when I fall asleep the tape will be another person’s job.

I don’t read the book. I sit on the floor with my back against the couch and watch dust climb a lamplight like a dance. The neighbor argues with someone on the phone about the right way to make stew. I get up to brush my teeth and have the thought—the stupid, movie thought—that if I look up and move my head at just the right angle I will see someone standing outside my window. I look up. There isn’t.

I sleep badly because I always sleep badly when left alone with the parts of my day that don’t understand they are allowed to end. At two, I wake to the sensation of my name. Not someone saying it. The shape of it. Like when you think of a song and then it comes on the radio and you convince yourself you did that with your mind.

Then the buzzer rings.

It is a sound designed to punish curiosity. It is not a doorbell, it is an accusation. I roll, find the edge of the bed with my feet and the switch with my fingers, pad into the hallway in my socks, ground cold through the thinness. The second buzz slices the night more angrily than the first, as if it didn’t get the attention it thinks it deserves.

“Who is it?” I say into the intercom, the metal grill cool under my mouth.

There is a breath. The buzzer is not meant to transmit anything nuanced. It is meant to squawk. The voice that comes through anyway is low and close and familiar in a way that makes my scalp tense.

“You still up?” it says. “Lila?”

My hand tightens on the button. The building pulls itself together around me. The radiator decides this is not its problem. I look at the peephole because that is what you do, even when logic tells you the intercom and the door are not the same thing. The hallway is empty through the fisheye glass, distorted by the trick of optics that makes everything seem both nearer and unreal.

“How do you know my name?” I say to the intercom.

Static. A soft cough. A whisper that hits my bones. “Because I had to tell someone,” the voice says. “Can I come up?”

Chapter One

The fog that came off the Graymire inlet had a way of making everything private, as if the whole town had been wrapped in cotton and whispered to stay quiet a little longer. It moved in smudged layers across the harbor road and haloed the sodium lights, and when I rolled down my van’s window at the police tape I could taste the salt before I could see the lighthouse.

“Quinn,” the patrolman said, leaning in, radio hissing on his shoulder. He had a baby face I didn’t recognize and the wary look of someone who thought locksmith sounded like a euphemism. “You’re cleared. That where they want you.” He gestured with his chin, the way people always do when they don’t want to let go of their hands.

“Thanks,” I said. The Quinn Locksmithing lettering on my van door had cracked last winter and now read Quinn Locks ithing with an unfortunate gap. I had put off repainting it the way you put off making a dentist appointment—too many reminders of what was boringly necessary. The fog beads on the paint looked like sweat.

Past the tape, Graymire Lighthouse ghosted up out of the rocks. It hadn’t lit a ship’s way in forty years, not since the Coast Guard declared lighthouses romantic and obsolete. They put a museum in its guts instead and rented it out for weddings to pay for repairs. There were seashell wind chimes hanging by the gift shop door, mute puppets in the damp.

I parked next to two cruisers and a coroner’s van with the back doors shut like a mouth trying not to say anything. A handful of people clustered near the stones, their shapes indistinct in the fog. One of them turned at my footsteps, the reflective stripes on his slicker catching light. Jonah Pike, his badge clipped crookedly to his jacket, the way it had hung crookedly on his father before him. Our fathers had played cards together in a basement that smelled of beer and machine oil. Mine taught me to listen to the stories metal told; his taught him to listen to the stories people didn’t.

“Eliza,” he said. He had a blanket draped around his shoulders that made him look like a pilgrim in a children’s book. His hair had gone prematurely gray at the temples, but his mouth still had the same crease it did in high school when he thought a joke was better left unshared.

“You look like hell,” I said.

“The humble glow of public service,” he said. “Thanks for coming out of bed.”

“Precious little to come out of.” My nights were often a television show murmuring to nobody and a cat who had adopted my porch but refused to admit it.

“Come on.” He started toward the lighthouse door. “We need the lower door, then the stair access to the lamp room. Door’s locked and bolted from the inside. Windows sealed. No second exit and no trapdoors unless they put them in since I was a kid and broke my tooth on the railing.”

“You didn’t call me to reminisce,” I said, but softly.

He ducked under the tape that someone had strung across the lighthouse’s stone steps. The lighthouse had two doors: a ground-floor oak door for visitors and deliveries and, farther up, a narrow iron door that, when the place was manned, had let keepers step out onto the catwalk and breathe on clear nights. The oak door had been sanded so many times it had lost its grain, but the iron one was pitted with rust and salt bite. We headed for the oak.

A uniformed officer stood by it, gloved hands clasped, eyes trying not to look at the field of dark water beyond. He nodded at Jonah, then at me.

The door was beautiful in its honest way. The brass escutcheon plate had a museum’s idea of polish, not quite removing the finger-thin scratches of a century of keys. There was a warded lock set in the old wood and, above that, a relatively modern deadbolt that had been added at some point in the last twenty years by someone who thought history’s charm should have boundaries. A chain had been bolted on at shoulder level years ago; it dangled now like jewelry nobody remembered to put on.

“No signs of forced entry,” Jonah said. “No signs of much of anything. McKay’s in there.”

“Docent?” I asked. The last time I’d been to the museum was to put a padlock on the display case with the harpoon in it when a bride’s kid tried to test its sharpness on a bridesmaid.

“Curator,” Jonah said. The word fell into the fog and sank. “Robert McKay. He took over when old Miss Pritchard had her stroke.”

What I remembered of McKay was an aversion to eye contact and a lot of talk about provenance. He had once described a fisherman’s logbook to me with a near-religious fervor while I was trying to fix a stubborn cashbox. The idea of him being past tense made something cold curl up under my breastbone. People who loved small things could be abrasive about it, but they were rarely the kind of people who acquired enemies.

“Locked from the inside,” I repeated. “Who called you?”

The officer shifted his weight. “A guard. Well. Not a guard. The volunteer who does Thursday nights in the gift shop. Woman named Geena. She tried to call McKay around eight to ask where the shipment of postcards got stashed. No answer. She stayed till ten because she didn’t want to close without okay from the boss—love that for the museum, by the way—and when he didn’t answer then, she got worried. She went looking. The door was locked. No answer when she knocked. She called us.”

That timeline gnawed. Eight, ten, midnight now. Hours were doors too; you could notice which hung open, which stuck, which whistled when the wind pushed under them.

“Everyone else?” I asked.

“He was alone,” Jonah said. “Supposedly.”

“I suppose I’ll have to let us find out,” I said. I knelt, every joint being loudly thirty-seven about it, and put my bag on the step. The fog beaded on the leather. I unrolled my picks—slim gleaming things in their slots—and shouldered my light. The first thing my father ever gave me was a pick set in a case made from an old wallet. The second was a lecture about how locks are promises, not guarantees.

I started with the deadbolt because it would make me feel better. It was a Schlage I had seen a hundred times, with a plug that could be persuaded if you made it feel it was in control.
