I set my tension wrench and listened. People think locksmithing is about sight; it isn’t. It’s hearing. It’s the difference between the minute click of a driver pin setting and the molar grind of someone forcing it. The fog settled into the crevices of the brass and into my hair. Somewhere out on the water a buoy struck its bell, a sound like someone tapping the rim of a glass to make a toast at a party where the guests had forgotten how to laugh.

The pins came, one, two, five, four, three. The deadbolt turned with a tidy snugness that satisfied my hands. No resistance. I didn’t like how clean it was. I glanced up at Jonah. He had his hands in his blanket as if he didn’t trust them not to do anything stupid.

“The deadbolt wasn’t thrown all the way,” I said. “It was set so it looked it from the outside.”

“Could someone have done that to make it easier to pick?” the young officer asked, then flushed when he realized he was suggesting that.

“Anyone could,” I said. “It’s arrogance that gets you caught.”

The warded lock was older. Older locks are honest in their deceptions. They admit that their mechanisms are a simple maze meant to catch a wrong key. Warded locks are theater; if you know the trick, the door opens. But this one had a custom keyway I hadn’t seen in many original fittings. The wards inside were likely not standard. I adjusted my picks, chose a skeleton key with ground-down post, and fed it in, listening for the scrape of ward against metal. There were narrow points that kissed the pick; I withdrew, filed a whisker off, tried again. The fog dripped off the brim of my cap and tapped the toe of my boot.

After a minute, the lock sighed and let me in. That was what it felt like: a sigh. I eased the latch back. It gave. The chain inside rattled against wood as I put my shoulder to the door.

“Wait,” Jonah said. “Let me announce.”

He stepped forward, raised his voice toward the seam. “Mr. McKay? It’s Officer Pike with the Graymire PD. We’re entering.”

He said it like a prayer. When no answer came, he nodded. I swung the door open and made sure to hover my light over the hinges, the jamb, the strike plate. No splinters. No pry marks. The wood was just wood, ancient and smug.

The stale tang of old paper and whale oil hit me first. The museum smelled like earnestness and dust. The gift shop’s shelves gleamed faintly with the sheen of things that want to be bought: postcards and snow globes with tiny brass lighthouses inside, mugs with slogans about anchors and hope. A rack of T-shirts whispered when the air displaced with the door’s opening. The door from the gift shop into the lighthouse tower proper was ajar. Something about that door made the hairs on my arms stand. The locking mechanism on that interior door was a steel slide bolt you could only throw from the museum side. It wasn’t engaged.

Jonah motioned the uniform forward toward the tower entrance, called for someone outside. I heard the murmur of radios. He gestured at me with gratitude that was half apology. I took it, because we owed each other those, small favors banked against larger losses.

The spiral stairs inside the tower clung to the wall, a corkscrew more treacherous with damp. Our footsteps echoed. The cast-iron risers were slick with condensation, and I took them slower than I would have ten years ago. On the walls, displays had been bolted—old photographs of men with faces like weather, a logbook behind glass with entries written in ink that had spread into the paper like bloom. Someone had placed little cards under each artifact with a certain fervid neatness. I had never seen McKay’s handwriting, but I knew it when I saw it. He made his letters too small for his fingers.

Halfway up, a drop of water hit my neck and startled me as if a hand had. It wasn’t rain. It was the lighthouse sweating.

At the top, the lamp room door wore an iron strap and a heavy mortise lock. The glass panes beyond, curved, made the fog look like something alive pressing its face to see in. The Fresnel lens sat like a holy thing, all concentric rings and facets, a glass bee’s eye that had once made a tiny flame into a scream of light. My father had taken me up here when I was nine and told me that something can be both obsolete and revered, like a grandfather at a wedding.

The door was closed and, according to Jonah, bolted from the inside. I knelt again, light in my teeth, and examined the mortise lock. It was dirty with age. You couldn’t fake that. Tiny tracks of salt had crept under the lacquer. I pressed my ear to the metal and rapped my knuckles near the keyhole. It sounded solid. The screw heads on the escutcheon were untouched, their slots filled with the same gray grime as the rest. No one had removed the plate to fish the bolt. But the bolt could be manipulated through the keyhole if you had the right mind and hand.

I slid my rake into the keyhole and drew it gently along the bottom. It came back with a smear of something black-green. Graphite, old, and a smear of oil that wasn’t museum oil. My father used to say that you know a locksmith by his oil and his lies. The museum used mineral oil because some donor had gifted it in bulk ten years ago; it had a sweet, hair-salon smell. This was machine oil, with a bite, and it was fresh.

“Jonah?” I said softly.

He stepped closer. “You’ve got something.”

“Someone oiled this lock tonight,” I said. “And not with what McKay would have on hand.”

“Could he have done it himself?”

“He could have if he’d brought the oil, or if he’d asked the lighthouse to please be modern.”

He looked past me to the glass. I knew what he was thinking. That somewhere beyond that glass, beyond the lens, was a body, and that everyone’s bad habit was to be sure a body meant a crime before we knew what kind of sorrow we were looking at.

“Can you get us in?” he asked.

I could. I didn’t like that I could, not this quickly, because it meant someone else could have too. The mortise had an old reversible keyway, and if you knew how to tickle the wards, you could catch the bolt mechanism. I fed a flat piece of spring metal along the bottom of the keyhole, hunted for the end of the bolt, and felt the slight give that meant it was, indeed, thrown. I lifted and pushed, and the bolt edged back, reluctant but persuadable, with a noise like a drawer being opened in a house where no one had been in years.

I stepped back. Jonah’s shoulders were taut, everything about him primed to either enter gently or kick in what couldn’t be kicked anymore. He opened the door with a careful hand.

The lamp room was all angles and ghosted light, and the lens made the fog into a hundred ghosts, each taking the shape of something you had believed and then lost. McKay was on the floor near the base of the light, his legs bent under him as if he had decided at some point to kneel and then run out of instructions. His eyes were closed. His face was too pale. The floor around him glimmered, not with blood, but with something that looked like scattered sugar.

The paramedic moved past us, then stopped at the threshold as if he had hit an invisible wall. He looked at Jonah and shook his head once, efficient. The earliest kindness we grant the dead is the efficient shake of the head. Jonah nodded, his mouth hard.

I made myself do what I was there to do. I looked, and I didn’t let looking be irreverent. The glitter on the floor was salt, I realized, coarse, grains of it catching the weak light like mica. It ringed McKay in a rough oval, as if he had been sitting inside a ritual he would have laughed at two days ago. On the table where the keepers once trimmed their wicks, the museum had placed a polished brass key on a velvet square and a placard describing the lighthouse’s original key set. The placard was at an angle, as if a hand had brushed past it carelessly.

There were no signs of a struggle—no overturned chairs, no broken glass. The lens was intact, its prisms dull with condensation. The narrow casement windows were shut and riveted, the rivets showing the soft-edged, generous look of metal left alone by the world.

“Time?” Jonah asked the medic.

“Hard to say,” the medic said. “He’s cold. The fog plays with the temperature. But it’s been hours.”

“Cause?” The word fell too quickly; we were all eager to categorize, to file away.

The medic shrugged, helpless. “No obvious trauma.”

Behind him, I scanned the doorframe again. On the interior face of the lock plate, on the edge where the bolt slid, I saw the faintest hairline scratch—a bright curve like a crescent moon. Someone had tried the bolt more than once. That could be me, except the mark was on the inside, where my pick hadn’t touched.

“Jonah,” I said, my voice strange to my own ears. “There’s something else.”

He joined me and followed my gaze. He took in the scratch with a cop’s mind. “From inside?”

“And this,” I added, crouching. He crouched too, and we looked ridiculous, grown people folding themselves into crouches like storks. Near the base of the lock, someone had stuck a sliver of wax as if to steady something while they worked. It had caught a few grains of salt and a single short thread of fiber. The fiber was red. Not a natural red. The fierce kind you only see in cheap tassels and uniforms.

He glanced down at his own jacket, its piping reflective, its lining black. He looked at my cap, the one with QUINN stitched in faded white. He looked back at the fiber and didn’t say the obvious: that red meant nothing on its own, but it would mean everything to us until it didn’t.

“We should—” he began, and then the medic made a small sound, something between a “hey” and a “huh,” the sound of a person who has found something in a pocket that didn’t belong to these trousers.

The medic had shifted McKay a respectful inch to see if there were any identifying marks, any signs of convulsion. In the cradle of McKay’s left hand lay a key. Not museum-polished. Cut. The bow was a plain oval, the kind I stock in a drawer next to the counter for people who come in because they’ve lost their spare. There was a little stamped Q on the bow, off-center, where my stamp always hits because my right hand has a habit I’ve never broken.

I reached without thinking, and the medic, saint that he was, put his gloved hand up until I remembered I was wearing no gloves at all. He dropped the key into an evidence bag, sealed it with a click, and held it where I could look.

It was one of mine.

I felt something give under my ribs like a latch slipping. I had cut a thousand keys with that little off-center Q. I could have cut this one yesterday. I could have cut it last month. I could have not cut it at all, and someone could have gotten my blanks, my stamp.

“You cut that?” Jonah asked. His voice had tightened the way it did when his puppy had chewed his girlfriend’s shoe and he had wanted to scold it and apologize at once.

“I didn’t,” I said, and I believed it. But the six lies one tells oneself about what one didn’t do crowded my mouth and made my tongue heavy. “But it’s from my blank. And my bench. That mark—see how the shoulder has that tiny crescent? That’s my cutter’s burr. I keep meaning to get the wheel dressed and I…haven’t.”

“Could someone else have used your shop?” He kept his eyes on the key, not on me, which was a kindness.

“I lock up,” I said. I could hear my father saying locks are promises, and behind that the laugh of someone who thinks gratitude is a trap. “I lock up. I set the alarm. I feed the cat. I turn off the radio. I lock up.” Nothing has the thinness of a repeated truth.

Jonah straightened and took a breath that moved his blanket. Outside, a gull barked once and then thought better of it. The fog pressed against the glass like a child wanting to be let in.

“Okay,” he said, and his tone was all cop now, the friend put away for later. “We do this right. We don’t make any more footprints than the ones we need to. We keep our stories clean.”

McKay’s hand, even in death, had left the faintest smudge of oil on the key, like a fingerprint of intention. I thought of him cutting his little card labels, of him being precise about where a comma goes in a sentence about boat length. The salt around him was undisturbed, the oval of it imperfect but not stepped in. I didn’t like that. Salt holds prints like a grudge.

I looked up at the lens, at the nothing beyond it. In the reflection layered upon reflection of my own face, it took me a moment to notice that someone had etched something small on the base of the lamp, where the brass met stone. It was a childish graffito, the kind the museum scolds had been trying to erase since the seventies.

My light caught it. A heart. Inside the heart, an initial. Not the romantic kind. A single neat Q.

The medic hadn’t seen it. The uniform’s eye slid past it. Only I, so trained to see my own mark in the world, could have seen that little capital tucked where it didn’t belong.

For a second, the lamp room felt smaller. For a second, the lighthouse had its old job back, not to warn ships away from rocks, but to tell me that the water was deeper than I thought.

I swallowed, felt my mouth go dry, and told my voice not to betray me.

“You should probably call the state,” I said. “I think we’re going to need a bigger promise.”

Mara Leland always rode the freight elevator with her mouth closed. The air tasted like old coins that had been licked and passed hand to hand for a hundred years. Even after three months, she could not get used to the mineral tang of it, the ancient salt that scratched her throat and reminded her, with every swallow, that she worked six hundred feet underground in a place that had once been a sea.

The elevator jolted, the gates rattled, and the box sighed to a stop. The doors scissored open onto a corridor that glowed with the modest confidence of fluorescent lights. White dust crusted the concrete walls, blooming like frost. A forklift rumbled somewhere farther down, its beeping softened by the mine. The air was the same as it always was — a careful sixty-five degrees, low humidity, a manageable carry of sound. Even the quiet here had been engineered.

Jake was waiting by the security podium, his hands deep in the pockets of his fleece. He didn't take out his gum when he saw her. He never did, not even when his chewing slowed to the lazy churn of a cow's jaw as they walked the long halls past rows of storage units. He had been in the mine for five years, which made him veteran enough to be her guide.

"Morning," he said. "I texted you, but—"

"I saw." She lifted the crate of nitrile gloves onto the desk and set her canvas tote next to it. The tote was printed with faded typewriter keys. "You smelled vinegar in C."

He gave a small, impressed nod. "Right off the bat."

"It could be a false positive," she said. "Some shipments you get adhesives, coatings. But if it's film..." She didn't finish.

Jake didn't need the lecture. In the first week she'd been here, he had learned that vinegar syndrome was not a syndrome at all but a breakdown, a chemical/paper rot. Old acetate film off-gassed acetic acid and collapsed in on itself until images curled and crisped and were gone. This was why you stored things underground. This was why you tried, anyway.

"I didn't open anything," Jake said. "I didn't even breathe down there. You could switch to a respirator if you want." His teeth flashed a quick smile, then he turned to badge them in.

They passed under the camera and walked, their footfalls muffled on the rubber runner. The mine ate sound, and yet everything felt loud to Mara—the hum of the air handlers, the forked lift of voices when two guys from Retrieval joked near an alcove, the squeak of her own shoe when she stepped wrong. She still thought of the prairie spread above them and the space of it, prairie and sky and miles of wheat country, and then she thought of the shape of emptiness down here, a place carved out and controlled. The mind staggered, sometimes, toggling between the two.

Unit C ran along the southwestern crosscut, beyond a set of double doors that closed with the assurance of a vault. The smell met them a full thirty feet before Jake stopped.

It was distinct in a way that was hard to explain to anyone who hadn't known it: bright and sharp, like a salad dressed too aggressively, and cutting through the flat as if someone had struck a match. It was faint here, a ghost of an acidity, but even the ghost made something behind Mara's eyes tighten.

They stood in the corridor, looking at the row of steel roll-up doors. Each was labeled with a number—C-1, C-3, C-7—each with a neat placard listing the client, climate spec, and date of last audit. C-17 was marked DECOMMISSIONED in red tape, and someone, at some point, had drawn an arrow in chalk on the wall near it that pointed down and then curved back, as if indicating a map that no longer made sense.

"That's not one of ours," Jake said, when he saw her looking. "Contractors way back, maybe. Before they put in the uniform signage. Another company had this unit until ninety-eight."

"You smell it most here?" Mara asked. She pulled a pair of gloves from her pocket and snapped them on. She took a breath through her mouth without thinking and tasted the remote sweetness of decay. "Or is it moving through the ducting?"

Jake rubbed his nose. "It's patchy. I walked the line twice. It spikes here and then dips, which... I don't know. Could be the air currents."

Mara crouched and pressed her hand to the floor. The mine expanded and contracted over time, squeezed by geology and money; somewhere, far away, she could feel the grumble of a compressor. The concrete was cool. On the floor along the base of the C-17 door, a faint line told of dust that had been dragged out under the rubber lip by negative pressure or rodents or nothing at all. She could smell the vinegar more clearly now, a steady thread in the weave of the air.

"They shouldn't have left it on the line if it was decommissioned," she said. She kept her voice even. "We should call Kline."

Jake was already pulling his phone from his pocket, then frowning at the bars. The mine was generous with its climates and frugal with its signal. He tilted his head, trying to find a sweet spot. "Eh. She won't pick up for me. You want me to see if there's a hardline at the office?"

Mara looked at the door. The padlock hung on the hasp like a shrug, its black-painted body flecked in white where salt had nipped it. The shackle, though, when she leaned to look, had a ribbon of brightness on one side, the metal clean in a way that did not match the rest. Someone had keyed it recently. Or recently enough that the mine had not had time to make it look old.

"Let's just look," she said. "We won't go in. Just check the interface seam. Make sure it's not a duct leak that's pooling."

Jake huffed and knelt, unhooking the lock with the casual intimacy of a man who had opened a thousand lockers. He rolled the door up a few inches. The smell hit like a smack.

"Whoa," he said, and rolled it down again, coughing. He gagged theatrically, then more genuinely. He stepped back and checked his watch, as if the time might have compassion for him. "I'm going to grab respirators. And a cart. If it is film and it isn't fused to itself, we should move it."

He trotted away, relief visible in the looseness of his stride. Mara hadn't asked him not to leave her. He would have stayed if she told him to. She stood alone for a moment with the door and with that line of dark, the tinny edge of acetic acid, the chalk arrow that had been scuffed once and then absent-mindedly retraced by someone hours — or years — ago.

She could have waited. She should have waited.

She rolled the door up.

The air that spilled out wrapped her in its hopeful hands. Film that had gone too far smelled not like vinegar but like death, a wet, flat reek that warned you away. This was not that. This was bright and alarming and still alive, the scent of something just beginning to go wrong.

There was a second door set back twelve feet, a standard fire-rated steel door without a window, chipped and painted over too many times. It had a push bar and a deadbolt, and a sheet of plastic slid under the threshold that someone had tucked with weather-strip to make a seal. The metal around the deadbolt had a white scrape that matched the lock outside. The hum behind the door was softer than the hallway's hum, a mosquito at the edge of hearing.

Mara set her palm flat against the door. It was not warm. Nothing here warmed, unless it was broken.

She slid her card through the reader. No red, no green. No reader at all, she realized; the small rectangular panel she had reached for was the ghost of one. There was only the deadbolt. She tested the knob. It turned.

"You are not going in there."

The voice was Jake's, dropped an octave by the acoustics. He was jogging back down the corridor with two respirators thumping against his chest by their straps, a stack of yellow biohazard tags under his arm. "We need to call it," he said. "We tag and we call. Kline will have my badge if we—"

"It's unlocked," Mara said simply.

He stopped, frowning, then came to stand beside her and peer at the seam the way one might look at the edges of a wound. "It wasn't welded, then. Idiots." He set one respirator on her bag, tightened the straps on the other, and tugged it on. His voice came out flattened. "I'm not joking. We should get someone. This smells... not good. But if we must." He offered her the second mask.

She took it. The plastic fit over her nose and mouth with a suction that made her conscious of her breath. Together, they shoved the bar and shouldered the door open.

The room was not large. It was not even very full. Its ceiling was low; its lights were strings of small bulbs with pull chains; the floor had been left concrete and not sealed. On the left, three rolling racks held steel canisters strapped upright with nylon. On the right, shelves contained bankers' boxes with the bland litany of handwriting on their sides: CORR, A-R, 1969. The air was thick with acid. There was a scattering of things that did not belong in a storage unit. There was a chipped metal desk with a green blotter. There was a metal ashtray like a shallow bowl. There was a gray wool jacket slung over the back of the desk chair. The jacket had a tear near the pocket.

"If I ever ran a horror movie," Jake said into his mask, "it would start like this."

"Don't," Mara said, but she was unnerved enough to be grateful that he had said what he had said. Naming things had power. Her gloved fingers smoothed the edge of the desk without touching it. A thin patina of dust lay on the blotter, even on the places where tide lines suggested cups had once sweated. The ashtray had a single stub in it, lipstick faint on the filter. It had dried and cracked into the dust like a small fossil.

She looked at the canisters. Some had cracked lids. A few had been wrapped in plastic. Something wet had bloomed and dried on the weldment of the rack, a rime of white that flaked when she touched it. She bent and lifted a canister from the bottom shelf, gauging the weight. Heavier than empty, lighter than full. It had no label. Someone had scraped it clean.

On the desk, under a paperweight made of a polished slice of agate, lay a manila folder. Inside were three index cards and a thin piece of leader. The leader was translucent and milky, the kind you used to pull a film through a projector. Someone had written on it with a dull pencil:

COUNTERMEASURES, 1973. DO NOT CATALOG.

"That," Jake said, "seems bad."

Mara picked up the cards. The first had a list of names that could have been a cast or a crew. The second had numbers, nothing else. The third had a post office box in town, printed neatly, and the words deliver if— The line cut off. The corner of the card was torn, as if someone had ripped away a thought.

She set the cards down carefully and bent closer to the leader. There was a faint print of something near the tape splices, as if someone had rolled across it with an inked finger and then changed their mind and wiped it away. The ink had resisted the wipe, had settled into the milk. The print looked like... a branch, almost. Or a crack in ice. Or a map.

"Mara," Jake said, a touch of unease in her name. He gestured toward the far wall.

She followed his hand.

The dust near the baseboard was disturbed. Not by mice. Not by the straight tail of a dragged hose or the broad heel of a cart. It was the shape it always was, the shape no one wanted to find: shoes. The prints came from the door and crossed toward the wall and stopped against it. At the wall there was a faint, darker line of difference, a mild misalignment in the paint where time had shrunk things unevenly. A door. A door within the room.

The prints doubled back once and smudged in their own passage and then were gone under the rolling racks, where the white dust insisted on its own continuity.

"You said it's decommissioned," Mara said. Her voice was too loud in her own ears, filtered and foreign. "Who has the key to this?"

"Kline," Jake said. "Facilities. The client, if there is even a client still. They're supposed to zero out buildings that get decommissioned. Strip them. Remove power, AC, all of it. They didn't do that, not all the way." He put his hand to the wall where the prints ended. "There is a cavity back there. I can hear it."

She could hear it too, now that she knew what she was listening for. A low, unsteady note. Not a hum. A breath. Or the echo of a breath. She looked up. The string bulbs shone like stars in low cloud. In the periphery, the canisters loomed, a small army keeping watch.

"We should go," she said. "We should call Kline. We should get this on paper and then let everybody whose job this is do their job."

Jake stepped back and toward the door as if to prove how amenable he was. "Finally," he said, kindly, but there was no real tease in it. He too wanted distance. He too felt the urge to place actual ground between himself and what they had crossed.

Mara looked once more around the room. On the wall above the desk was a photograph thumbtacked into the paint. It had curled at the edges in a way that told her nothing of when it had been taken and everything of the climate in which it had lived. It showed six people standing shoulder to shoulder in the wash of a headlamp's glare. They all wore hard hats. Two raised their palms to block the light. On the back, when Mara reached to take it down and then didn't, a bit of handwriting showed through in reverse.

Pick it up or leave it, she thought. Learn the first answer or the second.

She left it, but she allowed herself one trespass. She slid a hand into the jacket pocket, more a refex than a plan. Her fingers closed on a small hard shape. She drew out a key, flattened and stamped with a number, and a token attached to it by a short length of chain. The token was dull brass, the size of an old subway token. A bull's head had been stamped in the center. Around the edge, the words TEMPLE MINERALS CO. NO. 68 walked the curve in tiny, bitten letters.

She looked at Jake. She knew she should put it down. She slipped it into her pocket.

They backed out, careful of the prints, careful of the film, careful of everything. They pulled the door closed and then pulled the roll-up door down and jotted on a biohazard tag and looped it through the lock. The smell still pushed at the edges of the world. Mara took off her mask and tasted salt and then a sweetness that was not pleasant and would never be again.

"Tell me again how you're not here for the adventure," Jake said, trying for old mirth. He thumbed his phone. "I'll walk to the office and pull the hardline. You want to wait here?"

"I'll come with you," she said. "It's quiet."

They started down the corridor. Their footsteps had the orderly rhythm of retreat.

She could not help it. She looked back.

The chalk arrow on the wall glowed faint in the artificial dusk. The air moved nothing that could be seen. The hall was empty, which was the way halls preferred to be down here when no one was using them. It was not the arrow or the emptiness that made her stop. It was the touch of… change. A tiny difference the way an archivist knows a different hand in a ledger, the way she knew a chemical smell where it shouldn't be. The thin lifted hairs at the back of her neck knew it.

There was a new line in the dust. It was not big enough to be a footprint. It was not a straight drag. It was a tight arc, as if someone had turned abruptly, as if someone had pressed the toe of a shoe and pivoted on it. It traced a half-moon at the seam of the door she and Jake had just shut.

"Jake," she whispered, although whispering changed nothing down here and changed everything, if you needed it to. "Did you—"

From behind the wall inside C-17, the unseeable wall beyond the prints, came a soft click. Not a hum. Not a breath. The kind of small mechanical noise you might never hear above ground because the world had too much life to let it through, the kind of small mechanical noise that traveled like confession in the mine.

It was the sound of a latch finding its home.

They stood still in a place cut from the bones of an old sea, the air moving around them the way air always had and always would, engineered and predictable, and the idea that there was a second door behind the first door opened in Mara like a second mouth.

She did not say that they had made a mistake. She did not say that the mine kept what was given to it until someone came to ask. She looked down the corridor where Jake had already begun to move, fast and casual, his feet making bars of sound on the floor. She followed him because she had sense. She followed him because she had to call Kline and the client and the someone who had the key to door two. But her hand found her pocket without her permission, closed on the cool bull's head of the token, and did not let go.

The fog off Greyhallow Bay has a way of sounding like voices if you let it. All winter I slept with that hum in my ears whether I was in Boston with traffic under my windows or, like this morning, back in my grandmother’s house with salt under the floorboards and the old brass bedframe popping as the temperature dropped. I’d forgotten how much a wooden house talks. Heating pipes sigh. Stair risers remember feet. Out beyond the bluff, a bell buoy clanged every so often in a frequency that sat so neatly in my chest I could feel my ribs answer.

I wasn’t asleep at four forty when the engine started.

We used to say the town woke to coffee and the first ferry. Even in the off-season, when only a few year-rounders and the caretaker at Little Godwin Island rode the run, that diesel thrum meant the day was beginning—boats checked, traps mended, plow blades put back in the shed. But the ferry shouldn’t have started till five. And it shouldn’t have started at all without someone down at the slip.

I listened for the second, confident cough of an engine catching. It came. The sound flattened the fog, turned it from breath to wall. On the other side of that wall something moved—a white shape or a trick of the light—and the bell buoy answered twice, quick, as if interrupted by a hand.

The stairs complained when I took them two at a time. Everyone says you go right back to being a kid when you come home. In the half light the framed photograph of my mother tilted like it was watching me. I didn’t look back. I pulled on my boots by the door, found my grandmother’s rough navy pea coat on its hook and the old orange knit hat she’d insisted I wear in November and March, and I went out into air that tasted of iron and sap, as if someone had dragged a pine through the sea.

No one kept to the sidewalks on Winter Street. A thin crust of last night’s snow made print in the places where cats crossed. The world was two colors: the half lit gray of fog and the orange of sodium lights. I could only hear one thing, and it was the ferry.

At the top of the ramp the harbor’s shape revealed itself in flashes—mast tips, the low tarped humps of boats under winter cover, the stack of the Perigee with its peel of white paint. Frost tightened the aluminum grating under my boots. The ferry sat with its bow a careless three feet off the pilings. Its engine idled low, a reluctant animal.

“Hell,” said a voice behind me. “I was hoping I imagined that racket.” A flashlight beam hit my boots and climbed. Evie Pell wore a red knit cap so bright it cut a hole in the fog. She had a wool scarf tucked under a yellow slicker and the air about her of someone who could move a mooring ball with one hand and fix your tax problem with the other. “If this is some kid’s TikTok, I am going to make them scrape every line on this dock with a butter knife.”

“Do we have kids?” I asked before I could stop myself. “I mean—”

“I know what you mean,” she said. “And no, we do not. Even our mischief moved to Portland. You Nora March?”

It had been six years since I’d spent more than a long weekend in Greyhallow. I had expected some surprise at being recognized. I got none. In a place like this your face is a family tree.

“I got your email,” Evie went on. “About the boathouse key? We’ll find it. But first—” She flipped me a look. “Mind your feet. Frost’ll put you on your rear. And if your grandmother were alive, she’d yank that hat down over your ears. She always said you’d catch cold through your thoughts.”

“That sounds like her,” I said, and bit the inside of my cheek to stop whatever else wanted to come out with it.

Grief, contrary to the poets, is not a flood. It’s a tide that decides its own schedule. My grandmother had died in July, and I’d postponed dealing with her house until the lease on my place in Jamaica Plain was up and the cold made Greyhallow empty enough to be navigable. People who loved her left bread on the back steps as if I were a bird. People who loved a good story brought me other people’s sadness. I said thank you. Then, because I couldn’t sleep, I put a kettle on and brushed dust off the recorder I’d carried to interviews for years. I told myself I was here to clean out closets and list the house and get back to my life. Then the ferry started early.

Evie had a ring of keys and a confidence I would’ve trusted in a storm. She fitted a key into the small lockbox at the head of the ramp and took out the ferry’s passkey on its tagged coil. “Silas’ll love this,” she muttered. “Start a man’s boat without him and his blood pressure writes its own eulogy.”

“Silas Finch?” I asked. The name had come up in three stories I’d done on harbor towns over the last five years. Once because he found a brand new bag of heroin under a pile of lobster traps and turned it over to the sheriff and once because he delivered a woman’s baby halfway between here and the island while a tabloid photographer tried to take pictures and once because, at eighty, he still did the morning run in weather I would have called medieval. “He still has the—”

“Cap? Trophy for most opinions? Both. And yes, he still pilots mornings. Mateo runs afternoons unless he’s reading for his fancy medical classes. An empty boat is not a good look. You hear anyone?”

“No.”

“Let’s see then.” She stepped onto the ramp, keeled out and back for balance, and headed down to the float.

It felt wrong to follow. There are things that belong to a place—its smells, its complaints, the way the planks shift under weight—and you only borrow them while you’re visiting. I had left Greyhallow at eighteen with one suitcase and a scholarship. I’d come back for scattered holidays and once for a funeral that turned into a fight, leaving a hairline crack in my aunt’s front window you could only see in low light. But I stepped down behind Evie like someone who remembered where to put her feet. The Perigee’s fender knocked the piling with a halfhearted foam kiss. The engine’s noise felt like teeth.

We coiled one of the lines and threw it. The sound it made told me more about winter than any weather report; stiff as a snake in January, supple as a cat in July. Evie leaped the gap, caught the rail, steadied herself with a sailor’s grab and disappeared into the fog that whirled off the bow in little ghosts. “Well?” I said.

“Well what?” she called. “Nothing. That’s the problem. She ain’t tied and she ain’t manned and she sure as anything is running.”

The low door to the wheelhouse was open. Yellow light spilled onto the non-skid. I stepped aboard, heart doing something inappropriate in my throat. A coffee cup rolled to the edge of the deck and back as the boat shifted. I caught it without thinking and was absurdly grateful for heat against my palms, proof of how recently someone had stood here.

“I’m going to call this in,” Evie said, her voice already gone faraway on the phone. “If it’s a prank, I’ll skin it. If it’s not, I want people awake.”

I ducked under the wheelhouse hatch. Every ferry smelled the same, no matter the town: diesel and old rope, metal warmed and cooled too many times, coffee entrenched in the plywood like a religion. The chart was on the table near the window, folded and weighted by a rock painted like a ladybug. The rock made my mouth tilt. We’d painted those in fourth grade—small round bits of glacial smoothed granite turned into bugs and fruit and footballs to be used as paperweights during the Greyhallow Fair. The next thing made my mouth forget how to do anything.

Someone had tied the wheel.

It was a clumsy job, a figure-eight looped twice around the spokes and anchored off to the standpipe on the starboard side, but it was unmistakable. The rope was hemp, not nylon, a softer cousin of what the fishermen still used for someone’s father’s traps. Stuck through one of the knotted turns was a bunch of flowers.

At first my mind reached for a species and came up with wrong ones—baby’s breath, Queen Anne’s lace, no, too early, too cold—and then the right one settled like frost on glass. Sea lavender. Limonium. Even out of season, you saw it tied to the backs of chairs in town hall weddings and hung in sprays from the slant shelves at Fletcher’s Hardware because Mrs. Fletcher had decided decades ago that she was the kind of woman who dried flowers and this was the thing she liked to dry.

My grandmother had tied sea lavender to the posts on the wharf when someone didn’t come home.

It wasn’t a superstition. It was a message. The first time she did it I was seven and crying because Danny Walsh broke my best seashell. She wrapped my left hand around the slick, cool stems and my right around the red thread we used to bind old letters and she told me, steady as the tide, “If you tie this to a place that belongs to someone, it will catch their eyes. And if they are lost, it will point them to where they can be found.”

It was the red thread now, as if pulled from the old spool that lived in the junk drawer of my grandmother’s kitchen, that strangled my breath harder than the rope and the gray flowers. It looped the bouquet three times, knotted on the back with a seaman’s knot I could execute even half asleep.

“Evie,” I said, but she had gone out to the stern to take a call and the only answer was the radio’s patient, self-possessed weather report. The radio didn’t care about the thread. It said wind five to eight, gusting ten. It listed what it always listed: the names of the nearby stations, the points of safe harbor, the temperature of the air and the sea. I reached to touch the bouquet and stopped myself because what if I was about to smudge a fingerprint, which is the kind of thing I only remembered to worry about when I was standing in a place I wasn’t meant to be, which this was, which I was very much not meant to be.

I study sound, not crime. I could tell you the difference between a blizzard and a nor’easter by the way snow tattooed a window. I could tell you the month by the birdsong at five a.m. I knew the feel of a red thread between finger and thumb because I had tied it around a hundred lost things. I didn’t know if I should untie a stranger’s knot on a steering wheel, even if the thread wasn’t a stranger to me.

The coffee cup squeaked as it rolled. Something on the table caught my eye, a small white thing tucked under the painted ladybug rock. It was a paper tag, the kind you get on clothing or keep for stringing bulbs of garlic in a pantry. I slid it free with one finger.

There are three ways things disappear in Greyhallow. Tide takes them. The woods swallow them. Or you put them out of your mind. The handwriting on the paper knew that. It quenched and thickened in places, as if the pen had geared down, as if the hand that wrote it had done so on a moving surface. The letters were careful where you’d expect careless and careless where you’d expect a warning.

For the one who listens, the tag said. Below it was a single name in smaller script.

Nora.

My throat went tight as wind rope. The name on the paper was not a mistake and it was not about the other Nora in town—the one who’d married a fisherman and moved to Ogunquit and who always introduced herself as Lenora just to avoid what she called the Great Nora Wars of 1989 when we were in fifth grade and there were four of us with variations of the same name. The paper knew me. I didn’t have proof but I had a sudden foam of certainty in my mouth.

“I rang Silas,” Evie said, appearing at my shoulder so quietly I flinched and hated myself for flinching. “No answer. Called Mateo, too. Know what I got? Voice mail. Know what else I got? A deputy on the way with a fatigue jacket and a flashlight and opinions. Friday’s on the radio trying not to sound excited. You look like you swallowed a fishbone.”

The tag felt the way tags feel when you’ve paid too much for a sweater. I held it up. Evie read. She said nothing for the span of two full breaths, which for Evie was a paragraph.

Then she said, “Well. That’s a choice.”

“What's a choice?”

“Putting your name on it.” She had the expression of someone who had been supplied with a piece of information she didn’t want to own. “Do you know who’d—”

“No,” I said honestly. “Not yet.”

“Don’t touch anything else,” she said, which made me aware of my hands like I’d never had them before. She took a photo, quick, with her phone in its rubber case and texted it to someone. “And don’t go repeating it down the ramp to anyone with coffee breath until I get my feet under me. Where were you at four? Never mind. Don’t answer. That kid at the gas station will hear the word ‘mystery’ and print T-shirts.”

I found out you can both autograph something and arrest it by putting your name on it. The deputy on duty—Shaw, with a jaw he clearly shaved in the dark and a fatigue jacket too big in the shoulders—arrived eight minutes after Evie’s call. He had a flashlight and the face of a person who had been told to expect a laugh and found instead a family ghost. He looked at the wheel like it might move if he exhaled too hard.

“That knot’s old-fashioned,” he said, and even though I’d promised myself I would take up exactly none of the air in the wheelhouse, my mouth said it before I could stop it.

“It’s mine,” I said.

Shaw turned. “Excuse me?”

“The knot,” I said. “I mean, not mine like I tied it, but my grandmother taught me that knot. Sea lavender. The thread. We tied it to the wharf when someone didn’t come home. She liked her messages to be tidy.”

“You think this is a message?” Shaw had the particular careful voice of someone who called things facts only after the ink dried.

“What else is a flower on a steering wheel?” I asked. “A decoration? Sea lavender doesn’t say party.”

“Does it say trouble?”

“It says lost.”

Evie made a small noise that might have been approval or could have been a piece of her scarf trying to do murder by strangulation. “There’s nobody on board,” she told Shaw. “I walked the deck. The heads are empty. There’s coffee. There’s a ladybug paperweight because my niece painted half this town’s rocks last summer and we’ll be finding them in our shoes for the rest of our natural lives. And there’s that.” She jerked her chin at the wheel. “What there isn’t is our people.”

Shaw made a note. He did not touch the wheel. He did not touch the rope near the wheel. He leaned down and squinted, which seemed to be his current investigative technique. “Could they have fallen?”

“Both of them?” Evie asked. A thin humor sparked in her eyes like a match that knew better than to flame. “At the slip, on a windless sunrise? We’re clumsy in February, but we aren’t that ambitious.”

I stood with my back against the chart table to keep from leaning into the bouquet. The tag in my hand was suddenly too heavy. I could put it down, I told myself. It would be more honest. It would be more right. If I kept it, I was not doing a journalism thing. I was doing a taking thing. The thought turned into another thought: having something in your pocket isn’t always about taking. Sometimes you carry it because you have to walk it somewhere.

“Who has access to the keys?” Shaw asked. “Other than you, Evie.”

“Silas. Mateo. Me. It’s not brain surgery.” She added, in case that sounded dismissive, “You want to know how it actually works? We hide the passkey in the lockbox with a code that makes sense only if you knew who Evelyn Younger married when she was nineteen because she had to, which is not to slight Evelyn, who turned out fine and who also has a memory like a ledger. I got woken up by that engine same as Nora. Came down. Found this.” She waved a hand at the boat. “We haven’t had anything go truly weird on the water since—”

She stopped. I knew what she’d keep herself from saying. Everyone in Greyhallow eventually stops themselves from saying it. The town’s mouth tripped over the same stone and swallowed the same name. The last ferry didn’t come back empty. It didn’t come back at all. I was twelve, and I have never liked the dark since.

Shaw’s eyes flitted to me and away. “I’m going to need statements.”

“You’ll get them,” Evie said. “Deputy, pull this last line, please. We’re too far off the pilings for my comfort.”

We eased the ferry in. The rope made a sound against wood that was almost tender. Everything I did felt too loud. The fog forgot itself and parted in tatters, then drew back around us with a shrug, like a curtain reminding the stage that it was allowed to have a boundary.

On the way down the ramp twenty minutes later, Shaw writing diligently, Evie keeping pace like a boat herself, I kept my hand in my coat pocket. It was a childish posture. It made me feel like I’d stolen gum from Fletcher’s counter. The tag rasped against my middle finger, the hole-punched edge catching on skin.

We reached the top. The bell buoy answered something out in the channel we couldn’t see. I stopped. My grandmother’s house sat three blocks north on a cut of sand that let the light lay down in the afternoons. In my head she stepped out the back door, one hand on the jamb, and called me child, which she only did when she thought I was about to do something with consequences, and she didn’t feel like saying the rest out loud.

“Evie,” I said. “If it’s Silas, if he’s—if something’s wrong—”

“We’re going to find what we find,” she said, not unkind, which is what passes for comfort here. “Nora, go home. Drink something hot. Do not go on the internet. Give me an hour to call his daughter.”

She started toward the harbormaster’s shack to make the first of a dozen calls. Shaw took a breath that looked like it might fog the entire dock. I stood very still. I took the tag out of my pocket and looked at the back of it, not because I expected something to be written there but because it’s human nature to hope that if you flip a thing over often enough it will tell you the part you want to know.

There was writing. Two numbers. 43.748. -69.188.

Coordinates. The place they pointed to lived inside my body as a twinge, a remembered path underfoot. A rock shelf off Little Godwin where the water went green-black and the lobsters were as big as dogs when my cousin lied about them. A place you only went at slack tide. A place my grandmother had told me not to dive after spring thaw because the currents there kept secrets.

For the one who listens, the tag said. Then my name. Then a map you could fold and put in your pocket.

The bell buoy lamented like a throat clearing for a speech. The fog held its breath. In that brief, empty quiet, I heard the other sound the engine had threaded itself into. Somewhere far out, a gull laughed the way it does when it knows a thing before you do. And even if this was a prank, even if the story turned out to be two men who decided to play a game with the town for reasons that would make sense only after beer, even if the bouquet on the wheel meant nothing more than someone else’s idea of a good joke, I didn’t believe it.

There are three ways things disappear in Greyhallow. I had told myself that for years as a way to file information. It does not cover the fourth. Sometimes a thing never left and you did. You go away, and something waits inside the shape of you. When you come home, it does not rush. It hands you a small white tag and asks if you’re listening.

Chapter One: The Mirabel at Three A.M.

On the graveyard shift, buildings breathe.

You feel it in the carpet under the desk mat, in the way the air pushes softly from the vents and changes direction with a sigh. It’s different from the daytime breath—no hurry in it, no commuter exhale of coffee and cologne. At night the walls settle and the quiet expands. You learn where wood ticks and where plaster hums, where the chill climbs from the basement and how the lobby’s green marble collects every draft and keeps it like a secret.

I keep a small electric kettle hidden under the counter and I scrape a match on the underside of the desk bell when its piezoelectric button fails. On my third night at the Mirabel I memorized the pattern of light from Sixth Street, how it runs through the revolving door like spilled silver and prints the old mosaic floor with a moving map. On my tenth night I learned not to look at the gilded ceiling too long, because the paint wants to peel in your peripheral vision and make you think it’s breathing, too.

That’s the thing about an old place. It teaches you what to ignore, and then it tests you on it.

At three in the morning the Mirabel is at its thinnest. The last garnishes have been scraped off plates in the bar and left to shrivel under the red lamp in the kitchen. The housekeeping carts are parked in a neat line in the service corridor like a row of sleeping cows. The night auditor, Cray, has a tower of receipts and a headache and he doesn’t like to be interrupted unless a guest is bleeding or famous. Oleg, the overnight security guard, looks tall and impervious until he sneezes; then he looks like someone’s grandfather crumpling, which he very well is.

We have twelve occupied rooms, two weddings checked in for tomorrow and a convention of oral surgeons whose baggage will arrive without them at six. There are five elevators, which we call the west bank and the east bank because saying “Elevator Two” into the radio makes everyone suddenly deaf.

On the console in front of me the call lights are dark. The glass clock over the till ticks its dry, expensive tick. The coffee in the mug tastes like driftwood and the memory of something sweet. I bend to pick up a file I knocked down earlier and see the graffito again, carved with a key on the underside of the desk drawer twenty years ago if it was a day: DON’T ANSWER AFTER TWO. The letters are jagged, full of an angry leisure. I have a moment—nothing more than an exhale—of considering the superstition of it. Some hotels have a no-thirteen on the elevator panel and some have a superstition about peacocks, and we have the thing under the desk where no one sees it unless they crawl on their knees.

I’m back on my feet before I register the sound.

Ding.

It’s a polite sound. Nothing like emergencies. The kind of ding that used to mean a woman in gloves needed a porter to retrieve her hatbox. It’s not one of ours, because ours are computerized and cheap and all their dings sound the same. This one seems to come from behind the wall rather than from the console, and for a second I could believe the hotel wanted to play at being itself.

I look up at the bank of indicators for the east elevators. Someone had a good time with these in 1928—there are black glass panels behind the desk, all carved numbers and floral tracery, and each car has a little brass needle that creeps from B to 17. The needles haven’t moved in my lifetime. They’re disconnected, museum pieces now, and they hang a few degrees to the left like tired eyelids.

The needle over Car 3 leans right, just a whisper. I set my mug down very carefully. The needle leans right again, to the 1, like someone inching onto the stage from the wings.

The console panel is newer, a plastic grid that tells me what’s really happening. Four little green squares, one for each car on the east bank—1, 2, 4, and… 3 is supposed to be a blank space without a light. Nothing is supposed to light for 3. That car has been out of service for forty-seven years, welded and bricked and taped first with caution tape and then with contempt.

The blank space is glowing.

“Cray?” I call without taking my eyes off the panel.

“In what way is this interrupting me?” he replies from the office, the shapes of receipts reflected in his glasses.

“Car three just called the lobby.”

He makes the stage-grunt of someone who doesn’t believe in a line item. “That’s physically impossible, Samantha.”

“That’s why I’m interrupting you.”

He shuffles his seat back. Being the night auditor has given Cray a posture that looks like he’s already stuck in an elevator. He comes to the console and squints. “Maybe a surge,” he says. But he’s lowering his head to align his eyes with the old brass needle, and the needle seems to notice. It slides, slow as a minute hand, from 1 to L. It lands on Lobby. Ding.

Every instinct I have tells me it’s a glitch, a trick of wiring. Every rumor I’ve heard says otherwise.

There are three stories we tell about the sealed elevator. One is that a bellboy got crushed when the car misleveled during the winter of ‘78, and the owners, who were at that time trying very hard to convince the city they were solvent, paid cash to make it disappear. One is that Mr. Mirabel’s mistress, a singer whose stage name was Rose, went out the wrong door on the fourteenth floor the night he re-opened the rooftop bar and tumbled into the dark like a bottle from a lasso. The third—the one Oleg tells after precisely two bourbons—is that during Prohibition somebody ran numbers out of the elevator shaft and when the Feds finally pried it open there was nothing inside but a hat and two tickets to Havana.

I did not come to the Mirabel to collect stories. I came because I needed a night job that wasn’t serving drinks to men who confide in the bartender’s chest, and because the Mirabel’s manager, Ms. Lacey, had looked at my resume where it mentioned “former stage manager” and said, “You people know how to show up on cue.”

The panel emits a second sound I have never heard here: a warbling chirp that means someone has pushed the Emergency/Help button from inside a car. It’s odd enough to be funny in the way a dog looks funny when it says “hello.” The green light for 3 flashes. The phone on the console toggles automatically to speaker. The line breathes.

“Mirabel front desk,” I say, because no one can ever accuse me of not doing my job.

At first all I hear is static and the deeper hush of a closed space. Then a sound that could be a voice if it had anything to climb on. If the elevator had been open, I’d have said someone stood too close to the microphone and breathed hope into it.

“Hello? Hello, can you hear me?” I keep my voice level. Cray’s hand, very lightly, has found the edge of the desk.

The static tightens into a shape. “—help,” the shape says, as if it has been learning English by touching a dictionary. The voice sounds like it belongs to a man who sleeps on his side to stop the snore from waking his wife. He whispers something else. It could be the number eight. It could be my name. It could be a plea from a previous century.

“Hang on,” I say. “We’re coming right now. Are you injured? Can you breathe?”

Static. Soft, quick exhale. Then the line goes dead.

Cray swallows. The movement is visible in his throat. “Mickey!” he yells over his shoulder, forgetting that the building engineer’s name is Miguel and that Miguel went home at midnight. “Oleg!”

Oleg appears at the end of the hall in sock feet and security gray, doing up his belt as he walks. “What hurts?” he asks, because he is a grandfather, and I point at the panel.

He makes a sign of the cross without irony.

The east elevator lobby smells like old linen and furniture polish. The mirrors are floor to ceiling and shadowed with that mercury rash that makes everyone look like they’re fading. Car 1’s stainless doors are scuffed with baggage and the markles of bored passengers. Car 2 makes a sound like a playing card in bicycle spokes and has for as long as anyone can remember. Car 4 has a new sticker with a phone number that will go to voicemail. Car 3 is a history lesson. The center seam where the doors would meet is visible only because whoever taped the “Out of Service” sign to the steel plate forty-seven years ago picked bad masking tape that yellowed and left a rectangle.

The steel plate over the original doors is bolted not cleanly but urgently. My father used to say you can tell the kind of problem by the kind of work done to hide it. There’s an indecorousness to the bolts on Car 3. It’s the difference between a seamstress’s hem and a stapled wound.

Behind the usual metal, someone welded an additional smaller plate over the emergency release with eight mismatched screws. There’s no elegant way to go in. If anything chooses to come out, it will come out jagged.

The call button for Car 3—the old pearl push more appropriate for a private club—glows amber.

Oleg points to it like a tourist pointing out a rare bird. “No power to that one,” he tells me, and I know he’s correct because I sat in the back office last week while Miguel showed me the elevator schematics and tapped the dead lines with the kind of respect he doesn’t show to the living.

We all stand there a beat too long, the way people do at the scene of a minor accident, waiting for someone to make the first move toward the dented cars.

“Front desk to Engineering,” I say into the radio, out of habit. The radio waits. “Front desk to—anyone.”

“Call nine-one-one,” says Oleg, sober now in a way I like. “If there is someone in there, we can’t unbolt this fast. They send the fire department. They have saw for this.”

“Right,” I say, and already I’m moving.

The emergency phone under the console always rings too long. The dispatcher takes our address like we might have changed it since noon. I tell her what I heard and the fact of the sealed car. She does not argue about the impossible. Perhaps she’s had a night, too. She tells me somebody is on the way.

Back in the lobby my breath leaves visible when I exhale. It’s not so cold it should do that.

“We could try the inspection slot,” says Cray, who has pushed his glasses up and found a sudden bravery to fill the space between now and an arrival with lights and noise. “You know—the little hole where you can hook the release if someone is stuck between floors.”

He is right. In the corner of the welded plate is a hole someone has tried to cover with paint. It’s thumb-sized and deep. Every real hotel has a hook tool for it somewhere. Ours is in the office, in a drawer with rubber bands and the kind of pens that stop writing if you don’t coddle them.

“I’ll get the hook,” I say.

There is deep comfort in tasks. This is something stage managing taught me: panic can be put off if you have a list and a pencil. The drawer sticks. I jerk it and the pens rattle and there is another bit of someone’s message scratched in the wood, like a game of consequences from another time. It says CALL HIM ANYWAY. The hook is under a sheaf of old menus, thin and cheap and shaped like a snake that swallowed a coat hanger.

By the time I return, Oleg has fetched a flashlight from his belt. He hands it to me without saying anything and I take it the way you take a candle from someone’s altar.

Car 3 does not have an inspection slot in the ordinary way. You can’t poke and pull as if you were getting cereal out of a vending machine. The hole is in the steel and the steel is a second skin. Still, I can get the hook inside and feel the point of it skitter on old metal. I breathe. The building breathes back.

There is a sound inside the shaft like a cough.

“Hello,” I say to the door, because it seems polite. “We hear you. The fire department is on its way. Can you knock? One for yes, two for no?” I lean my ear to the seam.

A pause. A thud. A second one.

My skin prickles up under my jacket. I press my thumb to the hook, angle, push.

I get lucky. Something catches, a spring or a lever old as the hotel’s first chandelier, and the weld plate shifts a fraction of a fraction. It isn’t a door moving; it’s the door remembering it knows how.

“Careful,” says Oleg.

“I am,” I say, which is wrong. I am not careful. If anything is alive in there, the seconds scrape and are gone.

The seam opens just enough that a slice of stale air comes out, air sealed since before I was born or at least packed so tight with age it forgets how to leave. It smells of hot bearings and the wool of expensive coats after a night out. It smells like spilled gin. It smells like my mother’s red lipstick in the cracked tube she hid in her purse to touch up before my father got home. It smells like metal. Over all, faint but sure, is the iron scent you learn even if you don’t want to: blood gone a day, getting ready to settle into carpets.

It shouldn’t smell like that. Even if someone is—was—in there. Even if.

I put the flashlight to the slit and hit the button.

Light crosses metal then shadow then something like cloth. It flips face-down a talon of brass.

“Do you see—” Cray starts, and then he stops.

I angle the light further. The beam finds a face. The skin is pale enough to show the blue under it where the beard would come in later today if later days were available. The eyes are partially open in the way of sleeping passengers trying to make it until their stop. There is a neat dark line under the hairline, like a scratch traced with ink. Sometimes you judge a person’s life by how they die. Sometimes how they die refuses to say anything at all.

His hand is closest to the seam. It rests on the floor of the car, palm up as if asking. In it is a bit of brass that catches the light with desperate joy. It’s a key fob, the old Mirabel kind, oval and heavy, engraved with the crest no one uses anymore. The tag has a number stamped deep enough to be read by touch.

712.

I don’t move. The number sits in my brain like a coin dropped in a glass. Oleg breathes in. “That’s on seven,” he says, because he is trying to be helpful and because people will always say the obvious when they stand at the edge of something that is going to change them.

“He’s dead,” Cray says softly, surprising us all by saying it out loud before anyone else will. “We need to—” He gestures vaguely toward procedure.

There is no Room 712.

This is not superstition or rumor. It is not the Mirabel’s aversion to thirteen that skips it on the buttons. It is math and mapping. Seven on the east bank runs from 701 to 710. After 710 is the door with the linen closet and the iron staircase not used since a porter named Ernest fell down it laughing in 1959. There has never been a 712.

The building breathes again and this time the breath has a shiver in it.

I switch the flashlight off because I cannot make the man any less dead by lighting him. Oleg has his phone in his hand now as if he could photograph the moment and pin it to a board and label it with string.

Sirens arrive not like a chorus but one by one, as if even the fire engines have to punch in. The first two paramedics bring a tool that looks too cheerful for its job and a face that has learned how not to show waiting. They deal with our front steps, then the revolving door, then the way Car 3 is barricaded, then with me. Questions anchor them. How long since the call? We tell them. Has anyone else touched the door? I say yes because I am unwilling to live in a world where leaving your prints off a thing you have to get into to save someone is more important than getting into it.

More people arrive. There is a lieutenant with the kind of mustache that’s aligned to a code. There is a kid who should be asleep in algebra. There is a stethoscope that goes unused. They talk to each other in shorthand that sounds like a poker game. They pull their saws like violins.

The first shriek of steel on steel drives one of the dentists’ wives out of her room. She stands in the doorway of 806 in a robe too thin for the hallway, a silver necklace glowing at the notch of her throat, and says, “What is that noise?” in a voice that believes noise is a choice. I tell her to go back to bed and she actually does.

Ms. Lacey arrives in sneakers and a camel coat, and the coat is more shaken than she is. She stands between the paramedics and the wall and puts her fist under her chin and watches me watching her. She’s the kind of woman who rarely says your name except when she wants two things of you at once, once on duty and once on faith. “Report,” she says, and I tell her what I will later write in the incident log. She keeps looking at the door like it’s a table someone has put a cake on and told her not to cut.

When the second weld plate comes off it makes a sound like a bell with a stone in it. They get enough of an aperture to work in. One of the firefighters slides on gloves with a snap that ricochets. Everything is precise now. They are not here for the story. They are here because someone pressed a button and I answered and that is the only part that matters to them.

They widen the gap and air spills. The smell gets bigger. It isn’t worse, exactly, except that what was a suspicion becomes a fact that fits into your lungs. The young firefighter leans into the space, his helmet scratching old paint. He reaches, gently, for the outstretched hand.

“Hang on,” says the lieutenant. He squints, then squints deeper, then turns to Ms. Lacey and me. “Do you have a man named—” He pauses, because the face doesn’t immediately put a word in his mouth. “Identification?” he tries, neutral as eggs.

“We haven’t got inside yet,” Ms. Lacey says. “We don’t even know how he—”

“—got in there,” I finish, because the sentence, once started, wants a landing. We all look at the welded front and the blank place on the panel and the old needle pretending to be useful.

“Funny thing is,” the lieutenant says softly to no one in particular, “this looks fresh.”

He means the blood. He means the lines of scuffing on the steel near the seam. He means that if someone had died in 1978 in a car that hasn’t opened since, he shouldn’t be this color, this weight, this moment.

Cray is pale. Oleg shakes his head like he’s trying to dislodge a word in another language. Ms. Lacey taps her fingers against her elbow, slow as old jazz. I hold myself very still because there is a piece of me that believes if I move, the story will also move and I will not be able to put it back.

“Fire saw,” the lieutenant says to the kid, and the saw sings its bright shriek again, and the steel gives slowly, stubborn as a door to a house you once lived in.

When they pull the car open far enough to do what they do next, the world trims itself to a frame. The man in the gray suit has a good haircut and a bad day. There is a dark crescent under his left eye as if he had not slept, forever. His tie is loosened in that last-human gesture you make when nothing else will help. In his fist the brass key fob sits as if it has always wanted to be found. The number is the kind you could misread if you wanted to, but I am not confused.

712.

Someone will ask me later about the phone call, about the voice that might have been a word. They will ask what it said. I will tell them the truth: that I do not know whether it said help or hello or eight. I know only what the needle did and the ding that came after and the way the building took a breath that didn’t belong to any of us.

The lieutenant looks at me. The look is not unkind. It is simply square. “Has this hotel ever had a Room 712?” he asks, ticking boxes in his head.

“No,” I say, and my voice sounds as if I have been speaking into a door all my life. “We never have.”

“Well,” he says, keeping his eyes on me, as if in all this hardware and heat I am the thing that will either tell him the shape of the hole in the story or step neatly around it. “Looks like we do now.” He nods toward the fob. “And it looks like somebody checked in.”

He reaches for the key, but I put my hand out without thinking and touch his sleeve. The fabric is rough and reassuring. “Don’t,” I say, and then I don’t know why I have said it, only that if anyone touches that bit of brass it will change from being a sign to being evidence, and evidence belongs to someone who can take it away.

He waits a beat and then picks it up anyway, careful, with two fingers, like he is plucking a thorn from a hothouse flower. He drops it into a clear bag. The number, magnified by the plastic, looks even more emphatic.

We all exhale together. It could be called relief if you were new at this. The saw stops. The building seems to listen to itself.

Somewhere above us, on seven, the hallway light three doors down from 710 flickers as if a person is walking past. I know this because there is a camera there, and the monitor behind the desk does what monitors do: it watches. It shows me an empty hall and a shadow that can only be someone leaving a door that is not there.

At three in the morning an old building breathes, and if you are not careful, you breathe with it.

Chapter One: The Weight of Water

People like to pretend that time is something we make. We square its edges, etch it onto dials, pluck it from air and trap it behind glass. We count it off with lanterns and bells and schoolroom whistles. We arrange ourselves around it, drink it, pray by it, go mad because of it.

But the sea never asked permission.

In Marrowick they built a clock that bowed to the sea. They called it the Tide House—though it looks more like a narrow stone knuckle stuck up out of the harbor, ringed with iron balconies and salt-streaked windows. It is older than the bluff road that winds down past the church and the lobster pots, older than the split-level cottages that lean together against the gale. The tide lifts, the tide falls, and the Tide House swallows and exhales and its great handless face at the top—weathered brass with a single gilded pointer—turns to show the harbor when to launch and when to come home.

I had never seen it. I had only seen three photographs: one from a newspaper, one from a pamphlet with a seal stamped in blue ink, and one folded into a letter I kept in the inside pocket of my coat. In the photograph the sky was the kind of hard white that flays roofs and makes everyone squint; the tower looked like it was carved out of that brightness. In my coat, the letter had softened against my ribs from three months carried. It had been written in a hand that slanted heavy to the right and went ragged whenever a word had to be crossed, as if the pen bled. Eliza, it began, I am told you mend old hearts.

I got off the bus with the letter and one case. The driver—a woman with a cap so stiff it looked like a little fortress—set the case down on the damp cobbles with a gentleness that surprised me. Everything in Marrowick smelled like salt and diesel and winter-ready rope. It was late October, the kind of day that bides its time, slate clouds pressing down on a sea that considered being calm.

“You Eliza Reed?” the driver asked.

“I am.”

She jerked her chin at the Tide House, its windows filmed with the same salt rime that had gritted my teeth since we turned off the highway. “They’ve been asking, the lot of them. Council’s been in and out. Something wrong with the clock’s song, they say.”

“I heard.”

“They say it’s temperamental. I say it’s old. Old things sing wrong when they’re ignored.” She lifted a hand and then thought better of whatever blessing or warning she had almost offered. “Good luck.”

Luck, in my experience, was only ever a story you tell after the fact to make what happened look like it was part of a plan. I took up the case, turned my collar against the wind, and started down the road that hugged the bluff.

Marrowick is the kind of place built in layers. There are the old houses with their cedar shingles turned the same gray as the sea, huddled with their backs to the wind. There are the newer houses with their cheerful vinyl siding and flapping pennants—lobster, lighthouse, a red sailboat nested in a blue field. There’s the church with its creaking sign and its cracked bell that tolls a note no one in town can hear without looking at their watch. There’s the cannery, long abandoned and now painted with cheerful murals that the gulls bless daily. Children had chalked spiral tides across the road, the white lines blurred by damp. Somewhere a radio played a tune I remembered and couldn’t name.

I felt people looking. I always feel eyes. It’s a prickle at the base of my neck that either belongs to nerves or to a life spent being the sort of woman who makes people ask whose idea it was that she come here, do that. A man came out of a bait shop with three orange floats under his arm and paused to watch me go by. A teenager with a shock of bleached hair and a hoodie that read SIREN smirked reflexively and then softened to something like curiosity. An older woman with two small dogs raised her eyebrows so high they might have taken flight, then nodded once at me as if to say, Well, then. Well, then.

The Tide House had a gate and a plaque and an iron key scraped clean by a thousand hands. The plaque told me that the Tide House had been erected in 1871 “by public subscription and with gratitude to the sea”—which was the kind of statement a town makes when it hasn’t counted the dead in a while. The gate squealed when I pushed it, the exact pitch of three A’s braided. The key fit the door and turned, grudging and old.

Inside it was cooler, the salt damp doing the work of a cellar. The air smelled like oil and rope and a clean metal cold. My fingertips brushed stone that sweated a little. Light came in pale and steady through long, high windows, and the space carried every sound. Footsteps in here spoke twice, once for themselves and once for the tower, which answered everything. The floor was slate and warped wood, stained in crescents where decades of boot heels had pivoted, turned. The walls were hung with tools—wrenches with odd mouths, calipers with one jaw bigger than the other, brushes whose bristles had been trimmed to fussy little squares. There was a control table that would have been comical anywhere else, full of levers with porcelain handles and dials whose glass had fogged with age, labeled with words like FLOODGATE and WEIR and CHIME.

I set my case down and stood long enough to hear the place.

Every machine has its song. A watch movement’s is a tight, balanced back-and-forth: the tick-tock that isn’t really tick-tock at all but two shoulders of the same tooth touching different stones in careful alternation. The Tide House’s song was slower, cavernous. Somewhere beneath my feet water moved through a throat of metal and stone. Somewhere to my right there was the faintest sizzle, as if a fine strand of hair were burning. I turned to find it and saw that one of the porcelain-handled levers had arced a faint black kiss into its casing.

I heard something else, too: the faintest equivalency, a beat that should have been a beat and wasn’t. It caught like a skipped step in a stair. One-two, one—two-three, one-two. I could feel it in the soft place just below my throat.

“You’re early,” someone said.

The voice came from a door I had mistaken for a cupboard. It opened and let in a stripe of colder air, and a woman stepped through, both hands full of a coil of rope that had never seen a boat. She wore a fisherman’s sweater the color of old smoke and a skirt tucked up at the hip with pins. Her hair had gone to iron gray and then thought better of it, a few threads of black still threading through. She looked like the thing that is left, not the thing that goes.

“Am I?” I said.

“We were told tomorrow." Her eyes did a full survey of me—coat, case, boots, hands. “But your type usually comes when they get here. Paper says one thing, tide says another.”

“My type?”

“People with tools.”

I smiled. “I do like to be early. If that’s all right.”

“It’s more than all right, if you can persuade it to stop singing wrong.” She nodded toward the control table, which made its little stove-top hiss again in response. “I’ve had men throwing stones at this door saying it was bad luck. Never mind they’ve been hauling since before breakfast. There’s no talking sense when a tune rubs them wrong.”

“I can try.” I set a hand lightly on the nearest lever just to feel its hum. “Eliza Reed.”

“Agnes Crowe.” Her grip had the softness of someone who kneads bread and the strength of someone who can hoist an anchor if it comes to it. “Steward. That’s a fancy way to say I dust what isn’t metal and wipe what is, and if the council says we can’t afford to call anyone, I shake something until it behaves."

My mouth murmured a sound that wanted to be a laugh and wasn’t. “I was told the council called me.”

“They did.” Agnes tilted her head. “After six months of saying the tide was fine.”

“And the clock’s kept time for a hundred and fifty years,” I said. “It’s allowed to be tired.”

“And yet,” Agnes said. “And yet. Come on, then. If you’re early, you can see it when it’s honest.”

She led me up. The Tide House wasn’t built to forgive bodies. The stairs were mean. They had been designed by an engineer who didn’t expect anyone taller than five-six to ever climb them, or by an engineer who hated people. We went up a flight and then another, each landing an arrangement of pipes and gauges and wheels that had nothing to do with anything domestic. There was no place here to sit and catch your breath. The tower wanted, in its essence, to move, and it expected you to keep up.

We gained a level where I could see the underside of the face—the great brass disc that showed the tide. It was older than everything else in here, pocked and beautiful. The pointer that moved across its margins was attached to a shaft the width of my wrist, and that shaft disappeared down into the tower’s belly into the mechanism that listened to the sea. I put my hand on the brass. It thrummed and was cool.

“We should wait until low,” Agnes said. “You’ll see more.”

“When is low?”

“Half an hour if the sky means what it says. Less if she’s sulking.” Agnes glanced at the slit of window cut into the stone and then at me. “Five feet and change?”

“Five feet and half an inch in shoes,” I said.

“Mm. We’ll fit, then. If you’re not afraid of damp.”

“I grew up above a laundry," I said. “There is no damp left I haven’t met.”
