Agnes gave me half of a smile that might have been approval. “Bring your case.”

We went up higher than I thought the tower had room. At each landing the air changed. It got colder and wetter and then, as we went above the line of the clock face, warmer with oil heat and the iron scent of old bells. Somewhere deep inside there was a cavern that chewed and swallowed in slow, deliberate gulps. The not-quite-right beat sound grew clearer as it got slower, a drag in it, like one knee doing worse than the other. Two glass-fronted cases hung along a wall, each with a neat array of parts mounted inside: spare pallets, wheels, pinions; a set of keys labeled with numbered fobs; a tin of something labeled in ink WHALE (a lie; we aren’t allowed that anymore; still, I lifted the lid and smiled at the smell that wasn’t quite, that tried to be).

Agnes watched my hands. “You work by smell, too.”

“Sometimes. If something was bad once, it will be bad again. It’s nice to be warned at the door.”

She nodded. “My gran swore she could tell a storm by whether her tea tasted like pennies.”

“That sounds like a woman who paid attention,” I said.

We reached a landing with a low iron door inset into the wall. Agnes fished a key from the chain at her waist and turned it. She put her shoulder into the door and it gave with a sticky sigh, wet metal letting go. Beyond it was a ladder of rungs sunk directly into the stone, descending into a wet dark that smelled like low tide and money. Money, because everything here had been expensive and would be again.

“I’ll go first,” I said, because this is a thing that gets said and because I wanted what was under there to meet me before it met Agnes.

“Mind your boot,” she said, and tapped one rung with the toe of her shoe. It had crumbled at the edge, salt-fatigued.

We climbed. The stone pressed close around my shoulders. My case I wore like a backpack, its straps cutting into a place that already carried Henry’s ghosts. I counted the rungs—because I always count—and when I reached number twenty-three the air changed with the faint chill hiss of a place that had never been fully dry. When I reached twenty-seven my foot found water with a soft slap that climbed into my boot. The rungs ended against a metal platform that thrummed, faintly flexing. Agnes came down behind me with the steadiness of someone who had been born moving at the slope of a boat.

“It’s a float,” she said. “Well. There are floats, and there are the bones of floats. It changes as it needs. The old plans are in the archive and only good for making men say the phrase ‘in my day’ more times than anyone wants to hear.”

“The sea fills,” I said, peering along the gloom. “The float rises. The float pulls a chain. The chain turns a wheel. The wheel—"

“—snaps a pawl, lifts a weight, sings the tide,” Agnes finished. “That’s the poem we tell the schoolchildren.”

“Not bad,” I said, and set my hand on the support. It was slick and pitted and cold. Water moved somewhere close enough to think about touching me. I heard something like a bubble release; a small thing negotiating with a bigger thing. I breathed, trying to find the tower’s breath, to make the movement of my chest not an insult to its counts.

The beat that had been wrong above was worse here. I could feel it through the metal and through the bones of my wrist. When a machine decides to die, it doesn’t stop. It keeps going wrong until it breaks three other things with it.

I bent to look. There was a hatch, hinged, with a grid meant to keep out things larger than the rats the sea sometimes gives as gifts. The grid had been altered. Someone with clever hands had cut out one of the cross-bars and then welded it back in with a seam that was not original—a scar, crude but recent. Salt hadn’t gotten to it yet. I touched the edge. It was smoother than everything else in here and newer. It had been cut to fold up just so. A person could go through there if they were the right shape. A person had.

My breath did that brief high thing that says the body is remembering what it is to be animal.

Agnes’ hand came to my shoulder blade. “Are we seeing the same thing?”

“I think so,” I said.

She swore, but in the way the devout swear—in the subjunctive, as if she were asking permission. “Agnes,” I said, “does anyone else have keys?”

“Council has two. I have one. Elias had one.” She stopped, as if the name were sharp. “Had. Has. Lord save it, I’m tired of verbs.”

There was no help for it now. The hatch was there, the seam there, the water rising under our feet in a way a person could almost convince themself they were imagining if they wanted very badly not to notice. I wedged my watchmaker’s knife into the seam and it gave, grudging, then reluctantly pleased to prove what it could do. The hatch lifted with a slurp of suction letting go. I put my hand under the edge and raised it.

The smell that came up wasn’t rot. It was the iron smell that comes when a face has kissed something hard too quickly and for too long. It was winter pennies. It was not a storm in a teacup. I held my breath out of habit and out of respect.

Inside, the space was larger than I’d expected. It was an under-chamber to the float’s cradle, full of maintenance things—a wrench array mounted on pegs, a sack of rags, a tin of grease printed with a whale it had no right to wear. Someone had pasted a clipping from the Marrowick Courier to the wall with wheat paste that had run at the edges: HARBOR PARADE TO MARK FOUNDERS’ DAY. The float itself, an older piece than the other things around it, rose and fell gently, listing slightly toward the place where the weld was. When the float rose, it lifted the chain; when it fell, the chain took back a little.

On the mesh floor beneath the float was a man.

He was tucked in on his side the way a boy does when he falls asleep under an eave to listen to the rain. His hair—what of it I could see—had been dark and had grayed without anyone congratulating him for the dignity of it. His hands were large and blunt. The right one had a piece of paper clenched in it. A pale string of algae had draped itself across his shoulder like a woman fitting a shawl around someone she loved. He was wearing a coat I had seen before, not in person and not on him. It was the coat from the photograph in the letter, the coat a man wears when he doesn’t like to throw good cloth away just because the lining’s gone.

Agnes’ breath came in and then out and turned into something that had to be put down and dealt with later. “Holy God,” she said, and then: “No. No.”

He had a pocket watch, and if I had been the kind of person who did the wrong thing when the right thing is obvious, I would have taken it in my hand and listened to it for a beat that would have told me something about the person he had been. But I am wary of ghosts and grease. I put my hand on the nearest metal instead and let my fingertips drink in what they could. There was a bruise high on his forehead. There were smaller ones that meant nothing and something: marks along his knuckles that suggested a fight had wanted to happen and hadn’t; a scrape at his temple that had not bled much; a smear across his collar that might have been blood or might have been rust rubbed impatiently away by a man who hated rust.

“Don’t touch,” I said, because my voice needed to be useful to have any business being in my mouth at all.

Agnes’ hands, which had tensed into claws without her having decided to, opened and then closed again around air. “Was it the tide?” she asked. “Did he—”

“The tide lifts.” My voice had the manner of someone trying not to startle a bird. “If he—if he fell and the float came down—” My eyes went to the altered seam again, to the weld, to the way the grid had been made to fold. “He did not come here because the tide called him to look. Someone made a door.”

“We have to call Niles,” Agnes said, panic and discipline ricocheting through her syllables. “Constable Hart.”

“Call him,” I said. “Use my—”

“I’ve got it,” she said, and fished a phone from her skirt in a motion so practiced she could have done it in a sleep walking a gangplank. She looked at me while it rang. “You don’t have to stay.”

“I mended a nine-jewel Hunter in a rain barrel once,” I said. “I can stay.”

Her mouth did the half-smile again and then fell flat. She spoke into the phone in a voice people must tell the truth to out of habit. Whoever was on the other end must have done the sensible thing and not said anything dramatic, because Agnes rolled her eyes in a way that let me know she knew everyone’s lines before they said them and that for once she wanted something else. “The Tide House,” she said. “Under. Yes. Come now.”

I crouched nearer the body without getting within a foot of him, my hand braced on the metal of the hatch to keep from making the platform ring under my weight. The paper in the dead man’s hand had been crushed and wet and then dried again, edges crisped. The ink had bled in one place and not in another. What I could see of it made my ribs pinch: two lines of careful slanted writing and then a word in block letters the way a man who had been made to write copybooks as a boy writes when he needs someone to read him. It said—no: it would say, when someone with gloves and authority unfolded it. I curled my fingers away from the desire to reach.

“Who is he?” I asked.

Agnes was kneeling now and for a moment couldn’t answer. The sound she made was a ship’s rope shrilling under strain. “Elias,” she said, the word buckling a little. “Elias Fiske. He kept this clock since before my hair went gray. And then he—” She stopped, lifted her chin in a motion that had made stubbornness into a prayer. “He wrote the council saying it needed work. Then he stopped coming. Some said he ran. Some said he fell in. Some said the tide got tired of being told what. His brother put up signs,” and she gestured vaguely at the damp walls where the Marrowick Courier’s headlines were taped and pinned and then my gaze went to a nail where the water had warped a flyer into a curl and: MISSING in heavy type, a photograph above it that had put me on a bus.

Eliza, I am told you mend old hearts.

I had written him back and said, I do.

But my reply had not returned to me stamped UNDELIVERABLE, and no one had told me he had never received it, and the council’s letter offering me the job had not mentioned that the man who had asked for me was a ghost people took sides over.

“Six months,” Agnes said. The words were dull with the work of them, as if they had been dragged over gravel. “He’s been gone six months. Eliza—”

“I know,” I said, and felt foolish for saying it as if knowing were anything at all. “I read the sign on the church board.”

“You did?”

“You shouldn’t have to read much in a town to find its grief,” I said. “And besides,” and I tapped my jacket pocket where the letter lived like a small, stubborn animal, “he wrote me.”

Agnes looked at the pocket as if she could see through coat and cloth and what small defense I had made. “Then you’re part of it,” she said, not unkindly. Not kindly, either.

I could have said I didn’t want to be part of anything. I could have said I was here because my landlord’s tolerance had a limit and because the winter in the city where I had been was the sort that went on and on until spring could only arrive guilty. I could have said I fix what breaks because it gives me a way to believe that breaking can stop. There is always so much to say about why. None of it would have stopped the clock from being wrong or made the man on the floor stand up.

There were footsteps above, the sound traveling down the tower through the stone like a rumor. Voices layered themselves. The beat went on, stubborn as pain.

“Move,” Agnes said, and there was the constable—Niles Hart—with his hat in his hand and his eyes already doing what a good constable’s do, which is take in the situation and then refuse to let anyone perform it for him. He was younger than I’d expected and older, too, in that he had the careful movement of someone who had learned early not to knock over the wrong thing and had not forgotten that lesson. He had a scar, not the sort you get to be proud of, in the hollow under his jaw. He smelled faintly of pipe tobacco despite there being nowhere sane to smoke in here.

“Miss Crowe,” he said with respect and then, to me: “And you are?”

“Eliza Reed,” I said. “Horologist.”

He registered horologist as a word and put it on a shelf to be looked at later. “You found him.”

“Agnes did.”

“We did,” Agnes corrected. “And you aren’t going to say words like ‘we’ll see’ or ‘let’s not get ahead of ourselves,’ Niles Hart. That’ll keep for your mother when she’s convinced the school is cursed. You’ll give him his name, and you’ll do your job.”

Niles took his hat and set it on a peg like a person setting a prayer on a nail. He nodded once and then looked down into the under-chamber and there was the flinch that makes a boy into a man. He went careful to his knees on the wet metal and didn’t reach toward the body. “Elias,” he said. “We’ve been looking.”

He didn’t ask me to go. He didn’t ask me to stay. He said, “Miss Reed, if I ask you to tell me what you see, will you tell me also what you want to see?”

“Yes,” I said.

“Good,” he said. He took a long breath, let it out, found a piece of paper from his pocket, and wrote something down with a pencil that had been sharpened with a knife. Men like him can be relied on to have knives for pencils and for rope. “Because I don’t have the luxury of wanting, and if you do you won’t stop wanting just because I ask,” and he looked at me in a way that suggested he’d met women who refuse to be told what their eyes should do and was willing to make an ally of that.

We all watched as the float rose and fell and the chain rose and fell and the wrong beat kept wronging. Agnes stood with her back against the wall like someone holding up the world, and for a second I saw her as a girl who had run these stairs with legs and a mouth full of laughter. Niles took out his phone and took one photograph, and then another, and then put the phone away like a person putting a child down not because they want to but because there is something heavier to pick up.

“Elias Fiske,” I said, to use his name the way Agnes had asked that we do, the way the dead deserve when their names have been on other people’s mouths for months. A gull cried far off, a sound that is not sorrow but might be mistaken for it by a person looking for signs. I put my hand flat on the metal and felt the tower and the sea and the wrongness all at once.

He had written me a letter and asked if I mended old hearts. It had been a ridiculous line and had made me sit down when I read it. Now he was here under the part of the world that pretended to keep time, and the tide was lifting and lifting like a long-held breath, and as I watched the thin trickle of water that had been making its way along the seam of the hatch picked up as if the sea had heard our names and wanted to come.

“Hold,” Agnes said to the tower as if it were a person who loved her. The tower kept its counsel.

Niles put out his hand, palm toward us, and did that thing that men do when they have to take over because the next part is not a thing other people should have to see. I had never been good at that, at handing what came next to someone else, but this was his tide to manage. We backed up onto the ladder. I let him be the hinge the day swung on.

As we climbed, my eyes flicked once more to the piece of paper in Elias’ clenched hand. I could see enough to know what I had suspected was not the thing it would turn out to be. That’s the way with letters. They know when you think you’ve read them already.

I climbed into the damp light and into the room above where the brass face hummed and ticked and insisted, stubbornly wrong. I opened my coat and pressed my palm to my ribs where a folded sheet of paper lay against my skin. I will say this for time: it likes to arrange a good coincidence and then pretend it’s a coincidence. The letter had one crease along its center. It sounded like a wing when you unfolded it.

There are moments when everything that will happen later pulls backward through time like a tide makes all the pebbles whisper. It rattled, then. It rattled in the walls and in the little hairs on my arms and in the beat that was hurting the clock. Agnes leaned on the stone. Niles’ voice rose through the hatch with words that meant respect and plastic and tape. The song the Tide House sang shivered and caught on a tooth and paused and then went on.

Marrowick had been arguing for six months about where Elias Fiske had gone. Opinion is a kind of leisure and the right kind only until it has to be folded away. Opinion would be in poor taste now. He had gone nowhere. He was here. He was not missing anymore.

The morning after I eulogized Dr. Thomas Bell, he called me.

It woke me at five seventeen, that honest hour when your defenses are still soft and your heart believes strange things. The ringtone on my phone is a polite chime, chosen for days when grief sits in my living room and I need gentleness more than urgency. Half-awake, I got as far as a hand across the sheets before it stopped. The screen glowed: one missed call, no ID. Then the voicemail icon bloomed.

I didn’t play it. Not yet. There is discipline in my work. People hand you fragile pieces of themselves and ask you to say something true. I have found that if you rush, you crack things. I rolled onto my back and watched the light crawl under the shade, thinking of the day before, of clean black shoes on damp carpet, of lilies doubling the air.

Dr. Bell’s service had been at Seaward Chapel, which pretends not to be a funeral home by smelling like cedar and saltwater. The wind had pushed the rain onshore at a slant, and the chapel windows were a film of weather. I stood to the left of the casket, where the acoustics are cleanest, and looked out at a scatter of faces that knew him as father, as friend, as grant-maker, as irritant. He had been a man with edges, if you asked those who picked splinters out of their hands.

I thanked them for coming. That is how I begin. I anchor a room to gratitude so that sorrow has something to lean against.

“He taught me tide tables before arithmetic,” I said, which was the sentence I had decided would hold the speech. The one true thing. Dr. Bell had told me that himself two months ago, sitting in his kitchen with mugs between us; he’d offered a hard fiction about barely feeling things. But when I asked him—What was the first thing you taught someone you loved?—he hadn’t put up a fight. He had smiled, thin and a little embarrassed, and said, Tide tables. For the girl who stood on the breakwater because she thought the sea wanted to be tamed. He had looked at the window then, where a gull dragged a French fry across asphalt as if trying to find a perfect angle, and I’d known I had my lodestone.

So I carried that through. I told his grumpy jokes about calibrating instruments and calibrating people, how he had given money in lumps but time in slices, because he thought time should be tasted. I talked about his first research vessel, the rusting little thing that leaked dignity and oil in equal measures, and how he loved it anyway. I ran my voice over all the edges so that, for half an hour, he could be gentled in the hearing. That is the trick. I never lie from the lectern. I simply choose the truest truths and braid them.

The daughter sat in the front row with her head back as if the ceiling had answers. Maya Bell has her father’s mouth, wide and capable of meanness but better at laughter. She wore a dress that denied February and a coat that argued it back. Her mother—Judith, first wife and final friend, the way it often goes—had her hands folded like a stack of paper. In the second row, a man in an expensive raincoat held his sorrow like a lit cigarette he didn’t know where to put. I noticed a woman with a red scarf tied tight against her throat, the only color in a winter room. She had the alert eyes of someone who documents things. There are always people I clock without knowing why.

After we lowered him—lowered a polished box that claimed to contain him—people made a line and put their words on me like coats on a rack. It is another part of usefulness. “You caught him,” a cousin said, and I felt the word snag on me, strange and fitting. A colleague from his foundation shook my hand too long and told me what a relief it was to have someone else talk to fill the silence. The woman in the red scarf hovered, then didn’t come over. She waited with her back to a window, chin tucked. I told myself it was none of my business. It never is, not until it is.

When I got home, I took off my black dress in a dark apartment that smelled faintly of lemon oil and paper. My workroom is a narrow space with a desk that was once a library table and a corkboard full of pieces of lives: index cards with dates and favorite songs, photos with names scrawled on the backs, a brown envelope that holds a poem a grandson couldn’t read without crying. In the bottom drawer were three letters that never got used because their writers lived. People hire me for weddings too, sometimes. It evens something out.

I made soup. I listened to the rain articulate itself on the window. I wrote thank-you emails I never send and then delete because their very existence feels too presumptuous. Before bed, I opened the slim folder labeled BELL and put the notes back in order. Tide tables. Breakwater. He hated cinnamon. He believed mercy was a strategy. A corner of the page was smudged with what might have been gravy; he’d offered me meatloaf, because he said it was a meal that could not be made less interesting no matter what happened to it.

He had paid me in cash, which wasn’t unusual. He had told me he liked to keep his accounts beyond the appetite of algorithms. The bills had smelled faintly like old books.

At five seventeen, his voice sat inside my phone.

The cat—Sorrow, named in a fit of literalism after my first terrible year and then kept because she came when I called her—spread herself along the length of my arm as if to hold me down. I pushed her off gently and sat up. The room made that pre-dawn blue that feels colder than the day will be. On the street, a truck bellowed into motion. I tapped the screen.

“New voicemail,” the phone said, as if we were about to be introduced.

I played it.

A hiss like rain filled the first second. Then: “Ms. Page?”

It wasn’t the professional “Ms. Page” from the day he’d asked whether my name was truly mine and not a brand. It wasn’t the way salespeople say your name when they want to stand inside your house and appraise your coffee maker. It was exactly his voice, the one that had told me about the octopus he had bought at a fish market just to let it go. He swallowed a syllable like a man in a hurry. In the background, something clanged—a pot lid or the sound of metal on metal. Gull noise? Or just bad connection.

“It’s Tom Bell.” A breath. “I had your number from the cards. If you’re hearing this, there’s a chance I’ve made a mistake. Or someone else did. I need you to listen and do exactly as I ask.”

I was on my feet without deciding to be. Sorrow leapt gracefully over the dune of blankets and landed on the floor with a sound like a dropped sock. The room was suddenly a ship at night, everything moving by touch.

“Don’t call the police,” he said. “Or—if you do, wait. There’s a file.” Another clang, closer. Then a voice not his, muffled, like someone calling from the next room. He went on, lower. “In my study. Second drawer, right side. It’s labeled Kite. You’ll remember. Karachi. The black kite.”

The word landed in me like an anchor. The black kite in Karachi was not in the eulogy; it was in the hour we ate meatloaf. He had told me, unprompted, that he once stood on a hot roof in Pakistan when he was young and thoughtless, watching children fly kites made from newspaper and glue while the wind did not care what they were made of. He said he had tried to fly one with them and failed repeatedly, and a boy half his size took the string out of his adult hands and lifted it effortlessly. “I have never been more accurately put in my place,” he’d said, amused with himself. “It cured me of the idea that materials matter as much as skill.”

“That file,” his voice said now, too quickly. “If anyone asks you for my personal papers, you do not give them that one. You tell them you misplaced it, or that I destroyed things. You tell them—” The other voice came again, nearer. “Wait,” he said. “I am—”

A scrape like the phone against a shirt. A short, ugly sound like a hand over a microphone. Then nothing.

I stared at the screen like it could be coaxed into more. The timer had stopped at one minute and thirteen seconds. No second message bloomed. I hit replay as if it were a delicate switch that might work better if touched differently. The same hisses. The same “Ms. Page?” with that air of being startled to find me where he expected me to be. The same edges of other sounds, a conversation in the next room, or the ocean.

I sat down on the floor. The wood was cold under my thighs. Sorrow took advantage and claimed my lap as if I had lowered myself for her and not because my legs had given out. She kneaded me gently with her front paws, as if I were bread we were co-making. “Ow,” I told her, because the tiny points of pain were a relief.

There are rules for what I do. These rules are mine, and I made them because I want to keep doing this and not become someone whose voice is a tool for rent. I don’t take commissions where the primary motivation is revenge. I don’t speak ghosts into rooms where there are restraining orders. I don’t keep copies of speeches on my computer; I keep paper, so that when someone calls me at midnight to tell me their brother hates what I wrote and they need a new adjective, I can move my whole body through the act of changing it. And I don’t enter into the lives of the dead beyond what is necessary to do the work. I learned that last one the hard way.

So. Don’t call the police. A file called Kite. The black kite. He had said “if you’re hearing this, there’s a chance.” A chance of what? That he wasn’t dead? That the man we had lowered into the ground with nice winter shovels and practiced care wasn’t him? It was absurd. It was the sort of thing the mind plays with for warmth when it’s tired. It was impossible.

The thing about the impossible is that it is only a word your brain uses when it wants to go back to bed.

My apartment had a thin view of the water if I leaned out the kitchen window and didn’t mind that I might drop my coffee three stories into the alley. The foghorn’s bass hum made a slow seam in the air. The chapel was on the other side of town, behind the old shipyard that had become a craft brewery with ironic whalebones on the wall. His house was half a mile from there, in a row of narrow places built when men wanted to live cheaply at the edge of industry and women wanted windows.

I brushed my teeth. I put on a sweater over old yoga pants and then, offended by myself, I changed into jeans. Sorrow watched me from the chair with an expression that said she believed I was going to feed her again. I did not, and she marked me down as unreliable. I put the folder labeled BELL back in my bag. I checked the time again because checking the time is a way to feel as if you are being responsible when you are not. Five twenty-nine.

In the hallway, Mr. Alvarez was sweeping nothing into a dustpan. He sweeps whether there is dust or not; it keeps the building honest. “You’re up early, Ms. Page,” he said, as if I usually slept until noon like a cat. He is seventy and knows everything that happens within the perimeter of our brick.

“Client,” I said, because that is my word for the dead and the living alike. It fits in my mouth and in the mouths of others. It does not make people feel like they have been promoted to the main scene of their own loss.

“The ocean sounds wrong today,” he said, listening to something under the hum. “Too flat.”

In the street, the sky had not decided what color it wanted to be, and the puddles were opinionated. The bakery two doors down had its first tray of croissants cooling beside a cracked window, and their butter was a flag. I wanted to steal the smallest one with the least spiral and pay penance later. Instead, I stuck my hands in my pockets and walked toward Seaward, toward the house where Dr. Bell had kept time and secrets.

I hadn’t been inside his study. We’d done our interview in his kitchen because he said all important conversations happened near knives. The knives had been magneted to the wall in order of size, gleaming as if waiting for inspection. The fact that the file I needed was in his study felt like a deliberate strategy, a part of whatever game he was suddenly playing. He’d always liked strategy in the way of people who think they are the only ones allowed to make rules.

On Harbor Street, a man hosed down a sidewalk as if cleanliness could push back the morning. The wind lifted the water into a little storm and flung it back at him. The Seaward sign was off; the chapel needs sleep too, apparently. I turned at the corner with the mural of the blue whale whose eye followed you as if to ask if you had done your homework, and there was Dr. Bell’s house, as narrow and neat as a paragraph.

It looked the same, which offended me. I half-expected the windows to have comments. The mailbox had three catalogs folded into violence. I pressed the doorbell, because even if I was going to commit a crime, I didn’t want to be rude.

No answer. No footsteps. I tried the knob. It turned. In fiction, doors open like this with a groan and a frisson of fate. In life, they open with the quiet shame of someone who forgot to lock them.

Inside, it smelled like rosemary and dust.

The study was to the right, arranged the way studies arrange themselves in the minds of men like Dr. Bell: a desk too old for its owner, books that have been read mostly for their margins, a chair with a blanket he would never have called a throw. On the wall, a chart of coastal currents with the lines drawn in a hand older than printing. On the desk, not much. Neatness is a kind of camouflage.

I went to the right-side drawers. The second down stuck halfway, then yielded. Inside, everything had a label. Receipts. Maps. Post. And there it was, a folder with KITE written in a hand I recognized, because I had seen it on the backs of photographs and on the label of the Tupperware he’d given me meatloaf in to take home. I picked it up. The paper was warm from not being touched.

I had the prickling sense of being watched, but that is the nervous system doing its job when you open other people’s drawers. I pulled back the cover.

Inside, there were photos: a flat roof in a city that had never been cold, boys with spit-dark hair and hands like bird bones, newspaper kites tugging the sky. A younger Tom Bell, awkward and pleased, a creature not yet honed by money. A letter in Urdu that I could not read. A napkin with a diagram of a knot. A page torn from a ledger with a list of names and three-digit numbers beside them. And an envelope with my name on it.

I didn’t open it. My body had gotten ahead of my mind, and it had stopped. In the silence, something clicked in the house, the sound of heat turning on or off. I stood there with paper that had weight beyond its grams and thought: He is dead. He is dead and he called me. He is not dead. He is not dead and he is in trouble. All of these things were true in the same instant. People will tell you that only one thing can be true at a time. People lack imagination.

My phone buzzed in my pocket, a small, angry insect. I startled, because I was in another century. The screen lit with a number I didn’t know. I didn’t pick up. It lit again, and again. I felt perversely proud of my own spine, as if not answering a phone were a demonstration of moral fiber. The last call went to voicemail. The new icon appeared.

I put the envelope addressed to me into my bag. I closed the folder and the drawer and felt extremely neatly like a criminal. I walked out past his kitchen where the knives waited without complaint. I was in the doorway when I saw it on the table by the door: a red scarf, the kind of red that makes a rule about what else is allowed to be in the room. It was folded in half, as if its owner had meant to put it in a pocket and then had left in a hurry.

Outside, the morning had taken a position. The foghorn was a long line under everything. I walked fast, the way you do when the air behind you is full of theories.

At home, I fed Sorrow because both of us needed to feel like we had satisfied one creature with a simple need. I set the folder on the desk. I did not open the envelope. I pressed play on the new voicemail.

A woman’s voice, precise and calm as a scalpel. “Ms. Page. This is Zara Lanyon. We met yesterday. I was at Dr. Bell’s service.” I thought about the red scarf on his table. “We need to talk about your eulogy,” she said. “There’s a problem.”

She paused, and when she spoke again, the precision had bruised. “That was not him in the coffin.”

Chapter One

The keys to the Greenglass Branch should have clinked. In my hand they made a sound more like coins spilling onto velvet—muted, hesitant. On the ring they’d tied a paper tag with industrial twine: CITY PROPERTY, DO NOT DUPLICATE in blocky black. Someone had rubbed at those letters once and left a smear beneath the O. It seemed even the warning might vanish if you looked at it for long enough.

“You’ve got forty-eight hours,” the project manager said. “Tops. Demolition crew starts their equipment tests Monday morning. If you’re still ghosting around in there when the bucket swings, you’re buying me coffee.”

She was half joking, half not. Her name was Orla with a rusted laugh and a phone that chimed without breath. She’d met me on the city square, high-vis vest over a black dress, and thrust the ring at me like a baton. Behind her, the Greenglass lay across a length of street like something that had been left out too long in weather. The façade still remembered an age of white stone and leafed capitals; the windows were cataracted. The name was cut deep above the double doors: GREENG LASS BRANCH, the E and the second G chipped away by time or by kids with knives. The pigeons lined the sills like punctuation.

“I won’t be a problem,” I said. “You’re sure the utilities are off?”

“Everything but the emergency light in the main hall,” she said. “We’ve flagged the beams we think are spongy. Second floor stacks could be treacherous—watch where you step. And take him.”

She nodded past me. The building’s caretaker was a loose hinge of a man with a cap pulled low and a face turned permanent leather. He drifted over and took the ring from me without asking, as if that was the natural order.

“Henry,” he said, a small concession. “I’ll open. After that you’re on your own. I don’t like her bones.”

“The building?” I said.

“The things in her,” he said. He handed a second thing to me: a blunt little radio curled away from a charging cord like a sleeping beetle. “Channel one. If you go through the floor, I will call the ambulance. I will not climb in after you.”

“Duly noted.”

On the steps, a square of caution tape sagged in a tired loop. Henry flicked it away with a practiced wrist. Orla slipped a form to me, and I signed without looking—a promise not to sue, not to pry up the city’s history for resale, not to pocket. Archivists have whole codes about pockets. Mine were empty but for a pencil and a small flashlight I prefer to call a torch because it makes the work feel older than it is.

When the door opened, stale air exhaled from the building’s lungs and touched my face. It had the sweet dust of paper and the sour of long ago leaks and something else, a trace like old tea left behind the tongue. It stitched itself to the inside of my nose and pulled in.

“Forty-eight,” Orla said again, and checked the time on her phone like a curse. “Call if you find anything political. By which I mean any dumb statue or flag the newspaper would want to be annoyed about.”

Henry stood inside the threshold with the poise of a man letting a guest into a room where the wallpaper is mid-strip. “Don’t trust ceilings,” he said, and pressed the keys back into my palm with a strange tenderness. “They fall when it rains. And it always rains in here.”

He left number one on the radio of the sentence “good luck” and backed away. The door’s weight settled behind him with a sound like the building took me into its mouth and bit down.

It always rains in here. In my line of work—hired hands for paper, salvage, the last look before the first blow—every place has its weather. I’ve been in archives that condense grief on your forearms while you work, in attics with air that hums like the inside of a beehive. The Greenglass was a long dry throat. Even the emergency light hummed with thirst.

I switched on my torch. My beam swung across the circulation desk to the wall behind it, where the clock had stopped at 2:17. The faces of three busts glowed up from the shadow of the reading tables like pale apples—Milton, Jefferson, a woman with laurels whose name plate had been pried away decades ago. The ladder to the west stacks leaned at a lazy cant. Under it someone had left a ceramic mug with a lipstick thumbprint—a coral shade you can still buy, summer-salmon and determined. The marbled floor had a snow of plaster across it, fine as sugar.

“You and me,” I told the dust.

I set my bag behind the circulation desk and flicked the switches there, just to see, though I knew better. Something somewhere flickered like the wink of a coin; then nothing.

The first hour in a place like this is ritual. I walked the public spaces, my boot soles careful on the flagged tape Henry had laid across places where the planks buckled. I noted warping, noted places good for staging; I leaned into the corners and listened for trickles. The map of the building replaces the map in your head; you wear it like a second face. I touched spines in the first stack with my fingertip and left a line of clean brown in the dust like a healed scar. The card catalog sat with all its little eyes shut, each brass-pulled drawer a promise. A cat had walked on the next shelf sometime in the last month; there were paw prints curving along the Fiction L—Mc in the tired talc.

All the signs of a life cut short—or not short, necessarily, just ended. The Greenglass had been shuttered the summer before I was born; one wing had been repurposed into a file annex in the eighties and then abandoned again. People remembered its hours in gossip the way old men remember sine waves from weather radios. The official story: a patron went missing the night of the small fire in ’75; Mrs. Dryden, the head librarian, closed the doors that week and never opened them again. The city encased the building’s clean bones in red tape. Spiders moved in with the sad determination of squatters.

I’d been hired because Special Collections lived somewhere on the second floor and had never been fully cataloged. It was my task to walk the half-rotten corridors and say which pieces of the city’s past deserved a climate-controlled place to rest before jackhammers removed the rest. I was not the deciding vote. I was the person you blame when your favorite obituary is turned to pulp.

Henry’s chalk was on the newel post: 2F good stairs this way. The banister was slicked with wax and dust into a kind of gray silk. As I climbed, my footsteps sent a whisper under me, wood telling secrets to itself.

The second floor landing was a narrow rectangle with a bulging radiator and a gold-lettered door: QUIET READING ROOM—MEMBERS ONLY. The lock on that one was an old mortise, star-shaped keyhole, rust neat as lipstick. Past it the hallway ran east-west. The ceiling had water-flowers in three places, which Henry had circled in chalk like saints’ halos: SPONGY, CAREFUL, DON’T. It amused me that the last wasn’t a warning so much as a plea.

On my right, the first office still had a calendar on the wall, pinned through with a map tack that had bled red rust down the paper. The calendar had stopped at April. I traced the weeks with my eyes: someone had put an X through the 12th, and then just thrown the pencil—must have been a pencil; the faint gray arc still scarred the paper—across the desk and turned their back on the rest of spring. The blotter was the green of bottle glass; on it sat a date stamp, the metal kind with a handle like a toy hammer. I reached to ink my thumb and realized the pad was not quite dry.

The other thing on the blotter was a little open box. Library cards. My ribcage altered itself a fraction. There’s a sensation like coming across a box of postcards you meant to send ten years ago, browned to the color of tea. These were still white, their corners still biting.

The top card had a name typed on it.

Calder, Wren.

I stared at my own name the way you stare at a word until it loses its edges and dribbles down the bones of its letters. My address was below it—my current address, the one where the sink hiccups at night, where my neighbor plays the trumpet lovingly and badly on Sundays. The typewriter’s ink had been heavy; the S in STREET bled a shade at the corner.

I lifted the card and turned it over. In penciled caps, someone had written: QUIET ROOM, 4:17 P.M.

My watch read 4:05. I pulled off my glove and checked again to be sure, as if time in the Greenglass was not obliged to keep the same hours as the street outside.

“Henry.” I pressed the radio’s side. “Did someone else have access in here today?”

Static and then his voice, drier even through the squeal. “Door opened, door closed. The last person in there before you was me, six weeks ago, to put up the tape. And the inspector three weeks before. Why?”

“Nothing,” I said. “Just a…dated calendar.”

“You get out of breath, you holler,” Henry said. His voice clicked into silence around me. The note of the emergency light hummed on.

People do these things for a rush. People break into old buildings and leave notes because it makes them feel like they’re writing themselves into a story. The world is bored; the Greenglass is curious again. Fine. A prank. I answered myself aloud, made the practical: Someone at the city typed your name from an invoice. Someone got cute.

Except Orla would use her phone, not a ribboned Royal. Except the address.

On the inside of the desk drawer, stippled in dust, was a little tape mark—the ghost of something that had been stuck there once and yanked away. Old masking tape leaves behind its skin. I ran my fingers under and found, invisible to the eye, its twin square of gummy residue. Taped things leave cousins.

Under the ridge at the desk’s lip I found a brass hook with a single key on it. The key was older than my hands, long and with three teeth cut off-kilter. A dried scrap of paper clung to the bow. QR was scrawled across it in somebody’s urgent, slanted hand.

I put the key in my pocket. Not locked into the quiet room, then. Or someone had planned for a person like me, the type who pried open drawers and believed more in human frailty than in angels.

At the end of the hall I tried the door to Stacks East and stood with my ear to the wood. Buildings speak in water if you listen; they keep old weather in their joints. I heard the faintest drip. I heard the city breathing at the windows, buses waking and sleeping and waking again.

The key slid into the Quiet Room’s lock like it had been waiting for exactly this wrist. The mechanism turned with a soft metal complaint and something inside released with a sigh, as if the heavy old door had been leaning on its own bolt for too long.

It opened on twenty-by-twenty and two windows high. The carpet was worn through to canvas in the path between the door and the bay. The room had been arranged not for reading so much as for a tableau of thought—two chairs angled toward each other across a low table, a single lamp with a shade the color of tea after two minutes, not three. A square of sun wanted to push through the city grime and did not quite manage it. Dust was the room’s weather, finches of it lifting and going nowhere.

Someone had left a teacup on the sill. It had a chipped blue rim and the kind of crackle glaze that makes everything look sticky. I put my finger to the porcelain’s inside and found it cool. A line of tea had dried into a crescent so regular it could have been a smile.

On the center of the table sat a book.

Because I am not immune to theatrics, I let myself stop exactly where I was and take one step only when my pulse had come back to an even scold. The book was a naturalist field guide, the kind you see in schoolrooms and old glove boxes: City Flocks: A Guide to Urban Birds. The dust around it was thinner, a smooth oval where someone’s hand had slid the book in and set it down.

I turned it over and slid my hand under the paper pocket glued to the back cover. The checkout card inside was the thick heavy kind with the library’s name in blue ink and the pattern of beehive hexagons faintly pressing up from the stock. First Borrower: Vale, Lionel. 1975. The date stamps sat in a tidy column beside his name, dark numbers marching down to nowhere.

I didn't know him, not personally; I knew him the way anyone who reads knows certain names, the way you know the shape of a city you haven’t lived in. He had written essays that made people feel they had been thinking the right things all along. He had taken a walk one evening and not come back. The papers had called it a mystery for a month and then something else. His book at the center of the quiet room was a piece of sensational furniture. Or was it a plant, or a cruelty, or this building’s reflex?

Below Lionel Vale, someone had typed a second name: Calder, Wren.

My own name, under a dead man’s. Next to it the space where the dates go was blank, a small white rectangle into which the future could flow. Above the column of old dates, the little knuckles of the stamp had smudged a faint ghost in the ink like rain through a heavy dress. I turned to the date stamp on the desk behind me in my mind. The smell of its ink had been a thin line of environments ago.

My body folded into the chair without my permission. The wood was stable enough. I opened City Flocks to the inside cover. On the flyleaf, beneath a printed admonition about fines, an old, neat hand had written: MEMBERSHIP CONFERS OBLIGATIONS.

Obligations, I thought, and the room had the hard flat taste of the word copper in your mouth. I felt stupid, and then very alert. I could hear the building again—the pipes, the settling of old joinery where the humidity had swelled the wood and then the winter had taken it back down three notches. I could hear, under all of it, something like a mouse and something like a footstep. The building adjusted its weight around the absence of another person.

Had I left the door open? I’d meant to. I hadn’t. It had pulled itself almost shut, the latch whispering so sweetly you could forgive it. Now, as my eye moved, it kissed home.

My watch ticked. 4:16.

There are ways to be clever here. You set the book down. You get up. You leave. You call Orla and tell her someone is inside the Greenglass; she sends Henry and a patrol car and everybody stands on the steps and laughs about pigeon wings, and you add another line to the long dumb list of times people get spooked by something perfectly ordinary. The door behind me wore dust in the places where fingers would have brushed, a smear in the shape of a hand with the little finger stuck as if at a tea party. I told myself not to turn around because turning around is a pledge of belief.

There was a clock in the quiet room, a small mantel thing that had slumped inside itself. It gave a cough to the silence and then, very stubborn, struck four in a row and then one, as if to add them up and make sense of the hour. The notes sounded like a song played by a drunk.

4:17, my watch said.

On some days, the world has a talent for choreography. Somewhere below me, further back, the date stamp thudded the desk with a sound like an exclamation mark.

“Hello?” I said to the room, and to whatever had moved the old weight of air. It is a word with useless vowels.

Something on the other side of the door—the hall side—dragged softly. Not the step of toes but the body weight behind them. The brass knob twitched.

I held the book against my stomach like a borrowed baby and did not move as the knob turned a careful fraction, as if the hand on it belonged to someone who had been told, once, to enter rooms quietly because some people need quiet like food. The latch held. The key in my pocket shifted and made a noise like a coin recognizing itself.

I stood, finally, stupidly, because standing felt like an act, and those are the things that carry you from one moment to the next when you could just as easily sit still and be erased.

“Henry?” I tried.

The knob turned forward again and this time did not stop. The latch clicked, and the door opened in the breathy manner of an old stage prop. The light from the hall was colder and it threw the silhouette into the room in pieces—the line of a shoulder, the sharp of a collarbone, the hand.

“Mrs. Dryden?” I said, because my mouth had no better idea and my brain was still leafing through names that belonged to ghosts.

“Ms. Calder,” said the person on the other side of the door. The voice was not afraid. It was not city, not rural; it walked a careful middle line like a seam. “You’re late.”

The thing about other people's secrets is that they still need postage.

They come through in blistered envelopes with their corners chewed by sorting machines, in padded mailers that sweat the scent of another state, in boxes bound with so much tape they look like a mummy someone panicked over halfway through. They come with the wrong apartment numbers, the wrong zip codes, the wrong city, written in tidy cursive or shouted in fat marker by hands that believed ink could brute-force a path to the right door. They arrive late and heavy. They arrive stamped “undeliverable as addressed.” They arrive to my table like lost dogs, panting and hopeful, some of them already inches from giving up.

We call it the Mail Recovery Center because “Dead Letter Office” makes people think of tragedies, and it turns out people would rather contribute to a lost-and-found than a morgue. The old name was more honest. The fluorescent lights hummed like a tired organ. The conveyors rattled. The pallets sighed under the weight of promises. If you leaned your head at the right angle you could hear a thousand little voices: the tiny skitter of paper clips in a padded envelope, the thud of a book against cardboard, the hush of shredded tissue paper.

I had a label maker, a ceramic coffee mug with a chip on the lip, and a stubborn habit of reading the return address before the addressee, as if I could preempt a heartbreak by knowing who had risked it.

“Nora.” Reggie’s shadow fell across my table. He had a new necktie with tiny mailboxes on it and the same old impatient bounce in his knee. “Got a peach,” he said, which was what he called anything that wasn’t bills, catalogs, or hand-knitted hats shaped like avocados. He slid a manila envelope into my in-box with a flourish. “Also Janice says to remind you the inspector’s making rounds at two, so maybe keep the personal investigations under the table. I know how you are.”

“How am I?” I asked.

“Curious like a raccoon,” he said. “And cuter, but the inspector doesn’t care about that part.”

“I am at peace with who I am,” I said, and picked up the manila envelope.

It was old-fashioned, the kind of stationery you buy from an office supply store that still sells paperweights in the shape of globes. No return address. Three stamps—chestnut-brown forever stamps featuring some overlooked wildflower—marched across the top corner, postmarked out of habit more than necessity. What made me pause wasn’t the weight or the smell (a little musty, a little like a shed that had housed cans of paint somebody had once intended to stir). It was the address: MR. DORIAN GREEN, 311 CANDLE STREET, GRAYBRIDGE, GA 30312.

My city. My street. Candle Street ran four blocks south of the river and ended at what everyone called the Candle Factory, a brick warehouse that now sold cold-pressed juice. It did not have an address in the three hundreds. It barely had double digits. Somebody had written “311” with conviction in the crisp, neat type of an old manual, letters with their slight misalignments like a smile with one crooked tooth. The machine had pressed them hard enough that you could feel them if you closed your eyes.

I felt them. Then I keyed the address into the database. No such number. No Dorian Green listed on Candle Street in the past twenty years. There had been, once, a D. Green on Candle Lane, which ran behind a bakery and a shop that sold umbrellas in the rainiest city in the Southeast. He’d paid his water bill from that address until 1997, and then he hadn’t.

Policy said: If the address is wrong, if there’s no return, we open with a mind to find a clue. It wasn’t personal. We were allowed to look for a phone bill, a receipt, a snapshot with a familiar face we could show to the DMV. People think the mail is a straight line, from hand to hand. It is not. It loops back. It gets lost. It is found. There’s a reason we lock this place.

I sliced the envelope at the top, careful, the blade of my opener whispering along the fold.

Inside there was a letter. There was also a key, brass, on a thin wire loop with a stamped metal tag that swung light as breath: HARBOR STATION LOCKER 14. There was a flat box of Swan matches, the kind with a white bird sketched across cheap cardboard. There was a Polaroid, its square frame blurred at the edges with the kind of yellow only sunlight and time can teach, and in it three men on a pier who were laughing like they’d just gotten away with something. One wore a hat with the brim snapped down. One had sleeves rolled to his elbows the way people do when they want you to see what their hands do for a living. The third leaned back against the railing so far he looked like he might topple. He held a cane delicately, as if it were both habit and performance—tipped in silver, perhaps a bird.

I set the photograph down, very gently, as if the laughter inside it could startle and fly away.

The letter was typed on onion-skin paper thin enough to see the shape of the words on the other side. The font was the same as the address, patient, unhurried, the small errors corrected with red ribbon overstrikes that bled a little. It was dated in the upper right: October 14, 1997. I looked at the wall calendar without meaning to. Today was October 14. Not 1997. That trick of coincidence made the back of my neck think, which is always how it felt when something was wrong in a complicated way.

“Dear Dorian,” it began, and the air shifted around me when I read it, like the room had closed a door I hadn’t realized was open.

Dear Dorian,

If this finds you, I expect to be gone. I am late to tell you and later to ask your forgiveness, but I am not such a coward as to let you walk into our consequences blind.

You will remember the night at Lazarus Pier. You will tell yourself you do not. You will remember anyway.

By now you have learned the cost. I have kept an account of it.

Do you remember Harrow Square Station at dusk when the commuters go thin and the pigeons come down like gray snow? I have rented Locker 14 and put what proof I have there. The key enclosed will not suit any other. If you go, go alone at or after the last train, when the light over Track Two jitters even if no one breathes on it. Do not take the elevator; the security cameras see more than they show.

If you do not go, burn this letter. If you cannot burn it, hide it in a place water loves.

We were three, but we will not be three much longer. If you persist in thinking you owe no one debt, you will learn differently.

Watch your cane. There are men who will know it before they know your face.

M.

P.S. You will know it’s mine by the smell. It is impossible to rid old things of their ghosts.

I read it twice and then again between the lines as if the onion skin might yield another, more honest message if I narrowed my eyes and wished hard enough. I read the P.S. again. It did smell like something that had been in a room with old paint, with boats. The matchbox rattled when I picked it up. There were three matches left inside. The stems were damp blonde wood, the heads the color of blood.

“Peach?” Reggie said again. He’d doubled back. He had a sixth sense for when something interesting landed, which made him both a good friend and a terrible spy. “You get a taxidermied raccoon? Because if you did, I call dibs.”

“Just a letter,” I said. “Undeliverable.”

He leaned, and I angled my body so that if he wanted to see he’d have to be obvious. He was not the kind of obvious man. Instead, he tapped the Polaroid with one finger, quick. “Nice hat,” he said. “Looks like my uncle. All men in the seventies looked like my uncle.”

“Do you remember a Dorian Green?” I asked. “From the news, maybe? Like, a long time ago.”

Reggie scratched his cheek. “City side? Or state?”

“City,” I said. “I think.”

He shook his head. “Before my time. Ask Janice. She knows every councilman and their dentist.”

I did not ask Janice. I did what people in my position do: I typed his name into the feeds we were allowed and the ones we weren’t supposed to know about and then into the ones that used to be newspapers before they became good intentions. There he was in a black-and-white headshot in the Graybridge Ledger, a younger version of the man with the cane, hair combed in the uncomplicated way of someone who is handsome enough not to mind. Dorian Green, City Council, At-Large, 1993–1997. Crescent smile, eyes looking slightly past the camera as if something more interesting was happening over the photographer’s shoulder.

There he was again in 1997, the story swallowed by bigger national tongues but in our city the banner for weeks: DORIAN GREEN MISSING, read the headline. “Last seen leaving a committee meeting on public works,” read the story. “Known for his elegant cane—a gift from his grandfather, he has said—Green has not been located despite the efforts of the Graybridge Police Department, which urge any persons with knowledge of his whereabouts to contact them. Foul play is not suspected at this time.” That last sentence did the work of a dozen euphemisms. Nobody was suspicious; everyone was frightened.

There were other stories: whispers about a charity’s accounts, postcards sent to a reporter postmarked from nowhere in particular that said only, Wish you were here, and were attached to photographs of water. A grainy rumor about a pier out past the terminal where trucks idled all night, the kind of place named with temporary ambition that sticks: Lazarus, because someone had drowned there and then had not. A letter to the editor in which a man with too many commas complained that the problem with politicians nowadays was all the lying and the canes.

I looked at the key again: HARBOR STATION LOCKER 14. There is no Harrow Square Station here, I thought. We have Harbor Station, where the east-west line has pretended for twenty years it will reach the water. We have a locker bank by the vending machines where the air smells like spilled soda and hot brake dust, a lockable grid of metal cupboards rented by commuters who don’t want to carry their gym shoes home. The keys look like this. The tag looks like this. Someone had typed Harrow when they meant Harbor, or the other way around, or it had been a joke between two people who thought they would always know each other’s jokes.

“Nora,” Janice said in the doorway from the break room. “Two o’clock in six minutes and your desk looks like a crime scene.”

“It is a crime scene,” I said, which was both true and not the kind of thing you say to a supervisor. “I’ll clean.”

I slid the letter, the key, the matchbox, the photograph back into the manila envelope and slid the envelope into the locker under my table with the others that needed deciding. I printed a temporary label and stuck it on at an angle, the way I do when I am lying to myself about my intentions. I wiped my table with a damp cloth and stacked the envelopes in my in-box into a small, defensible hill.

The inspector came through with a clipboard and a casserole’s worth of suspicion. He peered at my table as if I might had hidden contraband under a coffee ring. He moved on. Reggie mouthed “hero” at me as if I’d just defused something.

At five, the conveyors shuddered to a stop and our building exhaled. Outside, the river smell was strong and honest. It smelled like metal wet from a long use, like the underside of a bridge, like the lingering breath of storms. The sky was the particular bruised color Graybridge gives in October when the light thinks about going early and then refuses to.

HARBOR STATION LOCKER 14, the key had said.

I walked.

Harbor Station was three blocks from the Center if you cut through the parking garage with the mural of fish and past the alley where the ice machine kept making ice even though the bar that owned it had been gone two years. The station had been renovated recently enough that the tile was still white. Pigeons bobbed along the ceiling beams like judges. The departures board flickered. I had always loved stations, even after years of being the one who saw what was abandoned, what didn’t arrive. People pretended they were liminal. People liked to think you could reinvent yourself between platforms.

The lockers were lined up opposite the coffee kiosk run by a man with a moustache like a paper cut. He handed a latte to a woman in a leopard-print coat whose perfume wafted down the concourse like a question mark. A guy with a skateboard under one arm clicked his tongue and made his heels do a little jumpy dance of boredom.

I held the key in my pocket until I was close enough to pretend I was checking the coin slots. Locker 14 was at knee level, a decent choice if you thought you might be watched and didn’t want to reach too high or kneel too obviously, and an indecent one if your back had opinions. The metal tag felt heavy. The slot looked like it had anticipated this key for twenty-six years and was trying not to let on.

I put the key in. It turned with a soft, practical click.

Inside, the locker smelled like dust and breath and the kind of sadness that comes from being ignored rather than mourned. There was a shoebox. It was wrapped in yellowed paper and tied with twine, as if someone had wanted to look quaint in advance. The knot had been done by someone who believed in knots. On top of the twine there was a business card.

I reached up without looking and pulled the locker shut so the echo wouldn’t travel. I held the box on my thighs like it might be a sleeping animal. I set the business card on top of the box and looked at it.

It was unadorned as a dare.

On one side: a name in the center. NORA KEENE.

On the other side: a sentence and a pencil scrawl so faint I had to turn it under the station’s hard light twice to make out the words.

Don’t turn around.

My name looked like something I’d dropped without knowing. My name looked like the kind of thing you never find again in cities this size unless someone wants you to. The part of my brain that runs ahead of me was already flinging questions into the corners: how could anyone have known I would open a wrong letter? How could anyone have known I would care? How old was the paper; who kept a locker; who kept paying for it; who put my name in a shoebox twenty-six years before I decided to be the kind of woman who was allowed to open other people’s mail? I put my thumb on the pencil scrawl to feel the pressure of the writing, the tilt and the speed that makes a hand its own signature, as if a fingerprint could communicate urgency.

The station breathed around me. Somewhere beyond the ticket counters a woman laughed, the sound bouncing off tile. The light over Track Two flickered, which is what lights do in old stations and what my brain does when it believes something even a tiny bit magical about coincidence. A train announced itself with a shudder. The pigeons shuffled their feet and considered their civic duty discharged.

Don’t turn around.

I turned my head the smallest possible amount and caught in the corner of my eye a reflection on the stainless steel of the locker bank: a dark coat, a hat brim, the suggestion of a shoulder. It might have been nothing. It might have been everyone. It raised the little hairs on my arms.

I slid the business card into my wallet. I slipped the twine loose, kept the knot intact out of superstition, lifted the paper away. The shoebox was white with a faint sheen where the finish had cracked. I took off the lid.

Inside there was another letter. There always is.

In the time it took me to draw breath, the station changed. I could hear it: the way the hum of people thinned, the way the announcements took a breath, the way a cane taps once when it meets tile.

It was that tap I registered first, a crisp punctuation mark two lockers down and half a foot back. Then the rasp of a breath through a throat that had known smoke or whiskey or both. Then the weight of an eye.

The letter in the shoebox had been typed on the same onion-skin paper, that see-through honesty, the red correcting ribbon blooming where it apologized. I did not read it then. The part of your brain that evolved to worry about tigers does not like to be insulted.

Tap. The cane again. Delicate. Precise. Once, as if to say, Here. Twice. Here.

I looked up. I did the thing you do when you are a woman and you have learned to be both polite and impossible to harm: I made my face into an apology and stood with my shoulders set to take a door to the chest. The man two lockers down was closer than a man should be if he wanted to be considered random, and farther than a man would be if he wanted to remark on locker prices. He leaned on a cane and the cane was beautiful. It had a slim silver heron for a handle and the heron’s head cocked as if listening, a bird trying to decipher a fish’s arguments.

The man’s coat was the kind that used to be called a topcoat when more men wore suits under them. His hat brim made a short, private shade. His face, what I could see of it, was the interesting kind: not handsome so much as constructed with a logic I wanted to learn. He was old enough to have missed a few wars by intent. He was young enough to call himself old when he wanted a seat.

“Miss Keene,” he said, and my name did a curious thing in his mouth. He said it like we’d known each other in a town where everyone knows everyone and are careful about it, like a tree leaning its branch just far enough to touch a neighbor.

He raised the cane a fraction and then let it rest again, the tap barely a sound.

“Don’t turn around,” he said, as if delivering a punchline to someone else’s joke. “They ask you not to make a scene when you meet a ghost.”

If we are honest, the first chapter ends here. But I’m not good at what’s sensible when it comes to kiosks and coincidences. I held the box closer with one arm as if it might ask to be introduced. With my other hand I reached into the shoebox for the letter addressed to me.

“Nora,” he said softly. The heron watched my fingers. “Do you believe in resurrections?”

“Only on paper,” I said, and did not look away from the onion-skin’s naked words.

It began, Dear Nora, and the station’s light flickered again like someone in the wiring remembered me.

Chapter One

In this city the complaints come like weather. You can feel a low-pressure system of pothole calls rolling in after the first freeze. Dog-barking spikes with the heat index. Streetlight outages increase by a third during playoff season, usually about the same time people begin to swear they’ve seen rats the size of toddlers. The phones ring and the apps ping and the emails arrive at two in the morning with all-caps subject lines, and it is my job to make the noise make sense.

My mother still tells people I work for the mayor. She says it with the same weight she used to reserve for “doctor” and “accountant,” as if power is a binary condition and proximity gives you a share. In reality, I work for the Mayor’s Office of Data Analytics, which lives in an old bank building that still smells faintly of lemons and money. The vault is a conference room now. The tellers’ windows are long knocked out to make way for an open floor plan that encourages collaboration and passive-aggressive headphone wars. We’re three floors up, with large windows that look over a block of discount cell phone stores, and after midnight the only lights on our street are ours and the bodega on the corner.

I’ve always liked this hour. Fewer meetings, fewer interruptions, fewer chances to say something that will end up in a council hearing. It’s just me, the hum of the servers in the closet we call the “machine room,” and the city’s heartbeat laid out in rows.

Monday night, late April, I was writing code to untangle noise complaint clusters in the North Gateway district—bars were using new outdoor speakers, the decibel meter app the inspector used had a calibration error no one wanted to admit to, and the bar owners had all discovered the same loophole in the sound ordinance. I was making notes on a legal pad beside my keyboard because I am thirty-five and refusing to learn to write on glass felt like my last stand against becoming the kind of person who clips their nails at their desk.

On a second monitor, an auto-updating map populated with fresh 311 calls bobbed with new pins. I should have ignored it. The day’s to-do list was long and I was already losing ground to tomorrow. But the glow of the map kept tugging at the corner of my eye. The pins are color-coded: orange for sanitation, blue for water, green for Parks, red for anything involving explosives, and so on. Tonight there were a lot of yellow callouts—noise complaints from the bars I was trying to fix for them without actually fixing it for them, if you know what I mean. And there were a sprinkling of gray, the catchall category for anomalies the system couldn’t classify.

If you want to know a secret: it’s not the big data that will get you, in the end. It’s the gray. The little burrs the system can’t catch that snag at your curiosity until you’re bleeding from a dozen tiny places.

I clicked on a gray dot out of reflex. The system opened a ticket.

Request Type: Other.
Priority: Low.
Channel: Web.
Logged: 2:18 a.m., Yesterday.
Narrative: There is a humming.

I frowned. Clicked the next gray dot. The same. There is a humming. There is a humming. There is a humming.

The tickets were nearly identical, down to the period. There were fifty from last night’s run alone, spread like a diagonal bruise from the northeast edge of the city down toward the river. I scrolled dates. The day before: forty-two, along a slightly different diagonal. The weekend before that: another line, shifted again. The lines arced with the grace of something planned.

“Remy,” said a voice at my shoulder, which made me jolt so hard I rattled my coffee cup. Priya was leaning around the edge of my monitor with one eyebrow up, the expression she reserved for either an impending disaster or the presence of food.

“How long have you been standing there?” I said, clutching at what remained of my dignity.

“Long enough to confirm that you are having a deeply meaningful relationship with the gray dots again.” She slid into the chair opposite mine. Priya’s hair was braided down her back, the braid so neat it looked like a rope, and she had a cardigan wrapped around her like armor. “Do I need to get you outside? Have you eaten today?”

“There’s this pattern,” I said, which was the kind of bait that worked on her every time. Priya had started out as a statistician in our department two years after me and stayed because she thought urban data was the last honest thing left in the building. She leaned in now, squinting at the map.

“What am I looking at?”

I toggled a filter. “Complaints with the narrative ‘There is a humming,’ filed between two and three a.m., for the last... I don’t know. Month.”

Priya’s mouth pulled to the side. “People are filing poetry now?”

“They’re all from different accounts. Different IPs so far. No obvious bots.” I clicked open a random one. “Names are different, addresses are different, and if it’s a coordinated social media stunt, it’s a well-organized one.”

She reached across to tap a pen on my legal pad. “You think it’s real?”

“I think the city is full of people who hear different things at night. Sometimes it’s eighteen-wheelers on the freeway, sometimes it’s the building settling, sometimes it’s the old refrigerator in the apartment next door. But this is—” I gestured to the screen. The dots formed a clean, almost seductive progression, starting in near the old cable car barns and stepping southwest night after night. “This is... moving.”

Priya tilted her head. “Weird,” she said warmly, as if it were a compliment. “Overlay the water mains.”

I did. The blue spaghetti of pipes and feeders filled in the map, and the line of gray dots cut across them without scruple.

“Rail lines?” she said.

“Light rail doesn’t run there. Old maps?” I pulled up a layer from Public Works with the ghosted routes of things planned and never built—subway lines canceled in the eighties, the proposed mid-level ring road that would have cut the city in half if anyone had ever listened to the man with the bulldozers. The line didn’t match those either.

“What about complaints the next day?” Priya asked. “If it’s construction at night, you’d see follow-ups—cracks in walls, broken sidewalks.”

I ran a quick query. “It’s not correlating. Honestly, it looks like—”

“Like somebody draws a line in their sleep and moves it a little every night,” she said, reading my mind written in code.

“Someone with insomnia,” I said, and because I had both hands in the wrong sort of curiosity, I added, “Time stamps are weird, too. Almost all logged at 2:17 a.m. Night after night.”

“That’s a lot of coincidences,” Priya said. “Or one tired person with time on their hands. Don’t go down the rabbit hole, Remy. We have the council meeting on Wednesday. You promised me figures that would make the noise task force feel like heroes.”

“I can be two kinds of hero at once,” I said, and she made a face like I had suggested kale at a birthday party.

“At least send it to Field Ops. Let them sweep a couple of tonight’s addresses. Maybe somebody has a generator running illegally.”

I thought of Torres in Field Operations, the inspector with the tattoo of a ship across his forearm and a tolerance for my questions that was somewhere between patient and filial. “Torres hates being woken up even more than I do.”

“It’s midnight,” Priya said. “Not everyone lives like a bat.”

She left it at that, the way she knew to leave things when I had that look. I told myself I would write the noise memo and leave the byways of the city’s strange alone for once. The memo got written. The gray dots kept pulsing in the corner of my vision. At 1:45, I took a jacket from the back of my chair because the office air conditioning ran year-round and the city has a way of spreading its temperatures inside.

On my way out, I stopped at the security desk. Edgar, the night guard, sat on his stool with a sudoku and a cup of tea that smelled like winter. He looked up and took in the jacket, the purposeful set to my mouth, and sighed in the practiced way of a man who sees another man pass the same fork in the road every week.

“Officer Duarte,” he said, because it amused him to pretend I had a rank. “Chasing ghosts tonight?”

“Just seeing something for myself,” I said. “If I’m not back in an hour, I’ve finally eloped with a data lake.”

“Congratulations,” Edgar said, not looking up from his puzzle. “You’ll be very happy together. Try not to drop your phone into it.”

Outside, the streetlights made puddles of light on the cracked concrete. The city was in the kind of mood where it couldn’t decide between winter and spring—it had rained earlier, and now the air smelled like wet pavement and car exhaust and lilacs someone had planted recklessly near the freeway entrance. A bus hissed as it knelt for no one. A couple argued with the quiet intensity of people who had already said everything and were now just tossing pebbles into a pond.

The address pattern for tonight drew a line that would cross Bower Park at exactly 2:17 a.m., if the math could be trusted. Bower Park is a small wedge of green where two diagonal streets meet, with a statue of a heron that looks like it regrets everything and three maple trees that turn a ridiculous orange in the fall. It’s not a place people go after dark unless they have to, or unless they’re young enough not to be afraid of the way the trees move when the wind decides to get creative.

I took a car-share because I could hear Priya’s voice scolding me if I walked alone. The driver was silent, which I appreciated, and the radio murmured something in a language that sounded like rain. By the time we crossed 14th, the windows had fogged slightly and the city had emptied itself of people who belonged in the middle of the night. Bower Park was lit by one working lamp—the other had burned out and put in a 311 call of its own that had gone unanswered twice already, because the world is an irony machine. The grass glowed with a sickly petroleum sheen. The heron looked past me at nothing.

At 2:10, I sat on the bench nearest the statue and felt the wood give under me in a tired sigh. Night air has a sound, if you listen long enough. You can pick out the freeway like a river on a far bank. The clink of glass ten blocks away. A siren starting in a minor key and drifting to major as it passes into the wealthy zip codes. The bench was damp enough to soak through the seat of my jeans, because the city likes to leave you small surprises. I checked my watch. My watch had belonged to my father and always ran a minute slow; a flaw that had made him late to everything and somehow made me the opposite. I hate late things.

I scanned the street. A man with a shopping cart moved along the far curb and stopped to rearrange something hard to see. Two raccoons argued near a trash can with the bitter insolence of longtime roommates. No one else. I kept thinking about how foolish I’d look if nothing happened at all, which was the kind of thinking that cupped its hands around your ears and whispered warm, practical things like Go home and Be normal.

At 2:16 and thirty seconds, the air changed.

That’s the only way I can describe it. I could feel the shift in the pressure inside my mouth first, as if the city had inhaled and wasn’t going to give the breath back. The bench seemed to straighten under me. The hair on my forearms rose in a single ripple. The raccoons shut up with a rustle and made themselves scarce.

At 2:17, the hum arrived.
