It was not loud. It wasn’t the chainsaw an old neighbor used to run at odd hours, or the thud of the club two blocks over. It didn’t have a pitch I could find in my throat. If I had to say, it was the sound of a refrigerator magnified to the size of a stadium and shoved underground. It was the sound of a cathedral organ only my bones could hear. It was the exact frequency that lives on the edge of your teeth, and it reached into my molars and tugged a tiny string tied to headaches. The bolts on the bench vibrated gently. The heron shivered on its pedestal as if it were alive and deciding not to show it.

The hum lasted thirty seconds, maybe less, maybe a lifetime. It moved across the park in a straight line so pure it made my neck muscles ache. It went under my feet and kept going, passed the statue, rippled the puddle near the drinking fountain, and disappeared into the street beyond. The man with the shopping cart stood very still as it passed on the opposite curb, holding his breath with the exact concentration of a person trying not to sneeze in a church.

Then—nothing. The night exhaled. A car alarm beeped two blocks away for reasons it could not explain to itself. My shoulders went down, and only then did I realize they had been resting somewhere near my ears.

“Okay,” I said to the heron. My voice sounded like I had been shouting, but I hadn’t. “Okay.”

Someone laughed softly behind me. I turned just enough to see the man with the shopping cart shake his head with the weary amusement of a person who has seen everything twice. “Earlier tonight,” he said to no one, or to me. He had a face like a map of places where the corners had gotten wet and run. “They moved it. It was south last night.”

“You hear it a lot?” I asked, trying to keep my voice casual. As if I were not the sort of person who would walk into a park at two in the morning to listen to something that wasn’t supposed to exist.

“Every night,” he said. He leaned down to adjust a bundle in the cart and then began to push it away with the sort of deliberation that says a person has learned to live on the edge of lines drawn by other people. “Some nights the foxes hear it first.”

He didn’t look back. He turned the corner and was gone, taken by the street the way a trick of light disappears when you try to claim it.

I stood up and my legs forgot themselves for a second. Blood made a slow parade through my head. I went to the drinking fountain and touched the metal; it was warm. The hum had left a memory of itself like a handprint gradually cooling. I walked to the curb and looked down into the iron gullet of a storm drain. The slots were a dark mouth. The map in my head ticked forward with the new point: the hum had been where the line said it would be.

Deep down, something made the sound of a drip that had been falling for years.

Thirty-one other addresses, if the pattern held, would have logged the same complaint at precisely the same time. People all across the diagonal—on couches and in beds and at windows—lifting their heads, saying out loud to empty rooms, There is a humming, and then pulling blankets up as if cloth could do anything about the part of the world that was a law unto itself.

“Remy,” Priya’s voice said in my head, you lunatic, go home.

“Okay,” I told the heron again, because it seemed polite to close the circle of conversation.

I sat back on the bench before I left because a bench has a way of insisting you sit on it when it’s two in the morning and you’ve just proven something to yourself that you wish you hadn’t. The wood was less damp now. My hand fell, fiddling with the gum-scarred underside out of habit more than curiosity, and touched something that didn’t feel like gum at all. Fabric. Or paper. And tape.

I bent and ran my fingers along the underside until I found the edge. The tape pulled away with a soft sound. Something fell into my lap. I held it in both hands because it felt like if I didn’t hold it, the night would take it back. It was a folded piece of white printer paper with the fuzzy softness that says it’s been handled more than once. No envelope. No dirt. As if someone had placed it there after a careful check of the weather.

On the outside, in blue ink, someone had written my name.

The handwriting made adrenaline go sideways in my chest. There are a thousand things that mimic your handwriting if you are not sentimental about it: long, narrow l’s and unambitious loops; the way the tail of the y in “Remy” swings too far right when you are rushing; the habit you have of never dotting your i’s in the middle of a thought. Things you don’t think of as yours until you see them in someone else’s hand. But this wasn’t an imitation. It was my handwriting.

I looked around because that’s what you do when evidence arrives. The park was empty in all the visible ways. The heron looked at its rules and decided they still applied. The machine hum of the city had returned to normal. I unfolded the paper.

You finally caught up. There were four words in the same restless hand that scrawled notes on my legal pad and labels on containers of leftover rice that I never remembered to eat. And below that, a date.

Three days from now.

I had the instinct to check the back of the page because sometimes life is a magic trick and you can catch the door to the trap if you know where to feel. The back was blank, and so was the rest of the night, and the feeling that presses on the bones at the base of your skull when something that should not be has settled itself in your lap did not go away no matter how many times I looked back and looked again.

I folded the paper, because my hands needed to be doing something, and slid it inside my jacket in the inner pocket where my father used to keep subway tokens and once, for reasons he never explained and frankly didn’t need to, a single slick green leaf. I stood, and the park moved forward one step in time with me, and the city let me leave because it had learned by now that if it held you too long, you started to think you owned a piece of it.

On the way back to the office, the streets had a washed look, the way your face looks after you stand with your eyes closed under cold water and think about nothing for a while. Edgar looked up from his sudoku as I came through the door.

“You drop your phone into the lake?” he asked.

“Not yet,” I said.

He squinted at me, then at the jacket I didn’t think was giving anything away. “You all right?”

“I heard something,” I said. There is a humming was accurate but not what my mouth wanted to put on the record. “Do you believe in coincidence, Edgar?”

He went to mark a number in his grid and then stopped. “I believe in it the way I believe in the weather. It happens to you whether you believe in it or not.” He put down his pen. “And you’d be surprised how much of it isn’t coincidence when you look long enough.”

I thought about telling him about the note. I thought about bringing it out and setting it on the desk and letting the light in our lobby make it ordinary. Instead I took the elevator back up, sat in my wheeled chair among the sleeping monitors, and pulled up the map again. The gray dots looked like a small thing from far away, like someone had spilled a handful of rice across a map of the city.

I created a new layer and added a single point at Bower Park and typed a few words no one else would understand if they saw it in the morning: It’s real.

Then I took the note out of my pocket, read it three more times to see if it would turn into something less specific the way dreams do, and slid it back into the place close to my heartbeat. The servers hummed in the closet the way they always do. The city breathed. And somewhere in the tangle below, something had written to me from a place that could afford to be three days patient.

Chapter One

In obituaries, the word “suddenly” is a negotiation.

People call us and put that little adverb between themselves and the disaster, because “suddenly” feels cleaner than “collapsed in the cereal aisle at Gristedes” or “did not make it past the red light at Flatbush and Dean.” It lets the facts change clothing. It suggests that the universe has a dimmer switch, and someone flipped it without warning, and all a family can be blamed for is standing in the room when darkness happened.

At Valediction, we use “suddenly” when the family insists, and we leave it out when the story does better without it. There are worse arguments to have at two in the morning.

That night it was a Tuesday, rain stuttering against the air conditioner in our single window, making the glass wrinkle with heat and noise. I was smoothing an unpronounceable middle name for a piano tuner in Richmond into something that would not trip a tongue, when the bell on the downstairs door gave off its rusted alarm. A breeze blew up the stairs like the sigh of a freight elevator.

We are a stubborn operation above a bakery, no sign, no reception. Our inbox is a nest of grief, our voicemail a chorus. The bell is purely for people who don’t know the form and don’t want to. Also, for couriers who smell like the rain they walked through and look relieved to deliver the kind of package that doesn’t tip.

“Ms. Cole?” the courier said, peering into our narrow room. He held a manila envelope like it might hop. The bakery downstairs had sent up the day’s unsold sourdough in a paper bag, and the room smelled like yeast and sugar and somewhere you could live.

“I’m Tamsin,” I said. I wiped butter from a corner of my keyboard. “You’re my six o’clock excitement.”

He grinned, looking at the dried lavender in the glass on my desk, at the smudged Chicago Manual of Style, and the sticky-note forest of names: Aunties, brothers-in-law, vigilant neighbors. He let the envelope go and fled down the stairs before I could dig in my bag for a cash tip I couldn’t afford.

On the front, in blue ink, my name and the typewritten address for Valediction. No return. The paper had absorbed the humidity; the edges were foxed with damp. I slit it along the top with a library card and slid out a single folio of thick cotton paper, folded once.

We get living obits all the time. People wanting to write it themselves, not trusting their sister to get the dates right, their church to remember the volunteer dinners, their errant son not to turn the summary of their existence into a budget item. We help them. We explain that a life is not a ledger, though we all keep accounts. We take the money, we make the words even, and we wait.

This was not that.

The letter was printed in a sober serif that made me think of wills and law firms. It was dated that day.

To Ms. Tamsin Cole and the editors at Valediction,

Please accept the enclosed obituary for publication at exactly 4:16 p.m. Eastern time on Thursday the 14th. Please do not before; please do not after. An automatic transfer for your usual fee plus a premium will be made to your account upon receipt of this packet and confirmation of your readiness to schedule the post. No changes to the copy are requested.

Pay careful attention to the fourth paragraph.

—A.P.

The fourth paragraph.

I had to fight the muscle memory that wanted to docket it with pre-needs, skim it, send the boilerplate email about our style. I read the letter again, then slid a fingernail under the staple in the upper-left corner of the second page. A single sheet, laser printed, twelve-point Times New Roman, nothing sentimental about the layout. The name at the top made me sit up, which is hard when you don’t realize you’ve been slumped.

Augustus Pell, 62, Horologist and Philanthropist, Is Dead

August Pelham Pell? August Pell. My brain did the real-time math: a watchmaker, sort of; a watchmaking empire, definitely. His name had been in Style and Business sections for twenty years. He had a museum wing uptown with his surname etched in marble like a horizon. My friend Cilla had once dragged me to a talk where he’d said time was a moral force, and I had made the face I make when people have the leisure to make aphorisms. The photos always made him look like an icicle in a well-tailored suit: that white hair combed to rational angles, that face like a coin rubbed smooth. He had a foundation, he had a collection of longcase clocks that could intimidate a cathedral, he had a daughter no one had ever successfully photographed because she apparently only went out at dawn.

We write famous people if their families or handlers want something personal that the wire services won’t touch. The Times was going to run a stock obit from a file that had been waiting ten years; this, one assumed, would be a companion piece for the memorial program or some glossy. We are not a glossy.

Paragraph one was as crisp as a check:

Augustus Pell, the watchmaker and art patron whose timepieces married physics with theater and who endowed the Pell Institute for Applied Chronometry, died Thursday at 62.

The verbs were mine if I had written them. Whoever wrote this had read a lot of obits.

Paragraph two secured the claims:

A spokesman for the Pell Foundation confirmed the death but declined to specify a cause. Mr. Pell’s exacting calibrations and showman’s instincts made him a fixture of the city’s cultural life and an evangelist for time itself. “He didn’t think of seconds as units,” said Mei-Lin Tan, director of the Pell Institute. “He thought of them as rooms.”

I knew Mei-Lin; she had once sent me a correction about the name of a minor Swiss town. That quote sounded like her; that metaphor, too on-nose not to be real.

Paragraph three stepped backward, the way the good ones do:

Born in Rochester to a machinist and a nurse, Mr. Pell sold his first pocket watch at fourteen and his first patent at twenty-seven. He is credited—or blamed—with inventing the Self-Winding Collection, which made his fortune and spawned a thousand lawsuits. In 2006, after an amicable divorce from actress Catherine Vale, he lowered his profile, preferring to lecture and collect.

I had never read “Self-Winding Collection” without a lawyer walking nearby. I glanced at the compliment sandwich and did not see a hand stuck in it.

Paragraph four.

He died at 4:16 p.m. in a fifth-floor walkup in Williamsburg, in Apartment 5B at 117 Lorimer Street, where he appears to have been alone except for a cat.

My hands went cold. The rain made the window hum.

Lorimer. My street. Fifth floor. 5B.

There are approximately eight billion apartments in Brooklyn, the way there are infinite stars in certain religions, but there is only one I fish my keys out for while balancing a coffee, a tote, regret. It is a narrow shoebox with a view of a brick wall the color of bandaids. The radiator hisses sympathetic stories in winter. I bought a rug off a woman online who wept when it was time to roll it up. The intercom is a rumor. The buzzer only works if you hit it with the meat of your thumb at the precise moment someone on the third floor flushes.

I read the paragraph again. The words were black and heavy on the paper, as if they could scar it.

People who write their own obituaries do not usually specify where they will die. They hedge. They say “at home” or “in New York” or “surrounded by the people who mattered,” which is a dodge, because there are always people who mattered who didn’t make the cut. They do not list an apartment number and make me picture my own doormat.

I pinched the bridge of my nose until I saw snow. My mouth tasted like a penny.

Time where? I thought, and then immediately hated the fact that I was being infected with his metaphors. Moral force. The child in me wanted to tell the universe it had full permission to leave me out of the moral meanings of time.

Paragraph five swallowed the “suddenly” whole:

According to the medical examiner, preliminary reports indicated drowning; a sealed glass vessel near the body appears to have been filled with water drawn from the North Branch of the Rogue River, in Oregon, a location of special meaning to Mr. Pell. How the water entered his lungs without submersion has not been determined.

What. I set the paper down as if it had overheated. It wanted me to exclaim. It wanted the type of gaze you bring to a magic trick when you know it’s practice for disaster. Drowning without submersion is one of those phrases, like “quiet riot,” that leaves a mark.

It went on, as if every paragraph were a corridor and the walls had gallery hooks:

He is survived by a daughter, Dr. Leda Pell, a physicist, and by the cat, name unknown. He is also survived by a city that, if not persuaded to regard time as a moral force, has at least learned to respect its decor from him. In an interview in 2019, Mr. Pell said, “I want my work to outlast my body, but if it doesn’t, I want it to fail loudly.”

He had a flair for epigrams that sound like refrigerator magnets at first and suicide notes later.

I read the whole thing twice and then read it backwards, which is a habit I picked up at the paper where I started, to make sure the names didn’t make different names when your eye breathed wrong. Then I put it face down on my desk.

The rain had stopped discovering the window and started streaming instead. In the bakery below me, there was the sound of proofing trays sliding, of someone laughing. My phone, propped against a chipped mug, showed me the time: 6:47 p.m. on a Tuesday, not a Thursday. The 14th was two days away.

I checked for attachments. The envelope had yielded only the letter and the obit. No check. I opened my inbox, counted to two, refreshed. An email had arrived nine minutes after the courier’s bell from a hush of a sender: ap@pellemail.com. The subject line: Scheduling Confirmation. The body: Thank you for your attention to the timing. Funds released. Please reply yes. There was a PDF of the obit. There was a wire transfer notice. I clicked on the bank app. The number in my checking account had more commas in it than it would until the next Thursday.

We don’t get paid like that. Even celebrities’ people do not pay like that unless they want you to use “passed” and a sepia filter.

I replied no.

That was the honest answer, on both principle and schedule. Also, the map of my mind had red circles popping up around any idea that led me to publish an obituary for a living man I had no proof was dead. Was. Would be. I did not want those verbs.

I called Cilla because she writes about arts patrons for a magazine that likes to remind the arts they exist. Her phone picked up on the second ring with the sound of traffic and someone in the background saying, “We do not comp that table.”

“Tell me you’re somewhere you can write something you will later regret,” she said.

“Possibly,” I said. “You like Augustus Pell.”

“I like his money. What’s up?”

I thought I could say it lightly, let the conversation turn into one of our towers of ridiculousness where we stack improbable things on top of each other until someone knocks it down with a laugh. I told her about the envelope. I told her about the paragraph. I told her about the apartment.

“Your apartment,” she said.

“My very own.”

“You’ll call the police,” she said, in the voice people reserve for when they know you won’t and want to be the good angel anyway.

“And say what? Hello, an obituary told me a man is going to drown in my apartment the day after tomorrow without any water. Please send patrol cars and towels.”

“Detective Mills likes you,” she said. “You flirt-talk about commas.”

“Detective Mills tolerates me because his mother reads my byline under pictures of carnations. Also, he has that scar near his eyebrow and I have a weakness for punctuation scars.” I swallowed. “Cilla.”

“Yes.”

“This isn’t one of those performance art things, right? He isn’t going to stage something for himself? A living wake in my living room? The cat is my neighbor’s? They filmed Law & Order in our hallway once; you could get lost in their fake blood.”

“If August Pell were staging his own performance-death, he would do it in the clock gallery at the Met, at midnight, with monks and a fog machine.”

“He did say he wanted things to fail loudly.”

“Everybody says that,” Cilla said. The traffic made a horn diagram. “Okay. I will ping his PR person. But Tas? Don’t go home to open your door and find a billionaire in your bathtub.”

It was a joke, then it wasn’t.

After I hung up, I printed the PDF and compared it to the hard copy because superstition insists on analog. The lines matched like teeth. I took a photo and sent it to the email address Monty gave me years ago when he’d pretended not to already know my name: mills@msp.nyc.gov. The subject line: You Love Strange Paper. The body: I received this. It might be nothing. It might be a violation of several kinds of law or taste. It also might be a prank. Or a rehearsal. Or a trap. Please advise. P.S. There is not enough water in my apartment to drown a billionaire. P.P.S. It’s a fifth-floor walkup; make sure you bring your asthma inhaler.

I did not hit send. I sat, my hand hovered over the key, and I thought about the shape of silence. If this was, somehow, a willful lie, and I brought the police to it, the end of the story would be me writing an apology to a man who had probably paid more in taxes than I would earn in my lifetime, apologizing for presuming his mortality and my proximity to it. If it wasn’t a lie, then no number of men with shields would stop a thing that had been arranged for an exact time, the way some illnesses have the nerve to arrange themselves.

I saved the draft. I set my phone face down.

There is a template for writing your own father’s obituary when he leaves your family and the only way you know how to absorb it is to fantasize the language that will make it orderly later. You do it at nineteen because no one can tell you not to mourn draft-first. You learn from practice that an obit is a kind of shelter. You learn from the bad ones that it can be a weapon. I did not write my father’s in the end. He didn’t die then—not that way, not all at once. He got new children in a different city. The obit in my head turned into something else, like everything does.

I pulled up our scheduling software. I hovered over Thursday, 4:16 p.m., a time I would be in the subway, probably, between stops, the cell signal most interested in other people’s phones. I scheduled nothing.

The bakery closed downstairs, the lock thunking, the last metal tray stacked. The only sound was the city’s thousand slow aches. I looked at the fourth paragraph again and made myself say the words aloud, the way you say a diagnosis to make it less of an enchantment.

“In Apartment 5B at 117 Lorimer Street,” I said, as if geography was a spell and saying it could change it.

There is an inventory of things in my apartment. A crooked print of a swimmer. A coffee table with one leg shorter, propped by a copy of a book I pretended to read twice. The plant that refuses to die or thrive. A cat dish, because sometimes my neighbor’s cat decides my sofa is an island and he is a shipwreck. The thought of that dish made the words “except for a cat” grow teeth.

I tucked the paper back into the envelope because leaving it out was like leaving a weapon on the table and then going to look for the bullets. I turned off the lamps one by one. The rain had finished its sentence. The night air felt rinsed.

By habit, I locked the door to the office and double-checked the deadbolt because grief sometimes walks in, and because the week before, a man had stood in our doorway for six minutes and told me a story about his brother that made me cry and then asked if he could have fifty dollars.

On the stairs, I stood for a second caught between floors. The city has an atmosphere that sometimes presses on your throat, and sometimes lifts it. In the second-floor landing where the baker kept the extra flour, there was a faint dust that made everything look lit from inside. I put my fingertips against the cool walls to steady myself as I went down. It was theatrical, that pause, and I am not theatrical; the city does enough theater on my behalf.

Outside, the corner where the laundromat had used to be was full of rubber vines. A boy on a scooter streaked past like a comet with bad intentions. I walked east, because that is where my apartment is in relation to the office; two turns and the bakery smell becomes the smell of hot bricks and cumin.

I have always believed in returning to your exact address the way you would return to your exact sentence, without changing it to see if it sounds better. I believe in the fidelity of small things. I reached my building, buzzed my own buzzer out of habit despite its ritual futility, took the stairs because the elevator is a mouth that doesn’t chew. My breath was fast by the second floor, and scolding by the fourth, and I had to put my hand on the wall to discourage the wobble in my knee—this is the choreography of getting older.

Outside my door, the hallway light flickered once, then held. I was holding my keys so tight the slot in the brass bit into my palm. Later, if asked, I would say that the phrase “at 4:16 p.m. in a fifth-floor walkup” was a hot wire in my head, sparking in time with the hall light. There was a leaf on the doormat, which I would register as a leaf only after my brain had discounted knife, shadow, rat. Someone’s cooking perfumed the corridor with garlic and apology.

I had the obit folded in my coat pocket like a confession. I set my grocery tote on the ground and pressed my ear to the door the way someone in a less well-lit movie might do, and I heard nothing. No billionaire breath. No cat knocking a glass off the counter to see if gravity was still good. Only the building, which purrs at night like it is trying to get you to sleep.

My key slid into the lock. I turned it. The sound was the sound of my life continuing.

When I pushed open the door, the apartment was as it had been that morning: plant with its edges theatrically browning, mug collecting a thin skin, writing desk with its accusatory stacks. The doormat rustled behind me when I stepped in, and a second later a neighbor’s door clicked closed at the far end of the hall, as if a watcher had leaned forward and then thought better of it.

There is nothing like the quiet after bracing for a noise that doesn’t come. It floods the body in relief and then leaves behind a hush shaped exactly like the absent sound. I shut my door and leaned my forehead against the wood.

In the kitchen, the cat dish was dry. I filled it from the tap, because if a cat was going to be in my apartment in two days without my planning and then not survive it, the least I could do was offer its ghost a drink.

The paragraph sat in my pocket like a folded, mechanical heart. I took it out and put it on the table, next to the plant and my mother’s postcards and a receipt for a cab. I ran my finger under the last line and let the letters nick.

It was the last sentence that would wake me in the middle of the night, though I didn’t know it yet. Not the where; not the when; not even the drowning that required explanation like a math problem. It was the note under the signature I had missed the first read through, because I had been overwhelmed by the geography of myself.

Printed tiny, at the bottom, as if embarrassed:

If this reaches you too late to stop it, please forgive me. If it reaches you in time, and you can, call me. A.P.

There was a number. It had nine digits I recognized as New York and one I did not. I stared at it until my eyes teared, as if it might shift. The clock on my stove blinked 12:00, because of a storm last week and my laziness since. The microwave’s clock said 6:58. The only accurate time in the apartment belonged to my phone, which I had left in my bag by the door.

I went to get it. The screen lit my hand an improbable color. On it was a new message, anonymous, a gray bubble that attached itself to my breath.

Are you home? it said. My apologies in advance.

By the time the first news van found Riverpark, the elm was already leaning toward the water in a way that made my stomach tense. Trees lean all the time. They cant toward light, reach over stretches of air for what their roots can’t find in soil. But a lean like this—the roots loosening from the ground, the crown pulled by wind and weight and rot—meant we were late. It meant tomorrow’s wind or the next kid with a kite could tilt the whole thing into the path and take a handful of tourists with it. The city would blame my name in the paper if that happened. So I signed the permit and blocked off the loop with saw horses and bright tape and let the mourners come anyway.

We work fast when a tree gets famous for dying. People bring their phones, their dogs, their stories. The Riverpark elm had plenty of those. It was the tree couples took engagement photos under before the river turned gray. High school kids had carved their initials in the lower bole when I was a high school kid, too; the scars were swallowed and resurfaced over decades like the marks on an old hand. It was the one everyone assumed would get Dutch elm disease and didn’t, a freak among corpses, a green lung by a busy bend. After last night’s storm it listed five degrees closer to the water than it had any right to, and anybody with eyes and a shred of arboriculture knew what that meant.

“Miss Larkin?” A camera appeared, a woman with neat hair behind it. I get called Miss, Ms., Hey You, Tree Lady. On my payroll forms I’m Cassandra Larkin, senior city arborist for Graybridge Parks and Streets: the one who keeps the lines clear and the phone calls manageable. On mornings like this I’m the public face and also the woman who will be blamed for killing an old friend.

“Morning,” I said. “Stand behind the tape, please.”

Her mic had a blue sleeve with a logo. She looked past me at the crew truck and the chipper. Julio and Bee were laying out the rigging ropes. A couple of teenagers sat on the brick rim of the flower bed, wiping their eyes like they’d lost a grandparent. The river smelled like iron filings and algae. A woman in an expensive coat tied a ribbon around the parking meter because she couldn’t reach the elm’s lowest branches anymore.

“Can we ask you a few questions?” the reporter asked. “People are wondering,” she did a small, practiced gesture toward the tree, “why it has to come down. It looks fine.”

“Looks are kind,” I said. “See the conks?” I pointed to the shoe-like shelves sprouting from around the root flare. “Ganoderma. And that shear crack above the first limb? That white line means the fibers have split. This is a hazard tree with a target zone that covers most of the north loop.” I try to keep it factual. Don’t hand a camerawoman phrases like We chose to end its life. “We’re going to take the crown in sections and reduce the trunk to a safe height. We’ll be planting replacements this fall.”

She angled her mic toward the fans gathered. “Can we film the work?”

“You can stay behind the tape,” I said. “Keep your dogs out of the dripline.”

I’d been walking the park since dawn, spraying my boots with the morning’s slick. The storm that ran through at two a.m. was a knife more than a blanket—brief, loud, directed. It tugged shingles and sent trash cans down the hill. The elm had been sick longer than anyone admitted, and this was the nudge that turned sickness into an obituary.

“Unbelievable,” said a man in a ball cap as I passed. “My father courted my mother under this tree.”

“I believe it,” I said.

My crew was my crew. Julio was twenty-three and had forearms like saplings. He had the gift of a steady saw and no urge to show off, which made him my favorite Oregonian in a city full of people who had never seen timber that didn’t come on a pallet. Bee wore her dark hair in a thick braid down her back and never took off her ear protection, which made her underestimate how loud she was. The third this morning was Hersh, older than me by a year and born with a bark-spattered laugh that scared pigeons. They were already inspecting the lean and the tension, glancing at me for the go-ahead.

“Good?” Hersh asked.

“The hinge is going to want to pull,” I said. “Let’s soft open on the east and hang that big limb first. I’m not trying to have the bar pinch.”

He nodded. Bee slung a rope over a lower branch with a throw line, then another. We’d take it in sections, lowering the big ones with the Port-a-Wrap so they didn’t crater the lawn. City parks hate us less when we don’t leave scars.

An old man in a light jacket stood just inside the tape, watching. His jaw had the tremble your muscles get when you tell them you’re not going to cry. He held a Polaroid of a class of children in front of the elm in what had to be the eighties: shag haircuts, a teacher with a name I almost remembered. He saw me see him and held the photo in a way that offered it without insisting.

“You can keep that,” I said. “If you want, the parks office is taking copies. We keep track of stories.” He nodded like that was a kind of losing, too.

Hersh fired up the saw and the morning filled with the burr of chain and the smell of chain oil. He set the notch, the face cut opening the direction of the fall for a limb that would weigh as much as a small car. Chips flew and clung to his chaps. There is a music to a good saw that I’ve tried to explain to the mayor and failed; it’s the steady, clean tone of power properly applied, of teeth taking what was meant to be taken, no more. When you hit something you shouldn’t, it is not that. It is a stumble, a metal-on-metal spit, a jump in frequency that makes the fillings in your molars ache.

He hit something we shouldn’t.

The saw hiccuped and threw sparks. Hersh let off the throttle so fast Bee was already reaching for the bar, like she could will it out of danger. He lifted his visor and swore, eyes on the newly opened face of the tree.

“Nails?” I asked.

“For what, an entire barn?” he said.

I walked to the cut. The wood inside the elm was pale as bread, the growth rings tight and even. It had lived a long, careful life, weathering drought with patience. There, in the buttery sapwood, something that wasn’t wood glinted dullly like an eye half-closed: not a nail, too round; not a fence staple; a disk, maybe, the coin-smooth edge of something the tree had tried to smother and couldn’t digest.

“Kill the engine,” I said. “Wedge the kerf and let me look.”

Julio tapped a pair of green plastic wedges into the back cut we hadn’t made yet, to hold the face open. He did it gently, his hands deft. I pulled off my right glove and pulled my hand pruners from my belt. I run cheap Felcos because I lose the expensive ones. With the tip I scraped the damp wood around the metal, freeing what the cambium had sealed.

The first thing to come free was the smell: not rot, but that wet-metal tang, like plumbing. The second was the edge of a key's head, greened over with years of tannins. It had gone in head-first, the shank and the teeth buried deeper where the tree had taken them.

“Well I’ll be damned,” Bee said, peering with me. Nail heads, bottles, a fork I found once in a sycamore behind the high school—trees eat what we hand them. Keys, though. Keys are something else.

I worked around it until I could get the pruners' jaws under the lip and rocking gently. The elm did not give easily. I sawed at it with my handsaw, a sliver at a time, careful not to gouge the metal. It comes back to me how my father slipped coins into the places he wanted me to look when I was five, and how I looked harder for the next ten years long after he forgot to hide dimes under couch cushions. Hoping this was anything like a coin was stupid. I kept going.

The thing came free all at once, slipping out with a wet sigh that pitched my hand back and nearly dropped it into the sawdust. I pinched it between two bare fingers and felt the cold of it, surprising after being inside wood. It was a key, not a house key like you pick up in a hardware store, but a longer one with an oval head, the kind that used to open lockers and mailboxes before everything grew a keypad. A thin stripe of bark had impressed into the brass, a vein line across its face.

“People always say trees remember,” the old man said, looking at it like it was an answer to a question he hadn’t dared ask out loud. “I didn’t think they meant…you know. This.”

“They don’t,” I said, before I could stop myself.

Hersh held out a shop rag and I wiped the key with it. It left a scar of green on the white. The head was stamped rather than engraved. I raised it until the light caught the letters so I could make them break out of the dings and patina.

PROPERTY OF GRAYBRIDGE CENTRAL was clean enough to read because it was already in my head. Below it, a number: 117. The tail of the 7 was faint where the stamp had hit a void in the metal. I didn’t realize I was holding my breath until I let it go and the words fogged in the air in front of my face.

“Well, hell,” Bee said. “That’s not a fence nail.”

“Old station?” Julio asked. The kids on my crew had never known Graybridge with trains—freight still crawled downriver along the flats, but the main depot had gone dark the year he was born. The station sat half-renovated now a mile up—the platforms turned into a café with draft beer, the headhouse boarded, the lockers stripped and auctioned as vintage. That year, 2005, I graduated high school and learned what it felt like to live with a vacancy that never filled.

A reporter’s microphone materialized at my elbow. “Can we get a shot of that?” she asked.

“It’s not safe to be in here.” I didn’t move the key and I didn’t open my fist. Around us, the elm creaked like an apartment settling. I nodded at Hersh, and he, blessed man, treated that as an instruction to start the saw on the other side and shoo everyone back with the motor.

I closed my fingers around the key and felt the green rub off on my skin in a faint gritty smear. I put it in my pocket because I didn’t know what else to do with it. Later I’d take myself to task for that. At the time, it seemed better than standing in front of a camera holding a piece of metal that made my stomach feel like the river smells on a hot day. I told myself the chain on the bar needed attention any second. “Back,” I said to the crowd, and they did, the way people obey when a machine’s voice is about to drown you out.

We took the elm down like we planned, except quicker and with more people watching. Section by section, lowering branches and trunk rounds, laying them in a ribcage on the grass. With every piece, a rain of sawdust drifted down and stuck to sweat and snot and tears. The old man had put his Polaroid away precisely and left when the first limb dropped, as if he couldn’t bear the idea that you could disassemble a thing you had loved. The woman with the ribbon stood with her hands in the pockets of her coat, jaw clenched so hard I could hear it. My shoulders pulled back with the saw’s vibration and stayed there all morning, hard as if the elm had climbed into my bones to argue.

When the big crown was down and the trunk stood like a column, we set the line higher and Bee got to go up in the bucket to set a pull. She swung in the cage, weightless for a second, before squeaking to a stop against bark. She loves being off the ground like some people love cafés. We built the hinge and guessed the weight and gave it the nudge, then fifty years of elm went down exactly where it was supposed to, with a thud you felt in your shins.

“So easy to end,” the reporter said to her camerawoman in that soft voice reporters use when they’re sure the mic is on and think they’re being elegant. “So violent.”

“Don’t talk about things you don’t know,” Bee said, but not into the mic.

We cut the trunk into rounds that four people could roll and two could ache about later. In the chainsaw’s wake the rings stood up, wet and gleaming. I counted from the soot-dark ring of a drought year I remembered into the years I didn’t. Somewhere in there was the spring a cheap polyester jacket sleeve left a smudge on my palm when it hit my shoulder. Somewhere was a fall when every tree in the city turned early because a cold snap surprised us with a lock and we’d all pretended we liked the sudden color. Time carved into circles, honest about it.

It was Bee who saw the second metal. “Cass,” she said, because in work I am Cass, and pointed with the tip of her tape measure almost against the cut face. “That look like another one?”

It did. A darker slug deeper in the heartwood, thin as a finger. My pulse did that sympathetic jump like it had after the first. I hacked slowly at the wet rings, cutting a clean channel, careful not to bump the thing and send a shock up my wrist that would be a week of ache. Splinters stood up and snapped. The heartwood released it reluctantly.

This wasn’t a key. It was a bit of chain, a link split from the rest. The kind you’d run through a bicycle wheel. The kind someone might have looped around a sapling because there wasn’t a pole, once upon a time, thinking only about the short future, and then a child grew up and left, and the chain remained, and the elm did what trees do—it took the shade and water and wire and welded them into itself and forgot nothing.

“Lock it, leave it,” Julio said, half-laughing, half nervous. “That must’ve hurt.”

“They don’t feel pain,” Hersh said, not unkindly. Then, with less certainty, “Not like us.”

We finished the job. The chipper ate what it could. The trunk rounds lay like thick coins waiting for a purpose. The volunteer coordinator from the parks office arrived with tea and a clipboard and asked the mourners to write memories on index cards and drop them into a shoebox like obituaries. The camera crew filmed without asking anyone else anything. The river kept moving.

When the crowd thinned and Hersh went to the truck for more wedge oil and Bee took the bucket to shake chips out of the cage, I leaned against the tailgate and took out the key. My fingers had left a new streak of green on my pocket liner. Up close the stamp was a little crooked, like everything made in this city before we learned a level was not a suggestion. I used my thumbnail to scrape a scab of bark from the head and thought, stupidly, about how many hands had held it before me and whether any of them had belonged to people I loved or people who had loved what I loved. That’s not how objects work, but I do this—assign echoes to things and listen to see if they reverberate. My brother says it makes me good at my job and bad at being at peace.

“Everything okay?” Bee asked, stepping down from the bucket with a clang, startling me into closing my fist so hard the teeth bit my palm.

“Tired,” I said.

“You never wear gloves when you should,” she said, as if that were the axis everything turned on. “Station key, huh? Think it opens the café now?”

“It says Property of,” I said. “We’d have to return it to the owner.”

She gave me a look that knew me. “Don’t joke,” she said. “Not about that.”

A woman came up to the tape then, like she’d finally gotten brave enough to speak. She was in her forties, maybe, her hair pulled back in a practical band. She had the kind of face that drinks in information and gives nothing away without being asked, and I realized I knew her from the library. Graybridge is big enough to be anonymous if you want. It’s small enough no one really does. She looked past me at the stump, then at the key in my hand, then at me again. Her eyes lingered.

“Ms. Larkin,” she said. “My name is Ellen Dawes. I heard—” She gestured to the littoral of sawdust. The noise had died down enough that the river felt louder. “I shouldn’t… I just thought I should come by.”

The air in my lungs took a second to find the exit. Dawes is a name a lot of people have. Here, with the river and the station and the number 117 cooling in my hand, it was not just any. If I had looked at my watch, I would have seen my pulse moving it. I didn’t look. It was that kind of day.

“I’m sorry about the tree,” I said.

Her mouth twitched into a smile that did not reach her eyes. “We all lose the same ones, eventually,” she said. It sounded like a thing she’d rehearsed for a thousand small losses, and it hurt anyway. “I thought you should know… I still get alerts when anything with my sister’s name comes up in the news.”

Someone knocked a round against another and the sound was a low drum. Bee turned her head, not hearing, or hearing and pretending she hadn’t. The microphone on the camera across the lawn had drooped like a flower and was pointed at the dirt. The rest of the world continued being itself, kindly indifferent.

I had a line I used during storms when the parks phone rang with men who wanted a branch removed because it shadowed their birdbath. I said, There’s a queue. We triage. The words rose to pretend they had purpose here. They didn’t.

“Ellen,” I said. I don’t use the first names of strangers often. I used hers. “You don’t have to—”

“She would have liked to be here,” she said quietly, interrupting a thing we both knew I didn’t know how to say. “She and her friends used to climb that first limb, the one that went out over the path. She carved a heart in it when the bark was smooth. We came in the mornings sometimes to see if it was still there. It wasn’t, of course. Trees heal.” She looked at my pocket like she could see through denim. “I teach now,” she said. “Fifth grade. My students love this park. They take their field trip here and touch the water and shout when their hands come out brown. I don’t know why I’m telling you all that.”

Because I asked people to write down their stories on index cards, because I offered them a place to put grief that had more shape than a box in a closet, because the line between the living and the missing is as porous as bark, because keys look like answers.

“Do you need anything?” I asked uselessly.

She shook her head. “When the paper calls you, tell them it matters that you took it down before it fell, will you? They’ll want to be angry at you because it’s easier than losing things we can’t keep.” She took a breath. “And if—if anything else comes up, would you let me know? I think the police have forgotten how to spell our name without checking.”

I looked at my hand and saw that without thinking I had closed my fingers around the key again. It was imprinting a crescent into the meat below my thumb. I loosened my grip. “If anything comes up,” I said, “I will.”

She left without taking a photo, without tying a ribbon. I watched her go until she reached the turn where the willow hides you from the river. The air pressed against me like somebody waiting for me to be done so they could say the next thing. It took me a while to realize that somebody was me.

We loaded the last round and swept the path, as if brooms could make any of this tidy. I signed the work order and told the volunteer coordinator to keep the shoebox of index cards dry. When the camera crew finally came to ask for a statement about the found key, I gave them the safe line about how “sometimes urban trees incorporate debris,” and that Parks would “work with relevant city departments,” and over my shoulder Bee said to the camera, “We’ll plant a maple,” like that solved anything. It did and didn’t. That’s most of life.

At home, in the bottom drawer of my kitchen where I keep rubber bands that have lost their mates, there is a bundle of things that aren’t mine and never were but feel like they could have been: a spare button from a coat I didn’t buy, a dry cleaner’s tag I found on the sidewalk outside the morgue when I was twenty and thought you could practice being brave, a lock of dog hair from before he ran away. I did not put the station key in there. I washed the sawdust from my hands, and I held it under the faucet, and the water ran green and then clear. I rubbed it dry with a dish towel and the letters shone a little better. Property of Graybridge Central. 117. I set it on the counter and it clicked faintly against the laminate, the sound keys make when you break a promise to yourself.

There are things you know because your body won't let you unknow them. The station’s lockers were sold in lots to three surplus dealers the year the trains stopped. My brother had dragged one into the garage because he said it “looked cool” and we’d mostly used it to keep the fireworks we pretended we were too old to care about. If he still had it, it would be in the back of the salvage yard behind a Ford tailgate and a ceramic deer and the promise of two hundred bucks if you could pretend any of it was rare.

It was almost four by the time I got there. The yard backs up to the river on a low stretch where the bank is mostly broken brick that looks like someone tried to press stop signs into a beach. Milo keeps an old mutt who’s supposed to bark at thieves and mostly barks at men in hats. The dog is named Hank. He knows me.

“You’re late,” Milo said when I walked into the cinderblock office. He had grease up to his elbows and a pencil behind his ear and a way of squinting at me that has not changed since he taught me how to ride a bike by letting go when he said he wouldn’t. “You hear about the elm?”

“I worked the elm,” I said.

“You crying on TV yet?” He lifted the pencil and drew a circle on a pad, then another inside it. “Hank, sit.” Hank ignored him and leaned against my knees. My brother looked up at me in the way he does when he knows I’ve brought something into the room that will need a plan. We were raised to be suspicious of plans and addicted to them.

“You still have that train locker?” I asked.

He frowned. “In the blue shed under the tarps. Why?”

I took the key out of my pocket and set it on his desk. He picked it up. The grease on his thumb made a thumbprint on the brass that looked like the fossil of an idea. He read the stamp. He whistled, low.

“Is that—”

“Found in the elm,” I said. “It had chain, too.”

“Jesus,” he said. “You call anybody?”

“You,” I said, before the rest.

He looked at me a long time in a way that made the room feel quiet. Outside, a forklift beeped in reverse like a toy that had learned to swear. In the river, somewhere, a carp turned over. He set the key down and it made the same small flat sound it had made in my kitchen, a little louder here among metal.

“Don’t hate me,” he said finally. “I sold it last spring.”

“The locker?” I asked.

He nodded. “To a guy who turned it into a bar. A real one. Put whiskey in it to be cute.”

I stood very still. I could feel the footprint of the key in my palm even though I wasn’t holding it. “Do you know which locker it was?” I asked. “The number?”

He shook his head. “I wrote it on a sticky. I threw it away because I am a fool,” he said, in the same tone he used when he confessed to breaking Mom’s stepping stool and we both pretended not to be mad. “But I know where it went.”

“Where?” My voice sounded like air forced through a flute’s wrong hole. He wrote a name on the pad and slid it to me. It was a name I recognized, the kind you see on the side of trucks and on donor plaques next to bronze benches that never got sat on because they were placed where the wind always hit.

Milo tapped the key with a fingernail. “Cass,” he said, soft with warning. “Whatever this is, it’s not going to be quiet.”

The thing about trees is they don’t hurry unless someone makes them. The thing about keys is they can open more than doors. I picked up the key and closed my hand around it and felt the cut of it start to make sense. I thought of the rings inside the elm, honest about time in a way people never are. I thought of a girl with quick hands carving a heart in smooth bark and coming back in the mornings to see if it was still there. I thought of the stations life builds into you whether you buy a ticket or not.

“I don’t think it’s been quiet for a long time,” I said.

And that was the day the city gave me a key and a tree died on my watch and the river kept going. I like to think the elm would understand that the things buried in us don’t always want to stay. I know it didn’t have a choice. The rest of us do, and we make them anyway.

Chapter One

By the time the pipe gave way over the stacks, the river had already been overflowing for three days. Graybridge pretends it knows how to take a soaking—the old granite buildings darken like whales and the storm drains talk to themselves—but a long rain loosens the place. The sidewalks tilt. The bridges hum. Paper remembers it is only wood.

I heard the snap the way you hear a bone go in a crowded room, before your brain knows whose. Then the sound turned to a hiss and then to a sheet, and I ran.

The municipal archive used to be a munitions warehouse. It still thinks in terms of war: thick walls, narrow windows, a single curved stair that squeezes you on the turn. The stacks are on the second floor where someone installed metal shelving gestures toward modernity. The pipe that let go runs along the ceiling like a second spine.

I slid on my way around the last bank of shelves, shoes skidding on slick concrete. The water poured in a pale horseshoe, splashing the floor and spitting off the lip of a shelf labeled B-13. I did the inventory automatically. Eighteen map cases. Five runs of newspapers. Fourteen shelves of boxes. My hands were already grabbing at a tarp that had been folded on a cart with a sense of foreboding even the tarp shared.

“You couldn’t wait until morning,” I told the pipe, and it hissed back.

Security was supposed to be a man named Miguel tonight. His chair was empty when I came in at six, a note clipped to his thermos: storm, be right back. At nine-thirty, I was still alone with the building and the rain. He doesn’t owe me his whereabouts. People leave notes. It’s the age.

I pulled the tarp over anything that looked like it would be sanctified by water and then unsanctified by emergency funding. The smell came on in under a minute—the glue in bindings waking up, the iron whisper in old ink, the fat of someone else’s hands from a hundred years ago swelling out of the paper. I pulled a library cart like a shield into the stream and let the water choose me instead of the shelves. It slicked my coat down to my elbows and slid into my sleeves.

The worst of the spray hit the three top shelves. Boxes marked with dates in my neat left-handed script, the kind of hand I had learned as a reporter before the newspaper died and I washed up here, where you get to touch things after the story is done. I pulled one box after another from the path of the water. The cardboard drank and then gave up, seams opening with a soft betrayal.

On B-13, third shelf up, a box didn’t move when I tugged. It felt heavier than its number suggested, and the water sheeting past it avoided it in a way that made my brain stumble. The label on the spine said: Property Deeds, Mill District, 1907–1911. The label was crooked. I don’t put labels on crooked.

I wiped my wrist across my eyes and tried again. The box came free all at once, as if it had been suctioned. My hip hit the shelf behind me. Water came off the brim of the tarp in a cadence.

I slid the box onto the cart, directed the tarp to cover what it could, and pushed the cart out of the fall. In the office—the one with the window that watches the back of the courthouse like an old friend—I flipped on the second lamp and set the box under the light.

There’s a sound I love, when a lid comes off something that hasn’t been opened in a long time. It’s hopeful and ruinous at the same time. This one gave me no sound at all. The lid lifted in silence, damp and cold along the edges, and the faintest breath of bleach met me.

We don’t use bleach in the archive. We barely get to use light.

Under the lid, the top layer was tissue—the kind we separate photographs with. The tissue was new. The hands that had cut it had had a small tremor; the edges were not clean. Under the tissue a ledger lay like a patient. The cover was linen, stained to the color of tea, with the word RECEIPTS faint under a darker blotch where a hand had braced itself over and over. The edges were thumbworn in two places.

I put both my hands on the table on either side of the box and breathed out the way I do before I take off the first glove. Don’t get precious, Mara. It’s a box in a city that builds levees out of boxes. Still, my stomach had gone cold.

The ledger came out heavy. Under it a small wooden object rolled and ticked against the side of the box with a sound too delicate to be part of this building. A spool, it turned out, when I lifted the ledger and watched something the color of a cardinal’s wing spin across the bottom and settle. Red thread. It was the thick, waxed kind used to bind book signatures or mend canvas. The end of it had been worked down under itself in a neat tuck. A needle was stabbed into the top and buried in a cork disk, so no one would find it by chance.

“Hello,” I said to the empty air, and felt ridiculous for the second time in a minute. It was only a spool and a ledger in a mislabeled box with a smell that didn’t belong.

I fit the ledger in the cradle we use for laboring bindings and opened to the first page.

The book had started life in 1929 as a series of payments and withdrawals, nothing glamorous, although I’d argue there’s glamour in a steady line of numbers no flood has smudged. Browns and blacks of two different inks, three hands—because you can tell by the loops and the pressure on the downward strokes—fading across the inside cover. Halfway in, the entries stopped and the rest of the pages were blank.

The blank wasn’t blank.

Someone with a light hand had used pencil as shy as breath. It was a grid, columns and wipes, with notations along the left margin: June, August, January. A line across page seventeen had a small, tight sketch in the corner—a knot drawn without lifting the pencil. It was the kind you learn if someone in your family had been on a boat: a bowline turned inside out, a sailor’s flourish. The mouth of it was closed with a loop that would never slip.

A caption, if you want to call it that, ran along the bottom of the page as if the pencil had walked its own cautious path: The river carries what we tell it to carry.

I touched nothing. It sounds like a lie, given that I was already touching everything by looking, but there’s a kind of touching you know when you’re going to remember the exact angle of your fingers later.

Under the ledger, tissue again. Then a photograph lay on its face. The back had a date. 1931. A thumbprint I would have matched if the world were inclined to give me two of one person. In the bottom right corner, a note in the same tiny pencil hand as the legend in the ledger: For when the water runs backward.

I turned it over and felt the building lean a degree closer.

The photograph was a night exposure of the river. The old footbridge—before the city had grown spines in the shape of steel—was a dark rib on the left. The water was too soft, the way water always is when you trap it in a lens long enough. A gas lamp on the far bank threaded light into the surface. And then, on the near bank where the land droops toward the laundries, something darker than night stood out: a line of rope from the posts down into the water. The end of the rope disappeared into the river with the tidy certainty of a sentence end.

I looked at the photograph until the edges of my own vision went white.

It is very easy, in my job, to start living more in the past than in the present. You can spend a long night with a letter written by a woman who calls her husband my dearest in the first line and sir in the last, because she knows where the letter will be read. You can learn the way the same place looks in five different shades of winter. You can tell yourself that time is a flat file and you’ll find everything if you pull the right drawer. But even the past doesn’t smell like bleach. That’s always the present.

I put the photograph back face down. I slipped the spool into the corner of the box without thinking why I didn’t want it rolling. I slid the ledger back into its soft cradle so the knot faced up. The room seemed to have somehow cooled in the five minutes the box was open.

The hiss in the stacks softened to a gleam. Somewhere downstairs the building sighed as the boiler kicked and then reconsidered. I shut the lid and wrote a note on the top with a pencil that had been whittled down to a worried nub: B-13 misfiled. Hold. —MO.

It was ten-thirty by the clock over the door when I dried my hands on the back of my skirt and went to find the valve shutoff that lives behind a cabinet they built without hinges. A trick of turning and then turning again and the water thinned from a sheet to a shawl and then to the thin persistent threads that all things leak down to. My phone, in my jacket pocket, had three missed calls from a number I didn’t recognize and one text message from my neighbor Mrs. Kerr upstairs, who lives another kind of archive: If you’re at work, don’t come across the bridge. Stay put. Police everywhere.

She adds an emoji to everything, little symbols like punctuation someone else invented for her. This one had the siren and a wave.

I walked to the office window and watched the backs of the courthouse, the rain rolling down their shoulders. The sound outside had changed. The river had found something to say.

I left the box under the lamp. I left the tarp trembling over the stacks like a creature sleeping under it. I locked the office door, the one with old chipped blue paint and a brass plate polished by the sleeves of four archivists before me, and crossed the empty first floor where the display cases hold the city’s war medals and also, inexplicably, a pair of women’s kid gloves with mother-of-pearl buttons that have nothing to do with war and everything to do with men leaving and women folding laundry. I closed the front door behind me and stepped out into the rain.

Graybridge at night in a storm feels like walking inside a throat. Everything is breath and pulse and the taste of iron. The courthouse steps plunged rainwater down into itself in orderly falls. The river below the bridge shouldered against the piers with a sound like hands rubbing together.

There were lights up on Pepper Mill Bridge. The new bridge has a green arch that the city decided would be inspirational when we built it. The arch looks like a wishbone and acts like a magnet. Police tape shivered between two stanchions, blue and white under blue and white. A crowd had started at the near end, the way a crowd grows without anyone deciding to. Some of them had umbrellas and some of them had coffee and all of them had their phones.

“Back this way, please,” an officer said, which is the most heroic thing you can say to a crowd.

I know one of the Detective Lieutenants out of habit. We did not have a grand romance; don’t get excited. We were both new to our jobs twelve years ago, when I was still with the paper, and Graybridge is a small city that pretends to be a bigger one. You run into the same people at the same coffee places and you learn the shape of their week. Janice Pinto has the patience of a person who built her life around listening. She used to tell me everything I couldn’t print. Then I didn’t have a job, and she had even less reason to talk to me.

She was there tonight under a rain hat that made her look more like a fisherman than a cop. The hat worked: she was dry, which felt like an accusation as I slid into the knot of people not breaking the tape. Her mouth was a line that carried rain to either side without letting any in. She was looking downriver, toward where the water leaves town and pretends it is generous in dropping its silt on someone else. The rest of her face was the shape of concentration all cops wear in the moment before they let the crowd see.

If I squinted past the arch, I could see the hunched shape of a boat riding the middle of the river, a little bow light like an insect eye. For a long minute there was nothing else. Then the dark thing at the end of a tether rose and bumped the current, and a sound like an animal and like a hinge went through the crowd without anybody admitting they’d made it.

Bodies change color fast in cold water. The river offers a kind of modesty. The face I couldn’t see, and I didn’t try; we leave people their secrets when we can. The hands were bare. The left wrist had a bracelet of something bright against the pale.

Three people in wet boots worked the tether. The rope lay along the surface like punctuation. The knot at the end of it had been tied so the loop would not slip. Even if the river changed its mind a dozen times about what it would take, the loop would sit exactly where someone had put it.

For when the water runs backward.

“We aren’t taking questions,” someone said, and then Janice’s eyes found mine the way you notice a book on a shelf because you’ve shelved it yourself. Something passed over her face and then nothing did. She lifted a hand I’m almost sure was as small a greeting as a person with a badge is allowed to make in front of a camera.

I should have gone home. I should have gone back to the box and closed the lid tighter and written a longer note. Instead I leaned under the edge of someone’s umbrella and watched the red ring around the wrist. It wasn’t a bracelet. It was thread, old-fashioned and deliberate, the kind you anchor with wax because you intend it to hold in wet.

I have a father who taught me knots and then left for places you need knots. He sent me picture postcards with palm trees and whales. I can tie a bowline in the dark. I can smell the wax on thread and tell you if someone used it for leather or for paper. I can tell when someone wants a knot not to slip.

A reporter close to me once said, You know too much about small things. It was not meant kindly. The small things tend to be the ones that stick.

The boat nosed against the residential dock below where the laundries used to stand. Men in orange vests because men always think orange will save them gathered the body in and the river tried to speak over them. Someone nearby started crying the way people do when they don’t know the dead person and are crying for someone else. The sky made the sound of its own piece of police tape torn.

If you are looking, you can see other things.

On the right side of the arch, under the light that turns the middle of the bridge sodium yellow, there was a damp, dark place on the railing where someone had leaned the wet of their coat and their patience. A line of drops on the pavement ran not with the slope of the bridge but across it, as if someone had turned and knocked water off a sleeve and the drops had listened to the call of home and walked toward the river. A cigarette end lay white and rotted in the rain, and that means nothing in a city of nervous smokers. The smell of bleach, though, came up hard in one breath and then was gone, as if the air had leaned past me with a cloth held too close to its own face.

My phone buzzed in my pocket. Another text from Mrs. Kerr: Are you safe? I did not answer. That’s what you say when you have to answer. I slipped my phone away and lifted my hand to the brim of my coat and felt grit. Fine grit, like the inside of a pipe. The feeling in my stomach returned. I had not washed my hands.

It is possible to feel ridiculous and frightened at once. It is possible to know you are going to carry a single page of pencil and a drawing of a knot in your head for longer than any sane person should. It is possible to stand in a small city and understand that your life has just been sealed into a box with a label that is not the label it will deserve.

Janice moved. There are ways people who know you move when they see you at a crime scene, where the rules are different and the talk has to travel through a thin place. She came to the edge of the tape and tipped her head as if to keep the rain off and keep the privacy in.

“You’ll read about it,” she said, and then, because she still remembers me when the information was useful instead of expensive, added, “We don’t have an ID yet.”

“I won’t write,” I said. “I don’t write.”

Her mouth did the thing a mouth does when it wants to be sympathetic and can’t afford it. She started to turn away. Then she looked back and said, because she couldn’t quite help herself, “You see anything?”

It is a dangerous question to ask me. The truth wants to come out my teeth.

“Someone cleaned something,” I said. “You can smell it. And the knot on the tether, the one at the—” I stopped myself from using a word like wrist. “It won’t slip.”

“Ropes rarely tie themselves,” she said, and I couldn’t tell if she was being dry on purpose or the job had made her this way. She had her notebook half out as if to make a shape of this that would fit in a report later. “Go home, Mara. You’re soaked.”

I nodded. She turned away because the living are always turning away from the living when the dead are listening.

On my walk back the rain made lace in the puddles and took it back. The city’s light put out its own clock. In the display case on the first floor of the archive, the kid gloves looked tender and disapproving. In the office upstairs the light I’d left on made a square on the desk. The box was where I’d left it. Someone had written a note on the lid in my hand. B-13 misfiled. Hold. —MO.

The damp of my hair folded itself into my shoulders. I closed the office door and sat in my chair and listened to the pipes settling into the shape of quiet. Outside the window the river was a moving black that seemed to ignore the concrete of the building and the metal of the bridge and all the palms and fingers people lay over it.

I took the lid off the box again. The spool lay where I’d tucked it, red as a warning. I lifted the ledger. The knot on the page waited patiently. I turned back to the photograph and read the words on the back a second time. For when the water runs backward.

We all think time only runs one way because that’s how we’ve arranged our records. With enough rain and a hole the size of a thumb in a pipe, time will burrow and find its own channel.

The phone on my desk—a landline the city refuses to replace—rang once and stopped. It was enough to make me jump. When I put my hand down, my fingers made a damp print on the edge of the photograph where a white scribble no eye but mine would ever find wrote the tiniest number: 1/3.

First of three.

The first time I saw the window it was already lying.

Not in any theatrical way. Stained glass doesn’t swoon or swear. It just suggests. It is made to tell a story the way water tells stories: by bending light until the truth looks more like a recollection than a fact. If you’ve spent enough years with it, the way I have, you learn where the lies like to hide—under a clumsy solder bead, behind a piece of flashed ruby, in the indifference of lead to history.

That morning, the west transept of Saint Severin’s was a cathedral of dust and hollow sound. Marrow Harbor was coming off a wet spring and the air smelled like old limestone soaked and then dried too fast. The scaffolding creaked around me with the occasional hollow grunt that comes from a tower that was never designed to hold a human’s wobbly faith and a conservator’s toolbox at the same time.

I was kneeling on the third level, close enough to the window that Saint Apollonia’s martyrdom spilled her glass blood into my eyes. At this hour the sun came through the alley of sycamores across Baird Street, skidded across the nave, and found the small panel I had been told not to touch. Which, of course, was why I had come.

I pried gently at the flaking putty, the kind that feels like old cheese between the fingers. The lead cames were original, I was sure of that—the profile and the tool marks were consistent with the Kalder studio, early twentieth century, working-class mysticism overlaid with competent math. But in the lower left, where a martyr’s ankle retreated behind a pillar, a splice looked wrong. The lead there was subtly thinner, and the came’s heart—if you can call that little ridge a heart—was a little too round. Someone had cut and rewelded, perhaps during some past repair after a windstorm or a war. It was reasonable. It was also wrong.

I leaned in until the world narrowed to a solder joint the size of a tear and breathed, putting a smudge of fog on the glass. There it was: a meniscus where the bath had cooled faster than it should have. The fix had been hurried.

A bell rang below me. It sounded small and forgiving, like someone’s idea of God after a long winter. “Ten minutes,” a voice carried up from the nave. “Donors at ten.”

“I thought I had until noon,” I called back without looking, because you don’t look away from a lie that pretends to have an explanation.

“Your contract says ten,” the voice said. The dean liked to speak like contracts had been carved on Moses’ second set of tablets. “And we have to hide the scaffolding. It offends them.”

I couldn’t help it; I smiled. “Should we hide the windows too?” I said, and slid my scalpel under the solder seam.

“I heard that,” the dean said, voice drifting closer even as he kept himself out of my sightline. Father Carrigan had a way of being both present and unseen, like a stain. “We simply want them to see God without any reminders of what it costs.”

“God doesn’t cut his fingers on century-old lead,” I said, and immediately cut mine on the soft lip of the came as if to prove the point. There was the sting, the surprising warmth under the chill. Blood rose to the surface and smeared across a saint’s sandaled foot. I swore under my breath and reached for the rag tucked into my back pocket. The old joke goes that glass is ninety percent gravity and ten percent injury. Today it seemed determined to be eighty.

“You all right up there?” Carrigan sounded unperturbed, which meant I was in visible bleeding territory and he had already calculated whether this might delay the donors or somehow guilt them into paying more.

“Fine,” I said. I licked the cut and tasted the faint sweetness of corrosion and dust. “Your Kalder windows have opinions.”

“They’re the best in the city,” the dean said with the casual pride of someone who had never had to scrub bat droppings off the sill between storms. “You know we found his signature on a cartoon rolled up in an old steamer trunk in the choir loft?”

“You told me,” I said. He had told me twice. “H. Kalder. Hermenegild. Born in Pomerania or Poughkeepsie depending on which doc you trust. Died in a fire.”

“That was the other rumor,” Carrigan said, and I could hear him step back, the hint of a scuff on nineteenth-century tile. “Anyway. Ten minutes.”

He left the rest unsaid: Keep it clean. Keep your opinions about iconography to yourself. Don’t find anything that changes our plan.

The scalpel worked. The tool is delicate enough that when you do it right, the solder yields like old bread. The seam parted just the way it should not have if this were all original. Under the bead was a saddle of lead that had been widened to accept a hinge. I said nothing, even to myself. I breathed. I slid the point under the hinge and nudged. The small piece of glass swung inward—no, not the glass; a false piece, flashed ruby over soda-lime, not as thick as its neighbors and cut on an angle to catch the morning light. Behind it, in the hollow of the lead where it met the rounded steel of the supporting saddle bar, something thin and gray lay curled like a sleeping moth.

“Donors at ten,” I said to the empty air, because when the world shifts, I like to pretend it’s normal.

I loosened the thing with an oiled toothpick and drew it out. It was not a piece of corroded foil or an old dead fly as I had half hoped. It was a roll of waxed paper, the kind they used to wrap sandwiches and protect secrets. It was small enough to disappear between my thumb and index finger. There was a smear on it that could have been soot, could have been the kind of smoke that takes a decade to settle. My hands knew better than to try to unroll it up here, so I slipped it into the breast pocket of my work shirt and pressed my palm there once, like a prayer.

Below, someone laughed, one of the lay volunteers with a broom. The organist, Ms. Dunn, ran a hand down the keys and let three notes climb the nave. The scaffolding groaned as it got used to me again. I looked at the window as a whole and waited for it to look back.

Saint Apollonia’s eyes did not meet mine. They never had. That is the trick with eyes in glass: unless you paint across the cames, which most studios refuse to do, the pupil is always broken up, the iris interrupted by lead. A face is a mosaic that you trick yourself into reading as whole. From the floor of the nave, from the donors’ angle, the saint looks upward toward salvation. Up here, with the lies at your nose, her gaze floats off to the right, over my left shoulder. Toward the triforium walkway.

If you got your start as a kid with comic books and stereograms, as I did, if you train your brain to ignore the lines and listen to what the light is doing behind them, little things stand out. The constellation of brad marks in the painted brown of the pillar wasn’t random. The angles of the lead weren’t just structural. I reached into my bag and pulled out a sheet of vellum, cut small for field work, and a graphite stick. I pressed the vellum to the lower panel, the one with the foot and the hinge and the moth secret in my pocket, and ran the graphite lightly over the lead lines, making a quick rubbing. The shape that emerged on the vellum was almost a fish. Almost a key. Its tail pointed to a small circle in the painted stone at the very edge of the panel. The circle had been tinted with silver stain—a golden halo in the midst of martyrdom.

“Hey.” The voice came from below me, a little sharper than the dean’s, a little less practiced at sounding like authority. I looked down. A woman in a navy blazer and jeans looked up, hand on her hip, the kind of posture cops adopt when they feel they’re supposed to be in charge of something. “You Rowan Hale?”

I nodded and held up a gray-smeared thumb like a flag. “He bleeds red,” I said. It was a terrible joke. I deliver terrible jokes the way other men deliver apologies.

“Sergeant Tenley,” she said by way of introduction. Her badge was clipped to her belt. The cathedral hired the city’s help when it needed to look serious. “You the only one up there?”

“Just me and Saint Apollonia,” I said. “Oh, and Father Carrigan’s expectations.”

She didn’t smile. “There was a break-in last night. Sacristy. Doesn’t look like anything’s missing, but the safe was open and there’s fresh oil on a lock that hadn’t been turned in a decade. If you see anyone who isn’t supposed to be up there, yell.”

“Anyone besides me,” I said.

She glanced up at the window the way people look at anything they know other people will try to explain to them later. “Is she the one that gets people’s teeth pulled?” she asked.

“I try not to think about that part when I’m leaning into the glass,” I said. “There’s hearsay that she once chewed up a man’s mystery and spit it back to him at the foot of a well. But that’s apocrypha.”

Sergeant Tenley let the joke sit between us and die. “I’ll be around,” she said, and her footsteps receded into the side aisle, quiet and purposeful, like a cat in a library.

I was alone. I looked at the hinge again and then at the small painted circle.
