I put my pencil to the vellum and drew lines I probably shouldn’t have drawn, tracing not the contours of the saint but the geometry under it. Kalder had been a man of his time. He had built a compass into everything he touched. If this window lay, it did so with intent.

The donors arrived with the sound of polite whispering. There is a particular hush to wealth when it enters a church; it feels like snow deciding whether to be storm or decoration. Father Carrigan met them at the narthex and steered them like a schoolteacher who still believes in field trips. “The west transept,” he said, “has been an inspiration to generations.” He said it as if the inspiration were his. He said everything as if it had waited for him to show up and narrate it.

I checked the time. Nine fifty-eight by my phone. I took out the roll of waxed paper. It was cooler than my fingers. The day might as well have turned on it. I rolled it open.

It made the small dry crackle of an old package. It had been folded over itself twice to keep the contents from rubbing against the lead. Inside the wrap was a strip of vellum the size of my palm. On it, in a hand that preferred small letters to big ones, someone had written in graphite so soft it had survived a century without working itself into dust.

Ask for Jonah, it said. The words were tight, the flourishes timid. Ask for Jonah, then a small cross, and then a date: July 16, 1913.

The vellum smelled like the back of a bookseller’s shop, like a certain kind of porch in the oldest parts of the city. July 16 was the feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel in that calendar, but the date meant something else to me. It meant something I couldn’t place. The cross was plain. The hand that wrote it did not have education to spare.

Herm Kalder had not been a literate man in English, if the rumors were true. He drew poetry; he did not write it. Jonah could have been a donor. A street. A pawnshop. The adage in this town went: ask for Jonah and you’ll end up on the water.

Below me, Father Carrigan said, “And here we have a remarkable example of early twentieth-century workmanship, the Kalder window of Saint Apollonia, which was almost lost to the storm last year.”

A woman said, “How terrible,” in the way people say how terrible when they mean what a good story, and then she asked, “Will it be safe to have it fully removed?” The last word was lazy, the way the rich let verbs be carried for them.

I slid the vellum back into my pocket and looked at the hinge. To the right of that little painted circle, the silver stain had been dabbed heavier, just enough to catch more sun. The angle of the lead came running up into it made a line that did not obey the narrative. It obeyed whatever compass had been in Kalder’s pocket.

Ask for Jonah. July 16, 1913. I had been nine the first time I sat in a museum with a Kalder cartoon rolled across my lap. I was not supposed to touch it. I did as I was told and disobeyed anyway, letting my fingers hover just above the charcoal. I remember thinking then that the people who made windows never expected to be read. They expected to be seen.

“Mr. Hale?” Father Carrigan called up to me, and this time he said my name like it belonged to a problem. “Can you tell us a little about what you’re doing?”

I clicked my tongue against my teeth and stood. The scaffolding always felt too dramatic when you became suddenly tall on it; your body tells you that you are in a tree, that this is a disloyalty. I put the vellum with Jonah and the date deeper into my pocket and stepped closer to the rail.

“We’re looking at a window that everyone in this city thinks they already know,” I said, because if you can’t conceal the lie, confess to a different one. “Hermenegild Kalder was a storyteller with glass. He used lead like a punctuation mark. These panels have survived one war, two fires, and a budget meeting last fall that nearly did more damage than either.”

The donors laughed. Carrigan beamed, or pretended to.

“What we’re doing,” I continued, “is listening. We clean. We shore up the weak points. We undo what time and amateur piety have done. If we find something, we preserve it.”

“Find something?” The woman with the lazy verbs had a scarf tied at her neck that looked expensive and uncomfortable at the same time. “Like what?”

I could have said this would not be the day I admitted to any hidden hinges. I could have said anything and made it true; I was up here, planner of light. Instead, I said, “Sometimes artists leave notes for themselves. Instructions. A recipe. A joke. Sometimes we find glue where glue should not be.” I looked at the hinge and then at their faces. “It is older than you think, and younger than you want it to be. It's exactly what you need it to be when you sit in the pew on Sunday.”

It satisfied them, which is to say it left them with something to repeat at lunch.

“Security is for the day,” Sergeant Tenley said quietly at the back of the group. I hadn’t noticed her return. She looked up at me with a neutral expression and then away, already scanning for different trouble.

Trouble found us faster than any of us asked.

It was stupid, the way accidents are stupid, which is why almost nobody believes in accidents. There was a footfall on the narrow walkway of the triforium, the low gallery that runs halfway up the nave wall. It’s usually roped off with velvet and polite language. The sound was light, too light for the dean, too hurried for a docent. It might have been a verger. It might have been no one.

I turned, the way Saint Apollonia’s painted eyes had already turned, and in the space between one breath and the next something dark moved where nothing was supposed to move. There was the sound of metal scraping stone, a cough of dust, a stifled half-shout, the kind of sound a person makes when they do not expect to need to use their voice to matter.

Then a human body fell.

He came down like a dropped coat, arms trying at the last moment to remember how to be wings. He hit the marble between the first two pews with the kind of sound that stops the heart of everyone who hears it, not because of compassion but because the body reveals in that instant that it is heavier than you have ever let yourself admit.

The donors became statues. The organist stood and then sat again as if remembering her knees existed. Father Carrigan reached out his hand as if catching mattered now. Sergeant Tenley moved, and I’ve never been more grateful for a person moving toward what needed a person.

I’d been on job sites where someone fell. Glass people fall. Roof people fall. It is a fraternity of gravity. The sensation that hit me was deeper and older: not horror, not even pity, but the practical need to keep the window from being shaken off its centuries. I braced myself against the frame and craned to see.

The man on the floor was veiled in dust, his hair gray when it had not been gray, or had not looked gray in whatever life he had before sky. His collar was black; a white tab sat crooked where the neck remembers what it was supposed to hold the face upright. Father Carrigan looked as if someone had stolen a line he had meant to say and said it for him, better.

“Don’t touch him,” Tenley said, kneeling, hand already at her radio. “Nobody touch anything.”

Then she did touch him, because human hands will move even when the brain has turned to instruction. She pressed two fingers under his jaw and then his wrist and then his shirt. She said a name that sounded to me like a prayer and then like a report. “Jonah,” she said. “Father Jonah.”

The word made all the pews into a map, every knot in the wood a place where a line crossed another line. Ask for Jonah, the vellum whispered in my pocket. The date July 16 flared in memory, silly with insistence.

Carrigan spoke and then didn’t. Somebody sobbed the way people sob when they need to be heard doing it. Somewhere up in the walkway, a velvet rope swung back and forth like a metronome trying to find middle C.

“Mr. Hale,” the dean said, and when he did, he looked up at me with an accusation I had not earned and did not like. “Were you working up there? Did you see—”

“I saw a man fall,” I said. It felt insufficient and brutally honest both.

“Can you come down?” Sergeant Tenley said without looking up at me, her voice calm as if calm were a tool she had spent a lifetime oiling. “I’ll have some questions for you.”

“Of course,” I said, because what else do you say when a city’s name climbs into your throat through different doors? I tucked the graphite, the scalpel, the toothpick back into their places and made the scaffolding take me seriously. On the second level my knee barked complaint; on the first I could smell the dust where the man had met the floor; on the ground the saint in the window looked up past me to a place where either truth or a very old lie was hovering.

I stepped off the last rung. The donors parted with the efficiency of people who have been taught by life to step aside when uniforms ask them to. Father Carrigan stood with his hand on a pew and his mouth closed and his eyes dangerously bright. Sergeant Tenley turned toward me with her notebook out like a passport.

“Tell me what you were doing,” she said.

As far as there ever was a beginning, I had it in my pocket. But I didn’t give it to her. Not yet. Not with the body cooling beside a shelf of hymnals and the hinge still warm from my breath. Not with the word Jonah hanging in the air like a rung wherein something had just slipped.

I told her about the morning. I told her about the putty and the lead and how sunlight can lie. I left the rest in my shirt, over my heart, a soft square that made my pocket heavy. Outside, somewhere in the brightness we had built this building to control, a siren wailed, a gull screamed, a city turned its head. I thought about a hand in 1913 writing a name in a careful, clumsy script, folding a tiny vellum note into wax paper, and sealing it into a place designed to keep both angels and drafts out.

Ask for Jonah, it had said. So I had, without meaning to. And Jonah had fallen from Heaven.

Chapter One

By the time the lake drew back far enough to show the bones of Graywolf, the name tasted like silt. You heard it in the hardware store and the feed shop, a soft, guilty word. People who had never set foot in the drowned town began using it like an apology. As if saying Graywolf let you share in it. As if names had weight and could bring anything up from thirty years of mud.

I parked where the road ended and the water used to begin, under a sun-faded NO BOATING sign that leaned like a drunk against air. The maples that had once shaded the overlook were dead columns, bark gone to parchment, leafless hands spread against an open, rainless sky. Beyond them the basin lay bruised with hard light, the surface a mosaic of dried clay plates and slender rivulets that glinted like veins. The receding edge of the reservoir had pulled inward and downward for months, exposing a pale, chalky ring around the basin that people in town started calling the collar. The collar scrawled itself on rock and concrete and wood, a line that said: here is the water’s memory of itself.

The morning was barely awake, but the heat already had the heavy intentions of a late August day. The smell was old—mineral and rot and sun-warmed metal. I slung my field bag over my shoulder and stepped down onto what had been the lake. My boots cracked thin skins of dried algae and left dark prints in the pale, sick mud beneath. A heron stood fifty yards out on an exposed log, prehistoric and patient. When I moved, its eye tracked me like a question it had asked other people and still not gotten a good answer to.

I’m a botanist by training, the kind who looks at a ditch and sees a calendar. I can tell time by what blooms or dies, by what sticks to your cuff. I taught for a while after my graduate work and then came home when my grandmother, June, started leaving the kettle on. For the last two years I have made a living out of two stubborn things: keeping her little farm alive—whatever anyone calls it now, because the sign that says June’s Herbs is more faded plank than readable promise—and consulting for the county sheriff and the water district when plants might be able to say something that people won’t. It’s a strange thing, to have a town remember you as the girl who worked the farmers’ market table and tie you to fieldwork with crime scene tape. It gives people weird ideas about whispered poisons and secret skills. Mostly I take notes in the heat and collect samples and tell men in boots and badges that the seeds stuck in their suspect’s socks came from broom sedge and ragweed, not from some dark conspiracy. It’s less dramatic than they think, except when it isn’t.

The water district had my name on speed dial when the first stench of algae rolled off the half-starved lake in June, and when kids started bringing home rusted things with sharp edges from the receding shore in early July. Fathers stood under holdovers of shade and told their sons not to go out there; sons went. We had all watched the drought grind on and the lake wither like a parent getting thinner in a hospital bed. When the roof of the old church broke the surface last week—the steeple canted and black-scarred, a piece of ruined piano left in the sun—no one told their kids anything. They put on hats and came to look.

I wasn’t out there for the crowd. I had a permit from the water district and a text from Sheriff Rios that read Graywolf? Are you available this morning. A pair of fishermen had found something tangled in their line near where the old state highway took its last breath in 1961. They said it looked like a bone. They also said it was a fish skull, or part of a fencepost, or a length of PVC, depending on which way you turned them. August was learning my number for things that might be bones and might be stories. I told him I’d meet him, then came early to walk the edges the way I like to do.

Plant succession on a drowned landscape is a palimpsest. The first opportunists arrive in the muck like gossip rushing to an open door. Spikerush and smartweed, little ranks of goosefoot with their lime dusting of lees. The non-native johnsongrass comes behind, maybe the same seeds that wrapped around someone’s socks the day they put the first load of furniture on the trucks for the long climb out of the valley. A person can think they are talking about history and then step on it.

I crouched and ran fingers along the cracked plate of ground beside a drainage ditch that had reappeared like a lost line of handwritten text. The mud under the dried skin yielded cool and dark. My field bag carries the same things it always does—little vials, flagged tape, a camera, forceps and scissors in a case that looks like it should hold someone’s reading glasses. The new growth was sparse on the higher parts of the basin. Closer to where the water still shimmered, I could see mats of algae clinging to wet, low places. The same bright green scum that had gnawed on fish gills in June lay here in soft, dry sheets like spent blankets. On a piece of concrete—what had once been a sill—a little tuft of Rudbeckia had the stubborn vigor I admire in people and plants both. Behind it, a gray cage of rootlessness: a willow skeleton, thrown into useless posture by a lake that had risen faster than roots could dive.

Graywolf had been a one-street town tucked along a shallow river with a name the department of water resources changed in the 1950s to something that sounded like a clean project instead of a living thing. They did that a lot then. There are pictures in the library—my grandmother June in a pressed cotton dress behind a table of herbs and salves in front of a shop with a striped awning. Next to her, a man with a white coat and a barber’s careful hair. HALLOW & WARD APOTHECARY, the sign said, in the kind of lettering they don’t teach anymore. Hallow was the barber-looking chemist, Ward was the doctor who went up to the farms, and June was the girl who knew plants. A photograph holds an arrogance: the idea that what it sees will keep existing because it has been seen. The dam burst that idea.

The block letters of GRAYWOLF MERCANTILE rose out of the hardpan as I walked, ghost-painted across a low wall like a sinking ship’s name. The frame of the building had held in the water for years; now it shivered out, ribs and rafters, the open mouth of a door that had been just so on unsaturated days and sealed under pressure on wet ones. I angled around a sinkhole that had appeared suddenly last week with an earthy sigh and felt for unexpected softness with the heel of my boot. People who had wandered down that far had been leaving coins on window sills like museum patrons and propping up coffee mugs as if ghosts needed caffeine too. Something about the exposed town made everyone polite. The footprints I saw were neat and careful, as if pressing down too hard might make the whole thing wince and go under again.

A dragonfly stitched the air. Beyond it, the apothecary was where the photographs said it should be: on the north side, next to the mercantile. The awning frame was still there, scalloped ghost. No glass in the windows, just ragged frames sticky with algae bloom that had dried into a crystalline powder around the edges and flakes to nothing when I brushed it. Inside, the bones of shelves leaned at affectionate angles. A jar lay on its side, old letters in a layer of lake filth beyond reading: MENTH—. A neat block of drawers had come unstuck from its case and lay around it like fallen teeth.

For as long as I can remember, my grandmother’s hands smelled like crushed mint and something dusty and good. She had a jar of comfrey root on the kitchen counter and a reputation for turning nettles into soup that wouldn’t hurt you. People came to June when their heads hurt and when they wanted to sleep and when they didn’t want to. There were parts of her that I have only found by going through her things now that she’s gone. A shoebox of notes tied with ribbon, a pressed sprig of yarrow in a book about county history, letters with a return address that said Ward, never more than two sentences long.

As the dam site creaked into place in the late fifties, as men with clipboards and women with casseroles argued in school gymnasiums about where you can move a whole life to, June had worked here at Hallow & Ward, with her sleeves rolled and a pencil tucked behind her ear. She used to tell me that the day the trucks came, someone put her apron into a box along with a set of cast iron measuring weights and a jar of licorice root, and that the jar broke on the trip out, and for years the smell of sweet root would surprise her in baseboards and in the pages of books and in the folds of clothes in an upstairs closet. I don’t know if she told me because it was true or because it was a way to give me the sound of her voice telling a story. In that voice there was always the river, patient and dull.

The doorway to the apothecary was open against nothing. I went in like a thief of dust. Under the quiet, the lake made small sounds. Tiny movements, things settling. The lake is never on your side; it only takes or it gives because it has to. Plants, also, tell you their version. They didn't survive under here. Their voices were elsewhere, in ferny gullies and in ditch lines that never got fully paved over, but their seeds had traveled, and you could read the compromise they had made.

A ladder lay on its side behind the counter, the iron feet sunk in inches. The old floor was a mosaic of broken tile and pressed playdough silt, the pattern of the footsteps of other people erased and replaced and erased again by water. On the wall behind the counter I could still read some hand-lettering, ornamental and careful: INFI- and the curl of an S for INFUSIONS. It might have been painted by June, or by Hallow. There was a trapdoor behind the counter, a rectangle of wood that had swelled and dried and swelled again for half a hundred seasons and now sat proud of the floor like a raised letter. I put my weight on it. It rocked, sucked dark water up from its seam, then settled.

“Don't fall through the floor of a building that hasn't had a floor in thirty years,” I said, to the dragonfly, or to June, or to myself.

With the toe of my boot I worried the edge of the trapdoor and then with both hands pulled it toward me. It wasn’t a trapdoor so much as an access panel to a root cellar or a safe place for bottles and samples during summer heat. It came up on the fifth try with a kind of wet reluctance. Underneath: a black square full of the richest mud I had seen in weeks. The light knocked itself out on it. I lay on my stomach on the counter and reached down into the square, my fingers walking over a shelf, pieces of wood, a glass lip. In the mud, edges are gentle. I found a tin—something with a lid—and teased it up like an egg out of a nest. It was heavier than I expected. Someone had sealed the lid with wax, sloppy dollops of it pressed across the seam with a thumb and string tied around like a promise. The tin was the kind with a goose on the side and a chip out of one corner, the kind you keep buttons or coins in until a child asks what’s in it and you say “nothing” and put the lid back on.

The wax had kept out the worst of the lake. It flaked away under the blade of my pocket knife. The lid came up gummy and slow. Inside, there were oil-paper packets tied with linen thread, and a small cloth-wrapped bundle. The packets were labeled in the slanting hand I have from photographs and family habit. Angelica, white willow, pipsissewa. Wards. The cloth bundle was the size of my palm, soft and heavier than it looked. I unwrapped it. Inside: a stack of envelope-sized, water-stained letters tied with that same linen thread and sealed at the knot with wax, the seal pressed with something that made a cross of little leaves. The wax had cracked, but it had been good. The ink on the topmost letter held some of its old black. J, it said, in a darting hand.

I felt the letters like a pulse in my palm. People talk about finding messages in bottles like the world sends them what it owes. This was different. This was not the world sending anything; someone had folded this up and pushed it into the dark to keep it from having to answer someone, and the dark had been showing its belly all summer.

I slid the top letter from the stack. The salutation was careful. June, that hand said, not J, not darling, not anything that had to cross a threshold. The date was a day in September of 1961, the kind of clean September day that the old men at the diner still talk about as if quail will walk out of that day and into their living room if they leave the door open.

I didn’t read it then. It’s a ridiculous acting in a novel when someone puts the letter in a pocket and walks away and the reader wants to shake them and make them read the thing, but the apothecary entire made my shoulders crawl, and a heat that had nothing to do with the sun came up my neck. There is a kind of knowledge that comes in from the corner of your eye before your mind translates it: something off-key in the place. The air changed with a weight I could smell. Algae, yes. Tannin, yes. But under it, faint and antiseptic, familiar to hands that have spent years with plants: oleander. It doesn’t grow here, not naturally. People set it along driveways and along fences for the flowers, not knowing or not caring that every part of it is poison. There was a sprig on the floor, beaten and browned, but the smell—when you know it—is a latch clicking. The apothecary’s floor does not hold any part of a living oleander plant, but my brain told me I smelled it, and then my body did. I put the letters back into the cloth, back into the tin, because if something is poisonous in a story, it will be there when you come back to it. It doesn’t evaporate on account of your curiosity.

I had meant to spend another hour looking at succession and at the algae bloom line, making notes on where the goosefoot gave way to bulrush, marking with tape a patch of knotweed whose seedheads looked like punctuation. Instead, with the tin secure in my bag under a coil of flagging tape and a field guide with a broken spine, I moved out into the open, into the glare, toward the seam where the old highway slouched down into the lake.

The road had emerged like a photograph developing—first a suggestion, then a line, then the confidence of two yellow stripes winking through the old, whitish skin of the basin. The county had posted little metal placards that said KEEP OFF, and people obeyed them like they do when a stranger tells them not to step on graves. The asphalt had been under water so long it had softened to something that looked like it would slide if a man with the wrong sense of humor put his weight on it. I didn’t go to the road. I went parallel to it, on the higher part of the shore that was dry and trustworthy and creaked under my boots with old shells and shiny flakes of something that had been paint once.

There was a car partly visible twenty yards downslope, exactly where you would expect someone to leave it if they had imagined the water was a clean blanket and that time could be paused by submerging it in the new forever. It was a rectangle of roof and a slope of trunk and the suggestion of a windshield frame. The rest of it wore a coat of dried mud and layered algae that had been a living skin last year. No one wants to be the first person to stick their fingers into a door seam that hasn’t been opened since Kennedy was president. We love old sealed things and we fear them, and those feelings don’t cancel each other out. They sit side by side and tug on you until one wins.

I put latex gloves on without thinking about it, the way you flinch from a hot thing before you know what hot is. Gloves get slippery in heat, but you get used to it. I knelt in the dry mud and brushed the trunk seam with a soft brush from my bag. It was just habit: take away the layer that might false your impression. When the brush whispered away the algae and drying lake, I saw the faintest suggestion of chrome, and where the handle had been, a hollow. The trunk had popped some time in the lake years the way drowned trunks do, water pressure doing dumb slow work. In the gap was a darkness no different from the other dark places around it, except that my stomach could tell it was different.

Sheriff Rios was half an hour away at best, maybe forty-five. He had a way of moving slowly until he didn’t. I had been the first to confirm a bone once—a leg that had floated down from the northern old farm with a story that nobody wanted to read. You don’t ever want to be the first person to see those, but sometimes you are and the seeing makes a loyalty in you to the truth that settles in.

I didn’t open the trunk. I put my call through to August and left one glove on so I could hold the phone without painting it with the lake. He picked up on the second ring and said, “Mara,” like he had already said my name in his head nine times.

“You told me to call you when I saw something that could be a thing,” I said. “I think I’ve got a thing.”

“You at the highway?” he asked. In the background I heard a door shut, a radio squawk, the sound the county cars make when their belts are off by a half-inch and summer is a mile wide.

“Parallel to it. There’s a trunk popped on something that might be a twenty-year-old Buick or a sixty-year-old Olds, and I don’t have any business telling the difference. I can see fabric. And—”

“And,” he said, because he has learned my ands matter.

“And a ring, August,” I said. “On something that’s not fabric.”

Silence. Not the kind that means nobody is there. The kind that means someone is giving respect to what you just told them. He inhaled and exhaled like he was counting to a number that both of us didn’t like.

“Don’t touch anything,” he said, the ritual line, the magical thinking sentence lawmen put between the world and disaster.

“I’m not touching anything,” I said. Then, because I never have been able not to tell him all of it when it matters, I added, “There’s something else. I found a tin in the apothecary. Letters. One addressed to my grandmother. June.”

He did not say, Oh. He did not say, We have to be careful. He did not say much of anything at first. He said my name again, different this time, softer and farther away, like a hand on the back of the neck.

“Mara,” he said. “I should have told you sooner.”

“About what?” I said.

He was quiet a beat, and in that beat a fish flopped in a slick rim of water twenty feet away and remembered a meaning it had never known.

“About how many of the old names are still fixed to this place,” he said. “I’m turning in by the feed store now. Keep your feet where they are. Don’t let anyone else near it.”

“There’s only the heron,” I said.

“Then ask him to stand still too,” he said, and hung up.

The ring in the half-open trunk caught the sun and threw a clean, stupid spark like jewelry in a store window. It had the look of a class ring or a lodge ring—heavy, a signet raised in metal and years. I couldn’t make out the seal in that light. The hand it was on was not a hand anymore but the suggestion of one, the delicate armature that remains when all the clever parts have gone. Skeletal finger, the ring so clean in its circle it made your mouth dry to think of it. Plants keep their circles in seeds and in years. We pretend to be different. We aren’t.

I knelt, the little vials in my bag clinking against each other like ice in a glass, and watched the shine and the bone and the water that had no loyalty at all.

Chapter One

The watchmaker died with every clock in his house stopped at the same moment, and two days later the lawyer sent me his key.

The envelope was thin courthouse stock, the kind that had paid for birth certificates and foreclosure notices in Graybridge since before my mother was born. It had my name typed in crisp, veering letters and a return address that made my stomach fold in on itself. The key slid against my palm when I pulled it free, heavier than the envelope had any right to carry. Cold. Brass teeth caught the November light. There was a note no longer than a grocery list: For the attic.

It was signed J. Hollis in the tidy ink I remembered from labels in his shop window: Regulator, 1889. French carriage clock, repaired. Not for sale.

I hadn’t thought about Joseph Hollis in years, not really, not like the town had. Graybridge never forgot him. He was a landmark you navigated around, a bruise you kept pressing on out of habit. People gave him their wedding watches and their grandfather’s pocket pieces and never asked why the sun set on his porch at a different angle than anyone else’s, why you could hear his workbench ticking when you walked past after midnight.

When my sister went missing, everyone asked him then.

“June?” The ceiling swam a little when I stepped off the bus and Graybridge staggered back into focus in that dizzy way childhood places do, half-scale and overbright. Tess Ellery waited near the station door, a candy scarf looped around her neck despite the temperate fall I carried in from the city. I had known her as Teresa in school, an elbows-and-knees girl who could draw precise horses from memory. Now she was Ms. Ellery, Probate Clerk, hair pinned in an efficient helmet that did not move in the wind. “I wasn’t sure you’d come.”

I held up the key like it might explain me. “This yours?”

“Mine?” She had Laura’s laugh—that little airless cough that all our mothers perfected when they were trying to be appropriate. “No, that’s his. He named you.”

I should have asked named me to what. Named me beneficiary? Named me burden? But saying his name in downtown Graybridge felt like swallowing a handful of needles. The lamplighter statue dripped from last night’s rain; the river held its breath under the bridge. The white-painted windows of Hollis & Son Watch Repair were blank across the street, their letters flaking like the bark of birches. Son was a lie. He had never married. He had been no one’s father.

Tess lowered her voice and glanced over my shoulder, unnecessary theater in a town with nothing posted that somebody’s aunt hadn’t read out loud at the post office. “I didn’t know if you’d want—”

“Want any part of him.” I pocketed the key. It bit my thigh through the denim like an accusation. “Me either.”

She didn’t say I’d left. She didn’t remind me that I’d bolted on a hot July afternoon after six months of searching turned into six months of casseroles, that I’d packed college and internships and a job that taught me where bodies turned up in the city when the first thaw came, and that none of it brought Rosie back. She didn’t prod the wound. “There’s no money. I want to be clear about that. Just the house, if you even want it. Or you can decline and it’ll go county. The shop’s inventory is gone. He never had much on hand except what was in repair.”

I glanced across the street again. The shop door was black-painted wood and old glass that had rattled like a loose tooth every time I shoved it when I was twelve and persistent and sure I could shake information out of hardware. Above the door a brass ship’s bell hung, salted green. “The house comes with the shop?”

“The shop is technically part of the estate, but it’s sealed. The house is what the key is for.” Tess’s voice softened. “His niece will contest it if you delay.”

“He has a niece?” It came out like a joke and felt like a knife.

“She moved away decades ago. Never came back. Different last name now.”

“Ah.” The niece I’d never heard of, who had never brought him pies or sat on his stoop while he smoked and watched the water darken. The niece who would fight me for a house I didn’t want.

“And he left you a letter.” Tess hesitated. “I had to read it into the record this morning.”

“Of course you did.”

“He wrote: For June Delaney, who always asked the right question, even when I didn’t know the answer. For the attic.”

I laughed without humor. “Is that flattery?”

“It’s a burden, honey.” Tess touched my sleeve and looked briefly like Teresa again, the girl who’d given me her sandwiches when I started bringing mine home untouched. “Don’t let the town get inside your bones again if you can help it. He stirred up old things. That’s not your obligation to carry.”

But I was home long enough to get the key and long enough to satisfy the ghost of a thousand little metal hearts that had once beat in that house. It cost nothing to walk down Front Street. It cost everything, but I pretended it didn’t.

I cut through the square where the farmer’s market used to be until the second big-box grocery rolled in. The coffee shop was still there, far too earnest for a town with one real street, chalkboard listing single-origin beans with names like Solstice and Riverbed. The hardware store smelled like oiled pine and dust, and when Mr. Barnett saw me he looked at me like a late snowfall. “June?”

“Still me.” I forced my mouth into shapes.

He wiped his hands on a cloth that might once have been white. “You look good. City agrees with you?”

“It agrees with everyone. Less personal that way.” We did not say Rosie’s name. People never said it in the present tense. They said when she was little or in the context of casseroles. Mr. Barnett’s eyes were the honest, guilty kind that couldn’t be helped. He always gave me two screws for the price of one when I was a kid, like he could fasten the town together better if I helped him. Now he offered me weather stripping and a door chain as if those things could keep me safe. “You be careful at that house.”

“I’m always careful.”

On the way to the house, the river breathed mist over the bank weeds. The white fence along Hollis’s property leaned like a tired old man. He had a narrow, salt-shingled two-story with a blind front parlor and flaking green trim. The maple that had stood in the yard since my mother’s hair was still black had dropped half its leaves in one storm; the rest hung like tarnished coins.

The front door stuck once, twice, then gave like a hand unclenching under mine. And after that, the sound. I’ve spent too many nights in too many quiet rooms not to hear things other people slide past: the way a refrigerator coughs every thirteen minutes, how old floorboards exhale when pressure leaves them, the radio frequency of your neighbor’s router sneaking through a drywall seam. The Hollis house had its own noise. The clocks. Though they’d stopped, though the papers said every hand had frozen at 3:18, their bodies held the memory of motion. The house sounded like a seashell does when you press your ear to it and lie about the ocean. The tick had been scraped away; the echo remained.

There were clocks on every surface. Big-bellied wooden mantel clocks with faces like pale, disapproving men; thin brass skeleton mechanisms like the bones of birds; cheap plastic schoolroom analogs he must have kept for parts. They all sat with their mouths open and their hands arrested. Glass domes smudged with thumbprints cupped dust the way hands cup breath. A longcase clock stood in the corner with its hood bare of glass, pendulum quiet.

I moved among them and they moved me back to being sixteen at his counter. “What time was it that night, Mr. Hollis?” My voice had been thin, knifed sharp by hunger and anger. “What time did you close? What time did you see her?”

He had looked at me for a long time like he was determining how many parts I would break into if he handled me. “Time is not the same as guilt, Miss Delaney.”

“Which you would know.”

“Which I would know,” he had said, with a softness that made me want to throw something heavy.

3:18. The hands were set there like a ruin you couldn’t live in, the single thing that got saved when the house burned. On the big one in the hall, the minute hand sagged just a fraction lower, worn at the fixing like a tired knee.

The house smelled like brasso and lemon oil and something wet that had gotten shut in too long ago and ruined. A line of sunlight limned the floor where a rug had always been and wasn’t. There were no photographs on the walls. His papers lay stacked on the kitchen table in neat piles under a broken bottle of cheap red wine as paperweight. A grocery list that read: salt, apricots, onions, fusible links. The last one made me smile in spite of myself, the way a word that has no business in a grocery list can make you. He must have meant for a clock.

The attic key stuck in my pocket like an insistent finger, tapping. I climbed past the framed map of Graybridge as it was in 1907, when the river ran wider and the bridge had a toll. The paint on the banister had been rubbed off by hands that never wore wedding bands. At the top landing the air changed, denser, like walking into a story you’d already told yourself. The attic door was narrower than it should have been. I could only wedge my shoulder through once it gave; it dragged along the carpet with a sound like low thunder. Cold dust settled on my face the moment I opened it, as if someone had been waiting to blow it under my eyelashes.

The attic was not the cartoon kind with a rocking horse and trunks and a birdcage. Hollis had cut it into a workroom with a long bench under the dormer window and bins of parts arranged in unmannerly precision: springs coiled like silver snails, little jars of screws and pins with hand-lettered labels so tiny I touched them to be sure he’d written that small. There were notebooks in a row as neat as the parts, black spines, no titles. An old tin that had held cookies once, the kind my mother bought at Christmas for the tin because the cookies tasted like powdered air.

For the attic. I'd expected the key to open something obvious, a trunk that glowed, a secret panel that breathed when I put my ear to it. The attic did not feel like it had secrets; it felt like an arctic animal’s den, stripped of everything that had once kept it warm.

The window had the kind of view that made poets lie. The river moved without seeming to; the bridge’s iron ribs held its belly in. On the far bank a row of light posts marched like soldiers toward the hill. And on the glass, a thumb-smudge in an oval, restless, where he’d leaned out to listen to the night. A brass ring lay on the sill. It was not a wedding band. It had numbers etched all around and a bit of chain fastened to it like a tiny leash. A compass bezel. It fit over my thumb like it had learned my shape and forgotten anyone else’s.

On the bench, the thing that did not belong: a leather case with a stitched strap fastened on the wrong side and a tag answered to where do I belong? by projectile virtue of having been left on top of everything else. The case was old, the leather crazed like frost. The buckle held. Inside, nestled in old cotton printed with violets, was a box made of dark, heavy wood with flowers cut in the lid and mother-of-pearl set like eyes. I hadn’t forgotten the weight melody could carry. I hadn’t known I remembered this particular one.

It took my breath with a punch. The first notes were tinny with age and still made the back of my neck go cold. Three measures, a flourish, three more, the roll into the familiar chorus. Rosie had eaten creamsicles on the curb and hummed with her mouth open when the truck rolled down our street, the song losing time with the squeak of its brakes.

“When you hear it,” my mother had said once, “you can measure how far it is by how long before the echo comes back.”

I wound the key instinctively, once, twice. The sound spilled like water into a cracked bowl. Little Tin Soldier. Or something like it. The ice cream trucks in Graybridge had played a dozen songs, and all of them sounded like this one. It was not a fine instrument; the comb tines buzzed. And yet my hands shook as if I were peeling back skin.

There was a false bottom under the velvet insert. You could feel the difference by the weight, the way a seam in your own dress will irritate you all day just because it is not where it should be. A little tug ribbon lay there like a dare. I pulled. The lid refused and then gave with a sigh. Under that, an envelope with my name in that same measured ink. The paper had browned to the color of tea. My name looked wrong in his hand.

June, it read. Everyone thinks I can tell them what time it is. I cannot tell you. But I can tell you where.

There followed a set of coordinates cramped into a square on the page, then again as if he didn’t trust my reading: 41.6428, -73.1092. Not far. The river bend above the old quarry. I saw in my head the half-road full of weeds, the No Trespassing sign written in spray paint that bled. He had underlined the last number twice. Below it, like an afterthought: Thursday. 3:18.

I folded the paper closed not because I wanted to but because if I could make the words not look at me for a second, maybe I could breathe. Hollis had timed his clocks to die like that. He had coaxed his little brass and steel hearts toward a synchronized death. For what. For me. For a map.

The workbench had a drawer with a lock like a stubborn child. I slid the square key into it and it fit, gratified, a very small triumph. Inside, a ledger in the same neat sweater of a hand. November. Repairs: Mather, Hermle. Returned: Finch, Elgin. Below that, without a date, written in a hand just a little worse, as if he had been in a hurry—that alone would have shaken anyone who knew him—a line that read: Do not set an alarm if you are not ready to wake.

The music box sang itself to quiet, the last note hanging in a way that made me think of unanswered questions. The house listened to me breathe. Below the attic, the silence changed color. It’s not a thing you can explain without sounding more haunted than you are, but some silences are blue and some are black. This one had a green underwash, like a pond no one had swum in for a long time. I told myself it was the river catching hard somewhere under the bridge.

I slipped the letter into my jacket, the compass ring into a pocket I could fasten, the music box under my arm because it felt like a promise the dead man had made to me personally. Tess had said don’t let the town inside your bones. It was already there, a warm animal burrowing.

On the stairs, the banister varnish stuck to my palm. In the kitchen, the paper piles put their shoulders against one another like livestock in a storm. I wanted light. I didn’t want to flip a switch. He’d wired everything himself, and you never know with men who think in parts they can hold in their hands. I pulled at the yellowed cord over the sink. A bulb that had known better days woke and hummed.

It should have been ridiculous to be afraid in a place whose most dangerous weapon was a screwdriver.

From the front room came a sound.

Not the house settling. Not the river chewing on stones. Music. Thin, unwilling, threaded with air. Little Tin Soldier, but from far away, as if the walls were singing it.

I went still the way rabbits go still, everything inside me gathering to a point. The box under my arm was heavy and dumb and quiet. I had not wound anything downstairs. I had not touched any lid but the one in my hands. The note I’d tucked safe had numbers on it and my name in a dead man’s hand and no explanation at all.

The music went on, a handful of notes, the turn and the little lilt.

The clocks were dead. The house was not.

“Hello?” I said, because it is the stupid thing the living do when they want to pretend what they are hearing is human. Air moved somewhere. A draft or a breath. The front room had no light and the afternoon had already given itself willfully to November. The darkness there was full of furniture I could not see. I reached into it and it put its weight against me, and for a second I remembered that when Rosie was very small she liked to hide behind the desk in Hollis’s shop, where I could see her shoes unpaired and think: if I were witch-fire or a fox, this is how I would look before I showed myself.

The music stopped.

My heart learned an instrument it had never learned before. I took one step forward.

And then something upstairs, above the attic, above me where nothing was, made a sound like a clock starting to tick. One hard strike. The house, all at once, held its breath. I did too, waiting to hear if the world began again.

Chapter One: The Blue Envelope

The sorters spit letters in thin, angry gusts, and by six-thirty the trays are stacked in metal ribs along the wall like a set of bleachers filled with muttering paper. You learn to hear moods in the bins—utility bills come in thick and humorless, glossy catalogs rustle, seed brochures whisper promises. Today the machine is in a generous temper. Everything slides. Everything falls where it should until I see the blue.

It’s a shade you don’t get much in winter, a blue like enamel washed a hundred times. The envelope is the size of a wedding invite but the stock is cheap. It’s always the same: top right, a single American Flag stamp, always pressed a hair crooked; address printed in slow, careful block letters that lean uphill, as if stubbornness keeps them standing. C. Dalrymple. 42 Arcadia Lane. Our blue.

I flip it in my gloved hand. No return address, but I know the zip they cancel from: 02790. That’s Westport, maybe. Paper has memory, so do hands. I’ve been carrying this blue for a year and a half now, longer than I’ve been carrying most of the homes on Route 12. On the first Monday of each month, without fail, it rides out with me in the top of my bag like a coin in a pocket, a rain charm. The first month I noticed it because of the way the sorting tech held it a fraction longer than the others, the way you pause over a coin to see if it’s foreign. After that, it was the steadiness of it that made it stand out—the way storms canceled school and closed roads and tore shingles off Cape-style roofs, and still the blue was there in my tray. The world doesn’t have many things you can set your watch to. On my route, I had two: Mrs. Hemmings’s lemon bar on Thursdays, and the blue envelope on the first Monday.

It’s not Monday. It’s Friday, early. The fluorescent chorus in the hangar of the Whitespire Post Office hums and flickers the way it always does, the concrete floor chalked with salt and boot prints. Somebody somewhere dropped a box of chocolate the day after Valentine’s Day, and the smell has lingered in the metal air. There is nothing different about anything I can name, which is how I know two things will be different before the end of my morning. First, that the blue has come off schedule. Second, that something inside the house at 42 Arcadia Lane will not add up.

Whitespire is a coastal town that has forgotten how to be one. The old cannery stood until last winter when a storm pushed it into itself. Now we have a new development where a grocery store should go, a mural where a cannery stood, a nostalgia we take like a vitamin. When people ask me why I like carrying the route, I say the obvious thing—being outside—but it’s really that I know the backs of this town, the lines no one meant to draw. You can learn a life from its mail. You can learn how many times a week a man orders at-home test strips, whether he still gets postcards from his sister in Sarasota, whether someone has stopped sending the card they always sent at the holidays. You can tell when someone is practicing being missed.

We load, we go. The truck’s heater has the manners of a drunk, going full fervor or not at all. I coax it because I’m greedy for warmth and try not to imagine my breath leaving the cab and freezing on the bitter edges of the sorting floor behind me. Ice fur is growing along every mailbox flag in town. There is promise of warmer weather later—always there’s promise. Right now, it’s a two-dog morning and I’ve got the good biscuits.

I swing through the mill road and down by the marsh where the cattails hold their rust still stubbornly high, as if shielding something. Mrs. Hemmings has outdone herself with the lemon bar. It sits in a waxed paper parcel on the end of her brick stoop, so yellow it’s a dare in the thin light. I slide it into my bag for later, leave her the latest seed catalogs. At Finnerty’s, the brass slot in the antique door sticks like the memory of a grudge. I wedge in a new credit card for the salon—they are changing their logo, the new envelopes say, a softer kind of pink. The world has a way of signaling small changes with expensive envelopes, big changes with calls you don’t want to make.

When I turn onto Arcadia Lane, I tilt the mirror to watch the hidden bit of road that swings behind the pines. The houses here are better spaced than in the mill neighborhood, with longer drives and lamps that look like lanterns, glass clouded on purpose to soften the harshness of bulb. Half the houses hibernate all winter waiting for summer people. Half the houses have people in them who can’t leave. 42 Arcadia is a saltbox with honest siding, paint gone soft where sun bleached it. The first time I came here I wrote a note to myself about the way the shutters were hung—they weren’t faithful to the period, but they were brave in their crookedness.

The blue rides heavy in my bag as if something in it sops moisture from the air. When I stop at the end of the drive, the whole street feels paused, a breath held. You feel that sometimes when a storm’s traveling over another town, when pressure drops but nothing here has changed yet. Now a silence pools around the place like the water fans you see in potholes after a truck passes through.

I pull the mail from the box and stack it neat in my hand. There are three publisher’s clearinghouse mailers, a thin padded envelope that has been resealed by someone who does not care, a postcard from the Natural History Museum in D.C.—the photo is of a mammoth bone, the writing in back not there—and two days’ worth of local circulars. Thursday’s mail sits in the back of the box, blue-edged with frost. That’s wrong. Mr. Dalrymple always clears his box. In eighteen months, I haven’t seen more than a day’s mail left sitting there. He keeps a dry tin in the vestibule with a bribe for the dog on the corner but he doesn’t own one himself. He wears a hat with a brim even when it snows. He has a dignified way of carrying his age—this was all from the glimpses, the steady pace, the neatness of the stacks I could see through the window when he took his letters. No dog, no children. The monthly blue from Westport. Yesterday’s mail remains.

I take the steps up to the small porch. The magnolia in a galvanized tub to the left of the door is wound with careful burlap. The doormat says SWEEP. Someone has a sense of humor. Normally, a bell would chime when you open the storm door, but when I press, the hinge gives and the main door moves too. Lock unlatched. Air sliding cold out of somewhere deeper. There is a moment in construction when a wall looks like a wall but is not, when the studs are up but there’s no skin on them yet. The air around the doorway feels like that—a shape missing its skin.

“Mr. Dalrymple?” I say, because the rule is to say hello always, even when you are not sure. No answer. My own steps sound too loud. The cat that belongs to nobody at number 40 stares from the hedge with a disgusted yellow eye, then flicks away into the meshed dark of the shrubs.

I know about thresholds. Once, not long ago, I crossed one I shouldn’t have. It didn’t go wrong in any movie way—no one got hurt, nothing got broken. After, I had to understand that a line is not always drawn in the sand for you. Sometimes the line is drawn inside, and you pretend you can’t see it until the day you walk over and can feel it under your feet. The postmaster would say I shouldn’t go in. The postmaster would also say call it in, wait, do nothing. My job ends at the box. But the box is full. The door is open. The air that moves past me smells like winter and something mineral and something like… lemon? A familiar tang that makes no sense until I remember the little bowl of citrus Mister Dalrymple keeps on the bookcase to the right of the hall—old habit from his mother, he told me once in the glance of a sentence, to keep the house bright.

“Mr. Dalrymple?” I say again, lower. I step inside.

Flow marks tell a lot. The hall rug has two stains, one blue from rain like an old bruise, one brown the crispness of coffee. The dimmer on the wall is set low. To the right is the doorway to the study. Papers are arranged in stacks so square I want to put a lily pad on each one to see if a frog will come. There is a map pushed with pins, but it isn’t cities. It’s the coast, and the pins run not up and down the roads but along blue lines that look like veins. Tide charts. The smell of lemon is stronger. There is a ceramic dish with pieces of seaglass, just one of each color, not a scrap of brown. On the far wall, above the low bookcase, a row of postcards are thumbtacked in a perfect line. Each one bears a picture of something ordinary made strange: a laundromat with all the machines’ doors open; a ferry with no passengers; a theater marquee with letters missing so the words say nothing.

He is in the chair by the window.

I’ve seen death a few times. Not enough for it to be ordinary, not so few that it is mysterious anymore. There is a way a body gives up when there’s no one to rally for. He’s slumped sideways as if listening to the floor. One arm rests along the chair like it got tired of having a hand at the end of it. His slippers don’t match; one is plaid, one a brown so worn it is a suggestion of a shoe. His glasses sit on the low table, folded, next to a book turned face down. The spine reads The Bird in the Machinery. A fair play detective novel if the title’s to be believed. There is no theatricality—no overturned chair, no dramatics, just the small disaster of a life interrupted while sitting.

The worst thing in that first breath is that he looks like my father did when I found him in the diner storeroom last spring, the same tilt at the corner of the mouth, the same stubborn residual expression that says I was doing something. I swallow and feel the cold in the backs of my eyes. My father died quietly and unfairly, and the world went on to lunch. Today, too, isn’t interested in reverence.

I take a step closer, because not doing so takes an equal number of muscles as doing so and I am already using them all. His chest does not rise. His hand rests palm-up on the arm, and the lines there are deep, deeper than I would have guessed. In his palm the skin is crumpled from having clenched, then unaimed. There is no blood, no disarray. The house has that set to it, the way a place is when a person is still inside it somewhere by habit but not by will.

“Okay,” I say, to no one, which is what you say sometimes to keep the sentence you’re not going to say from coming out. I back up to the doorway and hit 911 with my thumb. My voice steadies after the second word; the operator’s voice is clean and young. I give the address. I tell her I am a carrier. I tell her I found my customer. Her sentences make a neat block I can set my own against. Yes, I am safe. No, there is no sign of a break-in beyond the door unlatched. Yes, I will wait outside. Yes, I can check to see if there’s anyone else in the house. No, I hear nothing. No, I do not know his next of kin. Yes, I will meet them by the road. They are coming. They are always coming.

I close my phone and it looks wrong in my hand, plastic and light, surrounded by paper that has heft, paper that arrives by force of habit and weather and the grit of people who drove it into town or rolled it down conveyor belts with fingers split from salt. I will wait outside. I will obey the rule. But on the low table by the chair, next to the glasses and the book laid down half read, sits an envelope addressed in neat block letters to Ms. June Park.

It is inescapably and unforgivably mine.

There are a hundred reasons it could be there and I don’t like any of them. There are ten reasons I should not touch it. But the law that built itself in me while I learned these roads is simple: if a name is on a thing and I am the engine that takes that name to the thing, then I am a wheel on which necessary things turn. And in this case the name on the thing is mine. That tips the scale.

I bend, slow because everything in the room deserves slow. With one hand I ease the envelope toward me by its corner, not touching the table, and slide it from under the slight shadow where it rested. There is no seal on it. The flap is tucked. This feels like an apology from the universe for all the sealed things. On the front, my name is even, the P of Park as precisely proportioned as the everyday little railing on Mr. Dalrymple’s porch. In the left corner, no stamp. This did not go through. This did not leave the house. This is a thing placed and kept.

I slide my thumb under the flap. Inside is a single sheet of paper and, taped to the back with clear tape that has yellowed the tiniest bit along the edge, a key. The key is brass, flat, not a house key. It has the weight of thrift, the way a thing you’ve had for many years gets heavier because it has to hold everything you’ve asked it to open. The head is stamped with a number—12—and the word Harbor.

The letter is handwritten in a script that flies tight close to the line. I step into the doorway where the light is younger and read.

June—

If you are reading this, it means I’m late as well as imprecise, and both are offenses in our profession. I call it our profession because while you transport other people’s words for a living, I have been collecting them for mine. Forgive the presumptuousness. We have exchanged nearly nothing in words, but I have known your footfall on these steps better than some might know a voice.

I need to ask for a kindness that will not look like kindness while you’re doing it.

On my desk drawer you will find, taped underneath, a second key that matches the one I have sent you. There is a locker at the Harbor Depot marked 12. Inside is a ledger that does not belong with the olds down there. It does not belong with the living, either. I have kept it because it needs keeping until it doesn’t. If this finds you, please take the ledger from the Harbor and give it to no one in a uniform until we have had a chance to talk. And if we can’t talk, then please keep it for three days. After that, take it to the person whose name is written on the first page. You’ll know why when you see it.

I am sorry. You will hate me a little for laying it on you like this. I have no one else I can ask with so clear a conscience. The people who could ask me for such a thing are all inside the ledger one way or another.

You have always walked my letters with a particular measure. I am trusting that measure now.

—C.D.

Outside, a siren lifts like a gull and falls. It is far enough that a whole life lives in the space between its rise and its arriving. On the page, my name looks like someone took pains. A line has been drawn inside me, invisible until his hand wrote my name across it. I feel it then the way you feel a seam when a dress sits wrong. The key taped to the back of the page is cool. When I peel the tape, it holds on in that sticky, whispering way that means someone expected me to succeed at removing it.

Three days sounds long until something has to be done inside of it.

There are shoes on the mat by the door, a pair of boots that have seen salt, and beyond them the road that curves where the weight of the trucks has cracked the asphalt. The operator’s neat block of instructions sits in my ear like a calm room. Wait outside, meet them by the road. Do not touch anything else.

I glance once at the desk. Down here, the Harbor Depot hasn’t been a depot for twenty years. It used to be a ferry terminal. Then a storage facility. Now it’s a place with a row of lockers where high school couples hide notes under happier locks, and fishermen keep extra boots, and one woman in her fifties stashes her bad habits out of her husband’s reach. I know this because I deliver to all of them. I know this because Whitespire knows this about itself: everything goes out before it comes back in.

A locker marked 12. A ledger. A three-day vow. My name where it has never been in this house before. Outside, the increasing complaint of a new siren joins the first. Blue light slashes the snow-bent shrubs. I hear the crunch of tires on frost-buckled gravel. It occurs to me that at some point, I stopped being outside the room and started being inside that line, the one drawn in me. Later I’ll trace the exact second—the exact letter inside my name where I crossed. If I had to choose, I would say it was the part where he wrote we share a profession. That I transport words. That I am not just someone who turns keys in boxes, but an engine in the turning.

On the way out, I reach without thinking under the front edge of the desk drawer. There is tape there, the aged kind that fights you. My fingernail wedges under. It gives with a small paper sound. The second key is twin to the first. I do not give myself time to measure the ethics of it. I put both keys and the letter inside the pocket of my coat where the lemon bar would have gone if I had not been hungry enough to eat it on the way down Harbor Road. I close the drawer gently until the latch whispers. I step back into the hall, then out onto the small porch.

The morning air has teeth. The magnolia's burlap crinkles as if it were alive with some small thing inside. The road is everywhere that roads are, and coming up it are two cruisers and an ambulance, lights grabbing at the bay trees and dying there. I put my hand in my pocket and feel the shape of the key that belongs to the Harbor and the key that belongs to the bottom of the drawer and the folded letter that belongs to me, and I think: I am later and less precise than I should be, too. I am not late yet. Precision may still be possible.

The first cruiser stops with a grunt of suspension. Officer Ronson—who lost his house in the storm, who now makes a practice of lingering at traffic lights and letting two cars go through because he knows what it is to have to get somewhere—steps out and squints in the cold.

“June,” he says when he sees me. He doesn’t look surprised. I don’t know if that’s better or worse. “You the one called?”

“I am,” I say. The wind lifts my hair and slaps it back down in a gesture that feels like punctuation. The keys in my pocket lie against my leg and go warm against my skin. In the study behind me, a man who collected other people’s words lies listening to nothing. Out here, the morning arranges itself around what comes next.

Ronson’s eyes skip to the half-open door, then back to me. “You all right?”

“Not especially,” I say, because I find that honesty is easier to carry than its opposite. He nods and moves past me, one hand at the radio at his shoulder, and the little bell on the storm door, which never rings for me, chimes just once as if to say the expected thing when not expected.

Three days, the letter said. Later, if I am telling this to someone, I will say the first chapter of what happened started with a blue envelope arriving on a day it wasn’t supposed to and ended with a different blue flashing against a wall of postcards, but that’s not exactly true. It started with a door left unlatched. It started with thinking I knew the lines and finding out that the town had drawn new ones without telling me. It started with my name in someone else’s careful block letters and a ledger that does not belong with the living or the dead.

It starts, I think now, standing with my hand in my pocket and the sirens quieting as the engines idle, with the feeling of the key in my palm and the knowledge that I have already decided to turn it.

I never trusted empty rooms that remembered voices. They have a way of sounding like prayer: breath hitching where a person used to stand, tiny clicks in the wood as if syllables were settling there in the grain. When I unlocked the front door to the station, the air was cold and salty, and the room tone rushed me the way the ocean did when you took a step too close to the edge.

WQBR took up three rooms in a decommissioned customs house, a square of gray shingled stone facing the harbor, its roof line like a shrug against the weather. Someone had taped cardboard over the cracked pane beside the door. The sign under the eaves still said THE QUAY in faded letters; the T had peeled so it read HE QUAY, which seemed about right. I should’ve been happy we’d managed to sell the license. Now I could do what I was sent to do, and what I had told myself I was capable of doing: dismantle, box, list, sign, go.

But it wasn’t my city station. It was this one. My hometown’s radio noise. The boards were the kind you have to coax. When I touched the edge of the console in Studio A, the old laminate felt warm despite the chill, as if a hand had just left it. The monitor speakers were squat and scuffed, and the ON AIR light—once a blood-orange square—hung dead and dusty over the window. A coffee mug with our call letters sat on the windowsill, ringed by salt. The last playlist was still thumbtacked, all lowercase and abbreviations: joni. sirens from the point. psas. The handwriting was Robyn’s, round and stubborn. She’d left me a note under the mug: Iris, take whatever you want. Keys are in the sugar jar. Lock up.

The sugar jar was empty. The keys were in there anyway.

Outside, gulls sawed the air. It was off-season, late November. The boats had gone out early; by midafternoon the floats would be stacked in the parking lot like enormous mute bracelets. I hadn’t told anyone I was coming except the foundation director in Portland, who emailed a list of the gear she wanted salvaged, and the bank, which wanted the boxes to be packed, logged, and out by Friday.

I dropped my bag in the newsroom and went to wake the warm, slow heart of the board. I’d spent years in Chicago learning to ride boards that never slipped, that knew exactly who they were and did remarkably useful things like take commands. The Quay’s faders felt like pushing two coins through honey. I flipped the power buttons, and the counters rolled to life. The VU meters bopped lazily. Something deep in the equipment rack coughed and then settled into a soft whir.

Studio A smelled of curling paper, hot dust, and that strange acetic tang of old tape—vinegar from acetate when it gives up, a smell I learned here without knowing its formal name. It turns out you can leave where you were born and learn the names of things, but they don’t stop smelling the way they smelled when you were sixteen.

I set a spare mug with fresh water at the one remaining potted plant by the window—someone’s tired, victorious philodendron—and it did what plants do: it accepted that it would be neglected and would survive. Then I started opening cabinets.

We called it the archive, as if there was curation involved. It was a metal lateral file with three drawers, the middle one locked, the others a mess of CDRs in paper sleeves, DAT tapes in cloudy cases, cassette tapes whose labels had come unglued and stuck sympathetically to one another like remarried couples. The middle drawer had been labeled AIRCHECKS with silver duct tape and a Sharpie; below that it said DO NOT REMOVE. The key to the sugar jar also fit that lock.

A thin, tight smell rushed out when I slid the drawer. Inside, like neatly stacked loaves, sat four reels of quarter-inch tape in flat cardboard boxes, the kind with a little central window so you could see if there was any hope. Each reel had been labeled a generation ago when we pretended to log everything we put into the air. AIR-121210-L. AIR-042409-PLEDGE. Those. Under them, a bunch of loose label bands slipped like bracelets.

I didn’t come here for this. I came here to take the good CD players, the compressor if it still worked, the microphones if the rust hadn’t got at them. But the date on the top box had heat: 121210. December twelfth, 2010.

That was the last night we broadcast through a storm, and the first night in twenty years when the Chief had sent someone out to the breakwater to look for a body before the bad water did its worst. It was the night the tower went dead, and the transmitter cooling fans moaned into silence. It was the night Kit Bishop didn’t come home.

Of course, the box might have just held what it said—an aircheck, a routine recording of our output. That was what we used to do when there was a pledge drive or a new morning host, or when the FCC wanted to know that we were indeed running the mandated public service announcements about backflow prevention. Most of us forgot. Eli didn’t. Eli Marden had run this place like a garage where he tuned a single battered Buick to run forever. He believed in logs, in airchecks, and in the idea that if you were going to speak on the radio you should have something to say.

I turned around and looked at the empty doorway. The faintest draft went through. Nobody else was here. It was just me, and the boards, and a box marked with a date like a scar.

Reel-to-reel machines were better than people. They did exactly what you told them unless a belt snapped or the world intervened. WQBR had a ReVox B77 that we’d inherited from the Catholic station across the river the year they sold their frequency and moved to spots about insurance and God. It lived under a dust cover in the rack room. I pulled back the cover. There were three fruit stickers on the faceplate—Gala, Pink Lady, Braeburn—affixed to the right of the speed selector. Years ago, someone’s idea of decoration. I damp-wiped the heads with isopropyl, let the cold evaporate, threaded the tape with muscle memory: leader on the left spindle, wrap around the tension arm, across the heads, around the capstan, onto the right reel, two turns, snug, check the loops, clear the path. The machine’s buttons were brutal, square, and satisfying. I pressed play.

At first there was nothing. Then a soft hiss—the noise floor. The VU needles lifted. Something came in from far away. A song rose mid-bar, a baritone whose consonants were obscured by salt, which could have been anyone. After a few seconds it crossfaded to a station ID—one of Eli’s: “You’re listening to The Quay. We aim to please and occasionally we hit the target.” His voice occupied the comfortable register he reserved for announcing bake sales and city council follies. Then another song came in, some piano in a minor key, then out. A regular day.

I was listening to the past which meant I was already eavesdropping. The coil in my stomach that had been dormant in the car ride up—through the pine corridor, past the antique barns turned into stores that sold scented candles that smelled like the idea of woodsmoke—wound itself tighter.

After the second song, the phone line clicked open. On the air we had two ways of getting callers; Eli preferred to record and play, but sometimes he answered live. On the tape, I heard a ring, a pause, the click of a control button, the hollow of telephone space. “WQBR, you’re live at the Quay. Who’s this?” Eli said.

At first, only breath.

“Hello?” He kept it cheerful but not false. He had a way of making silence feel like a friend who was thinking of your question.

A voice came in then, high and small with the compression, like a bird. “We did it wrong,” it said.

Eli paused. He didn’t fill. I swallowed. On the tape the hiss seemed louder, as if it were wind pressed right up to a crack in a window.

“Say it again?” he asked finally.

“We did it wrong,” the voice repeated. I had the stupid instinct to look behind me, as if whoever said it had been hiding in our newsroom for fifteen years and was about to come out with a shrug, older and forgiving. The ReVox’s motors murmured.

“What is it that you did wrong?” Eli asked gently.

There was the sense of someone moving near the phone, or moving the phone. Then, so soft I almost missed it, a name. “Mar—” It clipped. A scrape. “Please tell him. He’ll know.”

Eli’s chair creaked across forty feet of tape and time. On air, once, certain names fretted him. He was a man with the old contagions: loyalty, privacy, a belief that some things traveled like fever. “You’ve reached The Quay,” he said after a beat, as if steering us back to the script. “We’re—”

“We did it wrong,” the voice insisted, and I heard it then, the tremor. Whoever it was, they were working to not cry, which in Telephone I learned early is a language all its own; you make your vowels smaller so they won’t come apart. Then behind it, another voice, low and close enough that the first picked up its consonants like a second signal. “Hang up,” the other said.

Eli said, low and off-mic, like a man turning away from a microphone but not far enough, “Do not use names. You listening?” Then into the board: “Caller, we can’t hear you. Call back.”

“What did you do?” he had asked me once when I was fifteen and trying to cut a spot, and I’d spliced the leader onto the wrong side of the tape so everything played backward. “Only one way to learn,” he said, and gave me back the razor blade.

I let the reel run another thirty seconds. On the tape, as if nothing had happened, a song started—a local band, a droning guitar—but beneath it, faint as freckles, I heard something else: the clonk and hush of the lobby door, the sticky hinge on the studio, a chair dragging. Eli had left the caller on the line. He was moving.

The rest of that half hour was nothing. Music. Eli back-announce. PSA about the library book sale. A call from Mrs. O’Keefe about adopting an old dog. Then more music. The end of the reel was leader. I hit stop.

My hand was cold. I was standing with two fingers on two buttons like a person trying to stop a train with a wish. This was a second. It could be nothing. It could be someone drunk. It could be a kid. It could be a wrong number. The night the tower went out there had been a dozen calls. I remembered the storm’s hum down the mic cables, how the castellations of the breakwater disappeared in the snow, how everything sounded like it was trying to find its own frequencies in order to leave.

But the date sat there on the calendar that had once been a piece of cardboard and was now a memory. And the voice had the tremor of the night. And the other voice. “Hang up.” So calm. The night Kit took the long walk out on the rocks, they said, she was calm. That was how people told the story who had never wept in a bathroom stall while their roommate pounded on the door and begged not to be chosen for that kind of love.

There are certain landings your bones learn to prepare for, even when you’re not sure how high the stairs are. I rewound, played it again, and listened to the vowel shapes with the part of my brain that pays my rent—my small talent for hearing under things. Radio teaches you to listen the way birds look at a field: alert, specific, willing to be wrong. On the third pass, the name was there. The missing piece of the syllable, scritched by the phone line. It wasn’t “Mark.” It wasn’t “Mary.” It was “Marek.”

That didn’t belong here. Not in Maine. Not in our town. Marek was a name I knew from the freezer cases at the grocery store: the white-bearded Polish man with the notebook who rented out rooms above the hardware store and bought two whole fresh cod on Fridays, cash. If you saw him at seven in the morning, he had already cleaned something—a sidewalk, a debt, a story.

Tell him. He’ll know.

My mouth went dry like I’d swallowed a fistful of the sugar jar. If I were the person I liked to imagine I’d become since leaving, I would have closed the drawer and put the reel back and told myself the story of process and property and moved my hands in steady, capable ways. Instead I cleaned the heads again, threaded the second reel, the one labelled AIR-121210-L 2 of 2 in Eli’s tidy block letters, and hit Play.

This one opened with a howl. The emergency tone we only used when the town’s volunteer fire frequency bled into ours, or when somebody pressed the wrong thing. I jerked the volume down and then back to a sane level. Under the tone, faint as a prayer, there were voices. The tone cut. Eli came back boyish and contrite, a smile in his mouth. “Sorry for the noise, folks. Weather’s got the gremlins out. Keep your pets in, get your cars off the street near the Point, and if you must go admire the feral ocean tonight, do it from somewhere it can’t take a bite out of you.” A song. Ads. Then more ring. The phone line clicked open.

“You really shouldn’t,” a man said. Not Eli. Close to the board. Maybe into the control room mic, the one we never used.

“I’m on record already,” Eli said, not joking. “Don’t do this to me.”

“Then cut it,” the man said. “Kill the transmitter. We’ll get the logs handled.”

If you’ve never been in a small station while someone uses the word logs in that tone, I hope you never have that moment. It’s like hearing a pastor say the phrase “technicality” while he’s holding a baby. The room shrinks.

On the tape, a fist hit a table. Paper jumped. A door opened. “Eli.” A new voice then, a woman. The phone line picks everything, invites everything. “There’s a call for you. It’s the Bishop house.”

I put a hand against the edge of the board because my legs had betrayed me once, in Mrs. Bishop’s kitchen, and I’d learned. Hot tea looks like ordinary tea right until it burns.
