Eli must have turned the caller’s fader down, or away, because there was a shiver of indoor sound, then music, then nothing anyone said could be heard like words. If the studio mic stayed live, it only caught chair-yawn and fabric and the near-silent screaming of a person who leaves a room with their mouth all clenched. After a minute the tone came again. Then the clean missingness of silence.

When the tape clicked through leader to clear leader and the reels spun with nothing on them but good intentions, I stood with the weight of that held between two fingers. I had to look away from the machine to breathe properly. The window to the soundproofing showed me a gull bellying into the wind, committing to a landing on the fire escape across the alley, changing its mind.

In Portland, where the bathrooms at the station have beeswax soap and a chirpy sign that says your pledge makes this possible, there is a glass conference room with a gigantic framed photograph of a ship’s wheel and the words WE NAVIGATE COMMUNITY. When my boss had asked me to do this—“We thought you could, you know, do it gently”—I had rolled my eyes when I hung up, at no one, at the idea that mercy could be applied like a sticker to a box.

I set the tape to rewind. While it did, I went digging.

I found the paper logs in the second drawer under the mixer—a ring binder fat with carbon copies. I turned past months of menial: missing carts, wrong spots, power dips and little notes from people who had loved this place enough to leave their tidy handwriting as a defense against chaos. December 2010’s sheets were there. And there it was, in Eli’s block letters: 21:42—POWER FAILURE, WEATHER. 21:43—ON GENERATOR. 21:47—TRANSMITTER LOSS. 22:30—SIGN-OFF DUE TO CONDITIONS.

Airchecks existed so that we could argue with our own stories. The tape told me there had been voices, and a tone, and a decision. The log told me the weather had taken us out. I had lived long enough in this town to know that weather is a beautiful lie because it is almost always true.

Footsteps came from the hall, the kind that are not sneaking. They came light and slow along the carpet, a rhythm learned from years of moving in that particular space and failing to announce yourself because you never had to. I didn’t turn. If it was the wind knocking something loose, I didn’t want to learn that it was the wind. If it was someone human, I wanted them to meet the back of me that they had always taken for granted.

A knuckle rapped on the glass.

“Iris?” said a voice that hadn’t changed. “I thought that was your car.”

Robyn had always sounded like she was calling you across a boat. That little lift on the end, the smile you couldn’t disbelieve even when you wanted to. She held a brown paper bag like it contained something moral. The bag read MARLEY’S DELI on it in green marker, which meant she had bribed Gary to keep the slicer on past closing. Her breath fogged the glass. She looked down at the ReVox and then up at me with her eyebrows making the old shape that said I know, and also, what did you do.

“I brought soup,” she said, as if that were an apology for some enormous, unnameable thing. “And because you won’t think about dinner. And because my mother said I should. Also, you can’t be here after dark.”

“Is that a law?” I asked, still bent over the reel as if it were the thing that could fall and break.

Robyn’s smile went to edges. “No,” she said. “It’s a courtesy. For Marek.” She leaned in so close to the glass I could see salt wear on her bottom lip. “He doesn’t like it if you play the tapes.”

Chapter One: Bearings

Maps are polite liars. They’ll show you borders and roads with such clean confidence that you forget how messy it felt to walk them. They promise that a channel is always navigable, a dotted line has agreed-upon meaning, a dash of green reliably becomes forest beneath your boots. It’s a comfort, the quiet authority of ink. It was also, depending on the week and the client, my profession, my consolation, and my practiced sin.

The ferry to Grayhaven groaned like a tired animal, its hull nosing through the last gray skirts of fog as the island resolved itself: a bruised hill, a scab of wharf, a row of pickets like teeth. Late October, the kind of air that gets into your bones and sets up a whistle. Twelve cars, eight passengers, a pallet of feed, a roll of hose, two crates of mail. My survey case was buckled to the passenger bench beside me—aluminum scuffed and stickered with places I liked to think I’d earned—and my old transit, wrapped in a wool army blanket, sat in my lap like a sleeping child.

“You’re meant for the Tanney’s fight, then?” the captain asked when he came out of the wheelhouse to stamp cold from his feet. He was a thick man with a burst of broken veins across his cheekbones and eyes so pale they seemed nearly colorless. He had the effortless nosiness of someone no one evaded.

“I’m meant for a map,” I said, which was true without being precious. “Who’s Tanney?”

He snorted softly. “If you’re making a map here, every name’ll be Tanney after an hour. Or Fitch. Or Bell—God rest him. It’s about the oyster leases. The spring storms shifted the sandbar, and everyone and their brother wants what used to be under the other fella’s plot now under theirs. They tell me you can sort that with lasers. I tell them—” He made a little circle with his finger in the air, some rustic charm of waves and weather.

Lasers were the least of it. In my case there’d be transceivers and base stations, tidal correction tables, soil compaction analyses, mean low water marks. Systems for turning a winter’s grudge into something measurable, a line both sides could sign. And if that line meant a man’s income for the year, his children’s rents, then the line had to be right.

“Bell?” I asked, trying to keep my voice casual. “Eamon Bell?”

“The map man,” the captain said, and his mouth softened. “Went into the sea two years ago next month. Some of us keep the day. He knew where we were before we were there.” He pushed off the rail with his fingers and went back into the wheelhouse without waiting to hear about how Eamon Bell’s transit sat on my lap now, its brass lens cap worn smooth by his hand. There was very little to say that didn’t sound like superstition.

The letter that had brought me here waited in the pocket of my coat, sour with salt and the memory of a practical hand. It had arrived two weeks ago without a return address, postmarked Grayhaven, the paper stiff as though it had been folded and unfolded many times before.

Mara,

Don’t laugh at me: you’ll want the old benchmarks, not the LIDAR. They’re discovered, not placed. Come soon. The tides have been wrong.

—E.B.

I had not laughed. I had written Eamon’s initials again and again on the back of an envelope as if I could force the hand to keep moving, have it climb back into itself. I had stared at the single line—discovered, not placed—and felt the old vertigo of the room at the Bureau in Portland, the day we’d opened their drawer of antique coastal markers, brass disks stamped with names like hymnals: US COAST & GEODETIC SURVEY 1932 DO NOT DISTURB. They had a density to them, a seriousness. Eamon had pressed my fingers to them and said, “If you pull one up, three states lean sideways. If you set one wrong, the world pretends it was always that way.”

He had drowned before I could come here and let him lead me to the oldest bones. Whoever sent the letter had waited until after.

We shouldered up to the splintered pilings of the ferry slip, the smell of creosote and old sea in my throat. A boy ran along the dock to catch the hawser. He was narrow as hunger and wore his hair like a question mark. A black dog loped behind him and barked twice for the pleasure of the sound. Onshore was motion and then the island’s stillness, a kind of restraint, like a held breath. The lighthouse at the northern tip, White Bell, blinked its single eye three times and paused. I counted the interval without thinking. My father had taught me: three seconds light, two dark, three light, seven dark, repeat. Every light had a signature the way every voice did. Eamon had used to time them against the beat of his own pulse.

My car made the thirteenth in the line of twelve and I took that as a small island joke. When we rolled off the ramp a woman in a denim jacket and a wool hat was waiting beside a sign that said POST & GENERAL. She was the kind of person you couldn’t stand next to without telling her something she hadn’t asked yet.

“You’re Sloane?” she said when I had my box in both hands. “I got your message. Nora Tanney.”

I wanted to correct her—Mara Keene, not Sloane—but somewhere between the dock and her eyes the name stuck to a felt of assumptions and I kept mine to myself. Names are part of the spell too.

“Welcome to Grayhaven,” she said, the words flat as a board. “Come on. You’ll want to drop your things. The fog will be back at dusk. It always is.”

Nora carried my tripod with the nonchalance of someone who had carried heavy things and admired herself a little for it. Her shop smelled of paraffin and coffee and salt. There were bins of twine, bundles of cedar shingles, penny candy for people who had lost the habit of treating themselves. She handed me a key on a carved bit of driftwood strung with red twine.

“Room at the top,” she said. “Bathroom’s at the end of the hall. If you’ve got a wish to write anything down, buy the notebook now because the books in the house you’re in will not be ones you want to write in.”

“Is that an advertisement?” I asked.

“That is kindness,” she said lightly, and then: “One more thing. My cousin’s the constable. If you find anything that looks like a bone, a boat, or a curse, call her before you look harder. She won’t thank you if you put your fingers somewhere and then have to argue about what you thought you were touching.”

It was so literal it almost made me laugh. “What if I find them all at once?”

“Then you’ll fit in,” she said, and the corner of her mouth flicked up.

The room at the top was as narrow and long as a ship’s berth. The window faced the harbor and the curve of marsh beyond. The island was not large; my field notes said three miles north to south and a mile and a half across at its widest, with a spine of spruce and rock, a half-ruined farm in the middle where someone with a dream had once tried to grow peaches on granite and fog, two dozen year-round families, two hundred houses that remembered summer. White Bell lighthouse stood at the far point of a bar that broke across low tide like a knuckle. It had not always been called White Bell. Names moved the way sand did, with storms and shame.

I set my box on the bed and unbuckled it. The new world smelled faintly of machine oil and coffee. My transit came away from the wool blanket with a sigh. It was a handsome thing, brass and glass, delicate as a violin. I checked its levels, rotated the scope, felt for the ghost of Eamon’s hand where his palm had polished the arc smooth. No one had ever found his body, only his boots washing up by the eelgrass, and a field book speckled with rain on the first page and nothing after.

Discovered, not placed.

On Grayhaven, as in many coastal places, the benchmarks didn’t live where I wished them to. People had used the same rocks and tree boles for so long they were part of their lore. You dug down beside a big granite shoulder and you’d find a brass disk once, twice, layered with the lives of surveyors who had come there year after year to make sure the baseline was still itself. I had planned three days of reconnaissance, two to place my base station, a day to argue with someone, and then the steady work itself. That assumed the island held still for me. Nora’s remark about fog suggested it did not.

I walked down off the porch with my tripod on my shoulder and the transit in its canvas sling, the letter in my pocket whispering its monotone. On the road two men stopped talking when they saw me and did not smile. A woman with gull-white hair pushed a pram the island did not need. A boy at the end of the wharf threw a line and hauled it back, threw it and hauled it, trying to pull something invisible to him out of sight.

I began at the wharf itself because there had been an old marker there according to the register, stamped 1936, with a little arrow and the number 1. It should have been in the lip of the granite block nearest the third mooring ring. I made myself walk and not count. It is a curse to think that if you do a thing in exactly the right sequence the world will leave your intentions alone.

The ring was there, black and smooth as ink. The granite was there, pocked with the history of barnacles. The disk was not. In its place was an oval of tar, like a healed wound. Around it the stone was scored in six neat crescents where someone had used a pry bar in the careful, patient way you’d use to extract a nail you didn’t want to break.

I balanced the tripod against my hip and put my finger in the oval. It was cold and slick. There was a grit on the edges that felt like the rime left when a wave pulls back and leaves the salt in your hair.

“Who would pull a benchmark?” I asked aloud.

“Someone with a grudge and a map,” a voice said behind me. I turned and squinted up at a tall man with a beanie pulled down over his ears and a face that had been arranged around the idea that other people were the problem. He had the shoulders of someone who had lifted lobster traps since puberty. The dog with the black coat had decided he belonged to him.

“You’re one of the Tanneys,” I said, because he wasn’t, and it is sometimes useful to let someone correct you.

“Fitch,” he said, and it sounded like a complaint he’d had to live with. “You’re the map lady. I’m guessing you’d prefer I didn’t say ‘map girl.’ Nora said you were coming. She also said you’d be nosy.”

“I didn’t pull your benchmark,” I said. “Though it would make my life easier to pretend it was never here. Who did?”

He stared at the hole. For a second something unguarded crossed his face, that mix of grief and calculation people wear when they realize they have lost a thing they want the credit for mourning. “Eamon told a lot of boys to leave things where they were,” he said finally. “The trouble is, when men grow up they don’t like boys telling them anything.”

“Eamon pulled his own anchor?” I asked, before I could stop myself. The word felt disrespectful until I said it, and then it settled comfortably in the air. That was what a benchmark was—the point everything else angles off, the thing that makes the crooked clear.

Fitch shifted his weight, deterritorializing. “He was a stubborn bastard. But he didn’t do this.” He narrowed his pale eyes at me. “You map people, you like your stories. Here’s one: my great-grandfather put in for an oyster bed when they were giving them out like pew seats. It got silted over by a storm in ’68, and they took it from him because the powers-that-be said the bed had moved. And then the ‘new bed’ that they gave him hadn’t got so much as a fucking shell. You tell me about movement. You tell me about the God-damned truth of it.”

“The truth,” I said, because flinching was worse, “is that the mean low water mark remembered it one way and your great-grandfather remembered it another. Neither one is wrong. One of them gets to be enforceable. That’s why I’m here. To pick which truth you can live with.”

His mouth twisted in something like respect and something like disgust. “You’ll want to talk to Ivy at the constable’s. And don’t let Nora make you pay for coffee again. She’ll say it’s a dollar because she’s trying to build character, but it’s a trap.”

He moved down the wharf with his dog flowing ahead of him. At the end he turned and said, as if it were an afterthought that had crawled into his throat and had to be expelled, “If you’re looking for the next mark, there’s one up by White Bell. Eamon liked to walk there. He called it his number two. He liked to mess with words like that, because he thought it made men like me more likely to listen.”

I stood for a while with my fingers in the tar and the unlatching sound of a ferry’s departure ticking through my bones. There is a feeling that some places have, as if the hinge is out of true. The sky above Grayhaven wasn’t any different from the sky over any other harbor, mawkish and hard to take seriously, and yet I kept wanting to lean. I set my tripod, put the instrument on, leveled it, sighted a set of nothing and a double-sighted second nothing for practice. I chose a datum in my head and told myself a line.

The path to White Bell runs along the north shore of the harbor and then out on a spit and then along a bar as if a finger had traced the sea and said, “Stop.” Twice I skidded on eelgrass slick as felt. Someone had cut back the beach roses recently and their smell stuck sweet and dark to my clothes.

There is a certain humility in walking with a tripod on your shoulder like something you are carrying to your own burial. The lighthouse got larger without seeming to move. We had loved lighthouses as children, and then adult life teaches you that their keepers were lonely and sometimes mean. Eamon had never seemed mean. Lonely could be a profession if you did it right.

The second benchmark was supposed to be at the base of the iron ladder that went up the side of the White Bell tower. The paint was newer than I wanted it to be, eggshell, careful. There was a padlock on the trapdoor at the base with a tag on it that said HARBOR AUTHORITY. The rest of the world had sneaked into the island and set its hand on things.

I knelt. This disk was in place. The rim was green with age, but the center shone where a thumb had worried it. US COAST & GEODETIC SURVEY STATION NO. 2. There was a triangle in the center. There were also initials scratched along the edge so fine they were almost decorative: E.B. I laid the edge of my hand next to them and my skin made a ghost of his. Something caught in my throat I did not admire.

“Come soon,” the letter had said. “The tides have been wrong.”

I glanced up at the ladder, at the silent glass above. The light had not rotated. I looked out at the bay, at the line the tide made in the eelgrass like a child’s ruler. I had not yet set a base station to tell me what wrong would look like, and yet it felt wrong. The wind was wrong too, coming off the sea in short rough pulls like a man trying to lift something he’d three-quarters given up on lifting.

I unsnapped my rod and my prism and did what I could without my team and my times. The island had no patience for people who needed others to decide what to do. When I stood to stretch my back there was a figure at the end of the bar, black against the gray, standing where the water fumed white. A gull, I told myself, then a person, then a trick of refraction. It did not move until I did. Then it lifted a hand—either a wave or a warning—and stepped sideways and vanished. The sea had no interest in registering my shock.

“Saw that, did you?” Nora’s voice came behind me. She had—without any theatrics—materialized like fog, her boots leaving clean wet crescents. She put a paper cup into my hand without looking at me. It was coffee. Against my better judgment I took a swallow and felt like a prisoner making a deal with her warden.

“Who is it?” I asked, but I’d made my sentence a set of sounds that could have meant any number of things. What had I just seen? Was I meant to have seen it? Would the island allow me to speak of it? How little of me counted here.

“Depends on the day,” she said dryly. “On Sundays it’s the ghost of my aunt who never learned to swim. On Mondays it’s the mainland with its pockets turned out. On Fridays?” She shrugged. “On Fridays it’s a Fitch, usually, stealing the world out from under me by pretending he’s the only one who knows where it was to begin with.”

I crouched again beside the benchmark, took out my phone, and opened the gallery to the photograph I had taken in Portland of another disk—Eamon’s hand next to it, though I had not intended to catch that part in frame. The scar along his index finger from some careless field day. The nails, clean and squared. The little crescent of dirt he would carry under the cuticle and pretend to be embarrassed by. Record of a human being and a habit, which is what most of us get.

“Did Eamon send you a letter?” I asked, keeping my voice light, failing to keep the tremor out of my words.

Nora’s eyes flicked to my pocket and away. “I saw it,” she said. “It was in a bundle of old mail that someone hadn’t posted because someone else told them we were never going to need his wry little sayings again. Before you ask, the someone is not who you think. Before you ask the second time: everything on this rock is who you think and not.”

“You don’t think much of me yet,” I said. I was not offended. I keep a tidy house around my feeling of offense, and let it out only on special days when I’m sure I can feed it.

“I don’t think much of anyone who arrives with a number and expects to be paid for it,” Nora said, with an honesty so clean I could have leaned my level against it. “But I like men who taught me things, and I hate how the sea snuck up behind one of them when he was showing off. So: I think I’ll give you a week.”

“And after a week?” I asked.

“You tell me where my shore is,” she said. “You tell me I can write my name on it in the frost and see it again in the morning. You tell me what belongs to me.”

“That’s not how—” I began, and then the light in the White Bell tower, which had been dark and then bright in steady, lawful sequence as the fog peeled back and the afternoon light lengthened, stuttered, jerked, went dead. It should not have done that. Even a bulb failing does not sound so much like a sound taken with its breath held.

From the harbor, a voice rose like a gull’s and broke in the middle where gulls never do. It was not a cry that called a name. It was a cry that tears something from the throat that you needed to keep.

I was already moving, my hand on the plumb bob because the human mind will always choose to secure a small thing when the large one is falling. The dog barked. The wind fisted where the water whitened over the bar. And at the base of the White Bell tower, in the little seam of shadow where the metal of the ladder met the paint of the door, something caught the light that had just gone out: a coin of brass, glinting. I bent and picked it up.

It was not a coin. It was the center circle from a benchmark, punched out with expert force and the indifference of someone whose job was erasure. On the rim, faint and fussy, there were letters: US COAST & GEODETIC SURVEY. In the slick where it had sat, where there should have been tar and granite only, the impression it left was filled instead with a curl of wet, light hair. It clung to the edge like a filament.

Nora made a sound under her breath that might have been a prayer or a curse. Behind us on the harbor a man shouted a single word—the name, finally—and then there were other feet and other breath.

“The tides have been wrong,” I said to nobody.

“Or the men have,” Nora said. “Come on.” She was already running, and I followed, because polite liars or not, there are few things more honest than the sound of someone calling for what they’ve lost.

On the morning my obituary arrived, the fax machine had been dead for three months.

It sat on a low filing cabinet, a beige fossil with the soul of a kettle, long since unplugged and sun-faded to the color of an old tooth. Still, people sent death the way they always had—folded into envelopes that smelled like lilies and car freshener, typed with the confidence of grief, scrawled in Sharpie by nephews who didn't know the right words for what they were losing. The dead came to my desk on letterhead and church bulletins, stapled to the kind of paper that made a noise like dry skin when you rubbed it.

I fed them into the living machines. I was a conduit and a sieve. I wrote the last paragraph anyone would read about someone else. The living forgot each other with alarming speed; newspapers paid worse than bar bands. Neither of those were the point. I knew the names, the little tangles of lives. I thought I understood endings.

The envelope was waiting for me when I came in, propped against my keyboard like a cat to blockade the screen. No return address, just my name—RAE MONROE—typed in a clean old font that looked like it might have been inked with a ribbon and not pixels. The newsroom was quiet in the early hour, a few lights on in the far corner, the copy desk asleep, the police scanner quiet. It was barely nine, and the Record woke slowly. Later, there would be the churn of the sports desk, features trying to make farmers interesting for the third time in a year, and someone complaining about the coffee. Now there was me and the sound of the HVAC clattering, and the ghost of cigarette smoke that lived in the ceiling tiles from decades ago.

I turned the envelope in my hands. There was something of a ritual in a thing like that: the weight of the paper, the tilt of the letters. Whoever had addressed it knew the building. The "O" in MONROE had taken on a little halo where the typewriter ribbon had hesitated. No postage. It had been dropped off, which meant the night guard let someone through or they timed it during the lunch rush when the lobby was a blur of messengers and irate columnists. The flap wasn't even sealed. Careless, or confident.

"Do you want coffee or blood?" Maryam's voice arrived as a disembodied question from behind the partition, followed by her head appearing above it, black curls pinned like a crown of question marks.

"Blood," I said, and slid a finger under the flap. "And a cinnamon raisin bagel, but that's just a dream."

Maryam gave me the kind of look that said she had four stories and a kid at home and no time for bagel-based fantasy. "You got two death notices bumped to this morning," she said, dropping a sticky note by my mouse. "The family for Nam said you spelled the wife’s name wrong yesterday, they spelled it wrong on the form and it's my bad but please fix. And Sonia wants to see you before noon. Something about 'tone.'"

"Tone is a trap," I said, but she was already moving toward her desk, leaving me with the envelope and the hum of the building.

There are ways we talk about the dead that aren’t true. Our style guide forbids "passed" unless it’s a kidney stone. We don't say "lost" unless it's a pet or a child, and even then there's debate. No angels get their wings in the Record; no one "bravely succumbs." We can say "died," and then we line up commas like matchsticks to hold up the names of the ones who remain and the ones who left first.

I slid the paper out. My hands knew the feel of the sheet before my eyes did—the expensive stock we ordered by the case; the weight of it, a little heavier than the rumors of ink allow. It was the Record's obit template, god help me. The masthead, the line of tiny boxes at the top we used for internal tracking. The font—Georgia for the body, Franklin for the hed. It was not a copy; you cannot mimic the way the slugs of our pagination leave a hairline in the kerning that only people like me notice. It was ours.

OBITUARY: RAE ELIZABETH MONROE, 36

A photo would have gone to the right, if there had been one. There wasn't.

The text began with my name, then "died Thursday in Darrow, of complications resulting from smoke inhalation." It went on to state I was known for my "accurate and humane portrayals of the recently deceased" at the Darrow Record. There were lines in it I could have written in my sleep. There were details about my education that anyone with a search engine could have verified. It named the year I transferred back from Chicago, the year I moved into my apartment over the laundromat where the machines thumped through the night like a slow heartbeat.

It did not list survivors. It said there were no memorial services planned. It said the family declined comment.

The cause of death looped back in my mind like a skipping track. Smoke inhalation. The phrasing was clipped, clinical. We didn't say "complications resulting from" unless there was a disease, not an accident. Fire was supposed to be "house fire," "vehicle fire," "residential complex blaze," whichever applied, and we hadn't run smoke inhalation since that apartment fire on Henley Street when Mr. Vasquez dragged his couch into the hallway and made a chimney.

Thursday.

Today was Wednesday.

"Look ashen," Maryam said, reappearing with coffee in a mug so chipped it looked like a relief map of the Rockies. "You okay?"

I held the paper so she could read. She narrowed her eyes, moved closer, and then did something I didn't see her do often—she went still.

"Is this a joke?" she asked, flatly, but the kind of flat that contains a wobble. She takes jokes like she does her coffee, with suspicion but open-minded.

"If it is, it's very on-brand."

"This is... Rae, this is creepy."

"You're telling me," I said, and tried to laugh, but my voice came out of my throat wrong, like I'd swallowed a spoon.

"Who would—" She stopped, scanned the room out of habit—Sonia hadn't arrived yet, the city desk was empty, sports had a new kid with the energy of a shaken soda already halfway into a phone call. "I'm taking this to Sonia."

She reached for the page. For a second—a strange, childish second—I didn't want to let it go. Then I loosened my hand and watched her carry it away like evidence. The paper was heavy enough to drag down on one side, pulling at itself.

"Don't move," she said over her shoulder, and disappeared into the editor's glass office.

The police scanner coughed a sting of static and then went quiet again. We didn't rely on it the way old newsrooms did, but we kept it as a talisman, a charm for when the power went out or the internet died, or when we wanted to pretend we could still beat Twitter to something that mattered. The light moved across my desk as the sun slipped behind the Prudential across the street. Dust lifted and settled. I looked down at my hands and saw that they were steady. Somewhere out there, I was already dead.

At 9:40, Sonia summoned me. She was taller than anyone realized until you saw her standing; she had a scarf collection that could have paid my rent for a year. She slid the page back across her desk with one finger, as if it might stain.

"Someone has a sense of humor we don't appreciate," she said. "You want to tell me why this would exist?"

"Believe me," I said, "if I wanted to write my own obituary, I'd go for cleaner verbs."

"Who has access to the pagination templates?" she asked. Her tone was practical, a bucket of water on a grease fire.

"Everyone in editorial, and anyone who ever sat down on a weekend and figured it out," I said. "Which is half the building. But this—this doesn't feel like someone who hates me. It's too..." I searched for the word and felt it land with the weight of it. "Intimate."

Sonia's mouth tightened. "Who knows your middle name?"

"Everybody who fills out paperwork," I said. "And the state. And the two boys I went to high school with who were convinced my middle name was 'Eleanor' because I look like one of those."

"Ever get threats?" She asked it the way she might ask if I wanted to switch shifts. Direct, no fuss.

"From the living? Sometimes," I said. "People don't like it when you fix their grammar. Once a man told me he hoped I died while misplacing a comma."

"And the dead?"

"They're generally very quiet," I said. The half-smile she gave me was for the attempt, not the success.

"We'll log this with security," she said, and used the phrase "log this" like it had teeth. "If you want to take the day—"

"I'm fine," I said, and meant it in the way you do when your mind is doing all the running and your body hasn't yet got the message. The part of me that kept lists had already started one—send an email to IT to check logins, call my landlord about the smoke detectors, ask Maryam if she could even be bribed to comment on a 'tone' meeting when she was the only person in this building who could use a semicolon without hurting anyone. "I have two write-ups and I told Mr. Nam's daughter I'd call her back at ten."

Sonia tapped the edge of the paper. "If this is a prank, it's mean. If it isn't—"

"It is," I said. It had to be. It was someone who could get into a building and wanted to make a point. The point might be as simple as "I can do this." The point might be an arrow pointing at me. I thought of the line about no memorial services, the small meanness of depriving me of ceremony. The small pleasure of making me see it, printed so plainly.

"Stay reachable," she said, and I went back to my desk.

At ten, I made the Nam call and corrected the wife's name and apologized and let Mrs. Nam tell me about the peach trees they had planted after they moved to Darrow thirty years ago. I rolled my chair with my foot to reach the micro-wavering of the fan, because the HVAC was always too much or not enough. I wrote the Walden obit with the detail about the cufflinks he wore to work every day even after the plant closed, because it mattered to him to remember who he had been. The work steadied me. That was one of the things I liked about it, too. Death is big and sticky, and arranging its words into a column was a kind of courage you could mistake for control.

Just before lunch, I traced the envelope. No prints that I could see, but I had watched enough television to know I wouldn’t, even if there were. The typewriter letters weren't even; some had bitten the paper deeper than others, the way old letters from my grandmother had once did, a ghost of the word bleeding through to the back. I imagined the machine, heavy, a feisty relic dragged out of a closet, its bell chiming at the end of each line like a toast. Who in Darrow still had a typewriter?

The city is old enough to remember when there were three papers here, but young enough to forget to salt the sidewalks when the first ice comes. It was built by the river and around it, and then the highways bent it into a new shape like a nail pulled out of wood. There are parts of Darrow that have families like woven fabric, threads crossing back and forth into patterns that have held for a century. There are parts that are empty lots ringed with chain-link, where the weeds bubble up with the kind of optimism that breaks your heart a little. There are buildings with names that matter. The Bellwether Arms is one of them.

The Arms started as a hotel when Darrow was in love with steel. It was all velvet chairs and brass and bandstands and cigarettes. Then it was a pair of apartment buildings for people who couldn't afford to dream about velvet. Then it was a place the newspaper wrote about when the roof collapsed in the north wing and even the pigeons left. Two years ago, there was a grant and a ribbon cutting and a speech about transitional housing for veterans and for the women from the shelter. The name stayed. They never take the names down in this city. They just layer them like paint.

I knew this because I had covered the ribbon cutting. I had a photo somewhere of a child in a blue shirt grabbing at the mayor's scissors as if they were a toy. I knew it because three months ago I'd written about the woman on the eighth floor who had taken in two cats and a kid when her sister went away for a while. I knew it because, in the obit on my desk, the rumor of my death happened there.

I didn't notice the detail at first. I'd skimmed the line and been arrested by "smoke inhalation." It was Maryam who fished it out when she came back from lunch with a paper bowl of soup and three crackers that looked embarrassed to be there.

"You read to the end?" she said, dropping her scarf and sitting in the visitor chair that had a broken arm and synthetic leather worn bald along one side. "It says where."

"It does?" I said, and reached for the page, and there it was, the sentence I'd missed, small and neat as a pin: "Monroe was found at the Bellwether Arms, where she had gone to conduct interviews for a story."

"I don't have a story at the Bellwether," I said. "I'm working on the feature about the guy who rescues parrots and the parks piece."

"You told me last week you were thinking about checking in on the eighth-floor woman," Maryam said. "The one with the cats."

"I said I might. That's not the same as a plan," I said, and heard my mother in my mouth, and had to squeeze my eyes shut for a second. She had taught me that we give ourselves away with verbs. Might, will, did.

"Well, don't," Maryam said, and reached out and put her hand on the edge of my desk, just far enough from mine that it was not a reach toward me and not away.

"I have never in my life let a printed thing tell me what to do," I said, and it was bravado, and we both knew it. The thing telling me what to do stood six three in flats and could close any story simply by putting the word "budget" before it. But the part of me that worked with words also believed in their weight. If a word was heavy enough, it could drop on your foot and bruise you. This felt like something you could lose a toe to.

"Tell Theo," Maryam said, and there it was — the name that lived under a layer of dust in the back of my mouth. "He might at least pretend to take it seriously."

"He's not my—" I began, and then didn't finish the sentence because any word you put there was a fossil. Friend. Ex. Cop. Coffee. I hadn't talked to Theo Park in a year. We passed on the sidewalk sometimes, that was all. Darrow is small that way. People you try not to know get caught in your peripheral vision and live there like floaters.

I worked the rest of the day with my shoulders tight. When I went downstairs for a soda at three, the security guard, Jeremy, pretended not to be curious about why Sonia had brought him a printout of my death. When I came back up, the copy desk had woke fully and swore in chorus at some councilman who had said he didn't say the thing he had absolutely said on tape. The afternoon slid to evening with a casualness that felt personal. Every time the scanner popped, I glanced. It was nothing: a fender bender in the south side, a welfare check that turned into a drunk asleep on a porch, a noise complaint that was really a birthday party.

At six forty, I walked home.

I live nine blocks from the newsroom, above a laundromat that never closes. The machines thump all night like a heartbeat. There's a tree trying to die in front of my building that refuses to. It's always in bud, always a little surprised at everything. The stairs smell like detergent and burnt toast from the apartment across the hall, where a man who's always polite and always tired burns something three times a week like it's part of a ritual. I like the sound of the washers. I like the feeling that the city is working while I sleep, that somewhere beneath me something is spinning everything clean.

The obit went in my bag because I couldn't not carry it. It also didn't belong anywhere. You couldn't toss it, not like a draft. You couldn't file it. It was a version of me no one had asked for, and now I had it.

I made pasta and didn't eat it. I checked my smoke detector and tapped the battery compartment like a superstitious pilot. I used my thumb to warm it until the test button clicked. The siren that sprang to life made me step back and then laugh at myself, hand to my chest, as if my heart needed the press of it.

At ten thirty, I went to bed with a book and fell asleep with the light on and the book on my face, because that was another ritual I liked. At eleven nineteen, a siren drifted through the window like a ribbon and then another, and then all of them, layered, their tones overlapping and separating, calling to each other across the city.

I lay there and counted them. You can tell who's coming by the voice of a siren if you've lived as a reporter long enough. The long low eel of an engine, the hiccuping urgency of an ambulance, the cops already angry without knowing why.

I got up and went to the window. The laundromat below was lit, the fluorescent hum visible as a halo in the glass. The cat that lived under the counter was alone, curled on the dryer like a comma. The street beyond was a scroll, waiting for words.

There was a glow at the end of the block. Not like the spill of a streetlight on wet pavement. Warmer. Someone's grill, I thought, because people treated fire like company in this city, like a reason to gather and talk politics in tank tops. Then the glow widened and pulsed, and swelled, and every part of me that knew a thing about light said no.

My phone buzzed on the nightstand like a fly under a glass. The notification banner brightened the room enough to show me the walls in strange angles.

It was a text from Maryam. It said: Are you seeing this?

I didn't know what "this" meant until I opened the news app we pretend we don't check after hours, and saw the words in the breaking banner. Large fire reported at Bellwether Arms. Multiple units en route. Evacuations in progress.

For a second, the rooms of my apartment tipped sideways. It was a trick of the eyes, a lurch in the little bones of the ears that tell you where you are. Then I was moving, because the body knows what to do when the mind refuses.

I pulled on jeans and shoes and a sweatshirt with ink stains that never washed out. I grabbed my bag because my keys lived there, and the obituary was inside, and I did not want to leave it alone in the apartment with my two plates and my long-limbed plant that always leaned to the window as if it could climb out.

By the time I stepped onto the street, the sirens were louder, nearer, the ambulance noise skidding around the corners like a coin. I followed the glow.

Security lines have elasticity. In a city, that's just a fact. Tape goes up, and people move it, and cops yell, and it gets pushed back, and someone who shouldn't be there is always there. I got as close as anyone else and then closer because I had the press badge I wear on a lanyard, laminated, with a bad photograph of me where I look like a person in witness protection. The fire had taken the south face of the Bellwether like a hand. Flames threw themselves out of the third-floor windows as if the building had been waiting to breathe. Smoke sketched itself into the sky and then erased that line as fast as it drew it.

None of the metaphors on my internal shelf had the muscle for a fire that close. Heat slid across the skin of my face like a palm. People were everywhere. The woman from the eighth floor with the cats shouted names and the names went up like sparks, swallowed by the sirens. A boy in a Spider-Man shirt clung to his mother like a question mark. The man from the corner store handed out bottles of water with the reflex of someone who had done it before and would do it again.

Firefighters moved like language: precise, practiced. A line of them disappeared into the building and then reappeared, changed, steam and soot turning them into punctuation marks, commas, periods, ellipses when they paused. Somewhere inside, something collapsed; the sound had a weirdly domestic pitch to it, as if a kitchen drawer had come out too hard and the cutlery tilled into the floor.

I had my notebook in my hand because of muscle memory; the pages looked like blank faces in the flicker, waiting to be told what to say. I wrote nothing. Instead I watched the mouth of the building and tried not to breathe too much of it. Smoke inhalation, the term in my head like a dare.

Someone shouted my name. It was not a firefighter; it was the voice of someone who has the right to be in a place like this and had just become aware of that right again. I turned and saw Theo on the other side of the tape, his shoulders the same, his hair a little shorter, a light at his collar where the reflective tape on his jacket caught the fire and hurled it back.

He didn't come toward me because there was a strip of plastic and the weight of an entire professional vow between us. He lifted a hand and flattened it into the air. It was a stop sign that only I could see. He had that look he gets when he is both angry and afraid and is trying to decide who to be polite to.

"Rae," he said, and I didn't hear it but I saw the shape of my name in his mouth.

Time does strange things at the edge of a fire. It stretches, folds, gets hot to the touch. At twelve-oh-six, a firefighter came out of the south stairwell with someone over his shoulder, the shape of a person in that limp that looks theatrical and is only acting because life has forced it into a role. A medic shouted something I didn't understand and then said "now, now," which is a word that looks different when you say it three times. A woman cried in a way that had no words assigned to it.

A clock on a nearby building ticked loudly in my ear like a metronome. That made no sense; clocks don't get louder near fire. I realized it was my pulse.

I don't know what I thought I would see. I don't know if I thought I would see myself. I do know that when the paramedic lifted her hand to look at the face of the person they had just taken out, I didn't look. I couldn't, because there is looking, and there is making a thing true.

Theo's hand was still up. I looked at that instead. The palm lines were blacked with soot. He frowned like the city does.

The smoke rolled and shifted, and the wind changed, and the heat touched me like an instruction. It pressed its words onto my skin: move back, breathe less, think later. I took a step. My bag thumped against my hip like a heartbeat. The obituary inside it made a small crackle of paper, a sound as common as a receipt, but I heard it under the sirens. It was a sound you can't unhear once you know what it is.

And then the first window on the fourth floor, on the corner nearest me, blew out with a popping noise like a cork, and for a fraction of a second, the fire shaped itself into a mouth.

If I had been someone else, I might have misheard the words I put into it.

If I were who the paper said, this is where the story would end. But I was still there, in the crowd, with smoke in my lungs and ink on my fingers, watching the building named for a thing that tells you which way the wind is going, and thinking that whoever had written my ending understood time better than I did.

Because it wasn't Thursday yet. It was Wednesday, and the clock over the corner store said 12:03. The kind of minute you can expect someone to die in, if you had a plan for such things.

I put my hand on the breast pocket of my sweatshirt, where my notepad lived, and felt the outline of a Bic and the hammer of my heart against the spiral binding. I thought of the line in the obituary that said I had gone to the Bellwether to conduct interviews for a story, and knew the shape of the story had already changed, and knew, worse, that I'd been written into it.

I took another step back, but not away.

They asked me to open a dead man's safe.

If you do what I do long enough, you develop a sense for what the steel is going to tell you. A front door with a chipped brass cylinder says divorce. A trunk with a custom hasp says drug money or guns. A commercial-grade safe dragged out of a burned antiques shop? That one says secrets. And the dead man who owned the shop, the one with the long bones in his hands and a habit of locking the display cases twice? He was full of secrets even when he was breathing.

The shop's bones were still smoldering when I parked on Dray Lane. Dawn had thinned the fog enough to give everything a damp, smoked-out look. Fire hoses lay like spent snakes across the cobbles, and the air tasted like pennies and wet drywall. A triangle of yellow tape marked off the entrance, but someone had looped it low enough for boots. I showed my city badge to the cop posted there and ducked under.

Inside, char had erased what didn't matter. There were little obelisks of glass where figurines had slumped and cooled, a fused lattice of spoons and forks, framed faces black-eyed with soot peering out where the flames couldn't quite lick through. The upstairs was an open mouth of rafters and sky. The sprinkler system had done what it could; puddles glittered under the emergency lights, and ash settled every time a beam somewhere sighed.

Detective Iris Larkin was waiting near the back, watching a thin stream of water thread down a beam into a bucket. She was wrapped in a coat that had once been cream and was now the color of dishwater. Her hair was pinned back in a way that made me wonder how early she woke to make it look that precise.

"Morning, Grady," she said. People call me Theo Grady unless they want something. Then it's Grady.

"Mornin'," I said, and stepped around a spill of glass microscopically sharp as sand. "You just couldn't wait until my coffee."

She tipped her chin at the heap against the far wall. "Didn't want you too awake. Might overthink it."

The safe lay on its back like a beached animal, its black enamel scorched to a mottled gray. The dial's face was blistered but intact. Two men in blue coveralls from the fire department had hauled it out of the crawlspace under the stairs. A wet drag mark ran from the hole they’d yanked it out of to where it sat now.

"Insurance is breathing down my neck," Larkin said. "The owner's nephew raised hell at the scene, then finally folded, said we could go in. I want to see what our Mr. Quinn thought was worth dying for."

Lysander Quinn. I'd replaced a padlock for him once, years ago, after a string of break-ins along Dray Lane. He had the kind of smile that meant he didn’t laugh often but meant it when he did. He was the sort who reflexively patted his pockets in public, catalogue of everything he owned and where it sat. You don't expect men like that to forget lit candles or bad wiring.

I crouched by the safe and brushed my thumb over the dial. Sargent & Greenleaf, model old enough to belong in a museum. Some of the paint cracked off under my hand. I pulled my kit from my bag: small stethoscope with a bell half the size of a dime, graphite, camera, a roll of cloth tape, a notebook so old the cover had gone soft.

"If this is evidence," I said, "we might be better off taking it in."

"Don't have the luxury," Larkin said. "Some structures in these old lanes go from singed to collapsed overnight. The building adjudicator wants this place empty by noon. Make me a way through that door, and I'll buy you a coffee big enough to swim in."

I smiled because she said that like she had never bought a coffee in her life and didn't plan to start. "Any idea who else had the combination?"

"Quinn lived alone," she said. "No wife, no pets, no roommate who did yoga in the living room. He didn't trust anyone to watch the counter when he used the bathroom. If he wrote it down, I'd like to know where and how."

I knelt and pressed the stethoscope to the metal, placing the bell just to the left of the dial. The trick with an old safe is not knowing the math—though God knows I can do it in my sleep—but knowing how to listen. Every soft click you hear through the bell, every tiny hitch, has a corollary in how the fence rides over the wheels, how the tumblers nap against the drive cam. You listen not to the sound but to the way the sound leaves.

I dialed it up, slow and patient, my muscles finding their own rhythm. The shop made a chorus around me as I listened: drip, drip, a siren down the street that grew thin and then was gone, the talk of radios, an early truck hitting third gear somewhere on river road. The wheel itself talked in whispers, and I leaned into them.

"Is this the part," Larkin murmured, "where I have to hold my breath because if I exhale, you lose the thread of the universe?"

I didn't look up. "Hold your breath for something useful," I said.

At thirty-eight, there was a tremor. I rolled back, forward again, testing. The tremor became a hiccup. Not bad. I locked it in my head. Spun past, found twenty-six, the same, and then there it was: the gate falling in the back like the memory of a hook. Thirty-eight, twenty-six, and—come on, old girl—something else that would make the set. I dialed clockwise and felt a little rise at ninety-seven that was almost certainly a lie, then a truer catch at eleven.

"Thirty-eight," I said, unwilling to admit that it delighted me when the numbers lined up like they wanted to. "Twenty-six. Eleven."

"Any chance those are Saint's days or a birthday?" Larkin asked.

"If the man was born in 1926 and eleven months later," I said, "he was a prodigy."

The handle was stiff with rust but moved. I leaned my weight in. The bolts withdrew with a groan that went up my arms like electricity, and the door peeled back.

If I had been alone, I might have paused and breathed into the space, the way you do with a room in a house no one has lived in for a long time. Not reverent, exactly. Just acknowledging that everything we lock away carries our scent. Larkin edged closer until her shadow cut into the rectangle.

Inside, it was tidy.

No stacks of cash. No velvet-lined drawers of gemstones. No damp packet of a pistol wrapped in oily cloth. Someone had taken the time to run felt along the shelves and label the boxes with little brass plates nicer than anything else left in this place.

Top shelf: a ledger bound in honest leather, the kind that would gain a scar if you looked at it hard. Beneath it, three small boxes not bigger than my palm, each wrapped in dull paper and tied with twine. Revised 2017 Novels, said a tag on one. I snorted.

Next shelf: a wooden tray with cutouts like it was supposed to hold silver service, except each cutout held a key. There were dozens. Some old pewter, some bright new, some the kind of cheap stamped keys you could buy with a silhouette of a cartoon on the back, some antique skeleton keys with hearts in their bows. Each had a tag handwritten in a tidy script: 119 King. Back Garden. Blue? and Sutter House - attic door and Lighthouse, South stairs and so on.

Larkin let out a low breath. "Huh," she said.

"Lysander ran himself a little business," I murmured.

"You mean he was a locksmith? Because then you're out of a job and might as well take up needlepoint."

"No," I said. "I mean he held the spare keys to this town like a priest holds confessions."

She pulled on a glove and reached in, lifted the ledger in both hands. It was heavier than it looked. Water had sneaked through somewhere and made the edges wrinkle, but the spine held.

"Don't touch the rest," she said, not looking up. "I want prints on those key tags. And the boxes."

I nodded and let my eyes move over the tray. The feeling that had stood the hairs on my neck up since I woke because my phone was ringing now went from a hum to a tone. The shop, the burned air, the soft scratch of Larkin's hand against the paper—it all went blurry at the edges for a second.

Because half of those tags were in my handwriting.

You spend a couple decades cutting keys for a living, you refine your hand into something that fits neatly on a sliver of plastic the size of your thumb. You develop certain tics. I dot my i's after I write the word, all at once, so the dots line up. My f's lean a little too far back. I had, on three separate, very public grins, responded to "nice handwriting" with "it pays the rent."

On the key labeled 41 Plover, Side Gate, the i was dotted like mine. On the one for 87 Baker, they had the same lazy f I always drew in if. It was my handwriting from a couple years ago, when I'd done a sweep for the neighborhood association, cutting extras for the old folks. My stomach tightened in on itself.

"You all right?" Larkin asked. She wasn't looking at me; the question was a habit, like blowing on a cup before you sip.

"Sure," I said. "Just cold."

"You and the rest of us," she said. "November doesn't play."

She set the ledger down on a steel table that had survived the night and flipped it open. The paper inside was thick, ruled with pale lines. The first page was written with a fountain pen, indigo ink looped with someone so patient that I felt obscene reading over her shoulder.

It wasn't an inventory. It was a list. Two columns on each page, names on the left, a date on the right. Some of the names had parentheses after them: "Emily Portman (knitting club)," "R. Drouet (for Mr. H)," that kind of thing. Some had a red tick next to them. A handful had a word in the margin. The words varied, but the ones I could see right off were Returned and Gone.

"Jesus," Larkin said.

"Let me guess," I said. "These are loans and these are returns."

"If this is what I think it is," she said, "it's not library books."

Two names down the list, the red tick had bled into the page. Larkin touched the corner of the book so lightly it didn't move. She traced a line with her eyes, then another, and the set of her mouth changed. She fished her pen from a pocket and clicked it against her thigh, once, twice. She does that when something needles under her skin.

I didn't ask; I waited for her to either close the book or show me. She did neither. She turned the page, and the next, scanning, not reading. The third page she stopped. The name on that page she covered with her palm as if it were something indecent caught in daylight.

"This is nothing you can do anything about yet," she said.

"That's a good way to make me reasonable," I said, and because she didn't move her hand, I glanced at the tray again.

My attention, when it's at work, is greedy. If I'm not careful, it eats everything, and then I forget to eat myself. I made myself count the keys like I'd count bolts in a door. Two dozen, three, then the second row, the third, the slotted tray neat like a fisherman's tackle box. At the far left of the second row, there was a key with a chip out of its bow that made it look like someone had hacked a bite out of a cookie.

I reached for it, and Larkin's hand snapped up.

"Don't—Theo, I said prints."

"I won't touch the tag," I said. "But I need to see that tooth."

"You need to—"

"It has a break in the second cut," I said, and heard my own voice go thin. "Look."

She didn't move, so I moved like I was old, slow enough there was no sudden behavior to spook her. I shifted the key with the tip of my pencil. It turned in its cradle. The cut was shallow where it should have been deep, and deeper on the third notch where whoever cut it—me—had compensated. The bow wasn't the key's original either; someone had broken the plastic novelty bow off fifteen years ago and slid a raw metal bow on to replace it.

Just above the last notch—if you knew where to look and if you could see in the ash-soft light—you could make out two scratches side by side, less than a grain of rice long. I made them with the tip of a needle and my left thumbnail to hold a dangle fob my sister insisted was bad luck unless there was a mark for every person in the house. Two marks in a row, one for me, one for her. We were twenty and sixteen, and June had the kind of certainty you mistake for wisdom when you're too young to have any.

I didn't breathe. If I breathed, something in me was going to shift, and once it shifted, I didn't know where it would go.

"Theo," Larkin said, very quiet.

"Don't," I said, except I was saying it to myself. The room went brighter along the edges, like a migraine coming on.

I had cut that key fifteen years ago on a machine that choked if you fed a blank too fast. I had handed it to June in the doorway of our old place, still warm from the grinder. She had stood with one foot on the step, one foot still inside, hair unbrushed, a chipped teacup in her hand because she refused to throw it away. She'd grinned and said, "So now we can both get back in when we get locked out," as if the world was that simple. The chipped bow had been a cartoon cat, later cracked when she slammed a door, replaced by a raw bow that had never fit quite right.

And then she was gone.

"You sure?" Larkin asked. Her voice had changed even more than her mouth had. It was softer in a way that made me dislike her, which made me dislike myself.

I nodded because my mouth wasn't a thing I trusted.

She looked at the ledger again. "This name covered," she said, "is June Grady."

I closed my eyes. I saw the entry in my head anyway. J. Grady. A date fifteen years ago. A red tick, a word in the margin. My whole life had been that tick and that word. I answered every lock for the sound it made when it was half-turned, the tumblers just beginning to rise. I kept my shop open later than any sane man. I called my mother every Sunday night to hear her breathe and ask if she still put the kettle on at six and seven. I didn't go to that part of the river where June and I used to sit on the cold stones under the bridge when summer was too hot for the apartment to be bearable. I didn't go there because I didn't trust what my body would do if I had to stand on the place where her bracelet had been found.

"What's the word in the margin," I asked. My voice was a match head; it burned out on the last syllable.

Larkin lifted her palm. The paper was old enough it had taken the ink into itself and not let go. The word was neat, the way the rest of it was neat. The word was Returned.

Someone who wasn't me and wasn't my mother had written that word next to my sister's name.

"You see the problem," Larkin said. It wasn't unkind.

"Returned," I said, and it tasted like a lie. June had not returned. June had disappeared on a Wednesday in October when I was measuring a door on Alder Street for a client who insisted his lock was haunted because it wouldn't roll smooth. June had taken ten dollars from my wallet and left me a note apologizing for stealing fries out of the oven and saying she'd be back before I got home. That was the kind of girl she was, apologizing for burnt fries. Then she vanished into the block of hours between four and ten, and the police told me that teenagers have ideas and will. They looked for a week and then waited for a body like people wait for weather.

Larkin shut the ledger. The thud was soft, nothing to it.

"I shouldn't show you this here," she said, "but if I take it back and lock it up and you find out later I stood in a room with you and didn't, you won't come through for me when I call. And I like it when you come through. I'm selfish that way."

She slid a card out from under the ledger's cover. It was an index card, the kind Quinn kept in his drawers, with a line drawn down the middle. On the left side was printed in the same tidy hand as the key tags: June Grady. On the right: 41 Plover. Side door. 5/12.

"I don't know what this system is yet," she said. "But I'm betting borrowed and returned weren't his only measures. Look."

She flipped the card. On the back, the same handwriting had drawn a tiny map. It wasn't a great map. The proportions were guesswork, the arrow pointing north crooked. But I knew, in the small heart of it, the shape of the alley behind our old place, the break in the fence, the trash cans with numbers painted on their sides. There were tiny Xs. One by the Plover streetlight. One by the alley mouth behind the El's support beam. One near the back door of the laundromat where we used to steal the heat in winter by standing in the cloud of air that blew from the dryer vents. The X by the back door of 41 Plover had a circle around it.

"This is what I think," Larkin said. "I think Quinn was a man who liked systems. He made himself a system that accounted for the things people lost, and the things they found again, and the things that should have been one of those and were neither. I'm not saying he brought your sister home. I'm saying at some point he wrote down that he believed something of hers came back. If he collected keys like old men collect pocketknives, then whatever this is, he thought he was, I don't know."

"A keeper," I said. "Of other people's doors."

Water popped somewhere behind me in the walls as a nail cooled at last. Outside, someone shouted and laughed; the sound slid in and evaporated.

"Take your time," she said, and when I turned to look at her, she was already handing me a glove without meeting my eyes. "And Grady? We don't throw ourselves into fires. Not unless it writes itself into the job description."

"Too late," I said. "I already have the jacket."

She gave me the kind of look that would put a word in someone's file if she still kept them on paper, a look that said we'd either had this conversation ten times before or were about to start having it once a week.

I pulled the glove on and lifted the key.

The weight of it wasn't a surprise. The chip at the bow fit my usual hollows, the same way a missing tooth fits your tongue. It had a smell like old laundry and a house that's been shut up for winter—that dry, woven smell of people you love who aren't in the room anymore. The second notch was shallow, the third deeper: my mistake, anyone's correction. The two scratches near the tip were as present as the back of my left hand, that little crescent at the base of the thumb where I'd cut myself on a screw when I was a teenager and had gotten bored while installing a deadbolt.

I pressed my thumb into the bow and closed my eyes and saw June trying to open the back door with this key the first night we moved into Plover, her breath showing in the cold, her muttering at the lock like it was a dog that wouldn't come. She'd say, Work with me, darling, and the door would consider it, and then, if it liked her tone, it would. The door liked her. A lot of things did.

Larkin was saying something to a tech about photographing the boxes. The fire guys were lifting a beam somewhere, men making noises to agree, disagree, or simply to fill the ditch a hard job can be. I forced my eyes open, set June's key back in the cradle where it had been, and swallowed.

If there was a map for this, Quinn had drawn one. He'd drawn it in his tidy hand with a fountain pen and a ruler, and he'd tucked it behind what was only half a secret because the people who came to him already knew. They knew he never forgot. They knew what he remembered.

"After you feed me that coffee you promised," I said to Larkin, "you can take me to see where they pulled the body."

"There was no body," she said. "Not of Quinn, anyway. He was out back in the alley. Smoke, quick as anything. Never knew what took him."

"Then what am I supposed to look at?"

She tapped the ledger. "Whatever this is, it didn't burn, and it didn't run. That makes it the part that doesn't know how to leave a room when it gets hot. That's either the best part of a thing or the worst."

"Both, usually," I said.

"Get your breakfast," she said. "Then meet me at the station. And Grady?"

"What."

"I don't know what your dead man was doing keeping people's keys," she said. "But from where I'm standing, it looks less like he was rifling through drawers and more like he was making a way back for people who forgot they had one."

"You practice these when you put your coat on?" I asked.

"Couple in the pocket," she said.

I followed her out into the wet light, the yellow tape snapping in the wind where someone had tied it too tight. Across Dray Lane, the coffee shop set out chairs the way they did every morning no matter what, their sleeves rolled like they meant business. The river beyond the block walls was gray and hard-looking. Somewhere, someone started a song on the radio, the old kind that counted the beat out loud before it began.

I stood on the curb and ate my breath down to steadier. The key was still under my skin even after I put it back. The ledger might as well have written my name there in blue ink.

There are mornings when you walk into the world and the world is the world. And there are mornings when you put your hand on an old machine and feel the tumblers rise, and you think, If this opens, it will bless me, and if it opens, it will curse me, and if it opens, I will not be who I was when I closed it again. This was that kind of morning.

I went to get coffee for us both, even though she hadn't meant it. I picked the seat by the window where I could see who came and who went, the safe men packing up, the smoke thinning to a memory you would smell again every once in a while years hence when a neighbor burned toast. I took my second sip and the third and waited for Larkin to call with an address, a room, and a question we might fit a key into if we were lucky.

And under all of it, a word written in a dead man's ledger. Returned.

You don't live in this town long without realizing how many meanings a word can carry when people are afraid to say the names of the things they lost. A soldier returns. A sweater is returned. A storm returns every fall. I hadn't seen my sister in fifteen years. But every time I turned a lock, I thought there was a world in which that click led back to steps down and the hallway at Plover and the sound of June humming, off-key on purpose to make me yell.

Returned. It could mean anything.

It could mean this was the first door I'd opened in a long time that didn't belong to a stranger.

Chapter One

They were shaving the football field down to its bones when the teeth hit metal. The backhoe’s bucket took a mouthful of clay and gravel and something else, and the sound of it made the men in neon vests freeze: a hollow, resonant shudder that didn’t belong to soil. Even from the edge of the lot, coffee sloshing in a paper cup I’d bought out of habit instead of desire, the wrongness of it prickled the back of my neck.

“Hell,” said the foreman, dropping his hand to halt the machine. He was red-cheeked and big in the way of men who’d been moving earth their whole lives, with a smile that stopped at his beard. “You hit a tank?”

The operator killed the engine. The field exhaled silence. The bulldozed slope was a raw wound, the turf rolled like carpet, the chalk lines from a season that never came curling dry at the edges. Graybridge High’s bleachers sat welded to their rust and memory, and beyond them the mills along the river hunched like patient animals. The town loved to bury things. We were all here to watch it unbury one of them.

“Reporters back behind the cones, please.” A kid in a fresh city-issued jacket—new enough to squeak when he moved—flapped a hand at me and the retired math teacher who wrote the daily column about yard sales.

“I’m not a reporter,” she said primly. “I’m the pulse of the classifieds.”

“Uh-huh,” I said. “And I’m just here to take pictures.”

He smiled the way people smile when they don’t remember they went to school with you. I stepped back behind the cones anyway. I was here on a last-minute assignment to cover the demolition of the football field for the Ledger—farewell, Spartans, farewell, Friday nights, farewell, the snack stand with its perplexing loyalty program. They were turning the back field into a stormwater basin and the main field into townhouses you couldn’t afford on a teacher’s salary. My editor wanted a slideshow of men in hard hats against an aching blue sky, something that said progress without reminding anyone which way the money flowed. He didn’t expect anything interesting. He didn’t know about the sound a blade makes when it meets a secret.

The operator climbed down, his boots slipping in the slope, and scraped at the chunk of unearthed metal with a shovel. Every scoop came up reddish and wet, the clay sticking. The scrape of metal on metal flashed up my spine. The shape wasn’t a tank. It was something curved, with a shallow angle that suggested roof over structure. A trunk. A hood. Something you could sit in, buckle up, drive away.

“Back it off,” the foreman called. “Easy. Don’t shear it.”

A forklift whined somewhere behind me. The math teacher stopped pretending she wasn’t taking pictures on her phone. The scattered audience—the curious, the retired, the ones whose houses would face new porches instead of end zones—tightened in. The rumor of it spread faster than the smell of wet earth.

“Maybe it’s one of those time capsules,” someone said.

“Town never had that kind of budget,” said someone else.

The operator swung the bucket around and levered it into the lip of its own hole. Another worker dropped into the pit with careful steps and tamped away more dirt. As he cleared, the shape became clearer. The slope of a windshield. The contour of a wheel well. The paint that remained was a dull bruise under layers of clay: a blue so deep it had to fight for its own name.

The world tilted. I knew that color. I knew it like I knew the old mill smell that rose off the river in July and the sound of sneakers scuffing a gym floor and the taste of cheap liquor up on Witch’s Bluff. People talk about foreshadowing like it’s a trick of literature, but your body knows a story before your head does. My fingers closed so hard around the paper cup it went soft.

“Get the Sheriff,” the foreman said, voice flatter than before, because even if it wasn’t what we all thought, it had to be something, and Graybridge didn’t have a lot of somethings that weren’t trouble.

They kept working. They were careful. They brought in a pump and in a few minutes the hole coughed up water, rust-colored, the ground giving back what had been pressed into it. It wasn’t that deep, six feet maybe, the car nestled like a bad seed in the earth. They revealed the back end first, the rounded lights caked in dirt, the place where a license plate should have been blank as a closed mouth. The rear window was crazed with the fractures of years spent under pressure.

I slid from one cone to the next, angling for the shot I’d say I needed for the paper, but really to see what I couldn’t be seeing. I told myself there were a hundred indigo sedans sold at Hardy Automotive between 2003 and 2007. I told myself the paint looks different under clay. I told myself that what I was feeling was old, an ache that had learned to live in my bones and was simply uncoiling in the familiar weather.

“Ms. March.”

I turned. Eli Cotton stood at the foot of the bleachers, boots already picking up mud, badge a bright note on his jacket. He walked like someone remembering how to move quickly without letting anyone see him run. He’d been two grades ahead of me, a linebacker with a soft heart. Now he was Sheriff because someone had to be and because Graybridge had a long memory for who showed up when called.

“Hey,” I said.

“You didn’t say you were coming back.”

“You didn’t say you’d grown a beard.”

He touched his jaw as if he’d forgotten it was there. “Stay behind the tape, all right?”

“Cones, not tape.”

“It’s about to be tape.” He nodded toward the machine. “Any idea what we’ve got?”

“A car without plates,” I said. “Rust. Regret.”

He didn’t smile. “Rowan.”

I held up my camera, lens capped. “I’ll stay out of your way.”

By the time the Deputy strapped saw horses together and fed caution tape through them, the rest of the car was up into view. The front bumper was scarred. The emblem was gone. When they washed it with the pump’s dirty water, a sliver of chrome flashed from the grill. A Hardy Automotive license frame clung to the back, bent and half-buried. The kind you could ask for even if you hadn’t actually bought the car there, because everyone asked for things from Mr. Hardy and he was always too nice to say no.

The trunk had a zip-tie around it. Blue, like what they used for electrical. It was cinched like a belt around the handle and the latch. The zip-tie was stuck fast in the mud, the little tab of it embedded so deep I couldn’t see the head. Maybe it had been put there to keep the trunk from flying open while a tow truck hauled it. Maybe someone had meant to open it later and couldn’t. Maybe.

They cleared around the doors. The driver’s side window was down three inches. You couldn’t see inside, not really, not through what water and time and clay do to a view. You could see your own face ghosted on the surface of the glass when the sun hit it right. For a moment the reflection lined up with the suggestion of a headrest and then I turned away and looked at Eli instead.

“Did you call the state lab?” I asked.

“I called them,” he said. “They’re en route.”

“How long is en route these days?”

“Long enough.” He looked at me. “You don’t have to be here, Rowan.”

“Neither do you,” I said.

He almost smiled at that. On the far side of the field, someone from the city parks department clanked the gate shut and turned away a van with a banner that read Graybridge Clean-Up Day. The woman driving threw up her hands and then, spotting the tape and the backhoe and the knot of people, parked anyway.

“Who’s your foreman?” Eli called.

“Joel Hennessey,” the big man said, pushing his hard hat back with the heel of his hand. “We got the first call into Dispatch. You gonna want me to shut us down?”

“I’m going to want you to put down the bucket and step away from the hole,” Eli said, not unkindly. “And if anybody else’s phone rings, you tell them I don’t care who’s offering what money, this site’s closed until I say different.”

Nobody argued. Graybridge didn’t argue with Eli; they argued among themselves and then did what he said. The tape went up, the kind that shimmers yellow and looks like it could be torn with a breath. I took two steps back to prove I could.

I hadn’t been planning to come back for more than a day. The Ledger paid for a room at the new motel by the highway and a tank of gas. I told myself I’d spend the afternoon taking earnest photos of the field, stop by Maria’s for a takeout sandwich that tasted like high school afternoons, and then drive back to the life I had made in the city where no one knew me as anything but my last byline. I’d avoid the river and the bluff and the house with the porch swing that still creaked when no one was sitting on it.

The last time I had stood here, there had been white folding chairs in rows and I had hated the shoes I was wearing. Kira had hated hers, too. She kicked them off after the ceremony and walked across the end zone in bare feet, green grass imprinting her heels, her cap tucked under her arm so the tassel didn’t hit her in the eye. The sun through the stadium lights made everything seem cinematic, like a final scene instead of the beginning of something else. We were eighteen and we thought you could tell which moments mattered.

“You won’t even miss me,” she had said, laughing, because she was leaving sooner than I was, because she had a car and a plan and we believed those things meant the same as a life.

“You’ll be back for the Fourth,” I said. “You never miss fireworks.”

She had pressed her mouth to my shoulder, the corner of a kiss between friends and not, and then she had pulled away already moving toward someone else who wanted her. There were a lot of someones. There always had been.

She drove a car the color of a thunderhead reflected on a lake. She named it, the way some girls named their hair straighteners and some named their dogs. She hung a cheap air freshener from the mirror that never smelled like pine and collected toll receipts in the cup holder, though there weren’t tolls within fifty miles. There was a chip in the windshield, right where the passenger’s eyes go when they’re laughing. I knew that car because I had been in it more times than I could count, in nights and mornings and afternoons that all feel like the same hour when you look back from a distance.
