When the state lab finally arrived, two hours later because the state lab is a hundred miles away and underfunded on purpose, the crowd had doubled and the coffee in my cup had gone cold. The techs wore coveralls and skinny wire-framed glasses. They had the patient hands of people whose work is always both urgent and late.

“We’re going to stabilize the soil,” one of them said to Eli, already setting up tripod lights as if the field itself had gone dim. “And then we’ll see if we can open a door without compromising anything. We can tarp it if we have to leave it overnight.” He glanced at the sky, which had clouded as if someone had dragged a gray thumb across a blue plate. “You get weather?”

“We get weather,” Eli said.

They took measurements with little white flags. They photographed the car like it was an animal that might spook, approached, retreated. When they finally worked a wedge under the passenger-side door and pried it an inch, the smell that bloomed out made a few people step back, and one of the parks guys put his hand flat against his own chest as if to hold himself in. It wasn’t rot, not anymore; it was earth and metal and time, an absence that had taken on a weight.

The tech with the glasses put on nitrile gloves, blue against brown. He slid a thin rod through the space, prodded gently, murmured something to his partner. They looked at Eli. They looked at each other. It was, I realized, a conversation in a language I had learned to understand without speaking: the choreography of bad news arriving at the exact speed of its making.

“Ms. March,” Eli said again, and there was something like apology in it.

“I’ll stay out of your way,” I said, and this time I meant it. I drew back three steps, then three more. I tried to be only a camera and the hands that held it, to let the lens make a frame the way a frame can make sense.

The tech pushed the door another inch. Water slopped out, slick and slow, thick with silt. The smell deepened. The crowd got quiet in a way that has nothing to do with respect and everything to do with fear. A piece of the dashboard came up in the wash, a softened rectangle that might once have been a receipt or a photograph and now was just paper that had learned to be water. It slid against the tech’s glove and folded like a jellyfish.

Something else bumped after it, caught for a second in the door gap, and then tilted toward the light.

It was a bracelet, the kind you get in the case near the register, silver-plated and meant to tarnish into charm. It had a tiny heart that had lost its shine and a letter stamped in the metal. It had a clasp that stuck, and a chain that always snagged thin sweaters. It rocked in the thin current and I knew how it would feel in my palm because I had held it there. I knew how it would look the first time it dulled, because I had watched her rub it with her thumb, trying to bring back the shine. I knew it like I knew the paint.

When it slid free and dropped into the reach of the tech’s hand, it turned once, twice, like it was remembering the wrist it belonged to. The letter caught the light.

K.

Someone behind me breathed in a way that wanted to be a sound. Someone else whispered a name they hadn’t said out loud in years. I didn’t say anything. I couldn’t, because my mouth had filled up with clay and old breath and the exact shape of a night I had worked like a loose tooth, worrying it until I thought I had learned to live with the gap.

“Bag that,” the technician said, and his voice was all edges, trying to make this ordinary.

I lifted my camera. The bracelet was blurred in the viewfinder because my hands had started to shake, and you can’t steady a lens against what lives inside you. I lowered it again. The world did not float away. The tape still hummed in the light breeze. Eli was still there, looking at the car like he could make it give back more than it had taken.

It wasn’t proof and it wasn’t a body and it wasn’t the whole of anything. It was enough.

“I know that bracelet,” I said, and only Eli heard me. “I gave it to Kira Dempsey.”

Chapter One

The dead send me mail.

They fold themselves into onionskin envelopes and heavy cream stock with wax seals and tasteful return addresses. They scrawl in fountain pen about how they want to be remembered, and sometimes, if they still can, they even call me to chat about it. Death, like weddings, is a logistical nightmare unless you plan ahead. On a good day, I shepherd three notices into print, field ten calls from people who insist their Aunt Mabel was “a saint, but put ‘she loved a bargain’ too,” and correct the spelling of eternity for someone who spells it like an Italian pastry.

On that Monday in April, the envelope was lavender and sat where none of the others did—right in the center of my blotter, on top of my coffee mug as if it wished to warm its feet. The stationer knew their craft: a crisp watermark of a bee in the paper when I held it to the light, the faintest chemical tang of something that wasn’t from our office. My name was hand-lettered with an elegant slant. No postmark, no strip of interoffice neon tape, no staffer scrawl. Just June Ellison. Obituary Desk. The Beacon.

The keys on my keyboard ticked in a neat metronome. The newsroom around me churned with the normal, survivable disasters—the morning budget meeting that had run long, the weather desk swearing at a radar map stubbornly insisting the sky was not as gray as the windows made it, the cop reporter trying to coax something useful out of a scanner that mostly coughed static and football games.

I slid my thumb under the flap and pulled out a single page. Onion skin, pale, translucent, a typewritten sheet caressed by a manual machine. The typed letters bit the paper, leaving tiny ridges you could feel if you closed your eyes. The R’s were weak. They had a stubby leg, faded at the bottom like someone with a limp.

Obituaries are formulas. You learn the pattern until a human slotted into it looks like a poem. Name. Age. Residence. Died. Survived by. Services. The one in my hands knew the template and also knew how to make it breathe.

ELEANOR QUIST, 62, of Garnet Street, died unexpectedly in her home on Friday, April 19, 11:07 a.m., after a fall. She taught Latin at Bayview High School for thirty-eight years. Her students loved her flashes of frost and fire, her habit of making them recite in the hall if they fell asleep, her mercy seen only by those who could translate it. She loved geraniums, the sound of rain on old glass, and the considerable silence of early mornings.

Predeceased by no one who ever understood her, she is survived by her sister, Nora Quist of Truro, and by generations who will still decline to use the passive voice in their essays. Services Friday, 11 a.m., Garner Street Chapel; internment south of the east wall, Garnet Street Cemetery, where the shadows do not linger as long.

No flowers, for heaven’s sake. Donations to the Bayview Scholarship for the Unapologetically Curious.

The byline, because we sometimes get them, was a flourish at the end, the way you might sign a dear friend’s wedding card.

—E.Q.

“Is that a fan letter?” Harlan leaned his hip against my cubicle wall, paper cup in hand. The Beacon’s editor has a face like the map of a small, hard county, all lines and weather, with eyes that still gleam when trouble pokes its head over the hedge.

“It's an obituary,” I said, and my voice came out flatter than I meant it to. “For Friday.”

“Appropriately cheerful,” he said, peering. “Who’s the lucky guest?”

I held it so he could read the first lines. His smiling muscles stilled. “We have a rule,” he said after a heartbeat. “No living obits in the paper except for heads of state, and even those are locked away until the Grim Reaper actually shows up. You going to call?”

The rule exists because people like to be dramatic. Lovers in a fight, exes with a grudge, kids who think it’s funny to kill off their teachers. It exists for the other reason, too: because I once ran an obit for a man who wasn't dead yet. The suit settled. The shame did not. It was an honest mistake, made with an honest funeral director who’d been given a false case number by a hospice nurse who later wasn’t one. Still, every time I touch one of these, my stomach takes the elevator down a floor.

“I’m going to call,” I said.

I typed the name and the smell of onion skin into our system, pulled up our subscription database where the city keeps everything that thinks it might someday need to be found. ELEANOR QUIST pinged back with a couple of hits. Teacher of Latin at Bayview for decades, retired three years ago. A letter to the editor from fifteen years ago insisting we stop translating “alea iacta est” as “the die is cast” because the nuance was wrong. A photo at a school banquet where a smiling principal held up a clock and Ms. Quist looked like the clock offended her personally.

With one hand, I flipped open the desk copy of the funeral homes list and punched the number for Garner Street Chapel. The receptionist answered on the second ring with a voice that could file your nails.

“Garner Street, how may I help you?”

“This is June Ellison at the Beacon. Do you have services scheduled for Friday at eleven for Ms. Eleanor Quist?”

“We do not.”

“Do you have a pending case for Ms. Quist?”

“Not that I see. Let me—no. No Quists. We did a Quentin, last month. He was ninety-eight and had better teeth than my husband.”

“Lucky Quentin,” I said. “Thanks.”

I dialed the number our system had for Ms. Quist. It rang eight times, which is a number that always makes me think of slow decisions, and then clicked.

“Quist,” a woman said. A voice like a winter coat, heavy wool.

“Ms. Quist, this is the Beacon. My name is June Ellison. I handle obituaries.”

“What an odd responsibility,” she said, and I could hear the scrape of a chair and the crinkle as she shifted the phone to the other ear.

“We received an obituary for you this morning,” I said, because there is no nice way to say it.

“Ah,” she said. “Well, I’m sorry to disappoint you.”

“It appears to be typed on a manual. The R’s are a little—” I realized I was about to tell a stranger her Rs limped. “Never mind. It says Friday at eleven at Garner Street Chapel, which they know nothing about.”

She was silent. Then she laughed, and it was not unkind. “Garner Street is a den of incompetence, but not usually that incompetent. I didn’t write anything for anyone. I assume you will require me to come prove it by being undeniably alive.”

“We can also verify with a funeral home if you prefer not to be inconvenienced,” I said. “I just—this is the kind of prank that isn’t funny. If someone is trying to harass you—”

“I retired; I no longer command enough attention to be harassed,” she said, and then, softer: “Though we are none of us as invisible as we think.”

Through the receiver, something chimed, a bright, mechanical ring, three notes ascending in a cheerful little ladder. I imagined a mantel clock, polished weekly until it winked. “I live two flights up,” she added. “End of the hallway. If you wish to laugh about my premature demise, come at four. That will give me time to put on lipstick and rehearse being charming.”

“I’ll be there,” I said.

“Ms. Ellison?”

“Yes?”

“Don’t print anything about my shadows,” she said lightly. “They’re private.”

After she hung up, I turned the lavender envelope over in my hands. No business’s return address, not even one of those coy embossed L.M.N. in the corner. The ink of my name made my finger pad squeak when I ran it across. I lifted the paper again, held it to the window; the bee watermark buzzed in the April light.

“Hand-delivered?” Harlan asked.

“Or dropped from the heavens.” Any messenger would have needed to avoid three yawning interns, the receptionist with the hair helmet, and a security camera that angles directly at the desk. A better trick than most angels manage these days.

At 3:45, the skies over Bayview had decided to drizzle. I bundled into my coat and walked the eight blocks to Garnet Street with my collar turned up, the rain rearranging my hair into a map of a small country in distress.

Garnet Street is our city’s answer to a lullaby—a row of brick shells with marble stoops and cast-iron railings that the fancy people scrape and repaint annually. The Delgado’s bodega was a few doors down and smelled like oranges and tired flowers. A church with a chipped bell tower watched the corner. The chapel loomed halfway down, a Greek Revival slab with pillars that would have impressed a dead Roman, and, opposite it, the cemetery. The iron fence was an honest one: pointy, unapologetic about keeping things in or out.

Eleanor Quist lived in a building whose foyer had seen better wainscoting. The mailboxes had been added whenever someone remembered there were laws, and no two were alike. I climbed two flights past a ripped framed poster of Pompeii, past a ficus that looked like it had given up politely.

Her door was the end of the hallway, as promised. The brass number had been polished until it believed in itself again. When she opened the door, she looked exactly like I imagined she would: hair the color of the inside of an oyster shell, cut blunt; eyebrows you could hoist a sail with; a mouth that did not take easy shapes. She wore a navy sweater and trousers, and the lipstick she’d promised looked like something from a department store, not a bargain bin. Behind her, the apartment smelled like pencils and lemons.

“Hello,” she said. “Come reassure yourself.”

“I’m easily reassured,” I said, and I wasn’t lying. Seeing a person alive usually did it. Usually.

Her living room was a museum of quiet pleasantries. Books shelved in actual wood, not particle board. Plants in terracotta pots. A framed print of a whale like a blueprint. On a table beside the window, a typewriter sat beneath a dust cover. The cover was the color of old raincoats. I could see the shadow of the machine beneath it, and my fingers twitched the way they do when they pass a piano.

“I assure you it has not worked in years,” she said, and when she pulled the cover off, dust languid in the lamplight like dancers, I could hear in her voice that she wanted it to have not worked in years, because the alternative would be to imagine it waking up at night to type you into the ground.

It was a Royal Quiet De Luxe, late forties, by the look of its curves. The keys were glass-top circles, three of the slugs mottled with ink scars. The ribbon was a fading red-black. She touched it the way you touch an old dog who hasn’t seen you yet.

I slid the carriage return in a way that made the bell sing. It sang the same three-note ladder I’d heard over the phone.

Ms. Quist watched me. “I taught sentence diagramming,” she said. “I am not afraid of weapons.”

I rolled a sheet of paper into the machine. Her eyes narrowed, but she didn't stop me. I typed THE QUICK BROWN FOX JUMPS OVER THE LAZY DOG, because some things are sacred. The R’s came out swollen at the hip and faint at the ankle.

“I didn’t write to you,” she said. “No one was here this morning except me and the radio. And that, briefly.”

“If someone typed this here and brought it to me,” I said, “they did so without you knowing.”

“That would suggest someone was in my apartment, Ms. Ellison.” She said the Ms. the way some people say ma’am, and some say dear. “And that is absurd. Unless ghosts have learned to use door locks.”

I looked at the lock: a deadbolt and a brass knob lock. The chain had been removed, screws filled neatly and painted over.

She followed my gaze. “I don’t like the sound they make when they dangle,” she said. “Like teeth.”

“Is there anyone who might think this is funny?” I asked. “A former student with a flair for theater and alphabet keys?”

She smiled with her mouth and not her eyes. “I have taught ninth-grade boys to decline ‘rosae’ for almost four decades. I have no shortage of enemies. But their revenge fantasies rarely involve punctuation.”

In the kitchen, a kettle began to whine. She went to lift it with a towel, set it on a holder shaped like a rooster. The radio on the counter was a small, angular thing with the volume knob offline, the cord pinched at the plug. Latin phrases were taped to the cupboard doors: nemo me impune lacessit. vita brevis. There were tidy piles of note cards, a discipline even in retirement.

“You make tea,” she said, setting a mug in front of me. “I always have trouble remembering how long to steep it when someone is watching me.”

“I can read a clock,” I said. “Quite. Were there any other odd things? Notes? Calls? A picture you did not take taped to your mirror?”

She gave me a look. “You sound as if you collect ghost stories.”

“I collect the mail the dead send,” I said. “Sometimes the stamps are interesting.”

She reached into the drawer beneath the stove and drew out three index cards. Each was the size of the palm of her hand. Each had a Latin sentence written in careful teacher script, and beneath it, an English translation in print like a textbook’s.

Mors certa, hora incerta. Death is certain; the hour is uncertain.

Non omnis moriar. I shall not wholly die.

Etiam capillus unus habet umbram. Even one hair casts a shadow.

“They were under my door, slipped sometime in the past week,” she said. “There is no neighbor who still reads Latin in this building. I took them as a compliment and a prank. Latin is a prank no one pulls anymore.”

“They’re not unkind,” I said.

“No,” she said. “But someone wants me to think about timing.”

Her kettle clicked as if satisfied. We sat for a moment with steam traveling past our faces, and I could hear the rain on her windows in its considerate way. The typewriter on the table watched us without being anything but metal, and I watched it back as if it were a dog deciding which of us would be its person.

Something thumped upstairs. Not a startling sound. A human one. The drag of a chair leg, maybe. Or a shoe dropped. Ms. Quist’s eyes lifted and then made a decision not to look alarmed.

“Two floors are empty still,” she said. “The landlord is persuading the world that they are a bargain.”

“You said no one was here this morning,” I said.

“No one you saw,” she said, the way teachers answer questions that seem self-evident. She set her cup down. “Ms. Ellison, are you going to print anything?”

“Not without confirmation,” I said. “And not on Friday. My paper does not kill people by ink. It’s bad for the brand.”

“Good to know The Beacon still has a conscience,” she said. “Tell Harlan he owes me a correction on Caesar.”

“I’ll send him yours,” I said.

When I left, the hallway smelled like bleach and old dust. I turned back once at the top of the stairs out of a habit that is part reporter and part fox. Ms. Quist stood in the doorway and watched me, one hand on the jamb, the other holding the door like the shoulder of someone who wanted to do what it was told.

I was two steps down when a different sound came from her apartment—the ding of her typewriter’s bell, sharp, three notes. I looked up. She hadn’t moved. For a moment, her eyes flinched toward the living room as if she’d seen someone who hadn’t been there before.

“You have a friend who likes bells,” I said.

“The building is full of ghosts,” she said lightly, and then she closed the door.

I walked the two blocks to the Garner Street Chapel purely because I am incapable of leaving alone the thing in front of me. The chapel’s double doors had been repainted a serious blue sometime in the last decade and were losing lungfuls of paint. Inside, a woman wheeled a vacuum in slow arcs along a carpet that had seen too many shoes. At the office, a sign said BACK IN TEN in a handwriting that did not know how to write fives properly.

I checked the board where they list services, a bulletin written in a hand that pressed hard: MARIE PERRON - WEDS 2 PM. WALTER H. - THURS 10 AM. Nothing for Friday. The woman with the vacuum looked up briefly and then went back to her circles.

Back in the newsroom, Theo in features had left a sardonic cartoon on my keyboard of a gravestone reading HERE LIES TASTE, DIED LOUDLY, and I taped it to my drawer because Theo's sarcasm is my favorite currency. I put the Quist obit in a file, wrote NO to the right of Friday, underlined it, and watched my inbox for nothing.

At 5:12 p.m., just as the newsroom was entering its second wind, the police scanner coughed a phrase that made the cop reporter sit up, which made me sit up. Garner Street, it said, in a tone that sounded as if the machine had learned to say words with its eyebrows. 10-54. Possible DOA. Stairwell.

I didn’t think of Ms. Quist first. I thought of the chapel. That’s how my mind works: boxes, lines, geography. I grabbed my coat, yelled “back in ten” at no one in particular, and trotted out into a rain that had gotten bored and decided to be fog instead.

A small crowd had coagulated by the chapel’s side gate. The blue lights smeared on the wet pavement like someone’s poor idea of art. A patrol officer held up his forearm to keep people from wandering in to see something they could not unsee.

I showed him my press card and he let me to the edge of the tape, which is the same as letting someone stand on the edge of a cliff if you trust their balance.

The stairwell in question was between the chapel and the alley, a concrete spillway down from the street to the lower parking lot. In that space, in the grim light that humans always find a way to make flattering to nothing, lay a man with his head at an angle that biology does not recommend. He was in his fifties, and he wore a black suit with the kind of sheen you see on uniforms. He had a face that might have been kind when it was not doing this.

Detective Torres stepped into view like someone you don’t want to see in your mirror. Torres is all square spaces and careful hands. We have known each other long enough to be honestly irritated by each other.

“Ellison,” he said.

“Torres,” I said. “You doing stairs now? Is that a promotion?”

“Find a better job,” he said mildly. “You live down here now?”

“Research,” I said, and looked deliberately at the dead man. “He looks like he belonged to the place.”

“He did,” Torres said. “Name is Michael Shepherd. He runs the chapel.”

“The director,” I said. “He’s the man you talk to when your aunt’s terrible life needs softening for public consumption.”

“So you two would have gotten along,” Torres said. He flipped his notebook without looking at it. “He fell. Or was helped. We’ll know when we know. You’re not writing me a poem.”

“No poems for you,” I said, and then, because the impulse that gets me into trouble is the same one that makes me good at this, I added, “Can I see his hands?”

He gave me a flat look. He knows I collect objects in my mind. He lifted the yellow tape with one finger, a gesture of reluctant permission.

Shepherd’s right hand was open, palm up, fingers still, the way hands are when they’ve forgotten their task. In it was a folded piece of paper gone soft from the rain. Torres unfolded it with a plastic bag as his glove and held it in the narrow space between us.

It was a slip from a receipt book. Garner Street Chapel at the top, in that solid ink that never fades, the kind you get from a stamp whose handle is smooth from years of being struck. Below, in a tidy hand: Friday, 11 a.m. Ms. Eleanor Quist.

Torres watched my face as if there were something written on it. There was. It said: You have got to be kidding me.

“You know her?” he said. He is not often that direct. It made me nervous.

“She sent me a letter,” I said. “Typed. Someone did. I went to see her.”

“Is she dead?”

“No,” I said. “Not as of four fifteen. She made tea.”

“She makes tea,” he said, as if I were telling him what golf course she favored.

“And someone typed their little ghost message on a machine in her living room,” I said, because I wanted to say it before I thought better of it.

He folded the paper. “You’re not my only headache today, Ellison,” he said.

“You say that like there is more than one,” I said. “Who found him?”

“Employee,” he said. “Going out to smoke. He stepped down into this and made a sound I have heard before.”

Beyond him, the chapel door stood slightly ajar, and inside I could see the edge of a room where flowers hung their heads in polite boredom. Rain frizzed gently in the alley. It was five twenty. In less than two days, at the time written on that receipt, there was supposed to be a service for a woman whose Rs limped and who had asked me, very cheerfully, not to print anything about her shadows.

“Friday,” I said under my breath, and the word stopped being a day and started being a threat.

Back at the office, the lavender envelope sat on my desk where I left it, the bee watermark buzzing quietly in my head. As I reached for it, because sometimes I touch objects to persuade them to explain themselves, my inbox pinged. The subject line on the new email was brisk as a teacher’s correction:

Correction to Quist obit.

I clicked. The body of the message was one line, typed in a font that tried to mimic a typewriter and didn’t quite manage it.

Not a fall.

On the morning the light was left on, the river had gone to glass. From the front steps of the Eleanor West Public Library, Mara Ives could see the pale spine of the water between buildings, flat as a mirror—no barges yet, no wind, only the ragged shape of a gull crossing like a thumbprint smudge. The streetlights clicked off one by one down Dannen Street while she fitted the brass key into the lock and leaned her shoulder against the heavy oak door.

Mara liked to be the first one in. It made something clean of the place, as if, in the hour before the public arrived with their strollers and damp umbrellas and questions and loneliness, the library could renew its intentions. She stood in the foyer and let the door fall closed behind her with a hush. The air met her: familiar cool, the cold dust of a century of handling, soap and lemon oil from last night’s cleaning, and, today, a thread of old rain.

It took a moment for her to understand what was different. Then she saw it, top left, in the dark pane of the second-floor mezzanine: a small, square light glowing where no light should be. The rare books room.

Mara pressed the heel of her hand into her sternum, a childish habit of steadying herself she’d never broken, and told herself to breathe. It could be nothing. Tess had mentioned last week, half-laughing, that the lamp on the rare desk was temperamental—as if finials and filaments possessed moods—but they both knew Tess had only been diffusing the fact that the west wing wiring needed replacing and there was no budget for it. If the light was on, someone had left it that way the night before. That’s all.

It would not be the first time the library had been injured by ordinary things. There was the toddler with the bubble wand in the map case, the teenage pair who’d found ways to leave inscriptions on spines without opening the books, the too-enthusiastic local history societies who wanted to borrow the city’s first charter for a potluck. Mara had been head librarian for three years and had become, unexpectedly, a negotiation specialist. But still, that little square light glowed in the half-dark like a held breath.

She went to the security desk and woke the bank of screens. The cameras fed her four angles: the lobby, the circulation desk, the main reading room—and a grainy shot of the rare books door at the top of the iron stairs. That angle was never good. The lens warped the steps into a fisheye, and the door itself looked like it belonged to a ship: heavy, old, a porthole circle of glass in the center. The time stamp on the rare books feed was blinking, frozen at 01:13. She tapped the monitor, as if it might reconsider.

“Of course,” Mara said out loud, to no one. The cameras had been installed in 2009 with a grant and had aged in dog years ever since.

She climbed. The ironwork stairs sang, a high whispery whine on every other step. The mezzanine circle, usually dim and private, was washed with a pale gold from the lamp on the rare books librarian’s desk: a deco thing with a square shade and a bronze pull chain. The chain swayed slightly, pendulum-smalls, as if someone had just touched it. There was no one in the room.

Mara put her palm flat against the glass in the rare book room door. Cool. The lock—a Yale from when the library was still a novelty in the neighborhood—turned for her key. Inside, the lamp made a little island of light that barely reached the nearest shelf. The rest of the room was shoreline: shadowy silhouettes of books in their case windows, the iron rail around the upright ladder, the ink-black rectangular mouths of Jacobs & Purdon’s locked archival cabinets.

She crossed to the desk. The blotter was clean. The pen tray was empty. The book log lay open, a neat blond rectangle of paper in the lamplight, a fountain pen set carefully across the margin. For a little while after Mara had been hired, she and Tess, who managed the rare holdings, had argued gently about the log. Tess liked the performance of certain rituals. She believed in certain talismans. The fountain pen was never supposed to leave its tray when the room was unattended.

The last entry in the log was written in a confident hand Mara didn’t recognize.

11:40 p.m., consulted Glass Collection Box 14 – E. Glass

Mara stared at the looping initials for an unreasonable number of seconds. “Ellory Glass,” she said, hearing how the name felt in her mouth. The city’s golden boy benefactor. The library’s namesake in all but name. Without Ellory Glass, the Eleanor West would have been a different building—fewer stained glass windows, no lunette of swans over the south door, none of the carved newel posts with their solemn owls. On paper, he had been lost forty-three years: a once-famous architect who vanished on a Thursday in April 1979, the same spring the river flooded high enough to touch the library’s front steps. His disappearance was one of those municipal stories you grew up absorbing, vague and enormous and flat. Over time it became trivia: what vanished men eat for their last meal, what vanished men liked to wear, whether they would have left as easily if they had known who depended on them.

You didn’t write his name in the rare books log as if you’d just signed out a mystery paperback.

The pen was wet. Mara smudged the lower curl of the G with her finger and felt the drag of fresh ink. She stayed very still. Her own breath sounded too loud. There were no windows in the rare book room that opened; the only draft came from the HVAC, which had coughed itself to a standstill weeks ago.

Behind her, one of the case lights flickered and died. The lamp on the desk hummed. That old rain smell threaded the air again.

“As long as you’re going to haunt this place,” she told Ellory Glass, “you could at least fix the wiring.”

A sound below made her look up. The building had its own vocabulary: the ladder-slide of book trucks, the thud of the reading room door, the low conversational murmur that seeped into the stacks and became a kind of heartbeat. This was different. A trickle. A single, slow drip.

Mara switched off the lamp and locked the rare room on her way out. In the bunker-cool light of the mezzanine she could taste the metallic tang of water. At the top of the iron stairs she put her fingers to the railing and felt dampness slick on the underside. The trickle grew louder as she descended, until she saw it: from beneath the baseboard along the west wall of the reading room, a thin, insistent line of water ran, catching the light in tiny scalpels. It gathered momentum at the corner and dripped from the lip of the marble step into the lower stack hallway. Somewhere down there the sump pump wheezed and coughed, as faithful and rickety as an old dog.

She followed the water. It led her past the shelved biographies of people who had survived worse, past the wall of framed photographs of the library’s construction, the one where the men on the scaffolding squinted solemnly into the sun and into some coming century. The air changed—more cool, more earth—and the smell of damp dust got bigger. When she turned the corner into the basement hall that led to storage and the boiler room and the staff lounge (which, if you were generous, could be called a lounge, though the couch slouched in a way that warned against confidences), she saw Lionel standing with his hands on his hips and his tool bag at his feet, bending his head to listen to the wall like a doctor.

“Don’t tell me it’s my turn,” he said without turning.

“I don’t know the rotation,” Mara said. “What’s my line? Something like ‘It’s yours if you want to make overtime’ or ‘How do we get the city to replace the pipes if you fix them too well’?”

Lionel didn’t answer right away. He was built to be underestimated—slight, quiet, with a face you’d forget in a crowd until he smiled and hit you with a dimpling charm. He’d been the building’s maintenance man for twenty-six years. He could take the elevator apart and put it back together more quickly than the fire department could walk over, and he had trained the pigeons in the south cupola not to land there by murmuring something to them that seemed to embarrass them deeply. He wore the library name on a patch over his heart as if it had been pinned there by a proud mother. He knocked on the wall and listened again. “That sound,” he said. “If you ever heard a wall cry, that’s what it would sound like.”

“It’s the west foundation?”

“Not if God’s good to us. It sounds higher, and it’s not spreading. Means it’s coming from one place. There’s pressure.”

“On what?”

“We’ll find out.”

He picked up the tool bag and started down the hall. Mara, who should have said she had things to do—unlocking the computers, answering the first email about the missing staplers, skimming Cole Porter lyrics for the afternoon’s teen music club—followed him.

At the end of the hallway, the wall changed. Here the plaster was a different color, faintly yellower than the rest. If you didn’t work in the building every day, you might not notice the seam running vertically, almost invisible unless light hit it from the side. There had been an old door here once. Nobody alive could remember using it. The rumor was that you could get to the old coal chute from here, and that the coal chute connected to the tunnels under West Avenue that had been used to smuggle whiskey during Prohibition—rumors so generous and contradictory they canceled one another out.

“It’s coming through at the baseboard,” Lionel said, kneeling. The water ran in a thin line, steady. “It’s not clean, either. See there? That’s silt.”

Mara crouched next to him. In the line of water she could see what he meant: a suspension of the river, a faint graininess, particles catching on the sheen of the marble.

“All right,” Lionel said. “We’re going to disappoint the mayor by not letting the building collapse today. Hold this.” He handed her a small pry bar. By the time she’d formed a question about what exactly she was going to do with it, he’d already taken a mallet and was tapping at the seam. The plaster here was old and more brittle than she would have thought. The seam widened, and an ache slid behind Mara’s eyes—the way it always did when a book’s spine gave and she heard it—something simultaneously wrong and necessary.

“There we go,” Lionel said softly, as if the wall were a living thing he didn’t want to scare. He set the mallet down, took the pry bar from Mara, and eased it into the gap. There was a groan from inside—as the pressure shifted, as whatever lay beyond resettled—and then the seam widened further, and a wet smell that was not like river water or the everyday damp of old buildings came out in a breath. Something sealed. Something stale. The line of water thickened and then slowed, as if mere relief of pressure were enough to calm it.

He widened the opening until the outline of the old frame showed. Beneath the paint, the wood looked honed and smooth. A door. Not bricked up. Not plastered over. Simply locked and painted to forget.

“That’s infuriating,” Mara said. “That we lost a room to a paintbrush.”

“We lose rooms to worse things.” Lionel ran his fingers under the molding. “Huh. Look at that.”

At eye level, a little to the left of where a doorknob would be, was a circle of brass the size of a quarter. Not a knob—a keyhole cover. It swung under Lionel’s thumb with a ghostly squeak and revealed an old-fashioned escutcheon, its interior dark.

“We get city locksmith down here?” he said.

“We could wait.”

“We could,” Lionel said, “or we could not.”

He took a folded set of picks from his pocket with the same lack of flourish with which he did everything. “You carry lock picks,” Mara said.

“I carry things that solve problems.”

He listened with an intensity that made Mara hold her breath without meaning to. The picks dipped, rasped, nudged. When the latch finally turned, it did so with a sigh that went into Mara in a way she felt in her ankles. Lionel stood back, and for a moment neither of them moved. The sense that they were trespassing on something felt so obvious it was almost funny; the library had trespassed on other people’s lives all the time—thieves who stole time from their jobs to read in the stacks, kids who hid in the holdings to feel safe, the homeless who would not say the word homeless out loud and sat in chairs all day to have a roof that had a name—but you didn’t usually feel, with metal in your hand, that you were on the lip of someone else’s century.

“Ready?” Lionel said.

No, Mara thought. “Yes.”

He pulled. The door dragged at first, paint sticking to paint, then let go all at once. The smell rolled out again—old paper, yes, and linen, and something else like the inside of a horn case. The room beyond was dark and rectangular. Lionel clicked on his flashlight and made a slow sweep. Its beam touched old wood floorboards, a coatrack in the shape of a tree, shelves built into the wall where the plaster had been left raw. The water had been seeping under the door, yes, but it had not soaked the room. It had sent its message and waited.

“Jesus,” Lionel said softly.

Tabloid headlines were not Mara’s instrument. Every year around October, when the city’s papers wanted to run their “Haunted Buildings of Ellsworth” pieces, they would call the library. She had collected their questions the way she collected flyers and magnets. Has anyone ever seen a figure in the rare books room? Do the lights go on and off? Are there cold spots? Can we get a photograph? She would grit her teeth and tell them the truth: no ghosts, no cold spots. The only faces appearing anywhere were in the window glass when the sun went down early on Thursday evenings and people lingered in the stacks longer than they meant to. She was aware, dimly and often with annoyance, that truth had cost the library attention those Octobers. She felt none of the satisfaction of that now.

The room on the other side of the door was not precisely a room. It felt like a memory of a room—windowless, a little narrower than it should have been, a little too tall. Someone had tried to make it comfortable decades ago and then, for reasons Mara found herself tiptoeing backward from, had shut it up. There was a table. On one corner of the table, a ceramic mug sat on a square of linen. A circle of the mug had pressed itself into the fabric in a faint brown ring. Beside the mug rested a pair of eyeglasses folded legs-in, with a flake of something pale caught in one hinge that might once have been paint. There was an armchair against the far wall with one arm worn darker where a hand had lived. Against the right wall sat a low trunk with brass corners, the kind you took to college in the 1920s if your feet never touched sidewalks.

“Look at the dust,” Lionel said. He meant its absence. A thin, even layer had settled the way it does when nobody breathes in a space for a long time. But the ring on the linen under the mug looked recent in the way of stains. It should not have been so clear. Blasphemously clear.

“Why is it dry?” Mara said. The water had licked under the door; they had both seen it.

“Because the room wanted to be dry,” Lionel said. Then he looked as if he would like to take that back and say something like gravity or sealed air.

Mara stepped in. The air was not as cold as she expected. She wanted, irrationally, to keep her voice low. “What was this?”

“Private reading room,” Lionel said. “Look here.” He ran his hand along the shelves. There were no labels. Only a dozen or so volumes: blue quarter-leather bindings with gold stamping. The titles, when her eyes adjusted, were not unfamiliar: the city’s founding diaries; an annotated copy of the charter; a first edition of Whitman with a bookplate she recognized from the special collections. On the bottom shelf, half shoved in so that the spine was protected, was a long flat box the size of a loaf of bread and very shallow. The label on the box had been removed. A square of pale where the label had been told its own story. In the corner where shelves met floor, under a drift of something like sawdust, a small leather tag lay face down, like a dog’s identification flipped by a paw. She picked it up. On the underside, filigreed, was a number: 14.

“Glass Collection,” she said. She looked back over her shoulder instinctively toward the door, as if the rare books room upstairs could hear her. She set the tag on the shelf and went to the trunk.

“Mara,” Lionel said.

“I’m not going to open it,” she said automatically, so automatically that if she had never intended to before, she would have had to now. She put her hands on the brass corners, cool and smooth, and lifted the lid.

It wasn’t empty. Why are you surprised? she asked herself, and then thought I’m still allowed to be surprised. Inside, carefully nested, were papers tied with cotton ribbon. On top, folded in thirds, lay a map of the library. It was an architect’s drawing on heavy cream paper, crisp creases preserved, the kind that made the mind think of compasses and rulers and neatly rolled tubes. The title block was in a hand she had seen only in reproductions and in the illuminated list of donors in the lobby under glass—the tall, confident letters that had once spelled out the future. Eleanor West Public Library, Proposed Plan, West Annex—Ellory Glass, AIA.

There was an X. Not dramatic. Not theatrical. An X like a reminder on a grocery list, down the right margin of the main reading room rectangle, along the west wall. Close enough to the basement door that when Mara did the math from memory, she felt the marrow in her arms go cold. The X was where the door used to be. The door in front of which she was kneeling. The X had been placed there on a date written in the same hand in pencil at the bottom right of the drawing: April 11, 1979.

Mara touched the pencil date and said, “No,” without meaning it as an answer to any question.

“Don’t,” Lionel said, which could have meant don’t say that or don’t move or don’t breathe.

The floorboard under Lionel’s right foot made a small sound like a tiny exhalation. He moved his weight back. His flashlight swept low, across the baseboard, where a slightly darker rectangle marked something that had been removed and replaced. No. A something that had been added. A panel cut and inserted and painted to look older than it was.

“We should call…someone,” Mara said. “The city. The board—”

“Let’s not call the board until we know whether to bother them,” Lionel said, not unkindly. “The board’s in love with making we-at-the-library statements.” He squinted at the panel. “And the city will want to turn this into a ribbon cutting before we know if it’s a leaky pipe with delusions of grandeur.”

Mara let herself smile and immediately lost the smile as her eyes went to the map again. The pencil marks were so ordinary. She was not a person who believed that objects trapped echoes, but in that moment she felt very close to believing.

She lifted the top stack of papers from the trunk and set them gently on the table. The ribbon nailed the bow of time in a nearly perfect square. She slid her finger under it and stopped when her nail snagged. The cotton fibers were stubborn and strong; they had not wanted to be untied. The bow’s knot connected to something else beneath—the ribbon wound down around the papers and came back through a hole that had been made purposefully in the cardboard. Somebody had tied these with a view to permanence.

She let the ribbon alone. Her hand was shaking anyway. The second thing in the trunk had sunk, so that you might not have seen it if you didn’t look from the side. She looked. An old library card. The thick card stock would once have been white. It had gone a color like tea, edges soft-fuzzed with handling. On its surface, in ballpoint blue, the letters had faded: Borrower: M. Ives.

She did not pick it up. The world went very quiet in the particular way quiet does when there are actually three more sounds in it than you can process. The sump pump coughed. Lionel’s flashlight clicked as he adjusted his grip. Somewhere upstairs a chair scraped and the sound traveled through the bones of the building.

Mara swallowed. “I never took books from here. When you’re a kid they don’t let you into—”

“That’s not the children’s room stamp,” Lionel said. “And that’s not our card format since before your parents were born.”

“My grandmother.” Mara heard herself say it as if answering a question on a test. She hadn’t meant to think of her. The M would have been for Marguerite or Mother and the handwriting would not be hers because the handwriting on the card was not human, it was the library’s distinctive printed label script, pencil neat. Her grandmother had lived two blocks from here and had worked half days mending coats in a shop in the winters when her husband’s work slowed. She had taught Mara to tie knots in yarn and call them what they were—square, clove, carrick bend—and to keep her nails clean. She had disliked fuss and had liked milk, cold, in the evening. She had died when Mara was eleven. “She had a card,” Mara said, as if it erased a decade and misplaced the room.

“So did everybody,” Lionel said gently. “So does half the town.” His light had swung, without meaning to, toward the corner. There was a violin case on the floor there, the old-fashioned type with a chipped varnish and a handle wrapped in tape so long ago the tape had become another kind of skin. Water had drawn a darker outline around the base of it on the floor, like a halo. “You tell me not to open something and I don’t,” he said, “because I am a creature of principle, but I think we should see what the water wanted us to see.”

He knelt and clicked the catches. The sound made Mara think uncomfortably of the lock on the door. Inside the case, instead of velvet, there was burlap evidently cut to fit, and nestled into the burlap, instead of a violin, was something wrapped in a coarse cotton, tied crosswise with string. Lionel looked at her. “You want to do the honors, boss.”

“Please never call me that,” she said. Her voice was steady now. She untied the string and turned back the cloth. Newsprint. Her fingers came away gray. The black was fresh somehow on her skin though the paper itself was brittle in the way you have to teach yourself not to breathe on. The headline was the same from three different papers in different fonts, all the same day:

LOCAL ARCHITECT ELLORY GLASS MISSING; WIFE SPEAKS

The photographs had been cut away. You could see the swoop where the scissors had gone, careful not to slice into the text. The three articles had been stacked and pinned with a rusty straight pin.

Mara set them on the table beside the trunk. They kept growing sides until the table itself felt like a stage for a story that had waited a long time. She looked down again into the violin case, expecting the bottom to be empty now that she had removed the paper, and saw, tucked at one end, a child’s shoe.

It was a small brown Oxford. The laces were tucked neatly inside. It had been polished to a shine once that had crackled and gone like glaze when something sits too long in a hot sun. She put a finger on the leather and did not press and felt, honest as a heartbeat, that she had trespassed into something the building had been told to keep.

“Lionel,” she said. “We’re going to need—”

He was not looking at the shoe. His face had gone a color she had never seen it. He had turned his light toward the lower wall, right of the trunk where the darker panel was, and the beam found something pale. It was small and round, and for a fraction of a burred second Mara thought of the handle of a drawer.

It was not a handle. It was a knuckle.

The panel had not been set back perfectly flush with the baseboard. In the half-inch gap at the bottom, in the line where water had licked and then receded, something had settled forward, a pale, reached curve, like a hand that had been asleep against a door for a very long time and, in hearing strangers in the room, had finally remembered to knock.

I mend torn things for a living. Paper is more forgiving than people; with paper, you can reconcile the past to the present with paste and patience, coax fibers back into line, smooth wrinkles with the soft heel of your hand. The trick is to do as little as possible and leave the least of yourself behind.

On the morning the city arrived at my office door, I was hunched over a nineteenth-century plat map of the Eastbank floodplain, tip of a sable brush dragging wheat-starch paste along a slit the size of an eyelash. The room smelled like what it always smells like: old paper—a hint of vanilla and dust—and the faint vinegar of cleaning solution. Outside the windows, the river made slow commentary on its way past the brick buildings of the old warehouse district. February meant the light was thin and slanted, catching in the floating flock of paper fibers and illuminating each one as if to prove that a single speck could hold a century.

"I'm looking for Ms. Ilyas?" A man in a hard hat blocked the doorway, cold air and grit rolling in with him. "Department of Records said you'd be the best one to ask."

"Ask what?" I capped the paste and set my brush aside. My hands remembered not to touch anything without wiping first; my mind didn't, racing a little at the thought of disruption. The plat had waited a hundred and ten years; it would wait another day. Most things do.

He was older than me, early fifties maybe, one of those foremen whose beard had gone white without losing its shape. His name badge—scraped and dirty—read Kavanagh. "We opened a wall on the Vesper site," he said. "There's paper behind it. Rolls of it. Someone said 'call Records' and they sent me here. Also there's—" He lifted his hand and let it prick the air, as if uncertain whether to say the word. "A room. We're not sure what it is. You should see it."

I had been a paper conservator long enough to have a small stable of questions for situations like this, starting with stabilization and ending with insurance. Instead, I asked, "The Vesper Theater site?"

He nodded. "They're doing the footings for the new condo tower. We cut into an old foundation—thick as sin. Found a bricked arch. We had an engineer look at it for gas, and it clears, but... there's stuff. Old stuff. It looked like your kind of trouble."

The Vesper had burned in 1913 and taken sixty-three lives with it. I knew this because I'd spent a summer two years ago mending thirty-six charred programs recovered from someone's attic, each resurrection leaving my desks covered in soot and my head full of names. The city had finally decided to do something with the lot where the blackened husk had sat for a hundred years: raze, stabilize, build. Every decade makes a different kind of amnesia.

"Give me ten minutes," I said.

I wrapped the plat in tissue and set it on its shelf, wiped my hands with a chamois towel and then again for luck, and grabbed my kit: a soft brush, nitrile gloves, a zippered pouch with spatulas and tweezers and a folded apron that kept the powder of older things off my clothes. There is probably a German word for the kind of joy and dread that comes when you are called to a place that will ask something honest of you. If there isn't, Greywater should invent one.

Kavanagh led me out into the river wind and down three blocks to where the street widened into a fenced-off construction site. The skin of morning had not yet thickened; the little flags that marked gas lines bowed as if in prayer. The Vesper rose bluntly from the mud, not a theater any longer so much as a suggestion of a doorway framed in blackened stone. Behind the chain link, an excavator held its steel mouth aloft like an animal hesitating over a kill.

We signed in at a trailer with coffee stains on the blueprints. "Don't mind the mess," the woman at the desk—Neve—said. She wore a jacket with the city logo stitched at the breast. "We've had four different crews through since Monday and none of them know what a trash bag is."

"You the conservator?" asked a man coming out of the back room. He was about my age, with dark hair shaved close and a face that looked like it had learned to be careful. "Mateo Ortiz, city engineering. We met with fire and utilities. Air read good, no methane, no weird voltage, but we haven't declared anything on the other side of the wall accessible just yet. You can look through the breach and tell us if anything is going to crumble if we sneezed at it."

"Nothing likes being sneezed at," I said, and then followed him out into the cold.

They had built a temporary staircase of bolted scaffolding that led down into what had once been a basement. As my boots clumped down the treads, my breath made a ghost in the air I could pretend didn't belong to the building. You could feel the difference when you passed the level of the original door. The air changed. There is a temperature to memory.

At the base of the stairs, the light went from winter to electric. Halogen lamps cast a false afternoon over the ruins: beams and brickwork, the metal skeleton of the balcony you could stand under and look up at imagination's ceiling. In one corner, someone had hung caution tape across a waist-high section of wall, yellow triangle paint pointing to a hole the size of a man. Bricks had been knocked out methodically, laid in a neat sacrificial pile. The mortar scars around the opening told a story of haste and quiet: someone had bricked up this arch fast, some long time ago, and then someone else had decided today would be the day to undo it.

"Did you get it on the first try?" I asked. My voice was lower now without meaning to be.

Kavanagh scratched his beard. "The wall was thinner there. We were cutting for caissons and my guy heard the pitch change. Hollow. It's like a bottle. You tap and it sings."

Ortiz held up a black box with a digital readout. "We checked O2 and CO. Oxygen's lower than out here, but not dangerously so. No carbon monoxide ping. The air is stale, though. Old. It's probably a sealed cavity. I'm wondering if it's an old coal chute or a servant's passage. The Vesper had all kinds of weird behind it. Auditoriums were front-of-house, but the real city was back here."

He swung his headlamp towards the gap and clicked it on. The beam spilled into the hole. I stepped closer.

On the other side of the wall, the light caught a curve of plaster dust, a strip of floorboards bleached to a bone-gray you only get when water has had its say, and, beyond, the outline of a low room that ran parallel to the basement. Not a corridor, exactly. More like a storage chamber, the way monasteries have cellars to tuck away their secrets. The opening offered a sightline into a corner that held an unexpected order. Someone had lined shelves along one wall. It was too dim to count, but I could make out the ghostly cylinders of paper rolls, bound with ribbon or string. That was what had raised Kavanagh's eyebrows. The smell that came through the hole was the shyest of breaths: dust; something faintly sweet, like when you open a box and the perfume of a long-gone owner has colonized the air. And under that—just a notch under—something else. The word formed in the back of my throat and refused the dignity of its letters.

"Is that...?" Kavanagh began, and didn't finish.

"Give me the light," I said.

He handed me a flashlight. I pulled on gloves and leaned in, bracing my shoulder against brick. The beam made white out of dust and turned my own breath into weather. The chamber beyond was maybe twenty feet by ten, with a curved brick ceiling that had been plastered over, then water-stained into an atlas of forgotten continents. The shelves were narrow and bowed, but still holding: rolls of paper, the occasional tin box, a little stack of what might have been ledgers wrapped in cloth and tied with string tight enough to make grooves.

Against the far wall, right in the center, was a chair. It was a wooden chair of no particular merit, the kind you could find in any secondhand store: four legs, back spindles, a seat that had seen wiser seasons. It sat like a punctuation mark under a small chalky circle on the wall where something had once hung and was now gone. On the floor beside the chair, glinting in the torchlight, a metal coin of some sort—no, not a coin, a watch, pocket-sized, its chain curled like a sleeping animal. And in the chalky dust on the floor, plain as any sign you don't want to read: footprints. They marched from the broken arch to the chair, two sets, crossing and recrossing, tracks with a diamond pattern at the ball and heel, and another with a smoother sole and a small nick that repeated with each step. In a room sealed by brick and time, the edges of those prints were sharp.

My back prickled. I was suddenly aware of my own shoes.

"What do you see?" Ortiz asked. He was careful not to let his voice carry.

"Paper," I said, because saying footprints would make us all no longer safe, and I am sometimes a coward. "Blueprints, I think. And a ledger."

"Any risk of collapse?"

"The ceiling looks sound," I said. "The shelves want to sag. If we move anything, they'll sigh and make us pay attention. There's a chair and—" I swallowed. "It isn't just paper."

Kavanagh did a chin tilt that meant go on. Construction men have a language as coded as archivists'.

"Footprints," I said finally, soft enough that the word had trouble getting itself together. "Inside. I can't say how old. But the dust isn't disturbed beyond the sets I can see. The edges are crisp."

Ortiz looked past me into the black. "There isn't another way in," he said. "We've scanned most of the perimeter now that we've exposed it. Solid all around. We took the O2 reading through the breach and got nineteen percent. If there were a hidden vent, we'd expect a different number."

"Maybe it's nothing," Kavanagh said.

"I just told you it's footprints," I said, and heard my own impatience, and flattened it. "Anyone go in after you broke through?"

"Not one foot," Neve said from behind, making all of us jump. She had a tablet tucked under her arm and an expression that reminded me of my sister when she caught you lying to her. "We taped it off all night. If a raccoon learned how to do the Macarena in there you'd have twelve photographs from six angles."

We stood in a cluster at the hole and looked at what we could see. There was a small miracle in the way the paper had kept its cylinder. There was a small horror in the way the chair sat waiting. I have been on excavation sites before. The past likes to make traps of expectation. Sometimes what you find is nothing like what you think.

"We need to document before we breathe too much for it," I said. "Anything we move will change the balance. Can you get me plastic sheeting and some boxes? And a gentler light. These lamps will cook the room."

Ortiz snapped his fingers at someone and a few minutes later I had laid the plastic in front of the breach to give us a clean threshold. I kneeled, headlamp strapped on, and wormed through the arch like a beetle. The dust on the other side had the fine cinder of a hundred-year-old winter. My breath sounded like someone else's. Behind me, their voices became a pattern of syllables I could hold like prayer beads.

The rolls of paper were indeed blueprints. My light caught the unmistakable Prussian tint under the dust and the white of negative lines. The top one had a label in an elegant hand: ORCHESTRA PIT VENTING, VESPER, 1909. The number 7 had a crossbar through it, the way my old mentor at the university used to write it, a habit I'd always teased him about. It made the 7 look like a letter that wanted more attention than it deserved. I told myself that all draftsmen of the period wrote that way. I told myself a lot of things.

The ledger sat on the second shelf, wrapped in muslin. I touched the cloth and it went to powder in my fingers, a sigh released after a long inhale. I slid the book out as if it might startle. It was bound in leather, spine cracked in one place like a smile that had not been practiced in a while. On the cover someone had written ACCOUNTS, 1911-1913, in a hand that didn't care about handwriting. The clasp had no lock. The weight of it in my hands was the kind of weight that belongs to words like "record" and "evidence." I set it on the sheeted threshold and told Neve, "Photo everything you can. Then get the evidence bags."

"I thought you didn't work for the police," Neve said.

"I don't," I said. "But I work for the city, and sometimes that's the same god."

Their lights shifted, making a little snow of floating dust. The chair grew more definite. The watch on the floor was gold-plated with a monogram. I moved toward it, careful of the prints. The dust scuffed under my boots at the edges, a soft apology.

The watch's face had spun to darkness. I turned it gently. 8:04. The glass was not cracked. The hands looked like they had stopped with intention. Someone had polished it not long ago; the metal was not as dull as everything else in the room. There was more. A thread lay on the chair seat. At first I thought it a stray hair. It was finer than that and dark, a cord of something I'd come to recognize in the lab under magnification: soot that had fused with a fiber. On the chair back, faint, two darker rings, as if something had rubbed or been tied there and left a whisper of itself behind. Rope marks, my brain offered, and then immediately gave the information a place to go where it would not be seen.

The smell in the room adjusted itself. It went sweeter by a notch, ripened by the heat of our lamps and our living. Some part of our bodies knows to catalog the air. There was the answer I didn't want.

"You smell it?" I asked, to no one in particular.

Kavanagh swore softly. "Christ."

"You should get your people out," Ortiz said, quietly now. "We'll call it in. We'll do this by the book. Neve, get the tape. No one breathes on anything unless we need them."

I looked past the chair to the far right corner. The light revealed a darker shape in the floor's shadow, a tumble of fabric and a shape beneath it that had the wrong geometry to be anything other than what it was. The cameras hadn't caught it from the angle of the hole. I took a step and then stopped myself, because there is a way to enter a room like this and I had just broken it.

"There's someone," I said. The words found their own quiet. "In the corner. On the floor."

Neve already had her radio up. The police like to say they respond as if it's the first time they are doing it. Sometimes it's true.

We pulled back, well-trained. Ortiz said something about sealing the breach to preserve air and I said something about letting the temperature equalize or we'd cause condensation, and we all fenced with our own kinds of knowing until we bordered the terrified thing that lives in any human room when there is a body in it.

Officer Neve put tape across the gap, a yellow banner pinned by plastic cones to brick. "No one in," she said with a voice that didn't tolerate annotation.

We waited for the detectives like people wait for weather to decide them. The crews stilled their machines. Somewhere above, the excavator sighed as if disappointed its work would be put on pause. The wind tugged a loose sheet of Tyvek and made a sound like a speech in a language you haven't learned yet. I sat on an upturned bucket and rested my gloved hands on my knees and tried not to think of the ledger that had been just a book until it wasn't.

I had wanted, foolishly, to be the first hands on the paper in that room. Not out of possessiveness, though maybe a little of that, too, the way any craftsperson wants to be first to speak with an object whose language they understand. Now I would spend weeks negotiating with other people's protocols and paper bags and chain-of-custody forms and the careful turning of pages under the watchful gaze of a camera. There are worse things than bureaucracy, I told myself. There are always worse things.

Detectives walked into the A-frame of the basement with the contained energy of people who have learned that posture is answer as much as question. The lead was a woman in her forties with hair gathered at the nape in the kind of twist you do when it's more for yourself than for other people. She took in the room and the breach and the way our attention pooled around it like tidewater. "Detective Tamsin Roe," she said. "Who's Ortiz?"

Ortiz raised a hand. "Engineer. Air is good. No gas. We haven't touched anything inside the cavity since we saw the—" He let the word dissolve.

"Who's the conservator?"

"That would be me," I said. "Mara Ilyas. Department of Records."

Her eyes went to my gloves, to the smudge on my knee where I'd leaned into dust, to the plastic she'd noted under two minutes ago. "You went in?"

"Yes," I said, letting the apology happen in my voice. "I identified potential risk to the documents and determined they were stable. I also observed footprints. Two sets. And a watch on the floor. And... in the far corner, a body."

She nodded once. "So I haven't arrived late enough. If you're both willing to come back through the whole thing twice, we'll try to do it without shaking the place to pieces."

Another woman from Forensic, Gus Haney, had a rolling cart with tripods and bags. She began to set up as if the room had always waited for her. She'd been to my lab two summers ago and had once let me use her digital microscope to look at a watermark in a pamphlet so fragile it might have been made of breath. She caught my eye and lifted her eyebrows in the worldless language of colleagues. It said: Can you stand it if I do my job in front of you? It said: I'm glad you're here.

We made our careful inventory. We crawled through in a choreography of caution, the way divers do when a cave narrows and you must make yourself smaller to pass. Photographs of the dust told the story of the prints with more authority than I could. One set was indeed made by a sole with a diamond pattern. The other set was the smooth sole with a nick. The stride length told us little. If I had to say, I would have said one person was taller. The edges of the prints told us more. Crisp edges meant recent, but not how recent. Dust does not keep a calendar. We measured the humidity and temperature and wrote them down because we needed to write down something that could be controlled.

The body was a man. He lay on his side, knees bent, as if he had curled toward his more comfortable self and found it gone. He wore a suit that tried to be modest about its expensive fabric, and a tie that had been loosened as if by an irritated hand. His hair was the gray of weather on river water. The skin of his face had gone to chalk where it wasn't mottled. There were no bullet holes that I could see, no obvious apocalypse. A ring on his left hand caught light and threw it back thinking no one would notice. I noticed. He had no shoes. The prints with the nick were small enough to have been his, but who could say. The pockets had been turned out: tidy little white tongues of lining sticking up accusatorily. He had been dead some hours and not more than a day. He had been dead inside a sealed room.

"If this was sealed since the fire," Kavanagh said later, "he's either a ghost or a magician."

Detective Roe looked at the watch in its little evidence bag and then back at the man's hands. "Or someone's practicing a different kind of trick," she said.

"Any ID on him?" Neve asked.

"Not yet," Haney said. "We'll print him, but for now he's just our Mr. X in a suit. Someone loved him enough to buy him that ring."

"I've seen that suit," Kavanagh said into his beard.

"You've seen all suits," Ortiz countered. He was grounding himself in joking now and I didn't hold it against him. You do what you do when your job is about not letting the earth surprise you.

"Something else," Haney said, squinting at the wall above the chair. She stepped closer, careful of the footprints. The little chalky circle had a faint rectangle of darker paint beneath it, like a ghost picture. "Something used to hang here. See the outline?"

"A photograph? A mirror?" I asked.

"A calendar," Roe said. She pointed to the faint numbers scumbled in charcoal on the wall near the circle. Vertical column, months abbreviated. There were Xs through some of the days like someone had kept track. 1912—no. The numerals were not old. 2025—no, either. The hand had an energy to it that felt uncomfortable against the rest of the room. The last date with a mark was three days ago.

I felt the small muscles along my shoulders pull tight. "Detective," I said, because someone had to say it, "what year is it in there?"

Roe looked at me with something that was not unkindness and not comfort. "Probably the same as it is out here," she said. "Which is the problem."

We went through the ledger in my lab that afternoon after I'd signed papers longer than the book itself. The pages were the crackle of good rag paper, onion-skin thin, lined in red, columns of numbers that meant coal and lighting and wages and, once, a payment to a Deputy Marshal with a notation so terse it might have been a threat. On the third page was a pressed leaf, not a fern, as my brain first said, but a piece of seaweed, brittle and improbable, a brackish offering a long block away from the river's saltless tongue. On the inside back cover someone had written a name and crossed it out with such efficiency it left the ghost of graphite in the fibers anyway. The name meant nothing. The way it was crossed out did.

I live in a city that has two faces. The first is the one in postcards: the river and its iron bridges, the hill with its park and its snow, streetcars with names painted in gilt. The second face is the one that stares up at you from the excavation trench when you lean over: broken bottle glass, a rusted hinge, a shard of blue willow plate, a newspaper headline from 1913 that says "Dreadful Night At The Vesper; Many Lost." You could live here your whole life and only learn one face. Or you could be unlucky like me and love them both.

The next morning, before I spoke with the detectives again, before the papers ran their photographs and the internet made its theories, I found a small envelope on the floor just inside my apartment door. No postage, no name. The paper was expensive, the kind of envelope that has a texture like honor. Inside was a piece torn from a blueprint. Blue, white lines. At first I thought it was of the Vesper. The paper tipped the smell of age, the late-Edwardian kind of glue they used on corners. But the scale was wrong and the notations notations were in a hand I knew too well: sharp, precise, with that cross-barred seven. Someone had circled a rectangle in pencil and written in the margin, two words like someone telling a joke they didn't care if you understood.

Wrong century.

Later, I would learn that the man in the suit had a name I had seen printed on the glossy programs for city fundraisers. Later, I would understand what it means to count days on a wall as if that would do anything at all to keep them from doing what they do. For the moment, with the city around me smelling like river and late winter and the news not yet arrived at my phone, I stood in my hallway, the blueprint scrap in my hand like a playing card in a game no one had taught me.

I mend torn things for a living. Some tears are not in paper. Some mendings do not keep. But I know how to read edges. And I knew, holding that torn blue square, that someone had gone into a room that had been sealed for a hundred years and come out long enough to leave me a clue and at least one other person had not come out at all.

The book came back on a Tuesday, swollen at the spine as if it had tried to hold its breath.

Mara Jensen heard it before she saw it, a soft, indecisive thud in the metal return bin behind the circulation desk. She looked up from the forms she’d been ignoring and watched the flap ease closed again, the lobby beyond it empty and still. Outside, someplace invisible, the tide was turning and the wind off the harbor found a loose seam in the western window and worried at it, first with a long, thin whine and then with a hollow cluck that rapped the glass in time with the old radiator’s ticking. It was March in Grey Harbor. Off-season tourist banners hung stunned on their poles and the gulls looked like folded paper against the sky.

She slid off her stool. The bin gave no resistance until the very last inch, then caught against the swollen edge of the book wedged under the lip. She pried, wriggled, and when it came free it left a ribbon of damp on her palm and a bruise of cold in the heel of her hand. Up close, the book smelled like low tide and a basement flood—wet nylon and salt over flannel and glue. The cloth cover had once been a dignified navy but had faded under bleachy sun to something like the underside of a stormcloud. The title stamped on the spine had sloughed off in patches; what remained read The Drow—Atla.

“Mystery returns,” she said to nobody. She had been on her own all morning. Dotty Walsh, who usually reported for duty at ten sharp to complain about her knees and sort paperbacks by whether she liked the author’s hair, had phoned to say her granddaughter’s car had chosen the exact moment she needed it to forget how to be a car. Mr. Cone, who came every day at eleven to read The Grey Harbor Standard and scowl at the obituaries as if they’d taken a personal risk by getting written, wouldn’t arrive for another hour. The town’s students were in school. The town’s tourist shops were asleep.

Mara carried the book to the desk. She set it down on a piece of butcher paper she kept for emergencies and patted its spine like you might a startled dog.

“Let’s see who you belong to.”

Grey Harbor had been proud of its library once, a red-brick edifice with a scalloped cornice and carved stone herring above the door. Half the town’s fathers had been fishermen and half of those had little boys who had been marched here by little mothers who wanted something more than nets for fingers. All that history had given Mara a card catalog with drawers that still smelled like cedar and an attic full of aging maps nobody used and—most unexpectedly—a handful of books that had slipped under the digital net when the old paper-pen rules had given way. The Drowned Atlas had one of those paper pockets pasted to the inside back cover, bubbled now under a film of salt. In the pocket, against a faded index card stamped with dates in red and purple ink, sat the squared-off shadow of time.

Mara tugged the card out with care. The ink was bled in places where someone with wet hands had slipped the stamp. She traced the dates with her eyes.

1999. 2001. 2003.

Her mouth had been dry all morning. Now it went dryer. The last stamped date had the library’s old hand-lettered due stamp and a name in tight, neat caps.

WHITCOMB, GREER.

She read it again. The outline of the letters pressed into the card’s surface where the ballpoint had dragged over, hard enough to transfer to whatever lay underneath. Her thumb found the indentation as if she could catch the shape of the girl’s name in relief.

Greer Whitcomb had walked into this building nineteen years ago and taken out The Drowned Atlas. Two weeks later, on the night of the regatta party, she had walked out of the world.

Mara had written that sentence once, long ago, or some sharpened version of it in a column for the Boston paper that had sent her out to cover a coastal town’s grief like it was a weather system. The Whitcombs were old money that had learned to pass in a town that pretended not to have any. They owned what had used to be the packing plant at the mouth of the river before it turned into a row of lofts with names like Net House and Wharfside, and they wrote checks to the school’s music program and let the fishermen’s wives hold their pancake breakfasts in their backyard every first Saturday in June. The summer Greer disappeared a reporter had asked Mara if there was a difference between a missing person and a missing princess. Mara had said no, which had looked brave in print but felt thin in the mouth.

She kept the card in her fingers and opened the back cover wider.

Something fluttered out and caught on the butcher paper with a soft, sticky sound. A Polaroid, the old kind with the white thick border at the bottom, the kind that developed color like bloom. This one had a tide of ruin across one corner where water had seeped under the protective film and turned the reds to rust and the blacks to aquarium green. The picture itself had been taken at night.

It was of the sea baths.

Mara didn’t need the caption to tell her; that cold slice of concrete bleachers stepping down to a square of trapped ocean water, the iron fence that tried and failed to keep the December storms from waltzing in, the half-collapsed diving platform whose ladder had been removed long ago and yet still carried rumors like barnacles—all of it was familiar in a way that made her jaw ache. She recognized the angle too. The Polaroid had been taken from the back, up on the promenade that ran along the top of the baths, under the sodium vapor lights that turned skin the color of old nickel. In the center of the frame, near the far edge of the pool where the sea slopped in, stood a figure. Dark coat. Hood up. The brim of the hood hid the face. The figure had one arm lifted toward the water as if to test a temperature or wave to somebody just out of the frame.

She could feel her heart beating in her wrists. She turned the photograph over.

Under the chemical sheen someone had written in pencil, letters the same tidy tightness as the name on the card, though she couldn’t know that, not really.

This time, start with the girl.

There was a small wet fingerprint in the lower corner, the spiral distinct. Without thinking, Mara raised her hand to her mouth and breathed warm air onto her thumb to keep from smearing it, an absurd, too-late reflex. She reached for the drawer that held the plastic sleeves the historical society insisted she use for anything older than their current board president and slid the photo into one with more gentleness than she’d given human beings in months.

The bell over the library door jittered a half-chime under a draft and stilled. No one came in.
