Her first instinct—a reporter’s, thick-muscled from years of having it rewarded—was to look for more information. Who had returned the book? Camera? Logs? The library’s security camera was a compromise between the town’s reluctance to be seen and their zeal for knowing: a single lens over the inner door, angled to catch faces coming and going. The book drop was in the vestibule under that sightline, which meant in theory the camera would have caught whoever opened the outer slot and pushed the book through.

“In theory,” Mara said. She tapped the stack of forms she’d been supposed to fill out—volunteer hours, interlibrary loan tallies, a questionnaire from a grant about community engagement that made events sound like disease—and moved to the monitor under the counter. The camera software was primitive and mean. She navigated to last night.

The image was grainy but good enough. The vestibule appeared and disappeared, appeared and disappeared, in ten-second bites of time. She watched customers come and go after school, teenagers shucking their jackets the second before the frame change to show bare arms. Dotty with her knitted bag. Mr. Cone with his hat on even indoors. Mara taking the CLOSED sign out of the window and flipping it toward night. Lights going to sleep. Dark.

At 1:13 a.m., the vestibule woke. A sleeve and the edge of a rain cape, slick and glistening as if oiled, came and went in the frame. The outer slot flapped open. A hand reached in.

The program’s poor resolution made the details ugly. She tried it in full screen. It helped a little. She watched the hand again. Knuckles large. The blunt-fingered confidence of someone who slept without worrying about breaking their nose. No wedding ring. On the index finger, the fat circlet of a signet. The ring’s face flashed only once, a little white place where the camera had not quite caught up with the fluorescent lights. In that flash was a suggestion of a shape. An anchor? A grill of some sort, latticework? She let the ten seconds run three times until she began to see what she wanted, then backed away and made herself remember that wanting was contagious, possibly terminal.

Under the desk, her phone skated against wood, buzzing the way it did when someone called from one of the numbers she had marked in her contacts as maybe. She let it buzz a second time and then pulled it out.

Unlisted.

She could let it go to voicemail and both pretend she hadn’t and remain the exact kind of person who didn’t. What she did instead was answer and say nothing.

There was a blip and the smallest sound, a held breath more than a word. The timbre of the line said winter and old wiring. In the space of that breath she thought of Rolland Brody—Eli, she had mostly trained herself to call him Eli now that they were both past high school and the things that had been attached to names had shaken themselves loose—of his coffee always two minutes too late, of his laugh. She thought of Greer’s mother’s bracelets singing in the light when she had turned her wrists the day they announced the scholarship. She thought of the sea baths in the dark, the shape at the edge of the water turning a face you couldn’t see.

“Hello?” she said to the line.

“You’ve been quiet,” a voice said. Male. Not young. No distinct accent, only the lack of one. The kind of voice that could set a term. “I was beginning to think you’d forgotten how.”

“I’m sorry?” she said, and then, because the years hadn’t sanded it down enough, “Who is this?”

Silence again, but not empty. A space filled with the pressure of someone listening and not bothering to hide it.

“I made it easy,” the voice said at last, almost mild. “You always think things are more complicated than they have to be. Same book. Same pool. Try again, Ms. Jensen.”

The click, when it came, felt old-fashioned. It had weight. It rang in the air after the line went dead. Mara watched the green square of the camera software cycle back to midday sun and the mayor standing in the vestibule last week for his photo op with Dotty and Mr. Cone for the Standard, all of them smiling in a way that showed teeth and no one’s eyes. The mayor, Noah Beck, had corkscrew hair he kept trying to bully into a part and the kind of hands that spoke to comfort out loud. He also wore his ring every hour of every day that Mara had seen him, a gold oval engraved with the town’s crest—the anchor threaded with rope, the rope knotted into a wreath. In certain lights the ring could look like nothing more than a pale, burnished flicker.

There was a line they drilled into cub reporters about numbers. If you see a number once it’s a curiosity. Twice it’s a coincidence. Three times and it’s a pattern. She wasn’t sure where rings fell on that scale, or warnings, or waterlogged books that felt like something had held them under. Patterns hid in everything if you were lonely enough.

“Who was that?” Mr. Cone said, materializing at the desk as only old fishermen and cats knew how to do. He had the Standard under his arm, folded to protect the masthead from the coming scowl.

“You move quietly for a man your size,” Mara said. She put the phone face down next to the mouse. She put the Polaroid inside the plastic sleeve under the blotter where it wouldn’t catch his eye unless he felt like being nosy. He often felt like being nosy.

“That’s what my last three wives said,” he said, as he always did. He tipped his chin at the book on the butcher paper. “Someone return us a fish?”

“Something like.” Mara slid the book a fraction farther from him, a motion so small it might have just been tidying. Mr. Cone had eyes like a gull that had read every tide chart in town for the last fifty years and refused to be impressed by any change in the moon.

He sniffed the air and then, to her brief relief, sniffed the day instead. “Sharp. You feel that? My grandmother always said March was the month with fingers. It know where you got soft. You want me to bring that space heater back up from my truck?”

“I’ll survive,” Mara said. “You need the paper?”

“What I need is for people to stop dying and then insisting someone write it down in a way that makes them sound good. But I’ll settle for the sports section.”

He took up his usual chair by the window, the one with the ring worn in the varnish where his elbow had fretted the wood before he remembered not to lean, and spread the paper with surgeon care. Mara watched him for the smallest moment and then returned her attention to the book.

She didn’t have to open the Atlas to know what was inside. The library had had two copies once. She’d shelved the second one last spring in Local History. Tide charts and maps and stories in the margins about storms that had named themselves by the damage they did. What had Greer wanted from a book like that two weeks before she went missing? Information about the sea baths? They had been there since the 1920s, a city idea translated to a town that was never quite sure it wanted such things. Even empty, they held an audience. Lovers wrote initials in the paint with keys and then, when the salt got into what they had done and swelled it, complained that the sea had ruined their promises.

Mara flipped the atlas open anyway, careful of the brittle binding. Pages riffled past. The endpapers had bloomed with fungal dragons in the years of damp, the spectacle for a particular kind of child who liked grossness, the kind who would grow up and learn words like patina to pretend they weren’t still delighted with rot. She turned the map of the harbor, the part of the river that turned green in June with eelgrass and light. The sea baths were a notch at the edge of one of the drawings, labeled in careful black script as Municipal Bathing Pool, which had always made Mara imagine men in shirtsleeves and women in caps with rubber flowers, a time when a thing could be both municipal and a place people wanted to go.

There were notes in the margin. Not many; just a few. Neat and tight. Not Greer’s—Mara refused to know even in private what Greer’s writing looked like. The notes belonged to some anonymous hand that had owned a different life before pencils went on their way. The pencil-gray had softened where water had kissed it and then evaporated, leaving salt stars at the edges. Near the sea baths, the anonymous hand had underlined something on the chart about currents and added one quiet edit: north when the wind is east.

Mara made a deal with herself very fast and very old. She would tell Eli. She would put the book and the card and the photograph in a box and she would carry it next door past the firehouse where teenagers smoked on nights they weren’t supposed to and into the squat little police building with its two cells and its bulletin board of charity car washes. She would set the box down on Eli Brody’s desk and say: This is yours. She would let him take the Polaroid in his big hands and look at her with that look that forgave and didn’t forget, and she would go home and eat the soup she had made and not tell her mother in the kitchen with the radio too loud that Greer Whitcomb had come back in a way that books did. In return, the universe would not require anything of her she had already used up.

The bell jangled. Dotty came in with hair blown sideways and indignation catching fire in her cheeks. Behind her, with that knack he had of arriving where the sound was thinnest, Eli Brody filled the doorway.

His coat was unbuttoned in defiance of March and his step. He took in the room in a glance and then took it in again more slowly, like a man training himself not to run. He warmed the lobby when he arrived and cooled it, too. Mara felt both and wanted neither.

“Morning,” Dotty said to the air, offended on general principle.

“Morning, Dotty,” Mara said, and then to Eli, unable to make the tone as even she wanted it, “Chief.”

He nodded at her and then at Mr. Cone and then at the book on her desk. Something in his eyes, which had always told the truth when the rest of him didn’t, tightened.

“You get anything interesting dropped in your slot last night?” he asked. Not surprised. Not quite casual. Like a man whose phone had gone off at 1:20 a.m. and had been thinking since then of what to say first.

Mara set her hands flat on the counter and learned again the weight of the wood. Her old deal with the universe folded in on itself with the ease of something that had always been paper.

“I was just about to bring it over,” she said.

“Good,” Eli said. He stepped closer. Up close she could see that someone had snuck a second cup of coffee into his day. He smelled like damp wool and cold air and the starch his mother had used on his collars when they were seventeen. He held up a clear evidence bag. Inside the bag was a yellow slicker, the kind sold for tourists who wanted to look like fishermen on festival weekends and for children whose mothers were smart. The slicker was torn along one sleeve, a small neat slice that could have been a knife or could have been the insistence of rock. On the cuff, in a spatter that could have been paint but wasn’t, were freckles of brown.

He lifted the bag a little, as if she might not have seen it. “We pulled this out of the sea baths at dawn,” he said. The little muscles around his eyes didn’t move. “And I think you and I should go talk somewhere I can shut the door.”

Chapter One

Buildings talk; you just have to learn their language.

Some people listen for music. I listen for plaster dust and fan belts and the slow settling of joists over a hundred winters. A room is never silent. It hums with what it was built for and what it has seen, and if you stand still long enough the echoes tell you who has been lying.

Morgan County Courthouse sat on the highest block of Brackenridge as if it had elbowed itself out of the brick row houses and set its dome to watch for trouble. It was a stern, beaux-arts contraption, all pilasters and patience, with two stone lions on the front steps and a ceiling mural of men in togas pretending to be miners. When they hired me in late October, the dome was swaddled in scaffolding and white drop cloth, giving the whole place the weird, theatrical look of a stage set half-struck. Three months of restoration had stripped away the grime and toothpaste-colored paint, cracking the old building open. Old buildings like that have memories folded into their cavities. You could smell it—lemon oil and wet gypsum, steel dust from saws, old paper that had slept too long.

I do acoustic surveys for a living. That means I come into spaces people love and spaces people hate and help them hear what they've been doing wrong. Is the choir getting swallowed? Does the councilman's voice slap back at him from the back wall? Are the jurors listening to the fans instead of the testimony? I find the frequencies the room favors and the ones it resents, and then I nudge them. It feels like solving puzzles except the pieces are air and time.

For the courthouse they wanted a clean report before they finished the ceilings and rushed to cut the ribbon in November. The judge who had hired me had called it "taking the room's temperatures," which she said plural like there were several. She wasn't wrong. In rooms as old as this one, the climate is a chorus.

That's why I was there at nine on a Thursday night, when the trades had gone home and the rotunda stopped heaving sawdust. I could control my own noise. I had my little work cart, the wheeled kind hotel housekeepers use, loaded with gear: my laptop and a battery pack, a soda can-sized omnidirectional speaker and its stand, a pair of condenser mics, my headphones, a coil of gaff tape I have probably spent half my life unspooling, and a bag of chalk pastels because someone had once shown me that if you rub a little chalk into the mortar lines the texture shows up better under flash.

"Ms. Stenger, you sure you don't want someone to stay with you?" the security guard had asked when I signed in and took my badge. His name tag said LENNOX, and the frown under his mustache said I reminded him of four daughters and a wife who preferred people to be careful.

"I'm fine, Mr. Lennox," I'd said. "It's easier without footsteps in the ways they shouldn't be. I'll be a few hours."

He'd nodded like he didn't like it but couldn't argue. He'd also slid a ring of keys my way with a plastic key fob labeled ROTUNDA/ARCHIVE/MECH, the way people do when they want to show you trust so you'll be obligated to be careful with it. The ring was surprisingly heavy. Keys for damp little rooms and doors with warped frames always are.

I rolled my cart into the center of the rotunda and looked up. The scaffolding was a lacework of steel poles and planks, rising in stages up to the oval of the dome. Someone had painted a test patch on one of the pilasters. It gleamed a complicated cream in the lamplight, richer than the chalk-white of the rest. The two stone lions on the steps behind me had been scaffolding-wrapped too, sheathed in blue tarps. Only their paws showed, huge and blunt, resting on the granite. People called the nearer one the Salt Lion because no matter how often they clean him, lime bloom and pigeon droppings crust his mane white by spring. Even under plastic he looked like he was bearing the shame of it.

I set the speaker on its stand and taped down the mic cables so I wouldn't catch a toe later and ruin both my equipment and my neck. My work always looks more impressive than it feels: a small speaker under a big dome throwing out a sound that climbs and curls and comes back with secrets embedded in it. Tonight I started with a swept sine wave at low volume, an ascending siren that makes everyone who doesn't know what they're hearing look for the train. The little speaker whined through forty to twelve thousand hertz while I watched the trace on my laptop build like weather over the waveform. I ran several sweeps at different positions: center, near the bench rail, close to the receptionist’s desk (which sat under a plastic shroud like a ghost had fallen asleep there), then at the base of the stairs. In between, I clapped and snapped, sending hand-bursts of noise into corners and listening to how the room answered. Every room has its favored notes. The rotunda liked sixty-seven hertz, a flabby, chest-deep hum that came from the void under the stairs and the way the curved wall concentrated the low end.

It was on the third pass, headphones belling my ears, that I heard the whisper.

The sine sweep had died away and the room was breathing the way rooms do when you leave them alone. I walked to the second-floor landing, curiosity tugging; acoustics are as much about shape as material, and the dome's elliptical geometry can play tricks. Whispering galleries are famous for taking a murmured word at one focus and piping it across to the other as if you're sharing a secret in someone's stall. When I stepped onto the landing, a draft of cool air slid down the back of my neck. The underfloor vents were open for cleaning, their grilles leaning against the wall and exposing black mouths beneath.

Someone spoke. A man's voice, close enough that the hairs along my arms lifted, but a footstep didn't follow.

"—told you, midnight," he said. The sound did that glassy thing whispers do in oval rooms, a shiver of words sliding over plaster.

I took one headphone off my ear and held my breath. My mother used to tell me ghosts wanted to be heard and liars didn't. I'd found both to be equally noisy in practice.

"Don't use that spot," a second voice whispered. The sibilants snapped like tearing paper. "You hit it, it sings. Carrick's dogs'll hear. Other end. Under the lion."

"Salt Lion?"

"Dumbass, we have two."

The first man huffed a laugh. "It's three o'clock in the afternoon to you, isn't it? Under the Salt Lion. Jesus. Keep up."

Footsteps creaked over wood somewhere above me and to my right. On the third-floor walkway, maybe, where the dome blossomed larger and the outer wall had those little arched windows that look like punctuation marks from the street. But the words had come as if whispered right into my ear, warm and confiding.

"Knew you shouldn't have let me leave it," the second man said. "I don't like it here at night."

"Then move faster."

A rustle, fabric against scaffolding. A clink, something metallic touching metal. Then my own breath got too loud and the sounds dissolved into the room’s morning memories and the murmur of distant air.

There are a dozen ordinary explanations for overheard whispers in empty buildings. Night watchmen talking into their radios. Teenagers who think a construction site makes a romantic place. Two contractors who decided to take advantage of an empty government building to do something that had nothing to do with county budgets. But "under the Salt Lion" lodged in my head like a burr. We were inland, two hours from any coast, and the only salt in the county came out of shaker tops in diners. You don't put something under a statue unless you think no one will move it. Or maybe you find it funny, which is a kind of protection. I had to move.

I might have left then, told myself it was none of my business, not my building, keep out, keep your job. But I found my feet carrying me up the narrow staircase anyway, toward the second floor where the courtroom doors were tall and heavy and the public gallery led right under the dome. My boots made polite sounds on the steps. I held my breath at each landing to see if my breath came back alone.

"Hello?" I said once, because old habits demand politeness and because there are places where if you don't announce yourself you will only hear door frames answer. My voice skated across the plaster. No one said hello back.

At the second-floor railing, I could see the rotunda below, my little speaker a lonely sentinel in the center. The scaffolding angled up from the floor to a catwalk that ringed the base of the dome, with ladders to the upper rails. Drop cloths hung in tabbed loops along the outer wall, sliding to the floor in soft columns. A work light burned on the far side, a single halo in a field of gloom.

A foot scuffed above me, urgent and near. Then a whisper hissed, not through the wall this time but on actual air: "Hurry up. He's—"

"I heard something," the first man said. "Shh now. Shh."

A hand—gloved, a smear of white caulk on the knuckles—gripped the railing of the third-floor catwalk, three yards to my right, and for a second a sliver of silhouette broke the line of the walkway: shoulder, head turned toward the dome where my speaker sat. He was leaner than the voice suggested. He wore a hard hat with a sticker on the back, one of those orange reflective ovals the foreman at Bastian Construction handed out for night work. Whoever he was, he knew the building well enough to move in it as comfortably as if it were his own kitchen at two a.m.

I sank into the shadow behind a drop cloth and listened to my heart throw itself around my ribs. It seemed like the worst possible moment to learn my pulse was an optimist.

Metal clinked again. This time it sounded like a lock face turning in a gate you can't see. The whispering stopped. I waited so hard I could hear the skin inside my ears flex.

One minute. Two. Then footsteps overhead receded. A door snicked somewhere on the third-floor level. Air moved in a different pattern.

The part of my brain that gets me paid reminded me that if I was hearing whispers, my mics were hearing them too. I edged out from behind the cloth, eyes on the third-floor railing, and slid along the gallery back toward the stairs. If I was quiet, if I kept my shoulders under the rail line, if I didn't catch a cable with my ankle, if I kept my fear from yawning into a hall of mirrors, none of this would be my business.

I wasn't quiet enough. A nail somewhere underfoot chattered under my boot. A squeak of the sort you remember at the worst times, the kind of childhood betrayal that rewrites a house map.

The silhouette at the railing returned. He looked down the way a man looks down a cliff he's forgot is under him, something sent up to him by whatever is below. Our eyes didn't meet. If they had, I'd be telling this differently. But his head tilted, listening, then turned toward the stairs where I crouched, small as I could make myself. He frowned. Even in shadow, you can hear a frown.

"Hello?" he called, a workman voice, pleasant on purpose.

I held very still. Breath quiet. Shoulders small. No answering.

He waited, long enough for my knee to begin a quiet furious throb. Then footsteps moved away, and a buzzy voice, a work light hum. A door opened on the far side of the dome and shut again, the slap of it immediate in the near. Silence folded back over everything like the drop cloths.

I counted two hundred Mississippi under my breath. I stood, knees arguing, and walked back toward the stairs like a person going to their own kitchen at two a.m.—casual, owning the space because that is how you don't startle whatever else thinks it owns it. At the bottom, I killed the sine sweep and unplugged my mics. My hands remembered their job; the rest of me was already halfway to the front door and the stony comfort of the lions.

The Salt Lion's tarp had come unhooked at the corner. It flapped a little in the October wind, making a small sound like someone shifting in their sleep. I thought about keys under stones and where a boy in a hurry might hide something he shouldn't have. I thought how hard it would be to move a statue no one ever moves and how the phrase under the Salt Lion would sound, said in a courtroom at volume, played back on a speaker as evidence.

I re-taped a loose mic cable and made myself do one more sweep, because my report in the morning wasn't going to write itself and I didn't want to explain to the judge why it was full of holes. The trace was fatter at sixty-seven hertz than it should have been. Maybe someone had opened a cavity behind the wall. Maybe the room had picked up a new condition, the way lungs do when the weather changes or you live with a smoker.

At eleven I locked the rotunda door, returned Mr. Lennox's keys to him, and signed the log. He watched the shape my pen made the way old men watch birds they are sure have flown before. There was a baseball game on the little screen behind him, men in white uniforms gathering themselves to crouch. It cast flicker across his face like a campfire.

"You be careful, now," he said, which is what certain men of a certain age say when they want you to know they are paying attention without condescending.

"I am," I lied.

Outside, the courthouse steps held cold like a hand from a refrigerator shelf. Brackenridge's courthouse square was as empty at eleven p.m. as a movie set after the extras go home: a neon slice in the window of the diner across the street, chairs upside down on tables, a bus that never had anyone in it parked at the corner, a stray grocery cart with a bent wheel. The lion tarps flapped again and went still.

On my way to my car, I looked over my shoulder as often as a person who isn't trying to look like she's looking over her shoulder can. I sleep alone. That means you learn to measure shadow, not because the world is full of monsters but because the part of your brain that didn't get the memo likes to make monsters out of everything. I didn't see anyone. Either the the men from the catwalk were gone or they were better at walking than I was at looking. I drove home with the windows cracked and the radio on low and my mind making its own loop at sixty-seven hertz.

The first ring of my phone in the morning jolted me up out of a dream about a stairwell with no bottom. The caller ID said MORGAN COUNTY COURTS. If I had been fully awake I might not have answered. Sleep makes heroes of us in small ways, and fools.

"Ms. Stenger?" It was Judge Carrick, voice taut enough to twang. "You were our last person in the building last night."

"I signed out at eleven," I said, because people say the things that make them feel safe when they're frightened. "Mr. Lennox saw me. Why?"

There was a sound on the line like a hand sliding down a face. "We found Mr. Lennox this morning. He fell. From the third-floor walkway. The foreman says you had access to the rotunda. I—"

"I—" The word hit a railing in my mouth and broke apart. In the same second, memory stepped forward like it had been waiting for its cue: gloved hand on a rail; "Under the Salt Lion"; the metallic clink of a lock. I was the last person to hear him tell me to be careful.

"We've called the sheriff," Judge Carrick said. "She'll want to talk to you. You're our professional; I know you were there to work, but my clerk—people are talking. I don't like rumors. I like the truth. You'll come in."

Of course I'd come in. Rumors eat truth like termites and I prefer my homes to stand. But standing there in my kitchen in socks with a coffee mug cooling on the counter, I had the urge to say I was sorry and then switch off my phone and run until the sound of the courthouse ceased to ring in me. Ordinary lives don't train you for the moment when a man you nodded to twelve hours earlier becomes a pronoun you have to speak around.

"Ten o'clock," she said, and then softened, a woman under a judge. "I know you are going to ask yourself if you could have done something. Let me have that job. We will see what the cameras saw."

The line clicked dead.

I went to the sink and ran the tap and let the water fill the metal sink in a circle that grew and grew. I have heard a hundred falls in a hundred rooms, played back in audio analysis software, blunted to numbers and decibels and durations. I know how sound wraps around a body, how a stairwell makes a cylinder out of a day. I know that sixty-seven hertz hum from the rotunda's under-stair void would have made an excellent bed for something heavy to sound against.

People lied. Rooms didn't. But it is one thing to listen to a building when it wants to tell you about its drafty corners and another when it wants to tell you about a man who shouldn't have fallen.

"They said he fell," my mother would have said, rinsing a glass and looking out the window into our old backyard the way she used to, as if the answers always hid under the lilac shrubs that refused to grow. "Do you believe them?"

I didn't know yet. I knew only the precise lightness of a gloved hand on a rail and that there were two sets of footsteps on the catwalk last night and only one body on the floor this morning.

I dried my hands. I found my notebook from the courthouse and flipped to last night's scribbles. My handwriting is tidy even when nervous, which is irritating in retrospect. Underlined in my square block letters, from muscle memory: 67 Hz — under stairs; whisper gallery strong at 2F; security presence: Lennox. Then, almost illegible because I'd written it shaped to my mouth; because I hadn't wanted, even on paper, to make it permanent: under the Salt Lion.

On the walk from my car later to the courthouse doors, the two stone lions watched as always. The tarps were gone. The morning crew had swung them off, rolled them up, and propped them against the rails. The Salt Lion's mane was filthy and beautiful, streaked white and gray, a river delta down his shoulders. People stood in huddles on the steps, shoulders hunched as if the cold was a thing you had to carry together. I thought of hands at two a.m. with caulk on the knuckles, of the orange oval sticker on a hard hat. Of midnight meetings because daylight makes some plans look silly.

Sheriff Inez Ritt was waiting in the vestibule with her coffee and her lack of patience. I've watched juries shrink from her stare the way people do from odd lights in the sky; if your alibi doesn't behave in daylight, she can make it come apart in the shade. She shook my hand, eyes moving from my face to my shoulder bag to my boots and back again, making a map of me she could understand later without me in the room. She had a string of rosary beads wound twice around her wrist, a habit and a weapon.

"Ms. Stenger," she said, nearly kind. "Tell me about your night. Start with the mundane. The mundane is where we all live until it isn't."

"There was a noise in the low end," I said before I could stop the truth from starting in the place it likes to start. "And I heard something you may want to hear too."

Later I would remember the way she went very still at that, the way old buildings go still when a heavy truck passes outside, not because they are afraid but because they are mindful of what they have survived.

They said he fell. The room had been there when it happened. And I had been there when the voices decided that would be the story. It is a terrible thing to realize you have become part of the acoustics.

Chapter One

The city is loudest where it pretends to be quiet.

Mara Quin sat in the Quiet Room, which wasn’t quiet so much as honest. It was a wedge-lined box in the basement of Bellwether City Hall where engineers calibrated microphones and where, on insomniac evenings, she went to be sure she was real. The foam swallowed the hum of fluorescent lights and the hiss of vents and even the ghosted shoal of traffic above, and what was left was the sound of her own body working. In the Quiet Room she could hear the blood in her ears, a private tide. She could hear the chirp that had been left there two years ago, a bright J-shaped whine that rose when she was tired. Sometimes she pressed her palm to the wall and hummed until the iron in her bones answered her.

On the table in front of her, the city had been made into a graph. Forty-three remote sensors, amber points on a map, streamed their numbers into her laptop. Each dot was a microphone bolted to a lamppost or a balcony rail, listening to an intersection or a park, a dog kennel, a nightclub strip, a row of waterfront warehouses the city didn’t admit it owned. The municipal code cared about decibels and time windows, about the rights of sleep and the rights of commerce; what it did not care about, officially, was the feel of a noise. That part was Mara’s.

There were burps and bursts on the feeds: a carnival ride squeal from Battery Park, the lilt of a drunk tenor on Rooke Street, basslines walking across the river like heavy feet. Sensor 04B on Division flickered, the landlord next door testing a new exhaust fan. Someone clanged a dumpster lid hard enough to spike 85 dB on Sherwood at 11:02, which wasn’t a violation but sure felt criminal. Mara watched the traces skate upward then settle as if embarrassed.

A little red banner bloomed over 27C at 11:11.

She tapped the square and a waterfall of frequencies unfurled, blues and greens and thin threads of yellow. Mara didn’t so much see the graphs as hear them—her mind had long since stitched sound to color and back. What flagged her wasn’t the amplitude; 27C was technically within limits. What caught was a narrow strip of alarm-yellow that shouldn’t have been there at all, a fixed tone too pure to be an accident. It sat low, at the threshold, the kind of thing you felt along your jawbone more than through your ears. It held steady for eleven seconds, vanished, rose again a few minutes later, vanished.

She cross-checked the complaint log because she could hear the questions already: yes, there had been a call. Two calls, actually, both from the same number in the new condos on Brackett Street that looked out like expensive eyes over a line of corrugated roofs. Caller reported “sub-bass pulses rattling glass,” sighting “unpermitted after-hours rehearsal” in the warehouses. The notes were filed by Elias with the dispatch code that meant If we have time.

Elias was supposed to be on call tonight. He’d sent a picture at ten, a beer bottle sweating on a pool table, and the caption: if you cover, i owe you my secondborn. “Secondborn” was a joke. Elias barely kept plants alive. Mara’s phone lay face-up beside the laptop, its screen blank and accusatory.

She checked a second feed from 27C, a diagnostic channel the field team used when a sensor misbehaved. There it was again, the tone, regular and measured. The graph marked duration; if she was making notes—and she always made notes, if only for future versions of herself—she would have put: 10.6 seconds; 10.6 seconds; 10.6 seconds; pause; repeat. Machines liked regularity. People liked patterns for different reasons.

The warehouses along the Emmett River had been ships once. Not literally, but the city had built them like hulls, tight and long, the wooden ribs curving under sheet metal skins flashed with a hundred seasons of light. As a kid Mara had ridden her bike down there, standing on the pedals so she could skim through the nets of rotting rope and breathe the sweet-sour grain that seeped from the old sugar silo. A nightclub had flared in one of the warehouses for a few months some years back, a beautiful illegal place that doubled as a church on Sundays and a boxing gym when it rained. The city had shut it down for lack of permits and faulty egress and because people with money had ideas about what the riverfront should look like when they ate dinner.

She signed out the field kit from the gold-wire cabinet behind her desk. The decibel meter was yellow and solid, its little screen a familiar square. The calibrator fit in her palm like a chess piece. She checked the batteries. She hesitated over the case that held a noise dosimeter and a spare set of earplugs, then took them both. Her own earplugs were on a cord around her neck. She put another set in her pocket, because if anyone asked she was the sort of person who prepared. She was wearing jeans and an old linen shirt, and one wrist smelled faintly like orange oil from the teak she'd sanded that morning until it shone.

Outside, Bellwether had decided it wanted to be summer again. Heat lay up against the buildings, peeling old posters into renegade curls. The Emmett was low this time of year, a thick ribbon cut with islands of wet sand. The big tugboats at the east anchorage were voiced in low vowels, a sound so deep Mara felt it in the hinge of her jaw. The sky was the color the city paint shop called “Public Works Blue,” the kind you noticed only when it chipped.

She parked three blocks shy of Brackett because it felt wrong to pull a city car into a mess a developer might be watching. As she walked the last distance, she could feel it: the nervous shimmer of a band practicing, the fundamental under the music that made windows complain. The warehouses kept their doors close-set and plain. The one with 27C on its lamppost had a paper sign taped to the metal that read NO TRESPASSING in all caps and the words BELLWETHER PROPERTY MANAGEMENT in a smaller font, as if quietly apologizing. She knocked anyway. Then, when the knock got no answer and the building did not make the micro-scrape of someone moving inside, she pulled on the handle and found it unlatched.

The air that spilled out was cold and smelled like lemon cleaner drowning out something metallic and fine as dust. Mara stepped into a square foyer where someone had looped thick curtains from aluminum rail like a theater’s black box. The fabric swallowed sound, and her tinnitus chirp sprang into the vacuum like a bird confused by a storm. She held up the decibel meter: it read 28 dB, impossible, like a winter night in the hills. She’d calibrated 27C herself last week to account for a bent grille. It wasn’t wrong.

She pushed past the curtains into the main room and understood the wrongness better. Someone had tried to make a studio out of a shipping shed, and someone else had made it into an exhibit. Panels of egg-crate foam zig-zagged along the walls, cheap tape gleaming where they met. The scuffed cement floor was new-clean, damp still in the corners. A row of folding chairs sat empty, all facing a low platform stage about the size of a bed. On the platform, a metronome ticked: an old wooden pyramid kind you had to wind with a key, its pendulum swinging soberly at a marking of 60. One beat per second. There was no music at all.

At the back of the platform sat a man in a straight-backed chair, his hands arranged on his knees as if someone had posed him and stepped back to assess. He wore a button-down shirt that might once have been expensive and was now a map of wrinkles. Headphones cupped his ears, studio-grade, the cable loose on the floor beside his foot. His eyes were open. There was a line around his mouth that had nothing to do with a smile. Mara’s first thought, ridiculous and automatic, was that he was listening to the click, steadfastly counting in a language only he knew.

“Hello,” she said, because it would have been worse not to. “Sir?”

He did not answer. The metronome said: here, here, here. Her tinnitus was a held breath in her head.

Mara put the decibel meter in her left hand and reached with her right. She knew the feel of cold skin; she had held her mother’s hand in hospice. It was not always like this, the body making its own rules. The man’s cheek was cool but not stiff. In the quiet she could hear the faint fizz of electric something from somewhere else in the room, a machine left running too long. She noticed, too, what was under his chair: a shallow, careful circle of coarse salt, as if he’d been placed in a ring. She saw a smear of black wax on the stage near his heel. On the chair’s rear rung, a strip of gaffer’s tape had been written on in a blocky hand with a fat pen: LISTEN CLOSE. She did not like that the tape had been placed where only someone behind the man would read it.

Her hands remembered the motions. She called dispatch. The call rang twice, the hold music bled in—Vivaldi scraping thin through a telephone line—and then the clerk picked up and said her name like a relief. “Mara. Tell me you’re on your couch.”

“Warehouse unit on Brackett,” Mara said. She named the number, because it mattered. “I opened the door, no noise. Inside looks like a studio. There’s a man here on a chair. He’s not responding. He’s—” She did not say the obvious word. “You need to send someone.”

“Paramedics en route.” The clerk’s keyboard made a chitter like rain. “Police, too. You stay where you are.”

While dispatch did its work, Mara walked the room. Not touching, not moving anything, just letting her eyes and her skin do the job the meter could not. Near the door someone had set a milk crate full of papers—flyers for a jam session that had never been, a sign-up sheet with only a first name on it, WREN, in careful block letters. A digital recorder sat on a stool with a wire run to a black box under the stage. Four cables ran from the box to a bank of speakers the size of refrigerators. The gaffer’s tape on the floor marked out squares like a chessboard or a dancer’s lesson; in the largest square, the floor was fuzzed with salt grains like frost. There were stacks of foam, a toolbox without tools, a roll of plastic drop cloth. No water bottles. No coffee cups. No cigarettes. Someone had worked here who did not make a mess, or someone had come after to sweep it away. The lemon cleaner smell wore a bitter aftertaste that made her tongue want to curl.

A faint stain ran down the wall by the far door, a whip of something darker. It was nothing. It was everything. Mara checked the exterior access to the river side; the door was not locked but it dragged as if the hinge had been oiled and then forgotten mid-stroke. She listened. Outside, a tug moaned, a gull laughed without humor. Inside, the metronome kept time.

Paramedics came first, a compact woman with a coil of black hair and a man who smelled like eucalyptus. Their boots made a noise that sounded wrong the way laughter does at a wake. They moved around the room with the easy choreography of people who had stepped into the middle of other people’s endings too many times to count. They went gentle, then less gentle. They tipped back an eyelid. They looked at each other with their eyebrows, which is the universal language of news not good enough for words. The woman stopped the metronome with a thumb, which was—Mara felt this like a snapped string—both practical and a betrayal.

The police arrived on the second wave, two uniforms and a detective in the kind of jacket that meant she kept a spare pair of shoes in her trunk. The detective’s hair was braided flat against her skull, and one sleeve was pushed up as if she had rolled it to avoid damp and forgotten to roll it back down. She was not tall but she carried tall. Her badge wore the number 141. Her eyes did a slow look around and came back to Mara the way a singer matches a pitch, testing.

“Who are you?” she asked, not unkindly.

“Mara Quin,” Mara said. “City Noise Office. I’m the one who—” She didn’t finish the sentence because it had too many ways to go. Found him. Called. Walked in.

“Detective Reddick,” the detective said. “Asha.” She glanced at the decibel meter in Mara’s hand and the lanyard that had swung forward with the weight of it. “You come out on complaints often?”

“On call tonight,” Mara said, because it was less complicated than the truth. “Sensor flag, two citizen calls. I saw a pattern on the diagnostics. I wanted to check the monitor.”

Reddick raised an eyebrow. “You saw what on a what?”

“A tone,” Mara said. “A fixed frequency repeating at intervals. 27C was registering—” She stopped. This wasn’t the time to ask a group of exhausted people if they believed in music. “It wasn’t normal.” She tried again. “I was worried there was unpermitted amplification.”

The uniform nearest them snorted softly and then turned that into a cough. Reddick didn’t smile. She looked at Mara, and the look said: I have seen stranger reasons to show up and a hundred worse excuses.

“Did you touch anything?” Reddick asked, her hand in her pocket where her notebook would be.

“Door handle,” Mara said. “Metronome? Not me. I called as soon as—” She made the shape of a mouth like she might breathe out and then didn’t. “There’s a recorder over there. A black box under the stage. And a strip of tape that says ‘Listen close.’ There’s… salt.”

“Salt,” Reddick said as if tasting the word. The paramedic with the coil of hair turned at that and lifted her chin toward the platform like yes, there is. “What is it with people and salt,” Reddick added, not so much to Mara as to the room.

The property manager showed up as if conjured by the words BELLWETHER PROPERTY MANAGEMENT printed on the sign outside. He was in his thirties and had the anxious polish of someone who told himself he wasn’t a liar because he only ever said what someone else had written down. He made a beeline for the uniforms.

“This is a restricted property,” he said promptly, the way a person says the only thing he has practiced. “There shouldn’t be anyone in here.”

Reddick did a slow pivot that made the room feel bigger. “There’s a dead man on a chair,” she said, calmly. “Who has keys to this ‘restricted property,’ Mr.—?”

“Thurber,” he said. “Ross Thurber. I’m with—”

“Property Management, sure,” Reddick said. “Keys?”

“Maintenance staff, obviously. Myself. The developer. The, um, the main tenant.” He gestured vaguely. “We’ve been showing the units. You don’t think—” He stopped because he heard himself. “Of course he’s not a tenant,” he amended, in the voice of someone who wants to both cooperate and disappear. “We don’t have the, um, the paperwork.”

Reddick looked at Mara. “You ever see this guy before?”

Mara shook her head. “Not that I remember.”

“You remember things,” Reddick said. Not a question.

“I file complaints,” Mara said. “I watch patterns. The—” She stopped. It was easier to do than to explain. “I have a stack of calls for Brackett. People who love their view and hate the noise that came with it, people who play music in empty spaces because it’s what they can afford.”

“Which was this?” Reddick asked. It might have been cynical. It sounded like curiosity.

“One way to know is to play back the recorder,” Mara said, and then waited to see what that did to the air.

It made Reddick think; Mara watched it. The detective glanced at the technicians setting up their canvas poles and lights and made a small circle in the air with one finger toward the recorder on the stool. A uniform fetched it in a bag, fingers careful as if the device might bite. They would bag the black box later and the salt, because you bag salt when it shows where someone cared enough to draw a boundary, even if the line was stupid or desperate or both.

“Stay close,” Reddick said to Mara. “I’ll have questions after I let the actual medical professionals do their thing. You hear any more of your tones, don’t leave town.” Her mouth crooked to show she knew she sounded like a line in a movie.

“I live here,” Mara said. “Where would I go?”

“You’d be surprised,” Reddick said. “The river’s right there.”

They moved in circuits around the stage for a while, the city doing its necessary dance. Mara stood near the milk crate of flyers and watched the metronome stopped mid-swing. She realized she had braced for the click to start on its own like a heart grown stubborn. It did not. The warehouse felt like a room a child had cleaned while waiting for a parent to come home, surfaces wiped, toys lined up, a single stubborn stain on the wall.

The clerk at dispatch texted a screenshot to Mara without being asked. Because she knew Mara. Because she sat under the same script everyone else did, and because at a certain hour in the night it hurt less to include people than to instruct them. The screenshot was of a page in the complaint log, dates and times for Brackett. There were more than a dozen in the past month, all between eleven and one, all referencing “pulses.” Six were from the condo number. Four were anonymous from burner accounts that used first names that sounded like wind chimes. One was from a payphone—there was still a payphone on Rooke, a miracle and a joke. The time stamps were neat in their way: 11:11; 11:33; 12:12; 12:24. Palindromes and halves, someone with a sense of humor or a need for order. The pattern reached out and tapped Mara on the collarbone the way her mother used to, lightly, to get her attention in a room.

She pictured the waterfall from 27C again, that thin yellow band lifting out of the noise, holding and falling, holding. She had the thought—not rational, an instinct that rose from the same place as the chirp in her ear—that somebody had been sending something and somebody else had answered. Not with words. With attention. With a chair and a circle of salt and a metronome set to the oldest time.

Reddick came back over, her pen capped, her jacket shrugged into the version that meant nothing would happen fast. “Who else knows you’re here?” the detective asked, and Mara felt the ladder of the questions beneath the question: who told you to come; who knew to get ahead of me; who might want you where cameras might see you.

“Dispatch,” Mara said. “My colleague. He texted me a picture of a beer, so he’s out. I didn’t tell anyone else.” She did not mention the way she had not told her sister about selling the violin, about the way she hung the bow above her kitchen sink like a warning. Those were not police questions. Those were the ones that could unravel you if you let them.

Reddick’s phone buzzed. She glanced at it, then lifted her head in sharp surprise, the first real break in her professional calm since she’d walked in. “Huh,” she said. “We got another flag.”

“Where?” Mara asked, before she could decide to keep her mouth shut.

Reddick turned the phone so Mara could see. The map was the police version of Mara’s—different icons, same bones. Another point had gone red. Not here. Not even on Brackett. On the opposite side of the river, at old Sugar Silo 5, a building the city had fenced off but which people always found a way to enter, because that was what people did to places that were supposed to stay silent.

“Two sites?” Mara said. She felt the J-shaped whine in her ear make a small greedy leap, as if it could feed on this. “At the same time?”

“Closer than coincidence likes to admit,” Reddick said. She looked at the metronome as if it might begin again. “You hear it?”

Mara closed her eyes and listened. The city did not have a single voice. It had dozens: wind in scaffolding, a siren two streets over smearing itself on damp air, laughter torn off by a car door. But underneath, if she knew where to press her attention, there was a note. It was not the metronome. It was deeper and not entirely sound, or not in the way people who hadn’t sat in the Quiet Room would understand. It came from the places where big metal met old concrete, from the ribs of the warehouses and the bones of the bridge, from the river when it got something in its head.

“Yeah,” she said, more to herself than to the detective. “I hear it.”

“Good,” Reddick said. “Let’s see if you can teach me.”

Later, when she tried to sleep, Mara would think about the tape on the back of the chair and the way someone had written the words in the precise uppercase of a person used to cataloguing. LISTEN CLOSE. As if the words were a kindness. As if not listening would be rude. She would think about the yellow line on the graph and how it had resurfaced after years of being taught to ignore the things that didn’t make bureaucrats happy. She would get up and pour water and stare down into the glass until her reflection blurred.

But that was later. In the warehouse, the air shifted as someone opened the door to the river side, and for a moment the smell of lemon cleaner was replaced by river silt and diesel and rain. The city breathed in. The city did not exhale.

If this was a message, Mara thought, then it wasn’t for the dead man. Or not just for him. The line had been cast onto water a long time ago, and everyone standing there had been tugged a half step forward before they knew it.

Outside, somewhere beyond the curve of the silos, something new started to hum.

The newsroom morgue always smelled faintly of paste and old rain. It wasn’t rational. The cabinets were steel and smooth, the folders crisp as cut cardboard, and our mice were wireless now, but every time I slid a drawer open the scent rose and the room felt older, like the damp basements where the first dailies were born. I liked it down there when the light was mean and the phones had stopped pretending to be landlines. I liked that it was called a morgue and no one apologized.

On Monday mornings, I took my coffee and my cleanest notebook down the service stairs and began the week with the dead. The living came upstairs and bellowed at each other about breaking news and click-through rates. The dead stayed where I could hear myself think.

I was sitting on the floor, my back against a file cabinet labeled C—Catastrophe—when the anonymous e-mail found me. The phone I’d stupidly brought to my sanctuary buzzed against my thigh. I thumbed it open without looking, expecting a note from Metro about a car wreck or a reminder about the editorial board lunch. It was an inbox rule of mine to never read e-mails in the morgue. The dead deserved that much. But the subject line stopped my thumb mid-flick.

Advance—Emmett Crane.

We keep advances on about a hundred people: senators, beloved anchorwomen, the more luminous philanthropists, famous crooks. Advances are prewritten obituaries we can run quickly when necessary. The famous crooks die, too. We update them and rehearse their endings like any other performance. If Emmett Crane had an advance, it wasn’t one I’d worked on.

Crane & Sons Horologists had a narrow storefront on North Boone, all oak and glass and small pronouncements lettered in gold leaf. The city had turned to Emmett when the courthouse clock stopped one March—he was the man who climbed into towers and coaxed stubborn gears back to rhythm. He had rescued wooden-faced schoolhouse clocks from dumpsters and restored them to solemn tick, and lately he’d become the kind of niche celebrity this city adored. He wore suspenders unironically and didn’t have a storefront Instagram. He had a face you wanted matted with matte finish in a feature spread: white beard neatly combed, eyes the pale blue of beach glass.

The e-mail came from a generic tip address that we publish on the site for crime scene photos and political hot mic audio. It included no text, just a DOCX. I looked at it too long. Even on a phone screen, the typeface was ours. The style was ours. My byline was mine.

By Iris Lowe.

I swallowed against a mouth gone suddenly dry and opened it.

The piece began with a sentence I might have written. It wasn’t that it had my turns of phrase so much as my restraint, the way it rolled back from the cheap flourish and left a space I trust readers to fill.

Emmett Crane, who restored the city's time to itself and was, in the end, undone by the steadying in his bones, died Tuesday under a new tin roof. He was sixty-seven.

I stared at the second sentence until the words went to pieces. Died Tuesday. Under a new tin roof.

The rest of it was careful, precise, as if it had sat atop someone's desk all day and been fed breadcrumbs. The obituary knew Emmett’s father’s name—Samuel—who had kept a watchmaker’s bench in a shed that sagged onto a river cowlick in Boone County. It knew that Emmett had learned to lay a hand flat over a moving clock and feel its humor the way veterinarians did with cats. There was a paragraph about the courthouse restoration and a quotation in which the county clerk said, He spoke to that clock; he scolded it like it was his favorite mule. There were dates in the right places and commas where I would have put them. It read like something I’d write two hours after a death, with quotes gathered by phone and a consistent clarity that you only earned by filing into a habit.

The last paragraph of advance obits is usually the most boring—survivors and services. This one was not. It was specific where it couldn’t possibly be.

Mr. Crane is survived by a sister, Lupe Alvarez of Jacksonville; and a shop cat. He will be remembered Saturday at Crane & Sons in a low-key wake with coffee, as he asked; his oak bench is to be left as it is until the courthouse strikes noon.

I was upright before I knew it, the cabinets pressing against my shoulders as I shoved the phone into my pocket and started for the stairs. On the landing, the newsroom opened like a diorama: the city editor hunched over an accident report, our political reporter arguing with a councilwoman who had wandered in with arguments the size of new city blocks, the sports desk assembling sentences like rooms in a dollhouse. Miles Tran saw me and lifted his chin in a way that said, Bring me the thing you have. I took it to him.

Miles had taken two buyouts in other lives and spent them starting a summer newspaper camp for kids, then getting divorced. He had hair he tried not to care about and an abiding affection for anyone who could write a nut graf that didn’t panic. He read the first paragraph, read the second, and then looked at the byline. He looked at me.

“Tell me this is some intern’s idea of a prank,” he said.

“It came to the tips address. And it’s—” I didn’t have the word. “It’s something.”

He scrolled, read the survivors, made a face. “We don’t have a sister for him in the file, do we?”

“We don’t have a file,” I said. “Emmett wasn’t on the list.” The truth was that our list of advance obits had shrunk with the newsroom. We kept it at a hundred because we could maintain that many. Emmett wasn’t, by any rubric, a national figure. He was, in the small radius of this city, important to people like me, who liked things that ticked.

Miles set the phone down carefully. “We can’t run this.”

“I didn’t suggest—”

“I know. I know you didn’t. But we can’t ignore it, either.”

“She—the writer—it’s in my voice, Miles.”

“You could sue yourself, get a settlement,” he said, absentminded, and then scrubbed a hand over his face. “Call him. Go over there. If he’s fine, fine. If he’s not—”

“If he is not,” I repeated, and the sentence felt like a plank underfoot that had shifted, revealing nothing under it but a long, grim space.

“Take Tino with you.”

“I don’t need a photographer to knock on a watchmaker’s door.”

“It will make me feel like I’m sending you into something with your hands not empty,” he said. “Also, if there’s a cat, Tino will get it to look soulful at just the right moment.”

“I’ll call him on my way,” I said, mostly to get out of the conversation. “If this is a prank, it’s a very good one.”

Miles looked down at the phone again. “And if it’s not. Time of death?”

“It doesn’t say. It says ‘under a new tin roof.’”

He looked at me. “Which is a sentence we’re not running, unless half a dozen people tell us they saw the roof.”

“Tin’s a stretch anyway,” I said, because it was what we did: we second-guessed the poetry out of things so we could see the facts.

The walk to Crane & Sons took me past the courthouse with its squared shoulders and the clock on its western face that had been still for my entire freshman year of high school. Emmett had given back what I came to college-town for—we like a bang at noon and the idea that the past can be coaxed to behave. North Boone narrowed into older storefronts with cornices that pretended not to be ashamed of themselves. It smelled like ground coffee and bike grease. Halfway down the block, a roof crew tacked aluminum sheets in neat rows. Lonpas Roofing, their shirts announced in a font that wanted to look like handwriting.

Tino would come, but slowly; he had a way of being on his way that involved a stop for better light, a different lens, a personal philosophy. I called Emmett from the corner, and he picked up on the second ring. The shop sounded like a pocket of rain.

“Crane.”

“Mr. Crane, my name is Iris Lowe. I write obituaries for the Register.”

“Oh,” he said, and then sound went to the edges around his voice, like he’d leaned away from the phone. “Am I—have I—”

“No,” I said quickly, and realized how stupid the only honest answer would sound. Not yet. “We maintain advance obituaries for prominent citizens. I wondered if I could stop by and confirm a few details.”

“Ah.” He seemed to expand again. “Advance obituary. That’s a dreadful euphemism.”

“It is,” I said.

“All right. I am here. The cat is asleep on my bench, so we will talk quietly.”

“I’m across the street,” I said.

“I have a bell,” he said, and hung up.

The bell was a brass ship’s bell drilled into the wood next to the door, with a length of blue rope for tugging. I pulled gently. The sound was clean, the sort of note you imagine continues inside the metal long after your ear can’t hear it.

Emmett held the door open a crack. He was smaller in person, not in a disappointing way but in a way that made you believe he could slip inside the back of a clock. He wore an apron that had once been white and now was the color of hands.

“Ms. Lowe,” he said. His eyes were kinder than any photograph had captured.

“Mr. Crane. Thank you.”

“You’re the first person who’s ever called me Mr. Crane and not meant my father,” he said, and stepped back so I could enter.

It was a long room that ran the length of the building, deeper than it was wide. On the left, a workbench crowded with grenades of parts: boxed springs, small open trays of screws that could have been beads. On the right, clocks fronted with glass blinked their times at me in an accidental kaleidoscope. In the back, a staircase went up at an angle steeper than common sense.

The cat was the color of spent matchsticks, all warm browns and a black forehead like a thought I hadn’t finished. She slept next to a magnifier lamp, a paw over her eyes.

“What’s her name?” I asked.

“Gull.” He said it without embarrassment. “She came with a sharp cry like the sea and a willingness to eat anything.”

“So, Mr. Crane—”

“Emmett,” he said, then stopped and glanced toward the ceiling as if he’d heard what I’d nearly asked. “Not yet, Ms. Lowe. Let us not skip ahead.”

“Emmett,” I said. “How long have you had the shop?”

He told me about the day he signed the lease, about the landlord who wanted a cigar store but had settled for a clock shop because clocks, at least, would look good in the window. He told me about the courthouse job, the way people had stopped on the sidewalk when the clock first struck, as if something out of joint had slid back and found its home. He did not talk the way people talk when they want you to write down their best self. He was not selling me anything.

I asked for his birthplace, his parents’ names. He paused before answering, not because he didn’t know but because the roofers, overhead, had paused between sheets. In the heavy air that lowered into the room—all that summer heat pinned by metal—I remembered the line.

Under a new tin roof.

“It’s aluminum,” I said, and before he could answer, felt like a fool.

“What is?” he asked, smiling, then closing his mouth when he realized my question had not been meant to be a good one.

“The new roof,” I said, instead of the thing I was going to say. “They’re putting up aluminum.”

“Tinned steel on the back portion,” he said, because he knew about metals. He lifted his hand and made a gesture in the air as if he were arranging plates invisible to us. “It’s Tuesday, isn’t it.”

“It is.”

“I am sixty-seven,” he continued, as though we were two actors rehearsing lines and we needed to test how they felt in the mouth. Gull’s ear twitched in her sleep.

“Is there someone we should call your emergency contact?” I said calmly, as if I had asked him whether he took his coffee with cream.

He put both hands on the workbench and looked at the grain. It was an old oak slab with nicks at intervals, as if he measured his work in damage. “Lupe,” he said. “My sister. She changed her name when she married. Alvarez now. Jacksonville. We don’t talk as much as we should. We say we do and then we don’t. My father would tell you he had a shop cat and three sons and the last one went west. That is not true. He had one son and a shop cat, and the son stayed.”

“Can I ask you a strange question?” I said.

“Stranger than having coffee with your own demise?”

“It may be the same question,” I said. “Has anyone from the paper reached out to you this week?”

“No,” he said. “I would have told them to call you.”

I took out my notebook, the one with the elastic band to keep the living from sliding out. “Tell me about the courthouse clock,” I said, which was a normal question to which he returned happily. He told me about shimming a gear with a sliver of copper, coaxing the hands to align with what the world believed about noon. He said, “When it struck twelve the first time, it sounded like the hour had been waiting behind that bell, cleared its throat, and then started over.”

He did not die while we spoke. The roofers resumed their hammering, precise and quick like a metronome that wanted to prove itself. Heat fell in curtains. Gull slept and then opened one eye, then the other, as if someone had told her the room might begin. I wrote until the questions I asked were no longer about the past but about the way his hand made a V when he moved his middle finger and ring finger together, whether that was from the arc of his work or from an old break. I write obituaries for a living, and what I learned is that the shape a body takes from its work is part of it.

When Tino arrived, he did the thing he always did: he moved around in an orbit, listing subjects he might photograph instead of Emmett, in case he had to console me later for the city desk rejecting everything: the cat, the cat’s nose, the cat’s whisker reflections in the clock face. “Gull,” Emmett told him, unprompted, and toothlessly obliging, Tino let the cat keep her name in the captions he was not yet shooting.

We made an appointment, at Emmett’s suggestion, for Saturday. “If you want to bring a photographer then,” he said. “It would be nice to pretend to have a reception.”

“You’d do that?” I asked.

“If we happen to still be around,” he said, “it will not hurt the clocks to be watched.”

“Saturday,” I said, because if you don’t make future plans in a room where death has been mentioned twice, you start to feel like you’re in a story someone else is writing.

Outside, the roof flashed heat. I thanked Emmett for his time and walked back toward the courthouse with Tino reading his light off the backs of truck mirrors and the shoulders of men in neon T-shirts. Halfway down the block, my phone buzzed again. I glanced at the screen and did not stop walking. The sender was the same generic address. The subject line was the same single word: Advance.

There was one sentence in the body of the e-mail. It was shorter than the last and harder to read.

3:17 p.m.

“What is it?” Tino asked, and I shook my head. The clock on my phone read 2:46.

“Spam,” I said, because in newspapers the way to keep a thing temporarily untrue is to name it ridiculous and move past it.

At my desk, where the air-conditioning kept things honest and the editors kept a jar of mixed nuts because no one had the nerve to say no to a thing called Deluxe, I pulled up the first e-mail again on the big screen. I looked at the byline. It did not blink. I printed just the opening paragraph and slipped it into a folder. I looked at the survivors paragraph, then opened the phone directory and found a Lupe Alvarez in Jacksonville who worked at a nail salon in a strip mall. I dialed. No one answered. I left no message. In the absence of a death, it seemed cruel to ask a stranger to confirm the name of someone she might no longer like.

Miles swung by with a packet of budgets and dropped them on my desk as camouflage. “Legal says,” he said, “if this is a prank, it’s not a funny one. If it’s not a prank, it’s not funny either.”

“I’m calling the roofers,” I said.

He looked very tired. “Why?”

“Because the obit says tin.”

He closed his eyes briefly and nodded. “My God, you’re worse than me,” he said softly.

“I know,” I said. It was part of why he hired me.

Lonpas Roofing put me on hold to the sound of a radio station that had decided it was soft summer and we were all in high school. I waited through three choruses and spoke to a man whose voice had layers in it like plywood.

“We do tin in town?” I asked, after introducing myself.

“We do whatever’s specced,” he said. “When they pay for it.”

“What’s on North Boone?”

“Back half is tinned steel,” he said. “Front’s aluminum. Back’s the old part. Front takes the weather.”

“It’s Tuesday,” I said, because it had become the wrong thing I said to strangers.

“Every week,” he said.

The courthouse clock struck three. We all paused. We do it without noticing; at the third hand of the hour we give up whatever we were pretending to be in the moment and mark where we are. The newsroom went quiet in the way all rooms go quiet when a sudden light goes out—without real silence but with a thinning you feel in your own chest.

Three-oh-one. Three-oh-two. The hands moved. My e-mail remained idiot-still. I opened a new document and typed “Emmett Crane, sixty-seven” because that much, regardless of everything, was true. I wrote three paragraphs that could, in any world where I did not hate myself, be folded into a feature if the prank resolved itself as harmless. I wrote, “He had a way of laying his palm on the chest of a clock that made the clock behave,” and then deleted the sentence because it was one of mine from the fake advance and I would not be stolen from and then indebted to the theft.

At 3:13, a summer storm came in fast from the west and tested all the roofs on North Boone. The newsroom windows filled with a color the photographers always called bruise-light. Miles stood up and looked at the sky as if it had just entered the room without knocking. The soft summer radio in my headset became rain.

At 3:17, my phone started ringing and did not stop. It was the stringer the paper kept like a loose tooth—the one who circled in his car and texted us pictures of men standing in front of thing that had happened behind them.

“You want to be down on Boone,” he said, when I answered. “Guy’s off the roof.”

“Which roof?” I asked, but I already knew. The desks around me had the same carefully blank look we get when the worst part of our job springs like a trap and we feel around in the dark for a way to do it with dignity.

“The clock man,” the stringer said, over the sound of rain. “The clock guy. You know, the—”

“I know,” I said. He was breathing hard, or it was the rain on his windshield, each drop a small hammer. “He’s alive?”

“Don’t think so,” he said, then, in a small voice that untrained men reserve for the moment when the world stops being their friend, “I watched him fall, Ms. Lowe. He went like a bag.”

He had no reason to lie to me. Mercy is not an efficient currency in a city like this. I didn’t move. Around me, the newsroom had the sound of a plane right before takeoff. Miles was at my chair and then at another, three steps that made a circuit in which he stashed his worry, then back with his hand on my shoulder and a nod I barely registered.

“Are you all right?” he asked, like a line a kind director gives to the actor he has to hurt.

“It said tin,” I said, helplessly, and realized how stupid the habit would be, now, of correcting the metal in a sentence that had just become true.

“Write the barest thing,” he said. “We’ll confirm the name. We’ll call the roofers. We’ll call the police. We do this the way we do everything.”

On my screen, the e-mail that had said only 3:17 sat like a pill I hadn’t swallowed and had no choice about anymore. I opened the original file again and read the first sentence through to the end, because if this was going to be the way it started, I wanted to know how the voice that had stolen mine wanted to begin.

He died Tuesday under a new tin roof.

Rain pinged against the windows of the newsroom, and out there somewhere in the bruise-colored afternoon, a roof accepted what we asked it to do, and something under it loosened and was done. I thought of Emmett’s hands making a V when he moved his fingers. I thought of a sister in a strip mall in Jacksonville, a cat who had been named for a cry, a workbench marked at intervals by the force of what he pushed against it. I thought of the bell the size of my palm at his door, which had been struck once, twice, a third time when Tino came in smiling. We would write about the ways he made this place more like itself. We would wait for confirmation like good people.

In my folder, the printed first paragraph rustled as if something inside it had changed position on its own. I did what I had always done, the only thing that ever made any of it bearable: I set my hands on the keys, the way you might lay a palm on a wild thing to settle it, and began to tell the truth that had, in the space of a thunderhead, become ours.

Every watch lies in its own way, my father used to say. Some lie fast, some slow. Some keep time like a guilty heart—steady until you pay attention.

I had the back of a carriage clock open when the storm rolled over Glasswick at last. Heat had been draped over the city for weeks, as suffocating as wet cloth, and everything in my shop had started to feel swollen and slow: the brass tweezers sticking in my grip, the wooden drawers reluctant to shut all the way, the felt mats damp beneath my elbows. When the rain came, you could hear it breathing relief over the canals, hissing into the water that wound past the alley like a dark ribbon.

Iqbal & Son, Horologists, sits at the bend of Blixen Lane, a narrow street that allows one person and one bicycle to pass at once if neither of them is fussy. The sign a carpenter painted for my grandfather in 1952 creaks when there’s a wind, which is most days. We keep the window glass bright because no one wants the person minding their time to live behind a smear. Inside, it is always the same time: the time of small tools and patience, the time of ticks layered as fine as dust, the time I have inherited.

The carriage clock on my bench had been in a family kitchen since the wartime, as its owner told me, moved from shelf to shelf to avoid splashes of oil and errant flour. You could tell. The case had a faint film of a thousand dinners, and when I cracked the seal I smelled onions and something sweeter, a ghost of marzipan. The escapement was fouled with lint. I was coaxing a fragment of thread from between the pallet and escape wheel with a sliver of pegwood when the bell from the Aurelia Tower struck twelve noon.

It is deep as a ship’s hull, that bell. Even with the cases cracked open on the bench, its note got into my watches and set them humming in sympathy. I held my breath and counted. Eleven. Twelve. The tone hung, rolled around the corners. The rain kept up its old song.

The bell had been mine, once—as much as a bell can belong to anyone. I had climbed the tower with my father, brought oil in a battered can to the bearings of the motion work, wiped verdigris from the faces of the big hands, listened to the whole mechanism talk to itself. I could still feel the tower’s stone under my palms when I let myself, though I hadn’t been up since the flood sealed the lower stairs in ochre silt and the City Commissioners gave a speech about modernity. They wanted electric chimes, not old iron lungs exhaling over the tide. So they wired a speaker somewhere between the slats above the belfry, and when the bell struck these days, what you heard was a recording from before the water came, perfect and wrong.

I set the bit of thread aside. The clock’s movement felt freer already, like someone had untied a knot from inside it. I was just thinking that my father would have nodded, his mouth tightening in the way that meant pride he wouldn’t name, when the shop door opened hard enough to ring the bells tied there and jolt the wall of glass domes that show off the antique pocket watches.

“Closed,” I said automatically. People come in when the rain gets bad because they see light and hope for hot sugar, a habit from when the baker’s was here before us. “It’s Monday.”

The man in the doorway brought the rain with him in a smell like coins. He was tall and goat-thin and his suit was the dark of a drain; drops hung on his brim like jasper beads. He took off his hat at the threshold and looked at me as if I were the person he had been expecting after waiting for a long time.

“You’re Ms. Iqbal,” he said.

“I am,” I said. “If you’re here about a repair, we’re appointment only. Or you can leave it; I have a—”

He lifted his hand and I saw the parcel. Brown paper, string. Rain had bled the paper dark, and the string had cut into it like a scar. He didn’t bring it too far into the shop, as if some part of him respected the fact that timekeeping instruments and sudden weather don’t mix.

“Found this,” he said. “Thought it should be you.”

People call or drop by all the time with fancies: a clock that stopped the moment grandfather breathed his last as if to mark his exit, a watch that started after twelve years when buried in a sock drawer, a barometer that only falls when the owner’s affairs do. I listened the way a bartender does when someone wants the version of themselves that makes sense. I gestured to the mat.

“Put it there,” I said. “Your name?”

He set the parcel down. The movement made the wet paper wrinkle. He took a step back and touched the brim of his hat with two fingers, which would have looked courtly done by someone with less bone.

“Penhaligon,” he said.

“From the docks?” I asked. It came out before I could stop it. My childhood had been sorted by the people who came through the shop: shippers with hands like rope, glassblowers with burns in strange places, teachers with overcoats full of papers. Penhaligon was a dock name. It sounded like the creak of planks.

He smiled to acknowledge that I had placed him and in no other way.

“From whatever I’m needed,” he said. “I won’t trouble you. The rain is enough.”

He turned and went without waiting to see my hands on the tied string, without a glance at the wall of clocks casting their steady beads of sound into the damp air.

The string had a knot more complicated than was necessary for a simple parcel. Someone had gone over-under-over twice, then put a half hitch through the grace note of their flourish. My father taught me knots as well as teeth on gears. I undid it quietly with the edge of my thumbnail. The wet paper peeled back reluctant as skin at the beach. Inside was a hard shape wrapped in the cotton worn thin from too many washings.

I don’t gasp often. My work teaches you to hold your breath with your hands instead of your lungs. But I let air out of me in a sound I recognized from the first time I looked through a loupe and saw a pinion gleaming like a thing alive.

The watch was an old marine chronometer, dress-sized rather than box-bound, a piece you could wear in your pocket and feel the ship’s heart beat against your thigh. The case was dented along one edge, as if someone had tried to close a door on it and come up against a truth. The maker’s mark on the face was still sharp: K. BRACE, GLASSWICK. There was an enameled moon in a window above the six, and its color was not the sky’s color yet it made your mouth taste like iron, like something lunar in a forgotten sense.

“Kellan Brace,” I said aloud to an empty doorway. “You lovely bastard.”

Kellan Brace had trained my grandfather, or so the story went. He had worked in the Aurelia Tower for decades, a slim, fine-fingered man who could look at a spring and see whether it would sing or sting you.
