He disappeared the year the bottom floors of the tower filled with brown water and the city learned to be poor in a new way. People said the flood took him. People said a ship did. People always said the water did the thing something darker did for us, perhaps because we felt better when our villains were wide and unblinking.

Under the watch lay an envelope, stiff despite the damp. No address. Just my name, written in a hand that stopped where it ought to have curved, as if its owner were stingy with ink: M. Iqbal.

My name on paper has always been a mixed thing. It is a beautiful thing when from someone who knows how to be careful with it, and it is a sharp thing when from the City, and it is a perfunctory thing when it is the signature on a receipt for a life that has to keep working in order to keep working. I eased it open with a knife rather than tearing and shook out a key that chimed against the counter like a small bell.

It was old iron, the kind you could cut your finger on without noticing. The bow was thin and oval. Someone had tied a label to it, the sort the city uses for evidence or for library returns, stiff and glossy so that oil won’t seep in from your hands. On it was written one word, the ink wicking slightly because it had been written in haste: Aurelia.

I wanted to sit. Instead, I stood perfectly still and listened to all the little clocks say nothing important enough to be fear yet.

There was also a slip of paper. Not a note, exactly. An old photograph, the sort my mother kept in a biscuit tin. On the white margin beneath the image was the impressed rectangle of a stamp that had been licked by a tongue that no longer existed. In the image was a boy and a man standing in front of a gate. The boy was holding both a wrench and his breath. The man, who wore a shirt with the sleeves rolled to the tender part of his arms, had one hand on the boy’s shoulder so light it might have been a closeness instead of a hold. The top half of the photograph had been eaten by damp or chewed by a mouse, but you could still see three things: the boy’s eyes, too direct for his age; the flaking paint on the iron gate behind them that spelled out —RELIA when the full had once read AURELIA TOWER; and the corner of the watch’s face peeking out from the man’s pocket like the bite of a white moon.

If you had asked me where I had seen that watch before, I would have told you I had not, because memories are venal. They sell themselves for smaller sums than pride will admit. But the minute I looked at that crescent of enamel, the entire room rearranged itself around my certainty that the watch in front of my hands had once been the watch my brother held up to the light and laughed at in the slanted attic where heat slept under the roof tiles.

I put the envelope down. I breathed. I lifted the watch to my ear.

Ticking is not always what people think it is. It is not a metronome. It is an animal—sometimes a mouse under the floor, sometimes a horse cantering, sometimes the blinking of an unfamiliar baby. This watch’s tick was new and not. It skipped and recovered, skipped and recovered, like a heart with a stutter it had learned to live with. The second hand moved in a precise arc and then paused too long at nine, as if something were pulling it from there.

The outside of the case was simple steel, not the gold you see on pieces meant to show people what you can afford for your wrists. The hinge had a bloom of rust. I eased the case knife into the join and opened it. The back popped with a breath of old air that smelled like wool and tobacco and the inside of a drawer no one has reached into for years for fear of what their fingers might touch.

The movement was a work of fretted plates and ratchets bright as the throat of a thrush. The balance trembled as if with fever. Someone had been inside; tool marks scratched the head of a screw near the regulator. There were hairline cracks in the jewels that made me want to re-house them immediately. And along the inside edge of the case back, the trap where dirt goes to die, there was a thin dark line.

I swabbed it gently with the tip of a cotton thread. The smear brightened like old varnish cut with spirit.

Blood, dried to that darker brown that hides in crevices. A curiously small amount, not the fount you get when a thing like this makes newspaper copy, but the sort of amount you find on cuff edges and ask no questions about unless it has found the wrong home.

I put the cotton aside carefully where it could dry on the porcelain saucer I keep for such salvage. I turned the case over to look at the inside of the front and there, scratched not with a steel scriber but with something in a hurry—maybe a nail—was a set of numbers: 12:13.

People knock 13 for superstition, but watch people know it can be a helpful reminder to make the day wheel line up. Still: the twelve and the thirteen side by side felt like the record of a bell striking somewhere it ought not. My throat felt thick with something that could have been old dust.

My father’s voice was a low thing, a thing made of coins and camphor. He and I had argued about the tower the last week he was alive. Not even argued, really. I had said I would go and look. He had said you go where the city lets you, not where you think you have rights, girl. He had always been softer with time than with permission.

The key on the counter was only a key. But the tag—Aurelia—made my palms sweat anyway. You could not go to the tower without thinking of water past your ankles on the stairs and of the time the city had rung fourteen strokes by accident on a night electricity had been thin and someone had started the recording with a greasy hand.

Rain rattled on the glass. The sound made the little chime inside the skeleton clock on the top shelf twang. In a pause, I heard it: feet in the alley, then the trundle of something wheeled past. Monday meant fewer tourists, meant more neighbors with their coats over their heads. Mrs. Dunn from the corner would come later for the kitchen timer she’d dropped in a pot, contrite as a child.

I turned the watch over again. The engraver’s letters on the back were half worn smooth with use. The little dings and scars were the livings of a thing that had been carried, not coddled. My brother had always wanted carryable objects, not ones boxed for high days. He was gone long before the city took its flood. If you asked my mother, she would tell you he left. If you asked my father, he would tell you nothing you could turn into a fact.

I set the chronometer on the mat where the cotton had folded away. Its tick continued, small as a moth in a vase.

I lifted the photograph by the edges so as not to touch the places where the silver halides might still feel my salt. The boy in the picture was not my brother, not when the face was what it was, but the slope of his shoulders and the way he held his tools, as if they were serious but not holy, was a thing I recognized. You recognize these things because your own hands are doing them even as you try to pretend you come from somewhere else.

The Aurelia took twelve strokes on the hour for as long as there had been months. When the city tried to bring it into modernity with recordings, the system skipped sometimes, the way a stylus will if you do not change its needle. In storms, the bell could double itself in the ear, which is the brain saying it knows something is wrong but cannot change the song. I stood from my stool and went to the window and pressed my palm to the glass so the fog of my breath could cloud it up and let me see out.

The rain had made everything the color of the river: stone, umbrellas, sky. The canal’s surface was stippled into an animal’s back. Mr. Penhaligon was nowhere that I could see, but a trail of darker wet marked where he had stood.

If you get a key to a place you have not been to in years, your body remembers the way the stairs feel under your feet even if you haven’t said they could. If you get a watch with someone else’s numbers scratched inside, you read them as if you had written them in a fever. I felt the tug that comes when the day moves to close a circle you did not know you have been walking.

The city has customs for weather. In heat you buy oranges and cut them across and eat them with salt in the afternoon. In rain you put saucers beneath everything you own that can take a saucer, because leaks will find you no matter your address. And when the Aurelia is wrong, you stop. It is not a law. You’ll see women with their babies swaddled tight in muslin stop with the pram wheels puddling, you’ll see old men with cigars not mind their ash, you’ll see sailors and schoolchildren and the girl who empties the bin behind the apothecary turn their head by half a degree, because a city is a made thing but it sings its own name when the bell is right, and you grow up knowing what it sounds like when your name is garbled by someone drunk.

I waited for the next hour without knowing I was waiting. I went through the motions of oiling the arbor on the carriage clock. I wrote Mrs. Dunn’s name on a piece of tape and stuck it to the kitchen timer with a concession to humor. I turned the sign on the shop door to Closed because rain makes people want to talk about watches as if they are cousins, and I did not have the energy for anyone’s family that afternoon.

When the light began to do the thing it does around four, turning the bricks in the opposite wall the color of a plum's bloom, I stood with the chronometer cupped in my palm. Its case was warmer than the air. I had not wound it; it ran on a cheerful arrogance, the way the models built for ships do, with their helical balance springs and their stubborn insistence on ignoring everything but themselves.

There is a second when a bell readies itself. You do not hear it in your ear but in your teeth. The Aurelia belonged to me that way whether or not the city admitted it.

The first stroke was a fraction low. It made the hairs along my arm lift as if the weather had stepped into the room. The second was truer. The third made the chronometer in my hand press its back into my palm, a little pushing animal. Four. Five. I could count by feel as much as by sound. Six. Seven.

My father would have said inventory is everything. Inventory your tools, inventory your excuses, inventory your losses. Inventory the ways time can put an edge on a day. Eight. Nine.

The rain had slackened. A single drip from the awning outside came slower, then stopped. Ten. Eleven. That should have been the end.

The twelfth strike lagged, like a man telling a story he had told too many times, watching his audience’s eyes go kind. It clanged and made the glass in the shop doors tremble in their frames. And then—there was a sound like someone drawing breath when they are not supposed to. A thirteenth blow fell out of the air and landed in the city’s lap.

The world around me paused in that particular way, the city’s animals and people and machines all taking that half step back you take when someone says your name too softly in the wrong room.

The chronometer’s second hand, which had been making its tidy open-mouthed rounds, shivered and then ticked once backwards, a tiny and precise defiance.

The key on my counter did not move. Of course it did not. Keys are not characters. But it felt heavier to look at it, and there are ways in which weight is as good as movement.

I have never been superstitious, unless you count the ways I work habit into the day until habit looks like belief. The thirteenth stroke shook something old, and the watch in my hand remembered a number scratched into its case, and the storm tipped a bucket somewhere that had been balanced on a beam waiting.

I locked the shop without thinking, because you do not leave time on a table and expect it to watch itself. I took the key and the photograph and the watch and put on my coat with its pocket mended in the lining because I am never happy with the first mend. Outside, the rain had washed oil into a sheen on the canal. I put my face up for one breath and tasted the city’s long habit of being built on water and argument.

When I was twelve, my father and I walked to the Aurelia with the morning inside our sleeves because we had been fighting in the night and thought repairing a mechanism bigger than our anger could make us both smaller and kinder. On the way there, he taught me the names of things that never came up in school: soling; mortise; verge. At the base of the tower, a boy had been waiting, grease already in the whorls of his fingers. He smiled like you do when you have given yourself a private task and you are about to do it well. I did not think of him again after the flood until I saw the photograph on my counter and counted twelve and then thirteen.

The tower stood across three bridges and four turns from the shop, but in a city like ours you do not measure distance by maps. You measure it by the degree to which your heart hopes to find what it has told itself does not exist anymore.

At the threshold of the door I paused and looked back inside my place. It was a room full of time, held open for people to walk in and say the things they could not say anywhere else. The rain made the light slow. Somewhere behind me, Mrs. Dunn called to a cat. The thirteenth strike was still in the glass.

I turned the key in my pocket against my fingers like a coin for luck and stepped out toward the Aurelia, carrying a watch that had learned, if only for a second, that time can inch back when it wants to.

When a writer dies, you can hear it in the sentences. They lose their gait, stumble mid-phrase, reach for a handhold that isn’t there. I am one of the people paid to find the handhold. “Forensic editing,” a client once called it, though what I mostly do is look for the place where a breath should go.

Tuesday morning, the breath in question came in a courier’s pouch with no return address and a printed label with my name. I signed with a pen that did not like the cold; the ink burred on the page and the courier’s breath ghosted in my doorway. I brought the pouch inside to the table by the window, where winter diluted South End light over stacks of paper. Outside, a plow scraped its eternal vow along the curb and a dog the size of a loaf of bread barked at its own leash.

The pouch had a knot of violet ribbon poking from the plastic flap, as if it had been gift-wrapped and then second-guessed. Inside, under a sheet of tissue so thin it was almost theoretical, was a manuscript with a rubber band around it and a smell like cedar and tobacco. Beside it lay a brass key fob stamped 417 and SYLVETTE in worn, serif letters. The key itself had been sawed off.

There was a single envelope, cream, with my initials—S.B.—lettered on the front in a hand that knew the difference between a flourish and a mess. Inside: a note on thick paper.

You don’t know me, but you will. The last chapter is in the wrong place. When you find the pool hall, ask for Esther. —I.V.

I read it twice before my body let me sit down. I know an I.V. like I know my own barista. Ida Vale had died two days ago. She was the sort of writer whose jacket photos became grad-student posters, the sort whose obituary included the phrase “prized reclusiveness.” I had never met her. I had never worked on her books. I had, however, read every one, for the same reason a locksmith keeps master keys in a drawer he never opens.

The manuscript was titled The Drowning Hour in the corner of the first page in the same hand as the note. There were thirty-seven pages, double-spaced, onionskin, with corrections in black ink and coffee rings that had not been protected by coasters. In the margins Ida Vale’s edits were surgical—kill this comma, move that clause—but there were also notations that were not mechanical at all. A tiny star next to a paragraph about a bellhop’s uniform. A name circled: Perlin. Two faint pencil Xs in the gutter, one page apart.

The rubber band had left a faint scar on the paper. I slid it off and the pages sighed into a fan. This is the part of working on dead writers nobody believes if you tell it. The paper carries heat or cold or the ghost of what was around when it was last touched. The fan of pages was cold, and smelled like someone had stapled winter between the lines.

I skimmed the first page.

The first voice was in third person, close. A woman named Nora counted the minutes between the end of a dinner shift and the start of her second job. The hotel where she worked, the Sylvette, was on the water in a harbor city never named but easily, to anyone who has lived here, placed. She described the blue wool of the bellhops’ jackets, the way the brass buttons seemed too proud for their station. She described a pool in the basement, not for guests—a training pool, a rumor, a secret. She described a boy named Leo who worked as a bellhop for three months and then did not show up for a fourth and was never mentioned again.

Halfway down the page, in the margin: Harbor Beacon—Sep. 12, 1975.

I stopped. I know the Beacon. It’s a column of a building a mile from where I live, the city’s old harbor paper, the one that runs on fumes and photographs. 1975 narrowed the air. I turned to the last page, just to know the shape of the cliff I was approaching, and found it ended in mid-scene. A sentence that bent toward a verb and did not find it. My heartbeat went up like stairs.

The brass key fob sat on the table with all the confidence of an object that had never been lost. 417. SYLVETTE. If keys could be ghosts this one had been exorcised; the key itself was gone. I turned the fob over. It had a gouge in the back where someone had once pried off a sticker. The metal was warm where my palm had heated it without asking.

I phoned the only person who could answer without pretending. Crispin Hale picked up on the third buzz. He had been Ida Vale’s agent for as long as she had needed one and several years past that.

“Sam,” he said, without hello. “Tell me you’re calling about taxes.”

“You sent me something,” I said.

“I send many—ah,” he said, as if a string had been plucked. “No. That was the executor. Or the executor’s assistant. Or a woman who keeps showing up and saying she is both. You received it.”

“You know what it is?”

“Ida had a box. She told me this—don’t write it down—her word was mess. She said there was a mess she could not leave in a drawer. She said it was for someone who'd know where to put the last chapter. She said she’d write a note.” He blew audible smoke away from the phone. “Does it have a…prop?”

“A key fob.”

He swore. “We argued about that. Who knows what. Look, you should bring it in. Today. Before the hive wakes up.”

“The hive?”

“The heirs have bees in their heads. The estate lawyer has bee spray. I should not be mixing metaphors this early. Bring the box.”

“There’s no box,” I said. “Just the manuscript and the fob and a note. It says the last chapter is in the wrong place.”

He laughed, short and not kindly. “Of course it does. Meanwhile you are exactly the person who knows what that means.”

“Do I?”

“You hear sentences fall,” he said. It was an old joke between us. “Say two. Say we meet at the café by the Beacon. Wear a hat. The weather has opinions.”

After we hung up, I looked again at the manuscript, at the underlined word: Perlin. I had a friend in grad school named Perlin who made marbled paper and accidentally stained my couch with indigo the week I moved in. I wrote Perlin now in a text with a photograph of the page and the shrug emoji my niece taught me. Perlin the person did not respond.

The door across the hall opened and shut. There was a whisper of a kettle lid. My neighbor, Mr. Osei, made tea at almost exactly this time every day since I moved into the building last spring. He was a man of cardigans and meticulously rolled rugs. We’d nodded at each other in the stairwell. We’d never gotten beyond names and weather. His door was painted a deeper blue than the others and had a brass fish for a knocker.

The kitchen radiator clanged into life like a train reluctantly waking. I put the manuscript back into its ribboned tissue—superstition, or respect—and slid the key fob into the pocket of my coat. As an afterthought, because the city likes to see proof of intention, I tucked the note from Ida Vale into the spine of my notebook. In my line of work, a note is oxygen; it proves the dead meant to be read.

The hallway smelled like floor wax and cold air that had practiced being snow and then decided not to. I turned my key in the great Victorian lock and pulled the door to without letting it click. The building’s habit of sucking doors shut had more than once taken my scarf prisoner.

On the landing, someone had scribbled a chalk 42 in the bottom right of the baluster. I do not go eagerly for numerology, but I notice numbers. In the manuscript, the circled word Perlin had 42 penciled next to it. Coincidence is a cat; it will sit on you if you invite it.

I knocked on Mr. Osei’s door. It was only polite; I’d left a box for him last week, misdelivered. There was the whisper-scream of a kettle escalating toward dictatorship and no human sound. I knocked again. The sound of my knuckles was too big for the hallway.

“Mr. Osei?”

If he couldn’t hear me because of the kettle, he wouldn’t hear me either if I didn’t knock. I turned the brass fish and pressed the latch. The door gave.

The kettle sat on the gas ring like a furious blue bird. The flame didn’t touch it; the heat rose around it with surgical discretion. The smell hit me only after I crossed into the kitchen: burned sugar. Not a smell I associate with tea. My brain does not file things under alarm in time; the body often goes first. Mine reached across the stove and turned the knob to off before I told it to.

“Mr. Osei?”

The apartment was neat in the way of people who did not want to have to look for things: newspapers stacked in precise columns, a row of spices that spelled a poem if you read the first letters. A window that had been cleaned with the kind of pleasure that does not announce itself. On the table: a single sheet of paper with a clipped newspaper article set neatly on top of it.

The headline read: Bellhop Missing from Harbor Hotel. The date was September 13, 1975. The paper was the Beacon. The photograph was of nothing in particular—two men with cigarettes standing in front of a loading dock, a door ajar, a smear of daylight. The byline was OWEN OSEI.

I said his name out loud because sometimes saying a person’s name pulls them from the next room like a thread. “Mr. Osei?”

Down the short hall, the bedroom door was ajar. The bed was made. The light in the room was the sort that makes you feel you have stepped into a photograph. He was not there. I turned in a circle I have taught myself to make when entering rooms that may hold more than you thought. All the while a small metronome in my head clicked: This is a bad idea. This is an excellent idea that will be retold as a bad idea in a different tone of voice.

I did not see him. What I did see, on a hook by the door next to a tan raincoat and a cap with the Beacon logo on it, was a brass fob. 417. SYLVETTE. The key attached to it was still a key, intact, not sawed, its teeth like a fence you did not want to cut your hand on.

I lifted it, the chain clinking quietly, like politeness discouraged from turning into song. It was the twin to the one in my pocket, except for the existence of the key, which here presented itself as a possible continuation of a sentence someone else had cut off.

Across the hall, a phone vibrated into my pocket, alarming me back into my body. Crispin. I let it settle. I could not, not yet, tell him that while he was blowing smoke about bees, the dead woman’s note had reached across the floor to lift the doormat on my own life.

On the table under the Beacon clipping lay a handwritten page beneath it. The handwriting surprised me; it was perpendicular to Ida’s, upright and unsentimental, made by someone who had written fast often. The note had no salutation.

I went back to the Sylvette when the library finally opened the archives. The clerk pretended not to recognize me. Esther—if that is her name—never worked there, according to records that have improved over time rather than gone away. I have been owed one truth for forty-eight years. Perlin moved. Orr said not to write it down. I wrote it down anyway. —O.O.

The pot on the stove ticked as it cooled, each sound a tiny betrayal. Steam unraveled itself from the spout of the kettle and dissolved.

I looked for the obvious—the wallet left on the dresser, a coat missing, a coffee cup with a lip print. Habits become evidence in the wrong light. A suitcase stood open in the corner, empty. I put my ear to the door out of the habit you are born with in apartments; the hall sounded like itself. The chalk 42 on the baluster stared its unblinking stare.

I should have called someone. I know how that sentence ends in other people’s mouths. But Mr. Osei’s kettle would go back on the flame regardless, and the Beacon clipping from my pocket’s sister lay on his table, and the key that was not missing had waited for my hand. So I did what my worse angels and my better ones both agreed on. I turned the gas cock on the stove and made sure the air was air and not something that might kill you if you breathed it, and I opened the kitchen window to the cold, and I took the handwritten page and slid it into my notebook under Ida’s note. I left the clipping. A familiar figure had taught me not to remove the bones from any crime scene you did not understand, even if nobody was dead yet.

When I turned to go, I saw something I ought to have seen when I came in. On the sideboard next to the hallway mirror, below a bowl of change that was honest enough to display its quarters and pennies, was a scrap of hotel letterhead. SYLVETTE at the top, again, in a font that was meant to reassure patrons that this was a location and not a story. The date typed in was August 14, 1975. The rest of the page was blank, but the indentation in the paper held the ghost of words once pressed hard enough to bruise. My hand knew to do it before I did: I tilted the paper, let the window light slide across it, and read.

…it wasn’t a pool at first. It was a tank, for fish or for stories. We dropped things in we didn’t have names for, and they sank, or they changed. Esther said the water had memory. I told her that was only true in poems. She told me poems are only the way we remember water. —O.

No pen had made those words dark, but they lived in the page anyway. I breathed in and tasted the iron of old type. Somewhere below me, a bus applied its brakes to the concept of a corner and complained. Above, a neighbor returned from somewhere and considered the idea of taking off their boots.

I stepped into the hall and closed Mr. Osei’s door until the latch caught. In the slice of dim between door and jamb I saw my own eye looking back at me, doubled and then gone. There was a motion at the end of the hall—a shadow negotiating stairs. I listened with the animal part of my attention and heard only the masks cities make of quiet.

On the sidewalk, breath swallowed itself and vanished. The Beacon building squatted across from the café like a ship that had decided against ocean years before I was born. Inside the café, Crispin sat with his hat on the chair like someone he was saving a seat for. He looked at the key fob in my hand and then at my face and then at the door behind me, where nothing followed.

“Tell me,” he said, and it wasn’t a request. He held up a folded newspaper like a card trick. The headline once more: Vale’s Legacy in Dispute. His cigarette had burned itself to ash in the ashtray; he had given up and then un-resigned. “How bad is it?”

“I have two identical key fobs,” I said, and the sentence felt like someone else’s story in my mouth. “One with a key. One without. And a note that says the last chapter is in the wrong place. And the name of someone I can’t find in the records, who might be named Esther. And a man across the hall who wrote for the Beacon forty-eight years ago and who is not in his apartment, but who left his kettle on and his door open and his note for himself in a place where someone would find it.”

Crispin has, in my experience, two expressions that are not actually expressions: pity in disguise, and calculation with a hat on. He made neither. He folded his hands on the newspaper. “Sam,” he said, and looked at me as if I were a piece of punctuation he knew he would need later. “Don’t keep this in your pocket.”

I reached into my pocket and closed my hand around the cold brass fob as if I could make that true by touch. The manuscripts I work on give off heat like animals. This one had cooled too quickly. Somewhere, the last chapter was in the wrong place. Somewhere else, a tank that had become a pool had given up one of its stories, and the story had learned how to walk.

The café door opened and a gust of air ushered in the smell of snow that had not yet taken a body. The barista called someone’s name as if names were something that could be warmed. Crispin’s eyes went over my shoulder. I did not turn. He exhaled and said, softly, as if in church, “Oh, god.”

I turned then. A woman stood in the doorway, the wind making a small argument with her hair. She was older than me by a decade only because time is cruel; her coat was the color of the whole fourth floor of a library, and her face had that set to it that grief gives people who have decided to keep moving. She saw Crispin. She saw the key fob in my hand. She saw me. She did not hesitate. She crossed the room and laid a folded letter on the table. Her hands were steady. The letter was written on Sylvette letterhead, stamped with a date from a summer before I was born.

“You’re the one they sent,” she said. “I’m Esther. And I told him, nobody puts the last chapter where they think they do.”

Chapter One

At the Mail Recovery Center, everything smelled faintly of glue and last chances.

They had tried citrus cleaner once, a bright artificial lemon that winked out after an hour and left only citrus mingled with dust and paper. Nothing overcame the sweet, animal tang of old envelope gum or the powder a thousand pages shed when they skidded over each other, rubbed, breathed out a little of their wood pulp. On dry winter days, static lifted the hair on the back of Mara Leung’s wrist and made the jittering conveyor belts crackle.

The building was a squat rectangle of concrete not far from the airport, a place you only found if you had business with things that had lost their way. Trucks unloaded palettes twice a day with the precision of aircraft, and the loading dock chugged like a world-weary lung. Inside, a pocket universe of bins and belts and tables hummed: Undeliverable–As Addressed. No Such Number. Insufficient Address. Forwarding Expired. Found In Equipment.

Found In Equipment was exactly what it sounded like: a catchall for whatever turned up when they shook out mail-sorting machines—letters that had folded themselves into hidden crevices, coin parcels wedged in rollers, once a whole pair of red shoes. Most of it arrived crushed, bruised along the edges, its journeys interrupted by the machine’s hunger and the small frictions of time. Pieces that might be worth something, that might have got lost in a way that could be reversed, wound up in the room where Mara worked, marked Research.

She made coffee in the break room the color of varnished walnuts, carried it in a chipped mug that used to say World’s Best Aunt but now read Wor Bes Au, and rolled her shoulders as she crossed the threshold into her section. The overhead fluorescents buzzed. A box cutter scratched. Across from her, June Nolan—a woman whose hair always seemed to be made of more hair than really fit on a head—was fishing a handful of tiny screws from the belly of a music box someone had mailed in a brown paper wrap.

“Happy Monday,” June said, which sounded a little like a dare.

Mara set her mug down, opened her own carton. “They keep coming whether we’re happy or not.”

“Personally, I prefer to be neither. It confuses them.” June gestured toward the bin labeled Found In Equipment with her screwdriver. “Got a new pallet. See if there’s anything with a return that isn’t ‘the machine decided to eat it.’ Oh, and management says to remind you not to fall in love.”

Mara smiled in spite of herself. June had been with the Center long enough to make rules. The one she repeated most often was that people who sorted dead letters were like divers—they learned how to hold their breath. You went down into other people’s lives long enough to pick up a name or an address and bring it back to the surface. You did not stay for dinner.

“I have terrible taste in mail,” Mara said. “You know that.”

“You have excellent taste,” June said, “which is the problem. The good stuff never writes back.”

The pallet was stacked with gray postal tubs, each strapped with an orange band. She slit the bands and worked through them tub by tub, taking in the quick silhouettes and exposures of other lives. A squashed envelope with something like sand inside that leaked out grain by grain from a tear at the corner—no, not sand, sugar, finely granulated, stick-sweet on her fingertips. A bubble-mailer that declared itself a URGENT GO PRO ACCESSORY, RETURN TO SENDER scrawled on the front in red. A square of corrugated cardboard with nine international stamps crowded into the top right like birds perched on a wire—someone, somewhere, had loved the look of it. There were envelopes written in a careful schoolhouse hand and envelopes scrawled in Sharpie. Envelopes that had clearly been addressed in a moving car. Envelopes that had cried in the rain.

She had been doing the job long enough that her hands moved even when her mind kept one corner for the past. What had started as a six-month contract after she came to Atlanta had turned into three years almost without asking her permission. The Center suited her, drew a line between her and the messiness of a city she had never meant to live in. It gave her names and addresses without giving her faces in the grocery aisles. It replaced questions with tasks. Here was a package with only a first name and the words “Your cousin’s place.” Here was an envelope addressed to General Delivery, MISS WREN, HARBOR POST OFFICE. A message that the mail no longer understood.

She paused.

The envelope lay half-hidden beneath a lump of padded mailers, almost modestly. It had the kind of quality that made your fingers tell your brain to be careful about it: not weight, exactly, but a density in the paper that resisted. The envelope itself was off-white, the sort of off-white you saw in wedding stationery shot at dusk, with fibers in it like tiny threads. The address had been written in pen that had feathered slightly at the edges of each stroke. The M’s and W’s had little extra humps, cautious and neat. It read:

MISS WREN
GENERAL DELIVERY
HARBOR POST OFFICE

No town. No state. No ZIP. Just a stubborn instruction to the universe, like a note in a bottle that assumed the ocean would understand the word harbor.

There was a stamp she didn’t recognize, or rather, she recognized it but hadn’t seen it in years: a lighthouse with a storm lifting at its back, the searchlight beam cutting fat white through a wash of blue. It had been one of those designs everybody used for a while in coastal towns because people liked the romance of it. Beneath it, not quite centered, the postmark had bled into the paper, rain having touched the ink. Only a few letters remained: …AFORTH. The date’s day and month smeared to a bruise. The year—almost clear—was fifteen years ago.

The blue coil in Mara’s stomach tightened.

There had been a dock in Seaforth, New Jersey, like the name pressed into the postmark where the smudged letters would fit. There had been a weathered wood sign when you came off the causeway that said SEAFORTH WELCOMES YOU underneath hanging baskets that never really took. The salt there climbed the metal of street signs and ate them alive from the inside. There was a harbor on the bay side and a mouthful of ocean on the other. When the wind got up it spoke in the cords of all the houses at once.

She looked up. June was frowning at a music box that would play no music.

“What’s the rule if the address says General Delivery?” Mara asked. “No town?”

“Without a municipality and state and if there’s no return, you’re cleared to attempt to identify internally,” June recited, then added, “which is bureaucracy for: open it with clean hands and a decent heart and don’t read more than you need.”

“Right.” Mara dusted her fingers on her jeans. She reached for a knife.

There were people who handled letters casually, tore them along an edge like they were cracking into something that had never been alive. Mara had been brought up to treat paper like cut flowers. She scored the top seam one neat stroke so that she could lift the paper away and leave the flap intact. It released with a small sigh.

Inside there was another envelope, thinner, made of what felt like linen pressed into paper. This one was sealed with a scrap of red thread that had been wound through two small cuts in the flap. A method she had seen only once before, on a letter her grandfather kept in a cigar box. Across the front, someone had written an address in a hand that made the hair rise on Mara’s forearms.

MARA LEUNG
IF YOU MADE IT TO THIRTY

For a second, she thought she had misread it. The words wanted to slide under each other, rearrange themselves into safety.

“What?” June said softly, hearing the breath catch.

“It’s—” Mara touched the thread. The paper seemed warmer than it should. “Someone put a letter in a letter.”

“Like a heart.” June didn’t come closer. She had earned her rule the hard way; she knew when to give space. “Is that a live mail piece?”

“It’s Found In Equipment.” Mara tried to make her voice a good-humored crisp that would carry away the tremor. “And it’s addressed to me.”

June straightened. “Here?”

“Not here.” Mara showed her the face of the envelope. “No address attached to the Center. No town, no return. It couldn’t have been meant for me here. Only for…for me.”

They both watched it, as if it might, like a skittish animal, bolt. The hum of the conveyors leveled into a plane of sound past which conversation felt like cutting paper in thin curls.

“You don’t have to open it,” June said. “The rules would back you if you routed it as undeliverable. We could document it and lock it up and pretend to believe it was meant for some other Mara with the same name and the same age and the same neatness in her life.”

“When have I been neat?” Mara said, and tried to grin and couldn’t find the muscles. “I need to see if there’s a sender behind it. That’s what we do, yeah? We find ways home.”

June watched her a second longer, then turned back to the gutted music box, perhaps not to watch if something broke.

The thread had been knotted twice. That detail was nothing. It stuck in Mara’s mind like a burr anyway, a small insistence. She slipped the point of the knife under the thread and eased, cut, saved the little red piece that fell and put it by her mug. Then she slid her finger beneath the flap and lifted.

The smell hit her first—salt. It would have been absurd to say so, and yet the idea of it filled her nose: not the spray of a breaking wave, not perfume, but the low-stuck scent of marsh when it’s warm, brackish and green and electric. Underneath it, paper, and something like iron.

There was a folded sheet of paper inside and something stiff behind it. Mara drew them out and set the envelope aside. She put the paper on the table with the reverence of a medic laying out an instrument. The stiff thing, when she turned it over, was a photograph, the old kind, a Polaroid whose white border had softened with time. The square was a wash of gray-blue and brown, the colors that never quite stopped being seventy-two degrees. It showed a stretch of salt grass and a post set in the ground—a weathered, splintery length of wood with a bell hanging from iron brackets. The kind of bell they rang in small places when the fog came in. The bell’s tongue was missing. In the right-hand bottom corner, in ink, someone had written: low tide. south of the bell.

Her stomach lit with cold.

Long ago, they had rung that bell on fog-bound mornings—the county didn’t do it anymore because people complained it started the dogs. She had once thrown a rock and hit it and the sound had come up through the soles of her feet. South of the bell was an unremarkable phrase until you put it in Seaforth, until you put it half a mile from where the causeway crossed the marsh. This is where you start, the handwriting said, and that felt like a threat and an invitation both.

“Mara?” June said again, carefully.

“It’s nothing.” The lie flexed reflexively between her teeth. “It’s—“ She put the Polaroid facedown, unable to bear its quiet. “I should document. Before I—before I do anything else there has to be a case number.”

There were forms for everything. There were even forms that acknowledged the forms were inadequate, and those were the best ones. She filled in the top half of a standard discovery intake: Date, Time, Pallet ID, Bin ID, Found in Equipment, yes. Description: Envelope addressed to “MISS WREN, GENERAL DELIVERY, HARBOR POST OFFICE”. Inner letter addressed to “MARA LEUNG, IF YOU MADE IT TO THIRTY”. One photograph enclosed. No currency. No checks. Possible personally identifying details; work to identify sender. In another space, meant for remarks, she wrote in block letters: Names in this item personally familiar to staff. Handling with oversight.

She got up from the table and went to the sink and ran cold water over her hands until the sensation of salt slid away—or perhaps smeared into another layer of memory and skin. She rinsed her mug and poured out coffee she had not tasted.

“What was her name?” June asked when she came back, not looking at the photograph or the letter so that she wasn’t asking with her eyes. June’s skill at the Center lay partly in knowing how to hold a question in the air like a coin.

“Wren,” Mara said. She did not mean to sound like a child saying a spell. Wren Baxter, whose actual name had been Renata before she decided at twelve that it was too formal for the girl she wanted to be. Wren, who wore a denim jacket even in August, the sleeves rolled to the elbow, the spare glint of a safety pin at the collar. Wren, who had stood on the causeway railing and let the wind press her shirt against her ribs and laughed like something halfway between a gull and a siren. People in small towns were held like arrowheads in resin: the light hit them and they were bright and fixed all at once.

They had been nineteen when the storm came.

The hurricane’s name had been Leda, a swan in the meteorologists’ mouths, and it had been one of those storms that gave the impression of choosing. It had looped out, inexplicably, then returned after everyone had reshelved their anxiety, and torn away roofs and decks and docks that people had only half believed were attached anyway. The bay had licked flat across the marsh and up the roads and swallowed up a shed and a yellow kayak and the idea that the island could be separate from the water. They had gone back over the causeway after, those who had left to higher ground, to find cars washed into corners and a pickup that looked like a toy, occupying the odd space of the bait shop like an uninvited guest at church.

After they counted each other, they realized Wren was missing.

Someone had seen her at the bonfire on the bay side around dusk, before the wind turned cold. Someone else had seen her on the jetty, or said they had. Her mother said she had called home and said the road was flooding and she would come in on foot. The sheriff’s people had gone up and down the edges of the island with dogs. They had brought in boats and men who knew how to read water like it was a book. The water said that people were things. That had been the cruelest part, how easily the bay could be talked into forgetting. Mara had stood on the marsh shore while a man in a faded baseball cap explained this like he had to say it to all the girls with frozen hands who wanted their friends back.

Her father had not said nothing or something wise; he had said, I told you not to go out after dark. It was simply how men who had grown up at the water made themselves safe. Keep to the trees. Don’t step where you can’t see the bottom.

Seaforth did not have a bell anymore. Or at least, if it did, no one rang it. The county had dismantled the frame after the storm twisted it. That she remembered like a rumor.

The letter lay on the table, still folded. The fold was the careful kind you made when you wanted to say, I took time to hide this from you and to show you I wanted you to open it, both things in the same gesture. Her name on the outside looked like it had been written by a hand that was trying very hard to be calm.

She slid the paper out and let it open.

Mara,

If you made it—if you made it to thirty, you said once you’d learn to keep your hands steady. You told me you’d cut your thumbnails straight and stop picking at the corners of paper.

They told us not to mail it. They said to pretend the thing didn’t belong. They said it was the water’s, and you can’t keep what the water wants.

But I was never good at listening.

Low tide. South of the bell. You’ll find the place because the old concrete is still there if you know where to look. We were stupid and brave and the wrong kind of careful. We were wrong in a lot of ways.

I didn’t leave the island.

The words walked themselves off the edge of the line and dropped, and then there was white space so large it felt like someone had taken a piece out of Mara’s chest and put it on the table with the envelope and the photograph.

She skimmed, not reading and reading at once. The letters were the letters of someone trying not to make mistakes: the way the g’s hung with their loops closed, the way the t’s were crossed early. It was Wren’s hand. It was Wren’s hand, aged as if someone had written it with a body that had forgotten how to be nineteen.

June said something. The conveyors changed their note as if a new order had arrived. The world did not care that something had shifted in it, or perhaps the world had done the shifting.

“…Mara?”

She could not answer. She could only feel the old math of the marsh lining up in her head, crackling and rearranging like the jigsaw of a satellite image. The concrete Wren had written about could have been the foundation of the bait shack that went out of square and then out of existence. It could have been the footings from the bell post. It could have been the old drainage culvert that people used to play in before everybody decided to be afraid of snakes and runoff. Low tide mattered. The marsh was a throat; if you went down at the wrong hour you could drown standing up.

She put the letter back on the table and touched the Polaroid with her fingertips, not to pick it up or to turn it over, just to confirm that it had not evaporated—which would have been the most reasonable thing in the room, a letter that self-immolated once it had done its slow work.

“Do you need a walk?” June asked, very normal.

“I need…” The sentence failed. Mara’s mind had entered a narrow hallway where there were only doors and no clues as to which one opened. What she needed, technically, was to step into a room with cinderblock walls and a metal table and a camera, to take photographs of the item, to call a supervisor, to file it in a locked drawer. What she needed, chemically, was for the adrenaline lying in wait beneath her tongue to burn off.

What she wanted, authentically, was to drive eleven hours up I-95 to the end of the causeway and walk into the marsh with a shovel.

She swallowed. “I need to make a proper intake,” she said, because saying that out loud would put a barrier between her and the other idea, fragile and terrible.

“Do that,” June said. She wound the screwdriver with a finaline motion, a spring clicking into place. “Then come smoke with me.”

“You don’t smoke.”

“I will take it up for you.”

“It’s a filthy habit.”

“That’s why they call them habits.” June looked at the letter then, a quick glance. “I grew up in a town where we knocked on wood we never cut. I know a little about islands. Don’t go alone, if you go. Don’t go without telling someone. And do not, under any circumstances, wade in without checking the tide table.”

Mara nodded. The fact that June knew her well enough to skip the part where she said don’t go at all made her feel tethered to the floor in a useful way.

She photographed the envelope and the inner letter and the Polaroid and logged them, hands steady between waves. She sent an internal message to her supervisor, escalating the item for review, using templates and polite verbs, holding the personal in parentheses. She put the physical pieces into a transparent sleeve, the kind with a flap that closed with two plastic buttons, so that nothing could slip without making a sound. Then, before she could overrule herself, she took out her phone and typed Seaforth Tide Table into the search bar.

The screen chewed the request, the little dots breathing, and then delivered the day’s tide times with the indifference of a god. Low at 5:41 a.m. and 5:58 p.m., increasing to 6:33 a.m. and 6:50 p.m. by Thursday.

A little voice occurred to her now, annoyingly responsible: You could give this to the sheriff up there, or the state police. You could mail it. You could push it from your hands like a raft and watch it go.

But the letter was in her name. It was not a raft; it was a rope.

She thumbed over to her contacts. She had not called home in weeks, careful as an awkward teenager in her thirties who had not meant to leave and had not meant to stay gone and had found herself in both conditions at once. Her father’s name sat pinned near the top, not because she put it there but because she could not bear it when it slid too far down.

She hit call before she could talk herself into waiting until lunch. The call rang three times, then four, then went to the old machine, which stubbornly refused to yield its recorded greeting to anything more modern.

You’ve reached Edward Leung. Leave a message and a number if you like messages and numbers. Otherwise, you’ll have to try again.

She did not leave a message. Instead she called another number. It rang once.

“Leung’s Bait and Tackle,” a voice said warmly that had once been a kid’s and now had gravel in it. “This is Luca.”

“Hey,” she said, and for all the words she handled in her day job, she could not get a second one. She had written scripts for this moment in her head and all of them fell apart when she tried to follow them. I found a letter, she might have said. Did you keep the bell? Did you ever really believe she ran?

“Mara?” Luca said, and laughed, startled. “Don’t hang up. People think of me like a curse sometimes and then they hang up.”

“I don’t think of you like a curse,” she said. He had been two grades ahead of them, someone who’d played drums in a garage band with Wren’s cousin and had worked the counter at her father’s shop when Eddie’s cough got bad. She saw his hands when he unrolled line or counted sinkers, competent and present. “Listen. I—“

“Is your old man okay?” Luca’s voice went on without waiting for her answer, the way small towns talked in circles until they landed on something. “He scared Marisol yesterday with that wheeze of his, but he wouldn’t let her call you. Said it was nothing to fuss over.”

“He always says that,” she said automatically, because worry climbed a ladder faster than any other emotion. “I’ll call him again in a minute. I—can I ask you something weird?”

“You could ask me to measure time in fish and I would try.”

“Do we still—the bell on the south marsh, the one that used to ring in fog. Does it still—“

“It went in Leda,” Luca said, and his breath made foggy noise in the phone, or else she only imagined she could hear the weather in his lungs. “They took the bracket off a month after. Why? You missing the sound, or you planning to bring it back by singing?”

She looked at the Polaroid. The bell in the photo was a survivor, its iron scarred but standing. Maybe the picture had been taken before the storm. Maybe—there was no maybe that mattered to the sensation tightening her chest like a swimmer’s chest at dawn.

“I got a letter,” she said. She heard the words as if from a little distance. “I think it’s from Wren.”

Silence. In it, she could hear the Center around her—the belts, the squeak of a cart wheel that always squeaked. Somewhere a bin crashed and somebody swore.

“You think,” Luca said, slow. He was one of the few people she knew whose voice did not curl up at the ends of sentences. “You think, or you know?”

“I know her hand. It was sent after—” She glanced at the faint postmark. “It’s old. It got lost. I can’t explain it yet. If I were coming up—if I get into town around evening, could you—“

“Low tide’s at six, give or take,” he said, beat her to it. “You don’t go out without me. You don’t go out without someone who can read that mud, even if you think you can. You don’t tell your father until we know we’re not chasing a ghost.”

She realized only then that she had been waiting for someone to say it for her. The whole room seemed full of birds settling at once.

“Okay,” she said. “Okay.”

“Bring boots,” Luca said. “The good ones. Leave whatever you’re city-wearing at home. And don’t tell Marisol or she’ll bring a casserole to the marsh.”

He was half-kidding, and wholly practical, and what she needed. “I’ll be there tonight,” she said, maybe and definitely.

She hung up and looked at June, who was waiting without waiting.

“Don’t say it,” Mara said.

“I was going to say, for the record, that you look like you’re about to drive twelve hours without stopping for the bathroom,” June said, dry. “I was then going to add that if you get pulled over in South Carolina with a shovel in your trunk and a photograph of a marsh bell, it would be immeasurably better if you also had a printed copy of your supervisor’s escalation memo. So you take a hard copy of that. And some water. And something to listen to that won’t make you cry too much and crash. And you leave me your father’s number.”

Mara breathed, laughed once, a small bark that startled her out of the hallway of doors.

“Also,” June said with plain tenderness, “I want to know if you need me to tell Hollis that you’re taking family emergency leave. Because that’s what you’re doing, Miss Leung, and I will fight someone with a letter opener if they disagree.”

“No letter openers,” Mara said. “You don’t have your tetanus updated.” She shuffled the paperwork, found the escalation on her screen, hit print, watched the machine spool out neat black words. She placed the letter she had found in the transparent sleeve into a lockable bag with a chain that would be wrapped through the handle of her travel bag. She had never been a person who wrapped chains through the handles of her travel bag. She had become one abruptly.

“You’re going to call me when you get there,” June said, as if repeating it could wedge that reality in place. “And when you leave. And if you step into mud deeper than the top of your boots, you back out slowly. I mean it. Watch for fiddler crabs. They’re spies.”

“I know,” Mara said. The shape of Seaforth—like a hand held out into the water, palm up—rose behind her eyes, overlaying the exit map posted in the hallway. Then she put the photograph back into the sleeve. The handwriting inside the transparent plastic caught the light, three words heavier than any parcel the Center would weigh today.

I didn’t leave.

On the nights the trains came late, the station breathed like a sleeping animal. It exhaled steam through its iron ribs, it muttered in the tracks, it shivered when a gust of rain found its way beneath the arched glass. The great clock faced the concourse like an old magistrate with cataracts, its hands moving with the solemnity of someone who had seen too much and decided to forgive none of it.

Mara Voss had long ago come to prefer those hours when the rails went quiet and the arrivals board forgot how to flip its tiles. The day brought people and their reasons. The night brought the things those reasons left behind.

She sat behind a low counter of scarred oak under a sign that read, bluntly, Lost and Found, though in the internal memos it was still the Department of Misplaced Effects. The old name seemed more honest; it allowed for grief as well as oversight. The lamps in her office had metal shades painted a tired green. They threw a workable pool of light over the counter. Beyond, the small room spread into rows of shelves and lockers, each cubby occupied by the consequence of a moment: a red scarf with moth pinholes, an umbrella with a broken rib, a brass key that had no lock left to seek. Mara knew their arrangement better than she knew the state of her pantry at home.

A storm hunched over the city that night, and the station magnified the weather. The glass roof stuttered with rain. Wind moaned somewhere high up near the iron trusses. In the bad days, when the coast pushed into the city and the river snarled with trash, the station would flood at track level and latecomers would wade to their platforms with tickets clenched between their teeth. Tonight the drains were doing their job. Mara could hear water boiling through them beneath the tiled floor.

Len Malloy appeared in her doorway, peering around the frame as if the room might bite him. He'd been a porter since before they put the kiosk for the city museum in the west hall. He still wore the cap even though the union had persuaded management to call them "assistants of loading" now. The peak of it was slick with rain. He carried a wooden trunk on a dolly, guiding it with his hip to keep the wheels from skittering.

"You got a special," he announced, as though he brought her sweets instead of someone else's burden.

"We're after midnight," Mara said. She checked the clock for the pleasure of being right. "Nothing scheduled in, nothing scheduled out. If it's drugged and ticking, I'll pass."

"Would've left it for morning." Len wrestled the dolly to a halt against the counter. The trunk was dull green under grime, with iron corners. Brass letters had once spelled a name. Somebody had scraped them off long ago. "But it came off Six just now. And it had one of your tags."

Mara leaned forward, interest snagged. "One of mine?"

Len produced a claim ticket held together by a rubber band that had given up elasticity years ago. The ticket was cut in the old style, the color washed from red to tea-brown. The Department of Misplaced Effects took a while to die; this ticket had survived its glory days. In ragged typed letters: Deliver to L&F — attention: Voss.

She didn't take it from him immediately. Her fingertips had a way of making conclusions before her head could. "Who put that on there?"

"I'll give you three guesses and the first two get drunk," Len said, which meant he didn't know. "Actually, I figured, no one. It was already there."

Mara laughed once as if he'd told her something both improbable and expected. "Already there how?"

"It was wired under the handle. The paper's older than us. The handwriting, you tell me. And there's this." He tapped a corner of the trunk. Against the iron angle, screwed down with deliberate care, a flat tin plaque read: To be opened on a Thursday.

"That's a joke," she said.

"What's today?"

She had to think, which embarrassed her. Lost and Found taught you the days that people misplaced things more than the days themselves. Mondays for umbrellas. Fridays for confidence. "Wednesday," she said.

"Now tomorrow will walk in, and lawyering that'll start a fight over whether midnight's a line or a field," Len said. The rain pattered a decision for them. "I wouldn't have brought it if it weren't—" He cleared his throat. Men in the station kept their mysticism tidy. "Well, it pushed back."

She frowned. "Pushed back."

"When I tried to pick it up off Six. Like the weight went wrong under my hands. Like it belonged to the tile." He shrugged before she could tell him there wasn't a fool-proof test for haunted luggage. Len had been here long enough to indulge his own folklore. "Then the tag. Then your name. Voss, the station says. This one's your problem."

"My the station talks a lot," Mara said, but her voice had softened. She reached for the old ticket. Her name was typed in that hoity typeface the Remington had given the department two heads of service ago. The date line had been stamped, but the ink had bled, and time and grime had conducted a marriage between the numbers. She held it under the lamp. June… something. The year? It was pre-merger. Maybe twenty-five years. Maybe thirty.

"I'll sign for it," she told Len. "Help me get it on the table."

He moved the dolly. Together they heaved the trunk onto the work table that legendary luggage had scuffed to anonymity. Close up, the trunk smelled of old oil and paper left in a damp room. The brass of the fittings had almost blackened. The lock was simple and rusted at the edges.

Len hovered. "You going to open it?"

Mara looked at the tin plaque. Thursdays had not figured vigorously in her life. Thursdays were for the sandwich you resented buying and the headache you resented having. "It's not Thursday."

"It's getting there," Len said.

Mara grabbed the lock and tugged it. The warded mechanism gave as though it had expected more patience. The hasp popped with a tired complaint. She lifted the lid half an inch and stopped because something inside whispered like tissue. They both held their breath, as if in ceremony. Then she closed it again with a decisive thump.

"I'm not giving you a show," she said. "I'll inventory it. I'll write the forms. You can come back tomorrow and pretend to be surprised."

He saluted with two fingers off his cap and retreated. His shoes squealed just a little; he'd tracked in rain. The station swilled it up immediately. The building did a better job of that than it did of kindness.

When he was gone the quiet ran its hand over her neck. The air held a taste of tin and wet stone. Somewhere out past the platforms, a late gull cried like a squeaky hinge. Mara stood still and listened to the station's noises sort themselves into compartments in her mind. She had always had a talent for compartments. It was why they'd asked her to run the department when they had gone through three managers in a year. It was why she'd once been able to sit at a desk in a different building and keep the cases of a city from gnawing through the paperwork. There were only so many failures of attention a person could take. The station required a different kind of attention. It asked you to remember that someone had once loved the person who forgot to take their rain hat, no matter how cheap the hat.

She pulled a thin pair of gloves from a drawer, stretched the rubber gently over her hands while keeping her mind sidelong from the act of opening the trunk until it was no longer ceremonial. Then she slid the hasp again and lifted the lid as if it weighed the moon.

Inside, old newspaper had been cut into squares and laid across the top, layer on layer. She peeled them back. The headlines were from The Courier, back when it was a morning paper. HARBOR PLAN DELAYED halting construction on the seawall that now held the river like the lip of a bowl; MRR CHIEF RESIGNS; BOY SAVED BY STRANGER ON TRACK TWO, unspecific about both. She put the papers aside, each older than the last. Beneath them lay a coat, navy wool with a high collar, folded roughly. Inside the coat, peppered moths had made lace.

The next layer was a ledger no larger than a book of recipes, bound in leather the color of a bruise. She lifted it. No title on the spine, no lettering on the cover. The pages fluttered dry. The first page had columns ruled with a light hand and headings penned with care: date, car, contents, destination. Underneath, entries in inconsistent hands, the alphabet betraying their writers. Thistle Ave to Portside. C/o Marris. Fabric bolts. The next: Stowell Barn. Clam crates. Back and back, the years unwound. The most recent entries—if recent could be used for anything written before the station refitted the tiles in the east tunnel—stopped abruptly mid-page. The line ended with a place she didn't know, or didn't know as a place. Thursdays, the line read in a cramped confidence, 14:00, Track 6.

She frowned into the ledger as if it might be lying. Thursdays aren't a place. Fourteen hundred was not when a local took Track 6 in any timetable she held in her head. The last column, destination, had a name she had to mouth to understand it: Inspector. Inspector of Thursdays, if the handwriting continued beyond the word. The nib had lifted, leaving a teardrop where the ink had clung.

She found the coat's inner pocket contained nothing but the powder of old moth work. Beneath the ledger lay a pair of men's gloves, thin leather spoiling to dust at the creases. And beneath those, wrapped in parchment that had gone soft with age but still crinkled, an envelope sealed with black wax. The wax had cracked and fallen into the envelope's own creases. The address was a perfect twin to the ledger's last word: To the Inspector of Thursdays. Mara ran a thumb over the words and felt, absurdly, the faintest lift of letterpress, though it was written by hand.

She did not know what lay beneath weird, and her mind had not invited guests there in some time. She had a habit of letting things flicker at the very edge of her acceptance until they either presented themselves as useful or bored her. She set the envelope aside. She cataloged the coat with a code she would remember and no one else would guess, noted the ledger in her inventory book, wrote words that might one day have to justify themselves to a superior's superior, the way words were asked to do when some other story blurred into the station's tidy world.

At the bottom of the trunk was a false bottom so blatant she felt insulted by it. A rectangle cut into the wood, made to lift with a bent nail, and beneath that a cavity with something long and wrapped and a coiled string. She used the nail. Her gloves squeaked against the board. The cavity had been lined with tin to keep the damp out. Someone had known this trunk would have to live too long.

The long thing was a phonograph cylinder snug in a cloth sheath stitched from a demolished shirt. The cylinder's surface, a deep pitch, bore neat grooves. On the cardboard ring at the end, in the same careful hand as the ledger headings, someone had written a name, and the name strummed her nerves like a thumb over harp string.

Thomas Wait. Track Inspector.

Once, a decade and the job before this one ago, Mara had read a file with that name threaded through it like wire. She had put its pages back together and not been thanked. The official story had tightened and the unofficial story had seeped under doors. The city is full of stories that end in approximation. She touched the cardboard ring again, as if it might spark.

The coiled string proved to be more than string. It was a thin length of wire with a small key attached, the variety the station used a lifetime ago for lockers. Those were gone. They’d torn the row down when a boy had climbed inside one to sleep and come out—well. She put the key in the dish she kept for keys too old to be called that. The dish was a chipped saucer from a never-existing tea service. She put the wire next to it. Under the cylinder, nothing else but the rough wood of the trunk's skeleton.

Rain worried at the roof. Somewhere, a platform announcement tried its best in a voice too cheerful for the hour, the speaker lisping around a consonant. Track Seven, last call, doors closing, mind the gap.

She retrieved the envelope. She broke the black wax, because in the end she could never resist a sealed thing. The paper inside was thick as a remnant of law. It wore the smell of cedar. Her gloves left the faintest outline of talc on the fibers. The letter was three sentences only.

If you are not who I think you are, burn this.

If you are, listen and come.

Thursday 14:00. Track 6. The place between.

Some days a detail jumps on a chair and waves; other days it sits modestly in the corner and you don't notice until you've half-swept the room. She had read "Thursday" so many times now that the word began to behave like a brick. The place between. Between which two things? The rails? The days? The city and the other edge of it, the one you only saw when the river ran low?

She put the letter down with care. She felt that fussy, hollow sensation she got when a thing had come too close to the shape of the life she'd decided not to have. She took off her gloves because she needed to feel the air with her fingertips. The gloves went into the bin they'd always gone into. She glanced about the room as though someone might be trying to catch her eye and clue her into a joke. Her calendar sat as it always did, wedged next to the phone, a calendar someone had given her as an apology, with pictures of the city's uglier buildings embedded in months that did not deserve it. She flipped it. Wednesday's square just done. Thursday stared up at her like a dare.

She slid the cylinder from its cloth. Her hand was almost too dry to be trusted; the rain in the station never made the room damp, only the edges of words. The office had a phonograph because of a donation from a man who'd died and left the station his nostalgia. It lived on a high shelf in her back room and had gathered dust like an obligation. She had refused to sell it to antique dealers who asked with their best smiles because someone had written her a letter once accusing the station of eating their grandmother's handkerchief, and that had been absurd and sad and accurate enough to make her cling to anything the station possessed that knew how to mourn.

She set the player on the table and wound it. The cylinder slid over the mandrel and nested into its taper. The needle, a trembling insect limb, poised. She reached out and let the switch loose. The wheel spun. The needle fell, clicked, and a wash of static like peeled-off tape filled the room. Then a voice emerged, thin and far and without room for hesitancy. It was a woman's voice, trained to speak against machine noise.

"This is for the inspector," it said. "Whichever one you are. If they haven't abolished it and you haven't gone the same way. If you haven't, be grateful to the station's accidents. They are better than its plans."

Mara leaned on the table with both palms, face turned toward the machine as if toward a storyteller at a low campfire.

"I am Emme Rook," the voice said. "I keep tracks of the tracks. I have no authority and less sense. You won't know me, or you'll think you do and be wrong. I am leaving this because Thomas didn't come back from a Thursday, and I am not patient, and I no longer believe in the kindness of leaving well enough alone. If you are who I think you are, you do not either."

There was a scrape sound. The voice moved closer as if the woman had leaned in, aware of time's drag on wax. "If you hear nothing else, hear this: do not stand where the rails mirror. Do not look left for your God. Do not speak a name twice. And if a man with a blue coat asks if you are lost, tell him your destination clearly and keep your hands where he can see them. It may save you; it did not save the boy on Track Two. I can't—"

The cylinder hissed and stuttered, and Mara had the swift sense of having missed a stride on a staircase. Words dissolved in fuzz then returned, a piece snapped off the end of a sentence with the clean edge of broken bone.

"—under track six, fourteen candles," the voice continued. "By the pillar where the paint falls away like old milk. That is where I will be on the other side. If you cannot find me, you will find Thomas's watch. Bring it back. Do not let the old men with the new coats catalogue it. They will write a number and the number will not be its name.”

The phonograph whined; the spring had opinions. Mara's hand hovered above the crank, but she let it run out. The voice softened, as if the woman had turned her head to talk to someone else. "Listen. The trains go where they go even when they don't. I am tired of that. Remember that we painted the line between place and time; it is not in the world. It is ours. If I'm gone long enough, they'll call it a myth. If that comforts you, let it." She laughed, the sound brief and untidy. Then the cylinder spiraled down to smoke. Sound shrank until it was only the machine's stubbornness, and then silence put its hand carefully over the room again.

Mara breathed in when she realized she hadn't. The station carried her breath away, pressed it under its floor. Emme Rook. Thomas Wait. She tried to put their names where they had been before, in a file folder with a misprinted label and a rubber band that had lost its conviction, in a cabinet two floors above a view of the river. A city inspector who had been found without his shoes on a platform without a witness. A stray boy who had slept where he shouldn't have and woken where he never would again. Emme Rook—no, she did not know that one. Names had a way of pretending to be strangers until you gave them a context they liked.

She looked at the clock. Thirty-eight minutes past midnight. Grease bled from the pin at the minute hand's base like mascara. She had been awake too long months ago, and it had kept on.

The phone on her desk rang the way station phones do: as if ringing were all they had ever wanted to be allowed to do. She let it ring twice to remind it who paid the rent, then picked up.

"Lost and Found," she said, and heard the fatigue in her voice make a small polite arrangement of itself.

"Voss," Len's voice said without preamble, breathy and thin at the margins. The storm's static pressed in. "You ought to come to Six."

"Now?"

"You'll want to see it before they move him."

Between, she thought, the word lighting itself in her, not a candle but one of those old flash cubes that went hard and white in the instant you needed it. "Who is it?"

"Don't know yet. He doesn't have his face as much as he used to."

"Len." Her voice climbed a step and stopped. "Don't be a ghoul."

"I'm not. I'm sorry." He swallowed, but the sound made it through the phone. "He looks familiar. And the watch—you'll want to see the watch."

"The watch."

"He's holding it. In his fist like he's late and trying to catch the minute. And it's...listen, just come."

An irritant like sand moved under the skin of Mara's patience. The station did not allow for much of that in the first place. She hung up gently, because she had learned the superstition that the last thing a dead person hears is the sound made by the person who will find them. She took her coat. The canvas was stained with rains. She slid the letter into a folder and slipped that into the coat's inner pocket. The key and wire she left in the saucer; one cannot bring each hint to a threshold. She flicked off the lamp. The room jumped to grey, and the great clock beyond the grille took itself too seriously again.

She walked down the corridor that backed the Lost and Found, the wall tiled to shoulder height in cream rectangles with black lines that threatened headaches if you looked at them too long. She had the move of someone whose place in a building was recognized by the building. Doors she had always found locked at this hour unlatched themselves with an ease she did not think of as magic; she thought of it as a system of favors paid down and up like debts. She reached the east hall and preferred its emptiness to the west's. The statue of the station's founder raised its arm to point nowhere useful. Someone had hung a scarf around its wrist last week. No one had taken it off. The museum kiosk's light hummed to itself, educating no one.

Track Six was in the middle of the twelve that fanned from the concourse under that arched glass. Its sign was black with gold letters that had peeled to show the primer like a second thought. When she stepped through the gate and onto the platform the cold came up at her like a dog, eager and toothy. Len was there, standing with his shoulders pulled in, his cap in his hands. Two uniformed transit officers stood farther along, one talking to the other with the careful blandness people employed when there are more than two truths available and you do not want to adopt the worst one for fear of being the first to admit it. Beyond them, under the friendly genesis of a platform light, the man lay.

He had a blue coat. Or the coat had once been blue, and the storm light made the cloth a color she'd seen on sailors' tattoos. His hair was a gray woven with wet, stuck to his forehead and the part of his face that was still a face. She recognized the shoes—not because they were stylish, they were not, but because in the department you learned markers like negative space. People who owned those shoes did not take trains. People who wore those shoes got sent by others to meet them. In his right hand he held a watch. The fist around it was a story: the skin already mottled, the knuckles not as hard as a fighter's and not as soft as a pianist's. You learned those too. The watch lay partly visible between thumb and first finger. It had a white face. There was something strange about the numbers.

"Don't come closer," one of the officers said as Mara approached. "We haven't—"

"It's fine," Len said. "She belongs here."

Mara crouched at a distance that would not cause later arguments. She tucked her hair behind her ear as though to convince herself she was making a procedural move. The man's eyes were open, but his gaze had chaired the wrong room hours ago. The watch. She angled her head. The numbers on its face were backward. Not mirrored precisely, but starting where twelve should begin and proceeding counterclockwise, neat as a reasonable mistake.

Her mouth went dry. The cylinder's static seemed to scurry at her ankles.

"His jacket," she said. "Do we have identification?"

"Not yet," the officer said. He glanced at Len as if to ask: how many of these does your station produce in a year. "Train came in late. Driver saw nothing. Someone paged the platform cleaner and—"

"And found him," Len finished. "And not a drop of blood near, Voss. Like when they pull a good rug and the dust keeps the shape."

His coat's lapel had a tear. In the missing triangle of cloth, a pin had once sat. Pins made grooves; her eyes found the ghost of metal quickly. The grooves were parallel. The pin had had bars, not a circle. Her stomach made a small, private motion.

"Do you know him," Len asked, quietly enough that he could pretend he had not if she said no.

Mara watched the watch. She could hear the great clock behind and above counting the same seconds in the way politics counted votes: however you arranged them, there were only so many. The man's hand had cooled enough to look like a hand again instead of something trying to become another thing.
