It turned out, the quiet hum of a lighthouse that no longer saved lives could still save one, if you let it.

She worked the chisel under the fresh slats and levered them free one by one, the sound of metal against nail a crisp bite. Knopf, true to her namesake, jumped onto the empty stool and watched with unblinking attention. Mara paused on the final slat and listened. Somewhere up inside the tower, a drop of condensation fell fat and echoing into the iron pan she’d put under the seam that needed repointing. The foghorn from the point let out a prolonged moan. The town went on, unheard.

Under the slats, the lid was nailed but not cruelly. Beneath it lay a layer of waxed canvas, brittle at the edges, smelling of paraffin and dust. She pulled it back and uncovered a flat bundle wrapped in brown paper and a smaller one tied with cotton string. There was an envelope, too, thick and old-fashioned cream, the flap tucked but not glued. Mara took that one first.

On the front, in a hand that slanted left and took up the bottom margin like it wanted to fall off: To the Keeper. No name. No address. Inside, a single page, yellowing but stiff, as if it had spent its life away from light.

If this finds you, the page began in the same hand, then I did what I could.

I don’t know who you are. There is a key in the box. The door is under the north stair by the oil room. I locked it the night after the September storm of '89. The girl is still there. We told ourselves we would do right by her when the weather settled, and then we told ourselves the sea would do it for us. I have not slept since.

The keeper keeps. I broke when I did not. It will not be my last night and I would like to go down knowing I set it right. Don’t call Ronald. He will tell you a different story. You will need a crowbar anyway.

— L. Oakes

Mara read it once. Athletes talked about heart rates; reporters talked about heartbeats as if they came down to sentences, to alignments, to the moment when the lead set. Her brain, trained on lies, caught the thread of truth that lined the note like a bone. The words were not composed with an audience in mind; they were confession, not performance. She heard a voice under it: not the narrative varnish people applied when they wanted to look good but the spare sentence of someone who was done being something to someone else.

“Oakes,” she said into the quiet, because the island liked a name said aloud to be sure of it. “Len? Leonard? Lenora Oakes?” Bernice would know; Bernice knew who had kept whose secrets for sixty years.

The key was wrapped in waxed paper and then in oil cloth, and it swam heavy into her palm when she untied it, like a fish that didn’t understand it should be dead. Brass, big as her thumb, its teeth irregular. Old. The other bundle, flat and paper-wrapped, revealed a book when teased free of its dressing: the lighthouse log for 1987 through 1989, its leather cracked, its pages onionskin thin, the entries in three different hands, then two, then a final one until one day in September when it stopped like the world had. She riffled until her eye caught on the last entry. September 24: storm. Lantern back-up. Visitors from town. No ships in distress. The entry was neat, patient, unexceptional.

Her eyes flicked to the note again, to the line we told ourselves the sea would do it for us, and a coldness like an ungloved hand in snow slid up her forearm to her elbow.

She could have called Sheriff Dan O’Malley. She could have called Ezra and told him to turn his truck back up the hill, never mind the ferry or the dockside courtesy two stops from the Blue Seal co-op. She could have said, “Mara, you moved to a place nobody locks their doors and now you’re going to open a different kind of door that has been locked for thirty-six years, are you kidding?” That voice in her head sounded like her mother and like Sam Whitaker, who had been her editor in Boston and also, for three brief and heroic months, something else. Sam had a scar you couldn't see that he wore on his sentences, and when he hired her straight out of a campus paper with four rooms and fifteen dreamers, he told her: “Don’t go where they point. Go where they look away from.”

She set the note on the counter, took the key in her fist, and crossed the wide room. Knopf landed lightly on the floor and flowed alongside her, a small gray river.

The north stair hugged the curved inner wall of the tower like a broken arm. The stone sweated in weather like this; the old whitewash had soaked up salt a hundred times and surrendered it back a hundred and one. Under the first turn of the stairs was what had been the oil room and was now a place she stored extra bags and a box of library sale discards. The door to the oil room was plain and newer than the rest, the tongue-and-groove pine Henry Lopez had hung for her last winter when the old one had swelled shut like a lip. She moved the bags and the box, and then squatted with a flashlight and the key.

There is no such thing as a seamless wall, she thought, and if there is, it is lying. In the whitewash there were hairline cracks that wandered like rivers on a relief map. In the boards of the stair, two of the risers were ever so slightly darker than the rest, as if a different hand had cut them and the varnish had fallen into them differently. At the angle where stair met tower, a seam made itself known when she ran her fingers along the skirting board and felt the dent-free line of wood turn into a line that had been split once and then married again.

She tapped with her knuckle. A hollow answered.

“Jesus.” The word left her with more breath than voice.

Knopf bumped her shoulder with a small, insistent head, and Mara set the cat aside. She crouched, got the chisel under the lip of the skirting board and pried gently. The finish had a modest heart and lifted with reluctance. Nails gave. There were more beneath, old black cut nails set deep. She worked at them. It took longer than she wanted. That was good. Hurried people made mistakes. She had made one, once, with a photograph she shouldn’t have run, a source she shouldn’t have trusted. It had cost her a man’s job and a woman’s marriage and all her trust in herself for a year and a half. The story had been right. The way she’d gotten there had not been.

When the board came loose, a shadow square opened where there had been none. There was a lock set in the edge of the board; it had been painted over, twice, maybe three times. The key in her hand matched it. She slid it in, felt the pegs bite, and turned. That sound—old metal yielding, old intent changing its mind—was the worst sound she had ever heard and the best.

The hidden door swung inward with a sigh like somebody else finally letting out a breath.

Cold came at her, not air so much as the absence of the warm draft she hadn’t known she was standing in. She turned on the flashlight. The circle of light cut a white coin out of the darkness and moved it over shelves that had once held oil cans and alkyd and now held nothing but a row of brown bottles with ghost labels and a tin of something that said SALT PORK with a price in cents. There was a rough chair with rope fraying where someone had sat and tied something while they waited for weather to pass. There was a coil of chain. There was the shape of the secret itself: not big, not dramatic, not the cavern that stories liked, but a space barely deep enough to hide a person if you folded them up.

Knopf pushed her small body through the opening and was a gray cutout for a moment against the black, tail up, then disappeared. Mara’s mouth filled with a taste like pennies. The flashlight’s beam found the back wall and then, at its base, a mound of something that had long ago dried and slumped upon itself. Fabric rotted into strands. Rope. The particular pale that bone took on when it forgot it had been alive.

She did not step in all at once. She didn’t call anyone. She did what she always did, which had not ruined her even when it had felt like it would: she named what she saw, quietly, to herself, as if the saying of it made the world stabilize around it.

“Cloth,” she said. “Canvas. Rope. Wood. Chain. Bone.”

At the last, the flashlight trembled in her hand. She set it down on the floor itself to steady the beam, and the light lifted the world into harder focus. A hand—no, a part of what had been one, the curve of metacarpals delicate as a tea saucer, wrapped in a rough loop of sailor’s twine. The bones were threaded through with something green-black that might once have been seaweed or that might have been ribbon. Above it, tucked into the fold of what remained of the canvas, a small oval glinted.

Mara bent and, with two fingers, lifted the oval just enough to see.

A silver gull, wings spread, unsubtle in that way jewelry sometimes was in small towns. She had seen one like it before. It had lived for years in the framed, fading photocopy of a missing-person poster thumbtacked to the wall behind Bernice’s counter at the general store. Angela Lively, the poster had said. Last seen September 1989 leaving the Clam Hut after her shift. Sixteen. Any information, please.

“Angela,” Mara said, and felt at once the intimacy and presumption of a first name spoken in a space like this. She had never met the girl. The town had never stopped talking about her.

The flashlight beam quivered again, but not from her hand this time. It vibrated as the floorboards above her head transferred a weight, then another. Slow steps crossed the shop. The faint chime of the door’s bell came belatedly, as if the heavy air had swallowed it and needed a second to find it again.

Mara’s heart stamped once and then again, hard, as if it wanted to be sure she was listening.

Knopf flattened herself and flowed into the corner like gray smoke disappearing into night.

“Mara?” came a voice, muffled, the floorboards turning words into a low instrument. “You still here?”

Not Ezra. Male, but not Ezra, not Sheriff Dan either. Ronald? The name from the letter sat up in her mind and looked around. But the voice was younger than the name she’d given it. Less certain of its own place in the room. The bell tinkled again as the door drifted toward shutting on its slowly-failing spring.

She put her hand over the flashlight beam, the circle of light collapsing to a crescent, then a slice. The dark came down, thick and complete, and for a moment all she could hear was the ocean, breathing in and breathing out, that long old body of water that kept all of them, even when it gave them up. She closed her eyes, though it made no difference, and then opened them again.

“Yes,” Mara called, and her voice surprised her by sounding like itself. “Just a minute.”

And then, because the keeper keeps—words from a dead hand, words she had never wanted to put on—she took her hand off the light and let the beam wash the back of the hidden room again, fixed the image of the silver gull and the small bones and the coil of chain in her mind like pinning a specimen, and came up out of the dark to meet the living.

Chapter One

Maya found the first body before she found the interference.

All the way up the switchbacks the radio had been whispering. Not voices, nothing so obligingly human—just a sheet of hiss and breath, the spread handprint of the universe against the station’s uplink. Every few minutes something slid across it, a tremor like a wet finger around the rim of a glass. It was so faint that even the tach needle of the pickup shivered louder, but once she heard it she could not make herself unhear it. Whatever was leaking onto their frequencies didn’t belong on this mountain. It didn’t belong anywhere.

“Stop listening to ghosts,” she told herself, and killed the driver’s-side speaker.

The array reared up in the last curl of the road like a herd of white animals frozen mid-sip. Two dozen dishes, each the size of a house, angled their clean throats at the cold, nowhere in particular. Everything was metal and shade and distance. The wind carried a powder of salt and old sun. There were hand-painted signs at the fence warning of oxygen depletion and electromagnetic exposure and pumas. The only thing moving was a patch of blue tarp slapping itself inside out beside a stack of cables.

The gate was open. It was always open up here; the mountain decided who stayed and who didn’t.

She parked in the wedge of shade thrown by the instrument hall and sat for a minute with the engine ticking itself cool. The roof of the pickup popped with heat. The sun was obscene: a sheet of glare dropped over everything. She had learned a long time ago not to rush the first breath, the second, the third. At five thousand meters every movement was a negotiation. She licked her lips and got dust.

A gust rolled dust over the hood. In it she could taste the nasty sweetness of antifreeze and something burnt, something electrical, the ghost of wiring heated too hard. Or maybe that was just the cab: nothing on this mountain was ever truly new. She took a packet of coca leaves from the dash, tucked two green tongues into her cheek, and chewed until her mouth was a flat, damp bitterness.

A man in a wool cap and wraparound sunglasses waved from the shadow of the personnel door. He had a badge clipped to a parka he wasn’t wearing. He wore the easy, weightless grin of a person hired to fix problems in a place where most problems didn’t belong to him.

“You must be Maya,” he called. “Dr. Kline said you were on your way.”

“Sorry,” she said, though she wasn’t. The drive had taken as long as the drive needed to take. “Road crew was blasting near kilometer thirteen. They waved me through.”

“Always the blasting,” he said. His accent stretched vowels to the horizon. “I’m Lucho. Everything else is broken. Do you have bags?”

“Backpack,” she said, lifting it. She traveled light. There wasn’t room up here for anything that couldn’t keep up.

He held the door open and the heat flinched. They went down a short corridor painted the color of old teeth, footprints in dust peeling away from boot-cleaners. Somebody had taped up a cartoon of a llama wearing a headset and scowling at a tangle of phone lines. Beside it, a printout from the national spectrum authority listed prohibited emissions in the millimeter bands. Someone had underlined a line in shrill highlighter: Personal electronics prohibited beyond this point.

“Is that a suggestion, or a rule?” Maya asked.

“A way of life,” Lucho said, tapping the lanyard at his throat, which held a plastic sleeve with a strip of foil in it. “We drop our phones in the Faraday pocket when we come in. People forget. People die.” He shrugged. “No one here, of course. Watch your step.”

He led her into a big room ringed with workstations, their monitors asleep in blue squares. The control room was a long, low ship with twenty chairs and only four bodies. It felt deserted in that way of rooms built to hold more conversation than oxygen. At the far end a glassed-in cube held the server racks, the lights within a small blinking galaxy. The floor hummed. The hum got into her bones. She liked it. The hum meant things that were supposed to be listening were listening, and the deathly hush of a dead cryo line was something she still heard in her sleep, seventeen months removed from the last time she’d walked into a freezer and found it warm.

A woman turned from the largest bank of screens. She had a face cut out of time in hard squares: deep lines at the mouth and sunburn laid down in layers. Her hair was ash-white and cut close to the skull with a soldier’s practicality. She wore a fleece embroidered with the observatory’s logo and a tiny brass saint pinned at her shoulder, out of place among the clean logos and industrial badging. The saint’s tiny face had been rubbed blank.

“Maya,” she said. “Irene Kline.” She did not add Doctor. She didn’t have to. The room was full of her voice. “Thank you for getting up here so quickly.”

“Flights out of Calama were clear,” Maya said. “Road, less so.”

“A Bernini construction crew is blasting an access road for a geodetics project three ridgelines over,” Irene said. “We’ve asked them to coordinate. They have promised to. In the same way my hairdresser promised not to take an inch and took three.”

Lucho laughed and drifted away. Maya shook Irene’s hand and felt those calluses particular to long-term instrument people: micrometer screws, steel wool, a life spent with both computers and very real bolts.

“I’m here now,” Maya said. “Do you still have the phenomenon?”

“If that’s what we’re calling it,” Irene said. “Evan, bring up the 41-gig window.”

A young man in a hoodie and a cap that read COMBINE AND CONQUER flicked keys. He couldn’t have been more than twenty-two. His skin had already succumbed to altitude, broken capillaries in his cheeks like faint maps. His eyes were the red-shot blue of someone who had been looking at graphs too long. He smiled at Maya in a way that said: You might, in the next ten minutes, save my dissertation.

He brought up a waterfall plot. Blue to green to yellow, the thin bands of ground-glass emission that should have been clean and black.

“There,” he said, stabbing a finger at a faint diagonal that whispered like a hairline crack in ice. “It’s not just at forty-one point three. It slow-drifts from point one to point three to point five, and does this weird sinusoidal beat if you watch long enough. See? It shouldn’t be there. It—it can’t be there.”

“Local?” Maya asked. “Have you done sweeps? Walked the grid with a sniffer?”

“Yes and yes,” Irene said. “We’ve had both crews sweep the instrument hall and the culverts. We killed the Wi-Fi. No phones past the Faraday strip. We powered down the vending machine after it tried to ensnare two people and then fritzed. We even cut the line to Rocío’s radio. She has opinions about that.”

The woman by the coffee urn, who had been watching them with amused contempt, snorted. She wore an apron printed with a field of little rocketships as if to remind the astronomers that they were, in fact, a species that cooked. “My radio was born old,” Rocío said. “It has vacuum tubes. It is not your witch.”

“It may, however, be your witch,” Irene said. “We’re not excluding any suspects. The signal appeared two weeks ago. It’s getting stronger.”

“Times?” Maya prompted.

“Always in the dark,” Evan said. “Mostly on the second shift. We tried to schedule the array around it, to avoid the band, but it bleeds into others. And it’s—look, if you zoom—”

He zoomed. The faint diagonal resolved into a broken line, a hand-shaken scribble. The beat he’d mentioned laid itself over it like the breathing of a sleeping animal. Now that she was watching for it, she could see that the signal wasn’t entirely arbitrary. It tightened and loosened, stuttered and fell back, like something running uphill, failing, and trying again.

“This observatory has weather stations up for two hundred kilometers?” Maya asked.

“Three hundred,” Irene said. “Why.”

“Any anomalous meteorology to correlate with this?”

“Dry as a bone and cold as my ex-husband,” Irene said. “Except—”

“Except three nights ago we had an inversion,” Evan said quickly, grabbing the ball and running. “Down here. Light winds at surface, high aloft. Nothing huge, but unusual. But the signal happened on nights with no inversion too, so—”

“So probably not weather,” Maya said, “though it’s good to know. What about ground?”

Lucho had come back without her noticing. He leaned on the back of a chair like it owed him rent. “The miners?” he said.

Irene’s mouth thinned. “There are old claims down the far slope,” she said. “Abandoned. Scrappers go in. It’s illegal. The municipality does not care to enforce, except when someone gets stuck and then calls their cousin who knows a cousin who works as a guard here.”

“And they bring radios and jammers and God knows what else,” Rocío said. “Too many of them. Not enough of us. We post the warnings. They wipe their boots on them.”

Maya filed it. Illegal mining wasn’t her problem unless it bled into spectrum. Spectrum was the only kind of border she’d been hired to patrol.

“I’ll need your logs for the last ten days,” she said. “And any changes that happened here. Even the stupid ones. Especially the stupid ones.”

Evan was already shoving a drive at her. “It’s all here, plus our installations from last month, even the, uh, trial of the, um—”

“The espresso machine,” Rocío said dryly. “Which we installed and then uninstalled when it began screaming.”

“It only screamed when you asked for a cappuccino,” Evan protested. He blushed the exact color of an angry avalanche. “It was fine for Americanos.”

“I will die before I drink brown water,” Rocío said, and took the urn off boil with a decisive click.

Maya slid the drive into her pocket and let the room breathe around her. The hum in the floor made a song in her teeth. Somewhere far down the hall a door shut, and the slight pressure change pressed against her eardrums. She could feel the signal, now that she knew its shape. It hung around the edges of the quiet like a mosquito in a dark tent.

“Do you have a spare sniffer?” she asked Lucho. “Something I can carry.”

Without looking, he plucked a battered antenna from a cupboard and laid it in her hands like a rifle. It had been branded by three different companies and repaired by a fourth. Its handle had been wrapped in tape and prayer. The LED winked when she thumbed the switch. The hiss of the room sharpened, grew teeth and edges, as the receiver cut out her own band-limited ears and replaced them with its own.

“Zones?” she asked.

“Exclusion around the cryo plant, obviously,” Irene said. “Most of your hunting you can do from here and the catwalks. If you go outside, watch your line-of-sight. Watch your breath. Don’t make me call your mother. We’re expecting wind later.”

“I don’t have a mother,” Maya said, automatically, and then wondered why she had said it out loud. She breathed, slow and even. The coca dulled the headache that bloomed behind her eyes. “I’ll start in the machine room.”

Evan half-rose. “Do you want company?”

“I’ll call if I need hands,” Maya said. He sagged back in relief. She remembered being twenty-two and offering help like a dog bringing a shoe, trembling with hope that it would at last be the right thing. She didn’t hold it against him. In a place like this, place was a thing you earned one task at a time.

The machine room was colder, the hum deeper, like standing inside a throat. On the way she passed the kitchen and made the kind of mistake you only made once: she took a breath and was hit full in the face by the smell of charring sugar. She flinched.

“Do not insult my flan,” Rocío called, though her hands were nowhere near it. “I will know.”

“I would never,” Maya said, because it seemed true.

The sniffer read high near the cryo compressors, as always, because nothing human had ever been built that didn’t leak a little. She bled that out in her head and looked for the ghost in it, the particular limp, the skip in the junk-thrum. The interference was there and not there, a shimmer behind the roar. She sat on her heels in the aisle between racks of cooling apparatus, closed her eyes, and counted the beat.

The beat went: fast-fast, slow, slow, hold. Fast-fast, slow, slow, hold. Any regular waveform would have been easier. The human brain loved rhythm, loved to call any rhythm a message. She made herself be dumb.

She moved along the racks. She held the sniffer against pipes and cabinets and felt the tickle of static across her knuckles, a thin hair-brush of sparking. She came up with dust on her hands that stained her skin white. Salt. In her head the signal flickered harder. She thought of all the ways waves found you even when you hid from them, even when you built a mountain of rules and posted them like a fence around your life.

When she came back into the control room an hour later the light had gone from horrible to merely indifferent. The sky outside the narrow slit windows was the color of bleached bone. A thin red scarf of cloud trailed over the peaks to the east. The saint on Irene’s shoulder leaned with it.

“Find my witch?” Irene asked.

“Not in the obvious places,” Maya said. “How well do you know your neighbors?”

“We watch their weather,” Irene said. “Lucho has cousins in the police in San Pedro. We are on the municipal smoking ban’s Christmas card list.”

“The Bernini crew uses millimeter-band tools?” Maya said. “Leveling something?”

“They are supposed to be coded to keep away from us,” Irene said. “Supposed to be. Their foreman says yes. Their foreman is a talker. His name is Carlo. He was born with an alibi in his mouth.”

“Signal’s too clean to be blasting timer bleed,” Maya said. “And the beat—the beat isn’t any timing I know. I’m going to need to stand outside when we get a spike.” She resisted the temptation to say that the signal made her scalp itch. It would sound like superstition. It wasn’t. There were things ears knew before you learned the math.

“Spike comes after one,” Evan said. “Most nights. You should get some sleep.”

“I slept in Calama,” Maya lied. Sleep in Calama had been two hours of intermittent blackout with a compressor groaning through the wall and someone’s television drilling holes in the ceiling. “I’ll nap on the couch. Wake me at midnight.”

“You really don’t have a mother,” Irene said, and for a second there was something not quite amused in her voice. It slid away like a fish. “Evan, Mateo and Cat will take the last hours of first shift. Lucho—”

“I know, I know,” Lucho said. “I fix the thing by kicking it.”

“Gently,” Irene said. “We are not barbarians.”

“Speak for yourself,” Rocío called.

The couch in the break room had a geometry designed to make any spine feel fortunate and then punished. Someone had draped a blanket over one arm and tucked a packet of aspirin under the corner, like an offering to a god of headaches. In the little library by the window someone had left a glossy magazine about vintage radios open to a spread of a cathedral set made of walnut. Someone had torn a square out of the page. Maya did not think you cut out a picture unless it meant something to you. Or unless you meant to hide something. Or both.

She lay down. She closed her eyes and saw the waterfall plot falling, and in it the diagonal line kept trying to hold itself straight and then sliding. The sugar smell of the flan had backed off. The metallic tang of the station persisted. She breathed, counting, until the number meant less than the breath and the breath meant less than the hum.

She woke in the stale dark to someone saying her name. For a moment she thought the hum had grown a voice.

“Maya?” Evan’s whisper, thin and papery. The clock on the microwave read 00:19. The sound had made a hole in the room.

“I’m up,” she said, not moving. Headache. The coca had worn off and left the familiar ache like a small strong hand behind her eyes. She sat up and the blanket slid down around her waist, dragging cold over her. “We’re spiking?”

“It’s—yeah,” Evan said. His throat worked. “It started. Dr. Kline says to—if you could—”

“On my way.”

The corridors at night had their own weather. The lights ran low, the emergency exit signs a dishonest green. The machine room sang its song in the cold register and the coffee machine sang its thin high one, even turned off. When she reached the control room, the glass of the server cage was dimmer than before. A converter hummed with sickly bass.

On the main screen the waterfall had deepened from blue to a bruise. The diagonal line had a partner now, shadowed and offset, a twin. The beat had doubled. Fast-fast-fast, slow, hold.

“That’s new,” Irene said, without looking away from the screen. Her jaw worked. She had rolled her sleeves up past her elbows and her saint had turned again, facing the window as if it, too, were looking for something. “Outside.”

She meant: Go. Find it. Be my dog and fetch.

Maya took the sniffer and stepped through the vestibule, through the bubble of still air that kept dust from the hard drives, and into the night.

The cold came like a hand. The sky had stolen the ground. The dishes were black shapes against black, only the thin white ribs of their struts holding any light. The wind had gone down: she could hear the breathing motors in the azimuth tracks as the dishes turned their faces. Somewhere a guanaco coughed like an old man.

She held up the antenna and turned in a slow circle. The sniffer’s LED ran from green to yellow without going through caution. The hiss ate her up. She crouched and let the wind pass above her and thought of waves, of how they wrapped around things and slid into holes. She moved to the edge of the pad and leaned over the rail and the sniffer ticked higher. There was a maintenance trail around the back of the instrument hall that hugged a berm and then edged along a culvert. She took it, boots scuffing grit.

Behind the instrument hall the wind was a little less. The culvert mouth breathed. The sniffer’s tone frayed and then reforged. There was another panel of servers here, a satellite rack, insulated and locked. She put her ear to it. Nothing but the low animal rumble of fans.

Something squealed, high and brief, and her skin tried to climb off her bones. She looked up.

A ribbon of light moved in the sky. Not a plane—too jerked, too obedient to some clumsy hand. Not a meteor—those did not stop and then judder forward, hesitate, and then course-correct. The ribbon made a little square of itself, like a child’s drawing of a kite. Then it went dead, went dark. The sniffer’s LED plunged into green and the hiss went soft and simple again, just night and the universe and the life support of machines.

Drone, she thought. Someone’s cheap little try-hard, in a place where drones had no right to fly. It had turned its light off too late. She got the rocket of adrenaline, that sharp now-there-you-are feeling, and then couldn’t put it anywhere. The night was hungry and ate everything.

She jogged back to the control room, lungs scraping. The oxygen was a rumor now, a promise somebody hadn’t kept. She palmed the door and the air inside swallowed the cold and gave back heat and bleach.

“I saw a drone,” she said when she could say anything. She leaned both hands on the console and watched the plot color itself. “Northwest quadrant. It turned and killed its light. That—if it had a transmitter, the Doppler—”

“Then whatever it is is here,” Irene said. “Not three ridges over. Mateo—”

The guard by the door had the mournful mustache of a man convinced that his job would never involve anything other than asked-for cigarettes and the occasional gun. He straightened like a curtain pulled. “I go,” he said, hand on the radio he absolutely wasn’t supposed to carry inside. He left anyway, the radio crackling softly, apology in every step.

“Call Bernini,” Irene said to no one in particular. “Wake Carlo up and tell him I am coming for his family.”

“Already on it,” Lucho said, somewhere outside the light, his voice dulled by the sting of cold air clinging to his clothes. “He says his logs are clean.”

“His logs are a fairy tale,” Irene said, and gave the plot a look that would have cracked granite. “If this is him he will confess in tears. If it is not him, I will make him cry anyway.”

Evan made a sound like a swallowed nail. “How angry are we allowed to get?” he whispered. There were rules, written and unwritten; they had had criteria and metrics for anger. Watching something you loved be used by something you didn’t understand made anger feel like oxygen. There was too much of it and not enough.

“Baseline fury,” Irene said. “Augment as needed.”

Maya was about to ask Cat, the night operator, to save off a high-res chunk of the last five minutes when she realized she had not seen Cat since she had left to go outside. Cat’s chair sat a little pushed back, as if someone had just stood up to fetch something. A mug with a leaping fish on it steamed faintly. The steam smelled of cloves.

“Where’s Catalina?” Maya asked.

“Head,” Rocío said. “She drank the tea that makes you run to the head on purpose. Do not ask me why.”

“How long?” Maya said. The sniffer lay quiet on the console like a sleeping animal.

“Four minutes?” Evan said. “Six? I wasn’t—”

The window of the server cage threw back a small, mean reflection of her face. She had not realized until that moment that the hum had changed. Not stopped. Not failed. But the pitch had shifted, a hair to the left. You could not do this job if you did not hear those sort of sideways things.

She stepped to the glass. Inside, the rack lights pulsed in an easy breath. The cable run on the bottom shelf, the one that fed the uplink to the dish control, sagged a little, as if someone had pulled on it and not quite pushed it back. That could have been anything. People tripped on things. People were the same everywhere.

She palmed the release; the server cage door clicked stupidly and then got its mind right and opened. The cold hit her again. Server rooms were never as cold as they pretended they were on television, but this one fought the heat with single-minded pettiness. Ice wanted to grow. Everything was set to deny ice its nature.

On the floor, behind the rack with the sagging cable, Catalina Huamán lay curled like she had been trying to keep a small secret warm.

For a second Maya’s mind did that thing it did, that mercy where it replaced what was in front of her with what it would have liked to see. She saw a dropped sweater. A cable looped like a sleeping cat. A damp bag of silica gel bursting like rice. Anything but the shape of a hand where a hand shouldn’t be.

Then the second passed and Cat was very much a body. Her hair had pulled loose from its braid and crossed her face like drawn wires. Her mouth was open a fraction and the lip was split and had dried in a little star. There was a dark smear under her ear that had crept in a slow tide to the floor tile. The tile had drunk it and drunk more and stopped. The mug on the console steamed. The clove smell was sweet enough to make the back of Maya’s throat water with nausea.

She did not touch the body. She knew better than to touch. She knew to look. She looked for the electrical burn, the arc mark that snatches at the eyes when something goes wrong in the way that happens to men who go into panels without ground straps. She looked for the bright little bead in a corner where someone had forgotten to tie in a remember-this wire. She found nothing. The rack was fussy but not malevolent, and it had never been able to get out of its own cage.

“Maya?” It was Irene, no louder than the room.

“Here,” Maya said, and her voice did a strange small thing. She cleared it and it did it again. “Don’t—don’t crowd the doorway.”

Irene was at her shoulder, and then she was not. She stopped herself the exact width of the door away. She had seen what Maya had seen and had been seeing it for a long time in other rooms. She made a small motion with her hand and the room at large stopped existing. Even Lucho’s grin fell off his face like a tool dropped when your finger meets the spinning blade and you are suddenly very interested in what you’ve cut.

“You called?” Irene asked nobody at all. Then she raised her voice. “Mateo.”

“Sí,” Mateo called from somewhere distant, and then again, closer. “Sí, doctora.”

“Call the carabineros,” she said, and then softer, “and shut down everything that can be shut down without endangering the dishes. No one leaves. No one arrives. If the road is open, it is closed. If someone is on the road, pull them in or turn them back.”

Mateo said something into the radio he wasn’t supposed to have. His voice had gone flat and very young.

“Evan,” Irene said. “Do not throw up.”

“I won’t,” Evan said, which meant he very much would, and then he didn’t. He bit the heel of his hand instead and stared at a fixed point slightly to the left of reality.

“Maya,” Irene said. “Tell me what you see.”

Maya crouched because there was no world in which standing above Catalina’s body and making pronouncements did not feel like sacrilege. The hum in the floor was behind her now, a thing with its own life that could not be called back. The clove steam made her eyes sting.

“I see Catalina,” she said. “No visible electrical burns. No scorch on the rack. Cable sag, here—not sure when it happened. I see blood from the right ear. A small impact wound on the occiput that looks old—no, not old. Dried enough to smear. No smell of ozone. No scorched hair. No signs of—”

She stopped. She was going to say: struggle. As if the absence of overturned chairs meant anything, as if the particular neatness of this room wasn’t its own trick.

“Her nails,” Maya said instead, and immediately hated herself for saying it because it seemed trite, as if she had been given a laminated card of things to look for and was reading from it. Catalina’s nails were short and clean. One of them had a crescent of what looked like pale clay under it. Pale clay should not exist on a mountain made of salt and stone. Pale clay was the color of riverbanks and school projects and Santiago sidewalks after rain. She put that thought down like you put down a piece of glass and looked at her hand to make sure she wasn’t bleeding.

“And the interference?” Irene said. She was the kind of scientist who sent condolences and asked about data at the same time.

Maya stood and had to put a hand on the rack to make the floor find her again. “It spiked,” she said. “It—”

On the main screen the signal had gone to hard, unapologetic yellow. It bulldozed from forty-one point one to forty-one point five like a thing drawing breath. The beat was regular now. Someone on a heart monitor. Someone walking stairs.

“—it’s not gone,” she finished.

She could taste clove and sugar and blood in the back of her mouth and in all of that, salt. The universe did not care that a woman lay on the tile behind the rack. The universe was always doing what it was doing. But in this small room on this high mountain, something else was doing something and Catalina Huamán, who had braided her hair and put a fish on her mug and drunk clove tea because it made her warm, had gone from being a person to being a fact.

Irene’s hand closed on Maya’s shoulder like a clamp. “It will take the carabineros three hours at best,” she said, softly enough that the saint on her fleece might just have heard. “The wind is coming up. The road will be closed. We—”

“We keep the logs,” Maya said. “We touch nothing. We watch. We listen.”

“Yes,” Irene said. She let go. The saint hung by its pin and could not fall.

Outside, on the mountain, the wind began to change direction. The dishes turned their faces like people trying to catch a whisper. Somewhere, where there should not have been any water, a thin, hidden seam of it moved and was very still again. The hum of the room went on.

Maya stood in the doorway of the server cage and realized that up here, where the air stripped you down to basics and machines were the only heat for miles, she was not going to be allowed to be just a hound for broken signals after all. The interference was present and loud and had killed the silence. Whether or not it had killed anything else, the night meant to tell her a story, and like all the best stories, this one had started before she’d arrived. It just had not decided yet how it wanted to end.

Watches stop for lots of reasons. Dust. Moisture. A magnet slipped too close. A shock that knocks the hairspring into a tangle the way bad news knots your gut. Sometimes a watch stops because the person wearing it stops, and sometimes it stops because someone wanted it to look that way.

By ten that morning I had three pocket watches in pieces on my bench, each one a tiny city of brass and steel. The shop smelled like walnut oil, old paper, and the faint metallic sweetness of polish. Outside, Oriole Street was its usual October self: leaves skittering down the gutters, delivery vans nosing into spaces that didn’t exist, the river three blocks away making its big gray sound. Above my door the sign read M. KLINE, WATCHES & REPAIRS, gold leaf and age-darkened varnish. It had belonged to someone else a long time ago. I had taken it and his workbench when he retired, and left the name as it was. The Kline wasn’t for him.

I had the loupe in my eye and a set of tweezers poised over a hairspring when the bell on the door trilled in three nervous notes. I lifted my head. The man who came in wore a messenger bag and had a clipboard he held like a shield.

“Mara Kline?” he asked.

“That’s me,” I said, removing the loupe and slipping it onto its hook. “If you’re here about the grandfather clock in Apt. 4B, I called yesterday. The pendulum’s bent.”

He blinked. “No. I have a delivery.” He fussed with the clipboard. “Sign here. And I need to see ID.”

“What is it?” I asked, taking in the unmarked cardboard box in his other hand. It was small and taped like someone didn’t trust tape.

“Says ‘Horological Device.’ Priority. Keep out of sunlight.” He turned the side toward me to show the caution sticker in black and yellow.

I took the box. It was heavier than it looked and something inside knocked dully against something else when I tilted it. There was no return address, just my name typed in neat capital letters. The tape had been circled with red Sharpie, as if to make certain the message about sunlight didn’t get missed.

“You really do need to sign, ma’am.”

I signed the rectangle he gave me, showed him my ID, and watched through the front windows as he climbed back into his van and left a hiss of exhaust in his wake. The shop felt smaller for a moment after he went, as if the box had stolen volume from the air.

There are rules with packages in my line of work. When an older client sends you a watch you’ve waited two months for, you put the box on the bench and cut the tape carefully because shaky hands often overwrap the green tissue they used twenty years ago. When a clock comes in from an auction house you don’t trust, you open it in the back under the camera in case pieces have gone missing in transit. When an unmarked box shows up with a hazard sticker and your name typed out by a machine, you don’t open it at all—but I’ve never been good with rules that begin with don’t.

I took it to the workbench anyway. The window was showing me slices of river between the buildings beyond the intersection. The water was moving fast from last night’s rain, slate green with white ruffs.

I got a utility knife and slit the tape where someone had made sure it was visible. Layer after layer of bubble wrap sighed under the blade. There was a smell when I freed the thing inside, a cold salt smell that made me think of aluminum docks and damp rope.

It was a diver’s watch. Old. The case was chunky stainless steel, the sort that was built like a hubcap and wore like a handcuff. The crystal was scuffed, the bezel’s black insert faded gray at the edges. The dial was matte, the lume on the indices a toasted almond color that comes from time more than tritium. No brand at the top. That was wrong. Every watch wants you to know whose face you’re looking at. Whoever made this had gone to some trouble to remain nameless.

I turned it over. The case back was brushed steel and engraved with the outline of a fish that was more imagination than species, all knife fins and needle teeth. Someone had added three letters under it with a nail or something like it: J.K. The letters were childish and deep enough to catch a fingernail.

There was a note folded into the bubble wrap, smaller than my palm. KEEP OUT OF SUNLIGHT. That was all it said, block letters like a printed label, as if my messenger had transcribed someone’s voice and nothing more.

I pressed the crown. It didn’t move. Screw-down. Good. I unscrewed it a turn, then two. When it popped I felt it in the bones of my thumb. I started to wind. The watch wanted to run. You can feel resistance through your fingers, the line between hunger and satiety. This one bristled like a cat being stroked in the wrong direction. After twenty winds I stopped and set the time. It started up immediately, second hand be-bopping its way around the dial with a lopsided happiness that told me its balance amplitude was off. It ticked loud.

“Hello, stranger,” I said. I’m not above talking to brass and steel.

Then I took out my case back wrench and fitted the three teeth to the notches. The case back was either cemented by godly torque or hadn’t been off in oceans. I put a leather glove over my left palm to hold the watch and leaned into the wrench until something gave with a sound you don’t hear so much as feel. It opened a quarter turn, then the rest with small scraping noises the way a can of paint does.

Under the back: a rubber gasket that was red, not black like I expected. Red means aftermarket most of the time, or someone trying to see if their arrangement is better than the one intended. There was residue under the lip of the back, like crushed salt or softened crystalline adhesive. The movement was a standard Swiss automatic, stamped on the rotor with a number. The screw heads were correct, the rhodium plating dull, the bridges showing the nicks and small stories all used things have.

I lifted the rotor gently and peeked. It had been worked on recently. A smear line where oil had gone places it shouldn’t, a tiny fiber trapped under one of the pallet bridge screws. I plucked it off with a tweezer and stuck it to a blotting pad. Red. Sewing thread, not watchmaker’s lint.

And then the light hit something wrong.

Beneath the case back, under the movement, someone had tucked a ring of paper coiled like a spring. If I hadn’t opened it over the bench the piece might have fallen into the black hole under my chair where things go to mock me. It was narrow, no more than an eighth of an inch wide, and wound around itself in seven neat turns. A very small ring, a confession slipped where a battery might have gone if there had been one.

“Keep out of sunlight,” I said aloud to the empty shop. The river answered me with a truck’s muffled horn.

I snapped off the bench lamp and pulled the shade on the window until the room was dim. The paper felt delicate and slick between my tweezers, almost waxy. I’ve seen my share of thermal receipts that yellow and go blank if you leave them on a dashboard. This had that same breathless, waiting quality. Heat makes a record. Time erodes it. Whoever sent me this wanted the record to last long enough to be looked at in the right way and no longer.

I have a red lamp I use for gilt work when my eyes need a break from white light. The bulb was an indulgence from an old camera supply place, a little nostalgia to go with a piece of history. I turned it on. The shop shifted to a world where everything was wine-dark and soft.

I eased the coil apart on a piece of black velvet. It opened reluctantly, like a fern. The words were dots. Tiny dots, each one a perfect uniform oval, arranged to make numbers and letters a person could read if they were patient and obstinate.

When I bent my head close, the dots resolved into four columns on a strip no longer than my thumb and a half. The first column had dates in a format no one uses in speech, the way computer logs choose to remember: 10-17, 10-18, 10-19. The second had times: 03:41, 05:10, 06:39. The third said things like LOW -3.8 and HIGH +4.4 and at the bottom SPRING TIDE. The fourth had coordinates you could type into a phone: 42.915, -73.092.

“Tide tables?” I said, because sometimes you have to say obvious things to make them less bizarre.

On the last line, below the rest like a footnote to itself: ROOK ST. BRIDGE.

I said a few other things under my breath that would have made my grandmother frown. The Rook Street Bridge was in all my windows. Not precisely, but you couldn’t be anywhere in this neighborhood without feeling its shadow. It carried six lanes of traffic across the river and it had stolen two blocks of houses from what used to be the waterfront doing so. It was one of the reasons people in this city had arguments about money after third drinks: because bridges cost and because this one had cost more than it should.

The dates were this week.

I set the coil under a crimson glass paperweight to keep it flat without adding heat and turned the lamp off. Sunlight shot like knives under the window shade and I thought of my man with the clipboard, his careful words. Keep out of sunlight. Whoever printed this had thought of dashboard receipts and August and had planned for me. Or not me. For someone like me.

My phone buzzed on the shelf. I looked at the screen. Rojas.

“Hi,” I said, and made my voice light, as if I hadn’t just found a message wound into a stranger’s watch. “Finn. What’s broken?”

“You tell me,” he said. The voices in the background told me he was in the squad room or somewhere tinny and fluorescent. “You in the shop?”

“Always.”

“I’m coming by.”

“When?”

“Now.”

“Okay.” I looked at the coil under the paperweight; it sat there like a living thing waiting for a domed lid.

He hung up without goodbye. That was his style. We had known each other for five years, since the case of the Riverwomen and the watch with the rust that wasn’t rust. He brought me timepieces that had been found on wrists in alleys and in pockets under seats and in puddles under accidents. I told him what time had done to them and sometimes what someone else had done. He thought I was a witch. I told him chemistry was only a religion that courted useful gods.

The bell on the door didn’t ring for another eight minutes. In those eight minutes I unscrewed the bezel from the nameless diver’s watch because it was either glued or it was hiding something. The former would be a nuisance. The latter would be a shock. It turned, grudging, then lifted in a jump that made me say out loud the frown-word I had reserved for my grandmother. Under the bezel, in the ring between the case and where the insert had sat, there was epoxy residue, yes, and there was also a second gasket. Who gaskets a bezel? People who expect to be underwater a lot and people who expect their watch to be thrown in a river and pulled out again.

My hands were steady but they felt like they were doing something a magician would be paid for.

I levered the gasket free and there was a thin metallic sound from inside the case that didn’t belong to gear or spring. A clink like a coin hitting porcelain. I turned the watch and tapped. A sliver of glass slid out and fell into my palm. Not from the crystal; this was greenish, with a bubble in it as if it had been poured quick. There were words on it. A partial: …PHALT & SONS. The font was a city font, a sign painter’s thickness.

I put the sliver on the black velvet next to the coil. The two of them made a pair in the same way a lock and key do, except I didn’t know which was which yet.

When the bell finally chimed in its little waltz, I straightened and slid the nameless watch into my pocket. I’ve helped Finn before in cases where people think they can be clever with a legal warrant. Being asked to consult doesn’t always come with courtesy. If the watch had walked in with him, he could walk it out. If it had walked in with a messenger who had made me sign for it like I was a hospital receiving a heart in a cooler, then it was mine until I decided it wasn’t.

Finn Rojas filled the doorway with discontent. He is taller than he has any right to be in a city built for short hallways and shorter doors, and he carries himself like someone trying to make himself smaller out of habit. His coat was the brown of a sparrow and fit well enough to tell me his promotion had been recent and real. He had a cup of coffee that smelled like the kind you get from a machine that hates you.

“Mara,” he said, and made my name sound like an accusation and a favor both.

“Finn,” I said. “If you drip on my bench I will make you buy me a replacement I can’t afford.”

He looked at the spread of pendant watches, the trays of tiny screws, the loupe lamp with its cyclops eye. “Can’t afford to buy you one,” he said. “So I’ll hold the cup.”

He held onto the coffee with both hands like a supplicant and then put it on the edge of a shelf that had nothing under it but air. I moved it before the gods of gravity could punish his optimism. He watched my hand going and coming and then his eyes moved to the thing under the crimson paperweight because Finn misses nothing and pretends he misses most things.

“What’s this?”

“Paper,” I said. “Flat. Letters.”

He gave me a look that said he could see a deflection at a hundred yards through fog. “I need your help,” he said. “Got a body.”

“I’m sorry,” I said. That much was true. Bodies interest me only in the way they speak in metal and glass. The rest belongs to the living.

“Joel Kantos,” Finn said. “He works—worked—for the city inspector’s office. He drowned.”

“In his kitchen sink?”

“In the river.”

I lifted an eyebrow.

“We pulled him an hour ago from the pilings under the Rook Street Bridge. Guy walking his dog saw something that wasn’t the usual turtle. Kantos’s car was in a lot by Riverside Market with the ticket that says he’d been there all night.”

“You want me to sympathize with the state of his wristwatch.”

“He wasn’t wearing one.”

“But you said—”

“He always wore one,” Finn said. “His wife says he never left the house without it. He told her the day he lost it was the day he wouldn’t be coming back. She says that like it’s a joke he kept telling, like a thing people own to be themselves. Kantos didn’t come home last night. She called it in this morning. She also called his boss.”

“And?”

“And the boss doesn’t want this to be a thing. City has enough things. There’s the new floodwall contract up for a vote. There’s a bunch of engineers on the radio saying if we build the wall the way they want the river will go ten feet to the left and drown Chinatown. There’s a developer with a grin I just want to—” He stopped, because Finn has rules about profanity around me like I’m some kind of auntie. “Point is, we don’t need a city inspector turning up dead. We don’t want a city inspector turning up dead with a note in his pocket that says EEL SONG.”

We looked at each other.

“My shop isn’t bugged,” I said. “Unless your people misplaced a surveillance van and it landed under my floor.”

“You would hear it,” he said. Then he frowned. “Would you? Is that something you can hear?”

“I can hear a watch with two seconds of amplitude running three rooms away if the building isn’t trying to talk to me. But vans? No. Finn. Eel Song?”

“Eels have songs?” he said. “There’s a place down by the docks. Not a place your mother would want you to go.” He rephrased before I could pounce. “Not a place my mother would want me to go. Bar. Real name is The Song. Sign out front is a cartoon eel someone drew on a Sunday twenty years ago and no one took down. People call it Eel Song.”

“Ah,” I said, and thought of the coil under the paperweight and the words I had said when I had read the last line.

“How did you know?” he asked, and I watched the question attach itself to other questions behind his eyes. He doesn’t like to think he’s predictable. He likes even less to think I am.

“Let’s put it in categories,” I said, and used that tone that makes him pretend not to be amused. “You have a dead city inspector who is or is not related to a floodwall bid. He had a habit of wearing a watch. He wasn’t wearing it. His wife is either wrong or he broke his own rule or someone took it. He had a note in his pocket that refers to a place your mother—”

He lifted his eyes to the ceiling.

“—would not want you to go. It could be the place where he had a beer before the river took him. Or a place he had an appointment. Or a place you would like to go later and pretend is work.”

He sighed and the sigh moved a small hair on his forehead like a breeze might.

“You see why I like to talk to you when anyone else would make me want to run my head into the wall,” he said.

“Because I’m kind and perceptive.”

“Because you are a witch.”

“Chemistry and patience,” I said. “Also, I listen. Which is what you pay me in coffee for.” I took a breath. “Finn. What time did you pull him?”

“9:22,” he said, and checked his notebook to be sure. “We think he went in sometime after midnight. He wasn’t bloated.”

“These are the details I didn’t have on my bingo card,” I said, and I meant it humorously but he flinched anyway. The dead do that to us. “Where are his clothes?”

“In our possession. Shoes were off. Wallet missing. Keys in his pants. No phone. We found two quarters and a paper clip.”

“What about his left wrist?”

“What about it?”

“If he wore a watch, there’s often a ghost. Paler skin. Less hair. Or a bruise if someone took it the wrong way.”

Finn opened his notebook. “Paler skin,” he said. “He tans easy, apparently.”

“And bruising?”

“None. Mara.” He leaned forward, remembering he was supposed to be making this official. “You seen anything unusual today?”

“Every day I see something unusual,” I said.

“Mara.”

I looked at my bench. The velvet gleamed under the red lamp even though I had turned it off. The coil waited with the patience of paper. The nameless watch in my pocket ticked against my leg like a small heart that didn’t belong to me.

“I got a delivery,” I said. Truth is a narrow blade. You can cut the right way and leave the fabric whole. “An old diver’s watch. No return address. Someone wanted me to keep it out of sunlight.”

“Why?” he said.

“Thermal paper in the case. Tide tables. Rook Street Bridge.”

I watched the way Finn’s face changed. He went from suspicion to anger to something uglier in half a breath. “You didn’t call me,” he said quietly. “You got something like that and your first phone call isn’t to me.”

“My first phone call was to the person who sent it,” I said. That was a lie. I don’t like lying to Finn, and I seldom do, so when I do it feels like swallowing a watch part. “No number. No name. You were my second call.”

I pulled the coil out from under the paperweight and pushed it across the velvet, a little stage with a small, meticulous prop. He bent his big body over my bench, and for a moment, with the red glass reflecting itself in his eyes, he looked like a man bending over a fire.

“Read it,” I said.

He did. His finger hovered over each line and did not touch anything because somewhere along the way he had decided my rules mattered. When he got to the bottom he swore without sound. He made a noise of disapproval in his throat that belonged to a man older than he was. “Someone wants to tell a story,” he said. “Somebody who thinks we need a map to it.”

“Somebody who thinks you won’t find it without a little help.”

“Somebody who thinks you won’t tell me unless they wrap it in something you want.”

“I want all of it,” I said, before I could stop myself.

We stood in my warm, cramped shop full of watches and silence. Outside, a siren went by at half voice, the way they do when the driver knows it’s not an emergency and the city needs to pretend it is anyway. The river made its glass-mouthed noise. On my wall, a cheap plastic clock shaped like a cat waved its tail with the smug rhythm of something that had seen enough time to know better.

Finn straightened. “Don’t go anywhere,” he said. “And don’t—”

“I won’t eat it,” I said. “I won’t take it out into the sun and hold it up like a transparent church window. I won’t photocopy it or put it in the microwave. I won’t use it to roll cigarettes.”

“People use paper to roll—”

“Not this person.” I went to the door and twisted the deadbolt. The bell made a small sound like a mosquito being reprimanded.

Finn took his coffee off the shelf and left a ring I would sand out later. He turned at the door. “You aren’t telling me everything,” he said.

“I never do.” I smiled. He didn’t. “Finn,” I said, as the door was already opening. “Who made that note on Kantos? About Eel Song. Did his wife mention it?”

He frowned. “No. It was in his front pocket. One line. No ink. It was the kind of paper that turns black when you heat it.”

“Thermal,” I said.

“Yeah.” He looked at the coil on my bench like he wished it would combust. “Why?”

“No reason,” I said, which was another lie. “Hurry up.”

After he left, the shop did a strange thing. It felt like it exhaled. The way a room does when you take a piano out and the corners relax. I put the paperweight back over the coil and the nameless watch on the bench and I let myself think about what I hadn’t told him.

There was an inscription on the inside of the case back, so faint I hadn’t seen it the first time. Not the J.K.—that was on the outside, and it could be Joel Kantos if you were a person who thought everything meant the thing you needed it to. Inside, along the curve where the case back met the thread, someone had scratched with a scribe a phrase in letters a child might have written if the child was very patient and had a magnifier.

EEL SONG. MONDAY. PAY CASH.

I had seen it when I’d gotten the case back off. I hadn’t told Finn because I had wanted it to be mine for six minutes more. Personal impulses are strange. You can love the truth and still tuck a kernel of it in your mouth like candy because you know you’ll have to give it away in a minute and you want to taste it first.

The other thing I hadn’t told him was the thing that made my skin feel like it was a half size too small. When I’d held the watch up to the window shade before turning the bench lamp off, for one silly second I had wanted to see if the lume still had any life in it. Old lume remembers light like old friends remember favors. I had cupped my hand over the dial and then pulled it away and in that curve of shade and red room light the little pips at twelve and six had glowed. They shouldn’t have. Not with that strength. Not unless the watch had been in bright light recently. Not unless someone had been in my shop and had lifted the shade when I was in the back taking a call I had missed without realizing I had missed anything.

I went to the front window and looked out. Oriole Street did its loose afternoon dance: a man with a pocket dog, a woman with a box of pastries she held like a child, a kid on a bicycle that had a front wheel too small for the frame. Across the street was a van that hadn’t been there earlier. No name on its side. It had a ladder bolted to the roof and a dent above the rear wheel. The driver had his hand on the wheel and didn’t move except to lick his thumb and turn a page of whatever he was pretending to read.

When you work with time for a living, you get good at noticing the places it pools. The van had the feel of a bottle left too long on a windowsill. Heat made the glass say what it was.

I took my hand off the window shade so fast the string burned my palm, and I turned the benchtop lamp back on, careful. The coil under the glass was still legible. The watch on the velvet ticked. I set the case back in place without tightening it and wrapped the whole thing quickly in a cloth that had belonged to the man whose name was on my door and then to me.

By the time Finn came back, twenty minutes later with a look that said he had yelled at a superior and had regrets about it, I had made a lot of choices and regretted none of them yet.

He said: “Kantos testified last month in a closed session about bid manipulation. The word bribe may have been used. He was scheduled to meet someone last night. It was not his wife’s favorite bar. You need to come.”

I said: “Let me lock up.”

He said: “What are you putting in your pocket?”

I smiled the kind of smile that has never fooled him. “A watch,” I said. “One of mine.”

He nodded like he was going to let me have that lie for another hour and then use it to strangle me. Outside, the van’s engine turned over, the driver leafed to a new page, and the city’s day took a half step into being night.

Chapter One

On the third floor of the municipal building, between the vending machine that ate singles and the window that never opened again after the winter of 2009, the dispatch room tasted like nickels. Static had a flavor if you sat with it long enough: copper and cotton, a humming band against the teeth. Mara Kincaid had been chewing it for years. She kept the lights dim on the night shift and the radio a notch louder than regulation because she liked to feel the invisible net flex when the city stirred—sirens uncoiling, tires hissing on wet streets, someone somewhere calling for help in a voice that darted like a paper moth around the bare bulb of the job.

The wall above her desk held a frame listing the ten-codes in stenciled letters, though most of them were a lie. No one said 10-13 for weather anymore. No one said 10-98 when they cleared. What they said instead, what they whispered or swore or typed into the notes field when the line went dead, was what Mara wrote on index cards and slipped into the manila box beside her keyboard. Phrases that snagged. Little burrs of panic or oddity that clung to the hem of her brain long after the units went 10-7 and the report filed itself into the dull alphabet of the day shift.

She was alone at the console except for Trip Connelly dozing in his chair with the sports page wilted across his chest, one of his shoes kicked beneath the console. The room’s fluorescent tubes made a high song of their own, an electric whine that rose and fell as the city exhaled the last of Friday night. It was late April and the river had swollen against the old wall that kept downtown from remembering it used to be a marsh. Somewhere a train was dragging its chain through the tunnels beneath the bluff, and the air that came through that once-open window seeped the sweet stink of creosote and mud.

CAD was quiet. Three accidents before midnight, one domestic that had resolved itself into a sullen no, a gas station robbery out on Fletcher with a kid so high he kept forgetting to point the gun. The calls had thinned into noise. Mara lifted her cup, sloshed cold coffee against her lip, and set it back down. She reached for the box without looking and flipped through cards with her thumb. People called differently in the dark; they confessed without meaning to. She had the way children described their world: The door is breathing. The road is asleep. The light around the lady is loud.

She found the one she wanted just as the call light flashed.

911, what's your emergency? Her mouth was already forming the words as her index finger hit the green bar, the motion so practiced she barely felt the button click.

A child's whisper seeped into her ear, thin as fishing line. "Can you hear me?"

"Yes, this is 911. What's your emergency? Where are you?"

A breath. Wallpaper silence on the other end, the sense of someone cupping the phone with two hands, hunched animal small.

"She won't wake up," the child said. It was a boy, or a girl with a boy's husk to the voice, maybe six, maybe eight. The high parts worn down by whispering. "Her hands are humming."

Mara did not look down at the card on her desk or the ballpoint words on it. She kept her voice low and steady. "Okay. Is she breathing? Can you tell if her chest is moving?"

"She won't wake up," he said again, like an answer to a different question.

"All right. Is she on the floor? On a bed? Are you safe right now? Can you tell me your name?"

There was a scrape like the phone had been set against fabric, the world of that room collapsing into scrapings and breaths. A ticking began, faint in the background, metronomic, something mechanical. It was the kind of artifact you got when someone called from a basement, from that half underground air with the water heater clicking to itself.

"There's a door," the child whispered. "It's breathing."

Mara reached without taking her eyes off the monitor and nudged Trip’s foot with her own under the console. He jolted, paper sliding to the floor, blinked at her. She made the hand signal for a live one and jabbed at the caller's number on her screen. No callback capability. Unknown. No ANI. No ten-digit string to hand off to the trace. But ALI flashed a hazy area—the cell tower on Harper and Third had sniffed a signal and thrown it back to them with an error margin a city block wide.

"Okay," she said, and her fingers were already arranging units in the CAD queue with a flicker: 2-A-12, 2-A-21, 3-B-9 for medical. "The door's breathing. Can you see the street outside? Any signs? Any numbers on the walls? The name of your building?"

A small exhalation she almost missed. "It says Crown."

Trip's chair creaked as he reached for his headset, snagged the mic off its hook. "Harper district? Crown? That's that old storage. Nobody uses it anymore."

"2-A-12 and 2-A-21," Mara said into her own mic, the one that made her voice a thin wire through the cruisers' speakers, through the bodycams and the thick vests and the sweat. "Dispatch. Respond code two to Crown Storage, Harper at Third, back entrance on the river side. Caller reports unresponsive female, unknown age. Possible child on scene. Use caution. Building supposed to be secured."

"Copy," a male voice said, the vowels flattened with boredom until she heard the quiver at the ends. "2-A-12 en route."

"2-A-21, copy."

"3-B-9 staged," the EMT chimed, female, crisp and already in the rig.

"Caller," Mara said, going back to the held breath on the other line, "help is on the way, okay? I need you to stay with me. Can you tell me if the lady is cold? Is she cold to the touch?"

"She's not cold," the child said, fiercely, and then, as if drained by that burst, softer: "She's supposed to be cold?"

"You're doing great," Mara said. "Can you tell me your name?"

Silence, then: "He says not to tell."

"Who is he?"

"He says he's fixing it now."

Her eyes flicked from the call time—fifty-six seconds, then one minute twelve—to the monitor where the nearest units’ little triangles puppeted across the digital map like migrants, their blue fields overlapping as they rounded the old luggage factory. She thought of the index card in her fingers, the one she'd slid from the box without looking because her fingers had known it by feel: Grace Pelley, August 5, 1999, 03:28 a.m.—Caller: male child. Phrases: door is breathing; hands are humming; he says not to tell.

"Listen to me," Mara said. "Is he in the room with you? Are you safe?"

The line crackled. Something metallic clinked, waiting to be told its next story. The ticking in the background had grown louder. It had a tinny, patient quality that stirred an old unease behind her ribs. Picture a metronome on a piano in a room with no piano, counting out a heartbeat for an instrument long gone.

"Can you tell me how old you are? Can you count to ten for me? One. Two."

The child took a breath and started to count, haltingly, like he did not want to be heard. He got to five. The call cut out.

There is a flavor to a disconnected line, too: the slick aftertaste of loss. Mara dropped her eyes, watched the seconds freeze, watched the unknown number turn into a row of dashes. She opened her mouth to rewind the recording and save it for the case file, felt something tug in her hand. The index card.

Trip’s voice came low across the desk. "Prank."

She looked at the card. The handwriting was ten years and a different life old, her letters smaller then, the loops careful as if she could contain the jitter in her own body by caging words. She had written at the bottom, in that old hand, Found later: nothing. No child. Blood on lint trap in utility room. Partial prints. No matches.

"2-A-12, 2-A-21," she said into the mic. "Caller disconnected. Last known was interior. Use caution on entry. Stage med until secure. Break. 2-A-12, be advised I have similar call on file from 1999 at this location. Unknown if related."

"1999?" The younger voice wavered on the repeat, the way rookies do when history reaches up and sets a cold hand on their neck. "That's before I was born, Dispatch."

"Copy," Mara said. "I'm old." She heard the brittle humor in her own throat and smoothed it with breath. "Alarm company isn't showing any opens. Crown is supposed to be empty."

At the edge of her mind, the metronome. The boy's whisper. He says not to tell. The thing about working nights is that memory is worse in the dark, or better. You never knew which until it had done its work.

She pulled up the old file, her fingers grateful for something they could do that wasn't thinking. The system groaned open the archived report, one of the gray ones with the format changed three administrators ago. It was spare to the point of insult. Someone back then had typed what they thought would matter to someone later: Date. Time. Type of call. Units dispatched. Location. It did not capture the singing in a child's voice when he said the door was breathing, or the smell the officers wrote down in a casual aside that kept her awake for a week—like a coin struck against stone, like rain hitting dust.

Back then, there had been a fire in the next building over. Back then, the night sergeant had thought the call came from a pay phone and they had chased echoes through stairwells until dawn. No one had sealed the scene. No one had believed there had been a scene to seal. She had been a junior then, lateral from the paper, and she had made clippings of the version of the world that got published and tucked the rest into a shoebox at the back of her closet. She had not known the river could keep so much.

"2-A-12 is 97," the radio said. On scene. The unit's voice was inside the tightness of his vest, a pitch that told her he could feel his heart beating the number on his badge. "Show us with the building."

"Copy, 2-A-12. 2-A-21, status?"

"Right behind you."

It is a peculiar sensation, hearing the door you cannot see open. The acoustics of old buildings made it worse. Her headset offered her the world as a set of earbuds might offer a symphony, bloated with frequencies that were not made for human wood. She heard, through breath and fabric and the oceanic rush of blood being pushed around, the long moan as someone pressed an iron handle that had not been touched in a decade. The hush that comes after is not quiet. It is full of choices.

"Dispatch," 2-A-12 said, voice low. "You got any intel about the layout on this place?"

"Crown Storage was used by tax records until oh-eight," Mara said. Her cursor flew. "Three-story, brick, open floors, interior office cubicles partitioned on the first two. Reports of transient occupancy but no recent calls. South side faces the river. Watch the stairwells. Old freight elevator is inoperable."

"Copy. 21, watch your left."

White noise rolled back, like someone had turned toward a wall eat with mold and mouse bones. Then: "Jesus," 2-A-21 said, almost kindly, as if it was a greeting he did not want to offer to what he saw. "What is that?"

"What do you have?" Trip asked, leaning forward. His knuckles were pale where they clamped his mic stand.

"A—" The younger voice stopped. When it came back, it was thinner. "It's a sneaker. Little red one. Left foot. Brand new."

Mara did not look at the card again. She tried to ground herself in facts as if they would tether her body to the chair. She pulled the property record for the building owner. She opened Google and street-viewed a truck captured in brilliant summer freeze ten years ago; two kids in the cab with their tongues out at the camera. It was a way to resist being dragged forward into the room where there would be a shoe and nothing else.

"Dispatch," 2-A-12 said. "We got—hold up. Hear that?"

The room breathed into her ears in a soundless way. Then she heard it, too, that patient tick, not like a clock hung right but like a thing counting down a long habit. Tick. Tick. Tick. She watched Trip’s eyes flick to her and back to the console. The old report did not mention a ticking.

"Follow it," Mara said, because the job is to send people into rooms because someone is inside and cannot call again. "No obvious hazards?"

"Smells like river," the younger one said, a reflex like the line about cats smelling like cat. "What is—"

"Door's shut on the office," 2-A-12 cut in. "Sign says Manager. Lock's busted. Moving to breach."

"Do it," Mara said. "Medical, hold."

The tick got louder. It pressed against her wrist bones. She had a sense, almost, of standing at the edge of something that had been smooth and was not smooth anymore. She could see a boy's mouth drop open into the phone as if he'd found a new way to arrange the air. Everyone keeps in their throat a jar of old silences you can break in case of emergency. She had broken hers once. It had not brought anyone back.

There was the blunt exhale of boots and wood, a fistful of sound. Then her headset filled with a confusion she recognized like déjà vu—the stunned moment when reality tilted fangs-out.

"Dispatch," 2-A-12 said. The word came out like he had been holding it under water. "We have— I don't know how to—"

If there had been a body, Mara thought in the open space where thoughts go to get dressed, he'd have said a body. He'd said body before, and his voice had not done that. He had seen a lot of bodies.

"2-A-12," she said. "Say again."

"It's a setup," he said. "It's—someone wanted us to find this."

"What is it?" Trip was on his feet, but he did not move closer, as if distance might discourage what was coming.

"A phone," the younger one said, strangled. "Like an old one. Rotary. It's on the desk. And there's— Jesus. There's a cassette recorder. The line is— It's rigged through the cell."

The ticking was a machine. That was worse.

"Don't touch it," Mara said.

Too late, the click of curiosity. The sound of the younger one's hand on chrome and plastic. The walls held their breath. The phone spoke.

"Can you hear me?"

It was the voice she'd heard sixty-eight seconds ago, a child's whisper freighted with the idea of the child's chest heaving and falling, a voice so present she could see vapor on cold air. It was the voice she'd transcribed in ballpoint ink twelve years prior and pushed into a box because the act of writing had tricked her into thinking the thing had been contained. The voice moved through time and settled in 2-A-21's mic like a bird on a wire.

"Please send help," the voice said. "Her hands are humming."

Trip whispered, "Jesus God."

The tape clicked. The metronome ticked. 2-A-12 swore softly, a sound barely in the world.

"Dispatch," he said, and the fear in his throat was grief-shaped, slow and hard. "Someone wanted us to hear this."

Mara made herself breathe in and out, as if oxygen were a spell. "Secure the room. Get me a photo of the setup. Watch for any—"

"There's a note," the younger one said. Paper rustled. "On the desk. It has— It's got your name on it."

Every muscle in Mara's neck folded into a knot. Trip stared at her not like he was seeing her for the first time but like he was trying to place where he knew her from in the story he had been telling himself about the world.

"Read it," she said.

"'Hear it again, Kincaid? Ask the river what it keeps. -H.'"

Mara did not know anyone who signed with an initial H on purpose, with its fat hook, its ladder to nowhere. She thought of the man’s voice in her earliest days at the paper, the one who had called after she ran a piece on the 1999 case. He had called twice from a pay phone on Butler, told her she was asking the wrong questions and then named the right ones and hung up before she could turn a yes into a thank you.
