She had never known if he had been trying to help or to watch her run.

"2-A-12," she said. "Do not touch anything else. Back out and hold at the door. Let's get CSU rolling. Medical can clear."

She hit buttons. The room filled with the rote good of procedure: codes translated into action, cars pointed like knives at a place where mystery had made itself a nest. On another channel, a man was complaining about his neighbor's dog. Somewhere out on Fletcher a drunk was singing to a clerk who did not want to be sung to. The city did not care that something had looped across a dozen years to lay itself at her feet like a gift she had not wanted, had not asked for, had trained herself very carefully not to imagine.

Trip slid his headset off one ear. "You think this is the same—"

"I think someone is playing games," Mara said. She put the card back in the box, careful, the way you lay a feather against bone. She closed the lid.

At the edge of her vision the river was a darker darkness beyond the glass. To get here it had passed under the railroad and along the backs of failing buildings with rusted fire escapes and windows full of chairs. It had accepted what the city gave it because that is what rivers do. Men thrown down the embankment. Bottles with burnt letters. A red left sneaker that had never been claimed.

The line that had carried the boy's whisper shone blank on her screen. The time since disconnect ticked up: eight minutes thirty-two, nine minutes. The tape in the office would be rewound. Someone would photograph the curled end of it like a tongue. They would bag the phone like an animal and label it and carry it with latex hands across the threshold of the room where nothing had happened, officially, in 1999.

"Dispatch," 2-A-12 said, quiet. "You hear that?"

She listened. Beyond the metronome, beyond the handling, beyond the breathing of the men in the room, a voice flared and went out again, a moth's wing. It seemed to come from the same tape, the same loop, but it had learned a new trick in the years since it had last been recorded. It had learned a name.

"Mara," the child's voice said, so distinctly that Trip's mouth fell open. "Mara, he's fixing it now."

The rest was ticking. The rest was river.

She swallowed. "Hold the room," she said again, though no one had moved. "Nobody in or out."

When she took off her headset for the half second it took to pull her hair out from under the band and slide it back on, the room became her body—the fluttering little hurt of her pulse in her neck, the unshakable sense that she had been here before. She had trained herself not to imagine the end of calls because imagination is where terror germinates. But there are some seeds you cannot keep from sprouting. The line tasted like nickels. The city rolled in its sleep. The river kept what it kept. And someone, somewhere, was winding a tape.

Chapter One

The dead never stop talking. They clatter. They whisper in paper fibers and thread. They slide along conveyors and bump into one another by the thousands, ink rubbing ink until every name is a smudge of someone else’s life. The Mail Recovery Center breathes that noise the way a person once breathed smoke, without thinking. If you spend enough years inside, you hear it even in your sleep.

Mara Lowe wrapped her palm around a mug that had forgotten coffee two hours ago and watched a gray tub of orphans come up the belt toward her. Padded envelopes slept against shoeboxes. A calendar curl peeped between two battered book mailers: March, a watercolor of aspen leaves. March had been October once and then June; time inside the MRC was always off, like the last station on a radio dial when you’re driving through the hills.

“New gaylord on lane three,” Kenya called over the belt’s roar. Her safety colors flashed when she turned, a neon safety vest lit up like a tropical fish under office fluorescents. She eased a forklift into a row of cardboard tubs chest-high and strapped—the gaylords—and settled one onto the rollers. “Be kind,” she said. “It’s a Friday.”

“Any other way,” Mara said, and managed a smile.

Lane three fed the rescue table, which meant anything on it had resisted every ordinary attempt at delivery. No such address. No such number. Recipient moved. No forwarding address. Postage paid with a chalky foreign stamp no reader had ever seen and no machine could approve. Sometimes what made a letter die was a human thing—a cursive that started brave and slumped into panic, a return address smeared because somebody cried into it, an envelope lined with glitter that took a cheap printer apart one grain at a time.

Mara pried loose the tape on the first carton as the belt sluiced past. She worked with a practiced gentleness. Knife out, blade dulled against the tape’s grit. Tape peeled back, noise of a sigh as the cardboard gave. People thought the biggest federal building in Atlanta stored secrets in vaults. Here they were stored between an old board game and a set of titanium cookware that never made it to the registry and a thousand birthday cards thinking their little confetti balloons were a unique idea. The dead letter office, the old-timers had called it, though here it was the MRC, corporate and impersonal. But the old name fit better. Dead things had rules. You didn’t look them in the eyes. You didn’t invite them in. And when they came, they came heavy.

She set aside a small box with a customs label she’d need to scan and popped open a padded envelope that crinkled like straw. Inside was a single baby sock the size of her thumb, hand-knit, pale blue. It had slipped out of its pair somewhere along a carousel and found its way, as everything here did eventually, to this limbo.

“Lowe,” Henry said from the next station, dragging out her name like a vowel changed at Ellis Island. Henry’s hair was the color of printer toner, prematurely gray, and he wore it clipped neat. He’d come here when the Airline closed and stayed because someone needed to translate addresses written in storms. “You doing the auctions next month? My cousin’s husband is looking for a big TV.”

“I try not to look at auction pallets,” Mara said. The MRC auctioned what never got claimed after a statutory period. There were entire pallets of unpaired shoes, new and unwalked, that left people on the floor wondering how all those lefts and rights were drifting alone through American life. There were urns that no one called about and never went to auction. Henry said the ghosts stayed in them and watched you pass.

Kenya texted something and laughed under her breath. “You two need water,” she said. “It should be illegal to be this dry this early.”

“It’s August,” Henry said. “It’s legal to be dry.”

The ventilation shook with the beat of a plane taking off from somewhere else. There’d been talk the past month about reservoirs dropping, the drought. National news cameras loved cracked earth and white fish bones. Caledonia had been on the news the other night, a lake an hour north exposing its own past. The reporters had stood on a wrinkled shore and introduced the world to a church steeple’s point and the tops of old sycamores that had once been drowned for electricity and a promise. The skeleton of the town looked surprised to be called upon again. Mara had changed the channel.

The next tub came and she caught it as if it could bruise. An old-style manila parcel rode the front, not quite parcel-post brown, not quite white. It didn’t belong and somehow that was the first thing she loved about it. She set it on her table. The corded twine around it was actual twine, not tape. Someone had used a fountain pen. The address on the front read, in a slow careful hand: To Whom It May Concern.

Her scalp prickled. No return address. Postage was a grid of Elvis Forever stamps that would not cover a newspaper, let alone whatever this weighed, and yet there was a faint smudge where a metered print might have been. She tilted it and the light caught a canceled bar code, half torn off, as if someone had cut a label away. There was an orange NIXIE label stuck to one corner: ATTEMPTED—NOT KNOWN / UNABLE TO FORWARD. The sort code on it said 30647. Habersham County. She didn’t have to look it up. She could hear the way that part of Georgia said its own vowels, mouth loosened by heat.

Someone had written, in a different pen, small and angry, along one edge: DELIVER TO THEM ALL. I’M SORRY.

She heard Henry’s voice before he spoke, the way you hear a chord you’ve been expecting. “That one’s got old bones,” he said, peering over.

Mara slid it into the open queue. “Old, but it came through last night,” she said, and forced her own voice to steady. The metering smudge was pale as breath. “You see the sort code? Twenty-eighty-seven. Caledonia Branch.”

Henry made a face. “Closed ten years,” he said. “They still have ghosts cancelling at closed windows. That’s a new one.”

He meant it as a joke. The Caledonia branch had closed when everything consolidating north of the perimeter had closed. She’d stood outside those glass doors once and looked at her own reflection against posters of winter packaging tips and a paper snowflake someone had stuck to the interior glass. She’d watched red clay grind into sidewalk seams in slow motion for a whole summer. She had told herself she would always be moving away, never toward. You could live your life like that if you kept your eyes down. If you were careful. If the dead let you.

Kenya fussed with a three-pound stack of mis-sorts behind her. “Y’all seeing this?” she said, and lifted up a bubble mailer that someone had addressed in gold glitter. “If I die of glitter, I want the headline to read Worker Did Not Sweat—She Sparkled.”

Mara breathed, and put the manila parcel to her left, where things waited until the sting left her fingers. She worked three more tubs the way you might work rosary beads, deliberately and with the same motion over and over until the mechanical steadied the unsayable. She noted a handwritten wedding invitation addressed to an apartment that didn’t exist and a bank document with a return address that had been a furniture store ten years ago. People sent faith through the postal service and paper was not dead because there were things you could not text, not properly. I’m sorry. I love you. I didn’t mean it. He’s gone. Those wanted a stamp and a prayer.

Finally there was nothing else to load her hands with; the manila parcel was a weight she could feel all the way up her arm. She moved it to the center of the table. Protocol first. Photograph the exterior with her station’s tablet. Tag it with the NIS identifier. Note visible data: weight, dimensions, the Elvis stamps. The words in the corner. Her breath stuttered when she typed DELIVER TO THEM ALL. I’M SORRY. It looked like shouting, even small on the screen. It looked like a man turning around and finally telling the truth.

She cracked the knot in the twine. The knot was a half-hitch that a person who’d grown up near water would tie and untie without looking. The paper peeled back softly, old envelopes making that dry whisper that visits you sometimes when you close your eyes. The smell inside was not the mold of a basement. It was lake water dried on denim. It was faint machinery oil. It was smoke, the kind of smoke that lives in paneling after a fire’s long gone.

Inside the parcel were letters bound with a strip of faded blue cloth. On top lay a motel key fob, green plastic, stamped with EBBSIDE MOTOR COURT 17. The number was white paint flaking off. The ring held a brass key worn smooth at the teeth. A receipt folded underneath bore the motel’s logo in cheap ink and a date stamp in last night’s date. Check-in 10:44 P.M. Name scrawled across the register in a hand grown used to signing lines: J. Kline.

The world went soundless. It was always loud in here. It was like that moment in a storm when the rain stops for a breath and everything on earth realizes it’s been holding its shoulders tight.

“Mara?” Henry said softly.

She stared at the key fob until her eyes made it blur, then she reached for the letters. The blue strip untied itself in her hands like the parcel wanted out. There were eight envelopes in the stack, all addressed by the same careful hand. One read Mrs. Portia Ames, 432 Ridgeside Lane, Caledonia GA 30647. Another: Deputy Harlan Fitch, Caledonia Sheriff’s Office. One with a Fayetteville address Mrs. Donna Lowe, in a looping, gentler script. Her mother. The envelope to her mother had never been sealed; the flap was loose as a sigh. Mara touched the edge with a finger that trembled and went cold. The fourth envelope said MARA LOWE in block letters a stranger had used to keep from breaking. He had added c/o MAIL RECOVERY CENTER, 6029 Fulton Industrial Blvd., Atlanta, GA 30336.

It wasn’t possible. She worked the address into the MRC every day and had never seen it written in someone else’s hand.

She set the letters down, all but the one with her name. She slid that one clear. There were rules about reading the contents of mail. The work had strict protocols around opening a parcel only to discover enough information to reroute it. You did not satisfy your own curiosity. Mara told herself she would open just enough to confirm where to send. Confirm the address. There were eight recipients. She could locate at least five. She could walk her mother’s out to her front stoop herself and slide it under the mat if she had to.

She slid her thumb beneath the glued edge. It was sealed in a mean way, two strips of tape crossing the flap like a bandage. She cut one strip with the blade from her table and pried the other. Inside there were three sheets of thin paper, the good kind old people buy and lawyers use, and a photograph. She saw the photograph first because light found it. It was a print with a white border gone cream with the years. There was a dock. There were six kids on that dock, summer-brown and not looking at the camera. One boy’s arm was up as if to wave someone over. A girl had her hair in two glistening ropes, water darkening their ends. The boy farthest out was all knees and grin. And the girl in the very middle squinted into the sun with an expression that said she had not yet learned to pose. She had a scar across one knuckle where a metal gate had slammed years before. Mara had never seen that picture in her life and she knew exactly where and when it had been taken the way you know the underside of your own hand.

Caledonia, August 2004. The dock at the old camp when the lake was new. The boy with all knees and grin: Jesse Kline.

On the back of the photograph, in the small precise hand of the letter-writer, there was a single line: For the ones who stood on the dock.

Her body did a thing it remembered from when she was fifteen—hungry and wanting to run and unable to decide which. The air tasted like pennies. She placed the photo down with great care, as if any rumple or fingerprint might spill whatever future was perched on it.

She slid the letter out. It was not long.

To the ones who stood on the dock,

I have written this wrong in my head for twenty years. I kept trying to start with the weather. It was hot. The kind of heat that makes you mean. But we were mean before that and hot makes no excuse. I have told myself the lake took him. That sounds like an act of God and it lets a man sleep easier. The lake took all of it, the church and the white oaks and that red clay road and your small stupid hopes. We called it progress and people talked about electricity and jobs. Then we built docks and boats and we floated over the steeple and we thought we were some kind of kings.

Here is the truth. We stood there and watched him go. One of us held the light and one of us didn’t say anything and one of us laughed. The water was black and the bulb in the boathouse had burned down to a filament and I turned the light away because I thought that would teach him and it did. I am not asking you to forgive me. I am asking you to meet me where the water used to be and hear me say it with my mouth.

Tonight, nine o’clock, spillway steps. Bring a light.

I’m sorry.

J. K.

Mara held the paper and every version of herself came to sit in a ring around her. The one who’d left Caledonia with all the doors open and none of them shut. The one who had tried to be so quiet that bad things would walk around her instead of through her. The one who knew how to read a story inside someone’s handwriting and realized all at once that this was not a prank, not one of Henry’s jokes, not a botched reunion invitation, not the wrong address that would belong to some other Mara Lowe if she just squinted long enough at the truth.

The spillway steps. She could see them in her mind’s eye not as television had shown them, cracked and exposed, but as the day the earthmovers had stopped and the water had first swelled around the poured concrete like greeting a stranger too close. The steps that went down under, like a hymn whose verses you never got to the end of because they drowned.

“You good?” Kenya asked, quick as a hummingbird, catching that tilt of the world around Mara the way good people do.

“Fine,” Mara said. The word husked itself dry. She set the letter gently back inside its envelope and pressed the flap flat even though it had been cut open. She put the photograph on top because she didn’t know where else to put it.

“Need to stretch your back?” Henry asked, more gently yet, which told her her face was doing something she was not aware of.

Her mother’s name on the second envelope was a spear through two decades. Mara slid it free with two fingers as if it had heat to it. The flap was not sealed. The first line was the same: To the ones who stood on the dock. It was the same letter word for word in the words she let her eyes jump over.

The other envelopes had their own names—Portia Ames, who had run cabins and rules with an iron voice that kids obeyed because they knew she loved them; Harlan Fitch, who had placed a heavy grown hand on a narrow adolescent shoulder and said, “He’s a good swimmer, we’ll find him”; a name Mara did not know, Beatrice Hall; another name she knew too well and could not look at long enough to keep in her head, because knowing it and not saying it was the only compromise she had ever made that worked. Each addressed in a hand that had looked up addresses and written them with care enough to get all nine digits of the zip code right. A man who had not slept, Mara thought. A man thinking of the right words.

She set the envelopes aside and picked up the motel receipt. EBBSIDE MOTOR COURT, GA 30647, the street address a remnant of one of those motor courts that the interstate killed and then some angler resurrected out of cheap paneling. The phone number was local. Someone had stuck their gum under the register line. J. Kline had paid cash. The stale-sweet stink of old smoke came up from the paper as if that alone could carry a person back to a room done up in wood paneling with those small soaps that smell like powder and loss and maybe a Gideon Bible in the drawer that hurt your hand when you opened it because the wood had swollen and stuck. He would be there. If she called now, the front desk would tell her if the room was still his or if he’d checked out and walked to the spillway like a man going toward his own verdict.

Protocol said: photograph interior, reseal the parcel, route it to Advanced Research for address verification and dispatch. Protocol did not say: hold a piece of your past dissolving at the edges like sugar and decide whether to take your lunch break in the hallway and call a small motel to ask for a name that has not been said in your house for twenty years.

Mara slid the motel receipt into the crook of the letter and the photo on top. She typed the phone number into the station’s tablet and hit call. The hum in the ductwork pressed down as if to listen.

Two rings. Three. Four. A fifth that caught and dragged at the end the way old phones do when the line heats up in August.

“Ebbside,” a woman said, and you could hear the cigarette between her teeth and the radio somewhere behind her playing a station that still did commercials for tractors. “Front desk.”

“Hi,” Mara said. Her voice did a thing like it’d been folded and unfolded all its life. “This is a strange question. Did a guest named J. Kline check in last night?”

“We don’t give out—” the woman said, a reflex that snapped and then softened. “Yeah, he’s here,” she said, furtive-crisp. “Already went out once this morning and came back. You family? He told me maybe some folk would call.”

Mara made her mouth remember how to work. “Maybe,” she said, and then despised herself for choosing the smallest possible word. She took a breath. “Will you tell him Mara called? Mara Lowe. And—” She heard the file-scrape of a Bic lighter. The woman had set the phone down on the desk, called across the lobby to a shadow. The radio sang about beer.

“You’re in luck,” the woman said. Her voice was close again. “He’s right here, sugar. You want me to—”

“No,” Mara said, fast, and did not know the person who had said it. Her free hand went around the edge of her table until her knuckles went white. She could see the underside of the dock boards in the photograph, the way a line of shadow fell across the boy’s shoulder who was about to become missing. “No,” she said again, and then, because that was not enough to keep the world inside its lines, “Tell him… we got it. Tell him we got the letters.”

There was a pause, a length of breath that could have included a hundred words.

“All right,” the woman said, and something in her tone said she’d heard the underwater in Mara’s voice and would act accordingly. “You can call back if you… we’re here.”

Mara disconnected and set the tablet down as carefully as she would have placed a crystal on a shelf.

“You okay?” Kenya asked again, softer.

“I have to—” Mara looked at the stack of boy’s clothing she’d been about to catalogue, at a bubble mailer that, for all she knew, contained ashes. She looked at the clock and then at the door and then at the photograph again. Her own young face had not known the camera would take it or that it would someday travel in a box to a federal facility and climb into the light and say her name aloud.

“I have to step out,” she said. “Air.”

Kenya nodded like a queen signing a stay of execution. “Take fifteen,” she said. “We’ll cover.”

Outside, the heat hit her like a sentence. It was the kind of August that makes a sound. The air over the asphalt shimmered and trucks idled in long lines, and the concrete steps held heat from back when the sun had first looked at them that morning and said: you’ll be mine today.

She stood under the loading dock’s lip and watched a swallow bring a thread into a nest it had made in a light fixture that no longer worked. There was a part of her that had never left the spillway. That girl had stood on concrete and learned a lesson about water that felt like a lesson about sin, and she had considered leaving town the same way water leaves a place when a drought comes—bit by bit, without anyone noticing until the boat sat on the lake bed like a stranded bull and the church steeple pointed its finger at the sky in a sing-songy accusation.

Her phone buzzed in her pocket, her own, not the station tablet. A local number she didn’t recognize lit the screen. For an absurd breath she thought: he will not call me. He had written when writing took more work than a call. He had mailed something old-fashioned and difficult into the world because talking requires you be moved by air and you cannot pretend you did not say a thing you said with your mouth.

She let it go to voicemail.

When the call clicked away and silence came back, she wouldn’t have been able to say what she had expected it to sound like. The dead, she thought, aren’t quiet; they aren’t even gone. They line up in tubs. They wait their turn on rollers. They arrive tied up with blue cloth. They put both their hands out and say: bring a light.

She looked down at her hands. They were steady. She looked back through the glass at Henry and Kenya and the blur of same. She thought about her mother’s porch, where a hummingbird came at four o’clock the way it did every day, and how in Fay it was always two degrees cooler and felt like forgiveness. She thought about the steps of the spillway and nine o’clock and every scrap of courage she had managed to save in a jam jar someplace.

On her way back in, she stopped at the dispenser, pulled a fresh roll of clear tape, and tucked it into her apron. She would reseal the parcel the way a person closes a wound that needs to open again soon so it can be cleaned. She would route the letters to their proper lives. She would, she told the versions of herself sitting around her and judging, break as few rules as possible.

The belt took up its chant as she returned to the station. The Elvis stamps stared back, black-eyed. The orange NIXIE label glared like a warning. She slid her hand over the photograph once, not touching, a hovering as if blessing. Then she breathed, lifted her blade, and got back to work.

Chapter One

The first obituary arrived before the death.

It appeared in my queue at 9:14 on a Thursday morning, sandwiched between a florist’s ad correction and a request from a grandson who wanted to add the phrase “She loved fiercely, never measured” to his grandmother’s notice for an extra fifteen dollars. The subject line was the usual perfect blandness—Obit Submission—no bells or sirens attached. I clicked expecting another life boiled to three paragraphs and a list of surviving cousins. Instead, someone had written:

Eleanor Hart, who believed in the sanctity of ordinary time, died Friday at her kitchen table, her teacup nested inside her saucer, a notebook open to a list of tomatoes she meant to plant. She was eighty-eight.

It wasn’t the poetry that stopped me. We get attempts, now and then—nephews with MFA degrees, uncles who parse their grief with adverbs. No, it was the date. Friday. Tomorrow. Today was Thursday.

The newsroom at the Ledger is forever suspended between apology and emergency: buzzing fluorescent lights, a printer that coughs like a sick dog, coffee that tastes like it’s been poured through a pencil. We still sit in pods like we’re on a sitcom about journalists—my desk with its teetering stacks, Len’s crime sponge to my left, empty chairs where features used to be, the back half of the room now a wasteland of unplugged monitors and coiled extension cords. The obituary desk, if that’s what you want to call my two-foot-square kingdom, is a rectangle of particleboard softened by years and elbows.

“Something good?” Len called without looking. His glasses were on top of his head and his eyes leaned permanently forward, even in rest. He spent years staring around corners.

“Define good,” I said. I was still reading.

We keep two kinds of obituaries at the Ledger. The ones people pay for—“funeral notices,” the kind you stick in the freezer with the casserole from a neighbor’s church—and “news obits,” which we reserve for judges, philanthropists, the man who built the light-rail bridge. Every so often a hundred-year-old teacher dies, and we give her a headline because we like the symmetry. I try to be kind to all of them. Someone once told me obituaries are love letters written by the living and I stole it, whole, because it keeps me from turning into a clerk.

This one wasn’t formatted like a paid notice. It had too much air in it. No boilerplate. No funeral home contact. And it didn’t arrive through our submission form. The metadata field was blank.

I read the second paragraph.

Ms. Hart came up in a generation that understood thrift as art. Her daughters remember the small salts of her life: the blackbirds she fed in winter, the cardboard she laid under the beds to hush the radiators, the way she sharpened pencils to tiny spears and kept them in a ceramic cup shaped like a lemon. She made things last. Her husband did not. He died in 1989 of a quiet heart.

There was a turn of phrase in there—quiet heart—that made me think of someone I used to read when I was young and believed newspapers were the opposite of hunger. I didn’t have time to dig. I scrolled to the end, breath caught in my throat. There was a line break and then:

She is survived by her daughters, Anna and May, two grandsons, and a hydrangea bush planted in 1964 that still blooms blue every June. Her mailbox holds three circulars she will never read and, as of 10 a.m. Friday, a letter she was brave to write.

I checked the time again: 9:15, now 9:17. A smear of light on my screen. I read the first line again: died Friday. Which would be tomorrow.

“Sloane,” I said to no one and everyone. “I need Sloane.”

“Editor’s out,” Julia from metro said, not without sympathy. She had mastered the small cadence of newsroom absence. “Budget meeting. The one with the CFO who smiles with his teeth.”

I leaned back and let the chair squeal. The photographs of people I didn’t know in frames I never dusted watched me back. In print above my desk were words I’d taped there months ago, my attempt at a thesis: Obits are the only stories guaranteed a reader.

“Okay, calm,” I told myself, which is what people who aren’t calm say. I opened the database and keyed in E-H-A-R-T. We keep a sprawl of advance obituaries—half-formed drafts on prominent locals that can be quickened with a date in a pinch. It’s not morbid; it’s a girded thing. I’m the one responsible for the rust on them. I’ve polished judges and philanthropists and a historian who, last I checked, still took his black Lab for a three-mile walk every morning. But we don’t have advances on eighty-eight-year-old women with lemon-shaped pencil cups.

The database returned nothing. I searched Google. No Eleanor Hart I could quickly tie to our city. I called down the list of funeral homes to see if any had a prearrangement on file for her. The youngest director at Wilcox & Sons, who has a voice like a towel rung out, said no. The others said no or let it ring.

I reread the address that wasn’t there and the funeral date that wasn’t scheduled and the phone number that didn’t exist. Then I called the one source always willing to take my calls: my mother.

“Ma,” I said, because I hadn’t been thirty-two in her mind for very long. “Do we know an Eleanor Hart?”

She thought for a beat. I imagined her in the kitchen of the apartment we’d moved to after my father discovered boats were better at leaving than docked, her hair wet, a dish towel slung over her shoulder like a sash. “No, honey. Should we?”

“No. I mean, maybe. Just… never mind. I’ll call you later.”

“What’s wrong?”

“Work thing,” I said, and invented, “Somebody wrote an obituary in the future.”

“The future,” she repeated, like a warning. “Watch your verbs.”

“I love you,” I said, and hung up before she could offer proof that the past is the only thing that behaves.

At 9:43, because I am a person who likes the path between points, I tried a new plan. I emailed the newsroom alias with the text and the subject line: Anyone know her? Sometimes the city is small when you need it to be. Julia’s reply pinged three minutes later: Nothing on voter rolls. Len’s reply: Hart as in Hart Farm? I called the city assessor, asked if anyone by that name owned property. The answer was ten seconds of keyboard taps and then a flat: nope.

At 10:05, a courier in the lobby buzzed up.

“Obituary desk,” the security guard’s voice crackled over the intercom, which meant the second floor, which meant me.

I met him halfway down the stairs because the elevator in our building is erratic and because I like to meet what’s coming. The courier was twenty, maybe, with a skateboard tucked under one arm and a manila envelope in the other. The envelope was thick and old, the kind of paper that makes you think of stamp collectors and letters that smell like cedar.

“This is for you,” he said, and even though I didn’t know him, I wanted to ask if it had occurred to him to look inside. He wouldn’t have. Courier ethics, another economy of secrets.

“Who sent it?”

He shrugged, flipped his skateboard to the ground with a practiced thunk, and rolled toward daylight.

Back at my desk, I slid a finger under the flap because my letter opener was buried in pens. Inside were five sheets of onion-skin paper, thin enough to lift light, with text typed in black ink. Typed, the old way. I know the way type looks when it’s not a font. I keep a drawer of proofs from the days when news was rearranged by hand, and this had the nicks and swagger of steel arms meeting paper, the imperfect e with a bit of its top shaved off, the slightly raised y. It smelled like library stacks. An undercurrent of dust and glue.

I dropped into my chair and read.

The first sheet was Eleanor Hart. The same text from the phantom email, only the margins cleaner here, the words more elegant somehow when your eyes have to do the work of holding them up.

The second:

Judge Malcolm Prescott, who could stare a man into a confession and a jury into rapture, died Thursday evening on a stage in front of the city’s finest. He was sixty-six. He wore a navy suit and a tie patterned with houndstooth. He made a joke about the wine. The microphone wobbled. He reached to steady what does not like to be steady, and when he fell, he struck his temple on the raised edge of the dais, which is an old Greek word for platform, which is another way to say: place to be seen.

My throat went cold. Judge Prescott was scheduled to keynote the library foundation gala that night. We had a calendar listing on page B2. He was very much alive at 10 a.m., as far as I knew. The obituary held more, the kinds of facts that feel like a friend is telling you a story before you realize the friend has never met the person: a reference to his law review note on the Fourth Amendment and “the way he loved the water knowing it could not love him back.” The cause of death, if you could call it that, was oddly exact. The aside about Greek etymology raised the hairs on my arms.

The third sheet was for a pianist I had once interviewed by phone to fill a gap in a Sunday Living. The fourth was a woman known for her dog rescue work. The fifth was blank but for a heading that read In Remembrance and a series of dashes like a score waiting for notes.

I got up so fast my chair rolled into the trash can and tipped it. Pens spilled, and a single paperclip made a sound like a tooth on tile. Len glanced over.

“What’s the fire?”

“Someone sent me five obituaries,” I said before remembering the fifth was not exactly anything. My mouth had a way of pulling ahead of my caution.

“Like the funeral homes do.”

“Not like that.” I held up the onion-skin like a magician with a scarf. “Typed. No return.”

Len’s eyebrows rose. “That’s... quaint.”

“Sloane,” I said again, and as if conjured, Sloane materialized, all long limbs and apologetic urgency, a stack of budget pages in her hand and a Sharpie tucked behind one ear. She had a way of moving like the ceiling was lower than it was.

“You bellowed?” she said.

I handed her the first page. She read. Her face did a thing—a shift, a leveling—and then did nothing at all.

“Where did this come from?” she asked.

“Courier,” I said. “No return. And there was an email that’s identical to the first one—Eleanor Hart—but it came from nowhere.”

“What do you mean nowhere.”

“No IP trail in the header.” I didn’t say that’s not my expertise, but I’ve done enough fact-checking to know how to look under the hood, and there was no grease to be found. “It seemed... clean. Too clean.”

“Judge Prescott has a gala tonight,” she said, flipping to page two. “Someone has a taste for theater.”

“You think it’s a prank?”

“I think we call his office and make sure he isn’t already dead.” She handed the page back, wiped her thumb against her skirt like she could wipe away ink. “And you lock this in your drawer.”

I didn’t argue. Sloane can make any word sound like a verdict. I found our latest press release from the library foundation, dialed the number at the bottom. A cheerful voice answered and put me through to a woman whose job, from her tone, was to recover from people like me.

“Judge Prescott is very much alive,” she said when I explained what I was calling about without insulting her intelligence. “He’s en route to meet with donors at twelve and he’ll be at the podium at eight.”

“You’re sure he’s—”

“Ms. Duvall,” she said, and because only my mother calls me Mara and the rest of the city insists I am a last name first, I did not correct her. “We are in the business of making sure our speakers are breathing.”

I apologized, thanked her, hung up. Sloane scrawled something on a Post-it that looked like a curse but was probably a budget line. “All right,” she said. “We don’t run anything. We sit on it. We do not give oxygen to the arsonists. If by some horrible chance something happens, we have a head start. You did nothing wrong and you didn’t show this to anyone but me and Len, who will now forget he ever saw it. Len?”

“Forget what?” he said, eyes not leaving his screen, which was compassion in his dialect.

“If you get another one, you tell me. If someone calls, you tell me. If someone sneezes weird, you tell me.”

“I’ll listen to all sneezes,” I said, and she left in that way of editors, leaving you with a problem and a plan and enough air to breathe if you remembered to.

I slid the pages into a manila folder and then into the bottom drawer of my desk, the one with the broken lock you have to coax by jamming a rubber band under it, which nearly makes it a lock. Then I did the only thing I could that felt useful. I called printing and told them to hold the page on the library gala until eight-thirty, a thing we would only do if we expected late art. The man in press grunted and said, “I like to print things while they’re still happening,” which is a private joke of his. I laughed because it’s important to feed people their lines.

By noon, I’d read the text of the second obituary seven times, the third three, the fourth once, because the fourth contained a detail about a factory fire in 1997 that only someone from the south side would know and I didn’t want to think about that neighborhood with the plant and the way the air tasted that week, which was like pennies and sermons. I answered two calls from funeral homes about garbled dates, one from a woman who wanted to know if we charge extra to run a photo because the only one she has of her husband is him holding a fish. I told her we do not. She said thank you like I had changed her life.

By two-thirty, I decided the best thing to do was to put my body in the way of it. Not stand physically between Judge Prescott and the dais. But to go and watch him interact with the night and make sure that the words on that paper didn’t have the power to pull down a stage. Journalism has made me into a believer in witnesses. If you can't change the story, you can at least be present when it turns.

When work wants us at night events, it gives us a taxi chit and a stern warning about alcohol. I signed out a chit and told Len nothing. If I told Len, he’d tell me to bring my flask, and then he’d tell me to bring him back a quote. I checked my phone—two messages from my mother, one from my ex that was just a link to a song and a shrug emoji. I ignored the ex on principle.

At five, on my way out, I stopped at the mailroom to check if the courier had left anything else. The room is a rectangle of stale air, bins labeled with departments we no longer have. The light flickers like there’s a ghost in the ballast. There was a single envelope in the slot for Editorial. My name wasn’t on it, but I knew, with that bodily knowing you don’t owe to thinking, that it was for me.

It was heavier than the first, and the paper had a ribbon of red thread stitched along the edge, a detail that felt like someone showing off. I took it back to my desk because I didn’t want to be seen reading it in the hall like a spy in a bad movie. I closed my drawer as if the act of shutting could make it all quieter.

I slit it.

Four sheets fell out. Three text-filled, the last folded in half as if it were shy. I read the first line of the top sheet and laughed because sometimes you laugh when your body's other options are limited.

The headline read, plainly, without a verb to soften it: MARA DUVALL.

I didn’t have to read more. Of course I did.

Mara Duvall, who wrote about the end of things and took notes on beginnings she rarely showed anyone, died Tuesday in a building where the windows had been painted shut for years. She was thirty-two. She kept a red ribbon in a drawer because her mother had told her once that pretty things should be saved, which is why she didn’t wear it. She was, to the end, precise about hats and careless with love. She did not believe in luck but kept a blue marble in the cup holder of her car, in case.

The ribbon in my hand, the red stitch through the envelope, seemed to tug at its own tail. My fingers touched the place where a ribbon would be if I kept one. In my desk, in the left-hand drawer above the broken lock, there is a red ribbon. I have never told anyone that. I don’t remember when I put it there. I just know it’s there the same way I know the way the printer sounds when it’s about to jam, the same way I know when someone is lying about a date.

I read the next paragraphs as if they were written about a stranger, and then about my enemy, and then about a version of me that might be improved by being dead. There was a line about a girl with her hair in braids reading on the floor by the refrigerator because it hummed loud in summer and that hum felt like safety. There was a mention of a sister. There was a mention of something that was not a fact and wasn’t a rumor and yet was there, typed with the certainty of keys on paper: she never forgave herself for something no one else blamed her for.

A cold came up from my feet into my legs, a tide in reverse. I looked up. The newsroom had thinned, everyone slipping off to their evening places. Light angled through blinds and made zebra stripes across desks. Len put his coat on, slow, half one sleeve then the other, a man moving around a stiffness. He waved without guilt and went toward the elevator and, because a thing loves a sibling, the elevator did not stall for him for once.

I took the page with my name and slid it under the stack containing other people’s deaths because it felt like a hierarchy I could enforce. I put the pages back in the envelope and then the envelope into my bag and then—for no reason that has anything to do with reason—I opened the left-hand drawer and took out the red ribbon. It was not the same as the stitch in the envelope but it was enough to make a word rise in my mind: watched.

On my phone, I typed a text to Sloane and erased it. I typed a text to my mother and erased it faster. If you tell someone the future they might make it true.

The city was damp when I stepped outside, the kind of damp that burrows into the metal of streetlights and makes them buzz. I hailed a cab because the chit in my pocket insisted on it and because, suddenly, the idea of waiting for a bus felt like an invitation to something I didn’t want to meet.

“Library?” the driver asked when I gave him the cross streets, and I nodded and tried not to look in the rearview where my face looked like a stranger's in a hood.

We passed the courthouse, which had columns like a Greek temple, and I thought about dais as a word and about platforms and about places to be seen. We passed Hart Farm, which is not a farm but a development with fake shutters, and I thought about Eleanor, who would tomorrow, who would—who. The driver turned the radio up and a man with a soothing voice told the city that there were candles available at the corner store made of beeswax for those who prefer them.

The library’s glass façade lifted out of the street like a ship tilted to show her belly. Inside, lights and people and a string quartet warming up on a piece that wanted to gallop. Out front, women in gowns that made sound and men with shoes that didn’t. A sandwich board announced that tonight the city would “celebrate stories.”

I paid the driver and stepped to the curb. I put my hand on the envelope in my bag like it might jump free and run. For a moment I stood there, as if I were someone with a choice about whether to move forward or not, as if choices are ever that patient.

On the steps, a woman I recognized from every corporate portrait made in the last decade smiled at me like I was part of things. Behind her, the doors to the library slid open, and I heard the busy murmur of a crowd, the clink of glass on glass, the bright apology of a microphone being tapped.

Inside, the night went on, not yet aware.

Later, when I tried to put the whole thing into past tense, it would resist me. The future hangs like a garment on a chair; you can pretend it’s not watching you, but it is. I took a breath and stepped forward, into the kind of light that flatters no one and reveals everything.

Everything in the property room smelled faintly of jet fuel and coffee, even the wool coat I kept on the back of my chair and never wore. Fluorescent lights hummed in a way I hadn’t noticed for six months and now couldn’t forget. We kept a dented aluminum kettle on a cracked hot plate under a sign that said Don’t Leave Unattended, which seemed like a joke until I found myself staring at the red coil and thinking of all the things we’d watched for hours and then still managed to lose track of.

Lost and Found sits behind a gray door at the end of a gray corridor, wedged between the oversize baggage room and an unmarked steel stairwell more people use as a smoke break than an emergency exit. This is to say: you only find us if you’re sent, or if you already know where we are. The city’s official site calls it Property Recovery Services, which makes it sound like we return heirlooms and DVD players with a tuxedoed flourish. In reality, we give a lot of chipped ceramics a second chance at life.

We’d just gotten our fifth umbrella of the morning—navy nylon, automatic, the kind that springs open like a startled bird—when Dex wheeled in the suitcase.

“Orphan on B,” he said, nudging the handle with his hip and trying to look like he wasn’t impressed. Dex is twenty-four, takes night classes, and has been in a documentary about air freight for long enough that if you pause at the right second, you see his elbow. He has a way of leaning like he’s modeling for someone’s album cover and always smells faintly of eucalyptus gum.

I looked at the suitcase. It was an ordinary carry-on, hard-sided, the kind of blue that masquerades as black until you put it next to something actually black and then it looks embarrassed. It was scuffed, the way suitcases get scuffed by love and concrete. Three old stickers peeled at the edges: a stylized gull, a Cyrillic word I couldn’t read at a glance, and a yellow triangle with a black wave. Duct tape wrapped one corner like a bandage.

“No tag?” I asked.

“Just this.” Dex held up a cardboard luggage tag, the kind from a gift shop. Someone had written, in neat block letters, B12. No name. No phone number. No airline bar code.

“Where was it found?”

“Against the column by the charging station. Cam shows it sitting there through the turn. Couple of people glance at it and keep going. No one touches.”

“HazMat says?”

“HazMat says, and I quote, ‘It’s a suitcase, not a hissing drum.’ He poked it. It did not explode.”

I slid the suitcase behind the counter with my foot. The handle was sticky with something that had once been sweet and dried there: orange juice, maybe. It was heavy enough to surprise me.

We triage, the way anyone doing this work does. Phones and laptops go in the locked cabinet by the back wall because even good people do dumb things when they see a row of iPads behind a secondhand desk. Wallets go in the safe after we inventory and call the last two numbers listed or the library if there’s a card—librarians answer before anyone else. Strollers, crutches, a surprising number of textbooks about accounting get labeled and lifted onto the gray metal shelves that wobble if you push them with your hip too hard. The top shelf is work boots, lined up like they belong to a chorus line of ghosts. The bottom two are umbrellas.

The suitcases are trickier. If we can’t find an owner in the first twenty-four hours, we open them and inventory, because the owner might call and say, It’s black, it’s Samsonite, it’s got clothes, which is what everyone says, and the only way to tell black-Samsonite-with-clothes from all the other black-Samsonite-with-clothes is to ask what else is inside. The Two Questions, which are really three: What color is it, what brand is it, what’s one thing inside that isn’t clothes? If you say “shoes,” I say have a nice day.

All this I could do in my sleep. Sometimes I did, and woke at three in the morning remembering a lunch pail or a shawl with moth holes and wondered if the person who left them behind had thought, briefly, that object might have decided it didn’t want them anymore. People don’t mean to lose things. They just mean to come back a minute later, and then a minute turns into a flight.

The door opened and a man stepped in the way people step into rooms when they already believe the thing they’re looking for isn’t there. Forties, maybe. Dark rain jacket with the kind of insulated lining that makes people sweat indoors. Hair clippered short, a little too close to the scalp at the nape. Clean hands, but a callus at the base of the third finger like a ring had lived there and moved on. He looked at me and then at Dex and then at the counter and then everywhere else.

“Hi,” I said. “Lost something?”

His gaze snagged on the suitcase because even when you think you’re playing it cool, your eyes tell on you. Then he wrenched it back to me. “Yes,” he said. His voice was low and even. No accent I could place, just winter in it. “A carry-on. Black. Samsonite.”

“Do you have your claim tag?” I asked, pleasantly, because sometimes people are frantic and sometimes they’re trying to bluff you out of an item and sometimes they’re both.

“I was in a hurry,” he said. “It’s mine. I left it at B—at a boarding gate.”

“B what?”

He blinked. “Twelve.”

“Lucky guess,” Dex said under his breath, and I gave him a look I meant to be a warning and he received as an invitation.

I smiled at the man. “We can check,” I said. “If you can tell me one thing inside that isn’t clothing.”

He stared for a second, clearly assembling a list and throwing it away in his head. “There’s a book,” he said finally. “Hardcover.”

“What book?” I asked.

“A—uh—Dan Brown.”

I waited. When you don’t fill the silence, people try to fill it for you. He didn’t. He had training or a stubborn streak.

“A specific Dan Brown?” Dex asked, helpful.

The man’s jaw moved once, a muscle in his cheek twitching. “Inferno,” he said.

The book in the suitcase—if there was a book in the suitcase—was not going to be Inferno. It wasn’t the wrongness of the guess that got me; it was that it was practiced wrongness, the kind that lands at exactly the level of detail someone thinks you expect. People tell you what you expect when they want you to stop asking questions.

“I can’t hand over property without the right identification,” I said, because that is what you say, and because it is true. “If you have your boarding pass and recall the flight number, that helps. If you can tell me more specifics about the exterior—a dent, a scuff—also helps. Your name?”

He didn’t give it. He set his hands on the counter and leaned in as if he could close the distance with posture. His eyes were almost the same dark color all the way through. “It’s mine,” he said softly. “I need it.”

“I’m sure you do,” I said. “Give me more, and we can help you.”

For a moment, he looked at me the way I imagine people look at airlocks. He straightened, put his hands in his jacket pockets, and drew them out again. Eventually he shook his head, a little, as if to dislodge something stuck behind his ear. “I’ll come back,” he said.

“Bring proof,” Dex said, and the man flicked his eyes at him as if he’d only just now noticed him.

He left with the same contained energy he entered with, as if he had to concentrate to keep from running. The door creaked and clicked.

Dex let out a breath. “Sketchy,” he said, the way some people say delicious.

In the first hour after that, we reunited a toddler with a pink stuffed animal that had clearly been an elephant before something hard had loved it flat. The father cried in an unembarrassed way that made the toddler look around like she was in the middle of a summer rainstorm, confused but enjoying it. We got a call from an elderly man who had left his only pair of bifocals at a security checkpoint and described them, when prompted, as “glasses-shaped.” We found a set of dentures in an eyeglass case and I opened it and closed it twice like I was practicing a trick.

The suitcase waited. Things always wait.

At noon the terminal kitchen sent down a tray of muffins that had missed their window. The raspberry had bled into the dough in a way I once would’ve called a study in saturation. I licked pips off my thumb and checked the manifest for Gate B12. Three flights in the last two hours, two delayed, one boarding. I flipped back through yesterday’s. Nothing jumped out. We live and die by bar codes; this thing had none.

At one-thirty, the man came back.

He had combed his hair. He had put on a lanyard he had not worn before, white, no logo, with a card in a plastic sleeve that faced away, blank side out. He moved slower. He set his elbows on the counter and looked at me in a way that said he had decided I was the obstacle and wanted to begin negotiations with himself about what to do next.

“Back with proof?” I asked. The copy point near Gate D makes fake proof for people in a pinch; the trick is that you can always tell.

“I can tell you what is inside,” he said. “A—blue shirt in the right side. There is tape on the corner.” He lifted his hand and mimed the gesture, as if the doing of it would conjure truth.

“Duct tape,” I said. “We saw.”

He swallowed. He smelled like rain. Or rather, he smelled like someone who had been near rain and then come into reheated air. “There is a key,” he said. “On a ring. Brass.”

“What’s engraved?”

He hesitated a fraction too long. “Nothing.”

He watched my face to see if he had passed. It is the hardest part, not being kind with your expression just because someone looks like they are trying, even when the trying is a kind of lie. “I still need a name,” I said. “For the log.”

He stared at me. I could feel Dex, behind me, a stillness more than a person, like the air in those seconds before the fireworks begin.

“Sir,” I said.

He said a name. It took him a beat and a half to choose it. It was common, forgettable, the sort I used to see on student rosters when I’d been twenty-two and believed a list of names could tell you something true about a person. It told me nothing about him.

“Wait here,” I said, and took a step back. I closed the door to the inner room not because I needed to—it’s still open at the top, and his voice would have come through if he’d called—but because it signaled a boundary. Inside, with the shelves and the safe and the little electric kettle, I leaned my head briefly against the cool metal cabinet and listened to the hum of the fluorescent light.

“You’re not going to give it to him,” Dex said, not a question.

“No.”

“He’s going to get creative.”

“Maybe,” I said, and looked at the suitcase.

There is a way some suitcases fly under the machine that sees through them that is more about human than algorithm. I crouched and set my palm flat against the hard shell. Cool. The handle rattled like a milk tooth in a child’s mouth. I flipped it and scanned for the zipper ends. Most of the time, if someone wants to hide something from us, they hide it in plain view, which never works. Now and then, you get someone who knows that handles, wheels, the molding at the seams are all places a person with a screwdriver can make a different shape of box.

“Do not,” Dex said, coming up behind me with an authority he did not possess, “open that.”

“I’m not,” I said, and felt for the likelihood of a double wall along the base. There it was: the faint give where there should be none, the seam that was not factory-straight. Awful at lying, good at metal. Whoever had done it understood both weight and patience.

I brought it back upright and opened my hands as if I were a magician who had never actually learned a trick in her life. “We wait,” I said, and took a breath and went back out to the counter.

The man had moved to the far end of the room, where the bulletin board was. People leave notes there sometimes: a granny-flat list of sublets near the airport, a guitar teacher’s schedule, a printed flyer for a support group for people who have lost things—the last one real, I checked it twice. He was not reading them, exactly. He was looking at the photos I had pinned along the bottom edge. I keep photos of the oddest found items, the ones we know no one is coming for but that I cannot bear to shove into a bin labeled Misc. without a moment of witness. The hand-painted boomerang. The green wool hat with a gold embroidered moth. The ring of keys with no door on the other end.

He turned when he heard me. He had put on polite. “Anything?”

“We need a little more from you,” I said. “If you can retrieve a boarding pass, even from the airline app—”

“I do not have it,” he said. “I do not have it.” He pressed his lips together as if the words were a thing you could eat to keep from starving.

“I can’t release it,” I said again.

He put both hands on the counter, palms down, as if to push himself forward and then thought better of it. He looked down. I saw what was in his eyes when he lifted his head back up. It was calculation and it was something like grief. For a second I wondered what it would be like to want something so much you would choose to be humiliated in public for it, and then I thought of a train platform in a different city, years ago, and a hand I had not reached for and how I wake some nights still with my fingers curved around the absence.

“Okay,” he said, and stepped back. He pushed his hands into his jacket pockets and pulled them out empty. “I’ll be back,” he said.

He wasn’t.

It got busy. A baggage cart’s axle broke at the outside doors and for thirty minutes there was a ballet of ground crew and wheel chocks and a woman in heels shouting into her phone that she was going to miss her connection and the person on the other end probably could do nothing about this. A damp child was ill and we had a mop and three extra T-shirts and none of them small enough, so I cut one with a box cutter and knotted it like I used to do with my own shirts when I wanted to be a different girl. The lights flickered once, the kind of flicker that registers in your stomach before your eyes clock it, and came back stronger, as if the room had made up its mind.

At three-fifteen, Dex took his break. At three-twenty, the phone rang, the direct line not from the main terminal but the little black phone we keep under the desk for the back corridor.

“Mara Kim?” a man’s voice said. Not the same man. This one was younger, or better at sounding young.

“This is she,” I said.

“Don’t give the blue suitcase to anyone,” he said. “Not the man who asked for it. Not anyone.”

The thing about a public building is that it makes you into a different species of animal. I stood up without meaning to and turned so my back was to the door to the hall. “Who is this?” I asked. I put my hand flat on the counter not because I thought it would help and because touching something steady helps.

“No names,” the voice said. In the background, a television murmured, that slippery cadence of commercials, high and bright. “Just don’t.”

“I wouldn’t anyway,” I said. “It’s not tagged.”

There was a pause, and I heard the edge of a laugh get built and then dismantled. “That’s funny,” he said. “And when he comes back with a badge he printed at a kiosk? When he comes with a cop and says ‘misunderstanding’? Read the bottom of the badge.”

“I don’t—”

“Just read it,” he said. “You will know.”

The line clicked dead. We don’t have caller ID on that phone and I decided I did not want to call back and reach security and have them tell me nothing had come into the back corridor line because then the phone call would no longer exist in a way I could hold in my hands.

Dex came back with a half-empty bottle of something green. “You look like you saw a mouse,” he said.

“Someone called,” I said. “Said not to give the suitcase to anyone.”

“Free advice,” he said, “the best kind.”

The man didn’t come back with a badge or a cop. A different man came, in a pilot’s uniform that had the wrong fit, the way a uniform does when the person wearing it has only bought the jacket and not learned how to fill it with authority. He stood in the doorway and looked at the ceiling and then his shoes and then asked for the bathroom and I pointed down the hall and watched him go past the bathroom sign and up the stairs to the door that says Roof Access Authorized Personnel Only and put a hand on the handle and then not push it. He came back down the hall, peered into the Lost and Found, and kept going. We looked at each other and didn’t say anything because sometimes the thing you know is more fragile for speaking out loud.

At four-fifteen, the terminal announced a delay in the careful voice it uses when it knows what it’s saying will make people angry. Dex went to help burst an overfull bin of strollers. I took the screwdriver from the mug that held our pens and shut the office door.

There are rules. There are also exceptions to rules, which is the wiggle that lets rule-based systems function as more than punishment. The exceptions save you or end you. You never know which until you flip it over.

The screws that held the interior panel were not factory. The heads had been ground down—to almost round but not quite—so you needed a driver ground to match. I did not have that driver. I had the little ones in the kit I kept for reading glasses and a flathead the width of my thumb that I had once used to pry a dime from an air vent. I had patience. And I had the specific stubbornness of a person who has lived with rules long enough to know when they were built for a world that had never existed.

It took time. I only hurt my palm once. When I eased the panel clear, it made a sound like a held breath.

Inside, the space was neat. People who make compartments like this are neat: it is psychological and it is practical. A layer of brown paper tied with twine. Under that, plastic—not the crackle kind of grocery bags, the soft kind that you get when you buy a sweater from a nice place and they wrap it in tissue you can turn into a ghost for Halloween. Under that, another layer of brown paper, heavier, like butcher wrap.

I untied the twine. If anyone wants to lecture me about fingerprints, you will have to stand in line behind the version of myself who does not make this choice and then lives the rest of her life in speculation.

Inside was a book, wrapped in an old knit scarf. The scarf smelled like someone’s grandmother’s house: cedar, laundry soap that came in flakes, a sweetness that might have been orange peel. The book was cloth-bound, green turned gray at the corners, the spine cracked in two places. No title on the spine, just a five-pointed star stamped small and discreet at the bottom. Alongside the book, nested in a depression cut in the soft foam that lined the compartment, was a key ring with three keys. The keys were brass, all old; one was a skeleton key with a fancy bow shaped like a bird with its wings tucked tight. One was the sort you get from a hardware store in a town where the hardware store also sells stamps. One was thinner than the others, with a notch near the tip that made it look, if you squinted, like a fish with its mouth open.

I sat down on the floor without meaning to and put my thumb against that notch in the thin key. It fit like I knew it would.

I keep other people’s keys on a nail under my desk. I don’t collect them because I love the idea of owning a thousand doors. I collect them because I don’t like the idea of throwing away the shape of what used to open something. When my father died, two winters ago now, the only thing of his I kept without thinking was a key he had worn on a cord around his neck for as long as I knew him. The cord had frayed so thin in one place that when I held it up to the window, it looked like a line drawn with a pencil that someone had erased. The key was brass and thin; if you put it on your palm and pressed your other hand over it, you could feel the notch—a small, particular bite near the tip. A fish, open-mouthed. It did not fit any door in his house. I had tried.

I slid the thin key from the ring and put it against the one that hung on the nail under my desk. They were not twins. Twins have symmetry and I didn’t think doors worked that way. But they were made by the same hand. Same blank. The notch matched exactly.

When I opened the book—because of course I opened the book—the first page had a list of months written out without dates, like entries waiting to be filled. February had a small penciled x next to it. Someone had drawn a map on the inside of the cover with a pen that had run dry and then been switched for one that had not. The paper had the texture of something that had gotten damp and then dried under weight with the windows closed.

The handwriting inside was neat and slanted, the kind of script you get when a teacher in a starched blouse watched you from the top of the room with her back straight and said things like no dangling. It wasn’t in English. I recognized it anyway, the way you recognize the shape of someone’s name in a crowd. Not Cyrillic. Not Korean, though my mother would have been delighted at the thought that her daughter, who had run so far from everything she had been given as a child, could still read a curve and know what it meant. The letters cut across the page like water.

I turned the page. I had not heard the door open over the hum of the fluorescents. I did not hear Dex until he said my name, which means I was further gone than I like to be.

“Mara?”

I closed the book. My hands were steady. My heart was not.

“What are you doing?” he asked, and then looked at the suitcase, and then at me. His eyes went from movie poster to person again, serious. He is a good kid. He has better instincts than he lets on.

“Inventory,” I said. “Sort of.”

“You’re not supposed to—”

“I know.”

“We’re supposed to call—”

“I know,” I said again, and held up the key with the notch so he could see it without me letting it go. “Look.”

He looked because I told him to, but he didn’t know what he was looking at. He was a kind kid, not a lucky one. He didn’t know that two years ago I had sat in my father’s kitchen and counted the number of times the refrigerator coughed and then went quiet and thought that might be the last time it did that with him in the room. He didn’t know about the door that didn’t fit in that house because the frame had been warped and planed and warped again. He didn’t know about the cord that had worn a thin ring into skin.

“Okay,” he said carefully. “Keys.”

Brother to his credit, he did not ask me why my face looked the way it must have looked. He just handed me a paper towel without me asking and then he stood with his back to the office door and looked out as if he were watching for someone who was not yet here.

A knocking rattled the front counter glass. It wasn’t the special knock we’d sometimes get from security or a courier in a hurry. It was the kind you do when you are trying to make someone jump. It accomplished its goal.

I put the book and the keys back into the compartment and laid the knit scarf on top and slid the panel in and pressed until the edges nested. I could feel the catch I had bent in the removal resist and then take. I stood and went out.

A cop stood at the counter. His badge was real. His face was realer. He had the look of someone who has made it through one long day and discovered it has doubled itself in the night. Behind him stood the man, hands in his pockets, shoulders down, a demonstration of not being a threat.

“Afternoon,” the cop said. “We’re looking for a blue roller bag. Gentleman says it may have been turned in here. Misunderstanding about tags.”

I looked at the badge. I read the name and then, because someone on a phone had a voice that had built a laugh and then taken it apart, I let my eyes slip to the bottom line that most people never read. The badge had been reissued yesterday.

“Let me check the log,” I said.

The cop smiled that particular tight public-service smile. The man did not smile.

I leaned back into the office, felt Dex at my shoulder, felt the hum of the light, felt my palm buzz as if the key had decided to become a phone. I took a breath and thought of doors you push and doors you pull and how, when it matters, people always try the wrong way first.

By the end of the week, three men would be dead and someone would ask me, sitting under a different humming light with a paper cup of bitter coffee cooling in my hand, if I understood that I had changed the order of the day. I would think of the scarf and the way the green had faded into a gray that remembered its original state and say yes, though I did not then and do not now know if it was true.

At four-seventeen that Tuesday, I did what you always do when you run a good property room. I reached for the log and bought myself thirty seconds to decide whether I was about to follow a rule or an exception.

By the time the letter found me, it had already been opened twice—once by the person who sealed it and trusted the system, and once by the machine that didn’t recognize it was alive.

On Mondays, the sorting hall hums like a hive that’s given up on honey. Metal trays ribbon past with dull clatter, a conveyor river carrying the apologetic wreckage of other people's intentions: envelopes warped by rain, packages bloated from smeared ink and melted chocolate, postcards from urgent vacations, brittle wedding invitations addressed to names that don’t exist. In the Undeliverable Mail Unit, we make a ritual of last chances. We angle floodlights. We squint at smudged return addresses under magnifiers. We cross-reference. We guess.

The posted rules—laminated, optimistic—are stapled at eye level by the badge reader. Rule One: Do Not Remove Any Item From Premises. Rule Two: You Are Not A Detective. Rule Three: If It Can Be Delivered, Try. If Not, Let It Go.

If you work here long enough, you begin to doubt Rule Three. We’re a room full of secular priests hearing about lives we will never meet, and we are expected to absolve the whole mess with a stamp that says No Known Address.

My badge light blinked from red to green. Cold air rolled toward me, smelling faintly of wet cardboard and the cleaning solution Silas uses on the letter-slicer’s rollers. Silas himself sat on his stool with his feet tucked up like a gargoyle, squinting at the slicer’s feed tray. He has been with the Unit long enough to remember when we'd steam open envelopes with kettles instead of heating wands, and still prefers the kettle for sentimental reasons.

“Morning, Iris,” he said without looking up. He can tell us apart by the shoes we wear. He says boots sound decisive.

“Morning,” I agreed. My voice sounded like a stranger's in that echoing hangar. I hung my coat on the back of my chair and nested into my station: magnifier lamp, tweezers, microblades for teasing open seams, the soft brush we use to coax grit out of the teeth of old typescripts. The avalanche had already started without me. A grey tub labeled ILLEGIBLE HAND—MANUAL sat fat and ready. I took a handful of envelopes and fanned them out.

Names floated like half-remembered songs. H. V….no, A. Y…Could be Ivy. Blue ink bled into the fibers like winter rivers. Some we can save. Most we can't.

Mags breezed in late, shedding a scarf that must have been six feet long. Mags is a woman who collects stray cats and stray opinions. She threw me a grin as she set down her lunch, a small mountain of Tupperware.

“Did you bring a sweater? They’ve turned the heat down. Rook says the budget's been shaved again. Lost half a toner box, I heard.”

“I’ll survive,” I told her.

“Only if you feed yourself. I brought apple cake.”

“We’re not supposed to eat over the bins,” I reminded her. It says that, in bold, right under Rule Three. Food attracts bugs. Bugs attract inspectors.

“We aren’t eating. We’re anticipating,” she said, and nudged my arm with her elbow. “See anything good yet?”

Good is not always good. Good sometimes means letters with photographs tucked inside, the kind that make you ache to meddle. Good is packages with rattling interior mysteries and no return address, the ones that make Silas put on his thick gloves and call Security.

“I just started,” I said, then squinted at an envelope in my fingers. The paper was not the modern peeled-back shiny stuff. It was slightly soft, cotton fiber, the kind you find in old desk drawers and scented stationary boxes. Pale gray-blue. I rubbed the edge and it gave under my finger like fabric. The stamp was the lighthouse from last year’s coastal set, but the postmark was new—three days ago. The address was in ink the exact color of the paper. The handwriting lifted off the page: tall straight letters, elegant dips.

My mouth went dry. It wasn’t the ink. It was the hand.

I haven’t seen it in ten years, except in dreams and in the margins of the recipes she left me, notes like “add more lemon if you’re feeling brave.” My mother’s name was on her birth certificate as Maren Gray, but everyone who loved her called her May. She had a particular way of writing an R that dipped below the line like a fish.

The R was there, right where Gray should have been, in the return-address corner. May Gray. The address: 31 Willowbank Road. The ink skipped slightly on the k of bank the way her pens always did. And there was the cheap little habit, the bracket she drew under the zip code to steady her wrist. She taught me to write mine that way when I was six.

Familiarity is not truth. Every day we see imitations. I know signatures can be copied with the right attention, that handwriting is a costume you can wear long enough to fool a stranger. But there is a feel to it, to the weight a person uses when they know a word like a small prayer. And it wasn’t just the hand. Willowbank Road.

I could have said the numbers of that house in the dark. The porch had gray paint that stuck to bare feet in the summer. I counted those steps holding my hands out to her when I was five, landing at the fourth one, where the paint was worn and where she laughed.

I think I stopped breathing long enough that Mags looked over. “You all right? You look like you swallowed a penny.”

“It’s nothing,” I said. “Just a…odd one.” I kept the letter face down under my left hand. My fingers shook.

“Don’t get attached,” she said automatically.

“I’m not.”

“It’s Monday.” She said this like it explained the world.

I licked my lips because this is what people do to pretend to be normal among other people. The rules clicked through me like teeth. Letters come to us because the machine cannot read them, because the barcode is wrong, because addresses are outdated. We open what must be opened in order to find a return address or contents that can clue us toward the sender. We do not linger. We do not investigate beyond reason. We do not—under any circumstances—take them home.

“Rook is doing a walk-through in five,” Mags said, sliding into her chair. “Hide your contraband.”

I slid the letter to the center of my blotter. I looked down at the printed placard that says UNDELIVERABLE—FOR MANUAL REVIEW in block letters, as if labeling could absolve us. The envelope had a smear along the bottom like someone had set it briefly in water. The postmark was from the city—our city. Not Willowbank. Not the small town where that porch had a gray step. Wherever it started, it had come close enough to us to be run through our machines, which had spat it here.

I flipped it over. The glue seam was intact. The slicer had not touched it. I could open it, legitimately. For information. For address determination.

Silas hates when we justify like this. He once said, kindly, that the difference between a sin and a policy is how good we are at telling the story to ourselves.

I folded the flap thirty degrees, then again, coaxing the old glue with a touch of hot air from the wand. The paper sighed. The inner flap freed and lifted. The smell that rose was not nostalgic. It smelled faintly of damp linen and something metallic.

Inside there was a smaller envelope, unsealed, with no stamp. It was the cream of cheap stationery. Across the front someone had written Iris, in the same hand, in the same ink.

I held still too long, long enough that the cold bit my knuckles where they rested on the desk. My breath fogged the magnifier. Somewhere beyond the island of light around my station, the conveyor belts worked and someone laughed at something Silas said. I had not told anyone here much about my life before this job. You sit in this room long enough reading strangers' emergencies, the impulse to keep your own secrets grows teeth.

A shadow fell across my desk.

Rook’s tie is always a quarter inch off center. He has two suits and alternates them with unconvincing randomness. He is, to his core, a bureaucrat, which makes him more honest than most men. He eyed my stack, did a quick count. He’s good at math; he carries an old Casio in his pocket to add insult to machines.

“Team,” he said, to the room in general. “We’ve had a query from Legal. The Agent desk received a phone call about an undelivered registered letter and wants to know our process on chain-of-custody for lost items with currency.” He sucked his head in between his shoulders slightly, as if bracing from a blow. “I said we have a policy.”

“We do,” Mags called without looking up. “It’s the one where we don't steal things.”

“That’s the one,” Rook agreed dryly. He nodded at me. “Gray.”

“Sir,” I said, hands folded like I was in school, the letter sandwiched between them.

“I need you to write up an example of best practice on the manual open. Photos, notes. Legal wants to see it. And put your name on it so they have a human to call.”

“Sure,” I said.

“I promised them poetry.” He moved on, the way a storm moves on, trailing paper clips.

When he’d gone, I breathed again and slid the inner envelope into my lap. The outer envelope had been addressed to 31 Willowbank Road, but in the corner, above the zip bracket, my mother had drawn a small symbol in pencil—the tilt of a maple leaf we used to use when we were playing spy games when I was thirteen. If I ever tried to mark a page nowadays with that leaf, the angle always came out wrong. Here it was perfect and small and all at once it was too much.

I tore the inner envelope clumsily. The paper inside was thin. The ink bled a little. It was short.

Iris—
