If this gets to you, forgive the method. There are things we didn’t say because there wasn’t time. I know how that sounds from me. I am sorry. There is a key in the starch of this paper. Soak it. Locker 217. Seventh Street Station. Tonight. After six. The locker is paid for until Friday.

Do not bring anyone. The river knows.

—M

M, in that looping, stubborn way she finished her name when she was signing notes for me to find under refrigerator magnets. There were tiny grease-ghosts at the edge of the page where the hand had paused. A corner was wrinkled, as if someone had pinched it between anxious fingers. In the bottom margin there was a faint dirt smudge shaped like a half-moon. I ran my thumb over it. It didn't smear.

“Anything?” Mags asked too briskly, popping the lid off her apple cake as if that had been my cue.

“No,” I said, my voice light, my heart drumming. “No return address.”

That was a lie. The return address was the outline of my life.

I moved the note from under the magnifier to the shadow of the desk like it would be less visible there. I tugged at the paper with my nails, looking for what “in the starch” meant. The old trick at sleepovers: soak a piece of paper and watch the gelatin in it release what someone has hidden between the fibers. I could not see anything embedded. Just words and a smudge and that signature like a music note.

Seventh Street Station is three blocks from us. It’s where I get my train home when I am too tired to walk the river path. The lockers there still use keys; they are old, dented, painted the color of moss. People store sneakers in them when they run the embankment. People stash grocery bags. Once, a woman left a cascade of paper cranes in one and watched to see who would open it, just to say to herself that luck can still spill out of steel.

Do not bring anyone. The river knows.

If you try to understand the logic of grief, it will refuse you. Don’t try. It will go around every rule there is.

I stood up suddenly, bumping my knee on the underside of the desk. Pain flared bright and embarrassed. “Bathroom,” I announced to no one in particular, and took the note with me as if I meant to put it in the trash on the way.

The Unit’s bathroom is the color of government thoughts. The mirror is always clean and harsh. I closed myself in the last stall because my hands were shaking and because on the back of that door someone had etched a tiny, defiant rose with the key end of a safety lock. Under the sink, beside the wrapped paper towels, there is a plastic tub labeled DISTILLED—EQUIP ONLY. We use it to top up the steamer.

I checked the hall and brought the tub into the stall. I poured enough to make a shallow pool in the bottom of the bin liner and set the note in. The paper darkened with a slow sigh. I waited, my heart thudding, counting my breaths, making myself go slow. Wet fibers release things the way old stories unbend their spines when no one else is listening.

At first, nothing. Then the bottom edge of the page puckered. The water clouded. A tiny, hard thing bumped against the side of the bin and flashed dull gold before it sank into the curl of the note. I fished it out with two fingers.

It was a key the size of a thumbnail with a punched metal tab stamped with 217. Locker keys are often this ugly. Ugly and very specific. Old vending keys are patterned differently. Apartment keys do not have a number like that on a plate; they are letters and cuts. This was station hardware.

There was a sound in the hall, a squeak of rubber sole, quick steps. The fluorescent light hummed and the radiator ticked like it was thinking.

I dried my fingers on toilet paper and palmed the key, folded the note into my back pocket soggy. I upended the tub into the sink and wiped it with a paper towel until it looked as if nothing of interest had happened in a government building ever again.

When I came out, Mags was at my desk snapping a photo of her apple cake with her phone. “Proof,” she said. “So when I send you a reminder at three and you say you forgot, I can shame you with evidence.”

“What do you want me to say? Thank you?”

“I want you to eat sugar. Sugar is good for people who insist on jobs like this.” She put the phone down and looked up at my face. Mags misses nothing she thinks she can tease you about and will miss everything you actually want to hide. That’s the bargain. “You’re pale.”

“Cold,” I said. I put my hands under the lamp.

She was watching my mouth like she was counting words. “We could skip trivia tonight,” she said after a moment. “If you’re beat. My nephew came down with whatever’s going around and I was going to bring him soup. Comes down to: I can be boring or I can be fun. You choose.”

“Go be soup,” I said, dizzy with decisions I could not tell her about.

“So bossy,” she murmured, and peeled the plastic off the cake. “One piece for me, one for Iris. And exactly four gilded crumbs for Silas if he is perfect.”

“You know I’m diabetic,” Silas muttered without glancing up.

“You’re dietetic,” Mags corrected with cheerful malice. “Not the same thing.” She slipped me a plate. I took it because my hands needed to be doing something other than clenching around a key until it left stigmata.

Rook reappeared, pointing vaguely with a clipboard. “Lunch at twelve instead of one. Union is doing a thing in the atrium.”

“What kind of thing?” Mags asked, alert like a dog hearing a of rustle.

“A meeting,” Rook said, as if the word itself was trouble. “Let them. And we will continue to make the mail less undeliverable, which is our actual job.”

I ate my cake and tasted nothing. The clock on the far wall made a noise like it was chewing.

People will tell you the river divides the city. It does not. It collects us. It remembers who we have tried to be. The year my mother died—no, that’s passive, that’s weak—the year my mother drove her car through the safety barrier and into the dark bowl of the reservoir, the river was full of its own story. It had rained for weeks. It was not her fault, said the police report; if the brakes failed, if she had taken that curve too fast. If. Her phone had no last message. Her purse was where it should have been. She was dressed for Tuesday afternoon. The story we told ourselves is that if she had meant to leave entirely, she would have said goodbye in her particular way: the way of lists, of labeled boxes, of a note on the counter saying there is soup in the freezer, there is cake, there is love.

There was no note.

Rule Two: You are not a detective. I had made peace with that. You don’t work here if you haven’t practiced letting go of other people’s threads. I am good at seeing but inarticulate at pushing. I hand the packages and the letters back to the system and wait for the green bins to empty.

The day stretched its bureaucratic spine. We opened letters to find receipts. We tossed empty envelopes into the shred. We saved postcards of sunsets because you cannot shred a horizon with a good conscience. At twelve, I stood in the atrium with the others and listened to someone talk about hours and the lack of overtime. I clapped when I was supposed to. I watched the glass ribs of the ceiling gather light.

At five-thirty, when the Unit thins and the night crew starts to ghost in, I signed my log. I put on my coat. I stood at my chair pretending to remember something in a drawer until Mags was distracted, until Rook went into his office and closed the door on the exact sound of a man who counts his breaths.

“See you,” I said to no one, and walked out into the blue part of evening.

Seventh Street Station smells like old coins and spilled coffee. Commuters swarmed, heads down. The lockers cluster along the west wall beneath a flaking mural of leaping salmon. Locker 217 had a dent near the lock that looked like a thumbprint. People have leaned here. People have pressed their bodies against cold metal and waited for a phone to ring, for a lover to arrive, for a panic to pass.

I slid the key into the lock. The brass was worn smooth where other people’s anxiety had polished it. It turned in my hand with a small, solid click, a practical music. A man in a knit cap the color of moss jostled me from behind and apologized without looking. Somewhere, a bus huffed and doors snapped shut.

Do not bring anyone. The river knows.

I wrapped my hand around the locker handle.

The door was heavier than I expected. It stuck a little and then gave. What was inside was not mine; nothing about this could belong to me yet. I pulled the door open on the breath I’d been holding all day and leaned in.

Dark metal opened like a mouth.

Something shifted, soft, like tide. Then I saw the first thing, and the second. And the note on top, folded once. My name again, in that hand that has no right to be here. The air in the locker was colder by a degree, a kept cold, the kind that preserves or warns.

Behind me, in the endless echo of the station, a child began to cry. I put my fingers to the edge of the paper and lifted it free. I didn’t read it yet. I counted the dents in the door because it suddenly mattered. I listened to the river of sound the city makes when it doesn’t know it’s singing.

“Okay,” I said to no one, to the station, to the tin cold mouth. “Okay.”

Old habits will take you only so far. I had broken Rule One already. Rule Two was next, or maybe it had been the first thing to go the moment I saw that R.

I folded the new note into my pocket, next to the key I no longer needed. I used both hands and moved what was beneath.

The locker held a sealed manila envelope and a small, neat coil of something like twine, but not twine—careful, white, and stiff. It took my mind a blinking second to name what it was.

By then, someone was watching me. I could feel it, a prickle between my shoulder blades. The station reflected its own crowd back at me in the long strip of dull metal, a ghost parade. When I looked up, a man in a black coat was on the far side of the lockers, turned away, talking into a phone that may or may not have been live. He had the posture of people who do not get jostled even when they are in a place where jostling is a way of life.

He did not turn, and I did not run, and I did not breathe. Outside, the river moved under its skin of evening and did not tell me which of us it knew better. I closed the locker quietly, like a prayer, and when the lock clicked back into place, the sound was too loud and exactly enough.

I collect other people's noise.

It sounds like a pick-up line or a confession, depending on who I’m talking to and how much they’ve had to drink. What it really means is boxes and drives full of wind and footsteps and birdsong, the hiss of audio tape lifting from spools, the small dramas you can hear if you know the kinds of silence that come before them. My lab at the university looks like a cross between a thrift store and a shipping depot—reel-to-reel decks with some of the chrome worn off, a tangle of headphones, stacks of battered cassettes and DAT cartridges, a wall of plastic bins neatly labeled in my little precise block print: 1969—Appalachian Ballads; Lake Huron Waves (Winter); Myers Field, Night Frogs; Grandmother Hollen's Kitchen.

On the morning I got my mother's tape, I was trying to name a bird that had been miscataloged into a box with "Kitchen." The bird was louder than the clatter of dishes, louder than the laughter. The tape hissed like a match thinking itself into flame. I was writing a tentative question mark after "red-winged blackbird" when Erin from Receiving poked her head around my door.

"You have a package," she said. She set a padded envelope on my desk. "Smells like attic."

The return address was my mother's, written in that meticulous cursive I'd copied and abandoned in fourth grade. The postmark was two weeks old. I traced the ink with my finger anyway. My mother had been dead for nine.

The envelope wasn't heavy. It had that particular flex of cheap plastic sleeving around paper. Inside, wrapped in a paper napkin with a ring of coffee staining its scalloped edge, was a black MiniDV cassette with a piece of blue painter’s tape across the top. Someone had written "4/14 2:13 AM" on the painter's tape in pencil, the tail of the 3 lost in a smear.

There was also a note, one of those spiral notebook pages my mother always tore from the back while holding the pad so the tear line was perfectly straight. Mara, it read. Call me when you get this. I should have done this earlier. M.

I turned the note over. No other words. No return number. No date.

I have a habit, when I'm nervous, of bringing things that frighten me closer. I slid the cassette into one of our old Sony decks, cradled a pair of headphones over my ears, clicked the dial to life. The tape spun, whispering even that sounded anxious. The digital counter ticked up. For eight seconds there was true silence—the low floor hum of the machine, my own blood. At nine seconds, breathing. Not mine. A woman’s, shallow and quick. At eleven seconds, my mother's voice, a whisper like she was bent over the microphone, her mouth to the strange little window of it.

"Mara?" she said. The way she said my name was the same way she'd called me to dinner when I was eight, except softer, like dusk had come early.

Something clanged in the background then. A low metallic strike like a slow heart. It was followed by another, perfectly matched in tone and decay. Even through the grit of the recording, I could hear its oldness. A bell, I thought, and then I thought: No.

By the fourth toll, my throat had gone tight.

On the tape, my mother whispered, "Listen," and the bell did what bells have always done. It marked time. Each strike hung, doubled back on itself, gathered the ruin and the river and whatever night air had been inside to carry it. On the twelfth toll, my mother's breath hitched. On the thirteenth, the hair on my arms lifted, as if sound could be a breeze.

The tape clicked and went blank.

There is a bell in my hometown that rings thirteen times only once a year, on New Year’s Eve, because it thinks it's clever. Teenagers clamber up the old mill tower and yank the rope on a dare. The sheriff rouses, threatens. The bell complains and settles, and the town yawns and goes on being itself.

But this wasn’t that bell. This wasn’t any bell that should have been ringing on any April night. The bell in Saint Casimir had melted ten years ago in a fire you could see from the highway.

I took off the headphones. The lab was suddenly too full of hum. I put the headphones back on and listened again. I slowed it. I watched the spectrogram bloom in oranges and indigos, that ghostly city skyline of frequencies. There was the bell’s fundamental, a deep A with an ugly warble where cast iron had never been perfect, and there were the harmonics climbing in unsteady ladders. There were distant sounds too—air moving over something, a rustle that could have been cloth or leaves, the faraway slap of water, and, if I wasn’t imagining it, a high-pitched whine where the tape was frictioning against its casing. There was no traffic. No voices besides my mother’s. No TV.

The tape counter had rolled to twelve minutes, but there was nothing more. I rewound. I listened again. I listened to the spaces between the sounds the way I had been taught, the way I actually liked to. In the blankness after the twelfth toll and before the thirteenth, a faint scrape, not a voice, not wind. Something metallic against wood.

At 2:13 AM, in April, my mother had called me down into her night and put a bell in my ear that did not exist.

I should have done this earlier, she had written.

"Okay," I said to the nothing in my lab. "Okay."

I made three calls. The first was to my mother's neighbor. The second was to the university chair to tell him I would be gone for a few days. The third, as my hand was on my office light switch and my bag over my shoulder, was to my mother’s old landline, because even dead numbers sometimes have a little afterlife.

It rang twice, and then a recorded voice told me to leave a message. I hung up as though I had gotten away with something.

It takes four hours to get to Graybridge from the city if the traffic isn't idiotic and the weather isn't prickly. The day was a strip of torn cloud that never quite committed to rain. Bare trees scratched at the sky. As the highway unrolled, my mother’s voice worked its way out of the headphones and into the car, and then, because the car's speakers made everything too bright, it settled into the part of my head that reproduced it without help. The third toll lodged itself somewhere behind my left eye. The thirteenth settled into the hollow at the base of my throat. After two hours, I took the tape out and slid it back into its sleeve, because I knew how obsessing over a single noise could make it less itself and more a mirror.

The sign for Graybridge is older than me—white letters on a green metal rectangle, the paint peeling around the G. The river runs under a short bridge the town never bothered to widen, which makes traffic in summer a polite nightmare. There are clapboard houses with their milky paint and their stubborn porch furniture. There's a diner that keeps changing hands and never changing any of its recipes. There's a mural of a sturgeon that some high school class painted across the Wasteway meant to hide the fact of waste. Saint Casimir Church used to be the tallest thing in town, with a copper cross that went green too quickly and a bell you could feel in your bones if you were unlucky enough to stand under it when it rang.

When the church burned, Graybridge stood in trees and watched the smoke line the sky. Somebody filmed it on a phone. You could hear cheering in the first thirty seconds, because someone had a private grief, and then you could hear, in the back of someone's breath, a wail. The bell fell second, they said. It sounded like a cry. I was in my dorm room, reading about the physics of instruments, when someone texted me a clip. I watched the building I had been dragged to on more Sundays than my mother would admit, my tights sagging around my knees, turn orange and then empty. The bell did not ring thirteen times that night. It rang once, and then it rang never.

My mother stayed. She watered her thrift store ferns, worked Saturdays at the library, pressed her coins into an envelope for the girls at the animal rescue, watched her watching things. When I visited, I stayed in a well-appointed guest room that still contained, under the bed, shoeboxes with my second-grade teeth in a Ziploc, fourth-grade dioramas beaten to dust, a shoe I had never found again and an apology note from an old friend for something I had both remembered too well and not at all.

If I had written a note to myself then, I would have written: Go more often.

Her house had the same number the realtor had taped up in the front window. RUTH KEMPER — CALL FOR INFO — 555-0131. The porch swing was listing to one side, the chain snapped from the weight of nothing. I let myself in with the hide-a-key under the frog statue. It should have been dusty, but my mother had made sure it never was. The air had settled, though. It had that long-closed smell like an attic thinking of cedar. I stood in the living room for a minute and let my eyes make the jump between what had been and what was: the lashed-together books, the picture frames turned face down on an end table, the dent in the couch where she always read the paper and fell asleep. The mail in a tidy stack on the hall table. A florist's card with a scrawled sorry again.

"Well," I said to the house. It did not say anything back.

"Is that you, honey?" called a voice from the porch. I started hard enough that the keys bit my palm.

Ruth Kemper from three doors down had aged into one of those lovely old women the town pretends out of whole cloth: narrow as a birch tree, face composed of soft folds and fierce eyes. When we were kids, she gave out full-size candy bars at Halloween and got away with it without anyone accusing her of anything. She was holding a Tupperware container, which she offered the way one offers a first drink to someone coming out of the cold.

"Lasagna," she said. "You look like you haven’t eaten since Easter."

"I ate," I lied, and let her in.

We put the lasagna in my mother's refrigerator to think about itself. Ruth made tea, the way my mother had always made tea, which is to say she boiled the water and spooned great sums of it into mugs until each string draped down like a flag at half-mast. The kitchen table had a scratch in one corner where I had carved my initials on a dare from no one. Ruth set her mug over it like she was shielding the damage.

"You got my message," she said.

"I did," I said. "Thank you for—"

"I didn't know the post would take this long. That's the thing about relying on the government. I told Eileen I'd run it to you myself, but she said no, she'll have the mail do it. You know how she was."

"Stubborn," I said, and realized my voice made it into a joke. The tape's weight in my bag made it into not one.

Ruth's eyes did a small glance to the living room. My mother’s photograph on the mantel had been turned face down too—some old superstition about souls finding their way back if you left faces out. Ruth noticed it and turned it upright with a sigh.

"They told her it was nothing," she said. "They always tell you it's nothing until it isn't. She said to me, 'Ruthie, everything in me feels like a hallway.'"

"I didn't know," I said.

"That's because she didn't want you to," she said. "She said you had your work. She said listening to old things was important. She said it like it hurt."

We drank our tea. The house settled. The river is close enough and busy enough with itself that sometimes you can hear it in these kitchens like a second conversation. You pretend you aren't hearing it because if you admit you are, you'll start to carry it around like an extra weight.

"Do you know what this is?" I asked her. I took the little black cassette out of my bag and put it on the table. Her eyes widened as if I'd put meat down between us.

"I do," she said. "I told her she was foolish for keeping it. I told her I'd throw it in the river myself. She said no, it had to go to you, because you had—" She fluttered her fingers, groping for a word she had never needed. "Ears for it."

"Did she say where she made it?" I asked.

"You know where she made it," she said, and her face did something angry for the first time. "Up there. At Casimir." She jerked her head in the direction of the hill. "You and I both know there's no bell there to ring. They took what they could salvage and hauled it away. They tore down the roof and left the stone where it fell. And still—" She broke off. The tea in her cup trembled a little in her hand.

"And still," I said.

"They came to see it, you know," she said. "The kind of people who hear about a fire and go to stand and pick what they can out of the ashes. They took pictures at night like they were waiting for it to light itself again. They told stories in the diner about the altar candle relighting, about voices. Sound carries in that hollow. Kids go kiss there now. The sheriff runs them off when she remembers."

"She?" I said.

"Sheriff March. Olive March. You were gone by the time she came up from Harper's Ferry. She won't love you wandering up there in the dark, but she can't stop you either. You're thirty-five if you're a day. You know how to put your hood up."

"I'm thirty-four," I said, because people like to hear you correct them down. Ruth grinned, which made her look briefly like the Halloween version of herself.

"What's up there besides stone?" I asked.

"Who knows?" she said. "A fox living under the stairs. Some boys' light beer. The ghost of a bell. My grandson says the starling flock goes through at dusk in October and it sounds like static."

The day slid down. The light in my mother's kitchen always seemed to get thin suddenly. I rinsed our tea mugs and left them in the rack as if the old habit could conjure someone to put them away. Ruth put her hand on my arm at the door and squeezed without saying any of the things you say when you are a person older than grief talking to a person standing at the lip of it.

At nine, I lay on the bed in the little spare room and scrolled my mother’s phone in the blue-dark. The last few texts were mundane in the way that seems like kindness after someone's gone: bring back the casserole; can anyone go to the post office; the horseradish brought tears to my eyes. One number with no name had sent a single message four months back: We should stop. Then, two weeks later: I’m sorry. I did not click through. I am not immune to the urge to draw connections where there might be none. I didn't need to invent a lover for my mother that night.

I set the phone face down and forced my eyes shut. Sleep, when it came, had the sloppy edges of jet lag without the geography. I was dreaming about the lab—mixing two tapes that shouldn't be on the same deck—when my phone's lock screen lit the room a gray more like water than light. I rolled over and squinted. 2:13 AM blinked back. A split second later, as if it had been waiting politely for me to consent to it, a sound threaded itself into the house.

Don't write this down like it sounded like something. Write it down as itself. The bell's first toll struck and was a layman's opinion about what struck three centuries ago might mean now. It came from up the hill. It came from the wrong place in my chest. It carried because sound always carries in fog, and the fog had come in off the river, a low roll I had not noticed until the bell told on it. A second toll followed, and then a third, like a thought repeating itself to be sure it was a thought.

I sat up. I could feel my face flatten into something useful. My jacket was on the chair. The flashlight that lived under the sink was still there when I went to find it, its beam a soft disagreement with the dark. I put on the boots by the back door that had always been a little too big for me because my mother had bought them a size up, expecting me to grow.

The air on the porch was cool and wet. The town was a smear of lights and fog. I thought, ridiculously, about the time in seventh grade I had snuck out and been caught by my own mother with a flashlight under this same swing. She had laughed, then made me hand over the flashlight like contraband and said, "What if you want to see?" It had sounded like a riddle then and like good advice now. The bell rang a fourth time. I glanced at my phone, at the 2:13 like a judge. When it surged toward 2:14, the fifth toll came and pushed back time like a hand on a fruit bowl.

The walk up to Saint Casimir is not steep, but the grass had gone wild in the months of no traffic. The path that used to be brick was interrupted by places where roots had decided they were old enough to insist on themselves. My boots slid once and then found grip. The bell rang the eighth time in the middle of the low stretch by the sledding hill. I paused because my chest had that bad parlor-trick feeling of having two hearts.

By the ninth toll I had the church's low wall in view. By the tenth I had my hand on the stone of the entry arch, which was blackened still in places where the fire had licked and been sated. The stain made my palm dirty with soot that was older than some people's children. I did not step inside at the eleventh. I am not immune to the power of thresholds. I leaned in and cast the flashlight across what used to be a nave and was now a picnic for ghosts.

People had done to the ruin what people always do: they had made it a place for their names. The walls were carved and inked and spelled with envy. The altar was a slab of white pocked with cigarette burns. The bell tower had been reduced to a frame of brick, the cavity where the bell had hung a cross-section of nothing. The twelfth toll rolled over the wall and into the absence like it had a right.

My mother had always told me the trick to finding what you want in the dark is to remember you are not the only thing there. I let the light move slow. I let shadows be. I listened to the quiet between the tolls like it might be trying to say something. On the thirteenth, the flashlight caught a scattering of white like broken shells, and then a shoe—the rubber sole of a work boot, the leather gone scuffled and wet. A leg. A hand curled as if the person it belonged to had died while asking a question.

I moved forward before I told myself to. There is a speed your body keeps for certain boats leaving certain docks, for corners you have already decided to turn. I did not step in the prints making a damp procession across the floor; they were recent and would be interesting to someone. The beam found the man's face and stopped there, because my face stopped there. It was Tom Halden, who had become caretaker of this ruin not because that was a job and someone had hired him, but because he was the kind of man who mowed rings into the grass around things.

He wasn't the kind of dead I had expected. I don't know what I had expected—perhaps a quiet untidiness, the stillness bodies make when they decide not to swear anymore. His eyes were closed. His mouth had a stubborn set I recognized from school board meetings. He looked like a man who had been arguing and then had forgotten how to find the next point. There was a long, shallow bruise along his throat like someone had put a hand there and set it back down. His left palm was open. In it lay a shard of something black and metal with a hole at one end and a broken edge at the other, a piece sniffed by fire and saved by someone's impulse to pocket it.

The little piece looked like a clapper does when a bell doesn't need it anymore.

I stood there and did what people do when they take a first breath at the lip of a wrong thing—weighed the weight of my name being attached to the finding of it. If I called, I'd be back in this town in a way that didn't end when I wanted. If I didn't, I would be someone else for good.

The bell ringing had stopped. It hadn't faded. It hadn't been swallowed by fog. It had gone from sound to no sound like a switch. I felt the tremor of it still in my chest and wondered if that was alarm or residue, if there was a difference.

My phone in my pocket had no signal here, not anymore. I turned and saw, through the arch, down the cut of the hill, Ruth's porch light like a dot in a dark map and, farther off, the blue blink of a cruiser light where the bridge wall met the river. Sheriff March had been pulled from bed by someone else's small emergency. I could follow my own footsteps back and wave my arms from the road like a person in a storm. Or I could wait with the dead man and the thrown-down silence and the little piece of metal in his open hand to see who else had heard the impossible sound and chosen to climb.

So I waited. The air pressed on my ears. In the blank that followed reverberation, you can hear the shape of what's left. The shape here was a long breath held. The red eye of my flashlight throbbed when it wanted to warn me of its dying battery, then quieted as if choosing mercy. Somewhere just beyond my hearing, the river made one of its useless arguments with the bank and lost. The fog settled, a shoulder over a shoulder.

Footsteps came up the path five minutes later, fast and unhappy. The beam of another flashlight found and then slid off my jacket. A voice called, not loudly, not with authority but with disbelief. "Mara?"

"Here," I said. I could have said a lot of things. I said the one word in my mother’s voice. And the sound of it, in that place, was another thing I would regret in a list I did not yet know.

The book drop had its own weather. It swallowed the day’s leavings in metallic gulps and exhaled little breaths of cold air through the chute, smelling of iron no matter the season. On windy nights, when the old brick walls hummed and the town’s flag snapped itself silly outside, the drop clicked and rocked and muttered, and I could convince myself that the library was as alive as any creature I had ever known—obstinate, benevolent, and tired.

Tonight, it was just past nine-thirty and the wind was out of the west hard enough to knock a last clinging maple leaf against the high arched windows, an arrhythmic tapping like impatient fingers. Down the hall, the boiler turned over in its sleep. I’d already shelved the newest donated paperbacks that smelled like suntan lotion and garage oil, turned the lamps off in the genealogy room where a framed portrait of the town founders insisted on catching a glint that made them look like they were wearing glass eyes, and walked through the stacks once without finding any rogue toddlers or teenagers.

“Closing in five,” I’d called at eight-thirty to no one at all. My own voice had surprised me in the quiet.

Gray Harbor’s Carnegie library was a stubborn square of granite on a hill, the kind of building that outlasted businesses and marriages. Alumni took wedding photos on the steps and teenagers smoked behind the statue of a muscled boy holding a tablet like a lunch tray. Inside, it creaked and settled and kept secrets the way old buildings do, gently, over time.

I am not the kind of librarian who shushes. I believe in noise on the right side of the afternoon, in babies who discover their echoes, in teens who argue about dragons. Tonight, though, I was an island at the front desk with the lights thrown low and the computer screens winking their low-battery are-you-sure-you-mean-to-be-here messages at me.

The drop thunked again. Not the papery swish of a paperback or the cheerful clatter of a DVD case. A single solid weight hitting metal and then sliding down to the bin. Even after two years back on the job, some part of me always wanted to say Bless you after a particularly good thump. The building had its own manners.

I took the keyring out of my cardigan pocket and went to the sorting room. The motion sensor light hummed awake. The bin under the chute was painted schoolroom green and had a graceful dent on the side, like someone had set it down on a hill in 1961 and never quite remedied the tilt. It looked empty.

Then I saw it, lying like a fallen brick at the bottom. An old hardcover, clothbound, the kind of book that throws off dust like a sigh when you lift it, only this one didn’t dust. Its edges were ragged, the corners charred. The spine had a strip of masking tape, brittle and stained, with a faded hand-lettered call number.

I know the weight of a hundred thousand books. I know the way paper ages and how glue goes and what mildew does. I know when something doesn’t belong. Standing there in the humming light with the boiler turning over again down below, I knew that book had not been in anyone’s tote bag next to a bunch of grapes. It smelled faintly of creek water and smoke.

I crouched and lifted it with both hands. The cover was once a handsome dark blue, but had been singed to a weary gray. The title was thorny with gilt.

“The Moonstone,” I read out loud. Of course.

My breath made a little cloud. The sorting room’s heater was a rumor, not a reality. I carried the book to the table where the book tape and stamps lived, the familiar rhythms ready in my hands. Cover inspection. Pocket check. Card check. Interior inspection. The ritual always calmed me. Tonight, the edges of ritual cut.

Inside, the book’s pocket was intact, glued in the old way, neat and square. There was a check-out card tucked into it, yellowed and thin as an onion skin. In the neat squares, rubber stamps marched backward: APR 12 1991, DEC 3 1986, MAR 27 1984. A child had once practiced writing their name under the lined space—looping, consonants too tall. At the top, above all those tidy stamps, the name in pencil: C. Hollis. Due date: SEP 17 2003.

My throat closed. I meant to set the book down gently. It made a choked noise when it hit the table anyway, because the table has a wobble I keep meaning to fix.

C. Hollis. Caroline Hollis. My mother.

I pressed my thumb to the corner of the card because it was either that or press it to my own lip to stop whatever wanted to spill out of me. The pencil had bitten hard into the fibers. Someone must have written it quickly, standing at the desk in the almost-long-ago.

My mother had been a substitute at the desk sometimes, when the head librarian’s early-onset arthritis was bad. She was not a reader. She was a doer. She had come into the building with a bucket and a rag after the winter storms to wipe away the tracked-in salt and had bantered with me under breath while I did my homework. There were people here who thought of her as the woman who straightened the chairs, and people who thought of her as the thief.

The map had gone missing the night the west wing flooded in the downpour of 2003. The longer story, the one that shaped me like a wrong shoe shapes a foot, was this: I was twelve. The river went up over the banks and curled itself around Main Street like a satisfied cat, and down in the basement storage Grandpa Reed—who had insisted on the title Facilities for thirty-two years—waded chest-deep to turn off the breaker. When they did the insurance inventory afterward, they couldn’t find the Gray Harbor survey map, hand-drawn in 1864 by a man with a sentimental mustache and a steady hand, a town treasure behind glass in the genealogy room. The story you could hear in the café if you lingered over a second muffin was simpler. Caroline Hollis had been the last one to see the map before the storm, and after the storm, Caroline Hollis got smaller, and then she left, and then nobody saw her again, not in this town or any other.

Boxes arrived addressed to me for a while—socks that wandered, once a ceramic owl. The postmarks were from places you can’t picture without working too hard: Wamsutta, Rhode Island; Cedartown, Georgia. Then the boxes stopped.

Even in my head I had reduced her to a rumor’s proportions, because it was easier to shelve without crying if the woman who’d left me was already only the size of someone’s opinion.

But here was her name, in pencil, my own letters in it—the loose C, the honest slant of the s. Caroline Hollis had checked out The Moonstone in September 2003 and, if the card was to be believed, never brought it back.

I slid the card back into its pocket and turned the page. The frontis had a woodcut of a hand holding an oil lamp. Someone, decades ago, had let a child draw a mustache on the hand. The second page was warped and discolored on the edge, as if it had drunk in a little of the flood and kept it. The gutter made a soft sjjjj noise as I opened it, the sound of cloth loosening its grip. There, pressed past the title pages and into chapter one, was an envelope.

It wasn’t library issue. Not the white woven kind we used to mail overdue notices to the address of a third spouse. This was a thin, brown, flaky paper like the envelopes my grandmother had used for cash to pay the electric. On the front, the writing was done with a fountain pen, real ink with that blood-warm semigloss that you can almost feel by looking at it. Two words, no address:

Caroline’s girl.

I set my fingers on the edge of the envelope and then put them back. No one else was here. The sorting room light hummed. The book drop sighed.

I carried the book and its envelope to the front desk where the big lamp threw a better light. The analog clock behind me said 9:41, though it has been five minutes behind for twenty years, so really it was closer to 9:46. I could feel the building’s weight leaning into the night. The wind plucked at the glass in the vestibule. I turned my phone over on the desktop so the screen faced me without lighting my own chin like a campfire, then I slid a fingernail under the envelope flap.

It had been opened before and closed with meticulous care. The glue, originally cheap and aggressive, flaked up like the edge of a scab. Inside was a key.

It was an old key, the impossible kind we always think are romantic and then are irritated by because they open exactly nothing now except decorative boxes. Brass, darkened where fingers had worried it, with a bed of grime worked into its grooves that I recognized as the honest work of years. On the round end, someone had scratched two letters into it with something sharp enough to do it and careless enough not to make them gentle. R.J.

In the bottom of the envelope there was also a folded piece of index card. Not a whole card—someone had cut it to a tidy rectangle. On one side, the library stamp bled through: GRAY HARBOR PUBLIC LIBRARY. On the other, typed letters, the kind you see in ransom notes in movies but without the melodrama: a typewriter’s steady characters, misaligned just enough to let me hear the small thwacks in my head.

813.5 • NORTH ROOM • ASK FOR THE SOUND.

My first thought was classification. Eight hundred thirteens are American fiction. Likewise, eight hundred thirteen point five—what, mid-twentieth-century authors? Newer than Wharton, older than Updike. My brain went there out of habit, filing the numbers into shelves, the way a mother puts a feverish hand on a forehead and thinks soup.

North Room meant the genealogy room. The north wall had family bibles and the local paper from 1899 forward bound in volumes too heavy for the new volunteers. There was a shelf there with fiction, yes, a strange leftover from when the library had fewer rooms and we arranged things where they fit, not where they made sense. I could picture the call number labels there, could almost see the O’Haras and the Oates in their ragged jackets, the Oglesby Novelists’ Club Self-Published Anthology a permanent shelf-sitter.

Ask for the sound.

As I read it again, the drop thunked. I jumped, then laughed at myself. The laugh was a brittle little bone. I went back to the sorting room. Nothing had come down now; it was the wind in the chute again, making the flap kick like a mule.

When I turned around, the shape on the far side of the main room made me freeze the way you do when you think you’ve seen a deer at the side of a road and it turns out to be a stump. The lamps were dim, so the long reading tables were islands of glow, and beyond them the stacks were shadows. Against the deeper shadow of the periodicals, there was a darker piece of shadow, too angular to be a person, too tall to be one of our chairs. I took two steps forward. The shape resolved into the book cart I had abandoned three hours ago, heavy with new donations. I exhaled again and made myself motion. The building turned on its heel and became familiar, which is another way of saying I let it.

I wanted to bolt the doors and go upstairs right away and paw through the north wall like a raccoon in a garden. The envelope was in my sweater pocket, the key warm now from my hand. I went to the front just to make certain the vestibule door was locked. The wind clawed politely at the glass when I reached for it, and a thin layer of leaves slid down the steps like flattening birds. Across Main Street, the bar gave a laugh like a dropped tray. Somewhere a dog started to talk itself into believing that other dogs existed.

I pulled the deadbolt, checked it twice the way I do and the way my grandfather had done (“Remember, Wren. Twice. We’re not Fort Knox but we don’t have to advertise”). The streetlight cast a slice of yellow through the door’s window and laid it across the foyer like something we could trip on. The placard with winter hours swung a little on its hook.

On the desk, my phone buzzed. Not a text. A call. Unknown number, local area code. I let it go to voicemail out of reflex. It buzzed again immediately, a second call, the device’s way of tapping my shoulder and insisting. I swiped because sometimes missing calls is a way to add to your pile of regrets, and mine doesn’t need help.

“Library,” I said, because it’s how you answer; it’s how I’ve answered since I was sixteen.

There was a pause long enough to filigree the air with my own breath. Then a voice, low, a men’s radio voice, a voice you trust when you shouldn’t.

“Did you get it?” he asked.

“Who is this?” I said. My tone came out professional-frost, the sort I use when someone calls at noon to ask if we have a notary and refuses to believe the answer is still no.

“You did,” the man said, as if I had answered. “Don’t say the name out loud. Not there.”

“I don’t know what you—”

“I’m telling you to lock up and go home.” The voice softened and got more dangerous. “Someone’s watching the doors.”

The line clicked like a tongue on palate. The connection ended.

I looked at the glass in the vestibule and waited for a shadow like you do when you don’t want it at all. There was no shadow, only the flattened birds of leaves, pressed into a glistening shape where the earlier rain had slicked the stone, and the slow parade of late people in coats like moving lumps of darkness. I set the phone down, useless, the way you set down a knife you aren’t ready to touch again.

“I think you’re being dramatic,” I said out loud to the empty room, because it is healthier to pretend aloneness is a choice.

I turned the desk lamp down. The place with the map in its glass case—that spot in the genealogy room where the sun had bleached the carpet in an even rectangle—glowed faintly. The case was still there; we had never bothered to replace the map with anything more than a framed photograph of it, like people who keep a picture of the old dog on the mantle after the collar is gone, because absence needs something to stand in for it other than an emptiness you trip over.

There is a peculiar courage in small-town nights. We are not so anonymous as cities and not so spread as true rural. We belong to one another whether we want to or not. I turned my collar up in my cardigan as if it were a coat and walked the long way around through the stacks to the north room.

As a child, I used to wedge myself back there and read under the table with my mother’s foot touching mine, a pressure like an anchor. As an adult, my ears have catalogued the small sounds—paper touching paper, HVAC doing a low sermon, those words you hear only when you can pretend you didn’t. Tonight those sounds had a layer laid over them, like someone had put tracing paper between me and the library and drawn the outline of me very carefully.

The genealogy room smelled like paste and cedar. The north wall shelves were original to the building, with a carved border along the top of them my grandfather had dented in one place with a ladder the summer they redid the lighting and never told anyone. I could find that dent in the dark. I let my fingers find it now, and then I walked them along the spines the way you do when you are trying not to delay and trying not to hurry.

There it was. 813.5. A row of novels with jackets gone and boards in utilitarian colors. I remember the book called Shore Leave by R. J. North, a local curiosity whose main charm was that the author had once thrown up in the back of the bar across the street and autographed a napkin about it. The call number labels were old, typed on with as even a hand as we could manage then, some of the adhesives giving way and the little white corners lifting like speak now or forever hold your peace.

Ask for the sound.

Ask who? What had been added to our old wood and paper that I was meant to hear?

I said, very quietly, “What am I supposed to ask?”

It was absurd, speaking to pine boards and cloth. It felt necessary. My voice got swallowed in the way small rooms swallow.

Under the shelf, where the baseboard met the floorboards, there was a grille. The building’s old vent system, closed off thirty years ago when the new ductwork went in. I had put paper over it once to keep out drafts. The paper was gone now. The grille was dusty.

I knelt. The wood floor pinched my knees through my tights. The grille’s screws were big slotted ones, the sort my grandfather had pretended not to mind stripping. I touched one with the edge of the brass key, because sometimes I am my grandfather. The key fit the slot as if it had been waiting to be more useful than decorative its whole life.

It made a small sound when the screw turned. Not a squeal or a protest. A click like a throat clearing.

In the front of the building, a door latch made a minute noise.

Every part of me wanted to flinch. I breathed instead. The boiler turned over again, six beats and then a pause that always made me think it would stop forever and then it didn’t. I turned the second screw. The grille loosened. The smell that came through it was old dust and a sweeter-thinner layer underneath, like flowers pressed in a book eighty years ago.

Behind the grille, beyond the slats, there was darkness first. Then my eyes adjusted that half-inch that makes the world appear. A small pile of reels. Magnetic tape, four inches across. The kind of reels you could load onto the portable recorder we keep under lock in the media room for when donors bring in old interviews. The reels had labels. They said, in someone’s careful hand, NORTH ROOM, 9/16/03—then the next, 9/17/03.

ASK FOR THE SOUND, the card had said.

I reached in. The tape was cool under my fingers, every turn of it holding something tight as breath.

When I stood, my knees cracked, and then someone knocked on the glass of the front door, knuckles flat, a sound like a simple fact finding my bones. My name rose into my mouth and I swallowed it, and in that one moment before I moved, I wondered if I was going to be someone who opened a door or someone who listened first.

The building waited with me. The library has always been patient with our choices.

Chapter One

By late afternoon the Halcyon Theatre looked like a ship caught mid-sinking. Its marble façade sloughed plaster in tides, letters of its name missing so that HALC—N gaped like a broken jaw. Pigeons kept watch from the architrave. The rain had tapered off, leaving the street slick and the scaffolding a grid of wet bones. I killed the engine and sat for a second with my hands on the steering wheel, listening to the tick of cooling metal and someone’s radio bleeding a bass line two blocks away.

Kade had said it would be unlocked. He’d said other things too—how federal tax credits made even the haunted places worth restoring; how any story could be sanded, shellacked, staged anew. He’d said my name the way he said square footage and cost overruns and demographic data: with an efficient interest that made me careful.

I tucked my hood up and ran for the brass doors. The first one stuck until I leaned my shoulder in and the seal let go with a gasket’s sigh. Inside it smelled like wet velvet and old cigarettes, mouse droppings and gilt, a sweetness like rotting fruit. The lobby chandelier hung in a grease-slicked net of chains, draped to keep its crystals from shattering when the ceiling had sagged. Someone—caretaker, security—had left a single bulb lit on a stand by the stage: the ghost light. Its filament glowed a threadlike orange. The rest of the house was dim enough to convince your pupils that there were figures in every aisle, just at the edge of recognition.

“Hello?” I called, because even people who work in sound try their voices first. It came back to me soft and rounded, like the room had cupped my consonants in the palm of its hand. After a second, in the habit I had since I was a kid, I snapped my fingers and listened. The tail of the reverb told me the story of the plaster curves overhead, the velvet rot of the seats, the portly columns that held up the second balcony. It told me what it could not tell other people: where the empty was.

I set my case on the lobby floor and flipped the latches. Microphones wrapped like swaddled moths. A little laptop. Balloons for impulse response tests. A coil of cable with its own inclinations, to be tamed. People imagine that acoustics is a matter of taste, the way wine is. In truth, so much is math and material. Reverberation time. Frequency absorption. Flutter echo. The ring in your skull when you sing inside a stairwell. I’d learned to trust my measurements even when my left ear—the one that didn’t quite pull its weight anymore—sold me a lie.

“Dr. Keane?” The voice came from the shadow of the box office window, and a small woman produced herself with a key ring like a curtain of metal hair. Her sweater was zipped up to the throat and had a little pilled hood with ears that suggested she entertained grandchildren, or cats, or both. “Glad you got in. I’m Pell. Sit guy’s on a coffee run. The downstairs is lighted, such as it is. Upstairs is—well, don’t fall. There’s still holes everywhere.”

“I’ll be careful,” I said. “I just need a few hours. I can manage the lights.”

She passed me a key on a blue lanyard. “Heard you knew this place, once upon a time.”

“Everyone in this city knew it,” I said.

Pell’s mouth did a little skeptical twitch. “Not like you, honey. Matinee baby, weren’t you? Your daddy on staff?”

On staff. That was one way. He’d been the head carpenter, the union’s loudest voice, the man who put a hammer in my hand as soon as I learned not to hit my own thumb. He’d been the one who let me sleep on a pile of drop cloths in the wings during tech week, who taught me to sit still and watch the fly system move like a skeleton, who told me that a building that big had to tell you how it wanted to stand up, you just had to be quiet enough to hear.

“Long time ago,” I said. “Back when it was still open.”

Pell’s eyes ticked past me to the scaffolding, to the empty street, to the fact of me there with my silver case. “You got my number if you need to come and go. After five the front locks itself, but the side door by the alley’s temperamental, you give it a knee it’ll common sense. You got a deadline?”

I smiled. “Don’t I always.”

She left with a squeal of sneakers and the door’s breath sucked back in. I stood in the muted fountain of the chandelier’s plastic wrap and looked up like I always did: the fresco ceiling with goddesses scumbled by water damage, the proscenium arch carved with laurel and those little fat men who look like they want to whisper in your ear. Halcyon, from the kingfisher who calmed storms, they said when they opened it in 1928 to a line down the block. Halcyon, from the year everything shut, when a soprano named Vera Glass fell from the catwalk during a strike and never made it to the ambulance. After that came rumors, then nails pried from the doorframes, then vagrants, then graffiti, then quiet.

My father left at two in the morning on the night of the closure, coatless. He’d been furious—everybody had been—and then he was simply not there anymore. A shovel of snow on the sidewalk with a trail of his boots leading away. Eighteen years. People learned to say this city out of their mouths without thinking of the Halcyon. I went to school, learned to hear the world, learned how little we notice about the way the air and walls are talking.

“Okay,” I said to the room. “Let’s start.”

I set microphones at the stage lip, at the middle of the stalls, under the balcony, up a top row where the oxygen thins. I walk-tested the aisles. I marked the spots where the carpet sank more than an inch. I blew up a balloon to a globe of pink and rolled it like a slow planet in my hands. Then I held it up and pinched the neck and let the rubber stretch and shriek until the world did what it does when you ask it, hard enough: it answered.

The pop was enormous, a crack with a tail. The ghost light quivered. The response washed around me in waves. It was still a good room, even with its decay. Two seconds to RT60 at the mid-frequencies, a whisper longer under the balcony, a flutter between two parallel walls at the rear, that could be broken with scattering panels, no problem. I watched the waveform flatten on the screen. I did another by the second balcony and listened to the difference stones make. I counted the blind seconds it took to die.

On the third test, at the foot of the stage, something issued back that didn’t belong there. It wasn’t the reverb. It was buried in the last inchworming of the sound, an articulation that wasn’t any of mine. A syllable that rode the decaying smear of energy like a fish moving upstream. It was not the trick the brain plays where it makes faces in clouds and names in noise. It was as if the room, tired of entertaining strangers, had decided to say my name.

Lin.

Just that, a small thing, two letters rounded off. A vowel opening like a door. I killed the meters and listened to the hush like it had become a new weather. Old buildings do this. They ask for your caution with every creak. Your pulse leaps at rats, at pigeons, at sheet plastic breathing in the world’s draft. My left ear translated the sound as metal scraping; my right ear insisted on the soft skin of voice. I told myself I was tired. I told myself I hadn’t eaten, that my blood sugar does few if any kindnesses after three.

“Hello?” I said again, and hated that it was the same word as before. I walked closer to the stage and put my palms on the boards, feeling for vibrated proof. The stage was an old bragger. It wanted a thousand pounds of chorus girls, a train set rolling at three miles per hour, a storm built out of foam and reachable with a ladder. It wanted to be cheered at. It humored my breath.

Behind the proscenium the fly system towered, endless ropes and counterweights, batten after batten above me like ribs. The catwalks were rigged with caution tape, the tape rippled by drafts from who knew where. The ghost light burned steadily, a star at stage center. There were names written everywhere if you knew how to look. Sharpied hearts on the masking. Cigarette burns on the 1928 muslin drop. Initials carved into the rail. The building had spent a century collecting people's insistence that they’d been here.

I went to the wings and checked my left monitor. I set another balloon free and popped it on the count of two and waited. The tail caught. It caught on a frequency that had a corner to it, as if reflecting off not the wide curve of the wall but something concave: a void, a pocket, a shell of space behind the plaster. The numbers on the screen did their math; the sense in my bones did a different kind. That empty I’d heard when I came in had a border.

You learn to map these hollows by ear. On job sites I’ve found brick wells under floorboards and false chimneys behind drywall. You knock and the sound comes back with a history. I knocked on the upstage wall. Two bright fingertip taps and then, between them, a darker answer.

The access to the fly loft was up an iron staircase that made noises like an old woman getting out of bed. My boots left tracks in the dust that had layered itself like pollen. Bees hadn’t made this place in a long time, but the feeling of humming held anyway. People think theatres are rooms. They’re not. They’re stacks of rooms, slices of air. The catwalks sighed when my weight stepped on them, metal exclaiming in its own language. I moved with the old caution, hand to the rail at all times, not looking down except when I looked down. The ghost light’s halo spread thin and buttery as a coin a long way off.

At the grid the space behind the proscenium narrowed to a throat. I squeezed through where once I would have run. The plaster molding from the other side revealed its chicken-wire skeleton. Dead birds lay like leather gloves. The void I’d heard was above the arch, a chamber the old designers had used to house lighting equipment and, once, a pair of horns that shot sound toward the cheap seats before amplification was anything but mechanical. The hatch to it had been closed and painted over. The paint had cracked along the seam, a fine net of channels like a leaf’s veins.

I laid my ear against the plaster and knocked. And there it was again: the hollow, the different reverb. I took out my little penknife.

Years ago my father had stuck me in just such a hole during a thunderstorm and told me to tell him what the building said. He was kidding, mostly. But he meant it, too. Buildings keep what we tell them, Lin, he’d said. They get fat on it. Some of it they never give back.

The paint flaked off under the blade. The plaster underneath had been patched and patched again. A circle revealed the shape of a handle, or had once. No metal remained, just the ghost of it in the way the plaster remembered. I edged my knife around until the circle deepened and the knife slipped through. The hatch gave with a little cough. I breathed dust and something sweeter, like powder. I wedged the panel free and pulled it away, trying not to think of how far there was to fall if I forgot my body in the theater’s history.

My phone’s flashlight made a cone. It lit a chamber big enough to crouch in, not to stand. Bits of rosined rope. A ring bolt embedded in brick. Someone’s two buttons. Somebody’s bottle cap worry-smoothed to silver. And on the far wall, in chalk that had lasted long past whatever hand had held it, letters leaned downhill in a rush:

I DID NOT FALL.

My hand shook like a badly tuned cymbal. I sat cross-legged on the catwalk and pressed my back to the nearest post because suddenly my legs were hollow reeds. The chalk had smeared at the tail of the L. I wanted to touch that smudge with my finger and know if it had been wet when the person had turned to whatever came next. The dust shifted, or I imagined it did, with my breath.

Vera Glass fell. That had been the story I’d learned like everybody else. Maybe not the first week, maybe not the first month, but at home, where stories were correctives to the things you couldn’t help hearing, and in the newspaper, when they still printed news instead of everything else. Vera Glass fell, and three stagehands were fired in the week that followed, one for drinking on the job, one for bringing a knife to a strike, one for threatening a producer. None of that mattered because the Halcyon closed, and the unions went to war with the developers and the developers won. And two in the morning, my father left with his coat on the peg because he thought it would take him two minutes to tell someone to go to hell and then he would come home, and instead he kept walking.

I got my recorder out and held it in the hatchway and turned it on. When you don’t know what to do, you set two steps of a ritual in motion. You listen. The small fan sounded like a moth. I noted the date and time into the mic like I always did, like I was steady. “Halcyon Theatre, stage house, upper proscenium cavity, unidentified chalk markings. Origin unknown,” I said. My voice sounded like someone competent. My right hand stopped its tremor to hold the pen. “Note: entry appears original. Ropes present. It smells like—” I paused, and felt ridiculous. “Like powder. Makeup. Is that possible? Pell?”

My phone had enough signal to scrape a text through. I told her I’d found an accessible hatch and asked if she knew about it. Then I waited, which is a thing a lot of people never learn and I had learned too well. The city’s hum rarely reached in that far. If you listened for it, you could tell wind from traffic from the train. If you listened hard enough, other things came back to you. I breathed. I tried not to hear my name in the quiet.

Footsteps scuffed below. They weren’t mine, and they were not Pell’s sneakers. They were shoes with a heel and weight, the weight that says: this person does not imagine a reason to sneak. That person moved across the stage, not hurried, and stopped directly beneath the ghost light. The sound changed the way it does when someone stands under a night streetlamp while you’re watching from a window two floors up. He or she put a palm to the stage’s center—sound tells you when a surface takes pressure—and then something heavy clicked against wood. Metal. A tool, maybe. Maybe a flashlight’s barrel.

I leaned out from the hatch, careful, and peered down like an idiot. The angle showed me the sightline between the ropes. The ghost light was a star and whoever was under it a planet that occulted it. A shoulder. A cap. A jacket the color of stale coffee. I held my breath until my left ear faulted the world to a ringing pure tone and my right ear had to work alone.

“Hello?” I called, and waited for the echo to lie to me or the person to answer.

The person didn’t. The person looked up, slow. The cap’s visor made a blade of shadow across a face I couldn’t see. He raised an arm and adjusted the brim like an old-fashioned gesture from some other decade, then turned away. There was a smudge of chalk on the back of his coat, a pale handprint at the shoulder that someone had left on him, or he’d left on the wall. He walked toward the wings with that same steady weight and vanished into the space where every magician you ever loved disappears.

My phone buzzed like a wasp in my hand. Pell: What hatch?

I texted back: Behind the proscenium. Looks original. There’s a message.

Another buzz, immediate: Get down.

I read it twice because my hands didn’t seem to understand the sequence of letters. Get down. My body took a second to choose a meaning. The old building breathed. The rain started again out there in the world, and the drip through the roof found its old channel and resumed the song it knew. I had not turned my recorder off.

I slid the panel back into place over the chalk like a bandage over a wound but I could not make it hold. The plaster was too old and the friction too low and the gravity too inevitable. It tilted, then stuck at the angle that meant it would fall if a cat looked at it hard. I backed down the catwalk with a hand on the railing and watched the not-quite-closed hole out of the corner of my eye like it was a mouth about to start speaking.

At the bottom of the stairs the ghost light burned and burned and at the lip of the stage there was a mark in chalk like a child’s drawing: a fish shape, two arcs crossing in the middle, a casual sign old Christians still scrawl on napkins. The chalk line blurred where a shoe had stepped through it. It could have been anyone’s symbol. It could have been someone’s house.

“Ms. Keane?” The voice came from the side door, Pell’s this time, and her breath carried the roughness of a sprint. She had her key ring out like a weapon, and her eyes were the tilted eyes of cats who know too much. “Don’t be upstairs alone,” she said. “Ever. Not this week.”

“Why? What—who was—?”

She shook. Her keys clinked like rain. “You hearing things? Don’t listen. No good comes of it. You want to do your clapping thing, you do it fast. You write it down. You tell Mr. Kade. You send him your invoice. You don’t listen, honey. Not here.”

Behind her, outside in the gray streetlight, a pickup idled with its hazard lights blinking and a Foreman leaning on its hood. Above us the chandelier’s chain creaked the way it does when the building neutralizes the night with the quiet movements of its own weight. You could chalk it up to physics. You could chalk it up to the wind. You could chalk it up to an old room that had a message written inside its throat, words pressed by a hand now dust.

I looked up past the ghost light to the velvet curtain that would never again rise and down along the stage’s seam where boards joined boards. I had come to measure how the Halcyon would sound when they made it into condominiums and a restaurant called Halcyon with a thirty-two-dollar ribeye. Kade would want data. He would want graphs. He would not want this.

“Pell,” I said, “who else has a key?”

Her mouth twitched the way it had when she said my father had been on staff. “Same people always had keys,” she said. “Anybody says otherwise, they’re new to town.”

I stopped my recorder and slipped it into my coat pocket, the way you put something that can hurt you where you can feel the shape of it against your ribs.

On the catwalk above us, something shifted, or metal settled, or a person took a quiet step and made the smallest sound a body makes when it commits itself to moving. The building gave it back to us in that indefinite way that might be a warning or a welcome.

Up there in the chamber behind the proscenium, the chalk letters waited in the dark. They would not be truer for being seen twice. They were either true or they were not. This was a city that had learned to live between those options without going crazy. I had left to avoid practicing that skill. Scripts we inherit find their way back to us anyway.

“Let’s go,” Pell said, and her hand on my elbow had the strength of somebody who had kept a building alive by making it decide to let her.

We walked out under the chandelier’s net and into the lobby where the posters still layered the wall, women in feather headdresses peeling away from brick, and a framed black-and-white photo of a full house, every seat taken, faces turned up to the stage with the same expression people probably made at church, back when. In the lower right corner a man in shirtsleeves stood with his arms crossed, face in sharp focus, and I knew him as well as I knew my own. He had my eyebrows and my chin and the dense look he always got when he was about to say something true.

He had chalk dust on his shoulder in the picture too, a faint brush. I put my thumb against the glass because apparently I had decided to have one cliché today.

Outside, the rain started to come down for real, and the hazard lights made two old coins of light in the wash of it. The Halcyon watched us go with its missing Y like a mouth lacking its forked tongue. Alone in the dark behind the painted gods, a sentence glowed in my mind with the cheap cheap magic of chalk under a blacklight:

I DID NOT FALL.

The church that lay sixty feet under Addison Lake came back the way shame does—slowly, in stubborn inches. It breached the surface with a black line around its belly and the roof shingles wearing silt like ash. The bell tower came first, then the cross, then the bevelled window that no longer had any glass. One morning, there it was: not a rumor under water anymore but a squat steeple poking at the sky, the drowned town exhaling through new gullets of mud.

Wren Calder stood on the shoreline with her boots half-swallowed and her clipboard damp, watching the way the wind shivered the skin of the reservoir. Every time the lake pulled back, it left a sheen of something that caught the light: mica, fish scales, a soda can so old the paint had worn to an accusing ghost. She’d marked a grid across the exposed ground in pencil and flagged the no-go zones with red tape. Beyond those lines, locals already ghosted around bent at the waist, combing for bottles and story-worthy junk, ignoring the signs, avoiding the county truck like it could give citations from a hundred yards.

“They’ll go home when the smell sets in,” Samir had told her that first day. He was her lead technician, a diver with the calm, slightly flattened voice of someone who’d learned to talk and breathe through a regulator. “You can’t argue with rot.”

He was on the far side of the ruined foundation, rolling up geo-fabric you could lay across the worst of the muck to keep your boots_ from being claimed. Wren didn’t mind the stink. She minded the stories. That was the part she hadn’t remembered about March in Dorning County: everyone narrating while they worked, a running commentary on weather and time and what the water knew.

They were drawing down the reservoir to do an intake repair and a full inspection of the dam’s downstream face. Wren had arrived with a small team from the state water agency and a binder full of acronyms; this was a project and she had it broken down in weeks and tasks, contingencies stuffed behind contingencies. The old town under the lake was an obstacle, not a ghost. She told herself that when she signed the permits and again when she drove past the diner with its handmade sandwich board: WELCOME BACK TO ALDRIDGE. BE POLITE.

“Aldrige,” Samir had said the first time he read it, squinting. “They spelled it wrong.”

“That’s how some of the old maps have it,” Wren replied. “The E falls off.”

“They do that here?”

“They do that here,” she said, and didn’t add that she knew because she grew up a county over, because she had heard elders apply or remove letters at will like conferring or snatching away blessings. She didn’t say she knew because her mother’s voice came back to her at the edges of this work, telling her not to be cruel about place.

Now the church was up enough to make itself a problem. Her email had been a mix of alert and apology to the historic preservation list: They had limited time before spring rains. They had structural priorities. If anyone wanted documentation, it would have to be fast. The reply from a grad student had come in brightly within an hour, full of exclamation points and requests for access. Wren had deleted the emojis from her printout with the side of her thumb.

“This is going to be all over the local news, isn’t it?” Samir said. He shaded his eyes, watching as a man with a metal detector wobbled toward the church foundation like a loon.

“I’m going to go tell that guy he’s about to get stuck,” Wren said, and started walking.

She liked the give of the ground. Even when it tried to suction her boots off, the mud spoke clearly. It told you where the river had run before they dammed it, where the silt had eddied and dropped its shoulder. It needed reading the way her father had taught her to read water, before lecture halls and budgets turned it into numbers. She’d come back to Dorning in a mood that felt like flight. She hadn’t phrased it to herself that way. “A good project and close to home,” she’d told her boss, carefully neutral. The levee failure two years ago had left a stain that still moved under her skin if she let herself think on it. She didn’t let herself. She walked into the wind and the stink and focused on what this job needed.

Halfway to the church, the metal detector man looked up and saw her coming. He wasn’t particularly old, but he had stooped into the posture of someone who bent—to lift, to search, to expect—so often that straightening up didn’t occur to him. He wore a baseball cap with fraying embroidery. The cap’s bill was damp with the same lake smell that had settled into Wren’s clothes and hair.

“No trespassing beyond the flags,” she called.

He thumped the detector against his shoulder like a rifle and nodded at the church. “My mother’s picture is in there,” he said, conversational as weather. “On a board with faces. Wedding party in fifty-four. The girls all with tulips. The tulips died before the photo took. That was the story.”

“That’s not a reason,” Wren said, but not unkindly. “Even if it was safe, you can’t go in. It’s not your site.”

He looked beyond her to the far ridge, where the dam cut a clean, blunt line across two hills, an unnatural geometry against mid-March softness. “Whose, then?” he asked.

“County’s while it’s exposed. We’re doing work. Please step back behind the flags.”

He kept nodding like it helped him take this in. He had a wedding ring and thick, winter-cracked hands and boots worse than hers. “You from here?” he asked.

“No.”

“Sound like it.”

Wren heard old habit in the question, a way of sorting strangers by how much attention to pay them. She pretended to look down to check her boot and when she looked up again, he had retreated three steps and was, she had to admit, where she had asked him to be. He pulled the detector back down and set its head against the ground, a mechanical dog eager to nose around, and she left him to it.

At the base of the church, the mud rose in a berm, oily with trapped gas. The front doors had stayed put, that was the first surprise. The right-hand door had shifted and twisted, the wood swollen to the shape of water’s bias. The iron strap hinges held in a way that was somehow more offensive than if they’d given up and let go. Silt had piled along the sill, turning the doorway into a lip. On either side of the doors, the brick had shed mortar like dandruff. Someone had carved initials in a softened patch years ago and the letters were barely there, like the memory of their author.

Wren slid her fingers under the strap of the pry bar she carried across the small of her back and brought it around to feel the weight of it. The smart thing was to wait. Call Samir, call the county sheriff, let them be present for the first breach, camera phones and pens required. But expedience dressed itself as responsibility in her head. She told herself they couldn’t leave a void like this unsecured even for an hour. She told herself she wanted to see how bad the interior would be to plan what to tell the preservation people. She told herself a lot of things and layered them until the rightness on top felt like it went all the way down.

She had learned, over the last two years, that this is how you got into trouble.

The pry bar bit at the seam. She worked slow, letting the wood know she wasn’t going to break it if she didn’t have to. The door sighed inward a fraction, a wet, sucked sound, and a smell came out that was not the general smell of lake. It was a closer, older thing—mice and hymnals and old varnish softened and baked in cold water. The door moved another inch, then two. Somewhere inside, something slid and settled with a hush like sand moving through a glass.

“Samir,” she called, although he wasn’t in earshot, a reflex of saying a name at thresholds.

She got the door open six inches and put her shoulder against it and pushed. The gap widened enough to admit a body if the body turned sideways, and Wren slipped in, holding the pry bar against her thigh and the clipboard up like a shield—which it wasn’t, but there is something about a rectangle of paper that makes people feel less exposed.

Nothing had the right color. The light through the broken windows was lake light, run through brown and green and churn. The floor—the idea of a floor—was a crust of damp dust atop something that had swelled and buckled in low ranges like the Appalachians. Pews lay tilted at angles, some still in regiment, most canted away. Every line had been softened by silt. Spider silk scratched her face, and her stomach tightened with the recollection of summer barns, hay and fear in equal amounts. There was a wooden support at the back, a buttress retrofitted before the flood, a brace against a sag you could still see. In the faint light, the shadow of it made a cross against the back wall, a little unkind joke.

Her first thought was that someone had propped her there, a training dummy for an exercise. Yellow glowed against the gray of everything else, a slicker collapsing around a human shape in the third pew on the left. Wren saw it the way her mind preferred to, as an illustration first. The head was bent forward, the hood empty. One arm had fallen into the aisle and the hand rested palm up like a question. The shadows around the hand were darker, a slick that had dried to a tack. She didn’t register the smell as anything new because it was braided into the lake funk, embedded, the way certain news only lands after a beat.

She stood very still.

There was a clicking sound. It took her too long—two clicks too long—to place it. On the right wrist, where the slicker sleeve rolled back half an inch, a watch ticked with patient competence. She could not see the face, only the crown and the worn silver band against black neoprene. A diver’s watch, maybe. The sound felt indecent in the open hush, like an animal eating.
