Fool that she was, Wren’s first motion was forward, not back. The lettered side of her brain supplied an explanation: training dummy for divers. They had used them sometimes at the spillway for ice rescue. The watch was some crappy promotional give-away. The yellow slicker was a style the last forty years had left behind, but one of the guys from maintenance still wore his grandfather’s. She reached the aisle and the smell took its full portion of the air, and the explanation wobbled like something stepping over weak ice.

Not a mannequin. Whatever else it was, not that.

She could see hair against the collar, a dark that had gone to lake color: brown to green. The hand in the aisle was not carved. A crescent of soil lived at the base of each nail. There were lines across the palm that fit a human story: some fine, some bold. The skin did not have the feel of months in water. She had pulled enough dead muskrats from screens and found a drowned deer once and the look was not this. This looked like last week. This looked like the kind of thing that still had names attached somewhere.

“Okay,” she said into the calm voice she had poured for emergencies. She put the clipboard down because it made the situation clownish, somehow, to still be holding a schedule in the presence of someone’s stopped life. “Okay.”

The watch ticked. Somewhere, water beaded and fell, the sound skipping forward through the empty. Wren’s chest pulled tight. She lifted her hand to the face of the dead person and stopped, because to touch would be a step over the line that training had drawn and well-meaning stories had reinforced since she was small. Don’t put your hands on the dead without authority.

She backed up two steps and pivoted to find the doorway and the light again. Her eyes adjusted and she saw more detail, whether she wanted it or not. Rust on the nails along the pew edges, dark veils on the walls that mapped flood heights and some other water logic, maybe that one storm in ’89 everyone remembered. On the floor near the dead person’s boot, a glint under gray film. She crouched, and with a stick, she nudged the thing until it skittered free. It was a key. Not old. Brass with a rubber head you could buy at any hardware store this decade. The rubber had a nick in it and a white paint smear like it lived in a kitchen junk drawer. Someone had pressed a V into its plastic with a pocketknife. Not a shape the old village would have created under the water and waited to deliver back. The sight of it and the ordinary heart of it did something to Wren’s breath that the sight of the body had not. Things that didn’t belong did that.

She straightened and reached for her phone and realized she had no service in the belly of the brick. Typical, she thought, and her mind went spinning off into petty, false anger at the carrier because that was easier than the shape forming behind her breastbone.

She went back to the doorway. The daylight came around her. She put a hand on the iron strap of the door like it had a pulse she could talk to. Then she turned around and called, voice steady enough: “Samir! Sam—” It tore and left her throat raw.

He came jogging across the mud with the rope bucket swinging. She had not realized that he had been looking at her the whole time, that her motion had told him a story and he had edited his own job to be on the edge of hers. Samir was good that way. He stopped at the doorway, looked past her, and swore under his breath. Not theatrically. Like the word tasted worse than anything else he had tasted on this site.

“Back out,” he said. “Outside.”

They took two steps into air and then three more, like distance had weight. The man with the metal detector had edged closer again on a tide of curiosity that was not entirely his to resist. He had good eyes despite the hat. He saw their faces and stopped, his detector held like a truce flag now.

Wren’s fingers shook. She set the phone badly twice before she got it unlocked and then her thumb hesitated over the contact list because the part of her brain that hated to be wrong wanted to find another number to call. Water Agency. Preservation. She scrolled like it might save her and then stopped herself. Sheriff, she thought. This wasn’t one of theirs anymore. This was one of the county’s. She dialed.

“Dorning County Sheriff.”

“This is Wren Calder with the water agency,” she said. It sounded bureaucratic, but she did not know how else to begin. She glanced at Samir as if he might supply a softer phrase, and he did not look away from the doorway. “We have a situation at the Old Alder—Aldridge church. We’re on the east shore of Addison Lake. It’s part of the drawdown site.”

“What sort of situation?”

“A body,” she said, and the word made everything else shut up. Even the birds on the far hill. Even the idiot wind.

“You’ve secured the scene?”

Sure, she thought. It was as secure as a hundred years of failure and flood can make a thing. “We’ve kept people back,” she said. “It’s inside the building. I went in—”

“You went in.”

“Yes.”

“I’m going to dispatch the closest unit. Stay put.”

She hung up and stared at the surface of the lake while Samir watched the door like he thought the yellow slicker might stand and walk out. The metal detector man’s mouth was a line. He did not ask to see. His detector beeped softly at his hip, an embarrassed sound.

“They’re going to eat us alive for touching anything,” Samir said.

“I didn’t touch,” Wren said, and then thought of the iron, the door, the stick nudging the key. “I tried not to.”

“Next time, call me first,” he said, and kept his voice gentle, the way he might talk to someone who had fallen not because they were clumsy but because they expected the ground to be where it wasn’t.

Wren nodded because agreement was the easiest thing to give that didn’t cost anything. She returned her gaze to the church. The door was open and the blank inside looked back. The watch kept tick tick ticking in the rhythm of someone else’s plans.

“You know,” the metal detector man said, finally, and it was not a question. “The church doors were chained when they flooded it. I remember my uncle saying there was a hearing about it. They didn’t want people going in to pray after—like we were going to hold our breath and solve it.”

“Chained?” Wren asked, stupidly forced into the small scope of one detail.

“Yep.” He swung the detector back down so he had the comfort of not knowing what to do with his hands either. “The county took pictures. I saw one up at the diner. A chain through the handles and a padlock big as my fist.”

Wren turned back to the doorway with a set of her jaw that she knew wasn’t about the padlock so much as it was about what people thought parts of the world owed their sense. In her head, the chain was not there. It was gone. Someone had cut it or unthreaded it with patience or replaced it with finicking and better tools. Someone had put a person in a yellow slicker in the pew of a drowned church and left them with a watch that kept time in the dark.

Behind her shoulder blades, a shiver crossed like a swallowed bird. She knew the feeling by other names from other jobs: this is larger than you, this is older than you, this is not going to go away because you say so. She reached up and rubbed at the back of her neck like she could smooth the feathers down.

A gull came down from the ridge and alighted on the peak of the church. If the lake had a god, it would have looked like this: mean and watchful and fine with carrion. The bird cocked its head, watched them watch the door, and screamed in a voice like a hinge.

In the hush after, Wren realized what had been needling her since she stepped inside. Mild and specific as a paper cut, it made the hair along her arms want to stand. It wasn’t the watch. It wasn’t the yellow. It wasn’t the fact of the body, though that would reach her later in the blue hour of the next day like a hand through the thin fabric of sleep.

It was the line on the wall.

Just inside the doorway, three inches above her head, the water had drawn its own horizon in a band of dark. Up and to the right, another line lower. Up and straight ahead, lower again. Years in stripes. Still farther in, behind the pew where the yellow slicker slumped, the wall was clean.

No lake stain. No algae bloom. No history of soaking and drying. Clean plaster with old paint, the color of a mid-century attempt at cheerful.

That pew had not been there every time the church had been underwater. The place where the body sat had somehow kept itself clear of flood. Or it had been dry until very recent rains. Or—

“Do you see that?” she asked, pointing.

Samir squinted. “Either the wall was sealed there better,” he began, then stopped, because he had the same map in his head that she had: water seeks its level, the simplest rule anyone professional or barely trained had, and this rule did not make room for a dry patch in a drowned nave unless someone had made it.

Behind them, up on the county road, a siren took a breath and wound itself into being.

Wren kept her finger on the air like she could hold the observation together, but it didn’t need permission. The strangeness lived on its own now, self-feeding.

She took one step closer to the doorway, as if proximity could unwind this. The watch ticked. The gull reeled and screamed again. The siren came around the nearest bend, awful and inevitable as weather.

“Don’t go back in,” Samir said.

Wren nodded without looking at him. She heard tires on gravel, radio chatter. She heard the metal detector man clear his throat the way old men do when there is a story to be told and they have realized it will be told by someone else.

The sheriff’s vehicle slid to a stop in a wash of grit, and a woman in a tan uniform got out with a notebook already in her hand. She had an expression like someone about to pick up something heavy with bad handles. Wren raised her arm to get her attention. The move felt ceremonial, as if it carried more than it should of an ancient upraised torch.

“Sheriff,” Wren called, and then, because this was the truth, clean as the wall where there should have been stain, she added, “It’s not old.”

Chapter One

The dead have better manners than the living; they never call back with corrections. On a good night that’s what I tell myself, as if tact were any consolation for the hours I spend coaxing names and dates out of strangers who hear me as a voice in the dark.

“Spell the middle name one more time?” I said to the woman on line two. It was midnight in the Ledger’s obituaries nook, which meant the phones were a chorus of grief and bad reception. The police scanner ticked like an anxious clock between bursts of coded urgency, and a fluorescent bulb over my desk hummed its dying tremolo. Control-Z had saved me from an unfortunate “beloved angle” earlier; angels take offense in print.

My name is Mara Ellery, and if your aunt or your grocer or the city’s most famous violinmaker has died, I am the one who will break them into sentences that fit between the car ads and a weather map. Most nights are a chain of small fidelities: verify the spelling, call the funeral home, consult the style guide to see if “predeceased by” is still frowned upon. When the grief is fresh, the living want to tell me everything; I give them three grafs and tuck the rest into the morgue where we keep clippings in manila folders with names Sharpied in a long-departed copyist’s neat American gothic hand.

The morgue is what we call the archive. We are either a literal-minded profession or we have been hanging around the dead too long.

“Eleanore with an e,” the woman said again. “Like the First Lady.”

“E-l-e-a-n-o-r-e,” I repeated, typing. I make a point of pronouncing spaces. People seem reassured when you handle absences carefully.

Dom slid a paper cup of coffee onto my desk without breaking stride. He’s been on the copy desk long enough to know better than to talk to me during a phone call. He also knows that when I am on my third obit in an hour my attention can be bribed by caffeine. I mouthed thanks.

By one a.m., I had filed a pipefitter, a kindergarten teacher, and a woman whose grandson had insisted we include the name of her parakeet, Moses. The scanner scrolled a bank of codes, the newsroom emptied, and the building settled into the old paper’s after-hours funk of ink, carpet cleaner and stale pastry. Beyond our corner, rows of desks lay abandoned; the overnight editors glowed blue in their orbits.

That’s when the envelope came.

It was one of those cream things you only get from stationers who sell wedding invitations and embossed thank-you notes. Thick, with the tooth of good paper, my name written on it in a black hand that leaned left as if the writer were dragging against a habit. It wasn't stamped; there was no courier sticker, no interoffice routing trail of initials. Just MARA in the center, a smudge of graphite on the M. Someone could have set it down while I was on the phone. Someone could have come in out of the elevator; our floor is never quite locked, because news never is. That’s the theory.

I stood up and looked to see if anyone was watching me watch the envelope. Dom had vanished. The design team glowed in their aquarium. No one looked our way, because I was just the woman who made sure names did not come back to haunt us via angry daughters. I slid my finger under the flap.

Inside was a sheet folded twice. Heavier than our stock, too stiff to feed through our laser printers. The first thing I saw when I unfolded it was the header: ADVANCE, centered, bold. The second was the name.

VOSS, AUGUST R.

If you live in this city and have ever read a profile of someone’s rise or fall, you know August Voss. He taught narrative nonfiction with a severity that made us better. He wrote the book about the waterfront fires, the one they assign in every class that dares to call itself journalism. He smiled with only half his mouth. When I was twenty-two and sure my words would save me from uncertain paychecks and mercy, he taught me to cut my darlings and string my facts like the beads of a rosary. Then he took a sentence out of me and kept it.

We hadn’t spoken in eleven years.

The third thing I saw was a line at the top right: Release upon 2:15 a.m., Wednesday. It was Tuesday night, edging into Wednesday, and all my body clocks said I had an hour and a half before a stranger’s name would take this line’s place.

I read.

It was not one of our advance obits, the kind we keep half-baked in case someone famous goes inconveniently early. Those live in the system and in a folder in the morgue with draft notes and ancient clippings; they are written by reporters who roll their eyes and lie to themselves about what else they could be doing. This was finished, polished, printed in a serif font that looked like it had been dragged out of a typewriter, complete with a faintly imperfect lowercase e. It was the kind of piece we might have run on A1 if we had wanted to remind ourselves we still knew what a sentence could do.

August R. Voss, whose exacting prose and ethical zeal shaped two generations of reporters in this city and beyond, died early Wednesday morning at sixty-seven, according to his publisher. There was a paragraph about his childhood in a mining town in Pennsylvania—news to me, he had been cagey about origin stories—where his father kept clocks running for people too cheap to get them serviced by a man with a storefront. There was an anecdote about him forcing an editor to print a correction that imploded an alderman’s career. There was a line, third paragraph from the bottom, that made my throat do that old muscle memory of shame and anger.

“Order,” Mr. Voss wrote in his essay after the river fire, “is the story we agree to tell after the flood.”

He had written that after he pulled it out of one of my drafts and slapped his name on the margin of it, which is where I learned that the flood itself could be editorial. The words were mine. The voice had become his in the way that teachers leave fingerprints on the best parts of you.

A few inches down, my name.

Ms. Ellery is among dozens of reporters who cite Mr. Voss as an early influence. “He made you want to be equal to the truth,” she said.

I hadn’t spoken those words. Or if I had, it had been the kind of wish you say to a wall when you’re nineteen and imitating someone’s walk because you think you will get to where they're going. Under it, in a smaller font meant to suggest neutral efficiency, was a list of survivors: a sister in Scranton, a dog named Vitruvius. An ex-wife—news to me again—with a maiden name that vanished briefly into a smear of toner, then resolved under my desk lamp into a familiar shape. Winship. The little stationer on Myrtle where we all bought our Moleskine obsessions before we admitted our addiction to notes on our phones.

I turned the sheet over. There was a line at the bottom you won’t see in print because it wasn’t meant for the public. In the thin cursive of someone who taught himself to write legibly after a cop failed to read one of his early notes typed: cc: M.E.

That gave me a quick cold behind the sternum. In newsroom shorthand, M.E. is the managing editor. In a different world, it’s the medical examiner. In this world, it was also me, if you were the kind of person who liked to make puzzles and salt your leavings with old intimacies.

“Everything okay?” Dom said, reappearing at my shoulder with a red pencil tucked behind his ear like he was already the ghost of a later era. I must have jumped because he put both hands up, palms open, as if from a safe distance he could make amends for surprising me.

“Fine,” I said. “Weird death notice.”

“You’ve got the scanner?” He was fishing. If the scanner was quiet, Dom liked to take his fifteen minutes with a cigarette and a podcast where two men with sadder microphones than ours argued about sports.

“Full of burglary calls and a cat in a wall on Mercer,” I said. “We are living in a golden age.”

When he left, I took the envelope and the sheet and set them on my keyboard like a dare. I pulled open the bottom drawer where I keep the bottle of aspirin I haven’t replaced since 2017 and a Tootsie Roll I’m saving for a blackout. I keep the ledger of my shift there, too—a composition notebook because it feels less compromised than anyone’s version of the cloud. In the margin of last Sunday, I had written AUGUST, in the tight, angry hand I thought was safely outdated, after I had dreamed of his chalk hand erasing my name from something important. I closed the drawer. With the envelope under my arm, I walked to the elevator.

We have an archivist named Louise who minds the morgue with a ferocity you’d not want applied to you. She clips and files and curses at databases that work exactly as they were designed to work. She takes her lunch at ten-thirty and reads romances with women smiling on the covers in front of buildings that are clearly Rome. She never, ever works nine to five. Last week she had posted on the bulletin board outside the morgue door a photo of a tortoise eating a strawberry; under it, in large letters: LEAVE THE DAMN FOLDERS WHERE YOU FOUND THEM. REFILE WITH THE SPINE OUT. PLEASE DO NOT FEED THE ARCHIVIST.

It is not my habit to go into the morgue after midnight because I like not knowing what the building sounds like when it's just you, the basement, and racks of bound volumes furring like survivors in a crime drama. But the obit in my hand had not come through any of the channels we use to keep mortality orderly. The morgue is where the paper keeps its premonitions. I wanted to see what was in his folder.

The elevator worked differently after hours; you have to use a key, and it grinds into the lower floor like a dumbwaiter from a kitchen that never stopped making spaghetti. The doors opened onto the corridor where the vending machine buzzed with Snickers bars and the Last Good Soda in the building. The morgue door was propped open with a rubber wedge that was really a rolled-up newspaper wrapped in duct tape. The paper on the outside of the roll was two days old. I knew because I had written the obit on the front page for a former city councilman whose greatest legislative achievement had been successfully renaming six blocks of Carver Street after himself. The tape had left a gray stripe over the e in Street.

“Louise?” I called, because you announce yourself to the dead, too. The overhead tubes, when they were on, gave the greenish light of a fish tank. Tonight they flared and took a breath and flared again. There are rooms that always feel five degrees cooler than the rest of a building; our morgue is one of them, though the summer’s loose grip had left the air damp. Somewhere in the bowels of the building, a sump pump sighed.

He had a folder, because of course he did. You get one if you are famous, or if you are an institution like the guy at the feed store who gives out lollipops, or if someone loves you enough to clip your clippings. VOSS, AUGUST R., 3 folders, a sharpie scrawl said on the tab. The top two were the usual: clippings of his big investigations, a profile in the glossy magazine that used to come bundled with the paper on Sundays when we thought that was sophisticated. The third was thinner, labeled in a more tentative hand. It held a half-finished advance obit written a very long time ago by someone who had graduated to national politics coverage or PR, with blank spaces where wives and books might go.

I laid the cream paper on top of the old draft. The new words looked like a good suit laid over an old coat. The fonts disagreed, the sentences had different spines. Someone not in this building had written it. Someone inside the building had delivered it, or permitted its arrival. In our world of bylines, very few things are truly anonymous.

Under the folders, at the bottom of the drawer where we sometimes find coins that fell from a pocket while someone researched a man’s life in quarters, a fountain pen rolled when I pushed papers aside. The color of the ink stained onto the nib was that particular blue-black you can't get in a ballpoint. Voss used a pen like that. He would take it out during student conferences like a surgeon unrolling instruments and look at you over the thing like he was deciding whether to amputate.

Something else slid flat on the drawer bottom. A square of Polaroid film with a white border and the soft focus that makes all memories look like they happened in better weather. It was a shot of a small model of a building: white foam core, a roof like a wave, columns too delicate for actual wind. Someone had scrawled in the margin: Lakeside Bank, preliminary. The handwriting had the same leftward lean as the envelope. I tried to connect model banks to professors whose idea of retirement was staying in the building until the young were too frightened to knock. The pen and the photo made a modest gravity in the drawer, more compelling for being unnecessary.

Behind me, something metallic chimed. The elevator had moved. I stepped into the aisle of file cabinets and listened. The building does a job of telling you it is old. Pipes tick and hiss; ducts vibrate. You tell yourself these are ordinary noises as long as there are at least two other people on your floor who could explain a fire alarm. Down here, the silence was a body on a slab waiting for you to come up with a cause of death you could live with.

I took the cc: M.E. line for the provocation it was and called his number from the main page of the faculty directory I had pulled up on my phone. It rang twice and then someone answered on the third ring with a noise like a chair scuffing a wood floor, the intimacy of it like the sound of a knife being set carefully down.

“Professor Voss?” I said.

He said nothing for a second. Then: “Who is this?” The voice was him. Older, the edges softened, but the scrape under the words like paper on paper remained. I felt all over again the stupid thrill of being noticed.

“Mara Ellery,” I said, and the name felt like I was reaching out with an old scar and asking someone to touch it. “I’m at the Ledger. I received something you might want to know about.”

“You’re an optimist,” he said. “You think wanting has anything to do with knowing.”

“You’d recognize this,” I said. “It’s your obituary. Or something like your obituary. It’s on my desk.”

He exhaled. It wasn’t a laugh. “And here I thought I was going to bed unsung.”

“Did you write it?” It sounded like a stupid question the second I asked it. But I have learned there is nothing people will not answer late at night if you sound both tired and polite enough.

“You think I’m the kind of man to write my own epitaph?”

“I think you’re the kind of man who would rather edit the inevitable than leave it to the hacks.” The old student in me enjoyed the insolence; the older version recognized it as a tell.

“If I had written my own obituary, it would be shorter,” he said, and I could picture the lift of his mouth without seeing it. “How did it begin?”

I read him the first line. He hummed once.

“And the quote,” he said. “Someone liked their Heraclitus.”

“You didn’t say it,” I said.

“Who did?” he said. He did not sound angry; he sounded like someone in a room turning in a slow circle, making a catalogue.

“There’s a release time,” I said. “Two-fifteen.”

“I’m fond of specificity,” he said dryly. “And of clocks. Who told you I was dead?”

“It says your publisher,” I said. “There’s a name. Winship. Does that make sense to you?”

“Everything that matters makes sense to me,” he said, and then he laughed once, a sound he had always reserved for other people’s bravado. “Where are you? The morgue?”

“In the building, yes.”

He was quiet long enough for me to think the line had died. “Bring it,” he said finally. “Bring it to me.”

“To you?”

“I’m at the old library,” he said. “The History Society. They love me there because I give them boxes of paper. I left something out for you years ago and then decided you hadn’t earned it. I’m a man of my appetites. Come make me feel like I’m not a complete coward.”

“I’m working,” I said, and even I could hear my reluctance trying out moves.

“Then take a break from memorials,” he said. “Bring my death to me so we can decide what it means.”

The line clicked. He hung up before I could ask him how he’d known I would be here on this shift to have my night rearranged by him again.

The History Society is two blocks down from the Ledger, in the old Carnegie library with a plaque that tells you how the city used to define generosity. They keep the lights on late because men like August give them boxes of letters tied with string and women like Louise go there on their days off to argue with docents about humidity control. Outside there would be a wheezing from the air system and the lonely uprightness of a building that used to know what it was for.

I took the elevator up again, which made a sound like a spoon in a glass when it arrived at our floor. Dom was not at his desk; a Post-it next to his keyboard gave evidence of his existence: pizza? it read, and a small box had been ticked and then unticked.

“Back in ten,” I told the copy desk that had become three people and a radio. When you are a woman no one thinks about that late, you can say back in ten and if you come back in forty very few people notice unless a billionaire’s death has stepped on a mayor’s press conference and everyone is waiting on the right hedge.

The city had cooled a little by the time I walked outside. The river made its afternoon glitter exchange with the streetlights. Two delivery trucks idled by the service entrance, diesel engines doing an imitation of sleep apnea. On Myrtle, Winship & Daughters had their metal grille down. A stray flyer wagged on the gate, slapping against it in a breeze that couldn't decide what it was doing. Under the single working bulb at the library’s front steps, someone had left a stack of magazines softened by a day of humidity. The reflection of the clock at City Hall puddled in the History Society’s windows. The time was one-thirteen.

The library doors were not locked. They were reduced to the weight of their swing. Inside, the air had a quality that all library air has: dust, paper, the perfume of slow decay. A city historian named Mr. Lahr sometimes dozed in a chair under the portrait of a long-dead donor when he stayed too late. He was not in his chair. The lights above the central hall were off, but a desk lamp glowed on a table in the reading room like the idea of safety.

“Mr. Voss?” I said into the hush. The hush drank it.

I put the envelope on the table and waited. There are scripts for these moments. The person you called arrives with theatrical tardiness. They make a remark about stalking their own funerals. They touch the paper as if this were all silly and then pull their hand back quickly, because the words have a heat. This was not that script.

There was a noise, a soft thump delivered through the soles of my shoes, not a bang—the regular, everyday kind of misfortune you file under gravity. It came from downstairs.

Basements in old buildings have their own climates. The steps down were narrow and lined with the kind of carpet that was brave even when it was new. On the halfway landing, a portrait of a woman in nineteenth-century black had been positioned to watch all arrivals. I looked away from her once too quickly and had to look back to prove to myself she hadn’t moved. At the bottom, the lights were on in a rectangle that framed the stacks where the History Society kept its oversize boxes of the city’s residue: maps, blueprints, handbills inviting you to ribbon cuttings at things that no longer exist.

“Mr. Voss?” I said. This time the hush made no effort to answer. The sound came again; a smaller sound on top of the first one, a jewel-snap, like something that had not been intended for weight taking weight, giving a little and then not giving at all.

He was in the wrong place for any of this to make sense.

There is a moment when you see a body and your first thought does not have the grammar for what you’re looking at. It’s a statue, your useless brain says. It’s too still to be a person. He was on his side at the end of an aisle between the metal shelving, one hand partly under him as if he had tried to catch himself with calculation and dignity. His head was not at an angle that suggested dignity had been available to him at the end.

The part of me that is always going to be a reporter took notes before my heart did. Jacket, gray. Shirt, white. Pen, blue-black ink stain on the cuff. Smell, something that was not yet the smell of death but its staging: varnish, dust, a thread of something sweet like eucalyptus gone sharp. His mouth was open, and it made his teeth look like a child’s block tower someone had forgotten to topple. I went to my knees because that is what you do in the world that still might be the living.

“August,” I said, and it was both for him and for whatever was listening that might count my familiarity against me. I reached to his throat. The skin was not cold yet, but it had confused itself. There was no pulse that would reassure the part of me that believes in do-overs. His watch—the same one he used to tap when you were six minutes late to class—had a shallow scratch across its face and had taken it upon itself to stop at a time it liked better than the one the city was keeping.

It is a measure of how much you loved a person—by which I mean both admired and resented—that you tell yourself you can still do something when what you can do is call a number and wait. I fumbled my phone out of my bag and the screen offered me the last call I had made. I scrolled down to the one you are supposed to make before you do anything else.

At the top of the stairs, someone coughed.

“Hello?” I called and immediately regretted the biology of the word. The cough did not repeat itself. The air circulated; an HVAC unit made a patient whisper like a nurse opening blinds. The time on my phone read 2:17.

Sirens are the one honest thing left in a city at that hour. They started far away, little falcons that got larger and nearer. I put my hand on the paper in my bag where it warmed my palm with the heat of implication. Release upon 2:15 a.m., its clean type said, as if there were nothing more ordinary than giving a time to an end.

When the first officer came into the reading room two minutes later at a fast walk that wanted to be a run and saw me at the bottom of the stairs with a dead professor and a cream envelope in my lap, the look he gave me had in it the beginning of the story he would tell himself about me. I had time, before the words started, to notice the ink on August Voss’s cuff, the way the stain had bled as if everything he had ever used to mark his pages had gone ahead of him.

I was going to be the one to write his obituary. And I had been the one to find him in the wrong morgue.

At two in the morning the sound becomes a thing you can touch. The fog folds itself down over Graywater Bay until the ferry pushes through it like a spoon through heavy cream, and the horn rolls ahead of us in a long, patient moan. The deck stinks of diesel and rain. Salt lids the rails. You learn the names of the different hums and groans when you work the graveyard shift—the engine’s steady thrum, the high whine of a sticky pulley, the hiss of the ramp hydraulics bleeding off as we nose toward the slip at Northcross.

I’ve worked the M/V Perigee long enough that I can feel the dock before I see it. The pilings knock a rhythm underfoot that tells you the tide, the angle. My chalk marks on sidewalls glow ghost-pale where I’ve hooked a finger to swipe moisture away earlier; the tires remember they were counted. I carry a stub pencil behind my ear because pens go to hell in fog, because my father kept pencil stubs like charms and because it gives my hands something to do when there’s nothing else except the water and the waiting.

We were light on the crossing—maybe a dozen vehicles, fifteen foot passengers who had the same reasons as everybody who rides at this hour. You can tell a lot by the kind of quiet someone wears with them. A kid asleep across a backpack under the lounge TV, a contractor snoring into his safety vest, a woman standing at the forward window with both hands clenched around a paper cup that stopped steaming fifteen minutes after we left the mainland. The island’s lights came and went and came again, blurred into a beaded line where the fog let them through. The bay had a second sky for a while, a hopping smear of phosphorescence behind our prop wash that I always watch when I can; it looks like secrets might.

“Two minutes,” Priya called from the crew cabin, leaning out with a braid plastered to her shoulder. She’s second mate and keeps the clock like a religion. Captain Garner’s boots drummed past me toward the bridge. I cuffed my gloves tight and split off down the starboard ramp to get the gates.

Docking is noise until it isn’t. Ropes thrown, caught, a bark of orders transmitted out of habit. The slip’s floodlights cut slices into the fog so we could watch ourselves doing our jobs. The ramp dropped. The bar lift clanked up. I took my post at the front cones. Garner gave the two-finger point to the tollbooth, and the booth crystal crackle answered back on our radio: “You’re clear to discharge, Perigee.”

They rolled off like they always do: a white work van with a ladder clattering on the roof, a pickup, a long low sedan that looked like a landlocked whale burning the last fumes of a cigarette into the damp air. The passengers came behind with their hands in their pockets and their eyes down. The kid was awake, rubbing a cheek creased from his backpack. The woman with the cup glanced at me and then away as if I was something she’d been warned about.

When it was done, the ramp stayed open, my breath made a cloud inside the cloud, and one car sat where it had when we left the dock a half hour ago. Black Subaru. Late model with the kind of clean that either means a lease or a careful person. Front left tire chalk-marked with my half C and the time I’d put it there. Windshield beaded with the infinitesimal rain of fog. My cones and chalk sat in their bucket like we were nothing but props in a picture.

You can tell stories by the refuse people leave behind. There wasn’t any to read. The driver’s seat was all the way forward, which could mean someone short or someone nervous and back on their heels. I went and knocked on the window with two knuckles. Standard: loud enough to startle if someone had drifted off, polite enough if they hadn’t.

Nothing.

The handle wasn’t locked. I slid my glove under it and eased the door open. The dome light blinked and then held, casting its weak gold over a cup holder with a plastic lid and a sleeve around it—the coffee still warm enough that our breath on it made a ring of dew. Air inside smelled like wintergreen gum and new upholstery, and under that the oily metallic faintness of tools. On the back seat behind the driver, there was a child’s car seat buckled in, the harness clasp latched and empty. A stuffed animal lay face down on the floor—something with blunt arms and a matted blue back, the label worn to threads.

“Ma’am?” I stepped back and raised my voice. “Sir? Anyone on board?”

My words went out and were extinguished. I glanced up. The lounge windows were black mirrors; my orange vest floated there like a ghost. The ferry’s horn boomed again of its own accord and then stopped as if embarrassed to interrupt.

Routine is religion, and the rules are gospel. I keyed my radio. “Priya, I got an unattended vehicle on the main deck, lane two. I’m gonna sweep.”

“Copy. Unit circle complete?”

“Everything else discharged.”

“Make it quick.”

We all think about the man who jumped last December, even when we don’t say his name. Winter made him break like a dropped glass, and he climbed the rail and let the water take him before anyone who was watching believed what they were watching. I always think about him when I walk alone through the lounge with my footsteps muffled by the carpet and the humming of the vending machines pretending to be company.

Up in the passenger cabin, the TV that plays the same looping footage of sunsets over the ferry system’s greatest hits was still running to an empty room. One of the plastic chairs was cocked on a leg as if someone had gotten up in a hurry. The forward observation windows were a hard blank. There was no one in either bathroom. I checked under the seats, checked behind the information desk where printed schedules curl at the edges from damp. The emergency phones sat in their glass-fronted boxes like red hearts waiting.

On the starboard promenade I found the only trace of anyone at all: a palm print smeared low on the salt-streaked glass by the rail, thumb and three fingers distinct and one finger a kind of drag. Maybe a kid’s, but kids at this hour don’t go out onto the promenade alone. The droplets that had beaded there had been pushed aside by that hand and were starting to melt back into themselves.

I leaned on the rail and listened, not because I expected an answer but because listening makes you look like you’re doing something. The bay moved underneath us; the ferry has its own tides when it sits in place inside the slip, slosh and draw with the breathing of the hull against the pilings. Farther out, some bell answered our horn—one of those older shipping buoys whose sound gets into your teeth if the wind’s right. The bell shouldn’t have been this close.

I went back down. The ferry without people is just a machine, and machines make their own company. The cars had painted stencils under them of shadows. The black Subaru waited like it had all the time in the world. There was a smear on the driver’s seat belt where someone’s shoulder had rubbed it—salt or chalk, a pale line across the fabric. The belt was buckled, the buckle latched into the receiver as snug as if someone had wanted the alarm to keep its mouth shut while the engine was off. I’ve seen that before, but always in cars with owners who hate being nagged by their investments.

“Still sweeping?” Priya’s voice made my radio fizz.

“Negative. I’ll need you here, Priya. Got a warm coffee, child seat, no driver. Nobody up top. No bathrooms. Ramp’s still dropped.”

“On my way.” If there was judgment there, it wasn’t for me. The worst part is when everyone acts the way they’ve been trained and things still don’t line up.

Garner joined us with his cap in his hand like he can’t make himself wear it when something is wrong. He took one glance at the car and the cup and the empty seat. “Call the port police,” he said to Priya without taking his eyes away from the Subaru. Then, to me: “Do not start moving anything until they clear it.”

He walked away again, making a long line under the floodlights, to talk to a man in a fluorescent slicker at the tollbooth. Business needs its little facsimiles of control. I rested a hand on the door and held myself very still. In my head the hour gained an edge, like the edge that comes on water right before the wind stirs it, a breaking of the skin without a visible hand.

We never mind waiting if we can be busy at it. Busy looks good on reports. I wrote down the plate: WJZ-8304, state of Washington, registration sticker current. I wrote down the time next to my chalk mark and my initials because the clipboard likes to be fed. The glove compartment sat in my peripheral vision as a neat blank rectangle. I could have opened it on a thought and half a finger. I didn’t. You learn when not to know things.

Priya came and we stood together like we were stakeout cops and the car might break down and confess. “Sucks,” she said after a while. Priya is younger than me by a decade and she still says things in single words that other people need whole paragraphs for. “You saw nobody pop on the last minute out?”

“No.”

“You break that cup seal?” She tilted her chin at the coffee.

“No.”

Her hand brushed the back of the driver’s seat. “Warm. Freshly warm.”

“You get the island end-of-night count yet?” I asked. Our tollbooth sent us numbers after every load. Ferry people trust numbers because they’re indifferent to us.

Through the radio, the booth squawked as if we had conjured it. “Perigee, we have sixteen foot passenger tickets collected on your arrival.” The number hung there for a second. “We had fifteen scanned on departure from the mainland.”

“So someone without a car boarded, and one foot passenger more got off than got on?” Priya said evenly. “Or someone with a car boarded and got off without it.”

“Copy.” I could hear the click of the booth’s keyboard as the attendant went back over their system to check for their own error, because that’s what we all do first—the penance of the double-check. “We’ll verify. Police are on their way.”

Northcross doesn’t have its own police at this hour; the port authority sends their two guys, and if one of them is on his dinner break then you hope the other one is close. The fog makes distances religious anyway. It stretches time out. It makes you think you have time you don’t and takes time you do. I looked down at the floor between my boots and the car and saw a darker wetness ghosting a pattern there. Everyone who knows me knows I can make something out of a stain. It was nothing—just a patch bootprints made when somebody’s feet had been damp and then dried as the fog pulled moisture out of any surface that would give it up. Still, the weirdness of them hit me, the way they came from the rail and crossed the deck and ended exactly at the rear bumper, as if whoever walked there had stepped up and then disappeared, and then I shook it off and told myself: you’re looking at them backward.

“Police want us to hold the ramp,” Priya said. “Garner’s not thrilled.”

“He’ll live.”

“Will he?” She smiled without moving her eyes from the car.

Everything that can be said gets said, and then there’s the part where your body fills in words for you. The skin between my palm and the leather-wrapped steering wheel itched with proximity. The car was one of those that does half its own thinking for you; they all do now. On the center console there was a phone. I saw it because the black slab of it made a darker black rectangle against the shadow cast by the cup holder. It had slid so the corner of it poked out. The screen lit, the way phones light when they think someone might want them, and I saw the lock screen—fingers arranged in a pattern that looked like a letter. 2:13 A.M. blinked in the top corner, the battery an angry red sliver.

“Don’t.” Priya’s voice and my hand arrested themselves at the same time. She hadn’t touched me, but if she had her hand would have hovered exactly where mine had reached, as if a conductor had frozen a piece of music in air. “Evidence.”

“I’m not—” I didn’t finish whatever lie I was about to tell.

The phone chose for me. The tiny speaker made a chirp that was almost apologetic and then began to ring, the noise thin and strange in the cold as if it was coming from under water. Some part of me—I don’t know which part, the part that hates unanswered bells—reached and tapped what it needed to tap to make the ringing stop.

“Mara?” The voice in my ear knew my name before I could decide whether I should be answering a stranger’s phone. It came in low and winded and pitched through some speaker that had seen better days. It could have been anyone’s voice, the way the bay flattens sound, but it knew my name.

“Who is this?”

“You’re on the ferry,” the voice said, not asking, stating, as if the speaker had just had his own eyes. A pause, a scrape like a chair moving and then a long breath. “You’re on the Perigee. Don’t let it leave.”

I looked at Priya. She looked at me, the fog and the floodlights turning her into something cut out of paper. “Who is this?” I said again, sharper this time, my throat tightening around it.

The line hiccuped. For a beat I heard nothing at all, just the ferry breathing and the far bell answering and the faint patter of droplets on steel. Then the voice came again, near a whisper now, so soft I had to press the phone tight enough to hear that I could smell plastic. “Please,” he said. “Whatever you do. Don’t let it leave.”

The line went dead with a click that sounded like a door locking from the other side.

I stood there with the phone against my ear and the car open and the bay making and unmaking itself around us. Priya reached past me and clicked the Subaru’s door shut with a clean little clap that sounded too final, and somewhere above us Garner’s radio barked like a starting gun. The fog moved a hair and shaped itself into something that might have been a person and then wasn’t, right where the passenger’s lounge window made its own night.

In the good old litany you say when you don’t know what to say, we are not late, we are not early, we are not anything we can see. Vehicles embark, vehicles discharge. The island takes what it wants and gives back what it doesn’t. But there was one thing the litany didn’t cover, one that nobody had given me a line for before now, standing with a dead phone and a warming cup and a shot of someone else’s fear raw in my ear:

There is nowhere to go from an island ferry at two in the morning. And someone had gone.

By midnight, the station sounded like tidewater in a pipe and the past unspooling at seven and a half inches per second.

Mara Lark was the only person left on the third floor of the old brick warehouse that housed Iverton Public Radio. The offices on the river side slept with their bruised blinds drawn, the production bays along the center hallway were dark except for a single green power light here and there, and Studio C—hers for the night by virtue of an approved request form taped to the door—glowed an aquarium blue. The building had once been a brassworks; the pipes still made themselves known. Sometimes they muttered like living things.

She leaned over the Otari deck and watched the world in miniature: the empty right-hand reel waiting to be fed, the left-hand platter with a pancake of brown tape circled around it, the silver capstan with its smear of light. Her left thumb kept the pressure steady on the tape as she threaded it through the heads: over the guide, under the tension arm, through the gap where, if you dragged your skin, you’d feel your fingerprint rising. The tape smelled faintly of wet cardboard and old pennies, the scent of shed oxide that every audio archivist learned to love enough to fear.

On the table, beneath a ceramic mug branded twenty pledge drives ago, lay a maroon shoebox with its top torn at the corners and a piece of masking tape across the lid. On that tape, in a hand that trembled not from age but from some contrary habit of haste, someone had written: City Hall Basement, Bid Committee, 1976-1977. Side A - B.

Earlier that afternoon a man had stood just inside Reception with that shoebox against his winter coat, like a boy waiting to give a teacher something not quite new. He wore an untidy scarf, his white hair combed forward as if to hide and then forgetting to. The girl at the desk had pointed down the hall. He’d found Mara by listening for sound in an empty building. “You’re the one who does the… with the tapes?” he’d said, drawing shapes in air, neither circles nor lines. “They said. Miss Lark.”

She had corrected him, but he’d kept calling her Miss Lark, like the title mattered.

“My name is Ernest Vale,” he’d said, “only nobody calls me Ernest. I was clearing a shelf in the old records room, behind the cabinets—only to find there isn’t a back after forty years, can you imagine? I bumped those things forward an inch and a half and—well. It fell.”

“What fell?” she’d asked, more to make him keep talking than because she didn’t see the box.

“Everything,” he’d said. And because he must have heard how that sounded, he’d adjusted: “A box. And a photograph that’s nothing now—faded. But this is what matters. I thought maybe you all… it was you people who did that lovely thing with the astronauts on the anniversary. My wife cried at the way it sounded like it was happening in the kitchen.”

“We can’t take everything,” she’d said automatically. Her desk already contained a drawer of cassettes labeled Uncle Mike’s Last Band and four DATs of sea shanties. “But you can let me look.”

He’d set the box down very carefully and then put both hands at his sides, as if recognizing a certain ceremony. Inside there had been four ten-inch reels, that same brown color that could have been chocolate or rust. Someone had written on the leaders with a highlighter that had faded to lemon. Side A. Side B. City Council Bid.

Or. Bid Committee. Or the scrawl was “Bird Committee.” You learned to hold two possibilities in your head until the third arrived and decided them both wrong.

He had watched her peel back the first protective wrap and had laughed without sound. “They told me,” he said, “I should throw it all away. The new girl down there—the one with the neat hair—she said none of it matters. But if I could—if you could just find something. You know? The thing at the beginning. It matters still.”

“What thing?” she’d asked.

He had stared through the window at the river making its march from west to east, flat as a blade. “There was a test, they said. A test of the sirens. The water was low that week. They said eight twelve, that was the time, we’d heard it at lunch a hundred times before, so why not. It would be fine. And then afterwards—everyone forgot in a hurry. I remembered in a slow way. I’ve been remembering for a long time. If there’s a tape that remembers too, I want to hear it before I can’t hear anything.”

She’d taken his number on the yellow-lined pad she kept around for people who believed in pads and pencils, and put his name in her phone when he wasn’t looking. She had promised nothing. He had pressed his hand briefly to the table near hers in thanks, but not touching.

Once he’d left, and after she’d waited out the afternoon news show and the thirteen voicemails about storm closings, in the late light that made the dust visible in the production bays she had gently pried up a corner of a reel and touched a fingertip to it. Sticky, she thought. Some older backings exuded their problems after time—sticky-shed syndrome—clogging the heads, rendering everything a squeal of failure unless you coaxed them into compliance. There were ways to do it: you could “bake” a recalcitrant tape in a low heat to drive off the moisture that made it gummy and deliver, briefly, a window of listenable grace.

At ten, after the volunteers for the jazz hour had left arguing about the difference between smoke and grit, Mara slid the first reel into the food dehydrator the station had bought on a half-serious memo three years ago and set it to a careful hundred and twenty degrees for three hours. She worked while it worked. She cleaned head stacks with a Q-tip and isopropyl. She answered two emails about levels on a documentary she’d promised to cut next week. She checked the city page to see if there had been any mention of a discovery in a hall of records. There had not.

When the dehydrator chimed—an absurdly gleeful little bell that belonged in a kitchen with a white linoleum floor—she lifted the reel out and let it sit. Warm, the tape gave slightly under her fingers. She threaded it, pressed REW, watched the tape spin back to the head.

She pressed PLAY.

At first the reel transported her nowhere special at all. The sound of room: the low hum of fluorescent lights, the out-of-phase rattle of cheap metal chairs, someone blowing their nose and trying to disguise it as a cough. A coffee mug set down too hard on wood. And then, in the slightly hollow midrange she knew came from a mic on a table and not at a mouth, a voice: “Okay, okay, I’m starting it. We’ll be official.” A little laugh. “Recorder on, it says. This is—oh for God’s sake, does anyone have the label? The label?” Papers shuffled. Chairs squealed. “City Procurement and Bid Oversight Committee,” one voice supplied, a woman’s, businesslike. “Meeting of August twelfth, nineteen seventy-six, Council Chambers.”

“Thank you,” the first voice said. “Present: Chair Alden Fitch. Councilmember R. Dorval. Evelyn Cho, Comptroller’s Office. Marcía—?”

“Mar-see-ah,” she said, the businesslike woman from before, patient. “Marcia Salazar. City Works.”

“Okay then. And an audience of at least five interns and one member of the press.” Mild laughter.

Sometimes, working with old recordings, you felt a fondness for ghosts you had no right to. Mara smiled despite herself and leaned closer to the monitor as the voices found their habits. There was banter and then business. A bid for new road salt suppliers. A formal thank-you to a retiring administrator who had made fewer enemies than expected. A request to keep to the agenda, please, because some of them had day jobs that did not run on committee time. The kind of civic content that had kept Iverton’s old papers in business for decades and then, when the papers went thin, kept their radio station useful to people who believed that knowing the dullest thing was how you kept the bright surprises manageable.

At fifteen minutes in, someone mentioned the river.

“Next,” said Alden Fitch—his voice a blend of rumpled charm and the strain of making his charm work for him—“we have... the River Works Improvement Project bids for the gating mechanism at Tanners Hollow. Remind me again why we are gating anything, Ms. Salazar?”

Marcia spoke as if this question had been asked and answered once a week since June. “Because, Chair, if we don’t, the Hollow floods every second spring and every big storm, and if we let the gates be simple instead of live, we have to send a human in hip waders to a box that likes to shock people and—”

“Point taken,” Fitch said. “All right. Bids. Who’s who?”

Mara watched the waveform drift along the screen, small mountains in a strange range. If someone had set a microphone on the committee table and turned it on and left it alone, that was one thing. But what she was listening to had a second sound riding under it. She turned up her headphones. There. Fainter than breath. A different moving air. The tape sounded like two things at once.

She stopped the reel. She let it spin back a few seconds and then forward. Again: the hum of a municipal room and then under it, a kind of whining line as if a cheap cassette deck had been recorded to and then erased to make room and had failed to forget entirely. She’d heard that in field tapes before. Amateur reporters recording over something else and getting a ghost for their trouble. But this was City Hall.

She made a note for herself, in a column labeled Pulls, that said: Undertrack? And then, because she could not help it, a smiley face that looked nothing like a smile, a quick curved line and a dot, her hand in shorthand teasing her day job for still having the power to surprise.

The table talk proceeded into the river. The Hollow. Gates. A subcontractor from Camden whom one member preferred because “at least they answer the phone.” A different firm out of Glenville that, according to Ms. Salazar, had “the technical chops to make a gate that differentiates between two inches and two feet of head pressure.” A rustle of impatience. A man’s shifting weight.

“We all appreciate the engineers,” Fitch said, “but let’s be honest—costs are through the roof, the taxpayers are through the roof, and if there’s a way to get what we need for less, we’re charged with finding it. Correct?”

“Correct, within reason,” the Comptroller’s representative said. “We’re charged with fiscal responsibility, not one of those carnival games where you guess the number of beans and someone else spends them.”

“You’re very vivid, Ms.—?”

“Cho.”

“Ms. Cho, thank you.”

Mara’s screen reflected back a watery version of her face in the glass behind the meters. She had late-show eyes. The habit of this hour was a second life. She yawned and then stopped herself and then took the mug that had “2011 Drive: You Belong” on it and drank lukewarm coffee without flinching.

At 22:18 on the counter, someone—she thought it might be Dorval—said, “Look, we can test it. They do the central test at eight twelve every day anyway, it’s not like we’d be surprising anyone. We just let the gate drop and see what the flow is. And if it’s ugly—God willing it won’t be ugly—we’ll have learned something without—”

“Without what?” Evelyn Cho said. “Without telling the rest of the Council? Without telling the Hollow? We’re not licensed to test on people’s houses without a vote.”

“It’s not on houses,” Dorval said, “that end by the culvert is practically weeds. Ms. Salazar?”

“It’s mostly weeds,” she allowed. “Depending on how much rain we’ve had.”

“And this was a dry summer,” Fitch added, so happily sure of this point it was almost a boy’s trick. “So this is the time when it’s as little harm as it can be. And anyone living out there knows what eight twelve sounds like; they’ll check their laundry lines if they’re smart.”

Mara took the headphones off and put them down very carefully on the table and then put them back on. The undertrack—if that’s what it was—had strengthened as if the tape had been recorded over and the earlier thing was bleeding through now that she knew to listen. It was a voice, but not near the committee mic. A voice on another day in another place. Whisper-low and then speaking in a rush and then cutting off. She put on the software filter that squeezed the center channel and widened the sides. The under-voice slid sideways.

“—not eight twelve,” it said. And then again, as if a second hand tugged on the first, “not accident.”

Her lower back prickled in that instinctive way she had never been able to talk herself out of, the prickle that said: something real. She took a breath in and let it out through teeth she hadn’t known she’d clenched.

Her phone buzzed beside the keyboard. It was a number without a name, just ten digits and the sense of something borrowed. She picked up.

“Miss Lark?” The voice was worn smooth but sure. Ernest Vale did not sound the way men sound when they call because their furnace has betrayed them or their child has; he sounded like a man who has been in hours of meetings and knows how far to lean forward to make the mice look at him.

“It’s Mara,” she said. “I started listening.”

“Yes,” he said. Paper shuffled on his end, the sound of his hand on… what? A desk. “If you hear the bit about the siren, you tell me. Please tell me. There’s a… there’s a number on the box. I wrote it there. If I don’t pick up this one—call that one.”

“Is everything all right?” she said.

“You know how the building feels when it knows you’re leaving it,” he said, and then, as if he heard himself, he half laughed. “Nothing. It’s nothing. Old buildings like company. So do old men. Eight twelve,” he said, not laughing anymore. “They thought that was so safe. Call me when you hear it. I’d like to hear it with you.” And then, in a voice smaller and younger than the one he’d arrived with, “I’d like to know I didn’t make it up.”

He hung up before she could say anything comforting that would have sounded like a lie.

She scrubbed backward in the file, set markers like pins on a map—14:02, 22:18, 33:09. She found again the phrases that made her sit up straighter. We can test it. Then the pushback. Then a compromise, the politician’s careful surrender: “We’ll call it a systems test,” Fitch said, “we’ll schedule it for Thursday, not put it in the agenda, keep it to staff as a routine check. I… I’ll take the flak if there is any. There won’t be any.” He said the last like a spell.

Marcia said something then, not into the mic but across the table to someone she hoped would hear, and the someone was not the recorder. “You don’t need to be the person it happens to,” she said, “to know not to do it.” It wasn’t on the tape so much as it was almost under it, like a thread too thin to hold by. And then there was the room again, the scrape of chairs, the meeting moving on to paint choices for the Avenue, the wages for part-time snow labor.

She listened through to the end of Side A and the click-click of leader and then the empty air running past the heads because long-ago someone had not wound the end of the tape tightly and the machine had got what it wanted. She let it slap gently against the post and then stopped it and took it up with her finger, touching it like hair.

On the edge of the reel was a torn-out square of blue plastic leader where someone had cut and spliced and cut again. The tape had been edited, crudely, at some point. She leaned closer to look at it. The splicing tape was the kind she recognized from old kits—the kind that dried out and pulled up a corner like a leaf.

She pressed PLAY on Side B. Hiss, then nothing, then a cough, then the sound of chairs again. Another day. The same voices, older by an afternoon. It was less legible, as if this reel had sat nearer damp, more of its stories softened in the bath. She put a hand on the left flange to steady its spin, an old habit to make the inertia behave. Under the room a sound rose up again, the undertrack. She adjusted the equalizer one notch at a time, listening for the squeal and listening around it.

“Thursday,” someone said. The voice wasn’t any of the committee; it was whoever had held the old portable and set it where it shouldn’t have been. “Test at eight twelve. Gate release at eight twenty. That’s… no. That’s not right, we—” And then, louder, as if someone else in that other room had come in: “You can’t be here. You can’t. I’m— I’m recording—”

Then the clatter of something hitting something else, and then the sound pulled itself into a shape and then tore itself apart as if a person had put a thumb in the reel and snapped it away from a metal tooth.

She took the headphones off again. Studio C seemed too large then, her breath a noise she could not tamp down. Outside the glass, in the hallway, the red EXIT sign made a worn neon promise.

Mara stood and flexed her fingers because one of them had started to sting, a tiny line of pain down her cuticle where she’d nicked it on the edge of leader. She walked to the little kitchenette and found the light that turned its humming refrigerator from black to brave white. There were two half-gone cartons of half-and-half and someone’s Tupperware labeled not yours seriously. She ran the tap until it ran cold and drank from her hand.

When she went back to Studio C, an envelope lay on the floor just inside the door, white against the gray carpet. She had not heard anyone step past the frosted glass. She had not heard the stair. She told herself she had left it there earlier, and then she told herself she hadn’t.

Her name was on the front in pencil, block letters. LARK. No dear, no Ms. She crouched and slid a finger under the flap and opened it.

Inside was a single business card from a restaurant that had gone out of business when she was thirteen: The Anchor, with a little lighthouse drawn in blue. Someone had written on the back, in that same shaky haste that had labeled the shoebox: 53 Calhoun. Side entrance. 8:12.

She turned the card over and over, as if flipping it would make it less impossible. The ink had smeared where a too-wet pen had lingered. It was not new writing. It wasn’t old either; the oil of the paper felt like right now. She put it down next to the Otari and used her phone to photograph it like a person at a museum.

She dialed Ernest Vale.

His phone rang five times and went to a courtesy voice that told her the mailbox was nearly full, and then invited her to leave good news. She hung up. She dialed the other number he had told her was written on the box. It rang twice and then a woman said, “We’re not here, leave it.” She left it. She kept her voice reasonable.

She sat down again and rolled the tape back and forth, marking the portion where the words not accident lived. She saved a copy of the file to a portable drive—the station’s idea of security existed somewhere between faith and even more faith—and then she wrote an email to the morning producer, subject: Unexpected find. She attached a ten-second clip. In the body she wrote: From a set of committee recordings from ‘76 I think, brought by source I can ID. It sounds like the river—like a thing they did or wanted to do. Also: there’s another voice under track, like someone recorded over someone else. Listen to clip. Want to talk at ten? And then, because she was a professional even when she felt like a person in a story, she added: We’ll need legal to weigh in if it turns into anything for air.

The rest of Side B was more of what she already had—chitchat, numbers. She fast-forwarded and checked every five minutes in case the past wanted her again. It did, in small, domestic bursts: a man telling a joke only he found funny, a woman reminding him that money wasn’t a joke, the squeal of a chair that had squealed its entire life. At the end there was another piece of splicing tape, this one cleanly cut and firm. She could have peeled it up and spooled the world back further. She had done that, here, weeks ago, on a firefighter’s oral history where he had coughed and cried and then excused himself for both. But not tonight. Tonight her hands were too warm and too shaky.

At three-forty-two she powered down the Otari and labeled the reels so she wouldn’t make herself scramble later: BASEMENT COMMITTEE TAPE A and B - FIRST LISTEN - DO NOT PLAY until after the dehydrator again. She slid them back into their bags. She put the maroon shoebox on the floor at the back of her desk because she did not trust it on a shelf. She shut off the overheads and left the blue of the board for last.

On the stairs her knees discovered how long she had sat. The building exhaled around her. Outside, the river told her nothing from under its skin. Iverton at four in the morning was a city in rehearsal, sets standing on their little wheels, the fog machines on low. The streetlights had halos. On Calhoun Street she could see the bridge’s black silhouette knifing across the water, and beyond that, the kink where the road turned toward the Hollow. Her breath went white and then gone.

She woke to three messages before dawn. The first was from the morning producer: what is this? But also: oh. The second was from a number she didn’t know: call me if you got that from Ernie. The third she saw after she turned off the alarm with her thumb and sat up too fast in her apartment that had a different hum than the station’s, less machine, more human.

It was a text from a friend at the Ledger, who had decided three years ago that the only way to be a reporter was to never sleep. Did you meet a guy named Vale last night? it said. He’s in the blotter. Found near Calhoun by the side entrance to the old Anchor building. Eight-twelve pm he’s saying in his notes? Weird. They’re calling it a fall.

She didn’t realize she’d said oh out loud until the sound stayed in the air and someone downstairs shut off a radio as if giving her silence to be surprised in.

Her hand reached for the edge of the bed and found it. Her other hand found her phone as it always did, as if that was where the rest of her had been looking.

Not accident, the under-voice had said, soft and then fiercely again. Not a test. Thursday. The words she had heard were not made of tape anymore.

She got up. Somewhere between putting one foot in front of the other and finding her shoes she decided that 53 Calhoun was a place a person could be without it being a mistake. The card from last night sat on her kitchen counter because she had brought it home without meaning to. The lighthouse on The Anchor looked like a thing a child had drawn to be friendly to boats. She slid the card into her pocket like a talisman people made from something paper to fight a tide made of more.

On the walk to her car the light was not morning yet but it had the idea. Pigeons made their case for the day on the telephone lines. The river had kept its last night shape. Mara thought of a voice in a room forty years ago, saying we can test it, and of a man whose hand had briefly hovered over her desk asking to hear something before he could not hear anything. The past, like tape, was physical. It could be cut, and it could be spliced, and you could heat it and coax it into letting you listen. But the cut places did not forget they were cut. The joins, if you felt for them, would tell you where the tear had been.

She started the car. She put the phone on the passenger seat without plugging it in and told no one what she was doing and told herself she was only going to look at a doorway. She had been a person who kept an ear on things for long enough to know that what you listened to changed if you told someone else to listen with you.

On the bridge the air was colder. Below, the river’s surface dragged over and around the pilings like a sleeve over an elbow. At the far end of Calhoun, the side entrance to the old Anchor had a steel door that had once been painted with waves. Under the paint, under the steel, under the concrete, the ground remembered rain a certain way in certain months. The city had asked the right questions in rooms and the wrong questions in others. She had the kind of night where you heard both at once.

She pulled over, parked half in the no, and got out and stood in a place where her breath made white and then made room for the day behind it. At the threshold to the Anchor somebody had taped up a squint of crime scene tape, not enough to keep anyone out, just enough to claim it. On the sill lay a smear that might be rust and might be blood if your head needed it to be.

She touched the pocket that held the card and thought of the way the under-voice had kept speaking under the official one, saying, insistently, even through the noise and the years: not an accident. You could decide to hear a thing as a mistake. Or you could decide to hear it as a message.

In her pocket her phone buzzed again. When she glanced at it she saw the morning producer had written back: Legal at nine. Also: when you said “river thing” did you mean river as in water?

Mara started to type and then stopped, because even language had catches and springs in it you couldn’t always see, and the first thing you said about anything in the city had to be right or it would always be wrong after. She put the phone away. She tucked her hair into her scarf as if she could hide from the cold and from the dictates of air. She looked at the door. Then she looked at the river. Then she decided that she had not misheard a man at the end of a life or a tape recorded over a day.

She put her palm flat against the steel. It was cold enough to hurt. She held it there until her skin told her the door was a thing and not the wall it looked like. And then she took her hand away and blew on it and laughed, a small ridiculous sound in the street where a gull’s cry could make more drama than anything.

On Studio C’s desk, a reel of tape cooled from its brief heat. Along its edges, in the places the splicing tape held it together, tiny lines of adhesive were lifting like the beginning of a thought. Stay together, they asked, and also: tell me what you were before they asked you not to.

Chapter One

The sea has a way of storing questions.

It keeps them tucked between tides, under the tongues of rockweed, in the shallow burrows where sand fleas scatter when a boot approaches. People think it takes, but most of the time it just waits. You can walk right past something that will change your life because the water is pretending to be polite.

I was thinking about that on the ferry to Blackcap Island, sipping coffee that had somehow gone both burned and lukewarm, while the deckhand looped rope around a rusty cleat with the easy grace of someone who had never not been on the water. The mainland slid backward into fog, the kind of fine, persistent mist that turns your hair to seaweed and your clothes to regret. A trio of herring gulls paced the railing and assessed me with their mean yellow eyes, like bouncers deciding whether to let me into their club.

“You Ellery?” the deckhand asked, wiping his hands on his slicker.

“Maris,” I said. “But yes.”

He cracked a smile. “Maris by the sea, huh.”

“I didn’t pick the name,” I said. It still landed in me like a nudge of fate sometimes. My grandmother used to say that if you named a thing it would always know when you called. She’d named me for water and then taught me how to respect it.

“You got Jonah meeting you,” he said. “He’s good people. He don’t talk much. That don’t mean he don’t know much.”

The gulls flapped into the fog as Blackcap’s dock came into view—a crooked ribbon of weathered planks, a stack of faded lobster traps like children's blocks left out in the rain. The island rose up behind the wharf, a hump of spruce and scrubby blueberry with a few shingled roofs peeking out like cautious turtles. And beyond the trees, higher than all of it, the white cylinder of Blackcap Light poked into the gray.

I stood up as the ferry bumped the dock and felt the small, familiar thrill in my chest turn into a steady beat. It had been a long winter of city noise and fluorescent ceilings and lines on spreadsheets that didn’t line up no matter how I shook them. I had told myself too many days that I did work that mattered, and then watched it disappear under budgets and politics and bad faith. When the Penobscot County Historical Society offered a contract to help stabilize and modernize the Blackcap Lighthouse for visitor access—harness the new beacon for demonstration only, upgrade wiring, install a solar array to make the place less of a fire hazard than it had been when they were running it off a generator—I signed before they finished their sentence.

On the dock, a man in a navy watch cap and a barn coat waited next to a four-wheeler hitched to an open trailer. He had the posture of someone who had spent a lifetime standing on moving things: slight lean, knees soft, eyes steady. He lifted a hand in a way that was almost a wave.

“Jonah?” I said, grasping the duffel handle and my rolling toolkit.

“Maris Ellery,” he confirmed. His voice was carved smooth by salt and years. “You got more than that?”

“There’s a crate coming tomorrow,” I said. “Panels. The rest I can carry.”

He took the toolkit like it was a paper bag and set it on the trailer. “Weather’ll hold until evening,” he said, glancing at the sky even though the sky was a uniform swath of damp. “Fog’ll thicken with the tide. You ever been on Blackcap?”

“Not since field trips,” I said. “They let the third graders in the tower then.”

He grunted, which might have meant yes or nostalgia or both. “They’ll be glad to have it open again. Folks like to be told where to look.”

We rattled up the dirt road through the low wood, spruce branches combing the air above us. The island was small enough that it all felt close: the house roofs blinked past, a patch of highbush blueberry, a glimpse of a deer’s white flash disappearing into brush. The path widened to a clearing of scraped earth and a scattering of old granite blocks. And there it was.

Blackcap Light didn’t look like anything much from town. They all kind of look the same from a distance: white cylinder, black rail around the lantern room, a silhouette on postcards and tourist sweatshirts. Up close it was different. The paint was new, but the stones underneath still bulged and dipped with their own weight, fitted like teeth by hands that were long gone. The door was iron and scabbed with rust around the bolt. A small brick building—once the oil house—squatted beside it. The foghorn trumpet jutting from the ocean-facing wall like a brass instrument gone quiet. Above us, glass panes like thick honeycombs made a prism out of the gray.

We clattered up the external iron stair, boots ringing. Inside, it smelled like salt and dust and a faint sweetness that always reminded me of old books. The spiral climbed like a ribcage. Jonah walked in front and the sound of his boots on the treads kept time, steady, unhurried. I could feel the weight of the tower around us, the compromise between wind and stone, centuries of wind trying to push it down and failing.

At the top, the lantern room was a bright little bubble. Even in fog, the light off the water found its way up and in. The lens sat at the center on its iron pedestal. It was a third-order Fresnel, its prisms fractured into a thousand tiny corrections, catching and bending until a candle could punch a hole through the night. I had seen photographs, but in person it was intimate and unnerving, a thing designed to be looked through that felt like it was looking back.

“She’s a beauty,” I said, because it felt like the right thing.

“She’ll bite you if you let her,” Jonah said. There was fondness in it. He ran his fingers along one of the glass ribs the way you’d touch a horse to let it know who you were. “They took the old lamp out. What they left is what we need to keep.”

“I’m not here to change her,” I said. “Just to make sure she can show off without burning down her dress.”

He made that half-grunt again, approval. He pointed at the floor, at the round iron hatch that covered the weight well.
