The original mechanism had been a clockwork: a descending weight turned the lens, which made the flashes. They’d long ago replaced it with an electric motor. Now, as part of the demonstration system, we were going to give it a slow, dignified rotation again when the schoolkids came, a memory of purpose without the risk.

“They never did get the horn back,” he said, tapping the rusted trumpet. “Hasn’t blown since ’98. Some say it’s quieter without it. Some say they can still hear it in weather, but that’s somebody else’s horn. Sound plays tricks out here.”

“What’s the old characteristic?” I asked. Every light has its signature—its own heartbeat so mariners could tell them apart.

“Flashing two every ten seconds,” he said. “Used to be three. Changed in sixty-three. You’ll see it on the card in the oil house.”

I crouched by the pedestal and ran a hand over the crank bearings. My head filled, as it always did, with a map of what needed to be done. The panels and the charge controller would go on the oil house roof. New wiring down the shaft, careful not to drill where we’d compromise stone. A battery bank in the oil house behind a locked cabinet. New glass for the cracked pane in the northeast quadrant. Check the ladder bolts. Safety cages around the stairs. It wasn’t glamorous work, but it was the kind that let things last, and lately that felt like rebellion.

“Do many people stay out here?” I asked, not looking up from the bearing. “At night?”

“Just me,” Jonah said. “And sometimes Beau on the weekends. House by the cove’s mine. You got the guest cabin, if you want it, or you can catch the last ferry back. But you knew that.”

“I’ll stay,” I said. “I work better when I don’t have to pretend I wasn’t thinking about something all night.”

He looked at me for a moment in a way that said he had heard something I hadn’t exactly said. “Good. You want coffee?”

“I’ve had worse,” I said.

It turned out to be better. He boiled it on a little propane stove in the oil house, poured it into mismatched mugs that said things like World’s Best Grandpa even though as far as I knew he wasn’t anyone’s. We sat in the doorway with our feet on the threshold, the rain by then a fine, deliberate brushing sound. A black guillemot sat on a rock near the shore and preened, its red legs like little silk ribbons. Somewhere out in the fog, someone’s bell buoy clanged, slow and mournful.

“You grow up here?” he asked me, like he had decided to pay me back for my question with a personal one.

“North of Bangor,” I said. “But my grandmother lived on Little Goose. We spent summers there. No electricity, no running water, one radio that only worked if you stood on the table and held a spoon above your head.”

He smiled for real, the kind that lifts the cheeks and softens everything. “You’re not going to be the one who cuts her thumb and has to be airlifted off because you thought a chisel was for butter, then.”

“I’ve read instructions before,” I said. “I’m not to be trusted with a microwave, but I can wire a breaker panel blindfolded.”

“I don’t doubt it,” he said. He took a sip and watched the fog like it might reveal a secret if he looked gently enough. “You ever think about how many lives it is, for a light? All those nights. All those eyes looking for it. Makes a person wonder how many people owe it a second chance.”

He said it like a man asking the water for a story, not expecting an answer. I didn’t have one anyway. We sat a little while longer and then I stood because the rain teased me into it and because there were screws to count and measurements to draft and I liked that part best, when nothing had gone wrong yet and the day was still wet clay.

By late afternoon I had a list with checkboxes and a floor covered in pencil shavings and a thumb smudged with graphite. I’d found a logbook in a drawer in the oil house—a fat, leather-bound thing with pages as soft as skin. The last entries were from 1973, when the Coast Guard automated the light and sent the keepers—they had called themselves keepers even then, though half the job was mending and painting and timing things—back to the mainland. The handwriting changed three times, one flowing, one meticulous, one a cramped series of numbers and short notes.

June 8: Fog, horn three times per minute. Herring full in the creek.

June 12: Mrs. Larkin sent pie. Rabbit got in the garden again. God save us from rabbits.

June 21: Flasher assembly inspected. Bearings greased. Characteristic good. Three in fifteen.

July 2: If he comes by sea, do not light.

The neatness of it, its lack of explanation, nudged my neck hairs. There were no later entries, as if the book had decided to freeze right there and hold its breath. I looked for another volume and found only insect husks and a coil of twine. The note wasn’t a secret; it was sitting there for anyone to read and imagine around. I rapped the knuckles of my free hand lightly against the doorjamb, a habit of mine when the past did what it does, which is wrap itself around the ankle and yank a person backward without warning.

“You hungry?” Jonah asked from the foot of the stairs.

“I could be,” I said.

“Beau’s making chowder,” he said. “You’ll think the angels learned how to peel potatoes. It’s not far if you don’t mind the walk.”

We picked our way along the path toward the cove, Jonah pushing past spruce boughs with a habitual shift of the wrist so they wouldn’t slap back at me, my head full of the smell of wet earth giving up its heat. From the edge of the path, I could see a sliver of the town dock, a smear of yellow that was probably Slick’s truck, a line of buoys—red and white, blue and black like candies—strung along the edge of a yard.

The chowder lived up to the marketing. We sat at a kitchen table scarred with cigarette burns and the bare map of a spilled beer and ate out of bowls big enough for a baby seal. Beau was younger than me and older than the kind of trouble that grows on its own; he had three silver hoops in his left ear and a tattoo of a cod that curved around his forearm and blinked when he flexed. He and Jonah didn’t look like family, and if they were, they never said so in my hearing, but they had the grammar of it—shared jokes with no context, the confidence that labels would be there when fingers reached.

“You here to turn the light back on?” Beau asked, spooning in more clams.

“Only when kids are watching,” I said. “She’ll keep her dark when she’s supposed to keep her dark.”

“You know how people get about that,” he said. “They think if it’s not always on, it’s not doing anything. That if it’s not loud, it’s not working. They want to be told.”

“Jonah says that, too,” I said.

“Don’t tell him I said he was right,” Beau said. “His head won’t fit through the stair.”

The fog pressed harder against the windows as we ate. Every once in a while a shape moved past that might have been a person or a tree remembering how to be one. When I stepped out onto the porch, full and warm and holding a borrowed raincoat too big for me, the damp touched my face like a hand.

“You sure you don’t want to ride back with me to the guest cabin?” Beau asked. “I can run you up, no trouble.”

“I want to look at the wiring again before I sleep,” I said. I wanted to touch the metal in the tower again, to feel its coolness anchor me.

“All right,” he said. “You see anything looks like a will-o’-the-wisp, don’t follow it.”

I smiled. “I read that story, too.”

“Weren’t a story,” he said, but he grinned back to blunt the edge.

By the time we reached the base of the tower, the fog had learned me well enough to try to climb inside my coat. I wiped a wet palm on my jeans and set my fingers on the iron door latch and felt it drag open, reluctant. The spiral stair rose ahead, dim, and the lantern room above it hummed with the particular quiet of enclosed space.

I was halfway up when the first flash came.

It wasn’t a sound. It was a sudden, specific brightness that turned the shadows to knives and then let them go. My body registered it a moment before my mind did, the pause you take when someone says your name in a crowd and you’re not sure if you imagined it. The light wasn’t wired yet. There was no power to the pedestal. No battery had been connected. I turned my head and another flash swept across the walls, scalloping the iron, touching and moving on. I counted under my breath without thinking. An engineer counts. A keeper counts. Three seconds, then ten of gray. Another. Two seconds. A pause. Two again.

“Jonah?” I called, my voice odd in the drum of the stair.

He was at the bottom. His boots moved on metal. “You see that too?” he asked, and something in his voice told me he wasn’t telling me not to be foolish.

We climbed the rest together, me a step ahead but not enough to pretend courage. The lantern room was bright like a mouth full of teeth. The fog beyond made the light larger, made it find edges where there weren’t any. The lens was a sleeping thing. The bulb assembly sat cold, its little polished throat as inert as a spoon. The flashes came from outside, sweeping the panes from the sea.

I moved to the seaward side and pressed my forehead to the glass. The world was white. But even in white, if you lived with it long enough, you learned to see. There was a smudge in the distance that was darker than the rest of the fog. It moved. It could have been a boat. The flash came again, from that direction.

“Not SOS,” I said, my mouth a machine turning syllables into calm. “Listen. Two short, one long, two short. Again.”

“You read it?” Jonah asked.

“I can try,” I said, and inside my head a scaffold built itself, the dots and dashes I’d learned working in signal timing for railways, the code of people who wanted to speak reliably in unreliable spaces. The timing wasn’t perfect. Whoever sent it didn’t have a keyer; they had a lamp and a hand and fog and hope. Three short, pause, one long, one short. Again.

“Two short, one long,” I said, half to myself, as the pattern, such as it was, repeated. “That’s U and T. UT… No. It’s not clean. Longer pause between pairs. That’s a new letter. S. S again. S. That’s SOS now, that cluster, but then—no—wait. That’s an A. BA? No. Dammit.” The fog got inside my head, too. The next set came slower—three long, pause, two short—and then nothing for a spine’s count.

I put my hand flat on the glass like it would help. The smudge in the fog didn’t resolve. I thought of a person in a small boat with a deck spotlight, his finger shaking on the toggle. I thought of the shape of an urgent hand.

“Sometimes,” Jonah said softly, “people just aim at what they know. A light sends to a light.”

A wave smacked the rocks below and reminded the tower we were small. The next flash was weaker, or else my eyes had tired. It stuttered. It flattened the white and then brought the white back. And then there was nothing. Fog and the low throat-sound of water pushing air.

“How far out?” I asked.

“Hard to tell in this,” he said. “Not far. Quarter mile maybe. Less.”

“Boat?” I said.

“Maybe a punt,” he said. “Maybe a skiff. Not big.”

“We should—”

“I’ll call it in,” he said. He had the radio and the right to use it, which is not the same thing. “I don’t want Islesboro or the Coast Guard mad we dragged out the volunteers for a gull sitting on a buoy. They’ll go quiet on you, the sun’s out tomorrow. They’ll go loud if you cried wolf.”

He was already speaking into the handheld while I watched the fog until my eyes hurt. He gave coordinates, calm and conversational, like someone asking a neighbor if they’d feed the cat. He was a person who understood that in a place where time is made of weather, urgency makes its own noise; you don’t have to add to it.

The fog ate light for another hour and then the daylight was also gone. We slept short and badly—me in the guest cabin with the room working through heat and damp, Jonah in a small house smelling of engine oil and rosemary—dreams full of flashing things and paper pages with impossible instructions. At seven, I made coffee and walked back down to the cove. The rain had wandered off. The island felt like a cat that had shaken itself and settled. The water lay dressed in pewter.

Two boats were already nosing around the rocks with men in them who wore orange and looked like they’d been awake all night. One was the volunteer rescue from Little Wren. The other was a skiff I recognized because Beau had painted it to look like a mackerel when he was bored one winter—wavy stripes fading to the bow. He stood in the stern now, jaw tight.

“You heard?” Jonah said behind me.

“What?”

“Tommy Rowe’s punt washed up at Needle Rock, empty,” he said. “His jacket was in it. No oars.”

“Rowe?” The name clicked and found places to anchor. A man at the diner who always sent his toast back. A face at the co-op who had once given me a towel when the rain blew in on me before I knew enough to sit far from the door. A brown dog that sat in his truck like a person.

“They’re calling him missing,” Jonah said.

“And last night—”

“Last night, somebody sent us a light,” he said. “Maybe him. Maybe some other poor fool. Maybe a trick of fog. That’s the trouble. Fog makes believers and liars of us.”

We stood on the shore and watched as the boats nosed, their motors breaking the morning’s stillness into chewed foam. A gull perched on a piling and shouted obviously critical feedback to everyone involved. Somewhere on the mainland a chainsaw started up, as if the world was keeping its appointments without us.

“What’s that?” I asked, pointing to a shape in the eelgrass at the high water mark near the base of the tower.

We picked our way over wet rock and wrack, boots slipping, and came upon the thing: Tommy's thermos, the battered green kind with a scuffed cup-lid. It lay half-buried, like it had washed up and decided to stay. There were marks around it in the kelp where the tide had rearranged its bed. I bent and picked it up because there are movements your body makes before you think on them, because it looked so much like every thermos I’d ever seen in every boat I’d ever sat in, because it was not a body and so was safe to touch.

The lid unscrewed with a protesting squeak. There was coffee inside, three sips worth. It was cold, and when I tilted the thermos, something clicked in the bottom like a coin or a peewee marble.

“Don’t,” Jonah said, but it was a gentle don’t, too late. I tapped the thermos mouth with two fingers and a curled scrap of paper slid out, brown and damp. I teased it open. The pencil had run some, but the lines were still there, blunt and dogged.

The clock stops at 2:17, it said. Bring up the clock.

“What is that,” Beau said behind us, breathless, like he’d run from the boat to the rock in one stride, as if wanting badly enough could make a man fly. His eyes went from the thermos to our faces to my hand. His jaw clenched and unclenched. “Christ, Maris, what is that.”

I lifted my head toward the tower, where the iron hatch over the weight well sat like a secret, where the lens had slept in the dark for fifty years and the prisms had not forgotten. I thought of the old log entry: If he comes by sea, do not light. I thought of a clock that had not turned in half a century, the click of pawls, the slow dignity of brass.

“It’s a message,” I said. “And I think it’s for us.”

I have three rules for writing about the dead. Spell the names right. Call the mother. Never run anything if the subject is still breathing.

The first two will keep you from having your desk set on fire. The last isn’t a rule so much as a superstition I stroke when the newsroom is quiet, a little prayer written in ink and coffee. I tell myself these rules make me a professional. I tell myself a lot of things so I don’t have to think about the fact that, on most days, my work is the last word anyone will get.

On Tuesday, the last rule arrived in a manila envelope with no return address and a perfume of lilies I couldn't see.

The envelope was waiting for me in the narrow mailbox under the Bellwether Chronicle sign, the brass flap clanking back into place as if it had just been fed. Our building used to be a bank; our mailboxes live in what used to be safe-deposit drawers. Some mornings the ghosts of old depositors line up in my head, all those careful men-who-wore-hats, all those women in white gloves, tucked away like the folded wills they came to hide.

The morning fog was still clinging to the river when I carried the envelope upstairs. The Chronicle’s newsroom sits on the second floor, a broad room with tall windows and a ceiling with a hundred small cracks that run to the walls like tributaries. The linotype machines are long gone; the presses are in a cheaper county now, and the noise at night is the quiet kind, the humming of the soda fridge and the police scanner’s murmur. There are fewer of us than there used to be, but the odd thing about a room built to contain words is that it never looks empty; the old headlines crowd in from the shelves, the framed front pages with one-word heds—Rebuilt, Flooded, Exonerated.

I put my bag down on my scarred desk, slid my finger under the envelope’s flap, and felt the tacky, old-school glue resist me. Inside was a single sheet of onion-skin paper folded in thirds. The letters were dark and precise, the way a typewriter makes them when the ribbon is new and someone has gone slowly, straight-backed, pressing each key like a thought.

The header read: Benedict Prosper Cole, 58.

Under it, in neat paragraphs that skipped just so from line to line, was an obituary better written than most of the ones families bring me. It had the shape we favor: a brisk first paragraph with the who/what/where/when, a second paragraph with the why-he-mattered, and then the orderly march backward to childhood and parents and the first job washing boats on the Yellow Dog River, which was a detail that managed to sound both invented and inevitable.

Benedict P. Cole, philanthropist, shipyard owner, and advocate for the Riverlight Conservancy, died early Thursday morning at his home on Hunter’s Quay, after complications from a rescue. He was 58.

He died twice that night, the body learning the lesson the heart couldn’t hold. The first time was at 1:17 a.m., when the river stopped speaking to him; the second was when we let him go.

That last sentence sat there like a stone on ice.

He is survived by his sister, Dorothea Cole Vance of Atlanta, two nephews, and an entire town's worth of small graces: the light on the lighthouse, the striped awnings on Third Street restored after the 2012 storm, the scholarships that made it easier for a handful of bright children to leave.

I read the rest quickly, my eye snagging on the sorts of specifics we salt our own pre-writes with when we know someone is frail and notable. We keep files in a shared drive labeled with names we never say out loud near the coffee machine. The mayor’s file is stuffed and frequently edited. The oldest file we lost by accident when the server burped three summers ago and nearly caused a lawsuit.

This was as if someone had raided our software and my notebook besides. There were quotes that sounded like quotes, set off properly and attributed to people who would give them: "Benny’s money turned our river outward again," Mayor Celia Hart said. "It’s not that he bought us a view—we had the view. He bought us the habit of looking."

There was an exact address: Hunter’s Quay, a crescent of rowhouses and brick mansions perched above the black curve the river made before it widened into harbor. There was mention of a quatrefoil window in his study, the one I'd seen once on a house tour, its mullions making a clover the color of late water.

At the bottom was a line we never use: Prepared by Family. In lieu of flowers, donate to Riverlight Conservancy.

My seat creaked. I put the paper down and went to the window. The river below was a gray muscle under the fog, flexing, then slack, as if somebody were lazily tugging at its anchors. A tug pushed a barge past, its horn low and patient, the sound rolling up into our office like a lullaby.

“You look like you’re tasting a lemon,” Tom said from beside the police scanner. He had a red ceramic mug in one hand and a paperclip in the other. His hair is grayer than spring when I first started here, but his eyebrows are still the kind that tell you not to waste his time.

“Pre-writes are on the second shelf,” he added. “Alphabetical. You didn’t lose Cole’s, did you?”

I handed him the onion-skin.

Tom doesn’t rush to read. He held the paper at a distance and let the first paragraph hit him. He has the kind of brain that can tell if a sentence is balanced from across the room. He raised an eyebrow at the "died twice" line and glanced at me.

“You write this,” he asked.

"It came in the mailbox,” I said. “No return address. Dated Thursday. We’ve never run anything on Cole. He’s fifty-eight. And that line.”

He flipped the paper. Blank on the back. He bent the edge near his thumbnail the way he does when he's thinking. The police scanner coughed and muttered about a truck stalled at the Second Street underpass, blocking a bus full of overtired second-graders. Tom put the onion-skin down carefully between two coffee rings.

“We do pre-writes,” he said, meaning that the existence of a decent obituary for a living person is not, by itself, a message from the dark. “His people probably typed something up and thought they’d be helpful. Famous men have assistants with folder habits. It spares the family the trouble.”

“A family friend who owns a typewriter and knows his window?”

Tom shrugged. “He’s our river baron. People talk.”

“Who says ‘the river stopped speaking’?”

Tom sipped his coffee. “Poets who forgot their rent.”

“I’ll call his office,” I said, already reaching for the book where we keep numbers that sometimes ring.

“Do that,” Tom said. His tone gave me the permission I didn’t need. “And Iris? Don’t you dare put ‘died twice’ in the paper. It reads like a dare.”

I found the number for Cole Maritime on a business card tucked behind a magnet shaped like a lighthouse. The receptionist was crisp; the line put me through to Elise Kline, who I knew by voice because in a town like ours, there are three voices you can identify by their hello—the mayor’s, your own landlord’s, and the assistant to the richest man in five counties.

“Cole Maritime,” she said. “Elise speaking.”

“This is Iris Flynn with the Chronicle,” I said. I’ve learned to put the next sentence close after the first, so people don’t hang up. “An obituary arrived at our office for Mr. Cole. Did your office send that?”

A pause. “An obituary for Mr. Cole?”

“It came without a return address, on onion-skin, typed, and it reads... it reads like something you would write if you had access to his study.”

Another pause, longer. Paper moved on the other end of the line. I pictured her in the building with the glass that takes on the river’s mood, windows reflected in windows until the whole place looked watery.

“We don’t… no. We haven’t prepared anything like that,” Elise said slowly, as if picking her way across a flat river stone’s wet face. “And if we had—I don’t know why we would—but if we had, we would have emailed it to the features editor with an appropriate note.”

“Would you like me to read you a line?” I asked. “There’s a phrase. It might ring a bell.”

“No,” she said quickly. “No, don’t. Can you… can you send me a copy?”

“I can’t,” I said, and was surprised to hear the stubbornness in my voice. It was faintly ridiculous to feel as if a single page were a bird I was protecting under a coat. “It came in with no instruction, and Tom—my editor—will want to decide what to do. You can come look at it, if you’d like.”

“I can’t take a cab to you to look at a fake obituary for my boss,” she said, and there was the Elise I knew, the one whose job was the firm and ungiving surface of things. “We have a nine a.m. with the mayor about the Riverlight budget. We have a donors’ lunch. We have… Mr. Cole is fine. Of course he’s fine.”

“Of course,” I said. “I thought you should know.”

When I hung up, I had the polite taste of nothing in my mouth. Tom had gone to tell the city desk that the school bus had found reverse. The onion-skin lay in my periphery like a polite letter from the future. I had once seen the inside of Benedict Cole’s house because the historical society had staged a fundraiser and chosen three houses with stories and expensive rugs. His study had smelled like lemon oil and river mud. I had looked through the quatrefoil and seen two men in a rowboat moving against the current like a slow argument.

By ten, I was at Saint Brigid’s, in the pews, because if an obituary is your beat, you go where the mourners are and listen to the way they say he truly lived when he did, and you notice the photographs blown up on foam board that always show the dead at a beach, and you write down the names of grandchildren, and you pull the advice from the way the choir director presses her lips together when the organist starts a hymn in the wrong key. Marcella Parry had been a librarian for seventy years. She could shush through walls, according to the second hymn read. Men in suits who hadn’t touched a book in years dabbed at their eyes because of the way one of her dozens of green-gowned nieces laughed in the third pew when somebody dropped a program and it sounded like a bird falling. It was a good service. It was better than most. When it ended, Benedict Cole shook hands halfway down the center aisle.

He was the kind of tall that made you think of ladders. He wore a gray suit and a scarf despite the warmish day, because men of a certain type put fabric by their throats to stave off the little drafts in the world. He had that slight ruddiness on his jaw that says I went out on a boat because it was mine. I had written about his regatta, the one whose trophies never looked as heavy as the engraving made them sound. He saw me seeing him and did what recognizable people do: came to me so I couldn’t come to him.

“Ms. Flynn,” he said, offering his hand. “The Chronicle told Marcella’s stories better than anyone deserved. She would have liked to lie about her age to you.”

“Mr. Cole,” I said. His hand was warmer than mine. He had a thin white scar on the back of it that flashed when he let go. “I’m sorry for your loss.”

“It’s a town’s loss,” he said. “The last time I saw your editor in a church he had hair.”

I smiled because one does at men who say you remember lesser versions of our elders. Behind him was Elise, her hair pulled back, her eyes doing the math of the rest of the day. When our eyes met, hers narrowed the way eyes do when they ask What are you about to say?

“Iris is writing a book,” Tom likes to tell people I’m not writing a book, so he can look like a man with good news. I wasn’t, but there it was, the thing that always gets asked now: what are you doing here besides the thing you do?

“I’m working,” I said instead. “We share a river," I added, because sometimes composing a sentence feels like throwing a rope. "Everyone shows up for the river.”

He laughed, a dry bark softened by the church. “The river shows up for us, when it wants,” he said. “Nice to see the Chronicle in a pew. Stay out of trouble.”

When he turned to shake hands with a city councilman, Elise took a half step in, a wedge of movement in a small space.

“There’s no obituary,” she said under the noise.

“I never said there was,” I said. It was the truth, in the strict sense, but as evasions go the river could have swum through it. “Is the view from your study as good as people say?”

“Which study,” she said, after a heartbeat.

“I’ll come by,” I said, because sometimes the only way to get someone to confirm a fact they shouldn't is to propose a reality in which it's already confirmed. “We can laugh about it in person. No lilies.”

She held my gaze long enough for me to see the tiny flecks near the iris that made her eyes look river-colored.

By late afternoon, the newsroom had filled to its afternoon volume. The city desk fussed about a zoning scandal. The features team debated whether the arts column’s new voice was insufferable or just young. Somebody had brought cookies that tasted like the tin they came in. I wrote about Marcella. I put Benedict's file in our pre-write folder with a name that would be hard to accidentally click. I walked to the river for a late lunch and watched an egret stand so still near the reeds that its reflection forgot to ripple.

At seven, the light leaned hard against the buildings at the far side of the river and then let go. Fog rose out of the water like a set piece arrived on cue. Across the room, the police scanner developed tension the way a person does when they remember a sudden appointment.

We keep it on for the cadence as much as the content. The voices of dispatchers carrying through the room is the city’s pulse. I’ve slept with it in my head for so many years now that when someone says “Unit four” in a new tone of voice, my hands know to find my notebook.

“Units to Harborview,” the scanner said. “Report of unresponsive male at end of Wharf Street. Caller states... repeat, caller states extraction in progress. EMS en route.”

Harborview is a name you give a cheap apartment building if you want people to think they live near boats. Wharf Street is the opposite; it does what it says. It curls under Hunter’s Quay, under the watch of the richer brick that sits like a calm judge above it. By the time I had my jacket on, Tom was standing.

“Truck stalled,” he said, because that is what he says when he doesn’t want to say the thing the scanner did. “You don’t need—”

“I know Wharf Street,” I said.

“I know you do,” he said. He looked at me with a face that softened and stopped. “Be a witness, not a hero. And for the love of God, spell the names right.”

Outside, the fog had thickened, the kind that takes an inch of distance from the face of anything solid and keeps it. The streetlights made cones of buttered light. There was the smell of the river—iodine and metal, something like pennies and ribbon. I walked quickly because there is a way to both want not to arrive and to arrive quickly, and I have learned it.

By the time I reached the bottom of Wharf Street, there were three cruisers, an ambulance, and one car I recognized as the mayor’s by its tinted windows and the way it had been parked like a thought abandoned mid-sentence. The river had come all the way up to the edge of the wharf and then stopped, gently making its case against the pilings. Yellow tape had appeared between a parking sign and a bollard. People had come out of the two bars—a scattering of men in white shirts and their dates in boots, and one very old man with a terrier that behaved as if the river had affronted it personally. The terrier snapped at the steam from the ambulance exhaust.

I could see the huddle near the water’s edge before I could see the person being worked on. A paramedic knelt and counted, two fingers pressing at the wind's throat. Another glanced at his watch every time the counting paused. Behind them, a man in a diving suit I would not have put on for any money held a coil of rope. There was a jacket draped over the railing, the scarf the kind of gray that looks expensive in fog.

“It’s private property,” a voice I knew said from my right. Detective Rowan Hale stood with his hands in his coat pockets, the kind of posture that looks casual until you have the cuffs on you. He had been a uniform when I wrote about the Fourth Street fire, a sergeant by the time the bus skidded on black ice and slid into a bakery. He and I have an understanding that could be called mutual irritation in a different key.

“Wharf Street belongs to no one and everyone,” I said, because this is how we are with one another when a scene is going to be bad and he doesn’t want to say it first. “Is it him?”

I didn’t say Benedict. I didn’t say the pronoun I wanted to say. I said Is it him because that way, if it wasn’t, I would not have put a name on an unresponsive male.

Rowan held my gaze long enough for me to see the weather those eyes held, to feel the air cool inside my chest. He didn’t answer me. He never does that for free.

A woman’s voice broke on my left like a branch. “Elise,” somebody said. “Sit. Sit.”

She did not sit. Elise Kline stood near the bollard, her mouth open as if the river had gone up and over her; her breath came in little shocked sounds. Her hair was out of its knot. The mayor stood beside her, saying nothing, which is how you knew it was bad.

“Back up,” somebody said in the cluster. The paramedic put both hands on the unresponsive male’s sternum and pressed down, and pressed, and pressed. The diver flexed his hands inside his suit as if reacquainting himself with the fact that he owned them.

Even when we don’t hear the words people say to one another by rivers, our bodies recognize the shape of them. Set. Go. Wait. Now. Stop. The paramedic checked the watch again. He glanced up, glanced down, pressed once more, and sat back on his heels. He put his fingers to the throat again and then did something with his mouth that was both a grimace and a kiss to the air, a gesture done for himself, like an apology.

“What time,” Rowan said, flat out into the fog.

The paramedic didn’t look up. “One seventeen,” he said.

The number landed like a coin dropped into my palm by a hand from a height.

I could feel the onion-skin paper in my bag as if it had a heartbeat.

There are moments when the sound drops all the way out of the world. In those seconds, you hear the part of your own mind that narrates whether you like it or not. Mine said: if this is what it looks like, you are standing at the first paragraph of a story that wants to be told in your voice and no one else’s. Mine also said: go home, now, and burn the envelope.

I didn’t move. My hands were the hands I bring to the dead, my listening hands. I had a pen. I had a notebook. The fog drew closer, curious as a cat. Elise made the sound of someone who has never cried in public before and is learning quickly. The river took what it had been given and said nothing.

Rowan put his hand out without looking and pressed his palm against my notebook—the kind of pressure that says I cannot stop you from writing, but I can remind you my body exists. His coat smelled like wool that has known rain. He leaned to the side so that his mouth was near my ear and said, softly enough that only I could hear: “Don’t make me read ‘the river stopped speaking’ in your lede.”

“I would never,” I said. I didn’t know if I meant the sentence or the promise. The line lay in my bag like a dare shoved down into a drawer.

“Good,” he said. He let go of my notebook.

The paramedics lifted the body. The shape on the stretcher was covered, present the way a concealed thing is more present than anything else on earth. As they moved toward the ambulance, the scarf on the rail breathed. Without thinking, I put my hand out to keep it from falling into the water. The fabric was wet and cold. It had the faint scent of lemon oil.

Somewhere up on the Quay, a light went on behind a clover-shaped pane of glass. The window looked like an emblem sewn on a coat. Perhaps no one was there; perhaps the house had learned to turn its own lamps on when the river wanted night. The fog took the light and tugged it through its fingers.

I watched the ambulance doors close. I watched the mayor straighten the line of her mouth so it would be ready for microphones. I watched Elise Kline begin to pick at her thumbnail, a small motion at the edge of the city’s big grief. I thought of a single sheet of paper folded in thirds, words arranged to fit a moment that had not yet happened when they were typed.

Back upstairs, a phone would ring in the Chronicle newsroom, and a press officer would ask us to prepare something dignified. The city would ask for a sentence. People would text names and question marks. The rules in my head had not changed, but the world had leaned up against them in a way that felt like the beginning of a crack.

When I finally turned away from the river, Rowan stood directly in my path the way a door would, his hands back in his pockets. He looked at me for a long moment.

“This wasn’t you,” he said, and it wasn’t a question. “You didn’t put words in the box and then wait for them to fit.”

“No,” I said. “I didn’t.”

“Then find out who did,” he said. “Before they hand you the next envelope.”

Back at my desk, the onion-skin felt warm in my hands, then cool, then just there, a piece of paper with a capacity for harm. I laid it flat and smoothed its curl with my palm. The words did not rearrange themselves under my touch. They stayed. They were exactly what they had been this morning: a map of a night I hadn’t yet seen.

I had always thought my rules were for keeping the paper safe from me. That was, perhaps, the first mistake. The police scanner changed its tone and said a street I did not recognize very well. The fog pressed itself against the window and did what fog does: made the world smaller and more exact and more like itself.

When I finally turned the paper over, there was, of course, nothing on the back. But along the top edge, pressed ghost-faint into the onion-skin by a typewriter carriage, a line of numbers had imprinted themselves, the way a heavy hand leaves a mark on the next page: 1 1 7.

I have three rules for writing about the dead. After I put the onion-skin back in its envelope, I added a fourth, written only in my head, in ink no one could see: if the future arrives in the mail, do not sign for it.

The clocks in Graybridge never agreed with one another. The ferry clock was five minutes slow because the ferry master preferred not to rush his afternoons; the bakery’s round porcelain-cheeked face ran a minute fast, which let the owner boast that his loaves arrived “still in the future.” Even the great tower in St. Aldwyn’s, whose iron tongue had marked the hours since before my grandmother’s grandmother stood on these slate-slick streets, lagged two minutes behind. Only I noticed that. I notice when time forgets itself.

On mornings when the river shouldered fog like a shawl and the cobbles echoed with the soft thud of bundles from the market, when everything felt just a little muffled, Hart & Sons kept the right hour. The sign said Sons because it was cheap to dust gold leaf off the old plaque than to commission a new one after my father died, and because Graybridge had known Hart & Sons for so long that people would have had to learn to walk a different way to speak of it. Inside the shop smelled the same as it had when I was ten and my father let my small fingers hold a balance spring for a daring moment: brass and oil and wood warmed by weak northern light.

I had a carriage clock open on the bench, swan-neck regulator glinting like a silver comma, the minute hand hovering over the exact moment I always loved best—when a machine agreed with itself, when everything met without apology. The copper kettle on the stove in back was just coming to its first impatient hiss. I could feel the thin shudder of the tower bell through the plank floorboards when it marked the half hour. Nine-thirty in the street, if you asked any of a dozen clocks; in my hands, nine twenty-eight.

The bell over the door chimed once. You would think, given the life I lead, that I would have replaced the bell with something more precise: a chime tuned to A, perhaps, or a spruce of silver rods. I never did. It sounded like a bauble, like something left over in a pocket, and I liked that about it.

The man who came in held himself together the way a bundle is held together by an extra loop of twine. He had a red scarf wound twice around his throat and a tweed coat that had been mended with loving indifference. Ink had lived in the grooves of his fingers; even his cuffs were freckled with it. He was not the sort of nervous that flutters. He was the sort that hums under the skin.

“Ms. Hart?” His voice had that cracked-leather quality men get when they have spent too many winters breathing cold air in. He glanced at the queue of clocks along the wall, at the glass-lidded display where old pocket watches lay in their trays like larks’ eggs, then at the window and the street beyond it, as if the street itself held its breath. “I was told—well. I was told you’re discreet.”

“You were told truthfully.” I set the carriage clock aside and folded the loupe against my collar. “Tea?”

The corner of his mouth considered a smile and thought better of it. “No. Thank you. I won’t take much of your time.”

He slid a small velvet pouch from his coat and set it on the bench as if he were putting down something that might wake. The pouch was stained near the drawstring with something darkened to brown; oil, I thought. The smell said smoke. Inside was a pocket watch. I have softened over the years on those who bring watches as if they were talismans. There are worse talismans.

It was a hunter-case, nickel silver case dulled by touch, with a dent like a knuckle near the hinge. When I pressed the button, the lid sprang with a polite little click. Someone had kept it clean. The dial was plain enamel, Roman numerals thinned in places from a century of eyes. The blued steel hands had been repinned, not badly. Someone had loved it enough to keep it working when it had no right to. It ticked in my palm with a stilted urgency, like a small animal out of breath.

“Family piece?” I asked.

“Business.” He had one of those careful Graybridge faces that could be any age between forty and sixty. The scarf made him seem younger, or an attempt at it. He took off his hat; the hair beneath was too long at the back and had gone white unevenly, as if time had taken practice runs. He set the hat on the counter and didn’t remove his gloves. “There’s something wrong with it. It—” He stopped, watching the second hand at my thumb chase itself. “It came into my possession yesterday.”

“It went hard on something,” I said. My father taught me to talk to customers as if they were the ones telling me the truth. “The dent by the hinge, an impact. Heat, possibly. The dial’s taken hairlines. Have you dropped it?”

He flinched so slightly that I almost missed it. “No. I shouldn’t… No. I want it fixed. Quietly.”

“I can fix quietly.” I turned it over. The case back had been opened with a blade at some point; you could tell by the faint crescent scratch near the seam. Old scratch, but not old enough. Someone impatient, maybe. Had they cut into it last night? I pressed the case knife into the groove and eased the back open. Inside, under the dust cover, the movement lay like a city viewed from above—bridges, jewels like small pond-berries, the balance wheel flicking itself into and out of frenzy.

There’s a thing that happens when you speak a language so well you’ve forgotten you know it. The smallest mispronunciation leaps out at you. On this movement, something mispronounced itself. It was a lovely piece by a minor English maker who never had the money for fancy and who, I sensed by the patient layout of his plates, would have disliked fancy on principle. The lever had been tampered with.

He watched me watch it. “Can you mend it?” he asked softly.

“I can. But whoever worked on this, recently, added a hack feature that doesn’t belong. See this?” I pointed, and he leaned in despite himself. “If you pull the crown in just so—here—the mechanism stops the balance wheel. Stops the watch exactly. It’s a soldier’s trick, synchronizing to the second. Only this isn’t a military watch. It wasn’t built for that.”

His breath did something I catalogued and ignored for the moment. “Is that significant?”

“What is significant is that whoever did it had steady hands and poor sense. They cut into the top plate to fit something that didn’t want to live there, and that’s made the pivots unhappy.” I peered through the loupe. The tiny steel screws had been polished and then, later, worried by a second screwdriver of a slightly different thread. Two hands, two times. “Also, that’s luminous paint on the hands. Old. Doesn’t belong with this case.”

He shifted his weight, the floor creaked, the kettle in back hissed again as if to say, well? The tower bell concluded the quarter hour and took a breath.

“How long will it take?” he said. His gaze kept rebounding back to the street. “I can pay in advance.”

“Two days, perhaps three, if it behaves.” I named a price that included how he held himself.

He nodded. He was the kind of man who did nothing with half measures; he took a bundle of notes from inside his coat and counted without looking, too quickly, then pushed them across. “Whatever it costs,” he said. “Whatever you find. Don’t—don’t give it to anyone else. If I don’t come in person, if someone comes for it pretending to be me or sent by me, don’t. Keep it locked.” The spill of panic in his throat made the words scrape. It made me look up and meet his eyes fully for the first time. They were the particular grey of the river in snowmelt, when the town thinks the water might decide to leave.

“I don’t mistake faces I’m meant to recall,” I said. “Your name?”

He hesitated long enough that the silence made two turns of the second hand. “Caspar Bly,” he said, and the name stuck in the air between us as if it was not the one he had been using lately. He fished for a card, found none, took a scrap of something from his pocket—an old library slip, stamped 1934 and overrun with newer stamps—and wrote a telephone number on the back. His fingers were trembling now. The ink blotted at the end like a bruise. “Here. I’ll call. Or I’ll come. Keep it running if you can. I need it to keep the right time.”

“We all do,” I said. I could not help it; the words made us both smile, briefly, ruefully. The shop was warm enough that the window had fogged at the corners because I had forgotten to wipe it after sealing the draft in autumn. Outside, the river gave the gulls something to complain about. On the farther slope of town, St. Aldwyn’s tower shouldered into the low cloud.

He took up his hat. “If anyone asks,” he said carefully, “I was never here.”

“If you were never here,” I said, “it will be difficult to return for your watch.”

That won a real smile. It made his face younger, just for the crack of a second. “You’ll do,” Caspar Bly said, and left with that looped-twine tension still holding him together.

After he had gone, I did something my father would have scolded me for: I wound the watch once and then, with the crown drawn out—feeling the slight catch as the hack engaged—I stopped the balance and put my ear close. The silence of a watch is one of the strangest silences there is. It suggests that even time can hold its breath.

Something else my father would have scolded me for: I loosened the two tiny screws that held the porcelain dial and lifted it, careful as a nurse with a newborn skull. Dials are treacherous; the hairline cracks that look like spiderwebbing are old injuries, and old injuries remember hands. Behind the dial, sometimes, there are maker’s marks, repairers’ cursive like graffiti under bridges, dates, little scratched prayers.

Behind this one, in the wide shallow space before the dust cover, someone had tucked a fragment of paper no bigger than a moth’s wing. If I had not been the sort to tilt things in my palm and listen to how they settled, I might not have heard it skitter. I teased it free with the corner of a clean cloth.

It was old vellum, yellowed and made brittle by something more than age. Heat, perhaps. The letters on it had been written in pencil and then, as if someone regretted even that, gone over with a smear so that the words had the wavering quality of something overheard across water. I shifted it in the light.

There were three words. They were plain words but they arranged uneasily.

Sable. West. Thirteen.

I said them under my breath and felt ridiculous for saying them out loud. Words in your own shop can be spells, if you let them.

“Mrs. Pell,” the bell over the door announced, and a wet gust of river air peeled across the counter with her.

Mrs. Pell and her dog arrived like weather. She was wearing her winter green coat with the fur collar that shed fur whenever she turned her head. The dog was some sort of terrier with the unfounded confidence of a small general. He snuffled every table leg as if there might be old biscuits folded into the wood. Mrs. Pell did her usual taking up of space.

“Miss Hart,” she said, as if she had thought of my name herself. “My nephew’s wedding clock. Two o’clock on Saturday. You promised.”

“I did and I will,” I said. I slipped the vellum scrap into the little tin where I kept orphaned screws and mismatched springs. The guilt I felt was disproportionate to the act. I slid the dial back, replaced the hands to the right minute, and closed the case with a precise soft click. “The arbour on the hand had been a touch loose. It’s tight now.”

“You are a marvel,” she said, and then put her hands on her hips as the terrier tried to climb into the glass case to investigate a silvered repeater. “Oscar, you brute, that is not for dogs. If that beast can tell the hour, Miss Hart, I’ll knock him into next week.”

“Please don’t,” I said. “I quite like this week.”

She humphed. Outside, a gull made a sound like grudging applause. Mrs. Pell tried to pay me in jam and indignation; I accepted the jam and refused the indignation. When I got her out with Oscar tugging at the lead in the direction of the fishmonger, my shop breathed in again.

The day stretched itself out like a cat. People came, people went, and their watches told me their stories the way people never mean to. A suit well-covered in chalk dust who was apologetic about everything except what he wanted. A girl in a rain cape wanting to know if I could make her grandfather’s watch tick like thunder. A young man whose grief made him careful with his hands. The kettle hissed and hissed and was poured and hissed again. At noon the tower bell dragged itself through twelve, each note a little more reluctant than the last.

At three minutes to four, the telephone in the back rang.

It has an old ring, the one that lives under the cupboard in the kitchen, the one that came with the shop and with which I’ve made peace. I left the watch I was adjusting with its balance cock half unscrewed and went to answer. The bell had that metallic applause again; a child outside, perhaps, clapping the air with his hands. It put actual applause in my head and I smiled as I lifted the receiver.

“Hart & Sons.”

“Ms. Hart?” The voice said my name as if verifying a rumor. It was male, crisp; a voice that lived in the habit of asking questions that deserved answers. “Eveline Hart?”

“Yes.”

“This is Detective Sergeant Rowan.” He said it with the certainty of someone who has said it many times to people who were very sorry to hear it. “Graybridge Police.”

A pause. The kettle was just beginning to think about boiling again. The little rhythm of it under the words made something in my chest go very still.

“Yes,” I said. “What can I do for you, Sergeant?”

“Do you do much work for passers-through, Ms. Hart? People who don’t give their addresses.”

“I do. Not because of any policy, just because it is how it goes.” I felt the shape of the watch on my bench as if it were in the room with me. I arranged my voice into something that would not spook either of us. “Why?”

“A man was found in the river by Westdock an hour ago. Drowned,” he said—the way he said drowned was a hand closing over cold. “He had a number in his pocket. A business telephone. Yours. Have you had a visitor today who you think might be him?”

Lots of men walked out of my door every day. Most of them were not going to be dead by tea. The words “West” and “thirteen” lined up with each other in the part of my mind that notices when bolts half-thread and pretend to be tight.

“I might have,” I said. “I can’t know until I know his name.”

“That would be helpful.” He sounded as if this reduced his list of potential difficulties by only the smallest amount. “Caspar Bly.”

I sat down because my knees went watery, which is not something I do for effect and not something I like in myself. The chair complained; it always does. The kettle finished deciding to boil and then stopped deciding.

“He was here this morning,” I said. “He left a watch with me.”

There was a quiet on the line like two people listening to each other breathe. “We’ll need to see it,” Sergeant Rowan said at last. “If you’d be so good.”

“For evidence,” I said.

“For sense,” he said. “There’s something wrong with the time, Ms. Hart.”

I could have told him that before he spoke it. The watch on my bench had been stopped at thirteen minutes past ten when I took its face off. It is a habit of mine, after I replace a dial and set hands, to return them to where I found them, even if only briefly. I had paused with its second hand poised at thirteen past, the old luminous paint faintly sugared with glow in the seam of the case, because I am sentimental. Thirteen past ten. The tower had rung ten poorly this morning, and then the half, and then the quarter, and I, idiot that I am, had whispered a child’s incantation—Sable. West. Thirteen—over a piece of scrap vellum and thought nothing of it but the sound the words made.

“Come ahead,” I said. My voice sounded as if I had borrowed it from a woman I knew slightly. “I’ll put on the kettle.”

When I hung up, the room had the feeling rooms have when someone has left them and you don’t know if they’re coming back quickly or at all. Outside, the fog had lifted and the river was the colour of lead and light together. The street had taken the afternoon’s shade. Across the way, in Mrs. Pell’s window, a clock with cherubs had decided to be industrious; they swung their hammers furiously as if hammering time into shape.

I went back to my bench. The watch casethought about reflecting my face and decided not to. I set it on a square of clean felt as if that could make it safer. It ticked now, a tick I had coaxed out of it, thin and stern. The dent by the hinge was smooth under my finger. I turned it over, not to open it, not yet, only to look at the engraving on the back. I had not looked at that properly. People sometimes carve their names or a date and you learn something you wish you didn’t.

The back had just a single line of text, so faint it had almost worn away from the friction of being in a pocket. Sable & Co., Leeds. I had never heard of them.

The tower bell struck four and then—after a pause I had never heard in my life on this street—struck once more, not as if calling the hour but as if clearing its throat. Someone outside laughed and then stopped. The dog across the street barked as if time had made a noise it wasn’t supposed to.

I have learned not to make omens out of everything. If I had not learned that, I would have had to stop keeping a shop. But there are days when the town speaks in its clumsy language and you are a fool not to listen.

Caspar Bly had asked me to keep his watch running, and I would. The rest of it—the river, the word that meant sable and meant black and meant fur, the wrong thirteen—would have to figure itself out around me. Some hours, like some men, arrive and refuse to leave until you have named them.

The bell over the door chimed, polite as ever. When I looked up, the woman standing on the threshold brought the smell of wet wool and lane dust with her, and behind her, across the street, a man in a police greatcoat waited with his hands in his pockets and his head tilted, listening to a town that wasn’t telling him everything.

By August, the lake had receded so far the bell tower returned.

It rose out of the dry basin like the spine of some ancient animal, a dark rib of stone with gaps where swallows had threaded nests, with long strands of lake weed pale and brittle from the sun. People had been walking out to it all week on the new ground the drought made, crunching over mussel shells and beer tabs and years of buried things. The bell itself was long gone. The old photos showed it lowering into the murk in 1952, Saint Elodie’s parishioners gathered on the hill to watch the men in rubber boots and felt hats lift their lives and their dead. But the walls were there. The arch. The idea of a church that refused to stay submerged.

June Park parked as close to the shoreline as she could without rutted tires and county liability being a story she’d have to write about herself. The heat was a mean, dull weight. Further out, converging around a stretch of the exposed floor where the earth had slumped and cracked, a knot of people stood in mosquito-numb stupor. News vans from Asheville had bled themselves onto the field like spilled paint. A drone buzzed over the bell tower with the conviction of a dragonfly.

“Park,” someone called. “Park, over here.”

Deputy Cora Whitfield was in uniform but had left her hat somewhere, freckles you didn’t see until, like today, the sun accused them. She pushed through the crowd without touching anyone and the crowd obliged because Whitfield had a tone you saved for snakes and ladies who wrote down what you said.

June got the camera strap over her neck and found her notebook in a pocket she’d sewn herself into liking. She snapped two framing shots—the tower to the left, the bodies of the curious balanced right, a tilt in the horizon to draw the eye. “What are we looking at?” she asked without looking up.

“You’ll see.” Whitfield didn’t smile. “You feel like you want to acclimate to the smell first. Hollis is trying to keep the city trucks back. Come on.”

June’s sandals sank an inch into what used to be the lake’s nerve. Her calves stung. A boy with a fish tattoo on his shoulder—bad shading, someone’s cousin learning—turned to watch her pass and tilted his beer in salute. The Ridgeway Sentinel hadn’t had this many page-two readers in a long time. She would have been grateful, if she allowed herself gratitude for work that didn’t have a mortgage attached, if she didn’t see her whole week turning into quotes from men sweating under baseball caps that read things like God Guns Grits, Hey SIS Where’s Your Mask? the last one outdated but kept for the joke.

Down where the earth changed color and sheen, Sheriff Hollis Garner stood with his boots planted and his hands on his hips. Garner had the quiet conviction of a man who fixed what was in front of him and was never paid to think about why it broke. He squinted when he saw June and made no motion like invoking privacy. The tape they’d strung between two sawhorses said Sheriff’s Line Do Not Cross and was already effectively a suggestion.

“Don’t tell me you found Jimmy Hoffa,” June said.

Garner tipped his head at the tower. “Hoffa would be easier. He comes with a city to bury him for free.”

The closer she came, the more the smell became itself: not rot in the way of a raccoon in spring, not the sweet of overripe fruit left inside a car, but the earthy, iron sting of silt that had held onto something it didn’t want and now had to give it back. June put a hand to her mouth because there were people watching and she had complicated feelings about giving anyone the satisfaction of seeing her flinch.

Inside the tower’s open arch, where the nave would have started before the lake drowned the idea of worship, someone had rigged slats across the gap during better times. A warning for the kids who boated close on dares. Those slats were broken now, three cracked and jagged, one knocked clean from its bracket. The remaining two formed a kind of awkward ladder up to the half-floor where the bell rope would have hung down, where stain on stone suggested years of hands. The light up there was the color of dirty glass.

Moving in the circle of that light, slow, like she had learned not to be noticed by deer, was a person in a wetsuit. He was broad across the shoulders, his neck raw at the seam from gear. Aquatic plants starred the backs of his knees. He used the rotted slats to brace himself and put something in a bag, a delicate private gesture like picking lint off a suit.

“Divers?” June said.

“We pulled one up from Greenville County who still owes me three favors,” Garner said. “I said there may be someone making pictures. He said make sure they get his good side.”

“Does he have a good side?”

Garner didn’t look. “Everything’s got one. We got us a bone up there, Ms. Park.”

June’s breath went sideways. She flipped her notebook open. “How big, how many, how… human.”

“Skull,” Whitfield said, voice flat but not unkind. “Piece of it, anyway. Maybe two. Enough teeth to look like a Christmas miracle in the worst way. I don’t have to tell you—please don’t—”

“I’m not posting pictures with dental forensics in the caption, Cora. Contrary to popular belief, I do know what line means.” June looked at the crowd. The boy with the fish tattoo had moved closer, a metal detector abandoned by his feet. A woman in a big straw hat held the hat in front of her stomach like that could keep what she’d seen from getting in.

June took a step closer to the tower and crouched, angling her camera through the arch. The divers had slowed. The man on the floor above had stuck a flashlight between his teeth and was reaching into a hollow. Something thin and pale uncoiled from behind a stone rib and drifted in the diluted sunlight. Hair. It moved like a warning.

No one said anything out loud.

They had not known Ivy Bell long. Ivy had been that last late-year addition to the missing posters that never stayed stapled straight on the board in front of the grocery. Her hair had been red, the kind that never looked brushed no matter how the picture tried to suggest she had brushed it that morning before the photo was taken. In the photo she wore a sweater with moth holes she loved like a joke about herself. She made scone dough early at the Fortunate Cup and didn’t mind the way the regulars ordered around her like she was the air condition. She also had a tendency to disappear for a week every time someone pushed too hard at the edges of her story. When she vanished this time, people had sighed and then, a month later, started cutting the sigh out of the sentence. Her car was found where town ended; her phone pinged a tower no one could agree existed; a fisherman said he saw a girl walking the shoulder of Route 21 with her shoes in her hand, Ashley furniture delivery said the gate camera picked up a fox.

The first time June wrote her name, she’d spelled it Ivy like the plant, not Ivey like the sheriff’s mother had insisted. Let the woman have her letters, Garner had told her, and June had walked it back in the next issue, blaming spellcheck. After that, she printed her name in big type once a week with whatever police were willing to say between poker nights at the Firehouse. She put Ivy’s sweater on the front page twice, because she didn’t have other pictures and because the sweater reminded June of a brown cardigan she had loved at nineteen, in the life before the paper printed her apology, before she drove west and then east again with the apology folded like a receipt she could never throw away.

The diver came down, slow. The bag he held was clear. Inside was mud and the suggestion of a shape. Teeth are obvious in a way nothing else is. We learn them early. June looked through her lens because a lens made things easier to look at. It made anything outside the edges not real.

Garner put gloved hands on the bottom of the bag like a midwife. He said something low to the diver that was mostly the sound of men who know each other working. Whitfield shifted her weight from one heel to the other and made like she didn’t want to see if anyone was trying to see. June took four pictures and then put the camera down by reflex.

“You’re thinking it’s her,” she said.

“I’m thinking someone’s granddaughter,” Garner said, around a breath. “Someone’s daughter. We’ll not do more thinking than that until we know. Any simple number of this county’s dead could have ended up in the church before the water took it.”

“This was underwater last month. Most months since 1952.” Whitfield had the tone of a cop explaining to a tourist why the view wasn’t free. “So it’s either old or… someone came out when the river level was low this year. Park, just write me like a normal human. That’s all I ask.”

June wrote that down, not because she would quote it, but because writing calm words made them feel contained. She scanned the bristly line of onlookers and found Mr. Llewellyn from the hardware store looking determinedly in the other direction. A boy in a tank top lifted his phone like worship. Whitfield moved to intercept him.

“Did someone call Dr. Bell?” June asked, and instantly regretted the consonants. “Sorry. I just—”

“He’s on his way.” Garner half-invented a way to put the bag down where it wouldn’t be a thing in people’s heads for the rest of the day and straightened. He was a tall man who had never had the chance to violate his own expectations. “He insisted, and I was not going to insist otherwise. You, Ms. Park, will be a professional or you will go write a nice piece about zucchini at the farmer’s market.”

“I already wrote that,” June said. “It’s not that nice.”

“Make it nicer. We’re going to call the coroner out from Marion. She knows the pH out here better than I care to. We’ll get some tarps up so the buzzards don’t insult us further.” Garner scruffed sweat off his forehead with the back of his knuckles and looked at June, not so much warning as consultation. “You can say bone. You can say remains. You will not say Ivy until I say Ivy. You will not say don’t go out to the tower because I can’t keep people from making bad choices and I do not want a body count in the ledger of your prose.”

“I can probably manage ‘respectfully curious citizens’ and a suggestion to bring good shoes,” June said. She glanced back at the ground behind her. Her sandals were ringed in gray. She had lived out of a suitcase in a series of sublets with nicer floors than this and had never felt the place she stood determine the shape of her day the way Ridgeway did.

“June.” Cora Whitfield had moved quick and quiet back to her side. She said her name not like the deputy and not like the girl June had written about ten years ago when she first ran track and fell on the last lap and still came back to win it. She said it like a woman who did not often say names. “Bigger than bone. He’s found something else. Just—be smart.”

June braced, but then there was no bracing because the diver was already coming, and he was asking Garner what he was supposed to do when the thing in the hollows didn’t want to be believed. He was young enough to remember the bell ringing because it was in a movie somewhere, not because he had grandparents who had recited stories with all the pronouns in the present tense. He held up a sealed plastic case like a magician revealing he had correctly guessed someone’s card. Inside the case was a rectangle the size of a hand, dark, with a kind of strangled glitter to it under the mud.

“A phone,” Garner said, blank as a chalkboard.

“Waterproof,” the diver said. “Some of them are. Not for long, the lake’ll eat anything. But this— Whoever was out here, Deputy, they didn’t come in 1952.”

June’s pen clicked by itself. Her skin did that tightening thing it did before storms, before headlines, before apologies.

Proximity did the rest for her. Memory drew circles around specifics. Ivy had bought a new phone in February because she kept dropping old ones in the wash sink at the coffee shop. She’d complained about it at the counter with her sleeves pushed up, showing a tattoo of a two-headed calf done bad enough to be charming. The calf looked a little smug. The tattoo had bled on the edges like someone who loved her had done it in a kitchen. June had asked to take a picture of the phone because Ivy had cut a sticker to fit the case: an egg with legs and a face. A thing from a cartoon June didn’t know. She had taken the picture and then deleted it because someone had told her the sticker was a sin against taste.

The diver’s hands weren’t steady. He turned the rectangular case, and the case turned its face, and June did not need a sticker to know what it was. The corner was cracked, the bezel marred, but there was a gouge where there had been a chip in the corner the day Ivy gave an old man his change and joked about wanting to throw everything she owned into a body of water and let the insects have it. The gouge looked like you could fit a promise into it. June had a photograph in a folder on her desktop called Bells. Bells for Bell, the pun she refused to admit. She had taken pictures of Ivy’s hands the last time she had talked to her, because the light had been nice, because that morning there had been room in June’s head for beauty, even if there wasn’t better a word for it than proof.

No one said Ivy out loud. They all said different versions of, “We’ll send that straight to the lab” and “Let’s get this under cover” and “Move,” to the girl in the straw hat who had decided to have a fainting episode near their better tarp. June lifted her camera again and lowered it, uneasy, the way the air had picked up the scent of something not the lake, not the mud, but a ripple of expectation.

The man who ran the bait shop swore and said he had known a girl with red hair. Mr. Llewellyn from the hardware store took off his cap without touching the brim. Somewhere behind them, a child asked, astonished rather than afraid, if there were bones in the floor of the church at home too.

“June,” Whitfield said again.

“I know,” June said. “I know. I’ll be careful.”

Cora didn’t look at the camera. She looked at June’s hands, which were steady on the outside and splotched with grit. “That’s not what I meant. You’re shaking.”

So the body was there, the idea of a body even if what they had right now were teeth and a phone and a kind of common sense that had nothing to do with the state making a certificate. So was Dr. Bell on the way, his mouth set, a man who had divulged maybe three things about his daughter in the last six months and had not been present for the last three. So was the tower, stubborn and sullen and barnacled with oaths. In the distance, the blue of the mountains did that habit it had of becoming the thing itself rather than a view. In the foreground, a dragonfly landed on the tape and did not care that it read sheriff.

June took one more picture while she was allowed and stepped back. Her phone buzzed in her pocket with the aggressiveness of a debt collector. She half-ignored it until it did it again and then again, insistent. Cora glanced down at June’s pocket with an almost injured patience, like she expected June to pick a fight with a fire alarm.

June thumbed the screen because she didn’t know how not to.

The text preview took up a bar across the top. No name. A number she did not recognize, starting with an area code that meant nothing in the story of this county. The message resolved itself before her eyes, gray bubble, three dots she had used in her own worst mornings.

I told you they’d find me where the bells used to sing.

For a second, she was offended at the presumption of it being poetic.

Then the text rolled up and she saw the line above. The last message from that thread was dated March 2, six months ago. There was a photo of a latte she had not answered because she had been in the middle of writing a paragraph about funding at the library, because she had believed there was time. The contact name at the top said IVY, because some part of June was a romantic, and because she had liked the rhythm of the letters in capital. The number matched, digit for digit, the one in the missing poster people had stopped stapling because it made them feel like bad luck.

Her phone buzzed again, as if it delighted in creating one more sound. The second message came.

Don’t let him tell a nice story.

On the day we opened the future, the past smelled like damp cardboard and vinegar.

I stood at the foot of the temporary stage on the town green, the Harbor Ledger’s camera strap biting into the tender spot on the back of my neck, my thumb working a smudge off the lens that I’d already cleaned three times. They’d strung bunting around the gazebo and erected a plywood podium that made our mayor look taller than he was, a detail he’d appreciate in tomorrow’s photos. Grayhaven’s December sun had done its best to reach us—thin, pale, apologetic. There were mittened hands and coffee in paper cups, kids who had been promised hot cocoa later if they stayed quiet through the boring parts. Somewhere behind me, a drone hummed. The town had hired a freelancer to make a sizzle reel, as if a sizzle reel were the sort of thing that might convince people to move back.

“I remember when we put that thing in there,” said Edda Pike, the town clerk emerita, who had claimed a folding chair front and center. “We had to get Milt Barnes to bring his backhoe, because no one else could get it leveled. He’d had a few, if I recall. He said the ground was an insult to a man’s spirit.”

“They don’t make insults like they used to,” I said, and Edda squinted up at me like she was deciding whether to smile. The wind tugged at the gray wisps escaping the pin in her bun.

On the stage, Mayor Hennessey adjusted the microphone with his pinky extended, which he thought made him look graceful. “Twenty-five years ago, our community—our families, our businesses, our young people,” he said, glancing around to locate the nearest group of young people—“placed their hopes, their dreams, and some very curious items in a stainless-steel capsule. Today, we open that capsule.”

A boy with a cowlick booed. Everyone laughed; the tension yawned and exhaled. The cameraman for Channel 6 panned past, and I ducked reflexively even though no one had asked me for a quote in years. The Ledger had been reduced to a Wednesday edition and weekend obituaries—the price of being a hometown paper owned by people who did not have hometowns. I was the last full-time staffer: editor, photographer, copy editor, half the layout team. I wrote the headlines and returned the subscription calls. When you run a small paper long enough, you learn to keep certain things out of print. A person’s worst day doesn’t have to be their public record.

We all watched as two DPW guys—Brandon and Luis, both in jackets embroidered with their own names, God bless them—worked a crowbar under the welded lip of the capsule embedded in the dirt before the gazebo. When the seam gave, the sound was a sigh you could feel. A few people clapped before there was anything to clap for. Brandon and Luis lifted the lid together, and there was the vinegar: twenty-five years of sealed air, high and stale and sharp.

“It’s like my Aunt Nina’s pantry,” someone whispered behind me.

Mayor Hennessey peered in, sniffed, and recoiled in a way that would not play super well on Channel 6. “Let’s see what treasures our younger selves have bequeathed us,” he boomed, recovering. He reached in and came up with a Beanie Baby in a plastic case that had fogged with time. “Ah! Vintage!” The crowd made indulgent noises. He set it on the folding table at his left, where Edda waited, hands ready. “We have… a cassette tape labeled ‘Harrigan Mix, Summer ‘99.’ I hope someone has a tape deck.” A Huntsman spider of a laughter. “A copy of the Ledger—ah—June 17, 1999.” He held the newspaper gingerly, the yellowed paper threatening to protest. I made a mental note to ask Edda if I could borrow it for the office archive. There were letters in a disintegrating manila envelope, bundles of polaroids crusted with glue, a flyer for the lobster festival that ended up getting canceled that summer because of red tide, a pamphlet from the volunteer fire department about what to do when Y2K hit the power grid and sent us all back to candles.

“Those boys put one of their Frisbees in there,” Edda announced to no one in particular. “Stood around like chuckleheads arguing whether a disc would throw well under the ground.” She pronounced disc like it had sin in it.

Mayor Hennessey reached in again and came up with a heavy envelope the color of over-steeped tea. It had been sealed with a swatch of red wax that had cracked and bent but not yet broken. On the front, in careful, formal print: To the Editor of the Harbor Ledger, 2024. Private.

My stomach dropped in a way that felt indecent in public. “That’s me,” I said, before thinking better of it.

The mayor searched the stage. His eyes passed over me, did double duty, came back. “Oh, Mara. Perfect. Why don’t you—”

“Private,” I said. I held up my camera as a shield, as if that had any institutional weight left. “It says private.”

He looked put out, then pleased. “Of course,” he said into the microphone, as if he had decided privacy would be his idea. “This town, our town, respects boundaries.” Brandon coughed. “Ms. Avery, if you’d like to come up and take custody.”

I slung the camera around to my back and stepped up onto the stage, aware of the way the boards gave under my weight, of the way the eyes of the town made a single warm pane against my skin. I took the envelope. It was heavier than it ought to have been, and cold.

“Everything all right?” Edda murmured as I moved toward the far end of the stage. She reached a hand to steady the wobbly table but caught my elbow instead.

“I think so,” I said in the voice I used for families of the recently deceased. I slid down the back steps off the stage and into the shelter of a banner advertising our town’s tourism website. In the shadow of the gazebo, it was a few degrees colder. The drone buzzed overhead and then drifted away to follow the mayor’s hands as he pantomimed pulling the future out of a steel box.

I broke the wax with my thumbnail. The letter inside was folded twice, the crease fibers white as scars. Something rattled at the bottom of the envelope: metal, small. I tipped it into my palm, and a key fell out. It was brass and old-fashioned, the kind that could belong to a clock or a cellar door. A bit of blue paint clung to the bow, a thumbprint’s worth.

When I unfolded the letter, the first line took my breath like a lungful of sea water.

Mara,

You won’t forgive me. I have stopped asking for forgiveness, so don’t misplace that on me. You can’t afford to.

Out on the green, Mayor Hennessey said something about community and letting the past inform our present. Kids clapped for the idea of hot chocolate, careful not to let their palms sting in the cold.

The handwriting was precise and confident, the long tails of the y’s and g’s clipped as if someone had been told, as a child, not to show off. The ink had bled a little but not enough to smudge. It was dated July 3, 1999.

You’ll have thought I died. It’s better that you did. But I’m not dead and neither is he. Saying that you can’t say his name is another thing you don’t talk about. I know how you run. You were always good at running.

There was a pause, a space on the paper where the pen had rested. I turned it to make sure I hadn’t misread the date. The summer of the storm. The summer Jamie went out in a black hoodie and never came home. August, not July, though. August 9, 1999, lightning finding the river as if it had been called by name. I had been seventeen and wearing cutoff shorts and sandals that made my ankles look delicate. My hair was braided and I kept a rubber band around my wrist to remind me to breathe.
