She looked down at the book tote where it sat shut like a well-behaved animal and thought about the certainty everyone had carried for half a century: that The Bellwether Glass was gone for good, that the fire had eaten it along with a dozen others, that the story of Iris Flynn had what stories usually have when there is no body and everyone gets older; it had the dignity of not being spoken and it had the ugliness of being used for scaring children senseless.

She thought of the note and its careful lines, the letters standing like quiet people at a bus stop.

I didn’t know where else it would be safe.

The bell on the door chimed again. The day opened its palms. Somewhere far off in the building, water ran behind a wall, then stopped.

Wren had always believed that libraries were for the return as much as the borrowing. People brought things back to the only place they could think to bring them. The book in her hands had been in the fire. So had Iris Flynn. Only one of those had come home.

The fax machine coughed up my name at 9:03 on a Thursday, the paper curling like a tongue out of a mouth that had already told too much.

It’s an old machine, the kind with an LCD that blinks exactly two characters when it’s thinking. I’d lobbied to get it hauled away three times, and three times Leo told me some variation of “It still works, Mara,” which is exactly the argument you can make for a lot of things that belong in the recycling bin. The obituaries desk of the Greybridge Ledger lives in a windowless annex off the main room, with a thrift-store rug and a door so frequently propped open with galleys that the hinge squeals like a gull every time anyone kicks through. The annex was once a storage closet and before that an actual morgue for the building’s original tenants. That’s not a joke, just a fact that comes with an office nickname: the morgue is where we keep our morgue, rows of cabinets with metal handles and a smell of paper dust and old glue.

I had a stack of death notices pushed up against my keyboard, overnight emails from funeral homes in a dozen fonts, some family-crafted (hotter with adjectives), some in the bare-bones language of “died unexpectedly” and “per his wishes.” There were voicemails from cousins straining through grief and brothers asking about rates. The police scanner on my right muttered about a two-car collision on the north side and then settled back into static. I was in that basin of morning work when your hands move faster than your brain, finding the names and dates, the survived-bys, the ashe-pronouncements from old congregations.

I only looked because the fax paper snagged against the plastic lip and I reached to free it, and my eye, dumb and dutiful, went to the first line.

MARA ELLISON, 38.

I reached for the mug I keep on the desk—a chipped thing from the newsroom’s Christmas party four editors ago that reads bury me in copy—and set it aside, then pulled the paper close. The machine whined. Two more pages slid out, long and damp, the ink blotty in places where the roller needs cleaning.

I’m qualified to pick apart an obituary the way an electrician looks at someone’s basement wiring. It shows, the style of a thing you read for a living. Your own DP history has a kind of fingerprint. The Ledger uses one kind of dash, not another. We italicize titles of shows but not albums. We generally prefer “born to” over “the son of,” unless the next sentence makes “the son of” the better cadence. My own obits—the ones with my byline—are full of oblique clauses and the kind of verbs that try to wake a life up for one last look.

This one used our dash, our italics, our cadence. It used the short hook at the top, the one we reserve for someone people might have known or should have. It used my address.

It was about me.

Mara Ellison, 38, a staff member of the Greybridge Ledger who wrote about the dead with a gentleness that made people call twice to say thank you, died next Wednesday at 3:17 a.m., after a fall from the Tully Street Bridge.

I touched that, the line about the calls. It’s a thing only we would know, the obits desk. People do call. Once, a grandfather’s second wife phoned back to fix the spelling of a maiden name, and then called again just to tell me the cake at his first wedding had been lemon, “and the dog took a bite right out of it.” I typed lemon between commas. She cried when she saw it in print. There’s a kind of ridiculous love in letting someone’s small truths stand where everyone can read them.

My hands were steady. They’re always steady in the crisis moments; it’s afterward that they shake. I flipped to the second page.

She is survived by her mother, Irene McCoy Ellison, 61, of West Greybridge; and a brother, Aaron Ellison, 31, of Tucson. She is predeceased by her father, Patrick Ellison, who died in 2009 at the age of fifty-nine, of a heart attack, on the 8:10 train, which never makes it to its stop on time. She is also predeceased by her ex-husband, Mark Ellison, who died peacefully at home on Tuesday.

I read that twice. Mark Ellison by marriage, not by blood, and Mark Eliot in real life, the way some people wear their surnames on weekends. Ex, too, three summers removed. And alive on Tuesday, which was yesterday. Alive last night when he texted me a photograph of a bowl of noodles that looked like intestines and wrote maybe this will put you out of a job.

“A prank,” I said, to the empty room.

“What now?” Leo materialized in the doorway with a stack of proofs in his arms. He’s a round man who should always be standing behind a deli counter, carving speeches. He has been at the paper longer than anyone and refers to our city’s politicians as if they are grandchildren he sees on holidays. He squinted into the annex. “Did the Collins family change the date again?”

“Nothing,” I said, too quickly. I slid the pages face-down under a folder.

Leo came in anyway because Leo believes in gatekeeping by virtue of his body. He put the proofs down, nudged the scanner back to its comfortable mumbling with a palm, and leaned over my deskscape like a cliff.

“You look like you saw a ghost.”

“I suppose I did.” I smiled. “Someone faxed us a throwback moisture festival flyer.”

“Again?” He scratched his jaw. “Call Facilities. The number in the header’s blocked on those things, but IT can trace it. If it’s that guy on 4th again—”

“It’s fine,” I said. “I’ll handle it.”

He peered toward the morgue cabinets and shuddered dramatically. “I swear they breathe. Little murmur of brown when they open.”

“That’s paper dust. And your fear of nouns.”

“You keep writing those pretty first paragraphs and they’ll put you out with the features people,” he said, not as a compliment. He slid his proofs toward me and tapped a headline that needed capitalizing. “Add this to your list. And call Facilities.”

When he was gone, I slid the pages out again and read. The language had that clean nothing hum we aim for, something like fluorescent lighting that doesn’t flicker. It listed facts I hadn’t told anyone I work with: that I won a small-town spelling bee once on the word catarrh, that I hate the gray stretch of winter in late February when everybody’s coats are exactly the same weight as their complaints. It did not mention that I talk to the dead when I type, which is something I would never tell anyone anyway—only Hello, only I hope I get it right. It cited teachers by name: Mrs. Kohn, fourth grade, who placed a loving hand on my back when I fake-fainted during our Revolutionary War skit because I thought you might as well go out dramatically if you are in a brown tricorne hat in a classroom with no AC.

The sentencing was correct; the spelling of Kohn was correct. So was the address of the apartment I moved into last fall when the landlord raised the rent on my previous place by three hundred dollars in a letter that arrived with peppermint scent. So was the name of my mother’s street, and the pet my brother had when he was eleven—a lizard he called Ink.

An “advance,” we call it when we have something prewritten for a person who will almost certainly need it sooner or later. The Ledger’s advance morgue is thick as a Bible. Actors, kings, long-suffering senators, mayors, a spry pizza scion who will never die. I update them when there’s time. They live in folders with names written on tabbed labels with a Sharpie and a nervous superstition. We only print advances when their subjects go. I put my hand flat against the place on the fax where my name appeared and waited for anything to happen—noise, the old building’s breath, a cue.

I fed the first page back into the machine to see the header. There was no number, just a string of Xs. Someone had turned off their caller ID—standard on a lot of faxes these days, especially if they come out of hospitals. There was a faint gray line at the bottom of the page where the drum had made a little hiccup. Ordinarily I wouldn’t have seen it. Ordinarily I toss faxes into the bin, recycle them into our notes pile, smear addresses out with thick black strokes, reassure sons who can’t pronounce epitomize.

I folded the pages and slid them into the manila folder I keep in the bottom drawer for the oddities: notice with no paying party, a man calling from a blocked number to ask whether we would print an obituary for a person not quite dead yet, a photocopy of a hand-scrawled death notice with only a first name and a map. I’d labeled the folder Strays, a joke that wasn’t a joke. Three weeks ago, I’d dropped something else there: a one-page email from an account with no name attached—not even a random string, just the blank box with the Auto-populated grey silhouette—and a short, correct obituary for a retired schoolteacher I’d never heard of. He died two days later biking home from the co-op when a truck turned left without looking. I wrote up his obituary and did not mention that someone had written it first.

Two days after that, a single-page fax, a nameless sender, for a city councilwoman whose constituents sent us potluck casseroles when she beat cancer a third time. She was photographed standing on an empty lot holding a shovel by the blade, smiling like a person who knew every photographer by first name. She died a week later of a clot on a plane to Phoenix. In the faxed obit, whoever wrote it referenced the shovel like it was an old friend. That detail is available to anyone who knows how to search Google Images, I told myself. Not everything is secret just because it feels like it should be.

Now I put my own name on top of that stack as if it belonged there all along.

I sat a moment, listening to the newsroom beyond the annex take its temperature. Phones, keys, sighs. Someone had ruptured a bag of peanut M&M’s and was cursing quietly into a drawer. The police scanner hummed with the indecipherable. The wall clock read nine-thirteen. I picked up the phone and dialed the number of the funeral home that handled our death notices from West Greybridge. When a receptionist answered, I asked casually if they had placed an advance for anyone with my last name.

“We don’t do those,” she said. “Not without a file.” She was a woman I had met at a holiday support event once, her hair always in a perfect helmet. “Not without a family.”

“You’re sure?”

“I’d know if someone did. We have a system.”

“Thanks,” I said. “Just checking on a typo.”

After I hung up, I opened my browser and typed obituary personal into the search bar like I might coax a ghost out of the pipes. An algorithm offered me paid ad slots for companies that print photos of your dead uncle on a mug. I thought of the lemon cake bite and rubbed my eyes.

The sensible thing to do would have been exactly what Leo told me: call Facilities, report the fax, get IT to trace the header. I could have walked the pages over to HR and had a humorless chat with a woman who, two years ago, had asked me to sign a Valentine’s Day card for an employee who had been fired. I could have called Mark and asked if he was playing some elaborate grief-edge performance art piece. He would have denied it easily; this seems too mundane for him, the man who once suggested we lie down on the floor of the grocery store and listen to the humming while the produce sprayers came on.

Instead, I slid the folder into my bag, typed my mother’s number, and listened to a cheerful recorded voice I had never asked to borrow tell me that the person I was calling could not come to the phone.

After that, I stood, stretched, and made a show of taking the headline proofs Leo had given me to the copy desk, because ordinary motions have a calming power. Theo, who tweaks our headlines and douses linguistic fires before they burn the entire city, took them without looking up from his screen.

“Your scanner’s got a judder,” he said. He is a young man who treats all office machinery like a temperamental horse. He speaks to printers with gentleness and makes them feed. Once he reattached a stapler spring with a prayer. “Ask Carmen to blow the dust out.”

“Hey.” I lowered my voice. “Can you trace a fax?”

He finally looked at me. He wears glasses like the villain in a late-night cartoon. “Depends.”

“Blocked number. Was wondering where it came from.”

He rolled his chair back and out, the better to see the annex, as if he could sight the question on my desk like a target. “Generally? If the sender disabled the header, you can’t. But you can sometimes get the trunk. Gives you the exchange it came out on. Why?”

“Curiosity. I get bored. Help me not be bored.”

He grinned because he thinks of me as a category of aunt. “All right,” he said. “But if this ends in one of those meetings where I have to explain what a trunk is to someone with a fast blink, you owe me a sandwich.”

“The long kind,” I said. “With peppers.”

He had a program for it, a little black-window thing he called his toy, a window within a window. He asked the machine to spit up the transmission log. We watched lines of barf appear on a screen and then still, like a heart pause, and then flicker again.

“There.” He pointed. “Came through a city PBX. Hard to tell which building. Government uses them like candy.”

“City Hall?”

“Could be any of fifty buildings within a mile,” he said. “The branch library, the clinic on May Street, the water department, the cat licensing office, probably. Might even be a school. You can go hand-to-hand, if you want. See which ones still have fax lines.”

“Thanks,” I said, and meant it.

I went back to the annex and sat. The obit lay in my bag like something living. I can identify cause-of-death phrases at twenty yards now, the way woodworkers can tell the difference between oak and ash from smell. We use “died after a long illness” when the family prefers to use the words long illness for reasons that are exactly both what you think they are and none of your business. We use “died unexpectedly” when someone’s heart stopped in the bathtub. When I have to write the word “suicide,” I step toward it as if it is sleeping. The obit in my bag said “after a fall,” and named a bridge I walk across twice a week at dusk for no reason other than that I like to watch the river fold on itself like satin.

I typed a quick, bare story for the man who had died of pancreatic cancer after outliving his doctors’ guesses by a decade. Then I slipped into the main room and did something I had never done in my time at the Ledger. I took a folder out of the morgue for reading pleasure.

The file was thick with clips, with the white edges of tabs like teeth. I took it to one of the tables under the window that faces an alley. It is a window with a view of a brick wall and a vine that will never make up its mind. I laid out the Strays. The retired schoolteacher: Harold Kent, who collected antique rulers and measured everything twice. The councilwoman, Josette LaRoe, who waved her shovel like a flag when they broke ground for a new clinic for kids who cannot afford ordinary things like braces.

The advance faxes had come with no headers, no way to see who sent them, the ink thick in places as if the toner had been shaken by someone with an old belief. They were correct in the ways that felt like trespass. They were wrong in two small ways. Josette’s sister’s name had been spelled with an h where there is none. And for the schoolteacher, the obit had listed a summer home in Sag Harbor he never owned. He had a brother with a little place by a lake in northern Maine. I had asked his wife if they had ever vacationed on Long Island and she had laughed into her napkin.

“A man came into the office,” she had said. “Last week. He brought a casserole and a card and asked if we’d help him plan. I told him it was bad luck. He said he didn’t believe in luck. He said he believed in being prepared.”

“What did he look like?” I’d asked, and the answer had been like a sketch.

He had looked like everyone else. Brown hair, brown coat, average. He had spoken quietly and well. He had written a check and then asked for a receipt, which apparently is something only men who want to be remembered do. He had left. And then Harold’s heart, which had worked for him without much complaint for seven decades, stopped behaving, and he was done.

I put my elbows on the table and folded myself small. I pressed my forehead to my forearms like a person praying to a horizontal god. I could quit. That’s the arc in the movie where she quits and then something drags her back in. I could go home and sit with my cat—a stray that had stayed, a creature that liked the typewriter sound of my keys late at night—and wait for a policeman to knock and tell me to come with him to a bridge. I could call my mother again. I could text Mark: Good joke. You are alive. I could tell myself that nothing written is true until it is lived.

My phone lit on the table. A message from a number I did not recognize, containing a photograph of a bridge at night. The Tully Street Bridge, its black arc and its lamps, a necklace over the river. The timestamp: last night, three seventeen. In the bottom right, a sliver of the concrete wall and the metal plaque with the names of the dead who had been memorialized by benches and trees nearby. It was like a postcard from a place you go often enough that no one bothers to sell postcards. There was no text. Just the image.

I stared at it until the light went out. Then I turned the phone face down and breathed.

The first time I met Mark, four years ago at a fundraiser for a literacy charity that needed money to keep a van running, he told me he remembered his ex-wife’s obituary by heart. She wasn’t dead. He wrote it as a penance. People collect their languages of remorse. They are mostly unusable and very heavy. He is not my suspect because I am not a detective and this is not a police procedural. This is a story about someone writing where there should be blank space.

At noon, I left for lunch, because that is what you do when your morning proceeds as usual; you get a chicken sandwich with the long peppers on the side and a bag of those vinegar chips that make your mouth feel like you have sinned. I took my bag and the folder and the phone and walked the three blocks to the small city branch library, because it is within three blocks of everything in Greybridge, and because Theo had said government and libraries are cousins with fax machines. It smelled like the past: carpet some color between brown and orange, the sour-sweet of a hundred thumbed books, children’s fingers on picture books with animals that smile with human teeth. A librarian with hair like a bun of planets looked at me over the edge of a desk where an actual fax machine sat, slumped in an open cubby, a patient asleep.

“Do people use that?” I asked.

“Like it’s going out of style,” she said dryly.

“We’re way past out of style.”

“Some hospitals only fax. Some of the older folks prefer it. There’s a sign-up sheet.” She slid a clipboard toward me. Hand-lettered lines, names written with pens that put down too much ink. People had initialed the hour and the need. A neat line at nine-fifteen: Stegner, L.—fax to city number. No phone attached. I ran my finger over the loop of the S. The librarian smiled without liking me yet. “You a reporter?” she asked, because after a while we all look the same. “You either are or you’re fifteen minutes early for a knitting circle.”

“I work for the Ledger,” I said.

She checked the clock and then looked back at me. “I like the obits,” she said, a confession after all.

“I try to make them true,” I said. “Even when they’re wrong.”

In the street outside, a bus inhaled and exhaled with a sound of weary doors. I put my name on the sign-up sheet, not because I had a fax to send but because I wanted a line in that list, something between those other names. When I turned away, there was a bulletin board with flyers for calligraphy classes and a poster about taxes. Tucked under a thumbtack was an index card, sharp-cornered and bright with blue ink.

It read: We will get this right.

It could have been about anything. Taxes. Calligraphy. Knitting. But not everything is what it is about.

When I got back to the newsroom, a siren was playing through the open window, the slow long moan of an ambulance that isn’t in a hurry because it doesn’t have to be. Leo had left me a note on a Post-it that simply said: CALL ME. His handwriting does a thing I think of as italicizing real life. I picked up the phone. He didn’t answer. I set it down.

The fax machine waited with its little green eye. The moment after you see your name printed next to the word died does not repeat. I am remedial at certain kinds of change, and excellent at certain other kinds. I had until next Wednesday, the obit said. It always feels obscene to look at a date on a page and think this is time, as if a life is a train schedule and the 8:10 will pull in somewhere to a bell and a platform where a man once took a breath and did not take another.

I slid my bag under my desk and opened a new document. It’s a thing I do to calm myself. You start with the name. You add the dates. You dig for the content that made this person stand up in a crowd and say absolutely not to whatever was ordinary. You call the people who loved them more than they loved themselves.

I wrote my name on a line and looked at it. I typed nothing else. I closed the document and pulled the folder back out of my bag. The obit for Josette. The obit for Mr. Kent. The obit for me, with its clean lines and its little crimes. I laid my hand on the paper like a promise.

I can trace a fax. I can sit in a library and wait for someone to walk in with a brown coat and the smell of a winter hallway. I can call my ex-husband and ask a question that sounds like accusation even when it isn’t, and then listen to his laugh that used to make me want to throw a glass against a wall just to hear it break.

I can drive to the bridge at three in the morning and stand exactly where the obit wants me to stand and say no.

I read the last line of the fax again because it had bugged me the first time. It was a standard line, usually almost a throwaway: Services are scheduled for—. Only this time: Services will not be held.

That was the part that felt like the dare. That was the part that made something in me sit up the way a person sits up when they smell smoke they cannot place, in a room that shouldn’t be burning. I reached for my phone and this time I didn’t call Facilities or HR or Theo. I scrolled to a number I never thought I would dial again and pressed the little green button because if you are going to reevaluate your life you should start with the things you know you should have done differently.

“Hello?” Mark said, after two rings.

“Are you alive?” I asked.

He laughed. “For the moment.”

“Someone faxed me an obituary,” I said. “It says you died yesterday.”

He was quiet long enough that I could hear the sound of water, in pipes or in a kettle on a stove or a shower hitting tiles the color of teeth. When he spoke, his tone had changed. He was no longer amused. “I got one of those,” he said. “Last week.”

“Yours?”

“No,” he said. “Someone else’s.” He said the name, and it was a name I knew, a name that had come through my inbox that morning without comment, and I did not write it down because there are some things you do not need to write to know they are real.

“Where did it come from?” I asked.

“Public library fax,” he said. “Downtown.”

Of course he could trace a thing like that without a Theo. Of course he would say something like that as if he were telling me where to buy good olives. “Did you tell anyone?”

“No,” he said. “I thought it was a prank. And then it wasn’t.”

I pressed the pages against the desk until the edges bent and whitened. It is a soprano note, the one I hear when I am about to do something that will go badly if I lie to myself about what it is. It made the old machines in the annex hum in pity.

“I have a week,” I said, because saying it made it sound like a challenge instead of a sentence.

“Then don’t do what it says,” Mark offered, with the helpful idiocy of people who do not write names next to the word died for a living.

“I never do,” I said, and hung up, because some conversations end not with closure but with a small slice put clean through.

After that, I opened the cabinet door of the morgue with the squeal and rolled out one of the drawers. Papers shifted like a hand on silk. Everything we have done in this room still breathes a little. There’s a kind of power in that. There’s also horror.

I took out one more folder I had never touched: mine. Somewhere in this building, for insurance purposes and tradition, there is a folder with my name on it that is not an advance obituary but a personnel file, with my hire paperwork and my emergency contact and the number you call if I am late and you think I might be concussed. I had never looked at it. I did not look at it now.

Instead, I wrote down a list of places with fax machines, starting with the branch library and moving out: clinics, schools, city offices that live above bagel shops, the cat licensing office Theo in his offhand way had conjured. I wrote a time: three seventeen. I wrote a date. I wrote a name: Stegner, L. For no good reason other than that it had been in front of me on a clipboard and was untidy in a neat way.

We call it a beat, the thing a reporter works, the terrain of their obsession. I had never thought of obituaries as a beat. You don’t think of gravity as a beat either. But I felt the shift. For the first time in years, I wanted to do the thing that had brought me into this building before I learned to be gentle for money. I wanted to know. Not because a page told me I would fall off a bridge, but because someone, somewhere, had written what they had no right to know, and sent it across a line as if it were a recipe.

I slid the folder into my bag and stood. I turned off the fax machine. Its little light blinked twice and went dark. In the main room, a copy editor cursed at the way the word referendum wants to be capitalized when it shouldn’t be. Outside, the siren had stopped. The day went on. They always do. For a while.

The dead don’t usually call the newsroom after nine. That was the joke, anyway, tossed across desks whenever the city desk was down to two blinking phones and a pot of coffee that had turned the color of shoe polish. If a line rang late, someone would lift the receiver with two fingers, as if it were hazardous, and say, “Obits, you’ve reached the far side.” Sometimes it was a son or daughter who’d waited until the house emptied to cry. Sometimes it was a funeral director with the spelling of a maiden name. And sometimes, if you were unlucky, it was the managing editor wanting one last rewrite on a mayoral candidate’s grandmother.

In the fall that refused to admit it was winter, I was alone on the tenth floor with the grid of windows at my back and the river knotted black in the distance. The rain had turned the streets below into lanes of crooked mercury. My computer screen kept dimming as if it, too, wanted to sleep. I had three obituaries stacked in my queue, all simple. A retired math teacher with polio scars from childhood. A bar owner who would be remembered for the way he salted the rims of his glasses by hand. And a woman who’d lived to ninety-eight and outlasted everyone who would have called to complain.

“Five more inches,” Miles had said on his way out, tugging his scarf up as if he were stepping onto a tundra instead of an elevator. “Give me something beautiful about the teacher. Make people like the multiplication tables again.”

“I’ll make people cry over long division,” I said, and he’d grinned and left me with his office plant, which leaned toward the fluorescent lights in a way that looked like pleading.

I’d once loved the way this job held still while the rest of the paper sprinted. Death notices did not break. They rarely lied. I could arrange a life like a mosaic and press it into print with the quiet satisfaction of someone smoothing a pair of sheets, the last courtesy. In my first decade as a reporter, I chased sirens and returned home glittered in glass dust. Now I chased dates and quotes and learned how to call late and ask for stories without sounding hungry.

On the city side, someone had left a radio hissing; the static made the newsroom sound haunted. All night, I’d been able to hear the freight trains moving across the bridges in the next county, low horns underscoring the rain. I angled my chair until my shoulder touched the cold edge of the window and typed “is survived by” three times with my eyes closed. After you write that enough, it starts to feel like the only true sentence in the language.

When the notification popped—a square of orange rising like a flare on my screen—I stared at it long enough to convince myself it was a mistake. Our content system liked to surprise you. It had moods. Orange meant urgent. Orange meant someone important had finally done the inevitable.

PRIORITY: Pryor, Calder L. (1939-—)

The dash stood there like a held breath.

I drew my hand back from the trackpad. Pryor. Even people who’d never been asked to donate to his foundation knew the name. It was on the wing of the children’s hospital, the lecture hall at the university, the Fleet Theater’s refurbished velvet seats. The Pryor Fund gave out scholarships every spring with photos in the Style section of the winner’s hand in a white envelope as if the money were secretly a blessing.

It was after ten. If the family wanted a private obit, they wouldn’t be calling this late. If this was a leak from the hospital—well, I didn’t like that sentence, so I didn’t finish it. I clicked.

The file wasn’t blank the way a new obituary is blank. It wasn’t a template waiting for “He married” and “She worked” to be filled in later. It was full. There were paragraphs already shaped, dates plugged in, quotes italicized, and the strangest thing was this: it read like someone had loved him.

“Calder Lionel Pryor, eighty-four, industrialist and philanthropist who changed the face of River City through his foundation’s work on literacy, medical access, and urban gardens, died on Tuesday at his home. The cause was complications of a fall in his greenhouse, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.”

I read it again. Urban gardens. The greenhouse. Tuesday. Tonight was Monday. I scrolled down. There were sections on his childhood in Clay County, on the shipping business his father built and he expanded, on his first wife—dead—and his second—divorced. There were quotes from a former governor, a rival, and a line he’d delivered in a commencement address that I remembered because it had been reprinted on T-shirts: “Saints are the ones who show up with a check and a shovel.”

At the bottom, below the boilerplate about memorial service details—which were left as PLACEHOLDER—there was the line I always looked for because it was where families decided whether the person would be funny, petty, or kind in death: He is survived by—

“—his daughter, Winter.”

I let the cursor blink inside that sentence.

Pryor didn’t have a daughter. He had a son, Jonah, who ran the foundation with a degree of grim efficiency that made donors feel like they were giving money to someone who would disassemble it and count the atoms. Pryor had been frank in interviews about regret and absence. “The work was my second family,” he’d said onstage one year when the paper still sent me to cover banquets and pretend to enjoy rubber chicken. Winter was not a name I recognized.

I backed up to the header again and checked the time stamp. Document Created: 2001. Modified: last week. There was a note in the upper right-hand corner where, in better-funded days, we used to leave annotations for fact-checkers.

Source: GK. On file w/ Eden ledger. Confirmed w/ CP.

GK.

The retired obituary editor had been named Gordon Keats. He wore suspenders and a hat like a prop and had a habit of telling rookies they’d be safe in obits because “the dead don’t sue.” He’d died in his kitchen making a sandwich two years ago. No one had unearthed this draft since then? It wasn’t possible. We prewrite the obituaries of public figures—we keep them on paper in the old file drawers and on servers—but they don’t just appear. They don’t blink orange at you at ten-thirteen p.m.

I picked up my desk phone and got the foundation’s night line. It went to voicemail. I called the number I had for the assistant we all dealt with, a woman who had mastered the art of making you feel you had asked for too much when you had simply asked for a pronoun. It rang twice and picked up. The voice on the other end was breathless and hard to pin down—young, I thought.

“Pryor Foundation,” she said, and then, without taking a breath, “Please hold, please hold,” and then she was gone. While I listened to a loop of piano music that made me think of elevators in anxious buildings, I opened the template for the math teacher and underlined the sentence that began with his habit of saying, “You can carry the one or you can carry your regrets. Choose.”

“Hello?” the assistant said, back in my ear. “Hello?”

“Hi, this is June Graves from the Herald. Has Mr. Pryor—has anything happened tonight?”

“What do you mean?” The piano stopped with a hiccup.

“I have a draft obituary in my queue,” I said, and waited for the hiss of outrage, or the word embargo. When none came, I softened it. “Is Mr. Pryor well?”

“He’s—yes. He’s at home.” She sounded farther away. “Working. Preparing for tomorrow.”

“For what?”

“The donors’ breakfast. In the greenhouse.” The last word made the hair lift on my arms, which was ridiculous. I was a person who believed what she could touch. Greenhouses were not ominous.

“May I speak with him?”

“He’s not—he’s not to be disturbed.” She hurried. “This is an internal foundation policy. Calls go through me except for family and his doctor.”

“I’m sure it’s nothing,” I said, “but if there has been a leak of any sort, it would be best if we coordinated. The draft mentions—” I looked again, as if the wording might have changed. “—a fall in his greenhouse.”

Silence. And then, low, “Who told you that?”

“You did, twenty years ago. Perhaps you forgot.” I could hear my own voice turning wry, and I rolled it back. “Listen, if there’s no crisis, then this is just a glitch. Are you certain he’s at home?”

“In the north greenhouse,” she said, as if this were a code word. Her breath ticked against the receiver. “If you have questions, you can send me an email. I’ll flag it for the morning.”

Before I could say another thing, my cell phone—the line almost no one had—shuddered with a call. No number. Unknown. I watched it dance across the desk while the assistant continued to say, “In the morning,” and I let the newsroom phone fall into its cradle.

“Graves,” I said into the cell.

“You opened it,” the man said. He didn’t ask. He had a voice like an old violin—thin and bright, the wood a hairline from cracking. “Don’t print it.”

I looked behind me, as if someone was standing in the dark between the pillars with his hand cupped around the receiver. “Who is this?”

“Who do you think?” He breathed once, and I heard something like wind. Not outside wind. The forced, wet breath of machines. Fans. “I’m reading my own death, and it’s very fine. I suppose I should be flattered.”

“Mr. Pryor.”

“Yes.” He sounded irritated, as if I’d kept him waiting. “Hear me carefully. Someone is obliterating me line by line, and they want you to help. Don’t. Don’t run it. Don’t touch it. Don’t even print the word philanthropist.” There was a small laugh in that word which made me think of knives.

“I’m not going to print anything until it’s verified,” I said. “What do you mean ‘obliterating’?”

“Do you know the word malum?” he said, as if this were all great fun. “Latin. Or Greek. Take your pick. An apple or a wrong. I walk into the greenhouse every night to keep the machines honest, and tonight every plant is labeled with its Latin name and a new little name below it. ‘Murderer.’ ‘Thief.’ I’m told this is an art project.”

“By whom?”

“That would be the wrong question for a woman who writes about the dead.” The sound shifted; he moved. When he spoke again, he might have had his mouth closer to the phone, the way people do when they want you to lean in too. “Come here. Come see. Bring no one. Come now.”

“I have an editor, and a policy,” I said. “And a very warm coat, which I’d like to go home and put on.”

“You think I’m calling to be profiled posthumously? The greenhouse is a body. It breathes at night differently. It keeps its own records. Do you know why I paid for urban gardens?” He didn’t wait. “Because people will excuse anything if you hand them a tomato. Ten dollars a pound at a farmer’s market and a group of schoolchildren picking basil, and you can sell them almost anything. I’d like them to like tomatoes for the right reasons.”

“You should call the police,” I said, reflexive.

“Police are people who carry their own gardens in their heads,” he said. “Do you want a story or do you want to sleep? Choose. But if you intend to write my ending, don’t do it from the tenth floor. Come to the north greenhouse. Come now.” And then the line was dead in my hand, and I was left with the whirr of fans in my ear like an afterimage.

I sat with the phone resting in the shallow cup my palm made. At the edge of the city, the river tightened its belt and the trains sighed, and because I didn’t trust myself, I tried to think of other explanations. A hoax. A prank. Someone hacking our system to mess with an octogenarian. Miles, who loved practical jokes and hated rich people. But Miles would not tag the file with Gordon’s initials. He would not type Winter.

I sent an email, thin as an alibi. Calder Pryor called. I’m running out to check something. Back soon. I put on my coat. It was damp from the sleeve down, where I had leaned on a forgotten puddle by the copy machine hours ago. I turned off my desk lamp and left the newsroom in the dim blue glow of the exit signs.

In the lobby, Eddie, who had watched this building empty one layoff at a time and still called people kiddo, looked up from his paperback. “You’re early to leave,” he said. “Either that or you’re three years late.”

“I’m going to get a tomato,” I said, and when he lifted his eyebrows in a graceful arc, I said, “It’s a story. Maybe.”

“You got your pepper spray?” he said, because he believed in ritual.

“Yes,” I lied.

“Take mine,” he said, and slid a can under the plexiglass with the discretion of a man moving contraband. It was light. I put it in my pocket with my dead winter gloves and went out into a rain that felt like someone had shaved it down to silt.

The Pryor place was only twenty minutes if the streets wanted to be kind. Tonight, they were an obstacle course of orange barrels and puddles so deep they hid teeth. The house was set back from the road behind a rank of trees that had been landscaped to look wild. The gate—iron shaped like the suggestion of leaves—was open, which was either civic pride or invitation. As I eased up the drive, I thought, as I always did around money disguised as good taste, that wealth liked to pretend it lived in the country, where your neighbors were deer and the night was a blanket. River City always made a racket, however far you ran.

The greenhouse was a glow ahead of the house, a rectangular breath. There were actually three, stepping themselves down along the slanted lawn like words in a sentence written diagonally. The north greenhouse was the one closest to the house, the biggest, its panes steamed with its own weather. The others were darker. The drive ended at a circle with a sleeping fountain. My headlights cut across glass and something inside caught the light and threw it away again: a string, a label, a white tag. I turned the car off and listened. Rain on glass becomes a kind of roar when you’re inside it; outside, it’s a shiver.

A man was waiting by the greenhouse door under the overhang. He was not Pryor. He wore a cap pulled low and the uniform of men who guards mistakes for a living—a dark jacket, boots that can grip. He looked at my car, then at me the way you look at someone who has committed to an error too late to reverse.

“Press,” I said, and held up my ID like a flashlight.

“Parking is that way,” he said, pointing past me, making it easy for me not to hear the rest.

“Mr. Pryor called me,” I said. “He asked me to come.”

“You’re not calling me sir,” he said, and I realized he was younger than I’d thought, his face barely shaved and a scar bisecting his left eyebrow like a mistake he’d learned to live with. “Even when you lie, you should call me sir. It’s respectful.”

“I don’t lie for free,” I said, because I have bad instincts when I’m wet. “Is he inside?”

The guard’s eyes flicked toward the glass. “You people,” he said. “Every story is a tax deduction.” He looked behind me, toward the house. “Ten minutes,” he said finally, and opened the door with a key he’d palmed so I wouldn’t see it.

The wet air that rushed out had its own flavor, humid and green, with a top note of something medicinal. I stepped into it and felt my hair give up. The temperature jump was a slap. The guard did not follow me inside. The door clicked shut behind me with the neat, expensive sound things here probably made when they completed their duties.

It took a second for my eyes to adjust. The cloudy panes filtered the outside into a gauze. Inside, things were lush and orderly. A straight walkway ran down the center with beds and benches on either side. I’d expected the adorable chaos of a community greenhouse—the twine, the mismatched pots, the chalkboard announcements of seed swaps and readings. This was a laboratory that wanted to look like a jungle. Vines rose to trellis. Palms fanned. The labels—white, crisp, embedded at angle in the soil at each specimen—were more numerous than any greenhouse should require. The labels had names in Latin and below them, smaller words hand-printed, which I could not read yet.

“Mr. Pryor?” I said, and my voice evaporated. The fans did what fans do: they took what you said and made a rumor of it.

The greenhouse had sections demarcated by changes in the air: cool fern damp, then heat like the breath of open mouths, then a temperate aisle that smelled of clementines, then the weirdly peppered smell of wet concrete. I let my hand trail along the railing of the walkway, which left my palm with a spray of condensation like someone else’s sweat.

I passed labels. Monstera deliciosa—’hole-plant.’ Nepenthes alata—’winged pitcher.’ A small slatted sign at the edge of a succulent bed: Crassulaceae—stonecrop. And below, in small block print that was not part of the official script, someone had added: swindler. thief. parasite. The words were not on every label but many. The handwriting changed. Some were careful printing. Some were calligraphic. On a tall, tree-like plant with glossy leaves: Ficus sycomorus. sycamore fig. Beneath: liar.

“Mr. Pryor,” I said again, louder. “I’m here. It’s June Graves.” My voice bounced off the glass and came back sounding sensible, which was unwanted. I preferred my sense of unease to be reflected at me.

He was seated halfway down, as if he’d simply stopped to admire an orchid. He wore a sweater that made me think of gentlemen in catalogues and shoes expensive enough to squeak even on concrete. He had one leg crossed over the other at an angle that would have made my knee scream, and he was looking at a plant with the concentration of someone trying to remember something important. When he turned his head, the thought in his face shifted to something resembling irritation.

“You took too long,” he said.

“You gave me fifteen minutes to break every rule I have,” I said. “You look alive.”

He grimaced, nothing that rich men do looking ordinary. “My obit says otherwise. My greenhouse is defaming me. Fans are sulking, or pretending to. Sit.” He didn’t offer his hand, which was just as well. He nodded at the bench slapped along the planting bed across from him. “You can listen for seven minutes, and then you will decide whether to do me a favor.”

“‘Favor’ is a big word.”

“‘Donor’ is bigger,” he said. “We traded in them for a decade. Sit.”

I sat. The bench was damp. The plant he’d been looking at was unremarkable except for its name. A small moon of a blossom tilted like an ear. The label said Cestrum nocturnum—night-blooming jasmine. Below, in the smaller hand, someone had written: confession.

“This is theatrical,” I said, because it was his style to be told when he was posing.

“What is a newspaper if not a theater?” he said lightly. “We print our lives and leave gaps for people to read themselves into. Listen. There is an Eden ledger.”

I thought he was joking until I saw the way his mouth softened around the words. “You know how it is with greenhouses,” he said. “Everything has a list. A schedule. You must feed and cut, water and starve. If the water that comes in is bad, the plants tell you. If the glass breaks, the plants tell you. Everything keeps a record. The Eden ledger is where we put the exceptions. Things that don’t fit and might be useful later. We have kept it under three directors. In times of trouble, it has had… uses.”

“For example?” I said, and he shook his head slowly. His eyes were gray in this light, bleached.

“For example, you might put away the way a councilman once asked for an exotic plant for his wife’s birthday, and you might remind him of that favor when he considers your zoning permit. For example, you might keep a record of donors who are late. For example, you might keep a list of enemies.”

“And mine is in there?” I said before I could stop myself.

He looked at me, surprised, as if I’d made a joke he hadn’t been warned was coming. “You,” he said, amused. “Oh, my. I forget you types think the story is coming for you. No, Ms. Graves. Tonight the story is coming for me. Tonight someone wrote my ending and decorated my glasshouse with footnotes. And somewhere in that ledger is the person who decided he was more alive than I am.”

“You could just throw out the labels,” I said, and he smiled with unpleasant delight.

“I could. But then what would I learn? The man who keeps the ledger is faithful. And now he is missing. He hasn’t gone home. He hasn’t answered. I called you, because every story of mine that might be worth keeping ends up under your hand. I want you to do what you do—go find the facts, make them smaller, put them in order. And then I want you to hold them for me.”

“Hold,” I said. “You don’t want to print them.”

“Not until I say.” He looked at the night-blooming jasmine and added, almost gently, “And there is one more odd thing. The daughter.”

“Winter.”

“You read it.”

“I read everything,” I said. “Is there a Winter, Mr. Pryor?”

He tapped two fingers against his knee, twice, measured. Rain ticked along the roof like breath. “That,” he said, and stood, and the bench shrieked again under his weight, and then something shot a crack across the air, not a gun’s noise but a fast, intimate sound that makes your blood think of bone breaking. The light overhead flickered and went out, and I was left with the afterglow of lamps dying and the soft edges of leaf against leaf.

“Don’t—” he said, and the word dissolved into the dark.

The exit sign at the end of the greenhouse made a mean little red mouth of itself. Somewhere to my right, water began in a thread and then found friends until it was a stream, then a sheet—a sprinkler system or a leak magnified by pressure. The fans coughed, settled, stuttered back to life, and in their wet breath I heard a sound that did not belong to them.

A body falling without hitting the floor sounds like this: a softer correction, a held breath let go.

“Mr. Pryor?” I stood, my knee knocked the bench, my hand caught the damp air. I took one step and my shoe was on something that rolled, round as a grape, and then my balance left me and I grabbed at the air and caught a wet vine that came away in my hand like a rope someone had cut. I swore, which felt like a prayer. “Calder?”

“Miss,” said a voice behind me, so close I thought for an instant it was my own voice thrown back wrong. A hand closed around my upper arm in a way that was not gentle and not cruel. “Miss, you should not move,” the guard said, and then the light—one of the emergency strips—flicked on low and green and made everything look underwater.

On the concrete two feet from the night-blooming jasmine was a puddle of water gone milky with soil. Beside it, a shoe had obscenely detached itself from a foot and tipped on its side like a fish. The rest of the shape was in shadow, a suggestion anchored to the floor by something I couldn’t see. I did what you do when your brain knows and refuses: I blurred everything I saw by focusing on the small thing nearest my hand. The label. The careful Latin. The small printed word below: confession.

Then, from somewhere deeper in the greenhouse, a sound like glass stressing under a change in temperature sighed through the structure, and the emergency light blinked twice and went black. The hand on my arm tightened.

“Don’t move,” the guard said. “Don’t say a word.”

I didn’t move. But in the dark, the names on the labels seemed to glow in my mind like an alphabet devised in secret, and in the space where the word is survived by sits, a shape whispered its name. Winter.

Chapter One

On the island, weather carries gossip faster than the mail. Everyone looks up at the same sky and feels the same pressure change in their bones. Still, most days, I trusted paper more than clouds.

I had the post office open before the first ferry pushed its bow into Sparrow Harbor. The lock on the door always protested, a zinc squeal, as if surprised to be asked to work again. I propped it with the broom and dragged the sack of undeliverable magazines in out of the mist. The heat had been left too low overnight—my breath was a pale ghost—so I thumped the baseboard near the radiator with the heel of my hand until it rattled itself into life. Spool, the orange tomcat who adopted the place last winter and me along with it, stirred on his pile of bubble wrap and one yellow eye slit open. He stayed where he was, compressing his own bed into a collection of small crackles.

Rain battered the window once and then gave up. Fog moved in without a sound, as if the harbor had decided to inhale and hold its breath. Somewhere out there, a diesel turned over lazily. The halyards on the sailboats made their thin, aimless music along the dock. On the counter, the brass dater gave off its penny smell. It was a low season morning on South Bower, where the summer people had gone back to towns with sidewalks and a person could hear their own footsteps three times between the post office and the store.

I slid open the drawer that kept the little weights, the good tape, the single roll of forever stamps with foxes instead of flags. The organizer for change, the hand canceler, the loops of rubber bands. The old canceler from the original South Bower Office—I kept that in the bottom drawer. The island office had officially been absorbed into Sparrow Harbor back in 1937, but every time someone rummaged in the cabinet out back, something old turned up. In May, it had been the canceler: a round brass head with SOUTH BOWER ME arched in worn letters and a blank space where a date once could be screwed in. The rubber had perished long ago. I had wiped it with lemon oil and kept it as a paperweight, which is to say, a thing to look at that had no more work to do.

I checked the registry book, even though nobody on the island had sent a registered letter in months. The page there was blank. Another book, the one for money orders, had three entries from yesterday: two slips from Marco Reyes to a scientific supply house in Portland and one from Nora Kavanagh for a recipe magazine in back issue bundles. I initialed in the margins because Mr. Holt in the district office liked to call and recite regulations at me if I forgot. Interim Postmaster, South Bower—he liked the interim more than the postmaster. I was only showing up for the winter; there wasn’t supposed to be any permanence to it. I’d told everyone that three times—but then people stop hearing your leaving when you’re still there every morning with their mail.

The ferry thumped. The door came open and with it a slice of the harbor. A man was a rectangle in the fog—Owen Madigan, cap pulled low, skin the color of varnished rope.

“You left the broom in the door again,” Owen said by way of hello. He set the canvas exchange sack on the counter, the brass lock tag clacking.

“How else will you know where to deliver it?” I asked.

He grunted something that might have been a laugh and had the same shape as disapproval. He never minded mixing them. He shivered his shoulders under his yellow raincoat and looked past me to the stacked mailboxes on the back wall like every time he came in he half expected to catch letters stealing each other’s secrets. His eyes slid to the radiator. “You going to freeze yourself on principle, Finn?”

“It’s warming,” I said. “Coffee?”

“You’ll make me miss the ten o’clock tide.” He watched Spool’s belly expand and contract. “Cat looks like a sack of mail you forgot to send.”

“He’s on island time.”

Owen shifted in a way that put more weight on his left leg. His right knee had never forgiven a November fall twenty years ago. He tapped the exchange sack with his knuckle. “Got a special for you. Handed off at the last second on the other side. Wouldn’t say who brought it. Didn’t like that.”

“You don’t like when the fog tells you to slow down,” I said, taking the tag key from under the counter. He did not argue.

I cracked the lock and pulled the sack’s mouth open. The smell that came out was one I knew too well—wet paper, rain, a breath of boat engine, the faint smear of wool. I could have navigated my old apartment in Portland blind by that smell. Someone, somewhere, had put rain on paper and handed it to someone else to carry for them. It was an intimate kind of trust, even if the letters were all bills.

Owen folded his arms. He stayed, which he usually didn’t. He liked to move. The ferry likes to move too. If it sits, it forgets how to leave.

I lifted mail out in manageable handfuls. A padded envelope for Marco, three catalogues for Nora, a thin but ominous notice for the school from the district office. A wrapped book addressed to me from my mother’s cousin—she hoarded mismatched teacups and must have decided I needed one. Then, in the tangle of plain white with window panes, one envelope that wasn’t.

It was heavy paper, the color of bone, slightly foxed at the edge as if time had been nibbling it. The address was written in an old-fashioned hand, letters that knew how to curve without showing off. There was no number, no street because South Bower had none. Just: To The Keeper of the Tide Ledger, South Bower Island, Maine.

The return address in the upper left corner was a neat block printed in the same hand: Enoch Gray, Gray’s Cape, South Bower Island, ME.

I held it without meaning to. A person is a thousand small resistances; you don’t know which ones will hold. At the corner, a splotch like a thumbprint traced with ink that was not quite dry. The stamp was a lighthouse—the current Forever, with the tidy, person-less sentinel in a storm. The cancellation mark was SPARROW HARBOR, ME with yesterday’s date around the circle. It had gone through the machine fine.

“He didn’t,” I said. The room shifted, and I corrected: “He can’t have.”

“Who’s he?” Owen asked, though he knew the name as well as I did the weight of the thing in my hand.

I read the return address again because that didn’t change a name. “Enoch Gray.”

Owen made a face that tried to be a smirk and failed because worry is heavier than mockery in the mornings. He rested both hands on the counter and leaned over to peer at the neat letters like it would declare itself a joke if he came at it a new angle. “Well. He learned better handwriting.”

“Not by practising.”

Enoch Gray had been the last person on the island who preferred to be invisible and was irritated to be seen. He’d lived in the shack up on Gray’s Cape—named for his grandfather, not him—among the gnarled spruce and the flat granite that remembered glacial ice. He came down into the village to buy flour and lamp oil and the occasional box of .22s, but he never stayed long. Winter had got into his lungs in February, the kind the clinic called “complications” when a person had no one who would sign their chart for them. He had died in March with the same stubbornness he’d lived with, as if annoyed the world dared change whether he agreed or not.

Owen shifted again and scratched at the stubble on his chin. “Could be somebody’s idea of a tasteless thing.”

I flipped the envelope over without thinking and rubbed my finger over the seal. It wasn’t a self-adhesive; it was wax. Not red, like the movies. A muddy, dark brown, like somebody had melted down a penny and coffee beans. The pressed imprint was not from a proper seal either. It was something textured, a crosshatch like a fish-scale pattern, and at the center a nick the shape of Maine. Oil lamp soot stuck to my finger.

“Who would bother,” I said. I did not say: Who else would know Enoch’s simple stride of letters, the way his G always looked like an animal turning away. “Who even knows what a tide ledger is anymore.”

Owen rubbed his hands together because they were cold or because they were empty. “Everyone knows what it was for,” he said. “Even if they think it’s stories. The old ones wrote the tides down. Straighter than weather.”

He was right. The tide ledger was something people said once existed. When South Bower had been a station for the men who watched and measured and recorded in careful script: water heights, moon positions, set and slack, tidal races that could tear a dory out of the hands of a man with forearms like ropes. There had been a book; the old fellows said so, big as a family Bible and bound with leather that had known salt. A boy had been made to stand and rink the bell with his palm when they recorded the king tides. The Keeper had been an official thing once, before the Coast Survey took their instruments away to other ports and the men who could listen to water like it was an instrument started dying.

Owen stared at the envelope as if it might offer up a second return address if he glared long enough. “If he posted it, the postmark would be from here.”

“He didn’t post anything from here,” I said, meaning he did not come in for stamps, did not come in for anyone, except to complain that the government was now watching him for buying lamp oil which I had explained to him no less than three times was untrue.

“Then who walked it onto the ferry?”

I did not answer because the answer would be a list and I had lived small enough in the last year to avoid lists.

“You’ll return it,” he decided, relief in the certainty of process.

“Wrong address,” I said, because that was true. There was no keeper, no ledger that anyone had, not officially. There was me and a wall of boxes and the power went out in nor’easters.

“So, slap RTS—” he made a rectangle motion in the air toward Enoch’s neat block—“and send it back to Gray the Great, which is to say, the county evidence room.”

“‘Return to sender’ goes to three places,” I said. “Back, dead letter, or the trash, depending on whether the address exists, the address exists but the person doesn’t, or whether there’s a stamp.” I looked at the stamp again because I could look at a stamp instead of look at Owen. The lighthouse stood there wishing it could choose its storms. “Owen, if this is a poor joke, it isn’t poor enough. Somebody cared to do this right.”

“How do you know what is right for a ghost?” he asked, and gave the counter one last rap with his knuckles. Then he was gone, leaving salt and damp and words behind.

Spool rose with deliberate reluctance, padded to the envelope and sniffed at the wax. He made a sound like an empty envelope making itself useful as a toy and yawned, showing canine teeth that had cost me $250 to have scaled last spring. I put the letter beside the antiqued hand canceler and felt like I had set down two stones that belonged to the same jetty.

It made no sense to hold the mail back, so I did not hold it. I sorted. People would come in. There would be talk. A woman of my own age might lean on my counter with the casual intimacy of people who share a remarkable nothingness in common, and say, Did you hear about so-and-so’s cousin’s lobster license. Everyone would say the name Enoch like they were testing it for rot. I placed bills in the slots, the glossy magazine for the tourist who kept paying to have mail forwarded to a summer address that was now a photograph by someone else. The parcel for Marco—heavy, bound with plastic strapping that cut into my hand—went under Off-Island because he would be along with shoulders wet from working on his traps and he would take it himself.

The last thing I did was slide the heavy envelope into my bag, under the counter, and tell myself I wasn’t doing anything with it. It had been addressed to a position, not a person, and there was no person. In the afternoon, I would call Elspeth Crowley over at the sheriff’s office on the mainland and tell her about it, and we would both make the small sounds people make when they are thinking about somebody who is dead once and might be dead twice because you cannot die and arrive in someone’s bag at the same time. I would log it. I had a ledger for anomalies in a notebook left by the last postmistress, who had gone to live near her sister because our clinic could not decide whether to call the thing in her brain a tumor or a cyst or a problem waiting to decide on a name. There was a box for it. Every box has another box inside.

By ten, the ferry had come and gone again. I had found the exact place to set my coffee on the radiator where it warmed without going lukewarm. Two people had come in for stamps. Nora Kavanagh came in for her magazine and told me what she’d told me twice before about why she had never married: because she preferred cooking for people who would leave her alone afterwards. Marco came in to sign for his parcel and left a slick trail on the floor, the rubber going squeak, squeak, the special sound of boots on soaked tile. He made a mess of my pen, and apologized, and then made a show of signing my book with calligraphic flourish to redeem himself, and I laughed because we were both pretending it mattered.

Around five past noon, after the door had closed behind the last person who could be said to have a reason to be there, I did the one thing I have learned to do when some quiet thing threatens to become a loud one: I took inventory of my own space. The dust on the windowsill wore the faint trailing haze of the tip of a gull wing where it had dipped under the eave this morning, looking for crumbs. The broom had left a thin slur of sand behind the door again where it had propped itself toward a purpose. The under-cabinet hinge was loose the way it had been since I moved in and the left side always hung lower than the right. The bottom drawer, where I kept the old South Bower canceler, was closed. The dust on its top was smooth.

The dust on the front edge had one place where a fingertip had been set down. Just the one, small, and there was no reason for me to have touched the wood there since Tuesday. I stared at the dot as if it might speak. It did not. The shape it made was the same as Enoch’s G turned away.

I told myself ten explanations, and the tenth one was that I would be ridiculous if I allowed a dot of dust to dictate my day. I closed up a little early—it was a day to be forgiven anything except perhaps ignoring the ferry schedule—and stepped out into the fog.

South Bower is two roads that become one when it rains. The pines keep their own weather under them; water gathers where you don’t expect. I had learned to step around certain puddles and discovered, in this learning, old habits. The city had trained me to look at the reflection of sky in the shape water makes in the street, to read traffic and human currents by how people alter their own wet. On the island, I knew where the sea pulled a bit harder at the bar because it was remembering a storm from another year.

The Clinic lights were on, but no cars clustered. The store had a hand-lettered sign that said Open, which in winter mostly meant Come talk to me, I am lonely, bring money if you have it. Past the church that had been repainted too white, past the teacher’s cottage which was only dim months where in summer it was full of cardboard rockets and glitter. I made myself walk past the turn toward my own cottage because I remembered the way my mother used to frown when my father brought his boat in and made a bad face at the House before he’d even stepped on the dock. Don’t give it to the House, Maeve, she would say. That will be the thing that kills you, not the sea.

I thought, for a moment, as I passed the trail that led to the eastern path, of simply delivering Enoch Gray’s letter to Gray’s Cape. It would be a kind of joke, and a way of refusing a new grief. If the Cottage had been my enemy, or my friend, maybe I would have. But I am prosaic in the ways that matter and superstitious only about promises I make to myself. I walked home with the envelope in my bag, the strap making a thin diagonal pain across muscle that ached on damp days, and made it up the steps to my rented cottage that crouched like a gull in the lee of the hill.

The porch boards had learned my gait. I set the key in the lock and sighed when it did not turn on the first try because the world is full of things that want to stick instead of open. I put my shoulder into the door and the door, like the lock, liked to complain before it relented. In the kitchen, I hung the bag over the back of a chair and set water on the stove for tea because I am, in all the ways that matter, a coward about coffee after noon. The old electric kettle hummed like a large mosquito. Spool circled my shins and made his small, questioning chirp. I ignored him in the way that makes a cat determined to be considered.

While the water pondered its boil, I took the envelope out and set it on the table. The table had a scar in it the shape of a fishhook, left by the last tenant, who had told me when we exchanged keys that he had always meant to sand it down and never did. The letter fitted the scar, which meant nothing I could put a name to.

To The Keeper of the Tide Ledger. The Keeper, which could be a person. The Tide Ledger, which could be a thing. The address, which assumed both existed.

On the back, the fish-scale seal. When I moved the envelope, it caught the light and, I realized, there were tiny speckles around it, not wax. Something gritty. Salt, like you’d find in the spray line of a rock when the tide dropped away, clung to the edges. A mistake of the maker. Or a message, if you were inclined to believe in messages. I have learned that it has to be one thing before it can be another.

I set the envelope down again. The kettle did not quite boil and then did. I made tea. I took down the mug my mother’s cousin had sent last Christmas, the one with a fox chasing its tail. I poured, waited, smelled. The smell of tea is the same as the feeling of an armchair in the houses I have loved. I went to the door of the little living room while the tea steeped and opened the window to the fog because my mother had taught me to air out everything I own at least once a day. I turned back into the kitchen, into the half-air, and saw the other envelope on the floor just inside the door, where the welcome mat scraped threadbare under it had tried to keep it.

It was the same bone-colored paper. It had the same tidy curves of the same hand. There was no stamp, no postmark. It had not been in the world enough to be touched by any of my little machines. It was addressed to me.

Maeve Finn, Interim Postmaster. Keeper of the Counter, it said, as if the counter were an altar and I its reluctant priest.

Spool made his interrogative noise because he had heard the sound paper makes when it meets wood and thinks of mice. Outside, the fog pressed its quiet face to the window.

I crouched. The buckled knee of my jeans complained, which is to say, my body told on the year and the miles. I picked up the envelope and, for reasons I could not name, held it to my nose. I expected paper and fresh ink. I got lamp oil and fish.

I stood very still with the door behind me open and the kettle ticking down behind me on the stove and the cat a punctuation mark at the edge of my peripheral vision. I whispered, “All right,” though no one had asked me a question.

The seal on this one was different. Not fish scale. The same wax, but pressed with something small and round, a coin maybe, so that the impression was a head in profile and the words around it reversed. I had a magnifying glass in the drawer because I am my mother’s daughter and because money order numbers are written in fine ink. The head was a Liberty dime. The words that went backwards around it were ONE DIME.

I broke the seal and the wax flaked and Spool leapt up, delighted, to paw at the pieces. I pushed them away from him and unfolded the single sheet inside the envelope.

Maeve, it began, in the same hand. It is a little late for me to apologize, but I am going to anyway. They told me that if anyone would listen to the words that are in a book, it would be you. You will be told to return what I have sent. Please don’t. Deliver the other one where it belongs, and bring yourself to the Balanced Rock at dead low on Sunday with a light and a rope. If you can bring the Ledger, bring it. If you cannot, then do not tell anyone you cannot. If you send anyone else, you will get someone killed.

I would write more but they do not all like that I am writing at all. It is not for me to explain. You will see. You always do. You have a way with names.

E.G.

P.S. I am, according to the island, dead. Let’s keep it that way until it is less useful.

The kettle ticked the last breath out of itself and went quiet. I reread. I do that when what is on a page refuses to be what my brain says it is. My mouth had gone dry as if somebody had opened the oven and all the moisture had rushed up and out. I reached for the tea and burned my tongue because I did not look, because I did not wait.

Balanced Rock is on the far side of the island—two slabs of granite arranged by an accident of glacier and time so that one leaned a hand on the other. A place where teenagers went to teach each other that Beltane meant kissing and where old men, those who still walked, went to look at water when a certain kind of memory swung its legs off their bed and sat with them at four in the morning. A place you could get in trouble if you happened to believe that the sea is a thing that is patient and it is only us that is hurried.

I put the letter down, face-up, and, without meaning to, put my finger on the ink of my name as if by pressing the word I might make myself heavier, harder to move.

They told me that if anyone would listen it would be you—who were they. I have a way with names—my mouth twitched at that, because my mother naming me Maeve had meant something only to her, and because my father, when he wanted to make a point, would call me by my full name, the one he gave me that no one uses, and because in law school for the quarter and a half I endured, the first thing they teach you is to name things properly so that they will either fit into a box or tell on themselves by the way they weep through its corners. I lost time in the notion of someone you could not see calling you something close to true.

The front door gave a small exhale as if something had leaned forward into it and then leaned away again. Footsteps? No, the sound of fog making itself at home on paint. But I was suddenly aware of the fact that someone had been near my door. Had bent, slid paper, walked away. In our little place, where an engine echoes differently if it belongs to the sheriff or to a fisherman or to a summer person with no muffler sense, I had heard no one. That does not mean nobody had come. It means I had been listening in the wrong direction.

I turned the other envelope over. To The Keeper of the Tide Ledger, it had said. It lay like a flat stone on my table. The wax on it threw no light back at me. If I listened hard enough, if I listened like I had as a child for my father’s boat, like I had last year in a city that never sleeps for the sudden absence of noise that means the worst kind of surprise, I could almost hear the tiny, imagined tick of ink drying. I had a number I could call to ask somebody else to make this decision. The number would ring in an office where a woman named Elspeth sat with a cardigan and a face that had listened to people crying at three in the morning and had gone on cooking her eggs anyway. If I called, she would say, Hold on to it, Maeve. We’ll come out after lunch tomorrow.

Tomorrow. Dead low Sunday. Whispered instructions in a dead man’s hand.

Spool climbed into a chair and knocked my bag off with the casual expertise of animals who have lived with humans and do not fear their reaction. The strap hit the floor with a small thunder that in my startled ear sounded too much like the stamp of a boot on my stoop. I told myself out loud, “You are on an island, not a crime show,” and picked up the bag and, for the first time since I came to South Bower, did what people on this island do without thinking: I locked my door while I was inside it. Then I sat down, put my palms on either side of the letter with the address that was technically wrong, and decided what kind of person I was going to be, at least until Sunday.

Outside, somewhere in the fog, a bell buoy rang. It was not quite on time. The tide took its own.

Chapter One

They called me because the organ wouldn’t stop breathing.

That’s how Father Anselm put it, in a voice pitched somewhere between apology and superstition. “Ms. Ellison,” he’d said on my voice mail, “the old girl’s sighing again. At all hours. Mrs. Phelps says it’s the Holy Ghost, but I’m holding out for a loose pallet. We’d be grateful if you could come.” He gave the code to the side door and added, “I know it’s late.”

St. Bartholomew’s sat on the granite knuckle that stuck into the harbor, a gray stone church in a town of clabbered whites and faded shingled blues. The storm had been flirting with us all afternoon, licking the ocean flat one minute and clawing it to slate shreds the next. By the time I parked on the loop of cracked asphalt beside the parish hall, the wind had committed; it banged the flag halyard against its pole and dragged the smell of salt and kelp into the curling leaves on the maples.

I locked my van, hefted my toolkit, and let myself in.

The vestibule smelled like old hymnbooks and damp wool. The sanctuary beyond was dim, lit only by the glass saint in the west window and whatever bruised light the storm let through. I stood a moment to let my eyes adjust. The organ was just where it had always been, shouldering itself along the wall of the chancel, a theater of pipes rising in tiers, its oak case polished by a hundred years of sunlight and pledge. The console hunkered at the edge of the choir stalls, like an animal that pretended to be tame.

The breathing started as soon as I crossed the aisle.

It was a pale, continuous whisper under the wind and the creak of the rafters. If you didn’t know organs—really know them—you might take it for a draft rummaging through the pipes. But organs are lungs as much as instruments, and wind on wood is a language. This sound wasn’t the hiss of an open toe or the wet, ragged exhale that means a damaged reservoir. It had weight. There was a body to it, the subtle thrum that only comes when a blower is moving air, when fans push and leather swells and tiny valves wait, nervous, to be asked.

None of which should have been happening at nine-thirty on a Tuesday night in a locked church.

“Anselm?” I said softly, out of habit. The stone made my voice into a stranger. No answer came.

The console told me what I needed to know before I touched it. The stop knobs—bone faces, cracked as old teeth—were all closed. The swell and great were uncoupled. The keys sat level. The on-off toggle for the blower was down, dark, where I had left it after the prelude last Sunday when Mrs. Phelps had indulged one of her fantasies and made the choir sing an anthem out of time and place.

But the whispers persisted. A silk sheet of sound. A suggestion of tone at the edge of hearing, like a whistle you can’t swear you hear until it stops and your head aches for it.

I set the toolkit under the bench and crouched to open the little door in the console’s side. The wiring was as it ought to be—swaddled cloth, my own neat splices from the spring’s rewiring—no gross, illegal jumpers to fool the safety cutoffs. I pinched the toggle switch and felt the clean click of it, off into on, on into off. Nothing changed. There was no relay thump, no blossom of a blower motor roaring awake or a reservoir flinching. The whisper stayed exactly itself, a soft persistent movement, as if the organ exhaled and inhaled without effort and without sleep.

I closed the door and stood. The hair on my forearms had stood too.

The thing about St. Bart’s is that she’s more mechanical than most. The action that connects keys to pipes is tracker, old-fashioned and honest: wooden rods and thin strips of leather, squares and stickers, tiny wooden levers and suspended wires that link your fingers to the little valves under each pipe. It means there are fewer layers to lie between you and the sound. It also means you can trace most problems if you’re patient and you listen.

I slipped off my boots and left them under the pew. The chancel floor is evil to stocking feet—splinters polished sharp by a hundred scrubbings—but I do most of my best thinking without shoes, the same way I play. Barefoot, you can feel the world’s hum.

The case shelf was cold under my hand as I pulled myself up onto it and ducked through the panel I’d left loose in spring. A smell rushed me: beeswax, murk, the faintly animal tang of leather.
