And under it, something else—salt, yes. Damp wood, yes. But also something metallic and sweet, like pennies held too long in your mouth. I paused, nose full, and realized it was copper and something else I did not want to name.

The internal organs of organs seldom look like their exterior promises. The pretty face of well-polished pipes hides the part that works: the windchest like an opened chest with ribs of channels, pallets like lips under each tone hole, a thousand tiny actions ready to open and shut. The big ranks that you can see from the nave are show, sometimes even dummies; the voices you love are tucked inside: the stopped bourbon with their hats on, the slender principals with their beards of solder, the reed shallots lined up like a calligrapher’s pens. I eased along the catwalk, my weight set on the beams I’d set a hundred times before. If you place it wrong, you scuff dust into the cheeks of the pipes and then make a fool of yourself trying to clean it without denting their faces. Soot and brass dust show where the last tuner went; I’m stingier than most with fingerprints.

The whispering was louder inside, the shape of it more distinct. It wasn’t random; it had the evenness of regulated wind. It also had a hitch in it, a periodic thinness, as if something soft was pressed and released, pressed and released.

“Don’t be weird,” I told myself. “You fix organs. This is an organ doing organ things when it shouldn’t.” When I talk aloud, it’s usually for the instrument’s sake. They like a voice. They sing better when sung to.

It had rained hard the week before. Tonight the wind pushed water in sheets against the stone. I told myself there was bulk water somewhere it didn’t belong, swelling a slip of leather so a pallet was ajar. And then I breathed and listened again, and the tiny hairs along my scalp prickled. Something about the odor, that copper-sweet like rotten apples, edged in.

At the swell box the louvers were closed, slicked with dust except for four thin streaks where fingers had touched them recently. My streaks are fatter. The blower trunk ran behind the windchest, a wooden pipe like a modest coffin. I crouched beside it and put the flat of my hand on the wood. The whisper traveled through my palm, but there was no vibration. No motor thudding in the basement. This was ghost wind.

There is no such thing as ghost wind. There are miswirings and bypasses and people who think they are clever.

Someone had been clever.

At the treble end of the great windchest, where you’d have to be narrow and determined to crawl, the belly leather on one of the reservoirs had a patch newer than the others—my patch, double-stitched, copper tacks burnished by my thumb on a Saturday in March. The patch bulged slightly. And under it—this was wrong—something pulsed against the leather.

“Hello,” I whispered, without meaning to.

The pulsing stilled. The whispering held, then flirted away, then ceased. For a moment there was nothing but the wind in the rafters and my heart’s stupid animal racket. The sudden silence from the organ hit me like cold water.

Something groaned.

It could have been the building settling. It could have been a pew complaining under its own weight. It could have been my nerve.

I set my hand on the reservoir again and pressed gently. The leather was firm, and the maple frame under it solid, the ribbing of the springs resisting my push. That ribbing responded to more weight than wind. The groan had come from the springs’ hooks moving, slow in their eyelets, the sound you get when someone heavier than wind climbs onto your system and makes it breathe.

“Anselm?” I said again, though my throat had decided it was tired of words.

No answer.

The narrow run between the flutes and the principals would take me back to where the wind enters the footboards and where—if someone had put their reflected cleverness where it didn’t belong—the bypassed blower line might be.

I moved sideways, a crab at a tea party, hips scraping the inner casing, my shoulder bumping the wooden bridge that carries the trackers across. Dust kissed my cheek. Somewhere, something knocked: faint, thin, hollow. The knocking came again in a rhythm that did not belong to wind or rain or men—tick, tick, long, tick. I stopped. It didn’t repeat. I tried to stand but there wasn’t room; I crouched, breathed, and felt it again through the bones of my ankles as much as through the air. Tick, tick, long, tick: a clock, maybe, tucked into a pocket that had lost its owner.

When I turned the corner behind the pedal rank, the smell unrolled like a banner.

I’ve worked on organs that have housed families of mice, a trapped raccoon, an apartment for a wasp queen. I’ve crawled into chambers where damp rot lay down like a dog at your feet. This wasn’t that. This was the tidy, shallow sweetness that meets you when you open the door to a room where lilies have been too long with the heat. It was a hospital smell without the antiseptic. It was candy if candy could dread you.

Part of my brain—the part that has kept me employed in a profession that conscripts every sense— cataloged it calmly. The other part made a quiet, inarticulate sound and wished for shoes.

I saw the leather first. A slip of strap, brown to go with everything, threaded wrongly around a pipe foot and into the dark between ranks. Then the cuff of a sleeve. The twill was good; even through dust it looked kind. The hand that hung below it was pale where the fingers weren’t black with something like oil, but not oil. The fingernails were squared, clean, clipped by someone who thought about how nails catch in felt.

I did not scream. I am not the screaming type. I did swear, but not loud enough that anyone but God heard it, and He’s used to better.

I backed up, taking care not to knock ranks out of tune or to step where I knew nothing would take my weight. Later, my body would make a note of every place I bumped and scrapped. For now, there was only the imperative that rose from animal to animal: out.

My phone was in my back pocket. I pulled it, immediately, like a person in a public service ad. No bars. This end of the town is a dead spot unless you’re standing on the belfry roof with a gull on your shoulder. Of course it was.

I breathed, twice, like I’ve been told to breathe when the world insists on being itself. Then I leaned in again, far enough to see what I absolutely did not want to see again and could not avoid.

He was wedged where no one would find him unless they belonged in here. The space between the fourteen-foot stopped bourdon and the paneling is a coffin if you aren’t thin or lucky. He had been both once, I guessed. His shirt was gray, the kind that comes with pearl buttons, though one of them was missing. I saw the loop of something—cord? strap?—crushed under his shoulder. His face was turned into the dim wood. His hair had folded away from his head in a style only privileged by gravity. There was no blood I could see, and I did not come blessedly close enough to smell anything but that sweetness.

His wrist was twisted against a heelboard. On it was a watch I knew too well.

I did scream then. A short sound, like something a chick makes when it’s fallen out of the nest and is offended more than afraid. The sound made me angrier at myself than I already was. I swallowed whatever the next sound was going to be.

I got out of the case, breathless without breathing hard, and fell off the shelf into the choir with less grace that anyone should. I slid on my socks and tore them on the splinters I had lectured my toes about. I put my boots on spreading their wet tongues at me, and after trying the toggle switch again, like a fool in a loop, I went through the sacristy and knocked with a ridiculous politeness on the rectory door.

It opened at the second knock. Anselm stood there in shirtsleeves and a cardigan like a grandfather who had borrowed fashion from a librarian. His hair stuck up in surprised silver.

“Mira,” he said, as if we had rung up an appointment and this was it. “You made good time.”

“Call nine-one-one,” I said. “And don’t go in there.”

He did not ask why. You can say many things about Father Anselm, but he is good in a crisis— because, I suppose, his work starts there. He stepped back, hand already in his pocket for his phone, while mine gripped the doorframe. The storm fumbled the gutters. Somewhere a loose thing clattered down the granite and went to sea.

I sat on the stair, and the cold came up through my boots slow and deliberate, as if the stone had all night to make its point. I rubbed my palms on my jeans, then stopped because I didn’t know if my palms had touched him. The thought of smearing any of him on the fabric of me made something in my chest give an unhelpful squeak.

The ambulance got lost in the maze of one-way streets. The police did not.

Brackett’s Point is a town that believes in two absolutes: the ocean will try to take you if you don’t respect it, and everyone knows everyone else’s middle name. I wanted a stranger to climb the church steps and bring a clean categorical voice into the room. Instead, I got Kellan Pike, who is adequate to most tasks and used to be adjacent to mine, though on boats, not inside instruments.

He had been a diver with the Coast Guard until he wasn’t, and now he wears a badge as if it’s another kind of uniform. He’s older than me by six years, tall enough that the church door made him a little smaller for a heartbeat, and he has a look like he has learned to expect that systems will fail in ways that make you swim.

“Ellison,” he said, and then seeing whatever it was in my face, “Mira.” He didn’t try to shake my hand. For that small gift I could have kissed him.

“In the organ,” I said. “Inside.”

He looked past me to Anselm. The priest nodded, set his phone on the table in the hall, and collected himself as if smoothing a prayer book. “She told me not to go,” he said. “So I’m obeying an expert.”

Kellan took that in with a flick of his eyes and then took me in, too. He knew my grandfather’s house and the shape of my childhood because that’s what this town is. He also, maddeningly, knew what my face looks like when I’ve played through dinner. It’s a look like a person concentrating and the edges of them a little frayed. He set his jaw in a way that tells you he plans to talk to you like you are both adults, in half an hour, when he knows where to step.

“Show me where,” he said. “Then you sit.”

I showed him the panel. I ducked onto the shelf and pointed where a person who is wiry and incautious could slide into the interior. I told him about the whispering, the springs, the not-blower.

He listened like you want a cop to listen—like he believes you even when he doesn’t understand the words. He tilted his head at the sound of the wind; somehow it had found its archetype and eased for a breath.

He slid in, not elegantly but without distress. I held the panel as if the case were a creature with ideas about closing on him. He was silent long enough that my body decided to begin quietly shaking and there was nothing to do but let it, because fighting your own muscles in the choir of God is performative and silly.

Then he spoke, low and flat. “You know him?” he asked.

“Yes,” I said. My voice found orphaned steadiness somewhere and brought it home. “I think so.” As if there were any doubt. As if you could confuse that scratched wide-banded watch, the face of it spidered across its bottom left quadrant, with any other watch in our small town.

“Name?” Kellan asked.

“Gideon Hale,” I said. The syllables felt too big, like stones so smooth from a pocket that throwing them hurts. “He’s—he was—the organ builder I apprenticed with. He retired here. You know that.”

“I know he bitched about the parking meters at town meeting,” Kellan said, voice still level. Then, because he may have a cruel streak or an honest one and they look the same from the outside, “You saw his face?”

“No,” I said. Relief and shame arrived in equal packets. “Just—his watch. The— the way he keeps his nails.” The little things betray you. When you learn instruments you learn hands. Gideon’s were beautiful in their particular ways: the pads warm and callused, the nails trimmed a tick shorter than fashionable, the cuticles ruthlessly neat. He had once told me that organ builders should not bleed into their work.

Kellan was silent again. The storm hit the stained glass, disturbed the blue saint so her foot broke into fish scales. Somewhere in the nave, a hymnbook resettled itself with a resentful slap.

“Gently now,” Kellan said, not to me.

He inched out of the case and they came in pairs after him, the EMTs and a patrolman who had the guilty look local police get when they know they are about to lay hands on a body that belonged to someone who used to complain about recycling schedules. The EMTs asked practical questions and did the ritual things that people do for the dead even when everyone knows the dead no longer require ritual. They wear their compassion like a uniform too, and it fits them. When they moved him—when they threaded the board where they could and coaxed him into a shape that would fit through a hole meant for sound, not flesh—I turned away. I stared at the hymn numbers on the board, which promised “Guide Me, O Thou Great Jehovah” as if someone had known we would need instructions.

Anselm stood with one hand on the chancel rail, not praying, exactly, not speaking. I had never noticed how long his fingers were, and now I was seeing nothing else about him except that.

When the gurney rolled past me toward the door, one of the EMTs paused. “You all right, Ms.—?”

“Ellison,” I said. Because if you don’t answer questions politely, this town remembers. “Yes.” It was true enough. The shaking had left. Something else had moved in to sit on my chest, radiating out in waves that made my teeth ache.

They left an absence and a smell. The organ had sighed once when they moved the weight from the reservoir. Then it had gone still, sulking, perhaps, at the indignity, or perhaps grieving in the only way that wind and wood can.

Kellan stood where he could watch both me and the hole in the case as if either of us might do something unlicensed. He waited until the door closed, until the ambulance flattered the night with its brief whine and then was swallowed by the storm.

“Okay,” he said quietly. The word was neutral, almost kind. “Tell me everything.”

There are different ways to tell a story like that. There is the version with all the fear words up front, and the version that clings to technicalities like a wreck to flotsam. I gave him the second. I told him about the call, and the side door code, and the smell. I told him about the blower that wasn’t blowing and the whisper that didn’t belong. I told him about the springs—a detail that made him tilt his head because springs are something he knows, too. I told him about the strap, the cuff, the watch. I did not tell him about the lily-sweet smell or the places my socks had torn my feet, because those felt like mine and because he is not a priest.

When I finished, he was quiet long enough to rummage a pen out of his shirt pocket and click it four times in a row. He doesn’t fidget except when he is writing the first line of a report in his head.

“Someone would have had to turn the organ on,” he said.

“I didn’t,” I said. The stupid toggle switch sat where it had always sat, innocent as a coffeepot. “It was on without being on. Someone’s bypassed the relay, maybe. Or there’s a manual pump somewhere I don’t know about.” The thought made me huff, humorless. Gideon had told me no builder worth his salt puts a hand pump in a church that no longer has a boy to work it. “No. If I had to bet, I’d say he sat on the reservoir to get himself more wind. Or someone sat him there.” My mouth made that shape without my permission and went dry doing it.

“Would that—” Kellan hesitated. I watched him reach for the place where his authority lives and then back away from it. “Would it— Could someone die that way?”

“Of suffocation?” I said. “Not from wind. It’s not an airtight system. These things breathe with the world. But if you were pinned—” I stopped. I had made the shape with my body already: tried to breathe with something solid under your lung’s needs. There are less ridiculous ways to die, but death is not interested in dignity. “There are easier ways to kill a man,” I said, as if my opinion mattered.

“Is that what we have?” He looked at me with something like apology. His eyes are the color of the granite when the tide is going out, which is an unhelpful thing to notice about anyone.

“I don’t know,” I said. “I found him.” As if finding were not sometimes a kind of guilt.

He nodded, as if that was exactly the answer he expected and was, in its way, content to have. He scratched something in a notebook that he had conjured from a pocket I wouldn’t have guessed. “You said you knew him,” he said, as if that were a different conversation he was laying next to this one. “When did you see him last?”

“Sunday,” I said automatically, then caught the reflex. That was when I usually saw him—after church, fiddling with the action, complaining cheerfully about how everyone breathed wrong, even in their singing. But our last actual meeting had been a month ago, at the coffee shop with the chalkboard that insists it makes the best lemon bars on the coast. We had argued about a horne stop in a north end church neither of us loved. We had not touched. Gideon did not touch people unless he was also touching wood and calling it demonstration. “A few weeks,” I corrected. “We email.”

“You argued,” Kellan said. Not like an accusation; like a fact he had observed in this town often enough to make him believe in recurring patterns: storms come on Tuesday, people argue at coffee shops, someone dies in a place where they did not plan to.

“We discussed,” I said. My mouth is sometimes petty.

His pen clicked once. “He was here because…?”

“He comes when the organ misbehaves,” I said. “He can’t help himself. And he’d been asked to do the upgrade this winter, if the capital campaign had their way.” I did not say “and if the anonymous donor holds.” Some details live in another box.

He nodded. “So someone who cares about this instrument called someone who cared more.”

“Yes,” I said.

“And now he’s dead in it.”

“Yes.”

We looked at the thing he was dead in, as if it could be persuaded to speak. The organ pretended to be innocent. Its pipes threw back at us the color of storm light. The stop faces read like titles on a shelf: Principal 8', Bourdon 16', Flute 4', Voix Celeste 8'. It was an honest organ, built by a man who had signed his work in places only a fellow tradesman would find: a small swallow carved under the manual, a cap on a pipe foot inscribed with the initials he finished hiding only twenty years ago. I had found them all when I learned her. I had found the swallow first and loved him for it. You sign what you love and what will outlive you.

“Stay put,” Kellan said finally, with a tired kindness. “Don’t go touching anything you don’t have to.” He gave me the look I used to give wayward choir boys who stuck gum under pews. The temptation to touch things I don’t have to touch is the defining essence of my work. “I’ll have someone sit with you while we—” He made a shape with his hand that encompassed the next hour.

As if I would leave anyway. As if anywhere else right now would be not-worse than this.

He stepped away to murmur in Anselm’s ear. The priest nodded and went to make tea because that is what priests do. I sat on the bench that had been my bench since I was tall enough to see over it, and I put my hands where they have always lived. I did not play. For the first time since I was twelve, the keys looked like something that could hurt me if I asked them for anything. My feet flexed and noticed that my socks were damp with someone else’s church.

When the tea came, it tasted like something steeped in nerves. I drank it anyway.

The rain remembered that it was water and wanted to be more of itself. The wind threw handfuls of it at the glass and then dragged it away, because the wind is greedy and likes to hoard the things it intends to spend. Somewhere in the building, a pipe ticked as it cooled. The tiny noise threaded into the small noises that were all that was left of us. And under all of that, behind the closed swell shades and the neat stop faces, the organ held its breath as if it knew it had been looked inside and was not ready to be fully honest yet.

The book of psalms lay open on the rail where Anselm had left it on Sunday. The text swam and settled, swam and settled until it was clear. The verse my eye happened to rest on spoke about breath and spirit and the bones of a house rising. It felt like a joke. The saints in the stained glass must have shared it because their faces made the particular expression saints and cops wear when they know more than they will say.

Kellan came back. He leaned against the pew opposite as if it was his pew. He had taken off his hat like a gentleman. He looked at my hands and then at my face and said, as if he had not asked me enough already, “Tell me something else, Mira.” His voice was too casual. “That little bird carved under the manual—what do you call it?”

“A swallow,” I said. My mouth remembered love even if the rest of me was all edges. “He always hides one.”

He nodded as if I had confirmed an ugly rumor he had not wanted to be true. Then he glanced at the open sacristy door as if someone might come through it carrying a thing he didn’t want to see. “There was a piece of paper in his pocket,” he said. He left spaces around his words for me to climb into if I wanted. “Folded small. Looks like a page out of a hymnbook, but it isn’t. Music, though. Know what it was?”

“No,” I said. “Not like I got that far.” The thought of going that far made my stomach think childish thoughts about ridges and ropes.

“Title says ‘Hirondelle,’” he said. “That mean anything?”

“It’s French,” I said. “For swallow.” I did not say what perched in my mind then and refused to be shooed: Gideon had called the little two-foot recorder stop he loved “Hirondelle” even though the donors hated foreignness on their stop faces. He had carved swallows in places no one would see if they didn’t know where to look. He had been a man in love with small birds and big voices.

He nodded once, the way a man nods at a thing that has cracked open in front of him exactly as he knew it would. “Okay,” he said again, and I did not need him to tell me that this had ceased to be a story with an end we could predict and had become a song with a line we would have to learn fast.

Outside, the storm laughed at a joke it had made itself. Inside, the organ kept its counsel. And somewhere neighboring and astonishingly close, a clock I could not see ticked and ticked and paused and ticked, counting something it alone had been asked to name.

The first thing you learn, if you stay in this job long enough, is that buildings lie. People think it’s sagging floors and cracked plaster and all the parts you can point to. For me, a lie is the second layer of paint that doesn’t match the first, the baseboard that stops a quarter-inch short of a corner, the patch on the ceiling that somehow looks too perfect. A building will swear to your face it has nothing to hide, and then you put your ear to the wall and hear the air moving where it shouldn’t.

St. Bartholomew’s was built when the city believed in permanence. The stonework was patient and pitted and furred in places with lichen that never seemed to dry out, even in summer. The bell had been silent for decades; pigeons rolled in the eaves. Now it was something called The Bart—a co-working hub with artisanal coffee and a logo that made the cross look like a minimalist ampersand.

I parked my city-issue Ford on the double-yellow anyway and left the hazard lights pulsing their apology. The rain had started up again—a cold, legalistic drizzle that made you feel like you’d missed a meeting. My name is Iris Cates, City of Lowry Building Division, certification badge clipped to my jacket like a dare. They’d assigned me the final on The Bart. The permit had been a political hot potato from the start. There were councilmembers who dotted their sentences with the word “vibrancy” and others who still crossed themselves when they drove by. And there was me in the middle, the person between old bones and new money, holding a tape measure in one hand and the codebook in the other.

“Inspector Cates,” said a voice that had practiced sounding spontaneous. “Finally.”

Silas Ward. Developer. Soft navy suit, soft leather shoes, a tie the same gray as the day. He made a point of carrying his own hard hat and wearing it like a halo. Behind him, the general contractor—a barrel-chested man everyone called Blue—turned his hat around in his hands as if deciding which way luck went today.

“You’re early,” I said, looking at my watch.

“I’m often punctual to things that cost me money,” Silas said, smiling, and held the door for me. “We’ve got pastry. Real butter.”

“Pastry is not a code issue,” I said, but I didn’t mind that he held the door. I stepped inside and smelled lemon oil, coffee, sawdust, and the faint undertow of damp stone. The nave had been transformed into a cathedral of productivity: long tables under the stained glass, pendant lights making their own constellations, whiteboards on wheels, a mezzanine that wasn’t on the original plans.

I tilted my head back and watched how the light hit the new paint. The old beams remained, sanded and oiled, their grain rising like a message. The windows—the saints and lambs and gilded flames—had been “curated,” Silas had said at a hearing, which I think translated to “retained wherever they were Instagrammable.”

“This is the last visit, right?” Blue said, and you could tell he’d rehearsed the casual part in the truck before I arrived. “Just a couple sign-offs and then we can bring the desks in.”

“You can bring the desks in when I’m satisfied you’ve met the terms of your permit,” I said. “Where are your as-builts?”

“Right here,” Blue said, sliding a roll of updated drawings out of a poster tube. He’d left a smudge of dirt on his cheek, like an athlete. My father used to come home like that from the firehouse, and the memory of it made me want to be kind to Blue. I try not to let my father be a part of my work. He had strong feelings about second chances; the last time I took one optimistic leap, it went wrong and a loft caught fire six months later. Two people dead. The city paid a settlement. I kept my job but got a stack of performance-improvement paperwork and a new supervisor who told me, “No more gut feelings, Cates. Code is not poetry.”

I unrolled the drawings on a long table, weighed them with my flashlight and my phone. Project sections: egress, sprinkler layout, electrical, occupancy. In fire protection, the nebulous words—“judgment,” “equivalent”—could save a life or end one. I ran my finger along a dotted line: new demising wall at rear, soundproof “focus rooms” along the south aisle.

“What’s a focus room?” I said.

“Phone booths,” Silas said. “Modern monks have their own vows.”

“And acoustic paneling,” Blue said quickly. “The good stuff. Class A.”

“Show me,” I said. The two men did what men do when they’re near a woman who can say no—they tried to charm the no out of me. I kept my hands in my jacket pockets so they couldn’t see me making fists.

We checked bathrooms. We checked handrails: returns flush to the wall, brackets at thirty-two inches, no gaps where someone could hook a sleeve. Occupant load signage: wrong numbers. Exit lights tested fine, glowing their calm red. I made notes. Every time I stopped to look at something, Silas forged ahead to the next point of pride: the coffee bar built out of salvaged pews, the mural commissioned from a local artist depicting the skyline with addition of motivational verbs. It was all very cheerful. I have nothing against cheerful; it’s just not the same as safe.

We paused under the southern clerestory. My pupils shrank from a saint’s indigo stares. The focus rooms were ranged along the aisle where parishioners would have once lined up for confession. They were little cubes of new drywall with glass doors and soft lights inside, furnished with a stool and a small desk. Someone had staged a ceramic succulent. The walls were inappropriately smooth for a building that had been rough for a century.

“Let me see the spec for the acoustic paneling,” I said. Blue flipped the drawings, then fished in a binder and handed me a packet. I looked at the numbers and at the logos of companies that stood behind those numbers and at the words “meets or exceeds.” They all said the right things.

I stepped into the first focus room. The quiet pressed on my ears. It smelled faintly of mint and paint. I leaned my shoulder into one wall and felt the give of it, the way a drumhead gives under a thumb. Drywall over studs, of course, but the rebound told me something was off, an elasticity where there should have been a certain dullness. I raised my hand and knocked. The sound came back wrong: not the crisp triple-tap of gypsum on air but a softened version, as if someone had hung a coat inside the wall to catch the echo.

I have a cheap thermal camera I bought myself because the city purchasing system takes three months to approve anything and then sends you the wrong color. It plugs into my phone. I pulled the phone out, clipped the camera on. The screen showed the world in gradients: blues and greens and a bright orange smear where a radiator warmed the way. I held the screen up to the wall. A rectangle of coolness showed in a field of merely cool, like a footprint on packed snow.

“What’s your insulation here?” I asked without looking away.

“Standard batts,” Blue said. “R-13. Nothing weird.” He watched me like I was a doctor reading a scan of his insides.

“What about that?” I said, tapping the screen. The rectangle looked the size of a door someone had decided to forget.

“Probably a stud,” Blue said. “Or, like, thermal bridging. You know how it is.”

I did know how it was. The as-builts showed these rooms were supposed to be five by five with a dedicated duct from the mechanical room to suck out stale air and a soffit gap to let sprinklers deploy correctly. I looked up. The soffit gap was there, a tidy inch of openness at the top of each cube. The sprinkler heads were pendant style, upright close to the old beams. The required coverage pattern was based on open rooms, not micro-caves.

“Your head spacing is off,” I said, pointing. “These rooms cut into the spray pattern. You’re creating shadowing.”

Blue’s ears flushed. “We ran it by our fire engineer.”

“He can sign whatever he wants,” I said. “We build to the stricter interpretation when there’s an ambiguity. That’s what the permit says. Also, I need to see inside the chase space behind this wall.”

“There’s no chase,” Silas said, smooth as cream. “These are just little productive cocoons, Iris.”

“That’s not my name to you,” I said, not looking at him. “Our relationship is based on the code, Mr. Ward. No chase? Then this is an unpermitted cavity, and I need to see inside it.”

Blue rubbed his forehead as if he had an itch his fingers couldn’t reach. “We can cut you a view panel,” he said, already looking around for a drywall knife.

“Good,” I said, and took two steps back. There’s a little bit of theater in inspection because sometimes the contractor forgets you’ve seen this city through a thousand holes. They’ll tell you a wall is full and solid and then, when you set your hand flat and make a circle against the paint, you feel the air moving behind it like the building taking a breath it was told to hold.

Blue scored a small square in the gypsum between the first and second focus rooms. Paper tore. He wedged the tip of his blade and pried. The square popped free and fell into his hand with a delicate sound like a teacup being set down. Behind it, darkness. I raised the flashlight and shot the beam in. The light found nothing for a second, a tunnel of black. Then it landed on something pale and fibrous—a tuft like mattress stuffing—but denser, with a sheen.

“You blow in cellulose?” I asked. “I thought you said batts.”

“No blow-in,” Blue said. “No blow-in on the schedule.”

The pale fibers resolved. Not spray-in. Not insulation.

Hair.

I didn’t say anything at first. And maybe Blue didn’t know what he was seeing, because men who build walls tend to think of walls as assemblies, not as places where a person might be. He leaned closer, squinting, and then punched the heel of his hand into his thigh as if calming himself. His breath came out hard.

“What is it?” Silas said, not stepping closer, not stepping away. “What are we looking at?”

I could hear the rain on the stained glass, as if someone had put a thousand typewriters on the roof and asked them to be a storm. The hair was matted with something and pulled against something else. The beam caught at a surface that reflected dullly, like leather. I put the light higher. The something else was a shoulder. Pale. The color of something that had once been the same color as the rest of a person and now had lost its idea of blood. My heart did a small, precise thing in my chest: a tightening and a release. My voice rose from somewhere steady.

“Step back,” I said. “Don’t touch the wall.”

Blue took two steps back and then three forward and then stopped himself with an effort. Silas made a sound that urban men make when their lives brush against the raw edge of reality and they realize money can’t file it down.

“How,” Blue said, almost to the wall, “how—”

“Stop,” I said, sharper. The codebook is useless now. There are other books I don’t carry, other rules. You call it in. You do not poke. You do not pull. You do not let anyone take a picture because they will post it before you’ve told someone’s mother.

I stepped out of the focus room and into my own body. I went to the long table and put my palms flat on the drawings to stop my hands from shaking. When you do that you can feel the table’s imperfections, knife marks and paint drips and a little heat from the coffee cup that had been set there earlier. The building around me had gone silent, as if embarrassed.

“Blue,” I said quietly, “go stand by the front door. Don’t let anyone in or out. Mr. Ward, please back away from that wall. You too.”

“Do you know who that is?” Silas said. He was looking at me as if he could get me to answer for him.

“No,” I said. And then, because Lowry is not big and because I’ve never been able to keep my mouth entirely clear of the rest of myself: “Do you?”

His face changed in the small way faces change when they have to rework a lie in public. His eyebrows moved a fraction. His lips did nothing. “No,” he said. “No, of course not.”

I believed him. I also didn’t care what he believed.

I stepped back to the wall and took one more look in, not for gore—I can’t handle gore and I don’t pretend to—but for context. The opening Blue had cut was too small. My flashlight took a journey: hair, shoulder, then the suggestion of a forearm pressed tight to a torso by the weight of construction. There was a sleeve, something dark, fitted close to skin. The light teased out a stripe—a narrow seam of reflective thread, the kind they sew into athletic jackets so runners don’t die under distracted drivers’ bumpers.

On the wrist, a bracelet. Simple, thin, with a disk that caught the light and flung it back faintly, a coin the size of a dime. A cheap thing. A charm at the wrong end of a wish.

It was familiar.

You don’t get to pick what sees you. I’d seen it on a flyer, tacked to the cork board outside the supermarket with a pushpin that wasn’t strong enough. The photo on the flyer had been brighter than real life, the way missing-person photos always are because the person is in sunlight, often laughing at something just out of the frame. Missing since June. Last seen leaving a night class. Two eyes that belonged to a person who believed they were going to see the other side of everything that happened to them. A bracelet that matched a coin I saw now in the dark.

My thumb had found the edge of the drywall square in my pocket without telling me. Blue was already on the phone a few feet away, repeating our address and the words “we’ve got a body” and “no, we didn’t know—no, it’s inside the wall,” and then, as dispatch made him slow down, “Yes, ma’am. Yes, ma’am. The old St. Bart’s. Front door’s propped.”

I backed up and my calf hit a pew turned bench and I sat. My knees felt as if someone had loosened their bolts. I looked up at the stained glass and enjoyed the way the colors rejected the gray from outside. In the sea of saints, candles, halos, there was a pane that had always delighted me: a small donkey with a ridiculous expression, halfway between humility and offense. The building had been made by people who loved humor as a discipline. Somewhere along the way, someone had invited secrets in.

I took my phone out again—not to record, not to share, but because my hands wanted a use. My thumb opened the notes app without my permission. Under “Final, St. Bart’s,” I typed: Sprinkler head spacing; verify acoustic panel flame spread; call in; don’t move anything; door hardware—panic bars installed? It’s a habit when my head is loud: make the quiet list.

The quiet didn’t last. The first siren sounded like a practice run on a day that needed practice. Blue stood by the door like a bouncer who’d suddenly been asked to keep out ghosts. Silas moved to the coffee bar and gripped the edge as if the bar were a lifeboat. He looked small, diminished by something that wasn’t even looking at him. We were each of us standing in a different part of the room, and the room was the old heart of this city, and in its walls we had found a piece of the city that hadn’t been given permission to be there.

I thought about my father, because that’s the kind of sentimental trip your brain takes you on when it wants you to step wrong. He’d stood in rooms like this after the smoke had gone away, after the water had stopped cascading down, after all the people had left, and he’d looked around and he’d made himself witness to it. He told me once, “The worst thing you can do, Iris, is pretend—to others or to yourself—that you don’t see what you see.” He also said, “Buildings talk,” and then, when I was fifteen and he took me into a rowhouse that had only its façade left and nothing behind it, he said, “Sometimes they scream.”

Blue looked like he wanted to peel all the drywall off with his hands. Silas looked like he wanted to peel his face off. The siren swelled and stopped. The door opened and a gust of outside came in. Two EMTs crossed themselves without doing it with their hands. A uniformed officer saw the cut square in the wall and stopped dead as if he’d stepped into a room where someone was sleeping and didn’t know whether to wake them.

Later there would be more lights. Later there would be a taped-off perimeter and the measured patience of detectives and someone with a scanner and a power saw who would extend Blue’s neat four-by-four square to a ragged wound. Later there would be statement and press and so much attention that would come to the wrong parts of the story, the logo, the irony, the wealth that had bought the cavity. Later, still, there would be calls from upstairs and downstairs, people who wanted the words “expedite,” “discretion,” “sensitivity” in the same sentence.

But right then, I turned my face away from Silas and away from Blue and away from the journalists who were still just thoughts in their own heads, and I walked to the rear of the nave, to the wall where the sacristy had been on the original plans. The as-builts had drawn a neat rectangle and an annotation: conversion to storage. The door was new, with a card reader. The old door had been wider, higher, a door that knew it was about to deliver processions to the world. The new door made you humble yourself to enter.

“Who has access to this?” I asked over my shoulder.

“No one,” Silas said quickly. “Well. Staff.”

“You have staff?” I said.

“We will,” he said. “It’s equipment.”

Blue hovered near me and then retreated as if the very act of hovering were an admission. “I got a fob,” he said, and patted his chest.

“Don’t,” I said. “Not yet.”

The officer had come over. He had a face my father would have recognized: careful, tired, good. His nameplate said B. Thorne. “Ma’am,” he said, and he looked at the hole and then at me and then at my badge and then at my eyes. “What do we have?”

“A wall that isn’t on the drawings,” I said. “And a person inside it. You’re going to want to call your detective unit. I didn’t touch anything. I didn’t even breathe improperly.”

He nodded like this had been enough for him. He took his radio and said things in clipped phrases, then walked to the hole and didn’t look in until he had his pen ready to write whatever not-looking gave him in return. When he did look, he made that same small adjustment of face and breath. He said nothing. He added what he saw to whatever ledger lives in men like him.

A part of me—the ugliest part, the one that had been on probation and hated every second of needing to be twice as clean as the men who didn’t care—was relieved that, for once, I had not signed off yet. The rest of me wanted to unsign the world.

A woman in plainclothes arrived, hair pinned back, shoulders squared for grief. Detective Harlow, she said. She had a voice that knew how to soften only around children. She looked at my badge and then at my face and then at the coffee cups cooling on the long table. She said, “You found this?” and I wanted to correct her because found is the wrong verb; the building revealed this, I just asked the right wrong question. But yes, I found it.

While Harlow studied the hole and made a call and Blue began the sentence “We didn’t” about fifteen separate ways, I stood at the back wall. A seam of new wood ran into old stone, and the seam put me in mind of sutures. The finish carpenter had talent; if you weren’t me, maybe you wouldn’t see it. The paint had been feathered well, the caulk smoothed with a wet finger, the line between then and now made into a gentle slope that didn’t snag the eye. But. The baseboard ended a hair proud of where it should. The nail holes had been filled with a denser putty than the rest. The air near the carded door smelled faintly of that lemon oil, and beneath it something else—the ghost of a cleaning product with a little animal content, like the world’s most defeated pine.

I stepped closer and laid my palm flat against the new wood. It was warmer than the stone around it. Not warm like a person. Warm like something recently closed.

People will say a thousand things about a death like this in a place like this. They will say it means something it might not mean. They will see patterns where there are none, and they will miss the patterns that cut your fingers if you run your hand across them too fast. The only honest thing I can say about that morning is that the building had tried to tell me something the way buildings do—through the thickness of air in the wrong places, the lie of paint, the unproductive quiet inside a box whose whole point was productivity—and I had listened because I no longer know how not to.

Outside, the siren lied down and caught its breath. The saints did what saints do and kept looking past us to whatever horizon they’d been assigned. Detective Harlow stood in front of me and said, “Ms. Cates. Don’t leave.”

“I wasn’t going to,” I said. My voice felt like a cheap pen that wanted to skip.

“You’re the one who noticed the wall,” she said.

“I’m the one who notices walls,” I said. It came out more bitter than I meant. There are some jokes you can only make when nobody else is around to hear them.

She studied me. “Ever known a building that kept a secret?” she asked, maybe trying to make me comfortable.

I thought of a loft on Addison where the ductwork had been painted, where a rooftop deck had been built without adequate load calculation, where a party had outnumbered what the floor joists wanted, where my signature sat at the bottom of a paper like the period at the end of a sentence that had already been written before I read it. I thought of the prayers that had been said in this room and of the ways rooms keep prayers in their corners the way some kitchens keep a smell of onions no matter how many times you bleach the counter.

“Buildings don’t keep secrets,” I said finally, and I realized I was about to lie. “They just wait for someone to ask the right question.”

I looked at the hole again and saw the coin on the bracelet wink at me, indifferent, like the eye of a small god who had slept through the last ten years and just woken up. The rain intensified. Blue’s palms were flat on his thighs. Silas stood with his hands in his pockets, the portrait of a man who has remembered his hands and doesn’t know what to do with them if they can’t sign a check.

And somewhere far away in a supermarket, a flyer still tilted on a pin even though it was no longer needed, though maybe it was more needed now than ever. It was a poor thought to end on, but that was how it went. The reading of a thing never matches the writing of it. The chapter does not end where you think.

The gotcha, if stories want one, will come. For now, the only person in the room who hadn’t been told and needed telling was the building. I put my hand against the wall once more, gentle, and under my palm the wood was not forgiving. Okay, I told it. Okay, then. We do it this way.

Chapter One

By the time Mercy Lake gave back the first bones, I already knew not to expect answers in straight lines.

At daybreak the surface lay in tatters, stitched with cattails and the wiry outlines of beer cans. The shoreline had fallen away so quickly that the new edge was a scab, ripping back in layers. Ropes of algae, a band of sticky black sand, then the bruised clay pocked with bubble holes; farther out, ribs of sunburned stumps and the ghostly foundation of a porch crouched where fish once drifted. Water had a way of making secrets look like accidents until it was ready to tell the story.

I watched the shimmer of heat lifting off the mud and adjusted a neon flag in the cracked earth. Two men were arguing on the washed-out boat ramp about permits and parking, their voices skittering across the empty water like bottle caps. Behind me, someone’s dog tore at something dead and flattened, then dropped it, ashamed or bored. Somewhere in the bay, a carp threw itself into the air with a slap that sounded like applause and disappointment.

“You’re early,” Burley said, coming up behind me with the easy wheeze of a man who had never had to argue with mud. He was carrying a clipboard and a half-empty travel mug that exhaled the bitter smell of old coffee. “Didn’t think you’d be here until nine.”

“If I’m not here early, the local news gets here on time,” I said. I had learned to gauge the presence of cameras from the whine of generators and the way people cleaned their sunglasses with the corners of their shirts. No generators yet, but the parking lot was already freckled with tripods, as carefully spaced as gravestones.

Burley followed my gaze. “They sent someone the minute they heard ‘drowned town,’ didn’t they.”

“They sent someone the minute they heard ‘bones,’” I said. The bones had surfaced yesterday afternoon in a narrow cove where the weeds looked like ropes. A fisherman had been casting for bass and snagged what he thought was a log, until the log turned out to be the leg of a deer with an elegant cloven hoof and a length of twine knotted around its ankle. The twine had been enough to bring the sheriff. Bones were bones, but twine suggested intent. Twine suggested work.

Burley shifted his weight and looked out across the desiccated bay. He was getting pink around the back of his neck, where his hair stopped pretending. “If anyone asks, you tell them we’re documenting historical resources exposed by drought conditions. Don’t get dragged into ghosts and gossip. People will want a ghost. We’re giving them flags and photographs.”

That was what the Office of Historic Preservation did in a drought: we triaged the past. We walked out into the places that had been underwater for so long that the water had become part of the story and we put little plastic flags in the places that were going to go away again. We measured, we photographed, we bagged what could be bagged and made notes about what couldn’t. We told ourselves we were helping, as if naming something meant keeping it.

The thing about Mercy Lake was that it did this every few decades. The dam had been finished in ’59, back when men smoked on scaffolds and shook hands without lawyers, and the first winter after that the water crawled over the road like a cat. It swallowed the town of Gray’s Vale piece by piece. Old photographs showed farmers moving porch swings and chickens, a man lifting a little boy so the boy could paint his name on a mailbox that would soon be visited by fish instead of mail. Not everybody left willingly. Some got paid, some got promises, some packed and drove away without looking back. Every time the water fell low enough and long enough, the town crawled out and blinked in the sun like a thing half-born and half-dead.

“Sheriff Rios is already cranky,” Burley said. “Try to make him feel like he’s in charge.”

“He is in charge,” I said. “We’re just counters.”

“We’re counters who can ruin his day,” he said, and then tried a smile that didn’t quite land. “You alright?”

“Fine.” The band of my hat made a pale line across my forehead when I pushed it up. Beyond the collapsed porch foundation, the mud field ran flat until it found the old highway. The asphalt showed through in hunched patches, a dark tongue all the way to the water where the new shoreline had cut across its old polite line. On the far side, the lake glared, a mirror with a bad temper. In the distance the dam looked like a wall somebody had forgotten to finish painting.

I was fine. And also: my sister had vanished from this county twelve years ago. Three days after a fight with our mother about money and finishing school and the man she was dating, she had gotten in her unremarkable white Honda and driven away. She had been twenty-two and furious and exactly Ava about everything, and then she had simply stopped being anywhere anybody could find. That had happened before my job, before my training taught me to run my eyes along edges and over surfaces until the missing edges told me as much as the present. It had happened before the first summer I spent counting flagstones on dead porches.

“Lina.”

I turned. Sheriff Rios was a precise man, even in mud. He walked like he picked his surfaces, like he had trained himself not to put weight on the wrong thing. The heat caught in the tan fabric of his uniform and made a dark line where his body pressed the shirt into his belt. His hat cast a knife of shade across his face so that his eyes were shadows that looked like bruises in something ancient and right-angled.

“We got a report this morning about someone walking out into the bell tower,” he said without greeting. “That sound like anything you want to do today?”

“I like my bones dry, Sheriff,” I said. “But if the bell tower is accessible, I should document it.”

He examined me the way people do when they’re trying to decide if you’re making fun of them and also whether it matters. He and I had done this dance before, different lakes, different exposed bones. He had the jaw of a man who believed in weight-bearing walls.

“Don’t go into anything with a roof,” he said. “Roof plus mud equals we pull your body out with a winch.”

“I’m not in the business of roofs,” I said.

“The bell tower’s not a roof. It’s a hole,” offered a voice behind him.

The woman who said this was small and upright and wore the kind of shoes nobody owned on purpose. She had the face of someone who ate vegetables not because she liked them but because she had always done what made sense. She lifted a hand at me like we were acquaintances at a report meeting. “Nettie Gray,” she said, though nobody had asked. She’d introduced herself to me yesterday with the effortlessness of a person who believed her name was a credential.

“Of course it’s a hole,” she said now, for me, for the sheriff, for the invisible people on the invisible camera crews. “It was always a hole. You can see it in the old photographs. My grandfather told me they put the bell on a scaffold over the crawlspace because of the weight. One of my uncles used to dare the others to crawl underneath. The floorboards were thin. The lid was loose.”

“Ms. Gray has asked to be present when we assess the church because of ‘family interest,’” the sheriff said, the quotes audible.

“My family built that church,” she said to nobody in particular. “It’s our name on the brick. We’re the Grays of Gray’s Vale, and if you think that’s a coincidence I can’t help your education. It’s always men who are surprised to learn some things are exactly what they are.”

“Ms. Gray,” Rios said, with the patience of a man who had trained himself not to put weight on the wrong thing. He looked at me. “Go. Don’t go under anything. Don’t take Ms. Gray anywhere she can’t walk back from with all her ankles.”

“I’m not a moron,” Nettie said, but she softened when she looked out at the skeleton of the town. I watched her face change, watched some private tenderness move through her the way a fish moved under water: visible only in the distortion.

We moved together across the mud. The lake had pulled back so fast the earth hadn’t learned how to be itself again yet. It was like stepping into someone’s mouth: slick and warm and surprising. My boots made careful little noises. Nettie’s shoes went in deeper than she expected and then she lifted her chin and pretended she had expected it. Sheriff Rios followed as far as the first line of flags and then stopped and hooked his thumbs in his belt like he was anchoring a boat. His radio hissed and sighed occasionally with the ghost of somebody else’s problem.

The church’s foundation came up out of the mud like the outline a child makes to keep her place while she goes for a drink. You could see the rectangle of it, and within that the smaller rectangle of what had been the sanctuary. A few bricks clung to one corner, red with rashes of mildew like the monstrous freckles of a boy who’d been in the sun too long. The ground within was different—dryer, the surface buckled in health in the way that sediment never is—because it had once been under planks instead of under water. At the near end, the stubs of what might have been steps pushed out like teeth.

“There,” Nettie said, with satisfaction and something like grief. She pointed toward the center, where a square hole cut the space into its own absence. The hole was framed by wet wood, warped dark. Iron bolts rose around it like spindly metal flowers, bent and eaten by this water’s way of going about its business. Across it, bridging the void as if it had been landed there by a careful child, was a single beam. A bell hung above, beached and mute, its bronze skin filmed with pale scum. It had a big belly and a narrow mouth. Size of a heart if you scaled the thing down into a body.

“People say you can hear it at night when the wind’s right,” Nettie said.

“Sound travels strange across water,” I said.

“It sounds like a warning,” she said. “It sounds like a promise.”

I shot photographs from a few angles, mindful of my own shadow, mindful of the way light opens secrets and closes them. The beam looked battered but solid enough to do what beams did. There was a crawlspace beneath the church floor—Nettie’s hole—and the lake had scooped it clean and filled it with air. On the far side of the hole something glinted, and unconsciously I glanced back to check the line of Sheriff Rios and heard him say through his teeth, “No roofs, Cole.”

“No roofs,” I said. It was always easier to say yes when the yes cost you nothing.

I crouched at the edge of the hole and peered in. It was only a few feet down, the walls of the crawlspace packed with the layered earth the original builders had kicked aside with their heels. The floor was silt, the color of old pennies, rippled by the last breath of retreating water. A length of chain lay like a discarded necklace, its links smiling their crooked smiles. There was something tangled in the chain, a shape that was too regular to be mud. I played the beam of my flashlight across it and the thing flashed back, not white like bone but glassy and green with filth. Near it, the fat thigh of the bell dropped from the beam with the serenity of a sleeping animal. The clapper was a dark tongue poised a finger’s width from speaking.

“I’m going to hook that item with the pole,” I said, more for the sheriff than for Nettie.

“What item?” he said.

“The regular one,” Nettie said, impatient and eager. “The something.”

I took the aluminum pole from my pack. The hook at the end had seen things I had not. I slid it across the beam like a tightrope walker who respected gravity and fished the hook into the chain, careful not to let my weight answer the beam’s invitation. The chain lifted with a wet sigh. The green glass shape came with it, bumping and making a little full, dull sound. I pivoted my hips to bring it to my side and Nettie reached without asking the way people do when they think we are in this together. Between us we wrestled it onto the dry plank and I eased the chain off with my fingertips. The glass was a jar, small and thick, goose-necked and clouded, with a lid as rusted as a story retold too many times.

“There’s something in it,” Nettie said unnecessarily. Behind us, the sheriff had moved closer, even though he stood at the same place he had always stood. The air felt different when he paid attention.

I set the jar upright and found the seam where the lid met the glass. Someone had sealed it with wax a lifetime ago. The wax had gone the color of nicotine and smelled faintly like candles after a birthday. I worked my pocketknife into the seam, careful so that if something broke it would be the jar not whatever it was protecting. The lid let go with a strong suddenness that startled me, and the smell that came out was mold and paper and something sweet gone wrong.

Inside was another jar, smaller, one of those little straight-sided ones you might buy so you can pretend to preserve your own jam. Inside that, visible through a layer of cloudy water, was a rolled piece of paper. I glanced at the sheriff and he nodded one of those nods that say nothing but suggest everything. I unscrewed the smaller jar with my fingertips slippery and fished the paper out, careful again in the way that has become instinct: how do you touch a thing that exists only because someone else believed it would matter later? The paper had been rolled tight and the water had done its best to lick the ink away. When I unrolled it as far as it would allow, it protested with a little sound that might have been a sigh in a different world.

“Don’t tear it,” Nettie said, and then was embarrassed that she had said a thing so obvious.

“I’m not,” I said. The letters flared and swam, the ink fallen into the paper like it had decided to take root. The handwriting was old-fashioned, generous, the kind my mother’s own hand had thought was what churches looked like. I read it half aloud because words that have been underwater too long sometimes need voice to get started.

“To the soul who opens this,” it began. “We put this where no one would find it because we were good and afraid. I ask you to forgive me and that you never will. We did a thing in the winter of ’59 when the first heavy waters came. They said she had no name. She had a name. We could not take her to the ground that would be ground no more, so we did as we had and we set her by the bell so that if the water ever went away the bell would tell it. If the bell is down, put it back up, and then dig where it points. Her mama was a singing woman. She used to sing to bring the rain. It came too late.”

There was no signature and there was nothing more to it, just the rising raggedness of paper dissolving into itself. I looked up. Nettie had her hand to her mouth as if to stop words falling out. Sheriff Rios had not moved at all. Far across the bright burnt flats of the lake something let go and fell with a far-off whump and a sparkle of water as if a child had dropped a bucket. The bell above us hung dumb. The two iron bolts nearest me were bent toward the hole like something had leaned on them for a long time.

“People do things because they’re afraid and then they hide them in a church,” Nettie said, fierce and triumphant and sad. “This county thinks it’s special but it’s like every other place. You put a fence up and people use it.”

“Ms. Gray,” the sheriff said, warning furring the edge of his voice. “The only thing it says is dig where it points. It doesn’t say what they did. It doesn’t say who. It could be an animal. It could be somebody’s idea of a joke.”

“Animals don’t have mamas who sing,” Nettie said.

The radio on his shoulder crackled and then spoke his name in the bored voice of a dispatcher who has not learned how to keep other people’s panic out of her day. “Sheriff? You copy?”

He pushed his finger into the microphone and said, “Go ahead.”

“You’re going to want to see this,” she said. “On the east side of Sawtooth Bay, where the old highway meets the water. They say they’ve got a chassis.”

Nettie and I stared at him like he was going to tell us it was a boat or a tractor or something that could be anything at all.

“Color?” he said flatly.

There was a pause, as if the person on the other end had looked at the thing and wondered what words were.

“White,” she said finally. “It’s a white sedan, partial under the mud. Model’s not obvious yet. There’s a…hang on…” Voices tangled with wind. “There’s a student parking decal on the rear window. From the community college.”

The world narrowed into the line of asphalt that ran toward the water like a dark decision. Everything that was not that line felt unimportant, the way landscapes blur when you look up at a hawk. For a moment I was not as good at breathing as I had been.

“She drove a white Honda,” I said to nobody, to both of them, perhaps to the lake. My mouth had gone dry so that the words were sticks cracking. “My sister. Ava. It was a white Honda.”

Nettie made a sound that might have been my name and might have been a prayer. The sheriff’s eyes had the same bruise of darkness but something old and human moved under it. He looked at the bell the way people look at a new grave. The air tasted like pennies and finally-days and the cautious joy of someone whose name is about to be said.

“Stay here,” he said, which meant nothing and everything. He spoke into his radio, low and fast. He gave coordinates I had walked in my dreams. He began to move the way men do when they have trained themselves not to put weight on the wrong thing but decide to run anyway.

“We are not going to stay here,” Nettie said, and then she did the most old-fashioned thing in this county. She reached for my hand in the bright ugly heat, squeezed it hard, and squeezed again, like you do when you don’t have a bell.

Chapter One

The night Grayhaven’s clock struck thirteen, I was awake for each wrong note.

I keep errant hours. It comes with the territory. People bring me their time in cardboard boxes and velvet pouches, in cracked shells and tangled necklaces, and I wind their seconds back into motion. It means that by midnight the shop has softened into a ticking forest, and by one in the morning there are only two kinds of sound to mark the world: the ocean worrying the harbor and a dozen different pendulums arguing with gravity.

When the tower bell boomed an extra blow across the roofs, the pendulums faltered.

I counted without meaning to. Ten, eleven, twelve… The thirteenth fell like a bad joke. The vibration climbed the glass in my windows and hummed under my teeth. Between one breath and the next, the hairs on my arms lifted. Then the town settled again—the fog outside thick as wool, the streetlamps burning halos in it, the gulls displaced by night and storm to the old cannery roof.

The clock in Grayhaven’s church tower is older than the paint on any of the houses. My father used to call it the town’s metronome. He’d kept it clean for thirty years. He taught me how to oil the pivots with just enough oil that a moth’s wing would drink it away, how to listen for a beat that had slipped to lame, how to measure a minute against what your body believes. “Machines will lie less than men,” he would say, straightening up slow because of the ladder in his back. “But they still need help telling the truth.”

On the night the bell argued with the number of strokes on its own brass heart, my father had been dead for five months.

I pulled the string to the blinds and squinted out. Fog sat in the street like breath held and refused. Somewhere beyond it, the tower was only a darker shape in a dark sky, its face faint as a coin. I could try to blame the thirteenth on the weather. Damp swelling wood, rope gone slack, sound doing tricks. But the wrongness was too clean to be a trick. Striking trains are fussy, but they don’t invent an extra number without help.

I thought of calling Amos Pike. The town had appointed him timekeeper after Dad’s funeral: a man with hands like smoked hams and a clean hawthorn cane, a veteran of shrimp boats and notched knuckles. We were supposed to hand over the keys to the tower, but Dad hadn't been one for lockers. He’d kept them on a nail by the back door the way his father had. Both keys were on my ring now. I set them on the counter in a neat circle of brass to stop myself spinning them.

Outside, a late truck muttered. Someone’s dog coughed and gave up on the idea of barking. Upstairs above the shop, my apartment was a narrow affair with walls that corkscrewed, the stair up it like a ship’s. I could climb into my thin bed and pretend I had not heard, that it had not been what it had been. Or I could put on my boots.

I turned down the lamps over the workbench, left the little marine clock from the seventies open and waiting in the lamplight, a tiny brass skeleton with its heart bared. I blew out the match, watched the smoke rise straight in the still air, and put on my boots.

The town at two in the morning belongs to those who are working and those who are hiding. The fishermen don’t start until three, unless the weather is in a mood, and the bar had emptied by one. There were still the summer people lingering in their porches with quilts and stories even in October, but fog closes a throat.

I locked up and stepped into the quiet. The world shrank to a circle—light from the shop’s front window throwing a trapezoid on the boards, then my breath turning visible, then the soft sound of my heels. The tower sits on a slight hill as if it wanted a view, the church at its base tidy white like a scrubbing brush. I knew the path up the hill. I had walked it in worse weather, with a heavier bundle on my shoulders. In the fog, sound does not travel the way it should. It hangs. You hear your own steps as if someone is pacing you. You cannot see trouble coming until you feel it.

I felt the hum again just before I saw the dark bulk of the church: that residual bees-in-the-bones feeling that happens after a bell is rung too hard. The front doors were latched. The tower door, set in the left transept and mean as a miser, took my key and thunked open like it always did.

The smell at the bottom of the spiral stairs was old stone and rain and something else: oil, the good oil, and the burnt tang of metal run hot. I have been in enough backs of clocks to know their scents. The spicy sweetness of orange from the wrong hand trying to do a right job. The animal musk of leather gone damp. The black pepper of old grease that has broken down and started to chew the teeth it’s meant to protect. This had a singed note I didn’t like.

“Amos?” I said, because even if it was the middle of the night and even if me and the dark have an arrangement, you don’t go talking to an empty tower and expect it to stay empty.

My voice came back to me in a smaller voice, but it came back. No one answered. I went up.

At the first landing, a window the shape of a bishop’s hat offered me fog and the pale smear of the streetlamp below, diffused until it looked like a glass blown too thin. The stairs are not generous; you have to tuck your shoulders. Halfway up, someone had marked a notch on the mortared wall—three scratches, old as I am. My father had done that with a nail when he carried me up here when I was small. He’d tapped the wall with the nail and said, “You’re this high in the tower,” and I had believed him. There was another notch an armspan higher. My hand found it without looking. It is a kind of map of leaving and returning, your palm remembering what your mind forgets.

By the time I reached the belfry platform, my breath made a little fog of its own. The trap door was thrown back against the oak. I could see the curved cheeks of the great bell, the yoke that held it, what passed for daylight all applied wrong. The rope that hung down through the bits and pieces to the nave was still. The heart upright.

And over it, under it, beside it, the movement.

If you have never seen the insides of a tower clock, you would be surprised. They are neither delicate nor clumsy. Iron on iron, plates and arbors, wheel teeth big as thumbs. The escapement is the part that makes a clock a clock. It is the governor, beating out intervals, letting the stored power out as something useful. There are a dozen varieties. Grayhaven’s is an old English pattern with a deadbeat escapement on a long wooden pendulum, the weight in a trunk, the drum wound by a crank that leaves your shoulders singing. There’s a striking train with a count wheel to record the strikes. You look at it and you think: a blacksmith did this. A clockmaker taught him where to file.

That is how I know what looks wrong.

I saw it as soon as I topped the ladder. Something in my chest went cold and heavy and quiet, the way it does in a bad storm when you realize you are maybe not getting home under your own power.

The count wheel had a bite taken out of it. Not a break. Not a missing tooth that would come from age or abuse. A segment filed, teeth shortened just enough that the rack would not be caught when it should, that it would drop once more than the hour ordained. Thirteen would not be an accident. Thirteen was a decision.

There was a wedge, too, where there should not have been any wedge. A hard bit of pale something—bone or ivory or even, absurdly, plastic—tapped between the pallets of the escapement in such a way that the pendulum’s arc took a hair longer on the part of its swing that lifted the hammer. A mechanic would say it had been retarded. A poet might say it hesitated. Either way, it would crawl the strike.

It was work done by a hand who knew enough to be dangerous.

“Amos?” I said again, softer—and then I saw him.

He was on the floor at the far side of the carriage of the movement, where the railing dips down before it meets the stairs. His cane lay across the boards as if it had been set there, careful, not fallen. His body had come to rest with one arm lifted over his head, the sleeve twisted, palm up as if he wanted someone to take it. There was a dark fan under his hair that at first looked like shadow and then looked like what it was.

You talk to the dead because it is rude not to. “No,” I said. “No, Amos. No.” It did not change the shape of him.

The clock spoke behind me with the imitation of a breath it always makes when the weight pays a little and the escapement releases it. It made the little cluck that can sound like a question. I could hear the lies starting in my head—He slipped. He fell. He hit his head. He came up here meaning to make a repair and the whole big patient mechanism did what machines do when they are tired and asked too much. But nothing else here was an accident. The filed count wheel. The wedge. The timing slowed just enough to be noticed by anyone who listens at night.

I went down on one knee. His skin was cooling. There is a physics to the dead you feel in your hands when you touch them. There is a weight moved differently from the way sleep moves it. I knew it from the hours with my father’s hand in mine at the final, when the hospice nurse stepped out to give me the time.

Amos’s pockets were askew. One bulged odd under his jacket. I did not touch it. There are lines for those of us who are not police to respect, even in towers where the police do not often climb. I put my fingers near his mouth anyway, because hope is more mechanical than time. It has only two settings. The false one and the other. He did not breathe. His tongue had a smell like metal.

I looked by instinct at his wrist. He wore a cheap digital on a nylon strap to save his good watch from salt. It blinked 12:04 in rude blue. It told me nothing worth hearing.

There was a scratch on the floorboards beside him. A crescent. A mark as if something heavy with a sharp edge had been dragged or dropped and then lifted again quickly. And scuffs in the chalky dust on the boards, because no one sweeps a belfry as often as it needs. Boot marks. Mine were the neat small prints coming from the ladder, the toes turned out slightly because I have a dancer’s gait and a father who teased me for it. These others were broader in the toe, the heel worn to the inside. Two pairs. A lighter set and a heavier. There was a smear where someone had braced a hand against the floor. Enough to have made a palm print if anyone with a kit was here to find it before fog did what fog does, even indoors, and softened everything toward sameness.

I have always been one for order. I carry a handkerchief because my father did and because cloth weaves a shame around your hands when you are tempted to touch what you should not. I took it out then and wiped my face. I was shaking now and wished I had a friend in reach. My father would have known what to do first and what mattered and what could wait. He would have said, “You are one person. Do the next good thing.”

There is a phone bolted to the wall near the staircase because the town does not trust cell signals through two feet of stone. It is the sort of phone that does not ring so much as startle. I cranked it—the crank is for show now; electricity is not so romantic—and got the dispatch, which is a woman named Iris at this hour.

“Iris,” I said, and tried to make my voice remember its ordinary shape. “It’s Mara Ellery. At the tower.”

A beat. “Mara? That you? It’s two in—did you hear it? I swear to God, my cat hid under the stove.”

“I heard it.” My eyes were on Amos. “I need Lionel.”

She did not ask why. “He on his way to yell at you?”

“He on his way to stand between me and something worse,” I said, which works out to the same thing.

“He’s out on Baker’s Lane with a kid and a four-wheeler situation.” I could hear keys in the background of her voice, the sound of someone who knows where things are kept. “I’ll ring him on the radio. You all right?”

Honesty is another machine with two settings. “No,” I said.

Five minutes later, Lionel Kittredge’s boots were doing the same thing mine had done, which is to echo more than they had any business to do on those stairs. He is not a tall man, which helps in a town that builds everything low and narrow, but he has shoulders and a way of walking that says someone owes him an apology. He had his hat in his hand, which told me he had gripped it between call and car and up the steps again in a way that made it a tool against what he was thinking. Fog had damped his hair into obedient waves. He is only ten years older than me, but the job had creased him earlier.

“Mara—” he started, and then he saw Amos and stopped saying my name.

He went to him, looked without touching, did the same inventory my eyes had done. The crescent scratch. The cane. There was something that lived at the corner of his mouth that came out then. The muscles that hold your face together so you do not fall apart.

“You,” he said, and his tone folded me into responsibility and witness at the same time, “didn’t touch anything?”

“Not him,” I said. “The door. The ladder. The phone. The air that was between things. I wiped my face so I wouldn’t go putting it where it shouldn’t be.”

“And why are you here.” It was not a question without an answer. He trusts me for the same reason I irritate him; I see what people wish I would not.

“Because it struck thirteen,” I said.

He blinked once and half turned toward the movement, as if it might answer him if he was polite. “So that was real. I thought maybe I was hearing double.”

“It was real.” I pointed with my elbow, careful to keep my hand empty. “Someone filed the count wheel. Someone wedged the pallets. It would take time. And a ladder. Or two people. Or one who could carry and come back. Amos did not do that on purpose. He would not humiliate a mechanism for the sake of a laugh.”

Lionel made a noise that might have been a laugh if you wanted to be generous to it. “You talk about that thing like it can take offense.”

“It can.” I looked at Amos. “And maybe it did.”

He holstered his hat under his arm the way some men holster a regret. “All right,” he said. “All right. Iris rang me all the way up those stairs with the kind of tone that says if I don’t call the county coroner and then the state man, she’ll find a stick big enough to do it for me. I’m going to set some flags and then I’m going to go back down and make that call. You are going to stand right there and not get clever, which is another way of saying: you are going to keep noticing things but not put your fingers on them. And tell me now if you see something that won’t leave us alone in an hour if we ignore it.”

“The wedge,” I said. “If we turn the clock off, the weight can stay there until morning. But if it keeps running, that wedge could chew the pallets. It will hurt itself for being hurt.”

“What do I do?” He looked at the mechanism like it was a patient with a wound and I was the only one with hands to stitch.

“Back off the weight a turn,” I said. “Let it rest on the ratchet. It will hold. Pull the wedge with your knife and put it on something that says ‘do not touch me yet.’ And for the love of what you love, don’t bump the count wheel.”

He did as I asked because that is our arrangement. He turned the winch slow, muscles in his forearms doing work in a tidy way. He slid his pocketknife into the little white thing wedged between iron and iron and eased it free, set it on a coil of rope. He waited while the clock sighed back into itself, the beat evening, a horse after a bad fence. He does not know that the sound a good escapement makes is meant to be called a tick; he thinks it is a tock; we are friends anyway.

His phone made the frog’s croak he refuses to change. He glanced at it and grimaced. “Don’t be offended,” he said to Amos, and stepped away to talk to the county.
