I stood. I went to the rope. There are wrong things and there are broken things and they are not always the same. I listened to the new-old beat with my head against the iron, felt it pass into my bones and move through them: equal, equal, equal. The tower breathed like something asleep.

When Lionel came back, he had his hands full of rubber gloves in a neat wad and a face that had learned some stiffness. “They’re on their way,” he said. “State man says to tell him nothing went missing. I told him we’re this side of decent and the other side of gulls. He will be here when the fog stops telling lies.”

I nodded. I pointed now, because he had put the gloves on and because he had told me to keep noticing. “There is orange oil in the air,” I said. “Amos used mineral. He never liked the fruit scent. Said it made him hungry. There is a scratch there that is not a scratch. It is a mark someone leaned and dragged something through. There are two kinds of boots. One drags a little on the right heel.”

“You are a comfort,” he said without irony. Lionel is a man who wants a map. I give him one when I can.

“Also,” I said, “we cannot unring a bell, but we can fix a clock. And whoever did that down there”—I nodded at the count wheel—“knew enough to do it in a way that would be noticed and not enough to do it clean. That is a person. Not an accident.”

“Which makes me feel better and worse.” He rubbed at the line between his eyes with a knuckle and left the glove on. “Who would do that? To Amos?”

You can make lists in your head. Lists are also machines, and they turn and they click and sometimes they grind. Amos had a son in New Bedford and a wife who had died before him. He had once captained a crew that cut another man’s line in a storm for the sake of the catch, and the man had broken his hand later over Amos’s jaw and both of them had gone to the same doctor and the same bar after. He had a quiet temper. He held grudges like rocks—weight and solidity, not sharpness. He had not spoken to my father for three months before the end because my father had told the council to hire someone younger for the tower, and Amos had heard “you” in “someone.”

The list will make itself. You have to write it down later or it will come back in your sleep wearing different hats.

“We’ll ask,” I said. “They’ll have answers. People love giving names when they believe it will keep them safe.”

Lionel nodded. The fog outside shifted, pressed itself against the slats, settled back like a cat. We stood in the tower with a man on the floor and a big iron heart made of gears and a whole town beneath us sleeping a little out of time.

It is unpopular to say out loud that noticing is a hunger. You say you’re only making yourself useful. It is less frightening that way. But I remember what my father said. Machines will lie less than men, and both will tell you small truths if you hold them gently.

I looked at the filed edge of the count wheel, at the neat ribbon of new bright metal against old. It had been done recently, not rusted yet. The file that had done it had not been fine, and the hand had been strong, and the person had not been afraid to climb. I thought of the thirteenth note moving over my skin like the flat of a cold knife. I thought of the way the phone had felt in my hand and Amos’s cane set careful as if someone had wanted to make his last gestures tidy. I thought of the wedge in the escapement, the bone-white of it, and the fact that nobody in town carried ivory. There was a place down on the harbor that sold those cheap asparagus forks with plastic handles the color of mayonnaise.

“I should get someone to sit with him,” Lionel said finally, like that was the thing that would make the moment decent. “Iris will know who gives a good hour.”

“I can sit,” I said, because it was true and because you do not leave a friend alone between calls you cannot answer.

He looked at me a long second, then nodded once. “Then sit.”

He went down the stairs and took with him a shape of heat the tower had made room for without comment. I heard his steps diminish, the door’s unhappy hinge, then the way the outside swallowed people. The quiet rose around me, and the clock made that formal business of its beat. A gull cried out somewhere blind and cheated.

I leaned my back against the cool iron of the movement and watched the hour hand think about moving. I told myself the same thing I tell the angry little alarm clocks with bad hearts and the grief-struck grandfathers with missing weights: we have all the seconds we have, and then we do not. I knew already that whatever had been done to make a bell tell the wrong number of the night was not the only wrong waiting. A person who files a count wheel to thirteen is not interested in sleep.

Grayhaven breathed fog. Down on the harbor, the boats made small noises as if they were talking in their dreams. A siren far off tried not to wake anyone. Above my head, iron ticked truth.

Clocks don’t lie, my father’s voice said like an old habit. People do. And I, in the first hour of a thing I had not consented to begin, sat with a dead man because it is rude not to. And listened for what the town would tell me next.

Chapter One

In the studio, the quiet wasn't empty. It hummed. It rode the air like a low tide, filling the spaces between the voice and the song and the red eye of the ON AIR light that looked, on bad nights, like it might blink and never come back. The tower out back sang its own thin metal note if the wind was coming off the river. The board under my palms was warm, a purr of cheap fans and memories, the plastic faders slicked by a hundred hands before mine, cigarette burns in the grey laminate from a time when you could smoke everywhere and nobody thought twice about what you left pressed into the furniture.

"You're listening to WREM," I said, because some things have to be said on the hour or the FCC wakes up and taps you on the shoulder. "Harbor City's own insomnia cure, where midnight happens as often as you let it. I’m Mara Finch. It's two-oh-eight in the morning, and if you're working, we're with you. If you're not sleeping, we're with you too. If you just made it to the kitchen and your cat is judging your snack choices, tell it that I said to share."

Jules snorted through the glass on the other side of the board. He wore noise-canceling headphones incorrectly, one cup on, one off, like the kids wore baseball caps now, sideways and ironic. He was twenty-seven and had been born in a year I remembered driving home from college with the windows down and the radio up. When I felt old, I looked at Jules and reminded myself that I started on nights younger than he was, playing songs and pretending that it wasn’t my voice coming back at me from the speakers.

"The phone’s blinking," he mouthed.

The phone was always blinking. I had three lines and a scheduled guest from a bakery that made bread you had to order a week in advance because they let the dough rise while the moon waxed, and a woman who called once a week to read poems about people she loved that she had not loved hard enough while they were alive. The phone didn't care. It cut through music like a metronome, insistent, mechanical.

We had a seven-second delay—the button was orange and would go warm under your hand when you held it. I cued it with the same care you use to lay scissors back into a drawer with bare feet. There are things you don't want to drop at two in the morning.

"WREM," I said, and twirled the swing arm so the mic faced Jules in case the caller was for him. He shook his head. "It's later than you think."

On the other end, the line hissed, a snake that had settled in for winter. "Long time," a voice said.

I expected hijinks, a bad midnight DJ prank. We get those. We get worse. The voice was neither young nor old, not strained, not drunk. A good voice for radio, if it hadn’t arrived there like it knew paths through the dark that people didn’t.

"Welcome," I said, the way I said it to every stranger. The word had weight, and like everything that can be used in a dozen ways, you could hide things in it. "What keeps you up?"

"Two-oh-eight," the voice said. "Perfect time. The numbers look like a pair of eyes and a mouth, don't they? Two little watches and an O that can't quite close."

In the main studio, the wall clock was a big round thing the station manager’s wife found at a yard sale. The numbers were black and a little faded, the second hand jerked like it hadn't found its rhythm yet. I had never considered it a face. I didn't like that I did now.

"We take all kinds," I said. "Music, company, insomnia poetry. If you need a weather report, I can make you one up that’s optimistic. What's your name?"

Jules waved at me from behind the glass, eyebrows up. He had that look he got when a call felt weird to him before it felt weird to me. He's good at people, even if he’s shy. He grew up with six sisters, he said. He knows the choreography of a room without having to think about it.

"Call me Nocturne," the voice said. I could almost hear the small smile. As if he had thought of it ahead of time and liked how it sounded out loud.

"That's not a name," I said before I could stop myself.

"Neither is Finch, not the way you use it," he said, and I stopped. The screen where Jules typed the caller info stayed blank. He didn’t have a number; the caller ID was a ghost.

On my sheet, for the two a.m. segment, I'd written Banter, then Local - bakery, then Play big band request that came in via email from a nurse on the night shift at St. Bridget's. I tapped my pen under the word Banter until the tip made a tiny staccato, like rain on aluminum.

"Somebody wants to hear Glenn Miller," I said to the caller. "You going to be generous and give up your slot?"

"No," he said, soft and firm, friendly like a good pastor or a bad gambler. "Play me something else. Something for the night animals."

I didn't look at the glass because I didn’t want Jules to see my face change. Because there are phrases that live in your mouth for years after you’ve said them, and there are phrases that lodge in you all at once like a shard. Night animals, and not in the cute way the bakery woman used it, owls on dish towels and foxes on baby onesies.

I had said that phrase three and a half years ago when my name still brought up ten pages of results more than it should have. We did an investigation, long and close, about a string of arsons on the north side, places that served the city when it wasn't beautiful: a halfway house, an old folks’ home with a broken heater they never could get the board to replace, the Orphic Theater with its velvet seats and sticky stairs and a sound system older than the war. Eight dead, eleven injured, a city that wanted a culprit and a reporter who kept asking questions until she wasn’t invited into kitchens anymore. I called the people who lived up under the freeway and in the creases of the park the night animals, the way you talk about creatures who survive in the unlit places, who eat what falls and what you throw away. I meant it kindly. It landed like a rock.

"Tell me more," I said, because nobody on the night line needed to hear my chest cramp. "What do they do?"

"They watch," he said. "They learn to cross when the light says walk, even when there’s no one in the intersection. They know what the chirp means."

I heard it then, faint under his words, too far for the mic but clear enough if you’ve trained your ears for trash. A crosswalk chirp, the kind the city had put in for the blind, but wrong. Not the peep-peep of most intersections, but a cuckoo, two notes that sounded like someone had wound the world up and forgotten to let it down. It was distinctive. I knew that sound.

It belonged to one intersection in the whole city, a corner that the budget committee had let a private donor fund because he had a daughter who walked there every day. The button had been custom. The city council made a day of it when they installed it. There's video of me on that sidewalk with a microphone and a ponytail that looks like I forgot what waterfalls were supposed to do.

"You on Lyle and Fourth?" I asked.

He laughed. "You've always been good with a map."

Always. A word is a bridge with rotten planks if you're not careful. A rush of smells hit me all at once, the weird way memory works when someone reaches in with a sentence and pulls something you thought you’d filed far away. Cold wet pavement. Burned sugar. The time I stood at Lyle and Fourth while a woman who'd lost her brother cried into my sleeve because I was the closest she could get to the person who had done it.

"Have we met?" I asked. The orange button under my thumb was warm, safe. I wasn't going to dump him. Not yet. "Because if we've met, you can tell me your name."

"Not properly," he said. "I passed you in a hallway once. You held a door for me a different time. You don't remember. It doesn't matter."

Jules scribbled on a yellow Post-it in block letters and pressed it to the glass: OK?

I nodded. The studio smelled like coffee and dust and the glue they used on acoustic tiles, which, once you know what it smells like, you can never smell anything else.

"What do you want to hear, Nocturne?" I asked. "I'll try not to disappoint you."

"Something nostalgic," he said. "A lullaby for the city. You know the tune. People used to sing it when the movies let out."

The Orphic was a movie palace before it burned, and then it was a column in the paper for three weeks and a scandal for six. Before that, it was a place people took their dates on a Thursday when they couldn’t afford Friday. The old men who haunted the newsroom said when you came out into the alley, tipsy on the light and the way you learned other people's lives by watching them pretend, you could hear kids under the fire escape passing a bottle and singing something about the river, that old song that starts with a lie and ends with a hope.

"Where the river meets the road," I said before I could stop myself. "Where the road stops lying."

He hummed two bars. His pitch was good. There was a whistle in one nostril, the kind you get after a broken nose that didn’t heal right.

"You do remember," he said.

"Every city has a song," I said, trying to slow my own hands, which had this fight in them they get when they think they have a puzzle and a deadline. "Pick a version. I'll put it on after the break."

"Put it on now."

"There are rules," I said.

"You used to break them," he said, like a confession and a dare. Then, easy, as if he were asking me to bring milk home: "I'll leave you something. Check your door when you go out."

The ON AIR sign looked like a wound in the dark when you stared at it long enough. I swallowed, dry. Jules leaned forward, fingers hovering over his side of the controls like a man readying himself to jerk the wheel if the car drifted over the line.

"What is it?" I asked. "What are you leaving me?"

"Proof," he said. "A memory that isn't a memory. Something with edges. You'll know what to do."

The chirp sounded again—cuckoo. Somewhere, a bus hissed its doors open, and line noise fuzzed like moths against a screen.

"Play my song, Finch," he said, the way a brother says a name when he's playing with you, the way a bully says it when he wants to try it on for size. "For the night animals. For the ones who aren't sleeping yet."

Then the line went dead.

I stared at the little green light on the console as if I could force it to come back on with will alone. The studio held its breath, and then the clock coughed up another minute and everything started again. I could feel the weight of the city outside the studio walls: the river bottlenecking against the piers, all the windows lit or dark, all the kitchens with their refrigerators opening and closing like gills. The bakery on my script had left a message saying the owner was sick and would we reschedule? The nurse’s request waited dutifully at the top of my inbox, all gentle commas and a smile I could hear if I tilted my head.

"Do we have time?" Jules said in my ear, his voice low on the break.

"To go to Lyle?" I said. My voice did a thing at the end of city proper nouns that I didn't like. It reached for them like the way your hand reaches for a rail when the stairs are dark. "After the show. Not now."

"Don't," he said. He meant be careful. He also meant don’t go by yourself.

"I'm not an idiot," I said, because I needed to say it out loud. There was nobody else to say it to.

I cued the old song, the version a barbershop quartet recorded in 1952, all honey and ache. It wasn't a lullaby. It was a promise and a threat and a lie you tell yourself so you can sleep. I turned it down under my voice.

"You know the one," I said, and my voice, thank God, sounded like a person on the radio and not a person looking at a cliff. "This is for all of you who have to cross when it's dark. For the ones who wait until the chirp."

I played it full. During the sax break, I checked the call log. Nothing useful. The number was masked, as if he were calling from a blockage in the city, a place where everything gets rerouted and nothing has to tell the truth. We have two payphones left within ten miles and both of them have been out of order for years because the city doesn't understand how to be broken gracefully. People made jokes about them in petitions to city council. They turned them into art. None of them worked at two in the morning.

Jules came in during a station promo, his headphone askew. He sat on the edge of the desk and rocked his heel against a dent somebody made with a heavy ashtray in 1993. He chewed the inside of his cheek, which was what he did instead of biting his nails.

"You think it's him?" he asked.

"Who," I said, and the word was impossible to keep neutral. You put your hand in a drawer for a utensil and set it down on the wrong tool. Your hand knows the difference before your head does.

"The one they never found," he said. "The Orphic guy. The letters."

I had a whole box of apologies in my basement, apologies that had started out as articles, sentences I wished I could reshape so they'd walk right out into the world and do their work without me. The letters, people called them like they were famous fiction, unpublished first editions that had gone missing and would show up at estate sales forty years after everyone had stopped caring. Half the city thought they'd been written by a cop. The other half thought they'd been written by me.

"Nobody ever wrote any letters," I said. "Not to us. Not like that."

"He said 'night animals,'" Jules said.

"It was a phrase," I said. "People say things. It doesn't make them who you think they are. If I told you you look tired, would that make me your grandmother?"

"It would get you in the will," he said, but his joke didn't chase the worry out of his eyes. "When you go, you text me."

"When I go where?"

He didn't dignify it with an answer.

At three forty-one, I told a story about a cab driver who had moonlighted as a baritone in a church choir and drove people all over the city on Saturday nights and then sang for them at their parents’ funerals. At three fifty-eight, the nurse from St. Bridget's called in tears because a patient she had loved, in the way you can love someone whose ache you've learned by heart, had died on her shift, and she needed me to say his name into the dark with her. I did. At four, the morning news guy came in early, hair damp and eyes small, the wrong kind of brave. He set his backpack down like it had something fragile in it. He always did that. He was gentle with his stuff, like maybe that could keep the rest of life from breaking.

When the ending music came in, when the board's lights felt like a far-off city at night and the ON AIR sign blinked down into red glass again, I said goodnight, the way I always did, the way you memorize a goodbye and repeat it until it acts like a blessing. "Be kind to the person you run into at sunrise," I said. "It might be me."

The hallway felt long in the quiet that came after. Sound doesn't just stop. It drains. You can hear where it was. It leaves a negative. We had posters on the walls for station events from the nineties, the edges curled at the corners. The carpet was new, like the manager says we’re trying, look at the carpet.

"Text me," Jules said, gathering his hoodie and his keys.

"I will," I said, and we both pretended I was a person who always did what people asked.

The door to the street was metal and badly repainted a shade of green that made me think of the first light on the river when the sun is stubborn and doesn't want to get up yet. It had a pane of glass at eye level, and it sucked the air out around it when you opened it the way doors do in old buildings that settle into themselves in winter and resist being disturbed.

Something was taped to it.

Brown kraft paper. If you've worked in news or radio or a grocery store that still wraps your eggs in paper, you learn to catalog the world by the tape it uses. This was painter's tape, blue, torn not cut. The paper was heavy, a manila envelope cut in half and re-taped into a rectangle. On the front, in block letters that tried very hard to be ordinary, was written my name.

Not my radio name. My real one. Mara Elise Finch, with the middle name underlined like a teacher or a parent or someone who had needed to use it in a room once to pull me back from something I had wanted too much.

"What is it?" Jules asked, behind me. He had come around the corner without making any sound at all and had the grace not to make me jump.

"A recipe for pie," I said, because the bravado comes out whether I want it or not.

I peeled the tape up. The envelope came free with a reluctance that gave me a fast, mean flash of relief: evidence, my old bones said. The old part of me that had believed in the worth of being the person who went first, who took the notes, who gathered the objects while they were still cooled by their last owner's hand. The city outside was night-sour and river-damp. Somewhere a late train coughed. Far off, gulls had started their shift early, their voices tearing at the sky.

Inside the manila, something slid, slick and cheap. I tipped it into my hand.

A cassette. Transparent plastic, the spools dull white. I hadn't held one in years. The label had been drawn on with a black felt-tip, sharp, bold, the ink bled a little like it had been written fast. NIGHT ANIMALS, it said. 1998. Under that, in smaller letters: for M.

There was something else behind it: a photograph. Polaroid, the white border smudged where a thumb had pressed. The image was too bright and too dark at once, the way Polaroids are when you don't know how to ape the sun. A marquee, letters missing, a few black gaps like missing teeth. ORPHIC, it said, all caps, and then CLOSED FOR PRIVATE EVENT. The rest of the shot was the street, the slick wet of it, the gleam of a puddle like an eye.

We didn't have a cassette player in the building anymore. The station manager had thrown the last one out last year in a fit of cleaning, like getting rid of it could make him younger.

"Jules," I said, and my voice had layers in it, some of which I hadn't used in public since before he came to work here. "Tell me you’re a hipster in one regard."

He reached into his backpack like a magician. He pulled out a Walkman that had never been called a Walkman, bought new last Christmas because his girlfriend had thought it was cute, because the eighties had got stuck in the throat of our culture and refused to swallow. He held it like a baby bird.

"Don't," he said. "Don't do it here. In the hall."

He was right. If there was anything on it that could be called evidence, I wanted to be careful. Also, I wanted to be alone with it. The wanting was an ache, old as bone.

"Then come with me," I said. "Or I'll lie and say you did."

He looked at the door like it had turned into an exit to somewhere less tangible. He looked at me. He could have said no. He could have said don't go or I quit or let's call somebody and wrap this in grown-ups. He said, "Fine. Coffee first," and headed toward the kitchen, because when the city asks you a question in the middle of the night, it's rude to answer without a cup in your hand.

The cassette was warm where it had pressed against the paper. It fit in my palm like a small clock. When I closed my hand around it, I could feel the spools shift, the little gears inside readying themselves, and the sound of that, imagined and mechanical, went through me like a promise kept too late to be useful.

On the chart, Hallowstone Island was the shape of a sleeping dog: head lolling toward the open Atlantic, back humped, tail curled toward the harbor. On the water, pushing through a soft soup of fog, it looked like something that hadn’t decided what to be yet.

Mara Finn stood at the bow of the little ferry and watched the world arrive in pieces. A bell buoy tolled somewhere off to port, disembodied and patient. A cormorant arrowed up from the gray, then sank again, leaving a split second of glossy, hard-edged water behind it. The deck smelled of diesel and salt and wet rope. She had run out of places to put her hands and finally settled them in the pockets of a jacket that wasn’t quite heavy enough.

“First time?” the deckhand asked, coming up beside her. He had a face made to look worried: deep parentheses around his mouth, brow permanently furrowed, a healed white seam cutting through one eyebrow.

“First time this year,” Mara said. “I grew up up-coast. Greyharbor,” she added, because it felt easier than explaining that growing up somewhere didn’t mean you belonged there. “I came out with my father once to check the range lights.”

“Ah.” He offered her a smile that wasn’t quite sure it should be there. “We’ve got one of those on the south point. Old Eamon had it fixed last spring.”

“Had,” Mara said.

The deckhand’s smile evaporated. “Right. Had. Like that.”

They were both quiet for a while. Mara followed the faint steps of surf on the pebbles ahead. The island teased itself out of the fog: a split granite spine, some pines, a strip of winter-yellow grass. A house sat a little back from the bluffs, lower and longer than she expected, as if it were deliberately keeping its head down. The ferry’s engine throttled back and everything took on a sheen of quiet, even the gulls.

“You’re here for the thing,” the deckhand said after a bit. “To measure it.”

“Map it,” Mara corrected. “Survey and map. Easements, boundaries, outbuildings. They said the courts want everything neat. For the estate.”

“Neat,” he echoed. He jammed his hands in his own pockets, mirroring her without meaning to. “It’s funny. You spend your life on the water, neat stops meaning much.” He jerked his chin toward the land the way a mainlander would nod toward a storefront. “You heard about Lathrop?”

Only what she could not avoid hearing. In Boston, you could spend weeks in a coffee shop without noticing anyone; in small harbors everybody had a tide chart of your life. “He died in his sleep,” Mara said. “Two months ago.”

“That’s one way of saying it.” The deckhand’s gaze drifted from the house to the narrow strap of dock. “They didn’t do viewings and casseroles. But I suppose a man like that, it’s different.”

“What other ways are there of saying it?” Mara asked, keeping her tone even.

He shrugged. The ferry kissed the pilings with a hollow clunk. He stepped forward to catch the bow line. “Depends who you ask. Depends if you liked how he spent his money.”

Mara didn’t say that money was one of the few things that could exist in both a ledger and in a breath, and that it changed shape when it crossed from one to the other. It was the kind of thought her father would have made mock-serious, turning it into a joke that ended with a lesson about baselines and datums while they ate sandwiches in the shelter of a breakwater, grease wrinkling the brown paper into little valleys.

They were tying off when a woman appeared at the head of the dock. Short, square, cream-colored in a sable coat that somehow didn’t look out of place. She had the sort of hair that only ever got cut in hotel rooms: precise, expensive, the color of Pearl onions. She watched the ferry catch and moor with the bright stillness of somebody who had been awake too long.

“Mara Finn?” she called.

Mara hopped down to the dock. “That’s me.”

The woman held out a gloved hand like a letter being offered through a slot in a door. “Vella Hart. Estate manager.”

“Ms. Hart,” Mara said.

“Mrs.,” the woman corrected, not unkindly, as if you should get the facts right even when no one else cared. “Let me take your bag.”

“I’ve got it.”

“It’s my job to take your bag.” Mrs. Hart’s smile didn’t reach her eyes. They were a clear, untroubled blue, like a winter sky that had decided it did enough. “And to answer sensible questions. I suppose you’ll have those.”

“Some,” Mara admitted. She passed over her duffel and shouldered the case with her instruments herself. Nobody carried the case if she could help it. It was childish and old habit and the weight of it pressed into her, a comfort, a reminder that the work was hers.

“Back by two,” the deckhand said in a voice meant only for her. “Weather turns quick here. You know that.”

“I know it,” Mara said. But the way he said it put a little hook in her somewhere, and she felt it catch as she followed Mrs. Hart down the dock, her boots ringing faintly on the planks.

They took a gravel path up to the house. The fog softened the edges of everything until distance was a rumor. Up close, the house had an expensive plainness: cedar shingles weathered to a silver the color of a good spoon, windows recessed to avoid the worst winds, low rooflines to keep from being peeled by nor’easters. It looked like it knew how to sit and wait.

“Mr. Lathrop built this as a holiday thing back in the seventies,” Mrs. Hart said. “Never quite managed to leave. Funny how that goes.”

“How did it go?” Mara asked, because asking was most of what the job was, and because nobody thought their story was interesting until someone else insisted that it was.

“It went as it goes for people who are smarter than is good for them.” Mrs. Hart pushed in the front door and stood aside so Mara had to walk through the air of her. Perfume, lemon furniture polish, and coffee that had been reheated too often. “He was very good at telling machines to do what he wanted. So he bought himself a life that wouldn’t argue back.”

“And did it?”

Mrs. Hart considered. “He was married once. That argued back.”

The entryway opened into a long hall that smelled faintly of old wool and cold ash. On one side, photographs of boats and people arranged so meticulously that even the chaos of youth in them seemed curated. On the other, maps. Not prints or quaint antiques either: real working charts and topo sheets, layers of pencil and grease pencil, annotations that staggered and tugged as if the hand holding the pencil had a thought its writer couldn’t keep up with.

Mara felt her shoulders drop a fraction. She knew maps, the way some people knew how to dance with strangers.

“He did his own surveying?” she asked.

“Oh, yes.” Mrs. Hart’s voice made the assent into a criticism. “He set benchmarks all over the place. Drove the grounds crew mad, tripping over brass disks where there ought to be nothing. Here.” She caught herself. “You know about those?”

“My father was a surveyor. For the state. Until I was in high school and the funding dried up and he took a job on a ferry because bridges still exist even when nobody wants to count them.” Mara let herself run her fingers in the air near a chart, the way you hover over a sleeping dog’s flank. “He taught me the alphabet of it.”

“Good.” Mrs. Hart reached for a folder on a side table, passed it to her. “Here’s what I could find. Copies of whatever permits he filed that might touch on boundaries. A list of outbuildings. If the county comes sniffing, which it will, they’ll want to know we’re not squatting on any rights-of-way. There’s a question about the south trail. It was his path since forever, but the Deans on the next island have a cousin who knows somebody in Lands. You know how that goes.”

“I do,” Mara said. She flipped the folder open. Inside, there were crisp tih-tih-tih typed sheets and Mr. Lathrop’s looser handwriting, shorthands and arrows and little faces drawn when the day had been long. Several items had been clipped and copied so that the corners of the pages had tiny black triangles, photocopied paperclips. “I’ll need to find his control points. If he set his own network, I should tie mine to it. Do you know where he logged them?”

“Logged?” Mrs. Hart’s mouth twitched. “He wrote. Mostly here.” She angled her head toward a room at the end of the hall. “The map room. I haven’t had the heart to—well. I dust. You can look.”

Mara followed. It felt like the house had arranged to have them go that way. The map room was small, close. Two drafting tables, one clear, one crowded; a few flat files; a narrow couch upholstered in something hardwearing and forgettable; a row of south-facing windows that had a pale sheen of salt on their panes. A nineteenth-century transit sat on a tripod in the corner like a polite deer skeleton. On the wall hung a topo of Hallowstone with pinholes in it thick as stars.

The second drafting table held the remains of a day. A half-empty mug; a mechanical pencil with its lead pushed down into its guts; an open notebook that had gathered salt dust along the top edge. Mara stepped closer. The notebook laid out a set of coordinates and bearings like a prayer, neat even when the hand had hurried. Between the numbers, there were words: South lintel rock — shift?; Old quarry lip collapsed (do not step near after rain); N field stone wall = older than property line?; Find BM 3 (up by fox grapes). The last note had been circled twice and then rewritten lower down in darker graphite: Find BM 3.

“BM?” Mrs. Hart asked behind her. She had come in without Mara hearing. The fog and the house had a way of making everything arrive gently.

“Benchmark,” Mara said. “The little brass disks you mentioned. He was having trouble finding one.”

“You’ll find it,” Mrs. Hart said. Her tone was flat, but it sounded like a superstition, or a challenge.

There were photographs too: Lathrop younger, beard darker, on a picnic blanket with a woman whose head was tipped back, her jaw a line of light; Lathrop older, in a heathered sweater, holding a drill while a teenager in a too-large orange life jacket squinted at him with the concentrating cruelty of kids. The edges of the photographs were worn. Someone had handled them more than was good for them.

“When did you last see him?” Mara asked, hearing how it sounded and not stopping herself anyway. It was the same impulse that had her pressing the pencil harder to get the line light just right: it looked wrong if you didn’t.

Mrs. Hart did not flinch. “The day before he died. He wanted me to order more pins. He was always running out.”

“Pins,” Mara repeated, and looked up at the topo. A galaxy of pinpricks around the south point. She stepped closer. Most holes were evenly spaced: grid control, or a tidy mind. But one cluster near the cliff wasn’t. They had that ragged look, sung at all day with the insistence of someone who didn’t like the answer he was getting. Little holes, deep, in a ring around—what? She squinted. The topo under the glass was a 1993 edition, revised 2005; the contour lines on the south side showed a gentle slope to a pocket beach that she could already tell, just by the way the fog muffled the surf, didn’t exist the same way now. The ocean insisted.

“Can I get to the south point?” she asked.

“Trail’s to the right once you’re out,” Mrs. Hart said. “You’ll see where. Mind the briars. The rocks after the pines are slick. We’ve had rain.”

“I’ll take a look before the tide turns.”

Mrs. Hart hesitated. “Do you know how to cook?”

Mara looked at her.

“Never mind,” Mrs. Hart said, the corner of her mouth bending. It was the first visible evidence that her face remembered how to do that. “If you’re staying past noon, there’s chowder in the blue pot. He liked it thin. He said it didn’t need to prove anything.”

“I’ll be back before then,” Mara said, because she wanted to be, because that was the kind of lie work made you good at.

She left the house with her kit and the island felt larger outside again. The fog had lifted a little; the horizon hunkered there, a darker stripe of potential. The path to the south point was obvious in the way worn things always are: a gap in the stone wall where hands had always gone to lift two stones and put them aside, a line through the grass where feet had argued with the earth for long enough that the earth gave in.

She walked the path with the practiced slowness of someone who knows that the ground looks different from different heights. She took bearings with her compass off the flat, blue smudge of the mainland and off a pair of pines that had grown too close together and baffled each other. She stopped twice to get down on her knees and look for the shine of a brass disk in the grass, and twice she let herself be fooled by damp leaves and a beer cap.

Her father used to tell her that there were only two kinds of lines: the ones people agreed on and the ones the ground forced on you. He’d said it over a plate of pancakes the morning her mother had decided not to come back. He’d said it at the next Thanksgiving when the pies were a disaster. He’d said it at the hospital when the morphine bag beeped like a starting signal and then went quiet. “You choose what to measure, kid. Or it chooses you. Sometimes it’s the same thing.”

She stepped out of the trees onto the south bluff and understood immediately that whatever the topo said, it was already out of date. The bluff had sheared away sometime in the last storm. You could see it in the raw, shocked faces of the roots dangling over nothing, in the way the granite showed a new plane like an open secret. The pocket beach was smaller than the map promised, the stones at its edge slick and new-looking, not yet rounded by the conversational wash of the sea.

Mara felt the tug in her stomach she always did when land failed to be where it had been supposed to be. It wasn’t fear; it was more like being called by a name you hadn’t used in years.

The bell buoy tolled again, closer. She could hear gulls working something on the flats of the next island over, their harsh satisfaction carrying like radio voices.

She moved along the cliff carefully, keeping a safe distance, sighting along the edge of vision to find irregularities. An old stone wall ran parallel to the cliff for a few meters then stopped where the land had gone. The wall was of that precise, casual local style where the stones seem to have been convinced into place rather than forced. Seams small enough to make a snake angry.

There, set into one of the larger stones, was a round of brass half the size of a playing card. Her heart hopped. She brushed away moss with her sleeve. A USGS disk, stamped with the year 1971 and a cryptic sequence: BM 2, Hallowstone. It had been hammered in with care; the letters were still crisp despite the salt.

The notebook had said BM 3. This was 2. She took a bearing, took a photograph, took one more just in case the first had some hidden sin. She worked a quick triangulation in her head. If BM 2 was here and his note said fox grapes for 3, then 3 ought to be—she looked around. Fox grapes liked edges: where the world changed its mind, where sun and shade negotiated. She scanned the trees above the bluff. At the end of a run of low spruces, a tangle of vine had clambered over a deadfall and made itself lord of that small chaos. Leaves thick and shiny even this late in the year.

She glanced at the path back. Going up to the grapes would take her an hour. If she went down to the beach, she could catch the bottom of the cliff where the wall had been and see if any fresh fractures told their stories yet. She could be at the beach in five minutes, out again in ten. She checked the sky. The fog had thinned, and a slice of sun tried at nothing and gave up. The air had that damp promise of rain that coastal weather has when it is trying to choose which of you to insult.

Down, then. She dropped from rock to rock with care, testing each with the heel and then rolling to the ball. The slickness was treacherous. Twice she put a hand out, and the stone she grabbed was cold and moss-soft and steady. When she stepped onto the last ledge before the beach, her boot slipped and she had to catch herself against the wall; her palm came away green and gritty, smelling faintly of vinegar.

The beach-let was a crescent of pebbles and torn-up kelp. The storm that had taken the bluff had also been profligate, tossing up lobster pot buoys, a once-red plastic gas can, wrack, a cool box lid. The world did not put itself away.

She was bending to look at a smoothed wedge of glass when she heard it.

It was not the gulls. Not a bell. Not the dragging hush of water over pebble. It was softer than a shout and harder than a sigh, and it came from the north end of the little beach, where the cliff’s new face made a cove the size of a bedroom.

“Hello?” she called, reflex overriding sense. “Hey.”

Nothing. She took two steps toward the cove and then two more, because it is impossible to take the first two and then stop. The kelp sucked at her boots. She rounded the corner.

At first, she thought it was a bundle of old rope. Then her brain rearranged itself with a click.

A man lay on his side in the angle of rock and seaweed, tucked there as if he had been placed by a careful giant. He was faced away from her, but she could see the sweep of a shoulder, the angle of an elbow, the dark hair caught in a mat against the back of his head. He wore a dark jacket. His right hand was up under it in a way that would have been comfortable if he had been asleep and choking if he had not.

For a second Mara did not move. The fog thinned and thickened and thinned again, as if the day were unsure what story it wanted to tell. The scrape of her boot on a stone sounded like a match being struck. She put her kit down. She didn’t want to. She did it anyway.

“Sir?” she said in the voice you use on the other side of a wall that you hope isn’t the last wall. “Hey.” She reached, then stopped and looked. There was nothing obvious and obscene. No red. No wrong angles. A pale strip of skin at the neck above the collar that made that little bowl where someone once would have put their mouth. She looked at his hand. The fingers were slack, cold-looking, gray with the fine silt that stuck to anything that rested here long enough to be claimed.

She touched his shoulder through the jacket. It gave, human. The cloth was damp but not soaked. The bone under it felt like it was supposed to. She pressed harder. The world was so quiet. Far off, the bell buoy made a sound like a stubborn thought.

“Sir,” she said again, and this time her voice was somebody else’s. She slipped her right hand under his shoulder the way you learned in a class, years ago, when you did not believe it would ever be you, and she rolled him toward her.

The face that came up was not a stranger’s.

For half a second she couldn’t place him and then she did, and the placement had a little shock to it like touching a door in winter. The crease through the eyebrow, the worried set of the mouth. The deckhand from the ferry.

Joel, she thought, ridiculous, because she wasn’t sure that had been his name. It was the one she had given him in her head for people she didn’t know well but wanted to be less clumsy around. She stared at his face. His lips were parted as if he were about to say something and had been interrupted by the ocean.

“Hey,” she said directly to him. “Hey.”

She put her fingers to the side of his throat. You always expected a little drum solo there; you expected the live comedy of a pulse. There was nothing. Or maybe there was, and her own had gone too big, too loud, an orchestra playing over a metronome.

She inhaled, hard, and that was when she noticed his left hand. It lay palm-up under the edge of his jacket, as if he had died in the act of showing someone something. In his palm was a round of brass the size of a coin, scored and bright in the places the salt hadn’t had time to tarnish. The word stamped across it was simple, almost disappointed in the effort it took to read it.

BENCH MARK.

Her breath pinched.

“What the—” she said, a prayer in some dialect.

He had found it. Or he had been given it. Or it had been put in his hand after.

A shadow fell across the cove.

Mara’s head came up. The light had shifted because someone had stepped onto the ledge above. She could see their boots first, expensive in a way only someone who had never expected to get them wet chose expensive. For a moment she thought it was Mrs. Hart. But the boots were wrong. The angle of the foot was wrong. The person above made the rocks look indecisive.

“Hello?” she called, loud, because quiet had suddenly become dangerous. “There’s a man—you need to call—”

“I wouldn’t,” said a voice she didn’t know. It was careful, like someone picking up a glass that might be cracked. “I don’t think you were supposed to find him yet.”

It was the kind of heat that made old paper breathe. Every time the fan on my filing cabinet oscillated, a slim curl of air rose from the pages spread across my desk, and with it the smell—iron, dust, a whisper of mildew that never really left this place. Beecher City Records sat on the fifth floor of a fourteen-story granite cube that had been ugly the day it was built. The windows were the old sash kind that stuck halfway up. Someone had painted them shut in the seventies. When I wanted air, I pressed my face to the crack and learned to be grateful for crumbs.

On the wall above my desk, a map of the city in 1904 had turned the color of tea. Small black type labeled districts in the serious, compact script of a vanished hand: Millers’ Meadow; The Cut; Warsaw Hill. When I got hired as municipal archivist, I’d pinned that map up before anything else. Twenty months later, I knew where its inaccuracies were. Streets that no longer existed. A bend in the river that had been filled and forgotten. I knew all the places the city had rubbed out its own handwriting and asked us to pretend it had never been there.

On mornings like this you could hear the building make noises—plaster ticked as it resentfully took on heat, pipes shuddered once like a fear dream and then slept. The clerk from Tax Assessments had a laugh like a soap bubble popping. Next door, they were digitizing old building permits. The scanner made a sound like a cat being indecisive: I want to go out. No, I want to stay in. My coffee had gone cold an hour ago. The clock in the hallway said ten. It had said ten for the last three weeks.

I was meant to be verifying parcel ownerships for a block on Barrow Street slated for demolition. “Partial demolition,” the letter had said, which in Beecher meant somebody important had smiled in the right direction and gotten to keep their facade. In my stack there were manila folders bound with rotten rubber bands, their corners furred with wear and the brown stigma of a hundred hands. I had resolved, at nine, to be efficient. At ten-oh-five I’d found the card telling whoever had assembled this collection that a box from the Forsyth Exchange Building had just been delivered by courier, and I’d stopped being anything of the kind.

The Forsyth was an old brick lump down by the river, once a telephone exchange and later a dozen other things, the way buildings here got reinvented by necessity and lie and new zoning. A sinkhole had opened at the edge of its parking lot in June, swallowing a blue Civic and the corner of a fence. Engineering had come and gone. So far as I knew the building was getting knocked down in two weeks, which meant that I had two weeks to write a letter in my delightfully stern government voice asking the demolition company to preserve any documentation found on site, including but not limited to ledgers, plans, signage, correspondence, and drawings, as per Code of Ethics for Municipal Archivists Section 3, subsection B. Then I’d have three months of emails explaining to my boss why we were suddenly storing nineteen dinked file cabinets, a termite colony, and a smoking asbestos condenser.

But the box was on the dolly by my desk, and the universe is not known for catering to resolutions.

Its sides were water-stained, one corner soft from a long-ago flood. Somebody had written FORSYTH in black marker and drawn an arrow toward the top, which was hopeful because the top had come loose and the contents were visible no matter which way you turned it. My name was on the shipping slip: ROOK, D. That would be me. People always asked: like the bird? I didn’t tell them that being named for a chess piece had never made me better at strategy.

I set down my pencil and slit the tape. Inside were the usual municipal survivors: rolled drawings in muslin bands, hardbound ledgers with black spines and gold-embossed dates, bundles of forms clipped with enameled paper clamps, pale blue onionskin. Under a sheet of brown paper was a shallow tray of index cards that had once been white. A corner fan of them had molded and conjoined, welded by time into a single concrete curl.

A single card lay free on top. I picked it up gently. Beecher Electricity & Telegraph, it said in a stuttering letterpress font, Service Requests. The edges were scalloped by nibs and impatience. On the back somebody had written in pencil, hard enough to leave grooves: 117 1/2 BARROW ST. SEAL S.B. MUST BE DONE BY OCT. and then the pencil had broken or the hand had paused, because after that the line skidded like a skater hitting a crack.

Barrow Street was in my pile. I set the card on my blotter and pulled the map drawer open with my hip, negotiating its willingness. My fingers knew where to find the right plat. I spread the sheet, smoothing its creases with habit. There was Barrow, running east-west, a block and a half from the river. House numbers had changed twice in a century, but if you’ve ever learned to navigate by the bones of a place, you can still feel where the arteries run.

There was no 117 1/2. There should have been 115, then 117, then 119: whole numbers, the odd side of the street, neat math for mailmen. Half-numbers belonged to alleys and awkwardnesses, to buildings born in the spaces between. But on this version, in 1944, the alley had no number and the lot to the south of 117 was a coal yard.

Maybe it was a clerk’s error from a day when the fan had broken and the clerk in question was spending more of their energy resenting their boss than writing letters. Maybe it was nothing. But I have an ugly weakness for maybes. My father taught me to read walls, and every city has a way of saying: look here. He was a mason by trade before he was a maintenance guy, then a night janitor. “They cover it, kid,” he used to say, showing me where a crack had been papered over. “They do what they have to do and they cover it. Doesn’t mean it wasn’t there.”

I looked again at the pencil grooves. S.B. Sub-basement, my brain supplied, pleased with itself. I stood up.

“I’m getting coffee,” I announced to the room at large, because I’d learned that people accept a lot if you tell them you’re on the way to an errand.

“You want mine?” Tom from Tax called. There was a beige mug on his desk that said TRIPLE ESPRESSO, because if you write it on a mug, it has to be true.

“Rain check,” I said. In the time it took to walk down the hallway I had my phone out and the City’s contractor portal open. The demolition company on the Forsyth job was listed as Red Hook Wrecking. There was a contact name: Nick Dallas. No number listed—of course not; this place believed in systems only conceptually—but there was an email address. I wrote the kind of email that has the right phrases in the right places and helps people believe you might be an obstacle later if they don’t answer.

Then, because efficient people are rewarded, my phone buzzed before I reached the stairwell. A unreadable number flashed. I tucked the phone under my chin and pushed the bar with my back.

“Rook,” I said.

“Dana Rook, Archives?” The voice had steel-toe boots in it. “This is Dallas. I got your email. You’re fast.”

“I was near my desk,” I said.

“We’re taking the skin off today. I got a guy with a jackhammer pounding like sin right now. You care to come down and point at what you want saved, be my guest. Otherwise it’s going in a roll-off.”

“I’ll be there in twenty minutes,” I said. “If they find any rooms that look sealed, don’t open anything without me. Photograph it. Call me.”

On the other end, a small silence. “You people ever happy?” he said, but he didn’t sound angry. He sounded like the only thing he feared was a bad review.

“I make my own happiness,” I said. I took the stairs, because the elevator had a habit of thinking over simple requests for half an hour before deciding the answer was no. On the third floor, the stairwell door had a sign that said AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. Someone had drawn a smiley face in the O with a sharpie. On the ground floor, the building exhaled heat; the revolving door thumped. The street felt like an oven you’d open the door of and stick your head inside to look. August had overstayed, and nobody had the courage to throw it out.

Beecher’s downtown is a grid whose gridness was softened by weak resolve and a bend in the river. The Forsyth was six blocks south and a little east, and halfway through block three of the walk a breeze came up from the water that tasted like old iron and the faintest hint of fish. Construction season had warmed the city’s appetite; dumpsters hulked at corners like battleships. Kids on bikes slalomed between pylons and potholes with a grace that made my teeth hurt.

Red Hook had made themselves known. Two excavators, one with its arm up as if asking a question, stood behind orange mesh fencing. White Tyvek wraps flapped like prayer flags where the facade had been stripped to its bones. It had once been handsome, in a heavy way; the bricks were a deep liver color and the window lintels were arched. The big double doors that had let vans in were propped open, and the noise inside was a catastrophe of enthusiasm. A man in a red hard hat stood just inside one of the doors, talking into a radio like he expected to win an argument with it.

I flashed my municipal ID and did the dance I always did: I’m the person who will make your day worse if you don’t let me in, but I promise to be grateful and quick if you do. The man in the red hard hat turned out to be Dallas. He had the tan that only men who worked outside have. His beard was going gray in a way that made him look trustworthy and tired.

“You the library?” he asked me. He had to pitch his voice to get it over the jackhammer’s ecstatic warble.

“Archives,” I said. “Different religion, same god.”

He grinned, brief and not unkind. He handed me a hard hat that had once been white and safety glasses without comment. “You wrote about rooms. We got a wall in the basement we can’t figure. Looks like it ain’t load-bearing, looks newer than the rest. I was gonna have Louie knock it down. Figured you might want to do your little photo shoot first.”

That you said my little photo shoot and still walked me there meant we were going to get along. He led me past a pile of ductwork that looked like a sleeping dragon, down a concrete ramp into cool dimness. The coolness was sudden and I could feel my shoulders unclench with it. Down here the smell was different—damp, old metal, something a little sweet like rotting fruit and not quite. The jackhammer was distant, a rumor of itself.

Basements are honest in a way that ground floors aren’t. Up top the Forsyth could pretend to be ready to be reborn as lofts with quartz countertops and exposed brick, but down here it had to tell the truth about how it was built. There were pillar lines, faithful as pines in a row; there was a tangle of pipes that had been the city’s veins. We ducked under a low run that might have once carried steam. We stepped over a puddle that had a rainbow skin on it, the way puddles sometimes do when long-ago machines have left their ghost behind.

Dallas’s guy Louie—skinny, every joint wired wrong, wearing a T-shirt that said OHIO in faded letters—was leaning on a sledge and studying a wall as if considering a chess move. The wall in question was newish brick, cheap, the color of bread dressed with ketchup. The walls around it were older, the mortar broader and sandier, the bricks more irregular, some marked with fingerprints in clay. Someone had taken real care, once. Someone had not, later.

“Here,” Dallas said. He bent, tapped a brick with his knuckles. It gave back a sound: dull, not hollow, but not the toothy click of old brick either. “We opened that little square up there.” He pointed to a patch near the ceiling where a few bricks had been knocked out, the hole loosely stuffed with insulation like a wound packed with gauze. “It’s a void in there. I don’t think it’s fill.”

I stood on my toes and peered through. Black. You can sometimes tell the age of a void by the way it breathes. This one did not. If there was space in there, it had been sealed long and good. A tiny trickle of air came back at me after a moment, like a thought too late to matter.

“Give me five minutes,” I said. I stepped back, taking pictures because the muscle thinks better if the hand is occupied. Brick lines, mortar joints, a faint scrap of paint in the corner, no color left to it.

“Take ten,” Dallas said. “We’re not digging to China.”

My father used to talk to walls like a doctor talks to patients. “What did they do to you?” I heard myself say quietly, not for the men so much as for the old brick. The mortar in the original walls was made of lime and sand and time. The new wall’s mortar was a hard gray stripe like epoxy. In one construction of bricks, someone had set a course on the half, wrong, in a hurry. They’d notched bricks haphazardly to make the line. That meant they were closing a hole fast.

“What do you think?” Louie asked. He had the kind of eyes people with dogs trust.

“I think someone wanted this sealed as if it mattered whether air got through,” I said. “Photographing the weird is my job. Opening it gently is yours.”

“Gently?” Dallas raised an eyebrow. “We got a slider out back and a bucket attachment.”

“Gently enough that if there is anything—papers, boxes, something—that won’t be turned into confetti. Please,” I added, because I have learned that the second word lets the first be heard.

“Fine,” Dallas said, which I knew in the dialect of men like him meant: I will show restraint until it bores me.

They set to. Science fiction in my mind would insert a dramatic soundtrack for the first bite out of a sealed room, but in reality it is a lot of brick dust and patient, petty work. Louie started at the top of the wall and began to unknit it, leveraging one brick out at a time, setting them on a neat stack because a person who slams heavy things for a living often has a secret love of order. Dust crawled up the light like a living thing. The first square they opened showed more black. The second showed the edge of something wooden. The taste of old air came through, a breath like breath held too long.

“Slow,” I heard myself say, as if they needed me to remind them that the past breaks hard. Louie nodded without looking. He knocked out one more brick and then one more, and then there was a hole big enough to push a hand through, except I am not the kind of person who reaches into dark holes with unknown corners.

Dallas took out a flashlight from his belt with the small flourish of a man who appreciates his own timing. He angled the light into the opening, moved it left, right. His jaw tightened.

“You got your photos?” he asked me, voice low enough that the question was for me alone.

I lifted my phone and took one more, because it felt like a sacrament.

“All right,” he said, for the wider world. He and Louie took turns. Brick by brick the hole widened until it was a doorway without a door, and then Dallas ducked and went in, and the darkness swallowed his white hard hat.

The room was longer than it had any right to be. It sighed at us when the wall let go, a stale exhale that made the hair on my arms rise. I stepped over the low lip of brick, a graceless hop, and my foot hit flat tile, the old kind, little octagons the color of smoke. My flashlight beam swept over floor, chair, desk, other chair turned sideways, bookcase. There was a coat on a stand, a proper hat with a pinch in the crown hung on a peg. A paper calendar was nailed to the wall, the month browned to the color of a bruise; days crossed off in pencil like count marks. October had been half-eaten.

On the desk was a telephone with a bell, the kind you answered by lifting heavy black up to your ear like you were taking an oath. A small metal fan perched on one corner. A stapler shaped like a squat animal sat next to a blotter stamped with a seal.

Behind the desk was a man who was not a man anymore, except for the shape you saw first: a collapse of suit and a long curve of bone where a hand had been folded over something. He had become what long-sealed rooms encourage—less than flesh, more than absence. The air had mummified him gently; his shirt had melted into a color that meant only: time. His jaw was hooked strangely, his head fallen against the high back of the chair. The small bones in the ear stood out, precise as punctuation. There was a lapel pin on the remaining wing of his jacket, bright as if it had decided color was a hill worth dying on: a gear with a letter in the center.

Louie made a sound the way I have heard men make it when a car almost clips them and does not. Dallas took off his hard hat without seeming to think about it and held it to his stomach for two heartbeats before jamming it back on his head. A fly that had somehow found its way down here through duct or crack circled once and left, uninterested.

There is a part of your brain that wants to write a neat caption when it sees a scene like that. Found: subject, desk, lamp, bones. There is another part that refuses and only notes the details because details keep your breath moving. There was a glass on the desk with two rings of dried liquid, one higher than the other. The desk blotter had a corner torn and the tear had been arranged to lie flat, the way neat people do when torn things offend them but cannot be thrown out. The chair legs had furniture socks on them—brown felt circles worn smooth. On the wall, a clock with a white face and black numbers had stopped at 4:12.

I had the list of the Forsyth’s past tenants in one of my folders back at the office, collected mostly because it made my boss sigh when I brought him things like that. I didn’t need it. There was a nameplate on the desk that time had failed to erase. HARLAN BELL, it said, Accounting & Licensing.

I had seen that name twice this week. On Tuesday, in a ledger from 1948, a crisp hand had signed it on a memo approving a parcel variance for a new highway spur that had bulldozed half the Cut. On Wednesday, I had scanned a three-sentence article from a microfilmed Beecher Herald that said City Accountant Missing, Family Appeals, and a grainy photograph in which a man with a Lily Munster hairline and a calm mouth stood with a wife in a small hat and a child done up like a cherub, all of them trying not to squint.

“Jesus,” Dallas said, not profane so much as awed. He kept his hands at his sides. “How long you think…?”

“Since October,” I said, because the calendar was easier than the question. Then I took a breath, because the heat of the world above had abandoned us here, because I was half a child again walking jobs with my father and feeling the way he would go quiet in the presence of something that had been done wrong. “Since 1948,” I added, and the year tasted metallic, like biting your tongue. I pointed at the calendar. He followed my hand, and then he did the math.

“They sealed a man in a room,” Louie said, with the peculiar bluntness of the excused. He made the sign someone makes when an old superstition puts its hand on their back.

“We don’t know that,” I said, because it was my job to say it and because the words are like salt you throw over a shoulder: they do their little juggling trick and reassure you for a second.

The door in the interior wall had a metal slide bolt on the inside. It was closed. That was not the kind of thing you notice second; it is the kind of thing you notice always.

“Whoever sealed the outside, he was on this side,” Dallas said, softly. We went quiet for a time that felt ordinary and wasn’t. Above us, the jackhammer had stopped. The silence was wide and thin.

I stepped closer, because the impulse to collect names is the same as the impulse to light lost corners. On the far end of the desk was a small metal drawer with a key in it. On top of the blotter, neat centered lines of ink had dried to brown. The last line broke off: Meeting — and then nothing. A paperclip had bent itself into a crude S and then thought better and stayed.

“Don’t touch,” I said. I said it for all of us. I took my phone out and photographed what could be read, what couldn’t, the gloss of the lapel pin, the calendar dates, the clock, the bolt. I took a photo of the neatness of the pencil lines on October. Somebody had marked the fourteenth with a red circle. There was a note in the margin: S.B. by 4:00.

“Sub-basement,” I said out loud, and listened to my own voice carry it back to me, from another time.

“Makes a mess of our schedule,” Dallas said flatly. He lifted his radio to his mouth, hesitated, put it down. He looked at me. “You calling this in?”

“In about three minutes,” I said. “First I’m going to call my boss and tell him I found the city’s past in a place I was not supposed to find it. He will yell into a pillow I can’t see. Then I will call the police. Then none of us are going to be able to leave for a while.”

“Been worse ways to spend an afternoon,” he said. “Been better ones too.”

I stepped back toward the hole in the wall to get signal, because even sealed rooms get bars if you stand close enough to a gap and hold your breath. Before I dialed, I looked once more. There is a thing that happens, when you have spent your life reading other people’s handwriting and their pencil’s pressure. It is not a gift. It is only a habit. You see a smear of ink and understand the seconds before it. The calendar squares had been filled in with a hand that pressed hard, that believed in absolutes. The last two days were tentative, the pencil faint. The last line of ink on the blotter had a drag mark that angled uphill to the right, the way it does if the pen lifts because your hand comes up fast.

October, I thought. 1948. Four and twelve. A half-numbered address for a sub-basement that was either a bad joke or a not-so-subtle instruction. A man whose name was a line in a ledger and a grainy photograph, who did not have a grave, who might finally have one. A room that did not breathe. Whole cities are built on welded lies that you can stand on and never fall through. Today I had put my shoe down in exactly the right place.

When the detective later asked me why I was the one who found him, I could have said: it’s my job. I could have said: coincidence. I could have said: because I mailed an email and a man answered. I could have said: because my father taught me to run my hand along the wall and listen. But I didn’t have those words then. I just looked at the man on the chair and thought: You were here all along. What did they make you know before they let the mortar dry? And out loud, because sometimes you have to meet a city’s eye when it looks at you through a hole you made, I said, “Hello, Mr. Bell.”

He didn’t get up. The clock stayed at 4:12. Outside, the city went on believing its new stories. Inside, we had found an old one that refused to be polite.

On the night the Verdigris sighed, Noor Calder was counting cracks.

She held her flashlight low so the beam skimmed the marble like a tide, picking out fissures, pitted places, the webbed hairlines that ran from the base of the ticket window to the edge of the vestibule. The rain had blown sideways all afternoon, and now the storm found its way into everything. It whispered under the doors and gathered into patient little lakes on the mosaic floor. The copper marquee outside dripped in a steady metallic tempo. Somewhere deep in the building, water tapped hollowly into a pan, a note that sounded like a gasp held too long.

“Even your bones are tired,” Noor said to no one. She said that kind of thing a lot to buildings, when nobody was around to hear.

Her official title was municipal code enforcement inspector, which made her sound like a person who counted things that mattered to no one until they did. She wore a yellow slicker and carried a clipboard because people expected that of her, and because it was a kind of armor. Tonight, there was no one to conjure authority for; the taped orange ORDER TO DEMOLISH notice flapped limply on the glass of the main doors, and the security guard assigned to make sure the Verdigris Theatre did not shake its last onto an unapproved passerby had gone home when the city told everyone to stay off the roads.

Noor picked her way around the fallen plaster and matched her boot prints to the salty footprints she’d made earlier. She checked off “mold,” “compromised handrail,” “exposed wiring,” “active leak—north vestibule,” in a tidy, compact script that kept strangers from asking if it was really her, and not some man, who made the call about whether a place was safe.

It was not nostalgia that made buying time worth the storm. It was a line item and a schedule and a temperamental contractor. It was also, if she allowed it to be, a memory of the first time she’d seen the Verdigris as a child, when her father had taken her to a matinee here for a film about a spacewoman and a flock of mechanical birds. He had held her up so she could see the painted ceiling better, the blue-green swoops and gold-leaf stars, his hands steady as machinery.

She flicked the beam over to a hallway where someone had spilled a whole bag of popcorn once, a hundred years ago, and the ghosts of butter and salt had set into the carpet forever. The lobby chandeliers were cold. The only light was what Noor brought with her and the faint emergency glow down in the aisle that had failed everything else. She’d verified twice that power had been cut at the main; contractors did stupid things in the dark.

Up on the mezzanine a velvet rope sagged like an exhausted smile. Noor stepped over it and went toward the staircase, her boots squeaking faintly. She had been up to the projection booth earlier that day, but the door had been painted shut from disuse then; there was nothing to see except the housings of two old 35mm projectors like sleeping elephants, their mouths open and teeth missing. At least that’s what she’d been told. The Verdigris had been shuttered before Noor ever worked for the city. She knew it through rumors and blueprints, its name invoked every election year like a talisman of some promised renaissance.

Halfway up, the smell changed. It went from wet plaster and cold marble to the tickle of something sweet and sharp that always made Noor think of hair spray and old books—acetic acid, the vinegar breath of dying film. She slowed, raised the beam, and panned it along the balcony railing, past the framed sepia photos of the Verdigris in its prime: marquee lit up like a constellation, men in hats and women in gloves, a spidery signature of a man posed with a shovel in front of a foundation trench.

Her light landed on the small square window to the booth. It was dirty, but there was a bloom of smear on the inside, a pattern where someone had wiped it with a sleeve, recently. Beyond the glass: a faintness, not light, not exactly. The suggestion of a circle like the ghost of a lamp on the wall.

Noor tightened her fingers on the flashlight.

The door to the booth was painted the same green as the rest of the mezzanine, a color meant to hide patina. The brass knob had the Verdigris V stamped into it. She tried the handle. It turned; the latch tapped in its bowl with a dry sound and then gave only a centimeter before the dead bolt bit.

She leaned into it, shoulder against wood, and frowned. She flicked her beam down to the threshold. Water hadn’t seeped underneath. The paint at the frame was cracked but intact, the head of each old flathead screw furred with dust so thick it had become its own protective coat. No forced entry, no recent repairs. No footsteps except her own and the ghostly scuff of a possum she’d scared downstairs earlier.

“Noor,” she told herself, and breathed like she did at the top of ladders. The smell of film was stronger. Someone had been in there. Recently enough for that smell to linger. Recently enough that her stomach tightened and then went cold.

She did not carry a gun. That was a joke contractors liked to make: what do you even have in there, Superintendent, a ticket pad and a whistle? She had a flashlight, and a pry bar, and the knowledge that doors did what they were made to do until they didn’t.

She set the clipboard down, slid the pry bar’s flat end between wood and jamb where the dead bolt had just that centimeter of play, and worked it with the patience of someone who’d once spent a month learning to coax rotten wood out of window frames without shattering the sash. The wood creaked. The bar flexed, and the bolt shot, and she caught the door with her hip as it swung into darkness.

At first there was nothing but smell and the dampness of old heat. Then shapes assembled under her light: the hulks of the two projectors, the stool between them, the narrow shelf arrayed with cans, an ashtray turned over and long ago emptied. There was an old reel of film kung-fu kicked against the baseboard, its leader unreeling across the floor like a ribbon. On the wall where Noor had thought she’d seen a circle there was a pale oval burned into the paint, a place once warmed by a lamp that had stood there for years. There was a ledger open on the shelf near the portholes. Noor’s beam caught the edges of scrawls, the silver glint from a paper knife.

And there was a man slumped in the operator’s chair, his chin tucked to his chest just enough that the edge of a jaw was all Noor saw for a heartbeat.

“No.” The word came without thinking. Not a protest. A diagnosis.

She stepped in. She could hear the rain better in here, hard on the roof, like someone flicking a thousand fingers against copper. A drip into a bucket somewhere else in the building counted her steps. She kept the flashlight on the man’s throat. Barely five seconds and she knew. The color. The laxity. She reached for his wrist anyway, because their paramedic courses insisted that you attempt even when you know the end of the story. His skin was cool. The pulse at the radial was not a pulse at all.

Noor stood still. The booth wasn’t big, but the silence around the rain was thick. She adjusted the light toward the face and registered what she could bear to take in: sixties, maybe. Gray hair, but too thick to be frail. A face made for being photographed: handsome in the way that once made people call men personable when they were out to ruin you. He wore a blazer like he had put it on five minutes ago, carefully, and a white shirt with a smear of something dull green at the collar. His left hand hung loose at his thigh. A ring glittered on it—an onyx square with a gold V that matched the door knob.

It wasn’t poison-green, that smear. Noor leaned in, smelled the metallic tang of copper compounds. Verdigris, she thought crazily, and then decided it must be paint from the door. But the paint wasn’t wet. The smear was too bright.

The auditorium porthole windows were to her right. She lifted the flashlight and peered through one. The house was black, rows of seats like a cave of teeth. The glass was scratched, the edges nicked, and on the inside she could see a ring of dust. She squinted; the ring had three clean arcs missing in it, the crescent marks of fingers that had gripped the porthole from the booth and left three clear moons within the dust.

The door had been locked. The windows were fixed. There was no other way in. Noor sent the beam up. In the corner of the ceiling was a register for a ventilation duct, bolted with four slotted screws painted over. The paint was craned and cracked around them, unbroken. The register was the size of her hand; maybe a cat could squeeze through. Not a man hard with sixty.

The ledger on the shelf sat like an invitation decided upon, its cloth cover stained with something darker at the lower right corner. The paper knife was stabbed into the wood next to it like an emphatic punctuation: stop here. The book was open midway. Columns of numbers, dates, the names of films and the costs of candy embedded with the tidy glee of accountants. And across the columns, running diagonal, a slanted note in a hand Noor recognized before her mind could tell her why it would:

Calder, she read. And below it, in the same hand, a number and a word: catwalk.

Her own name in someone else’s hand, here. Calder wasn’t uncommon. It could have been anyone. But Noor was not anyone and the name was both the fact of her and the echo of a man who’d taught her the word for any skeleton that held up something beautiful.

She touched the page with the tips of two fingers, conscious suddenly that touching anything was several kinds of wrong. She pulled her hand back, reflexive. The phone in her pocket buzzed: a small, unimportant cricket sound that startled her so sharply she almost laughed.

She fumbled it out. The screen was wet with condensation. The signal bar ebbed and returned. Dispatch had left a voicemail nineteen minutes ago—her earlier call about staying to check the roof drains and the east wall. She tapped out 911 anyway, then thought better and hit the non-emergency line she had on speed dial. The phone rang twice, then snagged into the recorded warning about storms and down trees. A human voice arrived at last, brittle with fatigue.

“City line.”

“This is Inspector Noor Calder, badge 3104,” she said. “I’m at the Verdigris Theatre on Third and Wayne. I’ve discovered a deceased adult male in the projection booth. The door was locked from the inside. I forced entry.”

“When?”

“Sixty seconds ago.”

“Is the subject breathing?”

“No. He’s cold. I did not move the body except to check for a pulse.” She heard the steel in her voice and was grateful for it.

“Cause of death?”

“No obvious trauma. No blood. Possible—” She looked again, resisting the idiot impulse to lean closer, to sniff, as though the body were a pan on a stove and she could tell by scent. She glanced at the mouth, the fingernails; her father had taught her once to look at the edges of things. There was no blue. The skin had the heavy whiteness of snow waiting for footprints. “Possible cardiac event,” she finished to get the operator on her side, though she knew she had no business guessing.

“We have multiple units tied up with weather-related events. Are you in immediate danger?”
