She thought of the locked door. The clean arcs where fingers had pushed the porthole. The fact that she was alone on a mezzanine in a building whose bones she loved and did not trust.

“No immediate danger. I can wait in the lobby.”

“Are you able to secure the location?”

Noor looked at the bolt. It lay like an accusation on the jamb. “I can try. It was locked from inside when I found it.”

“We’ll dispatch when we can. Stay on scene. Do not disturb anything. If you feel unsafe, leave.”

“Copy.”

The line died. The building inhaled. Somewhere a wet piece of plaster let go and kissed the floor with a sound like clapping once, softly. Noor took a careful step back out of the booth, then another, until she could pull the door toward her. The bolt was stripped now; it hung with a sulkiness she felt in her bones. She closed the door anyway, set the pry bar across the frame like a poor cousin to a brace, and told herself that it made a difference.

The faces along the mezzanine watched her move, all those black-and-white patrons with their perfect hats. Noor put the phone back in her pocket, picked up her clipboard, and walked to the velvet rope. Only when her hand closed around the tassel did she let herself think about the man. Had she seen him before? In the photos, maybe. There was a picture near the staircase: a younger version of that face, hair dark, eyes like a door on a hinge, one arm around an actress with a waterfall of pearls. The brass plate below read, GIDEON ROOK, OWNER, 1975–2009.

Rook. The name clicked like a die in a cup. The Verdigris had been insured—there had been fuss, the papers, the way the city could make a man famous for a week with the right verb in a headline. Gideon Rook had vanished one night on the river, is disappeared a verb, his wife had put up posters, and then the story had gone under with the rest. There had been talk—embezzlement, arson, the kind of romance a city uses to keep from thinking about bills. Ironic for him to end here, even more ironic for him to have never left. If it was him.

Calder, she thought again, not thinking Gideon but thinking of the tidy slanted hand in the ledger. Catwalk. In a building like this, the catwalk was an iron spine high above the stage, a place to hang lights and dreams. It would be long, narrow, lovely to someone with a head for heights and torture to someone else. Noor had grown up on job sites, with her father stepping out onto beams with a carpenter’s casual faith. She had pretended to that faith the way she pretended a lullaby of numbers could soothe her. She turned away from the booth door and looked down over the railing into the blackness of the auditorium. A stripe of emergency light washed the first three rows in an aquarium gray.

Her phone buzzed again. Noor glanced. A text, no contact name, just a string of numbers that meant burner or new phone or bad news.

Leave him as you found him, the message read.

She felt the cold climb her spine and settle there, an obedient animal. The water outside hit the roof harder, as if rain had opinions.

She tapped the number, her thumb moving without permission, but the call went nowhere. Straight to a mailbox that did not exist. She stood there, as the Verdigris listened, weighing the kind of fear that was useful against the kind that made you do foolish things.

Whoever had texted knew she was here, knew what was in the booth, knew what she might do next. Or wanted to make her think so.

Noor lifted the velvet rope and slipped back onto the mezzanine. She walked toward the door again, because she did not know how not to. A warmth had begun to gather in her—anger, that somebody had asked a building to keep a secret so long that it had forgetten its own language for telling. She put her ear to the door and heard nothing but the rain.

She turned, taking in the wall. The framed photo of Gideon Rook and the actress hung crooked. The brass plate, to her inspector’s eye, had four new screws where the mounting looked old. She reached up, touched the edge of the frame, and it moved under her fingers with a give that suggested it had been lifted recently and put back hurriedly, its twelve years of dust disturbed in an arc. She knew how to read old dust. It was the only script buildings wrote for those willing to translate.

Her light caught on something behind the frame—just a line, the edge of a cut in paint. Figurative lines, literal lines, they were all the same: they meant somebody wanted you to look and somebody else wanted you not to.

Another buzz. Another text. She didn’t check it; that felt like playing the game someone else had invented. She lifted the frame outright this time. It came free with a dry sigh. Under it was a rectangle inset into the wall, about the size of a shoebox, its edges neatly taped and painted over. Someone had carved a small notch into one side with the care of a person thinking he might need to get back in and would like the future to go easier on him.

Noor set the frame against the wall and put the pry bar’s claw into the notch.

The phone vibrated again, insistently, as if that could move her hand away. She ignored it. The paint cracked, the tape surrendered, and the rectangle of plaster lifted out, surprising her with how cleanly it detached, as if a piece of the Verdigris had merely been waiting for someone to ask.

Behind it was a metal box set into the masonry—a safe, very small, the kind used to hold things that would fit in a hand and make a life turn. It had a keyhole, no combination dial, and because human lives enjoy symmetry it had a tiny V stamped at its bottom corner.

Noor smiled without any joy at all. She glanced back at the booth door, as if it could watch her through wood. Then she brushed her finger over the ledger in her mind—Calder. Catwalk. Somewhere above the stage there would be another door, another lock, another person’s idea of safety.

Her phone vibrated, and this time she read the words without meaning to, because her body knew what to fear:

Do not touch the box.

Outside, the wind changed. The Verdigris tightened itself against it. Noor set her palm against the cool painted wall, feeling, as she often did at the edge of something important, that buildings remembered. And then, because everything had already been set in motion and because she had never yet learned to leave a living thing full of secrets in a storm, she slid the pry bar back into her belt and went to find the stairs that led up toward the catwalk.

Chapter One

The first thing they teach you in reporter school is that the record is never the truth. It is a meticulously arranged approximation, like a portrait painted with a broom. We transcribe everything—stammers, attorneys interrupting, the weary sigh of a judge—slapped down in characters and standardized punctuation until the mess of breathing people becomes a stack of pages you can bind with twine.

I have made a living from that neat falsity. It has the comfort of a ritual: open case file, plug in the steno machine, position myself like a piece of furniture no one sees until they need to trip over something. It lets you pretend that words are solid when, in reality, they are smoke and intention.

On Monday morning, the smoke came first.

I was in Department 44 fifteen minutes early, because Judge Vale liked the air to be calm by the time she swept in. She was a small woman with a complicated robe that she wore like a tailored suit, and when she sat down, you could hear the whole room adjust itself. I set my steno machine on the corner of my desk, wiped an invisible fingerprint from the keys, and adjusted my chair to the angle where I could watch both counsel tables without turning my neck.

The fluorescent lights hummed like thought. Somewhere in the building, a slow elevator sighed open and closed. I took a sip from the courthouse café’s coffee—over-brewed, comforting as a headache—and woke up my software. The day’s docket glowed across the screen: probation violations, a battered restraining order hearing, a pretrial conference for a theft case that had been pushed three times already. It was going to be an ordinary day in the municipal ballet of bad decisions and bored patience.

Three emails were waiting for me. Two were reminders to upload last week’s transcripts. The third was a configuration alert that my user dictionary had synced at 3:02 a.m. I blinked at that, checked the timestamp again. I don’t sync anything at three in the morning; I was asleep in my apartment, drooling into a book about train disasters, because if I read about anything cheerful before bed my brain interprets it as a challenge.

Thinking maybe IT had pushed an update, I clicked into my files to make sure nothing had exploded. There, between Friday’s sentencing and a transcript I’d started for an attorney who believed semicolons were a conspiracy, was a file I hadn’t created.

I knew I hadn’t created it because it followed my naming convention too precisely. I use a pattern: case number, party names, date, department, my initials. It’s the only neat thing about me. This file was labeled 22CR4901_State_v_Rivas_1025_Dep44_NQ. Today’s date was October 25th. The time stamp said 9:00 A.M.

It was 8:44.

I clicked it open thinking I had fat-fingered a shortcut and generated a blank. Words unfolded across the screen.

There was the caption line that my software spits out automatically—County of Ellis, Department Forty-Four, Honorable Harriet Vale, Presiding—then the start of a hearing. The voices were labeled the way I label them. SPEAKER: Vale, Harriet. SPEAKER: Prosecutor (Daz). SPEAKER: Defense (Unknown female). SPEAKER: Rivas, May.

The transcript was already paginated, each line numbered. The margins were the ones I use, slightly narrower to save paper when I print. The footers had my name and court reporter number. When the prosecutor said “kind of,” my dictionary had corrected it to “sort of.” My dictionaries are full of private quirks like that—corrections I decided on when I was a baby reporter and too stubborn to admit anyone else’s preferences might be valid. Seeing my style on the screen was like seeing a photograph of myself in a window I hadn’t walked past.

But the words weren’t mine. I hadn’t been in the room where they happened. That room they described—my room—was still empty around me. The vent over the gallery rattled as if to fill in a beat.

Reading transcripts cold is like eavesdropping on your own neighborhood from a rooftop. You recognize the voices even if they’re a line of text. Vale’s patience had a rhythm—slow, then the precise clamp of a question. Daz, whose full name was Desmond Dacey and who had a voice that always sounded like a man talking through a grin he didn’t feel, favored polite sarcasm. The defense wasn’t named. The defendant, May Rivas, didn’t speak at first.

Defendant seated at counsel table, the robo-voice of my software had annotated. Defendant is wearing a green sweater with a snag at the wrist. The bailiff closes the door. The clock ticks.

I don’t annotate like that. I don’t anthropomorphize clocks.

The hearing proceeded anyway. It was a pretrial. Daz wanted to push for trial dates; defense counsel wanted more time to review discovery. Vale asked for reasons and made a little joke about calendars being elastic. And then, through it all, as if entering the room like weather, the defendant—May—interrupted with a whisper that my software had printed as if she’d leaned into my microphone.

I did it.

Three words. I did it. Not in the defensive way. Not “okay, fine, I did it.” It leaped from the page, like words sometimes do when someone finally finds the thread they’ve been pulling in their sleep.

The translation of words to text is a miraculous flattening that I take for granted. Still, my fingers curled slightly above my keyboard as if they were going to start writing even though we were minutes away from the hearing itself. I read on.

What exactly did you do? Vale, of course.

May spoke slowly. There were pauses that in my text became ellipses because I force my ellipses to be three dots instead of awkward strings of periods. I took her pacing into me as if it were my own breath.

I killed Evelyn Hart.

I stared at the name until it wavered. I had never typed that name before. If you do this job long enough, you keep a mental index of names the way a bartender keeps a mental index of faces. Evelyn Hart was new.

Daz objected because Daz always objects when someone makes his life simpler in a way he didn’t authorize. Defense counsel tried to quiet her client. Vale ordered the record to reflect the statement and told May that maybe she wanted an attorney to advise her. May said she’d seen a string of green thread wrap around her wrist in her dream last night and she knew that meant she had to tell the truth today because truth was the only way to cut it.

That is not the sort of sentence a municipal court produces. It is poetry edged with nonsense. I looked down at the translucent keys of my steno machine as if they were going to be sticky with dream. My coffee had gone cool in three gulps.

May went on.

She said Evelyn had been her friend for six months. She said they had met at a bus stop on Ridge and Knox when May was wearing a jacket too thin for the weather and Evelyn had offered her half of a paper bag with a cookie and, later, work washing dishes at her brother’s restaurant. She said it simply, as if she were describing a bus route: we went to the river, we walked along the water, Evelyn slipped, I pushed her, it’s hard to tell which one happened. She said she had put her hands on Evelyn’s shoulders and afterwards she had wanted to pour the river out of herself but everywhere she went all she could smell was metal.

Daz asked when and where.

May told him. September 30th. The water by the foundry. Two in the morning.

Vale told Daz to stop talking like a drill and asked May if she understood that the court was not her confessor. May said, I thought you were. She spoke like someone delivering a line she had been practicing into a mirror for twelve years.

Defense counsel asked for a continuance, astronomical in length. Vale, understandably, told everyone to slow down and asked Daz why she had never heard of a victim named Evelyn Hart with a date of death at the end of September and a crime scene by the foundry. Daz said he hadn’t either. His words were neat on the page; in my head I could see his face when facts injured his plans.

The page broke there. At the top of the next one, beneath my standard footer with my license number and a greyscale seal, it said: There is a knock at the door. It is the building maintenance man with a plunger. He apologizes for the noise in the pipes.

That line did something to my stomach.

On cue, as if summoned, the pipe in the wall beside my desk clunked. I could not help the stupid laugh that came out of me—a little bark that sounded like a chair leg catching. I swiveled slowly and looked at the metal riser that ran like a spine up the wall. It clunked again.

Eight-fifty-one. The room was still empty. It wouldn’t be, soon. The bailiff would push open the door with his hip and the gallery would fill with people who needed us to assign a tense to their mess. The judge would settle in and shuffle a stack of papers in a way that telegraphed sanity. Between those ritual movements, something impossible had already happened.

I scrolled to see how the hearing ended. It didn’t. The lines of text broke and began again with something I never put in my transcripts: an italicized note, a stage direction.

The court reporter’s cough.

I felt my throat tighten at the exact moment I read it. I coughed. It was more reflex than affliction, the tiny cough I produce when the air turns dusty. I coughed and watched the instruction I had just performed, predicted by the text in my hand.

You will say this is the product of a deranged IT department, or a prank by a colleague with my password. You will say that what felt like a prophecy is just a mixture of coincidence and the suggestibility of anyone who spends this much time coding speech into symbols. Maybe.

On my screen:

Vale asks, Ms. Quinn, does the record have the correct date?

She calls me Ms. Quinn in court the way she calls Daz Mr. Dacey and calls defense counsel Counsel if she likes them and Ma’am when she doesn’t. I felt the soft heat rise on my neck the way it does when the judge speaks to you even if it’s the most mundane thing. I scrolled.

Yes, Your Honor, October twenty-fifth. 9:00 A.M. Department forty-four.

And then, three lines later:

The clock shudders. The power flickers. When the light returns, the defendant is standing.

I looked up. The clock over the double doors ticked in quarter-beats, a little stick insect of a thing that made everything under its sweep look essential. It did not shudder.

Three minutes to nine. For a second, I was twelve years old, waiting for the jump scare in a movie, unable to keep my eyes from the exact corner of the screen where I knew the monster would appear even though the adult in me wanted to stare at the carpet and pretend I was above it.

I saved the file, out of a mix of reflex and fear that my computer was going to purge it out of embarrassment. My thumb hovered over the power button. I didn’t shut anything down.

Instead, I opened another window and the public case docket. If one person in this courthouse knows everything that has happened and will happen, it’s the scheduling clerk, a woman named Deirdre who could make the entire county empty of cars if she wrote “roads closed” in the right field. I scrolled through the morning calendar. No State v. Rivas. No 22CR4901. Nothing. This was a ghost docket entry wearing my clothes.

On the screen, the transcript grew a last paragraph like teeth.

Bailiff knocks. Door opens. The hallway outside is full of people with umbrellas that they tap against their shoes. It has started to rain.

I hadn’t heard rain. The sky, visible through the high grim windows, was a hard November blue. The hallway, when I glanced out and left, was grey linoleum and pale walls and, at the far end, a man whose face I knew well enough to recognize by gait alone.

Harlin, the bailiff, was built like a corn crib and moved with surprising delicacy. He carried a mug the size of a flowerpot, and his belt creaked when he breathed. He was alone. No umbrellas.

He pushed the door with his hip and the hinge squealed in a key it only found when the building was about to surprise me. He nodded at me, at my machine. He does that every morning, a little salute like we’re both in on something slightly holy. The room smelled faintly of lemon oil because the night janitor had decided the judge’s bench needed blessing.

“Morning, Nora,” he said.

“Morning.” My voice sounded normal. That was a good sign. In my lap, my hands pressed flat together as if in prayer, probably because the transcript had my body remembering things it hadn’t experienced.

“You see the late add?” Harlin asked, moving to adjust the chairs at counsel table with an eye that made chaos look planned. “Daz sent a runner up five minutes ago. We got something at nine.”

I swallowed and tasted old coffee. “What something?”

“State versus Rivas. Pretrial consult, blah blah. Name ring any bells?”

The room did the kind of quiet that has an edge. My eyes were still on the screen. When I looked back at him, I could feel that my face had given myself away because he made his concerned-cow expression: eyebrows heavy, an attempt at humor at the corners of his mouth to ward off the possibility that he’d need to be serious.

“You okay there, Reporter Quinn?” he asked. He always switches to titles when he thinks someone is going to cry.

“It’s nothing,” I lied.

He put the mug down and the ceramic thumped. “You got that cough again?”

I coughed. It startled both of us, even though I swear my chest had been calm until that moment. The sound bounced off the empty benches. The clock ticked one more delicate notch toward the hour.

“Get a lozenge,” Harlin ordered, rescued by the comfort of admonishing. He went to the door again. “I’ll grab the judge.”

As he opened the door, the hallway revealed itself for just a heartbeat, full of people weathered by rain. Umbrellas knocked against shoes. Water chimed down the steel ribs of the stairwell. I watched one droplet fall from the rim of a green plastic umbrella and hit the floor with an impossibly precise pat.

It hadn’t been raining a minute ago. I swallowed the urge to stand up and leave the building and keep walking until the smell of lemon oil and old paper was something I remembered instead of breathed.

Judge Vale appeared at the threshold like punctuation. She did not look at me when she walked in, but I felt her presence straighten the air around my chair.

“Good morning,” she said to the room, which now contained exactly two people and a machine, and made it sound like an audience was applauding. “We have a late add. Mr. Dacey is on his way up. Defense has not filed. We will speak briefly; we will not make decisions we regret.”

“Yes, Your Honor,” I heard myself say.

I put my fingers on my keys. I waited for the door to open, for the defendant in a green sweater to take a seat, for my dictionary to take the messy attempts at truth and force them into the uniform spacing of ten-point font.

On my screen, the next line awaited my keystrokes like a dare.

When the light returns, the defendant is standing.

Chapter One

At nine in the morning, the light in my studio is kind—angled and not yet brave enough to show me every fault. It slants across the worktable and turns the dust in the air to a constellation I can move my hands through. I tell clients I restore maps. The truth is, I treat paper like skin. You learn where it wants to bend, where it will split under pressure, how to coax a curl out of a soaked corner with breath and patience. You learn to look past what’s on the surface to every creased memory underneath.

Today I’m finishing a late-nineteenth-century plat map of Harrowford drawn in iron gall ink. The river looks like a spine along its left edge, spinous processes of creeks and culverts splayed toward the city. The paper, cotton rag, had been stored badly—folded in the middle until the fold became a tear, tears became absence. I’ve been filling absence with Japanese tissue as thin as onion skin, painting lines of pigment to bridge the gap between then and now. On the Rook River estuary, someone wrote “Bottle Mill” in a neat copperplate hand, a mill long since burned down and replaced with condominiums that all have the same slate roofs and unhappiness.

The bell over the front door tings, and I hear the drag and scrape of cardboard across the threshold. Deliveries come through the alley. Clients who come through the front door are either lost or looking for a miracle.

“Just a moment,” I call, because miracles take time.

I put the brush on its porcelain rest, glance to see the paper’s not drying too quickly under the light, then wipe my hands on my apron and go out into the front. Palimpsest & Co. is three rooms: my studio at the back, a small narrow display room with a glass case of antique compasses and brass dividers, and this front space with the door and the bell and a scarred counter where I pretend business is straightforward. The man in the doorway is not one of my usuals. He wears a rain jacket even though the winter sky outside is crisp and blue. The jacket is unzipped, and he’s thin under it, as if he came inside and left half of himself on the sidewalk.

The box he’s set on the counter is a tube, thick-walled and water stained. There are two shipping labels, one pasted over the other. The top one is blank except for my name in block letters and the address of my shop, 611 Iron Street, Harrowford, no return address. My name looks like it’s been underlined by a hand that didn’t realize it was doing it.

“Ms. Arlen?” he says.

“Yes.”

“I was told to bring this to you. From a—” He looks past me, as if the name might be written on the ceiling. “She didn’t give me a name. Just twenty dollars and your address.”

“You took money from a stranger to bring a stranger a box.”

He shrugs. “I took the bus.” His voice carries a thread of local accent, the vowels muddy, the kind you only hear if you grew up here and stayed.

“Did she say when she’d be by?”

He shakes his head. “Looked like a student. Backpack. Short hair, some sort of—” He gestures at the air around his own head. “Stripes?”

“Stripes,” I repeat.

He nods. “Hair. Stripes. You’ll see.”

He leaves before I can decide whether to pay him for his trouble. The bell tings again, letting the winter morning in, and then the room is just me and the tube with its water stain like a country outline across the cardboard. I turn it in my hands. The water line runs diagonal, dried to a pale tide mark, and something about its angle catches in me like fish hook. It’s familiar. Everything is familiar in this town, and then sometimes, out of nowhere, it crawls out and looks back at you with new eyes.

The cardboard cap is intact. I ease it off with my thumbnail. Inside, the paper is rolled tight but not too tight, the way someone rolls a map who understands it is a set of possibilities wrapped around itself. I slide it out onto the counter.

The first thing that hits me is the smell, which sounds ridiculous, but people forget that old paper has a scent. It is wheelhouse and basements, dry ink, mildew chased by sun. If I believed in ghosts, I’d say they smell like this—like things left behind and kept. The second thing is that the paper isn’t paper at all but vellum—calfskin, scraped smooth until it can mislead you side-eyed in certain lights. It’s been wet and then dried, the tell-tale wave of it, but whoever dried it had at least set weights along the long edges to keep it from cockling entirely. There’s the faint pucker where water pooled, and when I run my palm above the surface I can feel the ghost ridges as a blind person reads faces.

I unroll it to the width of the counter and place bean bags along the edges to keep it from curling back up. The map is hand-drawn, black pigment with occasional notations in red. It’s a street plan, turnover-of-the-century style, the city’s grid stubbled across a part of Harrowford I know too well: the old tannery district along the Rook, north of Basin A. Six blocks squared, miniature rectangles for buildings, block numbers, street names with their municipal predictability—Thirteenth, Fourteen, Fifteenth. The river runs east-west here, bent like someone’s snapped its spine. There is a pale wash of blue showing the river’s shape twenty years ago when the city straightened part of it, a later addition that doesn’t quite line up. Whoever drew the base was precise. Whoever added to it later used a hand that almost but not quite matched the first.

My heart steps sideways.

In the lower left, by the title block that reads “Proposed Amendments to Survey of the Rook River NE Quadrant,” there’s a small black sign, a symbol, no bigger than a fly. Three prongs and a line through them. No surveyor uses it. No one, in fact, uses it except my father, who scribbled it in margins of his field notebooks when he was reminding himself to double check a measurement that made no sense at all. He told me once, when I was ten and trailing him down by the pump house, that the symbol meant: not safe to assume. I had drawn it in the dust with the side of my shoe while he locked the chain gate. He’d been laughing then, or pretending to laugh, because he’d been talking about the way the river never agreed to stay put.

He went into Basin A on a Wednesday night in March and did not come out. No explosion. No spectacular anything. He was there, and then he wasn’t, and the river ran on keeping its own counsel. The city called it an accident and wrote a check. The check paid for my last semester and most of the shop. It did not shut the doors behind the questions like they hoped.

I pick up the magnifier and bring it over the symbol as if my father’s hand will be there under it, ink ridges like thumbprints. The sweep of the line is clean, as if drawn slowly. The pigment sits high on the vellum’s surface, not wicked in, which means gum arabic in the ink—the older style. The title on the map is written in a mid-aughts municipal hand, though, not 1900. The map is wrong in time the way dreams are.

I turn on the raking light and angle it so it grazes the surface, shadows thrown by every line. Even old vellum sits up under raking light and tells you where it’s been touched. I can see where a pencil has been used and then erased, where a fingernail snagged and tore. There are pinpricks at the corners. Whoever used it tacked it to a board, shifted it, tacked it again. Each pinprick shines like a star.

I breathe in and out, slow, like I tell anxious clients to do when they hand me their grandfather’s war map and say, “Please don’t make it worse.”

There’s red pencil drawn across the streets in a jag—so faint I didn’t see it until the light kissed it into existence. The line isn’t smooth; it’s been drawn in a series of nervous stops and starts, as if the hand that held it listened to something else while it moved. It begins in the margin, as if coming from off the page, and it snakes up Thirteenth Street, turns toward the river, cuts through a block like the drawer couldn’t abide being constrained by buildings, then stops at the corner of Eleventh and River. That corner has no building now; it’s a fenced triangle of weeds where the city planted a sign about a future park that never happened.

At the corner beside the red stop, there’s a word written, so faint it might have been drawn with pressure only, the graphite having vanished to the oils of fingers. I turn the raking light until the shadows settle into letter shapes. It takes a minute for my eyes to translate the relief into words.

take nothing, it says. not even the mistakes.

The hair rises along my arms.

I turn off the light and go into the back and fetch the UV lamp. Ultraviolet is gentle and unforgiving. It will show me every oil stain, every path a moving finger took fifty years ago, fluorescence where someone traced a line with highlighter in a moment of modern vulgarity. I flick the switch and bathe the vellum in invisible light until the fluorescing details bloom. There is something in the margins that the visible spectrum did not show me. A date stamp, faint, in violet that glows under the UV: MAR 14 1998. I know the shape of the one that used to sit on my father’s desk because I used to stamp the blotter when he was at the door. The day before he went missing.

The shop bell tings again. I start, turning the UV off with a click. The map sleeps in its colors on the counter, looking ordinary and obscene.

A woman stands in the doorway, the bright cold woven through her hair and the shoulders of her wool coat. She’s mid-forties, a little younger than me, with a face built for withholding jokes until the right moment. The badge she shows me is discreet, leather-worn, and tells me what the posture would have already.

“Neve Arlen?” she says.

“Yes.” My voice sounds like I’ve been out on the river for an hour without speaking to anyone.

“I’m Detective Pallas Reed.” She tucks the badge away. “Can I come in for a minute?”

“My sign says by appointment.” When anxious, aim for dry. It’s a strategy that sometimes works.

“So does murder,” she says, and the dry slides off my mouth and leaves nothing useful behind.

“It’s a bad joke,” she adds after a beat. “I’m sorry. I never learned how to lead with the good part.” She glances at the roll of vellum unrolled on my counter and in the glance my entire body wants to step sideways in front of it. I don’t. If I step in front of something these days, it’s as good as telling someone where to look.

“What can I do for you, Detective?”

“Rowena Pell. Does that name mean anything to you?”

“No.”

“She’s a graduate student at the university, local history. Spends a lot of time with archival maps, according to her advisor. She called a number last week that belongs to your shop, left a message about wanting to talk to you about—” There’s a small notebook in the detective’s hand, and she flips it open with the muscle memory of someone who has done that motion in cars and kitchens and morgues. “—old municipal survey methods and the possibility of acquisition. That ring any bells?”

“I get those calls sometimes,” I say. “Survey methods are not as sexy as you’d think.”

“Everything is sexy to someone,” Detective Reed says. She drifts nearer without touching anything. Her coat is city-issue warmth. Her eyes are river-colored, a joke only to me. “When you didn’t call her back, she called again. Your message box was full. She came by. My partner talked to the sandwich guy two doors down; he says she was standing out front ten minutes yesterday. When the door didn’t open, she left.” She looks at me a moment like she’s affording me the chance to say that I opened it later and waved.

“I was at the county records office,” I say, which is true. “The old halftone atlas for 1902 is brittle as an oath. I told them I’d sit with it while it got digitized in case the binding went. My message box is full because everyone who owns paper thinks it is dying. Why are you asking me about a graduate student?”

“Because she’s missing.” Reed says it without embroidery. “She didn’t go home last night. Her phone’s off or dead. Her mother filed the report at two this morning. She says Rowena never doesn’t check in. The last ping off her phone was near the river.”

“What does that have to do with me?”

“She wrote ‘Harrowford Survey—Arlen?’ on the last page of her notebook,” Reed says, and there’s a brief mouth-twist that might be apology and might be an itch. “Also, you worked with her father ten years ago on a map of the Harrowford tanneries. Charles Pell. He wanted to hang it in his office.”

“The tanneries map was for a man who wanted to sell the land under them,” I say. “I only remember the way people use maps. Not their names.”

“A useful discipline.” Reed follows me when I move back to the worktable and flick on the small desk lamp. The plat map waits on the counter, unremarkable by its own standards, and I want the room to think about anything else. She touches the glass case with the compasses with one knuckle, the way a person politely taps a fish tank. “He committed suicide, Charles Pell, three months after he sold the land. Those condos are all the same slate roof you can see from the river road. You probably know them.”

“I do.”

Reed nods, and now I can feel the question that is not about condos tighten in the air like a wire.

“What do you think about the river?” she asks.

“It doesn’t hold a grudge,” I say. “It also doesn’t forgive.”

She looks at the map again, and her eyes do that tiny focus that tells me which direction trouble is traveling. I follow her gaze to the corner of the vellum where, despite my desire to seem casual, one of the bean bags has shifted and left the edge to curl up. The date stamp ghosts the curl. MAR 14 1998. I set my palm next to it as if I’m steadying the whole table.

“That’s an interesting piece,” Reed says.

“Client matter,” I say.

“Your client is missing,” she says. “Or she’s not your client, and this has nothing to do with her. In which case, I’m wasting both our mornings, and I could go back to the river and deal with the other matter we have down there.” She stops. Her jaw muscles ease and go hard again, a tiny weather pattern under her skin. “I’m not here to seize your property, Ms. Arlen. I am here to ask whether a young woman who pursues paper trails might have brought one to your door, and whether that trail leads to a place where someone can stop being a student and start being a statistic.”

I look at her for a moment because it’s my habit to see if a sentence will echo before I decide what to do with it.

“This came an hour ago,” I say finally, and I tap the tube with one fingernail. “No return address. Someone paid a guy in a rain jacket to walk it over. He says she had striped hair.” I touch the vellum, not the words. “It’s part old, part less old. And it carries a mark I recognize.”

Reed waits the patient wait of a person who has been taught to wait, who has leaned against railings, against bad coffee machines, against the side of grief and made leaning into a function.

“My father worked for the city,” I say. “Survey crew. He carried a stamp like that in his jacket pocket; he liked to do things in pairs—the real stamp on paper and then a phantom one on the inside of his coat, so he could feel the date pressing into his chest.” Talking about him feels like scraping something with a tool made for scraping something else. “He disappeared the day after that stamp was used, on Basin A. No one ever stamped that date again in my house.”

Reed’s eyes shift to the corner where the red line thickens with stops and starts. The line is the kind that draws your eyes whether or not you meant to look. “And that line,” she says.

“Whoever drew it took it to Eleventh and River,” I say. “They wrote ‘take nothing’ there, as if a map can be an instruction and not an observation.”

“Eleventh and River,” she repeats, not really to me this time.

“Yes.”

“We pulled a car out of the water there at dawn,” Reed says. “Silver Honda, license plate that belongs to Rowena Pell. It had been in long enough for the silt to find its way into every seam. There was no one in it.” She looks up, and her eyes are the color of a place where the river goes shallow and looks like it is thinking about light. “We were going to go public in an hour.”

“They left a map on my counter,” I say, as if Reed did not just say what she said. “With that corner circled in their way. And a date that makes anything I say about it colored untrustworthy.”

“Do you know what that symbol there means?” she asks. Her finger hovers above my father’s three-pronged line as if touching it would summon him, and neither of us expect anything that easy.

“Not safe to assume,” I say.

“Then don’t,” Reed says gently. “Don’t assume you have to carry this on your own. Let me help you hold it up and look under it.”

It’s a nice offer. It sounds like the sort of sturdy furniture someone else made in a different time, all mortise and tenon and no nails at all. I don’t know what to do with nice offers. People assume that because you fix delicate things you are fragile. They forget you spent years pressing weight onto paper exactly at the points it could bear.

“Do you have a card?” I ask.

She gives me two. The second one says her cell number and nothing else. “Call me when you breathe,” she says.

After she leaves, the room changes temperature by a degree that is mostly imaginary and entirely unignorable. The river might as well be in the walls, in the plaster, in the hair that has escaped the braid at the back of my head. I go back behind the counter and roll the vellum gently from one edge to the other, letting the images melt and reform under my hand. A street becomes a crease becomes a pale idea. The red pencil line moves with it, a vein under skin.

When I’ve got it rolled to the place where the title block is half-hidden under the curl, I see something I didn’t before: there’s another layer of graphite underneath the red, a shadow of the word not. Written twice against each other, then erased. Something in me tightens like the small muscles along your spine do when you watch a slow accident you can’t stop.

The phone on the wall vibrates angrily in its charger because the ringer is broken and I’ve never bothered to fix it. I put the map down, wipe my hands, and pick it up.

“Palimpsest,” I say.

Static. And then a breath. For a second, the old superstitions rise and try to put words in my mouth, the kind that say rivers can dial phones. I swallow them back.

“Neve?” It’s a woman’s voice, thin like it has been stretched.

“Yes.”

“I didn’t know if you’d stayed.” A laugh dissolves into the line and comes back strange. “If I say ‘striped hair’ you’ll hang up.”

“Rowena?” I say cautiously.

Silence and then: “I’m sorry.” The apology is so reflexive I want to reach through the line and move it out of the way.

“Where are you?” I ask.

“Answer something for me. When you touch the map, does it feel like a pulse?” A small wet sound, a muffled something. “They told me to ask you something you could only answer if you had it. I’m not—” The breath breaks. “I don’t have time. I thought I did.”

“Where are you?” I say again, and even I can hear the steady in my voice that surprises me when it appears, the same steady I used when the paramedic told me I couldn’t go in with her because they were doing all they could and Ambulance has rules.

“Between Eleventh and the river,” she says, and the line fills with a roar, not water, but breath and wheels and distance. “It’s never where you think. Tell her she should look for the part that was covered and write it down before someone tells her she imagined it. Tell her I’m not the first.”

“Tell who?”

The line dies like I stepped on it. I hold the dead plastic rectangle against my ear until my arm aches. When I put it back in the charger, the charger makes its angry beetle sound and tells me in its own way that nothing I plug into anything today will give me more power than I had this morning.

I stand in the quiet. There is a quality to certain days, an elastic resistance that tells you when you push on them, they are going to push back.

I take the map to the studio table where the light is honest, and I lay it flat. I do what I always do when someone brings me a thing that is part precious, part evidence, part threat. I square my shoulders to it, clean my brush, and begin with the edges.

At five-thirty on a Wednesday in late October, I have the back of a nineteenth-century repeater open on a velvet mat, and the tower that has slept for a century clears its throat in the fog.

It isn’t supposed to. The clock in the old mill tower hasn’t worked since my grandmother was young and the river still turned belts and gears. Folks in town used to set their bread to rise by its four quarters and a hearty twelve. The fire of 1913 took that and a lot else besides. A hundred years of birds, bats, and weather turned the mechanism into a sculpture. And yet this morning, somewhere up on Prospect, a hammer knocked against bell metal in a tentative way that went right through the glass of my shop door and through me.

“Don’t you start the day with omens,” I tell the repeater, because it’s the only thing I can say it to and not lose business.

The repeater says nothing philosophical. It’s still a little numb. I touch the tiny, knurled screw I freed an hour ago, then the polished bridge. The balance wheel is a sun on a spring, pulsing. When I draw the slide on the case, a coiled gong will spell out the time in sound. Minute repeaters are small miracles. They carry the idea that what you cannot see you can hear, that there is always another way to tell the truth.

Outside, the river braid below Hollow Street is black and flat. The fog on its back moves like breath. If I lean, I can see the smear of Prospect Hill, thin as if someone erased part of the town and left a thumbprint. The tower spears it. There are hawks that nest under its eaves, and there is a story older than me that says the brass bell up there can wake the dead.

The repeater begins to tick with a steadiness I haven’t managed all week. I lift the loupe from my eye, the world blooming from magnified brass to my small bench and my cat, who lifts his head and narrows his green eyes at the movement of my hand. His name is Balance because I never could afford on-the-nose. He is the color of tarnished nickel.

“Tell me,” I say to him. “When you dream, are you ever stuck behind glass?”

He yawns wide enough to show me every tooth he has. He is, unlike me, satisfied with the world as it is.

The bell on the shop door goes, a softer note than the repeater promises, and old cold comes in. I glance up and recognize Mr. Holt as he takes off his hat like a man who remembers his mother’s eyes every time he crosses a threshold. Eben Holt is older than my mother by fifteen years and older than everyone he’s ever befriended by ten in the mind. In summer he smells like hay. In winter he smells like wool and old books. Today, he smells faintly singed.

“Mara,” he says. I’ve been Mara to him since I fixed his father’s Cunningham after the hunting accident I still don’t ask about. He does not make a habit of buying new. He admires things that have been forced to last.

“Mr. Holt. You smell like a stove.”

He sets a small traveling clock on my counter, and for a second my stomach drops, not because it’s unfamiliar, but because it is.

It’s the size of my palm when it’s folded into its leather case, the kind of clock people took on trains when trains had dining cars with real silverware. The leather is scorched along the bottom edge, char blistered, the strap that keeps it closed cracked straight across. There’s a crescent missing out of the face crystal like a bite. And scratched very lightly on the polished back plate, almost erased by time and cleaning cloth, are three letters and a year: J.K. 1979.

I set my fingers on the counter so I don’t pick it up right away like a hungry person.

“Where did you get that?” I ask.

Eben’s mouth tightens. “A box of junk came in with old papers for the historical. The trust is doing that new display for the centennial, you know the one. This fell out in the basement when Mrs. Larkin tripped over the doorstop.” He looks down. “It landed on its back. It rang when it hit. Like a cough. Scared her half to death. I said I knew someone who could tell me if there was anything left inside it that wasn’t just memories. Can you see to it?”

I reach and run my finger along the scorched leather because I guess I need to touch it before my brain will sit with what it is. My father had two traveling clocks. One he kept perfect. One he kept in the glove compartment for emergencies. The perfect one was German, fat-bellied, loud as honest laughter. The glove-compartment one was English and compact, the leather like this, the mechanism thin. Once, when I was seven, we took it up to the tower because he said he wanted to see how wrong the dead could be.

It was misting that day too, the stone slick, and in the belly of the tower, pigeons cooed like old men. We knelt on the floor with the clock and a thermos of coffee and an egg sandwich wrapped in wax paper. He let me draw the slide and hear what eight-thirty sounded like. He showed me that sound is just a way of measuring small time with one’s ears. When we left, he put that clock in his coat, and it smelled like tobacco for a week from his clothes. That was the winter before he took a job in Boston on the Red Line and stopped being a man everyone in Morledge waved to and started being a man people felt sorry for when they saw my mother on Church Street. Six months after that, he took his toolbox to a house call on High Garden and never came back.

I open my hand and take the clock without more conversation. It is cold, as if it has been sitting out in the night. It weighs less than memory suggests. The hinge is gritty. I half expect Balance to hiss. He only sniffs the air like smoke has stories.

“You can try,” Eben adds grimly, almost as if permission needs to be softened with a warning. “Don’t, you know, do that thing you do where you decide you know how it was made and then make it that way no matter what.”

“I am a humble servant of original intent,” I tell him, because we have joking long enough to make it count. “Is the trust really done in time? The town is having a party, Mr. Holt. I’ve seen the bunting.”

“They hired a man from Worcester with a laser level to take charge of the tower.” His tone makes taking charge sound like theft. “Got a degree. Has opinions about lubrication.” He lifts his hat now that he’s inside and stands holding it like an offering. His hair is a halo of white around a scalp that the weather does not touch. “Your grandfather put that mechanism to rights twice before the fire and three times after. Your father… well.” He doesn’t say wasn’t asked. He doesn’t say you weren’t. “They wanted new eyes. You understand.”

“I understand,” I say, which is true in the way understanding is an engine that you keep running so it doesn’t lock.

He nods and waits while I set the clock on my mat and take the back off the traveling case. The tinny smell under the leather is old salt and scorched glue. The brass inside looks tired but not destroyed. The mainspring is intact. The gong coil, the heart of the repeater sound, is still tight against its tiny pillar, an uncanny blue that metal gets when it’s seen the wrong kind of heat and refused to break.

“You might’ve got lucky,” I say.

“I’m eighty-one,” Eben says. “Luck at this stage is a man who remembers where he put his shirt.”

I laugh. “Come back in two days. That’s what I tell all the big donors. And I’ll tell you what she wants.”

He lays money on the counter before he thinks better of it. I don’t push it back. There are weeks I polish the same carriage clock twice to calm the books and still ask Lucia two doors down to add an extra day-old bag of rolls to my bag.

“And Mara?”

“Mm?”

“If it does speak,” he says, and some of the wool falls out of his voice, the bookishness burned off by worry, “listen fixed. Not like a story. Like you might listen to a machine that remembers more than you want it to.”

“I always do,” I say, even though that is exactly the opposite of how I do it, and he knows.

When he’s gone, Balance hops up and puts his front paws on the counter to stare at the empty place where Eben’s hat was. He is affronted by hats. Then he climbs to the display in the window and writhe-naps among the pawned wedding gifts. Fog condenses in fine beads on the glass.

I put the traveling clock under the lamp. Someone has hammered the screw that ought to be a screw flat, as if the last person to open this had only one tool and forward motion. The lever that lets the repeater engage has a burr. The rubber that braces the back plate has become sap. I fix all the obvious insults first. The work is old work, not difficult, almost soothing. The pieces respond to being seen. When I draw the slide that first time, the sound is hesitant but clear. Eight low thunks and one high chime, so it thinks it is eight-oh-five. The notes ring under my nails. Sound travels through bone.

When I look again, the letters are still faint on the plate. J.K. 1979. My grandfather was James, not John, and he didn’t scratch his work on the pieces—he said the repair should disappear behind a flawless face. My father was Joseph. My father did scratch, because he always liked coming back to his own ghosts. The year could be the winter we took it to the tower.

I set it aside and make myself work on the repeater under my loupe because paying jobs win, and the money from Eben will keep the oil circle on the ledger page another month. Sound in this shop lifts and falls. You don’t notice how loud silence is until you spend your days in a chorus of ticks. People imagine a clock shop is quiet. It’s not. It is like being in a roomful of content birds.

Lucia comes in at nine-thirty with a paper bag gone a little transparent with butter. She sets it down where dust is not allowed and pulls a roll from the top. She is the only person I permit this. Her cappuccinos are crimes against decency. She has hands like a sculptor’s, strong with flower and heat. Her hair frizzes. In this building, everything frizzes.

“Have you heard?” she asks around a mouthful. “They took the tarp off the western dial. You can see the new gilding from the square like it’s a coin in the sun.”

“It’s foggy,” I say.

“Like a coin in a wet pocket then.” She plops into the chair opposite the counter as if the shop were her kitchen. “You going to the dedication? They were pasting up posters at dawn. The mayor hugged the bell like it could hug her back.”

“I’m working Saturday.” It is not a lie. I recess two brass bushings and pinch my tongue at the same time so I won’t say the other part, which is that watching someone else wind that mechanism would be like being forced to watch a stranger make your mother laugh.

Lucia swallows and wipes her fingers on her jeans. “You’ll regret being stubborn when there’s free cider. Oh, hey, I found this in a box of sugar packets.” She pulls a folded paper out of her pocket and hands it over. It’s old, brittle at the edges. The town crest is on the top in black ink from a ribbon. Below, in a hand I recognize because it taught me to count heartbeat seconds, there is a list that says: trap, missing tooth, south weight clevis cracked, something unreadable where a coffee ring ate the ink. And then in my father’s little backhand, three numbers underlined twice: 12:13.

“Where did you—”

“I told you. Sugar packets.” She is unconcerned about the provenance of things. “Maybe your dad liked his coffee sweet.”

“He used sugar when he was trying to give up cigarettes.”

“Would you look at that,” she says, as if I found a four-leaf clover, not a line of numbers that will wedge in my head like a song. “It’s like he never left.”

I fold the paper along the old fold marks and don’t say anything.

By noon the fog has risen and spread, so we are in a pearl. The light in Morledge is always particular—long winters, short summers, a river that makes its own weather. Crows own the afternoon no matter what the weather does. They come to the alleys and shout at dumped stock and half-eaten bread. I eat two rolls and fight the impulse to stand on the porch and stare up Prospect at the tower the way you stare at an ex in a shop window. People pass my door with their collars up, and I fix another watch whose face someone sat on at a wedding.

At three, a man from the trust named Burr stops by to say there will be a second gala if the mechanism runs. He leaves a flyer I put under a book to keep the paper from migrating into my head. At five the bank teller whose mother collects clocks brings in one with a cat that chases a mouse around its face. I tell her I charge extra for cats. She says the cat hurts no one. At six, the streetlights pop and hum up the road, cones of light damped by the fog into lemon stains.

I should go home. My home is an apartment above this shop and two down, a scoop of rooms under the roofline that make me stoop in the corners. I should feed Balance fish that smells like the sea was angry at the can. I should take my boots off. Instead, with the street gone soft and the glass of the door dim with the breath of the river, I wind the traveling clock and let its mainspring catch. I draw the slide. Thick silence pools. Then a single high chime.

The cat lifts his head. The hairs along my forearm lift too.

“There you are,” I say to air and brass. “You remember the one.”

I take the back off again and wipe the coil with a bit of soft cloth in circles until I can feel when its skin stops resisting. When a thing has been partially burned, it wants to be all the way one thing or the other. You have to tell it it’s still what it was and always will be.

By eleven-thirty, my eyes ache from the loupe and the light, and I give up the shop for the apartment. The stairs smell like old varnish and yeast. Upstairs, the radiator ticks like a metronome that has lost its sense of humor. I put a pan on for soup and stand in the darkness of my own kitchen while the tower gets ready to do what it’s going to.

It is easy to be alone in Morledge past ten unless you are under the bridge or pressing a glass in Lucia’s kitchen while she puts away the day. If you stand in my window at this hour, though, you can see the smear of the square and the taller shape at the hill’s edge. You can hear the river in different languages: slap, hiss, chuff. Somewhere someone laughs and it carries to me like something heard while underwater. I feel the old itch in my hands that always arrives when I’m not working. I don’t pick up my phone. I don’t call my mother. I don’t make a list. I don’t feed the part of me that wants to drive up Prospect with a flashlight like a tourist.

My soup scalds the top of my mouth. Balance does the cat thing with his jaw like the air is flavored. He perches on the back of the couch and watches the window the way cats watch fresh kill fields.

At twelve, the quarter chimes echo. They are bright and slightly off—too new to be music yet, the new gold too eager, the hammers finding their memories. I set my spoon down. The hair along my arms salutes again, but not just from the sound, from the knowledge that someone with hands I don’t know is up there, has been up there, is petting a mechanism that knows my name.

Then the hour.

One. In the beating of the first strike, the metal declares the air around it a body. Two. The sound grows a spine. Three. The glasses in my sink tremble like they are a chorus called to stage. Four, five. I count in my head without meaning to. Six echoes like a boot in a stairwell. Seven marches the crows out of the trees. Eight. Nine. I put my hand on the window because I am an idiot and think feeling it is a way to be closer to it. Ten. Eleven. Balance’s tail fluffs. Twelve.

Silence. The kind that means the end of something. On the other side of the glass, the fog holds its breath with me.

Thirteen.

It is not like the others. Not just because it shouldn’t be there. It is longer by a breath. It finds the pipes in my walls and sends them singing. The glass over my stove fractures itself at the corner with a worm of white. Somewhere on the street, a man shouts, and then someone laughs, and then someone else swears. A dog whines two buildings over and an engine dies. For a moment, under it all, there is the faintest sense that the sound comes from below rather than above, a bell rung underwater.

Balance leaps flat-footed from the back of the couch and hits the rug, then shoots under the chair with his belly dusting the floorboards. My hand prints on the window. I don’t realize I haven’t breathed for a count of three tens until I have to sit.

My phone rings.

It is a dry ring, not one I’ve chosen, the setting I never changed. The number is hidden. It glows white in my hand like a coin sunken somewhere and found by a diver.

“Hello,” I say. I don’t know why I keep my voice low.

For a second all I hear is the line, the small electricity of connection. Then I hear it, almost like it’s far away or caught under fabric. A tick. It’s the cadence of a clock, but faster than comfort, fifty beats a minute like an anxious heart.

“Mara?” says a voice. Male, mid-older, roughened by time and something that rubbed it the wrong way for an hour too long. The voice that says my name holds it like a tool I handed over and should never have.

“Who is this?” I ask. My mouth is dry. Balance’s eyes are two coins in the dark under the chair.

“You hear it,” the voice says, as if it’s not a question, as if time has only two categories now: people who heard and people who didn’t.

“I heard the bell,” I say. “If that’s what you’re—”

“No.” The word is small. “Not the tower.”

Silence blooms, then something like breath, then the tick louder for a moment, as if the phone has been lifted closer to the body of a clock than a mouth.

“What, then?” I ask.

“The same mistake,” the voice says. Each syllable feels laid down careful, like a watchmaker setting jewels. “Don’t let them wind it again.”

The line crackles. Under the words, under the tick, there is a sound like water finding a grate. I am standing at my own window with my fingers going cold, and the fog outside moves as if it has just been told a secret.

“Who is this?” I ask again, and I think my own voice sounds like new glass does, waiting for what the world will do to it.

There is a low noise and I think he is going to answer. I think he is going to say a name I haven’t had in my house for ten years. What I get is the click of a line disconnecting, the extraordinary suddenness of a world without a ticking on it, and the long echo in my chest of a thirteenth chime that has nowhere to go.

The town came back the summer the lake died.

It didn’t return all at once, the way a dream lands intact in your head on waking. It rose in suggestions: a line of stones that used to be a wall, the shoulder of a road resurfacing like a pale bone, the stumps of the old orchard with black teeth of bark grinning at sky. When they first called me in June to say the reservoir had dropped below sixty percent for the first time in a decade, I’d stood on the intake tower and watched gulls walk in places that used to be water. The air smelled like coins and rot. We were supposed to be tallying shortages and arguing over allocations. Instead, by July, the lake was retelling everything it had tried for forty years to forget.

I hadn’t seen Graycap since I was nine, since the day my mother packed our lives into cardboard and left notes on our bright refrigerator door for the neighbors who stayed to the end. The state offered money and the state took the valley, and Graycap—the school with its polio-shot tiles, the blue-steel bridge that trembled over the river, the clapboard houses with their low, stubborn roofs—slid under that obedient flood in the spring of 1983. The brochures called the new waterline a shore. People called it a future. They called my father an obstructionist. He called it a killing.

He died that September, chest weak as dust. We all left in a slow kind of panic. But memory is portable. The map of home rolls small in your back pocket whether you want it there or not.

“This is what I was talking about,” Sheriff Harlow said. He had a way of saying my name with too many consonants in it, like it was snagging on his tongue. “Ms. Vale. We got something out there you should look at.”

It was early, a white rag of fog across Trevino Lake, sun still sifting through. I parked on the dam crest, flashed my badge to the roadblock deputy, and followed Harlow’s pickup as it crabbed its way down the access road to the drawdown fields. The reservoir’s edge looked ragged and wrong, like a garment hem ripped up. Grass that had been underwater for four decades lay in pale mats. Where the waterline had dropped, delicate rings of salt dried to a chalk. Somewhere a heron made a vowel of itself and stalked through the shoals. The smell was sweet and dangerous, decomposition buttered across the heat.

I’d worn my boots because I know the kind of mud these places make—fine as flour until it swallows you shin-deep. The Sheriff had his hat on and that damp halo you get at the rim when the day pretends it will be kind and won’t. He carried his authority like a folded coat. His deputy, Sanchez, kept skirting the worst of it, eyes fixed on his own footing, like looking up was a sin.

The lake had pulled back forty feet in eight weeks. Where the blue water used to shoulder the dead trees, the stock of the old county road revealed itself, snaking along, disappearing, then reappearing as if it were shy. We walked along that remembered line, past a traffic sign so corroded it had become art. Someone had once painted over the words SLOW with a mustache. A brown, half-sunk rowboat rocked on its side in the mud, its bow pointing at the shore like an accusation.

“It’s just past where the bridge used to be,” Harlow said. “Or maybe it’s the bridge. Not like there’s enough left to call it anything.”

He gestured with his flat palm to the right. I could see the pilings, four of them, old concrete cylinders like blunt fingers, water-stained and now cut off at the knuckles. There were stories of kids diving from those pylons into the river to prove bravery, before the dam. I had stood on that bridge holding a wind-twisted cone of cherry ice and my father’s rough hand. The river had been full of power then, a wrinkled muscle.

“Mind where you step,” Harlow said. “It sucks you in worse by the pylons.”

“I know,” I said.

“I figured you might.”

We went slower. The mud gave perilously. My bootheels made a sound like a kiss each time the suction let go. Harlow pointed with two fingers at the far side of the nearest pylon, and at first it was just another shape in that shape-heavy landscape—angles where there shouldn’t be, rust like bruises. Then, as we drew closer, the geometry resolved. The sun knifed through the fog and laid a strip of brightness across it.

The car lay on its belly, half-spun, the driver’s side angled slightly downward, as if the last thing it had done was to attempt a turn it never finished. The paint could have been red once; now it was more rust and fisket-slime, a kind of living brown. The windshield had cracked like a spiderweb but held. The grill had the smile of a thing caught in embarrassment. There was a dent on the passenger fender like a fist had lost an argument with a mailbox. The water had carried silt into everything: the headlight cavities were cups of dirt; the wheel wells were bowls of it. A slick of oil rainbowed over a puddle at the low side, a grotesque beauty.

Sanchez stopped ten feet away, hand on the butt of his holster for no reason but habit. “We think it’s been here since,” he said, and trailed off, as if all those years had a hard stop, since before I was born, since my wrong marriage, since the last good winter—choose a hinge.

“Since we filled it. Since always,” Harlow said. “Most likely. Weren’t nobody noticed nothing go missing in any recent time.”

He squinted at me, trying to read the expression I refused to let move my face. I kept my voice in the place it goes when it’s just me and slurry and numbers. “Did you call State Bureau?”

“Not yet. We wanted you to see first, what with...”

He flicked his hand out toward the ribs of stone showing half a field beyond—what with the past trying on its bones.

“What with the hazard,” I said, to give him a way out. “A vehicle this close to the old crossing, you’ll get people coming down to look. You’ll have teenagers going home with their shoes on in their hands.”

He huffed a laugh. “You think they wear shoes anymore?”

“Sometimes,” Sanchez muttered, and then, unusably soft, “I hate this.”

I hated it too, in the particular way of someone whose job is to translate the problems of the physical world into things you can measure. In the spreadsheets back at the regional office, Lake Trevino was a shape and a volume. It was numbers with four decimals and big red warnings that policymakers ignored until their lawns went brown. It was nothing like this thing before me. It was nothing like a car sleeping under water for decades, the lake floor linted with the lives of the people who’d given way.

We stood a moment in that scoop of silence. A breeze moved across the mud in a shiver. Far up on the rim road, a news van idled, waiting. It would be a day before I’d see the helicopter.

I dragged my attention back into work. I looked at the slope, the way the old road fell toward the pylon and then dropped to the original riverbed. The river had used to be narrower here, fretting itself through a clutch of glacial boulders and then spreading to a calmer reach. People parked by the shoulder and walked down to fish. That was the habit of it: a man who had enough beers in him to tell his wife later he’d lost his wallet set his last one on the hood, forgot to pick it up. A boy in a letter jacket dared a girl. A girl, who assumed she was plain because everyone told her so, smiled down the girl with the braces and said it was impossible.

“Water’ll be down another foot by August,” I said. “I’ll get my crew to stake the perimeter. We’ll need a sign down on the road. Falling hazard, unstable substrate. The Bureau will want this taped off until they can—”

“Find a way to get the door open without it falling apart,” Sanchez said, as if he was afraid of adding the word body to the air.

“They can pull it,” Harlow said. He had taken off his hat and scratched the hairline groove it made in his forehead. He was a compact man. He had the permanent squint of someone who’d had too many summers on the baseball diamond. “We get a flatbed down enough—”

“Wait.” I stepped closer, then stopped, the mud making a treacherous suggestion. “Something’s...” I felt my heartbeat in my gums.

You expect the car to be empty, even when you know better. You expect the lake to have erased whoever it took, because erasure is simpler to carry. But there it was, in the driver’s seat: a posture that said person even before it said anything else, the geometry of the narrow shoulder bone lifting the cloth of the old shirt. The lake had swallowed and preserved and softened. The right hand was still on the steering wheel, a gesture frozen in the tenderest part of intent, the second before impetus resolves into action. Silt had gathered along the wrist like a bracelet.

“Oh,” Sanchez said. “Shit.”

“Don’t use that word,” Harlow said, but his voice broke on it like a cousin.

The truth is, you can’t look away. Thousands of days ago, someone drove this car with their knee, scratched under their chin with the back of that right hand, sang too loud to the radio. In one of the salvaged files from the Graycap public library, the list of people who borrowed the new John Grisham is my mother’s and Mrs. Trisano’s and a third that is a smear, probably Vance. Names are one kind of ledger. Water keeps a different ledger.

For a long minute I did not look at the face because I didn’t want to reconcile my memory of faces with the fact of what water does. I looked instead at small things: the bit of cracked vinyl in the sun, the way reed grass had trapped itself across the hinge, the chain that had once held the mirror dangled onto the dashboard and ended in a clot of something dark.

“Don’t,” Harlow said, when I took a step left, into a better angle for seeing.

“I won’t touch,” I said. “I just need to look and then I won’t need to, again. All right?”

He gave me a look that was both the sheriff’s and the small-town boy’s. He knew who I was. He had been two classes over me. He had held the door to the church basement the night they gave us cider and folded maps of the new lake and told us how many recreational opportunities we’d have. He’d watched my brother tuck his chin into his collar and make a list of places he’d never see again.

“All right,” he said.

I edged forward onto a hanging knob of gravel where the mud had dried to gray scab. The low sun thrown through the windshield made patterns of light and shadow across the interior. The figure in the seat was, yes. A buckle strap crossed the pelvis. The shirt had been blue once, I think, something with a small plaid, the kind my father wore when he wanted to look like he was going to a meeting instead of a fight. The jaw had the collapsed look of long time. The left hand, I saw now, rested not on the shifter but on a book thickened to pulp.

A voice that was mine but not smoothed and professional said in my head: Not him. Not yet.

The mirror had fallen. It lay between the front seats to one side, its chain kinked like a knotted fishline. At the end of that chain, a small coin of metal glinted where the sun found it. The metal was darkened, its surface scummed, but worn smooth at the edges. In the middle the stamped image rose, familiar as the inside of my palm.

It was a bird with its wings sloped and open, a wren maybe, its beak pointed upward. There was a scar right across the bottom arc of one wing, a groove where the file I’d used had slipped, making a mark I tried to sand away and couldn’t without thinning the whole shape to nothing. I knew the exact curve of that scar because I’d put it there.

The chain was the cheap brass I’d used for everything I made in middle school. The way the jump ring was crooked was the way my rush and lack of good pliers made things crooked. I could see the one place where my father had pressed his forefinger to tilt the metal while I hammered, leaving a little clean crescent in the tarnish that never quite lost its echo even when years scabbed over it.

Something moved in my chest, not a breath. It was an old bird beating at the inside of a box. I had made that charm in the Thistle Middle School shop room the winter my father died and given it to Link because everything I made went to Link by default. He had smiled and said he’d hang it in his car when he had one, which had been a joke because he’d been fourteen with no way to get one, and then he was seventeen with a borrowed one he never brought home and then he was gone.

“Ms. Vale,” Harlow said. “Mara.”

I knew every person who had left Graycap angry and every person who had left Graycap in the way they could. I knew the kids who spit in the dirt when the county graders came and smoothed our street for the last time, and the men who stood around the coffee counter at the gas station like a chorus, and the women who screamed quietly into dish towels. I knew who had cars then and who didn’t and who borrowed and from whom. I knew the feel of my brother’s shoulder when he was trying to make himself be the kind of man our father would not call weak. I knew that we had never found him. We had painted his face on signs and taped them to telephone poles in a place that was going underwater. I knew that I had taught myself to expect my past to stay in its place because that was the bargain we all made when the dam was poured. I knew now how poor our bargain had been.

“Mara,” Harlow said again. “You all right?”

“I think I know whose car this is,” I said. My voice felt like I was scraping a shovel against frozen ground.

Sanchez looked at me with eyes that wanted instructions on how to be gentle. “Do you...?”

“No,” I said, and swallowed, and was embarrassed by the way my mouth didn’t want to work with me. “Not for sure. Not yet. It might not be. It’s an old red Ford. Lots of boys had red Fords then because red is cheap and Ford is always somebody’s uncle’s discount.” I could hear the dissociation in my own voice and hated it; I wanted to be my competent self and here I was, being a child in boy hand-me-downs because our mother had found another sale. “We’ll know when the Bureau pulls records. When they haul it and get the plate. When someone looks and tells me I’m wrong.”

“Or right,” Harlow said, and then, as if he wished he hadn’t said that. “Do you need me to walk you back up?”

“No,” I said. “I need to stand here a minute. Then I’ll call my crew and tell them to bring barricade tape and cones. I’ll put language on a warning sign that will make the county lawyer happy. That way when the teenagers come to look, they’ll know they have to skip period four to avoid the news vans.”

Harlow gave me the long no of a man who knows every kid’s tricks because he invented them. “I’ll get Sanchez to put up crime scene tape. The bureau’s on their way. Do you—do you want me to call your mother?”

“She doesn’t pick up before ten,” I said. “She teaches water aerobics to women my age who have already done the hard parts.”

“Those ladies will riot without her,” Harlow said.

We all stared at the car like it might do something, and it did, in a quiet way: something small inside, trapped when the windshield refraction shifted, made a tiny sound against the glass, a sand-grit rattle that made me flash on pennies on a school desk, the kind our principal counted when kids brought in candy money for the nurse.

I found my phone in my pocket. My hands were shaking now—fine tremors like I was cold. The heat was already so much that my shirt stuck to the small of my back and gathered in my armpits. I typed with care because I refused to have any of this be messy. I texted my crew—Ward, Ngozi, Lourdes. Stakes, tape, no-sag barrier, weighted cones. Old road, pylon one, bring the long poles. I texted the foreman who ran the maintenance yard to set aside more of the warning signs and decals and orange vests because reporters always think they can walk where they please and sometimes turn into caution cones if no one tells them different.

“That bird,” Sanchez said, too curious to stop himself but too decent to make the curiosity look like prurience. “The thing on the chain. What is that?”

“A mistake,” I said, and he straightened a little, stung, so I tried again. “A gift, from someone who was bad at making things and loved someone who was unfair to love. It’s a wren. Or I meant it to be. The wing’s wrong. My father said it looked like a quail who didn’t have enough to drink.”

Sanchez nodded solemnly, as if admitting a quail to the lake’s ledger.

“Okay,” Harlow said, settling into something that was work. He put his hat back on. “We put the line up. We get folks back from the edge. We wait for Glenn at Bureau to show and do his measuring and his tsk-tsk. We keep the damn kids home. If the press asks, I say that time is a circle and I’m not surprised by anything anymore. And you, Ms. Vale—”

“I’m going to walk the old road,” I said. “Only as far as where the bridge proper used to be. I want to see how many other things the lake is ready to spit out at me today. If it’s just the one. Or if it’s a season.”

He didn’t like that. I could see his jaw do the little shift men do when they understand they will not win. “Just don’t make me yell at you,” he said.

“You’re going to yell at me anyway,” I said. “Because later someone will hand you a transcript when this is all court, and it’ll look like I got too close.”

“And did you?”

“Probably,” I said, and started forward along the narrow strip where the gray scab of dried mud held. I passed the pylon, ran my hand, dictator-gentle, along the edge of it, felt the grit. Beyond, the old road sloped down until it disappeared into the kind of blue that isn’t water but a sky’s rumor reflected. I squinted, trying to read the topography the way my father had taught me, surfaces speaking their slow language. In the distance, the husk of a house’s foundation made a right angle no one had bothered to raze. It would be a million degrees by noon. The insects would set up their electricity. The law would come in and do their work and my job would be to keep people from sinking while they watched.

And somewhere past all that, all that protocol and signage and numbered photographs, I would tell my mother what I think I found. Somewhere in the afternoon, I’d call a number I hadn’t called in years—Link’s oldest friend, the one who had not gone to the lake the night Link did not come home—and say his name into that old space. The past had made its strange offering. I could feel the knot of it under the islanded ribs of my maps.

Behind me, Sheriff Harlow said something to Sanchez about coffee. The news van door thunked shut on a high sound of chatter. A dragonfly stuttered and hung and gave me a look as if to say I had no standing here. I kept going until the mud made its first treacherous noise and then I stopped, because I am not that kind of foolish, because the drowned keep their own counsel and I am only in the business of measuring their saturation.

I turned back and stood one more time exactly where I had stood before and looked at the car and the shape in it and the small coin of metal on its chain.

“I made that,” I said, in a voice so low it might have been only inside me. It didn’t matter. Even at that volume, the lake heard. It always does. It keeps what we give it and gives back at its own low tide.

On Founders’ Day, before the brass section had even warmed their mouths, the Council Oak started bleeding.
