That’s what the caller said, breathless and triumphant and way too awake for five-thirty in the morning. I had my boots half on and my coffee not yet poured. Trees don’t bleed, I told him. He assured me that this one did.

By the time I got to the green, a saw had already chewed a bright mouth into the air. A three-man crew in neon shirts stood on the sidewalk with a truck, cones, and a toolbox that looked like it had just lost a fight with a hardware store. A coil of yellow caution tape sagged between two park benches. On the other side of it, the Council Oak rose out of the town center like a ship’s stern, its limbs holding up the sky. The trunk had a girth that took two of my wingspan to hug, which I knew because I’d done that once, alone, on a dare I made to myself.

Red-white bunting scalloped the gazebo. Vendor tents slept along the far edge of the common, their sides fluttering. Someone had chalked parade arrows in white on the pavement. The air smelled like low tide and bacon fat and lilac. Seagulls cut the sky into white commas. Wake’s Point dresses up for Founders’ Day the way some people dress for job interviews: over-earnest, hoping to be chosen.

Addison Cho stood by the truck with his hands in his pockets and that smile that made you feel like you had just both been photographed from your good side. He wore the kind of navy jacket you don’t wear if you plan to do any work. A few months earlier he had bought the old shipyard at the edge of town and renamed it Wake Harbor, because developers always need to rename the thing before they dismantle it. He had also dumped a lot of money into the Founders’ Day fund and a new set of swings for the elementary school, and I would have liked him better if he hadn’t kept telling everyone how much money he had dumped into things.

“Ms. Harrow,” he said, as if we were friends. “This is an emergency.”

“I can tell by the chainsaw,” I said.

He gestured to the base of the oak. “Look. It’s sick.” He lowered his voice. “It’s dangerous.”

He was right about one thing: something was wrong. At the root flare, where the buttress roots broke the ground like humpbacks surfacing, a slick redness varnished the bark. It had streaked down into the mulch in ribbons, the way juice runs down a chin. A cluster of flies had convened with the kind of focus they usually reserved for picnic tables and trash cans. The gnats over the lawn had drafted in too, a thin haze caught in the sunlight.

I crouched, and the wet damp of morning soaked through my jeans. I pinched the bridge of my nose, and the day to my left came into focus—parade, kids, a brass band tuning, bunting—while the day to my right slid away. I reached out and touched the red with the back of my fingers. Warm. Sticky. It did not smell like maple syrup or the sour tang of slime flux. It smelled faintly metallic. It smelled like pennies.

“Where’s the wound?” I asked the tree. Then, to Addison, “Show me where this started.”

One of the crew, a guy with a goatee and the kind of hands that kept the memory of every job they’d ever done, knelt beside me and tapped a spot just above the largest buttress root. “Right there. We saw it on the pre-trip. Boss said it looked like a split.” He pointed to the thin, dark crease in the bark. “Then the…stuff.”

I wiped my hand with a rag from my back pocket until the red gleamed under my nails. “Turn that thing off,” I said to the guy holding the saw. “Now.”

He glanced at Addison.

“She’s the tree warden,” Addison said, with magnanimity, as if he were acknowledging a small, determined nation. “But we have the parade in three hours. And if that thing sheds a limb over the route, it’s on me.”

“I’m the tree warden,” I said, in case the neon shirts didn’t hear it the first time, and because saying it out loud always made the words sit square in my chest. “By the authority of Ordinance 14.3, no pruning or removal of any public tree can happen without my assessment and a permit. That” —I pointed at the chainsaw— “is not an assessment.”

Addison’s smile thinned. “Eliza—”

“Ms. Harrow.”

“Ms. Harrow, the town is going to be here. People. Children. My son will be on the fire engine, for heaven’s sake. You know we can’t have a hazard on the route.”

“No one is under this tree for the next ten minutes.” I set my clipboard on the mulch. “Give me that mallet.”

The mallet fit my hand like a familiar bottle. I rapped my way around the trunk, listening for hollows, listening for that drum-thud that says rot has eaten the heart away. The Council Oak answered with solidity. Dense. Sound. The wound, if you could call it that, creased the bark like a wrinkle around a mouth that had smiled too much. I tapped above it, below it, either side. The same thump. I bent, put my ear close. The gash was not big enough to be bleeding like that. It was barely a shave in the cambium.

The redness came thinner now, dark where air had already licked it, brighter where it had just slipped from the seam. It caught sunlight and made a gemstone color I had last seen on a stained glass window. A drop swelled, detached, hung from bark, fell into the mulch with a wet cuff.

“Tree doesn’t do this,” I said, mostly to myself.

“Then what is it?” Addison said.

I looked beyond the trunk to the sidewalk. The roots had lifted the concrete slabs in that slow, stubborn way roots have, turning them into ship hatches. The town had skim-coated tripping lips to appease wheelchairs and joggers. A vandal had spray-painted a smiley face over one of the slabs. A white ribbon of chalk ran right past, listing “PARADE ROUTE” in a hand I recognized as Bev Ramsey’s, who had taught third grade when I was ten and who could never resist labeling anything that might wander off.

A fly landed on my wrist and worried my skin. I flicked it away and reached for the little hand shovel I kept in my bag. “I need to check the root collar,” I said. “And the soil. Something could have leached in.”

Addison blinked. “Leached in?”

“From the sprinkler system. From the lawn treatment. From your conscience.”

His laugh was two notes too high. “Ms. Harrow,” he said again, “please.”

“Step back,” I told him, because whether I would find fungus or drainage or vandalism or some idiocy involving ketchup packets, I needed room to see. He stepped back. The chain-saw guy tried to look invisible. The goatee guy squinted, curious, the way people do when their day might still be a story later.

I scraped away mulch to expose the flare, the first big roots. Some bright genius had mounded mulch like a volcano around the trunk last summer, which would suffocate the bark if I didn’t keep digging it out. I made neat piles with my shovel, the way my father had taught me to sort screws—keep your line clean. The metal in my hand made a low whisper as it slipped through moist soil. Earthworms tensed, then settled. The mulch smoked a rich, green smell, and beneath it the dirt was dark, threaded with white mycelium the way veins thread an old hand. I paused when the shovel clicked against something not root, not stone. Something that gave a little and then resisted.

“Careful,” the goatee guy said reflexively.

“I supervise careful for a living,” I said.

“It’s like the time with the cedar by the library,” he said. “When those kids shoved fireworks into it? Remember that?”

“I remember the cedar,” I said. I also remembered the way the char had gone deep, the way the cylinder of rot had followed the wound and carved from the inside a dark perfect column, and the way the town council had argued about whether the tree’s ruin was an opportunity to install a new walkway. If you want to know how a place values its trees, wait until one becomes inconvenient.

I eased the shovel out and set it aside and used my fingers. The cool dirt sank under my nails. The thing under there was slick. I pushed the loam back and my hand found a curve, smooth and gritty. The sun was on my neck. A cheer went up across the green where the high school baseball team had just walked onto the lawn in matching jackets, and somewhere behind me Bev Ramsey started practicing on the megaphone.

I brushed away a layer of packed soil and the thing glinted, a thin half circle catching the morning light. For a second, my brain flicked through its catalog. Mason jar ring. Pull tab. The rim of a bottle. Then my fingers found the tiny snag of a prong, and I couldn’t breathe.

I had a flash picture, sharp as a postcard: a notice tacked up in the post office seven years ago, printed on someone’s home printer and then reprinted on three better printers as the weeks went by. The smiling woman in the picture looked past the camera with a squint that made her seem like she might laugh at any moment. Lenora Pike. Thirty-two. Five foot six. Last seen outside the town hall after the Save the Oaks meeting, wearing a yellow raincoat and an anchor ring on her right hand. Please call if you have any information. The first time I saw the poster I had rolled my eyes at another anchor in a town drowning in them—our coffee mugs have anchors, our underwear probably has anchors—but the ring in the picture had been different: hammered silver with a fat little anchor, the loop a perfect circle, the shank thick as a nail.

I wiped the curve clean. The light flicked. It was a ring, lodged half in dirt, and it was caught on something pale.

“Ms. Harrow?” Addison said, and the words were far away.

I brushed the dirt with my fingertip and a length of white showed itself like a secret. It was small as a pencil and smooth, and there were ridges, three of them, shallow scallops in the curve like the faint memory of knuckles. My mouth tasted like pennies. The flies rose and fell.

“Everyone back,” I said, but my voice had lowered, not for authority now, but because you lower your voice in church and at graves and sometimes even in kitchens. “No one touches anything.”

The goatee guy had the sense to set his hands up and step back. The chain-saw guy had gone white. Addison’s mouth was open, his tongue pressed to his top teeth as if his next argument had jammed there.

“What is it?” he asked, and because there were witnesses and because the words mattered, I didn’t say it. I took my phone from my pocket and dialed the non-emergency police number with a steady thumb.

“Wake’s Point Police,” said a voice I recognized as Officer Marty Bowen, which presented the possibility that I was still asleep and dreaming the part where high school and adulthood kept tripping over one another.

“Marty, it’s Eliza,” I said. “I need a unit to the town green. By the Council Oak.”

“What’s going on?”

“I have what looks like human remains.”

There was a small, precise pause, as if he had just found a hair in his breakfast. When he spoke again, his voice had adjusted. “Do not touch anything. Are you alone?”

“God, no,” I said.

“Put someone at the edge of the sidewalk to keep people back. Don’t tell anyone anything you don’t have to. I’m two minutes out.”

I slid the phone back into my pocket and looked up. A cluster of early walkers had drifted over and collected themselves at the sagging caution tape, as if it were the barrier between the real and the not. Bev had abandoned the megaphone and was craning on her tiptoes. I nodded to the goatee guy. “Ray, right?”

“Yeah,” he said, eyebrows climbing because I remembered.

“Can you keep people off the sidewalk there? Just until the officers arrive.”

“Uh, sure.”

“Don’t say anything.”

“I never do,” he said, and then looked over his shoulder at Addison and amended, “Mostly.”

I leaned back on my heels and looked at the root. The ring had a dent in the band, a tiny moon. In the scooped dirt, an ant explored and then changed its mind. The white curve under it—bone—hugged the root the way a child’s hand hugs a wrist. I wished, for once, that I believed in the green, kind world Nora Shaw used to talk about during yoga, where things returned to things and none of it hurt. The world had returned a lot here. It had returned fireworks to a cedar. It had returned gulls to the trash bins. It had returned a married couple’s rare china to the consignment shop and a fishing boat to the marsh with no one in it. It was returning this now.

“You can’t be serious,” Addison said softly. He had that look of a man whose day had been a straight line and then suddenly was a water's edge. His eyes slid from my hand to the ring and then up to my face. “Is that—”

“Back up,” I said.

“I’m not—”

“You want to be on the wrong side of this?” I raised my eyebrow in a way that would have made my father proud. My father had a way of weighing a person with his face. Conscience is heavier than most people can lift, he used to tell me, usually when loading something into the back of a pickup.

Addison stepped back, but only one step. The saw guy set his machine down like it was a sleeping animal. The other two crewmen retreated to the truck, where they studied their shoes with the profound attention of men who prefer not to see.

Two minutes, Marty had said. Two minutes took longer with the smell of pennies and damp soil and the sense that some enormous thing had shifted under the ground and we were standing on the lid of it. Across the green, the band finished playing the scales and struck a chord that made the hair on my arms lift. A kid ran past the far side of the oak with a streamer. His mother reached for his collar and caught him and pulled him back and hissed something do-not.

I breathed through my mouth and tried not to see the poster in the post office. The anchor ring. Lenora’s hair in the wind. The night in the town hall when the meeting had gone until ten-thirty and felt like two in the morning. I had not run the Save the Oaks movement—that belonged to the kind of people who were loud and brave and believed that standing in front of a machine with a banner could stop it. I had stood in the back with notes and ordinances and the town code open on my laptop. I believed in knowledge and in natural enemies: contracts, procedures, public outcry, fungus. Lenora had been the one who believed she could talk anyone into anything. The profiles said “advocate,” as if that were some kind of crime. The rumors later were mean, the way rumors get when a body won’t show up and grief has nowhere to sleep. She took the cash and ran. She got on a boat. She had a boyfriend in New Jersey. Everyone on a peninsula thinks escape means water.

I knew better. Water only ever brought things back.

Marty’s cruiser pulled to the curb with the economy of a man who had parked on this green his whole life. He got out and wiped his hand on his pants and looked ten years younger than the last time I’d seen him up close, which was absurd because he had been ten years younger then, too. He had the kind of face that had made high school easy and then turned into the kind of face people told things to before they meant to.

“Eliza,” he said, and then looked down. “All right. Okay. All right.”

“Cordon,” I said.

He turned, lifted his hand as if he went everywhere with an invisible megaphone, and said in a voice that was remarkably calm, “Okay, folks, the parade’s going to take a detour around the south side of the common. Please give the officers some— thank you— yes— no photos here, please.” The no photos part was sweet and doomed. Three camera phones already pointed at the ground in that greedy, acquisitive way. I stepped to block a woman’s angle without looking like I had stepped there.

“Do you want CSI?” Marty asked under his breath.

“Whatever passes for that in Wake’s Point,” I said.

“We’ve got Margo and a kit.”

“Get Margo and a kit.”

He keyed his radio and said the words. Addison took a breath. “Officer Bowen,” he said, moving in the space he thought was available to him. “I called Ms. Harrow because there’s a very, very, very dangerous—”

“Mr. Cho,” Marty said. “Now is not the time.”

“When is the time? We have a parade in—”

“Marty,” Bev said, as if they were still ten, “what’s happening?”

“Bev,” Marty said, “step back, please.”

“I run this parade,” Bev said, indignant.

“You can run it from ten feet further away.”

She recoiled, wounded, and then set her jaw and marched off, already dialing.

I crouched again, not to touch, but just to be near it. Sometimes you see a tree your whole life and never get to see the way it holds the ground. The Council Oak’s roots spread like a skirt. Each buttress was as wide as my thigh where it entered the earth, and the soil between them had humps where the fine roots breathed. The ring was lodged in the top inch of earth and snugged under a small feeder root the thickness of a pencil. The bone—was it finger? was it something smaller?—had either been placed there and trapped, or the tree had grown around it slowly, as trees do, incorporating fence wires, lost toys, and war.

The red slick had slowed. It caught in my fingerprints and dried sticky. Not sap, I thought. Not slime. And if not that, then—

“Could someone have—” Addison stopped, embarrassed by the words even as he made them. I knew the theory turning in his mind: that some ghoul had staged a thing under his nose to drag his name into the grave with the tree. The politics of accusation were already sloughing into place. There were cameras. There would be reporters by noon. If he had once texted Lenora, someone would know by dinner.

“No one poured a bucket of blood into the base of the Council Oak,” I said, keeping my voice even.

“Then how—”

“You asked me not to use words I don’t have to,” I said to Marty without taking my eyes off the ground.

He grunted assent. He was watching the crowd; I was watching the root.

“What are you going to do?” Addison asked, and for the first time that morning he sounded less like a man giving a speech and more like a person trying not to be cut in half by whatever this was.

“I’m going to stay with it,” I said. The breeze ran through the oak, and the leaves turned their pale sides up in a ripple, the way fish do when the sun moves. “And I’m going to listen.”

“Listen to what?” he said.

“The tree,” I said. It was only half a joke.

I don’t like second-person in my head, but sometimes it comes anyway. You did this, it says, and you did this, and there was that time you cut the root of a maple on County Road 3 too close to the trunk and you killed the thing even though you knew better. And also that time in high school with Marty that you never talk about because it would not be interesting to anyone but your own ghost. The rest of the time my head is full of Latin names and hazard ratings and things that can be measured with an increment borer. It felt good, even now, to have those lined up. Quercus alba. Heritage tree. Sound wood. Unexplained fluid from a superficial wound. Human remains present. Reported to authorities. Scene unsecured. Wide public exposure. Dripline resecured. Parade diverted. Words like stones in a pocket.

Margo came into the circle with her kit then, her gray braid looped and clipped against the back of her neck, her mouth tight in a way that said she had left her coffee on her porch with only one sip out of it. She looked where I looked and then looked at me.

“We can’t not see it,” she said.

“We can’t,” I said.

“Jesus, Eliza. On Founders’ Day?”

“That’s what they’ll say.”

“What will you say?”

I looked up at the oak. Its crown was full and even. There were no dead branches up there, no widow-makers poised. The thing had held this town together in storm and calm and weird teenagers and men with ideas. It would have kept doing it if we let it.

I wiped my palms on my jeans. The red had dried darker. “I’ll say the same thing I always say,” I told Margo, and when I said it, I believed it, and I wanted to. “The tree is not the hazard.”

But then I glanced at the ring again and the bone and the slow seep and felt the earth tilt under us in the smallest way. There are roots under this town that don’t belong to the oak. You learn the path of them by where people don’t step.

I stood up. “Marty,” I said.

“Yeah?”

“Call Detective Moreno,” I said. “Tell him that Lenora Pike might not have gone as far as we thought.”

The first thing you learn behind a counter like mine is that most people don’t think about a lock until it refuses to return the favor. Keys, levers, pins—those are abstractions until your door won’t open and your life is on the other side of it. I live in that space between intention and impediment. My shop smells like brass dust and cuttings oil, the sunlight walks across the pegboards every morning, and if I lean back in my chair at the right angle I can watch the street in the glass of the display case without anyone knowing I’m looking.

My father used to say, people think doors are the decision. The door is the theater. The decision is hidden in the frame.

He taught me on a dented practice cylinder when I was nine, my chin level with the vise. He would set me to work on a Schlage and go out to the lot to chain-smoke and talk to whatever car needed coaxing that day. When he died two summers ago, I kept his name on the window because I didn’t know how to be a shop by myself without something to hang the promise on.

Calder & Daughter, Locksmith & Safe Specialist, stenciled in gold leaf that has begun to bite at the edges. Marin Calder—me—alone in the stink of metal and the quiet, answering the phone with “Calder” on the second ring because first ring is too eager and third ring means you’ve lost them.

On a Tuesday in late October, the first person through the door was a man with a key bent like a question mark and a story to match. The second was a woman who didn’t come in at all.

She only looked at the hand-painted Hours sign and then at me through the glass—gray coat buttoned wrong, hair that had lost an argument with the wind, one hand already up in apology. I made a motion through the door that read some version of you can make me aware of your existence and she nodded, fished a phone from her pocket, and called.

“Calder,” I said into the handset, looking through the glass at her mouth shaping my name.

“Ms. Calder,” she said, and her voice was made of two things at once: fatigue and urgency. “This is Irene March. I’m calling on behalf of the estate of Professor Ezra Whitcomb.”

The name brushed something in the back of my mind, the way a finger grazes a shelf of spines and stops on the book you hadn’t remembered you’d read.

“He died last night,” she said. “There’s a safe.”

There’s always a safe. Or else there’s a door with ideas about itself and a landlord who thinks fifty dollars and a stiff shoulder will fix it.

“It’s in his house,” she continued, as if houses were not where safes naturally sat pretending to be furniture. “It’s personal property, not university. The will stipulates it be opened within twenty-four hours by... by you. Specifically you.”

I was glad I was sitting.

“Me,” I said, tasting the word as if it, too, could be misshapen. “The will says my name?”

“It says Calder & Daughter,” Ms. March said, glancing down—at papers in her hand, at a lawyer’s lips, the reflection told me. “It names Nikolas Calder or his daughter, Marin.”

That was my father’s full name, proper as he never was out loud. People were always making him into a Nicholas or a Nicky; it would have delighted and annoyed him in equal measure to find his formal self alive and well in a dead man’s paperwork.

“What’s the address?” I asked.

She told me. A Greek Revival two blocks east of Harvard Square, the part of Cambridge that refuses to believe it is a city. The kind of house that has moldings that have seen things and stairs that complain in meaningful ways.

“How soon can you be here?” Irene asked.

“How soon do you need me?”

There was a sound like someone swallowing the idea of a clock. “Now would be best,” she said.

I took a lockout kit, a small roll of cloth that looks like a travel-size carpenter’s sin, and the tools I use for polite safes and ones that aren’t. I zipped my jacket and killed the lights. On my way out I touched, as I sometimes do without meaning to, the worn initials carved into the counter where my father had braced a mug. N.M.C., cut into wood one winter with the same care he would take opening an old safe he respected—quick and exact and almost invisible unless you were looking.

The address on Irving Street had a hedgerow that wanted to be a wall. I let myself in the gate and wrapped on the knocker, a bronze lion who had gotten used to biting his tongue.

The door opened on a woman whose face I recognized from the glass two miles back. Irene March had an oval face made more angular by worry, her eyes that steady gray of New England mornings. Behind her, the hallway rose with the house like an intake of breath: runner carpet, photographs of men with hairlines that told the story of their discipline, a clock ticking in a tone that had been described at some point as sonorous and never recovered.

“I’m so sorry for your loss,” I said, because that is what people like me say to people like her even though we never knew the person being missing.

“Thank you,” she said, a reflex that lit and extinguished at once. She stepped aside. “Mr. Pierce is in the study. The safe is there.”

She led me down a hall that felt like the word mahogany. The study was a reader’s room, the air broken by dust and light and paper. Books to the ceiling. A globe large enough to sit on and too small to hold the world. A desk with a green blotter and a pen whose cap had been worried at until it sighed and gave up. There was also a safe—or what appeared to be a stack of drawers, the bottom of a gentleman’s chest, quartets of brass pulls politely arranged.

“Calder,” said a man with a tie that thought it was Sunday. He was in his sixties, tan in a way that doesn’t happen in New England without travel or deceit. He rose from a leather chair and put out his hand. “Harland Pierce. Counsel.”

We shook and agreed silently not to like each other.

“It’s behind the false drawers?” I said, walking the perimeter the way a dog would stake a claim against an intrusive squirrel.

“It is,” Pierce said. “We believe it is a Herring-Hall-Marvin from around 1920. Professor Whitcomb enjoyed—” He hesitated, choosing a word. “—mechanisms.”

“Don’t we all,” I said. I set down my bag and crouched. The top row of drawers was real enough—lined with felt and pens, the kind of pens that announce things like retirement and maritime achievements. Midway down, the woodworking took on a caution that told the truth. I tested the veneer at the corner, felt the give of a hidden hinge. To the right, a small keyway pretended to be the hole for a missing pull.

The keyway was oblong with a warding pattern like a small puzzle trying to be polite. I took out the pick with the thin, patient hook and the tension wrench that my father had filed until it felt like a second thumb. The lock would be wafered—Herring liked the cheap elegance of it—so I set the wrench, lifted, felt the wafers rise and drop. Second and fourth stuck, which told me someone had ignored it on purpose and filled the chamber with old smoke and fear of fingerprints.

“May I?” Pierce said, leaning forward like a man who has leaned forward his whole life to see how things work while others work them. I did not answer. The wafers were talking, and if you interrupt a person who whispers you only ever get the truth after they decide you deserve it.

The lock opened like a book that had been waiting to be read. The false front swung on a hinge hidden in a darker history of glue, and there it was: a round safe door behind the veneer, its dial set at zero, its handle a short polished T like a coat hook thrown on the wrong wall. Raised letters read Herring-Hall-Marvin Co., Hamilton, O.

I took the stethoscope from its case and the house quieted itself. You can learn a person by watching how they manage silence with you in the room. Pierce became worthy. Irene turned into a statue that remembered it had once been warm.

Dial manipulation is not magic. It is listening for travel and tolerance and counting the oddities of metal made to be exact. I rotated the dial through counts of four until I found the scrapes of the drive cam, the faint bump of the contact points. The wheels spoke in the hazy way that old things do—resisting explanation and asking politely to be convinced.

On the second revolution, the fence dropped. I set the handle and turned it, and the safe let go like a breath someone had forgotten they’d been holding.

Inside was not the kind of wealth Mr. Pierce’s eyebrows had been rehearsing for. No cash bands, no watch boxes, no velvet trays. The cavity was deeper than it had any right to be and lined with wood instead of steel. On the top shelf, a red leather notebook sat as if it had been posed by a photographer who understood how often cameras win. Beside it, a flat envelope, thick with paper and tide-wrinkled at the edges. An old microcassette recorder the size of a deck of cards, with a tape inside. And, nestled in a cutout of black felt, a key.

It was a key that did not pretend to be part of a household. The bow was round, stamped with a star the exact shape of the ones kids draw. The blade was too long by practical standards, its cuts irregular, a reverse paracentric profile that made it look like a blade that had decided to argue with itself. A small sticker on its bow said in blue ink, MARIN CALDER.

My throat closed. The room seemed to tilt in the smallest way, like a dock would if a single gull decided to take the whole thing personally. I reached out and then, because I was being watched, I reached instead for the envelope. On its front: For the Locksmith. In handwriting that tried to be straight and occasionally succeeded.

“You have to inventory everything,” Pierce said, but in a tone that meant he knew he'd already lost this round.

“It’s addressed to me,” I said.

“It’s addressed to a profession,” he said.

“Which is, for our purposes, me.” I held the envelope in my palm. The paper felt thick, the kind of stationary on which people once practiced failure in love. I broke the seal. The paper smell was linen and age and my father’s desk drawer when I was small.

Ms. Calder—

If you are reading this, I am either dead or in a stupendous amount of trouble for reasons with which I have become intimately familiar.

It is a frightening relief to address this to a Calder. Your father opened the first lock I could not in 1999, and did it with the precise rudeness of genius. He called me Ezra and never Professor after the first hour, which was possibly why I trusted him.

I should like your discretion and your impatience both.

At the bottom of the campus there is something called the Sluice. It has not sluiced in a hundred years but it remembers. In 1998 a student named Eliza Hart drowned there with water up to her knees. Factually impossible, said the coroner in a note he did not attach to the official report. Accident by intoxication, said the file. An unfortunate girl, said everyone else, because that is what people say to tidy the part of the story with hands in it.

I have been looking, like a fool, at a door everyone believes is a wall. Someone has been, in consequence, making things difficult for me.

If I have died what they will call a “natural death,” I will ask you to assume it was not. If there is still time to open the wall and remove what is behind it, the key I have left will be essential. It belongs to the water gate at Winthrop Bridge. I do not mean the iron gate under the arch that keeps undergraduates from proving themselves. I mean the narrow door adjacent, which you would never call a door unless you loved doors or had cause to fear them.

Please do not go alone. I would ask your father to go with you, but the last time I asked him anything I believe he told me to light my own damn cigarette. I apologize for the presumption of naming you, but my memory insists that talent follows blood as often as it moves in its own direction.

If you don’t open it the week I die, it will be boarded over again and we will have to wait for someone else’s curiosity.

You will be watched. Do what you always do in a room full of strangers: look for the person looking for you.

If you find nothing, burn this. If you find something, bring it to my office and lock the door. The book is for you. The tape is for you. The key is—well. Find out.

With nervous admiration,

E. Whitcomb

P.S. If a man named Harland Pierce is in the room, he will be unhappy that this is personal. He is not a villain. He simply enjoys putting lids on boiling pots.

I read it twice because the first time I only managed to read the part where my father’s name appeared and then everything else turned into noise. Irene watched me with a concentration that felt medical. Pierce did exactly what the postscript predicted and tried not to show it.

“Is this a will?” he asked in the tone of a person who feels a hook in the foot and chooses to argue with the lake. “Because if it is not a will, it may not be pertinent to—”

“It’s a letter,” I said. “To me.”

He breathed through his nose, a muscle moving at the corner of his jaw. “Then we will note that it exists.”

“Good,” I said. I put the letter back into its envelope and slid the red notebook into my bag with the kind of theft that isn’t theft because your name is on the thing in question. I picked up the microcassette recorder. The plastic was cloudy, the buttons dulled by fingers that had probably smelled like library glue and nicotine. There was an A written in black marker on the tape’s spine. There was a second tape under it, labeled B. On its label, the date from last week.

“Is there anything else?” Irene asked, and there was something in the tremor of her voice that told me she had not immediately brought herself to names in the letter, our unknown Eliza Hart had introduced herself not like a person but like a problem.

“A notebook,” I said, which was technically true.

Pierce cleared his throat. “Ms. March, will you accompany me while I make a list?”

Irene gave me an open look that I read as please don’t explode anything. “I’ll be back,” she said, and made a motion at me the way you would at a cat to let it know you’d noticed it was still there. They left the study. I was alone with the smell of dead flowers and Ezra Whitcomb’s absence.

The safe was not empty. On the second shelf, behind where the notebook had sat, there was a shallow compartment that you wouldn’t have noticed unless you knew the furniture of safes the way surgeons know how skin behaves when it tries to hide something. I eased my fingers along the seam and found the pressure point. The back panel slid toward me with a muffled sigh, and I saw—just for a heartbeat—the corner of a photograph.

A blue sky and a brick arch. The Cambridge River with a long-limbed bridge. Two figures in the midground, one of them a girl in a red coat with her hair blown sideways by a wind not unlike the one that had found Irene’s earlier. Her face was turned, not fully toward the camera, not fully away. There was something written across the bottom in a hand different from Whitcomb’s, angled and quick, a scrawl that looked like someone running downhill with a pen. I had time to read the first two words—Red Gate—and then—like any good ghost—the picture was gone.

The compartment snapped shut with the sharp resentment of a mechanism that has been told all its life what it is supposed to do. I cursed under my breath and reached for the seam again. It would not open without more persuasion and more time than I could afford while a lawyer talked about inventory in the next room. I left it as it had been and took an even breath to replace the uneven one I wanted.

Harland returned with a clipboard. Irene behind him with a face that had aged an hour in ten minutes. “We will need to establish chain of—” he began.

“Of course,” I said. I shouldered my bag with more ease than I felt. “Chain on. I’ll bring the key and the tape back when I’ve finished confirming that they are not booby-trapped with snakes.”

He made a sound that started out as a laugh and then reconsidered. “I’ll expect an accounting by morning.”

“And coffee helps,” I said. “For both of us.”

I left the same way I had come, the door’s heavy air kissing my back with a sigh. On the street, a woman with a baby pushed a stroller that made the same noise all strollers make no matter how rich the zip code, a squeal that sounds like an apology. A man across the way stood with a camera pointed at the house, his lens not quite the house and not quite me. When he saw me see him, he smiled in an exact, empty way and took a picture of the sycamore instead. I filed him in the drawer marked They Are Not Always About You.

Back at the shop I locked the door, pulled the shade halfway, and stood for a long moment with my palm on the counter. The quiet was the good kind, dense with sawdust and something like memory. Across from me hung over a thousand blanks—their profiles like a city skyline made of potential. I have always loved the moment before a key is cut; it is a calendar of promises.

The microcassette recorder clicked when I pressed Play. The motor whirred with the particular tremor that says this machine has lived long enough it can choose to misbehave on its own terms. Ezra Whitcomb’s voice unfurled into my shop: a tenor smudged by years of chalk dust and lecture halls.

“If this is A, it means I have failed to say something to your father in person without being overwritten by our mutual tendency to be delightful during discussions. Marin, if it is you who hears this instead of Nik, I apologize in advance for addressing you in the tone of an old man who knows better. I am an old man who knows better. It has never stopped me.”

A rustle of paper. A breath. A match being struck and then not used. The kind of sounds that make a man real when he has been otherwise replaced by cultural shorthand.

“You grew up in that shop. I came to it on a rainy day and watched your father open a safe that had been built to shame the people who believed in cleverness. He did not shame the safe. He conversed with it until it agreed to reveal itself. I have been in conversation with a wall for twenty-five years, Marin. It is rude and it lies and it pretends that water does not climb when it is told to.

“I think that whoever killed Eliza Hart knows those things. I think they have been discouraging curiosity since. I think—”

He stopped with a small exclamation that was not fear yet but recognized fear. There was a knock in the tape—not on a door so much as on wood that had ideas about doors. Then his voice, smaller because distance does that to men: “One moment.”

Footsteps. The tape whirred onward because older machines do not care what happens to you; they are clocks and they are on their way to being dead. A second knock, closer. The sound of something being set on a desk too carefully. A whisper, not a word, a breath that had the shape of the letter s.

Then a voice I didn’t know and wouldn’t recognize if you set him beside me on the T. Not loud. Not the voice of a villain auditioning for a role. Patient, almost kind.

“Professor Whitcomb,” it said. “We need to talk about your knack for keeping things open.”

The tape squealed, an old belt giving up. The sound curved inward, a slow collapse like a building deciding to become dust. Then a click that was not a click on the tape but the world I live in: the bell on my own door.

I hit Stop, and I turned the way a person turns in a house when they are alone and the house has told them otherwise. The shop door was still locked. The shade hung exactly where I had left it. Another knock, soft. The second one is always worse.

“Calder?” said a voice outside, a woman’s, stretched and sharp; my name became thinner and more precise. “Marin? It’s Irene.”

I let air back into my body because it had left without telling me. I walked to the door and stood with my hand on the latch. Through the glass I saw her face, pale and already speaking, and behind her, in the street, the man with the camera no longer bothered to pretend he was photographing trees.

When I opened the door, Irene leaned in a fraction, as if the threshold could pull truth from her if she crossed too suddenly.

“They’ve changed the locks at Whitcomb’s office,” she said, the words running one into the other as if she could outpace the meaning. “The university. They say it’s standard. They say—”

She looked over her shoulder the way people do when they have been taught by that afternoon to develop new habits.

“They say the tape is missing,” she said. “And Mr. Pierce is looking for you.” She swallowed a thin laugh. “I believe he thinks he is a villain now.”

The man with the camera lifted it again, his stance slightly off, like a dancer a beat behind the song. I felt, irrational and correct at once, the gravity of a river, the memory of water where it should not be, doors that would not call themselves doors unless I confessed to loving them.

“Come inside,” I said to Irene, and the bell over the door said hello and the lock slid home like a word that feels right in the mouth.

The ledger arrived the way most ghosts do—in a box no one wanted to open. Someone had scrawled in black marker across the cardboard, LOCKMASTER, and then struck it through hard enough to nick the lid. Under that, in a smaller, meeker hand, was written: Donated by Caldwell’s Antiques. Please handle.

I lifted the lid anyway.

The Municipal Archives shares a building with the old ferry station on River Street, a brick cube with windows painted shut against the Mississippi’s moods. You can smell the river in every corner—silt and iron, damp rope—and underneath it the sweeter, papery scent of lignin breaking apart in older books. In the front lobby there’s a faded mural of Gadsden Falls as it never was: browner than it is now, a few umbrellas, men in hats, a luminous river, boats steaming purposefully toward a horizon smudged with promise.

I rolled my cart into Processing. Mel glanced up from an accession form and the sandwich she wasn’t supposed to be eating at the table. She has white hair like steel wool and a way of waving you over that makes you feel like a stray cat she’s taken in. There was a smear of mustard on her thumb.

“What’s the tide bring us?” she asked.

“Some ghost’s book,” I said.

“Should have called us twenty years ago, then,” Mel said briskly, setting her sandwich aside. At the Archives, almost everything comes twenty years too late.

I pulled aside the packing paper, careful as if it might bite, and exposed the ledger. It was big—twelve by eighteen at least—and bound in buckram that had gone the color of over-brewed tea. The cloth at the corners was fraying, the spine half-detached. It had the heft of something that had once mattered to people who never imagined it might matter to anyone else.

Under the ledger were three folders, a handful of photographs stuck together with albumin and neglect, and an envelope fat with metal. The envelope rattled like bones. I loosened the string and a small brass key slid into my palm. FLINT N° 2, it said, which meant nothing to me, but the weight felt old, confident, the way older objects do when they have done their job long enough to be sure of themselves.

Mel leaned in over my shoulder, her glasses low on her nose. “From Caldwell’s? That the one with the limp who smells like mothballs and carnations?”

“That’s him,” I said. I knew Caldwell only by sight, a narrow man with a cane and a scarf even in August. He kept the antique shop two doors down from the bakery, the one with the bell that sounded like a swallow when you went in. He would appear out of nowhere whenever I lingered near the cases of pocket watches, telling me how all timekeepers shared a guilt. I never asked him what he meant by that.

“Lockmaster,” Mel said, peering at the red label pasted to the inside cover. “Lock and Dam Twelve.” She tapped a finger. “Used from 1919 to 1923. Before they put in the new gates.”

“Caldwell said it came out of the lock house,” I said, pulling a letter out from under the string. Caldwell had typed it on onion-skin paper, and the keys had bitten through. Donating the enclosed ledger and associated materials pertaining to Lock and Dam Twelve of the Gadsden Falls Division. Items recovered from estate of Mr. E. Pennington, deceased. Provenance unclear regarding photographs and key; however, the ledger’s origin seems obvious. Yours etc., J. H. Caldwell, Proprietor. At the bottom, a little theatrical flourish of a signature and a phone number.

I lugged the ledger onto the foam supports and brushed the dust off with the softest brush, the one that feels like stroking the belly of a sleeping cat. With my palm flat I felt the slight resistance of grit embedded in the cloth—the river has a way of insinuating. The first page cracked a little when I turned it back, and the ledger exhaled—ink and glue, the faint sourness of mildew.

The entries were in a neat, blocky hand in iron gall ink gone brown-black. The Lockmaster had recorded river heights, gate settings for each sluice, barge passages by time and tonnage. It was a meticulous—almost loving—catalogue of what the river did and what the men did in answer. Along the margins were notations in pencil that looked like numbers, a column of dates with a slash through each.

“If you’re lucky,” Mel said, “you get the person who minded their columns. Some of the lock books are chicken scratches.”

“I like this one,” I said, surprising myself. It wasn’t unusual for me to be charmed by someone else’s old structure. Order makes a certain kind of sense when nothing else does. On the second page a coffee ring had bled into the paper like an eclipse.

I flipped, fascinated by the tide of it. September 12, 1920: three barges loaded with wheat, one tug, no incidents. October 1: left gate jammed, men at it with crowbars, resolved by noon. January 13, 1921: ice. The iron gall lines were so even they almost hummed. Here and there, in faint pencil, were notes I couldn’t place: LOUISE—11/3, T. MORA—7/28. I ran my finger above those two names without touching.

A trick of my mind. I blinked and looked again. Mel was putting her sandwich back in its wax paper, the sound of it like leaves.

“What?” she asked, catching the knot in my throat. She has that kind of hearing.

“Nothing,” I said immediately, and then because that was a lie and we don’t do lies in Processing, “There’s a T. Mora in the margin.”

Mel glanced at me. “Not so many M-o-r-a’s in town. Your father was—”

“Tomás,” I said. “But he was usually T. or Tom. Around here anyway.” The ledger hummed in my hands. In 2016, my father had disappeared working a tug in a storm without a body, without a clean ending, and that sort of thing does not end. Not really. There is always another door in the brain that you shake and shake, even after it is nailed shut.

Mel put her hand on my elbow. “Let me make some tea.”

I shook my head. “Let me check something.”

I went back. The pencil was faint, the paper toothed. I angled the desk lamp low for a raking light, the way my old boss had taught me. In the skewed light the page changed: you could see every ridge where the iron gall had eaten its tiny canyons, every indent where the pencil had pressed hard. The T. MORA, the LOUISE, the other names, were not written in pencil at all. They weren’t written at all. They were indentations—the sort that get left when you use a sheet of paper to write something and that paper rests atop another.

I breathed out, feeling the odd delight of being right about something that had no business making you happy. Somebody had used the open ledger as a writing surface. The pencil had been applied to the paper above, and the pressure had sunk through. These names were echoes, ghost writing without the writing. The dates next to them were more than a hundred years ahead of the last entry in the ledger itself.

“You see that?” I asked.

Mel was already nodding. “Get your film.”

You’re supposed to use an electrostatic detection apparatus in a real lab. We have Saran Wrap and a number two pencil. I cut a square and laid it over the page. With the side of the graphite and the light just right you can bring up impressions. It takes patience and a certain touch, which I have because I file my feelings until they behave. Mel watches me do it with the fondness of watching someone knit.

One by one the names surfaced: LOUISE PENDARVIS—11/3—NAT, FRANK B.—5/12—HANSEN, T. MORA—7/28, HECTOR LORRY—8/02. The list wasn’t long. It ran down the left margin and curled around the bottom of the page like a footnote. The last three were without dates. Next to CARO LEVITT, only a little dash. Then MAYOR L.

I sat back. My chest hurt like I’d been holding it tight for a while.

Mel came to my side and read the names with the kind of solemn mouth she uses at funerals. “Tomás.” She didn’t touch the page. “Caro Levitt’s our mayor. What do you suppose a fool list like that’s for?”

“Obituaries,” I said, and I felt my stomach drop when I heard my voice. If you work in archives long enough you learn the cadence of names that people have had to say out loud while crying softly. LOUISE PENDARVIS had a sepia portrait in the Gadsden paper’s online edition beginning of November two years ago. She made the best chess pie in Tanglefoot County. Frank B. Hansen had died last spring. Hector Lorry ran the bait shop by the pier and had his heart attack in August out in the marsh; he hadn’t been found until the pelicans had dispersed. I knew because I collected these things. I put them where they went in the city’s story, which is the closest thing I have to religion.

“And your father,” Mel said, as gently as if the words were a fragile emergence. “He went July twenty-eighth.”

“He disappeared July twenty-eighth,” I said. “The coroner signed him dead in September.”

“Still,” she said, and she wasn’t wrong, but this ledger felt suddenly like it was looking at me.

“I’ll call Caldwell,” I said. “Ask where he got the ledger exactly. See if he knows who used it as a notepad. Maybe there’s a note in the envelope.”

Mel had already seen me slide into a sharpness that meant I was going to pursue the thread. It’s my better self, the one that kept me in town when leaving would have been easy and kind. She nodded. “Do that. Don’t do it like a stranger. He likes attention.”

I dialed the number Caldwell had typed beneath his elaborate signature. It went to a machine with a mechanical voice and no name. I left my own name and said the words Municipal Archives, which usually summon people with curious donations quite quickly. I returned the ledger to the box for someone else to process the accession: I am not supposed to take personal assignments, not even when they feel like they are knocking at your teeth from behind. But I did slip the brass key into my pocket. I am allowed to hold keys. It’s practically in my job description.

I went to the window and cracked it an inch against the posted building rules because the room had become too warm. The river sighed against wood pilings. A barge blew low and mournful as it rounded the bend. On the far bank, the cottonwoods glittered in a wind that we did not feel yet, because things arrive late in this town.

“Eat,” Mel said, sliding her sandwich across the table toward me like it was a prescription.

“After,” I said, and I meant after I took three more steps.

By the time I walked down River Street, the noon bells from Saint Raphael had rung themselves out of breath. The river had pulled away from us the way it does in late fall, flaring bright and then going gray, an old coin in a shallow dish. The shop called Caldwell’s Antiques had a window display of maritime nonsense—oars, a ship’s clock that had not worked since the 1950s, a handsome brass spyglass. The bell over the door had been tuned to be charming. The door was locked.

There were two men on the sidewalk in front of the shop in close conversation. I knew one of them by reputation: Detective Isaiah March, who had the kind of face that made you confess to crimes you hadn’t committed just so you could stop looking at him. He was younger than the stories made him, with a barbered beard and a coat that made his shoulders look larger. The other man was from the medical examiner’s office, the one who always wore bright socks like a secret. Both looked up when they saw me and did that subtle adjusting cops do when a civilian appears in a place that is about to matter.

“Ms. Mora,” Detective March said, as if we were old acquaintances. We had never met, but it felt like he had seen my face on a corkboard somewhere. “It’s a day for librarians.”

“Archivists,” I said.

“Right. You and Caldwell are pals?” He nodded toward the door.

“We aren’t anything,” I said. “He donated a ledger this morning. I was coming to thank him and ask a few questions. Is something wrong?”

He didn’t say yes or no. The medical examiner’s man adjusted his bright socks in a nervous hop. Detective March turned his head to the side like a dog hearing something at a register I couldn’t.

“How long have you been working at the archives?” he asked.

“Nine years,” I said.

“You grew up here.”

“It’s a small town. Everyone grew up here.”

“Fair enough,” he said, almost smiling. “We’re waiting on a keyholder. Did you happen to bring a master key to all troubled doors?”

“Only on Thursdays,” I said. He liked that, which made me like him more than I should have.

He held up a hand and peered through the window. From where I stood I couldn’t see beyond the glare. I recognized the barber pole reflection, my own face floated over the antique dressing mirror inside. Detective March knocked once on the glass a way no polite person ever knocks—assertive, tempo odd enough that anyone alive would reveal themselves by responding. No one did.

He said into his radio, listened, nodded. He didn’t fidget. March had the centering stillness of someone who had been taught to breathe a certain way under a certain kind of pressure.

When the keyholder—a woman with too much ring on her fingers and Caldwell’s camphor-scent on her—arrived and made a trembling business of opening the door, the bell made its pretty bird sound. We all stepped back to let the professionals go in. March went first. The scent that gusted out wasn’t camphor or mothballs; it was river. The kind that lingers after a flood, that fine silt smell, metallic and faintly sweet, threaded with rot.

“Stay here,” March said to me without looking.

I stayed, because despite my qualification I am not entirely feral. The ME man went in next. The door closed with soft ceremony. Fifteen seconds later, I heard the bell ring again as the keyholder changed her mind about coming in and retreated to the sidewalk, hand over her mouth.

“Don’t look,” she said, eyes wet. “Don’t you look.”

I looked only when Detective March came out again. He had the face they get when they are thinking while also laying groundwork for later. His pupils were a little smaller than they should be. He scanned the street, saw that we were nobody special except for me and did a small mental adjustment for that.

“Mr. Caldwell is deceased,” he said.

The keyholder made a little sound in her throat like a hinge. March inclined his head. “I’m sorry. The scene is... unusual. We’ll be speaking to everyone who interacted with him this morning. Ms. Mora, you said he donated something to you today?”

“A ledger and some papers,” I said, doing that thing I do under stress where I flatten out emotions into notes and order. “From the Lock and Dam Division. He delivered them himself or had someone deliver them. We received the box around nine.”

“Did he say anything unusual?”

“He didn’t speak to me,” I said, and his eyes tightened slightly as if speaking to me was the unusual thing. “The envelope contained a key labeled FLINT N° 2 and a note. The note said he got the ledger from an estate. Errol Pennington.”

“We’ll want to see all of that,” he said.

“You can,” I said. “It’s at the Archives.”

March nodded, as if he had expected a fight and found cooperation disconcerting. He looked back into the dim shop. The brass spyglass glinted. On the floor, I could see the faint sheen of moisture catching light.

River water dries with a different pattern. It leaves behind a fine lattice of minerals that looks like the skin of a dragonfly under magnification. It dries fast, unlike floodwater.

The ME man stepped out with blue booties on and nodded to March in a language of professionals. March said “Uh-huh,” and then to me: “We’ll take your statement now. And we’ll need you to identify Mr. Caldwell if you have met him. We don’t like to rely on strangers' eyes,” he added to the keyholder kindly, who looked seasick.

“I don’t know him well,” I said.

“That’s okay,” March said, and there is something strangely intimate about following a stranger into a room with a dead man in it.

The shop was cool and overly composed. Movement made dust leap in the single shaft of light from the rear skylight, the particles floating, shining and being nothing. On the front counter there was an old register that had not rung up a sale in a decade and a blue porcelain bowl with calling cards in it, as if we were in a century under glass.

Caldwell was on the floor behind the counter, on his side, in the precise posture of someone who has just realized he is lying down. The side of his face that showed was pale, his mouth a little open. His cane was six inches from his hand. His scarf had come undone and lay like a shed skin. His other hand rested palm up, cupped toward the ceiling as if offering something to air. There was a smear of blue-gray on the pads of his fingers. Particles sparkled on his cuff. His shoes were wet with a thin slick of fine silt, and the pattern of his tread had imprinted the moisture in scallops. The smell was stronger here: the river in your teeth.

“No obvious trauma,” the ME man said to March. “No glass, no contusions, no hemorrhage. He’s wet, though. Socks soaked. Trace silt.”

“Stroke?” March said.

“Maybe. Or maybe someone brought the river in,” the ME man said, and March did not smile, which is how you knew the joke wasn’t one.

It was small, the thing that snagged me. On the floor beside Caldwell’s open hand, someone had set something down and lifted it again when it was still wet. The silt left a hollow pattern and a fine edgelike dusting where the object had rested. It was not the shape of a glass or a bottle or a book. It was a shape I knew because I had my hand in my pocket and my fingers were parsing an old brass key like prayer beads. The negative space on the floor was the shape of my key.

I looked up. March was following my eyes because that is a skill he has. He raised a brow. I could feel my own pulse in the pads of my fingers.

“What is that?” he said.

“A key,” I said, and heard how idiotic that was, so I took the one from my pocket out and held it up. “Or the absence of one.”

“Ms. Mora,” March said, like a reprimand and an invitation, and I felt suddenly like I had done something wrong, which is another skill he had.

I cleared my throat. “Caldwell sent the Archives a key with the ledger. I didn’t think it had anything to do with anything. The impression on the floor there is the same shape.”

March made a sound that might have been a sigh. He didn’t reach for the key, which made me trust him. He said, “Tell me again about the ledger.”

I told him about the ledger as much as I had told myself, but I did not tell him yet about the names in the margin or the dates. I wanted to keep something small for myself until I knew which way was up. That is not what honesty looks like, and I know it, but I could feel something shaking inside me like birds trapped in the rafters of a church.

On the walk back to the Archives after the statement, the weather changed. You could feel it. A wind came off the water cool and quick, snapping flags, making the river’s surface pebble. My phone buzzed with a voicemail from a number with no name. Caldwell’s machine, I thought, but when I pressed my ear to it I got only a faint burble, as if the mic had been left open on a glass held up to current. Then the line went quiet.

In Processing, Mel had made tea anyway and arranged it on the table with an order of cookies she thought she could pass off as purchased on her break. She had a sixth sense for when I needed sugar. I set the brass key on the table between us as if it were a reliquary.

“So?” she said.

“Dead,” I said. “On the floor with river mud on his shoes.” I told her about the shape on the floor, and she did not look surprised. It takes a lot to surprise Mel. She has been in love five times and hates two of them less every year.

“Don’t let them take the ledger,” she said.

“They have to take it,” I said. “Chain of custody. March will come. He wants to see it.”

“Then hurry,” she said, which is Mel’s way of not saying please hide the thing and never tell anyone. She is not unlawful; she is protective.

I lifted the ledger back onto the foam, ran the raking light again, and slid the Saran Wrap over the page like a second skin. The names rose when I shaded in graphite. LOUISE PENDARVIS—11/3. We traced with our eyes the list as if reading it too quickly would offend some rule of the dead.

“You going to tell March about—” Mel began, and then stopped. She had seen the last impression at the bottom of the page. So had I. It was shallow, the pencil lighter there or the pressure less, as if whoever had written it had hesitated, or had known what it meant to write it. It said MAYOR L and then a name in impatient capital letters: CARO LEVITT. Next to it was a line. Not a date. A line. It was the oddest thing. A thin pencil dash and then, in very faint pressure, the ghost of an eight and a one. The eight was perfect. The one was merely a scratch. I laid the pencil on its side and breathed like I was going to practice scales.

“It’s incomplete,” I said.

Mel squinted. “What is that? Eight-one?”

I looked at the calendar on the wall. Today was the thirty-first. Mel looked too. We both looked back down. The graphite told us nothing. The faint impression was just that—faint.

I stood, walked to the window, and looked down River Street. In front of City Hall, the flag did its work with the wind. Three police cars had parked at stupid angles in front of Caldwell’s, their lights revolving lazily as if bored.

When Detective March came to the Archives an hour later with a box and a form, I showed him the ledger. He did not touch it. He leaned in with his hands on his knees, like a coach talking to someone shorter on a field. I showed him the names. I showed him my father’s name without saying my father, because I did not want to watch pity cross his face like a shadow. He looked and his eyes did a quick tick when he got to T. MORA.

“You think that’s a list of—who?” he asked.

“Obituaries,” I said. “Or something like them.”

“How do you think the ledger was used?”

“As a writing surface,” I said. “The impressions are from a page that sat on top.”

“When?” he said.

“Recently,” I said. “The paper fibers under those indentations are clean. The ledger itself is old. The impressions are new.”

“We’ll take it for examination,” he said. “You can visit it on weekends.”

He tried to smile. He did not succeed entirely.

After they left with the ledger swaddled like an infant, Processing felt too big. Mel went to call her daughter because that is what you do when someone in your town dies and no one knows why. I turned the brass key in my hand to see if it still said FLINT N° 2 when you held it at an angle. It did. I looked at the photographs in the Caldwell box again.

One was of the old lock house, taken from downstream. You could see the iron gates like teeth and the men standing with their caps in their hands on the concrete apron. Someone had written on the back in a scrawl: E.P. and the boys, ’23. There was a child at the edge of the photograph in a dress with a big white collar, looking up with her chin to the sky as if daring a cloud to drop anything on her head. The river behind them was the color of lead feathers.

My phone buzzed again. Unknown number.

I answered. Someone was breathing, close to the mic. A sound like water touching something smooth, lapping, rhythmic. Then a voice I did not know, a whisper more than a sound. Just a single word.

Key.

“I have it,” I said, because sometimes you cannot help but try to complete a stranger’s sentence. The line went dead.

That night after the sky went ink-blue and the cat three doors down began its nightly argument with the oak tree, I sat on my fire escape with a mug of tea that went cold in my hands. My father used to say the river keeps its promises. He meant the floodplain would flood; he meant the barges would come on the hour if you set your watch by the whistle; he meant the river did not recognize obligations it did not create. He did not mean it would deliver its debt to us.

Caro Levitt was on the six o’clock news, smiling the smile that had got her elected—wide, trust your auntie—and talking about the city’s new riverwall improvements with the Army Corps. She wore a dark suit with a brooch shaped like a lock and key. I watched the brooch more than anything else. When the camera cut away, they did a human-interest piece on the oldest pecan tree in the county. That is how we do things here. We put pecan trees between you and whatever you should look at.

At ten-thirty, I could not sit still any longer. I went to the drawer where I keep the things I should not keep at home—notes from cases, a jade button, my father’s cheap watch. I dropped the brass key into that drawer with the sound of everything that matters. It did not sound guilty. It sounded like a key, which is to say it sounded like possibility and metal and the weight of opening things and the responsibility for everything that comes in.

I slept poorly with the ledger in custody and a list in my head like a song. I dreamed of a lock gate opening underwater to let current through. In the dream I could see fish drifting backward against the pressure, eyes calm, bodies silvered.

In the morning, Mel texted me a picture of the whiteboard in Processing with a drawing of a key on it and the word bread. She likes to mix messages.

I got up, put on the same shirt I had taken off, drank half a cup of coffee and walked to the Archives watching the river the entire way. The city was setting up tents near City Hall for the annual Fall Fest. Someone had strung paper lanterns in the sycamores. A man with a leaf blower chased leaves in a circle like he had all the time in the world.

By the time I reached my desk, there were two voicemails from Detective March and one email from a city address I did not recognize. March’s first message was bureaucratic. His second had a gulp in it. The email subject line said: Calendar.

I opened March’s first voicemail. “Ms. Mora, March here. We’ve taken custody of the ledger. Do not discuss its contents with anyone outside our office. Please bring the key to the station at your earliest.”

His second voicemail was shorter. “We have a date. Ms. Mora, call me.”

The city email was from someone in the Mayor’s office, a scheduler named Daphne who had once called to ask if the Archives had any photographs of Caro Levitt that made her look “less wide” which is the sort of thing people think they can ask you when you work with their pasts. The email said: Per Mayor Levitt’s request, please confirm your availability for a meeting today at 4 p.m. Re: Archives partnership for Riverwall History Project.

I looked at the clock, then at my calendar, then at my own facedown palm as if there were words written there.

I called March. He picked up on the second ring this time. In the background people were talking low and crisp.

“Ms. Mora,” he said. “The impressions—you might be right about obituaries. Homicides looked at your list. We cross-referenced with the papers. Some of those names were flagged in internal files. That’s not your concern. But the last—Mayor Levitt—there’s a faint date next to it.”

“Eight-one,” I said.

“It’s not eight-one,” he said. “It’s eight-slash-one. And the day count shows it wasn’t written in August. It was pressed recently. There’s a second number we can lift with lab light. Their guy is good. It’s very faint, but they think it says eleven-one.” He paused. “That’s tomorrow.” He let the word settle. “Ms. Mora?”

“Yes,” I said.

“Where do people go,” he asked me softly, like a man about to step onto ice, “when they want to bring the river inside?”

Chapter One

The first thing the tower did was lie to me.

It loomed over Graybridge like it always had—four weathered faces, hands black against the pale, and that shabby slate hat that the pigeons preferred to the Civic Centre's polished steel. It had been telling the hour since the town was gaslit and the river still ran green most summers, but now it said ten past nine and my breath was steam in the cold. It was after midnight. The rain had the river the color of worn coins and the cobbles shone like gristle.

“It stopped sometime around nine,” the city engineer had told me on the phone, covering the mouthpiece against the noise of traffic. “It jammed. We can’t get it moving. The mayor is threatening to do the ribbon cutting without a working clock. I told her I would get her someone quick as a key. Mister… Finch, was it?”

It was. I arrived with my satchel and a thermos of tea because it seemed like a long night, wiping the handle before I pulled the tower’s side door open. It smiled at me with old hinges and stale air. Somewhere above, something heavy knocked against something else with the slow patience of water.

The tower smelled of rust, pigeon dust, and the kind of oil that tries to be sweet. My shop smells that way after a day with antique movements—sunflower oil the old men still bring me because their fathers used it, alive with stories and particles that never truly wash out. The tower took that smell and made it cathedral-sized.

“Finch?” a voice called from within. A beam of a flashlight jittered down the spiral steps. Boots on stone. The light found my chest, slid up my throat to my face. “God. You actually came.”

“Ortega,” I said. Detective Sergeant Maya Ortega in a tweed coat that had seen better winters, hair pulled back and cheeks chapped from the wind. She reached me and the beam flinched away.

“I thought you were on nights with your little cog museum,” she said, but the smile tightened in the way that had always meant not tonight. “The city’s people rang us when the caretaker called it in. Then engineering rang us. I rang you. It’s like clockwork.”

“It would be, if it worked.” I tapped the face of the tower from the inside and felt the glass cold and thrumming. Somewhere above, something tried to turn and couldn’t. “What did the caretaker call in, exactly?”

“Jam,” she said. “And a smell.”

“The oil?”

She was already lifting the beam to the stair. “You’ll see.”

We climbed, our feet speaking to the stone. The steps were narrow and the kind that don’t handhold you kindly, passing arrow-slit windows where the wind pushed its damp nose through and made the flashlight halo mist. I listened because that’s what I do, to the talk of moving parts. There was the slow tick of a tower mouse in the wall near my ear, the drip from a crack into a bucket a floor above. There was also something sharp and fine, like a harp string out of tune, which in my trade usually means a spring that’s been given something to resent.

Maya’s light found the caretaker at the landing below the mechanism level, perched on a stool that looked like it had been dragged out of a church basement. He was a man with too few teeth for the whiskers he kept and an attitude to match the tower: “We used to wind her by hand,” he said by way of hello, as if Maya had been born a minute ago and had bothered him with her existence ever since. “Young ones put in a motor, now they gripe when she don’t sing.”

He looked past Maya at me like he was grading me for dust on my shoes. “You the one who fiddles with the little ones?”

“I mend watches and clocks,” I said. “All sizes.”

He sniffed. “We don’t have all night. Or we do, but I prefer to spend mine with my kettle.” He gestured up. “Go on. She don’t like strangers.”

“Neither do I,” I said, and the corner of Maya’s mouth twitched.

We went up the last set to the clock room. This was where towers like to keep their bones: timber beams black with oil and hand-grease, gear wheels taller than a man with teeth like iron thumbs, a fly fan pale and still. The escapement—a familiar signature in any mechanical clock, the see-saw that regulates the release of energy into time—sat like a stalled catechism, its pallets frozen against the escape wheel’s set of teeth. Above, through the slats and catwalk, the great bell waited like a sleeping animal. Maya played the flashlight about the room and caught the dust, which hung in the beam like it was having a meeting. The rain tapped at the tin roof. Somewhere up there, a pigeon muttered a short curse.

I could tell you everything I know about clocks in one breath if you don’t mind drowning: any clock is simply two arguments having a ritual—something heavy or tight pulling something in a circle, and something clever saying, Wait. In towers, the heavy thing is a weight or a motor pretending to be a weight. The clever thing is old and patient and shaped like the letter every religion prays to. And all of it, in the end, is in love with friction.

“Don’t touch anything,” Maya said, which is the kind of thing people say when they have said it to me before and know it never works.

I touched the escape wheel anyway. It was cold and had the kind of stick that comes from something foreign. I glanced at the teeth. One was shiny in a way the others weren’t, and there was the faintest fray of red when I ducked and held my breath close. Not paint. Fiber.

“What is it?” she asked.

“Thread,” I said. “Wool, maybe. Someone’s scarf got too intimate. Or someone fed it this on purpose.”

“People go poking things in here all the time,” the caretaker grumbled from below as if hearing through wood. “Kids. Lovers. Tourists. Council members.”

“What time did you notice it stopped?” I asked him. “Exactly.”

He rolled his eyes. “Exactly. It was nine and seven, because I have two wrists. And it smelled wrong. You learn her scents. Grease, pigeons, wet stone. That night it was like the things we put to keep the things from rusting, but sweeter. Flowers. Disgusting.”

I leaned over the guardrail and looked down at him. “Orange blossom?”

He shrugged. “Like old candy. The kind in tins lightning strikes.”

“Camphor and citrus,” I said, half to myself. There’s a horologist in the next town who makes up little stoppered vials of oil in his kitchen and insists on scenting them so he can tell them apart in the dark. It clings to every movement he touches and makes his shop smell like summer. He is also the only one I know who will tell you with a straight face that he can tell the hour by how a gear tastes. If the tower had that on its face, someone had been here with more than enthusiasm.

“What about the bell?” I asked.

“It rang late,” the caretaker said. “The bell knows when dinner is. Last night she thought supper was at ten past. That’s not the motor. That’s the lever. That’s interference, that is.”

“Who else has a key?” Maya said, and we both looked at her because it’s always the right question.

“Half the council. Me. The priest for weddings if he wants it jangling when they kiss. That boy who runs the tours with his hair and his teeth.”

“When did you last lock up?” I asked.

“I don’t leave,” he said.

Maya’s light landed on a small stool beneath the dial. On it was a handkerchief folded like a napkin at a bar you’re not sure you want to sit at. I reached for it and Maya said, “Finch,” in that tone again, but I had already taken the handkerchief between thumb and forefinger. It was monogrammed with an old-school humility: B.S. The thread stitching that had once been white was gray with oil. The smell of orange blossom nudged my nostrils like a girl in a photograph.

“Benedict Somers,” Maya said immediately. “Barrister for the council. Likes to give the mayor advice in expensive paper and eat other people’s sandwiches. He has keys for everything. Including my patience.”

“This could have been here for weeks,” I said. “Or last night. And it could be a decoy someone dropped to be thorough.” I opened it carefully, and a single shard of glass slipped out and gayly tried to leap to its death. Maya snapped a hand out and caught it. It glittered like a piece of the day.

“From the dial,” I said.

“Then whoever had this was inside the faces,” she said. “Up there.”

It was a simple thing to push open the trap to the crawl between the clock and the face, but simple things are often the ones that make you taste your breakfast again. The beam of the flashlight went first, and then my head, and the smell hit—wet plaster and iron and something that had thought about sugar for too long. The space was close. The glass of the dial was a white moon an inch from my cheek, the painted numerals giant, reversed and strange. Behind them, a man’s face looked back at me through the six, eyes (inverted) half closed and ultramarine in my light.

“Finch?” Maya’s voice behind me, at my ankle.

“There’s someone here,” I said. “He’s not going to ring the bell.”

He was wedged between the slats and the braces, not posed, not tossed, the way someone lands when they have had their expectations changed by gravity. His coat was the kind of blue that hides ink stains. His trousers had a crease still pressed into them like a regret. His hair had gotten wet and dried in argument with itself. His mouth, which had likely been good at persuading, was open enough to tell me he had not had an easy last sentence.

“Don’t touch anything,” Maya said again, and I forgot that sometimes that means anybody.

“I’m not,” I said, although I had to shift something to see his hands, which were, I discovered, holding something clasped to his chest so tightly that death had made it permanent. A watch. Of course that was what the tower had to show me.

“You’d know him?” Maya said.

“Not personally,” I said. “But professionally? Yes.”

I moved the light gently. The watch was a man’s pocket watch of a sort I had seen in three states and seven attics: brass plated in silver, glass crystal, crown worn by a thumb that had worked a profession. The case had the faint ghost of an engraving polished away near the hinge. The minute hand was missing, the hour hand hovered between five and six, and someone had replaced the luminous points at the cardinal numerals carelessly at some point in the last half-century; you could see where the old radium paint had been scraped away and modern, safer paste had been daubed, a shade too green. It was stopped. The second hand had fallen off entirely and sat like a comma near the center post. The dial had a hairline running from the nine to the small seconds. It was an old thing that had lived three lives. Like most of us.

Maya squeezed in and looked long. “Benedict Somers,” she said again. “Barrister. Without limit of impatience.”

She tucked the light under her chin and looked at the man’s hands where they clenched the watch. The fingers were stained pale green at the cuticles, new enough to be from handling fresh luminous paint. His nails had half-moons of dirty chalk.
