There was the faintest smell of something that wasn’t the tower’s old oil, coming from the metal like a whisper at my teeth. Orange blossom again. And under it, the tinny bite of cheaper lubricants, like what men thin with spit when they think persistence can stand in for skill.

“He fell?” she said, because that’s the second question after the first has been asked.

“Maybe,” I said. “But if he did, he caught himself with both hands on the watch and nothing else. He also found time to change a hand.”

“What hand?” she asked.

I reached with the tip of my pen to tilt the watch very gently. It hissed to me in metal vowels. Where the minute hand should have mounted, something thin had been slid through the post. It was a shard of colored glass, shaped with a file. The red was not red; up close, in the white light, it was a kind of wine color laced with black bubbles.

“From the dial,” I said. “Same as your handkerchief shard. Whoever was here took a piece of the clock’s face and made the watch tell time with it. That’s not something you do unless you have a sense of theater. Or unless what really matters is that there’s no minute hand and you don’t want anyone to notice.”

“You like this,” she said.

“I like when machines tell the truth,” I said. “I don’t like the bit where people get in the way.”

Maya glanced back down through the hatch, toward the caretaker area, where the man had no idea yet that someone he knew a little had come to the tower to be a problem. “How long?” she said. “Dead.”

“Hard to say in the cold,” I said, automatically. It defaulted to testimony in my throat. “But I would say before midnight because of the blood in the hand that’s lower stopping where gravity made it stop, and after nine, if the caretaker is right about the bell being late. And his watch is a liar.”

“How do you know?” she said.

I pointed to the crown. It was pulled out one notch, stopping the movement if it had been running. Someone had stopped it deliberately. If you are dying in a tower and you want us all to know when, you do not have the presence of mind to pull out the crown—unless you intend to lie more elegantly than the tower had.

“The crown is out,” I said. “He stopped it. Or someone did it for him. And the glass for the minute hand… that’s careful. That’s time spent. He wasn’t running from the top of the stairs with a scarf stuck in the wheel.”

Maya’s breath huffed whitely in the space. The rain drummed, harder now. The bell above us loomed, a yawn. It occurred to me to look at his shirt and the skin I could see where his collar had gone crooked and there it was, faint and crescent: a burn that had been baked into people who slept with radium dials in their waistcoats in the 1930s, the glow-in-the-dark treachery of ore. Except this was new, the edges clean, the surface unscabbed. He had been handling luminous compound and got it on himself in a way a man does when he is in a hurry and doesn’t have a sink.

“I want to know where he was before he got into my tower,” the caretaker said from below, his voice small and ugly eddying into our space. “And who he came with. And why he thought he could keep secrets from the old girl.”

“Put the room under,” Maya called down. “No one in or out. Call your boss. We need CSU, the medical examiner, and someone who can carry without complaining.”

She touched my sleeve. “And you. Don’t go back to your bench.”

“When have I ever,” I said, because she had pulled me out of warmth the week after my father died to look at a kitchen clock with a melted belly and told me I would either hate this work forever from that day or never be able to quit. “Do we like him?” I asked, nodding at Benedict. It’s always relevant, the way people felt about the soon-to-be late.

“We liked him enough to give him several retainers,” she said. “He liked himself twice that. And he liked being in places he wasn’t recorded to be. You’ll say he lies and I’ll say he had hobbies.” Her eyes caught the monogram on the handkerchief again. “Beatrice Somers,” she corrected herself. “His wife. The one who keeps him in a house I can’t afford to imagine. Different B.S., same embroidery.”

“So he didn’t bring his own handkerchief to his secret after-hours tinkering,” I said. “Either he used hers, which is domestic in an ugly way, or someone brought it later and put it somewhere it could make a point.”

“Why would he be here at all?” Maya said.

“For the inauguration,” I said. “To pull a lever in the morning and be photographed. Or to jam something and be paid twice by someone who wants footage of clocks lying to the public. Or—”

“Or to hide something and forget gravity,” she said.

We were both watching his hands now like they could write to us. Something else caught my eye—the faint dusting on his sleeve, not the gray of the tower but a pollen yellow that glittered when the beam touched it.

“Chalk?” Maya said.

“Pollen,” I said. “From lilies. Or from orchids. Or from those gaudy things the council buys for ribbon day. He took the time to lean on a bouquet.”

Maya smiled without humor. “He always did.”

Behind us, the big minutes gearing ticked over by a tooth. The sound happened like a jaw cracking. Maya’s light shivered over the iron and the glass numbers went dull bright dull with the rinse of headlights from the road below. I felt the room more than I saw it, the old wood thinking about the weather and the bell thinking about everything.

“Tell me something I can use,” Maya said, and when she says it like that I go into the place I keep for juries.

“His watch was stopped on purpose,” I said. “His fingers are stained with luminous paste and chalk dust, which means he was pretending to fix the dial or was making it look as if he had. He handled oil that smelled like orange blossom which is not standard, and a shard of the dial glass has been filed into a makeshift minute hand. Whoever did that had time and intent. There is wool fiber in the escapement, red. It isn’t from a pigeon. He died here, but I don’t know if he was killed here. If he fell he did not catch anything he should have except a lie. And your caretaker’s bell chimed late, which is a kind of note.”

Below, a door slammed in the tower’s belly and men’s voices climbed the stone, heavy with official purpose. The first drop of water found its way through the roof and fell on the bell with a sound like a coin in a brass bowl. That was when the tower lied again.

The escapement was locked where I had found it and the power should have been let out before we arrived. The weight motor was switched off at the panel with a neat turn of a black lever. The bell hammers were secured with pins. And yet the bell made a small, intimate sound, one a person shouldn’t hear unless his ear is pressed to the metal.

Then, clear as a hand on your shoulder in a room you thought you’d left, the bell tolled once. Somewhere in the gear train, something shrugged. The hands on the nearest dial twitched without committing to a minute. The sound went down through the stone and out into the rain. The city took it into its bones and decided it meant nothing.

Maya looked at me. In her eyes: You locked it.

“I did,” I said.

“Then someone else didn’t,” she said.

We both looked up through wood at the belfry, at the trap that led to the world of the little weathervane and the tangled aerials. The beam of her flashlight turned and climbed like a question. The caretaker’s breath stopped. The rain did not.

There was the scrape of something not a rat on old stone. Not a part of the mechanism unless the mechanism had learned new tricks. A person’s shoe on slate. A whisper of fabric. The faintest ticking that was not a clock at all.

“Don’t,” Maya said, but she was already moving for her radio.

I took one step onto the ladder and the ladder accepted me the way old ladders do: with regret and assistance. I put my face into the sulfur glow behind the iron and I said, quietly, for my own comfort, exactly the thing men with watches say.

Time, I thought. People will do anything to it. And then they will do worse to each other.

Chapter One

The first time the train came home empty, the gulls had the platform to themselves.

They stalked the paint-peeled edge of Platform B at Grayhaven Station like parsons at a funeral, muttering and scolding one another in the fog. The sound reached me before the horn did—thin, reedy, like a metal chair dragged across concrete. Then, far out of the fog, something sighed, and dull silver slid where there should have been people.

I was still halfway down Grove Street when Ezra Finch called, breathless, to say that the morning six-oh-eight had arrived without its driver.

“You’re joking,” I said, because it felt necessary to make a scale model out of ritual, even with the dawn blowing salt into my teeth. Ezra didn't joke about trains. He’d been the stationmaster since I was a teenager loitering under the departure boards and, back then, he’d watched me the way people watch dogs who might bolt into traffic.

“I’m not,” he said. “We’ve got red on all signals, it pulled in alone, and nobody’s getting on until you tell me.”

By the time I reached the station building, my breath had knitted itself into a steady pattern. The old clock over the ticket office insisted it was twenty-eight past six; my watch promised twenty-three. Ezra stood on the concourse pacing a rut between two vending machines, pale eyes vivid in his small, foxish face. He had pulled a blazer over a janitor’s zip-up hoodie, and his right hand kept worrying the plastic name tag that said EZRA in conservative black capital letters. The early commuters who hadn’t yet given up were clumped around him and at the ends of the platform, faces turned toward the fog as if toward God.

“Through here,” he said, ushering me along the edge of the turnstiles, murmuring the small spells of apology that get you past startled crowds. “I called Ortega. He said he’s on his way.”

Sergeant Luis Ortega and I had been playing a long game of professional ping-pong since he came back to Grayhaven and I accepted a job that almost guaranted I’d stay entangled with his paperwork. It was supposed to be temporary: three months to clean up a backfile at Coastline Transit’s safety office. That was four years ago. The trains stayed and so did I.

On Platform B, the gulls watched me in furious silence. The six-oh-eight sat with its doors closed and its lights breathing calmly, like a creature at rest. Seven stainless-steel cars, the windows banded with advertising, not the newest on the line but not old enough to be finicky. The Harbor & North logo—H&N in a restrained loop—was damp with dew. The nose of the lead car wore a veneer of salt, as if the sea had licked it and let it go.

“Signals?” I asked Ezra automatically. My voice felt like it belonged to someone older.

“All red from Southwest Junction straight through,” he said. “I watched it on the board. Reckoned it had failed, radioed the yard. Then it just… came.”

“Speed?”

“The track sensors show twenty-two as it rolled in. Slower than it should have been.”

“That'd be the station decel,” I said, though I didn’t like trusting a system without a hand on it. “Deadman’s?”

Ezra blew a breath out, shaping it toward patience. “Modern alerters. No pedal. It should have required acknowledgment.”

“Right,” I said, and touched my scarf to my throat, to give my hands a task. The fog tasted the same as it did every dawn in Grayhaven: clean as cold iron, even when the harbor cranes were grinding and the bait-shops had that secondhand ocean smell.

“This way’s sealed,” Ezra said, pointing at the doors. “We’ve got one at the tail end that popped. Sandoval kept it propped with her foot until backup arrived, then pulled it shut. I put tape on it and told everyone to stay back.”

“You didn’t go in?” I asked.

His eyes flicked at mine as if to check whether the question had an accusation nailed into it. “No, Mara. I didn’t. You told me, after that brake cylinder thing? First person to touch it writes the story of what happened. I wanted you to tell this one.”

My name sounded faintly unfamiliar.

Just then the fog peeled back at the far end of the platform and a siren wound down to a civil register. Luis Ortega emerged from it, broad-shouldered, coat unbuttoned, paper coffee cup balanced on his palm like an offering. He always looked as if he had just come from a room where a dozen people were shouting at him. We nodded at each other the way we had learned to—flat, efficient, as if the nod itself were a form the agency liked signed.

“What am I looking at?” he said.

“Six-oh-eight,” I said. “From Southpoint. No engineer. No conductor at the rear. All doors closed except one at the tail for a moment. Docked clean. Lights on. No passengers.”

“Bomb threat?” Ortega’s eyes traveled the length of the cars. The fog obligingly cleared another arm’s length.

“No call,” Ezra said. “No radio. It came in like Sunday.”

“We’ll need to clear the concourse,” Ortega said, scanning the cluster of delayed commuters. “Get statements. Video.”

I nodded. Everything we were saying was for someone else to hear later, typed out and slotted beside an invoice in a manila folder. That was fine. I preferred to find the thing itself unsaid and pin it open.

“Let me go in,” I said.

I walked the train as if I could pretend we did this every day. I put my ear to the metal before trying the lead door; the mechanical quiet on the other side angled the hairs along my arm to attention. Ezra gave me the key to the manual override. My fingers did what they were trained to do, and the door gave with the sound of a breath being carefully held and then let go.

My father used to take me to see the trains at the North Yard on my seventh birthdays. He had a thermos that smelled of coffee high up in the top register—the kind of smell you could fall through and never hit bottom. “Listen to them,” he used to say. “They’ll tell you if they’re right.” He taught me to hear when the brakes were singing in the wrong key, when the cooling fans were trying too hard. He taught me that machines had a posture. The six-oh-eight’s posture was obedient and wrong.

A draught met me when the door edged aside, smelling faintly of damp wool and stranger. The empty is always different than the vacant. Vacant is a room that hasn’t been lived in; empty is a room that has, and everything has gone away.

“Hang on,” Ortega said. I turned back to see him tugging a pair of nitrile gloves into place, then offering me a pair with two fingers. “If it’s a crime scene, we won’t be the ones who home-decorated it.”

We ghosted inside together.

The first car—the lead coach—still had Wednesday piled around it like drift. A coffee cup rode the incline of a seat, a tongue of foam dried in the lid seam. A tablet lay face down on the floor; a pair of reading glasses perched cockeyed on it as if a hand had set them there and never came back. An advertisement for a dental practice smiled at us, all small, white relief.

“Where are the people?” Ortega asked.

I listened, which is not the same as answering. The HVAC hummed in brave ignorance. The overhead lights ticked faintly; the way fluorescent fixtures tick when the ballast is thinking about aging. From farther back in the train came a single electronic cough and a clatter. The sound evoked the reflex memory of puppies and made me hate it.

We moved forward together, me on the right, Ortega on the left, Ezra hovering behind in the vestibule. Our breath made low intermittencies in the quiet. I stopped to look at the armrest nearest the aisle, and saw where a woman had pressed her fingers absentmindedly into the vinyl a hundred times, leaving a polished place paler than the rest.

The second car was a mirror. Gum pressed under a seat like a secret. A shopping bag with two lemons, one rolling around loose and dimmed by a film of condensation. A knit scarf looped into itself so neatly I wanted to put it around somebody’s neck. We reached the joint between the second and third cars and I felt it then: not a temperature change, not a smell, just the sense that we were on the other side of something ordinary.

“Wait.” Ortega put up a hand and tilted his head. Somewhere inside the train, a phone was ringing.

There are a hundred reasons why a phone rings in an empty car. Forgotten purses, forgotten lunches, a person on the concourse calling the device location he can see circling on a map. But this was not a cheerful chirp. It rang slow and resolute, the way my grandmother’s phone used to ring in her house: insistently modest.

We stood for a moment, listening. It rang again.

“Third car,” I said, surprised to hear how certain I was. We moved toward it. The fog tapped a rhythm on the windows. The ring came again, nearer.

It was on the aisle seat, two-thirds of the way back, nested in the groove where a human thigh would go. The screen lit the carriage up ghoulishly for a heartbeat and a face bloomed there in miniature: a woman laughing, someone’s hand mid-swipe across her cheek. The caller ID said UNKNOWN. It had been ringing a long time. The battery icon scowled.

“Don’t,” Ortega said softly, just as I was reaching for it. “Let’s not turn it into ours.”

He wasn’t wrong. He pulled his phone out and took three photographs, then lifted the ringing one with a delicacy that I would have teased him about on any other day. The ring broke off as soon as the angle shifted. A second later, it began again, stubborn. He held it for me to see the background better.

The woman without the swipe-hand was wearing a dark-blue work shirt with a name patch on it. She was standing beside a man whose hair had gone white early. He was kissing her temple. They were both wearing safety goggles. Behind them was a wall of numbered metal drawers. I shouldn’t have known the place, but I did: the yard tool-locker at Southpoint, the kind with the padlocks replaced every month because someone always kept a copy of the key.

God, I thought. Lanie.

Alana Perez, assistant yard manager, Southpoint. Thirty-four. The kind of competent that makes other people forget to be threatened because they’re too relieved. I had signed her completion certificate for the CR-04 rolling stock orientation two years ago. We had eaten donuts together when Ezra turned sixty and refused to let anyone sing. The last time I saw her, she was swearing to bring me a grapefruit from her neighbor’s tree the size of a toddler.

“Do you know the owner?” Ortega asked.

I didn’t answer because I was looking at the lockscreen and underneath the picture and the UNKNOWN the faint okra-green smudges of a broken tempered-glass protector spiderwebbed across the lower-left corner. The cracks were clean and new; I have never met a woman who wouldn’t pick at a crack like that until it became a hole big enough to catch on a pocket.

“I do,” I said. “It’s Lanie’s.”

“Do you think she called herself?” He meant, is it a back call from another device, is this some automation we can explain with a chart.

“I don’t know,” I said.

He silenced the call and slid the phone into an evidence bag, discomfort flitting over his face as if he’d just done something impolite to a stranger. The quiet that fell after we stopped it was weighty, as if it were sitting in the aisle and breathing.

We moved on.

Car four had a pebbled scattering of salt on the floor by the window, a wayward map of the bay, like the sea had leaned in and shaken itself. The fifth had a lipstick in the wire tray under a seat, the bullet blunted flat from being pressed too hard into a mouth. The sixth had the smell of oranges for no good reason. We passed through each like divers who had not yet decided whether the surface was home.

At the far end of the seventh car—the cab car—Ezra said something under his breath that might have been a prayer. The cab door had a narrow rectangle of reinforced glass at head height and in the glass a pale reflection of my face was waiting. The door itself had an old-fashioned keyhole below the panel, more for tradition than necessity, but the lock cylinder showed the telltale unscarred circle that meant nobody had put a screwdriver to it. A strip of security tape ran across the seam and had not been broken.

“Locked,” Ezra said unnecessarily.

I leaned closer to the glass. On the far side, the driver’s chair sat neatly tucked back from the console as if someone had ducked out for a moment, as if someone had given it the courtesy they give a seat before leaving it to someone else. The console hummed like bee-loudness. The radio handset lay in its cradle. The digital clock on the panel said 6:24. The master controller was in the neutral notch. The emergency brake handle was where it should be: pushed in and rotated ninety degrees to set. No human anywhere.

“Key,” I said.

Ezra passed it to me: a fat old brass thing that could bend an argument. I slid it into the keyhole and heard the small, serious clunk of hungry pins. The door yielded an inch; then the resisted give of a thing whose edges stick by virtue of being in place a long time. When it opened, the smell hit me: a little like dust that has never seen the sun, a little like the inside of my father’s tool bag. And lying on the floor directly in front of the chair, as neatly placed as a bookmark, was a thin rectangle of cardstock with a pastel stripe across the top.

I bent and lifted it. Standard H&N stock ticket, printed on the kiosk in the Southpoint concourse, today’s date—like the universe needed that there—and a destination corrected twice by an impatient finger on the touch screen. Someone had swiped the strip with a thumb as they pulled it free and left an arc of something on it—a half-inch curb of dried red-brown along the left side. Not the amount you’d have if you overwhelmed an engine with panic. The amount you get when you don’t notice you’re bleeding and you do something you’ve done a thousand times.

“Blood?” Ortega said.

“Maybe,” I said, because my router didn’t want to go there yet. When I turned the ticket over, there was writing on the back, in pencil. The graphite had been smeared by a heel or a hand, and it made the letters a little furry.

Signal the river, it said. Then underneath, more faintly, two small, neat words with a care that made my stomach remember what falling felt like: SORRY, MARA.

My name again. Now it sounded like it belonged to me, and I wanted to give it back.

Ortega had leaned in close enough that his shoulder touched mine. “You’re going to tell me why someone would leave your name in a locked cab.”

“You're going to tell me why there is no one on this train,” I said, because it felt like a ladder that would get me off the ground.

Ezra stood at the door, hand on the frame, strung tight with the sort of nervous flyer’s tension that can make a person squeeze armrests long after the turbulence is gone. “The cameras,” he said suddenly, relief at something he could offer, something uncreepy. “Car cams. Cab cam. We can see who was in here.”

He was right. The cab camera would have been running from the moment the six-oh-eight left Southpoint. The event recorder would have had everything: throttle position, brake application, horn, location down to G.O.P.S. coordinates, radio logs. I turned to the console and checked for the small telltale LED that indicated the recorder had power. It glowed green. When I pressed the RESET, it did what it should, and my body admired the fact almost in spite of my mind. Ezra’s hands were already moving over the panel the way a priest might handle a Bible, careful, reverent, practiced.

“You'll dump it?” I asked.

“I'll dump it,” he said. “No one’s pulling this chip until the paperwork is a tower. But we can pull a live feed now from the buffer.”

He navigated the menu tree with more grace than most of the twenty-year-olds in our office, because this was the church and Ezra had done his confirmation here. I watched the corner of the screen where the thumbnail would show, where a frozen frame was waiting.

It came up in black and white. For a second, because my brain is a living thing that sometimes wants to be wrong, I thought the camera had failed and given us nothing but a confession of emptiness. Then the figures resolved: the driver’s chair, the none of a person in it, the console, the window. The time code in the bottom left flickered like a hamster heartbeat. The date stamped itself gloomy and unarguable over the entire lower third.

“Reverse two minutes,” I said.

Ezra did. The numbers counted down like someone tiring. The picture jiggled once as if someone outside had thumped the nose of the train with a palm, to see if it were real.

“There,” Ortega said reflexively, although nothing had changed except our expectations. Ezra finessed the play. The supervisory computer data painted a parallel story on a smaller strip: throttle settings, brake set, door cycles. The last door close mark ticked over. The intercom had been used at Southpoint with a hiss and a “Doors closing,” in Lanie’s voice, because she liked to give the morning a clean line. The event that brought us here—somebody, somehow, vacating a moving train of all its humans without leaving a rip in the air where they went—did not present itself.

“The conductor radioed a shift handoff at five fifty,” Ezra said, voice going flat to keep the devotional in check. “Lanie was on the rear car. Engineer was Nora Wyle.”

My mind filed that name with the clean, painless accuracy of a machine. Wyle. Wyle, Wyle. Forty-six. Signed off through grade crossing modules, slow-order compliance, last five-year re-shift two months ago. No demerits, two commendations. Lives in a two-flat on Juniper Street near the old bakery that always smells like cinnamon enough to make you irritable. Played kingdom on the back deck with her daughter while the gulls mapped the slats.

“What happened between the bridge and here?” Ortega asked.

“Between the river and here,” I corrected, and then felt idiotic, because there is a way to be precise that is useful and a way to be precise that is a shield.

Ezra gave me the look of someone who has been waiting to ask me something unnoticed. “What does ‘signal the river’ mean?”

My mouth had an answer ready that had nowhere to go. It could mean a dozen things in a dozen small dialects: we sometimes refer to the drawbridge telling us a way that isn’t closed; sometimes, I had heard the older engineers talk about the river as if it were a person who needed the courtesy of a horn. On my father’s runs, signaling the river had meant tapping the metal railing twice when he crossed the marsh-spine, a private superstition he pretended was part of the rules. He had told me it was to let the river know we meant its crossings politely. I could feel the thunk of his ring on the rail in my wrist bones.

Before I could find the right shape of not-answer, Ezra lowered his eyes to the console again. The camera image jumped. There was a smear across the lower left quadrant now that I hadn't noticed before, a finger’s worth of blur, the kind you get when someone passes too close to a lens and the oil from skin makes a halo. It was too diffuse to be useful but too human to ignore.

“I'm going to want that dump and a print of the passenger manifest,” Ortega said. “And I’m going to want to know who’s got the footage from the last station stop before here.”

“Halvorsen is at Bayview,” Ezra said. “He can sit on the footage until we pry it out by form.”

“Make the call,” Ortega said.

He stepped back to give me room to pass him in the little cab. I put the ticket with the apology into an evidence sleeve because my training had taught me about the parts of my own hands I cannot sterilize. I looked once more around the small, precise space where the absence sat, orderly and emphatically present. Machines do not keep secrets. They are bad at it. The people who run them, though—we are very, very good.

When we stepped out onto the platform again, daylight had decided to admit it was involved. The wet edges of things glowed. The cluster of would-be travelers had been moved back off the concourse; a few of them had started the business of turning this into narrative with their phones. A boy of twelve leaned against the vending machine like he wanted to be seen leaning. A woman in a pencil skirt spoke into her front camera with the calm of a person who has never yet seen something that did not eventually end up in a story she understood. In the new light, I could see the river like a seam under the city, as if someone had unpicked Grayhaven and laid it out flat and the stitch that had held it together was slack.

“Do you know why you’re sorry?” I asked the cardstock in my pocket, as if it could answer me, as if it could shrug and say: for what I did, for what I didn’t, for all of it. As if the ticket could tell me what the absence took with it. As if the river were listening.

Ortega tapped the toe of his shoe against the yellow line at the platform’s edge and looked at me. “I hope you brought your boots,” he said. “We’ll be wading for this one.”

I looked down at the metal, at the fine line of rust that grows even on stainless steel if you let the salt talk long enough. Outside, a freighter sounded a horn three times, and in the small cell of the cab behind me a camera continued to watch a seat that did not have a person in it, obediently making a record of how nothing can be the biggest thing in a room.

The first time it rains inside City Hall, it comes through three sets of locked doors and a stairwell we keep padlocked for “safety and aesthetics.” By the time I get the chain off and throw my shoulder into the swollen door, the water has decided for itself. It barrels past me in a broad, flashing sheet and goes happily down to the lowest level like a dog that knows which lap is allowed.

“I told you the gutters were a joke,” I say it to the water, and to no one. The building listens, or pretends to. It’s one of those brick piles that sits on old maps like a paperweight, our Hallowell City Hall, built when things were made to last and budgets were set by cigar-smoke and handshakes. The storm finds every crack those men refused to see.

“Ms. Liddell!”

Davon, my part-time assistant, appears behind me with his palms up like he can stop physics. He’s nineteen, with a hairline lightning bolt tattoo behind one ear that, in a different city, would keep him from getting hired. Here, you’d better have at least one if you expect to be listened to at Planning Commission meetings.

“Grab towels,” I say. “And the food-service trays. If anyone asks, you didn’t take them from the breakroom, I did.”

He grins and vanishes. I step gingerly into the flow. It’s not deep yet, just enough to soak the hem of my dress and make paper a disease. My basement—the Records Division—stares back at me through the open door: gray rolling shelves, tan acid-free boxes with their smug little labels, that smell of dry breath and old gum wrappers. The ceiling is sweating, the fluorescent tubes emitting the exact flicker of a first date with a bad idea. In here is birth, death, taxes, permits, follies. The items deemed “permanent and vital” by the indifferent god of the retention schedule sit on the highest shelves. The luckless reside lower. We keep regrets in various formats.

Davon arrives with an armload of towels and two cafeteria trays. We skim the rolling river into the mop sink, dam off the low shelves, speak to the building like it’s an old woman refusing a sweater.

“Turn that one,” I say, pointing at a shelf. “If water collects, the bottom ones will swell. The boxes will think we’ve decided to bury them for real.”

“You okay if I document?” His phone is already out.

“Yes,” I say. “Thank you.”

I taught him to photograph our failures. I taught him to timestamp, zoom on mold threads, to note where the metal has bloomed into orange lace. Documentation is the curse and charm of my life. My mouth can lie or forget. Paper is a quieter accomplice. It only tells you where you didn’t look.

Rain gives way to a hard tattoo on the sidewalk overhead, a sound like a crowd banging on the glass. The drains make confession noises and then, miracle of miracles, give up gurgling. We stand in the new silence, wet shoes precisely where no one will step except those who are paid to.

“We should lose electricity by half-past,” I say. “You might as well go home.”

He flinches but not in fear. “My mom said I could stay. She said if I came home and found her basement covered in boxes, I’d be tempted to start alphabetizing.”

“Your mother knows me,” I say, and he laughs.

We continue triaging. We put “Building Permits, 1973-1981” on the second-highest shelf and “Dog Owners Licensed in the Year of Our Lord 1956” on the floor to dry. We move the rolling stacks because the mechanism sticks in humidity. The records sing if you know their voices: brittle-ledger leaf-thrum, manila whisper, the heavy whisper of cloth-bound books with names on their spines that don’t fit on gravestones.

“A bunch slid.” Davon points to a low, the lowest, shelf. He kneels with unwarranted confidence in the puddle and feels underneath. “There’s one severed.”

“It’s not a salad,” I say, but the word severed makes me look. The roller track wobbled when the water came in, and a box that used to be braced by a neighbor has pushes out from the wall. It is not a box from my inventory. I would have remembered a box like that. It has no label, which is one of my dislikes. It has no standard hand-written scrawl in blue Sharpie that says, for example, “ZONING COMM. 1989-90 DO NOT TOSS!” Instead, this is a dressed object, wrapped in heavy paper and taped with a kind of attention that borders on love. A thick ribbon of red wax seals one side seam like a scar.

Red wax is dramatic. The last time I saw it, it was on a wedding invitation shaped like an apology. I crack it with my thumbnail.

Davon makes a sound that could be awe or hunger. “Are we allowed?”

“When there is water, we are allowed to do anything we need to keep information alive,” I say. “Also I am the keeper of keys. Watch me keep.”

We haul it to the worktable. The paper unfurls like a sail. The box inside is metal. It’s heavier than I expect, which is never good news when you are wet and everything turns to soap in your hands. I lever the lid up with a butter knife I keep in a drawer next to pencils and spare Bone Folders.

Inside, everything has been wrapped again—this time in waxed cloth, like sandwiches from a romantic era. Whoever packed this wanted to keep the damp out. Whoever packed this believed that they might fail. I unzip one bundle. The first thing I find is a letter sized envelope with the words EMERGENCY PACKET written on the front in block letters that look nothing like the curl of the labels here.

“Should I take pictures?” Davon asks, and then adds the thing I like about him. “Or do you want to look first.”

“Documentation is dessert,” I say. And then I take his phone, because hands shake less when they have a machine between them and the thing that is new.

The envelope is thin. Inside is a folded sheet of City letterhead—the old kind, with the line drawing of a bridge we tore down ten years ago, and the slogan no one would approve now. On the paper:

If you are reading this it means someone is dead in a way they are not meant to be, and no one will call that crime by its name.

If you are reading this in the year 1979 I have made a mistake.

If you are reading this in some year beyond that then you remember me. Please tell the mayor I was right to be afraid.

The name at the bottom is written in one go, a slow firm hand. Etta Voss.

I know the name the way you know a song your mother hummed while doing dishes. It’s in the index of a hundred binders across the shelves. Typed on memos to four different City Managers. She worked here, once. I have never met her and yet I have built entire afternoons on the idea that she sat in this room, or one like it, the paper the same. The last file with her initials is from August of 1979. After that, a thread gone.

Davon leans over my shoulder, risking his status as a living person if he drips on the page.

“Oh,” he says, like the letter bit him.

I read it twice. Then I turn it over because sometimes people write more on the back. There is a phone number from before there were area codes, written and then scratched out and written again.

“Keep going?” Davon says.

We do. Beneath the letter is a passport photo of a woman in her late thirties. She has a blunt jaw and eyebrows that meet if she is tired or mad, and hair cut into a pageboy that looks like a choice, like she told the barber to do it and he stopped saying are you sure after the first inch. Another bundle holds a small day diary with a black faux-leather cover and the year 1979 stamped in gold. It is zippered shut; there is nothing inside except entries that stop in July. “Dogwood” appears four times, underlined twice, followed by “1st floor foundation cavity—ask K,” then “Ask J? J unreliable,” then nothing. One more packet holds three Polaroids. In them, two men stand in front of the Dogwood Court sign as if they built it. Their sunglasses are as large as hands. The third photo is of the sign without the men. The corner has been torn and then re-taped in the way that suggests the tearing had a ritual.

“Is that the old Dogwood?” Davon asks. “The apartments?”

I nod. Dogwood Court was a cluster of low brick rectangles jammed into a triangle of land between the Vance River and the railroad. The buildings had numbers instead of names and the blacktops grew silver in the heat. People got fed, housed, harmed, married there. I was a kid then. My father got work there once, patching roofs that made tiny lumpy mountains as they bubbled in August.

Dogwood came down in 1982 in a flurry of lawsuits and dust. There had been all the normal reasons—mold, inefficiency, the new idea that we could do poverty better by not seeing it—and three unusual ones that no one ever named in writing. We put “URBAN RENEWAL” on letterhead. The morning the wreckers came, a crowd watched from the sidewalk as if the bricks might do a trick. They didn’t. It rained that day too. By afternoon there was only a field of broken teeth.

“I was three,” I say, to the envelope. The paper does not care about my milestones. “This is before I knew what paper could do.”

From the far end of the basement, where the microfilm reader sits by itself like an insult, the light blinks. Rain has reached some breaker. The fluorescents hum, dim. Then one row of bulbs gives up entirely and when it does the room feels as if it has swallowed itself.

“Maybe we should go upstairs,” Davon says.

“In a second.” I flip the letter back to its face and read the next line as if it appeared by itself while we weren’t looking.

There is a ledger they will not let you see. It has numbers that do not add and men who never stop smiling. It belongs to the office called ANNEX 79—DOGWOOD PROJECT, which is what you say when you want a name to be a shed and not a street.

They think they can hide something under a new coat of paint. They are wrong. People like me have keys. People like you will be given a mop.

When you need to find the ledger, ask for the foundation logs for 14-B, but say you are looking for 14-A. They will correct you and show off. That’s when you watch their face. It will be either a J or a K.

She does not explain J and K. The way the letter moves makes me suspect the explanation is a person and not a policy and people decompose faster. The last sentence reads, as if she ran out of space and breath at the same time:

If this is about water, believe me.

“Ms. L?” says a voice from far away, the sound travelling down the stairwell and through the wet. “You got a call.” It is Steve from the security desk. He is the kind of man who has introduced himself the same way three times, twice to the same person, because introducing himself is his job.

I wipe my hands on my skirt and sprint up two flights, dodging the spots with the most rain memory. The lobby smells like damp wool even when it hasn’t been raining. Old marble sweats. Paint flakes into delicate bones.

Steve holds out the black desk phone like a librarian offering a warning. “He says it’s urgent.”

“Who?”

He shields the mouthpiece with a palm he could have used to palm my head. “Your ex.”

Evan.

The phone is older than some of the interns and has that gravity they sometimes lack. I put it between my ear and shoulder and brace myself with an elbow against the directory.

“Liddell,” I say.

“You at work?” His voice is exactly the same and completely different. The City pays him to talk not quite like a cop but not quite not like one, and all I hear is how much he has learned to pull words out of the ditch and set them upright.

“Yes,” I say, although if he is calling me at the desk phone he knows. “We’re taking on water down here.”

“Everyone is,” he says. “Listen.” He waits, and the waiting tells me this is not a feud, this is not a question about who gets to keep the good towels or whether I will return his mother’s casserole dish. “We found a body.”

Every city has the sound it makes when someone says that. Hallowell has wind down a long alley that shouldn’t exist because there is river at the end of it, and a freight train horn that has been bending in the same place for forty years. They both arrive at once in the lobby.

“Where?” I ask.

“Dogwood,” he says.

It takes a second for the word to mean what it means now and not what it meant in 1979. “The site? The new development?”

“The… proposed one,” he says, and the word proposed is an insult and a prayer. He is moving—I can hear his breath do a thing, the thing it does when he is walking quickly indoors and being careful not to sound like he is. “The rain made you think of me?”

“It made me think of disasters,” I say. “And then Steve said my ex and I figured someone had done something to deserve me.”

He is quiet long enough for a statement to fill that space by itself. When he speaks, he has adjusted.

“We haven’t called it anything. We haven’t told anyone anything. But we need someone to look at what he had in his pocket.”

“Evidence,” I say, from habit. We learned the same language once, then opted for dialects. “Who is he?”

“Councilman Rook,” he says.

There is a bench under the directory sign. I sit because that is what benches in City Hall lobbies are built for—someone to sit on them and pretend that the information they have just received is not an ocean.

“Rook,” I say, and it sits in my mouth like something it doesn’t know what to do with. Rook the long-serving councilman who has been running for mayor for so long that sometimes even he forgets there isn’t a mayoral election every year. Rook whose signs have stayed up through three winters on badly nailed posts. Rook whose face you could sketch from memory because his smile was a brand and his wince a habit.

“We’re securing the site now,” Evan says. “I’ll send a car if you don’t want to drive in this.”

He remembers something about me then. I do not drive in rain like this. I do, but I do it badly and with the radio off so I can hear the road argue with me. When someone you loved used to sleep in your bed and then didn’t, there is a book of things they can still read in you. You spend the rest of your life deciding which sentences you want edited.

“I can get there,” I say, although we both know I cannot get there quickly. “What did he have in his pocket.”

“A note,” he says. “And something else you should see.”

“Read me the note?”

“I’d rather you saw it,” he says, because that has also become the language. “But I can tell you one thing. Your name is on it.”

“My…?” I stand up because when you are about to be hit by a wave, that is what you do, even if it is the wrong thing.

“It’s your card,” he says. “Your business card. The new ones. The ones with the city seal in blue because the black looked cheap. He had one in his jacket pocket.”

“I have never met—” I start. “I’ve never put a card in his hand.”

“Maybe he was in here,” Evan says. “Maybe Steve gave him one.”

I look at Steve. He looks back at me with the personal interest of a person who is in charge of doors, which is to say, all of them.

“I don’t hand out cards for her,” Steve says. “I am not her receptionist.”

I put my hand over the mouthpiece. “Do you remember Councilman Rook?” I ask.

“He comes in through the back when he doesn’t want those people to see him,” Steve says. “Whichever people those are that day.”

I put the phone back to my ear. “What else did he have.”

“A photo,” Evan says. He is moving again; the echo of his shoes says gym, concrete, tarp, water. “Dogwood. The sign. It’s a Polaroid. Your guy from Records will tell me the film type and date later.” He is teasing me, also not. “It’s torn on the corner and taped back together with yellowing tape like somebody was keeping kindling.”

My skin goes hot then cold. The sensation is precise. It picks up where the storm left off and sits on my shoulders.

“And the note?” I ask.

“A name,” he says. “The name Etta. And a phone number with no area code.”

The lobby is not built to rock, but it does, in the way boats do even tied to docks. I swallow and taste metal.

“I’ll be there,” I say.

When I get back down to the basement, the waxed paper is still spread in gentle curves. The letter with the old City seal lies with the careful arrogance of a witness. Davon stands by the table with his arms crossed over his chest as if he is holding himself in.

“Everything okay?” he asks.

“Nope,” I say, and I smile at him because I am not a monster. “But for once it might be the useful kind of not okay.”

He looks at the letter, then me. “Do I touch nothing until you get back.”

“You touch nothing,” I say. “You take photos of nothing. You sit at the desk, which is elevated, and you read something printed after 1990 so your lungs don’t learn anything. If anyone asks what’s down here, you say Christmas decorations and a broken microwave.”

“I can lie with the best,” he says, and then, because we have known each other just long enough to reach for the same tool at the same time: “What did he have.”

He means the body. He means what we will all mean until this shifts and becomes actual.

“My card,” I say, and show him the face I make when something is technically true and emotionally absurd.

“That’s flattering,” he says.

“And a photograph of the Dogwood sign,” I say.

He nods like the world makes sense if you tilt it a certain way. He has not learned yet that sometimes it only pretends to, the way a dying appliance pretends to be quiet because you are on the phone.

“What do I tell people,” he asks, “if they call and want to know why the Records Manager has gone to stand in a field of broken teeth.”

“That she is doing her job,” I say. “Tell them it is raining in the basement and someone who might know why is lying in it.”

I slide the letter back in its envelope. I don’t trust myself to leave it here, but I also cannot take it. It belongs to this room the way a confession belongs to a church even if the church leaks. I take a photograph of the letter’s top half—a sin I have already committed a thousand times. Then I put the metal box back together, layer by layer, and seal it with blue painter’s tape because we are modern people and wax is for people who still have illusions about how long things last.

On the way out, I stop at my desk and pluck one of my business cards from the small, heavy stack. Hallowell City Seal in navy so it looks like a thing and not a joke. My name in full. Records Manager, which makes my mother tell people I am a librarian because that sits easier on her tongue. I turn it over and look at the white side. I write Etta Voss in the corner because it will matter, and because when you write something down you tell the universe you intend to remember.

It is still raining in the stairwell. It will be raining in the stairwell when I come back. Outside, Hallowell is a show of light on wet streets, brake lights blur into a dragon that does not sleep. Down river, at a brown field where an idea used to live, men in City windbreakers will be putting up tape where we have been trying to put up condos. There will be a tarp over a shape, and some part of me will still want to check the retention schedule to see how long we’re meant to keep it. There will be a camera pointed at my face, eventually, and a question about why my card was in his pocket, and a longer question about what it means that when it finally rains inside City Hall, it rains like this. It rains like someone promised it would. If this is about water, believe me.

On the desk by the phone, Steve has put a paper cup with coffee and a napkin under it because he is an artist. He taps the top of the cup twice with one finger as if to seal it.

“Bring me back something interesting,” he says, and I almost say I always do. Instead I tuck the napkin in my pocket and walk out into the kind of storm our city uses to scrub itself.

“Tell Evan,” he calls after me, “to stop calling you here like he owns the number.”

“I’ll put it in an email,” I say. I put everything in an email eventually. Some of them get printed and put into a box. Some boxes get sealed with drama. Some boxes sit where the floor sags until the storm finds them and asks if they still want to be secrets. Some secrets burst like the wax on a letter, then cool, then hold their shapes for a very long time.

Dogwood waits. The street I take to get there has two names: the official one with its dead politician and the old one everyone still uses—River Road—because it goes where everything does here. Down. Toward the water, where we keep the stories we couldn’t bear to tell upstairs. Where tonight something is lying that should not be. Where a woman who vanished in a year with a number I can recite like a prayer has written me a sentence from the past, and the rain has carried it like a rumor to my bare toe.

The lake had always been a mirror, a flat coin of water that held the sky by its throat. This summer the sky wrenched itself free. What remained looked like the underside of a scab—cracked mud, pale ribs of old foundations, the black bones of stumps that had done fifty years under silt and ice. Even the air felt picked clean. When the wind blew, it brought the smell of pennies and old rot that clung to the tongue.

I parked by the rusted chain across the access road, hopped it, and walked. My shoes took the lakebed like an apology. Behind me the dam kept its square face turned toward the day, concrete unmoved by the drought or anyone’s grief. Half the county had been out here in the last week to gawk and carry pieces of what the water had returned, and somehow, this early, I had the place to myself. News moved faster than water.

At the edge of a ravine that had been West Church Street, I stopped and took the first pictures. The case had felt too heavy on my shoulder when I’d packed it before dawn, but my hands know what they’re doing even when the rest of me has questions. The sun came up behind Gray Ridge, made the broken house rectangles look important for a moment. If you knew where to look, you could see the faint line where the old sidewalk had been, a sliver of brighter mud with chips of pink gravel. Someone had set three mason jars along that line, each holding a clenched fist of wildflowers. Most of the flowers were already tired.

Graybridge had been two towns even when it was whole: the part that now lived along the highway with its pizza and auto parts and interrogative billboards, and the drowned part whose bones the drought had bared. People had told me last week—old men dropping their cigarettes into their palms as they spoke, women tucking hair behind their ears with fingers chapped from the coin wash at Benny’s—that they’d come back to see where their grandparents had long-ago shopped, kissed, waited for buses. They never said buried. Drowned sounds like something that tried to breathe and failed. Buried is tidy.

I used to lean over the lookout fence at the dam as a kid, hook my elbows and throw a penny south toward what we were told lay below. It felt like buying a promise. When I moved to Boston and then New Haven and then, briefly, anywhere that wasn’t my town, I stopped throwing pennies. It didn’t help anyone.

I knelt at the steps to what had been the church. The steps kept going down into a rectangle where the basement had once kept casseroles warm and secrets colder. Someone had been here before me to brush off a piece of tile, bring up a blue-and-white pattern that remembered something ornate. The tile flaked in my hand; and there, underneath, a shard of glass with a bevel, like from a frame, still squared enough to catch the sun and throw a foolish flash into the emptiness.

“Dad,” I said to nobody, the way I sometimes did out loud when a shade of him passed across my brain. He would want a photo that turned the mud romantic. A picture you could paste across the top of the Graybridge Ledger with a headline that made you pause. I took the photo anyone would take—wide, lonely; the steps, the suggestion of a nave—and then a photo only my father would print. Near the bottom step, tangled in silt, a child’s necklace of flat glass beads lay like a fossilized smile. The beads were the color of an old sky. I got close and filled the frame with it. Somewhere in my knees, a popping told me I wasn’t nineteen anymore.

The sun shouldered higher, warmed my neck. Down the ravine that had been Church Street, the slick remains of a hand-painted sign drooped against a crooked post. All that showed was RAIN. It could have been something else. It was nice, though, to believe in omens.

I heard an engine long before I saw the truck. It sounded wrong out here, loud and ordinary. The truck coughed up dust as it took the access road and then braked beside my car. Owen Knox swung himself down, took off his ball cap, and beat it against his thigh like it was going to misbehave. Owen had been operating the dam longer than I’d been back in town; I could chart time by his mustache—thick, then vanished for two years, then returned as a thinner line like someone had drawn it in with pencil. He shaded his eyes, looked down at me.

“You’re out early, Hannah.”

“Reporter’s hours,” I said. The Ledger didn’t pay me anything close to a full-time wage, but my father was still learning how to be a person who didn’t leave at five a.m., and the paper had been his spine for thirty-seven years. I couldn’t let it curve now.

“Got someone from the state coming at nine,” Owen said. “Hoover this time. Water Resources. That woman with the hair that could take an eye out. She wants a look. You stepping around by yourself makes me nervous.”

“I’m careful.”

He gestured at the ravine. “Careful would be not falling into a root cellar that’s waited half a century to take you down.”

“I’ll be out of your way before your meeting,” I said. “Need a photo. People like to see where they used to pray.”

He snorted, not unkindly. “People prayed for rain. I got men sending emails like I control a faucet in my basement.” He squinted at the wide bowl of exposed town, then winced as if he’d stepped on a nail. “Hell,” he said, and the sound barely made it across the distance. “It ain’t right.”

He waved once and left me to my work and my thoughts and the careful navigation of half-seen edges. The truck after him made no pretense at quiet: shiny, lifted, with an Instagram handle stenciled on the tailgate in pink. The woman who drove it was my age, maybe a little younger, wearing a baseball shirt with a retro logo and a ring light folded like a white bird in the bed of the truck.

“You’re here too?” she called, cheerful, as if we’d made an appointment.

“Early bird,” I said. “Worms and so forth.”

“Careful where you dig,” she said, as if quoting a movie no one else had seen. “Jessa Quin,” she added, though she said it like I should know. She picked her way down beside me, sticking her boots into my footprints. “I do the channel,” she said when I didn’t take the bait. “Finding the forgotten? Ghost towns are magic. Everyone’s rediscovering roots this month.”

Her hair was a wound-bright red that could not exist by accident. She had a GoPro clipped to her jacket like a badge.

“Try not to take anything,” I said. “They posted signs.”

She made a face. It belonged on camera. “We can’t leave this stuff under the mud when it fills again. It’s basically a museum.” She pointed the GoPro toward the steps. “Imagine the comments.”

“Imagine the sheriff,” I said. The Ledger rarely ran photos of Sheriff Hollis Kline smiling. He had a mouth that went flat, like a ruler laid across an unserious statement.

“Ugh. The sheriff. He DM’d me,” she said, as if she were telling me about a man who had tried to sell her life insurance on a bus. “I told him I was an educator. He told me he had a shovel and didn’t mind the work.” She waved the GoPro. “I’ll blur faces.”

“Don’t blur mine,” I said. “I work for the paper. The Ledger. Tell people to buy it and I’ll owe you two favors.”

“Print,” she said, and for a heartbeat I saw actual curiosity soften what I’d thought was permanent brightness. “That’s kind of punk.”

She drifted away, narrating to her lens. I watched her place her feet carefully. The mud here took in stories and didn’t give them back easily.

Farther down, nature and history had conspired to create a dark mouth where the mud shelf had slumped into an opening. I almost missed it; a collapsed corner made it look like nothing, just a dusty softness. There was a piece of plywood, gray as old bread, off to the side, damp fuzz of moss still clinging. Someone had moved it to look. Someone had put it back and not exactly lined it up. The hair went up on my arms. There was no reason. There was a reason.

“Hold up,” I called, too casually, to Jessa, but she was pretending not to hear me for the benefit of a sound mix later. The bile taste of adrenaline touched the back of my tongue. I looked around—Owen far, Jessa farther, no one else yet—and crouched.

The opening was a square leading into a space that had been, by the old maps I’d copied and taped over my desk yesterday, the pantry of the parsonage. Not quite a cellar, but an underground coolness. A root cellar would be deeper. This was a place you put preserves and, if you had them, secrets.

The damp that had not yet left the earth made the smell come up—soft rot and a sweeter disgust. Summer will do that. It makes anything left too long announce itself.

“Hey,” I said, not believing I did, the old bone habit of talking to empty spaces making my voice smaller. “Anybody in there?”

I put my palm on the dirt and leaned. The edge of the mouth held. I slid my camera down first and then my feet, lowering myself slow, testing each bend and tendon. The rectangle admitted me with only one complaint: the scuff of my jacket against something embedded that had edges. The air inside was three degrees cooler and half a century older.

It was only a few feet deep. Enough to stand with your head down. Enough to feel like a trespasser if you didn’t belong to a story. I let my eyes adjust to the struck-match light and saw the rope before I saw what hung from it. In photographs at crime scenes there is a trick of the eye that always comes; ears do it too, with sirens, the way they start far away even if they’re on you. You see what you don’t want to see and your brain tries to give you a ladder down into anything else.

It was a ten-foot length of cheap nylon, bright yellow where it hadn’t taken on the color of the mud. It wrapped a beam that had not expected a rope in its old age. The knot was neat, strange—tidier than the mess below it. She was not old. She could have been anyone. Her hair had been, once, a careful color. It now was a dark rope that the rope crossed. Her hands hung straight down, knuckles loose. Her boots were brown and expensive and new in a way nothing submerged should be. The rope cut her neck a precise line. Her eyes were open just enough to be almost closed.

I wanted to say something. I wanted to say, no, sit, wait a minute, you cannot be here. The sound that came out of me was the sound the man who’d called from the back room of the hardware store had made last winter when he’d dropped an axe on his own foot. In the tight cool space the sound had nowhere to go and came right back.

The mud beneath her boots showed diagonal lines from where she had kicked and then stopped. On the shelf to the left of her head—this had been a pantry, it had, because there were still rust patterns where jars had sat for years—there was an unlit white candle under a saucer that had been blue when it was fired. It had been burned once, recently, the wick a crisp black question mark. There was a droplet of wax on the shelf that had caught a hair. My stomach made a small, ugly leap behind my ribs.

I made myself do the things. Camera up, hand steady. A shot from the entrance. A shot of the feet. The hands. The knot. The shelf with the candle. My mind took notes the way it had been taught to long before I’d ever thought I’d need to remember anything like this. The rope was a clove hitch at the beam and a perfect noose at her neck. The person who made those knots had known what they were about. The boots were a brand I could see in the eyelet detail, a little crescent scratch deliberately distressed by someone in a warehouse in Portugal. The left boot had a diagonal scuff bright against the brown where it had swung against a nail on the far wall. The nail wore a smear of something that glimmered faintly like glue and was the wrong color for glue. The candle had dripped once and then the drip had been wiped, the smear a dull arc the width of a thumb. There was a line at her wrist as if something had been there, a fit of pressure, recently removed. Her ear, partly visible beneath hair, held no jewelry, but a line where a hoop had been, healed over, new enough that the skin still shone. I told my stomach to wait. It went on with its own plans.

Above me, the daylight held itself very still. The world had a shape you could lean on one minute; in the next, a piece of it popped like a plank under your foot and you fell down into it. Somewhere out in the bright bowl of mud, Jessa was probably narrating the beauty of ruins to a lens that would later add soft heartbeats. I tried to push the air in and out of me in equal amounts and found my hands again.

I went back up as slow as I had come down. The light was too bright. I put my hands on my knees and the lake that wasn’t a lake inched sideways. Then I went on autopilot, which had saved me in a courthouse hallway once and in a snowstorm later and, once, digging a garden in August when the shovel had struck something my mother had buried long before. I dialed.

“What’s your emergency?” said a calm voice I didn’t recognize. They train them to have voices like that, weather that never tells you it’s about to rain on your only suit.

“This is Hannah Lowry,” I said. “I’m at the reservoir. By the old church steps. There’s—there’s a body. A woman. It’s recent. She’s—she’s—she’s hanging. It’s a crime scene.”

“Are you safe, Ms. Lowry?”

“I don’t know,” I said honestly. “The ground is safe. Physically. No one is here. I think. The ground is safe,” I said again, because sometimes you repeat a thing until it believes you. “I didn’t touch anything. I took pictures.”

“You’re a reporter,” the calm voice said, not accusing, just placing. “Stay where you are.”

“I will,” I said, because I wasn’t going to go anywhere my shoes had not already been. “Tell Sheriff Kline. Tell—” I almost said my father and then did not. “Tell them to bring the people who know about knots.” I heard myself say it and would remember later and wonder which part of me had known to say that.

Sirens sound wrong in an empty place. They come as if the air has been rolled up and you’re inside it. Jessa looked up when the trucks kicked up their band of dust along the ridge and then tried to frame them as they slid down. Her mouth formed a perfect O behind her perfectly sharpened teeth.

“Hey,” she called to me, hushed and somehow louder for it, “what did you do?”

“I found someone,” I said. “I didn’t do anything.”

She came closer, and I lost my temper, not at her exactly, but at the idea that I was going to be turned into a clip. “Back up,” I said, sharper than I meant to. “It’s real. Turn your thing off. Don’t put this behind a buy link.”

Her mouth went flat. For a second the camera wasn’t between us. She nodded and dropped the GoPro to her chest. “Okay,” she said. “Okay.”

Sheriff Kline’s truck slid in, braked in so much time it made an ugly dry sound. Hollis Kline got out slower than his truck, as if there were no point in running toward something you couldn’t fix. He had his hat in his hand and his eyebrows lower than usual, which is how I knew this would not get beautiful anytime soon. Benji Dunn, who had been a grade ahead of me in school and had taught me to roll joints in a culvert when we were both too serious about pretending not to be serious about anything, tumbled out of the passenger side and would have run if Kline hadn’t put a hand on him that was not unkind and made him walk.

“Lowry,” Kline said with a nod. His voice was a saw cutting a slow line through something old and dense. “You called it in.”

“Yes,” I said, and started to tell him my hands were clean of it and realized how that would sound and stopped.

He took the path I had made with my shoes, his weight finding the same places mine had. He didn’t ask where. I pointed.

“We’re going to do this carefully,” he said to the air and to Benji and to me and to whoever else had ears. He didn’t look at Jessa. He knows what a camera looks like even when you put a coat on it.

We went in the way I had gone in. We did not go into the opening. He crouched, working at knees that had more years in them than mine did, and looked. I watched his face watch what was in there and saw a small muscle in his jaw flex once, as if it lifted a weight and then set it down gently for fear it might break.

“All right,” he said to Benji without looking at him. “Circle this like you don’t want to break it. Get me tape. Get me a line on Knox to keep the councilman out when he shows. Call Doc Merritt. Tell her to bring her cooler. And send someone to the north gate because you know every man who’s been griping about this lake since before you were born is on his way with a pair of binoculars.”

Benji went like a dog that had been named good boy for the first time.

Kline looked at me and finally his mouth had something that was not a line, though it was no more pleasant. “You go in?”

“I had to see,” I said.

“Why?”

News, I could have said. Curiosity. A ladder in my head that had dropped me down rung by rung into things since I’d been small, the thing that made me find all the baby mice under the lawn chair when I was eight and carry them in a shoebox to Dad and make him explain why they were still and then not anymore. “The candle,” I said instead, because it was what I knew. “There’s a candle. New. Burned once. Someone was there with her.”

He nodded like I had told him it was Tuesday. “You take pictures.”

“Yes.”

“I’ll have to ask you for the card,” he said, and waited for me to argue.

“You can ask,” I said. My mouth was dry enough to powder a room. “Let me copy them. They’re the paper’s.”

“The state will say chain of custody,” he said. The nod now meant that he disliked the phrase as much as I did but we both would say it like a prayer because the church steps were over there and everyone lies to themselves somehow. “You can be there when we do it. Consider yourself invited.”

“Consider yourself sued if my name ends up in your story,” Jessa said from a careful distance. We all ignored her, her own jaw set, her handsome head turned away as if privacy was a thing she could put on like sunscreen.

We waited together, four people and a dead woman and the sun. Doc Merritt arrived with her white hair woven like something that would hold a ship to a dock and her cool eyes that made you feel both looked at and not yet judged. She spoke to the dead woman the way people speak to dogs, soft but not ridiculous, as if there is a thing you could say and you should say it.

When the state woman came, she had her hair back in a weapon of a braid and the kind of sunglasses that put you into a version of yourself with your mouth slightly open. Her name was Hoover. She shook my hand like she knew where my bones were and I had not hidden them anywhere useful.

“Ms. Lowry,” she said. “We’ll need your photographs. We’ll also need you to tell us everything you saw and how you reacted to it.”

“How I reacted,” I said.

“People don’t always tell the same story twice,” she said without heat. “And I like to know if the sound someone made was an oh or an ah. One time a man whistled. I still don’t know why. It has told me more about that man than anything else.”

“I made a noise with my throat,” I said, because it was true and because I did not trust my face. “It wasn’t a word.”

“Did you move anything?” she said.

“No.”

“Did you touch her?”

“No.”

“Did you know her?” Doc Merritt asked this time, her voice like linen.

“I don’t know,” I said, and then, like a fool, I looked at the boots because they were trying to tell me something about a store that didn’t exist here and a woman who had bought them to walk on other ground than this.

We set up tents and tape and the word perimeter. Men with gloves appeared, and women with clipboards, and the shape around the opening changed from a hole in the past to a place you could rub off with your thumb and never get clean. People came to the fence and leaned. Some prayed. Some took photos. My father would have said, get their names, their faces, their ages, their reasons, and then he would have gone home and stared at the ceiling and not told my mother why he wouldn’t sleep till two.

I stepped to the side, into a square of shade the tent offered that was more idea than help. Owen stood there already. He had taken his cap off again. He had the look of a man who has come up under a deck to find a family of raccoons glaring at him and was grateful, later, that it was only animals.

“You good?” he said to me.

“No,” I said.

He nodded, somehow relieved by honesty. “You going to put this on the front page.”

“Yes.”

“Try to make it useful,” he said, and the way he said it made me want to cry worse than the woman had. “Something people can act on instead of just bleeding over every breakfast table.”

“I will,” I said, because I could promise intentions from here to sundown.

He rubbed his upper lip where the mustache used to be a decade ago. “You remember when we flooded it.”

“I wasn’t alive.”

He sighed. “Feels like so long ago I was a different person. The day they closed the gates. We stood there like people at a wedding who know what the bride is going to do and can’t say anything. Took three days to get to the roofline of the school. Over a week for the rest. People said goodbye to their porches like they were something to say goodbye to. That’s what this lake is made of. Long goodbyes. Not water.”

He walked away before I could answer. He always did that, left you to fill in what he had refused to finish. It’s the same move a certain kind of hymn makes: it leaves you on a note that could rise or fall and then lets you decide how much to care about where it goes.

They got her out just before noon. There are words that make people look away—when flesh turns to evidence it is one of them. They put her on a sled because a stretcher would take the air out of the word and they had none to spare. Doc Merritt did not look at anyone. Hoover did not change her face, which is the face she had chosen and practiced. Kline put his hat back on because it was time to put a lid on. I put my camera to my eye and did not press the shutter, just watched the world in a rectangle until it made a kind of sense, and then when the rectangle lifted my hand pressed the button and it made the lie of turning this into a picture for strangers.

I saw, as they carried her, the edge of something in her jacket pocket, a fold of paper or a fabric handkerchief that had been ironed once upon a time. It was triangular with a corner embroidered in a color like summer thunderheads. A small thing. I did not say anything about it then. I do not know why.

By afternoon, the heat had turned the mud into a skin again. The crowd had learned to stand back and feel holy in the ways people can when death is close enough to shine your shoes. The trucks moved off in a slow procession that would be reported as respectful. The Instagram truck stayed longer, then left. Jessa walked up to me in the silence after the sirens had gone and put her hand up as if to touch my sleeve. She didn’t.

“Hey,” she said. The camera was back on, but she had turned it sideways to take photos of her own knees as if that was the thing to point at. “You okay?”

“No.”

“Want coffee?” she asked. The offer was so human it was almost funny.

“I have to write,” I said. It felt like a thing I could do that would keep me from crawling into a hole and lying down with the mud. “The paper goes to print at five.”

She nodded. Her mouth did that thing your mouth does when you don’t want to say you’re sorry in case someone says for what. “Okay,” she said. “I’ll send you my email. If you need to see what I shot. If they take your card and you have to remember things without it.”

“Thanks,” I said. It was something like kindness, whether or not she meant it.

I walked back up the slope, the dam keeping its face. The chain was no more substantial than it had been at dawn. My car had a film of dust that you could write your name in and I did not. On the drive back, the radio said nothing because I turned it off. The ledger office smelled like hot paper and ink and my father’s cologne that had sunk into the fibers of everything. I sat down at his desk, which is mine now, and opened the blank document, which was also mine.

The cursor blinked like a heartbeat. I listened for a long moment to make sure my own still was.

The lake had started giving things back. But today it had returned something fresh, something that had no business belonging to it. People will tell you that the past lies quiet under water. That is not true. The past is a throat, and when it opens, what comes out is not always what you expect.

The city's night had a sound the day never bothered to learn. Under daylight, everything was a clatter and a shout. After eleven, it turned honest. The traffic thinned. The sirens stretched and softened. Houses exhaled. The radiators confessed. Leftover music leaked from the backs of bars and spilled onto the empty sidewalks, where it mixed with the hum of things that had been told to stay on: the soda machines, the fluorescent lights, the endless breath of vents on roofs.

I sat beneath one of those vents at a desk that was always a little sticky, answering calls nobody wanted to make to an office nobody believed could help. My supervisor, a man named Walt who lived on menthols and crusades against modern coffee, called it civic triage. What he meant was that if you had a raccoon in the attic, a neighbor parking on your lawn, or a pothole big enough to eat a tire, you dialed three-one-one and someone like me talked you back down to earth.

"Three-one-one, non-emergency services," I said for the third time since midnight, the words as automatic as the blinking cursor in the system that logged our calls. "This is Mara. What's the issue you're reporting?"

"That noise outside? It's two in the morning," a woman's voice hissed. "It's—hold on—it's like a beeping. I think the city put a machine there to spy on us."

"Where are you located?"

It was the block with the public pool, I guessed before she said it—there's a security system there that chirps like a smoke alarm when the back gate's open, a new thing the parks department installed in August and forgot to recalibrate. I could hear the exact frequency riding behind her voice, a perfect B-flat with a pulse like a second hand.

I dispatched an after-hours request to Parks and calmed her down. Another call about the construction site on Kottage. A man who wanted to know, at 2:03 a.m., whether he'd get towed if he left his truck in the winter parking zone because he had to be at the shipyard before dawn. I told him no, not before six. A woman who whispered, laughing, to ask whether the city could do anything about “the fact that my boyfriend thinks I’m asleep.”

My headphones pressed the room into a soft tunnel. The call center itself was always too bright and too cold, the overhead lights turning even the potted ficus into a pale suggestion. Someone had left a container of powdered creamer uncapped in the break room. The fridge whined in concert with the ceiling vent, a unison A that would have made my old boss in sound design proud. Walt’s chair squeaked higher than middle C every time he leaned back, which was often, which irritated me more than it should have.

Three years ago, I spent my nights behind a mixing board, listening for the way a footstep can change the meaning of a line, the way air vibrates in a set designed to look like a church but breathes like a basement. After the accident, after the long day that turned into a long week of ringing—real ringing, punishing and relentless, like a rusty kettle that never quite found boil—I stopped. Stage used to be my living. Sound used to be my whole language. When the city posted for a night operator, I took the first job that offered a different kind of listening.

At 2:17, the call that mattered found me.

"Three-one-one, non-emergency services," I began.

"Can you hear me?" The voice was female, low, not old but smoked-down. There was no greeting, no pause. The way she said it wasn't casual. It bunched tight in my ear.

"I can hear you," I said. "You're calling three-one-one. Are you safe?"

Silence held for a beat. Behind her, something breathed. A fan, slow, with a wobble at the bottom of the arc. I clicked the "trace" function with my index finger without looking. The system takes the first three seconds of every call like a dog lapping a puddle and then waits for more.

"I need to report a—" She cut herself off. A sound came through, quiet and far away, as if it had to find its way down a hallway before it reached her phone. It wasn't a siren. It wasn't a television. It had that fried sugar curl of a calliope, that oiled-wood thickness of pipe organ. And it was wrong.

"Are you near a carnival?" I asked before I could stop myself, because that's the kind of thing that will make a person hang up—strange, irrelevant questions that prove no one's listening to the right part.

The woman didn't hang up. "I can't talk long," she whispered. "They smell it now."

"What do you need to report?" The cursor on my screen blinked in its blue box: Describe Issue. The trace function hummed but the number refused to resolve, stubbornly flagged as Unknown. Most pay-as-you-go carriers did that. Burners did that. So did old buildings that swallowed signal, spitting it back when they felt like it.

"The smell," she said. "Like pennies, but rotten. Like—"

Something knocked metal, a tapped ring on a railing, a small bright clink. The wobbly fan kept its faithful arc under everything.
