Bring me home, he had said in the bloom of the sound. Or I had made him say it because it was the only sentence I wanted from him now. It is the risk you run when you can hear what water wants: you start to give it the answer you need.

The next person cleared her throat and slid into the folding chair across from me. She had a wrinkled folder and eyes like a deer in a spotlight but in a good way, if there was a good way for that. I smiled with all the teeth I had left. The fan turned its slow interrogations across us. The drizzle that had been nothing for an hour gathered itself into a grammar and began to speak against the roof.

What I did not know, not yet, was that the box would not wait for my break. What I did not know was that the river would not either. That afternoon, while the fan crossed us and crossed us, while the stamps found their colors and hit and hit, the weather opened its mouth the way a knot does. And if I had been listening more closely to the way the room changed its breathing, I would have heard—under the rustle of papers, under the printer’s cough, under the murmured, we’ll do what we can—the soft, steady clicking of lead weights in a tin tray keeping time, like the sound a man makes on a porch when he calls a dog in from the rain.

Chapter One: First Snow

On the first night of the snow, the dead stood up out of the drifts and knocked politely on doors.

Miren had been awake for hours, listening to the air tighten. It made its thin glass song against the windowpanes, which meant the cold was honest, which meant the snow would not be ephemeral. Honest cold laid a base. Honest cold made the dead coherent enough to speak.

She’d set a blackened kettle on the iron stove, not for tea but for steam, to test the leak in the kitchen window. A seeping draft could lull a snow-body into sleep and then the head would slough when it hit warm room air. People didn’t like that. It made them feel guilty for weeks. The remedy was simple: an old rag rolled and stuffed, a glass of salt near the sill to drink the spare damp. Miren’s hands knew their motions before her mind fully woke; she rolled the rag, breathed through the sting of the cold. The clock, a gift from her father years ago when he still gave gifts, shuddered toward midnight.

Across the room her coat hung like a dark animal with antlers—the cedar twine looped over the peg above it, the twine braided from bark and someone’s grandmother’s patience. In the corner, the knotted harnesses lay sleeping, the bells muffled in felt pockets for later. Everything had been cleaned a month ago and laid out three times since then, not because she was a romantic about her work but because beginnings mattered, and some years the dead needed you to seem larger and more deliberate than you felt.

She drank from the kettle carefully when it started snarling, let the steam climb into her face. She didn’t watch the clock. There was a first knock; there always was a first, and Miren always tried to hear it right.

Three soft knocks from the next street over. Then one at the Faroe house, two short hard ones at Maite’s. The whole town of Urtza held its breath with the falling snow for a moment like a shared, ridiculous secret: it had all happened before, this measure of the first night, and yet this was the only time it would be this way. Miren looked around her kitchen and saw the chip of blue paint missing from the nail she’d hammered in for the aprons, the onion with its greenish, determined spear quietly trying to become its own new plant, the jar with the coins for the new boots. Then she blew out her lamp with a random wish because her aunt had taught her to, and put on her coat and stepped into the white.

Urtza is not high enough for real names on maps, which is how Miren liked it. The mountains around it were deciduous and bruised in three seasons, only showing bone in winter. Red roofs went black under snow. The old schoolhouse, slouching, wore its drifts like a shawl. The first snow was never blizzard, never drama; it was the cautious hand. It sifted. It accumulated in quiet declarations. The lights all through the village were toned down and warm the way voices go in sickrooms. One by one, doors cracked open and faces leaned out. The dead were already in the street, learning their weight.

“Evening,” one said, a man, polite as a shopkeeper. He lifted his hand—his mittened hand—and examined it, amused. Then he looked down at his feet. He had no feet, only shapely ends that suggested boots, because boots had mattered in the last few years of his life. The snow had remembered that.

“Blessings,” someone called from a stoop. “Heitor?” A woman stepped forward and the dead person tilted his head toward her voice and smiled as if meeting a person he’d heard only good things about from a mutual friend.

Miren walked past them toward the House of Sinks.

The House sat low and square near the pump station. In summer its shutters were hot and the paint peeled, and goats leaned themselves against it as if it could cure sweet itch. In winter someone always remarked it looked like a cradle. Inside, the sinks—a dozen long basins cast from iron and lined with salt—waited. Copper pipes wound the room like ribs, humming. The basins would be tepid by morning. The dead liked that, liked the ease. No one said exactly why. Miren didn’t ask. You did what kept the village and the valley and the pipes and the spring all in accord and let mystery be one more kind of weather you endure.

Maite was already there, gray braid a thick rope down her back, fingers—two of them missing their tips from an old frost—tapping her ledger. She had been Miren’s supervisor for eleven years and her friend for fewer because it did not do to count your friends among the people you might have to argue with at dawn. A large apron was bound around her waist as if anything could splatter at a melt.

“The first ones are generous,” Maite said by way of greeting, meaning the dead were not crabby, not clinging, not apt to physically lean into people’s doorframes and refuse to be moved, but were letting themselves be named. “The road’s good past the estanco. You have Ila with you tonight. Slowly, Miren.”

“I always do it slow,” Miren said.

“Slower,” Maite said, and slid the ledger across the table. Miren put her glove on the paper to keep it from curling back up; her breath condensed in the cold room as a mild astonishment at being alive. The ledger had the town’s names in rows and the first night was always a lottery. Who came up first? Who came composed? Who did not come at all? Urtza kept its own amateur anthropology. Patterns comforted people who needed to think they could infer mercy.

“Is Jon on your sheet?” Maite asked, mild as lukewarm tea.

“Don’t,” Miren said.

“Don’t what?” Maite said, not looking up, and then she lifted her face with a look that was not unkind. “I ask because it would not be right for me to send you to your own door.”

“No,” Miren lied, though she had not yet looked. “He’s not.”

Maite took this and tucked it away. They were good to each other like that. Miren folded the ledger back into her bag and turned when she heard a sound like an eager cough. Meanwhile the House of Sinks had filled with their first two callers, a young woman with bird-boned wrists who kept wringing her fingers as if ringless meant something essential had been mislaid, and an old man whose knit cap had grown from the snow in perfect detail down to the loose thread near the crown.

“Ila,” Miren said. The apprentice was a long bendy person with a face that looked lost without a smile and thus wore one much of the time like a protective amulet. Ila had moved up from Elsai in the spring and had never seen a snow-body in the round. She had practiced on the straw men in the shed, which the goats had eaten between lessons so their wrists came away always smelling of cud.

“Present,” Ila said, trying to keep her voice steady with gravity. She wore her scarf wrapped three times around her throat. Her hair had frozen at the tips.

“No tugs,” Miren said softly. “If you lead them, keep the twine loose until you feel the want. They follow their names more than they follow your hands. You don’t want to insult that. And believe them when they tell you what hurts.”

“They’re made of snow,” Ila said.

“They hurt more than you think,” Miren said without heat. “And if you know who they are, say their names into the twine. It likes that.”

Outside, the street had settled into its new population. Snow-bodies moved with the articulated care of people who had had a recent surgery and did not dare look at their stitches. The living made way. The old woman from the post office—Choli—had a snow-body leaning against her shoulder as if to borrow her opinion on something. There was a feeling like wedding reception in the air, except no one had cooked, and the good potatoes were still in the cellar.

Miren made her circuit. The job was to gather the first ones, see who among them was warm to the idea of the sinks, who needed coaxing and a story, who would break. The ones who broke had to be minded longer. They cracked at the joints and drifted around corners and tried to put themselves back together, and some of them managed it, but afterward they were as haughty and brittle as kings and offered no one a farewell. It was better—safer for the pipes, safer for the gullies come spring—to get everyone through in those first hours, to plant an idea of smoothness and consent in the town’s head before the valley called to say the gauges were siphoning light.

“Heitor,” Miren said to the man with the mittened hands, because Choli had said his name first and made it public. He turned toward her; there was recognition in the way he lifted his chin. He had been a mason. You could see that in the accuracy of the hands, the careful way his fingers were made of sharp snow—no mush, neat edges. “We have your sink ready if you want it now.”

“I felt so good walking,” Heitor said apologetically, as if to turn down hospitality were impertinent. He touched his shoulder and then his face, struck by his cheekbones. The dead were always surprised by what the snow chose to keep. “The stairs don’t feel like anything. Imagine that.”

“The stairs are for the living,” Miren said. “We’ll take the ramp together. Do you want to hold the twine or shall the twine hold you?”

He laughed at that. “Do you talk to all of us as if we were toddlers?” He said it kindly. His eyes had no color at all. The snow did not bother with eyes—there was a hollow there that you had to pretend to yourself was pupil. It was unnerving the first week and then something in you understood how little of seeing had to do with wetness in the socket.

“Only the ones who need to be reassured of their own wisdom,” Miren said, and Heitor nodded and took the twine and turned toward the House and walked.

“Do they remember much?” Ila whispered beside her, not knowing whether it would insult someone to be pointed at with a whisper. Her breath made a halo in the air. She was the kind of person snow would love; she had the itch of longing about her and longing gave the snow good shapes to work with.

“Some do,” Miren said. “Some remember the story of their death. Some remember exactly what they forgot while they were alive. It’s not fair. But it does not have to be fair to do the work. See the way Heitor lifts his feet?”

“That bounce.”

“That bounce is a man who had a heavy body and now does not. He’ll go easy. You can tell the hard ones because they look as if every step costs them a coin.”

“Like your father,” Ila said, without thinking, because the gossip of Urtza traveled like a hand-carried loaf, warm and desirable, and who in a village can keep a loaf uneaten.

Miren did not flinch. She had known Ila to be clumsy and good both. She had asked for her because all of them—the old wardens and the middle ones—were tired of the way the valley men from the water company behaved when they came up for the year’s final counts. You needed someone who could smile through the right rage without deciding smiling was the whole life. “My father is not the snow’s to keep,” she said evenly. “He’s never been fond of being held.”

It wasn’t even a lie. Jon Ortuza, whose legs had survived a thing that had killed his friend and whose rage had found a long narrow corridor to walk down for twenty years, was terrible at being held. He had not picked up his child much. There had been the one time at the orchard when he had lifted her by the armpits at the urging of her mother, and his grip had bruised and he had looked so surprised by the bruise that he never did it again.

They took Heitor in and he melted with gratitude, which is to say he looked at his own dissolution the way a person looks at a warm bath after a long walk and began to talk about mortar. Maite wrote it down. She always wrote it down. People thought she’d sell the ledger. To whom? There is no buyer for what keeps you awake at night.

Miren and Ila went back out. The snow had added a thin new layer while they were inside, a syllable. A girl stood near the lamppost with her hands together as if to keep a moth in them. She’d been dead six months; Miren had known her. Everyone had known her, which was the trouble with loving a small place. The mountain gave you back what you lost while other people watched.

“Nati,” Miren said softly, not because she was trying to keep the town from hearing but because she wanted the name to travel well. “Did we make your lamplight a good height this time?”

The snow had hooked the girl’s nose just so—sweet to see. The first year Miren had gotten that wrong. She had gone around telling people, as if a problem could be solved by naming it loudly in front of witnesses, that the snow did not know faces. The snow knew shapes of feeling—the feel of a hat—you got a hat. Nati’s nose had been the most argument the snow had ever had about itself that anyone could remember. It had put half the town into science or religion, for three weeks at least, arguing one proof against another.

“It’s all right,” Nati said. The voice was always hard. The sound came from a soundlessness. Maybe that was why the snow liked her nose and found her laugh, which came out of her like a bluebird.

“Are you going to walk with us, or run?” Ila asked, in love.

“Oh,” Nati said. “With you. I want to tell you something.”

“Tell me now,” Miren said, because when the dead said they wanted to tell you something they often wanted to tell it to you while there were still edges to their mouth. Afterwards you had to interpret eddies in the basins. You learned. It was not as satisfying.

“Later,” Nati said, and who was Miren to say she did not have the right to desire a later again, that luxury, that lie. She held out the twine like a hand. Nati took it like a promise.

So it went: the young ones who wanted to see each other again as if even the vanished could be bored of being alone; the angry ones who hissed that no one had told them it would be like this and then loved the first time they heard their name from a friend and were softened; the stubborn ones who had bad reputations while alive and were not going to change their brand for a season, and who required the presence of someone they had despised to say, “Come,” and then they melted out of spite. There were apologies in the street the first night that softened knees the same as the slope of snow did. And the small oddities that made Miren love the work beyond its bureaucratic edge: the woman whose ears were made only of air and were somehow perfect ears anyway; the man whose mustache had become an animal in its own right and had to be coaxed separately into a basin and dissolved with its own lecture.

They had taken two handfuls of people to the Sinks when the weather did what weather does and changed its mind. The wind turned mean. The snow narrowed, sharpened. It began to make bad shapes, little screes of grief in the alley mouths, hard mounds against doors.

“We keep going,” Ila said, which meant she was feeling the sweetness of her own courage.

“We do,” Miren said, pulling her scarf up so the wool bit the bridge of her nose. She felt the weight of something coming that she could not name in the older part of her body that had known her mother’s hips, and she did not like the mix of old and new in that sensation. The street had emptied a little. They were going up toward Pelay’s, who had not come out yet, who had said loudly in the store last week that he didn’t hold with the sinks, that the dead should be left to the forest to walk out their own weather. He said this every year and then came the first and stood on his stoop and cried like a stubborn child. Miren liked him for the predictability of his faults.

The knock came then. Not on a door. On Miren’s shoulder, from the air. It was the slightest bump, the way a bird will correct itself mid-flight and tap your coat with its wing. She stopped. Ila stopped because she had learned that much of this work at least.

The snow had piled at the base of the old hedge behind Miren’s house in a sloped curve like a shoulder under blankets. Now it shifted. The wind seemed to go somewhere else in order to give what was happening enough room. The drift unlearned itself. In a way, this was all Miren’s mother had ever done—unlearn. She unlearned the valley. She unlearned the idea that a person with a mountain could just go down into the plain when a company had a set of blueprints and a song about progress, and say yes, by all means, drown what raised me, drown the goats too, drown the lilacs and the school with the ink still fresh. She unlearned that you said “please” when you wanted something you already owned. She unlearned fear until it surprised the rest of her and took a bite.

“Amaia,” Miren whispered before she meant to whisper it, a whisper that got into the bones of the hedges and lived there all winter.

The snow made a face. It did not do it the way a sculptor would, from the forehead down, chiseling detail into the brow like a decision; it did it from the mouth up, the mouth that Miren had thought of every time she’d entered the Sinks for years and watched the mouthing of vanished things. The mouth was familiar in a way that knocked Miren’s sternum with both its fists. There was no fairness in the world. There was also this.

The hair was wrong. The hair was always wrong. Hair is what memory lies about in order to flatter its own ability to transform loss into something portable.

“Miren,” said the snow, and if she had needed the voice to be exact she would have failed her own adulthood. It was the instability of the voice that felled her—the part that almost slipped apart and was remade.

Behind her, half a dozen practicalities assembled like birds on a fence. There were the rules Maite had written, which were not laws, which were better than laws. There was the part where you did not usher your own mother into the House. There was the part where Amaia had not had a body when she went; there had been the blue water and the men with their waders, and then there had been nothing, and Miren had kept nothing in a drawer the way other girls kept love letters. There was the part where Jon had gone quiet and stayed. There was the part where the valley men would ring the bell at dawn to say the gauge at Bridge Two had a new concern, and a woman could not bring herself to be a metaphor and also do her work.

“Miren,” the snow said again, and the twine in her hand slackened, slackened, and she let it fall. Ila complained about everything and anything under her breath, a soft generational commentary any older person should have been irritated by, and she went absolutely still now. The stillness of an apprentice who has wandered into scripture.

“Ama,” Miren said. It violated her to say it. It fixed her in the year a woman left without choosing her leaving. Miren found the edge of the new thing with her own hand, which is what she had always done. She pressed her palm to the snow cheek, which was not a cheek, oh no, it was not. It was not skin. It would leave her with aching tears as if the cold had eaten the water out of her eyes. She pressed anyway. The snow took the heat and the imprint of her. A dimple. Her mother had always had the same. Trickery. Or mercy. Perhaps there is no theological difference when you are wet to your elbows in the basins and somebody’s ring rises to the surface with no finger in it.

“Maite will say you can’t,” Ila murmured.

“Mhm,” Miren said. She did not remove her hand.

“She will say it to you with the voice that makes people obey because they remember their first attempt at disobedience and the equal measure of the shame and the thrill,” Ila said, which was very good for a person who had not had the valley men lick their teeth at them yet. “And I’ll just—well, I’ll follow you.”

“You’ll stay out of the doorway,” Miren said. “You’ll speak to Heitor and keep him from feeling that we left in the middle of a thing. You’ll tell Maite that I have a pipe to check. That the pipe is screaming. Give me one of those bells.”

Ila gave her a bell. It was a small one, meant for a goat. Miren held it tight until the cool sound went into her palm and settled there.

She had thought a hundred times she would do this—disobey the gentle rule, give the snow what the snow wanted and take what she had wanted since a black day—but wanting something for a long time does not prepare you for the moment it takes a shape. She was not a child. She felt ridiculous. She felt a person who had a helmet on their head for the first time and kept turning their head too quickly, surprised that the world did not move with them. The snow-Miren—no, she would not. The snow-Amaia leaned from the drift without swagger. She was—thank God, thank somebody—not holy. She still had the trick in the mouth that meant she was about to lie in service of something she thought larger than truth.

“You can’t come in,” Miren said. “Before you think to ask. You can’t come in and be what that room is. Ama. It matters. I will take you round the back.”

“Which is the front when you are small,” Amaia said, with her old act of transforming everything into a parable. “And you were very small when you began to lie to me in defense of your father. Hello, my love.”

“Don’t,” Miren said, not unkindly. She took the cedar twine and looped it around the body, not to bind but to suggest the idea of a tie. She took the bell and put it in her own pocket with her hand around it. She did the thing she’d told Ila not to do and tugged. The snow grain followed not the tug but the heat of her. It shivered as if the wind were fingers.

People saw. You can pretend in a village that you go unseen if you give nothing to people to point at, but you are wrong. People saw. It would be at Maite’s door to reckon with in forty minutes. There was a specific indignity in being observed doing the thing you had told them not to do for years. Miren did not flinch at that either. The weak satisfaction of being right in front of witnesses had ruined more than one person. She turned, and very carefully, as if she had balanced a full bowl on her head, she led her mother around the back of her own house.

The backyard was small and full of old habits. There was the shed where the straw men went to be eaten by goats. There was the pump where Miren had leaned into the handle and thrown her back out last summer and then had to pretend to the valley men that she was strong because their eyes had weighed her in front of her door. There was the woodpile with its low, essential brag. There was the stump where she had put her face and told it a thing on the day the blue water had calmed too quickly and the last search had become truly polite. The snow here had gathered deep because this was a wind-break. It took shapes that would need encouraging. She laid the twine down in an S in the snow and watched the body settle onto it slightly, a child who does not know whether to honor the ribbon you have put out for them to run along.

“Is it wrong,” Amaia said softly, “that I am relieved you are not older than me?”

This was exactly her. It was exactly not. It was something the snow wanted. It wanted to align with the soul the way a magnet moves iron filings in a school experiment.

“It is wrong,” Miren said, and forgot to be generous, so even now she was her mother’s daughter. “You were supposed to be older if only so that I could forgive you cleanly, and now you have taken this from me.”

Amaia began to laugh. It was a bright sound. Miren had not allowed it into the house in years. It was balm for a moment. Then it made things hurt. “Forgive,” Amaia said. “You think that word belongs to you? You give it away the way your father gives away screws—to make friends with men whose hands are always closing around you like boxes.”

The bell in Miren’s pocket pricked her palm. “If you are going to scold me while you are a weather, go back into the wind. It can finish the sentence.”

“Don’t be cruel because you can be,” Amaia said, which was an arrow buried in the proper place.

They stood there, two stubbornnesses on either side of a slow leaking heat, while the snow tried to remember the way a person shifts their weight when they are about to say something they will regret and then never admit regret about.

“Tell me,” Miren said at last, not because she thought there would be good news but because secrets breed worse things in small places than they do in large places.

“The dam,” Amaia said, and Miren wanted to say the words herself as if to steal the power from them. “They have cut new channels under the old river and built teeth in the dark. In spring they will hold back the thaw until the gorge breaks at the orchard. They will call it unexpected and ask us to be patient and they will show us numbers that lean in their favor and they will not recognize the name of a single person we bury afterwards, because they do not think our names are made of the proper stuff.”

“You’ve been here two minutes,” Miren said. “You’ve always been like this. Your appetite for doom. Is this your penance, Ama? To be made of frozen water and still find a way to be fire.”

Amaia moved in a way that said the snow was remembering her shoulders for the first time. She had had a good pair. She had carried Miren on one more often than she should have when Miren was ten and too old for that kind of foolishness. She had done it to make a point to Jon, which is why it hadn’t worked. “I have been here,” she said, and stopped and remade the sentence in a way Miren recognized, because you had to be careful what you said when you were the weather. Words over-somethinged themselves when they touched too much metaphor. “Listen. I will ask only this: you must make them measure before they cut. You are the measure now. They will ignore the snow. The snow is only story to them. You must stand with their meters and make their numbers answer to facts.”

“I work water,” Miren said, with very great patience, with an irony so precise she wanted to keep a piece of it for her pocket later. “I do not work men in suits.”

“Not at first,” Amaia said. “You will look good to them when they have to walk into breath with teeth in it. You will make hot tea and you will forget to offer honey and they will think you have been rude and then they will be ashamed of thinking that and you will reward them by showing them the good pipes. Meanwhile you will be the bowl we always wanted to be that makes a thing visible by holding it.”

“I am not your parable,” Miren said. “I am not your second chance, Ama. You of all people don’t get to—”

“Stop,” the snow said, and Miren did, not because she was obedient but because the air this time ordered it in her lungs. Something had shifted in the street. The call bell at the House of Sinks was ringing—a particular call, the one that meant an argument had become sharp and needed a warden’s voice. It was not Maite’s way to ring that bell more than once. It rang three times. The sound came across the snow like a black thread pulled through a white cloth with a needle too big for the job. Somewhere down by the pump a pipe coughed. Somewhere a goat shook its back-end and the bells on its strap sang.

Miren thought, once, big as a church: I should not have done this.

Then she thought: There was never a year I was not going to do this.

“Wait for me,” she said to her mother, to the snow with a borrowed mouth, to whatever the mountain had appointed to test her arithmetic. “I will be precise." She was talking to herself as much as anything. “Do not walk,” she said, as if the snow would obey like a trained dog. “Do not join the wind. Do not be a decent person and spare me.”

“I taught you to lie,” Amaia acknowledged. “It pleases me that you are lying well.”

Miren took the bell out of her pocket. It did not sound in her grip. She went around, up the two stairs, into her own back door, through the kitchen where the heat had made a small, irresponsible heaven for her cheeks, into the front where the cold cut everything it touched and left it shining and manageable. On the porch she could see Maite’s big shadow in the House of Sinks doorway, her legs apart like a sailor’s, her head a kind of lighthouse turned now toward Miren’s own ridiculous house.

Later, people would say that the first snow had come on hard that year but it had not been unfriendly. The unfriendly came after. Later, there would be a sign stenciled in black paint on the bridge over the ravine that read not Bridge Two but Second Chance, which would have been a miracle if miracles didn’t always irritate people after they exhausted the first flush of being used as an anecdote.

Now, Miren went down the steps and felt the shape of a fight the way you feel a bruise before you see the color of it. She put her hands in her coat and secured the bell and the coil of cedar. She met Maite’s eyes across the tidy yard and saw that every story she would have to tell had already made a home in them.

“Miren,” Maite said, her mouth not moving much, the way the old women talk when they are quilting gossip into a blanket. “Do the pipes scream as much as Ila says they do?”

“They are in their right,” Miren said, which was not an answer and thus an answer.

“Bring me your ledger,” Maite said. “And bring me the names you will not write down.”

Miren had never minded being caught. It made the next thing clear. She crossed the few yards of snow between them, not yet thinking of the way a river is just snow that forgot the rules. She had left her mother in the back. She had written nothing yet in the ledger that mattered. The bells in the village all sounded alike and different: goat bells and sink bells and the little chime of wind through the pipes and the iron alarm that made the valley men hustle up with their hats in their hands pretending that hats could solve anything.

She reached Maite and did not look away. She lifted her bag. The snow fell on her eyelashes the way eyelashes love to be loved. The House opened its mouth and the heat reached for her knuckles. She did not step in. She stood there with her breath a flag and waited to be told what she already knew she would do.

In the backyard, the drift shifted again. In the street, the dead looked up when their names were spoken and smiled as if hearing themselves was this year’s miracle. In the valley, in a heavy room with lamps too bright, a man watched a gauge bleed numbers that made a lie of what the company had promised and began to practice the speech he would give at dawn.

There is a point in the season when all the waters agree on a story. It had not come yet. Miren would be asked to make it come. She would spit in her hands and lift. That was the work. That had always been. That had never been enough.

“Miren,” Maite said, not unkindly. “Now tell me what you have done.”

On the morning the sea gave us back the church bell, my mother bit the orange in half as if the rind were nothing. I watched the juice thread the lines of her palm and drip from the point of her elbow onto the tablecloth, where it spread into one of the faded flowers. She swallowed and said, without looking at me, What a day for returns.

She had always eaten oranges that way—like a fruit was a piece of news that could not wait to be peeled, like it might walk away if not enough urgency was shown. I set my lavender lunch tin on the chair, though I would not be needing it. My mother flicked the half-eaten orange back into the bowl, where it rolled among the others, shining with her saliva.

From the window we could see the line of the seawall, the edge of the early-spring fog. Little else. The gulls had made a braid of sound that tightened and loosened by the minute, as if they were trying to remember a melody they used to know. A black kite hung and swung above the harbor cranes. Beneath it, human figures bobbed and lined the promenade, dots in a schoolbook margin.

I hadn't slept. We'd had a storm at midnight that knocked out the eastern lights, which meant I lay in bed counting seconds, then losing count, listening as the house moved in its old ways. Every nail and beam knew how to take a wave, but that knowledge had been hanging on by its teeth lately. The storms were coming more often, like calls from a relative who'd been quiet for years and now wanted to go back over everything.

The bell had been gone for thirty-four years—since winter after my sister left. The cliff behind Our Lady of the Fathoms Church gave way and took what it could hold: mud, gravel, the bell, the lintel with its painted saints. They found the saints floating for a while, waterlogged and kind-eyed, before they went down too. The bell dragged itself deep and quiet. There were men who said you could hear it on some nights, underwater, answering the bells of the other towns. The idea used to wake me from a sleep I had hardly managed to fall into, and I would go out with a towel on my shoulders to the cliffs and stand very still, waiting. If I heard anything, it was my own blood.

My mother wiped her hand on her apron and finally looked at me. Did you hear? she said. She couldn't say the word bell; she circled it like it was the name of a person we had no right to invoke.

I nodded, feeling the hush reaching us even with the windows closed. There is a particular silence our town knows. It is the silence that prefaces a return.

Every child in Bahía Espera grows up hearing about returns. We are not supposed to speak the word with the superstition that naming will invoke it, but we have pet names: la devolución, the bringing-back, the balancing of the ledger the sea keeps with its cold and patient hands. It took my father's boat one spring and returned the mast in pieces three summers later, the paint scaled off as if it had lived a hard life as a fish. It returned a knitted hat that clung to a pipe at the sea-bottom and grew a sleeve of green hair. It returned a shoe that had belonged to a man who drowned; his widow, whose hair had gone white in a month, put the shoe on the stoop and planted basil in it, and the basil grew thick and obscene.

And then there are the impossible returns. A man I knew, a baker with hands like loaves, swore the sea returned him a dream once, the night after his wife died. He woke with the salt still drying on his face. The old women shook their heads, half out of pity, half out of the thrill of it. There were years the sea returned nothing and years it returned so many small things that the registry office could not keep up with the recording and the foundry in San Gerardo could not take any more metal to recast.

I am the record-keeper of returns. There is a ledger in my office that is older than I am, older than the rebuilt overlook, older than the iron fence that runs along it with the paint flaking off in long curls. The ledger's pages are a thick, fibrous paper that takes ink like skin takes a scar. I have my pens that I do not lend. I have my drawers labeled with names: Flood, Collapse, Ferry, Anger, Accident, Misunderstanding. They make people laugh when they see them. They ask what goes in Misunderstanding. I tell them, Anything you are not sure of. This is usually where the strange things go. I am careful with the strange.

I looked at the clock. There is a habit in me that cannot help but count toward the office. Once my mother kept clocks like some women keep plants. They were all hand-wind or pendulum, clocks with faces like eyelashes, clocks in the shapes of birds and spoons, but after my sister left, she stopped winding them. Time pooled and caught in our rooms like rain along the baseboards. She threw the clocks away one by one, except for the kitchen wall clock, which ticked too loud and kept poor time, so that it seemed like time was good only in very small sections and wrong in the larger sense. The clock we had now was new. The storm had shaken it forward by four minutes. That was all the difference there was between me and what would happen outside that morning.

We heard Hernández's whistle—two notes, one sharp, one like a sigh. My mother braced her hands on the table and stood. She wiped the juice from her elbow and took her shawl from the hook beside the door. Her hair was gray in long streaks that made her look as if the sea had pulled its fingers through. She wrapped the shawl and tied the ends in a knot you could trust to hold while you crossed a river. In the hall, I found my municipal jacket and my ring of keys, which hung on a hook shaped like a fish. There was a time when my mother had a hook shaped like a girl in a bathing suit. She took it down after my father drowned on a day so calm it still makes people laugh.

We stepped into the street. The air had that taste it gets when the wind changes direction and comes from places unlike ours. There is a little bakery on our corner; it had its awning pulled in and its window dark. The door of the watchmaker's was ajar, as if he had run out without finishing his shirt. Fish scales studded the cobbles from where the night boats had dragged nets and spilled.

I could see already that the crowd was moving toward the harbor. People went toward the sea automatically, like blood returning to the heart. There are some things we do not need to call each other for. A woman passed me with a baby strapped to her chest and a string bag with oranges in it, and for a second, unreasonably, my mouth filled with their oil.

They had set the bell on the wet stones where the tide had been an hour ago. It looked smaller than it had hung in the church, as all things look smaller once they have been put down on the ground—kings, secrets. It was green with a bloom of coral and growths that had made a calendar of its years under the water. The tongue was missing. A man named Salvador had his forearm pressed to its rim like a lover. He was trying to hear if it held any veins. The patina left a dark stripe across his shirt when he pulled away. The rope, a fat new one that did not yet have salt knitted into it, still hung from the crane hook. Weird scab-like barnacles dotted the curve like a sentence written in a language we refused to learn.

It had come up with the kelp from the trawler's deep net, a kilometer off our usual grounds, farther in the direction of San Gerardo than we thought our things traveled. If the captain had not been cautious with his winch, the bell might have swung and crushed someone's leg. The bell's shoulder bore a dent where it had carried the weight of its fall. On the lip, though, I could see the old inscription when I knelt and wiped the green with my sleeve: Hear, O people, and hold. The letters were mostly legible. The metal around them had been eaten away in swells and troughs, like the sleep of a person who cannot give in to it easily.

Ribera found me by the crane. He squeezed my shoulder once. He is even-tempered and has a face that can look stern even when he is playing cards. He gave me a slim notebook with a pencil run through the spiral and a cloth tape measure. He does not trust phones for these matters, and I have learned to respect that. Measure her, he said. Then he caught himself. Measure it. He glanced at the bell, back to me. I wrote his misstep into the margin. There was something in me eager for it to be a her too. We are all superstitious in our own ways.

By the time the first picture was taken—a tourist with a camera who did not realize the weight of that act—the fog had thinned and the sky was the color of quartz. The bell, in that light, looked less like an apology and more like a heart. Children with sticks wrote their names in the sheen of algae on the stone. I could smell the hot metal of the crane, the diesel, and beneath all that a sweetness that surprised me, like the breath of someone who had just eaten sugar.

My mother stood on the low wall and left her shawl folded on the fence post, as if trusting the world not to take it. Hernández leaned on his boot heel and squinted. The watchmaker had not gone back to his shop; he was as eager for this as any of us. The baker. The women who clean the fish. The barber who never cut a straight line in his life. All of us in different clothes, the same posture.

For three breaths, I thought that if the bell sounded, the sound would come not from above but from the stones beneath it, where the years had puddled. That it would bring old words back with it. When I put my ear to its side, it was so cold it burned. And there was nothing in it. No sound like coins. No heartbeat. Just the ring of my own blood against my ear.

Sergio, the priest from the church that now met in the community center when the rain's direction allowed, pressed his palm to the inscription. He is younger than the marble in his chapel's altar, younger than the earnest lines around his mouth. He looked at me as if he would ask my permission or as if I would ask something of him. I dipped my chin. He closed his eyes and spoke a blessing that felt like he was talking into a bottle to throw into the sea. He almost said a name, then did not. I respect this in a man with his job.

There is a tone the air takes on in our town when a return is recognized as itself and not as a one-day wonder. It is the tone of something that must now be moved and measured and assigned, as so much else must be. It is the sound of a thing that will get a ticket in the ledger and acquire obligations. Everywhere my job comes with obligations. I am not a collector. I am a witness, and then I am an assigner. That morning, as I measured the bell's circumference and noted its weight as an estimate (five men and a teenage boy to lift one side grudgingly), the gulls were a white punctuation in the sky. They did not come down and peck. They held themselves apart, as if in respect, or hunger, or bird-thoughts none of us knew.

You might be thinking: but what of your sister? I was thinking it too. On the day the cliff fell, we had been sitting on the seawall with our feet over the side, our sandals slapping against the stone. We had almond cookies. She had braids that my mother had woven the night before with a speed and patience that you would not believe in the same pair of hands. A priest in sandals and a soccer jersey had jogged past and laughed and said to us, Half the hill is moving. We looked back at the cliff and did not see it move. People always say after the fact that they could see it. We could not. He shouted again and we stood and began to run toward the three little brick steps that led to the church where we took confession like medicine. When we turned back, the cliff fell—not as a slide, not as a sheet, but as if someone had let go of holding it up one piece at a time.

We were not crushed, or we would have been two names on the brass plaque in the atrium of Our Lady of the Fathoms, where the angel with too much gold leaf and too little face kept watch. But in the sound and dust, my sister let go of my hand. She did not come when they pushed me away from the edge into a passing body's arms. When the dust thinned and the day took shape again, I held a braid in my fist.

It would be a tidy story if this were the day she disappeared into the sea. She did not. She washed her face in the fountain, put on my sweatshirt, kissed my hand where it had been in hers so tight the grooves showed, and went to stay with our aunt for a week while the walls of our house were checked to see if they meant to stay. She slept with her back against the door because of dreams. And then, some months later, she stood on the quay with a bag and a ticket and a mouth set a certain way and said something I have never repeated to anyone, and the ferry took her and the ferry brought back others and did not bring back her. She went inland. There are people who cannot stand to be heralded by the noise of one familiar gull. She sent a postcard that had a picture of a statue with a sword and never sent another. If I saw her again, it was only in the ways you see someone you love if you spend enough days looking at faces in line for bread or standing under bus shelters in rain. I made furniture out of the absence of her. I hung cups. I put my household gods on it. I dusted it.

It would be another kind of tidy story if the bell came back carrying some part of her, like a cuff of her coat or a stray word. It did not, and I was relieved, and I was furious at that relief.

We hauled the bell to a flatbed with a winch that yelled the whole time. The men did the thing men do, which is lift and shout and curse and then grin at the hurt their bodies made, as if they like to confirm what they are made of. The women did the thing women do, which is tell them where to place their foolish hands so nobody loses a finger. I signed a dotted line on a form that placed the bell in the custody of the Registry Office until such time as the parish of Our Lady of the Fathoms is deemed stable enough, architecturally and metaphysically, to rehang. When I screwed my signature tight and neat in the lower right corner, a gull screamed overhead in a voice like a child. This, too, I wrote in my notebook.

Between one task and the next, I glanced down at the film of water that collects in the gaps of the stones where the tide rests. In the shiver of sunlight that made it look like a trick, something lay there like a book. Paper does not keep long in the sea, not even if you think it will because you wrapped it in a bag and a prayer. There was a boy with bare feet trying to catch a crab with a chip bag; he had stepped in the puddle already and muddied it, and I thought the book would come apart at his small heel. But when I crouched and reached, it held.

It was the size of my hand, wrapped in oilcloth that had gone gray. The corners had softened and the string binding it had frayed until there were two strings and the suggestion that they had once been one. I carried it to the flat stone by the seawall and put it there, and my mother made a sound in her throat, a sound I had heard the night my father's boat did not come for the late tide.

It was my field guide. The one my grandfather had given me the summer I turned twelve, when I thought I would become a person who knew the names of shorebirds so exactly that I would stop feeling the need to lie. I had carried it in the pocket of the denim jacket that my mother said made me look like a small statue of a god from a bad museum. I had underlined the parts that talked about migration. I had pressed sea lavender in it and stained the pages with butter from a sandwich. One winter my mother lit a fire that ate that jacket and the field guide with it. We had watched through the glass as the pages took on black lace. It is not known for burning, my mother had said wildly, and then had gone quiet. The fire had slid toward the knitting basket like a hand down a leg and left it alone. The knitting had survived. The field guide had not. We buried it in the green metal trash at the end of the street and heard the truck take it and had toasted that night to, We will buy another, and had not.

And yet here it was. There were no burn marks. There were water marks where there had once been oil. When I undid the string—the string my mother had tied for me with a sailor's knot and a look on her face as if she were sending something over land that meant more to her than land ever had—it loosened as if it had been waiting. A crab the size of my fingernail skittered out and back under the rock.

On the inside of the cover, in a child's hand, was my name, written with a certainty that embarrassed me. MIR EN, the middle letter separated like a broken bridge. Beneath that, because my grandfather always made a game of suspicion, he had written in his the phrase you must be willing to be wrong and crossed out three words, so that it read: you must be.

I thumbed it open. The pages smelled of the drawer where we kept knives. There was my underlined passage about migratory patterns as old as moonlight. There were my notes in pencil that had not washed away. There was the small faint smear of blood where I had cut my thumb on the staple of a pamphlet and bled without knowing. There was a pressed gull feather—impossible; feathers do not press without turning to dust. The field guide held itself in my hand as if it had been made for it. The place where the spine had cracked when I dropped it from the seawall to the bench below was still cracked. There was no ash. There was no smoke. If you believe me, you have to believe me entirely.

I looked up and found my mother looking not at the book but at my face. The look she had was the one you have when you take out a dress to find it has not molded, though you had every reason to think it would have. Hernández urled a gull cry with his mouth; he likes to do that when he is happy. People had begun to move toward the fish market, because you cannot stand with your neighbors and perform awe all morning; you have to go buy mackerel and ask after someone's mother. The bell sat on the truck bed and drew light to itself as if it could eat it and store it and burn with it later. Ribera was on his phone making a list of who had the equipment to move it without taking chips out. A small part of my brain was enumerating the steps that would follow: call the carpenter in San Gerardo, assign two volunteers to brush, designate an area in the registry for drying, arrange the chairs so that those who wanted to sit and tell how it fell could sit and tell. Another part of my brain had been blown open and was letting in birds.

Who else would write their name like that? my mother asked, finally. She had her hands in her shawl again. The knot had slipped slightly. I moved to fix it, then let it be.

No one, I said. The truth is not hard when the thing sits in your hands.

She reached out and rubbed the corner where the oilcloth had been worn away by years of being taken from a pocket and returned. She rubbed it the way you rub an elbow you have bruised and cannot help but check again. I wanted to say something tight to hold us together, like a joke or an errand. Instead I said: I burned this. You burned this. I did not know which version would be less likely to make something break.

She nodded. Then a small flame of defiance lit in her eyes, the way it used to when the women at Mass would look at her with pity as if pity were a shawl you could drape over someone to make their shoulders warmer. She said: Perhaps we are wrong about what fire knows.

The priest had come closer, as if drawn by the gravity of things behind understanding. He looked at the field guide, and because he is devout in as broad a sense as you need to be to live here, he closed his eyes and crossed himself. His hand in the air made the sign slightly crooked. He said nothing. I would like to pretend that I preferred this to his blessing, that I found silence more honest, but if he had held the book and called a saint's attention to it, I might have felt steadier.

I slid the guide under my jacket, inside the lining where a pocket had been sewn by my mother when I was fifteen because she did not like what pockets mean for a girl in a city. The book was cool against my ribs. Its edges made a square that I could feel with my palm. Keeping it there made it possible to stand where I stood without falling apart into water. There are times when your body requires a weight to hold it in place, the way you put a book on paper when the window is open.

Ribera had turned the truck toward the municipal building. The sun broke fully from the fog then and skated itself across the water the way a thrown plate might spin before settling. The bell, on the flatbed, shone in patches. The dent caught the light and made a thin bright line. I have seen broken things flash like that. It is how they keep you from throwing them out.

When my mother looked at me next, she had the face she wore when she was pretending we were all right. There was the mouth, a little wider than most women's, the cheeks with their salt maps, the eyes that could hold anger as long as a glacier holds a summer. She said: Work. As if the word were a rope we could both hold. As if it were a raft that would not turn over when the wave came.

Yes, I said.

We began to walk up toward the Registry. The boy with the chip bag had given up on that crab and was now standing with his hands full of sunlight, the bag behind him dark in the wet. The watchmaker was telling a story that would be different by the time we were back for lunch. The harbor cranes had hoisted themselves into a question mark. The bell rumbled over the cobbles, and every loose screw in the bed sang. A woman with a face as thin as a sickle knelt and kissed the bell's side before her nephew pulled her back for fear of the truck.

A thought slid into me then and laid itself down quietly. It was a thought as ordinary and as blasphemous as wanting to lie to a child. I wanted to bury the field guide in the yard. I wanted to put it in the tin with the saved nails and the loose buttons and the gold ring my sister forgot to wear the day she left. I wanted to write nothing about it and dare the sea to bring it back again or, if it would not, to prove to me that it had not meant what I thought it meant.

Instead I said to my mother: You'll come by later. There will be people. They will have their stories. She gave me a face that said: I have always come by. She waved with her fingers, the three with the small scars from cutting squid, and went on ahead of me down our street, the shawl slipping, the knot holding, the orange in the bowl we had left perhaps rolling a little and then deciding to be still.

In my office, the ledger sat where I had left it yesterday, open to a blank page, the left side heavy with what had already been said. The afternoon would fill with voices that thought it important to repeat to me how they remembered the bell's tone, as if memories were not real unless they had been passed over a desk and written in ink. I turned the ledger so it faced the light and uncapped my pen. My hands smelled like my childhood. When the nib touched the paper, I wrote without pause or ceremony:

Entry: Devolución—major.
Object: Bell of Our Lady of the Fathoms.
Year of loss: 1987, winter. Collapse of cliff.
Condition: Patina, marine growth, dent at shoulder, tongue absent. Inscription legible: Hear, O people, and hold.
Circumstances of return: Recovered by trawler off San Gerardo grounds in calm water after storm. Brought in with rope and crane. Witnessed by seventy-three persons (approx.), gulls, one priest, registry staff.

I paused then, pen hovering. The choice was a simple one and also not. The field guide, small as it was, insisted. You could ignore it as a strange coincidence and place it in Misunderstanding. You could put it on the shelf with Lost Causes and pretend there was a consistency you would not let something unsettle. You could open the drawer labeled Flood and Adsorption and insert it between law and faith.

I wrote:

Addendum: Return of field guide, personal. Date indeterminate. Item believed destroyed by fire, 1994. Current condition: dried, intact, bearing annotations by Miren Arriaga (age 12) and A— (see page 14; fingerprint visible). Circumstances of return: low-tide pool. Witnesses: self, Estela Arriaga, Father Sergio. Note: The sea is not consistent in what it refuses to keep.

The ink spread just enough to make me breathe out. The nib left an island where it had rested longer. I turned back the cover of the ledger and closed my eyes for the length of a bell tone I had not heard but could imagine, a note we would all pretend to understand and would disagree about in detail for decades. I could feel the square of the field guide against my ribs like a seven of hearts.

People began to come. You never have to wait long for a town to find its feet and bring its eyes to bear. I stood and straightened my back. When the door opened and brought with it the smell of wet rope and hair, I did what I always do: I raised my pen and invited the first story in.

I notarize endings.

Every morning, I lace my boots and polish the face of my stamp—copper darkening where fingers have learned it, the center etched with a ring of concentric circles like a cut trunk remembers its years—and I go out into the city to witness what will not be again. The work begins before the heat, while dew still makes the herb sellers’ palms shine, while the fishmongers’ voices carry farther than their catch.

Some days it is a grand farewell, with a mayor and a ribbon and over-cooked speeches and someone’s aunt wailing into a handkerchief for the cameras. Some days it is a quiet apology to a cupboard. We close a bakery whose sugar has become a rumor under dust, or a tree whose roots have found the pipe under a woman’s floor. I have certified the last errand run for a man with a hip like cracked porcelain. I have stamped the last linen sheet pulled across a laundry line that had been a border in a courtyard argument since the seventies.

They tried at first to call us Archivists of Closure, to see if a brighter word could make a ritual of losing feel like a civic achievement. But the city knows its own names. In the market, in the cafés, in the places where the river licks the quay and the boys practice their dives, they call us notaries of last things. They press our arms for help. They joke: If I cut this mole, will you stamp it? If I quit her, will you stamp me free? We laugh when appropriate. We point to the law carved on the inside of our leather folders, as if law were a thing that could float.

My mother, who did not believe in law except the one that comes from winter, once told me that everything can learn to float if you teach it slow. She meant grief. My mother had strange instructions for grief—braiding it, feeding it boiled lemon peels, placing it under a sleeping child’s pillow so it would give up its shape by morning. She had a kitchen full of jars and a window ledge with basil and a story for everything. Then one afternoon when I was nine, she put on her good coat with the missing button and went to buy cloves and did not come back. There is no closing ceremony for a door that keeps waiting.

I press the stamp face to my hair to feel if the sun has warmed enough to start. Then I begin.

On the docket the first day of flood season: one doorway, one dock, two stalls in the old market, one parrot and the voice it learned. The doorway belongs to a tailor named Hrvoje who cannot keep his rent, who once traced my arm to take a measure and told me the only true things left in the city were shoulder blades. The dock is Pier Fourteen, which requires a delegation and a brass band and a municipal photographer with a ladder. The stalls are sisters, literally; their father wrung chickens with thumb and forefinger and the younger sister, Lila, can wring the necks of arguments with the same dispassion. The parrot’s owner is eighty and thinks the bird remembers the word for a lover that nobody says anymore.

The river has been getting wider like a skirt being let out, one stitch at a time. It isn’t just the rain farther north or the docks rotting; it is the crust under us deciding on its own terms where to lay down. We shore up this and brace that. The planners make gestures and curses. They draw lines on a transparent sheet that slides over the city; they move it. We move with it. The water learns us, and we learn it. I have a graphite pencil tucked into my braid that I call the river—soft, smudging, cannot be sharpened past a certain point without snapping.

On the way to the market I pass the wall of the Office of Attestations and read the chalked slogans left from last night. They are not clever. They are questions. Where do you put a last bowl of soup? Who stamped the first stamp? Do your fingers hurt? Yes. My fingers hurt. The joints. The heart is a joint if you think about it. Every morning I want to write back and the janitor with the stooped shoulders—his name is Ahmed, he has a new grandson—has already scrubbed.

At the market, the sisters have taken down everything that can catch a spark. Their stall is a wooden ribcage. For twenty years they have sold scarves and belts and the little bracelets woven so tight that if you cut one it throws a lash. Now everything is in cardboard boxes, except a scarf hanging alone in the draft, blue as an unmade promise. Lila climbs a chair to pull it down when she sees me. “Not you,” she says. “I thought they would send someone crueler.”

“They are out of cruel.” I set my case on the counter and unsnap it. The stamp sits in its velvet bed like a well-behaved child at a funeral. Inside the case are also my papers, the ink pad in its tin, and two small stones that have traveled in pockets from other shores. I do not think of them as lucky. I think of them as heavier than they look, which is a quality I admire.

Lila’s sister, Mirna, appears from the back with a tray. Coffee cups the size of thimbles. She used to keep a fig leaf pressed under the tray to make jokes about modesty. Today she has pressed nothing. She puts a cup inside my splayed hand like I might drop it. Around us, the market is coughing itself open. It smells of mint and wet rope. The fishmongers pour gray water from buckets to keep their tables honest. Someone upstairs is beating rugs, and the dust spills like prayer.

“Say your words,” Lila says without rancor.

The words are written in the book I carry, but I never read them aloud. “You have the right to speak your own words,” I say. “My words are print. They cannot hold what your hands have held.”

Mirna sighs like an old hinge. “Speak for us, Sima. For once I want to listen to the city telling me what it thinks I have done.”

I place my palm on the stall’s counter, under the line where they measured their sons’ heights in pencil. The graphite river. “On this day the stall of Lila and Mirna, known for the braided belts and the rumor of discount, has ceased to do business at (I check the clock) nine thirty-seven. The owners have tendered their keys to the Market Council and received a receipt. They acknowledge that the stall number will be reassigned. They release the city from further obligation.” I look up. “It is wrong to say ‘release.’ It implies we were ever holding each other correctly.”

Mirna laughs, a small, honest sound. “Stamp your stamp,” she says.

I ink the copper. I choose a place on the ledger and press down until the circles catch. When I lift it, the rings shine wet, receding. There is a little ceremony I do only for those who have given me their listening: I touch the edge of the ring with the pad of my thumb until some of the ink comes away, and then I touch the wood we are closing, leaving an almost invisible echo. It is nothing the law requires. I tell myself it means the wood will recognize itself, if someone rebuilds it into something else.

When I step back into the aisle, a man with a child on his shoulders is trying to teach the child to spit cherry pits into a paper bag. “Better to spit out than hold in,” he tells the boy. The boy misses the bag prophetically. Lila and Mirna turn the sign to read Closed and then keep standing there, because what else does one do with hands that were always busy.

I walk around the corner to the tailor’s.

Hrvoje’s doorway is narrower than it has any right to be. A heavy woman cannot enter without her breasts brushing his coats, which he pretends not to notice and notices fully. He is already waiting in the threshold with a spool of navy thread, unwinding and rewinding it around his fingers like a private rosary. He has hung the Open/Closed sign on the handle of a suitcase from 1974. The suitcase is scabbed with stickers of cities that used to mean a passport in the mouth: Odessa, Tunis, Thessaloniki.

“You will say my name, yes?” he asks.

“I will say all names written.” It is a rule of ours not to invent, not to fill in. The city is made of absences; it does not need me to bring it new ones.

“You will say my father’s.” He points to a gold-lettered plaque above the mirror. The letters lean. His father was a man who could sew a dart into your despair and nobody would notice the repair except you when you exhaled and noticed you could.

“Yes,” I say.

I stamp his lease with the ring. He strokes the stamp’s face with a fingertip when I am done, as if the metal were a saint. He takes a photograph from his drawer and hands it to me without explanation. It is a picture of the city taken from a ferry, twenty-six or twenty-seven years ago. In the foreground a boy has his foot on the lower chain of the railing like everything is a climbable ladder. In the background Pier Fourteen is still straight, the water quiet as a lie.

“You look like your mother in the mouth,” Hrvoje says, as if speaking to the photograph, and then he puts his hand over his own mouth as though he has spilled a needle.

“So they want you at the pier for noon,” he adds. “There will be a song. Also maybe eggs.”

“Eggs?”

“Thrown,” he says.

The pier has been on the docket for months. Repairs were counted and discarded. Braces put up and lifted with relief. We have been swallowing the money for it and then putting that money toward the flood walls upriver and then borrowing more. The pier is a mouth full of soft teeth: beautiful from a distance, unreliable when you bite.

At ten forty-one I stand at the gate of the parrot’s courtyard. The old woman’s name is Zofia, and she has the shoulders of a water-bearer and the voice of someone who knows how to pinch a boy’s ear and make him grateful. The parrot sits on the back of a kitchen chair, one foot tucked up, the other foot splay-toed like a dancer. It is a green that is not found in the market but in the place where bottle glass remembers sand. “He lived in my son’s bedroom,” she says, “and when my son died, he moved to the kitchen. I cannot have his voice caused by a saucepan.”

“You have a form,” I say gently. “There is a part of the law about voices learned, voices that belong. If you can say the word you want to close, the city will hear it. I will witness.”

Zofia nods. She strokes the parrot’s back with one finger. “He says the word for ‘come back,’” she says. “But he says it in my mother’s Polish. Not in the Polish they speak now on television when they make the jokes and smile like teeth. He says it like an invitation from the other room.”

“Say it,” I urge.

She does. It is two syllables, the first one a little pause, the second one like a latch lifting. The bird hears the shape of breath more than the letters and repeats it perfectly. For the bare width of that word, a woman who is not Zofia stands in Zofia’s kitchen and asks a man to return to the bed that is warm on his side. It is the most intimate thing I will ever certify. When I stamp, the bird beaks my knuckle, not as punishment but as an anchor.

By the time I reach the river, the sun has turned water into something that has its own skeleton. A policeman with one eyebrow directs me toward the dais with two fingers. The brass band is tuning circles into the air. The municipal photographer is already on his ladder, already speaking to us from a height as though we have shrunk, and the mayor’s aide is reading my paperwork over my shoulder as if he can catch me out and save a future he will not walk in.

“You will read the withdrawal, and then the mayor will say the civic thanks, and then the band will play them out,” the aide instructs. He has the mouth of someone who bites his own cuticles raw and blames the teeth.

“Who’s ‘them’?” I ask.

“Fishermen,” he says. “And…people.”

There is a crowd. Not as large as the old pictures on the municipal website would hope, not as small as the cynics expected. They have come in shirts that remember the pier. People who did first kisses in its shadow. People who got yelled at for taking the rope without permission. People whose grandfathers whispered a prayer into their hair when the boys jumped. They stand with their hands ostentatiously in their pockets so that they will not reach out.

When the band takes breath, a boy—no older than the one in Hrvoje’s ferry photograph—climbs the railing where the wood goes soft. He is skinny enough to look like hunger, strong enough to make the mothers suck their teeth. The policeman pretends not to notice, and the boy pretends not to see any of them. He leans out and spits, expertly, a cherry pit into the river. There is nowhere in law that covers what that is the last of.

The mayor speaks of continuity and of hubris as if he had discovered the words in a drawer and was pleased with them. He thanks donors who do not use this pier. He thanks my office without looking at me. I am glad of that. I do not want to be looked at and mistaken for a reason. At the corners of the dais the boatmen who have paid their licensing fees three times over mutter. The old men who sit on packing crates with newspapers in their back pockets hiss the same breath as the geese. Lila and Mirna are here; I see them, holding hands like girls lost in a fair.

When they gesture me forward, I take the paper that says, in the dry language of law, that the pier’s designation is changing from “active municipal port appendage” to “recreational walkway, access denied.” It also says that section seven of ordinance nineteen will be applied to any person who continues to use rope or ring on said pier after this hour. The ordinals make it sound like the pier is a person who committed a small offense. I clear my throat and choose, as I always do, to read what is true if you turn your head slightly and look at it slant.

“On this day,” I say, “the city asks the river for a favor. It asks it to remember what this wood has held—the feet of children and the weight of boats and the first time somebody took your wrist and said wait. It asks the river to take into itself what we cannot keep straight, not because we never tried but because we were built on a seam that moves. We name this ending not to make it real—it is already real—but to say we saw it. We say your name, Pier Fourteen. Pier of the missing nail. Pier of the knot nobody could teach with words. Pier of the night we stood under fog and knew there were lights.”

A murmuring like bees. The band, with their mouths ready to call the notes into being, glance at their leader. He is crying and trying to look like it is the wind. I reach for the stamp.

The man who has been standing near the dais with a rolled poster under his arm moves then, quick as a thrown fish. He is not big. He is practiced. He darts his arm into my case, and before anyone understands this is happening, he has my stamp in his hand. For an instant our fingers touch around copper. For an instant the rings cut both of our skin. He meets my eyes and there is no hatred there, only a proposal: come with me into this mistake or stop me.

He throws the stamp into the river.

The aide screams. The band lets out a single, orphaned note. The crowd makes the inhale a crowd makes at a falling, a so-called collective gasp that feels to me like the city drawing breath to say our name.

The stamp hits the surface with a polite plop. It is not heavy enough to make a drama of sinking. It vanishes the way shame does.

There is a full second in which I do not move. I am not a leaper. My mother always said: think before you put your feet where stone stops.

Then someone who is not me moves: a teenage girl in a black T-shirt with a silver whale on it, hair braided down her back with bright thread. She is on the railing and then not, she is in the water that has more current than its face shows. The policeman swears like a prayer. The band sets down their instruments carefully as if sound has become too heavy. The mayor bends and looks worried in the direction officials practice: vaguely, toward the scene of the problem, toward what camera they sense.

I am at the edge before I have thought of it, my hands out and foolish. My forearms have that gooseflesh that is not cold but a warning. The girl’s head bobs up where the pier’s shadow makes a darker water. She has the wrong shoes. She has clenched her mouth tight so the river cannot come in. Her hand goes under and comes up again with nothing, fingers opening as if in disbelief. I do not see the stamp. I see only circles where things fall disappear.

There are men with poles, and I hear Lila’s voice say: here, here, stupid, the current takes, it does not give. The boy from the railing runs without his shirt and throws himself from a lower rung with a whoop that belongs to three hours ago. Someone laughs in the way a fear laughs to keep itself awake.

After, after the girl is shivering on the planks and the boy is being slapped on the back by men who want to remember their own spines, after the mayor has stumbled through a reconfiguration of the ceremony, after I have announced the closing with nothing in my hand but a pen like any other, a small box is set on the dais where the ink pad had been.

It is the size of my palm. Someone has wrapped it in brown paper and tied it with blue string, the kind I would loop through my belt when I was apprenticed and sent to measure alleys. There is no name. There is my name inside, which is a different matter.

I wait until I can be alone. I take the box to the shadow of the crane that has rusted itself into one last, benevolent gesture. The string is one of those that knots itself in the night, so I use my teeth, the way my mother would scold and smile at. The paper gives with a sigh.

Inside: a cheaper ink pad, the wrong kind of tin, and a piece of folded newspaper that has kept the smell of onions as if it were saving a taste for later. Inside the newspaper, a card. Not an official card—no embossed crest, no seal—but heavy, thick as someone’s insistence. The letters on the card are printed in blue. There are two words only.

Forgive me.

Underneath, another thing. It is a sheet torn from a spiral, damp but legible; it bears a diagram of the stamp I had lost, drawn with the care of someone who knows exactly the weight of other people’s names. Around the rings there are notes. It says: Radius one centimeter. Radius two and a half. Space between rings matters. There must be exactly what each year would have laid down if it had been cut. In the margin, a hand has written, in a slant that has visited my dreams every spring since I could count: The tree we used to sit under would be nine rings now.

It is my father’s handwriting.

Chapter One

The morning the river sent back my name, I was cataloguing knives.

It’s a tedious category, knives. They come up in baskets, tangled with rope and water weed, their edges softened by silt, their handles swollen with other people’s kitchens. You can smell the rooms they once belonged to if you hold the steel close enough and breathe slow: onions confiding their sharpness, marinades turned wetly sweet, the sour patience of vinegar. Some of them still carry bits of grit lodged into grooves, a dark rime that might be resin or might be blood. My role is to look and smell and touch, to weigh the knife in my hand like a thought, and then decide who it belongs to now that the river has scraped its history off.

We are the Bureau of General Recoveries, though the city calls us the Lost Office when we assemble in the courtyard for audits. We sit in a brick warehouse at the bend of the water where the river widens and remembers it is not ours. The windows bloom with condensation in winter and with pollen in spring. If I bring my mother here, which I have done twice and will not do again, she will reach for the glass with both hands and think the fog is trapped between panes. She’ll leave her fingerprints in it like markings, and she will hum the hymn she learned at nine in the village no Cadastral Map was allowed to show. She forgets the lyrics. She repeats the tune. It fits the hum of the river more than the river fits it.

I had my head bent to the ledger when the boatman thumped his crate down on the intake table and called, Sima, this one’s you.

Half the boatmen know my name only because I sign their manifests. This is the way most of us are known in this city: by paper, by the stamp a man in an office says makes a life official. So I did not look up at first. I had my stamp between forefinger and thumb, and the rhythm of stamping had become the rhythm of thinking. Then he said it again. Sima, it’s your name.

I glanced, annoyed, and saw the label on the crate. In the space where the origin should be, someone had inked a single word in a purple that had run. SIMA.

The boatman grinned, showing the little gold stud in his canine that he pretends he got in the navy and probably got in an alley off Dafoe Street. He can be cruel when he’s bored, like anyone who lives on the river must be, but his teeth are kind. “You’re famous,” he told the room. “The river’s returned our dear archivist.”

Only two of my colleagues laughed; the rest were too tired or too careful. We work, in general, with what the river gives us: calendars turned to the same month forever, shirts with all their buttons but one, a mother-of-pearl comb with every tooth intact, charred rafter fragments freighted with the sweetness of sap. The river takes the labels. It eats them first. We live on a water that keeps only the shape of things and will not keep their names.

Gorse came out of his office, shaking his newspaper as if it were a small creature he was trying to wake without scaring, and said, “What’s this racket?” He is a tall man who wears cheap suits as if they are expensive and never sits without crossing at the knee, careful of his socks. He looked at the crate, then at me. “It’s not hers. She’s only responsible for the second intake on Wednesdays.”

“It’s her name,” the boatman replied, tugging at the rope knots with a showman’s flourish. “I didn’t write it. The river wrote it.”

“Rivers don’t write,” Gorse said. But his voice landed on my face and stayed.

It is superstition, of course, to say the river writes. It is superstition to say that it takes what it wants and returns what it cannot bear. It is superstition to place coins in the cracks of the wharf so that, when the night tides rush up, the river will swallow the metal and spare your child. The Mayor has issued three proclamations about superstition in as many years.
