Still, when children scrape their knees, their mothers dab them with river water, half-believing the silt remembers what skin should be, and when a thing you love goes missing, you walk the banks with your hands behind your back so that you will not, in your desperation, offer other things up to be taken.

“Open it,” I said.

The boatman lifted the lid. Inside, on a bed of reeking weeds and the tatters of a tarp, lay a stack of soaked papers tied with cotton string, a half-stuffed muslin pouch, two keys fused together by some chalky accretion, and a leather book swollen to almost twice its size from water. The leather had been tooled when it was still new and hungry for marks; you could almost smell the tannin under the river, as if the cow still breathed. There were little rosettes stamped into the corners, petals in a geometry even the river had not managed to blur. No title. No clasp. No ribbon. This was not a Bureau ledger. Those we order in lots of fifty, their spines green as an old bruise, their pages ruled. This was something someone had loved.

And on the inside lip of the crate, in a hand that belonged to no one in this room, someone had written: SIMA, SEND IT BACK IF IT’S NOT YOURS.

The cotton string of the papers had burst with wet and had to be coaxed, gentle as I could. A brown cloud rose from the bundle and curled under my fingernails. No one spoke. Outside, the river muttered to itself, the same syllable over and over. The book I saved for last—not out of professionalism, but because the sight of it made the muscles in my forearms ache with a desire I did not know I still had. To read something that someone meant. To read anything that had once been meant for anyone.

I untied the pouch. It contained teeth. Six, human, the roots chalked and lovely as tiny stalactites. Three were molars with the little decks of silver in them.

“Jesus,” Kaya said, leaning over my shoulder. “Why would anyone keep their teeth in a—”

“For the charmer,” whispered Anselm, who does the watchwork and still believes every superstition applies to him. “Some of the old women keep teeth for the charmers. Even now.”

“Teeth are before superstition,” I said. “Before any of this. They’re what we hate to lose that will not stay lost. They will be here after us.”

I said it without thinking. I reached for the keys. The chalky fusion was brittle and broke easily with a twist, leaving me with two discreet iron bodies, one long and one squat. The long one looked like a cathedral key, the kind for a lock that expected its doors to be heavy. The squat one looked like the kind you find under a mat even though everyone has heard the warnings about putting keys under mats. I set them aside and turned my attention to the leather.

It resisted, as wet leather does. It clung to itself as if that were all it knew how to do. I slid my fingers under the covers and pried, and at last it gave with a long sigh. The first page was blank, except for a faint watermark in the shape of a flowering tree. The second page too. On the third page, someone had drawn a neat chart of dates, except the years were wrong. They had written dates as you would dream them: 22 Orchid, 23 Ox, 7 Iron, 8 Iron, as though the city were keeping time by its own calendar and had forgotten to tell us.

“Look,” Kaya said, her breath touching the damp paper. Her scarf was wicking the river into itself like a wick.

Names had been recorded in two columns: given names, by some order that did not go alphabetical, and on the right, a single word that kept repeating and repeating: delivered, delivered, delivered. There were ticks next to some of the names, as if the book-keeper had won a small victory over someone else and had done himself the grace of marking it. The names themselves were not remarkable till I saw mine.

I am thirty-five. I am my father’s only child. I am my mother’s only child. I was named for a woman my mother’s mother never knew, who is mentioned in our family with the reverence you give to a rumor that finally goes and becomes a person. And there it was, my name, written in a hand that belonged to the time when the boy who wrote the first proclamation about superstition was still learning not to lick the glue off envelopes.

Sima, delivered.

Gorse coughed. He has an unpleasant, private cough, as if he is rehearsing his old age in an empty theatre. “Well,” he said.

“Well,” I echoed, but it came out softer, as if I were not standing exactly where I stood, as if someone had called me from the other side of the room. The string of my body went loose. I thought of my mother humming at the window, her fingers leaving whorls of fog. I thought of my father stepping onto a ferry in a navy sweater, his hands in his pockets as if the cold could be handled by posture. I thought of the year the river worried at the footings of the west bridge until the city woke one morning with the bridge slightly crooked, like a smile.

“It’s an ordinary name,” Gorse said. He always goes for the ordinary when the extraordinary will not submit to paper. “There are a dozen Simas in the registry.”

Kaya made a soft noise. I knew her well enough to hear the way that noise meant I’m here, next to you, I’m asking you to meet my eye. I looked at her.

Under my name, there were five blank lines. Under other names, there were not. Some had addresses added, initials in parentheses, notes like wrong door, moved, cross with the charmer. Mine had nothing. It had the simplicity of a stone dropped into water, with no ripples around it. It had the honesty of an object that belongs to no one.

The boatman looked suddenly abashed, as if this were a holy thing and he had made light of it. “I can take it back,” he said quickly, as if that might undo whatever had begun.

“It came here,” I said. “It’s already ours.”

“This office is not a chapel,” Gorse added, which was curious, as no one had said it was.

We’ve had the chaplains come through, once or twice, to ask if we might return certain things before the Bureau’s holding period was up—embroidered cloths, bells, a wooden icon with the paint blistered away from the face like a finger had touched it over and over again. They stand in the courtyard and preach the gospel of letting go properly. They make the river sound like a mouth that needs to be fed. I never go out to listen. I stand at the ledger and stamp and stamp until the pulse in my wrist has forgotten its other rhythm.

Gorse told me to take the box to my desk and to record and lay out the contents for drying. He told me to note the condition and to make no assumptions about provenance that could not be supported by the witness of what I held in my hands. In this, he is a good manager.

I lifted the crate. Water slopped onto my sleeve and soaked through; I felt the cold like information. The crate was heavier than it had seemed the last time I carried something that mattered.

At my station, I unwound the string of the diary with care I reserve for few things. I had already come to think of it as a diary. That is not a category we use in the Bureau. We are taught to say journal if we must say anything at all.

When I set the book open on the blotter, the pages parted grudgingly, their edges blooming into soft curls. Between the damask pattern of the paper and the first entries, there were faint pencil lines where someone had once meant to draw a map and had instead given up. A river ran down the middle of the almost-map. It forked toward the bottom. The hand that had made it was sure until it was not, and then the pencil lifted. You could almost hear the person erasing the thought, deciding to be practical, to keep records instead of making them.

I turned the pages slowly. Names and dates, all in that same small hand, like a school certificate. Addresses appeared, then stopped appearing. The ink changed from brown-black to green, then back again to brown. A page was torn neatly out and left in its place, like a gap in a grin. Across one page, as if in fury, the book-keeper had gouged through not with ink but with the nib itself, a thick seam of ruin. I passed my fingertips lightly over it the way I had touched my mother’s temple the day the doctor told me the name of what was happening to her. The name had five syllables and an air of inevitability, like the law of gravity but more personal.

“Lunch,” Kaya said after a while. “Come down with me.”

“In a minute.”

“You always say in a minute.”

“I mean it this time.”

She sighed. “If you find your birth certificate in there, at least give me the privilege of being the second to know.”

She left the way she always leaves, with one finger touching the objects on my table not to claim them, not to steady herself, but as if to bless them: a spool of thread, a marble, a brass clasp that had long ago lost hold of whatever it once closed. When we were younger and you could still be scolded for this, she pressed her thumb into a cake of sealing wax until the shape of her fingerprint sat shiny and perfect in it, and then she put that bit in her mouth and softened it again and pressed her fingerprint next to the first. “Now there are two of us,” she said through wax and tongues. I have loved that audacity my whole life.

I read until the letters started to jitter. Then I looked up and found that the light had changed. The early shift had gone long ago. The room had the grainy feel of afternoon, like a fruit left too close to the window. I got up and took the book to the back with me and turned the dehumidifier on and set it in front of the fan with the wire guard missing from one of its blades. A pulse of air pushed the pages as if to say, We are not finished with you.

At home, when the river is high, my building creaks as the water speaks to the shore piles. Tonight, the river was sleepy, and the creaking was my neighbor practicing scales on a trumpet he had picked up two winters ago when his wife left. I took the stairs two at a time because the lift was still out; it has been still out so long we have given it a gender and a history. The smell in the stairwell is a little like milk and a little like rain. When I open my door, I always think, simply and without any flourish, that I am glad to have a door.

My mother was waiting in the chair by the window with the plant she calls violet even when it is geranium, and the cardigan she calls mine even when it is hers. She had put two cups on the sill and forgotten to fill them and was rubbing the hem of the cardigan between forefinger and thumb, as if coaxing it to make a noise.

“I’m late,” I said.

“You’re late,” she said. Her mouth remembered the shape of scolding even if her day had not contained any waiting.

I filled the cups. I put the cups in her hands. I told her, as I do, a story about the river that is true and feels like a lie. She nodded in the middle of it and then again at the end, as if the beginning will never be the part she keeps. When I told her about my name in the book, she frowned in a way that made me think of rain.

“You have my name,” she said. “I lent it to you because you were small and had nothing.”

“No,” I said, smiling. “You gave it to me. That’s different.”

She worked this. She took the idea between her fingers like wet wool. “Gave,” she said finally, and grinned a grin that the world could not ruin. “I gave it to you. That’s an act. That’s a kindness. Not a lending. If I lent it, you would owe me, and you don’t owe me.”

I thought of all the things I owe her. They spooled out behind my ribs.

She leaned in, conspiratorial. “Don’t give it back,” she whispered. “Not to any book. Not even to the river. Keep your name in your mouth where it belongs.”

I wanted to tell her that the book had said delivered. That I owed something back to someone else, and the verb for the owing had a courier in it. But when she looks at me this way, the girl who waded into the canal to fetch her mother’s stolen scarf returns to my chest and takes my tongue. I said only, “Okay.”

On the way back to the Bureau after I had settled her in bed, after I had set her pills in their blue case and twisted the lid till it clicked like a toy, there was a man under the bridge selling birds in cages made from old tomato tins. The cages swung from the underside of the arch like lanterns. “Listen,” he said, “how they mimic the river.” The birds’ calls sounded like coins shaken in a glass. A boy crouched at his elbow, counting something. The man wore a hat that had once belonged to someone who would never sell anything for less than exact value. I did not want a bird. I wanted not to want anything.

When I came into the Bureau, Gorse was waiting for me with two men in plain jackets whose faces had nothing exceptional about them except the way their eyes slid past me too quickly and then slid back. In our city, there is a department no one calls by its proper name. We call them Recorders. Or, when we are pretending irreverent safety, we call them Ears.

“Ms. Rahimi,” one of them said, and already I disliked him. He had the voice of a man who has never had to call anyone by anything but the name printed under their photograph. “We’ve received an alert about an item of potential interest to Municipal Safety.”

“Everything in this building is of potential interest to Municipal Safety,” I said. “We keep the city’s private tragedies in alphabetical order.”

Gorse made a growl in his throat that meant, Please. He is always consoling the world on our behalf so the world will not bite us. It is a service and a habit. He looked at me with a small ache in his eyes. He rarely allows himself one in public. I couldn’t tell whether it was for me or for his own sleep.

“The ledger,” the other man said. He was the nicer of the two, you could tell not by his mouth but by the way his shoes were scuffed in a pattern that meant he paced in small circles while thinking. “The one that came in this morning. We’ll be taking it.”

“It is not dry,” I said stupidly, like a student doing her first day at the Bureau, sweating through her shirt. “The pages will stick if you close it.”

“We will manage,” the first replied. He smiled without the corners of his eyes smarting. “Things like this belong to all of us.”

“The river belongs to all of us,” I said.

“In principle,” he said. “In practice, certain bodies must hold certain responsibilities. We are a city, Ms. Rahimi. We are not a wish.”

Kaya stood up from her table, pushed her chair back with a sound, then sat down again because she is braver than I am but knows better how to spend it. The room had that concavity it gets when power enters it, the pressure that makes you think you should whisper though no one has asked you to.

I walked to the back and stood in front of the book. It lay flayed open, caught in the mid-bloom of drying, its edges turning up like tongues. The fan drummed a little. The names shimmered as they dried, their ink lighter around their letters as if each letter had grown a white aura and then lost it. I could tell that the page with my name on it wanted to be turned again, though no wind had moved it. I could tell that if I closed the book, even gently, some of the names would weld themselves to their brothers and would never be legible again.

I put a scrap sheet over the top page, as we do, to keep dust from settling, though there is never dust in a room that humid. I turned and held my hands out to show they were empty of defiance. I said, “It is the policy of the Bureau that all items must be recorded before removal. I need an hour to finish the intake.”

“You have fifteen minutes,” the first Recorder said. “In the spirit of cooperation.”

Fifteen minutes is not enough to save anything. It is enough to decide whether to try.

I took the intake sheet and filled in fields at a speed that felt like faithful translation. Object. Category. List of contents. Condition. Provenance: unclear. Notes: Contains a list of names in long hand dated according to unknown calendar. Contains my name among others. There was a place for Significance, a blank we almost never fill. I hesitated and then wrote, simply: The handwriting is someone’s. It is this that feels important.

I slid the intake sheet into the folder. I slid the folder into the drawer. I took the diary in both hands and lifted. Water dripped onto my wrist, then down into my sleeve. When I passed the book into the first Recorder’s hands, the air around us went cool. He took it without flinching at the wet, which is how you know he is good at his job. He tucked it under his jacket as if into a rib.

“We will return it when we are done,” the second one said, and for a moment I almost thanked him.

They left. The door closed in a gentle way, like someone finishing a sentence too soon and being pleased with that. Gorse looked at me and then, to his credit, looked away.

On the wharf, the light had gone fish-belly pale. The boatman had his hands in his pockets, looking out into nothing, his gold tooth making a small star when he turned. For a moment, the city was only breath and the sound of the fan spinning with the slightest wobble. The ledger had gone, and my name with it. Still, when I bent to my ledger and stamped the next document, I repeated my name silently, the way my mother had told me to do, the way a person says a word until it becomes sound, and then says it again until it becomes theirs. I stamped until the red ink made the world official, and when my wrist ached, I thought, delivered. I did not know whether I meant the book or me. I did not know whether I had just kept faith, or broken something that was not mine to break.

Chapter One

The day my father became light enough to lift, the orchard turned white.

It was not frost. Frost would have melted at sunrise, would have shown itself honest with a drip. This was a rim of crystals along the leaves and the irrigation lines, a sugared edge on every lemon, as if someone had dipped the whole of our land into a brine and set it out to dry. The men from the church stood in the middle row, hats in hand, their boot soles slipping on the crunch. My aunt Rosalba stood by the open van with her rosary wrapped twice around her wrist. The funeral director kept apologizing for the state of the vehicle, for the way the door stuck when he tried to slide it shut. He had a mole on his cheek like a misplaced seed, and when he smiled at me—condolence-tried, professional—it jumped.

“You okay, Mari?” he asked.

I had his paperwork folded in my back pocket, still warm from my skin, my father's name smudged from my thumb. I was not okay. I was what you are when you have flown for seven hours over clouds and drought and returned to find that the air above your childhood is so dry it stings. I was what you are when the desert has crept in like a rumor and the rumor has turned true.

The men lifted my father with the caution you reserve for an object you understand is unforgivable and fragile. He had lost weight in the months I refused to measure. The hospice nurse had said he was in no pain. She had said this gently, with the practiced cadence of a person who has learned the grammar of last things. He looked asleep. He looked as if he might sit up and tell us where the pressure valve stuck and which of the old valves you should never touch. I stood by the van until the door gave in with a sigh and slipped along its track and closed him away.

“Let me get the casseroles inside,” Rosalba said, because men and women here had always divided grief into tasks. “Before the cats run off with the cheese.”

I followed her past the spigot where my father had tied a length of blue cloth so he could tell the difference between cold and hot with a glance, into the kitchen where the tile grout had given up and turned the same dusty color as the world. The counter brimmed with foil-wrapped pity. People had written their names on masking tape and stuck it to the lids. Love, Mirtha in black marker on a tray of enchiladas. From us, Los Nuñez under a trembling hand. Some elderly neighbor, trying to be funny with his felt-tip, had written Not poison.

“Eat something,” my aunt said. Her hair was gray now, the black of it surrendered with a grace I could not fathom. “You’ll make yourself sick.”

So I ate a spoonful of beans, and I chewed, and I felt like a machine that had been restarted after a long time sitting in its own dust. There was a humming in the walls I had not heard in years, and for a moment I thought it was the old swamp cooler, but then I realized it was the thing in the shed, the desal unit, doing its low animal purr.

“Did you turn it on?” I asked.

Rosalba shook her head, hands busy unwrapping an idea of comfort one aluminum fold at a time. “It started up by itself this morning,” she said. “Woke me. I thought there was a truck in the yard.”

I set the plastic spoon down. “Alone?”

“He’d leave it off at night because of the light,” she said. “Because they watch, you know they watch. After he went, it sat like a dog that knows the voice it should be listening for and doesn't hear it. And then today, it… I don’t know. Machines have their own type of missing.”

I thought of the way the unit had sounded when I was a girl, how I’d put my ear to the corrugated tin and felt the cold of the process, the push of water through something smaller than a prayer. My father had built it himself from old irrigation parts and a membrane he'd bought off a man with a catalog who had promised it would make even the dirtiest water sing. He'd called it his organ. You just have to know which key, he used to say, tapping a pressure gauge like a tuning fork.

We had called this town La Ciénaga when it wasn't a lie. There had been a lake once, before my time, a broad one that didn't know yet it would end up a story. The old men at the feed store talked about it like a woman, the lake that used to put her lips right up to the road, the lake you could fish with your eyes closed. Then the projects came and the canals were straightened and siphoned, and the lake, obliging as a good host, left. It left salt. It left a powder you could see from space, they said on the news, like a scar the size of a city. When the wind is terrible it picks up that salt and throws it into lungs and vegetables. People here carry inhalers in their bib pockets. Children cough and cough. And the companies came too, with blue trucks, with tankers, with the way that men who own water walk. Blue Barons, someone had said once at the co-op, and the name stuck to them like calculus.

My father had not sold his allotment, which was both a point of pride and a point of need. He had kept his acre-feet like a Catholic keeps rosaries, each bead a thing to count when he couldn’t sleep. He had built the illegal unit in the shed so that he could pull up what lay under the earth, a fossil brine thick as old soup, and make it into a ribbon of clean water that could persuade a tree to keep trying. He had called the brine what it was. He had said it like a curse.

I went out to the porch. The air was the taste of a penny held too long in the mouth. Our trees—lemons, a few stubborn oranges, an experiment of guavas that never truly believed in this latitude—stood like people mid-argument, arms up, waiting to see how the other would react. A dove pecked in the baked dirt and shook its head as if trying to dislodge an idea.

He had lined the north fence with pale succulents years ago, after it became clear that thirst was going to be an adjective for everything. Over the fence, at the neighbor’s, there was a collection of old cars that had dreamed once of movement. The wind chime from their porch banged and clanged, no melody, all percussion.

“Mariela,” a voice called. A boy stood at the end of the path that used to be softer. He had a face that was someone’s nephew, always in our house for tortillas or advice. He had been seven when I left. He was not a boy anymore.

“Checo?” I said.

He smiled, and time stuttered. “I go by Sergio now,” he said, which meant he had tried to leave like all of us. “I heard. I’m sorry.”

He had a crate, and in the crate he had newspaper. He unwrapped the paper and showed me what was inside: three jars of lightning-yellow spheres, lemons, ours, floating in oil and spices. “My mama said these are good for keeping,” he said. “I did them with her. Even if the trees go… She says you can make eggs taste like good years.”

I wanted to cry then, not because of my father but because of those jars. I didn’t. The water stayed somewhere inside me, pooled behind a dam of better manners.

“Help me with something later?” he asked. “Before all the old men take over your table and tell you how to feel?”

I nodded. He looked toward the shed. “That thing is humming like a saint,” he said, and there was something like awe in it. “Is it true your father could make the pipes talk?”

“He could make me think they were,” I said. “He could lean his ear to the floor and say, she’s thirsty, and I’d believe.”

He put his hands in his pockets and nodded in the way of someone holding a story that belongs to others. “A man with a white truck was here two days ago,” he said. “Not a company truck. Before he went.” He tilted his head toward the house. “Leather shoes. He asked if your father was willing to consider. He wouldn’t say what. Your father said he had already considered and that we are not chickens, we do not sell our water by the pound. He made a joke about feathers. The man didn’t laugh. He left driving slower than he came.”

He looked like he wanted to say more but didn’t. He handed me one jar and walked back to the road, which had more weeds in it than cars. There was dust in the air that might have been a warning, or might have been just the day scouring itself of attachment.

Inside, the old men came after lunch, as predicted. They sat at the table with their hats on their knees and told me things I knew and things I didn’t. That my father had pulled his first canal water as a Martin Luther King speech played on the radio in a neighbor’s truck. That he had picked peaches as a boy in orchards so thick with morning that he couldn’t see the ladder in front of him. That he had fought a man once behind the feed store over a debt of three dollars and lost on purpose to keep the peace, and then paid the man’s bill anyway. They said he could remember every leak he'd ever found, every hairline crack in a schedule 40 pipe, every sin he’d committed in the name of keeping a graft alive.

“He taught me to listen,” one of them said, not looking at me but at the ceiling fan. “Not with the ears. With the feet. You feel where the vein is. You feel where the water wants. It wants the low places. It wants to colonize the dark. It is the most patient thing. It will take the shore from you one grain at a time. You think you are making choices. Water is making a map.”

Rosalba made coffee strong enough to hold a spoon upright. Someone said “blue barons” with the kind of contempt that is also fear. Someone else said, “Everybody has to eat,” and nobody argued because we were eating. Mirna from down the lane brought a picture of herself and my father standing in front of a row of baby trees that were now dead. He was wearing a hat you could have used as a boat.

There is a kind of laughter people do at wakes because if they didn’t they would drown in their own bodies. I listened. I washed cups. I let the old stories pull the new grief into shapes I recognized.

When the house emptied in the late afternoon, after the heat had reached that particular bright that lucid dreams have, I went into my father’s room. The bed was made the way he did everything, with a stubbornness that looked like artistry to people who didn’t know better. On his dresser was the watch I’d sent him when I got my first paycheck as an engineer, the one with too many functions for a man who never used a calendar. It had died at 2:12. All of his paper had been left in stacks that seemed accidental but weren’t.

There was a cigar box under his pillow as if he’d meant to keep it warm. Inside were envelopes with labels in his thin, staunch handwriting. There was one for Rosalba with a note about the mortgage. One for me with no name. When I opened it, a small jar rolled into my palm. The glass had the tint of something recycled from a different century. The water inside was clear with a green memory. A two-digit year was written on a piece of tape on the lid: 78. There were small flecks at the bottom, sand maybe, or pieces of leaf that had outlived their plant. My father had a habit of keeping history in jars. He had a jar of the first rain after my mother’s death. He had a jar of run-off from the year the mountain burned. He had a jar labeled Cienaga Before.

Under the jar there was a folded page with a hand-drawn map of our land and a single line arrowing across it like a remark you might make to a lover. The line started at a spot near the shed, dipped under the row of old pecans that had given up three summers ago, and ended in a circle with an X in the middle at the back fence where the ditch we called a ditch even when it was a trench should have been. Underneath he had written: old canal? or wish.

I carried the jar to the window and watched the dust move through the light like flocks. 1978. The year I had been born. The year the snowpack had been so generous that people thought maybe the long thing had broken, the curse undone. In the picture album, there is me on his shoulders in the yard with the grass still believing in itself. He is wearing the same watch. We glow like wet.

The hum from the shed deepened and wavered. I felt it under my feet, a tug at the ankles, like the gravity had decided to run in a new direction for a while. I set the jar back in the box and went out.

The shed's door stuck and then relented with the sound of water wrung from a towel. Inside, the desal unit crouched like an animal. Its pipes were patched with things that had not been designed to be patches: napkins, pieces of bicycle inner tube, an old leather belt. The membrane housing gleamed with a clean that did not belong to this family. The sight gauge flitted between numbers with the agitation of a trapped sparrow.

A braided hose snaked toward a sump dug into the floor, and in that sump the brine sloshed. The surface of it had a skin that wrinkled when I blew on it. It stank of the sea in a way that made the word sea seem like a fantasy, like a cousin you only ever heard stories about. There were crystals clinging to the rim that looked edible. I tapped one with my fingernail and it broke and fell back with a sound like sugar.

He had been feeding the brine to the salt trees, to the weeds that didn’t care. Or he had been sneaking it into the old ditch at night, lighting no light, walking with care, meanness toward his own ankles, so nobody would see. He had always said you can’t make a thing vanish. You can only move it to where it hurts someone else less, or you choose yourself to be the hurt. Choose, he said to me once, when I was old enough to stay.

There were notations on the wall in pencil, dates, gallons, little victories. June 3: 225 gpd no leaks. Sept 17: membrane fouled, flushed. Dec: frost like salt. It was my father’s whole faith written on a wall where he could touch it when his other faith failed.

The unit's hum stepped a note and, from some far seam of pipe, a trickle began. The clean-water line trembled with the thrill of being. It did not look like salvation. It looked like a compromise, clear and thin and luminous. I put my finger under it and it made my fingertip cold and clean and sting. I tasted it. In that drop was a river that had thought it was done.

Behind the shed, the ditch ran empty as a promise. The dirt had been scoured so smooth by old water that it looked like the interior of a long animal, ribs showing. Dry weeds did a brittle choreography in the slightest wind. Under everything, you could feel a shape, the absence of a thing. Below, an old channel of the old canal, or the old lake’s willingness still, a memory laid in silt and bones.

We grew up in a place where adults referred to the aquifer like a person they had wronged. She’s tired, they said. She can’t give like she used to. We need to let her rest. And then they dug anyway. Sometimes I think this is the story of the world—wanting what is under and making any story to justify the hole.

When it was finally dark enough that the stars here could do their full work, Sergio came back with a flashlight and two shovels, as if the day had been an intermission, as if we had always been on our way to this.

“I told my mama I’m at the swing,” he said, which is what we used to call the mesquite whose lowest branch someone had put a rope on in the late eighties, and which no longer had the strength to hold even a mockery of that weight. “You want to see what your father wanted you to see?”

We walked along the back fence, where night made the salt glow faintly. The flashlight made tunnels through the air. I could hear dogs arguing with their own courage in yards up and down the lane. We stopped at the X from my father’s map, which felt like voodoo and math, both.

“You dig here,” he said. “I’ll dig here. He showed me once when we were patching the ditch. He said one day you’d come. We found something, and he said it wasn't ours yet. My father said not to say. But he’s gone too. Maybe secrets expire like milk.”

We dug. The earth fought me. It was clay, then softer, then a layer of something that broke in plates like old china. The shovel hit wood. He looked at me like we had discovered a violin. We cleared more. A board. Then another. A lid. My heart did the thing it had learned to do on flights in turbulence—grab at its own ribs, think of passengers and the uselessness of prayers and then breathe through the driver’s competence.

Sergio put his ear to the wood and closed his eyes. He did not move for a long time. “It sounds like maybe a room,” he said at last, embarrassed by the magic of what he had done. “Or like when I was little and I’d put my ear to the table to hear my mother cut vegetables.”

We pried at the boards with a rake head and a stubbornness that could have gotten us to California in a different life. The boards had been hammered down from the other side. Someone had wanted a thing to stay gone. Near the corner, there were rings in the wood, metal, the kind you might tie a rope through. When the first board came up, it let out a smell like old rain.

We shined the light. There was space. Not a cavern. A passage. Lined with brick, coated in the calcified memory of water. It went under the fence, toward the neighbor’s lot, and the other way, under our shed, under our house, maybe, under our kitchen where the casserole dishes had been stacked like strangers.

“An old lateral,” I said. “From the river diversion. The kind the old maps forgot. He drew a wish because he couldn’t bring himself to write down what he knew.”

There was a trickle, slow as guilt. It ran along the lip of brick in a thread that might have been nothing at all. But when Sergio put his finger to it, he smiled like someone tasting a language for the first time. “Cold,” he said. “You feel that? Like a new idea.”

We lay on our bellies, two grown people, our shoulders touching as if we were kids again hiding from adults who were no longer looking for us, and breathed in the sour-life smell of water that has been moving in the dark for years. We didn’t talk about what it meant that he had known and not told. We didn’t talk about the men with their white trucks and their leather shoes. We didn’t talk about the brine’s patience, about where it had gone all this time, about the illegal unit singing to itself in the shed. We looked into the throat of something and listened.

After a while the flashlight dimmed, and we lay there anyway, watching the dark be honest. Somewhere in town, a train cried out as if the earth had pinched it. Somewhere a woman yelled at a man and he yelled back and then their voices fell into the private quiet of a door closing. Somewhere the salt lifted and settled back down, undecided.

When I finally went inside, I passed the table where the old men had drummed their fingers. I touched the jar my father had saved for me with its date like a speech. I lifted the cigar box to my face. It smelled like his shirts had when I was a child and fell asleep against him after we’d brought back the last of the crates. He had his own smell and then the smell of everyone he had tried to be for me.

In the night the desal unit’s hum grew softer, then surged. The house creaked as if settling into a story it had told itself so many times it believed it.

I lay in the bed that had once been mine and pressed my ear to the mattress as if the pipes could speak through the springs, as if they could tell me how to be now, as if they could give me a word better than daughter. This is what I heard: a far-off rain, someone else’s weather deciding it would belong to us for a while; the inching of an old canal relearning its lesson; the salt singing its slow bright song, and under all of it, the faint unignorable rhythm of a heart that was not mine.

Nobody talks about how a house dies. We make lists and tape them to the fridge, we sell the good chairs for less than they deserve, we stand in empty rooms and clap to hear the echo like a flat laugh. But the dying itself is a quiet industry. It happens in the walls, in the nail-holes that look like pupils. It happens in the way the floorboards learn to take your weight and then forget.

On the first morning that the river swallows the edge of town, I go out with my coil of copper wire and the little blue book from the Ministry of Resettlement and Antiquities, and I listen for what each house has left to say.

“Do not anthropomorphize,” the manual begins, as if our wrists and tongues can be disciplined by a paragraph. “You are not therapists, you are record-keepers. You are collecting residues of utility, not sentiments.” On page three there is a diagram of a wall cross-section, a rectangle sliced into grain and plaster and cavity. On page four, a caution about personal property: do not affix your wire or your ear to anything you are unwilling to lose. The river has a temper; the wind that runs its corridors does too.

I am not supposed to begin with my own house. There are senior listeners—men who wear ID badges and the clean boredom of authority—who have said as much. “You will get starry,” one of them told me at training, speaking in a tone he might use for a niece with a small, forgivable addiction. “You will get in the way of what must be done.”

So I begin with Mr. Ghosh’s house. He is the first to be scheduled because his house is the first the chalk line touches. Out in the lanes, the Authority’s boys have been chalking all month: a bright indigo that clings to your fingers for days. They choose the stones first, marking them with numbers and red arrows. Then the walls get marked, the eaves. Even the mango tree has a little slash. It looks as if the town has been prepped for surgery.

Mr. Ghosh is a fisherman who no longer fishes. He sits on a small pillow on his veranda with his elbows hooked over his knees, wearing the same white undershirt he has worn in every season of my childhood. It has a yellowing map beneath one arm, a continent he refuses to recognize. His house is light-green in the way of a leaf kept too long in a book. It was painted the year his son left. Or maybe the year his wife died. People here take their griefs to the same man with the same bucket of paint.

“You brought the wire?” he asks, as if there is a parallel world where I would show up empty-handed and ask his house to speak to me on the strength of my name.

“I did.”

“Shoes off,” he says, pushing himself up in a way that looks ostentatiously painful. “Come. This room.”

He leads me into the front room with the lightened rectangle where a framed picture used to hang. The walls are crowded with the absence of the things he has taken down and wrapped in newspaper. On the floor there is a line of jars. He has labeled them carefully with dates and names in black marker. The first one reads: Dried chillies, 1998. The second reads: Lakshmi’s buttons, 1983. The third: Fish bones, assorted. He has always kept things with the gentle hoarder’s conviction that another day will come when he will know what to do with them.

I kneel and unspool the copper wire. It gleams like a snake that has outgrown its skin. The wire has been passed down in my family from the days we did it for ourselves, before ministries and badges and forms. My mother kept it coiled above the kitchen door, a living talisman, and sometimes she ran it through the sink to keep the drain from clogging, because in those days a thing had to be useful twice to be kept. She called it the listening rope, though of course it is not rope. She has been misnaming things more often, lately. I offer her new words like spoons; she takes them and lays them neatly beside the old ones.

I find a place on Mr. Ghosh’s wall where the plaster has cracked. The cracks look like a net left to dry, which is the kind of mistake you only make here, where everything is always also something else. I push the pin through the plaster, then I wind the copper around it. I wind the other end around my index finger until it tightens, then looser, until I can feel the thrum in the wire like a low, responsible hum.

I close my eyes. Lean my head against the wall.

Sometimes the houses speak immediately: a rush of voices, the sound of spoons chiming in a drawer, the wind of many feet going by. Sometimes it is only a whisper of temperature, a knowledge of sun. Sometimes it is nothing at all, an expensive silence.

Mr. Ghosh’s wall smells like rain under a tarp. The voice, when it comes, is thin with dust, like a child talking from inside a tent of sheets. It says: December. It says: rust. It says: light entering a bottle.

“What?” says Mr. Ghosh, too close, as if he could share the hearing.

“Shh.”

“Don’t tell me to shh in my own house,” he says, but softer.

It comes more steadily now: In the year when the flood took the porches and left the rooms, there were footsteps, then sleeping. There was scratching. Morning warmed the varnish and loosened the piano keys so that one of them would sigh, E flat, whenever the door swung shut. There was a bright magenta ribbon that fell between the dresser and the wall and stayed there, smelling like soap.

“Do you have any magenta ribbons?” I ask him.

He pinches his lower lip. “I will look.” He does not ask why he should look for one small piece of cloth among the partial archive of his life. Maybe he believes me. Or he believes the wire. He has been married. He knows that faith is less about the object than the hand.

The wire vibrates, then goes slack. The house is resting. I loosen it from my finger so the blood comes back in a slow prickling. In my blue book I write what I heard, in the careful block letters the Ministry likes. I don’t write the colors. I never write the colors. The Ministry is not fond of abstraction, and in their minds everything that cannot be weighed or counted is abstraction.

Mr. Ghosh returns with a ribbon that is not magenta, but could have been, once. He holds it with two fingers as if it might bite. “Used to be Lakshmi’s,” he says. “From the wedding.”

“Your wedding?”

“Her cousin’s. Our wedding had nothing to do with ribbons.” He slips it into one of his jars without looking at it again. Then he leans on the wall where my ear just was, as if he could overhear the residue of what I heard. His cheek has fine white stubble, like frost on stone.

“Tell me if the house said anything else,” he says, the way a child says I didn’t cry.

“Not today,” I lie. “I’ll come back.”

Outside, the sky is low and complicated. The river is throwing up a foam like milk gone over, and the current is braided with twigs, with petals from someone's flamboyant tree that has been losing its grip. The Authority's trucks are parked at the edge of the road, their noses pointed toward the water. Men in orange vests smoke in a nervous circle. One of them flicks the end of his cigarette into the river. The current whips it into its mouth, an old addict grateful for anything that burns.

I carry my coil in a cloth bag that used to be a curtain. It still has the damp, heavy smell of rained-on fabric. The bag slaps against my leg as I walk, a familiar reprimand. I could take the car, but there is nowhere to put it that will not soon be underwater. Anyway, the roads have begun to think badly of their own surfaces. They buckle in the afternoons like tired men. Potholes bloom in the night and then parade themselves in the morning like oddly shaped flowers.

My mother’s house—my house—sits on a little rise, a proud chin in the valley. When the floods began, she said: I did not raise you for this. She meant: I did not raise you to listen to strangers' houses for money. She meant: How dare you use our rope for them. Two days later, when the Department posted the list of houses to be submerged, she told me, with an expression I would later understand as relief: Good. It will drown and I will stop hearing it. I told her we would get an apartment on higher ground with cold air that came out of the walls and had no smell. She asked: whose ground, whose air. She was very good at questions that had correct answers but no right ones.

By the time I climb the steps to our verandah the chalk line has already come, a thin blue vein above the last stair. Someone has dutifully marked it with a number and a slash, as if grading our home. My daughter sits just inside the door, a book face-down on her lap. She has inherited my mother’s posture and my mouth, a combination that makes strangers want to ask her for directions.

“How many?” she asks, nodding at the blue book. She is making an effort. There was a week last year when she refused to speak to me at all, and I learned for the first time how quickly a house becomes hostile when a woman in it goes silent.

“Three,” I say. “Ghosh, Singh, and the old clinic.”

“They still having babies there?”

“No, baby,” I say automatically, and she lifts the corner of her lip into a weaponized smile. “They stopped when the generator went. There isn’t enough cold in the town anymore.”

She closes her book and (this is how well I know her) sets it down open, as if to say that we are only a pause in something that is larger than us. “Dida sleep?”

“She’s listing,” I say. “Mangoes this morning. All the mangoes of her life.” My mother has been creating inventories that have no use beyond their own recitation. She was an effective listener before it was a job. People came to our kitchen because they heard she could make a house tell the truth; she had a voice that made walls less shy. She would put her palm on the spot where the plaster had given up and she would say: There is a key behind the westmost baseboard. And a tray of almond sweets under the stairs that your grandfather pretended not to know about. Now she spends her afternoons naming fruit: Sindhuri, Banganapalli, Badami, Malda. She gets to each name the way a tired person gets to a chair. She stops and sits. She waits to be called back to the next.

I take off my shoes. The house feels the muscles of my feet with the intimacy of long marriage. If you have lived in a house long enough, you can walk through it in the dark. That is not the same as knowing it. This is what I tell myself as I take out the coil of wire.

“You’re not supposed to,” my daughter says, without lifting her eyes from the television that is off.

“They won’t know.”

“It’s still not allowed.”

“Then you keep watch.”

She nods solemnly. I love her with the kind of frustration that makes room for humor. She has been rehearsing a moral superiority since she learned how to use a pencil without breaking it. I hold the rope like I’m about to plait someone’s hair. The copper has warmed from being in the fold of my arm; it unwinds obediently.

In the oldest part of the house, the plaster is sugar. If you lick your finger and press it to the wall, it will come away sweet with mineral dust. My mother says when this house was built, the men who made it mixed jaggery into the lime to make the white look whiter. Sweet bones, she calls it. She tells me not to run my tongue along the wall like a goat.

I press the pin through under the wooden lintel that still bears, in pencil, the measurements of my daughter’s growth. The newest mark is the almost-ghost of her eighteenth birthday. She wrote it herself, a misery of numbers. I wind the wire around it twice. Then I wind the other end around my finger, once, twice, thrice, until my fingertip goes purple and alarming. The Ministry’s men would wag their fingers and say: No color is the right color for blood but blood. But I trust the pressure. The listening is better when the wire has to negotiate with the pulse.

I breathe until the house and the air are the same temperature. I breathe until my eyes ache a little, the way they ache when you have watched something bright for too long.

At first it is, as it has always been, the sound of my father’s boots finding themselves on the threshold. The boot he wore at the heel. The way the grain in the wood welcomed his weight as if it had missed him. Then a soft roar: the kitchen’s remembering. The fan coughing itself awake and then pridefully steady. The sink like a throat clearing. Then the light of mid-prayer. Sandalwood. A heavy cloth lifted from a shelf to let the dust go up.

“Anything?” asks my daughter in a voice she thinks is a whisper. The wire carries it; my mother has always complained that the living are much too loud in a dying room.

“Shh,” I mouth, and she raises her eyes to heaven in that precise teenage way that suggests a personal acquaintance.

Then something that is not ordinary arrives. It is a cold current under the warm one. The sensation of an old draft. A shape that hasn’t been in this room for many years taking up its space as if it never left. The wire burns my finger with the smallest sizzle. My heart skids, then answers.

Come back, the house says.

“Who?” I ask it, because I have not yet learned to be quiet with my questions.

Bring back the spoon, it says, with my mother’s voice.

I take my finger from the wire as if it has bitten me. It has not, of course. Not like that. My daughter leans forward so fast her hair blurs. “What?”

“It says—” I am old enough to know that speaking aloud gives a shape to a thing, and that shapes have a way of convincing the future of themselves. “It says something stupid.”

“Like what?”

“It says: bring back the spoon.”

My daughter laughs, a short, relieved noise. “All this for a spoon.”

“It doesn’t say which spoon,” I say, because I am suspicious of relief. “We have twenty spoons.”

“Nineteen,” she says. “I took one to school and it did not come back. I emancipated it into the wild.”

I look at my mother, who has fallen asleep behind the curtain on her charpoy, her breath like a moth’s. She has been waking at night and walking the rooms. I have found little fingerprints in the dust on the highest shelf where she keeps the pressure cooker. I have found the wire coiled in her lap like a cat.

We stand in the doorway as if we are in an expensive painting and the painter cannot decide whether to make us central. I wind the wire around the pin one more time to keep it there until I know what to do, and as I do, the house says, with impatience I recognize: Do not pretend you don’t know which.

In every family there is an object that is both ridiculous and sacred. For us it is a soup spoon with a bone handle worn smooth by the grip of cooks who, for three generations, understood appetite better than sorrow. It belonged to my grandmother’s mother. It was the only thing my mother asked for when the relatives divided up the meat of the house where she grew up. She carried it down to us like a relic. “Every broth that saved a throat,” she said, “has met this spoon.” When my father died she stirred grief with it, lifting and lifting without tasting.

The spoon has not been in this house for nine years.

I do not tell my daughter the story of the spoon, because I have already told her and because I do not want her to put this new hunger together with the old theft. The spoon left on a winter afternoon when an old friend came to say a loud goodbye. We drank tea until the sugar turned our mouths blunt. My mother went to rest, suddenly too tired for company. I took the friend into the kitchen to show her my cupboard of jars, my respectable array of labels. And then we were saying goodbye at the gate and the sun made a navel out of the puddle by the step, and when I went back in the spoon was not on its hook. I did not notice until evening. By then, why ask? Whom? I chose a suspect and married my suspicion to her as if suspicion could be a husband. Years later I would see the friend across newsprint and the bottom of a courtroom door, her eyebrows newly militant, and think: things acquire new uses when the river changes course.

“What’s all this about a spoon?” my mother asks suddenly from behind her curtain, her voice thick with sleep and a peculiar joy. She is the only person I know who can wake in joy to a sentence she has slept into being, as if the sleeping were part of the saying.

“You were right,” I tell her, because she likes that, and because she has been wrong so gently it has not mattered. “The house wants it back.”

“Then give it back,” she says, as if I could reach into the past and fetch it like a toy from under the bed. “You always think things live where you left them.” She pushes herself to sitting with small, fierce noises. Her hair has come out of its braid and moves like a weather system around her head. “Who took it?”

My daughter looks at me, then away. We are a triangle in a small room, and the smallest movements are always the most catastrophic.

“It walked out,” I say.

“A spoon will not walk,” my mother says. “It will skate, if you push it.” She smiles at this small, precise joke of hers. She has always liked the way language slants.

She insists on rising. She moves to the doorway and puts her palm on the lintel where the pin is, as if checking a fever. For a moment the three of us—old woman, middle woman, young—are held by a little piece of copper and the idea that the dead thing we live in is listening back.

“What did the first house say today?” she asks, the way some people ask: what is the weather.

“December, rust, light in a bottle,” I say.

“Good,” she says. “He will be able to find his breath in the night.”

“Don’t start with your breath jars,” I say, but my voice is fond. There are jars of her breath on the highest shelf, each with a date. Some in winter, fogged. Some in summer, bright as nothing.

That night it rains. The rain is thin and hard, as if it comes from a place that dislikes us. We put pots under the gaps. After all our preparations—the making-high of important things, the putting-low of unimportant ones—the water finds new intentions. It wicks up the table legs. It anoints the bottoms of books. If I were a better kind of person I would believe that everything knew what to become. The broom under the water becomes a fish. The mug becomes an air hole. The bed becomes a boat with a bad dream.

In the half-quiet between thunder and its own answer, I hear a tap against the step. It is not rain. It is not a rat. It is not the boys next door practicing their command of profanity. It is a polite sound. The sound a person makes who has arrived too early and knows it.

I take the lantern and open the door, and the door opens with soaked reluctance. The verandah is a kind of island, and on the island float small things the river has decided to bring back. There are three oranges not from our tree. A child’s sandal with the face of a cartoon rabbit, the face worn smooth where it has been kissed by sand. A feather from a peacock you cannot confuse with any other bird; arrogance has a particular weight. There is also, wedged against the last stair, sticky with green, the spoon.

It has come dull from the river’s pocket. The bone handle is the color of old milk. The curve has taken on a new story of scratches. For a ridiculous moment I think: maybe the river bought an imitation and hopes we will not notice.

I pick it up and the cold goes through my palm and up the underside of my arm very quickly, as if I have tripped backward through time and landed, ungainly, on my elbows. I stand with my legs braced because the ground beneath us is a rumor, and I raise the spoon to the yellow lantern light and beneath the slime the metal winks, and I know it like I know my mother’s scolding breath. There is a nick on the rim that used to match the nick on my father’s canine. There is the faintest shallow dent where a hungry hand struck the pot without meaning to. My name is not on it, but mine is the throat that leans toward it now.

My daughter appears beside me in her bare feet, her toenails bluish in the cold. She looks at the thing in my hand with the appropriate awe and confusion of someone who has read many books but not this one. “Is that—”

“Yes,” I say.

We stand there long enough for the lantern to sputter twice and catch itself. Behind us, my mother says, from her bed: I told you. Not with her mouth, but with her satisfaction spread through the house like warm air.

I lay the spoon on the table and the house becomes, for a moment so short only my skin notices it, taller. It takes a breath. The breath is familiar as the sound of a child’s shoe being shaken free of sand. We always underestimate how much a building wants to be itself.

In the morning the men in their orange vests will come with their clipboards and their braided tape. They will knock and we will sign. I will borrow a broom to sweep the verandah because I was raised to be embarrassed by any dirt my eyes can see. I will sit with the spoon in my lap and the spoon will make me remember the other thing the house said, the thing I did not write down: After the spoon, bring the rest.

But for now, in the night, with the river at our knees and the water counting the bricks, I rinse the spoon in the pot under the leak. I say, as if greeting a guest who has always known the way to our door: Come in. Where have you been.

The spoon does not answer. The lantern burns a smooth hole in the dark. My mother breathes her catalogues under her breath: sixteen mangoes, possibly twenty, the green ones that refuse to ripen until you forget them. My daughter, who believes she is not anyone’s child at this hour, touches the rim of the spoon with one finger and smiles. Outside, the river rearranges itself like a body in sleep, finding a position that is both comfortable and fatal.

On the morning the houses began to weep, my mother sugared the thresholds.

She pinched white crystals between finger and thumb and drew a thin line along our doorway, a ribbon of sweetness against all that salt. “For the good spirits,” she said, though she had never been sure whether the good ones were the ones who stayed or the ones who could be persuaded to leave. When I was small, she used to tell me that sugar called the rain closer and salt called it away; that if I licked the wall, I could taste the story of what the sky had done the night before. I tried it once, secret and slow: pressed my tongue to the chalk-cold bricks and tasted only the ache of my own foolishness. Salt was like that. It made you certain of things that weren’t entirely true.

That morning, though, our walls needed no coaxing. They had learned, somehow, to draw water from air. Windows pearled. Doorframes slicked. Our house stood in the lower ring of Erisar, near the pans, and the air always held the damp breath of brine, but never had it beaded itself and run. We watched the first clear drop fatten, tremble, then fall from the corner of the kitchen shelf to the packed earth floor. We watched another birth itself and slide down, leaving a darker track that the salt tried to reclaim even as it glistened. It was like seeing a person who has not cried in years discover how to sob.

“The old summers are gone,” my mother said, not to me, but to the room. “They’ll take away the rest of our customs and leave only our bad habits.”

I could count the times I had seen her cry. Twice when Father left for the high ridge and did not come back. Once when a crane from the city side took a bite out of the far pan and chewed a family’s livelihood under its iron teeth. And once, quietly, when I told her I had cataloged her wedding veil, that I had written its story on chip-mulberry paper, stamped and oiled and tucked into the archive where the damp could not find it. She said she didn’t have a story, but when I opened the notebook later, the page smelled faintly of a stranger’s perfume and summer oranges.

“I should go,” I said. “The archive will be sweating.”

My mother made the sign over my head that she reserves for the fragile work I do. She thinks it protects the past if you make a little excuse to the present as you pass. She says: forgive us. She says: we’ll be back in a minute. She says: you won’t even notice we were gone.

In Erisar we have names for the whites: the skin-thin glaze that settles on our hair and shoulders on the walk down to the pans; the rubbled snow that trembles underfoot at midday; the pearl fizz that coats our tongues when the wind shifts from the south. We have names because this is our work. We gather, we scrape, we rake. We break crust. We dry crystals as long as thumbnail moons and bag them by the kilo for caravans heading north. It is our inheritance and our penance, our great pride and our constant irritation. Salt eats the seams of our clothes, opens our hands in a hundred paper cuts. Salt pays for weddings and funerals. Salt turns our boots white and our hair silver decades too soon.

Erisar was at the edge of the Great White when it still deserved that name. In my grandmother’s time, she said, the pans went on past the reach of an afternoon’s walk, and at night the moonlight made a false horizon. She carried a lantern and a little bell to find her way home by sound. Now the salt has retreated into basins we could count. After a long dry age, the weather has started to misbehave—rain out of season, fog that refuses to lift, heat that sits down on your chest and will not leave until you’ve spent half the day begging it. The White is stranger, patched with spiny plants and collapsed pools. Children from the City come on buses in creased uniforms to take the open air toxicity of our place into their stories about other people’s lives. They buy little bags of our labor tied with ribbon and say the word artisanal like a prayer for goodness.

I walked with my scarf up over my nose, my satchel swinging against my hip. The morning’s first light made the pans look bruised, purpling in places where the brine lay thin. Out in the middle somebody’s dog, a red-bone mutt with a brineburned tail, stood and barked at his own reflection. The bell from the topmost house—that steep little chapel with its slat roof and its chipped saint—gave a single flat note: the warning we use for weather, for fire, for strangers. Its sound knocked the air the way I imagine a bird knocks at a window. People appeared in their doorways, eyes narrowed, hands shading their faces, and then vanished again to hustle children indoors or pull tarps over the baskets of drying fish or climb up to the flat roofs to sandwich tar between bricks where the leaks had already started. I saw Jaca from the second ring and he saw me and lifted his chin in that way of his that says both trouble and hello.

“You’re going to the old school?” he called. The wind chewed his voice and spit it back, thinner.

“Somebody has to,” I said, and continued before he could offer to come with me. How could I explain that certain places obeyed me better when I went alone?

The archive isn’t a building of its own. It’s rooms that have been emptied of their old use. Classrooms are good, with their straight rows of windows and their blackboards for chalk notes. We store the town’s papers in the southern wing of the disused school above the flats, two rooms with cracked cement floors and high ceilings, given over to me because nobody else asked for them. I keep the windows shuttered and oiled, the shutters patched, a snake of binding around the gaps. The lock is stubborn. The lock likes me.

Inside, the air was wetter than I liked. It had that fat feel of breath that has nowhere to go. I unbound the first window, then the second, opening them just enough to set the air moving without inviting all the damp inside. The light came cautious and a little yellow across the tables. Stacks of ledgers and boxes of documents and baskets of photographs took on a low sheen, as if they, too, were preparing to sweat. I moved among them with my palm open, a brush of greeting for each. Good scribbled order. Good cotton-thread binding. Good grease-stamped notepads with the yellow that doesn’t run. I kept a cloth in my mouth to wet with my breath and then rubbed the corners of papers with it, a trick old Archivo Maddon taught me: oil keeps the wet from eating the paper; our breath gives the oil a reason to stay.

“You are too attached for a person,” Maddon used to say, in his lake voice, slipping and sure. He had come from a place where water did not have to be boiled twice before you drank it. “You love thin things. A wind will carry you off in the end. We’ll lose you like we lose our hats.”

In the back room there is a cabinet whose lock is not stubborn. It’s a stupid lock, a flat metal tongue in a slot so clumsy a good-kneed child could bully it. I keep our worst ideas there, and our most beautiful. From the shelf I took down the Book of Thaws. I named it that in a fancy mood during a year when the weather disappointed us so gently we hardly noticed the harm it was doing. It’s a leather book, blue going gray, with soft pages. I record days when Erisar changes. When fog stays. When a stranger arrives with the same face as our last stranger. When a girl born nameless in the upper ring is named at last. When the houses begin to weep. A town should know how it is different this morning. How else will it speak to itself?

I was writing—Date this. Bell gave one. Breathing walls; clear tears; sugar at thresholds; do not sleep on your back; talk to the doorframes—when I heard the first tapping.

At first I thought it was the shutter bumping in its latch. I went to the windows and set the wooden pegs more firmly, snugging cloth around the gaps. The sound continued, regular and small. Scrap scrap. Count of three. Scrap scrap. A pause. The bell gave another flat note and then was silent. When it stopped, I felt its absence on my skin the way you feel an ache only when you move. The tapping went on. It was coming from below.

The school was built with a long crawlspace where winter cold and summer heat could go to learn each other’s language. That space had been dry since before my mother was born. In the prolonged dry age, the floor of the crawlspace had grown a fur of salt crystals, like a winter pelt. Children used to dare each other to slide under there, to come out with the rime dusting their eyebrows and eyelashes, white as old men. When I first took these rooms, I had asked the men from the northern ring to carry out the broken desks and the map-stands, and one of them had said, Now, girl, you should check your boards. A crawlspace like this sometimes caves. He had stamped his boot and the floor had held. The sound it made was not sound I would call trustworthy.

I set the Book of Thaws under the wrapped bell on the table and went to the cabinet where the snake of binding cord lived and took it, and the bent hook I use for fetching objects from high shelves. I went to the tiny door behind the back shelves that opens onto the crawl. It was set down a good knee from the floor and framed in brick that had crystallized along its edges like hoar on beard. The door hinge squealed its old complaint. Damp came out, cool as breath. The tapping stopped and then started again, louder in the opening. Scrap scrap. Count of three. Scrap scrap.

The air down there was wrong. Not wrong like rot, but wrong like a room you have known all your life and which someone has turned a quarter turn while you were asleep. I went down anyway, because the work we do makes us less careful of our own skin than we should be. If you spend your days keeping fragile things from breaking, you come to think of yourself as blunt enough to manage it.

The crawlspace was taller than I remembered and shorter, both at once. Salt had grown there like chandeliers, like jaws. Often the crystals make little square cities, polite and geometric, full of corners and reflective habits. Down there they had made themselves wild—long ferrous-shine stalactites that looked more like teeth than minerals should. A few of them had been cut once, I could tell, their severed ends duller, and had sprouted back fingers beyond the cut, reaching down as if they liked the feel of my hair when I passed under.

The floor was wet. That was new. Not puddled with water, but wet like dough that has had too much salt folded into it, sticky and giving. The soles of my boots made mild sucking noises. The tapping had become a knocking now, stone on stone, metal on metal. The sound called a rhythm from my grandmother’s time: a work-song women sang when they cracked the first crusts in spring. I felt it in my chest, like the bell had migrated into me.

“Hello?” I called, ridiculous as that felt. “Is there someone?”

Scrap scrap. Count of three. Scrap scrap.

I moved toward the far wall where the school had been built over one of the old brine cisterns, a round stone-lined pit where the water had been gathered and measured and allotted back when we still had to argue about who owned thirst. The cistern had a short rim that rose just above the ground, like a little wall, and a wooden lid in three pieces: a central piece that could be lifted entirely and two side pieces hinged like ears. The central piece wore a ring of iron.

No one has used that cistern in years. There are better wells. There are tanker trucks from the City with their rubber hoses. Still, the lid was damp, the rim glistening. An error in airflow, I told myself. A trick of weather. Erisar loves tricks.

I tied the cord around my waist and hitched it to the leg of a desk. I tested the knot with my weight twice. I hooked the iron ring with the bent hook and levered the lid up a few fingers. The sound of its seal breaking reminded me of the first time you open a jar of preserved summer and the fruit smells like it has been waiting for you under all that sugar. The air that came up was cold, and it had a smell that was not rot and not sweetness and not brine. It was a smell like the metal of a key held between your teeth.

The knocking stopped.

Silence can be worse than any sound when you expect sound. The quiet made me aware of my heart and then, after a beat, of the other, smaller sound inside the silence: a breath that wasn’t mine.

“Hello,” I said again, quieter. “If you’re a person, say so.”

At first the only answer was that metal taste of the air finding me. Then there was the slightest scuff of something against stone. Not a rat. Not a fish. Something that had hands and had forgotten for a while how to use them.

I put my face over the opening and breathed out once. My breath fogged the air and then was eaten by it. My eyes took a moment to find the shapes. The cistern was a throat of stone, with a shoulder of water slicking it a few feet down. The water was not water the color I expected. Not brown and not clear. It was the color our old clock face goes when the day is full of heat and the edges of things give up trying to keep themselves.

Below, not quite under the lip, I saw a shape that was somebody’s, curled and heavy with crystals. Salt had grown on a person the way it grows on fallen boards in a storm season, building a second body around the first. The hair—if that word belongs to those strands—hung like white kelp. One hand had found a small ledge and then had let go and then found it again, over and over, making the only sound I had been hearing. The hand did not look like a woman’s or a man’s or a child’s. It had the shape of a hand used hard by weather.

The mouth was above the little edge of water, barely. The crystal had grown around the cheeks and the bones near the ear and had left the lips bare. I tell you now that I have seen dead people in the time since my father did not come back from the ridge, and I can tell the difference between a face that has ended and one that has stopped to listen.

“Hold on,” I said, like anyone needs advice as simple as that. “Hold on. I have you.”

The ring of iron was no help, only decoration. I had the bent hook and the cord and the knot that I had tested and the idea that even if my arms failed me, my legs—stubborn as my lock—would not. I hooked the cord under his arms, the crystals cutting against the rope like they wanted to saw themselves free. The hands on that ledge let go long enough for me to pass the loop under them, then found the stone again as if that were their job and they had been hired to do nothing else. When I hauled, the salt body moved like a heavy piece of furniture, something with its own gravity that has never liked to be asked to change rooms. I put my shoulder to the work. I talked as I pulled because my mouth didn’t know what else to do with itself.

“You’re heavier than you look,” I said. “Old man. Brother. Father. Guest. Whoever you are. I am not the best person for lifting, but I am the one who is here. That counts for something.”

When his face came up to the lid, I could see his eyes. The lids were rimed; the lashes clumped with little crystals that made a lace no woman would wear for fear of losing her vision. The eyes were open and unfocusing, like shallow water over stones. I thought for a moment that they might be ice and that I had dragged a statue from the days when we used to put up saints everywhere and leave them to winter. Then he blinked. In that one slow lift-and-fall, I saw a person come back to the room.

He was younger than the way he had gotten suggests. Not child, not old. His nose had been broken once and healed a half shade too far to the right, giving his face the look of someone who smiles while thinking of something else. When he finally took a full breath, he made a sound that emptied me and filled me at the same time. Like he had been underwater in his own life for a long time and now had bumped his head on air by accident and decided against drowning.

He did not struggle. When I said, We have to get you out, he made the smallest nod. I lifted and he let himself be lifted. When I hauled him to the lip, I thought: I am going to tear off his skin, the salt has made its armor and I am going to peel it with the rope and that will be that, we will make a new entry in the Book of Thaws for the death of the man who came back as a statue and then did not. But the skin is stubborn too, and whatever made the crystals give him up that morning had given them a soft heart.

He lay on the floor of the crawlspace, on the wet salt dough, and made a sound that was not language and was not pain and was not gratitude but was something at the root of all three. He closed his eyes and opened them again and found the little rafters of the school, the poor childish painting of a bird on the far beam, the knot of cord attached to my waist and then, following it, me. He had an earring of thick wire in one ear. Not a City man’s wire—ours. Practical, the sort you bend yourself when you want to keep something close.

“What is your name?” I asked.

He tried. He would have said it if he could. He made a little shape with his lips and gave up before the first sound could be turned into a letter. Then he said nothing and instead reached for the hem of my skirt the way children do when they need help standing. His hand was warm. Heat flowed from him into me or from me into him, I couldn’t tell which. It is like that with certain shared tasks; you do not know who is supporting who.

He stood with the kind of grace that belongs to people who used to fall for a living. He was one of those, I thought, before I knew anything else about him. A salter, a net-man, a roof-er, a goat boy on the ridges. One of ours. His knees shook. He set his shoulders and the shaking stopped. He took a breath and tried again, the first word he had a right to say under another person’s roof.

He didn’t say my name. He didn’t say his. He said one word in my grandmother’s language, the one she kept for the world before the White took its breath.

“Home,” he said.

The bell at the top of the hill gave another flat note, and then, after a long beat of listening, a pair of quick bright ones. Not fire, not strangers. Weather. The kind that makes and unmakes a town. My mother would be putting pans under the drips that had become leaks, insisting to herself that if she could manage a house she could manage an age.

“What is your name?” I asked again, softly.

He touched the place under his broken nose and then the hollow at his throat where a pendant might have hung, where a mark of belonging sometimes sits. He looked at his hand as if expecting to find something written there. There was nothing but the pale frost of salt and the long dark lines where work had taught his skin to be strong.

“Tide,” he said, in our everyday tongue this time. His voice was hoarse and somehow rich, like the inside of a bell. “I am tide.”

“We don’t have tides,” I said, before I could stop myself. This is what you get for loving thin things: you supply them with their definitions when all they want to do is be.

He smiled then, with the right side of his mouth more willing than the left. It was not a happy expression but it was certainly not unhappy. “You do now,” he said.

Behind us, in the room where I had left the Book of Thaws, a page turned with a sound that paper shouldn’t make by itself in a closed room. And then, under our feet, the crawlspace floor sighed—not settling but expanding—the way a person sighs when they have decided, at last, to tell the truth.

I tightened the knot around my waist as if more rope could make any part of this safer and said, “Come on. Let’s get you out of the ground and into a chair. I think today will be for remembering more than we expected.”

Outside, the houses of Erisar went on weeping until the noon bell, and then they stopped and waited, polite as guests, for whatever came next.

Chapter One

The first map I ever lied about was my mother's face.

I was twelve and she was thirty-nine and the sea was steady as a held breath. I traced her on butcher paper with a school compass I had begged from my teacher, skidding the point along cheek and temple, the pencil making a taking sound on the torn edge of the page. I gave my mother two identical eyes and left out the nick on her left brow where a mango fell when she was a girl. I refused the fine lines that had started to spider at the corners of her mouth. I smoothed everything. It felt like kindness.

Years later, bent over rolled charts on other tables, hearing the thrum of engines under my feet, the smell of diesel knitting itself to salt, I learned a word for what I had done.
