The officers called it generalization. You omit the obstinate, the particular, so the picture will hold. You make it tidy so the world can fit flat.

Outside the cabin window the island I refused to call by its government number rose out of the water like the spine of a sleeping animal. A low strip of green and tin roofs shouldering the wind, the white bite marks of surf on its eastern side. On the ferry's loudspeaker a recorded voice kept repeating the safety instructions in three languages and then an approximation of ours, in a voice that had learned the shape of our words but none of the breath.

Block 12A, the ferry schedule said. Block 12A, said the letter with the seal that had found me in the city, just as the first winter rain turned the air to iron filings. You are requested to assist in the preparation of risk maps and relocation diagrams for Block 12A, known locally as Niranam. Known locally as a place that had put me in a boat and waved with both hands and then raised them to my face in blessing and then if the stories are to be believed never quite lowered them.

"Do you know it?" the man across the bench asked me. The bench was sticky with salt, the kind that works up from metal. He had a new file holder wrapped in plastic on his lap and wore his ID badge like a borrowed word.

I looked past him at the line of water, that false horizon that kept lifting itself a little farther off at every blink. "I know a place that used to be here," I said. "I don't know Block anything."

He smiled without malice. He was younger than me and his smile had not yet learned regret. "We have to number things so they can be accounted for."

"We have other ways," I said. My voice surprised me. The ferry cut a new seam in the sea; the water stitched itself behind. As if it would be as tidy as that, the healers said.

He reached to steady the file as we listed. In the swell the light made a ceiling of coins under the water. I thought of my father's hand on my head, the way his thumb had always found the bone behind my ear to anchor me when I was small. The hand that had learned the weight of a net and a paddle and the gentle slapping rhythm of a child's shoulder blades when the crying would not end. The hand that had relaxed only in the moment before the boat tipped. Some mornings I still feel his thumb there, steady as a compass point.

"The letter said you've done coastal work," the man—Officer Devan, his badge said—continued in a way that attempted casualness and achieved politeness. "We are lucky to have you. Very few both speak here and speak there. The maps need to be understood in both places."

He meant the city and the island, the air-conditioned, and the air that tasted of falling fruit, the offices where the walls didn't sweat and the kitchen where the walls did. He meant the government and the rest of us. He meant the language of forms and the language of old women calling to each other across the docks. I thought of my mother’s ledger book with its red-ruled lines, the one she kept wrapped in cloth, with columns for date, borrower, item, return. Priya, two cups rice, returned. Kanthi, pestle, lost. Sea, Rafi, boy, no answer.

"I'll do measurements first," I told him, to get away from all of it. "We'll need a baseline, some triangulation. Tide tables for the week. Where are your benchmarks?"

"We have four official points," he said, pleased to be asked. "Their coordinates are in the file. One is on the church steps. One on the water tank. One on a rock that used to be on the beach but is now in the sea. They'll be easy to find."

It would have been funny if the air didn't already feel thin. Easy to find was one of the more dangerous phrases an officer could use about an island. Rocks remembered, yes, and steps kept their mouths, but nothing was easy to find when edges refused to stay. We would come in on spring tides. We would measure over their shoulders. We would write down our version of their hem.

On the day I left for the city, my mother did not speak to me when I left the house. Not because she was angry. She had lost the word good-bye the day before and did not want me to see the empty space where it would have been. She touched the ledger and then touched my face and said, "Write to me like a foaling." She meant often, in small bursts, with urgency. Instead I sent her steady, useful boxes: a pressure cooker, a reading lamp, a raincoat. As if a coat could help with the kind of rain that starts at the ankles, as if lamps could trick time when time was already at the door.

The ferry steered for the gap in the reef as if it remembered my body weight. Along the east shore, shack roofs were measured in patches of light, squares of scavenged aluminum and tar paper reflecting the sun. The boys had always learned to walk wide-legged to balance the water and the wind. The new men wore trousers rolled to the calf that looked like the sea had licked them. I pressed my palm to the window for heat and found it wet. We were sweating out of the world.

Perhaps you think I am exaggerating. You think the city trains us to dramatize where we come from to make it legible to donors and departments. Here is a number, here is a child, here is a color photograph of a woman with a distance in her eyes. But listen: We learned our measurements from the water. We knew how long it took for oil to ribbon itself across a bay. We had a word for the iridescent skin on a bucket of rain collected in April. My grandfather could taste the difference between the rust of two shipping companies. That was our education. When I say the window gave back water to my hand, I mean somewhere the sea had already entered a new absence, and my palm took on the possibility of it.

We docked in a crowd of small salt-hardened faces. A man with a fishing line coiled around his wrist shouted to no one and to me. Children saw me and then the case for the theodolite on my shoulder and decided I must be a kind of magician. They would ask for words like "azimuth" and make them into jokes later. I opened my mouth to find the air that had once known the shape of my name.

"Mira," someone said. Not a call but a confirmation, like a boat ceding space. "Look at you."

My mother had not come to the dock. That was sensible. The heat would have undone her, and the dockers would have undone her with questions. It was my aunt Kalyani who stood with her sari hitched to her knees and her slim calves streaked with mud in the way that makes us look like we are growing back into the earth. In her hair there were three pins that did not match. She kissed my sleeve instead of my cheek, in consideration of my cityness. "The officials," she said under her breath, sliding her eyes at Devan. "They were here yesterday too. They walk with mouths. Come, your mother is counting. She is on second rice."

Devan introduced himself with the hospital politeness they teach in their trainings. "We are here to help," he said. He pushed a paper at her that had been signed by someone whose name looked like a river. My aunt raised her chin in the old way that had stopped policemen and priests, and said, "We will help you," which was not the same thing.

The path to the house was thinner. The reeds had leaned into it. Mangrove roots looked like hands blind in a bucket. The house itself had learned some small worry at its foundations; the back corner sloped as if it were listening to gossip. The roof was new in patches. The netting over the veranda had been mended with blue plastic string that did not match the old rope and so read to me as both hope and rude.

In the kitchen my mother sat in the cane chair that used to belong to my grandfather. She had tied one end of her sari to its arm as if she feared drift in her own house. When she saw me she did something with her mouth I'd never seen; the left side lifted and the right refused. I went to that wise, refusing mouth and put my cheek against it, the way we do to test if the water is too hot for a child's bath. She smelled like fenugreek and damp pounded walls. I had brought her a new jar of turmeric because I still believed in talismans.

"My girl," she said, finding girl easily but not my name, and then, "You look like someone else's daughter." She laughed—there it was, my mother's laugh, uninvaded—and then she left. Not the room; just the present. Her eyes traveled to the ledger on the shelf and her hands began to count the way they do when nothing is owed and everything is missing.

"She's worse in the afternoons," my aunt said, as if I had asked, as if I had any right to be told the shape of what I had abandoned. "In the mornings she will ask if you are hungry, if the fishman is late, and she will call you. She will call you by all the names she has known you by. In the afternoons she counts. The debts remind her there was a time when people returned things."

I took my mother's hand. The skin was thin as onion. In the city, when I thought of her, I thought of her hands, of their ferocity. She had pulled a man off my father in a fight at the dock once, her fingers wrenching the man's ear so hard he forgot how to walk. Those hands now folded over nothing. I slipped my thumb under the bone behind her ear.

"We have to go see the church steps," I told Devan, because work felt like a garment I knew. "And the water tank. I'll need to see the old rock too, even if it thinks it is a fish now. We should start before the light opens."

"And in the evening," he said, looking at the ledger, not understanding what he was seeing, "we will meet with the committee."

"Committee," my aunt repeated, trying the shape of the word on her tongue like a new fruit, checking for sour. "They had committees when I was young too. The result was the same as a quarrel, but with more paper."

We left the kitchen through the back where the ground has always been honest. There are places you can’t lie, however useful it would be. The well is one. The line of ants is another. If they have moved, something has shifted that has nothing to do with funding. The well had a new crack on the northern lip. The ants had changed their street. These are the kinds of measures you do not write on a report. These are the kinds of measures I know make a life.

By the time we reached the church the sun was already boiling entire creatures out of the lagoon. Small fish stepped on the surface for mercy. The church wore its usual eye-roll of seagull shit and its bell, which has never rang on time, rang anyway, convincing no one. On the fourth step someone in a yellow vest had nailed a small aluminum plate that read BM12A-CH. It was the kind of plate that would outlast the sermon and the steps and us.

"One," Devan said. He touched it with a kind of ceremony and I didn't know whether to resent or appreciate the gesture. "You said you need three points."

"We'll need at least three to get a line we can pretend to trust," I said. I set the instrument on the most level part of the wide step and told him to stop talking. "Tell the fathers to keep people off this area until we finish. I don't want a procession wandering through my sight lines."

"That's a sentence no one in my family has ever said," he said, again without malice.

He was eager. This made him dangerous and useful in equal measure.

From the church we walked to the water tank. It was taller than I remembered. Memory shrinks infrastructure. The tank had been painted the blue of old mouths and new flags. On its base someone had drawn the outline of an island and written Home. Someone else had tried to cross out the e and write o in its place. HomO. It read as insult and biology and then as humor again. The plate on the tank read BM12A-TK. Two.

"And the rock?" Devan asked. "You will not take a boat?" He was trying to be kind. He thought the sea would keep its manners for me if I stepped on it in my first hour back.

"We'll walk," I said, and he followed me down the path that had shifted into water and back into path so often it had a memory like fabric. On the far edge of the lagoon the old basalt the fishermen called Grandfather tilted under its new circumstance. Half of it still lay on the sand when the tide supped itself out. The other half belonged to the sea now, black with the kind of green that looks like hair until you touch it. The aluminum plate, ridiculous in its aspirant words, read BM12A-RK.

"We had our own name for it," I said.

"And now it is a rock with a number," Devan said, as if there were comfort or fairness in saying everything twice.

We set the tripod, levelled, pointed, read. The instrument made its delicate robot noises as if it could talk the sea into a hold. The heat softened my ears. The numbers came into the notebook obediently: angles, distances, cautions scrawled in ink. The water flattered the sky.

When you make a map of a thing that would rather be moving, you learn to bargain. There are formulas and yes, we brought them, in folders and in our heads. There are tide charts and yes, we laid them flat and held them down with shells. But then there is the bargaining. If I take this point now against that wall, if I cheat the instrument two degrees to account for the ducking child, if I resolve to return at dawn for a confirmation shot. These are not the lies of my mother’s face. These are the kinds of cheats all cartographers perform to keep the paper from wobbling off the table.

"Tell me about your father," Devan said, as if he had been taught to ask that on page three. Maybe he had been. They recruit boys like him at universities where the rice has no stones and the handwashing sinks always have soap. They give them a list. The list has questions in it that never dream of the answers they will find.

"He did not like the idea of maps," I said. "He said if the sea wanted to keep a secret, it was impolite to draw it. He said the only person whose business it was to know where the reef cut deeper today was the person whose ankle was already in its teeth." I looked up into the white. "He taught me to read the lazy ripples that tell where a big fish is pretending to be sand. He taught me the taste of a rag left overnight on a boat. He was not there on the day the net weight slipped its rope and he went with it. He had been sick that week. He didn't listen to his lungs."

"I'm sorry," Devan said, reflex more than feeling. Then, younger than his badge, "Do you hate it? The work? The side you're on?"

I took my eye off the scope. My unfathered father would have told me not to. "The side is a line I keep persuading to be a circle," I said. It sounded like a lie and a hope.

"Officer," someone called from up the beach. Committee, I thought, the word already tasting of paper. Two men and a woman were walking with the confidence of wardens. They were not of our island, and my aunt would have told me that without the way they placed their feet. Their shoes were relevant. The woman shaded her eyes with a folder; her arm hair glittered. Behind them, someone small followed, imitation heavy in each step.

"Later," I told Devan. "Let me finish this traverse. We need something we can say as if it were true."

He went to meet them with the relief of a person sent a handhold. I turned a degree, wrote, breathed through the smell of warm algae and old plastic and the peculiar clean gratitude of a fresh cut on an adult toe. The child who had been following the officers came close enough to touch my sleeve. He had the earnest belly of the not yet scolded. His hair had been cut at home by an aunt. He wore a charm, twisted red thread, that would have struck a donor city as primitive and all the rest as prudent.

"What are you doing?" he asked.

"Measuring the island," I said.

"How big is it?"

"As big as the stories you tell at night," I said, because I am my mother's daughter when we are approached by a child we cannot protect. "No bigger than the breath you forget to hold when the wave goes under your boat. Do you know how to keep a straight line?"

He squinted into the telescope eyepiece, his breath making small clouds on the glass. "You can't keep straight lines here," he said, as if reciting from science class. "Only the path to school is straight. And even that goes around the old tree."

"Even straightness has to travel around somebody," I said, and he laughed and then went serious again in a way that made me want to hide him in a jar.

The officers had reached us. The woman took off her sunglasses as if her face were a privilege. "Ms. Nair?" she said, reading the name from a list that had me in the wrong quadrant. "We have a preliminary meeting at six. There will be representatives present from the Health Unit and from Housing. We will be presenting options."

"Options," my aunt echoed later, when I reported. "They bring adjectives with their pens." We were still by the rock, the day leaning over us, when I decided to stop for the afternoon, to keep something unmeasured for the stubbornness of it. You learn that with the sea. You learn to leave a thing.

At my mother's house my old room still held the mosquito net that once made me think of veils and weddings and then made me think of traps. The walls had been repainted that careful green that announces a new start or a hospital. On the shelf a gap where my atlas had been. Under the bed a box that, when I pulled it out, rasped like paper wet and dried again, warped into the memory of water. Inside, the ledger wrapped in its fading cloth. My mother had written in pencil in the years after my father's death as if that would give back any of what was taken. The entries grew stranger. Fire, one napkin, returned. Crow, two chilies, paid with song. Sea, teeth in dream, left at door.

That was when I found it. Tucked into the ledger not as a page but as a plea. A small square of brown paper, sweet shop paper, the kind that takes oil like a tattoo. On it, in a young child's tilted capitals, one sentence that lifted the hair on my arms.

MAPS ARE WHEN WE CHOOSE WHO WILL BE RESCUED, it said.

And under it, a line drawn in blue crayon that began at the edge of the page and did not stop by the time the paper ended.

In the evening, as the officers unfolded their options under the strung light above the schoolyard and the men who had once taught me to slip off a boat and into the sea without shaking it too much crossed their arms like oars, a wind rose that smelled of metal and lightning. It had been a hot day and the kind of silence that follows heat had settled like a wet cloth on everyone's mouth. The woman with the sunglasses said a word that made my mother laugh from inside the house: stakeholders. From the lagoon there came a sound like a hand slapping a cheek and then another, then a rhythm, like someone remembering a song.

We all turned our heads toward the place where the old rock had rested for most of my childhood. The light took a long time to agree to show us what had happened. When it did, there was a new shape where the water had been. Short, black, jagged, teeth set into the mouth of the shore. Someone said the word reef and someone else said the word proof and someone else said the word omen. My aunt lifted her chin. Devan wrote something down that I should have been writing but couldn't, because at that moment my mother stepped through the doorway into the yard, her sari untied from the chair at last, her hair falling from its pins like something that was never meant to be contained. She looked at me and she found me and she said my name with a voice that had not forgotten anything.

"Mira," she said, like a point closing a triangulation, like the kind of lure that gets you, always, to turn.

Later I would think, this is where our map chooses. It isn't made of lines, it is made of what we can call each other while the water tries to teach us its own names. I stood up to go to her, and the sea, as if it had been waiting for a single step, climbed the yard and took one of my mother's ledger pages in its hand and left us something in exchange. A smooth, blue-white bracelet of shell with a cheap clasp, the kind my brother had worn on his left ankle when he was eight and trying his first swagger. I did not know whether to recognize it or to think the sea was cruel in an entirely human way.

The wind carried the officers’ paper into the canna lilies. The lantern swung. The map on the board flapped and gave up one corner. And I thought of the child’s sentence in the ledger, and of the line he had drawn that did not end, and of how even the kindest lies are simply delay.

"We cannot leave," someone said.

"We cannot stay," someone else said.

"We must decide," said the lady with the folder, and the word must came out like a cough.

My mother held the bracelet to her ear like a shell and listened to what she had lost. I wrote the tide of that moment into my book in a shorthand that would make no sense to anyone later. We would build a map with circles if they let me. We would choose nothing alone. The clouds fissured. The new reef argued with the shore. A dog began to bark at the dark as if it had a job it could perform. And then the first drop came, big as a word, on the back of my hand.

People bring me their lost minutes wrapped in tissues, like teeth.

They slide them across the counter as if they might bleed through the paper. Some have written the dates on the outside in a careful hand: “March 12, the hour between the ultrasound and the call.” Others cannot say what day it was, only what it felt like: “The half-light when the snow wouldn’t stick,” “the dry clicks of the radiator,” “my father’s sleeve.” Either kind gives off the same little hush when I open the tissue, like a church door swinging closed. Inside: a flecking of light, a pine-resin smell, a smear like oil on water. Sometimes the minutes have weight and I feel them pull my wrist down; sometimes they’re all bright chaff and skitter off my palm with a sound like a breath taken in too fast.

People come to me with seconds they’d forgotten on train platforms, with hours siphoned off by waiting rooms. They bring me years they didn’t consent to lose: the years they worked two jobs and slept in their car; the years that went missing because a country decided to rearrange itself without asking. They bring the time they borrowed and couldn’t pay back, sheepish and hungry. I take them all. I have a ledger and a license, a rubber stamp and a hand steady enough to add up lives without trembling. The city says this is the work, and it is, but most nights it feels like prayer.

The shop is a narrow space on the block between the pawnshop and the laundromat, with an iron grate I roll up each morning like lifting an eyelid. The glass reads Exchange & Repair in gold paint, so old that the & has long since flaked into an infinitesimal galaxy of curls at the window’s edge. The bell over the door is a misfit: too sweet, more music box than hardware store, and when the air is damp it sticks and sings. I keep the counters polished with lemon oil because the woman who owned the place before me did—Mrs. Goto, who repaired watches so delicately I once watched her coax a hair out of a pocket watch’s throat as if it were a swimmer’s last breath—and because the smell hides the faint tang that time leaves behind, a coppery thing like pennies pressed against gum.

Clocks line the walls, none of them telling the truth. I let them be wrong. It keeps customers from negotiating. The only piece I trust is the brass scale on the counter, heavy as a baby, with a tiny nick in its pan. I calibrate it at the start of every day with a weight marked One Good Hour. The hour was poured by the city from summer’s metal, in a little ceremony that involved a man in a sash and a string quartet and a sonnet. This was before my time, but the official gave me the hour with a gloved hand like a holy relic when I got my license, and we all pretended to believe in poetry.

Rules are posted on the chalkboard by the door, handwritten because printing them makes people feel as if they were accused of something:

1. No claims on another person’s purchased time.
2. Lost time will be returned with proof of loss and associated sounds if available.
3. We do not take time from animals, plants, children under seven, or the dead.
4. Unclaimed minutes will be redistributed after nine years to the common pool for sleep, sickness, grief.
5. The house keeps a commission of one memory, chosen by the claimant.

The last rule makes people flinch. They imagine I’m a thief, and perhaps I am. They ask if I will take their worst, and I tell them no, those have to be carried. We take something small: the taste of a pear eaten standing up, the hum of the elevator cables in the old building where you used to live, the sound your neighbor made when she laughed against her scarf. You live without it. My ledger lists them all: from Miriam B.—one forgotten pigeon; from Hector R.—his first unbroken strand of spaghetti; from Tae-min K.—the white dog’s bark.

Outside, the sky was the color of wet paper. The gutters ran. The laundromat’s steam came in through my transom and hung in the air with the lemon oil and the faint metallic sweetness of people’s sadness. I unlocked the till, wiped the brass weight, unfastened the cover of the great book. It is a ridiculous thing, the ledger—too large, with a spine like a poorly set bone, paper that feels like old skin—and I think sometimes the city chose it because anyone would be cautious around it. Its pages hold the official record of all time that passes through my hands: by name, by date, by reason. There is a column for who took it and one for who brings it back, though often they are the same.

The first was a small woman with a coat that had been dark blue once. She carried a paper bag clamped to her chest the way you hold a loaf. We had known each other as children, in the way city children know one another, by nodding at the same streetlights and seeing the same pigeons. Now she always gave her name as if she were trying something on. “Janelle?” The bag held four hours, lumpy and warm like bread. She hadn’t wasted them; she’d rolled them into balls and kept them in the top of her closet during her husband’s chemo, taking them down when the day ran thin and there was nothing left of herself. Now he was in remission and she had regret like a burr on the tongue.

“For you?” I said, because I like to ask twice. Taking anything back changes how you understand it. Returning something can make you what you were not.

“For my grandson,” she said. “He just turned six. He wants to know why everything is always over.”

She placed the bag on the scale. The pan tilted and steadied. I opened the ledger and wrote: From Janelle D.—Four Hours, Household; For Devonte D.—Birthday, Waterpark. I stamped the page: RETURNED. The stamp made a sound that never stopped feeling like an answer. She watched me, and when I slid the bag back across she pressed her palm to mine through the paper, a small child’s game we used to play with tin-foil and window glass, and for a second I saw her face with two missing teeth. People think it’s the time that undoes them, and sometimes it is. More often it is the way the past refuses to stop behaving exactly like itself.

The bell did its sugar-song and the next was a boy, thin and electric, with a haircut that wanted to hurt somebody. He had a shoebox wrapped in brown paper and twine, which meant he was trying to be good. He pushed it to me and said, “I took afternoons. From them.” He swivelled and pointed out the window with his chin, to the laundromat across the street where a woman I assumed was his mother fed shirts into a mouth of light. I untied the string. Inside there was a warm smell and three rolling, marble-dark hours a little larger than the others, each one with a sound in it like rain on a different roof: shingle, tin, that corrugated plastic that kitchens and sheds wear everywhere children never stop being children. I looked at him.

“Yes,” he said quickly. “When she was sleeping on the folding table. I wanted her to have time for me. I wanted to see if that would help.”

“It did?” I said. This is a question I ask not because I cannot guess, but because it matters whether people can bear to hear themselves.

“A little,” he said, and looked at his knuckles.

“Afternoons taken without permission are still afternoons,” I said, and wrote carefully: From Malik H.—Three Hours, Trespass; Held Pending Parent. He stared at my pen the way children stare at anything that will not let them in no matter how good their reasons are. Then he unclenched and the boy who had stolen for his mother became just a boy again, with a scab on his knee. “I’ll hold them here until she comes. They’ll stay warm,” I said. “Do you want to keep a minute?”

He glanced up, and looked at the shoebox like he could see into it. “Just a little one,” he said. I pinched off a sliver with the edge of my hand. That’s what it felt like: pulling a splinter of sweetness out of the greater sweetness. When I dropped the minute into his palm, it ticked once, a mouse-sized sound. He put it in his mouth like sugar. He went out into the rain and practiced being brave, which is to say he didn’t look back.

Between customers I make my own coffee on the hot plate, pour it into the chipped mug that says This Will End Well. Someone left the mug in exchange for an appointment when the power was out for a week one spring and I’d lit the counter with votive candles, placing minutes into people’s hands by touch. On mornings like this I remember the weight of those nights, all of us scooping time in the dark like water.

The mail arrived. The government’s brown envelope had two barcodes and the faint smell of dust that all buildings downtown share; you get a whiff of courtrooms and cafeterias when you open them. Inside was a sheet of the city’s seal, which is a cormorant with something in its beak that used to be wheat and is now a cell phone tower, and beneath it a list of reassignments: time taken by the City for work stoppages, digital outages, miscounted polling hours, administration error, etc. The word “error” does a lot of work in our city. It lives like lichen in every crack. I stapled the sheet into the ledger with the tiny stapler the size of a beetle that used to belong to Mrs. Goto and tastes like chlorine if you lick it, which she told me and I tried in the year I started, just to see if everything she said had the ring of truth or if it was the way truth makes sound when it hits you from a height.

The rains deepened. The laundromat’s owner propped her door with a bucket and the heat rolled out, hackles up. The taxi dispatcher next door cracked his window and coughed like somebody should apologize. The street wore its thin coat of weather and kept walking.

A man came with a sealed note from a court that gave permission to return the three lost mornings he had put inside his wife, and in the space where his wife should have been there was a pocket of air that smelled like cloves. A woman came with an appointment and a dog, and I told her we don’t take time from animals, and she cried politely behind her collar. I gave her a matchbook with the name of a woman across town who will tell you exactly the dream you are about to have if you cannot stand to be surprised by it. The matchbook went into her mouth like a lozenge and I pretended not to see.

Between all of this the door opened and closed on the rain, and the chalkboard rules sighed when the damp touched them, and I did the work, which is the right way to talk about it, because it feels like something you hold with both hands. Doing the work keeps all the other doors closed that want to swing wide inside my head. I like the narrowness of the shop, the way my hand knows where the scale sits even when I’m not looking, the way the lemon oil smell sits just barely inside the smell of rain. When I am working I do not think of the jar wrapped in the yellow scarf, at the very back of the top shelf where the wood bows and splinters, the jar that is not in the ledger for anyone to claim. I do not think of the fact that I have taken the great-grandmother of those rules and put it up high and told it to keep quiet.

At ten past two, the bell stuck and sang. I looked up.

She was younger than me by—what?—fifteen years. That happens, these past years; people who look like they are coming into their faces, into their own gravity, and mine already in orbit. She was damp to the elbows, her hair the color that birch bark goes after rain, which is another way of saying it didn’t belong to one thing or another. Her umbrella—yellow, the ordinary city bright of caution—dripped quietly into the rubber tray by the door. A small dark mole sat brightly on her left cheek like a bird at a feeder. She had that look I recognize in people who have come to me alone with something they cannot believe is important enough to ask for and cannot bear not to ask for. It is a look that keeps a person at a distance and brings them to the counter in the same motion.

“Can I help you?” I said, because all language is ritual, and sometimes the second sentence of the day is the one that makes the first true.

She took a folded paper from the inside pocket of her jacket and shook rain from it like a hand. It was one of the city’s forms, tear-off edges still frilled and proud, the ink dampened into soft edges by the weather. She pushed it across, and when I turned it toward me I had to keep my hand from moving too fast.

CLAIMANT: the name said, in a handwriting not hers, and then the name in print beneath, and the name was my daughter’s name.

The room didn’t tilt. The clocks did not change their wrong minds. The lemon oil kept up its small work in the air and the woman’s umbrella continued to bead water very politely into the tray. None of the things books would have you believe happened, happened. What happened was that I put the tips of my fingers on the paper where it said Sora Kline, the way you touch a baby’s face through a glass window. The way you touch a word you haven’t said out loud in nine years. I could feel the rivets of the perforation biting the pads of my fingers. I could feel the woman across from me watching me feel nothing.

“I’m sorry,” I said. It came out clean and shaped, like a cup you can put something in. “Can you—what would you like to claim?”

She looked up then, and whatever had sent her here moved across her face like a weather front. “I was told,” she said, and her voice had the slight hoarseness of any voice used mostly to talk to one person, late at night, “that you’re holding minutes for me. For this name. That there are unclaimed minutes in the ledger and they belong to me.”

The paper fluttered when the door, doing what poems always say doors do, swung a little in a draft. The city seal on it looked suddenly like a joke, a bird with a reed in its mouth staring down at both of us as if we were supposed to be ordinary.

I have done this long enough to know when there is an answer as slick as a deck of cards and when there isn’t. “We can check the ledger,” I said, and my hands were steady because the body is obedient first and a person second, and I turned the stupid book toward me as if it were a teacher I had done my homework for.

In the logic of our work, time is entered twice: once when it is lost and once when it is found. Most of us go through life with two hands missing different things. I ran my finger down the pages for the last nine years’ worth of S: Sada, Salwa, Sam, Sana. Sides of the page turned up a little where people had cried into them. The paper rasped my finger. I licked it without thinking, a childhood habit that tastes like chlorine. Sian, Silas, Simone—then I hit it, the shape of the letters striking up off the page as if they were a sound I knew: Sora Kline, three lines, once in the year my daughter’s shoes moved under the bed like animals—do you see how I tell you things to keep myself from telling you them?—and twice the year after.

Time Taken: Seven Minutes, Kitchen; Time Taken: Six Minutes, Hospital Corridor; Time Taken: Twelve Minutes, Crosswalk Outside 9th & Tamarind. Reason: Administrative Reassignment; Reason: Medical Overflow; Reason: Traffic Management.

Under “To be returned” the lines were blank. Beside them, in small black letters written by the city’s person with the tidy hand, stamped almost into the paper, was License Holder: Kline, Mara (authorized). My signature was there, careful and unhurried in a way I do not always recognize as my own. I had signed for the taking. I had told the city yes, take these.

“I’ve just moved back,” the woman said, as if we had been speaking all along. “I didn’t even know this existed, this office. My mother said there’s a place you go to ask for what you lost. She said, Go downtown. She said, Say the name on your birth certificate. She said, Tell the lady you have come late. I am late. I know. I am trying to catch up.”

She was not my daughter. The thought went through me cleanly like a shotgun pellet, shattering nothing but itself. My mind knows the difference between the thing and the name of the thing even when my breath does not. The piece of paper lay quiet under my hand, bright and completely convinced of its own reality.

“What is it you think I have?” I asked, and the steadiness of my voice made me feel cruel to me in the way that work often does when you do it well while your heart tries to do something else.

“My minutes,” she said, and finally an impatience rose in her because she was a person and not a form. “The ones someone took. The ones I was told would be here because a woman named Kline signed for them and this is the office.” She put her finger to the ledger in the place where her name was not, the blank where the returning signature would be, and tapped it to make the blank confess.

Behind her a taxi honked once, a punctuation mark that meant nothing and would be remembered by no one. The rain changed its mind and became something like a sieve.

There are two versions of the rules, every place like mine has them: the one on the chalkboard and the one in your bones. The written ones say unclaimed minutes revert to the common pool after nine years because time does not like vanity; it likes to be spent. The unwritten ones say that if something you love has gone into the jar at the back of the top shelf, you do not open it, because love rots in jars. You keep it there and the love continues to be love by being potential. You do not try to lay it out on the counter like slices of wet apple. You do not put your mouth around it and swallow. You do not trade it for anything. You do not.

I stood with my hands on a book that knew more than the woman in front of me and more than any city has a right to know, and I thought about the crosswalk at 9th & Tamarind. There was always a man there selling oranges that smelled like new pennies. I thought about the hospital corridor, the scuffed floors and the machine that sounded like a small bird trying to escape a locked room. I thought about a kitchen, the old one, the one with the cracked tile in front of the sink where a person’s weight always surprises you because you do not think you are as heavy as you are. I thought about seven minutes, six, twelve. Twenty-five minutes. A small pocket of air. A handful. A life.

“You’re certain,” I said, because I wanted any out—hers, mine, the city’s.

She laughed. It was not the laugh I have been carrying around in my chest for nine years like a warm stone. It was a new laugh, with its own ruin and its own luck in it. “No,” she said. “I don’t think I have been certain of anything in some time.” She looked at the umbrella in the tray as if it might be a way to talk about all of it. “But some time is exactly what I am here about, isn’t it?”

Sometimes when people come and we find their name, they cry in a way that is precise and directed, like returning a library book you loved to the shelf you got it from and walking away. Sometimes they go hot all over and say I don’t want it any more and leave with their hands in their pockets because a person cannot stand to hold the thing they thought they wanted. Sometimes they want to fight because fighting is easier than feeling and also more acceptable in a world where the acceptable gets you applause and the true gets you strange looks on the bus. This woman stopped and waited. Some people understand the dignity of asking and the work it takes to wait for the answer like it might be news and not confirmation. That kind of waiting fills the shop up with a listening you could sleep inside.

I reached to the shelf with the ledger and then past it, to the higher shelf where the wood is darker because the landlord painted the walls once and painted around the furniture. I stood on the little stool that says Milk on the side because it used to be a crate. The jar was where it had always been; it had folded itself into the place back there as if the shelf had been built for it. The yellow scarf was the color of a sun you see from the subway, a softness dyed onto a cloth that somebody took time to get right. I had wrapped the jar once and then again, in an attempt to teach my fear to make itself useful and put its hands to work. The knot had a way of always being exactly as complicated as whatever you think you are ready for.

I could feel the woman below watching me. There is nothing quite like the weight of someone else’s watching when you stand on tiptoe and ask yourself whether you are going to be this person or some other. I took the jar down.

“To be clear,” I said, back at the counter, not opening it yet, the glass cool a little in the way a snake is cool and clean. “These minutes were taken by the city. Whatever is inside—” I touched the glass—“will not lift any day that has already happened out of where it sits. You know that, yes?”

“I came here and not to the church or the bridge,” she said. “I know where I am. I’m not asking you to—” She lifted her hands and placed them on the counter, palms down. Her fingers were ink-stained the way people’s fingers are when they write someone else’s letters for money, or copy parts of their lives by hand to make them feel they belong to them. “I am asking for what you owe me.”

It sat between us. The jar held nothing visible, if you were the sort of person who only believes you can see what can be seen. If you were not, it held a current of air that curled around your wrist hairs and made them stand. It held the sound of my daughter’s feet on the old cracked tile at the sink. It held a bird’s frantic machine. It held the breath of a crosswalk, the oranges, the name. It held the small thing I kept back, because there had to be something I kept back or else I could not keep doing this work, which is only a way of saying that every job requires an altar of some sort and the sacrifice you put on it in order to keep from lighting the whole building.

I unscrewed the lid. The gasket stuttered, then let go.

The air that came out smelled like wet wool and the faint vinegar of hospital food and the last half-inch of tea in a mug you forgot to drink. Under that, the clean ozone of rain hitting a street just dirty enough to deserve it. The shop filled with it. The clocks all continued to lie. Nothing in the world’s clocks changed. But the third thing, the thing that is not clocks and not weather, adjusted itself. I thought: it has been nine years since I heard this, and the nine years went like a wave on muscle and left everything it touched brighter or more tender or simply different. It is possible, I thought, that grief itself is a kind of minute we keep because we are not allowed to spend all our time at once.

The woman did not lean in. I respect her forever for that. She closed her eyes and held her palms open and did not move, the way you do with a steely horse. I tipped the jar toward her. The minutes that were hers—but whose others were they as well?—lifted and went to her as if they were remembering. They touched her wrists first—everyone thinks it will be the throat, because that is where the words live, or the heart, because the poets taught us nothing if not that—but minutes always go for the places the blood announces in a whisper. She listened. I watched her listen. At the laundromat across the street a dryer door opened and clanged, a noise like a bell that thinks it is a boat. The rain became a sound I could not get my hands around.

When the jar was empty of those particular minutes, the bottom glimmered like any jar. I set it down. It made a sound like a jar set down. Not poetic. Just the sound.

She opened her eyes. There are looks a person will give you that you should put somewhere safe in case the world gets a little hungry later and tries to eat them. I put that look somewhere I cannot name because if I did it would come out like telling you my pin code. “Thank you,” she said, and I could see she had arranged her thanks in a way that made room for the places in her that would feel something about what had just happened later.

“What memory do you want us to keep?” I said, and I regretted it even as I said it. But the ledger was open between us and the city keeps the rules with more dedication than it keeps its promises.

She did not hesitate. She lifted her hand and touched the little mole on her cheek with the pads of two fingers like she was seeing whether it was real. “The taste,” she said, and smiled, not on purpose, “of that terrible pear I ate yesterday while I was walking. In the rain. It was like licking knives.”

“You’ll never know a pear is terrible again until you’ve finished it,” I said, because the rules also require we use something like gentleness to hand people the thing they are about to lose, and because the thing I wanted to say—Sora, Sora, how many times—was not mine to say to her. I wrote it down: From Sora Kline—One Memory, Fruit; For the Common Bowl.

She made to take the jar with her, and I put my fingers on it. “I have to—” I said, and flicked my eyes to the ledger. The blank lines beside her printed name where my name had signed for the taking waited to be filled. “I have to record the return. Will you—” I made a little half-circle with my hand and she closed her hand on air as if I had given her something and put it in her pocket the way people put their hands on talismans they are not ready to call by their names.

When she left, the bell did not sing. It was damp enough that the spring had given up and held the door open with an indifference that felt briefly like relief. She went out into the gray with no umbrella, having forgotten it, and I watched the yellow shape fold itself politely and wait on the tray. The jar gleamed on the counter. The ledger lay open to my name in black and to hers in a hand someone else had taught themselves to shape.

I signed. Under “To be returned” I wrote the date, and the city’s stamp came down and pressed my hand bone to bone. The sound of it took its place in the shop’s air as if it had been there always.

When I put the jar back on the shelf, I did not wrap it. I stood looking at the yellow scarf. It has always been the color of a sun seen through glass. It is a manufactured color. It is not the color the sky gets of its own accord. I folded the scarf, once and then again, the way you fold a shirt you hope someone will someday borrow, and I put it in the drawer where I keep the stapler that tastes like chlorine and the rubber stamp that says RETURNED in a font I dislike.

Someone was at the door. They tapped the glass with the side of their finger the way annoyed people do. I looked up, thinking of clocks and rain and Janelle’s grandson’s wet hair. The man by the door had a bookshop vest and wet shoulders. He patted his pocket for his pack of cigarettes as if he needed permission from the rain.

“Hey,” he called through the glass. “You open?”

I nodded, because I am, because the work is a rope you pull hand over hand and because the woman had left her name and her umbrella with me like the kind of omen you only call such when it’s already come true. When I lifted the bell from its stuck place with my knuckle, it sang sweetly twice, as if it wanted to make up for an earlier silence.

“Tell me,” he said, coming in, “do you take minutes spent in line at the post office or is that just life?”

It is life, I wanted to say, in the way everything is life until it isn’t. But I smiled, and pointed to the chalkboard that says we do not accept time from the dead, from children under seven, from animals or plants, and from the federal government. He laughed, because laughter is sometimes wool and sometimes knives. I weighed his patience and stamped his page and took a memory he will not miss until he reaches for it and finds the cupboard bare.

All afternoon the rain stitched the street to itself. Every time the door opened, a thin seam of cold worked across the floor and vanished. In the advantage of work I allowed myself a piece of knowledge salt-small on my tongue: the name in the ledger under mine was written now in two places. Once for taking, once for returning. Names are what a city has instead of family. I sat there and watched the light change, and the hours people brought me moved across the counter the way my daughter’s hand used to move across a table when she wanted to show me not what she had but what I had missed by looking somewhere else. The umbrella stood in its tray like a word I could not use yet.

When I finally turned the sign to closed, the street had the thin, metallic gleam it only has after a rain has spent itself without ever committing to the idea of cleansing. I stood on the stool and put the jar back up and put nothing with it. Down from the shelf, the yellow scarf was an ordinary length of woven time, and I touched it, and it did not tell me anything.

That night, after the wind began and stopped and began again and the taxi dispatcher coughed a long, high cough like someone calling to someone he was not sure would answer, I dreamed of a crosswalk in the dark, of oranges in a bag tearing their way out, of a bird in a locked room whose beak struck glass with a sound like a metal weight set gently on a scale. When I woke I had lost the taste of pears entirely. I lay there in the not-day, my hand on my ribs. It is possible this is what slowly winning looks like when you cannot tell who is keeping score.

I tell you all this to say that the first chapter of what happened in this city with this shop and this woman began, as things always do, with a door you have opened so often you no longer see it as a decision. With rain. With lemon oil. With a bell that meant to sing and sometimes did not. With a name folded and unfolded until it was just paper. With a jar lifted down. With a small keeping and a larger letting go. With me, in the middle, practicing the narrow art of returning.

Chapter One

They told us the mill would stop breathing at noon.

By ten the heat had settled into the corrugated roofs, and the air inside Shambhu Spinning #3 tasted like a spoon handled by too many mouths: metal, salt, a little grease. I stood in the caged stairwell and ran a cable through my hands to keep it from knotting. The cable had a memory for wrists; it coiled back on itself the way old women plait their hair even after the hair is gone.

"You're the one from the Registry?" the foreman asked, watching me with the narrowed expression of a man who'd been told to cooperate against his better instincts. His name tag said RAJESH in chipped enamel, and someone had once soldered two letters back on with a trembling hand.

"The Registry of Last Sounds," I corrected, because you never knew which words people heard and which they didn't. "I called Tuesday. You said the whistle is on the roof?"

"It was," Rajesh said. "Everything here was. Give me that."

He took the cable from me and looped it around his forearm with a practiced flick. Above us the metal staircase kept on climbing, a spine through a body that was no longer sure of its hands and feet. Floors slid past with their particular weathers: ground level with its dark tide of oil and machine sweat, the first with its thin sunlight slitting through broken windows, the second with its thread fluff, the third with its surprised coolness, unexpectedly sweet. Soot and cotton dust hung in the beams like snow in a city that had forgotten winter.

"Was your grandmother here?" Rajesh asked, as if this was a question you could ask in a place like this. "You look familiar. There were women like you, a whole line of them, rope-boned and quiet until the siren. The siren made them loud."

"My grandmother worked in jute," I said. "By the river. She did not think of herself as quiet."

He grunted as if noise were a kind of weakness. We went up another turn, and a strip of sky slid into view. It looked like a page torn from a book that had been left too long under a lamp: bleached at the edges, a little warped. The roof doors were chained, of course, but the chain had learned from all the others that had girlied to the foreman over the years; it yielded to his bolt cutter with a resigned pop. We stepped out and the brightness scalded my eyes.

Once, when I was seven, my father took apart an old radio on our kitchen table to show me the stations inside. He had laid out the guts carefully: tiny screws in a bottle cap, a wafer of circuit board like a city seen from very far away, and the dial face propped in a saucer so I couldn't smudge it with my fingers. "You think stations live in the air, Mira?" he had said, not teasing. "They live in here. The air just remembers the way to them." He held the radio's coil up to the light as if it had a soul. He had already begun to lose his hearing then, in the way people first lose keys before they admit they are forgetful; he still smiled when my mother called his name, but I could see him aiming his attention like a flashlight in a dark room, trying to catch everything at once. He taught me how to hear with more than my ears. That was before the blast at the docks took what was left.

Up on the mill roof the siren sat like a small torpedo braced on its cradle, a dull green shape with a grill shaped like a forgetful mouth. The paint was blistered. A black kite reeled in the bright heat, writing and rewriting its signature on the sky. Beyond the mill roofs and telephone lines and marigold flags drooping from a temple dome, the river lay like a blade. Someone on the far bank had put up a billboard of a family wearing sunglasses on their veranda, staring into a future made of patios and white crockery. If we had been able to hear it, I thought, the billboard would have sounded like a plastic bag.

"Power's on till noon," Rajesh said, kneeling to check the connection box. He had that careful economy of movement that comes from spending too much time around hungry machines. "The developers said twelve. I told them if they wanted the whistle to say goodbye, they could call you people. The developers said, 'The whistle is your heritage! You should be grateful we let you play it one last time.' I told them if they used that word in front of the women downstairs, they'd learn exactly what heritage can do."

"Thank you," I said. "We can't do our work if people don't tell us in time. So often, by the time someone calls, the water has already left, or the birds have flown. Or they didn't expect the last time to be the last."

He glanced at the black case at my feet—my recorder, my boom mic wrapped in its soft cover like a sleeping grey cat, headphones coiled neatly, silica gel polite as dry rain. Tools are another kind of bone. I took them out and laid them on the roof in an order that made sense in my hands: low frown of foam windscreen here, a shallow pile of fresh batteries there, the recorder itself resting where the cable could find it in one motion. I put the headphones on and the world narrowed the way it does when you form a cave with your palms. The noises sharpened: men coughing somewhere in the mill; a scooter dribbling past; footsteps climbing the stairs.

"We have two minutes for levels," I said. "When it's time, can you give me a count? Or is it just on?"

"It's never just on," Rajesh said, and something inside him softened. "Even dying things need coaxing."

Down in the city, morning was going about its business without us. I could feel it in the way the air moved—the long breath between bakery ovens opening and school bells; a bucket carried down a narrow corridor hitting the doorframe with a damp knock; chai debating its own intelligence in a battered kettle. The Registry trained us to notice, but I had always counted by listening. After my father lost his hearing, it's what he left me. You count a room by its echo. You know when someone has lied because your skin finds the space where their words have not landed. You know your own name in a crowd by the way it refuses to belong to anyone else. When we go into a place like this, I tell the new field recordists, the first thing you do is shut up. The second thing you do is listen to what the silence comes made of.

I walked around the siren to find its voice. Metal sounds complicate; wind complicates; and the city would do its best to complicate everything. On one side, the edge of the roof was close enough to catch the river’s mutter. On the other, a skinny electric pole tapped out its message in the sun. I set the mic low, under the siren's mouth, at a diagonal to cut the wind. I clipped a secondary to the back for the low-end rumble that comes free with any old machine suffering nostalgia. I taped the cables where the corrugations could not scrape them raw. I checked the recorder’s red lights and my lungs.

In my right ear, the city shifted from a smear to a nameable: trains and their small apologies, a dog debating whether to commit a crime, the unmistakable sound of someone dragging a chair across a floor to stand on it. In my left ear, my own blood. The first time I put on these headphones, in the Registry training room with its hissing air-con and soft mold smell, I heard that river inside me and wanted to fling the headphones off and run. It turns out you carry so much noise inside. The trick is to know which of it is yours.

"Your people always come late," Rajesh said. "The last time I heard your name, they were trying to record the old monastery bell, and it cracked the day before."

"I was on that team," I said. "The bell didn't crack because of us. It cracked because the rain came hot that year and the bell wasn't watching. We kept the crack. We always keep the crack."

The Registry of Last Sounds began as something like a joke, the way useful things sometimes begin. A sound artist named Elena made a small exhibition of the clicks you hear in fluorescent tubes before they go out, then the cough of a dying refrigerator, then the sigh an escalator makes when the mall closes on Sundays. People came and cried. They cried over the exact whir of a sewing machine's pedal that had lived under their grandmother's foot, they cried over the particular thwack of a cricket ball on an abandoned colony's cement pitch. Someone in the Ministry saw numbers; someone else saw a way to turn grief into a ribbon-cutting; and now there were six of us, two in the city and four itinerant, carrying equipment and blank forms into the last seconds of things. We did good work, mostly. We had a code: we did not record people without consent; we did not romanticize what had been cruel; we did not set up a funeral where there might still be a possibility of fight. You could break those rules and still get a clean sound file. I didn't like the noise that made in me.

"We're ready," I told Rajesh. "Will you—"

He had already put his hand on the lever. It was a brass lever, worn down where a hundred thousand fingers had grabbed it morning and noon, thin as a prayer. Below us someone banged on the doors with something heavy—an idle demonstration, a way of testing whether the doors remembered their responsibility. "You—what's your name?" he asked, abruptly.

"Mira."

"Mira. You'll send us the recording? We can’t pay you."

"You don't have to. It will be public. We put it up on the site with context. Anyone can listen. We will give you a copy yourself."

"You think we have computers?"

"I can put it on a little card that works in your phone."

He did not appear to understand the words. He placed the lever all the same in his palm, as if he were giving his hand something to remember.

"For your grandmother who didn't think of herself as quiet," he said, and he pulled.

The siren coughed.

Not the cough of the unreliable—the cough of someone who has lived with their mouth open for too long. It sputtered once, twice. The first breath scratched my headphones like a pencil starting a test. The second turned into a sound so old I found myself bracing my feet as if a big wave were coming. It wasn't the loudness. Loudness is a civility, a courtesy. Loudness tells you what's happening. This was a sound for which loudness had not been invented. It came up through the bolted frame and pushed the sky out of its way. I felt it in my teeth. I felt it in the cartilage of my nose. Birds rose from all the roofs with startled harmonies. Windows shook while pretending not to. Somewhere down in the weave of streets and courtyards and alleys someone dropped a pan and someone else said "Hai, hai!" and started laughing and cried while laughing.

I kept one eye on the levels, letting the needle climb just to the place before harm, holding my breath the way you do at the peak of a ladder. I tilted the mic half a whisper. The siren held on. It had the muscle memory of call and meal break; it had the habit of itself, which is another way of saying a soul. People talk about sound as if it passes through you and is gone, but if you've been inside sound you know it leaves a little of itself behind, a sheathing, a rind. The whistle's rind had lined this city's lungs for fifty years. You do not take that out without a scar.

Half a minute passed. The whistle hit that seam where iron remembers ore. Something else slid under it—something lower. Not the river. The river in this city has a three-note song, learned after the dam: ache, ache, stop. This was older and more patient and more unreasonable. It flickered at the edge of the range like a name you think you know and then, when you turn, it isn't there. I pinched down my headphones over my ears and opened my mouth to bear it better, the way divers do, and the foreman saw the look on my face and for a second we were both children again and the siren was God.

Then the siren failed.

It wasn't dramatic. No sparking, no smoke. Just a gentling and a slowing and the doppler of all the pigeons arriving back where they had meant to be. A man on the next roof took off his cap and swatted his face with it, suddenly embarrassed to be sweating. The air near us felt taller.

Rajesh let the lever drop. He wiped his face with his sleeve. He looked down through the grating into the bright dark where women had stood until their bones remembered the beat of picking, where men had learned to cough with their mouths closed. More banging came from the doors, but now it was the developers, impatient for public dying. I took the headphones off and the world widened, feral.

"That's it?" Rajesh said, as if there might be some remainder we were being mean about not sharing.

"That's it," I said softly. My voice felt foolish against the air. I unplugged the mics and fitted them into their nests. The battery light was still green. The recorder was warm as a small animal. Habit made me check the file twice, limbs, file name, timestamp, all the little bureaucracies of memory that keep chaos and comfort from calling each other in the night.

"You can go down and let them in," Rajesh called to a supervisor appearing in the stairwell below, helmet on, clipboard raised like a shield. He turned back to me. "What happens now?"

"You cut it free?" I asked. "You leave it up there to be smashed? You put it in the foyer of the new luxury complex so young people can plan their hot yoga under it?"

"You make good jokes for someone who looks like somebody's daughter," he said. "They will cut it down. They will put it on a truck. If they have a soul they will take it to a museum. If they do not, they will sell it for scrap and bring their wives trinkets bought with that money. I will go downstairs and explain to the women that there will be no more whistle, which means there will be no more clock, which means we will have to learn to count the day with the sun like our fathers, except the sun has learned different hours. We will listen for the muezzin and the temple bell and the price of vegetables and the time it takes to boil rice. We will tell the children that when the whistle blew, we knew who we were."

"We recorded it," I said. "Our children can listen."

He looked at my case as if it were a very small coffin. He looked at my face as if the coffin were mine. "You will do what you have to do," he said, and he went down.

They bill us at the Registry as technicians, archivists, a gentle civil word for what we do. My card says: Field Recordist, Last Instances. I carry a second card, in case someone doesn't know us: It says, simply, Listener.

There is always paperwork after, in the same way there is always water after rain and a bill after a feast. I sat on the roof a moment and filled out the fields on my screen with my thumb: location, coordinates, date, community contacts, notes about wind and habitat and any interference that didn't exist on the spectrum. I typed the names of the women I'd seen on the stairs, because sometimes a name is all you can give somebody and it is a better gift than almost anything else you have. I marked the file for urgent processing because the developers would be adding their own story and I wanted ours to be louder in the rooms that matter. I wrote, in the box for observations, "Underfrequency present, inharmonic, unknown source. Might investigate older signal?" I could hardly explain it to myself. The Registry had taught us to be alert for "crosstalk," the way signals bleed into one another—a radio station climbing into an amplifier and stamping its feet, a cell phone negotiating with a pacemaker. This was not that. It was the audio equivalent of seeing somebody you loved at your bus stop and realizing, slowly, that it was not them. I closed the form and let the city wash over me.

By the time I reached the ground floor the developers had come. They had that look: men in clean jeans with measuring tapes clipped to their belts like holsters, women who held their water bottles like microphones. They had bailed out of SUVs and were attempting self-effacing jokes about their cars while finding their angles for photographs in which they would be small and the mill would be wide. I did my best, slid along the perimeter, let Rajesh catch my eye once and look away. In the doorway a girl in a pink school tunic was pressing both palms to the rusty jamb as if she could memorize its texture into her hands. You will lose so much and not even know it, I thought, and smiled at her because that was not a thing to tell a child. She did not smile back. She looked at my headphones and then at my face the way children do who haven't been taught yet that there are some looks too honest to be allowed in public. I reached into my case and took out the small card reader and handed it to her mother's hand instead, because gifts given to children by strangers become complicated parents of stories.

The street outside moved sideways while pretending to go straight. A man selling guy ropes wove through with a coil on his shoulder, crying, "Hold! Hold!", his vowel drawn long, and nobody listened. A truck scraped by a cart, and the cart owner examined the scrape as if he were looking at a cut on his own body. The mill's guards stood fitfully, trying to swell themselves against the tide, and the tide washed around them and left behind snack wrappers and small cartoons of spit.

At the tea stall I ordered a glass of lemon tea and another of water and stood to the side like hugging a pole. The owner nodded at me the way somebody nods at a regular who has been away too long. When the lemon tea sang its high clean note against my teeth, the whistle uncurled behind it like something that had slept too long under the tongue. The tea man watched my face. "You were up there," he said, as if I had climbed onto the moon to tie a ship.

"We were up there," I said, because I have learned to include people who can hear me.

"You will put it on the internet," he said. "My son will play it to me and I will say, This is how the day sounded when your mother first came to this city. He will roll his eyes. He will say the day always sounds like this: click, clack, ding. He will spell it for me: C-l-i-c-k. Then he will go and stand where nobody can see him and he will cry."

"If he cries, you must pretend you do not know," I said. "It's the only honor left to the young."

"Your father, he worked in—" the tea man gestured, his hand a blurry forenoon of burn scars. "Mechanic? I remember him."

"Radio," I said. The word came out wrapped in cotton. "He taught the radios to speak. Now he sits and the radios talk only to each other and not to him."

"Give him this," the tea man said, pushing the second glass into my hand even though I had already paid. It was melty sweet, goat milk thick, boiled to an agreement. "Tell him Kishan says, we still hear him when he warms his hands near our fire."

My father's hands had learned the language of warmth and the language of cold; the exploding dock had taught them the language of loss. I walked east through little rotten nets of shade, the recorder in my bag a weight like a sleeping child, and took the long way home past the river because it was the day for pasts. At the bridge, the wind carried fertilizer and fish and something bitter from the new plant upriver. The water lay sunstruck and sullen. Children flung themselves off the pilings in their underwear and came up with hair like sea creatures. A woman in a sari tied her skirt between her legs and waded in, quick as a fish, to grab a floating coconut. She looked up once and met my eyes and for a second we were in the same job, salvaging what the city had set free.

In my apartment the walls held onto the day the way cloth holds onto steam. I put the recorder on the table in the place where, if I died, a neighbor asked to describe me would say, "She kept that thing there like a shrine." The cat from the next building, who had adopted me because my windowsill was at a good height and the person living with me was often out, leapt up and sniffed it with suspicion. I set a bowl of water for him and he refused it with dignity. I washed my hands and the lemon tea left me. I stood by the table and listened through my headphones again.

It is one thing to hear in the field. The world commits crimes in the field; everything is urgent and everything is unrepeatable, and your gut makes executive decisions you do not understand until the line of the waveform appears on your screen. At the table, with the refrigerators humming their agreements and the neighbor's television teaching you a laugh track in a language you do not speak, your ear becomes a different animal. You hear the places where a motorbike's chain reads its own prayer aloud. You hear where your hand trembled and you can guess what you were thinking then, like a pen pal reading the fat of your letter and not only the ink. You hear the places where the air wore sandals, and where it went barefoot.

I queued the file, named: SHAMBHU_3_SIREN_1206HRS_LAST. I took a breath of the kind my father's doctor would approve. I pressed play.

You never get used to it. The whistle came up like a mountain does when you are still far away: blue at first, not yet a place, then its sides resolving, then its ash and its burn and its rock. The first cough of it scratched the small hairs around my ears. The second breath found my chest. I let my teeth chatter a little and the space behind my eyes loosened. The cheap glass on my table sang. The siren went through me. Then under it, the other thing. I stopped the file, returned the scrubbing line to a second before the seam, and played it again. I have learned to place my right index finger on the table in front of the speakers when I listen for sub-sounds; the wood conducts what your fingers know before your head does. The unknown tone slid like a fish under the siren's hull and then laid itself along its bottom. The siren didn't notice. The city didn't notice. It had decided to be here anyway.

I isolated the low band and magnified. Waveform pulled like pulled silk. It was not the 50 Hz hum of old circuits or the 60 of foreign machines. It wasn't a train at distance or a plane pulling at its own doubt. It had a shape like a breath held and then not given up. It had familiar edges to an unfamiliar body. And threaded through, thin, occasional, no bigger than the hair of a violin bow, a little high pattern like—no.

I took the headphones off. I put them on again. I used the scrub to run only the high frequencies, so the whistle fell away. I had heard it from the kitchen in my grandparents' house, when I lay under the table pretending the tablecloth was a field, and my grandmother smoked her bidi and flicked the ash into an old seashell. I had heard it from the riverbank, when my mother hung the clothes on the line and the wind refused to help her. I had heard it when I sat too long with my father after the blast, and we listened to his silence together. It had never occurred to me that it belonged in any file, that it could be coaxed out of air into this little box. I played it and there it was again, the high pattern in the bone-white space: a child's hum with a mountain in it, a three-note fall like the first three words of a lullaby I had not heard since I was nine.

Everything after that became slow.

The wall clock imitated an old man making up a joke. The cat leapt to the windowsill, spotted something in the invisible world and hissed. A balloon popped across the courtyard and somebody swore across three floors of old fights. I walked into the kitchen and put my palms flat on the warm wood of the counter and put my head down on them in that hollow and listened to the way breath gets stale when you hold it. It wasn't a lullaby. If it had been a lullaby I could have convinced myself I was a fool with too many mothers. It was a signal we used at the Registry in the field, our old signal when we didn't yet have our hands full of phones. Three notes called and three notes answered: I am here. Are you? I am.

We had stopped using it years ago when one of the undersecretaries heard it on a file and got upset about the "unprofessionalism." The only people who would have known it now were those of us who had been there at the start, those who had stood with Elena in rooms and on hillsides and in small vessels of wind and agreed that if you ever find yourself alone in a sound you do not understand, you ask your herd where they are. You call and answer. And here it was, threaded under the siren of a mill that had decided to be old politely, and I could not remember calling, and I could not remember answering. And it was my voice inside it. A child's voice, thin as aspiration.

The recorder sat on the table and did not explain itself. I reached for it, then pulled my hand back, not out of superstition—I don't keep that kind of superstition in the house—but because I am careful about touching things that might redraw me. I thought of Elena, who had taught me to hear and also to keep what I had heard from the people who would make it small. Elena had left us three years ago when a grant took her inland, somewhere dry and fierce. We texted on holidays and when a sound made me giddy I sent it to her and she sent back a wordless emoji that meant, to me, long hands holding my face. I could call her. I could say: Listen to this recording. I could say: In the low band the river would not know itself. I could say: Did you ever hide your child's voice in a file and then forget you had done it?

Instead I opened a new form. Under Project I did not choose "Shambhu Mill: Decommission." I chose "Uncategorized Single Instance." In Notes I wrote: Underfrequency queries—possible crosstalk from earlier fieldwork? Please check for similar in: GLACIER_KHAM_09; LAKE_BARUA_17; also check love-song at 3k-5k for hum. Caution: this may be my own error.

After I hit send the little progress bar crawled across the screen like a thoughtful snail. There would be meetings now. Someone in the Ministry would decide this made a good summary line. They would say: In a city where nothing is allowed to end, the Registry captures the last moments before change. They would not say: Sometimes the last thing isn't the last, sometimes it is the first time you hear yourself unleave a place.

I washed the cup from the tea I had drunk and put it on its base to dry. The cat knocked a domino of air off the sill, pressed his forehead into my shin and forgave me for being a person. From the street below, a boy on a bicycle rang his bell three times, thinking of nothing. The sound came up and sat in my mouth for a second and then went away as if it had somewhere important to be.

When the phone rang, it was Rajesh.

"You people take everything, don't you?" he said without preamble. His voice was stripped. "We stood and watched them take the whistle down. It was a good whistle. It didn't want to go. There is a room where they put things before they take them away so they don't have to look at them while they eat their lunch. We went in there. There was a box on the floor. The box was making a noise. I asked the supervisor, Did you hear that? He said he did not hear anything. I asked the boy with him, the new boy, if he heard it. He said his grandmother used to sing like that when she was frightened. I told him to go and drink water. The box was yours. If you want it, you will have to come and take it."

"My recorder?"

"No, some other people's," he said, impatient with my stinginess. "The developers like to record things, too. They recorded the women laughing when it failed, saying it was the sound of resilience. They recorded your voice on the phone. They recorded me telling them to leave. They put everything in a box and closed the lid. I didn't touch it. We don't like to take what's not ours."

I thought of the underfrequency and the child's hum and the rule about unromanticizing cruelty. I sat down because my body thought I might lie down if it had the chance. "I'll come," I said. "Don't let them—don't let them turn it on again until I get there."

"You think I can stop them?" he said, laugh and remnant of whistle in the low syllable. "You people think you can stop anything. Come, then. Bring your cards. Bring those little jars you keep the crickets in. Bring your ears. The box wants a witness."

"I'll be there in twenty minutes," I said, already putting on my sandals, already reaching for the case, already reaching for the habit of myself that had driven me through streets and rooms and arguments for seven years. The cat watched me and closed his eyes as if to keep me safe.

The city picked up its unmatched pair of shoes and resumed its walk. The river threw its shoulder into the afternoon like a wayward son into a doorway. Somewhere, a woman sang for no one's benefit, and the song turned corners to find the ears it needed.
