Somewhere, old cotton lifted from the floor on the boots of the young and attached itself to their laces and went to see the new city with them. On the stairs, the light was polite, as it always is to those who hurry.

In my bag the recorder, warm now as a pulse, held the whistle's last breath and the little trick of our old signal humming under it like a confession, and as I ran I heard, once, from the deep places where sound never settles, three notes that might have meant I am here. Are you? and I answered, aloud and stupidly, to the ceiling, to the railing, to my own feet: I am.

On the morning the sea returned my handwriting, the tide was wrong.

At Saint Bridget’s the tide is as much a calendar as the one nailed to the fishmonger’s door. It slacks and floods with a punctuality that can be read by the line of rot on the shingle and the green that rings the pilings. Even the widows can tell you when to set the pot for cockles without checking the almanac. But that morning the sea stood in its own throat, hesitating as if it had forgotten a word.

“It’s late,” Ren said, hopping from rock to rock to keep out of the black weed. He was small and summer-bruised, with a habit of collecting disastrous things. Last week it had been a gull’s skull with the beak still attached, the week before a set of trestles from somebody’s drowned garden.

“It’s not late,” I said. “It’s thinking.” I stepped into the sash of wet sand and felt the pull under my boots, the way it tries to take you by the ankles if you don’t make your steps decisive. The clouds mirrored the flats, a pewter over a pewter, gulls writing their rude letters across both.

He was old enough to hear the difference between words meant to soothe and words that meant something, and young enough to ask anyway. “Can it do that?”

“It can do anything,” I said, and that was not kind, because it is the kind of sentence that gets into a boy’s bones and changes the way he stands by doors.

My name is Ellis Morrow and my work is keeping the ledger of what the sea gives back. Since my mother began to leave herself behind, it has been me at the tide line with a hook and a basket and a pencil tucked behind my ear, looking for all the things I did not know I was missing. There are villages down the coast that consider any salvage fair game; their lane walls are mortar pocked with blue tile and glass smoothed by the tide, their children toe rings of copper fished from foreign wrecks. But here at Saint Bridget’s we keep a simpler covenant: Everything found belongs to the water until it’s been named.

It began fifty-two years ago, when the bell came up in an eel skin. The church had burned in a winter gale and the bell was lost with the tower and four pews and Barbara Fenway’s girl. In spring a fisherman walking the flats to yank up his knives before the sand took them found the bell lying on its side like a drowned ear. It clanged when he prodded it with his heel. When he went to fetch help, he found his name written in sea chalk on the smooth of it; he was poor and thanked God for a sign. The vicar thanked him, took the bell, and started a larder for sea returns. There have been lanes full of such larders since — baskets of keys, shivved spoons, medals, a clutch of postcards bound in hair ribbon yet unmailed, five teeth not all of them human, hundreds of shoes because something about the way shoes fit water is irresistible.

We made a book. We called it the Book of Offerings until the Dean came down from the cathedral and wrote “Remembrancer” over our door in chalk and decided we should have a title with more respect. If you come to Saint Bridget’s with a prayer, and that prayer is small enough not to trouble the cathedral, you will find me. I will bring you to a cedar chest with lines cut into it by wet rope and we will look together, and if the sea has returned what you lacked — which it sometimes does, uncannily and at its own pace — then there is a coin to be dropped into my jar and a line to be drawn in the book. Some years the jar fills and some years I hold the lid closed with an elastic.

Ren carried my basket, which he believed made him my apprentice, though there is no such station. You can’t apprentice to a thing that is mostly waiting and talking and being polite to grief. He had a blade at his belt that I had dulled and forbidden him to use for anything more ambitious than twine. He had the blunt end of it between his teeth.

“Spit that out,” I said, as I’ve said every day since Midsummer. He spat and the blade hit my cuff in a way that promised pain later if I moved wrong. “You’ll need your teeth.”

“For what?”

“For lots of things.”

He made a face. “You chew like a gull, Ellis.”

“If a gull chews at all, it does it beautifully,” I said, and nodded toward a cut in the flats where eelgrass lay in a tangle, thready and glossy as if dredged out of someone’s throat. Something shinier than weed lay inside it. We went the long way round because the sand there is treacherous and can go liquid under your feet. There is one thing about Saint Bridget’s that will never be written in any almanac: you must not make the sea change its mind about wanting you.

The shininess was not bottle nor coin. It was the tied seam of an oilskin packet, rubbed slick and green with time, sealed at the corners with triangular tacks. It had a glass drop set into one edge, a makeshift window. That was new. We do not set windows into things we expect to put in the water unless we want the water to look back out at us.

Ren worked at it with his fingers. “Careful,” I said, and pulled my dull knife from my boot. The wind was from the north and tasted like cut steel; behind us, the town’s chimneys wore their own thin scarves. Saint Bridget herself stood on her pedestal at the end of the quay, stone hands lifted as if to hold a sheet to wind.

The packet came open as if it had been waiting. Inside the oilskin was paper wrapped in flour cloth. The paper was lined. I could see that much through the glass drop, lines ascending and descending, a page that had been written on in a hand too familiar and too neat for a fisherman, too patient for the library girls, too stiff to be Ren’s mother’s. Ren’s breath went sharp beside me. He stuck his nose to the glass and fogged it.

“What is it?” he said.

“Nothing you can smell,” I answered, and there was something wrong with my voice. The sea had shifted decisively now. It slid back a foot, then two, then more, salting the sand with the hiss of its apology.

We take what the sea gives where it lies. You do not carry a thing across the line from wet to dry unless you intend to name it. Some things want to go over the line and some do not. I’ve seen a wedding ring slide as if of its own power the last inch to safety; I’ve seen an entire cabinet-latch set drift backward like a hand refusing help. We bring a mirror on days when the sea is in a mood. We put the mirror on the sand under the object and coax it to admire itself. Vanity is as ancient a force as tide and carries as many away.

This page came across without needing help. I cut the cloth and the oilskin and slid my fingers in under the paper with the delicacy I’d learned from my mother before she began to mistake me for her sister and then, later, for the girl who helped her in my father’s shop before I was born. My fingertips touched the edges and then the face of the page. The paper was a kind that sells dear in the stationer’s: weighty, with a deckled edge, meant for formal letters. The writing on it, blue-black and precise, was mine.

It was not writing I remembered writing. I keep a flat hand, the loops tight, the descenders severe. On the page were the margins I make and the tiny flourish I add on the tail of my capital R when I sense someone is watching. Between the margins was a date I had not yet lived to: two weeks hence. And then, a little lower, my name.

For a second I thought of Aleister Baines down the lane doling out his hoaxes, a twine-taut man who could not swallow a whistle without making music. He had served up Spanish silver two years ago as a dare to the parish council and claimed the sea had given it for the annual pig race. We found his topsoil lodged in the coin’s cross. But Aleister is slapdash and cannot stay out of his own jokes. The neatness of this thing belonged to someone who keeps ironed handkerchiefs and thinks about weight.

“What’s it say?” Ren said, his voice stretched as he balanced his curiosity against the rules. I had told him too often that we do not read at the shore. We take and name and draw the line; the book is written only when the water is a memory in our hair and there are mugs of tea sweating on the counter.

“It says I should put my boots on before my feet start a union,” I said, and tucked the page back into its jacket. I could feel the letters through the paper like a name scratched into a tabletop. Ren scowled, which made me forgive him a little for being young.

We stepped back over the line. The sand there is fuller of shell and broken pottery, the small dead clatter of a land where the sea has made old towns into walls. My shop is on Swithin Street, two doors up from the ropewalk. It used to be my father’s, and before that it had been my grandfather’s, and I kept the hook and the creel and the three-legged stool and put my own ledger on the shelf where the tobacco once sat, because if you replace everything at once you’re only entering a new room in the same house.

My mother’s house is above the shop. This is a terrible arrangement if you want a steady life and a perfect one if you none of you care about how often the kettle shrieks. When I let us in, Ren rushed to the back to shake his boots into the yard without being asked. He had learned after the second flogging I got from Mrs. Inderwick over sand on the stairs. Stairs hold onto sand the way a sick man holds on to breath.

“Ren’s not staying,” I called up the stair. “He’s going to school and I’m going to have a large argument with a kettle. Is there tea in the pot?”

There was a shuffle and then a rattle and then my mother’s voice asking something I had not yet learned to hear as the wrong name. “Ara?”

“Here,” I said, because fighting a name is like trying to teach a tide lessons.

She came to the landing in a dress with buttons she couldn’t do and a cardamom seed cleaving to her cheekbone. “You were meant to be home last night.”

“So were you,” I said, without heat. In her time, which is a time we only share sometimes now, my mother had kept the best kitchen within five miles of Saint Bridget’s. She fed men whose hands had no nails left, men who could only taste with the spit of their fingers, men born to death by water and with no taste for it. She fed them pies with the fat crimped careful as coin-edge and laughed when they smacked her behind and called her captain because she bossed them better than their boats did. Then, in a winter that came in great heavy teeth, she began to forget the way to her own pantry. She called me her sister. She put brandied cherries in her tea and pretended not to notice their color.

“I made fritters,” she said now, triumphant. “We ate fritters in Pembroke on that blue day when the church had daisies on its steps.”

“We did,” I said, which is the truth in both times. “Ren, say goodbye.”

“Bye, Miss Morrow,” Ren yelled, and she peered down at him with an interest she would not have had when she was herself. Children interested her only when they were about to fall into stew.

“Mind the cart,” she told him. “And the dog.”

“Which dog?” he asked, but she had already retreated up into the room where the wallpaper is full of ships that will never make harbor and where, when she is tired, she calls to her father as if he might come if she makes the right shape with her mouth.

Ren stood in my doorway with his hands shoved under his armpits. “Are you going to open it now?”

“I am not going to open anything now,” I said, with a seriousness meant to impress him into school. “I am going to read the list Mrs. Pye left of all the things she lost last week.”

“She lost her cat and her spectacles and the way to her own door,” Ren said, rolling his eyes with the tender ruthlessness of children. “I met her looking for her house in the pub.”

“And if the sea returns any of those, I will put them on the table.”

He went, throwing his weight against the door the way he liked to, a small crash he would call a punctuation. I could hear him whistling down Swithin, fierce and off-key, the sound of a boy trying to be bigger than his own boots. I boiled the kettle twice and poured the water out when it smelled wrong the first time. My mother sang a song to the kettle she had used on me when I was a child — a thing about blackbirds that made no sense and that I have never been able to sing back to her, because she watches my mouth too closely when I do and sees me failing.

There is a bell on my shop door. It is the bell the sea returned, come down from the tower with its ear tuned now to human footsteps. It rings differently for different people. When Mrs. Pye came the day after she became thin as glass, it rang a thready note like a lost spoon. When Maudie Hey kissed her Henry over the counter, embarrassed, the bell rang three times and a laugh. When Olly Pike came the winter his brother went out and did not come back, the bell did not ring at all. It had never done that before and I thought, briefly, that it had learned his grief.

Now it rang a sound like a hand in a pocket. Soft and not wanting to be remarked upon. I put the kettle on the trivet and wiped my hands on my skirt as if I were the kind of person who always had her hands clean.

“A place for prayers no one wants heard,” said the man at the door, looking around my little room with its glass jars and its cedar box and the pile of things waiting to be persuaded to assume common names. His coat was good wool and his collar held like something bought in a city; he had the distinct air of someone who might be from the cathedral. I quailed without knowing why.

“We have a book,” I said. “And a jar.”

“Everyone has a jar,” he said, and smiled. Not unkindly. “My name is Ansel Sharp.”

“Of the cathedral,” I said. “Sharp as in skulls.” There are two headstones in our yard with arched tops and an angel spreading its wings like a housemaid shaking a sheet. The angels’ mouths are sharp; their chisels are sharper. You learn the names of men who do beautiful harm.

He looked surprised and then pleased. “My uncle.”

“You want to name something,” I said, and he flinched a little, because men in good coats are not used to girls in aprons reading their intention off their shoulders. He looked toward the cedar box. “The sea brings things. It brings what you ask for, sometimes. That’s what they say,” he said, and his voice had that tightened quality — as if he were holding a bowl full of water and trying not to spill it.

“It brings what it is ready to remember,” I said. “Sometimes that looks like what we think we need.”

He laid his hat on the counter. “My brother went over a wall forty miles south last November. Black ice. No body. The river is impassable this winter. We have held a service and my mother has put his childhood shirts in a drawer and my father yells at the cat like it is an argument he can win. There is a — I am told there is a protocol, here.”

“There are a great many protocols,” I said, because the worst thing we can do for grief is make it feel unspecial. “Write his name on a paper and put it under a stone on the quay. Wait until it rains the kind of rain that leans. Find someone who loved him who will not come to your house. Bring a penny and a shoe that no longer has a mate. Bake a loaf and cut a slice for a stranger.

“And then?” he whispered, as if afraid the cathedral would hear him wanting something it could not provide.

“And then,” I said, “you wait.”

He closed his eyes. Men look naked when they admit to waiting. Their faces smooth, their eyelids show the child in them that grew up loving lit windows and coming home. I think the only gift the Remembrancer can truly give is permission to be patient.

“I will write his name,” he said. “Now? Or is that something we—”

“Do alone,” I said, and handed him paper and a blunt pencil because the good ones are for the book.

While he bent over the page, the kettle went from hummed promise to boil. My mother’s song rose to meet it. Upstairs, she forgot the words halfway through and started again, and I felt the ache of it the way you feel a missing tooth — with your tongue, uselessly. I poured tea and it smelled right. The man folded his paper as if it were a garment.

I set my own oilskin packet on the counter and looked at it as someone might look at a letter left under a door. In the corner where the glass was set into the skin, a blot of dry sea-mud cracked like old heels.

“What’s that?” asked Ansel Sharp, in the unembarrassed tone of the curious, not yet credentialed by need.

“Accounting,” I said. “Would you like your tea?”

He would. I poured and pretended not to see his hands shake as he took the cup. Your eyes grow polite if you’re around grief as much as mine have been. They learn not to make contact the way a surgeon’s hands learn not to flinch.

There was a protocol for this, too. We do not read the sea’s letters on an empty stomach. We do not open the sea’s knots before we have set our shoulder against the door. We do not bring it upstairs. We do not call anyone’s name while the letter is open unless we are prepared to hear a voice that may not be the voice we love.

I broke three of these rules in an afternoon in my thirty-first year, but not then. Not yet. I undid the ties of the oilskin while Ansel fished for coins he did not need to pay yet. The paper slid out and lay there, blue and exact, my hand on it twice over — the hand that had just set the kettle and the hand that had written the words that would tell me something I ought not know.

Around us, the shop breathed. The jars held beads and bent nails and a single stub of candle that a girl had brought in as if bringing a finger. The cedar sap in the box rose in my nose like a thing that might keep me standing. Outside, Saint Bridget wore the wind as if it were a custom, the gulls wrote insults in a clear hand, the tide considered, then committed, then came.

I unfolded the page and read my name in my own hand and below it, three words I had not written.

Do not follow him.

The first apple I pick after my grandmother’s funeral tastes like rain that hasn’t fallen yet. The skin is green with a cast of silver, the bloom still dusty under my thumb. When I bite, the flesh gives with a sound I have not heard in years, a small tender crack that lives in the mouth longer than it should, and the juice stings the soft places behind my teeth. I lean on the ladder to catch the drips with my wrist and think, ridiculous as it is, that she has arranged this—her last trick—to remind me that something can be both tart and kind.

We bury her on a slope between the orchard and the road because that is where she said the hill holds the dead closest. Our pastor mumbles in the state language; a bird coughs once in the ashes of the persimmon tree. I stand between the beekeeper and a cousin I do not know and I say the words the old way, as best as I can put them back together, fingers closed like she taught me: let the wind not mistranslate you, let the earth hear your right name. A few women nod although I am not sure whether at the sentence or at the effort.

After, when the plates have been put down and lifted up and the laughing done because carriers of grief pretend laughter is a pitcher you can pour from without spilling, I walk out alone. The orchard is unlocked. The wire we braided around the gate fifteen years ago because my uncle said the goats had brains for knots hangs loose, good wire gone slack. The path is the same care I used to give it as a child with a broom, only what I swept then was the idea of leaves, not the cut of them against my feet as it is now.

Everything is smaller and larger than I remember. The trees come to meet me and stop short, the way animals do when you have been away and return in a different skin. From the road comes the vinegar hum of tires, but the rest is its own old noise: bees combing the air, sap thinking about pushing up again, a tin pail rolling where the wind takes it. That pail still carries the story of the morning my grandmother made me kneel to catch a leak from the rain barrel. I put it upright now and it is the same flaked red with a white handle, unexpectedly fierce with the scent of apples you can no longer buy.

Her ladder lies where she fell from it last summer, not the fall that broke her but the fall that taught me to watch her more closely. The rungs are smooth in the spot where she set her foot and then me, and then my cousin Leno for one month before the city took him and kept him, as the city keeps so many things. There is no reason to keep the ladder except that it seems wrong to lift what knew her weight. I sit on the third rung and let the ladder take mine, small as it is.

The first apple I eat is dzenka, if the tags are right, and in this orchard they almost always are. Dzenka is the one you eat when you leave the house so your mouth remembers how to come back. The tag is a bit of tin cut from an old flour tin, punched and wired. The letters are her neat sloped ones, stubborn in their refusal of the modern alphabet, the kind that turned every language into the same door. When I was little, I thought script itself was a kind of magic: anything you wrote would be heard by the right ear. Now I know the state has two ears and they never agree.

Grandmother’s ledger is in the house, under the woven rug that is not pretty enough to make anyone think of looking there. But first I make myself walk the whole orchard. I mark with my body where the old fence lost itself in the blackberry, where the spring still lifts its muddy mouth and gives the cold I cannot get from a tap. I say the names out loud again after all those silent city years, as if I am one of those witches my grandmother insisted were an honest profession when done correctly, stirring back the ingredients of a language. Vrash, for winter’s keen. Melki, to set beside a window for a wake. Stolni, whose flesh you whisper into and who will carry your message wherever you cannot go. Ladova, that keeps its shape after frost. Hele, that bruises in the shape of whatever you were thinking when you picked it.

We did not call them varieties; they were trees and neighbors. The state has its own names and numbers for the ones it cares about: a string of letters and a code in the nursery catalog, a patent name stamped on a stake. I cannot fit that catalog over this place without tearing it.

On the far western edge, where we pushed the rows too close because the hill tries its best to slide down every spring, I find the first new thing: a notice nailed to the sycamore, the one with bark that peels like a child who never stops growing. The paper is a blue I know well from my years reading municipal threats. There is a seal with the grain sheaf and the river.

Property owners in within-district agricultural lots are reminded of the Standardization of Product and Yield Act, says the paper, and then it says a great many other things, none of which are false if you only consider the law’s language and none of which are true if you consider a mouth. Remove noncompliant plantings. Register varietals with accompanying genetic certificate. Submit for inspection or risk levy. There is a date and it is soon.

I take the notice and fold it until the seal cracks like old lacquer. When I slide it into my pocket it makes a stiff corner against my thigh as if it would like to be a knife and do the cutting itself.

My grandmother did not teach me to fight governments. She taught me to cut grafts in moonlight and tie them tight as a promise. She taught me that the cider press must be cleaned so well you could put a new child through it and not worry. She taught me that every language has more names for hunger than it admits. But even though she would spit and say, that is not our problem, my hands feel heavy with the problem anyway. This is how it is to inherit anything: you inherit the names, and the kneeling, and the debts, and the notices.

I force myself to keep walking. The sun lets itself down between branches and turns the leaves bright from the inside. I pay attention for the trees that speak first because I know that if I cannot hear them now, later I will pretend they were always quiet. In the stand of melki, the bee boxes are fewer: Leka the beekeeper must have moved some to the buckwheat field. Even so, the air is stitched with bees as if my grandmother spent her last winter crocheting them. Melki are for wakes; you set them in small bowls by the bed and the house will not smell too much of dying. My grandmother once said that melki work the same trick when you have fallen deeply in love. It keeps the air sane, she laughed, because some joys will burn you out of your house if you let them.

Behind the melki is the row of salvaged trees, the orphans from the north slope that belonged to a church no one will admit to now. We moved them after the last thaw when the concrete was poured for the new road. It is not true that trees are quiet when you move them. It is not true that a machine does not know what it is breaking. They came out whispering, all roots and soil, and my grandmother said put them where the wind cannot bully them. Sprout-of-ashes, she wrote in the ledger. She had a word for the line you draw back to a tree you do not know the name of. It is not lineage and not regret, but something narrow and tough as rope, and it does not break where you think it will.

I am tired by the time I turn back toward the house and the heat has almost turned itself inside out: the day’s core cooling, the air lifting. Smoke from two chimneys. A boy’s laugh from the road. And then something else: the sound of a motor coming slow, wheels finding their way despite having been told what to do a thousand times. The county truck. I recognize the lazy cough of it as if trucks too were cousins who never did come to the city.

I watch it through the hedge because part of me is not a person at all but a deer, all eye and ear. It eases over the ditch and stops at the shoulder by our gate. The door opens, then closes, and a man walks around to check the hinge. He is small in the way of people who wear too many official shirts, but the way he moves is easy. The gate is not locked and he opens it with his knee and takes a step inside before he remembers to call out.

Anyone? he says.

I do not answer because for a second my mind stutters between languages and there is a ridiculous urge to shape my mouth around his mother’s tongue even though I will do it badly and he will see who I am before I can decide what being seen means. He repeats himself, which tells me he is good at his job, or at least not a coward. I step out of the hedge.

I am Mara, I say. My grandmother kept the place.

He tips his cap. I’m Nenad, from the district. I saw… he touches his pocket. He has one of the blue notices, but he also has something else: a roll with percentages on it, a tape measure, perhaps to show that number is a thing you can stretch and wrap around a living limb until it fits.

She died, I say, as if it is the kindest address: not the title on the deed, not what the ordinance calls us. She died this week.

He nods and his face agrees: there are times to put papers away. I only came to make sure someone was here, he says. We had trouble with… he looks toward the road, which sometimes is how our people name the state. There was time last winter with the theft of the bee boxes. People who think they’re free help themselves to sugar they don’t understand. If you need… he says, then stops. It’s good to have someone keeping things.

I resist the urge to tell him that the bees are better thieves than any of us, that they will find sweetness under your floorboards if you let a jar tip over, that I have a scar on my ankle from a summer when I thought I could move a hive by asking. Instead I nod and ask whether the notice has a specific person’s name on it or if it is from the floating head of the department.

He almost smiles. We do have heads, he says. The law’s been around. They are serious now. The farms up the valley went through it last year. They let you register some things. Others they say are… he touches the paper as if it might catch it from his hand… volatile.

Do you know my grandmother’s orchard? I say. The way you are supposed to talk to someone who might need to hear your voice leave your body and stay in the air between you. He looks down the rows as if reminded of his own grandmother by the shape of the shadows. I used to come for cider, he says. It was like music. She would tell me the names of apples when I brought her the bottle and I pretended not to understand because I liked the way she would repeat them.

He is not my enemy, but he will bring his own bees here if asked. I thank him, and he goes, and when the truck starts again the first three apples above the gate shake as if nodding and then do not move at all.

The house holds its heat the way old women hold their breath when someone says you are beautiful even though you do not need to be. I push the rug aside and lift the ledger. It has been repaired with tape twice, on the spine, and the green of the cover is the same green you find in moss and old schoolroom paint. The pages are thin and in places worn into lace by her hand. She writes the old way, with ink she mixed herself from walnut hulls and vinegar, so even death will not make the words go away.

When I was a girl, I sat at the table with my pencil and said I can read this, let me, and she set her finger over my hand and said, not yet, not while you are still afraid of mistakes. The mistake was not to write the words at all, she would say later, pouring cider that sloshed like a clear lake. Take your fear and put it where the cold keeps the milk. If you cannot find it, good. If you can find it right away, do not drink from that shelf.

The ledger opens to a page I know because my grandmother loved the way the ink gathered in the tall letters here. Dzenka. The old script arches and returns like a person turned toward the door. Under the name, a sentence in the home language and then one in the state’s: Eat before leaving home. The practice keeps your tongue elastic. Under that, the kind of notes that could be jokes or rules: pick with shoes on, never count to fifteen when the ladder is leaning, do not force the knife to cut what the branch will give. About midway down the page is the drawing of the graft we made the summer I thought I would run away. That was the same summer she told me, write down the names even if you think you will never forget them. You cannot remember what you did not write, not because your hands are cruel but because your mind is.

It goes on for pages and pages, the orchard’s mind in her hand. Vrash, to be stored where the house remembers it has a cellar. And notes: apples do not like to be called fruits in winter. Melki, set for the dead and the newly married. Ladova, cut thin with a grater and draped over a slice of bread with salt. I run my finger down the columns as if I am learning another person who happens to be myself. I do not know all the words in the older parts of her writing. She must have learned them from my great-grandmother, who kept books in the language no one will own up to now, the one that the pastor says was never respectable and therefore worth saving.

There is a page near the back that is not like the others. It is written in block letters as if she wants some future hand to read and not mistake a long tail for an s. She writes a word I do not know: krezna. Under it, in the state language, a translation: the duty owed to the dead. She has never explained this to me; she has always said grief is personal cargo, not a legal weight. But here, under the name, is her neat precise list of the reasons anyone might plant an orchard in the way we did even when the state said to pull it up and begin again with clean stock. Krezna, she writes, as if the word itself is a tree whose roots she is mapping: because we keep people alive with our mouths, because sweetness is a kind of law older than law, because if we do not conserve their names they will come to us at night and ask where we put them. Below these sentences she has drawn a line and below the line she has written the state’s word, a word so bureaucratic it sounds like metal: compliance. She has written in small letters, under that: the opposite of compliance is not disobedience but memory.

I close the ledger then, not because I am tired of reading but because I am full. What do you do when your dead hand you a duty they hid until after they left? This is how they keep living: they fold a sentence into a page and you open it when the light is a certain color and you have already thought you are alone.

I light the stove. The kindling catches slow and touches the logs as if testing. The kettle hangs and makes the familiar voice. I slice two apples and a third because that seems like the right number to put into tea when death is in the house. The knife is the one my grandmother used to cut grafts. It has a notch where it caught a nail in a fence post. The blade is the stiff kind you cannot buy now unless you go to the flea market before dawn. The apples fan into pale crescents on the board and the paring curls in smells like the sound of heat on metal.

When the water boils I pour it over the apples in the old enamel pot, white with blue flowers, chipped by the handle where I once dropped it. The tea goes the honest color of autumn ditches. I drink and it tastes of grief and sugar, which is to say there is nothing in it you cannot survive.

Someone knocks—not at the front door where family comes but at the side door by the shed where strangers and deals come. It is nearly dark. I wipe my hands and go to the side, feeling the old tiles press their old language into my feet through my socks. The person on the step is a woman with hair cut in the way of people who are tired of hair. She wears a jacket that smells like a new car and holds, wrapped in paper, a small square as if it is her own pulse she is offering.

You are the granddaughter? she says, and when I nod she shifts to the home language in a way that makes me feel skinned, because her accent is careful in places people my age are careless. I’m Elka, she says. My mother was Vara who cleaned your grandmother’s stovepipes. She died too, long time now. I came for… she looks down at her hands. We always came for melki but your grandmother would not take money for that, she said it was not a thing you could sell. This is bread. I made it. I thought—well. You know how it is.

I do. I take the bread and it is still warm. I break it and that is the first time since the funeral that my throat tells the truth and I am crying in the doorway like a woman in her first year of grief. She looks away the way women do when crying is a private language, then looks back anyway and touches my sleeve.

They nailed something to your gate, she says. I saw it when they went by our house because they nail to everything they see now like men who do not know how to love anything without making it still. You will need someone at the hearing if it comes to that.

I do not tell her I know all the words at every hearing and none of them are enough. I do not tell her my job in the city these last years has been to turn what people say into what judges can stand. I say yes, and she nods and says, I know a man, and laughs because that phrase holds its own joke, the joke that every story has a man who can fix it until he cannot.

Before she leaves she looks at the row of shoes near the door—the old city habit of me keeping them neat even though here we kick them off wherever—and lifts one the way older women do when they have something to say that is not gossip. That apple, she says, nodding toward the bowl on the table where I set the last of the dzenka slices, that one is for coming back. Did you choose it on purpose?

No, I say, but even as I say it I can hear my grandmother laugh, not unkindly. And I think of the sentence in the ledger, the line where she wrote that the opposite of compliance is memory. I tell Elka about the notice. She spits into the yard and says a word we use only with relatives and magistrates. The flowers of the enamel pot float like tiny boats in the sink behind her. The light has gone the gray that is not yet night. She touches my sleeve again and says, I am across the road if you need hands that do not write but will pry out nails.

I sleep badly in her bed because everything that held her holds me too tightly. At some hour past the train but before the foxes I sit up and see the orchard out the small high window, a darker dark below the lighter one, and think of the way she told stories when she thought I was asleep. She never told them to my face, never in the day. She told them into the air above me where I could catch them or let them go. That is not true of how she did anything else. Even her cooking was direct: if she meant you to taste something, you tasted it. Names? she sighed once, blowing on the lid of the soup as if that would cool the whole world. Names are slyer.

When morning is actually morning and not the idea of morning you ache toward in the night, I put on boots and go out before tea. The grass makes that cold seeping sound into the leather my foot will remember all day. The bees are asleep or pretending. The trees look like cities a long way off. I think, this is the last day I will be able to be here before the machines make their own sounds. That is not yet true but it will be, and ahead of the fact my body leans as if bracing against it.

I go to the row where the letters in my grandmother’s hand have been eaten the most by weather—the oldest row. The tags tell me what I already know by the tilt of each tree. I say their names out loud anyway. The saying will not save them, I am not a fool, but I will not let the silence do the work we should resist. At the end of the row is a gap where a tree fell in a storm when I was seven and my grandmother let us climb it as we would climb an animal that would not throw us. She did not cut it for years, out of respect, as if the trunk needed to think about being wood before becoming heat. In the gap now there is something I do not expect. It is a small tree no one planted, lithe and shameless, strung with beads of dew. It has pushed through the mat of roots like a child through a crowd and found its space. It is topped with a flag of leaf that looks like both of its parents without belonging to either.

Volunteer, my grandmother would say, as frankly proud as any commander. There is also a word in our tongue for what rises where you once lost something. It is not miracle and not vengeance. It is closer to apology, but not because anyone asked. I pull the weeds around the base so the shoot can breathe. I touch the tiny bark with the back of my finger so I do not harm it. The leaf says hello back in how it holds sunlight.

The state will not like this in the way it does not like a defect that turns out to be a new design. The volunteers are the mess the ordinances were written against. They bear surprise. They do not carry certificates. They are not the children of anyone registered.

I stand and talk to it anyway; it is lucky that there is no one to watch. I say, you are trouble, and I feel the answer run up my arm: so are you. I think about how to graft faster than paper can move. I think about how to register names that will not be registered. I think of all the days my grandmother made me repeat the word for what you owe your dead, a word I did not know she had given a page to, and how plainly disobedient it turns out to be.

By the time the sun lifts and my tea is cold on the table where I left it, I have done the first thing I can. In the ledger under dzenka I add in my careful block letters, as if someone a hundred years from now will need to hear me unmistakably: eaten upon return also, the practice keeps the mouth brave. I write it in our language and in the other one. Then I lift the pen and hold it against the air above the page where her hand would have been and I whisper her name and the name of the duty until I can taste them both, and when the taste settles in my teeth like the first bite of the day’s first apple, I stop. I go outside. I run my fingers over the wire of the gate and it bites my palm and I do not let go. The notice is no longer on the sycamore because my pocket knows how to hold things. The bees begin again. The volunteer leaf trembles as if remembering an instruction it never received. In the road there is the sound of a truck I recognize and also the sound of a truck I don’t yet.

This is how it starts: not with a vow spoken in front of witnesses, but with the small practice of saying the right names to the right ears. With a tree that arrived without permission. With the taste of rain in a green apple, and the ledger spread open on a table set with bread given by a neighbor who learned the old words for kindness even as everyone else forgot. With a page that says there is a thing between compliance and defiance, ancient and tender. With me, in my grandmother’s boots, making the stupid brave choices of people who love what might be taken.

Chapter One

By the time the city learned to drown without fuss, we had learned to dive without asking.

I marked the morning by the sound the river made through the under-bridges. In summer, it chattered like a wheel of glass. In winter, it chewed. Today it was a low, steady breath, pulling at the pilings of the Upperwalk, worrying the ropes of our moorings the way the old women at market worry prayer beads. On that breath we loaded the boat: coils of nylon, the weight belt, my mask with the hairline crack I kept meaning to replace, two cheap air tanks battered oil-blue. Once, this city had arranged itself around avenues and traffic lights; now there were canals and the narrow decks between apartments, and cranes whose rust-dripped arms lifted groceries and furniture instead of freight. On mornings you could still hear bells—that was what people said when they needed to make a promise seem sweeter—but I knew better. The only bells left in this parts of the drowned wards were underwater, their mouths grown quiet with silt.

“Don’t waste your breath on an empty bell,” Tolin told me, sticking a piece of dried mango between his teeth and my glove. He had run salvage before there were licenses. If you could fence it, he had ducked after it. He was thick around the shoulders and careful with lies.

“It won’t be empty if I get to it,” I said.

He squinted across the flat green of the flooded street, where the sun turned paint blister into mirrors. The city across the water was rumpled and layered: roofs like discarded plates; balconies sprouting steel ladders from one to the next; a vine of laundry climbing a stairless wall.

“You are sure the priest promised cash,” he said. “Not crowns in heaven.”

“He showed me the envelope.” I tapped my chest, feeling the thickness of it with an acquisitive animal’s satisfaction. Money has weight that stays with you after you give it away. “He wants the bell from Santa Fina,” I said. “He said the new parish can’t call itself a parish without something the old parish recognizes. Old saints are worse than old men.”

Tolin barked, short as a gull. “Santa Fina.” His tongue clicked against whatever memory that stirred. “She was the one with the grapes.”

“That’s a song,” I said. He worked the engine loose with a cough; it coughed back; we dribbled forward between the spine of a smashed sedan and the jut of a stop sign. Below us, the river swelled like an animal turning over. “And don’t look at me like that. I know what you’re thinking. The registry keeps civic artifacts on the Preservation List.”

“I’m thinking nothing. You unscrew what you can carry. If the registry man asks, we went to fetch a pot lid and came up with a family story instead.”

Family stories were safer to pocket. If you returned to a client with the pot where their father boiled fish heads into suppers or the enamel bowl the mother used to catch rain, they paid you twice: money and a place in their memory. Our yard was full of those small loyalties. It was not full of bell towers.

We ground to a halt against a rail that had been a balustrade once and now was a mooring. A boy with hair bleached pale as flour sat on the ledge with his legs dangling. He flicked water at a fly. “Which saint?” he called. He was barefoot in the cold and grinning like it didn’t matter.

“Fina,” I said.

“Bless her frozen hands,” he said, as if she had just dropped something. Everyone in the drownward had a proverb for the saints. Saints were built to carry what water could not.

Santa Fina's church had not been as spared as some. There were those buildings that the water loved, which it carried up and set down like a grandmother lowering a sleeping child into a bed; Santa Fina had been one of those it hated. The right wall canted, the steps were a notch like missing teeth. The rose window was a wrecked eye. The tower had fallen into the nave gull-first, the bell poured out of the wreck and into the green. And there it stayed, an upside-down mushroom, mouth in silt, sleeping.

“I don’t like that you’re going alone,” Tolin said. “He should have brought us men, pulleys. Men to stand on things and make the city scold.”

“You don’t like a lot of things,” I said, and tried not to think of the way the undergovernment men could appear when you tugged a rope that looked like it belonged to them. A woman in a yellow dress had once tried to teach me breathing exercises. “Imagine you are a bellows,” she had said. “Imagine you are a river, slow, then fast, then slow.” But I had always been a bell. You cannot unlearn the work your body does: you ring when struck, you do not apologize for it.

He kissed the air between my eyebrows, old superstition, and I let him. “Find the rope I left last spring,” he said. “Take care of your lines. Don’t wrap yourself in somebody else’s grief.”

Underwater, the city stood exactly as it had the day it gave up. That’s what unnerved me most talking to the people from the hills: I would describe the way curtains still hung, or a bowl on a table, or the string of rubber bands that had been saving chip bags in a kitchen drawer, and they would bring their hands to their mouths as if I had shown them a ghost. But of course it is all right there, dully faithful. You go under the skin and the wounds are still wet.

I wore my mother’s rings under my gloves because that is what a person does when her hands do the work her mother’s didn’t get to do. She had been a teacher of difficult children, drum on the desk with the flat of her hand when a room needed ordering. She had loved the piano like it had more particular mercy to give to the world than any instrument. I am not superstitious, except for the things I am superstitious about, so I keep her rings and do not talk to her while I’m below. The river does not like it when you talk to someone else.

The chill of the water took my scalp first. The breath from the regulator was mechanical, my ribs doing what they had practiced as a child swimming down between stilts when the tide fattened. There is a kind of hearing that arrives underwater, different from sound. You feel the city in your bones. The groaning of cabled things. A soft-ticking where the fish have nested themselves into suit pockets and light fittings. The prayer of a fan turning on nothing.

I kicked past a window that had turned into a doorway, past an advertisement painted directly on cinderblock—TINNED PEACHES FOR ALL SEASONS, the peaches now furred with the thin lace the river makes. I stopped and listened. A bell rumor, if a bell is under silt, is not a noise but a pressure. You hum the note back and if you hum the right one, the river hums with you—your humming, through metal, through water, through yourself—until you feel a seam give way. I hummed, low, a note under language. A dull answering thickness came from my chest rather than my ears. There you are, I thought, and the river was by then inside my mask and crawling cold down that place a mother used to call the back of the heart and then farther down.

The nave of Santa Fina was all splayed ribs, wood beams like the thawed skeleton of a whale. The tower’s stump lay like a sullen drunk across the pews. The light came down in bands broken by dust and fish, coinish, greenish, a liturgy of imperfect things. The bell had fallen on its lip. It had cracked one of the stone tiles and settled into its wound. Silt had fluffed up around it. It wore a shawl of algae. It was heavy the way a promise made to a frightened person is heavy: not in any way you can distribute.

The rope we had tied in spring was still wound around the bell’s flank, bleached where it crossed open water into the nave light, dark where it sank into mud. Something had chewed the line near the post and left cursive gnaw-marks. If Tolin had been here he would have tutted. I put my palm against the bell. It was barely gritty to the touch. My mother would have chastised me for that—do not give consecrated things your fingerprints—but that sort of consecration had gone out with dry feet.

There were scratches of a chalk arrow on the stone—three marks at the doorjamb, a sign divers left for one another. It meant, roughly: don’t go this way in a hurry unless you like bleeding. The arrow whisked toward something darker than shadowing by the old confessional. I turned my head to look. Down here the bubbles roped off a small patch around my face and the rest of the world happened at a distance. A net. Fine, nylon, meant for fish but eager for anything. One of the occupational differences between us and the tilapia was that tilapia do not worry about getting their tanks torn.

I ran my palm over the bell until I found the slots where the clapper pin had gone. If I couldn’t pull the bell today—and I couldn’t, not without gear and men and a skiff rig—then I could take the clapper. Not because it had more value separate, but because I had a feeling and because feelings are not reasons and we are embarrassed to admit we use them to make decisions when we are alone. The pin was rusted and the rust had flowered into the wood of the fallen tower. I made a mental list: saw, wedge, whalebone shim. It is always a gift to know what you will need later while you cannot do anything about it now.

I hummed again, because I am that sort of fool, and let my fingers rest on the mouth. A warmth moved through the bridge of my nose, an almost-pain, the way you feel a storm come on days before it breaks. It wasn’t the bell exactly; bells don’t hold voices, only the shape for voices to grow in. But beneath the sludge I heard the tone that had woken me when I was a child raising nights at the window to watch the storm boats run their lanterns along the river’s throat. It was lower than my neck and the color of dust on water. The tone shivered once in my bones and then another thing reached for me.

The net came out of the confessional like a rumor. The edge of it caught on my tank and kissed my lip where the mouthpiece met my skin. Don’t thrash. Don’t get bigger. That’s the first thing. The second is cut with the small knife you can rock open with your thumb without taking your other hand off whatever keeps you here. I had cut rope on outriggers and in stairwells and around the ankles of men who thought drinking was a softer way to drown. Rope is honest. Nylon is not. Nylon holds a grudge. It remembers where your skin will catch.

I made my breathing deliberately dull. I slid two fingers under the fine line where it tightened across my hose and held them there so the pressure would take my skin and not the rubber. The knife was in the other hand now, small scalloped blade, ridiculous for kelp and miracle for grocery twine and everything in between. I made three neat cuts and the net let me go the way a mouth lets go of a word when it has said it too many times. The knife went away. I felt stupid and old, which is to say: lucky.

On the far side of the nave something else moved. Not fish. Not the cat’s shadow that sometimes becomes your own shadow when you catch it out of the periphery of your face. I stilled, because my body has always known how to be a deer when it needed to be. The man was older than me, which is not a proof of anything. He had a shaved skull and a line of rope burns dark against the white of it and a thin mustache that looked drawn on with a finger dipped in oil. His fins did not belong to anyone who bought them from a shop. He put two fingers to his mask in the signal that either meant peace or look. You can say look a lot of ways underwater. He said: look where I am going, look who I am not, look how I could take this. I looked down at my hand on the bell and realized I had been making a fist.

He raised a hand, a little bow. That was an unambiguous signal; it meant, Are you also a thief with a job, or are you a thief without a job. I gave him open palms. He rolled over in the righted slow way that those who have been diving since they had ribs thin enough to show have, and he slid out through the broken frame of a saint, his tank not dragging on anything, the net not interested in him. He had made it his business to learn this church already, then. In the way he knew not to snag himself there was the intimacy that made me feel a possessive flicker of anger. You hated him for sleeping with your city first.

Fine, I told myself. The world was full of inconvenient others and if you killed them all you would never have someone to pin your anger to. I unspooled a length of line and made a lark’s head knot tight into a notch in the bell’s shoulder. The lark’s head is a little sorrowful knot; you make it and unmake it so many times in your life you could tie it in your sleep. I put a second loop over the first and went to the butt-end of the rope to set a hook in fallen beam. These were small things that would save hours later if the river didn’t decide to move an unsubtle tree through here by morning.

On the way out I picked three small things because ritual demands tribute. I took a handful of tile blue enough to salt a sky. I took a silver spoon that had the chew set deep in the handle from a baby and in the bowl from a poison tester, because no good spoon only has one mouth on it. I took a brass ring that might have been a curtain ring and might have been a lover’s ring and held it with my gloved hand and felt nothing particular. Sometimes things speak; more often they look at you like you should know it without them telling you; you put them in your pocket anyway. I left two coins in the sacristy drawer, because we are all superstitious about the things our hands do over and over.

When I broke surface, for a moment the world forgot which way air should move. Then the Upperwalk rumbled back into being, that plank shiver you get when someone four moorings down jumps back in with a coil of hose that he swore he left on his boat. The city above water was bright in the way cities are when someone has cleaned them too hard. The laundries flapped. The boy with flour hair had moved because boys like that do not stay. Tolin was chewing his mango down to a string.

“Well?”

I held up the ring, the spoon, and the blue tile, which glittered wet in my palm like a handful of small, obedient skies. “Tribute,” I said. “The clapper will need a saw and a new word for leverage.”

“And the bell?”

“Sleeping,” I said. “Where else would it be.” I pulled at the cuff of my glove with my teeth and freed my hand. The imprint of the glove ridges on my skin pleased me. It meant my body had done something.

Tolin stared past me. He was looking at the tower’s bitten-off face the way you look at a tooth you’ve spit into the sink. “When you were little,” he said, “they rang Santa Fina for the first flood. Everyone had ropes. You remember? Your mother tied three of you together and made you laugh while she made three little knots.”

“I remember,” I said. That was partly true. I remember the knot. My mother used to tie a knot and say, “This is for the future. This is for the future. This—this is for the day after that.” She had been wrong about which day came after which. That is what happens to good women.

He took the tile out of my hand and held it up. A gull wheeled through its slice of blue. “We should sell this to someone who thinks blue is the last honest color,” he said.

“And the boy with the head,” I said. “Did you see him again? He asked which saint.”

“The boy is in seven places at once,” Tolin said. “He will ask which saint until we make one up to satisfy him.”

The priest from the new parish came at dusk to the yard. He wore his collar like an apology. The yard is not much to look at: a heap of usable nails. Doors that still took their handles with grace. A kitchen hutch whose glass had shattered and been replaced with a web of chicken wire and the heavy leaded rectangles from a bar back somewhere across the river. What no one ever expects is how dignified a broken sink can look if you get the angle of light right. People who have lost things think the world is made of proof that they have lost more than anyone else, but really the world is made of small things that will outlast your grief so thoroughly it feels like disrespect.

“You went down,” he said, as if it was us who needed confirmation. He stepped around the heap of rolled rugs the way a man steps around a snake, slow, appreciative.

“Yes,” I said.

“And the bell?”

I didn’t like to say no and I didn’t like to say later and I didn’t like to say we could try, for twice that number you have not paid anyone in a hurry to pay. “It’s there,” I said. “She fell on her mouth. We’ll need men and a crane—"

“Please don’t say ‘she’,” he said, quickly, sharply, the mask ripped off the politeness. “If you say ‘she’ I will feel like a man who has, I don’t know, left someone in a cold bed.”

“Bells are stubborn daughters,” Tolin said. “You kick them and they sing about it for years.”

“I can get you the clapper by tomorrow,” I said. “You could ring a bowl. A butter churn. Your church stovepipe until the neighbors throw cushions out of their windows.”

He pressed his lips together. “They will say it isn’t proper.”

“They will say whatever you tell them to,” I said, and didn’t mean it. I had seen the hill parishes and the way they carried their sacred up off the floodline like goats, sure-footed, their god heavier with each step, their hands blistered. “If your people hear a tone, they will think you have gathered some kind of real back to them. While we fetch your symbol, you might as well purchase a sound.”

He looked down at my hand. My fingers had left a wet slick on the blue tile. In it he saw his reflection, drawn out by water, rippled. “You talk like someone who loved a church,” he said.

“That’s funny,” Tolin said. “She mostly loves the things that aren’t allowed to leave.”

I wanted to say I loved my mother’s piano and the way when she played, our small apartment shifted around the notes and became briefly the right shape for living. I wanted to say that there had been once a church whose balcony had been good for kissing in, if you liked the smell of someone else’s grandmother on the wood, but I didn’t. I said, “We love work here.”

He gave me the envelope then, not all of it, but more than most men would have offered before we cut a single bolt. Hand over coffee. Hands have always known the simplest treaties. “We need that bell by Saint Bruno’s night,” he said. “The hill people will come down with candles. If we don’t ring something they will say we are only staging the performance of worship. They will say we are pretending at belonging.”

“Everyone is pretending at belonging,” Tolin said. “Why should a place be different from a person.”

“It isn’t,” the priest said. “That is the trouble. The city will remind you of it if you let her.”

He left with five loose nails in his pocket; nobody leaves without a gift if they came to us with empty hands. I watched him go past the edge of what had been our street before it became our dock. The river’s skin wrinkled with small winds. When Tolin had closed the ledgers and tied the blue tile into a ratty bit of cloth, when he had taken his blanket to the office couch and pretended as a younger man that he slept in a house with walls thick enough to keep a dream in, I went back for a minute to the edge of the yard.

What I mean is this: you can stand at the edge and think there is edge. Later you discover that nothing has edges anymore. Even your name dissolves a little in salt.

I put my hand on the post and felt the grain of the wood, the place where the rope had been tightened so many times it had left a groove. I closed my eyes. That humming—the one from the nave—nested itself again in the bones inside my ear. I could not have heard it from here; no one could; that is not how sound travels through water and distance and two killed streets. And yet. And yet there was a sense of something tuned, of some great metal wanting. It had nothing to do with God. It had everything to do with people who refuse to stop naming each other across impossible spaces.

I remembered my mother saying, as she tied the knot I have tied a thousand times: this is for the future. I thought, not in words, that these small hands of mine would carry a bell if they had to carry it piece by piece, because I had learned this: the city didn’t ask us for faith. It asked us for stubbornness that could sing.

Something out on the water gave a sharp flick, like a fish turning, like a sheet set loosely that snaps itself taut. The wind shifted. Far away—too far—the cough of a generator turned over, tried, failed, tried again. The sky did one of its diluted opera tricks and went coral briefly. I thought of the green light through the nave and of the shaved-headed diver rolling himself out along the length of a fallen saint. The river touched the foot of my shoe, then drew back.

The first time you actually hear a bell in this city, you always think you imagined it. There was a tremor that ran through the post under my palm and into the plane of my hand and then made itself a felt thing in the skin over my ribs. The sound rose. It was not the shape of the bell; it was the shape of the air that would have been moved if air had been where the bell was. It was a ghost rung on nothing. It made the stray hairs at the back of my neck stand up. I could have said: some boy is banging a wrench on a pipe far down the row, and that would have been true enough. I could have said: maybe I have a fever. I could have said: street noise, water trick. But the tone that lifted the night had iron in it, and too much of my life was made from it to pretend it could be mistaken.

I did not call to Tolin. I did not kiss my fingers and press them to the post and call it a vow or a dare. I did not think any word with the boldness we think words when we mean them to bind us. I only stood there, and the river breathed once like a very old animal made of ruins. Somewhere below, a stubborn daughter turned in her sleep. My bones answered her without my permission. That is what I would learn: there are callings bigger than faith. Here is a city. Here is a bell. Here is a woman who will go back under for it.

Chapter One

On the mornings my father took me to the bridge, he would bring a pocketful of bolts, smooth-headed and cold, and lay them along the dashboard like a row of small moons. While we waited for the light at the foot of the span to turn green, he’d rap them one by one with his knuckle and say, Listen—this is E, this is F, this is the note of wet steel. He claimed every length of metal sang if you let it. It was the first lesson he ever gave me about the work: how to find the sound in what looks like silence.

I keep a rusted bolt on the ledge by the window of the booth, as close to an altar as I allow myself. It’s pitted and unsound, something that ought to have been thrown from the workbarge into the estuary and left to grow its fur of green. Instead, it’s traveled with me through apartments and lovers, was tucked into my father’s jacket pocket when we buried him and then taken out again when I could not bear to imagine the weight of hardware on his chest.

It is shortly after four when I unlock the booth and flip the breaker. The lights come with a gentle indignation, the way old dogs rouse and blink at your intrusion. Outside the glass, the city is still a gradient of dark—San Perdita, with its scalloped hills and stubborn bridge that has carried five decades of errands and elopements and moving vans packed with the certainty that is youth. The newspapers call the bridge obsolete. On talk radio, it is a financial ulcer. In the blog of an eighteen-year-old I will never meet, it is a beautiful, stupid thing.

I have been here for eight years. That is long enough to learn where the drafts creep in under the metal seams in winter, long enough to know the trucks by sound. Long enough to be the last.

“Performative nostalgia,” the city comptroller said on television when they announced the ceremonial final week of cash tolls. He tried to make a joke of it and then, seeing how poorly it landed, shook his head as if at a child. But people have come, in droves, to hand over coins and tokens and damp bills with tears trapped like fish between their fingers. They have come to feed a story through a slot and receive a story back: a receipt, a smile, the brief static of being seen. After today, there will be only auto-debit and velocity. After today, the bridge will be cut in sections and lowered like stiff limbs into the waiting barges. After today, the water will learn that light in a new way.

The booth has a smell I have come to think of as loyal: scorched coffee and hand sanitizer and the faint tar breath of the road. I boot the register, count the wrappers of coins. The last tray of hexagonal tokens the Commerce Office found in a storeroom—heavy pieces with a heron stamped on one face and the year the bridge opened on the other. The tokens were retired when I was still in high school; now parents spill them from red velvet jewelry bags into their children’s palms as if they were pirate gold. The kids lick them and make faces. Money tastes like everyone who has ever needed it.

At four-thirty the gulls start their maraud over the water. Their cries sound like laughter and argument and glass breaking in the next room. A pelican takes up his post on the stanchion halfway between my booth and the far bank. I have named him Captain, not because he leads anything but because he looks as if he has somewhere better to be. In a few hours the demolition crews will arrive and put up the last of the fencing. The countdown will begin. For now, the world holds still as if to increase the distance between before and after.

When I was nine, my father took me to the central seam between the lanes and told me to press my ear to the railing. People thought he was a crazy man dragging a child into traffic, so he did it at two in the morning. The bridge sang, not one note but a layered chord: engines and tires and wind and the less explainable hum of mass held by faith and mathematics. He told me about the crews lowering the caissons, about men in dive suits feeling for bolts with their fingertips in water with the temperature of bone. He was not there when the ribbon was cut. Men like him never are, his friend Luis said and laughed without humor. My father said only, The first morning of testing the fog came in so fast it shrouded the last span and nudged the birds right into the struts, and the sound they made was like hail. He loved the bridge the way men are allowed to love wars and teams and objects: publicly, without apology.

I’m not supposed to take coffee into the booth, but I do. I am supposed to stop every person who says This is free now, right? and give them a lecture about municipal budgets. I am supposed to notify the foreman if any of the regulars who live in their cars have not been seen for three days. I am supposed to be neutral, kind, tidy. Mostly, I am.

At five, the first car is a white sedan with a backseat full of succulents wrapped in newspaper. The driver is a woman with a face like the word careful. I can tell she has packed a home. People think they hide everything in boxes, but it gives you away, the way you drive when the sum of your breakables is behind you. She rolls down her window and holds out an old token with her fingertips, as if it might make a mess on her. “Last one,” she says. “For luck.”

“If you’re moving east, you’re going to need more than one of these,” I say. The heron on the token is worn smooth to an idea.

“I’m going north,” she tells me. “The map at the realtor’s had blue behind the house. But when we went there it was only a thin ditch with tadpoles. Still. Better to pretend.” She looks at the water. The tide is a low belly at the moment, restless but contained. “It used to be different.”

“Everything did,” I say, and take the coin.

Here is something I have never told anyone: I hear the coins when they handle them like this. Not all of them and not in words, exactly, but in a heat, in a pressure in the inside of my hand. The ones taken from a change dish without thought are cool and slap down with no more memory than a pebbledrive. The ones that come out of old cigar boxes or fruit tins from the top shelf of the pantry pulse once, underneath the skin. I have convinced myself this is not magic, that it is nothing more than the body keeping a record of the body. Maybe the metal remembers warmth. Maybe I invent what it remembers. Still, sometimes the palm fills with an image: a man spitting a piece from between his teeth and handing it over to a cashier with a grin, a child holding one to her eyelid and saying See, now I’m a pirate, and the smell of an ocean she has never seen.

The woman breathes in once through her mouth as if trying to memorize the air, then drives on. Fifty feet up the road she taps her brakes lightly and then continues, a person who has decided to hurt no one if she can help it.

Between six and eight, the morning accumulates. Men in fluorescent vests walk the length of the median in pairs, talking without moving their heads. A boy in a hoodie comes over the crest of the rise on a skateboard, pushes himself along the grit at the shoulder for a thrill. The bridge is a mouth on days like this, taking in cars and letting them go, tasting the city in each.

An old man in a hat whose brim has been stitched with fishing line lifts his hand to me before he’s fully pulled up. He keeps it in the air as if he has a question.

“Tell me,” he says, “do you keep them?”

“The coins?” I glance at the tray as if to jog his meaning.

“The stories.” He holds out his palm, and I see the awkward curve of a ring finger. He is missing its ring. “Everybody’s got one to give a bridge.”

“I keep what gets past the glass,” I say. I don’t know if it is an evasive answer or the only true one. He laughs and shakes his head, as if to say fair enough, and sets down three quarters and a button. The button says VOTE YES ON SCHOOL MUSIC with a music staff printed upside down. He has forgotten that it’s in his hand along with his money, and I hand it back. He blanches, thanks me, then leans forward to the lip of the window.

“Long time ago,” he says, “I threw mine right over there. I was so dramatic. Then I had to go look for it like a dog the next day. Spent two hours with a magnet on a string.” He laughs at himself again, but softer. “Three days after that she came back without me asking.”

“That was good of her,” I say.

“She didn’t stay long. But she came back,” he says, as if this is the threshold in a story that makes everything else possible. He puts his hand to the naked ring finger. “My granddaughter tells me when she has to go anywhere hard and fast on this side of the city, she goes over the footpath and throws up. Some people make do with less.”

The lane behind him is empty as far as the far bend, which stretches like a thigh up into sky. He starts his engine again with his hat still in his lap.

“I hope they save a piece of it,” he says, and I know he doesn’t mean the metal.

“They say they will,” I tell him. “They say you’ll be able to buy commemorative paperweights in the shape of herons and ashtrays in the shape of the curve.”

He shakes his head. “I don’t smoke,” he says, as if this were the part that mattered, and goes.

When the sun clears the eastern hills without apology, the light through the booth glass looks like old film. The flaws in the pane make a map. In the gap of cars I walk a little circle in the booth to shake the acrid sleep I have not quite caught, touch the bolt, check for a second time that the novelty siren works, the one that makes a basso foghorn when I push the red button. Its proper purpose is to alert the crew if a car catches fire or a tire comes loose and does its stupendous metamorphosis into weapon. The boys who do nights sometimes press it at two a.m. because sirens sound different when only the sleeping hear them.

The workmen arrive. Their trucks come up the far side with no hurry; they are the kind of men who ocean their way through hours. This is not the dangerous day; that is for later. Today they will finish the last of the barriers, consult the plans, stand around large rolls of paper that are not really paper anymore and draw loops on them with greased fingers. They are younger than my father was when he told me to put my ear to the rail to hear whether the bridge was sad.

A white pickup slides in without stopping. It has a municipal sticker on the windshield and the look of vehicles that think they are invisible.

“Hey there,” says the driver, rolling down his window with three cigarettes on the dash like companions on a road trip. “You the one they wrote the thing about?”

I stiffen like the booth is my body. Two days ago a reporter with the kind of patience that brings stray cats to the door sat for an hour on the curb and then wrote four paragraphs that were mostly about my hands. He made a reasonable case that they were similar to the hands of every other woman who has ever stood between a city and what it thinks it deserves and what it can afford. He quoted me saying that sometimes I think people choose a bridge over a boat because bridges ask you to do your part. That was the only line I liked.

“Maybe,” I say, blandly.

“Here,” he says and passes me a canvas bank bag. It is heavier than it should be, dense in the way of something not meant to be hoisted by one person. “You do me a favor? We cleaned out the lockers from the old paint shed. Guys left all kinds of tokens mixed in with washers and bolts. Figured if anybody wanted to say goodbye in the old way, you probably ran out of souvenirs by now.”

I set the bag on the counter with a grunt. The side of it has the ghost-stencil of a defunct bank’s logo: a yawning vault door. Our boredom that year was such that we pressed the ink to everything, my father said once, and showed me his jeans, faint rings on the thighs where the stamp had bled through.

“You were on paint?” I ask, although it is obvious. He has a widow’s peak etched by a hard hat and a faint scattering of persistent green on his forearms.

“Back before they switched to spray. Back when it took all summer just to get one panel feeling grateful,” he says. “Forty feet in the air in a swing with a man named Avelino who sang like God invented him just for that, and gulls who had the decency to wait their turn to shit on you.”

He laughs when I wince. “The water makes comedians of us all,” he says. “Anyway. Use what you can. Toss what isn’t.” Then, as if embarrassed by his offering, he digs around in the glove compartment and pulls out a lemon. He wipes it on his shirt and hands it to me. It is cool and yields its oil to my palm. “From my neighbor’s tree. She said don’t bring fruit to a tollbooth, but I told her you got to give something people aren’t expecting if you want to be remembered.”

I put the lemon on the ledge next to the bolt. The two of them look like an idea.

“Thank you,” I say. “For all of it.”

“Don’t thank me yet,” he replies. “Half the bag is bottle caps. Guys used to put a cap under the edge of the bolts when they didn’t feel like you could tighten down any more. Makes you feel like you’ve got room to go when you hit it again after the winter. It’s not in the code. But it’s in how things get done.” He reaches across and taps the bag with the back of his fingernails. “Don’t go getting your jobsite shut down,” he teases, and rolls forward.

The bag sighs when I open it. He is right: a cataract of things. A handful of dull washers that have seen the inside of teeth. Bottle caps stamped with brands that no longer exist except on t-shirts in bars. And tokens. Not just the herons but older ones from ferry days—small discs with square holes punched through their bellies, the kind you thread on a string and wear around your neck during wartime. My palm warms as it sifts. If the other coins and tokens are a crowd in a train station, these are a family reunion where you know just enough names to humiliate yourself completely.

I pick up a thin disc with a nick in it like a crescent moon. The metal soft as thought. The instant I touch it I feel—no, I smell—the salt of a secondhand coat, the wool the same age as me. And then a word, not spoken so much as already in the mouth: Marta. Not the way my mother said my name when I was in trouble, not the way men said it after I cut my hair too short to hide inside, but the way my father said it when he found my name in the margins of the newspaper because I had circled it to show how often a name can be asked for in a day in a city this size. He’d traced the O of the printed A with his fingertip, turned it into a fruit on the page. Mártica, he said, stretching the vowel like a hammock.

I make a noise I would not know how to spell. It is as private as rapture and as small.

The booth is not empty. There is a queue of three cars and a cyclist who has made the mistake of thinking he can buy a bottle of water from me. I set the coin down. My hand wants to cling, to stick like performance gift wrap to whatever it has touched, to say No, wait. But being a person is mostly the art of not making a thing about the things you could make a thing about.

“Do you sell water?” the cyclist asks through the glass.

“I can give you a paper cup,” I say, already reaching for the stack. “It’s for the handwashing station but bored men who think of themselves as canyon-far from boring have drunk worse.”

“Happy last day,” he says, accepting the water and finding a way to be on my side without knowing anything about me. “We used to come out here to see the fireworks. Did you get those? The big chrysanthemums?”

“We got the smoke the next morning,” I say, and he laughs and pedals off with the self-satisfaction of the virtuous.

An SUV purrs up.
