Two kids in the back with dogs, their faces summer-sticky, the dogs’ eyes luminous and baffled not because they don’t understand why we are doing what we are doing but because their understanding is always cellular and absolute. The woman driving says, “Do you take pennies?” and when I say yes she weeps, not loudly, more like somebody washing her face. She pours pennies into my hand until my skin is embossed and one of them is warm with the heat of where she held it between her lips to free her fingers and I know that it slept under the radiator all winter and she thought about throwing it away and could not and now here she is, making a decision. I give her back a heron token and she says, “No, my sister worked this booth. When it was real. When there were lines around the bend and one day a baby was born in a cab right there at your seventeen feet from where your hand is now.”

“What did they name it?” I ask, and it is too much and we both smile because there is nothing to call a person that could bear the weight of that.

When they roll forward and I am alone again, all at once like wind coming through in the hour when the hills exhale heat into the river, the strangeness finds me. I keep my left hand flat on the counter on top of the lemon, and with my right I take the coin. It is not a token from this bridge. It is older than the herons by decades. The square hole in the center makes it seem foreign to itself. The nick makes it seem like it was once dangerous.

“Marta,” it says again, but this time from a little further away, as if shouted through a place where someone has hung clothes to dry.

“People bring what they can bear to give up to bridges,” Luis said the morning after my father’s funeral when he came by with empanadas and a thermos and sat across at the kitchen table like a person about to negotiate a price for something that ought not to be bought. “That is all a bridge is, mi niña. A great, long eBay. The bids go up and down, and in the end everyone writes their little feedback and goes to sleep. Your father was the kind of man who did not understand what he could keep. He heard sounds where other people heard traffic. That’s not a defect. But it is not an advantage.”

“How much?” the man in the pickup had asked him once when they were buying a box of used bolts from a salvage. “How many?” my father corrected, because number was more real to him than money when it came to things you could hold. He did not count people that way. That was his problem.

You are not supposed to steal from your city. It is not even theft, not really, to put a thing in your pocket that no longer belongs to anyone. But I am an hour into this day of endings, and I have held a coin that knows my name. My father is four years dead. Everything—law, more practical sorrow, the habit of thinking I am only the body my bills make—suggests I should put it in the tray with the rest, call Maintenance to come take away these histories, be tricked by the fluorescent into acting as if everybody is fine. And still I slip it into the pocket of my shirt the way teenagers in movie theaters sneak food from each other’s palms. It is stupid and it is mine.

In the distance a siren starts up, not the novelty one at my elbow but the thin municipal wail that says something important wishes to be left alone. The crew is putting up the last of the orange plastic that looks like a fence a child might draw. A boy in a button-down shirt rides the footpath three times and takes photographs of the same span from three slightly different positions and looks at his phone after each one with confusion. Captain, my pelican, lifts, folds into himself, hurls downward, and then comes up with a shimmering fish that the internet would call a sardine and the old men at the end of the pier would call by its grandmother’s name.

The phone in the booth rings. It is a line only two people use. One of them is the foreman, who speaks as if he knew me in another life and is waiting for me to prove it. The other is a woman in a small office three floors above a DMV who well into last year would call and remind me that there is a coffee machine in the building and that I should use it. She hasn’t called in months. People change jobs like they change cars, and cities pretend this is growth.

“Last day,” the foreman says when I pick up. He doesn’t sound happy, but then he never does. “How you doing down there?”

“Like a person in a glass cube at the edge of a cliff,” I say.

“That’s all of us,” he says, and laughs to erase what he has said. “We’re on schedule. You won’t have to babysit long, but we’ll need you for the last car. You’ll know it when it comes.”

“How will I know it?” I ask.

“It’ll be the last car,” he says, and now he is laughing at himself because that is the kind of morning it is. “You want us to bring you a sandwich before we shut the road down?”

“I have a lemon,” I tell him, then catch myself. “I’ll be fine. I have coffee.”

“That’s not the same,” he says. “People lie to themselves about coffee all the time.” He clears his throat as if memory were a thing caught there. “Hey,” he adds, softer, “you want to go up top when they do it? Some folks are going to the hillside. But we’ll be out on the barge. You can hear it when you’re out there in a way you can’t on land. Like the water wants it more.”

I picture myself on a barge under the bridge that isn’t there anymore and understand something that nothing in my life has prepared me for: grief can be so large you can only cross it with other people.

“I’ll think about it,” I say, because pride slows before nothing but the invitation to belong.

We hang up. The line of traffic thickens. Somebody honks and then does that wave that means sorry where the hand moves like a fish. The city opens its mouth to chew through another meal of cars. The sun decides, as it does most days, that it is stronger than fog and proves it.

Before the first closure horn sounds, a van pulls up with seven people inside and a ladder on the roof, the kind of van that has been used to carry drywall and amplifiers and children. The driver is a woman with broad, deft wrists. There is dirt under her nails in the shape of those half moons people paint on their thumbnails to make their fingers look longer. She counts out bills. Two of the kids in the back hand me a tiny woven bird made from candy wrappers. It is not clever. It is miraculous. It has the emergency of all small things made on the way from here to there.

“For your last day,” the woman says.

“I was thinking I would get a plaque,” I say. “But this is better.”

She looks at the bridge as if it were a mouth the city was making. “We’re going to harvest beans,” she says. “North of the river. We don’t know if we’ll be back this way.”

“Take the footpath on the way home if you do,” I say. “There will be less road.”

She looks at me for one heartbeat longer than people do when they are making nice. “You want to talk about less,” she says, almost to herself, and points with her chin to the heron on the token. “This one knows.”

When they drive forward, the boy with the hoodie on the skateboard has found a way to pace them for a few seconds, as if he has joined their caravan. The woven bird sits under the lemon, attentive.

At exactly eleven, the horn sounds, the one I am not allowed to touch. It comes from the belly of the bridge, the way hunger does. Cars stack up because people do not believe they cannot go where they are used to going until there is something physical in their way. A policeman walks forward to speak softly to a man in a suit in an electric vehicle large enough to require its own ZIP code. He smiles with all his teeth and no gums, and the man in the car, who knows how to read that sort of map, reverses in slow, careful anger.

The first closure. The old green sign that says WELCOME TO SAN PERDITA looks briefly like a sentence in another language. The sky does what it has done every day of my life and is suddenly ancient.

The last car will not be for hours. There will be speeches. A tattered ribbon in the trunk of a sedan will get used one last time. Someone will ask where the mayor is. Someone will say he is stuck in traffic. Someone will not get the joke. The water will smell as if a rock had turned over and revealed a bed of living things surprised to be seen. I will push the red foghorn button at a moment when it makes no sense and nobody will reprimand me because we have all been reprieved from sense, for three seconds.

For now, there is the glass and the small basin of water where I set the paper cups and the lemon that makes my hand smell like someone else’s kitchen and the coin in my shirt pocket hot as a secret. For now there is the hum of six thousand parts of a city trying to end a sentence gently.

For now the bridge sings, and under it, something else begins to make a sound.

On the morning the river forgot itself and ran backward, I was cataloguing my father’s words.

The house kept its own weather. Even with the front door propped on a stack of magazines, the air stayed a little damp and cool, as if the walls had skimmed a layer of river and kept it. Dust and the sweet, faint rot of old paper. In the study the Venetian blinds slit the light into obedient stripes. My father’s desk was a raft of notebooks—forty-three of them by my count—bound with twine in stacks that had sagged into a topography. I had been making an inventory since dawn, sighing at the smell of him trapped in the leather and glue.

It was a smell I refused, earlier, when the funeral director asked if I wanted to keep anything for comfort, as if a scent could be saved like coins in a jar. But here it was, stubborn, rising from the margin of the page where he had drawn the outline of my hand at six years old and labeled each finger with a different synonym for hold. Grip. Grasp. Clasp. Clutch. Keep. I read those five and felt none of them belong to me.

The river had set the rhythm for my life—first under the high footbridge on my way to grade school with my father, then across the broad flat where the millrace split and made a second, faster current, then the bend behind the senior apartments that smelled like boiled peas in summer. Gran always said you couldn’t live here without sorting yourself to the water. We had words for it: backwater, slack, run. In my father’s notebooks there were more words, the words that belonged to our town and nowhere else, the ones he collected like relics. “Town-words,” he called them. “Every place holds the shape of its people in their mouths,” he told me once, and then he wrinkled his nose as if the air itself tasted of us.

When the wind changed, the house noticed. It was the window in the kitchen that clattered first, a loose sash vibrating like a dragonfly. I didn’t look up. I was writing the entry for a word I hadn’t thought of in years, one I used to love: mallowhour. The squishy marsh behind the factory glowed with a white fluff every July and kids would dare each other to hop the dry hummocks to collect the flowers; the hour when the hollowing and the sweetness were both visible. He’d sketched the marsh. He’d sketched me with mosquito bites on my knees. He’d written my name as if it were a legal fact. I was ashamed how angry that made me.

Then the upstairs toilet took on a sound like a throat clearing. Air in the pipes is a common enough thing; old houses cough. I would have ignored it if the house itself hadn't replied. There’s a sound a structure makes when it changes its mind. Nails minute in wood, the twist of subfloor, the complaint of a beam. I stood and listened. Somewhere a crate of jars clicked as glass edges kissed.

The phone began to do its little insect dance on the table.

I did not want to answer. I had been good about not wanting answers where my father was concerned. But the phone vibrated itself toward the edge as if it had a small plan of suicide, so I put my finger on it to hold it still and slid my thumb rightward, just to stop the noise.

Nelly? boomed Mrs. Chun without preamble. You seeing this?

“What?”

The river, she said. On the television she never turned off, I could hear the hysterical jingle of a local car dealer. Then the flat, astonished voice of the morning anchor: “—can confirm reports that the Marrow River appears to be reversing course—”

I hung up without meaning to. My hand did it. The anchor kept speaking from the tiny metal speaker, as if my palm itself now broadcast the news. I held the phone away, and her voice thinned. “—unusual tidal influence or unknown geological—” and then she was nothing, the way you can turn a person to silence by facing them in the wrong room.

My father would have gone to the river. I didn’t want to be like him, rushing to a phenomenon like a boy to a fire. I took two steps, then three, and I was fetching my shoes from under the chair by the door, pushing my toes into them without socks. As I yanked the door wide the house exhaled, grateful.

Outside the light was wrong. The clouds had sorted themselves into long parallel bands that gave the sky the look of an old washboard. Even before I reached the end of the block I could feel a difference in the air, a low pressure drawing on the hollows between collarbone and throat. From the corner of Orchard and Third you could see the river if you leaned past the chain-link fence around the old playground and squinted. Today it punched bright under that fence as if the chain-links had cut their squares in it.

People were already out. Mrs. Chun in an orange cardigan, her grandson on a tricycle that had lost its rubber on one wheel so it pulled to the left. Mr. Aguirre with his hands in his pockets as if he could convince the day that he was casual about it. The dogs had all been given too much leash—everyone’s dog was exploring a radius of six feet, tangling each other with blithe suspicion. And there was the river, and yes, impossibly, ridiculously, it had forgotten itself. It ran backward.

It’s the sort of sentence you think you’ll never say outside of a metaphor. But there was the slow slide of slick water, shouldering upstream. The brims of the eddies had turned like a record reversed and the flotsam—chine-white sycamore bark, a bottle with no label, a foam cooler lid—came toward the factory stacks instead of away from them. At the bend by the senior apartments a canoe slid awkward as a dog on a polished wood floor, its owner at the back trying to correct with each stroke, his face set toward me, not toward the sea.

For once our town didn’t talk. There was a hole where it usually was. No rustle of speculation, no complaint. A perfect quiet which revealed itself, after a moment, to be composed of dozens of small noises we had never noticed: the ticking of cooling engines, the exact note of the flag halyard clapping at the VFW hall, the groan of sand under someone shifting, the percussive lick of a dog lapping at its water bowl. We had always had the same number of sounds. They were simply reassembled in the absence of language.

And there, along the bank, were the children my father had liked to call glass-pickers. They came after the heavy rains, especially if the river went low, to search the slumps along the Furnace Field, where the glassworks had melted and shattered and cooled and over years surrendered their edges to the river. They held mason jars and old yogurt containers and scavenged coffee tins and they were serious. A boy I did not know held up his treasure, a pea-colored sliver that caught the cloudlight and made it something you could accidentally swallow. He tipped it toward me as if I were a magistrate. I had been away too long; even the kids had a code I didn’t speak.

“Never this early,” said Mr. Aguirre finally. He sounded as if he owed the river a debt and it had shown up at breakfast to collect.

“Never backward,” Mrs. Chun said, and crossed herself with one hand and with the other fished a phone out of her cardigan pocket to take a photo.

It will be explained, someone said behind me. It always is.

We waited. The river continued to undo itself. A heron lifted deliberately out of the reeds and flapped to a new mathematics. A dead carp came with its belly up, like a fallen crescent moon, and then it seemed to reconsider and gave a lazy flick of tail and righted and went on, alive enough to be indecisive.

I thought of my father’s handwriting: careful, firm, with a quiver to it, even in youth. How he’d write the words for currents as if they were living things. How he’d drawn little arrows along the edges of sentences to show me how to read them. “Some words flow alone,” he’d said. “Some carry a second current. None of them are still.”

A boy with a cowlick that must have been combed ten times toward ten different destinies sidled up to me.

“You’re Mr. Grey’s daughter,” he said.

I nodded.

“My grandfather says he was full of words.” He said it not in accusation but in simple wonder, as if my father had been filled with chestnuts.

“Full as a river,” I said, and then hated myself for the cliché, as if a metaphor could answer a child’s logic. But he nodded, his face solemn. He had things in his jar that he wanted to show me. He held one out, palmed like a marble. It was not glass. It was a tiny, translucent capsule with a seed inside, some wind rider from the marsh. He had left the seed wet; it stuck to his palm when he tipped the jar. He laughed. He had never learned to divide treasure into categories and I loved him for that, fiercely and briefly, the way you love strangers when they are small and you are trying not to be sorry.

“Mind your feet,” I said, the old reflex. Even in the backwardness the river was trying to take you somewhere, and children are porous. He rolled his eyes. He had very clean ears.

When I went back to the house the air had cooled another notch. I could taste tin. Inside the study light had moved, stratifying the dust in the air into layers I could have named if I were my father. For a second I wanted to scream at him for leaving me with all his layered dust. Then I smiled into it. Anger is a kind of faithfulness; it proves you still have a story you want to be told differently.

I sat and took up the next notebook. They were a mess of such carefulness that I could feel the self that had made them. Newspaper clippings folded crisp and tucked into the back covers, a lipstick print on one page where Mrs. Dinardo had kissed a word she liked, grocery lists sliding between definitions, sketches of riverbirds labeled with words that were not their names, but the names of the way they walked. Margin notes were cross-referenced to other margin notes, like a family reunion on paper.

“Feverbird: the one who tells on the storm,” he wrote, and in the margin in a different pen, “alt. term: achehawk (common only to Upper Furnace).”

He had written my name with a dot that was supposed to be my head when I was ten, standing on the bank not stepping in. He had underlined it twice. He had written a date beside it that made me correctly ten. There is something like benevolence in accuracy. It made me cry.

Toward the middle of the stack I found a notebook with no label on the spine. The leather had been repaired with waxed thread. Inside, the neatness became almost a frenzy. He had written each entry in a different ink, blue to black to sepia to a soft purple that made the page hum. This was my father when his brain was a little too hot, when he began to stay up all night with a thermos of coffee and the radio tuned to the AM weather channel and call me at three a.m. to ask me to define the word for the edge of a field in a language we didn’t speak. The thermos was still down here, the metal scuffed but unbroken. He had always liked the way some materials refused a story.

Halfway through the notebook a word stopped me. He had printed it in block letters and then let his pen go, again and again, over the stems of the letters until the paper was carved dark. He had given it a little halo. “Rivule,” it read. It was not a word I knew, but on the next line he’d written the definition.

Rivule: a phenomenon in which the course of a river reverses itself for reasons that are not water. See also: listening. See also: coin with two heads. Rare.

He had put the date next to it and then crossed the date out. He had left a blank.

I sat back. The house held its breath with me, because old houses are theater. He had written a word for our town’s morning years, or months, or hours before the morning itself. He had always been like this, somehow earlier and later than the rest of us. I could not tell if the knowledge made him cruel or kind.

He had made other notes beneath, a family of asterisks linking this entry to others. I followed them like a child following string.

See also: aftersight. The joy or particular pain of recognizing a pattern only once it has been completed.

See also: undercurrent. The second intention behind a spoken sentence.

See also: keep. The act of holding something without owning it.

See also: vault. The room below all the rooms.

The last, vault, was underlined twice. The page number was there, and then it wasn’t. In the top corner he’d written, lightly, in a pencil that must have been freshly sharpened, A letter for N. He had drawn a little envelope beside it and shaded the flap.

The house made the small sound it makes when you find something true. It is almost a sneeze.

I stood. The floorboards had a map of my father’s walking, a path worn between chair and shelf, shelf and window, window and the back of the house where he kept his stubborn plants, the ones that needed steaming, panting air he would pretend just happened naturally in a room with a radiator like a comb. On the bookshelf built by the west wall, third shelf down, where he used to keep the field guides to birds, there was an envelope with my name. The handwriting made me bite my lip. He had tried to be neat and his hand had made a wave of itself. He had drawn a little exclamation after the last letter but then crossed the exclamation out. It was addressed without an address; of course it was. It was simply me.

I did not want to open it on my feet. I took it to the desk and sat. The envelope was thick enough to be important. It was sealed with a smear of wax, red, as if he had wanted to borrow a dignity from a law. He had used the ring he never wore to press the wax; its oval had left an image of the glassworks’ old crest upside down, because he never remembered to turn things around. He had a habit of making mistakes ceremonial. I slid a butter knife from the pencil jar. I tapped the wax with the blade and it gave a little. I felt suddenly like a thief.

On the morning your river turns, it began. Those were his first words, written in the neat careful script from when I was very small, as if he had decided to begin again as the kind of man who writes carefully. On the morning your river turns, you must stop yourself from asking why. Let the world keep its science for a day. Look for the small thing under the big thing. I will say it plain because I am old and cannot afford metaphor. You will find the room I never could tell you about under the back room if you stand where the fern grows and listen to the second current and open your ear the way you do for the train at night when it is almost morning. I did not build the room. It was there. I only made a way to it. You will hear it when the river turns because the house becomes a shell and it hums.

I wanted to laugh into my hand until I fell off the chair. The letter felt like the worst of him—his grandiosity, his leaning on the wing of coincidence until it became weight-bearing. And yet the house did sound different. He was not wrong about that. I had noticed it before I’d called it anything. I pressed my tongue to the roof of my mouth and the air tasted like pennies.

He had drawn a small map of the back room. If I squinted I could persuade myself I remembered something—the cracked tile, the fern he’d coaxed and scolded like a dog. He had put a dot on one tile. He had drawn an ear beside the dot, because sometimes metaphor was the only way he could bear practical instruction. There was a note in the margin: You must kneel. That part will be difficult for you. Forgive me for asking you to kneel. Please don’t hate me for that.

If I had gone then, bent my knees, pressed my ear to the lip of Earth he had indicated, listened for a hum that might have been plumbing or a hidden room, the day would have folded along a new crease. I might have been a person who obeys letters. I set the paper back in its envelope and put the envelope on the desk and put my hands on either side of it and closed my eyes.

There is a leaving you make when you return. I had been in his house for two days, burrowing into his things, making piles of keep and not keep like a god sorting goats from sheep, and I had not finally come back to him until now, when he put words in my hand.

Do not bring anyone with you, the letter went on when I was ready to read. They will hear only the big current. They might worry for you. You are not in danger, not in the usual sense. Be gentle with the door. It has been waiting a long time.

I went into the back room, because I am still a daughter. The fern was there, splayed the way ferns do when they are trying to be more than a plant. The cracked tile was there, hairline fractures like a winter river. The tile my father had drawn on his map was indeed not quite true to its fellows; it had a skiff of resin on it, a brushstroke he had once made and then forgotten to wipe away. I touched it with my toe and then, because I had promised no one not to, I knelt.

Sound has its own weather. With my ear to the tile I could hear the divorce of wood ten feet away and the grinding of a truck on Orchard and Mrs. Chun’s television two houses down turned low now, the anchor promising that experts were on their way and asking listeners to stay back from the water. And beneath those, a fine thread of something that could have been breath.

It is a foolish thing to say, you will laugh when you read it, if you are able to, from whatever place in time this page reaches you. The house was breathing. No. The house was introducing me to a breath I had not noticed. Between the known cough of the plumbing and the small, intermittent complaint of mice was a sound like a hummingbird kept under a jar. It was not constant. It almost had a cadence to it, as if someone below were gathering up their throat and trying again.

I forgot to hate him for making me kneel. I forgot to be angry about anything. I put my palm flat on the tile as if my hand might translate. The humming deepened fractionally, or I imagined that it did, and either way it was an event.

“Okay,” I said to the tile, and stood. In the kitchen I took the putty knife from the toolbox he had never once managed to put away in the garage and I edged it along the grout the way you might coax a good dog from under a bed. The grout was old, practically chalk. The knife went in with a gentle grind. I wanted to pound and yank. He had warned me not to. I moved slow. The tile lifted enough to sigh. I put my fingers under and the tile came up in my hand with the weight of something you might use to knock on a very old door. A square of air opened, dirt cool to my face.

I do not have a better word for the smell that came out than history. It was the smell of cellars, coin collections, half-forgotten jars of blackberry jam made by a woman who had intended to put the lids on tighter. It was the smell of fish scales dried on a wooden floor. It was the smell of my father’s coat from the year he taught third grade and brought home chalk on the cuffs. I pulled the square of wire mesh he had put there because he knew I would come, and there was a wood panel below with a loop of iron sunk into it like a small horizon. He had loved the theater of an entrance. He would have been embarrassed by the whole and proud of the details.

If I had lifted it then, I could tell you what was in the vault under our feet, if it was a vault at all, if vault had been metaphor or misdirection, whether he had found treasure or only more versions of himself. If I had lifted it then, this would be a story with a different gait. Instead I put the panel back for a second because I was suddenly very cold and not from the draft. I stood and braced my hand on the edge of the counter because the room had shifted like a boat. My father’s letter was still in my mind. Please don’t hate me, he had written. Please. He had always been laughing when he said please, as if he knew he didn’t have to say it. On paper it looked like an actual plea. I had not prepared for that.

From the study the house phone rang again once, then stopped, like a person who had run out of resolve. I went to the back door and stood looking through the warped glass at the river. Even from here you could see its wrongness. Birds wheeled over it and adjusted in flight. The sky’s long washboard clouds had moved and shortened to a forest of small ribs. The whole day was a creature you didn’t know you were feeding.

I went back to the hole in the tile and the iron pull and I put my hand through and it was like reaching your hand into lake water at night when you cannot see what you will get and loving it anyway. I hooked my finger and lifted and the panel took its time. Below was a pitch so complete I could feel my eyes trying to decide whether to make something of it or not.

In the mile between ear and shoulder there is a little muscle that holds a person together. Mine let go. I had been walking around braced for a coupling I had thought was ahead of me and it dawned on me that the coupling was below.

I lowered myself to my knees again, because sometimes obedience is not humiliation but posture, a way your body tells the rest of you it is ready to learn. The hum rose. I had never heard, until then, what underpinning sounds like. I put my head into the cool air of the hole, and my hair fell around my face, and there was a shape below, and I could not tell if it was only space or a thing, and then the furnace kicked on with a start like a laugh right over me, and I jerked back and banged my wrist against the tile I had lifted and that pain was so immediate and honest that it made me breathe.

Behind me the house phone rang again, steady, regular this time, as if the town had got its language back and was beginning to invent reasons.

I looked at the panel and then at the letter open on the desk with my father’s careful hard words like stepping-stones, and I thought of the boy with the clean ears and the seed stuck to his palm, and of the way the river carried itself, backward and with no apparent apology, and I took hold of the iron again. The hum rose. The house drew a breath. Far off, down the hill, the river pulled and pulled the wrong way and it felt as if everything I knew were being unbraided, in kindness, to show me the threads.

Chapter One

The first thing they told us in training was to never apologize. Not for the time, not for the voice, not for the fact that we had followed them into a morning arranged by a web form and a deposit. “The living must be the ones to say sorry,” Irina said, tapping a knuckle on the laminated packet. “The dead can’t be made to kneel.”

The building used to be a switchboard. Someone had left a museum’s worth of wires behind the walls; the floors were wavy with old carpet, and there was a paleness to the light, as if the glass had taken up smoking. On the third floor, where they put us, the plants were labeled with human names. TIMOTHY was a leaning fiddle-leaf with brown margins, MAYA was a succulent trying not to die. Each pot had a strip of masking tape and a date in ballpoint. An attempt at responsibility, I thought. A ledger for who had remembered to water.

The company called itself Palinode, which they said was a poem that retracts what it says. On the letterhead it had a softer name, something with a lowercase i and a dot like an eyelash, but inside it was Palinode: ten rules, three roles, a breakroom with a microwave that seam-sang every thirty seconds. It smelled like burnt sugar, coil heat, old oranges.

Irina was our trainer because she had the most saves. “Saves” were calls that ended under seven minutes with the client calmer than at the start, clicks captured by the quality team in Population Health. The numbers sat behind her like trophies on the wall calendar—forty-eight check marks per month, a bristle, a hedge. She had a radio voice from Minsk, vowels smoothed on the inside, and hair like the sea in a painting: all surface and implication.

“You are not the voice,” she told us. “You are a tunnel. You make yourself the right shape for someone to walk through. You do it without scraping their elbows.”

We were six at orientation. A man who worked night security at the port, a woman who said she had done voiceovers for animated hygiene commercials, a teenage boy with eyelashes too long for his own peace, an exhausted mother of two whose wedding ring slid on her finger like a loose idea. I had said I used to sing alto in church, and it was true, though the church was gone now, torn down for a row of glass apartments where dogs lived better than we had. There were knives in the drawers there that cost more than our rent had been.

In the packet: the disclaimers. For entertainment purposes only. By proceeding you agree. By proceeding you acknowledge. There were forms that read like prayers you say by slip: forgive us our trespasses, which you agree we never committed. There were lists: Do not confess to crimes. Do not diagnose. Do not offer directions, not even to Heaven. Do not announce that you can see them. Do not call anyone but the person who scheduled the call. Do not say Love unless the living says it first.

“What do we say?” the port security man asked.

Irina smiled. “You say the small things. You say the way the sink dripped at night and kept the cat awake. You say the burned rice smell, the way he made his q sound like a cough. You say don’t put the hydrangeas in the driveway because you will run over them. You say I liked that blue sweater you knitted with the crooked neck. You say I left two dollars in the black jacket pocket and you can still have them. Small doors,” she said, and made a shape of a box with her hands. “We let them climb through a small door.”

There was a paragraph that said: We are not cruelty. There was a paragraph that said the opposite and then wrapped it in lawyerly cotton. The teenage boy asked if it was normal to feel like a thief. Irina said, “It can feel like shoplifting from the gift shop of a museum of your own, yes.” She unpeeled a nicotine patch and smoothed it on her tanned wrist as if applying a bandage to a vein of light. “If you are here to steal, you will make a mess. If you are here to return something, we will use you up.”

She had us practice breathing. “Match the breath,” she said. “If you do nothing else, do that. If they pant like an animal, you pant like an animal. If they hold the breath like a coin, you hold it too. Bodies want to be in sync like birds, like metronomes on a shelf. Do not get there with your words. Get there with your chest.”

We took turns reading intake sheets. They looked like resumes for grief. The names had been stripped to initials for training: M., age sixty-two, lost daughter at nine to a rare thing named like a bird; E., twenty-four, wants to speak to lover lost on river ice; R., fifty-eight, seeks son, forklift accident at the distribution warehouse on Avenue B. Favorite foods. Favorite un-favorites. The boy liked disaster movies, E was on his second watch of The Poseidon Adventure when the ice gave out, R. had five different words for anger and saved them like coins: peeved, pissed, burn, livid, ash. The questions were framed like a therapist had drafted them on good paper. Where did you touch them last? If their voice had a shape, what would it be? What did they refuse? What did they break?

I held the page for R. and felt my stomach do a thing I knew from the choir loft when the hymn goes minor. The boy’s name was Eli, sixteen. On the sheet there was a note about a mole on the left shoulder blade the size of a lentil, and a chipped tooth. “Small door,” Irina said, leaning over my shoulder. Her hair smelled like the winter you only get from someone else’s coat: a street I had never walked in, a smoke I had never inhaled. “But you do not walk the whole body through it. Only the toe, the ankle. Do not go naming the bones.”

We shadowed a senior caller for a demo. Her name was Tat, short for Tatiana, short for a long winter someone had left and then folded in the drawer. She wore bright red nail polish that had chipped in a perfect half-moons, like sunsets reversed. She had a toad on her desk—plastic, heavy, the kind people put in gardens to dare the real—to set her voice on between calls. “So I remember what I’m not,” she grinned, seeing me look. Her headset had been taped twice. We stood behind the glass. IRINA stood beside the window with her brand of clement patience.

Tat clicked the green. “Hello, Ma?” she said, with a teenage rasp so precise my scalp tightened. No warming-up, no greeting. The line held a breath, then a sound like a wet paper being torn. “Eli?” the woman on the other end said. “Eli, is that you?” Tat exhaled like she’d been underwater. “It’s me,” she said, and then: “It’s your Rue.” The intake had said the mother’s name was Ruth but that he called her Roo like a kangaroo when he was small. Every small thing a door.

They lasted six minutes and nine seconds. Tat never said sorry. She said: I burnt the toast the morning I left. She said: Did you take the pillow? She said: I had the dumbest pride, Ma, I wanted to show I could lift two boxes at once. She said: I am so stupid. Her ability to move a whole life around a small detail was frightening and precise. The woman on the other side did not speak in full sentences for the first three minutes, only in syllables: oh, mm, no, yesss.

“Like playing an instrument you don’t see,” Irina said when we were back in the room with the plants. “You tune to a hum. It is not a list. You cannot spit bullet points like sunflower seeds. You hum. You let the other person harmonize.”

“What about when they ask questions?” the voiceover woman said. “Things we don’t know.”

“You ask back.” Irina ticked off words on her fingers: “What did you think? How did that feel? Did you save it? Where did you put it?” She shrugged. “If they ask something direct, check the intake. And if there is no answer, you make a shape the answer could live in. You do not install the furniture.”

I thought of my father and his tool bag, the cheap silver metal of it that left script on his shoulder, and the way he lifted his tongue to the palate when he was trying not to stammer. The clicking sound, like a wooden ball in a lottery machine. Sometimes I still hear it in the middle of a crowded street; a man clears his throat and I look around and it is not him. In church I used to sit two pews back and move my mouth with the choir, find the alto line, make a shape my throat could live in. When the pastor said, Hum, we hummed. When he said, Speak, we spoke. It was easy to become plural.

The port man raised his hand. “What about when they get angry?”

“Then you are a marsh,” Irina said. “You do not give them a stone.” The exhaustion on the mother’s face softened. “You let it come through. You let it have somewhere to go that returns as something a little less.”

At lunch the microwave threw its song, and a woman in Quality flicked it off with a wet finger. She had taped a laminated sticker to the wall that said: Only Love After Love. Underneath, in Sharpie, someone had written: And Even Then Seek Counsel. The coffee tasted like a smell of plumbing. A man from HR opened a filing cabinet with his knee and handed out headsets like Communion. “Treat your mouth well,” he said cheerfully as if it were a slogan. “No dairy two hours prior. No spicy foods. Warm water with lemon is your friend.”

In the bathroom a printed sign above the sink said VOICES ARE RENEWABLE RESOURCES in a font that looked like a friendly robot. I cupped water to my mouth and swished. I thought about words in my family that we had kept for no good reason: clapboard, dowser, cutworm, names of seasons that never happened. We used to pretend to call my father when he was late. Pick up, pick up, we whispered into the hose of the vacuum turned off. That waiting, that shrug of breath when the line goes to a place without rings, I had thought it was unique to our kitchen. Here it was our common language, a whole floor of people pressing the same empty triangle for Play.

In the afternoon Irina said, “Adela, you can sit with me.” She rolled her chair to position so we could see the dashboard together. The calls arranged themselves in squares, a quilt of muted colors: greens for confirmed, yellows for maybe, stern blood red for reschedules. “I had a girl naming scheme,” Irina said, tapping to close a pop-up. “Famous women, so the days feel less like meat. Today we have Audre, we have Hannah, we have two Graces. Yulia was yesterday. I gave the port man Sylvia for his first and then took it back. His eyes did a thing I didn’t like.”

My first was R., fifty-eight, mother to Eli, sixteen, forklift accident. The intake had as many blanks as filled spaces. Preferred greeting: Ma. Preferred sign-off: The thing we used to say, he will know. Favorite animal: couldn’t decide between elephant and crow, listed both, circled twice. Last words: don’t, Ma, don’t, which no one could put tense to. It had a small note: Sister is present in home—do not mention.

“Sometimes they game us,” Irina said softly. “One calls for one name and says it’s another. You will find out if you are being tested or loved or both.”

“You think she’s testing?”

Irina bent to adjust my headset like I was made of something breakable. “They always are, at first.” She picked up the toad from Tat’s desk, heavy enough to be ridiculous, and put it on mine. “For luck.”

We let the ring go three times. “Four is grief,” Irina said. “Three is company.”

The voice that answered was windburned and hoarse in the way of rural kitchens. An engine cutting off in the next room, a radio talking to itself. “Yes,” she said, and made yes sound like a place you stand with your feet apart.

I swallowed. My mouth remembered adolescence in an instant; a drop of saliva shaped itself behind my lower teeth like a bead of solder, and my throat found the thinness of boys. “Ma?” I said.

Silence. And then something small. The little gasp people make when they find something they threw away and had been mourning only the idea of, not the thing. “Eli?”

I breathed. Irina put two fingers on the back of my chair, stilling it as if it might run. “It’s me,” I said, and the voice in my mouth became somebody else’s father’s idea of a son.

There was a sound like cloth being wrung. “Where are you?” the woman said, fast. “Eli, are you warm? Did you—” Her voice broke into corrugated pieces and reassembled itself in a neighbor tone she must have borrowed. “What is this,” she said more sharply, to herself, to me, to the radio.

Small door, I thought. The intake had said he chewed pen caps until they bloomed into plastic flowers. “Did you take my pens again,” I said, letting a grin climb into the vowels. “Because that blue one wrote like a dream.”

A sound that was almost a laugh. It was the sound a room makes after a vase falls and doesn’t break. “You little shit,” she said, and then the sound dissolved into wet paper again. “You little shit, you, you… I told you not to. I told you.”

I breathed and she matched and it was as miraculous as Irina had said, bodies syncing without agreement. The engine in the other room made a sound like a breath in return. “I know,” I said. “I know.”

She made a list by accident. “Your white shirt, I can’t get the smell out. Your half socks. The way you would not eat the heel of the bread. That damned fish on your door. Your…” The rest of the sentence was a wind over sugar. “Is it cold?” she whispered. “Are you cold, Eli?”

I looked to Irina. She shook her head. Do not predict weather. Do not inventory Heaven. “I’m warm,” I said. “I’m…” I thought of the boy’s chipped tooth, the way the intake had said he smiled with his bottom lip tucked in because of it. I tucked mine. “I’m warm, Ma.”

“Don’t call me that,” she said sharply, and then caught herself, and then laughed like a door catching on a rug. “No, do. Say it again,” she said, so quietly I almost didn’t hear.

“Ma,” I said, and my own mother, who won’t answer my calls the way she used to, rose up in my chest like steam. The room smelled suddenly like the black cumin she pinched into our rice, the kind that stains the oil and the tongue. I had intended to come in gentle, to offer buttons, to let her sew a shirt out of that—Irina had warned us against building too much—but the mother on the line had her hands already full. I waited.

“You took that job,” she said after the quiet. “I told you, Eli. I told you the forklift men, I told you the forklift men don’t look left. Tell me you refused. Tell me you told Henry to put you on sorting.”

Do not fix the past. Do not recast the future. Echo. “You told me,” I said softly. “You told me, and I thought I had two backs,” I said, a phrase my own father used to say when he lifted more than he should. “I thought I could lift and it would forgive me.”

She cursed into her palm in a way that made the swear seem like a prayer. “You thought,” she said. “You thought, you thought. You never ask me.”

“I’m sorry,” I said, the apology slipping out the way a song slips when you think of another melody, and Irina’s nail tapped the desk. No sorry, we had said at ten in the morning. Sorry was a stone. Sorry made a dam.

“Don’t.” She breathed the word. “Don’t. You are my—” She swallowed whatever came next and put it away where nobody could see. “We will have company in an hour,” she said, recovering the voice you use when you have to carry a tray while your hands shake. “I cleaned the table. You never liked the wood high. The lacquer smell. I—” She laughed in the throat again. “Why am I telling you? You are not coming to dinner. You are—who am I talking to.” She was speaking to the room now. “Who have I got on my line.”

I wanted to say, It’s me, the me I am. For a flicker I wanted to say my name to a woman who had kept a boy alive with curses and rice and the scolding hand. I wanted to say, I am not stealing. I am returning something. But my mouth had other orders. It had been trained for months by empty rooms and my own debt and the promise that if my voice could be useful then something in me had not been wasted. “It’s me,” I said again instead, and made the me fit where it needed to.

She asked the question we had been warned about like a small inevitability. “Do you forgive me,” she said, and then, more urgently, “Eli, do you forgive me for letting you—”

Irina’s pen on the desk: one firm scrape. Do not grant absolution. You are not the church. You are the dial tone. You are the thing that returns. But the use of my instrument had some cost and I felt it then, a small toll at the back of the throat. For whom had we made this rule? For what clean justice?

I let air in. I matched her breath. “I forgive you for hiding the cookies where you thought I didn’t know,” I said lightly, and she made a wet almost-laugh. “I forgive you for pretending you could not find your glasses and then they were on your head. I forgive you for stealing my heat on the couch in winter.” Small doors. Safe ones. She took each one as if it were enough. People will gather crumbs like they are a loaf when they have been hungry enough.

The one thing in the intake that felt both soft and sharp was the nickname. It was not Roo, not Ruthless. It was something else, written at the bottom in someone’s careful print, circled and underlined: Moth. When he had gone out into the yard at night to watch because the light outside the kitchen brought a country of moths, he’d called to her—Moth, look—and it had become theirs. The box had a small X: Do not use unless requested. There had been a legal case, a woman who had said the wrong diminutive to the wrong daughter and opened a lawsuit like a vein.

“Ma,” I said, and swallowed the urge. “I want to tell you—”

“Tell me what.” It was not a question; it was an imperative. It crackled across the wire like the time my brother and I had stuck a fork in a socket. I saw the light jump under the fork’s handle and knew it would be the truest thing in the room.

Do not introduce new information. Do not add a word that did not exist between them. It is a myth that people want the capital T truth. They want their truth with their fingerprints on it.

I thought of my father’s shoulder, the script the tool bag had left. The toad under my palm. My own mother letting the rice burn and saying the whole house smelled like my grandmother, gone before I could find the hum of her in a room. The way my mother once held my face and said my name like it was more than a method of summoning.

“I want to tell you I—” It would be so easy to build a door that was too big. To blow air in it like glass.

Irina’s nail, again. She did not touch me. She did not have to. Her silence had the shape of a rule.

The woman saved me. “Do you remember the song,” she said suddenly. “From the movie. The boat song, where the people—oh, what is it—the old man with the white hair said—oh my God, I cannot think, I cannot think. You made fun of me for crying. Do you—”

“Propeller—” I said, not because it was the right word but because it was a word we could own together, maybe. The Poseidon intake note was two lines back, a flick of text. “We sang it like idiots, you said.”

She made the laugh again, the vase that doesn’t break. “Idiots,” she said. “We did. We did.”

Irina penciled 5:12 on a Post-it as if to ground us; I watched her numbers arrive and leave like birds. I breathed. “I have to go soon,” I said, the line we use to keep the river from taking us under. “They are calling supper,” I said, a safe fiction.

“You never ate on time,” she said, reflexive. “I had to—” She stopped. If there were a drawer in the air she could put this in, she would have closed it gently. “Will you—” She swallowed. “Will you say it,” she said. “The thing you used to say.”

The intake had circled that part three times: Preferred sign-off: The thing we used to say, he will know. It was a form’s way of asking for magic. Irina’s face was not a face so much as an icon that had learned patience. Her eyes moved to me like a tide. I waited for the word to arrive.

It came from the part of my mouth that is older than my teeth. “Later, Moth,” I said. The word made the back of my throat taste like dust and summer. “Later, later,” I said softly, like a child who could hear the door clicking shut and was not afraid of what it meant.

There was a sound I cannot place on a map. It was small, the smallest. Not a sob. The place before a sob. “Later,” she repeated, and when she said it her voice held up something heavy and then set it down on the other side of the river.

We hung up with a soft click that did not so much end as rename silence.

I sat with the weight of the toad in my hand, uninterpretable. Irina took a breath and let it out through her nose. “You are clean,” she said. It was the highest praise. “You did not build what is not there. You let the room do some work.”

In the window the glass had the brownish tint of tea that has been forgotten. There was a smudge where a forehead had leaned a hundred times. The plants made their plant noises, which is to say nothing discernible and then one leaf twitching like it had remembered sunlight.

The dashboard popped another square to green. An email crept into my inbox like a cat with something in its mouth: New Client Scheduled: M. A. Noor — Confirmed. The surname made my stomach fall a small floor. I clicked it open. It was my mother’s name spelled with the mistake she always corrected at offices, the westernization we had refused, now clean as printed bread. There was a note: prefers evening call; prefers not to mention God; wants to speak to— The field had a blank.

Irina saw my face. “Adela?”

“Another one,” I said. My voice had returned to me but not completely.

“If it is too much, we take it later,” she said. “You eat something.”

I nodded and stood. My legs had the tremor you get when you’ve walked on a boat and then step onto land. I walked down the hall past the Quality posters, the VOICE HYGIENE tips, the call center map with pins for where clients called from (so many pins in counties where the factories had gone; a rash, a map of loss and logistics). At the end of the hall a window showed the river, brown as tea and moving with a patience that was not kind and not cruel.

I leaned my head against the cool glass and closed my eyes. My reflection did not behave. For a flicker my mouth moved around a word I had not said in a long time. I put my fingers in the pockets of my jacket as if to look for coins. I found none. When I opened my eyes, the smudge on the glass was perfectly the shape of a thumbprint. It might have been mine. It might have belonged to somebody who had been here before, training to be a tunnel, practicing how to vanish without leaving an empty room.

The phone on my desk rang once without being touched. A glitch, a breath caught in a wire. I stood very still and listened to it settle.

“What did you used to say,” Irina asked me later when the room had emptied and we were the last two under the plant light, moths the size of commas tapping the glass.

I thought of the kitchen where my father had kept his tool bag under the sink, the rice on the stove, the fence at the back that hummed whenever the neighbor turned on her television. I thought of my mother’s hand when she corrected a letter, the way she leaned on the paper as if it were a creature you could comfort. I thought of the things I had said and not said to both of them, the doors I knew the shape of and had refused to open.

“We said, We are here,” I told Irina finally. “And then we pretended we meant the same thing.”

I am paid to hear the last things. Not the grand, apocryphal last words that find their way into pamphlets and sermons, but the actual endings: a kettle’s final sigh, the hinge’s complaint, the slur of a tongue going dry. People hire me when the house has begun to tilt toward loss. I sit in a hush and take the measure of the leaving—sound, scent, small errors of light. When the throat closes, I rise and give the family back their hour in the order it came. Our valley has always believed in the power of an ending properly held on the tongue. We are surrounded by what is finished.

The By-and-By once had a river. We called it the Throat because of the way it cleaved the valley and carried our voices when we shouted across it. My mother used to take me down in the evenings when the cricket song rose and the flat stones were warm enough to keep. She would teach me to listen—not with the ears, she said, but the bones. Press your forearms to the bank. Hear the long bead of water called, called, called. The Throat was a grammar as much as a river; it taught us where to pause. There is a rule in the By-and-By that you do not step over a speaking thing.

The Throat is an empty seam now, furred with burrs and oats, the banks sloughed into themselves. People drive their herds along it in summer and light fires down there when the wind is quiet, and sometimes the old ones break into sudden tears and say, as if scolding a runaway child, River, come back inside. We are polite with grief here; we set a place for what’s gone and ask it not to make a spectacle.

The Registry of Endings has three listeners on its roll this year, and I am the only one who is paid in coin more often than onions. It feels arrogant to say so. I am careful with the way I sit, with the way I fold my hands. If I didn’t keep that small austerity, my head would balloon with every grieving person’s rawness, and grief is heavy as wet wool when you take it home. I keep a length of twine in my pocket. Once a last hour is witnessed and spoken, I tie a single knot in that twine and thumb it hard so the hour does not fray.

On the first frost morning of the year, the Quim family sent a boy banging on my door with a heel of bread and the news that Elieta Quim was failing. He was ten or so, goat-run and breathless, his eyes erupting some private joy at being entrusted with death. “She went soft in the night,” he said, tapping his own chest with his fist as if testing a melon. Then he held out the bread like a promise he didn’t yet know he would break.

The Quim house sits on the southeast of the old bridge levee, where the stones make a low wall against an absence. The door was unlatched. Inside, the heat wore a handmade smell—soap, cinnamon, wool. Someone had tucked orange peels along the windowsill to discourage mice. There were bins of beans under the benches and a coil of blue hose hung like a sleeping snake on the pegboard. I have noticed people tidy before a death, as if they hope the neatness will translate, as if God were a fussy aunt and might be appeased by a swept hearth.

They had moved Elieta’s bed into the main room. She was small as a bundle of kindling, skin drawn fine on her bones. A woman I knew to be her daughter-in-law knelt by the bed, smoothing the edges of a quilt with one hand, and the other was pressed flat on the old woman’s chest, counting. Three sons stood back, clumsy in grief, cracking their knuckles like firewood. A boy—the messenger—had shrunk to the doorframe and was watching me with the satisfaction we reserve for rituals that behave themselves, for the predictable lift of a priest’s hands or the exact way a baker scores his loaves. In the corner, the stove coughed and a pot sent up a wet, beanish breath. The clock above the sink had stopped at a quarter past something.

“I’m the listener,” I said to the room. I never say my name first. The work comes before the person who does it.

“Then hear her,” said the daughter-in-law. She had a braid you could tow a boat with. She smoothed it as she spoke. “She wanted you. We put aside three silver for you. Please don’t make us wait to hand it over.”

I nodded and took my place on the low stool by the window. The frost on the glass had come up like writing, loops and misbehaviors of cold we’d be punished for if we were schoolchildren. I stared at it the way I have been taught to. There is a wrong intimacy in looking at the dying while they die. They should feel free to be ugly, to be trivial, to kill the fly that has landed. If I look at the frost and listen, the dying will know the room safely goes on being a room, that the broom in the corner is still a broom, and the chair knows its own legs.

It was a quiet hour. Quietness is not the same as silence; it carries weight. The bedframe ticked. A moorhen called on the riverbed where there is no river. A horse shuddered a stall door and then surrendered to stillness. The son with the hairline fracture of a heart—that is to say, the youngest—began to cry and then stopped himself by looking at his own hand like it had made the sound. The beans bubbled again as if thinking of an idea. The frost scribbled deeper. Elieta’s breath had a slant to it, like wind always meant to go elsewhere and got tricked into a house.

And then, the ending. The last inhale—an acquisitive sound, greedy and surprised—and the last exhale as if she’d decided to tell someone a secret and had fallen asleep mid-sentence. I do not believe in souls leaving. I believe in heat and in the thing that heat allows and in the way a body forgets, after so much practice at staying, how not to. When the exhale was done, the daughter-in-law let her hand rise and fall once, testing for a reconsideration. There wasn’t one. She arranged the old woman’s mouth, and she and the sons let themselves be empty for ten seconds before filling with the wails they owed their own story about themselves, about being good children who loved their mother and would continue to love her in the approved manner.

I stood and set my palm to the wall and counted the last hour back. It is a work of attention and internal measure. I do not have a gift; I have a practice. Each sound stitches itself into a lattice if you let it. Each scent clings to a different die in the mind. Sweat goes to the wrist, soap to the tongue, smoke to the inside of the left elbow. That is how my mother taught me to hold a place without writing. When I was a child, she made me tell her the street we had just walked back again—every dog, the smell of every bread, which window was a mouth, which was an eye. When I got one thing wrong, she would pinch my ear so I would know how it felt to be mistaken.

I recited for the Quims: the ticking, the horse, the beans, the moorhen’s decoy call from a dry river. I told them the exact time the clock had been wrong and the way the frost wrote, if such a thing can be said. I said the last thing she looked at, which was not a face but the orange peels on the sill, curled like commas. I said her last breath was generous and did not cut. These are the parts I can embroider a little—not in their content, but in their stitching. The room must feel like a room you can live in again.

They paid me the silver, and I put it in my pocket where the twine lives. I thought I would leave then. The beans were beginning to want salt, and there were already two other people waiting in the street with the particular thinness of those who have not had a death for themselves yet but have stood near too many of them. Then the daughter-in-law pressed her hand against my elbow and asked in a voice that had been sanded by the day if I might stay a while.

“Why?”

“She asked after you,” she said.

I had never spoken to Elieta before. She was not somebody who bought my work; she had not married nor buried anyone I had listened to. But the Registry is small and we are heard of, and often the elderly take us on as mascots. We are a piece of furniture in the valley’s understanding of how to behave in the presence of the precipice. There are houses in which my name is a noun for any woman who can keep a last thing from slipping away. Oh, look, someone might say when she drops an egg and catches it—well, aren’t you a listener.

“She asked after me,” I said, uncertain if this meant something more than the obvious. The daughter-in-law nodded too quickly and turned away. She was the kind of woman who mistranslates her own feelings into work. I have that habit too.

The sons carried their mother to the table, where the washing could be done in a way that spared her the indignity of being flopped upon. In our valley, the dead are scrubbed with nettles boiled and cooled, as a way to raise their last flush and to remind us that pain is not only a thing that goes; it can be given and taken, and even then it can sting or soothe. The men would do the lifting and the daughter-in-law would do the fine work, and I would be a piece of cloth draped over a chair. I settled myself.

It was while they were busy that the room bent toward me, and with it the peculiar concentration that attends all secrets at the last. The daughter-in-law glanced at me and then glanced toward the bedroom doorway. Even when the dead have been lifted from the bed, we call the room by their current name. It is hers now, someone will say a month later. Don’t sleep in her room until the air is done with her.

The daughter-in-law pursed her lips and shooed me with a jerk of her chin. The goat-run boy had followed the men toward the table. I went where I was sent, a little misgiving making a rope of itself in my throat. The room was still warm and shaped to the old woman’s size, which startled me—how rooms decide which person they fit. A moth of sunlight had been trapped between the curtain and the window. I sat on the bed as if it could remember me and be surprised.

There on the nightstand was a brush with a handful of gray hair in it. It was the right kind of hair—that is, it was ordinary. Our stories like to imagine old women with queen’s hair, pewter waterfall hair, the kind wind will not undo, but most of us braid what we are given and make it do. The brush had hair snagged at its base, and when I put my thumb to that hair, it was damp. I put the pad of my thumb to my tongue and tasted only salt, nothing else. The restless thinking in me went briefly still in the way the river had when I put my forearms to it, as a child. I should not have tasted it. But I am in the habit of tasting what is about to be gone.

Under the brush, there was a piece of paper folded the way our mothers teach us to fold a wish when we will not trust a mouth to keep its shape. There was a word on the outside—Mara. My name looks chiseled when someone else writes it. I am always astonished at its consonants there, at the rasp of the two syllables as if they must be dragged. No one writes to a listener on the day of their own death. We are spoken to; that is our business. I put my ear to the hallway and heard only water running over a body that could not protest and a whisper of nettles against skin. I unfolded the paper.

The hand was not one I recognized. The words did not tilt but leaned back against themselves, as if each letter had backed up to shore to take a run at the next. A hand certain of its own uncertainty. The letter said:

This is not an ending I will swear by in front of my children. I am writing to you because you keep your own ears and do not sell them to the first woman who weeps. Do you remember how the river stopped? Of course you remember, you were a girl. You were knee-high and angry and your mother made you hold a pail bigger than your chest and walk behind me across the bridge. You are the last person I saw with a wet mouth after it went. This is a wicked thing to say and I say it: the Throat did not dry. It was taken and braided. I put my hands in my daughters’ hair and felt the small pull of current. The town took what it feared and hid it in the mouths of women. We tied it up to keep the fields from taking the house. You think I am being fancy because I am dying. I am not. Go to the old well on the Brin farm. Bring a sharp comb. Your mother is the last who can undo it. Your mother is not below the river, Mara. She kept nothing you gave her except herself.

I read it twice and a third time and then, because I am an honest woman, looked around to see if the old woman was anywhere, to say aloud into a room that had no hearing left in it that she was a liar. Then I put the letter inside the lining of my coat with the twine and the coin.

It is not unusual for the dying to write odd things. They write down recipes and revenge—he is not your son, keep the recipe behind the big pot, the man became a fox and left me with nothing but the holes. Dying turns people into their youngest selves; everything not yet decided becomes the only thing they care to decide. But I have never known one of them to throw their rag over the town like that: the river was taken and braided. A valley is made of what it believes about itself. We believe we were struck and punished; we believe we were undone by the weather as if it were a deity with childish moods. It is easier to live under the sky if it is capable of temper. To say we did this—that we took what shunned us and wrapped it into hair—requires arrogance or clarity, and dying gives you one or the other, sometimes both.

There are things about my mother I don’t say aloud because if I say them they are heard as accusations and I mean them as measurements. She was precise. She wouldn’t count out a tablespoon of flour when a thumb of flour was needed for weather like this, for a day like this. She was a woman the town used to talk about in the ways that towns talk when they have not been challenged in a while and need to flex their old cruelty: she wears her skirts too clean, she thinks she can tell a fish not to die when it has been in a trough too long. My mother did talk to fish. She talked to everything. She tied our laundry high when the Throat rose up and she pushed it low when it shrank back, and the day the river went, she took my hand and we stood there and put our forearms to the bank. I waited for her to say the flippant thing that would make the bone-hum resolve. She did not say anything. She lifted her arm away as if she had been burned, and she went home by herself. Three months later my mother went down to the riverbed and did not come up, and the town said drowned and I said no and we stopped speaking to one another for a while after that.

The daughter-in-law came to the doorway then, her sleeves pushed up and her arms littered with nettle burns. I had tears on my face that I could not account for. The way grief behaves, it will take the nearest excuse. She reached out as if to wipe my cheek, then remembered who I was and the rules of who can touch whom when, and pinched her own forearm instead.

“Do you think she was ready?” she asked, and there was real curiosity in it. It is a question I hate for how little it asks and how much it aspires to measure.

“No one is ready,” I said. “We just become easy to carry.”

She nodded, not because she agreed but because she had decided to be a person who agreed with things today, and I took it as a kindness. I stood and tucked my twine deeper into my pocket and felt the corner of the letter press my ring finger and leave an immediate white impression, which felt like a joke and also like a promise.

Outside, the frost had gone from writing to water. The boy who had fetched me had grown an inch with the news he had delivered and was walking as if his knees had new hinges. He would tell this day back to himself every week for the next year until he had it in a shape he liked. The houses along the levee were halfway to themselves—morning has that effect on roofs, loosening them and then tightening them back down. I could hear the sound of a comb through hair from two doors down, a mother making something neat for school that would be undone during the first lesson, because learning is a kind of storm.

I walked toward the Brin farm along the old footpath that pokes at the edge of the Throat like a child stealing raisins from a cake. The Brins had once owned all the land from the red silo to the ridge, but then they forgot how to marry and they forgot how to grow daughters. Now the farm was two men with ruined hands and a cousin from the Low who owed somebody a debt and was hiding. The well on their land is a square thing with a lip like an ashlar and a winch that whines like a widower. No one draws from it anymore. The water table changed when the river left us, and there was a bitter chalk at the bottom of the Brin well that made soup sigh wrong in the mouth when you used it. Even cows have preferences.

At the gate, the elder Brin lifted two fingers off his mug by way of hello. His dog was a goitered thing that barked as if he had been paid not to. “You come for us?” he called, half-joking, the way men do when they place themselves in line to be relieved of something and pretend they do not want to be.

“Not today,” I said. I am impatient with their jokes. They are the old kind that think the only way to be soft is to be mean. “I need to look at your well.”

“It’s ugly,” he said. “It will make you feel better about what you have at home.”

“I live in one room with a chair and a bed,” I said. “Your well is probably fancier.”

He gestured for me to go. The cousin was sitting on the stoop with one bare foot in his hand, worrying at the sole. He glanced up and then back down the way rabbits do when they are not convinced you are a hawk and are not convinced you aren’t. I walked the length of the yard. The well was more polite than I had remembered and the rope across its mouth had been tied by someone who believed in knots, which is not the same thing as someone who knows them.

I took the comb from my bag. I carry one because the smallest girls we stand for at the Registry always want their hair done in the first quiet after a parent goes. I sit cross-legged on their floors and part their hair with my forefinger and say I am very good at making a head into halves and then halves into halves again. They laugh because the math seems like a trick in the mouth, and it is.

The stone around the well was cold. I pressed my ear against it and heard nothing. I do not know what I was listening for. I looked into the square of dark. A fly spiraled up, ruined by the light. I leaned farther and thought of the day my mother walked away from me on the bank, her bones wiping themselves of a river’s grammar.

When people in town tell stories about the Throat, they talk about the day it stopped as if the river played a game of statues and froze in the act and then became the act. But water does not behave that way. It is not the kind of child you can catch pretending to be your stone. Even dry, a river remembers movement; its bed wants to become aged in a particular pattern. Even in the Brin well there was a sense of accustomed falling, of distance knowing itself and then being known again every minute. I put my hand into the square of dark as far as my shoulder until my skin prickled with the cold. I brought the comb down through the air, and something caught.

Something caught. The comb snagged like a fish tooth on a net. This is only language, I told myself. You are not special for believing it is more than language. But there in my ordinary hand with the knuckles that complain in rain, I felt a pull that is not apparent in a stone and a rope and a shaft. It was the kind of pull that belongs to things that go toward their habit without asking.

When I drew the comb up, it brought with it a single hair, gray and fine the way an old woman's hair is fine, and in that hair was a small wetness that did not taste of chalk and did not taste of my hand. It tasted like nothing I have known how to name for a long time. The word my mouth made was river before I could look for a grown-up synonym.

A woman behind me made a small noise. I had not heard her approach, which meant I had been more interested in what my hand did in the dark than in being the kind of person who notices where her body is. I turned. The cousin from the Low had come closer, his foot held close to his chest like a small animal he had rescued and was trying to decide what to feed. He had a scar that went up into his hairline and then disappeared the way a path does when the grass overturns its memory of the walker's feet.

“That well is finished,” he said, softly, as if he were telling me that I’d mistaken the door for a window. “It’s only pretty to stones now.”

I put the wet hair to my tongue and he watched me, then looked away as if he were embarrassed to be the kind of person who watches what women do with their mouths.

“Everything will be finished someday,” I said. “I just wanted to hear how far.”

He nodded. He was younger than I had thought at first. He had the old men’s shape of endurance but not yet the old men’s surrender of hearing.

“I heard something,” I said, and he shook his head in a way that meant he had a type of loyalty to his employers that required him to falsify what was right there. Men love their codes for the way they ruin their useful sense.

I put the comb away. The wet hair had begun to dry and curl back into the decline of memory. Under my coat, the letter warmed itself against my body as if it wanted to live. I would have to make sense of a sentence that could not be sworn to in front of anyone. I would have to find my mother or fail at finding her. The two tasks are different kinds of religion. I walked back into the part of the day that pretends it is not happening yet to any of us.

In the Registry ledger, there is a space after the name and the fee where we write a single word to carry us into the next call. It is a habit like any other habit that stands in for faith. Today, without thinking how it would feel to see it there later, I wrote down my own name. Then I put my head on my arms on the desk and for the first time since I was knee-high and angry, I said out loud to a room with no hearing left in it: well, then.

Chapter One

The lake gave back the church in pieces.

On the first morning the steeple rose from the wrinkled skin of Harrow Lake like a finger pressed up through plastic; by noon the carpenters’ nails in the clapboards had caught the sun and flashed, and by evening wind had threaded itself through the empty casements and made the rusted bell mouth a wordless hum. The men from the salvage company stood on the bank in their rubber boots and squinted, forearms folded, the way men look at a stranded animal they know they have to put down.

Mara was already there. She had been taking measurements all week—tape unfurling, survey flags blinking red against the dun—trying to make the ever-changing both precise and public. The county had asked her to show up with clipboards, laminated hazard maps, the bare scaffolding of order.

“Twenty feet in one week,” Felix said, the county supervisor, a man who wore his tie like a dare even now, surrounded by brown grass and grasshoppers that threw themselves against pale ankles. He had a way of stating a number like it could be a promise kept or broken by sheer tone. He rocked back on his heels. “We’ll never hear the end of this.”

“From who?” asked June, the reporter from the Herald, already writing. She had freckles and a manner that turned every answer into a footnote.

“Everyone,” Felix said. He waved his hand in a circle that took in the few houses on the ridge, two rusted mailboxes, a horse chewing the post like it was sugar, the salvage trucks, the lake—so much of it now plains of cracked, black silt skin in shapes like continents. “They’ll say we built a drowning and now we’re building a drought. They’ll want somebody hung by the steeple.”

Mara didn’t say anything. She had learned already that silence could be a kind of professional language, that men in ball caps and sunburns felt steadier when there was one person among them who counted and didn’t look like she didn’t sleep at night. She looked through the field glasses anyway, because it mattered, because it was hers to name: a line of pew-backs loosened by the changing chemistry, floating like vertebrae. The bell’s yoke still intact. Cattails collapsed in brittle heaps at the margin, their cigar-tops creasing like chewed pencils. If you are precise enough, you can keep the panic to a small room inside you, separate from the room where the papers are.

Felix’s phone buzzed again. He’d been getting calls all morning. When he’d invited Mara to the county building the first time, two counties over from the university where she’d learned how hydrologists use words like dead pool and bathymetry as if they were not also metaphors for a marriage, he had called her “our drought liaison,” as though the drought were a city that had chosen in bad weather to send a legate.

“Press will want to go out on boats. We say no,” Felix said now, shading his eyes. “You’ll put that in the plan. Liability.”
