“There aren’t boats,” Mara said. “There are people in chest waders and a jon boat that’s more hole than metal. And anyway, the silt is like pudding under there. It’ll suck you if you stand still. Liability goes both ways.”

Sloane from salvage—ruddy, quiet, not the slicer-for-hire type his company’s name suggested—spit into the dirt and mangled a stalk of foxtail into his cheek. “We can run the cable out, hook from shore,” he said. “Church’ll come easy enough.”

“Easy?” June said.

“It’s only heavy if you lift it,” Sloane said, like it was a proverb, and the men with him laughed without letting their mouths open much.

They were all waiting for the woman with the cane to arrive. She’d been on the radio that morning, and people in Harrow—a place grown used to not being a place, to being a margin on a map of a reservoir and then a smear on the screen of a storm report—had passed her voice from car to porch to feed store. Ruth O’Donnell. Last baby born in Gander Creek, the town drowned to make the lake. Mara’s mother, which is something June did not yet know, the reporter as much intrigued by the lineage of a rumor as the lineage of a person.

“You’ll call me when she gets here?” June said to Mara, low, putting names to faces in her notebook. “So I don’t miss the first time she sees it.”

“She’s seen it,” Mara said. She was thinking of the way her mother’s mouth had thinned when Mara told her yesterday, about the steeple, about everything pulling itself up wet from the place where Ruth had learned how to tell April from May. “She rides out to this ridge and sits in her car and doesn’t get out.”

“Yeah, but not like this,” June said. She smiled, like what she wanted from that line was not cruelty but shape. “Not with the bell.”

At eleven the wind changed. The smell that rose off the lake was not rotten fish—those had long since been carted away or become shapes under the sails of gulls—but the iron smell of wet earth drying, the alchemy of drowned loam. Mara’s throat tasted of pennies and schoolyard dust. She used to try to describe that smell to people, made a taxonomic mess of it, ended up saying it was like the inside of a cow’s nostrils, blood and grasses, and then she’d laugh to show it was a joke so they wouldn’t pity her for what she couldn’t name.

She was walking the graded slope when the boy planted himself in her way. Skinny, long knees, fingered a rubber band until it snapped and he didn’t glance down at the welting. He had something wrapped in his T-shirt, cradled like bread.

“Is it true we can keep whatever we find?” he asked. “Sloane said first finder’s keepers.”

“Sloane said no such thing,” Sloane said, from behind her. “Sloane said stay on the bank unless you got a reason and a rope.”

“Name?” Mara asked the boy.

He shifted, and she thought he’d give her a false one, that grease of adolescence, a dare. Then he said, “Theo,” and tipped out what was in his shirt.

A clutch of mail. Envelopes tanned to the color of old teeth at the corners and the flaps still gummed down tight by what the lake had not quite unmade. The top envelope had a stamp with a bird on it folded at the corner, a postmark: June 1952. The address: Mrs. Abram Sledge, 228 Milkweed Street. Gander Creek. Gander Creek and the county was enough to find anything then. There was a line, scratched by rain, that had begun to erase the return address.

For a second, nobody spoke. Objects found in lakes had their own weather. A kind of hush named less by religious temperament than by the sensation of proximity, the proof of other people having breathed in the same world but named it differently.

Sloane didn’t reach for the letters. He had already made enough enemies without declaring by a hand that anything belonged to his company.

“Found them wedged under a rock up by the old boat ramp,” Theo said. “I didn’t go out. They was just there. My Grandpa says he remembers that woman. Mrs. Sledge. She made pies.”

“Everybody makes pies,” Felix said, as if saying it would return propriety to the scene. He adjusted his tie. “Hand them here, son. We’ll establish a chain.”

Theo took a step back. He shook his head in a tiny way, the kind of shake that indicated not so much a refusal as a rehearsal. Mara crouched, the lake smell in her head. She had an optional, in moments like this, to be an employee or a person, and on good days she felt like she had found a way to be both. Today her head felt like a kept room with too many doors.

“We’ll make sure they go to someone who can find Mrs. Sledge’s people,” Mara said. She held her hand out, palm up, not the grab of authority, but like she was asking for something delicate or hot. “You’ll be in the paper for it, for doing the right thing. And if we start with chaos, everything will be chaos. There are nails and bottles and the lake doesn’t always give back the way it took.”

Theo chewed his lip. He looked at what was in his shirt like it was a nestling bird it would be on him to feed. Then he put the letters in her hand. His fingers were cold. After, he made a noncommittal sound like he’d been asked a question he hadn’t heard right and loped away in a lopsided jog, knees first, leaving a trail of foxtail seeds stuck to his socks.

Sloane straightened and said, not unkindly, “You got a way with em.”

Mara didn’t answer. She held the stack of letters and imagined their tongues inside, stamped by someone the summer before the place became a pool and then a lake. The summer when warnings were notices but not yet the end of a space. The thing her mother had never been able to convey to her—what it felt like to watch a town dig up its own graves to move them to high ground. “If the lake had been the size they promised,” Ruth said once, rubbing a circle on the wood where a glass had been, “it would have been just inconvenience. But they kept adding. Like a story you tell and don’t know where to end it, so you keep talking even when you’ve said the important part.”

A pearled truck came rattling up the ridge. People moved as if the truck could change the weather by its presence. Ruth didn’t park straight. The dust she had brought with dragged after her, lazy. It took Mara a second to see the way her mother was moving: slow, not because she was old—she refused it as a word—but in a contained way, as if the planet might tilt without warning and she would need to brace.

Mara had never called Felix dad, and had never called him by his first name in his presence; Mara had never called Ruth anything except Mum, and this was a town that would never call her anything except Ruth O’Donnell, in full, the last baby born in Gander Creek.

Ruth’s cane was a blackthorn, not pretty. It was a stick Napoleon might have knocked down a soldier for because it would make a better story later. She planted it and looked not at the steeple but at the ground under their shoes, as if that were the threshold. People often think memory is a sky you lie back into. It is rarely sky.

“You could have called me earlier,” Ruth said to Mara, not moving to hold her, not making a face. They showed their affection sideways, over a sink full of plates, in chaff, in the way a head leaned back in a shared car.

“I did call,” Mara said. “Before seven. And again.”

“You know my phone,” Ruth said. Which wasn’t untrue. Ruth kept it in a biscuit tin. Sometimes it rang five times in a day from people wanting to know if she remembered a thing they needed to make themselves whole; sometimes it rang not at all. Sometimes the phone was in the tin in the pantry, sometimes in the oven, sometimes under the passenger seat because she’d tucked it aside to put a jar of honey where she wouldn’t forget.

“You ready?” Felix asked her, the cordial and the political caught in his tie knot.

Ruth finally put her eyes on the lake. It was as if a slow hand had turned her chin. She adjusted the strap of her cane. “You’ll not touch that bell until I say,” she said, to no one and everyone, each word like she’d soaked it in vinegar.

Sloane lifted his arms in surrender. “We’re on your clock, Ms. O’Donnell.”

“Don’t Ms. me. I got a name. You might have read it,” she said, and that made June smile, because there it was, the line.

They walked down to the flagged limit. Everyone knew the flags meant nothing now. The lake would take their meaning back and give its own.

Ruth breathed with her mouth a little open, air on her tongue like she was trying to taste the past and knew she could not, only inhale its outline. “That’s the tower,” she said. “Father Blix was not the physical type. He wheezed. He used to pay my brother a nickel to go up there and ring the bell properly on Christmas and for marriages. My brother wasted his nickels. Boys do that. You know, the day they started the fill, we ate cake for no reason.”

She knelt with the cane across her knees and put her hand on the new black shape of the lake edge. The silt took her fingers like a mouth. She didn’t pull back. “My mother said they’d need our faces for a brochure. She made me brush my hair. They put us all on a truck bed and made us wave like a parade of the conquered. Lord, this smells like the feed shed after a hard rain.”

“Were you eleven?” June said, soft, and when Mara looked at her the reporter looked back with her pen in the air as though it were a barrier she hadn’t realized she was carrying.

“Twelve,” Ruth said. She looked up like a woman might look for a bird she had named as a child. “Thirteen by the time it took all the porches. The Goshen girls swam in their slips. We threw horse apples into the water to hear them kersplunk. Men walked around like they’d had something stolen they couldn’t report. You see that?” She pointed with her chin. “That’s the old road. Look how it remembers a straight line.”

Silt had slumped away and the surface features had reappeared: the macadam of Milkweed Street, heaved by ice layers, a metaphysical highway. To either side, like a child’s map, had come the square lashes of old foundations, stone and concrete and in places just hard tamped earth. The pattern made Mara’s stomach drop in a way that felt like a carnival ride she had lied to herself about not liking.

“People lived right,” Ruth said. Her voice brightened with indignation as if the indignation powered the remembering. “Do you see? There were lilacs. Judge Henley had himself a formal hedge. That’s his. My sister Agnes stole his mail for a week once. She was never sorry.”

The lake breathed. It felt like a library in summer, reading the rot of bindings. Sloane motioned to his men and they moved with braided rope that shone with use. They were careful. They had been told to be. They threw the hook and it clanged and they went quiet. Above them gulls sat like punctuation on the power lines.

The salvage crew had done this before—hapless piers after storms, old equipment dredged up in a drought so that it would stop snagging fishermen. The ethics of a bell were new to them. Sloane placed his foot against the bell tower’s visible part and his men kept the rope slack. “We can stabilize without pulling it all,” he said. “Keep it from falling onto itself. Lady,” he added, softer, to Ruth, “we don’t have to take it. We can leave it so you can see it until the water comes back.”

Ruth laughed, a sound that wasn’t humor. “And will it?” she asked, as if you might ask someone if God would, in fact, make a door where there was a wall if you prayed sideways. She turned to Mara. “You promised me you wouldn’t talk to me like a child,” she said. “You can answer me straight. Will it?”

“We have models,” Mara said. She hated that word coming out of her. It made her sound like a store clerk. “Nothing like this is the way it has been.”

“Meaning no,” Ruth said, and patted the mud next to her, companionable with the impossible. “Your father wanted me to move to his house on the back of his flat land. But the first thing he said to me when they were putting the forms in the ground for that place was he’d always wanted to be a river man. This is what a man is. He’ll dream himself a boat when there is no river.” She looked at Felix like he was nothing to her and everything both. He took it, this looking. He had never been the villain Ruth made him in a story at the laundromat but that never meant he was not to blame for some weather.

“Ms.—Ruth,” June said, catching herself, trying not to look at Mara when she said the name, a little economy of press ethics. “Do you remember what Mrs. Sledge made?” She was trying to make a loop from the letters to the living.

Ruth closed her eyes. She gave the question a try. “Chess pie. Everyone says it’s sugar and no chess but I remember a lemon rind there somewhere. Her husband had a limp from the war. He used to count out loud in church until Father Blix told him it wasn’t a ledger. They moved with their daughter to Utica. How did that turn out, I wonder?”

Mara held up the stack of letters. “Theo found these,” she said. “We’ll try.”

Ruth put her palm flat on the envelope with the bird and it left a prints whorl in the silt that had dried there. The bell hummed when the wind came again. Mara felt the sound in her ribs. It was not a note. The tone that pretends there is a key to grief and that you are simply not skilled enough to hang with it.

Her brother had gone into this lake eight years ago on a smooth day in June. Jonah. It was a fact they said like they said the name of a fish. He’d gone under while Mara was at a meeting two counties away about how to share the water out of season. The meeting had had ham sandwiches brought in and coffee that lit her up in a way that seemed manageable and then the phone had rung and she had driven without realizing to the wrong side of the lake first. The divers had said words like “visibility” and “temperate stratification.” After, she’d written the phrase “thermocline” on five file folders because that is what the brain does when it is given the chance to name the thing that killed your brother in a way that can be put in a binder.

Jonah was not in the mud. Mara knew that the way you know by the body and the way you know by hope, and sometimes those were the same. But it was still true that her feet in the damp edge sent a shiver up her like a warning you feel in a crowded place before anything has happened. Her legs remembered how the lake takes you by ankles and says, stay.

“Let’s not make a circus,” Felix said, which is what a man says when the circus has already set up its tents inside his voice. “Sloane, do what you have to do without cruelty.”

Sloane nodded. He had a foreman’s fear of becoming the story in the wrong way. He and his men waded in a cautious reckoning. The rope snagged, then tightened, then loosened; a piece of something came up bellowing air, what had been a pew leg, the air colored like tea.

A woman in a sun visor with a dog that looked like a rug tugged on the flag. “My great-aunt’s hope chest is under there somewhere,” she said to no one in particular. “It had silver in it. Do you think the lake took the tarnish off or just put another kind on?”

A man who had never said hello to Mara in the grocery store elbowed her now like friends do in tragedy. “You a praying sort?” he asked, and seemed to care what she’d say.

“I make a list,” she said. It was true. She had a list in her shirtsleeve of things she could say to people that were not lies and did not make her seem like she was trying too hard.

He nodded. He seemed grateful, as if the lists of strangers might stand in for the things he’d never written down.

Ruth had let her cane fall sideways. She bent forward and touched the road. It was uncomplicated. It was a hand meeting a thing. Her hair had come undone and the wind took a strand and stuck it to the wet wheel of her cheek. For a second, her shoulders shook, and Mara put her hand on them and felt not smallness but a kind of fury that had no voice. There are angers you don’t waste on names.

“Take it slow,” Ruth said to the bell and to the men and to the lake and maybe to Mara as well. “We waited to be flooded. We can wait to be dug up.”

A kid ran past with a farm bucket sloshing. “Lookit!” he said. “Mussels!” His mother’s voice came after him a beat too late. “Don’t you! You’ll get the itch!” Old instructions were crows; they learned to perch on new fences.

The rope went taut. Metal ground against stone—not the bell but its cradle. The mouth moved like it might speak. The sound it made was not pretty, not even melancholy; it was effort given voice. The men cursed pleasantly. Sloane’s boot sank and he swore in a way that included his ancestors and God and then apologized to Ruth for the breadth of it.

“Pull,” he said, and his men pulled, and the bell, which was not a bell to him but an object in a problem, heaved another inch into time.

On the shoreline, something glass winked. Mara saw it because she stood still. In emergencies, people move and move and it looks like help; stillness is also a kind of help, but the praise for it is thinner. The thing in the silt was once a doorknob, the kind you see in houses with stairs narrow enough to make a coffin go cocked. The glass was pebbled from water’s arithmetic. She bent and pried it out. The cold of it made a ghost in her palm. It had a short stem still bolted to what had been a door. The stem’s screw was a tiny world, shaved by someone’s earnestness and then abandoned to a lake that takes. She thought of the hands that had turned it. She thought of how many hands have turned any knob and how many of those hands had ended up anywhere near the thing they loved. She should have put the knob on the table they had set on the bank for found things. She put it in the pocket of her jacket.

Her face knew she had done a wrong thing before her mind did. She kept her eyes on the lake. She did not look at Felix, who would say, later, in his reasonable voice, that procedures exist for reasons that are larger than any single object and that she had made a bruise in a place that would show. She didn’t look at June, whose profession was seeing and making seeing contagious. She let the weight of the knob in her pocket press against her thigh and thought, it weighs less than I do. She didn’t know why she had thought that. She did not try to explain it to herself. She breathed in the iron air and felt the bell’s vibration like a thing you can’t wipe off.

Ruth said, “Look. That hole right there? That’s where the Luttrells kept their septic. He swore he’d not go before the lake took his house. He sat on his porch and smoked right up to his last morning. They found him in his chair with his shoes clean and his wife said, knew you’d do it your way.”

“Do you remember,” Mara began, and stopped, because they were not in the business of remembering together, because this was a morning that had too many possible hinges. She tried again. “Do you remember the day Jonah…?” she said, tasting the name that had so few forms left.

Ruth nodded without taking her eyes off the bell. “He put his face down to the lake like it was a pocket mirror,” she said, and then made a sound the ear can’t bear, so it decides it is a laugh. “Do your work, Mara.”

“I am,” Mara said, and wondered if she was lying, wondered if her work—this moving of rope and shore and language—could ever be called work in the face of a lake like this. Where does the day end when the work is measuring a change that does not intend to be measured in human hours?

The bell came up enough to catch the sun. Something small in it rattled. Somebody crossed themselves. The dog barked like a tambourine. The rope creaked, threatening. For a breath, the whole town, or what the town had become in this new season of itself, held still. In that quiet, Mara heard it. Not the hum of wind through the mouth, not Sloane swearing poetry, not Felix on the phone with a state man, not June’s pen. A tiny sounded chime, stubborn as a spoon against a jelly glass.

“Did you—” Mara said.

“Sh,” Ruth said, without looking at her. Her hand tightened on the mud like it was somebody’s hand she meant to bother. “Let it.”

After the day would become tellable, June would write about the bell in the paper. She would say the wind had been a brush and the lake a throat. She would say the sound made the hair on her arms stand up like a field of wheat in hail. She would skip the doorknob in her notes because what mattered and what could be printed were different, because even in the pursuit of the public there was room for the private thefts of a morning that felt like someone opening the spine of a book and being shown how even paper can be a country.

“We’ll have to keep people off,” Felix said under his breath when he found a space that did not need him to be loud. “They’ll be down there with crowbars and greed.”

“Greed and grief look similar from behind,” Mara said. She had a finger on the letters in her pocket and glass in the other, a weight on each thigh that made her even, as if balance could be purchased.

“Leona’s coming,” Felix said, with a nod toward the road, where a woman in a denim jacket with a hawk stitched across the back was getting out of a car. The tribal liaison. “We’ll need to do this right,” he said. He meant permits, cordons, a lot of poster-board notices. He meant speeches. He meant what they all meant, which was that you can set up a table under the sun and put your forms on it and write hazard in red, and the lake will still teach you something that does not have a form.

Leona came and stood shoulder to shoulder with Ruth without asking permission. “I told you, I’d bring you if you wanted,” Leona said.

“I know the way,” Ruth said. “I know the way when the way is back. There’s no tool for that.”

Leona looked at the places where the water had drawn back like a sheet pulled off an unmade bed. “They call it wholly behind and wholly ahead,” she said. “On the radio. Like a child might sit with her feet in a creek and ask if she can be in two places at once. They make it sound like science. Perhaps it is the science of not choosing.”

“What is?” June asked, because that is what reporters do—they take a line someone else is living and ask it to dance.

“Dragging,” Leona said. “Flooding. Staying. Naming. All of it.”

And so the bell hung there, a mouth full of silt and a voice that had once summoned people to kneel and now called them to a bank. Behind them, the sun moved on its track that nobody elected. A tractor coughed somewhere up on the ridge and started nothing. The gulls waited and judged without bias. A dust devil wrote itself briefly down the old main street, raising a skin of ash from what had been the feed store and the three steps to the barbershop, and Mara had the sense that if she were quick enough and brave in the right direction she could read in that dust the words people had spoken in that place, and she could gather them, and she could hand them back, and her mother would be a person she could help in a way that looked like help and not like the paperwork of it.

But then the dust shifted and the sound from the bell changed, and the day went on, as days do, both prize and punishment, awarding nothing neat. And Mara, who had made herself a list-maker, who had learned to feed the part of herself that loved ratio and gauge because it could be fed, pressed the glass in her pocket with her fingers until the ridges bit, and said out loud, because it was the only thing she could say that could bear being said, “We need a perimeter,” and people nodded, because even when a lake spits up its own church, someone has to lay down flags.

The day the lake came back, it brought fish older than our names. They rose from the cracked white pan with their mouths opening and closing like church doors, bewildered in air that had forgotten them. Dogs ran circles, slipping on wet gypsum, teeth to scale, children shrieked and someone shouted for a bucket, as if there were a bucket big enough for what was happening to us.

I was standing on the porch steps with my mother when the sky loosened. Heat had been a long arrogance over Harrow’s Dry. We had learned to fold dust into the idea of home—dust in the seams of bread, in the threads of blankets, in the hollows behind the ears. We grew our tomatoes in barrels with bottoms cut out; we hung wet bedsheets over screen doors like additional lungs; we drank water with the mouthful reverence of church wine. There were stories, drifting from the older men at the co-op like the smell of motor oil, about the time before, when Gullarm Lake was a bruise of cold blue at the town’s feet. None of us believed it belonged to us. Water is something you owe, not own.

“What’s that sound?” my mother asked me. Her voice was papery. My name, lately, was also slippery to her.

“Thunder,” I said, though there was a freight to it, a heavy rolling. Something between a freight train and a long exhale.

She frowned. “Is it the boys with their car again?”

“Maybe,” I said, because it was easier than unpuzzling it with her. Her hair, white and sparse, kinked around her ears like cotton pulled from a pill bottle. In the early days of her forgetting, I bought a label maker and began naming everything: drawer, tap, cup, stove. I stuck little words to surfaces as if language could anchor them to reality. Now, the labels peeled and curled at the corners with heat and time. My mother would pick at them the way she had once picked at scabs, slowly, then all at once.

“Your father would not have liked that car,” she said, in the tone of assuring herself of something.

“No,” I said. “He liked tractors.”

“He liked tractors,” she repeated. Then she glanced toward the shimmer at the end of our dead street. “Hear it?”

I heard it. Not thunder. A gathering, like a rumor turning into a parade. I could taste something strange on my teeth, an old metalness, the faintest lick of something like algae. The air changed its shape. The heat had been a lid; suddenly the lid lifted.

The street had always ended in a low swell of salt, a dune flat as a bitten nail, and beyond that, distance. If you climbed the berm at four in the morning, carrying a stool and a thermos, you could sit and watch the sun drag itself up, a slow coin from a poor man’s pocket. You could look out over miles of flat, white brilliance where gulls used to hover and where we now flew kites, where teenagers burned their tires into shredded rainbows, where my friend Gus collected scrap aluminum from the ribs of abandoned boats and turned them into kitchen tables. That morning, the flat was darkening.

“Stay,” I said to my mother, the uselessness of the word like a penny on the tracks. “I’ll be right back.”

She went to the kitchen anyway to put the kettle on for a tea she’d forget to pour, and I slid into my shoes and took the switchback path behind the house, the one that used to be a deer track before the deer gave up on us. Yard bindweed slapped against my ankles; the ants were frantic, drawing sudden lines between their hills and ours. The moment I reached the crest, I saw it.

Water doesn’t arrive like in the movies, one great wall with a curl at the lip. It returns by insistence, by a series of compromises. The distant horizon was smeared with a dark band, wrong and right at the same time. Where there had been white crust and a lace of wind-carved ridges, there was movement. The wind ran its hand across the surface and the surface moved back. The sound was a mouthful of small sounds, the scrape of pebbles and the soft slap of wavelets finding the idea of shore again.

At the bottom of the berm, a cluster of neighbors stood at an angle, as if bracing themselves against something enormous but not wanting to show they were bracing. Lina’s boy had a colander; he was scooping the twitching bodies that made it across the first lip of the dune and shoveling them back, as if he could save them when the thing saving them was saving us. Old Man Vickers wore his VFW cap without understanding its dignity, and Gus, who had hair like tumbleweed and a laugh like a crow, had his sleeves rolled past his shoulders, his tattoo of the girl with the fox head puckered from all the sun. The boy with the colander was telling the fish nothing as he ferried them. Everything that was once a myth had turned literal.

“Jesus gulps,” Gus said when he saw me. He lifted his arms in surrender to a god he didn’t believe in. “She’s really doing it.”

“She?” I said, forgetting, too, how to speak about permanence.

“Gullarm,” he said, and his voice went soft. “You know how when women decide?”

“Water doesn’t care what we call it,” Vickers said. He said it with a tremor, though he would later spit on the idea that he had felt anything other than contempt for nature’s insolence. “It’ll take what it’s always taken.”

A small carp, metallic and shocked, flailed in the boy’s colander, then leaped and smacked itself onto Gus’s boot. He bent and scooped it with both hands. Its slime parted on his fingers like a revelation. He grinned down at it, this dumb creature inheriting the world again.

“Look at you,” he said. He dropped it into the nearest runlet, where it shuddered and was gone.

Lina’s boy looked at us with frank, amphibian eyes. “Will it be deep enough?” he asked.

“For what?” I said.

“For boats?” he said, and when we laughed he wasn’t insulted. He’d never seen a boat move across water. He knew boats as metal furniture, as roofs propped over shade gardens.

I thought of the maps I made for people who wanted to remember where they were. I wasn’t a cartographer in any grand sense, not the kind whose work appears in museums with glass over it and an elderly docent in a tidy silk scarf explaining isotachs and isobars. In college I’d had a crush on a girl with an accent like a soft violin; she convinced me that maps were just the sexiest lies we agreed to tell. When I came back home, I got a job at the real estate office drawing little neighborhood maps with perfection: every cul-de-sac, every dead end, every imaginary buffer between neighbor and neighbor. I was precise to the point of pettiness. I labeled the dry wash behind the school, the unspoken fence lines between Maxwell’s goats and Edna’s: goat wander begins here. I put a cartoon papery blue where the lake used to be, a gesture toward the fiction that we were still a lakeside town.

Now the map insisted on revising itself. You couldn’t pin this. The water came in fingers, testing. It reached reeds remembered in the mud as if it had left notes for itself. The stubs of old dock pilings, silver and termite-riddled, trembled and then relaxed as coolness slicked them. A heron, where had it been all this time, blew in like a note from the old hymn book.

“Should we call somebody?” Vickers said, which made Gus snort.

“Call who? The Bureau of You Get What You Get?” he said. He put his hands on his hips in a posture I recognized from when we were twelve and the melon truck overturned at the edge of town and we’d eaten ourselves sick because the idea of bounty was so insulting. “We can tell Ortega, I guess. He’ll need to move the carnival. And the RV park, and the Pentecostals.”

“Ortega knows,” I said. I’d seen the big man drive by with his window down, smelling like cologne and worry. He had built his carnival out on the flat, wheels on ancient axles that had once sweltered in lake water. Tilt-a-Whirl seats repurposed from a defunct planetarium. Goldfish prizes that had never known a home. We laughed at Ortega the way you laugh at the man who is more honest than you can bear. He built hope on our loss, and when the wind gusted he let people think it was the ride.

My phone, which I had shoved into my back pocket, vibrated twice: the hospice nurse confirming Tuesday, a reminder from the pharmacy to pick up my mother’s rivastigmine patches. Memory was a condition with a monthly copay. I frowned at the coincidence and then told myself there were only so many kinds of coincidence.

“I need to go back,” I said, and the men nodded, not because they understood my particular urgency, but because there were so many urgencies at once.

On the way down the path I passed the rusted sign that used to say CONSTRUCTION SITE AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. The dust had eaten all words but ONLY, which felt like a rebuke. The only today was different than the only yesterday. A grasshopper startled onto my shoulder and clung there, a small soldier waiting for orders.

In the kitchen, the kettle had boiled itself quiet and the stove light blinked patiently. My mother had found the drawer with the spoons but not the cabinets with the cups. She stood in the doorway with three spoons in her hand, and a fourth between her lips, like a cigarette.

“I was looking for the small ones,” she said around the metal. “The ones for eggs.”

“Teaspoons,” I said gently. “Those are them.”

“They’re not for tea,” she said. “They are for eggs.”

“Right,” I said, and took the spoon from her mouth. I put it in the sink and turned and kissed her forehead, which was cool and damp. “You hear the frogs?” I asked, and then stopped, because I had asked the question as a joke. For thirty-two years there had been no frogs. The first summer after the lake dried to a bruise, the frogs had died in a matter that made my father go quiet. I remembered him carrying a five-gallon bucket of them to the ditch and tipping them in gently, as if he were burying them upright.

Outside, they began. Not a chorus, not yet. A tentative calling. The sound crept through the screens like gratitude. My mother’s head tipped.

“Where did that come from?” she asked.

“The lake,” I said.

“It had a different name,” she said, with the small ferocity she brought now to things she could grasp. “Before they changed it. It had a good name.”

“Ciénaga,” I said. “You liked that one.”

She shook her head. “Before that.”

“Before I was born?” I smiled, and it was too much, and her face softened as if I had pressed it gently with a fingertip.

“You were always born,” she said, and I tried not to be wrecked by that.

She walked past me to the back door and put her face to the mesh, the way cats do. The frogs tuned themselves. Somewhere, a man who’d been sleeping day shifts woke to the wrong night and there was swearing and then, above the swearing, laughter.

“You write it down,” my mother said, as if remembering my job. “Write it down so it doesn’t go.”

“I will,” I said. I pulled the small notebook I kept tucked into the drawer with the warranty for my toaster oven. I had once written down the names of streets; later, when the forgetting began, I wrote down the names she called things. It amazed her that a spoon could be a boat, a word could capsize and still arrive at shore.

I wrote: frogs return, shy at first, increasing. Under that: water tastes like a coin pressed to your tongue; smells like what it says on the side of a new refrigerator — fresh.

The door blew inward with a soft thud and we both turned. A wavelet, nothing more than a rumor of a wave, had reached the bottom step and slapped it as if in greeting. We had been fools to love what we’d had. Here came something we could fear properly.

The first line of water that reached our yard had in it a few red ants, one bottle cap, a cigarette butt swollen to a sad white worm. The second line carried a cluster of seed heads, the kind that used to make children wish toward what wouldn’t happen. The third brought everything else.

There was a glass jar, the old kind that had been in the pantry since before I was born, the kind with a blue tinge no one can fake anymore. It banged once against the bottom step, as if knocking. It rolled fully into the low pocket that once hosted a kiddie pool that never stayed full for lack of water. It lodged against a nail, and turned, and with the impatience of the lake bumping its back, it righted itself as if it meant to be found.

“I’ll get it,” my mother said, and before I could stop her she was already stepping into her sandals, that old nimble way of slipping, and moving across the uneven paving stones.

“Mamá,” I said, but she was good at moving through her house even when it had become a different house. She knelt, and her kneecaps popped and then settled. She put both hands around the glass as if this were a baptizing. Fish scales glinted in the water inching past her wrists; a worm attempted to crawl and then simply turned itself into a question mark.

She brought the jar back to the table with a solemnity that made me stand straighter. The lid was coated in an old wax; the wax had taken impressions of fingerprints that were not ours. There was a paper inside, curled like a pillbug, and the ink had bled a little but not so much that it had become river.

“Oh,” my mother said, and the sound of it required me to look at her face. There are times when a face is nothing but younger versions of itself passing quickly like birds in migration. I saw the woman who used to stand in this same doorway in winter in a sweatshirt that said UNM LOBOS and snap beans into a bowl while snow drummed the roof like tapped fingers. I saw the girl from a grainy photo, hair in a rag scarf, biting the laugher from her lip to keep it inside because the camera had been meant for seriousness. Then she became herself again, the current stoppages and puddles.

“I think,” she said, and touched the jar with two fingers, “I sent that once.”

“How could you?” I wanted to ask softly, and then didn’t. The last thing you learn before a mother becomes a weather pattern is when to let her be the climate.

We unscrewed the lid. The wax had cracked at the first turn, old sadness. The smell was of age but not rot. It was the smell of cupboards that haven’t been opened in a while, of dresses that still keep your shape after you’ve lost it.

Inside, the paper unfolded with care. It had been folded so deliberately that it seemed a map in the wrong direction. The first words swam up even before the paper had completed its small unfurl.

Isidro, my mother had written, in a hand that had learned English with a stubborn patience and refused to be scolded by it. It was her handwriting from before I was born, round and forward-leaning as if always late to the party.

Isidro, forgive me. The water is rising. If you are reading this, the thing I promised not to do is done.

My mother put both hands on the table as if it were a boat and she were steadying it. She said his name again into the room in a way that made the room have to answer.

“Who?” I said, because of all the questions some people are given to carry, asking the right ones early is hard. “Mamá? Who is he?”

She touched my cheek with the back of her fingers, a tenderness so old it made a sharp intake in me. “He could swim under the floor,” she said. “He could hold his breath for minutes. He could find coins by listening.”

“You’re not making sense,” I said, and then hated myself for wanting what she couldn’t give.

“Inez,” she said, and the way she said my name made it new again, as if she had just named me. She tapped the paper with a fingernail. “Write it down.”

I wrote: Isidro. Forgive me. The water is rising.

In the space between us and the returning lake, the frogs tuned from tentative to fervent. The first boat—no, the first thing that could be called a boat—floated past, a plastic kiddie pool with two children belly-down in it, crying with delighted terror while their mother, waist-deep in denim, scolded and laughed. From somewhere toward Ortega’s, a generator coughed to life, and then you could hear a man praying, and then you could hear someone telling him to shut up, and beneath it all the body of water speaking to itself after a long vow of silence.

I took the paper and read it again. Isidro, forgive me. The water is rising. The handwriting sloped more quickly after those words, as if the writer had stood up from the chair while writing, as if the land itself had tilted. There were names. There were the kinds of details people only write down if they know they can’t go back to tell them in person.

I looked up at my mother. Her eyes were fixed on the doorway where water would soon stand and then move through and out. She was somewhere in a house I had never lived in.

“We should put sandbags,” I said, because even in disaster some parts of us prefer errands.

She shook her head no, a little smile like an apology. “Let it come,” she said. “I have been dry too long.” She reached and patted my hand, quick as a bird’s tapping. “We’ll write it down. You always were good with maps.”

“I do the little ones,” I said, but she didn’t hear. The frogs lifted their song until it stitched the air, and under the table, the floorboards answered, a tremble like breath.

The jar, empty now of its one secret, had a ring of old wax around its mouth. I could not help but touch it. In the chalked ring on the table the jar’s base left, the circle of it was exact. You could put a compass point in that ring and draw a thousand miles of coastline. You could make a lake from that shape. You could name it after a saint or after an old woman or after the person you loved and failed or after a word for marsh in a language your grandfather had once spoken to your mother across a border that would not hold.

Outside, the water took another step. Inside, my mother pinched the edge of the paper and began to read aloud what the younger version of her had written to a man I had never met. The lake caught the sound of her voice and, hearing its name in it, continued.

On the morning the whales entered the harbor and refused to leave, my grandmother decided to die.

She said it the way she said everything else that mattered, with her eyes on some horizon I could not see. “I’ve finished with this,” she told me over the crackle of her radio, the one that still had a dial and a mouth like a tin can. “Come home. The tide’s wrong.”

I was late, of course. The train broke down outside the city and I watched a flock of starlings turn into a single black thought over a field of winter wheat. When the speakers hissed For your safety, please remain seated, a woman across the aisle began to cry softly into her scarf, and I could not tell if it was grief or habit. By the time I arrived, the morning had become a thin, sullen afternoon, and the whole town was pressed up against the rusted rail of the harbor, staring at the water as if it had finally offered an answer.

They looked like ruins in the smooth gray body of the sea. Dozens of them, maybe more—humpbacks, if the knobby heads and long white wing-fins were any indication. They had slid into the harbor in a procession, rising and vanishing, a strange, hungry tide. People had left their shops mid-transaction. A butcher’s apron hung streaked with blood on a nail, a sign in the pharmacy read back in five that stretched into hours. Children crouched on the railing like cormorants, necks craned. The whales were so close you could count the barnacles on their throats, pale constellations on dark skin. When they exhaled, the breath rang the metal in my ribs. Even the gulls were quiet.

“They won’t move,” a man whispered, as if his voice could do what the harbor pilot’s horn could not. “They came in and they stopped.”

“That’s not stopping,” a woman said. “They’re singing. Can’t you feel it?”

I could. The song moved through me the way thunder moves through the ground. It made the air tremble. It rattled windows and church bells and the red enamel pot in my grandmother’s kitchen three streets away. It shook the last pears from the backyard tree. The sound was not just sound; I felt it against the inside of my teeth, a hum loosening a screw.

I bought a paper cone of damp fries out of habit and did not taste them. Salt gathered in a cold ring on my upper lip. Across the harbor, the offshore wind farm, a new line of white stems installed the year I left, turned their arms slowly, indifferent shivers against a low sky.

“Get out of the way,” someone shouted down the dock. “Harbormaster,” someone else murmured, and people stepped sideways and left nothing clear anyway. There were always too many of us when something happened to the sea.

“Luca!”

Mira, hair tucked into a knitted cap that darkened in spots where the drizzle found her, touched my arm with a mitten and then folded her hand back into herself. To look at her you wouldn’t know she had put the turbines out there last spring, wouldn’t know that her name had been cursed with a slice of fish knife in more than one kitchen the day a net tangled with a cable and a boat capsized. She had always been slight, but the city had carved angles into her, patience into her mouth, a calculator behind her eyes. We did not mention the last summer we had been here at the same time, mouths salt-shocked and clumsy. We never mentioned the summer after, when I left.

“You made it,” she said.

“I did.”

“She called you.”

“Yes.”

“The whales came at dawn,” Mira said, as if reporting a minor mechanical failure. “They’ve been here ever since. Near as we can tell, they’re holding a line.”

“As if we need another blockade,” a voice behind her sniffed. A winter hat with a pom-pom. A mouth that no longer belonged to her. The harbor always belonged to somebody else and that somebody never named themselves.

“Don’t let them start the sonar,” my grandmother had said on the phone. “Don’t let them crack the walls of their heads.”

I let the fries drop into the nearest trash can and turned to go. The song pressed my spine like a hand. Mira caught my sleeve.

“You’re going to her,” she said.

“Of course.”

“She’s been telling people the whales have come for her.”

“She’s been telling people stranger things than that since before we were born,” I said. It was meant to be a joke, a soft place between us, but it found nothing to land on.

“She asked me for a battery for her radio last week,” Mira said. “She didn’t say why.”

“Do you remember,” I asked, “when she would take us to the point and make us put our ears to the rocks?” The memory was already there, a fossil in a certain shape: our skinny stomachs pressed to cold granite, lights out of our bellies, the sea conversing with the stone beneath us, the low rum of it. “She said you could hear all the ships that had ever passed if you were patient. You didn’t have to know the words.”

“She told me once that if you listened long enough the dead would introduce themselves,” Mira said, and then bit her lip, as if she had not meant to be so tender in public. "Be careful," she added, as if I had ever been.

I cut through the back gardens to avoid the people who would want to put their hands on my shoulder with either pity or anger, past the laundry strung like flags between porches, the sheds built out of pieces of other sheds, the rosemary bush that had survived four winters when it should not have. Grandmother’s house had a lean to it, a slow surrender toward the sea, as if it had been walking and remembered mid-stride it had forgotten its shoes. The paint had given up pretending to be blue. The window beside the door was open an inch, as it always was, no matter the season.

I did not knock. I did what I had always done. I said, “It’s me.”

“It’s your mother you sound like,” she answered, from somewhere not far, and my chest hurt with a very old ache for something that had never properly existed.

She was in her bed by the window in the front room, the one that had once been meant to show off good furniture to the street and had instead become the right place to watch storms. The bed had been my grandfather’s. The bed had belonged, before him, to some other man unrelated to us, its headboard carved with curling leaves like a grammar of something we never quite learned to speak. My grandmother was propped among pillows and three blankets, one of which I had knit as a child and which still held the shape of my uneven patience. Her hair, white as anything, lay thick and unbraided beside her head like an unspooled rope. On her neck, purple blooms where she had bruised herself getting up when she should not have. The radio sat on the windowsill, a square of dented metal, its dial lit with a watery green eye. It hummed even when it was off, anxious to find something.

“Do you hear them?” she asked.

“I think the whales might be inside my throat,” I said.

“Good. Let them in. Don’t shut the door behind them. It’s manners.”

She patted the bed. I sat. The mattress sighed under the geography of us. The smell of her was lemon candies, soap, old wool dampened by the air. The walls wore a lattice of maps with pins stuck in their edges, the strings she had once thumbtacked between our town and South Georgia, Mauritius, some tiny part of the world that had to do with birds.

“They woke me at four,” she said. “I felt them come before they sang. The floor shook. My good glass rattled to its rim and stopped. The pine needles lifted their heads. It is polite to announce yourself.”

“You told me to come.”

“I would have told you to come if goats had walked into the kitchen and sat down at my table,” she said. “It is time.”

“Time for what.”

“For me to leave. For you to choose a thing. Take that box.”

On the table beside the bed was a box of oiled wood I had never seen, though I had lived in this house a half my childhood. Its lid fit as perfectly as the lid of a mouth. When I opened it, I smelled salt and something like old teeth. Inside, wrapped in a flannel shirt of my grandfather’s, lay a bone.

I had seen a whale’s ear bone once. The year they beached three of them on the shoal, the town women had taken knives to blubber while men moaned into flasks, and the bones had risen out of that work as if conjured, dense stones with the complicated swelling shape of a fist. This one was like that, white with the yellow of age, a geography of ridges my fingers wanted to read. It was heavier than it had any right to be. When I tilted it, the room tilted with it. The bone was not smooth, but it had been touched so often that every roughness had become instruction. I held it and felt the song more strongly, as if an inlet had been carved in me, as if all sound tired of the air and wanted to lie down somewhere denser.

“I took it,” she said, matter-of-fact. “Years ago. This is my shame and my joy.”

“You—”

“From the cow on the shoal. She had cast her calf and did not want to leave without him, and of course she did not leave, because we did what we had always done when a thing bigger than us presents itself. We took her apart as if she were made to be taken. Your grandfather’s knife had a curve that suited it. Someone would have kept her ear if I had not. I told myself I was a better thief than the next person. You know how we sweeten our mouths.”

“You kept it all this time.”

“Some things need a keeper. It sang even then, quiet. I thought it might teach me something, and I was right. It taught me my cowardice. I listened to it every night. Put it beside the bed and let it hum my bones. I dreamt of cities I had never seen. The train conductor who killed a man in the war. The girl on the pier in a red coat who did not know her own name. I heard people who spoke in languages I did not know I knew. I heard your mother.” She said that carefully, as if placing a glass on a table. “I heard her when she left and I heard her wherever she went. I kept thinking, if I listen long enough, she will turn into a direction and I will go there. But it is a fool thing to think. It is not a map. It is a door that opens onto a hundred rooms, and each room is a grief that belongs to someone else.”

I turned the bone over. The tide pulled and released the house. The whales were loud enough that the air had a taste. My grandmother closed her eyes and opened them again, as if she were practicing.

“You want me to take it back,” I said.

“I want you to put it where it belongs. It is their instrument, not ours. It is what the world gave them to hear themselves and we have used it like a shelf. You return a borrowed thing when the owner asks for it. It is the only rule I never broke.”

“And they are asking.”

“They are asking,” she said, and her voice did not wobble on the fence between certainty and wish. “Do not give it to the men with their trucks and their vests. Do not let them lock it in a glass box in town and put a brass plaque under it with the wrong story. If they take it, they will call it history and it will be dead in a month. I want to go with it.”

“You can’t—”

“You will take me out in my shroud like a parcel,” she said, briskly, as if she were ordering sugar, “and you will put me somewhere under the shelf at the point where I could hear the shipping lane when I was a girl. You will not burn me and scatter me on pizza like we did to your grandfather when we could not bear to do the harder thing. Do not look at me like that. I am not trying to make poetry. I am trying to make sure that when I go, I am not kept. Do you understand? It matters what we do with the parts of us that can still listen.”

“Nan—”

“You can say no later,” she said, and her mouth did that thing it did when she had used up tenderness for the day. “But first, put your ear to that thing and tell me what you hear. Humor an old woman. You were always my best listener.”

We had sat on this bed with my ear pressed to her chest, my ear pressed to the wall to hear a rain I could not see, my ear pressed to a shell the size of my head. Each time, what I heard was either nothing or a kind of world. I lifted the bone and felt stupid and felt eleven again and put my ear to a shallow curve.

It was not like storm or machinery; it was not blood. It was a hum that contained other hums, a braid too fine to unpick. As I listened, the rest of the room fell away the way a hallway falls away when you decide which one of the doors you want. Sometimes you can’t tell if a sound is outside of you or inside of you, and sometimes you realize there is no outside or inside to begin with, that everything you’ve ever held to your ear has been your ear teaching you its own name.

Then I heard it. A name. Not spoken—there is no tongue in those mouths—but shaped in the air nonetheless, the way a bird shapes flight. It touched the part of me that my grandmother had always said was a harbor no matter where I lived. It was not my name, not the one I used for people, not even the one she used for me when she remembered who I looked like, but it was mine and I was unmade by it.

I flinched. The bone rang my teeth.

My grandmother watched me with the serene, vindicated look of someone who has made a proper match between a word and a thing. “There you go,” she said. “There you are.”

“I can’t carry you and the bone at the same—” My mouth, always practical when I was frightened.

“You push me in the old wheelchair and put the bone in your bag and you do not tell anyone where you are going,” she said. “You go when it is dark enough. You go when the harbormaster is tired. You go when the moon is the same size as the eggs my hen will not lay. You will know. If you do not go, then you will not go, and I will rot in this bed like a saint with no pilgrims, and I will forgive you while not forgiving you at all. There is very little dignity in being human. At the end you choose the story you can stand to be told about you when you cannot raise your voice to correct it.”

“You could wait,” I said. “You could stay until—”

“My body does not know how to wait anymore,” she said softly, and it was the first time her voice sounded like the voice of a person with a body. “It is finishing with me. Think of it as a house that knows when it is time to fold up the furniture and blow the lamps out. I would prefer to go while the song is playing.”

The glass in the window trembled. Beyond, the afternoon had turned the color of pewter, and a rain had begun that did not announce itself on the roof, only appeared on surfaces until everything darkened by a shade.

“Will you call—” I started, the list of people who thought they ought to be called unspooling like chain: the minister, the woman who organized the casseroles, the neighbor who had brought her glossy magazines and left them in a stack that kept sliding onto the floor, Mira.

“I have called myself,” she said. “I am here. That is the only person I owe.”

She closed her eyes again and this time they were more reluctant to open. Her breath had a pattern, then it did not. I had imagined there would be one thing momenting from the next like beads that made a necklace I would recognize later in the dark, but there was no sense to it, not any you can count on.

“I took you from the water when you were born,” she said suddenly, as if she had forgotten we had begun this conversation and were picking it up as we always had, the years between us accordioning into ordinary time. “Your mother went to the harbor because she had decided that she would be the sort of woman who did not bother anyone when she hurt. Can you imagine how silly. I walked down there in my apron with my hair not pinned up, and the men looked at their boots, because there are certain thresholds a woman crosses and even a man who is ignorant recognizes that he should look away. You came out like a fish surprised to find air. I said, Oh, you. You were already listening. Your ear was the first part of you I loved. Isn’t that a ridiculous thing to say. Your mother looked at me as if she had betrayed me. I said, No. This is not betrayal. This is a gift. She had a mouth I recognized. She had your father’s hands. There. I have said it. You will not get the rest of that story out of me unless you dig me up, and I doubt you will find the shovel.”

“You could write it down,” I said. “You could tell me and I would translate it.”

“For whom,” she asked, with such unbelief that it melted my courage to be glib. “Language is a toll you forget you are paying. Take me to the point and toss me in. Take the bone with me. All our stories will be understood by whatever hears us then.”

We lay like that for a while, two animals breathing in a room. The whales sang and pipes in the walls answered in their own octaves. Somewhere down the street someone laughed the way people laugh when they are very frightened they might believe what they have always said they do not believe. The radio lit its green circle as if it hoped someone would give it a job.

When she went, it was the small sound of a door’s latch, not the door itself. The silence that followed it was the kind that is never entirely, because the body continues to do small, impolite things. I touched her forehead with my lips and felt the skin cool in the seconds it took my guilt to find me.

I sat very still because I had been taught that stillness was a form of respect. The light leaned across the floorboards and fell apart. The whales made a note like a bell someone had lowered into the harbor and I felt it grip my spine and shake. I put the bone to my ear again and this time what I heard was not a name but a map with no numbers. I did not know where on it I stood, only that there was a line and I was on it. I stayed there long enough to feel foolish. I stayed there until I began to understand that foolishness is just the word we use when our love is showing.

After a while, I stood. I closed her eyes, a cliché that turned out to be true: it is like it is in the films, you run two fingers lightly down and something in the lids takes the cue. I did not cover her with the sheet. She hated that, the reduction of it. I took the blanket I had knit and tucked it around her shoulders the way she had tucked me into the basket of the red bicycle she rode until she was sixty-two. I turned off the radio because I could not stand the way it was trying to make itself useful.

Then I went to the back door and stepped into the yard and breathed the rain. A neighbor saw me over the fence and lifted her chin. I lifted mine back and then went inside because to stand there would be to become a news the town could consume with their tea.

I packed the old canvas bag that still had one handle mended with my blue thread. Into it I put the ear bone wrapped in the shirt, a loaf of bread and two apples, the flashlight with the batteries that rolled when I shook it, the key to the gate at the point because my grandmother had never returned keys to anything in her life. I found the chair with wheels in the shed behind the house, cobwebs netting its spokes like something the sea would approve of. I washed my hands because it felt like a ritual and because there was blood under my left thumbnail from where I had pinched the bone too hard. I did not look at myself in the mirror above the sink. The person there would have an expression I did not have time to interpret.

By the time I wheeled the empty chair through the front room and into the hallway, the light had gone fully to ink. The whales were still there. The song quieted and rose, quieted and rose. It sounded like patience if patience were a direction. Three times I opened my mouth to call Mira and three times I closed it. I would have to live with the words that would come next. I would have to live with the fact that I had set something in motion that could not be put back on its shelf.

I stood at the door and listened to the wheel squeak and the rain make its small speech on the walk and the sound inside the bone, which had settled into a hum that matched my pulse. Then I went to where my grandmother lay and slid my arms beneath her shoulders and knees, and for a moment it was years ago and I was small and she was large and then it was now and I was strong enough and she was light. I put her in the chair. Her hair fell over the blanket like the loose end of a rope thrown from a boat to the dock, asking.

Outside, the whales lifted and fell, lifting a world with them. I pressed my hand to the bone through the fabric of the bag, as if I could steady whatever in it was unsteady and ask it to do the same for me. The hum answered with the particular arrogance of the truth. I did not know if I was about to commit a small sacrilege or repair an old one. Above us, the wind farm turned and turned, their red lights blinking in an idiot reassurance. The harbormaster’s horn tried again and failed to be bigger than a whale.

“Come on,” I told my grandmother, who would never again look past me to the horizon I could not see. “Let’s go while they are singing.”

Chapter One

In the morning after the storm, the island smells like iron and fennel. The cliff path is slick with blown needles and the foam looks like torn letters pasted back into a page. I walk with my apron tied twice around my waist, tin shears in one pocket, a coil of bright twine in the other. I go down to the striated beach, where the sand changes color the way bread does when it's first cut, and I begin to see what the sea has decided to remember.

When strangers ask about Vespera, I tell them it is an island shaped like a hand that doesn’t know whether to wave hello or goodbye. We used to make our living out of what we could coax from the water—inkfish, octopus, the bones of old ships—and for a while it seemed the sea was a generous grandmother. Lately she has been moody. Lately she has started sending people back to us, or parts of people, or the lives they meant to live.

Mano is already down there, boots sunk deep into the damp, trousers rolled to the knees, his hands like knots of rope. He is always first. He says he comes to count the gulls, to curse the kites that take fish mid-leap, but really he comes to see what came in on the night. He believes the sea keeps count the way priests believe God takes attendance, and if there’s an extra thing on the shore that wasn’t there yesterday, it means we’re in someone else’s story now.

“Don’t do it today,” he calls, without turning his head. His voice is the rasp of a barnacle on the hull. “Leave what she leaves.”

“She” is the only pronoun allowed for water. On the island even dogs are male or female only by virtue of who calls them.

“You say that every time,” I say, and because I want to ease it for him I add, “I only take what no one comes to get.”

He snorts as if I’ve told a joke I don’t understand. He is nearly seventy, skin freckled with old sun like spill-salt. For as long as I’ve known him, he has not gone farther out than the pilings. He wears three scarves in winter and a saint under his shirt. He is kinder to lobsters than to men.

He nods with his chin toward the southern end of the curve, where the kelp lies roped and snagged and a black thing sits among it like an animal at rest. “That one,” he says. “Not yours.”

It is a suitcase. Or rather, it looks like a suitcase looked in the photographs in the post office, the sepia ones of the men who left for the cold countries and the pale-faced women who followed with children asleep on their shoulders. Leather, darkened and bruised by water. A strap with a green ribbon tied around it, like a wrist asking to be taken.

My museum is an accusation, people say. Or a consolation. They use the words as if one could be the polite version of the other. I say it is a ledger. The lighthouse had been empty since the new one was built, electric and machine-minded at the point. When I inherited the post office from my father, I inherited as well a room behind the sorting racks filled with envelopes that had never been claimed, packages with addresses written in foreign hands. There were postcards that had become a series of skies, stamped year after year and never sent; there were notices from capitals that kept losing their capital letters. People began to leave things by mistake and because they had no choice. The boat overfilled. The ditchwater rose through fields. They left their shoes, their cups, the boxes with their boys’ drawings. They left the things that weren’t a person but were attached to a person, the way a shadow is attached to a body if you stand up before noon. I took the lighthouse key from my father’s chain. I put shelves along the walls, doors back on the cabinets, a bell at the entrance. I wrote labels in my neatest hand, the letter loops fat as fishhooks. I left space after the word belonged to. I called it the Museum of the Unreturned because there was no reason to handle the facts gently.

It isn’t only strangers’ things that wash back. There are our things too. There was once the wooden toy my father carved for me, a turtle with a shell made of bottle caps, vanished at the bottom of the bay when I was seven and too proud to cry. Two winters ago it turned up under the pier in February, the caps still clicking. There was once a yellow scarf that my mother wrapped around her hair, and I found a corner of it in a rock cleft the year I turned twenty-eight. Whether that means anything depends on whether you think the sea is a storyteller or a thief.

Mano goes back to his slow trawl for thick rope and intact buckets. I stand by the suitcase and listen before I touch. Ridiculous, but you learn to hear the difference. Sand whispers around glass. Seaweed makes the sound of hands clapping underwater. A suitcase full of clothes sighs. A suitcase full of paper is quiet in a way that draws quiet to it, the way a mouth draws spoon.

I lift the strap. It is heavy, but not above what I can manage. It leaves a rectangle in the wrack. The leather leaves my palms wet, and there is a taste in the air like a coin held too long between teeth.

“Don’t put it with the others,” Mano says without looking at me.

I think of the place I keep the newest things, because they have not yet agreed to be old. On the lighthouse’s third floor there is a glass room where the lens used to sit, where we have built a light out of LED strips donated by a boy who was once our boy and now isn’t our boy, because he has a job fixing planes in a country where snow comes in only one size. I keep the newest there in case their owners come quickly and we must show them how we kept faith.

“Was there anyone?” I ask him. “In the night?”

“Wind,” he says. “Water. One boat that went where it shouldn’t. That’s enough anyone for me.”

He does not say what he means: small boat, too many, the filament of a light far out and low, the absence you see in the morning as foam on a black gull wing.

I carry the suitcase up the cliff path because the stairs at the pier are still slippery and I am fond of both my legs. The dog that is not mine but calls me his with his eyes, a thick-shouldered creature with ears like torn sails, shadows me and then darts ahead to scare the lizards. My father used to offer me a shoulder when we reached the steep part. He would say, The rock is like an old mother, Amália; she won’t mind if you lean a little. He said this in the years after my own mother walked out of the long shadow of the lighthouse into a fog that did not exist and was not seen by anyone else.

People say all sorts of things about her leaving. That she went with a man with a boat big enough to carry the moon. That she heard a song the rest of us can’t hear. That she drowned six meters from shore the way brave men sometimes drown when they go to rescue other brave men and there is no one left to pull them out. My father said none of it. He kept his jaw where it was supposed to be. He kept the post office open Monday through Saturday, eight until two, because grief is easier with hours.

I move the suitcase into the museum’s middle room, where the walls are painted the same white the inside of a conch is painted and the floorboards creak like a man trying not to wake a child. I have dusted. I dust every morning. It is a way of asking permission. The labels are lined up like prayers. If I could fit an ocean into a drawer I would have cataloged it by now.

At the door, the small bell shakes. Juno arrives with two baguettes and one piece of gossip, as is her habit. She runs a café that never knows whether it is open or closed, and because she likes to lean on counters she is always falling in and out of love.

“What is it?” she asks, eyes going immediately to the dark thing on the table.

“A suitcase,” I say, unnecessarily.

She sets the bread down next to a colander and a row of marbles that had once lived in a pocket now empty of the boy who carried them. She stares. Her mouth tilts the way mouths tilt when people are counting what they have left.

“Don’t open it,” she says, which makes it the only thing I can do.

The strap resists, but not terribly. The green ribbon leaves a ghost line on my hand when I slide it free. The brass clasps are dull. There is salt in the creases like an old secret. When I lift, they complain—a small click, a not-quite sigh. It’s strange: the leather is wet, but the hinges are smooth, not crusted the way they should be with crystal crust, the hinges of all the sea-opened things.

Inside, the lining is a faded blue, printed with small moons. Paper, yes. A layer of paper, edges straight, as if this box has been carried from office to office and kept under a desk. I feel ashamed to be disappointed. You want a story to be glamorous even when you know better; you expect coins, a ring wrapped in cloth, something with the romance of rot.

On top, a ledger. A worn cloth cover, corners bruised to board. It is the kind of book they wrote hours in, here, years ago, back when days could be counted in flour or fish, not in tourists or storms. I lift it, and the dog puts his head on my knee. He has gotten old without my consent, silver at the jaw. I make a note to give him the soft part of the baguette later, even if Juno glares.

Under the ledger there are envelopes. They are addressed in a hand that belongs to no alphabet I know, which is saying something; I have learned to tell, in my work, how the A sits in a hand from Algiers and how it sits in a hand from the capital; I can tell a mother’s L from a father’s L without looking at the names. These envelopes turn my competence into a child.

There is a sweater folded small, the kind you knit when you believe winter will be a story you tell and not a place you live. The color is marigold. I put my nose into its cloth and smell lemon and smoke. No sea. Not even the borrowed salt of someone’s neck.

Next, a bracelet of dried seeds, a chipped cup, a tangle of green laces, a key attached to a ribbon that matches the one outside. The key is square-shouldered and worn where lots of hands have asked it to do an ordinary grace. It warms as soon as I hold it, but that could be because of me. It has numbers stamped into its flank: 11, 19, 7.

I open the ledger. Juno has moved closer without moving; you know the way people do that. She is behind my shoulder but it feels like she is inside the hinge of my own breath.

The first page is a list. Date, time, coordinates in neat columns. It looks like the ugly part of a poem. I have seen pages like this. Our coast guard keeps these. NGOs keep them. Women on the mainland keep them when they begin to track what happens to the migrants who are told they are not their husbands or their sons, who are told husbands and sons are accounted for elsewhere. But the handwriting is not state. It is small, fierce, like a person afraid not to be believed. At the top: Inventory of Passage. As if suffering could be enumerated.

I turn the page. Names, now. Two to a line. A child’s name next to a number. A mark where someone was tall. The notes are tender, like the way you would describe a bird that is tame enough to trust you. I skim, because my own name work has taught me this: to read every line is to become drunk on other people’s lives. You can’t deliver letters if you are always drunk.

I look, and I do not look. I look, and then I stop. The names begin to become a single sound. Then, like a fish turning at the edge of a net, one catches one eye and stops.

Luzia Pinho, it says, in a hand that makes the Z into a loop like a lark’s wing. Next to it, a number that could be a date or could be a room or could be a nothing. There are coordinates in the margin, written later, in pencil. They lilt like a song.

I am still. I have learned, from the men who taught me to swim, that sometimes stillness keeps you alive when thrashing would not. The room is white, and in the whiteness the small black letters look suddenly extravagant, excessive, like too much jewelry on the skeleton of a woman who used to prefer a clean collar and a simple dress.

“Say it,” Juno whispers.

“Luzia Pinho,” I say, as if I am being asked to confirm my own name for myself.

“Your mother,” Juno says, because she is incapable of reverence even when it is the only safe language we have. “Your mother’s maiden name. Your mother who—”

“I know who she is,” I say, and for a moment it feels like I have never said the sentence before and perhaps I haven’t. Perhaps I have only ever said who she was.

The dog lets out a sound that is almost language. Somewhere in the top of the lighthouse, a gull beats against the glass with both its wings. It makes a thud like an impatient heart.

There are more names. I could turn pages and find my own again, my own name, my own face, as if the book is a house with all its doors standing open. I could decide that this is someone's Luzia not ours, like those children who share names with saints and criminals and our sons. I could decide that a hand like that would loop Zs with loops like that for every saint in the calendar and every bricklayer who ever came through our port. I could decide.

I close the book. My palms are damp. When I lay the ledger back into the suitcase, it makes that whisper paper makes when it loves where it sits.

“Who brings this?” Juno asks the ceiling, which is to say the God she believes in when she is frightened and sometimes when she needs money. “Who writes that? Who writes that and puts it where you will find it?”

“It may have meant to go somewhere else,” I say. “Everything is a detour until it isn’t.”

This is how we do it here: We answer important questions with small truths, the way you would put a child's shirt in the sun and say, See, it is warm now, without talking about heat in general.

I lift the key. In my palm it seems to pulse, but that could be my blood trying to pretend it is a thing. I see that the numbers on its side are not arbitrary. They are coordinates too, written in a language that exacts a subtle revenge: 11 to mean day, 19 to mean month, 7 to mean the year my mother was born or the year she left or the year the world will choose next to be cruel. Or maybe they are not numbers but letters, standing up like soldiers: K, S, G. Maybe they are the depth of a certain place at noon.

Mano’s head appears in the doorway without his knocking, his cap dripping a little rain that has been waiting all morning for the courage to fall. He sees Juno. He sees me. He sees the suitcase, the ledger, the way my hand holds the key as if we have been introduced.

“No,” he says.

He steps in with his boots still wet and the dog pretends to sleep. There is a look people share when they have chased things away together and now must pretend to be enemies for the sake of custom. He and Juno exchange that look and then stop pretending.

“The thing you have, menina,” he says, using the word for girl even though I am not one and he knows it, “it brings back, but it also calls. Take care what you ask back. The sea is very careful with verbs.”

I could say, I know. I could say, I have been careful my whole life. Instead I say nothing, because I understand that silence is also an instrument. He leans his knuckles on the table as if ready to push or pray.

I think of my father cutting stamps along their perforation and brushing his thumb along the edge to feel the way separation leaves a burr. I think of the morning my mother went out into the fog that was not there and did not take her scarf because she said she would be back for lunch. I think of the museum, full of small careful things trying to remain themselves against the tyranny of weather.

“Bring it up,” I say.

I do not say what. I do not need to. I wrap the ledger back in its paper skin. I carry the suitcase up the spiral stairs, where the corners wear the footprints of our ancestors in shallow bowls. My shoulder finds its old place against the wall. Juno follows, wood under her feet, the dog behind her, old and gallant. Mano comes last, muttering to the saints he keeps for emergencies.

In the glass room the sea flings its shoulders against the horizon like a great tired animal. The new light at the point blinks its bored electric blink, indifferent to the old stories. I set the suitcase on the floor and the key on the sill and the ledger on the table where we have signed so many guest books and so many petitions.

I take a breath into the part of my body that always knows when to be patient and I say, quietly so as not to scare anything away, “If you have something of mine, I would like it back. If I have something of yours, I will keep it safe until you come.”

The glass holds the reflection of my mouth forming the words. Out on the water, a line of light travels as if someone is dragging a spoon along the surface. It is probably a fish breaking. It is probably nothing.

The key warms in my palm. The dog puts his head against my thigh and sighs the long sigh of someone who finally recognizes a song. Juno curls her fingers around the balustrade. Mano looks at the sea the way a man looks at a door that is about to open and will not say for whom.

We wait. The museum waits with us. On the table the ledger sits like a heart. The island holds itself in a practiced shape, the way a hand knows how to carry water if it keeps very, very still.
