The bus creaked down out of the hills as if it were remembering how to descend. The driver had strung a plastic rosary over the rearview mirror, and each bead clicked like a metronome gone dull. I had been watching the river since the ferry stop, the way the light settled into it, the way the water moved with the slow insistence of old arguments. The bridge our bus would cross was a flat tongue of concrete, unlovely, an idea someone had had about spanning distances. Every time I left as a child, my mother would stand at the window and say, Go past the river and it will forget you. Every time I came back, she’d say, But it forgets like an old person—slowly, in parts.

We were almost to the midspan when the driver eased the bus to a standstill. A line of cars piled behind us, horns muffled the way a warning sounds when it is given by someone who doesn’t quite believe it. The driver leaned forward, hands on ten and two, and the rosary clicked once more, then was still.

“Watch,” he said. To whom, I wasn’t sure. Maybe to himself. Maybe to the river.

The air had that iron taste storms bring, though the sky was washed clean. A heron traced a line so straight I thought of the pencils they handed out in first grade, new and waiting for a mistake. The river slackened. That’s the only word for it. It loosened, like a belt pulled one hole out after dinner. The surface unwrinkled. The sound — always there even when you weren’t listening — thinned until I could hear the click of the rosary beads again.

People on the sidewalks stopped. A boy ran forward to the railing and stood on his toes, and his mother grabbed him by the hood the way you’d pull back bread before it burned. The bus driver breathed out — I could see the fog of it against the windshield — and then the water tugged itself in the opposite direction. It was subtle and then it wasn’t. The wavering weed at the embankment, the bottle snagged under the pier, the oil-slicked filament of fishing line that had been caught on a nail since winter — everything admitted to being touched by the same new force, a hand the size of a town placed under the surface, dragging.

“Early this year,” the driver said. In the mirror, my face was thin and my hair smaller than I remembered. I made a sound in my throat I didn’t mean to make and the driver’s eyes flicked up to meet mine. “You picked your day,” he said, not unkind.

“I didn’t pick anything,” I said. My voice came out too stiff, like it had slept under an iron.

He let the bus roll forward. On the far side, people were already carrying down the long rake poles, the nets patched with string in colors that told you who had done the mending. The chalkboard outside the Office of Returns was blank for now. It would be full by nightfall: names, objects, years. You could pass by and read lives scratched in powdery letters: ring, silver, 1997; lunch tin, enamel, 'sings when struck', 1973; bone knife, no sheath, belonged to someone no one would admit to remembering. Outsiders stood in small clusters, phones held up like sparrows, trying to catch the moment water admitted its little frauds.

My aunt’s house had once been blue, the kind of color that had a name for boats, not for walls. It had faded to something you couldn’t place, the sun taking out the salt and the salt taking out the rest. She had left the door unlatched the way we always did on reversal days. “Mara,” Aunt Lila said, stepping out of the kitchen with a dish towel thrown over her shoulder like surrender. She was exactly as I remembered, which is to say she carried twice as much as she should and did it without complaint. A pot hissed in the corner where beans were losing their stiffness. My cousin Tomas was on the floor with a spool of orange twine and a box of rusted hooks, his tongue out the corner of his mouth in the fixed attention of boys and surgeons. He looked up at me and then away, embarrassed by having grown.

“You made it in time,” Aunt Lila said, and then her eyes slid to the place over my shoulder where the idea of my mother usually stood. It wasn’t there. Grief, I’ve learned, leaves an outline the way flames do, a darker, precise shape in which absence is lit up.

“I made it because the bus didn’t break,” I said. It was an attempt at humor. It turned into something like a flinch. She nodded, understanding what I hadn’t said.

“Eat something,” she said. “We’ll go down.” She glanced at Tomas. “You have the ledger?”

He held it up. It was the same old thing: leather, soft with use, the corner chewed by a dog that had died before Tomas was born. The Office had a ledger too—the official, iron-backed book that lived under glass and smelled of the wet wool of history—but every house kept its own. You always wanted your own version of the truth.

We walked down together. Voices found a register they only had one day a year, a baggy, careful loudness. People touched one another more. When the river remembered, neighbors became the kind of kind they regret the next day. The silt had a clean smell today, fresh-baked and metallic. On the far bank, reeds trembled with a wind I couldn’t feel.

“You were small enough to fit in the bait bucket the first time you saw it turn,” Aunt Lila said. “You kicked your foot in the water and your mother slapped your ankle and then cried because she had never lifted a hand to you. Do you remember?”

“I remember the duct tape she put around my wrists,” I said. “So if I fell in, she could hook me easy.” What I didn’t say was that I remembered the pride in being considered salvage at all.

“She believed in it,” Aunt Lila said, a shrug doing poor work as a sentence. She meant the river. She meant this day. She meant anything that could be believed in because it was too large to be held alone.

“She had a box,” I said, without planning to. “Tin. Letters. Photos. Buttons from coats that didn’t fit anymore.” I had been eight when the flood came up past the stoop like a dog that had grown too familiar. The box had slipped from my mother's hands in the second hour of her carrying everything she could carry. I had seen it hit the water and then not seen it at all. My mother had said, It will come back when it knows how. That was the last year she insisted we watch from the bridge, then she watched from the window instead. You can be superstitious and still be tired.

At the Office, the Registrar stood on a fruit crate to be heard above the whisper. He wore the same vest every year, an eggplant-purple thing that never fit any time but this one. He spread his arms like a bird who knows it can't fly but wants everyone to agree about the feathers. “Splitting,” he called. He meant the river, but people made way for him as if he meant them. “Keep your poles low. No leaning into momentum. If it comes to your hand it was meant. If it runs past it never was yours.” The same rules as always. The rules kept us from fighting, mostly. They made a ritual out of what could have been only greed.

Someone’s radio crackled to life with the morning announcer from the city above us, his voice surprised and pleased, the way men are when nature does something they didn’t schedule. “Reports of the reversal coming five days before equinox,” he said. “Call in with what you’ve netted. Someone’s grandmother says fish swim belly-up on days like this. That true?”

“Fish don’t care,” the Registrar said, to no one in particular. “It’s people who care.”

An old man with a cap pulled down to his nose held up a bottle full of letters, the kind of bottle you find only in movies and in our town once a year. The bottle had a lopsided cork and a wax seal the color of smoked cherries. It had no right to be intact. He handed it to the Registrar with two hands. The Registrar, wiser than the story demanded, held it up to the light and looked for names. He didn’t find any. He set it on the table under the tin sign that said Holds, the plural thin because the s had been rubbed to almost nothing by years of forearms.

“It ain’t magic,” someone said in a voice that invited the river to disagree.

“I know,” said someone else. “It’s just what it does.”

We threaded our way forward. You could feel the tug of the water even on land, a lean in your calves, your body wanting to fall into agreement. Tomas zipped in front like a small dog that doesn’t know it’s supposed to heel. He had the hook he had filed on the back steps all spring to a gleaming, mean point. His hair was too long because Aunt Lila cut everyone’s hair in town and never her own. He’d written the year on his arm so he could copy it into the ledger without asking anybody.

“Mara!” I turned. It was Neri, who had sat behind my mother in church for thirty years without believing in the same God. He had the habit of turning his hand over when he spoke, showing you what he wasn’t holding. “I told them you’d come,” he said. He had told us many things when we were little. I had learned to believe him only when he talked about other people’s chores, where he was often right.

“Did you,” I said, and he thumped my shoulder with his knuckles the way men beat on doors.

“Your mother,” he began, and then stopped. He pulled his lower lip between his teeth and worried it a moment. “She used to stand in the back and make a note every time someone lied. Little marks in the margin of the hymnal. You were that kind of person once.”

“What kind of person is that, exactly?” I asked.

“The kind that thinks the ledger should be true even if we aren’t,” he said, then smiled like he hadn’t said it.

When the first thing came in it was not a thing anyone could own. It was a spot of oil the size of a hand. It slid up against the pilings and then reversed, slid backward as if someone had cupped it from behind. The surface of it was that rainbow you always pretended you were too old to love. A child reached for it, and his father held him, held him, let him go. We watched the oil slip back under the bridge and out of view. People pretended it had been a good omen to see it.

The second thing was a hat from a store that had gone out of business before I was born, the name lettered in the brim by a clerk long dead whose forearms had dust on them that had never come off. The Registrar held it, turned it, called out the name. A woman with a scar shaped like a comma at the base of her throat laughed, a sound that had sharp in it. She took the hat, held it against her side like a child.

“Twenty years,” she said, to no one. “It still smells like his work.”

“Is that good or bad?” the Registrar asked.

“Both,” she said. The laughter fell out of her mouth.

We took a place on the warped boards by the boathouse. The river moved against us, and in it there were pieces of sky we hadn’t asked for. Tomas crouched, line deep in the water, his tongue doing its thinking. Aunt Lila had her chin up like a person who has cried all she will cry for the year and is working out how to breathe for the rest of it. I could not help it: I reached for the water with my hand and then stopped, my wrist prickling in memory of the duct tape my mother had wrapped around it, the rough silver edge hot with her breath on it as she tore it with her teeth.

“She’d box your ear if she saw you do that,” Aunt Lila said, soft.

“If she saw me at all, she’d do worse,” I said.

We waited. Waiting is the work of this town. It’s what we’re good at. We wait for the wind to change directions, for the tide, for our children to come home full of someone else’s ideas. We wait for the bureaucrat to stamp the paper we require to do the thing we were already doing under a different name. We wait for the rain everyone said was coming in May and arrives either not at all or on a Tuesday in September when no one has a bucket handy.

A jar knocked against the dock twice, like a visitor asking to be let in and then losing their nerve. Tomas hooked it clean, the point of the tool shining like a feeling. He lifted it with something like reverence, though he would deny that word. Things that arrived in glass seemed pleased to have held together long enough to see us. Things that arrived in wood carried a patience so tired it made me want to nap.

The jar had a red rubber ring and the metal clasp rusted with a kind of elegance, the way old men’s knuckles look when they clasp their hands together in church. Inside the jar was something wrapped in waxed paper. Tomas put the jar in my hands as if it had, in fact, arrived to see me. The glass was colder than the air.

“Read it,” Tomas said, and Aunt Lila cuffed him lightly.

“You don’t read jars,” she said. “You open them.”

“They open us,” said Neri, who had sidled up as if we had invited him, which, to be fair, we always did. He reached two fingers to the clasp and pinched. It came free without a fight. He lifted the lid and a smell came up that was not river, not silt, not old. It was laundry dried indoors, cheap soap, fennel seed, the talc my mother dusted into her shoes in summer when the heat blunted her steps. The smell made a place under my breastbone and widened it.

Tomas slid the waxed paper out and handed it to me because sometimes boys like to see if you’re brave. The paper was cockled in waves, the folds so sure they had become their own geometry. My name was written on the outside. My name. MARA. In my mother’s hand, which was not a neat hand or a beautiful hand but was a hand I would have recognized if you had written with it on the wall of a cave caves hadn’t taught themselves to be until the week before.

“Wait,” Aunt Lila said, but I had already opened it. Sometimes the story won’t be told slowly, however you tell it. The wax pulled back and something slid into my palm: a comb, simple bone, the teeth worn smooth, and along its spine what looked like scratches that wanted to be a sentence but hadn’t yet learned. They weren’t scratches. They were notches, deliberate and small.

“Your mother’s,” Aunt Lila said. She had parted my hair with that comb, pulling the river of it in two as if it were always meant to separate. When it had gone missing, she had accused me of swallowing it in a fit of childish envy, and then cried and apologized and made me tea I was too old to be soothed by. We had not found it then. We had not expected to.

“Did she carve it?” Tomas asked. His voice had the whisper of people inside churches this town might like to have.

I put the comb to my ear the way my grandfather used to do with shells he would bring back from the drying lakes, a joke no one laughed at but him. I did it because we do the wrong things first. Nothing. I turned it in my hand. The notches were not alphabet in any sense I knew, not numbers the way clocks count them, not ticks the way prisoners mark days into walls. But they were a pattern. You held the comb in your palm and each notch sat under a finger if your hand was my mother’s hand. You pressed and it made a story told by pressure.

“Is this…,” I began, and didn’t finish because what I meant to say was Is this what I think it is, but to be honest I didn’t know what I thought.

“Things come back with a stubbornness,” Neri said. He was watching us the way he watched fires: at a distance that implied he had once learned something too closely. “Sometimes they come back wrong.” He turned his face up to the clouds like he wanted to see if they believed him.

“You think it’s wrong?” Aunt Lila asked. Her voice had an edge I knew too well. It was the edge of someone who will fight the idea of loss until it tires and goes to sleep.

“I think it’s here,” Neri said. “Right or wrong is for people who have time.”

Tomas was already writing in the ledger: jar, glass; contents: comb, bone. Found by: Tomas Lila’s boy, handed to: Mara returns. Date: he copied off his arm. He looked up, eyes shining, and said, “We did good,” the way children share credit for the moon.

We stood there a while with it. I put the comb against my lip and breathed. The bone warmed to my skin the way stones in the yard kept the sun’s heat long after the tomato vines had given up for the night. In the glaze of the jar there was a smeared reflection of my face that looked like a stranger holding my features together like a bouquet. I reached into the jar again to see if there was more. The waxed paper was heavier than it had any right to be. It had a second fold. Of course it did. My mother always folded things twice, once for the world and once for herself. In the second fold there was a scrap of ribbon, yes, and a stick of pencil worn down to the nub, yes, and a strip of cloth from the dress she had been wearing the day we had thrown our furniture up onto the roof like an offering, yes. And there was a note.

It wasn’t paper. She had never trusted paper on the river. It was cloth. The weave tight, the letters big, blacked in with ink that had bled along the threads without losing their shape. It was two words at first, then three, then the sentence made itself out of my mother’s breath.

Don’t let them.

“That’s not a sentence,” Tomas said, dissatisfied with cliff edges.

I folded the cloth until those words faced inward and the rest of the world was hidden. I pressed the comb hard into my palm until I felt each notch. It hurt in a way that made me think of stair rails and broken jars, of laughter in the wrong rooms. On the far bank, a boy picked up a fish that had no business in this river and tossed it back in with tender disgust. Someone down the way shouted about a watch that had never stopped and wasn’t starting now. A siren wailed uptown, the polite kind that moves traffic and soul only if you let it. The river kept pulling the way long ropes do: steadily, with a knowledge that you will tire before it will.

“Don’t let who,” Aunt Lila said, plainly. She had no patience for pronouns.

There was a second line on the cloth, smaller, the stretch of it cramped, less certain, the kind of writing done in a hurry with hands that bleed and never say why. I angled it toward the light. I thought of the bridge, the midspan where the bus had stopped like a heart. I thought of my mother in the window, her hands lifted in a gesture I had, as a child, called prayer and as an adult called surrender. I thought of the drawers in the office where I worked in the city, where we kept maps of the proposed dam, neat as bones, measuring the undoing and calling it progress. My tongue tasted pennies. The letters stood up like small fence posts.

Stop the memory.

It wasn’t a sentence I had been expecting from my mother, who kept recipes in the seams of her coats and names in the hems of her skirts. We were a saving kind. She had written it to me, who had left. She had written it in cloth because she expected it to get wet and need to be read anyway.

“What does it say?” Tomas said, eager. He jumped a little with the contained force of it. He was too young to understand abbreviations of pain. He would learn. We all did.

I did not want to invite the river into this. I wanted not to speak beside it and mean it too. I wanted to go back to Aunt Lila’s kitchen and put my head on the table the way I had when I was the size of an argument between adults. I wanted, and I also lifted the cloth higher because the sky had decided to dim a fraction and I was not yet willing to invent shadows.

“Don’t let them,” I said, because repeating the first line was easier, because saying it wrong would make it less true. “…stop it.”

Neri whistled between his teeth in the way men from our town did when nothing else made sense. It sounded like a kettle arguing with itself. Aunt Lila closed her eyes briefly, as if to consider whether closing them would stop anything. Tomas looked from me to the cloth to the river, and I could see the story forming in his head the way streams make their beds and are surprised to find themselves in them.

“She could have meant the winter fishing,” he said, wildly, bless him. “Or the bakery closing. Or…” He didn’t say the dam because he wasn’t supposed to know about it. Children know everything you hide badly.

“It’s a sentence,” I said, and did not say mine. The comb sat in my hand like an instruction. The bone warmed and then cooled and then was my temperature. Out beyond us, the water slipped past like a book being opened to the right page. Boats that had been stubborn all summer came untied as if obeying a word. The chalkboard outside the Office of Returns already had a list of what had come in and what had been claimed, and there were empty spaces left that people had a terrible, beautiful hope about.

Behind us, the bus made its way back across the bridge, slow, sincere, beads ticking against a dangling mirror. High up on the hill, above our flat part of town, the office where I had drafted the first lines of the proposal to measure and harness the river’s work — beneficial diversion, flood mitigation, energy capture — glinted square and glass-eyed. I had kept my name off the public documents. I had told myself this was how you kept faith with two worlds: you cut your signatures like bread, and no one went hungry.

“You always were your mother’s child,” Aunt Lila said then, and I couldn’t tell if it was a praise or a sentence. She meant the way my shoulders shifted as if I had been assigned a thing to carry and was already calculating corners.

“I don’t know what I am,” I said, and it came out truer than I intended.

The Registrar, at the far end of the dock, banged a spoon against an enamel mug to get attention for a thing that had been washed up that was large enough to require fifteen hands. The sound clanged in the thinness that comes right before noon in a town where the sun is a fact and the facts are unforgiving. People came, dutiful, curious, hungry for a story that wasn’t theirs.

I folded the cloth until the words were inside themselves, safe or at least contained. I put the comb in my pocket where it bit thigh each time I took a step, reminding me of its teeth and of mine. I set the jar under the bench at the edge of the boathouse, the way you would set a sleeping child where it could still hear its family moving. The river tugged backward with the patience of a thing that has read all the books and is pulling its favorite story up again to the beginning. I thought of ink bleeding along thread. I thought of my mother’s mouth and the way she would set it when she had decided something she knew would cost us both. I thought, ridiculous and absolute as a prayer, that we name what we love, and then we try to fix it in place. And that the river, unkind and faithful, gives back what it has held only to ask us — with the weight of things, with their smell, with the indentation bone makes in the palm — do you know it now. Do you know it yet.

Before evening, if the pattern held, someone would pull up the box my mother had dropped when our furniture floated like promises no one believed in. Or they wouldn’t. I was not patient in ways that counted. In the afternoon, some newsman from the city would stand on our dock in clean shoes and pronouncements, and a child would drop his microphone into the water and laugh, and no one would be angry at her because she had been right to do it. In a week, the river would turn itself properly and forget our names again in the way you always forget somebody who refuses to be introduced twice. And somewhere between now and then, I would climb the hill into the office with the glass eye and put my hand on the blueprint table the way a person checks another for fever, and decide how much of the world I was willing to write my name on.

Don’t let them stop it, my mother had said, in cloth because paper hates water and because she knew. She always did. The reversal had come early, like a child that cannot wait to be born, and in that hurry there was a kind of warning. The sky clouded and cleared its throat. The river pulled, and the people who lived with it leaned, and the ledger pages turned, and the bones of the comb pressed against my leg: small teeth asking what I intended to chew.

The river ran backward the morning my mother left. People said it was some crooked trick of the tide, though we were forty-seven miles from any honest sea. They said it was the dam burping. They said it was wind. They said a great fish rolled in its sleep and the whole water bowed to it.

I was eleven and on the footbridge behind the old Atlas plant, where the boltheads had rusted to the size of knucklebones and the rail paint came off on your palm like an old bruise. Harlan—my father—had walked me there because he didn't know what else to do with my hands. I wanted to carry something, a box, a bird, a rope. There's a choreography to leaving that everybody knows from animals. The dog paced and cried; crows gathered along the power lines like black-coated judges. Even the neighbors came to the porches and leaned on their hips with dish towels draped over their shoulders, watching our yard as if we were their television. Mom—Marin—had suitcases and a red scarf she never wore, tied uselessly to the strap of the largest bag. She was all motion until she wasn't, and then she was gone.

We watched the river unspool itself. There was the mudline in the winter grass on the bank, eight inches up, a careful lick of dark like a second horizon. That line had always promised where the Marrow had been, where it might be again. That morning the water edged backward and lowered, like it was drawing breath between its teeth. Leaves, fishkill, a syrup of junk—foam cups and a glove and a snapped-off broom handle—all of it turned on its axis and took a few hesitant kicks upstream. The men from the night shift at Atlas hung over the rail with us, their sleep creased and shuttering in their faces, their thermoses fatter than their wrists.

"No way," one of them kept saying, his voice pitching higher until it squeaked. "No way, no way, nuh-uh."

"It isn't possible this far in," Harlan said, but he said it gently, like you might say, The dog isn't dead, she's asleep. He had been forty-two that spring and looked at least fifty, the marshy tissue of his nose threading red as if threaded with veins of coral. He smelled always faintly of solvent and mint because the church had managed to make him quit drinking but hadn't found a way for him to forgive his own tongue for liking it. He pressed his hand to the crown of my head and swayed it. He had a habit of steering me by that soft place, like a bowl you keep from sliding.

At the far bend, near the willow where boys went in late summer to jerk bluegill from the heat, the surface slicked and blistered. The willow hair was winter-dead and looked like the broken spine of a old broom. A snapping turtle like a polished rock lifted its head into the reverse slick and let it carry its mouth backward. I had always thought of the river as a road that didn't care for us but tolerated us along it. That morning it lifted its skirt and revealed its ankles and showed us that it had joints we had never asked to see.

"Why does it do that?" I asked.

"Somebody up there pulled the plug," the man with the thermos said, and laughed his creaky laugh and then stopped, as if someone had told him that laughing is a kind of food some days and you shouldn't take it from a child.

My father looked at the surface like he could remember equations. He had once been good at those—my mother told me the numbers used to come off his pencil as if they couldn't wait—but at some point the sum had stopped landing. "Rivers don't have rules," he finally said. "They have habits. And bad days."

He took the thermos man's cigarette and ground it under his heel, not meanly but the way you'd snuff a candle before wading the dark. When the wind—there wasn't much—threaded through, you could taste salt on your lip. I had tasted that only in tears and in the little white packet of Morton my mother kept, blue girl with her umbrella, to sprinkle on tomato. But all of Atlas had brines and vats and an evaporation pond that looked like a winter-lake even in August, a flat glare where no birds landed. The town's gossip was salt even when we were sweet to each other. A decade of salt in the ground, they said, gets into the dog and the beans, into the bones. Babies cut their teeth early here and old people lose them all at once.

She had not left a note. I know how this sounds later, and I want to say that my mother was not the kind to leave without words. If you met Marin on a Tuesday she would tell you about a Wednesday from when she was nine and the weather had been like the throat of a flute. She layered her speech. When we were little-little—me and my brothers, the twins dead before two breaths long, and then just me like a survivor of a vanished family—she would turn everything into a map for us. Salt roads were old buffalo runs. Crest of hill was a whale's back. The ditch behind the school was where the soldiers had dug their hunger. We walked the mud in boots and she would instruct me in invisible things. In June, star-thistle; in September, white aster. "You need to know their names so you can ask to pass," she'd say, and then say it again, half to herself. "You always ask to pass."

It wasn't a note. It was the sound of the river reversing itself, and us watching it, and the zipper of the largest suitcase that stuck and then, with her grace, didn't.

She left us the red scarf, intentionally, I thought later. Marin was the kind of person for whom a scarf was a sentence. That one meant: you tie a thing to a thing so it doesn't blow away. The scarf was silk, which made no sense for here, for us, but then she had come here as if she'd pointed at a map with her eyes closed and when she opened them she said, Oh. All the stories about my parents were like that. Oh, we chose this. Oh, we didn't know but then we did. Oh, it was an accident and we married it.

After she went, the whole town found something to say to us. The women said, We'll bring casseroles, but don't eat the one with peas unless you're starving. The pastor said, God tests the horses He intends to race. Harlan said nothing, and the silence was a room in our house you could walk into and forget your own name. That evening, the river went back to its old habit, as if a blood pressure had shifted and stabilized and we had returned to someone else's normal. We could tell where it had earlier reversed because the scum had a second layer. Even the dullest water keeps a record if you know how to look.

If I am telling this like a scientist, it is only because work has taught me to speak without weeping. I left Ellis Bend when I was eighteen on a bus whose bathroom door would not latch and nobody ever figured out why it stank like rain at the end of a summer of drought. I took my loneliness to a city where nobody cared that I didn't understand that traffic meant it was Christmas, that nobody there pronounces pecan the way we did, that there were far more names for coffee than for a river. I became the thing my mother had taught me, though in a different uniform. I measure. I pin things to elevations and hold them long enough to know if they'll slip. I tell the water where it ought to behave and then live with myself when it laughs. My badge says Bureau. Once, a man at a bar said, Oh, Boring, and then tried to slide his hand down my shirt before he remembered I was made of teeth.

I am thirty-three now and my title is cartographer, a word that fits in the mouth like a hard candy you haven't decided if you like. I've mapped drought lines across states whose names sounded romantic when I was a child—Sonora, Platte, Bitterroot—and I've watched gauges tick to zero while the reporters ask me what it means that the river has turned into a string of shiny stones. I've stood in good dress shoes in a hearing room and told an old man in a bolo where he can no longer take water because the invisible ledger is red. I've listened to women in broken trailers tell me that their children smell like sulfur even if she triple-rinses the sheets. I think of Ellis Bend in those rooms. I think of Atlas. I tell the truth in the most mathematical way I can and then sit in my car and put my forehead to the steering wheel and breathe.

The letter came in February, folded like a bird into itself. The return address was a place I could not find on a map, which is the kind of thing that makes a person like me go cold. The date stamp was last week, and the paper was the thin kind that war veterans prefer. The handwriting was Marin's. I would say that there is no doubt, but I know doubt nests in everything. Her hand was a tidy slant with loops that never closed, because she believed the end of a word should be a window.

Cass, it began, as if there had been no years where we were not making each other eggs and mistakes.

Then as if she had turned to the side and said something to someone else, and then returned to the paper:

I owe this to you, at least. I am downstream but coming back. If you decide not to be here when I am, I will understand. Get the spoon that was your grandmother's out of the third drawer, the one with the notch. It has a fish engraved on it. Take it to the river and put it in. Not the spoon. Your hand. The river has a question for you. Be patient with what it asks. It will not sound like a human voice because it doesn't have lungs. It will be the voice of something pulled tight and plucked. I am sorry about the scarf. Keep it this time. Or bring it.

She signed it M like she always had, a monogram she had invented as a girl that had three points, like a mountain. There was a dab at the end where a drop of tea had landed and bled into a tiny watercolor.

By then, Harlan had been dead three months, the house turned quiet in a new register, as if a radio station had slipped from its frequency into something root-toned you couldn't dance to. He died the least theatrical way someone can die around here—a knee giving up its blood and a plug of fat finding its way to his brain—except that's not fair. There is nothing routine about a body deciding it is tired of being a body. At his funeral the pastor quoted something about sheep, and afterward men slapped my shoulder, too hard, the way they'd slap a refrigerator to admire its sturdiness.

I had come back because there were papers to sign and a roof to check and houseplants to forgive. I had told myself I would stay three days and then slip out before anyone had to tell me I looked like my mother. The letter turned those three days to a blind thing that unfolded like an animal from a box. I opened all the drawers in the kitchen and found the spoon exactly where she had said it would be, which made me want to put my head in the sink and run the water until I couldn't hear why that was the thing I wanted.

It wasn't fine silver. The spoon was pewter, dull and comfortable. The fish on the handle had a simple eye and a body of four scales, as if a child had designed it and a grown man had realized the design with his thick hands. I polished it with my thumb until the fish shone like a memory surfacing.

Outside, the late winter had thawed into what people around here, when they're feeling like poets, call false spring. Day for day, night for night, it will punish you. The grass had forgotten its manners and gone bright in patches. You could hear the slack in the river's voice before you saw it, a low mutter like someone behind a door trying not to wake the baby.

Ellis Bend in February smells like bleach and mud, like my father when the group met in the church basement and he came home with the chemical confidence of a man who didn't yet know he'd fail again by Friday. The Atlas plant had shuttered four years ago, the windows now scabbed with plywood and the catwalks broken and the sign that still said A L A S because the T had fallen in a wind that ate the women's hair from their heads. Before the closure, we had all rehearsed what we would say when the paychecks ended. Then it ended, and we said other things.

I'd parked by the lot where the teenagers show each other new scars. The footsteps of my boots had that hollow winter-river sound, snowmelt soaked in the sand. The sky was the old blue enamel saucepan we'd used to pop corn, the paint chipped to a white it never had been. This is to say that it was perhaps too pretty for what I was hoping for. A letter like that wants a dark day.

The footbridge was still there. They'd bolted a new sign to it that said Not Maintained and somebody had drawn a smiley face in the rust with a finger. There were stickers from bands. The handrail gave off the cold of old metal, which is different from the cold of fresh frost; it is a gray with a smell of hands. I tucked the scarf into my jacket. It was the same red. I had been carrying it around the house like a hot plate, touching it, dropping it, changing its place, the way grief at first scurries from room to room pretending to be a different animal in each.

I took the spoon from my back pocket. It had warmed to my body. I held it for another minute because I was afraid that if I put my hand in the Marrow it would bite. People have their stories about this river. It takes kids in June. It is generous with catfish. Once, it brought up a bicycle so old that the frame had bloomed like a great iron flower. It has never in my life been exactly what it looks to be. If it had turned and asked for a name the way a dog asks to be called, I would not have given it mine.

When I was small, Marin brought me here and showed me how to cup my ear to the rail to feel the huff of freight that had long ago stopped. "Everything leaves a draft," she said. "You can learn to feel what's not there by practicing on what is." I didn't know then if she was teaching me to listen or to miss her.

There were ducks farther upstream, the early ones who don't read the almanac and show up like a surprise guest with a cake. They moved crookedly, as ducks do. The willow, skeletoned, raked its twigs in the slow current. The river's top looked as if something had dragged a fingernail across it, not hard enough to cut, hard enough to know it had been touched.

I leaned and let my hand down. The water took its time. It wasn't ice, but it had that winter-thickness that laughs at tips of fingers. When it finally came around my knuckles, it made me gasp. It was not so much cold as a suggestion that something greater than cold existed and we had named it wrong. And then—I am trying to say this plain—I heard something.

It was a low thing, not a voice, exactly. Imagine you might pull a string that runs through the earth. Imagine that string running through you too, through your hand into your ribs. pluck and release and there is a humming the size of a bedroom, the size of a field, the size of a year. In that humming, something like syllables. Not in any language I know, not even in the language of scientific reports and maps, which is wicked with numbers and yet refuses to weep. The syllables were stretched like the colored rubber bands we used to twist around the jars of my mother's salt-in-progress.

I turned my palm and let the water pool into it as if my hand were a spoon. It slopped over my skin, and in it little flecks of mica and powdered rust turned and clicked. I thought, stupidly, of the fish on the handle in my back pocket and had the thought you have when you're grateful you don't believe in anything, because what happens if what you don't believe in knocks.

It did not say my name. But it asked it. I don't know how else to write that. The way a teacher will pause at roll call and glance up as if to say, Are you here, then? And I said—out loud—"I am," because sometimes the body is its own priest.

The pull under the bridge shifted. The ducks lifted their heads all at once, like someone had thrown up a flag with their mother's face on it. The water around my wrist climbed, a fraction, and then I felt it slide the way a hand might slide under yours on a porch swing when you didn't know someone had sat beside you.

I took my hand back and stared at it, at how plain it looked. Some place on my palm had woken. My fingers stung as if I'd touched a coin. I held my palm to my mouth and tasted it, like you do when you're not sure what worse thing is on it. Salt. Of course.

A boy on a bike came along the path, braking suddenly when he saw me. He was twelve, maybe, his hair too long for his ears, a line of acne along his forehead like a halo. In his right front pocket, something heavy tugged the denim. The kids here all carry a knife and a lighter by twelve, and by fourteen they've found a reason to use both.

"You good?" he asked, trying on deep-voiced concern the way boys do when they suspect you might be old enough to be their mother.

"More or less," I said. "Do you ever put your hand in and hear things?"

"You high?"

"A little dizzy," I admitted. "It's just the winter." And then, because the truth wanted to slide out of my mouth: "My mother told me to."

"Mine tells me not to," he said. "So I'm gonna do it all the time." He looked at the spoon where it hung halfway out of my pocket. "That's neat," he said, and then, even though the word neat has not been cool since someone wore a poodle skirt, he said it again with conviction. "That's neat."

There was a sound like a dropped bucket upriver, a hollow whomp. The boy turned his head. We both stepped at the same time toward the center of the bridge. The wind shifted and brought the smell of the Atlas evaporation pond, even though the pond had been drained and filled and drained again with somebody's money. It was a sweet chemical that tried to resemble the sea and failed.

Something floated into view just around the willow. It was a white plastic lawn chair, the kind that cracks in triangles and leaves patterns on the back of your thigh. It had leaves caught in the seat like someone sitting with a lapful of winter. It bumped against the pilings and turned and then, with a small decision, began to move backward. The boy shifted on his bike, making the front wheel lift off the ground like a horse.

"Cool," he said, and then, perhaps because he thought he was supposed to be hard: "Weird."

The chair lodged against a rock, considered itself, and then went under. For a moment the water made the shape of a chair without the chair. Then the shape pulled out of itself and became river again.

The plucked string under our feet tightened. I could feel it even through the soles of my boots. Sometimes when I can't sleep, I stand barefoot on my apartment floor and feel the hum of the building. This was like that, and also like standing on a chest and waiting for it to rise. The boy's freckles stood up on his nose like little seeds.

"I'm Cass," I said in the voice you use to talk to a skittish animal. "What's your name?"

He hesitated, as if a name was a thing to risk. "Danny," he said. "Dan."

"Don't put your hand in without warming it up first," I said, and only after the words left me did I hear Marin's shape in them, her caution wrapped around a dare. "You don't want to surprise it."

"It?" Danny said. But he surprised it anyway. He plunged his hand in before I could stop him. He jerked it back and shook it, laughing, because he was twelve and anything that bites your hand and doesn't draw blood is funny. Then he said, "Huh," and leaned over again, sloppier this time, the hunger in him thickening the air between us.

"Do you hear it?" I asked.

He cocked his head. "Ducks," he said. "My blood in my ears. Somebody's truck on Harlan Road. The plant rattling even though it's dead. No offense if your dad worked there."

"He did," I said. My father was all through this town. His name on the road. His shoulders in the siding he nailed to houses that still stand because he refused to do it quick. His joke in the bar about the bartender's eyebrows migrating like geese. His quiet at the dinner table like a living thing that we fed with potatoes and silence. "No offense taken."

We leaned there for a while, strangers, until the boy's phone hollered at him from his back pocket and he rode away standing on the pedals. The bridge trembled as he left, not much, just enough to remind it might one day fall.

I stayed until the light changed from spoon-silver to tarnish, the way it does on winter afternoons when something in the city starts cooking dinner and someone out on the farm is burning something they called brush until the county told them to stop. An egret lifted like faith from the bank and moved upstream, the wrong way, or the right one, depending on when you learned your directions. And then, because I am slow, I finally did what the letter had asked.

In your life, there are very few times you will be given an exact directive. We crave them so much that sometimes we trick ourselves into thinking someone's casual wish is instruction. This wasn't that. Put your hand in. Be patient with what it asks. It wasn't the river I was worried about. I was worried it would ask me to forgive my father for saving only himself most days. It would ask me to forgive my mother for saving no one at all, not even herself.

I leaned again. The scarf tickled my neck like a hand that had never learned to be gentle. The cold came up. The humming gathered. If you had been there, if I had thought to bring you, you might have said later that I had induced this in myself. I am willing to hold both truths—that I caused this and that it came.

The syllables made a shape. They didn't resolve into letters, but they did into something like a map. A bend, a cutbank, a little triangle that in my work would mean a culvert. I could see it inside my head as a field of white, the clean of paper before you pencil something that makes it less perfect and more real. On the white, a line, making a loop that did not close. And a single word, not written but felt: return.

It is one of those railroad words. It is one of those words you can do with your body and also with your mouth and also with a package and also with a kind of ticket. It is a kindness and a threat.

"Where?" I said, to the river, to the scarf, to the part of my mother that sits still in the cartilage of my ear.

The water tapped my wrist as if it could reach farther if I would only go deeper. I went to the second knuckle. The ache went boneward. The hum thickened until I could have lain down on it and slept. I saw the loop again, and the triangle, and the word. Return. The arrow of it was not pointed here, not to this exact stupid bridge and its foot bolts and its boyish graffiti. It pointed toward the old ferry slip, down by where the river once had allowed men to drag it from one bank to the other. The place where everybody's grandfathers had stood in checkered shirts and spat into the water and argued which team in what year had won by the grace of God.

"All right," I said. "All right."

I took my hand out. The air bit at the wet like a jealous thing. The skin had gone the white of old scars. A grain of something—sand, salt—clung to my line of fate. I let it dissolve. I held the spoon in my fist. The red scarf flashed in the corner of my eye like an animal crossing.

"Mom," I said to the railing, and then to the river because it had asked first. "Okay."

On my way back to the car, a woman I didn't recognize stopped me on the path. She had one of those faces that seems to be trying on grief as a new skin and not yet sure if it fits. Her hair was coiled under a knit cap. She had a stain of something green along her sleeve, the shade of baby food or moss.

"Are you Harlan's girl?" she asked.

"I was," I said, which is not what people expect to hear and not what I meant and also exactly the truth.

"They say the river did it again," she said. "This morning, my husband swears he saw minnows on the road like the sky had opened and put them down wrong." She leaned in, sniffed. "Did you…did you put your hand in?"

"Yes," I said, and saw her flinch and then consider whether to be impressed or frightened. "Did you?"

"I don't swim," she said, the way people of a certain age say I don't dance. "I don't even bath if I can help it." She looked at the scarf. "That's a pretty thing," she said. "Too pretty for this place."

"It doesn't belong to this place," I said. "But it keeps showing up here."

She nodded as if I had said something reasonable. "Doesn't everything," she said and went on, siderailing me with her hip like a sister.

I sat in the car with the heater on and the engine off because I am suspicious of movement after feeling called by anything. In my lap, the letter. On the passenger seat, the red scarf coiled like a sleeping snake. The Atlas plant stared at me with its window-eyes, plywood pupils growing mildew. Once, when I was very small, my mother took me into a room inside where all the dials were lined up like moons and the men stood with their hands respectfully by their sides, not touching anything because touching is how you die. Marin nodded at a gauge and told me, "Here is where they keep track of how much vanishes." She was wrong, of course. That gauge was measuring what was still there. The vanishing keeps its own counsel.

I had planned to go back to the house and finish what people had asked me to do, which is a thing I am good at. Their lists sit in me like metals. But the word in my chest was not the word List. It was the other one.

The old ferry slip is where children go when we are fifteen and need to see how far our mouths can open without swallowing someone's open, ruined future. It is where I learned to kiss and was told that I did it right like a woman my age should, and I didn't yet know to lampoon that as rude. It is where I took a bottle on a night when the past and the present both wanted a drink and learned what the third drink does. Nobody had used the ferry in my lifetime, but the river remembers being made to carry us in other ways than itself.

The road to it is scatter, gravel that leaps from under your tires and tells you how much heavier the world is than you want to carry. I drove slowly. In the ditches, snow clung where the sun hadn't yet bothered with it. Somebody had dumped a couch on the right side, a green thing with exposed guts, and a crow sat on its armrest rearranging a snack. If I could teach crows to read, I'd give them this letter.

I left the car on the tongue of a turnout and walked the last piece. The slip itself is a slope of poured concrete chewed at its edge by frost heave. The river is deeper there, and the bottom goes from chocolate milk to steel. The far bank is a woods that belonged to nobody until Atlas said it was theirs, and then to the county, and then to hunters, and then to nobody again.

There was a shape on the concrete, some child's chalk that had been half-rained. It was a circle with a triangle in it. A sign that means hazard in most places. Here, a game. The chalk had been pink. The triangle pointed upstream.

I half expected someone to be there, a body leaned against the trunk of a car with their arms crossed. Nothing human could match what the water was doing. It had slowed in a way that suggested not laziness but deliberation. If you've ever watched a hand that knows how to do something you're learning, you know the difference.

"Okay," I said, to the air, to the letter, to the woman I couldn't decide to love unless she had been my mother and even then you can't decide.

I pulled the scarf tight around my neck. I put the spoon in my mouth for a second, the way my mother once put pennies in her mouth to test if they were real, the heat of it an animal, and then took it out because this was about hands.

I stepped down where the concrete still had some of its tooth, squatted, and reached in. The cold that took me was a story. It came from far. It came from before.

The humming was immediate, urgent, as if it had been waiting all afternoon and I was late for a flight I didn't know I'd booked. The map unrolled under my ribs again, clearer this time. There was the loop and the triangle, and now not just a word but a sense: not just return but reconcile. The loops did not close because they were meant to be tied to something else. The triangle was not a hazard. It was a boat.

"How?" I said. "What can I possibly bring that you don't have?"

The water tongued my wrist as if tasting—not for sugar or fear, but for intention. Every time in my life someone's asked me what I want, I have named something that fit on a plate or into a bank account. Now the thing in me that is older than me—call it marrow because I am simple—opened its mouth. I wanted what everyone wants when they walk toward a ferry: to go and to be kept, simultaneously. To be allowed to go without being punished for possessing a foot.

Something bumped my fingers. Not a fish. Not junk. It was cloth. It was a ribbon of something that slid along my skin with that whisper of silk I have only heard when I move in another person's dark.

I grabbed because I am not that kind of poet who lets a symbol pass and says, Ah. The silk came up, red, bleeding river. My mother's scarf, of course. Not the same, because the same is a wish and wishes are a way of making yourself small. But the twin. The long red mouth of something that wanted air. It wrapped itself, I swear to you, around my wrist like any snake saying hello.

It was not pretty. It was river-scoured, its edge fringed like the bones of a fin. It seemed a foolish thing to weep over, but here we are. I did. I put it around my neck and felt the weight of it less than a pair of pennies. The letter in my jacket pocket pressed to my heart like nothing like a hand.

Behind me, on the bank, something shifted. A foot, a cough, a calling. I turned in a way that made the world go from water-colored to human.

She stood three trees back from the slip, her coat wrong for the weather, an old wool with buttons that were not a set. Her hair was threaded with winter and a bad night's sleep. Her face was a face I could have picked out of a lineup drawn from the dead. Down by her shoe, a little pool where the concrete had settled collected the river and made a second moon.

She had my mouth. Or I had hers. She had the red scarf's twin around her wrist like a tourniquet, like a ritual, like a way not to lose her own hand.

"Marin," I said, and then I could not say anything because sometimes the mouth is a fist.

She lifted her hand. The river tugged at everything in me that is meant to be overlapped. "Cass," she said. Not with apology. Not with triumph. Not with the gratitude I have collected for people all my adult life like sugar packets I plan to return. With the plainness you bring to the door of a house when it belongs to you. She said, "We have a thing to do."

You think the first chapter would end with an embrace or a slammed car door or a sentence about forgiveness braided like hair. It doesn't. The river hummed, a string plucked under the bridge and under our feet and through my bones and through hers. The scarf warmed against my neck. And my mother, who had left the day the river showed its secret habit, stepped down toward me and toward the water that had no rules, only bad days and good ones. I put out my hand, because I have always believed in maps, and because sometimes a line only learns it is a bridge when it is crossed.

On the day the river turned and began to climb back into the mountains, my father told me he had been saving my mother's voice in jars.

He said it like he was mentioning a new brand of flour, a small household preference. He wiped his hands on a rag that had once been a shirt of mine, blue gone to a hard gray, and met my eyes as if to see whether I would love him less for it.

Outside, the Alder unstitched itself from its accustomed logic. The surface, usually obedient, began to show the wrong kind of hurry. We could hear it before we knew it; the hum in the stones, the way the windows seemed to breathe out and hold. The woods were full of people walking faster than they meant to. The horses in the fields turned their heads toward the gorge and forgot to chew. Even the tea in my cup leaned north.

"You should have warned me you were going to say something like that," I said, and set the cup down because my hands were not entirely my own.

My father nodded. "Well," he said. "I thought if I sent a letter you'd just not come."

I had not come in ten years, not in the nine between then and now, not even for the half holidays that other families made the river's climb to be, caravans of cousins and coolers and fold-out chairs dotted like migrating birds along the banks. I had not come for the town's spring potluck, for Aunt Iva's third wedding, for the time Teddy Callow broke his leg and the whole town signed his cast in the square. I had not come when he wrote that he had fallen on the back steps and lay there for an hour remembering the year my mother taught me the names of clouds and none of them were right. I had not come for his birthday. I had not come because he wrote, five summers ago, that the eraser head pulse of a tumor had lit up the scan like a coin in the dirt, and he seemed, in the letter, to find this amusing.

"I came," I said, which meant I had rented a car I could not afford and driven through three nights that smelled of diesel and hummingbird sugar and motel disinfectant, and bought a bag of peaches from a roadside stand with a little girl on a stool and a jar for cash. I came.

He leaned over the stove and lifted the lid on the pot. Steam, cinnamon. He was making pears, because he always made pears for the turning. They were not our pears; our tree had died the winter after the last climb and I had not been there to watch, but I had gotten a photograph from him of a young sapling lashed to a stake, and then another of an empty circle of dirt. The pears in the pot had a taste of aluminum and town water, and I knew they were from a woman up the ridge, the one with a laugh like gravel who never seemed to age.

"All right," I said. "Show me."

He wiped his hands again and went to the pantry door. It had always stuck, since the year my mother painted it yellow and the wood swelled. He had never gotten around to shaving the edge. He put his shoulder to it, the small grunt he made almost exactly the same as when he heaved me onto his back when I was little and the fair came through town. I watched his shoulder through his shirt and thought of the bone underneath, the hinge of it, the ways he had told me a body betrays you in increments and then all at once.

On the shelves where we had kept sugar and salt and stores of beans in coffee tins, he had made space for glass. Jars in spaces where light gathered itself and became something else. I counted without wanting to: twenty-seven of them, labeled with his square block letters on masking tape, some with dates, some with names, none of them names I recognized. One he had written "north bend." One said "survey stake below limestone cut." One said "Vesta's field." One said "behind the girl's ear," and I wondered which girl and whether she knew she'd been behinded.

"They're empty," I said, because why not be unkind. "And what if the food inspector saw this mess."

He sighed, and in the sigh there was something like relief. He reached for one at eye level. It was not dusty; he'd been touching them, moving them. It said "7:30, below the spill," which put it right where the river, this morning, had begun its wrongness. He held it for a moment, and I saw the hesitation take his wrist. The lids were flats and rings, the old kind, finger-tight. He looked older in profile; the bones of his nose were my nose. He cupped the jar to his ear.

"You'll not hear it like this," he said, and spun the ring and popped the lid.

For a heartbeat there was nothing but kitchen and pears and the small click of cooling metal. Then the jar breathed. It was like listening to a seashell, if the sea in the shell had learned to talk. Not a single voiced word, not a sentence, not my mother, but a movement of vowel that lifted the hairs on my arms. The sound had a shape, and a shape has intention. It was a woman's voice, or I decided it was, at least the shadow of a woman. A laugh pulled inside out. The kind of sound you make when you first step into a cold stream and bear it.

He saw my face and nodded. "You see," he said, and there he was, the man who showed me how to coax bees without being stung, how to break a fever with a washcloth and a song, how to stand still so the deer would forget what you were.

"You can't just," I began, and then stopped, because he could. How do you say to a man that he can't hold air.

"No," he agreed. "I can't. But I can try."

I had heard the stories like everyone had, but only as a child can hear them: as if a story belongs to someone else and therefore is true. Any thing thrown into the Alder on a day it climbs will show itself again in time. Whole rocking chairs had come back left-handed. A bicycle had washed up with more than its original spokes. There were rings and holy medals and sacks of flour snagged in branches like strange pale fruit. Once, there had been a coffin, and this town we are, with our particular sense of humor and our tenderness toward old grief, had walked the coffin home to the cemetery without opening it, because the dead should decide their own timing.

People had run their own tests, because people do: initials carved in a stick, a painted boot sole, a message in a child-hand with a drawing of a dog. Sometimes it came back, sometimes not, and when it did it was never in the same day or the same form. My father loved the river as if it were kin. He did not worship it. He would never have called it a god. He would have called it a neighbor with bad memory and a good heart.

When I was eight, on the morning of the climb, my mother had plaited my hair and tied a red ribbon in it and told me that if I lost the ribbon the river would take my patience for good. She had been laughing when she said it, but she had a way of laughing that sounded like a warning. She had a way of looking at the river like a woman looks at a man who knows how to dance and chooses not to. At noon she had walked down to the water in her rolled-up jeans and stood at the edge where the thin ropes tied off boats went taut like veins. She had said she wanted to see how fast a stick would run backward. It had been an ordinary stick, picked up at random. She had said to me, "you count," and I had counted, and at twenty-eight, because I'd learned to slow down my counting to keep things from ending, she had stepped in and the river had lifted around her like hands. She had turned her head to say something that got lost in the sound. She had gone a little deeper than anyone expected, and my father had called to her, not by her name but by the old nickname he had for her when they were shining and twenty-two. She had smiled. I remember this: she had smiled, and then she was not there.

This is not a dramatic river. It does not have falls or cruelness. It has the patient face of a grandmother with her knitting. People drown in it because they forget that patience is a strength. People leave in it because that is sometimes easier than leaving by the road. For years, when I told the story to myself, I changed the sequence—first she smiled, then she slipped, then the water turned to a different country, then my father went in up to his chest and came out holding somebody else's shirt. I told the story different ways to see if there was a way I could make us keep her. Children are magicians until they learn where the seams are and then they are spies. I learned the names of the rocks and the runs, the way the midges show their hatching above the riffles like punctuation. I learned that my mother had left a drawer full of lists, in a hand so neat the teacher used them as an example: honey, vinegar, needlepoint cotton, winter onions. Each list had something crossed off and something added, so each list was a day that had happened and could not be taken back.

Now, in my father's kitchen, the long whistle of the kettle cut through the half-voice from the jar. He half-laughed and half-swore and slapped the lid on again. The sound inside kept moving a beat longer, as if looking for a body to live in, and then it went to ground.

"Where did you get that one," I asked.

"The last time," he said. "On the evening of the climb. Down by the spill, where the old tree fell that spring but kept leafing out for a few years because it didn't know it was dead yet. The air was full of them. You could just hold out a jar and catch one. Like lightning bugs. Only you had to be quiet. Everyone tries to talk to the voices and scare them away."

"You caught voices," I said, as if catching voices were like catching rain. As if words had shape enough to be kept. But then I had gone to school and studied acoustics and built rooms that were softer inside than snow and harder outside than debt, and I had listened to the physics of resonance that tell you every place has a key and everything you say is a string. I had stood in a chamber designed to swallow sound and heard my own blood. I had fallen in love once with a person who refused to be recorded. This was not stranger than any of that.

"This one," he said, and nodded toward a jar on the top shelf. "This is your mother."

The tape on that jar was old. He had written only "E." next to a date that was, to the day, exactly ten years today.

"You haven't opened it," I said.

"Can't," he said easily, as if he were saying he cannot eat apples because of his teeth. "If I open it and it's not her, then I've lost more than a jar."

"And if it is," I said.

"Then," he said, and shook his head as if to clear a fly. "Then we will have to be people we do not know how to be."

He went to the sink and rinsed the spoon and set it in a place where my mother would not have set it. It is impossible not to inventory. He had always dried the dishes right away; now the rack sat in the sink and the glasses were dotted with the town's lime. The geranium was gone from the window. In its place, a pile of rubber bands like a nest and a single dead bee. The kitchen smelled of William's tobacco from two doors down. I could see my own hand on the table, the scar down from the thumb where I'd cut myself on a broken microwave at nineteen, the callus at the base of the ring finger some ex-lover used to touch with a thumb while we waited for the kettle to boil. The kettle boiled again and again; this is my father's way, to make tea whenever anything is bigger than his body.

Outside, a car honked the sharp three-note that meant more a warning than a greeting. A woman called to a child with the caution people are taught to put in their voices today. The river, when it climbs, winds everyone tighter but no one says so.

"They're saying," my father said, not looking at me, "that this might be the last year."

I laughed without meaness; I couldn't help it. "The river will forget how to go uphill?"

He shrugged. "The new people. They don't like the spill. The inspectors say it's inefficient, what with the turbines and all. They've been talking about damming the north fork. If they do that, there'll be less pull. Also the weather. You hear them. Anyway. People say things."

He had been saying them in his letters, in his careful hand. The town with the old factory waking up and wanting to be an art school. The meadow behind our house measured and then measured again, as if measurement alone could make it valuable. The men who came to the Brown Owl with maps and gave a talk about the future like a sermon, and how in the future we would all be happier because we would stay put and have predictable rains. The river did not listen. It was a poor listener, and that is perhaps why my father loved it.

"When we were small," he said, as if both of us had been, "we believed everything returned in the same mood we had lost it. You remember how Aunt Iva beat her rug to dust every week and then threw, on climbing day, the dust over the water, as if the river liked to keep dirty secrets too. She swore the dust came back cleaner."

"My mother," I said.

He put a hand out, the way you put a hand out to a bird or a skittish horse. He did not touch me. He did not say stop. He is not one to correct a sentence's direction.

"She went. I know she went. You know that. And also," he said, and breathed, and when he breathed I could hear in it the whistle in his chest like wind through a small hole in a pane, "also the voices came and I caught them. I have lived for ten years not opening that jar because I could not be the person who opened it and I could not be the person who did not. I thought I'd wait until you came home and then the decision would have a second spine."

"You want me to open it," I said, but he didn't answer. He lifted another lid instead, and a man's voice, or possibly a crake, sang one note like a saw and then went. He smiled, the real smile that makes him look like a boy who has held lightning in a jar.

"I want," he said, and now he met my eyes and did not look away, "to ask you for a favor, on the day the river climbs. I want you to take that jar, the E. jar, and I want you to carry it to the black tooth and stand on the flat rock and open it there when the current is the most wrong. That is the place she liked. That is the place she went. I am not strong enough to go out that far now. And I think if I open it here it will be only a story. At the black tooth it will mean something else."

The black tooth is what we call the basalt that juts up midstream like a molar too big for the jaw. Children wade out to it in the summer and stand with the water in their shorts and shout to hear their voices change. Lovers kiss on it and the river eats their balance. Men have carved initials into it with knife blades that turned at the grit. I could see it from the kitchen window if I stood on tiptoe: the river drawing its strength from an old buried fire, the tooth like a punctuation mark in the wrong place.

"You think," I said, and my throat had a catch, "you think her voice, opened in that place, will call her."

He lifted his hand, let it fall. He did not say yes. He did not say no. He said, "I think I need to hand this thing forward in time in such a way that I am not crushed by it."

"You're asking me," I said, "to be a pulley."

He smiled, surprised I had named it. "A good pulley," he said. "The kind that doesn't screech."

The people I work for in the city build rooms that are like organs in cathedrals: the sound is meant to behave, to take its shoes off at the door. We calculate the escapes and we trap them. We bottle the unpredictable. Sometimes I have hated myself for being so good at it. Sometimes I have loved the clean honest math. The man I loved who would not be recorded left not because I tried to record him but because I did not, and he said that meant I didn't want him to last.

My father took the top jar down, the one marked with a single initial that could be mine. He held it as if there were heat coming through the glass. He didn't look at it; he looked at me. He stepped toward me and the jar crossed the air between us as if it were an animal that had seen my hand and decided my hand was safe.

I held it. It was heavier than it should have been. Or perhaps my arm was tired, from holding off so much gravity for so long. The glass was cold because the pantry was. There was a smell like old fruit and something else I didn't know. My father's breath made a small fog in the kitchen the way it does in winter, although it was not winter. He had the habit of winter.

Outside, a low whistle started: the civic band, tuning. Old man Grover from the lumberyard practicing his cornet. The children down near the rope swings beginning to chant the chant they make up every year as if their particular words will keep everyone safe. The sound of rope pulled through raw hands. Somebody shouted a warning, but whether it was about a plank, a dog, a child, a cloud, I didn't know.

"Don't open it now," my father said, because he knows me and because he did not quite trust himself not to look.

"I won't," I said, though of course I wanted to. I wanted—what did I want? Not my mother, not exactly. The idea of the jar as a thing that could unmake absence. Whoever invented jars should get a prize. The man who thought of bending sand into something you could see through and shut.

We stood with the jar between us like a baby, like an altar. My father had always been most himself when something needed fixing. When a hinge was cracked he would split the difference between what the wood wanted and what the door. He had a beautiful patience when he wasn't asked for more than he had. Now he had less than he wanted and he was trying not to show it.

"They posted the Rules for the Climb," he said, as if reminding me to take a sweater. "Same as always. Don't wear something you'd hate to lose. Tie down anything you wouldn't look up for. If you value your hat, don't wear it. If you love anybody, tell them to sit with you and not to move unless something moves first. Do not invite the water to remember you by name."

"You sound like my mother," I said.

He smiled without showing his teeth. "She was a person made mostly of rules and exceptions," he said. "She thought you should have a soft palate and a steel spine."

"She thought I should learn to swim," I said, and we both laughed. Neither of us did.

The windows rattled a little. In the sink, the glasses chimed. My father moved to the stove and turned off the pears. "Leave them to steep," he said, though no one had asked. He lifted the pot and carried it to the cool back of the counter. He moved in that careful way he did now, as if the floor might get ideas about shaking.

"Will you stay tonight," he asked, not like a question but like a hope that knows itself.

"Yes," I said. "Of course I will."

He nodded, as if relieved, as if I had made a promise. He put a hand on the back of a chair, the chair he sanded the summer my mother left, and stood with it the way a man stands with a cane he refuses to have. He looked at the pantry, at the jars, as if they might misbehave. Then he looked back at me, and the look had in it all the way we had failed each other and all the ways we had not. He cleared his throat and said, "I'll go down to Vesta's to see if she has more cloves. You wait until the band has passed, then go. It's best when the sun is wrong. The black tooth—" He didn't finish. He didn't need to.

I tucked the jar in my bag as if it would bruise. I thought of the black tooth, the slick of it, the way the river hammered at your shins if you stepped wrong. I thought of my mother stepping and smiling and perhaps turning her head just so.

When you live away from a place long enough, your mind preserves it like a photograph that fades only at the edges. Coming home you see the difference not in the houses—painted, unpainted—but in the spaces between them. Where there had been field there was now concatenation: fenced rectangles, driveways that gleamed with the suggestion of money. Where there had been a sycamore there was a flyer with words on it about a new menu at the old diner and three new bands with names like jokes. The river itself was not more water than it had been, but it was more named: someone had put signs along the edge telling you what birds were what and warning that the current had unpredictable features. We had always known that, and now the signs knew it too.

The band struck up something that could have been "Onward" but with a hitch in the middle. The first swell of backwardness took a set of leaves and ran them uphill like small lost gossip. A woman in a hat the size of a plate laughed the kind of laugh that says I am not afraid. Two boys acquired a tire and a rope and a plan. A man in a yellow shirt set his lawn chair in a puddle and did not notice.

I stepped out onto the back stoop and the air cut through my shirt, full of small brightnesses. My father's yard had grown a certain wild. He had always kept it tidy as a clock, with the kind of pride you have when you own something bigger than you can explain. Now the grass had opinions. The space where the pears had been was a circle of other green. Bees moved like punctuation through the mint, the last of them drunk on the late bloom. The fence he'd mended a dozen times held because it did not know another way.

Down at the bottom of the yard the path to the water had been worn in by generations of deer and our feet. I followed it. I could feel the jar thrum faintly against my hip. I told myself it was the movement of walking. I told myself not to listen. I told myself to watch where I put my feet, because the river was turning and everything wanted to be part of it.

At the edge, where the alder trees lean their faithful lean, I stopped. The water had not changed color, but it had changed attention. It had the look of an animal that has decided, for a little while, against its habit. The black tooth sat where it always had and always does. It is not the tallest. It is not the bravest. It is simply there.

Behind me, because this is a small place and we all believe in pretending we are alone until someone wants to be not alone, no one called my name. The band marched past on the road above, and a line of children banged wooden spoons on pans. My father's house breathed. The jars on the pantry shelf kept their counsel. The jar in my bag did not.

I took off my shoes. I rolled my jeans to my knees and then to mid-thigh and then, because I am not my mother, I stopped. The water at the verge was cold the way the air at the top of a ladder is different. I stood for a minute with my toes in the edge, and I thought of all the ways this might go. It is hard to be a good pulley when the load is yourself.

"All right," I said to the jar, to the tooth, to my father up the hill listing the spices in his head, to my mother wherever the absence had put her. "All right."

Then I stepped in. The river took my calves, and then the river took me higher. It leaned on me like a friend who has not told you everything. I went forward because the only way out of a pull is through it. The world above squeaked and shouted, and I put my hand to the round gin of glass in my bag, and I let my body remember what it knows about balance. The black tooth stood a few strides out. It is good that there is something to aim for, even if it is slick.

Behind me, the low thrum of town went on. Ahead, the wrong-way sound of water was a voice I had not learned to speak. In my bag, in my hand, there was a jar with a letter on the tape, and I had to decide where to put my feet. I kept going, one more step, another, and the river, the dear old neighbor with a bad memory and a good heart, kept trying to lift me. I laughed, and the laugh blew away. The cold made my teeth ache. The stone was near enough I could have thrown the jar and struck it, but I would not. You do not throw a mother. You do not throw a promise. The glass against my palm hummed like a hive.

I reached, and my fingers found the first edge, and the river, because it is sometimes kind, did not disagree. I pulled, I stood, I half-stood, I slid a little, I set my toes into a shallow abrasion I remembered from a summer when my legs were shorter, and I stood up on the black tooth with the water slapping the back of my knees as if to say, you again.

I took the jar from my bag and looked at it. The tape was lifting at one corner. The lid had a small dent in it the shape of what could have been a thumb. My thumbnail worried the edge of the ring.
