I thought of my father at the stove, of the way he had said pulley, of the old rules about names. The chant of the children rose up in the wrong key. My own voice, when I found it, sounded like someone else.

"All right," I said again, because sometimes the second saying is the one that counts, and I held the jar like a person holds a bird that could leave.

I lifted the ring. I felt the world pause, just a fraction, the way it does when a storm is deciding where to go. The river rushed backward around my ankles, and I put my other hand to the lid, and then, with all the care I had, not the kind that tries to keep things the same but the kind that allows them to become what they always were going to be, I turned.

The first fish to speak did not open its mouth.

It lay on the table with the others, a pile of quiet silver, scale on scale like the backs of coins. The morning was already warm, the kind of heat that drained the salt out of your skin. My aunt Salma had just come back from the shoal with her skirt wet to the knees and a net thrown over her shoulder like a cape of nerves, and I was sharpening the long knife she liked because it sang. She always said: a dull blade is just a promise to cut your own hand. She liked to say things that could be fixed with your own careful attention.

We kept the table by the window to catch the light. Out there the sea tried on its many faces and the houses blistered with white paint and gulls indicted the world with their screams. The first fish slipped as I held it and rocked on the board, rainbowing oil in the low bowl beneath its tail. I put my thumb under the gill flap to steady it. It was breathing still, barely, enough to shiver that little membrane inside. I hate that moment, when the animal is too alive to be meat and too dying to be spared. The trick is to be quicker than that distance.

“Be quick,” Salma said, as if I needed reminding. “This heat will turn the air before the onions do.”

When the blade went in, the fish let out its last, the weight of it settling, and the scales along its flank caught the light and spelled a word I had known since the first day my father taught me to write. My name.

Naila, the scales said. Then the shimmer shifted and broke and it was only a fish.

I could have told myself it was the light, or a trick of heat, or that my mind had been dusty with sleep and the fish had written what I wanted the world to say. I have told myself all kinds of things. But that was not the first time, or the only fish. The second one I opened that morning told the butcher’s daughter, who had still not forgiven anyone for the way her husband died, to stop leaving bread at the edge of the old pier—it was making the rats bold and no rat had ever been made into a saint. The third was an apology for burning the neighbor’s tree when he was thirteen. It was written in the careful unsteady angles of a boy after punishment. The fourth said: the rain will come for the thirsty girl, but don’t drink the first cup. And the fifth said nothing and I was relieved.

You can see it if you stand at my shoulder and look along the scales, not straight at them, but through a thin door between light and angle. The markings are not letters like ours, not the hooked script we learned on school slates that blisters your lips with its s’s and t’s, but I read them as easily as I read my own face in a window at night. People say the words are there like the tide is there, because it keeps coming, and because even if you don’t believe it, you will get wet. People say a lot. We are a village of mouths.

For years after he went out and did not come back, my father was a story boys told each other to prove they could pronounce the names of storms. Khatima took him, they said, but others said it was the trawlers from the capital, dragging high and deep, that snapped his line and cut his life as clean as any rope. There is a bureaucrat somewhere who keeps a ledger where my father had a place and then, one day, a drawing of a line, and then a stamp. My aunt Salma will spit every time she says the word stamp. She spits precisely, into the corner behind the oven, the pelvic corner where the kitchen’s hips meet, blackened with salt and soot.

“We were supposed to have been born inland,” she told me once, after she’d drunk a little and the fog in her mind became generous. “We’re not built for this tide in, tide out. Our people had fields, and the wealth they counted was not in salt.”

“And how did you forget to be born inland?” I asked.

She laughed the dry laugh I love. “Like this,” she said, and pretended to smoke her fingers. “We sold three goats for a single tin mirror and we wanted to see ourselves from the front.”

I have never been inland. I have stood on the broken wall at the far end of the old port and looked toward it, toward the green and the red grit and the heat rising from things that do not move. It is a direction like any other, with a way of being threatening and mostly theoretical.

After the fifth fish refused to say anything and died with dignity, Salma stalled me with a touch on the elbow. She felt the way I did when the scales lit for my name, the way the small hairs on my arm rose up like wheat in a wind. She might say she didn’t believe, but her hand told me she believed enough to pull me back in, to make me show her again, to make sure.

I turned the first fish in the shallow pan of water and tilted it so the light had to admit itself.

“Naila,” she read softly. Her mouth worked around the sound, tasting it. “Like when you were a baby and we wrote your name on your ankle in kohl to trick the jinn into thinking you were not ours.”

“I remember,” I said, and she smacked me with the back of her hand because, of course, I do not remember.

She took the bowl of offal away for the cat. Its name is Colonel and it cannot be bothered to come when you call it. It is not a colonel of anything except its own appetite, which has the discipline of hungry soldiers. The cat’s ears quivered when Salma stepped outside, and so did all the birds in the sycamore. Even the birds knew this heat would make things sacred or rotten.

By the time the sun was up like a coin jammed in the slot of the sky, we had a basin full of songs, curses, sweet scents, grocery lists, advice, maps, the taste of an apple you ate in a summer with your first lover, a woman’s inventory of her pain that stretched longer than the eel we caught in the spring. My head thrummed. The fish lay in their own pale and the drains sang to themselves like they remembered other water. When the scales speak, it is not the fish that do it. Their mouths stay closed. It is the light knocking its knuckles against each lip of silver, it is the tiny rivulets of oil captioning the day.

I kept a ledger on the highest shelf, the one my aunt had to stand on a chair to reach. It was wrapped in an old shawl of my mother’s, embroidered with a pattern of roses like the kind that grow where there is such a thing as rain. The ledger is for what is for everyone. It is for the words that want to be known. I write them down for people who are ready and for those who are not. I am careful with names. It is not my duty to upset or to comfort. It is my duty to listen and not to invent.

We used to pretend, when I was smaller and would make games out of the empty, that the sea tried stories on us like dresses, held them up against us to see if the fit was good, if the seam sat where it should. Then it found out we liked the stories more than we liked the work and it took them away. Now it gives them back, in this sharp cheap way, and expects us to do something with them.

By noon, Salma had left, because when her day held too much of one thing she would push the boat out and row until everything small in her mind sorted itself like shells in a basket. I know she went toward the shoal with the good rocks because she always goes there when she is trying not to tell me something. She is not much of a liar. I say this with love. She comes home with a face as obvious as a tide chart and thinks she has kept her secrets.

I kept gutting. Sweat stuck my shirt to my spine and pooled in the hollows of my collarbones. The cat sat beneath the table like some minor god, breathing rot with religious devotion. The beads of brine on my fingers turned the edges of my fingertips into prisms. It is one of the reasons I can read the scales; my nails are shallow spoons of saltwater, and the light goes in and comes out knowing more than it did.

I had just told myself that I would stop after the next three and drink in the shade of the lemon tree, the one that keeps fruiting out of stubbornness, when the fish I had been reaching for twitched, ruining my intention to be kind to its dying, and thudded its head against my wrist. The knife slipped and bit my knuckle. A bright, immediate sting. A little blood blushed out and mingled with the fish’s.

The scales flared and resolved. I could feel my heart knock against the word it made. The script was a slope I had practiced as a child, standing beside my father as he wrote lists of expenses and the price of oil, the names of men he owed and those who owed him. He wrote with his left hand, and so the tails of his letters all leaned like grasses after a long wind.

Naila, he wrote, and the breath went out of me. Naila, don't speak us to them.

I pressed my thumb into the bleeding and the fish into the water and the light into the scales until the words steadied. There is always a moment when the meaning does not want to hold, like it is shy. If you look away or blink too fast or let your mind slide toward fear, you lose it. I learned this the year I turned nine and found a girl from the inland lying on the beach, her face pink as if she'd been boiled. I wanted to look away and I did and afterward all I could remember was the way the sand had stuck to her eyelids. I failed her. My aunt said there was no way to succeed her either, but still.

Naila, don't speak us to them. Keep your mouth shut as if you've seen your bride before the wedding. We are not yours to sell.

Fish have always said things like this. Don’t sell me. Don’t tell my mother. Don’t tell her that I was not where she thought, doing what she thinks I was doing. But the slant of the letters, the way the long notes of the script pulled up at their ends like a man surprised he could be kind, that was my father. Sometimes a handwriting is the only body left.

An old fisherman once told me that the sea keeps certain kinds of things, and it is not choosy. It keeps rusted anchors and the anger you swore would sink if you threw it hard enough, it keeps shoes and prayers, it keeps the names of ships and men and gods who thought they were bigger than currents. If it takes you, it does not digest you. It lets you lie inside its vast stomach for as long as it takes to make you stop insisting. Then one day the day is calm and it has a thought like anyone else, and it coughs you back up.

I read my father again. He had written more. They come to weigh our voices. They want the weight not the words. Hide what you can. How do you hide a thing of water from a government? You pour it into something more mortal than it is and you call that hiding. The ledger under its shawl felt suddenly like a swollen thing. I wanted to throw it into the oven and bake our dead into bread.

Years before, after the tenth week of my father not coming back had passed like a plank floated by, a man from the Bureau of Losses came in a car the color of gut, a pale pink with a sheen like meat. He had a stamp and a pen and a face that had never belonged to a boy. He measured our house with his gaze and found it adequate to our grief. I am not being fair. He was gentle in the way they teach them to be gentle, a sequence of soft words that have been used to keep people compliant for a long time. He made our house official. He made our absence official. He told my aunt to sign, and she did not sign, and he stamped something anyway. That night she sat with two candles—one for her brother and one for her anger—and let both burn so low the wicks smoked.

Once the fish started to speak, the Bureau came back with a different car, the color of a dry leaf. This time it was the Department of Phenomena and Other Public Risks. They had a ledger that looked like mine but heavier, a black book that could probably eat my book and still want a second course. The woman who carried it had arms strong enough to carry two. She walked around our table and did not touch anything, which is a way of touching everything. She asked me questions I pretended I did not understand. There is an art to playing your own fool.

“Do the fish carry names?” she asked.

“They carry salt,” I said.

“Do you write things down?” she asked.

“I cannot read,” I said.

She smiled. Her teeth were neat as soldiers in a photograph. “You are very polite,” she said, as if I had complimented her dress.

We said we were busy. We said the heat would turn the air before the onions did. We said someone had to clean the fish and our someone was us. Finally she closed the hungry book and looked at me as if I was the day’s catch in a basket she intended to buy.

“Everything speaks,” she said, which is true and a way of making you look foolish for noticing. “The trick is to teach it to speak to you, and only you.”

Now my father’s hand had come to me and it was shaking, or my hand was, and outside the house a car made a sound like tires chewing quiet. I do not know how time plaits itself in a place like ours, braided between weather and intention. I stood with the knife still open and sharp and my blood drying like red salt on my knuckle and the fish (which could not be bothered with any of this) breathing its last and the scales changing, changing, and for a long moment I forgot that anything could come toward us from the road, because all my life what World we have has come over the water line.

He had written his name below mine, as if we had to be reintroduced. Hassan, he wrote, as if I had forgotten how to say my father’s name. Those are letters that have lived in my mouth. If the scales had allowed me to, I think I would have put my lips against the fish and kissed his handwriting. What he wrote after that was not like him. He had always been a man who believed in the miracles that his hands could make—nets, ropes, a mended hull, the manner of a knot. He did not believe in warnings. He believed in weather reports and gut instinct and the way a man who has a daughter cannot wait for grace.

Mouths will come to measure you, he wrote. They will come with their questions and their precision and the weight of their paper. They are empty. That is why they are hungry. They will put your words on a scale and call it a service. They want the gravity that holds you to the living. Don’t give it to them. Keep your ledger for the ones who bring you bread and for the one who brings you lemons no matter how stubborn the tree is. Bury the rest.

With remorse a thin and dangerous thing, I reached up to the high shelf and found my mother’s shawl. It smelled like the old cedar chest we keep for summer’s few nice things, and like cloves because my mother would boil them in winter with orange peels for the god of flu. The ledger was heavier than it had been in the morning, which made no sense and made perfect sense. Words gain weight when someone intends to take them from you.

The cat looked up as if it knew this too. In that moment the heat changed, a shiver going through the day like the rumor that a stranger has entered the room. The gulls turned their heads to see who it was and then remembered that they were gulls and did not care. I wrapped the ledger in the shawl and took it into the back room, the room with my mother’s narrow bed. I knew where I would put it, not because I had thought this through, but because my aunt and I have a way of tucking our worries into the same crevices. There is a loose tile behind the headboard. If you press its left corner, it lifts. Underneath is a hole we pretend the mice dug and that we did not improve.

I slid the ledger in, and with it went half a dozen little packets of paper covered in salt stains and my own handwriting pretending to be neat. Copies. I had started to make copies in the spring when a man from down the coast came and offered me money for my book. He had fingers like driftwood and a voice like velvet. I listened to him and saw my aunt light her cigarettes on the stove and I thought: a ledger is a net like any other. Maybe it’s greedy to fish twice. But I did not sell. The copies slept like smaller scavengers in the same dark as my secret. I felt the weight of my father’s disapproval settle very gently on my shoulder like a shawl of its own. It was almost nice to feel him again anywhere except in the dark behind my eyes.

I had just slid the tile back when there was a knock that did not come from the sea. There are many kinds of knocks. There is the neighbor’s knock, which does not ask permission, and the cousin’s, which goes on and on and expects you to open because time is something it eats, and the knock of a man who wants to sell you something that will not keep. This knock was new and did not quite remember the code for a door. It was like someone killing a fly very politely.

I stood for a second, hand on the headboard as if the bed could be a wall. When I did not move, the knock came again, practiced, then a woman’s voice. “Naila? Salma?” The sound of my name from a stranger’s mouth is one I am learning to recognize faster than I would like. She added, as if we had always been friends, “It’s Alder from the Department.”

She did not say of what. She did not need to. There is a way a government uses its name like a father uses his, expecting your attention to go from whatever it was loving to the face that made you. I looked at the half-gutted fish in the kitchen and the bowl of shining alphabet. I looked at my bleeding knuckle. The knife trembled and spoke to the table in small taps.

The front room had gone bright and flat, the way it does when there is a shadow at the threshold. I walked toward it with the light both blinding and instructive. The heat leaned in like a neighborhood woman, eager to hear. The cat considered abandoning us and then remembered the bowl of guts and stayed. I had to wipe my hands. I reached for a towel and realized my fingers smelled like coins and oranges and pages turned too quickly.

When I opened the door, there were three of them. The woman from before, the one with the soldier’s teeth, with a dress that made her look like a schoolteacher whose class never learns to spell. A man with a face like old rope. Behind them, another man with a notebook, the kind that can write through rain. They had eyes that did not bother to apologize for being where they were. They had empty hands, which is sometimes more threatening than hands with guns. The empty waits to be filled.

“Good afternoon, Naila,” the woman said, so pleasantly I forgot for a second that she was the reason I had just put my father back in a hole.

“You look hot,” I said, because my mother has been dead long enough that I have to remind myself what manners are supposed to be.

“We are,” she said. “Will you have some water for us?”

The thing with water, here, is that you cannot say no. We do not have much of it. That makes it sacred. That makes it ugly to refuse. I turned and poured from the jug into the three cups we own that do not leak. I gave them water as if it were kindness and not obligation. The woman watched me like I was spelling a word she had almost forgotten.

“We hear you’ve been keeping a ledger,” she said, without any of the breath wasted on compliments.

“We hear a lot of things,” I said.

She laughed. “Yes,” she said, as if this was witty. She took a drink and did not grimace, which is how you know her face had been trained. “We’d like to help,” she said. “If you let us, we can make sure everything only goes where it is supposed to.”

“Where is that?” I asked.

“Where it serves the public,” she said. “Where it does not hurt anyone. Where it does not offend the memory of the dead.”

My father wrote: don’t speak us to them. He did not say why, because he did not like why questions. They were either a map back through pain or a map toward something you could not control.

“I do not think the dead are easily offended,” I said.

“Still,” she said, and she nodded toward the table, where a fish had arranged its scales into the word for patience and then, as if it, too, was being watched, changed its mind and flashed only silver. “They must be cautious. They do not want us to read them wrong.”

“I do not read them wrong,” I said, more sharply than I intended. The man of rope-face noticed that. He stepped forward like a sailor testing a knot.

“No,” he said, his voice full of salt. “That is the point. That is why we are here.”

He looked at my hands, the left one with the blood on its knuckle and the right one with the line down its palm that all the old women in the market had sighed over when I was small. “This girl,” they’d said to my aunt. “She will do a thing no one else should do.” My aunt had given them the onion eye and said she had already done it, by being born.

“We’ve had reports,” he continued. “The scales have carried certain…sensitive messages. Names. Admissions. Predictions.” He looked up at me then, and his eyes were the exact color of the sea two days after a storm, when it is thinking about being kind again. “Some of these messages involve the safety of the region. The state.”

“Safety,” the woman said, and the word ate up the room’s air more efficiently than our cooking ever had. “We are mandated to consider it.”

I wanted to tell them about the way the wind hollows a day. I wanted to tell them about the time Salma pulled a boy out of the waves by his hair and he thanked her by running away. I wanted to tell them about the old man who comes every Thursday and asks if I have a fish that will speak to his second wife, the one he loved, not the first whom he married. I wanted to tell them that the fish do not care about the state. That they do not know about our maps. That a tide is not a border. That a scale is not a page.

I did not say any of that.

I said, “What do you want?” which is always, with these people, the most boring and important question.

They glanced at one another, sorry to be forced into the inelegance of being direct. The woman set her cup down on the table beside the half-open fish. She rested her hand on the table as if it was a Bible. Her fingers were long and clean.

“We want your ledger,” she said. “We want to make copies for the archive.”

The word made something in me stand up. Archive. It made me think of a cold building with walls thick enough to store other people’s summers.

“And in exchange?” my aunt would have asked. But my aunt was not here. She was out where the rocks are good, telling the sea secrets it will not bother to keep. I made my voice old with her.

“In exchange,” the man with the rope face said, “we ensure the safety of you and your family. We can guarantee that certain…unhelpful items do not circulate. We can help you—”

“You can help me keep my mouth shut,” I said.

They did not laugh. Their faces did the thing that says: we do not pretend we are not listening to you, but we will take what we can. The woman touched her book in a way that made me want to snatch it and put it in the oven. I felt the tile under the headboard grow heavier, as if it had its own little gravity.

From the table, a fish flashed up a word like a coin lifted in a palm. Hurry.

I looked at my hands. In the palm of my left, where the blood had dried, the imprint of one tiny scale had glued itself to my skin. When I pulled at it, gently, it came away whole, a little mirror, so small it did not belong on a body that had ever been large enough to swim. I held it up. Light struck through. On its surface, as if my hand were the sea, a single letter leaned like a man I knew. I managed not to tilt it toward them. I managed not to put it in my mouth.

“Would you like to see?” I asked Alder. I watched her eyes to the left, to the book, the calculation, and I wanted to tell her that her name was a tree. I wanted to tell her to go grow.

“Very much,” she said.

I smiled at her, the kind of smile I have learned from my aunt. It offers you the ocean and gives you a coin. It is the kind of smile that might even win you a prize if someone was giving out prizes for who in the village did not drown today with their dignity still on. It said: I am here. I am not yours. It said: Yes.

“The light will be best at the window,” I told them, and the three of them turned as one to where the late Bolts of the day were warming the glass. They went to where I wanted them, with their backs to the room and their faces to the sea. They leaned forward, as if the horizon would answer.

Behind them, the bowl of offal gleamed and finally brought the Colonel to his feet. He finicked at a piece of lung. He interposed himself between me and the cupboard where my mother had kept the good spices and I had put the second ledger I had always pretended I did not have. He did not know this. He knows almost nothing. He knows he is a cat.

“Careful,” I said, and when they turned half their bodies to look, because people cannot resist the small catastrophe of a cat, I slipped the tiny scale into the seam of my shirt, where the hem had come loose. The scale was colder than the rest of me. It sat against my skin like a vow.

Then I watched them watch the light. The scales of the fish on the table did what scales do. They mirrored. They moved when the fish did not. They took the world and made it look like silver, then gave it back. I felt my father’s slanted hand at my throat. I could not tell whether he was catching my voice or telling me to swallow it.

“What did you say your department is called?” I asked, letting my mouth do what it would now with what he had written.

Alder’s smile was the kind that softened asphalt.

“Public Safety,” she said.

“Ah,” I said, because a word like that wants to be there.

Behind her, the sea rolled its shoulders. The lemon tree shook its little fists. The air made a sound like a dress being slipped out of. Somewhere up the coast, a boy threw a stone at a bird he would later love. Somewhere inland, a field waited for rain. Somewhere under the tile, the ledger thought its own heavy thought and the ink dreamed of becoming tree again.

I put my hand on the table, on the wet wood with its palimpsest of knives. The word the fish had made for hurry broke and was gone, as if it had merely been a wave that looked like an instruction and not the other way around.

“Sit,” I said to the Department, because I needed more time. “Let me show you how the light must be for the scales to give anything away.”

That was the first time I lied to them with any real elegance. It felt like taking a breath I had kept for too long. Outside the window the sea lifted one long blue hand and reached for our shore as if to touch our faces and say, remember.

The morning my machine told me the truth, the ceiling fan stuttered, and we all pretended it didn’t.

The courthouse was always like that—everything a little broken but very dignified about it. The plaster blistered in pale moons above the judge’s dais, the velvet runners had been brushed threadbare by the years, and the long windows caught street noise like pollen and let it drift in: the hawker’s bell, the exhaust cough, a child laughing as if air were a thing you could own. Even the air smelled respectable, like mothballs and lemon oil and the old hymnals at my mother’s church, as if everyone who entered had been rubbed down with a cloth.

I sat below the bench, as always, at my little desk to the left, my knees exactly where the groaning radiator would blister them winter after winter. The machine’s carriage pressed warm against my right forearm, the way a cat finds the part of you that won’t move and leans. She was old, older than me, with keys like tiny teeth and a green enamel nameplate that had lost its name. My mentor had given her to me ten years ago, his only extravagant act. “This one listens,” he had told me, wiping his thumb on his tie and then polishing the empty plate again. “Don’t laugh. Some machines listen.”

The bailiff intoned his open-throated call. All rise. The room stood; cloth sighed; benches creaked like ships leaning into current. Judge Kato swept in with her iron hair making a sensible wave behind her, her robe immaculate, her mouth set in the way that reassured the city’s fragile notion of fairness. I liked her because she read the transcripts. It’s incredible how many of them don’t.

She gave the slight nod, and we all sat. My foot found its place on the machine’s pedal, the familiar pressure like a matched weight easing.

The case was a misfit in every way, a body of a thing that did not want to be held. A boy dead, a police officer on the stand, a jury that looked like someone had shaken a jar of buttons and poured them into the box: two bright, one dull, one cracked, one missing a hole. They had been told not to read the news and had nodded with their faces. There was fear in the room, shapeless and polite. You could feel people rehearsing their own neutrality. Even the cop’s shoes, black and buffed to a prayer, had been arranged toward the jury as if to say: look how clean.

I set my fingers. I tapped the keys without looking; the braid of motion and sound came up in me, the way teeth find each other in the dark. If I do not think about it, I am my best self. If I do not think, I can hear everything.

The clerk held out the Bible. Do you swear to tell the truth, the whole truth, nothing but?

The officer’s thumb touched gilt. “I do,” he said, and I found the strokes for I and do, my fingers falling through the habit of years. The keys made their small noises, lime seeds in a glass.

On the paper, my machine wrote: I don’t.

I paused. The fan thumped its once-per-rotation hiccup. The officer was standing very still, a cutout of a man in a catalog. The words on the page were my strokes, my shorthand, my little vowels and lines, but when I watched the ink bloom, I could read them as if someone had translated from a language I had forgotten I knew.

I could have blamed coffee. I could have blamed the man shifting in the second row whose jacket zipper rasped like a wire saw through my attention. I could have assumed my hand had stuttered, that a letter had slipped, the way a mind slips when it sees what it expects. But the machine wasn’t a typewriter; it wasn’t letters. It was pattern. It was a net thrown across the mouth of a river to catch anyone who said anything worth keeping. My net should not throw back fish.

The oath ended. The first question went up like a thin smoke. “Officer Koenig—” the prosecutor said, his tie a column of migratory birds. “Walk us through your training.”

“Five years on the force,” Koenig said, and I hit the stroke. “Two at the academy before that. Certificates in,” the faintest pause, “conflict de-escalation, field response.”

My machine wrote: I was taught to live.

Judge Kato’s pen clicked once and clicked twice. The juror in the near corner was blinking too much. The air moved and did not move.

I do this work because when a voice enters a room, it leaves two of itself. There is the one with teeth, conjugated and correct; and then there is the one that isn’t language yet, a warmth, a lull, a crack. My mother taught me that, though she would have put it differently. “Listen past their mouths,” she said when I was twelve and had snuck under her desk at Legal Aid to read the names off the file spines, “and you’ll hear the part they can’t close their lips around.”

She was an assistant and therefore invisible. Later, when a lawyer told her to smile more because clients didn’t like chatting with a mop, she smiled less. I watched her hands while she set coffee for men who did not say thank you. I have to tell you this to explain how the machine felt under my palms. It felt like a door opening into that other voice: the one people keep caged behind their teeth.

The prosecutor moved along his path. The defense attorney smoothed nothing over and called it cross. A juror coughed and disguised it as a sneeze and then looked guilty. Outside, a siren wound itself into a knot and undid. I kept up. When I don’t, I dream the errors later, the pages sprouting mouths to tell me I failed them. I can’t afford that. I was taking down my own breath.

“Where were you at 2200 hours?” the prosecutor asked.

“In the patrol car,” Koenig said. The machine wrote: In the quiet before.

“And what did you see when you approached Jericho Street?”

“A male,” the officer said, and my stomach went cold, because I knew what word the machine wanted to write and also what words it could not, in a court transcript, be seen to write. “A suspect,” Koenig corrected, his eye flicking sideways at his lawyer, “standing near the alley. He had something in his right hand.”

The machine wrote: A child. He had a phone.

I let my foot ease off the pedal, just a fraction, as if less weight could soften the sentence. The keys didn’t care. Ink is honest in its own stupid way.

I had a practical thought. If I was sick, if I was losing whatever small, salvageable thing in me that made the job possible, then I would need money. And then I had a stupid thought. What if this was that, the thing my mentor had said in the tone he used for horoscopes and the stock market: some machines listen.

He died in his sleep on a Sunday, the paper lying to him by the door. There were fifty-seven pens in his desk drawer. His wife gave me the machine because she did not know how to throw it away. During big trials, I sometimes still hear him in my head, sucking sugar out of a mint and dictating. He said: Don’t be interesting. You’re a pipe. Let it flow through.

I was a pipe. Beneath everything, my hands did the work they knew. The sound of Koenig’s shoes creaking up the witness stand never got in the transcript, though it should have. The sound of the mother in the back row swallowing her grief so it would not embarrass this whole room of strangers never got in either, though there are days I think our archive would be truthful if we typed nothing but the noises that hurt.

“Describe the suspect,” the prosecutor said.

“Tall,” Koenig said. My machine slurred in: Bright. “Black.” The machine wrote: Boy. “Hoodie.”

“Hood up?” the prosecutor asked, and Koenig nodded, and my keys made the shape that stood for yes, aye, affirmation.

He didn’t say: I was tired. It was the end of shift. There’s a way the street looks when you’re two hours from bed. He didn’t say: I had to split the world into threats or it would multiply. He didn’t say: I was afraid of the dark boy, because I had been taught fear like grammar, without knowing I knew it. The machine did not write all that, of course. It is not a novelist. But it wrote what was under the words the way a pond writes wind on its skin.

When he described raising his gun, a ripple moved through the courtroom that was all the bodies remembering what arms can do. Someone in the hall cracked a joke that arrived from the far end of the corridor as a smear of joy, against my better judgment, into the room. It is indecent, the way happiness refuses to keep to its borders. It is a good thing it does not, or we would all die of famine.

“Did you identify yourself?” the prosecutor asked.

“Yes,” Koenig said. The machine: No. He swallowed. There was a tiny clack as his tooth met glass in his mouth. Why do so many men chew ice? It makes their gums flat and mean.

“Did you issue a command to drop the weapon?”

“Yes,” Koenig said. The machine: I said hey.

“Did the suspect comply?”

He hesitated. “No,” he said, and the machine finally agreed. No. It did not write the step forward, his weight on the ball of his left foot, the scrape inside his head where he had to choose or the world would tell him who he was without him. It did not write the name the boy had been called when he was four. I did not know it to write it. The boy’s mother did, and she sat and did not say.

I have a brother. Eli is six years younger than me and loves me as if my name were a word he invented. Once he stole a mango from the vendor at 3rd and Marlowe because he had counted his coins wrong and could not bear to put the fruit back. The vendor’s hand clenched around his arm as if he was the sum of every boy who had ever taken anything from him without paying. I stepped between them and bought the mango for twice its price, and the vendor let go his arm slowly, as if skin could fuse to skin when you weren’t looking. Eli held the mango contorted against his belly like a contraband god and said I’m sorry to me, not to the man, because I was the person he did not want to disappoint, and because children reorder guilt toward the people who love them. He lives in another city now, and we speak on Tuesdays, and sometimes he is quiet in a way I am learning to take on faith, like an oath.

“After you fired,” the prosecutor said, and the fan hiccuped. “What did you do?”

Koenig’s lips did a strange thing. They sorted themselves into a lie and then did not use it. “I shouted for backup,” he said. My machine wrote: I waited for the world to become the one I had acted in.

When it was the defense’s turn, they rearranged their papers so that the jury would believe in order. “Officer,” the woman with the pearl earrings said, and I liked her despite myself; she wore sensible shoes and did not do her hair small to look less determined. “You feared for your life.”

“I did,” Koenig said, and the machine wrote: I feared being wrong.

The judge rubbed her forehead with one finger. The mother clasped and unclasped her purse. When she looked at her hands, a small liturgy happened there that no one else saw. My mother used to do that when we were on the bus and she was looking for exact change, her fingers trying to make a whole out of coins that did not fit. We had never had exact change for anything. The year we lost the apartment, my mother said, darling, if we make ourselves quiet, the universe will forget we are here and we will cheat it out of suffering. I was nine and believed her, because if a person you love promises magic, your mouth learns the shapes.

I tell you these things because the machine had never done this before. Or it had, and I had not looked straight at the page while words were hot. Or I had looked and pretended, as we did the fan, because many things in this city kept their small lies and we survived by none of us being the one to tug at the loose thread. I was thirty-five and might have only then become a person who could read what words wanted from me. There is no miraculous age at which you will become generous. It is always now if it will ever be.

When the morning recess came, I carried the unfinished transcript to the copy room. It is not a room, truly; it is a space between two dead elevators where broken cabinets go to consider whether they deserve a second life. The copier lives there like a heavy animal nobody wants to name, and someone had taped a sign to it a year ago—Do Not Breathe On The Glass—that nobody has taken down because it makes them laugh. I shut the door behind me. The hallway noise did not enter. The machine’s mouth was warm. I slid the sheet into the slot and watched the black spill into shape.

What do you do with a disobedient page? If I sent it up to the judge as it was, with the underwords written into the margins, with the machine’s added sentences like someone else’s handwriting on a test, I would be called a liar or a miracle, none of which the court had proper forms for. If I corrected it, as I always did, translating shorthand into words that matched the audible voice, I’d be safe, and the boy would be a boy again only inside his mother’s chest, where heat goes to live after it stops being a life.

I did what people do when they need time. I made busy with precision. I put the morning’s pages in order and clipped them with the good black binder clip that closes like a wave taking back a shell. I sharped my pencil and put it parallel to the pen with the blue cap. I unfolded and refolded the parts of my body that had gone numb under the pressure of my job and my own absorption. And then I did something I had not planned to do and had been planning since the first line wrote itself wrong: I made a test.

At the edge of the page, where the stabler would bite later, where no eye but mine would usually land, I wrote a single extra line, because there is a place between silence and noise where a person can choose. It was a small thing. It was a sentence that did not change verdicts. It was more an exercise of grammar than rebellion. After Koenig’s “Yes,” I wrote the NO I had seen in my machine in parentheses, as if it were a cough, as if it were breath. The world did not resize itself. The building did not shudder. I made a clean copy for the judge and a dirty for my drawer that I told myself I would burn.

When I came back into the courtroom, everything had rearranged itself by atoms and the blueprint unaltered. The mother’s hands were folded as if she were in a train, waiting for stations. Officer Koenig was answering a question about the training manual as if the manual could keep him from drowning. The defense attorney’s pearls glowed and did not give off warmth. The ceiling fan stuttered its brief dissent and continued as if persuasion were possible with machine parts. I sat.

I did not have an exit plan for the experiment. I thought, monstrously, childishly, that possibly the truth belonged in the record not in the sense that would satisfy a philosopher or a priest but in the sense that would satisfy an indexing clerk. I thought, if the paper will take it, it must have a place to live.

We gurgled along toward lunch. The jury paid attention for three and a half minutes and then fell in sequence like keystones asleep in their chairs. The judge asked three questions that came from a place in her unlike the city had made her—soft, almost motherish—then tucked that away and made herself the law again, because a woman cannot walk around with her softness showing in a room like this and expect to keep her job. When the noon bell dinged from the church across the park, I could have cried. I could hear the first floor waking up: the probation kids slapping each other and getting told to quit it, the woman at Records shouting that she closed at twelve-thirty and meant it, the intern in Corp Counsel’s office learning the art of carrying coffee and documents like both were fragile gods.

Judge Kato dismissed everyone for the hour. Her clerk gathered her papers. The jurors funneled past one another, a little flock wary of own its feet. I stood slowly to keep the blood from rushing away from me. I am not noble about fainting.

“Ms. Quaye?” Judge Kato’s voice came down from the bench. It has always startled me when a person above me speaks as if we are horizontal to each other. Something in me expects only weather from that height.

“Yes, Your Honor,” I said, projecting just enough to be heard, not enough to be interesting.

She tipped two fingers under the first page of the morning’s transcript, the way you might lift a child’s chin to see whether a lie fit it. She tapped. “Is this yours?” she asked.

“It is,” I said, and thought of my name on a warranty card taped to the inside of my own ribs.

There are a thousand ways the face tells you what a woman is about to do. Judge Kato’s went strange the way an instrument does when it is tuning and you are not its pitch. “Stay,” she said, not unkindly, and swept out, leaving her clerks in her slipstream as tidy as train cars.

The room emptied. The fan muttered to itself. I could hear the cuffs on someone somewhere in the building closing around a wrist. The mother of the boy stood at the edge of the aisle like a woman who has forgotten how to push a door. I didn’t know if anyone had sat with her during recess, held water to her mouth, said her son’s name thinking it would keep him from evaporating into a noun in this building. I wanted to step down, to sit in the second pew and say his name back to back to back until time bored of me and looked away. I did not. I am a pipe. I let it move through me.

“Excuse me,” a voice said from the aisle. It sounded like smooth gravel, the sound of a person who has told stories at every table the city owned. I looked up. The man had the kind of face that loses at cards on purpose to make friends. He wore an old suit that had seen someone’s wedding and someone’s last day at work. He was holding, of all things, a red folder with a piece of string around it, compliant as a child.

“You’re Mara Quaye,” he said, not quite asking, and a bead of sweat broke loose at the base of my neck, a small slide.

“I am,” I said. If you say your own name, you prove you still exist.

He looked past me at the empty bench and then down at the little machine at my hand. The enamel plate caught a thin stripe of noon and offered it to him like a coin. His mouth softened, the way mouths do when they have found a thing to love that cannot possibly love them back. “You put it in,” he said.

“I’m sorry?” I said, and my throat opened as if for water and received air instead.

“The parenthesis,” he said, as casually as people talk about bus schedules, then glanced toward the door where the bailiff leaned, bored and suspicious, in a way I would have called a posture of the city itself. “You were not supposed to,” he added, almost gently. “But you did. Good.”

He laid the red folder on my desk, close enough that I had to step back or let it land on my hands. The sticker on the tab read: City of Hallowell v. Unknown Parties; Petition for Injunctive Relief and Other Remedies. It could have been any old file in any old creaking cabinet. He tapped it with one finger like a doorbell without a door.

“I need you to write something down for me,” he said. “And I need you to be the kind of person who sees what a thing says when it doesn't open its mouth.”

The bailiff shifted. Somewhere up the stairs, someone laughed at a joke I would never hear. The fan breathed its error, patient and patient and patient. I looked at the folder and then at his face and then, because I am a stupid woman who cannot help herself, down at my machine.

She sat there, faithful and green, as if she had been a hedge at the edge of a garden long before I was born and would be there after lightning ate the house. I put my hand on her nameplate. The metal was warm. I thought of my mentor’s fat hand polishing it, of my mother’s hands smoothing down a dress she’d worn to two jobs, of Eli’s fingers sticky with mango sugar and guilt.

“Lunch is only an hour,” I said, because if you can make a problem small in a sentence, sometimes it will agree to be small in the world.

“Then we shouldn’t waste it,” the man said, and smiled in a way that did not make me want to run. “You like to listen,” he said. “Let’s start there.”

Chapter One: The Brine Thief

Salt remembers. That was my father's claim, and it was the only argument he never lost.

By the time I turn down the pitted road to the old saltworks the weather has gone to a thin glare. Spring here is all reflection: white on water, water on white. The road buckles and settles, and the wind lifts salt-dust so it crackles in my teeth like sand I’ve chewed in childhood. Out on the flats the wind farm leans and pivots and murmurs to itself, blades drinking the light without ever getting full. Gulls hang and reconsider the air. The marsh chuckles where it still can. The only shade lies in the ribcages of the abandoned evaporators, those long low houses where brine was coaxed into crystals before they closed, before it was cheaper to drag salt from somewhere else and ship it here in bags with cheerful blue logos.

His place is at the edge of all that; a shed stitched from scavenged silver. The padlock is the size of my palm, its gut rusted. I don't have the key, but the door doesn't seem to care, bowing in when I push. There is a smell as if an ocean died here days ago and no one has decided what to do with the body—iodine and rust, old wood’s fat grief, the hot spelt-scent of dried salt and something sharper, like lemon oils gone bitter.

"You're late," I say into the empty, because he always said it to me. You’re late as if lateness were a quality you could bring in from the outside, like a raindrop clinging to your hair.

Inside, his machine sulks, silent and enormous in the half-light. He had never named it, not out loud, not to me. To everyone else it was fool's aluminum and aquarium hose, the mischief he spent himself on after the company let him go and the city declined to put him back on any of its lists. He built it from the bones of centrifuges and chest freezers, from cracked condenser coils pried off ice cream trucks, from the irrigation pump that used to thump on our neighbor’s melon patch. It has the improbable grace of a thing that should not stand. The center is a steel drum with windows cut into it and covered over with safety glass and soap—shallow portholes. From its flanks, pipes run to three shallow basins lined with black tarp. Above each basin he once hung small glass bottles from string, a hundred of them in a pretty arc, tiny cathedral bells. The glass is clouded with vapor. The strings sag. The bottles are mostly empty.

When I was small he let me count them: the bottles, the valves, the luminous meters he found at the Goodwill. Counting what does not belong to you is the beginning of belonging, he would say, tapping my hairline with one salt-scratched finger as if winding me up. Even then he was veneered with salt; it collected in the corner of his eyes and the bend of his elbows as if he were petrifying from the outside in.

We buried him two weeks ago on the inland side of the levee, the ground unwilling and damp, my aunt clapping a hand on my shoulder as if to fasten me down, my cousin whispering that she didn't know which prayer to use for a man who refused even the cheap ones. I had not seen him in two years. I thought it would be easier to begin after the funeral. It is not.

On his workbench there is a jar of lemons he salted in winter, colorless now, pocked and collapsed, the liquid around them a tight gold. Next to them, the last notebook. He always cleaned his pens by sucking salt into them and spitting it out again, a habit that scalded me with disgust when I was twelve and elegant when I was twenty and distant. The notebook sits where his hand left it, a heavy rectangle of responsibility, made heavier by the grit that hides in the gutter.

I do not want to open this part of my life and have it flick like a fish and die in my hands, but there is the practical matter: the machine must go. The saltworks lease is overdue; I cannot keep paying on something that does not produce. The county will come with papers. So I hang my jacket on the red wheel of a valve and I roll up my sleeves and I listen for the trouble inside me to quiet.

Across the door someone has chalked a looping warning. I rub it and sniff my fingers. It is chalk, nothing more. I blow it off and watch the ghost of it drift into the room and vanish into the sun-shafts.

I walk the machine the way a shepherd walks a fence, testing for weakness. I talk to it. You don't have to answer. I’m here to learn where you end.

In the brine basins the water waits. Some of it is clear enough to watch the wind make ovals on the surface. Some of it has gone to brown, as if a tree fell into it and thought better, withdrew its body and left its idea. In the third basin something glimmering moves, then stops. I lean in. A fish? Of course not. Nothing alive could live here. He would never allow it. He believed in clear lines: this for living, this for binding the past like an ankle so it cannot run.

My god, the heat. My scalp prickles, and the sweat that rises on my back is not clean; it inherits the room. When salt is in the air, the air remembers it. You can taste what your lungs have done. You can feel your heart go a little hard.

He used to say: They will tell you the sea takes and takes. But it gives back. Not what you asked for. Not what you meant. That is the nature of returns.

I kneel and peer through the nearest porthole at his drum. The inside is a closet of glass coils and meshes, a child's drawing of cloud, some filters made of capillaries stolen from an enormous beast. On a shelf to the left he has laid out his sound. Each of the small glass bottles holds a label with a date and a name written in his scratch: MARCELIA 4/19, TIDE ALLEY 7/2, UNMARKED BOY 10/8. Some labels he has written and crossed and written over. A few he has stuck with questions instead of names. From them a faint deterritorialized scent rises, as if somebody spilled spice in a library.

"Don't," I tell the air again. "Don't make me part of this."

"Don't what?" a voice says from the door.

My aunt Salome. Her silhouette is a dense bird against the glare, her blouse blisteringly white, her skirt the green of money you don’t spend. She steps inside with the caution of a woman who has had her hem wet by more than one tide.

"I thought you'd be gone by now," she says. "I thought you'd send men to do this."

"You thought I'd behave better than he did?" I slap the notebook with the back of my hand. The sound is too loud. Everything here amplifies. "You thought I'd delegate his sins."

"Don't be clever." She doesn't come closer. "We gave him rest. Now give the place rest. Sell what you can. Let the rest fall back into itself."

"That's the plan."

She looks at the basins. The surface claims the glare and hurls it back. "Then begin. Don't pretend it's church if it's only a shed. Don't pray to him inside or outside your head."

When she goes, she does not leave the door ajar. I take a breath of the room's salted breath and I open the notebook.

His handwriting has always looked surprised to find itself on paper; letters slope like drunks leaning into each other at last call. The first page has a tidy list, as if someone else wrote it for him: inventory of valves, gauges, phrase "approx. head loss at 4 m lift," and then, in his voice, one of the strange formulas he made to satisfy the indifference of his work to the mind behind it. Later, instructions, numbered, as if he expected me.

Begin with Basin Three. Uncouple line D3 first. Open slowly to fail. Not the others. Three first, then the drum. Avoid noon. The salt remembers loudest then; it is indecent. If what you see is yours, spit it out. If it is not yours, swallow.

At the bottom of the page, an arrow, pointing not to anything but away from itself. He never liked endpoints. He trusted arrows.

I stand up and go to the third basin. The glimmer I saw earlier is only a coil of plastic catching light. I think of the summer I was nine, when the flats turned so white even the gulls looked embarrassed flying above them. He had just begun this contraption then, laying out the parts like bones on a sheet. He lay on his back under the drum and handed me a wrench as if he were reaching up from a grave and I were some ministering angel. He had salt in his beard, and when he laughed the salt flew. Our neighbors came to witness his misdemeanor joy. Later the same neighbors would come to demand his apologies, his accounting, his mind. That summer they brought mussels and beer, made a circle, and told him stories of days that had sloughed off. He wrote them down in the pocked cheap notebooks he preferred. "Something got me," old Marcelia said. "I woke on Friday and Thursday had never happened. But my sourdough knew. It had bubbles for a day I didn't feed it." Tomas blushed at the gift of this. He said maybe there was a way to coax Thursday back out of the salt. He said salt holds memory the way a cathedral holds breath.

He never said where the days went. Only that the sea took them because we had taken from the sea without paying right. He had not always been a man for paying. Except he was. Except his morals were just not the ones other people recognized.

"D3?" I ask the machine. The hoses are a tangle of patient snakes. Someone—probably him—has found a label-maker and enthusiasm. I follow D until it forks into four, damp with brown, then three, then two. D3 sulks under the drum, bolted with a clamp that has lost its wingnut; instead there is a little wrench tossed in the nook as if to say patience will be rewarded. I loosen and loosen. My knuckles choke on the crust. The clamp gives in with a dry sound like a moth. The hose sloughs free.

The stopcock for the basin is a heavy red wheel. I lay my palm on it. He had the same habit—laying his hand like that before a turn—as if he repented what came next and needed to ask forgiveness from the machines that never forgave. I turn, the wheel complaining, then shouting, then deciding to be obedient, and the brine begins to mutter down the exposed pipe, the basin pulling itself toward empty.

I wait for nothing. Nothing happens for a polite amount of time. Then the air changes, a notch downward; the salt fizzles aloud; the wind lists. Something unspools in my head the way an old cassette tape goes slack and the music warps and limps and then comes back hyperreal, the singer’s breath so close you could begin to believe you have spent your life inside her throat.

I see a ferry hold with a ripped poster of a girl laughing at a car she can't afford. The lights flicker in the way of fluorescent when the current is bad and the sea is planning to meddle. Water beads on everything; a man I don't know is peeling an orange with a plastic knife with the quiet competence of someone who has killed. He lifts the peel to his nose, eyes shut, reverent, as if preparing to deliver the orange back to the tree. Behind him, a boy in a blue shirt kicks a crate of clams until his mother shouts and the boy laughs and knocks his shin and then bites the pain before it can find him. The knife in the man's hand is from a bait shack I know. The ferry is one that stopped running when the bridge came, that my father insisted was better because on a ferry you cannot pretend you are not surrounded. Everyone takes up the same shape of fear.

I have never been on this ferry. Or I have, and I have not been that small blond woman leaning her forehead to the window while the rain tries to come through it. The air in the room goes heavy, my lungs go particular, the ventricles knock, the wind outside sharpens like a joke that cuts too close. The vision shakes itself like a dog, then carries on. The man halves the peeled orange carefully in his palm and hands one to the boy. The boy considers it as if considering a planet. He says something I cannot hear because he has a peel in his teeth as a pirate mustache, because the boat brakes and someone has dropped a bucket and there is laughter—my father's laughter, rasped by smoke and salt and contempt, a sound I could pick from a wreckage, a wedding, a riot. Except in the vision he is young, too young to have me, and he has no beard, and he is looking at the blond woman with his mouth undone in simple adoration, which is a word I have never safely associated with him. He is in a blue shirt, but not that blue, and he is standing as if he has not sat for months. His hands are clean. He does not turn when someone beside him says his name.

Tomas.

The brine says for him. Or the room. Or I do. The sound is disgusting and holy. The boy eats the orange. The ferry hits something low in the water and does not know how to tell anyone useful about it.

"Stop," I tell the wheel. I turn with both hands. The pipe coughs and sighs and the noise in my head dials down, the vision going thin as tissue and then tearing. For a second there is dark, the precise dark of an animal's closed eye. Then the shed is itself again with its soft rot of wood and salt. The wind farm murmurs in patient circles. My hands are shaking.

On the notebook the page turns by itself in a draft the door could not have made. I can hear my aunt's footsteps outside, not moving toward or away, just measuring the distance the way a cat measures a high leap.

Avoid noon, he wrote. It is indecent then. I check my watch. Three minutes past. Of course. Of course he was right with the kind of precision that makes you want to smash a cup on the floor just to have the sound of something not right.

I look back into the basin. The water winks as if it knows something and won't. On the black tarp, eight copper pennies glint in a loose circle. He was always dropping coins into water to test someone else's law. These are old, one with a cut through it as if someone tried to see what a penny is made of when you get past the surface. I reach in and pluck it up, rub the cut. It stains my thumb. For a moment I smell blood. Then only brine. The power it has to make everything only brine terrifies me.

I should stop. I should call the scrap man who will come with his sons and dismantle this contraption while lecturing me about hazard and regret. I should find the deed and the rent receipts and veil this place in paper. I should go down to the wharf and drink a beer with two limes plunged into it and tell a story in a voice with nothing to recommend it. I should, I should.

I lay my hand on the red wheel and think of all the things that can be coaxed out of solution.

When my mother left, he told me she had not gone. "She has precipitated elsewhere," he said, with a shrug that might have been science or cowardice or both. He refused the language of leaving. He refused the language that would have found him culpable. His truer language he saved for water, the forms it liked to take, the forms it could be forced into, the forms it remembered when we were not decent to it. He made his apology to salt and none to me.

What he wants, I think—the old rage rising bright and hot and quick as a boil—is for me to finish his penance. To take his device and sweeten it into proof. To watch the town bring their empty mouths and fill them. To prove I am my father's daughter in a way that will sting for generations. To swallow what is not mine and spit what is.

The light in the shed thickens. I am not alone, not exactly. The machine is a body we both have to live with for a little while longer, and bodies keep their gossip. A fly that cannot find enough fresh thing to justify itself clings to the window of one of the bottles like a dot of punctuation, then abandons grammar altogether and knocks itself silly against the glass.

"All right," I say, and let go of jaw and fist and all the other small muscles I have been holding shut. "But not at noon. You win that one, old man."

I turn the wheel the other way and I watch the water rise to fill what’s been emptied, because after the taking there is always a little seepage, always a secret pocket that refuses to give up, always the trick of the tide. The pipe coughs and then stills. The basin stops muttering. The shed leans back into itself.

Outside, the flats shine as if the earth has been shaved and polished. A man on a scooter buzzes by, one foot pushed back in an aristocracy of balance, a box of cigars tied behind him with twine as wet as hair. In the distance, higher ground, the new rows of houses facing away from the water, meant for people who wish to be near the idea of water without the accident of it. The wind farms carve and carve and never get smaller.

On the bench where he salted lemons there is also a photograph I have not seen. It is facedown. I flip it. On it: my father's open hand, palm up, a closed screw lying on the lifeline. No face, no context, only a cheap liturgy of skin and metal. On the back in his scratching: If you are reading this, then I am wrong in one way and right in another. Begin with Three.

I put the photograph back. I close the notebook. I wash my hands in a bucket of fresh water that tastes like the holy. I breathe. It is not noon anymore.

When I turn the red wheel the second time, the machine wakes without shame. Somewhere the pump thumps. Somewhere the sea inside the drums remembers it was once muscle. The basins summon, the strings twitch, and the tiny clouded bottles tap themselves together in an untranslatable language, a soft music like bones knocking in a velvet pouch. The water goes, the air answers, the past comes into the room and sits down and makes itself comfortable.

When the vision rises up, it does not come in pieces. It comes like weather. I hold on. I keep my eyes open. I do not swallow, not yet. I take what I need of its salt on my tongue and I tell myself that prize or penance, magic or machine, this is where it begins: not with belief, not with love, not with a story, but with the sound the brine makes when it gives up something it has guzzled down and carried and carried until now.

Chapter One

By dawn the city has a thin film of yesterday on it, same as grease on a skillet you forgot in the sink. It clings to railings and to the bent backs of the benches along the Malecón, settles in the lace cutout of the ironwork, coats the bronze horse of the general so the general looks like he has ridden through milk. Some mornings it is glitter-fine, so light you only know it's there when you pass a storefront and see yourself fuzzed by a bright haze. Other mornings it comes down heavy, the kind that slides when it warms into drifts, the kind that will pull a small child back through a door they only meant to lean against.

We teach the apprentices to taste the air for it before they step off the truck. It's not the way rain smells—rain smells like wet coins. This smells like burnt cloves and old apples, like your grandmother's chiffon scarf when you find it after twenty years and bring it to your nose before you think about who did the washing, who did the leaving.

"Keep the scarf out of your mouth," Tío Lucho says now, and taps the bottom of my chin with his glove the way he always did when I was a rookie and couldn't help breathing in, greedy. "You don't need to bring anybody else's Sundays into your lungs."

"This isn't a scarf," I say, though he's right. The mesh of my mask has a backyard barbecue taste to it this morning, and the hair on my arms has stood up from the minute the truck turned off the highway and we saw the first glitter on the sugar mill, the first thickening around the eaves. "This is a proper state-issued filter rated for—"

"For nothing." He grins, all gums and the one tooth that is gold. His cheeks are cracked leather, his smile a crease cut into old boot. The sun breaks over the cranes in the harbor, laying out a road of gold like a bribe. "The state issues lies, niña. You know this. We keep tomorrow walkable."

He says the motto like a joke, but his hand goes up and touches the patch on his chest, same as I do. The patch is a blue broom wreathed by laurel, same as the coin now worth less than bus fare. The union has been around as long as my mother, and my mother was born when there was still a trolley and my grandfather's mother would shake out rugs onto cobbles and men in white shirts would wave their hats and no one knew yet that time sheds skin and leaves it on everything and we would become the ones who sweep.

We unload in the plaza because the plaza is a bowl where yesterday collects. The pigeons sit already with their heads tucked, content as old men with soup, because they don’t get pulled backward by what they don’t remember. I stretch the kinks out of my back and look at the halo around the statue of the general, thick as soap scum, making all the edges thick and soft. On mornings like this, even the bells of San Jerónimo sound like they were rung last week.

"Map says heavy drift overnight from the old cinema district," Zel says. He's the new apprentice, hair all angles, seventeen and making his voice thick in his throat, trying to find his own weight, his own age inside himself. "Green line is our perimeter; orange indicates a seam near the Luna."

"They marked a seam and sent us with a broom?" I say this too soft for him to hear, only loud enough for time to take it and tuck it somewhere. You're supposed to anchor a seam with a silt net and call a crew with a luger and a spool, someone with a badge that lets them climb the inside of years without getting sealed in the wall. But budgets only do math in one direction. "We can go have a look," I add, and nod toward the triangle where four streets notch together and the Luna sits with its mouth open, sign still promising a matinee that's fifty years late.

"You're shift lead," says Tío, lifting the pole from the truck's bed. He hefts it like a spear, tests his shoulder. He shouldn't even be here. His lungs are a moth-eaten sweater and his granddaughter is due next month, but if he sits at home he coughs wealth dust, finds the morning on the cushions and can't get up. Out here he can walk and curse and teach the new ones to keep their wrists loose.

"Zel," I say, "start at the gutters on the west side, work downhill toward the fountain. Watch your step around anything that looks like it's frozen and isn't. If you feel the ground remembering, move your feet, okay? Do not put your hand out to steady yourself; it's not your hand it's going to take. Call if you get the hollows in your knees."

"I'm good," he says, but his eyes dart to the place by the fountain where the red tiles never warmed again after the last century squall, where your bones ring if you stand there at noon.

"Your mother is good," says Tío, unhelpfully, and then laughs when Zel flushes. He always laughs at the wrong time. I don't mind. It makes a little hole in the morning you can see through.

We sweep. "Sweep" is what we say, because it sounds simple and clean. It is both and it is neither. The poles have bristles that are not bristles, filaments that aren't quite there, threads you can't look at too long or you find them wriggling into a word you almost remember. You hold the pole with your palms loose and you coax the drifts into the silt pans, you tease a sticky spill from a stoop, you clear the lines of the zebra crossing because if you leave the zebra crossing thick, a bus won't know what year it's supposed to stop, and the bus will stop for a woman who isn't yet looking both ways.

We wear masks; we wear rubber that isn't rubber. We wear little charms pinned to the inside of our collars that women made in kitchens, old women who have been doing neighbor magic since before this work was a job that paid, work that was someone's aunt calling you at dawn with a pot of coffee and a basket of bread and twelve boys with brooms and the kind of tired you tell stories to and push away. My charm is a circle of linen with a single seed sewn inside it. The seed knocks against the inside of the circle when I walk. My mother sewed it into a coin for me the night before I started here. She didn't go to bed with my father while I sat and watched her fingers and listened to the news say the river would flood again. I held the bowl where she kept her pins, caught the pins when they fell, tried not to fall asleep and be the kind of daughter who drools on her sleeve on her first shift.

It's not bravery, sweeping. It's not heroic. It's work. You do it with hands and wrists and humor. You do it because if you don't, the bankers feel like their Christmases come twice and the kids on the hill slide backward mid-laugh and their mothers catch only the idea of their shirts, a shape in their hands that never fills. You do it because the city paid your father in back wages with a mason jar of twelve good afternoons the year before he got sick, and you took that afternoon and poured it into his tea, and the color came back to his face, and he carried you to the porch like he did when you were four, and the way he laughed then could cut the dark. You do it because the city refused to pay for the medicine he needed the next month and your mother counted the jars on the shelf and then she disappeared the next week, and the next week went with her, and the weeks after that stretched like taffy and snapped hard.

The plaza scrapes clean in the first hour. The sun climbs. The old men by San Jerónimo play dominoes and the clack hits me like nails in wood, sound of a door. A woman in heels edges around the edge of the caution cones, raises her voice in a way that is supposed to be bright and is only sharp. "My car," she says, showing me her keys, as if keys are a passport. "I parked last night next to the badger statue. I have a meeting at nine."

"The otter," I say. "That's an otter. You need a receipt from the district office. They'll store on G Street until the sweep team releases." I point her toward the turquoise door, the woman with red braids who will stamp her papers with a stamp that looks like it came from kindergarten. The woman in heels is from the new condominiums by the salt plant. They called them "Skylofts" even though the sky is an open sore above them and the salt plant never sleeps.

"I pay taxes," she says, like she is saying "I am someone's daughter, too."

"And you'll get your car," I tell her, because she will. She'll bribe the warehouse man with a day of last summer and he'll come home and smell like mango, and his children will climb him like a tree and rub their faces in his shirt. "Go on. If your meeting's at nine you have time to drink water and think about the otter."

She stares at me like I'm a bridge she isn't sure will hold and then she goes away and her heels tick out a code on the red tiles.

"You're soft," Tío says behind me, bending to scoop a glittering handful of yesterdust into his pan. "Soft makes mistakes."

"Soft makes tips," I say. Behind either of us, a boy we don't know ties a rope to the bronze base of the general and leans out over nothing to wipe the thick powder off his hat. He isn't union. He isn't anyone with a badge. He's a kid who charges tourists to let them feel a breeze that isn't a breeze. He calls it "standing in last Thursday," five bucks each. He holds their hands and tells them when to step and means it. He hasn't fallen yet.

We move toward the Luna. The Luna's marquee still has the letters for the last picture show that played when I was eight: A BESOS SABE LA NOCHE, some doomed couple kissing under a bridge while a clock turned to ash. The metal ladder up the side is rust but still holds weight, though I can't let myself think of Tío on it. He broke his shoulder at a seam on Calle 12 three summers ago when the years hiccuped and his foot found a rung that wasn't there thirty years ago and then was again.

"Seam marked at the northeast corner by the ticket booth," Zel reads off the tablet. He has the tablet because he has young eyes and those eyes track scrolling things with confidence. He is striding. He wants to be seen being in charge of something, anything. It makes me want to put him in my pocket with the charm so no one can take him.

"Slow down," I say, and then I feel it: the hollows inside my knees, the little tug behind the breastbone like my body is remembering how to fall. A seam whispers. It's the sound of a stove cooling, of a book closing next to your ear. It's the sound of your mother in the next room when you aren't sure if she is crying and you don't want to know and you need to know.

The seam is not where the map says. It never is. The map marks a seam that's old, a healed scar. What we find is new. By the ticket booth, tucked in the corner where two walls meet and the paint bubbles, there is a place the air is thicker than it should be. The thick shows like the heat above the grills on the pier. Inside that mirage is a color that is not a color, like oil drizzled on a puddle, like the blue of the blood inside a wrist if your wrist were a sky.

"Don't touch," I tell both of them, as if they're both seven. Zel's cheeks go stiff. Tío's grin broadens and he leans closer. His mask fogs. His breath draws in and I can tell even through the filters he has given in and he is drinking it a little, taking the sweetness, letting it catch at the back of his throat.

"Seam net?" he asks, voice a fraction rougher.

"How much net do we have left?" I ask. "Three meters?"

"Two and a half," he says, without needing to look. "We used four on the last one on Calle de las Flores when the sidewalk tried to go home."

"We'll need six," I say. "We need to call it in."

"And they will send the boys from Norte," he says, meaning men who wear suits under their safety vests, who are paid three times what we are, whose masks hum faintly because they have real filters and the city wants to keep them alive. "And they will take our names off the report and attach theirs, and the money goes in the Norte pension, not ours. Your father would be so proud."

He says that one like a knife. He can, because he carried my father on his back when they both were sixteen and the river pulled my father under that winter, because he remembers my father with his hands up and the laugh that bounced off the bridge. He can do it because he watched me learn to walk and bought me a tin horse when I was three and ran alongside while I made that rattly thing go.

"We need to call it in," I say again. My voice does not shake. It doesn't get to. "Zel, radio. Channel three. Request a crew."

He starts to tell me his radio code, voice proud, and then he looks at my face and says only "Right," and his fingers go fumble in his pocket. He curses under his breath, a hiss, a prayer.

While he is talking to a woman who sounds like she is peeling an orange with her teeth, I stare. The seam flares, just once, like something behind it opened and let a door swing wide and then shut again, slow. Inside, for a second, I see a fish. It isn't a fish from here. It has scales like broken gold and it moves in a way that makes my heart hurt, like each flicker backward is a word I have forgotten how to say. The Luna was built over a tributary and the tributary was built over a freshwater vein that runs out of the hills and the hills were once a flat plain where the people with the blue tattoos came to sit and sing and forget their dead for an hour. Everything shakes hands underground. If you are lucky, you have someone who taught you where to put your fingers.

"What's the protocol if the seam starts to gape before the net's in?" Zel asks, voice pitched just on the good side of panic. His eyes are big, earnest. He looks like a boy I sat next to in school who would take any punishment that was only on paper, any detention that meant sitting and writing, but would cry if the teacher raised her voice.

"You leave it alone," I say, because that is the only possible answer. "You get everyone out of the radius. You call the loudspeaker. You keep the children from playing king of the hill."

"And if someone is inside?"

"They chose," says Tío, and something in me goes to the door and closes it and leans my back against it and holds there.

"They did not choose," I say, once.

We have all known someone who has gone. Some went to the gleam of it, sure, reaching in for a love letter they saw rise like a moth. Some stumbled when the curb changed century under them. Some chased their dogs. Some were pushed. The city sells nostalgia by the ounce, but it also sells amnesia.
