The men from Norte have a contract with the developers from the salt plant to keep the seam nearest the new condominiums shallow and safe; the seam that opens under the hilltop shacks can gape for two days before anyone sends a team, because the people on the hill always owed someone something anyway.

"Permission to deploy net?" I ask the air, the radio, the woman peeling her orange with too-white teeth. "Net length inadequate," I add, because if I am asking, I am telling. Because when I walked into the job my mother told me if I never made any other mistakes I should not make that one, not the mistake of asking when the answer is all you need to move your hands. And because the seam has flared again, and this time what I see through it is not a fish.

It is a swatch of red cloth, caught on something like a nail. It bobs in a current and then subsides and the cloth is not just red like any dress, it is the exact red of my mother's scarf the morning she said she was going to the district office to see a man about the medicine, red like tomatoes you bite in summer, the red that soaks your fingers and you lick it and then your fingers are a tongue.

I move forward and my stomach drops. Tío puts his hand on my arm and he doesn't squeeze. He has taught me more than my father did, and that is not his fault and not my father's. He does not say my name because he knows that sound holds weight and to speak my name here is to put a coin on the scale.

"It isn’t hers," he says instead, and I can tell by the way he says it that he knows it is. His voice tricks like a good rope, gives you slack and then catches you.

"It isn't," I say back, because we tell each other stories that hold. "It could be anyone's scarf, because women have red scarves, and men too. It could be anyone's."

I could reach my hand. If I reached my hand right now, I could catch that cloth. The seam has opened wider, the mirage thickening to a film you could push your fingers into, a membrane that will leave glitter on your knuckles. It is illegal to retrieve through a seam without a permit. It is not even illegal; it is one of those laws written in italics as though italics can shout, a law with a shape like a stick. The law exists because we have lost too many who reached for the obvious and then kept going, and the next obvious, and then they forgot how to stop reaching and their bodies forgot to be here, forgot to be touched, forgot to be fed.

Zel says into the radio, "Team on scene. Repeat, team on scene. Seam is hot. Net insufficient. Request reinforcement."

"How hot?" The woman on the other end yawned as if she didn't know she was doing it. I want to slap the radio against the side of the ticket booth because my body remembers what happens when I get impatient and my mother is a red sleeve.

"Hot," I say, so she'll hear me. "Temperature outside variance. Surface pressure deviation. Drop in barometric. The air tastes like cloves and old apples and the kind of record you play until you can't hear anything else."

"I can send Norte in forty-five," she says. "We have a developing surge by the stadium, priority."

"Forty-five minutes," I whisper, because in forty-five minutes someone will have already remembered themselves into the seam, someone will have brought a folding chair to watch.

"We deploy net," says Tío, and his hand lifts mine and places the net in it because he knows my bones will do what they practice even when my mouth says the right things to the wrong people. "We anchor it there and there," he points, "and we pull wide, and we tell her to wrap her scarf around her throat so she will keep her voice with her and the seam will be tired and will not pull her by her edges."

He does not say the word "her." Neither do I. Zel does not ask who we are talking about; he is young enough not to see the thing you hide by standing in front of it with your shoulders square.

We anchor. The net is filmy, a thing like webs that isn't made by a spider. It crackles faintly, like sugar on your tongue. I count aloud because counting warded off monsters when I was small and because I count when I do anything that matters: "One, two, three, four." The anchors bite into the old mortar with a satisfying sound, like biting into toast. The seam brightens. It hates the net in the way a cat hates a bath, entirely, with back arched and claws out and a howling that makes your scalp ice.

"Talk to her," Tío says. He is in a place that is between the place where he learned that talking can pull a man off a bridge and the place where he knows whispers cost.

"I don't know what to say," I say, because the last time I tried to talk to my mother I broke the wheel on the microwaver and told her I didn't need medicine for my father if we just let it be, that time is time and you can't put it in a jar; she laughed like broken glass and a week later she disappeared into somewhere not on the map and since then I have learned what you can put in a jar and what you cannot.

"Talk about breakfast," he says. "Talk about anything but the thing you want."

I have always done what people tell me if they tell me in the right tone. "Do you want coffee?" I say to the seam. "Do you want coffee and bread? We have yesterday on the bread and I will scrape it away with the back of a knife. We'll sit on the steps if the pigeons have left room. Today the pigeons are slow. They are fat, their necks pulse in and out and look like they are made of coins. You always pretended they were our ancestors, coming down to be a nuisance. I used to call them tíos and you would tell me not to be rude because there were enough rude girls in the world, we did not need another. We can be patient. Let me give you coffee."

It flares and the red swatch whips and something that could be a hand brushes the inside of the net.

"Don't pull," says Tío, too soft to hear and very loud.

"I am not pulling," I say through my teeth.

A siren starts up on the far side of the plaza. The storm siren is a deep-throated thing that can make your teeth ache if you stand too close. The tone slides up and then down, like a whale calling God. It is early for that sound. They told us noon. They told us that we had until noon before the progress front came over the salt plant, before the hot wind from the north tangled with the swell coming up the estuary. But the siren doesn't need to be right to be reason. Heads tip up like flowers. People stop walking. They look for an explanation. We have trained them to look for us when that sound goes, the way we have trained them not to look too long at what shines in the corners of their kitchens at four in the morning.

"Was the map wrong," Zel says, even though he knows maps are always wrong and you marry a map only if you want to die of boredom. "Do we—"

"We pull and we go," I say. The red cloth is now an arm. I almost say "Mamá," and swallow the word whole. The seed pin in my collar knocks against my skin like a heart that is not mine. I think of the night she sewed it. I think of her mouth making the knot. I think of how a knot is just two ends of a thing promising to hold.

"One," I say, and my hands pull in the net. The seam presses back like a belly.

"Two," Tío says, and braces his back against the ticket booth and his boots splay in a way my grandmother would scold as vulgar.

"Three," says Zel, his voice cracking high in a place it never leaves and then deep down in a place he hasn't grown into yet.

The net takes the weight. For one hot second I am holding the whole city like a blanket. In that second, I hear a radio jingle for a brand of laundry soap that hasn't been sold for thirty years. I smell the inside of a bus. I hear my father's laugh on the bridge. I hear my mother when she is twenty singing something she doesn't think anyone can hear. I hear my name said in the voice she had when she thought I was sleeping and she would talk to me as if to a saint, a little bit scornful of what saints are good for and a little bit hopeful too.

The seam sighs. I would swear a seam cannot sigh. I would sign a paper. It sighs and then the pressure eases, and the red cloth slips forward and into the net and I reach with two fingers and I catch it. The fabric is wet, or my glove is. Water runs down my wrist and into my sleeve and it is cold. I didn't know that kind of cold lived here. It bites and then it burns.

The scarf is not whole. It is a torn piece the size of a handkerchief, frayed on one edge and knotted on the other. The knot is tight as a word you can't say in public. I slip the thing inside the chest of my suit without thinking, instinct and theft, against my shirt. It sticks there like a hot coin. Tío sees me do it and does not stop me. He does not nod either. He doesn't move his head, for fear of tipping the balance we have acquired by charm, by pleading, by lying to the radio.

"Reinforcements in thirty," the radio says in my ear. "Repeat, Norte ETA thirty."

"We'll be gone in ten," I say, and throw a lie back at her. I have twenty-eight years to learn how to lie better.

We hook the net under the anchors we can save. We leave the anchors we can't. The seam has tightened like a mouth being stubborn. It wants to spit. Good. Spitting is better than swallowing. I wrap the loose line around the bronze wrist of the general, who looks west forever with his nostrils flared because he knows the future stinks. The siren on the far side has picked up a rhythm. The pigeons lift in a wave and settle on the theater roof, then lift again when the wind hits them.

"I saw her," Zel says, breathless, his mouth open behind his mask, fog making a flower on the filter. "I saw a woman—"

"You saw nothing," I say, too quick and too sharp. He flinches, and I hate that I made him. "You saw yesterday. That's all. That's what comes through. It's sticky. It looks like people because it uses your people to talk to you. You don't know anything until it's in your hands."

He looks at my chest without meaning to and then away, as if my shirt front is a secret or a sin. He is polite like that. I didn't teach him to be polite. Someone did. Thank them. I will find them and give them oranges.

We coil lines. We shoulder poles. We step back from the gaudy mouth. The plaza is brighter. The sun is high enough now that the glitter is meaner, showing wrinkles, the cracks in paint that we haven't had time to fill. A boy is on the red tiles by the fountain, knees on the ground, crying because the soap bubbles around the rim are grabbing at his fingers. His mother is trying to lift him under the arms without touching the foam herself. When she catches sight of us, her mouth opens like a fish's. I nod. We go. I lift under the boy's knees. Tío takes his shoulders and says, "Aquí, campeón," and lifts him clean. The foam disapproves and then lets the boy go because the foam respects a routine done right.

"Thank you," the mother says, breath rolling out. "Thank you, kori," she says to me, a word an aunt would use. I am no one's aunt yet. I will be if the baby Tía Isolina is carrying makes it; we are all aunts to that one already, we argue names in the break room like bargaining with the saints. The boy hiccups. He is fine. He has a ring of white around his mouth where he touched and then touched himself, a moustache of last week.

"Don't lick that," I tell him. "You'll only make yourself want to keep licking. Eat bread instead."

"With butter," he says, offended that I would imagine otherwise, and his mother laughs for the first time this morning.

We head back toward the truck because the map is blinking new marks, because the wind has turned and brought the smell of salt whether or not the tide has, because you can hear the stadium when people talk loud there as if the stadium is a bowl with our city in it like soup and we are the spoon and the spoon sometimes is a blade. We leave the anchors. They will hold for an hour, perhaps two. Norte will come and put their name on the final form and get their photo taken with the general at a slant so you can see the skylofts behind them. They will gesture. A paper will print their suits.

"You're pale," says Tío, which is funny because I am always pale the way flour is pale, like flour hasn't decided yet what it will be.

"I didn't breathe enough," I say, which is true and false. I breathed. I am breathing now. The scarf burns against my skin. My chest feels like a house with a stove on. I don't look at the place where it presses. I don't look at the theater because if I look I'll go back and if I go back in a storm I have earned what comes to me.

Back at the truck, there is a paper cup of coffee someone has left on the bumper. It has a lipstick mark on it. A woman with hair in a hard oval nods to me from the sidewalk and lifts her chin and I don't know if the coffee is for me but I take it because it is in my hand and because it is not good to refuse gifts this early in the day. It is sweet. It is too sweet. Someone has poured something into it from a jar that was not coffee. It is yesterday coffee. For a minute I am sitting at the kitchen table at eight years old and my mother is peeling a mango with a knife no one else is allowed to use, the peel coming off in long yellow tongues. A fly bumps the window. A radio plays a song with eight syllables in the word for love. My father's laugh comes from the porch like a wave. The coffee burns my mouth and I do not stop drinking it. The sweetness makes my shoulders drop. When I finish the cup I am still here. Good. I am not forgiving coffee that easy.

"Union tomorrow," Tío says, like he reads my mind when it's tired. He taps his patch again. "They want bodies to go to the courthouse, make noise when the Norte boys bring their list for the pension. You coming?"

"I always come," I say, and don't add that lately when I go I stand in the back and press my hands together tight and think about a seam in the shape of a door and whether there is a knob on the other side and whether it is cheap metal that will always show fingerprints.

We ride. The truck is old. It shimmies at thirty and sings at forty-five. The breeze lifts hair at my neck and I let it. I press my palm to my chest once, flat, feeling heat through cloth, and the knot of the scarf presses my palm back, a little ghost of a fist. I press again, harder, as if to press it into a softer part of me where it cannot go.

When we turn the corner by the pastel factory, the wind makes a sound that is not siren and not bird. The sky to the north has gone the color of the inside of a lime, sick and bright. The progress front runs along the horizon like a new wall built where no one asked them to build. The cranes creak. A traffic light shows all three colors at once and a boy on a bicycle shakes his head at it as if it has said something that offended his mother. The air tastes like sugar burned to darkness and something like metal shaved to dust.

"It will be a good one," says Tío, with pleasure, and shakes his shoulders like a man walking into a dance. His joy is not madness. It is preparedness. He knows that the thing that comes to take will come whether he sings or sulks, and if he sings, at least his lungs keep time.

"It will be a storm," says Zel, unnecessarily.

"It will be a day," I tell them both. "We keep it walkable."

No one answers. They're both busy. The radio crackles like it has something to say and then doesn't. The stadium whoops in the distance as if someone has scored a thing that matters to them. The eyelashes of the city quiver.

I close my eyes for a breath and in that dark my mother steps around me as if I am a table, minding not to spill soup on the floor. She tucks hair behind my ear. She smells like mango if mango were a color that doesn't exist, like a red you can put your finger through. The scarf in my shirt cools, just for a second, like a fever finds a window. I open my eyes and the day is exactly where I left it. The broom is warm in my hand. The road ahead is dirty.

We go.

Chapter One: The Hour of Redrawing

At six-oh-seven each morning the Anthem for Accuracy rose from vents and culverts, from elevator shafts and bus intercoms, a civic lullaby in a key no one could hum. It was always three notes too long, a ribbon of sound wound through our tea steam and toothbrush foam, and when it finished the city put on its new outline like a shirt that had been cut overnight.

From my window above the print shop I watched the first corrections unspool. The plaza at Fingerling Station widened by a palm’s width, which would be enough to glance sunlight off the bench into the eyes of the woman who sold parrot eggs, if she returned. The little temple that never made it onto any official edition slid one centimeter east; it did not move, but the lines around it did. Across from it the waste-to-heat unit acquired a shadow it hadn’t had yesterday, meaning the municipal drone would scold passersby for standing in a “nonperson trajectory” that hadn’t existed yet by old measures.

Streetlights blinked in sequence. The devout turned their prayer rugs to face the newly computed central coordinate. Riders checked their phones to make sure their addresses were still addresses and not just words. You developed a sensitivity to it, the way you do to storms or pregnancies—if you lived here long enough you could feel the redraw in your cheekbones. Children, who took to change as ducks to water when it was offered as a game, ran to the nearest blue kiosk to watch the pixels consoling them that the world was accounted for.

I drank from my chipped enamel mug and waited. The press below me was still warm from last night; I could feel it through the boards. In the gilt frame over my sink hung an antique surveyor’s chain that had belonged to some man who had cut canals and names into places I would never see; when I moved in, the chain had smelled of oil and old rain. This morning it smelled of tin.

I keep my own maps on paper so old the fibers are part breath. I keep them rolled, cloth-bandaged, hidden in long drawers that used to hold bolts of wedding lace. I do not hang them, though sometimes I want to. The unrolled world has a way of asking to be confessed.

On the street below, the pigeons started their morning circuit, turning as one above the newsstand where, through a habit of negligence or defiance, the vendor still sold last week’s provincial. He held up a small paper map the kiosks had printed for him in error last month, a square of streets with the round edge of the river slicing through like a crescent moon. His stall had never been granted a blue dot or an official polygon; legally it did not have corners. He called to the pigeons as if they could read, which maybe they could. If I had learned anything, it was that living things were not as stupid about coordinates as we were.

My phone chimed with the morning’s digest from the Ministry of Vectors. As always it began with the pledge: Our map protects us. Readability saves lives. Report irregularities immediately. There were exhibits of streets corrected, slums threaded into service, parks granted proper shading. The cynic in me, which had been fed and fattened under employment, watched the ad for the new MapClock—a smart wallpiece that would display your status in shades of friendly green and could be calibrated with a tap to the hour of redrawing—and wanted to throw my mug. The draughtsman in me, which was harder to kill, admired the curve weighting on a new projection of the harbor.

Even after three years, I could not help feeling some small joy when a line was clean.

The last page of the digest announced a Consolidation scheduled for next month. Three neighborhoods on the east end, spurs of two rivers that braided in the rainy months, were to be absorbed into a larger, more serviceable unit. The word serviceable glittered like a knife. I folded the message into a shape with crisp corners and put it in the drawer with the other cheerful amputations.

My neighbor, a man named Caspar whose job, he once told me, was to teach ant colonies to go around construction pits, emerged onto his balcony in a bathrobe and scowled at the part of the street that had become illegal for our feet sometime in the night. “They stole my corner,” he said without looking at me. “Now I have an edge.”

“You can plant thyme along an edge,” I said.

“They'll come measure it and decide it’s a walkable slope. Don’t laugh. It’s happened.”

“I wasn’t laughing.”

Caspar leaned on his rail, making a careful practice of not setting his cup on it; it was one centimeter too narrow now. Rules turned simple actions into small acts of performance. When the geometry of the city changed, the rest of our behavior followed suit. You adjusted, or you were adjusted.

My orange cat, who had come with the shop and took no interest in human arguments, pawed at the stack of proofs on my table. He liked to sit on the draft of the thing I most needed to look at. His name was Sum. He had one ear scarred from some algebraic fight with a dog.

At six-thirty, while the Anthem’s last spiritless echo was still trapped in the stairwell, my private map trembled.

You would laugh if I told you how I keep them. The official kits gleam with glass fiber reels and drones and code. Mine are inventories of smells and sounds and human tongues; written on onion skin and receipts; scored by heat. In one drawer I keep a catalog of the city’s public brass—railings next to the river, rims of trash receptacles, the belly of a bridge crossbeam—under my hand they have given up secrets of the people who leaned into them. Under the table, tucked where Sum likes to sleep, is a wooden box of strings. Each string is the length of a path, with knots for corners and shells for elevation and things that look like accidents but are not. A lime slung inside a damp cloth tells me the sum of the day’s moisture; a wheat stalk tells me which way the alleys breathe. I had a sensor once that did these things without theater or fuss. It died in my pocket the day my mother went off the map.

And then there is my hand. At some point, when I was still employed, I began writing coordinates on the skin of my left palm. I did it the way people draw hearts or knives or draw boxes to keep lists. When I resigned, I had the faint white scar of a single place in the pad below my thumb. Now, on mornings when the redrawing is particularly ambitious, the very pale, very shallow marks there prickle, as if the city were murmuring under my skin. I told no one. People have been committed for less.

My phone pinged again. A different sound, halting and rude, the tone I had assigned against my better sense to push calls that would be work but would also be harm. I let it ring twice, then answered with my name. It is always easier to be lent a story if you wear a syllable people trust.

“Lina?” A voice I knew and did not. The first three letters carried every fight we had had as children in our mother’s hot kitchen, every time I had split a fig and given the sweeter half to myself.

“Jao?”

There was a noise like a lorry passing. The call flickered. I stepped closer to the window.

“I need you,” he said, and then I heard a scrape, the long dragging sound of something heavy being moved along tile. “Where are you? Say it. Say your coordinates.”

My heart stood and did not sit down again.

“I’m at Merton and Fifth,” I said, because that is what you say now when someone asks where you are. “This is— Jao, where are you?”

There was air on the line, which meant he was somewhere without roofing or with roofing perforated enough to let the sky through. “Here,” he said. “I’m here.”

The tone under mess and bravado was fear. He was the one among us who had taught himself to set men's boxes on fire with nothing but a bowl of sunlight and a mirror. He was the one who had once walked home from a beating with blood in both of his shoes and could still crack a joke about the way the city had measured him. I had not heard fear in his voice since we were little and the neighbor’s boy had told him that if you swallowed watermelon seeds your belly would grow a red fruit.

“I’m sending you my location,” I said. “Walk toward me and don’t argue.”

He said a thing I had been making him say since he was eight: “I’m on the map.”

We waited for the lie to take. I could hear nothing but the friction of his breath and the static that comes of being bracketed by machines.

“Jao? Respond to this. I am— I’m here.”

He laughed then, a highly inappropriate laugh, the kind that made me, even now, want to put him in a basket and send him down a river. “I don’t know how to respond.”

“Tell me what you see.”

“A wall.”

“Describe it.”

“Two meters by forever. Concrete. After that, nothing.”

Outside my window, the sun found a gap between buildings it liked and came through. A girl on a scooter paused at the blue kiosk, read some instruction, and turned a sharp circle, adjusting herself to the morning’s reality in a single movement that would have sent my ankle bones chattering. I wrote on my palm without realizing it: two meters by forever. “Is your block...” I could not finish. You never said vanished or erased. The official language was neutral. Off-page, someone in policy once explained to me over eggs and a full bottle of rain-chilled white that there are places the map is not, and therefore to consistent instruments there are places that are not there.

“Wiped,” he said, cheerful as matches. “We woke up, and my house was a clean card. My kettle makes noise, but the water is pretending it does not know about fire because the grid has— I don’t know. No drone. No nets. The street past the wall is... I think it is a place where I am not.”

“Do not,” I said, “step off anything.”

“I am not a fool.”

“You are. Stay still.”

“Lina,” he said, and there it was, that child-appeal. “Don’t bring the police.”

“As if,” I said. “As if I have them in my pocket. Keep your call running. If the line breaks I will hate you forever.”

The line laughed of its own accord in the little hiccup way it does when a tower isn’t certain. The Ministry would not come for him. He no longer existed under their eyes. If you went off-map you were to queue at a particular window in a particular building and wait for someone to ask for your mother’s maiden name. The window had no clear hours and people set up tents. You could wait until your legs made other plans, and sometimes after that. The people in the tents cooked with illegal fire.

I put the phone on speaker and set it on the table while I looked for my bag. The bag is an old postal sack I stole from myself when I still worked in a building with smoke detectors funded by foreign grants and wall televisions that never showed the dirt on the floor. In it: chalk, a coil of red grosgrain, a paper shuttle for paying out line, a sliver of mirror, an old transit level with a crack I know how to look around, a jar with holes in the lid. The jar was for the bees, which ought to be saved for another chapter; for now I only unscrewed the cap and held a breath over the lip and screwed it back on again. All maps begin with breath.

Caspar watched me from his balcony with his lips moving through a litany of things he wanted to say but would not because he knew me. “Who is it?” he called, finally, as if it would help to give him a shape to fear.

“My brother.”

“What did he do?”

“Someone drew wrong around him.”

I locked my door, although when you work where I work you understand that locks are declarations of faith rather than masters of outcomes. On the street, the kiosks were still busy. It is a small sort of entertainment to see your shop or your house or your little bit of roof assigned a shade of permissible. A silver-haired woman in a blue skirt stared at the screen and then up at the building and then back again, the way you might look at a lover who has just shaved and the mouth is not the mouth you recall. “They trimmed us,” she said to no one in particular. “We are cleaner.”

I took the stairs because waiting for the lift made me feel like the city was in my ear. On the landing above the print shop door, someone had pasted a flyer for a lecture at the academy titled Zero and the Citizen: Why Absence Is a Gift. The speaker’s face was everywhere the last few weeks: a man with well-apportioned eyebrows who used to teach at the place where I had knocked my knee against desks and dreamt of lines straight as beliefs. I tore the corner of the flyer to clean an old glue smear and put the piece in my pocket because you never know when you will need somebody else’s certainty.

When I reached the street the pressman had propped open the shop door and was oiling the old machine in a way I had had to swear not to learn because he thought I would take it to bed with me and sleep under it like a carriage. “Do you have work?” he asked, which was a tender way of asking if I had enough money to pay for the ink I borrowed from him and the light I stole by leaving things plugged in too long.

“We will see,” I said. “Call me an ambulance if you don’t see me by nightfall.”

“God,” he said, crossing himself out of superstition, not habit, “if I called for an ambulance on this street they would ticket me for blocking a bus that never comes.”

I went left. The pedestrian algorithm ran at shin height along the curb, light spilling like toothpaste. I stepped out of it. It made a sound like a deflated balloon. Drivers respect the maps more than they respect human bodies. If you walk in the light, the cars will stop. If you step into gray, you are only as safe as your face.

Jao lives—or lived, or will again live—in the district of old factories that had been turned to student housing which had been turned to small apartments where single men and last old people share walls. The buildings there have beautiful bones: iron ribs and windows that were once eyes big enough to confess. On firm mornings you can see the pennants of past affiliation painted under the cheap stucco. Some of the stilted houses along the river look like they have pulled their skirts up to wade.

On Rotter’s Street I passed a hole you cannot lay a plank across, not because of width, but because the hole is not a hole. It is a kind of absence the map designates as Corrections Pending. A woman sat on a folding chair and read a holy book beside it, because absence makes for privacy. Farther south the scent of sesame and hot oil from Mr. Kin’s bun cart made every arguing detail of the city go quiet behind my face. I bought two. I ate neither. The bread keeps better if you keep it waiting for someone.

As I walked, the shapes told themselves to me. A line of kiosks set at intervals just shorter than comfortable, which meant the Ministry expected people to be waiting to see if they were still included; the benches had had their arms redistributed to discourage lying down, which would tell you if you were listening that the new illegal plank cities—wound under overpasses and around the ankles of official housing—had been counted, measured, and assigned to the category that has no food aid attached. A new kind of camera had been installed on the corners of the two streets where dogs always forgot their names. Somebody had washed the statue of the woman with the basket, not an official wash, but an ordinary city wash: someone’s hand and a rag and a basin of water that had been fetched on a shoulder.

I do not carry white when I go where I go. White is for doctors and brides and those kinds of men who must be recognized at once. I was a slate color and a dark green and a stripe of orange that nobody had claimed.

At the edge of where the city acknowledged itself, there was always a mood. Sometimes it was the smell of pennies. Sometimes it was the sudden quiet when machines believe they are alone. Today it was the sound of paper rubbed with the flat of a wooden pencil—the scratch that is not a line but the texture of line. The antennas above my head went still. The drones pulled back, as if the air itself ended. The sidewalk stamped its last little emblem of compliance. Beyond it there was pavement, and then there was not.

Jao had not mentioned which way the wall faced. There are practical reasons for that—when you are scared, you cannot tell east from the other east—but also a superstition: if you tell the wall where it is, it will take offense and move.

I stood in front of it. Two meters by forever, yes. The concrete looked poured late in the day by someone thinking of supper. It was a different color than our walls, a lighter gray, the gray of long-washed lint. On our side there were marks from hands and shoes. On the other side there was no sound at all. The official word for that state is unencumbered by network; I have always preferred blank.

“Don’t come through,” I said, although there was no door, “not until I test.”

A danger, with blanks, is that they look like the country you grew up in. Your feet remember things your bones do not. But if you step wrong, you might learn that gravity has an opinion about where it is allowed to operate. Or you find that a block loops back to the start like a board game a cheap uncle has purchased to save himself grief. Or you are measured and found wanting by a tool that believes the city is shaped like a square and will not be convinced otherwise.

I blew air across the top of the open jar to wake the bee. It was one of my mentor’s tricks, and she had said, even after the disaster with my mother, that tricks were just strong tools that had been embarrassed. The little animal had been numb with cold and glass. It staggered up, crawled around the rim, and lifted. Bees do not like static, and they do not like the smell of burning without fire. They will veer away from both. This one flew out over the line where official services had stopped and hovered as if sniffing. Then it went up, straight up, steadied, and set down on the blank side of the wall, right at the seam where poured concrete met air.

“Do you see me,” I asked Jao, “or do you hear my bee?”

“You,” he said, without confidence. “No, the bee.”

Something like relief makes noise in my body like the cracking of sheets hung to dry. If his senses registered the bee, we were contiguous, which meant a particular set of risks rather than the other set of risks, which I despise more.

“Talk to me while I do the stupid part,” I said, and tied the long red strip of ribbon to the brass ring on my belt. I fed it through my hand to make sure it would unspool without snarls. I chalked my right shoe along the sole, a habit older than anything I had learned under the Ministry because my grandmother had believed it would keep her from falling into wells.

“You’re old,” he said, hearing the sounds of my superstitions. “Listen to you making knots like an aunt.”

“The manual agrees with the aunt,” I said, and then I stepped off the map.

Here is the sensation, which I am convinced is different for each of us: the weight of the air changes. There is a cold that is not cold, a dryness that is not between skin and skin, but between measurement and your body. Sound becomes too intimate; your own breath has nowhere to disperse and so swells. The light is a flavor different by a molecule—milk that has gone one hour too long without chilling. The city is not gone, exactly, but a version of it has veiled itself. The red drift of my ribbon stayed red. My hand went hot where the old faint coordinates were. Once, stepping into a blank under rain, I saw drops begin to move in a direction no human would have named down. Today, the dust rose as it always did.

“Keep talking,” I said, because silence here means the shape of your skull will speak to you in whatever voice is most cruel.

“Remember when you tried to leave flowers at the corner where they put the tower down and someone told you you had to apply for grief?” Jao said. “Remember when we were six and we drew a map of our building hallway because mother told us the landlord would put our doormat on the other side so the devil would come to the wrong door? Remember the coin I swallowed and you told me the Ministry would send a man to retrieve it with a spoon?”

“My most successful policy recommendation,” I said, and put my palm to the wall. It felt not like concrete but like the idea of concrete, built of a thousand other walls that had been considered and not poured. The seams were wrong, shallow. Someone had thought about engineering and stopped. Just beyond it, a smell of burnt sugar. Farther right, something sour; left, a draft that had no source, which meant an opening that did not admit human bodies would admit air. The ribbon paid out behind me like the tongue of a red animal that loved me more than I deserved.

“Keep talking,” I said again.

He said a list of small crimes he had committed as a boy. I took out the chalk, marked an X where my hand told me the wall stopped being wall and began being name. I put my shoulder against that name. The concrete gave as if a family had leaned on it at dinner every night for twenty years. Dust fell inside the blank like confetti at a parade no one was attending. My body remembered making itself narrow between stacks of paper down in the pressroom during a heatwave, hands on either edge to keep from touching the ink.

“Do you see my ribbon?” I asked.

A pause, then: “It is the color of a bus.”

“Pull gently.” I fed out line until I felt not resistance, but attention. There is a difference.

He tugged, mild as a fish. I stepped, heel to toe, into the quiet. The ribbon brushed my hip as if to say I was still connected to something that had a language for me. I moved parallel to the wall until the chalk mark was behind my knee and then I stopped and turned my head the way my grandmother had taught me to turn it when I smelled night rain—one ear toward the inadmissible, mouth closed so the tongue did not argue with the air.

I heard him. Even though sound in a blank travels as if each syllable must push its own cart through a bureaucratic corridor.

“Jao,” I said, and he said my name, say a spice.

“I can’t see you,” he said.

“Good. That means the wall isn’t letting the stupid kind of trick through.” If he could see me, it would mean that light and object were currently in the kind of argument that ends with broken plates. Where there is light that acts without matter you do not bring your soft parts.

I put one hand forward, palm open in case there was a change in pressure that would hurt. There was a draft of air again, a seam, something human. I took two more steps and felt the world loosen around my ankles, like water yielding. I saw the corner of a kitchen table that was not in my world and then I saw my brother’s face.

He had the eyes of the boy who had chased coins along gutters and the stubble of the man who had, in fact, once set a box on fire with a mirror. He looked thinner. There was flour on his shirt, which meant he had been baking, which meant he had used the last of what he had to make a thing that would make strangers forgive him. He lifted his hand. He was six inches away and a kilometer.

“Don’t move,” I said, and almost laughed because it is what the police say; we have borrowed all of our sentences from people who have never been to the blank.

“I told you not to bring the Ministry,” he said, as if I had, because on my worst days I look like I belong to the people who measured him without asking permission.

“I brought bread,” I said, because there are places the city will not recognize but bread speaks through them.

“Why are you crying?” he asked me, gentle as a bee.

“I’m not,” I said, and truly did not know. The chalk X on the wall behind me glowed as if it were pleased with the part it was playing.

Somewhere outside the blank, a siren started its long practice of not arriving in time. The sounds of the mapped city came in and laid down on the floor like cats. The ribbon pooled at my feet. The Anthem had ended a half hour ago and still my bones hummed with it. The morning was a quarter eaten. A fly cut figure eights through a beam of light that had found a crack in the official shade and was pouring itself into the wrong category. In my palm, the old coordinate rose like a question.

“You found it,” Jao said. Not the path. Not the seam. Not me. “The place where the walls let through the names instead of the hands.”

I did not ask him how he knew. I had a rule once about never believing anything that could not be printed and folded and placed under a wedding cake for luck. I have broken all my rules one by one until they sound the way the press sounds when you take your finger off the button: relieved, but a little bereft.

On the other side of the blank, the kettle whistled in a tone slightly wrong for metal. Behind my brother, through a window that gave onto a street that did not connect to ours, I could see the sky. It looked like ours except for the way it did not make promises about tomorrow.

“We have to do this carefully,” I said, and lifted the bread with both hands as if it were an instrument that could fail and started to speak the names of the corners between us. The names are what the maps have always forgotten.

Behind us, beyond the wall, the city went on redrawing itself, working itself into a shape it could face in the mirror. I said the names of drains and thresholds, lintels and lint, the proper names and the ones children shout when they run past a place without looking. The air took them. Somewhere, I was sure, a woman at a blue kiosk blinked up at her changing green. Somewhere, a man oiled a machine. Somewhere an ant colony learned the contour of a hole.

“Start with the door,” my brother said, because he remembered, and the word door, which had so often failed us, hung for a second between our two worlds like something you could measure and trust. We both smiled, and then, because it was a blank and because every entrance is also a test, the wall breathed. The ribbon answered. Sum, on my table where I had left him lording it over the proofs, sneezed. I had stepped off the map; I had not yet returned. The first chapter of any rescue is this: you teach a thing to recognize a name you can stand in.

“Door,” I said again, and the seam in the world widened the exact width of a human hand.

Chapter One

On the morning the pigeons learned my mother’s last words, I was performing a calibration.

You don’t learn this job from books. You learn by learning the weight of pauses, the dialect in a cough, the arrangement of vowels a throat chooses when blood is full of morphine. You learn the sound of a compliment sent to keep the living from breaking. You learn how to coax speech from the throats of creatures that don’t owe you anything. You learn to listen to birds the way some people listen to rain—without assuming it’s about you.

I was standing in a courtyard off Nargis Lane, ankle-deep in blue shadows, tuning my ear to a myna’s inventory of a dying grocer’s opinions on mangoes. The myna was perched on the metal bracing of an awning, pecking at a strip of peeling paint between sentences. Below, a narrow house lay open like a mouth with one tooth; between kitchen and living room a white sheet flapped on its line. On the balcony opposite, a woman in a faded sari spilled rice onto her wide palm and shook it to make the sound that brings pigeons.

“The Totapuri is a liar,” the myna said, in a voice like the grocer’s, a little watery, a little too proud. “It says it will be sweet and then it is thread and fiber, too many strings for a tongue that has done its work. If you can carry something in your hand that looks like a promise, do not trust it.”

I nodded. I wrote it down. I have a pen whose nib I sharpen with fine sand, and a notebook that smells like the herbal powder my mother used to keep in the cupboard for cockroaches. The page drank. I date everything; the Bureau insists. The light from above wasn’t light, exactly—more like a heat that had learned how to glow.

“There was also,” the myna added, turning its head toward me and showing a bead-black eye, “that time with the girl from the cigarette shop in the college lane.” Then it hopped three steps sideways and coughed up a kernel. “But that is not last words. That is before.”

“Before doesn’t belong to me,” I told it. “Just the end.”

The woman on the balcony clicked her tongue at a pigeon in a way that was almost scolding and almost affection. You can see love in a hand when it flings small things to the hungry. It looks like absolution. The pigeon—particular pigeon, with a notch in its left foot, as if a piece had been bitten away by a rusted wire—floated down, fanned its tail, and pecked with the ferocity of a sentence being found. The morning had the sound of metal being folded.

“You wrote the mango part,” the woman called down. “But he also used to curse the Ambika chutney because they put sugar and not jaggery. That used to make him furious. Doesn’t that belong.”

“Did he say it with a foot inside tomorrow?” I asked. Sometimes my tone makes me sound like a clerk preventing a complaint with a rule. I don’t mean it that way.

She pushed rice into the space between index and middle finger and slid it out into the air with the violence of an accusation. I think of myself as gentle. But this city has taught me how to be regular. Try bringing mercy to an office and you will find yourself lifting boxes alone while your supervisor reads the paper. Try ordering the last words of the beloved, and you will find yourself building shelves in your sleep.

“You know how he was,” she said. “His whole life he was saying last things. Like he couldn’t stand a day unless he killed it with a sentence. Then he lived tomorrow anyway. So who knows when it’s the last.”

“Let’s check the formal testimony,” I said, to be kind. Formal testimony is where we pretend there is only one ending.

I set the quiet bell in the middle of the courtyard. It looks like a tin bowl, dented from some older use, with a tiny hinge and a tongue of owl feather inside that never moves. I opened its lid and let it collect voices. The bell’s job is not to quiet the world; the world rejects being told to hush. The bell quells the inside of your head that wants to fill in blanks. We call it calibration so that the City will pay us. I took a shallow breath. The myna cocked its head, and for half a second every rooftop slept. Then:

“The pickles are under the mahua syrup,” the myna said, then giggled with the grocer’s exact giggle—a heh-heh-heh as if humor were a spool that had to be unwound.

“Under the mahua,” I repeated. I looked up at the woman. Her mouth had turned line-like.

“Was he—I mean—was he alone when he said that?” she asked.

“Our witness indicates proximity,” I said, because I have a way of not answering questions that would open other questions. “We will certify these words. Will you sign the record?”

When she came down the stairs with her pen, she looked at me like she wanted to ask whether words were enough when all she had left were things that had held words: his shirt with the missing collar hook, the chair where his hips kept their shape for an hour after he rose, the space his slippers left at the bottom of the stairs. But we were both inside the Bureau’s ritual now. I tilted the notebook toward her and she made a mark that might have been her name if names were birds and ink were sky.

The pigeon with the notched foot hopped onto the lip of the bell, put its head into the quiet, and, without prelude, said in my mother’s voice: “Under the blue tile.”

It was not a line. It was the way she would say it when she wanted to pretend the fact of a thing could be made holy by turning it into a secret. She had a pale scar above the bone on her right wrist where a buffalo once stepped on her by accident. When she was excited, she would rub that place like a worry bead. Her last days had smelled like antiseptic and cardamom. The pattern of her breath had had a hole in it. “Under the blue tile,” said the pigeon, and the courtyard fell away and all the sun’s heat tumbled into the space inside my ribs that exists for sudden loss.

The city has a thousand false prophets. Every utility pole gives a speech. Every auto-rickshaw knows your father’s faults. When the monsoon comes late, you can hear twenty-seven interpretations given outside the same tea stall. I do not, as a rule, let myself be invaded by coincidence. But my mother’s voice had a particular warble at the end, a tiny rise like a hand lifted to wave it away. The bird lifted the word tile on that wave and put it down in a tone that was mostly apology.

The woman with the rice drew in her breath and made a low sound that could have been envy or fear or sympathy. She looked at me and looked away because we all participate in the pretense that we are doing a job and not a sacrament. The myna, perhaps insulted, picked at the railing and recited, in the grocer’s voice, the price per kilo of okra if the leaves have brown spots.

“Who does he belong to,” the woman asked finally, nodding at the pigeon as if he were a bowl passed around a circle and not an animal that refuses ownership.

“No one,” I said. “He belongs to the sky. But I need his utterance.”

“You want to catch him, Miran,” she said, and there was tenderness in how she said my name, a neighbor tenderness, one that recognized me from the time I was the boy who cried for a whole night because a kite string cut my ear.

The pigeon fluttered to the ground, cooed a sound that could have been a laugh or hunger, and made a soft motion with its head as if to tell some invisible partner that the conversation had become too much trouble. Then it lifted in a kind of half-hearted way, smacking the air twice with its silver wings, and perched on a television antenna above the lane. The sky was the color of a bruise a day old. Don’t run, I told myself. People had opinions about Bureau men who ran after birds.

In my jacket pocket, I keep a little bag stitched by my sister from the hem of my mother’s old nightgown. Inside it are a handful of millet and a penny that is not from here. The millet is for luring the past near without letting it climb onto your face. The penny is for remembering the way metal can lie. I took the bag out. I raised my hand to throw.

“Miran,” someone said behind me.

I turned. Tavi, my junior from the Bureau, stood in the alley with his shirt sticking to him and his lanyard fallen behind his back like a noose. He has the infuriating optimism of someone who has not yet been told to sit down and look at his hands. He’s very good at hearing through windows.

“You’re supposed to be at the General Ward by ten,” he said, pushing his glasses up his nose. “There’s a doctor who hates birds but likes forms. He says if we don’t show, he’ll propose a rule.”

“What sort of rule means anything in a ward,” I said. “People break rules with their lungs.”

Tavi looked at the pigeon, listening to the slow grinding of my jaw the way he might listen to a rumor. He has a little notebook too, because all of us in the Bureau begin with the idea that our job is holding other people’s words away from rain.

“Is that your pigeon?” he asked.

“Nothing is my pigeon,” I said. “That one is dangerous.”

Tavi squinted. “Dangerous with what. Droppings. Disease. A sharp look.”

“Dangerous with doors,” I said, and did the terrible thing of speaking a metaphor like it was literal, because inside me the air was tightening against my ribs. The pigeon shifted on the antenna and made a sound with its throat like a fountain being turned off. “You go to the Ward. Tell them I will come when I can.”

“You will come when you can,” Tavi repeated, not as sarcasm, as a habit of capturing my way of speaking for later mimicry. This is how we teach. This is how we ruin and bless each other.

He left. The myna recited the registration number of the grocer’s old ration card. The woman on the balcony began collecting the grains the pigeons had ignored with a pinched hand, as if withdrawing a loan from a generous aunt. I told myself to do nothing. But I took two steps into the lane anyway and the pigeon lifted again, crossed Nargis Lane with a line drawn between two rooftops as if pulled by string, and settled on the iron gating outside the clinic where my mother had coughed the first cough that made our neighbor turn his face away.

I know exactly when I stopped believing that the city would hold me upright if I handed it the right papers. The afternoon my mother died, the nurse who had developed a love for rules pinned a paper sheet over the lower half of the bed to cover my mother’s legs, as if modesty were something the dead could feel. The sheet had blue squares printed on it, the color of swimming pools you cannot enter. The wall opposite had a strip of tile that didn’t match the others: six inches of sky in a sentence of sea. If I trust the bird, I am trusting a trickster that eats fallen lint. If I don’t trust the bird, I am refusing the only testimony my city believes has no motive.

“You and your work,” my sister had said two days after the body was delivered to us, without a wreath because the men at the wreath shop had been drunk after the local team’s victory. She sat at our kitchen table with a hard tear in each eye that refused to fall. “You collect last words for strangers and you didn’t even bring me one of hers.”

I did not tell her that I had gone to the balcony outside the ward at dawn and whistled under my breath the way we whistle to each other between aisles in a market. I did not tell her that the only bird that came was a crow with mischief on its beak. I did not tell her that the crow had looked at me with a gaze of fierce pity and said, in the voice of a boy we once knew, “I was joking.” The joke of death is that it knows a hundred voices and uses all of them until yours confuses their faces.

“Under the blue tile,” said the pigeon again, softer, like a rehearsal.

There was a line of ants moving along the rim of a broken pot near the clinic’s gate. The clinic’s watchman, who loves to have the last word on anything that enters his sight, yawned and let his baton clatter against a metal chair. He works nights in a different place, some place that sells bottled kindness to people in checked shirts who sing on a stage about the women they forgot. During daytime, he watches us with the resentment of a man whose sleep was interrupted by sunlight. He saw me but chose not to see me because one afternoon I had filled out a form in his name for his mother, and then I had not been able to retrieve what was not there.

“Shoo,” he told the pigeon, waving his baton as if the air were dust he could rearrange. The pigeon ducked, pecked, stayed.

I took one step and another, and heard a scooter behind me come loose from its rider and scrape its own paint along a wall. Across the lane, under a window where someone had pasted a calendar that showed a god with eight arms and a very modern haircut, a pair of schoolchildren were being kissed by the older version of time known as an examination. Their mothers barked instructions that would be mistaken for love in a different language. In the sweat that had collected in the hollow between my chest and my shirt, a series of small worlds were being born and dying.

I stopped under the antenna. The pigeon bent down, made a tiny clicking sound, and put its beak to the rust. I held out my hand the way I had held out my hand to my mother five days ago and felt that old humiliation I had felt as a child when a stray dog sniffed at my fingers and declined to lick them. “Come, then,” I said, and my voice did not sound like mine. “Come tell me properly.”

People hate that there is a Bureau of Avian Testimony. They hate it for its premise—birds as archives of the dying—and they hate it for what it makes them do—write, stamp, attest. They hate it because you can’t bribe a pigeon. They love it when it offers them something no one can argue with. They hate it when it does not. Our funding is renewed every two years by a committee that looks like tired schoolteachers trying to decide whether to adopt a new map. At the last hearing, a man with a beautiful voice had presented a box with a cylinder inside it. He had pushed a button. A boy’s laughter had spilled into the room, bright as marigold dust. “Stop depending on birds,” the man had said. “Record the living. Then you will not need scavengers of speech.” I had tapped the table with my nail and watched a beetle dying on its back behind a glass pane of the window.

I should have gone to the Ward. Instead I walked to our old house.

There are streets that put their hands around your throat gently and ask a question. The path between the clinic and the house where my mother used to live holds its tricks like a conjurer who does not like applause. At the paan shop the size of a cupboard, the man who had once told me he liked my shoes watched me with the special interest reserved for other people’s sorrow. At the corner, Mr. Nair was thwacking a mattress on the wall like the city was a drum he was arguing with. A girl dragged a stick along a metal grille—chink, chink, chink, a sound that calls you back when you want to leave. I let everything rise and fall around me without making space for it and then I turned left under the guava tree whose fruit had learned, over the years, to hide from boys like us with aspirations toward theft.

Our old house is not ours now. We rent the lower floor to a family whose living room holds a sofa that has learned the exact slope of three different bodies. The upper floor is occupied by the kind of silence that collects in places where noodles have been boiled for ninety seconds too long. The outer gate’s latch had broken last year and we had not fixed it on the theory that a broken thing announces having been looked at. The pigeon with the notched foot sat on the gatepost and watched me try to pretend I was doing anything other than making a pilgrimage to an altar I had built myself.

When you are a listener by trade, you develop an intimacy with doorways. At a threshold, everything is trying to tell you something. The wind says: why did you forget your grandfather’s skull had a dent you loved as a child. The smell says: someone with sugar on their hands came here yesterday. The hinge says: you will lose me in your budget if you do not oil me with a cloth that belonged to a woman who laughed with her whole belly. I touched the wooden frame and it touched me back with the memory of my mother pressing the lintel with turmeric the week of my sister’s wedding, lifting her four fingers like the city’s flag. The door pushed open as if it had decided on me in advance.

Inside, the air was cooler in the way of rooms that have decided to be patient. I do not think an emptiness is an absence. It is a presence you have to learn a vocabulary for. Across the small hall, a row of tiles along the baseboard, white with a blue stripe at the top the width of a thumbnail, marched their way toward the kitchen. I stood in the place a person stands when they are in between thinking and doing and I did not think.

“Under the blue tile,” she had said or did not say. Under the blue tile can be a direction, an apology, a dare, a question dragged by one shoulder across several days. When we were children and we played at hiding coins, my mother would pretend to helm the world as if it were a boat and announce that treasure isn’t really anything but a friend you can’t find until you think you’ve lost them. She would hide a copper coin under the pot of rice on the stove, and my sister and I would sniff the entire house into a fever.

I put my hands to the lowest row of tiles and pressed. The edges were cool. The line where one ended and another began had collected a thin sediment of skin and spices and the bodies of very small lives. I ran my finger along the grout. In the kitchen, there is a place where the pattern breaks, where my sister’s child once slammed a spoon on the wall so many times a chip flew up and cut her forearm and she wore that mark like a necklace she forgot to remove until a boy kissed it. The blue stripe there is thinner, as if the maker's hand had shaken.

“Don’t let him cut the lemons,” my mother used to say when she was angry with me for saying something too sharp, and to this day I cannot hold a knife against citrus without feeling like a thief. The pigeon had said something else once and I had been too scared to write it. If I had written every last word I have ever heard, I would have had to give up my hands.

The tile near the corner moved when I pulled. I had to use both thumbs and the underside of my will. It gave with a sound that I will hear when I am old even if the rest of me has swallowed its own tongue. Behind it, darkness the width of my palm lay waiting. I put my finger into it like someone putting a question into a well. Dust made the old smell of paper that has decided to leave its letters.

I touched a bundle. Not large. Wrapped in plastic that had aged into a yellow you could mistake for virtue. I brought it out and I sat on the floor and a sound came out of me that was not my voice. We have a word in our city that means the kind of crying that is not for the thing that broke but for the part of you that believed it would not.

Inside the plastic was a handkerchief, white, hemmed by my mother, threaded in the corner with the letter S for her name in the way she believed initials could keep a body safe. Inside the handkerchief was a key. Old-fashioned, with a round head and a toothed end that had kissed one lock so often they had trained each other’s mouths. There was a slip of paper too, lined, with the ragged edge that comes from ripping a page out of a child’s notebook. On it, in pencil, in a hand that wanted to be neat and learned that neatness is sometimes rude to speed, was written: “Miran. If I do not show you, go to the roof on the first of no moon. Take off your shoes. Listen to the ants.”

I sat on the floor with the bundle in my lap and the idea of my mother’s voice in my ear and the pigeon outside laughing at my need like a god who wants an apology from a believer before he will give him what he was going to give him anyway. Somewhere outside, in some part of the city where the air carries the sound of steel against steel, a train announced it had done something unavoidable. I held the key with both hands like a question.

At the Bureau, when a testimony yields not solace but complication, our manual instructs us to contact the family liaison office and schedule a mediation to prevent the escalation of grief. At home, when a dead woman directs you to put your ear to an ant, the manual is your memory and you will disobey it.

If anyone asks me later when the story started, I will say: with a pigeon that broke a rule. Or with a blue tile that expected to be a tile for the rest of its life and instead became a door. Or with my failure to be the kind of person who believes coincidences can be asked to wait.

The notch-footed pigeon made a low sound outside, something between a lullaby and a complaint. My phone vibrated in my pocket, an invisible insect demanding I admit it built a life inside me without permission. Tavi had sent me a message with six words and a full stop: The doctor says he has time.

I put the key in my shirt pocket. I reset the blue tile as if I were putting a body back into its bed. I stood up. Everything I have done since has been a response to an instruction that came from a throat I loved that was already becoming stone. If there is a prize in this city for anything, it should be for the people who keep walking when being told to stop feels like devotion.

On the way back to Nargis Lane, a myna on a wire told a boy below that he would fall in love with someone kind who would trouble his sleep for a decade. Birds can be cruel. It is not their fault. We teach them. The pigeon was gone from the clinic gate. The watchman had fallen asleep in a way that suggested he had a fight with rest and lost. The woman with the rice had folded her balcony into shade. Above the lane, between one building and the next, the sky had the look of a lid put lightly on a pot that refuses to boil.

“Under the blue tile,” I said once, to the quiet bell in my head, and the bell quivered and settled and was no use at all. I wiped my hands on my pants. I took a breath that tasted like the last bit of someone else's prayer. Then I went to the General Ward to do what we are paid to do: listen to what the living say as they leave.

Chapter One

It begins with the sound of small clocks.

In the gray hour before the sun unpeels the horizon, the breaking tide is a scatter of ticks and tocks as wristwatches knock and rattle across the pebbled Strand. Their hands have stopped at inconvenient times—2:17, 11:03, a quarter to dawn—but they keep their habit of sounding important. The gulls, in their slovenly wisdom, fall back to watch, and the volunteers in their thrifted orange slickers wade in with nets and long-handled scoops. There is a hush like the inside of a bell. If you listen closely, you can hear the objects naming themselves.

I am the first to step onto the wet stones, as always. The leather of my boots drinks the brine up past my ankle bone, and it is as if the sea has reached out to touch the tendon that ropes me to its tide, pulling and letting go, pulling, letting go. “Morning, Inez,” calls Ayo, from under his hood, and his voice is as careful as his feet. It is a morning to speak softly so we do not drown out what is trying to be heard.

We work the Strand with measured choreography. The city has marked off the perimeter with red twine looped around metal stakes, a gesture toward control that the sea finds amusing. Before the twine, crowds would surge and wail when they thought they recognized something. Now they surge and wail from behind the line. It is the unluckiest job I have ever loved, to stand between the water and the people and say, Not yet, or This will hurt you, or Yes, I know.

A wave withdraws with a huff, leaving behind a neat row of cutlery nestled in silt: a knife with a bird etched into the handle, a fork with bent tines like a broken comb, a spoon that has collected a moon of rainwater even though it is not raining. I kneel and lift them, one by one, with the respect you give to things that have been elsewhere. My fingers remember more than I do; they know how to cradle a thing so it does not remember the fall.

Behind me, a murmur swells. Even without turning, I can feel the weight of waiting. People come with their pockets full of names. Names used to be enough; once, a name could seat a child at a kitchen table or send a letter across a war. Now you must bring paperwork. There is a laminated sign duct-taped to the barricade: CLAIMS REQUIRE PROOF OF RELATION. Beneath that, another line in smaller font: The Archive is a secular office and will not accept prayers. The tape has peeled up at the corners, and the spray has inked salt punctuation into the rules.

A boy’s voice shivers clear through the air, rope-thin and taut. “Is that his hat?” he asks. “Is that my father’s hat?” The hat in question is a thing like a flung shadow—black felt, battered crown—but when I glance toward it, the fear in my chest flutters like a trapped sparrow. It is not a hat; it is a cormorant wing, sleeked with oil and spread in an unkind mimicry of a brim. The boy is small enough that the world can, and will, lie to him.

“Not a hat,” I say, gentle without looking him in the eye. Eye contact can solder hope to a single, unkind object. “Look how it shines. That is a bird who will go on flying.”

His mother’s hand tightens around his shoulder. She is the kind of woman who has learned to keep her jaw soft so that her sentences do not crack. “He thinks—” she starts, then stops. The rest of her sentence wraps around the boy and will demolish him if spoken. I nod instead, half a bow, acknowledgment of all that cannot be made rational in front of the sea.

They say the returns began the year the breakwater was built and the scoured ships finally dozed in the ship graveyard without banging their ribs against the piers. Or they began with the storm that left jellyfish in the traffic circles and squid like torn umbrellas in the cypress. Or they began the first time someone shouted a name at the water and the water did not leave them unanswered.

The scientists papered the thing with currents and probability. The believers tied ribbons to the fence. Fishers, with their butchered tongues and eyes lined by wind, called it what we call everything we cannot buy or sell: a thing that belonged to us before it came.

The first time I stood on this Strand with a plastic crate strapped to my hip, I was twenty, and the older volunteers watched me with a mix of pity and suspicion, as if youth were an excuse. Ysa was still alive then, the fierce woman who had signed the papers and started the Archive with a yard of shelving and a ledger salvaged from a closed school. She had taught me the rules: don’t pick an argument with a grieving father; always mark the time using a watch that never touches seawater; if you drop something and it breaks, that was always going to happen.

There are the official rules and the rules that carry a notch rubbed smooth by use. When the tide starts to go slack and the water lies like a breath held in the throat, you must stand still and lift your eyes. If you don’t, the sea will pry them up for you and show you something you cannot put down. When a woman from Far Mar walks into the Archive wearing black and salt-crusted shoes, do not offer her a chair unless you are prepared for her to sit in it for hours. If you find a child’s shoe with sand worn into the stitching at the heel, do not catalog it until you have eaten something and told a joke to someone you love.

This is the season of returning. The equinox has passed; the nights are hoarding minutes. The smell has shifted from sunburnt metal to kelp and something like the rind of an old lemon. Gulls drop mussels onto the slick black rock until they shatter and leave a halo of meat. Ayo mutters to himself as he works, all vowels and religion he believes in enough to argue with. He wears the same blue cap all season. It has a safety pin holding the back strap together. When he thinks I am not looking, he kisses it for luck, the silly man.

I spot the first good thing of the morning, good meaning something that will go in the small front room under glass rather than the rows behind the swinging doors, where I keep all the things that have not yet decided. It is a coppermusic tin the size of my palm. These tins are odd because they make no sound when you shake them and ring like coins when you swallow. I took the last one to the university, and they looked at me over the rims of their lenses and called it interesting, which is the word you use when you would rather be sure. I fish the tin out from under a fringe of foam. It has a nick on one edge, as if it has been opened by someone impatient and only just stopped in time. I can feel the small airless song it carries. Ysa used to call these a mercy.

I set the coppermusic prefacing everything else in my crate and begin to build around it: a length of fluted iron that might have been part of a bedframe, a cosmopolitan coin sealed away from any economy, a plastic comb with a line of beachgrass threaded through the spine like a forgotten crown. The inventory tags in my pocket are stiff with starch. I tear one free with my teeth to write: copper tin, etched, no lid, found widthwise to the tide, no visible seam. Beside me, Ayo holds up a pair of spectacles in triumph. The lenses are clouded with a mineral bloom that will never scrub clear. He looks at me over them, a comic professor, and then slips them into his bag with delicate reverence. He has a grandson who likes to put everything on his face. The Archive has learned not to call him out on small thefts that make the world kinder.

We are ankle-deep in salt when I see the sandal.

Not see: know. Some objects look back. This one looks through. A thong of worn leather, brown once, unbuckled, the buckler flattened into an oval as if a heavy machine parked on it. There is no pair. It lies the way a dropped thing lies—in the posture of having been held, and then not. The strap is embroidered with a row of tiny shells in the style that came from a market near our old apartment, where women in bright saris had sat on mattresses while men brought them long flat boxes tied with twine. They had shown you everything except the thing you had flown across a city and two buses to buy, so you would stay longer and describe the body of the person you loved and let them choose.

When I was nine, I watched my mother bend over a table under a blue light, a needle in her hand, threading shells onto a sandal. The shells were wrong, their holes drilled rough with a cheap bit. She had bought them from a vendor she did not trust, because the woman she was making the sandals for handed her a note with an address and a sum of money and said, from now on, the child will be measured in these. It is foolish to fall in love with these details when your life is about to rupture. It is not foolish at all; it is what saved me.

Under the rank of shells there is a charm—no, not a charm, a knotted thread the color of saffron and saffron’s smell, like floral hay and the fine dust of a saint’s hair. The kabbad’s thread. My mother tied it on when she crossed the threshold of any dwelling that was not ours. It was easier than refusing a person’s food. It gave the neighbors something to point to and say ah, then turn away.

The sea has no right to her shoe. She is not dead.

I almost hear myself say it out loud. The Strand’s voices pause. The gulls tilt their heads. Ayo glances over. I crouch so fast I splash my socks and lift the sandal free, trying, stupidly, to keep it from touching the water, as though that will make it less a part of the tide and more a thing from a closet we have yet to open.

“Inez?” Ayo’s question is not my name. It is Are you through? Are you steady enough to stand? I manage a nod that cannot possibly look like what I think it does.

The thread looks new. Even through the salt, I can tell it would stain a wrist if you pressed it. The shells knock softly against one another the way teeth do when you sleep with your mouth slightly open and dream of cold. I turn the sandal in my hands and, without meaning to, lift it to my face. The leather is warm.

It should not be warm.

Another wave moves up over my boots, and my hands reflex back against my chest. Something sharp pricks my thumb. It is a sliver of glass, caught where the sole separates from the footbed. The sole is not the original. It has been resoled twice, at least. My chest aches. The last time I held this shoe, the woman who wore it tapped the arch against the floor of the bus to shake out grit. The grit jumped like fleas of gold. She told me, without looking at me, that we were going to be poor in a way you could not explain at school. She confessed this to the window. Bus windows, you could trust. They were where you took your deals and your forgiveness.

I only have to tilt my palm and let the water touch the sandal to make it not mine to decide. I do not tilt. I slide it under the fold of my slicker, against my ribs. Wet leather kisses my side. I cannot tell if my heart speeds up or if I have started counting again and every number is the same.

The line groans, the groan a wooden ship language. Do they sense the breach? We all know the word for it, and how small and common it is. When Ysa caught a volunteer pocket a pendant once—an ugly thing, plastic, cloudy with scraped glitter and a smiling whale—she cuffed the woman awake with the flat of her hand. Not because it was a theft, but because it was foolish.

“Enough,” I say to myself, to the sea, to the history of being loved into cowardice. I pluck three more things quickly to blunt the shape of what I have done: the fork with the bent tines, two subway tokens zipped into a transparent bag like a specimen. One of the tokens is drilled and strung on black thread. I will write in the ledger later: two tokens, city of origin unknown; one adapted for necklace/luck. I glance once more at the water, because there is a superstition that if you take, you must look back, the way you would look at a house you are leaving.

A weight of bright catches the edge of my sight. A child, not the boy who sought a hat, tugs at his mother’s sleeve, pointing at a gleaming chain. It is a bicycle chain. He will want it with his whole, greedy, good heart, and his mother will tell him to wait until the lady says. It is its own sharpness, that children obey rules at the mouth of the sea.

By the time the tide slumps into itself and the first sunlight comes like something spilled and the gulls decide to be ordinary birds again, our crates are heavy and our shoulders hurt. The volunteers are not supposed to joke during the return, but we fracture anyway, laughing low about things that would be nothing if said slightly louder. “What does the sign say again?” Ayo asks, his voice gone rasped, and someone recites, “The Archive is a secular office and will not accept prayers,” and we all grin at the wording, because what we do all day is pray over objects and not expect God to stop us.

On the way up from the Strand, the official path is a switchback lined with new signage and native grasses the city planted and forgot. There are painted footprints telling you how to walk, one in front of the other. By summer, children will have peeled the footprints up at the corners and stuck them to their cheeks. The crates cut marks into our arms. The morning’s crowd drifts back to the bus stop and benches and the hopefulness of coffee. Some stay. They have the look of people who understand that waiting is the work.

The Archive is an old wharf office that acts like a body in winter and a mouth in spring, leaking in the places that matter. The sign on the door is hand-lettered, and you can tell because the second R in RETURNED is a different animal from the first. I turned my apartment out gradually until this place became that place and then the reverse. I can sleep upright in the bentwood chair behind the counter if I need to, with my feet propped on the parcel scale and my coat like a blanketing adjective. Ysa’s portrait hangs on the wall behind me. It is just a photocopy of a cutting from the local paper, her hair huge because that was what hair did then. She is squinting into the sun. A girl is beside her in the photograph that we know is me because Ysa wrote Me + Inez on the bottom with a violet pen that never dried out.

The lights hum with a sound like bees locked in a mason jar. The front room holds the glass cases for special things: the coppermusic tins, a tin badge from a club that closed before I was born, a handkerchief embroidered with a star chart that maps a sky that has not existed for a hundred and thirty-three years. People come in and put their hands on the glass and call me a curator, and I laugh because they mean putterer, tender, idiot, liar. They mean someone who will open a drawer and say, I think I know what you are.

Ayo hauls the crates onto the central table and unloads them with the reverence of a man who has learned not to skid a human soul across wood. Each item goes on an unbleached cotton cloth.
