We leave space between everything so they do not argue. I log the time on the wall clock, then on a watch face propped inside a teaspoon. The watch does not work. It never has. That way, it cannot betray me.

“Councilman Domen’s office called again,” Ayo says, like a person telling you their tooth has begun to ache in a new way. “He wants a tour for his donors on Saturday. ‘Heritage engagement,’ he said. ‘Story assets.’ I wrote it on the pad.”

“I saw it.” I had turned the pad over. There is a list on the back I do not want Ayo to see. It includes: new box of gloves, soft kind that do not squeak; camphor for drawer six; track down a woman named Zamina who left two months ago without her kettle. The list has: tell my aunt’s portrait that I am still here.

“You working the counter?” he asks. He always says it as if what he really means is, You going to remember to eat?

“Later,” I lie. My stomach is a small rude fist. I put on the white cotton gloves that never stay white and take up the copper tin. It feels like a withheld word. I write: Copper tin, etched with waveline design, lid absent; hum present but mild; found north of lamppost number three, 05:41. Then: Spectacles, steel wire frame, lenses mineralized; possible claim by N—? (ask Ayo’s grandson). The Archive makes me precise in ways nothing else ever has. When you have nothing that is certain, you take certainty where you can.

When I reach the sandal, my hands confuse themselves. I do not put on the gloves to touch it. My ungloved fingers find the welted seam and the stitched-on shells and the thread that is not thread but the tightness of survival made visible. There is grit lodged between the sole and the upper, and I pry it loose with the scribe we use for writing in damp. It is not grit. It is a shard of brown glass with letters on it: DARJEELING SOME SUCH. My mother loved tea like everyone who had to love something you could buy in a shop and make with water you did not own. When we first moved into her apartment with the walls that flaked when you laughed, she kept her tea in a jar with an elastic band around the middle and a label that said “DON’T BE A THIEF.” Now a piece of that kind of jar is in my hand, washed unreadable.

I should catalog it under G: glass. I should put it down and write: Sandal, size unknown, brown leather, saffron thread, damage to sole; probable early twenty-first-century manufacture. Instead, I slip my scribed thumb under the edge of the strap and lift it, cat quiet. The lining gives slightly. A paper peels away as if shedding. Under the strap, where the leather once lifted before the cobbler stitched it back, my mother has left a folded strip the size of my little finger. It has stayed because the place was made for it.

My name is written there in her handwriting: not cursive but that half-loose print she had, each letter a little tipped, as if she had written their names when they were already a little drunk. INEZ, it says. Under that, a line: Third step.

I look up, dizzy with recognizing something I have never seen. Ayo is making tea on the hot plate, which is a spitting beast. “Do you want—” he starts, and stops, as if the air between us has changed density. “What is it?”

I cannot tell him. Not because he would go to Domen with it or because it breaks a rule. Ayo knows what rules we are allowed to break. I cannot tell him because to put it in his mouth would make a taste, and once he tasted it, he would perch there on the edge of my past and fall or forget to jump. “A note,” I say, which is both generous and untrue. “Somebody wrote a note.”

He brings me tea anyway, in a chipped mug that says CITY HALL in navy letters with the A smudged into a blunt triangle. There is sugar, but he does not add it, because he has stopped trying to sweeten things for me before I ask.

Third step. There were twelve stone steps from the street into our building, because it was built when people had legs like boats. There were three steps up into the room we called the kitchen. The third step in my mother’s care was a kind of roof—the place where she taped under the lip, out of sight, rent money, an extra key, the list of women who would take you in if the night came too fast. Third step. Third step, that she had to write to me as if she might not ever have the chance to tell me with her mouth.

“You all right?” Ayo means the kind of all right you have to scan for with a device. He means, on a scale of one to broken, where do we put you now?

“Spell out the tea,” I say. “If you drink it, it makes letters on your tongue.” The joke is small and unworthy. He laughs the way you laugh when someone hands you rope in a flood, because rope is smaller than a boat and sometimes it is enough.

The bell on the door rattles. A woman enters, trailing wind. She holds herself like a promise someone else has made to her. “Am I in the right place?” she asks, which is what we all are asking, just with different nouns.

I smooth my face into the expression Ysa practiced in the mirror when she first took me in and our grief made our faces undomesticated. “Welcome,” I say. “Yes. Please tell me your name.”

“Zamina,” she says. My list shifts over in my head. She is the one with the kettle. I write her name down, the Z like the beginning of a lightning metaphor and the rest of it like rain. “What can we help you claim?”

“Oh,” she says. She steps toward the table as if the things on it are sleeping animals and she will not spook them. “Not claim. I came to return something. It’s been on my shelf for weeks and I think it is making me dream somebody else’s life.”

She opens her tote bag and pulls out a small ceramic bird with a crack along the wing that is mended with gold. It is a common thing, the bird. They return in flocks and none of them are alike. You set them on a windowsill and they stare out at the day, polite with their beaks closed. They stay warm in cold rooms. If you wake in the night and forget your name, and touch one, it will tell you something true in your language. If it is not your bird, it will tell you something true that you cannot stand.

“It told me,” says Zamina, “it told me the first lie my husband told me, which is a long way back. It told me the rhythm of it, and after that I cannot not hear it. I would prefer to be permitted to forget.”

We are not a forgetting office, either. It is not written on the sign only because there was not enough tape. I reach for the bird and my fingers pass close to the sandals. The paper with my name on it burns unburning under the strap. Third step. Third step. I nod, keeping my head on my neck. “We’ll take it,” I say to Zamina. “We’ll find the right window for it.”

She exhales. That is most of what I give, here. I let people exhale while I count.

After we have closed for lunch and Ayo has gone to fetch us two rolls he will make me split and a wedge of cheese that tastes like lake water, I lock the front door and take the sandal, dishonorable as a thief, through the swinging doors into the back room. This is where the drawers are. Each is labeled in my hand on the fading blue tape Ysa liked because it made everything look like the kind of nautical that gets printed on sheets. Bone. Glass. Cloth. Wood. Unknown. Unknown, Not to Be Touched by Children or the Mayor. Unknown, Domestic.

My mother’s shoe goes in no drawer. I set it in the middle of the work table and stand over it like a spell.

“Third step,” I say, to the lightbulb and the errant breeze that wriggles under the door and the sea pressing itself against the window as if curious. “Third step, and you don’t write a second instruction. Did you think I would know what to do with that? Did you think I would be the same person who knew where the bobby pins were?”

The shoe is still warm.

I take the paper fully from under the strap. On the back there is something I could not see before, ink that the damp has made shy. When I lift it toward the light, pale letters float up. 27 Broadwater. Back stairs. The O in “Broadwater” is a heart that has been corrected into a circle by a second pass of the pen. My mother’s need to neaten, even in the middle of hiding, even in the middle of what I know now was departure.

27 Broadwater is a place. It is a building three blocks south of the market where a woman once handed me a spoon and told me there was no reason for a sorrow that did not cook. It is a place where the steps will have been measured by legs that are not mine. It is where my mother meant me to go when she could not tell me how. It is either nothing or it is a map, and maps keep their own time.

I slide the note back under the strap. I do not want to, but I do. The Archive is a secular office and will not accept prayers. If you are going to leave, you leave with what was found.

Outside, the sea ticks and tocks and resets its watches. I press the sandal against my ribs again under my coat like a small, compliant animal. The back door that opens to the alley sticks when it rains, which is a particular cruelty in this season. I hip it loose and spill into the brightness. Above me, a string of laundry shivers. Someone has hung a line of shirts like stolen flags, everything moving, everything saying enough.

27 Broadwater is brown brick with the roofline of a grin and two windows that look like somebody closed their eyes and left them there. The back stairs are metal and slanted and could be climbed by a cat just by thinking it. There are weeds in the cracks of the step-pans, weeds so green they look impudent. The third step has a strip of duct tape folded double and stuck under the lip. I reach under with two fingers, held like tongs, and pry. Something unsticks with a sound like a word you should not say in front of a child.

Inside is a key. It is a key I know. It is the key to the room we left when we left everything, the key that my mother pressed into my hand the day she told me I could not sleep, not yet, we had to wait for the neighbors to turn off their radio so we could hear which of our names the building would call. It is a small key with a scalloped edge and a single good tooth, and on the metal is stamped a number that does not correspond to any lock in this city’s memory. It is a key to back doors and to rooms that smell like people who never discovered bleach. It is my mother’s joke and warning and making sure.

I put it on my tongue. It tastes like old pennies and rain. If this were a story with mercy, the key would go into a lock within the hour and turn.

A gull screams from a rooftop like a woman being fed good news she does not trust. The world goes on: a bus whines and shifts gears, someone shouts “Don’t forget the pie!” in a voice that is the same in all languages. I close my fist around the key and stand with my back to the building and look up at a sky that is thinking about being blue.

“Okay,” I say to the wall, to chance, to what comes when called and what comes when it is ready. “Okay, Mother. We can do this together. Or I can do it now without you. The tide is in. It will go out. There will be more clocks.”

Back at the Archive, the bell rings of its own accord. Sometimes it does that when the heat changes or when a person we used to know comes to stand on the other side of the door and change their mind. Ayo is behind the counter drinking his tea and scribbling a note to his grandson on the back of a receipt. It says: tell the boy the glasses work better if you pretend.

“You went out,” he says mildly. He knows where. Of course he does. He is a man built of well-placed guesses. “You came back.”

“For now,” I say. The key in my pocket is a small, honest weight, the weight of a single letter spelled correctly, the way a life can be corrected by a second pass of the pen.

The day proceeds. People walk in with hands open and leave with their fingers closed around nothing but air and a length of red twine, the kind I keep beside the register that makes a knot mean something. Zamina returns at four to say that her kitchen is quieter without the bird. A child loses his tooth in the sugar jar I keep for the tea and holds it up like a pearl. The tide turns out; the gulls go crooked on the wind; the clocks begin to pucker their mouths.

And in the middle of it, behind the glass of the front case, the copper tin hums until the hum becomes a tone low enough to be a floor you cannot see. A man walking past hears it and pauses, one hand to his pocket where a watch ought to be. He will think it is a truck downshifting. He will forget it. He will dream tonight of stepping onto a stair that is not there and catching himself. He will call himself foolish when he cannot hold a fork without seeing a comb in his hand.

The sandal warms. I do not write that on any card. It is a detail that is only mine and my mother’s, and maybe the sea’s. The afternoon smells of lemon cleaner and kelp and the lemon hangs like a trick. Men in suits will come Saturday and call what we do an asset, and I will smile the way Ysa taught me to. And later, under the metal breath of the back stairs, I will put a key into a door that will open or not, and I will remember how it feels to hear a lock say yes.

In a town that measured wealth by the weight of glass on its shelves, I kept my money in sunlight.

The shutters were half-closed to keep the heat from laying its full hand on my jars, but there was always a seam, a slow gold blade that cut the dust and lay lengthwise along the rows. The light moved across each jar as the day lengthened, and I could tell time better from the way September’s jars lost their marrow of blue than by any clock.

We called it the rain bank, though the county register still had me down as miscellaneous retail, subcategory: curios. The sign outside said Romo Rain, but the old women who never learned the letters said, with their hands, the place where the girl mixed weather. Everyone else said Inez’s. Children were not allowed inside without one of us, and even then they were taught to breathe only in the upper half of their lungs, to keep their breath from shaking the shelves. A dropped jar is not the same as a spilled coin. It can be mopped. It can be forgiven. But the sound it makes is a sentence.

Rain has taste. People think I say that to put a price on what should never be priced, but they don’t hear what I hear. When I put a drop of October on my tongue, I know whether the wind came across the sugar factory or over the char of last year’s fires in the hills. First rains after a long drought bring up the smell of everything that happened while we were waiting: thorn, powdered brake, creosote shrugging off its dust. High-desert storms sit butter-fat on the palate. Fog rain has no edges. Rain from the prison yard carries a whisper of ammonia and hand soap. I have a mouthful of maps and a ledger that could drown a person if they leaned too long over its pages, all that handwriting, all those dates.

I was rinsing the sand out of a row of dropper tips in a gallon of old fog — people bring me their broken jars’ remnants, and I keep a poor man’s bin of cleansing rain — when the bell over the door wrote a line in the air. The bell is tin and flat and sharp as a surprised sparrow, and though I had propped an umbrella of cloth over it to tamp the sound, it still made that certain brief confession any metal makes when it knows it is being struck because it is the only one who can be struck.

He stood just inside the door until his eyes found their way in. Children do that; men who spend their days outdoors do not bother. He was neither and both. Thin like something had already been taken from him, hair that hadn’t yet decided to be recalcitrant or obedient, a clean shirt with a dark circle deepening beneath one arm. He had wrapped his right hand in waxed cloth, not from any injury. He held it like one holds a baby or a bomb.

“You’re late,” I said, though I hadn’t been expecting anyone. It is an old shopkeeper’s ploy to skip over “hello” and take a person into the sentence after their guilt. I could tell from the quick lift of his chin he had had an aunt who loved him once and scolded him enough to make him proud.

He came forward two steps and held out the bundle. A bit of grit in the cloth whispered as he shifted it. He did not put it down. It is a test. The hands will tell you whether a person has come to buy or to pretend.

“You the rainsmith,” he said, and there was the north flats in his mouth, the way their Spanish stays lower and makes friends with the vowels. His voice stuck to the room like the first damp.

“My mother was the rainsmith. I keep the ledger and I mind the jars.” My hands were wet to the wrists. I could feel the cooler’s breath wrenching at the drip from my elbow. “What have you brought me?”

His left hand worked at a fold in the cloth. He was not laughing but he had that treason of a smile people get in my shop when the memory of the first time someone let them taste their own first rain came back through their teeth. He unwound the cloth, slowly, and set the jar on the counter between us.

I knew it was wrong the moment the light hit it. Not wrong like a forgery — we get those, men who bake gravel with a piece of copper pipe to make something taste old — but wrong like music that has lost a note and keeps going as if we have all agreed not to notice. The jar was my jars’ shape, a mouth wide enough for a woman’s thumb, shoulders like a bird’s chest, glass thick with the littlest green the old bottles have. The wax at the rim was my wax, the particular wrong color of berries boiled in the same pot I use for tortas, because the wax is the last thing we make in this town and it gives itself to anything that will hold it. The stamp was my stamp: a moth, wings like a wet dress clinging to the shy of a woman’s hips.

It wasn’t the stamps or the glass or the competent way the wax had been turned. It was the label. In my mother’s hand, labels were slow and made of breath; in mine, quicker, the g’s fat-bellied, the s’s leaning into whatever came next. The label on that jar was mine. The ink was the watery black I make when I’m careful and the girls from the school are watching. I knew that because my hand went looking for the shape of a mistake it had made — that extra tremor in the z of my name — and found it there.

INEZ ROMO — 14 APRIL

The year, if it was written, had been pinched under the tape. The tape, a lovely perverse thing, coiled like the skin of a kettle burned dry. I looked at the calendar on the wall by the door so my face would not show my search for a paper I did not remember writing. The calendar still had my father’s club’s logo, though the club had been gone thirteen years. The month was March. The family of green squares had its fat child around the fifteenth, where someone had drawn, in a hand not mine, a little ear.

I leaned in enough for the water to speak if it wanted to. Sometimes it does, without a taste, through the glass. Altitude is a tone. I put my ear close enough to fog my own stamp. I felt the hair go up along my arms. The jar was cold.

It is never cold in my shop unless I beg the cooler to take pity. The coldness was not the kind that comes from a machine. It is a rare thing to be able to point to an absence and call it a weight, but that is what this cold was. It settled on the counter. It found my bones and lay along them like a mother who has come in the last hour and cannot turn back the bed for fear of waking the debt.

“Where did you get this,” I asked, my voice lower than before, and I did not put a question mark at the end of it. He watched my mouth when I spoke, a thing people do when they have lived too often with lies and need to be sure which way the words go.

“We found it in a house.” He lifted his chin toward the east and the empty where the river used to run. “Down by the canal. It was under a sink, behind the rust pan. It was wrapped like that. My uncle said bring it to you. He said it looked like money.”

“Was your uncle born in this town,” I asked.

“Him and my mother were born where the flood made a bend,” he said, and not everyone remembers there was a bend. He needed me to believe him.

“You didn’t open it.”

“No.” He took his hand away from the mouth of the jar. The cloth left a faint meniscus on the glass. “We don’t drink from jars with names we know.”

He had a kindness I had not expected. I was terrible suddenly with the wish to ask him what he had called rain as a child, when his grandmother had pointed to the haze that isn’t a cloud and said, look, it’s thinking of us. I could not. There was a jar on my counter with my name’s breath on it and a date whose morning had not yet dissolved in tea.

There are rules. The rules are very fine-voiced in this valley, and they live in people who would swear they are godless and loud. You do not open a jar that isn’t yours unless you are the rainsmith and you have written the reason in the ledger and the person whose name is on the glass has consented and has a witness who is alive. You do not taste while angry. You do not sell smart rain for idiot uses. You do not tell men what you have tasted in their weather unless they ask twice with their hands open. You do not toss out a jar that has a name. There are more. When I was a child, my mother made me say them like prayers, and then as jokes, and then not say them at all, because the town knows what to do with its weather better than a girl brought up on syllables.

The ledger sat under the counter, the way my mother put it, because the ledger belongs where dark keeps it honest. I stared at the jar instead. The wax had been turned by someone who knew to dampen their fingers. There were no stray threads of wick, no thumbprint in the red. The moth in the wax had landed tilted. That was mine, that tilt. The date. Fourteen April. It had the sound in it already of someone saying it, six weeks from now, in a hurry.

“I can tell you what you have,” I said, and I used the voice I use when I am trying to save a person from buying two ounces of December for their child’s fever, when we both know that if I sell it, and the fever breaks, they will bring me a chicken and the chicken will lay small eggs that taste of closeness and loss. “But not yet. Leave it.”

He took an involuntary step back, the way a person does when asked to undress in a room with a window. “We brought it for you.”

“For me?” I said, and my mouth, traitor, turned the words toward the easy path, toward please take it away.

He cleared his throat. “Señora Altagracia said to tell you you put it aside.”

Altagracia had been dead two summers.

There are sounds glass makes when it is moved by a hand and there are sounds it makes when it shifts by itself. My jars are like a choir who will sing to the wrong music if any bossy woman in a pretty scarf comes in and coughs. I do not allow coughing in my shop. Even so, every so often the lower shelves decide they are river rocks and lean into one another and make that small, quick, trapped sound of something changing its idea and not wanting to be caught at it. While he stood there with his dead woman’s message and my label in my face, the shelf to my left flexed and put its shoulder under a jar from July of the year the sky had made a choice about us. The jars there are all shorter, they had been filled from dishpans when the clouds dropped by accident after the commissioners said they could not. That shelf edged its wood forward and the jars gave a small, high sound as if they were clearing their throats.

“I can tell you what you have,” I said again, to the room, to my own hand, which had begun to sweat and print itself into the wax. “But it will cost you. Not money. Don’t look like that. It will cost you whether or not you open your pocket. That’s the kind of cost this is.”

I took the jar toward me three inches. He did not stop me. He put his hands in his back pockets and watched my shoulder. “We thought,” he said, his voice finally letting the worry in, “we thought maybe it has the first rain from—” He did not want to say the name of the boy who had died in the pit that January. He looked at the floor. “From that day. My aunt said maybe it should be taken to the church.”

The moth in the wax was so precise, its junior wing almost free of the stamp, that for a moment I could not remember if I had stamped it myself and forgotten, or dreamed of stamping it so often — hundreds of jars — that dreaming had worked itself into the matter. My tongue pressed the roof of my mouth. “It is not from any day you remember,” I said finally. “The stamp is mine. The hand that cut this string was mine.” The cold had moved through the counter into my belly. It was not a good cold; it was a promise made by someone who had never had to redeem such things on a morning when clocks forgot the difference between minutes.

“What is it, then?” He took his hands out of his pockets. He was ready to run and he was ready to stay in the same body at the same time, and there is nothing sadder.

I went to get a needle.

My mother used sewing needles for breaking wax. I like the thin filaments from the stripped wires people use to strengthen fence, because they are hard to see and they sing when you pluck them. I plucked one to make it sing and it made no sound. The cooler shuddered when I pulled at it, as if the air was water and some fish below the surface had turned in its sleep. My hand wanted to get it wrong. It rose toward the mark on the label where the date had been pinched under the tape. It rose toward my own name. I set my hand down and picked it up again.

“In the ledger,” I said, to say a thing out loud people think you intend to do it, and their belief holds your spine up, “I’ll write that I opened in extremis.”

“What is that,” he asked, but softly, as if the word might break.

“It means the whole town’s throat is in the same hand as mine.” I breathed out. “It’s one of our excuses.”

The wire found the seam between wax and glass. Wax is stubborn until it isn’t. The first time a needle slips in, the whole world remembers it has a seam. The line opened with a tired softness. I could smell my own stamp as it gave up its oil. Under the wax, a square of cloth. My mother always used cheesecloth, bleached with a lemon under the sun until it was the color of something that never made a choice. This cloth was darker, like the rag my father kept for checking oil, always a little black no matter how hot the sun. I turned the mouth of the jar to the light. I had that small dizziness you get when you look down from a height and remember your feet are traitors.

I lifted the cloth. The top of the water was as clear as any answer. It did not have the small slick some rains get when they have listened too long at metals. It had no skin. It held a sullen stillness, the way water in pipes holds itself back from its own weight. When I moved, the water did not move. It had that old river trick: its surface made me go away, and then made me again, less.

I put the jar to my mouth.

There are drips I let fall first, for luck; there are drops I catch with my nail and bring to my lip as if we are two shy people touching for the first time. There are tastes I take and then spit because the mouth goes numb and you must not let yourself be anything but a mouth when that happens. I did none of this. I put my mouth to the glass and took the barest shine of a sip. The water hit my tongue like a word I had been taught never to say in front of my father, and my father was sitting at the kitchen table.

Ozone is too common a word for that taste. There was iron in it the way the first time you smell your own blood is iron, not meat. There was the green of a date palm cut at the wrong hour. There was a sweetness like nothing exploded in a barrel behind a mechanics’ shop and everything exploded if we looked at it that way. There was a cracked leather, a dog’s ear. There was the aftertaste of a laugh someone tried to swallow. There was—no, I say I do not trade in the dead—but there was a body in it, a particular boy’s and not the one from the pit and for his mother I will not write his name here for you, she deserves her own loss and not my version of it.

More than that, away under and hidden where the tongue cannot reasonably have nerves, there was the throat of a thing getting ready to open.

When I pulled the jar away, the room took a breath so fast my ears rang. My eyes were watering. The boy—he still had not told me his name—had stepped back without moving. The edge of the counter had turned into a ledge he was balancing on. The small hair on the backs of his hands was trying to remember another animal. The shelf to my left made that shift again. The cooler coughed. Something tiny and glass gave up and fell and did not break but landed on its side and rolled three shelves down like a cricket running from the dark.

“You don’t sell that,” I said to myself, to my mother, to the ledger, to the forty-six jars of August I had stored high in the backhouse to keep them from the fingers of children with dreams. “You don’t put a price on that.” I put the cloth back. The cloth slid into place as if it had a maker’s mark.

“What is it,” he asked again, and I could hear now that he was past polite and moving toward the place men go when their sister is not speaking and you need to tell them something that will make them forgive the weather for being indifferent to love.

“It’s rain that hasn’t fallen yet,” I said, and the words were too big in my mouth the way a baby feels when you lift it and it decides to be air for a minute and then goes heavy without telling you. “It has my label because I put it there. It has the date because… because that is the day it will fall. Or would have, I don’t know. Sometimes the world is incorrect and gives itself a chance to change its mind.”

He laughed once and it sounded like a man stepping through brush in a suit he borrowed. “That doesn’t make sense.”

“Correct,” I said. “It does not.”

“Who sent it?”

“You did,” I said, because sometimes the straightest line is the knife you have to put through the joke, and because I was already tired of being careful, and because it was true. Not him; him older, his hair more decided; his mouth at the corner bitter. He had brought it because I had asked him to, and I had asked him to because my mother had once told me, when you run out of miracles you have to use the ones that have you in them.

We stood like that for a time the length of a light ray moving across a jar. The dust sank. My tongue tasted itself and found it strange. Outside, a truck went by very slowly, the driver counting the houses. Beyond that, further than the river, further even than the old flood lens that turns summers into the inside of a tin, the sky had been trying to decide itself all morning. Now it took a stance. A bruise rose on the horizon. Not a cloud, not at first. A thickening. The old men at the domino table across the street, if they had been there instead of home waiting for their wives to find what there was to cook, would have stood up with their hands at their backs and watched very carefully. It is not the color that tells you what the sky intends; it is the way it pulls at its own borders.

I put the jar down very gently, the way you put down a sleeping child when you know the floor is not to be trusted. “Go home,” I said.

“To my uncle’s?”

“To whichever woman fed you this morning,” I said, and he started, and his hand went to his pocket because the only obvious thing I had told him all morning had been the thing I should not have known. “Tell her to bring whatever jars she has, the ones with the tape that is giving up, the ones with other people’s names. Tell her today I’ll take them without asking whose rain it is. Tell her to be fast but not to breathe hard. Tell her if she runs one will break.”

“What about—” He nodded at the jar. He swallowed and his throat worked like rope. “What about the rain you said.”

“I will keep it where only the ledger can see it,” I said. “I will taste it again when I am not angry. And then I will ask it what it knows of me.”

He was halfway out the door when he turned and said, because he wanted to leave the room with something he could hold, “My name’s Javier.” He was waiting for me to give him mine though he knew it as well as any man knows the name of the thing he thinks will save his mother.

“Inez,” I said, though I had been tasted by that name across the counter my whole life. “Run, Javier, but walk.”

He nodded as if I had told him a secret, and then he was gone into the light, which had gone thin.

The wind that came after him into my shop was no wind any of my jars had ever held. It smelled of white cloth hung on a line and then never brought in. It smelled of hot copper. It smelled of what the first cactus smells when it realizes it is full of water and someone without the nerve for knives is still going to live.

I wrote in the ledger: Opened the jar with my own label dated 14 April. Immediate taste of ozone, iron, salt not ours, oil house, fruit tree sap, riverbed sigh. Body. No measurable altitude. Cold. Not anything. Felt known. Extremis.

The moth in the wax cast a tiny shadow on the counter even though the light had moved. Outside, as if taking the jar’s side in some argument I did not remember starting, the sky gathered itself together and said my name in a voice no one else could hear. Then it said everyone’s, all at once.

The day arrives folded small as a paper bird, slipped through the gap under my door where the wood is chewed by winter. The hallway smells like the noodle shop downstairs, broth and clove and a clean seam of steam. It is early enough that the windows across the alley still wear sleep, and when I bend to pick up the day, it is warm against my palm. Someone has walked fast to get it here. Someone didn’t want to be seen.

I sit at the workbench under the skinned lightbulb and set the day on the wool cloth. The paper is good stock, not the bureau’s pale green but the thick kind you buy in calligraphy shops for confessions and vows. They have folded it the way my mother taught me to fold receipts, into a crane whose beak will not tear until you ask it to. The edges sweat a little, as if the day is nervous, or as if it knows something about what was bent into it. I know better than to love the object; it won’t be an object for long. But I like the way the crease around the eye has memory.

The city wakes like it’s embarrassed, noise muffled by fog, a broom on wet stones, the first line of a song. My fingers tilt. The crane stares back at me with the cartoon patience all small folded things have—the patience of trapped time, which can outwait anything. I crack the beak and thin air hisses from the fold, carrying a smell that unhooks my breath: salt, and the ghost of oranges.

I lean back. There is no sea here. Not for two hundred miles in any direction. The only time I smelled salt like that was the day cheap soap ran out in the bathhouse and old Mr. Huang poured a scoop of pickling brine into the water and we all pretended we were at the coast. The city has names for the river it lost and stories about the port it deserved, but those are games we play to teach children desire. You don’t expect a day to lie to your face.

There is a note tucked into the wings, skinny, folded around itself three times, as if privacy could be a matter of geometry. No name, no mark, just the pencil letters thin enough to have been written on a knee: a debt returns to you.

I let my finger rest on the sentence. When you deal with days, sentences like that get written at you. People want to believe that time can be balanced like a ledger, that the days you sell will make a house somewhere, that the days you take will learn to be gracious. They want to believe the bureau will keep them honest and the laws will keep them safe and the conscience will keep them upright. It isn’t true. Nothing keeps anything where it belongs. Not even the paper it came on.

I uncrease the crane and lay the sheet flat and smooth and turn it. In the middle there’s the signature swirl from the spiral press that fixes a day inside the sheet, a faint iridescence that looks like oil in a puddle. I hold it under the bulb, tilt, tilt again. The colors move. I imagine an ocean rain and my throat fills. If this is a day I knew once, if this is a debt that belongs to me, I should be able to find my name in it. We leave fingerprints in days we live. If you know where to look, you see the whorl.

Mrs. Ku taps the ceiling with a broom handle from below. She’s been my landlord for eight years and she bangs when she wants something and only knocks when she wants money. I call down "What is it?" and she calls up "Soup," which is love in this building, and "Cilantro or no," which is religion. I yell "Yes, and lots." I will tell her later that I answered incorrectly.

The big copper bowl in the corner is as old as my grandfather’s stories and would have been worth more than the shop if he hadn’t punched a perfect half–moons’ worth of dents around the rim by christening it with a hammer the day I opened. He said, now time can’t see itself. He was Pashto and musical and believed in tricks. I fill the bowl from the kettle, the water just under boiling. The steam reaches for me like something that has been waiting and I set the sheet, face down, oil-slick swirl touching the meniscus. The paper goes pliant and heavy. I count under my breath, because if you are not counting, time will count for you.

One hippopotamus; two hippopotamus; three hippopotamus.

The swirl unspools like it remembers how. The day leaves the page and arranges itself across the water’s surface, not visible as light but as a tremor under the skin of things. When the shimmer stabilizes I lean and breathe in it. There are rules, and I follow most. Don’t enter a day that’s been sharpened to take you with it. Don’t stitch a day into yourself if you’re running a fever or a war. Don’t do more than one a day, unless the second one belongs to someone you love. Don’t charge someone who is paying you in grief. Do not ever enter the first day a person no longer believed in the body, because you will bring it back with you where it will make a home. I break some rules. Not that one.

Breathing a day is like sharing a secret with a blackbird. It is not your language and it is not your throat. Some of it sits in your lungs and watches your ribs thicken and some of it darts past the gag reflex and leaves a ring of heat like you have swallowed a coin.

There is wind in the day. Cool, steady. The taste is bright. There’s the sound of shoes, a scatter of kids, the hint of a market—the specific metallic chime of carts being dragged over stone. Somebody yelling Hey. Someone else laughing from their chest, not their mouth. That laughter. The smell is oranges, yes, but also old rope, wet wood. No river has wood like that, like the bones of a dock. No river in this city. My heart does the ugly thing it does when something you thought was fact lifts up and floats two inches above the table. Then there is a note—a long one—from an instrument I don’t know but want to know. The day flares.

Then, so fast it feels like theft, it closes.

The paper in the bowl turns gray, then white again, empty as a starved plate. Water stills. The room tilts back onto its hinges. The idea that it was mine tilts with it.

A debt returns to you.

If someone is returning my day to me, it means they took it. If someone took a day from me, it means I had it to begin with. It isn’t as simple as that. Nothing keeps anything where it belongs. But the thought, even in the cheap sandals of the morning, walks well.

I set the paper to dry and pour the water into one of the copper channels that lead to the sink. Somewhere I have a bottle with a screw top where I keep the sediment of days I don’t know what to do with. There is money in that bottle, if someone ever learns how to coax it into language. We all have cabinets like that. My grandfather’s cabinet was birds.

He built cages so beautiful even the birds who had been born inside didn’t know they were in jail. He let them free for an hour each day and he named them after people he loved. When he died we opened the doors and a few of the birds just sat there and then died along with him. Some creditors are loyal like that. Some go to the sea.

"What is all that?" Mrs. Ku says, because she is in the doorway with a bowl and even her bony kill-you-later shoulders are kind. I don’t know why I don’t hear her come up the stairs. She moves like good news, silently and all at once.

"Tea," I say. "Steam. The weather visiting."

"You smell like an argument." She sets the bowl down and shakes her head at my room, the way she does every time. She thinks I own too many jars and too few chairs. She thinks the copper bowl will be my ruin. She thinks if she doesn’t look at the orange thread tied around the knob to the back cupboard, the stories in there won’t climb out. She has seen me come home wobbly with other people’s days and the only thing she’s ever said about it is "You short people want too much." I am not short, but the comment is love.

She leans over the bowl, then shifts her face away quickly, as if the steam is rude. "Ah," she says. "Your mother."

I bristle like a cheap brush. "No," I say, and then realize that she means the smell. "The oranges."

"She used to stand at the corner and buy them even if they were sour, even if it was rain and the man wrapped them up like shame." She pauses. "Your shoes are wet."

"My shoes are always wet."

"Tear the cilantro," she says, and I do. The soup is good enough to invite sin. "Master Chen is asking for you," she adds, as if it were dessert. "He says bring your honest face, not your buyer’s face."

"Is he selling?"

"Buying."

"Impossible."

She shrugs. "That is what he whispered. If a tiger whispers it is only because the forest is crowded."

She goes. The bowl radiates all the feelings a bowl can radiate. On the wall, the little clock that runs on my thumbprint ticks just out of pace with the big clock that runs on the city’s hydro. The small one is more accurate. Accuracy is no use; what matters is whether a thing agrees. The day lies like a divination on the towel, a faint shine left where it lay. The note darkens as it dries. A debt returns to you. There is no signature to hold.

I don’t have a buyer’s face. I have three faces: the face that gets me noodles in a storm, the face that makes people want to confess kindness they haven't done yet, and the face that makes men decide I’m not the kind of trouble they’d hoped for. I put on the middle one. I pin my hair into something a comb would recognize. On my way out, I touch the bottom edge of the cupboard in the back, where the orange thread is tied. My fingers find the knot the way they find prayer. It pulses.

The street is the soft weather of early summer, the kind that is all exhale. The shops unscroll. The woman who sells belts unhooks sunshine from her awning and shakes it out. The alley by the pawnshop hosts a cat that looks like it has forgiven its last five lives and will not forgive the sixth. Boys play an invented game with stones and chalk and the fluid arithmetic of bodies that go where they haven’t been allowed. A bus coughs up old men.

I walk east toward the water that is not there and on the way I pass the exchange and look anywhere but at its door. The exchange is an old bank with its windows polished until the air is a mirror and its letters carved deep enough to draw blood. Inside, the people who buy days and sell days perform concern for one another in a choreography no one rehearsed. There is a woman whose job it is to make tea for remorse. There is a man they keep on a stool near the front who looks so ordinary you think you must have met him on the street and you will be safe; he arrests you without standing. The bureau has its offices upstairs. I have a license the way a bird has a leash.

Master Chen stands outside his shop with his head halfway tilted like he’s listening to the ground. He is a small man held together by relish and rage and his wrists are always wrapped in stained rags to keep his skill warm. He fixes broken instruments, which is to say he is god for sound and devil to silence. When he smiles his gold tooth looks like a coin he intends to spend twice.

"Little Sera," he says. "Your hair is a nest. If you lived in it I could sell tickets. Your face, however, is correct. Come."

His shop is a forest of necks. Fiddles hang like birds killed and dried and made perfect again by hunger. A pale man with hands so thin you could see a fugitive thought traveling through them sits in the corner, his hat in his lap, as if he has been told if he shifts he will lose the last animal that comes when he whistles. He lifts his head when we enter and his eyes are that specific gray you get after you have pulled a boat ashore by yourself in the rain. His suit is beautiful. His shoes are not.

"This is Sera," Chen says, and he says my name in the old accent, the one that makes it taste like a medicine. "Sera deals in days. Sera eats fools and excretes advantage. Sera can tell you what you’re buying, and what you’re selling, and why your bones creak when the wind is southerly. Sera owes me money for a broken window."

"I paid you for that window."

"Not the spiritual cost."

The man smiles like a cello. When he stands he brings a bow with him, as if his hand can’t remember how to stop, and then shakes mine, warm and dry. His skin smells faintly of rosin and coffee. "Celestino Duarte," he says. "Tino. I used to be the first chair at the Municipal until I was not and then I was a studio donkey until I was not and now I am nobody until I am something again. I hear you can find things inside of time."

"I can find things inside of days," I say. "Time is ambitious."

"Days, then," he says, as if days are a reasonable compromise.

He takes something from the inner pocket of his jacket and unwraps it from felt. It is another crane, but the abusive work of one of the bureau clerks—office paper, bureau stamp, no gentleness. It has been folded and unfolded many times the way addicts fold things when they want to keep their hands from praying. He lays it in my palm and what should surprise me is that it hums like the last part of a note. What surprises me is that it smells like soup, but not soup anyone who has ever lived poor would eat. Stock. A chorus line of bones.

"I bought this from a man who said it was the day after my son was born," he says, and then waits, perhaps to see if I will tell him something true. I can hear the reverence he has in the word son and the careful distance in the word man. He is holding himself like a violin so he won’t crack.

"I take it you remember the day your son was born," I say.

"I remember the hospital and my wife’s hand and the way the rain tried to come through the glass," he says, and his eyes go far off and then return like they paid the toll. "I remember the nurse who looked like a child and the way the doctor kept saying nearly and I remember the way something in me split like a string when the room went quiet and then the way that same split cord bound me when he cried. But I…" He breathes out and when he does you can hear the note in it. "I sold too many days, Sera. When we were young and had no money and thought life was long like a road and not short and vertical like a well. I sold days around his birth, thinking days were days, that they were adjacent, that if you hugged the days around something holy close to you it could not be stolen. We needed a refrigerator. We needed to pay rent. I tried to keep the exact day. I did. But poor men trying to be fathers do not get to keep exact things for long. I am now greedy to hear my wife laugh the way she laughed that day. There is no other day with that laugh."

"And you think this is it?" I ask, to hear what he will say.

He looks like a man standing in front of a house he grew up in that no longer exists. "I don’t know what it is," he says. "But when I breathe it, I feel the floor tilt the way it tilts in a room where a child is new. The man who sold it to me is gone. I went to his apartment and there was a mattress and a fan and a shoe and two roaches discussing jurisprudence. The building manager told me the bureau took him in for registration irregularities. That could mean a thousand things. Or nothing. I don’t want to take this to the exchange because I don’t want them to laugh me out of my hunger. I came to Master Chen because all day he eats the ghosts of notes and I thought maybe he knew a woman who eats ghosts of days."

"She eats them," Chen says. "But sometimes she chokes."

"I want to know if this day is the day I bought," Tino says, patient and raw. "Or if it is a counterfeit. And if it is a counterfeit, I want to buy the man who did it a good drink and then break his hands."

The bureau calls it Fraud when a day is what it pretends to be but from someone else’s life; it calls it Theft when a day is not what it pretends to be and from no one’s. The language doesn’t make it true. I look at the crane again. It hums at a frequency that tickles the old part of the ear, the part that knows thunder without looking. The stitch is sloppy. The spiral is true enough, but it drifts like drunk walking. I could taste it. I could tell him something he already believes. I could tell him something I will regret.

"I can only tell you a day has been what it has been," I say. "I can tell you whether it is empty or full and sometimes I can tell you whether your name sits inside like a coin in a pocket you wore thin. I can’t tell you how to live with it and I can’t tell you how to stitch it in. I do not stitch babies."

"I am not asking you to." He runs his thumb along the edge of the paper the way you might run your thumb along the edge of a scar and I can see that his hands miss the idea of string the way some people miss a god. "If you can tell me if it is the day I bought, I will pay you in money. If you can tell me if it is the day I want, I will pay you in the opposite of money. I am not sure what that is called where you come from."

"Grace," I say, before I can stop myself. "Or salt." Where I come from, my mother called it enough. She’d say, you have enough days to last until more days. She sold one once, or five, or twenty. When I asked her how many she had sold, she said, the number does not matter. What matters is which ones.

I could take him back to my shop and pour this day into my bowl and breathe with him and hear the sound of his wife’s laugh and then teach myself how to wish for something that was never mine. I could give him a story that would keep him alive longer than bean soup. I could also bring the bureau into my afternoon. I could also step two feet into a river I don’t recognize.

"A debt returns to you," I hear in my head, and almost say it out loud. It could be the city speaking. It could be my mother. It could be nobody but the cheap paper on my table leaking its bravado through my nails. I look up and Master Chen is watching me with the intensity of a man who loves his own teeth.

"I’ll need to do it at my place," I tell Tino. "My bowl is bigger than the one the exchange lets you borrow and my kettle boils faster and I like my own ghosts when I’m working."

"That was going to be my suggestion," he says, and tucks the crane back into his jacket. He has good wrists. The kind of wrists that learned to be beautiful because something else would have broken if they weren’t. "I have a rehearsal at two for a concert I will be paid nothing for unless strangers like me. After that, I am yours."

"I am not anyone’s," I say, because sometimes the body remembers how to be contrary with a speed that surprises me. Then I smile to make a house for the offense to sit in. "But come at half past three."

When I step back onto the street, the city has decided to be louder. The bus has arguments in it. The boys have switched to a game that has more throwing in it, less strategy. A couple argues gracefully with their hands. The exchange’s door opens and someone I know a little by the angle at which she lies walks out—Inspector Vita, bureau, hair like the haircut you get when you let a law make you handsome. She sees me and stops walking and looks as if she is deciding whether to cross the street or take the air out of my day with a paragraph.

"Don’t," Master Chen says behind me in a whisper that is almost kind. "If you talk to her, your soup will get cold."

"Master Chen," Vita calls, because she is polite. "Sera. You look domestic."

"I am practicing," I say.

"For what?"

"Old age."

"It won’t take practice," she says, and then the smallest sliver of a smile, the kind that doesn’t count. "I’m looking for a man who sold a Brahms day to a fool."

"Lots of fools in town," Chen says. "Narrow it down by the idiom of the laugh."

"Celestino Duarte," Vita says. "Tall."

"Not tall," I say, because I can be helpful without being useful. "Polite."

Vita tilts her head. "If he comes to you, Sera, and he will, tell him to call me. Before he spends anything he cannot earn back."

"I make soup," I say.

"That makes you more dangerous," Vita says, and is gone, because she is a person the wind would like to keep up with and rarely does.

Upstairs, the day I steeped earlier has dried into something that could pass for a receipt for nothing. The note is heavier now as if it had been watered and took the water the way a seed takes it. I stand a long time looking at the copper bowl the way you look at the door you have to walk through.

I try to remember a sea I have never seen. I try to remember where in my childhood a dock could have been. I try to remember my mother’s laugh. It comes to me, ridiculously, as a thing with mittens on. Safe, muted. Then it takes the mittens off and becomes a noise that startles cats and opens windows and makes men in hats speak gently to her even when they plan to be cruel. She sold days and she never told me which ones. When she died there was a jar of sugar on the counter and she had left a spoon in it, reckless.

I dip a finger into the copper bowl and touch the ring of wet it left where a day was. The metal is cool. My hand smells like salt and oranges. I go to the back cupboard and open it and the thread goes slack like a rumor. Inside are nine things I do not tell anyone about, and the tenth is a photograph of a girl at the edge of some water that is not this city, her hair lifted like a blessing, her mouth open wider than is polite. You can’t see the person who took the photograph but in the angle of the girl’s head you can see how much she loved them. On the back, written in my mother’s impulse, is only this: remember what we did not have to pay to learn.

There is a knock on the door that is not a broom.

When I open it, the hallway is a line of damp air and the man standing in it holds his hat in two hands like it is full. He is not anyone I have seen before, or he is everyone I have seen before after they have run for a long time. He says my name the way you might say the name of a city you mean to spend money in.

"Ms. Sera," he says. "Do you still collect stray days?"

"Do you still bring them barefaced to women you do not know?" I say.

"My name is Omer," he says. "I was sent with this." He takes from his coat a small jar with a screw top. Inside, viscous and sly, is the sediment of time—the lees at the bottom of the barrel, the syrup left in the copper after a day is wrung. People carry it when they do not have language.

The jar is labeled with a strip of blue painter’s tape. On the label, in pencil, is written only this: for the day you were born.

My landlord coughs gently in the stairwell below, because the world cannot bear for a moment to go unoverheard.

"Come in," I say.

Later, I will tell myself this is where the story starts. But I know better. It started the day my mother wrapped three oranges in her shawl and told me she had once seen the sea and that when we could afford it she would buy it by the cup and pour it over my head and I would wear it like a new way to believe.

It starts whenever something returns and brings with it the noise of a place you have sworn never to need. It starts wherever the exchange sits in you like a tooth you can’t stop touching with your tongue. It starts with the day you decide to taste what someone else says is yours and with the burst of salt that says, yes, you have been lied to your whole life and here, here is the mercy in it.

"Come in," I tell Omer again, and the copper bowl waits on the table like a circle you do not cross until it’s too late to go back.

Chapter One: The Animal in the Fountain

By the time I reached the square, the pigeons had already given the news its language. They flapped and rose from the rim of the fountain as one gray body, as if the sky itself had been startled, and then settled back, curious and unafraid. There was a child on a father’s shoulders, two elderly men arguing in a dialect I could almost understand, and a woman who sold sweet tea from a dented samovar, watching with her ladle held mid-air like a question mark. And in the stone bowl of the fountain—a bowl I had measured for pressure and cracked tiles, a bowl whose plumbing I could draw with my eyes closed—there lay a whale.

Or not a whale. An orca, a killer of fish with a head like a softened arrow and a flank of black that reflected a thin, bruised blue. It filled the fountain the way a dream fills a morning. Its pectoral fin draped over the edge like a tired hand. The white field around its eye was not an eye at all, I knew. I knew things, even when they didn’t belong to my life: that the white was a trick of pattern, that inside the dark there were teeth built for raking, that this thing needed salt and depth and a story it was born into.

Noor, they had called me, at an hour so early the moon was still pale in the west. Engineer Noor? Come quick. It’s your fountain. We thought. You’ll know.

As if any degree had prepared me for the possibility that the sea would climb a hundred and ten kilometers of earth and stairs and alleys to lie down in our town’s lap. As if plumbing could argue with miracles.

The first thing I did was smell the water. The fountain was municipal, fed from the mid-city line that we chlorinated three times a week. I leaned in and inhaled the sharp, swimming-pool bite, the sweetness of algae scraped from stone, the brass-proud scent of coins. A film of pollen from the fig trees along the square feathered the surface. No salt. The orca’s skin had a dull, dry cast, and along the leading edge of the dorsal fin a gray, filmy look like old soap. It turned an eye toward me—an honest, wet stone—and made an exhale that felt like a slap. Not on the face, but lower, under the ribs, where I had kept every emergency since childhood.

“Don’t touch it,” someone said. “My aunt says they curse.”

“I read they’re very intelligent,” someone else said, as if intelligence could be poured back into the unlucky.

“It’ll die,” the tea woman said to me, simply. She was wiping her ladle on her apron. She had returned her question mark to its line.

It would. In this heat, with this water, in a shallow bowl designed for coins, it would die the way fish die under a sun, slow and deliberate. The orca’s breath had the smell of rot baked into bread. It was too afraid to thrash. The fountain’s statue—a bronze general pointing forever at a horizon the town had never reached—looked like a brave fool, posed above a thing that would not know his name.

I took out my surveyor’s tape and tossed it to a boy. “Hold this.”

He blinked like I had offered him a crown. His fingers were quick. The tape cut the air between his hand and mine, and I measured the width, the depth, the distance to the street where a tanker truck could back in. I called Hassan at the North Pump Station. “Where are your trucks?”

“Full on the east line,” he said. “We’re moving water for the hospital.”

“Move one here.”

“El-Safa fountain? The one with the statue?”

“Yes.”

“You think he needs a shower?”

“Yes,” I said. “A long one.” I moved aside as a policeman pushed through, the leather of his belt squealing. He placed a hand on his own stomach unconsciously, a gesture men in this city made when they felt their authority challenged by a problem bigger than their palm.

“What is this?” he asked me. He knew me. The way city servants know each other: by the curve of shoulders, the scratch of heels on stairs. He knew I could be made to say no to things that wanted to be yes.

“An orca,” I said. “A whale.”

“But we are not the coast,” he said, frowning up at the vanishing moon as if it might be hiding a backdoor.

“Tell the waterpeople to come,” the tea woman said, as if we were in a folk tale with a chorus. There was already a crowd. I watched as the orca’s side rose and fell, as a cat might watch the breath of a sleeping horse. It was a slow, foreign movement, an animal that took up space in time. Its skin—the part above water—was drying. When I reached to slide a wet cloth over it, the crowd edged forward and back, a tide.

A little girl reached out and, against her mother’s hissed warning, pressed the tip of a finger to the glossy black. She withdrew it with a look on her face like prayer and triumph had both failed to explain something. The mother didn’t scold. She was crying without making sound.

Hassan called back. “I can send you one truck, maybe two. But Noor, the water—”

“I know,” I said. I couldn’t give the orca brine from the municipal lines. We had deep wells and a stolen river, and the salt inside our bodies made us loyal to the old coast, but our pipes were pure. I looked up at the buildings that held a stare over the square. A man leaned on a balcony in his underwear and called to his wife that there was a whale in the fountain. Birds wrote sentences between eaves.

My mother used to say that in the long-ago, the desert had been an ocean and the bones of fish still slept under the sands. She said this when I was small and afraid of the dark, so that when the city lost power and the lights died like a field of stars, I would imagine not thieves and monsters but a low, shelving beach, black as it is before the first edge of day. She said once that the city had a vault under it where the old water turned in its sleep. She said it without evidence. As if memory were a pipe that sometimes whistled and sometimes sang.

I thought of her now, in her chair by the balcony, her mind making and unmaking maps, her tea cooling with a skin over it like shame. I had told myself, in a hard, child’s voice I could still borrow, that I was a woman whose job was to measure flow and loss. That my work was the rationing of miracles. That morning, though, I could feel the city’s water in my hands like a live thing. I could feel where it was sullen against rust and where it ran bright. And somewhere under the northern warehouses there was a pickling plant that had been shut down last winter, with tanks of brine thicker than soup hiding in the dark. I had signed the closure reports myself. I knew exactly how many liters.

I pointed at the policeman’s leather belt. “You have the keys to the plant permits? The padlocks?”

He bristled. “There’s a process.”

“There’s a whale in my fountain,” I said gently. “Today is the process.”

He looked beyond me to the bronze general. He counted the crowd. He scratched his belly. “I’ll get the paper,” he said. He didn’t move.

A boy—no older than my nephew would have been, had I ever had a brother or a sister—waded into the fountain to place a bucket near the orca’s mouth. He poured water onto its skin, a ritual of comfort. The animal turned again and made the sound. His mother’s face crossed from pride to fear. The officer put his hand out, not quite touching the boy’s shoulder, as if trying to stop a thing already done.

“We need shade,” I said to no one. Someone ran. The tea woman and the child’s mother began to unfurl the stalls’ woven awnings, tying them to fig branches, making a makeshift roof over the fountain. A breeze lifted the reed mats, and for a moment the square looked like a ship’s deck. The orca blinked. A fly landed in the corner of its mouth and the soft, ridged lip muscle twitched. The breath again. Wet bread. I thought of my mother’s kitchen and the loaf we never cut before it cooled, which crumbled in punishment when we did.

Two trucks rumbled into the square and I felt their weight through my shoes. The drivers leaned out. Their faces were shining with the pride of being called into a story. I shouted at them to stay back, to keep the engines going but not to run over anybody’s feet. I had grown used to speaking in choreographies, in the declarative mood of traffic. I climbed onto the nearest bumper and removed the cap. The truck smelled of metal and chlorine, the old, faithful stench of the city doing what it could.

“Fill it,” a man shouted. “Flood the thing.”

“And drown it?” the tea woman said. “Your head is a cupboard with no sugar.”

Another woman, in the wide skirt of the upriver towns, pushed a box into my hands. I looked down. Bananas. In this town, everything that could be given was a fruit. “If it needs food,” she said.

“Thank you,” I said. I handed the bananas back. The skin was stippled like the orca’s dorsal, I thought, then hated myself for finding metaphors while the animal was drying to death in my familiar, useless fountain.

We kept it wet. We lifted water with buckets from the fountain itself and poured it over the orca’s back, left, right, left, like a prayer. The buckets clicked on the rim. The boy was tireless. The little girl came back with a plastic watering can shaped like an elephant and emptied it in a generous, comic stream that made even the policeman smile. I put my palm against the rubbery curve and felt the vibration of breath, what fishermen tell you is the rumbling song of a ship before it docks.

Hassan came at last, his body in its blue work shirt, sticking with heat. “Brine?” he said.

“Pickle plant,” I said.

“Closed,” he said.

“Yes.”

He squinted. “You’ll break things.”

“Yes,” I said. I was already dialing. Hasan tapped his cigarette on the roof of the truck and lit it, even though in the yard there were signs about oxygen, about sparks. He blew the smoke away from the awning the way a man blows a fly off a cousin’s face.

My mother, the voice reminded me, the voice I called mine. I sent a message to Sami, who sat with her in the mornings when I had early calls. He worked nights at the market and had hands that could make a tea kettle sing with a single touch. Keep her inside, I wrote. Draw the curtains for the heat. And he, who knew my days better than I did, replied: And you?

A municipal van skidded into the square and a young woman from the Environment Office spilled out with three interns wrinkled as laundry and a man in a tie whose title rolled off his tongue like a contradiction: Deputy Assistant. He put his hand on my arm and made a politician’s face. “Noor,” he said. “This is unfortunate.”

“That’s a new word for it,” I said.

“Public safety.” He gestured vaguely at the crowd, at our city, at the idea of his job.

“Public wants it to live,” the tea woman said. She had that ladle still in her hand, and I saw him flick his eyes just once to the weight of it. She would ladle him across the ear if he made the wrong call. I felt a quick, wicked joy.

The interns began to take pictures with their phones, their mouths open, their foreheads slick. The orca breathed. The deputy smiled, as men do when they want to be forgiven in advance. “We will form a committee,” he said.

“We will open a padlock,” I said. “And bring me salt.”

He looked as if I had asked him for a thing obscene. “We’d have to get approval.”

“You are the approval,” I said. I was taller than him, and I am not a tall person.

He laughed, and in that laugh I heard all the permits that had held back blood and bulldozers both. I turned away. I was not going to spend this animal’s minutes rehearsing our bad habits. And the interns, who had the full appetite of their age, had seen something in my back, because one of them—dark-haired, with the soft upper lip of countryside boys—said, quietly, “I have a cousin with a truck. He knows the lock on the pickle plant because we used to play soccer there. The guard sleeps.”

“Go,” I said. I said it in a way that was no longer polite. The city, too, said go, in the creaking of a pulley somewhere, in the low talk of the fountain’s outflow pipe, in the way the awning’s shade trembled, in the way the orca did not yet die.

The boy who held the tape measure up to me earlier looked at my face as if it were a weather vane. “Should we pray?” he asked, at the same time a man with a book began to recite verses into the heat, and someone else sang a tune I knew from the stadium. Everyone brought what they thought would help: bread and water and rhyme. A woman unwrapped a string of plastic fish she had bought for the Eid and hung them on the fig tree, as if the tree could learn from their stubborn, glittering idea and bear something inedible and miraculous.

I remembered a story my mother had told me once about a village far upriver where the men, in a drought, had carried a boat over their heads into the middle of the market and sat in it and pretended to row. They did this every day at dawn until it finally rained. They said it made the sky remember. When I had laughed at the ritual, my mother had asked me what I thought a pipe was if not a way to remind water of its shape.

“Bring me a wrench,” I said to Hassan. He reached into the truck’s back and handed me his biggest. I took the ladder we used to clean the bronze general’s sword and leaned it against the fountain’s valving as if it were a more reasonable task: a squeaky tap, a leak. I moved through the knots of people. They made space for me, which is a grace I was taught to be suspicious of and accept. My hand on the wrench, the metal under my palm hot enough to sting, I closed the feed from the municipal line—there would be shouts later about who had turned off whose water—and opened the outflow, the one that ran into the old stone drains under the square, the ones we had not mapped completely because they belonged to older cities built beneath ours like a pocket in a pocket.

The orca sank a fraction, the water lowering around it, everyone crying out. “Not to drown you,” I said, as if it spoke my language. “To make space.”

“Space?” the deputy asked doubtfully, sweating like the rest of us.

“For salt,” I said. I imagined the brine moving in the dark, a lazy animal roused. I had never opened the sluices under the pickle plant. We used those drains to carry storm water away in the last monsoon. They were brick and temper and blind turnings. But water knows a slope like hands know bread, and brine is heavier than freshwater, and there was, under this square, a place where the two could meet and argue in my favor.

It ran faster than I thought it would. There was a wet sound rising through the brick, a sound like throat-clearing, like a whale’s low, distant speech. The interns came back with a borrowed truck, dented blue, its bed sloshing with a swashy, evil-smelling tide. They had threaded through back alleys, their laughter like barked seals. The guard at the plant had stirred, perhaps, and then gone back to sleep. Or he had pointed at them with a cigarette and waved them in, understanding the grammar of this day.

We tipped the brine into the old stone mouths. It rolled through the darkness with a slowness that felt dignified, a posture of goodness. In the fountain, the line between fresh and salt appeared before you could feel it, a sheen like oil, a liar. Then there was the taste, clean and old, and the smell, pickles, sweat, funerals, sea.

The orca shifted. Its eye turned again, and this time it felt less like a cornered thing and more like a listener at a door. The black gloss of its skin took in the brine like news. Hassan made a small sound under his breath that I have only heard men make in mosques when they believe they have been seen by God and forgiven for having been born too human.

“Good,” said the tea woman, and she lay her ladle in the brine and tasted it and said, “Better,” though I did not recommend that to anyone else.

The deputy dabbed his forehead with a folded document. “This is highly irregular.”

“Today,” I said, and I didn’t look at him because I was looking at the orca’s chest. There is a V there, where the black and white meet, that looks like a door that is always slightly ajar. When I was a child, I had a lock my father had brought me from a port town, heavy as his pocket, with no key. My mother told me some locks are better that way, to remind us not of things we can open but of a good closedness. Since she began to lose names, she worn that lock on a ribbon, touching it as you touch a prayer.

In the brine, the orca took a breath that lifted water and awnings, and for a moment the square smelled exactly like an ocean that was not ours. The pigeons rose again and fell again, and the child on his father’s shoulders clapped, and the bronze general, already green with time, glowed. I put my hand to the smoothness under the orca’s jaw. I didn’t know if it could be saved—not here, not by what an engineer and a handful of neighbors could do—but the animal had shown us our own mouth opening.

A siren began to wind up in the east, the kind the coast guard uses when a ship hits a shoal. A siren that doesn’t belong in this city, except here it was, coming through the alleys on a truck borrowed from a port three budgets away. I looked up to find the deputy watching me with a face I did not expect. He wore a look like a boy who has lied on behalf of a friend and has liked it.

“It will not be enough,” Hassan murmured, and he said it not as a condemnation but a weather report. He was a man who knew that something can be good and not be enough and that both of those sentences can be held in the mouth without tasting of failure. “We will call the coastal people,” he said. “We will call everybody.”

“Call my mother,” I said to Sami on my phone. “Tell her about the whale.” I wanted the story to find her before the rumor did, wanted to thread it into that vault under her mind before her mind flooded.

I stayed at the fountain until the heat turned the square into a stage set seen through glass, until the boys with ropes appeared and the television van and people with clipboards who use the word triage. I stayed until someone brought me water and then, because they did not know better, poured it over my head as if I were burning. I stayed until the brine settled and the orca’s breathing slowed and the city’s usual noises found a way back in: the crank of a bicycle, a man selling greens, a baby’s outrage. And still the animal lay in my fountain like a gift or a dare.

No one asked me if I had caused it. No one asked me if I believed in omen or if my mother was getting worse. I would have lied to both questions. What happened mattered more than why. That’s a lousy position for a person whose life has been an alphabet of reasons, of valves and volumes and metrics, but it felt right and raw. It felt like being a child again at a door that had no keyhole, with my ear pressed to it, hearing something alive arrange itself on the other side.

When I finally stepped away, the tea woman touched the back of my hand with her ladle handle, as if knighting me. The boy with the tape looked like a person who, when old, would tell this story as if his telling had saved the animal more than the brine. Let him. The deputy had lost his tie. Hassan opened his second cigarette. The pigeons had learned the shape of us around the fountain and adjusted their paths accordingly.

I walked past the fig trees, past the man who had been measuring us with his balcony, past the shop that sells plastic buckets and dishracks and miracles for ninety-nine piastres, down the street to my mother’s building. The siren the coast people had brought howled once and then died, humbled. The square behind me thrummed like a heart two sizes too big for the day.

On the stair to my mother’s apartment, the light was out and someone had left a broom leaning against the wall. I knew, stepping past it, that the brine would scar the fountain’s pipes, that I had already written six letters I would never send to the accounts office, that what we had called in would not go back into the quiet like a guest. I knew that in years to come men would curse the day I had made of that morning, and others would bless it, which would amount to the same thing. I knew the orca might die despite everything. I knew all this and climbed anyway.

When I opened her door, my mother was on the balcony despite my message, the lock on her ribbon resting against the soft of her collarbone. She had the posture of a person listening to a long story told by a friend too far away to make out the words. Her tea had grown its thin skin and she had not disturbed it.

A whale, she said without turning. Her voice was clear as a bell at a burial. She had remembered something she had not been told, or perhaps the city had told her itself. I went to stand beside her and we looked toward the part of the sky that lay over the square, and though the buildings were in the way and the awnings’ fabric too, I saw the shape of the day moving there. The orca’s breath rose again, one more time, like the city trying its best to be a coast.

If I were the sort of person who believed in signs, I would say that was when we began to shift, to tilt on the stubborn wheel of ourselves. If I were a scientist, I would point at the brine and the valve and the trucks. I am both, and neither helps. What I had, after, forever, was that sound: breath where it didn’t belong, and our hands making space for it.

Chapter One

They came home heavy that morning, slow with it, their abdomens shadowed and their legs furred with whatever the city had been saying to itself. When they banked into the wind and staggered across the lip of the rooftop, the sound of their bodies made a little pressure in my ears, like when you swallow too fast and the room has to accommodate you.

It was the third day without rain. The canvas water collectors we used heaved and shivered in the currents of air over our block, the rooftops a ragged plain stitched with laundry lines and satellite dishes and, on ours, six wooden boxes narrowed to the cunning of bees. I had named the hives after things that could rescue a person if you could find enough of them: Bread, Fire, Names, Weather, Time, and Mercy. Names had been a weak colony for months. You could tell by the way their hum was frayed at the edges, the flight line to their entrance thin and jittering. Mercy, on the other hand, was a monster. The frames I pulled from her were gold and heavy. I had set aside half those combs for the clinic to dilute into their tonics, because the nurses liked the way Mercy’s honey laid a hand on the chest and told a body to hush.

I worked early, before the heat bruised the city into a single exhausted flavor. The veil itched where it touched the back of my neck. Smoke from my can drifted up in a thin domestic ribbon, blue as writing ink. The jar of water by my knee caught the light and threw it back in moving pieces. Across the alley the lottery office was opening its shutters, and the woman inside, who knew me enough to raise a hand but not enough to know me, began singing into the empty.
