It was only six notes, the start of a song that Youssef the vendor had rewritten about bread and luck to make it legal, but in those six notes the pathway to the old thing was still there. I watched for any of the official cars. There were none yet. You could sing, if you were careful about the dialect and if you cut it off before it looked like a prayer.

My brother, Miro, came out with a mug of coffee for me and set it on the crate by my elbow. Sixteen last month and expanding in all directions, bones, opinions, the length of the startling hair he refused to cut. He was barefoot. He is always barefoot on the roof no matter how many nails I pry up with my new wire puller and no matter how often I say, You want to die of tetanus? That the city has invented new verbs for infection?

“You’re late,” he said cheerfully. “It’s nearly hot.”

“Weather doesn't know what late is,” I said. “Weather just treats us all the same.”

“That’s what we say when we’re the ones late,” he said, and grinned, and the grin startled me because our mother had that same grin, a break in the face like sunlight through a fence.

“Don’t hover,” I told him. “They’re moody.”

“I’m not scared.”

“Good,” I said, “but fear is evolutionary and I would like you to use some.”

He crouched anyway, tilted his face toward the hives. When he was a child he used to fall asleep with his ear pressed to the wood, listening to their winter songs. On a thick night, the sound traveled through your bones and went right on traveling, like a train in a city where nobody had ever seen a train but everybody had learned to dream of them anyway. Even now, if there was shouting in the street or if a fight broke out in the building, Miro would go to the roof and lay his head against Mercy, and say later that he felt better, which is how you know that the old laws still work even when the government tries to replace them.

He put his palm flat on the lid of Names. “They’re different.”

“I know,” I said.

The bees fanned their wings along the entrance, the collective exhalation like the hush that moved through a theater when the lights went down and the hand of the first note was lifted into the air. Bees fan to cool the brood or to circulate a smell. I told myself, as I always did, that there were a hundred simple reasons for a change in the hive’s sound: a storm moving in from the marsh, grain trucks belching ethanol at the corner, the municipal turbines sending out a current almost but not quite audible to human ears. The girls pick up everything. They taste with their feet. They choreograph themselves to the invisible.

But the first frame I lifted from Names had a weight that resisted more than gravity. The comb was dark as tea. When the sun struck it, the light showed thin lines traveling through the cells, a faint geometry, a kind of skeleton under the sweet. I thought at first it was the brood pattern. Then I saw that the lines were too regular, too slanted and straight, like the leftover bones of letters after ravenous winter.

“What the—” Miro breathed.

“Don’t—” I said, because even your breath can alarm them.

I tilted the frame. The honey swam. The light came. We both leaned in. In the cup of three hexagons together I could see strokes gathering, dripping their serifs as if someone had written quickly above a candle and then folded the paper before the ink could dry. I could make out a vowel, a shape like a weeping eye, a slash. It did not surprise me. This was the city. Our bees fed on whatever flowered here. In spring, the apricot trees along the canal. In summer, the border of clover by the school, the spilled soda under the train bridge, the handfuls of sugar children tossed at weddings when they had forgotten why their grandmothers used to toss rice. They would also work the paper trees. Every public board, every window with a notice taped to it, every handbill, every sticker, every scrap of stenciled law that insisted on itself. Words release a kind of sweetness. That is a true thing. It is why people lick their fingers after reading a letter and why some cannot read at all without whispering.

But this was different. These weren’t the block-printed proclamations our bees had learned to harvest from walls. This wasn’t thin bureaucratic sugar. What hung in those cells had weight. It was made of the air we had been forbidden to shake.

“Get me a jar,” I said.

Miro ran to the crate stacked with sterilized glass and lids. He handed me a jar still warm from its bath. I slid the uncapping knife along the wax and the comb broke with a sound that, if it had been a word, would have been the word for a promise allowed to be broken. I scraped slowly, letting the honey fall. It was darker than Mercy’s, redder somehow, with smoke in it, though I had smoked as little as possible around Names this month to keep their temper delicate. It smelled like rain that had visited a long time ago and still refused to leave.

Bees thudded against my veil, impatient. I could feel their legs on the skin of my wrists where my sleeves had rucked up. “Keep them away from my hair,” I said, and Miro held out his hands, fearless enough to cup my neck.

It took both jars and half my steadying breath. When the frame was bare, it looked obscene, an architecture denied its content. I hung it back into the hive. I marked the lid with a blue dot. I wrote on my clipboard: pull two frames Names; flavor unknown. Then I added smaller: maybe Gray.

I didn’t like writing it. Graytongue was what the old men in the courtyard called it, half-joking, touching their ears as if what had brought them through would break them now. It had a real name of course, but the law had taken that name into a room and closed the door. You didn’t say it. You could ask for your grandmother in many dialects and the nurses would nod and find you somebody with hands. You could say bread in seven ways and mean seven kinds of hunger. But there were some words that the city took away five years ago, along with the statues of the men who had made those words with their mouths. They were polite, in the way that the government likes to pretend it has invented politeness. They did not cut out your tongue. They only inscribed. They wrote down what you had said. They wrote your name under it, neatly. They wrote the amount of the fine and then, if you could not pay, they wrote something else on a separate sheet, folded it, put it in a folder, put that folder into a drawer.

They called it the Quieting.

Over in the lottery office, the woman stopped singing and read the numbers for yesterday. People's names rose in her throat and went out into the morning like birds with their beaks taped.

I put the lid on the jar and slid it into the hollow in the crate where the dust and the shadow would keep it from admiring eyes. I stood on the roof and looked at the bright terrible city. The old floodplain spread itself around us like a map of the past, flats of water that were supposed to be a lake and weren’t anymore, whipping up fine grit that found its way into your pillowcase no matter how careful you were. The new tower on the other side of the canal had finished its skeletal first story, and the men who ran the elevator had built a shrine inside it out of bottlecaps and a picture of a let’s not say who. Laundry flapped in every available breeze. The radio from Joris’s kiosk emerged and then subsided in static like a friend climbing a bad staircase.

Miro touched my arm. Through the thin muslin of my shirt I could feel the heat of his palm and the bones inside like small oars. “Did you hear it?” he whispered.

“Hear what?”

He stared at the hive, and then at the jar. He had our mother’s superstition about looking at certain things directly. “When you cut it. There was a sound—”

“A breaking sound,” I said.

“No,” he said, and shook his head. “I don’t know the word. In… you know.”

The word he meant was a word we were not allowed to admit we’d kept. The little dialect our mother had let slip at night when she was bent over the pot, the small sharp words that punctured the room whenever she stitched herself to her own remembered life. The breath under which she taught us to count, to pray, to curse. After the Quieting, she had stopped. She had pursed her mouth like a child refusing medicine. She had started waking in the night with a hand on her throat. She had smiled more, but it was the smile of someone who had once known how to tell a story about a river and now faced a glass of water she was not allowed to drink.

“You think you heard Gray,” I said. The bees rode the air between us. The hum raised and folded, cloth making itself into a garment.

“It said a thing,” he said.

“What thing?”

He flushed, and now I saw that under his bravado, my big boy was still a boy, still with the trespass in him. “I think it said home.”

A word like that is silly with context. It means everything. It means nothing. It is what babies learn to perform with their mouths when they are promised applause. But there is a door in the word that opens only in a body that was taught it a certain way. The door was there. The other side was there. It hit me under the ribs. It would be so much easier if we had not been that mother’s children, if our lives had not begun in a building where the stairwell was painted like a forest and the kitchen floor was always sticky with sugar because people were always pouring sweetness over one another’s hurt just to survive.

“Don’t say it again,” I told him, and couldn’t keep the softness out of my voice.

“I won’t,” he said, and to his credit I think he meant it.

We came down off the roof with the honey hidden under my shirt in case Mrs. Soare from the fifth floor was hanging laundry and felt moved to do her civic duty and remind everyone in the courtyard we were not supposed to traffic in illicit feeling. A pair of kids took turns pretending to be a police van. The one who was the siren was very convincing. I nodded at the girl with the pigeon. She was always walking around with that bird on her shoulder, the bird’s head tilting in the exact rhythm hers did. It was making a mess of her mother’s blouses. The old men along the wall were playing a very tense game of dominoes and adjusting their hats. The courtyard always smelled faintly of fried onions and the communal lower tank that refilled whenever the lake got it into its head to be generous.

Inside, our rooms were small and close and honest. My mother had painted the walls a color she called blueglass, though it was more like river if you poured milk into it. She said she missed the heat of the place she came from, and so she made heat a room. She had hung fringed cloths around the light bulbs so that nothing hard could fall straight down on our heads.

I took the lids off the jars with their little telltale tongues of wax still caught along the threadings. The honey bent light. It was gorgeous. It made me angry. Not at the bees. They are not politic. They bring home what needs to be brought. I was angry at the morning. At all the right now in it. At my own hands.

We have a back room we call the library. We call it that because you can’t lie about what a room is and then expect it to become that thing. We call it that because when Miro and I were small, our mother whispered to the room until books appeared. The spines lined themselves along the shelves, a slow miracle. Poems first, because you could hide them in a loaf of bread. Novels after, because their sheer weight protected them. A box of his and her theology because our parents liked to argue and this is how they liked to arm themselves.

In the third cabinet my father—before he left for the camp and the camp swallowed him the way a mouth swallows a cherry and you can remember the ball of sweetness and still not find the pit—had built a set of narrow shelves with slats bored through them, like a hive. We put the books face-down in the slats with their pages open, and the bees came through the tiny holes and drank the words nobody was allowed to drink anymore. Sometimes if you left your hand resting on the wood, you could feel the language leaving.

The law said this was collaboration, harvest, useful work for the state. The law said we were doing a public service: gathering the harmful dialects and distilling them into medicine. The clinic made a tincture that settled the shaking hands of the widows of the last war, a syrup that poured fog over the tongues of men who needed to stop wanting to die. The law said this was good. I believed that it had some good in it. I believe a lot of things that are in arguments with each other. This does not make me a liar. It makes me local.

I slid the jar into the back of the cabinet behind a row of cookbooks. Old women in the market watch cookbooks the way some men watch the horizon for the first sign of a navy. I breathed through my mouth so that nothing about me would scent the honey with fear.

“What if they test it?” Miro asked.

“They test the quotas,” I said. “We’ll break this down, cut it with Mercy. We’ll match the notes to something legal. I know a woman at the clinic.”

“You know everyone at the clinic,” he said, with an adolescent scorn for my reputation that he had earned the right to.

“Because mothers know the people who know where the aspirin is,” I said.

“Don’t call yourself that,” he said, and then tried to rub the word back out of the air. “I didn’t mean—”

“It’s nothing to apologize for,” I told him. “Somebody has to find your lunch money.”

He looked at me from under the curtain of hair. “What if you kept it,” he said. “What if we kept it whole. It was saying things, Yara.”

“And who would you give it to?” I said, too sharp. “Who would you trust to put it on their tongue and not call the whole neighborhood down on us?”

“I didn’t say—”

“You don’t say,” I said, and then made myself a smaller person and put my hand on his shoulder. “I know. I know what you are like. So you must know what I am like.”

He lifted my hand off his shoulder and turned it palm-up and put his mouth on the heel of it, a little ridiculous adolescent gesture that made me want to weep and laugh. “Don’t die,” he said. Teenagers say this to the person who has become their mother. They say it not because they think you’re actively auditioning for death but because they recognize the exact quotient of danger in your day.

“I have an inspection at nine,” I said. “If anyone knocks before then, you don’t open.”

“Nobody ever knocks that early,” he said, which is the kind of statement that tempts the gods.

When the knock came, it was less like knuckles and more like a statement from a person who had the right to open any door they liked. It wasn’t nine yet. The clock over the stove said eight-forty. The eggs on the counter softened their edges in the heat. Somewhere in the courtyard a glass broke.

Miro looked at me and I looked at him. He put his thumb between his teeth to keep from shouting. He has this habit because if he says the wrong thing, it will be the wrong thing for a year.

“Go to the roof,” I said. “Take Bread. Take the spare queen, put her in your pocket. If they ask later where the spare is, you tell them she died last week, which is almost true because we thought she would. Go.”

He went. For all that he is slow with his mornings, he can go quick as sunlight down a narrow hall when a door closes for reasons he does not trust. I wiped my palm on my skirt and went to the door and opened the first lock, then the second. I tucked my hair behind my ears because my mother told me once that this is how dignity arranges itself.

The woman in the doorway wore the jacket of the Linguists’ Bureau, summer-weight, the kidney shape of the state embroidered on the breast pocket in a thread that insisted on itself even when you looked aside. She had taken off her cap already, a sign of politeness. Her hair was gray and chopped short, probably by the same hand that did my hair when I did not sleep well and forgot to go to the barbershop and told myself that self-sufficiency was simply efficiency in drag. A second person stood behind her, a young man with a clipboard, his eyes bright and feverish the way people’s eyes get around a profession that can make numbers out of anything.

“Ms. Haddad?” the woman said.

I have been Ms. Haddad since I was twelve and my father stopped coming home and my mother did not stand up fast enough from the couch when people knocked. There are names you inherit as a warning. “Good morning,” I said.

“Good morning,” she said. She did not smile. She did something better. She looked around my doorway at my kitchen and let her gaze linger on the three cups on the counter. “My name is Shirin Abadi,” she said. “We scheduled an inspection for—” she took a neat little breath that said she was about to say “nine”— “in twenty minutes.”

“I didn’t change any clocks in the night,” I said.

“No,” she said. “We’re early. There was a fire on Third and we had to move our morning around it.”

“Of course,” I said. “Come in.”

The young man with the clipboard didn’t. He took care of the new politeness for both of them and stood in the hallway so that if I attempted to run he could have grasped my elbow and prevented me from falling. Shirin looked at my walls. She looked at my books. She looked at my mother’s blueglass. Her face did not betray disgust or affection. She had one of those narrow faces that seemed to have been intended for the desert.

“We had reports,” she said, as she sat at my table without being invited to, “that you had begun keeping more queens than your license allows.”

“That’s quaint,” I told her. “We require more queens than the government currently imagines it does. They die. Sometimes the whole city feels like a hive that needs re-queening.”

The corner of her mouth did a very small thing. “Your humor is noted,” she said.

“What’s your humor doing right now?” I asked the young man in the hall. He blinked at his clipboard and found that there was no response page for that.

Shirin took the jar of Mercy from the counter and turned it so that the light ran its hand along it. She did not open it. “You have always have been cooperative,” she said. “Your batches test clean. You have a good hand. We appreciate it.” She did not say the next thing. She had been instructed not to show her hand before she knew where mine was.

“Thank you,” I said.

“My job,” she said, “is very simple. I take from wildness what can be kept, and discard what cannot.”

“My job,” I said, “is the same.”

For the first time she smiled, small as a knife laid flat.

“What if,” she said, and paused, a courtesy to herself, “what if a jar came to you that had a word in it your brother would recognize.”

From above us, very faintly, the roof hens—that is, our neighbors’ birds—clucked in their flock-sad voices. The fan in the bathroom rattled. A bee landed on the lip of the sink and walked sideways, reading.

“You should be more precise,” I said. “Words do not fit in jars.”

“They do,” she said. “That is the problem. Words will fit anywhere a person puts them if they want to live.”

It was then that another sound reached me, another speech, not in the room and not on the roof and not in the street. It was a rubbing at the back of my ear, a trouble, like the memory of the time my father put his hand up to catch the glass he had knocked off the table and slit his palm cleanly and calmly remarked that he could see his own life-line as a piece of white meat now. I lifted my fingers and found, because this is a house where certain creatures can come and go as they need to, that a single bee had crawled through the hole in the screen and into the conch of my ear and was walking there, tick-tick, telling me something in the language of legs, which is older than law.

She said, this one is yours.

Of course I did not say that aloud.

I looked at Shirin and she looked at me. Maybe, once, somebody had put a bee in her ear and told her the same thing, and she had listened and then gone and gotten herself a jacket with the kidney on it because the world is complicated and love travels by weird routes. Maybe not. Maybe the only hum she had ever trusted came out of a machine.

“Ms. Haddad,” she said, “can we see your roof.”

“No,” I said, surprising myself. It was a soft no. A polite no. It was the kind of no that invites a third word to sit beside it and complete the sentence with something like today.

Her eyebrows made a small cathedral over her face. “Ah,” she said, and stood, and placed her hand on my table like a person in an old play swearing to a god outside the scene. “Then we will have a look ourselves.”

And it was only then that I realized, because this is how small our lives had become, that the sound I had thought was just a morning had swelled while we were speaking, that bees were pressing themselves against the window screen so thickly that the blueglass no longer looked like anything but sky, and that down in the courtyard the dominoes had stopped clacking, because somebody had lifted their head and said, Listen.

They gave me a cart and a ledger and told me to save the weather.

“Seasons are municipal property now,” the deputy said, barely looking at me as he slid the brass key across the counter. His office smelled like boiled starch and old raincoats left to mildew. Behind him, a framed print of our harbor in better days showed a harbor that probably never existed—blue water like enamel, gulls arranged politely on the horizon. “People hoard,” he added. “People sentimentalize. Do your work.”

My cart listed to the left the way feral dogs do after too many kicks. On its shelf rode a crate of empty glass, clear jars with rubber seals like mouths poised to swallow. The ledger was the size of a pillow, with paper the color of tea. Someone had penciled in the heading in careful block letters: TEMPERATURES REMEMBERED (VERIFIED). Beneath that: Personal logs are legal documents. Falsehoods will be prosecuted.

It was spring by the old calendar, but the sun felt like the rim of a spoon pressed too long against skin. The city had been this way for months now, holding its breath at the top of an exhale. A billboard on Dock Road showed a model wearing a sweater and mid-thigh boots, hoping to conjure a cold that would justify them. Around the model’s knees a plastic snow of soft drink logos fell in pixelated flakes. Real snow was a story told by exiles and a limited edition postage stamp. One of the jars on my cart had held snow once, sealed by a fisherman the winter I was nine. I had kept it beneath my bed all that season, cracking the lid to catch a smear of whiteness. This is how you breathe in cold, my father said, cupping my hands around the jar. Inhale it like a prayer so it can bless your ribs. He could make even miserliness sound like generosity.

The city smelled of warm bread and diesel, iodine and rust. I pushed the cart past the shuttered florists who painted artificial tulips with chalked veins, past the barbers dragging stools into shade, past the nana on the corner selling bottles of cloudwater that were only tap water with a story. On the municipal radio from an open window, a man’s voice described the planned seawall in numbers and metaphors. Thirty-two meters at its tallest, he said, the height of seven stacked elephants, to help you imagine it. The ring of teeth that will keep the sea from chewing us. They never called it what it was yet: a border through our bones. Someone had taped a hand-lettered sign under the radio, where people coming to renew their licenses could see it. No wall without witnesses, it said. The tape peeled at the corners like dried mouths.

On days like this I tried to walk like my mother used to walk, a glide that turned pavement into something she owned. She’d slip through markets and bureaucracies with the same light impatience, never quite stopping, catching a name here, a rumor there, staring down the officials who wanted her to stand in line. I am a line, she’d say, and watch them fluster. She’d had a stand near the ferry terminal selling fried fish and gossip. She is housed now in a building where air conditioning hums night and day so that the temperature can be kept at an average citizens are meant to find comforting. My mother always hated averages. The nurses text me photos of her smiling beside plastic plants, of her palms raised like a traffic officer’s to emphasize the punchlines to jokes she doesn’t quite remember. When I have allowances for the commute, I go. Once, at the end of a visit, her eyes slid away from me toward the window as if embarrassed to be seen. “Don’t start with me,” she said, in a tone I remember from my teenage years. “It’s your memory that’s slipping.”

Three streets down a boy flagged me like a taxi, two fists in the air. He stood under a tamarind tree the city had decided to spare because it had insinuated its roots into the foundation of the municipal god you’re not supposed to covet but everyone covets anyway, the one that looks like a chrome acorn. The boy wore a shirt that used to be white. He had the reckless smile of a person who had lost something and then found a way to sell its replacement.

“You’re the Weather Woman?” he asked.

“Close enough,” I told him.

He tugged at my sleeve the way kids do when they believe you’re in uniform. He led me into a courtyard that used to be a parking lot for scooters, now hemmed in by buildings whose paint had peeled down to honest concrete. In a plastic basin by the tap, something shimmered like possibility. It was just water, but then everything necessary is.

“My aunt says it’s winter,” he said, reverent. “She had it in the freezer. She said you’d trade.”

His aunt looked like every tired aunt in our city, every woman who had learned to keep a family from boiling over by turning herself to a simmer. She came out of the doorway wiping her hands on a towel that had once had roosters printed on it. The roosters were faint now, ghosts fighting. “They said on the radio to bring our Remembered Weather straight to the office,” she said.

“They said many things on the radio,” I said. The ministry’s van that collected contraband jars was a rumor that kept old men alert at night. People hid their seasons under beds, in hampers, in the back of cupboards. The season-clock had fallen off the wall, and the same month had crawled over everything like ivy; so when people found a pocket of another time, it was not simply nostalgia. They were collecting alibis.

“I’ll log it if that makes you feel better,” I said, opening the ledger and smoothing the page with my forearm. “What makes you call it winter?”

“I remember winter,” the aunt said. “When I was a girl in the hills, we had a tree that turned its leaves to smoke in the cold and an old man with cracked hands who sold paper kites shaped like snails.” She looked past me at some kitchen only she could see. “I carried my father’s shoes to the river and broke the ice with the heel so I could wash them. This—” She nudged the basin with her toes. “This is colder than our electricity, colder than our fridge used to be when it still sang. Put your hand.”

I put my hand in the basin. The water was indifferent. But the cold was like a question asked against my wrist, persistent and odd. The aunt watched me the way people watch magicians in case they can learn the trick.

“It’s colder in the middle,” the boy whispered, as if the water could overhear.

We had a procedure for this. Identify, discreetly, the source. Persuade citizens that their memories were safe with the state. Open the ledger. Make the case for donation with dignity. The ministry had speech cards for us with words that had been tested in focus groups, words that tripped over nobody’s throat—Contribution, Heritage, Resilience. But the aunt’s forearms were crossed now like pontoons under her breasts. She blinked the slow blink of a person who has answered enough questions and will not answer one more.

“It was my husband,” she said finally, and tapped the basin with her knuckles. “He brought it home a long time ago from a job up north. He died last year. We were cleaning. The freezer swallowed itself.”

I crouched, and the boy crouched too, as if cold demanded a lower posture. In the basin, something thinned the light. I thought of one winter when I was small and my father had strapped knives to his shoes—not knives, he had said, laughing at my wide eyes, but old blades from the factory—so he could slide with me across the flooded ice of the football pitch as if we had been born into that country. He had fallen, and the laughter had cracked into something else. A woman had stood at the edge of the field calling a name that was not mine, and when no one answered she had let the cold into her lungs until her voice turned white.

“Okay,” I said. “Let’s see if we can catch it.”

The boy clapped once, then covered his mouth as if even joy might scare it off.

I chose one of the smaller jars and rinsed it with water from the tap whose handle squealed as if reluctant. Then I slid the jar into the basin and waited. The old men who taught me how to do this were rail-thin and smelled faintly of sugar and night shift. They had learned on different apparatus—leather gloves gone stiff with cold, hose valves that stuck open, stopwatches with cracked faces—back when our weather tried to kill us per the old contract and the state paid people to fight. Now the job was mostly paperwork. But there were days like this when the old craft returned, the skill of simmering the air down to an essence. It is like catching a fugitive, one of the old men told me once. It wants to run through your fingers, so you make your fingers compassionate. You show it you remember it. Place your hand above the jar but don’t touch it. Leave a roof it can be persuaded to live under.

It is useful in life, to persuade something to live under your roof.

The water in the basin sighed as if relieved its shape could be held. The boy leaned so close his breath blew ripples. His aunt set one hand on his neck for ballast. I lifted the jar and sealed it with the rubber ring and the lid and then wrote their names in the ledger in block print: INA GARCIA and JOCELITO GARCIA. My supervisor had told me not to include children; they had their own separate book that gathered their names like rain. But it felt wrong not to write the boy’s name on the page that described the world as stoic adults met it.

“What does the city give us?” the aunt asked. Her voice was almost a shrug.

“Receipt. A small stipend.” I took out the printed notice with its fussy border and slid it under her thumb. “Your name will be kept confidential if you request it. The jar will be housed in climate at the Archive for all residents to access. If you wish, we can arrange a supervised visitation so you can—”

“Breathe,” she said.

“Yes.”

She stood there for a long time, looking not at me but at the basin empty now except for water that made broken pictures of our faces. Then she nodded. “You’ll come back?” she said, and I did not know if it was a request or a warning. She put the stipend in her brass sugar canister and did not offer us tea.

The boy followed me as far as the gate, carrying the jar with the tender care of a ring bearer weighted with a future he could not predict. “What’s it like, where you keep them?” he asked.

“Cold,” I said. “It’s very clean. The jars stand in rows until they look like a building themselves. Sometimes when the lights are off I can hear the water arguing.” I stopped. Not everything that is true is helpful. “It’s like a library, but for people’s weather.”

He nodded as if libraries were the sort of thing that could hold you accountable. “Can I visit?”

“When you’re older.” This was the line. I hated it. The boy’s hands tightened on the jar and he nodded as if an oath had been made against him.

When I pushed the cart away, it wobbled more. Maybe my hand on the handle had turned anxious. Rooftop pigeons, bleached by the sun into a shabby kind of grace, shuffled across eaves. A hawker with a bucket under a parasol called out items I couldn’t afford, inweights that were the correct names of their long-ago wholes—mango tongues, belly sugar, tea leaves that had never seen tea fields. The sidewalk boiled with women who had wrenched a city out of their bodies and now had to feed it.

At noon my phone pulsed with the city’s standard alarm. Heat advisory. Please stay in shade. Please hydrate. Please report the elderly and unaccompanied. And because the city had learned to speak like a friend, it added, Thank you for weathering with us. A nurse from my mother’s facility called, the number flagged with orange in my contacts. “Your mother is in a remembering mood,” the nurse said. “Can you talk?”

“I’m across town,” I said, shading my face with my palm. “Put her on, if she wants.”

There was a clack as the phone transferred. “Hello?” my mother said, the vowel long as if speaking into a tunnel.

“It’s me,” I said. “Mira.”

“You always say that like I should be impressed,” she said, and afterward her laugh was a sound I did not recognize. She used to laugh like a door banging their way into our kitchen with the wind. “There’s a man here who says he is a doctor. He keeps opening and closing the shutters for no reason. I tell him stop it. He says that they are just buttons and not shutters. He thinks I am an old fool.”

“They’re changing your bed, probably. He’s testing the remotes. Let him show off.” I angled my body to make a sliver of shade from the truck that dripped cold water beside me.

“Is that your father?” she asked abruptly.

“Which he?” I said, and after I said it I bit my tongue. My mother had had many hes. The father I had lost to the sea and the father who had come after and taught me the names of oil stains on asphalt as if they were saints, and the string of men who had stood in our doorway bringing fish, bringing bills, bringing promises.

“The one who took me to the fair,” she said. “With the pig. He put me on his shoulders so I could watch the auction.”

“I don’t know him,” I said softly. “But tell me about the pig.”

“It was not a pig,” she said, triumphant. “It was a bull dressed like a bride. But that tells you the sort of man he was. You do not owe anyone anything, Mira. Do you hear me? You owe them exactly what you want, my mother said that, and my mother was wrong half the time but she was right about that. They can build walls and say please and say thank you and put stamps on it but they cannot grow the winter back.” She was breathing harder; the nurse must have come back into the room. “I have to go,” she said in a little girl voice. “There is something in the window.”

“Love you,” I said, because there are some things you say not to be reported but to keep your own pulse steady.

“Drink water,” she said, and hung up.

Afternoons in summer-as-spring are when the city turns into a creature with hot breath and a low belly. Exhaust mounts the air like a rider. I turned toward the port where the air tastes at least like salt and not like pennies. A cat lay on a concrete eyebrow of roof with one paw dangling, the way my mother dangled her hand out of the bus window when she used to smoke and pretend it was someone else’s mouth.

I was cutting through the alley behind Camacho’s Bakery when the bell on my cart’s frame rang by itself. The sound was small and precise as a coin dropped into a glass. I stopped. The bell only rang if the jars clinked. The jars only clinked if one of them had something in it aching to leave.

I lifted the crate’s cloth cover. The aunt’s jar rested among the empties. The tin lid sweated. I set my palm flat on the glass as if taking its fever. It felt like a stone pulled from a river’s throat. I bent down so I could say the truth without embarrassment. “Not yet,” I told it. “Wait while we get you a safer room.”

The jar calmed against my hand. People might correct me about the science if I said that out loud. I do not use science for everything.

In the Archive lobby, the air conditioners coughed their white noise like polite old men clearing their throats before they offered opinions no one had asked for. The guard at the desk had fallen asleep, her mouth open just enough for the city’s heat to sneak in and wreck the cold behind her teeth. On the far wall hung photographs of the old firefighting squads, men posing with hoses and women with their hair pinned up inside metal helmets, their eyes full of the practical romance that happens when danger looks like a job and not a disaster. The Archive had been a fire station once, and before that a fish market, and before that a fort. There are buildings in this city that just keep holding, no matter what you pile inside them.

I carried the aunt’s jar down the narrow staircase to the vaults. The metal rungs were slick with condensation, the green kind that makes your shoes behave like arguments. Below, the vault rooms were blocks of regimented cold, each with a bone-white number painted on the door. The new security contractor had installed biometric locks that read palms, but the oldest doors still had keyholes. I like keyholes. They admit the idea that you could be wrong.

Room 12 was where we kept the early winters, back when donors were old men who remembered the hill country and women who remembered the year it snowed once on this shore like a rumor that found us by mistake. The jars sat on metal shelves in labeled rows. Some had strange things in them: a button, a black hair caught in the threads of the lid, a medicinal leaf that someone had pushed into the throat before they remembered the rules. Once, in a jar donated by a couple who had married in a cold snap, there was a platelike fossil of a moth pressed against the glass, all its equations suspended, its body preserved as if it had chosen death where intimacy offered no exit.

As I logged the jar into the ledger, my phone vibrated three times with a pattern I had trained myself to fear. When I saw the notification, I almost dropped the jar. Delivery attempted. Package will be held at neighborhood kiosk until close of business.

I had not been expecting anything. It is a mark of our times how quickly an unexpected package becomes either a promise or a threat. I closed the vault’s door with my shoulder and took the stairs two at a time. Upstairs, the guard had woken and was gnawing at a cuticle with the kind of concentration some people use on chess. “You’re making me cold,” she said, as I passed.

The kiosk stood in the shade of a banyan that had eaten three meters of sidewalk and a municipal bench and now had roots like an exposed nervous system. A clerk with a neck tattoo that looked like a skyline scanned my ID and slid the mail across to me through the bullet-proof glass. People liked to pretend we didn’t need bullet-proof glass in our neighborhood. People like that didn’t live here.

It was a small padded envelope with a tear in one corner where you could see the plastic inside like a second skin. It had been forwarded through a chain of scratched-out addresses, like someone with a new set of teeth trying to learn how to pronounce us. The postmark was so faint I had to tilt it toward the boy behind me to catch the date. The stamp was a special issue I hadn’t seen in years, a snowflake that made its own argument for geometry. On the back, just above the seal, a careful hand had written a return address that no longer existed: North Base, Kilometre Marker 19, beneath the words Temporary and Authorized. Under that, the name of a training camp they had renamed three times. There are places so temporary they last forever.

I held it for a moment in my palm, weighing history. There are people who tear things open. I thought of my mother, how she wrenched the plastic ring from a bag of sugar as if it had insulted her. I considered being that person now. Instead, I carried the envelope home. I do not know why. Superstition. Reverence. Or because some things, even in our ruthless heat, deserve shade.

My building smelled like dried fish and spilled laundry soap. The old man upstairs had hung chiles along the railing to blister in the sun, and their smell had soaked into the concrete so that even rain could not wash it out. I climbed the four flights to my door and remembered every other day I had not wanted to leave this city, and some days when I had. In the hallway, my neighbor Mr. Costa sat on a plastic chair with one broken leg propped on an upended crate, smoking a cigarette without the cigarette in it. “They told me not to,” he said, though I had not asked. “So now I do it without the fire.”

“Does it help?” I asked, unlocking my door.

“It helps the boredom,” he said. He peered at the envelope as if it were gossip. “From a lover,” he guessed, delighted at his own boldness.

“From an administrative entity,” I said, to dampen his appetite, but my hands were not the hands of a woman receiving a form letter. They were the hands of someone holding a story like a bird.

Inside, my apartment had the quiet of a place that was not waiting for anyone. The spines of books tilted on the shelf with the crooked fortitude of distant cousins in a photo. A fan turned in the corner with such poor success it should have been pitied. Through the window, my laundry on the line tried to take flight and failed. Sometimes when the wind catches the sheet, I see for a second the petting motion it makes against the sky, and I want to cry. The body sometimes gets confused about how it is meant to grieve.

I sat on the floor under the open window where the light made a rectangle on the tile like a prayer rug and I weighed the envelope in my palm again. I tore it carefully along its seam. Inside, wrapped in two squares of soft paper, was a letter on thin blue aerogramme with perforated edges you lick to seal, the kind my father had sent when he worked on ships that went north and docked at ports with names you wanted to pronounce with your mouth close to the paper. The paper had phantom lines showing you where to fold. The ink had bled a little from damp somewhere in its travels.

Mira, it began, and my heart made the sound of a jar lid being loosened, the little pop of air being admitted. Then, after my name, there was a space as if the writer had had to reach for me across a room in his mind.

I read the date—four years ago, almost to the day. The letter was not long. He had never written long letters. He used to say you could sum up a good day in two sentences and a bad day in one. He wrote about cold like a creature that had walked into his tent and curled itself in the corner and refused to be shooed. He wrote about work—how the men who were boys at home made worse mistakes at the margin of sleep, how the diesel smell got into his prayers until he was saying the names of God with fuel on his tongue. There was a line about me that made me set the paper down and press the heels of my hands into my eyes in the way you do when you want to hold your face together. He had something for me, he said. He had found a piece of the old calendar. He had found a winter small enough to mail.

The paper unfolded again in my lap. I reached into the envelope’s torn mouth and drew out a square of stiff clear. For a second I thought it was nothing, the ridiculous elegance of nothing you can touch. Then the light caught it and broke. The form was too precise to be accidental. Six arms, six smaller arms splayed from each of those, the geometry that can make a person believe in the information inside cold. It was not ice. That would have been a parable too cheap even for our city. It was glass, spun so thin it caught and released the sun in pulses. In its center, a pinprick where a string might have been. It was too perfect to be mine.

The fan spun and the air shrugged against my skin and outside a woman was scolding a child who scolded her back with a confidence that made me proud without knowing why. I held the glass flake up to the window. The light that came through it landed on the wall and quivered, a small, trembling flower that had never grown here until now. I thought of the aunt’s jar downstairs in the vault, condensing its insistence against the lid. I thought of the seawall men with their measuring tapes calling the ocean a number to prove they could hold it. I thought of my mother saying There is something in the window.

On the aerogramme there was a last line, added in the margin as if an afterthought. Come if you can, it said, in my father’s hand that had taught me once how to catch a coin behind my ear and how to read a map as if it had been made specially for me. Then, after that, a coordinate. Not an address. Latitude and longitude, as if what he was giving me was not a place but a moment.

I stood and watched the small unseasoned wind press its mouth to the glass in my hand like a person practicing a kiss. For the first time in months, a cloud dragged its shadow over the buildings across the street, making a bruise that moved and then healed itself. I set the snowflake on the windowsill and the light on the wall moved as if to accommodate it.

In the hallway Mr. Costa coughed in the thoughtful way of a man considering fires he could not smoke. Somewhere below, a door slammed with the force of news. I pressed my palm flat to the window pane the way I had pressed it to the jar, and the glass cooled a little under my skin. I thought of my cart, the jars with their rubber lips, the ledger with its tidy lies about permanence. Evening would come and give people permission to say the things they could not say under direct light. I thought of a border that was a wall with a name like an oath. I thought of a coordinate written on blue paper like a prayer bead.

There are days when you carry the city on your back like a sleeping child. There are days when the child wakes. The first time I felt the pull of a tide I could not see, I had been standing waist-deep and grinning, not knowing to be afraid. The water had kept going. I had not understood then that to go with it was also a choice.

I looked at the envelope with its traveled stamps. I took the aerogramme to my mouth and breathed on the place where the paper had been folded and licked and held. Then I turned to my desk and drew out the map that was not official and so more accurate. I put my finger on the place where the lines met and the paper wore a smudge, not yet, I told the part of me that was always already leaving. Wait while we get you a safer room. Then, when the feel of it in my chest did not change, I understood that this had been a message from a past that had finally found its way through every redirection. What do you owe a ghost? my mother would ask in the tone she reserved for fruit sellers who were trying to cheat her.

Exactly what you want, I answered her in my head.

Out the window, a gull nobody had invited to our part of the city circled with the caution of a tourist, then pitched itself toward the harbor and the unbuilt wall. The light on the wall trembled but did not go out. In the corner of the room the fan kept turning. The city outside listed and then righted itself. On the sill, the glass snowflake did not melt. But my palm, when I lifted it, held a scent of cold so faint I almost missed it. It smelled like iron and clean teeth and a word I had not said in years and was ready to learn again.

Chapter One: The Sounding

The marsh does not keep our calendar. In the municipal ledger we write equinoxes in ink, and we draft notices on boiled paper with the crest of the old water tower pressed into the corner—soundings approved for the twenty-third at dusk, bring blankets, no alcohol on public land—but the marsh has its own arithmetic. It counts by tide and hush and the barbed whisker of wind that scrapes the surface until it shines. Sometimes it keeps the appointment. Sometimes it arrives late with its hair wet, shaking a storm out of its skirt.

On my desk at City Hall, beneath the framed oath and the yellowed photograph of a ribbon-cutting we no longer remember, a milk crate of cassettes rattled when the north bus coughed by. I took the crate with both hands. The plastic handles had cut little semicircles into my palms by the time I reached the door.

“Lark!” Paulette called from the switchboard. She acts like her chair is a horse, like every call requires spurs. “Your professor called twice. He says he’s already at the tower.”

“He’s not my professor,” I said. “And it’s not a tower. It’s a tank on stilts.”

Paulette twirled the phone cord and winked. “Same difference to a grant man. He'll name it after himself either way. The Amanu Tank. The Amanu Sound. Never trust a man who takes notes in pencil.”

“You taking notes?”

“Always,” she said, and redirected a call with a gesture like feeding a violin.

Outside, noon light lay on Main Street like a sheer curtain. You could see through whoever walked through it. The awning over the bait store flapped, the hooks on its underside clinking like teeth. Last year, city money had replaced three smashed panes in the public notice case. Behind the glass the paper looked like a pinned moth, spreading its wings to directions and prohibitions. It would be torn by morning.

I loaded the cassettes into the trunk of the city sedan and slid behind the wheel. The seat still smelled like Deputy Bell’s Old Spice from when I borrowed the car for the spring clean, when I hosed mud off mannequins abandoned behind the thrift store. The radio was dead, which was an omen if you were that kind of person and only a broken wire if you were me.

My name is Lark, which is not my fault. Around here you get names like Rowboat, Flick, Polly, Bug, names that start as jokes and then the jokes go to school and carry lunchboxes, take arithmetic, get jobs like city recorder and learn to keep the jokes straight on paper. On my birth certificate my name has more letters, but the marsh trimmed them down the way it trims the edges of the town—gunnels splintered, paint lifted. People look at you until your name fits you. My mother insists I was named for the bird and not for any of the other reasons you might guess. When you work in a town that listens to the dead, strangers guess a lot.

At the end of Main Street, where the asphalt thins and the boards begin, the water tower stood like a stork on its long legs. A skin of rust had reappeared along the seam that we painted in June. The tank shadow cut across the mown strip that the town maintains for the Sounding and fell into the cattails. You could step from shade to sun and feel, in the skin under your wrist, the marsh making a small decision.

Two figures had already taken up positions under the tank, in the three o’clock wedge between leg and ladder. Zeke Holcomb, who runs the shrimp co-op and keeps one foot on land like it’s a promise he might withdraw, waved his hat when I pulled up. Beside him stood a man with a clipboard and two cameras strapped to his chest like infants.

“Lark,” Zeke sang out. “You brought me a crate of your finest hits. A tune for every occasion.”

He points to the cassette deck that sits on an old card table we hauled from City Hall. The deck is older than I am; we had to special order belts for it from a woman in Ohio who listens to vacuum cleaner motors for pleasure. It has survived baptisms of beer and brine. I keep it wrapped in a towel in my hall closet when it’s not in use.

“Dr. Amanu,” I said to the man with the clipboard. “You were scheduled at three.”

He looked relieved that I knew his name and simultaneously affronted that schedules had standards. “Traffic was clear,” he said. “I wanted to get a sense of the… acoustics.”

“You can get a sense of the acoustics when they arrive,” Zeke said, cheerful as a knife. “Until then you can get a sense of the birds.”

The new man tipped his chin up to the tank and the ladder; his hair was damp at the temples though the day wasn’t warm. He had flown in last week with shoes like polished bread and a grant in his briefcase. He was staying at the Albatross Motel, where the towels smell like toast. He had come to help us preserve our heritage, which meant he wanted to tame it and sell it back to us.

“It is not a tank,” he said, and laid his hand against one of the legs like he was feeling a horse’s flank. “It is an instrument.”

“We have one of those in the humane society office,” Zeke said. “It is of an incredible temperament. Shall I fetch it?”

“You fetched me instead,” I said.

Zeke took the crate from my arms. My fingers flirted with numbness and then went blunt. He glanced at my hands and made a face. “You don’t have to carry it alone,” he said, for the twentieth time.

“It’s lighter than last year,” I said, because it was. He didn’t answer. He knows the difference between lighter and lighter because half of the older folks went under the winter flu like so many cattails in a hard frost, and my sister—Liddy—has been gone four years. Every time I manage to think a thought that doesn’t touch her, somebody says something about weight, or weather, or time, and there she is, a slice of song in my ear, unasked.

Dr. Amanu peered toward the trail where it enters the marsh and the boards begin to knock underfoot. He had the look of a man who expects to be greeted with garlands, and we were greeting him with a card table and the carcass of an old tape deck. He lifted his camera and snapped a photograph of the tower leg, as if the leg might change.

“Do you have enough outlets?” he asked.

I pointed to the generator behind the municipal bench. “If we need it. Usually we don’t like to lay cord in the grass where folks will walk. We have one primary speaker up on the platform, and these smaller ones—”

“Birdhouses,” Zeke said.

He smiled at me, the worry line in his upper lip softening. Before Liddy disappeared, before we had to start counting money with the diligence of prayer, Zeke sometimes took us out in his boat to an island of cypress and barnacles, where we pretended we were arriving at a country that required no visas and had never hosted a war. He shared strawberries with us that he claimed he stole from a ship in port. He was never mean until he was.

I set the birdhouse speakers on their posts, five of them like patient little owls facing the path. A spider had built inside one since last season, and I tried not to think about what it meant to evict an occupant just when the season turned. The idea of displacement is tender around here. Too soon after a storm to joke about who keeps which house.

From the marsh there came the sound of a dozing toad, the quick hitch of a rail, the shake of dry reeds like gossip. The laugh of a child floated from the path and was answered by a gull. When wind slides across the water, it trembles at the edge of audible, a fish at the surface. You can hear the difference between an incoming cloud and incoming men. You can hear your own heart argue with gravity.

A couple from away arrived along the boardwalk with their arms full of folded camp chairs and their assumptions. The woman’s hair was the color of oyster liquor. The man’s shirt had little anchors. They nodded to Zeke and gave me a smile like I was the clerk at a deli. Behind them, Reverend Hobb came grim as a kneeler, his throat already red in patches where the sun bites first. Reverend Hobb belongs to the church with the bell no one can bear to ring. At Sounding, he stands at the edge and threatens to ordain the air. He wants the Sounding in his sermon, and the sermon in the Sounding, like a hand pushing a bird into a cage with debate about whether the door will remain open. He and my mother had three small wars over this in the first year after Liddy. He thinks grief must be visible to count; my mother thinks grief is like water and steals any vessel you put it in.

“Miss Poe,” he said now, unsmiling. He calls me Poe when he is particularly set on his point. “You are aware of the clause in the regulation regarding the reading of names?”

“No lists this year,” I said. “Like we discussed at the council meeting.”

“We did not discuss it. You declared it.”

“Declarative sentences are the best kind at a certain point,” I said, and I must have sounded brave instead of brittle because he leaned back, surprised.

“The town expects to hear the names,” he said. “The Sounding must be anchored. Otherwise—” He opened his hand, and a fly went out of it. “Otherwise it is just a noise.”

“What about the names the marsh already speaks?” Zeke asked. “That’s what it’s for.”

Reverend Hobb shot him a glance that contained, in a space the size of a pinhead, all their old grievances about a borrowed truck and a broken promise. He looked back at me. “You have no authority,” he said. “To take names off a list.”

I do not know why that was the moment I thought of my sister’s shoes the day she disappeared. They were white canvas sneakers with a stain on the left toe where the berry bled, and she had tied them with that elaborate double loop she learned in first grade and never abandoned.

“Then file an appeal,” I said, and turned away as if there was an urgent knot in a cable I had to untie, which there was not. I can outlast anyone if we both stand very still. It is one of the few things I learned early and well.

By three, the field had salted itself with bodies. Blankets in patches of color across the mown grass like a quilt our town has been stitching since the first year, when we thought this could be controlled. Children dragged their palms along the tops of the grass like they were testing a piano. An old man, a veteran of a war that didn’t ask him which side he preferred, wore his ribbons on an undershirt and never sat. A pack of teens with hair in their eyes took turns confessing to a phone. The Albatross Motel supplied plastic cups of water for a dollar ninety-nine, and a boy from the bait store wandered with a tray like a steward, selling sausage rolls with mustard in sullen little packets. When the sun made its long decision to fold, the color of the light shifted to the one that makes you think you are a better person than you are.

I set the last cable, tested the deck with a recorded voice instructing us to mind our children, and spoke into the municipal microphone.

“Good evening,” I said, and the field answered with a hundred little coughs and shifts. “Welcome to the thirty-seventh annual vernal Sounding. If you brought a blanket, spread it. If you brought a child, hold onto it. The marsh is moving water and will take what it is offered. Please keep the boardwalk clear. Please, if you are tempted to speak loudly to a Ghost, remember there are others trying to hear their own.”

A man near the front raised his hand and half stood. His nose looked like a strong opinion and his hairline like a tide line. He wore a jacket that had been new in another city. “Who chooses what gets amplified?” he called, and a few people turned in a way that meant they liked this kind of question and would eat it if you served it on a plate.

“No one chooses,” I said. “We do not choose, Reverend Hobb does not choose, the council does not choose. We amplify what is already loud. We try to capture the quieter ones for the Archive.”

“And who keeps the Archive?”

“I do,” I said, and the man sat back with a small smile as if he had discovered what he needed to know.

Liddy would have laughed at that. Even in death she cannot resist a neat ending, a jar for the fireflies. Maybe that’s why she left the way she did. You could argue the Sounding is our town’s attempt at a neat ending, the white envelope you tuck the mess into. Around here, we do not believe in endings. We are strong on continuations.

At the treeline, I saw my mother arrive, her head wrapped in the scarf with brown moths. She moved slowly but not tentatively. People stepped aside the way they do for firefighters and widows. She took a place near the back and sat on the ground with her legs folded like a girl.

Zeke stood to the left of the ladder. On the landing, the primary speaker sat. It looks like the mouth of a fish. If you stand directly beneath it, you can feel the air of the Sounding on your scalp. We waited. I watched the hands of my watch. A fly walked across the dial and stopped at the seven.

Nothing happened, and then something did. The temperature shifted as it does when you step through a doorway into a room where a stove has been left on. The reeds began to talk to each other, and then they hushed. The birds took inventory and left their last words hanging on a wire. A hush thickened that was not silence. This is when your chest tightens even if you do not believe, even if you have never lost anyone, even if you think suffering is a story told to sell you insurance.

“What is that?” Dr. Amanu whispered. For a man seeking to name, he had no label. I liked him better for a breath.

It began as it always begins: with the little ones.

Every year there are children and there are not-children. The former run forward and put their palms to the ground like it might answer a question in the language of ants. The latter stand with their arms crossing their ribs like they must hold themselves in. Voices come thin at first, like bees, as if the ground is trying different throats. It clears itself. A shape tries to occur.

Then the big voice came, the one the tower catches, the one the deck knows how to drink. When it lands on the speaker it sounds like someone turning the knob on a radio you didn’t know you owned. It sounds like drowning and laundry and a hand on your coat, tugging. Sometimes it says names. Sometimes it says numbers. Sometimes it breathes only. Sometimes it tells a joke no one understands and the field laughs anyway. Tonight it said:

Bring me the knife in the silted drawer.

It is another thing when the voice uses your house.

I did not realize I had gripped the edge of the table until afterwards, when the lines across my palm had made impressions in the damp wood. The phrase came not once, but twice, with the cadence of a grandmother’s instruction. You will not find a drawer without silt unless you live in the new houses on the ridge, the ones that look like teeth. But there is only one drawer I know of that earns the description by right. The drawer beneath our kitchen sink sticks, and if you pull it too fast the whole thing will come out and scatter spoons like fish. Everything in our house is slightly damp and slightly salty. After my father left (or left; the marsh is particular about words), my mother grew careful with knives. She taught us to keep them in a separate jar, blades sheathed in cardboard, but our grandmother had kept hers in the silted drawer, with the patent paperwork and the peach stones.

The field went very quiet. Not the holy quiet we like to sell. The other kind, when everybody is looking for how to be the audience for a thing but they do not know if they ought.

Bring me the knife in the silted drawer, the voice said, and the smaller speakers answered it like the wind might carry a piece of a sentence and assemble it for a different ear.

Reverend Hobb’s hand went to his pocket like he was looking for a Bible none of us would tolerate in this air. Zeke glanced at me. I shook my head a degree like we are mice conferring in a wall. Dr. Amanu fumbled with his camera, kept deciding and undeciding which button was the correct one to press. He did not press any. I loved him in that moment. It seemed an appropriate sin.

Bring me the knife, the voice said, and there, under the sound of it, I heard a laugh. Not a laugh. The inhale your sister makes when she is trying not to laugh at you and loves you anyway.

In the first year, when we were still learning what to say to the marsh, there were fights about what the voices were. If you make a list, people will think that a list will save them. The fishermen said we were hearing pressure in the pipes. The professor at the community college said we were hearing interference from foreign radio. The church said we were hearing a temptation. Someone from the university said a thing about tectonics. The fourth year an Army colonel came with a device and then did not come again. Regardless of what you think you believe, you come once and then you decide if your heart can make the shape Sounding requires.

Who do voices belong to. Around here we are particular about property. The marsh returns what it wants. The town returns cash with a receipt. The law returns the favor. You cannot own a voice the way you own, say, a boat. You cannot brand it or pen it. We have tried. We try, when the voices come, to be polite.

“Now,” I said into the municipal mic, and my voice was not mine but the town’s voice, the way you wake with your mother’s name in your mouth though you swore never to call it. “Now we listen.”

The voice on the speaker went on. It told a story about a window, the way the rain makes temporary rivers on glass, the way one river always chooses another no matter how you tilt the pane. A woman put her forehead to the grass. A boy gasped and said Dad. A stranger reached toward the sound with his hand and then curled it into a fist without touching anything. The marsh tried a dozen throats and then found one it liked. It said a list of herbs my aunt once grew in coffee cans. It said a number that was the lock on Reverend Hobb’s office. The field was full of people pretending they were alone in their kitchens. The field was full of people so alone they could not bear it.

Bring me the knife in the silted drawer, the voice said, a third time, and I was not mistaken. The laugh under it was the laugh of Liddy. Not because it sounded like her—Sounding does not do impressions—but because something in me opened the way it only ever has when Liddy pointed to a cloud and assigned it a part in a play we had not rehearsed.

I turned the dial that feeds the little speakers less air than the big one. You would think more, when something belongs to you, but it is not ours. I set the recorder to record. The deck whirred like a cicada. Zeke shifted his stance, half ready to hold me and half ready to catch me if I bolted. He does not often look younger than me. Today he did.

When the thing ends, it ends abruptly. Sounding will go six minutes or sixty, and then it snaps like a line. You stand dumb with your hands out like someone was handing you a baby and then there is only air.

The light thickened once, then thinned. A red-shouldered hawk made an appointment with a pine. Somebody cried out a name that was not on any list. The voice faded the way a boat goes away from you, making no sound that belongs to you.

Reverend Hobb, polished by safety, cleared his throat. “We will now say—”

“We will not,” I said, into the mic. That was not policy. That was not written. “We will not say anything for a minute. We will let the marsh make its afterword.”

Zeke, God bless him, began counting in his head with his mouth closed, which the children nearby imitated, lips moving, an arithmetic of silence. For sixty seconds the field held itself. Even the tourists found a piece of reverence that fit them and held it. I counted three breaths and three beyond that, and then I breathed.

It is possible I imagined it. It is possible, once you are in grief long enough, that you learn to carve signs from plain wood like a prisoner. It is possible that the laugh under the voice was not Liddy’s but the memory of her. It is also possible the marsh uses what it has to speak with, and what it has is us.

After the sixty seconds, people stood. They shivered, as if what they had heard had passed through them and was leaving. They folded chairs. They spoke softly, in the tones used near sleeping babies and men in cuffs. Coins went into the jar by the card table that says repair in my handwriting and then says please in a steadier hand afterwards. A little boy stood by the leg of the tower and refused to move as if maybe the next voice would be addressed to him and grief had already found him and he was staking his piece.

“You look like a person who has seen a ghost walk into her kitchen and ask for a sandwich,” Zeke said. He put his hand on the corner of the card table so it would not collapse if I leaned on it. “Talk to me.”

I thought of the drawer, how its handle used to be kissed by our greasy little hands, how once Liddy filled it with shells and declared we were living from the sea from now on, which lasted three meals. I thought of her sneakers, that double loop, the way she would plant her feet when she had decided a thing. The marsh had tried her voice in its mouth and found it comfortable. Bring me the knife, it had said. Why. To defend. To cut. To slice fruit. To pry open a stuck window. In our family, knives are for utility. We are not dramatic. We save drama for the church steps and the checkout line.

“Lark.” Zeke’s voice cut through a net I had not known I was holding. When I looked at him I saw his brother standing behind him like a ghost sometimes does when two faces rhyme. I saw the day we took his boat to the cypress island and how a storm came up fast and pushed us into an inlet and we were not afraid because we were children and everyone we loved was on the boat.

“I heard her,” I said.

He nodded as if he had been expecting me to admit it. “Where?”

“In the space between the big voice and the little one. In the part that makes no sense to the professor’s microphone. I heard her laugh, Zeke. I heard—”

Dr. Amanu approached as if he believed politeness could be a door. He carried his clipboard against his chest like a question.

“That phrase,” he said. “The one it repeated. That isn’t… that isn’t usual?”

I swallowed. I watched my mother pick up a piece of trash that was not hers and tuck it in her pocket. Her hands are always busy. She says it keeps the voices out of the wrists.

“It isn’t,” I said.

“Does it have specific meaning? Is there an oral history—”

“It is a drawer,” I said, and he blinked. He blinked in a way that said he will go to the Albatross and write that down and research our drawer for his book. He might even come to our house and ask to see it. He will be sorry if he does. My mother will feed him soup too hot and tell him about the seasons you cannot see.

“If you hear it again,” he said, with a gentleness I had not offered him, “will you tell me?”

“If I hear it again,” I said, not unkindly, “I will bring a knife.”

He half laughed and then saw that I meant it and closed his mouth. The professor did not know that a knife in our house is a sign of remedy not harm. He did not know that when the marsh names an object, you do not bring its cousin. You bring the very one.

The field exhaled. The children ran. The Reverend called for names and a few, the ones who like to be seen, went and whispered theirs into his collar. Zeke began to coil the cords. I wound the microphone wire around my forearm and hand like my grandmother wound yarn. The sun drooped its shoulder toward the trees.

“Do you have it?” Zeke asked.

“Yes,” I said.

“Do you want me to go with you?”

“No.” I imagined him in my doorway, looking around the kitchen like a man who is afraid of knives. I did not want anyone in the room when the drawer spoke.

I put the deck into its towel and lifted it into the trunk. People were still leaning in close to each other, reporting what they heard like travelers from a country no one else believes in. The professor touched the leg of the tower again and then thought better of it, as if the leg had scolded him. Reverend Hobb stood under the speaker and looked up like a man who had lost at a game he had never consented to play.

When I turned the sedan’s key, the radio sprang alive. It has not worked in months. It has not worked since the winter I used it for warmth long after the heat died in our building while we waited for the city to release funds. A woman’s voice came through, staticky but sweet as bread.

Lark, it said. Lark, Lark. If you’re coming, be quick. The tide.

That was not Sounding. The dial wasn’t even set to anything. I reached for it and then did not touch it. You learn, in a town like this, how not to touch the thing that is perilous because you might end it if you do.

Zeke had not yet walked away. He saw my face and tilted his head. I lifted a finger without looking away from the dashboard, as if to say: wait.

The voice continued, soft and bright like it had climbed a fence. It named the bend past Canaan Road where the marsh throws up driftwood after storms. It named a sweetgum tree with a spoked scar like a wheel on it. It named, last, the old iron ring hammered into the rock by men who had misremembered where the river would always be. Liddy and I had used that ring, once, to strap a raft we built to something that would not move if the river begged. We had been twelve and thirteen. We had believed in rings.

Mother, I thought, and then, traitorously, I did not. I thought, Liddy. I thought, if the marsh has our birthdays it will have our ring.

When the voice ended, it ended like the click of a light switch. The dashboard went quiet. In the rearview mirror I saw my mother’s scarf move, and I do not know if it was the wind or if she lifted her hand. I think now that she knew before I did.

I put the car in gear.

“Where,” Zeke said.

“The old iron ring,” I said. “If I am not back by dark—”

“If you’re not back by dark,” he said, “I will go to your mother’s house and eat the soup too hot and I will lie to her about what color the moon is.”

“You will not tell her where.”

“No.”

“Thank you,” I said, and then, because the day had been generous with me in a strange way that might have been cruel, I added, “I think it is her.”

“And if it isn’t?”

“Then it is something that knows how to make me think it is.” I paused. “Either way.”

“Either way,” he said, and stepped back. He put his hand on the car roof like a prayer and then he took it away. If you leave such a hand too long, it becomes a mark.

I drove. The road east trembles where the marsh undermines it, like a story told too often. Kids on bikes chased me until their mothers called them back with spoons on railing. The air had that smell, the one that means crab molts and violets and a storm somewhere you won’t have to admit you want. I carried, on the seat beside me, a kitchen knife wrapped in a sack, the one with the nick on its back that our grandmother says was a blessing.

The marsh does not keep our calendar. It does not owe us our memory or our dead. It does what it wants with the nouns we thought we owned. I have the privilege of writing it down. I have the burden of not mistaking my handwriting for the law.

At the sweetgum with the spokes, the road goes to dirt. Grass grows in the middle, the way it always does when a road decides it is tired of humans. I parked at the ditch. I heard a bird. It was not a lark. It was not a bird I could name.

Bring me the knife in the silted drawer, the marsh had said.

So I brought it.

Chapter One: The Accumulation of Almosts

On my first day at the Ministry of Unfinished, the elevator refused to close. It yawned with bureaucratic patience, as though considering whether to take me in at all, then twitched its doors together, then relented again at the slightest choreography of my hands. I had not yet learned that this was policy: nothing here was allowed to complete with a clean click. The sixth-floor button glowed without lighting the others, a private conspiracy, and in the metal panels my face looked like a sentence that kept changing tense.

“You have to say please,” said a man behind me, his voice as dry as a file. He wore a cardigan as if it were a kind of armor. He shouldered his way into the stall and pressed the sixth-floor button with his knuckle. Then, looking up at the gap between door and jamb as though addressing a superior, he said, “Please. We’re late.”

The doors closed.

I laughed—my laugh always arrives before my doubt does—and he did not, and the elevator took us up through floors that hummed behind their walls. Somewhere inside the building the sound of a saw started and stopped and started again. The Ministry was in a former textile factory, and the hallways had the habit of holding onto drafts, as if ghosts carried swatches from one case to the next.

“First day?” the man asked. His badge said MAREK K., CASEWORKER III.

“Yes,” I said, “and I’m hoping for cake.”

This time he smiled, the way one does at a child learning a dangerous game. “The cake here never sets,” he said. “Welcome.”

The doors opened to a panorama of shelves. I had expected to enter an office, with chairs that rolled nowhere and desks that had belonged to some previous government. Instead, I stepped into a kind of museum without labels. There were objects with the unrepaired look of a wish: mittens without thumbs; a ladder missing its top rung; a bicycle renovated into a stationary tribute. On one table sat a line of glass jars containing clouds of words, cursive still raw inside them: letters people had never sent, caught in mid-sentence, as if they had been snapped by a particular kind of thunder. There was half a chess set. There were recipes written without quantities. There was a teacup that was all handle.

All morning the Ministry cross-ventilated with the street, and the smell of damp pavement moved inside us, then moved out again. A weekly farmer’s market was setting up on Modesty Square across the way. I could see, from one window, an old woman negotiating with a grocer about the price of arugula as though arguing for her late husband’s name—softly, with precision, a little menace. Somewhere a cat chose a lap. Somewhere the river turned on its back to be warmed by the autumn light.

We were seven new hires in a circle of folding chairs. On the wall behind the Director’s desk, the Ministry’s motto had been painted in letters too fine for the room, a sentence so thin and fervent it made me thirsty:

What remains behind remains with us.

The Director herself appeared to have been compiled out of unfinished things: a wire for a spine, a collection of small, purposeful wrinkles, hair that surrendered only to clips. There was a rip in her sleeve that had been repaired with red thread. Her smile was a digression. “Good morning,” she said. “I am Director Lenka. I wish I had a better word than ‘director’ in my title. It suggests a conclusion.”

She looked around, counting us for an unfamiliar denominator. “Is everyone sitting? Wonderful. I’d like to welcome you to the Ministry of Unfinished. The newspapers have had their fun with us—no need to pretend you haven’t seen the cartoons. We are not the Department of Laziness,” she said, and beneath her humor the tenderness in her voice made me want to confess. “We are not here to scold anyone for failing to make a bed. We are the keepers of the nation’s remainder.”

A goose marched by the open window, pursued by a boy bending under a kite he could not seem to get off the ground. The boy took two running steps and the kite lifted and wrote the letter L on the air and then sat down again, stubborn as a cow. I felt the pull in my own arms: that movement, that insistence, that failure.

“You have all read the manual,” Director Lenka continued. “It will help to imagine that what you will handle is not pieces of trash, but pressure. We are in the business of pressure management. Your job is less about finishing things—the word makes me swell like a blister—and more about recognizing what has already begun to end. Culture has a terrible backlog.”
