She took a stack of thin folders off her desk and hugged them to her flat chest, like a stack of prayers. “We receive unfinished buildings, unslaked apologies, hobbies that never made it to competence, proposals that were choked in the throat, half-knit baby sweaters. We receive interrupted jokes. We receive silences too large to keep at home. When we can, we return things to their rightful places, where they can be tended or dismantled in safety. When we cannot, we classify and store them. We do this not to hoard, which would turn us into a museum of failures. We do this to make room.”

She handed a file to each of us, one at a time. The man next to me—he had a birthmark shaped like a thumbprint on his cheek—opened his at once. Mine sat on my lap like a lunch I was not yet hungry for.

“I know why you’re really here,” Director Lenka said into a sudden silence, as though she had been in our kitchens yesterday, watching the knot we made of our keys. “You are here because you came to this building and felt an ache ease. Because the thought of all that is unfinished, unsaid, unbuilt, untaken, began to feel like a tide, and you wanted a wall against it. This is not a wall. This is a harbor. It is windy. Hold your hats.”

Marek, the cardiganed man from the elevator, began passing around our badges, each with our shy photographs. The words on mine looked too committed. The plastic was thicker than honesty. I began to peel at the edge with my thumb until the laminate squealed surrender. I stopped.

“Each newcomer is paired with a senior caseworker,” the Director said. “Do not fall in love with your mentor. It does not end well.”

Someone laughed, and someone else did not.

“Leila?” Director Lenka said. My name hung patiently in her mouth as though it had been trained by a tailor. “You’re with Marek. Marek, don’t let her file all night.”

“I never file all night,” Marek said. “Sometimes I file at dawn.”

“Do not file at dawn,” the Director said. “I will come and pour coffee in your lap.”

We followed Marek past a row of desks that resembled bodies waiting for their owners to admit defeat. The desk he indicated was made of two mismatched boards set on saw horses. Someone had built a drawer out of cardboard and tape. When I slid it open, the entire desk made the sound of a cello agreeing to be moved.

“You might want to reinforce it,” Marek said. “We’ve had incidents.”

He had a way of speaking in which every so often a word would turn the corner into another corridor. He set a half-glass of marbles on my desk, pushed it an inch to the right, and then pushed it back. His orderliness seemed more tender than fussy, the love that a monk might bear his broom. “These are to remind you,” he said.

“Of?”

“Gravity.” He set down several forms. “This is the F-13: object descriptions. The D-4 is for degenerate urgency. You’ll recognize it when you see it. The W-25 is for weather-related interruptions. Try not to invoke it to excuse a personal life. Never confuse a person with their thing.”

He looked at my hands, and I hid them in my lap. “You’ve nervy hands,” he remarked. It didn’t sound like a reprimand. “Do you play an instrument?”

“I play the panicked telephone,” I said. “Badly.”

“Ah.” He pulled out the chair at the desk opposite mine and sat, as though lowering himself into water he knew would be cold. “You’ll improve.”

The first phone call arrived before I had arranged my pencils by despair. It was the kind of phone they give to mothers and detectives: heavy, expensive-feeling, guilty. It rang with what I would come to recognize as one of our tones. We had seventeen. This one was the sound of a barn roof in wind.

“Ministry of Unfinished,” I said, reading the wall behind my desk to make sure I got the words in the right order. “This is Leila speaking.”

A man cleared his throat on the other end, as if his doctor had told him to behave as if he had a throat. “Am I calling a person,” he asked, “or a machine?”

“I think I am a person,” I said. “But I have been wrong before.”

There was a pause in which he decided to be charmed, and then he was. “All right,” he said, almost to himself. “All right. I’d like to register an apology.”

“Of course,” I said, reaching for the F-13 and then reminding myself this was not an object. “Could you tell me the intended recipient?”

“That is sort of the problem,” he said. “It keeps changing in my head. I’m calling because I am not sure who deserves it the most.”

“Would you like to list them and we can start with an order?”

“Sensible girl,” he said. I flinched on the word girl. “Let’s see. There’s my mother. The dog. A woman in a blue coat I never met but whom I blamed for something she did not do to me. There’s my wife, of course.” He said of course like someone listing allergies. “There’s an oak tree behind the house. There’s a taxi driver from the summer I turned twenty-three. There’s my son. There’s the older version of myself, asleep with his glasses crooked on his nose, who should not have been left alone so long. There’s my neighbor for whom I borrowed—no, stole—salt. There’s the person I once promised to become.”

“Was that last one hyphenated?” I asked. It was satisfying to make marks. The pen sounded like rain.

“Do you make jokes so that you won’t cry?” he asked me, gently.

“Do you apologize so that you won’t have to finish anything?” I asked back, too quickly.

We were both quiet then, as if people we had not invited had entered the room. Marek glanced up at me over his mug. He had a way of raising one eyebrow that did not question me so much as remind me that I owned my mouth.

“Let’s put them all down,” I said. “We can assign a weight to each and then see where we are.”

“You assign weights,” he said, simultaneously startled and relieved. “That makes sense. I’ve been walking around like a chandelier all this time.”

“It’s not about guilt,” I said, reciting something the manual offered for this situation. “It’s about pressure management.”

“Ah,” he said. “So I’ve heard. I’ve heard you’re building a wall.”

“More a harbor,” I said. I did not know if I believed it yet, but my voice did, and my voice has always been ambitious.

The line hummed. I could hear him thinking, which sounded like meat resting. “Let me add another,” he said. “I should apologize to my sister for pretending her hair if given to me would make me brave.” He inhaled sharply. “And to the person whose shoes I fill. And to the shoes.”

I wrote until the names made a column whether they wanted to or not. “We can process this,” I said finally. “We’ll send you an A-7—a preliminary certificate of apology—and a time for a possible handover if any recipient is willing to attend. Or we can hold it for you.”

“Hold it,” he said quickly, as if apologizing were how he breathed and he feared he’d be deprived of air. Then, after a moment softer: “No, that’s not true. If it is held by you, I will come to visit it and will never have to think of it again. Send the certificate. Let me be civilized at least in my first steps.”

“What’s your name?” I asked.

“Does that matter?” he said. “It feels as though I should apologize for my name, too. People have stumbled over it. Let’s say that my name is kept in a drawer somewhere and only the right person knows which. Would you be the right person?”

“I am this person,” I said. “It will have to do.”

“Then I am a man who has one good coat and a house that is too warm. I am someone who inherited a brown suitcase and a history of turning on the radio and thinking the music is for me. I am ashamed of little things. I am ashamed of being ashamed.”

I carefully wrote: One good coat; house too warm; brown suitcase; radio; little; little. Then: ashamed of being ashamed.

He made a sound, a small shift of breath that I would learn meant someone had reached the end of what he could say without help. I said, “We will do our best,” and he said, “I’ve left it late,” and I said, “We are patient,” and he said, “I am not,” and I said, “Then meet me halfway,” and he did, in how he hung up with a thank-you and not with silence. It was a decent small ending.

Marek had been listening with the false disrespect of someone reading a page while a neighbor dies. “Good first call,” he said. “You will learn to reduce your adjectives.”

“I am better at doing that for other people.”

“You’ll have your chance,” he said.

He pointed to the shelves along the walls. Cases with labels in a code that would become my second alphabet. On the lowest shelf, so low you would only see it if you fell, there was a manila envelope with a black ribbon tied around it. I would not notice it until later. For now there was only the feeling that in this room, beginning had its own smell. Dust with sugar in it.

All afternoon I practiced describing without finishing. There were tasks subtle as hairlines. A woman came in with a locked journal and asked us to keep it unopened for ten years, “and then read it out loud in the square.” A boy left behind a small, filigreed bell that had belonged to his sister and asked us to ring it only when it rained but never when it poured. An old man brought his wedding toast, composed on blue paper nearly transparent from folding. His wife had died on a Thursday; the toast was written on a Thursday; the word Thursday had been circled three times in green. “I never liked that day,” he said simply. He left the toast with us and took, from our shelves, a pocket mirror that had belonged to no one. “I need to see my mouth,” he explained. “It is the one part of me I understand the least.”

Midday, the power hiccuped. In the sudden quiet, the building went intimate. People wrote faster, as if the darkness were an inspector. The shadows in that room were so orderly they could have been counted. Somewhere in the next room, someone cried in the way of adults: a series of asthmatic acquiescences, an apology to the lungs for needing air. When the lights returned, there was modest applause, which made me forgive this city for the year it had almost been my home and then refused to be.

“You write too big,” Marek remarked, looking at my forms. “You’ll run out of paper before anyone runs out of grief.”

“I’m conserving,” I said. “I skipped entire vowels.”

“You are not at the post office,” he said. “We do not charge by the letter.”

“What do we charge by?”

He lifted his shoulders. The idea of a shrug sat oddly on him, like a borrowed coat. “By the breath.”

“Do we bill that weekly?”

“You make jokes,” he said again, with the cautious fondness of someone diagnosing a manageable condition. “It’s useful. Just don’t marry them.”

Toward four o’clock, when the sun began to lose interest, a courier brought in the late post by hand because the Ministry’s mail chute had jammed on someone’s stubborn letter. His leather bag was scarred with stamps from places that existed to remind this city it was not alone. He set the bag on my desk as though placing a child who had woken into someone else’s bed. “For you,” he said, touching the bag’s mouth as if it might bite.

“For the Ministry,” I corrected, smiling the smile women use when they love you but do not yet know whether to forgive you.

“For you,” he insisted, and turned to go. On his neck, a thin scar rose and fell, as if a fish had once been persuaded to be a necklace.

We do not open items without authorization, the manual said sternly. We do not allow our personal lives to insinuate themselves through the standard procedures. We were told this sentence in training, and it had the fairytale cruelty of a quest: do not turn around. do not eat the fruit. do not stop to tie your shoe.

“Someone loves you,” said the woman from the next desk over, who had not yet told me her name but had already decided to adopt me. “Or hates you. Same handwriting.”

“It’s for the Ministry,” I said again, though it did not sound like a spell.

There is a part of me that believes in rituals louder than any religion, and that part reached for my letter-opener with a gravity that had nothing to do with my hand. The letter-opener was in fact a butter knife and had belonged, the tag said, to a boy who never made it past eggs. The knife’s edge was dull and forgiving. I slid it under the flap.

Fealty to the Manual made me lift it out gently, like a newborn, a loaf, a cat. Marek stood, and then sat, and then stood again. “If this is personal,” he said in a voice like a pencil drawing a line you might later erase, “you should not read it here. Or perhaps you should only read it here.”

Within the envelope was another envelope, inside of which lay an unsent letter. It had been opened once before, resealed; the seal was red wax in the shape of an onion, a joke I did not understand. Even before I turned it over, I saw my name on the front, the way a person sees a house out of the corner of her eye and knows it is hers because of an angle, a crookedness, a porch that leans the way her father leaned. The handwriting was not astonishing. It did not promise genius or hurt. It made my name look ordinary, and this shocked me more than anything could have. No one had managed to make Leila ordinary before. My teachers had said it as if it were a boat setting out. Lovers had moaned it as if it were a command. Here, my name was a cup without a handle. It had been written by someone who believed my name belonged in the inventory of everyday.

The return address was our old apartment on the quiet street where the fruit seller left apples with small bruises on the stoop for my mother, who considered bruised fruit evidence that capitalism had hesitated on our behalf. The date was the year after she had left. The sender's name was not there.

Time changed its shape around me. The light went long. The sound of someone rolling a folder cart down the hall became amplified, a parade, a storm. I was very aware of my own calves.

“Are you all right?” Marek asked, then waited. He was the kind of man who had learned that the answer to that question is not a noun but a story. He arranged my marbles in a rough circle and then, embarrassed by his own whimsy, returned them to their straight line.

“If I open it,” I said, “I am both this person and that person at the same time, and I do not know if the floor will hold us.”

“You don’t need to,” he said.

“But it’s already here,” I said, looking at the letter. “It has arrived. I have a duty to move things along.”

“You have a duty to not swallow hand grenades,” Marek said.

“My mother used to say that letters come older than the words inside them,” I heard myself remark, as if someone else had placed the sentence in my mouth and taught it to swim. “They’ve been traveling in the world. They’ve met rain. They’ve been left in bags at the feet of buses across mountains. They have changed their minds. The person who wrote the letter is younger than the letter itself.”

“But you’re older,” he said.

“I’m older,” I said.

We sat there like two statues employed to mislead pigeons. In the room behind us, someone was explaining to an inspector why a half-built wedding arch had been delivered four years late. He was using words like supply chain and subcontractor, and there was a handmade sign that nobody could see, hung in the window of his voice, that read: I was afraid.

My hand knew what to do. My hand had always known. It turned the letter over. It slid the butter knife under the wax onion.

“Leila.” The first line was a line I had once thought I would never see, and then had stopped thinking about, and then had conducted my life around anyway like a river around a rock. “I am writing because I cannot finish not writing.”

I read the letter the way the body reads shame. I will not tell you everything she said. Not because I am greedy, though I am, but because the letter was an object and not a testament, a thing built with rules that were not mine to break. But I can tell you what I will never be able to forget. The way she leaned on a gerund and made it do the work of repentance without demanding apotheosis. The three mundane instructions that felt like rope: warm the pan until the butter is quiet, then break the eggs; do not sleep with your earrings in; when the first snow falls, go outside before the plows and listen for the way it muffles the birds into thinking the sky is a room. I can tell you that she said the name of the man who took her away. That she did not ask for permission to be forgiven. That she did not offer me the trick of a reason that I could pull out of a hat and call a rabbit. At the bottom, there was a question, and it was not one I had a form for.

I put the letter back in its envelope. I looked up. The building bent around us, old plaster holding itself together for the sake of our moral education. I imagined the elevator, its mechanical patience.

Marek was not watching me. He was giving me the privacy of his distractedness. He was rearranging the paperclips in his dish according to a system of his own devising, each bent into a letter, making a word only he could read. For a moment I hated him with pure gratitude.

“What do you want to do?” he asked, and it was only the absence of the gentle that told me he was being kind.

“I want to say that I cannot process this case,” I said. “I want to recuse myself.”

“You want many things,” he said. “We are almost out of paper.”

“I want a harbor,” I said.

“We are not one,” he said.

“I want her hand to be allowed to be older than the letter,” I said.

“Good,” he said. “Write that down. We will assign the case to someone else. You will not decide her fate, or your own. You will eat bread you barely deserve. You will go home.”

“I don’t know where that is,” I said, which is a thing people say when what they mean is that home has become a verb.

He nodded. “Then you will walk,” he said.

From the farmer’s market, the blue tents were being folded like unsent prayers. Across the square, the old woman had won the argument about arugula; she walked with a bag with two sprigs jutting out like antennae she did not intend to hide. A small dog, off-leash, carried a glove it would never surrender in its teeth. The river kept moving, grateful for the delusion that moving is the same as finishing.

I slid my mother’s letter into the bottom drawer, beneath the map of the bus routes I had never taken, the keys from apartments I had left to be someone else’s threshold. I tried to close the drawer. It stuck.

“Please,” I said, to no one in particular.

The drawer eased shut, plus a sliver. I left it there, almost closed, a measured gap. It was what we did here: leave a breath and call it policy.

When I locked the office that night, I did it with care. The key turned with the effort of someone who had been made to stand all day and then asked for a dance. I did not look back. I did not look back until the corner, and then I looked back.

On the wall behind the Director’s desk, the motto had changed while we worked. Perhaps the paint had dried and darkened; perhaps the hand that had painted had come back to bring herself to her own ending. Now it read, unequivocally: What remains behind remains with us, until it does not.

Somewhere a bell was rung though it was not raining. The sound went into my ear and made a small room and sat down and waited politely for supper. The air was the kind of green that makes the city forgive itself.

At home, the houseplants had been living without me for some time. They had not finished dying. I filled a glass, I poured, I apologized to their stubbornness without knowing which one deserved it most. Then I stood by the window with the glass still half-full and thought of all the things that might not get done if I stopped pretending the work was a faucet I knew how to turn.

I am trying to be honest. If this story is going to win any prize, let it not be for what it pretends. In the morning, my desk would have a new file on it, pale as a cheek: An Unfinished Lullaby, Address Unknown. Someone had already penciled my name on the tab. Someone had decided what I should do next, before I had finished naming the things I would not be able to do. And my marbles, because I am not careful, would roll and some would fall, and one, the red one, would wedge itself under the leg of my desk and hold it steady. Only then would I know what it had been for. Only then would I know that sometimes we are held up by what we were not careful enough to keep.

That night I slept with my earrings in. I wanted the holes to remember me. I wanted, in the morning, to have to begin again with a small pain. I wanted that to be enough.

Chapter One

The bell rang the day I came back, though there was no bell to ring.

It was a dry sound, a brushed bronze hush, as if someone had run a damp palm over the lip of a glass. The wind settled in the cottonwoods and the lake took a breath it had been holding for sixty years. The first reports came over the radio while I was still fifteen miles out, a voice from the bait shop saying the old church was showing its teeth. The station fizzled to static and came back clean on the word miracle. On miracle it always came back clean.

The truck’s air-conditioning had given up two hours before. August stacked up in the cab, hot as breath. My son slept with his head tipped at the angle that always makes mothers ache. Mateo’s hair stuck to his forehead in wet commas. I reached across at a stop sign and slid one fingertip along the back of his neck where the skin has not yet decided if it will be tough or tender. He stirred but did not wake. We turned back onto the highway, and the world unspooled flat in the way it does out here—ash-colored scrub, a scavenger hawk too busy with heat to lift its wings, the far blue rumor of mountains.

Every summer of my childhood was a story about water. We watched monsoons stand up on the horizon and then sit back down again, the lightning trying its keys in the lock of the desert. We counted the white scars left on rocks when the river retreated, the mineral memories of floods that came the year before anyone could drive. My mother used to say, Water does not forget anyone who has touched it. This is why it terrifies me and why I trust it.

The lake lay ahead, a polished shard in its concrete cradle. A pale ring clung to its edges, a whitening that made it look elderly and embarrassed. San Felice Reservoir, named for the saint of felled things. When it was new the brochures called it progress, wrote about the dam in the tone reserved for a gift from a rich uncle. The labels downtown framed the photographs: men with their hands on their hips, men with names carved into stone, the river corked like a bottle.

Technicians use other names. Operational level. Dead pool. The day it reaches dead pool, the lake becomes a confession of rock and mud. There were weeks, even months, when my work had me in the back of a helicopter counting bathtub rings, like a maid told to inventory what has been used up.

I had not been back to Las Palomas in nine years. I told myself I lived elsewhere because there was more work "elsewhere," whenever elsewhere was not simply a place without my history in it. The Bureau needed bodies, degrees, people who could speak bathymetry and politics. I learned to put the words out where they could be seen like wrenches in a roll. In reality I had left because the lake had my mother inside it, and even though I knew better—I had seen the divers’ logs, the murky photographs of silted pews, the nightmare of old cottonwoods drowned and somehow still standing—I could not unsee the way my town could not stop looking at that water.

We crossed the bridge they renamed for the congressman who lost his seat. From up there the lake’s surface looked harder than steel. Light steamed off it. Far below, I could just make out the skeleton of a fence, the wire still strung, now draped with pondweed, a winter coat forgotten. Beyond it, something pale and angular stabbed upward where there had been only the blank mirror last year. I slowed to a crawl. The truck was state-issue and rattled like a birdcage. Mateo blinked awake.

“Did we get there?” His voice was stringy with sleep.

“We did,” I said, and lied immediately. “No one will make you swim.”

“I didn’t cry last time,” he said automatically.

“No,” I said. “You didn’t.”

He pressed his face to the glass. The truck rumbled onto the far side of the bridge. The lake wasn’t the only thing exposing what it had covered. In the town itself the peeling billboards—DRIVE TO THE DAM!—were not even trying anymore. On the corner near the diner, a coyote had given up pretending to be a dog and trotted across Main Street at noon. My grandmother’s house sat at the top of a brief hill, as if it had pulled itself as far as it could get along the dry wash and then stopped, winded.

I parked crooked; the paint on the curb was gone and the rules with it. When I opened the door the heat rolled in with the smell of geosmin, that petrichor you think is rain but is really bacteria telling you they are there, the earth’s own cologne. It came at me off the reservoir in a damp sheet and brought with it a fishy rot, another small grief we now took in, unremarked upon. There is a smell to loss when it breeds in water. Ask any floodplain, ask any mother whose baby put a pebble under her tongue.

My grandmother was as small as she had promised to be in her last letter. She had always been straight in the way desert women are, folded arm to folded arm, ankles lined up, but now she had taken up living in parentheses. She kissed my cheek and the air behind it. She said my name like she was reading it off a prescription. Iris. You will stay with me. There is no argument in this, her hands said, urgent and soft. Her porch was a bowl of dead bees. She flicked them off the rail with the back of her fingers, quick as snapping at flies.

She and Mateo took each other's measure, as if they were buying each other at a market and wanted to be sure the goods were fine.

“You got tall,” my grandmother said to him. “Your mother was tall by seven and then stopped exactly there and turned stubborn and heavy. We put books on her head to push her down but it did not take. Come in. The swamp cooler functions like an old man—he works a little, complains a lot.”

Her front room had not made any accommodations for time. The crocheted afghan had the same snags I remembered; the Virgin watched us from behind her glass like she had been called to jury duty. In the kitchen, a jar of chile pique had taken on the dignity of an antique. My grandmother fed us ham and sugar bread and called it a compromise with the doctor. She asked me no questions for fifteen minutes, and then suddenly all of them.

“How is your work? Do they pay you? Are you safe? Do you carry a gun? Do they make you fly? They want to spray silver on the clouds again? I told the priest if God wanted our clouds to be different He would’ve made our desert another way. He laughed. He thinks I am a comedian now.”

The radio on her kitchen shelf was turned low but I heard the word bell twice, and the phrase under the water. I looked at the counter so she would not see my face do whatever it was doing.

“Don’t start that,” she said. “You know how the town likes a ghost. Eat your bread. Tell me if you like this salt. It’s a new one. I cannot afford it but I prefer a salt that tastes like failure.”

“Abuela,” I said, and my mouth went warm at the old word. On the other end of the table, Mateo tapped a rhythm on the rim of his plate with his finger pads. He looked toward the window as if sound might be visible, a wave he could catch with his hands.

“They say it rang.” She said this to the sink, to the sponge, to the busy sponge. “They’ll be at the water in a narrow line. Everyone in town will try on piety like an old suit for a wedding. If the bell rings without a hand on it, Iris, we are meant to know something. That is what they will say. You know better. I know better. But I lit a candle anyway. I am not interested in being left out if something is being given.”

Our priest had been a young man with acne and a jaw fixed for righteousness. He had a way of blessing the lake with his whole shoulder, like he was throwing something toward it. I remembered the first time the divers brought up a body. The hard white folds of the tarp made the shape of a folded person on the dock, and for weeks I dreamed of laundry as if this were a new category of tragedy, cotton made of grief. The town had not looked away. We had never been good at that.

“Do not go down there today,” my grandmother said, and in the same breath, “They will expect you to do something.”

“I have a meeting,” I said. I had one tomorrow with the man who ran the dam in his shirtsleeves, a person you could never catch off-guard, whose wife bought pies from my grandmother and never saw me. Today, though, there had been no plan except to lay down my bag in the room with the yellow curtains and invent a way of sleeping that did not involve listening for my mother’s voice in a faucet. I could feel sleep at the edge of me even now, like a tide tugging you out whether or not you meant to swim.

“The Sheriff called here,” my grandmother said, and we both looked at the phone where it sat, innocent and fat. “He asked me when you were coming and I said when she comes. That should be enough for a man with a gun.”

After lunch, when the air outside the swamp cooler’s cough felt almost mortal, I took Mateo down to the edge of the lake. He wanted to go because it was forbidden. Or—worse—because I had been reluctant. Either is irresistible to a nine-year-old. We walked the long road like it was a slow thought. The asphalt had troubled up into blisters. Grasshoppers knocked our shins with the soft clack of wooden beads. Two boys in the shade of a mesquite played with a pocketknife, passing it back and forth as if passing it were the whole point.

The reservoir was lower this year than I had ever seen it. Old habits in my body muttered about inflow, about unseasonal releases upriver, about the fight that had been fought two counties over where a man chained himself to a gate until they cut him away like a sturgeon. The far shore lifted out of the haze like a shoulder. Boats lay beached in ungainly white rows in the dust, the marina’s floating dock now an exposed vertebrae. The line of people my grandmother had predicted stood along the bank in reverent disarray: a clutch of women from the Holiness church, the fisherman who wore a hat made from an old cereal box, the teenage girls who had never left; a child in only a diaper clapping, not because anyone had taught him but because something in him understood applause. There was a gap in the water where the light was different; this was not even human superstition—physics makes a place you cannot name inside a place you think you know. The drowned church lived there, and when the wind dropped, its angles showed themselves.

I had seen it in pictures before, in milky underwater photographs where silt is a fog and the light is not from a sun but a machine. To see it now with the sky above it made my mouth dry. The building had been brick and nobody had bothered to take it apart before the water came. Men had dragged pews and lecterns up the hill the year they told Santa Rita to move, but the shell was a stubborn thing. The steeple had been topped once by a spire, later by a lightning rod, later by a cedar post wrapped in tin. Now the post was there, a rusted lance, and below it, the bell. It lay on its side like a sleeping animal. I could just make out the rope’s frayed tongue, slicked and stiff there inside the metal’s dark mouth. It was a big bell—bigger than my bright child’s memory had made it, bigger than the one that rang the school to us every morning. It wore the sand it had been packed with like a second skin, a fine bright coat that glittered as if the lake had made of it a thing it loved.

“Why are they—?” Mateo began.

“Shh,” I said, and regretted it. He had not asked a question that could shame anyone. He is not a boy who takes forever to learn things. He looked at the bell as if it were a throat that would sing if he but touched it.

“Your grandmother says it rang,” I told him. “When bells ring for no reason people are certain it is a reason.”

“There’s always a reason,” he said, borrowing my voice for the second half of the sentence.

“Not always the one you can use.”

We stood and watched along with the town. The Sheriff was there in his used-up shirt. His hairline had made a cautious retreat. He nodded at me in that way men use to convey forgiveness for things you did not ask to be forgiven for.

“Vargas,” he said. This is what they called me again here: my father’s name. Iris was too intimate in this place to be used lightly. I had not decided whom I would allow to say it. “You heard it?”

“I was on the highway,” I said.

“That’s a place to hear things.” He tilted his chin toward the bell. “Old Mrs. Cantu says it’s the sixth time. I told her it was the first and she said that’s because you weren’t listening all the other times, which is my point.”

“Somebody hit it?”

“I took wants,” he said blandly. Wants: statements. “Not a kid among them who would venture that close. There’s mud like soup down there. You step wrong and you’re stories for the winter.” He looked at my son, whose face had the open intentness of someone trying to draw a map as they walk it. “Keep your boy up here.”

“Up,” I agreed, and put my hand on the firm plug of Mateo’s shoulder.

We watched a long while. The water made the noises anyone who has sat with it knows it will make, the shiver and slap. The fish made larger, more impatient thoughts beneath those. When the wind came it did so as an argument we could not quite hear, talking to mesquite, talking to reeds. The bell did not speak again. People began to perform excessive slowness—taking photographs and pretending they were not, blessing themselves and pretending it was a stretch. The mothers picked up the babies, the teenagers pretended to be bored, the men looked far away and thought about money, the same liturgy as every other day. The Sheriff lifted a hand as if we had been talking and said we would talk again. He had the politeness that comes from proximity to law and sudden death.

“Look,” Mateo whispered. A fish, a carp thick and yellow as melted butter, pushed at the bell’s rim with its mouth. It did not understand the object the lake had offered it. It tried again and again to eat the bell’s perfect circle of shadow.

“The bell doesn’t work anymore,” he said, a little disappointed.

“Not yet,” I said, and was surprised to hear it come out of me like that.

We walked the edge and I walked, also, a farther route that had nothing to do with feet. I counted the old street lines exposed like palm creases. I could have put my hand on the ground and a palm reader would have had me married and alive in sixty years, if she believed in asphalt. The church had stood across from a feed store, and the feed store across from the house where my mother grew up. Nothing much of it now—some bricks, a warp of the line, a place where the earth felt burnt if you stood there long enough, as if memory gives off heat.

The last week my mother was alive she took me out in the shallow part and made me hold my breath until I could hear the thing under things—the churning of silt, the small crackle of living. “Just past the fear,” she said, “there is always something to learn.” When the divers found her car at the bottom they said the windows were up, the doors closed, the seat belt undone. No sign of struggle. She was at the back of the car, as if she had been looking for something she dropped. It is possible to make of a detail a great religion.

We turned back when the sun moved past the place where it forgives your skin. Stretched across the road on our way home was the oil stain in the shape of Texas I had stepped over my whole childhood. I stepped over it again. The men at the engine shop had just left a rusting transmission like a shrine on the gravel outside. The grocery store had formed a confederacy with the flies. The grandmother and her windows waited for us with the curtains pulled to that angle where they look afraid for you. My phone had collected messages with a stunned enthusiasm, and I ignored it.

On the porch that night I sweated and listened to the town rehearse its song. Every house keeps something and lets go of something else. People next door were fighting in that sibilant way intended for privacy and meant as advertisement. Somebody’s radio played music that had been popular when the men who built the dam were alive, as if their ghosts had tuned it. A dog barked once, as if to make that fact known. My grandmother had gone to bed with a rosary and a magazine I had seen under her bed for twenty years that did not appear to have any words in it, only rooms without owners. Mateo slept on his stomach, superhero shirt stained with the day. He is a good sleeper in any town. I have always envied that in a person.

The sheriff’s cruiser idled just past midnight in the street long enough for me to notice it. He did not get out, and then he did, and then he got back in, and then he left. It felt like old girls used to feel when they sat on the curb and waited for a car to stop. I wanted a cigarette and I have never smoked.

At three there was a knock at the door that was not a knock. My grandmother is a person who sleeps light and still it did not wake her. It was a touch inside a wall, a weight on something. I sat up and I said my mother’s name, and I hated that about the body, how it will always name the person it needs even when it knows that person cannot be the one at the door. I went to the porch, went down the steps, went barefoot into the street, heat still coming up from the asphalt through the meat of my feet. The lake lay a darker dark in its basin.

Sometimes the desert sends a wind that is like a person you do not know bending into your ear. It came then, not to cool us but to speak. It touched the cottonwood leaves in my grandmother’s yard and made a sound not unlike the one I had heard through static on the radio that morning. I put the heel of my hand against my sternum as if reminding it to stay, as if offering it a seat belt. From the lake there came, very faintly, as if from a thing across a lifetime or water or both, the bell speaking.

It was a quiet sound, nothing like the howl people were already telling. It was like the throat of an animal dreaming. It could have been the settling of the metal as the night cooled it. It could have been the slow untangling of the rope in the small movements of a world that never stops moving. There is always, as my son said, a reason. There are also the other reasons—the ones that run beneath the lake like old streets.

I listened until my legs told me I was in fact standing and might consider doing something about it. I went back inside and stood in the doorway of my son’s room and he had both of his hands tucked under his face and one knee up, the precise position he had slept in as a baby. I stood in my grandmother’s doorway and she exhaled, and her breath sounded like a small engine deciding. I went back to my bed but not to sleep. In the morning the news would come as it always does here—in a voice that believes it is weaker than the event it carries. They would tell me what the lake had given, and I would go where I did not want to go, and the town where my mother had been born and my mother had gone to die would arrange itself behind me like a jury and watch as if watching were any kind of mercy.

I lay on my back and waited for the light to come through the thin yellow curtains. I watched for the moment where the day hooked into the house and pulled. I had come home because there was less and less elsewhere, because the work had finally delivered me to the body of water I had always been working around. I had thought I would make it easy on myself by coming before the lake came for me. I had forgotten there is no choosing the order of the things that surface.

Chapter One

On the morning the river returned my childhood dress, the tide laid it on the stairs to my boat shed like an apology. Pomegranate red, with a row of mother-of-pearl buttons marching exact down the spine. The hem fluttered in the breath of the water, as if it hadn’t been buried twenty years in silt and gossip.

I was halfway through scaling a redfish that had died with its mouth open, surprised, when I saw the fabric caught in the reeds. Even through the water’s brown—the color of tea where the leaves had been left to argue—I knew my own stitches. I was seventeen when I sewed that dress from a pattern in a magazine with a blond woman on the cover and a price higher than any of us could afford. The thread was cheap and stubborn; I broke three needles and pricked my thumb until my blood made a little constellation on the bodice. For months the women watched me in the evenings, their knees shining like river stones in the lantern light, offering advice by way of insult. Our town could needle a girl into womanhood if nothing else.

I hung the fish from a nail and waded. The water in June is warm as a body and carries everything it touches. It lifted the hem to my fingers like a dog bringing back a stick it wasn’t allowed to have, pleased and panting. Then in the next breath I saw the curled hand beneath the cloth, the fingers pale and puckered, the palm turned upward as if to ask for something I did not know how to give.

I have pulled my share from the river. The living, when the current has knocked them against pilings and stolen their sense of direction. The dead, when the river is done arguing and gives up its claim. I run the mortuary because someone must. Our town has a physician for stitches and births and the occasional infection, but we have me for the rest. People say it was fate because of my name, Mara, which the old women like to remind me means bitterness. Then in the next breath they bring me jars of their pickled okra, their last jars in some cases, and say sweetness belongs to whoever stirs it into their coffee. That is how living goes here: everything is bitter and sweet together.

I slid my hands beneath the cloth. The girl was small, too small to be Lila. That was what my thinking said, while my body, old stupid body, said Lila out loud in a voice that shook. I knew the dress by the unraveling at the hem where my thread had never learned to lock. I knew the drop of dried pomegranate on the left shoulder from the day the fruit slipped out of my hand and broke against the flagstones and my sister laughed until she hiccuped. People think fruit stains are innocent, but some are as permanent as names and they travel like rumors.

The girl’s hair was braided, not with ribbon but with eelgrass, and in the braid a tiny silver hook had caught and held fast. Her skin had softened in the river until the freckles looked like something you could wipe away. The dress fit her badly. It had been made for a body that was taller in the leg and wider in the hip. A hand-me-down from someone who never got to hand it down.

“Who are you?” I asked her, because even if they can’t answer, it is polite. Her fingers were cool through the wet cloth. I lifted her and the river made that sucking sound it makes when something comes away from it that it intended to keep. A great egret stalked three yards away and watched with the offended dignity of a waiter refused a tip. On the far bank, the willows drooped their leaves in a pose of exaggerated grief our pastor would have envied.

In the shed the wood smelled of salt and oil, of all the goodbyes that had passed through. I stood her on the table and wiped the silt from her hair. Her eyes were closed. I do not open eyes; they fight you, every time. I talked to her as I worked. It is not for them, but for me.

“We’ll find your people,” I said. “No one gets burned alone here. No one goes into the dirt without a name to fold over them.” The river birds shrieked and bickered, and under their quarrel the steady thrum of the pump that kept my shed’s stilts from becoming stylish gravestones.

In town they say the river forgets. That is a nice story for children. The river does not forget. It misplaces. It misfiled my father, it misfiled Lila, and sometimes, just to be contrary, it returns a thing at the wrong time and in the wrong body, wearing the wrong dress. The day the oil company came to talk to us about relocating, the river pushed a velvet couch onto the landing with barnacles on its wooden feet. It was extravagant and wrong for the place, and for an hour we sat on it and pretended we were people who had couches by rivers on purpose. But by evening it had soured and sagged and we hauled it back in the dark. The river keeps its jokes short.

I lifted the girl’s head to see the back of the bodice. The buttons were the same mother-of-pearl I had found in a tin beneath my mother’s bed, a tin that also contained two flat stones that fit each other like lungs. I had polished each button on my shirt hem before I sewed it on. They shone now with the kind of shine that is only partly light.

There were voices outside, scuffing footsteps on planks. Ree came in without knocking, as she always did, a streak of mud on her cheek and her hair braided in two plaits that made her look twelve and fierce. The other girls had left to work in the city or to have their babies in houses with roofs that did not drip on them. Ree stayed and ran errands for me in exchange for stories and the chance to apprentice. She wants to learn the bone names and the trade of the dead. I told her the trade of the dead is mostly telling the living to eat and sleep. She said she had been telling people to eat and sleep since she was six.

“That’s a dress from the old photo,” she said with her sharp eyes. She meant the photograph in the frame behind my clock, the only picture I own where I am young and laughing. In it, Lila is blur because she never stood still. She is tilting her head like a willow in wind. You can’t see the pomegranate stain in the black and white, but you can see the shine of those buttons if you know where to look.

“Who’d give it to her?” Ree asked. Because the people who rummage where the water has reached have no business rummaging where the water hasn’t.

“I don’t know yet,” I said. “Go get Frankie. And tell him, and only him. No one else until we know.” Frankie ran the bait shop and the gossip shop depending on which hand you watched. He has the right to scowl at me because I once took his brother from a party where the boy had drunk himself sideways and then let him walk home alone. The boy never made it. The levee was a rumor that night with a mean sweet breath, and people who say the river doesn’t speak have never heard it drunk. In the morning they dragged his body out near the black stump where the cranes nest. If Frankie carries kindness in him, he carries it in his pocket, hard as a stone, and takes it out only when you’re not looking.

“Miss Ruth’ll see the dress,” Ree said, hesitating. She meant my mother. “She’ll say Lila walked out of the trees.”

“She says that every day,” I said. “The trees are full of my sister in that house.”

“That don’t mean it won’t be cruel when she sees this,” Ree said, and there she was, older than me for a second.

“Go,” I said, and she went, because even when we are oldest for a second, we still obey the structure of the day. I lit the blue flame on the small stove, put water on. Later there would be washing and combing and the slow work of returning shape to the places the water had softened. For now, I looked at the dress and then at the girl and then at my hands and thought of all the times I have not been ready and did the thing anyway.

I cupped the back of the girl’s head in my palm, gentle under the braids. There are people who will say this is morbid, that it is better to leave the dead to the river, to the gulls, to God. Those people have never loved anyone whose father went out for shrimp and never came back. The dead weigh the same as the living when you carry them up a ladder, and that weight is a kind of prayer you can’t refuse and still call yourself human.

By the time Frankie arrived with his hat punishing his forehead and his shirt untucked like a flag in wind, I had made tea, braided the girl’s hair again without the eelgrass, and cut the stitches in the hem where something made a hard little knot. It is a habit of mine to feel hems. Women hide things in hems when they have no pockets. Men hide things in their mouths until their tongues turn black. We do what makes sense with the bodies we have.

“What’s this?” Frankie asked, but he wasn’t looking at the girl. He was looking at the dress like it was a bad debt.

“You tell me,” I said, and held up what I had found: a strip of oiled paper folded so tight it had become its own opinion. I pried it open with the edge of my thumbnail. Inside was a pencil drawing in a hand I would have recognized even if it had been drawn with a toe: Lila’s. She drew like she was talking, quick and impatient, the lines leaning into one another. In the corners she always drew a little fish with a dot for an eye and another dot where the heart should be. It was small enough to be missed if you didn’t know to look. There the fish was, stupid and brave in the bottom right.

The drawing showed the curve of the river where it braided around the cypress stand we call Widow’s Fingers. It showed three Xs where there should have been none, and a thin arrow pointing upstream, toward the new gate the oil company installed last year to keep their piece of the river obedient. And there across the top, as if she had wanted to write a sentence and then changed her mind halfway, the pencil had pressed down hard enough to dent the paper. Whatever was written there had been rubbed out, but the ghosts of the letters remained. When I held the paper to the light, they rose like fish.

He will come.

“Who will?” Frankie asked, reading it over my shoulder like he had every right, which he did if you counted everything we had shared and lost.

“The one who thinks he can shut a river,” I said. It was easy to hate a corporation with a name like TideCo because it pretended to be the thing it was choking. But corporations don’t show up at your shed with their hats in their hands. A man does that. A man with fingernails you could clean your teeth with and a suit that will not stand wet. A man named Arden Royce or Buckalew or any of those names that taste like dry cereal. The letter had come last week with his name on it and five figures typed in a font that made numbers look like they weren’t real. Relocate, it said. Reimagine. Rebuild. As if we were Lego we had scattered in the night and could pick up now and rearrange while the house was still on fire.

“You need to tell the sheriff,” Frankie said.

“The sheriff is his boy,” I said, and we both stared at the girl like she might argue with us.

It is necessary to pause here and say what our town looks like, because you will imagine a place and it will be wrong. You will picture a postcard. You will picture pelicans on pylons and painted shacks with planters of geraniums and a sign that says Oyster Po’boys in a cheerful, crooked font. You will imagine our water clear enough to reflect your face back at you like a compliment. That is not the way of it.

We live in a place where the land is in the act of leaving. You can hear it: the long slow swallow of mud, the whisper of roots as they let go, the slap of boards as they go adrift. Stumps move around like rumors. The sky is too big, being half water, and sometimes the thunder sounds like a truck driving over your house. We have three streets that matter and six more that used to. The school has been moved twice because it kept standing up in the morning and finding the river had crept into its shoes. The church stands because the pastor nailed it to the bones of his belief, and no one has told him that wood does not listen to a man’s God if physics says otherwise. If you fall asleep to the blowflies and wake to the egrets, you are lucky. If you fall asleep to the egrets and wake to the blowflies, you are less lucky.

We love it. We do. That may be the truest thing I know. If you ask us why, we will tell you the reasons that sound good to outsiders: because the shrimp are sweet and the gumbo is gospel and the sunsets could bless the dead. But if you sit with us after dark and you know enough to be quiet, we will tell you the real reason, which is that our people are buried here. There is not a way to love a place more than to have it hold your bones. There is not a way to leave it without taking something of it into your lungs and your hair and your blood.

I folded the paper back into itself and put it in a jar with a screw top, because the river has a long reach. I do not own a safety deposit box. I own jars. Jars and twine and a voice I have learned to pitch a certain way when people start to wail. My mother says the jars make me common. I tell her common is how we survive a thing.

As if called by our talk of her, my mother’s voice came from the door. “Mara.”

She was standing with her hand on the frame like a woman about to perform. She had dressed herself in yellow and tied a scarf around her head. The scarf was blue, and the blue and the yellow made me think of the macaw we once saw in a traveling show that came through when I was nine. It had said hello in a man’s voice and then said help in a voice that was all bird.

“Don’t come in,” I said, too late. Her sight went straight to the dress. She took three steps and touched the hem with her old, precise fingers. They were still the hands that had shelled a thousand shrimp and mended a thousand nets and punished me for running with my skirt rolled at my waist.

“She’ll be hungry,” my mother said. “Go cut her some bread.”

“She can’t eat, Ma,” I said, soft. “She’s gone.”

My mother tipped her head, as if listening. “Lila?” she asked.

“No,” I said. “A girl. A stranger.”

“She’s wearing Lila,” my mother said. “Where did she get that?”

“We’ll find out,” I said.

“Are you lying to me?” she asked, and there it was, the way she has of opening me with a phrase like a can with a key. People think forgetting is mercy, but my mother’s forgetfulness is carnivorous. It leaves her teeth for the things that can hurt. On the good days she tells the same joke about a crab and the priest twice and then laughs as if she remembers why it was funny. On the bad days she ties the good silverware in a pillowcase and says we are leaving before dawn because the men will be back with their shovels. It is not that she simply cannot recall. It is that she remembers in the wrong order.

“I’m not lying,” I said. “I don’t know yet.”

“Find out,” she whispered. “Find everything out.” Then she sat on the stool by the window and held her hands in her lap like she had been tied to herself.

“I’ll walk you home,” Frankie said to her, and her mouth softened, because my mother likes a man who offers to walk when his feet are already tired.

“Let me look at her,” she said to me, and I nodded, because I have learned not to deny her. She reached and touched the girl’s cheek and then withdrew her hand as if the skin had burned her. “Cold,” she said.

“It’s the river,” I said. “The river does that.”

“It’s the river everything,” she said, and stood, and let Frankie take her elbow. At the door she turned and aimed the full weight of her attention at me for the first time that morning. “If he comes,” she said without looking at the paper I had folded away, without looking at anything except me, “oh my girl, if he comes, you do not give him even a finger. He will take the whole hand. He will take the arm. He will take the shoulder. He will take whatever you think is your pride and wear it like a tie.”

“He’s just a man,” I said, because it was easier to say something flat than to tell her the truth, which was that I was not certain whether I wanted him to come.

After they left, the shed felt larger by one ghost. The girl on the table lay still and small, and the dress clung to her like a color holds a fruit. I set the kettle back on and poured myself another cup and stood at the door and watched the river breathe. Out beyond the cypress, the clouds had gathered in that intent way our clouds have, like women crowding a doorway to see what trouble has come.

Names matter. When the first men came with their poles and their unquestioned hands, they named this place after a saint who had never set foot in water. Before that it had a name in the mouth of the people who knew how to move from marsh to marsh without sinking, a name that meant the color of the egrets’ cry or the taste of the air before rain. When I was a girl I kept my treasures in a shoebox with Lila’s handwriting on the lid. At thirteen I crossed out her letters and wrote my own name in their place. At twenty-three I scratched my name off with a knife until the cardboard tore.

If we are judged by our keeping, I have kept poorly and I have kept well. I have kept a jar of my father’s voice in my head for twenty years: “You listen to the middle, Mara. The surface is noise.” He was talking about the river then, but it works for people, too. I have kept Lila’s bite marks on my forearm where she bit me the summer we were children and she could not bear the thought that I might leave her. I have kept the taste of the pomegranates the grocer started bringing after the hurricanes became regular—like a dare someone dared the weather to take.

I leaned my forehead against the doorframe and let the soft damp of the wood cool my skin. A dark shape moved in the water beyond the pilings. A gator, probably, or a log imagining it was a gator. Or the couch, returning for its second joke. Then I heard the clatter of truck tires on the gravel of the road, and the sound of a door slamming, and men’s voices, confident and bright. That particular brightness men have when they arrive intending to help you.

The first chapter of any story is the one where you still think you can stand in the doorway and keep the weather outside. I wiped my hands on the hem of my shirt and went to meet them. In my pocket, the jar with Lila’s map clinked like a small bell.

Chapter One

On the morning the dam authority stamped Wetland Conversion Approved over an entire valley, I signed for a satchel of glass lungs and a train ticket.

The satchel was technical, army-green canvas with buckles scarred by other hands. Inside, each bell jar shivered against its felt cradle as if it remembered breakage. We called them lungs because they learned the air of a place and held it. The official term was volatile organic compound capture units, but in practice you carried them like you carried any living thing—close and aware of what you might drop.

The letter that came with the satchel was stamped with the seal of two ministries that disliked each other, which meant I would be paid. It said: You are hereby tasked with the collection and preservation of primary olfactory signatures associated with the Araslı orchard, the last extant stand of Crimson-Seed apples, prior to the scheduled controlled inundation of the Lower Hol and tributaries at fourteen hundred hours, fourteenth September. The signature was a slur of ink from a man whose last name I could not pronounce.

In the lobby of the Institute of Olfactory Heritage, the floor cleaner had been working before dawn. The halls smelled of things both aspirational and bureaucratic—lemon disinfectant, polished wood, old library dust, and the faintly pleading sweetness of drying orchids. The intake desk smelled like burned toast. I know these things are not complimentary, but it is my job to notice.

“You got the orchard,” said Sevda, whom I had once loved and now avoided touching by mistake. She leaned against the door of Analysis, her hair pulled tight and high, a pencil lodged like a stake behind one ear. Her wrists were tattooed with bands of tiny numbers, each corresponding, she said, to a beloved molecule. Everyone had their way of hiding their devotions.

“I asked for it,” I said.

“Of course you did.” She pursed her mouth. “That place. They had to send an envoy last year to read out the expropriation. The village women lined the road with juniper branches so Death would get lost. The envoy called in sick for months.”

“I’m not an envoy.”

Sevda laughed without pleasure. “You carry glass lungs. Same difference.”

Every assignment soured our coffee with its own particular fear. The markets—spices stuffed in sacks like sleeping birds, the fish grids winking with silver—had been easy. Fire scenes less so, if the plastic also burned. Once I collected the smell of a library after it was bombed, and I dreamed for weeks of pages lifting up and leaving as ash moths, of glue’s sweet death. Smell walks into you without your permission, into the old part of your head that remembers fruit from poison. You learn to carry your protection like a second skin, to dial the filter down or up with your left thumb. And you learn the old truth that no one believes: what you breathe in does not leave you. It sits in your marrow, in the silt of your lungs, taking names.

I had been ten when the ocean came inland. It came with the smell of coins and wet dog and something alive trying to become air. My mother took me to the roof. We watched crates of oranges pivot and spin like wrecked suns and then lose their skins. The water never reached our street. Afterwards, everything had little salt teeth. For weeks, it was just salt—on hair and doormat, in the eyes of strangers, salted again by their crying. It was there I learned how smell tells the truth about a thing, which is often too much of the truth. My mother used to say: it will leave you first when the body decides it can no longer afford the world. Then she stopped smelling entirely. There were leaks in her brain that every doctor named differently, and none could fix. Its thief took the smell of coffee and winter rain and my hair when I was older. She died in a hospice that smelled like cheap soap and winter fruit, and after, I stole her apron from the laundry and sealed it in a bag under my bed. Sometimes I take it out and let it breathe, and her hands are there, and the burnt almonds she never meant to burn, and the forsythia she used to bring home from the wet market and call barbaric because it bloomed too early.

The train erased hours cleanly. The city poured backward into bathrooms of small stations and chickens tied by one leg. Once we cleared the cinders of industry, the hills began. The river tracked us, widening itself in rehearsals for what it would become. In my compartment, an old man opened a jar of something that could have been pickled walnuts or could have been grief, and I dialed my filter one click towards distance. On the opposite seat, a schoolchild pulled a blue scarf from her backpack and then breathed it in, not for warmth but because her mother had sewn inside the hem a sachet of tea leaves and a clove, nothing expensive, something home.

After the town of Demirkent, we had to take a bus. The river lay stretched like a muscle. The road climbed, then detoured around a hole that was so clean a circle it could only have been made by law. At checkpoints, the guards barely glanced at me, so certain were they of the inevitability that arrived with my paperwork. The valley turned towards itself. The air changed. People say the countryside smells like cow and hay. They have never been to a valley about to be drowned. The smell is of the things that don’t want to leave their positions: the field magnetized to the idea of field, clay that has learned the weight of what grows on it, the mineral memory of stone.

The orchard was not visible from the road. It made sense. A good orchard holds itself close, like a story told in a family that knows who wants which part of it. The bus driver let me off at the brick sign that said Araslı in letters that had been painted over too many times to be childish or proud. Beside the sign was a shop that sold twine in loops and tins of oil. The man inside looked at my satchel and shrugged as if to say: we have all carried something heavier.

I walked the path down to the trees. It was a looser path than I’d expected, a long conversation of dirt and stone. There were bees even this far out, or a sound like bees, and then the trees began. The leaves were half light and half dark as the wind moved, and the apples let go their shapes in the air long before I reached them. People think apples smell like sugar and schoolyards because they have been raised on those two smells. These smelled like the bloodundergrin of green wood touched by frost, like grass with a grandmother living under it, like secrets told too close to the ear.

A boy ran across the path and then froze when he saw me. He could have been nine or he could have been eleven. His shirt had been mended twice, beautifully, as if someone had run thread through it with intent to make of his small body a map.

“You came to take it,” he said.

“I came to keep it,” I said. “It, them, the smell.”

He looked as if this was a trick. People are most afraid of the idea of losing something twice. “My aunt said you would come with glass,” he said. “She sent me to tell you that she will meet you among the old ones, but not the very old one. You will know the difference because the very old one has something thrown over it to hide it from you.”

“You memorized that?”

“No. She wrote it down and I memorized what it felt like to read it.”

“Your aunt is wise,” I said.

“She is tired,” he said, and led me to the trees.

The orchard gathered as we entered it. The light around us went green. The path braided itself around trunks and then vanished, the way a person stops pretending in company when the person they love arrives. I took out one of the lungs and set it, carefully, over an apple that had already declared its readiness with a bruised halo. The glass made the normal world’s texture change—everything outside it went less, and everything inside it went more. I checked the seals and waited for the small huff the machine makes when it begins to drink. Just then the old woman stepped around the trunk of a tree and said, “If you breathe too much of us, you will never leave.”

She was smaller than I had imagined and more powerful. Her body had that gravity that comes from being used for work not the gym. Her hair was not white but the color of fog. From her wrists hung three keys on a ribbon, and I did not dare think they opened anything as dull as boxes.

“Aysel Araslı?” I said.

“If there is another, she will contradict me,” she said. “I made yogurt for guests. You will drink it. After that I will decide if your glass can take a piece of us. If your glass is scared, it may go back to the city. We will not be offended. We have offended better things.”

The boy, whose name turned out to be Halil, ran ahead, looking relieved that I had not been turned away on sight. He touched the trees as if counting them. The old woman walked on a line she invented. I carried the lung, which had already begun its work, and three others, and the kit of caps, and my fear, which I had stopped calling by its name when I was twelve because it liked attention.

Their house was within the orchard, not beside it. It was made of stone that had pulled light into itself for decades, a knotted old structure of additions and refusals. The kitchen smelled like sumac and old lemon peel, smoke that had learned obedience, iron pots scoured too hard by grief. Two other women sat at the table with cups. They nodded the way the last two birds will nod to each other at evening without needing to prove they are birds.

The yogurt was thick and sour and good. It had a skin like the surface of a lake at dawn. Aysel watched me drink it as if she could judge my intentions by how my throat moved.

“You’ve come to steal truth,” she said.

“I’ve come to keep what can be kept,” I said, and felt ashamed even as the words worked. “In a vault in the city, we have shelves that smell like rain that never fell. Like books that went to ship. Like the breath of a mother giving her child to the aunt while the aunt gives her child to the river because the river is hungrier and will accept the trade.”

Aysel’s line of a mouth twitched. “Who told you that we feed the river?” she asked.

“My grandmother,” I said, though I had no grandmother from here. It was how one answered. “Where I am from we fed the sea. Everything eats to live. You tell yourself a story about which mouth is the biggest.”

Aysel lifted her wrist. The keys chimed. “We will let you take the easy parts,” she said. “The summer fall. The bees’ talk when they have run out of insults. The bruises that have decided to be sugar. But there is one tree that is not yours.”

“The very old one,” I said.

“There is the very old one,” she said, “and there is the old one. The very old one knows names. Her roots have knotted themselves around the bone of this place. If you put your glass over her, she will speak you, and you will not make it out carrying anything but yourself, and yourself will be too heavy.”

The other women watched me with a frankness one might reserve for a doctor in a faraway room. Halil’s eyes were black, unpersuaded, pure.

“We cannot take everything,” I said. “We never do. There are laws. And there is what we keep the laws for. If I promise you I will not go to the very old one, will you let me do my work among the old ones? Will you sign the paper so that I can do it without dragging some man in uniform through your house?”

Aysel considered. She lifted her cup and drank a little from its rim. Her throat moved like the throat of a working river.

“I will sign nothing,” she said, and my fear clicked up one notch, an automatic machine I could now hear if I tried. “But I will walk with you and show you who will forgive you. You must promise me one thing in return.”

“What thing?”

“When you make a vault of us,” she said, her eyes on my face like hands, “and people who have never been wet listen to what they think is only fruit, you will speak our names aloud. You will say: I took this from the Araslı, who held this valley under its breath like a coin. You will say: this is Aysel’s apple, which was her mother’s apple. You will not call us by number. I have listened to the radio. I have heard what numbers do to people.”

I thought of the shelves in the Institute labeled OP-119, OP-120, OP-121, tidy brown boxes, brilliant smells inside, held down like animals help themselves to sleep. I thought of the catalog, the clipped language we had invented to describe a fallen pear: top note sour-sweet; undernote bruised chlorophyll; ghost note of sun-warmed leaf; presence of bee chaff; modulation by rain. I thought of taking something that makes the mouth flood and working it until it is safe for committees.

“I will say your names,” I said.

Aysel nodded. “I liked you when you asked if I was myself without introducing yourself,” she said. “What is your name? Say it as if the trees will use it later.”

“Mara Orhan,” I said.

She lifted her hand. “Welcome, Mara Orhan, who thinks glass can do what mouths do and sometimes is correct.”

We went back into the orchard together. Halil ran ahead as before and then slowed as he approached an arc of trees deeper in. There was a place where the land let go of its slope and felt briefly like a ship’s deck. The wind moved from side to side as if it were thinking. The apples here were red in a way that was not market red. Or rather, they were teaching me how many reds I had never seen. Some carried within them the brown of a rope after a rain; some held a pulp color that made me think foolishly of newborn lungs. When I set a lung over one and turned the dial back to real, the smell came fast and complicated. It had time in it. It was not only now-smell. It was ripenings that had happened on this same branch forty years ago, and a little of the iron water of a well I did not know, and honey with the wings still in it. It moved the lever inside me that, when moved, releases both joy and sadness in the same liquid spill. They are not opposites. They are how we are sure we are awake.

We worked silently. Aysel showed me which ones wanted to be taken. People call it superstition when those who have never had to listen to a field speak notice the conversations it is having without them. It was not a superstition. If I had leaned my head against the bark I could have heard the upward push of sap like distant clapping.

We had filled three lungs and were working on the fourth when I saw the very old one. You cannot throw cloth over a thing like that. And yet they had tried, fixing sheets with clothespins, draping old dresses, a suit jacket, a child’s blanket with a cartoon bear. The tree under the clothes was massive in the stubborn way stones are massive. It had a seam along one side where lightning had fingered it years ago as if it were deciding that it was not hungry today, after all. The cloth moved a little in the wind and I smelled a strand of something that went straight through my nose and touched an object in my mind at the center that is mostly protected by bone. In the moment that strand touched me, the room that holds my mother’s apron opened its door, and I let out a sound.

Aysel’s hand was on my arm before she knew she had put it there. “No,” she said, not angry. “Not yours. That is the Bitter Bride. She is the tree we feed when we are not feeding the river. You would not like what she owes you.”

“I’m not going,” I said. The smell braided through the cloth again, showing itself and then hiding, like when someone dear you thought gone passes you while you are talking to someone else. It was not sweetness. It was the smell of rain on a roof that will not last the winter. It was the smell of a small pocket inside a wooden bureau where a ring had been kept, without the ring, for decades. It was not nostalgic, which is an insult you give to a smell when you do not want to admit it has teeth. It was, quite simply, the smell that lives under my bed inside the plastic bag my mother’s apron sleeps in. It took me a full breath to close that door. When I opened my eyes, Aysel was watching me as if I had confessed to a crime that was also a prayer.

“You knew I would smell it,” I said.

“I did not know who you were,” she said, and there was curiosity in her voice, not hardness. “Now I know you are one more person this valley did not get to keep. I can feed you lunch, at least. After the water comes, the only people who will come here will come in boats.”

We moved away from the covered tree. The wind brought us yellow sweet clover. A grasshopper jumped and failed to clear my boot. Halil was trying to teach me how to shake an apple loose without poking at it like a fool. “You must make the branch think you are the weight of an old storm,” he said, with the patient viciousness of the young. I lifted my hand just to the point where the apple kept pretending I had not touched it. I felt, stupidly, that if I succeeded, if it let go because I had asked correctly, the dam would empty itself, the river would go backwards like a scribe scratching out his own decree.

We took what we could take until the light bent itself differently and made our arms look like someone else’s. In the far distance, the concrete where the river would be held had a smell I could taste even from here—new, difficult, limestone crushed and burned, water that would be taught to hit the same architecture each time. It already tasted a little like laws.

Back by the house, a man I hadn’t seen before sat on the step turning one of the keys over in his fingers. He stood when we arrived. He had a badge in his pocket, and when it came out, it immediately began to smell like someone’s office, like pencils recently sharpened into points that wanted to break their own shavings.

“Madam Araslı,” he said, “we must begin preparing the area for the surveyors.”

“We have been preparing the area since men like you learned how to button shirts,” Aysel said without looking at him. “This is my niece.”

“Niece?” He looked at me, and in the second before his face arranged itself into something polite, I saw that he had not slept well. “We were not informed of extended family.”

He meant: Are there more people to pay, in fruit, in notes, in pity.

“I’m not family,” I said. “I’m the Institute.”

This had its effect. He nodded and glanced towards the satchel where the lungs sat like sleeping animals invented by a careful god.

“You will need to sign,” he began.

“You will need to listen,” Aysel said. “We are being preserved. It is not the same as agreeing.”

He stared at her. You could watch him trying to fit his sentences into the shape of this place and failing by a hand’s width. He put the badge back in its pocket, and the smell of the office lessened. Somewhere near the covered tree, a bee began a complaint and then forgot what it wanted.

When I lay that night on the pallet they gave me in the corner room, the window open to the orchard, I did not sleep. The air wore the day’s heat differently in the dark. Every hour a different smell came into the room as if keeping watch. At two a dawn hawk took something that had squealed, and the air said metallic, blood bright. At three the creek turned over on its side and the stones made that water-on-larynx sound that made my throat go tight in sympathy. At four an apricot somewhere let go and bruised itself on purpose, as if to hasten a sweetness it deserved. And between them, thin as a needle you could sew yourself shut with if you wanted, the bitter thread of the Bride. The house breathed. The trees breathed. My glass breathed, the faint whistle of it filling. I lay and named what I could so that it could not say later I had not paid enough attention. Sometimes paying attention is a way to alter nothing and keep yourself alive.

Just before the sky made its first mistake towards morning, I remembered the names I had promised to say aloud. The room in the Institute. The shelves. My mouth. I said the names I knew.

“Aysel,” I whispered. “Halil. Araslı. Mara.”

I said my own twice, in case the trees had not been listening. What I wanted next was too much, and I kept it in my mouth anyway: Keep me. Keep me even when the water comes. I am tired of the city and its lemon floor. Teach me the right weight to be an old storm.

The orchard exhaled, and somewhere in the orchard a sheet sighed and lifted and settled again. The breath that reached me tasted like metal and grief and the inside of my mother’s apron pocket, where she kept a slice of apple for me to find if she had to be elsewhere for a minute, those minutes that, added together, made the rest of her life. I lay on the pallet, still, and let the thing that tied me to the city loosen one knot. It would be a good day tomorrow. It would be a terrible day tomorrow. The glass lungs slept beside me, and they dreamed the orchard in.

Outside, not yet a river, the river rolled over the river bed the way a hand strokes a child’s hair before waking them. It was a killing and a kindness both. It was what the world does when you are not watching, and also when you are.

By the time the city hired me to write obituaries for houses, I had already buried three kitchens, two porches, and one marriage. It was easier to eulogize a structure than a person.
