Bricks did not ask for forgiveness. Windows did not stare back with the wounded insistence of a lover's eyes; they only let the weather through and held onto fingerprints until the light changed.

They put me on the fourth floor of the Department of Structures and Remembrance, a name that sounded like a dare. Our building was a retired high school whose auditorium now hosted council meetings and stage plays about river spirits. In the office elevator, every button stuck. In winter the heat growled out of ceiling grates like an animal we had accidentally trapped. My desk was by the window, which overlooked the sliced throat of the freeway and the river beyond it, the river that dragged itself through town like someone returning from a long trip without a suitcase.

If you had asked me when I was younger what I'd be doing at thirty-eight, I would have told you something with a beginning and a respectable end: teach literature, write a small book that twelve women in two cities would clutch to their hearts and tell one another about in mirrored whispers, eat dinner at a table with a man whose socks matched. But there had been a flood, and then a recession, and then a new mayor who liked ribbon-cuttings and invented departments. You could get hired if you had a way of naming things. I had always named things.

Our mandate was to attend the municipal unmakings—to stand in the presence of what was going and give it a shape suitable for mourning. We logged the angles of staircases, the local reputation of stoops, the names carved into wet sidewalks in the years when babies wore shoes heavy enough to leave an imprint. We collected recipes hand-written on the backs of water bills and scanned them into the public archive. We noted the pattern of mold on basement walls, whether it was maplike, as if the house had been remembering the country it left, or whether the damp rose straight up like the necks of herons.

"This is a city of departures," Mr. Ballentine, my boss, liked to say, tapping the glass of his office door as if testing a melon. "It is our job to keep what leaves from leaving the language."

He believed, against evidence, in ceremony. On my second day, he gave me a glossy black notebook and a pen that refused to write until it warmed in my hand. "You have to learn to listen to materials," he said. "They do not always speak in words."

I learned to listen. Plaster listens back if you give it time. Brick is shy but dependable. In the presence of metal, you have to lower your voice. Wood is gossipy and always remembers who tracked mud in.

That morning in early March when the air tasted like old pennies, a request came through the internal system with the stamped urgency that meant someone had leaned too hard on their keyboard while angry. OLEK HAD CHOSEN the subject line, which meant it was indeed urgent and probably complicated.

OLMSTEAD AVE, read the file. 139. Demolition scheduled for Thursday. Code violations on violations. Owner unlocatable. Neighborhood council loud. Media probable. Please do a swift and sympathetic. —OB

I clicked open the attachments: a grainy photo of a two-story house, its face missing in several places as though it had misunderstood the definition of a smile. Vinyl siding peeled like a peeling back. Two upstairs windows glared at me like old women suspicious of everything new. The front yard was a small tamped square of earth which, in the picture from August, held a tireless dandelion that had insisted on being the center of a life.

"Olmstead, huh," Olek said when I turned to ask if he'd been to that street. "It's the one where the pigeons do a parade at five if you give them popcorn. I used to take my baba down there when she thought we were going to Mass. Do not underestimate the theater pigeons."

"I wouldn't dare," I said. "Any idea who owns 139?"

"We are all, in a cosmic sense, owned by the river," Olek said in his tone that meant he didn't know and had already looked.

Mr. Ballentine had leaned out of his door. "Mara," he said, his soft tie testifying to a morning spent trying to tie it and then, halfway through, deciding to accept God's flawed world, "Mara, this one—be careful not to pick a fight that forces us into a lawsuit. We are memorialists, not enemies of the bulldozer. We do not blockade. We remain behind the caution tape and make the tape feel seen."

"I know the job," I said, which always meant I would fail at its limits.

In the old days, when I still left coffee cups in peoples' cars and every Thursday bought flowers with the certainty that flowers could keep a body buoyant, I did not see the appeal of this work. But grief changes what we love. In grief, the blue of a tarpaulin seems like religion. You would kneel to a broom if it knew how to talk. The year after the flood, I walked for days down streets where couches were finned with mold in the sun and children's drawings curled on chain-link fences like flags of lost countries. I wanted to give those losses a place. We all did, in our different ways. Some wrote checks. Some learned how to sand. I learned to listen.

Olmstead lay east of the freeway. The sky above it had always been a little lower, a taut skin stretched across the incline of land where the factories used to breathe. If the west side was where the city kept its postcards, the east side kept its receipts. We had, over the years, given Olmstead more phrases than it had trees: starches and smoke; onion-skin light; street cats with the faces of philosophers; a corner store with fried chicken good enough to convert the baptized. People said this with affection or with mockery depending on their audience. People said it because saying it was a way to remember that the street was real.

I parked a block away because there were three cones in front of 139 and a sign that said FOR YOUR SAFETY DO NOT ENTER ALL CAPS. A boy in a red knit cap sat on the porch across the street, bouncing his heels on the top step. In front of him on the sidewalk, four pigeons paced a square with gravity, like judges practicing their route. The boy held a paper bag whose grease halo had spread to the edges. He made a flick with his fingers and the birds surged and then pretended they didn't care.

"You the house lady?" he asked as I stepped under one of the cones and into the yard.

"I'm one of the house ladies," I said. "There are three of us. I'm more of a kitchen woman personally, but my title is House."

He considered this. "You don't look like no bulldozer."

"I left my treads at home," I said, then pushed my palm flat to the door. It was locked, of course. The city had to pretend to keep the public out. I had a ring of keys that could open half the doors in town and the other half if I was patient and the hinges had already given up.

"Miss Dora says I shouldn't let you in in case you get dust all in your throat and then sue," the boy said. "Miss Dora says the news likes to film that."

"Is Miss Dora the neighborhood council loud?" I asked.

"She is the loud, yeah," said a voice behind me. I turned. A woman in a calf-length quilted coat in the exact green of winter resistance stood at the edge of the yard and watched me. Her face was the kind that had spent the last thirty years in the sun and the kitchen and had not asked which was worship. She wore hoop earrings and her hair was wrapped in a scarf that looked like it held ten remembered nights.

"I'm from the Department of Structures and Remembrance," I said. I flipped open my badge because sometimes the official emblem, which was a spackled wall with a small stylized heart, soothed. "We're here to document 139 before—"

"Before it becomes another photograph on a banner. We know," she said. "We got photographs. What we don't have is the down payment the city wants for memory."

The pigeons had begun to parade in earnest, their beaks tapping the sidewalk like the smallest kind of drum. The boy held his breath as if he could balance the moment with his own stillness. He looked at me and then at Miss Dora and then at the house and in his eyes I saw the map of an inevitable that had become so familiar he could fold it with his eyes closed.

I am good at speaking three languages: bureaucracy, sorrow, and whatever dialect a block speaks among itself. "I'm not a reporter," I said. "I won't record your bad hair day for eternity. I am here to ask this house what it needs to have said before it's gone."

"And what if what the house needs to have said is 'don't take me'?" Miss Dora asked. "What then?"

"Then I write down that the house said what almost every house says," I said. "And I write down who else is saying it. And somewhere, twenty years from now, a girl will read the file and she'll know that her grandmother stood in a green coat and said a sentence made entirely out of "no" but with different vowels."

Miss Dora's mouth did the thing that is not a smile but is the corner of something warmer. "You're a poet," she said, dissatisfied with the category but unwilling to fight it in front of the pigeons. "You can go in, then. Twelve minutes. If you're not out, Elijah here will start the choir." She lifted her chin at the boy, who made his eyes go the size of saucers as though he had swallowed a miracle.

Inside, the air was one of those old smells, intricately layered, like a meal cooked by a family in which nobody had agreed what celebration was for. There was damp and eggs and the sweet ghost of a pine cleaner. There was an undertone of iron. There was the settled presence of dust that had learned every name this house had gone by and now had opinions.

"Hello," I said to the entryway. I know how it looks, to greet emptiness. But emptiness never stays empty. It fills with your voice if you are not careful. "I'm here to listen," I told the banister and the worn baldness on the second step where someone had learned to leap. I told the rug stain that looked like someone had dropped a star and the star had dissolved slowly into the warp. I told the electrical panel, which wore the tattoos of a careful hand.

The door tried to close behind me, but the hinge caught on the puffed place in the floor and it stayed there, ajar and disapproving. Beyond the living room, a dining room was squared off with a cheap paneling that had turned the color of tea. I moved slowly, not to be polite to spiders but to give the rooms time to decide what to say. When you rush, houses defend themselves with cliché: cold spot, creak, a toy that rolls on no floor. If you wait, they will give you what you weren't brave enough to ask for.

In the dining room, a radiator ran its tongue along its coils and went quiet. The overhead light had a dangling chain with a porcelain pull shaped like a pear. I reached up to touch it and the chain broke off in my hand as cleanly as if it had been waiting for the privilege. I put the pear in my coat pocket and went on.

The kitchen was a chapel. Most kitchens are, though no one likes to hear so. The refrigerator was an older model with a rounded face like a grandmother once beautiful and still capable of making a man nervous. The stove had four gas eyes, two of which looked blind. The sink had a curve that made it smile whether it was tired or not. Above the sink, a window gave onto the yard and through it I could see the boy—Elijah—shape his breath into winter smoke and cup it in his hands like a thing that might ask to be raised.

On the counter, under a dust-gray plastic flower, lay a folded grocery flyer. On the front, someone had circled in blue ink a sale on potatoes, and written beside it in the good careful second-grade cursive of somebody slightly prideful: Scalloped is best. In the margin: Auntie T.

I recognized the handwriting before my brain knew where to put it. Recognition operates like an older sibling, barging ahead and then turning and shouting back the truth over its shoulder. The T had a flourish at the end, as if the writer tossed her initial into the air and trusted it to land correctly. You could tell, just from the curl of the line, what music she listened to when she cleaned the floor.

"Auntie T," I said, to the sink, to the absent aunt. "Teresa."

Walls, when they are startled, contract imperceptibly. The temperature drops the smallest bit, the smallest enough to raise a trace of something on your skin. Houses mortified by being recognized often assault you with the past without warning: a faint tune coming from nowhere, an onion skin that stuck to your shoe in defiance of time, a phone ringing in a key that the last person who lived there would have answered with "Who this?"

In the corner of the kitchen, near the back door, a cupboard crouched. You know the sort: low, five inches deeper than you thought, painted shut and then opened and then painted shut again. Its knob was missing, the circle of wood bare where someone's aesthetic had once been. I crouched and pressed my fingers to the edge and felt the warp release with a reluctant sigh. Inside was a glass jar with a lid, and inside the jar: a ring.

It was a cheap ring, thin and silver, the kind you could buy outside the courthouse from a man whose store lived inside a rolling suitcase. It had a tiny yellow stone, plastic pretending to citrine, and on the inner band, as I ran my thumb over it, were engraved two letters, not quite even: M.T.

I sat on my heels until my calves complained. The light from the sink window made a small trapezoid on the floor, sliced diagonally by the shadow of the faucet handle. Outside, the pigeons made a unanimous sound and Elijah turned his head sharply as if someone had called his name. I put the ring in my left pocket, the one I used to use for house keys that were also my keys and weren't marked with an angry city number.

When I stood, the radiator cleared its throat. The unmistakable sound of a foot upon a stair came from the front room. I left the kitchen, because the kitchen and I knew each other now and I could come back. The front room had a space that used to be a parlor. Somewhere in the wall, perhaps behind the place where someone had hung a family of crooked frames, something small scurried, a reckoning of mice.

"Hello," I said again, because once isn't a greeting, it's a mistake. "If there's anyone left who wants to tell me what should be written down, I'm here now. I'm not a clipboard person. I write on the backs of things. I write on my hand. I write on whatever sentence doesn't resist me. You get to choose what gets saved."

I always talk too much at first. Houses find this comforting. It makes you look like the kind of person who will keep talking even when the roof starts to loosen its ribs, and that means you are the kind of person who will also keep listening.

On the narrow staircase, paint had checked itself into a mosaic. On the fourth step, someone had scratched PRINCE into the wood with something sharper than a key and then drawn a crown over the P. It was not careful work, but it was not careless. Upstairs the air deepened, couch cushions and dryer lint. The first bedroom held an orphaned mattress and a tangle of extension cords. The second held a mirror leaned against the wall. In the third, a patch of ceiling had fallen and the plaster dust lay like a wedding dress somebody had decided to take off at the wrong moment.

In the mirror, my face was gentler than I felt. There was that line at my mouth I had refused a year ago and then met at a dinner I couldn't leave. The scar at my temple where the cupboard corner had reminded me not to rush. In the glass, a corner of the hallway reflected a blur—a movement, smallest, like a cat's tail you almost imagined. I turned and saw nothing. When I turned back, the mirror had shifted infinitesimally to the left. I closed my eyes and counted five. When I opened them, dust motes were doing a procession in the light, small priests with nothing to bless.

The third bedroom looked onto the back alley. In the back alley, a blue car with one green door had been abandoned and then adopted by the morning glories; they had decided it was a trellis and no amount of municipal notices could convince them otherwise. There was a dresser under the window. The top drawer had no pull. It was stuck at that point drawers get stuck: where the promise of opening is so present you would like to bite the wood to make it confess.

I ran my fingernails along the seam, cursing in the voice my mother had used when she had missed the bus by seventeen seconds. Mother. Teresa. I do not say her name often. The problem with names is that they are the kinds of things you can be persuaded to keep saying even after the person no longer answers. The drawer released its breath. Inside, there were receipts for groceries from a decade ago, a church program with the corners chewed off, a photo—my breath went sideways—a photo of me and someone else in the backyard of a house with a fence I did not recognize. I had my hair in two braids. I was eight, glaring at the camera with my entire body. The someone else had a mouth like mine. She had written on the back in blue ink: M. don't make that face, it'll stick. —T.

I did not come apart. It is one of my few skills. The room did a small tilt toward me. My ears filled with the sound of my own blood.

It is an ordinary thing, to arrive at a place where, unbeknownst to you, your mother has once stood and to find a letter leaning toward you from the decade when she still belonged in the category of the living you could call and ask why she had never taught you to make scalloped potatoes. It is an ordinary thing in a city where people have always left. And yet. And yet the room, sensing me, pulled itself together.

From the hallway, the murmur of voices floated up. Miss Dora and the boy had entered, despite their arrangement, because neighborhoods make rules and then transgress them together. I could smell the cold on their coats like a spice. I came to the top of the stairs and the house, in satisfaction, gave a small click somewhere deep within what had been its mouth.

"Time's up," Miss Dora called, but softly, as if not to scare a thing that might not be fully formed. "I let you have thirteen. I know what thirteen means in this house."

"What does it mean?" I asked, descending. None of us looked at the pear pull that had fallen from the light. Miss Dora had the kind of eyes that took in everything and pretended to take nothing so you would not guard yourself from her. Elijah held one hand in the other as if he had caught something and wasn't sure yet whether it would bite.

"It means," Miss Dora said, "that this house was lucky and didn't know it until it forgot. It means I had my first kiss on the stoop in a snow like this and it meant nothing in the moment and then meant too much exactly five years after. It means the landlord got tired of replacing door glass because certain girls with careful handwriting liked to tell certain boys their names belonged in a heart. It means nobody ever baked a cake in that kitchen in the afternoon because the sun came in too hard and made the frosting fight you."

She looked at me a long time. "It means your mother used to sit on the second stair from the bottom," she said without warmth or meanness, only the way you say the weather in a room. "And she used to fix her stockings before she left for evenings that made her useless the next day. Teresa with the yellow ring. I see it, keep it. You won't have time to come back for it."

Elijah looked at me, them, me again. He was too young to hide how much he liked knowledge that made adults uneasy. The pigeons outside had started a second parade, richer, as if a drummer had joined the band and was only going to get better.

"Do you want to come to the community meeting tonight?" Miss Dora asked. "The Goodmans from the development corporation will be there with their cookies and their charts and their 'we love heritage' mouths. You can sit and take notes and pretend you're Switzerland. Or you can just eat a cookie and hear your mother's name said by five women like a proverb."

"I'll come," I said, not sure whether I was agreeing to a meeting or to the rest of my life.

At the threshold, the house let out a breath that was not mine. The doorframe brushed against my shoulder like a relative who had never learned the difference between affection and ownership. I stepped onto the stoop and the winter day folded itself around me, crisp and ridiculous, the street glinting with old ice in the cracks. Elijah tore a corner off a piece of bread and held it up. One pigeon went absolutely still, the way he had seen his elders do when something was good enough to deserve a body.

"You write this one nice," Miss Dora said, pinching the bridge of her nose as if she could press a headache into hiding. "You tell them this house had company when it needed company. You tell them it smelled like somebody knew how to cut an onion without crying. You tell them the roof leaks where roofs always leak and you pass me the bucket when I call you from bed."

"I will," I said. My hand was still in my coat pocket, holding the pear-shaped light pull. The ring in the other pocket dug into my thigh in a way that would leave a faint red half-moon. From somewhere inside the house, the faintest sound came, like a small portion of laughter from someone thinking of something a long time ago.

At the car, I looked back. The upstairs window had fogged with our breath or the breath of a memory stubborn enough to refuse evacuation. There are things I do not believe in, like grand gestures and heaven. There are things I cannot help believing, like the persistence of certain rooms and the desire of some houses to get the last word. And so when, just before I turned my key, a whisper came through the door—soft, the way a person's voice sounds when she is pretending to be asleep and wants you to come closer—I stood still and let it open the skin between my ribs.

The house said my name. Not the one the city used, or the one my husband had used when he was trying to be kind, or the brisk syllables of coworkers. It used the one my mother had used when she had still believed in the child's version of me and the possibility of soup. It was the name that belonged only to certain afternoons and a turquoise plastic bowl. It was the name nobody had said in twenty years, not even me.

"Marita," the house said.

The day I came home, the fog had already let itself in. It lay in the bowls on the table as if someone had ladled it there; it beaded on the spine of my mother’s cookbook and curled under the door like an animal that had learned the latch. Every cloth in the house was damp. The jars that used to hold peaches had their mouths open, gathering, gathering, as if the season had never ended.

Out on the road, the fog licked at ankles, lampposts, the low stone walls where ornamental poppies had once swayed. People stepped into it the way you step into a memory you cannot quite bear to finish, and let it stick to their lashes. The island hadn’t changed its habit of feeding itself from what couldn’t be owned. It had changed the price. It was my first thought when I stepped off the ferry and my hand slapped the salt-gritty rail: someone had finally started charging the fog.

“You’re longer than you said.” Aunt Kittie met me at the dock with a paper cup of coffee I didn’t want and pressed it into my hand as if it were language itself and I might have forgotten mine. Her face was browner than I remembered, or else her hair whiter. The coffee was sweet enough to pull the teeth out of my head.

“The bus broke down,” I said, because that was true and easy, and because the other reason—that I had stood for ten minutes in the hardware aisle on the mainland, staring at the display of fog knives and wondering which edge was the one my mother would have pointed to—felt like something the island didn’t deserve yet. The knives were illegal here anyway, except by license.

“I thought you of all people wouldn’t be squeamish about a ferry.” Kittie lifted my suitcase before I could. She had the arms of a person who lifted things all day and called them by tender names. “Well. You look like the mainland.”

“Do I.” The hair I’d cut myself in the bathroom mirror two nights ago was still too uneven to be a choice; the sandals were ten-dollar foam and kept slapping me back for every step I took. “That seems unfortunate.”

She laughed and then remembered herself. “There’s stew,” she said. She always opened conversations like that, with food and then regret. “At the house. If the fog hasn’t eaten it.”

“The fog eats stew?” I imagined lifting the lid and finding white, a new skin, the shape of our scoops preserved like fossils. When my mother was a girl, there were stories about fog that picked up the cries of any child and took them wandering—the island simply took things and made itself heavier with them. We all pretended not to have fed it. We all fed it.

“Everything eats stew if you leave it.” Kittie took the cup back and finished it herself.

The ferry sounded its horn once, a long note that made the antique shop cat rouse and curse. It felt obscene to me that so much was exactly as it had been: the gas pump that blinked out 00.00 and then clicked uselessly; Mrs. Chu’s hair in the window of the seamstress shop, a cloud in its own right. If the island were as unchanged as it appeared, then my leaving and my being gone had been as unimportant as I had hoped they would be. If not, I had failed it and not even noticed the failure.

And yet: the posted signs were new. Each place that used to wear a painted mermaid or a child’s name now wore metal: FOGGING PERMIT REQUIRED; DO NOT SYPHON WITHOUT REGISTRY; REPORT ALL CONDENSATION THEFT. Someone had stenciled a blue raindrop on the side of Kittie’s van, which I remembered as green and serviceable and now was blue and just as serviceable as ever. The raindrop had a serial number under it. Kittie saw me looking.

“They fined us for not dressing like a business,” she said, with half a smirk. “So I put a dress on the van.”

“You own a business now?”

“I own what your mother refused to, which is a license. She was happier pretending no one was watching.”

We walked the long way back to the house because the short way went by the school, and even now I couldn’t stand the smell of pencil shavings through those windows, or the taste of blue chalk when you talked with your mouth open and it drifted in. Also the short way went by the statue of the man they said had built the first fog fence. He had the bland concentrated face of a person in love with an idea. I didn’t want to look at him looking at us.

“And you,” I said, to keep us to safe familiars, “are you still stepping onto roofs at night to shake the gutters?”

“At my age?” She sounded offended, the way she did whenever I implied she might be considered old. “Never mind roofs. They built the new fences so tall we can walk right under the gutters without touching them. All the water goes where it’s told, now. We spend our nights writing down how obedient it was.”

“Who gets the water?” I had listened to the mainland news on the bus and tasted dust through the filter in the air-conditioning. I knew already, in the way you know you are being played with as a child and pretend to enjoy it out of love. It was still a question I wanted my aunt, who wore her answers like a sweater, to answer.

“Depends on the day.” Kittie set my suitcase down on the house walk so she could reach for the door. The screen’s bottom corner had the same tear it had when I was eight and newly permitted to come back from the shore without a sister. “On the wind. On the quota. On who was seen at the meeting. You’ll learn.”

“I won’t be here long,” I said quickly, and then, because that had sounded cruel even to my own ears, “I mean, I don’t want to—”

“I don’t expect you to want.” She pushed the door open. “It wants for you.”

Inside, the house was both mother and not: the same stain on the table where bleach had met cherry juice and decided to be a map; the same crack across the back of the sprawled green couch. But I had expected the dishes to lobby for her, piling in a sink the way they used to, growing white fur like things neglected and cherished in equal measure. I had expected the trailing plants in their macramé hangers to clack their wooden beads together in irritation. The counter was clean. The plants were cut to nubs. The air was all honeysuckle and iron.

“I didn’t know what to do with the plants,” Kittie said, when she saw I was looking. “They got brittle when she chose. So I cut them back and told them it was for their own good.”

“When she chose what?” I stood, not sitting because if I sat I might be the same person who had sat here and thrown a salt shaker at someone for saying my mother had climbed into fog the way some people climbed into beds. If I didn’t sit, I could be someone else: the visitor who wiped her feet and asked real-estate questions and pointed at floorboards and said, There is a dip there, did you know.

“When she chose to walk through,” Kittie said.

“You mean die,” I said, and the word felt adolescent and defiant in my mouth, like profanity that had been carefully saved for an occasion not worthy of it.

“I mean what I said.” Kittie went to the stove and lifted the lid on a pot that always had a lid—always had something under it left over from the finest last meal in the world. Steam lifted and found the air was already full. It hesitated and then made itself smaller, negotiated a space between the other wetnesses. “You think fog is only a matter of water. Maybe that was true before my grandmother. Maybe that will be true again when they iron the island flat enough to fit their numbers. In the middle we get to be wrong.”

“She drowned.” I was twelve when Tommy Kline told me he had seen her feet leave the ladder on the western fence and go up instead of down. I had shoved his face into the sand until his mouth found grit and tears. He didn’t take it back. No one ever takes anything back here. We would rather choke.

“She didn’t drown.” Aunt Kittie stirred with a wooden spoon, and the fog braided itself around her wrist where the old wristwatch, my grandfather’s, had clung so long she had a bony pale ring to show where a circle had been. “Bodies drown. Your mother was a body when it suited her. When it didn’t, she was not.”

I felt a sudden exhausted fury, a child’s, pure and helpless. I wanted to climb onto the counter and shout into the poor stew. I wanted to make the shelves speak. “You speak like that because she was your sister.”

“I speak like that because she was my sister and your mother,” Kittie said. She turned off the flame and the house sighed with it. “Would you like to see what she left.”

“Is there a body?” My exhaustion melted at the edges and dripped onto the floor by my shoes.

“There are the things that made a body look like her.” Kittie wiped her hands on a cloth and then remembered the cloth was one of the ones that wasn’t allowed to be wiped on. She folded it neatly, scolding it with her hands as if it had misbehaved. “There’s a letter if you want to call it a letter. She never could make a single sentence without giving it two jobs.”

“All right,” I said, like agreement could be a door and I was pushing.

We went into the little room at the front of the house where the fog liked to sit—which is how you knew it was older than our houses, more stubborn, because the front room views the road and what you mostly see through that window is your neighbor’s throat clearing. The glass was thick with breath. People’s names were pushed into it. I hadn’t ever noticed before that this was a calendar. You wiped your own name away the day you were forgiven.

On the table were things that might have been a child’s treasure pile: a shard of blue china with a chrysanthemum that didn’t know it was a flower; a bottle cap with a bird on it that had not flown since I was seventeen; my mother’s fog knife, the handle worn satin under her thumb. I picked it up and then put it down, and my thumb wanted to go after it.

“She left the knife to me?” I asked, though it was foolish as questions go. Tools pass to hands in this family. You don’t list them in the will as if they were land.

“She left the knife to whoever would pick it up,” Kittie said. She reached under the table and brought up a brown paper package with string around it. The string was the kind from the co-op that never quite knots and has to be held in the mouth while you maneuver the rest. She tugged it loose and the paper sprang like a thing badly wrapped to start with, which was my mother’s manner of protecting anything: badly, quickly, with the assumption that anyone who wanted it could have it. Inside was a notebook, its cover greasy from years of counters and pockets. It had been hers the way handwriting is yours even when you copy your best friend’s Gs.

I did not touch it.

“Another time,” I said, appalled at myself.

“There may not be another time,” Kittie said, with a gentleness I stood against because it made me want to lie down.

“What is it,” I said, because my aunt had always liked to be asked.

“A map,” she said. “Or music. Or both. She took the fence into herself and gave it back out as a line of places to step. There are marks where she tested the knots. There are marks where the fog was thick with dead men’s breath and there are marks where it was thick with living men’s greed. She drew a way through, is what I’m telling you. And then she walked. And she didn’t drown.”

There are times in a life when a person you have loved in one way offers you the possibility of loving them in another, where you can turn your face like a sunflower. I stood in my mother’s front room with the fog tasting my skin for salt and felt the possibility lay itself down in front of me like boards over water. The planks had gaps. The water had teeth.

“I only came,” I said, and my voice had gone baby-soft and awful, “because the man on the phone said I had to sign for… for the… my mother’s… for legal…”

“For the right to leave without them calling you every week.” Kittie nodded. “They want your signature on how little you know. They want you to say yes to a number that will make you quiet, so they can hammer some new metal into our shore and listen to it ping. The mainland likes its song with no words.”

“Did she—what did she do with her—” I couldn’t say the words bank account, ring, dress. They felt like the pieces of her that had chafed.

“She left you the house.” Kittie did not indulge me with a pause. She set the knife down with a clack that startled me out of my chest. “And whatever is in it that she couldn’t name. And her license.”

“I don’t want, I can’t—”

“You can sell it to Mr. Pereyra, if that’s how it is. He’ll put a fence through the kitchen. He wants to make a demonstration of how civilized we are. People will tour. They will lean on the doorframe where you scraped your knee and leave their gum in your mother’s teacup. It will be some of the best workmen he’ll ever hire. No offense to workmen. I am one. But I am telling you, it will be said to be for the good of us all, and it will not be for your good in any way that matters. And anyway, you can’t sell it until you notice the fog has already got in and laid claim.”

“It isn’t a person,” I said, and felt foolish immediately. You can make anything a person by talking to it. That was one of the things that had made me leave. The other was that the island had given me a name I didn’t want, and the mainland had been willing, for a while, to call me by any name I chose.

“Mireya,” Kittie said, her voice suddenly different. Factual. “When the fog came in this morning, it had your breath in it.”

“What.”

“It knew where to go.” She picked up the notebook and held it like bread. “And—never mind. You’ll hear it yourself if it’s for you.”

I did not mean to say, Stay. I said it to my feet. I said it to the stew. I said it to the door, which had always been the third person in any conversation in this house, because of how it did and did not line up with its frame. “If I stay, it doesn’t bring her back.”

“If you leave, it doesn’t send her farther,” said Kittie. “Stop trying to manage distance with your body.”

I laughed, because the alternative was a sound that would have had to be called by the old name for keening, and the island does not like to hear itself called old. “I am hungry.”

“That’s more like it.” She lifted bowls and laid them on the table where nothing else was allowed to be. “We can show the fog how to eat properly.”

We ate with the window open and the fog put its hands on our shoulders like a great-aunt who is always too cold in the theater. Beyond the yard the fence showed itself only by its supports, thin spidery poles that began somewhere that had once been gardens and went down the slope to the west where the cliff breathed tides like a sleeping chest. The net that hung between poles was a silk so fine you could not see it until the fog touched it and the whole lace became a garment. When I was nine, I ran into it full tilt because I believed in furniture’s honesty. My mother had lifted me out of it and plucked the strands from my cheeks and said, You say thank you to the thing that caught you, which is how we keep the things that catch us from wanting to close their hands.

Now, between mouthfuls, Kittie told me in a voice that meant she had told herself many times already, “There are men who come in suits and say, You could be rich. They say, You could sell the fog by the ounce with little gold labels on it and people will drink it at their parties and think they have swallowed a weather. They say this because they have already built the boxes to hold it. They have already labeled the boxes. They need nothing from us but our air. It makes them hate us that we have something that is not theirs yet.”

“And you,” I said. “What do you say.”

She tilted her bowl to get the last of the stew and banged the side with her spoon like I used to. “I say, Personally, I enjoy being hated by a man in a suit. It reminds me that I have mass. But I also say: I do not see any reason to put a label on what already knows my name. The fog comes when I call. It does not come when they do.”

“You talk as though it listens.”

“If it didn’t, all our dead would be just dead.” She did not soften it for me. I loved her for that and hated her as a person who had been allowed to stay. Out the window, a finch hit the net and bounced off with indignant competence and flew away, and I was relieved to have a thing I could love without complexity: the embarrassment of small birds when physics surprises them.

After we had rinsed the bowls and argued about whose house this was, and lost, and found the night with our hands instead of a switch because the electricity had forgotten us for the moment, Kittie went to the door and put her hand out waist-high.

“Say I will be back at supper,” she said, like a polite borrower.

“You live here,” I said, and then remembered she did not. She lived two streets down, with a woman named Ila who named all her plants after famous swimmers and who had upgraded their mattress the way you change a car part: exactly, without romance, with excellent results.

“I live where my work lives,” she said. “The rest of the time this house is yours or the fog’s, whichever is less fussy. If you are frightened, you can come sleep with the top of my head.” It was what she had said to me when I was six and afraid of the story about the boy who had drowned in his own tub, incredulous, face toward the ceiling.

“I am not frightened.” The lie was so efficient it made me proud. “Thank you.”

There is a way people leave on this island where they are not really leaving you; they are walking into another room to get the sugar. Kittie went like that, with her hand still saying I will be back and the door taking her in bites. When it closed, the house made a small bell sound. The fog trembled as if someone had whispered across it. I stood and let my ears fill.

It will seem invented when I say that what I heard was my name. Maybe it was only the wind and the soft knocking of dowels in their sockets and the way ears insist on pattern because patterns keep us upright on stairs.

Still. It came from the back room, where my mother kept her boots and the grocery list that had groceries on it even when we didn’t. It came not as Mireya, the way people on the mainland tried to make my name taste like their tongues, but as the way Kittie used to call me when I went too near the edge of the rock that grew the blue barnacles and the eelgrass you could braid into your hair if you liked slime: Miri, said fast, twice. Miri Miri, like a bird you could teach to say two words but not grow tired of them.

I went as if a rope had been tied to my ribs and someone had given a polite pull. The back room had the weight of coats. The smell of them was ours: fish oil, lemon in the winter, cigarettes in the summer when my mother liked to forget herself. On the bench was a letter with my name on it in her handwriting. The handwriting had the grace of someone who thinks the future can be held down and still. Under the letter was a flat of jars that had been prepared and not used, their lids ringless and bright.

Outside, the fence wire pinged. The sound is what you hear when a ship changes its mind.

I stood and did not take the letter.

“Miri,” my name said again, and this time it did not bring me toward the bench. It brushed the back of my neck and blew a strand of hair into my mouth and opened. There is no word I’ve learned on the mainland for that opening. There is a word here, but it was not made of an alphabet. It was made of standing in fog and feeling it take your shape and then not.

“Not now,” I said, to everything.

Someone on the road laughed and threw a bottle. Somewhere a gull picked up a thing that was not food and insisted. The letter was weight on paper. The fog was weight without paper. My mother had been both and had left me both and I had come back intending to sign something that meant I didn’t have to think about either.

The second time my name came it was not a calling. It was a telling, the way you say the name of a tool before you use it, to remind it what it is for. My skin did its small disloyalty to me and thrilled.

“Fine,” I said, and sat on the bench as if it were a new religion and crossed myself in the old way that belonged to no church but habit, and picked up the letter and broke it at its fold. The fog leaned as if to see. The house, which had wanted to be anyone’s more obedient child than mine, endured.

My mother’s first sentence was not a sentence. It was a direction.

Go where the fence sounds thinner than your breath, it said. Then it will hold you.

Every Thursday I carry the future in a tin that stains.

The label on the side reads Tidefast #17, but in the Bureau we call it Remainder, a blue that refuses to dry the way it should. If a sunbeam hits it wrong, it looks wet again. If the air grows thick with salt, it darkens. Children say the line blossoms at night, that it seeps like a bruise through plaster and brick and the names penciled on doorframes. People will insist that is superstition as they slide their wardrobes a few inches away from my marks.

Our trucks started out white. Now, no matter how often the interns scrub them, there is always a drift of blue along the doors, the wheel wells, our cuffs and nails. The city marks us the way we mark it. Once, when I stopped by the clinic for Father’s blood pressure tablets, a woman in the line touched my wrist and pulled her hand back, stained, as if prophecy were contagious. She laughed, embarrassed, asked if it would come off by Sunday. I told her to try vinegar and patience.

Today, three boys with a plastic football jog around my ankles while I unload the measuring pole. One of them mimics the grinding sound the Bureau truck makes when the transmission doesn’t quite catch, a funny, wicked imitation of anything governmental. Another calls me Señora Blue, which is a promotion from the last neighborhood’s choice: Plague.

Above us the parrots brag in their pepper leaves, little bright bureaucrats of their own. Their colony moved into the ficus when the last utility pole was removed in this block, and their nests hang like rough sacks, twined with wire and fishing line and strips of garbage bags. They speak in other people’s voices, a chorus of misdirected calls, long-ago arguments, passwords whispered too near an open window. “Mother’s maiden name?” one of them asks the street, almost sweetly. Another answers itself: “I decline.”

The house I’ve come to measure is the fourth from the corner, lime plaster and a cornice of molded vine leaves. The portico will be hip-deep, according to the model, in five years; the kitchen tiles, in eight. The municipal archive gave me a sheet with the family name, the parcel number, and the coordinates where the river will cross itself and remember it used to be ocean. My job is to get the line right. Someone from the Bureau of Mortgages will handle the loan forgiveness paperwork; someone from Cultural Heritage will come for the ceramic saints in niches and anything with an old signature; someone from the Department of Rehousing might, if the lists ever shorten, find them a place further uphill. People think I am all those other someones. People think if they argue long enough with me, the water will take pity. People think if they kiss the heart tattoo on my wrist—my late mother’s initial—I will aim one centimeter higher than I should. I do not correct anyone anymore.

The door opens before I can knock. The woman on the threshold is the age of my father but straighter in her shoulders, with a scarf knotted at her throat in a precise bow. She is holding a cup like a weapon.

“This is my daughter’s house,” she says, as if to posit that she has no business with the future, she is merely passing through for the afternoon to water the plants.

“I’m here for the line,” I say.

“The line we did not ask for,” she says. “The line that is an excuse.”

She does not step aside. Behind her, a hallway widens into a sitting room where velvet sofa backs face away from the door, as if the furniture has been caught in the act of turning its back on strangers. A lace doily rests on an armrest with the neatness of grief.

“It’s protocol to accompany me while I mark,” I say.

The parrots, as if bored with us, volley, “Name of your first pet!” and “Fourteen!” The boys have drifted to the end of the block where a woman is peeling mangoes with a knife that gleams like a prayer blade. Juice makes her fingers glow.

The woman on the threshold sighs and shifts, lets me in, but her gaze lingers on my tin. “Will you at least do it low,” she says. “Quiet. My grandson is sleeping.”

“The height is calculated from the tide gate at Puerto Chico, the storm surges, the rate of subsidence.” I could say more: the error bars; the weatherman who cried the night the estuary swallowed the bus stop; the way our models fatten like pigeons over certain districts and starve over others. “I will be as quiet as I can.”

“Quiet,” she repeats, as if that were the insult. “No one warns you loud anyway. They mail you a soft envelope.”

I set down the tin and the pole. The pole is an instrument we pretend gives authority to what is essentially an act of faith. A brass float, two glass vials, a laser level, a bubble like a green pupil that must be kept centered. It hums when I turn it on, its small mind calculating tilt and distance. In its hum I hear all the Bureau’s directives, my boss Velasco’s kind and ruthless voice: Do not round. Do not console. Do not assume you bring news. You are a recorder, not a herald.

I touch the wall at the foyer and feel damp tucked behind the paint like a secret. “I can mark outside,” I say. “Kitchens, on the cabinets. Bedrooms, on baseboards. Nothing at head height, where it will greet them every morning.”

“It greets you either way,” the woman says. “Blue at your ankle is still blue in your head.”

I open the tin. The smell is chemical and coastal. A nervous, metallic ocean. My brother once said it was the exact shade of denial. He only ever came to my apartment when he was in trouble, and last year he slept three nights on my couch because he had tagged the steps of the Ministry of Planning with his own angry blue, a row of little fish skeletons climbing the marble. “They banned the trucks from our street for a week,” I told him, furious because when he did something, he pressed both palms into it. He smiled like a bruise. “I just wanted them to see what they are doing.”

Now he is somewhere I cannot measure with a pole. Now we say gone as if it were a place he bought a ticket to visit.

“Señora?” the woman says. “If you are dreaming, I cannot stand here all day.”

We go outside. She fidgets with her scarf. “My name is Inés,” she says finally. “Doña Inés, if you want courtesy.”

“Mara,” I say, the name quick between us. I check the bubble, the laser’s tiny pink dot that makes my stomach turn every time I see it on plaster, on concrete, on periwinkle paint. The children loiter a polite distance away now, sensing ceremony. This is what we have become: a city that recognizes ritual in bureaucratic gestures.

At the right-hand corner of the house, someone long ago embedded a tile of the Sacred Heart into the wall, brim in pink rays. It is a good tile—the kind with the glaze that crazes but does not flake. The laser dot lands just beneath it, a throat’s width.

“You can go higher, perhaps,” says a voice behind me. A man in a soccer jersey that strains across his stomach, a toddler propped against his hip. “We run a shop,” he adds unexpectedly. “Groceries. We will lose everything if you mark that high.”

“Your packet has the appeal form,” I say gently. “If other data becomes available, if this year’s storms—”

He is shaking his head before I finish. “Appeal to who, Señorita? The same desk that gave you your blue?” He laughs, but he isn’t wrong.

“Do you think she can put it lower,” says the woman with the mangoes to no one in particular, “and the tide will listen like a dog?”

Doña Inés folds her arms. “Let the girl work. You won’t bribe water with conversation.”

I dip my brush. The first stroke is always too careful. Velasco says it should be an unbroken stroke if possible; an unbroken life. The bristles climb the plaster and leave that improbable blue behind, the color of surgeries and parrots, the color of news anchors’ earrings. I exhale. The line is a quiet thing and it is also a siren. It looks like nothing and then, once it exists, like everything.

A child has his hand on the wall before I can stop him. His palm comes away blue, five petals. He grins, then frowns and rubs it on his shorts. The stain smears. I offer him a rag and he takes it, disappointed that magic has such easy undoing. Later he will go home with a pale echo on his thigh and a grandmother who sighs and says so now we know, and a mother who scrubs until bedtime and it is still faintly there. In their sleep they will move away from whatever touches that place.

My phone vibrates twice in my pocket: Father. I ignore the first call because he sometimes butt-dials when he sits down too quickly. He has opinions on momentum now, as if all his life were an argument with physics: why a body should touch chair and then immediately renounce chair. The second call I answer with paint still on my fingers, holding the phone a hair away from my cheek.

“I found the book,” he says without preamble.

“Which book, Pa?” I keep my voice even. There is the book he has misplaced every morning for a month, the one with the escapement diagrams we used to pore over when I was a girl and we made up names for the shapes of gears.

“The one about the fish,” he says triumphantly. “The one we never returned to the library. Your mother loved the drawings, remember? The little mouths, or maybe the fins.”

“The field guide?” I say. “Pa, that one we donated when—”

“Donated,” he interrupts, sourness thickening the word. “When we had to trash half the shelf because mold had come to live with us. Mold pays no rent. The landlord said buy bleach, as if bleach can teach manners.” He breathes into the phone. “Anyway, it was under the sink. There is no sink under the sink. Did you know a sink can be mostly pipe?”

“I’ll be home in an hour,” I say. “Do not drink the bleach.”

“Who drinks bleach?” he says, offended. “Your brother drank seawater once. He said it tasted like everything we were not allowed to say.”

I hold the phone to my cheek without noticing. The screen leaves a faint rectangle of blue near my ear that will follow me until I scrub with a brush. “I love you,” I say.

“I love you,” he answers automatically, then adds, softer, “Do not bring me any of those lines, Marita. The walls are tired enough.”

When I lower the phone, the parrots are at it again. “Your first teacher?” one calls. “Your first street?” Another laughs, a sound that is a perfect imitation of my brother’s laugh. For a second I forget to breathe. I look up into the leaves as if the laugh could be in there, as if Davi is a green body dipped in sunlight and feathers. But the swift bodies are only birds. One of them has woven a silver cassette tape into its nest so it glints like a fish each time the air moves.

I finish the line across the front face of the house, the brush laying down blue that means later we will box these rooms and lift them piece by piece into a truck or boat or nothing. The grocery man has retreated, the toddler asleep against his shoulder, his hand patting a rhythm that will outlast his anger. Doña Inés has the hubcap of her concentration on.

“The kitchen cabinets?” I ask her.

“If you must,” she says, and the two words contain half the history of the city.

Inside, it is cooler. The tiles have a little green in them, a lean-to shade someone chose fifty years ago against glare. On the countertop, near a bunch of plantains brooding in a bowl, a framed photograph of a graduation: a thin man in a hat too big for his face, a woman in a red dress whose happiness makes her eyes look younger than the rest of her.

“My daughter,” says Inés, noticing where I am looking. “She is in the mountains now. the city is no good for breathing because of our neighbor.” She means the river. She says neighbor with a grim love. “Do you know what they do to wives in the mountains?” She raises an eyebrow. “They make them pick coffee and sing.”

I measure, I mark. The cabinet takes the blue like a bruise. The house does not make any new sounds for me. Some houses talk. Some leak secrets under your hands like a low fever. This house endures.

On my way out, a girl is leaning against the gate across the street, the bakery gate. Her hair is thick and black and braided down one shoulder, flour dusting the braid like a snowfall somewhere improbable. Sol. She and I played a game as children on the bus where we pointed at strangers and invented their jobs. She always made people into soloists. “That one is a tuba player,” she would whisper, which meant unrequited. Now her forearms are scalloped with little burns, tiny moons catching light. Her bakery is called Pan del Día painted in white on a teal wall, but everyone in the area calls it Sol’s.

“Don’t,” she says when she sees where my hands are heading.

My brush hovers. The model tells me her ovens will be shin-deep and then knee-deep and then we will rescue what can be moved and arrange it elsewhere, perhaps under a new sign, Sol’s Again. “I have to,” I say. “You know I have to.”

She looks up at the parrots as if to ask if there is a world where we can refine our choices to the angle of a wrist. The parrots are too busy with their rehearsals. “Dock nine,” one says suddenly, my brother’s voice pitched one register off. “After dark.” Someone throws a seed at them. A parrot drops it and says, gently, “No, thank you.”

My mouth goes dry. It is a phrase I haven’t allowed myself to say out loud in months, those two words and the time. They were in the last message he sent that was not a picture of something raw or triumphant: Dock nine. After dark. By the time I found the message, the phone had chimed with a dozen newer irrelevancies. The timing was wrong, and my mind did not rise quick enough to meet it. The department of Fisheries and the Port Authority and our own Bureau argued for weeks about whose business it was to search the water by the pilings for a long, lean thing shaped like hope. I stopped going to the dock after the third day of nothing, which felt like betrayal and survival at once.

“Mara?” Sol says softly. “Your face.”

“It’s fine,” I say, not fine at all. I dip the brush. I draw the line across the bakery wall where the flour will later not reach. Sol watches, and then she touches the wet paint with the tip of her finger, leaves a dot. A pinprick of proof.

“Leave it,” she says. “It’s like the border of a photograph.”

“You will not be able to sell bread if you are below the line,” I remind her, Bureau reflex. “The inspectors—”

“The inspectors love bread. I will give them the ends of the crust. I will give them coffee. I will place a tin cup on this line and catch the sun in it every morning.” Her laugh is bare. “Do you remember when you and I swam at the soccer fields after the rain? When we pretended we were the first kind of fish, the kind who grew lungs out of stubbornness?”

“A salamander,” I say. The memory tastes like bright grass, a fever. “We got ringworm.”

“My mother said the water was insulted we had enjoyed it,” Sol says. “She said we should apologize to the field. It is not easy, being a witness.”

Outside, someone is arguing about a parking space. The parrots are quiet, as if the phrase they have thrown down has exhausted them. Inés appears behind me again, her scarf looser, her eyes on the bakery window where two loaves sit naked and a third is wrapped in a plastic bag that clings as if it loves bread the way a glove loves a hand.

“I will make coffee,” she says, announcing a truce with the day.

I agree only because my legs have gone weak and coffee is dignity when you have nothing left to lay down between you and the floor. We sit at her small kitchen table with the plantain bowl between us like a timepiece. The coffee is black and hot and I swallow it too fast. It wakes the anxious animal that lives behind my sternum. I let it move.

“You cannot bring him back by painting prettier,” Inés says, surprising me. She doesn’t say his name, but we both know the shape she means, the absence that takes its chair without asking. “You can bring your father a fan that does not rattle.”

“He says the fan lies,” I say. “He says it tells him his papers are flying away.”

“Your father likes to collect the wind,” she says. “He always did.” This is the first I realize she knows who I am, not just the fact of me but the trail that leads from me backwards through house drawers. In a city this size it is hard not to be known by at least three old women in every block.

When I leave, the line is a necklace on the block and we are all wearing it. A man is washing his car with a hose that twitches like a flower stem in the heat. He lifts the jet and, for a moment, lays the stream across the blue, and the water pushes the pigment aside without removing it, as if it respects the tint. He shakes his head and returns to the wheel wells.

At the truck, a smear of blue across the seat matches the smear on my forearm. I have been careful, but the work finds the body anyway. A message from Velasco waits on my screen: a polite reminder that this week’s lines must be uploaded with photographs, that this month the minister wants figures to the tenth. Do not round. Do not console. I snap the pictures in the approved framing, upload over a network that flickers each time a bus passes, because each bus now is a rumor of power.

On the way to Father’s, I drive along the river road because I am weak for it. The water is low today, the bottom visible where it should not be, a suggestion of ribs under a shirt. Children run down and try to pick up stranded fish with their hands, squealing each time the slick bodies torpedo away through the shallow to a brief reprieve. A billboard by the ferry dock offers us boots with a guaranteed lifespan: “the last pair you’ll ever need,” which is an unkind promise in a city where feet outlast soles and love outlasts boats. Someone has already scrawled a skull over the boot.

At Puerto Chico, the fishermen sit on milk crates and mend their nets with needles the size of pencils. They look up when my truck passes, then back at their hands. Dock nine is further down, beyond the warehouse that used to sell a brand of paint no one wanted, beyond the piles of pallets where teenagers kiss, beyond the angle where the river forgets to be polite and pushes its hip into the land.

At red lights, the parrots from other neighborhoods practice other secrets. “Name your favorite teacher,” one says in a voice that might have taught me long division. “Name the month your mother was born.” I do not answer. The red becomes green and then yellow and then green again. I imagine the dock in the dark, and my stomach turns as if it cannot settle on a time either.

Father’s building is five floors with a grill at the entrance that now stays open more often than not because the key mechanism is insulted by the salt and refuses to click. On the landing, someone has stacked four buckets and a broom in preparation for a leak that is not yet visible. My father has taped a piece of paper to the door: Beware of Mold. It flaps when I open, as if it wants to leave.

He is at the table with a glass of water and the field guide to fish, which is, as I told him, impossible. He has a good imitation from a street vendor, a book with neat drawings of fins that look like leaves. He lifts the glass in a toast. “Water,” he says solemnly. “To our neighbor.”

“Do not flirt with the neighbor,” I say. “She will chew your shoes.”

“Youth,” he counters, as if that is an answer to all things.

The apartment smells faintly of bleach and onions. The fan is on and humming. It is not rattling as much as yesterday. There is a damp rag on the back of a chair. He has placed a bowl under the corner where the ceiling wishes to be a colander. It is a good bowl, blue around the rim. He would never put a bad bowl under a leak; you must meet water with dignity or it will scorn you.

“I saw Sol,” I say, to begin him with a safe picture. “She says hello. She put her finger in my ruin.”

“You two,” he says with fondness. “You burned my pot once, do you remember? You made sugar melt to see if it could. It could.”

We eat the plantains I bought on the way up, fried until their edges crisp and turn the color of fortunate pennies. Father tells me about the news he did not watch. I tell him about the parrots and the phrase they dropped: Dock nine. After dark. He flinches but only a little, as if the air moved and the hair on his arm noticed. He looks at me the way he looks at the fan before turning it off at night, as if he knows it will turn back on but for this moment he can master a small thing.

“Don’t go,” he says. He is not the kind of man who has ever told me that. He always let us run, me and Davi, even when the running cost him money, sleep, face. “I mislay my things when you are gone too long.”

“I won’t go today,” I say, a lie I believe for two hours. We watch the little television, where a woman with perfect hair talks about a promotion the water company is running: send us your old pipes and win a year of new ones. The parrots somewhere outside our building practice their funnies: “Your first kiss?” “Your birth month?” “The secret place.” Father falls asleep in his chair with his mouth open, which is how he slept the night he brought me home from the hospital. He would sleep like that in a flood if no one closed his mouth, catching the water with his face.

When the dark arrives, it arrives quickly, the way it did in those afternoons when I worked the late shift at the registry: five minutes and the queue turned into night. I stand in the doorway of the bedroom watching my father’s chest rise, counting the breath the way I count the feet between my line and the floor. I write him a note he will not see: I am buying milk. I put it on the bowl under the leak because at least the bowl looks at us.

Downstairs, the door is stuck; I lift and tug. The street is full of evening conversation, a lightness that might fool me into forgetting the line I drew this morning. The parrots have tucked their heads into their greenness; they sleep with one eye open. My phone is plugged into my palm like an IV; Dock nine, I type into a blank note, and the letters look ridiculous like that, amputated from meaning.

The dock road is almost empty at night now, ever since someone said the pilings creak like bones. The warehouse doors are down; the pallets are bare; the teenagers have gone to roofs where they can accuse the moon of being nosy. My truck sputters once and then catches its breath because it wants me to choose a different narrative for it, one in which it is dependable.

At Dock nine there is always a man who sells cigarettes and boiled eggs from a cooler because you never know which vice you will need. Tonight, he is not there, or he is swallowed by the dark. I park under a light that is both too yellow and not yellow enough. The water is black with sharp shoulders. I think of the phrase like a secret poured into my ear in the wrong year: After dark. It feels too simple now. It feels like something someone would say to a parrot to teach it mischief.

I sit in the cab with my hands on the wheel, my eyes on the plane where the water meets the air, which is the city’s oldest lie. The pilings creak like bones. A figure moves on the far side of the dock, a lanky shadow, a rope over one shoulder. My heart leaps and I do not follow it fast enough. The figure turns into a boy who works hauling crates for the market in the morning. The rope over his shoulder is a belt he bought too large at a stall and has not yet cut down. He yawns. He does not see me.

I should go home. I should go back to my father’s fan and the bowl under the leak and the field guide to fish that is a forgery but at least an honest one. I do not. The parrots are asleep, and there is no one above me to hand down instructions.

When the sound comes, it is not dramatic. It is the slow thrum of a motorboat that has been tuned in a backyard, the way you tune an instrument with love and guessing. It approaches without lights because lights attract a kind of fish you do not want. The man at the tiller is wearing a hat with the brim pulled low against the bugs. He sees my truck even though my headlights are off. He slides the boat along the pilings and ties the rope we all pretend is stronger than it is.

“Mara,” he says. He knows my name and I do not know his, which is one of the endless balances the city strikes, power like a sea-saw. “You were expected.”

“By who,” I say, and the question tastes like a thing I should have asked months ago.

He taps the brim of his hat with one finger, a salute to something I cannot see. “By anyone who finds the future in a can,” he says. “By the sort of city that breeds parrots who gossip.” He nods toward the dark water. “He left you something.” He says it gently, the way you place your palm on a dog’s head when it is shaking.

I step down onto the dock, the wood under my shoe sealing my weight in an agreement with itself. I reach for the rope that is used by everyone and keeps us all in place. I do not know if I am walking toward a letter or a mistake or a beginning. I only know that the line I drew this morning trembled when I put my brush to the wall, as if a house could flinch, and that tremor has followed me and is inside my wrist. The river breathes. The city shifts her shoulder like a woman tasting a new dress.

Somewhere, in a tree, a parrot wakes and asks the dark, “What was the name of your first street?” I am thinking of how, when I was small, I traced the shadow of my brother on a Sunday morning as he stood with his arms out against the brick, because I had read a story about a woman who did that and kept her lover from being lost. The line I made then did not save him. The line I make now will not stop the water. But here is the dock, and here is a boat, and here is my foot, and here is the stirring below us, like a throat clearing before a speech, and tomorrow I will carry the future in a tin again, and tonight I will open my hands to whatever the water has memorized in the steps we take to meet it.

Chapter One: The Ladder

The first thing to vanish in our town was not a creature but a way of moving.

Before the good roads and the new factories, before the river was straightened like a scolded child, the eels used to climb. They were taken by a fever every spring, silver-eyed glass slipping through the locks and up the rain-black ladders our grandfathers built out of stone and willow. My mother said you could hear them at night, a soft beadwork of sound as they writhed over the rungs and into the brown of the canal, as if the water couldn’t bear to be still and was inventing a way to tremble.

Now the ladder lies dry most days. The men, when there are men left to stand with their caps off and curse at the sky, call it useless as a broken zipper. The eels don’t climb anymore; they drift by on their ancient mission, their bodies remembering one direction and forgetting the other.

I stood at the base of the ladder in the blue before sunlight, my boots sunk to the ankle in silt that smelled like iron and old brine. In the pocket of my coat was a notebook with carbon paper and a pencil sharpened to a false point. I had a lure in my other hand that used to belong to Mr. Pacheco—just a handful of willow switches bound with twine, their ends softened with oil. You could tickle the water with it and the eels, once upon a time, would believe the stones were a mother’s belly and begin to rise.

“You won’t coax them,” a voice said behind me. The fisherman had come as a courtesy, he’d said on the phone, though I knew it was because he wanted someone with a title to see what he had been saying for years. He wore a sweater so old it had mended itself, his knuckles the color of walnuts, a cigarette that had been smoked only to a belief in heat.

“I only have to coax one,” I said. “Just to see.”

He laughed with his bones. “The girls from the Institute,” he said, not unkindly, “always only need one. The river’s not obliged to give you even that.”

I am thirty-five and I have been called a girl in laboratories with ten million dollars’ worth of apparatus. Out here, with the cold under my fingernails and the luna moth of the moon going white behind a haze, it didn’t feel any more inaccurate than inside under LEDs. I am a taxonomist for the Department of Remnant Behavior. In the big city where our building stands, all glass and restrained trees, that title fits on an embossed card. Here it felt like the lie that all work is when you stand it up against water and hunger.

I put the notch of the lure into the first rung and brushed at the surface of the canal. The turbines in the plant upstream were still for the moment—the company’s one concession to the town was to turn them off for two hours around dawn. In the old days, in certain moonlight, billions of transparent bodies would press themselves against the ladder, each with nothing in mind but upstream, upstream, upstream. The fisherman said he had seen that shimmer once, when he was a boy and someone put a cigarette into his hand and he tried to pretend it was a way to keep warm. He used to lie about it later, the number of eels, as all men lie about their flocks of girls and fish and enemies. But it had happened, and the boys had thrown a net across and then thought better of it and let the net go slack. It swung like laundry and the river undressed itself.

I tickled the water. The surface believed me only for a moment; little circles went out toward the cut bank, and then nothing.

Sweet-sour air rose off the silt. A heron, statuesque as a noun, watched us from a rusted pipe. The fisherman flicked his cigarette into a bottle cap. He had brought the old coil pot with him—the one like a wicker cornucopia that the men set against the current, in case the night sent back a meal. It was lined with a small miracle of knowledge: a splatter of chicken blood, a smudge of anise seeds, a scrap of the shiny wrapper from a child’s toffee. Eels are catadromous, I could say, unspooling the words like a prayer or a curse; they go down to breed and rise up to live, their lives inverted to our sense of direction. Once that had felt like romance to me. Now it felt like the stubbornness of an old habit that would kill you.

I tickled again and counted to forty under my breath. In my pocket the phone vibrated. The fisherman raised his eyebrows. “Could be them,” he said, meaning the turbines.

“Could be my mother,” I said, more to the water than to him.

The Department taught us jokes for the field, little wards you could rub between finger and thumb to keep from becoming the kind of person who says elegy at the dinner table. The best one was that we called ourselves coaches. Coaching is what you do when a thing has forgotten how to do itself and needs a ladder built in its mind. In the office, in the rooms filled with recordings of bees dancing and cranes bowing and slick videos of wolves teaching their pups to cut elk out of the herd, this seemed almost practical. Even the donors could understand the idea that if you could archive a behavior you could return it, like a scarf left at a bar.

Behavior is not a scarf. It’s a bridge with no pier left standing. There are things you can try: you can bring a bridge to where a pier once was and let it remember its shape. You can call out across the gap. You can sing. Some evenings in the lab we played migratory alarms to a map of a sky and the ceiling trembled with recorded wingbeats, as if we had called down weather.

In the cold by the canal I tapped the lure on the smooth and waited with the old man. A siren sounded far away. A dog barked twice, like someone remembering to say something and then not.

The phone in my pocket trembled again. I let the water quiet and then took it out. The number was from the care home. I felt the small drum in my chest that meant I already knew what it was before the voice said my name.

“She wandered again,” the attendant said. “She walked five blocks barefoot before a boy on a bicycle saw her and circled her like a bird and kept circling until someone noticed. She was humming. She wouldn’t let us put the shoes on. She told the boy he had left the kettle, which frightened him.”

“Is she hurt?” I said.

“No. We brought her back before she reached the intersection. She had a handful of—” a rustle—“of salt.”

“She doesn’t like it when you take the salt,” I said, picturing my mother’s hands, the folded-paper bird she used to make from napkins to drop into soups, as if a bird could teach water how to sing. “She thinks you’re seasoning the weather.”

The attendant took a breath that might have been patience. “She had written your name on the door with it. Please come when you can.”

“I can come now,” I said, though now meant a bus at eleven and two transfers and a walk, and my supervisor, when I called her, would say it could wait a day. Every time you leave a field site you carry a cud of failure inside your mouth. It tastes like the metal of bitten pennies. But I put the phone back and lifted the lure and brushed it softly once more, and then, because magic and patience had kissed in the shallows exactly so often as never, a long, slender shadow unmoored itself from the bank and undulated toward my hand.

“There,” the fisherman whispered, already moving with the coil. The eel was no longer glass. It had taken on that adolescent smokiness, blackness the color of rain. It brushed the wood as if to answer and then in an unconscious movement that had more to do with memory than with me, turned its head upstream. For an instant its whole length rippled with intent. My heart did that thing a heart can do when it confuses a hired trick with a sign. I bent low and, without touching, I matched its undulation with my wrist and forearm, my shoulder, my back, as if I could dance it onto the rungs.

A current shifted. The turbines hummed alive. The eel made a choice. It flicked its body and gave itself to the pull. The fisherman swore softly. The water shrugged and the eel was gone. The river was a face that had mistaken us for someone else and returned to its expression.

“We should have come last week,” the fisherman said. “They had better moon.”

“We did our best,” I said, and I said it to him and to the world and to the embarrassment inside my chest that had nothing to do with him. He set the coil pot gently against the current and watched it settle, then turned to me and squeezed my shoulder with three fingers, an old men’s blessing.

“They had better mothers,” he said, as if he had not meant to say that, and then he walked away with the gait of a man who saved his speed for when the weather demanded it.

Field note: The tendency to ascend is present in the body even in failure. The tremor I want to call yearning occurs before direction.

In the care home they keep the windows open in any weather until someone complains. “Circulation,” the head nurse says when family corners her in the corridor. No one ever thinks to ask what they’re trying to circulate—the air, the memory, the smell of cumin and bleach. The first time I visited, two summers ago when Ma began to switch her verbs around like kitchen magnets, I stood under the ceiling fan and felt my childhood go by like a deck of cards the dealer had gotten impatient with.

Ma is living now in a room with a corkboard and a bed she calls a table. On the board is a map of the world folded into a shape that could be a hat, or could be nothing; a spineless plant in a cup; two pictures from a magazine of a woman holding a loaf of bread to her cheek like a phone. My mother has never baked.

When I let myself in she was sitting on the floor with a plastic bowl and a spoon. She had a halo of dark hair still—streaked with white, an elaborate astonishing language all its own—bundled into a clip that looked like the fossil of a bird. Bare feet, one heel smudged with something. A salt shaker sat on the table. The trail wasn’t there, because the cleaning staff is skilled and tired, but I saw it anyway: the faint white line on the brown door where she had written my name.

“Mara,” she announced, before I said anything. Somewhere inside her, names lived with the stubbornness of eels. “I have been making the soup.”

“What kind?” I asked, squatting, putting my bag where she couldn’t see it and begin a ritual around it that would involve unraveling the zipper and feeding it a shell. In the early stages she would ask me to close the window and open the door as if we were releasing something and catching the same thing in a better container. Now we had arrived at the stage of soups that would never boil, meals built out of attention and water.

“The green kind,” she said, stirring nothing. “You didn’t come last week.”

“I was working,” I said. If I had said I was coaxing eels she would have said, of course you were, and then asked me to fetch garlic, or asked me where her own mother had been buried. Sometimes she asked without knowing she had asked.
