There were mornings when her face was so young it hurt me to say good morning; there were afternoons when she wore her grief like a coat of armor and made the room feel six inches narrower.

“I stood outside,” she said matter-of-factly, the way she used to tell me she had gone to market and bought brinjals the size of pistols. “It was cold. The boy on the bicycle went around like this.” She made a circle in the air with the spoon. “And then he went around the other way. I told him it was no use if he went only one way. He had to un-net it.”

“Un-net what?” I said, though I knew.

“The forgetting,” she said, and shrugged. “It gets stuck in the corners.”

“Did you bring the salt?” I asked.

She glanced toward the shaker, guilty the way a thief is guilty when stealing what already belongs to them. “It’s for the door,” she said, as if I had never met salt before. “They are very strict about the edges in this place.”

People are strict about edges when bodies fail. It gives us something to enforce. The rules of the care home were posted with a cheerful brutality: No candles, no knives, no glass, no names on the doors that could be read by visitors who could teach a mind to walk down corridors it was better off not knowing. My mother had always hated rules. As a girl she started fights with the nuns in school about the hem of her skirt; as a woman she arranged spoon, ladle, jar in a way that made the kitchen feel like jazz. When the neurologist told us, in a voice made of velvet and statistics, what the scans suggested, my mother listened with her head high and then came home and turned every jar in the cupboard so that their labels would face out, a pageant of peaches and plums smiling.

“We will mark everything,” she said then, with the ferocity of a general. “If they insist on forgetting, we will insist on the opposite.”

The opposite of forgetting is not remembering. The opposite is attention. My mother, who never wanted anything more than to be left alone to pay attention to the particularities of the day—whether the goats at the end of the street had been painted a new holiness for some festival, whether the neighbor had switched the place of the basil and the mint, whether the boy who delivered the milk had decided to part his hair on the left—was now in a place where attention had become a violent luxury. The building was designed to soothe and the soothing had sharp elbows. At night, the halogen glow bled onto the street like a clouded story. Inside the residents told each other things any which way. Discipline of the anecdote unspooled. You could walk through that house with a notebook and end up writing a book you wouldn’t know how to end.

She stirred the air in the bowl. “You’re not married,” she said, out of nowhere, in the tone of a meteorologist informing me of the temperature. “You are very good at birds.”

“I’m all right at birds,” I said. “I’m better at fish.”

“Birds, fish,” she said. “They all need ladders.” Then she looked at me as if she had found the joke and we had both been in the same room the whole time. I felt something move in my chest that might have been grief loosening its tie for a moment.

“I brought you jam,” I said. I held up the jar, a squat glass antique with a dent in the lid that my mother would have noticed even if she hadn’t been a person whose life was a liturgy of noticing. “Fig. From the market near the station. It tasted like it remembered something.”

She peered. “It has a bubble,” she said. “Bubbles mean someone tested it.” She set the spoon down and reached for the jar with both hands. For the briefest of instants her fingers looked like my grandmother’s fingers. It is strange how a woman can arrive at old age through a tunnel that takes her backward through her mother, her mother’s mother. I thought of the eel whose shape is a type of remembering. I thought of songs taught to children and later given to birds over headphones in the laboratory. I thought of the fisherman’s hand on my shoulder, three fingers pressing into muscle as if to pin the world down long enough to name it.

“Have you been writing?” I asked. There were papers on the bed-table with loops and miniature mountains. Sometimes Ma’s words came out as elsewheres—fewer anchors, more weather. I liked to take those papers home and read them out loud when my apartment felt too ordinary. I told myself that if I learned to speak my mother’s new language, I could teach it back to her when the old one failed. This is the sort of thing you say to yourself during other people’s appointments, when you are sitting in a waiting room with a plant whose leaves are polished and you keep finding the wrong questions to ask.

“I did something better,” she said. She dusted the lid of the jam with two fingers as if she were blessing it and the fig. “I rearranged the shelves. I put the books about water on the bottom so that the water wouldn’t run downhill. The nurses don’t like it because they don’t know where to look for mercy anymore.”

“Mercy isn’t shelved,” I said, hearing the old rhythm of her voice in my own. She had been a schoolteacher for thirty years, specialist in nothing and everything: those small people with sharp eyes, the geography of the desk. She taught them the names of rivers as if she were introducing unstoppable friends. The first time she forgot the name of our river I pretended I didn’t notice. The second time I said it with her, and the third time I looked at the map on her corkboard, the world crumpled into a hat.

On the way out, after she had kissed the entire air around my ear as if tasting the climate and declared the soup to be finished, the head nurse caught me by the hand. “A letter came,” she said, drawing a folded paper from her pocket. It was addressed to me in the curved handwriting my mother had when she concentrated. The stamp was from the city, the kind the departments use. The seal, when I turned it over, was the Department’s, two cranes kneeling.

“Left at the desk for you,” the nurse said. She had new lipstick, a pink that belonged to a different decade. In this place everything performs its own time.

I read the letter leaning against the window while my mother made small kitchen noises to herself in the room behind me. The letter was from my supervisor, rather than from the poor intern who usually sent memos. The formalities were there, as always, as precise and polite as clothes chosen for a funeral: Dear Dr. Bernal, Hope this finds you, etc. Then the meat of it, the thing she would have circled if she had sent it as a memo:

We have been contacted by the Ministry regarding a case in your hometown. It does not fit squarely into our remit, but I would like you to assess. The community choir has ceased to sing. As in: they assemble, they open their mouths, nothing. The doctor insists there is no damage to the vocal cords. The conductor wrote to us because they suspect the loss to be behavioral rather than structural. There is also the matter of the eels, but that may be beyond us.

Additionally—and this part was written as if my supervisor were speaking quickly, knowing she shouldn’t—there was a note from someone at the care home about your mother. The Ministry has a new initiative called the Personal Archive. They are cataloguing domestic practices at risk of extinction. They would like to assign a recorder to document your mother’s rituals and phrases. If you are agreeable, I would prefer that the recorder be you.

My supervisor had enclosed her card. On the back she had written, in pencil, as if knowing I would prefer it: Do not feel obliged. Although you are the only person I trust to recognize a habit dying and not confuse it with a quirk.

I folded the letter into my jacket pocket and looked out at the parking lot where the river threw light up at us. Two gulls were standing breast to breast on a car roof, knocking their beaks together with a sound like small wooden instruments. The boy on the bicycle a few hours ago, circling my mother, had been making the same sound with his wheel; a chittering, as if telling anyone watching that a word had been dropped and needed to be found.

I went back into my mother’s room. She had poured exactly three teaspoons of jam into the empty bowl and was stirring it into the ghost soup with serious attention. When she saw me she smiled and held out the spoon as if to feed me, and I opened my mouth because this is what you do: you allow the ritual to pass through you, you become one side of a behavior that cannot stand by itself anymore. The sweetness in my mouth was more than fig; it had the salt of the door in it; it had the cold of the morning ladder. It is not a good time to be alive if you like things to stay still. It is, however, a good time to learn the difference between keeping and holding. The first makes fists. The second lets the shape of the other thing tell your hand what to do.

“What is the soup called?” I asked, because names are ladders.

She tilted her head. “Same as everything else,” she said, without cruelty. “We call it what we have left.” Then she laughed—clear, bright, my mother’s laugh—and the sound rang along the corridor into the transverse hall, where someone, somewhere, was humming a note that refused to turn into song. Outside, the turbines went on turning. The river, remembering everything and nothing, bent itself around the town and went on.

On the low road, where asphalt bruised into salt and the bracken gave up trying, Miren counted hands.

The bus shouldered the tide like a tired animal swimming broadside. On both sides the marsh lay glossed, lap marks clotted along the reeds, and the causeway shimmered under a film of water so shallow it pretended to be air. There was a sign warning that the road flooded at spring tide, but the driver, who had been ferrying the same handful of souls twice a day for twenty years, drove by the habit of tide tables and hamstrings. He wore a threadbare cardigan with buttons carved from limpet shell and when he took the fare from her he cupped his palm high so she could see it by accident: nine-fingered, missing the left index.

"Back for the neap," he said, as if that was what she was back for. "You'll want the last stop."

She nodded. Her coat cuffs were long enough to be indecent, swallowed the half-moons of her thumbnails, hid the fact of her. Ten. Ten in a village of Nines.

She kept her eyes on the causeway, on the place where the brackish water opened its throat around the road. The bus's tires pressed small wakes, parted a line through shoal fish. Silver bodies flicked out from under her reflection, their scales catching the sky. Miren remembered how as a child she had tried to lie flat on the road in summer when the water washed over, imagined herself as a boat, imagined the sea deciding whether to indulge her foolishness or to sidle itself over her in a slow-cold sheet. Her mother had laughed then and said, Get up, Miren, that stone will take the ones who think they're clever.

The last stretch of the road grew narrow and then narrower still, shouldered between slumping dunes and a ragwork of gorse. The bus crested and there was Grey Banks, hunkered on its spit of land like an animal that had learned to sleep facing the wind.

It had always seemed older than time to her: scalped salt-painted roofs, timbers silvered by the patience of weather, the church steeple blunt as a finger. Nets hung like a tangle of spiderwebs behind sheds. The tideline was tattooed on the houses in pale scallops.

People were moving at that hour, an in-between time when fishing boats had come in with the early trawl and the afternoon's work had not yet begun. They turned when the bus came up the incline and their hands rose in automatic greeting. Miren saw the erasures in them—index fingers gone smooth at the knuckle, banded sometimes with rust-red thread as if remembering were a kind of jewelry. The absence was as familiar to her as the smell of creosote and iodine. She had spent the first thirteen years of her life with that absence pressed up against her skin.

The bus jolted to a stop by the Harbor Store and heaved a sigh that seemed to empty its lungs of diesel and patience. Miren stood. The driver thumbed the meter and handed her a paper ticket without looking, because it never mattered who was coming or going; the maths of the road had no faces.

"Hold your coat," he said, low. "You know how they are."

"I know how they are," Miren said, and stepped down into home.

The air here tasted like something you should humbly ask permission to breathe. It left a mineral stripe on the tongue—salt, kelp rot, a whisper of fish blood—and the wind folded sound, gulls scissoring the sky above the wharf, the slap of halyards against masts, the soft chime of a glass buoy someone had not yet brought in for spring.

She walked, the soles of her shoes remembering every nail that rose in the boards of the jetty, every fat-slick of algae to step around. The Harbor Store’s bell gave a small hysterical ring as someone came out with a jar of boiled sweets. There was a dog she remembered only as a descendant—a grey-white melee of fur—who lay on the walkway with its chin on its paws and watched her as if considering a guilty verdict.

And then there was the house.

The house was at the end of a lane with a vanity of shells planted in cement along the garden wall. Miren had made those with a spoon when she was seven, had pushed the shells into the wet mix in a crooked pattern that her mother called a crown and Miren called a failed sun. The wall had become scabbed with lichen and bleached to the same gray-blue as the sky. She could see the window where the nets had always been mended, the chair that had belonged to her grandmother and then to her mother and had, in the packing of the past fifteen years of Miren’s life, been just another absence to inventory.

The door was unlatched. She knew because the key’s gone-dead weight had been in her pocket for three weeks, a padded gravity. When she turned the porcelain knob she expected a resistance that did not come. The door swung gentle as a wrist, letting in air and the muffled sound of someone sitting very still.

Aitor was in their mother’s chair.

He had their father’s stubborn nose and their mother’s commas-at-the-corners eyes. His hands were folded on his knees. The left showed the neat absence of bone, the soft glossy tissue where index met nothing. The right hand was whole, because it didn't matter which one you gave at thirteen: there was a ceremony of choice, a weighing, a delicate cruelty in letting you decide how your future would be compromised. Miren made herself look at his left hand without flinching, because hiding her glance would have been worse.

"You shouldn't have come," he said, in the voice of someone who has rehearsed a sentence and now has to hear it sound like a stranger.

"She was my mother," Miren said.

"And mine," he said. He shifted his hand—nine-fingered, nine-fingered—and the gesture was a small flinch of himself, as if even he was startled sometimes.

The living room smelled of salt and orris root. Their mother had kept bunches of it tucked everywhere, to hide the fish, she said, as if a village could hide from itself. On the table there was the ledger with her neat columns. On the back of the chair, her shawl. It still remembered the slope of the shoulder it had warmed.

"She asked for you," Aitor said after a moment, emptied of malice by the practice of grief. "Twice. When the late tide came in. You would have been at the field station, she said. You would be too busy to get to the phone."

Miren swallowed. The field station was two hours up the coast and might as well have been on a different planet. A meteorologist's life had a language of its own: isobars and occlusions and the beautiful cruelty of certainty. The last storm had chased itself along the coast and she had been in its eye on a bluff with instruments humming like bees. She had looked down and imagined the flood like the filling of a mouth. She had thought, not of Grey Banks, but of the math of water.

"What do you need me to do?" she asked.

"We're laying her out tonight," Aitor said. He glanced at the clock. The minute hand was a fishbone. "The women are coming. Sola will be here any moment."

Miren felt the old unspooling of the name in her body like the memory of pain. Sola, who had held every child in Grey Banks at birth and at thirteen. Sola, who had a foot in both the church and the sound, who wore the sea on her as other women wore brooches, who had once spanked Miren for taking the boat alone and then left her a slice of bread and jam on the thwart and turned her back so as not to witness the gratitude.

"I brought the papers," Miren said, because in her world everything came down to papers. Wills. Death certificates. Signatures.

Aitor stared at her as if he was trying to focus on someone moving behind her. "I don't care about papers," he said.

"We should care about papers," she said gently. "I signed for the headstone. We'll need to decide—where. Which plot."

"We're not burying," he said, and then every one of the words found a place in her head and laid itself down. Of course. She had been away too long. She had allowed her mind to arrange her mother into a town with a hedge and a churchyard. As if Grey Banks would cede one of its dead to dirt.

"They want to take her to water," she said. She did not put a question at the end of it. She heard the chords of its inevitability.

Aitor rubbed his thumb against the place where his finger wasn't. "She wanted it," he said. "Said she'd been waiting for the calm that comes after the neap. Said you'd come. Sola'll say the words. But you can't stand in the circle."

Miren heard the tapping of rain that wasn't there. The room had corners that collected silence the way some corners collect bugs. "Because I'm a Ten."

He flinched again, as if she had used an obscenity. There were words that felt like punches even when whispered. Ten was one of them. The children said it on the rocks to one another with a cusp of daring in their mouths. Ten was noisy as a bottle breaking. Ten was the thing you could not help noticing if you stepped on the bus, the thing that a driver would try to hide with a small kindness. Ten was her.

"Because you refused," he said.

The didactic fairness of thirteen had never left him. The day of the Tithe drew its head back in her memory, a gull with its beady eye. You were given the choice. You were given time to sit with the stone and consider it. You could run. She had run, sea tangle in her hair, her ankles cutting themselves on heather and her heart a bird. She had borrowed a skiff, pushed it into the slick green of the harbor, and rowed in a very small circle as the women watched from the shore and did not call her back because calling would have been indulgence. It had been Sola who waded in, who caught the skiff’s bow, who held it with one hand and the stone with the other and whose voice had been the sounding line of that day: We do not force. But the sea remembers.

"The circle is for those who have given thanks," Aitor said now, his tone paled by repetition. "It's not for you."

Miren set her bag down. She had packed it with clothes that smelt of electricity and deodorized soap. Standing there in that room, she could smell the newness like a kind of disrespect.

"I came home," she said.

He didn't answer. In the silence the harbor found ways to creep inside, an insinuation of scent and sound. A lull and a lift.

There was a knock at the door like someone tapping with their knuckles against driftwood. Then, without waiting, the door opened a palm-width and Sola came in.

She was smaller than Miren remembered, tightened by time as rope tightens when it dries, but her hair was still the indecent black of women for whom sorrow had been a winter coat instead of a wedding dress. She wore a cardigan with cerements of salt in its pilling and a skirt that had once been red. A basket was looped over her arm with something woolly and white folded inside.

"Girl," she said, and Miren was thirteen again, the word landing on her shoulder with its old weight. Sola put her basket down and put both her hands on Miren's cheeks for a moment, her palms dry and warm, her fingers callused from the calibration of blades. Sola's left hand was the strangest part of her: the missing finger had made a cradle in which she'd learned to balance eggs, babies, burdens.

"You took your time," Sola said. There was no cruelty in it. The words were the weather and Sola was naming it.

"I was in a storm," Miren said.

"You are always in a storm," Sola said. "Come and see your mother."

They had laid her in the bedroom, because the house had no coldroom and there was no space for lying in state in the small square of the parlor with its net and chair. She lay on the bed with a sheet to her waist and a knitted shawl over her chest, blue and yellow like a child's drawing of the sea. The women had combed her hair and pinned the front from her face. Miren's mother had always had the kind of mouth that looked like it was about to speak; even in death her lips seemed to be making a fate. On the bedside table there was a pair of scissors, the big ones with the names of all three grandchildren scratched into the blade.

Miren stood and did not cry. She had cried on the train when the woman with the container of live plants had made excuses to the conductor and the conductor had smiled with the weary good nature of someone who has decided, in the absence of anyone else deciding, to be kind. She had cried in the field station when she had pressed send on an email and written, I can't make the meeting. She had cried to the dull blue light of a vending machine in a service station when she couldn't make the yogurt choose between banana and peach. She had used up the sentimental allowances of strangers on her way and now she gave her mother only the silence she had inherited.

"She looks like herself," she said.

"She agreed to the netting," Sola said, voice practical. "Last week she told me. I know you would have wanted something else but sometimes the sea wants back fast. And anyway it is cleaner." She touched the shawl. "We'll tie her as the tide turns. The fish are noisy."

Miren looked up. "They're noisy?"

"You've been away so long you forget how to listen," Sola said, but not unkindly. "They sing when a big one goes. The choir's here every night, but mostly it’s just a rumor, a shiver. Yesterday, since she went, they've been up close, dense. You'll hear them soon enough. They remember their own."

Aitor had come to stand in the doorway. He watched his sister look at their mother's face as if she were reading a language that no longer admitted her.

"There's more bad weather coming," Miren said, reflexively. "The pressure—"

"Always with your pressure," Aitor said, exasperated into affection. "You and your numbers. We've been in bad weather since before you knew how to scowl."

"It matters," she said, and then all the old arguments rose up like a sudden squall and she let them fall again because there was no time. "I want to stand in the circle."

Sola turned her head. The grandmother muscles in her face moved like someone handling bones. "You want, little fish?"

Miren straightened. "She's my mother. Maybe I owed the sea a bone. I didn't give it. Maybe it has been waiting to make that debt into a story it can tell, I don't know. But it doesn't stop my wanting."

Sola's mouth did a slow, private thing. "Wanting is a currency that spends badly here." She came closer, the hem of her skirt whispering. "I told your mother I would hold the rope for you. I said if you came with your ten, I would hold it on the outside. I can do that once. The sea does not like us making new rules. But for births and for deaths, it sometimes looks away because it knows it will get the rest of us in time."

Aitor made a sound that might have been disapproval. Sola lifted her right hand a fraction and in that small movement was all her authority, volcanic and casual. "I'm old enough to bargain," she said, and then smiled in a way that made Miren want to put her head on her lap like an exhausted child. "Don't look so afraid. The dead don't want your shame. They want your hands."

For the rest of the afternoon the house filled with women. Some Miren had danced with at weddings, steps called out over the roar of wind; some had tightened their lips and refused her left-overs as a principled act of neighborly judgment. They moved around a body the way people move around a fire, cautious and drawn. They stopped to say how sorry they were, how much she had been loved. Tulla, who had once stitched Miren's knee with a sailmaker's accuracy when she split it on the iron ladder at the dock, held her hand for a moment like a rope.

Outside, the day softened. The light turned the color of something you could eat too fast. Herring gulls threw their shadows like knives across the yard. The first sound came thin as wire.

At first, before your ear learns the grammar, it sounds like a malfunction. The harbor has its own metallic lexicon—bolts unscrewing somewhere you cannot see, chain dragging chain, anchors complaining in their sleep—but this was a thread of sound that slid under those, held them up, made them suddenly mean something else. It quivered like a glass tuned.

Miren stood at the kitchen sink with a dish in her hands, and it shivered her bones from wrist to shoulder. She set the plate down. In the front room the conversation faltered, and then there was a mutter like knitting needles in the dark.

The fish were singing.

She had always thought it a kind of story the old women told to give shape to the ridiculousness of grief: how else do you explain that the water grew thick at your making and your unmaking? She had been out on the boats at night when the water held its breath, when constellations were inverted and the plankton lit with a drop of your finger as if you were God. She knew fish could make noise—croaks and grunts and clicks, vibrations traded like secrets in a nightclub. But this was not the biology of it. This was a sound that called you by your broken names. This was the voice your mother used when she wanted you to come home.

Sola came to the doorway and said nothing. She didn't have to. Miren took her coat and didn't bother to pull the cuffs down over her hands, forgot herself enough to be who she was. She followed Sola and Aitor and the dog and the neighborhood to the shore.

The boats had been pulled up on the shingle. Ropes were coiled with the idiosyncratic excellence of men who had learned to be precise to save their lives. The sky had become a lid with a chipped edge. Out beyond the line of rocks the water seemed to be seething with light, a scatter of cold cooking oil in a pan, and then you realized it wasn't light, not quite, it was movement; that the surface of the harbor was soft with bodies. Fish rolled and shouldered at the surface in a press of silver, their mouths opening to vowels of air, and from them a sound came that made the bones behind Miren's ears ache for recognition. It was a song without a language and then it wasn't. It was the timbre of a voice she knew.

Her mother's voice had not been pretty. It had been low and rough as the underside of a boat. But in the choir of the sea it was as singular as a black rock at low tide.

Give me your left, it said, and then—no, that was the old grief making meaning out of noise. She put her hands in her pockets until her knuckles pushed at the seams. Give me your left is what her mother had said on the day Miren ran, saying it with her mouth and her eyes and her hands. You'll learn to tie knots with your ring finger, and you'll forget to miss what you don't have. You'll be here with me, Miren, and the sea will know you belong to it. We'll eat bread with our silly pincers and laugh. Give me your left.

Now the sound came again, more specific, the way that echo can trick you into thinking the original voice is speaking. Bring me to the stone, it said, in her mother's voice without the smear of consonants you get from wind. Before the ninth wave.

A murmur moved through the women like a small weather. Sola made the sign she made, which had nothing to do with the cross. She picked up the coil of the funeral rope. It glittered with salt.

"You'll stand outside with me," she said to Miren, low. "And when we take her, you'll be the weight on the shore. You'll be the gravity. You'll feel her leave and you'll not try to follow because I have your belt in my hand and because you trust me."

"I trust you," Miren said. She heard what she was saying and swallowed. She had always trusted Sola because Sola did not ask for persuasion. She provided reasons the way she provided soup: put your spoon in this; there is salt and heat, and it will keep you until morning.

They bore her mother down between them. The women took the corners of the blanket, moving with choreography ironed into their bones by the families of the dead. Aitor took his place at the head because that is what you do when you are the son, even if your sister is a meteorologist and knows the names of winds you will never feel.

At the edge of the slipway Sola looped the rope around Miren's waist and tied it with a competent ugliness. "Nine waves," she said. "Don't lose count. When you take a breath, count the next one as one."

"It asked for nine," Miren said.

"I heard," Sola said. "It's an old number. The ninth wave hearts or wrecks, depending on who is counting. We will not drown a woman who is already where she needs to be."

They went into the water. The women waded first, skirts making a brief show of modesty before darkening, heavy with salt. The men stood aside, their faces bowed, as if the sea made widows of them in advance. The first wave broke around Miren's knees, the cold a shock that made her cough. One. The second climbed, her thighs went to stone. Two. The third found the seam of her coat. Three. The fish pressed closer, a corporal body with a grammar of movement that insisted on a communal clause. My mother, she said in her head though no one had asked, as if she were queuing and someone asked who she was waiting for and she had to make the answer tidy and small. My mother.

On four Sola said, Wait. The word was a hand between Miren's shoulder blades. Wait. And then, All right, go now. The women leaned into the water as one and set the wrapped body on the surface as if it were a child learning to float and the sea, with a suddenness that would have looked like cruelty had you not been raised in it, accepted. The shawl took on a darkness and then it was only shape and then it was only light on water. Five. Miren felt the rope go from being something that held her to being something that held Sola. She felt in her bones the way in a storm a house feels the flex of itself.

The singing shifted. The arpeggios changed their angle. Six. Seven. At eight, the fish surged in, bumped their bodies against her knees, a nuisance of grief. Nine.

Miren breathed. She had not realized she had been holding all of herself in. The women stood, their skirts plastered against their legs like repentance. Sola tugged the rope and Miren came a step backwards, obedient to the authority in the hand on her back. She turned to see Aitor, his eyes salt-brimmed and very clear.

"It’s done," he said, as if checking the fronts of his cupboards.

"Nothing is done," Sola said, and her voice made the air around them warmer. "Everything is only what it is. Come on. Come away while your mother is safer than you are."

They walked back to the shore. The fish continued to sing, loosening into their own sentences. Someone started a tune that required only humming. A child put a hand into Miren's and did not notice that there were too many fingers.

She could feel the call of the house on her, the insistence of a kettle, the comfort of walls, the way grief is easier to pour when you can aim it at a table. But she did not move. She stood with her feet in the rocking margin, the curl of foam laying temporary lace on her boots, and felt the precise and appalling perfection of the place where she was, how you stood on your own shore and in someone else's story.

The tide took in the voices and returned them smaller. Sola looked at the sky the way a woman looks at her pantry and counts jars. "You'll stay the night," she said to Miren, casual as a command. "Tomorrow there's talk we'll be needed at the point."

"For what?"

"There's been a tearing. The sea took the east fence. A calf went through."

"That's not my job," Miren said, and immediately felt the heat rise into her face at how childish it sounded. "I—"

"It's everyone's job," Sola said. "There is no job in a place like this that doesn't belong to everyone. You can tell us where to put the fence so the next storm won't suck it out like a whelk. You and your numbers can make yourselves feel useful."

Miren opened her mouth to answer and the sea interrupted. A small fish—a sprat, perhaps, or a smelt with its delicate underline—leapt, impossible, from the foam and hit her just above the collarbone with an apology of force. Her hand closed around it without meaning to, warm and alive and panicked. It wriggled there and she felt the slick of its scales and the beat of its stupid, furious heart.

She thought, wildly, of ceremonies, old women, offerings. She thought, This is ridiculous. And then, because she knew when ridiculousness had turned its head into something else entirely, she felt with her thumb a small hardness at the gill, a bead threaded through flesh by the sea itself. It was black as the pupil of a cat and slick with salt.

"Don't," Aitor said sharply, as if she were about to commit a sacrilege and he was tired of being the one to point such things out.

She didn't listen. Of course she didn't. She put her nail under the bead—it was like a knotted pearl—and prised it free. The fish sang or screamed and then loosened in her hand and slipped back into the water with a flick that made her wrist sting. The bead sat in the bowl of her palm, a ridiculous thing the size of a pea.

Sola leaned in, her eyes suddenly very old and very young. "What is it?"

"I don't know," Miren said. "It…"

The bead moved. It didn't roll; that would have been fine and rational and subject to laws she had made her peace with. It throbbed, a heartbeat that was not hers. And then—it split. A seam opened like a mouth, and from it, a sound came very small and perfect and not meant for a crowd.

Bring me to the stone, the bead said, in her mother's voice, with the measured patience she had used when teaching Miren to plait rope. Before the ninth wave. You will know which one. You always did.

Sola put her hand over Miren’s as if capturing heat. "Well then," she said, conversational as supper. "It seems the sea is not finished making demands of you. It seems it has learned your number."

"We just did nine," Miren said. Her tongue was clumsy in her mouth. She looked at the horizon where the water lay sudden as slate. "We counted to nine. We did what it asked."

"There are always more nines," Sola said. "Don't stand there like a woman in a painting. Get your things. The light goes, and the tide will turn again. You know how she is."

Miren closed her fingers around the bead, feeling the stubborn pulse, the syrupy insistence of her mother's voice threaded into stone. She thought of papers and plots, of field stations and storm charts, of balances you make with old places that have no patience for modern apology.

"All right," she said. She did not say what this meant. She did not say what she was afraid of. She said what one says when the sea asks, with an intimacy that is barely less impersonal for being absolute.

She turned, and the village leaned toward her as if expecting a performance. Aitor lifted his chin because he wanted her not to fail and wanted her not to succeed and didn't know which would hurt less. Sola had her hand already on the rope. The dogs, who have no gods but motion, quivered.

The stone had been there since the first boat came cortex-deep into the cove, before a village made of wood and sky and net accreted around it. The old engraved lines were worn to shadows and the basins were smoothed by the thirst of salt. Children ran their tongues along it in dares and announced that it tasted like blood even when it did not. They called it the Thanking Stone, because you could not say Tithe without making a filing cabinet in the head of God. Miren had avoided it for fifteen years as if it were an ex lover she might see at a party.

She walked toward it now with the bead in her fist, her coat kicking against her legs, her breath making fog in a sky too sharp for fog. Behind her the choir lifted and shook itself clean of grief to make way for something else: the sound of metal warming in fire, of a coast curling up its lip to see who had come back.

Before the ninth wave, her mother's voice said against her palm, smaller now, as if the stone were greedy and sucking it down. As if the sea, which had waited a patient lifetime, had suddenly grown impatient. Before the ninth wave. And Miren, who had been built by rules she had chosen and rules she had refused, who had learned to measure storms and been unmade by the aftermath of a day when a tide table was not enough, counted ahead. She made a map of breaths in her head and in that map all the paths from the house led, as they had always led, to the edge.

Chapter One: The Dome That Forgot the Sky

The morning the city opens the old planetarium for the displaced, the sky goes paper-white and refuses to carry anything as delicate as a horizon. People stand in a line half a block long, their bags humped like extra vertebrae; they breathe in a particular way that is not quite waiting, not quite holding breath, but the somewhere between when you have been left behind and you have decided to leave.

The planetarium never belonged to our century, not really. It was a dome’s idea of a world, the world’s idea of a dome: concrete, circular, windowless, a blunt fruit fallen among cracked sidewalks and pepper trees. When I was a child, you slid through the blacked-out lobby and the ceiling fell away into a velvet that never cracked or leaked, and instructors with soothing voice timbres taught us our inheritance. Polaris, they’d say, and north became a bead you could swallow. We leaned back at once and were organized.

Then Meridian changed its mind about its sky. Smoke sat over the bay as if it had decided to lay claim, storms came in the wrong months and forgot who they were; the streets learned the slope of water; the donors turned to new necessities, desalination and battery storage. The planetarium went dark. I touched the main projector last on a Sunday six years ago, when there were still news articles about “the pivot,” about rehomed institutions and the end of stargazing as a public good. Its lenses were heavier than my forearms could understand. I put the covers over the star plates, turned the key, and listened to the hum click down into a sound like absence making itself known. I told myself it would be temporary.

“Temporary” is a word you hold in the back of your throat for so long it learns how to taste like permanent.

The city’s Relief Coordinator—a man named Elias with cardstock-colored hair and a laugh that never touches the tip of his teeth—found me three weeks ago, my name in a drawer of dusty files, and asked if I would look at the dome. “We need square footage and plumbing,” he said. “We need what keeps happening to us to happen under a roof. Also, if there’s light? People like light.”

We stand now at the top of the low stairs, a sagged ribbon fluttering between two collapsed stanchions. Elias makes a joke about cutting it, realizes no one can hear him over the traffic and the wind around the corner, and drops it instead. “Welcome home,” he says, and the doors open with a complaint like a wooden instrument clearing its throat.

The smell is first: dust woken up, old carpet glue, a ghost of machine oil. Then the sound: the friction-shush of a hundred shoes, the rasp of zippers, the thousand tiny collisions of metal against metal in bags, the way any crowd is a percussion instrument even when it tries to be careful. I am not sentimental; my work is almost always in the joints of things. But when the dome swims into view beyond the vestibule and the old seats curve their patient backs toward a center of nothing, I feel the only word that will do. Oh, I think, as if someone has opened a box and inside is a night kept safe for you, safe and at last.

We have sliced the seats down the middle to put in tables. Folding chairs flock like nervous birds. Volunteers with good handwriting sit with clipboards and the welfare tablets the city acquired secondhand from a bank; their wrists glint with their personal lives. On the far wall, the cramped little café I remember from field trips has lost its espresso machine and taken on a bulletin board: hand-drawn maps with paths through dry neighborhoods, names and phone numbers in trades (anyone have a wet vac? anyone have a truck? my mother needs). The dome breathes over all of it like a paused cough.

A child in a red sweater drags a duffel over the carpet, staring up with her mouth open so wide I can’t tell whether she is happy or about to cry. “Look,” she says, pointing. “The holes.”

“Not holes, angel,” says the woman behind her, the kind of weary tender who always chooses the softer word even when she has no energy left. “Just the ceiling.”

“They’re holes,” the girl insists, “where the dark drinks water.”

I find myself smiling. The metaphors children adopt are so much more honest than ours; their grammar negotiates with the world in equal amounts of surrender and nerve.

“Is it going to work?” Elias whispers. He is standing too close in the way of administrators who can only be intimate when they are worried. He is holding the strap of his bag with both hands, as if anything anchored will help.

“It does not work or not work,” I say. “It was not made for our kind of success.” He does not laugh, which is not a failure on his part. I am not always a person who says what will be understood.

In the center of the room, under the small circular platform where the projector used to rest like an animal whose species evolved into night, there is now a folding table with a pot of tea that tastes like mint and recent memory. Someone has put a jar of flowers next to it. Not store flowers: stems with their names still in the dirt they were pulled from, city weeds, the thin yellow courage of mustard and something blue and wild that leaned over the back fence of my childhood.

A woman in a floral headscarf stands near the first intake desk with a jar of soil in her hand that she holds like a baby. Next to her, a man whose left cheek has the map of a particular scar looks around with sharp, efficient eyes, inventorying exits. The child in the red sweater has discovered a wedge of sun slicing through a rip in the blackout curtain and is making an optical bluebird in the dust with it. The volunteers write. They ask: Name, and again for spelling. Date of birth. Last address. Number of dependents. Medical needs. Allergies. Languages spoken. When the city was prosperous, our forms loved to complicate themselves. Now, in our mild apocalypse of wet electrical outlets and stubborn mold blooms, we have pared back to the nouns.

There should be a way to register the unregistrable. “Do you have any constellations you carry in your head?” I want to ask, walking between tables. “Did your grandmother teach you the difference between the crying of crows and of gulls? Have you inherited, from anyone, a method for looking at a map without believing it?” The forms do not ask this. They ask what things must ask when they have a timeline and a budget.

“You did this?” says a voice, a pleasure of a voice, with an undertide of iron filings. “Back then?”

“Back then,” I say, turning, “I turned the key. I did not do this. The sky did this. The sky and the lens design of a man named Spitz.”

Dr. Ko smiles at me, the careful hello of a colleague you knew in another life. She is fatter than she was and more beautiful for having ceased pretending otherwise. She was a postdoc when I started; her hair has gone pepper-drift at the temples. Rumor says she owns a bakery now, because a person who watched stars teleport into history sometimes needs the alchemy of flour and water to return them to the earth. She gestures with her chin toward the dark hulking outline on the cart behind the velvet curtain where the machine is waiting. “You think she’ll wake up?”

“She’s been sleeping too long,” I say. “She might be a different person.”

“We all are,” says Dr. Ko, and it is not the kind of line that would sit comfortably in a poem, but here, among cracked armrests and a hundred small exiles, it is the truest sentence anyone says.

Early fresh arrivals stream in, then lull, then stream. The trickle-tide of a Sunday line. I put my hand on the plaster of the dome, palm flat, and feel the faintest temperature difference—cold at the top, warmer near the vents, the old breath of the building exhaling through its nose. I remember the way light crawled here when it began, the way we timed the dim to the minute the fifth-graders would stop rustling and the teenagers would stop daring each other to touch hands. I have a small wrench in my pocket and keep touching it, a habit I learned in my twenties when the world seemed like a series of delicate bolts that could be tightened before they fell apart.

I told Elias that I’d come early to test the system. I came at dawn with a bottle of rubbing alcohol and a stack of lintless cloths, and slid the cover off the main lens as if I were preparing to meet someone who would judge me, and me alone. The gears swore at my hands; the panels I removed had screws which identified the last person who had turned them by their conviction. Metal remembers; there are fingerprints you cannot wipe off. I told the machine a few secrets I had been keeping too close. Maybe I hoped it would ask less from the people under it if I gave it this.

Now, a child starts to cry, and then stops, because someone has offered her a hard candy from a pocket, and the dome breathes again. The intake desks continue: “Can you tell me the street you left from?” “Do you have a family member we can call?” “Can you describe any medicines you need?” In the back, near the old volunteer closet where we kept cushions that children with sensory sensitivity could hold, a man unrolls a blanket that is too clean not to have been saved against the day. He lays his cheek on it, face down, and doesn't sleep, exactly. He listens to the floor.

There is always a first crisis, and it is always a small one. A woman whose papers were in the freezer at her old address, because a radio show once told her that if your house burned the papers would be safe there, and of course it was water that came. A boy who has a rescue dog but the form says “no animals,” and the volunteers are very sorry, and the word “no” is a thing made out of three letters until it is the thing on which your whole life rests. A man who cannot find a word in our language for what he is allergic to because he never had it before and only knows the particular feeling in his throat, like a door unable to decide whether to stay open or close. A first-time volunteer with polished nails and a desire to be good who says, “We’ll figure it out,” and means it, and then looks for someone in a green vest who understands the limits of the figuring.

“We can do a show,” I hear myself say. My own voice is a stranger to me. It has not spoken to so many people at once in a long time.

Elias stops writing and looks up. “A show?”

“Just to calm things,” I say. “Ten minutes. Remind the ceiling.” There is a grin I cannot help; it might be hope. “If you give people something to look at that is larger than their own inventory, sometimes they can set their bags down.”

There are murmurs. The child in the red sweater says “Yes, yes, yes” as if her tongue itself is jumping up and down. Dr. Ko holds her hands out in that universal “what can I do?” She is my favorite scientist because she never demands that an instrument be more than it was designed to be. I tilt my head and she nods; I go behind the half-curtain to the crow’s nest of switches and faders and delicate toggles that made me feel, when I first started, that the world might actually respond if you knew where to stroke it.

The old projector sits like a rusted god, wings folded. In daylight, it was always ugly. Useful things often are. I ran my cleaning cloth until it stained gray, and even now it bears a skin of grime that resists both solvents and apology. The tiny brass shows their age. But when I turn the switch, the belly hum begins and the hair lifts on my forearms. It is the sound of something older than the last emergency waking up and clearing its throat. A sweetness pinches the back of my nose, that particular odor of heating dust and relit filaments.

“Ladies and gentlemen,” I say, picking up the mic with its foam top fretted by a thousand nervous thumbs. “And anyone who has needed a new name and not known what to call yourself yet.” A small wave of laughter. I let it break. “Welcome back.”

I do not give the speech the museum wrote with grant money. It referred to “our shared terrestrial home” and “everchanging skies” and belonged to a different kind of disaster. I say instead: “Once, this building was an hour you came into on purpose. You made a plan. You sat back and let your perspective be managed by a person like me. Today, many of you have had your perspectives managed by chance or by decisions that were not yours at all. I cannot return to you what has been taken. I can only show you something older than us. It is not the same; I am not confused about this. But sometimes seeing the larger keeps the smaller from swallowing you whole. If you need to look down at your hands, please look down at your hands. If you need to look up, the ceiling is here for you. For the next nine minutes, this is the sky.”

There is movement under the words, the way there always is—the half coughs that people press back, the click and drag of people sitting forward or back, the ragged breath of a lost person finding a rhythm they can pretend is theirs for a while. I kneel next to the panel and push the sliders forward with the tenderness of first touch. The room dimming has always been my favorite applause. Light retreats from the corners; the room’s edges become the inside of an eyelid, then that eyelid becomes an ocean, and then there is the dome.

Stars flower, not all at once but in bursts, as if they are a memory being remembered in the wrong order. I have dialed the plates to late summer, from a time when the city still had evenings; Vega and Deneb find their places, and the air inside the dome quickens, an organ with which some of us have not breathed for a long time. I trace with the pointer. “Summer Triangle,” I say, and my finger jittering in the air sparks a small blue arc. A few heads tilt back as if their bodies know what to do: how to afix themselves.

Hands unclamp from bag straps. A woman wipes her mouth with the back of her hand. The child in the red sweater lies on the carpet, arms straight out, her fingers making a windmill in the air.

I talk about light-years and how they are a unit of what falls between us and patience. I talk about old photons, the ones that set out before we named what they were, and the idea that everything we see is late in arriving. “Many of you,” I say, “know what it is to be late, and to be told that your lateness is the problem rather than what delayed you. The sky does not scold. It labels the distances and then goes still.” I am not sure if I am saying this for anyone but myself. It is good, sometimes, to be honest among strangers.

And then something happens. It starts small enough that it could be an error, a human error, or a lovely coincidence: a faint extra brightness between the projected Pleiades and Pisces, a seed pearl of light in a place my machine does not know to carry one. I squint. I am like a mother asked, How could you not know your own child? The patterns we spend our lives with can become the air, and we can be fish.

I adjust a dial. The old machine protests in a high whine, then obeys. The light takes a breath. Another point appears, where Cygnus is not. It is like the first at-home pregnancy test when you are not sure you want to be a parent; lines bloom where no one promised them. I look down at Dr. Ko. She is looking up too, her brow tensed in a way that, in the years I watched her write code and calibrate a spectrograph, meant: something is either wrong or about to become even more right than we have prepared for.

“Did you add a plate?” she whispers, as if I have been hoarding stars.

“Do you think I have been in here soldering them by hand?” I say, my voice too flat, too startled to pretend.

On the floor, the child in the red sweater sits up as if she has heard her name spoken. “There,” she says, and points not where I see the false star, but toward the far southwestern quadrant where the glow of a city always intrudes, even in a simulation. In our dome, the city’s old light is a faint ache, written into the calibration of our memory. But now, inside the faintness, something shapes itself. A line, and another, connecting what is not supposed to be connected. A pattern builds itself as if it has been waiting in the plaster, shy and stubborn, for the day when the lungs below it would breathe the way they are breathing today.

When I first learned the constellations, they were the diagrams of myths I did not love. Strong men, animals too ornate to have a smell, a woman forever forgiven and forever punished. When we grew into better versions of ourselves, we taught children how to draw their own constellations, how to decide that a scatter of lights could be a bicycle or a dragon or their aunt’s laugh. There is power in renaming. There is also power in what refuses to be renamed. This shape, forging itself in our unpromised sky, is neither the old myth nor a child’s assertion. It is a kind of happened-upon.

“What does it look like to you?” I hear myself say, because the planetarium taught me years ago that when the world changes you ask this question first, as if you are teaching a tool its own purpose, when really you are quietly begging it not to leave you behind.

“A net,” says the man with the scar, in a voice that, now that he is speaking, sounds like a river with a rock in it. “But broken.”

“A hand,” says the woman with the jar of soil, and the way she says it tells me the hand she sees is both a help and a taking.

“A map of cracks,” someone says, and people laugh, a sound that breaks like crushed ice.

The shape—the net-hand-cracks—extends. I let the projection run in real time. The ghost stars appear where there are no light outlets on my machine, where no holes have been drilled. Something is feeding it. Somewhere, either in the wiring or the atmosphere, someone is drawing the new lines. It is not that the dome is making the shape; it is that the dome is finally accepting it.

“Could it be interference?” Dr. Ko says small into my ear. “From the new cell towers?”

The planetarium always had to fight. Light pollution, the city’s hum, the new fashion for headlamps the size of fists. Electromagnetic noise got into our wires like gossip. But this does not feel like interference. This feels like the opposite. This feels like intention.

There is a rumor that in the late nineteenth century a small rural church discovered faces in a windowpane, faces that would not wash out no matter how much soap and vinegar they tried, faces the local mothers’ union eventually held meetings in front of to see if among them they could find their dead. It took scientists and skeptics, and then later the heat of the sun itself, to admit defeat: no process could be named. The window was renamed miracle and was left alone. I think of that while I watch the plaster make its claim. I am not religious except in the ways that require silence.

The shape resolves. As I watch, accepting around it the older stars I can name—Altair, Deneb, Vega tired and proud in their points—the new lines knot themselves into a figure I cannot disbelieve: it is our city. Not in any map the newspapers used to print, with neighborhoods named after developers, lines and block numbers and the shy shy of cul-de-sacs, but in the way the city lives in our bodies. The rise up Sixth, where you measure yourself each summer against the heat. The toothed edge of the old seawall like a jaw. The broken streetlight at the corner of Spruce, where teenagers learned how to be seen by one another and not by their parents. The triangle where the food trucks park when the tide is wrong. The way the drought tore the grass out of the parks and left a map of the games we play anyway. Streets that no longer exist under water. The dome shows all of them together, the way time shows itself when it has to.

I am not the kind of person who stands transfixed by coincidence. I love what can be tightened, oiled, calibrated, made obedient. I love a faithful machine. But I am also a citizen of Meridian, which means I know how often we have been promised certainty and given guesses. I look at the dome and crouch closer to the panel and twist a dial I have twisted a hundred times and I watch our city tilt above us in crisp white points and I remember where my brother used to live.

He lived in a building at the corner of Grafton and Fifth, a building whose landlord turned the water off in summers to make a point. He lived there with a woman who never learned to like me. He left from there one morning in a borrowed skiff with a crate of batteries he’d bought from a cousin and an idea about islands, and did not come back. This is categorized, in various file cabinets, as a private loss. It was also one among a thousand. Still, it is the one my hands shake for.

Above us, the map glows quiet. Between the points that mark the grocery with the good radishes and the pothole that makes the buses whisper to themselves, there is an extra brightness, and then another, making as small a triangle as can hold an address. It is something like an arrow. No: it is simply like the point your eyes make when they refuse to unfocus.

“Do you see that?” I say. My fingertip draws a circle in air. I have never been a person whose voice shakes in public. Today, my voice is a thing stored in a body.

Elias, who had his hands on his hips fifteen minutes ago, who said the word “deliverables” as if it could be reconciled with need, steps closer, his eyebrows like marks someone drew with a pencil and forgot to erase. “I see…points,” he says, his voice apologizing to every thing it is not trained to see.

“It’s pointing,” says the child in the red sweater, sitting cross-legged now, her hands perfectly still for the first time. “It’s pointing where the dark drinks the water.”

The woman with the jar of soil clutches it closer to her chest. Dr. Ko puts her hand on my forearm and squeezes, once, as if she is reminding me we are made of the same material.

There is no reason to believe that the dome is speaking. There is no reason to believe that it is pointing to anything but our hunger to be directed. But there it is. A brightening in a shape the old maps did not authorize, insisting on a small triangle of brightness no one else is naming, one that overlays exactly on a place my body could walk to in under a quarter hour, if my body were still the body it was when I was twenty-three.

Time resumes when the lights come up. People remember they have papers to fill, children to quiet. Elias rubs his eyes with the back of his hand and then glances at his palm as if he expects it to come away star-littered. The room takes a breath that is not collective but ends up being synchronized anyway. Someone says, “Thank you.” Someone else says, “We were fine before,” and then laughs at the unkindness of the sentence, and says, “I mean, we were as fine as.”

The woman with the jar of soil comes to me. “Thank you for the hand,” she says. “It looked like the hand of my mother, once. When she told me where to put the basil.”

“It was a net,” the man with the scar mutters, a man not interested in being softened. “We got caught, that’s all.”

There is a thing I could do or not do. It is a small thing, like refusing to take the pill such-and-such doctor says will not hurt you if you do not know why he wants you to take it. It is a thing that involves a wrench and my pocket and the idea that some shapes are insistences. I could shut the machine down, name what we saw a glitch, file it under “theaters of the overwhelmed.” I could leave it there and live inside mechanics for the rest of the week. This would be my right and my relief.

Instead, when the dome brightens and the volunteers press on with their questions and Dr. Ko heads toward the café to help refill hot water and Elias works the door with his practised nod and voice, I pull the stretched black curtain closed again around the platform and crouch and unscrew the panel where the old green schematic shows the circuits I pretended to understand when I was twenty-six. Under the metal, there is a mess of wires tied with twine in the dark. A previous me or a previous somebody has made do in here. This is what keeps us alive and kills us: our capacity for mending.

I touch the place where the extra light would be coming from if extra light were a thing that followed wires. Heat pulses. Not enough to be ashamed of; just enough to prove it was not a dream. I imagine bringing a diagram to Dr. Ko and asking her to name which elements of our disaster might be sympathetic to projection. She would say (I can hear her) that I am looking in the wrong place for answers. How many times did we work together when the data needed to be asked questions no instrument could form?

“We’ll do another ten minutes at noon,” I tell Elias. It occurs to me that I have given myself a new job without asking permission. His face, which is built for conditions where he can confess he does not know while moving forward anyway, opens in relief. “People liked that,” he says, not needing to say that he liked it too and did not know what to call why.

I stand alone under the dome when the lunch lull comes. The volunteers eat crackers they found in a carton and a woman in a medical mask who was a chef before she lost her kitchen has found a way to arrange two carrots and four pickles on a plate in a manner that makes everyone feel fancier for ten seconds. Dr. Ko leans, eyes closed, on the wall under the “EXIT” sign, as if she is charging.

I think of my brother. I think of the boat. I think of the way he made the word “Mara” into three syllables when he wanted something, and the way his left front tooth had a chip he got when he was five and fell off the stoop while trying to see if the rain would let him part it. I think of a triangle of light that a building somewhere thinks belongs to him.

I think of the child saying “where the dark drinks water,” and of the man who could not name his allergy, and of the way my hand felt on the dome like touching the belly of something that might one day have to choose between us. I think of the ten thousand things the city says it cannot do and the one or two it does without asking. I think of how any prize worth winning is not the prize but the permission it grants you to keep talking.

The dome is quiet. The machine’s saucers sleep like tired eyes. I pull the curtain open an inch and look out at the city’s approximation: clipboards, jars, fatigue like a made bed. The woman with the soil now has a roll of duct tape someone gave her; she has taped a note to her jar. Basil. Hospitality. Remember. The child is asleep with her head on her duffel, her red sweater bunched up toward her face like a scarf. I could go to Grafton and Fifth. I could follow a point the ceiling made like a proffered hand. I could be wrong, and it would break nothing that isn't already a little broken.

I tell the machine: You are not the oracle. I tell myself: Neither am I. I tell the dome: Do not point unless you are willing to be followed.

At noon, I dim the lights again, and the ceiling does what ceilings do: it holds. The room quiets, and for nine minutes the hydraulics of attention take over. The sky returns. The new shape waits, barely there, the way grief is when you live with it long enough to set out two bowls at supper without thinking and then put one of them away.

On my way out, I put the wrench in my pocket and the key to the door on a string around my neck, and I walk toward where the shape pointed. There are three streets that will get me there if I decide to are, but there is only one I can take without walking through a place I no longer belong. I choose the broken sidewalk under the sweetgums because I want to step on their spiky fruit with my heels and feel the not-pleasant pain that tells me I have a body not made for stars. Someone has chalked, on the asphalt near the old bus stop, You Are Here, with an arrow pointing down at a tidy circle. As if to gently correct whoever needed reminding it is so much harder to locate yourself when you have not been keeping track.

I am not sure what I will find. There is a part of me that still thinks the dome, like any instrument, has been hijacked by a story I have not yet heard. But I am walking toward the story anyway. People in the city pull their own children out of other people’s puddles and put their groceries back on the shelves after the earth shakes and learn the names of clouds that will hurt them and the names of the people who will show up with blankets. We triangulate with what we have.

On the wall of the planetarium, when I close the door behind me, the shadow of the dome falls in a way that makes the word MERIDIAN look like a question. The white sky hovers, bright and empty, above the low buildings. But the dome knows which holes the dark will drink water from. It is a start. It is the first chapter of what I will have to tell if anyone ever asks how we learned, once again, how to look up.

Chapter One

The memory I take from Edda Ruíz tastes like boiled sugar and diesel, a carnival ride stalling midway over the river. I’m not supposed to taste them. The handbook is clear: observe the subject’s posture and pulse, watch the filament for color shifts, keep your mouth shut. But it’s like standing in a bakery and pretending you don’t smell anything. Some days the scent reaches into the back of my throat and drags a feeling up with it, and I can’t help it. I swallow. Later, I’ll pretend the burn is from the tea.

Edda sits on the edge of her gray sofa, feet not touching the floor. She is smaller than I remember, a dried fig of a woman in a blue housedress with pockets deep enough for secrets and peppermint. Her hands, knuckly, stay busy worrying the hem. Behind her, a wall of frames glitters with faces turned toward one another. So many parties in one room—baptisms, quinceañeras, graduations. The Ruíz family throws more celebrations than the rest of Palmar put together. Or they used to. Some of those faces are braced against blank panes where images have faded, bleached into clean squares like missing teeth.

“You don’t have to be nervous,” I tell her, because the faster I say it, the more gently it lands. People hear what they need to hear if you don’t give them time to argue with it. “You’ve done this before. It doesn’t hurt.”

“Teo,” she says, and the way she says my name makes my shoulders drop. Her voice is the sound of a stone rolling down into a well. “Hijo, you always say that. It’s not the hurt of it. It’s—” Her fingers pull another thread free. “It’s the empty after. I always walk to the kitchen and forget what I came for. And then I stand there and look at the window, at the trees, at the glass. And I—” She flaps one hand. “I stand there, and I am waiting for someone to come tell me what I wanted. Like a waitress with her pad out, writing down nothing.”

I nod and open my case. There are twenty-seven names on my docket today, and only two of them pay cash. The rest will pay in increments of themselves. The filament lies coiled against the velvet, a whisper of gold. When I feed it through the condenser, it hums awake, brightening to a thread of sun, fine as a hair. The handbook says the filament has no sound. The handbook lies about a lot.

Edda leans forward, offering me her wrist. Her skin smells like orange blossom water, like the past hiding in plain sight. “You and those hands,” she says, staring at them. “Like your father’s. I used to tell your mother—”

I touch the filament to the soft skin below her thumb, and her words snag, unspool. The current leaps. For an instant, we are a circuit closed under winter light, and I feel the heat of it run up my arm into my teeth. It is always like this. The filament warms, and those small brown flecks in the gold wake and rise like fish coming to the surface.

I was a child once. People remind me of this. I remember it like you remember a street you haven’t walked in years: the potholes are deeper, the paint is flaked off the curbs, the bakery has new owners. I remember the sense that everything around you is taller than you are, even the light. But mostly I remember my mother’s hands catching my face when I came running too fast, palms against my jaw. She would say, “Despacio, Teo,” and the word—despacio—would break apart in her mouth into soft pieces, the way bread falls, the way clouds do, into practical weather. This is how memories arrive to me now: not in order, but in what they’re made of.

Edda gasps. On the thread, a darkening, plum-pulp purple. Taxable.

“That’s enough,” I say. If you take too much, the person will go flat on you like an old soda. I am not supposed to think about it that way. The handbook says: You are a public servant. You are the steward of fairness. No one likes paying taxes. We are the bank that keeps the city’s faith. But you work long enough in this office and you learn the metaphors that help you sleep.

The condenser purrs in my lap. The purple gathers, thickens, beads. I touch the thread to the gate of the ampoule, and it slides in without any indecency at all, a marbled drop that settles in the glass like a fruit preserved in syrup. The ampoule’s seal bites down and clicks. On its belly, the ledger stamps a number that will match the one on my report. The City is a lover of numbers. Numbers tuck under its tongue. Numbers let it forget our names.

“What did I give?” Edda asks, without looking at me. Her eyes are on the frames. One of them has turned soft with mildew at the edges, a place where the river crept in, a little.

“Nothing you’ll miss,” I say, and it’s almost true. What she handed over had the feeling of tin roofs in rain and the smell of corn cobs charring on a brazier. It tasted like diesel and sugar. That’s how I knew it was the carnival. Forty-seven years ago, a man in a hat with a white feather guessed her weight and gave her a stuffed bear for lying. She lied; he lied; everyone laughed. There was a kiss behind the bumper cars. Beyond that, something with a bridge and a cigarette and a wristwatch’s ticking. She won’t notice it’s gone unless she goes looking for it.

“I always miss it,” she says. “That’s how missing works.”

I might have said something to her. I might have told her about the day after my first collection, when I walked out into the courtyard of the Office of Equitable Contribution and didn’t understand where I had put my car. The weight of the autopay schedule, old muscle memory, carried me past the car, past the nearest bus stop, until I was standing at the river with my hands empty and a feeling in my mouth like I had eaten oranges with the peel on. I might have told her how I have learned to walk around the empty spots like potholes, sometimes with dignity and sometimes, there is nothing dignified about it, with my ankles wet.

Instead I take my pen and sign my initials—TM—on the line below her name. The machine zips out a copy for her. I lay the ampoule in its slot in my case among the others, a tray of candied plums.

“You’ll send a receipt,” she says.

“It’ll arrive before the end of the month,” I say. “New system now. They’re faster.” I stand and my knee cracks, a small private thunder. Twenty-seven today. Twenty-nine tomorrow. The numbers stay constant; the names swap out. The City tells us the algorithm is fair. Edda’s sofa exhales when I get up. She looks at the framed faces again and puts her hand on the glass as if she could warm it.

“You look tired,” she says, mothering me despite the fact that she is not my mother. “You must be careful with your heart. Men think they only have one, but that is because they are cowards. We have many.”

“I’ll be careful,” I tell her. I want, for a second, to put my hand over hers on the frame. Instead I close my case. My hands are not for comfort. My hands lift memory out of living bodies and send it to a place with turnstiles.

Outside the building the day is the kind of white that makes you think of a fresh egg cracked into a bowl and whisked until it holds peaks. The evergreens planted by the Rotary Club stand too still, like men at attention, collared by their little iron fences. A poster is glued onto the sideline of a telephone pole: a simple black fist and a slogan in orange paint you can’t miss even if you are late for everything—REMEMBER WHAT THEY TOOK. Someone has tried to scrape it off, but the orange clings stubbornly. A second hand has written under it, in blue ink, smaller, like a whisper: Does it help?

On the walk from Edda’s to the Bureau, I pass a man selling prayer candles that have been burned and refilled. They are full of lumps like kneecaps. Children run with sticks dragging behind them, drawing stutters through the dust. A girl with a braid down her back is carrying a jar that glows faintly despite the daylight. The jar is stoppered with wax and string. Inside, a small storm turns and grumbles. Those aren’t supposed to be out here. Weather has a chain of custody now. The City says the storms give us power. The farmers say the storms are tired of us.

At Ninth and Beryl, a boy in a yellow raincoat stands on a milk crate and holds up a cardboard sign with the price of days: Today 1.2, Tomorrow 1.4. He is joking; it is a joke so old it has become a service. People laugh at him, and some of them give him coins because their laugh feels like a purchase. I do not laugh. I keep my chest steady, the way you hold a bowl full to the rim.

The Bureau is a building from the 1970s that smells like all 1970s buildings do—hot dust and dry paper and coffee that is never the right temperature. The floors have been polished to a greasy shine, and the windows are always half-open because the air carries better that way. The City prides itself on circulation.

“Teo,” says My supervisor, who hates being called my supervisor because she has a name—Ariela—and a gold tooth and a laugh like someone dropping cutlery onto tile. She leans around her doorway and snaps at me with two fingers to come in. On her desk there are three stacks of forms, and the stacks are slumped against one another like tired men. She points to the top one and taps the corner with a short nail. “Assessment Week,” she says. “You heard?”

I set my case on the chair and keep my face as polite as a spoon. “I heard they’re moving it up,” I say. “I heard rumors are good for morale.”

“They’re moving it up,” she says, and does not apologize. “There’s to be a holiday fair. Old music. Trucks. People give better when the drums are loud.”

“You think people give better when there is free popcorn,” I say. Ariela smiles without showing her gold tooth.

She slides a paper over to me. I watch the sheet’s edge travel across the desk. The list is only five names long. Five names are trouble where twenty-seven are not. Five names have a weight to them.

“Special Extractions,” she says, and says it like it is nothing. “From the backlog.”

Two of the names are out in the North Orchards. One is near the riverport, the buildings there leaning into one another as if they all have something to say. The fourth is a dentist. The fifth sits on the page like a nail you’ve found with your foot—Delia Sereno.

“Is this a joke?” I say, keeping my voice level because there are other kinds of pain besides the theatrical. Ariela knows my mother’s name. Everyone in this building knows it. I bring in the best numbers in my division. This is not because I am hungrier, though I might be, but because I have learned people’s ordinances. I collect from them what they can give. “I can’t take from my—a relative,” I say, and the handbooks are suddenly quiet.

“You can,” says Ariela. “You will. We’re short on special collectors, and your assessments come in clean. The auditors like clean. They purr.” She leans back and looks at me, and in her eyes something softens the way a light will go soft before a storm breaks it up. “It’s a back tax, Teo. You know how it is. The City let Delia’s account float. And then add and add, like dough left out in a hot kitchen. It’s no good once it sours.”

“My mother has never been late,” I say, and it feels like a lie even if it is technically true. No one is late if their note is forgiven. No one is late, either, if the note never arrives.

Ariela watches my hands on the leather of my case. The case was my father’s, the handle worn into the shape of his grip. It is the only thing of his that did not go into the water. “If you don’t go,” she says, “someone else will. You can tell yourself which someone you would prefer. The young ones drive the numbers up because they think success is a math problem. The older ones drive them up because they are tired of chewing their food.”

“If I go,” I say, “I’m taking only what is owed and nothing more. Nothing from her body that she needs to get through a day. None of the good things.”

Ariela’s laugh is quiet, knives on tile far away down the hall. “You think you can tell the filament where to go? It goes where the heat is, like a cat. If you do your work, it takes what is richest and most offered. That is the mercy in it. You will not rip her apart. The work does not permit it.” She looks up at the clock as if time could be persuaded to sit down. “Before Assessment Week starts,” she says. “Do not make me chase you.”

On the walk home I cut down under the bridge because I need the river. The underside of bridges is where people tell the truth. There are initials carved into the pillars that hold up the westbound lanes—MS + AEM; TONY; Una vida—and there are hearts around some of them and a slash through others. A boy sits on the bank with a line in the water and no hook on it. The way his jaw is set says he knows: sometimes the point is not to catch anything.

The river is the Rasa. The Rasa is older than all our paperwork. We built the City around it and pretended we were the ones doing the holding. In the spring it comes up over its own edges and reminds us. People come down to throw stones, letters, pieces of bread. The activists—rememberers, mem-hustlers, radicals with jars—bring contraband to the arches at night and toss in bags they’ve cut loose from the chain stores. The City says this is illegal disposal.
