The posters say it is a giving back. I stand and watch the water move around a broken shopping cart. The water comes, goes, comes back. It does not remember me. It does not have to.

“Teo,” says a voice, and when I turn, Lark is there, rolling a cigarette with her fingers like she is making a fortune-teller from notebook paper. Her hair is the same as it’s been since we were children, the color of damp rope, the length of a promise that keeps being kept. She wears her protest on her sleeves: safety pins, an enamel button with a hand opening, yesterday’s orange paint. “You look like someone told you your house is going to fly away.”

“Assessment Week,” I say.

“I know,” she says. “We've been working the phone lines. The lines tell us back how tired they are. It’s like singing into a closet.”

“I have special assignments,” I say.

“You always have special assignments. You’re special.” She says it lightly and then looks at the chain-link fence as if it has answers. “You could come with us tonight. We've got boxes. The good kind. No alarms. We’re going to throw a little party for the river.”

“I’ll be home,” I say. “I have—” I stop. It is a superstition among us that you do not say the word mother on the under-side of things.

Lark nods. She licks the paper, seals it, slides the cigarette behind her ear. “Come if you need the noise,” she says. “It’s better with drums.”

On my mother’s block, the jacaranda trees have gone slightly wild. Their purple is too much for the street, a kind of rash. Kids have been stomping the fallen blossoms into paste; the driveway margins are slick with it. The Ruíz family’s little house is three down from a place where a door has been painted with prayers, a calligraphy under glass. My mother’s house has a roof like a knitted cap. Someone has patched it since I was last here. The new shingles don’t match the old, but they sit together politely.

She answers the door before I knock, as if she has been standing with her hand on the knob since I was born. She is wearing a yellow blouse and a skirt with little stars. In the gathering dusk her face shows as a version of mine sanded by weather. Her earlobes, I notice, are bare. It is not a thing someone else would see.

“Teo,” she says, and I put down the amulet I’ve been carrying under the skin of my tongue all day. My mother says my name like she made it. She steps back and lets me in. “Mijo. Mira. You are thin. Come, come.”

The house is smaller than I remember and bigger than it has any right to be. Every wall has been persuaded into holding up more than it should. Receipts are clipped to string and stretched from corner to corner, a zigzag of paper. There are lists pinned to lists. The couch has a spilled soup of pennies pooled in the corner where the cushion sags. On the table, a vase with one gladiolus leans its whole gladness toward the light.

“You got a letter,” I say, because avoiding is a cruelty we reserve for strangers. “From the City.”

My mother looks at me as if she is translating. “I did,” she says. “Teo, sit. Drink. I have hibiscus water. It is too sweet.” She pours and pushes a glass toward me. Her hands tremble only slightly. She has trained them better than her heart.

“I can go with you,” I say. “To the office. We can talk to Ariela. She—”

“I went,” my mother says. She sets her glass down exactly in the wet ring left by the last glass. “I am not a child.” Her voice is kind when she says it, which makes it worse. “They told me what I owe. It is a big list. I told them I would pay. I am a woman who pays.”

The hibiscus tastes like the inside of a red blossom. It is too sweet. On the sheet of the table there are faint pink drops like a language of warnings. “When?”

“Today,” she says. She doesn’t meet my eyes. “I gave. The boy with the hat. The one who does not look at women when he does this. He had…a cardigan. He was polite. He asked for a good day. I tried to give him a boring one, but—” She shrugs. “How do you know what is boring, Teo? Today in the market, a man cut his finger and bled into the guavas. That is interesting. He was ashamed. I wanted to say Listen, we are all dropping ourselves into the fruit. I wanted to say, Do not cry. But I did not. That is a boring day. Not saying the thing.”

“What did you give?” I say, and my mouth is so dry with the sugar that the words come out soft. “Mama.”

She looks up as if I have asked her the name of her oldest friend in a language she once knew. There are shapes moving across her face, the shadows of birds passing in front of a window. “Your birth,” she says after a long breath. “I thought I had paid that already. It is on every list. It is on the backs of all the lists. It is a thing I have already paid. But the boy with the hat said no. He said we are new inventory now. He said, Tell me the time, Señora. And I couldn’t. I don’t remember numbers. I remember the water and the scream and the way the morning smelled—my hair. The taste of the mint they made me suck. I thought I would die of mint. It made everything else…far away. And then your father cried because he cried at good weather and at bad weather and at your name. He wanted to name you River. I said No, he will only be called back.”

My hands are on the table. My hands are not for comfort. My hands want to break every ampoule in my case and pour what’s inside into my mouth just to see if I have the shape for everything. “They took that,” I say, and cannot keep the break out of it.

“I gave it,” she says, a correction as gentle as the first rain after a dry month. “Do not make me a child.”

Behind her, on the wall, a picture of my father is hung crooked. He is leaning against the hood of a car he never owned, smiling like he knew the camera loved him. The light at his left ear turns into a flare. The paper with the City seal sits on the shelf below it, heavy, officious, official. I can feel the numbers inside it like a headache.

“I will talk to them,” I say. “They can’t take something like that. It is—” I have no word that will not make her look at me with pity and amusement.

My mother reaches into the pocket of her skirt and takes out something small wrapped in tissue. She puts it in my palm. It is dangled and fragile. “I wanted to give you this,” she says. “Before they come again. Your father left it in the plant by the door, like he thought it would grow if we watered it. It is not mine to carry.”

Inside the paper there is a small ampoule, glass with a seam like a flaw in the air. It is old. The seal is waxed, not the click-snap of now. Inside the glass the liquid is a thin gold, not yet darkened, not yet eaten by its own sugar. I hold it up to the light. In it I see something move like a fish, then vanish into the sweet. On the belly in a shade of ink that has gone gray: T. SERENO, it says, in a hand that is not the City’s.

“It’s yours,” my mother says, and because she has given a day in which I first came to her and because I cannot stop the hunger in my hands, I take it.

“How long have you had this?” I ask.

She lifts one shoulder like a bird adjusts a wing on a perch. “How long have people been paying?” she says. “We did not always give our days in jars. Before, you threw what you did not want into the river or the fire or you told it to the priest. He said Hush and said God and then took the sound of it into the archive of his chest. It is easier now. The jars break when they should. They break when they shouldn’t. I am old. I have learned to like the sound.”

When I close my hand around the ampoule, it warms, not with the filament’s impersonal warmth but the heat of something waking up. The glass hums. For a second I taste oranges. I think of Edda’s carnival. I think of my father putting money into my pockets when my mother wasn’t looking, as if I were a jar. I think of the poster on the pole, the question written under it with the blue ink: Does it help?

My mother looks at me over the lip of her too-sweet glass. “You can sleep in the back room,” she says. “Your old bed is not there anymore. It was never very good. You are too big now for that kind of arrangement. You can have the floor. Floors are honest. They tell you what falls.”

She moves through the kitchen, her skirts whispering to the cupboard doors. I sit at the table and put the ampoule down and turn it under my finger, like a bright coin. In the glass liquid is a trick of the eye: when I tilt it, images seem to gather and recede, as if I am looking through the bottom of a bottle at a familiar street. I should not open it. There are laws written by people who wear better shoes than mine, and there are other laws written by rivers and mothers. The house smells like hibiscus and dust and something else, something green starting up.

When night falls, it falls all at once, like a door closing. The jacarandas outside the window have turned into dark hands pressed against the glass. In the quiet, the City’s distant machinery takes a deep breath and lets it out. For a long while, my mother moves through the house, checking locks that are already locked. She hums, off-key, the song that makes new things right with old things.

On the table, the ampoule makes no sound. How many things I know that make no sound until they break. I look at the numbers stamped into the City letter. I think of Ariela’s tooth and the way the filament bit down on Edda’s skin and drank like a cat. I think of the boy with no hook and of Lark with a cigarette behind her ear and of a poster that orange could not outrun.

When I lift the ampoule to my mouth, I am no one’s public servant. I am my father’s son. The glass is cool on my teeth. I bite until the seal gives, until the taste empties into me like dawn into a room. The sweetness is so sharp it stings, and there is diesel in it, mint, the arc of a bird from one tree to another, the exact weight of a hand on my head. It is a day that could have been mine. It changes the place behind my eyes where the paperwork lives.

It is not the memory they think it is. It is not the memory anyone would inventory. It is not yet a story. It is a door. When it opens, the house around me shifts, breathes, becomes new. My mother pauses in the doorway and looks at me and tilts her head, as if she is listening to the same thing I am. The quiet has shape.

“Teo,” she says, and this time the way she says my name has me in it twice.

There is a way certain days take you and stand you where you can see how you have been carrying yourself so far. There is a way the river looks when the bridge lights come on in a line, one after the other, like a sentence starting. There is a way a city empties its pockets and finds in the lint a gold coin it had not meant to save. I sit at the table in my mother’s house with my hands on the wood and the ampoule and the sound of the filament in my teeth and I know: the work I learned how to do can be undone. Or not undone. Remade.

Outside, far down by the arches, a drum starts. Then another. It is Assessment Week on its way to be moved up. It is a party for the river, for the night, for the city that believes in its own fairness. My mother takes my glass and washes it and sets it upside-down on the drying rack. We look at one another and then look away, because neither of us knows yet whether we are about to do something brave or something that will undo us.

The ampoule in my hand says nothing at all. It sits and waits for me to decide what a first chapter is worth.

Chapter One

On the morning the city lifted its white tongues to the sky, Miren woke to the sound of cloth filling with weather.

She rolled onto her side and watched the fog nets from her window. They had been hoisted above the alleys in the blue before dawn, stretched from rooftop to rooftop with the practiced economy of a fisherman’s hands. Now the wind combed the nets, combed the thin hair of fog that had huddled overnight in the spoil of the old estuary, and the cloth bellied and sagged and glistened. Light skimmed the threads and turned each droplet into a tiny, trembling coin.

The air had a taste then that it only had once every twelve days, when the fog came low enough to catch: a chalky sweetness, like biting the seed of a green peach, and under it the metallic breath of old anchors. In the street below, the Fogwardens walked with their lanterns unlit and their hands softly out, keeping the children from dancing under the swaying nets. Above the nets the cranes of the saltworks were still, every hook at rest, the cranes’ shadows long and thin as tally marks.

“Close your jaw,” Sabela used to say when Miren was small and the fog was a joke they weren’t in on. “You’ll swallow a moth.”

Miren closed her jaw. Her mouth was an instrument she kept clean and quiet these days. She lay for a while, listening to the city gather itself, feeling the filtered weight of the fog settle into the cloth and thread its way into the cisterns that kept a million throats from cracking.

In the workshop below her room—the room that had been the pantry when the sea still came up to the second step—someone knocked a wooden handle against a surface in an off pattern. It was the knock they used in drought years on doors they were unsure of: three, pause, one. Miren sat up.

Her boots were cold, the gloss of last week’s brine still at the seams. She sealed her mouth with the strip of linen she wore when she worked and slid down the stair, keeping each step out of memory’s exact crack. In the stairwell the air smelled of lard and salt and the faint peppery ghost of Sabela’s tobacco. Miren had scrubbed the walls with the ash of mule clover for years to exorcise that smell, but the stone had taken it badly, the way salt takes a stain, holding the shape of the thing that fell on it clear long after the thing itself is gone.

She opened the door.

A boy stood there, skin the color of wetted earth, hair speared flat by fog, eyes too alert for his age. He held a basket bound with rush and blue wire, damp enough that drops had rolled down and made circles on the threshold. Miren’s mouth changed; against her will, it opened.

“You’re the reader?” he asked, sounding proud to have memorized his line.

“I read what hasn’t melted yet,” Miren said. It was the answer she gave to keep people from thinking she could read anything.

He looked at the linen on her mouth as if it were a superstition. The basket smelled of flesh.

“You’re Miren Sera. They told me to put this into your own hands.”

“Who told you?”

“A man with mildew on his shoes,” the boy said, with a child’s relish for small authority. “He didn’t like the fog. He said his lungs had been tired since the rains turned into a rumor. He gave me bread for the errand and said someone would make a blessing if I gave it to you right, but not the church kind. The kind with both hands.”

Miren took the basket. It was heavier than she’d expected; the rushes creaked. Under the damp scent of the weave was the cold, unmistakable breath of something that had been under water that was not domestic, not harbored, not pumped through the city by pipes. The hair at Miren’s nape lifted and then smoothed itself.

“Do you want to come in and watch me open it?” she asked reflexively, because when she was a girl the opening of bundles had been for the whole street. You weighed the twine, you guessed the sender, you judged the way the knot had been tied, with love or in haste. But the boy took a step back and put his hands under his armpits and shook his head.

“My mother wants me to show my tongue to the Fogwardens so they know I didn’t swallow real dew,” he said. “They don’t count spit.”

He squinted at her face one last time, as if to take something away from it and tell it at home, then darted up the alley. Miren watched him weave past the laddered legs of the Fogwardens stilling themselves to pull the nets down when they were heavy. The city had learned to move like that: quickly, in the openings, the way fish once moved through light.

She set the basket on the table by the window and loosened the blue wire. The rushes opened their breath. Inside, wrapped in three tight turns of something that glittered, was a fish.

For a moment Miren forgot that the room was not the room she had been born in, forget even her body. The fish lay there simply as if it had lifted its own lid, as if someone had conjured it up out of the old water and set it on her table. It was no desert breed from the brine pans, not a tight-shouldered carp from someone’s emergency pond; this was a fish whose muscle had been taught by tides. Silver yellowed at the belly, the line along its side pale blue as breath held too long, an eye that should have reflected a ceiling of boat planks but instead reflected the cracked lime of Miren’s workshop. The gill fluttered once, an after-argument with death, and stilled.

Miren had never believed the city’s stories about the sea sending things back to the people who missed it. She believed in what the salt kept and what it lost. She believed in what it said when you put your tongue to it and waited for sense to dissolve. But her hands trembled around the fish like hands around a warm bowl.

She didn’t touch the thing that glittered. She stood for a while and watched the way the light from the window fell on that glitter, and because she was who she was, she could not stop herself from cataloguing the reflections. Lines radiated in a repeating pattern that was not the pattern of fish scales but something brittle and regular. The pattern fell into her like a remembered prayer.

Salt leaf.

No one pressed salt leaf like that anymore. It broke if you breathed on it wrong. You needed a humidity like a held mouth and a patience like a saint’s to work that thin. You needed a way to keep your fingers warm and dry at the same time. The last person Miren knew who had been able to make salt leaf that thin had died seven years ago when a salt storm took the market roofs and the walkway and Miren’s mother.

Sabela used to slice one thin sheet of salt leaf and let Miren hold it up to a candle. The sheet would blush. In the light you could see the inclusions: specks of mud, flecks of kelp, the shinier grit of shell. “This is how the sea remembers,” Sabela would say. “This is the alphabet we have been given.”

Sabela had not invented the alphabet of flavor, but she had learned to hear it. She said that the tongue could read the way a fingertip reads. That what a child was told were tastes—sweet, salt, sour, bitter, umami—were only untrained families, like calling all birds birds. From childhood, she had taught Miren what the tongue could differentiate if it sat still long enough: the iron of old blood from the iron of nails, the chalk of bone from the chalk of fish scale, the funeral-ash salt that clung when a shoreline burned, the limewash that a priest had scraped from a church wall and sold. Each flavor was an inclusion, and each inclusion was a mark. With a sheet of leaf as thin as the blister on a heel, a hand could lay down marks no eye could see, and a tongue could read a name tireless as a repeating wave.

It had been years since Miren had put her mouth to any leaf. She had sworn off tasting the day she had put her tongue to the last sheet Sabela had made and felt—on that slip of salt, smooth as new ice—the cold flat taste of tin. The letters had spelled her own name in a pattern Sabela had never used for her before: MIR ENSER A, broken, Sabela’s mistake or her intention, Miren would never know, and then under it the word RUN, a pure, unalloyed copper that had not come near water in decades. She had run to the market. The roofs had been lifting like pages. She had not been fast enough to keep a sheet of corrugated tin from coming down like a word on Sabela’s shoulder.

She reached for her scalpel.

With the point, she loosened the bridge that had sealed the leaf around the fish. The sheet eased free. She slid the sheet onto the window and pinned two corners with little rice-weighted sacks. The light from the window made the inclusions flicker. The city’s fog light is gentle; it has no spine to it. It makes everything wish to be touched.

She washed her mouth in brine, once, twice, as the old practice demanded, and dried it carefully on the inside of her forearm where no lint would cling. She sat on the low stool Sabela had carved for her when she was nine and the floor was still damp at dawn and tasted the air with her smile hidden behind the linen. Her heart beat a small wing in her throat. She reached out, pulled the linen down, and pressed her tongue against the leaf.

People believed, dangerously and incorrectly, that readers like Miren were like anyone else with a tongue, only more so: that we had been born, somehow, with a scale in the palate, a tuning fork in the flesh. The truth is that we are taught. We are taught to quiet the alive of the mouth. We are taught to keep saliva where it belongs. We are taught patience. We are taught how to wait for what is not at the surface. And in the waiting, the distinctions are a kind of mercy.

At first there was only salt. Salt is not a taste, not anymore; it is a way the mouth understands the world. The leaf softened. It yielded the lightest shade of rust: river iron, not long water. That was a stroke, not a background. Miren held her breath. She closed her eyes and let the sequence unfold across her tongue like beads drawn through a hand.

The first line tasted of lime, very thin: a house. Then bone, bleached of smoke—she could see the pale ribs of the fish without trying, that was almost unfair. Then ash from carob, bitter but with a sweetness that dried into sugar at the end. Then copper, laid so fine she almost missed it. Not pure copper—there was a wire taste to it, a city copper handled by many palms. The pattern of strokes spelled a familiar beginning: MIREN.

She pulled her tongue back from the leaf and put her mouth back under the linen to rest it. Her hand had learned not to tremble. Her hand trembled anyway.

She drew the leaf closer and pressed her tongue again.

Under MIR EN, a taste like an unripe pomegranate—that was the way Sabela had always marked her own initial. It was how she had signed the sheets in the early years, when words were too obvious and the world too small for secrets. And after it, a night-of-rain taste, a taste that had not run down the walls of this city in Miren’s life. Sabela had always said: I will not use flavor to mean what flavor means. Yet here was water used to mean water. The stroke thickened at the end. A well.

She read the strokes aloud in her head, not in the alphabet that everyone agreed on, but in the older alphabet that Sabela used for the ones she hid even from herself.

Miren, the salt remembers the wrong things. Follow the water that does not look like water. Under the old track, past the stalled crane, where the woman with one ear sells soap of no smell. Bring a bone from the oar.

Miren pulled back. Her mouth floods when she reads; the body thinks it is eating. She swallowed the extra and tasted shame. She had thought the hunger in her mouth belonged to words. It belonged to hunger.

She stood up, wiping her lips carefully with the back of her hand. The fog nets had begun to lower, full bellies groaning. The Fogwardens’ voices had shifted from night tone to morning. In the alley, someone coughed a cough that ended with a spit on the stones and an apology. In the workshop, the fish lay on her table and did not bleed.

A woman with one ear who sold soap with no smell. Miren knew her. Everyone knew her, like everyone knew the rats with white blazes and the boy with the cobbled knee and the cranes that had never moved again after the sea left. Iria, whose brother fell through when the salt bridge under him gave way, whose left ear had been bitten off in a market fight over a bowl of clean water when Miren was still too young to understand why you would bite to draw blood when what you needed was not in the blood. Iria boiled soap in the alley behind the collapsed bell foundry and kept her head turned when people were unkind.

Under the old track, past the stalled crane. The cranes were stone now. Their hooks were good for hanging meat and hammocks. Sabela had marked meet points in stranger ways before. But water that does not look like water? Bringing a bone from the oar?

Miren walked her hand along her shelf until it rested on the long drawer that held the things that had survived the night the market roofs went. Sabela’s pipe lay there with one crack like a river drawn with a child’s certainty. The tape Sabela used to measure for leaf. The foxed notebook with nothing in it but four pressed leaves of the old sea ivy. And a small, curved length of osseous pale wood that Miren had always told herself was from some instrument, because instruments had the bright shape of hope even when no hand tuned them.

She lifted that bone. It was smoothed where a hand would have gone. The oil of the hand had gone into it. The grain of it—lack of grain—was like the endlessness of waves. Miren had never been out far enough to feel endlessness, but she had inherited a bone from it anyway.

And then, because not eating the question would be worse than any answer, she bent again to the leaf, and read the last line.

Tell no one who counts fog for a living.

She sat down on the low stool in the fog light. She did not know how to tell the leaf that she had been someone who counted fog her whole life. She had counted drops in the nets with her tongue. She had counted how many cups of it would keep her from answering people with unkindness. She had counted Sabela’s steps to the stall and back and had not reckoned on the gust that would miscount her mother. She had counted her own guilt.

She looked at the fish on the table. There were things that could be done with such a fish in a city like this. It could buy her clean water for a season. It could buy a child’s first shoes that were not made of stitched salt leaf, a knife that had known a throat. It could buy a man’s memory out of a salt block and back into his granddaughter’s face. It could be sold in slices to the rich on the hill who held their noses against the brine of the market and pretended they were eating something delicate instead of a miracle. Or it could be carried through the streets under a cloth and laid at the foot of a woman with one ear as proof of message.

She went to the window and looked down on the alley. Iria’s corner of steam was where it always was, as constant as the stump of the bell. Iria had a way of thinning the fog with her body, of making a pocket in it where she could be almost alone. A child stood on a stool to watch the froth. A Fogwarden paused and then moved on. Iria did not look up.

Sabela’s letter had tasted like lime, like bone, like copper, like rain. But beneath all that, under the alphabet and its comedy, there had been a taste Miren had not tasted in seven years. It was not a flavor the city had a word for. It was the taste of hands that were always warm because they would not admit the cold. It was the taste of the little notch Sabela had cut in the edge of a sheet when Miren was thirteen and thought she could hide the way she flinched at the taste of grave ash. It was the taste of Sabela’s breath the night before she died when she had eaten a piece of sugar full of ants and laughed, the ants’ bitterness making sweetness strange. It was Sabela herself, because there are some inclusions even the sea cannot leach.

The Fogwardens started to call out the wards of the city, numbering them so that if a net broke or a girl climbed a roof or a man forgot and reached with both hands for what he should have taken with one, the city would know where to look. Their voices moved in order, like prayer.

Miren wrapped the fish again, close and tight, in what leaf she could salvage, and bound it not with wire but with strip of the cloth Sabela had used to wrap the handle of the blade she preferred. She set the bone along the fish side and held them together with that cloth until her fingers were sure. She put both into the basket with rushes and the damp smell of old water, then covered the basket with a tray so that if anyone peered they would see the working of a woman who read things, which mostly looked like nothing.

She thought of telling Jun, who worked three alleys over tincturing algae into something that resembled olive oil if you held it at tilt. In their youth, when hunger was still an hour, they had once laughed at a man who had tried to sell clay molded into the shape of bread. They had bought the clay anyway for the shape of it. Jun had a way of turning the obvious into something kinder. But Sabela, in salt, had said Tell no one who counts fog for a living. Everyone in this city counted fog. Some counted it to sell, some counted it to stay alive, some counted it to know when to leave. You could think yourself the exception and be a fool.

On the threshold she stopped. The taste of the message was still in her mouth, a long light thread humming between her teeth. Her body wanted water. She did not drink. She spread a little ash across her tongue and pressed her lips together and breathed through her nose until the hunger lay down.

Outside, the fog had come down enough to touch her hair. It beaded there, then ran. The alley was a hallway of hung cloth, a white tunnel with a seam of people down the middle like a spine. They moved around her with care, recognizing the shape of a basket carried level, the shape of someone paying attention. To her left a woman cupped her hands and someone shook a net like a pitcher and poured a fistful of water into those hands and the woman lifted them to her child’s mouth. To her right a man knelt in the mud with a notebook under a splatter of wax and tried to invent a new way to tally drop by drop. The fog horns in the distance spoke to each other, deep-bellied, as if under water. The cranes stayed still.

Miren moved through the alley as if the alley had been laid for her, as if the day had been a sheet of salt leaf stretched between two things she could name, as if the taste in her mouth would persist long enough for her to carry this strange, impossible, almost holy cargo across sixteen doors and one small square and past the boy with the cobbled knee who would look into her eyes without a question and then forget her as a kindness.

At the juncture where the old track buckled up over the road and cracked the stone into the shape of a sleeping animal, she stopped to let three women pass. The women carried buckets on their heads and sang in a language that had rolled pebbles smoother than any paper would make you think. At the base of the stalled crane, a man with mildew on his shoes was teaching a child how to sweep without making dust. Miren kept her eyes on the place she was going. Good luck is a squirrel in this city. If you turn toward it hard, it is only air in your hand.

Iria saw her first. Her eye was a human eye, brown and ordinary as wet dirt, and then it narrowed and glittered and made Miren think of scales. She lifted a hand and made a space.

“If it’s soap,” Iria said, already reaching for a coin that might help Miren bear the weight of bringing it, “I have use for it. If it’s prayer, I’ll take it if it doesn’t tattle. If it’s a word, you can keep it until I’m old.”

“It’s a fish,” Miren said, because you begin a miracle with its true name.

Iria laughed then, and wiped the laugh away with the back of her wrist as if it were something that might sting. “In this city a fish is not its true name. In this city that is a map and a way to get lost. Put it down.”

They slid the basket onto the shelf by Iria’s boiler. Miren took away the tray. She loosened the cloth. Iria leaned. When the first sliver of yellowed silver showed, Iria did not reach to touch it. She put her hand to her chest and let her mouth open, forgot her missing ear for a moment and let her head turn full. In that instant she looked like a storybook queen who had been taken somewhere she did not choose and had found on her lap something she recognized.

“Who,” Iria began. She could not find the rest.

“A man with mildew on his shoes,” Miren said, and it was true in one way but not the way that counted.

“And you brought it to me.”

“My mother wrote to me in the leaf wrapped around it,” Miren said, and her voice shook, and she let it, because she was done apologizing to anyone for the miracles their mothers made. “She told me to bring a bone of the oar.”

Iria looked at Miren’s hands. Her gaze fell, as eyes do when they trust hands more than faces, to the bone laid along the fish as if sleeping there.

“You carry the oar bone like a spoon,” she said, not unkind.

“I’ve never rowed out,” Miren said. “I have not had water enough for that.”

“We rowed in canals once,” Iria said. “Small. No tide. A child could do it in a skirt. The oars were ugly. The water smelled like old teeth. But you could go somewhere without taking your feet with you.”

Miren hadn’t known Iria had been a child in a city with water. Iria had the look of a person born too late for her own memories.

“There’s water under the ground,” Miren said, because saying a thing makes it less likely to be taken before you touch it. “She said, the water that does not look like water.”

“Dark water,” Iria said softly, as if reading a label in her mind. “There are stories. There are holes. Your mother told you to go to one of the holes?”

Miren nodded, and Iria nodded back, and for a moment the city made a line through them like a skewer through fruit, and Miren thought, not for the first time, that the only reason anyone lived here still was that the people made spaces for each other to stand in.

“I can pretend I didn’t see you,” Iria said after a moment, and her voice had changed to the voice she used when she talked to Fogwardens. “If anyone who counts fog asks. Don’t take a light if you can help it. The holes don’t like light. They eat it and leave nothing to see with.”

“And the oar bone?”

“That,” Iria said, and she smiled, and the smile made Miren see the child Iria must have been, the one with both ears and a row of teeth like white beans, “you will know where it fits by the way your hand stops wanting.”

Miren put the bone back in the basket, laid the fish against it, bound both. She did not tell Iria that her hand had wanted always. Some hungers did not deserve to be fed. Others were maps.

“Under the track,” Iria said, and glanced, and in the glance there was a grace Miren would not forget. “Past the crane. Keep the wall to your right. When you feel the wall sweat, stop taking steps.”

In the square, someone started to sing a fog song, one of the new ones that was only numbers and the names of streets. Miren stepped back into the alley and into the song. The basket pulled her down like a promise and kept her upright like a secret.

There would be time to be careful. There would be a way to tell Jun. There would be a day when she would be able to slide the sheet of leaf into a book and name the lines without thinking of bone. There would be a night when she would not dream of roofs lifting. There would be a place under the city where the water did not look like water.

Her mother had tasted like rain. The air had the chalk of promise and the iron of warning. The fog lifted off the nets and ran into the mouths of the cisterns, and Miren walked toward the old track, the stalled crane, the wall that would sweat when it was almost time to stop, carrying a fish that should not be and a bone that had been waiting, the taste of letters humming still in her mouth like something alive.

Chapter One

At dawn, when the kettle began to beat its small drum and the window gave back a pale square of day, I noticed the absence where my other life usually lay. I lifted my hand to wipe the steam off the glass, and nothing lifted with me. The wall behind the sink was blank, the floor stretched clean of me. My shadow had not gotten up.

It is such a quiet betrayal you can believe you dreamed it. The child in the other room was breathing evenly, her slow drift of sleep like tidewater. The kettle quivered. I aimed for ordinary. I ground the coffee, I set a bowl and a spoon, I took the bread from the tin and worked the knife through its heel. My movement should have been doubled, should have had that loyal smear of dark, a faithful stain. I have lived a life doubled: what I am above the tile and what I am on it. I have angled my sewing straight by it. I have kept myself company at night by it. I have learned the weather from it, and the time of the year, and whether someone was standing too close behind me.

It was early, the kitchen square still soft with dawn. Perhaps in that light it was all around me, very faint, clinging to my skin; perhaps it had slipped somewhere only children see in their milk. The kettle, impatient, skipped toward a boil. I bowed my head, and a chill reached through me that had nothing to do with air.

"Nene," I called softly.

"Five," she said from the couch, five in child-speak meaning five more minutes, five more miles of abandoned dream. She is eight years old and making numbers do what she wants is her favorite trick. The couch springs croaked as she turned over. When I had pulled her into my life, she had been the only thing I could not duplicate on a wall. The only thing that did not obey the sun.

I poured the coffee, sat, and put the bowl of cereal near her head. The spoon clicked as she hunted for it in her sleep. Her eyes opened, brown and blurred. She ate without looking up, the slow, careful chewing of a small animal that knows food could go away.

"You're missing," I said.

She squinted, rolled off the couch, and stood between me and the light. The wall took her whole. She put her hands on her hips and made a fierce shape. "Not me," she said, and laughed and stepped aside. She has a gap between her two front teeth that whistles. "You," she added, watching the blank where my piece of darkness should have gone. She waved her hand through the emptiness. "You're a ghost."

"Not funny," I said. I put my hand out; there was the warmth of the window, the cool of the tile, the thud of my pulse. I felt as present as the coffee cup. I felt like someone who had slept badly and would be punished further for it. I took my palm up to my face. It was as it had always been: calluses, the bluntness at the finger from where a needle had gone in and broken, the pale scar like a crescent near my thumb when I had tried to cut open a jar with a knife and slipped. All of me answered when called. But the wall did not consent.

"Maybe it's behind you," Nene said, and walked around me as if I were a statue to be appraised. "Maybe it got embarrassed."

"It?" I said.

"She," she amended. "She didn't want to come out for work. Sometimes a body doesn't."

Nene has a way of speaking like a very old person who lost track of which things she had learned and which things she had always known. I leaned my forehead against the window and looked down into the street.

Our building faces east. The light comes up and catches on the laundry lines like birds caught midflight. The street is narrow and collects morning like a cup. On an ordinary morning you see cats, a man who sweeps with a bad broom, the boys who sell cigarettes one by one, the neighbor woman in her blue robe pinching basil. On our street, the day is begun by those who cannot permit themselves to want.

What I saw now was a seam of dark pulling itself along the pavement. It was not the trick of cloud or the boredom of a branch shadow. It was moving like thought. The long, elegant smudges of human shape were sliding away, many of them, hundreds perhaps, gathered out of their apartments and leaning forward toward the boulevard. Under bare feet, under boots, under Women's House of Pam's glitter sandals, the shadows hurried. Some looked back, the way you look back when you're leaving for good and you can't help yourself.

"Do you see?" I asked. My voice went up around the last word like a kite string catching on a nail.

Nene's breath went quick. She pressed herself to the glass, her hands like starfish, leaving prints. "They go," she said. "They're going to school."

"Of course," I said, because when your child names a new world you let them be right. "And me?" I asked, surprised to hear my own voice break.

She looked at the wall at my side the way a doctor looks at a wound. She sucked her teeth gently through the gap. "You're late," she said, with less accusation than wonder. "Hurry."

I put my coffee down and tied my scarf. It was one my mother had embroidered with red thread, small stubborn flowers that always looked a little as if they were a second away from wilting. My mother's house is three bus stops away and full of warnings. She ties her news to the beams of her house like turmeric hung to dry. She will have opinions about what is missing and what is not.

"Come," I said to Nene.

She danced. "No, I'm going to watch from here. The cat will be lonely and cry."

We have no cat. It is a running argument between us, fur versus bread.

"You don't open the door," I said. "You don't open it for a talking flame or a man in a hat you like or a girl with a basket of peaches. You don't open for me if I forget my keys; you call out and make me name your middle name."

"Yeraldina," she said, grinning, drunk on the power of it. I have regretted since the day of her birth that I gave her that middle name for my favorite aunt. It is like a bell, a ridiculous bell I will never stop ringing. She took the phone and plugged it in and put it face down like a good luck charm. "I'll watch the school go by," she said.

"You holler," I said, and opened the door.

It was a strange morning to go down stairs. The pipes in the walls were ticking. A neighbor, a man who always held his grocery bag as if apologizing to it, was standing there with his shadow still attached, his eyes on the floor. "Lucky," I said.

He shook his head. "I pissed into the basin?" He held up his hands. "He was disgusted. He slid under the door like oil. Maybe today this, tomorrow he will not be able to take me spitting. What will be left for me?"

"Keep your light low," I offered, and stepped around him.

The stairs pitched me to the street. It was dazzling with a kind of movement that made my heart skip in an unsteady way. There is no exact word for what you feel when you see the familiar split open. Awe is too church. Fear is too tight. It is like laughter, the kind that uses your stomach. I stood in the doorway—my mother would say doors and mouths are the same—and watched the boulevard fill.

Shadows do not have eyes, but I swear to you they were looking at us. Some kept their hands, their lightless fingers, at their sides. Some walked with palms upright as if to prove they were empty. Some, arrogant, put their hands behind their heads and strolled. They were not not human. There is always a little theatricality in the body that has always played second to a louder twin.

Then I saw her.

That is the only thing you need to know: you know your own. It is in the tilt. It is in, forgive me, the way even absence can adopt you. My hair was up; hers had the little ear of it knocked loose and falling. There is a curl over my left shoulder that never obeys, that my mother used to tape down. It cannot be a coincidence and yet it always is. The fingers of her right hand were not quite smooth; I broke that joint when I was a kid, falling off a wall, and when I make a fist my fingers align like a bad army. That misremembered bone was there in the darkness that crossed the street. She was long in the dawn, elegant, not burdened by gravity at all. She walked, and my body ticked, as if attached to a dog that has suddenly seen a rabbit.

"Ma'am," a voice said from the street.

It was the man with the broom, the one with the bristles always blown out like a witch hair. He held the broom against his chest as if it had an opinion. "I don' think you should step too close," he said. "If you're not ready."

"They belong to us," the neighbor woman protested ten meters down. She was in her slippers and her basil was tucked into the pocket of her robe. "She belongs to me." She reached for her shadow as it elongated along the curb, and it lifted its chin and slid away. The woman made a sound I had heard before in the hospital when someone realized what the doctor was truly saying.

"I just want to see," I said, and stepped to where the light shadowed the curb. I turned my foot sideways like a dancer. My shadow—this shadow—tilted her head. It was so intimate I felt heat rush to my face. There is a way your own double listens to you that is forgiving and impatient and a little mocking. It is the attention you learn from sisters. She lifted her hand. I lifted mine. Her fingers fluttered, and I heard something in my chest move, the kind of small click you hear when a jar opens.

"Stay," I said, ridiculous, as if training a puppy. The sound we use when we are too scared to ask for what we want. My blood ran toward her like a dog after a van.

She stepped back from the curb so that my foot found nothing.

"Later," I whispered, and she gestured almost not at all, a tiny shrug, the smallest possible no. Then she turned, and when she turned she turned the way I do, on the ball of the foot, heel lifted. She was not stumbling or caught by the lip of a stone. I have always caught myself on lips of things. She had the virtue I have tried to learn: motion without apology. Then she joined the larger river, and the street swallowed her, and the light moved, and she was many other shades.

"You see," the broom man said. "Now you are missing."

"They have a right," the neighbor woman argued. "Don't you dare tell me they don't. But he doesn't have a right to do it like this. He stirred the porridge in the mornings. Now what? Cold porridge? No."

A siren bucked and then held. Down on the corner, a police car nosed into the street very slowly, like a cow that has been convinced it is a boulder. The officers inside were young, their eyes the wrong kind of bright, the kind that looks for a forked path and sees only a cliff. One had a remnant of a night club stamp on his hand. They did not know where to direct their training. There were no bodies misbehaving, only manners of light. Besides, the city had not given the police scourges for things like this. The police carry night sticks and guns, which, for once, seemed useless. I saw the driver reach up and cover the dashcam with his palm like a man piously covering his hat in a church.

By then the boulevard was throwing off heat in a way that had nothing to do with temperature. People were out on stoops and balconies and leaning off the sills, some like saints in their frames, some like thieves. On Mira Street, someone had brought a folding chair. An old woman sat and crossed her legs delicately at the ankle as if to show she was prepared. A boy on a bicycle rode slowly, his shadow still loyal, pedaling out of time so that for a moment he and his darkness were at war. A girl ran down the street with a spool of red thread, thinking of fairy tales, and tried to tie her shadow's ankle. That is the kind of thing you invent when you are eight. A father descended in bare feet with his baby tucked to his chest, whispering apologies to the ink that left him anyway. I do not mind telling you that the city wept on its first try.

"Nene!" I called, and craned to see our window. She had her face pressed against the pane, her mouth dropped open, her hand flat. She looked like a fish that had become a sermon. I waved, and she waved, and then she held up the phone and made the sign that we should be recording this or it would not be true. I made the sign that we should be eating or we would not be forgiven at noon, and she stuck her tongue out. I could see my own lower lip in the set of it. My traitor.

I had to go to work. You cannot stop working just because something impossible is happening. Or, more precisely, you can, but you call poverty down on your house like a howl.

My shop, the Evening Mender, is seven blocks away, two blocks past the church named for a woman who once ate only poppy seeds for a year, if you believe the story. I sew for people who are tired of their clothes in the way they are tired of their faces and cannot afford a new face. I fix hems, I change a button for its nicer twin, I mend a seam where life has hectored its thread. The work is honest without being noble. My landlord is not impressed with nobility. He is impressed with money that does not argue.

"Lock," I told Nene when I came back up. She had the news on low and the sound of a woman in a high voice saying we must all stay calm and inside, as if the dangerous thing were a dog with rabies. The woman had a pearl at her throat that sat there doing nothing. I packed my bag with needles, the good scissors, a coil of chalk. It makes my hands feel right to know where those things are. "You go to Lola if the electricity goes," I said. Lola is our neighbor across the hall, who sews banners for demonstrations and has a grown son who calls only when his rent is due.

"I can't go to school," Nene said, primly sad. "I was going to learn the map of the world."

"You will," I said. "You will learn the one we have and the one we are getting. Two maps. Your head will be heavy with them. Lock."

She kissed the air toward me three times, because three gives luck weight, and then made a trumpet shape with her hands and blew as I climbed down the stairs.

By the time I turned onto Livingston, someone had put black tape on their heels and was walking as if he had caught his shadow by its hair. The tape glinted, a silly shiny like a child’s sticker. His companion shook her head at him and he said loudly how a man had to manipulate the constructs of his own existence with whatever tools he had at hand. There are always men like that, narrating the scene as if the words were wires holding up the sky. I wanted to tell him to lower his voice; the sky was listening for once.

At the Evening Mender, a sign was taped up crooked: No Entry Without Proper Accompaniment. The letters were stern and fat. I tried the handle. It stuck, then gave with the embarrassed groan of a door used to easier conversations.

"Maribel," my boss called, seeing me hesitate. "We didn't know what to expect. But here you are. Good." He is a man who keeps his hair slicked back in a way that makes it look like a new kind of fish. He is careful with women the way you are careful with glass.

Publicly, he treats me as if I am excellent and the world is the criminal that doesn't see it. Privately, he and I know that you could be excellent in this city until you are blue and it will still knock you into a ditch and tell you to apologize for dirtying your dress.

He was holding a bolt of cloth, black as a sentence. All the curtains I had hemmed were stacked in bags, tagged with names and promises. "Cosmina cried when she called," he said. "She has an event. The event still exists. She cannot arrive in a naked window. Imagine the rest."

"You see what is happening," I said, and gestured toward the door as if the street would stroll in to testify. The light outside had turned brighter, the kind that looks sharp enough to cut. If you have ever worked a double shift and then walked into sunlight you know that light can be cruel. "You know I cannot be here today."

He looked at my feet. You see? Those of us used to refusing apologies will look at your feet to find the truth in them. He noticed then, not rudely, but with the shock of someone discovering that a spoon is dangerous. "You too," he said softly. He touched his chest with the end of the tape measure, a child's gesture. He had his, you could see it nodding under his shoes, wonderfully obedient. He looked at me as if I were someone who had shown up without my voice. "Insurance."
"What?"

"That's the word they used. We cannot be insured against the actions of the... absence. If you injure yourself while not in accompaniment, the policy does not cover. If you injure someone else." He spread his hands as if to show me the ways I could swing.

"We learned this in twenty minutes?" I asked.

"Emailed after the press conference." He jabbed his chin toward the little television near the irons, where the pearl-throated lady said, "...while investigations are ongoing, we advise citizens to minimize exposure to direct light if they are experiencing separation."

"Separation," I repeated. "Like a marriage." I laughed, and it was the wrong laugh for the room, and he winced.

"It is temporary," he lied, because the cloth doesn't much care if you lie into it. "They always are, these oddities. The river ran backward; the City Hall clock stuttered; the pigeons did their circle in the other direction. It gives us something to tell kinds of reporters. And then it stops and we go back."

"My mother says," I began, and then shook my head. You do not want to be the woman who blames her mother for anything after a certain age. "I saw her," I said. "She shrugged at me. She shrugged."

"At least she shrugs like you," he said, a small attempt at a kindness. "Take the day. Take two. We will—"

"We will not be paid," I said, finishing him like a seam.

He looked downward because he was halfway decent. "I have Cosmina's curtains," he said, as if offering me his cough. "She offered extra. People who have extra do this when they are afraid, because it feels like they are building a wall."

"Give them to me," I said, before I could tell that voice to lie down and be still. "I'll do them and bring them back tonight. I'll be careful."

"At home," he said. "If the window is—"

"My window faces east. It is early. I'll angle the lamp," I said, and we both smiled at the idea that you could angle a lamp away from consequence. He put the bag in my hands like a baby he did not entirely trust me with.

As I left he reached as if to touch my sleeve and then did not, his own shadow brief and obedient in the fierce light. "Maribel," he said, and the way he said my name made me feel both chosen and dismissed. "Are you frightened?"

"No," I said, and he cocked his head as if to say we were doing a play badly. "Yes," I corrected. "But since when has that mattered."

On the way home the city had advanced by an hour. By then, the march of shadows had turned resolute. On the boulevard, they poured toward the stadium as if it were a bowl placed for them. It made sense. You go where the light is clean and unbroken; you go where a human cannot easily pinch you. Under the stadium floodlights installed for night games that were always rained out, the dark would gather and not blur. Even if you turned them off, it would take a time for the light to forget its habit. They would form their own bright noon and settle within it like fish under an unforgettable bridge.

A woman was walking along with a parasol up and crying. A boy with religious hands was making a sign of the cross at every third shadow, deciding he would baptize the multitude if no one else would. A small girl had a chalk rock and was kneeling in the street, tracing herself around and around and then standing in the middle of the chalk shape and grinning as if she had discovered something ancient. I wanted Nene's hand in mine and my other hand on my missing shoulder. I wanted something that did not exist: to be one and divided at once.

Back upstairs, the television had become a lit face speaking in puzzles. A visiting professor with a tweed jacket told the pearl-throated woman that there had been cases in texts from the eighteenth century of anomalies in the behavior of light. He did not say who had written these texts or where the light had gone. He used the phrase collective psychosomatic event. He used the term emergent properties. He used his hands too much, arranging invisible flowers. The crawl at the bottom said: Citizens are advised to remain in shade if separation occurs. Avoid driving. Please postpone weddings. I set the bag of curtains on the couch and Nene planted both hands on it in the way of children guarding something that is not theirs.

"They are singing," she said, pointing toward the window.

"Who?"

"Listen."

It is difficult to describe the sound of many shadows together. It could have been a low wind. It could have been the ocean in a shell. It could have been a thousand pages turning, at exactly the same second. It was not singing and yet we call many things singing when they approach us and make us aware of being made of skin.

"Can they—?" Nene began, and then stopped, because finishing the sentence would make it into something smaller. We held those first sounds together the way you hold hot bread: palms cocked, careful not to waste.

When I was a girl and still my mother's daughter in a way I am not now, I lay on the roof in summer and tried to keep the mosquitoes from learning me. My shadow lay alongside like a sister who has moved to another city and is home for only a short week. When boys whistled ten stories down, our dark bodies pretended not to hear. When the parade came down our street each spring, we used to watch from up there so the girls with the hips would not know we were measuring ourselves against them and failing to sum. If I have ever felt owned by anything it is by the knowledge of that second self. She held me together when I left the house at night and when I came home with a baby and when I did not answer the door to the man who insisted he knew my future better than I did. Shadows teach you refusal, if you let them. They are not just your outline; they are your practice.

That evening, after I hemmed the curtains crooked and unpicked and hemmed them again and my eyes went heavy and I scolded them for their laziness and Nene fell asleep with chalk dust on her fingers, the news reported that the shadows, the majority of them, had gathered under the stadium lights. A helicopter showed them, floodlit and writhing, but I could tell it was not writhing. It was concentration. It was a long decision coming to its mouth. There were men in orange vests carrying barricades. There were priests with stoles. There were girls with bullhorns. There were mothers pulling toddlers by the sleeve. There was a man with a giant balloon of the mayor with no shadow under him; the balloon bobbed and the crowd shook.

I put a stool by the window and took my mother's scarf off my neck. It smelled a little like garlic and rain. I tied it around my arm. It is a foolish thing, a bandage for a wound no surgeon could recognize. Then I took the flashlight we keep for power cuts and turned it in my hand. The beam felt heavy. It is a misuse of a thing to turn it into a flag, and yet: I wanted to offer a sign.

I stood in the rectangle of the open window with the flashlight at my side. I waited until the light in the street went low and kind, until the neighbor boys' voices rasped quieter, until our building sighed in the way it does when it realizes no one else is coming, and then I lifted the light and drew a circle slowly on the ceiling.

She came. Not all at once; not in a rush; not captured. The edge of her brushed the floorboard near my toes and then, impatient, she made a long line of herself along the baseboard where the paint chips. She did not attach. I did not force. We stood next to each other as we have done a thousand times. I turned the flashlight so that we lay together along the far wall, a double made by a cheap trick. It is something to make your own double if the world will not do it for you. She cocked her head and I did too and for the length of one breath we were exactly ourselves.

"Tomorrow," I said, and the word filled my mouth with its soft o and made me think of every promise anybody had ever made to me and kept and not kept. She put her hand toward the window as if pushing some curtain aside that I could not see. She pointed nothing like a finger toward the stadium that was a white bowl full of dark. She did not need me to learn what would happen there. She was telling me where the city had placed its hope. Or its demand. Or its story.

"Tomorrow," I agreed, and turned off the flashlight, and stood in the dark and felt like someone who had lost her companion at a fair and had, at last, grown up enough to go looking without crying.

On the morning the city ate my address, I was lying to a stranger about names. I told her my name meant light, when really it meant wolf. She was vanilla-skinned, flinty-eyed, one of those surveyors who keep string in their pockets as if seen from above we all make sense as angles. Reva, she said. We were in my apartment beneath the waking thrum of pigeons and laundry lines, and the ceiling bowed like a prayer about to be forgotten.

The call came while she was tracing a scar down my calf with a fingernail, a light-colored canyon from a summer when the river was not yet bridled. Unknown number, a municipal cruelty. There are people in this city who will never answer a call they do not recognize, because history has taught them their names can be taken in a voice.

“I should get that,” I said, and Reva turned on her side, facing the wall, as if to give me privacy, which we both knew was impossible in rooms like mine.

We regret to inform you, the voice said, in a tone like pennies dropped into a jar, that your parcel has been reclassified as Null. At eight past nine this morning, pending review and seal, all civic services—address, voting district, waste removal, postal—will be rescinded. Please report to the Bureau of Rectification to discuss resettlement.

The voice did not say my name. It did not have to. It said my parcel.

I sat up too fast and the pigeons startled on the eaves. Reva’s eyes flicked toward me and away again. “What is it?” she said.

“I think I don’t live anywhere anymore.”

She laughed. The kind of laugh the educated keep for bureaucratic errors, the custom of believing that mistakes happen to other people in different parts of town. “You’re here,” she said, pressing her palm into the mattress as if to anchor me with its hollowness. “You exist.”

In City Hall they answer to existence. The papers do the rest.

The thing is, we’d always joked about it, this idea that the map ruled us. Two summers ago, during the plague of crows, the council moved our district boundaries so that the new mayor never had to hear us drown when the storms came. A line, a pen, a new reality in which our boats turned illegal and our windows no longer qualified as windows. But that was gerrymandering, a word that has a nice slither to it, a way of saying we were being rearranged like cut fruit. What had been happening these past months was something else, and it curdled inside me like a suspicion finally coherent enough to shame you.

I didn’t put on shoes. Reva reached for me and missed my shoulder. “Luka,” she said, which is not what the wolves call me. We all have two names in this city: the one you can pin to your lapel for offices, and the one your grandmother breathed into your fontanel like a warning.

Outside, the sky was that summer gray that promises a storm and delivers only heat. The pigeons repositioned on the eaves with the world’s oldest gossip. Men were already arguing over bread at the corner—bread has become political; we have learned to butter ideals. Somewhere a truck was reversing with the sound of urgency in slow motion. I ran, which in this city means I navigated. Up alley, over steps, along a bridge where the slats in the wood had memorized my soles.

At Market Square the woman with the velvet strawberries had a new sign that said two for one, as if a future existed in which one could afford to eat two strawberries for breakfast. She lifted her chin at me in acknowledgment of my sweat, my urgency, the civic tone that makes strangers step aside because they recognize something is happening to you that might someday happen to them. We have learned triage as a neighborliness, the way we used to lend sugar.

The Bureau of Rectification smells like mildew and ironed shirts. It is housed in an old bathhouse the city saved from demolition by filling it with paper. The marble is clean in the way that always makes me sorry for marble, which is a stone that wants to be a mountain, not a file cabinet. I pushed through the brass doors and my mouth filled with the taste of cloth. Inside: benches from a church, a deli ticket system, clerks with haircuts like temporarily tamed grasses. Above it all, in a glass-fronted room like an aquarium for zeal, the Master Map.

If you have never seen the Master Map, it will be difficult to explain why people cry in front of it. It is not a single map, not really; it is an accretion, a chronology of guesswork and greed stitched together with horsehair and tape. You can see the hands in it—men who wrote like priests, girls who wrote like soldiers, a signature on the coastline from a time we believed in signatures. Boats inked with a hope disproportionate to their size. The river, thickened and thinned with history. Patches where the city’s wounds were repaired with new streets, their names optimistic as birthdays. When children visit for school, the teachers ask them to spot where their grandparents bought ice or umbrellas, and then leave flowers under the laminated notice that says Do Not Touch. That’s not an allegory. People bring flowers. People bring candles. People stand in front of the glass and count backwards from where they are to where the city made them.

I pressed my forehead briefly to the cool of the vestibule’s marble because it felt like consent. Then I climbed the stairs without waiting for a number, past the guard who looked at me the way you look at a person who is obeying you in advance. Ms. Varga was behind the desk in the map room, a woman with wrists like foreign currency—not meant to be touched, luminous with exchange. She has this way of speaking that makes you straighten your spine because grammar is a kind of attention.

“I received a call,” I said, forgetting to say good morning, forgetting to say please. “They said my parcel—”

“Null,” she said, not unkindly. She had already pulled a file from a drawer by my hip bones. It had my name on it in my father’s handwriting, which meant nothing except that paper goes where it wants. “Sit down for a moment,” she said. “We are still learning the shape of it.”

The map behind her had developed what the clerks, with their appetite for mild metaphors, had been calling the winters. Pale patches in the southeast first, an innocence like frost on glass, the kind that you can blow into a heart with your breath. Then the patches darkened, their borders softened, and something feathery bloomed along the docks. Mildew is an ugly word for such intricate hunger. It made lace out of our industry. It ate the N orth out of N o rth, and so south swelled. It did not respect concessions or walls. The first time a street disappeared on the map, the committee convened a study to determine whether the map was failing the city, or the city was failing the map. They wrote a paper with footnotes like pajamas made of ice. The nights were warm; a boy fell into a blank place where the map had been scrubbed for restoration and came out on the other side of history, which is to say he drowned in the old river that used to be there before we moved it.

“What is the shape of it?” I said because I have learned that sometimes what people call patience is the unsaid word.

“I cannot say shape anymore,” said Ms. Varga. “I can only say sway.”

She led me to the glass. There is a particular elation to the feeling that you are about to prove to someone that you have been telling the truth for years. It’s not triumph, exactly. It’s grief with a point. She indicated with a wooden stick—the kind teachers used to tap maps in a century when wood was less endangered—the part of the city that had been my street. No one moved when Ms. Varga lifted a piece of new vellum and placed it like a veil over the Old Town’s scuffed auburn, her hands so steady the paper did not argue. Under the veil: the bright apostrophe of my building block, the coal-smudge of our alley, the little hatch marking the balcony where we tie our laundry like flags of a country that refuses to become paper. Someone had annotated the margin in pencil with my building’s height, which is an absurd fact to die with.

I watched her search for my address the way a magician pretends not to know where the coin is. And then, as if shivering itself to privacy, the corner of the block went gray. Not gray like ink. Gray like breath on glass. The pencil notes blurred. A clerk in the room said oh the way people say oh when the baby’s head emerges.

“You see?” Ms. Varga said, lifting her eyes to mine as if to check that I had understood that she did not take pleasure in this. “It has learned to go faster.”

“I live there,” I said, which is not an argument but a spell.

“We are not making value judgments,” she said softly. “We are measuring. We are triaging. We are extremely sorry.”

“Can’t you do anything?” I whispered, the way my grandmother asked for her teeth when she was forgetting.

There are rules, and then there are the secrets the rules require in order to appear reasonable. We are a city built on measurements; we trust the toothiness of gears. The secret this time was not even a secret. They had tried bleach. They had tried fan and sun. They had tried freezing the vellum and hovering prayers over it with a humidifier because the archivists, like beekeepers, live with instruments as if they are loved ones you have to learn. Every time they dabbed at the bloom with a swab soaked in something sterile, the mapped street on the table smeared, and when it smeared, the street outside developed a fatigue. A railing went missing down by the fish market. A stoop lost a step. A door that had always known to be aubergine forgot its color and woke up the gray of boiled bone.

Once, during the trials, they scrubbed at a lane in the northern quarter that had been misnamed a century ago for a general who never existed. They told themselves they were removing an error. The lane went blank on the map. Outside, the people who had always been almost invisible walked to work that morning and found that the alley they called home had become a shine, a gleaming plane of unthing where the sun went into itself and did not return. They stood with plastic bags of oranges and the day’s good intentions lifted their hands to shield their eyes and saw only their hands absorbing the light. The oranges melted to rind scented with elsewhere. A boy reached out, and his fingers came back with a paragraph missing.

We do not talk about that boy because what would we say. We say the word accident until it stops being a loss and becomes a way to walk around silence like furniture.

“Look,” said Ms. Varga.

Where my building was, the mildew had blossomed. It moved like time-lapse film: the petals of a carnivorous plant unfurling to show you their lack of appetite in real time. It wasn’t beautiful, but it had the morphological sincerity of a fungus, which is to say it did what it did without maliciousness. There is a comfort in systems that do not pretend to love you.

Behind us, one of the clerks put a hand over her mouth and then removed it because protocol. The guard outside cleared his throat. Somewhere in the building, a printer coughed a paper it could not spit out.

“Don’t,” I said. “Please don’t touch it. Please do nothing.” My voice was too loud and rang against the glass.

“You think we cause it,” said Ms. Varga. Her eyes were very tired. Under their lashes, the skin had the translucent shame of someone who is forced daily to be the instrument of inevitability. “You are not wrong. You are also not entirely right. It wants what time wants.”

“What is that?”

“To continue,” she said.

In that moment I remembered my mother telling me to never carry myself as a person who is owed. She said the only reason we ever kept a house was because we learned how to leave it. And I remembered my grandmother sitting out on the balcony in her slip, her hair braided to her hip like a letter from a shore where no one writes, combing it with the long wooden comb her sister had given her before the border moved and gave them different sisters. She would comb and hum to the pigeons a song that did not have lyrics so much as topography: a descent, a flat, a turn by the old peach orchard that became a stadium. When I was small and wanted to fall asleep and could not, she would pat the mattresses and tell me where we were in the city by naming the things we could reach with our bodies: the tin of anchovies under the sink, the green bowl with the chip shaped like an idea, the neighbor’s rooster that crowed at two because no one had taught him clocks.

Luka, she would say, and I would only answer if she said the wolf-name, because the other one belonged to school. Luka, if someone shows you a map first, they get to choose what is far. Memorize your own near.

“What do I do?” I asked now, dumb as a church pew.

Ms. Varga handed me a paper, because there is always a paper to be handed. Rectification Initiate: Consequent Reassignment Options. It offered me three suburbs I had never seen and am already ashamed of how quickly I judged. Replica Gardens, where each house is a version of elegance supported with pretense; the Flood Plain Heights, which is a very funny joke because it is neither; and the Green, which is not. There were allowances for sentimental objects. There was a line for pets as if the city would reimburse you for a cat’s decision to continue to be a cat.

“People are still in that building,” I said.

“You have until nine.”

It was eight-fifteen.

Out in the street I tried to call my neighbor, the old man on the first floor who always smelled of thyme because he fingered the herbs in the window box whenever he spoke to anyone, as if each conversation required seasoning. The line did not connect. My phone showed me the kind of panic that disguises as a blank screen.

I ran again, which is to say I betrayed the laws of pedestrian courtesy and knocked my shin on a planter and apologized to nobody. On the bridge, a boy hawked bottles of water labeled river and I could not tell if he was honest or the kind of liar who convinces you that your thirst is a personality. The churches let out a sound like teeth. It wasn’t bells, exactly; anybody can ring a bell. It was the sound of marriage to ritual, a reminder that we have ways of noting the hours that are not beholden to electronics. A gull dropped the carcass of a fish in front of me and scolded me for not being dead enough to share it.

The closer I came to my block, the cleaner the city grew. At first I thought someone had washed the windows, had finally swept up the glass that time produced every weekend when somebody mistook an insult for a requirement. But then I saw it wasn’t clean in the way of soap. It was clean the way blankness is clean. Graffiti there, not there. The poster of the actor who broke everybody’s heart twice—first by love, then by politics—had faded along his lips. Paint lost its nerve. The trash bins had their names removed. There is nothing more unnerving than a bin without a label. Even our garbage deserves to know which of us we are.

A woman carrying a purple chair was talking to herself and to the chair. “Come. Come along. Don’t be stubborn.” Behind her, a man rolled an empty water heater like a barrel of regrets. People craned their necks with the morbid curiosity that is a neighbor to tenderness. When the city suffers, we keep our front doors open in case the hallway forgets itself and needs reminding what a threshold is.

At my street there was a smell I have learned to hate because it is the smell of salt without sea. On the corner, a boy had set up a folding table and was selling old photographs of people we did not know. The black and white faces looked unbothered by permanence; it’s the cruel thing about photographs, how they preserve not only the face but the face’s belief in the future. I asked him where he’d gotten them and he said the attic, and when I asked whose attic, he said, whose does it matter now, exactly as if he had graduated from the city’s Academy of Resignation.

Then I saw it.

The first time you meet absence, you think it will be like night. Shadow with possibility, the smell of sleep. It is not. The blank at the end of my street was as bright as new bone. It was a whetted thing. Where the cobbles should have been there was a smoothness that made your eyes water. The air had a temperature but it did not behave the way air should: it did not carry sound with courtesy. People stood three feet from nothing and shouted the names of their children and their voices laid down like obedient dogs at their own feet. Dust on the edge of the blankness made a line that a hand could not cross, the way sometimes a grief is inscribed in a body and a person learns to put their hand down on the table and not move it because to move it is to admit a before.

I was still a block away when I saw my balcony. The balcony was not there. The nails that used to hold it in place made a soft suggestion of themselves and then reconsidered. The window was not there either, which suggests the wall was not, which suggests the room where I had lied about my name was now a very ordinary piece of history: a place people used to talk.

“Luka!” someone called, and I turned, because we are conditioned to behave when called. It was Tomi, the kid from the second floor, the one with hair like he’d been frightened by electricity. He had his backpacks arranged across his chest and back like ammunition. “Mamá’s inside,” he said. “She’s asleep. She works nights. She will not listen to me.”

I had never loved my feet so much for their fidelity. They carried me across the street to the stairwell, which was intact in the way a saint’s toe bone is intact inside a reliquary: by agreement. I put my hand on the banister, which had been smoothed by a century of palms, and there was no splinter, which is when I knew we were really in trouble. The banister’s job is not to be safe; it’s to remind you who else has gone upstairs.

On the first landing, the tiles that spelled out Felicidad in chipped blue were unmoored and simply read LI. That made me laugh, because maybe we are always telling ourselves only the essential part of a word. The door to Tomi’s apartment was ajar. Inside, the fan turned uselessly above the bed where his mother slept with the authority of people who have had to put themselves further away to survive. Her hand was on her forehead. She breathed like a delayed metronome. I touched her shoulder and name and rising, in that order. She sat up with the ease of a soldier waking to the signal.

“It’s time to go,” I said.

She looked at the window, which was a window. “But it is morning.”

“Everything is morning when it wants to be.”

We packed poorly because what matters is changing size inside a catastrophe. Tomi took his books. His mother took the folded photographs she kept under the mattress, shoved a plant with a cracked terracotta base into a tote as if it would break more gently if contained. I was surprised by the thing my hands found: the wooden comb from my grandmother’s braid. It lay in a dish with coins from countries that no longer existed, which is the most reasonable thing to do with such coins. I put the comb in my pocket because I am who she made me.
