We went down the stairs as a unit, which is the only way to use stairs if you wish them to remain stairs. In the hall, Mrs. Imane from the attic apartment was trying to lock her door and finding that the lock was ornamental. She wore her yellow dress that made even the pigeons look drab. “It is not just us,” she told nobody. “It is not just us.”

Outside, on the threshold, Tomi stopped. The line of blank had advanced. It moved with a slow confidence, a tide in a lake pretending not to be a tide. The old man with the thyme came out onto his stoop and put his hands on his hips and said, “I have paid taxes,” as if that were a charm. He stood on the last definable step and looked down into the bright and there was nothing of him in it, which is perhaps the worst thing you can see of yourself.

I took the first step toward the blank and felt the air resist my leg, not like a wall so much as a friend who has decided to not let you leave a party with someone who will be bad for you. I took another and the resistance pulsed, a tide trying to teach me that water does not hold the same thing twice. I picked up a pebble because this is what we do, we throw small things at the unknown to see if the unknown has a sound.

When the pebble met the edge of the blank, it did not fall. It did not burn. It did not bounce. It simply un-made. I do not have better language than that. It became the idea of a pebble, then an earlier idea, and then the absence of pebble. The sound it made was a kind of yes.

Behind me, Ms. Varga’s guard cleared his throat again in a building a mile away. Reva, somewhere on a site north of town, adjusted her tripod and missed the way the light let go. My grandmother, on an old balcony in an old city that was also this one, hummed the part of the song where you go under the bridge and pretend it is a river and not a question. My mother, somewhere without my address, measured flour with the accuracy of an apology.

“Luka,” said Tomi’s mother, whose name I did not know because we are stingy with intimacies when we assume people will remain. “Now.”

It was eight twenty-nine. The pigeons on the eaves blew their grayness against the morning like the first page of a book shaken open. I did the ridiculous, tender thing. I put my hand in my pocket and felt the teeth of the comb, and then I stepped forward.

On the last Sunday my father belonged to us, the city came with a silver bowl and a written apology.

They arrived early, before the church bells, before the neighbor’s pigeons had found their morning thermals. The woman wore the city blue—jacket too stiff, shoes too soft—and carried the bowl against her chest like something that could spill. Steam from the pot on the stove curled around her as if trying to read her name tag. M. DESAI, it said, in thin letters that looked as if they would rub away with the oils of the hand. Time does this to names, my father liked to say. He said many things he only half believed.

“Good morning, Mr. Nayar,” she said, and set the bowl on our table. It struck wood with a sound like a small bell. The bowl was plain except for the inside rim, where someone had etched a rope of minute-marks, a careful loop for each unit. It reflected our kitchen distorted: the faucet looked bent enough to pour at right angles, and my father’s face, when he leaned over it, broke into two.

My mother wiped her hands on her apron, then wiped the table again though it was clean. The spoon she’d been using lay on a saucer, a comma in the long sentence of that morning.

“I thought it would be a briefcase,” my father said, and grinned to show there was nothing in his mouth but what he’d always carried around: words, small kisses, the false gold of reassurance. He’d set his best pen by the placemat, as if what he was about to sign might look handsomer written with a fountain nib.

“It should have been,” said the woman, glancing at him and then past him, to the four bowls my mother had set out, one of them with the blue rim that only ever appeared on Sundays. “We used to bring a briefcase, back when it was paper. Now it needs to be a bowl.”

It made more sense than any of her other explanations would have. Our city had decided that it could not keep up with itself; that something was wrong with the way hours pooled in rich quarters and drained out of others; that there were surgeons who couldn’t finish stitching because their shifts dissolved at midnight and children whose birthdays arrived three times a year, because their parents kept buying the same Friday nights for different celebrations. There were accidents that clotted in the mornings like traffic, because time ran narrow on weekdays, and old men who hung their chair outside their doors and sat in it through every afternoon until dusk, the chair as worn as if they had carried it down from their father’s slippers.

The Time Redistribution Act sounded like an algebra problem when the newsreaders said it. The city would collect unused hours and borrowable days; it would pay people to sell their Sundays and their Mondays by the square, the yard, the cupful. They called it chronoequity. It sounded clean. The pilot program was the first of its kind in the nation. There would be good oversight. There would be a rubric. There would be bowls.

I was ten that year; I had a gap between my front teeth and a notebook where I had drawn a map of our apartment and marked the slow spots. The slow spot in the hallway where a draft made the calendar sag, where you could feel the morning like a weight. The slow spot under the table where your bare foot met the cool tile and knew that afternoon would come, but not yet. The window, which was the fastest place in the house. You could look out and see time in other windows, reflected, repeated, windows in windows, people watering their plants, shaking out shirts, washing their old teacups and new babies. Sometimes I thought if you climbed into enough windows you would reach the place where hours are made before they are distributed. That was the place all the officials faced when they spoke at press conferences, trying to learn the formula.

Mrs. Desai, with the bowl, sat at our table. My father sat across from her and showed her where to sign. He had the finger-smudged copies of his early refusal letters bound with a clip. He had refused for months, saying we would make do. Then the letter with the number came—the house insurance, recalculated, the number that could have been a phone number or a code but was just how much more we had to pay for living where the river could reach us if it got big ideas. My father took his mug to the window and watched the river for a long time, so long that the tea cooled to the exact temperature it always was when he said, too late, it’s too late now. He knew how to arrive late and how to catalogue the reasons, how to outline all the better versions of himself who would have done it differently. He was tender to the ghost of the man we needed, and he signed anyway.

“What happens to them?” I asked, though I knew how to ask in a way that seemed like I wasn’t asking at all. That’s how you learned in our family: you were nosy and you made yourself small.

“They go into the common pot,” Mrs. Desai said, not unkindly. She had a mole on her cheek that made her look as if she was always about to make a point. “We allocate them to critical services. And we allot so they are fairly—”

“No, I mean—when he sells the Sundays. Does he go somewhere? Do we put him in the bowl?”

If she laughed she swallowed it. She had good throat muscles for her job. “He will be at work on those days,” she said. “Because others will be at work. Because the city will continue. You will not perceive his Sundays. They will not occur for you.”

“There’ll be stew,” my mother said, quickly, as if pushing a pot between my father and my question. “I’ve already started the bones.”

My father picked up his pen as if it were something that might squirm away. He had the sort of face people confided in, and sometimes he looked upset about this, even if he was the one they were paying to take their words seriously. “Think of it as if I’ve put them away,” he said to me. “Like when we used to put your sweaters in the cedar chest for summer. They’ll be there, out of the moth’s reach.”

He hadn’t put anything away in years. He packed badly, made piles that tipped. He was still the man who bought one extra scarf in winter because he had lost the one from last year, then found both in spring, braided around each other like a pair of snakes.

He signed, and Mrs. Desai checked the signature against the one on her file as if this might be the part that saved us from something bigger than handwriting fraud. She took out a device that looked disappointingly like a kitchen timer and set it on the table. The lights in it blinked once, irregularly, like a heart failing to telegraph something and then managing. She turned it toward him.

“Place your palm here,” she said, “and look into the center. There might be a brief sensation, a sensation of being subject to bureaucratic processes. Many people report that the sensation is like a static shock.”

“Or a haircut,” my father said, because the room was too serious for its own good.

He pressed his palm, and the device lit the bowl from beneath as if it contained some shy candle. The light ran around the engraved minutes. I had the sudden feeling that everything that made our house ours was being warmed gently, and that the warmth would climb into the bowl and stay there. The light brightened. My father’s eyes watered but he did not look away.

The bells at the church two blocks away rang the half-hour. The river threw the sound back at us, softened. Somewhere, the pigeons lifted and set down again, deciding there was no emergency. What I remember most vividly: the sound of soup just before it begins to boil, the small noise like a hand dreaming of being clapped. The way my mother’s knuckles whitened around the spoon.

“It’s taking,” Mrs. Desai said, soft enough that maybe she meant for herself. “It’s taking.”

When the device dimmed, she tapped a sequence and picked it up. The bowl stayed, heavy and ordinary.

“That’s it?” I asked. “Is he no longer—”

“On Sundays,” Mrs. Desai said, “he will be otherwise allocated. It’s a contract. Contracts are mostly a way of making people agree upon what they will pretend is true. They’re very effective. You’ll get the deposit this afternoon.”

My father blew on his hand as if it had been pressed to a stovetop. “Worth it,” he said to my mother, as if the word could brand the air and make something stay. “I’ll be home for the rest. You’ll hardly notice the difference.”

He was right. That’s how it works: you hardly notice the missing until you do, and then you can’t stop noticing.

The first Sunday my father did not belong to us, a cat walked into our kitchen as if it had always lived with us. It sat in the absence where my father’s chair made a small hollow in the rug. There was always something to fill absences. That was one of the city’s deeper theories. If you removed a slice, the rest rearranged. If you pulled Sunday out like a card from a deck, Monday might learn a new trick.

“It’s quieter,” my mother said, stirring. My brother and I set out bowls and then set them out again, because we had done it without thinking. The ceremony of spoons seemed important. We were not church people. Our sacraments were the oil on the lentils, the palm we set to each forehead around the table. The embrace of stew.

My father’s bowl stayed empty. Part of the contract involved leaving the places of the missing untouched, especially on former days. It had something to do with calibration. Later I would read about it: how hunger in a house helped the city measure where to put what it had bought. But that day it was just an empty bowl, blue rim bright as if unused glaze loves light more.

At the end of that first missing Sunday, my mother turned the bowl upside down. We clucked at her, the way people do when they love someone and are afraid if they speak plainly they will break something brittle inside. She said, “Dust,” as if that explained it, but we knew she was trying to stop something from settling in it that wasn’t dust. The blue ring looked like an iris shut to keep from seeing.

We learned the tricks. We learned how to say “Your father is at work” as if it were not both a lie and a truth. At school, I learned that no one else in my class had sold the other parent; that some had sold mornings, the better to sleep through them, and some had sold the slice between two and three in the afternoon which they claimed not to feel anyway, because of the way days yawned there. We traded minutes the way we traded candy, stuck to the bottoms of our desks until a teacher found a small cache of them—thin coins printed with the city seal, stacked like a broken watch—and made us return them to the office. My brother learned to take naps on the rug between the sofa and the low bookcase during news hours, so that the words on the TV didn’t catch him. He pressed his ear to the floorboards as if the neighbors were below and he could get their time to seep up.

The Sundays came with a particular light. I think the city arranged it, a way of making it plain that something real was happening. The light on our kerosene can looked unusually kind. The balcony looked like a postcard of itself. The world kept showing us the edges of things.

On the fourth missing Sunday, I followed my mother into the backyard to hang sheets, a job my father used to make three times as long because of the stories he hung between the clothespins.

“Don’t put the pins in your mouth,” she said, and they clicked between her teeth anyway, the old habit holding on, the fungi of habit too stubborn for the light. Her hair had come out of its knot in strands that looked like stray threads pulled from the day, and I wanted to tuck them back in. She thwacked a sheet to loosen it, and for an instant the world behind us was only a pale sky full of wind, and it seemed so tender, and I felt that if my father walked through it he would show the shape of himself the way a fish shows itself beneath turtles in clear water, and I would reach out, I would touch.

“What are you thinking?” she asked, because she had eyes in the back of the skull made for spotting both head lice and grief.

“I don’t like that the bowl is here,” I said. “Is it always here?”

“The bowl.” She looked puzzled, and then it was as if a sun rose in her face: she had not thought of it since she had put it in the cabinet, practical woman that she was. She had been busy with laundry and breakfast and the neighbor’s way of knocking as if the door were to blame for whatever she had come to say. “It’s just a dish.”

“It’s not just.”

She hung the sheet. The wind wrote a fox across it, then erased it. She said, as if to the cloth, “We won’t do this more than we have to. It’s a stopgap.” She loved that word. It made everything seem like a temporary fix on something permanent, a tidy plug in a leak behind which was a seawall shaped like morality, democracy, the peculiar bravery of cities.

“It’s a hole,” I said.

She smiled at me, and in her smile I saw how many hours she had already moved around like furniture, trying to make rooms, trying to find the slow spots where we could stand steady. If time was a city program, my mother was a small city and a good one.

He was the one who suffered the most from his absence. That’s what happens with sellers. The loss swims back, knocks against them like a fish against glass. He started to fall asleep on Tuesdays in meetings. He came home smelling of other people’s Sundays: rosemary, chlorine, the warm version of beer. He started writing notes to himself on his arm in the evenings, as if he might wake in the night and forget how to be in a day he still owned.

When the deposit hit, it did what all sudden money does: it made a list of itself on the fridge, impatient to be spent. We paid the insurance and a month of the hospital bill and bought a metal rack for the shoes we had been keeping in a crate since the hinge broke. We ate fruit out of season with a small sacrilegious thrill.

Mrs. Desai came back once to check on our compliance. She sat in the kitchen with the bowl cupped in both hands as if it was her grandmother’s. She told us there were people who were already trying to sell half-days on the black market, and someone who had sold so many hours he seemed to be living only in the thin slice between late night and dawn, loving it, becoming a legend at the all-night diner, his hair smelling like coffee, a rumor made of waffles and bacon.

“Does the city buy them all?” my father asked.

“The city has a budget,” she said, and laughed into the bowl. The laugh came back at her, small and tinny. “It turns out you can’t just print time. Everyone says the city should run more like a business, until you ask them to pay their taxes.”

He made her a cup of tea. She blew on it and kept blowing. She was young; it occurred to me then, violently. Her hair hadn’t yet learned to be hair that slept standing up. Her hands hadn’t yet learned to love paperwork more than dough. She had a ring with a matte stone. She watched my mother spoon stew into bowls and then realized what she was watching, and looked away, and you could see the first nick in her professionalism, the first place where her job met a person she might have been if she had been born to our family instead of to a different apartment.

“It’s not my business,” she said, “but if you pick days, pick ones you can stand to lose. It’s a lot, to give up a day.”

“What did you sell?” my father asked.

She smiled as if the question was unorthodox but permissible. “Evenings,” she said. “Just a few. I grew up working nights in my parents’ place. Evening never felt like it belonged to me. I was always à la carte. So it was easy to say yes.”

He nodded. “We picked Sunday because—”

“No school,” I said.

“No work,” my mother said.

“No crisis,” my brother said, because in our family if you said the word often enough it would dissolve into letters that could be repurposed. Cries. Sir. Sic.

My father lifted his bowl and the steam wrote his name in the air. He carried the bowl to the table and set it down as if it held bones that could heal. “Because of the river,” he said, which was not an answer to anything, but we took it, the way you take a foreign coin just to feel it.

After the city bought our Sundays, time became something we could not talk about without sounding like we had taped a program to our tongues. People I overheard at the market said, “They extended the peak hours and I missed my train right through it.” They said, “We’re saving up for a summer,” the way people used to say they were saving for bicycle tires or braces. The newscaster said, “In other news, the council approved an hourglass on the courthouse lawn to mark the city’s extra hours,” and laughed politely.

Less politely, the cartoonist in the morning paper drew a poor person trying to push a minute into a slot machine shaped like City Hall while the mayor, a sausage man with a tie like a noose, leaned on the lever.

In the tenth week, a family in the building down the block hung a sign on their balcony that read: MONDAY DINNER AT SIX. WE OWN THIS ONE. The next day, the sign was ripped, and nobody could tell whether someone had reached up and torn it or if it had simply worn in half, the way fabric does when you hope too much with it.

On the Sunday before my father’s birthday, a letter came from the Department of Chronoequity with a note pinned to it. The note said: Reminder of Obligations. The letter listed them as if they were groceries. There was one item in a column of its own: Core Derived Time-Tax, due February, calculated based upon utilization of municipal hours.

We were paying to lose, in other words. We were paying to watch our own hands empty. My mother put the letter under a magnet shaped like a tomato, because she refused to make papers more important than the recipes they covered.

“This is where it gets hard,” my father said that night, when we lay on the floor in the living room with our feet on the sofa, a way to trick our hearts into calm. He told us stories the way he always did, but they were thinner. They had holes. Bats flew in and out of them. “Not the money, though that’s already not easy. It’s that once they can price things, they can call anything a luxury. Once they call it a luxury, they can make it our fault.”

“Whose fault is it?” I asked.

He considered. He had grown up in a one-windowed room over the tailor’s, seven people to a bathroom, he had told us this often enough that the white of the bathroom and the smell of the bleach lived in our house like a cousin. He said, “Fault is the laziest word. It’s a mattress. You throw it down over a hole and jump on it and think you won’t fall. But you will.”

He did on a Tuesday. Heart, two flights of stairs from the office, his bag with his notes spilling like fish as he went down. They got him back. They cut Sunday inside him and shoved it into Wednesday and made him a week of a man. He came home with the back of his hand bandaged and a serious look that would have made strangers think he was steady when he was really a man whose steady sat outside him like a bench.

“This city,” he said to me, the next morning, sitting at the edge of my bed as if that edge could tell him something about strength, “owes you more than law about bowls.”

“Dad,” I said, because he was naming a thing he couldn’t build, and where do you put that kind of promise but on the shelf where you keep paint and old screws.

The city never did send another bowl, but it kept sending notices. After he left us on a Friday, later—more later than I am ready to tell you about now—we learned there is a kind of time you don’t sell, a time that leaves anyway, the unauctioned hour that looks over its shoulder at your house and keeps going.

By then, I worked for the city. There’s a sentence that deserves a paragraph on its own and gets it: By then, as if a hand moved across a calendar at the speed of fungus, I wore the city blue. I had a badge with a number that contained the last two digits of the year my father taught himself to type because his own father’s fingers had been the kind that broke grain and tore the small hairs on the back of chickens. I had a title that sounded like a threat: Reclamation Officer. I had a feeling I carried under my tongue like a seed you don’t tell anyone about because you’re not sure what it will grow into: a little bitterness, around the rind, where the pith is.

You don’t need to hear about my training, the coffee, the rooms where we said the same sentence until it stopped sounding like something you could fit a person inside. You don’t need to hear about the men who wore their hair cut short because some kinds of short make the world read you as kind. You only need this: the first file I was assigned had my mother’s street printed on it. Not her building. Not her number. The street with the figs that fruit too early because the sun hits the brick in winter. The street with the window whose reflection I used to count as a child as if the house were a hand of cards.

“No,” I said to my supervisor, a woman with a mouth like a slot. She had been at this long enough to know when to blink and when not to. She had learned not to try to smile and had invented a new expression for herself, less ambitious than smiling, like the faint satisfaction one feels when a drawer shuts without catching on anything.

“It’s a nuisance account,” she said, pushing the file back over the desk to me. “Not a conflict. She’s three months overdue on the Derived and adding late-fee interest I don’t love the look of. There’s a petition. Some elderly. We prefer human contact on these. A person with a face.”

“My mother has a face,” I said.

She lifted an eyebrow. It was an elegant eyebrow, sharply triangular, the opposite of mine, which my father used to say looked like two moths that were considering leaving. “Remit, reassess, rehabilitate,” she said, sing-song, the act-name in our mouths like the alphabet in a child’s. “Maybe she will pay. Maybe she will yell. Both would be, for our purposes, fine.”

On my way out, I stopped in the bathroom and watched my own face in the morning bar light. There’s a moment when you start to look like your parents in a way that isn’t flattering: a shadow beneath the eye, a line between the eyebrows that has nothing to do with kerfuffle and everything to do with the kind of thinking you do when the meter is running. My father’s line was there, the one that deepened on Sundays we didn’t own. I put a fingertip to it. It did not rub away.

Outside, the river was the sort of green that makes people on bridges stop and decide to be philosophical. Men in hard hats leaned over the railing as if it were an altar. The courthouse hourglass had been installed on its lawn, and people were taking the kind of picture that involves you standing in front of a thing to prove both the thing and yourself. In the extra hours section of the day, the glass glittered. More sand than I liked had already sifted down. There’s an art to not looking at what will be empty. I had as much of it as anybody.

I took the long route to my mother’s street, the one that carried me past the park where boys played the sort of basketball that wasn’t really, where the hoop was just a shadow of itself on the wall and each boy decided whether to treat the shadow as if it could receive. It was a city trick: we made do with outlines. We pretended the unowned could still be ours. It was warm, then chill, that spring, in the way that made everyone’s coats look like indecision instead of warmth.

My mother did not live there anymore, not really. She lived in the one-bedroom off Beale with the sliding door she couldn’t make slide that faced a parking lot made of glittering trash. But the file wasn’t hers; this was someone else whose name I read and did not recognize, a woman named Tam in a building I knew with my feet like a song. She had fallen behind on time-tax. There was a petition. She had written in erratic cursive that she had given enough to the city already, that the city had eaten her brother, that the city could eat air. She had printed beneath her letter a small drawing of a bowl.

When I turned onto the block, I could smell tomato leaves, which you cannot smell unless someone is pinching them between finger and thumb, which meant someone was tending a garden early. The figs on the corner tree wore their little hats. A dog barked at a pigeon and apologized. On one of the balconies, a pair of hands sprinkling water looked like a miracle, and then the water fell and the hands were just hands again.

Her door had a brass number that had been polished with unnecessary care: someone in the building loved a rag. I knocked, and knocked again, and heard the sound of something being dragged across the floor. I had a folder with official stamps. When she opened the door, she wore a sweater the color of a bruise you are proud of. She had hair the color of loamy soil and eyes the brittle, merry gray of a pan left on the stove a second too long. She looked at my badge and then up at my face and called me by my father’s name.

For a moment I thought I had time wrong. Not the clock, the private kind. There are seconds I can feel my way back to blindfolded: a sweet’s sugar in my mouth the day we found out the second baby wasn’t stopping, the feel of a new pillowcase on cheek the first night I didn’t sleep in any bed that knew me. The sensation then was unmistakable: a bowl lifted and the bottom dropping out.

“He isn’t—” I said, and then did not know which verb to pick. Among the verbs in the language, some are polite to the dead and some aren’t. Some are honest to the absent and some are shorthand for a story you will not tell a stranger on a landing.

“You have his face when you are trying not to admit you are lost,” she said. She had left the door open, which is hospitality and also a trap. “You are late,” she added, as if I was delivering a package of clean minutes and not a notice. “I was expecting you yesterday. The city always comes a day earlier than it promises.”

“Ms. Tam,” I said, smoothing the paper that had crinkled in my damp hand. “We’re here about—”

“Your father bought a goldfish from me when you were little,” she said. “He wanted it to teach you that mourning had a limit. He was wrong about that. But the fish was pretty. Come in.”

There was a bowl on her table. There will always be a bowl on a table in any story worth telling in this city. This one was cracked and mended, kintsugi lines like veins running through it, gold where breakage had been. The bowl was filled with Sunday light, though it was Tuesday. It was the oldest trick in the book and the best. She dipped her hand into the bowl as if to rinse something the day had put on her.

“You have something to tell me,” she said. “Tell me it later. First, sit. Then I will tell you something that will change the story you think you are in.”

On the street below, the church bell rang a half-hour that did not belong to it. The sound came through the window wrong, like a name almost remembered.

“You hear that?” she asked, cocking her head.

“I hear the wrong hour,” I said.

“No,” she said, smiling, and pressed the rim of the bowl with her finger so that it sang softly. “The right one, finally. They slip sometimes, when people keep too much polite in their throats. Today, time has decided to be impolite. Good. You brought it.”

She slid a piece of paper across the table. It was a photograph. My father, hair blown off his forehead, mouth a small surprise. He was standing in front of a shop whose sign had been painted over twice. The picture was dated. It had a thumb print in one corner. It was stamped, faintly, with the city seal, an accident or a dare.

“You see,” she said, as if I had sat down in the first chapter of a book and found my own name already underlined, “you’ve come about a debt. But he came about a secret. You shouldn’t ask people to pay for what they were promised for free.”

And there, the bell in my chest struck Sunday. The light in the bowl slipped and settled and rose again, like breath in a sleeping house.

Chapter One

Before the road, there were only paths: the dirt ones the goats made with their idiotic insistence, the footworn traces between water and house, and the ribbon of shade you learned to craft if you walked at noon behind the tallest person and kept perfectly to their step. People say paths make themselves. Roads require permission and maps and men in vests the color of peeled mango, and a minister with a microphone who smiles as if he is giving you weather, not a decision.

On the morning they began marking the cemetery, the storks had already gone. The acacia trees held their nests like empty hands. The grass was a bristle of end-of-dry-season fatigue, the blades giving up when you pressed a palm to them, a soft ceding. The earth was a ledger. Between stones, the ground sloped to a ditch that the village boys had widened over years to catch frogs during the rains. The frogs were out in their pale shells now, clickable as marbles. It was the sort of morning that punished tenderness. Everything you touched became a wound.

I carried the tin box with the oil pencil and the roll of rice paper and the contract with its shiny seal. I had borrowed my aunt Salme’s hat, the wide-brimmed one, though the hat was more a story than a shade. It had the crease where she crushed it under her belly when she slept on her stomach back in the days she said she didn't mind dreaming she was drowning, because in dreams she always grew gills and carried a basket of fish to the surface and woke with the taste of salt on her tongue. The hat smelled faintly of tamarind and smoke and the kitchen at dawn.

The minister’s man, who had introduced himself as a coordinator and then told me not to worry, was waiting with two boys in neon vests and one girl with a tablet that turned the sun to a glimmering glare. The coordinator’s face was the way official faces are, well ironed and prudently empathetic. His name was Gidou, or that was what he offered. He was the sort of man you could imagine doing any task neatly: folding an envelope, washing his hands, lying. He shook my hand the way you hold the handle of a heavy pan: with intention.

“Thank you for coming,” he said, and then added a little half bow as if he’d done me a favor I should acknowledge. He gestured broadly. “We are merely staying ahead. We respect, of course. We are not moving bones. Have we not assured? Names, that’s all. To bring forward. The records, to keep. For the families and the archive.”

His mouth made words like a fisherman throwing a net: wide and practiced, catching mostly light.

I touched the seal on the paper again, though I knew it by heart. The contract had a per-name fee and a per-page fee and a clause that said if I miscopied, the fault would be solely mine. It congratulated me on my literacy and my service. It did not say my grandmother’s name or my mother’s, but it had both their shapes, in the way it understood that a woman would come with a mouth, that the mouth would open, that breath would leave and be entered in a ledger.

“We start here,” the girl said. She was young enough that the pillar of hair she kept balanced on her head, bound in gold thread, seemed less style than an experiment she had dared herself to maintain. She pointed to the first row of stones, newer, the ones families still visited on Fridays with sugar and thin leaves. The vests fanned out, placed numbered flags at the foot of each plot so it looked like a parade halted with the dead mid-step. A drone passed whispering. Its eye, dark and reflective as an animal’s, hung over the name that was my neighbor’s child and then bobbed to another.

I knelt at the first stone. Heat rose up through the knee of my trousers, through skin. Someone had stained the letters with boot polish and the ‘a’ had a sudden shine to it I didn’t like, as if the vowel were slick with something too alive.

The work, as my aunt taught it, was simple. Consonants are bone. Vowels are breath. You hold the bones in your fingers, you cradle the breath in your mouth, and you return both to the world with more care than you were given when you arrived. There is a kind of cruelty to the way we name the living, my aunt said once. We stamp them too early with the hopes of a family, with the ghosts we want to appease, with the debts we intend to collect. But the dead, she said, are tender. The dead deserve to be called without wanting anything in return.

I unrolled the paper, smoothed it. I traced the letters with the oil pencil until they pressed up through the thin sheet, their curves filling with black. Then I spoke. The boy’s name on the stone had been home for three summers. I remembered his father’s hands the day we washed the car together for a trip that never happened. The foam like weather at our ankles. I said the name. I don’t speak names carelessly. But the dead take their own meaning of care.

The air shifted, a small coolness like the feeling when you open the lid of a pot. And then there it was, the taste. It always begins for me in taste. This one was an orange dragged through ashes. On my tongue, the grit and the high sugar. He had been burning something when he died and someone handed him fruit, or he imagined fruit. The memory settled against the back of my teeth. His laugh came into my ear amid the clatter of a spoon. His joy was my mother’s kitchen, though that wasn’t possible. I swallowed and let him go. The paper took his name, the pencil took his shape, the drone, the girl’s tablet, the ledger on the fold-out table all took their versions, and the ground accepted what it no longer had.

We went like that for a while. I made the rubbings. I spoke the names. The others tapped scribbles on screens and occasionally paused for the angle of the drone to adjust. At one stone, I tasted iron rain, which meant someone remembered their roof in a storm when they died; at another, I tasted salt too old for our inland, which meant a grandmother had been ferrying a story of the coast along her blood as if it were a precious contraband she feared to lose. Between the voices, there were intervals that felt like the bare spaces between songs on a cassette, a faint hiss the whole way through. Aunt Salme called that hiss patience. If you cannot listen to hiss, she had told me once, you cannot listen to the dead.

The heat settled its hands into the tops of our heads, the way an old teacher will lean on a desk and say, show me. Time loosened and thickened. We paused for water. The coordinator made an announcement about the magnificence of progress that the frogs answered by clicking twice.

“You don’t have to say them aloud,” the girl said to me as she handed me a bottle. “You could just write. We have the photographs, anyway.”

“I have to say them,” I said. I did not say because I am what I am, because my mother stitched this into me, because when your sister runs away you teach your mouth to keep her anyway.

We worked into the second row. These were older stones, the ones that had never belonged to a family that stayed. Some had been taken from older buildings and repurposed as markers, their letters half another language, their edges rubbed smooth by years of heat and harm. There was one with a broken corner that cast a triangular shadow in which a tiny lizard lay in the exact shape of a folded paper.

The heat made me think of my mother’s back, a map of lines and knots. She used to sit on the steps in the late afternoon and have me pour water from a cup slowly down her spine, cup after cup, the water running like a brief relief. “My river,” she would say. “You have to keep my river from breaking.”

We came to the stone I didn’t recognize. It had been placed in the second row but its color was wrong, a dull greenish granite you only see in the city, not the sandy limestone from the old quarry. No family would have brought such a thing here; moving that kind of stone costs money, a particular kind of painful money like the kind you borrow from a cousin who will ask you to pay back at a wedding. The letters were shallow, almost tentative. The surface was not burned or oiled, no fingers had loved this name. The number flag stuck in the earth by its foot flapped once and then went still.

I set the paper down. The friction of pencil against stone played up through the tip of my fingers into my knuckle as if it were telling me how it had been worked. There were tiny points where the carver’s chisel had slipped and been corrected. A hurry. Perhaps a fear of being seen doing what he did. I leaned closer. The letters were familiar. Not in the way letters are familiar, but in the way you know the arch of a particular eyebrow from across a room.

I traced the first character. It formed itself under the pencil’s sheen. I traced the next. The third sprang from the texture into visible black. The lizard made a noise like a cough. The drone sidled closer, its spinning wash making the hair on my forearms rise.

“What is that one?” the young woman said. Her tablet waited like an open mouth. The coordinator was shading his eyes as if watching a ship approach. There were men in vests arguing about whether the road should tilt left or right by two degrees as if it were a wristwatch they were strapping to the earth.

I could have walked away. There are moments that announce themselves ahead of time and give you the courtesy of being able to ruin your life very slowly instead of all at once. My aunt would have said not to be dramatic. She would have said sip, don’t drown. But she wasn't with me, and all I could see was the top of her hat in the corner of my eye, a circle of frayed straw.

I rubbed the final letter. The name became a thing you could not unsee.

Laleh.

It sat there with more gravity than stone. It pulled the air into a particular silence, one in which you could have heard the sound of a sleeping person remembering their own name beneath blankets. I did not move. Sweat ran down the inside of my arm, found my palm, soaked into the paper’s edge. It made the pencil’s line a hiss. The dirt at my knee gathered into a damp patch and held my kneecap the way a hand does. The world was now split into between before and after this shape.

“Laleh,” the girl read, careful, looking at the rubbing as if it might refuse. “Is it a Laleh? From which family?”

I did not know, for a long moment, what my face was doing. My mother had a face she used for grief that was also the face she used for spices, concentrated and invisible. My father’s grief was a ruin above water. Mine was always a small door opening where I did not know there was a wall. I had not practiced the face for it. “It is a common name,” I said. It was lying in its worst form: the sort that tries to mean harm to no one and therefore drenches everyone.

“Do you know the surname?” the coordinator asked. There was a casual note to his voice he could not quite nail to the air.

There was no surname on the stone. Only the first name, the date of death, and the narrow river of an etching that might have been an attempt at the symbol people carve when they are too poor for the full shape of faith, or it might have been an artist’s flourish, or a child’s drawing that someone preserved by mistake. The date beneath the name was six months ago.

Six months ago, on an evening of thin rain, I had heard a knock at midnight that I refused to answer because I was being stubborn about something that now I cannot remember. In the morning, there had been a single line of footprints pressed into the red earth outside the door, a goat nibbling at a scrap of newspaper, and a small, wet flower under the lintel. My aunt said it was no omen, only bad timing. I said an abundance of brave things to prove that I could refuse the irrational. At noon, a bolt of cloth fell from a high shelf at the tailoring stall where I was collecting a shirt and landed on my shoulder, and my shoulder felt bruised for days. None of that, I told myself now, meant anything. You can make a pattern out of a map of falling fruit if you want to.

“The records,” the coordinator said. He made a little gesture that brought the girl with the tablet to his elbow. “Search the parish. Search the hospital. Did you… you only need the name for your ledger, yes? We can proceed, if you are comfortable.”

Consonants are bone. Vowels are breath. If you hold them too tightly, you crush. If you let them flap loose, they fly away and you are left with the use of your mouth for only eating and refusal. My aunt said to spit out the vowels you don’t need, to keep your mouth honest. She never had daughters. She had me.

Laleh had been two years older and so beautiful people said her name with the last letter curled the way you might keep a secret on your tongue as if it were a spice too expensive to eat. She had a laugh that made men forgive themselves for the things they had not done in time. She tied her hair back with the red string that came on sacks of flour because she claimed any ribbon would spend its whole life pretending to be more than it was. She had left the village when I was nineteen, the week the rains never began. She said she was going to the city to learn something that wasn’t waiting tables. She asked me to come, and I didn’t. When I asked her, months later in a letter, what she had learned, she replied in a hand unfamiliar even to me: patience, this time, the kind that breaks teeth. Then the letters stopped. She sent no address. Someone said they saw her at a march with a sign like a sheet snatched from a clothesline. Someone else said the minister had smiled at her and that it had meant nothing but it had meant everything.

Sometimes at night I dreamed I was following her braid down a street in the city. In the dream, her braid was a path, and at the end of the braid there was a hand, and in the hand a stone, and under the stone a coin, and under the coin a beetle. In the dream, when you lifted the beetle, there was a tiny hole in the earth and in that hole a voice. The voice was speaking my name back to me, syllable by syllable, the way you speak to a fish underwater when you hope not to startle it.

“Names only,” the coordinator repeated, almost with kindness, as if he were offering me a slice of a dry cake. “Then we will … take care of the rest.”

The wind, which had been polishing the edges of everything all morning, went slack. The frogs stopped clicking. The drone faltered and hummed itself a nervous song. It was a show, the way weather will stop when it remembers you have said its name out loud. I did not look at the coordinator. I did not look at the girl. I put my fingers on the edge of the paper and I spoke. I said it in the way I would have called her from the riverbank when we were children, when she stayed under too long to scare me and then came up like a miracle, laughing. I put breath where breath belonged. I took the bones into my teeth. “Laleh,” I said. “Laleh.”

The taste was instant and terrible. Not terrible like rot, not terrible like a secret blade, but terrible like a color you cannot name entering the root of your tongue. It was the taste of unripe fruit that had been bitten by a wasp. It was the taste of rusting metal you put in your mouth when you are ten and you want to feel brave. It was a street opened by rain for the first time in months. It was a mouthful of thunder without the anger.

Then the voice. Not from the ground beneath my knees the way most voices come, climbing through dirt as if the soil is their throat. This voice came from the air just above my right shoulder. It spoke not into my ear but into the little hollow under my jaw that the edge of your hand touches when you cup someone’s face. It was my sister’s voice, not as it had last been but as it was when we made forts of bed sheets and forgot to come out until my mother knocked a wooden spoon against a pot and said, If you are going to live in a house of cloth, you had better learn to eat vapor. It had the break in it where laughter always eventually lodged like a seed.

“You took your time,” she said. If I had been standing, I would have sat down, and if I had been running, I would have stumbled and learned all over how to fall. I was on my knees already. The voice used a second breath, the way you do when something important needs to be held in the lungs a moment before the mouth gives it away. “Do not let them write the river wrong,” she said.

“What river?” I said, and then I was embarrassed, because there is only one river, and it is not like me to feign ignorance. But in that moment there were at least eleven rivers: the one my mother used to keep in her back, the one under the road in the engineers’ minds, the river of people who had left and never sent word, the river under my tongue where names move from living to paper and then to air, the river that runs in the ditch the boys widened to catch frogs, the river of black wires that go from house to house with a gossip of light, the river of chance, the river of a road itself, the river that the minister will cut and claim he has made it straighter.

“Promise me you will not,” she said, and outside the word promise there was the smallest sigh, the weary happiness of you catching someone you have known all your life at the exact moment they become themselves again, despite everything—like a stitch pulled out and then, by some miracle, the cloth mending itself back.

Speakers do not like to tie knots with nothing. Words require a listener to catch, to wind, to set aside for a time when they can be needed. I realized, not for the first time, that my mouth had been arrogantly believing its work alone enough. I closed my eyes. I saw, as I always do when I close my eyes and someone says my sister’s name, the neck of the road I dreamed she was walking along, the way dust can flex and behave like muscle when a truck passes.

“I promise,” I said. In front of me, the stone warmed as if it had been held in a lap. I put my palm against it and felt the slow, animal heart of something that is neither alive nor dead but insists on beating anyway because of love. It’s a word my aunt always refused to say, as if by not saying it she could keep it from getting trapped and misused. I said it now, silently, to the stone, to the air, to my own mouth.

The coordinator cleared his throat, a paper noise. The girl with the tablet wiped the corner of her mouth with her thumb in reflex to nothing. A vest said “Number two-nineteen?” to the other vest as if perhaps he had wandered into science by mistake. The drone, bored by our lack of motion, drifted to look at a tree. There are times when the world refuses to announce the hinge. It turns, and since it makes no sound louder than that of a lizard’s cough, you can claim later that nothing changed. I have lived long enough to stop consenting to such claims.

On the paper, the black letters of my sister’s name shimmered with oil. I rolled the page up because I could not bear the thought of the sun reading it more than it already had. I slid it into the tin box. The clip caught, the metal made the click that gave away nothing. I stood up slowly and realized my knees had dyed themselves to the color of the ground, an old woman’s skin. The hat shadows tangled over my eyes.

“Everything all right?” the coordinator asked. We say all right when we need to keep the world from breaking while we gather ourselves a ribbon or a rope. He kept his voice in that place between officious and kind, the way the new politicians had been trained to hold themselves like waiters with less soap on their hands and more practice with expensive cutlery.

“We will have to,” I said, and I found my own platter of words and my own napkin and I laid them gently on the coordinates he would understand. “We will have to check with the families before we enter certain names. It is the way.” I said it in the tone people use when they mean you may be in charge but of this you are not in charge.

“Very well,” he said, because the drone could not record a brand of defiance that small and the frogs had resumed their metronome and his sunburn was beginning, and because he was the sort of man who liked to take time as his tool and not as his master. “Very well. We are ahead, still. The road is not until the end of the month.”

The end of the month is a mathematical fiction. Time in a place like this does not honor the squares you draw around days. There is heat, there is rain, there is some How—some plucky How—you practice to get you from the worst morning to the part after the afternoon when the sky turns briefly the color of old iron and a new wind comes down like generosity. The road will come when the men with their shaved heads and their invoices finish arguing with the men with their religion and their invoices. It will come with a machine that makes a sound like a house growling. It will come over the cemetery like a fact.

Aunt Salme would be home making soup of the things that had been saved from spoiling by being turned into other things. She liked to say, when she peeled garlic, that the most honest way to convert the past into a future is with a knife. If I brought her a copy of the name, she would put her thumb on each letter as if measuring its pulse. She would say, You must let the world be brutal but not in your presence. She would say, Promise me, and I would. I had.

I lifted the tin box. It was heavier by more than paper. Muscle remembers weight before the mind admits it. I nodded to the coordinator in a way that pretended we were on the same side of a river I now understood would need to be named all over again. I put my hat better on my head, my aunt’s smell of smoke and tamarind arranging itself in my nostrils like furniture. I took one more rubbing, a name that tasted of parched mint, and I was careful with it, because care is a river also.

As we walked back down the row, my foot hit a stone and it shifted and under it a beetle scuttled, glossy and necessary, finding the small hole it had been looking for all morning. I thought of the crater in my dream. I thought of a promise. I thought of the road, which is a straight line only when you convince the land to stop speaking.

By the ditch, the boys had gathered a bowl of frogs and were arguing over whether a frog, if named, would live longer. I wanted to tell them about vowels and bones and patience. I wanted to tell them about thunder that tastes like iron and sisters whose voices arrive like weather you forgot you loved. I wanted to tell them that the worst thing to do with a road is to confuse it with a future, because roads, like names, can only deliver you to your own undoing more efficiently if you walk the way someone else decided your feet should go.

Instead, I said: wash them and let them go. Which is what my mother would have said, and on the days I wanted to be heroic, I remembered that she said it again and again into an ear I now wished I had favored with more attention. The boys rolled their eyes in that way children do when adults insist on mercy. They tipped the bowl. The frogs slid out as if in one wet thought.

On the path home, a woman coming in the opposite direction recognized me. She put a prayer folded into a piece of paper into my palm as if it were a coin and she were paying me for bread. “For my father,” she said. “They said you are doing the names. Say his again to be sure he has it.”

I put the prayer into my pocket with the tiny stone I keep there to remind me what the world owes no one. “I will,” I said. She touched the brim of my hat to steady it as if the hat were an animal that could bolt.

The clouds had gathered into a suggestion of rain that might, if they thought kindly of us, unwrap themselves later. In the distance the only palm bent to the right all the time was bending to the right as if being acquire d took place in small, incremental surrenders. I put my hand to my throat and felt the warm place still holding Laleh’s words. It would be days before anyone in the ministry noticed there was no record of her death. It would be days before anyone remembered that dates are often ideas we put on the world to ease the ache of not knowing when to cry.

Consonants are bone. Vowels are breath. Between them, we walk. The road is the sound of a mouth making a straight line where one did not want to be. I did not know yet how to disobey a machine. I knew only how to put a name in my mouth so that if anyone ever asked me to spit, the name would be caught behind my teeth like a bead, warm from being held. I knew—and this I had learned in the old kitchen with my aunt when we kneaded dough until our wrists begged—that a promise is not a word, it is a work.

At the gate, I turned and looked back. The cemetery sat hunched under the heat. The boys’ flag numbers made enamel fantasies of order that would fade before the year was out. The drone, having discharged its duty to the replayable, turned again into a dragonfly and went to find a puddle to imagine. The stone with my sister’s name lay flush and unreadable from this distance, which is the way love keeps itself. If you stand too far from it, it looks like everything else, a rumor of a surface.

There is a sound the air makes just before rain begins. It is less the sound of water arriving than the sound of heat being evicted. As I put my hand on the latch, the sound began. I was not ready. I said aloud to the empty yard, which is sometimes braver than saying it to a person: I will not let you write the river wrong. The yard did not answer. The first drop hit my thumb like a small sentence. I went inside to learn how to keep a promise I had made to a name I had pulled from a stone, to breath I had borrowed, to bone I had held, to a sister who spoke into the hollow under my jaw and, like all good ghosts, asked not for mourning but for work.

The first time she heard her name from the dead, the vault was cold enough for her breath to show.

It wasn’t supposed to be cold. The building had been a bank once, meant to hold the warmth of money and the warmth of men who counted money. Now the Commission rented the basement, concrete on concrete, with a metal door that shut like a jaw. On damp mornings the walls held their own weather. She wore a cardigan over her blouse and the cardigan held the ghost of the ginger tea she had spilled on it last week. The air smelled of old plastic and dust that had been taken apart molecule by molecule and rearranged into the precise shapes of other people’s lives.

Mara worked with her hands. There was a deck from the 1980s, Tascam 122, that she talked to the way people talk to stubborn animals. Don’t do that, she told the capstan when the tape refused to thread cleanly. Be nice to me. She cleaned the heads with a Q-tip soaked in isopropyl until the cotton came away gray, then black, then finally almost white. The machine purred and ticked, the two sides of its mouth ready for anything she might feed it.

The labels on the cassettes were parchment-colored and furred with fingerprints. The hand that had written on the one in front of her this morning was neat, slanted, unadorned. R-4827. Box 18-B. March 12, 86. The ink had bled when the writer’s hand had sweated or when the tape had sat too close to some spill. The number struck a match in the drawer of her memory. They had been working through the R-series for two weeks. R was for Room, someone had told her when she started at the Commission, until someone else had said no, it stood for Registration, and finally Dr. Varga had put both palms flat on the table and said, “R is for whatever keeps you moving from number to number.” The interns snickered. She had liked him a little more for that.

“Mara,” Ilyas called from the far end of the room. “The machine is sulking again.”

He said this every time he didn’t want to admit he had put a tape in upside down, but she obliged him, wiping her hands and walking past stacks of cardboard boxes stamped with dates and decades. The vault got quieter where he was, the air so flat it sounded almost like silence. He had a cigarette behind his ear that he would not smoke; the Commission had a sheet of rules on the door that began with No Smoking and ended with Everything You Do Here May Be Used Against You. He looked up at her with his lopsided grin.

“Look,” he said, and hit play on the deck. A man’s voice came out, so faint it could have been an insect, pitched high with speed. Squeak-squeak-squeak. Ilyas winced. “Chipmunks.”

“Wrong speed,” she said. “You’ve got a sixty-minute tape and you’ve set it for forty-six. You’re compressing their lives into a cartoon.”

He blushed and flicked a switch. The chipmunk relaxed into a human. She leaned over, adjusted the azimuth screw with the little jeweler’s screwdriver she wore on a chain around her neck. The sibilants came into focus. A chair scraped in some other room, multiplied by echo. She pressed her finger into the deck to give the tape a bit of drag, feeling for the steady pull, listening for the point where the voice stopped sounding like metal moving over metal and started sounding like a person unscrewing his own words in order to hand them to someone else.

“Thank you,” Ilyas said, his voice making a question of the last syllable the way he always did.

“Don’t beg the machines,” she said. “They’ll make you say please forever.”

A laugh, small and genuine, floated up from where Sofia was crouched beneath a table labeling an index of “Non-Spoken Sound: 1978-1991.” Sofia had the high, intent patience of a cathedral candle. Her dark hair fell over her cheek as she wrote. “Can I be on chipmunk duty next?” she asked without looking up.

“You can if you promise not to record over anything by mistake,” Mara said.

“I’ve only done that twice,” Sofia said, earnest, which made Ilyas choke badly enough that Dr. Varga lifted his head like a bird from the corner office and squinted.

The Commission’s logo had been painted over the vault’s old door, but the old world bled through: a faint crest of a lion with a coin between its teeth. Outside, there was a street of barbers and a man who sold false teeth on velvet. There was a statue of a man on a horse who had been unhorsed three revolutions ago and now stood on the ground next to his empty plinth. There were gulls, too, even so far from the harbor, because gulls are nothing if not opportunists. The city had stuffed its dead into the walls and then painted over them, and now men like Dr. Varga and women like Mara were meant to take the paint off carefully and say, Here, look, a shape you recognize.

Back at her desk, she took the cassette R-4827 and turned it in her hands. The clear window was clouded by years. Inside were the small brown bricks of magnetic tape, spooled neat and even at the factory, then unspooled and respooling, each pass lifting a little of the oxide and laying down a little of the past. She wondered, as she always did, at the faith of it: the belief that iron filings would keep the soul of a sentence in their bodies forever if you only kept them cool and dark and dry.

She slit the tape’s cracked case with the little knife she kept in her pocket and inhaled the chemical note that had sunk into every sleeve in the vault. She slipped the cassette into the deck. The deck sighed. Her fingers found the familiar controls. There was a sweet moment, after she pressed play but before the sound arrived, a breath held, as if the dead were licking their lips.

It was a room. You learned to imagine the rooms by their breath. This one had high ceilings and a geometry that made a man’s cough bounce back too quickly. Along the floor a heater hissed as if a snake had built its nest there. Someone clinked a spoon against a cup and then remembered that the tape was rolling and set the spoon down quietly. Someone else shifted papers, unable to remember anything without something to shuffle. It could have been a primary school classroom if the space between the sounds weren’t so careful.

A woman coughed, a short sound, the cough of someone who is not allowed to be ill. “State your name,” a man said. His voice was low and too close to the microphone, which gave it a softness that was not his own.

A flood of sibilants: the woman’s name. Unknown to her. The woman’s age. The year. The year uncoiled in Mara’s stomach. She knew the date from the label, but hearing it said out loud made the room recalibrate itself; it was not March for her. It was one of those late months when the light goes a long way toward forgiveness and then gives it up.

“Do you know why you are here?” the man asked.

The woman breathed. She had one of those breaths that had once belonged to someone who sang. “I’m here because you sent for me,” she said.

Mara adjusted the volume. The voice was familiar in the utility of its vowels, not foreign to this neighborhood, the neighborhood where seven bakeries survived in a row even though nobody ate bread anymore. She leaned closer. Voices in the vault were like coins in your hand: you wanted to bite them to see if they were real.

“You are here,” the man read, “in relation to events that took place on the third, fifth, twelfth, and twenty-one days of the month of February, one thousand nine hundred and eighty-six, specifically pertaining to the distribution of… pamphlets of seditious content, and the… organization of gatherings in the Plaza of Memory without… authorization.” The man’s voice had to fight its way through words that had been making the rounds for years, worn smooth as soapstones. He was bored by them. He was excited by them. Both.

“I distributed what I was given to distribute,” the woman said. “I brought soup to the plaza. I went home.”

There was a scrape of a chair. A second man leaned in, or perhaps the first man stood and the second man took his place, as a way of reminding the woman that voices were interchangeable and that bodies didn’t matter. “State your children,” a new voice said—he meant number; he meant name.

“I have two,” the woman said.

“What are their names?”

There was a pause. In it, a bus passed outside some window. It laughed like buses laugh down a long block. The woman said, “I have one son.”

The man sighed. “What is his name?”

“He changes it all the time,” she said. “He calls himself Pirate. Astronaut. Housefly Seven.”

“His actual name.”

“I don’t use it. It’s possible he forgot it too.”

“Fine.” The sound of a lighter. The hiss of the flame close to the microphone’s sinew. He lit a cigarette because some men believed smoke belonged in every room. “And the other?”

The woman exhaled. It wasn’t smoke. You could hear it. “My daughter,” she said.

“What is her name.”

The end of the last word scraped itself as if the man were exhausted by the grammar of her refusal. There was another pause, longer. Someone’s watch ticked with a tyrant’s insistence. The woman said, clearly, as if she were calling across a courtyard, “Mara.”

Mara’s hand slipped from the volume knob. The sound leapt. The voice went on. The word hung everywhere it could hang. She brushed her thumb against her lip as if a bee had landed there. The feeling came over her that she had as a child when she flattened a coin on the train tracks and went back to find it: that the thing that you made flat was not the thing you started with, and it was still yours whether it wanted to be or not.

She stopped the tape.

Her name was not so rare as to be hers alone. She had two classmates called Mara when she had been in school, both of them with hair that lay obediently down their backs. A woman at the market had once leaned over to her mother and said into a basket of cucumbers, “Mara, those are not lemons,” and her mother had laughed and said, “I am not Mara. I am Vida.” The woman had laughed harder, as if a private joke had been told in public.

She wound the tape back with a finger on the spool and pressed play again. The hiss again. The small cough. The man’s lighter. The woman’s voice without gasping. “My daughter,” the woman said. “Mara.”

A body knows its names. There were times she had woken because in a dream someone had called her a name that was not hers and still the body had brighted into alertness. This was not that. This was a syllable that had sat at the bottom of a well and been polished by water for years and then raised.

She played the next seconds with the volume low. The man said, “Write that down.” A pen found paper. The woman said, “You don’t have to say it as if it were a weapon.” The man said, “Everything is a weapon or nothing is.” The woman’s laugh was the kind that happens with your mouth closed and therefore was more terrible.

Mara’s fingers had gone cold. She sat back in her chair, which complained with a high wooden whine. She looked down at her sheet, at the column where she should write: R-4827 – place, date, speed, condition. She wrote: noise floor low; interference minimal; head alignment adjusted. Her handwriting was angular, disciplined, as if it had once been someone else’s handwriting and then it had been left to her.

“Everything all right?” Ilyas said softly from behind her shoulder. His voice had learned how to enter a room without knocking. He had come up without her hearing. He had a face that could do sympathy without condescension. It annoyed her and calmed her.

She took the headphones off, letting them hang around her neck like a mechanical jaw. “Yes,” she said. “It’s a mother talking about her children. Nothing unusual.”

“Unless the mother is the unusual part,” he said.

“Unless,” she said, and put the headphones back on without looking at him. It was unkind. He withdrew at once, his body receding from her the way a shadow recedes into the brighter shadow of a wall.

Outside the vault’s thin windows—six panes let into the concrete like mistakes—day moved. The children who were too young for school and too old for the hang of their mothers’ skirts kicked a flat ball against the statue’s empty plinth. From the fruit stand at the corner the smell of guavas came in waves as the man cut them open with a knife he sharpened on his trouser leg. The gulls angled over the city with their patient, idiotic faces. The city was in love with itself the way a scar is in love with the finger that presses it.

Her mother called at eleven past eleven, which was her mother’s favorite time to call because her mother believed in symmetry when it was free. “I’m at the market,” her mother said without saying hello. “Do you need tomatoes? If you do, you have twenty minutes. After twenty minutes, price is a different animal.”

“I’m at work,” Mara said.

“Work is work. Tomatoes are tomatoes.” The sounds of the market crowded the line: coins, yelling, a radio playing a song from long before. Her mother did not sing along out loud; her mother hummed through her teeth, like a kettle not really interested in boiling. “Your landlord called.”

“What did he want?” Mara said, as if landlords ever wanted anything else.

“He wanted an answer last week. I told him answers are like apricots. They come when they come.”

“You told him that,” Mara said, and a smaller part of her wished she had been there to see the landlord’s face as her mother said that to him, head to the side, rings shivering. “Thank you. I will call him.”

“And your work,” her mother said, not curious not at all, but not uninterested either. Mara had told her a version of the truth when she was hired at the Commission: that she was working with tapes, that she was making the ghosts of stations speak again. “Do you put on songs and sit in a chair with your eyes closed?”

“Some days,” Mara said. She pressed two fingers to the page with her notes as if it could bleed through to her mother. “Mostly we make lists.”

“I made a list this morning,” her mother said. “But then I bought a string of amber at a price that was an insult to amber. I will wear it to the church on Sunday so the women can be angry.”

“You don’t go to church,” Mara said.

“I go where there are women,” her mother said. Behind her, the market yelled with the joy of trading insults. “Don’t forget to eat. I made soup.”

“What kind?”

“The kind that remembers you,” her mother said, and then she had to go because a woman was stealing pears with the fantastical boldness of someone who has been told she will never be caught.

When her mother hung up, the room did not change its shape, but Mara could feel in her bones the tiny reorientation the world did after every conversation. Her mother had been like this for as long as she could remember: insisting on being the current that ran under the city’s stones, not the stones themselves. The last time the Commission had been on television, her mother had turned the sound down and eaten her stew with concentration, as if the men’s faces were themselves pieces of an animal she had to chew carefully to avoid the bones. “I was busy then,” her mother had said afterward, meaning the time when the tapes were first made. “I was not making history. I was making your shoes fit longer.”

If she said the name, her mother would say a thousand other words first to protect it from being heard.

She pressed play again. The conversation on the tape had traveled down a road she could now follow in the dark. The men asked for places, for times. The woman answered and did not answer. Every now and then the woman’s necklace hit the desk with a sound too small for jewelry and too heavy for an ornament.

“Sing it,” one of the men said suddenly, as if he were tired of the game. “Sing us one of your songs from the plaza. We have it here.” Paper rustled. A cassette case clicked open and snapped shut. “Sing.”

The woman said nothing, so the man did: he hummed the first line, badly, and here was the betrayal of the human: he sounded almost shy. The melody was one of those made to be remembered by people who had neither instruments nor choirs, to be sung while peeling potatoes. The woman exhaled, and then she sang a few notes back at him and their notes collided in the air like two birds.

Mara knew the tune. She did not know how she knew it. It was not the anthem they all knew and pretended not to know. It was not any of the lullabies that had been smuggled past bedtime. It was something between. It had the shape of a lament and the engine of a marching song. And then the woman stopped in the middle of a phrase as if someone had caught her by the throat.

“No,” she said. “That is ours.”

The men did not move. You could hear their not moving. “Yours?” a man said.

“The plaza,” the woman said. “We sang it with our mouths open. You cannot ask me to give it to you with my mouth closed in here. It belongs to air.”

Mara’s hand had gone to her throat without her permission. She took it away, laid her palm flat on the page with her notes. She wrote: song – Record? Source? Check. She was supposed to be making neutrally useful marks. She was supposed to be the narrow bridge between one thing and another. She was not supposed to feel anything as the people on the tapes insisted on the texture of ownership.

She listened for another ten minutes without hearing her name again. At intervals there was the scrape of a pencil. There was the small intake of breath that people do when something has just held a knife to their pride. There were the sounds of a courthouse where the courtroom had been dismantled and distributed into offices and waiting rooms and hallways and kitchens, in order that it would be everywhere and nowhere and therefore invincible.

At noon, the interns went up to the street to buy shawarma from the man with the red umbrella. Ilyas stood in the doorway with his head tilted back, sniffing at grease, and said to her, “Do you want a sandwich?”

“I’ll come,” she said, because the tape had given her the feeling you get before an exam you have not studied for.

The street peeled her eyes open. The man with the red umbrella had a scar like a country’s map around his mouth; he told the same joke every day and it was a good one for morning and a less good one for evening. He said it again and the students laughed again. Mara chewed her bread and watched a dog watch a pigeon with the intensity of undying love. A woman at the corner looked at her exactly long enough to be recognized and then looked away. The sky was the kind that cannot decide whether or not to rain and makes a career of thrilling itself with the possibility.

On the way back down, Sofia said, “When you go home, what do you hear?” She was the kind of person who would ask that question and require a precise answer. If you gave her a word like “neighborhood,” she would make you hold it up by its corners until it dripped.

“Lately,” Mara said, “the man downstairs is teaching himself the accordion. So I hear the inside of a whale in distress.”

Sofia made a thoughtful sound. “As a child?”

“As a child,” she said, and the stairwell gave the words back to her with its own varnished shape, “I slept under a piano.”

“Oh,” Ilyas said with terrible admiration, as if she had confessed to an exotic illness. “That explains something.”

“My mother rented a room in a house where the landlady kept the piano in the front because her dead husband had been a small-time composer and she wanted a big-time reminder. Twice a week there was a boy with a hat who came to play scales. The rest of the time I slept under the belly of that animal. The wood made all the other sounds into the sound of wood. Even the voices were timber.”

“Do you know any of his songs?” Sofia asked.

“They were recipes,” Mara said. “My mother used to say they didn’t keep.” She put her hand on the vault door and felt it vibrate slightly as if it were its own animal with its own blood. “Let’s go back,” she said, because the air was warmer out here and her head felt too light.

She did not put her headphones back on right away. She made herself look at the form as if it were a piece of laundry she had to fold properly or else the drawer would never close. She filled in the box that asked: Language. She wrote: Ours. Then crossed it out and wrote the language the Commission expected to see. She picked up her pencil and sharpened it and sharpened it until it was dangerous.

She pressed play.

The tape, cooperative as a vein after hot water, gave up another room. It was the same room; it was always the same room. The men had changed cadence. They were past patience and into repetition, which made their voices soft with practice, like the hands of the women who had ironed shirts for thirty years. They asked for dates again. Today is the twelfth, they said. What happened on the twelfth. The woman answered. The bus. The square. The soup. The rain that came and went. The men shifted tactics like dice in a cup.

“Tell her the thing about the nursery,” one said softly, as if the microphone were deaf to the word softly. “Go ahead. Tell her.”

A chair scraped. The second man’s voice moved closer to the woman’s breath. “We are very patient, Mrs. —” He paused. “We can wait for your song to finish. While you stop singing, we will tell you a story. Yesterday, we visited a place where the walls are painted yellow and the doors are narrow and there are small beds in a row. We visited with a man who is allowed to take things away with his hands. We asked him for a list.” Papers. “We will ask you for names soon. But first.” He paused as if to let her picture the beds. “First, to save our time, tell us the one you would like us to ignore.”

The silence changed shape in the room. It did not grow. It did not thin. It began to sit on the table.

“I have three nephews,” the woman said at last. “They do disgusting things with their noses. They would give your lists a headache.”

“And your daughter,” the man said.

“She is taller than me now,” the woman said. “She tells me I am not allowed to wear red.”

The man made a noise that could have been laughter if laughter were not banned in warehouses. “She sounds like a revolution,” he said, and then the cassette caught, the tape buckled slightly, the woozy wobble of oxide passing over a less-than-perfect wheel. Mara leaned in and nudged the side of the deck with her knuckle as firework adjusters nudge the fuse. The sound cleared. With it came the ghost of a melody. Not the march, not the plaza song. Something else. A few notes. The woman was humming to herself as if it were the only way to close her mouth without breaking her teeth. The tune ran under the men’s words like water under a bridge.

Mara knew it. Not from the plaza. Not from the boy with the hat at the piano. From somewhere nearer. From the winter she had the flu and lay on the couch while her mother moved through the rooms. A tune like a river not in a hurry. A tune with no words because words were expensive. It was possible, in that moment, to believe that all songs are one: that you can walk into any room in any city and find that the song you learned by accident is being sung by a stranger to keep her hands steady. She felt again the coin she had pressed to the track and the train running over her fingers.

Something shifted inside her. Not conviction. Not knowledge. Something like a small hinge applying itself to a door it had not known was a door. She took the pencil from where it had rolled to the edge of the table and wrote in the margin where there was no designated box to write such a thing: Do not include.
