Then she struck through the words with a neat line and wrote in a neat hand: Sheet shedding—surface damage. Head alignment unstable. Consult prior to use.

She breathed. She let the tape run until the end of the side. The man said, softly, “Thank you for your cooperation” the way men say “This is an arm” and hold up a weapon. The click of the stop. The dull head of the tape against the spool. She turned it over. Pressed play, then stop. She pushed the cassette back into its case and felt the crack in the plastic find her fingertip like a mouth finding a lip.

“Mara,” Dr. Varga said from his door, his hands in his pockets as if to remind them he had nothing up his sleeves. “If you finish with Box 18-B today, we can begin to build the listening station for the public. The opening is in two weeks.”

“I finished the first two,” she said. She had finished one and a half. She slid R-4827 into the small basket on her desk labeled: For Review.

He nodded, too used to her precision to check it. His face had learned a patience that probably felt, inside his mouth, like holding a hot stone. “Good,” he said. “Good, good. People will want to hear. People will not want to hear. Either way, they will come.”

The light glanced off the small bald patch on the back of his head. It made it tender. She wanted to be kind to something.

At four, the gulls tore someone’s bag of bread open and the bread scattered like promises, and the sound of the city rearranged itself again. She worked more slowly than she could have. She wrote notes that were more precise than they needed to be. She wrote the truth again and again until her hand ached: head alignment optimized. tape formulation high. hiss constant. She wrote and did not write. She put the two cassettes for the day into the tray and left the third under her blotter. On the yellow paper under the blotter was a phone number she had written last year in an unsteady hand when she thought she wanted to call a man she used to know. She had not called him or thrown the paper away. She liked to imagine a world in which she had done both.

The vault began to close itself around her. The others went one by one, the small noises of their departures as ordinary and final as the sound of a book back on a shelf. Ilyas lifted a hand without turning his head. Sofia put her palm flat on the table as if blessing it. Dr. Varga shut his office and the vault echoed in that particular way that meant the city had become more insistent above it. The last elevator’s cable sang its single low note.

Mara sat alone in the chair with the bad spring. She took R-4827 from beneath the blotter and put it back into its cracked case and took it out again. She held it up to the light as if the dead, like children at windows, might press their faces to the clear plastic and make a shape with their breath.

She stood. She took a clean label from the drawer. She wrote in her precise hand: surface unstable. consult. Her pen hung over the last letter. The liquid in the pen made a round, glossy well.

When she left the vault, she did not put the tape in the tray or in the basket. She put it into the pocket of her cardigan, the one which smelled of ginger, the one in which things had gone to live for years: a ticket stub, a bead from her mother’s broken necklace, a stone the size of a thumb joint. The tape pulled her cardigan to the side, a small proof of matter. It rested against her body above the shape of her hip as if it had always known how to sit there.

On the street, the sky had decided not to rain after all. The man with the red umbrella took the umbrella down. The statue’s horse stood beside its man as if it had never known any other configuration. The gulls found an organization suitable to their talents and obeyed it. She walked toward the bus stop and did not look up at her mother’s building, where every window was an eye. She would call her landlord. She would eat soup. She would not mention the Commission. She would not say, Did you ever sit in a room and say my name to a microphone? She would not say, Sing. She would not say, That song belongs to air.

A child on the steps of the barber’s shop blew a strand of hair from his mouth and said to his little brother, “Pirate.” The little brother said, “Astronaut.” Their mother, pinning their cardigans with mouths full of safety pins, said, “Housefly Seven,” and did not know she was telling a future she didn’t believe in.

Mara got on the bus. She kept one hand in her pocket the whole way home. She could feel the old plastic warming a little. Not enough to turn, not enough to soften. Just enough to make a place where the dead could settle and begin, very quietly, to hum.

The river began to say our names the summer I came home to pack the house.

It had been a dry year everywhere; the radio crackled news of distant fires and reservoirs drawn down to a seam, airplanes flying over moonscapes where lakes used to be. In our valley the river narrowed under the bridge until it showed its spine—the pale sandbars that made the fishermen swear and the children wade out so far you could stand in the middle and not be taken. The old-timers said you could step across with a good run and a prayer, though they still took the long way, still paid the toll because the man at the booth had a voice like a hymn and because the bridge, with its lattice of rust, was a kind of religion.

Of all the things I thought might drag me back—marriage, debt, a teaching job that had fallen through—it wasn’t the notice from the electric company about the dam, or even the text from my cousin saying, he’s worse this week, he keeps asking where the atlas is. It was a voicemail you could barely hear over the hum of the hospital oxygen: Mina, he said, then again, Mina. Like a person practicing a foreign word. And then, as if the air between us were water and he was afraid of drowning, he said a third time, My girl, your name.

In the city where I’d been working I held other people’s names in my palm all day. I recorded elders whose children had long since ceased using the words they carried; I wrote phonetic guides for tonal rises that could mean “rice” or “mother” or “ghost,” depending on what your mouth did. I listened to a woman who had fled across two borders tell me the name of a black bird we never see where we live now, and as she said it her hands cupped a shape that wasn’t there. We talk about languages dying as if breath were separate from body, as if whole lifetimes didn’t go quiet with them. Sometimes, leaving the archive, my clothes smelled like mothballs and something else I can only describe as old rain. Sometimes, in the subway, I’d mouth the syllables I’d just captured until the people across from me began to shift their knees away.

“Our river is a language,” my father used to say when I was very small and he could still sit cross-legged and drop me an apple from the knotted pocket of his sweater. “You read a river only if you remember its grammar.” He was a surveyor for the county back when work was work; he carried a transit and drew lines on maps with a pencil so sharp it could cut your finger. He walked our land in a vest full of pockets, measuring a world that refused to stand still. The dam people came in his last decade of working life—hard hats, clipboards, plans rolled up and banded like cylinders of meat—and he measured for them too because it was what they paid for, and because if he didn’t it would be someone else. He could tell you to the inch where the new water would reach. On the kitchen wall he had penciled a line and written ninety-three feet above summer flow, which is the way he dated us, the way he kept time.

The house was cooler than the air outside because my father would not turn on the stove since June. The June before this one he’d put his tea kettle on every morning and then leave the burner cold until the afternoon, as if he were gauging how much heat nostalgia could provide. Now he was on the sofa, wedged into the crook his body had made. He wore the oxygen tubing like a second set of veins. Pale dust, not dust—silt—had settled on the mantlepiece, fine grit blown in from his open windows, and when I brushed it with my finger it left a clean line like the mark of a ruler.

He had always been small for a man, even before the lungs shrank and the shoulders fell: narrow hands with square nails, the kind of hands that can hold a pencil and lay fence. “Seven pounds, thirteen ounces,” he liked to say when someone asked what he carried home from the hospital that day. “A good number. Lucky. Easy two primes.” You’d think luck would depend on more than arithmetic. You’d be right. But in this house the world made sense most when it could be measured back to something that would not lie: the circumference of a tree held in his arms like a beloved; the speed of a current tied to a rope around his waist; a squint through the eyepiece until lines converged like promises.

“Atlas,” he said when I leaned down and he felt my hair against his cheek. The oxygen machine hiccupped. He smelled like the medicine that turned his spit pink. “Where did it go?”

“In the office, Daddy. On the low shelf.” I smoothed a place on the blanket that didn’t need smoothing. “How are you, my heart?”

He made the face that meant why ask and also I am still here. Three small folds under his eyes. “The river’s showing itself,” he said. The words were breathless, like leaves in a dry wind. “Have you been down? I can hear it from here.”

I could hear it too. The back door had been propped open with an old grammar book that had belonged to my mother: Latin, with phrases underlined in her careful hand. She had written margines on the flyleaf and drawn a leaf in the margin. Beyond the screen, the cottonwoods thinned the light. Somewhere a dog was crying the way dogs do in this part of the world when they have seen the end of a day they cannot change.

“I went by the bridge,” I said. “The sandbar is out. There were kids.”

“They aren’t supposed to swim,” he said, and then smiled, because we both had swum there first at eight, at ten, at twelve when our bones needed something to set them, then at sixteen when our bones needed something to unsettle them. He was not a scold, my father. He believed in signs more than rules. “It’s saying names,” he said. “They come up on the little stones. I’ve put them all in the bowl.”

On the table by the sofa was his chipped blue cereal bowl. Inside it lay a handful of smooth pebbles like the backs of river fish. On each, in either black or a deep green not unlike the river water when it’s happy, was written a single word in a hand that could have been a child’s first careful attempt. It was my father’s handwriting except not: less canted; rounder; as if written by light. He picked one up with his fingers as if it might leap and wriggle. “See,” he said. He held it so I could read.

Sahar.

If he had wanted to test me, he could not have chosen better. A string of breath and heat and a place I would not have put in our valley. I knew a Sahar from the archive, a woman who laughed from the back of her throat and whose son never answered his phone. She had said her name meant dawn in the language that built the words for God like ladders. But that Sahar had moved to the city because she could not bear the distance of small towns, she said, the way everyone in them says hello with their whole face. She’d described our valley when she saw the river in a picture on my desk. The color of your water, she had said, those long goats’ll drink anything.

“You wrote them?” I asked carefully, because the pills were new and he had been awake in odd hours.

“I would not write a name I did not own,” he said in the old way that meant don’t make me be a fool, Mina. He held up his forearm, where the skin had thinned to paper. The blue of his veins drew neat tributaries. “Promise me you won’t bring a marker down there. Promise me you won’t play a joke on an old man.”

“I promise,” I said, because I am not unkind and because I could feel the same prickle rising at the back of my neck that came when I was a child and the first thunder clattered its copper pot. “You found these on the bank?”

“They found me,” he said, and then seemed embarrassed by the drama of it, the way the words ran together like he was quoting a book he’d once mocked. “I went down to see how far out it had gone. I was only going to the lip. I can count in my head how many steps from the back stoop to the break in the slope. Thirty-six. I can do thirty-six and back. But I went an extra six, and then there the first one was. Round as a kneecap. The name was looking up at me like a fish’s eye. I thought it was a trick by those boys—Palacio’s sons, you remember? But the next one was by the willow they cut down three years ago, and I figured if a boy had hidden them, he’d have been hiding a hundred. I brought it to the house because my head was spinning. And when I turned around, there were three more on the path.”

“There are more,” I said.

“So many,” he said softly. “So many, my girl. You know how in April you walk out in the pasture and the ground that looked like one thing is suddenly another because of the violets? There were violets made out of names. I couldn’t carry them, so I came back with your mother’s apron. The one with the snail on it. Don’t be cross. It was in the pantry. It’s a good apron.”

I hadn’t been cross in a long time, is the truth. Whatever anger I had left, I used for other things—the women in the archive who had not been paid after the deli closed, the boy in our hallway at three a.m. who’d lost the language of his own name in the bathroom mirror. If I had saved any anger for my father it was for his grief which refused to behave itself and get smaller. The gray sweater that wasn’t clean but wasn’t not; the way he left oranges on the steps for the foxes and then complained of fox shit in the yard; that he had learned how hot dogs came to be and then ate them on Monday because it made sense to put all ugliness in one day; his insistence that you could walk every day to the river and never learn it completely and how he would demonstrate this in the rain.

He set the stone back into the blue bowl as if laying down a spoon he had finished with. I touched it with my fingertip, the way you touch a candlewick after it has burned.

“We should tell somebody,” I said after a moment. “Someone at the paper. Or at least Lisa. People will be… I don’t know. Sad. Or glad. The ones with uncommon names will be thrilled.” I didn’t know, in truth. We come from people who have spent lifetimes not wanting their names on lists. And yet to be seen is an ache that does not choose its medicine.

“They’re not names we know,” he said, as if he were offering a riddle. “They are names we have to learn to pronounce. They don’t belong to the churchyard or to the war memorial. I thought maybe they were of the men who poured the footings for the old bridge. But I took two to Ellen. She wrinkled like a shirt. She said there was a girl in her class called Sahar once, and that she left before fifth grade because her father took work in the next county. Sahar Ali. Skinny legs. Always had ink on her finger from the chalkboard. Ellen said she had forgotten that girl’s name until she saw it on the stone.”

“You took them to the store?” The grocery’s new owner had painted the sign a different green than anyone liked. He was from Ohio. He carried quinoa and called it keen-wah with a happy certainty that made you love him a little while still despising the price of bread.

“I wrapped them in my handkerchief and put them in the pocket with my wallet,” he said. His voice was defensive in the way of honest men who have nothing to hide and yet are no longer believed. “I bought milk. I paid with cash. I took out my handkerchief. It is linen. People don’t use linen anymore, because it is not as easy as a towel and the washing machines make a fist with it, but your grandmother—”

“I’m not scolding,” I said. I could feel the hook of weariness catch behind my ribs and tug. “If the river wants us to know these names, it will tolerate their being seen at the grocery. Did Ellen know the other one?”

“It said Valeriy,” he said carefully, as though the y at the end might cut us if he turned it wrong. “A man with a voice like a train. He used to stand by the chain-link at the ballfield and sing to himself in the language of broken metal. Do you remember?”

I did. Girls have a way of cataloging the men who watch games. This one had been tall in the way that means knees. He had hair like the grass that grows next to the range of a propane truck. He always wanted to carry more than his paycheck would allow at the store, and people in line would fall silent. Valeriy had taught himself how to ask for the brand names of olives and then, on a Friday, had stood at the end of the meat case with tears in his eyes because the word he needed for his mouth was not there.

“What does it mean?” I asked, lower, because the air between us had grown sensitive like a bruise. “What does it mean, Daddy, if the river is doing this?”

“It means,” he said, and he closed his eyes as if to get help from somewhere warmer. “It means the ground is calling a roll before it is covered over. It means the grammar is changing. Or it means nothing and I am old.” He opened his eyes again and looked at me in the direct way he had taught me to look into an eyepiece, a way that insisted the world would not lie to you if you didn’t lie first. “You’ll go to the meeting tonight?”

“I’ll go.” The dam company had posted notices with glossy photographs of kayakers on white water and a woman in a visor standing next to a field of solar panels that had nothing to do with anything. The room would be the firehouse, because you cannot refuse people in a place that has saved their ovens and dogs. There would be plastic chairs and the dais would be draped in a flag, as though democracy were a table we kept forgetting to set. The company would say what it always says. Easements. Energy independence. Jobs with hats. The river would be called Resource until you wanted to throw your body across its mouth.

My father let his head fall back against the cushion as if he had been holding it up by force. “They’ll bring the map,” he said. “It is almost beautiful. The blue of the water, squared and tamed. You can’t put ugliness in that blue.”

“I know,” I said.

“Look for the line,” he said. “Ninety-three feet above summer flow.”

“I will.”

“And if they give you a number to write on your mailbox, don’t you write it,” he said fiercely, his voice the old voice, the one that could put a nail in with one swing. “Don’t let them number you. A house is not a grid. It’s a mouth.”

I raised my hand in surrender. “I’ll be your bad daughter,” I said. It had been our joke once that when I left at nineteen, I took with me the version of me he loved most and left behind the rest. At the window a jay called once and then was quiet, as if it had tried out a voice and found it wrong.

In the afternoon while he slept I walked the yard and then the slope, counting steps in case the river wanted to compare. Thirty-six to the break in the hill where the ground fell away in a ruined shoulder; then down through sumac and into the small of land where the beetles had written their thin tracks in the fallen ash. The river was lower than I had expected, bowls of mud with their rims exposed. The willow’s stump was a molar. It smelled like the bottom of a drawer that has held cloth for too long; like iron left to sigh itself back to dirt. You could see the old tire someone had rolled into the current in 2006 because the dog had died that week and boys do what they can to stop a howl with a splash.

The stones were everywhere once you knew to look. They were not larger than plums and not smaller than your thumbnail. No two were the same color. I could see the hand that had written on them as surely as I could see the little snail in the apron my father had tied in his lap: a hand that did not rush. A hand that did not hesitate when it came to the old letters or to the hooks that belong to languages that never learned to worship straight lines. I hissed when I first bent to take one, as if the mud had a voice, but then there it was in my palm, light and holding its ink as if ink were part of it: Naza. The n had been written with a tremble. Or it was the way the water has when it looks calm and then shows you the ruffle under it.

I put the first stone in the pocket of my jeans the way you pretend not to weep by putting the edge of your ring under your tongue. The second I held and I could feel nothing and I could feel my whole life. Hanna. The third was a name in the old country alphabet, the one my father could not see and my mother could read in a single sweep the way a swallow will learn the map of a barn. I imagined, without meaning to, her wrist when she wrote grocery lists, the little straight mark she made when we needed milk. A name is a handle, she had told me when I was seven, but you must be careful how you carry things by their handles because sometimes the inside is fragile.

The day went orange as if seen through honey. I filled my pockets and then my hands. The river made sounds the way a throat does when it has been crying. Two boys solemnly installing a row of stones on the clay like teeth looked up to see if I had sanctioned their work. One of them had drawn the letters on his own hand, copying, I realized, what he saw in the mud. A before it knows it is an A. He showed me and I nodded and he smiled a gap that said he had lost a tooth and somehow found it again out here and put it back and it had taken. Across the water the tracks where the old ferry used to tie off were showing, indentations like a cuff. If I could have kneeled and spoken to the land I would have asked it whether every name we ever spoke went down into it whispering, and which ones came back and which ones never did.

By the time I climbed the hill again the house had folded into the dull heat. The oxygen concentrator let out a sound like a small animal contemplating a leap. My father had left the bowl of stones on the table and a pad of paper that was one of his old field notebooks, its cover soft with the oils of his skin. In the corner he had written inventory and under that, in the careful way of a man who has three hours and a purpose, he had started a list.

Sahar. Paloma. Valeriy. Keoni. Ann. Ardashir. Kiko. Old Mr. Pollard was right about these letters.

I picked up his pencil. I wrote the name off my palm. I wrote three I could carry in my mouth and another I would need to practice. The pad took the shape of a day. Somewhere in the house, behind the old quilt in the guest room closet or under the box of postcards, there was the atlas. My father would wake up and look at me and ask me to fetch it, and we would open it to the page where this place is a brown stripe with a blue thread, and we would put a finger down as if we were stopping blood, and we would say together the words for what was there.

On the chair by the door my mother’s apron hung, still marked in one corner with the ring of a jar. You mustn’t keep all your jars full, she used to say when she put up peaches, because the season you make a pantry of your heart is the same one the ground will shift. She had left in a season of flood—the last time the river was a parent and took what it wanted. She went to check the culvert at the bottom of Lewis Lane because if it clogged, the road would wash out. By the time anyone remembered she had said she was going, the rain had grown teeth. That is not the way it happened, and also it is the only way it happens.

I stood at the threshold and realized I had not brought any water up from the bank because I had put it all in my pockets. I was laughing before I knew I was, the little hysterical laugh that no one believes is laughter in the moment. Then I did what I had wanted not to. I reached into the bowl and pushed the top stones aside soft as one does with shells. Underneath, along the curve of the ceramic, a piece of river lay with its back to us. I flipped it. It was the color of bone and on it was written a name in a hand that was not mine and was not his; it was the hand of the river if a river could write.

Sae.

My mouth made the sound the way you make a sound into your skin to see if it can be contained. In our house we had never agreed what that syllable stood on. My mother had been five languages by the time she was twenty-two. Here she was three and in each she was something else. The name on our mailbox was the English one, which was simplest and could be pronounced by men from Ohio and women from Alabama. The name on the birth certificate was a hyphenated transcript of a promise. In the kitchen my father used the small vowel that does not take up room. In the night, when he woke from a dream, he would say two more syllables after it which no one else had the right to use.

I pressed the stone into my palm until the bone hurt. The light had changed. The air had the feel it gets when people begin walking toward a place where decisions are supposed to be made. I put Sae back in the bowl because you do not turn everything into proof. I found the atlas and carried it to the sofa because I am obedient and because I needed to put something on my lap. I wrote my name at the top of the inventory because if the river wanted to count me, I would be counted. Then I pinned my hair back and my father woke and said, “My girl,” as if he had learned a new word, as if it had been given to him by the current itself.

At the firehouse that night the fans made a sound like wings that would not lift. The company men unrolled their plans and our faces gathered like weather. But even as they made their case, polite and practiced and accompanied by slick, even as a man in a crisp shirt whose cheeks were too smooth tried to say “riparian” and failed to make it lie flat, what I heard was the low work of the river, a throat clearing. Back home, under our windows, the river was practicing its new grammar, raising a hand in the dark and saying, present, present, present, until the call was answered.

By law our tears belong to the city until noon.

Every morning the Harvest Hall opens like a mouth. The doors yaw, their brass hinges dark with old brine, and people step in with their grief folded neatly the way one carries clean linen. The booths are tiled in a pale blue that looks like the inside of a shell. Names chalked above each stall turn into a soft blur by ten, the chalk dampening in the shared breath. At six, when I let myself in with the night key and switch on the banked lights, the room is a grid of salts. The tiles bloom white. Tears dry on the walls in ridges, in lace, in maps that pretend to be countries. By noon, if I’ve stayed ahead of the drip, everything will be harvested and sacked. The City Office likes to say that grief is a resource, that salt is order, that the sea itself understands the virtue of keeping.

It takes both hands to lift the first sack. The canvas is always a little damp and always smells faintly of lemon oil and bodies. Blue 17 had a wedding party last night, six hours booked and the bride had thrown her bouquet into the far drain. Fake eucalyptus, pale silk roses, a few buttons shaped like bells. The bouquet had caught and hung there like a fish. Someone with no sleeves shows up in every season in Blue 17. You can tell because their salt is fine and hot and clumps as if trying to hold itself. I take my spoon—steel, chipped, older than my hands—and scrape from the top-left corner to the right, cutting through the crust and letting the flakes fall into my apron, then the sack. The motion wakes up the muscle in my shoulder. I breathe in the faint taste that aerosolizes off the wall. Onion tears go to the kitchens. The salt my city hires me to find is not for meat.

My mother used to tell me every tear had a flavor: grief like coins, shame like copper roofs, relief like the first ice of winter. She could cry on any cue. She was valuable in a way that made men polite. At the Weepers’ Theatre she would stand in a white chair and let the songs make a ladder up her throat. Women paid good money to sit in the dark and listen to someone else's pain tapped like a cask. It was an old art—older than this hall—and when the city made weeping municipal she said, now they’ll put a meter on it. They did. She stopped performing and the blankness in her look scared me more than any of her enacted griefs had. After the illness, the ducts dried. She could not summon one drop. She laughed because it was foolish and then she kept laughing for a long, long time as if the sound were a bucket dipped into an empty well that still somehow came up wet.

I cannot cry. Or not in any way that the city can catch. It’s like a perverse inheritance. Mother and daughter: one a faucet, one a drought. To keep Van’s name from appearing on the black notices tacked to doors for arrears, I come here. I scrape what other people have left.

The tiles hold stories. There is a strictness to certain griefs. Soldiers cry in grids. Children cry in clouds, the salt meeting the floor in arcs. The night our neighbor’s boy fell off the back of a truck his mother used Blue 3, and I had to stand on a stool to get the vertical streaks where she had pressed her head high and kept it there as if to leave a dent. After she left, I found her fingernail half-mooned into the grout. I kept it until it softened indoors, then it dissolved. There are losses you keep as a lesson. Everyone here pretends to be practical because the scale waits in the back room and nothing is as practical as a weight.

At seven, the schools send their children to observe. They come in to smell their fathers on the walls and then laugh because nothing in this place should be funny and so it is. Five little boys line themselves up at the edge of Blue 11, shoes squeaking, hands gripping the rope that keeps them out. Their teacher—thin, an ink stain on one cuff—reads from the Council pamphlet in a voice full of red stamps.

“This is where we harvest communal salts,” he says. “Do we ever cry straight into sacks, Yosef?”

“No,” the boys say as one. They’ve practiced this. “That would be unsanitary.”

“And who owns your private tears?”

“Private tears belong to the household until noon, at which time—”

“—unused portion is remitted to the City if not stored properly,” I say, and they look at me because I am the adult with the spoon, a rare beast. The teacher flushes and lets me have the line. “We keep this place clean,” I add, because it’s true and because the cleanliness feels like a benediction. It’s easier to work with grief when it doesn’t stink of its body. “Full booths are marked with chalk. See here? Someone signed Ada. Someone else wrote just an X. You must write the name you want the salt credited to. If you don’t, it goes to Common. The hour of crying, the type of tear—if you can note it—go in the ledger out back.”

A boy with a cowlick raises his hand, though he doesn’t wait to be chosen before asking: “Do all tears taste the same?”

I dip my finger into a bare patch and touch it to my tongue. It is all metal coins this morning, pockets of the poor. I think of saying this and then choose kindness.

“No,” I tell him. “But you have to learn the differences slowly. Some salt is for illness, some for birth, some for war. You will taste only what’s left of a feeling after it has dried.”

“I thought salt killed,” another boy says. He is the kind who looks at drain holes and imagines them bigger. A future engineer. When he grows he will measure pipes with his stamp in his mouth.

“It preserves before it kills,” I tell him. “Most things do.”

The teacher herds them on to the next shuttered hall. I go back to Blue 17, set my stool under the bell, and reach for the high lip of crystal that has grown along the upper tile. The spoon knocks something loose that falls, too resonantly, into my sack. The sound is like a hard candy clinking against a bowl. Curious, I fumble my hand into the damp canvas and feel it: a shape not like any salt I have touched here. When I close my fingers around it, my skin reports a map. It has the exact curves of an ear, small as a child’s.

We have all heard of ear-salt. Folk songs love them, little talismans that shore up listening. They are not supposed to be real. A woman at the fish market swore her third child’s left ear was a salt ear, say he could hear the tide plan the week. My mother would sing a verse about a girl who left an ear in the sea to spy on sailors while she stayed home and cured their grief. Songs do not make things true, but they do make them durable.

The thing in my palm hums. It is not a sound so much as a pressure that insists on itself behind the teeth. I glance toward the open doors. No one is watching. I could put it on Thalia Rui’s desk and fill out the anomaly form and watch it get spirited away by men in coats the color of wet rope. I could.

Instead I slide it into my apron pocket and keep scraping, gooseflesh like salt itself up my forearm.

When the sacks are full, I drag them to the back, one at a time. The Weighing Room has a heat that makes the hairs in my nose singe. A big scale sits on a plinth like a docile animal. There’s a ledger open to a fresh page. The first column reads Name, the second Booth, the third Notes, the last two Weight and Credit. A stylus lies in its groove like a thin bone. Before noon the book is everyone’s book. After noon the book is evidence.

Thalia is doing sums with her finger in the air and a cigarette unlit at her bottom lip. She is never without the cigarette; she does not smoke. She looks like a child was told to draw a severe woman and did not understand that severity is not a haircut. Her hair is a straight block. Even her eyelids look sharp.

“You’re behind,” she says, not unkindly.

“The tile up top was thick,” I offer. My pocket hums and I shift. The hum doesn’t care about my lies.

“There’s a rumor, Vera.” She taps ash that isn’t there onto the ledger so that tiny white flakes pepper the black. “The northern clinics say they’ve found half a dozen sweet-cries this month. Sugar on the wall. Bees. I told them it’s just syrup spilled from cones. Don’t bring me a hive. You do, I’ll dock you enough that you’ll cry for me in my office and then we’ll see what the meters say, eh?”

“Yes, Thalia.”

I am careful to look incompetent enough to be left alone and competent enough to be retained. This is the only math I do without the ledger.

I heft the first sack onto the scale. It tips to seven kilos and three hundred grams. In the booth column I write 17. In the name column I look up at the chalk I copied in my head. Ada. X. Whole names. Half names. A little ear of salt pulling at my apron like a dog. My stylist slants to Ada, Booth 17. In the notes I write wedding, probably out of habit, as if the word makes and unmakes the feeling it is.

The second sack is from Blue 11. The chalk had been careful there, no smudges, a square drawn around one word in a hand like a stair: VERA KOST.

I stare at my own name on the paper as if I’ve written it without my wanting to. I look up and through the half-open door to where my stool splinters a shadow across Blue 11’s tiles. My name sits above the stall in a clean white print that is not my writing. The letters are a shade neater than I deserve, the K turned inward like a prayer. The salt on the wall, when I had scraped it, had come away mosaic-brittle and bitter as winter tin.

“Who the hell put me on the board?” I ask aloud to nobody who will answer me. The ledger, obligingly blank, waits to be informed that I have cried.

Thalia looks up like someone who has heard the tone of a question but not its words. “If you don’t want the credit you can put Common and the City buys us soap. It’s always soap, Vera.”

“I want the credit,” I say, my mouth full of something that doesn’t taste like coin. It tastes a little like keys.

“Hm,” she says, and goes back to making numbers with her fingertip on the air. “Write your own name. Claim your own grief, why not. Women are allowed to these days.”

The stylus doesn’t shake in my hand but the bone of it feels like something alive now, a fish in the grasp. VERA KOST, Booth 11, I write. Notes: unknown remit. Weight: three kilos even. The numbers line up obediently. They do not care that some facts sit wrong in the mouth.

Claiming salt that is not yours is a low crime. It is the kind of thing men in wet ropes decide to elevate to a high one at whim. If someone used my chalk—if someone wrote me where they wanted to be remembered or disguised—then this credit will land at my door later like a bird and peck. There will be questions. Did I authorize a surrogate weeper? Did I barter my tears? Do I owe, now that I have a surplus? All the verbs the City loves will be applied in neat stamps to me.

My pocket vibrates again. I feel for the edge of the ear. The inner curve fits the pad of my thumb. When I press lightly it ceases its humming, as if soothed by being handled.

At ten, my shoulders ache. At eleven, men with mustaches come to roll the exhausting barrels out of the back where the saline bars are pressed for the market. On the street at noon, women with brittle hair tilt their faces up to judge if the weather will take their wash. Salt hangs in the air here like a law we inhale. It makes the peonies in Mrs. Lou’s yard tie themselves tight and refuse to open. It keeps fish honest. It makes certain men believe they cannot rot.

On my walk home I pass the Weepers’ Theatre. It looks smaller every year, the paint cracking at the seams of the painted curtain over the door. People go to watch the old shows out of habit and out of the kind of hunger that eats its own hunger. There are posters brittle on the brick: The Sobbing Wife, The Siege, The Nine Streams. A boy who once asked me for a slicer at the butcher’s runs with a paper cone of almonds, licking his fingers in a way that makes me want to grab his hand and wash him at the pump. He has sat in those dark seats and he will sit there again and the city will tax his sorrow and he will not notice until the floorboards ask him who owns the things that leak from him.

Home is a second-floor flat the color of old fingernails. The steps are quick to complain; they try to tell the neighbors everything. Our door sticks by design. My mother is asleep at midday the way she always is now, a sheet over one knee and the heel of one hand pressed under her jaw to keep her mouth closed. A postcard of the sea flutters above her on a nail, held by a magnet shaped like a spoon. Her hair has escaped its tie and lies on the pillow like a stubborn rope. I stand for a moment in the doorway and watch her chest rise.

There is a jar on our little kitchen table that we keep for the municipality: a cut glass bowl from someone’s wedding, once. If we gather private tears (rare) we tip them in there to mitre with the other sifting things. Today there is a lemon on the table next to it, bright-headed; its skin holds an old thumbprint of hers. I lift it, roll the soft rind against my palm, and press my thumb into my forearm just to see if there is any drop left in me that wants to be caught. Nothing.

It is not wrong to be dry. It’s only unusual. The City has a pamphlet for everything but for this they have none. If you are dry you are asked to contribute in other ways, and those ways multiply until you are contributing with your knees as you mop the floors with your hair.

I can’t keep the ear in my apron. The hum feels like a new kind of weather. I sit, ease it out onto the table. In daylight it is less like an ear, more like a knot of salt that has been told a secret and kept it. The curves are exact where they matter and fanciful where they don’t, as if the body’s memory is good enough for poetry but not for anatomy. I hold it up to my head and it warms against my skin. For a moment I imagine Agathe next door arguing with her husband in the courtyard is drowned out and that I can hear instead the underwater boil of blood. Then the hum becomes clear in my molars and I set it down too fast. It clicks against the glass of the bowl and we both flinch.

“Don’t break your salts,” my mother says without opening her eyes.

“I thought you were asleep.”

“Don’t break your salts,” she repeats. “Once you break them they are just pieces. And pieces do not buy bread.”

I sit very still until her breathing floats back up to its sleep tempo. Once, when I was ten, she taught me how to make myself cry. It involved a list of questions: What do rabbits eat? What do you know by heart? Who taught you to tie a knot? Which one of your hands would you keep if you had to? It also involved onions and sometimes a spoon on the bridge of the nose. “It is not that the body dislikes tears,” she told me then. “The body is stingy because the world is greedy.” Counting starts with a coin. We counted. It never worked.

The ear sits in the bowl like a small drowned thing not designed to drown.

Outside, a bell down in the square marks noon with a procession of tinny notes. The city lets out a breath, a thousand backs straightening as work reprieves—or changes shape. I stand, go to the sink. For something to make sense I need the tap running. The stream is thin at first, clouded with pipe rust, then it clears to a steady thread that sings against the tin basin. I hold the bowl under the faucet and let water sluice over the ear. It sits there. It does not dissolve. Salt should give up. It does not. The humming in my pocket—that phantom hum, now that the ear is out—relents into a quieter insistence, like a baby three rooms away.

The bowl changes temperature. My hands register heat and then the absence of it. Now the water itself hums. I shut off the tap with a quickness I hope is not fear.

A small greenness appears in the salt’s curled concha. The kind of green you only see in new leaves before they learn municipal dust. A thread as fine as hair unbends, feels the air as if it were testing for a draft. This is impossible. This is scientifically disgraceful. I fight the immediate, childish urge to put it in my mouth. Instead I lean down and blow, as if my breath could spare it or spare me. It trembles. Another thread follows, a twin. In the ear that should hear, something is growing that speaks.

There is a tap at the door. Not a fist. The polite knuckles of a neighbor. I reach for a cloth to cover the bowl out of stupidity and then stop because idiocy is sometimes survival. I pull the bowl off the table and slide it into the gap under the counter where we keep empty jam jars we mean to fill with things that never need a jar.

“Who is it?” I call, too quickly. The cloth I ended up grabbing is in my hand like evidence.

“Vera Kost?” A voice I recognize but cannot immediately place rises through the wood, turning our name into something official. A man standing too straight to be a friend. The door complains at the look of him.

I think of the chalkboard at the Hall. Of my name in someone else’s hand. Of the ledger open like a wound or a mouth. I think of my mother in sleep looking like the child she was when she left the harvested fields and came to the city believing a job that pays you to feel is a thing that will leave you with something in your hands.

“It’s your City Office,” the voice says, as if anyone could own that ugly brood. “There’s been a discrepancy. You’ve been credited with tears. Quite a sum. We need to talk about your surplus.”

Behind me, under the counter, in a bowl that was never meant to be more than decoration, a plant in salt presses itself slowly, stubbornly into the air.

1

On the morning the city names a street for a river it buried, I wake to water drawing lines under my floor.

At first it is only a darker grain in the wood, a bruise traveling east to west, a thin slick that catches the light as if the boards are learning to breathe. My building is old enough to remember when the word loft meant light and the word district meant something you could cross on foot before the rain caught you. I live on the third floor, both above and below everything. The windows face a row of warehouses turned gyms, and beyond them a crown of scaffolding where glass climbs another story before the next storm.

I lie flat on the floor and press my ear down. It has always been my habit to listen before I look. The city’s drowned body speaks best through wood. Under the varnish, under the paste of old renters’ lives, there is a hum I recognize: not the thin, impatient buzz of a pipe or the ragged rattle of someone’s washing machine leaning loose from the wall, but something low and patient as a long question.

You learn the city’s water the way a child learns to read the faces of adults. You learn how a throat sounds when it is about to lie, how shame sounds like a pause. My father used to lay his cheek to manholes and say, Shh.

That’s not a memory I summon often. It comes in with the humidity, an unrolled spool.

I get up and follow the line where the damp has lifted dust into paste. The apartment is one long room divided into sleeping and not sleeping by a bookcase I never finished painting. My brushes are in a can by the sink, clean for once. I reach past them and pick the cheapest one, the one with the split ends that turns anything it touches into weather. When I’m working I carry water in jars — river water, mostly — but today I wet the brush under the tap and drag it through the first sheen of damp. The bristles darken, drink something more than what they were given, come away tasting faintly of iron.

When I was ten my father kissed my mother on the shoulder in our kitchen and told us he was stepping out to listen for the downspout. He put on his too-light jacket like a man going to be measured for another job. It was a summer of heat, then rain, then heat again, storms that came stacked in threes. He did not come back. My mother invented a new tense to hold him in, one in which he would be altering a pipe, turning a corner, looking for a manhole key. When the rain came thick at four in the morning, she lay awake naming the shapes the drops made on the roof — pennies, then buttons, then beans — so that the sound would belong to someone.

I was supposed to be asleep; I was counting, without knowing it then, the short silences between noises. I learned that from him too. His maps, rolled in a tube behind our couch, were full of blank spaces where he said the water would have wished to go.

I reach the end of my perfect line of damp and it keeps going through the wall. Of course. In this city your boundaries are never truly your own. I stand with my palm on the plaster and feel the cool of someone else’s room. My neighbor on that side is a musician who sleeps by day and practices by night when all our dishes chatter.

My phone vibrates under the pillow on the not-sleeping side, as if it has tunneled there for warmth. I let it get three pulses in. Then I answer.

“Mara, tell me you’re awake.”

Only one person says my name like a pin pulled, and I am already watching her hair in my mind: black, decisive, cut to the jaw. Nadia manages the project. She manages me in the way of people who are fond of a thing and afraid of it in equal measure.

“I’m awake.”

“You sound like you’re trying to hear if your floor is pregnant. Are you coming? The wall is crying out for you.”

“I’ll be there.” I look down at my shirt, paint-freckled, my jeans with a hole in a knee I have revised and let be. Outside my window a crane draws a rectangle in the air, a square of frame that will soon be a window through which someone else will stare at yet another new crane.

“They installed the letters last night,” she says. “Canal House. There is no canal. It’s very honest.”

“Names are cheaper than water.”

“I’ll put that on a tote bag. Ten minutes?”

“Fifteen. I need to wipe my face.”

“Bring the blues.”

I hang up and go into the bathroom where the mirror still carries the last tenant’s tape outlines of where he wanted to put a cabinet. My toothbrush watches me like an animal with its head in a trap. There is a small rust-colored crescent at the base of the tub where the enamel has gone thin and the pipe peeks through like a knee. I wash, pull hair into a knot. My coat hangs by the door like a curtain that refuses to fall. When I step into the stairwell the smell of other people’s breakfasts greets me, eggs and cardamom and that scorched edge of bread we all pretend means home and not lack of attention.

Three flights down I pass the glass case with the red metal tube behind it. The word Break is stenciled in white above a little hammer on a chain. Some days when the city’s sirens are more insistent than usual, I stop and look at the water map behind the glass: a tangle of pipes with arrows as if an artery diagram in a science classroom. The arrows are always going places they won’t.

Outside the air is tuned higher than the room I left. The street named for the buried river runs one block over. I can see the new sign at the corner, fresh green, white letters crisp as teeth: Minnow Street. The developer paid for it, a gift to the neighborhood. The city accepted on the condition they would also add a plaque explaining that no actual fish lived there now. It is affixed to the brick of a building whose first floor is a café with a chalkboard that says Wildflower Latte, which contains no wildflowers and no latte.

At the fence around the site, a woman in a high-visibility vest checks my name against a list as if I might be smuggled in inside myself. Inside, the air is the air of raw gypsum and the tire tracks of small machines. Nadia is standing in front of the wall that is our direction, our client, our site of attempted persuasion. She is wearing her red boots because she believes in talismans that are both symbolic and waterproof.

“You’re late,” she says, and kisses my cheek. “You smell like rain.”

“Talk to my floor.”

“I will add ‘plumber’ to your bio.”

On the wall, in pencil, I’ve laid the bones of a river that used to cross this very lot, permitting no one to build on it. We had the city’s map, a copy of a copy of an eighteenth-century drawing that made the water too wide, then not wide enough. The developer wanted me to paint a river as a ribbon, a flourish. Something children could pose in front of while their parents pretended to imagine living here.

I told them a river is not a banner, it’s a muscle.

There are shades of blue in my case I keep for work that must sell, and shades for work that must not. Nadia gestures toward the most practical of my jars. “Use the responsible azure, not the melancholy one,” she says. “We can’t have buyers thinking their bathrooms will whisper to them at night.”

“They will.”

“I said buyers, not prophets.”

She is right that I sell enough of my belief to pay for heat. But I keep aside the small well of ultramarine my father kept in his box — war treasure, I called it, because he bought it with money he should have used on something else — for the deep curls at the edge of every mapped bend. It’s showy, it’s wrong for modern taste, and without it the water looks like a lie.

I open the jar with my thumbnail. I choose a brush that will let me make a line that looks like what it says it is. I begin at the bottom because I distrust impositions that come from above.

There is a kind of silence that happens in a room when you put paint to wall and everyone decides to be glad for a minute. Even the men hanging duct move softer. I am in it, and then I am in the thing itself. The line goes, in the old drawing, under what is now the freight road and then under what was once a church sold for condos with small balconies just large enough for a bright bicycle no one ever rides. It leaves the block at an angle and goes toward the place where Nadia looks when she’s doing numbers, the corner of the sales table. A woman in a scarf walks in with coffee and stops in front of our river like she has arrived at a barrier. She is carrying a clipboard that tells me her name in a font chosen to be lightly friendly. There is an O where I would have put an A. Names have gone that way in this city; vowels lilt depending on market.

“Beautiful,” she says. “I mean, not beautiful beautiful, not picturesque, but… credible.”

“It’s not a compliment if it ends in procurement language,” Nadia says.

“Everyone’s a poet today. We’re putting out the racks with the miniature kitchens at two. Are you done by two?”

“I was told I’d be done by last week,” I say. I am smiling the way I learned from my mother: with my teeth pressed softly into my tongue.

While the day collects behind me, while I lie a line into memory and hope it stays, my phone shivers against the table where I left my bag. Nadia glances at the screen and her mouth does a thing that is most of the reason I like her, which is to say it becomes a sentence without sound.

“Your mother,” she says.

“I’ll call later.”

“She will leave a message and then leave you a hundred more about the meaning of the message.”

“Let her.”

“Do you need to—”

“Give me ten minutes.”

I lengthen a bend as if I am uncurling a sleeping animal. The client says, “It flows,” as if flow is a favor I’ve done to a word we all know.

I step back. I like it in the way you like the image of a person you will not get to meet. Nadia whistles low. “If anyone asks, we can say a historian cried when she saw it.”

“Which historian?”

“You, for a fee.”

We laugh in the way people in open spaces do because the ceiling insists. Then Nadia says, softer, “She called three times. I think it’s about the announcement.”

Right. The announcement. My mother reads the city news the way other people read horoscopes. Today the Council votes on the transit expansion: the new line that will run beneath the western neighborhoods no one used to go unless something you needed was stored there. The line that, if the old drawings are true and my ear is not lying, wants to cross a river that isn’t supposed to be there anymore. The maps that they released show the tunnel skirting the known culverts. But maps are a way of speaking, not always of telling.

Some nights the people in the planning office ask me to paint the idea of something so hard it begins to exist. I should not be trusted with that.

We break for lunch when we are told to. I eat a sandwich of bread and bread with an oiled leaf in between. The woman with the scarf tells a man with a haircut about a couple from upstate who fell in love with the fixtures. Nadia reads a letter on her phone and does not read another. I step outside because the inside is too full of future tense. On the sidewalk, just beyond the shadow of the sign with its impossible canal, there is a woman of the kind who waits in all weather with a stack of papers that no one wants to take because they might have to talk after.

Her coat is gray and has been good at its job for a long time. She has arranged herself beside the “No Standing” sign as if it’s a rule for other people. On the cardboard at her feet someone has hand-painted words that tilt, which makes me love them more: Don’t let them flood us twice.

She watches me like a person watches a crosswalk, not looking at the faces but the currents. I look back because my father taught me that only cowards watch with their eyes half-closed. She nods, once. It is a gesture that means You hear it too.

“Do you have a minute?” she asks, as if minutes are coins and our pockets are full.

“For what?”

She lifts the papers like a waiter showing me a tray. “Do you make maps?”

“I make pictures of maps that make people behave as if a thing existed.”

“Then you make maps.” She smiles; her teeth are square and uncompromising. “You’re the one with the river on the wall inside there.”

“I am.”

She looks up at the letters I painted in pencil and then in paint. “Pretty,” she says, an indictment.

“What can I do for you?”

“You can look at this.” She opens a folder like a mouth. Inside is a stack of photocopies that have their own hunger. The top one is a city map from 1921. Someone has drawn in ink a line that is not on the printed page. It is not one of mine. It is a line that behaves like an animal that does not owe you its shape.

“Where did you get this?” I ask. It is always the first question with a map.

“My husband worked for the Department of Sanitation for thirty-four years. He took pride in what other people threw away.” There is a tenderness in the way she says it that makes me want, inexplicably, to protect her shoes. “He kept what he shouldn’t have. He said if he didn’t, the city would forget what it was made of. When he died, I put his name in the paper small because he would have hated a fuss. These were in a box marked Tools.”

Tools can be anything. I look at the line again. It runs from the edge of the industrial district north to the old park and then into a tangle of printed streets whose names have changed twice and never in their own language. It intersects the new transit line as drawn in the press release last week like an argument nobody at the meeting wants to have.

“I’m having a meeting tonight at the church on Hadley. Seven o’clock.” She says “church” not to tell me where prayer happens but where heat does, free. “You should come.”

“I don’t go to meetings.”

“You don’t have to speak. Just bring your eyes.”

“Why?”

“Because your eyes are already wet.” She says it without cruelty. “And because you can help me say my son existed where the city says he did not.”

There it is, the bank where the water drops fast.

“What is your name?” I ask.

“Doris.”

“Mara.”

“I know.” The corners of her mouth go up, not like a smile but like the way a door lifts when the lock remembers its job. “You painted the cold-storage warehouse on Fifteenth with the rope of blueberries.”

“That was for a jam company.”

“You painted the old slaughterhouse with the white birds.”

“Egrets.”

“They were pretty and wrong as hell. But people came to look.”

“I’m not sure that’s a compliment.”

“It is what I have.”

She hands me a copy of the map and then another of a typed letter with a coffee stain that has turned, over time, into a country. The letter is from 1991, on city letterhead formatted in a hierarchy of obedience: To the Families Affected by the Flooding of July 12. It speaks about “extraordinary weather events” and “unforeseeable conditions.” It uses the word sorry as a synonym for unfortunate. It does not say We built a road over a stream and forgot, and your boy was good at running short distances.

“My David,” she says to the air. Her voice alters; it folds a little. “They said he fell in a ditch that was not supposed to be there. I told them it wasn’t a ditch; it was a river with its name taken away.” She taps the hand-drawn line. “I want to give it back.”

Nadia’s boots appear at the edge of my vision. “Friend of yours?” she asks, gently, as if I am a person who grows friends like moss.

“Not yet,” I say.

“I’ve invited her to church,” Doris says, “to hear what the city will not tell her in clean words.”

“Good luck with the city,” Nadia says, affectionate in the way of a native skeptic.

“Luck is for scratch-off tickets,” Doris says. “I am offering work.”

I fold the map into a square and slide it into my coat pocket where it makes a new angle in the fabric. It warms to me as if it, too, can adapt.

“I’ll come,” I say.

“Bring that thing you do,” Doris says.

“Which thing?”

She points at my ear. “That one.”

When I go back inside, the river on the wall is waiting with the patience only painted things have. The developer’s people have arranged a small cluster of chairs as if the chairs have something to say. A photographer takes a picture of a man in a suit holding a child in a hat in front of the word Canal and nobody feels the need to apologize in any language.

By two the room has a new sound, a money sound, a sound I cannot make less true with brushwork. We are told to sign a thing asserting we have not built a hazard. Nadia signs and then blows on the ink like it is an old trick. I sign with my left hand because superstition tells me that way the letters cannot be used against me. When I leave at four the blue is dry enough to own its first darkness. The angle where the line crosses the corner of the room seems to lift when I look away.

Outside the sign for Minnow Street is casting a shadow two inches short of the curb. It takes a city a while to get its shadows right. The afternoon has become more itself. The sky is the color of a child’s drawing of a sky. On my walk home the hydrants wore scarves in winter and hats in summer, but today they are simply their iron selves, kneecaps for giants. A dog paws one like a saint’s knee and looks embarrassed about religion.

The block with my building has two trees pretending to be a row. Someone has tied fabric to the trunk of the one on the corner with a handwritten note: Not trash. My landlord has used three locks that do not relate to one another. Inside my mailbox is a pamphlet from the city with a stylized map of how the new line will save lives and time. It makes ghosts of the blocks it does not wish to address. The letter says We listened in a font that has never heard anything softer than an argument.

Upstairs, my floor has continued its slow declaration. The line is wider now, like a vein after work. I take off my shoes and step around it in the way you step around a sleeping animal. The window is open an inch. The air that walks in is wearing the park; someone has fried onions in it.

I take the photocopy from my pocket and spread it on the table, smoothing the corner where the staple once held. The drawn line runs where stories from my father end in a pause. I hold the paper up to the light and the ghost of the map on its other side shows through. For a minute there is a river that crosses itself. My phone blinks. It is my mother this time, the subject line an aria of alarm: CALL NOW.

I do, because otherwise she will call the landlord to ask if I am alive.

“Finally,” she says. I can tell by the way her voice wraps itself around the first syllable whether she is alone in the room. Today she is. “You sound out of breath.”

“I walked.”

“You should take a taxi. Is your painting dry? Don’t breathe those chemicals. They say it becomes part of you.”

“It’s paint, not language.”

“Language becomes part of you too.” Her mind runs ahead of her mouth these days and it is a lovely, terrible thing to watch. “The news,” she says, putting a capital N into it. “They’ve put the route on the news. They’re going to dig under Hadley. Under the market. Where Mrs. Singh sells the balm. Under Mr. Li’s barbershop. He has that sign with the woman’s face cut out of paper that scares your aunt.”

“I’ve seen it.”

“You must do something. Write a letter. Draw their attention.”

“I already have their attention. They want me to give them a river.”

“They want a swimming pool and a boat parked in it so they can say they are sailors,” she says. When my mother is at her best she can fit the city into two nouns. “Don’t help them.”

“I have to help somebody.”

“Help yourself,” she says, blunt and kind because she knows how hard it is for me. “We are running out of… what is the word. Preparedness.”

“Time,” I say.

“That too.”

“I’m going to the church on Hadley tonight,” I tell her. “There’s a meeting.”

“You don’t go to those.”

“I’m going to this one.”

“Good. Take a sweater. People speak longer when there is heat.”

I laugh in spite of myself. The river on the map hums under my hand. Through the wall the musician starts to tune a guitar or a machine. For a second the pitch matches the pitch under my floor and the chord makes a new color in my brain.

“Do you remember,” my mother says suddenly, “the man by the school with the balloons? The ones shaped like horses that looked wrong from the side?”

“I remember.” The balloons were always almost full, never quite. Like lungs in a waiting room.

“His brother calls. He wants to sell the cart.”

This is what my mother does when she is afraid: she inventories possibilities. “We do not need a balloon cart,” I say.

“You never know,” she says. Then, quieter: “Do you dream of him, lately? Your father.”

I look at the line at my feet, at the paint under my nails, at the place on the wall where the light always leaves a little later. “Only when it rains.”

“Then it is going to rain,” she says, her voice a smile without teeth. “Be careful.”

“I will.”

When I hang up, daylight has moved into the place where it becomes indecent to stay alone without turning on a lamp. I set the map on the floor where the damp is becoming itself. I lie down the way my father taught me to when he wanted me to learn between noise and sound. The boards have warmed me for years; now they bring me news.

Below, something runs that does not care about us. It is not malevolent. It is not kind. It is a body doing what it did when it had a name and when we painted over it and when we called what it did an accident. People say a city is a machine, but machines have off switches. The old water curls under my shoulder blade and hums there, asking none of my permission.

I close my eyes and the map on my chest lifts with my breath. For a second, because Doris has asked and because my father didn’t, I imagine a way to measure what matters without making a chart that anyone can sell. I imagine painting a door where the river used to be and opening it, and a boy running up through the tile into the light.

The sound rises, or I sink into it. Or both. The hard wall between remembering and imagining resolves and then dissolves. In it there is a long, low note I have never heard before. It is not a pipe or a truck or a musician tuning toward a pop song. It sounds like a train speaking under its breath to a thing it can’t see. It sounds like the city asking itself how not to drown again.

At seven I will walk to the church on Hadley with the map in my coat and sit in the third pew and listen to people say what they have needed to say for twenty years without anyone official hearing. For now I touch the place on the floor that is trying to become river and say, out loud in an empty room, Okay.

Okay, I hear you.

By the time the river let go of the house, it had learned the taste of us.

It was late September when I came back to the peninsula. Ferry decks were still dotted with tourists in raincoats and pitying eyes, all craning to see the slick slump of my town, the bruise of the flood. Someone had taped a hand-lettered sign to the ferry snack bar: WE ARE NOT A SPECTACLE. A young man in a volunteer vest tried to enforce a kind of order, but grief finds its own route. The rain set in, thin and meticulous, the kind that makes begonia leaves glitter and skin itch. The ferry horn sounded as if through gauze.

On the other side, trucks idled in a long line. A woman with a bulldog in a knit sweater handed me a mask and a box of contractor bags without my asking. “Mold,” she said, and pressed her lips flat. Her sweater was impossibly white.

I drove slowly, because the road had been turned in places into a kind of new river, a flat brown slick with this sheen that makes you look twice, thinking you saw a fish. On the left, the cedar mill had become a silence with a sign in the middle, We Will Rebuild. On the right, there was the Thai place that had always smelled like star anise and garlic—its front window was bellying out. In the little gravel lot behind the old Catholic church, men with chain saws stood huddled like birds. The church’s steps were slick with algae. A paper sogged to the railing announced that Sunday Mass would be held in the gymnasium until further notice. Rain braided the letters.

In my grandmother’s front yard, the salmonberry canes were bowed with mud and silt, leaves cupped like green hands. Halmeoni’s picket fence, which she had made me paint every August with a brush so small it felt like a pen, was flattened on one side, as if a giant had decided to sit for a while. Her mailbox pointed at the neighbor’s maple in a kind of accusation. The maple itself held a plastic kiddie pool high in its branches, sky-blue and very cheerful, the way foolish things sometimes survive the worst.

I sat in the car a minute longer. In the glove compartment was the spare key, hung on the same teardrop of smoky quartz it had been attached to since I was twelve. Between the seats, the cleaning supplies I’d piled in without thinking: bleach, vinegar, a whisk broom. A yellow legal pad. The county had given us all orange tags to fasten to the front door: NAME, ADDRESS, ESTIMATED DAMAGE, IS THE RESIDENCE HABITABLE. I’d brought a Sharpie for the certainty I didn’t feel.

The porch steps sucked at my boots, cheeks of wood swollen, slick. The front door opened on the second try, having swollen itself into a tight fit—wood that had drunk too much and wasn’t going to pretend otherwise. The smell that hit me was a layered thing: river, rot, something sweet and familiar trying to pretend it hadn’t been afraid in the night. The floorboards had curled up at the edges, cupping the river like the salmonberry leaves outside. The entryway rug—a red one I’d always tripped on as a child—had splayed itself open, pattern bleeding, like a cut pressed too long to the wound.

Kimchi jars bobbed in the kitchen like fat glass buoys. We had always called them onggi even though they were not; she used mason jars with blue lids now, the same kind she stored buttons in. The river had unshelved cookbooks, a volume of essays with a dried ginkgo leaf utilized as a marker fluttering like a fish on its back.

On the piano—a spavined upright that had traveled from Seattle in the back of a neighbor’s pickup truck in 1986 and had never been in tune—small white mushrooms had sprouted between the keys. They were little tongues, or little ears. They shone with the kind of luster that makes you think of soap. My boots left glossy half moons on the floor as I moved toward them. When my sleeve brushed them, they leaned, damp, resilient. “Do you hear that?” I said out loud, as if I were asking the mushrooms for their side of the story.

In the wall above the piano, the framed needlework my grandmother had hung the year her arthritis first flared sat crookedly, floss darkened. It read in an off-kilter font, if you have two loaves of bread, sell one and buy hyacinths to feed your soul. The corner had grown a bloom of mold that looked like a very polite country of Antarctica. Beneath the needlework, water had creeped under the paint in a way that made the wall look like it had been breathing.

I picked up a jar.

The label had been applied neatly, of course. She had never learned to be messy on paper. CABBAGE—JUNE 2022 in a neat stairstep of letters, a little flourish on the 2, the same little flourish she used to end her signature on checks. The jar was cloudy and inside the cabbage had gone vague and pale. Up close it was worse—the rot and vinegar had made a new thing together, a sweet, chemical musk. Something in it was alive. Something in it was dying. I turned it and turned it again, seeing my own face through the shifted glass, the warping making my mouth oval, the way a child draws mouths.

The last time I had been in the house had been in July, the day before I took a job in Reykjavik cataloging speech accents in Northern immigrants and my grandmother told me in English that she was happy for me, and then in Korean that she wished I would stop running. I understood about one in four words. I understood the tone, which rose in the middle of a sentence and then fell as if down a long, gentle slope. That was how she wished you would love something: slowly, inexorably, without hurry.

I set the jar down. It left a dry circle on the piano’s finals and in the circle a few flecks of plaster had settled. The mushrooms between the keys trembled again, just slightly. It was the air, I told myself—the way I had come in and changed it. The house was a body. We had known that all along. It inhaled and exhaled. It had a liver. Its bones had been wounded. The river had mistook it for a thing that it could take. It had been right, for a while.

The floorboards in the hall were the worst: heaved up in the middle, there was a ratio there, the calculus of long slow damage. I stepped where I remembered the nail heads were less likely to be proud. My grandmother’s bedroom door was ajar, and beyond it the quilt I had pieced with her—crooked squares of my father’s shirts, a floral pattern she had bartered for, a swatch from a dress I had loved until it loved me back to threads—was tumbled to the floor. Her orchid, a station at the window that had always faced east, had gone, pot tipped, its roots like fingers lifted in surprise. In the closet, things had fallen in an order that felt like a decision: cardigan on cardigan, the good coat we’d taken to my aunt’s funeral in a blue plastic bag that had held bread at some point, a vacuum-sealed pack of seaweed noodles that had floated up onto the shoe rack and lodged there as if shy, bright.

Her nightstand held its small and unsurprising altarpiece: a photo of my mother and me on the dock the summer of the barnacles, my mother’s dark hair pulled back, my head tilted as if I were physically trying to take her in, the way you tilt a glass at the tap. The rosary the woman from the Catholic church had given her in March, shiny like new spoons. A jar of tiger balm with the lid on crooked. A book on wild mushrooms with notes in the margins in pencil, the neat stairstep again, her guess of Latin names, her confidence tender and rationed.

It was the book that made my mouth go wet with tears. How many hours had we spent at the edge of wet places, her pointing with a stick—never a finger—saying the same thing she had said since I was a child: We look with respect. We look with care. We never take the first one we see, because it might be a guardian, it might be lonely. When I had been eight, and then twelve, and then twenty-two and smug, I had resisted the idea of mushrooms as anything except something to name and not eat too many of. Now, with the river’s work around me, the remark about the first one seemed less silly than spare. All those old meanings, laid up like jars on a shelf. You bring your own hunger to the shelf. You pick.

The county tag lay on the kitchen table, half stained. This was the part they didn’t put in the forms: when you mark a box, you are describing a body to a doctor who will never touch it. Habitable. Uninhabitable. I filled in NAME in block letters because they made me feel brace-faced and twelve: JUNE SEO. ADDRESS, though a kind of joke, because the street sign had been twisted and then removed altogether: 187 Seal Cove Road. ESTIMATED DAMAGE: there was a drag box with insufficient room to write: all we are handed and all we keep. I wrote what they wanted: structure compromised, mold visible, floorboards warped, wall swelling. It all turned into a squint of letters in the end. The form gave me an option to declare if I intended to rebuild. I left that blank. I drew the tip of the Sharpie gently over the cap of a shiitake jar. If I told a different story, I thought—if I said the house wasn’t a place but a body, and the river had not damaged it but had spoken through it as through a throat, would anyone give me money for a new foundation?

On the second day, Orlando came by with a sump pump and his oldest daughter. “I can give you two hours,” he said, and he was already halfway inside, which I loved him for. We had shared a fence our whole childhood and a science fair ribbon one sixth-grade spring. His daughter, who wore earbuds and a sweatshirt with flames licking up its sleeves, offered me a box of granola bars as if it were a hot potato she hoped I’d fumble.

“I’ll get the crawlspace,” Orlando said, and he stripped to a tank and old basketball shorts and I watched him uncoil the orange hose like a line used to lay out a story. “The rest of these houses,” he said, prying a cover off with a screwdriver and a gentleness that made me want to cry again, “they’re all calling the same number. Nobody answers.”

“Thank you,” I said. He knew my grandmother had fed him noodles on nights his mother worked late and his father stayed until closing. He knew the old culvert on Seal Cove Road sat higher than it used to, and the new culvert, expensive and shiny, had been installed too late and too small. He knew the taste of our water. When he sat back on his heels and a smell of the crawlspace rose up—cold, loamy, vaguely mineral—he said, “Oh,” softly, a person who used words with caution.

“You smell that?” he said without looking at me.

“What is it?”

“Earth,” he said. “But different. Like a garden down there hired a violinist.”

We ran the pump until the river that had made itself comfortable under the house was forced to relocate. When the pump sputtered and sucked air and protest, we turned it off and blew on the motor as if it were a child. Orlando’s daughter took a picture of the mushrooms and barely smiled and then took two more.

“Don’t post,” he said to her without turning.

She rolled her eyes. “I don’t post,” she said. To me: “I could draw them. For school.” Her voice was carefully bored. Her sweatshirt’s flames licked.

“Bring over some paper,” I said. “I’ll pay in kimchi.”

She looked at the bobbing jars. “No offense,” she said. “Pass.”

They left a plastic tarp, a stack of towels, a bag of rice. “We’re staying at my sister’s,” Orlando said at the door. “Call if you need a couch and a place that doesn’t smell like... like this.”

“Like a violinist,” I said.

He grinned as if we had reached a difficult answer. “Exactly.”

That night I slept in my grandmother’s room on a camp mattress that smelled like my aunt’s garage. The rain wrote its long essay against the roof, and every so often a tree threw a handful of it into a different rhythm. The pump had done its work; the sound of the house changed. It was a relief that made me giddy and then nervous, as if a fever had broken and now we were in new peril. I dreamed what the house had always let me dream: I was in a forest where the trees grew in pairs and you could tell from the way one lifted its leaves how the other had slept. In the dream, I had two tongues. One spoke easily and one spoke with tiny clutchings, like a hand finding a pocket in a coat it did not own.

I woke in the hour that belongs to bowls. My throat felt lined with mown grass. I lay there with the camp mattress’s plastic seams pressing into the backs of my knees and tried to hear what the house was doing. Houses at night have protocols; anyone who has ever loved one will tell you so. I wanted to hear the old ones, the ones from before the river had made its amendments. Instead there was a noise that was a texture, a sound that you wanted to see. It raised the hair on my forearms in a way that was both fear and recognition.

When I was thirteen, my grandmother had fallen asleep on the couch while watching an old drama, a tidy woman on the screen crying in a kitchen where all the jars matched. I had wanted to go out with Orlando and Laura to the abandoned cannery, where there was an elevator shaft that made you think of all the ways we had hoped to move upward and the walls etched with declarations left by bored boys we knew. Instead, I had hung back. The house made a sound I didn’t know, a small whistling at the baseboards. I laid my ear to the floor. The house answered.
