I pressed the air return gently and the whistling ceased. I lifted my hand and it began again. It had been like learning the piano when I was seven and finding out the keys were heavy and then light, depending. My grandmother had woken and I had told her it was singing. Eh—she’d said, a sound that means a dozen different things depending on how you pinch it. Maybe the house is lonely for the dirt, she’d said, and then she had laughed at herself and sent me to wash rice.

That same feel came back now, that sense of a thing that was not language answering a call that was also not, strictly, a word. I padded to the hallway. The floor was cool. I pressed my palm flat to the boards. I felt nothing but the residual warmth of my own body, the memory of pressure.

And then: the smallest vibration pressed back against my hand, a pulse like the ones nurses count and pretend not to worry over. It was not rhythmic; it came in three and then five and then two, irregular, as if the house were learning the sentence lengths we love.

Ridiculous, I thought. And then that other word people use when their mouths go dry and they remember to kneel somewhere: listen.

I went to the kitchen and opened the drawer with the towels. I still had my grandmother’s old headlamp in there, the elastic stretched out and permanently smelling faintly of fuel. When I crouched by the floor vent and lifted it, the smell rose up at me: the dark clean of unpainted wood. And underneath that, something mushrooms smell like only if they have been actively thinking. I told myself I would not say that word. Thinking. I told myself the flood had seeded the crawlspace and I would find what any person would find: a net of mycelium doing the ancient job of undoing. The headlamp made a tunnel out of my gaze.

In that tunnel, the beams that held up my grandmother’s house had been rimmed in a fine white frill, as if stitched with a skirt. Enough water had been driven down there to swell the underbelly of the house and then, when we pumped it out, there was a coolness like a drink poured and saved for later. In and around the seams where wood met wood, the white had gone thick, as if it had exhaled and was not embarrassed to be known. Across the dirt, lines ran with a purpose I recognized without understanding, as if the floor of a city were revealed and traffic was suddenly light and visible. Threads met threads. Some threads braided and then untied. There were small outcroppings where the threads thickened into nodes. On one of these, water had gathered, a held breath.

I put my hand on the frame of the vent and the house pressed back into my palm: three small, separate pulses, a shy consonant. It seemed less like a machine than like a met. Not any one I could name: not a heartbeat, not a distant walking, not a train I couldn’t see because fog had made itself lord of the town for the night. I held my breath to see if the pulses were something my body was inventing to put reason into the dark. My breath made a shallow sound. The pulses went on, unrelated to me.

The first word came the way all first words do: wrong—both in tone and in context—wrong enough that you struggle because you are already in love with the idea that someone wants to talk to you.

“Joon.”

The sound was little, stitched together out of the whistle of the air in the vent and the distant hum of the refrigerator and something I will not pretend I knew the name of. I jerked back and hit my head on the cabinet hard enough to see a damp confetti of sparklers.

My grandmother’s voice in my head was three-limbed. It existed from three different times in her life, and when she said my name, each limb carried a weight. In the first, she was thirty-four and in a kitchen in Tacoma where the sink coughed every eight minutes and she wore a sweater with a hole she would never fix. She had kept my mother and me alive with the same care she had thrown rice into water: practical, precise. In that voice, my name had been a thing you called a person you had decided would live. In the second, she was in this kitchen, in this house, and there were small jars lined up and the piano going out of tune more aggressively each year, and in that voice my name was a tool. Joon! Hand me the salt. Joon! Stop. Joon. Again. In the last, she was two years from absolute forgetting, and she sang my name more than spoke it, a way to keep the chain bright: Joon—ah—where are—yes.

The sound that came from the vent belonged to none of these fully. It had a chastened quality. It was like a child holding a heavy object and trying not to drop it. I lay on my stomach on the kitchen floor and put my mouth close to the gap the vent had left. The headlamp made light pool on the edges of my cheekbones. Everything in the house smelled carefuller than it had a few hours ago. The floorboards were cold. Water moved somewhere polite.

“Halmeoni?” I said. The kitchen’s night noises leapt to attention. A drip developed somewhere, having found courage at the sound of my voice. One of the jars burped and then regretted it. Something—a mouse? my grandfather’s watch springing itself loose?—shifted in the wall with a small gut cough.

Down in the chill belly of the house, something gathered itself. I felt, not hand but impulse, like the sense you get that someone who does not wish to wake you has stepped into your room. The threads in the dirt gleamed a fraction brighter, which was ridiculous because the headlamp could not have altered itself. I did not move my head. I did not blink. I waited because sometimes the waiting itself is a kind of speaking.

“Joon,” the house said again, and this time the vowels slid together with more confidence, a river rounding off stones into shapes that fit a hand.

I did not cry. That was the first generosity. The second was that I said something a person would say from the other side of a door.

“I’m here,” I said. “I’m here.”

In the morning I would find the note she had written on the back of an envelope in the desk by the piano—a list: call Orlando about gutters; buy more salt; don’t forget the starter; June coming? In the morning, I would walk outside and look at the cedars, their feet black at the base, as if they had been walking in their sleep and had wandered into ink. I would see the county truck on the next street tagging the Johnsons’ porch with orange like a wound on the skin of the town. I would look at the legal pad and write a word in the blank. Rebuild. I would pretend for a few minutes that rebuild only ever meant wood. In the morning, the town council—three of whom had eaten kimchi at my grandmother’s table and gone home to find it a little too spicy and later asked her again for the recipe—would call for a meeting: federal money, a developer, a wall we could build to keep the river in its place. And Lisa from the library, with her hair in the same braid she had worn since she was nineteen, would tell me that the university had put out a call for research on bioremediation, and would I, with my degrees in languages I never used for asking anyone anything, know anyone who might know anyone.

All that waited.

On the cold floor of the kitchen, my cheek to the boards that had held my grandmother’s footsteps longer than the dirt would, I listened to the house remember how to say my name. The mycelium made a gentleness out of ruin. It spoke the only way anything ever does, with what is at hand. In the walls, the nails compacted their rust and said nothing. The river shifted where it had lodged itself in the yard. The mushrooms on the piano lifted their precise heads as if to yield the note.

I thought I could feel my grandmother’s hand on the back of my head, fingers as gnarled as driftwood, tender as the way you pick up an egg you are not sure is boiled. You come back, she had told me on the phone in July, before the river, before the slow undoing. Promise me you come back.

I had not promised. I had told her I would call on Sundays. I had told her and told her.

“Say it again,” I said to the belly of the house, into the damp and the insistent earth. “Say it one more time.”

And the house, in its new careful language, did.

On the morning the river changed its mind, the first thing it returned was a blue shoe.

It drifted past the rusting bollards and the vandalized kilometer marker like a small hesitant creature, toe pointed upstream, laces trailing in the water like whiskers. A man with a paper bag under his arm leaned out over the quay and tried to catch it, and the crowd breathed as one when the shoe slipped just beyond his fingers and continued, stubbornly, against the current that should not have been. A cyclist rang his bell as if the river might step aside for him. Someone laughed, startled and high.

By the time I arrived, the blue shoe had already passed the ferry stairs, had already been remarked upon by three separate women who had once owned a blue shoe and were relieved, and then unsettled by that relief, to discover it was not theirs. The quay smelled like bent coins. The Admiralty clock-tower, which had run ten minutes slow for as long as I could remember, was wrong in a new way: it had stopped, as if time itself had stumbled on this reversal.

“I told you,” Mr. Uspenski from the fireworks shop said without greeting, startling me. He was perched on the rail like a boy, his trousers rucked up around his stick-white ankles. He and I had an arrangement: I would buy sparklers from him on my birthday and he would tell me stories that were almost, but not quite, memories. “I told you the river was all appetite. I told you one day it would be full.”

“Full of shoes?” I said, trying for a laugh. He grinned and shook his head like a dog coming out of water. The paper bag beneath his arm let off the sour-sweet smell of pears.

It was the color of it that startled me most, not the direction. The water had taken on a metallic clarity, like tin was dissolving under the surface. The scum that usually collected at the bend had been swept backwards, leaving the pebbled shallows visible, the old coins glinting among them like fish scales. What you hide in a river is not the same as what you hide in a drawer. I felt that in my teeth.

“I thought you’d be at work,” he said, meaning the map room.

“I thought the river would be at work,” I said, and that made both of us look at it again, as if it were a pet we had shared.

At the Imperial Cartographic Services we never used the word “work” in relation to the river. We said “motion.” We said “behavior.” We said “tendencies” and “volition” only after a drink. My job — the clean part of it — was to repair old maps. I sat beneath the skylight on the fourth floor and lifted pasts off paper with a thin blade, coaxing latitude lines out of glue, softening signatures with steam. I can tell you the smell of prewar starch the way a perfumer could tell you bergamot. I know where the apprentices used flour when money ran out and what lakes were invented to satisfy a rumor.

The other part of my job was private. It began with an incorrect atlas when I was eleven. A printing error had sent a river through a mountain. On the page it looked like a miracle — the thin blue line threading itself where no line could be. When I showed it to my mother she didn’t laugh or correct me, she tapped the mountain with her nail and said, “Wouldn’t that be something.” There was a hunger in her voice. I have spent my adult life collecting maps with errors in them. I keep them rolled in the bottom drawer of my desk, beneath the scratch paper and the jar of oxidized pins, and sometimes between binding and paste I feel that same hunger work its way up to my mouth, and I need to bite something.

The blue shoe went on ahead. The rumor went faster than the shoe.

By ten-thirty the quays were crowded. The Pioneer’s Union had dragged out a banner that said WATER DOES NOT BELONG TO ANYONE LIKE A CAT, which I suspected was a mistranslation but could not argue with. The ferry, moored and sulking, creaked at its tethers. I could hear the brayed orders of men who had suddenly discovered authority in themselves. A baby started to cry and someone shushed it in five different languages. A tea vendor did brisk business and refused to add sugar unless pressed.

Ayo found me by the stairs. He had the same cautious gait he’d had since we were twelve, all knees and careful angles, as if the world were an instrument you could knock out of tune if you weren’t gentle with it.

“You’re here,” he said. “They said you’d be here.”

“I thought you’d be on a boat,” I said, nodding at the water. He worked for the hydrology division now, though when we were in school we were going to be everything together: paleontologists, guerrilla journalists, two-thirds of a band. Ayo touched the rail with the back of his fingers as if to ask permission of it.

“The boats are all upside down in the captain’s heads,” he said. “Half the drivers refuse to take them out. The other half are waiting for a decree. Everyone is practicing being reasonable. You know what that sounds like.”

I did. I had grown up with that sound in my kitchen, postures set like porcelain, a cooling of voices around the most heated thing. My mother had the kind of quiet that could be used like a knife. The last morning she was home had sounded like that — kettle, heartbeat, breath held around a piece of news too sharp to swallow. She had embroidered a list of everything that had ever been lost in our city on the back of a pillowcase, and when the laundrywomen refused to wash it she soaked it herself in the river, wringing it out carefully above the darkest current. “For luck,” she said. “For remembrance,” she said, and those were the same thing to her.

“Do you remember the story she used to tell us?” Ayo asked now, and it was as if he’d taken the thread from my mouth. “About the river knowing names.”

“I remember,” I said, though I wanted him to tell it again.

“She said if you threw your name into the river it would carry it to the sea and back to you with all the other names it had met on the way.” He grinned with one side of his mouth, the way he had when we were boys eating fruit in the sun until we were sick. “I said that was why names were heavy sometimes. All the other names clinging to them.”

“That’s not why,” I said. “But it’s not bad.”

He nodded toward the water. “This one has got tired of carrying them downhill. It wants to see where people keep their umbrellas.”

As if to prove his point, a black umbrella came tilting on the currents, spokes catching the light, skeletal and cheerful. A woman threw out a hook on a string and reeled it in to applause. She opened it and it let itself be opened, a wide and improbable flower. It had a single word stenciled on one panel: SORRY.

“They think it’s a prank,” Ayo said, squinting. He had his official badge pinned crooked to his shirt as if he had done it left-handed in the dark. “They think we can’t do this by ourselves, so someone with machinery behind him is turning the river like a key.” He looked past me to the clock tower that had stopped. “Or they think it’s the beginning.”

“Of what?”

He shrugged, and all around us people practiced being reasonable.

By noon the river had given back three tires, a jar of pickles, a stack of damp newspapers from 1978, four plastic bags with infant clothes folded inside them, a small suitcase of letters tied with string, and twenty-three fish that were not ours, bright and panicked and stupid with travel. The fish threw themselves into shadows, into hands. Children chased them as if they were balloons. Someone stepped on one and cried the way only a person who had never killed something by accident could cry — a shocked, hurt noise, as if the world had committed the injury.

On the bridge, city officials in their hard hats pretended not to be delighted to be on television. A minister made an announcement in the middle of the bridge that no one could hear. The pigeons, who have never believed in us, sat it out with their heads tucked under their wings.

Two men brought a wooden door out of the water like coffin-bearers. It had a circle of glass set into it, and I saw my own face ringed in salt.

When the call came from Cartographic, my phone vibrated muted, urgent, then muted again. I let it do that three times before I answered. I was still in the habit of ignoring it on difficult days, or perhaps I was letting it feed me. There is a cold power in neglecting a summons.

“Mara?” said the director. His voice had the taped-together quality it got when he was shouting and whispering at the same time. “Are you where you can see the river? Of course you are. Bring yourself here. Bring yourself now. I need you to make a map of this before someone else does.”

“Before who does?”

“This is a rhetorical before.” Paper shuffled. In the background someone found a stapler and achieved something exquisite with it. “We need lines. Do you understand? Lineage. If we give them a shape, they will stop restoring to it their mothers.”

“I’ve been thinking about mothers,” I said, and he made a noise like a stamp.

“Bring your eyes,” he said. “Bring your wrong drawer.”

He hung up on his own finality. Ayo watched me put my phone away.

“You’re going to make a map of this,” he said, not quite asking.

“I’m going to make a map of the river going backwards,” I said, and wished I had a cigarette to say it through, though I didn’t smoke. “I’m going to measure something that refuses to be measured and claim I have done it.”

“It won’t refuse you,” he said. “You smell like the river.”

“I smell like pears,” I said, because of the bag Mr. Uspenski had abandoned on the rail when someone told him his cousin had fainted. I picked the bag up and left it at the base of the bollard, where a sign asked us not to tie boats. There is obedience and there is obedience.

On Brickmaker’s Lane the posters that had been advertising a circus no one could afford to attend had already been replaced by posters with watery metaphors. I watched a trio of young men slap paste over a woman in a glittering blue costume with a headline that said: AQUIFER OF THE SOULS. Their new headline was something about management. I preferred the glittering woman. The city believes good things are vulgar.

By the time I reached the building, our lobby was full of civil servants. People who had never looked at a river except to glide their eyes over the surface of it were exchanging terms like “run-up” and “weir.” The elevator was not to be trusted, so I took the stairs, which smelled like the kind of soup that is made by someone who loves you against her own better judgment.

I have lived long enough in the map room that I can tell when the light has been touched. People move the light without knowing they have done it. Today there were fingerprints on it everywhere. The interns had the special taut faces of the newly excellent. The director stood at the long table with a martingale of rulers looped around his wrist. He held himself like a curtain.

“We must be careful not to produce a talisman,” he said to me in the tone of a man who knows he is going to produce exactly that. He sniffed, always allergic to feeling. “Where have you been. Never mind.”

I shrugged off my coat and let my hands take inventory. I took down a roll of the city from five administrations back, one whose brown dust I loved. I took a pencil soft enough to admit it didn’t know everything. The director started to hover and then realized what a poor idea that would be and drifted away.

“Do we even know where it began?” an intern asked from the copy desk, as if we were discussing a civil war.

“There is no beginning,” someone said.

“There is always a beginning,” I said.

“Toward the sea,” Ayo said from the doorway. “It began toward the sea.”

He had not waited for me by the quay. I thought he had left for one of his meetings to practice reasonableness with other reasonable people. Instead he looked as if the river had sent him here with a stamped address.

“Go,” the director said, throwing an indulgence into his voice like a coin to a performer. “Take her. Take measurements. Take a photograph if someone makes the mistake of being beautiful. Don’t get wet.”

We did not take the elevator. We descended into the brown and woolen heart of the building and came up on the fish-shining river as if it were the end of a tunnel. The first man I saw fell to his knees when he caught a silver thing in his hands, and his face — he had the face of a child. His wife did not like that.

“Where should we begin?” Ayo asked, and I said, with the ease of someone who had rehearsed this so often in her mind that it felt like memory, “At the bend where it threw her.”

“It never threw anyone,” Ayo said quietly, almost as an apology to the water.

“It threw spoons,” I said, and if he smiled at that I did not watch him do it.

My mother loved the river the way other women loved the kinds of men you don’t bring home. She thought it was faithful. She thought it went one way. She thought if you gave it something of yourself it would make more of it and bring it back to you changed and improved, the way a good cook improves broccoli. When she stopped believing any of that she tried to prove herself wrong with her body. She walked out in the early morning with a parcel under her arm and that parcel returned empty at my feet, bumping the quay-pile like a cat, with my mother’s blue sweater snagged on its handle. The sweater had a hole at one elbow where desire had rubbed it thin. Desire rubs everything thin.

We stood now at that bend. The quaygate still rattled as if the wind had been given orders not to open it. The iron posts still smelled like a storm. The hut where the ferry ticket-seller had kept his birds — three budgerigars with names like ancient gods — was gone, sold to pay debts that had the international smell of vodka about them. There was a new man who made cigarettes not quite out of tobacco in the lee of one of the uprights. He had scars arranged like a constellation on one cheek. He was telling anyone who came near that in his village they had caught three aggressors in the act of reversing the stream by hand. He had a face that asked for purchasing and received assent.

Ayo held the tape. I took the angle readings. We could have been amateurs making a shared future. The river slid under us, upstream, flung itself around the bulkheads like a shy animal who cannot help showing how fast it can move when it is watched. When you have loved something with your eyes as long as I have loved this river, you develop a feeling for its spine beneath you. We were learning it again. We were embarrassing ourselves in public with our awe.

At my ankles, a boy from the neighbor’s bakery, Kamil, squatted and watched me mark a point on my paper. He had flour under his fingernails and the serious eyes of someone who had had to lift things that were heavy for a long time.

“Why are you doing that?” he asked.

“So we can say what happened,” I said.

“So you can say this,” he said, and moved his finger upstream.

“Yes,” I said, and was surprised by how pleased he made me.

“What did you lose?” he asked, as if we had already had the other parts of conversation and we were finally where we would have ended up anyway.

“Kitchen knives and my mother,” I said, because you can’t lie to a boy who smells like yeast. “You?”

“An uncle,” he said. “He was only an uncle the way a shirt you like is a shirt,” he added hurriedly, as if he did not want to lie either. “I brought him cigarettes sometimes. He told me I had eyelashes like a horse. He taught me to play cards. When my Auntie found out she slapped his face so he would blush for the first time as an adult. He walked along the quay and did not stop walking.”

“What will you do if the river brings him back?” I asked.

“That depends on whether he is the same,” he said, with the same cramped wisdom all the children in our town develop when their parents spend the groceries on something brighter.

The cigarillo man laughed and the laugh had the clatter of coins in it. “Why would the river bring anyone back?” he said, not looking at us. “We are not worth the effort.”

A man in an orange vest waded out to his thighs and argued with the current. His boots were heavy and the river held him as if he were a word it did not particularly want to use. The laughter spread, an oil-slick on water.

The current jilted the foot of a rope against the quay. A flock of starlings coalesced above the clock tower and turned not as one but as many. Ayo anchored the tape and I marked the distance between ignorance and declaration. You could measure it any number of ways.

“Do you hear that?” he asked suddenly, the left side of his mouth paling.

“What?”

“The chime.”

I listened. It wasn’t until then I realized how loud it had been in my head, the mere fact of reversal, the rattle of people locating each other in it. Beneath that, there was a sound like a bell struck underwater. It was not the clock. It came from the silt and the pilings and old anchors. The sound of water recognizing itself.

“Maybe it always sounded like that and we never listened because it was going away from us,” Ayo said. “Maybe you only hear bells when the procession comes toward you.”

“Maybe,” I said. Kamil had stopped looking at us and was scanning the water with his neck craned, looking not for a shoe or a door but for a person.

If this were a story my mother was telling, this is the moment where she would have paused to look at her hands and then she would have said, “And then.”

And then a boat came around the bend. It was the old kind of boat, the kind we had nearly finished getting rid of, with a keel that remembered wood, that remembered hands that made it. The man who rowed it had the tender, furious face of every ferryman who has ever been press-ganged by circumstance. He was rowing against an upstream current that wanted him. The crowd, God help us, clapped. He did not look left or right. He brought the boat to the ferry stairs that had been contemplating idleness and pinned it there with an unforgiving elbow against wood.

He had three passengers. I will tell you the first two because they mattered: a woman who looked as if she had been peeled, and a boy who carried a broom as if it were a flag. The third passenger had her back to us. She wore a coat that had once been expensive and was now only precise, a coat with a belt that made a promise about her waist and then forced her to keep it.

The boy hopped off the boat with the broom held high and the peeled woman sobbed once — a dry sob, like someone who had practiced – but she still had tears, and I envied her them. The third passenger sat without moving, and it began to feel like an accusation. The ferryman’s jaw moved. He put his hand out for a fare, and with that rude gesture he gave everyone permission to speak. The crowd became a crowd. The woman with the SORRY umbrella held it open as if it could keep back everything.

The boat pitched slightly. The ferryman either changed his mind or his arm grew tired. He flung the passenger’s suitcase onto the stairs and it hit the stone with a lover’s thud. The passenger rose, her coat making a sound like a page turned carefully. Her hair was pinned up in exactly the way a woman pins her hair up when she knows she will have to make a point with it later. She stepped onto the stairs and the water paid her no mind.

It was not my mother. I have to say that. I have to lay it down like a straightedge: it was not my mother. The woman’s hair was darker, the posture younger, more sure of its own small boundaried kingdom. The hand that went to the suitcase was ringless. She looked up and her eyes gathered the quay, took inventory, spent and saved all at once. She did not look at me long enough to see me. If she had been my mother she would have known where to place her gaze in me to make a house.

But.

But her coat was the same color as the sweater that had returned empty in a parcel to my feet — a particular blue that only appears to people who have sat up all night with a sick child. It was the blue people invent to talk about the morning when the tide turns. It was the blue of maps when they have bled their oceans into land.

Kamil tugged my sleeve. The adults were already pushing forward with questions that had no words and no pause, and the ferryman had found his. He planted his oar in the stair as if he were defending his home from invaders. “One at a time!” he shouted, and it was the sound of his own father coming out of his mouth. He looked startled, as if he had discovered a trick with his tongue.

“Where did you come from?” cried the woman with the umbrella that said SORRY, as if she were being brave on behalf of the rest of us.

The ferryman lifted his chin upstream, into the city, toward the part of it where the river threaded itself past the old dye-house and the meat market and the power plant that had turned itself into a school as if ashamed. “There,” he said. “Where else.”

“But why?” someone waded knee-deep in that question. “What is the reason?”

“We have never known what is reason about water,” the ferryman said, his chest heaving. “Do you want me to lie?”

The woman in the precise blue coat stood still on the step with her suitcase, which had no wheels. The peeled woman behind her put a hand to her mouth, only to remove it again quickly — as if she had remembered a rule. The boy with the broom had already darted into the crowd, where he was collecting “raise your hand if your name is…” and turning it into a game.

I stepped toward the steps. I would tell you that I was pushed, and that would be true, but it would not explain it. A gravity was at work that had nothing to do with flesh. I slid my palm along the rail the way I had done when I was twelve and my mother had laughed and told me to stop polishing it with my skin. The iron had the right temperature. The right temperature would be the one I remembered, so perhaps I am not a good judge of heat.

The precise blue coat turned at last. Her face was no one’s. It was what faces are when they have just crossed: a set of decisions temporarily relieved of their obligations. She looked down at the suitcase and something in her softened — something only a person could see. The crowd leaned with me, as if to hear the contents.

The latch gave as if it had been handed to this moment. The suitcase opened and a wet smell rose that made my spine think of basements and my mouth think of coins. Inside, wrapped in river paper, was a doll. The kind with porcelain cheeks that crack if you look at them too hard. The same doll my mother had lost as a girl during a sudden storm in the market when her father had lifted her onto his shoulders to keep her from the press of legs and later she had gone quiet over soup and her mother had loved her less for a week in that complicated way love reduces itself to a budget.

It was only a doll. It was, also, precisely that doll. There are two kinds of knowledge: the kind you would put your tongue under oath for and the kind that would not survive in a court. I stared at the doll in the suitcase and could feel its heft in my childhood hand the way you can remember the weight of somebody else’s pain even if it’s been years since you held it.

“Do you see?” I said, and realized I had pressed a thumbprint into the foolish soft pencil the way a child presses berries into paper for color.

Ayo looked at my face, not at the suitcase, because he is a careful person and because he has learned not to look too directly at the things that undress you. “I see,” he said, and if there was pity in it I was not offended by its flavor. If you do not want pity, stay away from rivers.

The ferryman’s boat knocked hollowly against the stair. The boy with the broom had climbed up on the low wall and was announcing his gift: “Raise your hand if your name is Raisa!” And three women did, and then were ashamed of the coincidence, as if it made them complicit.

A low humming passed along the quay, a sound like electricity failing to decide. People began to say the names of the lost under their breath — as if the river had not heard them the first time, as if you could coax water the way you coax a sleeping child back down to sleep. I thought of the wrong atlas in my bottom drawer, the blue line cutting through the impossible, and for a moment it was not a defect but a permission. Who would stop a river from being its own legend. Who would draw that line.

My phone, which had died of indignation twice, made one last thin noise. The director, of course, and the city and the stooped future that belongs to all of us: we’re waiting. We’re waiting for you to turn this into something that can hang on a wall without making people ill.

A voice came over the loudspeaker attached to the clock tower and declared we should go home, as if you could ask a person to walk away from their right face returning to them. The voice tried again in a different language, and then again in another, and we could all hear the patience widen, crack, widen again. None of us moved. We had married this river in poor times and now it had remembered our vows.

And because there is always a last thing — a coin you did not know was between your fingers until it flashes — Mr. Uspenski came panting down the stairs towards me with pear juice slicking his chin and an expression of someone about to sing very loudly in a quiet room. He thrust something into my hand with a ceremony that shamed the ceremony.

“I found this,” he said. “It seemed like yours.”

It was not mine. It was a brass token from a ferry that no longer ran, stamped with a year that had not happened to me yet. The edges had the rubbed, earnest comfort of prayer. On the back, where you would expect to find the raised relief of a boat, the water, was a map. The river cut through the city the wrong way.

When the river said my name — or the ferryman said it and the water occurred to me at the same moment, and names are a kind of water — it was like someone opening a window in a room where I had learned to breathe stale air and calling to me from the street.

“Mara!” The precise blue coat stood too far away to be honest. She had not looked at my face long enough to own my name. But she knew it, someone had given it to her, or the suitcase had, or the doll. “Mara,” she said again, not question, not command.

I could have moved. I could have stood where I was and let the city break around me. I did what I always do. I made a line. I put my pencil on paper and I drew the path between the place where I was standing and the stairs where she stood. I traced it with my foot. I put one foot on that line.

Later, when people would tell the story of the day the river changed its mind, they would mention the shoe and the fish and the peeled woman and the boy with the broom. Someone would remember the minister choking on his own reasons. Someone would say what a shame about the pigeons never looking up. If they said my name, they would not get it right. That is proper. Names are heavy with all the other names that got wet with them.

That afternoon, which had been on its best behavior until then, leaned forward, and the light — touched by too many fingers — fell toward evening and then lifted, undecided, and then fell, like someone wavering on a bridge. The river carried not away but toward and we learned in the way of citizens and children and survivors to call that forward. I stood very close to the water and did not get wet. I made a map not because it would save any of us but because paper takes ink with more humility than we do.

“Mara,” the woman said once more, and the syllables she sent me were the ones my mother had used when it was late and she had misplaced one of my teeth in a handkerchief and did not want to confess the loss. My body, unasked, believed her.

“Do you know me?” I asked, and in the arches of the bridge the bell sounded again, underwater, a sound like a low warning from an animal that has decided to let you live.

“I know a way,” she said.

On the morning the Equinox Squall went missing, I was polishing the fingerprints off the hailstones we kept for the public. Hail is a bad borrower. It dings roofs and bruises gardens and goes slick with the oils of whoever touched it, even after you’ve stored it properly in felt-lined trays. If you do the job right you can almost see your face in the milky marbles, distorted the way your reflection looks in a rain barrel—cheekbones wavy, hair a dark river. I liked the work. There is an honesty to water when it has forgotten which future it is meant for.

The Larkspur Public Weather Library and Archive occupies what used to be the train depot, a long red brick building with a green tin roof and a clock that never agreed with itself. When the Bureau privatized the sky, they sold off the trains at auction and gave the depot to us in an apology. It was the sort of apology that looks generous if you don’t read the fine print. We got a roof with hieroglyphs of soot in the rafters, a platform where people still come to watch imaginary departures, and a freight room we turned into the freezer for flurries, with a thermostat that sulked if you looked at it.

I opened at seven as I always do, turned the deadbolts that have never been breached by storm or man, threaded the security chain through its choreographed loops, and walked the aisles of jars and cages and carefully labeled drawers. Lemon oil does something to the smell of thunderglass, and it unfrets the breath. I learned that from my mother. She used to rub a cut lemon along the rims of our drinking glasses, then drop them into the pot drawers so they could sing when you opened the cabinet. “Glass likes to be a bell,” she told me. “If you let it.”

The archive hummed. I say that as if it were on purpose. We have the dehumidifiers and the thermostat, the compressors from the cold room, and the occasional impatience of rain pressing its face to the panes. But there is a deeper sound here, like a sleeping animal. It comes from all that is captured and waiting to be needed. A drizzle for a graveside, the kind that makes people put their faces up and say yes of course this is how life goes. A righteous north wind for the county championship when the boys want to feel their jerseys snap and anybody’s grief can be turned into something you yell into. The wedding fog that softens unwanted edges and makes flowers look like they have a secret.

Larkspur was never the kind of town that kept to a single season. We used to take what we were given—long gold summers, then springs that arrived in a rush and dropped their suitcase in the hall, late winters with thin light and a shrug. When sky became commodity, everyone got careful. There were forms. There were the new hierarchies, who you could call when your street needed a thaw, who signed off on breezes for block parties, what counts as an act of God. Some people moved away. Some people took to hoarding small weathers in their basements: a saucer with frost long as eyelashes, a mason jar with two inches of fog you could release on your birthday because it made the candles look like ships. And some of us got jobs we didn’t know we would be good at.

When I applied to be a weather librarian, they asked if I knew how to keep quiet. I said yes. They asked if I could carry more than I thought. I said I had carried my mother’s last thunderstorm down the stairs in my arms because I was nineteen and she didn’t want it to wake my brother. They took me on the spot.

I was working my way down the hailstones when the door opened and Mr. Fenn shuffled in on his impatience. He is one of our regulars. As a young man he used to paint houses in town, all those exacting brushstrokes, whites that could never be too white. Now he lives in the blue house with the roof that peels like a summer foot. He had in his hands a plastic grocery bag that writhed with cold and damp.

“Edda,” he said, in that guilty way people say your name when they are confessing something small, like taking three peppermints or stepping on your newly planted bed of basil. “I’m returning Friday drizzle. A day late. It didn’t want to leave the porch.”

“It rarely does,” I said. “Any seepage?”

He untied the bag as if he were about to release a captured bird. The neat thing about drizzle is that it doesn’t panic when you give it back to its jar. He tipped it in an elegant thin ribbon, his hands steady the way they must have been with a brush, and I screwed on the pewter lid and tilted the glass to make sure everything was sitting where it ought to.

“I think there was a laugh,” he said, looking at his shoes. “A child’s. Just once. When it hit the empty chair. Is that outside of policy?”

His gaze skipped up to mine in quick apology. There are not many parts of the job that break your heart outright, but the places where weather collects what happens around it—an echo, a phrase, a scent—those get me. People don’t mean to give anything away. The atmosphere wears us like a sweater for a while, and then later, someone like me hears the sleeve whisper.

“It’s not unusual,” I said. “We’ll note it.” I took the ledger out from under the counter and wrote: Friday Drizzle, 4 hours, minor laugh.

He nodded with relief, then leaned on the bar for a moment as if there were a beer coming. “Do you think,” he said, “I could put in for the first frost? Next week. I want to do something nice with the garden before it knows.”

“I’ll see what I can do,” I said. “You know we’re low.” It has been a stubborn autumn. The Bureau is thirteen counties over, on the other side of the river where we can’t afford a bridge. They have a way of announcing scarcity that makes the scarce feel inevitable, like saying the moon is simply out of town. Meanwhile, the fish shop on Main posts a sign: out of ice, ask for snow by the handful. The high school homecoming game smelled like copper and dust for days because someone released a stillborn storm in the parking lot and the smell of sky-blood left.

Mr. Fenn held his hat in both hands and turned it like a wheel. “Right,” he said. “Well. If there’s any way. I won’t be here in November.”

He said it in the same simple tone people say the forecast, and I didn’t ask. We learn not to. When he left, I wrote him on the Frost List and underlined his name.

By nine I had fielded a phone call from the elementary school requesting five minutes of breeze for the kindergarteners’ leaf project; a voicemail from a woman in Godfrey who wanted to know if we had anything “less wet than rain”; and a knock from a teenage boy with a kite tucked into his hoodie. He wanted wind. He had that particular teenage boy look in his mouth, as if daring the world to be as good as the expectation he had for it.

“For today?” I asked.

He lifted a shoulder, which I have learned is the genderless sign for I’m not going to mother you into admitting your plans. “I think,” he said, “just ten minutes. It’s not fair, there’s no wind. We’re supposed to fly them in PE but Coach says unless we can make a current out of nothing we’re doing sit-ups.”

“I could give you a small northeast,” I said. “Grainfield speed. It will tug.”

He nodded gravely at the word tug, as if we were discussing the correct amount of salt for soup. I took him into the courtyard to explain the rules in person. You cannot open wind indoors. You have to be away from power lines. You have to say thank you, even if you think nobody is listening. Wind enjoys being appreciated like any other thing, and it behaves better when it is acknowledged.

Inside, my desk phone lit up. The bulb was out so I had to watch the dial pad for the pulse of light. It was the county clerk, who always sounded like he was telling you the punchline of a joke you might not approve of. “You got the request, Edda?” he said.

“Which request?” I had a small pile of neon forms on my blotter; requests leak fluorescence onto your skin the way figs stain your fingers with sweet.

“From Albright. Albright Leisure, Albright Holdings, Albright My Pockets Have Pockets.” He didn’t like Mr. Albright. Most of us didn’t. “They want your Equinox Squall.”

“That is an archive item,” I said, the way we are trained to say it, with caution and pride. The Equinox Squall of ’99 is one of the few things Larkspur shares across its many versions of itself. It washed the mill’s chimney clean in one hour. It sent the painter’s ladder sliding and the painter laughing as he slid, unhurt. It bent the lake into the shape of a thought. My mother made us take off our shoes and stand barefoot in the hall. “You need to know,” she had said, “what arrives for itself.”

“They say they’ll give a donation that starts with four and ends with zeros,” the clerk said. “The teenagers are baking scones to keep the library lights on, and this yahoo thinks weather is something you garnish with. You could refurbish every dehumidifier, I’m not telling you what to do, I’m just telling you that this is the weather we live in.”

“What would a waterslide park need with an equinox squall?” I asked.

“Atmosphere,” he said. “So people will say, you remember the time we went on the Helix and the sky spoke. They’ll taste their own teeth. He wants a reputation that feels like risk. People always want what you can’t give back.”

I hung up and went to the vault.

We do not have a vault to impress. Someone once told me that vaults either want to be churches or tombs. Ours is a glorified pantry. We can’t afford the biometric scan that the Bureau uses; our security is a padlock my father replaced every spring. But inside it is another world. The air is older. The floor buckles slightly where the flood licked us two years ago and then had the decency to apologize and leave without taking any books.

Each Archive Item has a glass built for it by my mother—that was her work here, before her last thunderstorm. The glass that holds Hurricane Gentle—the kindness of a storm that (like one man in town) left without breaking anything—swells like a lung and has a spiral seam. The glass that holds the Little No of ’85 is a child’s lunchbox lined with silver; it argues when you open it, and then decides you were right to ask. The Equinox Squall waited on its middle shelf, wrapped in the quilt of its clouds, the mouth of its vessel sealed with the metal clasp that makes a particular sound when you press down. I stood with my hand on the glass and felt the familiar prickle up my wrist. People think the prickling is electricity, but I think it is a memory trying to get home.

There is a kind of inventory you perform with your body. You learn to feel the heat through your palm that means a storm is persuading itself to be weather instead of being an idea. I closed my eyes and listened for that sound, like a room that has its windows open one inch. Nothing came.

At first I thought I was the problem. My body had been too long with lemon oil and ledgers. I pressed my hand to the other items: the Lunchbox No, the Hurricane Gentle, a jar of April Moths that you were not supposed to jostle. Each answered. I pressed my hand again to the Equinox Squall, and what met me was hollow, the kind of absence that isn’t empty but buffed.

I opened the latch.

There are things you cannot mistake. The smell of ozone bright as copper pennies, and underneath it the iron sweetness of a torn earthworm after rain. The way your face dampens without a single drop landing. The hair on your arms in applause. None of those arrived. Inside, there was a cotton cuff where all the squall had once rested, a white that stubborn people would argue was blue. The cuff was flattened. The label my mother wrote—EQUINOX SQUALL, BLACKBERRY YEAR—tilted in its sleeve where someone had hastened the glass closed without the ritual of aligning tags. There was a small notch on the lip like a toothmark.

For a minute my thinking did not have words in it, only weather. An empty of that size wants to be a shape. I carried the vessel to the long table and set it down where the sunlight makes a road. Then I went to the windows and looked out at Larkspur, as if a missing squall would show itself like a boy with jam on his face.

Main Street was as it always is, sincere and blessed and ridiculous. The fish shop owner’s daughter had opened the door wide to let the smell of heat out, a noble but useless gesture. The yoga studio across the street had put out a sandwich board: Namaste and Stay Dry. A crow took off from the roof of the old movie theater, which shows films on Tuesday if the demo crew is late on Monday. A bus went by, which is to say a man in an old van stopped at the same corners he always stops at and allowed people to treat his vehicle like public infrastructure instead of personal charity. None of it looked like theft.

We have rules for when weather goes missing. They are written down on the same paper we use for card catalogs and on the sticky side of my heart. 1) Check the ledger. 2) Check the obvious hiding places. 3) Make tea. I went to my desk and pulled the ledger to me and let it open to the page where we keep the Archives log. There was my mother’s handwriting, square and ready, on ninety-seven lines. There was mine, smaller, trying to make itself be serious. The most recent entry for the Equinox Squall was seven years ago, when Mrs. Yara’s husband died and she asked for something that had been powerful once so that she could believe power becomes gentler with use. She returned it with a sprig of rosemary under the clasp, which the squall had allowed. It had refused a sprig of rosemary from anyone else before, and will again, because weather likes personality to be even across conditions.

Nobody after that. There was no form for request from Albright. The margins were ordinary. I licked my thumb and turned back a month just to be sure. The ledger tasted like dust and cherry because the woman who made them chews gum when she binds and it gets into the glue.

Tea. We do not keep fancy tea, but the act of making it tells your mind what to do with itself when it can’t fix what is wrong. I set the kettle on the hot plate, and that’s when the phone rang again, not the desk phone but the red one in the corner inside the wooden hood that used to be the conductor’s call. The red phone is not for the public. It rings when the Bureau decides to remember we exist.

“Larkspur Public Weather,” I said, and put the smile into my voice because there is no sense handing your enemies a storm.

“We have a discrepancy,” said a woman in a tone that had been steam-ironed. “You are currently two units of wind above winter allowance.”

“We haven’t logged any wind since the pumpkin festival,” I said.

“Then you are using it without telling us,” she said. Paper sounds traveled down the line like the sounds of winter coats in a hallway. “Or someone is using it for you.”

“You’ll have to take it away then,” I said, because that is what you say to a woman who irons her voice. “Take away our excess.”

There was a pause. “We can’t retrieve wind already in circulation,” she said, which was the ordinary truth. “But we could reduce your snow.”

“Is there anything we could increase instead?” I asked. “People are raw. Grant us fog.”

“We do not negotiate at retail,” she said, and hung up.

My kettle began its small riot. I poured the hot water over the bag and stood in the steam of it as if that counted. The door opened again and a girl came in, hair wet though her shirt was dry. She had a violin case on her back and the expression of someone who believes in the correct angle of things. “Do you rent silence?” she asked me. “For practice.”

I wanted to say, what a lovely mercy, to offer your house silence, but I said only, “We have hush. It’s not complete.”

“I’ll take it,” she said, as if kindness could be casual. Then she looked past me, toward the vault. She had the gaze children have when they know where grand fires live. “Do you ever take the big ones out?” she asked.

“We don’t,” I said, because the rules are stern here, and because words shape behavior. We is a word that pins you to the world. “Besides, I’m dealing with a missing.”

“Missing weather,” she said, with a respect that did not have fear in it. “Where does it go?”

“That is always the interesting thing about what goes missing,” I said. “It forgets the obvious exits.”

She nodded like a tiny mayor and put her coins on the counter for hush. Her palm smelled like resin and rain at the seam. When she left, a drop of water fell from the sleeve of her jacket onto the floorboards and did not break. It sat there like a glass eye. Some water knows itself better than we do.

By noon the news had moved through the small invisible pulleys that pass it here. A man from the paper came by and leaned on the bar and asked if he could photograph the empty glass, as if it would look instructive. I said no. He took a picture of my hands instead, the lemon oil in the creases. Two high school girls came in and stood with their heads together and whispered loudly and made their whispering obvious so anyone could hear that they thought Mr. Albright’s wife had made a phone call last night to the county clerk and cried, which made the girls harsh in their compassion, the way that particular age is. Mrs. Yara stopped for her noon walk and let her palms sit on the counter for a minute, her wedding ring cool as a moth.

The absence of a squall has weight. Every time the door opened, air didn't exactly rush in, but it adjusted itself with a click, as if the building had changed hands and the windows noticed. I went into the vault three times and stood in front of the empty glass and put my palms out to either side and tried to feel a direction. If a stolen storm is released improperly, it will go to whatever remembers it, the way birds who have never met will find the same sugar tree in a yard that was not there when their great-grandparents were birding. I looked at the route light took across the floor as the day turned, and I thought about Mr. Albright’s construction site on the hill, about water that does not want to become a thrill, about how my mother used to put her ear to the jar and listen to the soft tick, counting the pressure as if she were counting my fever.

On my fourth visit to the vault I noticed it. Not the obvious kind of clue, nothing cinematic. A crisping across the cotton cuff, a subtle yellowing the size of a thumbnail, distinct from any bruise of hand or shadow of age; a stain that smelled, when I lifted the glass, not like anything the squall had ever smelled like, but like pool. Chlorine, the ironed-white of it, the towel smell of a municipal afternoon. The thing that breaks bodies to fit it. A water that forgot river and ocean to become rectangle. The stain kissed the lip of the glass with its ghost.

When I was nineteen and carrying my mother’s last storm down the stairs, she told me a thing I didn’t understand. “The wrong container makes a good thing cruel,” she said through the thunder. “Don’t let anyone confuse weather with ambition.”

I set the glass down and looked up as if the answer would be written on the ceiling in leak marks. The clock argued with itself. Two crows conducted a small fight across the roofline. Down on Main, Mr. Albright’s men in neon orange swung their hammers against a sky that tuned its instrument behind the hills.

My father still keeps a set of locks in a drawer he doesn’t tell anyone about. At night sometimes, when sleeping refuses me, I get into my car and drive to the river and count the buoys that used to warn the ferry and aren’t needed now that the ferry doesn’t run. Water keeps passing even when we choose not to. I thought of those buoys when I picked up the phone and dialed Mr. Albright’s assistant, who would answer in that cheerful way you answer before your life has asked its worst question.

“Albright Leisure,” she said.

“This is the Weather Library,” I said. “Tell your boss if he has something that belongs to us he should bring it home before it remembers the hill and eats his fence. Tell him we know the smell of his water. Tell him it’s not a donation if he breaks it first.”

She made a small polite sound like a light switch, but I had no wish to humiliate either of us further, so I hung up and went to switch the sign on the door from Open to Be Back Soon, which, in Larkspur, is a kind of vow.

I locked the front and lifted the hinge on the side gate to the courtyard, a trick my mother taught me, a hinge that carries a secret weight in its middle so it does not cry out when you do not want it to. Outside the light felt like glass again, hot without mercy, almost white. Under the climbing roses someone had left a child’s galosh. It stood with its opening upward, a little well for orphan rain.

When I was small, my mother taught me to hold my breath under a pot. You invert it over your head and wait for the sound of your own air to change, and in that dome you hear the world truer, the way a house hears wind when every window is shut. Practice, she told me, so that later when the world tries to take your air you will know you have your own. I lifted the pot we keep next to the gate, the one that holds the wandering cat’s early spring, and put it to my ear and listened. In the hush I found it, faint and stubborn: the Equinox Squall’s particular click, that open-one-inch sound, not here, not inside the pot but running parallel to my listening, up the hill toward the machinery of leisure.

I put the pot back over the cat’s hopes. I went inside for my keys. I wiped my hands on the lemon oiled cloth because I didn’t want to carry that scent into what I had to do. I left the tea cooling on the counter. I wrote a note for the front door in my ridiculous square hand: Closed for Retrieval. People said later they liked how that sounded, like a mercy.

On the way out I passed the shelf of hailstones. I touched one that had taken a thumb’s oil and learned my fingerprint. It was cold and clear and mean and honest. It had not asked to be put to use. Neither had I. I locked the door behind me, checked it twice, then a third time, as if doors are the kind of thing that fail by almosts.

As I walked up the hill, the air changed. There was no breeze but the trees told me movement anyway, silver-brushing the underside of their leaves like someone passing a hand over a field of hair. Somewhere the county clerk was moving a pencil the way a man moves a boundary. Somewhere Mr. Fenn was standing in his garden deciding if he had a week or three. Somewhere the teenage boy with the kite was telling his friend that the wind had listened to him and he had believed for a second he deserved that. Before I reached the top I heard it. Not thunder, not rain, not yet. The pre-syllable a storm makes before it names itself, a small legal sound, a sound that says, I am learning the shape of you so I can break you only where you are made to be opened.

The Best First Chapters take a character across some line that looks like a crosswalk until you’ve stepped into it and then it is a river. The equinox is a hinge and a dare. I took my foot and put it down where I would not get it back. My mother always told me that weather is a library too; some people read it for the plot and some for the paragraphs. I would have to remember both.

By the time I reached the gate to the construction site, I could smell the pool. Under it, faint as rosemary, the squall. I squared my shoulders as if there were an ethical way to carry a storm and reached out to unlatch a fence that did not want me. Behind the fence, men in orange shouted to one another about measurements as if numbers had ever saved anyone from water. The hill, my hill, the town’s tender cup of a hill, wore scars of new roads. As I stepped through, the temperature shifted the way a small animal shifts when you pick it up and it decides, for now, to be held.

Across the field, a glass shape glinted in the noon like a secret where sunlight had been cut into pieces. The sound was louder. Somewhere back in the depot, the hush would be weakening under the violin. Somewhere ahead, the wrong container waited, and my hands—my lemon hands, my carrying hands—asked quietly if they knew how to lift the lid.

The morning the river forgot its name, the clocks in my father's shop began to run backward.

At first, I thought it was the light. The shutters threw ribbed shadows across the workbench, and in that dimness the second hand on the brass regulator seemed to hesitate, shiver, then tremble into a new direction, a spider retracing its web. I held the loupe to my eye as I always had when I was a child — out of habit, out of superstition — and watched three seconds un-happen.

Beyond the open door, the Ruelle lay the color of pewter and salt. A fog had settled so early and so thoroughly that the ferry horn sounded like something underwater. There should have been birds. The river always made a sound with the birds: the white noise of gulls, the quick stitch of swallows over the bend. That morning there was only the ferry horn and, beneath it, a low, unplaceable humming that made my fillings ache.

"Do you hear it?" I asked the empty shop, because I’d learned to talk to absence the way my father taught me to talk to gears — softly, with all my breath.

The place smelled the way it had when I was eight: tin oil warming on the radiator, the licorice of old rope, the sour draft from the wharf. The front room was all glass — gone foxy with age along the edges — and shelves of clocks with faces like moons. The back room held the other business, the one that had no sign and never needed one.

Anyone from Gleaves would have told you that my father was two merchants folded into one. He could fix the watch your grandfather forgot to give you, and he could put your unsayable into a jar.

He called them silences. He collected them in clear glass, as if they were preserves. When I was small, he'd take me into the back room and show me the rows upon rows of jars, each with a cotton plug tied with twine, each with an ochre label scribbled in his neat printing: Mrs. Anwar, 2 May — for the news about her son. Petra Lavigne — the night by the quarry. There were rules, the way there are rules for any instrument with teeth. Don't tilt a jar too quickly; the silence will shift and bite. Don't store one near the stove; heat wakes them. Don't give a silence you might later need back.

People from upriver came on market days with wrapped bundles under their arms — a ham, a bunch of late plum, a galvanized bucket of oysters — because my father never took money for the jars. "Money talks," he would say, smiling, "and we are in the business of its opposite." He took barter, and he took vows of secrecy. When he died, the ledger on his desk was full of IOUs written in floury hands: a ream of paper once the pressman’s back healed, a pane of glass cut to fit that uneven window; three winter mornings spent in silence together. He liked to be paid in the same currency he gave.

It had been twelve years since I’d left. The last time I’d stood in this doorway with a valise at my ankles and the taste of the river in my mouth was the night I was nineteen, and I told him the thing that couldn't be jarred. I was not coming back, I said. I said it louder than was necessary, because so little else had been said between us after my mother stepped into the Ruelle in her white dress and never returned. It's funny, the lies people swear not to tell. I was gone for twelve years. And then I came back because the ferry carries grief as well as fish, and there are some businesses they won’t let you sell.

The backward clocks were a new phenomenon. All morning, townspeople had been walking past the shop and slowing to look in without looking at me. That was another Gleaves rule. You do not stare at the grieving. You respect their privacy by seeing right through them. But I'd grown thin enough since the call from the vicar that I could see through myself, too — the joints of my hands like hinges, the burn of the weather under my skin. The fog made everyone ghostly. It eased back like a curtain and then fell again. The ferry horn cried out. And that hum under everything — like the sound an empty jar makes when you blow across its lip.

The bell over the door had been disconnected ages ago, when my father said he preferred to meet interruptions on equal footing. So I heard footsteps first, slow and deliberate, and then the door creaked and Madame Estève came in, bringing a gust of damp that smelled of dockweed.

"You've let the clocks go wild," she said, which is how the old women in Gleaves offered condolences. I remember her as a hawkish shadow at every Sunday market, the keeper of the stall of hair ribbons and candles and small, sharp candies shaped like leaves. Her hair was a sheet of iron, braided and coiled into something like a knot of anchors.

"I'm still finding where he hid the keys," I said. It wasn’t untrue. The clocks were mostly wound by hand, but there always seemed to be a key behind a painting or under a mat that fit a lock you did not expect to have.

She placed an object on my father's counter as one lays down a weapon. It was a glass jar, the kind my father used, and I knew at once what it contained not because of any sound but because of its silence — the way the air seemed to lean in around it. The label on the side was an old one, the paper whittled by the years into translucence. She had brought it wrapped in a towel embroidered with grape leaves. When she unwound it, her fingers trembled.

My name was written there. Not in my father's hand.

For a moment my stomach climbed into my throat in a way that felt exactly like boarding the ferry as a child in high wind, when the planks shivered under my shoes and everything went half-soft. My father had never labeled a jar with my name, and if he had, he would have written it in that steady script I could see in my sleep. This was a different intimacy — crooked letters, crowded.

"Who—" I began.

"Don't say it out loud." Madame Estève raised that hand that had taken my cheeks between her palms when I was sick, her knuckles like stones. "Names wake them. You remember the rules."

I remembered the rules. "Names wake them; heat wakes them; time wakes them," my father used to chant in the back room as if he were lulling. "Do not store them near a clock. Do not open in wind."

"Sit," she said, and I sat on the stool behind the counter because I could not say no to a woman who used to wrap black ribbon around my scraped knees and tie it like a present. She set the jar carefully on the worn wood and pressed her palm flat against the grain beside it. That, too, is how people in Gleaves offered comfort: by placing a hand to a thing and listening to the knock.

"You'll want to know what you are inheriting besides dust," she went on. Her voice had always sounded to me like the river in winter — less water than iron. "Your father, he kept careful ledger of the jars, God rest his clever but infuriating soul." The glance she flicked at the ceiling was an old woman's compromise with faith. "But there are some that will come to you outside of that book. People, they entrust silences to one another, too. We are not a solitary species, no matter how we pretend."

"Who wrote my name?" The question slammed out of me before I could stop it. The jar did not tremble, but the hum under the ferry horn swelled as if the river had heard. Outside, the fog fluoresced, then dimmed. The old woman laid a finger to her lips.

"It's good he did not teach you to be patient," she said. "The patient drown with their eyes open."

"You haven't answered."

She sighed, and for a moment I thought she would refuse entirely to tell me anything, which is her right, which is the right of Gleaves. Then she traced the label with her cracked thumbnail. "The one who wrote your name is not the one who gave you this silence," she said. "The giver is gone — where all such go. The writer is not. He is waiting, as we all are, to see if you will open what is not yours."

"Not mine," I repeated, and there was that ferry again, nosing through fog. The clocks behind me clicked. I could hear them taking the same second twice and eggshelling it on their faces. "Then why my name?"

"Because," she said, and here for the first time her voice softened into something I could not name, "people believe in a certain justice. They believe that silence seeks its own heart, eventually, and that if we cannot carry our own, we carry the ones that rhyme."

She didn't stay long. She received the tea I made, though I could see from her face it was too weak, and she touched the glass with a knuckle as she left as if to see whose bravery would prevail — hers, mine, or the jar’s. The door closed behind her with its old sigh. The room hummed. I picked up the jar and felt the thin-animal heart inside of it tick.

The label was written in blue pencil, the kind schoolchildren use for maps. The "e" in my name had three loops in it, like a treble clef. The twine holding the cotton swell in place had gone a little brittle. It would have been the work of a moment to tug it loose.

On the wall behind the counter hung my father's photograph. The vicar had chosen it for the service because it made him look like a saint of the second order — not flashing gold but working stiff in his sleeves. He was sitting at this desk with his hands folded in his lap as if he had never touched a tool in his life. He hated to be photographed. He used to say that pictures stilled the wrong thing. "I don't want a stillness that won't unstill," he'd tell me. "It makes people lazy. It makes them think they can hold breath forever."

The day my mother walked into the river, he put a jar on the counter without a label and told me not to say her name. I was seven years old. I bent toward the cotton and blew. The jar sang like a bottle. He smacked it away from my mouth so sharply I cried.

After Madame Estève left, I brought the jar into the back room, which felt both smaller and larger than it had when I was a child: smaller because I wore my father's weight, larger because there were many more jars. The shelves stretched in new, slender spans right up to the ceiling, and my father's ladder hung crooked from its pegs. A fly was trapped against the high window, and its small body thunked and thunked again in determined rhythm. On the table lay the green ledger with the black spine. I ran my finger down the columns until I found the last entries my father had made.

4 March — M. Estève: the night in the boathouse. Trade: quince jam, nine jars.

5 March — A. Cressy: the choice. Trade: dredging permit stamped, no fee.

10 March — P. Lavigne: the word he could not say. Trade: month of lulls.

12 March — The river.

In that neat printing, as if the river were a client like any other. I touched the page and felt my hair lift as if I'd stepped onto an escalator. The hum under the town tremored once like laughter or fear. The river had been in this room. Of course it had always been here — in the wood of the shelves, in the silt between the floorboards — but my father had written it down as if he had taken its breath and tucked it away.

The back door opened on the alley where my father used to stand smoking in those seasons when grief pressed sour against his gums and made him reach for one vice or another. He never taught me to smoke; he taught me to wind clocks and to wind myself. The alley smelled of diesel and rosemary. The rosemary bush had broken through its terracotta pot and had spread raw green into the crack by the drain. The cat that people called Nobody was sleeping upright on the overturned crate, one paw hanging like a misremembered word.

I set the jar on the workbench and kneeled to find the box of matches. My father struck a match for every jar he opened and then blew it out. He said the river liked to be told it was night, so it could see better.

But the rules. The rules are how people in a small place pretend they can outrun their fate. The rules were carved into me like letters into a school desk. Do not open a jar that is not yours to carry. Do not open a jar alone. Do not open a jar in wind.

I unstrung one of the workroom windows and pushed it up. The fog pressed its face into the pane like a child. When I put my hand through, the air was damp in a way that felt more like breath than weather. Somewhere down in the fog a motor coughed to life. Over the roofs, the bell of the Saint's church attempted to ring noon and got tangled in its own sound.

I left the jar and took the ledger and the box of matches and walked to the river. That is how decisions are made in Gleaves: in motion, with a book.

The streets in the lower quarter were as I remembered them, except they were not. The earth seemed shifted by a hand. The cobbles were not where my foot expected. A house whose shutters I once kicked with my thin summer sandals had gone; in its place, rebar grew like weed. Near the wharf a new building had risen — squared steel and glass, no patience with the wind, no give. Someone with money had arrived and decided to teach the rage what to do with itself. A board nailed to a fish stall announced in blue paint: Riverfront Redefined! Come see our Vision. The fishmonger had put a sardine on each letter. They had leaned over to look at their names and dried there, astonished.

I passed the ferry house, whose window was blind with condensation, and the man with the red beard who smoked down to the filter looked at me and away. The vicar stood in his wedge of sunlight like a spoon in a jar. "You are going to do something unadvised," he said when I passed, not as an accusation but as a report. He had the kind of eyes that believed they were washed with mercy and were in fact washed with rumor.

"You’ve been reading the ledger again," I said.

He held up both hands. "I have not touched your father's book since the day I prayed over it."

"And did you think prayer would lock it," I asked, "or unlock it?"

"Both," he said. "Always both."

On the Ruelle, the fog parted briefly and then closed again. A fisherman was coiling rope into a pattern so neat it looked printed. The water near the pilings was not moving. The Ruelle was always moving, even when it pretended to rest. It had a way of pretending. But right then it lay with the flatness of a held head. The word for fear rose in my throat in the language my mother sometimes spoke to me when she was tired. The word meant the thing you cannot undo and must do anyway.

There are people who will tell you a river is unnameable. They have not lived beside one. They have not stood on its bank and given it a nickname because the true name felt like a pet name whispered into a collarbone. Our river had always had too many names. The Trench, the Thread, the Ruelle. When it ran wide and slow in summer it was the Lady. In winter when it picked up a taste for iron it was The Knife. When my mother walked into it it was God. The men who made the maps wrote "Ruelle" as if they were leaving a space between buildings. And then one March morning the mouth of it opened and no sound came out. Your tongue can slip on your own name. So can your town's.

I set the ledger on the low wall at the edge of the wharf and laid the unlit match on top like a bookmark. The jar I had brought I did not set down. I held it with both hands as if it were a newborn. I could feel the pressure of it. My father had always said silences, like fish, have weight. That is one way you know they are alive.

"All right," I said to the water that did not ripple. "If you wanted me home, congratulations."

A boy about eleven with a rucksack too big for his shoulders had the gall to snort as he ran by. That was how I knew the town was not dead. The ferry moaned long and low, and the fishermen stopped coiling their neat rope to look upriver, toward the bend where the Ruelle caught its breath. The fog did not move like fog. It moved like intention.

"Idiot season," the fishmonger observed to a man who was not buying the cod.

At the far end of the wharf, a woman in a red wool coat had hung a placard on a stick and planted it between two cleats. No more dredge, the placard read, in letters that had run in the damp. When I was younger, the only people who planted signs in our town were men with titles. Now everyone with a coat thought themselves a title. The woman made eye contact with me because I was holding a jar and therefore looked as if I had already taken a side.

The side I have always taken is the river's. That does not make me noble. It makes me practical. The river is the only thing here with a memory longer than our grudges.

"Well," I said, and the vicar’s "unadvised" rang in my ear. I took the match in my teeth and struck it on the wall. It flared stubborn and then went clean. I blew it out and let the smoke write its quick calligraphy in front of my face. The air changed. Those are the moments we live for, when something fine and thin threads through and we feel ourselves threaded with it.

I did not open the jar.

Instead, I took the ledger and, with the bottom of my shirt, I polished a bit of river grime from the S in Ruelle. I thumbed through pages until I came to 12 March — The river. Below it there was a line my father never wrote before. In his hand again, precise as the tick of a metronome: If unnamed, none of it counts.

Fogs have moods. This one had stepped into the street intending harm and then caught itself in a mirror. It hesitated. The immobility of the Ruelle shifted toward something that could be mistaken for a breath. A strand of eelgrass lifted, considering. A gull that had been perched on a piling, waiting like a debt collector, stretched one wing and returned it to its side.

"Fine," I told the ledger, the river, and myself. "We will do this in order."

I went home by way of the Saint’s church because my feet have their own devotions. The vicar had gone inside to speak to a child about first knowledge. The church smelled of beeswax and damp wood and the stubborn not-quite-sour of old lilies. My father did not believe; he did not disbelieve. He wanted a god who could be timed and wound and given a proper key. He made do with the river. My mother believed in water, which will reveal its own god if you let it drown you.

At the shop, the backward-running regulator had turned itself forward again. On the counter the jar with my name sat with the patience of a cat. I put the ledger beside it and, with a pencil checked from the vicar's bowl, wrote my name where my father would have written it if he'd been the one to label this silence: M. Clouet — the morning the river forgot its name. Trade: to be determined.

If you want to become your father in order to bury him, you can. It is a mantle heavy enough to crush. I did not try it on. I took off my coat and hung it on the back of his chair, which is to say, my chair. The weight of the chair was familiar. I set the jar between my hands and leaned my forehead against the cool glass the way I used to lean my forehead against my mother's temple when she had headaches, while she told me, in that other language, stories with endings that were not guaranteed.

"Not yet," I told it. "Not until I know how to ask."

There is a way to open a jar in this town so that the silence slips out and stands as tall as a person and makes itself visible like a fog that has decided to take on a face.
