There is a way to open a jar so that the silence becomes a node of heat and burns the inside of your chest a little, making room for something you didn't admit was still alive. There is a way to refuse a silence and send it back into the river the way we send ashes from the wharf, with bread tied into the cording and a coin in the mouth.

How do you open a jar with your name that does not hold you.

That was the question that would take me, before the end of anything, to the dredger's yard with a rope around my waist and a case of matches and a debt I did not know I owed. That would put the vicar’s finger in a book where no finger had been allowed before. That would teach me to call the river by the name it had been trying to speak with its mouths of silt for longer than we had measured time. There is a very old practice in our town of inviting trouble in and giving it a chair. I have never been good at otherwise.

Before evening, a boy came with news.

He was small enough that the bell I'd left silent would have rung for him anyway because his body was all bones and echo. He had sandy hair and a ear too big for the other, the way children’s parts grow on their own schedules. He put both hands on the counter and panted and then remembered his manners and removed one, wiped it on his shorts, and put the other back.

"You Anaïs?" he asked, and then, seeing me see his mistake, winced. "Mireille. Sorry. Your father called you Anaïs when he talked to the cat."

I didn't correct him. I loved my father's incorrectnesses the way one loves a person's scar. "What is it?"

"They said," he reported, eyes big with the importance of the saying, "a man came into the ferry house and forgot where he was going. He handed the ferryman a jar. He said to give it to you if the river made no sound. That is what he said. And then he went back up the hill and then back down the hill and then back up again, like a tide. And then he took the road that doesn't exist."

"The—" The word slid in my mouth. There had always been a path behind the Saint's church that went nowhere and everywhere. Children took it and returned with nettle welts and a changed expression. "What was the man's name?"

The boy looked at me like a cat who has seen both mice. "You know I'm not to say."

"Of course," I said, because I had asked a child to break the rule I had been polished with. "What did he look like?"

"Like a man," the boy said, seriously, which is the funniest way anyone has ever described my father.

When I handed him a sweet from the bowl — they were the citrus ones shaped like wedges, hard as fates — he took two and put one back and then changed his mind and took the one back again. He left with the jar pressed to his chest, the one from the ferry house, and I realized he had not come for me at all but for the jar itself. The jar had sent him. That is what you learn, if you live long enough in a place that is seldom quiet. You are not always the carrier. Sometimes you are the carried.

When the fog lifted at last, it did not go away. It stood at the end of the street and looked back at us as if to memorize what we looked like when we believed ourselves alone. It is a funny kind of fortune to be seen at the moment you think yourself unseen. That is what that day felt like. The river trying to unremember itself; the town trying to recall its rules; a woman trying to decide which way the second hand addressed her.

I closed the shop at dusk and went upstairs to the rooms where my father had stopped living and I had begun to sleep again. They retain a body, the rooms of the dead. His shaving mug sat in its circle of dust. The comb with one missing tooth lay on the windowsill. On the table beside the bed was another jar — he had left it where a man might leave a glass of water in case of thirst. This label was in his hand. M. Clouet — for when the river forgets.

It was smaller than the others, meant for a spirit or a child. The cork had been paraffined. The twine was new.

I took the jar in both hands and pressed my forehead to it and smelled wax and the faintest breath of violets, which is how my mother had smelled when she braided my hair.

"All right," I told the room and the two men I had lost to water, which is cheating because only one had made it all the way into the river. "All right."

If you believe that a first chapter should end with an opening, then you will be disappointed. If you believe it should end with a promise, you will be less so. I set both jars side by side on the table, took off my shoes, and lay back on the bed with my socks still on like a child who has run through ruin and been told it is enough for today.

I listened to the river forget and begin again. I slept with the taste of wax in my mouth. Somewhere beneath me, in the shop, the clocks crept forward and then back as if practicing for a future neither of us had agreed to carry yet. The town turned its face to the fog. The jars did not sing. I dreamed of a woman walking into water, and for the first time she turned around before she submerged and looked at me only. She opened her mouth, and silence poured out — not emptiness but a freshness like the first part of a storm. There is no saying what she said. In Gleaves, we pay attention to what cannot be told as if it were the most expensive thing.

The city hums in three keys in the dry months. Rooftops make one, thin as a coin held to your ear, the sound of heat boiling quietly off tar and grit. House walls make another, rounder, a ceramic note that tastes like chalk on the back of your tongue if you press your teeth against it. And the third is the pipes, always the pipes—bright and secretive like glass, a river in a throat, a flute you were sure was silent until you leaned close enough to be kissed.

I sit on the ledge at the edge of Block Seven with my stethoscope pressed to a cast-iron downspout, sweating through my shirt. The tin beneath my hand has the three-day rasp that means the line is thirsty. Faraway, a trolley grinds and waffles its way along the coast road, and someone below me is frying onion paste in oil. The city smells like that when it’s parched: ghost rain and onion and the brooms’ brooming.

This is how the morning goes. I listen. I sketch the shape of each block’s throat in my ledger with a graphite stub. There’s a tenderness to it. Each building has its own distortion, its dent in the song, the way a hard childhood will make a laugh come out a little sideways forever. Old Settlement has deep bowls of sound from the low-set cisterns. Riverside has hissy lines from sand that found its way in and will never be gotten out. The Port Authority goes like a metronome when the ships are in, and like a batwing when they aren’t. Weddings make a sound I can hear even through stone.

“Code?” calls the rope-mender below from her doorway, without looking up.

“Seven-Kappa-Nineteen,” I call back.

Numbers are safer in a city like this. Numbers are clean to stack and count and lay under your tongue. Numbers pass across stalls and desks and the throats of the police like clean water, which is to say—tightented, tunneled, carrying with it what the Ministry wants it to carry.

The rope-mender’s boy has a tin cup he rolls back and forth so it clinks along the lip of the gutter. He’s been doing it since dawn; a rhythm the pigeons have accepted with the resigned dignity of pigeons everywhere. Children’s play has a sound too. Children have a dozen secret keys, and I haven’t yet learned all of them.

I move along the ridge, three houses to the left, and settle my cup against another length of pipe. I close my eyes because it helps. Appreciable silence gathers. Then it becomes the kind of silence in which anything at all can happen. The trick—the one they couldn’t automate, the reason they keep us—has to do with that moment. The city has its hundred thousand small adulteries; its unauthorized spigots, its rainbag hoarders; its washers who pretend to be laundries in the dark of night. They are my notes in the margins. If I listened like a policewoman, I would fine them. If I listened like a poet, I would go under; the weight of all that water wanting to go where it is not supposed to go would drown me. I try to listen like a decent liar.

This pipe is a little too bright. The cadence suggests a foreign coupling in the third-floor bathroom—a ceramic pot nested into the junction where the Ministry's blue pipe meets the building's black pipe. The sound is thinner where the illegal pot steals a little pressure, like a place in an old song where a child claps one clap too soon. I mark the address and the hour and use the shorthand for quietly harmless: a loop with a tail.

Between us and thirst, a hundred rules. This block is average: twenty-three badges tied to belts, five with worn edges from being touched too often, one cut in half the long way, which always means somebody ran away and somebody is holding the other piece like a promise. An old man sells dumplings made from the dredges of flour that come to the markets once a week under Ministry seal. Water trucks purr and glitter against the notion of relief.

“Hey, Listener,” Auntie Salt says from the corner where she sits selling her salt in little bags twisted shut with a single hair plucked from her own head. She is not anyone’s aunt but it’s what everybody calls her. She quicks her fingers in greeting and makes the sound of a bird with her tongue.

“Hey, Auntie,” I say. She knows my number and also the names people call me when they think I can’t hear them—Pipe Girl, Ear, Quiet-Kappa—that I pretend not to know because pretending is part of how we all live here. She blows salt from a pinch in her palm onto the ground. A blessing against a slip, a spill, a sudden forgetting.

At midday I fold my ledger away and climb down via the drain ladder. By then my whole body is tuned. I can tell you when a kettle begins to wake on a stove three houses away; I can tell you when the wind has brought us the smell of real rain and not pipe-water rain. I can tell you that Block Seven’s big belly women will be sweating heavy by the time the bells call third meal; that one of the longshoremen has peed in his shoes.

The Tracery Office is three streets over from the Old Prison, which we have repurposed into a junior sports complex with a queue for water cans like a parade of silver ghosts. Every morning the Office spits out its printouts with their delicate red lace of anomalies and sends them by boy with knife-paste to stick on certain doors. But the Office also listens through us. We’re the ones who draft made maps on cheap paper with borrowed pencils and our knees under them, and turn what we hear into a speech the city pretends to understand.

The Office is all neatness and cool tile. The ceiling fans make my hair tickle my neck with their breath. The Director, who is called Director and also Old Pike when he isn’t listening, looks up from his desk and saws open a grin with his dry mouth.

“You are late,” he says, which is our old joke. I have never in my life been late to the Office. Time slides for me but never loses its place; I think in rhythm, and the city keeps the beat for me whether I want it to or not.

He taps a ribboned printout. “We got a shout from Bath Lane.”

“Bath Lane always shouts,” I say.

“This isn’t their usual bakers’ nonsense. High frequency, inside a low supply window. We can’t chalk it up to forty girls washing hair at the same time.”

“It’s Wednesday,” I say, because Wednesday is discount hair day in the Old Laundry because the owner—Haja—gambles on boats on Tuesdays.

“Exactly,” Director says happily, because contradiction both pleases and wounds him. He likes puzzles, which is why he never left this job even when his friends all went on to the big water, to the Labs behind the Blue Glass, where there were chances to name things.

They tried to teach us not to want names. They took the old ones away, said that way everybody stood in the same line, drank from the same spout. You know the slogans. They hung banners like skins. Names were how the war began, and names were what the war had eaten. So now when you are born they give you a code and a card and a little bracelet made from a polymer that looks like coconut shell, and if you lose any one of those you are a trouble, and if you use any else you are a danger.

Bath Lane lies down three flights of stairs into a quarter that pretends, even in heat waves, to have a tide. Laundry hung from every balcony slaps like sails; fat bars of soaps like bleached bricks gleam in nets; the alley smells not like onion but like lemon and animal fat, ancient and merry. The buildings there are ninety years old, which is practically primordial in a place that has been rebuilt twelve times in my father’s lifetime alone.

Haja is there, skin loose as a paper bag and hair like a nest of grey eels. “What took you,” she says, because this is how they see you when you are the kind of woman I am. You are always not yet here enough, and what you do cannot possibly be skill because skills are men’s things in a city that has forgotten so much. We are all unfair in our own directions.

“Your lane is singing,” I say. “Haven’t you heard it?”

She snorts, which bounces her whole self up and down once. “We hear money, girl. If there’s a song money is later than it used to be.”

I kneel, not in deference but because the old stone under my knee has its own memory. The floor is stained with a hundred thousand years of soapsud and sweetgrass, footsteps of egg-sellers and boys with charcoals, the bleached calluses of women who came here with their mothers and are old now and bring their own daughters. I set my cup against the junction where the Ministry’s supply meets the old laundry’s overstone basin and still as a heron.

The noise is wrong. No—it is constructed. It isn’t someone stealing a little more pressure to splash their hands. It isn’t someone pressing palms over mouths to laugh in the night. It’s—there, around the eight-second mark, a repeat. The sound loops. A human brain will always put pattern where there isn’t, and I am careful of that, but my skin has the little lift it gets when it hears something assembled. The pipe makes three steps down, two up, and holds.

“Not hair day,” I say, without meaning to, and Haja makes a motion which is for luck and for warding off bureaucrats and for babies who have not yet got a name.

“How bad?” she says very quietly.

“If I wanted to find the source I would go under the stairs,” I say, not answering.

She looks over my head at the corner where four yellow and green shirts—men’s—hang. Small men. The shirts have been washed long enough to become almost weightless.

“There’s been a lot of talk about prayers,” she says, looking no one in the eye.

One must be deliberate with Bath Lane. They will cut the control valve if the police come too fast; they will flood the place with suds and slip ten men away under the cover of unsure feet. The Director would call me back for a raid, a showy one, red capes and warnings out of bullhorns. Everyone would look relieved and go to bed hungrier.

“Give me a minute,” I say. “Fetch me a kettle.”

“You are not tea,” Haja says, and skitters away anyway.

I slide the stethoscope’s cup along the seam where the main line takes a ninety-degree turn. The wall is damp like old bread; the mortar is furry with something that likes damp. The Reverend used to say that the city was wicked and God made it thirsty to scour it clean; that if we had been good people we would not live in a place where brick goes green just by thinking about water. I never liked him, and God never struck me down for that, which is how I measure the kind of God I will tolerate.

In the narrow under-stair space the pipe changes character. It is nearer the skin of the building, and I can hear the rush of footsteps over my head as variations on a theme. It is more intimate here, as if a throat cleared and soft speech were about to come.

Pressure, repeat, rise. I hold my breath, my ear bone pressing the cup so hard it will leave a ring. The kettle clatters as Haja sets it on the outer counter. The boy with the cup from this morning has followed me, his tin now hung around his neck like a hungry medal. He clicks the rim with his fingernail impatiently; it is part of the percussion.

I hear it before I know I hear it. Not language yet, but shape. A glass bead dropping into a wooden bowl. Then the vowel opens, thin and long, as if a door. It slides across the cavity in a way that can only be a deliberate stringing.

A note under the sound like a thumb across the top of a bottle, and then, gently as someone saying it while moving your hair, a syllable inside my head.

Mi—

I jerk away so fast the cup falls and Haja curses because the leather strap goes slap into the wet and picks up the stink. My own voice is somewhere between my chest and throat, unfit for polite company.

“What,” Haja says carefully.

“Someone’s teaching your pipes to talk,” I say, and laugh in the wrong place, because fear and joy are sisters if you look at them slant.

“Talk how, Kappa?” she says. She never uses the K. She calls me Girl or Listener or Nobody; to use my letter is to put a finger on my pulse.

“Like you’d talk to someone you don’t want other people to know you’re talking to,” I say.

She nods, once. The boy with the tin cup watches me the way boys watch snakes—half hoping, half prepared to run.

There are, in the city, many ways to say a thing without saying it. People who love in the wrong direction leave nail marks in doors in certain patterns. Women braid the right color ribbon, or the wrong one, into daughters’ hair. The old men with their morning chess have rocks carved into the pawns’ bellies, and the others with the same disease know the rock and do not say the word for it. You could say it was cleverness; you could say it was cowardice. You could say both and be mostly right.

“Bath Lane will be raided if we flag it,” I say after a second that feels like an hour. I can suddenly hear the thirst of the whole block; the pips of washing machines saving up their water spoon by spoon; the voices of girls off-key singing to soap. “If there are prayers in it, it will be raided twice.”

“That’s not our word,” Haja says, too quickly.

“Prayer?” I say.

“Raid,” she says, and has the gall to grin at me, which is why I like her.

The kettle screams. Haja lifts it with a cloth and pours the water into an old basin, and I watch the steam make fingers. She will use it three times. She does not look at me as she does. She does not have to beg. Neither do I. We too are women with small rebellions we do not name.

At the Office I could translate a slight variance in pitch into a leak rate and a fine. My hand knows the equations like lullabies. But what I heard under Haja’s stairs was not a leak. It was a ladder. A set of steps for a sound to climb to become a word.

I walk back. I do not go to the Office. I go the long way, past the sea where the lemon light looks like a lie, past the under-market where three men pretend to argue about shirts while watching for the red hats, up the stairs carved into the hill that used to have a name. I go to my father’s apartment because when I am unsure my feet go there the way a creature goes to ground.

He is at his window with the plant I have repeatedly told him is a weed and which he insists on calling, with heartbreaking obstinacy, a tree. He is humming along with the street. The melody is not one the city is actually making; it is one his head adjusts the world toward.

“You are early,” he says.

“You are sober,” I say.

We do not discuss the other conditions. We do not say, for example, your mother has been dead seventeen years and the bed shows the shape of that every time I make it. Or, the Director sent a boy to find you and you were under the stairs in Bath Lane with your cheek pressed to the pipe because you thought you heard something you did not have the right to hear.

“You will not like that plant any better if you call it a tree,” I say instead, and put the kettle on our little square hob. Our kettle has a voice like an old cat.

“Names change things,” he says, which is the sort of thing he says when he is trying to be clever and to remind me that he was once not only clever but useful, and that the city used to pay him for it.

My father used to be a Namer. He never says it like that. It’s a word you don’t say. But it was his work before they made us all stop. He was the last man in the district to go building to building with a paper map and write, with a pencil that needed sharpening twice a block, the names of places that had been bombed flat. He had the gift of hearing what was still there in the dust when others could not. It is, I know, a kind of sin I am committing, to go to him now with my hunger.

“What was yours?” I say, because we do sometimes, in the shelter of our one room, tempt a god with our foolishness.

He smiles a little and does not answer. He does not have the sound of it anymore. He traded it for me to live, or if not that, then something like it. We have different myths about it. He calls me by my letter when other ears are around. He calls me sweet names he didn’t have with my mother when nobody is. Whatever I was once, in that wet fever night when she whispered me into the curve of his neck and then into mine, is not for the air we have now.

I pour tea. We do not waste milk on anything but children and funerals. The water tastes like sugar bitten too long on the tongue; the desalination plant has been acting up and the Office alerts say there are new minerals in the flow. I don’t mind. I like the bite. It reminds me that the line between sea and cup is thin as a foil around a block of butter.

“Did you know,” my father says, exactly as if we had been talking about this all morning, “that if you put your ear to the heater you can hear the neighbors argue about fruit.”

“I can,” I say. “But that’s because the pipes run under their kitchen. You’re cheating.”

He sips his tea and sighs and finally looks at me properly, the way he does when he has decided he will go down the stairs with me into whatever mess I have brought home. “So,” he says.

“So,” I say, because I am my father’s daughter in that way and several ways I wish I weren’t.

“Are we going to pretend you didn’t bring me the smell of Bath Lane on your shirt?”

I breathe in. Soap and lemon and the iron of old water. “Somebody’s teaching the pipes to speak,” I say. “They’re shaping the pressure into a pattern. It is—” and here I have to stop, because to say it would be to offer the god my throat.

“Go on,” he says.

“It is like a name,” I say. “No. Not like.” I close my eyes, because sometimes you can say a forbidden thing better if you take one of your senses away. I say what the pipe said. I say the one syllable I heard in the under-stairs dark, with the smell of lemon in my nose and the sound of a boy tapping tin like a clock.

“Miren,” I say into our rented room, into the water-worn air. “It said Miren.”

The kettle pops in the quiet as if it had just remembered something crucial. The window slides a little open of its own accord. It is a window that sticks when it’s hot, but it changes its mind under my voice.

My father sets his cup down so precisely the sound it makes is a note on the scale we used to sing before school. His hand has begun to shake in the last year. It doesn’t shake now.

“Say that again,” he says, and I cannot tell if he is asking me or begging me.

I do not. Because I am careful, because I have learned with bones the difference between a thing you want and a thing you should give, even to those you love. I reach for our ledger instead and draw onto a blank page the shape of what I heard under the stairs: the rise, the repeat, the gentle pressure that was not pressure exactly. The line looks like a river if a river could learn to write its own name against the stones.

My father watches my hand, not my face. “You won’t report it,” he says.

“I’ll report a variance,” I say. I can tell you the number for it right now. I could mouth it in my sleep. “I won’t report a word.”

“You’ll go back,” he says.

“Yes,” I say, because some things live in you like a second pulse.

He opens his mouth and closes it. We are a house with two chairs, two cups, one spoon. We are not a house with a Bible or a shrine. His missing word hangs between us like a rain that will not fall.

After he has slept and I have washed our two cups and set them to dry on their sides like ears, I lie on the floor with my cheek to the cracked tile and listen to the building breathing. Above me, the boarding house girls turn in their beds and someone cries out into his pillow. Next to me, the heater coughs. I press my palm flat against the pipe until it warms to my heat, and then the city in its thirty seams comes in like a tide over my skin.

At first there is the noise of evening cooling, the house emptying water like a body in the dark. Then a wash of narrow sounds I know too well, that make the map in my head purl and nip. And then, a minute, two, three—there. The same pressure-ladder. The pause. The careful thumb at the bottle. It rides the building’s throat like a net hung off a boat.

“Miren,” the pipe says, intimate and small. It says it the way you would say it if you had taken care not to say it for ten thousand days and then could not help yourself.

Someone in our city is teaching the pipes to carry a name they never meant to be taught, and it is mine. Or it is my mother’s for me; or it is the one my father never says. Or it is a trap and I am exactly the fish for it. Or it is a prayer and I am, to my horror, who it is for.

On the street, someone’s heel sharp against stone. On the corner, Auntie Salt coughs into her fist and swirls her little plastic bags like charms. On Bath Lane, Haja will be smelling her knuckles of lemon to make herself brave, and the boy will be rolling his tin back and forth across the sill because his body knows time better than his mind. The Tracery Office will be drawing its red lace. The sea will be busy pretending not to want us.

The pipe says my name once more. The third time is always the dangerous one if you grow up in this city. Three is when the gods who don’t exist but do anyway get interested.

The radiator ticks as it cools back into silence. I pull my hand away and put both palms flat on the tiles, the way you would on a stalled animal to reassure it that you know what you are doing. In the morning, I will go back to Bath Lane and I will go under the stairs and I will be slower and I will listen harder, because this is the way I have learned to survive. Between us and thirst, a hundred rules. Between me and the sound I heard, there is now only the night.

Chapter One: The Arithmetic of Water

The island kept its own time, a wet arithmetic of moon and stone. I remembered that much even after ten years on a mainland where the clocks were smooth and electric and did not smell like salt. On Farrow, the hours were measured by the roving shadow under a gull, by the pitch of the rope when the tide went slack, by the small brass hands on the tide-clocks my grandmother tended in her kitchen. The tide-clocks did not count the minutes; they counted the waiting. They told you when the water would lift the skiffs and when it would place them back on their ribs in the mud, when the causeway would drown and when it would show its spine again, and whether you had enough time to cross it if you did not stop to talk. There is an honesty to a clock that counts only what a body can feel.

The ferry ride was short enough you could taste the rain in the spray the entire way, and long enough that the mainland light let go of you and you had to face the island’s. I stood at the rail with my bag between my shoes and watched Farrow lift itself out of the fog like something remembering. The line of black rock. The rag of field with two horses like apostrophes. The houses close to the harbor, their shingles silvered like fish scales. And above the roofs, above the dock where Bowline Joe always pretended he’d never seen you before, the mast of my grandmother’s windvane with a tin bird that turned in no wind at all.

Nell Farrow died in her chair in the kitchen, halfway between low and high tide. That was what my cousin Dory had written in the message she sent me with a picture of the tide-clock above the stove, its hand exactly on the cusp of flood. She was wearing her rubber boots when she went. The chair was the blue one with a crack through the back that made your spine buzz if you leaned wrong. On the ferry, I tried to remember the last thing I had said to her, but all I could call up was the sound of my mainland life: the bright chat of the espresso machine at the transit station, the artificial birdsong piped into the lobby of the finance firm where I had helped run the city’s quiet numbers. I could not think of a single question I’d asked my grandmother that wasn’t answered by a shrug across a long distance, a voice that worked like a weather report: wind light and variable, fog beyond the bell.

“I didn’t think you’d actually come,” Dory said when she met me on the dock. She had her hair in the same red handkerchief she used to use to tie up the flopping mouths of the fish her father brought in, and on her left wrist the tattoo of the rope we had given each other when we were eleven. The rope had faded into the under-skin color of belonging.

“You asked,” I said. “You said she left me—”

“Left you what she always said she would leave you if you ever stopped pretending you weren’t made of water,” Dory said. She looked at me, at the long black coat I put on when I wanted to armor myself against the old places, and she smiled with the sad tilt of the island pull in it. “That coat won’t stop the damp.”

“This was all the dry I could bring,” I said.

Behind her the dock was the same and not the same. The gull that used to hop on a single foot because the other had been lost to a rope was gone, but the young men sitting on the bait barrels had the same knot-sharp faces as their fathers, and the old woman who sold butter and pomegranate tea from the back of a truck was the daughter of the old woman who had sold egg sandwiches and coffee with grounds thick enough you could read them afterward, if you had the stomach for it. The ferryman, who had refused to let us ride free unless we promised to sing him a song when we were little, wore a black band of cloth around his arm now, and when he saw me he lifted his chin in greeting and then hawked a rope of seawater off the deck. The island does not say I missed you. It says Here is work; here are your hands.

“You’ll stay with me, you hear?” Dory said. She took my bag before I could stop her. “At least until the spring tide. You know how it is. The funeral has to keep to the water.”

“I booked the noon ferry back on Monday,” I said, lying in the way you lie to someone you know will call you on it, the way that builds you a tiny raft just in case.

“You can unbook as easy as you booked,” she said. “There’s no ferry back in thick fog. Or in a wrong tide.”

“Is it wrong?” I asked. It was an old habit between us, to call any complication wrong-tide.

Dory’s mouth did its island tilt again. “You’ll see.”

We walked the length of the harbor road with my bag knocking against Dory’s thigh. Two small boys ran past us carrying a net strung with seaweed as if it were a captured constellation. A man with hands like a pair of barnacles nodded at us from the door of the bait shop. An orange cat sat in the window of Mrs. Sketty’s old house and licked the salt out from between its toes as if it had more sense than anyone else. The wind had the soft tongue of a south wind on it, and the air was somewhere between rain and not-rain, the way Farrow liked to keep itself.

We turned up toward my grandmother’s place, which sat above the harbor like a bird with three wives. The siding needed stain. The steps remembered each foot that had walked them and complained accordingly. There was a new crack through the yard where the ground had settled last winter. The tin bird on the roof vane turned twice and then went still.

Dory pushed open the kitchen door with her hip like she had always done. The kitchen had not changed. The same table with salt in its grooves like old tears, the blue chair with the cracked back, the stove with the tide-clock above it with its small brass hand pointing to the place where the paper had been tacked. In childhood, I thought the clock was simple. Low tide here, high tide there. The moon’s breath. The perfect pendulum of water. But that was mainland thinking: that the sea could be kept on a schedule. Nell Farrow’s clock was not one clock but many gears with names like listening and hush and reckoning. You wound it with a key that was smoothed by her thumb. You did not ask it yes-or-no questions; you asked it the kind that left room for change. What will the water do if the wind shifts south? If the river throws its house down? If the moon is in a kind of mood.

“She kept it going,” Dory said, seeing my eyes go there. “Even last month when she fell with that cold, I found her here at four, winding the hush gear like she was the only one who remembered the island would drown if she didn’t.”

“She always said it would,” I said, remembering my grandmother’s voice, low and calm, the way she could lay a card on the table and all the men in a room would look to her for how to play theirs. “Drown and then spit us up again. She liked the spitting part best.”

“She liked the part where she got to be needed,” Dory said, which was fair and a little unkind and what cousins can do.

“What did she leave me?” I asked. The question sat in the middle of the room like a wet dog.

Dory reached over the stove where the kettle had always sat and pulled down the jar of salt from the shelf. The jar was old, its lid rusty, its glass not perfectly clear so it made the world behind it ripple. She unscrewed the lid and poured the salt into a bowl. In the white cone of it was a small brass key with a thin neck and a top shaped like a captain’s wheel.

“The listening key,” Dory said.

“Listening to what?” I asked. It was a cruel joke because she know I knew. She only smiled and put the key in my palm. It was heavy for its size. Oily, like it had been held by almost every hand on the island at some point. The weight of a thing that had been used rather than loved.

“There’s a letter too,” Dory said. She reached into the jar again and brought out a folded piece of paper that had taken on the salt’s softness. It had my name in my grandmother’s careful black ink across the outside: LUCE. She had always written print like it was a field she had to fence in.

I did not open it. Not then. My hands were not ready. Instead I looked around the kitchen and let the small ghosts have me for a minute. There was the jar of buttons that had belonged to my mother before she left, the blue ones still in a threadbound coil. There was the chipped bowl Nell used to make mustard like a curse. There was the map of the island Nina Roke had drawn when she was thirteen and fancied herself an explorer, the secret places all labeled with names that meant nothing to anyone but us.

“She wants you to wind the listening stones,” Dory said after a while, her voice doing the thing it did when we were children and we had decided to tell the truth even if it got us in trouble. “Before spring tide.”

“Those are just stories,” I said. My mouth said it. My tongue had salt on it. I wanted to be cruel to something and I didn’t want it to be Dory.

“Of course they are,” Dory said. “And also not. You think your grandmother spent all those nights out on the point in the rain to humor the dead?”

“Careful,” I said, the old argument rising. “Careful where you walk with words like that.”

“We’re in the kitchen, Luce,” Dory said. “They know the difference between a cuss and a prayer.”

We were quiet then. The clock above the stove gave a small click as the hush gear let go of the minute. A rope of fog curled under the door and went away again. It was almost funny that Dory was the one telling me to listen. When we were eleven, I had been the one to lean my ear against the listening stones and swear I could hear the slow choir of the drowned, and Dory had kicked at the barnacles with her cracked heel and said I was just hearing my own blood.

I opened the letter. There was no point in dragging it out. Nell’s handwriting came up off the page with all the pressure of the grip she’d always taken on her pen, as if the ink might otherwise try to run away.

Luce,

If you are reading this, I am the kind of gone you can’t bring a pot of soup to. Do not light the stove until you open the windows. The flue never did right after the winter of ’99 and I never made the boys fix it because I liked the way the house remembered its own smoke. The tide will change in seventeen minutes. You always hated how I could say that. You thought it made me god. I am not. If I have taken any of god’s work it is to admit the ways I was wrong and to offer you a job you don’t have to take.

Wind the listening stones before the spring tide. They have gone dull in my fingers. The gear of the hush is stiff. The voices are getting faint like a radio signal nobody holds their breath for anymore. There are things the water took that belong back in the mouths of the living, and if we don’t wind the listening that memory will silt over, and we will forget not only the dead but the reasons we kept the living.

I am not asking you to come back to the island. I know you left for good reasons. I am asking you to do this because you know what water is, even if the city has taught you to eat your lunch at a desk. When you were six and I told you to watch the way the eddies made their little decision trees, you said They’re choosing. You were not wrong. The water is choosing without me now and it is choosing faster. The clocks are confused and I can’t make it right with cussedness anymore. Wind the listening stones. Keep the tide from swallowing the wharf on a wrong Friday. Tell Dory you will stay until the moon is fat and then you can leave and never speak to anyone again, and you can be the mainland woman with good boots and a calendar with a different spice each month. But wind the stones.

The key is in the salt. The other key is in the place you don’t want to look. Don’t be clever with me about that; you will know what I mean when you are standing there. If you get stuck, talk to Joe. He knows more than he lets on. If you are frightened, do not go alone. If you are proud, remember I loved you like a stubborn harbor loves its boats. Wide-eyed and refusing to admit the storm.

It would be wrong to say I am sorry and not say what for. I am sorry for not telling you who your father was. He was a summer storm. He was the first good cherry of the season and then the rot. He was the sound of a coin going through the slots at the carnival and never coming back. You are not him. You are water and you are me and you are whatever you have taught yourself on the other side of the bridge. I should have had the nerve for it. I didn’t. Do not make my cowardice a kind of skeleton you carry around to show people how honest you are. Sometimes history is bone and sometimes it is mollusk.

Wind the listening stones.

Nell

I read it twice because once was not enough to let all the sentences lay down where they were meant to go. After the second time I put the letter on the table and put my hand on it and the paper felt like a warm thing because I had made it that way.

“What are the listening stones?” Dory asked, because she wanted to hear me say it.

“The stones out on Gannet’s Point under the old bell, the ones that go hollow when the tide turns,” I said. “The ones that used to hum when we were little if you laid your ear against them and held your breath and put your tongue to the roof of your mouth like you were tasting the rain.” I had not thought of the bell on the point for years, the way it had a voice whether there was a rope on it or not. Old men used to tell us it was the bell the whales rang when they came to look at us. Old women told us it was the bell the drowned climbed if they wanted to speak to someone obstinate.

“Don’t be clever with me,” Dory said, exactly in her aunt’s voice, and we both laughed, and in the gap of laughter I felt something in the house ease, like a knot you were not aware of loosening.

“What did she mean about the other key?” I asked. My eyes went to the blue chair without my permission.

Dory followed my gaze. “She never told me about it,” she said. “She always called you her second skeleton. I don’t know whether to be insulted or proud.”

“Both,” I said. I took the brass key and threaded it on the ribbon I wore around my neck under my shirt, the one I had forgotten to take off for three years and then decided to pretend was a style. The key was cold and then it was my temperature.

“You hungry?” Dory asked. “If you don’t put something greasy in your stomach, the island will think you hate it.”

“I could hate it for a few hours,” I said.

Dory fried me two eggs in olive oil and we ate them with yesterday’s bread, which was better than most people’s best bread. The salt on the eggs made my eyelids go soft. Dory ate like a person who still had things to lift after lunch. The clock above the stove clicked in its throat and then sighed which meant the tide had turned, which meant the men at the dock were thinking of the gut they had to steer through, which meant the causeway would show its back for two hours and you could drive across it if you believed in the lights on the other side. I did not look out the window. I was trying to be a person who could leave, in case I had to be.

“Come on,” Dory said when she had washed the pan and set it in the rack. “You’ll want to see the water. Otherwise it will come in here for you.”

We walked down the path that skirted the back of the house because if you went out the front door the gulls would think you were the kind of fool who did not know they were standing guard, and they would take your hat. The blackberry canes were brown like old string. The willow at the corner of the yard had dropped its green the way a woman drops her hair in a grief you should not look at. The ground was softer than it should have been, spongy in the way that meant a spring had found a new place to speak.

“Wrong,” Dory said again, almost to herself.

“At the funeral,” I said, “will there be the carrying?”

“Four boys on the board,” she said. “Joe’s boy and Roke’s oldest and the new man who is not from here but we allow him to pretend on Sundays and the one with the scar through his eyebrow who used to sleep in the boathouse until his mother let him into her kitchen again. They’ll walk her around the harbor on the board so everyone can say thank you. Then we’ll set her out to the slack and push.”

“Push what?”

Dory looked at me as if I had not read the letter in my hand. “Her.”

“I… I thought—we’re not Church,” I said. It was ridiculous after all those years, how my mouth could dry up on a simple sentence.

“We’re not anything and we’re all things,” Dory said. “We don’t put a person in the ground when it’s full of water, Luce. We give them to the place that taught them to speak.” We had always been a town that put its dead into boats and untied them and watched them go, let the current decide whether they would fetch up against another island’s pines or whether they would go out to where the water was a blue so deep it let you know what you were made of. When I was seven I had watched a boat with the bones of an old woman in it move in a way that made me understand the word mercy for the first time.

We reached the wharf. Joe was varnishing a mast with a rag like he was polishing a story he would tell later for cigarettes. He wore the same hat he had always worn, the brim torn where the wind had tried to eat it. He looked at me and looked at my ribbon and the way it bulged under my shirt because of the key and nodded as if some small arithmetic had checked out.

“You stayed,” he said. It was a statement and a forgiveness.

“For now,” I said.

“You remember where to press?” he asked.

“I remember where the stone wakes,” I said.

He nodded. “It’s ringing faint. The fog has had its hands on it too much. The young ones are too polite with it. They lay their heads down like they’re asking a favor of a sleeping aunt. Your grandmother used to slap it first. Wake up, she’d say. If the stone didn’t like it, it could stop being stone.”

I remembered Nell opening her palm and setting it on stone as if she were checking a child’s fever. The island had never been sentimental. It loved you or it taught you or it let you go.

“Do you have the board?” I asked.

Joe nodded toward the boathouse. Through the open door I could see it propped against the wall. It was just a board. Also it was not just a board. It had the dark gloss of the oil rubbed into it over years. It had the mark of each body that had been carried on it like a wear spot on a step. It would hold my grandmother like it had held the others, and it would feel like it was built for her and only her because that is what a board like that does, if it is used right: it remembers everyone and it remembers no one and that is what you want when you are going to be carried.

“You’ll be there,” Joe said. It was not a question.

“I’ll be there,” I said. My throat was a strip of kelp. I could not keep the mainland out anymore, not in that sentence.

We walked past the wharf to the path that went out to Gannet’s Point. The bell out there was redundant, everyone said, because the electronic sensor on the buoy did the same job without rust. But still the bell rang in fog because it wanted to. Nell had not been the only one who kept it going. Dory and the Roke boys had made sure the clapper hadn’t rusted straight through. They had taken welders out there in the rain. They had said there were other things to spend money on, and then they had spent it on that because sometimes you have to keep the thing that keeps you honest, even if the city says it’s nostalgia. I put my hand on the rail at the first bend to feel if the iron had held. It held.

Out at the point the fog was thinner because the wind had somewhere to go around the rock. The bell stood on its iron legs with the stubbornness of a goat. The stone under it was dark and wet and went to a hollow in the middle like the breath of an animal that had lain there for a long time and then gotten up. The sea on the north side of the point was as mild as a child. On the south side it showed its teeth and then tucked them away as if that had been a joke it did not commit to.

“Go on,” Dory said. She stood with her arms folded across her chest in the way that meant she was making herself into a post I could tie to if I wanted to.

I stepped onto the central stone. It was colder than I remembered. Someone had painted a small white mark on the underside of the bell, the kind of practical thinking that makes an art of itself: the mark lined up with the listening place in the stone when the tides were right. I knelt and laid my ear to where the stone had a slightly different tone, the way a body has a soft place behind the knee.

At first there was nothing but my own pulse, which sounded too quick. Then the stone made a small sound the way a shell makes a small sound if you remember how to ask it. The sound was a river at first and then a wind in pine and then something like a graveyard of spoons. I wanted to sit up and say, See? Foolish girl. But Dory put her hand on the back of my neck the way she used to when we were children and I was trying to look in two directions at once, and she kept my head on the stone and the bone behind my ear tuned.

People will tell you they do not believe in listening stones. They will tell you water is just water and a bell is just a bell. Those people are not wrong. They are playing the safe odds. But if you have laid your head on the right rock at the right time and had the right stubborn woman’s hand on your neck, you might hear the kind of voice that has no breath but still finds a way into bone.

I heard my name. It is stupid to write it. I will write it anyway, because otherwise everything after might as well be a joke. I heard my name the way a thin string hears its own note in a chord. Luce, said the stone, not like a call but like a report.

“What the hell,” I said, and my voice got swallowed and came back to me like someone had decided I could be left alone with my shock for now.

“Don’t look at me like it was me,” Dory said.

I heard, behind the string of my name, the shape of something Nell had always said when she lifted a pot with her bad wrist because she had refused help: There, there. Not as a comfort but as a command. And I heard something else, almost lost in the rummage of water and bell: something knocked. The kind of knock a nail makes when it drops in the bottom of a tin can.

I put my hand on the stone. The small hairs on my arm lifted because the air went cold around the warm. When my grandmother used to tell me a storm was coming she would say, Taste your teeth. I tasted them. I tasted iron and the first two minutes of a nosebleed and the crust of a good pie.

“What?” Dory asked. She smelled it too. That first odd sit-up in the air when the pressure changes.

“Wrong tide,” I said, not because it wasn’t rising but because it was rising without the right permission. The bell swung without wind. Something was moving under the rock. It is silly to say the sea was listening back. Perhaps what I mean is this: there are places where the world remembers you without your dignity on. This was one of them.

We stood back while the bell rang itself three times. On the third ring the horizon went from the gray of a pigeon’s belly to the gray of a church its lights just coming on. You cannot tell anyone that a bell moved the light and expect them to invite you to the good parties. But I am not interested in parties now.

Dory had brought the small mallet Nell always used when the bell sulked. She handed it to me. It was just a stick wrapped with a piece of an old glove. I held it and did not hit anything with it yet, because I had the sense that if I hit the bell I would tell it something I was not ready to say.

“You could go back Monday,” Dory said, practical as a pan. “You could say we’re ridiculous and bury her in the city with those little maples that get planted with people. You could say the listening stones are a way for us to make a living off tourists who come to be told that sound is the same thing as meaning.”

“I could,” I said. The mallet was heavy. Not because of its wood. Because of the hands that had held it.

“Or you could wind it,” Dory said.

“We don’t wind bells,” I said.

“Don’t be clever,” she said. “You know what I mean.”

I put the mallet against the bell and the bell took that contact like a relief. The stone under my feet went from being stone to being bone. I don’t mean in any mortal terror way. I mean in the way something becomes itself so entirely that you cannot get your metaphor around it. I was tired of metaphors. I hit the bell lightly. It did not ring. I hit it again and it rounded the air and the air held it, and who knows if anyone heard it out past the point. Maybe the whales. Maybe the women in the kitchens holding eggs in their palms like choices. Maybe my grandmother, wherever she was, looking around at the physics of things like she had been right only accidentally and finally finding that a pleasure.

At the third strike, the small knock in the stone sounded again. I knelt. I put my ear down. The sound was not the sound of a person, not the sound of words at all. It was the sound a key makes when it slips into the right tooth of a gear.

In my pocket, the brass key shifted against the ribbon like it had found its way to a map. I had the impulse—hallucination, if you’d like—to put the key into the hollow place in the stone, to fit it where there was no keyhole. It was a stupid, child thing. Child things have saved my life.

“Don’t do it if you don’t want what happens,” Dory said.

“I never want what happens,” I said. And then I lay down on the stone and pressed my cheek flat, and as the sea rose around the point, in the arithmetic that was both just the moon being a rock and something else being a chord, I slid the key against the stone until it found the minuscule sadness in the rock that was its slot. And the whole point shivered like the first time a newborn tastes smoke.

You could say I turned a key in the island. You could also say I got water in my hair. Both are true. Both are ridiculous. Both are the beginning of the kind of debt that looks like a life.

By the time they move water into a place, they move the names out.

On the road into our valley, someone had nailed a plank over the county’s blue highway sign and painted NEW LAKE in white, slanted cursive, as if renaming were an act of mercy. On the other side of that curve the hills opened, and there it was, the basin cupped like a palm, the river like a vein glinting in the afternoon. The asters had gone lavender along the ditches and the bee-balm had browned, heads ragged. A yellow plane made loops above the ridgeline, counting, I guessed, the last roofs, the last silos, the last voices to be coaxed or pushed out before the cut and fill began in earnest.

They called the dam The Promise up at headquarters. As if its whited letters on a T-shirt rigged on a consultant’s back could keep it clean. Most promises depend on silence. I’d learned that much by the time I signed my first non-disclosure form.

I downshifted at the long stone church, the one with the lightning rod that had kissed enough storms for three lives. Orange surveyor flags showed up where they never had before—zigzagging through the graveyard like the idea of a future.

My father’s lane had more grass in it than gravel. Apples had dropped from the wild tree by the culvert and crushed under my tires, their scent sour-sweet in the heat. At the mailbox, a black bear had left a mud print of its snout. The lid hung open, full of flyers. WE BUY ANYTHING. CASH FOR ANTIQUES. There was one from us, too, COMPANY NOTICE stapled through parchment leaves of burdock. Sectioning off the valley by parcel and deadline was an art. A map is a mouth, one of my professors had told me, that eats what matters until only lines remain.

For the last two miles, bees came and went across my windshield like stray punctuation. A few bumped their bodies on the glass, tasting the world with those tiny tongues set between their teeth. My father used to say that bees never hit windows unless they were trying to show you yourself.

The house looked smaller than my mind had kept it. It had been painted barn red long before I was born. Now it was the red of tongue blood after biting it. A green hose ran from the spigot to a water trough. The porch had a new sag. Four hives stood up on cinder blocks near the overgrown lilac, roofs weighted with bricks. The air had that noise it always had here in late summer—bees tuning the day somewhere between C and the inside of an ear.

He wasn’t in the yard. He wasn’t in the kitchen where the door stuck for the same two seconds it had my whole life. The floor was soft by the sink. A damp chunk had fallen out near the plumbing, and someone had set it back like a loose tooth. A jar of honey sat beside the stove with the cap off, a spoon stuck in its throat. It had sugared up. In the far corner, a plastic pale blue cooler had collapsed in on itself, the lid cracked and the sticker gone to ghost outlines.

“Dad?” I called, and my voice did that strange thing voices do in places that made them—the echo was not an echo, but an accompaniment of my smaller self.

On the table, between a coffee cup and a roll of baling twine, lay a folded piece of butcher paper. He had written my name on it with a carpenter’s pencil: Mara. The graphite was soft and fat where the pencil had been sharpened on the edge of a cinder block, as if anything might need to sharpen anything. A smear of dark honey had made the M look wounded.

Under that, in smaller script: You came home strong.

The third line had a little drawing of a bee. He’d never been whimsical. The lines were careful, anatomical. Wing veins, three segments on each leg, the stamen of its body held in a disciplined arc.

I touched the paper to be sure it was paper and not a memory.

“Myra! Myra?” He used to call from the hives and I’d correct him. I had been nine. It had felt essential. My name was the one thing I could keep sharp.

Now I followed the hum.

He was in the back field in the same old hat, the one embalmed with smoke and propolis and sweat, the brim patched with a piece of leather held in two X-stitches. He had tied a veil on top of it with twine, but the veil had not landed properly and a small dome of bees had pooled along his crown like thinking. He stood in shirtsleeves. The smoker had gone out. He had the hive tool clenched in his hand and his lips moving as if to a psalm.

He saw me when I was five feet away and did not move his feet. “If you stand there, you’ll funnel them,” he said.

“I got it,” I said. My palms knew the phantom weight of frames, of boxes, of lid bricks. He would always, I think, assume my body could not do what his had done. I stepped to the side so the bees had a lane. They poured past my ear in a kind of precise panic. There’s a tone bees find when their queen is off her throne; the day had it.

“Your smoker’s out,” I said.

He breathed out through his nose. “Been trying to go easier on the smoke. You know how it is with the season being wrong.”

“The season being wrong,” I repeated. It was how he spoke of droughts, late frosts, rain that fell on the wrong side of the tree line. Any harm had a season, and the season had simply showed up at the wrong address.

“You look like you’ve been fed,” he said, finally, letting his eyes hold on me. They were the same mossy brown he’d had and his hair a shade thinner. He was older in the way of thigh muscle going away. His arms were still a story about the work he could do with a few pieces of iron.

“I’m fed.”

“You go fancy?”

“Hell no.”

“There you are,” he said, as if he’d been waiting for me to claim an identity he could stomach. He took off the veil and it snagged on one of his ears. He didn’t smooth it. He didn’t do anything slowly that day. He lifted the inner cover of the hive and a snap of propolis broke like a note. I let my hand go to the frames. A wash of bees lifted and settled, their little faces twitching. Bee faces always had made more sense to me than dogs or newborns. I knew how to look at them.

“What’s wrong?” I asked. It was there in the bees’ mood, the way colony is a mirror.

He tapped a frame. “She’s laying like December. Half the brood. Drone cells where they don’t belong. Hear that?” The tone again, almost dolphin high, complaining.

“There are so many.” I pointed at the tall yellow weeds beyond the fence. The field had gone to goldenrod, a sea at calf height, every panicle heavy with pollen. Everything in a bee year leads up to this, then down from it.

“I think they know,” he said.

“What do they know?”

“Whatever the river keeps,” he said.

He said it without looking at me. He slid a frame out and leaned it on the brick, then pulled the next and the next. The music of bees on wood. I could smell the faint solvent of propolis, the yeasty sweetness of ripening nectar, the damp of his shirt. In the brood the baby bees sat curled white and new, like punctuation, like the little commas I used to draw between words when I was a child and wanted everything to stay very connected.

“The company,” he said, not naming it. “They came by last week with the map.”

“I know,” I said. I had signed off on that delivery. Not by choice. Not without half the room thinking of my maiden name. Somehow there is always someone who recognizes.

“Boy with a soft mouth. He called me sir in the way no real person ever calls anyone sir.”

“Emmett,” I said, then immediately regretted calling him by his name in our lane. “He’s just doing his job.”

“And you?” he said. The hive tool was pointing at me like a small, rough knife.

“I brought your relocation packet.” I nodded at the truck. “But I didn’t come as the company. I came for you.”

“For me,” he said, as if pronunciation could put quotation marks around me. He slid the frame back, his hands trembling a touch in the wrists.

“I’m not here to tell you to be grateful,” I said. “I’m here because the water is coming and I want you on the right side of it when it does.”

He shrugged. “Does it matter which is the right side when the water is done with you?”

He had always been able to sound both wise and obstructive in one breath. I had once taken that tone and grown up inside it until my way out was the architecture of someone else’s idea of a world—a dam, a reservoir, an engineering drawing with circles of crosshatching so neat it made my teeth hurt.

A bee got itself under his shirt and he held still while it decided whether it was lost. “Besides,” he went on, “I can’t lift like I used to. Moving the piano would be an insult to it. And where would I even put—” He bit the thought. He had never liked thinking about afters.

“You could put your chair anywhere,” I said. “A window is a window.”

“A window is a particular window,” he said, and in that line I could see all the days he had jumped up from the table to look at the way the snow was falling, or the way the sound of a truck was different because of humidity. He was a man cored out for detail. That is something to love and something to be exhausted by.

He was not good at saying I missed you. He was a genius at placing blame in the open air until anyone might put their hand under it and feel its temperature. Once he had told me our valley was nothing but a long pew and the mountains around it were a congregation of shoulders and sky. Once he had told me the river wrote names on the undersides of stones, that if you turned them over you could read all your dead. Once, when he was not drunk, he had told me that my mother left because she had a taste for air travel that he could not afford.

“Do you still do it?” he said now, as if picking up a thread from the kitchen table, from eighteen years before when I had turned a stone and said a thing I should not have known.

“What?” I said, pretending it was not a thing to ask in a field.

He set the cover down. The bees came back. One pinged the lobe of my ear like a sifted piece of light. “Read,” he said.

My throat went dry in the way of a name stuck. I was not prepared for this version of him, direct and unbluffing.

“I never did.” The lie objected to itself in my chest. “You did,” I said, correcting the lie with another lie. “You have the better eye.”

“You could line a ditch with only your mind,” he said, half smiling as if we lived in a story where praise made goodness safe. “We took you up to the spring, and you said how many stones there were with her in them and I could not count them the same even when I looked.”

Her. He would not say our mother out loud unless there was a third person in the room to witness. Language’s own superstition. Names invite the named.

It had been one spring where the tadpoles blackened the shallows and the maple keys spun in a red-brown fall. I had put my palm in the stream and felt a hum. That was how it was. It was not witchcraft. It was not angel-status. It was a skilled listening, the kind you can train into yourself if you believe a thing will keep talking when no one answers it. But I never wanted my body to be used for anyone else’s proof. By the time I was ten, people were leaving little notes in the creases of the screen door, just a first name and a date. I stopped going to the spring.

“You still have the ledger?” my father asked. He did not look at me when he did, which was mercy.

“The ledger is a myth,” I said, and this time the lie was tidy. The ledger was a myth because we had always made the ledger a myth.

“They’ll put it in the water,” he said. “Everything we don’t carry.”

“They’ll put it under water, yes,” I said. “Not as a punishment. It’s physics.”

“Physics is a way of naming the hand you won’t admit holds you,” he said. “You always liked the part of a field with the orange flags because that was where thinking held still.”

“I like knowing where not to step,” I said. It was a small joke. He didn’t take it.

He peeled a bee off his knuckle with the hive tool, gently. “Do you know what they did, once?” he said. “They made a neat rectangle of land and they cut the trees down in the neat rectangle and they burned the stumps and the rocks and everything inconvenient, and they laid a foundation for a house with white soapstone and they set the first course of brick and the second, and then the war came and the man who had ordered the house never got on the boat. All winter the foundation waited. And in spring the field buckled. The dead tree roots, unbothered by brick, heaved the corners out. Ten thousand bees nested in the gaps. The house never was. The bees did not care about intentions.” He adjusted his veil over his ear. “Intentions are what people with money call a place.”

“Your car’s lease is done,” I said, to interrupt what had started to feel like a sermon. “You’re going to be pedaling the highway if you want to go anywhere, which I do not recommend.”

“There’s nowhere to go that is not here,” he said.

We worked the hives in companionable silence for a while. I had not realized how my hands had missed this: the slight flex of wax in hot weather, the soft grit of propolis. It is a liturgy, a box. Life, in its billions, can be made patient by the shape of a frame and a steady hand.

When we were done, he went to the barn and came back with the metal pail we used to take to the river when we were careless. “I thought we might go down,” he said, as if it were an idea. “See how she looks.”

We walked past the sumacs with their fuzzy red torches, past the old pigpen with its collapsed fence. The path was the same but narrower, grown in by knotweed. The bees followed us as far as the wild grapes, then turned back. That had been my measure of distance all childhood: how far the bees came, and no farther. I had learned to love the exactness of a radius.

The river was lower than any September I remembered. The water had pulled back from itself in wide terraces, each darker band showing the last height it cared to keep. The engine of new water still made its throat sound on the rocks near the bend, but the middle ran thin. Pursed. The small fish hung their questions under the surface, all fins flicker and flash.

He crouched on a boulder and dipped the pail. He held it up to the light like wine. A thin strand of algae trailed from the lip.

“I don’t drink it raw,” I said.

“Always the lady,” he said. He scooped and let it go, scooped and let it go, like a man convincing himself of the point.

There was a tree whose roots I knew better than my own. When I turned around, its exposed claws made a map of nothing and everything—river undercut, storm anger, the way a belly lives on a slow hinge of hunger.

He said, without preamble: “Do you dream in ink?”

Sometimes when he had a thought he behaved as if the thought had its own heart.

“I do not dream,” I said, which was the only untrue answer.

I dream in everything I will not say awake. The house backfilled with river, the pantry floating jars bumping their shoulders like women in a small hallway. The dam a hand. The men I worked with wearing smiles too tight to be honest, their teeth stacked like the white rocks we used to collect and pile by the road. My mother’s knees in a red dress. A ledger in which every name is written twice, forward and backward, as if folding could save.

He set the pail down. He put his palms on the same stone he’d held since he was ten. “When your mother left,” he said, and the air went flat, as if the bees, who were not here, had sensed a cage dropped. “When your mother left, I found in her bureau a paper. It was nothing much. Like you would turn a ledger sheet into a grocery list. Corn. Needles. Two train tickets. It was in her hand but not. It looked like who she would be if she was trying on a person she thought I would forgive. I put it in my wallet and carried it until it wore a hole in its own corner. Then I stopped. I stopped carrying things because they made holes. That is my science.”

“Dad,” I said, because a person has to say something when a person says that, and the name was the least ruinous thing I had to offer.

He nodded, the kind of nod that means I hear you not that I agree. He turned to the water. The surface had that late sun shimmer that looks like waiting. He put his hands in. He lifted them full, then empty, as if baptizing. He said, quietly: “They start talking to me.”

“The bees,” I said, heading toward what was manageable.

“No,” he said. “The ones in the water.” He left off any other qualifier and it made my ribs feel like the pew they resembled.

We sat there until the light slid. The mosquitoes were slow and regretful. When we walked back, the house had taken on its evening shape—a creature who had learned how to darken at the edges first. A mourning dove called from the neighbor’s naked larch. The sound was nothing like a human call for the same thing and exactly like it.

He went inside to make eggs. He was a scrambled-everything man. I went to the truck to get his paper. The folder had my return address on it, as if the company had a home.

Inside, he had lit the gas with a match as he always had, because he had never trusted the clicker. The frying pan was the same one my mother had dropped on her foot once, leaving a bruise she had showed me like an island on a map of a leg.

“Don’t,” he said when I set the folder on the table. “Not yet.”

“Just look,” I said. “There’s the base rate and the bonus we can argue for because of the repair to the roof you did when the ash tree dropped that limb. I know the codes. I can do better for you than you’ll do if you bring that soft-mouthed boy a plate of cookies.”

“I wasn’t going to make cookies.”

“You will.”

“And if I did, I’d keep two,” he said, because he could not let me have a line untested. He cracked the brown eggs and their yolks were the color of ideas that have not been dismissed by any room of men. He threw in onions. He had pulled them weeks ago and hung them and now they were sweet enough to convince any person to stay.

We ate, and he asked the questions he would ask if I were any daughter with any job—how many tires I went through in a year, whether the boys told jokes at my expense, whether the motel smelled like freon when it was hot. He listened like the good man he could be. It is an easy thing to forgive a person for not being able, all at once, to look the piece you need looked at.

At ten he went to bed. He left his glass on the windowsill as if it had to catch a certain number of night sounds. I made up the couch. The couch Springs said older woman, every time I moved. The house breathed the way a house breathes with someone in it who believes it has your back.

When the lights were off, the river turned up in my ears. The first ear to hear it is your molar teeth, I have learned; they amplify buds of sound. The names come as a kind of clotted syllable; you have to be patient to pull them apart. Years ago there were so many I used to count them as sheep. Now there were few enough I could tell who had moved away.

I thought of the ledger I said did not exist. It was a school composition book with a marbled cover and a black taped spine and the first page was for our house and the last for our house because that was how a circle could be made and kept. The entries were hard-won and easy. You had to write down the names of everything that had ever mattered and the date between the first time and the last time. Last time you saw your blue bicycle. Last time you watched a flock of starlings make a whole sky into a thought. Last time you told your teacher a lie that made her cry. Last time he scraped his knuckles raw on a radiator. Last time she hummed the song about larks. Last time the river broke and wrote you back into the stone. I had kept it in the bottom drawer of the desk that used to be under the window in my old room, behind the socks I never wore because they had too much acrylic. When I left, I took the book and hid it, and when I could not bear the thought of years passing without an entry I brought it back one night like a thief and left it under the stove where the mice would not gnaw it for lack of salt. That is the kind of myth that keeps its own mouth shut.

The couch made the shapes of every sleep I had not slept in this house. I lay growing stiller than a person in a field of clover. The moon was on the wane and it threw enough light to let the table know it was wooden. When I could not pretend to not listen any longer, I got up and went out.

The night had that kind of thinness the first nights of cold get. The bees had curtained themselves over their doors to hold in the day. I had a sweater but not enough. I went barefoot across the porch, safe in a knowledge I never knew I kept: where each splinter would be and wasn’t.

I walked to the river by the shortest path, the one you only think of when you cannot think for staring. It cut past the old foundation where the beebalm used to grow, then down the steep bank where the black shale had always kept its smell of wet pencil. The crickets were burning down the last of their summer fuel.

At the bottom of the hill, between two exposed stones, a mason jar sat like a cheap moon. My father had told me to stop believing in signs when I was seven and found a nickel in the church parking lot after asking for a sign. He had wanted me to save myself for the things that were real. I had tried. I had found too many jars.

This one was a Ball wide-mouth, cloudy. The ring was rusted and an old square of wax had been pressed over the lid like a thick patch of new skin. It had the strange, faint light of something with a purpose. In other years I might have stepped over it. The new lake had come and put its damp hand on the back of my neck and said: nothing casual now.

I picked it up. It was heavier than it needed to be. Inside, folded paper. Outside, something smeared that was not honey and not grease and not anything I could name without compromising it to someone else’s word.

I looked down the river. It ran in the dark, its borders drawn by what did not run.

The jar was childproof in the way of things that want to be opened. The wax came up in my hands in two pieces, flexing, releasing its particular breath. I unscrewed the ring and the lip squeaked. Somewhere an owl announced an idea about mice. I slid my fingers into the jar and the paper was damp and cool and a little slimed with whatever time puts into glass. I unfolded it as if it might tear for the sake of theater. It did not. It was a page from the ledger. No, it wasn’t, I told myself. It was an identical human-sized twin of a trick we had refused to teach. The ink had bled a little in places, as if it were still making up its mind about how thick it wanted to be. There was my name at the top, written not in my hand and not in my father’s. Mara Deming, it said, and then there were six lines of neat, deliberate items:

First time you lied and thought it holy.

Last time you chewed your hair.

First time you made a man shut his mouth without raising your voice.

Last time she wore the blue, with the buttons like flat teeth.

First time the river used your real name.

Last time you refused the keeper.

At the bottom of the page, written at a slant as if someone had not been able to bring themselves to push their chair in fully, it said: Keep the ledger.

I stood with the paper and the jar and my body, which was feeling every degree of itself. The river said something that was almost, and then not, my mother’s voice. The bees back up at the house would have been asleep if bees sleep. My father would have been in the posture his shoulders had taught him to keep, top of a hill, waiting without calling it waiting.

There are promises. There are the names of the promises. There is what holds the dam up. There is what dam breaks mean the morning after. There is a person who leaves and a person who refuses and a person who gets called back to hold the ledger and hate it and love it and lose it and find it and put it under a stove to keep mice from learning the names of the dead.

Someone had inked my life like it was a place you could map. Someone had put into a jar the thing I had told myself did not exist. And at the second turn of the river, where the water scoops its shoulder and goes off, a black shape lifted and shook itself, and I thought for a second it was a deer. It was not. It was a person who had been waiting for me to stop pretending I did not know how to read water. I did not call out. I kept the jar. The paper whispered in my hand as if wind had learned my skin from the inside and was practicing it. I could have washed it all out then. Instead, I walked back to the house as if my feet were older and my name was heavier than it had been an hour ago.

Inside, the ledger under the stove, if that was where it was, kept its mouth closed. On the table, my father’s note with the bee anointed my name with a sticky shine. Upstairs, the old bed where I’d kept my loving to myself remembered a weight that had been a different girl. The new lake hung outside the windows in its unborn way. The Promise, the company said. As if that word was a dam that could hold. I put the page from the jar inside my shirt, over the same ribs that had once sounded like a pew in an empty church, and I lay down on the couch and let the river unspool. It did not stop, as it never had. It said my name once. It tried out another that I refused to hear. Then it said a third that belonged to someone who had not yet died, and that was when I knew that any map I ever drew from this day forward would either save a thing that did not want saving, or give a name to the ruin that might at least be told.

Chapter One

They say when water leaves a place, it drags the past up by its hair.

In the mornings the valley wore its new braids: ropes of mud laced with stalks of yellowed reed, staircases leading nowhere, the roads reacquainted with air. The dam operators had been opening the gates in increments, a widening mouth that exhaled the reservoir’s years. Far below our scaffold the water uncurled itself from the concrete with a sound like tearing fabric. The river that had been tethered obedient for four decades gathered itself, shook, and ran.

I stood on the spillway with a clipboard and tried to keep track of numbers that had once meant everything to me—cubic feet per second, stage height, turbidity—while the air steamed with the smell of pennies and algae and something older, like an attic flung open. Gulls had come from nowhere and hovered above the outflow, shrieking. Beyond them, the slope of the reservoir wore a new low-water line, a pale ring marking every drought my father used to pretend wouldn’t last.

“Seven-thirty,” Jo said beside me, tapping her watch with a grit-streaked finger. “Mark it.”
