I wrote 7:30 a.m. Gate adjustment; drop of 0.8 ft. Jo, the chief engineer, had a voice that could cross scaffolding through wind. She had inherited the job of undoing what men like my father had built, and she carried it in her back and her jaw like a weight she meant to set down carefully. She did not know me well enough yet to realize the temptation I felt to shove the board into the river and let the numbers go sliding under. She only knew I read a river the way some people read palm lines.

“You grew up here, right?” The intern asked. She was twenty-three, with the bright boots of someone not yet resigned to mud working its way into everything you love.

I glanced at Mei, then back over the shoulder of the valley. “Here adjacent,” I said. “Up on the ridge.”

“Before the dam,” she said, wincing as if the word were a bruise. “Sorry. That’s probably—”

“It’s just a noun,” I said. And for a moment I saw my father’s hands in the air, measuring a span no one else could see. He used to sketch in the air like that when he was thinking—if I were to cross this river where it breaks, if I were to shore it here, if I were to make a box that could hold a century.

“Fine drop rate,” Jo said, her eyes on the readout. She had not asked about my father, and I was grateful. In other versions of this morning, I could have chosen a different life entirely, one where I was still cataloguing benthic macroinvertebrates in desert creeks two states away, and a former student would send me a link to some article about Kingsley Dam’s decommissioning with a note that said, Did you ever know this place? and I would not have clicked.

But when the county hired a crew to shepherd the river home, my name got passed along with the other old artifacts. The Finch girl knows this water. The Finch girl can read mud.

Down in the valley the tops of old fence posts showed themselves like rotted teeth. There were apple trees too, ones that had survived four decades of water standing to their waists. The first to sneeze out leaves were ghostly, chlorophyll-starved, as if they’d been practicing photosynthesis in their sleep. Someone’s red roof had come angled out of the slope last week, and a deer had stood on it. I could see the curved shadow where the old church would be if we kept pulling at the plug: its bell would be full of silt. The playground would keep its midnight-blue slide. The grocery’s canned peach sign, if it hadn’t dissolved, would remember everybody’s favorite brand forever.

“We’ll move the line down another foot by noon,” Jo said, “if the fish stay off the intake.” Everything lived in odds here: the chance of a landslip, the chance of a low-grade toxin blooming out of its deep sleep, the chance that someone would bring us a coffee that wasn’t all sugar. Everything kept its ledger whether we tallied it or not.

“Where’s your sister?” Mei asked, mouth careful around the question.

“Not here,” I said. It came out sharper than I meant. Mei had no idea that my sister and I spoke the way neighbors speak across a hedge, nodding from our distance, waving when we can’t be misconstrued. She didn’t know that Naomi had written the first paper that made anybody with a badge pay attention to dam removal in this part of the state, that she had been the one in waders at meetings, reading fish charts with a finger like a metronome, naming the species that had vanished upstream as if she could call them back. She didn’t know my father used to lay my sister’s op-eds facedown on the kitchen table and rest his mug on the pushover photo byline.

He died two summers ago, which is how some things happen. A plaque somewhere near the entry road has his name on it, and on clear days I can stand beside it and see both of us reflected in the steel. There is a photograph in the county records of my father tapping the first wet concrete into place—he has my mouth and Naomi’s brow, his sleeves rolled above his thin wrists, a red scarf around his throat because it was March and cold enough that the men’s breath could be seen. If the photographer had turned to the left that day, they might have captured the two of us. We were nine and eleven, and Naomi would not stand still. I watched her run along the riverbank toward the bend where the water made a sound none of us heard anymore after the pool filled. She threw sticks into eddies and named them things: kingfisher bone, willow spine, the color of a bruise. She wanted the words in her mouth so she would not have to swallow the river itself.

By nine o’clock the mud had changed color. It went from a black that ate light to a ruddier shade that accepted it, grudgingly. The taste in the air had shifted too. I noted it in the margins without meaning to: sulfur reduced, iron rising. A man in a faded hat—Larkin, the town liaison—crawled a backhoe down toward the old road, his tires leaving ribbed signatures. We’d marked paths with stakes and flagging tape to keep people from sinking where the mud had the memory of quickness. Yesterday, a woman from the historical society cried until she hiccupped when we pulled a cast-iron stove out from a tremble of muck. The stove’s door had rusted shut around the last soot.

Down on the slope a boy in a yellow hoodie—illegally here, a teenager who had found a hole in our fence or simply ignored it—stood watching the water draw itself thinner at the base of the gates. He had his hands jammed in his pockets and the angle of his neck said he could stand that way, in defiance or awe, for a long time. When Larkin shouted he trod backwards the way herons do in shallows, feeling before placing, then slung himself up toward the oak line and vanished as if he’d been an errant thought.

I had expected a kind of relief when the drawdown began. I had expected it to feel like unfastening a button that had been digging into my sternum—oh, here is the breath I was made to take. Instead there was the ache that comes when a tourniquet is loosened and everything you have learned to live without finds its way into the bright again and insists it has always been yours. I wanted to call Naomi and say, There is a smell that is both rot and resurrection. You would have known the word for it. I wanted to say, I am sorry about the call I did not return three Novembers ago, the one where you left the first sentence and then swallowed the rest.

“You okay?” Jo asked, and because she was a woman whose questions wore no embroidery, I trusted the space she offered into which I could set anything I wished.

“This valley is louder than I remembered,” I said. The road on the far slope had a tire on it that had grown moss fingers. A lizard, pale with the indignity of light, made a purposeful line toward a scrap of shade, its ribs visible, its tail unscrolled like a ribbon. The river below us took the rocks back into its mouth the way a person takes their own name, slowly at first, then with relief.

At noon, wind. It should have helped, pushing the smell down and away, but it only stirred deeper layers and carried them up. We ate standing with our sandwiches folded into paper towels, and Mei told us how, as a child, she had lived beside a lake that wasn’t a lake, either—a gravel pit that the water insisted upon. Someone had hauled a sofa down to it every summer, she said; by August the cushions would have enough green fur to look like animals sleeping.

“Artifacts,” Larkin said, coming up the slope and blowing his nose on something that was either cloth or the ghost of one. “The volunteer table’s full.”

He meant the folding tables under the canopy we’d rigged at the crown of the slope. Every day people came with their mud-gleaned offerings: a jarful of buttons made slick as pebbles; a soup spoon whose handle had been bitten into by rust as if gnawed; a toy car with one wheel; the metal ring a cask once sat upon. We would label them, photograph them, bag them. We had a system for what belonged to whom if anyone could prove anything, and another for what would be set in a glass case in the library or returned to the river, which had a better memory than we did.

In the afternoon, clouds shouldered each other into something like a plan. The drawdown made the air feel cooler even on sun-baked days—the reservoir had been a sheet of body, and the river was bones underneath. The intake gates sighed again, and I watched the surface of the pool tilt, a new line honing itself along the shore. That was when I saw the root cellar.

It was only a suggestion at first, a mouth in the hill that had lost its teeth, a rectangle of absence where the ground had remembered that it had been carved. The trapdoor, heavy planks banded with iron, had swelled with water and then, starved, shriveled. Jo had said she expected collapse and we had a map to show where we should not walk; this was outside our pencil-marked boundaries, just to the left of where the general store’s foundation should be. I would have missed it if the cloud’s shadow hadn’t laid itself over the slope just then, making the darker hole darker.

“Do you see that?” I said.

Jo shaded her eyes and squinted. “You want to wait?”

“We should check it now before kids go poking,” Larkin said, already half in motion toward it, the part of him that had put his name down for weekends and weathered his wife’s look and put on his boots again winning over the part that wanted his lunch. I had never liked volunteers before this—people whose love for a place made them soft toward its dangers—but Larkin’s practicality had a beauty to it. He treated the valley like a kitchen he had worked in for years: he didn’t mistake knives for friends, but he knew how to handle them.

We picked our way down the slope with our weight in our heels, the mud taking us in one shallow breath and letting us go in the next. There is a way to love what can kill you without asking it to stop being itself; that is what I wanted to remember for Naomi once I could lay the right words in order. Outside the mouth of the cellar the ground had hardened into plates. The trapdoor lay cocked like an eyelid. I could see the iron ring, brown-sugared with rust, and the place where the wood had been nibbled by something small with a persistent hunger—muskrat, maybe, or memory.

“Careful,” Jo said, because she’d promised someone somewhere she’d say it.

Larkin wound his hands in the ring and heaved. The door lifted with a wet ripping sound, then gave, then came up altogether and flipped back, knocking out a shower of small black stones that weren’t stones at all but desiccated something. The hole breathed.

The air that unrolled out of that cellar was not the same air that rolled in. Cold, even in July. Sweet in a way that made the back of my throat ache. It smelled like last year and the year before and the year before that, pressed together in the dark. Apples. Summer earth. The potassium hum of potatoes. People forget that air itself can age.

“Jesus,” Mei said softly, because the inside was nearly intact. The shelves were still shelves. The hooks were still hooks. The rings where jars had sat were circles of dustless wood. There were jars too, remarkably, lined like small soldiers along the back wall, their tops leaded and waxed, their bellies clouded. The labels had sloughed themselves off, but someone had written directly on the glass in grease pencil; the dark lines had held.

Larkin crouched, his knees cracking audibly. He picked one up and turned it carefully as if he held a sleeping thing. You get good at reading handwriting in places like this, where it survives in odd patches—on calendar backs, on the inside of drawers. This was clean block print, letters pressed confident into the present tense: Beans. Beets. Peaches. The same hand had written in smaller letters along the base of one jar, as if to tuck the words where only someone looking closely would find them: September 1978.

“They salted them well,” Jo said, peering through at the pale spears in one. And then she straightened. “We should let the historical society—”

“Wait,” I said. My voice had gone odd in my mouth. I reached past the first row and then the second. There, at the back, was a jar smaller than the rest. Its top was blacked with wax, overkill, as if the maker were afraid of the world pushing in. It was set a little apart, and someone had slipped a folded thing—a paper—against its side before the long shadow of the decades pressed both into an arrangement.

“What?” Mei said.

“My father told us that once the water came it would be pure,” I said, and heard how strange that sounded. “That it would keep everything safe.” I should have known then what he did not: water’s idea of safe has never matched ours.

On the side of the small jar, the grease pencil handwriting had slid, as if the glass had cried and the letters did not want to stick. But they were legible. Someone had printed there, in letters smaller and more private than the word Peaches: For M.

Larkin looked over his shoulder at me, his eyes quick. “Is that—”

I set my clipboard down in the mud. My name has never been rare; it is not a name you wouldn’t find on someone’s extra key or somebody else’s graduation cake. Still, I knew this jar was not for every M that had ever lived here. The angle of the F had Naomi’s candor; the way the R lifted before it ended was mine.

“Don’t open it,” Jo said reflexively, and then, reading my face, changed tense. “Or not alone.”

“We’re not going to, like, unleash botulism ghosts, are we?” Mei whispered. She was trying for levity, but her eyes were full of the thing she would later learn not to show in bureaucratic meetings: belief.

My hands knew the jar before my mind caught up. My memory had the relief of recording its weight into the ledger of myself—this is how heavy the past is; this is how cold. The wax around the band was cracked in two places. I looked up the slope out of habit to see whether anyone’s gaze might pin me, but the canopy was far and the gulls had gone elsewhere. A short way down the bank the river was busy with its own return, shouldering gravel aside, tasting old beds as if to see whether they still fit. Larkin’s breath made a small steam in the cellar’s air.

I eased my thumb under the hard ridge of the lid and felt the give, the way you feel in a tooth filling the place it left. The band came first with a gummy reluctance. Beneath it, the lid held for a second longer, then popped up with a sound as tiny and enormous as the first bubble in a pot that’s going to boil. We all flinched because we are animals and we know that small sounds can change the room more than loud ones. A bead of something that had once been wax slid like a tear.

Inside, there was no liquid. Time had done what it always does. There was the paper, curled to itself, and below it—the glint of something red that I recognized by the way my heart moved before my eyes identified it. It was a hair ribbon, clotted now, the woven red bleached rust at one edge, tied into the same sloppy bow Naomi tied because she never looked in mirrors long enough. Underneath both, flattened to the glass, a coin.

I pulled the paper out very carefully. It had the softness of bodies do when they are old. It wanted to stay folded. On the outside, two letters again: M. my name shrinking in the ink, or my sister’s hand learning how to speak to me in smallness. The fold lines were not quite straight. The room had gone quiet in the way rooms do when the past is present, respectful but curious.

“Mara,” Jo said. It wasn’t a warning; it was permission.

I opened the paper. It had kept a dry smell, like the inside of a dictionary. The first line was in pencil and had that insistent tilt our school taught. I read the letters as they turned themselves up out of the years and arranged themselves on my tongue.

If you are reading this, it means we did not leave right.

We kept our weather in glass because nothing else would hold.

On the long shelves that followed the curvature of the old cannery’s staved walls, there were ranks of jars whose sides had breathed thin fog-circles into the wood. Each jar wore a label in Miren’s hand, small calligraphies of air: Short Rain, citrus after; Heat 42C, hospital corridor; Wind, mother laughing, loose around the edges. She wrote as a way of forgiving the weather for what it had done and what it might yet do, the way you acquit a family member because they are your family.

The Museum of Broken Weather occupied the last brick building at the end of Gullhook’s only road, where the blacktop dissolved into mussel-shell gravel and the land gave up trying to pretend it wasn’t mostly water. The old cannery had been a place that ate light. Fish had poured through it in ribbons and come out disciplined into tins. Now, the light came through in slices and pools. It lay on the floorboards like pelt, slid off the brass railings in amber ropes. Miren had coaxed spotlights to find the jars without startling them, to persuade an old storm to stay the night.

On the morning the snow arrived, the museum had run out of labels. The printer on her desk made a small mewling sound, a kind of apology. Miren had fed it a last strip of card stock and watched the three remaining blanks slide out. July’s intake had been worse than spring’s — too many visitors wanting to air out their childhood thunderstorms, excuse me, could you, I brought the morning my son was born and lightning was a wide blue seam, I’ve been keeping it in a spaghetti jar and I think it’s going off. It was a truth universally known in Gullhook that if you loved something and if it endangered you at the same time, someone would devise a way to tax it or a way to preserve it in a museum so that others could pay a fee to come and feel sad in public.

The first person through the door that day was a man with a shoebox of fog. He set it down carefully, as if something inside could bruise. “It’s the fog from my grandmother’s street,” he said, once Miren had invited him to open the lid. “Mornings she would go outside with her coffee and the fog would let her see farther, if that makes sense.”

“It does,” Miren said, and it did. Heavy fog let you see the immediate, the exact, the bead of water on the thorn; it took away the hills, the causeway, the ferry schedule; it returned your street to you. She wrote Temporary Sight into the small box on the label and pasted it to the glass. As the man lingered, she showed him where they kept similar fogs, allowing for variations. Fog with diesel. Fog, orchard. Fog, Catholic schoolyard. He took a picture of his fog on the shelf and cried decorously, his face tilted away from the lenses of others’ sadness. Then he touched her forearm as if she were also made of glass. “Thank you,” he said, in the careful tone people used for the living at the edges of a wake. She had learned to answer without deflecting. “You’re welcome.”

By ten, there was a line at the acceptance counter that bent around the bell jar of early thunder and down the corridor past the informational plaques about barometric pressure and loss. The interns moved up and down the queue with pamphlets explaining chain of custody, donor anonymity, volatile weathers, the snack policy. Ena, the new one, wore a sweatshirt that said THERE IS NO PLANET B in letters that had washed to pale. Ena was not yet old enough to remember the snow here. She and the gulls had come up together on a diet of french fry ends and overheated summers. She had a painful way of looking at Miren when anyone mentioned winters their grandparents had known, like wanting to apologize on behalf of the entire century.

“You have three labels left,” Ena said, leaning across the desk to count. Miren made a rueful sound and tucked the blanks under the blotter as if they were cash. “The vendor won’t deliver more until Monday,” Ena added. “I called.”

“Then we’ll take down in pencil,” Miren said. “We stack more descriptors and rewrite them pretty later.” She tried to say pretty, not legible. She didn’t want the interns to get the clerical habit of thinking beauty was an indulgence.

At eleven, the door stuck as it opened and admitted a girl with her hair caught up in something that was not exactly a scarf and not exactly a net, some contraption of thread meant to keep things from escaping. She had brown elbows and a careful expression that refused the museum’s invitation to narrate. She carried a white polystyrene cooler in both hands, chin tucked down almost against its lid. The cooler had been wiped clean of marker with a solvent that left a faint lemonade smell, or maybe she’d brought that in with her—lemon soap in the skin, sugar in the breath. It took Miren only a second longer than it should have to notice that the girl’s shirt had been turned inside out. There are things, Miren knew, you could make look intentional when they were mistakes; there are other things that were instructions to the world that you hoped the world would disobey.

“You do intake?” the girl asked, standing at the edge of the desk, peering around at the rooms as if there might be a more official counter lurking in the shadow of a rain exhibit.

“I do.” Miren lifted the hinged section of the desk and came around because she didn’t like to make anyone offer her the thing they feared drops. “I’m Miren,” she said.

“Sabi,” the girl replied, not waiting for the question, like you would if you’d been on a list too often. She eased the cooler onto the table with a tenderness that hurt.

Do you have an appointment, do you understand our compensation policy, is your weather stable — none of those were the first question. It felt indecent to ask a woman in labor for her insurance provider while she was between contractions. “Would you like a glass of water?” Miren asked, and then realized how idiotic that sounded in a place where water had to be coaxed from almost everywhere. But they did, under the desk, keep a gallon for headaches and the dried-out throats of people who tried to tell their weather’s story more quickly than they had breathed it.

“No,” Sabi said. “Can I—should I open it here?”

“We can step back to the intake room,” Miren suggested, and Sabi nodded. She had a tiredness about the eyes that wasn’t sleep; it was the baggy look of someone whose attention had been kept at a very high pitch too long.

The intake room was small and had once been the cannery manager’s office. The paint peeled in long flensing strips, and the single window showed a rectangle of the new sea below the old seawall, an arrangement the sea had already found hilarious. Miren set the cooler on the table there and pulled on gloves.

“We accept only original,” she recited for the recording device’s benefit, and for Sabi’s. “No reproductions, no second-hand. You certify what you’ll tell me is true to your knowledge. I’m going to open this now. You may stop me at any time.”

Sabi nodded. Her fingers tightened around the strap of her bag. “Okay,” she said.

There is a cold that is merely the absence of heat, and there is the cold that is a species you could list in a field guide. When Miren unlatched the cooler lid, what rose up met her like a cautious animal. It smelled of pennies and milk. It might have been her own memory leaning in; it might have been the weather itself. She lifted the lid.

Inside the cooler was snow, and not just any snow but an arrangement of it, a wrapped parcel. It had been packed into a shallow metal pan and covered with a rectangle of aluminum foil that someone had lifted and relaid, perhaps again and again over the years, briefly exposing it to air that had no business that close to it. The foil crackled like hard leaves as Miren folded it back. Beneath, the snow made a tight white, granulated like a good frost on a cold marrow bone, and the light in it was high, the kind of blue-white that burns the retinas of the burned. Snow from around here had always had a little grit in it, a small impatience in the mouth. Miren inhaled, reached out, and held her hand above it. The air above the pan was ten years ago, twenty. There was the faint whisper of things wanting to be steam and knowing they weren’t allowed.

“Where?” Miren asked, because the labels loved the Where almost as much as the When.

“South of here, outside Rook,” Sabi said. “On our porch, year we got the blackouts. It was the last big snow. Mama put it in when the power came back on. She wrote the month on the foil, it was…” Sabi squinted, as if this should be easy to remember. “She said it would be for something.”

“How long have you had it?” Miren asked.

“Since that winter,” Sabi said. “It’s been… it’s been in the freezer. She died last week. I thought I should bring it before—before the house goes. They’re knocking it down for the new road. I didn’t tell them I had this. I didn’t want them to fine me.” And there it was, the small lawlessness of grief: it makes the polite into smugglers.

It had been twenty-seven years since the last big snow at Gullhook. There had been flurries like apologizing, powder that found the night and did not make it to breakfast, but the last time the town had laid out oven trays on porch railings to catch enough to promise children and animals, to prove to themselves that weather could still be kept, Miren had been a new archivist and still a daughter. She felt the way the cold reached up through her bones, the old ache in the wrist she had broken once. She had not expected to ever see this again.

For a very long time after the cannery stopped and the money that had been made of fish had traveled away on highways to a different coast, people here had not known what to do with the weather. It went on as if it had always been the landlord. The museum had started as a joke in the back corner of the city hall; it became less funny when the insurance maps were redrawn and the word flood turned into a suffix for ordinary nouns: houseflood, streetflood, schoolflood. The Board had voted to give them the cannery, cheap, like giving your grandmother her own room in the house you were already planning to sell. Miren had been in the first class of trainees. She had learned the hard work of coaxing an afternoon into a jar.

At the intake table, she felt the old training settle into her shoulders like a scarf. “I’m going to sample,” she said to Sabi, and took up the thin spoon and the vial. She scooped a small portion into the glass. The tiny grains rang like stars against the side where they struck. She sealed the vial and wrote what she knew: Snow, porch; Rook outskirts; blackout season. She longed to write the adjective for the color—a whole encyclopedia had splintered into adjectives on her tongue—but the museum did not recognize color as unit. It recognized coordinates, dates, names. It had to pretend to be a place without metaphor in order to be allowed to exist.

Outside in the gallery, a small aquarium pump that kept the humidity near the rain shelf stuttered and resumed. The room whispered like a seashell pressed to ear. Ena’s laugh, a little unkind because she hadn’t learned yet to be kind ahead of time, drifted and was caught in a jar with Laughter in Rain already on its label. Miren’s hands shook as she wrote. Snow did that, set your blood to fast talk.

“Who taught you—” she started, and then stopped. Who taught you to carry something like this. Who taught you that keeping a weather was something you could be fined for. Who taught you to wrap.

“My mother,” Sabi said anyway, as if Miren had managed the question. “She said everything is going to move one day. She said we should keep a part that isn’t. She thought you should have it here, so other people could see it. Is that okay? Will you keep it?”

There were rules about acceptance, and there were rules that lived in the same room as grief and would not be told what to do. The Board would not like that this had been in a home freezer; they would not like anything about donors that smelled like poverty. They liked the glass to look all one kind. They liked the jars to remind them of apothecaries, not cafeterias. Miren thought of the Board’s keenness for early thunder; their gratitude when a donor of means with a house on the original bluff had given them a whole summer wind. She thought: this snow owes nothing to anyone. It owes even less to the men up in the city who write the letters to the museum reminding them that the museum’s tax exemption is a privilege that can be revisited.

“Yes,” she said. “We will keep it. Thank you for bringing it to us.” Her voice was steady and then it wasn’t; she heard how it went soft on us. It was a way she betrayed herself, including herself in the safekeeping.

Sabi watched the vial with the sample as if it were a capsule of something a doctor had drawn. The tip of her tongue pressed against a canine as if she were trying to keep a teeth-bite story down. Miren set the vial upright in its little rack and covered the pan with the foil again, flattening the wrinkles lightly, reseating the snow in its cold. She stood for a second with her gloved hands on the edges of the pan and let the old winter run its cold into her. Cold that had nothing to do with the fan in the corner chattering on. Cold that had looked at her once when she was a girl and told her she would owe it. You could owe a winter. You could spend a lifetime paying it off without ever finding out the original charge.

“Do you want a receipt?” Miren asked, because it was in the script and because sometimes orderly pieces of paper were a way of saying I believe you.

Sabi shook her head. “I get a discount, right? If I come to see it?” Her face shifted to the side she had not shown yet: the one that could afford to be a little funny in her grief.

“You don’t have to pay at all to come and see your snow,” Miren said. She had invented that rule and had argued it into existence in the boardroom by using their own glass phrases against them. For a while, donors can return and visit their weather without charge. For a while was undefined and she liked it that way.

“Good,” Sabi said. Her stare flicked to the square of the window and away. “They’re knocking the house down tomorrow. I thought I’d come after.”

“You live in town?” Miren asked, because the map loved the Who almost as much as the Where.

“Across the inlet. Two buses. If I run for the one that skips the loop.” Sabi smiled one. “I know that’s not your problem.”

“It is now,” Miren said, and she surprised herself. “Can you leave me your phone number?”

She took down the number and wrote it on the edge of a tourist map of Gullhook because there were no more labels. She made herself a promise that she would find Sabi again if Sabi did not come back, because some people made offers to the museum in the voice of the last attempt, and if the museum failed them there, they would not try again with anything, not weather, not the next good day, not anyone.

When Sabi had gone, Miren stood for a long moment with her hand on the cooler before she carried the pan to the cold room. The cold room was not as cold as it had once been because the compressors were tired and because the Board had nearly won the argument about shutting it down. There were grants for fog and there were grants for heat, performative, interactive. There were no grants for the blue-white of the word winter written in a small steady hand across a piece of foil.

She slotted the pan between a tray of frost scraped from the window of a train in the Alps by a man who had kept it in his suitcase for two days like a pet and the velvet block of hoarfrost that had been lifted, whole, from the bristles of a broom in a barn. She let the door seal and heard the gaskets take a breath. Out in the gallery, a family had arranged themselves for a selfie with the bell jar of early thunder, which was the museum’s most popular exhibit because it made children feel important and made parents feel that they were doing education.

She did not go out to greet them. She went upstairs to the office where the window let out onto the roof and the roof let out onto the idea of collapse. The roof had been replaced once in the museum’s tenure. It would need it again sooner than the Board would allow, because roofs were like people: they were what stood between the real and the everything, and nobody wanted to spend money on that.

She set the three remaining labels on the desk in front of her. She wrote on the first, in pencil because the printer had wept itself empty: Snow, porch; Rook outskirts; blackout season. Then she turned the second over and wrote a note to herself about Sabi’s number and the demolished house. On the third, she wrote a name that was not yet an exhibit and that she was not allowed to write.

There is a class of weather you cannot accept publicly because you cannot prove it. There are words you cannot get grants for. The storm that took her father should have had a name, and because it didn’t—because the year it came there were other things happening and the men at the weather service had been sleeping in cots under their maps—it became a rumor at the longer tables in the bars. Not the big one, the one after. You know. That gray day. Because she couldn’t place him in a jar, he existed around the museum like a smell of something the ocean left behind.

When the phone rang, she answered with the museum voice. “Museum of Broken Weather,” she said. “We accept what you cannot keep.”

“Ms. Ochoa?” a voice said, surprised to find itself speaking to someone alive. “This is Tillman from the Board.” He always said Board like it was heavier than it was. “We’re getting letters again about your intake policies. Are you open to discussing them? We think you might be taking in instables.”

“Instables,” Miren said. She saw from the corner of her eye what the sea was doing, and it was the oldest thing it knew how to do. It tried the low wall, tested the seam where brick met mortar, searched out what didn’t belong. “Is that a weather or a person?”

Tillman hissed a little. He disliked having jokes applied to policies. “Both, in a way. We need you to be more circumspect. The museum cannot be seen as a catchall for every sigh someone’s got about the climate, excuse me, about weather events. There are donors that— There are optics.”

“We can discuss it at the next meeting,” Miren said. “We can discuss it, Tillman.” She could almost see him straighten his tie, even though he was a voice.

“And there’s this other matter,” he said, softening. “The newsletter wants a feature on your most important exhibit. They asked if it could be the early thunder again. The thunder photographs well.”

A wind fingered the side of the building as if choosing a place to put its mouth. Miren looked at the labels on the desk. The third one had in pencil the word her hand had left without her permission. Winter, last. She put her hand over it. She had learned to make her palm a lid.

“Maybe,” she said. “We’ll see.”

When she hung up, she did what she sometimes did when the museum felt like a body with too much remembering in it. She went down to the jar of Field, post-harvest, stored below the level of an adult’s waist so children could see. She unscrewed the lid. Ena would scold her later for doing it without logging the exposure, and Miren would pretend to be sorry. The smell came up—sun’s arc on straw, mouse urine, patience. The air that had leaned all day on a flat place and made it into a sentence. She put her face over it and closed her eyes and let that time instruct her lungs for a few minutes. When she sealed it again, she felt steadier.

Outside, the sea struck the rocks like a hand clapping. The gulls braided themselves through it, brilliant stupid acrobats. The town carried about its business, which was to say it tried to do things that had no obvious future. In the cool room, a small square of snow from a porch south of Rook did not think anything. It did not remember the porch rails under it, the breath of a child above it. It simply resisted the shape the world had chosen lately and held its own for an hour, then another.

At closing, after the last family had been persuaded to buy a postcard of fog in order to feel they had done commerce and not merely reverence, Miren stood alone at the cold room door. There are keys you keep on your person and keys you leave on hooks. She held the key for a second before she slid it into the lock. She could feel, through the steel, the old winter leaning patiently on the other side. It was not cruel. It did not forgive. It waited like debt, like love. “We’ll make room,” she told it out loud, as if she were promising the porch or the girl, as if she were promising the version of herself who had last stood in snow without doing math for the roof. The compressor thudded and their breath made a kind of treaty. She understood, suddenly, that taking in Sabi’s snow would not be the worst of what the Board would forgive her for. There were storms coming that could not be lidded. There were laws and there were laws.

Downstairs, the jar of early thunder hummed with its own small weather, the way an instrument hums after you set it down, to remind you of the note you asked of it, to tell you there are more. Outside, the sea rehearsed. In the morning, she would bring in three more folding chairs from the shed. In the morning, someone would come with a shoebox of wind. She would write what she could in pencil and later, when the labels came, she would rewrite them pretty, believing still that if you were careful with your hands, the world would learn from you.

The Loren remembers the mountain once a year and goes home.

That’s what my grandfather used to say, his mouth half full of pipe smoke, the tobacco charred to the taste of summer’s last plum. He’d point with his chin toward the gray water, not the smoke, and squint as if the river might squint back. Every person who grows up within hearing of the Loren’s cough of current has heard some version: the river is a body with a heart that refuses to be told what direction to beat, the river is a cat dissatisfied with the arrangement of furniture, the river has a calendar pinned behind its eyelids and keeps the appointment even if the town forgets.

We don’t forget. The backward day is written on the chalkboard in the bakery, in the calendar at the municipal office where the clerk keeps her spoon in a jar of sugar and clutches her chest when she laughs, and on the wall of my little ferry hut, where the paint curls away from the wood like fish scales. All morning I’ve ferried people across who have a reason to pretend they don’t believe. By ten a.m., a line of figures trails down the narrow road like a braid unraveling.

“You think it will be noon?” Arta asks. Arta has the kind of voice that leans in to tell a secret and then decides to sing it. He holds a bunch of reeds that rattle when he shakes them and calls them lucky. He is not lucky, or else his luck is a different species, because last night he lost the key to his lockup and this morning the lock gave up and opened anyway.

“People say noon,” I say. “People say dawn. People say when the swallows drop low over the mill chimney and your hair stands up. People are full of bells.”

Arta grins and taps his reeds against the railing. “Full of bells,” he repeats, as if he could swallow them and chime. He’s wearing a shirt that used to be his father’s, the shoulders not yet taken in, the cloth shiny from years of carrying hay, or prayers, or just the weight of having been needed.

On the far bank, Alder Street points its crooked finger toward the hills. The loricaria trees there have learned the shape of the prevailing wind the way some people learn the shape of grief. Their roots go down like a handwriting I can’t read. All along our side, the fishermen have staked their poles deep and looped the lines across the eddies, a harp across the river’s throat. The first cormorant of morning watched them set the lines, then dove and came up with nothing, then dove again, stubborn.

On any backward day, nobody brings anything across who doesn’t intend to bring it back. There’s a superstition about it, but also a practicality; the ferry is a flat-bottomed wooden thing and I am a small man with bad wrists on low-pressure days. Four generations of my family have poled it, then pulled it by line when the river was petulant, then installed an outboard engine that rattles so much you feel your bones will come unscrewed. This morning the engine starts, then coughs and shivers and waits, nervous. I understand. Even metal has an opinion about today.

“What time did it happen last year?” asks the girl with the jar of bees. She holds the jar like a lantern. The bees are slow, as if they woke in syrup. Their bodies hum a first paragraph, try a second, erase it.

“Three,” I say because that’s what you say to children. Three is when you believe anything becomes possible or safe or both.

“What if the bees get confused?” she asks.

“They are bees,” I say. “They are confusion with wings.”

She laughs, the kind of laugh that makes a man want to earn it again. I take her across first because she asks the most questions, and people who ask questions are a species of anchor. A woman with a basket prayers under her breath the whole time. An old man with a paper-wrapped package holds it in both hands, as if it might decide to fly or bite. A boy with a shadow longer than his sense stares over the edge, daring the river to claim him earlier than it is scheduled. The mayor’s nephew in a pressed shirt and polished comb-over takes my picture each time I lean into the pole, and I decide not to charge him double for the offense.

Most people who cross do not look back. The far bank has the market advertised in chalk, the violin maker who lines up his instruments in the sun like fish to dry, the house with blue shutters where someone has painted the lintel with the date love arrived and the date it left. On backward day, the far bank also has the expensive things: charm sellers, bottle-sellers, the woman with a stall of clay jars shaped like jaws, each with a painted tongue inside. She promises to keep a name safe until you come to collect it. If you forget to collect, the jars are buried in a field where the wild carrots grow and the foxes dig them up and run through the night with a half-dozen names in their mouths.

About ten, Evi arrives at the ferry, her hair pinned in her garden way, two forks crooked in like they got tired of the kitchen and needed to hold something else. Evi is the one who will tell you that the river isn’t a god, it’s a piece of furniture someone decided to pray to because they didn’t know where else to put their hands. I am in love with Evi the way a winter window is in love with the first hand that fogs it.

“You slept?” she says, handing me a parcel wrapped in brown paper. Inside is a hollowed-out loaf stuffed with shredded lamb and mint and the finish of lemon. Evi feeds me and makes sure there’s always too much; she is practical about hunger and other unfillings. Her husband died in a normal month on a normal day, walking from the mill to their kitchen with flour on his sleeves. A truck came around the corner and folded him like a letter. That was four years ago. She does not wear black, and no one who loved him complains.

“I slept some,” I lie.

She watches my hand on the pole. My bad wrists telegraph like boys from the mountain with messages written on their skin: storm coming, a mother sick, a girl says yes, the inspector changed his hat. “You can look for me around three,” she says. “Bring me back before it goes dark.”

“Before it goes dark,” I echo. We do not say, the day the river runs backward, it might go dark at a time that is not day.

I lie and Evi allows it, and this is our kindness to each other. She tries to teach me more verbs for the ways of water: to roil is different than to fester, to foil is not to churn. She knows these things like a second language she learned because the first one betrayed her.

At noon, Arta’s reeds are shredded by small hands and the smell of bread names the air. Some of the schoolboys from the upper town come down, smug with the unassignable permission granted by a day that breaks rules. They carry their uniforms folded over their arms and turn the pleats with fingertips so neat it almost makes me like them. A woman I do not recognize puts a folded paper in my hand and says, “If you see him, tell him I have forgiven him the small things.” The paper is thin, the words heavy like coins.

The Loren is restless by then, the surface pocked with wind, a murky muscle forgetful of its size. A snapping turtle surfaces and rolls an eye that knows the whole story and is bored. A dog runs into the shallows, stops short at the sudden touch of cold. The little spinning whirlpools we call the river’s thoughts collect under the pier and mutter.

When I was six my mother stepped into the river on the backward day because she believed the river could undo, and she was a woman who didn’t understand that the body does not take orders, that it is a mutiny machine. She smiled at me, or I remember it as a smile; memories are thieves with sentimental scores. She wore a dress that wasn’t meant for water and held her shoes in one hand like a pair of small animals she was setting free. My grandfather said not to stop her because it was her only decision she wanted to make alone. She walked until the water touched the hollow at the base of her throat. She said something I couldn’t hear but will hear forever. Then she went where the current was new. The river gave back three buttons and a hair tie that smelled of oranges. There are years I hate the river. The backwards day arrives and I say, histrionic in the privacy of my hut, not this year, keep walking, leave us out of it, you’ve done enough. But the Loren does not speak my language, or else pretending not to understand has always been its coin.

In the early afternoon, the municipal man arrives in his little hat. He is small and precise and smells like pencil shavings. He unrolls a piece of paper that says, in a language too tall for the pier, that due to safety concerns there will be no crossings permitted between contenders and contraries, which is to say between east and west, which what other choices are there. He has ink on his fingers and sighs, a man who has fallen into the kind of job where he must mispronounce the names of people who will not forget it. I fold the paper around a sandwich and say, “There will be crossings.” He nods, because he has to make a note about that, because notes are the only way he sleeps.

The sky goes cloudy, not with rain but with the kind of weather that can’t decide, which is a mercy. On the opposite bank, the man who paints birds on the backs of shutters paints a bird bigger than a door. Its beak is a small scythe. Its eye is a walnut of flame. He keeps stopping to light a cigarette, draw, forget the cigarette, watch the smoke until it troubles him into remembering, and put the cigarette back between his lips to draw.

Halfway through the second sandwich, something like quiet climbs up from the riverbed and sits on the pier. It is not the absence of sound so much as sound reconsidering itself. Even the bees in the girl’s jar slow, a thought halfway decided. The dog at the end of the road picks up its paw and puts it down like a magician. Everyone is speaking. No one is listening. Then the listening begins, the way a room can decide to be a room and, in doing so, it decides what to hold.

“Now,” says Arta, almost lovingly, as if now were a person whose shy hand he wished to take. He always says now at least three times before now.

The Loren’s surface shines with a skin that is not water. The current pulls once, twice, then a shiver climbs the length of it as if a fish the size of a town brushed its side. I have watched this happen on thirteen backward days. Some years it is a polite hinge, a door closing and opening on the usual room. Some years it is a wrench so abrupt everything in the world seems to be on the wrong shelf. I brace my hand against the pole and feel the ropes from pier to pier take a breath.

The empty bottles tied to the uprights turn and bump against their knots. Leaves snagged along the shore lift, flutter, commit to coming home. A pelican skims low and suddenly has to work to keep its place; its wings, all duty, slap a new kind of air.

There is always a moment, short as a cigarette, when the river forgets both ways. It slows to a standstill, astonished that motion is an invention, not a requirement. It is then that the children run down to the edge and frantically throw in what they want back: buttons, coins, a tooth, a paper boat with a drawing of a mother with impossible hair. Arta throws in the stub of the key that broke off in his lock yesterday. Evi throws in nothing. She tucks her hands under her arms as if she is afraid of what they might let go.

Then the eddies smooth and curl in the other direction, and the Loren, with relief, begins to climb uphill.

It is not dramatic, unless you have spent all your life with a map in your head of how water works. The first evidence is the way the green film along the stones peels back and adheres to the rock upstream. Then the long ribbon of pollen floating under the pier hesitates, shrugs, and goes the other way, a parade turning around. A duck, indignant, flaps and angles its tail as if that alone could rewrite physics. Downstream becomes a word I do not trust.

In all the clatter and hush, I almost miss the jar that knocks gently against the ferry. Not the bees. A pickle jar, mayonnaise jar, one of those drawers of your grandmother’s with saved jars for reasons no one asks. It is scratched and fogged and stoppered with red wax as if someone feared the thing inside might climb out again. I lift it and it is heavier than the body suggests. It could be a rock, it could be a baby sleeping, it could be the entire contained mood of someone who never learned to write and asked the river to write for them. I hold it against my chest and feel a tremor through the glass like a bird remembering.

“Found something,” I say. People look and don’t. There is so much to look at. On the far bank, the violin maker has stopped pretending to quell his wood. A woman with a row of flowers, each in a tin can with the label still on, has sat down in the dirt. An officer in the sort of uniform that means and doesn’t mean anything has taken his hat off and is looking into it as if a fortune might explain his scalp.

“Stay,” says Evi, the first time she’s ever told me not to cross. “Wait until the first return.”

Arta scoffs. “First returns are wishing wells.”

“Only when you don’t know what you’re wishing,” Evi says.

On the backward day, the first return is an apology. The river sends a thing back not because you deserve it but because it is easy to carry. It starts with small absolutions: a shock of eels in the shallows, a doll without an eye, a photograph of a boy whose ears are too big. Once, we got a hat with a letter tucked in the band. It said, in the handwriting of someone who worked with his hands, I will come back to you as soon as I am done being no one. He did not. Or he did and we didn’t know him.

I hold the jar and don’t open it.

“I’m not going to,” I tell Evi and Arta, and also the part of me that has no patience for suspense. I am not a man who enjoys withholding, but there are silences that, once broken, cannot be made again.

The water begins to deposit what it has kept under its tongue. The first thing is a comb with a cracked middle. Then a string with two keys, a kind that tells you what doors it once wanted to be. A rusted bicycle bell. A set of teeth. The river is short on poetry today. Children race and shriek and pick and pass their hands over with the carefulness of thieves who prefer not to get caught, and all the while the water is doing something it does not do, and the town is making noises that belong to both birth and fire.

“I dreamed your mother last night,” Arta says, and regrets it as soon as the word mother leaves his mouth and becomes the kind of thing that will not fit back in. Evi turns her face from me, correctly. It is a mania of my people to stare when a hurt arrives, as if we might find the pill inside it that makes it edible.

“I dream her every night,” I say, so softly that it is almost a forgiveness.

“You should open it,” a boy, not the bees boy but a different boy, says, his voice snot-bright. “Maybe there’s money, or a snake.”

“Money would be more useful than a snake.”

“You could train the snake,” the boy says, earnest. “You can train anything if you tell it enough stories.”

My grandfather used to say that stories are just the long way to every place that matters. He would light his pipe and let everyone in the kitchen pretend we didn’t know where he hid the matchbox. He would tell about when the bridge was wood and it groaned with carts and brides and the boots of soldiers. He would tell about the winter the river froze, not all the way, but enough to let a family cross with hands held. He would tell about the girl whose mother hid her in a wicker trunk under the bed when the men came looking for boys, because what is a boy in the blue dark under the bed except a shadow. He would tell about the time he and my mother stole apricots from old Man Renzo until he came out with a broom and they ran and my mother fell and scraped her knee and Grandpa had to put the fruit back, every warm one, in the crate where it would be sellable again, the fuzz smoothed in one direction, his indignation the other direction, the facts never quite in the middle. He would not, he would never, tell about the day she stepped into the river, because that was my story. That was my eating. Someone else’s hunger could not help me.

I do not open the jar. I set it on the shelf next to the spare rope and the ripped life vest with the three fraying ties. Bees girl watches the jar as if she could see the thing curled inside its cloud. Out there, the backwards current takes on the confidence of any decision that no longer needs your approval.

By three, the air has a different seam. Arta has sold all his reeds as tokens and now has nothing to do with his hands. He sits on the crate with the word oranges despite it decades ago having held only nails. Evi wears that look of watching that is indistinguishable from prayer until you hear no one’s using God’s name. The municipal man keeps making notes on his paper as if his pen will someday testify. The water keeps ascending. Every backwards day it climbs up something that surprises me. Today it climbs the memory of my wrists.

The first return of consequence is a dress, snagged on the end of the rope looped around the third pier post. It is simple and blue, the kind of blue that only happens to an object that has been in water long enough to forget what it was for and become only color. Evi sees it before I do and her mouth makes a shape I have never seen it make.

“Careful,” she says, because she has to say something. The river bumps the dress twice, impatient. I reach with the hooked pole we keep for this, as if we are fishermen and what we fish for is the past. The cloth is heavier than it should be. When I bring it up, water unthreads itself from the hem and returns to its home and the dress collapses in my arms the way a body does in a dream when you are trying to carry it to safety and your legs are filled with sand.

“It’s the wrong blue,” I say out loud to nobody, because my mother’s dress was a blue that smelled like oranges, and even thirty years of silt cannot change a smell into a color.

“It is a blue,” Evi says gently, which is not the same as correction and not the same as kindness and not the same as surrender, but partakes of all three.

I stand there, holding a dress like a ridiculous man in a sad play, and the town goes on about the business of believing. On the far bank someone is singing an old river song about boys who went to sea when there was no sea and men who looked at the sky as if it were a terrible menu. On our bank someone is arguing with the municipal man about whether a river can be fined. The wind changes to bring the smell of fried fish and cinnamon and iron. Somewhere a child loses a tooth and does not notice.

I drape the dress over the railing to drip and reach again with the hook because the current has snagged something else under the boat, a stubborn weight that knocks three times and stops, as if it has considered the etiquette and finds it wanting. I kneel and balance and can feel Evi’s hands hovering a respectable distance from my back, ready to catch a man if he decides to fall. The hook catches. I pull. The thing comes up reluctant, then sudden, and in the instant when water releases anything, the world lifts a little around it, and in that lift is a space where something could speak.

When I have it on the deck, there is more water than jar, more rope than clock, more silt than skin. I am staring at a wooden crate, small enough to carry, big enough to mean. The slats are tight. The nails are old. In one corner someone burned a letter into the wood. I wipe the face of it with my sleeve. The letter is M. For many things. For mother, or marriage, or mouth. For mountain, perhaps. Or my name, which is not a letter people burn into anything.

“Why is it here?” Arta says.

“The river is no archivist,” Evi answers. “It doesn’t care about your categories.”

The crate has a lid that was hammered in with an enthusiasm I respect. I pry at it with the hook, then find the crowbar under the bench. The lid lets go with a sound like regret. Inside are bundles wrapped in waxed cloth. My hands go careful as I lift the first and the second, and the third. I could pretend I don’t know what they are, but pretendery only works when the stakes are low, and the river, even backwards, does not lower anything.

Letters. Letters waxed and wrapped against what was certain to happen. This is not a family’s tragedy; this is a town’s. I recognize the s of someone’s hand, the white of the police blotter paper, the fussy loops of a schoolteacher who wanted to be recognized however she signed. The fourth bundle is smaller. The wax has been sealed and re-sealed. When I move it, something skitters inside, and I think of bones. I set it down, ashamed of the jump of my heart.

The fifth bundle is not wrapped. It has the shape of a book and is bound in oilskin. I keep my hands from shaking and fail. I unroll the cover and the first page is a map drawn on cloth, inked with a thin, neat instrument. The map is our stretch of the Loren, from pines to reeds to mill, the pier drawn as a boy would draw his house, too tall and not enough windows. But this map is wrong. Or not wrong—older. The river is curled like an animal at ease with its own lines. There is a note in the corner in my mother’s hand: you are here even when you are not. My name is not there, but her hand is there, and I am suddenly and completely upended.

I do not fall. The world cannot be so kind. I sit. My knees take that as permission to stop being knees. The municipal man calls something to me that has no meaning. The children are kneeling in the shallows, making pretend cups of pretend tea and pretending to be invited to a life. Evi puts a hand on the back of my neck and says nothing. Arta looks at the letters as if they are birds he might fling into the air and see who they come to.

The jars of bees hum in their new language. The dress drips the last of its travel onto the boards and makes a shape that looks like a door. The sky finally chooses a direction to be. The river, superior and ridiculous, continues to walk up the hill it has always wanted. On the far bank, a woman raises both arms and then only one, like a semaphore for which I never learned the code. She could be anyone. She could be no one. She could be my mother, who was not the sort of woman to wave, and that is how I know that it is her. My hands fill with heat, which is the worst kind of hope, the kind that cooks the palms and leaves the fingers hungry.

“Do you see?” Arta asks.

“I see,” I say, and the word is a net.

It is the first chapter of the day and the river has already given back more than it meant. The boat rocks and finds its balance. The letters wait, the map breathes, the jar on the shelf quivers in that small way that makes you think of sleeping animals and clocks. Evi says, softly, “If you take me across now, we may not come back the same.”

“Good,” I say, though I don’t mean it. I mean, we will go, because the Loren once a year remembers its mountain, and it is polite to remember in turn. Because my mother on the far bank is an arrow drawn to its length. Because there are letters in a crate that were meant to arrive before they did. Because I am a ferryman and the backward day is the only day when the water is honest about loving both shores.

I pull the rope into my palm and taste iron. The engine quivers and then commits. In the shallows the eel’s backs gleam like negatives. The boat noses into reverse as the river and I agree for once which way is home.

The day June Keys came home, the river was breathing in the ditches again. The tide had learned the routes of the culverts and the culverts had learned to cough; every hollow in the road carried a thumbprint of sky. Mosquitoes lifted their thin churches from the shade and conducted a small, hungry service around her as she stepped out of the car. The house—raised on old brick piers, porch sagging like a mouth after a tooth—was exactly where it had always been, and yet it had the look of something that had kept still too long and collected a weather of its own.

You don’t know a house until you’ve sealed and unsealed it a hundred times, Alma used to say. Some walls keep air like lungs. She’d said it idly, in the kitchen, one of those summer days when the talk rose and fell with the kettle. She had been drying mason jars then, turning them open-mouthed into light.

June stood now beneath the porch roof with the funeral lilies shivering in the backseat, and the keys warm in her palm. Rain had fallen that morning because the sky here had always eavesdropped on grief, dripping respectfully onto cheap suits and small town dresses while casseroles congealed. They had buried her mother with hands on the tombstone that no one would admit were shaking, and then the church ladies had boxed the leftovers in foil. June had eaten nothing. It was enough to watch the potluck heat evaporate into the bright, and to think: another weather that would not be kept.

The front door stuck in its middle age, a shoulder required to convince it. The smell the house exhaled was not exactly familiar: some mildew, some lemon cleaner, the sweet dryness of old books, and underneath all of it the brined breath of the river. The tideline had crept past the marsh line these last years with a patience no human could have tolerated; rushes drowned and then adapted, growing their feet longer. When June left at eighteen she had promised herself she would never become one of the silhouettes you could see at dusk on Airplane Road, staring past their fences, gauging the water with a broom handle.

She put the lilies in the sink and turned the faucet to fill their throats. The kitchen window opened to the narrow yard where her mother had once tied strings of white shirts to a line and watched them snap like gulls. No shirts now. The line hung like a sentence with the subject missing.

On the kitchen table: a manila envelope in county-issued tan, stamped with the lawyer’s name in clean, mechanized letters. The will had been short because there was little to inherit. The house. The insurance money in a sum that would keep the house up a little longer, though not against water. The contents, which the lawyer had gestured toward in a way that assured June he had no idea what that meant in this particular case.

Contents: the cellar, locked since June’s seventeenth birthday. Contents: a key heavy enough to dent your palm. Contents: what Alma had spent three decades gathering, labeling and arranging with the kind of ferocious order some women applied to quilts or grudges.

June took the key out of the envelope and turned it over. Its teeth had accrued the tarnish of disuse. The weight of it pulled on her hand as if it had learned gravity too well.

She put off the cellar.

She walked the rooms that had been designed by the river’s breath: the front room with its two windows facing east, the faint square of lighter paint where a picture had hung; the hallway with its run of nails that had once borne coats, oaty in their absence; the bedroom where she had woken to storms and to the smooth, unreasonable dawns after them. Her mother had left everything arranged properly for a quiet departure. The bed made. The two glasses by the sink washed and drying. The magnolia leaves she had pressed in a dictionary thirty years ago still there in their pressed season, the flesh of them a polished brown.

The barometer, a weatherglass her father had found at a yard sale and given to her when she was fourteen, hung crooked. It had a crack crazing its crescent face. In the years since she had left, she had trained herself to learn weather by other means—pressure maps, satellite images, the calibrated data of a profession whose work was to control the uncooperative, or at least make infrastructure pretend to it. She had a job inland in a city with brown dust on its horizon, designing detention basins and drought-friendly berms to urge a reluctant water to wait. Out there, if rain came it came with the brittle smell of static, and people stood under overhangs and let it have at them like they were trying to remember. Here, there was no remembering without damp.

Eventually the house pressed her, as idle old friends will when they’ve been made to wait too long outside the real subject. June found the door in the hall that led to the cellar—a step down, then another, and the wood underfoot no longer finished. Alma had slid a deadbolt over this door with a seriousness June had resented at sixteen, had shouted about privacy and arbitrary rules and old-woman superstition while the river breathed patience at the end of the road. The lock had other ideas and no interest in adolescent justice. Things had been said that could not be put away, and then things had not been said at all. The lock had won and stayed closed. That was the closest June had ever come to violence in this house: throwing a fist of bobby pins at a sealed door, crying in a dry voice.

The key went in with a cold tolerance, turned. The bolt sighed back. When June put her shoulder to the door it held a second, then gave like a held breath let go.

The first thing that hit her was not the smell she expected. It wasn’t mildew or mold, the ordinary rot and seepage of southern basements. It was chalk and rain and the green cold of shade under grass, a bouquet of different hours and geographies staking the same small room. The second thing was the way the air changed as she took the first step: the foot on the top step stood in a late-July attic, the foot on the next in a March in a city with no leaves yet. At the bottom her skin pimpled. Gooseflesh lifted on her arms as if a hand had passed above her.

Shelves, floor to ceiling, filled the walls and the freestanding aisle in the center. The jars were there in their hundreds: mason glass and patent glass, old florist vases stoppered with wax, olive jars with their fuzzed labels scraped away. On each one, a strip of paper inside the glass with her mother’s square, stern handwriting in pencil that could not be erased by time it had never planned to negotiate with. Outside, adhered to lid and neck, was the sealing wax. Different colors. A small code June had never been taught all the way.

Three things clicked together in June in that second: the click of having been wrong for years, the click of comprehension arriving like a key in the right lock, and the softer click of grief, which was always a series of small shut doors. Old rage and old love shuffled to make room for a new guest.

She put a hand out. Glass sweat on her palm and damp made the label blur for a second before she focused: July 3, 1996. Fireworks at the Turnaround. It was sealed in blue wax. A safe jar. Harmless. June slipped her nails under the wax and it gave with a sound like the peeling of an orange. She unscrewed the lid.

The room exhaled a night warm enough to keep on skin. Pop. Another little sound, not in the jar but in the remembering space the jar made. The air made itself early-July precise: the blacktop soft, the barely-legal fireworks blooming like bruised peonies over the Turnaround where the road gave up and the river began, teenage arms bare and a boy’s laugh that she could not mesh with his later voice. The smell of hot dogs rolling on a kiosk grill ran its grease-laced line through the memory, and the tight-silver itch of mosquito spray on her forearms seemed to reappear.

And there were, undeniably, fireflies. Not insects that would have starved in a jar for twenty-seven years and turned to crumbs, not any living thing. But the quality of light did a trick of its own. In small corners of the cellar, at bread-box height, at shin level, spheres of dim greenish light went on and off irregularly, as if someone were blinking directly into June’s memory.

She shut the jar quickly.

The cellar remembered the closed shape of the jar and collected itself. The idea of summer left her skin but not her. She stood very still. She had come to bury or itemize, to be stern with herself, to do safe things with paper and signatures and never, ever to admit to the possibility that Alma’s hobby had been anything but a neat way to assign shape to the unshapable.

June had watched her mother make the jars all through childhood. Alma would catch the day by standing on the porch at dusk, holding a jar to the shimmering, and then she would bring it down in both palms, careful as a person carrying a full bowl and not wanting to spill. There were unconsidered days, of course, Monday days and days when she had a headache and had to lie down or the washing machine decided it would walk itself across the kitchen. But the bottles proliferated on the shelves and the handwriting stayed steady. There had been rules for opening, as for everything. Don’t do it alone. Don’t do it in anger. Don’t empty the jar in a place that wasn’t yours. People were less careful with their words than with their jars, she’d say.

June moved along the shelves now, reading, slower than she’d walked the rooms upstairs. The town’s history was arranged here in a lexicon of clouds. October 29, 2012. The day the church roof caved. May 14, 2000. Azaleas like gossip. February 3, 1993. Your father’s boots thawing by the vent. April 21, 2002. Smoke over Saint Therese. July 6, 1995. The day the twins fell into crabs. The labels were both exactly and insufficiently what they described; they were a life written in nouns and weather.

She found herself padding the air for some unthinkable name the way her tongue hunted a lost tooth. It was too much and she had wanted too little. She had sworn her adult life would be made of things you could measure: rain in millimeters, flood stages in feet, the amount of time it took a detention pond to let a storm go.

On the bottom row, on the furthest shelf back and left like a children’s book’s secret, a set of jars had been sealed in iron wire to their shelf. June crouched to see. There was nothing mystical about the wire—a hardware-store pragmatism. Her mother’s square knots in the fastening convinced June more than any incantation could have. These were not to be opened by someone curious and lonely at night.

The wax on them was red. The handwriting neat even where the pencil had worn thin. August 28, 2005. Wind learns your name. September 1, 2005. All the phones are tired. There were other years. Later storms. A winter that had broken pipes and dignity. A day the river had taken Mrs. Simms’s Newfoundland and returned it three days later full of marsh grass, making Mrs. Simms a story she would tell as long as anyone would listen. But the ones for late summer 2005, for reasons the whole town could have guessed at, had extra layers of wax and her mother’s caution like a smell around them.

June slid her hand along until she stopped on one she had not allowed herself, tuning up from a loose string in the back of her chest. August 31, 2005. The last day we saw your brother.

He’d been nineteen and ox-shouldered, sweet in the face. He had always made a little game when they went to the river bank together, stepping down to the water and then stepping back fast, letting the tide lick at his sneakers, retreat, come again. For being such a tall person he had been able to make himself air; he could vanish in a group of kids or in a grocery aisle and materialize humming next to you holding a packet of gum. This was not something a person could do to a river. But Appalachio boys had turned themselves into smoke for years—dust, enlistment, work, ghost—and then the water learned how to do it better.

We don’t use names as hooks, Alma had told them as children when she hung their pajamas on the line and wind made them proof that bodies existed. The river doesn’t mean harm by yours. It just likes to practice.

She closed her eyes and imagined the day entire—the sky low but fast, the branches making a racket like a stadium, the cupboards taped and the porch furniture brought inside with difficulty while they laughed at their own cursed luck. She had been working at the gas station then, programming the pumps to go to credit only, hearing the hush-hush about price gouging, watching people fill three tanks and drive away with a look that made her decide not to ask anyone for anything ever again.

June was reaching for the jar, her fingers fitted to its corona, when someone knocked at the cellar door.

Her body stood her up before she knew she meant to. The knock wasn’t Hannah’s—no impatient woodpecker tap of a friend trying to let you know she was more entitled to your time than any other job. It wasn’t the lawyer’s in that swollen way of men with clipboards. It was a careful, almost courtly knuckle-rap: I know this is a house waking up. I won’t wake it much more than I have to.

June walked up the stairs into the hall. The light from the kitchen made a path and definitely did not look down onto a cellar containing weather. She could have stayed a little longer and turned the jar, the way a person holds a coin under water to decide if it’s gold or gum wrapper. But the knock came again and she wanted to be a person who always answered, if only to prove to herself that she owed human reality precedence over weather.

On the porch stood Mr. Venn from two houses over, holding a pie.

“Miss June,” he said, though she’d never been called Miss anything by him in her life. He rotated the pie, the way old men do when the world was designed before they were and then reinvented while they weren’t looking. “What they make us put under foil, I swear. If you wanted to make a thing taste like a whisper.”

The pie under the foil had the damp look the inside of a cooler acquires. A condensation ocean in miniature ran along its pebbled surface.

“Come on in,” she said, because there is always script. He stood inside the doorway and looked toward the kitchen and then toward the hallway beyond it; his gaze brushed the cellar door and then it looked away respectfully.

“We all of us were sorry,” he said. This was something the town was good at: plural grief, practiced enough to be useful without becoming art. “Your mama kept a garden out back long after any of us would have given up. I told her the salt’d have all our tomatoes, but she said she’d boil it out of the dirt if she had to.” He smiled. “Told me not to tell her what the river could do. ‘The river,’ she said, ‘has nothing new to teach me that I don’t know the old way.’”

June gestured toward the table. “Thank you,” she said. She wanted him to say the other things people said. She wanted him to say there was a casserole of a memory somewhere, maybe in his wife’s pantry, that explained why a person would keep weather. She wanted him to say, your mother did not mean to be cruel. Or: she did not mean to teach you that the most important door in your house would always be the one you had been told never to open.

“She had a letter for you,” he said instead.

June looked up. “Did she give it to you?”

“She made me promise I’d deliver it if you didn’t turn up by the second of the month.” He cleared his throat. “She thought it would be decent if I brought a pie along so it wouldn’t be just an envelope at a door. I told her you’d come the day after her service. She said that was a river question, not one she wanted to answer.” He set the pie down and pulled a small envelope from the pocket of his jacket. Someone had folded it three times so precisely that the creases lined up like fence slats. On the front, Alma had written in the same hand as the jars: For June, when the pressure drops.

“If you need anything,” he added, and June wondered if he meant a tide table or a person. He took his hat off and then put it back on, a gesture that accomplished nothing except its own familiarity. She thanked him again and he humbly escaped.

The envelope had grit of graphite on it from the pencil that had made its lines. June slid a finger under the flap. The paper inside was the kind the county used, too thin. Alma had always written on both sides and that discipline had made her letters denser, like weather maps.

I won’t tell you not to be angry, it began. You can be whatever you want. But give yourself a place to be it that isn’t the river.

If we could have put better things in jars we would have. I mean money. Promises. Your father’s boat. I tried to keep for you what I could. It got out sometimes. Nothing is perfect.

There are jars you do not open and jars you do and neither kind will save you. You have to decide which hurt you came for.

If you are holding this it is because the pressure has changed. You know what that means better than I ever did. People in town think what I did was something like knitting. They use a needle word for it and say stitch the weather or catch a storm between your hands. I’ll let them call it that because they want it to be smaller than it is. I kept the day your brother went into the water. It is yours, not mine. You can open it when you can stand up straight in it. Don’t open it to fall down in. It knows which is which.

It isn’t all memory. That’s just what it does to us, to make itself reasonable. There is a thing bigger than that, and sometimes it gets into houses.

June held the letter closer. The handwriting faltered at the end and then recovered, as if the pencil had run out of itself and then been sharpened.

If you mean to sell them, sell them carefully. There is a woman will come to you who pretends to be the kind of person who would call them specimens. She isn’t. She works for a room with no windows. They would keep your brother in there longer than you can stand.

June did not realize until she set the letter down that she had been holding her breath. She put her finger against her throat. That was how you learned as a child whether the jar you were supposed to be filling with your voice was full yet—Alma would say stop singing and if the hum was still under your finger then keep it, keep it until it stood in your bones and made you taller.
