The phone buzzed on the counter and made a small throat of its own. A number from out of state. She let it go to voicemail. The ringing left the house emptier than silence had. She went to the sink, took the lilies out, shook water off their stems. Through the window she could see the back line of the yard where the ground leveled into marsh, and the narrow channel the neighborhood raccoons had walked all summer as if on pilgrimage. Water glittered there in a thin library of pages catching light in different languages. Beyond that, farther than morning sight usually let you see, a freighter was going by out on the river’s proper body, moving with that arrogant grace ships have when they carry everything you do not have.

On the hall wall beside the cellar door, there were three small dimples where Alma had once hung something heavy. June pressed the pads of her fingers there, as if to understand the negative of a thing might be enough to conjure it. She almost laughed. Rough magic.

The voicemail was from a woman whose voice moved politely, as if through cathedrals it owed, but was not devoted to. Ms. Keys, I’m Dr. Celeste Pereyra with the Institute for Domestic Climatology. First, my condolences. Second, I realize this is a difficult week to field inquiries, but I’ve admired your mother’s work as a student of ephemeral structures for some time. Her jars represent not only the persistence of folk meteorology under environmental stress, but a unique archive of affective atmospheres, as it were. I’d love to talk about preservation. The phone did a small digital bow and the voice ended.

June played it again, this time for the way the word preservation had to push its edges wider to make room for what it did not yet know. She thought about a windowless room. She thought about the blue wax jars that had seemed soft enough to open like eyes and the red wax jars that made the air at the back of her throat go cold.

She went back down.

On the third step she stopped. The cellar was not different. It was a cellar. But the air inside it had clothed itself in a small intention, like a person walking toward you who has decided at the last second that they will say your name after all. A thing bigger than memory, Alma had written. Sometimes it gets into houses.

When June reached the red-wax jar with the date that had been said in this town like the name of a mean cousin, she put both hands on it. The wire held it to the shelf with a stubbornness that June recognized in her own muscles. She slid the wire off. It said a sound against glass that was almost gratitude.

She didn’t open it. Not yet. She held it the way a person holds their breath until they can’t decide whether they’re hoarding oxygen or sorrow. She put her face close to the glass and her own breath clouded it.

“Danny,” she said, into the cellar air that kept so many versions of his voice, that would keep this one too. When she said his name, the barometer upstairs made a quiet tick. The pressure had dropped again. Outside, the light changed. Women in houses along Salt River Road moved to their doorways and, in the accustomed way of those who have learned to keep vigil without the word for it, they looked up and measured. The river exhaled in the ditches and then, with the unpretentious authority of an old god waking at dusk only because a human had said its name, drew breath to see what kind of jar it would have to make of the night.

On the twenty-third morning the sea laid out a wedding dress, six keys not belonging to the same door, a toy horse with its paint scorched to a smoky blue, and the kind of letter you can't put back once you've read it.

By then it was easier to believe the sea had found a system. On the first morning of returns, things were flung along the wrack like an argument—beer tabs stuttering into the eelgrass, a brass cuff from another place, a child's mitten, a watch still beating with someone else’s minutes. People had gathered with coffee and a city hall disbelief, hands on hips and phones lifted. A boy in red pajamas ran barefoot down the sand to show us the spark plug the ocean had coughed up, grinning as if it had coughed up the idea of sparks. The pastor had bowed his head as if we were at a wake. No one touched anything without looking left and right first, the way you do at an accident. We called the state, the state called the county, the county promised to call back. They still haven’t.

By day twenty-three, the items arrived in quiet arrangements, as though someone found the town's junk drawer and emptied it with an archivist’s hand. The dress was draped across the silvered bones of a pallet, sleeves pinned by seaweed. One heel of a satin shoe had lodged in the plank, and sand had risen to cover the toe. The keys made a flower—six spokes around a center shell. The horse was posed as if mid-whinny, its nonexistent mane arced by tide. The letter was folded tight in a plastic sandwich bag that had been knotted with fussy care, the knot fat and clean as if made in a kitchen. It had not been sealed with salt. Maybe someone put it in the sea that way. Maybe the sea had learned to protect certain things.

“Your sea is getting tidy,” said Rennie from the lifeguard chair. He had turned forty three times already, by which he meant he’d been turning forty all spring, telling anyone who’d listen and anyone who wouldn’t. He wore his whistle and the same sunburn as last year and kept his toes curled into the rung of the ladder. He calls me your when he means ours.

“Maybe it hired a clerk,” I said.

“Then it should pay you double. You're the only one getting up to meet it.”

He wasn’t wrong. Most of us had trained our alarms to the tide. People who’d lived six weeks of their lives without touching the beach now had a habit of walking its margins at dawn, their expressions set at worry or hope depending on what they’d lost and what they’d done. They came for people, mostly, which made the presence of objects feel indecent. The sea kept to itself about bodies. It returned other things in a teasing abundance: receipts that should have stayed in pockets, license plates from distant states, hairpins with a webbed cuff of somebody else’s scalp hair. It had sent us two teeth, gold-capped; three letters addressed to Grayhaven that had never been mailed from within it; a violin bridge; thirty-three jars—if you counted jars as it counted them, including a chipped ceramic sugar bowl and a glass ashtray the color of iced tea. This was what the sea admired about us, perhaps: our talent for keeping, our talent for losing.

I had a list. I am a person who makes lists, a fact both cause and consequence of my job. I carry a pencil behind my ear as if I am a carpenter and the town is something I am building true. I make a list of items to be retrieved and a separate list of things I notice and a third list of names that fall out of people's mouths like coins.

Today's list read: dress, keys (6, various), horse, bagged letter. Side list: terns above the channel have learned the noise of zippers. Smell of fish gut, smell of old glue, smell of the particular metal in those keys.

The horse was small as a hand, the paint bubbled from heat as if it had been too close to a stove. I turned it in my palm and a flake of blue came loose onto my skin. My mother had owned a horse like this, my grandmother said, when she was the kind of girl who’d tie her hair with a ribbon and not care when it slipped. They’d keep it on the knotted runner beneath the television, where dust lived. My mother kept nothing, not even the girl she had been, but my grandmother kept the hitching post: photographs glossy with fingerprints. I had looked for the horse among those pictures after my mother left, but it was never posed within reach. Here it was, a replica from a parallel shelf. I worked it into the evidence bag with my breath held. Salt has a way of sharpening memory, of tricking you that remembering is a skill you once had and simply forgot to practice.

Rennie watched. “My cousin thinks it’s some current we caught. Says there’s a gyre out there the size of Vermont and someone poked a hole in it.”

“And your cousin should apply for my job,” I said, and smiled in the direction of the water so he’d know I meant it kindly.

“But if it’s a current, why is it only landing here? The breakwater down at Coleman’s is bare as my kitchen table.”

“Grayhaven always was greedy,” I said, but he wasn’t wrong about the particularity of it. The tideline for half a mile bent its shoulder to us and no one else. The Coast Guard stationed on the point had chalked the wind on a slate and shrugged. A woman from the state lab had come with vials and a taut mouth, then gone again with a cooler and a promise to email preliminary reports. Meanwhile the town appointed me Keeper of Returns, a title which embarrassed me and then took my hand like a dance partner. The clerk at City Hall had printed it on card stock and taped it to the glass. It made people settle when they saw it. We like to believe our grief has a window to lean on.

Three girls in identical pink shorts were watching me from the soft slope of the dune, knees tucked, toes buried. They came every morning, which meant their mother woke them, which meant she had her own list she was trying to check—children, present and accounted for; the past, located and turned safely into story. The girls’ hair was damp at the tips. You can always tell who has slept with their head on a wet pillow. When I stood, two of them stood too, reflexively, as if they could be of use. I gave them each a task, because children bark like working dogs when you ignore their instinct to pull: hold this, carry that. They speculated as we walked. One’s father had lost his ring and was convinced the sea would hand it back only if he came alone; he had taken the habit of walking toward morning with an engaged intent that made strangers side-step him. The girls told me he had cried on the back step once—this was reported with equal parts awe and scorn, as happens at eight, as happens even later.

“Do you think it knows what we’re looking for?” the tallest of the three asked, not about the ring.

“I think it knows more than we think it does,” I said, which was both evasion and a kind of truth.

“Do you think it knows Nana?”

I did not answer. I had a rule against answering the questions whose answers make the air heavier.

Behind me, Rennie whistled. “Mara,” he said softly, like he was telling me I had dropped something. The letter had been angled by a shift in the tide, and sunlight was piercing the damp fold. The knot remained crisp as a new boy’s tie.

“Don’t," I said, and no one moved nearer.

People began to arrive in twos and threes. Mrs. Costa, who had taught me to read, who had a husband last year and a husbandless couch this one. A cluster of men who smelled like the back room of a hardware store. Two officers, who had learned to keep their hands low and open, who had learned to say please and maybe and not right now. Jonah was one of them. He walked with his shoulders quiet, and when he saw me he made his mouth into a line of something polite. He had a way of looking at my lists without looking at me. He had been mine, once, but it was an ownership that hadn't held across weather. The other officer, a stranger with a catalogue face, stooped to the keys and then looked up at Jonah, as if to ask whether they should be allowed to gleam there a little while. It had taken us a week to learn that sometimes people needed to see the thing before we bagged it. They needed proof that the sea had hands.

“We got a radio about a crowd,” Jonah said, unnecessary as always in his courtesy.

“Look,” Mrs. Costa said to no one and everyone, “who is that letter for?”

I glanced down, and on the outside of the plastic bag, someone had written, in pen that had run to blue with the water: For the One Who Let Me Go. I did not like the way the words sat there, unspecific and correct, like a dress you could fit yourself into if you breathed right.

“We’re logging it,” I said, too quickly, and picked up the bag as if that urgency could sew a seam around the privacy inside. The paper had browned like the crust of bread. In the Arc Room, I have a humidifier and a dehumidifier and never feel like I am using the right one. I have gloves and envelopes and a scanner that refuses to be bored. I am good at not peeking. I am good at leaving other people's truths folded until they are ready to be unfolded. But the label, their expectation that we make a ritual of the untying with witnesses—that was new. The first week, people kept their items and their secrets close, vaulting them like children over their ribs. Then it began to feel to some like a sacrament. The opening of a letter at the town hall was something like communion, the communal taking into yourself of one body. If there is blasphemy in that, please write it down in a gentle hand. We will file your letter in the drawer marked Doctrine and then lose the drawer.

“We can take it inside,” Jonah said, because he understood my rules and liked to make me enforce them.

“I’ll wait,” Mrs. Costa said, and stepped back, patient, as if she had all day for the sea and its chores.

“Better bring the dress too,” the stranger-officer said. “Before somebody decides it's theirs.” He had not yet learned the tone we used to keep people from circling a thing into an argument. Lafitte, his name tag said, black letters on a gold bar, which did not match anything about him and therefore fit.

I took the dress. Sand let go of the hem as if it had been meaning to all along. It left a damp outline on the pallet, a dark body, and I wanted to put the dress back where that dark body was, to pretend possessions have their own shock at losing their place. Its weight surprised me. It was heavy the way wet things are, dense in the belly. I turned my face to keep the smell off it. It was an old smell, not of salt but of closets and sugar. The satin had yellowed toward the seams, but the lace along the collar was fine as a breath caught on a cold morning. I thought of the photograph in the library’s local history cabinet, of the run of silk at Miss Hafferty's haberdashery, lengths falling like long punctuation marks, and how once, decades ago, a young bride might have stood in a dress like this and said the words for always and now someone had stood at a shore and let the dress go and been done with it, or someone had never stood anywhere at all and the dress had lived only in a promissory note, and the sea, not caring about narrative, offered us only the nouns.

At the City Hall, the Arc Room is just the room with the worst windows. We called it the Arc Room because a letter went to the paper announcing the Archive of Returns and someone at the Clearview Journal mistyped. The town liked it better. They like all our mistakes better when they come with a story attached. The room used to hold the assessor and his maps of lots; now it held people who were not their lots and my tables lined in craft paper. We had strung a clothesline from beam to beam, and on the line hung slips with codes I had invented and then expanded and then made ugly by adding letters in: GRH23:13 for Grayhaven’s thirteenth item on the twenty-third day, GRH23:13b for the second item in a bundle, because the sea sometimes tied things together and who was I to disband them.

Rita from the bakery had brought me coffee with a lid I couldn't tame. It wept onto my knuckle as I tugged the letter's knot. We had overflow detectors in the ceiling already; water found ways. I had put on gloves, thin ones you could see your hangnails through. The girls had followed me inside with their glossy seriousness, and Mrs. Costa stood with her handbag on her forearm like a small animal. Jonah leaned against the door, his radio finding its own reasons to speak. He had a new scar on the ridge of his wrist. He caught me catching it, and tucked his hand out of sight, his mouth making that shape again. He had told me once that every job is an apprenticeship in deciding when not to touch. We had been a job for each other, once, and passed that test sometimes.

I put the letter on the table under the light, the way you lay a person in a photograph: gentle, as if the gentleness makes up for something terrible that happened already. Mrs. Costa breathed out. The knot loosened like it had been waiting for me; it came apart with a small noise. The plastic uncurled, and the paper crisped as it breathed new air. The ink had slipped, making a stain under each letter like a shadow.

For the One Who Let Me Go, it said again at the top. There was no date. There was a salutation, Dear, and then a name, and the name was not mine. It was a name I would learn, because the letter was like a stone in a hand you can't pass to someone else without feeling its weight for yourself. I read the first line because everyone had turned their faces to me and the read in my mouth seemed the same size as the read they had come to do.

I read it aloud. “I am writing from beneath,” I said, and stopped. The word made the room tilt. The letter was not mine, which meant it likely belonged to someone who would come, person after person crossing our threshold with their eyebrows up, their palms nervously oiled, hoping the bottom had a voice hired to their own beating.

Beneath, we understood, could mean water. It could mean earth. It could mean the way a past sits under present things and presses its chill upward until certain moments have to be warmed. People would stand in front of things and try to decide whether they could survive knowing.

“I should stop here,” I said, and looked to Jonah because his job was to be my muscle when my no grew thin.

He nodded, and made a slow open of his hands. The girls sighed as if I’d shut off a cartoon.

“We'll catalog it,” I said. “We'll call names. We'll ask you to raise your hand if—” and then I couldn't make myself say if the letter is yours, because if it was theirs, it would be because the one who let them go had thought to fold paper and seal air and test the ocean's mail system. That felt like an act more intimate than the letting had been. I thought of the letters I had not written and could not now.

The line at the door had deepened. People had learned the signage, had learned that patience meant better information, and better information meant a better chance of leaving with the thing they had woken up wanting.

“Do you know your nose bleeds when you’re thinking too hard?” a small voice said, and I looked up, startled, puzzled at the truth of my face. The smallest of the pink-shorted girls stood on tiptoe on the backs of her sandals. She made a delicacy of arrant facts, as children do—say the odd thing, receive love, repeat. I touched my upper lip and came away red. If it is possible to bleed politely, I did.

“Oh, Mara,” Mrs. Costa said, fishing in her bag for a tissue as if this were a classroom and she were still my teacher. The bag had a wealth of tissues, fruits of a lifetime of preparedness. She pressed one to my hand, and I tilted my head back as if laying myself down, the ceiling’s water stain finding me with its map of a continent we do not have the fare to visit.

The blood felt like a message you can't read. It made green taste in my mouth. Jonah stepped to the table and turned the letter back onto itself, a kindness. He reached for the dress then, though it lay at a careful remove, and his fingers brushed the lace and then recoiled and he put his hand to his wrist like he was swearing an oath. We were all learning the way a thing will talk to you if you let it—the way the dress could briefly be everything about the day you were meant to have and did not, or everything about the day you had and are now trying to forgive.

“Put it in A,” I said through the tissue. Drawer A was for the things that spoke too loudly. We had made it up the day the sea returned a rusted bicycle bell that belonged to a boy who had pedaled out of town with his breath a wheeze and never pedaled back. The way his mother's face reacted to the bell—how it closed and then opened like a door shoved against a soft drift of snow—made us decide there must be a drawer that let us pause. You never think about the ways you will need to make time kneel for you until the day presents its knee.

After the letter and the dress settled into their temporary alphabet, I went back to the beach because there is always something new where the line of foam unfastens and then refastens its work. The sun had climbed into confidence. By ten, everyone’s shadows hug their shoes. The beach smelled like low tide organizing itself for a party. Down by the point I saw a man kneeling with his back to me, his hands up to his hair. He was making the movement of prayer without the necessary language. From the curve of him, I knew him. There is a way a person from home holds their spine that even a decade cannot edit.

He heard my sand and turned. The hair had gone thin along the crown; the face had learned a shape called father; the eyes were still the particular gray of a day with weather. “Noah,” I said. He lifted his palm out of reflex. We had told the sea other names, but the sea was not present for that. The name we had kept for each other was still allowed to stand.

“Something came for me,” he said. His voice was low and polite. He had a politeness that made people trust him without cause. He was not wearing his badge—it was his day for the other job, the one where he laid flooring in houses that would be second houses for the kind of people who put their second houses on the calendar like a dentist appointment.

“Do you want company,” I said, and did not add, you don’t.

He tilted his chin to the sand. There, where the sea had drawn a curve as neat as the inside of a shell, lay a small plastic wristband threaded with hospital air. White, with blue printing. The words were simple as broth. Name: M. Qadir. Date: 03/13. Time: 06:54. Sex: F. Above those, the name of the hospital where we had never met a nurse like the one who told us jokes as if we were people who would respond to kindness by staying. Grayhaven does not have a hospital. To be born, to be mended, we drive.

It was my name. It was not my date.

“Before you say anything,” Noah said, because he will forever believe he has the right to speak just before me, “I didn’t put it there.”

“I know,” I said. And I did. Noah was not a person who could manipulate water. He once cried in the triangle space behind his mother's shed because of a picture of a dog with eyes like something on fire. He is a person you could love if you were prepared to be watched by a witness.

He rubbed the heel of his hand against the back of his neck, smearing sand. “I thought you should see it before—before someone else decided it was theirs. I mean, it is yours. Except it isn’t.”

The band was cool to the touch. The plastic had not silted with salt. It had an elastic give as I pressed my thumb against the barbs that would tighten it around a newborn's ankle. My date is in September. My mother told me I arrived with the smell of apples on her skin. The bracelet suggested otherwise, suggested a March dawn. As if I had been born twice, or as if what I knew about myself was a story someone had folded and slipped into my mouth the day I learned language and I had been chewing it ever since.

“These are for infants,” I said, as if he didn’t know. I turned the band in my hand, trying to coax it into another answer, trying to read a message hidden in the plastic’s seam. The girls from the dune could have slipped it over their wrists like a joke. The date printed under my name was three digits uninterested in my personal theory of myself. I became suddenly aware of my mother, of her hair against my cheek, that one time on the wharf when she lifted me as if someone else had wanted to see my view and she was willing to carry me higher until they could. For all of my adult life, my mother had been a narrative I layered onto small objects. A river stone rubbed thumb-thin with softness; a tin of throat lozenges from a winter when she believed in the medicinal properties of sugar; a barrette in the shape of a whale that she had held in her mouth while the boat lines bit her fingers. That barrette had washed up on day two and I’d put it in Drawer A and then I’d taken it out when the Arc Room was closed and laid it on my palm and spoken to it as if it were a shell.

“Maybe it was another M. Qadir,” Noah said weakly.

“There are not many of us," I said, which I meant about my last name and something else. My father carried it into town like a storm front—curly hair and a laugh like a caught oar and a family in Karachi who wrote letters that took three weeks to arrive and always began with rain. He left with the boat one August and didn’t come back, which is the way you explained things here: he just didn’t come back. My mother left via land. It is the sea's fate to be blamed for everything we cannot count.

“What are you going to do,” Noah asked, the sentence not quite a question.

I slid the bracelet into the mouth of my bag. It vanished with a small clack against the zipper pull, a sound like fate being tidy. I said, “I’m going to put it in a drawer,” and I did not specify which.

When the wind came off the bay, it carried the smell of kelp and something faintly sweet. People were still at the line where the water put down its throatful of offerings. I could see Mrs. Costa's handbag glint white where it caught the sun. I could hear Rennie’s whistle, and how it pretended to be in charge of anything but the air it pushed. I could feel the bracelet prick against the fabric of the bag, like a child loosening herself, like an idea.

“The sea remembers everything,” my grandmother always said, and then she’d smack the table as if memory were a fly she could kill. She believed in forgetting as a civic duty, like paying taxes. Remembering had gotten her into trouble. It got me into a room with a sign that spelled Arc and meant Archive. It got us into a season where items arrived with a logic that was not our own, where the daily work was to make meaning or make do.

Back in the Arc Room, I set the bracelet on the table and stared at it until it warmed under the light. I wrote down the name, the date, the time, my own skepticism. I wrote the phrase admission band and circled it, because that was its official name, because the object demanded it. I printed on a slip GRH23:19. I hung it from the line to dry like a thing that had been washed. Above my head, the line dipped with the weight of other people’s wanting.

Outside, the sea took a breath and lay back down. Inside, the dehumidifier hummed, uncertain whether what filled the room was water or something that behaves like it. I pressed my fingers to the corners of the table and stood that way a long while, as if bracing as we turned into a next thing.

On the morning the river changes its mind, a letter I should not open is rasping in my bag.

The zipper teeth nibble it all the way down River Road, where moss knits the guardrail into a green scarf and the mailboxes lean like old men at a bus stop, shoulders to each other. It’s not a miracle, what the river does. The tide rams itself up our throat twice a day, and at the turning it can drag even the most stubborn current back toward the mountains. Still, after a week of unseasonable heat and then a bark of wind overnight, the surface is a sheet of opal in the early light, and it is disorienting to see our ripples uncurling the wrong way, unspooling their braid, like someone has reached into your chest and reversed the pump.

I tell myself not to look at the bag. I tell myself to look at the road: at the foxglove in clotted bloom, the scatter of beer cans moldering in the ditch, the stump that last winter’s flood stooped into a chair for crows. My father taught me to keep the route in my bones. The river will try to pull your eyes, he said, and it’s not your job to go where it goes. That was when we still used sorting cases the height of our ribs and pushed a canvas cart in shoes that leaked after two months. When you had to read the weather in the paper and your patron’s marriages in their handwriting. When a letter from the Bureau of Rural Services wouldn’t come with a little blue map at the bottom showing the exact angle your town makes with the national grid and a tidy square around it. The tidy square means something is about to be tidied.

I’m not the first in my family to carry other people’s words. My father walked this route for thirty-three years, and before that my grandmother carried a pouch of prayers to doorways in a place that is no longer on any map except the one she kept inside her mouth. In that language, our language, the word for river is the same as the word for throat. “Because it is where the voice of the land comes out,” she told me once, cracking a walnut against the heel of her hand, the table sticky with the syrup she had boiled out of fir tips. “And because you can drown in either if you do not listen.”

We used to practice listening for whole afternoons. She’d put out six cups and fill them with different waters—tap, well, rain barrel, snowmelt left too long on the stove so it smelled faintly of iron, runoff slicked with wood smoke, an old bottle of water my aunt had brought back from the sea. She’d cover my eyes with the dish towel. Taste and tell me which is the one that has seen fish. Taste and tell me which is the one that remembers a root. I could tell, I swear I could, though maybe that’s only what she wanted to teach me: that a thing carries its path inside it. That if you learn the path of a thing you can know where it is, even when you cannot see it.

The first box on my route today belongs to the Everlys, who bolt and unbolt their sign in front of the farm depending on the season, block-printing what they pull from the fields in black. In February it says “EGGS.” In June it says “EGGS AND FAVA” and the fava pods hang like green tongues from their trellis. During August and September it says “EGGS AND FAVA AND TOMATOES AND PLUMS” and there is an exclamation mark. People think farmers are simple until they try to grow anything. The Everlys have ten different words for the soil after rain.

Mrs. Everly is in the yard when I pull up, bent over her rows. A tuft of white hair escapes her bandanna and her hat is tugged down over her eyebrows. She is either older than the river or younger than her hands. She hears the gravel crunch and stands and uses the back of her glove to mark a line across her forehead, leaving a comma of dirt.

“You hear?” she asks before I can say good morning.

“Hear what?” I ask, and I know what she means, but when you are carrying a letter you shouldn’t open you learn how not to say yes to anything.

“The river,” she says. “It’s arguing with itself.”

“I like to think it is practicing a new song,” I say, which is a thing my father once said. I tuck a seed catalog into her box between a bill and a postcard from her granddaughter, who is making a careful empire of succulents on a fire escape in a city that has four bakeries on one corner and a pawn shop around the other. The postcard is of a cactus with hair like a little old man. It says “lol is this you.”

“You and your jokes,” Mrs. Everly says, which means she will bring me a paper bag of green beans at the end of the week if the rabbits don’t get into them the night before.

I pull away and the bag whispers against my ribs, and I rehearse the argument I will need: that it is not my letter. That it is addressed to the Postmaster of Shoals, and even though I carry the key to the office and I sign the timesheets and I sweep the grainy sawdust of paper into the trash and I am, for all practical purposes, a postmaster—I am not the Postmaster. The title belongs to a man in a town I have never visited who signs forms in blue ink. There are rules even in things that are dying.

Shoals is not a town so much as a congregation of stubborn continuances. Four streets spider-webbing from an intersection the locals insist on calling “the four corners” although there are only three because the river used to be a road before we learned better. A post office with seven boxes and the rest general delivery. A school with four grades in one room and a teacher who commutes from Cinder Bend and is always leaving us for long weekends and bringing back little treats for the children like dried mango or stories about the dinosaur skeleton in the museum there that you can walk under and feel forgiven. A church hall that’s been a kitchen for more funerals than weddings. A handful of houses that look as if they grew where a hand set them down in a hurry, which is precisely what happened. A diner that opens when Ruby can find eggs. Once there was a cannery, and before that there was a docking point, and before that there were holes in fir bark cut by hands that never learned the names of their own moths. The Boreal Development Company has sent men out twice in three years to take pictures of our shoreline when the tide is low. The second time they brought a drone and forgot to keep it above the tree line. It went down in my neighbor’s cedar like a weird silver crow.

I take my time with the next boxes. At the second box, the dog is a scuffle of fluff trying its best to remember the duty its lineage has given it. It barks to let me know it remembers. I smile to let it keep its pride. At the third, someone has tied a ribbon on the little flag and the ribbon is already rain-puckered and beautiful, and I know it is their boy’s birthday. At the fourth, I find a magazine with a woman on the cover drinking green juice out of a jar that looks like one my grandmother would have used to trap nail polish smell in the bathroom. The woman on the cover is stretched like a rubber band into a shape no spine could hold. For a moment I feel the old bite of envy I used to feel when I was sixteen and the town would be invaded by girls in shorts thinner than thought, their laughter like little bells as they lay on the river stones that drank and drank and never looked sated. That queer, bright ache that I learned late to name. I slide the magazine into Mr. Forten’s box, say the weather in my head in three different tongues.

At the fifth box, the box is dented. At the sixth, the box is full of poems printed off and folded into squares I don’t have to read to know are about how the sun touches the hill. At the seventh, the box belongs to Toma.

He lives in a house that used to be a bunkhouse and before that a barn and before that a tree. It is sinking into its own shadow and he has propped it up with anything he could find: a bright yellow road sign with a bear on it that he says fell off a truck, a length of cedar trunk he peeled himself in the spring before his knees went bad, a pile of books that don’t notice their service. My mother says people love this kind of thing until storms come, and then they complain the state didn’t save them from themselves. I think it is a miracle to see what holds us and know it is not what it was meant to be. The yard is a tangle of berry canes and boat parts. The boat parts have not belonged to a boat for a long time, and maybe that is how boats always end: spread out like ribcages around a yard, the memory of a keel under every rain.

He hears my truck and is already on the porch, his hand raised like a schoolboy’s. He wears the orange knit hat that belonged to his wife even though the morning is too warm. A fish hook winks from the brim where she had stuck it for luck and never took it out. He is holding a wad of letters as if to hand them back to me. On days when his fingers are far away he gives me his outgoing in a crumpled bouquet, and if I do not pull in each paper one by one they will all drift to the floor like leaves.

He says, “Come,” and the word is in our language, and I drop the brake and get out and climb the four stairs that are all different heights because his nephew ran out of wood and good sense halfway through building them. I greet him in the old words, the words that taste like salt in the back of the mouth, and the skin around his eyes dissolves into twenty years ago. The lines there are so delicate they look like lifting fog. It is like watching somebody take off a heavy pack.

“Tell me,” he says, with ceremony, and holds his hands out, and I pretend I am giving him something grander than the electric bill, the pension check, a letter from the hospital with the red mark on it that says what red marks always say.

He takes the letter from the hospital and leaves the rest in my fingers. “Later,” he says. “Always later.” He puts the red letter under one thigh. He taps the seat of the rocking chair beside him with the back of his fingernails. “Sit,” he says. “No, wait.” His eyes brighten. “First.”

He disappears into the dark of the house and returns with a small object wrapped in wax paper. When he unwraps it, the porch smells like candles at the bottom of a drawer. It is a little piece of driftwood carved into the shape of a bird, smooth with handling. He has carved a bird like this for every child born in Shoals for forty years. He carves them even though the little ones get smooth too quickly, in their mouths, in their little fists, and fall between the boards. Some of the children have moved away and sent him pictures of the birds on white mantels in cities where the mantle is for candles you are not supposed to light. Some have put the birds on shelves in trailers that move with the wind. He does this because his own child was a little bird who did not stay.

“This one is for the new one,” he says. “The Everlys’ nephew. They brought him home in a blanket you could see the future through. Name?”

“It’s Rowan,” I say, and he says the word and rubs it into his mouth like lotion.

“Rowan,” he repeats in our language, as if to see how the syllables sit in there.

“And how are you,” I ask, and he cocks his head the way he does when he is listening to a small noise behind a big one.

There is the fizz of the cottonwoods and the heavy hush of the river going the wrong way. My truck cooling. A mosquito with a tiny violin. His breathing.

“I am,” he says finally, and grins with a kind of brightness that is not a lie but not the truth either. He pats his own chest with the flat of his hand, the old sign for beating heart, for still here. Then he frowns, and for a moment his face is as blank as a plate. “I forgot the word for—” He searches. It is an old thing to watch him search, like watching a dog try to remember where it buried the bone two winters ago. He lifts his hand and pinches the air in front of his nose like he is plucking a hair. “When the name hides behind a door,” he says, “and you can hear its feet but it won’t run out, it only laughs.”

We do have a word for that. My grandmother used it at the stove when she couldn’t find the word for the wooden spoon, when she turned in her chair toward me and then laughed at herself and said, “I put the thought down somewhere too careful.” But I do not say it. Sometimes people need the mercy of making a thing together.

“Let’s make a word,” I say. “What does it taste like? Does it taste more like smoke or like coin?”

“Coin,” he says immediately. “Cold between your fingers and one side smoother than the other.”

“Like the note in music where the throat winces,” I say, and hum it. “Like when you mean to knock but your knuckles are soft.”

“Like the cat went into the room and you shut the door but the cat is on the other side looking at you with eyes that are not sure if they belong to you anymore,” he says rapidly, thrilled, the way he always is when a new thing is being birthed.

“Laka,” I say. It comes up my throat like a bead blipped up by a diver. Not sure. Raw. But good in the mouth.

He nods. “Laka,” he approves, and says it four more times with different longings in his mouth, the way you try a shoe in the store. He points at me. “You keep a list, June,” he says. “Tell me where you write them down.”

“In the blue notebook with the bent corner,” I say, and he smiles because he knows it is under the breadbox.

“You keep it safe,” he says, serious now. “You keep it even safer than the letters.” He points at my bag, and even though he doesn’t know what is rasping at the bottom of it, he probably does.

“Do you know what the word is for when the river goes backward?” he asks suddenly, as if he has been holding it in his mouth since I pulled up but it has turned to lightning in there and he has to get it out.

“I know two,” I say, grateful, unexpectedly, for the solid fact of them, the way they make a little shelf in my head to put the morning on. “There’s ‘ulufa’ for when the tide pushes the top and the underneath keeps going where it always went. And there’s ‘sulur’ for when even the rocks at the bottom are thinking about giving up and following the moon.”

“‘Sulur,’” he says reverently. “The foolish wind. The second son.” He sighs. “I love that one. It sounds like being pulled by your shirt.”

“The tide has sharp teeth today,” I say, and we listen to the long hiss of it through the reeds.

He picks up the red-marked letter from under his thigh, not because he wants to read it. He points to it the way you might point at a snake sunning itself on a path. “They say my blood has made too much of itself in one place,” he says in the normal tongue, careful now, because sometimes the bigger nouns in our language take a toll on his breath. “They burned it a little. It did not behave. It has cousins. I am a party.”

The porch slats press into my palms. In the language he taught me, there are seventeen words for kinds of water and nothing for “insurance.” In the language the hospital speaks, there is a word for everything except the thing I want to ask, which is: what will you leave me, and what must I carry.

“You let me know if you need to go,” I say instead. “We’ll get you there. I’ll drive you myself, I swear.”

He nods, and his eyes skip from my face to the river to my face. He is not listening exactly, he is taking a picture to put in a room where he keeps things he might need later.

“You will do a thing for me,” he says then. He reaches into the pocket of his coat, where I expect to see a clean handkerchief or a boiled sweet he will pretend he bought for me. The thing he brings out is a small book the size of my palm, wrapped in oilcloth like a sandwich. He places it on my knee. “When I can’t find the rooms,” he says. “When I look at your face and I say, ‘Girl who brought me the bird,’ and you are standing there with your hands like that,”—he mimics me so perfectly I feel my hands curl—“you bring me this. You tear the red ribbon from it. You read the first page to me. You say the old name of the river and the name of wind that sounds like a goat, and you keep going until I wake up.”

The book is heavier than it looks. It has my grandmother’s idea of neatness: good enough, and then a flourish at the end, a little rope of ink that drips out after the knot. I realize with a kind of clattering surprise that this is a book I have never seen.

“What is it?” I ask, forgetting for a moment everything else I am holding—the bird in its nest of wax paper, the student loan bill in my pocket that hasn’t been paid since last fall, the way the blue envelope in my bag hums against the zipper like some strange moth.

“A word-net,” he says simply. “From the island. Your grandmother never showed you because by the time you were born she had decided it was for those of us who had already crossed. But she told me if she died before me then I must give it to you. She made me promise,” he says, and he pronounces the word “promise” like a dry twig, snapping it.

The book in my hand is a damp stone. The oilcloth is a promise of not letting go. A part of me that I didn’t know I still had lifts up and shows itself like a fish touching the surface. It has a slit of a mouth and a little silver smile.

“Thank you,” I say, and he bats the words away as if they are flies.

“Do not thank me,” he says. “If you thank me it will mean I am not here to see you open it, and then I will be dead twice.”

We sit. The river pulls and pulls in the wrong direction, practicing its other life. The scarf of moss on the guardrail shines. A boy’s bicycle goes by with a bent wheel that kisses the fork with each revolution, a silver chime. Somewhere downstream, the Boreal Development Company’s men will be polishing their drone.

“I forgot something,” Toma says, and laughs.

“What’s that?”

“Your name,” he says cheerfully, in the ordinary language, as if this is very funny. “It went behind the door. There is a word for that,” he says, bright again, triumphant. “Good. We are fine. I am not an old fish. I can smell the coin. Laka,” he says, proud of himself.

“Laka,” I say, and I say my name for him the way I would say it to a customs officer, careful with its edges. “June.”

“June,” he repeats, and puts it on his tongue and then in his pocket.

I stay longer than I should. Every minute I stay makes the blue envelope in my bag heavier. It is addressed to the Postmaster of Shoals in a font that thinks it is helping. It is exactly the weight my father’s hat had in my hands after he died, and if I open it, I might wring water from the paper.

At the corner where River Road meets the old mill track, I stop and watch the water. It is easy to see a force for malignance in something so sure. We put our picnic blankets a foot farther up the bank every year and pretend we always liked that patch of shade better, that the grass is softer there. Last fall, a girl whose mother I know only because she used to work at the diner and made me grilled cheese with a tomato slice as if I were a special kind of citizen fell from the rope swing when a knot gave way. She landed in three feet of water and broke her arm at an angle that made me sit down on the grass. Later she said, “The river wasn’t thinking about me,” and I wanted to tell her how comforting that is, in the right mood.

I go back through town, past Ruby’s diner. The sign in the window says “We Have Pie” even though all she has is tart, and today it’s lemon. The chalk of the words is a little smeared from when she forgot it was raining the day she wrote them. There is a new notice on the corkboard outside the post office, printed with a logo that looks like a wave wrapped in a ribbon. “Public Hearing on Shoreline Redevelopment,” it says. “Opportunities for Community Input.” Below it, someone has written in ballpoint, small enough that you have to go close to read it: “Water doesn’t go to meetings.”

Inside the post office, the air is its own kind of cool, a little sugar to it from the envelopes. Our sorting case is a shelf someone made in shop class and left unvarnished so the wood has been drinking anything we spill on it for twenty years. I put the little carved bird on top of the discarded label maker that we keep because it makes Toma laugh to imagine what it would label if we let it: river, bird, regret. I hang my bag on the hook behind the counter and reach into it without looking. If I look I will open it.

There is a feeling like swallowing a spoonful of water and finding it too clear. A feeling like the river moving in my throat.

I break the seal.

The letter is three pages and says what I knew it would say in the voice of someone who has practiced sounding sad. The budget has budgets inside it. The routes have been recalculated. The needs of the larger body have been weighed. “Staggered transition to centralized service,” it says, and “residents will be advised of their new pick-up location,” and “thank you for your decades of dedicated service, which, though no longer fiscally sustainable, remain an important part of the story we tell ourselves about who we are.”

At the top right corner there is a tidy square around our town. The tidy square has a little number in it that corresponds to a legend farther down the page, where, if the print were just a little bolder, you could read the note that says we are a pilot project. We have always been a pilot project, for anything that looks good on paper from far away.

I set the letter on the shelf. Then I set it on the counter because it looks less official there. Then I tuck it under the blue notebook with the bent corner. The notebook is warm, as if it had been sitting in the sun.

Outside, the afternoon makes a sound like a held breath. Ruby will pull down the shades to keep the diner from heating up. The Everlys will lie down for twenty minutes and then get up like they are still tired. The children will go to the blackberry patch with bowls and come back with bowls of blood. Toma will sit on his porch with his hat on and try to decide whether to open the red-marked envelope, and then he will feed the envelope to the stove. The drone will study the fringe of reed canary grass and report that it is invasive. The river will tilt and practice its other name.

When my father retired, he took his hat off and held it like an egg. “The thing about carrying something,” he said to me then, the night before he died, because he was a man who practiced the words he needed ahead of time, “is that if you set it down too fast it will crack. You have to figure out how to put it somewhere it won’t break before you’re done holding it. That is the whole job.”

The bell above the door rings, a bright little apology. The first person to come in is Mr. Forten, magazine tucked under his arm, who says, “June, tell me you saw the river this morning,” and the second is Ruby, holding a paper bag of lemons that she will forget on the counter and come back for at closing, and the third is a woman I have never seen before, with boots that probably cost more than my truck and hair that looks like every hour in a salon is a lullaby. She says, “Hi! I’m here to see about a box,” in a voice that puts exclamation marks where other people put breath.

“Of course,” I say, and pass her the form, which asks her name and whether she understands our hours, which are written in a way that suggests we mean them.

She says her name in a way that makes me accidentally try to speak it in my grandmother’s mouth. It will not go. There is no word for her in any language I have.

“Welcome,” I say. “We don’t have much,” I add, “but we have everything we need.”

She looks at the walls, squinting as if there might be a treasure she has heard rumors of, something not nailed down.

“Except maybe a little more light,” she says, and smiles, like we are in on the same joke.

“Light costs,” Ruby says over the lemons.

The woman laughs. “Doesn’t everything?” she says, and on that we agree.

On my way home, I stop beside the river again and say the old words under my breath because there is no one to hear me and because sometimes you must say the thing its right number of times to make it visible. “Ulufa,” I say, for the surface trying on a new dress. “Sulur,” I say, for the rocks thinking about walking. “Laka,” I say, for the name that hides behind the door, which at the moment is “Shoals.” Which at the moment is “post office.” Which at the moment is “June.”

When the sun gets low enough to set the tops of the firs on fire, I go to my kitchen and set the little oilcloth-wrapped book on the table. My cat puts one paw on it and looks at me to see if this is a game. It isn’t. In the next room, the radio says words like “heat dome” and “historic,” as if history is something someone else did and we get the dome. I untie the red ribbon. It is true red, the kind of red that, when you were a child, you would use too much of because it looks like fruit. The knot is tight and then it yields. I fold the oilcloth back.

The first page is not paper. It is a thin piece of wood shaved like a page. It has a grain in it like a fingerprint. My grandmother’s handwriting runs across it in a script that sits squarely on the line and then leaps. The words there are words I have not seen since her mouth moved. The first one is the old name of the river. The second is a wind that sounds like a goat. The third is the word for a thing you carry too long and forget it is not your heart.

Chapter One

In the museum, the weather was not allowed to touch the visitors.

Signs said so in a friendly font, blue and soft as a sky you could trust: Please Do Not Touch The Weather. The docents said it too, because someone always reached out. Here, thunder lived in velvet boxes and the storms were tamed, swaddled into jars with rubber seals. The children filed past, fingers twitching, as if the air itself were the temptation.

Mara made sure the air was obedient. She watched how it moved in the halls—where it pooled, where it rushed when the doors breathed, how it skimmed the glass displays as if looking for a seam. She wore her hair pinned up in a steel clip because loose strands thrilled to static, and her keys hung on a blue lanyard between her ribs like a small ocean.

“Is this all real?” a boy asked, pressing his nose to the panel that held a slice of fog collected from the western ravine. The fog floated behind glass like a ghost forgetting what it had come for.

“It’s real,” said Mara, and kept her voice somewhere between lullaby and fact. That was the tone the museum required: the kindness of a map, the distance of a storm seen from another country.

“You stole it?” another boy said, almost gleeful.

“We borrowed it,” said Mara. “We promised to return everything we keep.”

“Can we touch it?” A girl with chipped purple nail polish held her hand a centimeter from the fog’s barrier. Her eyes were wet and bright. It had been a month since the last rain; the city’s public fountains were turned into planters.

“We don’t touch the weather, and the weather doesn’t touch us,” Mara said. “We look. We listen.”

The museum had been a power station once. Its windows were tall and skeletal; light slid along the concrete floors. You could still see the ghosts of old turbines in the marks left behind, the clean arcs on the floor where metal had taken a decade to decide to leave. The river was a block away, and sometimes you could smell it: mud and cold tin, a faint sweetness where algae screamed at the sun.

Mara walked the group through the Rooms by order of risk: first Heat, then Winds, then Precipitation, because people were easily dazzled by anything that fell. The Heat Room was a corridor lined with panes of treated glass; behind each pane was an afternoon, labeled with its year and coordinates, its former sky: 19 August 2032, 110° F, Salina. The Salina afternoon was amber with wheat and flies; standing near it felt like feeling your hair grow. The children slowed, eyelashes damp with sweat that belonged only to themselves.

“Who measured it?” asked a boy with a backpack shaped like a shark.

“People like me,” Mara said. “We have tools.” She did not say that the tools made her feel like a thief: funnels and mesh boxes and copper gutters set along roofs around the city, where wind and vapor and heat could be coaxed to enter. Etymologists might have envied her instruments, for their delicacy.

The Wind Hall was Mara’s favorite. Its corridor was a set of rooms with narrow thresholds, each containing a wind with a name you could speak. Half the winds in the museum were borrowed from the sea, and half from deserts, and some had been gathered from the edges of fires, where air leans in and leaps away. The exhibition text had a humor that the board had not liked: “Please tie down any loose ideas before entering.” Mr. Hsu had kept it, in the large way he kept small rebellions. He had pink, tender ears and an affection for inappropriate levity. “These winds,” he always said on his tours, “have paid their fees.” Children loved him. He retired last winter, but wandered the office anyway like a man who had left his house and forgotten why.

Today, Mara guided alone because Mr. Hsu had an appointment at the Ministry—what he called, with weary courtesy, the tall patience of government. The Ministry had begun to count the museum’s storms as if storms were money. Ten years ago, when the city was still perforated with scaffolding, people had brought weather here because they were tired of weather in their houses. Now, the weather was given a number and the numbers were put in a ledger. There were quotas and audits. Even the rain in the Drizzle Room had to justify its existence.

In Precipitation, she stood the group beneath a hoop of pipe hung from the ceiling. She let them watch as the fine mist brightened, then thickened into drops and then decided against falling. The mist quivered above their heads as if tasting them.

“Is it heavy?” asked the purple-nailed girl, looking up.

“It’s as heavy as the day it came from,” said Mara. “That day was light.” She had collected that day herself from the roof of the old library, with her hands sunk in a duvet of damp linen that filtered the air, the droplets stepping through. She had known by touch when to stop—when the first notes of rain, the very preface of it, had gathered and had not yet fallen. It had felt like catching someone in the act of changing their mind.

“Why can’t we touch it?” said the shark boy, now calculating offense.

“Because even when they’re caged, storms are storms,” said Mara. “They remember themselves. They’ll go home with you in your hair, and we will have to come to your house with a net.” Laughter, the teacher’s rebuking glance, a file of children swinging their bodies back toward the floor.

At the end of the tour, she led them to the Listening Wall. It was a slab of pale wood, worn as a pew, that held a field recording: a minute of the first rainfall after the thirteen-month dry. The Museum played it twice a day at the times that the city was most tired. People came to see the weather here; they came to listen for forgiveness. Mara stood with them and closed her eyes with them as the sound unfurled. The recording started with the throat-scrape sound of the sky deciding to speak. Then there were rooftops and leaves, cement, shoulders, the silence of a person stepping into a garden and not breathing because if they breathed they would break the spell. A single, small shout. The microphone had caught the word Mama.

She had been at the edge of that crowd, a rookie then, her measuring tools still stiff and new. She’d held an umbrella like an apology and never opened it. She could still taste the rain’s first syllable: iron and dirt and a green that had not been born yet.

After they left—handprints like greasy moons on the glass—she walked the emptying halls and saw what needed to be resealed. A seam in the Typhoon Case had whitened like sugar. The vault’s lock was gummy in the heat. She made a note to talk to Maintenance; the new man worked with a slow care that made Mara itch. She cleaned the smudges from the Fog panel with a microfiber cloth that told her it was made of future technologies and a certain measure of hope.

When the doorbell brayed at the loading dock, she wiped her hands on her jeans and went down. This is what they brought her, on pallets and in cradles: weather at the edges, weather that had slipped under doors. Jars with tea-tin lids, mason jars with rubber rings, wine bottles with corks held down by twine. Someone had once delivered hail in a violin case. Once, a man had handed her a grocery bag heavy with a punishing heat; she had kept it and found his address and written him a note.

Today it was a crate lined with ripped newspaper. The paper was old—big headlines, a book review, the photograph of a man smiling with all his teeth. She lifted the top layer and found glass. Three jars, two bottles, a tin. The invoice in its sleeve said: Donation, Private Collection, Estate of L. Kestrel. Items prepared at Aster House, 2017–2021. She read it twice, then a third time, as if the words might decide to arrange themselves into something else.

Her mouth tasted like the sound of a coin struck against a tabletop. Her hands felt louder than the room.

She pried open the crate further and took out the first jar. It was brown glass, old medicinal. On its label, in tidy block print: Late summer gust, the day the awning tore. She could see the gust: a small energetic shadow moving over the surface of the liquid air inside. Gusts, unlike winds, sat uneasily in jars. Their shoulders hit the sides. They knocked under the lid. She soothed it with her palm. The jar cooled.

The second jar was a clear mason with the rubber ring intact. The label said: 4 September 20, 3 a.m., distant thunder. She held it up, and the thunder rolled in its own throat. The sound was the size of a kitchen. It was the size of a person lying awake and listening to the floor tick.

She knew the handwriting. A woman’s neatness, leftward lean. The long tails on g and j. The way the t was crossed below the bar, impatient, stubborn. She had practiced that hand on the blank backs of envelopes, when she was twelve and wanted to write like someone who knew where letters were going. The label on the tin said: Dust from under the rosebush, before rain. Who else would think to collect dust before rain? Who else would consider dust a kind of weather?

Her chest shrank. It was not news. It was a thing that had always been true but that she had so often been able not to know.

Lina Kestrel had collected weather the way other mothers collected recipes, remedies, reasons to say no. It was her mother’s handwriting on the labels.

The crate gave her three more hours of anything but this thought: she had to log items, scan them, assign them accession numbers. She had to test seals with the pressure gauge the Ministry sent, an apparatus with snouts and dial faces like a set of metal mice. She had to sort by risk. She had to fold the newspapers and slide them into the recycling, but she did not throw away the photograph of the smiling man. She put it on the desk that had once been Mr. Hsu’s desk and would always be his desk, with its cup of desiccant sachets and its fossilized jellybean.

She put the crate’s last jar in her hands. She stopped breathing for two slow beats, as if breath were a price she might be charged.

This jar was small and heavy, the glass thick. The lid had been tightened with something like love; it wouldn’t budge even when she held it with the hot towel and the special wrench. The label was rough paper, edges feathered. It said only: For Mara. Open when it chooses.

Her hand shook. At the bottom of the label, Lina had drawn a little crooked heart, the one she had drawn on napkins when she signed for deliveries, as if hearts were receipts you gave the world for what you took. Marinara sauce, toilet paper, roofing nails, a heart. Later, empty jars, rubber rings, mesh, copper. A heart.

When Lina had left, she had left in increments. First the late evenings at Aster House—what the city called the research center but what Lina called, with quiet certainty, the roof. Then nights she had not come home. The last morning, her mother’s purse had sat on the kitchen counter, its strap a parentheses around a tangerine.

Mara had called. The phone had answered itself as a recording. A voice had cleared its throat and said: I’m out feeling for it. It will come if it comes. Leave the back door unlatched.

She had been twenty-four. She had left the back door unlocked for a week, then for a month. After a year, you didn’t get to call it dread. You called it your life.

On the jar, the ink had bled very slightly when it dried. Lina had never waited long enough for anything to dry. She had hung laundry in rain. She had smoked cigarettes under the bathroom fan because the fan was a polite fiction, and it pleased her to behave as if all lies were small and elegant.

“Do not tell me you are opening something you haven’t measured,” said Mr. Hsu, from the doorway of the loading dock. He had let himself in with the sound that certain people made, which was none. He was carrying a paper bag that smelled like oranges and dill. His retirement had happened in name only. He had kept his keys.

Mara closed her fingers around the jar. “I’m logging donations,” she said. She held the jar like someone who had been given a glass bird without instructions.

“Donations,” he repeated, and put the bag on the sorting table. He looked at the crates like a man looking at a stack of letters. “Is there a rain with my name on it?”

“You hate rain.”

“I hate the institutional experience of rain,” he said. “I hate what rain in a city has become.” His fingers walked along the edge of the crate, and his eyes softened. For all his complaints, he loved the museum. He loved its premise: that attention was a kind of mercy. “Make a list. I will take that to the Ministry’s patience, and I will count some storms in my most official pen.”

She should tell him. She should feel the word mother climb to her mouth and go out to him like an animal that had lived in a small room and was now being invited to a field. Instead: “There’s an estate,” she said. “L. Kestrel.” She made her voice an errand. “I’ll need you to sign for the accession sequence, while I catalog.”

“Kestrel.” He rolled the syllables as if testing their weight. “Bird of prey.”

“A bird that hovers,” Mara said without meaning to. “It beats its wings so quickly that it seems to be standing still.” She had been given a book once. The pages were soft with reading. On the flyleaf: a heart and a sentence that said, Be better than the world deserves.

“You know the donor?” Mr. Hsu asked.

“She—” Her mouth said nothing else, which in itself was a sentence. “It will be a good addition,” she said. “She kept unusual items.” She lifted the tin with the dust under the rosebush. He saw the label and smiled without expectation.

“Let me do the Ministry,” he said. “You have the eyes for glass today.” His kindness was that he believed this to be an ordinary thing to say. He patted the oranges in his bag. “I brought fruit. These days, if I bring an orange anywhere, a child looks at me as if I have walked in with a comet.”

After he left, she put the oranges in the staff fridge. She put the paper photo of the smiling man in the top drawer so that she wouldn’t throw it away. She wrote numbers on tags with the black pen that bled too much, then rewrote them with the precise pen Mr. Hsu used for Ministry papers. She pretended the jar with her name on it had simply not been in the crate. It waited. She knocked her keys against the edge of the table just to hear the small metal clarity of yes and no.

The museum had been busy this year. Flood headlines had put them in the news. A morning show had brought a host who had peered at the jars with a bright, spayed curiosity. He had cried when the Listening Wall began to rain. He had held the tears like a trophy. “Catharsis,” he had said to the camera. What the wall had given had not been catharsis. It had been a wooden bench and a moment in which a city had remembered itself with embarrassment. But you could not put that on television.

At five, the last visitor left. Mara locked the front doors and put the signs away. The walls hummed as the building made itself smaller for the night, safety systems turning on, cases taking their own small breaths. The river sounded like a coat being shaken. A siren went by on the street—blue light on concrete like mercury.

She took the jar with her name on it to the Typhoon Room. There, when she was alone, she could see without being seen. A small camera watched the hall, but it did not watch the fifth step under the maintenance ladder, which was where she stood when she needed to feel outside of time. The ladder’s metal cooled her back. She put the jar on the step above her knee and rested her fingers on the glass.

Heat passed through like a truth.

Inside the glass, something moved the way a fish moves when it guesses a hand above the water. A curl of air swam. A smell rose, so faint that perhaps she made it: iron and petals and something like old paper.

“Hey,” she said, without thinking.

She had not spoken to her mother in six years. She had spoken to the absence in the house—Hello? Leave a message? Are you there?—but she had not said a word into the world with the expectation that it would find Lina’s ear.

The jar, being glass, was honest. It made no pledge. It was a mouth that had been sealed shut with a ring of sky.

Her job required procedure. Accession numbers, measurements, safety checks, two staff present when opening anything. Open when it chooses, said the label. She could define choosing as a measure on a dial, and then the words would be law.

She checked the gauge. She fitted the snout of the mouse apparatus to the lid and watched the dial settle. Pressure: nominal. Seal: ninety-eight percent. She held the wrench in her hand until her skin printed on the metal.

She loosened the lid a fraction, as a person unbuttons something tight after dinner.

Air came out like a glass breaking under water. It was a soft, astonished hiss. A smell flushed her face: petrichor, that expensive word the Ministry preferred, and the cheaper word behind it: wet dirt. Not the smell of the city; the smell of somewhere with space to burn. Then a thread of cool laid itself along her throat.

A sound followed the air. It was not thunder and not breath. It found the shape of her name in her ear as if her name were a shell and the sound were a sea.

Mar.

Her mouth filled with water. She remembered the word Mama caught on the microphone in the Listening Wall and felt as embarrassed as a city.

She closed the jar again, hard enough that the jar felt scolded. She held it against her sternum and counted until the water in her body stopped behaving like weather.

“Don’t measure me,” the sound in her chest said. It was not a sentence; it was her mother’s voice making no sense. It was the kind of instruction Lina had given, which had always been a way to see who Mara was. “Don’t let them. They will count and then they will keep.”

Mara slid down the step and sat on the floor. Her knees made a shape she did not recognize. The jar sat beside her and sulked or shone; she could not tell which. The museum breathed around her, its machines settling, its vents turning like slow birds.

The museum wanted her to log a number. The Ministry wanted her to sign for it. Mr. Hsu wanted her to eat an orange. Her mother wanted her to disobey, as a form of love.

In the Typhoon Room, the walls were thick; sound did not escape the way it did in the Precipitation Hall, where you could sometimes hear rain talking to itself. From the fifth step under the ladder, you could see the top of the Typhoon Case: a square city of glass that held the typhoon’s eye as if it were a gem. Hairs lifted on Mara’s forearms in agreement with a wind that was no longer in the world.

She put the jar in her canvas bag. She had never taken a piece of weather out of the building. A person who took weather out was other than what she was; that person belonged to the market that sold snow in cones on blued corners in summer, to the people who shook heat out of rugs like gold. That person belonged to her mother.

When she reached the lobby, she stood still. A group of teenagers had pressed their faces to the glass. They looked in because the museum was part of their walk home and because the building was beautiful and because everyone always looks in when you turn on the lights after the dark. She pressed a hand to the glass and smiled at them in the way of a person who worked in a place children came to and who had to be the proof that adults existed in a state other than rage. They moved on, laughing like coins shaken in a jar.

She turned the deadbolt. She turned off the front desk lamp. She stood with the smell of the river and the orange breath of Mr. Hsu’s oranges and the feather of cool on her throat and the jar in her bag.

On her walk home, the sky was the kind of blue that made you taste milk. The jacarandas choked on dust and insisted on blooming anyway, purple like extravagant bruises. A neighbor had put a bowl of water on the sidewalk for dogs, and a cat drank there with quiet mastery. Two boys were trying to kick a ball hung in a tree with a rope. Every time the ball swung, the rope burned the branch, and a shower of brown fragments fell like confetti you felt ashamed to catch.

In her apartment, she placed the jar on the kitchen table. The table bore the scars of everything that had come before. If wood keeps a record, then her table knew her better than anyone.

The refrigerator hummed a note of contented stupidity. A moth made of dust touched the edge of the lampshade and turned itself into light.

“Okay,” she said to the room, to the jar, to her mother, to the part of herself that had hoped not to be a person who did something like this. “I hear you.”

On her phone, four messages waited. The Ministry. A friend with a baby. The bank. Mr. Hsu: Did you take your orange? He always sent the questions without punctuation; it made them more affectionate. She texted him a photograph of the orange halved, light caught in its pulp as if a small world had been cut open.

Outside, a car’s music made the street briefly heavier. The jar sat in its halo of kitchen light and emanated a patience that was not human. For a moment, she believed in forgiveness. For a moment, she believed this: that you could keep a storm in a jar not to own it but to keep it safe from being owned; that the point of a museum could be to hold something without naming it to death; that a mother might leave a daughter a thing that was as much warning as love.

The jar inclined, infinitesimally, toward the window, as if it were listening for weather beyond the glass. It had its own gravity. She could feel how the night leaned. She set her hand on it, just to steady. The glass was cool, the way a forehead is when fever breaks.

Somewhere, not on her street, sirens started and then made themselves thin. The river turned over in its bed. In the distance, clouds thought about coming north and then changed their minds, as clouds do. Above her, someone rolled a chair and laughed into a telephone. Two floors down, a child asked a question that even walls could not prevent from climbing.

In the museum, there were rules for the distance between human and storm. At home, there were none. She had been a city’s daughter and a museum’s daughter and a drought’s daughter; there was a chance, very small and very bright, that she could also be a weather’s daughter and make something of that of which no Ministry had thought.

“Open when it chooses,” her mother had written.

From the jar, a single drop ran down the inside of the glass, slow as a road. It left a clean path behind it. It hung at the lip like a thought unsure of itself. It made no move to fall.

Mara waited. She did not reach for a measuring cup. She did not write down the second the drop began, the rate of its descent, the exact temperature of the glass. She counted neither beats nor breaths.

The drop trembled, learned her, made its first decision in her house.

When it fell, it was only itself. It touched the inside of the lid, made a sound that might have been laughter, and became air.

The last word the river learned was my mother’s name.

I heard it in the objects that had once belonged to water—the bowl of a chipped spoon, the hollow of a long-dry snail shell, the bell of a broken bottle rooted into clay. If you stay long enough, the stones begin to lift their throats. They rasp the syllables they were polished on. When the light comes level across the bed of Bitter Run and you press your ear to the earth where it used to rattle and sing, you can sometimes catch a list of us: the names of all who once stood shin-deep here, who hid their feet in the cold and thought themselves forgiven. Children learn to smile into their cupped hands; old men go off to piss in privacy and return quieter. Lovers swear holes into their pockets.

Salma. The river never said Mother. It is precise with what love costs.

I was where I’m most at peace: belly to dust, a string of twine in my teeth, needle in my fingers as I threaded the skeleton of the river. This practice isn’t necessary, but it makes it look like I know what I’m doing. The truth is worse. I can feel the way a current once turned by the way the ants move and the taste of the dust: it has the chalk of long fish and the copper of a child’s coin when the channel was shallow enough for wishing. My mother taught me that. The twine is for them, the ones who hire me and need to see a ritual to believe in. I unspooled it along the river’s old spine. Each knot was a bend she would have named differently than the maps do. The bends have names like church gossip: Widow’s Rib, The Argument, Coyote’s Eye. The bend where, in spring, the owners of the almond groves knocked back the levees and let the trees drink like animals. The bend where a man from the Company drowned on a clean day. The bend where the school bus slid a little and made us saints.

“Is this where you’ll tell us no?” Mr. Sada asked from the bank. He didn’t climb down. His knees were bad. His hands were river hands and root hands; the last of the old boys in Hallowbridge who could make something stand without nails.

“You’ve paid me to tell you yes,” I said. “That isn’t a promise.”

He squinted the way people do when they don’t want to see the future too clearly. The lines around his eyes pulled tight, then let go. He held a jar of rain like an apology.

“I brought you this,” he said. “From three springs ago. I kept the window open all night, and it filled. As if it knew where to go.”

He’d sealed the lid with wax. I could see the little particulates of weather as it turned in his hands: the dust of the porch, two gnats, a speck of white paint. He wanted me to drink it. They always want me to drink what they bring, to fold their hope into my body so that when I say yes, they can believe the yes is theirs, or that some exchange of fluid has welded me to their thirst. I thanked him.

“It doesn’t work that way,” I said, with love. “But I’ll keep it near. Water knows you when you keep it near.”

He passed it to me without argument. He had an old man’s understanding of superstition. He’d been raised in a time when people believed in weather as a person who needed greeting. He carried a little charm in his pocket that clacked when he walked; if you stared too much he closed his fist.

“You’ll find it underground?” he asked. “Some new branch? Enough to give the school a tap? The children could stay after lunch again. They could wash the clay from their knees. That would be a mercy. I’d be obliged.”

He was not asking for himself. If he was, I would have told him to dig a barrel and catch the fog in the mornings, to cut his shower time to a song, to learn how to wash a body with a rag and a bowl and be grateful. For the school, I said I would try.

He nodded, and the hope stood up in his chest and looked at me.

“Lark,” he said, and the river answered him with my name from somewhere deep in the baked earth as if air had been caught there waiting. He flinched. His eyes glassed to a boy’s for a moment. He had grown up two towns upriver and had not heard his name like that in forty years. The sound loosened something in me. The twine gave under my hand and slid over a smooth rock, notched with grooves that only water can carve.

“Look,” I said. “Here is where she used to slow. And here is where she learned to run again.”
