The river is a she in our town, except to the men in ties. To them, a river is a system, a source, a cost. To us, she is a creature whose appetites are older than our habit of measuring. Bitter Run used to carry trout, used to carry the taste of iron and nettles. She carried silt that made corn hands fat. She carried gossip and beer and pigs when they flooded, and she carried our tenderness when we needed not to be seen giving it. We walked into her when we confessed, and we walked out feeling as if we had been baptized in something we had earned. When they put up the dam at Cedar Gate thirty miles above us, the first signal we received was a silence. The goats bleated at it. The dogs went down to the bank and lay with their heads on their paws. The second signal was that the elders in the drift church started to speak in tongues again, and then they stopped, ashamed; what’s the point of tongues without water to be blessed in.

I am a cartographer of what isn’t there. I make maps of the vanished and sell them to people who want to keep losing from feeling like failure. I draw the ribs and old fingers of streams that no longer surface. I label the bends with our names: The Place Where I Was Asked, The Place Where He Laughed, The Place I Learned I Could Not Swim. I am paid in coin, in jars of rain, in bread, in promises. I am paid in secrets. The Company pays in folded checks that smell like ink and heat, and I cash those too, because I have a room to rent and a mother who may still be alive somewhere beneath the grammar of the land, and news costs.

“Aperture is drilling again,” Mr. Sada said, not quite at me. “You’ll have seen the flags.”

“Yes,” I said. Red pennants at the top of the gorge, like the ears of a nervous animal. The men there wear hats that shade nothing and cut their sleeves to show scars. Their tires make a language in the dust I’ve learned to read only enough to know when to walk away.

“They sent a girl who said she was me,” he said, and he laughed. It was splintered. “She had a clipboard. She had a voice that kept going even when she ran out of sentences. She said she cared about the community. She said we could truck water down from the reservoirs all summer for a ‘preferential rate.’ I said to her, you can take your preference and throw it to the coyotes.”

“I would’ve liked to see that,” I said.

“She wore a suit,” he said, as if that explained everything. “I couldn’t tell if it was cruel or if it was a shield.”

I knew. It was both. I have one like it, in a garment bag under my bed from a time I thought I could learn to be an interpreter between blue and brown. I wore it to a meeting once when my mother was still walking. Aperture had laid out pastries in a room too cold, the air-con a virtue signal. They gave us pens. I don’t remember what I signed. I remember my mother’s face when I came home crinkled with their fabric: how she looked at me like I was a child who had licked a battery.

“They’re not drilling for us,” I said. “But they’ll find something that has our names in it anyway.”

I left Mr. Sada at the bank with his hat in his hands and a little of my pity tucked into the band. I climbed the dry ladder the river had left in the clay and turned toward town. Hallowbridge lay across the bowl of our valley like something flung. The houses had grown extra skins to keep the heat out. Curtains in windows had darkened from white to bone to something that remembered milk. My office is a smaller skin inside another small one. It used to be a barbershop. The mirror is still there; sometimes I draw the channels in soot on it so I can see if the lines know their own faces.

On the walk, I passed the drift church. Its doors were open. The fans inside beat their steady wings. A new sign had been propped up on an old pew dragging the grass: Evening prayer, 7. Bring your own water for blessing. I thought of how my mother used to spit into her palm before braiding my hair and how sacred and vulgar that had felt at once. We are inventing new sacraments in the absence of old ones. We pretend they took us by surprise.

In my office, a map was still drying on the table: a carefully inked litany of absences. My inks used to be good. I could afford the imported ones that glowed blue even when the light was mean. Now I make ink from soot, from boiled oak galls, from tea. The company check I hadn’t cashed yet lay under a paperweight along with a note from the post office that I had a package waiting. The check looked like a sentence I would have to say out loud to the wrong person to receive sugar for it.

I hung Mr. Sada’s jar from a hook over the table by a little length of ribbon. It caught what light there was and made a shape on the wall like a child’s idea of a sea. I took off my boots. I unrolled yesterday’s work and today’s and laid them together. There are days when the lines let themselves be faithful to their old course, even as you know they’re whittled off underground by the new flows in the pipes that feed the orchards behind the fences that say Security is a Conversation. Today was a refusal. The lines kept sliding off the page as I drew them. I tried to close the loop around the school, to find a place to dig where digging would not be stolen by some larger mouth a mile away, and the loop wandered like a cow.

I took out the tools that don’t belong on the table when other people are here: the brass cup with the crack down its side, the spool of wire my mother pulled from an engine and calls Salvaged Lightning, the little box of bones I pry from the belly of the riverbed when the coyotes have finished with their feast and the sun has cleaned what they leave. None of this is necessary, and all of it is. I wound the wire around the cracked cup and the bones around the wire and held the whole thing up like a witch at a fair. The bone knows thirst. The metal knows the way it wants to kill us with thirst if we forget the original bargain. The cup remembers being full and how full felt. If we had kept to the old bargain—take what you can carry with your arms, leave what you can’t—it would be fine to spill into superstition. But we invented machines for thirst and the machines learned to beg.

The wire hummed, the smallest version of itself. I held it over the map. The hum lowered almost to silence at the places where people had been laying black hose in the night, tapping those fenced runs of the Company’s feed like thieves stealing from thieves. It rose in the places where the clay under the school was still unclasped enough to hold some shade of water in its knuckles. I breathed onto the paper. My breath stained it slightly. My mother taught me that, too: make your body part of the instrument or the instrument will not love you.

When she was still around, she would go down into floods as if the current were a conversation between friends who argued and laughed. She would come back with a branch that spoke in leaves and a story about how stupid she had been and a new scar on her thigh that said otherwise. She never forgave Aperture. She said what they were doing couldn’t be called theft because theft implies the thing is portable. “They are erasing,” she told me. She had a voice that made the word mean both chalk dust and a child’s name being rubbed off a door. The day before she disappeared, she went upriver with a book of hymns, as if she meant to sing at them. She walked with her pants rolled to her knees because it made them angrier when she remembered to laugh.

Sometimes in the mornings I think she ran. Sometimes in the evenings I think they held her while they told her that water does not belong to people who say it has a soul, and in the gray between I think there is a place under the bedrock where the river still visits, a little dark room the Company’s drills have not found and will not, because they have never loved anyone enough to know what do not enter feels like when you touch it. The bed of Bitter Run holds secrets like an old woman holds pins in the hem of her dress. When I lie below the bridge in the honey-hour, the pins prick through the cloth of the century and remind me to get up.

The post office had closed by the time the lines on the page agreed to anything. I inked it quickly when it did, before it changed its mind: a path from the east edge of the school property to a depression behind the freight yard, a shallow vein of sand that stains darker at night. “Dig here,” I wrote in pencil, then erased it and drew a little magnolia blossom instead. The men who would read this would not need the instruction. They would need a shape they could find with the memory of sight rather than with arguments.

I took the map and slid it into a tube. I drank from the jar of rain. It tasted like body heat and porch. I left my office as the sky turned scrap-metal and the road collected the cool like a rumor. The air had gone thin enough to be honest. You could hear the trucks at the gorge like teeth.

When I came back by the drift church, the doors were still open. I went in and sat in the back, not because I am pious but because it was not a bad room to be poor in. The pastor’s wife stood at the front with a bowl. It was only water if you believed in it. People came with their jars, and they touched the bowl, their hands still wet with whatever they had gathered: laundry sink, pot, hose, spit, prayer. We are learning to bless the sources we used to curse. It will make us obnoxious when this turns, if it turns. One of the children raised his hand and said, Can I bless our dog? The pastor’s wife said, Yes, bring him. The child said, He’s dead. She said, Yes, bring him anyway. The whole room made a sound like a choked joy.

On my way out, the boy bumped me and looked up with a face like his mother when she was sixteen. Everyone we love becomes everyone we loved if we stay long enough.

“Lark,” he said, and held up a battery with the copper torn clean. “Can you make this sing?”

“Everything sings,” I said. “Sometimes we don’t have the language it uses yet.”

He made a face like he might spit or he might learn. He ran off, battery clacking in his pocket like bones. It was a good evening for ghosts. They were tired and thin. They put their mouths to our ears and asked only to be recalled correctly.

The night felt like a hand flat on my back. All its fingers said, Be quick.

I went to the school alone with the tube under my arm and a shovel slung with a rope. The fence was a suggestion. There is not much crime except the kind that is now policy. The grounds had gone brittle. The sand pit where the children used to dig and be told No, not here had cracked in the shape of a drowned city. I walked to the place my line had traveled to in my mind. I put the shovel in with my foot and lifted the first watch of dirt. The sound it made was domestic. The second sounded like the first time you fold a letter. The third sounded like someone taking a breath after a long explanation. I have listened to the ground long enough to know when I am about to cry and when it is.

Four feet down, the shovel cut into something that gave like bread. I knelt. I brushed with my hands. It was a layer of sand the color at the center of a magnolia flower, fine as flour. I pushed my hand into it, and it sank sweetly up to the wrist. The sand moved through my fingers like a whispered swear. When I lifted my hand, the hole filled a little and then stopped. If we had a well here, the village would gather like geese. There would be fights. There would be a need for someone to keep lists of who came and who took how much. There would be recipes for what to put in the evening rice based on whether the water tasted like wild onion or like coin.

And then there was the cool.

It rose first as a joke, as if someone stood out of sight with a glass, blowing across the mouth of it. The hairs on my arm stood like a field before harvest. The cool had a body long after water had been a mouth. It came from the east, from where the freight yard is. It tasted faintly of oranges and diesel, like a Christmas from the wrong decade. I threw my head back before I could stop and opened my mouth, and the cool went into me, and it said my mother’s name in a way air should not. Salma. The sound of it leaned. I grabbed the edge of the hole with my dirty hands and swore in seven languages, most of them mine and one of them water.

When the wind stopped, the cool went back to being a trick. The sand was just sand. My arm was wet to the elbow. That was the part I couldn’t answer to myself. I looked up to the fence. Nothing had moved except the arrogant grass that thinks it can outlive a drought. I put my hand flat on the sand again and waited. Nothing but the old childhood noise of blood and fingers.

I don’t know what I expected when I walked back to Bitter Run, but it wasn’t a light on the far bank. It wasn’t that small, unwavering glow tucked into the ribs of the slope. The moon wasn’t up; there was nothing to give a lantern back its self-regard. The light said, I am mine.

I went toward it as if it were a person I had trouble with. I took the path that remembers being a dock because the wood is kinder to feet that have already been in the earth. When I reached the lip of the bank, I could see that the light came from a jar like Mr. Sada’s, set into a niche the river had once made in the clay to keep itself amused. The jar was the kind of thing you’d keep pears in. It held light the way the old jars held peaches. There was a label. The ink had bled in a way I recognized because it is how my ink bleeds when I hurry.

It said: Spring, Mouth. Not a date. No apology.

Next to it, pressed into the clay, was the wet print of a hand.

It was the size of my mother’s hand, which is to say it was only a touch smaller than mine with more stubbornness. The edges had already begun to dry, the way cake does when you forget to cover it. The lines in the palm were clean as new maps. The middle of the print had left a little lake behind. It made a shape like a magnolia blossom while it lasted. Above it, written with a finger, before the clay could return to grammar, was a sentence that stopped my doubt and then set it on fire.

It said: Stop looking where they want you to.

There was no signature. There didn’t need to be. The river does not say mother. But I do.

I sat with my feet in the dry, my hands on my knees, and for the first time in years I admitted out loud to the open that I was not mapping river to river, grief to grief. I was walking toward a person. The night took that into itself. It did not argue.

Behind me, toward Cedar Gate, a truck downshifted with the self-importance of a god. Down the slope, a coyote laughed as if it had been sitting there all evening waiting for me to speak. The jar’s light had the tenacity of hunger. My mother’s handprint dried around my work like a blessing, and I remembered how she used to correct me, gently: Blessings are obligations with prettier clothes.

On the map on my table, the lines would not close. They ran off the paper into whatever comes after paper. I should have been scared of that then. I wasn’t. I was only thirsty, and I was only furious, and I was only myself, which is to say, the daughter of a woman who thought she could name a river and be answered.

On the morning Mrs. K came to borrow light to bury her brother, the cloud had dropped so low I could feel its damp throat on the back of my hand each time I reached for the ledger. The building took the weight of it differently than people did. In the night the beams learned to stretch; the glass learned to stay quiet. The Bureau learned to be patient. I leaned my forehead against the front window and left a clear oval that fogged and unfogged, my own private weather pattern, while I watched the lift bridge across the canal cough up one slow barge the color of old coins.

“Are you open?” Mrs. K asked, before she’d even been able to make a shape in the doorway. Her voice felt around the edges of the room the way a hand would. She wore her grief in a way I recognized: not black clothes, not the stiff public shoulders, but a looseness in her cardigan as if her buttons were now merely suggestions. I had seen her in the market on good days, haggling over cucumbers and mussels with both hands and a laugh that made the fishmonger throw in a sprig of dill. The laugh was not with her today.

“We’re open,” I said, because I had unlocked the door and put the blue flag in the window and arranged the pen on its little brass chain just so. It didn’t matter that we had no customers for days. It didn’t matter that my supervisor sent notes that said, in ink getting thinner by the month, make yourself useful and reminding us that what we do is work even when there is nobody to see us do it. Open was a kind of promise we made to the block, to the city, to each other.

“It’s for my brother,” she said, flattening her palms on the counter as if to keep herself steady. “They’re doing the service on Friday at Saint Evangeline’s, as you know. Do you know? Anyway. We can’t—” She swallowed. It made a tiny sound I tried not to hear. “We don’t want to do it by matches. You understand.”

We had catalogued light for births and weddings and blood transfusions and the painting of a mural on the east school’s shattered gym wall. We had a shelf labeled for emergencies that wasn’t for emergencies; we had everyone’s birthday filed in a drawer in the back as if it could keep them safe. We had what passed in this city as brightness. Yes, I understood.

“Have you got your stubs?” I asked, because the ledger loves ritual and ritual keeps the world from skidding. Mrs. K unsnapped the coin purse she kept on a ribbon inside her sweater and shook out a thin fan of paper stamps like the gills of a fish. Every month, the Ministry of Illumination ladled out allocations in the same way my grandmother once ladled out soup to the men who built the flood wall—heavy-handed some days, stingy with onion on others—and we lined up as if flavoring were the law. You could argue, in the early days, with the clerk at the substation about whether a sprained ankle counted as two hours of morning or whether the thin light counted toward cooking time, but the clerks now had that tired look of people who had run out of exceptions to make.

“I’ve saved some,” Mrs. K said, and I saw how careful she’d been, tearing the stubs with a fingernail to keep the serial numbers intact. Tuesdays and the odd Sunday, each stamped with a gray sun that looked like a thumbprint.

“I can make it work,” I told her, and meant it.

Under the counter, our laminated menu, printed before I came to work here and kept despite its inaccuracy, said: Daily Dawn, Midday: Neutral, Winter Midday Tone: Cool, Summer Midday Tone: Warm, Dusk, Evening, Candle Supplement, Needlepoint Extension, Baking Glow. Somebody had drawn a smiley face beside Baking Glow. Somebody had crossed out Needlepoint and written Surgery in a different handwriting. All of it was a lie now. I kept it within reach anyway, like a child who keeps a map of a place that’s been renamed.

“What did he like?” I asked, uncapping the pen. “What kind of day was he?” It seemed foolish, most days, to put personalities on hours and sell them by the jar, but grief has its own metaphysics.

She looked up, surprised. “Apples,” she said. “Apples and dogs. He hated the lice checks at the school nurse, like everybody did. He loved the fair even when all the lights were false, bless him.” The word bless came out as a cough. “He liked that time of year you know the smell of the river from the bridge. That light. Forgive me, I’m not making sense.”

“You are,” I said. “He sounds like September.”

“I can afford Friday through the interment,” she said, glancing at the stamps like they might walk away. “I’ve got a cousin bringing a jar from her pantry for the wake. The mind can adjust to the dark, you know, but I want our faces to be visible to him when we say goodbye.”

I wrote: Funerary allotment, Saint Evangeline’s, Friday, 1400 hours through 1700 hours. I gave our side of the agreement the same careful loops I give my name when I sign it in public places. The pen ball clicked. The whole thing felt obscene and holy. “Wait here,” I said.

The vault had been the jellyfish room when this building was an aquarium. If you squinted, and Lord knows we all did, you still could see the sinuous swoop of the letters painted high on the tiles. MEN AND WOMEN OF A CERTAIN AGE could point out to you toward the corner where the blue light once made lovers’ faces seem honest. The floor sloped gently, so anything that broke rolled toward the grate. We learned early to set the crossbars in the doors. You can’t be too careful with light.

I unlocked the vault and stepped into the lives of others.

The walls carried shelves. The shelves carried glass. The glass carried degrees and flavors. If you think that light is all the same, you’ve never held dawn from the same month over two different years and felt the temper of them in your hand. You’ve never tipped a jar and watched a December gather itself like a thin scarf and tried to decide whether it’s more blue or more honest. You’ve never held a smuggled noon so dense it sat in the glass like a cat, leaving you with singe marks for your trouble.

I placed my fingers against the cool alphabet of tags. There is a grammar we use: Year-Month-Place-Quality-Use. I’m not supposed to say the names out loud, but inside my head I always do. 19-06-Bridge-West-River-smell: Traffic compromised. Saved from a window breach by three of us with buckets and a sheet while we cried for no reason but the joy of being suddenly wet. 22-09-Orchard-Eel Road-warm: Cider day. Apples tumid and generous as knuckles. 17-01-Barber-Street-cold: Threaded and pure. Good for stitches and careful conversations.

For funerals we keep to the sober and clear. The celebrant’s face shouldn’t look like a saint’s painting and the widow’s cheeks shouldn’t look like raw tomatoes. We want edges without cruelty. We want to see the fall of the priest’s sleeve over his wrist. There is a jar we use that we call, among ourselves, The Honest Noon, and we dilute it with water in a jug so that it doesn’t stab anyone in the memory.

I found the Honest Noon on its shelf and gave it my cheek for a heartbeat to wake it. The glass looked empty; all the best ones do. It’s the difference between light as a thing to see by and light as a thing that pushes back your hunger. Some jars hum; this one didn’t. At my hip, the ledger rustled with the movements of other clerks upstairs. In the metal door of the old filter pump, I caught a shimmer of my face: wide mouth, hair plaited so that it wouldn’t tangle with the hooks, eyes darker than they ought to be at this time of day.

My own mother used to say that the only time she felt truly safe after the cloud came was when she knew exactly what day was bottled in her palm. She worked in these rooms when it was still illegal to bottle anything except government hours. She was a “fielder,” a person sent out to the perimeters with a length of glass, a pocket of salt, a blessing, and a rigid set of rules about what you do and don’t collect. The rules were sensible and human and broke easily under the weight of unfiltered noon. When she had been gone four years some man knocking rust from the flood wall stepped on a bottle like stepping on a snake and it let a sigh of summer into a February. The ice on the canal congratulated itself and did nothing. Nobody knows if she did it on purpose, in the end. There are people who worship those who went into the field and didn’t return for supper. There are people who spit when they say their names, like it was a choice. I carry her face around the city and sometimes someone tries to hand me a blessing or a bit of tobacco and sometimes someone tries to hand me a bill.

I set the Honest Noon on the trolley and added, because I am a person and not a bureaucracy, a jar of 14-04-Window-Sill-North: a small, easily diluted spring morning that does exactly what you ask it to do and then goes home. It smelled faintly, when I cracked its seal to check integrity, of metal and toast.

On the way back I passed the shelf that holds the returns we don’t put back into circulation. There is no legal language for this shelf. On those bottles the tags are wrong, or absent, or written in a hand I know then refuse to know. If there is a crack I can fix, I fix it. If there is something that has become too much like a story, I leave it alone. The top of my ear burned as if a match had been struck near it. Someone had walked past the front window upstairs. Someone’s coat had moved shadows across the wall down here like fish.

“You’re a good girl,” Mrs. K said, when I rolled the trolley up to the counter. “The kind of good that I pray for when I have nothing left to pray with. Write it all proper. I don’t want to owe anyone anything.”

“We’ll stamp you,” I said. “And we’ll do the two-for-one if you bring the glass back clean and unchipped on Saturday morning, like a saint.”

We have bromides like that, little jokes that pass for smiles. Bring it back clean. Don’t drink it. Don’t put your lip to it. Don’t pour it into your neighbor’s shed. Don’t sit under it and tell stories. Don’t mix. Don’t save. Don’t save. Don’t save.

She took the jars in their padded hamper and I watched the Poplar Boys from the corner cock their hats and pretend not to see that light was being ferried past them like a swaddled infant. They have what passes for grace in this part of town and what passes for teeth, mostly. I blew on the oval of my breath and erased it with a sleeve.

The day trickled. You’d think the cloudy days would feel the same, but the temperature of a silence changes. Morning’s quiet is different from three o’clock quiet is different from the quiet of a city that knows you’re leaving. There are days when a thread of singing carries all the way along the canal, across the wet roofs, and lands near your elbow without breaking. There are days when the only sound is the scratch of my pen, adding Hilde K’s code to the ledger and blotting it with the blotter my supervisor keeps polished with lemon oil. There are days when my supervisor herself descends, clicking, her heels announcing themselves because something in her upbringing refused to learn to be soft. She didn’t come down that day. I had the jellyfish to myself.

I should tell you the rules, in case you’re visiting and you plan to borrow anything bright. The glass can hold an hour and a half in jars big enough to call jars. There are little vials that go for a minute, the length of the Lord’s Prayer and one deep breath. We do not label anything holy. What you do with it is your business, unless you’re bringing it into a school, in which case we ask you to sign the pledge that you will not uncork it in the presence of children under five, who will try to catch it with their tongues. We dilute everything. We presume good faith. We wrap everything in old newsprint because there is always old newsprint. We do not ask why.

That afternoon, there was the brief shiver of the mains and a bubble of official light, the kind that vibrates at the joints and makes everything look like paperwork, pushed itself reluctantly into the Bureau from the street lamps. It made the fish in the tile mural look like policemen. I turned it off, because it makes our stock nervous and our clerk’s eyes ache. The cloud whispered on the roof the way a mother who believes in discipline will whisper your name of an evening.

It was almost closing, the hour when you can reasonably put a soft scarf over the bell and flip the flag, when a stranger came. He had a coat that had once been expensive and had learned not to mind damp. His shoes apologized to our floorboards when he crossed them. He didn’t take his hat off, and I didn’t call him on it, because he carried a jar like you carry a sleeping cat: with humility, with attention.

“Am I too late?” he asked. His voice sounded like cigar boxes and rooms with shutters.

“For what?” I said, and only then thought that what I should have said was we close in eleven minutes, which would have given the ledger something to do besides sit there like a watched clock.

He set the jar on the counter and we both felt the counter adjust. Even empty glass weighs what it weighs, but this—this had a heaviness that glass alone could not carry. It looked ordinary. The seal was dark red, not the Bureau’s municipal brown, not the glossy black I’ve seen from the fielders with a sense of theater, but a wax an ordinary person could purchase from an ordinary stationary stall. The tag was the part that made my throat close. It had been torn from the corner of a flyer of some kind. The writing leaned left, as if it didn’t want to be seen.

“I’ve come to return a loan,” he said.

I looked at the jar without touching it. It is a skill we teach the new clerks. Do not touch. Do not touch. “What kind of loan?” I said, standing still so that he would feel how much was already in the room.

He tapped the tag with a torn fingernail, a nail with a fan of oil embedded in it, a worker’s nail. It read: Noon, North Sluice Road, Tide High, Illegal, Keep.

The wax had been pressed with a small oval seal. Within the oval was a crude shape of a fish with a diagonal slash through it. I closed my eyes like a child does when she wants to hear better. I knew that seal.

“I’m not the right person for returns,” I said, because that is something a person like me says in a situation like this, to give herself time to understand why her heart had just remembered, all the way to her fingers. “There’s procedure.”

“I watched a woman hold up this jar to a square of sky where the cloud had opened,” he said, with all the worried dignity people have when they tell you the first part of a confession. “I watched a woman say the words under her breath that the fielders say when they’re not being listened to. I watched her put the lid on with both hands. She wrapped it and gave it to me like giving me a ham on Christmas. She said, you give this back when you can. She said, you give it to my daughter if she’s old enough to stand behind the counter by then. If she isn’t, you give it to the Bureau. She said daughter like it had twelve syllables, the way women do when their daughter will have to carry rocks with her bare hands and try not to drop them. I carried it for twenty years. I’m trying to put it down.”

There are moments the Bureau trains you for. Someone fainting. Someone drunk. Someone so poor you would upend the vault in their lap if you could. Someone with a gun, once. The Ministry gave us a certificate after that one. We probably still have it, if the paste hasn’t given up. There are moments the Bureau never trains you for. In the kovsh of his hat brim, as he tipped it up, there were the stains of salt that had dried and been wetted and dried again.

“What’s your name?” I asked, because the ledger likes to begin at the top left of the page.

“Jan Mal,” he said. “Nine Poplar Court, east side of the bridge. Shipwright’s apprentice until there were no ships. Cooper, when there were barrels. Runner of errands when there was weather that needed errands run in. I brought you her jar.”

I touched the wax. The shape of the fish, the slash. The patience of it. The clumsy insistence. My mother had had a thing about small defiant icons. I had, in a box under my bed, a matchbook with a tooth drawn on it and a slash through it, a way of joking about the dentist that had kept me sober through two molar extractions. She had stamped everything she made for her own kitchen with the fish. No fish wasted, no fish forgiven. She had told me herself that the fish was the oldest sign there was for people like us. She had told me that symbols are a way of saying you don’t want to buy a thing that already belongs to you.

“Wait here,” I said, the way I’d said to Mrs. K. I carried the jar into the vault on both palms, keeping it level, listening. Sometimes you can hear a noon purr. Sometimes a dawn will talk to you because you are tired. This jar kept itself to itself. On the shelf of returns that we do not catalog and do not discuss, I set it and tucked the torn tag between my cheek and my teeth to free my hands. The taste of the paper was clean and then suddenly bitter, like biting the pith of a lemon.

On the back of the tag, in a different ink, in a different hand, there was something written I had not expected.

For Ina, it said. It will be less heavy when you carry it. 

If I were a different person, I would have run my thumb over the wax again and again until the fish wore away to nothing. If I were my supervisor, I would have rung upstairs and said, we have a violation that is also an inheritance. If I were my mother I would have tilted the jar toward the slant of the pump room’s window and caught whatever fell out with my mouth.

Instead I stood there with my hands so empty and so full that it was a kind of pain. The cloud dragged its damp sleeve across the skylight. The building remembered the weight of water and leaned into it, the way old buildings do.

When I came back up, I laid the tag on the counter and slid it back to Jan Mal with one finger. “Thank you,” I said, because there are not many words that do their work as well as that one. “You’ve kept your promise.”

He set his hand flat on the thrice-polished wood. His lungs made a sound like a stair. He looked to the left and the right, in the way of all men who do not want to cry in a public place and will betray themselves with their politeness instead.

“If you needed a jar,” I said, because kindness is another ledger and one that likes to balance itself in surprising ways, “for yourself or someone—”

He shook his head. He tapped the side of his nose. “I am all night now,” he said. “It’s all right. There are people who like the afternoon more than I ever did.”

Outside, a boy ran with a paper pinned under his shirt to keep it dry, and some little burst of unregistered light in his pocket made him shadowless as he passed. If my mother had been alive she would have had something stern and funny to say about that. If my mother had been alive, I wouldn’t have the jar in the vault making a new gravity under the smell of wet tile and old brine.

The day folded itself smaller. The city did that daily trick of believing its own faintness was an evening. I stamped the top of the page with the square stamp that leaves behind a rectangle of dust the color of the Ministry’s blush. I put the blue flag away. I covered the bell. I waited in the doorway while the long barges came and went, each with its orange eye at the prow. The cloud lowered its head again until it could read our street names upside down. Mrs. K’s hamper glowed a little through the towel as her nephew carried it through the gate to Saint Evangeline’s. Jan Mal walked the slow walk of someone who had learned to redistribute his weight.

This city built its house on borrowings. Borrowed stones from farms now under the water. Borrowed children from villages upriver who wanted a wall built. Borrowed names stitched from other tongues. Borrowed light, and borrowed vows, and borrowed till we could pay and borrowed past the point of paying. The first chapter of a life is bending your head under the weight of all you’ve been given, whether or not you asked for it.

I locked the door and checked the jars whose seals had bubbled and tapped each one with the nail of my smallest finger. The pumps in the old tank took a breath. Somewhere, three floors up, somebody rolled a chair back and scraped the spine of the Bureau’s day against the cement. I sat down on the stool with its wobble, and I took the paper tag out of my pocket to read the four words again. For Ina. It will be less heavy when you carry it.

It wasn’t true. But for a minute or two, knowing it wasn’t true felt a lot like light.

Chapter One

The museum drowned and called it an act of God, as if the ocean had filled out a form and left a forwarding address.

I arrived after the water receded, when the floors still gleamed with the kind of shine that makes you think of surgeries rather than art. The salt had dried to a crust along the baseboards, white as orphaned teeth, flaking wherever the mop couldn’t reach. There was a soft, remedial smell in the galleries—bleach, wet paper, the iron breath of rust beginning. Someone had dragged a dehumidifier to the center of the atrium and the machine labored like an old man climbing stairs, a constant, drowning inhalation that made the quiet heavier.

“You’re late,” said the night guard, though it was only a minute past the hour. He stood behind the admissions desk in a soaked uniform, pistachio shells arranged in a half-moon around the base of his stool. He was the kind of man who had never outgrown the shape of a boy—ears a little too big, wrists thin, eyes that looked at you straight as a ledger line. The name tag fixed crooked to his chest read: M. Halim.

“I’m insured against lateness,” I said, and flashed the lanyard with the bland authority of someone who has been sent. There is a look people recognize: you are the person who writes numbers down beside their ruins.

“Hollis Mutual,” he read. “Sounds like a marriage.” He snapped a shell open and coaxed the meat out with his tongue. “Masud,” he said, not offering his hand. “We’re supposed to minimize contact.”

He had a point. The policy binder in my bag had a page about oils from human skin and what they do to works on paper, which I had skimmed and then highlighted anyway. The truth is most forms of touch are less a danger than the idea of them. You cannot insure against an idea once it has entered a room.

He slid a laminated sheet toward me. “Sign in. The curators left in a hurry. The basement is a lake, but we locked the doors. Entities of record? That’s what they said you’d ask about.”

“Entities of record,” I said, and pretended the phrase didn’t make me want to wipe my mouth.

I was supposed to be grateful for the job. Loss assessor, junior level three. A steady salary and hazard pay, plus an algorithm that turned empathy into a bar graph on my performance review. “The empathic quotient is predictive,” my supervisor Joyce had said my first week, tapping the screen. “Customers who feel ‘met’ are less likely to litigate. Just meet them, but not too much. Think of yourself as a bridge. A bridge can’t follow everyone home.”

She was on her third divorce and had a laugh like breaking plaster. I had nodded. It is not difficult to learn to be a bridge. The secret is that most of us already are.

There was someone else I should have been bridging toward that morning. Two missed calls from my brother Idris, his name stacked twice on the black glass of my phone, like a promise or a threat. The night before he had texted: She is asking for you. He didn’t mean our mother as person; he meant a collection of needs in a bed, unslept.

I put the phone back into my bag and looked past Masud to the drowned atrium. The museum had been built glassily, an announcement in angles. At the opening ten years ago we all came to have ourselves reflected—small people inside jagged light—and I’d thought at the time how arrogant it was to make a building like this on land that had once been marsh, as if the mud would suffer such geometry. An architect on a stage said the words you can say when money is listening: dialogic, sustainable, future-proof. The mayor’s wife wore a dress the color of limes and later my date took a picture of me standing under the whale skeleton, my mouth slightly open, as if that ancient ribcage had something to say.

That skeleton hung above us still, its shadow rafted across the wet. The string of halogens along the ceiling had survived. Art had been slurred to the higher floors, a tide of canvases and plinths shoved into the elevators with their tongues poking out. On the stairwell landing a bronze had been left with one foot in water, the toes electing not to rust out of sheer stubbornness. The museum had raised funds in the aftermath and posted a video of an intern in waders rescuing a lithograph of a girl with a yellow kite, her hair forever obeying a wind that came from inside her. In the comments, the architect left a note that said, “We are resilient.” No one replied.

“Basement,” I said.

“There’s an archive,” Masud said, lowering his voice as if the word had a religion. “If they’ve got sense, they put the archive upstairs. If they’ve got donors, the archive stayed downstairs and the donors went upstairs.”

“And which do we have?”

He cracked a shell so neatly it came away in two perfect halves. He cupped them, admiring, shells like little parentheses holding nothing. “We have both,” he said.

He handed me a key ring with a wobbling assortment of tags. The keys were small and obstinate with use. He nodded toward a door marked STAFF ONLY and I went.

The thing is, water is a storyteller. It takes the shape of whatever disappoints it. It remembers, just not for our benefit. My mother used to say this into my hair when I would wake shaking from dreams I couldn’t keep. She would comb the dream forward, coax it word by word into daylight until it was tame enough to release. Water remembers, and saints keep the lists. In a city that has forgotten both, what you get instead is insurance—memory turned to tables, to premiums and deductibles, a ledger against forgetting. You are paid to write the shape of what is gone.

I thought of the day my father took Idris and me to the bay when the ships were leaving with families braided into their rails, when my mother stayed home and washed the walls. I thought of the way he counted the boats under his breath, as if saying the numbers out loud would pin them to the surface. He wore his one good shirt and the wind moved through it. At the time I didn’t know that leaving has a weight, that you can hold a departure in your hands if you’ve been trained. My father died later, in a smaller body of water than he deserved. When they found him his watch had stopped at a good hour and they said he had a peaceful face, which is what people say to themselves about the dead so they do not have to revise them.

In the staff corridor, the lights flickered and steadied. The walls had that artless yellow you find anywhere choosing not to be seen. I opened a door labeled ARCHIVE, expecting boxes and ledger books and a smell like old basements begetting each other forever.

Instead, I found a room of jars.

Not a few, not the tidy dozen you might keep for winter, but hundreds of glass bodies lined up like a battalion, each with a white label and a date, some with a clumsy annotation in faded ink: Opening Day; Governor’s Visit; First School Tour; Rain—Late February; Rain—June, Warmer Than It Should Be. They were onion-jarred and Mason-jarred and jam-jarred—a museum made of weather and the habits of someone who believed nothing should be thrown away. Light from a high window fell over them and they answered with a softened shine. There was a particular quiet in the room, a quiet that not only held sound but held itself, as if the air were bracing.

On the floor, water still stood in a shallow shine a centimeter deep. The bottom shelves had already lost two lives: labels softened and peeled, handwriting blurring to tear-ink, the glass under the water singing when my shoes touched the wood.

“How did they think this was upstairs?” I said aloud and then remembered I was alone.

There is a form called a Statement of Loss I am supposed to fill out. There is a number that completes every sadness, if you go about it with enough endurance. The form has a line for Physical Damage, a line for Ancillary, a line for Emotional Value that we are instructed to leave at zero, for that is not how the world works under signature. But as I stood there with my binder tucked under one arm, I wanted to put a number in a place that did not exist.

I stepped closer. The labels nearest me were a steady year, a full rotation of holidays and attempts. Opening Day—September 6. Gallery East—September 7. Few Visitors But Enthusiastic. The handwriting was careful, leaning slightly forward as if it had somewhere to go. When I held a jar up to the light, the liquid inside stepped toward me like a shy animal. I could smell metal, and something else: a faint, sour sweetness like old raincoats.

“Don’t open that without me watching,” said a voice at the door.

I turned, ready to apologize and explain and justify all at once, which is to say I was ready to be me.

The woman in the doorway wore a cardigan that might have been ivory before the day began. She had a rectangle of plastic clipped to the edge of it, the kind that holds cards and also tells you you will never wash this cardigan free of your job. The card said: CURATOR. The thing about that word is that it once meant to care for, someone who tended the troubled in their rooms. Now it means to arrange the troubled in agreeable light. Her hair clung to her head in a holy pattern of damp. She was breathing too fast.

“Hollis,” I said, and lifted my lanyard as if it could ward off curses.

“I know who you are, Mr.—”

“Samir,” I said. “Just Samir. There’s no Mr. in our training manual until the file closes.”

“Yes, well,” she said. “Do not open them without me. I am supposed to be nowhere near this room and I have already been nowhere near it for two hours and the idea of someone opening these alone makes my hands—” She looked at her hands, which were trembling with precise energy, as if the tremor had a schedule. “It makes my hands do that.”

I put the jar down. “Did you put them here?” I asked, though I knew the answer was older.

She shook her head. “The first Director did. He kept rain the way some people keep grudges. It was his little private sacrament. It was meant to be a joke, I think, and then he kept going. When he left, he forgot to forget them.”

“He kept rain?”

“He kept days,” she corrected, and the correction landed so gently I felt it for a few seconds after it finished. “It is not scientific. We have no protocols. There is a note somewhere that says they should be stored away from heat and hubris.”

I smiled despite myself. The label did not say Rain in an ironic script. It said it in a hand that believed if you named a thing carefully you might keep it.

“I wasn’t going to—” I began, and she lifted one shaking hand to stop me.

“It’s fine,” she said. “You are the first person to walk into this room in two years who hasn’t looked like a calculator. I would almost like to see you open one.” She glanced at the high window. “I would like to see something today that behaves.”

Down the hallway, something metallic shuddered, and a moment later the building gave a quiet sigh as a system found itself again. The water at my feet shivered as if it had remembered its job and then forgot.

“I’ll need to list. Photograph. Value,” I said.

“I’ll need to grieve,” she said, not unkindly. “We can do both. Isn’t that what we do, the two of us? Measure the breakage and then look at each other over it like it’s a chessboard.”

Up close she had the sort of face that makes you think of a particular day in early spring when everyone still wears their winter responsibility but the light is warmer than it has any right to be. I wanted very much to sit down on the floor with her and begin with the easy parts: laugh at the labels, compare odd donations, tell each other the worst thing anyone had said about art and money in our hearing. But there is never time inside of a form. The danger of working in catastrophe is that you begin to address a person by the thing that has happened to them. Hello, flood. Good morning, fire. I told myself another day I would say hello properly to the woman named without a name card. Today I would say hello to this.

“I will file a preliminary,” I said, flipping open my binder. “We can call it that until we decide to call it something else.”

She nodded toward the shelves. “If the number is not zero, I will find a way to be surprised.”

I took pictures of the jars with my phone, my screen turning them into little moons. The camera app took in the light and patted it down. I counted, though I would count again later. Counting is a way to avoid feeling rearranged.

“This one,” she said, and pointed at a jar on the top shelf, third from the left. “He wrote something extra on that one. He said it was the first day he believed the museum existed.”

I stood on a crate to reach it. When I balanced it in my palm, I could feel a tremble in the glass, a suggestion of waiting. The label was more careful than the others, as if his hand had considered itself. Rain—September 6, 1986. Opening Day. Borrowed Umbrella.

“He borrowed my umbrella,” she said, startling me. “I was an assistant then. I had written down nothing that mattered to anyone. He realized he would get his suit wet, so he took my umbrella and walked around the building like a benevolent beetle, greeting everyone. He said hello to the donors, and their wives who are never donors, and the woman who does the floors, and a bus driver who had stopped out front just to look. He stood in the rain with that ridiculous umbrella and said hello to everything. He had a voice like a kettle just before it boils. Then he went home and, presumably, poured that day into a jar and called it sacred.”

It was such an ordinary holiness I could have kissed it. Outside in the atrium, Masud’s dehumidifier inhaled and exhaled industriously. The rain in the jar looked like any other water. It didn’t matter.

“Do you ever open them?” I asked.

She shook her head. “No. We learned. Once. We were afraid it would change. Isn’t that ridiculous? As if something like that could change because we asked it to. The fear was superstition. The fear was respect. Sometimes I confuse the two.”

I thought of my mother lifting the lid of her pot to release a spoonful of steam and make a room smell like cumin and apology. I thought of my father and his watch, the perfect second stretching on its spool. I thought of Idris’s two missed calls. I thought of the city listing slightly under its own language.

“Do you have power?” I asked the curator. “At home?”

“I live in the building with the olive tree in the lobby we are not supposed to pick,” she said, which meant a neighborhood I could never afford unless my company paid me for something unforgivable. “We have candles. This morning the candles looked like people bent over work. I almost apologized to them for calling them in early.”

We were quiet. The kind of quiet that has a choice. The labels around us breathed the names of days under their breaths. The room had waited a long time for an occasion and had received one. There is a difference between a flood and the sea coming in to take back an old room, but I have learned not to say that out loud where anything can hear me.

“Would you like to open it?” she asked, suddenly, the earlier fear turned into a brittle invitation. “We could say I asked you. We could say it was necessary, for the claim, to assess the interior.”

“It would not be true,” I said.

“No,” she said. “That is not what we are doing today, is it.”

But my hand had already found a willingness inside itself. I felt the screw of the lid under my fingers, the small resistance of a faithful seal. I felt younger than my body. The line on my performance chart that would measure reason pulsed faintly in my mind.

“Maybe just a look,” she said. “Maybe just the edge.”

I met her eyes. The disks of her irises were almost the exact gray of the water in the jar, which is a trick of light and nothing more and also a miracle.

“On a different day,” I said, putting the jar back on the shelf. “On a day we are not standing in the ruin of good intentions.” It was the unargument I offer myself when I know that what I want is too expensive.

We worked. She opened drawers and produced lists that would make someone at my office clap. I asked the questions Joyce had taught me to ask but in a voice that did not make the answers sound disposable. The numbers were too small. They were always too small. When I moved a second shelf to raise it off the wet, my shoulder burned in a specific old way. I put my hand to it and then did not.

We were almost done when the lights went black and the room slipped into itself with a sigh. I stopped, the way you stop when an authority enters, and we both listened. The dehumidifier in the atrium wound down with the melancholy of an engine that has realized its life has been wasted.

“Generator?” I asked.

“Being begged,” she said.

In the dark we both smelled the room more. The old water and the new water ghosted about each other. I thought of you again, my mother, your way of cataloging smells as if they were relatives, and I realized with a fatigue that made my knees doubly real that I had to call Idris.

“I need a minute,” I said, as if I had anything more dignified than that.

“Go,” she said. “I will stand here and be counted by the jars.”

Out in the hallway, my phone found a thin lobe of reception. I leaned my back against the institutional paint and pressed the thing to my head like a cold cloth. Idris answered on the first ring, as if he had been holding the phone like a prayer.

“She is asking for you,” he said by way of hello, and I closed my eyes to soften the distance.

“I’m at work,” I said, and immediately hated the thinness of it.

“I know,” he said. “I saved your voice messages. I could recite them to her and pretend. She would not know the difference. Or maybe she would, with that particular cruelty the dying have. She keeps reaching for the table and then forgetting the table is there.”

I listened to his breathing. I listened to a world where a table could be both there and not. “I will come,” I said. “Tonight.”

“There will be no busses,” he said. “The road flooded at the hospital and the bus thinks the flood is contagious. People are walking on the median as if it is a new faith. Bring bread, if you come. The good kind, the expensive one. I want to taste today as it passes.”

“I will bring bread,” I said. “The expensive one.” I did not say her name. We had turned her into a pronoun some time ago to make her more portable.

“And Samir,” he said, before I could end it, as if he had been waiting for permission to say the part that mattered. “She is forgetting languages in reverse. This morning she barked at me in a word our father used when he dropped a cup. Then she tried to ask for the window and said the word for knife. I opened the knife. She looked at me like I was a miracle and an idiot. It would be easier if she didn’t laugh. She laughs when she finds herself.”

The hallway felt longer than the building. The museum groaned thinly somewhere like a boat under strain. The city outside kept its own counsel. There are all these ways of meaning to go home and then not.

“I have to finish one thing,” I said, and meant it the way you can only mean it when you are already failing. “One thing and then bread and then you.”

He sighed, and for a moment I was on a wharf with him again, a boy at my shoulder, both of us counting boats we had no business counting. “Today is long,” he said. “I will make it longer. Do not worry. I saved her this morning. I kept her from a fall. She wants to know if you are still making your little lists.”

He said it kindly. I felt my face do something I would fix later. “Tell her yes,” I said. “Tell her I am writing the names of the days down so we don’t lose them.”

“We always lose them,” he said, softly. “That is the part you never learned. But come anyway.”

After we hung up, I stood in the dark until the dark felt like a decision. The generator rumbled to life and the lights returned with the guilty surprise of someone who fusses over the check at dinner neatly enough to lose. I took a breath that did my heart no particular favors, rolled my shoulder as if it had a voice, and went back to the room.

The curator had not moved. The jars had not moved. That is their job: to wait and pretend that waiting is a virtue. Somewhere farther up in the building, a voice murmured something calming in the way only people with jobs can afford. The dehumidifier found its wheeze again and resumed its Protestant work.

“I’m done here,” I said. “I’ll have to come back. The numbers need to be proven to someone whose fingers have never been wet.”

“They like that,” she said. “Numbers that have stayed inside all day.”

We stood together in the middle of the room and looked at the shelves the way people look at the sea in movies. I couldn’t tell whether she was about to open one of the jars and drink or baptize herself or fill the room with a storm that would wash every list to zero. Sometimes what you want is not to be good, but to be faithful to the original mistake.

“Do you ever think,” she said, not looking at me, “that we will run out of days?”

“Not in any way we can afford,” I said.

On the way out, I slid the jar with the borrowed umbrella off the shelf and tucked it into my bag without knowing I had decided to. It made a shape against my hip that felt exactly like someone pressing a hand there to lead me through a crowd. The binding of my policy papers rasped against the glass. I would tell myself later that I meant to return it, that I needed it to do my job, that the claim required everything. Even as my fingers closed around it, they were already telling me that future truth.

Masud watched me sign out and made a mark of his own beside mine as if he were writing an amendment. “You look like someone who has been carrying water for too long,” he said. “Put it down sometimes. It feeds no one, the water you carry in your arms like that.”

“And you,” I said, gesturing to the shells.

“They keep my hands honest,” he said. “They keep me from putting them places they should not be.”

Outside, the afternoon had decided to become evening without telling anyone. The sky had that exhausted copper recipe the city has taught it. People moved in the street with care, carrying plastic bags that bulged with the weight of cautious choices. Somewhere not far away, a siren realized itself. The building across from the museum had a mural of a woman carrying a river on her back; someone had spray-painted a whale jumping it, wrong side up.

My car had a fogged windshield as if it had been breathing without me. I sat behind the wheel and pressed my palms to the glass and left my hands there until the heat made a shape of them. When I pulled onto the avenue, the tires hummed a sound I recognized from childhood, the sound of VCR tapes rewinding, everything running backward fast, faces smearing to their beginnings.

At the first red light, I opened my bag to check that the jar had not broken, that it had not decided to return to wherever it was before we were a species with hands. The water inside held itself as if it had been practicing. I unscrewed the lid a fraction, just a laborer’s quarter-turn, and leaned in as if I could hear the difference between what has been kept and what merely is.

Something like faint applause rose to my ear, or perhaps it was only the vibration of a truck rolling through the next block, something large and ordinary on its way to the flood. A thread of cool air traced my cheek, and then, so soft I could have called it inventory or made a note to call it later, I heard a voice inside the jar say hello in a kettle-just-before-boil register, the exact note of a man who believed naming a day could rescue it.

Then the light turned green, and I closed the lid. I drove toward my brother and the bread, the museum’s day in my bag speaking to itself about umbrellas, and the city, which does not care, listening in its sleep.

Chapter One

The first thing I inherit is the weight of the keys.

They hang from a frayed blue lanyard, each one a different shape, a different decade of a building’s stubbornness, and when I close my fist around them the metal is hot from the sun and the press of strangers’ hands. Halina’s keys. The seed library has always sounded like a small claim, smaller than a city library, smaller than a church, yet somehow its keys weigh the most. They settle into my palm like stones drawn out of water.

We bury my grandmother on a day that refuses to be anything but sky. The ground is a cracked plate that rang when the backhoe bit it last week. The gravediggers did their best and everyone acts like they can’t hear the distant complaint of metal on clay, the dry rattle under the minister’s words. There is one old cottonwood in the corner of the cemetery, its leaves turned the color of loose tea, and it sifts the hot wind over our heads in a tired, papery sound.

People come because Halina taught them how to save what was left to save. Pike farmers with faces shaped by wind, town kids who sprouted in her after-school programs, a mayor with her hair just so, even the new folks in polo shirts who bought the old Keho farm and introduced themselves as “from the city, but we’re learning.” They bring food and stories and envelopes of seeds that have their own names written in shaky ink. On the folding table under the tent, next to the ham loaf and the sheet cake with the piped blue roses, people leave their packets like offerings. Pinto, October, Hutterite Soup. Names like spells. A child upends a jelly jar of bean seeds into my hands. They are mottled, so white and brown they look like things that can’t happen at the same time.

“Your grandma started this family with a handful from her mother,” Mrs. Suchak says, patting my wrist, then offers me a paper sack with two jars of pickled carrots, the brine cloudy, the sprigs of dill like calf legs swimming in the vinegar. Her palm smells like Sta-Flo and pie dough. “Such hands she had.”

“She did,” I say, and after fifty condolences I can keep my voice even. The keys coast along the bones of my wrist, click at my pulse like insects.

They were Halina’s because Halina never lost anything important. Her cheeks were papery when she died. She took my hand and asked me to come home. She said, They’ll take the seeds if you don’t stand. She said, Don’t let them rename what we already know. She said, The seed is not an object. It’s a verb you haven’t watched finish moving.

I left this town seven years ago because I couldn’t stop listening to things that weren’t said to me. In Iowa City they call it synesthesia. In Split River they called it being a strange child. Touch a row of black-eyed peas and feel a metronome thought—count, count, count the days. Prick your finger on the sharp of a broken corn husk and there is the old tractor cough—coax, coax, coax the engine. Sit down to dinner and hear my mother hum though she is gone. Touch a seed and it begins to speak. Not words, not the tidy radio of sentences. Seeds are thick with breathing. They keep it. That is what a seed is: an attention, carefully folded.

The minister says uplift, resilience, and the whole town glances at the riverbed beyond the hedgerow. Once Split River thundered, carved a basin that gave the town its name. Four summers ago it moved underground like something that had finally decided it was done with us. A ditch now. An absence. In June the wind bowls dust from the old channel into windows we forgot to seal, into the mouths of sleeping children, into coffee cups on porches, into unfinished lives.

When the speeches end, a man in a dark suit that doesn’t know how to sit on a human body crosses the grass with a precise motion. Heat turns his face shine-soft, but he’s proud of not panting. He is the reason I kept one hand on the keys during the service.

“Ms. Trumbull?” he says. The name lands like a chair pulled out in a quiet room. “Do you have a moment?”

He says Trumbull like a file number, and it takes me a second to remember that was once my last name. I have been Lark Halina since the day I left. I turned it into one word, like an address I could fit in my mouth.

“I’ve got several,” I say. “But I’m using them.”

He offers a fraction of a smile. I see myself reflected in his sunglasses, small and sun-warped, hatless while everyone else has scarves and caps, because Halina always left her scalp to the weather with a kind of ferocity, and I had gotten used to being the person who matched her. The man’s suit is Navy Department dark; his badge is clipped to his belt even though he’s already in the cemetery. Department of Agrarian Compliance: there it is, assessed and laminated.

“I want to offer condolences,” he says. “Ms. Halina was an asset to this community, and to the state.” He pauses. “We’ve been in conversation about the proper custody of the vault.”

“It’s a root cellar with shelves and a dehumidifier,” I say, though I can feel him measuring the denial in my disgust. “A wooden desk if you go by the front door. A bulletin board with faded notices for lost dogs. You could call it a vault if you were shy around words.”

“Our office calls it a seed bank,” he says. “With function in emergent times.”

Emergent times. The phrase has the same expression as a closed door. There were rumors about the Department for years. The clean seed list they mail out, the knock-inspection-pry logic of their visits. They used to keep to the big farms and the so-called research institutions. They used to keep out of places like ours that kept our own lists. Halina penned her own in blue ink, unruled paper covered in a tight, precise hand. Absolute, he could see that hand and panic, or he could see that hand and want to hire it.

He shifts his weight. “As you’re likely aware, when a registered custodian passes—”

“She didn’t register,” I say.

“—the keys are to be returned to the state,” he continues as if finishing the sentence is an act of mercy. “We can provide a compliance number now and schedule an inventory. It will ease the transition.”

“You came to the funeral,” I say, which is not a question, but he answers anyway.

“It seemed the efficient time to connect,” he says. “And respectful.” His sunglasses make him look like a bird who has stolen a mirror. He removes a business card from a thin denim wallet and extends it. His palm is pale inside. “Ms. Pruitt,” the badge had said earlier. Not a Mr. at all. She takes off her sunglasses. Her eyes are neither apologetic nor unkind. They are tired in a way that looks practiced.

“Do you plant anything?” I ask, taking the card. I can smell the paper, a chemical brightness that always feels like being lied to gently. The card says Marla Pruitt, Field Supervisor.

“Raised by a farmer, myself,” she says with the tone of someone asked to present a credential she had already placed on the table. “My brothers still run our acreage in Franklin County. But the weather doesn’t ask for nostalgia.”

“The weather doesn’t ask for a department either,” I say. “But here we are.”

Ms. Pruitt’s mouth does something that involves both sympathy and impatience. “You can be angry later,” she says. “For everyone’s sake, it’s best to follow protocol. It protects you more than you think.” She glances at the keys with open frankness. “We’ll need those.”

“We?” I ask. “You brought a chorus?”

“The state is never one person,” she says, and then, as if another line had been rehearsed and this is where it belongs, she adds, “I’m sorry for your loss.”

She turns and moves away across the grass with that small, exact step. The minister is wiping his forehead with a folded handkerchief and losing details from his eulogy that he will never find again. The cottonwood keeps talking to the hot wind. People linger at the table and the open coolers, because it is what you do after you lower someone into earth. Eating at the mouth of the ground is a human tradition older than a lot of departments.

Jude doesn’t come. My brother told me he couldn’t get off work, which might be true, if work is the word he’s using for the hollowing out he lives inside. He went west to chase a girl once and found a different thirst. He sends postcards sometimes, photographs of mesas with one hand and his return address with the other, and in both hands there is a tremor. Halina never gave up on him returning the way you never give up on rain even the fourth summer in when your rain barrel is a memory more complicated than water. I loved him once in the way you love the person who climbs the silo to get a better look at the comet and then disappears into a night you did not invite.

I wait until the last spoonful of potato salad has warmed into danger, until the mayor claps me on the elbow, until the tent flutters and sighs, wanting a storm that will not appear. And then I go to the library because there is nothing else left that feels like an action.

The seed library sits behind the high school in a low cinderblock rectangle my father always called a fixable building. He said that as if the word fixable lived on his tongue like a mint. He said it about everything he loved: his truck, my mother’s shoulder, the old shed roof, the town’s cracked fountain, me. But the thing about fixable is that it is not a promise. He left when I was nine and died when I was twenty-two and I am still listening for the after-sound of that word.

The door is painted a color that someone thought would say cheerful and says the shade of a robin’s egg after it’s been dead a week. I fit the oldest key into the top lock, the one that sticks, and hold the lanyard taut so the other keys don’t jingle and tell everyone in the parking lot where I am. The air inside is twenty degrees cooler than outside and smells like cumin, dust, the inside of a pencil. The hum of the dehumidifier in the back room is a thin, determined line. Fluorescent lights click on and the room becomes what it has always been, a patient array of small containers. Shelves along the walls carry metal drawers with ceramic knobs. There are mason jars and envelopes and pill bottles with labels scissored from typing paper. Tobacco tins with tinny lids and rubber gaskets turned brittle. Flip-top freezer boxes that once stored ice cream bars. Each holds a collection of future.

Halina never believed in alphabetizing. She had her own way of sorting, which she explained to me once and said, “You will get it, or you will hate me for building a system out of weather.” Beans next to sunflowers when they were grown by people who taught one another how to trap the first runoff in spring. Tom Thumb popcorn next to Hungarian heart peppers because once in 1999 a woman named Bea had a bumper crop of both and brought them to the harvest exchange in a wicker laundry basket and we had to switch to the gym because people kept showing up with more. The shelves stood in patterns of connection you would not notice if you were looking for an index because the index was a story.

I set the keys on the desk, on the thin blotter where Halina kept the loan log, written in the blue fountain-pen ink that had somehow not run out for twelve years. The desk still has her jar of borrowed pens, the rubber bands that have given up on stretching and hold the place of purpose without doing the work. The chair is as narrow as my waist when I was sixteen. In the bulletin board there are thumbtacks, a Polaroid of the fourth grade field trip where my hair was the color of wheat and stuck up in a piece of private weather, a flyer reading LAST SEED SWAP OF THE SEASON in all caps. There is a clipping about the second summer the river left. The headline is neutral to the point of insult: Riverbed Exposed, Study Planned.

I take off my shoes and step into the back room. The floor is laid with those rubber tiles meant for gyms and hospitals, something forgiving that can be cleaned, that does not care what you drop. The dehumidifier exhales like an animal. Once we found a garter snake in here, coiled in the quiet under the barley. She raised her head and regarded us as if we had interrupted her reading. Halina loved that story enough to repeat it to anyone who visited: We got a snake librarian. The crop failure that year was less catastrophic than we had feared, and everyone said, See, snakes are good luck, as if luck were a reptile you could coax indoors if you left a door ajar.

My hand reaches for a jar the way a hand reaches for a glass in the dark in a kitchen you haven’t lived in for a while. Murky muscle memory. I find the Painted Pony beans by shape, by the sound the lid makes when it screws on. The label says, in Halina’s small script, that these came from Elva Proulx’s grand-daughter two summers ago. I open the jar and lay five seeds on my palm. They are the size of the first knuckle of my thumb, half cream, half a chestnut brown that looks like it could have been invented by a tree. They warm immediately, because seeds run toward heat the way stories do.

I don’t so much hear as become porous. You let a seed talk like you’d let a creek undercut your thinking. It is there whether you find it or not, until it is not. A Painted Pony does not tell you about drought. A Painted Pony gives you the number of days it takes to set a flower. It gives you the moment before Elva’s granddaughter was born, when Elva was checking her breathing, and her husband’s boots were by the back door and the radio was saying there’d be a storm at four, then changed its mind without apology. It gives you the weight of a child’s hand asking for more.

I hold my breath without meaning to. The metal of the keys on my cheek is a stripe of heat, a brand cooling.

When I was thirteen, I told Halina that the seeds were loud and it made me tired. She said, most of what you call loud is somebody else’s hunger. Then she made me drink tea that tasted like weeds and shut all the library windows and let me sleep in her office on the couch where a friend of hers once sobbed, kneading the cushion like dough. When I woke up, the room was the same size but my body fit it differently, as if sleep had been a carpenter.

Three knocks, open knuckles on the doorframe. I start so hard one of the seeds jumps from my palm and lands on the floor tile with a plastic click. A hand appears, white-haired and slow, and lifts the bean with the care you give a tooth from a child’s mouth.

“Sorry,” says the hand’s owner. Mr. Herzog. He used to have a print shop in the space that’s now the tax-preparer with the pink sign. He’s wearing a fishing vest that has small objects braided into every pocket. A brass key for something else. A whistle. A level that acts like a charm against crookedness.

“No apology needed,” I say, heart still going fast. See: this is why I left. I can take a city siren and make it a chord. But a knock in a beloved building is a panic like a fox.

“I was walking by and saw your car,” he says, sheepish but with the confidence of a man who has seen seven iterations of this town and can call himself a contributor. “Wanted to get you the milk vetch from Doris. She said if she died it had to go through me, and then she went on with the business of not dying. Woman’s stubborn. Still, I like to keep my end of a bargain ready.”

He produces a pill bottle with a label for a cholesterol medication and shakes it. It makes the music of small authority.

“Thank you,” I say, and when I take the bottle, the little tan seeds press into my skin. Milk vetch: poor soil’s friend. Even the name sounds like persistence. I touch the cap and get a scene in late spring. Mud. A little boy with a tooth gap. A handful of seed that looks like sand. Tiny possibility. I close my hand around it, gently, to keep from drowning.

“Your grandmother gave me my first little printer,” he says, looking not at me but at the shelf of onions, at the brown paper sacks where the seeds make sorcery of something as dull as an envelope. “Everybody thinks I was born with a business in my hands, but I wasn’t. She traded it to me for flyers. Save this and we saved the town a year. That was the flyer.” He laughs. “She liked a joke you had to live with.”

“She did,” I say. I can see her hand drawing a little cartoon bean at the bottom of the flyer, smiling in a way that meant Don’t smile at me, I’m busy. Halina disapproved of cute. She trusted only ferocity, but she knew how to dress it for public.

“You got company,” Mr. Herzog says, thumbing back toward the hallway. “Woman with a badge came to my shop to ask if I’d seen you. Ten years ago I’d have told her to go fry her clipboard. Now, well. She looked like a person who eats her lunch in her car.”

“Ms. Pruitt,” I say.

“They ain’t going to let it be,” he says. “It’s too sensible. Town hands, town seeds. An archive that returns to itself. The government can’t see something circular without wanting to make it a straight line and then own the ends.”

He sets the bean he saved back on my palm with more gravity than I feel fit to carry. “This place holds everything that made sense about Split River. Don’t let them make it a museum.”

When he leaves, I close the door until it is only a narrow invitation. I stand in the aisle between the legumes and the squash, where the air is a little cooler, as if the seeds are evaporating a memory of rain. Halina never locked the inner door. We had nothing anyone wanted to steal. She used to say that like a dare. We have precious things but not expensive ones, that’s the trick.

The room’s noise sits up around me. The tiny, overlapping hum. Not actual sound, but whatever name you give to the friction between breath and time. Sorghum whispers about the hands that threshed it, honest hands, worried hands. Sunflower hums Bee. There is a tangle under everything that is not a plant’s voice. It is older. It is the logic of hoarding when you come from hunger. It is the logic of sharing when you came from the same.

On the desk there is an envelope in Halina’s hand. It is not a surprise. Even as a child I knew she stored future in paper. For Lark, it says. Do not open until you are inside. Obedient, I slit it with my fingernail.

There are two things inside: a key on a ribbon of red seam binding, and a note on a yellow index card.

The note says, in her hand that could have been a font except fonts have no mercy: If you are reading this, you know why you had to leave and why you had to come back. The state will say a thing is safe if it can be counted. Sometimes that is true. But safety is a poor god. Use this key when you cannot tell if you are being careful or small.

The address is not an address. There is no P.O. Box, no street. There is a drawing, the way we used to draw maps when we played the treasure game in the elementary school playground. Here is the gym. Here is the line of the fence. Here are three trees like buttons. Here is the earth where we buried the box because we could not keep it above ground without inviting a different kind of trouble. She has put an X where a person who loved certain shadows would know to look at sunset.

The ribboned key is old iron, heavy, with a hole at one end where someone has worn it into a story. It looks like it would turn in a lock carved out of limestone. It looks like it would sing in a door that has not been opened in a long time.

Under the index card she has slipped a small glassine envelope with a dozen bean seeds. They are a color I do not have a word for. If brown is a low sound, these are a note higher, the color of a river when it carries soil it only just met. On the label Halina printed a name I have never seen written anywhere: Oriole’s Heart.

As soon as I pour them onto my hand, the room tips. It is subtle, like a rowboat taking someone into it you were not expecting.
