The Oriole’s Heart is warm before it meets my skin, as if it were trembling to be held. I press my thumb to a single seed and it moves against me like a small animal. Then it opens.

I hear my mother.

Not a word. But the exact salt of her skin I have not smelled since she went away. The hum she made when she looked over her shoulder to see if the pot was boiling. The shape her mouth made when she read silently. And the shadow of a car at dusk, the interior light catching the wrist of a woman with a blue birthmark in the shape of a bean. I hear Halina say a low no, not the word said out loud in the kitchen but the thought said in a different room. I hear the door closing. I hear a promise being rearranged.

The seed leaves my hand without moving. There is only my palm, empty. The sound stays. It is like listening to a past that has been made into a room and then locked from both sides.

The dehumidifier clicks and shudders, its small labor louder for a heartbeat. The window’s light will change in ten minutes. I am inside. I am inside and someone wants this place like it wants my bones.

I pocket the ribboned key and the Oriole’s Hearts, and then, with both hands, I lift the heavy ring of the library’s keys and feel their weight differently, not like stones now but like birds that consented, somehow, to land. I say, out loud to no one, We are closed, and lock the front door. Then I do the thing Halina taught me when all you have are the smallest tools: I sit at the desk and I begin to write down the names. The list is the first defense. It is also a prayer. And if I am praying to anything, it is to the shade of the cottonwood and to a bright bird that always knows a way back to a nest you have hidden so well even you begin to doubt it was real.

On the morning they bless the dam, the river lies flat as a held breath. A dull light leaks through the cloud, enough to turn each droplet on the reeds into a small bead, enough to pick out the geometry of wings as the first terns begin to work their circuits over the water. They find the upstream breeze and tack into it, sharpening and softening, making and unmaking the same shapes as if they are drawing a message only their own bodies can read.

I stand in a line of men in orange vests and one woman with a clipboard who keeps tilting it to keep the paper dry, and beyond us is the dais with its garlanded microphone and the plastic chairs waiting for officials. Someone behind me mutters that the canopy should have been larger. Someone else lifts a brass plate and checks the ceremonial lamps—a domestic gesture in the wrong place, the same way eyelashes would look wrong on an excavator. Diesel and incense lap over the wet. Far out, a boy in a narrow boat trails his hand in the current, and a thin dog's ribs show like a shuttered window as it watches him. If this were the city I could forget I have knees and shoulders. Here everything has muscle; nothing holds still for long.

The terns skim low enough that their shadows cross the new concrete, and I have to fight the childish urge to throw something into the air, to test whether the shadows will take that, too.

“You came,” Dhanu says, arriving as if the river had coughed him up. He hasn’t shaved, and he smells of fish and the smoked tea he keeps in a thermos, and his eyes have the unkempt attention of a dog that still knows the world belongs to it. “Bird-sayer, you came early.”

“I don’t have much to say,” I tell him, and offer him a smile I hope he will ignore. I have not forgiven his non-names for me—bird-sayer, bird-cheat, bird-wife—as if loving something that does not love him back has a name that hurts me more than it hurts him.

He looks past me at the dais, the bunting pinned into the river wind. “It will rain,” he says, though the sky is not gray enough yet. He drags the toe of his rubber sandal through the mud until it makes a narrow canal, diverting a rivulet from where I am standing to where he is. “Do they know? The ones with the garlands. Do they know what they are telling this water to do?”

“They say the reservoir will be the size of three hundred thousand fields,” I say. “They say we will have lights that don’t die at the first storm, and a clinic that doesn’t drown in its own smell. They say the terns will breed on the new islands.”

“They say,” he repeats, in the slow way he would say a curse. A tern breaks free of the line of its own flock and hangs above us, a fixed piece of sky with points. “And what do you say?”

I don’t tell him I wrote the paper and nothing in it was untrue, only unlived. I don’t tell him how I fed ten years of counts and nest maps and hatching data into a model and asked it to speak for me, and when it did—tidily, with numbers packed together wrinkless as new bedsheets—I let it. I don’t tell him that I turned common nouns into italic names and the river into a solvable thing. I only say, “I say they will adapt.”

His mouth opens as if to spit, then thinks better of it. He squints at the smallest tern out over the far bank and says, “Look.”

He has a fisherman’s knack for seeing other things through movement—wind under wing, not just wing. He sees the difference between current and drift in the way a single scale of light turns on the water. I follow his look. The terns are flying in a figure I have not seen in years, a pattern of short scissors and low skims, as if snapping the surface to test the membrane between worlds. A wedding figure, my mother would have said. Or a funeral one. She had names for their arrangements that never matched the occasions to which people wore them.

I can’t say I speak their language, not in any way a person like Dhanu would recognize. When I was six, my mother and I took a spool of string and a piece of chalk out to the old jetty where the wooden posts still smelled of people who had passed down fish and bananas and wrapped newspapers to one another. She tied the end of the string to my wrist, then laid the same string on the boards and pulled it until the chalk line was straight and white across the wood. Now, she said. Watch. Each time a tern crossed, I made a mark where its shadow cut the line. At the end there was a clumsy constellation: a series of overlaps and empty spaces that meant nothing by themselves. Only when she lifted the chalk line and snapped it again, and again, and we layered a dozen mornings together until the wood was a pale ghost of lines, did a pattern appear. The terns had their habits, the river its own. Over time we learned what they did when shrimp came into the shallows, when a new sandbar rose, when a storm spun a dirty wind over the flats. It was not their language. It was a kind of listening.

Later, when grant money arrived like a fat fish and I was already good at writing software that dreamed of describing nightmares, I fed all my lines and shadows into a machine that could make much prettier patterns. When it spoke—I mean when it gave me graphs—I trained myself not to hear my mother in them.

“They think the one with the hat is a predator,” Dhanu says, which makes no sense because there are a dozen hats out here and all of them are ugly in different ways. He points. On the dais, the district secretary has arrived, and the hat is a stiff white, folded like a boat. For a second the terns hesitate, a sharp jerking in the pattern, like a stutter in a song. They have long been unconcerned with us unless we go near their eggs. People in hats have been on this bank since birds invented wings. But then the hat turns so its brim catches the light, and the flock lifts as a ribbon lifts when pulled, and I feel something that is not the hat’s doing at all: under my sandals, the tiniest shiver in the mud, like a heartbeat under skin.

“They’ve started closing the far gate,” I say to nobody in particular. The man with the garlands on the plate gives me a quick, startled look, as if he thought I was a courtesy and not a mouth.

Dhanu’s eyebrows tangle. “Without notice?”

“They told me yesterday,” I lie. I did get an email last week. A polite note with a file attached: test sequences, dates, times. I dragged it into a folder full of other polite notes, then went to count nests. I would have thought, I tell myself now, that the test gate would make the same drop and rise as the old sluice did when I was twelve and the flood took the sugar factory and the lower school and half the mango grove. I would have thought there would be time for the fish to find their way back and for the birds to fall into a new habit. My thinking has never been the problem. It’s the thinking I throw away.

“Jaya!” someone calls, using my name in public like a hand at the back of my neck. It is Mr. Thakkar from the Department, tin-framed glasses, a quick sideways smile like a boy who has a pen behind his ear and likes that he does. He carries a file even out on the mud because this is how we know he is not the kind of man the river can mislay. “You’ll come up and say a few words? Just after the ribbon.”

“What can I possibly say that the chief engineer cannot?” I say. I am good at this, the skip and twist, making language a fish that stays forever just beyond the net.

“Whatever the birds are saying,” he says, blushing a little, as if the request is both silly and indecent. “You are the one who understands them. People love it.”

“I sell it to people who love it,” I correct, but not out loud. Aloud I say, “After the ribbon.”

He glances at my shoes. “Do you want something over the heels? You’ll sink.”

“I’ll float,” I say, and he laughs as if I am someone he has chosen. He goes back to the dais. On the far bank, the boy stands up in his boat and looks at his own hands as if they have done something remarkable without telling him. His dog makes one small anxious sound.

The shiver comes again, a larger one, like an old engine catching. The surface of the river creases. Around us the terns level out and the figure they were making dilutes into a long slow line. They begin to call, a brisk mechanical sound. When I was a child my mother used to imitate them with her own tongue and teeth, and the dog would tilt its head, and the buffalo in the field would glance up and then go on chewing. The terns do not call for us. They call to one another like women on different rooftops practicing a language that never appears in any book.

“Will you come tonight?” Dhanu asks suddenly. The question is an old knot: the monthly meeting in the back room of the tea shop, a circle of people who build each other out of worry and butter crackers. They have invited me every month and I have made every excuse. Bird-sayer, bird-sayer, come sit. You are needed. My excuse is that I am needed elsewhere. It is a true excuse; they like their needs to be religion and mine to be theft.

“I have the nests to check up near the ferry,” I say. “And the new island looks like it may have taken a shift. The wind is going to turn. I have work.”

“Your work is to hear,” he says. “You can do that in a room. You can do that with other people in it. You think we will contaminate your little ear.”

“If I wanted ugly friends I’d join a chorus,” I say. He cackles. He slaps my shoulder and his hand is warmer than the morning. He drinks from his thermos and then offers it. I want the tea so badly I could bite the cup, but I shake my head. If I take the tea I will be in his mouth for the rest of the day, and I want to keep my own taste.

The minister’s convoy arrives. It is the wrong vehicle for riverbanks: a long shining animal that wants roads. Men run in front to find its path across the pocked earth, and a small boy with a flag and no shirt tries to outrun all of them. Then there is a phalanx of umbrellas, black and serious, though the rain has not yet decided. The terns throw one last shape and break. They rise, then settle on the sandbar like sharp gray stones. A few keep working the water, steady in their business, the thin bills dipping, the tiny white spoon of their underbellies flashing as they bank.

The brass plate is lit; the ribbon is tied across the two stainless posts which someone has wiped five times in case the river smudges them; the dignitaries take their places. The minister is smaller than the television makes him, more like a man. He presses his hands together and bows and the cameras applaud him noiselessly with their red eyes.

Mr. Thakkar glances at me. His eyebrows lift. It is my cue to become the interesting animal that makes everyone else seem practical in comparison.

“Ladies and gentlemen,” I say into the ringing loudspeaker that, like all loudspeakers near water, thinks the water is its true audience. “We gather today on the bank of a river older than our meetings, our houses, our names. No one can bless a river, but we can ask to be good to it.” I hear my mother’s unkind mutter—Who is ‘we’?—and push on. “Those who live by this water know there are voices here that do not carry through microphones. The river terns have built on these stones season after season, and will build on the new islands we are creating for them upstream.”

He loves that, Mr. Thakkar does. He beams.

“They are speaking to us now,” I say, because this is what every crowd wants: to be addressed by the non-human. “They say”—the terns lift like a blown sheet and my mouth goes dry—“they say eat while the water holds.”

It is not what I meant to say. It is what my mother would call a grammar mistake. To share the imperative of another species is a kind of arrogance, but there is a cousin to it: to clean someone else’s words and lay them back at their feet like a washed bone. If I could I would make my words as useless and trinkety as any blessing. But the terns have changed their figure again; they are cutting short, quick angles over the little sandbar in front of us, and from here I can see the pale speckle of eggs that look exactly like their background if you look with the wrong kind of wanting. Something in the water has shifted; the surface no longer shows its true wind; the low upstream gate is taking a bite of current and holding it for a later chewing.

Back down in the mats of rushes, a small boy screams. He is knee-deep in a place that, yesterday, I could have walked across with dry ankles. The minister’s bodyguard steps forward into my line of sight and blocks him out and then they are lighting the wicks and the smell of kerosene fights with the stink of river and wet earth. The ribbon trembles as if it knows more about tide than about ceremony.

“If we build with care,” I say, and immediately hate my mouth for its smoothness, its habit of placing cushions under everyone’s feet, “we can share this place with the more-than-human and with each other.”

There is a smattering of applause, quick and grateful that someone has said something that belongs in a file, and then the minister takes the mic and begins to talk about numbers, which are the only poetry that moves budgets. I step back into the shallows of the crowd and feel the edge of a stone under my heel, and that pain convinces me, briefly, that I still have nouns the river can understand.

I hear the splash before I see the change: not a surface splash but a belly one, a whole-body gesture. The boy in the boat is standing now, and his dog is baying, and silvery flashes break the river skin as fish rise and then fail where air is. It is too early, too sudden. For a moment the terns stud the air like buttons and their calls become a tearing. They toss themselves into the air and down, the way women throw themselves toward a door that cannot be opened. They catch three fish, seven, twenty, a flurry, and the river continues to flatten like a sheet being smoothed by a large, indifferent hand.

The motor of the far gate catches again, and I feel—through my sandal soles, through the braided strap, through the soft of me—the thud of a decision made somewhere else arriving here late and untranslatable.

Dhanu is already moving, the way he moves when a net needs more hands, without thinking first. He sloshes into the water to his shins and then his knees, and there is a parting like hair around him. He reaches for the boy in the rushes and pulls him up under his armpits and tosses him into a drier patch. The dog swims with an open mouth and stupid courage. The minister keeps speaking, because it is not his business to stop speaking while other things are happening, and because there is a camera, and because he has worked on these lines and they will not fit anywhere else.

A tern lifts straight up from the sandbar as if something has lifted it on a sudden current of irritable air. It is close enough that if I reached I could unthread a feather. It hangs for an instant in the sweet place between effort and fall, then banks and darts toward me and, because I am human, I flinch. It is a ridiculous motion, ridiculous the way it would be to duck under a ceiling of thatch you have known all your life. I am more ashamed than afraid. But the tern does not strike me. It lets go.

Something small hits the back of my hand and slides into my palm. The impulse to throw it away is one part superstition, one part the skill of someone who has handled birds long enough to know when to let something fall. I make a bowl of my palm and look down.

It is not a fish. It is a ring, plain and thin, with a small notch on the outer edge where it once met a stone or a pipe. There is river grit in the groove where a finger would go. If I turn it in the watery light, I can see the faint ghost of someone’s knuckle in the shine, the way jewelry remembers its owner and you can feel the rent through it. My mouth goes completely dry. For a second my body is exactly the shape of the child I some mornings still am: bare feet on the old jetty, the chalk string, my mother’s wrist. A ring with a notch like a worry, which my mother pushed up her finger with her teeth when her hands were wet. A ring the river took twenty-two years ago on a night when the sugar factory’s wall went and the lower school went and half the mango grove went, and my mother’s hand caught on the lip of the little fiberglass boat and then slipped, and the ring went tick into the water, and the sound of it was so small that I did not hear anything else we lost because I could think only of that sound and how it was the most arrogant sound I had ever heard.

The tern circles once over my head, then rises and joins the line over the sandbar, as if it has delivered both a message and the proof that it was not the messenger after all. I feel the shape of the dam in my palm; I feel the shape of my mother’s absent hand. Mr. Thakkar has turned back toward me with triumph in his face because the minister, in the slow helicopter of his speech, has said my name. He wants me to be where I will be visible. The ring in my hand makes me the opposite of visible. It makes me an absence, a hole in the figure.

Under my shoes, the mud shivers again, and the small line of terns along the sandbar lifts one by one, up down up down as if practicing a more anxious alphabet.

If you asked me to translate what they are doing, I would say: not fear, not even warning. An accounting. They are adding the weight of fish in their bellies to the weight of the air under their wings to the weight of the water drawn away and held at an invisible height, and they are setting it against the weight of shells that will not crack. They are doing the kind of math that kills the stories we tell ourselves about generosity and leaves only the fact of time and hunger. They are measuring, and in their measuring I hear the bright angle of my mother’s laugh when she took the ring off to knead dough and put it in her mouth and pretended to swallow to make me scream, which I always did, which she always loved.

The minister cuts the ribbon. The plush sounds ridiculous under the blade. The crowd claps. The cameras lick and blink. A thin rain begins, the kind that cannot make up its mind whether it is responsible for anything. Dhanu shakes water out of his ears like a dog and looks at me in the moment when he can still be just my neighbor and not my jury.

“Bird-sayer,” he says, soft enough that I could refuse him hearing it. “What do they say now?”

I open my mouth. The ring bites my hand with its small cold and I close my fingers around it as a person would close their fingers around a secret for warmth.

“They say eat while the water holds,” I say, which is not an answer and not a lie, and behind me the river begins to shiver in earnest, as if something very large has turned over in its sleep.

By the time the lake gave my mother back, it had learned the shape of every bone in the valley.

I stood where the waterline had been last summer and smiled at the fresh knife mark the drought had carved around the basin—clean and pale, as if someone had sliced a rind from the hills. The shore was no longer shore but a confounded seam, a band of chalk and salt that made your tongue taste iron. The wind came off the cup of Marrow Lake with a schoolyard’s breath—warm, dusted with dried algae and the copper throb of coins—and all along the newly birthed flats, things rose up that I had been told belonged forever to forgetting. Fence posts that had sprouted barnacles grinned with old wire. The steeple of the First Tabernacle of Grafton tilted like someone listening. A fishing chair polished by years popped its legs out of the mud, and a ladle, and a bicycle frame, and the rib cage of a sedan that had gone silent under a president I no longer remembered liking.

They had strung caution tape, the fluorescent plastic plucking lightly in the breeze, because of us—the watchers with our styrofoam cups near our mouths, townspeople I knew by the shape of their shoulders even after fourteen years and strangers who came when water receded anywhere, drawn to the spectacle of absence. There was a news van already. A child kicked at a caked catfish skull until his mother cuffed him. The smell was wrong and true at once. It held something of the cellar of my father’s house, something of pennies, something that made the back of my palate remember the night I turned eighteen and drove out of here with my hand on the radio knob, hunting a station that would not betray me with a song about home.

Sheriff Kline stood with her boots ankle-deep in the exposed silt, hair the color of hammerheads now. Leona had been two years ahead of me in school, had once laughed so hard at a joke I made during a pep rally that milk came out of her nose. We hadn’t spoken in a decade until her voice earlier that morning through my Phoenix half-sleep, the air already gathering its heat against my apartment’s windows. We need you, she had said. No prelude. We found her.

“Ruth,” she said. She did not hug me. Neither one of us had that in us for this. “Be careful. It cakes.” She gestured at the ground, and when I stepped beneath the tape, the lakebed answered with a soft catch at my heels, a loverly give that was not love.

“How far down?” I asked, because saying anything else would make it real.

Leona tilted her chin toward the ghost of water, toward the line the lake had kept like a promise for generations. “Twelve feet’s worth of summer,” she said. “We haven’t seen the roadbed in my lifetime. You can make out the hash marks now. The old county road that ran through Grafton. The way folks used to drive into town to buy screws and pie.” She shaded her eyes. “My mother says she can almost see Mrs. Fenn’s quilt line from here.”

The Bureau chart would say Coleman Basin—Marrow Lake to those of us who had never liked the word basin for anything but a bowl—was at forty-two percent of capacity. I had access to those charts more easily than most. I filed water rights claims three states over and listened to men whose shoes never saw mud argue over acre-feet like children divvying a pie. In my desk drawer there was a translucent ruler I had used to measure the gentle bloodless slope of falling, the last five summers in particular a graph of hunger.

“It was near the old church,” Leona said, stepping, and I followed. “A fisherman snagged a jacket last week and next day came back with his cousin and a dip net to see if they could turn up tackle. Turned up your mother’s ring instead. Caught the sun.”

I wanted to say people have been mistaking rings for proof since the beginning of rings, but all that rose in my throat was the taste of sugar dough and lake water, the afternoon my mother had brought me to Fenn’s Bake Shop for the last time and then taken me to the dam to see what a wall could do to a river.

Marrow’s dam was a brown wedge at the far end of the arid cup, planted half a century ago during a season of confidence. The men who set its bones in concrete had called the work Reclamation, as if the river had taken something from them first. In the photographs in the county office, you can see them grinning in their shirtsleeves atop the curved wall with the valley spread behind them like a bed they had made themselves. My mother had stood me there when I was ten and said, Look. Watch what men convince water to do. She did not say at what price. She did not say whose couch they pulled out from under the water and whose couch they left to mold.

We walked past the bent spire and something ghost-white that turned out to be the shell of a turtle. A flock of dragonflies stitched the air with blue thread. The earth had opened into a miniature of its own gullies, new as a scar, and I was grateful for the way my feet had always known this ground. You could stand here blind and know the angle of the wind and the smell and the give. It was not the same as comfort, but it was in the same family.

They had draped a tarp over the body, a cheap blue that made the whole thing look like a child’s game, and there was a generator thrumming behind the county van, and the undertaker’s boy—who was now a man with the same red whiskers his father had had, the same inability to find a hat that fit—standing and watching his fingernails. When Leona lifted the edge of the tarp, flies rose like a small prayer.

She had come back wearing green. That was the first true thought that landed in me, stupid and clear: my mother had gone into the water wearing a green dress. I had known my mother’s clothing the way a small animal knows the scent of a path. I had slept inside her sweaters when she left them on chairs. The dress was there in shreds, fabric the color of junegrass, gone soft and then stiffer in places with silt. The ring glinted—a hammered copper circle with a nick where I had once, as a baby, bitten it. The skin had a pallor that was not decay, not yet, but the lake’s idea of preservation, and there was river silt matted in her hair. Her hair. There was too much. In my shoulder, a stitch began, the pain you get when you run too fast after not running in months.

“We can do this in the office if you prefer,” Leona said. Her voice had learned a step down, a floor lower than it used to be. People who speak to grief every day find that lower floor.

“I’m all right,” I said, which was what you say when you are absolutely not.

She did not say Are you sure. She did not say I’m sorry again, which she had said on the phone and which had passed through me like radio static. She said, “Your father can’t come; you know that.” I nodded as if that had been a question.

I did not touch my mother’s face. It felt like a sacrilege I would not be forgiven for by any god I had stopped believing in. But I looked at the mouth that had told me stories I now could not retell without hearing how much of them were about escape—roads heading west at dusk, trains that took you to cities where your name meant something else. I looked at the wrists, and the second true thought landed like a stone thrown into water: there were marks there, not purple bruises any longer, but grooves.

“Don’t say anything yet,” Leona said, too late, tipped forward into the place between ritual and report. “Just take a moment. We believe it’s her.” She swallowed. Her throat had thickened since I knew her last; everything about her had thickened. “Your mother’s dental chart is in storage. We’ll do our care.”

I was trying to remember the day she disappeared and the day after and the week after, and all I could get were the edges, the chores. The bowl of undercooked beans. The two grey socks rolled together on the floor. The way the porch boards gave a little at the second-nailed end where my father had said he’d go back and fix them and never did. My father’s silence that became furniture. The rumor in my torso that I would one day build a life somewhere that baked you dry, that nothing could seep into. As if that would save me.

I hear you’ve got a job in an office, someone from Marrow had said to my father at the feed store when I came back for Thanksgiving my sophomore year. Like a real one. He’d nodded without using my name, and then had looked at the sacks of seed like they were going to tell him secrets. I had decided in that moment to stop coming back on holidays, because there are only so many times you can take a dead man to a living altar.

“Was she near the road?” I asked now, voice steady because good training is bone-deep by the time you can name it. “She wasn’t a wanderer.”

“Near as we can tell,” Leona said. “The mud doesn’t give back clean, Ruth; you know that. But her heel—see here—she wasn’t far from what used to be Main. And there’s… listen, I’m going to show you something, and I need you to be a bench when I do. All right? Not a daughter. Not yet.”

I nodded because I wanted to earn being told.

She peeled the tarp further and eased the jaw with two fingers that had built fences and birthed a colt and written tickets and called an ambulance for the boy who flipped his ATV at the quarry. Leona’s hands, like all our hands here, were a ledger.

Inside, nestled like a child’s secret, were three smooth stones.

“Gizzard stones,” the undertaker’s boy said, although he was a man now and his voice failed him at the end. He’d thought to make it lighter, to make it a farmer’s joke. No one smiled.

We were raised on stories where men in the old country put rocks in the pockets of the women they did not want to rise. We were raised on a version of church that told you weight was a solution. But this was not pockets. This was a mouthful against speech. One stone the size of a robin’s egg. Two like dice. I thought of my mother’s voice caught between them and wanted to tear the sky.

Leona pulled the tarp down again slow, like an eyelid. The generator coughed, hiccuped, caught again. A gust of air almost blew the tape into my hair.

“Leona,” I said. I did not know where the strength came from in my throat. It was the same place you sing from if someone in your family plays an instrument and asks you to fill the room.

“Mm.”

“Do you think she walked in like this?” I asked. “With stones in her mouth.”

She watched me the way a nurse watches the moment between medicine and its work. “No,” she said finally. “I think she was put under. But I’m raw, Ruth. I could be wrong.”

I had the oddest desire to apologize to her because my mother had come back in her county. As if grief were a thing that made clerical work for public servants. We somehow always make women sorry for the trouble our bodies make. I pressed my fingers into my palm until crescents bloomed.

The crowd shifted, the way wheat shifts, a collective sigh you hear with your skin. The news van’s satellite dish squeaked. Somewhere far across the dry dish of the lake, a dog barked a bark that ricocheted.

Do you want to see the ring, Leona had asked me on the phone. Hadn’t you made that ring with her from a kit she bought at the craft store? Copper sheet, little mallet, letter stamps. A Saturday at the kitchen table hitting TINY HARD THINGS. She had stamped LARK on hers and LARK was my mother’s name. And I had stamped MINE on mine. We had laughed like thieves, like women who thought we might leave and take only ourselves.

“Do you think anyone knew?” I asked now. It was an absurd question. The answer to every question here had always been: yes. Someone saw you buy that shirt. Someone counted the hours your father spent in his truck outside the bar. Someone noticed Lark stopped buying cheese. But knowing and saying were different countries.

“I think some of us thought she ran,” Leona said, as if she could afford the verb we does. As if she had lived through those weeks of casseroles gone cold. “I think some of us hoped she did.”

My mother, in a town’s mouth, had been a woman with a tune in her. Some had called it rebellion the way they call a field that won’t take seed uncooperative. Others had called it danger. She was the wrong temperature for this place, which made her a rumor and a cure. I had wanted to be her and not be her so badly the inside of me throbbed for years.

“You need me to say?” I asked. “That it’s her.”

“I need you to tell me if you believe it is. And then we’ll do the rest with the clean attention it deserves.”

I bent without bending, the way you do when you try not to lean toward something and can’t help it. I looked at copper, at the joining, at the nick where a child’s teeth had marked time. The groove across the knuckles as if someone had held her hand too tight. There was a thread looped around her left wrist—red, faded, the kind we used to tie around each other when Mrs. Perino told us in fourth grade to make friendship bracelets. I had made it while pretending my pencil was a reed and my desk a river and Mrs. Perino hadn’t seen my eyes sliding out the window to the cottonwoods. I hadn’t given mine to anyone. It wasn’t the kind of bracelet you gave to a mother, but I had tied it to her wrist one afternoon, a joke. Later she had tugged it back and forth while we watched the evening news—a nervous feed. In the cool gleam of the damp silt it looked like a story someone had started and abandoned.

“It’s her,” I said. My voice did something like it had to remember where to put the weight. It found the old path. “It’s my mother.”

Leona nodded and then she was law again, giving orders low and steady to the undertaker’s son, to the deputy whose shadow I recognized from basketball games in a gym that smelled of oranges and sweat. Document. Bag. Do not drop anything into this mud if you can help it; it will take it and never say thank you. The crowd behind us hummed, and I heard my name once, twice, then in a whisper that lifted and curled, Like the wind was picking it up and sending it to someone else.

I stepped back. The lakebed held me with a reluctance that felt biblical. I thought of the morning Leona had called, how my apartment had been full of light already, so much light in that city you paid for screen shades to pretend it was less. I thought of the teeth that were stones. I thought of the sound the lake would have made when it took her, which is no sound at all—just the busy whispering of water doing its work.

“Are you staying?” Leona asked, not looking at me as she asked, because looking is a kind of permission we grant and revoke a thousand times a day. “We’ll need you for some days at least.”

“My father—” I began.

“He’s where he is,” she said, not unkindly. “They have him a routine. We can bring him here if that’s what you want but he won’t see what you want him to see.”

I’d last visited my father in the spring when the snow had melted off the high road but they still served soup in paper cups in the visiting room because you couldn’t trust a metal spoon with men like him. He had watched a static TV show and I had said I got a raise and he had nodded and said, Good for you, like a left bench coach who’d forgotten the score. There had been a smell in the place I could never place until I realized it was all the old brands of aftershave I had ever known commingling.

“I have a room,” I said. My mouth said it. My mouth knew where my body was going before I did.

“Back at the house?” Leona asked, and she pressed the back of her wrist to the sweat at her hairline, leaving a smear of silt there—war paint, if you wanted it to be. “Is it all right there?”

I hadn’t been inside my childhood home in eight years. The last time, I had gone in with a key I’d never returned because we never had a talk in our family about the ethics of keys. The plastic runner was still on the hall carpet. The jar on the windowsill still held the turquoise buttons my mother had bought for a coat she never had the money to own. Dust had laid down in a way that suggested it was tired of being always wiped away.

“It’s a roof,” I said. “It doesn’t have to be more for a while.”

When I turned toward the hill, the sun made a brilliant white band on the lip of the basin, the kind of brightness you want to put in your mouth even though your mother once warned you not to lick knives. The people stepped aside. A woman I didn’t recognize placed a hand on my arm and then took it away. Another offered me a bottled water as if that would be an irony the universe might enjoy. I took it. The plastic crackled. My hands smelled like lake.

When I looked back once—because that is what the body does at thresholds, it looks back—Leona had her palm on the tarp, not in a benediction, not in any formal gesture I could name, but like a woman trying to tell another woman with no useful language that she would stay until the work was done. It occurred to me that if this was going to be a story, if one day someone would write a book and say, In a small town in a drought year, a lake gave back what they thought it had kept, they would try to make the scene pretty. They would find something noble in the tilt of the church or the ragged way the blue plastic held its place against the wind. But this wasn’t pretty. It was thick and mean and ordinary and full of flies. If there was any noble thing here, it was in the small, boring doing—photographing, lifting, bagging a thread.

As I climbed the slope, my breath got shorter. My chest recognized the climb before my mind did. Heat lived inside my shirt like a second animal. At the top, where the road turned from new dust to old, I could see the white scrape of the waterline on the far hills like a ring someone had forgotten to take off and now couldn’t, and beyond it the shimmering heat rivers that rose up from the asphalt, making everything interesting and far.

I had no plan but the one laid out for me by habit: go turn the key; open the window; see what lives where you left it. I wanted to be grateful for something specific, so I chose the dragonflies, the blue absurdity of them. I chose the way the undertaker’s son had tucked a strand of hair behind his ear and then remembered it was not his hair to touch and flushed a color he would always remember.

When I reached my car, my phone was a small animal panicking in the cup holder with messages. A number from town. A number I didn’t recognize but could tell from the bloat of digits was a reporter. A text from a man in Phoenix who had become my occasional winter, sent at 7:12 a.m.: u ok? And then, later, another: I saw the news. Call. He was good enough that sending that made me love him a little more and also want to drive the car into a tree. My thumb hovered and then went to airplane mode because there are times when the sky is the only thing that can stand you.

There had been other droughts. There had been other remnants. People had found a hairbrush, a waterlogged book from Grafton’s library that had swelled into a soft brick. Once, when I was twelve, someone had found a mailbox with its door sealed shut with mud. Inside were postcards, their colors bled to elegies, addressed to Raymond and Hazel and a PO box no longer real. I had taken one and propped it against my mirror until my mother said either keep it or lose it and I had lost it. I wished now for the small impunity of theft.

As I drove the curve that would take me up to the house, the stand of cottonwoods on the left made their old sound—the silvered rattle that to me is the sound of being alive—and the skyline of my childhood rose up. Someone had bolted a Go Easy on the Water sign to a post where the teenagers used to carve their initials. Beyond everything, the dam sat in its seat in the canyon like a tongue pressed against a hole in a tooth. It had seemed exciting once, that control. It had seemed adult. It had seemed like what the world was about when I was a girl who thought rules were the way you kept meeting one another possible.

I stopped where the shoulder widened and looked out one more time across the shrinking skin of the lake. The blue wasn’t blue so much as the lake’s memory of blue. Boats that had once cut it had been pulled on trailers to garages where they would be covered and dreamed about. On the shore someone had planted a sign on two cracked legs: Pray for Rain. Someone else had spray-painted below it: Pay for Rain. Then someone had crossed that out and written: Pay Who.

In that moment, before the rest of the summer unspooled, before the weighing and the press and the inside-outing that would have to happen, there was a small, sharp quiet. It lasted the space of a held breath. I could feel the shape of my mother’s hand in mine from a hundred afternoons, as if the bones of us were horses that knew how to find the barn.

Marrow Lake had been a blue sentence across our lives. Now it was a blank with a bared subject line. The heaven I had learned as a child had been so far away, it had made the idea of reaching it both a joke and a threat. Now everything important had plunged down to this basin.

She was put under, I thought, and for the first time since the phone rang I let myself imagine that I might one day say that out loud in a room where someone would have to answer.

On the morning the river turned backward, I found my mother’s voice curled in a tin box.

The box was the kind that once held imported biscuits, roses stamped into its dented lid. It had lived at the back of a cupboard my whole childhood, behind tea tins and the emergency torch that never worked. When I pried it open with a butter knife, I tasted rust in my mouth, the way you do before a storm. There were six cassettes nested in a rag my mother had bartered from a wedding sari when the seam split. Each cassette had a strip of paper in my mother’s cramped sloping hand, words crowded around the spool-holes as if afraid to touch the edge.

Outside, the tide moved against its own history, as if it had made a decision overnight. The Inai had always been capricious. It crept up the steps of our stilt house some seasons, licked away our old shoes, then lay flat and sulky for months, the mud flats a dull shining pelt. But this morning, the water heaved itself toward the mangroves, back toward the salt, and the bamboo poles the fishers had sunk at low tide shivered and pointed inland like useless compasses. The men in yellow hats on the western bank took photographs none of us will ever see and made notes in their binders. One of them drew a line in the air with his finger and nodded to the others, as if the river could be taught to stay.

When my mother died, the Authority sent us a form. I filled it out in black ink and printed, because you cannot trust cursive with grief. I signed my name in the square they had left for it—my name, not hers—and posted it at the old station where trains used to stop, where now the platform was a gallery of warning posters: danger of subsidence, danger of wild boar, danger of non-compliance. I waited two weeks and began to sleep at odd hours, wedged into the netted cot like a dried fish. The third week, aunties I had grown up with began to knock on our door with bowls of curried jackfruit and the kinds of news nobody wants to wear alone. They oiled my hair and said the Authority wore polished shoes even to the mud, which told you everything.

On the fourth week I opened the box.

The cassettes had dates written on them in a brown that had once been black. The earliest—1987—smelled faintly of camphor and damp paper. The latest had two dates, one crossed out. March 15, March 22. The week between those Mays when the river had roared like a lion in a painting and my mother had stood on the veranda steps waist-deep with her arms crossed, daring it. She had died after the last flood, not in it. The difference felt important, though I could not say why.

I carried the tapes to the low table by the window where my mother’s recorder rested like a sleeping animal. It was heavy and scarred, an instrument from another century, with buttons that took your whole thumb to press. In the old days, when our electricity came from a coiled wire hooked in ingenious ways to whirring illegally from a pole, my mother would record by day and listen by night, her face usual when she collected the voices of others and small when she was left only with her own. She wore the headphones the way sailors wear binoculars in films, as if about to see something you would have to explain too many times.

I had always liked the first few breathy seconds before a track, when the machine felt its way into sound. I pressed Play and waited for that thin ribbon to become a river. Static introduced itself like rain on metal, and then there was the scrape of a chair on a concrete floor, a cough she thought she could hide from the tape.

“Test,” my mother said, her voice younger than I remembered. “Date twenty-two April nineteen eighty-seven. Location: Kuttipalam ferry hut. Speaker: Lakshmi P.” She paused and the tape breathed, the river on the tape louder than the river outside. “Word: pamiya.”

Lakshmi P’s voice was smoke. “Pamiya. That’s when you hold a cup of tea and it is too sweet, but you drink it anyway.”

My mother: “A preference for politeness over pleasure.”

Lakshmi laughed. “No. It is a sweetness made of obligation.”

The tape clicked and whirred. I glanced at the door, where someone had stuck a government sticker across the carved wood. The sticker said you are a temporary occupant. The sticker said your tenancy is conditional on the success of the Project. I wanted to peel it off and lift the grain with my thumbnail like a confession. Instead I cupped my hands around the speaker as if warming my fingers on a kettle and let the old words pour through.

My mother had been collecting the words that did not travel well. Words that pulled a whole fogged landscape behind them. She taped them to index cards and pinned them to the wall above the kitchen, where grease and salt browned them slowly. If a word returned to the house, it returned crooked, dust in its spine. After she died, I took all the cards down and stacked them in a shoebox, but I could not throw them away. Some of the words had no definitions; some had only sentences. Some were just names.

Una: when a fish calls the net by your mother’s name.

Karamaan: a shore that appears in the wrong season.

Sulkai: a new cut in an old tongue.

The words made a country on the wall, a country that you could only live in with your ears. When I was a child, I wanted to add words too. My mother would laugh and make room with her chalk, scissoring twine between her teeth. If I half-remembered a word from a dream, she would scrunch up her face and say, no, but tell me anyway. She taught me that sometimes a thing exists only because you claim it.

The second tape was not labeled. It opened on a wheeled rattle like a bicycle on a bad road and the background chatter of a tea stall, spoons clinking lazily, a radio murmuring a cricket score.

“What word?” said a man. The voice pleasantly sour, a lime squeezed too hard.

“Morai,” said my mother. A car honked somewhere like a distant cow.

“Ah,” said the man. “You will have trouble with that one.”

My mother drank loudly to record her presence. “Say it anyway.”

“Morai is how my wife’s aunt looks at me when I come home too late to cut beans. It is not a scolding. It is not fear. It is an inventory.”

“That’s specificity,” my mother said. “Difference between a word and a story.”

But the man—his name might have been Bigu, or Biju, she would have spelled it three ways—would not be ruled. “Morai is when a boat tied properly is found floating in the next canal, in perfect position to be tied again. Morai is the smell of clothes dried in a room with only one small window. Once there was a god who did not have a temple; he had only a memory. That memory? Morai.”

“What is its opposite?” my mother asked.

“You tell me,” said the man, and someone swatted a mosquito hard enough for its death to be a word too.

I listened and added my own definitions, the way a child adds just enough salt to make a soup her own. Morai: when the river unlearns a person but leaves his sandals. Morai: the shape of a house when the furniture is gone. Morai: the face I made getting off the train in February with a blue suitcase, and how the platform took an inventory of me right back.

The third tape was labeled with the double-date. It had a coffee stain that spread from the label into the spool-hole like an unhealed wound. It was heavier in my hand, which is impossible; it was plastic like the others; still, it held a present tense more tightly. The wind rose and slapped the palms behind the house as if awakening them. On the far bank, the men with hats raised a red flag and then lowered it again.

I hesitated, my finger above the button. The room breathed around me, the house settling into its stilts, the fans turning their indifferent faces. From the kitchen came the sound of something soft giving way—maybe the sack of salt had bowed to humidity, maybe the jar of pickles had sighed and decided to become a new kind of vinegar. The house sounded like a throat clearing itself.

I pressed Play. The tape swallowed air, and then my mother’s voice arrived—older now, the joy worn into caution. “Date: March fifteen, two thousand and nineteen. Location: house on the Inai. Speaker: self.”

I stood up without meaning to.

“I know,” she said, as if answering me. “I know you like the other tapes more. I know you don’t like my voice in the house. But listen.” She paused. The recorder had picked up the river beating itself to a consistency we were supposed to consider progress. “Listen. Word: vancham.”

A page flipped. I could hear her rings click against the plastic. “Vancham: the betrayal the water makes when it comes to take what it supplied. We say we are protected by vancham when a nephew’s loan is forgiven in a public place where forgiveness looks like cleverness. We say the Authority is practicing vancham when they build the steps we have to climb to collect our compensation. We say the river’s vancham is not the river’s fault.”

She coughed. “You are there, on the veranda. You are peeling a pomelo with your teeth. I can hear you judging the fruit.” A small laugh. “You are impatient. This is how you hide tenderness. If I stopped speaking, you would call to me. You would say, Amma, come. It is too hot today. You would say, Amma, what is the word for when a man promises you a bridge and gives you a plaque?”

I do not remember the pomelo. I remember the way my molars hurt when I was angry, the iron taste that meant I had kept too much in one place too long.

“Inai used to stand for consort,” my mother said, her voice a careful boat. “Then they said it meant infrastructure. They said it meant we would be the mouth of a river they could put their hand in and make speak. They promised us less salt in the air, which is like promising a person less blood. Word: nilaipanam. This one I invented, because the world required it.”

She laughed again, but there was sand in it. I found myself smiling in the unsmiling way you do when someone you love has used trouble as a tool and found its edge.

“Nilaipanam: a money whose denomination is your place in a line. The kind of currency they designed for us. If you come on the fifth day, you will get two hundred; if you come on the sixth, you will get one hundred and the rotten tarpaulin. If you come on the seventh, you will get a gum-boot with a smile painted on it. The boot will be left-footed. You will be expected to make your inconveniences match.”

In the yard below, Saroja called a greeting. There was a ladder to the yard; she never used it. She believed in keeping her feet on the same plane as her intentions.

“Naila,” she called, “the boys say the water is wrong.”

“I know,” I called back, and then turned my attention to my mother again, as if she were the one who had called out. I lowered myself to the mat, crossed my legs, and placed my palms on my knees the way she had taught me to sit still when I was small. The mat had a memory of my mother’s weight and took mine grudgingly.

“I have been trying to fix a word that keeps escaping me,” my mother said. Her voice had the flatness of someone speaking while writing, her pen skating. “Aranam. It is not, as you will want to make it, the name of a tree. It is not a prayer. It is when a thing is named prematurely. When you say ‘home’ too soon and the place hears you and disappears. When you throw a person a rope and call it promise. Aranam is the bruise you make by giving shape before the skin is ready.”

The tape should have ended there: the words, the small weather of the room, the river not quite the same river. But there was a click and then a sound I could not place at first: a person shifting their weight, an inhalation taken too close to the mic, a scrape of wood against wood. It was, after a moment, my own voice.

“Amma, what is the word for the opposite of aranam?”

I did not remember this. The sound of myself was younger and sharp at the edges, like a coin fresh from a mold. I pressed a hand to my own throat, as if to stop a future.

“Does it have an opposite?” my mother asked me on the tape, and then, softer, “I hope so. I hope my mouth has not broken anything by naming it. Your father says I should stop putting things in jars; he says there is no point archiving the humidity. I tell him I am not a museum. I am a boat.”

A pause. A chair. The thud of a hand on a table that knew our family better than the temple did.

“Word,” my mother said. “Let’s go to the opposite of aranam. Kaatri.”

She said it with tenderness, as if the word were a cat that would come if you offered milk and silence.

“Kaatri: the naming that protects a thing by generalizing it beyond recognition. The way we called the big fish simply ‘fish’ the year the temple pond dried up. The way you call any woman who does not belong to us, ‘aunty,’ so that she will. Kaatri is the veil you make to stop malevolent interest. We say it when a child is beautiful, and we say, alas, this face is only a face.”

A sound like the recorder being moved. The river hit a part of itself that answered back. “Naila,” she said then. “You are older, when you listen to this. You have decided I am inconvenient. You are wrong, and then you will be right to say so. The Authority will come with blueprints rolled like goatskin in their fists, and they will offer you a stenographer’s job. They will say your knowledge of the local language makes you a treasure. But I need you to listen to me first.

“Word: magei. Magei is the promise a river makes to a woman with a list. It is not debt, but something more supple. It is what we owe the mouth that fed us and the ear that noticed. That is what you have to keep. Not the house. Not even the tapes. The angle of noticing.”

She coughed again. “If you are hearing this,” she said, and now her voice was low enough that the house itself leaned forward to collect it, “then I have done all the things I could do. I have refused to go to meetings where they take our photographs. I have gone anyway and put my face into their machines like a handful of sand. I have told them yes and no. I have told them no and yes. I have lit the stove. I have boiled water. I have made rice for three and eaten for one. I have called your name to the river when you would not answer me. I have gone quiet. I have spoken too much. I have said the name of the man who sits in a building without windows and calls my house a number. I have, this morning, said to the river that I am not ready to be a story, and the river said, we will see.”

The tape ended as if someone had taken a breath that refused to be categorized. I did not realize until the white of the hiss went on too long that I had been waiting for my voice to speak again, to ask another question I did not remember asking. The urge to rewind and listen once more was the same urge that makes you scratch a scab, admiring and harming the same small new skin.

Outside, Saroja had begun to argue with someone about boats; the argument sounded friendly. Children snatched something from the water, shrieked, then giggled to prove their continued existence. On the opposite bank, a digger yawned and set about insisting on the shape of earth. The day deepened and the smell of mud lifted, as if the river’s backwards trick had taught it to move its odors differently too.

When I was little, the word my mother had most loved to collect was a word that meant almost-but-not-quite. You could use it for a stitch that pulled but did not bind, for a sneeze interrupted by politeness, for a light falling in such a way that you could see dust and feel like a god. So much of my life since leaving had been almost. Almost enough money. Almost enough sleep. Almost enough love to make the leaving look like a choice. In the city, I woke sometimes to the memory of the river and reached for the curtain, and found only brick and a billboard and the neighbor’s kitchen window where a woman I did not know sang to a pot with a voice that gossiped with mine through the piped air. I had promised myself I would not be ridiculous. I came back anyway.

There was a knock, and Saroja came in without waiting. She moved quickly for a woman her size, her bright cotton sari gathered up at her waist, her hair an argument with the pins that held it. She set a basket on the table. The basket smelled like okra, which is to say it smelled like patience. Her forearms were wet to the elbow with the river. She looked at the recorder and then the box of tapes and then my face, like a priest reading a reaction. She did not touch the tapes. She had always respected my mother’s devices as if they contained actual gods.

“You saw the water,” she said.

“I heard it,” I said.

“You always argue this way,” she said, not unkindly. “You’ve been listening to her old things?”

“They’re not old,” I said, more defensively than I intended. “They’re as now as anything.”

Saroja nodded, as if this settled something for her. She bent to the basket and pulled out a banana flower she had convinced into a perfect tightness. She held it up to the light, turned it, nodded to herself, then set it down. “They came to the yard already with their paint,” she said. “They put a mark on the mango that came with my mother as part of her trousseau. Can you imagine? They tell me that if I plant a new tree somewhere inland they will give me an allowance to watch it grow. They will give me a photo of myself with the sapling. They will put it in their calendar.”

She took the tapes one by one and arranged them in a row without touching them, the way you arrange the steps of a dance in your head. “You know the last flood?” she said. “Do you remember the sounds that came with it? Not the furniture moving. Not the neighbors calling. The other sounds.”

I remembered late nights when the house groaned, when words slid between the slats of the floor, words I had not been taught to hear. If you put your ear to the pillar you could listen to your own name approach. “Ghosts,” I said, half-joking.

She smiled. “Yes. But specific ones. My mother says some floods bring back only the voices that said what they meant and were ignored. That is why they are louder than the ordinary dead.” She looked at my mother’s recorder. “Your mother’s voice is one of those, I think.”

The river struck the house’s underbelly with a sound that took root in my stomach. For a second I was small again, waiting on the ladder for the water to decide what kind of visitor it would be. The Authority men pointed at the house with the determined courtesy of officials trying not to see people. They had the look of men proud of their knowledge of tidal charts in a place where the tide tells you if you are allowed to wake up.

“What will you do?” Saroja asked, her hand heavy on my shoulder suddenly, as if testing the ripeness of my intentions.

I wanted to say that I would box the river and send it somewhere safe addressed to myself. I wanted to say that I would climb to the roof and break off a piece and put it in my mouth so I would never be hungry for this place again. Instead, I said, “I will finish her list.”

“The Authority doesn’t pay for lists,” she said, and laughed, because we were both still sentimental enough to find humor in our wrongs.

“They will pay for the labor of not having to learn our names,” I said. “Maybe I will let them. In exchange.”

“Exchange for what?”

“For time.”

Saroja frowned. She hated math that tried to act like morality. “Time for what?” she asked.

“For one more flood like the last one,” I said, and surprised myself. “Not a big one. The kind that brings the right ghosts.”

She pressed her lips together, making her face a crack that let out light. “Be careful,” she said. “You know how the river is with requests. It pretends it doesn’t hear you. Then it gives you exactly what you asked for, plus everything you forgot to imagine.”

After she left, I rewound the third tape and put my finger on the reel as it turned, a trick my mother had taught me so that a mouth opens just where you need it to. When I heard myself ask the question I did not remember asking about aranam’s opposite, I closed my eyes. I tried to remember the day it was said. The mouth of the thought; the heat; the way the house shifts in the afternoon; the mangoes on the tree that the Authority would put a mark on; my mother’s feet, always cold on the slatted floor. I could not find my place in the memory; the memory would not let me own it. That happens with grief: you cannot possess even the parts you paid for.

When the tape ended this time, the recorder clicked and then did a small jerky thing it had never done before. It coughed out an extra second of magnetized air in which a word glided through the room and found my skin. The word was not one either of us had put there. It was a word I had carried with me to the city and back without noticing. It was the word the river uses for the moment before it changes its mind.

The box did not contain a label for it. My mother, in all her urgencies, had left that space open, as if she wanted me to decide. The men on the opposite bank made a new mark in their book and then corrected it, and I realized the tide had shifted again while we stood here defining it. The backward morning had ended; the river resumed its old insistence. It had only been borrowing a gesture from the sea.

I took a card from the shoebox, the kind my mother had hoarded from the stationery shop when it closed. I wrote a word at the top in my own hand, letters round and stubborn as I had been at five. I wrote its definition as if I had always known how. I pinned the card to the beam above the kitchen with the rusty nail that had held pamiya and morai in place for years, each rust mark a map of a previous thought. I stood on the ladder while I did it, one foot half into the house, one foot half out, the place where our floor became air and then water. It was not a ceremony, but it felt like one.

Evening moved in with its unnecessary clarity. The palm leaves began their conversation with bats. Saroja’s boys let a boat loose and pretended to be alarmed when it drifted beyond their reach. The men with hats rolled their plans back into their polished cylinders and drove away with the assurance of people who think time arrives only in straight lines.

The river figured out its own shapes and kept them to itself for the night. I washed my face in the tall blue basin and tasted salt that had been in the air longer than any government. I pressed the tape with the double-date to my chest like a book you can only read backward.

On the morning the river had turned backward, I had found my mother’s voice in a tin box. On the evening of the same day, I lifted a word from out of the air and made it stay. I slept that night with my ear to the floor, the way a person sleeps who knows her house is a boat and her body a cargo and the water beneath her an animal and a god. The ghost flood took its time arriving. When it came, it did not apologize. It brought a chorus of clearings of the throat. It brought a hundred women saying no into a room that never had enough windows. It brought my mother saying my name in the way only she did, not as ownership and not as permission, but as if retrieving me from a place I had already entered: Naila. Naila. Come back with all your words.

Chapter One

On mornings after the river remembers its name, we take the nets and go out before the city is awake. The only sound is the guttering of water returning to pipes, the after-rain ticking of leaves, and, always, the river itself, speaking in the language it invented for everything that falls into it: the language of arrangement. If you pay attention, you can hear how it sorts a city.

Aya waits in the doorway of the workshop with a thermos the color of bruised plums. She is so young she hasn’t yet learned to pretend not to shiver. Her hair is pinned back; she wears my old waders that balloon at her knees and smell faintly of camphor and last year’s red water.

“Too early,” she says, which is what she says every time, rubbing her thumb along the burst seam of the thermos cup.

“It never waits,” I tell her. “Not even once.”

She looks past me to the river road. The streetlights blink two by two and then surrender to gray. All night the rain had thrown itself down in sheets, like someone flipping through a book in a hurry, trying to find their name. The gutters filled by midnight. The culverts spit by two. And now the river ruins and hushes all at once, its surface as stitched as the scalp of an old summer.

We go because people will call us by noon, and because sooner is kinder. If we wait, the weight of silt may erase the names on envelopes, and the water will rot the corners until they become a taxonomy of dissolves. We go because something in the river wants to be read. Because everything that floats has the will to be remembered.

“You could have slept; I could have gone alone,” I say to Aya, knowing what she’ll say.

“And miss it?” She smiles, small and beginner-tough. She pushes her hands into her pockets. “Last time you brought back a cassette tape that had—what did that woman say?—her husband’s voice from 1984.”

“From before he was her husband,” I say.

“Exactly,” she says. “Exactly.”

We are sentimental, both of us. I blame the river for this. Or perhaps it is the city’s fault—any city built along a brown water learns to reconcile itself to accumulation. Ours is an old river city; the sloped streets still remember the tongues of animals. The buildings were designed to be hosed down, and every seventh of them contains a back room where someone keeps a box of paper they cannot throw away.

The workshop, at the bottom of the hill that used to be the town’s first sandbar, is mercifully empty in the morning, the air the fine damp of the inside of a cucumber. We leave the lights off and only the window fills with color: a ripening rectangle of river going from iron to pewter to the certain green I can never properly name.

We take the nets and the bucket with the drainage holes, and the old orange life vest that has lost its buoyancy but still knows how to be binding. I leave a chalk mark on the door as we go out, a habit I learned when the workshop was just a locked room behind a locksmith’s shop. A white mark meant gone briefly, a blue one meant gone all day. No one follows these codes now, not even me, but the chalk feels like a way of telling the building we’ll come back and occupy it again.

When we’d first opened—my mother’s sewing table tilted on a sawhorse to make a long desk; a fan that coughed up flakes of dead ceiling paint; a sign that Aya had lettered with a nervous hand: The Archive of Wet Things—people had come by to laugh. To peer in and make guesses at what we were doing. “Fish?” one man had asked, pressing his forehead to the window. Another said, “My cousin collects nails when the river goes down. Are you like that? Witch nails.” “No,” I had said through the glass, and then, without meaning to, “Yes.” And I thought: it will go like this. We will be the neighborhood’s good weird thing. People will come to us when they are already the kind of people open to being surprised.

But then the first two weeks we carried back a small stack of envelopes wrapped in white towels, and the stack was full of things that people were already missing: an accordion-folded letter a teenage boy had dropped from the bridge before deciding not to die; a stitched packet of hair and rose thorns that had been thrown off a ferry in 1977 and surfaced because part of the ferry ramp fell into the river and shook everything cheerfully loose; a ledger page with a list of women’s names in a necessary hand and an address in white chalk: a place that was and was not a brothel. We delivered what we could. People cried. Someone spat. The city inspector came and asked if we had a permit for hope.

“Listen,” I said to him that first time in the workshop. “What permit is there for catching what comes back?”

“Salvage,” he said, flipping his little book. “Or waste management. Or miracle. But you’ll need to register either way.” He was not unkind. He was not anything at all in the room. He left a pamphlet that was an index of rectangles.

Now, Aya and I step down to the river road and cross the flattened grass to the culvert where the rainwater mouth had been roaring the night before. The culverts on the east side intake the language of divorce: things people throw out of car windows on the way to leaving. The culverts on the west side keep their secrets longer; the water there is daily and slow—laundry water and bath water, water with shampoo in it and the hair of newborns. The north culvert, the one by the old mill with the crumbling stanchions where swallows make nests, carries the first fierce truth of the storm. We go there first.

Aya sets a basket of gray rags on the grass. She has learned the way of her hands from the river, which is to say, she has learned to be particular without making a show of it. I tie the nets to the ankle-high steel posts along the culvert edge, knotting in a way that Teo taught me when I was very young: two loops like ears and the tail pulled through and then the whole thing kissed with a tug. Teo belonged to the river in a way that no one can belong to any person, and when he died last spring I walked to the bend he loved and said a few sentences that, from a distance, might have looked like a prayer.

“Look,” Aya says, making her voice small to match the smallness of this good thing. The throat of the culvert gleams like the inside of an animal. On the lip, a line of sticks and leaves has arranged itself into a private handwriting. We pull our nets through this scrawl first and catch what we can: ticket stubs softened to tissue and the odd coin; a fingernail in a pale crescent that makes us both look at the water with new suspicion; an envelope with a pearl in the top-left corner, as if the stamp was a small, tame wound. I take the envelope and slide it into a plastic sleeve.

In the bottom of the net, trapped in the crosshatch like a single good word, a photograph clings—one of those passport-office photographs where the face is trying not to invent itself. The woman is almost smiling, which means she had been told not to and did so in spite and then got afraid in the split second before the shutter. I do not let myself look too long, not now. I slide her into another sleeve. We will dry her, we will breathe her flat again and see what she wants.

When I first begin to speak in front of people—schools, library classes, the women’s club that meets in the back room of the pharmacy where there’s a faint smell of mint that even grief cannot smudge—I tell them there are two kinds of wet. There is the wet that leaves, and the wet that decides to stay. River water is the second kind, despite what happens to it through the alchemy of evaporation and return; it is a wet with opinions. It seeps and stains and recolors. It changes the taste of a secret. If a thing wanted to be destroyed, the river would oblige it, but a great many things do not want that at all. When we bring them back up, they carry their wetness with an authority that sometimes looks like shame.

“Today’ll be good,” Aya says, not meaning good exactly. She means full. She means the shelves will fill and we will have to lay ropes across the room and clip letters to them with clothespins the way laundries used to, the way churches do with certain dignities. She means that afterward we will sit with our backs against the cold of the floor and eat tamales folded neatly back into their own breathing.

“It will,” I say, because there’s no undoing it now.

We drag the nets a second time. The culvert is less frantic. The swallows begin their stitch-work above us—each bird a needle that believes in the act of going and returning. In pulling the net up we bring with it, for a moment, the scent of the storm’s belly: coin-metal and yeast and diesel. The net coughs. It nestles down what it is carrying like a mother who is trying to be casual about how much a child is suddenly asleep. In the middle there is a glass jar, round as a skull and the faint green of old Coca-Cola. The lid is sealed with wax, though the wax has been water-dimpled, like skin after a bath. A red string is tied around its throat. Inside, something pale bends like a folded heron’s wing.

“Who throws a jar in a flood?” Aya says. Her voice is less small now. Not awe, not yet, but a leaning forward.

“Someone who wanted there to be a jar at the end of it,” I say, and the words feel thick around my teeth. I take the jar and hold it where the light makes it a place. Inside, the paper, if it is paper, is surprisingly whole. The jar is heavier than it ought to be, the way winter is heavier than it looks when you first open the door to it.

“It’s—” Aya starts, but there is no good word, so we do not try. We put it in the basket not gently but with the respect of normal handling, because I was taught that reverence makes you clumsy.

We make one more drag. Then I untie the knots, cracking them loose with the heel of my hand. After rain, everything wants to be twice itself. The road is two roads: the one we know and the one that believes in a river the way a grandmother believes in recipes. We carry the nets and the jar and the plastic sleeves back up the hill. Old Mr. Calderón, who sells radiators and trumpet valves and the idea of order, opens his shop and wishes us blessings. Bless your wet things, he says, because he is a man who would bless a splinter just for being honest about what it does.

In the workshop we switch on the lights, which flicker as if auditioning for a different life. The fans are already set out on their low hums. The racks are empty and hopeful. There are lines strung across the room with tiny wooden pinchers clipped to them like a row of thoughtful birds. The dehumidifier gurgles. This room has invented a weather of its own.

I set the jar on the high table. “Should we open it?” Aya asks. We both glance at the rules we wrote in permanent marker on a strip of masking tape above the sink. The rules were born from the mess the first few weeks made. They have the sternness of children’s manners.

Dry before you read, the first one says, one of mine. Then hers: No judgments. And: Gloves if there’s blood. Mine: Do not try to fix the writing, only reveal it. Hers: No phones when the names are saying something.

“And here,” Aya says, tapping the last one, which Teo dictated to us and we did not argue with because grief is persuasive: You are not a detective. You are not the police. “Which means we don’t need to open that right now,” she says, but we both know we are going to open that right now.

I go to the sink and run warm water over a cloth, then wring it out and wrap it around the wax. Warm is kinder. Warm recognizes effort. The red string is looped through a notch in the glass and has swollen its own authority. When the wax softens, I pull at the string and it gives with a small, obscene sigh. The lid has rust where the metal meets the glass. I twist it and it refuses and then changes its mind. When I get the lid off, the workshop smells like rain the way the inside of an old wardrobe smells like a wedding. Aya stands on the other side of the table with her fists pressed into the wood.

Inside, the paper has been folded in four, each fold burnished into a tearless seam. The top sheet is splotched where it touched air through the inadequate seal; the lines on the page are school-blue; the margins are narrow. The ink, what I can see of it through the glass that still fogs a little from its own sudden future, is the brown of tea forgotten on a windowsill.

“Gloves,” Aya says, and I put them on and then, mindful of how the paper might have taken on characteristics of damp things that never wholly forgive handling, I slide the letter out of its jar and onto a clean tray. The jar makes a small chime against the metal edge, as if to say that to contain is labor. I lift the first fold with a spatula and ease it open. It is the work I know, the careful un-creasing of words someone folded with worry. The paper resists in the way of paper: with all its quiet determination. I open the second fold. The third.

The letter lies in the light. The handwriting slants like a field that cannot help its own drainage. The date is in the top-right corner: September 10, 1999, which is a date that rides the back of my tongue like a coin. I was twelve. Teo’s brother had married a woman with a wolf tattoo on her ankle. The river had gone low that summer, low enough for boys to throw their bikes in to see if they would stay upright.

“Well,” Aya says, and then stops.

“Tea,” I say, and I say it to buy us both a moment.

“No,” she says. “I mean—read it.”

It is addressed in Spanish and then, as if the writer thought better of it, in the English he learned as a second thought. Querida M—, he begins, Dear M—. I feel the vowel stick in my throat and stay there. There are many Ms in this city; it is a good letter to begin a woman here with. My hands are neat in their second skin.

I have held this for too long, the letter says in careful, stubborn handwriting, and I do not know anymore if the river took you as she takes all the slow things or if you took her like we did that night at the weir and made a way out of it. Forgive me if I am asking forgiveness. I am not sure what I am doing. I learned that year that there is no single right way to tell a truth. There is only a way not to tell it. He writes around it as if walking a dog around a tree and the leash is too short. The next paragraph is precise: a description of a woodpile stacked so diligently that it became a wall, of a lamppost that was a place because two people said it was, of a level being held flat by a thumb. He names the stones of the weir. He names an awkwardness that sounds like devotion.

And then: There was a child.
