“What kind of letter,” Aya whispers, “begins by confessing it doesn’t know the way to confess?”

“The kind that took a jar to the river,” I say, but my mouth’s gone dry.

There was a child, he writes, and she was a still thing and then she was a moving thing and the way you looked at me is the way a person looks when they make a promise aloud and also in their body at once. The river bumped the stones and the water got new hands. We thought we could change something back by changing it forward.

We have dried worse than this. We have dried letters written in the ink that is really ash washed from the bottom of a cooking fire. We have dried letters that were written with chewing gum spit and then hidden by a wife under a floorboard and discovered by the new owner’s son who thought the floorboard was a secret door. We have dried letters in which nothing is confessed, only described, a description so relentless it becomes an apology.

I read. Aya watches my face to learn how to watch. The writer finally names himself: E. de la Cruz. That is a name that does not belong to me, but the city is old with that name; it is hung on the backs of many men. He signs it in a hand that breaks the strength it had in the first lines, the way a person loses their posture when they think they are alone. He writes, If you have not climbed back, if the river is not full of you, then you will need to know what I did, and if you have come back but not to me, you will need to know what I did anyway. I would send this to a place, but places moved. He writes the name of a street that had been a street and is now a parking lot for a hardware store that sells windows that never see the river. He writes the name of the hardware store. He writes the name of the house with a blue door that smelled like bees.

“Do you know him?” Aya says. The innocence of the question knocks me hard. It is full of the belief that the river might be naming something we can simply go and ask about. She is not yet the age where she knows that the end of a letter can be the beginning of a long burning. She is not yet the age where you learn that the person you are looking for is not necessarily in agreement with your wanting.

I do not answer because I am a little bit inside the letter, the way you can be inside a song that you stepped into accidentally on a city street. I reach down and stroke the edge of the paper the way you might stroke the back of an animal to reassure it that it is here.

There is more. He writes, That night the river tasted like pennies. The child was the first to know that there are more appeasements in a city than the ones a map tells you. I took her—I do not know the right verb; the river delivered her to me, perhaps, and I did an impious thing: I kept her as if she were bread and I was hollow. You did not ask me to; you had your hands in the water. You said her name. I have her name. It is a name I have never said aloud since because it is a live wire still.

“Who writes like this?” Aya says, and I almost tell her the truth: the men who work with their hands and are forced in trouble into a different eloquence. The ones who say less until the day they say too much. The ones who think if they just describe the hinges and the width of the boards, they will be forgiven the door they made.

There is a sentence that I do not want and I read it anyway: Inez, he writes midway down the second page, and seeing my name where my name ought not to be is like lifting a sack of flour and finding it full of bees. I must, he writes, explain to your mother—he drops the M; he writes it: Mariela. I must explain to your mother what I have done.

The room makes a sound that is not audible to humans, a lock opening in a pocket of the wall where tools begin to believe in their own angles. All through my body, a feeling opens and does not pause to introduce itself. The letter is a stranger and also it is in here with us now, breathing and wanting.

“Inez,” Aya says, my name a small thing in her mouth.

I do not reach to turn my name over where it lies. I stand very still. In my mind my mother is already at the sink of our old kitchen, her hands in the water, a pale circle where her ring had been. The kitchen had a window that looked over a neighbor’s lemon tree and the river from a tilt. The kitchen had a clock that ticked in the way of a person limping bravely through a crowd. My mother had an apron that was really a shirt she had cut in half. She had letters she wrote and did not send that lived in a box so flat and so bossy that I never dared to open it until she died. I had their ink under my fingernails for weeks. I could not get her words out of me in a sanitary way.

“It’s a common name,” Aya says, alert and kind.

“It is,” I say. It is not. It is as common as a lightning strike.

We read the last paragraphs as if we are walking on a floor that someone has apologized for in advance. He writes—E. de la Cruz—that he cannot keep quiet under the labor of his own keeping. He writes that he has watched the girl whose name is mine walking on the river road with an orange dog and he cannot tell if that is the girl we are both thinking of or another girl shaped by the river’s insistence on recurrence. He writes that he has taken a house across from the green church, that his knees hurt in the winter, that he knows what he is is not a father, and has been and may be cursed for the portion of father he mis-stepped. He writes that he lit a candle until the wax ran out and then held his hand over the flame, which is not a confession so much as a man thinking the body is a ledger and not an instrument. He writes, Forgiveness is not the currency I can afford to ask for. I will, however, come each Tuesday to the bench near the fig tree and wait.

“1999,” Aya says softly. She looks at the date as if it is a living thing. “If he went to the bench—”

“He would have waited,” I say. Teo had once told me the river is full not of apologies but of rehearsals. People throw practice letters and watch them ride down and away and then they go home and write the proper thing or they do not. Practice and the proper thing are siblings who stop speaking to one another after a while. I put one hand on the table and the table holds.

“Are you all right?” Aya says, and then, before I can find the speed my mouth uses when it is speaking truth, she says, “This is your mother’s name?”

“It is,” I say. “It is my mother’s name.”

We do the right thing then. We dry the letter. We do not reach quickly for the jar to see if there is a second page or a third. We have learned that the river gives at its own speed. If we rush what it has offered, it will refuse us a later mercy. We lay the paper on the blotting sheets made of the felt of something else’s former life. We lay cheesecloth above like a fine winter. We weigh it down with the sandbags that my mother had once used as pattern weights, bags the size of her hand, each one made from a sleeve cuff.

The room performs its tiny weather. The fans hum and the dehumidifier does its thieving. The words do not move under the cheesecloth; they look like sleeping. I stand and put my hand flat on the old sewing table, which still has the little nick on the edge where my mother slammed a pair of scissors down the day she found out that the store would no longer carry the thread brand she liked.

“Who is he?” Aya asks.

“De la Cruz?” I say, and I try, unsuccessfully, to keep my voice out of history. “Everyone,” I say. “No one.”

She reaches for the jar and places the lid back on it, loosely. “So,” she says, as if she is supposed to say so because we are not supposed to be detectives but surely some next thing wants us. “You’ll…?”

“I’ll sit,” I say, though I mean something else. I mean that I will take out the box of my mother’s letters and look for the bench near the fig tree and see if she mentioned going there on any Tuesday that summer. I mean that I will put the letter’s name—E. de la Cruz—next to the names in that ledger of women in the first stack of returned paper, and see if any of the men who come to me to pick up their sorrow have that name stitched into their being. I mean that I will go tomorrow morning to the green church where the paint is the color of old lettuce when you peel away the darker leaves, and see if there is a bench.

“We could call the number,” Aya says, always, at the end of every small crisis, this suggestion: use the devices, use the provided coordinates, trust that the world can be rung like a Bell System. But there is no number to this. There is only the shape of handwriting that will be recognizable if it moves in the world again.

The phone rings. It rings with the definitive chirp of a bird that knows one note and one note only, a call that is an announcement of itself. It is ten o’clock almost exactly. The calls never come before ten; the river itself respects business hours. I go to the phone. “The Archive,” I say, and because I cannot stop myself from making us plural, “We’ve received a few things already. Yes, we’re open. Yes, I’m sure.”

“My grandson,” a woman says in a voice that is more air than sound. “He threw something. He threw something and then ran. I saw it; I was sitting at the window. He throws things when he doesn’t have words and I thought—no. I thought, let it go. Let it be the river’s. But then I thought he throws things when he doesn’t have words, and he will need those words back eventually. If he threw his words, he will come to me like a little bank and ask for them with interest. Do you pick things from the river?”

“We do,” I say.

“Do you pick words?” she says.

“If they’ve become things,” I say. “Yes.”

I take down her name and her address, scribbling it with the pencil that never gets sharp enough. I watch the cheesecloth not move and the letter beneath it be a fact. When I hang up, Aya has written the date of the letter on the whiteboard under New Arrivals. Beside the words she has drawn, small and wonderful, a jar.

“People will tell us what to do,” she says, meaning the phone, meaning the city, meaning the river, meaning all the things that ask to be answered. It is a young person’s thesis that the world is a machine that responds to questions with the courtesy of answers. I am not so old that I do not sometimes still believe in that mechanism myself, but there is another machine that I have learned to trust more: the one that puts an old rumor on the tongue and asks you to taste it.

I sit. I pick up my mother’s scissors from the weighted corner of the table and I weigh them in my palm. I am as my mother was in this one way: when presented with a thing, I meet it with my whole attention. I do not own a dog that needs walking, and there is no one who will text me to ask me if I am on my way; I am full only of this and breakfast. I have, if I am honest, avoided for so many years looking at the portion of my mother’s life that included whatever is now here and the name he signed. It is a particular cowardice to run a place like this and have its central artifact and never take it all the way into yourself.

“Tea,” I say again, because that is what a person says who is not ready to say what she ought to. Aya turns the kettle on. It clicks as if counting. Outside, a bus sighs at the stop; an impatience of pigeons makes their point on the windowsill; the river lowers its voice to talk to the stones that remember it best. The jar sits where we left it, a stranger we invited home. The letter rests and becomes itself again.

There was a time when I thought a person could choose the world she needed to live inside. It seemed reasonable, then: you look around at the things and the people and the events and you take what you can bear. You make a collage of the tolerable. But that was before I knew what the river knows: that everything rises to the surface eventually, altered, softened, speaking a dialect of water, but speaking. Ties you thought you’d cut float back to you like weeds that have learned your name.

The kettle lifts its voice. Aya pours and the steam hairpins upward and then is gone. I do not tell her to go to the green church, to sit on the bench, to see what the fig tree remembers of that September. I do not tell her not to. In the end, even the people in my life are currents and eddies, and what they carry past me is mostly not mine.

“I should tell you,” I say instead, and my voice sounds like it has been wrapped in cloth for many days. “When I was six, my mother told me there were stories about how I got here.”

Aya, to her credit, does not rush to the water, does not lean too fast as the river gestures. She brings me a cup and sets it down and says only, “There are always stories.” She places her hand on the edge of the table, close to my hand and not touching it.

And then we work, which is the only way to keep from imagining each thing all the way to its most seismic conclusion. We lay out today’s catch. We put clothespins on a string and hang up a line of wet names. We coax, with the tips of our fingers and with a patience I did not know I possessed until the day I first needed it, a city’s silent things into their new speech. I leave the letter under the cheesecloth as long as a person would need to breathe underwater and still be alive.

By noon the workshop has become a smell: old water turned toward air. The phone has rung twice and I have said yes to both. The sun, such as it is, has remembered its job. There is a dark spot on the floor from my wet boots that looks like a map of a country that wanted to be oval and learned to be more interesting. I lift the cheesecloth at last and the letter reveals itself with the indifference of something that has already decided its path. My name is there on that second page, a longer word than the other words. My mother’s name is written without apology, plain as the wall. I do not know yet the shape of the person who wrote them, but he exists now in the room as if he is another jar we have taken the lid off.

We have a way, here, of not deciding too soon what anything is. I tuck the letter back into its glass. I put the lid on but do not twist it all the way tight. I have learned to let air sit where I cannot. The river, indifferent and infinite, presses its body against the banks, and the city, contrite and needy, places its hand against the river’s rib and calls that mercy. On days like this, when the first true thing comes to your door in a jar, you must resist the instinct to shape it into an answer.

“Let’s eat,” I say. Aya is already unwrapping a tamal, the cornmeal damp like a new secret, the filling smelling faintly of cumin and a house I used to live in. We sit with our backs against the table, and the fans hum and the letter waits for me the way a creature might wait for the person who found it to remember how to go home.

Chapter One

They always said the city would shrink to fit our forgetting. Not suddenly, not with apocalypse, but like a belt tightened by another notch each winter, like a house whose doors hung a little looser year by year in their frames. A street name would fade first; the paint chalked off metal. A shop would stop opening for lunch. A window would go black. Then the pavement would change temperature in one place, warmer, or cooler, as if the ground were mulling a decision. We would wake to a notice slip under the door: Correction to Map 48-A, please see revised scale. We were good citizens and we folded nothing.

In the Department of Small Geographies, folding an official map was an offense that carried a fine equal to a month’s rent. There were reasons for this—superstitions that had hardened into protocol. “A crease is a suggestion,” my first director told me when I started in the drafting room eight years ago, his mouth stained with coffee, his hands the gray of erasers. “Suggest too many lines and the ground bites.” It sounded ridiculous until the week someone rolled up the plan for the Southern Market to swat a fly and the eastern aisle shortened by three stalls. Every vendor swore it. We bought our flies traps and kept our maps flat on the long wooden tables that bowed like exhausted boats.

I measure my mornings by the way the light climbs the brick wall across from the department. By the time the second pane goes from ash to honey, the clerks upstairs have emptied their satchels and the building smells like damp wool and pencil shavings. Someone laughs into a handset. Someone curses a blot. The city presses itself into our rooms: the cleft stones of the milk warehouse, the pocked surface of the bridge over the drain, the vacant lot where someone once grew sunflowers big as plates. We copy them with small gestures and pretend they will stay.

On the day the third staircase fell, I was repairing the scale bars on Map 67-K, the one that covered our patchwork of apartment towers along the river and the curl of warehouses that held a hundred years of unsold paper. The river in that quadrant was not a river anymore, but a trough of silt and green bottles. We still drew it as if it moved.

Kasia, who had the voice of a gull and shoulders like a boy’s, brought me a stack of notices bright as arils. “Edge reports,” she said, and tapped her nails against them to make them fan like a deck of cards. “Four from Mallow Street. Two from the Old Quarry. One from a woman at Twenty-Three Quince. Says her corridor opens onto air.”

“Old pipes bleed out, plaster goes, floors sag,” I said. “How sure is she?”

“She sent a photograph,” Kasia said, putting it on my drafting table, where it lay like a mouth. In the picture, a wallpapered hallway ended in an absence you could not name. Beyond it there was nothing: not brick, not sky, not the bruised layer of the city that we knew proved in all soft places. Her slippers were in the foreground, one pointing toward the void in a way that made my palms itch.

My father taught me to see. He put a pan on the stove and filled it with water and shook salt into it by careful pinches, while I dragged a finger through the crystals that spilled and tried to arrange them into continents. “Everything is coast,” he said, rolling up his sleeves, the hair fair with flour, as if it held memories. “Even the inside of you, where one certainty ends and another begins.” He is why I do not trust edges that arrive in photographs.

I rubbed a nub of kneaded eraser along the grain of the paper and watched a margin soften, then sharpen again. I thought of Miren, who would have liked the name of the Department and hated what it meant. She used to tell me to fold maps, to see what mountains we would make if we dared hard lines. The last night we slept in the same room she said the scale of our city was wrong. She took her marker and drew a tree three times taller than our building, then sat on the sill and swung her bare feet. Beauty was no protection; she left anyway.

“Put Mallow and Quince at the top,” I told Kasia, and she looked at me sideways, careful not to scrape her flank against a map.

“How’s your day?” she asked, and it startled me, her kindness. Since Miren, only my immediate work touched me without stinging. I pretended I had not heard and reached into the drawer where we kept the labels for our field kits.

“Six hours,” the glass clock above the door said, and somewhere in the building the old printer coughed a ream of card stock like a lung and righted itself. In the corridor, the bulletin board wore the week’s admonitions from the Municipal Council: Prefer rails to wheels. Chalk your house numbers in case of metal theft. Do not say aloud the names of areas already corrected; this may induce nostalgic compaction in listeners of unsteady temperament. The last always made Kasia clap her hands like a child. She would lean around the door and whisper the forbidden words anyway: Frost Gate, Orchard End, the Bathing Pools, her mouth reddened by mandarins. Someone had written under the last notice, in lilac ink: A city is not a season. When I glanced again, the line had blurred, as if the board itself had moved in memory.

A call came, then another, then the office vibrating in its frame. “Don’t send the boy,” Mrs. Kline from Twenty-Three Quince was saying into the receptionist’s handset. I could hear her even without putting it to my own ear; when the city thins, sound carries like it has been pared down enough to travel. “Send the one who was married. Send the one who keeps his shirt half out of his trousers.” Her specificity amused even as it disarmed. The receptionist, with her soft tortoiseshell eyes, looked around and pressed the button to hold. “She means you.”

On my way down Grist Lane, I passed children chalking stars where the last of the bread carts had wheeled; by supper, those starbursts would be scuffed into smudges, the flour or the chalk mingling in an ordinary whiteness. Two pigeons stared from the window of the bakery as if they’d spent the night reading a book they didn’t understand. There were fresh cracks in the corner where the lane met the old tramway. Men dug the cracks for copper, the red thread that binds the city in heat and voice; they had sharp tools and scars that made their arms look mapped to the bone. Above them a woman stitched a curtain in the window with such intent that if we had a survey for focus, the needle would have pinged.

The closer I got to Quince, the worse the numbers behaved. Twelves repeated. Eights were missing after six. Sevens had turned their heads and were threes. The paint grew thinner, then gave up. Someone had chalked their pride in a careful school hand on a door that had lost its digit: WE LIVE HERE. BE SPECIFIC. A pair of socks, stuffed into the letterbox as if it were a mouth, breathed in the wind. The three towers of the estate loomed, each with its own variety of weather strapped to it: a corner full of hail, a corner with fuzz like dandelion seed, a corner with a glitter like colored sugar. I took the rear stair, out of habit. I counted my steps and my breaths. I did not name the floors as I passed them. Naming intensifies attachments; attachments cause weight; weight drains a city of its small flexibilities. These were the sorts of things the Council printed in pamphlets. I had even written a pamphlet once about the ethics of maps. I cannot say it saved anyone.

Mrs. Kline met me at the door, a cardigan as bright as persimmons wrapped around her like a small animal. She was younger than her voice, though that could have been the trick of the apartment where the squares of evening laid themselves obediently across a neat carpet. She cracked the surface of the table with her knuckle to show it was real. She poured water assuming I wanted it. She led with hospitality because fear likes to be made to sit with its hands in its lap.

“Through here,” she said, and we walked past pictures that were not exactly pictures: pieces of fabric with words stitched into them, profound of needle but vague in meaning, and driven through with tiny knots where the thread had balked. Salt in saucers. A jar full of screws. In the bedroom a cradle took up more space than the bed, and had never been filled. I did not need the cradle to tell me this; you can tell where presence has worn a dip; you can tell where the dip is long and has never known a weight.

Her corridor offered itself like a dare. Wallpaper with a marching pattern of reeds. Electric sconces that had teeth marks on their bases. The smell of laundry. And at the end, the kind of hush that needles your ears, the kind the ear interprets as threat. Air pressed differently against my skin there. My little field meter ticked and then thought better of it and went quiet. That meter has two needles and neither of them is supposed to go left.

“I’m not fooling,” she said.

“I never assume someone is fooling,” I said, though people often were, presenting cracks with flour dust shaken into them to make them glamorous.

The edge had no color. It was not black or white and it did not seethe. If you looked straight at it, you could not see it at all. I had learned this long ago, the way hunters learn that you must look at the space just to the side of a thing to understand its movement. When I softened my focus, the end of the corridor quivered and I saw how the pattern of reeds did not reach a seam but simply ended, reed heads half-painted and then air.

“Did you… push?” I asked, knowing how poor the word was and the expression it dragged behind it.

“Of course not,” she said, but her hand hovered near my sleeve, as if she thought anyone could go with a gust. “It started small. A missed step’s worth. By dawn it was like this.”

“Who lives beyond?” I asked. This is a question of courtesy and of law. Not that it matters, ordinary law cannot pass the way the light doesn’t pass past an edge.

“A young couple,” she said. “Roku and Rin. He fixes bicycles. She bakes the sugared dough that tastes like air. She wears her hair like a veil when it’s windy. They are not home.”

“Have you spoken to them?”

“You think I would open this, if it is an opening? You think I would put my voice inside?” Her anger was a lantern and it warmed me. It meant she might obey instructions. Some of them matter.

I took out the line from my kit. “Chain,” we call it, though ours is not brass, it is silken, dyed crimson to be obvious in photographs. Every eighteen inches, someone has tied a knot, and every tenth knot is marked with a bead, bright blue. I shook it once and the knots woke and announced themselves along the floorboards with a dry sound. I threw the first knot at the floor just before the edge and it bounced and came back; I threw the next and the next and when the fourth crossed the threshold of absence, it did not come back. My fingers burned in the pause before the chain came abruptly easy. I took in what it had to say: there is no such place as beyond.

Miren sang, when she was happy, from the throat rather than the chest. She believed land and water were aspects, not kinds. I had met her at the municipal hearing where a developer argued that we should move a hill and she had not laughed, she had stood in the aisle and suggested that if we were moving one hill, we should move them all so as not to leave our city unbalanced. Her hands were a geography, the broken bone in the left pointer telling the story of a friend’s door badly locked when she was seventeen, the scar on her palm an illustration of the time she tried to rescue a pan from burning. She liked the smell of developing fluid, the taste of oranges, the cheap umbrellas with entire skies printed on the underside. She liked the border of a page more than what it contained. The day she left, there was a note in blue pencil on my map that I will not tell you because I am not who I was when I read it.

“Will you fix it?” Mrs. Kline asked, and there was the hunger. We were naked when anyone asked us this, with our little tools, our clipped pencils.

“There is no fix,” I said, gently, and it is the hardest thing I say in my work. “There is only acceptance, and then we redraw.”

“You and your maps,” she said, but there was no heat in it. She went and brought me a glass of water and put two biscuits on a plate and set the plate at a distance suitable for a guest who might still not be family. We stood as if we could convince the hallway to change its mind by witnessing it hard enough. My field meter woke and ticked its two needles together. Through the wall, a baby cried, though the cradle had told me there was no baby here. I have learned to trust both.

When I slipped my thumb under the skirting, the wood met my nail, then did not. I lost the shape of my thumb beyond that. Panic is a small animal that can be quieted with breath if you catch it early; if it grows, it becomes the kind that bites. I took my thumb back and wiped it on my trousers. The nail seemed to have lost some insistence, as if the edges of me had learned something from the edges of the city about how to blur.

On the floor, where dust and stray hair made a record of what had passed in the last two weeks—an earring back, a sesame seed that did not belong to any of us—someone had written in chalk, small as if they were trying not to involve the fibers of the world: DO NOT TRUST THE SCALES. The handwriting was familiar enough to painful. The neatness, the way the D refused the usual loop, like a city at war with a plain letter.

Miren had said it often, in different rooms. Do not trust the scales that are printed for you. Do not trust the scales that your hands pick up without asking. I looked at the chalk a long time, and Mrs. Kline, watching me, watched me become someone else and did not remark upon it with any kindness or cruelty. She had been in the city long enough to let people be their own storms.

“Do you know her?” she asked finally, with a caution that made me love her and everything she would never be to me.

“No,” I said, and then, because it would be worse to let that untruth live between us, I said: “Yes.” I put the chalk into my pocket. This is a violation. I did not care.

“Will you mark it in your book?” she asked, and I nodded. I drew a rectangle, then half erased it and left the smudge. The map is an act of grief and we are never advised on the etiquette of grieving for places. I noted the time, the temperature, the fact that the crack in the ceiling had not widened in the hours since morning. I measured the distance from the door to where the corridor ceased, the way one measures a loss because once you have measured it, you can move around it without bruising yourself every time. I asked her if she had anyone to stay with. She told me she would be fine. She had been a child once in a part of the city that had stopped recognizing itself and had lived: this gives a person an odd kind of authority. I left her the chain for the day and told her to anchor it to the radiator. There are rituals; sometimes they work because we do them.

On the landing I met a boy with a self-inked star on his wrist, bright as a new bruise. He blocked the stair with his foot and told me, with the seriousness of the unusually young, that he had counted a different number of steps going up than coming down. He seemed to think I held an answer that would keep his mother from tightening her mouth at night in the way she had picked up from hunger.

“Do not count,” I told him. He sneered. He must have heard me tell other people not to do other things in the language of the boards downstairs. I took the boy’s hand and I closed his fingers around the chalk out of my pocket and I said, lower: “But if you must, mark a line only you can see.”

Bureaucracy prefers that we pretend the personal is a rumor; grief makes a path of its own and drags its own cartographers. I returned to the Department with my notebook and my depraved pocket. In the afternoon Kasia brought me a plum and a piece of paper pinned with five addresses that had become difficult in the last hour. She could have left them on my table, but she put them in my hand and closed my fingers and looked at my eyes as if she could read more there than I had ever intended to print. We used the city’s old coffee pot to scald the smell of damp off our coats. We traced the lines of Mallow Street deepening. We drew the Southern Market again, less, though the fly had died three years ago and there was no one left to blame.

In the blueish early dark when everything in the building looks like part of a photograph that has failed to fix, the Municipal Council announced changes by paper megaphone at the corners: Avoid the footbridge at Cotton Row past midnight; its hinge was not to be trusted. Do not name your addresses aloud if you still live on Ghost Lane. Return library books with apologies for the books are reading themselves to save us the trouble. The whimsy was not new; what was new was the crack in the voice that read them.

And I, who had trained for the modest precision of squares, felt the pull to go again to Quince. The chalk in my pocket had a heat as if it had its own blood. The weight in my chest had become the odd lightness of a balloon lifting itself against an open palm. There are nights when a city asks a small favor. We pretend it asks it of all of us and that the favor is blind. I packed my field kit, on top of it the old folded map I am not supposed to have, the one with Miren’s blue pencil still haunting it like the scent of someone’s hair in a sweater. I tucked it away beneath the official paper because I am not stupid. I went down the stairs and opened the door to air that had been flavored by the river’s low tide and the sugar factory’s sigh. Somewhere behind me a chair scraped; somewhere ahead a child lost its handle on a name and called out mother, mother as if the word itself could build a platform under us all. The hallways of memory are full of ends, and I had been cautious my whole life at the edges of things. It was not caution now that made me stop at the threshold of the Department’s door; it was the new knowledge that there are kinds of stepping we cannot practice for.

Outside, the city had not yet flinched at my intention. Good. I walked.

Much later, when I would think of this night, I would remember stupid things, as one does: the way my bootlace frayed at the end, the oily glint in the gutter too bright to be water, the two men under the lamplight opening a tin as if the tin contained very small birds they meant to save. I would fail to remember the names of streets and have to go back and write them down, ashamed. I would draw differently. But then, in that hour, all I had was my small chain, my faith that measuring could be tenderness, and the note in someone’s hand that told me, against all training, that the scales we were given were not scales at all but stories that had forgot they were stories.

When I turned onto Quince, the hallway I had left had spun itself another inch of air. The radiator hunched. The chain trembled. Through the plaster, the boy upstairs was tapping in a rhythm that belonged to a song I knew and could not place: a simple melody children teach other children when they need to remember how to be in time with something. The room was warmer. Or perhaps it was the chalk. I did not ask permission; I leaned, and I wrote, on the skirting board, in my not very good hand, a line that did not say a name and did not try to summarize anything, a line that might be mistaken tomorrow for damage.

We are here, I wrote. We are here; be as exact as you can.

Then I put my kit down and reached for the space where the reeds did not complete themselves. I did not put my whole hand in. I am not a fool. But I spend my days drawing the limits of people’s folly. I know how deep they go. The chain kissed my wrist. The city inhaled or I did. The edge was neither warm nor cold and had no charity, which is perhaps the closest thing to true I have known, and when I withdrew my hand, for a half second the skin wrinkled as if I had had it in water that my father had salted as if for soup. I licked my thumb. It did not taste like anything at all.

Back in the Department, there are drawers where the old maps lie like bodies do when they believe they will be woken. I slid one out. I opened it flat. My hand shook. Interference, the Council would call what I was about to do, as if the course we had chosen for ourselves were a train and I were the idiot goat on the tracks. I took Miren’s map and I laid it on top of Quince, and I let the light from the lamp make the two cities one. Where they fit, it was an accident. Where they failed, it was a proposition. On Miren’s paper, in her difficult, mathematical script, along a corridor she had made longer just by looking hard, was a tiny arrow and a note not in blue pencil, not the sentence that made me love her before I even met the person she advertised with it, but this: Stand where you are too frightened. Look back.

The edge did not move. I moved. I stood in the place Mrs. Kline had smoothed with her hand as if to iron out the wrinkle of catastrophe. I looked back, past the plates she had set out, past the photograph of a man and a dog who had each belonged to each other twice over. The city arranged itself at the perimeter of my fear, as if waiting to be allowed. The scales, if that is what they were, trembled like fish.

You will want me to tell you that something happened then, that something opened or closed, that a light did some acrobatics of meaning, that my hand went through and pulled back a thread of Miren’s hair, a smell of oranges, a cheap umbrella. I am making the mistake, already, of anticipating and smoothing. I am drawing a line where there are two kinds of sea and pretending they do not fight.

Nothing happened. The edge did what it does. It stayed. It will surprise you, then, that I count this as the last hour of a peace I had not known how to name, and the first hour of a work that would make of me a person with a better mouth for saying what I mean when I say here.

On the way home, at the bend of Grist where the children had chalked their stars or their bread wheels, a new notice had been pinned to the board, likely in the hour I was in that corridor with the chalk and the foolishness. It read: Bring your own light.

I had never considered that possibility. It shook me. My father’s hand on the pan. Miren’s difficult D. The boy’s tapping from the ceiling. Mrs. Kline’s cardigan with its animal warmth: persimmon, persimmon in a city that has never grown a persimmon tree. I looked up. My window at home was dark. The moon had not come; it had been busy elsewhere or had become too light for us to pull, with our poor gravity.

I went upstairs and opened the drawer where we keep things we are not supposed to need. There was a flask half full of clear spirit and an old candle stub wrapped in paper printed with a holiday from a decade ago. I put both in my bag and slept with my hand on the bag’s strap and dreamed of a man standing at the inside of a map and kissing it as if it were the face of a lover, careful not to crease.

On the morning Candlefish Lane was erased, I was the one who had to pronounce its absence.

It’s a ceremonial word, and we say it plainly, no throat-clearing flourish: Departed. The brass letter D hangs on a nail by the door of the Department of Maps and Departures, and whoever is first in must carry it through the rain to the bell and ring, once. It is an old bell, green with salt, struck so many times it sounds like a throat murmuring to itself. After the ring we mark the map—small bright pins that are not so much celebratory as cautionary, threaded with red string that begins to look, in certain lights, like a system of veins.

Candlefish Lane had always been a thin wrist of a street, a sliver that only the winter sun remembered, lined with narrow two-storey houses painted the colours of seashells. People there salted their own fish and hung streamers of eelgrass from the gutters—good luck, they said, good luck against the water because the water respects what returns to it. The city surveyed Candlefish Lane last spring and decided it was not worth the cost of raising. Decision codex 1187: low-lying residential. Subject to reversing brine. Short-term mitigation only. Thus, Departed.

I walked its length with the measuring wheel the way you walk a child around a room to introduce it to company: this is the table leg, this is the window, this is the curl of dust in the corner. My breath fogged the instrument’s little glass as if I were kissing it. Every few steps I stopped to write, as precisely as I could, what the world there had said. A green door with a handprint in flour, the last baked morning. A tile with a blue chip, shaped like a continent. The beige cat that moved on, finally, like a tide receding from one particular stone.

We teach ourselves, in this department, to collect what’s going to disappear without troubling it. We collect what cannot be bulldozed or moved: the argument of wind in a hedge, how bread smells when the salt dampens the oven, the exact way Mrs. Pell at No. 7 wraps a fish so it doesn’t leak on the bus. People call us sentimental. It’s not sentiment, I want to say. It’s accurate. It is the record of the world as the world had the decency to be.

At the end of the lane a man in a high-wader suit hammered a sign into the earth. We add these signs as much for the sea as for the people. The sea pays attention to markers, to intention. We are polite to one another, the sea and my city.

“Take a look,” he said, stepping back, tipping his chin at the word I already knew. He had a face like the side of an old cupboard, a dent where you’d expect a knob to be.

I crouched to align the picture in the public archive app. In the photo the word Departed leaned a fraction to the left, the way people lean, unconsciously, to hear better.

I have a job because the line where water meets land refuses to stay where someone put it sixty or a hundred years ago. The water has begun a gentle, methodical audit. Every day it takes something small to see if we notice: the bottom stair, the hinge of a gate. We noticed late. Now we send people like me to observe, to ask our questions and keep our mouths closed over our grief like a pebble.

“What did you want us to remember?” I asked the first woman who opened her door. The asking is part of the process. You’d think people would want us to remember the big things—birth and marriage—but in the document of a place it’s the small that stays. Like how in your body you think of your skin or your breath, but when the doctor asks what aches you say: a tooth, the back of my knee.

She pushed her hair behind her hat, considering. “The water used to shy away from Mr. Pell’s boots,” she said. “A little lick of a wave. Never more than that. He said he had an agreement.” The woman laughed, a short sound that implied the world had not kept its side of many agreements recently. “And that my stairs were always crooked. You can put that, you can write that the stairs were crooked and never worth straightening.”

I wrote. It’s good when people give you an offering right away. You can make the shape of a place out of those first words. You can see how far the shape will reach.

The opening in the sky widened reluctantly. The gulls hovered at the exact height where the wind would deliver their hunger to them. Children from the uphill school, who were meant to be inside, used the slant of the street as a runway. One slid a piece of plywood and caught a wave at the lip of Pell’s yard, scudding with an ease that made my heart climb into my mouth, as if my heart, too, wanted to reach the long water.

“Do you mind if I come in?” I asked Mrs. Pell herself, later. I knew her from the paper where, for sixty years, she’d advertised herrings and hope. Not in those words, but that was the grammar of it. She had become one of those faces you could punctuate a sentence with.

“You’ll step out with more on your shoes than when you came,” she said. “But it won’t belong to you.”

I stood on her square of mat and smelled river and vinegar. On her mantel there were three photograph frames with nothing in them. Empty frames are more honest than full ones, sometimes. They tell you the person hasn’t had time to choose which memory to live in, or the person is waiting for the right light to pour through the window and spill into the old faces.

“What did you want us to remember?” I asked again, because the asking is a sacrament, not a form.

She pressed the bridge of her nose with her finger and then drew a line in the air, as if dividing something from the rest of the room. The line hung there, a glimmer I couldn't see, only sense.

“Not the stink,” she said. “People will say Candlefish was always stink. Don’t write that. Write instead that on some mornings, right on eight, if you opened all the windows, you could smell sugar. The bakery uphill, they used to burn the first batch of sweet buns because the oven was old and nobody lived there to scold the oven. And the sugar would throw itself down the hill as if calling hello. I liked thinking of it that way. Hello, it would say, and it would rub itself on my curtains.” She smiled, which told me she had liked other things too, even if she wouldn’t offer them in this minute.

“What about the sea?” I asked.

“What about it?” she said, and we both looked to where it peered into her kitchen as if it were a neighbor considering a pot left on the stove. In the picture I will keep in the archive it looks innocent. Water tends to look like itself.

When I rang the bell back at the office, the sound was swallowed like a pill. More people had been moved to the long buildings uphill, where every row of windows looked like a mouth trained not to speak. My supervisor, a woman who has never once told me not to carry work home with me because she knows the map has its ways of traveling, slid a black envelope across my desk. On its flap the city sigil—a blue fish with its eyes closed—glinting like something pressed down hard.

“Tomorrow,” she said. “Harrowgate.”

Harrowgate had been a district, then a gated set of blocks for magistrates and travelers, and now a zone. When something becomes a zone, it means there are rules inside it that do not apply outside it that the water, also, does not accept. Harrowgate had three fountains that had never once run dry in two centuries. Every geographical miracle we have remains under-lined in old legislation, surrounded by words to keep it from spoiling. Nothing holds, finally. The cords chafe from where we hold too tight.

“Why the envelope?” I asked.

“Because there is still someone left there,” she said. “Warden would like you to observe with him. You speak quieter than I do.”

The Warden of Names is not the highest rank but it is the rank that hears the most. He has his office in the old post, where the bags used to arrive heavy with letters that smelled of salt and train metal. He reads the register of the dead every morning and pauses over the names that have been used more than seven times in a century; he says those names are trying to tell us something about ourselves. He says the city is only a city because we say its name the same way every day.

“I’ll be there,” I said, and tucked the envelope into the pocket of my wet coat. It was lighter than the others. It had the sense of being a piece of paper with words that didn’t know yet how much they would weigh.

On the way home the rain advanced to a new agreement with gravity. It came down with intention. The market vendors tied their tarps tighter, and the tarps made a sound like the sea makes under a pier when it practices its speeches. The old men who measure everything with their eyes stood beneath the arch of the courthouse and noted, with the tips of their mouths, that so many people had misjudged the season again.

My apartment is on the third floor of a building that leans into the wind the way an old woman leans into a countertop. The plaster is not original, nothing is original but the way the light moves on the boards, which is to say: time is the only architect we all share. I have collected things that seem too light to sink. On the sill: a feather, an old ribbon, a piece of bread cracked so hard it pretends to be bone. In the cupboard: jars of dried lemon peel, tiny paper bags with labels, not because I am precise but because I like to let certain things go slowly.

There was a package set just inside my door. I knew it was there before I saw it in the way the room arranged itself around an absence of its own.

I did not touch it for five minutes. I peeled off my coat and hung it from the hook, which sagged as if carrying a confession. I filled the kettle. I took the envelope out of my pocket. I opened the window to convince the room it wasn’t only itself. Sometimes this is the only way to continue being a person. You have to behave as if nothing is extraordinary, as if water boiling is the most pressing thing in your life.

The package was wrapped in oiled cloth and bound with twine I recognized from a kind of fishing we don’t do here. The knot had been tucked under itself with a care that suggested a habit. My heart, which had been standing politely somewhere near the window, came to the doorway between my ribs like a neighbor with news. There is a small shape that lives on the front of my shoulder, a shape that is not visible and not imaginary: the shape of a hand. My father’s. It has no weight, usually. When the package touched the table, it did.

I am not sentimental about my father. He enacts in me the same effect that weather does: certain days I feel myself unwilling to be inside the way he was, certain days I look at the horizon as if that were a line drawn by a human hand. He named me for a bird that does not migrate. One year—this was before the water began asking us questions—he took me down to the quay and made me touch every boat that had a name. He said, see how names sit on things? As if you could take them off and knot them elsewhere. He was not a cruel man. He simply lived as if he had been born between the parentheses of something that mattered more than the room he was in.

I untied the knot.

Inside the cloth there was a sheath of paper that smelled like the inside of a drawer that had once held possible lives. There was a map on top. It was not a map of the city as we draw it, from above, with our lines and our pretenses of knowing where the land stops. It was a face-on map, as if someone had laid down on the ground and drawn at eye level.

He had always drawn that way. He would put his cheek to the table and, with the pencil clamped like a compass, trace the way the street looked when you were six inches above it. A map for people who walk, he said. A map that remembers the slope where you hesitated the first time you rode a bicycle, the lump in the road that taught you to lift your feet when you were being dragged somewhere you didn’t want to go. The map he had sent was a map of the harbor wall, drawn in segments with the kind of attention you give to a sleeping thing with a knife nearby.

Behind the map was a letter. His handwriting startled me. It was clean even where the rain had gotten in. He did not use my name. He never does in letters. He thinks names belong to the mouths that first spoke them.

He wrote: The tide will forget to turn, sooner than you think.

He wrote: Do not make a noise where the stones speak.

He wrote: Find me where the barnacles have eyes.

He wrote in a smaller hand beneath this, as if apologizing to the paper: Find me where the tide forgets to turn.

There are sentences that stand upright where you put them. There are sentences that immediately lie down, drunk with their own implication. These lay down. The space in the room shifted. The kettle screamed as if just then it remembered what its purpose was and was ashamed of all the time it had spent on the stove idle.

The barnacles in our harbor are as blind as pain. Their mouths open and close like indifferent hands. There is no place I have ever seen where the tide does not perform its ancient mathematics, its perfect subtraction and addition. Always I have counted on that rhythm to anchor the rest of the ways we must lie to ourselves. The tide is a metronome, we say. The tide is a heart that belongs to everyone.

Was he teasing me? Had I been softened sufficiently by the small kindnesses of my job to fall for a myth? There are old stories that the sea pauses—only pauses—on the nights when whales pass who are older than the idea of whales. There are places in our records where the handwriting falters, in that part of the book where the clerks used to copy the measurements of dawn, and a note was added: Struck with a feeling. But a forgetfulness? A tide in error? A tide with its mind elsewhere?

Find me.

You could hollow out a life with those two words and build a boat from the wood, and it would sail.

I put the kettle off the ring and wrote to my supervisor: A family matter requires my attention. Too formal. I wrote: Something has come up related to the harbor. Too casual. I wrote: I will be at Harrowgate. Honest, nearly. I did not write: If a person were to go where the tide might fail her, would you come too? She’d ask me to bring a second rope and a man who had been a man long enough to not try to decide anything, and there are fewer of those than there used to be.

I stood on my stool and pulled down my father’s copy of the Boundaries and Indices, a volume the Department keeps in a glass case as if it were the heart of an animal that keeps our building alive. We have three editions. This one was the oldest. On page 118, the first mention of Harrowgate: A hedge pulled up and replaced where rain falls more evenly. On page 200, the surveyor’s complaint: The tide is not to be relied upon as informer of all things. On the back board, in my father’s careful pencil: not if asked rudely.

He had, of course, drawn his own indices and inserted them in the binding. A flimsy paper, thinner than onion skin, with small eyes in the margin to suggest where a person should look. He drew not just for himself but for the reader he knew he was raising. This would be sentimental if it weren’t true that I’ve cursed him for the places where, too, he drew his little arrows as if they would take me where I wanted to be. For months, when I was twelve, I believed he had hidden maps within other maps, and that if I found the precise point where his pencil had pressed harder—a pothole, a nail hole in the drawing—I would be let into the room where he had slept since he left us. I had to teach myself, over and over, to be the person I am and not the person his absence could make of me.

Do not make a noise where the stones speak, he wrote. The wall has been speaking all along. You can hear it on mornings when the sky has a thin skin. You can hear it when a ferry slides by and the water gives its little hiss like a secret wanting to be told. The wall says its long, low word, and the word is not a word for people. It is a word in the grammar of weight.

I unfolded the other sheets. There were not many. One, lined faintly with the outline of a fish, edges salted into lace, a list:

where people put their feet when afraid
where the dog sits but only when the moon is less
places made of iron that believe in themselves
the crack at Number 3 where a child hid a tooth
the nail that remembers being silver

This could have been anyone’s list, except for that last line. Nails do not remember being silver. They remember the hammer. They remember what they hold. Silver is something my father thinks metal becomes when it can no longer tolerate the company it keeps.

I put the papers back in their cloth, the cloth back into the drawer where I keep the candles and the seeds I’ve yet to trust to the earth. The rain leaned with its full weight against the window like a person you love who has done something you cannot accept and whose forehead you cannot stop touching.

Night is a tide too, and when it comes in my part of the city, it drags the smell of creosote and moss with it, and all the lights along the harbor smear on the wet like the undersides of fish. I lay on the floor to feel the building’s sway, imagining the wall as my father had drawn it, close as a body, whispering its great untranslatable word. On the ceiling, the bottle glass in the roof above me made ovals of green light, one of which drifted from the seam where the plaster cracks toward the corner where the spider makes arithmetic of dust. I thought of Harrowgate, of the fountains that forgot to be coy, of the way water can be convinced to pretend it is tame if it is asked properly. I thought of the envelope on my table, official and black, and the twine knot my fingers had found as if of their own accord.

In the morning I would go to the zone with the Warden, and we would stand where the law still believes itself more than salt. In the afternoon, perhaps, I would find the part of the wall where men with patience have taught their sons to tip their hats to stones. In the evening, if the math we have all agreed upon failed, I would wait on the edge of the pause.

Find me, he had written.

The bell in the office would ring without me if a street somewhere else had been erased by the water’s logic. My name would be called, twice perhaps, and then the register closed over the space where I should have written what was lost. The city, which has been so careful to pretend it knows nothing of me beyond my signature, might allow this lapse if, afterward, I delivered them an absence they hadn’t yet tallied: the day the tide forgot to turn, and what it said when it remembered.

I slept with my boots by the bed and the letter under my pillow like a superstition I had outlived and was doing for the comfort of the person I had been. The rain moved away in its dignified way. Somewhere far off a siren practiced hope. In the marrow of the building the water rose, and then it fell, and then, perhaps, for the smallest fraction of a second no one could measure with our instruments—you could almost have called it kindness—it held completely still.

The first number that betrayed me was three.

It was stamped in black on the corner of my mother’s death certificate: “Survived by 3.” I stood in the municipal office under a fan that moved only the heat around, feeling the slowness of ink. We were four. My little brother had slipped out of the count, being born without the paper that would welcome him into the state’s math. He was a soft-cheeked boy who smelled like cumin and rainwater and, by any measure that mattered, he existed. The clerk did not look up when I told her. The fan made a sound like a goat’s laugh. I held the page to the light and the three hung there like a fly, refusing to shoo.

Years later, when people asked me why I took the job, I lied. I told them I liked the order of it, the columns and boxes. I told them that weighing a life in digits was cleaner than in tears. The true thing is this: I wanted to keep a private ledger that would settle my debt with that first treachery. I wanted to write the names that were forgotten, and I wanted to write them in a hand the state would never get.

The road into the valley counted itself in switchbacks that made the bus breathe like an animal. It was late August and the hills were the color of old brass. From a distance, the valley looked like a bowl you could drink from—two ridges cupping a thread of river, terraces bitten into the slopes, houses clustered like teeth. The driver kept a lemon wrapped in a handkerchief and bit into it at every stop, the flesh shining, his lips quivering. At the last bend he tapped his horn twice, a ritual, he said, so that the valley would allow us in.

The Directorate had sent me because I was less noticeable than the usual men. Women did not think to hide from me. Men thought less about lying. Mr. Falou, my supervisor, had called me into his office a week earlier and closed the door with theatrical gentleness.

“They’re expanding the irrigation, finally,” he said, pushing a folder across his desk. His fingers were stained with nicotine and ink, as if he lived off what the pen exhaled. “The minister wants every head counted. All registered males over twelve, all cattle, goats, sheep, donkeys. Number of fruit trees. Which families have radios. Which houses have roofs.” He smiled at his joke. “You will bring me a valley in rows and figures, Leila.”

“And the women?” I asked.

“The women will be wherever they belong,” he said, not unkindly. “Do not waste ink.”

I slid his list under the thin blistered leather of my case and held my tongue against his word for our work: head. It made a clean sound when he said it, as if heads were something you could stack in a neat pyramid with no eyes in them.

The bus coughed us onto the square at the valley’s center, a broad plot of thorns and hard-packed dust presided over by a mulberry tree that had seen more dead donkeys than weddings. A faded mural on the souk wall showed a man in a peaked hat shaking hands with another man in a peaked hat. Between them, in a blue ripple, the river. It was true that the water there did not know where to go; it changed its mind twice each year, as if embarrassed by its own direction. In spring it ran hard toward the plain in a green rush, carrying the mountain’s melt. In autumn it turned back and ran up toward its mouth, which everyone agreed was ridiculous but also, somehow, right.

I rented a room above a shop that sold flatbread and cigarettes. The shopkeeper coughed without trying to hide it and called me daughter on the first syllable. His name was Jabril. In my room, the bedframe was so narrow it made my body remember how to sleep small. From the window I could see the mountain path switch up between two stones everyone had likened, for as long as anyone remembered, to a pair of thighs.

That first evening the air was the temperature of hands. The sound of a radio drifted up from the square—someone reading the news like it was a sad sacred story—and somewhere a goat screamed as if its own skin had surprised it. I took out the Directorate’s ledger, heavy as a breath you can’t release, and placed it on the table. It had a thin red thread looped through its spine and a watermark of the emblem: a lighthouse rooted in wheat. I turned to the first page and printed neatly:

Qal‘a Valley. Survey Year 38. Agent Name: Leila b. Sanaa. District: Southwest.

Then I took the other ledger out from the bottom of my case, the one I’d bought with my own money, its paper thick and soft as an old shawl. I wrote nothing on its first page. I have always believed that if you start with an empty line as your first sentence, the rest of your words will be gentler. I placed a pencil between its pages and shut it.

In the morning, I went to the river.

Children were already there with pails and baskets, girls coaxing shrimp out of holes with their singing. The river smelled like iron trying to be sweet. It had the look of a ribbon that had been folded too long in a box: pleats, a little shame in its creases. A woman in a black dress stood knee-deep and lifted one foot then the other as if teaching herself to dance. When she stepped out, her legs were crosshatched with the bite marks of little fish. She laughed and went back in, displaying the map the fish had made, as proud as if it were a lover’s bruise.

“Fewer this year,” one girl said to another, and because the river was stingy with loudness, the words came to me.

“Fewer shrimp?” asked the girl.

“Fewer of us.”

The girl tipped her basket and let the shrimp tumble back in. “Then be two.”

The houses up the bank were stone and mud and old patience. Doors were painted blue because blue would keep everything at bay—evil, drought, envy, snakes. The first door I knocked on had a rooster carved into it, its comb encrusted with black finger-grease from years of touching. An old woman opened, resting the door against her thigh so it didn’t scrape the stone.

“Good morning,” I said. “I’m from the Directorate.”

“Good morning,” she replied, having nothing to say to such a statement.

“I am here to register,” I said, lifting the official ledger a little, not like a threat, not like a relic.

“The state has a long memory and short ears,” the old woman said. “Come in.”

Her name was Hajar. She was the kind of old that made you wish the word for it were something cleaner than old. She had a face like a walnut—every line was a rumor of winter—and her hair, which had been dipped in henna sometime in the last week, flamed on her head. In a pan on the earthen stove she was stirring a handful of stones with oil and garlic.

“For the mouth,” she said when she saw my glance. “It is good to trick the mouth in the morning. It will be too busy to complain.”

A little girl sat under the table, chalk dust in her hair, making marks on the underside as if the table were the sky. She held a shard of slate and had already covered every corner she could reach with tiny white scores.

“My granddaughter, Narin,” Hajar said. “She likes to write where writing is not expected. Come, sit, take tea, I know how you people work. You will ask as your paper instructs, and I will answer as my God does.”

I turned to the first page of the Directorate ledger. The pages were heavy, lined in faint blue, the columns printed ruthlessly straight.

Name of head of household: Hajar bt. Salim.

Registered residents: 2.

Men over twelve: 0.

Cattle: 1 (OX; name: Red).

Donkeys: 0.

Sheep/goats: 4/3.

Fruit trees on property (bearing): Fig (1), almond (2 dead), pomegranate (1 surly).

Radio: yes, sometimes.

Roof type: yes.

On my own ledger I wrote, in the left margin very small, because the left margin is a place that numbers cannot see: Narin. Draws the sky on the underside. I thought to myself: bears the wrong number on her wrist; and then I saw that she had numbers indeed, small ones, written in blue ink along the river of her veins. 1 1 2 3 5 8. Fibonacci, an old cousin whispering to himself on her skin.

“What’s that sequence?” I asked her, forgetting my script.

She stuck out her little arm happily and wiped her nose with her other hand. “Grandfather told me about it,” she said. “He said it can tell you how rabbits fall in love.”

“Grandfather is dead,” Hajar said, as if this was a gentle correction. “He is in the fig tree now. Math is a language that makes people arrogant. The fig tree has never learned to count beyond wants.”

“Where is Narin’s mother?” I asked, because my page wanted to know, because my other page wanted first to know.

Hajar’s eyes slid toward the stove. She shook the pan gently so the stones clicked and oil popped. “My daughter went up with the gophers two seasons ago,” she said. “We find their mounds and bury her words in them. Sometimes they answer us in the morning.”

I did not write anything for a moment. The Directorate’s pen hovered, obedient, waiting for me to tell it what to do with a woman who had gone up with rodents.

Narin looked out from under the table. “Mama went over the ridge with a clay jar and came back with a jar without a bottom,” she said. “She caught wind in it and then the wind ran away. We made soup in it anyway.”

Hajar laughed, showing me teeth as gray and soft as the end of a good pencil. “You see,” she said. “Math makes the world less handsome. We are done with it.”

I asked the other questions. Who owned the land. Who held the mortgage. Whether there had been any boys born in the last census year. I asked with the meekness of a person entering a room where the light had already decided where to sit. Hajar’s answers were a string of truths that refused to tie themselves into a bow.

“My sons are salt in the city,” she said. “They make people thirsty, then go home and drink nothing. My neighbor’s son was taken to the barracks and came back as a shadow on the wall. Once a soldier gave Narin a coin with the minister’s face and now she thinks all coins have that face.”

Narin pressed her lips together and made a mark on the table’s underside so hard that chalk broke under her finger and fell like snow into her lap. She rubbed it into her knees.

When I left their house, Hajar pressed a small cloth wrapped around warm stones into my hand.

“For your mouth,” she said. “So it will not begin to tell you that all you have is ash.”

I went to nine more houses that day. At each door my knock learned a new sound. At each table I learned what would never fit. There was a woman named Isra who kept a goat inside the house because it had once saved her grandchild from a hawk by butting it off course. She fed the goat dates and spoke to it more tenderly than she spoke to her husband. There was a boy called Sami who rehearsed silence so well he was almost good at it. In the second house after that, there were three brothers who slept on the roof all summer to keep the stars from leaving, and a mother who wore an apron with the road from her village printed on it so she would never forget how to go home.

On the plaster of many rooms I saw writing in pencil low to the ground where only someone sitting would think to look. A list of spices. A line from a song whose melody had lost its shoes. A number circled and circled, as if circling could contain it: eleven. In the sixth house, above the stove and too high to read easily, there was a prayer written in charcoal. I craned my neck and read it slowly. God, let my child be counted by bees and not by men.

At midday, a pause—that old holy instrument, used by grandmothers to beat back hunger—worked on the valley. A woman in a gold scarf sold sesame flatbread from a basket, and a boy ran after her calling: Aunt, the sesame is escaping. I sat under the mulberry tree and ate the bread with the stones Hajar had given me, rolling each in my mouth until it learned to be walnut, learned to be olive, whatever the teeth wanted. I washed it down with tea from my thermos, tannins staining my tongue the color of argument.

Mr. Falou’s list waited in my case, but the soft ledger in my lap cooled my knees like a sleeping child. I wrote there: Isra—goat saved baby. Prayer on wall. Narin—numbers on wrist. I will never embarrass these names by letting them become statistics. I wrote the sentence and immediately wished I had not. Writing an oath makes you a liar, sooner or later.

The first man from the Directorate found me just as I finished my bread. He was tall in a way that made his tallness look like a misprint, like someone had stretched him to the wrong ratio. He had on a beige shirt that announced its newness in every seam. His hair had a leftward opinion. He smiled before he knew what he would say, which meant the words arrived out of breath.

“Agent Leila,” he said. “Of course I would find you under a tree.”

“Because that’s where women go,” I replied, and he laughed as if I had given him a gift that did not require reciprocity.

“I am Riad,” he said, offering me a palm that was damp in the way of men who have tried to wash themselves of cigarettes. “Mr. Falou sent a runner from the city—there is some business—but he delayed in the heat and so I bring it. You are to note the irrigation canals precisely. Which ditches are dry. Which farmers are leveling on their own without permit stamps. The minister is making a map. They are calling it Widening.”

He handed me a flimsy top sheet, copied by a machine that had been coaxed into functioning with violent prayer. The words blurred a bit at their edges, as if they had been written under water.

“And the rest?” I asked.

He shrugged in a way that said the rest would happen itself. He leaned against the mulberry’s trunk and shook one of its branches to make a purple rain. He held out his palm with berries in it and I did not take them. He did not seem offended. The purple stained his fingers.

“There are many women here,” he said, as if I had not noticed. “More than the numbers say. The valley is famous for that.”

“Famous,” I repeated, and he nodded.

“For what is not seen,” he said. “My mother used to say some places collect the rain, some places collect what the rain whispers.”

“Your mother is a poet,” I said.

“My mother sells thread in the market,” he said. “She teaches herself to sleep with her eyes open so thieves will feel ashamed.”

He straightened and dusted his shirt as if mulberry juice could be dissuaded by discipline. “They sent me with a shade,” he said, pointing his chin toward the alley. In the little rectangle of shadow between two walls, a boy stood with a slate and a stick of chalk, looking like someone had told him to grow and he was trying to obey politely.

“This is Amin,” Riad said. “He will help you carry. He will lead you to the men who think they have nothing to hide.” He tipped his head. “And he will stand behind you when people retry their lies.”

I nodded to the boy; he nodded back. He had eyes like wells that had been covered with boards for years, then lifted and found to be clear. He wore a shirt too large for him, more idea than shirt. His feet were black with honest dirt.

“Do you know this place?” I asked him.

He nodded again. “I know which doors say they are closed but are not,” he answered. It was the first time that day I recognized my own language coming back to me from someone else’s mouth. I liked him for that immediately.

By dusk my official ledger had weight in it. I had written rows that would become decisions made in rooms with carpets. The other ledger lay hidden, waiting to be made dangerous by love. I had found the first irrigation ditch, caked with the crows’ footprints; I had measured its width with my foot, heel to toe, in repeating units of Leila. I had been told by a man with a plume of white hair that he had had seven sons and no daughters, and then his wife had come to the door with a girl on her hip who had inherited all seven laughs. “She is a mistake,” the man said, smiling like a wound. The girl bit my finger, gently. I wanted to tell her to bite harder.

When I returned to my room, the shop was crowded with men exhaling smoke and news. Someone’s brother had been detained. Someone’s cousin had bought a television set with a screen so large it felt like you were on it. Someone had seen a stream of dust at the ridge, a caravan headed toward the frontier. The shopkeeper Jabril made me a plate of eggs, their bottoms crisped nearly black the way my mother did, and a wedge of cheese shy with salt. I ate in my room with my back against the wall and my case at my feet.

I opened the secret ledger. On its second page I drew the map that I draw every time I arrive in a new place. I drew the river as a thread pulled through too-tight cloth. I drew the mulberry tree as a sun. I outlined the ridges with my finger before giving them ink. I marked a dot for Hajar’s door, a dot for Isra’s goat, a dot for the house with the prayer on the wall. I drew a small circle the size of a coin where Riad had stood, because it is useful to know where a man’s shoes have made a thought.

The room dimmed as the square below entered its evening. Someone tuned a radio and found not a station but a space between two stations, where the voices of both persisted like a conversation between two old men who had decided not to agree. I listened to them argue while I wrote the day into margins. Names are a currency that only gets more valuable when hoarded. I hoarded them with the precision of a miser. Then I blew on them gently to help the ink forget it was blood.

I slept badly. The bed was made for a thinner, more obedient woman. Midway to dawn I woke to the feeling that my ledger had moved. This is not metaphor. On the table, the soft book had slid closer to the edge, as if it had wanted to see what the night was doing. I reached out in the dimness and put my hand on it, and at my palm the cover was cool, like the forehead of a child who is either very well or very ill. The street whispered a little and I slept again.

In the morning I woke to a small sound at my door. Not knocking. Not a voice. A smoothing, as of cloth. I opened it to find the girl Narin sitting cross-legged on the landing with a stone in her lap. She was drawing on it with a piece of white chalk, and her tongue peeped out of her mouth with the effort. She did not look up until she was done. When she stood, she placed the stone in my hand.

It had a number scratched into it, zigzagged and careful.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is who I am here,” she said.

“And somewhere else?” I asked, because I was tired and because my mouth always betrays me first.

She shrugged, and the shrug was as old as the valley. “I am a number in my grandfather’s mouth,” she said. “He liked to count me twice. He said some things get closer when you count them wrong.”

I held the stone. It was warm. The chalk was not chalk; it was the tiny scratched residue of lime mortar, the table’s underside given to me, infused into a stone. I closed my hand around it.

“Will you put me in your book?” she asked.

“Which book?” I said.

“The one you keep under your dress,” she said, delighted that I had a thing to hide.

“I have only one book,” I lied.

She shook her head. “I am clever,” she said. She looked down the stairs to be sure no one had suddenly invented themselves there, then met my eye again, solemn as a syllabus. “If you count me, they will come and take me to the city,” she said. “They will give me a number and I will belong to the number, and then whenever my mother tries to call my name, the number will answer instead.”

“No one is coming,” I said, which is what I always tell children who have asked questions that are too good. “No one is coming for anything that is not theirs.”

“The river comes for what is not its,” she said. “In the spring it comes red, and in autumn it comes clean. I have seen it take a goat that did not belong to it, and a scarf that did, and once it took our neighbor’s shout and did not bring it back.”

I do not know what possessed me then. Perhaps it was the rhythm of the valley, the way air here made a half-promise of cooling, how every word seemed not born but laid like an egg. I went to my table and took the soft ledger. I opened it to the map. I took the stone from my hand and placed it on the page, under the mulberry’s inked sun.

“What number is this?” I asked.

She told me. The number was too precise to be ceremonial, not pretty enough to be lucky. It was a number you would give a medicine dose. It was a number full of humility. I wrote it, as she had given it to me, in the margin where numbers do not like to go.

Narin put her finger on the word as if to keep it from running away. “If I live on this page,” she said, “will you bring this page when you count? Put it under the other one, so the number they see is not the number that decides me?”

I almost told her that this was not the work of paper, that what she wanted was larger, that numbers are cathedrals you can exit only if you leave your shoes inside. But I remembered the way Hajar had stirred stones to trick her mouth. I remembered the coin with the minister’s face biting into a little girl’s hand. I remembered my mother’s certificate and its stubborn three. In the alley below, a man shouted for his wife to bring a spade, and his wife shouted back for him to learn the shape of her name.

“Yes,” I said. “I can do that.” The answer sounded like a spoon touching a bowl.

She nodded with the gravity of a judge. Then she smiled, and the smile was the first thing in this new place that did not seem like a wall or a door.

When she had gone, I sat on the bed and held my one ledger and my other one, knees leaned together like a single organ. The work of the day was already knocking—but the knocking was like rain, in the sense that you could turn your head away and still be made wet. I stood, tucked the official ledger under my arm, slipped the soft one between my dress and my ribs where all my secrets stay the right temperature, and went back into a valley that pulsed with numbers and names, both of which wanted desperately not to be mistaken for each other.

On the morning the river decided to go the wrong way, the apples fell with their blossoms still clenched.

At first it sounded like wind. A low, listless rush through the flats of the Borrow, a thread of sound you could follow with your head tilted as if a bird was passing somewhere you couldn’t see. I was standing by the pump house with my father’s ledger under one arm, still wearing my city shoes even though he told me to put on boots, and a cloud’s shadow was crawling over the lower rows.
