The men were moving ladders in their careful two-person way, the Echevarrías laughing about something private and small, the kind of laughter that keeps work from turning into a grind. Maria stood by the sink, washing the dust off late peaches we’d found tucked under leaves like lost coins. We were all, in one way or another, looking down, letting the morning do what mornings have always done here.

Then the apples began to patter quietly through the trees, their stems snapping, one after another, as if some hand far away tugged the world a little too hard.

“Listen,” my father said. He was looking over the ridge of his shoulder at the gap in the cottonwoods where the river showed itself, a slate blade. He wasn’t wearing his hat. In the pale light his hair looked like frost that had thought better of itself and kept living.

“What is it?” I asked.

“Not wind,” he said, and he lifted his chin like a dog catching a scent. “Not today.”

The pump house coughed and rattled and died before I could set the ledger down. The little red light that meant the intake was pulling shut itself off. Everyone heard it. The men stilled in place. The quiet rushed in with its own noise. Maria set a peach carefully on the towel and wiped her hands and said, “Pilas,” to no one in particular, and we all began to move toward the gap.

The fence on the far side of the lower rows was a halfhearted thing. The orchard wanted to be in the river and the river wanted to be in the orchard; fences here were more like polite reminders. We stepped over, walked the weeded path to the levee, the ragged edge where sedge pulled itself thin and the old flood marks stained the trunks of the cottonwoods like forgotten sleeves. The air smelled of penny and stone. The river lay in its channel quietly, as it had for my whole growing up, that mumbled, steady song, always, always, toward the sea.

Only now it wasn’t. At first it was just a trick of light and the mind’s insistence on patterns. The surface looked like a curtain in a breeze, and then the brightness of the other bank slid upstream as if someone had tugged a mirror. We stood and watched fish pitch in the wrong direction, their backs hooking out of the water in flashes like thrown spoons. You could see the reed heads dip and bow in a new way. A branch with last night’s swifts’ droppings on it floated past and then slowed and turned and shrugged itself back up toward the old bridge, toward town, toward the high, blank wall of the dam we all pretended didn’t exist until the county sent out a notice about scheduled releases and the sacred hours when children should not play.

“Is that supposed to be happening?” Maria said, and then, because she trusted us to have an answer, she asked again, quieter. “Is that supposed to be happening, Nora?”

I have never liked when people make me the answer to their questions about home. I am not the kind of daughter who writes to the town paper or shows up at meetings with a neat folder. I had come back because Baba’s handwriting was collapsing into itself and because Mrs. Shaw from the farm supply called to say he had been buying things twice, sometimes three times—a row of identical fuses, three valve keys in a week, a box of nitrile gloves the color of the sky on the last day of summer—keeping each purchase tucked in different pockets of the pump house as if he could hide his forgetting in separate rooms.

A man down the levee, Harlan Caldwell, had his phone out and said, “The dam must have—” and didn’t finish. People who were not supposed to be at the river had already begun to gather. High school kids who should have been at algebra hung from the bridge like cormorants. Old Mrs. Penn, who owned the bait shop, kept saying, “Well I’ll be,” as if the words themselves might keep something unlucky from swallowing us. I saw a county truck park crookedly on the far side of the bridge and a woman in canvas pants get out with an orange case that looked expensive and official.

Behind me the orchard waited, grid by grid, an old sheet of music the river had always hummed underneath.

Baba stepped down the slope as if the earth had remembered his weight overnight and had hardened just for him. Even from behind I could see how loose his belt had become, how he had not re-threaded it from the hole his waist had known for thirty-five seasons. He still had his field knife at his hip. He held his hat in both hands and bent its brim and flattened it, a ritual like worry beads. When he spoke, his breath grazed the tiny hairs by my ear, the way it had when I was small and he taught me to tell the different calls of birds by shape and not by sound. “It’s forgetting,” he said. “That’s all. It’s the remembering that hurts.”

“Baba,” I said, because one of us had to be the one who didn’t speak in riddles, “we have to call the county.”

“They’re already here,” he said, as if he knew before I did. He was right. The woman with the orange case had reached us. There’s a look that people who do important work wear when they come into places like ours: a gentleness that reads as consideration until the moment it hardens into certainty. She had already clipped her badge to the pocket of her shirt and so the first thing about her I knew was her name.

“I’m Pia Rook,” she said. “Hydrology. I don’t know what you prefer to be called.”

“Orchard,” Baba said, and his mouth made a crooked shape that could have been a smile if he’d had the energy. “We prefer to be called Orchard.”

I said, because there are always two languages where I am from, and it is a kind of kindness to answer both, “I’m Nora. This is—”

“I’m not his,” he said, quick as a slap, and then he laughed at the look on my face, that old, mischievous laugh I knew from the time he tied a rope to the back of the pickup and dragged my first sled through the meadow. “Hers,” he said, and he put his hand on my shoulder, heavy, warm. “Forever.”

Rook touched her glasses. It was the gesture of someone who was about to try to say news gently. “We have some flows scheduled for tomorrow at noon, but this—” She dipped her head at the river as if it were a person and she needed permission to speak about it. “This is not us. There’s been a surge in the canyon. Some sloughing. We think—” She shook her head, checked the orange case, took out a coil of cable, a yellow thing that reminded me of a snake. “It’s a pressure difference. It will adjust. You should keep the pumps off.”

“They already died,” I said.

She looked at me with her lips pressed into a reasonable line. “Then we’ll talk about alternate schedules if this persists.” Her gaze flicked to my father. People do this sometimes, when they can’t tell who is the voice that carries the weight in a family. I stood a little taller in my city shoes. It made no difference to the river.

Behind us, apples popped softly against earth. It sounded like rain from a far body of water.

“Please stay away from the bank,” Rook said. “Especially old folks and children. There can be boils in the water, odd undertows.” She paused, and because she was not from here yet had the sense that this was not a place where you told people what to do and expected them to listen, she added, “We’ll send a notice.”

Harlan made a noise that could have been assent or the beginning of a joke. Maria said, “Vamos a ver,” under her breath. The Echevarrías crossed themselves in the careful way of men who had made a bargain with weather and luck long ago and tried not to show they were keeping their end of it faithfully.

We watched for a long time. Things you see only once in your life must be watched the whole way through. The river greeted debris it had already met last night. Its old coils uncoiled. A ladder somebody had knocked over by the old mill inevitably slid toward us and then paused and tucked itself back up, its yellow feet new again. It didn’t feel like a miracle, or catastrophe. It felt like a mistake the earth would correct if you gave it a little time and a clean corner to put itself back together.

When the first siren went, the kind with that particular county wail that makes your mouth fill with sourness whether you like it or not, Rook checked her watch. She gestured to the other side of the bridge and her partner hustled down with a spool of caution tape that looked, from a distance, like a pale streamer for a parade nobody had quite decided to have.

Baba touched my elbow. “Don’t let the men work the lower rows,” he said. “It’s all wrong. They’ll break fruit. The ladders will sink.”

“I know,” I said.

“You have to tell them,” he said.

“Okay,” I said.

He slipped the hat on his head. It was the wrong hat, almost too small, the blue one from the time the county had given them out as if a free piece of shade with CHARLES BORROW CLEAN WATER stenciled on it would make everyone forgive the dam. He had nicer hats. He looked like a kid playing a role. “I’m going to check the gate,” he said. He kissed my temple, casual, as if there had not been three months in which he did not recognize my name when I came to the door, as if he had never asked where Nora had gone when I was sitting at his own kitchen table with his favorite mug in my hands. “Don’t fall in love with any hydrologists,” he added.

I smiled because I wanted to. “That’s not how it works,” I said.

“It’s all how it works,” he said.

By noon the sun had hardened everything into angles. The men moved to the upper rows. The apples in the lower rows lay on the ground like a spell you were not supposed to break by stepping through it. Maria made sandwiches from things we had in the house: grilled cheese, tomatoes sliced so thin they looked like stained glass. She put a plate on the pump house desk next to Baba’s ledger. We ate standing up. Work tastes different when your mouth is the only chair you have.

I checked the ledger before I checked on the men, because there are some rituals the body carries out without the mind’s permission. His handwriting had always been tidy. The kind of tidy that never calls attention to itself, steady as winter ribs in a horse. Rows were laid out in exact rectangles. Intake was scratched with arrows in the margins where he wanted to remember to close one gate and open another. On the last page his letters came apart like houses in wind. The numbers were no longer lined up. He had written the same word three times, each time worse, the last entry so faint I could barely read it even when I held the paper to the window, even when I pretended there were fewer nights between what he was and what he had become.

The word, when I saw it, was my name. Written without vowels. NR.

On the inside of the pump house door, where Baba and all the foremen before him had tacked up calendars with big-chested women in bikinis holding buckets and wrenches, and later, when I moved home the first time after college, calendars with comical goats in party hats because I had huffed every time I came in to turn on the tap, there was a new page. It was not a calendar. It was the thin brown of a paper grocery bag, cut open along the seam. He had written along the top, in a hand that was both his and younger—so maybe he had copied it from an old thing, maybe this was what it looked like when memory was borrowing itself—a list. It said:

When the river goes the other way—

then, as if he had forgotten to finish, he had drawn a square, and inside it, the map of the orchard, the blocks a quilt, the paths numbered stupidly in our family’s peculiar way, where we named 1 after the west row because that had been the first one he had planted, and 2 after the north row, and then 3 came in the middle because his back had given out that summer and he had to plant what he could where he could reach it.

I traced a finger over the square. The lower left corner had a circle around it, and in his scavenger’s writing, the kind printing he’d used when labeling jars of pickles, he had printed: Gate.

I found his watch hanging on the nail inside the door. The leather was cracked where he preferred the third hole. The face had begun to fog. He had never in my life gone anywhere in the orchard without it, not even when he slept, not even when my mother left. In the old story he told, like fathers tell daughters, the watch was from his father and his father’s father, from a market in a city with so many lemon trees the air itself tasted yellow. In the real story, I bought it for him after his heart attack. It had a second hand he could count when the world went thin. He had taken it off. He had not taken it off. Something had taken it from his wrist.

“Nora?” Maria called. It was the third time. I always took the third time seriously.

“I’m here,” I said.

“The man from the county is asking if we have an old map,” she said.

“Do we?”

“No,” she said, and then, because she was Maria and believed in grace, she added, “Yes. But not the kind he wants.”

Pia Rook was standing at the bottom of the stairs with a smile on her face. I have never been good at reading a certain kind of woman, the ones who carry confidence as an intention instead of a nature. She had wrapped her hair up in a rag to keep it away from the wind. Her eyes were the color of certain rocks you pick up without meaning to. She looked like every person who chose a life with measurements and equations I could never quite trust unless a hand had touched the thing and told me how it felt.

“Do you have an old irrigation schematic?” she asked. “The original.”

“Everything original here is under dirt,” I said.

“That’s what I mean,” she said. “The old intake in the bend might be exposed if the pressure keeps acting like this. There were stories in the archives. I think—”

She stopped because something was happening to my face. I don’t know what it did. It must have betrayed me like a dog. The word original made the back of my throat taste like the inside of a well. I could see, as if a page had been held up to the lamp, the day my father and mother walked the bend with the county man, and how the county man had a way of folding his paperwork in half and then again so that it was smaller than his decisions. I could hear my mother’s voice saying the one thing she ever said loud enough for neighbors to hear: If you take a thing’s mouth from it, what do you expect it to eat? And then I could see her back, her scarf bright as a bruise, as she lifted her suitcase into the back of the car and did not look at the house where she had taught herself to cook love out of flour.

“I’ll look,” I said.

Rook touched her glasses again. “I’m sorry,” she said. “I didn’t mean to—I just think the old gate could be pulling. When the river does this, old things wake up. It has something to do with the low pressure over the ridge. It’s not—I know how it looks. But it isn’t alive.”

I had the sudden desire to put my hands on the ground. To press my palms to the dust and ask, the way a child asks, how do you know.

Instead, I said, “If it isn’t alive, stop talking to it like it is,” and then wished I hadn’t, because she flinched as if I had taken something from her and broken it without meaning to.

“We’ll be careful,” she said. “We’ll keep people back.”

“What does careful buy,” I said. It was not a question.

By afternoon the sun went strange. A haze walked down the valley as if someone had set a field of hay on fire and then decided to carry the smoke somewhere else. The cows in Calder’s pasture lined up and faced west, which meant weather but not which kind. A child ran along the path with a paper airplane and the airplane, against all rules, flew upriver on a steady line until it was level with the old bridge and then, in an instant, the same instant the child’s mother hollered his name with that particular rope in her voice, the plane folded in on itself and fell into the water and the river, like it had not eaten for years, swallowed it whole.

By three the men had put away their ladders. By four the county truck had left. By five Pia Rook’s orange case was gone and there was caution tape curling like party pennants at the places where the bank undercut most. By six the Echevarrías had gone home to wives and babies who would smell river on their clothes and decide whether they loved it or hated it. Maria wiped down the sink with a ferocity that made me think of every woman I have ever known and the way we try to clean the uncleanable when our hands are the only thing we have any authority over.

By seven, Baba was not back.

“Does he do this?” Maria asked.

“Walk the gate?” I said. “Yes.” The number of times I had watched him do it, under every kind of sky. The number of nights he had taken the old flashlight and walked the line and checked each tie and came back with river pebbles in the cuffs of his jeans like small planets.

“Forget to come home?” she asked.

I wanted to say no. When you want to live in a place where men are dependable, you learn to say no even when the answer is making a bed in your mouth with its shoes on. “He’s late,” I said.

We waited another hour. I went out to the road and listened for the sound of his truck because the truck, like all true things in my life, has a sound you can tell even from far away. The sky purplish. Orion not yet risen. The moon, not ours. The neighbor's dog that hates everything making a private prayer. Cars from town with the windows up and the tinny ribbon of someone’s radio like a ghost.

By eight I could hear Mrs. Shaw’s front porch swing in my head. I could hear my mother’s suitcase wheels. I could hear the watch ticking softly on the nail. The ledger had a spot on it I had not noticed before, an oval like a thumbprint in oil.

I took a headlamp and put on the boots Baba had told me to wear. They were too big. When I tightened the laces, the tongue of one boot pulled away from the body as if it rejected me. The buckles felt like something someone else should touch. I left a note for Maria in my careful city handwriting that said: In the lower corner by Gate. If you don’t hear by ten, call Harlan. There are instructions stuck to the inside of the cupboard door, written when I had first come home the first time, when we believed instructions could keep us from the kind of night when the world went blank-faced and took what it wanted.

The river sounded tired and mean. The levee was slick with tough grass. I kept the beam of the headlamp low so it wouldn’t scare whatever might decide to be gentle if I let it be itself. Downstream—upstream?—the old names of distance had gone strange. The lower corner was where he had circled on the mapped bag. When I bent down to check the tie-off, to see where the pipe’s mouth opened to sip, my hand met emptiness. The bank had washed out, undercut as if a mouse had decided to live there. The pipe was hanging exposed, like a limb.

“Baba,” I said. It was not his name in public. It was his name for kitchens and thunderstorms and that one time we had gotten muscle bold and dragged a canoe overland because the river had decided to put a new tree in our way. “Baba, this is not the time.”

The beam of my light slid across the water. The surface skipped like film. And there, snagged on the limb of a willow that had decided to grow sideways, was a hat.

Not the blue county hat. The good hat, the one he wore to weddings and funerals and to shake hands with new men so they would know he was the kind who didn’t run from an eye. The ribbon had unglued and drifted down like a snake shedding its skin. There were two things inside the brim that made no sense because for a moment I could not reconcile them with the hat, the willow, the water. The first was his little suede bag, the kind he kept seeds in, even though no one had sown seeds in this orchard in a decade because the trees bred true and their childrens’ children were their best argument for staying. The second was the piece of paper I had taken off the pump house wall and folded neatly and put into my back pocket like a charm hours ago.

The bag couldn’t have been there. The paper couldn’t have been there. The bag was in the pocket of the jacket on the hook. The paper was in my jeans. But there they were, nested like the twin halves of a fruit, and the hat rocking in the wrong kind of current like a bowl somebody had set on a table even though the table was not level.

When I tried to reach the hat, the bank leaned toward me as if it wanted to kiss me, and then the whole world tipped and the mouth of the river said its last quiet word and let the ground give way.

I did not fall in. I am not, despite what this story might think, a woman who pays no attention to advice. There was a root. I had the boot. I had the sense not to lean my whole head into luck. I lay there with my chest pressed against the wet dirt until it made a brown ribbon across the front of my shirt and hauled myself back up to the grass on my elbows. My body shook like I had already fallen and the river was still holding me underwater somewhere else, in another world that had already happened.

“Nora?” The voice came from the path. It was thin and high and undecided. Harlan’s son Miles, who tied tin cans to the back of his bicycle because he liked to sound larger than he was.

“Go home,” I said, but not unkindly. The wind carried my voice sideways. He stood at the top of the levee fence with his arms hooked over and looked at me the way children look when they haven’t yet learned that adults don’t like being watched when we are caught doing things we do not know how to do.

“Is Mr. Aziz okay?” he asked.

“Yes,” I said, because the word made a small bridge over the breathless place inside my chest and I wanted to walk across something.

When I slid down again a few feet away from where the bank had given way, the hat was gone. The little bag knocked against the willow, then fetched up and stilled. I used the hook of the field knife to pull it closer, cutting my thumb in the process, and then sat back on my heels and opened it.

Inside were seeds I did not recognize. Thin, papery, like the husks of a moth. Two apple pips, shriveled. A handful of grit that could have been river or orchard or the hinge between. And one small tooth. Human or not I could not tell in the lamp’s light; it looked like something the world grows when it needs a point.

I reached for the pocket of my jeans for the paper, to measure it against the one that had been inside the hat. My pocket was empty. In the bag, folded into the seeds, the paper was damp, the brown grocery color gone to the weak tea color of old bandages. I smoothed it against my knee anyway. The square of the orchard was there. The circle around the lower corner was there. Beneath Gate, the word I had not seen before, the one I would have sworn was not there at noon, had appeared.

The word was Door.

A fish surfaced, took air, vanished. On the bank above me, Miles said something I could not make out and then said my name, the real one, the one my father had given me before school polished it into the version I offered the world. In the river something turned itself around once, twice, like a creature making a bed.

I tucked the bag and the wet paper into my shirt, under my bra where nothing could take them without speaking to me first. I stood to face the darkening water and to say my father’s name to it plainly, the way you say grace in kitchens, not because you expect anyone to be listening, but because the sound is what keeps you from becoming the kind of person who lets the dark do all the talking.

“Farid,” I said. “Enough.”

Far away, the bridge hummed with the dull sound of tires. The insects in the grass whispered with their bodies the old language they had always spoken. The river was the river, wrong in its bones. Behind me the orchard breathed in and breathed out. The first stars pulled their damp eyes open.

If I tell you that I felt the ground answer me, you will think that this is a story where the earth is a person with a mouth to kiss. If I tell you that my father stepped out of the reeds and said, “What?” you will think this is a story that gives back what it takes because it is afraid of what it has asked you to hold.

Neither is true. What happened was much simpler and worse. The current slid along the bank and took my voice between its hands and carried it the wrong way, upstream, toward town, toward the old dam, toward the place where the river’s throat narrowed to speak through concrete. And in the carrying I heard, not the river answering me, not the earth, not any of the saints I have never learned to recognize, but, faint as sleep, my father's voice, as if it had been trapped and was finally pulling free.

“Here,” he said. And then, so quietly I could have pretended I heard nothing at all, “Now.”

Chapter One

On the day the jar of honey began to sing, I had been assigned to Liquids.

I’d been in the basement long enough to know that assignments had their own weather. Blades were dry; you could keep a distance from them. Cosmetics were a fog of floral claims. Toys were bright and sticky and often surprisingly violent. Liquids were their own tide: they sloshed and seeped and seeped into you. They required patience, a steady hand, the ability to read labels distorted through glass. They required faith in lids.

At the Retained Items Repository there was no natural light, only the ceiling’s humming grid and the green exit signs that promised a way up and out if we ever needed to escape the airport’s stomach. Above us, bodies and their carry-ons circulated through the building the way fish move through reefs, while we skimmed beneath, netting what could not pass. We worked under the concourses, under the runways where the tarmac men wheeled their orange wands, under the tang of cinnamon pretzels and the duty-free’s perfume fog and the departure boards whose numbers clicked like teeth. We were the trapdoor beneath the theater of departure.

The older workers called it the House of Almost. “It almost met the size restriction. It almost had a declaration form. It almost was under three ounces. Almost belongs is one kind of heartbreak,” Dot told me once on a slow afternoon, filing nail scissors in a rolling drawer that had been three different shades of beige. Dot had been with the Repository twenty-two years and called everyone sweetheart and kept a clean handkerchief tucked into her sleeve. She believed that objects had no moral character. “They are what we make them, sweetheart,” she said, peering over the half-moon glasses she wore on a chain, which made her look as if she were peering over a very small gate.

We took things from the public ask-no-questions, their contraband pulled off conveyor belts by purple-gloved hands above us, boxed and barcoded and ferried down the service lift. We sorted them into their categories—liquids, weapons, foods, perishables, electronics, valuables, prohibited cultural materials—and logged them into the system with their date, flight, and the flimsy reasons the system assigned: volume, blade length, external battery, agricultural risk. We were instructed to record without commentary.

Our inventory reads like a poem of renunciation: honey, shampoo, grenadine; ceremonial knives, pocket knives, butter knives; olives in brine, goat’s milk cheese, pomegranates wrapped in newspaper; power banks, e-cigarettes, a curling iron that looked like a flute; a carved figurine of an ancestor with his hand raised in a vow. In the cells the system gave us—tiny prisons with fields for color and dimensions—I wanted to add annotations no one asked for, like: sliced into a thousand thin mornings; smells like my mother’s hair; if you hold it up to your ear you can hear your uncle laughing three years ago in summer.

That morning, a bin came down full of liquids that had been surrendered or taken or, in the case of the jar, coaxed. The jar of honey was glass, squat and shameless, with a paper label bleached to the color of the airport’s coffee. The top had been dabbed with something that looked like wax and glittered like varnished sunlight. Its label said: Thessaloniki Honey, Aidan & Sons Apiary. Below that, in smaller print, honey tastes like where it is from.

“You cannot bring liquids over one hundred milliliters through security,” said the man above, and his voice had been recorded in ten languages to play to the lines of people who pretended not to know. Honey is sticky and slow, homeland in the mouth. An agent had set the jar on the table in that half-second before the traveler could plead. They always plead for honey, for gifts that translate easily across languages, for sauces and oils and perfumes that mean, this is what the place smells like. And because honey poured out of a plastic bear can get on everything, the agent had moved it aside, put it in a bin with other liquids that couldn’t fly, and called for a basement pickup.

Beside the honey there was a snow globe with a tiny capitol building inside, forbidden because of the water. There was a bottle of perfumed oil from a shrine somewhere in the subcontinent, the faintest veggie green of coriander dresses. There was a squat plastic jar of homemade ajika thickened with walnuts. There was a liter of rose water the exact clear of a letter never sent. Many strangers’ kitchens. The basement smelled like an international wedding—sour coltish wine, sweet almond pastries, the musk of tourist t-shirts, a little bleach in the corners.

“Liquids for you, Ani,” Mr. Halprin said, sliding the bin onto my station, his mouth already in apology for the memo he was about to give me. He was a careful, papery man who always smelled faintly of thrift stores and who wore ties that suggested he wanted to be taken seriously by higher managers but did not have the budget to be. He had been promoted from Knives only last year. “You’re good with labeling.”

“I like nouns,” I said, and he blinked rapidly, either amused or unsure whether he was permitted to be.

“We’re starting with the new spectral arrays upstairs,” he said, holding a paper like a rosary. He tapped it as if to keep time. “By the end of the month. No liquids at all. No exceptions. They’ll see in your heartbeat. We’re going to have an uptick. Just a heads-up.”

He meant: more work for us. He meant: more things almost belonging. He meant, perhaps, no more singing soon, though at that moment nothing was singing yet.

I weighed the honey. The system wanted numbers and the system always wants numbers to be confident. Material: glass. Fill level: near full. Color: amber. Weight: negligible compared to the weight of what it meant.

When I set the jar on the cool metal table, I heard a sound like what I had thought was the air conditioning. A humming, faint and high as a mosquito, threaded through with notes that belonged to kitchen sounds—the tap of a spoon on a rim, the chime of small plates, the hush of boiling water being shushed. The sound specifically avoided syllables. It wanted me to lean in. I stuffed my ponytail back through its elastic and bent closer. The label had been pasted poorly; a corner lifted, and under it I could see the ghost of another label that had been peeled at some point like a scab. I pressed the corner down with my thumb to feel the jar’s warm-cool, the way glass keeps a room’s temperature even if it has been outside.

The honey’s voice, if voice is the word, braided itself with a melody my mother used to hum when she stirred the pot of milk before bed, not so much because we were thirsty but because rituals did the work that prayers failed at when the house was aching. The melody went up and down like a good staircase. I knew, as certain as I know the feeling of a fabric’s nap, that the tune was older than the label, older than Thessaloniki, older than the basement itself. Older than the rule about liquids. Older than the word for honey.

“Do you hear that?” I asked Dot, who was logging a pound of cherries in contraband produce as physical evidence of desire.

Dot looked up from her screen with her eyebrows in a question. “Hear what, sweetheart? You gotta be more specific here. You know I’ve got that tinnitus, sounds like the ocean if the ocean had bees.”

“Bees,” I said, too fast. “No, I thought I heard—never mind. It’s just the air.”

I was not a fanciful person. People at airports cure you of that quickly. They do not want stories. They want new rules to apply to their old ones. I had taken this job because it made sense. Because after years of applying for translation fellowships and teaching jobs and editorial assistant positions that would have unitized my days into emails and galley proofs, the Repository had offered a salary near enough to living and a health plan and a degree of anonymity. Anonymity is a country of its own. You can cross into it and spend years there without learning the word for “home.”

My mother had wanted me to be either very safe or very brave and had raised me so that I would be just brave enough to attempt safe things. When I changed my name to Ani on the application form so that people would not ask me how to say the rest, the old part of my name did not stop being mine. Anahid lived under my signature like an older city under a modern one, paved over but full of staircases to anywhere.

Dot returned to her cherries. “People think honey never goes bad,” she murmured. “They’re not wrong exactly but they’re not right either. It just doesn’t apologize for changing.”

“Dot,” I said. “Dot, if an object could—” I stopped. The word would ruin what I’d only barely heard. The word would make it sillier than it was.

Mr. Halprin drifted by again, his tie an indecisive green. “And remember,” he added, as he always did, because the training videos required him to, “no personal contact, no removal, no commentary. Document and dispose according to the chart. Do not anthropomorphize.” He said it softly, like an apology. He, too, had a basement voice. We all do, if we’re here long enough. We learned to speak as if a bright light were behind us, as if we might be observed.

At lunch, I took my Tupperware to the service corridor where a painted metal door opened onto a staircase up to the tarmac. If you stood on the landing and held your breath between bursts of wind, you could see wedges of planes lifting their noses. Even when I didn’t look, I felt them in my jaw—the way a high-speed train vibrates your teeth when it passes you so fast you don’t realize you’ve been separated from your life and then reattached. The sky above the airport was always a single shy color. Nothing was up there except departures and weather; no mountains, no cranes, no church spires to keep things anchored.

I ate a hard-boiled egg and half an orange and thought about the way the honey had sounded like the hairline crack in my childhood apartment’s kitchen tile where heat had raised a line like an old river map. I had not, until that moment, realized that I had been waiting for something to call out to me by name in a language I did not know I still understood. You can live in a city for ten years and never see your neighbor’s eyes. You can live in your name for thirty and suddenly remember it belonged to other mouths before yours.

When I came back from lunch there was a small knife on my work table, a bone-handled thing someone had thrown in with the liquids, as if, at a certain point, the confiscations were all one large idea: take what isn’t permitted until it is all the same shape of not permitted. The knife was the kind used for peeling apples, who taught children finesse, who had peeled so many fruits in its life that its blade looked tired of sweetness. There was a pomegranate carved into its handle with a pin. I held it between my fingers the way we were told never to hold knives and felt something else, a feeling like when you come to a word you don’t use often and it turns your mouth into a perfect O.

“Who sent the knife?” I asked Halprin. He checked the barcode on the bin with his little reader and shrugged. “Came down with the jar,” he said. “Somebody’s gift basket. Somebody got time for a picnic before security.”

I lifted the knife to read the tiny mark near where blade met handle: a maker’s mark filigreed into metal so thin it had become nearly memory: H. S. Sahak. The S had been scratched by long use, leaving only two hooks facing away from one another, like swallows.

The blade was warm. It had been in a hand recently. Or perhaps things remember hands longer than we admit. Its warmth lasted exactly the time it took for a name to cross a room.

Anahid, the knife said in a voice that was not a voice, that sounded like the exact friction of bone and metal. It was not a question. It was a greeting. It was a refrain.

I put the knife down so carefully that it did not clink, and then, because sometimes there is nothing else to do, I lay my palm over the honey’s lid and closed my eyes. I am not sure what I thought might happen. The fluorescent lights hummed. The upstairs conveyors, the ones that pretended to be rivers, clattered. A child screamed at a line. Someone kissed someone near a pretzel. The air held together its own mix of breath and the little aerosolized histories of everyone’s lunches. The honey, when I touched it, relaxed in its crate. And then it sang, not louder, but more itself.

Behind the label of the honey, under the paper where someone’s damp hand had lifted it and smoothed it again, there was another label. The old label was in a language that had been taught to me by my grandmother on an apartment couch that had given up on standing. She was eighty-nine and signed her name in letters that were all corners. She said the words were good to have for when the mail came, for when the radio said a name we recognized, for when the pots needed words the way dinners need salt. It had been years since I’d said any of those words to anyone except the woman upstairs at the halal grocery when she slipped me a bag of the good apricots merely because I had pronounced apricot like a woman who had peeled a thousand of them for other people.

The old label said: honey from the hills above our vanished town. It said it in a scissored, persistent script that reminded me of hands that stubbornly refused to become the language of a passport.

“How,” I whispered, which is a word both too large and too empty for most uses.

A man wheeled in a cart of confiscated meats, hovering in the doorway because meat had its own shelf and no one liked to rearrange shelves. Dot waved him like a woman directing a ship into harbor. “Right there, Rudy. I’ll change the tags. Make it quick or Mr. Escamilla will smell blood and call the disposal team.”

The electricity in the room stretched like a cat.

I cataloged. There is always a way to find refuge in a list. I entered weights, noted flights, signed my initials where the agency asked me to. The knife went under Weap—Small-Everyday, which was something the system created to keep it from thinking everything that could cut was a threat. The honey went under Liq—Food-Sweet. I added a note in the field for spoilage: “None.” In the comments I wrote: “Viscous. Clear.” There was nowhere to record a song.

That afternoon, a woman came down the service elevator with a hand to her throat, escorted by an agent who thought she might throw up. She was not authorized to be in the basement. We were not authorized to care. Her eyes were the kind of glass that breaks without sound. “A jar,” she said. “It was my mother’s, my mother kept bees in the city when no one would let her, she strained the first honey in a curtain and even the curtain was sweet, I didn’t know it was too much, I didn’t know we couldn’t, it’s a gift, can you—”

“I’m sorry,” said the agent, the way agents are taught to say a word hard enough that it will bruise. He had freckles on only one side of his nose as if he had once fallen asleep in the sun with half his face.

“Policies,” said Mr. Halprin, arriving with a brochure he kept for moments when lives needed pamphlets. He held himself like a man trying to prevent a train from rolling with nothing but the back of his sensible shoes.

“I know how to bury them in the ground so that the earth keeps them cold until spring,” the woman said, as if that were what we were refusing to let her do. “I know when to take their soup away and when to wrap their house.”

“We can donate it,” I said before I remembered the chart. The screen would not allow donation of anything home-canned or unsealed or past the point where two different labels indicated a transfer of ownership. It had been a long time since I had let my mouth run the red lights like that.

“We can’t donate,” said Halprin. He did not say cannot, as if to soften the directive with vowels. He showed her the brochure, where there was a picture of a smiling TSA agent handing a smiling man his belt, and beside it a graphic of a gallon of milk with an X over it, and a small child holding a teddy bear who looked as if he had learned very early not to attach too much of himself to anything that could be taken. “We dispose,” he said. “We’re not allowed to take custody of food of unknown origin.”

“It’s honey,” the woman said, as if honey were its own kind of passport. “It is not of unknown origin if I know it.” She was neither naive nor entitled; she was pleading in a way that knew how to make itself small without becoming voiceless.

“What flight?” I asked, and she looked at me as if I had offered her my hand from a dark roof.

“106 to Newark,” she said. “My mother is going into hospice. They said no food. They said she cannot taste anything. I thought—just a little on her tongue so that the last thing she tastes is what we kept alive.”

How we were supposed to be impartial, when people bring us the exact shape of longing that looks like our own?

“Policy,” said the agent again, and Dot said, “You want water, sweetheart?” and the woman shook her head and wiped her nose with the back of her hand. Her sleeve was grubby with travel.

In my mind, the honey was singing. Whether it was this jar or another I had not logged yet, the song had found its words: a low line about bees who returned regardless of winter, a high line about roofs that remembered footsteps, a counter-line of vapor that said slowly without consonants.

“You can write a letter,” Mr. Halprin said in his hopeful tone. “We have a form.”

We have so many forms. We have forms for redress, for complaint, for post-fact permissions, for item recovery which is rarely more than a gesture toward hope, for the illusion of process we offer in place of mercy. People collect these forms like kinds of rainfall.

The woman wrote, I believe you tried your best, which is the sentence people have learned to write to those of us who stand at the places where rules are enforced, because it is the sentence that keeps us from closing the door too quickly on our fingers.

The agent brought her back to the elevator. She looked at me the way people look at windows where they once lived. It was not a plea exactly, nor was it forgiveness. It was the recognition between people who know that customs are sometimes very old violence done up in flags and stamps.

After they left, Dot said, “Go on. Take five.” Her voice was marshmallow. “You got your 2:15 call.” It wasn’t a real thing. I did not have a 2:15 call. But Dot had made it up when she realized that sometimes the only way I could be human was to be allowed to call my mother at exactly the same time every day in case her heart needed a schedule.

I went up to the landing by the tarmac. The planes were lined like fish at a market, their stripes and names repeating, as if there were only six words for flight and we had run out of new combinations. My mother answered on the third ring. The third ring had been ours ever since the year that sirens took us too often and too near and we learned to measure safety in threes.

“Are you eating?” she asked, and then without waiting she said, “Do you hear the geese? They come early this year.”

“We don’t have geese. We have machines who pretend to be,” I said. “Mama,” I added, and then did not know how to say, I heard honey sing and it sounded like the way you used to stand with your hand on the kettle as if you were checking the heart of our building. “What does it mean if an object knows your name?”

“It means you have been touching too much. You know your asthma,” she said, and I laughed, the way daughters are allowed to laugh at mothers who try to cure everything with logic. “Names are not secrets,” she added, maybe to try to meet me where I stood, maybe to guard me from whatever trick my mind was trying to play. “They are coins. Other people spend them.”

I sat on the step and pressed my face into the sleeve of my sweater. I tasted last week’s laundry aroma, papery lemons and a false thing called Blue Sky. “Tell me again the thing about honey.”

“It keeps,” she said. “It will keep you if you let it.” She was silent for a moment, calculating whether whatever game I was playing with words would bring me more harm than joy. “You should come Sunday,” she added. “Mariam is bringing the boy and he is going to be taller than my sink and pretend he is not. I will make those little cookies you burn.”

“I never burn them,” I said.

“You forget them in the oven because you think you will remember without a timer because your grandmother remembered without a timer and we are not our grandmothers anymore,” she said. Her breath clicked, a hinge that needed oil. “Should I be careful? Is something there?”

“There is always something,” I said. “But you do not have to be scared of this one.”

When I went back down, the honey jar’s label had peeled itself another sliver. The under-label showed more. A little drawing of a hill. A line indicating distance, like the measure on an old map. A small star. I pressed the label back without thinking, as if to keep a skittish animal from running into traffic.

I stayed late under the lights that do not dim, finishing the logging for that day’s intake and then starting to cross-check the tally for Disposal. Items marked Expired or Unsafe or Perishable were to be destroyed in the evening, by a contracted truck that would arrive at a discreet hour, its driver whistling the kind of tune that belonged to men whose work is made easier by pretending they do not carry other people’s sweets to the dump. The Distribution list—what we could legally auction or donate—was shorter and shrinking as policy tightened toward an ideal of zero liability.

The longer I sat at my station between the lockers and the rolling cages and the shelves of things that would not be allowed to move forward, the more the particular voices of the day found their pitches. A bottle of cologne muttered to itself in Arabic about the kind of man who bought it. A snow globe told me of a girl who had turned it over and over in the gift shop while her father talked too loudly on his phone. A sealed plastic bag of soil, brown as bread, held steady silence that did not so much refuse to speak as keep a confidence given by someone who had dug it up in darkness. Make no mistake: I knew it was my own brain, layered by years of listening for the click where languages share a hinge. I knew also, with the same certainty, that my brain had not been making this kind of music until something changed. Change hums. It is not shy forever.

Thirty minutes before disposal, I unscrolled the day’s list. Honey, the list said. Note: break. That was the standard. Jars were to be broken to prevent reuse. Liquids poured into the bin. Bleach added to make all the world a uniform diluting.

It is not a crime to hesitate. I wrote: break at end.

A spill is a different kind of mortifying than a theft. If I had been the kind of person who broke things on purpose, my life would be different in ways I cannot imagine.

Dot collected her cardigan and her pocketbook and kissed the tip of two fingers and pressed them onto my forehead like a blessing she would not call a blessing because certain words did not fit us. “Home,” she declared. “Go. This place will be here when you come back.”

I waited. The men from Disposal were late, their truck slow or their route diverted by something aboveground—the protest I’d heard about on the radio at lunch, a slow-walking string of teachers with paper fish hung around their necks that said Save the River; or a man who had walked into the security line with his baby strapped to his chest and his hope like a sentence written in chalk; or simply the thickening of a day when everyone wanted to be somewhere else.

Alone in the aisle between Liquids and Small-Everyday I unscrewed the honey jar’s lid.

The first turn was glue-stuck. The second turn was easy. The air in the jar smelled like a place that had made a long promise. My thumb sticky where the rim kissed me. I did not tip it. I did not take anything. I only held it open to hear.

Sound broke over me the way warm water does when someone dips a bucket from the public fountain and pours it over your head. There was no language, there were languages. A woman laughed in the kitchen of a building whose corners had held through five owners. A boy recited the names of the streets he could go alone now that he was ten. Bees invented opinions about clovers. A man in a field sang to himself to keep his breath even as he lifted hives—there was effort in the way his voice sloped at the ends of lines. Somewhere, a bell told you what time it used to be when the world worked in time. And threaded through all of it, like a string through beads, my name the way my grandmother said it the night I mispronounced her lover’s name and turned one vowel into another and she had looked like a person who had found an old door in her house.

Anahid, the honey said, and as it did, a memory rose so distinct I almost reached for it with my hands. A river with a real curve. The bank under my bare feet grainy with bottle glass and the shells of things too small to be anything but hunger. My father lifting me by my armpits and setting me on a rock because the water had decided to forget itself that year and had reversed flow under the influence of a wind that had not been measured yet. “Watch,” he said in that voice you use when you give a child proof of magic or science. “Watch how even a river can change its mind.”

The honey said, They didn’t search the river.

I put the lid back on and for the second time that day acted as if I had not done something irreversible.

On my way out, I passed the bone-handled knife. Its maker’s mark gleamed like a tiny constellation that had become stuck in a sharp thing. I thought of how many women had peeled fruit with it, the way the edge separated skin from flesh with barely anything spilt. My hand reached before I could act the sensible person. I wrapped it in the paper I kept for breakables and slid it into the pocket where I kept my grocery list and my chapstick that tasted of something called Bora Bora.

At the doorway, I stopped and took it out and set it back on the table, my throat tight from the effort of being good. Then I broke the paper in half and wrote in the half I kept, in the smallest letters I could make: old name. river.

When I got home that evening, the apartment smelled like last night’s cumin and the kind of evening that has resigned itself to humid. The window above the sink refused, as always, to decide whether it was a thing for letting in air or a thing for keeping it out. The radiator pinged even in June, as if it was telling the story of a winter it had survived and suspected another.

I placed the paper with my two words in the drawer where I keep the corks and the rubber bands and the passports and the funeral cards. I closed the drawer. I leaned my forehead against the cool of the laminate.

Under all the crunch and drone and instruction of the airport, something had spoken with the calm of those who do not ask for permission to exist.

In bed, I fell asleep thinking of bees in a city, bees on a rooftop whose owner goes up in slippers to ask them, softly because bees understand weather and breath, to keep. I was very nearly asleep when the phone on my nightstand lit with a number I did not recognize. I did not answer. It swam into messages. The screen showed: a picture of a jar that looked like mine except it had a red ribbon. Then a single line of text, no name attached.

I heard it sing when you turned the lid, the message said. Bring it back. Or bring you.

The morning the city asked me to print your name, the river climbed into the gutters and the pigeons learned a sound like the hinge of a door that had not moved in years. I had oil on my hands and the ink was warming in its tin. The press was still asleep: the platen slack, the tympan curled like a tongue in an old mouth. A damp fog had crept down Alleyside, that confident sort of fog that has no intention of leaving.

I unlocked the front shutters and yanked on the cord until they rattled up, letting the morning in by increments. Behind me, the cases of type watched with their blind, reversed eyes. I said good morning to the O’s, which always seem surprised at themselves, and to the ampersand, asleep on its side. There is a particular chill that lives in a printshop even in summer; it lives in the slots between letters and the thumb-polished handles of the composing sticks. My father taught me to work with my sleeves rolled, even in winter, not to feed a press anything I couldn’t bear to have bitten off.

Lo & Daughters Printworks has had no daughter but me for thirty-six years. My father kept the name out of stubbornness, and after he died I kept it out of defiance. The window still says Lo & Daughters in gold leaf I touched up myself two springs ago, when my grief had grown a muscled back.

By eight, the city clerks were already heading up Mint Street with their briefcases like brick loaves. Forgettings always bloom early. There are mornings you can tell what sort of forgettings you’ll be printing before anyone walks in; the fog glows a shade of green when a teacher remembers every student but her own son, a faint lilac when twins wake up and only one of them knows the other. This morning was pewter. Pewter means the old. Pewter means a quiet sort of subtraction.

There is a way to make a Notice of Forgetting live. The law requires the posting, and the law’s language is as dry as the back of a stamp. But a good printer can thread mercy through serif and leading. I set the words in generous line spacing for wives forgotten after fifty years: let her name breathe. For brothers: tighten the letters until they hold each other up. For the loss of a child, I use the small type that looks like seeds.

The bell at Saint Vict’s tolled nine, then nine again. When bells repeat themselves in our city, it is to correct for the wind. Or God. People who pray here pray to windproof gods; you must.

I had one hand on the wheel when the door banged open and a man with a municipal pin on his lapel came in, his breath dragging fog behind him. He was one of the new ones. His face was familiar the way a bank note is. He took off his hat like who he took it off for was someone behind me.

Morning, Ms. Lo, he said. The office sent this one straight. Time is of the— he made a hand cut in the air, slicing invisible bread. —Time.

He slid a blue folder onto the counter. The folder was not the city blue, but something bolder, the color of the bottom of the swimming baths the one summer they drained them for repair and the city had no water to spare to fill them again. The color itself felt like pressure behind my eyes.

I wiped my fingers on the rag and opened the folder. The form inside wore the seal of the Office of Record and Correction, embossed so deep it made the paper pucker into the air. The lines were blank.

Is this a joke, I said.

He leaned in. His breath smelled of peppermint and an eager sleep. It’s coded, he said. Heat activates it. New policy for sensitive entries.

Sensitive. The word landed like a coin that didn’t belong in our currency. I could smell the paper—starch and something like cinnamon. It was thicker than the usual stock, too stiff for wheat paste and the rough stones we nailed notices into. The city does this sometimes: experiments in how the official word meets weather. Last year they sent a batch of water-resistant sheets that turned to lace anyway at the first rain. The notices bled polite apologies down the brick and smelled, disconcertingly, of pears.

Do you require these posted today?

By noon, he said. He spoke with the righteousness of someone personally aligned with noon.

I lifted the form. It was hot under my fingers already, as if my touch were a pocket I had been keeping it in. There was a faint thing like hair caught in the paper fibers—a thread from the shirt of the person who cut it, or the life of a plant that wasn’t certain it wanted to satisfy our need for squares.

I’ll see what sort of heat it wants, I said. I set it on the proofing table. The municipal man watched me with a poised attention that might have been politeness or fear.

You don’t have to stay, I said.

He started to protest and then swallowed the protest. I’ll be back in an hour, he said to the door.

When I am with paper I think better. It makes demands one cannot ignore. I lit the little alcohol lamp I keep for such problems and held the form over it, not so close as to scorch. The heat slid through the sheet, and I watched nothing happen for longer than felt reasonable. The nothing thickened. Then a color appeared at the top of the page the way bruise colors rise: yellowed letters seeping upward, shaping themselves into our city’s standard header.

Notice of Forgetting.

I have inked those words enough times to feel their weight even when my eyes are closed. As the rest of the text emerged, it was as if I watched a face I should have known learn its own name for the first time. Lines found their lines. The legal phrases took their positions with the fatigued dignity of old soldiers.

Citizen Formerly Retaining Memory: —

To Be Forgotten: —

Relationship: —

Effective Upon: immediate.

I waited for the names. Paper can hesitate; it has no obligation to us. A thinness came into the air, the way a room feels after laughter leaves. The first name resolved, letter by letter, with a carefulness that made me want to put a hand on the page to steady it.

Citizen Formerly Retaining Memory: Mara Lo.

For a heartbeat I saw another name—my mother’s perhaps, or a name that belonged to me when I was someone else. Paper does that. It can sheet all your possibilities as if misnames lay under your skin like a nest of fish. The name settled into the surface calmly, sibilants and thin vowels and the soft capital that begins mine.

I stood and leaned my hips back against the table to keep my body from thinking it should run. The dust in the corners of the shop retreated, as if the smallest particles available to me were careful to make space.

There are names that are possessed of a density, like a fist closed tight around some small treasure. Mine has always been the opposite: light, with room in the vowels to hide. I am a woman who has learned to put a weight behind that lightness, to swing the hammer of the press with my whole shoulder, to control the speed of ink on roller so that it does not spit. But I am not used to seeing myself in the place where other people’s losses begin.

I didn’t realize I was holding the paper closer until the warm made my face flush. The second line was slower to reveal itself. It stood up out of the blank like a person rising from a pew, uncertain if they’d been called.

To Be Forgotten: Please see attached designation, withheld pending clause six review.

No name. In the space where the city asks to be told who is to be put down like a misfiresome dog, there was only bureaucratic trickery and a clause. The clause was new to me. The clonking of the press metal on metal carried wrong from the back room, the way a child slams cabinet doors to test what can bear what sound, though no one had touched it. The forms talk to the press sometimes. Paper that arrives with a bell has a weight the frames feel.

I turned the page. Clipped behind it with a brass clip was a smaller slip: a thinner tissue, the sort we use for proofs, stamped with the seal of the city’s Legal Innovations division. It was opaque as milk.

Apply heat at point of delivery only, the slip said. This was its whole instruction. Beneath that, as if someone could not resist politeness, it added: Thank you for your discretion.

The last time the city had thanked me for anything it was because the dog had been alive when they came to retrieve it. The dog lay by my door for two days. He had the look of a thing that had come someplace specific to die. I set out water in case he changed his mind about the specifics, then called the office because if there is one thing we do here it is document, collect, and make a display of what hurts. The clerk sent a man who apologized to the dog and to me. He said someone would return to spray the stoop. He made the sign some people make in this city when they feel God noticing them.

I set the magic paper aside. If it wanted heat at point of delivery, then I would give it heat at point of delivery. It would be my hands doing the delivering; that would be a glitter of power I liked for about a second, then didn’t.

I first drew the feel of my mother’s hair braid when I was five. It was longer than my forearm. I remember this true as anything: how heavy a braid is. We rolled it into a button on the back of her head and stabbed through it with sticks we whittled from a broom. My mother bound flowers with raffia thin as her own patience and sold them under a blue umbrella in the market. She smelled like damp dirt and the sweet rot of things that choose despite us to live. She was what you might call a forgettable woman in a city that makes a business of forgetting. She made herself small in the way of those who have learned how much space costs.

By ten she was gone. Some days I think I remember the day she forgot me. Some days I think I only remember the day a woman with the same wrists as mine did not answer when I said mother. My father pretended I had never said it. He pushed the roller across the ink and the ink made a sound like shoes on wet steps. He said: mind the sorts, child.

I stopped the memory before it made a fool of me and set about the day’s work. Ink does not care for the drama of its deliverer. It wants warmth and it wants patience. It wants you to want nothing from it but what it can give.

The pewter thickened into the sort of gray that has weight. People came in with their hats and their early-morning forgettings, and I took the orders and wrote the specific names in the log. The log is a long book with a spine my shoulder has shaped to fit into the slit between it and my neck. It is the old leather, and it is always a little greasy. As a city we are unclean with our longing to name. It’s an oily living.

The first was a carpenter who had fallen asleep in his chair and woke to the smell of oak and no knowledge of the woman who had set his eggs on a plate waiting for him on the warm part of the stove. He brought his wedding certificate and a photograph of two people with their mouths open to catch thrown rice. I did not pretend to recognize the woman or the past. Do you know what you have lost, I asked instead. He turned the haberdasher’s hat in his hands like a bowl he was deciding to drink from or not.

They tell us to say that, the office. Do you know what you have lost seems like a cruel question until you hear the answers. Sometimes the knowing is worse. Sometimes the not knowing is a mercy. I write and set and print. I prefer my preachments to rise from ink to paper and join the rest of the world at eye level on the brick.

A mother came in with no coat and the dried crust of baker’s flour on the cuffs of her sleeves. She had a child on her hip and another attached to her knee. The new one’s hair stood up like a surprised field. She held a notice from three years ago, tattered and folded so many times the creases had become ridges. How do I reverse it, she asked me, holding it like a passport. How do I name him again. His name was Petru on the paper. It might still be.

We cannot reverse. We can only record. We can only ask whether a name has a back door and if so whether it will open for you. I gave her the petition form with the red stripe along the edge and lifted the forms in the drawer in search of the softer pencil. I keep the soft pencils for those who cannot push hard any longer. She held the paper the way people hold a sleeping cat they do not own.

By ten the line had bent and then unbent and the municipal man was back, the shape of his hat first, then the breath. I had his folder on the counter, closed. He set his hands on the wood as if expected to pray.

You can leave those sensitive attachments with me, I said. I’ll take them on the route. Less errand for you.

I should… he began, then let himself be made of less.

He had small bites taken out of his fingernails. They were half moons. Nail-biting is common among those in the Office of Record and Correction. There is always something to have undone.

The city does not require the printer to be the poster, but I have always liked the errands. My father sent me with a hammer and a pocket of tacks when I was small, and I learned to find the good wood beneath the plaster of the old buildings so the nails go in like a surrender instead of a squeal. I learned which walls take paper like water takes water. I learned where the wind makes its paths. Posting is the last part of the ritual that keeps this place calling itself a place. This is what I tell myself when my loneliness wants to be useful.

By noon, the fog had decided to keep to its origins and go lie down over the water. I bundled the notices with twine. Names. Dates. Instructions. I tucked the folder with its heat-hungry slip deep in my satchel where I keep my lunch and the wool in case evening says cold. Outside, the street sounded like a tongue trying to remember a tune. The bells kept up with themselves. A boy with a ladder walked past carrying a bag of nails like a prize.

I started at the corner of Mint and Third, where the old bakery still has blackened letters on its brick from before the fire in ‘04. A fresh blue notice requires the wall to give something of itself over to the word, and this place had been generous with its giving. I hammered and the hammer told me what wood lay beneath, and I tapped the paper into the building’s memory. The mother had asked how to reverse it. If you hammer long and sincerely enough into the city, you start to believe you can make anything go in and stay.

The second corner was the shoe repair, with its window display of married shoes and widow shoes. The man who owns it knows the names of all the old last shapes. He says the city once had feet that knew where to go. He says everything he says like just now matters. He watched me post Fernando Alvarez’s notice. To be forgotten: Mrs. Alvarez’s sister, who taught Fernando to sew on a button with a left hand. The forms make it clean. He came out and stood with his hand on his heart and called me daughter, which is what he calls all the women he thinks should look out for themselves better.

When I got to the wall opposite Saint Vict’s where the city keepers do not like us to post because they say it interferes with prayer, I always post there anyway because the church’s wall is one of the only walls left in the heart of the city that will take a nail without complaining. The saints and I have had words. I took the blue folder out of my bag. The slip lay above the form like the thin skin on soup. I could feel the intention of it before I even touched the flame to it. There is a violence in modern paper. It wants to be a witness.

It asked for heat at point of delivery. I am point of delivery. My hands. My eyes. The place where my pinched shoulder rests the log. The living ink that runs in my wrists. I lit the match and the sulfur smell came and went. I held the slip to the little blue orange of the flame. For a second nothing. And then the letters came up white on white like bones through skin.

To be forgotten, the line read. I read my name again above. We do not deserve to know this, the law had decided. In an avalanche of kindness, it had granted the comfort of ignorance. The white on white letters made their own light, a shy lit, like glowworms that do not know about sky.

Your name appeared. Not mine. Yours.

It is useful here to say that the name was not a thing I had ever heard said out loud. I had not written it in the log—at least, not that I knew. But I felt my hand know its shape. I felt my mouth move the letters like it had been speaking them in a house I do not live in. It was one of those names that carry a geography with them: a grain of northern sand, the clipped contraction of a language from before we were polite. The vowels were the kind that require you to open your throat. The consonants clipped their own shadows as if they would not be followed home. The skin on my arms decided to be understood. I said the name under my breath and it changed something about how the square of the street and the church made a right angle with each other. It made the angle a little larger, so you could walk through without touching.

Wind made a quick noise, the waiters at the cafe lifted their hands to save napkins, the bell fell into its next toll and corrected itself, then corrected its correction. The city, which had thought itself done with my mother, looked up.

I could have folded the slip and put it back. I could have stood there rehearsing the many ways to refuse what comes to your door with a blue seal and a hat. I could have decided the magic had failed, as all magic fails eventually in a town too practical to build a wall it does not intend to school you against. My fingers smiled at that plan. They are better than me at refusing to be lied to. I burned the edge a second time and watched the letters grow more legible. Your name sat there with its frown of meaning, and I heard in it my father’s voice on a late night, the ink rich and sticky, telling me a story about a boy who invented his own alphabet so he could be sure he was not understood. He said: language is a lock and a door at once.

Notice of Forgetting: Citizen Formerly Retaining Memory: Mara Lo. To be forgotten: [your name]. Relationship: unknown. Effective upon: immediate.

Unknown. I have rarely set the letters for unknown. They feel like a curse when you stick them in the composing stick, the k biting the u like correction. Unknown is a declaration that a space exists with no bridge over it. My father used to say there is no room in a good sentence for unknown. He knew nothing of the life sentences I would find myself composing.

I posted the rest of the blue slips slow, my eyes seeing nothing but the space where your name had sat. The corners of the paper curled the way thin hair does, acknowledging humidity and its own eventual end. Aunties pulled their carts along the sidewalk and did not notice me. A girl in a red jacket climbed the horse of the iron fountain and pretended that it was anything but iron. The city’s breath beat in and out. I have always trusted it to do this.

By the time I returned to the shop, the afternoon had snuck into the door ahead of me, thin and brassy. The municipal man was waiting, turned in profile to the window so he could practice an expression of concern upon his reflection. He achieved a sort of practiced sorrow that is taught in the office two floors above my shop, where young clerks learn to soften their mouths before delivering bad news, to widen the eyes slightly.

Well, he said when I set the empty folder on the counter.

It is done, I said.

He reached for the folder and then stopped himself, as if we had both remembered there were rules about touching. I placed the log between us and turned it toward me. We are not required to write our own names next to our own forgetting, not even in pencil. It is considered an unkindness to ourselves, to write your own name on a list like that. I opened the drawer and took out the soft pencil I was sparing.

Under Citizen Formerly Retaining Memory, I wrote my name anyway. It looked like a lie. Under To Be Forgotten, I left the line blank. My hand hovered. I was careful to put the tip of the pencil down, to show willing. The graphite made a dot so precise my father’s ghost would have been proud of the point. I was proud of it, who am alive.

Then I shut the book.

Ms. Lo? said the man, his voice pitched high in the range where worry lives.

I’ll need a plate, I said. Make ready for the run. The usual posts. And a few extra to be sure.

His mouth opened to say there was only the one, only the one, but the city doesn’t know itself. It believes in singularities. It forgets how forgettings multiply. He closed his mouth and nodded. When he left, he had his hat in his hand.

I washed my hands as if ink were a contaminant and not my work. The soap smelled like lemons that wanted to be wood. I looked up and for a second my father was standing at the table where the forms leaned toward each other like men at a bar, and when I blinked the trick of light learned better.

The press waited. The rollers waited. The frame of the room waited. I pulled on the chain to turn on the overhead lamp and the hum of it made a circle you could count your wishes with. I put my hand on the wheel and felt the cold like a fencepost after frost. I set the lines of type into the stick: Notice of Forgetting. Citizen Formerly Retaining Memory: I set my name and it rang a small bell in the bones of my wrist. To Be Forgotten: I did not set your name, because I did not have it, because the law is a complicated man who eats alone.

There used to be a rule when I was a child: we do not print what we do not see. If we cannot see it, we write it by hand. If we cannot write it, we say it to someone as the bell rings and trust that what is spoken under a bell cannot be entirely lost. I put the empty space in the composing stick where your name would go as if the absence itself were a character.

You learn over a life of letters that absence has heft. Paragraphs balance on it.

I inked the rollers. The ink had learned the day and stood up to be counted. I pulled the sheet and tucked it under the frisket and pulled the handle and the press leaned into the work like a creature teaching itself a language that requires you to push. The first impression came up clean: my name, the legal phrases, the space like a tooth gone. The city requires twenty copies. I ran twenty-five.

On the last copy, something shifted. The press made a noise I had only heard once, the year the great flood came as a whisper and then as a shout and people rolled the rugs and put the table legs in soup cans and hoped for manners. A shudder in the wood, as if the tree that had given itself to the frame decided to recall the flexibility of sap.

I lifted the sheet. Where the space had been there was now the faintest dark, the suggestion of letters like moss in the shape of a sentence on a stone. Not ink. Some other kind of pigment. Some other way of making the world visible. I held the paper up and walked it around the room to find where the light would lend it the most. On the back table in the corner where the window does not know how to be a window, in the narrow slice between shadow and the slant of the afternoon, your name appeared on my print.

The letters rose as the heat rose off the derelict radiator. It was the same white-on-white as on the slip, but this time the paper had something to do with it. The fibers drank the light and held it and gave it back through the shape of what I had not set. It was a trick. It was a cruelty. It was an answer. It was your name in my shop.

The first chapter ends lots of ways, my father used to say when he put a story in his mouth to see if it was ripe. Usually, he said, with an arrival or a departure. In the quiet, the shop held the even breath of the thing that knew it had been seen. I said your name again and the press shivered. Somewhere, three streets away, someone forgot the face of the person who had unbuttoned the top button of their collar every hot season for twenty years.

I laid the proof on the drying rack as if it were a skin. The letters hovered there a moment longer, then settled. The ink took its set. The absence learned the presence it was up against.

They came for the posters at two. I gave them the lot and kept back the proof, because some rules exist to say you are loyal to something besides a city. When they asked me if everything had gone as expected, I said it had, because expectation is a thing I have never been asked to print.

That night, as I shut the shop, the pigeons on the wires made the sound again. If you tilt your head, it is like a door translating itself from one hinge to another. I locked the shutter one lock at a time. I laced my boots. Out in the street, Saint Vict’s corrected itself twice before it believed what it was saying. And somewhere across the water, the fog took a breath like someone about to speak.

Chapter One

On low tide days the city remembers itself.

Steps return to meet the air—their edges furry with weed—doorways reclaim thresholds, balconies show their ribs. You can see the faded paint where shop names once were, blue letters licking out from barnacles: tobacco and starch, a pawned violin, a tea shop that became a welding place and then nothing at all. The water exhales, and in the slack between tides the drowned quarter, the Below, rises two or three palms, a breath, enough to make you think of ankles and the pale parts no one expects to see.

It is a day like that when my hammer finds the ring.

The hammer is not heavy and not made for striking; more like a tuning fork married to a moth. My father made it when I was eleven, showing me how sound is just a body deciding not to keep quiet. He made me close my eyes and strike the bell in our kitchen—just a clay bowl with a spoon would do—and said, Tell me where it hurts. I learned to hear what the brass refused to swallow. I learned to hear the seam where the bell holds a city’s throat.

There is no bell here, only water and silt. The house that hired me was a stilt thing: four rooms, iron mesh hung across the porch to keep egrets from nesting, a laundry line that never dries. They told me their grandmother had lost her ring last night. She’d taken it off to knead dough in salt water, as she had all her life, and the bowl teetered and the ring went over the porch and down between the planking with a small noise nobody could agree on afterward. She had been married fifty-eight years and didn’t sleep at all.

I am the sort of person the city calls when something falls into the Below. This is a job and also a faith. I have a license that says Municipal Recovery and Salvage, and a photograph where my hair looks grim, and red stamps from the Office of Claims. I carry my hammer in a wool sleeve like a saint’s bone. I go into things. I come up with other things that do not always match.

“Is that your mother?” I say to the man who hired me. He nods and doesn’t look at me. The old woman sits on a plastic chair with both hands pressed flat between her knees, as if the ring were that soft and could be kept from falling simply by the pressure of a life. Her palms are the color of tide.

“She says it is her duty to die with it on,” the man says. “She says my father will not greet her otherwise.”
