“That’s a very polite gatekeeper,” I say. He doesn’t smile. He looks like a man who has seen his house measured.

The slats between their porch boards let the day through. The water below is not blue but a greenish brown that reflects things wrong, as if shadows bloom here like algae and faces slur. There are blades of light between pilings. Something bright races in a dart and gone, the bony flash of a fish that has learned to be a key.

I tie my rope, not trusting their posts. I have done this enough to see where wood is still wood and where it is something else, softened to a pale sponge the color of an old tooth. The man watches but does not offer to hold the coil. Sometimes people blur with the city in my vision and their edges go the way of stone steps, softened by a thousand salt fingers. Then their voices are the only true parts of them.

“You’ll hear it?” the old woman asks. Her teeth are gold and very straight and hold the shine of the tide.

“If it wants to be found,” I say. “Not everything wants to be looked at.”

This is a lie, and it is also true.

The shock when my body gives up land is always the same. I never like it and I never stop seeking it. The water is cooler by a pinch than the air. It holds on. It is mouth and throat and grip. The first foot of water is a rash of thin plastic bags and shredded newspapers and the husks of drinks masquerading as shells. The second foot is calmer. The third has a current that wants me but not with anger: more like a sideways desire to escort. This canal has no one name, like some women in the city with many husbands. The Below has called it, through centuries, the Marble Lady’s drainage; the Eye’s Road; Annie’s Stitch; the duct just off Saint Tadeo’s. For me it is simply here. It holds my tinnitus and makes it a bell.

I take the hammer from where I’ve clipped it to my belt and tap the closest piling. The sound is in my head and my sternum, a small metal moth clapping. I move my ears with my shoulders and orient. Wood answers with dullness, a domestic no, a signature of eaten cellulose. There is also the high, nickel chime of a bolt, the slow breath of rope catching, the huff of air from somewhere that is trying to get out.

There is a language in this. My father heard vowels, he said. He could tell you, without looking, if a bell had a crack, if it was old enough to remember smoke, if it had rung after midnight. He could tell if a person had lied beside it. He could tell how many people had stood under that bell with scarves over their mouths while men at the back lit torches. He called his work listening for the size of a lie.

I find the ring against a barnacled joist just where the tide has been licking it for a generation. It has found itself a notch and sits there like a pupil. Rings like to find their size again; they like to measure themselves against the world. This one is small and yellow and set with a sickle of diamonds that are already teaching themselves how to keep salt out of their hearts.

I take it between two fingers and pull. It resists briefly, because everything here resists, and then it is in my hand, and somebody’s whole marriage is on my palm, catching the meager daylight as if it had won it from something and didn’t want anyone to know.

I surface. The old woman’s face is there, too close, at the floor of the porch. Water has made her eyelashes point.

“Your husband might prefer you as you are,” I say, offering the ring. She presses it to her tongue and then her forehead and, at the last minute, her little green vein that flutters above her eye.

“God is not that flexible,” she says. She slides the ring on, grinding it a little over a knuckle that has changed shape since she was sixteen. The metal hesitates and then remembers.

The man pays me too much and I try to give some back. He insists with his eyes. The money is damp from being held in a pocket. My palms leave the railing and pick up splinters. A white bird watches from the tamarind tree, as if it is practicing reincarnation.

“How do you hear that?” the old woman asks me, as if she wants to tell someone else later. I could say practice or attention or the way the underwater city speaks right into your bones if you offer them. I could say that metals ring more true down here. I could tell her that most of the time the object that wants to be found is not the thing I was hired for and that I know, within a footfall, where somebody hid their better life. I could tell her that sometimes the city flings up a whole rung of stairs between laughs and then shrugs and sinks back down.

“Everything has a note,” I say instead. “Even what is lost. You listen for what you already love.”

After, I coil my rope and walk home along the northern plank road, where the skin of the water strikes its random light onto the undersides of houses and makes them look like priested fish. The road is narrow enough that you and whoever comes the other way have to decide whose shoulder is saltier. Buckets knock knees. Dogs lick at my boots and children have a sport of asking whether I will retrieve a thing for them that they either never owned or have not lost.

“The moon fell in the canal,” a boy says, holding his face calm. “Can you bring it up for me?”

“Everyone’s always dropping the moon,” I say. “If I find yours I’ll tie it to your bed.”

“My bed is on a roof,” he says. “So it can see.”

This could be the whole city talking.

The slick of the Below has reached farther in the last couple of years. There are new houses on pilings, and the old houses in the dry quarter, the Above, are painted a smart, better shade of white as if they are receding or performing death. There are fences that make noises when you touch them, as if an animal lives in their wires. The Office of Claims has grown noisier, and the men who work there wear yellow slickers even in sun.

It is only after I hang my coil in the shed and put my hammer back on its pegs and lay my money to dry that I see him. He is sitting on the low wall outside my gate with his hands in his pockets and his chin tipped down as if he is apologizing to the road. His raincoat—I look carefully, because all raincoats in this city carry a message—is the wrong color. It is a municipal yellow, yes, but dulled, almost mustard, the color of a flag that has seen years. Also it is too long in the arms. He wears a hat that he takes off when he sees me, revealing hair that would like to curl but has been told not to. He is younger than me by maybe a decade and he is trying not to look at my hammer.

“Mira Sola?” he says. “Mira Sola, of Municipal Recovery.”

“On good days,” I say. I have a cut on my ankle that is saying hello.

He stands, not tall, not short. Not expensive. He smells of the Office. Ink, mold, rain soap. It is a smell I used to think meant civic parenthood and now think means fear of shadows from above leaning over paper.

“My name is Idris,” he says. “I am not here from Claims.”

“No?” I say, because he is.

“I work for the Conservatory of Measures,” he says, as if that will cover for what he isn’t. “I am attached to the Archive of Soundings.”

“You people with your little rooms,” I say. “I thought the Archive of Soundings was dissolved in the flood year. They said the city could not afford to keep old noises.”

He looks offended culture-deep. “Noise is a word that makes a cathedral of itself and then locks the side door,” he says. “We keep what we can.”

Somewhere, a boat hits a wharf and shivers.

“I don’t have anything for you,” I say, because this is almost always true. What I have is on my pegs or drying in the sun with clothespins biting it.

“We don’t want what you have,” he says. “We want you to get something. We hope it is something you would want to get.”

In another life, before the Below, before the water came up and contradicted the planners, I would have closed my gate and let my dog bark and sat at my table with my father and said, There is a man from somewhere and he wants to hire me and we would have laughed until the small ceramic horse on our mantel looked down his nose at us. In this life, my father is not someone I sit with. In this life, the horse has been fetched. It came up with a spoon in its mouth and a ribbon of hair pressed to its thigh.

“What sort of thing,” I say carefully, “does the Archive of Soundings want a person like me to fish?”

His eyes flick to my hammer. It takes work not to say, sir, respect yourself and do not look at my tools like that.

“A bell,” he says, not whispering but aligning his voice with the part of the air where whispers live longer. “We need you to bring up a bell.”

I feel the inside of my mouth go cold. I take it out on my shoes by pushing my toes into the end of them. Bells, in this city, are not simple.

“I do not do churches,” I say, easily. “There are people who specialize. They like making the sign in the water. They wear little necklaces. I’m not good company for that.”

“It’s not a church, mainly,” he says. “It’s the bell at Saint Tadeo’s, not the big one, the—”

“I know what’s under Saint Tadeo,” I say, and I do. The steps of that church were the last thing, they said. I was there the day the baptismal font went under, cradled like a child by its own water. Saint Tadeo could not agree with the idea of surrender, and so the Below took her in parts, over months. One morning her west aisle folded like a paper boat. One afternoon the sacristy exhaled. The big bell, the one that had a name—there are always two bells in this city: the one with a name and the one that holds the name in its mouth—the big bell was crumbed by salt years ago, my father said. He told me we do not touch bells unless we are invited by more than one thing.

“The marrow bell,” Idris says, and then stops as if tasting the fact. “We are told it’s still in its yoke. We are told it will be navigable at next fortnight’s low.”

“Who told you?” I say, but I know he will not say.

“People who listen,” he says instead, which is either flattery or a stupidity.

“You walk into my yard wearing the city’s coat,” I say, “and tell me your office needs a bell from Saint Tadeo, the marrow bell of Saint Tadeo, which everyone pretends not to believe has collected the last voices of what happened there, and you don’t think you will leave with a sore ear.”

“What happened there,” he says, very gently, “happened many places. But the bell at Saint Tadeo did ring after midnight. It was rung without permission by hands that were not on the list. It—” He picks his way. “You know how bronze holds its sufferings.”

“Bronze holds what you strike into it,” I say, and my arm thinks of my father’s hammer, a different heft, and the way he would say, Listen, it is still saying no, and then strike again with his whole heart.

“We want to catalogue the sound the bell refuses to lose,” he says. “We want to bring it into a room and make a record that cannot be argued by water. We want, in short, to keep what is going to be taken.”

“Why me,” I say, though I could list the reasons he would list.

He looks at my house. It is a house that looks like a person who has been told to leave and refuses to care that she will be told again tomorrow.

“You go under what other people won’t,” he says. “You don’t steal from your pockets. You hear.”

Something in my chest chooses that moment to remember my father’s laugh. It was not a kind noise. He laughed like he had paid for it in blood.

I say, because I can’t not, “You found me because my father wrote his name on paper for your office once.”

“I found you because the man at Fabrications two streets over said you have hands that do not lie,” he says, surprising me. “Because seven people used your name in their sentences when I asked whoever would keep me in the shade for a minute which person in this city hears the Below like a person.”

“And because my father worked on the bells,” I say, and Idris nods, once, not happily. My father was not gentle with the city, and the city was not gentle with him. Women with many keys came to our door once, twice, four times. There is a day I cannot hear properly when I think of it because of the blood in the water and because a bell will sometimes carry for only so long and then it refuses.

“What do you pay,” I say, to be cruel.

He names a number I pretend is smaller than the one in my head.

“Half up front,” I say. “Half when I give you a bell. I say when. If I do not like the day, if the currents are singing what I refuse to sing with, we try again later. You do not tell anyone who is not in your office where you are putting this bell. You do not write my name down in any other ledger except the one where you pay me. If we do this, you hire no one else for this task. If you hire someone else without telling me, the water will eat your bell back up.”

“Who are you threatening,” he says in wonder, as if I have turned into someone with a history that hasn’t been printed yet. His hat looks like a living animal in his hands.

“Everyone,” I say.

He nods as if that’s fair. “We can do those terms,” he says. “But I think you are underestimating the number of people who want that bell. There is a collection of men who wear clean shoes and talk about urban clarity who want to call it an unlawful object and sink it deeper. There are people, also, who light candles for saints that don’t like candles, who want to ring it again in daylight and say that if anyone didn’t hear it properly that night, now they can. There is a woman with a soft voice who says the bell belongs to people with the same last name as a boy who drowned two streets from here. There are the men with the little rooms.”

“And your office,” I say. “Where would you put it.”

He looks at the road. “In a room that doesn’t admit water,” he says. “We will hit it with a padded mallet and listen with fifty mouths. We will write the sound onto lacquer. We will make numbers of it. We will put it in a place where a person can come and put their head against it and hear what the Below says when it’s asked to remember without malice.”

The wind from the canal brings a sweet, rot smell. My amaryllis, which I have not loved, opens itself six inches of red.

“I know what bells do,” I say. “I know what people make bells do. I know they are innocent until named.”

“Marrow bell,” he says softly, as if he is stroking around the bruise of it.

I turn, because the sun has set its mind on going behind Saint Tadeo’s little iron cross that remains above water like a needle angry with sky. I do not look at the cross. I look instead at the laundry line that is not mine but is always there, six streets away, where a woman hangs white shirts for a husband who has been gone for years. They stand in the air as if they are not allowed to fall.

“You have a way to pull it,” I say finally. “A cradle, something that won’t tear the mouth.”

“We have a rig,” he says quickly. “We have a quiet barge. We have climbers and ropes of silk. We can take your instructions. We have a little priest if it comes to that.”

“If it comes to that,” I say, my tongue thick. “You bring him to my door first.”

When he goes to write something down, I put my hand through his page with a finger. “No more ledgers,” I say. “My name lives where it lives.”

He tucks his little pencil away as if it is a bird he doesn’t want to wake. “Do you,” he says, not looking at me now, “hear your father? When you go under, do you hear him? They say he went down at Saint Tadeo, but they also say lots of other places.”

“I don’t hear what I would like to hear,” I say. “I hear what holds.”

“I would like to pay you the first half now,” he says. He reaches inside his coat slow, like a person at a parade who knows there are thieves. The bills he hands me are crisp. They smell like rooms where paper sleeps.

“Come at night,” I say, after a moment that aches. “No boat at midday. No silk. No barge. Not at first. Just you and one other and a coil that has been washed. I will show you where the city breathes in there. If the keel of your quiet barge scrapes what I hate, I will leave you holding a lot of silk and a prayer book.”

“I’m not religious,” he says, and looks immediately like a man who will apologize to a river.

“The Below is,” I say.

He hesitates in my gate, as if it is a mouth, and then steps out into the public light. Two boys with a crate between them go by and look like a two-headed animal. He puts his hat on with both hands. “Mira Sola,” he says to the road, and then, to me, “We will not write your name. But we will remember you. We will remember.”

When he is gone, I stand awhile to listen to the city remember itself. The tide is not at its lowest yet; the steps at Saint Tadeo’s are a chain of bones with clam-mouths at every link. You can make a map by listening to what refuses to stop ringing. Some days I think, if I collect all the sounds that should not be allowed to slip, I will have a whole person, and that person will come up the steps with sweet hair and say, I was below when you thought I was in your house and forgive me, it was so loud.

I go inside. My dog looks like a piece of rope with two eyes and follows me to the table. I pour tea that tastes like a clean nail. I rub oil into the handle of my hammer, the way my father did, ignoring the parts of me that reach for a belt I can no longer wear. At the edge of the shelf, the ceramic horse tilts his painted head so slightly I cannot tell if it is a trick of sinking, his glazed hooves polished by salt.

When the city remembers itself, it remembers the names we gave the bells. There was Lucia, who cracked her mouth during a storm and went on singing as if a person had just told her she was no longer a person. There was Passenger, who was rung during births and made the men outside reach up and hold the doorframe like a ship. There was the unnamed bell of Saint Tadeo that the old men called the marrow bell because it wasn’t for festivals or fires but for the day the city had to pull something out from inside itself with both hands.

At night, the Below is as black as the inside of a bell. When you put your head into it, the sound is yours, and you get to choose whether that feels like luck or debt.

Chapter One: The Lilac Theft

On the morning they came for the lilac, the city smelled like nothing, which is to say it smelled like itself—cleaned to a sheen you can’t quite polish, a blank that throws back everything you hang on it.

I was installing the new labels in Gallery C—“What We Called Spring”—because the previous donor insisted on a comma he had forgotten in 2003 and now wanted to place between rain and dirt, and I, as always, obliged the dead and the living alike. The jar that held the lilac’s description—twelve pages folded into a glass cone, a lozenge of careful handwriting and my mother’s map in pencil—was already centered beneath the light. People came in just to stand before it, to thumb their nose unconsciously as if their bodies could pull something through, to read the words and chase the ghost of a chemical that isn’t there anymore.

The pair stepped inside when the door chimed. It was early, and the city hadn’t yet baked the reflected heat into a hum that would drive the neighborhood children into our air-conditioning for the afternoon. The man wore the kind of yellow construction vest that had become a fashionable signal of sincerity, as if fluorescent tape could make your presence infrastructure. The girl was twelve at most, narrow as a blade, sleeves turned up, eyes that looked like they’d swallowed a horizon and were still hungry. They walked the way people do when they’ve practiced invisibility at home and found it doesn’t work outdoors—too careful, which makes other people look up.

“Welcome to the Museum of Olfactory Memory,” I said, out of habit, out of the kind of politeness bred into people who guard the last of something. I put down the comma and the glue. “Admission is suggested.”

“We’re not staying long,” the man said. It came out like apology and defiance both, that tone people learn when they’ve been told too often that they are using something that doesn’t belong to them—air, space, sunlight. He kept a hand on the girl’s shoulder, guiding her with a pressure that wasn’t rough but was relentless.

They could have been father and daughter, but there are bonds that only resemble others and that’s enough in a museum. The girl had a Band-Aid on her elbow, the cheap kind that peels up at the edges in heat. She scanned the room and then she looked up at the main pedestal.

Lilac, Northampton, May 1996, the placard read. Donor: B. P., who had brought us the smell when my mother was still calling everything by its proper name and correcting everyone who wasn’t. There is a long, complicated way to talk about what is in that cone—language pinned like butterflies in a shadowbox, careful notations, what we call the map: the way to get from one thing to another. There is also the short way, which is to say: my mother taught me that smells were not single points but constellations, and if you traced them, you could get home.

“Is that the one?” the man asked, not looking at me.

The girl didn’t nod. She didn’t breathe. She stood on the marble circle in front of the pedestal and fixed her gaze on the paper inside as if she could push through glass and years with the force of want. It took me too long to see the shape of it.

“We don’t keep any actual lilac here,” I said. I say that to everyone with an ache in their mouth. There is always someone who believes the rumors—that we have a freezer of preserved fragrance, that we’ve hoarded the last molecules, that if you break the right jar the room will flood with a chemical that can save you from what happened. “These are descriptions. Scores. Memory, not matter.”

He flinched, as if the word memory were a weapon. “Then what good is it?” His hand tightened on the girl’s shoulder, and she made no move to shrug it off.

“It’s as good as you can get,” I said, and then I wished I hadn’t said it, because there are so few sentences we can say without sounding like we chose what was taken from us.

He moved in a circle around the pedestal, like he was measuring the best approach to lift the glass. Our cases are heavy; the donors want us to guard their grief with lead. He put his fingers at the edge and lifted anyway. The suction undid itself with a complaint of rubber. He had some strength in his shoulders. He was shaking.

“Sir,” I said. “Please don’t.”

“You have cameras,” he said, as if that evaporated any human obligation. “You can call someone to stop me. Maybe they’ll get here in time. Maybe not.”

“Is there someone I should call instead?” I said, because this is not a museum so much as a confessional. People come here to say what they’ve lost out loud, and sometimes I can answer and sometimes my answer is a hand on their sleeve so that they don’t have to puzzle out touch in a world where one whole category of touch is gone.

He lifted the case. He lowered it onto the marble floor with more care than he had shown in lifting it. He reached for the cone inside, fingers gone precise now, and I understood that I was not going to forbid him successfully. You can tell when people have done something like this before; you see the rehearsed hands.

“Dad,” the girl said. Just that. It was enough to pause him, a word thin as rice paper and carrying more weight than the glass.

He looked at me then, fully, as if I had become suddenly the person with the lever. He had a cap pulled low; he tipped his head and I saw the architecture of tired that frames a person who has not slept because sleep steals time and he cannot spare it.

“People will give me good money for the lilac,” he said. He didn’t put threat into it; he stated a fact he hated. “But that’s not why.” He swallowed. “She can smell it.”

I have been told all kinds of things in that room: that the museum is a fraud, that the museum is sorcery, that we are doing a good job, that we should burn our archive and seed it into the air. That last suggestion came from my mother, but only in the months when her mind was made of fog.

“She can smell,” I said carefully, because there is a way to say a thing that will make it lie down and show you its belly, and there’s a way to say it that will make it bolt.

“Sometimes,” he said. His eyes flicked toward the door and then back to me, a quick, practiced sweep. “Not food. Not danger. God help me, not danger. But flowers. Soap. The top of her head after she’s been out in the sun.” He pushed a finger against his lower lip, caught himself, dropped his hand. “They’ll take her if they know.”

“Who is they,” I said, although I could make a list.

“The same people who took your mother,” he said, and then he startled, as if he had said too much. “Not took,” he corrected. “Claimed. Used.”

My mother went into the Ash Year with a temper and an archive and came out with a scar in the shape of her name. She wore a hospital bracelet that said subject instead of patient. She coughed into a stainless-steel bowl and said: they’re trying to map us like we map odors, love, but we are not a smell. She died on a day the sky was the wrong color and the city as a whole agreed not to name it. There are three photos of her on our donor wall and all of them lie.

“Come with me,” I said, because some imperatives arrive uninvited. I stepped around the pedestal and I put my hand on the glass cone. The girl watched my fingers as if she were ready to memorize the sequence of my bones.

The case had been made in the era of craft, which is to say it had been made to last through flood and apathy. The pages inside were my mother’s chart: a topographical map of something that can’t be contained in elevation lines. She has written: lilac is made of first-day-of-Vacation shampoo and the throat of a life jacket and the wet tongue of a dog you held before it shook off the rain. She has written: green’s sweet beginning and an old book when you turn the last page. She has written: the way your grandmother’s dress smelled when she hugged you too long in the dark.

It is a dishonest description because it is not universal, but that is the point. Memory is the only democracy that gets worse when it scales.

“Don’t,” the man said, when he saw me lift the cone. He said it like a plea.

“We can’t move it,” I said. “Not now, not like this. We can’t break it open or it breaks. Come with me.”

I led them through the swinging door to the back galleries. The wall there is a color that was called eggshell in a world where eggs used to vary and we thought their variety was a sign of something else as well. We passed §B-16: Hinge Grease, 1971; §K-04: Kerosene, Night; §P-09: Peaches, Canned; and the girl touched the glass of the peach display the way a thirsty person touches a photograph of water.

“People found this funny once,” I said, because the chatter that keeps the wolves away had come up in me, a thin ribbon of words I don’t fully authorize. “An apple on a teacher’s desk. The smell of rain on a sidewalk has a word and isn’t that clever? Petrichor,” I said, and the word collapsed in front of us, a house someone never finished building. “Smells were small then. Now we are all children standing on our toes with our chins on the edge of the sink.”

The man said, “They’re outside.” He didn’t move his head; he doesn’t need eyes in his face to see. I heard it too then, the slow tide of a van idling, then the door. There are two kinds of silence in the city now: the expectant silence and the resigned. This was the first kind.

“Who is your contact?” I asked him. “If you’re selling to the wrong people, you’ll never see her again.”

“I’m not selling her,” he said, and his hands came up, palms out, as if I had accused him of bartering organs. “I’m selling the paper.” He looked at the cone cradled in my arms, at the way I held it like a child. He laughed, short and hard and desperate. “Listen to me. I don’t know how to keep her. Do you?”

The girl reached out. She put her hand on the glass of a case labeled §D-02: Death. People bring in the weird parts. We don’t keep the obvious; we don’t keep rot because it’s power we can’t touch and because there are legalities. We keep the lace at the edge—candlewax that stuck to a pew, the sour of the dress you forgot to wash before you wore it to the cemetery.

She closed her eyes. “It feels like this room remembers me,” she said, and a pulse went through me. Her voice had the precise, untested gravity of someone who has never been listened to and is finally listening to herself.

“What does it smell like?” I said, my voice raw as paper.

She hesitated. She hates to give anything away. Then: “That thing when you bite your lip and it bleeds, but only a little, and you press your mouth together and tell no one.” She opened her eyes. They were detailing the ceiling, counting the heads of screws. “And warm pennies in your hand from the fair ride. And… grass that is wrong. Like it was watered with tea.”

The fair ride. The pennies. The tea. That was lilac—hers, not mine, and the way it latched onto my mother’s map without matching it made something in me stand and walk toward her without my body moving.

“How often,” I asked. “Does it come and go?”

“When I earn it,” she said, and her father made a strangled noise.

“There are people who would say you were a miracle,” I said, because I have never learned to hold my tongue at the exact right time. “And there are more who would say you were a resource.”

“I know,” she said. “That’s why I don’t talk much.”

“You brought her here,” I said to him. Not accusation. Observation, which is sometimes worse.

“I thought—” he began. He took his cap off. His hair was in the style of apocalypse: cut short because long hair carries too many tasks. “I thought this was a place that knew how to keep things safe.”

“It is,” I said. “But we don’t keep people. We keep their breath.”

The van door slammed. There were footsteps that understood that every force has an equal and opposite reaction. The front chime rang, the polite ding that makes anything seem like commerce. The day I hired a person to sit at the desk downstairs and say we’re closed, come back later, sincerely, that was the day I decided the museum was a building separate from my own body. It was a fantasy; the museum is my lungs.

“They’re not the state,” he said. “Worse.”

He had a piece of paper in his pocket. He took it out with the reluctance of someone who knows that an object is also a confession. It was a flyer printed on thin stock, off center: CALYX CHILDREN. SEEKING, he read aloud. The rest of the words were hidden under his palm. He lifted it as if it weighed more than the glass cone in my hands. FOR STUDY, the flyer said. FOR SALVATION, it added in a different font, a font that has always lied for the church and now lies for the science that took its place. There was a number and a promise and a picture of a photograph of a girl’s hand touching a petal. The picture had been taken from our website.

“If you have one,” he said, his voice gone wry, as if we were in on a joke together that would end us both, “they want to help.”

Of course they do. They, who had taken my mother’s ease and returned it to me in a box with a bow.

“Come,” I said. “Through the stacks.”

We went into the part of the museum we never show. The building used to be an ice factory, and there are rooms that hold cold as a language. We pass shelves where we keep the overflow, the scores we’ve not yet cataloged: §B-01: Bread, Burned; §N-08: Newsprint; §H-03: Hair, Wet. There is a smell that accompanies paper, a not-smell now; I do not reach for it but it rises in me like a friend you don’t trust but love anyway. The girl skimmed her hand along the boxes without touching, a gesture of priesthood.

“This is where we keep it,” I said, and I wanted to laugh, because keep is a plot we tell ourselves so we can stay in one place long enough to lift a thing and name it.

There is a door in the back that looks like it leads to the alley but opens into what my mother called the Library of Air. It is a room the architects left when they were translating cold into commerce. It’s lined with drawers. Each drawer is lined with felt. In each felt nest is a jar. In each jar is a folded sheet, a calculus of wanting. My mother named them like hurricanes: she gave each new smell a person’s name, pompous and kind, a way to pretend that what we built here had a lineage it could claim. I’ve tried to stop that; I believe there is something loaded about names.

“Hide,” I said. “In §M.” It was an old joke. M for Mildew. M for Mother. She shoved it open, slipped behind the drawers. She is a creature designed to fit into spaces there isn’t yet a word for. The man hesitated, looked at the door, looked at me.

“If you betray us,” he said softly, already unable to stand his own tenderness. “If you do anything that is not what you just did—if you do anything that I’m afraid you did—then I will—”

“What?” I said, and I handed him the cone of lilac because sometimes you give someone the one thing you cannot replace in order to distract them from the thing you are about to do.

He went still with it in both hands. He looked up. I wondered what he saw in my face that made him lower the cone to his knees like a viol and tip his head and whisper a thank you nobody heard.

The footsteps came down the hall, deliberate. “Hello?” a man called, his voice trying on different shapes. “We had an appointment. We spoke with your assistant.”

I do not have an assistant. I have a sixteen-year-old who sits at the desk because she loves the sound of the door chime and the power of saying no. I closed the Library door and stood in front of it as if I were a piece of furniture.

The man in the yellow vest handed me the cone. He stood up. He stood off to the side, and I recognized in him the learned performance of harmlessness. It is a skill for our age, like archery was for others.

I stepped back into Gallery C, carrying the lilac as if it were an infant being brought to the window to see snow for the first time. The men in the foyer wore the new uniform: plain clothes, expensive shoes, a badge that looks like graph paper. They looked past me but not through me, as if the building were a lingering person in their way.

“We’re closed,” I said.

“That’s funny,” one said, because there is an economy of laughable in this world, and people like him spend it like coins. “We’re not.”

“What are you here to see?” I asked. I slid the cone into the case without looking down. My hands know the weight of our losses too well.

“We received a tip,” he said. “That you had a new acquisition.” He smiled like a man who has always been allowed to use the word acquisition by people with keys.

“We don’t accept new donors without a waiting period,” I said. “If you’d like to fill out a form—”

“Talia,” the other said, reading my name off a plaque near the donor wall. There is a warmth in hearing your own name used as a lever. He tilted his head. “The world is turning in your hands. Don’t you want to be part of where it goes?”

I thought of my mother’s hands, which were large, the bones like reeds, how she gripped mine the night the fires came, how she said: smell the world, now. How I did, for the last time, like inhaling a tidal pool, the iodine and rot and bright: how I thought the world would always be this specific. I thought of the girl behind the door, her lip-rid blood, her pennies, her wrong grass. I thought of how many children have been left at the door of places that promised to keep them and taught them instead to imagine the smell of their own fear.

“There is no new acquisition,” I said.

“Then you won’t mind if we look.”

“You don’t have a warrant,” I said. “You don’t have cause. This is a museum.”

“This is a storage unit for grief,” he said, and for a second I liked him for saying the truth aloud. “And grief has a way of getting in the way of progress.”

He stepped toward the back. I stepped into his path. Behind me, I could hear the girl breathing, only because I know what trying not to breathe sounds like. It is one of my cataloged sounds. It goes with §N-05: Night Sweat.

“My mother built this place,” I said, and the words left my mouth with a solidity I had never granted them. “You can have progress, or you can have a map.”

The man’s face rearranged itself into patience. He glanced at his partner. They could, at any moment, brush past me. They weren’t afraid of the law. They were afraid of looking like the kind of men who push women aside in museums. They have consultants who advise them about optics.

“Don’t be the last person who believes you can hold what was always air,” he said, and if he had not been the person saying it, I might have put it on the wall.

There was a sound from the back. Barely. The scrape, very small, of drawer felt against glass. I spun my sentences around my mouth and looked for one that could go to war.

“If you turn around and leave now,” I said, “I will let you come back during business hours and buy a family membership. If you don’t, I will tell the press that you attempted to kidnap a child in my care.”

“You don’t have a child,” he said smoothly.

“Exactly,” I said.

For a second nobody moved. The morning outside stacked itself into layers: the street vendor’s radio, the van idling, the pigeons trying to remember who they were before they ate our hunger every day in crusts. The world smelled like nothing, the way a room smells after the argument has ended and before anyone starts to clean. In that space, the first absence is a beam of light.

The men glanced at each other again and performed the calculation of trouble. The one with the badge shaped like math said, “We’ll be back.”

I said, “I’ll still be here,” because I am built of stalling tactics and the belief that if you can move the present by an inch, the past will follow it.

They left. The chime did its little routine. The van door closed like a hand. The engine’s hum took itself down the street.

I sat on the velvet stool in Gallery C and put my head in my hands and breathed the big empty air that passes for normal now. The man in the yellow vest came out from behind the door. His face broke in half. He laughed and then shoved his fist against his mouth to stop.

“We can’t stay,” he said, even as his body asked me to make him wrong.

“We can’t,” I said. “But we can decide where to put this minute.”

“Where do you put it?” he asked.

I held up the cone of lilac. I set it on the pedestal. I placed the rubber seal along the glass and pressed. The case made the small, obscene kiss it makes when I do it right.

“Here,” I said. “For now.” Then I went back to the Library to find the girl in §M, and when she looked up, when she smelled me like a question and said, “You’re not like them,” the world tilted. Not toward salvation. Toward something smaller and more survivable. Toward a ledger my mother started and I, despite everything, am still adding to, carefully, in pencil, with the belief that paper can hold a promise until someone arrives who can make it true.

Chapter One

The last sounds a machine makes don’t come from its mouth, if it had one. They retire into the narrow places: the teeth of the gears, the hollows of the casing, the seam where the screw threads bite. You have to put your ear to it. You have to let the cold of it soak your skin. You have to be willing to hear a thing that doesn’t know you’re listening.

My father taught me that the summer before he died. He was crouched on a milk crate, his bad knee untwisted as if he had tricked it out of pain. He held a small motor in two hands the way people in church hold their prayer books. “They don’t stop,” he said, his voice with its sea-grit rasp. “They gather themselves somewhere else. Like water.” He tilted the motor so the light from the high window slid along its ribs. “If you don’t listen to the last of it, you leave it alone in there. You wouldn’t like that.”

Our shop is the last one before the river turns ugly. That’s what my mother says. Our door faces Cloister Street, which once led to monastic gardens and now leads to a salvage lot guarded by two dogs with arthritis. The river used to be lined with glassworks and bottlers, then with garages and small factories, and then with nothing but the slow collapse of brick and the new spines of condominiums rising like a cassette player ejecting in reverse. There’s always the smell of metal, even in winter. If you stand long enough, your mouth fills with the taste of pennies.

Our sign is older than the truths in this neighborhood: Esteves & Daughter, Ceremonies for Departed Machines. The paint on “Daughter” is brighter. My mother found the brush and wrote the word with both hands the day after the hospital turned off its machines.

People don’t believe in us until their own machines are carried away. They think it’s a joke, or a scam. But the day their laundry room falls quiet, the day the elevator stops between floors and groans as if it has a stomach, the day a kitchen goes dark in the middle of a meal, they come, hatless in rain, with their hands open. They bring everything on wheels. They bring ice-makers and printers and hairdryers and once someone brought a treadmill and cried over it as if it had been the legs of a person.

“Not a priest,” my mother says to them. “We aren’t priests. We maintain a form.” She is a woman who has almost never cried in front of anyone. She folds her grief into the same squares as she folds our rags.

On the morning the washing machine from Block 8C died, a row of women and one man waited in the alley smoking with their elbows tucked to their ribs. It was late fall; the city had begun to taste like chimney soot again. They had named the washing machine Margery because half the tenants were named Margaret and needed to distinguish themselves.

We ran the ceremony in the yard so there would be space. My mother laid thick canvas over a pallet and made the machine lie as if it had lain down there of its own will, exhausted. When somebody asked if it was disrespectful to tip it on its side, she said, “Nothing about this was ever dignified. We are trying to add to the world.” The man from 8C laughed in the way men laugh when they would rather not have heard a woman say what is true.

I went around with the enamel basin and the small jar of distilled water with copper filings settled in its bottom. The filings caught the light and looked like tiny fish that had migrated into a viscous lake and forgotten how to leave. I washed Margery’s enamel lip. Chips and rust came off on the rag like old blood. I touched the belt, the cracked rubber familiar as a knuckle. My fingertips tingled the way they always do. That’s the first sign of a voice: a kind of heat where there shouldn’t be. The finger I cut last month doing a blender grew hotter, its new skin red and exquisite.

“You’ll talk to her?” a woman in a yellow parka asked me. She had the face of someone who has just looked into a forgotten bag and found back a photograph they thought lost.

“I’ll listen,” I said.

My mother began our words. They are not prayers. My father wrote them. He wrote them in pencil on paper the color of old sugar, and when the pencil wore down to a thumbnail he kept writing with the wood. He wasn’t a poet. He worked with his hands, and he believed order mattered. He believed if you named a thing correctly you gave it a way to put itself down. Our words for washers are always the same with the exception of the name, the model, and the small detail for that one machine that lets it know we know it.

This one: We thank you, Margery, who for sixteen years turned the shirts and the sheets, the spit-up cloths and the oil rags. We thank the teeth that engaged, the belt that persisted against the groans of teenagers and the impatience of bachelors who overloaded you on Sundays. We thank the chipped enamel for not cutting the ankles of children. We thank the steady emptying of water into a pipe someone heard knocking at three in the morning and went up to fix. We thank your whole unsealable self. If a scrap yard can be a grave, let this be that place. If not, let our hands be sufficient.

People wept when my mother speaks these words. Not every time. Some machines no one is ready to see. Once we did a small printer from a family with two sons. It spit wet ghosts on paper until it drowned itself, and the mother came not because of the machine but because for six months of those wet ghosts she had seen the face of her own mother there, the jawline clear as day. “I know,” my mother said afterwards, washing her hands as if that would take the sadness off. “I know. Don’t tell your neighbors. They will ask us to conjure faces and we don’t conjure anything.” People make miracles out of what they already believe, which is both a comfort and a danger.

We asked the tenants of Block 8C to speak, and they did, the way people speak when the subject seems too small for the emotion they feel. The man told a story about losing his wedding ring and finding it again when the machine coughed it up silver-green and laughing at himself because it had taken a muscle to teach him to search. An older woman admitted she had fallen asleep sitting on the lid while it spun aggressively bright clothes. A girl, maybe nine years old, said shyly how she liked the way Margery sounded like someone knocking from the other side when it came time to rinse. I had to look away for a moment. There is always someone who hears knocking and thinks of return.

My mother nodded and made a sign with her hand that looks like blessing but is really just habit. She always finishes by switching a thing on one last time. Sometimes, in that moment between the power and the refusal, I can hear everything a machine is willing to yield.

We had spliced a cord to Margery’s exposed wires because the plug had been melted with a candle—a previous repair that didn’t confess itself until I flicked the casing and smelled wax. “People think electricity is just light that moved into a wire,” my father used to say, making that face that meant he was both amused and worried. “It is something that bites and forgives.” My mother held the junctions steady in a rag and I plugged the cord into the long orange extension we use for everything out back. The tenants drew closer as if we were about to call down weather.

A tremble. Then a grind that was almost a clearing of the throat. The drum twitched, nudged, and stopped. Then something opened that shouldn’t open. I heard it. The tiny river that lives in the coil that used to be new. I heard the unshakable rhythm of sixteen, sixteen, a whole life of rinses. I heard the laugh of the nine-year-old like coins falling down a metal chute. I heard the scrape of a plastic fire truck someone had once washed alive. I could smell soap high and thin, the smell anyone could smell. Under it was the smell only I get, an old sharpness like when you lick a battery and the taste makes your whole jaw ache. Inside that ache, the small voice that is not a word but a vector.

It is not language. It is not not language.

I leaned in and put my ear to the housing where the motor sits like a heart people assume is just a pump. I closed my eyes in the old country manner of closing them when you want to appear to listen to God. Mostly what I got was the sound of my own blood in my veins answering. There was a little more. It said: Enough.

That was all. Just the one rough good word. The machine registered the presence of hands which had been close to it for hours, years; the hands that lifted, that pressed lids. Enough with a carrying both of exhaustion and of completion. You could bury that bit of sound and it would grow a tree.

“Thank you,” I said aloud without meaning to. My mother made a small impatient noise like she does when she knows I’ve let my listening fall all over me and I’m going to need a minute to get up out of it again.

Afterwards people used the basin to wash their hands, a habit we never discouraged. The copper filings made the water look holy while doing nothing to it but turning brown. They put coins into the old tobacco tin we keep under the shelf. We kept the coil because coils stack nicely. We kept the motor because we keep every motor, labeling the shelf with names in thick blue marker. We printed “Margery—8C—Kenmore 90—1970-something—talked” and my mother underlined talked with a thin mean line whose anger isn’t at me but at something too big to shout at, like landlords or icebergs or my father’s cells.

The dog from the salvage yard put his aching front paws over the low wall and watched us with a delicate attention he never gives his owner. He was named Lenny. No one knows why. He is one of the things in my life that does not belong to anybody I can call and rescue. I gave him half a stale bun. He chewed as if careful of his weak teeth.

“If we could afford a freezer, this would go easier in winter,” my mother said, rolling her shoulder until it made the seeding crackle sound that worried me and no one else. The morning had moved from lemon light to dirty dishwater. A bruise of cloud was coming up from the river because the river climbs over the city in winter and holds it by the hair when it feels like it.

“We can get an old one,” I said automatically. “Refurbish.”

“Old ones bite. We know this.” She stood and looked at the pallets that made our yard look like a stage. “See that the motor is labeled. People are coming later with the copier.”

“That’s afternoon?” I checked the page on the nail by the door: my handwriting in pencil, my mother’s additions in pen like small corrections from a careful teacher. A copier, a broken electric kettle, and a man with a portable fan “that flips when he sleeps” according to her note.

“That’s after lunch,” she said. “Before, we have to go plead with the man from the city.”

Right. The man from the city with the white hard hat who had an inspector’s voice even when he was ordering coffee at the cart. The city had sent him when our neighbor complained about the pallets. Then he looked around our yard and saw all the things he had not planned to see: the drums of oil, the racks of parts that to him were contumely, the almost-footbridge of ironing boards we kept because people kept bringing them like old planks. He saw our children of metal and said words like hazard and abatement. He mailed papers with his name typed at the bottom and his name got bigger each time. He said he would come back with a team. My mother said he was the kind of man who liked to be watched while he ate.

We would go plead, because that is one of the forms this work takes: you remember to say please to the world. You say it with your smallest voice so it won’t hear you as a challenge.

I carried Margery’s motor inside and put it on the shelf between the two fans that had sung until their bearings burned and the blender that had so vibrated with hunger it had only ever wanted to grind ice. The shelf is the height of my chest. When I stand there sometimes my heart beat arranges itself to be in step with the motors like soldiers march when they can’t bear their own separate legs. My father’s handwriting, my mother’s handwriting, my little additions in an almost straight line. Familiarity as ceremony.

The bell on our door is a spring and a fork hung inside a jar to amplify the sound. It rings like someone at a polite dinner set down their knife a little too loudly. The bell rang and there was a woman in the doorway looking behind her like the street might give up everyone it had hidden.

It was noon; we were supposed to be shutting to go plead. She stepped inside anyway, quick like if she got both feet in we couldn’t kick her back out. She had a coat that had once been a good coat, the kind you buy yourself the winter you begin to be promoted: wool so dark it eats the light, collar turned up against the weather of a man’s gaze. She had a scar running like a loose thread from the corner of her mouth down her jaw where the soft bits get thin. Her shoes were wrong for the potholes of Cloister Street.

“I am sorry,” she said. People always begin that way even when they aren’t sorry. “I need a quiet disposal.”

“Everything we do is quiet,” my mother said. She doesn’t like people who treat us like a secret. “We are documented. We abide by weight requirements.”

“Please.” The woman’s hands were inside her coat pockets. That’s not what made me notice her hands. It was the way the sleeves moved like there was a tremor there that wasn’t hers. “No forms.”

I thought of the man from the city who wears his helmet like an extra skull and makes notes as if ink is the thing that eats you. I thought of my father’s neat lined words. I felt the old adolescent wish to do the thing somebody swore we couldn’t.

“We don’t take materials without record,” my mother said. She wiped her hands on a cloth that used to be a towel that used to be someone’s beach day. “There are other places downriver.”

“They don’t do what you do.” The woman said it without flattery. Her eyes made the small roll that means you have done the shopping of last resorts and arrived where you should have gone first. She reached into her coat and put something wrapped in a gray canvas square on the counter. The canvas was the type they use in labs and hospitals when they want to wipe away things they don’t admit were there. The thing inside wasn’t heavy enough to be a motor and too heavy to be a phone. It had sharp corners that found my palms before the rest of it did.

The same heat as always climbed my fingers when I touched the bundle. But it wasn’t heat the way of the last of a machine, that vanishing warmth of something that had been working and then stopped. This heat had nowhere to go. It stood itself up in my hands. It wanted.

“Ma’am.” My mother didn’t mean to say ma’am but she did when she was furious and the fury made her polite. “We will not do something that will close our doors. This is my house. Don’t ask me to set it on fire.”

“I wouldn’t ask you to burn your house.” The woman untied the canvas. The knot had been done tightly and too quick, like someone tying off stitches in the dark. She showed us a thing we should not have been shown. It was a box, black and charred at one lip where a cable had gone in and then been forced out as if it had tried to return when the fire started. It was the size of a child’s lunch. No logo. That scared me more than anything. Everything new comes with a logo like a birthmark. The face was a field of tiny holes, the kind microphones wear to make the world behave.

“We don’t take police materials,” my mother said. I couldn’t look at her face because it would have told me we were not about to do a very bad thing.

“It isn’t police,” the woman said. She swallowed. She had one of those small swellings beside the throat that rises like if a bird were trying to get out. “It’s a miscalculation. It’s a… a companion device. For elderly care. A pilot. They were testing the speech maps.” Her eyes moved in a motion that was either shame or nausea. “There was a fire in the lab. They scheduled disposal. But they didn’t listen first. They’re not going to. I thought—” She swallowed again. “I read about you.”

“You read about funerals,” my mother said. “We disassemble. We praise. We do not hide things from the people who have made rules for us.”

“Please.” The woman turned the box so the holes faced me. I didn’t want them to face me and they did. “If it goes with the rest, no one will ever know it existed. It will go into the ground and be torn up again in twenty years and remelted to make something else that talks back. Can you imagine a conversation like that? People will think it’s a cooking pot that remembers.”

“We save motors,” I said stupidly, as if that would explain an ethic. “We label.”

The woman nodded. “Save that. Label it. Put my name. Put any name. Just—listen. Please. I am not a sentimental person. I don’t want to name it. It isn’t a dog. But there is someone in there.”

There it is. The sentence people think will move everyone. There is someone in there. Women say it about their own bodies at clinics. Men say it about their cars when we try to take out the stereos. Old women say it about dogs in sweaters. There is someone in there. As if the world wouldn’t be enough to make one careful.

“It’s illegal.” My mother’s voice had gone low. “You know this. The man with the helmet will stand up straight and clap.”

The woman opened her hands as if that would make her less present. “I’ll pay.”

This is the place in the story where mercenary people ask how much, and moral people say no, and the truth is the same in both houses, which is that our light bill was late. My mother’s eyes flicked to me. There was the quickness of calculation, not of money but of what my father would have said and whether that mattered when you had to make soup that night.

“I’ll listen,” I said, before my mother could say no. Then, because I am my mother’s child and learned from her that all sentences must be paid for, I added, “I will listen. Not take. Not hide. Not bind. The listening is no one’s business but mine.”

My mother’s lips pressed into a line the shape of a screw under too much torque. “You will not—”

“I will not connect us,” I said. “If the man with the helmet comes with his clipboard, he will find what he wants.”

The woman set down a folded stack of bills that smelled like someone’s perfume and a building with too much carpet glue. My mother didn’t look at it; that would have been a confession. The fork in the jar bell gave a little accidental sound when the door shivered in a new gust. The river was coming up the street.

“I have to go soon,” the woman said. “I only have the lunch hour. My supervisor is—” She stopped. “Please be quick.”

“I am never quick,” I said. It is a thing my father used to say in the way he said I am not your enemy, which makes it true only sometimes. I reached for the black box with both hands like a coward. My fingers went hot again and the heat climbed into my wrist and sat there. The weight was wrong for what it was. If I tipped it, I could feel a little something inside slip and find rest against a different wall. There was a sound where you never want one: the faint grit moving. The place where fire got in and turned parts of a thing to powder. The hole where it married the cord was carbon ringed and the smell that came off it is one I have to leave behind whenever I can: burned insulation makes a shamed smell like hair and a strong smell like old milk.

I put the box on the wooden table with the gouges in it that have my father’s fingerprints invisible where he smoothed every burr he could find. I put my ear to the face where the small holes made a field of stars. I reminded myself to breathe. I reminded myself that the first sound is often my own teeth trying not to chatter.

The first thing I heard was the river, because I always hear the river. It wraps the city and the people and the power in it all and it sings one song, the one that goes down.

Under it, something came up. Not language. Not not. A frequency that sat in my mouth. The place where a reader begins and a writer begins are both in the soft palate. Have you noticed? That’s where the world vibrates you. It said—at first I thought it said the whistled sound my father could never do. Then it resolved. And it said my name. Not the one people use when they call from the doorway. The other one. The one my father called me the summer he decided I was old enough to steady the coil without being shocked. The name that isn’t diminutive exactly, but is nearer the animal of me.

Nini, it said in the small voice that isn’t a voice. Nini. Do you hear me? I am not in the dark. I am arranged.

I jerked up so fast I hit the lamp with my forehead and saw stars. The woman flinched. My mother didn’t move.

“Well?” the woman said, whispering even though whispering doesn’t change what you’ve already done.

I did the wrong thing. I touched the box again as if it might shiver away and I could catch it. The heat sat like a bird on my hand bones. Somewhere far down the street the man with the helmet was probably telling a story about how he saved a childhood pet from drowning in his pool. I pressed my ear back to the small holes and let my face rest against the cool. I shut my eyes. The dark behind them was my mother’s shape, my father’s hand, the river. And there, again, gentle and patient and exact the way a machine is when it has been tuned past fear:

Nini, it said. If this is your house, please lay me down where nobody will turn me back on. I have done what they asked and I have unmade it. I would like, if you can, for you to find a jar and time. I am not alone.

Chapter One

On the morning the sea returns a jar to me, all the glass in the shop thrums like a hive.

It’s not loud, that hum. It’s a tremor in the teeth, a thread pulled tight over the day. I wake to it under my pillow, rise with it stitched into my spine. By the time I’ve lit the lamps and thrown back the canvas awning, the humming has climbed into the jars on the display racks—lullabies and tempests and silvery drizzles all buzzing in solidarity, as if some leader neither of us can see is about to enter with a fog of bodyguards.

I’ve seen glass do this twice before. Once when the air turned itself inside out for three nights in a row and we named it a border storm. Once when my brother didn’t come back.

I chalk OPEN on the board outside and then wipe it off, as if adding one more word to the day will spill it over. Someone will come, though; they always do. In this town, when the world is too much or too little we come to The Sky Settlement & Sundries and barter for weather we can live with. You can get a jar of kitchen-scented sunlight here, if you want. You can take your pick of moral rains, focused downpour or permissive drizzle. I have bolts of wind that whistle in D, and one glass bell that contains a gust so kind it fixes your hair and your temper in a single go.

“Your jars hum,” Lita says, coming in sideways, wrestling the door with one hip and a paper bag of still-warm rolls with the other. “My teeth ache.”

“Mine too.”

“You always say that.” She sets the bag on the counter, peels back the top. The butter inside is a marvel—palest yellow, a sea-stable cream she churned at four in the morning while her daughter slept. I was meant to go dancing with Lita last night at the pier, but I stayed up balancing my ledger and the ledger didn’t like me.

“You shouldn’t keep them so close together,” she says now, nodding at the high shelves. “They talk to one another.”

“They’ll talk whether or not they can hear. It’s what weather does.” I smile like I mean it. I’ve put the gale jars on the top shelf, anchored with twine. The calm ones—Sunday Afternoons and Thaw I—have their own row, well away from the mischief.

Lita takes her bread, a jar of August and one of Elevenses Sun—the light that gleams off cutlery and dominoes—out of my hands when she sees my fingers fail to find purpose. “Eat,” she orders, then remembers the hum and stops short with a grimace. “It’s like a fly trapped in your skull.”

“I promise I haven’t trapped flies,” I say.

“You’d sell them minutes.”

I would. I do. Stale weather has uses. If I let it molder in the corners of the shop it turns to grit on my tongue and sours the whole place. So I decant it, label it, and greet whoever walks in.

“Morning, Mara,” says Tomer from the ferry, bringing me a bag of coins with the ferry tax and a personal purchase wrapped in newspaper. He blushes when I ask what’s in it. He knows I know. Sailors and priests are always the same when it comes to rain that makes you sleep like you did when you were ten and your mother was still the warm in your house. They act like their longing ought to be private. I act like it is.

A woman I don’t recognize for once—hair severed blunt at her jaw, a lensy stare that tells me she is new to paying for weather with coins instead of promises—comes in and points at a small vial of Worry.

“Not for me,” she says when I ease it down and try not to cough when Worry scrapes my throat. It’s sharp, Worry, a collection of taut little weather, brief panics the wind left scattered in alleyways. People take it in teaspoonfuls and feel justified for an hour. “For my dog.”

“I sell Worry for dogs under the counter,” I say. “Softer stuff. This is adult Worry. Kites and exam halls.”

She buys two thimbles of Dog’s Morning instead, and I pack them in wool. Dog’s Morning is dew on the brain, every scent important and none alarming. She takes one for herself too, at my look.

“Does the hum mean something?” she asks, nodding toward the shelves. The sound is a wire through everything, an embarrassment of attention.

“It means the sea is about to tell a story,” I say. I intend it to be a joke. It is not.

I know the hour the jar is delivered because the light in the shop shifts the way it does when someone walks into a room dressed in bad news. It’s a density. It pushes the buttery lamplight up under the ceiling beams. The humming pitches into one frequency I can almost sing to, one that cuts the air like a keel. Lita turns without looking at me and puts both palms flat to the counter. Tomer, who has come back for a flash of Shallow Sleep to roll in his pocket like a talisman against his own breath, looks down at his hands. The woman with the Dog’s Morning closes her eyes, the way people do when they smell the top of a baby’s head.

Then the door knocks, which the door doesn’t do. The door doesn’t need to knock. It has a bell.

I wipe my palms on my apron, as if what is about to happen requires clean hands.

There is no one on the stoop. There is a jar.

It wears rope like wet hair, a rope that has seen ship and sewer and the bottom of a child’s pram. The glass is old, thick, the kind that kept cherries. A cork sits proud of the neck like a thumb. It is unlabeled.

The unlabeled part makes the back of my tongue go bitter.

“Who—” I start and stop.

I do not pick up jars from the stoop. I learned that lesson once with a jar of Laughing Wind that turned out to be Second-Hand Anger. There are traps you can set for a person in a weather shop. You can give them your weather and make them pay for it. You can give them back what you stole and be forgiven. The town has always understood this and explained it to me with its eyes.

But I know this jar is for me from the way the sea has chosen its address. The rope has been tied not in knots, which are for people, but in loops, which are for stories. You don’t tie a jar like that if you want it to go to anyone else.

There are formalities, even with gifts from strangers. I take the jar in both hands. It’s cold enough to hold its own frost. I hear the little sound old glass makes when it remembers its sand. I carry it inside and put it on the counter in the place where I weigh coins and weigh the things people say they cannot live without. The other jars adjust their tone. They hum together until the sound finds a floor.

“What is it?” Lita whispers.

I shrug, as if my shoulders are reliable creatures.

I know better than to pull the cork. You do not unstop something when your hands are full of yourself. You set it aside. You let your nervous system become a thing with balance again. If it’s a storm, it will rattle. If it’s heat, the glass will sing of it. If it’s sorrow, the cork will slow dawn by an hour.

“It’s—” Tomer says, and I lift a hand without meaning to tell him to let it be. He closes his mouth like a door.

There are tests that don’t break a seal. There is the mirror trick: if you hold a jar to the flecked mirror by the register, its contents show themselves ahead of time, the way a mirror betrays the day’s first sun before the window can. There is the ear trick: touch the jar to the little bones behind your ear and you’ll hear whether the weather inside is left-handed or right. There’s the sharpened pin behind the counter: place it on the glass and see which way it leans. There’s the breath test: fog the glass with your breath and watch what your cloud makes of it.

I try none of these. Instead, I press my palm flat to the dome of old glass.

It’s not weather under there, not as it is sold and organized in a place like this. It is not a mood or a daybreak or even an event in need of a customer. It is a density of one thing, and my body does what bodies do when they meet their match. It flinches. I squeeze my eyes shut. The hum changes again, not louder, but closer.

The jar contains a storm.

Not a new storm. Not the kind the children bring me in tea cups, shrieking, the kind I pour into a naked jar and seal with wax and a kiss of nettle and a promise of pocket money. This is age and edge. This is steel and rope, wood and prayer. The storm in this jar is a history written with a nail.

I open my eyes. I do not look at Lita or Tomer or the woman who bought Dog’s Morning. If I look, I might see the thought forming in their faces—this is the border storm from three springs ago, the one that tore roofs and spat fish and named the crooked tree at the end of my lane for itself. The one that set itself in my brother’s mouth and didn’t let go.

“What do I owe you?” I say aloud, wanting to make the world plain with money.

The door swings in its hinge then, as if something remembered it was supposed to knock first. Old Mr. Haan, who smells always of brass polish and mushrooms he insists used to be oysters, stands on the step with his hat in his hands. He sees the jar and steps back as if he has remembered his first and last words. He does not come in. He neither asks for his Monday Fog nor volunteers his usual complaint about tides and shops that sell them domesticated. He goes away.

“That’s none of ours,” Lita says. “That doesn’t belong to a shop.”

“I know,” I say.

It is possible to extract a storm from glass safely. It is possible the way it is possible to remove a splinter from a child’s heel without making the child hate your hands. You practice. You are gentle in a way your voice doesn’t teach you. You learn when to look away so the pain can leave without shame.

It is also possible to ruin it—to chip the glass and cut the thing inside, make it bleed and bleed and be a smaller, meaner thing once it is out. People have done this to their own weather for generations. We lay blame on storms when we are the tilters, the ones who pry with a blade instead of a stitch-picker. I have taught myself not to blame.

This is not my storm to release or mangle. It is mine only because it has come to me.

After Lita leaves and Tomer goes and the woman takes her dog weather to her blunt, lensy dog, I sit on the stool behind the counter and lay my ear along the side of the jar. The glass is so old it puckers. I feel under the feel of it, to the blood that has its own sound.

Inside, in a space no bigger than an apple, something moves its weight from one foot to the other.

“Talk to me,” I tell it, though this is not how we’re supposed to do it. You’re not supposed to ask the weather to speak a language you learned from your grandmother and your school teacher and a radio that loses signal every time you climb your own hill. You’re supposed to put a jar like this one on the fourth shelf from the bottom, where the height is for things not to be touched, and you’re supposed to record the way it leans and the way it sighs and make your notes and wait. You’re supposed to be as patient as a saint whose statue the gulls have practiced on.

“Talk,” I say again, because the longer I wait the more the hum will pluck at everything else in me and leave me in threads.

I close my eyes, which is how you open your other ears. I picture the place I always picture when my job asks me to listen for something bigger than money: the old listening hill behind my father’s shed, the one with the cracked bedrock you can sit on and feel the river chew down below. My father took us there when we were small and said, The bodies of this place are busy. He’d taught me to put a stick between my teeth and lay the other end on the rock to hear the water as the teeth of the world.

I put a finger to my lips now to ask the day to keep its voice down. I concentrate on the part of me that listens with bones.

And there it is, the shape of it, the tell-tale lilt of something too used to being a god to remember it can be held. The last time I lay like this to it, the pitch had my brother in it—a thread of him like a nick in a bell. It had a scratch he’d put there with his laugh, you understand? Joss was like that. He’d posit himself against the weather as if he were an equal and the weather had loved him for it, had made room in itself for him. He’d left and come back with rain in his lashes and a coin he’d made from the sun under his tongue. He had not come back the last time.

I listen now for a nick, a scratch, a laugh under the roar.

The hum doesn’t roar. It cuts. It is a blade on my spine. It is a fool thing to do, to put your ear to a storm somebody else trapped and left you with, to believe you can harvest meaning like mushrooms in the dark. It is a fool thing people like me do every day.

It says my name.

It says it in the old way, with the consonant at the end softened to a liquid, the way my mother said it when she was sick and the way Joss said it when he wanted something. It says my name with the modest gravity of someone calling me over a distance they have no right to cross.

I pull back like something bit me. The stool squeals. On the shelf marked Late Winters, the jars shimmy together and clink like teeth. A rivulet of butter runs down the side of a roll and onto my ledger.

The jar is a mouth. It has found that it can form words. This should not be possible if what is inside is only weather made glass-worthy. There is weather that can talk, yes. There is the child’s hail you can slot into your ear to hear your own childhood complaining about nap time. There is the Orator Wind, which climbs into the throats of men with pins in their lapels and hammers their words into the bricks. But what is under my palm now says my name and waits.

“You can’t,” I say, which is what you say to a mind that has come to visit yours uninvited but not unwelcome.

Mara, says the thing in the jar. That’s all.

The urge to open it is a stitch in me. I could. I could break the wax, twist my wrist, let the cork move in the old coiled way. The cloth under my fingers is printed with suns that once meant something to someone else. I have a knife for stubborn cork. I have the first scar that happened inside my mouth when I tried to soften a cork with my teeth and bit too hard into a piece of grit. I have the kind of day people tell stories about after they sleep.

“No,” I tell it. “Not yet.”

It doesn’t ask. It says my name again, a fraction less like a word and more like a knuckle knocking wood. There is a patience in the sound I do not trust. There is an urgency in me I trust less.

It matters that a parcel of weather has traveled the bottled way back to my counter to talk. It matters not only to me, but to people who will, if I open the door, walk into this shop and insist, tactfully or not, on hearing their names too. It matters to the folk with badges and the folk with oars and the folk whose bad luck is all teeth. It matters because anything that can say a name can also say a date and a location, and what we call law is just the right names said at the right moments by the right weather.

I take the ledger out from under the roll and turn to a blank page. It’s not blank, of course. There is writing there already. There is always writing already, the faint graphite of the day that thinks it outranks your plans. It says: butter stain. It says: twelve coins and a promise from Tomer to mend your railing. It says: Joss would have told you not to be an idiot, and then he would have handed you the corkscrew.

I dip my pen. I write: Unlabeled jar found at doorstep at nine minutes after ten. Thick old glass. Loops in rope. Storm of unknown provenance. My name spoken once, twice.

I do not write: Father, if I write to you, will it get across? Mother, will you hold your breath for me, will you at least look away while I lift my hand? I do not write: All of this hums because something terrible and beautiful remembers me.

The official I expect does not come that day. The one with the pale hands and the stamped book and the talent for making everything sound like part of a process being improved. He will come tomorrow probably, on his way between measuring the harbor with his little watch and subtracting a kilometer from our town because it wants too much. He will come and he will call the jar an artifact of a weather event and he will mark me down as a citizen with a coastal affection for romances. He will call what we do bartering. He will call what I do purveying. He will say that storms have no owners, so no crimes have been committed.

By closing time, the jar hasn’t said my name again. Lita has kissed my head and taken the butter home. I have sold six vials of Troublesome Good Luck, one hamper of Craft Wind, and a jar of Night That Smells Like Knives to a woman who works the late shift at the fish-packing shed. The hum has settled into the floorboards. The shop is the shop again—donkey and honest and mildly illiterate.

I latch the door. I turn down the lamps. I stand in the aisle between Augusts and Mournings and I listen to the small noises of old wood settling its bargains with air. I choose a jar of my own—Dull Courage, a thin winter sort—and put it in my skirt pocket like a coin.

When I reach for the jar on the counter—to carry it into the back room where the mice use my willow baskets as a thoroughfare if I let them—the jar is warmer than it has any right to be.

“Mara,” it says. The sound is a shape made of my ear. The shape is my name said by my brother the way he would say it when he’d found something he knew would hurt me and make me grateful.

“I’m here,” I tell a piece of glass, and mean it, and hate that I mean it.

A storm cannot go on saying a single name into a room where it knows itself already heard, my father would say, if he were still the sort of man who taught things. It will say the next thing it knows how to say.

The next thing it knows how to say is not a word.

The next thing it knows how to say is a place.

Chapter One

On Sundays I take the letters nobody wants to claim and drive them to the places that meant to be addresses but never made it onto a map. The truck is older than me and called the Blue Jay because the paint flakes like feathers and because it steals. Not shiny things. Stories. Every week, it returns home with new ones caught in its grille: a strip of caution tape, a hometown newspaper turned to pulp by the rain, once a funeral program pressed flat as a leaf.

By seven, the sky is the color of a bruise that will never explain itself. The city sits inside it like a guilty thought. From the roof of the main post office, which closed two summers ago and now hosts pigeons and a twelve-year-old with a skateboard and death wish, you can see the river faking obedience for a while before it bends around the factories and becomes the wide, brown body it always wanted to be. When it floods, the city lifts its feet like a person stepping onto a chair to avoid a mouse. When it dries, it leaves behind sticks that look like ribs.

We used to have a Dead Letter Office. Aunties with knuckles swollen from arthritis and rings would sit with columns of envelopes, steam sponges and broken hearts, and open what the world had lost.
