They became cartographers of the messy human wish—right turn here at desperation, left at pride, straight on pure stubborn. They'd reseal everything with the foamy patience of bakers. They ran names like rosary beads. When the office closed, I inherited their work not because I am a saint but because I am stubborn and because grief has made me tolerant of tasks with no promised end.

People leave me their undeliverables in a decommissioned newspaper box outside the Viva Mexican Grocery. The box still says TAKE ONE, as if clarity was something you could grab. The lid sticks on humid days, which is most days in summer. I pry it open with my house key and lift out the mail, cradling it like someone else's sleeping child. I do not wear a uniform. I do have a satchel that used to belong to my father, leather softened by years of sun and rain and other things that soak in and leave marks: motor oil, lake water, whiskey. On the inside flap he wrote his name in a blue so bright it hurt. AUGUST, he wrote. He liked to make sure a thing knew to whom it belonged.

The first letter in the pile is addressed to "Jordy 'Peanut' Alvarez, State Correctional Facility," and the postmark is our neighboring town, where all the buses to the prison begin. There's no return address. The handwriting is careful the way a person writes when they're trying to be someone else. The corner of the page beneath the stamp is damp, as if the envelope had been held in someone’s mouth. Inside the grocery, Mrs. Alvarez stocks hot sauce with hands that never stop moving, as if the shelves will collapse if she stops. She calls every boy under twelve "Peanut" because if she says the name enough, maybe her son will come running.

I tuck that one into the flap of my satchel next to a fat envelope addressed to "The Three-Story Yellow House, west side, with the porch where a girl skipped rope till midnight." A letter to "Vashti who sells mangoes from her car trunk, Saturdays by the bus depot." A final notice stamped in red for "Occupant," a word that wants to be a body and isn't. A hand-drawn postcard that is not a postcard at all but the back of a cereal box carved into a rectangle with a steak knife and scrawled with a message to "Mom, who lives over the bakery that sells the bread with sesame on it, I am OK, please feed my cats." A stack of flyers for a missing dog, the dog smiling out at the future no matter what the future plans to do to him.

"More came," Mr. Padilla calls from two storefronts down. He runs the last payphone in the city. The sign above his shop reads REPAIR in letters that have faded to the color of breath on glass. He sells clocks and fixes nothing but hope. He keeps a ledger of long-distance calls nobody will pay for, numbers with faraway area codes underlined twice. He hands me a paper bag with a flourish as if it's something he baked. "People slide them under the door at night," he says. "Like I'm a priest."

"I'm bringing you cookies next time," I tell him.

"You say that every time and you never do," he says. "Which is all right. Empty promises still sound sweet, August. How's the Blue Jay?"

"Still loud," I say. "Still flying low."

He laughs, showing a gold tooth. "Go," he says. "Deliver all the secrets."

On the corner by the bus depot, Vashti’s trunk is already open, fruit heaped like a bright promise against the morning. She has a tattoo of a mango across her collarbone, the skin splitting, inside flesh the color of a sunrise. She sees me and whistles. "Dead-letter August," she says. "Come buy from me so the others believe this is normal."

I hand her the letter with her name on it. She doesn't even feign surprise. People pretend they don't know about me but that's just manners. She slips the envelope into her bra. "From my brother?" she asks.

"From someone who is unlearned in the art of lying," I say, because the writing trembled not with age but with a new fear, a hand unused to confessions.

She nods as if that makes sense and offers me a mango the size of my hand. "For your work," she says. "Green or ripe?"

"Green," I tell her. "So it lasts."

"Good luck," she says.

"You, too."

The air by the river smells like metal and mown grass and, faintly, the sweet plastic of beach balls gone to seed. Boys fish with their shoes off. Girls show them how to bait the hooks without flinching. I park the Blue Jay where the gravel meets the mud and sit a minute with the engine ticking like a nervous clock. The life of the river would seem to forgive us if forgiveness were her hobby. A fish flops and leaves behind a wet comma. Bubbles rise, as regular as a prayer. The city council would like to plant more trees along the banks. They say shading the water lowers its fever. They say new paint can cure the sorrow in a neighborhood. They cut ribbons with big scissors while the brown water licks the shore with a tongue the size of a house.

I do my rounds. The three-story yellow house got painted gray last spring but the porch remembers the jump rope, a scar in the wood left by thousands of tiny scuffs and the weight of a girl whose calves were stronger than someone's patience. She is a woman now with a baby on one hip, eyes that do not lift from the child to my face. I do not tell her I remember the rope. I do not tell her I once hopped that beat, that my sister laughed at the way I counted, fast and quiet, as if numbers could hear and would stop if you bragged. I do not say her house will always be yellow to someone who hasn’t lived there in a decade. I hand her the letter.

"I don't like surprises," she says, but she peels the envelope open with one neat finger. She reads. The baby's breath warms the paper. Her lips part. She does not cry. The porch light has a bee’s nest inside it and the bees know what to do. The woman folds the letter with care. "Thank you," she says, and I nod as if I deserve the thanks. I feel like a thief who returns a wallet and pockets the change for his trouble. I am always paying myself in shame.

Sometimes I deliver to people who don't know they've been waiting. The envelope to the prisons I bring to Mrs. Alvarez. It’s a Sunday, bread day, tortillas and gossip. I step into the fluorescent hum and the smell of cilantro and meat. She moves toward me before I’m in the aisle, apron ghosted with flour, eyes swollen with a grief that looks like an allergy. "Came today," I tell her. "No return."

"It's him," she says, touching the paper as if it could burn. "He cannot write, but he learned, maybe. He learned." She holds the envelope to her forehead briefly, a prayer. She does not open it then. She slips it under the counter. She will read it in the stockroom, alone, pretending she is looking for jalapeños.

"Do you want me to bring it out to the prison next Sunday?" I ask, because there are things I can move around a city and there are things I cannot transport at all, no matter how many stamps I lick.

"Next Sunday," she says. "I will go. You will drive me? The bus takes too long. He can see me in the morning through the glass."

"I'll be here at seven," I say.

She grips my forearm, her fingers an accusation and a forgiveness. "Bless you," she says. I have not been blessed by a priest in twelve years. Grief has made me accepting, if not religious.

The work isn't always noble. Sometimes I bring child support checks to the wrong door on purpose. Sometimes I misread a plea and what I deliver instead is an end. Once, a letter came to "The man who sings in the stairwell." That could be anyone on the south side, but the stamp was older than anyone who would bother to send a joke, and the return address was a shelter three towns away. I opened the envelope with my steam kettle and sweat, placed my ear to the paper. There was a whistle trapped there, clean as a bird call and thin as a blade. I found him—old Mr. Cyrilio, in the building next to the laundromat, singing to the mold so it wouldn’t grow. The letter was from a daughter he had taught not to cry, telling him he was forgiven for using too much of himself for strangers. The gist of it, anyway. He held the paper like an altar and I left and cried on the landing because my sister had died in March when the river thawed and the ice broke and she stepped wrong and went under and when they pulled her out she was full of sticks and I could not forgive anything at all.

That is how I came to this work. If I cannot pull people out of water, I will pull their words out and lay them on doorsteps like bread.

Before noon, the Blue Jay grows less insistent. We are in rhythm. We travel to addresses you will not find: The porch with the plastic swan planters even in winter. The house with the little library built from a microwave. The third step that squeaks in Etta’s house, which used to be my house. My house still likes to pretend it belongs to me. It floods in April when the river wants attention. We used to stack sandbags and watch them drink the water like thirsty dogs. It has a window that is always blind, can't see out, can't see in. The mailbox is a tin sugar box from my grandmother's kitchen, bolted to the railing, still smelling faintly of sweetness when it rains. Etta and I do not speak. We are not enemies. We are former neighbors in the body of a friendship. She watches for my truck when the storms come. She texts me weather reports as if there could be a new kind of rain and we should not miss it.

A box awaits me on Etta's porch, blue twine like a belt. On top of it is a note: For the boy with the red bike, who helped me carry groceries last week. No address, no name. I check the contents: a book about planets, a pair of bright socks with rockets on them, a lollipop the size of the boy's palm. He lives behind the old school, third door, upstairs, mother with the hair that looks like wind. Etta watches me from behind the curtain. I wave. She doesn't wave back. She is trying on bitterness like a dress she can't quite fasten.

By one o'clock I'm on the north end, where the highway makes its permanent apology to the lake and no one believes it. The wind smells like old paper and algae. The mall died and came back as a church. The church sells smoothies. A man in a suit with a microphone waves at traffic. He looks sunburned and sincere. I park and take my only selfish detour: the library.

The library isn't a library anymore. It's half a daycare and half a community center and the books choose you rather than the other way around. The woman at the front desk, who wears three pairs of glasses at once depending on her work and mood, has a basket for me under the counter. The basket is filled with cards the children made for "Abuela, who is sick and lives four blocks away and always smells like cinnamon, please take this today August please." The children draw addresses the way they draw faces: with two big eyes and a smile that takes up too much room.

"You're late today," she says. "You have company."

"I have secrets," I say.

"Same thing," she says, crossing off my name and adding a star. "There was a man asking for you. He left something."

"A warning?" I ask, half-joke. The city council's latest memo calls my work "beneath the dignity of municipal service" and "counterproductive to the ability of citizens to accept loss." They are correct. I am beneath. I am counterproductive. I am a city creature who pushes against his cage and calls the rattling a song.

She reaches down and slides an envelope to me on the counter the way you'd pass a drink to someone with a trembling hand. I look at it and time drops a wrench into the works.

The paper is cheap. It still somehow has the appearance of money to me, because that handwriting belongs to a person who could turn a list of apples and milk into a letter you'd keep in a drawer for the rest of your life. My name is on the front in her hand: AUGUST, like my father's satchel, like the month she drowned, like the end of summer pretending to be a beginning. There's no return address. The stamp is an old one, the kind with the goose curled around its own neck. Across the top, a postmark like a bruise, black and unhelpful. My fingers go cold and then too hot. I do not need to see the back to know how she sealed it. She would have pressed both thumbs along the edge the way our mother taught us, like a blessing, like a lock.

My sister's handwriting. Three years gone and the river still in her lungs, and this envelope says she has something to tell me.

"You all right?" the woman with three pairs of glasses says softly. She hasn't called me by my name; she doesn't have to. Names feel too heavy all at once. Everything inside me unshelves itself and clatters to the floor. I set the envelope on my palm and it gains the weight of a stone.

I could open it here. I could stand in the lull between two songs on the radio in this library that isn't and break the seal and let whatever voice lives inside it into the air. I could run with it to the river and hold it under and watch it bubble. I could tuck it back in the basket and pretend the name belongs to some other August in some other undeserving city. There are a hundred ways to do the wrong thing gently.

"Is there—" I start, and then I stop. Above the postmark is an address, written in the way Lena invented after she got tired of the post office losing our mail every spring with the floods. She said if what you sent is true enough, it will find you. We used to test this with postcards when we were twelve. We wrote: To the house that smells like lemons in July. To the place where the hallway light flickers in an unkind way. To the girl with the scar that looks like a comma. And the mail came. The aunties in the Dead Letter Office laughed and let us keep living.

The address reads: To August, at the house that floods in April. The tin sugar box.

"Who gave you this?" I ask.

She shakes her head. "It was in the overnight basket. No one wrote a name. The cameras don't work, August. They're decoration."

"What time?" I ask, though it doesn't matter.

"Early," she says. "Before sun."

The library hums. Outside, the highway apologizes. The Blue Jay, in the sun, matches no known color. My sister's name is not on the envelope but her hands are. I could pick them out of a crowd of a thousand hands. I can see her pressing the stamp onto the corner with that extra push she gave to every task, as if the notch would do more securing than glue. Everything in me leans. The wind shifts. Somebody’s child laughs in the daycare. Somewhere, Mrs. Alvarez is in the stockroom reading her son's voice. Somewhere, a man in a suit believes in salvation because there are no other choices left to him.

"Do you want to sit?" the woman asks.

"No," I say, because if I sit I will likely drown in whatever chair I choose. "I have deliveries."

I slide the envelope beneath my father's name in the flap of the satchel. My hands feel unfamiliar, as if they have tried on someone else’s life and it does not fit. The thought that arrives is not noble. It is not even true. It is: Maybe there has been a mistake.

Maybe the letter is for someone else. Maybe handwriting can learn to haunt. Maybe the river keeps secrets and I have been delivering them back and forth my whole life, mistaking them for other people's love.

I step into the afternoon and it feels like stepping into the mouth of something large and patient. The Blue Jay coughs, then steadies. I put my palm to the envelope through the leather of the satchel, as if heat could pass through both and tell me if what has arrived is alive. The city has turned brighter, somehow, all the edges turning to knives. Every address I have ever made up gathers itself in a corner of my mind, ready to be called on.

In the mirror, my face looks like my father’s and my sister’s and someone I do not yet know. I ease the truck into gear. We go. There's still mail to deliver. There is always mail to deliver. There is always at least one thing that will not wait.

Chapter One

The river turned around the week my father died, as if it were reconsidering the whole arrangement. By noon the water was shouldering back toward the hills, pushing against the usual grain, wearing a new expression—apologetic, maybe, or just tired of listening. People at Dean’s Diner on the bend ate their fried eggs with the yolks broken and said it was an omen. The feathers on the geese pointed the wrong way. Floats bobbed in place like they were waiting for someone to tell them what to do.

I came home on a bus that sighed and overheated and listened to the driver talk to his mother on speakerphone about pot roast. My father had been dead four days by then, and I had not yet decided whether to tell the woman who raised me that he had left me the building and not her. It was not the sort of decision you can make in the rhythm of a bus. I tried to think about the river instead and all its new ideas, but every time I looked out the window it was hidden by brush, or the gray of warehouses, or a billboard that said Don’t Quit Your Quitting.

The bus hissed into our town the way a lung gives up: slowly, reluctantly. The water tower perched on its stilts like a fat bird, the words HARLINGER painted along its side in the same font as the high school yearbook. Someone had taken a line of black spray paint and put a question mark after it. It made me laugh in a short, mean way and then stop, because laughing like that here felt like telling a joke at a hospital bed.

Harlinger had not changed enough to be kind. The same neon sign flickered at the bait shop across from the river—my father’s sign, my father’s jag of blue saying MINNOWS—one bulb always out in the W. There were still tire ruts worn into the clay behind the shop where someone had tried, once a year since the seventies, to launch a boat without a trailer. There were still cigarette burns on the railing from the men who flicked their ash with their thumbs while they told stories about fish that got away. The gummy residue around the door handle was still the exact pattern of my father’s impatience.

The only new thing was not really new: a vinyl banner drooping across the porch across the way, showing a rendering of a future that had lost an argument with reality. Riverfront Lofts. Brick the color of bread, balconies overlooking the water, little potted trees arranged in lines. The banner buckled in the middle, where a nail had pulled loose and the river’s breath had gotten underneath. Someone had added a mustache to a woman in a linen dress, a perfect swash of Sharpie that made her look like she knew something the banner did not.

“Luce?” someone called. “Lucinda?”

I turned, and the sound of my own name tasted of rhubarb, tart at the edges and good in the throat. That’s how it always was with names. Numbers were lemons. Words were smoke. The smell of hot newspapers. My father used to laugh at me when I told him that eight tasted like burnt sugar and that his handwriting sometimes tasted like brass. He would lift his eyebrows and say, That is a fancy disease you have there, and then he’d be careful not to say the word disease again.

Blue Ike came around from behind the soda machine and hugged me. His overalls smelled like earth and diesel, like the underside of a lawnmower. His beard was gray and yellow, as if two kinds of weather had passed through it. He was called Blue because, when he’d been young, he’d fallen through the ice so many times that people were tired of calling him Lucky.

“You look the same,” he lied. “Just a little taller.”

“Ike. How’s your back.”

“My back’s dead,” he said. “But the rest of me refuses to take the hint.”

We stood with our hands on each other’s elbows, polite, and then he let go. His eyes flicked to the banner across the way and back to the shop door, as if the building might take offense at being caught between.

“Place wasn’t open this morning,” he said, his voice lowering to a church whisper. All the men did that when they were talking about a thing you already knew. “We had a sign up. MARGARET’S ARRANGING THINGS. FUNERAL FRIDAY. That was what it said. We wrote it on cardboard from the new shrimp boxes. Big letters.”

I had seen the sign, taped crooked on the inside of the glass with the white duct tape my father used for everything. The handwriting had been mine.

“Winds out of the northeast,” Ike went on. “That’s what turned it. You could see the eddies like a man walking against a crowd. Never seen it so strong, though. Kitchen got a tub full of it when it came up through the drain. Ethel thinks it’s a sign he’s trying to come back, but I said no, you have to have been gone to come back, and he never went anywhere. You know?”

“He went somewhere,” I said. I meant it as a joke, but it came out solemn.

“Well,” he said, after a moment. “We’re all sorry.”

The key to the shop was heavy, and the lock had a hitch in it from a time my father drove a screwdriver in there and said, There, I taught it who’s in charge. The door stuck, then gave up and came open in a rush, and the smell was exactly as it had been: equal parts dead things and new ones. Coffee, gasoline, minnows, wet newspaper, blood. A sweet rot threaded through like a thin ribbon. Whatever oil you use on fishing reels has its own smell, faintly like crushed leaves and burnt hair. That was here, too. It hit a place behind my eyes that I had grown a scar over.

The lights stuttered on. The radio on the shelf over the counter clicked alive and offered me a commercial for lawn service in a jubilant baritone. My father had never listened to the weather unless it was bad. He could sniff the air and tell you when the barometer changed. He could tell you when the fish would bite by how the minnows held themselves—restless near the top, or drifting and private. He believed in the river the way other people believed in calendars.

I walked down the aisle where he kept the lures, past their rows of iridescent, curved ribs and eyes. The hooks all faced the same way. He had always said the fish on this river were like anyone else: they wanted to be tricked, but they wanted to be treated with dignity. He hated a cheap hook, a cheap knot, a cheap lie. He said, We catch and we eat and we tell it right, Luce. That’s what we do here. We tell it so that when the fish is gone and we are sorry, the story still tastes like what it tasted like.

I put my hand on the glass lid of the minnow tank and felt the condensation, the cold of it. The little bodies flicked below like punctuation marks at the end of a sentence that wouldn’t end. In the corner, the big cooler hummed, and I knew without looking that there were Styrofoam tubs in there stuffed with black dirt, each of them with a rubber band around its mouth like a purse. The worms were all coiled in themselves, tasting the cool dark. Worms, my father said when I was four and incredibly wise, do not have thoughts like ours. To them, the world is just a series of news items. Wet. Warm. Stone. Danger. This is either comforting or not, depending on what you prefer.

I set my bag behind the counter. The stool still had the bite marks from when I’d been seven and furious and wanted to leave a record of myself without having to tell anyone what I was recording. Above me, the wall calendar hung open to April, as if it were surprised to find itself in any spring at all. In the square for the twelfth, my father had written Arrangements, then drawn an arrow pointing to a little fish he’d doodled in March. His writing that week was small and neat, the way it always got when he was trying not to be loud.

Behind the counter, under the shelf where he kept the sinkers and the cash register he never trusted, was the ledger. It was the same red book he had used my whole life, the edges of the pages stained by his hands. There was a lot of him in this shop. His coffee cup on the windowsill, with three rings of brown, each at a different height. His winter hat on the hook in the back, even though it was April. The boots lined up under the bench like compliant dogs. But the ledger was the most him. He put things there that had nothing to do with money. The ledger was maybe the only place where he apologized.

I ran my fingers along the spine, and the texture tasted like wintergreen gum. I pulled the book free. I have to say it took me a moment to open it. Not because of grief but because of argument: my most private way of talking with my father was through that book, and once I opened it after he was gone, the argument would have to change its terms. The last time we’d argued, it had been about a ditch, and a city inspector with soft hands who wanted to fill it, and how long you could keep a thing on your land even if everyone else said no. The inspector had said liability. My father had said privilege, and meant it as a threat.

The ledger fell open to a page from winter, where someone had put down a cup with a ring of mud on the base and marked December 3 in a perfect wheel. Mr. Krauss, it said, two dozen shiners, paid cash, bless him. Small mouth, midstream by church pier, careful. Then: I owe Harriet for the plow, next time. Then: Eaton boy says he saw a pale deer near the tannery, and I told him that deer do not make us special, only hungry. Then a grocery list: tea, mustard, wood glue. There was a line about me that tasted like cinnamon and tin. Lucy said she would come soon, and I did not ask her when because when has always made her slippery. And he was right. When was the worst question anyone could ask me. It required me to conjure a future in someone else’s thermos.

I turned the pages, greedy and careful. He had always kept the names the same way: their last names in all caps, their first names lowercase, as if to call them by their familiar selves but also put them where they belonged. MRS. JAREK came in with a crocheted hat, and he wrote she looked like a Marine. TAMMY GIBSON dropped her change and we searched and searched and found it later in the cuff of her sleeve. The GIBBS boy wants a knife, small, which I will not sell him because I am fond of his fingers.

And then, three pages in, a line that made my mouth flood with the taste of fennel and copper, like swallowing a penny you ground between your teeth. STURGEON, he had written. 0.0 lbs, seen. Then the date. Then: four thirteen p.m., bridge.

We did not have sturgeon anymore, not here, not since before I was born. That was the story of the river they told us in school: what we had done and what was gone. The picture in the faded textbook showed a fish like a cartoon of a dinosaur, blunt and armored and impossible. They had been hunted until there were none left within the county line, and then the state went on building dams and pouring useful things into other useful things until the river made a noise most people stopped hearing. The boys used the word sturgeon the way they used the word love: to see who would turn their head.

I looked at the date again. It was only two months ago. The taste in my mouth shifted, and I thought of the way my father considered certain words weapons you should keep cleaned and hidden. If he had seen one, he would write it down as if it were a bill. He would do everything except tell anyone.

Ike came in from the porch with a breathful of cold. “You want me to bring up fresh of anything?” he said, but he was fishing around it, too. He knew about the ledger. Half the town did, half wanted it to be mystical so they wouldn’t have to take responsibility for anything written there.

“In a minute,” I said. “Did he… Ike, did he say anything about sturgeon, lately? I mean, recently?”

“Sturgeon,” he said, and made a shape with his mouth as if he were biting into a thought no one had fed him. “The old ghosts? Well. He always said they were better than us. He always said if there were a judgment we’d be weighed against one and found wanting.”

“But did he say anything else,” I said, and now I could feel the hunger rising, mine, the old one, the one that made me take things apart and arrange them on the floor in lines until the world made more sense. “I mean, did he say he saw one.”

“Ain’t nobody sees a ghost and shuts up,” Ike said, but his eyes went shiny and evasive. “Except him. If he did, then that would be him. He got real lonely about what he saw, that last month. He’d stare at the minnow tank like it was a TV you could fall into. He’d say the river was trying to tell a story to a person who could listen. He’d say but the person is tired. He’d say but the river can wait. He’d say some things he had no right to say.”

I nodded, as if what Ike had said didn’t matter, and turned the pages again. STURGEON. 0.0 lbs, seen. STURGEON, 0.0 lbs, seen. It went on, once a week, sometimes twice. He never wrote a weight. He did not write caught. He wrote, on Valentine’s Day, STURGEON, low near Wickham’s; I think there are more than one. And below that: Do not be sentimental. He had been writing to himself to take his own temperature. He had always done that when he felt his habits trying to take him. He would say, Robert, do not succumb to superstition; save it for Sunday. He would say, Robert, do not talk to your daughter as if you are a boy. He would say, Robert, for once try to let your hands do the thinking and your head go outside into the sun.

Behind me, the radio was talking about a lost dog. A golden something named Sunflower who answers to Sunny. The woman on the recording sounded like she was trying not to cry. I thought of the word sturgeon sitting under a poster over the freezer that said BEER IS CHEAPER THAN THERAPY. I thought of our river, turned and pushing back against what held it.

The bell at the door jingled. Margaret came in with a box of paper cups, which she put down and then, before she saw me, pressed her hands flat on the counter as if to steady herself on the edge of a lake. She had cut her hair in the six months since I’d seen her and dyed it the color of molasses. It made her eyes go dangerous and kind.

“There you are,” she said, and then caught herself and made the same face she made at the grandchildren when she realized she’d told them they were wrong about something small. She was only my father’s wife in the municipal sense. She had raised me without nursing me, and I loved her in a way that felt like a good coat: something you could rely on, not for glamour but weather.

“Here,” I said.

“You open up?” She reached for the ledger and then pulled her hand back as if she’d been about to touch a stove. “Sorry. I was going to bleach the counters. Is there a service for ledgers.”

“We will not bleach the ledger,” I said.

“We will not,” she said, repentant and amused. “I wrote out some ribbons for the wreaths, but I know he thought those were nonsense. Your father loved anything that had dinged edges and a job to do. Ribbons are always getting into trouble with him. I told him once that a little decoration doesn’t hurt, and he said, not on fishing, it does. And then I told him he could decorate his own coffin and he said one step ahead. Which he was not.”

I could hear the rhythm of the thin grief in her voice, the part that had not made its way to the bones yet. She had not been in the room when he died. I had. It was an accident, both ways. He had finally agreed to see the doctor about the cough, and I had finally agreed to come. He had laid his palm on the curtain as if it were a wall between two parts of a barn. Then, a small interval, a sound like he was clearing a stone from his throat and didn’t want to bother anyone with it. Then nothing. We stood around him in disbelief like mourners at a party. The nurse wore a pin shaped like a heron that seemed unkind, since the river had never loved those birds.

“Did he leave anything weird,” Margaret said, gently, in the way some people will say are you okay to mean I know you will lie but I will prefer that to making an actual demand of you.

I slid the ledger back a little, my hand still on it. “Define weird.”

She laughed, and this one tore a little. I could see her put herself back together and stand in the position of what was left. “He left a note in the coffee can for the plow, did you see? He wrote Get Roy before it snows again and then wrote, in parentheses, no say it differently: get Roy and then, under that, Roy will turn up, he always does. He trusted Roy to exist more than he trusted me to buy onion powder. That is not weird. That is just him.”

“He wrote about sturgeon,” I said.

She met my eyes, and her mouth did a thing I recognized from when I had told her at fifteen that I had dropped out of chorus, or from when I had told her last year that I was thinking of selling the apartment I had only just learned to tolerate. The mouth gathered itself to ask a better question.

“He wrote seen,” I said.

“Seen,” she said.

“0.0 pounds,” I said. “Like it matters. Like the scale was ready, but the fish took no interest.”

“Lucinda,” she said, and now she was praying, or something like it. “Listen to me. We are sad. You are tired. Your head will make quilts out of anything if you let it. You always did. Remember when you put all the blue things in a drawer and then could not think about anything else because there was one blue sock you could not find. And what did we find it in? The bread.”

“The freezer,” I said, smiling, because she was trying to rescue me.

“The freezer, yes. I said, why the freezer, and you said, I do not trust places that are warm when they should be cold.”

“He wrote it,” I said.

“And he could have meant he saw one on TV,” she said. “Or on a sign. Or in a dream. You know he half lived in his dreams. That man would have married the river if it had a courthouse."

I wanted to argue with her about that, and then I wanted to be glad that she was making him ridiculous so I didn’t have to. The ledger was heavy on the counter, warm from where my hands had been. I pulled it toward me again, as if it were a door I could hide behind.

A man came in to buy lures and left without saying anything to either of us, even though he had been my geometry teacher. Ivy from somewhere had made its way into the corners of the window and gone brown over winter and looked like someone had glued the idea of a forest to the glass. Outside, the river made a noise I had not heard in years: a little whispering slur as it went the wrong way, a child’s idea of rebellion.

I turned to the last page. The last entry was the day before he died. He had written STURGEON again, but his hand had been shaky, and the R slid into the G like a boat sliding back into the water. He’d written soon, too, and underlined it twice. Then: we did not do right by them. And below that, smaller, in a line that made the lemon taste of nine go sharp on my tongue: heard singing.

It is sentimental to say the water lifted then, or the minnows chorused, or the banner across the way let go of its one remaining nail. That did not happen. What happened was that the light shifted, a cloud went across and then off again, and in that small weather I could hear on the other side of the glass the river pushing its shoulder into the town.

Margaret set a paper cup on the counter and filled it with the coffee she keeps in the back for old men who think their hands shake less if they’re holding something. She slid the cup toward me without asking. “All right,” she said, more to the room than to me. “All right. Let’s take inventory.”

Of what, I wanted to ask. Of hooks and worm dirt, yes. Of rope and bleach and the gray rag he thought made itself clean if you hung it up overnight. But also of the things that get under the skin of a place and lodge there like grit, becoming pearls or sores depending on the season. If there were sturgeon, if there had ever been, then there had been a congregation at the bottom of all our mistakes. If there were sturgeon, my father would have hidden them like a man hides a suitcase of money he knows will buy him no peace. If there were sturgeon, then the river had not forgiven us but had simply carried on, the way rivers do, without our permission. If there were sturgeon, there would have to be a reckoning. The word tasted like cloves.

The bell rang again. A kid with a skateboard and a wet flannel came in and asked if he could have change for the vending machine out front. He was all elbows and privacy. He did not look at the ledger. He did not look at me. Margaret counted out a dollar and told him to bring her the quarter back if the machine ate more than it gave.

As the door swung shut after him, I lifted the book and tucked it under the counter, into the drawer where my father kept the good line. Neither of us said anything. Neither of us had to. There are things you put away not because they are secret but because you want to keep them near and under your hand.

“You don’t have to stay open,” Margaret said. “We can put the sign back up. We can go home and fight about where to put the photographs. It won’t be any use, but we can do it, if that’s what you need.”

“I need to see the bridge,” I said. “What he saw.”

She sighed, and her breath was a small field of white in the air between us. “Take a hat,” she said, because love often sounds exactly that ordinary. “He’d have told you to.”

I pulled his winter hat from its hook. It smelled like sweat and river. It made a noise on my hair like someone rubbing a balloon on wool. When I stepped back into the unseasonably cold April, the banner across the way snapped once in the wind and lay back with something like relief. The river ran east to west and then, at the old church, made its turn. The town had been built along that turn, as if to watch. What it watched for had changed. There had been a time when it watched for logs, for ice, for flood. Later, for barges. Later, for anything to do.

At the bridge, I put my hand on the iron and felt the cold come into me as if it were saying, I have a job, too. Downriver—a word that, for the day, made no sense—I could see the boys who fished after school even when they were men, their bodies pro and stubborn. They cast into the current and got their lines knocked back to them. One of them laughed and threw his arms wide, like he’d been hit with a compliment. On the far bank, a blue truck sat with its lights on, a radio ticking, a white paper sack from the diner on the seat.

I stood where my father might have stood and saw what he might have seen and thought of the thin bones in the fins of a fish that had once dined on dinosaurs, now sliding past the pilings like a rumor. I did not put my hand to my ear. I did not lean over the rail hoping to fall in. I did not want to become any more like him than I already was. The water was brown and urgent, and the light on it made a kind of armor.

On the way back to the shop, a girl in a red jacket with a snake sewn to the back walked past me holding a bouquet of grocery store tulips, and the smell of them was faint and bruised, like hands clap-smacked together and then parted. The wind off the river had an iron in it. It tugged my hat. It made the glass over the minnows inside vibrate so they turned, once, all at the same instant and then forgot why. This was not any sort of proof. This was just the day holding itself up to us without apology.

Inside, Margaret was writing in a little notebook she kept in her purse, the one with birds on it that looked like they were arguing. She did not glance up when I came in. She was making a list with care and then, between bottle of bleach and chicken broth for me, she wrote something and crossed it out I could not make out. And because it was Margaret, and I knew the way she believed in putting things in their right place in the body, I made her a cup of coffee without asking, and slid it toward her, and we were two women in a bait shop with a ledger under the counter and a river that had decided, for one afternoon, to break an old habit.

The bell rang again. The day went on. Somewhere down under the bridge, something that remembered us moved the way old things move: very little, but with a kind of absolute. I put my fingers on the drawer where the ledger was, and it was warm, and I did not open it, because sometimes you honor a thing by letting it be heavy without making it prove anything to you. The boys made one last cast. Someone drove over the bridge and the whole place hummed. The coffee tasted the way it always had when my father poured it: too strong and exactly right. In the margin of my mind, in the place where I kept other people’s secrets because they never fit in my own pockets, the last entry in the ledger kept its small music: heard singing.

Chapter One

They stole the monsoon at dawn.

I know because I’m the one who wakes the rooms each morning, and when I walked the corridor toward Six there was a hush where there should have been a kind of low, unspooling hunger—the patience of dark water gathering its own weight. I tasted the air (it has gotten so I can taste it, salt, copper, brick dust, the slight sour of algae) and I tasted nothing. No damp, no shiver, no threat. On the observation glass were the faint runnels where last night’s condensation had stood in beads, leaving a tide line as clean as a vanished shore.

The door to Six was ajar. Someone had unscrewed the antique brass hinges. They wrapped their tools in cloth, smooth-handed and careful, no scratches on the varnish. They knew the alarms and their blind spots. What set my skin prickling was the smallness of the gesture left on the threshold: a folded square of paper, the creases oily from fingers.

We return what you hoard, it said in tidy block letters. Sky belongs to no one.

I could have told them the monsoon we held never really belonged to us. The Museum calls them holdings, acquisitions, as if you could cup a season and mark it on a ledger. We curate microclimates, we say. Specialized exhibits. A place a city might come to borrow a small rain for a funeral, a steady wind for a regatta, a fog for a play wanting to deepen its mystery. We press them between panes of reinforced glass, wrap them in the language of stewardship. We speak of civic good. And still my grandmother used to say, on the nights the dehumidifiers hummed like a hive below our apartment, that the sky will never be obedient for long.

Someone had wiped their fingers on the lintel, leaving faint arcs of gray. Chalk from the old riverbed—the activists mark their routes in stone dust, which is almost funny if you think about it, because we are all breathing ancient ground all the time and the city declares it an act. Why not just sign your name with air?

“Oren,” I said into the com. “Six is empty.” I said it the way a person would say a room is empty, a chair, a drawer, as if a monsoon is a thing with edges. I leaned my head against the cool glass and listened to the not-sound, which is a kind of sound if you’ve spent enough years learning how to hear it. It was like waking up in a house and realizing a wall’s been moved overnight; everything the same, and not.

From the lower gallery came the early rattle of the queue. We open at six and a half; the line forms before first bell. A smattering of ration-keepers, a choir director with her rolled score, a boy in a school uniform gripping an empty inhaler like a prayer. The roofs of the city throw heat like another sun. Even at dawn, people are thirsty.

“I’m on my way,” Oren said, and then his footsteps were in the corridor, slow because of the knee he won’t let be replaced. He caught my eye and then looked beyond me, out through the glass into the held emptiness. His hand went to the latch of reflex and then fell. “But the locks.”

“Not forced.” I held out the note.

“Sky belongs to no one,” he read, and he snorted, a tired sound. “The Commoners again.”

“Or people who listened to your niece,” I said, and then I was sorry because the child in question is not a child at all but a woman older than me who had slept last winter in a tent on the museum steps as part of the hunger vigil, and on the fifth day, a boy who looked like her out of the corner of my eye came and fed her spoonfuls of broth while the cameras watched and then the cameras forgot. She had brought Oren a knitted hat when the frost came, hand-dyed, a gray that flashed green in certain light. He had worn it inside when nobody could see.

“Call Dr. Hye,” Oren said. “And shut up the lower floors until we’ve swept this level. I’ll lock down the vents.”

I slid the note into my pocket. “Do you want to be the one to tell the Borrowers we have a—” What? A gap? A theft? A crime with a victim made of two thousand kilometers worth of water waiting to happen.

He scratched his beard, white with iron filings from the workshop. “We’ll be measured. We’ll be careful.” Which is Oren-speak for let me take the yelling. He is soft with me, in the way of men who have loved a daughter and lost her to a coast on the far side of a closed border. Once, after a double shift, we went to the roof and watched an old lightning storm trapped in a test tank throw itself against the glass. He told me about his father’s hands, the stubbornness in his line. He said my work made sense to him because he had never been able to plan for anything and here you could at least rotate the cycles, turn a key, regulate. He did not say regulation is not the same as control. I let him believe it for both our sakes.

Dr. Hye was in when I called her office, which meant she hadn’t slept or she had slept in the little cot behind the broad desk, the way she did during last year’s heat bloom. “Tell me slow,” she said. “Tell me as if I cannot see.”

I told her as if she could not see. When I hung up I did the stupid thing and walked into the empty of Six. I stood there, expecting nothing and receiving it. The walls are lined with hand-blown glass panels that ripple like lakewater. We position them so that light moves. The floor is grooved with channels feeding into a cistern the size of a whale’s skull. When the monsoon is here, there is a particular odor of green numbed by rain, like crushed stems. The room feels made of breath. You can smell earth waking before it takes the first drop. Some days the pressure will bring tears to your eyes for no good reason, which is one way to learn that there was always a reason.

My grandmother brought me here when I was eight, a day so irradiated that her sandals stuck to the tar. She was not interested in museums, as a rule. To her, history had a smell like wool scorched by iron, and she had burnt enough of it out of garments to be done. But she had heard that the Museum kept the first rain, which was a marvel where we came from, and she wanted to smell it again and see if memory would oblige. I remember the cooler air of the lobby with a gratitude that felt dangerous, the way you feel taking an extra cup of water from a jug that is not yours. I remember the Hall of Named Winds with its brass placards: Simoom, Mistral, Harmattan, Föhn, Santa Ana, the names like a litany of friends who will blow your house down if you anthropomorphize them too much. “I dislike this part,” she said, and clicked her tongue at the archaism of it, “as if naming meant taming,” but she touched the letters as if she knew them in another alphabet.

She would not let me queue for the Schoolchildren’s Shower. She would not let me stand under the manufactured drizzle, would not let me cup my hands for the curator’s voice teaching fun facts about surface tension and scent. “Rain has a job,” she said. “Rain belongs to the soil it wakes.” But she stood for a long time at the window of Six, watching a storm pass itself between two panes of glass. “And if I tell you we met in such weather,” she said to me then, meaning my grandfather, an absence I had presumed into myth, “if I tell you the rain was like a drum and he walked without a hat, you will not know the texture of the hair on my neck and how it stood.” It was the first time I understood that a story was a room you could lock yourself in forever.

Outside the Museum, the city lifts its scaffolds into the sun. Someone will set a fire in a trash barrel somewhere because they have run out of other things to do with their hands. Someone will break a bottle. There is always a courier on a bicycle tagged with black-market wind. There are children on a roof with buckets, their mouths open to catch the dew. You could live here your whole life and never see a real rain without a ticket.

“Do you want me to close the vents?” Oren asked from the doorway. He knows better, but he likes to ask.

“Even if I said yes it would make no difference,” I said, and he smiled without looking at me.

“You make me feel useful,” he said. He goes to his panel anyway. Buttons are comfort. Locks are a religion one can afford.

By seven, word had bled through despite the staff shunting. When I slipped away to the Borrowers’ Lobby (an ugly name for a pretty room, all white plaster and skylight, the light itself our most popular exhibit) there were three messages from the registry blinking red. I passed the long ledger desk where the docents do their work, that cheerful army of retired teachers and retired meteorologists and retired anyone who could bear to explain once more why the fog is safe, yes, it will dissolve before you get home. There was a boy on the bench with a paper cup. He swished the water back and forth. His knuckles were pale as tallow.

“Mara,” called out Ms. Delgado, who has run the registry since I started, who has a voice like polished wood. “Should we be telling the queue to go home or what?”

“Tell them nothing for the moment,” I said. “Tell them the Museum is experiencing a routine systems recalibration and we appreciate their patience and that there will be vouchers.”

Ms. Delgado rolled her eyes so that I saw the white all around. “Always with the vouchers,” she muttered, then raised her head and used the voice sometimes the sparrows stop to listen to. “Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your patience while we recalibrate certain systems. We regret any inconvenience and will issue—” The crowd made its noise, the sound a large animal makes when lifting. People are kind until they are not, and then it is not kindness they withhold, it is an assumption that anyone is in charge.

“Can you help with this one?” Ms. Delgado asked quietly, tapping the screen that held an open application. I glanced at the file. A request for micro-fog, quarter-hour, for a hospice room. Dying in heat is like being sanded from the inside; we do what we can. The address was near the old canal.

“Yes, we can do that,” I said, feeling the shape my mouth made around the words. Fog lives down the corridor in Nine and is never in danger of being stolen because fog is humble and nobody stages a heist for humility. I printed the authorization and the spool keyed and spat out a square of thing-film embedded with the release chain. The film is an ugly brown, like chewed paper. We conjure nothing beautiful without dressing it in something unbeautiful to keep it from running away.

I was heading back toward Nine, authorization in my pocket, when Dr. Hye found me. She’d changed from her usual gray suiting into a shirt the color of bruised plums as if to be the opposite of a sky. Her hair was pinned in the knot I had seen her tie in the dark at three in the morning, flat-handed and certain.

“Walk with me,” she said, and did not slow to see if I would. We went down the long corridor where the walls curve in with the weight of water behind them, past the Hall of Winds with its names, past the staff kitchen with its stale coffee and the mesh bag of withered lemons. “They did not trip a single alarm,” she said. “They did not appear on a single camera.”

“They used the vents,” I said. “You need a body small enough. And the soot under the hinges was—”

“Riverbed,” she said. “Yes, I know what chalk looks like, Ms. Sima. I was born in a city with a cathedral made of the stuff. Do you think they knew what this would do?”

“What this would do,” I repeated, as if the phrase could be arranged into a different shape. It is not that our monsoon would be released whole from the room and sweep out into the street. That is not how the containment works. The confluence is a delicate composite. You cannot liberate it and expect it to remember itself. It would tatter like wet paper, shred into drafts and pockets; it would be like tipping a jar of river water back into the sea and claiming to have saved the river.

“However,” Dr. Hye said, “people will think the rains are coming back. They will look at the sky and believe it owes them.”

“They are not wrong,” I said, before I could make my voice behave.

She stopped. She turned toward me. It is a terrible thing to be looked at with attention by a person who spends their life choosing where attention will land. “I chose you,” she said, not unkindly. “You know why I chose you.”

“Yes,” I said. “Because I can tell the difference.”

“And because you know names and the right distance to hold them at. Slow releases, measured entries. I do not run a prison. I do not run a circus. I run a museum.”

I said nothing. The difference between a prison and a museum can be as small as who has the key.

“You’ll have media in the atrium in an hour,” she said. “Avoid them. Oren will say what has to be said. You will coordinate immediate substitutions—you will ensure no one’s morning is worsened because of this. You will not, under any circumstances, use your station to issue statements.”

It is a precise pleasure to be told what not to do and to know you will likely do it anyway. But I nodded and said, “I’ve got a hospice fog to issue,” and she let me go.

At the door to Nine I breathed through my mouth so the sweet rot wouldn’t feel like a hand. Fog is gentle but it can also hide the way your child will hide—too well for comfort. When we were little in our apartment on the ninth floor of the building that had never meant to be a home, my brother used to crawl under the bed and hold his breath until the air in the room felt like a thing you might eat. I would press my face to the slats and murmur names of winds to him like fairy tales. Zonda. Nor’easter. Khamsin. He would put his finger to his lips and make the smallest sound of refusal I have ever heard. He was a good hider. He is very good, it turns out, at disappearing.

I engaged the micro-release, watched the fog pool against the glass and then travel, a gray animal, into the delivery channel. We send it along the old pneumatic tubes that used to carry messages and coin between the floors of the city’s first department stores. We are a museum of air in more ways than one.

In the monitor, the fog arrived at the hospice room. I saw a nurse with a green braid down her back lift the pane. The fog spilled and climbed politely to the ceiling. In the bed, a very still person made smaller by a great many things. You get used to the shapes people make at the end. I watched for the breath. I watched for the relaxing of a clenched jaw. There is a measurable change. Behind the nurse, someone stood with both hands on the window frame as if to hold the building up. Their mouth opened. Later, perhaps, they would say there was mercy in the room, and I would be glad they had words for it, however wrong.

When I stepped back into the corridor Ms. Delgado was waiting with her enamel cup of tea. “For you,” she said. “And there’s a man in the lobby with a jar.”

“That is not unusual.”

“He says the jar is ours.”

“That is extremely unusual.”

“He says it’s part of a set. He says he bought it from a boy on the quay last night for a swallow of whiskey and he woke up this morning with a taste in his mouth like dirt and coins and he does not want it.”

In the lobby the man was two breaths into a story that had already lived in him for years and had simply changed its final paragraph this morning. He smelled like rope and salt. He had the drifter’s shuffle and the clothes of someone who had once owned a good shirt and worn it every day until the idea of ownership had worn off.

“It doesn’t belong out there, does it,” he said, as if he were confessing. “It belongs in a place with labels.”

“Not everything does,” I said, because I should not be the mouth of the Museum when I haven’t even swallowed my tea. “But tell me anyway.”

He set the jar on the counter as if placing a child there. It was a squat glass thing with a rubber stopper and a clamp so blunt it had to have been sealed by a hand aching with a long job. The glass was cloudy. There was a ring of chalk dust around the neck, a polite collar. On the glass, someone had scratched a number with a key. It meant nothing to me. It meant a great deal.

“Where did you get this?”

“I told your lady,” he said, nodding at Ms. Delgado. “The boy.” His mouth tightened. “Thin like the reddest pine. Eyes from nowhere. Sold it me for a swallow and a story. I give away more than he did.”

“Who was he?” I said, but what I meant was: how did he move; what did he do with his hands; did he look like a person who might have once hidden under a bed and been the best hider.

“Wore a scarf even though it’s the hot season,” the man said. “Talked with his head tilted as if to keep something from falling out. Had a laugh like a door sticking and then giving way.”

My mouth went dry in a clean way, like fear. “Wait here,” I said, and took the jar to the back.

In the small exam room I sat on the stool the interns roll around when they are dropped into our hurricane days and think the chair has wheels so they must have wheels too. I set my ear to the glass. I am not something special. I do not hear voices. I heard a memory of sound, the way you hear a sea when you put one of those carved tourist shells to your head and all it is is your own blood. I smelled something. Not green. Not stone. Not the sour sweet of fog. It was iron, rain on the tongue. It was the faint mold of a closet that has been closed too long. It was cumin. It was the first room I remember, where the windows stuck and my brother pushed his hands into the gap they made and whistled to the pigeons. The smell of summer thunder six blocks over on a night where you are small and sure nobody will ever pick you up again if you sit down on the step. And under it, a kind of purpose. It made the skin on my arms sting as if I’d come too close to something meant to burn me.

I turned the jar to look at the scratched number again. On the bottom of the jar, a stuck label: Museum property, a faded stamp. Ariadne Reiss Foundation, our founding. A silhouette of a kite and a lightning bolt. Somebody had taken this from us; somebody had given it back.

There was a note under the stamp, folded into itself, a trick Elias had learned to entertain me when we had no toys except the ones made of paper. I pulled it out with tweezers because the oil from your fingers is part of how a thing begins to change.

Mara, the note said in a hand I had seen only in the margins of recipe books and scrawled on the underside of maps and once, in black marker on the inside of a pillowcase when he was ten and let the thought of leaving for good possess him for a hot afternoon.

You smell it, don’t you.

Meet me where the floodgate sticks. Bring nothing. Leave the alarms asleep. If you tell anyone, the river decides.

I put my throat to my collarbone and waited for my pulse to quiet. “You stare like you lost your keys,” Ms. Delgado said from the doorway, which is another way to say a person looks like they are subtracting thirty years from a single breath.

“Do me a favor,” I said, and my voice knew enough not to crack. “Tell Oren I’ve gone to inspect the old intake valves.”

“That’s a lie with better shoes,” she said approvingly. “Shall I tell him to take a lunch when he gets back to the desk and to call his sister and to drink water and to consider the possibility of joy? And shall I tell the cameras not to see you?”

“Tell them to misplace me for an hour,” I said.

“And the boy with the jar?”

“The man with the jar can have three more vouchers. He did not know what he was buying.”

“None of us do, baby,” she said, and touched my arm, just where the skin is thinnest, with the wisdom of a person who has issued too many tickets for small reprieves to believe in rescue anymore but does it anyway, which is a kind of faith. “Go before the river changes its mind.”

I went.

If you have never been to the old floodgate, you have never watched the city pretend it can say no to its body. It is a rusted mouth that refuses to close no matter who tightens the instruments. Children like to dare each other to touch it. Lovers write their names in the silt where the water licks when the tide is wrong. There are the hinges, thick as calves. There is the list of dates when the gate did and did not do what it promised. A museum of failing. We are very proud of it in the way of things we cannot fix.

At the last stair the air changed the way air does when it decides to belong more to a river than a road. The chalk dust in the corners had been rubbed with a thumb. He was there, of course he was, thin enough to fit inside a narrow thing, in a scarf he did not need because he believes rituals stop us from becoming other people too quickly. When he heard my feet he did not turn. He had the gift of withholding that is the opposite of pride. He put his hand on the iron as if it were an animal that might bolt. I looked at his wrist, where the skin is pale. It was my brother’s wrist. Once he had held my hand so hard the bones popped like the knuckles of a child one by one and we laughed because it sounded like dry peas hitting a jar.

“I smell it,” he said without facing me. “All the time. Does it smell different in there?”

"It smells like then," I said.

“Then is the most dangerous scent,” he said. “You asked me once what I wanted. I said a pocket to put the cold in. I didn’t know you were already keeping one.”

“You stole a storm,” I said. “Or part of one. Or a label. Or a promise.”

“I opened a door,” he said finally, and turned toward me. He had a face like mine with the angles changed by weather. He had a laugh coming that he did not let out. “Which one of those is a crime depends upon where you stand.”

“Where you stand is under arrest, Elias,” I said even though my hand had not so much as twitched toward my com. He looked at the black bead on my shoulder, as if he could make of it a witness that would choose its own testimony.

“You won’t call,” he said, because we had never built a world where that would be the ending. “And besides, you need me.”

“For what?”

“For the thing that’s already coming. For the fact of it. You think you can hold absence as well as presence. You cannot. They didn’t just steal a monsoon. They left you a hole with teeth.” He put his hand in his pocket. He brought out a key I recognized. It fit our oldest locks, the ones they keep for display. Ariadne’s key, the founder’s, with the notch that looks like a swallow’s tail.

“Those keys are museum pieces,” I said.

“So are we,” he said. He touched the iron gate, the rust lifting in a soft red cloud like old blood in water. “Why are you shaking?”

“Because,” I said, and in the breath before I thought better of it, “it’s not yours to do, to decide, to open. You left and you left me and you left her and you left and now you come back with a pocketful of weather and a speech.”

He leaned his forehead against the metal. “You know how I said I wanted a pocket to put the cold in,” he said. “What I meant was I wanted a place to stop time when it got too fast. The problem with all your rooms is time still moves. It keeps its own weather inside its own glass.” He turned. In his eyes something unclenched. “I took the note from the throat of a jar because the city cannot live like this anymore, because you cannot do what you do and be the person you are without breaking, because they were going to steal it anyway and make worse of it, because I wanted you to hear a sound again. Choose one. Choose all.”

A gull cut the sky with its bad grammar. The river slapped a gnawed pylon. Above, a street vendor rang a bell nobody uses money for anymore because rings are free.

“Come with me,” he said, and I did, because every story we told each other when we were children began with those words and only some of them ended in a scar.

We slipped into the shadow that the gate makes at particular hours, when the sun and the river and the memory of a storm held too long align so that anybody standing just so looks, in the right photograph, as if they were walking into a different weather. There is a photograph like that in the Hall of Founders. Ariadne Reiss stands in her boots and her skirt with a teacup in a hand that should hold a wrench, and she is smiling, the smile of a person who has found a way to keep a thing that ought not to be kept and thinks she has solved something. People stand before her plaque and see genius. I see a woman who never once had to decide between water and reputation.

“What did you open,” I asked. “What did you let out.”

Elias’s hand closed on my elbow, hard enough to hurt. He smiled then for real. “What did I let in,” he said, as if the distinction mattered, as if the hole with teeth were a door after all and not a mouth. He lifted the latch that sticks if you are unsure. He was never unsure. That talent is another kind of cruelty.

Behind the gate, the river took a breath. It is a funny thing to see, a body of water breathing—the surface goes tight, then eases, the way a shy dancer steps into the arc of a partner’s arm and allows herself to be led.

“Listen,” he said.

I did. It sounded like weather remembering its first work. It sounded like a promise my grandmother made and then broke, and I could not forgive her and I loved her all the same. It sounded like a city practicing a kind of prayer it had forgotten.

For the first time in years, without paying, without a permit, without the rub of a stamp on my wrist, I thought we might be about to get wet.

Chapter One

On the day the river gave the dead their words back, Nia had dried ink beneath her fingernails, the kind that does not yield to soap but fades only with time and care. It was the first real thaw, the brief window when winter relinquishes its hardness and the city remembers it has a pulse under the crust. The Roža ran different in that season—milk-white from the ground meal of ice, cold to the eye, the way grief is cold.

She was on her way to the North Quay building with a paper-wrapped packet of returns tucked under her arm. She had taught herself to carry the thing like a loaf, as if it might grow stale if handled with indifference. The sky was the pale blue of stationery. Men in rough coats were testing the strength of their boats and the cracked boards of the quay. And at the far end, a boy with a stringer of silver fish in his fist saw something snagged in a whorl of eddies.

It was a canvas bag, silt-bruised and bunched tight with a strap. It knocked against the quay, a low, dull sound like a shoulder against a door. There was a brass plate riveted to the leather: POSTAL SERVICE—WINTER SERVICE—NO. 73. The rope that had secured it had frayed to hair; where the fibers ended, frost glittered in the sun. The boy squatted to reach, slipped, recovered, and then the boatman with the scar on his lip hooked the bag with a gaff and hauled it dripping into view. The bag bled glacier water onto the wood with the slow insistence of a thaw.

By the time Nia reached them, there were seven or eight watchers, the kind who materialize when luck—good or bad—runs at the surface. She knew men like that had watched her father when he hauled crates out of the Roža in flood-time, back when they were building the second bridge and the river kept throwing back what it did not want to bury: boards, barrels, in one case a whole wardrobe with a mirror inside that had survived the fall intact. "The river is a selective archivist," he had said, cigarette behind his ear, moustache lifting with the words.

Now the boy pointed with the dirty pride of finders. "Look at the tag," he said. "Winter Service."

"That would be from the mountain run," one of the boatmen said. "The passes. Maybe they used to sling these across on wire." He eyed the bag. "What good is winter mail now?"

"There are people to whom loss is never out of season," Nia said without thinking, because that sort of sentence lived beside her tongue when she was tired. She saw the look the boatman gave her—small, amused, vaguely annoyed by poetry getting to the front of the line—and softened. "It's postal matter," she added, to no one and everyone. "It should come with me."

In her head, she was with her father again, in the smallest room of their old apartment, which they called The Cupboard and which was where he kept his uniforms and his stamps. He had taught her to love the things that moved quietly. Words on paper. The smell of glue. The way a stamp adhered if you warmed it between your fingers first, and then smoothed it from the center outward with the pad of your thumb. He had always said, clean hands for other people's words. As if shame could transfer through handling. As if their lives required wholesomeness even if hers did not.

The bag was heavy. Two men lifted it with equal parts ceremony and curiosity. It sloshed against the boatman's knees. The brass plate had oxidized in a way that looked deliberate, sea-green around the letters like someone had shaded them. The strap creaked as if shrugging awake. There was a lock, but it had corroded open.

Inside, she had expected pulp—a gummy, illegible mass—but whoever had packed Post No. 73 had known his weather. The letters were in bundles wrapped in oilcloth and wax. The wax had cracked where the leather had rubbed against it. When she lifted a bundle, cold threaded between her fingers. It smelled of beeswax and mold and something older, buried wood.

The watchers drew in their breath in the same communal way they would have done if she had raised a hand full of gold coins. Even the boy leaned forward quietly. They were of the city; they understood that sometimes the only treasure is a story no one else has heard.

She carried the thing like a baby across the quay and into the North Quay building. On ordinary days, the building did not look like anything that special; it was a municipal hulk with a history of shingles. But the way it had settled—slightly atilt, stubborn in the mud—made it feel like a barge that had gotten tired of floating. The whole first floor was sorting; above that were rooms for the clerks and inspectors, a canteen with an oilcloth table, and at the very top the room that the original plans had labeled Dead Letter Office and later, when euphemism was a public policy, The Division for the Handling of Undeliverable Mail.

She had a key to the top room. The lock was new, because people thought relics needed security; she respected that but sometimes thought it betrayed a misunderstanding of what was valuable. Inside: shelves, pigeonholes, a long worktable with embedded knife marks older than she was. A high window gave onto the river, which she loved because it meant that if she lifted her head from her work she saw water moving, a reminder that even the unmoving had a current to it. She propped the window. The room exhaled.

She cut the string on the first bundle with a letter opener that had belonged to someone before her, its handle smoothed by other hands. She placed a blotter under her hands the way she always did. Her father would have liked that.

The oilcloth peeled back with a reluctant sound. The top envelope was addressed to a Mrs. Eliska Fiala in the north quarter, in ink the color of bruises, the letters slanting to the right with a confidence that read as prewar. The ink had not bled. The stamp was a post horn with a 3 in the corner. On the back, the wax seal had impressed a dove. You could almost see the hair of the clerk in the wax, a stray. She turned it over and over in her hands, examining the way time leaves fingerprints, then set it aside and made a note on her ledger: Fiala, Eliska, North Quarter, stamp three crowns, dove seal.

The second was to a Maria Varjak on the south hill, an address that no longer existed since they had taken the ridge for the reservoir. She had a map in her head of the city, but hers had too many topographies layered on it: the city of her father's steps, and the city of the brochure, and the one that existed in a hundred brittle photographs in the Archive, and the ghost city with its streets under water. When she placed Maria Varjak's letter in the stack for addresses that had gone under, the sound of paper on wood made the two boatmen who had followed her to the door straighten. They had the solemn faces men wear at births and burials.

"This is where the dead words go," one said, and then, as if remembering he was speaking to a clerk, added politely, "With your permission."

"With mine," said Nia, and the formality relaxed them. She gestured to the two chairs against the wall. "You can sit if you want. I just need to log what's here. After that the Inspector will wring his hands and talk to the papers about heritage and the duty of state. He will promise everyone something that will satisfy no one. Meanwhile I will do the work."

The older boatman laughed quietly. The boy stood with his fish turning slowly on the stringer like a clock.

She worked. It was the kind of work she was built for. The letters had lives; she acknowledged them. She breathed fewer times per minute when she was doing this—she had measured—and she ate standing up less and slept better. It reconstituted her.

On the fifth envelope she paused. It was addressed in childish careful capitals to Army Post Unit 17, which had meant to find a boy somewhere in the mountains with a bowl haircut and the conviction that the world could be negotiated with. On the back, beneath the seal, someone had written, in a smaller hand, if the war is over, break the news to him gently. Time had done that.

She cracked a seal to see what state the paper inside was in. It was a simple sheet, blue lines, the corners nibbled by mice in some brief dry era in the bag's long sleep. The ink was iron and smelled faintly metallic when you lifted it to your face. She did not read the words, because that was not what she was authorized to do; she just breathed them.

By noon the Inspector came in with his usual array of intentions, smoothed his moustache, and said the things he thought he should say. He was a man with a consecrated paperweight.

"Have you any idea what this is, Nia," he said. "We have been given a patrimony. These will be—"

"—people's mail," she said. "They will be people's mail, sir."

He disliked being cut to a plain term. It thinned his blood. "We will need to calendar a press call. The Minister will want to be seen. The public loves stories that make history seem personal."

"It is personal," Nia said. "So personal they are addressed. We should attempt delivery."

"Delivery," he repeated, as if the word had recently been removed from the language and she had smuggled it back in. "To whom? A Mrs. Fiala who is a hundred and thirty if she is lucky? You are thinking like a clerk when you should be thinking like a storyteller. We can make a commemorative exhibition. Work with the Museum. Stamps. A fountain pen display."

She had never been good at letting her face be the thing she did not feel. "We will do what is proper," she said, each word carefully folded. "We will try. Where there is no recipient, we will find the nearest living kin. Where there is no kin, we will find the place they belonged and mark it. There are stories, yes. It is not your job to corner them. They will unfold if allowed. The public likes stories that behave like people."

"And the one thing we cannot do is guarantee satisfaction," he said, taking his compromise out of his vest pocket and polishing it. "I will send you an assistant. It will take more than your hands."

"Ira is enough," she said. "And the boy, if he wants to ferry." The boy looked up, startled to find himself in the future, and then nodded gravely, as if he was accepting a conscription.

"Ira is too sentimental," the Inspector said.

"Yes," Nia said, because with the exception of her father, everyone she had admired had been described that way by men like the Inspector. "Yes, she is. It helps."

After he left, she pried open the second bundle. Names were a brief nation under her hands. Varjak, Kehr, Paun, Botoș, Vacek, Sulejman, a mix as rough and genial as the city. She had dried a dozen with blotting paper, had separated three dozen by the shape of the addresses into manageable stacks, had written the same words—undeliverable, to be located, unknown street—in a column she had invented as a girl for the pleasure of columns, when she saw the envelope that would change the grade of her breathing.

It was not beautiful. It was an envelope like others of its age and kind: cream gone to yellow, corners rounded, the side seam with a small tear. The stamp was cheap. It was all in how it was addressed that her skin understood something before she did. The script was tiny and deliberate, as if the writer had no faith in the postman but an obscene amount in the future. The address read:

TO THE KEEPER OF UNDELIVERED LETTERS
NORTH QUAY SORTING OFFICE
CITY

On the back, the wax was black—not the killed black of funeral seals but a muddy black like lamp soot mixed into beeswax with a spoon. The impression was a small key. Underneath, in another hand, was an instruction: if found after the thaw, open only with clean hands.

Her father laughed in her head without moving. Then he said, even though he was five years dead, or five hundred in the way that certain kinds of dying make of a man, "Nia, mind you wash."

There was no date, not visible. No return address. It could have been from yesterday, if yesterday had learned to disguise itself as a hundred years ago. It could have been a joke, a planted thing—if the paper had not smelled faintly of resin and packed snow when she raised it to her mouth as if it were a piece of fruit. She held it too long. The boy stopped humming over his fish. Ira, who had drifted in quietly, glanced up from her stool by the window like a deer at the scent of rain.

"What's that?" Ira said. She had white hair she wore like a hat and hands that were gentle even when they were rummaging. Nia had once watched her coax a letter out of the belly of a book like a midwife bringing out a breech infant.

"Addressed to us," Nia said. She said it dryly so as not to alarm the room. She placed it on the table the way a careful person places their palm on the flank of a horse they do not yet trust. "To the office. Unsigned."

"Time behaves badly," Ira said, smiling into her collar. "Life only pretends to make sense to soothe men like Pavek."

"Don't call him by his name," Nia said, reflexive, and then, because she was honest even when no one asked it of her: "This is nonsense at a high volume."

"Open it," the boy said.

"Not yet," Nia said. She turned it over again and again as if agitation could be pressed out of it like water. She imagined it had been written by a clerk with the same job she had, hunched over in a cold season with a handkerchief in his sleeve, his mother alive and cooking cabbage, the city in the same place but a different age, someone who had thought as seriously about addresses as she did. She thought of it addressed to her not by name but by function, and felt that particular intimacy that was not personal but cut deeper because it was not. Use. The kind of affection that is not about you but about what you do.
