All afternoon, the bag kept bleeding its past onto the blotters and rugs. She logged. She made a list of streets that no longer existed and then, because she was not in the practice of only listing defeats, a list of names that still appeared in the phone directory. She assigned addresses to apartments in her head. She watched the river in the window bruise itself against the west bank and fall back, then try again. She did not open the letter.

At five, the Inspector returned with a photograph crew and discovered that she had moved the bag to the far table and covered it with a clean sheet, which made him say "Ah!" as if she had hidden something valuable. She said, "No," and he said, "Yes," and she said, calmly, no again, and because her calmness was the sort that opens a door and not the sort that closes one, he found himself stepping through. He took his photographs of the edges, of the idea of the find, and did not ask to hold the letters themselves. She liked him for brief seconds at a time when he remembered what he did not know.

By seven, the building was quiet. The boy had gone home with his fish, one eye bright, one dim. Ira had gathered her skein of errands and drifted away like a river plant. The Inspector had gone somewhere indoors to turn himself into statements. Nia lifted the window. The river sounded like torn paper. She put the letter in her pocket because if it stayed on the table it would become communal—not legally, but by the laws of rooms. It did not fit her lambswool cardigan well; she would have to be careful not to crease it.

Outside, the thaw had loosened everyone. The air had the taste of a coin held in the mouth too long. She walked upriver past the bridge and the little park where the trees were still suffering out their buds, past the woman who sold shoelaces and the old man who fed the brutal swans broken cake, past the corner where her father once tripped and fell in a way that made a memory, because he had laughed as he went down. She climbed the three flights to the apartment she had not been ready to leave after he died and had therefore furnished, in an act of defiance, with nothing new.

On her windowsill there was a white envelope that she had not opened in two weeks. Her mother had written her after a period of silence that Nia had ended in the way a person does when they have written the same letter in their head for a year and cannot stand one more day without its existence. Her mother’s reply was in a careful script she had improved at night classes in her sixties. The envelope had gone a little soft where she moved it each day to dust and put it back. She had told no one this. It sat under the plant that was trying to be an orange tree.

She washed her hands. She scrubbed her nails with the brush. She did it the way her father had taught her after the day she had adopted the letter with the mud and the blood on it: thumbs, web, back, clasp, rinse, each finger pure. She thought of the admonition on the back of the letter in her pocket; she thought of all the hands between then and now and the ones to come. She dried them on the cotton towel with the faded initials that were not hers but had belonged to the woman who had lived there before her, who had left it as if to say that things do carry on even if.

At her table—a plank with legs that creaked when you set down anything heavier than your hand—she set the letter. She set it not in the center but to the left, closer to the window, where the light was thin but honest. She took the butter knife because she could not bring herself to use the letter opener on something that had traveled through time. She touched the wax. It felt like skin. When she leaned down and drew in the scent of it, there was a sweetness she wanted to name and could not. Smoke, yes. A note of Tony, the beekeeper from the canal, no. She was making up elements to distract herself.

She slid the blade under the flap, carefully, carefully, and paused, the way a person pauses on a winter morning to consider whether to put both feet on the cold floor. She thought of clean hands. She thought of the way that, some mornings, her father had stood in the door of The Cupboard and called her by her whole name, like a prayer and a verdict and a greeting from someone who planned to see her again.

Down on the river, a barge blew three notes, and the room trembled. The beeswax of the seal gave the way an apple gives under a tongue. She saw the sound of the tear before she heard it. She told herself there was no right order for things and yet there it was, the opening, the tiny surrender. She thought of the unopened envelope on her windowsill and of the unopened places in her, and of how she lived on the ridge-line between them.

The flap lifted. Inside, she could just see the edge of the paper: thick, rag content, the texture of old linen. She slid her fingernail under the first fold and then—she laughed because the page resisted like a chair with a trick leg. There was a single sheet. The ink was brown to the point of black. The hand was not the same as the address hand; it looped when it could and compressed when it was shy. There was a date in the corner, faded as if time had licked it: 3 November 1918. There was no name at the bottom. At the top, it began without salutation, like a conversation resumed in the middle.

Nia put her hand flat on the table where the paper would lie. She did not start reading. The city pressed itself against the panes. A drop of meltwater slid off the toe of the envelope and darkened the wood, a perfect circle. Somewhere, over the reservoir where the old neighborhood slept with its streetlights forever dark, a bird made the sound of a hinge.

She blew out a breath she had been saving since the quay, tasted iron, and set the paper down. The river kept moving. The future, like a small animal, had come closer without her looking at it directly. She bent her head and began.

The year the wind forgot us, I opened a shop for scents that weren’t there.

People brought me their rooms in shoeboxes. They brought walls, folded up on slips of plaster. They brought quilts sealed in plastic, cedar chests still sweet where someone’s hands had not been. The air in the city hung like laundry that would never dry. Flags stiffened and stuck to their poles; a swarm of gulls, confused, took up a permanent roost on the rusting crane by the ferry terminal and blinked at the tepid horizon as if waiting for a cue that didn’t come. On days when the heat climbed and the canal went its particular algae-green, the whole waterfront smelled faintly like a mouth slept in. Men in suits stooped at the corner to lay their palms against vents; they wanted to feel anything moving.

On the first day I propped open my door with a brick, out of habit. The bell tied to the handle jingled once for bravado and then fell quiet, as if embarrassed. Tiny things betray you when the big ones do. Without the draft from the river, the bakery down the block kept the sugar of its morning buns to itself. The tannins of the tea shop stayed in their tins. A small boy in a bicycle helmet stopped at my postcard display and spelled out the name I had painted on the glass. Olfactuary. He kept stumbling on the f. His mother corrected him and then slouched in the shade in a way that meant she had not slept.

Inside, I had arranged the shelves like ribs. Heptagonal, light blown glass, each vessel obese with anticipation. I had scoured salvage yards for the right stoppers, the right cork. I had tuned my ventilation until the room was a quiet lung. On the back table I kept my books, ledgers with onion-skin pages and field notes about the things people said they remembered: the metallic vote of lightning right before it arrives; the powder under a grandmother’s breasts; the fat, clean sugar of August corn; a father’s nicotine, slept-in wool, anise. There were formulas beside some of the entries. Beside others, question marks, or angry lines where a customer had gone blueshift and then resolved into tears, all of which I tried not to layer into the tinctures. My nose knows when someone has cried. Grief has an iron shape that comes through no matter what flower you float it on.

Clients sat at the small iron table where a café would’ve given them coffee. I had glass droppers and white blotting paper and the habit of asking them to hold their breath. Not for long. Just enough to empty themselves of whatever they had been breathing while they crossed the heat-sprung street, whatever argument they last had on the phone, the hair of the last stranger who brushed past them. A pure inhale, I told them, once, so that what we made could be as close to a time machine as the body allows.

A woman named Edwina came in carrying a winter coat in a trash bag. She had bucked the trend for summer—most people wanted warmth, they wanted citrus to trick themselves into a rising sun, or grass, or the salt you get from the first good wave breaking on your shins. Edwina wanted the smell of the inside of her father’s sleeve when he came back from the fisheries before they closed. I lifted my dropper above the back of her hand and watched the very finest hairs there tilt to the room’s soft currents. They were still. I thought she might cry. She didn’t. She sucked her lips in like she was tasting salt.

“Can you do it?” she asked.

“Yes,” I said, because yes is the currency. Yes gets you in the door of other people’s rooms. Because I had been the one with a bag of useless clothing once, too, and the person behind the counter had been twenty-three and made of kindness and certainty in a way that contained whole governments.

Anchovy, oak, diesel, mended wool, a touch of gasoline for the outboard motors that waited to hum under the dock in the gray morning. There is a way for a smell to smell like a metal boat without actually smelling like metal. I explain more than most people want, which is less a sales strategy than a genetics I cannot help. I explained how our brain holds on, how volatile compounds hitch a ride. I said it as calmly as I could, so she wouldn’t remember anything new here that might come between her and the thing we were building.

When Edwina left with the little blue bottle labeled daily, evening, no more than three drops, she pressed her coat to her face like she had scored against winter. It was eighty-six degrees outside and the sky was a chalkboard. She walked into it like a figure in a diorama.

My mother did not come by that morning; she had promised, and broken promises lately with a sort of gentle, befuddled surprise that made me want to put my head on the table and sleep for days. She used to be the one who remembered the day of the week by its bread. Tuesday was the seeded braid; Thursday was the rye I had to promise not to eat while it was cooling. My mother could pull a loaf from an oven, thump its belly and declare its mood. Now she stopped sometimes in front of a cupboard for minutes, just hand on the knob, something working behind her eyes and not finding purchase. Her making had been the axis of my childhood and the smell the weather of it. It turns out I opened this shop for her as much as for me, though I will not say that both to myself at once.

I poured water into the kettle so I would have an excuse to call her. The phone rang five times before she picked up. The wind’s quiet made the call sound like I had climbed into her kitchen and put my ear against the breadbox.

“Ma,” I said.

“Oh. Mara. Thank God. There are small moths in the pantry that I think are ghosts.”

“They’re not ghosts,” I said, because she knew that, once. “You have to put the flour in the refrigerator.”

“The refrigerator is full of music,” she said. Sometimes she was a poet. Other times it meant the actual radio was in the refrigerator. “I have your father’s hat.”

“Do you,” I said, the way you say it when you want to ease yourself up to an edge and look over without moving too fast.

“I found it in the shoe bin,” she said. “It had a spare key under it. Why did we have a spare key under your father’s hat?”

“I don’t know,” I said. I could picture the hat. A straw fedora with a battered ribbon, left out in the front hallway for years after he went, until one day when I was nineteen and angry with myself for counting such things, I took it into the back bedroom and put it under the bed as if it had died, too. I had never known about a key.

“The wires hum out here,” my mother said, her voice dimming toward the window like she had turned away. “Do you hear them? The trumpet thing?”

“The what?”

“The trump—oh, for heaven’s sake, never mind. Do you remember lemon oil on the dining table? That you had to make those little circles be full-sized circles, if you wanted—”

“Ma,” I said. “If you want, I can come by at lunch.”

“The moth ghosts,” she said. “I will put the flour in the refrigerator, but I need you to say it again.”

“Put the flour in the refrigerator,” I said. “And the rice. And the oatmeal.”

“I will,” she said, and then, nearly into the mouth of the phone, “That hat shouldn’t be in a shoe bin.” People’s priorities were not wrong when they came by illogically. They were simply rearranged.

When I hung up, the kettle had boiled. I made my tea strong just so my tongue would feel something. The day leaned on itself. The heat gathered in the brick until the brick began to sweat. The gulls down the block adjusted themselves along the crane like beads sliding on a string.

At noon a little girl in a school uniform tugged her grandmother in by the elbow. She stood silent until I crouched, so our eyes were on level ground.

“Do you do dog ears?” she asked. The grandmother had the look elders get these days when the children know the names of things the elders never learned existed, like iCloud and the idea of a fog farm upstate.

“I do dog everything,” I said, though ears are strong and can easily result in wanting to bite a table leg, which I have found is unpopular with parents. “Whose ears?”

“Moxie’s,” she said, and showed me a tiny tuft of fur in a sandwich bag. Moxie, apparently, got carsick and cried when he was picked up and liked to sleep between the girl’s ankles at the bottom of the bed. Moxie was a person. Dogs are often the most person in a family. I took the fur to the back. I didn’t need it—the oils were on the bag already—but people like the gesture. It makes them feel they have given me something I can touch. In truth, I could have reconstructed Moxie’s ears in the dark with my own dogless ankles. But part of what they are buying is how still I stand, the way I lift a stopper with both hands, the way I close my eyes. I gave the grandmother a tiny brown bottle with a buckle on it and instructions not to drink it.

I jot down recipes in the margins when people are still themselves enough to offer them. In my ledger there’s a list headed bread that my mother’s pen started before my pen took over. It runs out of ink halfway through the phrase pinch of salt. I have tried pinches as big as my whole hand. There are notes that say too brackish, not unlike the channel. There’s a drawing of a whisk. Under it, in a shaky version of my mother’s hand where the loops go wide and then fall inward like they are tired, there is a line that says what if the missing part is the part where we waited.

At four, the clouds stacked on the horizon in a way that only meant heat. The door had the stubbornness of a sleeping child when I pushed it. I had already given up on the bell making noise for anyone but me. A man in a lemon-colored shirt opened the gate to the park across the street, then closed it again because somewhere someone had decided the trees should only be looked at and not touched. The idea of a breeze was a rumor we told each other. We looked at the little ripples on puddles when a bus went by and tried to take it as comfort. If you held your hand out of your car window, if you had a car, you got a breeze, the rumor said. If you were very rich, you paid for air pumped through your vents with piped-in sea-salt scent and pretended you were on a boat whose anchor was a mortgage.

I wiped down the table again. Even without wind, dust knows what to do.

When I looked up, a man was standing halfway in the doorway as if there might be a membrane there that would resist him. He was tall in a quiet way. His shirt was the crushed-ice blue of a lake in the back of a postcard you never sent. He wore no hat. There was something of the old work about him—the posture of someone who has lifted sacks onto a truck, who has wiped rain off the back of his neck and then kept going. His hair was not gray but had the feeling of gray. He had a paper in his hand, folded twice.

“I thought,” he said, husky with not speaking, “that if I brought you the thing, you could find the smell of the thing.”

“We can try,” I said. Though it is easier if they bring me the memory before they shape it. Things lie, more than memories do. Objects have learned to go polite from sitting on desks.

He held the paper out. Not a letter—two photographs, glued side by side. On the left: a wooden kitchen table, bright with flour, a pair of hands whose fingers wore rings they forgot to take off before kneading. On the right: the same table, empty. The light had moved between pictures. In both, a chair was tucked in, slightly askew, the way someone does it when the day is a habit.

“What do you want?” I asked, soft. Because he might say anything and my job in that case is to make the question less certain.

“The second takes the first with it,” he said. He tapped the empty photograph with one big, cautious knuckle. “It’s wrong to look at. I used to know how it felt to smell something like bread in this, and then the bread was gone and it was the same air without… I want the second to smell like the first,” he said. “I don’t care if it makes me hungry. I should be hungry.”

I gave him a stool and he sat on it like he was waiting for a bus whose route he understood by bone. He did not cry. He did not even lean. He folded his hands in his lap and looked at the floor so that the floor might feel useful.

Sometimes what you add to an absence is nothing. What you have to find is the polish on the wood, lemon oil, a touch of rag. Also the ghost of yeast. The thin bitterness of a scraped-away burn. A person’s ring clacking accidentally against the rim of a bowl, the blue heat of the stove reaching for a pan. But if I gave him all that, I knew too that he would take it home and it would stand beside the empty photograph and the empty photograph would be no less empty, because what had left the room would not be the smell. Loss is not accessible by dropper. It is a season. And yet my job, if it is to be worth the word, is to give people what presses away the edges of their vigilance long enough for memory to come in.

I met his eyes. “Hold your breath,” I said.

He did, obediently. The vessels shone like eggs on the shelf. In the corner, a spider the size of my thumbnail had made a lucky home. I was building a structure to hold heat that is only ever useful early in the morning and late at night: a family kitchen. Counter after midnight. Bread for the morning. A person who can no longer sleep bent over it.

When he left, the man in the blue shirt checked his pocket twice to make sure the bottle was still there. He paused on the sidewalk. He closed his eyes and tipped his head back and the sun hit his throat. Somewhere behind his ribs a small thing unlaced.

Near six, the street changed its sound. You learn to read this, even when sound is the only thing that moves. My neighbor from the poster shop dragged his rack in. Teenagers on backs of bus benches slid down and stuck their shirts to their chests. The gulls let go of the crane one by one and the only reason to do it was maybe for the feeling of falling. I turned my Open sign to the language of sleep and then closed the door with the bell cheating out its little sound, as if it wanted credit.

On the counter by the till, a plain envelope lay as if it had always been there. Someone had slid it under the door when I had my back to the shelf. What I noticed first was that the stamp was from June of last year and not canceled, because the post hadn’t known wind was going to go on vacation and take its postmen with it. There was no name on the outside. Inside, a single line, written by someone whose letters leaned left like a person walking into resistance:

Do you keep the ones you cannot name?

I set it down like it might ignite. I have discards, orphans, near-misses, the things that cling to the edge of language like barnacles when your boat has not moved. I keep them in a tray in the back. They are quiet. If I put my ear to the glazed dish I keep them in, I can hear the ocean there. This is not a metaphor. There is a layer of salt in this city that cannot be explained by tears.

I flipped the envelope over, looking for fingerprints like a detective on a show with better light than this. The paper had the faintest bit of grease on one corner, as if someone had held it while they ate. Fish and chips, maybe, if you could find fish anymore. I licked my finger and touched the grease and then the tip of my tongue, which is how people like me commit crimes. Old oil, approximating new. Someone had been careful and then careless. The careless is always where you fall in love.

The day waited. I thought of my mother and her refrigerator of music. I thought of the hat in the shoe bin and the key under it. I thought of the look on the face of the man in the blue shirt when he inhaled the idea that would let him sit, later, at his own table. I thought of my father, who had once stood with me on the back stoop of our house when I was seven and explained that the wind had a name for each of us and that some days if you listened very hard to it you could hear it say yours. He had put his palm on the top of my head and said mine, out loud, so the wind would know it. I thought incorrectly of opening all the windows in the shop and then correctly of the spider who would be ruined by that.

When I stepped outside, the heat had become something you could lean your shoulder into. I walked the four blocks to my mother’s, past the boarded-up storefront that still had a painting of a hamburger in the window, so big it looked like a planet you could live on. Past the barber who had trimmed the same one man’s hair for twenty years and now swept out a shop that had stopped being cut by the geography of draft. Past a woman on a stoop with her hand between her breasts because a necklace she had worn there forever felt like a stranger. As I went, people sat with the posture of checking. Maybe this was the day something moved. We are ridiculous animals that way. We look up when everybody else looks up.

My mother’s street leaned seaward. In August, when I was a child, the fog would climb up it like something out of breath. My mother kept a basil plant that survived every apartment by sheer will. Now the basil was, like most things, a crease of itself. She had put the radio in the refrigerator once, but now it lived on top of the fridge like a crown. The pantry door was open, and two small moths did a lazy ballet in slow motion, as if somebody had turned the gravity up.

“Ma,” I said. “I’m here.” I put my palm on her cheek and found it cooler than mine. She had flour on her shirt but no flour spilled on the counter. She had a piece of paper in her hand and the paper was a recipe in my handwriting. She was underlining the words let rise as if they were an incantation.

“I want to do the part where we waited,” she said, not looking up. “That is the part that tasted like something.”

I took the bag of flour. I put it in the refrigerator. I took out the stale loaf from yesterday and cut it into squares and set it in a bowl to dry so we could make something else out of it. The small moths bumped into each other professionally. Outside, something loosened, but that was wish. We stood in the kitchen and waited for the part where waiting mattered.

There was a sound. It was a tiny thing, smaller than a trumpet, less than a whisper, the sound a paper makes when you drop it and it falls not straight down but with the idea of diagonals. It came first across my forearms—little hairs, long patient citizens of their own street waking up and turning their heads. It made my mother’s recipe quiver almost imperceptibly. The basil lifted its spears as if saluting. The curtains moved.

Then it happened the way the first rain after thirsty months hits the road and the road answers like whatever you had been doing was so small. The window I had left cracked for luck clattered softly in its frame. The dead plant on the fire escape let go a single seed head, light as a map of itself. For an instant, there was a smell like the inside of the ferry at dawn, when the fishermen still took their boots off before boarding. There was salt. There was engine, but kind. There was something else that knocked my chest once like a stranger saying your name on the street.

My mother stood very still. Across her face came the expression she used to get when the loaf answered her knuckles back. If the years of breathlessness had not happened, I would have said she nodded at the wind as if making an agreement. She put a hand out and the air went through the spaces between her fingers. She looked down at her palm, surprised and delighted in the exact measure a person is when they get their own joke.

“It smells,” she said, “like something is about to begin.”

It died almost immediately, the way you put a shell to your ear and what you hear is not the ocean, never was, and yet who is to say the ocean doesn’t live there for you because of it. The curtain settled. The basil remembered the law of it. Far away, a gull let out a single skeptical laugh and went back to being a statue.

Out in the hallway, under the hat in the shoe bin, I found the spare key wrapped in the paper of a business card for a store that had not been open in years. Open hours printed in a font that had believed in future Tuesdays. On the back, in my father’s hand—his printing was mostly vertical because he hated to lean—was a line. In case of wind, it said.

In my shop, there is a small tray of half-fails that I never put out, that I never give away, for fear of their contagion. They are the right notes in the wrong order. They make a person hear the past with the doors shut. People write me notes like the one on my counter. They ask me if I keep them. As if there is any other way to live.

That night, after I got my mother to sleep and killed the moths with a guilty flapping magazine and put the basil on the fire escape because it had asked politely with its leaves, I went back to the shop to close the window I had cracked. The city’s heat was a cooler shape. On the crane, the gulls reconsidered democracy. On the counter, the envelope waited. I held it up and caught the air that was left in the room—the slow moving water of it, the thick smoothing of it—and thought of the line my father had written. The door moved under my hand like something that could go. For the first time in a year, the bell on the handle woke of its own volition. It rang like a word you could build a life on. I could not name the smell that rode in with it. But I knew it. It had been there the day I was seven and he had put his hand on my head. It had been there the night he walked down to the ferry and did not come back. It stood in the room like a friend you thought had gone to another country and now was here, carrying something in his hands.

Do you keep the ones you cannot name?

Yes, I thought, though there was no one to hear me say it. Yes. I had just written the first line of a recipe. I had just put my nose to the glass. I had just felt the part where we waited turn into the part when everything begins.

By the time I got back from the northern banks, our house had been given an orange X, fat and sun-bright, the way children draw treasure on a map. It slashed across the wall between the two windows that never shut properly, dripped through the little crack where the bricks had turned powdery as biscuits, and stained the scalloped edge of my grandmother’s ganja plant with a bright, sickle-shaped bruise.

“Mm,” Nani said, looking at it as if considering embroidery. “They put their ideas where rain used to come. Come in, come in, your feet are full of river.”

I was still in the habit of stopping at the threshold to slap my palms against my ankles, as though river water had hands. Sand clung to the creases of my toes. In my satchel, the tin recorder bumped and clicked—there was a nick on its mouth that sometimes shrieked when wind blew against it, so I kept it wrapped in a thin handkerchief that smelled of fennel. The house smelled like turmeric, and the slant of mid-afternoon lit the jars of rain along our living-room wall in a row of long-necked ghosts.

Nani believed you could taste the difference between monsoons. Over the years she had done what everyone does with the little useless jars that live forever in kitchen cabinets, the ones worth less than their lids: boiled them, bleached them, and set them along our highest shelf with dates painted in her nail-bitten, red-lacquer letters. 1988, 1995, 2002, 2010, 2013. The oldest had a soft blue halo where the water had kissed glass and forgotten to pull away.

“Your shoes?” she said.

“I left them by the neem.” I looked past her to the mark, as if it could be made to move by being stared at. “What did they say?”

“They said a lot and very fast. That we must not cook after tonight, that someone will come to measure, that if we sleep we will be sleeping where we shouldn’t be. You know this, Lila. They have been saying it in the papers for a year. Their tongues just now arrived.” She turned toward the shelf. “Sit. By God, you are thinner. How thin you must make yourself to fit into other people’s stories.”

She kept a favorite jar, 2002, which she said had smelled of raw mango the first day the sky broke that year. Even now, she would unscrew it on afternoons when the roofs were blistering and hold the rim under her nose like a flower. It wasn’t the water itself that she worshiped, it was the air the water had sealed inside. “You trap a cloud,” she always told me. “You listen.”

The orange X on our wall glowed. Across the lane, Nasim-uncle leaned on his bicycle and watched me like I was the first rain that knew how to answer back. There was a thin boy with a paint-can across his shoulder still standing two houses down, looking apologetic. A hired wrist. He had given our home an X and then paused to drink from someone else’s steel cup. Two municipal men in sky-blue shirts had gone on ahead to the corner, where the banyan’s aerial roots had been bound up together like a plait so the bulldozer could pass.

I pressed my fingers to the wet paint. It came off dutifully, obedient to touch, and bright against the lines of my hand.

“Don’t put that in your mouth,” Nani said instantly. She was barefoot, of course, and unafraid. “It tastes like traffic.”

She had been eighteen when she married into this house, thirty when she hung the first rain jar after a monsoon that sank entire goats in the low fields. My father was born here. I was born in the back room furthest from the street, which is the cool room, where the wall sweats even when the rest of us are parched. A woman can hold a map in her spine, Nani always told me, and live in a place like an animal lives in its home: all angles and shortcuts, all kindnesses and hazards memorized. She knew which cracked tile sliced heels, which wooden beam hummed with termites after August, and which part of the roof sang when the sun was high. She knew which parts of herself belonged to which corner. Watching the X being painted, I knew she’d been counting.

“I heard the loudspeaker from the ferry landing when I was interviewing Meena,” I said. “She said this was coming.”

“And before that we heard it from the doctor’s clinic,” she said, “and before that from the school yard, and before that from your own mouth like you were a messenger carrying a heavy basket that could not be put down anywhere sensible. They sent a boy to make the mark anyway, so we know it’s time.”

Across town, along the river’s western bend, the dam had been blooming like a white sore for months. People there had stopped calling it a dam and put different shapes around it—wall, tooth, help, monster—depending on what they needed to say and what they needed to keep down. Next to our house there was a crack across the street like a vein, where the municipal men had measured and measured and mumbled, stepped over the mark, measured again, gone home to choke on onion chutney, come back.

“I wrote down two words today,” I told Nani, because it was what we did when things became too big to put in our mouths. Language had always been her way of holding the hot end of a stick without blistering. “One is for that curl of river around your calves when you step in backward. It’s not the same as how the current feels when your shin is forward. There’s a word. Did you know there’s a word?”

“Of course there is,” she said, and then added, “I don’t know it. But of course there is.”

“I have it,” I said. “It’s something like sikri, but not quite. Sikiri is the tassel at the end of a chela’s scarf. This is a weirder curl.” I drew a snake in the air with one finger and then gave up, because you can’t draw river with air. “The other word is for that particular ache when you try to move a large stone that has been settled a long time in silt. It’s not your body’s ache. The word means the stone’s.”

“That word probably wants a home more than we do,” Nani said. “What home can you give it? Where do they keep such things, these people you work for?”

“They keep them for a while, to make it clear that they kept them,” I said, and then felt the strange, sour laugh rise in me that I’d learned to keep down around her. “They keep them in big folders made of paper stiff as new bangles. They keep them in digital places, which means nowhere you can put water. They keep letting me keep them for a little while in here.” I tapped my satchel.

Nani gave me her old face, the one that refused to let me be clever in front of it.

I was used to the horror of loving my work. I had been hired by the Institute for Cultural Resilience, a long-coat name passing through town like a stranger, which everyone said was funded by the company building the dam. They said many things. Maybe it was the government. Maybe it was an American philanthropist with a soft heart and a hard head. Maybe it was the river itself, paying reparations for all the years it had been everything’s excuse. My first week on the job my boss told me to carry my own water, to keep my hair tied, and to remember not to arrive with my notebook in the obvious hand. It was a woman who taught me to listen without changing my face. I learned that too. I would sit cross-legged in courtyards and leaning against shop counters and perched on low temple steps while old men and women told me words they had kept in their mouths like seeds. They did not always believe in me. They believed in their words.

Every word I wrote down made a noise, like a dropped bead, in my head. Some nights I could not sleep because the words rolled across the floorboard of my mind and clinked against the walls. In the places where the orange X had been painted for weeks and weeks and the white-marked trucks had begun to be warm with furniture, people were still joking, still feeding stray dogs, still shouting from doorstep to doorstep. In our end, there were still hens. It was easy to think the river had promised us extra time. It was even easier, because we had jars.

“Do you want to open one?” I asked her.

She stood beneath the shelf and reached, not for 2002 like I thought she would, but for the shortest jar—2013, which was an unremarkable monsoon except for the way the sewer had backed up near our block and sent frogs into the primary school toilets. “Today needs a small rain,” she said. “Don’t fight me, Lila. Sitting makes storms in your back.”

There were dents in the lid where her thumb had learned the stubbornness of rust. She padded a towel around the jar and let me help, and when it gave with a tiny pop, something inside our little room changed temperature. It is hard to describe air you cannot see. It smelled of roofs going soft, of cow dung melting into field, of the one time a lorry crashed near the bus stand and a barrel of molasses spilled into ditch and men ran, laughing, with their open palms. I could swear I heard the whipped sound of sheets brought in from a line just before the first drop.

We did this once, sober and without reverence: unsealed a monsoon and let it warm our visit, sat with it until it went flat, and then at evening poured the water into the tulsi and told it to keep our names. We did this because the jars were not gods, only containers for a world we were trying to explain back to itself.

Now the air from 2013 washed against our faces like a dog’s slow nose.

“Eat,” Nani said, and when I said I wasn’t hungry she put my saucer on top of my thigh and said, “Eat as if eating makes the ground hold you.” She scooped the last of the pumpkin and new potatoes into my bowl. “They put paint on my house,” she said mildly. “So I opened a small rain.”

The boy who had made the mark on our wall drifted into our lane again, looking very much as if he had been told to bring himself back for a scolding and was resigned to a scolding. His hair stuck up in three ridiculous points and he had that air of being the youngest at home, a sort of determined humility that comes from washing everyone else’s tea cups. He looked at the jar in Nani’s hands as if it were illegal.

“You went too close to our tulsi,” Nani told him through the window grille. “Do you want to kill an old woman and a plant on the same day? That is too much for your karma.”

He blushed. “Aunty,” he said. “They gave us the line.”

“The line is crooked,” she replied.

“Your drain made me walk at a slant.”

“The drain was here before your line was a gleam in someone’s chalk,” she said. “Tell me your name.”

He said it, too softly. She made him say it again, again, until it sat on both our tongues properly. I have noticed that if you say a person’s name the way they want to hear it, some of the fog between you clears. The boy’s name was Rohit, which means red, which made him laugh a little bitterly and say, “It also means the name you shout when someone needs to carry something heavy.” He had a smear of orange on his cheekbone that looked like a thumbprint.

“Go wash your face before you touch your mother’s gate,” Nani commanded him. “If she faints, I will have to wake her, and I have no patience to wake strangers today.”

He grinned, sudden, and left, the paint-can thumping. His orange thumbprint remained on his own face like a prophecy.

When I had eaten the last bite and licked my fingers, to make it clear that I understood food and love were the same, I took my satchel to the back room to plug the recorder into the one working outlet in the house that did not make sparks. The back room smells of cassia and damp stone. It has a low chest with four drawers where my mother kept our papers: ration card, bank passbook, photographs she would not show, the school fee receipts that had always made Nani run a thumb down the right side to check what we owed. My mother left when I was eight. We do not, in this house, say “left,” we say “took the better bus.” In my first memory she is laughing with her eyes closed, holding up two bangles and guessing which one I should want. In my last, she is walking along the highway’s shoulder with a blue shawl and a smaller body beside her like a shadow that finally has a person for company. It stands to reason that she is somewhere on high ground, that she learned to make her tea with salt instead of sugar like the women in that direction, that she has not read the papers in some time. Every woman deserves the grace of being unknowable to the people she could not stand.

I opened the top drawer to put away the handkerchief that smelled of fennel and my notebook with all its little scribbles and saw, under the heavy envelope with the Institute’s name in English and Gujarati printed too quickly, a slice of paper that had not been there this morning. It was a page torn from a child’s rough exercise book, lines faint, grey-smudged, neatly ripped. On it, in pencil so faint I could only find the marks by angling the paper toward the window, someone had written: Don’t write me down.

I pressed the paper to my face and smelled chalk. The handwriting was almost perfect, each letter pretending to follow a ruler, as if whoever wrote it had been swatted very early for wandering. There was no name. No address. It could have slipped under our door from anyone’s hand in this block, even from a ceiling through one of the long cracks where geckos come and watch us.

You would think a historian-in-training would thrill at the arrival of a secret message. I felt only a sinking. Most things do not want to be kept. Most words live better on the backs of teeth and in the muscle of the cheeks. My job was to catch the ones at risk of drowning in the immediate future. The Institute had given me a bright paper for my satchel that said I was qualified to collect the last of anything. Old crafts. Terms for agricultural practices that needed a year of a year to explain. Songs. Small expletives. I did not have a permit for the names of the living.

The orange X on our wall dried like an idea.

At four, the light through the alley turned the dust as fine as spun sugar. A man came by and read names from a form. He had a voice made for arithmetic, precise and bored. Nani stood at the doorway and refused to be assigned a number. She told him she had a birth certificate, a marriage certificate, and a certificate from the municipal council that excused her from the late fee on her water bill because of her age, and that if he wanted to pin a number to her, he would have to pin it to the sari she wore for my mother’s wedding and he could do that only if he could find it, which he would not, because it was under the head of her bed in a trunk under the oldest rain jar. He wrote a number on his paper anyway and did not meet her eyes. He asked who else lived here and I stepped forward deliberately, like a shadow discovering it could move independently and wanting to make a point of it.

I said my name.

He wrote: “Lina.”

I spelled it and he dented his paper with a new letter, irritated. He said it back to me, still wrong.

“How do you get to name the water that pays you?” Nani asked him, barbed and sweet. He left a second X on the corner of our wall as if to bless us against ourselves.

When he had gone, the lane sighed. People went back to peeling cucumbers, beating rugs, oiling bicycle chains. People kept one ear for announcements and the other for gossip. That is the split all towns teach. Somewhere on the other end of the river, near the cantonment, someone began to play a flute very badly.

I went to the roof and lay my palm flat on the hot plaster for a while, convincing it of my existence, which is a trick I learned at school when I had a teacher who hated me and would only call on me after I had surrendered to the idea of disappearing. The river looked like a belt left on the floor after a long day. The dam threw back light like a tusk. There was a curl of smoke out past the brick kilns, blacker than anything else. A kite lifted, paper-thin, a shadow of something called fun. A little girl was climbing the banyan by our corner, working her body through the bound aerial roots with more patience than strength, already learning to make her path fit whatever the world had tied up.

When I came down again, Nani had fetched an old cardboard crate and was putting in it, with absolute stubbornness, the least portable objects in the house. The brass mortar whose pestle had made a dimple in her palm, the iron tawa that had belonged to her mother, the big glass jar full of buttons that no one had thrown away since 1971. Some objects nestle. These might as well have had nails.

“You can’t carry the stove,” I said.

“I’m not carrying the stove,” she said. “I’m carrying the circle where roti has been made.” She dropped the tawa in so it thudded like a small drum. “You will take the rain.”

I turned to the shelf and looked at the line of jars with their numbers and their tiny imperfections—the bubble in the glass of 1988, the twist in the metal lid of 1995 where it had been opened and re-sealed after a cousin’s wedding, the smear of clarified butter from someone’s fingers along 2010. I thought of rivers moving to embroidery in other people’s mouths, the way everything becomes myth when it is taken out of its calendar. I thought of the note in my top drawer: Don’t write me down.

There is a word, I know there is a word, for the refusal to move. Not stubbornness, which is noisy. Not defiance, which looks up too sharply. This word knows how to sit. It knows how to make tea. It wraps a shawl, not because it is cold, but because it will not be told to uncover its shoulders. It knows, in the dark, which jar to open and why. It must exist in some mouth. I have not found it yet.

Down the lane, someone began to cry with that particular creaking sob that means a child, and another person laughed, high and surprised, as if they had found a coin. The boy with the paint-can had wiped his cheek. There was a faint, wrong-season breeze.

“I will go and give Rohit tea,” Nani said. “His mother will not have time this evening.”

“Let me,” I said. “You have to keep putting the world in that box.”

“She belongs in the box,” she said, meaning my mother, and then looked at me as if she had slapped me and wanted to apologize. “Not her, but the shawl. The smell of it.”

“The shawl is not in this house,” I said, and she nodded as if to say, I know; it is in your voice.

I poured tea into two steel tumblers and carried them out into the lane, the hot sleeves burning my fingers in a way that felt like penance for something I had not admitted to myself. Rohit was sitting on the curb with his paintbrush held like a tail. I handed him a tumbler. He lifted it to his face, grateful and shy. We sat, a girl with a job like a net and a boy with a job like a mark, and we looked at our feet.

He said, “Some of the houses have been marked twice. Some not at all.”

“Nothing is fair if it happens to you,” I said.

“My sister says if you get to choose your pain our God is kind,” he said. “If you don’t, we must make our God learn.”

“Tell your sister to write that down,” I said, and he shook his head. “She will never. She says words inside. She says outside there are ears.”

We drank. People passed us with bundles on their heads and hands, with boxes, with a fish in a newspaper, with a dog, with a child with a dangerous eye for glitter. The river arced its dirty shoulder around us the way a mother arcs her body to make a cave, at least in the stories we are told and wish to be true. Above us, high and white and very far away, a man pointed in the sky as if he could direct the angle of a bird’s wing with his finger. On our wall, the X dried completely and became something you could not wipe away with the edge of your shirt.

That evening, I took down one jar with both hands, not because Nani told me to, but because something in me wanted to know the weight. It was 2002. The glass had a fat lip. My palms fit around it the way you hold an awkward baby. It was not heavy, but it was heavy enough to make you promise yourself you wouldn’t drop it.

I did not drop it.

My left sleeve caught the corner of the shelf as I turned, and that was enough. The jar next to it—1995, with its caved-in lid—tilted, tried to catch itself on the lip of wood, failed, and let go. Time makes a particular sound when it breaks. You can deny that it breaks by saying, It was only glass that made that sound, water doesn’t fall that way. You can deny anything, if you practice. But urgency has a noise. It is the hiss and smack of breath taken in at the wrong moment. 1995 exploded on the floor in sharp wet. The water went in every direction the tile would allow, a slow and determined spreading. It found the little channels we did not know were there.

We both froze, our hands like birds that had been looked at too sharply and didn’t know whether to lift or fold. The smell came like a slap, like the first time I had turned down a chance to go somewhere far because there was a test the next day and I had wanted to be good. School uniform after long rain. Mud tickling the roots of our toenails. The sorrow of a cricket who had crawled into a classroom to die. Nani made a sound I had never heard from her—a laugh, maybe, or its opposite—and then crouched and pressed her palms into the broken deep.

“Let it go,” I said, although I was talking to myself, to the boy with the orange thumbprint, to the little girl in the banyan, to the man in the sky, to my mother’s shawl.

We cupped the water back into a small island on our floor, neither saving nor losing it, neither gods nor authorities. There are some moments that are not metaphors even though you want them to be. Who was I to make this one mean more than a broken jar, a wet skirt, and the delicious, merciless smelling of a year when mangos went soft too soon?

I took my notebook out and opened to a fresh page. I wrote, in my untidy script that only I and an aunt in another town can read: the word for refusing to move when you have been marked to move. Then I left the space after it empty enough to fit both our hands.

Chapter One: The Cartographer of Loss

We had spent three years learning the grammar of loss when the sea decided to conjugate return.

On my first day at the Bureau of Vanishing—a clapboard building with a roof that sang in rain and a door that stuck at low tide—there were seven of us and one long table that bowed under maps. The maps were of everything that had disappeared: a spit of sand that used to hook into the lagoon like a thumb, a single date palm, a goat track, the blonde house of the shoemaker’s sister, two pirogues swallowed in the same storm as the shoemaker’s sister. The head of our office, Dorotea on her third set of reading glasses, told me we were not here to make anyone feel better. “We are in the business of measurement, not balm,” she said, dipping her nib into a bottle of ink that darkened like an old bruise.

I learned how to measure the shrink and fray with a hand steady enough to translate grief into centimeters. I learned how salt eats paper if you let it breathe long enough, how the wind off the water steals lines when the window is cracked. We logged the vanishing not because anyone would come to fix it, but because writing it down felt like laying a hand on a pulse and saying the name of everything that slipped beneath. The law had decided we should be precise about our diminishment. We were precise.

By the third year, my hand had learned to wait at the shore for a wave’s thought to change. The water on our side of the archipelago had begun to behave like a tired horse, stepping forward and back with more hesitation than I remembered from my childhood, misplacing its hoof, then trampling too far. People started tying their boats in two places. Babies born during those years learned to sleep through the long hiss of retreat.

There is an art to drawing an edge as if the world might move while you look at it. It taught me about marriage, about rage, about the way even the most determined love can shrink and swell under a moon you did not pick. It taught me to face, every morning, the knowledge that I could not keep what the sea wanted. I would say I chose this work, but the truth is that after Hana vanished I could think in no other tense.

Hana was my mother’s name. She taught mathematics at the secondary school and smelled faintly of graphite and cloves. She had a way of using chalk that made you believe a proof could be coaxed into docility. On Sunday afternoons we found shapes in the sky that were not there, assigning meaning to collections of vapors we would never touch, arguing quietly until the world darkened into its night names. The year the western wind stopped arriving on time, she took our little wooden skiff out past the point while I slept. In the morning the boat returned, but too light. It knocked once against our dock and then let the tide take it into mangroves like a child who could not decide on a game.

There were five of us who had lost someone with no body to bury. We met twice a month near the cracked fountain in the square and called ourselves The Ledger because some of us needed humor to stand its own weight. We brought each other things we could not eat but that comforted the room with their existence. Olives in jars. Preserved lemons. A cake made by the baker whose date palm we had recorded in the Bureau with a neat cross. We did not believe that telling our stories aloud would make them smaller, but we were convinced that not telling them would turn them into weeds.

I mention this now because one of the members of the Ledger, a fisherman named Joaquim who had a talent for looking at the weather and knowing when a joke could be made without consequences, is the one who first said the word that turned the morning for all of us.

“It’s back,” he said, standing in the doorway of the Bureau of Vanishing with his shirt sticking to his body and his hat in both hands like he had a younger version of himself sitting in it. “A house,” he added, as if that part were the less surprising. “You have to come.”

Dorotea did not look up at first. She was trying to make a straight line where the shore had bitten into itself like a lip. “We log disappearances, not debris,” she said, and filled in the gap with a pale gray wash. Then she did look up and saw the way Joaquim’s set of his mouth had exchanged ease for something stitched. “Whose house?” was what she asked.

“Morales,” he said. “Blue porch, tobacco jars in the kitchen. The one with the rooster carved into the lintel. From before.”

It was like saying a holy name. Everyone in the room paused—not for the house itself, which had belonged to a family too numerous to count and resilient in a way that annoyed other people at elections, but for the phrase “from before.” On our island, “before” divides time into colors. There was before the storms began to drive north instead of east. Before the mango trees started bearing more fruit than anyone could eat and then died of it. Before Hana’s boat came back without her. Before we made an office for measuring what the world had decided, again and again, could not be ours.

We took our measuring cases because we had no other way to carry our lives down to the shore. The cases held string, chalk, pins, brass weights, and three different widths of handmade paper to be used depending on how stubborn the wind was that day. My case is scuffed in two places by the same coral head near the western pier that catches everyone at least once if they are looking up instead of down. Someone in another century would have called our cases net bags. In ours were not fish but lines.

On the way, the town put itself in our path at the pace of heat. The woman who sells vinegar under the dyeing rack held out slices of cold green mango that numbed the mouth after the first salt. Two children chased a bird with a ribboned tail too long for its body. Old men on a bench turned their heads as one, their faces like maps of arroyos we had not yet drawn before flood. The sound of Joaquim’s boots became the sound of someone trying not to run.

At the top of the beach the world turned white: foam, sweat, the paper in my case, the glare of afternoon lit like a promise I did not believe in. People were gathered along the dry line the tide had just stepped back from, hands up to shade their eyes, their mouths curiously quiet. The Morales house rested in the shallows as if it had always been a boat. It was unmistakable. Two stories of weathered plank, shallow eaves, a porch painted the old blue that used to be made from crushed shells and a pigment one of the Morales girls had ordered by post before the post turned traitor. The rooster above the door was there, beak open as if mid-complaint, comb scalloped, the wood chipped at the tip where everyone used to hang wreaths out of habit more than faith.

But no one in any century builds a house to sail. That was what I could not fit anywhere. The base of the house was torn and swollen like a damp book. The kitchen window was broken and I saw glass no longer green but the kind that goes clear as a held breath when water has had its time with it. A line of seaweed had drawn a scar across the front door. The smell rising off the place was sweet and wrong, like fruit left too close to a radiator in another life.

“It’s the wrong size,” Dorotea said, thin as paper, the way she spoke when she was measuring something she didn’t trust. “Morales’s didn’t have such a long porch. And the roof pitch is wrong.”

“It could have warped,” someone said.

“Warped transforms, not invents,” Dorotea said, and I thought I would remember that sentence until my hands forgot their names.

I stepped forward because it seemed like the only thing to do. A crab made a decision near my foot. The sand took my body weight with interest. One of the Morales boys—I suppose he is no longer a boy and yet I have not seen him long enough to change him in my memory—stood near the porch steps with his arms around his ribcage as if to avoid falling apart. He had the brown eyes of his mother and the same scar on his right forearm where a pig had made a point about fence etiquette when he was ten. He did not say my name when I came up beside him and so I pretended, for a few seconds, to be a stranger.

“It knows the sound of waiting,” he said, and because I am ridiculous I thought he meant the house.

“What do you think happened?” I asked. It was a stupid sentence; you cannot fit this event into a question. But questions are what we carry when we have nothing else that will not sink us.

He shrugged with his whole back. “Maybe the world got bored with disappearing,” he said. “Maybe it needed a new game.” His mouth quirked in the old way, quick and mean to hide something soft. “Maybe it never left,” he added, and when I turned he was looking not at the house but at the place in the water that had cut us so precisely and so gradually we called it a surgeon.

The Bureau exists to put numbers on things that resist numbers. Still, all those afternoons had taught me a kind of thinking. If the sea returned a house which was not exactly the house that had gone, then either the sea was not a reliable archivist or the house was a different noun altogether. If more things were going to come back bent, we would need a new language. I put my case down in the sand and unlatched its worn brass toggles. The paper came out well-behaved for once. I took my line and my pins and measured the front step.

I know the exact dimensions of grief. The step was three spans wider than it used to be.

“Is it wrong to hope?” one of the Ledger women asked in my ear. Eira, who had lost a nephew she raised as her own and then discovered she could not tolerate the pity of oranges in winter. I wanted to say yes, that hope is a solvent that makes you forget the shape of what you are holding, but what I said was, “We will write it down.” It felt cowardly and true in the same bone.

A boy with a face like a fist darted past me and leaped onto the porch, leaving wet prints like punctuation. The house held. When he grabbed the edge of the door, someone yelled. The boy flinched, then pulled anyway. The door opened with the stiff, wet breath of a cellar after rain.

Inside, the air was cooler. It should not have been possible for another climate to exist in the space where we all kept our feet, but that is what it felt like. The kitchen ahead was a darker square. Skewed to the left where Morales’s butcher block used to sit was instead a table with a mosaic of green glass in its surface, the pieces arranged to make a shape that wanted to be a map but had lost its north. Two tobacco jars did sit where they were remembered, which made my heart do something unkind to my ribs, but there was also a lathe against the far wall that no one on the island would have owned because no one here trusted machines you could not explain to a child.

Eira made a noise. “They didn’t have a lathe,” she said to no one in particular, and in the saying made us all believe there were rules for this, even now.

Each of our bodies knew someone else’s loss had reached out its hand to ours across the space that separates definitions. There were things that were precisely the same as photographs and things that had no counterpart in any memory. The rooster had a chip at the tip of his comb, but the chip was on the wrong side. The paint on the porch was so exact it revived the particular scraped knees of every child who had played there on days when grown-ups were too tired to shout slow down, except that it was two degrees bluer than we remembered, and those two degrees felt like a betrayal of something we had only learned to name.

I was not the first to see the scarf. It hung from a peg by the door the way, once, my mother’s scarf had hung from a peg by our own. My scarf too is green, but the green of moss in a riverbed where the cows go to drink. This scarf was red. A red so precise I could taste the pomegranate it was not made of. The scarf was Hana’s. There is no way to explain how a red scarf could belong to a woman who wore a green one all her life, any more than there is a way to explain how you hear your name behind your ear at the market and know it is a voice that has not spoken in three years. I knew what I knew. The knot at one end of the scarf had been tied by someone who learned to tie knots from my mother, who was patient only with certain tasks and precise about the ones requiring hands. My lungs did the thing they do when I remember the day I found her chalk handprints on the patio wall after we’d fought about nothing, the prints already fading under sun.

My hand reached without my consent. The scarf was dry. It smelled like clove and graphite and a kind of cold, which is the smell of the inside of aluminum in winter. My face did an arrangement I would not have allowed in public if I had known I was capable of it. I took the scarf down and looped it around my neck the way you loop words you do not trust to stay said.

“We’re making a new ledger,” Dorotea said softly at my shoulder. She does this often: speaks not to me but to the room dressed as a person. “Things returned that are not exactly themselves.” She had a pencil she did not trust in her hair and her old hands held open the book she uses for field notes. The book is the black of the inside of an eyelid and it has one edge stiffened with glue from a year the damp would not leave us. She wrote under our first heading.

A house.

A scarf.

A lathe.

Someone else said “A teacup with a crack on the wrong side,” and another person laughed in a thirsty way and wrote “The rooster” as if he were a person who might mind not being mentioned by name.

“Where was it all this time?” a child asked. Because we cannot help ourselves, three adults responded at once: “Under,” “Inside,” “Between.” The child looked disappointed at the abundance of wrong answers.

Outside, the sun leaned toward a thought about going. The sea tried a new sentence on its tongue and then thought better. People took their time leaving, willing their bodies to be slow enough to stretch the moment into a cloth they could use later. The Morales son touched the banister the way one touches a fevered forehead: pity tangled up with anger. Eira stood with her arms folded tight to keep from undoing any knots she could not redo.

“What if everything comes back,” Joaquim said to me. We were at the waterline again; cruel shells beneath our feet did their impartial work. “What if people, too?” He had always been able to say the questions that wanted saying. He did not pretend his voice didn’t break exactly once.

“We will write them down,” I said, and knew we would also drown. It was either an answer or a habit.

When night came, we nailed the door of the Morales house shut not because we believed a house could run away when you turned your back—as if houses had not already done so—but because the sea was louder after dark and men like to do something with their hands after their day’s work has been taken from them. Dorotea numbered the boards. Eira lit a string of cheap plastic lights from the market and draped them along the porch rail with the exaggerated care you give an old woman’s hair. We are not fools: we know talismans do not hold tides. Still we tie them to our days.

I slept not at all. The scarf lay folded on my table in the room I rent above the vinegar seller, where the curtains smell of brine and sweet rot and old dye. Every time I closed my eyes I saw the house’s kitchen with the not-map table and the lathe against the wall like proof that the future had crept into the past while we were out getting more water. I thought of the sound of a pencil on paper. I thought of the way my mother used to keep score of something only she was playing. Dawn arrived damp and without apology.

There is a sound the Bureau’s door makes at low tide when you force it. That is the sound that woke me. It was not a thief. Thieves open doors with dignity or leave dignity out of it entirely. This was the sound of someone who did not believe doors could say no. I pulled on my skirt and went down the back stairs that smell like vinegar and old wood to the lane, where I stopped because something was in the wrong place and my brain had to slide around the fact to find the sense.

The Morales house was gone.

The beach had not smoothed over the place where it had sat; our footprints had not been rinsed. The nails we had hammered into the door were there in the sand as if a carpenter had squatted down with his tools and made a tidy offering to a god who did not eat iron. The string of lights Eira had hung lay in a loose suggestion of the porch railing. One of the bulbs had cracked; a tiny curl of filament looked like a hair caught in a comb. At the edge where the shallows begin, the water had taken on that dense, blue jealousy it gets when it wants to pretend it has always been everywhere.

We did not speak for a long time because we were not sure yet which language it wanted.

On the horizon a long, low shape considered us. At first I thought it was one of the flat fishing boats that come between our island and the next, the kind you can always identify by the way the men on board lean as one. But it did not move like a boat. It did not move like anything I knew. It had edges like a thing that had taught itself to be edged from rumor. It took me ten counts to understand what I was seeing and I am not slow. The thing was not far. The thing was a house. Not the Morales house. Our house. Mine.

Our house, which had been swallowed when the mangroves decided last year that roots were not a sufficient prayer. Our house, lifted in the sea like a word you think you heard a friend say across a loud room and then realize you were wrong and the word belongs to you.

It was coming toward shore. Or it was floating away. With here and there changing their minds about each other and the tide leaning into its afternoon desire, I confess that even with all my paper and pins I could not tell which direction it had chosen.

The Bureau teaches you to stand still and watch until you can see what is there and not the memory of what was. But after three years of learning how to write the world down, I broke myself of everything and ran. I ran toward the water, scarf knotting the morning to my neck, the day answering with a bright, hard heat. Behind me people named my name and the names I used to carry when I was small. The surf said something which I understood and then pretended not to. I reached the wet with the easy pain that says this is a body and you still own it.

Before my toes went numb, I stopped. There is a line none of us can say who drew. It moves, but we feel it. I have honored it so long I could no more cross it than I could tell my mother’s laugh from any other sound in the world. Beyond that not-line, our house waited with its roof at a tilt that was ours, with the dent in the gutter where a coconut fell the year I turned ten, with a pattern of cracks above the kitchen window like a constellation I had named once with someone who taught me to see shapes and then left.

I might have crossed. I might have risked the sea’s sudden thought. I might have let the world change me.

Something on the porch glinted. I shaded my eyes with my hand though the sun was behind a cloud. On the rail hung a length of cloth, green as a riverbed moss where cows go to drink, tied in a knot I knew as well as the word I used to wake a sleeping child. The scarf was mine before it was anyone’s. It had been a long time since hope felt like a person. But there she was, standing in the doorway of the old morning, framed by wood swollen with salt, her hair pulled back the way she wore it when she needed both hands free, her mouth not smiling and not not. She lifted a hand and neither of us said the other’s name. The sea lifted an edge of itself at our ankles and set it down again.

Behind me, the island breathed. I did not. We were going to need a new ledger. We were going to need a way to count how many times a heart can break and not be the same word.

“Do you see her?” Eira asked from the shore. Joaquim made a sound like something had been lowered into him. The rooster above the empty door in the empty sand, chip on the wrong side, watched me without mercy. I took one step forward into what was almost water—a centimeter, a breakfast spoon of sea. I did not make the second step, not yet.

Not yet.

The day my mother’s voice comes back to me, it rides the throat of a wren.

It is a small bird, the size of my palm, an ordinary scrap of brown that once rattled at the eaves without consequence. Now it perches on the rusted rim of the listening pole as if on a stage. The pole stands over our lane like a stripped tree with metal fruit, a crown of microphones that flare out like peonies. In their season the peonies were showy and vulgar and loved by my mother, who drank from chipped cups printed with their sudden blossoms, who called them foolish flowers for opening too soon. The microphones are nothing like that. They were planted by men in gray shirts who counted our words as if they were bulbs.

The wren bows, throat trembling. It clicks, it spills a run of notes that tumble and stop abruptly, like someone catching herself in the act of naming a secret. Then, clear as water poured into an enamel basin, comes the shape of my name. Not the syllables the city used in my file. Not the clipped, bureaucratic Li-en that the clerk had called out to a waiting room full of women chewing their knuckles. The sound is the one my mother used when I was small and sunburned and spent my afternoons cataloguing shells by the riverbank. It is a name made of two notes, linked by breath. I hear the breath in the throat of the wren and I do not remember moving until my hands are damp with the side of the listening pole.

No one else is in the lane. The mangroves at the bend hold their shadows like a mouthful of dye. Aunt Hoa’s shutter is half-down; her basket of washing breathes in the late heat. A drone passes overhead with a patience that makes me think of rain, of all the slow things we were taught to count. Its rotors stir the leaves of the guava tree; its camera, I am convinced, is the cold seed in its belly that will fall where it wants. The wren bows again. My name falls incomplete this time, chopped by static.

I step backward, away from the pole, away from the wren. The lane tastes faintly of iron; the smell of the river at low tide carries its own inventory: mud, oil, papaya peel, old fish. My key sticks in the lock and I have to lean my shoulder against the door. Inside, the house is smaller than my memory had the mercy to make it. The air is stale. A line of ants has erected a daring highway across the edge of the sink and into the mouth of a teacup someone left to dry, a brown ring of tannin like an eclipse.

It has been six years since I was here. It is a small house, two rooms and a strip of yard where my mother grew a determined failure of tomatoes. When I turned fifteen, she began leaving me alone after school on Thursdays to supervise the weeds. On Thursdays she went to the city to sell the silk scarves she dyed on our kitchen table. She would come back with stiff shoulders, smelling like everyone else. When the inspectors came to ask how she had learned to make dyes that did not run in the rain, she laughed and told them she had secrets, as if secrets were a seasoning any widow could afford. It was her way of living, to treat surveillance as weather, to take it personally only insofar as she chose her clothes.

Now, the scarf she had half-woven hangs from the beam where she liked to stand in the evenings. The threads at the loom are brittle with dust; when I pinch them, they leave a little stain on my fingertips, like pollen. I open the windows and the river’s breath folds into the house, blunt, heavy. A gecko clicks once from the corner where the plaster has swelled and lifted like the skin of a sting. Outside, the drone’s hum thins and passes away.

I unpack slowly. I am slow whenever I come home, as if that could change the elapsed years. The city taught me speed: it taught me subway stations with unpronounceable exits, coffee that tasted of exhaust, the minute schedules of academic extraction. It taught me to produce the right nouns on command and to pretend a certainty that I didn’t feel. It taught me to sleep in a way that never involved dreaming. When the collapse came—which collapse, you might ask, because they layer upon one another like last year’s mud under this year’s—there were notices and committees and suddenly-empty offices, and what I knew about the way small throats learned language was no longer necessary to those who paid attention, so I packed a suitcase and a book of debts and I came home to tend to the one collapse that had belonged to us from the beginning.

On the kitchen shelf where my mother kept the oil and the salt is her radio. It is an old model with a cracked dial. It used to sing once the sun gave up its height. She tuned it slowly, never arriving at any station, never settling on a voice. “There’s more than news in the static,” she would say, as if she could pull a sentence out of the snow, as if a sentence could pull her back. On the back of the radio, the screws are fresh; someone has opened it. The only someone was not me.

I find the spare sake bottle under the sink where she hid her extra cash. There is no money, only a cassette wrapped in a strip of blue cloth. On the cloth she has sewn a small patch of red thread, a signal we agreed on when I was twelve and afraid of the school’s guidance counselor. Red meant this: I remembered what we practiced. No words on paper.

I carry the cassette to the window. It is labeled in her hand, three numbers that mean nothing, a date that is months before the government delivered the listening poles like gifts to the lanes and the markets and the little squares where old men carved birds with knives and fed them to the fire. There is no player in the house. The university sent me home with a stipend that ended at the station, and a letter recommending patience with myself and with history. I have patience for neither. A cassette is an old traitor and a faithful friend. I turn it in my hands. It is heavy for what it holds.

“Lien,” says a voice from the yard.

I sink the cassette into my pocket and close my hand around it. I have never been quick with my face but I have practiced neutrality the way I used to practice scales: slowly, with attention.

Aunt Hoa leans on the low wall that separates our patch from her papayas. Her hair is piled on her head with a pen jammed through it. In certain light she looks like a woman I might have loved and in other light she is simply my mother’s friend, who taught me to braid green onions and to keep a blade under the mat. She studied me when I came up the lane an hour ago and made no comment. She studies me now.

“You smell like the city,” she says.

“Only on the outside,” I say.

“You’ll bring yourself inside,” she says, and pushes open my gate. “I made bitter melon with egg. Your mother used to say it tastes like regret. She would finish all of it and then drink a fist of water, as if she had won something and was trying to rinse her mouth of the victory.”

“I don’t think I’ve ever won anything,” I say.

“I’ve seen you watch things until they gave themselves away,” she says. “That is winning of a sort.” She lowers her voice; she has always lowered her voice as if the air itself were listening to her. “The men in the shirts were here in the spring.”

Of course they were. Of course their shoes were too clean for our hallway, and the prints of their soles lasted for the length of a week. “What did they want?” I ask.

“Your mother’s recipes, among other things,” she says. She has a small scar on the inside of her wrist that I have never asked about because I was a coward in those days. “They asked about your work. I told them about the papers you sent and the way your forehead grows a vein when you are lying.”

“I have never been good at lying,” I say.

“You have been good at speaking the truth to those who cannot translate it,” she says. “That is a cousin of lying, in these times.” She puts the bowl on the table and slides me a spoon. “I do not like to eat alone.”

We sit with our backs to the window and our faces to the wall where my mother’s shadow is not. The bitter melon is sharp and soft all at once, like a grief held in the mouth. I think of the wren outside, of the exact shape of my name. The first time my mother taught me to whistle, she slapped my hand away when I shaped my lips too proudly.

“You whistle to call things,” she said. “You do not whistle to applaud yourself.”

“What does a whistle call?” I asked, a child with a vocabulary like a net with holes in it.

“What is listening,” she said. “Never forget that. You whistle accordingly.”

“Aunt,” I say now, when the bowl is almost empty. “Did you hear anything unusual this morning?”

She takes her time. She turns the spoon in the last of the egg as if it were silt. “The birds have been different,” she says. “They have been trying on voices that do not belong to them. It is unsettling, like seeing a neighbor wear a soldier’s cap as a joke.” She looks at me. “There have been fines.”

“For the birds?” I say, and I shouldn’t, because making jokes is one way the city taught me to stay safe, and it is not safe here now.

“For those who encourage them,” she says. “As if encouragement were a leash.” She wipes her hands on her skirt and stands. “No need to borrow danger your first day. I brought you a pillow. Your mother’s smelled like a nest. You would not sleep.”
