She takes her pillow away from her ribs as if it were a baby she had stolen and sets it on my bed. On her way out she pauses at the loom. She touches the warp as if it had a pulse. “She waited for you,” she says. “Until waiting itself was a second occupation.”

“I didn’t ask you to say that,” I say.

“I did not ask permission,” she says, and leaves before I can decide if I am grateful for the hurt.

After she goes I wash the bowls and set them to dry. The gecko clicks again. A bicycle bell rings on the road and a child’s laugh answers it. A fly discovers the rim of a jar of preserved lemons and immerses itself with enthusiasm. It is a day like other days, except that on the table, next to a coil of blue thread, under a paperweight in the shape of a bird (for my mother did not find the obvious embarrassing), is a small notebook of hers with a red patch sewn into the corner. Red meant: remembered. Red meant: we are not writing. I open it anyway, with the care of someone unwrapping a delicacy they are ashamed to want.

The pages are filled with marks that look at first like embroidery patterns. Rows of small x's, circles, slashes, and arrows, drawn with a dull pencil that has smudged and softened at the edges. Beside the rows are dates and, sometimes, the names of places: the east canal, the ferry corner, Aunt Hoa’s papayas. I run my finger along the sequences and the room tilts slightly. It takes a moment before I can unlearn my training and remember the way my mother taught me to listen: to hear not only pitch and sequence, but the space around them, the breath. I begin to see that the symbols are her own, a notation for what she could not bring herself to describe to anyone else.

A series of slashes. A small circle. The same two marks repeated, a soft arrow. It is a stutter made of line and throat. It is a short phrase with a stop. If I say it in my mind, if I imagine the timbre of a wren and the way it perches like a question mark, I hear my name again. I hear the way my mother would separate it when she was angry, and hinge it together when she was tired. I put the notebook down and open the cassette with my fingernail like a thief.

I am not a mechanic, but I am the daughter of someone who could coax sound from wire. I take the radio from the shelf and lay it on its face. The screws give in easily; the back comes off like skin from a fruit. Inside, someone has soldered a small cassette player to the radio’s spine. The wires are neat, uncharacteristically neat. My mother never did anything tidy without folding a little mess into it as insurance against envy. Someone else did this. Or else she did it in a moment of uncharacteristic fear. I slide the cassette in.

The tape is slow to catch. The voice that emerges is hers and not hers. It is her voice in the way a signature is a person’s name, a shorthand for a living thing. It is the voice of someone who knew where the floor creaked. It is the voice of someone speaking at a distance from her own body.

“I am practicing saying nothing in a way that might be useful,” she says in the recording. There is a soft rattle under her words: the noise of the ceiling fan when it was failing, a season when the electricians were punishing us all with half-days. “Lien, if you are listening, it is because I have broken my own rule.”

I sit on the floor. I hold the radio’s guts together with my palm, as if any sudden movement might dislodge a syllable and drop it behind the cupboard.

“The men came and asked me what you are doing,” she says, and laughs a small laugh I know. “I told them you were a clerk of small mouths. I told them you filed vowels. They have no imagination. They do not believe that a thing can change its shape because it is watched too much. Maybe they should not be in charge of so many things.”

The tape clicks. It whirs. The gecko clicks back, involuntarily sympathetic.

“I am recording the songs as they shift,” she says. “I go to the places where they used to sit and do as they did. I sit. I watch. I write. The wrens are the most stubborn. They like the edges of nests better than their centers. They like gutters better than roofs. They do not take to repeating back what I offer them, but they listen to my breath. When I scatter the crumbs of words you carried home in your hair, they taste them on their tongues and make their own flour.”

I shut my eyes. There is a nausea that comes with excitement, the feeling of being pulled toward an open window with the knowledge that there are men on the street below in the posture of uniforms. In the city, a professor once told me that we anthropomorphize because we are lonely. Perhaps. Or perhaps we recognize structure when it knocks on the door of our own mouths.

“I do not feed them,” my mother says, in the cassette. “Only because that would be an admission. The women who feed pigeons have been made examples of. It is not wise to be an example these days.” Her breath thickens. “But I whistle when the inspectors have gone. And they whistle back something I have not taught them. They have been listening to other things besides me.”

There is a soft thud on the window. The wren, or not the wren, has decided to attempt the glass. It leaves a pale smear of fog. I press pause on the tape, and the sudden silence is cavernous. Through it comes the drone again, farther away. A boat engine starts at the quay. A child cries because children cannot always be coaxed from their own private disasters with a biscuit. The listening pole outside the window hums almost imperceptibly as it drinks the echo of the world.

I take the cassette out. I tuck it under the mat. I think of all the ways I have been taught to be careful, and all the ways it has never been enough. In the schoolyard a boy once told me that when catfish are shocked by lightning they sing. This is not true, but I believed him until I was old enough to know the shape of a lie that had weather in it. Now I press my ear to the screen and listen through the hairs of it, as if through grass.

When the wren sings again, it uses new words. Not words, not exactly. The pattern is one my body recognizes—a cadence that belongs to the bread knife on the wood, to the way my mother used to count the whites when she beat them into a foam. It gives me the beginning of a sentence and leaves me hungry for the rest. It does not say my name. It says, I think: don’t write.

It does not matter that I am already writing. It does not matter that I am writing in a place without paper, on skin and on air. My mouth fills with saliva as if I am preparing to swallow something difficult. I swallow nothing. I watch the bird tilt its head in two delicate increments, look down at the space where I must look like a dark shape settled in the window of an empty house, and then it lowers itself into flight. The light catches the underside of its wings. They are not beautiful in the way the feathers of books are beautiful. They are busied with life.

I am the clerk of small mouths my mother told the men I was. I am not brave, not yet; bravery is a velocity you can only measure in hindsight. But I can listen. It is a poor thing to set against the devices and the salaries and the patient machinery of men, but it is what I have. I retrieve the notebook from under the paperweight, the pencil from the jar. The red patch blinks in its corner like a wound sewn shut. Outside, down near the bend, the mangroves shift their hips and the river gossips to the silt in a voice too low for anyone to gather as evidence.

The drone circles once more and goes. The first mosquitoes invent me. Evening leans its elbow on the roof and looks in. The listening pole watches without blinking. On its crown a wren returns, impossible and ordinary, and opens its throat. The first notes stutter—old, honest confusion—and then, with the exact tremor of breath I cannot forget, the voice of my mother slips out of its beak and lands on the sill between us. It is my name, the whole of it, and in saying it she teaches me again the shape of my mouth. It is both a call and an instruction.

I do not whistle back. I whistle accordingly.

Chapter One: On the Classification of Small Losses

The Ministry taught me that anything can be archived if you name it gently enough. That is the secret and the sin. We learned to coax the world into drawers with brass handles and card catalogues whispering their paper syllables like prayer. Even a life, if it is shattered finely, will fit.

On my first day as a junior registrar, they rolled a rusted cradle into the intake hall. It had traveled to us on the river trucks from Basalt Parish, lashed to a pallet with rope braided out of telephone wire. The mattress was gone; the hood was a frame scalloped with salt, the paint blistered into petals where a hand would once smooth it to quiet a baby who is always, in the past, crying. Tags swung from every rung. We moved around it with our pencils tucked behind our ears and murmured the codes that we would later write on the survivor sheets. The foreman in his yellow slicker laid his palm on the hood and said, without looking at any of us, Type R, Subcategory 9. Remains: Domestic.

I had never known there were so many ways to lose something.

People imagine the Ministry as shelves and dust. We have those, we have dust that tastes like coins. We also have air that buzzes with cold because everything that comes through has already learned the language of water. We have machine rooms where salt is brushed from spines that once were books, bearings that once were shoulders. We have the big doors on the river side where they reverse the flood—a high green smell, silt in the hinges. We have the intake bell that rings when a shipment arrives, which is the same tone as the bell that used to call children to school in the parish where the cradle was found. Maybe it is that which keeps me loyal, the way each sound contains the size of itself.

I began on a winter week when the light was thin enough to seem catalogued. The weather hung off the river like a coat that didn't belong to us. We wore our fingerless gloves and our patience. Mrs. Hollis, who had worked there since long before losing became an industry, watched me tilt a wet photo, blotting it, trying to make out the faces: two girls on a jetty, one mid-laugh, her mouth a dark pearl.

"You will think your job is to save things," Mrs. Hollis said. She unscrewed her thermos and tipped broth into a chipped enamel cup. "It's to bless what cannot be saved by calling it what it was."

"I thought naming was a way of taking," I said, because I am built for argument, not obedience. My mother had once said that to me with both fondness and warning, and in that way I am my mother even now, ten years after the day the river refused to give her back.

"Sometimes." Mrs. Hollis sipped, and steam lit her eyes like a foggy street. "But better taken this way than by forgetting."

The ledger is where we put the names. There are computers and cloud storage and six separate redundancies, but there is also the ledger, bound in leather that once was a chair at a mayor's desk, its edges darkened by hands that begged, bribed, voted on whether Bittern Avenue would get a new culvert. I love it more than any person in my life, except perhaps a person who is no longer living. In its pages, written by a hundred hands, are the hush and stubbornness of entire towns. The ledger knows the difference between an urn and a pot because one of them was hidden behind a loose plank and the other was simply misplaced. The ledger knows that the fisherman who lost his boat also went back for his wife’s knitting; the ledger knows that a man from my town insisted we categorize a bag of acorns under Assets, not Debris, because he had promised his grandson they would plant oaks together.

In it, too, are mistakes: the wrong name for a child's shoe; a ring that might have been a washer from a pipe, unless the way it warmed my palm was not imagined.

It was in the ledger, on a Thursday that seem to have been boiled until it was gray, that I saw the entry that should not exist. Unit 47-D, Estuary Nine. Item: Resin mass, translucent, honey-amber. Inclusions: insect wings. Bubble with acoustic quality. Note from Field Agent: Hum audible at close contact. Suspected vocal encapsulation. Code: Unknown.

I read it standing up at the tall desk under the intake clock. My fingers went cold.

We have codes for many impossible things. We have a code for bones found in tree roots, a code for coffins that rise and travel on their own to lodge against a bridge with the insistence of grief. We have a code for salvaged perishable harvests which, though ruined, are claimed anyway because they are the last fruit a person picked with a parent. We do not have a code for a voice in amber.

Before I was a registrar, before my mother drowned and my father left us like a note under a windshield wiper saying, I'm sorry, I have no more words, before the river ate the lower streets and people began to say the water had an appetite and a preference, I was a child who knew the amber-colored sap in the pines by its smell. On August afternoons, the resin beaded on the trunks and the sun went visible in it, a small animal trying not to breathe. My mother taught me to press my fingertip to it and then touch my tongue. "Taste it," she said. "It tastes like sweet ten thousand years ago. It tastes like the world rehearsing amber."

"They're conifers," I said. I was proud of the word. "Conifers in this climate are stressed."

"I know. We are all stressed." She ran her palm over the bark, a lover's rub that made me jealous. "There is a story. If you speak your name into the tree when the cicadas first start singing, it will keep you. The pitch will close over the sound, and if someone finds it and listens, they can take you back."

"That's not how sound works," I said. I wanted to be an oceanographer then, in the way a child wants something in the language of a brochure. I drew diagrams of currents, returned the waves to our kitchen table with a ruler that had a brass edge.

"Of course it's not how sound works," she said. Her laughter was a creek talking to itself. "But it is how hope works."

Her name was Tanis. She once told me she chose it like a window, because people would always ask, Where's that from? and in the asking there would be air. She sang in our kitchen as if the sound were also flour she sifted into the batter. I am not being sentimental; it was like that. Her shoulders were units of measure. When she died, there were no units that fit.

Estuary Nine is what the maps call my home. We called it Greyhook. It had once been a fishing town and then it became the kind of place people whose kids left accused the government of forgetting. The government arrived, eventually, with a program and a logo and a ribbon-cutting for our new levee. The ribbon trailed into the water and the man with the scissors realized what he had done and laughed, which is the sound of a man looking for where the cameras are.

Greyhook is where my mother walked into the flood and did not come back. Someone said she was trying to get to our neighbor's house because they'd seen him on the roof with the dog, and if you were Tanis you would never leave a dog. Someone else said she tripped when the current took the planks from under her. We did not stand on our porch and watch it happen. We went to the window when we heard someone shout and by then she was part of the river's thought. My father howled like a beagle, and then he took the shovel to the wall and dug us a mark six feet up where the highest water had been, because we would never forget. And then he folded in his chair like he was a paper somebody meant to reuse, and then he went away.

I left Greyhook the way a tide leaves: as if I were compelled by another moon. I didn't mean to become a registrar, someone whose job is to make a place for lost things. But when you grow up in a small town where disasters come with names, your horror and your talent find each other.

When the intake bell rang that Thursday, I went to the river door with the others. The shipments arrive bound, labeled with coordinates and a docket that tells us the story without telling us anything. The foreman whistled at the size of it—crates and crates from Estuary Nine—and Mrs. Hollis crossed herself, which she always does when the town name matches the one on her birth certificate even if she stopped believing three disasters ago. We cut the straps and breathed in the smell that, if you had one word for it, would be December, and began.

Keys. Always keys. We tie them onto the grid with ribbon: house keys, car keys, mailbox keys with numbers etched into their faces. A dictionary swollen with water and rapture. Boots with the imprint of the big toe like a planet pressed against the rubber. A black bag of medicines, their labels gone, the good strong chemical names washed to ghosts: methylenesomething, some other something that ends in -pril.

Then a crate that had been lined with cloth, as if whoever troweled it from the silt knew we were the kind of people who notice care. The docket number matched the ledger entry. Resin mass. Inclusions unspecified.

"I want this one," I said too fast.

"You sure?" Dimas asked. He chews his pencils. His fingers are always rimmed with graphite that won't wash off because he will not stop working long enough to go to the sink. "Looks like a paperweight a giant would use to keep his gazette from blowing off his table. Code unknown is where interns go to die."

"Let me," I said, less because it would be good for the Ministry and more because the word Estuary had bloomed through my coat and found the skin under my shirt. "You can have the copper chest that smells like fish."

"I hate you," he said cheerfully. "Take a respirator. And holler if the unknown code blows are we are."

The resin was exactly the size to fit both my hands. It was not smooth; its surface had been buffed by sand until it seemed to glow from beneath. You could see insects forever falling toward their deaths and never arriving. There was a shape inside that was not leaf, not hair, not air. It made my pores close, the way a breeze can do through a shirt you had not expected to be so thin.

It did hum. I pressed my ear to it and I heard humming the way a tooth sometimes lets you hear the root of yourself. I did not, then, hear the voice that would make me leave everything I had named my life. I heard a note, and that was enough.

"Vocal encapsulation," Dimas said, mockingly formal, his pencil twirling behind his ear like a baton. "Is that when somebody's song gets caught in sap?"

"Don't be cruel to your seniors," I said. We are all the same age. "Hum audible, note says. They make it sound like we're listening to bees."

"Better than when it says Vermin present," he said, and nudged a fabric-wrapped parlor chair with his foot. Something the size of a thought darted under the slip in answer.

We have rules about attaching ourselves. It is unprofessional to turn a crate into your own history just because it shares a map or a smell. It is unprofessional to identify a brooch as your grandmother's without proof. We call it "inadmissible intimacy," and we sign statements that we will avoid it. This is how the State keeps a hold of its own throat.

"Should go back," Mrs. Hollis said softly, watching me watch the stone. "If it belongs."

"It doesn't," I said. "It belongs to us now."

"Us being who?"

"The ledger," I said. "The logic of what happened."

"Logic and history," she said, kind not to laugh at me. "You were not there the day the river woke up and took out the food pantry because somebody had told it there were people in line inside the food pantry who were in pain. Logic is an afterword. Take it to classification, registrar. See what name fits and then give it back."

"To whom?"

"To the person it is an answer for."

I could keep describing that day and it would be water that doesn't end. Illustrations of salvage, stacking and stacking. I slept with sap in my hair that night, smelling like a summer even though it was winter; I dreamed of cicadas singing with throats that were rings of amber.

In the morning my boss called me into his office. He is a kind man named Ferris with a voice that has the sturdy grain of a board that used to be a porch. He wore the same pale blue shirt he always wears, which has a triangle of pen stain at the breast pocket that makes me want to hand him a needle and thread. He gestured at a chair and I sat, hands on my knees like a student. On his desk was a letter with the Ministry crest. The seal looked like an eye that had found a reason to believe in itself.

"Greyhook is my home," I said before he spoke. "If this is about a conflict of interest related to Estuary Nine, we both know the statute says registrars are disqualified only from evaluating property claims when there is provable kinship, and—"

"Mira," he said. "Take a breath."

I did, and the air tasted of dustpollen and coffee.

"The Estuary Nine shipment needs field verification," he said. "Too much arrived without proper coordinates. The taggers were young or the flood was wild or both. We need to go back, match some of what we have with what's left there. And you—if you want—should go."

"Because I grew up there," I said. The word grew puts leaves on any sentence you put it in. He nodded. He waited, letting me decide which part of myself would answer. "Is this," I asked, "because of the resin?"

"Partly," he said. He does not lie to us. "We aren't equipped, here, to determine whether a humming stone is a curious bit of pressure or..." He glanced at me. "They sent a photo of your mother in with one of the crates, Mira. I saw it when I went to initial the intake. I thought you should see it where the walls are made of the same salt that did it, before you saw it on our table. I thought you should go as a registrar, not as a daughter, while you still have the choice."

"I don't," I said.

"I know. But we'll pretend you do, for a day. There's a truck at noon. Take the resin. If it was made there, someone will have a story about it. Bring one back that fits. We'll make a space for it if there isn't one."

He passed me the photo. The water had swollen it until the faces were almost unjoined. But there she was on the jetty with me beside her, my mouth broken open with laughter at something I can no longer name. Her hair was dragged across her cheek by a wind that existed on that day, at that hour, like a person. I could not stop my thumb from pressing the damp image as if to check for warmth.

"Ferris," I said, because I didn't know what else would hold the room steady.

"There is a line item on the docket," he said, and from the wrinkles around his eyes I could tell he had saved this as a balm and didn't know whether it would sting. "'Resin mass likely from pine stand north of Greyhook. Local note: Resin collects words. Do not call it that around them. They will say you don't respect them if you call it that. Let them call it that.'"

"What do they call it?" I asked.

"It's written here," he said. "'Hush.'"

I packed what you pack when you are going home as a person with a job. A change of clothes. The ledger's traveling copy, less beautiful than the original but with the same bones. The respirator. The resin wrapped in cloth like a baby I had convinced myself I would not claim. A sandwich that Mrs. Hollis had pressed into my palm, its bread collapsing like knees. I put the photo in the map sleeve and told myself I would not look at it between here and there. I looked at it at every red light.

The drive to Estuary Nine is a journey through the country's lessons. There are towns where the church is now the tallest thing and the church is an empty steeple. There are places where spray-painted Xs on doors have been painted over with a cheerful yellow that is not cheerful for long. There are miles of new levee and then sudden breaks in the levee where the engineers misread the older language the land was speaking. There are cattle standing on knolls, ankle-deep, confused that the world has turned bovine everywhere but under their hooves. There are billboards advertising agencies who will help you claim what you cannot prove you had. There are, newly, signs for the Ministry.

I crossed the bridge where, once, my father lifted me onto his shoulders to see the fireworks. He had not planned for how heavy I would be, or for the way the barge horns would tremble through us like a second heart. I remember the feeling of being too large to be carried and not wanting to climb down into a world where that would always be true.

Greyhook is smaller than any map admits. Its houses, when I was little, had all been built by men who later smashed them with their own hands, cursing the nails they'd set. It has since been remade and unsolved three times. When I drove in, my car sighed over potholes that were ponds by another name, and I braced my hand on the dash the way my mother used to do without knowing she was doing it.

The salvage yard sits where the cannery was. You can still smell the fish if you step into the wind wrong. An antler of rusted conveyor belt arches like a rib out of the weeds. Boats are stacked on their sides and the grass grows through them like hair. Men and women in rubber boots move with the quick carefulness of people who know the river has eyes and remembers insults. I parked under the only tree, which was a cottonwood that looked surprised to be alive, and slid the respirator into my bag because if you put it over your face here in front of them they will forgive you but not forget.

"Help you?" a man asked, wiping his hands on a towel that once was a flag.

"Probably," I said. "I'm from the Ministry."

He squinted at my badge and then at my face. Greyhook does this to me. It tries to put me back into a girl it knows and does not find and then treats me accordingly. "Oh," he said, as if he had found a coin he once dropped. "Mira Tanis."

"Tanis was her first name," I said automatically. "Mine is Mira. I'm a registrar."

"People are allowed to be two things," he said. "You and your mother. I know the difference."

He was older than me by some years. His hair had given up. His smile built and then didn't. We had gone to school together; he had been taller then, or perhaps I had been shorter. He said his name and it clicked—Noah Pruitt, who once swallowed a penny on a dare and waited out the whole summer to retrieve it because he believed money had memories.

"You run this place?" I asked.

"If by run you mean I call out numbers with a solemn voice and pretend I know how to price a broken wedding," he said. "I do that. The actual running is the river's. You're here to take our treasures and send them up to the men with pens."

"I'm a woman with a pen," I said. "And I'm not here to take anything. I'm here to match what we have to its place so it can return, if returning is possible."

"Always nice when the returning is possible," Noah said, kind but also not. "What are you looking for?"

I unwrapped the cloth and showed him the resin. He did not reach for it. He made the sign he would have made as a boy when lightning struck close and he wanted to scare it into seeing him.

"Who brought this in?" I asked.

He looked at my face the way a person stares at a horizon deciding if that is a storm or only the way land is when it meets the sky. "Hush," he said. "That's a good one. We've had a rash of hushes. People pry them off the pines with butter knives. They keep them by their beds. They say it helps them sleep. Sometimes they say it keeps the dead from walking through."

"Does it?" I asked.

"Do dead people not walk through your dreams?" he said. "If they don't, teach me. Old Eveline Brant made more of them than anyone. Used to talk to the trees. We'd laugh at her and then she started selling them off a table with hand-lettered signs, like she was a farmer and words were produce. Then the flood," he gestured, a wordless sweeping. "Now people buy them because they need something to touch that isn't a screen and isn't their own salt."

"It hums," I said, and held it toward him. "Do you hear it?"

He leaned in. He put his cheek to it the way you do to your child's forehead to check for fever. He went very still.

"That's new," he said softly. "Eveline would have bragged if she'd managed humming. She'd have written it on her signs. Hush that hums. Guaranteed to keep the names where you left them. Five dollars extra."

"Who is Eveline?" I asked.

"Old woman. Been alive two hundred years as far as I'm concerned," he said. "Lives north. Pine stand past the oysterman's road. She's been here longer than any of us. She has an eye like a nail. We can go see her if you like. But not today. She'll be sleeping or pretending to. You never wake Eveline on a Thursday."

"What's wrong with Thursdays?" I said.

"They don't hold," he said. "Best to let them pass without making any plans at them."

A dog wandered up and sat on my foot. This was the neighbor's dog my mother had gone into the water for, her dog's grandson, perhaps. He leaned his entire attention onto my ankle. I put my palm on his head and the small warmth of him felt like a permission I had not known I needed.

"Do you still have your house?" I asked. My mouth did not tell my mind before it moved.

Noah's attention learned a different river. "No," he said. "My house is a place where fish graze. We have a trailer. We have a deck built out of everybody's old porches. We like it. We hate it. We're alive."

"I—" I started, and stopped. I am trained to ask for what I need while acting as if I do not need more than anyone else. People are tired of needing. People are tired of the humility of asking. We all resent each other. "I need to find who held this last. The hush that hums."

"We can ask the pines," he said. He looked away when he said it so I could pretend he had not meant it. "Or we can ask Eveline. I'd bet on her. If I were you."

"I am me," I said, smiling despite myself.

"I can see that," he said. He glanced at my bag. "They sent you with a respirator. Good. The mold in Eveline's house will make you forget your mother's name."

"It won't," I said, the way you say something that cannot be true.

We made a plan, and then we unmade it because it was a Thursday and he had convinced me on that small superstition alone not to give the day more than it could carry. I walked down to where the jetty had been. Children were flinging rocks into the water and screaming as if they had invented gravity. The river made its syllables around the pilings like a cat weaving your legs.

When I held the resin to my ear that evening in the motel room with the mildew that had personality and the curtain that had ideas, I heard the note again. I listened long enough to learn its shape. And then it broke—no, it opened. It is hard to write in the ledger the moment a rule becomes porous. I lowered my head the way you would lower your head to a friend who is about to tell you the part of the story where they cried in public and you didn't know that about them.

"Mira," my mother said, and it was not like that but it was exactly that, the way a smell is not the past but opens it like a door. "Mira, if you found this, you have to stop calling things by their shapes." She paused, and I could hear the insects in the resin pause with her, the whole pine stand clamping its mouth. "It wasn't the river," she said, and then the hum rose the way a kettle tells you it was boiling all along.
